description: Functional claim limitations (including those potentially invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f)) must be assessed for adequate written description and enablement; if construed under 112(f), structure corresponding to the function must be sufficiently disclosed.
guidance: Assess whether the specification conveys to one skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the claimed functional invention at filing and provides sufficient structure/algorithm (for computer implementations) to support the claim scope. See MPEP § 2181 for means‑plus‑function guidance and related subsections on algorithms and structures.

name: ‘Essentially the same’ products test for preclusion/Kessler doctrine
description: Accused devices are 'essentially the same' where differences between them are merely colorable or unrelated to the limitations in the claim of the patent.
guidance: If products are essentially the same, Kessler may grant a product noninfringing status that carries to subsequent versions absent material differences. Courts review district findings for clear error on whether products are essentially the same.

name: Kessler doctrine scope
description: Kessler grants a product a noninfringing status that prevents repeated harassment for continuing its business as usual post-final judgment; that noninfringing status can apply to subsequent versions of the originally accused products if there are 'no material differences.'
guidance: Kessler fills the gap between claim and issue preclusion doctrines by protecting adjudged non-infringers; courts examine prior precedent to determine Kessler's applicability based on product similarity.

name: Collateral estoppel (Eleventh Circuit four-part test)
description: Collateral estoppel requires: (1) the issue at stake must be identical to the one involved in the prior litigation; (2) the issue must have been actually litigated in the prior suit; (3) the determination of the issue in the prior litigation must have been a critical and necessary part of the judgment; and (4) the party against whom the earlier decision is asserted must have had a full and fair opportunity to litigate the issue.
guidance: Federal Circuit applies regional law for collateral estoppel issues; for patent-unique questions (e.g., whether claims are the same), the Federal Circuit applies its own law.

name: District courts must perform claim construction (intrinsic evidence focus)
description: Before concluding two suits present the same infringement issue for preclusion purposes, the district court must assess claim scope by conducting a proper claim construction using intrinsic evidence.
guidance: Reliance on extrinsic evidence (expert reports) in place of intrinsic claim construction is error. The appellate court is ill-positioned to conduct claim construction in the first instance when parties have not provided claim construction briefing.

name: Collateral estoppel and differing burdens (IPR vs district court)
description: A finding underlying an unpatentability decision in an IPR (preponderance standard) does not automatically collaterally estop a patentee from making validity arguments in district court where a different legal standard (clear and convincing) applies.
guidance: Collateral estoppel may not apply where the second action involves application of a different legal standard; courts have distinguished cases where a claim was found unpatentable and affirmed (which may bar assertion) from those where claims were not found unpatentable.

name: Pleading standard for patent infringement at the motion-to-dismiss stage
description: A patent plaintiff is not required to plead infringement on an element-by-element basis; the complaint must place the accused infringer on notice of the accused activity and plausibly allege infringement.
guidance: Review of district court categorizations of allegations as well-pleaded factual (entitled to presumption of truth) versus conclusory is de novo. Detailed infringement theory and claim charts, along with the technology's simplicity, can satisfy notice pleading. Defendants' operational roles that are contested factual issues cannot be resolved at dismissal.

name: Types of disclaimers — statutory vs terminal
description: There are two types of disclaimers: a statutory disclaimer (relinquishes legal rights to one or more claims of an issued patent) and a terminal disclaimer (disclaims or dedicates to the public the entire term, or any terminal part of the term, of a patent or patent to be granted).
guidance: The historical usage distinguishes statutory disclaimers as disclaimers of claims of an issued patent and terminal disclaimers as disclaimers of patent term or a terminal part thereof. Both are provided for by statute, but are used differently; e.g., a statutory disclaimer cannot be used to amend or add claims.

name: Statutory disclaimer content and recordation requirements (37 CFR 1.321(a))
description: A statutory disclaimer to be recorded in the Office must: (1) be signed by the patentee or an attorney/agent of record; (2) identify the patent and complete claim(s) or term being disclaimed (a disclaimer which is not of a complete claim or term will be refused recordation); (3) state the present extent of patentee's ownership interest in the patent; and (4) be accompanied by the required fee.
guidance: A statutory disclaimer is binding upon the grantee and its successors or assigns; notice is published in the Official Gazette and attached to printed specification copies. A statutory disclaimer is not a vehicle for adding or amending claims.

name: Terminal disclaimer content and recordation requirements (37 CFR 1.321(b))
description: A terminal disclaimer to be recorded must: (1) be signed by the applicant or an attorney/agent of record; (2) specify the portion of the term of the patent being disclaimed; (3) state the present extent of applicant's ownership interest in the patent to be granted; and (4) be accompanied by the required fee.
guidance: Terminal disclaimers are binding upon the grantee and successors/assigns. The disclaimer must be of a terminal portion of the term of the entire patent to be granted — disclaimers of the term of individual claims are not accepted.

name: Content requirements for proper terminal disclaimer language
description: A proper terminal disclaimer must disclaim the terminal part of the statutory term of any patent granted on the application (or the statutory term of the patent) which would extend beyond the expiration date of the full statutory term, shortened by any terminal disclaimer, of the patent that is the basis of the NSDP. It must state that the agreement runs with any patent granted on the application and is binding upon the grantee, its successors or assigns.
guidance: Permissible exculpatory language (e.g., 'In making the above disclaimer, the owner does not disclaim...') may be used. The disclaimer should identify the disclaimant and their interest and specify the effective date. A terminal disclaimer of individual claim term is improper; conditional disclaimers (tied to PTA determinations, litigation outcomes, etc.) are not acceptable.

name: Effect of terminal disclaimers in continuing applications, reexamination, and reissue
description: A terminal disclaimer filed to obviate an NSDP rejection is effective only with respect to the application or patent identified in the disclaimer unless by its terms it extends to continuing applications (in which case applicant must file a copy of the disclaimer in the continuing application). A terminal disclaimer filed in a parent normally has no effect on a continuing application claiming benefits under 35 U.S.C. 120 unless properly extended.
guidance: Applicant must file copies of the disclaimer in continuing applications to achieve the intended carryover. Examiners should check whether a terminal disclaimer should be filed or has effect in related/progeny applications and CPAs.

name: Prohibition on using disclaimers to add or amend claims or as conditional instruments
description: A statutory disclaimer or terminal disclaimer is not a vehicle for adding or amending claims; the statute and rules provide no mechanism to add claims via disclaimer. The statute does not provide for conditional disclaimers — proposed disclaimers contingent on PTA determinations, litigation outcomes, allowance of certain claims, or grant of a petition are improper and will not be accepted.
guidance: Examiners should refuse recordation of disclaimers that attempt to add/modify claims or are conditional. Applicants must use proper claim amendment procedures rather than disclaimers to change claim scope.

name: Cannot rely on a generic desire to 'build something better'
description: A generic desire to improve or that one reference 'obtains better image quality' is insufficient standing alone to show motivation to combine prior art.
guidance: Cite ActiveVideo Networks v. Verizon and related authority: evidence must connect the asserted improvement to the specific features the petitioner relies on, not just a general superiority claim. Petitioner retains the burden to prove the claimed advantage of the combination when that is the theory of motivation.

name: Attorney arguments cannot substitute for evidence
description: Arguments of counsel cannot take the place of evidence lacking in the record.
guidance: Unsupported attorney argument is insufficient; the record must contain testimony, demonstrative evidence, or prior art statements to support claimed rationales (Estee Lauder, In re Pearson).

name: Comparisons must be between relevant types of art (context matters)
description: An asserted superiority in one context (e.g., still-image deblocking) does not automatically translate to superiority in a different context (e.g., real-time video deblocking).
guidance: Petitioner must show the prior-art comparison is to appropriate, comparable techniques; Huang’s claims about still-image performance could not be assumed to apply to video without supporting evidence. Consider practical differences like real-time constraints and edge-map reliability.

name: Need to show asserted improvement is attributable to the relied-upon feature
description: If a reference claims an overall improvement, a petitioner relying on only one feature of that reference must show that the improvement is attributable to that specific feature.
guidance: The Board requires evidence linking the claimed benefit to the particular element the petitioner substitutes (e.g., show Huang's classification, not just its nonlinear filter, causes improvement).

name: Obviousness requires selection/combination as part of ordinary research and development
description: Obviousness requires showing that a person of ordinary skill would have selected and combined prior art elements in the normal course of research and development to yield the claimed invention.
guidance: Piecemeal combination of portions of different methods requires showing that such piecemeal combination would have been part of normal research activities (KSR, Unigene Labs).

name: Nexus requirement and coextensiveness presumption
description: Objective indicia are relevant only if there is a nexus between the claimed invention and the evidence; a patentee may get a rebuttable presumption of nexus by showing its products are coextensive with the challenged claims.
guidance: The Board uses a two-step analysis: (1) determine if patentee's products are coextensive with the claims (presumption of nexus), and (2) if not coextensive, patentee can still prove nexus by showing the evidence is the direct result of unique claimed characteristics (Lectrosonics, Fox Factory).

name: Claims or limitations unsupported by petitioner may be deemed waived
description: If Patent Owner does not respond to petitioner's arguments directed to particular claim limitations, the Board may find those arguments waived and accept the petitioner's showing for those limitations.
guidance: Where Patent Owner does not specifically respond, the Board may treat arguments as waived (see examples where Patent Owner did not respond to arguments for certain limitations and Board found them satisfied).

name: Best practices for patent claim drafting and prosecution
description: Best practices for patent claim drafting strategies and prosecution
guidance: Broadly promises guidance on drafting and prosecuting claims (strategies, examples, and recommended approaches) with full details available in the downloadable presentation and recorded webinar.

name: Elimination of proposed drawing correction practice
description: The proposed drawing correction practice has been eliminated. For any changes to the drawings, applicant is required to submit a replacement sheet of drawings with the changes made.
guidance: A letter to the official draftsman is no longer required. In response to drawing objections, submit replacement or new sheets with the corrections made. Drawing submissions without any amendments to the specification and claims after allowance should be forwarded to the Office of Patent Publication.

name: Content and authorization for examiner's amendments
description: The examiner's amendment should include the reason why the amendment is non-compliant and indicate how it was corrected.
guidance: Authorization from the applicant or attorney/agent of record and extensions of time are not required if the changes are not substantive (e.g., corrections of format errors or typographical errors). Authorization and appropriate extensions are required if the changes made in the examiner's amendment are substantive (e.g., cancellation of a claim or change in scope of claims); such authorization must be given within the time period for reply set forth in the last Office action.

name: General handling of non-compliant amendments (Form PTOL-324)
description: If an amendment fails to comply with 37 CFR 1.121, the Office will notify applicant by a Notice of Non-Compliant Amendment (Form PTOL-324) identifying: (1) which section is non-compliant; (2) items required for compliance; and (3) the reasons why the section is non-compliant.
guidance: The type of amendment determines whether applicant is given time to comply and whether the reply must include the corrected section or the entire corrected amendment. The notice will identify required corrections (e.g., a compliant claim listing) and the applicable time period or consequence.

name: Non-compliant amendment: preliminary amendment present on filing date
description: If a preliminary amendment that is present on the filing date fails to comply, the Office of Initial Patent Examination (OIPE) will send a notice setting a two-month time period for reply. Extensions are available under 37 CFR 1.136(a).
guidance: Failure to reply will result in abandonment. Applicant's reply must include either a substitute specification under 37 CFR 1.125 (if amendment to the specification) or a complete claim listing under 37 CFR 1.121(c) (if amendment to the claims).

name: Preliminary amendments must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 and timing rules
description: A preliminary amendment is received on or before the mail date of the first Office action (37 CFR 1.115). Any preliminary amendment, regardless of when filed, must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 (e.g., include a complete listing of all claims and each section begin on a separate sheet). Preliminary amendments in a transmittal letter will not comply.
guidance: If a preliminary amendment fails to comply, applicant will be notified and given a non-extendable one-month period to correct (or two months if present on filing date per OIPE practice). Filing preliminary amendments is generally not recommended because changes may not be reflected in the patent application publication if not entered before technical preparations for publication. Applicants are encouraged to incorporate desired amendments into the specification at filing instead of using preliminary amendments.

name: Timeliness and disapproval of preliminary amendments
description: A preliminary amendment may be disapproved (not entered) if it seeks cancellation of all claims without presenting new/substitute claims, or if it unduly interferes with preparation of a first Office action.
guidance: Factors for disapproval include (i) the state of preparation of the first Office action at date of receipt; and (ii) the nature of changes to the specification or claims that would result. Entry of a preliminary amendment will not be disapproved if filed no later than: (i) three months from the filing date for an application under § 1.53(b); (ii) the filing date of a continued prosecution application under § 1.53(d); or (iii) three months from national stage entry under § 1.491. These time periods are not extendable. If filed after these periods, disapproval may be denied subject to supervisory patent examiner approval, and the two-factor test above will be applied.

name: Functional equivalence in combinations (equivalents)
description: A device which, both mechanically and practically, performs the same precise office of another device, in substantially the same manner, is the equivalent of the latter for purposes of a combination claim.
guidance: Even if the alleged equivalent also performs additional functions or has different mechanical features, if for the purposes and in the operation embraced by the claim it performs identically in the same way, it may be deemed an equivalent and its substitution can constitute appropriation/infringement. Improvements that add functions do not necessarily avoid being equivalents.

name: New combination of old elements may be patentable
description: A new combination of old and well-known things may be a proper subject for a patent if the mode of combination was new and produced a beneficial result.
guidance: The specification must claim the new combination, not the old processes individually. Prior knowledge of the separate principles does not preclude patentability where the mode of combination is novel and yields a beneficial effect.

name: Description not claimed may be dedicated to the public
description: If a previous patent describes something but does not claim it as new, there is a strong (perhaps conclusive) presumption that what is described and not claimed is given up to the public.
guidance: This presumption can in some cases be removed only by surrender and reissue under the statute providing for such correction. A subsequent patent cannot cover what was already validly claimed in a prior patent, but where the first patent's claim was invalidly overbroad and did not validly embrace the subject, a later patent on a distinguishable improvement may be allowed (e.g., O'Reilly v. Morse).

name: Effect of prior patents on joint invention claims
description: Prior separate patents held by inventors are strong evidence against a claim of joint invention but are not necessarily conclusive an absolute bar to a joint patent.
guidance: The facts and statutory context matter: courts have allowed joint patents following inconsistent prior separate patents where the circumstances (e.g., innocence, mistake, or subsequent joint application) support it. Remedies for conflicting outstanding patents may include equity proceedings to declare patents void or other statutory remedies.

name: Substitution that produces reciprocal action distinguishes patentable combination
description: A combination is patentable where there is a reciprocal action or operation of the parts upon each other and conjointly upon the entire machine, each part giving increased support and efficiency to the other, producing a new efficiency due to the combination itself.
guidance: Contrast with mere aggregation where parts operate independently. The example of flanged collars combined with tenoned spokes: combined they provide mutual support and a stronger wheel; that reciprocal interaction supports a combination claim.

name: Surrender and reissue as remedy for undesired dedication
description: Surrender and reissue under the statute that provides for correction of inadvertency may remove the presumption that parts of a specification not claimed are dedicated to the public.
guidance: If an inventor described but did not claim subject matter in a first patent and wishes to reclaim it, surrender and reissue may be the available statutory route, subject to the limitations of the reissue provisions and the status of prior claims.

name: Procedural limits on invalidity requests prior to publication
description: Prior to publication made per specified paragraphs of Article 99, the court shall not decide invalidity requests made pursuant to certain grounds (subparagraphs (a), (b), (c) of first paragraph).
guidance: Claims that the patent owner does not have right under Article 109 may be alleged only by the holder of the invention or successors. The invalidity proceeding may be instituted against those registered as owner during protection or within five years following termination.

name: Grounds and procedures for termination of patent right
description: Patent right terminates upon: (a) expiry of protection period; (b) waiver by patent holder; (c) failure to pay annual fee within specified periods.
guidance: Office publishes termination. Subject matter of a terminated patent belongs to the public from execution date. Waiver can be partial (one or more claims) but requires notification to Office, is effective from registry record date, and sometimes requires permission of registered right/license holders or third parties with interlocutory injunctions. Waiver decisions are published.

name: Utility model procedural requirements (formal exam, search, corrections, grant)
description: If application lacks elements of Article 90(3) it is not processed. Deficiencies (including foreign-language elements) must be corrected within two months or application is deemed withdrawn. Applicant must demand search within two months of notification of formality consistency or correction; a search report is issued and published. If subject falls into excluded types or description/claims unclear, no search report is prepared and applicant must file objections or changes within three months or be rejected.
guidance: Applicant can appeal search report contents within three months from its publication; third parties may present opinions. If Office decides to grant, decision and utility model are published. Amendments requested as condition of grant must be fulfilled within two months. After granting, appeals per Article 99 are not available; only invalidation actions before court. Granting is not a guarantee of validity or usefulness; implementing principles are set by regulation.

name: Available claims/remedies for right owners in infringement actions
description: Right owner may claim: determination of infringement existence; prevention of possible infringement; stopping infringing actions; remedy and compensation for material and moral damages; seizure of infringing products and instruments exclusively used in their production; being granted property right on seized items; measures to prevent continuity of infringement including altering shapes, erasing trademarks, or destroying items; and announcement of final judgment at infringer's expense when justified.
guidance: Value of seized devices/machines is deducted from compensation; if value exceeds compensation, excess paid to opposing party. Announcement scope and form determined in the ruling; claim for announcement must be made within three months after final ruling.

name: Compensation rules and pre-litigation evidence-seeking
description: Those who commit infringement are obliged to compensate the right owner. Additional compensation may be claimed if reputation suffers due to inferior use/production or improper market launch. Before instituting a compensation proceeding, right owner may ask the court to order the person responsible to submit documentation related to the use of the right to determine evidence or damages.
guidance: This provision allows obtaining business records/evidence prior to filing substantive compensation claims.

name: cDNA can be patent eligible subject matter
description: Complementary DNA (cDNA), created synthetically by excluding introns (exons-only strands), is considered non-naturally occurring and therefore patent eligible under §101.
guidance: cDNA results from human intervention that creates a molecule not found in nature. Drafting claims directed to cDNA (as opposed to isolated genomic DNA) may survive §101 challenge, though careful factual analysis is needed.

name: Very short cDNA sequences may be ineligible if indistinguishable from natural DNA
description: Eligibility for cDNA may be denied where the cDNA consists of very short series of nucleotides without intervening introns and is indistinguishable from natural DNA.
guidance: When claiming cDNA, evaluate whether the claimed sequence is practically identical to the naturally occurring sequence; if so, §101 ineligibility risk increases. Consider sequence length and presence/absence of introns in claim drafting and prosecution strategy.

name: Isolation alone does not create a new 'composition of matter' (Funk Brothers principle)
description: The Court relied on Funk Brothers to conclude that simply isolating a natural material does not necessarily produce a new composition of matter for §101 purposes.
guidance: Claims that rest on purification/isolation alone should be scrutinized; show how the product differs in structure/function from the natural counterpart or how inventive techniques materially change the composition.

name: Prior USPTO practice is not dispositive for §101 eligibility
description: The Court dismissed the argument that the Patent and Trademark Office's prior practice of awarding gene patents is entitled to deference for determining §101 eligibility.
guidance: Historical PTO allowance of claims does not guarantee constitutional or statutory validity under §101; courts will independently assess whether the claimed subject matter is a product of nature or the result of human invention.

name: Claims must define DNA sequences more precisely than 'isolated' to survive §101
description: The decision suggests that gene claims framed merely as 'isolated' may be invalid, but claims that define DNA sequences more precisely or in different terms may still be patentable.
guidance: Draft claims to recite specific sequence boundaries, functional limitations, engineered changes, or applications rather than relying solely on the term 'isolated.' Consider claiming cDNA, altered nucleotide order, or application-specific inventions to avoid §101 rejection.

name: Patentability of DNA with altered nucleotide order not decided
description: The Court explicitly stated it did not decide on the patentability of DNA in which the order of naturally occurring nucleotides has been altered.
guidance: Altered-sequence DNA (e.g., engineered or modified nucleotide order) may present stronger arguments for eligibility; however, absence of a ruling means careful claim drafting and factual showing of non-naturality are important.

name: Myriad is a relatively narrow ruling but has consequential effects on existing gene patents
description: The Court's holding is narrow—genes and the information they encode are not patent eligible merely because they have been isolated—but it affects many existing patents and pending claims.
guidance: Interpret Myriad in the broader context of case law (e.g., Mayo, Chakrabarty, Funk Brothers, and Federal Circuit decisions like iNO Therapeutics). Use an integrated case-law strategy when assessing claim validity and during drafting to mitigate downstream litigation risk.

name: 37 CFR 1.312 — general rule for post-allowance amendments
description: No amendment may be made as a matter of right after mailing of the Notice of Allowance. Amendments filed before payment of the issue fee may be entered on the recommendation of the primary examiner and approval by the Commissioner; amendments filed after payment of the issue fee require a petition with fee and a showing of good and sufficient reasons under 37 CFR 1.312(b).
guidance: Examples of amendments falling under 1.312 include changes to the specification, drawings, claims, inventorship, and submission of prior art. The Commissioner has delegated approval of 1.312(a) recommendations to supervisory patent examiners.

name: Primary examiner authority on formal corrections
description: After the Notice of Allowance, the primary examiner may make examiner's amendments and may enter amendments that merely correct formal matters in spec/drawings or formal matters in a claim without changing scope, or cancel claims, without forwarding to the supervisory patent examiner.
guidance: Amendments other than mere formal corrections require SPE approval. The examiner should indicate 'Enter Formal Matters Only' for such entries.

name: 37 CFR 1.111(c) novelty statement requirement applies to 1.312 amendments
description: Amendments under 1.312 that add or amend claims must comply with 37 CFR 1.111(c) by pointing out the patentable novelty of any claim sought to be added or amended.
guidance: Remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state the reasons relied upon to show patentability; see MPEP §§ 713.04 and 713.10 regarding interviews and claim support.

name: Entry of amendments correcting only formal matters
description: Amendments that merely correct formal matters in the specification or drawings, or formal matters in a claim without changing scope, or cancel claims may be entered by the primary examiner (notation 'Enter Formal Matters Only').
guidance: Such amendments do not require SPE prior submission. If disapproved in whole or part, SPE signature is required. PTOL-271 is date stamped and mailed by the examining group.

name: Amendments ordinarily denied entry — drawing changes alleged to contain new matter
description: Amendments to the drawing held by the examiner to contain new matter are not entered until the new-matter issue is settled; this practice does not apply to specification and claim amendments.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 608.04 and 706.03(o) for new-matter drawing practices.

name: Claim amendment limitations (37 CFR 1.121) — addition of words and rewriting
description: A claim may be amended by specifying exact matter to be deleted/inserted where changes are limited to deletions and/or addition of no more than five (5) words in any one claim; otherwise a claim must be cancelled or rewritten with underlining for additions and brackets for deletions.
guidance: When rewriting, underlining/bracketing are applied relative to the previous version; parenthetical expressions 'twice amended', 'three times amended', etc., must follow original claim number. A canceled claim can be reinstated only by presenting it as a new claim with a new claim number.

name: Disclosure correction and prohibition on new matter
description: The disclosure must be amended when required by the Office to correct inaccuracies and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings. No amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure of an application.
guidance: Ensure amendments do not add new subject matter; corrections should be limited to securing consistency among claim/spec/drawings.

name: Reissue application amendment rules
description: Amendments in reissue applications must comply with special requirements: provide entire text of newly added/rewritten paragraphs with markings (or a statement deleting a paragraph), indicate precise point in specification, use underlining/brackets for changes, and follow strict rules for claim amendments including presenting entire text of each amended/added claim with markings, not renumbering patent claims, and setting forth status of all claims.
guidance: Each amendment must be accompanied by explanation of support in the disclosure on separate page(s). Drawings amendments to patents follow substitute sheet practice and must be identified as 'amended' or 'new.' No reissue patent shall be granted enlarging scope of original patent claims unless applied for within two years of original grant; no amendment may introduce new matter or be made in an expired patent. All amendments must be relative to the patent as of the reissue filing date.

name: Meaning and use of brackets and underlining in claim amendments
description: The term 'brackets' in 37 CFR 1.121(a) means square brackets [ ]; parentheses () are distinct and may be held not fully responsive. Underlining indicates added matter; brackets indicate deleted matter. If a dependent claim is rewritten in independent form, subject matter from the prior independent claim is considered 'added' and should be underlined.
guidance: Ambiguous use of brackets/underlining that makes it unclear whether markings are intended to appear in the patent should be clarified by applicant; see form paragraph guidance for examiner notices.

name: Purpose of the double patenting doctrine
description: The doctrine of double patenting seeks to prevent the unjustified extension of patent exclusivity beyond the term of a patent. The public should be able to act on the assumption that upon the expiration of the patent it will be free to use not only the invention claimed in the patent but also modifications or variants which would have been obvious to those of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
guidance: Double patenting results when the right to exclude granted in one patent is unjustly extended by the grant of another patent or patents. The focus of analysis is on whether grant of a second patent would give rise to an unjustified extension of rights; examine claims for scope and obvious variants. Citations: In re Zickendraht; In re Van Ornum.

name: Two types of double patenting rejections (statutory and nonstatutory)
description: There are two general types of double patenting rejections: (1) the 'same invention' type (statutory) double patenting rejection based on the statutory language that an inventor may obtain a patent; and (2) the 'nonstatutory' (obviousness-type) double patenting rejection, a judicially created doctrine intended to prevent prolongation of patent term by prohibiting claims in a second patent not patentably distinct from claims in a first patent.
guidance: Statutory double patenting is about claim identity/coextensiveness; nonstatutory focuses on patentable distinctness (obvious variants). Nonstatutory also addresses equitable concerns and risk of multiple suits by different assignees. Examiner must analyze claims to determine which type applies and apply appropriate remedies (statutory cannot be obviated by terminal disclaimer; nonstatutory can often be obviated by terminal disclaimer).

name: Claim-centered analysis (focus on claims for double patenting)
description: The focus of any double patenting analysis necessarily is on the claims in the multiple patents or patent applications involved in the analysis.
guidance: Compare scope of the claims (identity, coextensiveness, patentable distinctness). Nonstatutory double patenting can be based on anticipation, a one-way obviousness determination, or a two-way obviousness determination. The obviousness-type analysis is similar to but not necessarily the same as that under 35 U.S.C. 103. See In re Braat; In re Longi; Geneva Pharmaceuticals.

name: Use of prior-art status and transition (FTI vs AIA) in charted analyses
description: When analyzing conflicting claims, examiners must consider whether the earlier reference (application or patent) is prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 (FTI) or AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103, and use the appropriate chart versions (I-A_FTI, I-B_FTI, II-A_FTI, II-B_FTI versus I-A_AIA, I-B_AIA, II-A_AIA, II-B_AIA).
guidance: In transition cases, an earlier-filed application may require use of FTI version for one application and AIA version for the other; consult MPEP §2159.03 to determine transition status. Determine if earlier-filed application or patent is prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) or AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) before making anticipation/obviousness rejections. Consider exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(A)/(B) for inventor-originated disclosures; case-by-case analysis required to establish inventor-originated disclosure.

name: Provisional double patenting rejections (when allowed and how to use them)
description: An examiner may make a provisional double patenting rejection (statutory or nonstatutory) against a pending application when aware of copending applications or published applications that claim conflicting or indistinct inventions, provided confidential status and other statutory constraints are respected.
guidance: Provisional rejections are used to notify applicant of potential problems if one application becomes a patent; they may be maintained until obviated. Published applications unredacted may be used; unpublished or redacted published applications may be used only when there is at least one common inventor/applicant/assignee or deemed common ownership per 35 U.S.C. 102(c) or pre‑AIA 103(c)(2). Replies to provisional rejections must overcome them by showing patentable distinctness or filing a terminal disclaimer; such replies should not be held in abeyance. See MPEP §§2136.01, 2154.01(d).

name: Required responses to provisional nonstatutory double patenting (NSDP) rejections
description: A complete response to a provisional NSDP rejection is either a reply showing that the claims subject to the rejection are patentably distinct from the reference claims, or filing a terminal disclaimer in accordance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or (d) with the reply.
guidance: Such a response is required even when the NSDP rejection is provisional. Terminal disclaimers or a showing of patentable distinctness should not be held in abeyance; an application must not be allowed unless compliant terminal disclaimer(s) is/are filed and/or the rejection withdrawn by the examiner. See MPEP §1490 and §804.02 subsection VI for filing terminal disclaimers for applications filed on or after June 8, 1995.

name: Patent term filing date determination for double patenting (utility and plant patents)
description: For utility and plant patents issuing on applications filed on or after June 8, 1995, the patent term ends on the date 20 years from the date on which the application was filed in the United States, or if the application contains a specific reference to one or more earlier-filed application(s) under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), 20 years from the filing date of the earliest such application (the 'patent term filing date').
guidance: Patent term filing date is the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)/386(c) is properly claimed. Benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) and foreign priority claims are not taken into account for patent term calculation. For reissue applications, the patent term filing date is that of the original application. See 37 CFR 1.78 and MPEP §2701 and §211.01 et seq.

name: Statutory double patenting rejection and permitted responses
description: A statutory double patenting rejection (same invention) is overcome by canceling or amending the conflicting claims so they are no longer coextensive in scope, or by a reply showing the claims are not the same as the reference claims.
guidance: A terminal disclaimer cannot be filed to obviate a statutory double patenting rejection. A complete response must point out specific distinctions, amend claims, or cancel conflicting claims. Provisional statutory DP rejections follow similar examiner actions with regard to patent term filing dates as nonstatutory provisional rejections.

name: Double patenting in reissue and reexamination proceedings
description: A double patenting issue may arise in reissue or reexamination between claims being reexamined and the claims of one or more applications and/or patents; it is necessary to determine whether the patents are subject to double patenting considerations in that context.
guidance: Consult MPEP §2258 for double patenting rejections in reexamination proceedings. Determine ownership/commonality and claim relationships, and apply statutory vs nonstatutory analyses as appropriate. Consider whether terminal disclaimer or amendments are available remedies depending on statutory vs nonstatutory.

name: Section 121 protection (restriction/divisional) limiting nonstatutory double patenting rejections
description: When a claimed invention that was the subject of a restriction requirement in one application is presented in a divisional application, a nonstatutory double patenting rejection cannot be applied to that claimed invention unless the restriction requirement was withdrawn.
guidance: Section 121 shields claims against a double patenting challenge if consonance exists between the divided groups of claims and an earlier restriction requirement; if restriction requirement does not clearly set the line of demarcation or consonance is lost, Section 121 may not apply. If multiple patents result from an examiner's restriction requirement, Section 121 insulates resulting patents from nonstatutory double patenting rejection. See Geneva Pharmaceuticals v. GlaxoSmithKline; Applied Materials v. Advanced Semiconductor; see MPEP §804.01 for details.

name: Impact of Patent Term Extension (PTE) under 35 U.S.C. 156 on nonstatutory double patenting
description: Nonstatutory double patenting does not invalidate any patent term extension granted under 35 U.S.C. 156, provided the claims are otherwise valid under the pre-PTE expiration date.
guidance: If the patent, under its original expiration date without a PTE, should have been terminally disclaimed because of obviousness-type double patenting, then usual NSDP principles apply and the patent could be invalidated. However, if the patent is valid under pre-PTE expiration date, it is entitled to the full PTE. See Novartis AG v. Ezra Ventures LLC for court precedent. Examiner should apply these principles when PTE creates potential NSDP issues.

name: Procedural handling of provisional DP after PTAB decisions or reference status changes
description: If a PTAB decision does not reach a provisional NSDP rejection but reverses all other grounds for a claim and applicant has not filed a proper terminal disclaimer, the examiner must determine whether any reference application used in the provisional NSDP has issued as a patent and act accordingly (re-issue as nonprovisional DP rejection if reference issued; withdraw if reference abandoned or not matured).
guidance: Examiners should re-issue provisional rejections as nonprovisional where appropriate and may make them final if otherwise proper. If reference abandoned and no other grounds remain, withdraw the provisional rejection. See subsection I.B.1(iv) and MPEP §1214.06.

name: Generality/abstractness (claims that are 'so abstract and sweeping')
description: Assess whether the claimed invention embodies a 'general concept' presented in such an abstract and sweeping way that it covers both known and unknown uses of the concept.
guidance: The PTO identified this as a factor. The article notes that extremely general concept-claims are likely not 'new' or 'useful' at the statutory level, may be incompatible with §112 requirements for 'clear, concise, and exact terms' and particularity, and may therefore be treated as abstract ideas excluded from §101. Example: Bilski's high-level hedging concept was characterized as a fundamental economic practice long prevalent in commerce.

name: Tie §101 analysis to other Patent Act provisions (structural/textual arguments)
description: Consider the text and structure of the whole Patent Act—especially §§ 112 (written description/definiteness), 102 (novelty), and 103 (nonobviousness)—when assessing §101 eligibility.
guidance: A textualist analysis can legitimately ask whether the invention is such that other statutory requirements can be meaningfully applied. If a claimed invention is so abstract that statutory requirements (e.g., precise claiming under §112, novelty under §102, nonobviousness under §103) cannot be rationally applied, then the structure of the Act supports excluding it from §101. Thus §101 eligibility should reflect whether the claim's 'true merits' (new, useful, nonobvious, precisely described, definitely claimed) can be evaluated under the Patent Act.

name: Emerging_field_rigor (fit within a developing scientific/engineering field)
description: Evaluate whether the claimed invention fits within an emerging or established field (e.g., financial engineering) that provides rigorous terminology and standards for identifying and defining new contributions.
guidance: If the claim lies within a maturing field with robust prior art and technical standards, it is more likely to be sustained as patentable; by contrast, methods that are merely general advice or practices without a rigorous disciplinary foundation (e.g., 'How to Win Friends and Influence People') are unlikely to be patent-eligible. Claimants seeking Supreme Court validation for business-method patents must demonstrate the emergence of such rigorous fields.

name: Use prior-art/practicality indicators (long-prevalent, well-known, taught in introductory classes)
description: Consider whether the claimed idea is a 'fundamental economic practice long prevalent in our system of commerce', 'well-known', or taught in introductory classes—indicators that the claim may be an abstract idea or obvious/anticipated.
guidance: Bilski used such factual characterizations of the claimed hedging practice to support finding the claim abstract and unpatentable. These indicators cut against novelty and nonobviousness and support exclusion under §101 when the claim merely recites longstanding commercial practices or commonplace techniques.

name: Exhibit compliance; public use/on-sale and best mode review
description: Exhibits filed as part of an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 must comply with the requirements of 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into an application file. Any affidavits or declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.131 and the accompanying evidence must be reviewed carefully by the examiner to determine whether they show that the claimed invention was 'in public use' or 'on sale' in this country more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)). Where the 37 CFR 1.131 evidence relies on an embodiment of the invention not disclosed in the application, the question of whether the application includes the 'best mode' must be considered.
guidance: Exhibits that do not comply with 37 CFR 1.91 may be disposed of or returned. A best mode rejection should not be made unless the record, taken as a whole, establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the specification has not set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (see MPEP § 2165 et seq.). See MPEP § 2133.03 for public use/on-sale statutory bars.

name: Use of form paragraphs (¶ 7.65/7.66 series)
description: Use form paragraph 7.65 or 7.66 and applicable subparagraphs (7.66.01–7.66.05) when commenting on a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit or declaration to indicate whether the submission is sufficient or insufficient to overcome a rejection.
guidance: Form paragraphs contain bracketed fields for filing date, affected claims, and the statutory grounds of the rejection. When using an insufficiency paragraph, follow with detailed reasons (e.g., untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane; showing not commensurate in scope with the claims) and include a full explanation as appropriate.

name: Insufficiency: Untimely / fails to set forth facts / not germane / not commensurate in scope
description: When an affidavit or declaration is insufficient to overcome a rejection, the examiner should state the insufficiency (categories include: --untimely--; --fails to set forth facts--; --facts presented are not germane to the rejection at issue--; --showing is not commensurate in scope with the claims--; etc.) and provide a detailed explanation of the reasons why the affidavit or declaration is insufficient.
guidance: General conclusory statements like 'lacks technical validity' or 'not commensurate with scope' without supporting explanation are insufficient. Follow with applicable subparagraphs detailing the particular deficiency.

name: Insufficiency reason (7.66.03): Refers only to invention, not to claims
description: Affidavits or declarations that refer only to the system described in the application and not to the individual claims do not show that the objective evidence of nonobviousness is commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Must explain why the submission fails to connect the evidence to the claimed limitations; use 7.66 and give full explanation when appropriate.

name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpected results and to explain proffered data
description: The burden is on the applicant to establish that the differences in results are unexpected, unobvious, and of both statistical and practical significance. Applicants must explain any data in declarations proffered as evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: Direct and indirect comparative tests that are commensurate in scope with the claims are probative. For intermediates, applicant must identify the contributing cause for unexpected end-product properties and establish a nexus between the intermediate and the end product (see In re Magerlein).

name: Commensurate in scope: objective evidence must be commensurate with claimed scope
description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support — e.g., results must occur over the entire claimed range or be justifiably extrapolated from tested species/ranges.
guidance: A showing of unexpected results from a species or narrower range can support a genus or broader claimed range only if one of ordinary skill could reasonably determine a trend allowing extension of probative value. To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, compare sufficient tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show criticality.

name: Comparison with the closest prior art
description: When assessing unexpectedness and rebuttal evidence, comparisons should be made with the closest prior art (i.e., the most relevant prior art reference) to determine whether claimed results are unexpected relative to what would have been predicted.
guidance: Use direct or indirect comparative testing commensurate with the claims and explain why the particular prior art is the proper baseline for comparison. (Section heading begins here; details/illustrations follow in adjacent MPEP text.)

name: First-inventor-to-file priority rule
description: Replaces the U.S. first-to-invent system with a new 'first-inventor-to-file' system in which, when more than one application claiming the same invention is filed, priority is based on the earlier-filed application (filing date is most relevant).
guidance: The filing date (including effective filing date) becomes the objective determinative date, eliminating the need for costly interference proceedings to determine who invented first. The change is described as harmonizing with other industrialized nations and simplifying priority determinations.

name: Derivation proceeding to ensure true inventor
description: Creates a new administrative 'derivation' proceeding to ensure that the first person to file an application is actually a true inventor and to resolve disputes about who actually invented the claimed invention.
guidance: This replaces interference proceedings (which determined who invented first) with a proceeding focused on whether the filer derived the invention from another (i.e., is not the true inventor). Derivation disputes are to be resolved administratively by the Patent Board.

name: Inclusion of patent-owner written statements in reexamination limited to claim-meaning
description: Expands the category of documents that may be cited in a reexamination proceeding to include written statements of the patent owner filed in a Federal court or USPTO proceeding, but such statements may only be considered to determine the proper meaning of the claims that are the subject of the request.
guidance: The Committee specifies these statements are not to be considered as a basis for instituting a reexamination proceeding; their use is limited to claim construction issues to prevent inconsistent claim interpretations across forums.

name: Substance of submissions under 37 CFR 1.129(a)
description: A 'submission' under 37 CFR 1.129(a) includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement (IDS), an amendment to the written description, claims or drawings, and a new substantive argument or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: No amendment considered as a result of payment of the fee may introduce new matter into the disclosure (35 U.S.C. 132). Previously refused IDS may be treated as filed within allowed time periods if they comply with 37 CFR 1.98 and certain statement requirements. Examiners may introduce a new ground of rejection based on information submitted in the IDS and make the next Office action final, provided no other new ground of rejection (not necessitated by claim amendment) is introduced. See MPEP § 706.07(a).

name: RCE submission content requirement
description: A 'submission' for RCE purposes includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: If reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of § 1.111. A previously filed amendment after final (whether or not entered) may satisfy the submission requirement. Previously filed appeal or reply brief arguments may be incorporated by reference or copied into the submission. Arguments entered after final but not found persuasive may satisfy the submission if they are responsive within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.111.

name: Pre-interview submissions to facilitate special dispatch (35 U.S.C. 305)
description: If the patent owner desires to initiate an interview, the patent owner should initially contact the examiner to indicate issues to be discussed and determine if an interview will be granted; if granted, the patent owner must file at least three (3) working days prior to the interview an informal written statement of the issues and an informal copy of any proposed claims to be discussed, unless the examiner waives the requirement.
guidance: Submit copies by facsimile or hand-carried to avoid delay. The informal copies considered by the examiner will be made of record as an attachment to PTOL-474. These steps provide structure to the interview and facilitate the statutory mandate for special dispatch.

name: Standard for granting a second/subsequent ex parte reexamination request
description: In order for a second or subsequent request for ex parte reexamination to be granted, a substantial new question of patentability must be raised by the art (patents and/or printed publications) cited in the second or subsequent request.
guidance: See MPEP § 2240 for discussion on determining whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised. The second request is decided based on the claims in effect at the time of the determination (37 CFR 1.515(a)).

name: Consequences of failing to make claims identical after merger
description: If an amendment to make the claims the same in each file is required by the merger decision but is not timely submitted, any claim that does not contain identical text in all of the merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite as to the content of the claim.
guidance: This rejection is for failure to particularly point out the invention. Patent owner will be given 1 month to provide the housekeeping amendment to make claims identical when required by the merger decision.

name: Lapse of time and abandonment
description: “there is no limitation unless the lapse of time be sufficient to show an abandonment of the invention, which is a question for the jury and not for the Commissioner.”
guidance: Delay between invention and application does not automatically bar a claim; only when lapse indicates abandonment (a factual question for a jury) may delay defeat rights. Commissioner should not treat mere lapse as conclusive.

name: Commissioner’s opinion is not conclusive; board/judge may reverse
description: Section 7 (1836) contemplates that when the Commissioner considers a specification/claim not allowable, he may order a board of examiners whose opinion may reverse the Commissioner: the legislature did not intend the Commissioner’s opinion to be conclusive.
guidance: Administrative decisions include procedures for internal review (board of examiners) and external appeal; the Commissioner’s written grounds must be furnished and can be revisited by the board or judge.

name: Interference must concern patentable matter and claims are limited to their specification
description: “The interference mentioned... must be an interference in respect to patentable matters; and the claims of the applicants must be limited to the matters specifically set forth, as their respective inventions; and what is not thus claimed, may, for the purpose of this preliminary inquiry, be considered as disclaimed.”
guidance: Only overlaps in patentable subject-matter as specifically claimed trigger interference; unclaimed subject-matter should be treated as disclaimed for interference analysis.

name: Test for whether an interference exists: compare claimed patentable matter
description: “The question then is, does Mr. Bain claim a patent for any matter now patentable, for which Mr. Morse claims a patent? To answer this question, it is necessary to ascertain for what patentable matter Mr. Morse now claims a patent.”
guidance: Determine interference by construing each party’s claims/specifications to see if they claim the same patentable subject-matter; focus on what each party actually claims as their invention.

name: Patentability of combinations vs elemental features
description: The Commissioner found that elemental features (single circuit, prepared paper, marking by electro-chemical process) were not new, so they were not patentable alone; but a novel combination of known elements producing a new or better result can be patentable: “it was only a new combination of the several parts so as to produce a new result, or an old result in a better manner, that either could patent.”
guidance: Do not claim monopoly over long-known elementary devices or natural forces alone; instead, claim a novel combination or application that yields a new/result or improved operation. Assess novelty and patentability at the combination level when elements are known.

name: Claims must be read in light of specification (claim construction rule)
description: The court analyzed Morse’s claim language (use of a single circuit to mark telegraphic signs and the machinery described) to determine the scope and whether Bain’s claims interfered.
guidance: Claim construction is central: read claims per specification to identify scope, elemental features, and whether the competing claim falls within that scope for interference and patentability analysis.

name: Definition: invention information and use of claims for guidance
description: Invention information comprises all novel and unobvious subject matter in the total disclosure (description, drawings, claims) that represents an addition to the state of the art; 'invention information' should usually be determined using the claims of the patent document for guidance.
guidance: Determine invention information primarily by reference to the claims but consider the total disclosure in context of the state of the art.

name: Structured metadata availability
description: Structured Metadata: Each application includes application/publication numbers; title, abstract, claims, background, summary, full description; filing/publication dates, decision status; inventor, examiner, attorney information; primary and secondary classification codes (CPC/IPC)
guidance: Presence of these fields is required to enable linkage to outcomes, examiner-level analysis, subject-area classification, temporal studies, and other quality-relevant analyses.

name: Summarization (task)
description: Summarization models can be used to evaluate whether patent abstracts accurately summarize the claims and convey the technical contribution.
guidance: Quality abstracts should be extractable by models and align closely with claim content; automated summarization performance is a proxy for clarity and faithful communication of the invention.

name: Drafting Quality — specific embodiment descriptions
description: Drafting Quality Markers: Specific embodiment descriptions
guidance: Concrete embodiments in the description increase claim support and facilitate summarization and claim–description alignment checks.

name: Drafting Quality — consistent terminology across sections
description: Drafting Quality Markers: Consistent terminology across sections
guidance: Terminological consistency aids subject classification, claim mapping, and reduces anomalous perplexity; inconsistent terms across sections are a red flag for drafting quality.

name: Patentability Quality — claims calibrated to disclosure
description: Patentability Quality Markers: Claims appropriately calibrated to disclosure
guidance: Claims should be supported by the specification; automated checks compare claim scope to described embodiments to flag overbroad or unsupported claim language.

name: Strategic Quality — continuation potential / open-ended disclosure
description: Strategic Quality Markers: Continuation potential (open-ended disclosure supporting later claims)
guidance: Open-ended language and broad embodiments signal ability to pursue continuation practice; measure via presence of generalized disclosures and multiple dependent claims.

name: Strategic Quality — international family / PCT-friendly drafting
description: Strategic Quality Markers: International family planning (PCT-friendly drafting)
guidance: Drafting that facilitates international filings (clear priority claims, standardized structure) is a strategic marker; datasets can track family formation and international prosecution.

name: Strategic Quality — litigation readiness / claim construction support
description: Strategic Quality Markers: Litigation readiness (clear claim construction support)
guidance: Clarity that aids later claim construction (definitions, consistent terminology, clear embodiments) increases value and reduce ambiguity in enforcement contexts.

name: Operative Quality Test — Claim–Disclosure Alignment
description: Do summarization models extract claim content from the description? Misalignment suggests support issues.
guidance: Use automated summarization or information-extraction to align claims with descriptive passages; lack of extractable support indicates potential written-description or enablement problems.

name: Operative Quality Test — Section Coherence
description: Are background, summary, claims, and detailed description coherent in topic and terminology?
guidance: Measure topical and terminological coherence across sections (e.g., via embeddings or topic models). Incoherent sections are a sign of drafting weaknesses and reduce model-based quality signals.

name: Identify what applicant invented and establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim. (MPEP 2103(I))
guidance: Use a separate worksheet for each claim. It is suggested the worksheet be used with the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance Quick Reference Sheet, which includes an overview, flowchart, and form paragraphs.

name: Step 1 — Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter)
description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter) (Step 1).
guidance: Choose A or B: A. If yes, continue with SME analysis. B. If no, make a rejection of the claim as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record. If no amendment is possible, conclude the SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements.

name: Step 2A — Is the claim directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea)?
description: A claim is 'directed' to an exception when the law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim. For this analysis, it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception.
guidance: Courts have identified laws of nature and natural phenomena to include naturally occurring principles/substances and products lacking markedly different characteristics. Abstract ideas include, by example, fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. Refer to the case law chart and the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance for assistance. Choose A, B, or C: A. No — conclude SME analysis. B. Yes, but streamlined analysis appropriate — claim is self-evidently not focused on an exception and does not tie-up the exception; conclude SME analysis. C. Yes — identify limiting elements that recite the exception and explain why the recited subject matter is an exception; then continue SME analysis.

name: For product-of-nature exceptions: explain marked-difference analysis
description: For 'products of nature' exceptions, explain why the claimed nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics compared to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: When asserting a product-of-nature exception, the examiner should explain why the claimed nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics versus the natural counterpart; use case law and the guidance materials to support the determination.

name: Identify the claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why
description: If Step 2A indicates the claim is directed to an exception, identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe the law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea and explain the reason(s) they are considered a judicial exception.
guidance: Document the specific limitation(s) and provide a rationale explaining how those limitation(s) map to the judicial exception (fill-in fields provided in the worksheet).

name: Step 2B — Presence of additional elements beyond the judicial exception
description: Determine whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the exception identified in Step 2A.
guidance: Choose 1 or 2: 1. No — there are no other elements in the claim in addition to the exception; conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. Also consider whether elements in the disclosure could be added to render the claim eligible and identify them for possible suggestion to applicant. 2. Yes — list the claim elements in addition to the exception and continue the SME analysis.

name: Additional-element significance: improves another technology or technical field
description: One basis for significance is that the additional elements 'improves another technology or technical field.'
guidance: If the claim's additional elements produce a technological improvement outside the abstract idea (or other exception), that supports a finding of 'significantly more.' Document how the improvement is concrete and specific.

name: Additional-element significance: applies the exception with/by a particular machine
description: Applying the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine can support that the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the exception.
guidance: This is not satisfied by a generic computer performing generic functions. Do not accept 'apply it' or equivalent language as sufficient. The machine must play a specific, meaningful role beyond generic implementation or mere instructions to implement the abstract idea on a computer.

name: Additional-element significance: adds a specific limitation beyond well-understood, routine, and conventional activity
description: Adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field can show the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Do not treat appended well-understood, routine, and conventional activities specified at a high level of generality as sufficient. Also note that merely using a generic computer to perform these activities is insufficient.

name: Additional-element significance: adds unconventional steps confining claim to a particular useful application
description: Adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application may indicate significance.
guidance: The steps must be more than insignificant extrasolution activity (for example, mere data gathering). Show how the unconventional steps meaningfully limit the claim to a practical application.

name: Conclude SME analysis and appropriate next actions (if elements amount to significantly more or not)
description: If any elements, individually or in combination, amount to the claim reciting significantly more than the exception, conclude SME analysis and continue with examination under other patentability requirements. If not, make a §101 rejection.
guidance: If concluding a §101 rejection, use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (or 7.05.01 where indicated). The worksheet provides a sample rejection template: 'Claim __ is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception ... without significantly more.' Include the identified exception and explain why additional elements are not sufficient. Consider clarifying remarks in the Office action about claim interpretation if needed.

name: Consider and identify disclosure elements that could be added to render claim eligible
description: Identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to the claim that may make it eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant.
guidance: Where additional elements currently in the disclosure (but not the claim) could supply an inventive concept or meaningful limitations, specify those elements in the record and consider proposing amendments to the applicant that might overcome a §101 rejection.

name: Use of streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
description: If eligibility is self-evident and the claimed invention is not focused on an exception and does not tie up the exception, a streamlined analysis may be appropriate and a full eligibility analysis is not required.
guidance: Refer to the February 2015 Training Slides for examples of when a streamlined analysis is appropriate. If using the streamlined analysis, document the basis for concluding the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up the exception such that others cannot practice it.

name: Patentably indistinct / indistinctness standard
description: A later claim is not patentably distinct from an earlier claim if the later claim is anticipated by or obvious over the earlier claim.
guidance: Indistinctness may be established by anticipation (e.g., genus/species relationships where a genus is anticipated by an earlier species) or by obviousness over the earlier claim. Courts construe claims to determine differences and consider inherent results and admissions. Indistinctness is a threshold requirement for ODP.

name: Policy rationale: prevent unjustified extension of patent term
description: ODP is intended to prevent unjustified timewise extension of patent exclusivity when related patents claim patentably indistinct inventions that expire at different times.
guidance: If a later-expiring patent claims indistinct subject matter, the patentee effectively extends the exclusionary right beyond the original patent term, which ODP seeks to prevent. Examples: Vogel (meat vs pork) and the general bedrock principle that when a patent expires the public is free to use the invention and obvious variants.

name: Policy rationale: prevent harassment by multiple assignees
description: ODP also aims to prevent multiple assignees from filing multiple suits based on patents that claim patentably indistinct variations of the same invention.
guidance: Courts view this as a theoretical but real concern; terminal disclaimers promise common ownership to address harassment worries. The doctrine guards against multiple enforcement actions for indistinct claims assigned to different parties.

name: Practical prosecutorial responses to In re Cellect and Allergan
description: Prosecutors must understand that ODP can arise within a portfolio due to PTA differences and adjust prosecution strategy accordingly.
guidance: Possible responses include filing terminal disclaimers (often disclaiming later-filed continuations to earlier parents), increasing claim coverage in single applications to rely on divisional safe harbor, and careful management of continuations to avoid creating later-expiring indistinct claims. The market value of added term, particularly in pharma, drives litigation risk.

name: Purpose of examination
description: At each stage, perform a thorough analysis of the patent application to determine whether it complies with the requirements of the Patent Act and Patent Rules.
guidance: As part of this analysis the examiner performs a purposive construction of the claims and considers a search of the prior art. If compliant, the examiner will approve the application for allowance (notice of allowance); if not, defects may be communicated via an examiner's report, examiner-initiated interview, or a conditional notice of allowance. An application may be examined before being laid open, but allowance or conditional notice will not be issued until laid open.

name: Purposive construction required for claim interpretation
description: The Commissioner’s identification of the actual invention must be grounded in a purposive construction of the patent claims.
guidance: Purposive construction must take into account the role of the patent examiner and the purpose and context of examination. It is performed to determine what the person skilled in the art would have understood the applicant to have intended as the scope of protection as of the date of publication of the application. Once a claim has been purposively construed, that construction is used to determine compliance with the Patent Act and Patent Rules. If there is no disagreement as to construction, the examiner may choose not to provide detailed purposive construction analysis in a report.

name: Steps of purposive construction
description: When examining a claim, an examiner must read the claim in an informed and purposive way, performing specific preliminary steps before construing the claim.
guidance: Prior to construing a claim an examiner will: identify the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) and identify the relevant common general knowledge (CGK) of that person at the time of publication. Once context is determined the examiner will identify the problem addressed and its solution as contemplated by the inventor, and determine the meaning of claim terms and identify elements essential to solve the identified problem.

name: Use a fair, balanced and informed approach to construction
description: Claim construction requires a fair, balanced and informed approach considering the specification as a whole and the common general knowledge of the POSITA.
guidance: Terms of a claim receive technical meanings in light of CGK. The specification provides the context and must be read through the eyes of the POSITA. Foundation of knowledge comes from applicant submissions and the examiner’s technical expertise. A properly informed purposive construction considers the specification as a whole against the background CGK at the relevant date.

name: Identify the person skilled in the art (POSITA)
description: Before construing claims, the examiner must identify the person skilled in the art: a fictitious construct representing an average competent worker in the relevant field(s).
guidance: POSITA may be an individual or a team; is logical but unimaginative (not a creative expert); in highly technical fields may be presumed to have expert-level knowledge; need not be a manufacturer or designer but must understand the problem and means to address it; reasonably diligent, may be multilingual; may have knowledge from outside the field but not presumed. Exact educational background or experience is typically unnecessary. If POSITA is relevant to resolving an issue, the examiner will determine who this person is by reference to relevant fields and consider applicant comments; characterisation should be careful but generalized.

name: Identify the problem and solution
description: The identification of the problem addressed by the inventor and the solution provided informs purposive construction: an invention is an inventive solution to a practical problem and must be disclosed to provide an operable solution.
guidance: The problem need not be explicitly stated; paragraph 56(1)(d) requires description to permit the technical problem and its solution to be understood even if not expressly stated. Identification is guided by the examiner’s understanding of CGK and teachings of the description. Focus in description on particular details can indicate the problem; the examiner should consider the background, objects, specific problems, needs, limitations or disadvantages stated by the inventor. Claim construction cannot be determined solely literally — it must consider the application as a whole to avoid 'pitfalls of language'.

name: Determine essential elements that solve the identified problem
description: One must identify which claim elements are essential to provide the solution to the problem; this is central to purposive construction.
guidance: Essential elements cannot be identified without first identifying the problem and solution. Some elements that materially affect an embodiment may nonetheless be non-essential if the skilled addressee would have appreciated they could be substituted or omitted. An element is essential if required to provide the solution regardless of whether it is known. Essentiality is not determined merely by whether an element distinguishes over prior art or is part of CGK. If a claim omits an essential element, it may be defective for over-breadth (lack of support) and/or lack of utility. Superfluous (non-essential) elements are not a defect per se but could render a claim ambiguous.
