If a claim includes solutions to more than one problem, examination should focus on one solution, guided by the description's emphasis. Aggregation (elements not interacting) versus combination should be considered.

name: Examination after claim construction — reporting and reasons
description: After purposive construction, examine whether essential elements clearly define subject-matter that complies with statutory requirements and provide reasons where relevant to perceived defects.
guidance: Examiners need not explain conclusions in a report unless there is disagreement; parts of analysis not in issue need not be detailed. Where conclusions about specific elements are relevant to an identified defect, the examiner should provide reasons (emphasize problem and solution and elements essential to that solution). Specific statutory requirements addressed in later chapters: clarity and form (Chapter 16), subject matter (17), utility (19), novelty/obviousness/double patenting (18).

name: Use of illustrative examples to apply purposive construction
description: Apply the purposive construction guidance through concrete examples to determine POSITA, CGK, problem, solution, essential elements, and whether claims are statutory.
guidance: Examples (skillet and spoon with specific identifier; outdoor playpen with sensors; board game scenarios) illustrate how to identify the problem and solution, distinguish essential elements, and determine statutory subject-matter (e.g., purely aesthetic 'specific identifier' leading to non-statutory claim). Examiners should follow the analytical steps shown in examples when assessing similar fact patterns.

name: Prior art search scope and content
description: Patentability must be assessed in view of the prior art, broadly including all information made available to the public prior to the claim date, with limited exceptions for applicant disclosures.
guidance: In practice prior art relied on during examination generally comprises published patent documents, journal articles, textbooks, manuals and the like. An application may result from a national filing or PCT national phase entry; scope of a Canadian examiner's search at national phase is influenced by earlier searches. Examiners are not required to search claimed matter having defects relating to unity of invention, divisional requirements, or new matter. Where a comprehensive international search exists, a Canadian examiner will nevertheless perform at least a Canadian patent document search for double-patenting or anticipation concerns.

name: Step 2A — directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea)
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicial exceptions). "Directed to" means the exception is recited in the claim, i.e., the claim sets forth or describes the exception.
guidance: If no (not directed to an exception), the claim is eligible and examination should continue for patentability. Examples of concepts courts have found to be exceptions are provided in Parts I.A.2 and IV of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

name: Use streamlined analysis when claim does not 'tie up' an exception
description: If the claim when viewed as a whole clearly does not seek to 'tie up' any judicial exception, use the "streamlined analysis" discussed in Part I.B.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.
guidance: Streamlined analysis applies where a claim clearly does not preempt or monopolize the exception; see the referenced part for procedures and examples.

name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' (additional elements analysis)
description: Determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception. If no, the claim is ineligible; if yes, the claim is eligible.
guidance: Additional elements should be considered both individually and as an ordered combination (elements that do not appear to add significantly more individually may do so in combination). The Supreme Court has identified considerations for determining whether additional elements amount to significantly more; examples and applications are in Parts I.B.1 and III of the Interim Eligibility Guidance. Examination should continue for patentability in either case.

name: Evaluate each claim separately
description: Consider each claim separately based on the particular elements recited therein — claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application.
guidance: Perform the eligibility analysis claim-by-claim; do not assume the outcome for one claim dictates the outcome for another even if similar.

name: Handling claims directed to multiple exceptions
description: If a claim is directed to a plurality of exceptions, conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions.
guidance: Additional elements that satisfy Step 2B for one exception will likely satisfy Step 2B for all exceptions in a claim. Conversely, if the claim fails under Step 2B for one exception, the claim is ineligible and no further eligibility analysis is needed.

name: Form paragraph 7.05 — §101 rejection heading and procedural placement
description: Form paragraph 7.05 is the §101 rejection heading to be used when rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Examiner note: (1) This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.04.01 in first actions and final rejections. (2) It must be followed by a detailed explanation of the grounds of rejection using one or more specific form paragraphs (7.05.01, 7.05.015, 7.05.02, 7.05.03, or another appropriate reason). See MPEP §§ 706.03(a) and 2105 - 2107.03 for additional guidance.

name: Form paragraph 7.05.015 — rejection for judicial exception without 'significantly more'
description: Use form paragraph 7.05.015 when the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea) without significantly more. The template requires identifying the claim(s), identifying the exception as recited in the claim, and explaining why the claim(s) do not include additional elements sufficient to amount to significantly more.
guidance: Examiner notes provide detailed bracket guidance: (3) identify the claim(s) that recite the exception; (4) in bracket 2 identify and explain how the exception is recited in the claim and why it is an exception (examples: 'Arrhenius equation' or 'series of steps instructing how to hedge risk'); for products of nature explain lack of markedly different characteristics (example: naturally occurring DNA segment conveying same genetic information); (5) in bracket 3 identify additional elements and explain why, separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more (examples: generically recited computer elements that would be routine in any computer implementation; routine data gathering steps used to apply a correlation). This form is for use with all claim types and any judicial exception.

name: Provisional protection after publication of application (Article 67)
description: From publication under Article 93, a European patent application provisionally confers upon the applicant such protection as conferred by Article 64 in designated Contracting States.
guidance: States may limit this protection but must ensure at least a claim for reasonable compensation for use between publication and grant. Non-official-language States may require translations of claims to be public or communicated to users. The effects never arise if the application is withdrawn, deemed withdrawn, or finally refused, or if a designation is withdrawn.

name: Extent of protection and claim interpretation (Article 69)
description: The extent of protection conferred by a European patent or application shall be determined by the terms of the claims; nevertheless the description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims.
guidance: Up to grant, protection is determined by the latest filed claims in the publication; the granted or amended patent determines retroactively the protection conferred by the application insofar as such protection is not thereby extended.

name: Deposit does not substitute for full description when product can be defined
description: The fact that a biological deposit has been made does not of itself mean an invention has been adequately described; a claim to a desired product does not merit protection simply because reference is made to where the product can be found.
guidance: If the product can be defined in clear and explicit terms (e.g., DNA sequence), a deposit is not a substitute for a full and correct description. Whenever possible, include both deposit information and a clear explicit description of the product or method of making it.

name: Anticipation considerations for prior art requiring biological material
description: If a prior art disclosure requires access to a biological material in order for the matter described to be practised, the biological material must necessarily have been reliably available to the person skilled in the art before the claim date in order for that prior art disclosure to be anticipatory.
guidance: Examples illustrate that a prior art document disclosing a strain without a deposit may be non-enabling (and thus non-anticipatory) if the strain was not reliably available. Conversely, if prior art enables construction/isolation by known methods from publicly available elements, the claim can be anticipated even without a deposit.

name: Antibody claim characterization: generic vs particular
description: A claim to 'an antibody which specifically binds to antigen X' typically represents a generic group of structurally different antibodies sharing binding specificity. A claim defined by nucleotide/amino acid sequences or by reference to a deposited hybridoma encompasses only the particular antibody.
guidance: Distinguish between genus-style functional antibody claims (broad) and structurally-defined or deposit-defined claims (narrow); the scope affects support and enablement requirements.

name: General support and enablement requirements for antibody claims
description: A claim to an antibody must be supported by a specification that correctly and fully describes the antibody invention and its operation/use and must set out clearly the steps in a process or method of making/using the antibody in full, clear, concise and exact terms so as to enable any person skilled in the art to make or use it (subsection 27(3)).
guidance: The specification must enable and correctly/fully describe the invention as of the filing date. Claims must also distinctly and explicitly define novel, non-obvious, useful, and statutory subject-matter.

name: Support for generic antibody claims (antigen characterization/antiserum)
description: Generally, a claim to an antibody specific for antigen X will be considered supported if antigen X itself has been fully characterized and either antiserum has been prepared, or if antiserum has not been prepared there is no indication that producing such an antibody would be unlikely.
guidance: A fully characterized antigen (e.g., complete amino acid sequence for a protein) can serve as a correct and full description of corresponding polyclonal antibodies; other characterizations (formula, chemical name, properties, deposit) may also be adequate if they allow skilled persons to understand the scope of the antibody claim.

name: Polyclonal antibody disclosure expectations
description: Polyclonal antibodies are treated as a generic group representing the family of antibodies in antiserum capable of binding a target antigen; methods for preparing polyclonal sera are well known and a specification generally does not need to describe them in detail to be enabling.
guidance: Describe the antigen sufficiently (sequence, properties, deposit) so that the person skilled in the art understands the scope of the claim. If antigen X is known/obvious in prior art, polyclonal antibodies reactive with it are generally obvious.

name: Monoclonal antibody enablement factors
description: Enablement for monoclonal antibody claims is fact-specific. Examiners should consider factors including: whether the applicant actually prepared a monoclonal antibody; where not prepared, whether the target antigen was fully characterized; availability/ease of antigen production; absence of indications the applicant/others were unable to produce the antibody; absence of indications undue experimentation would be necessary; and whether the scope of the antibody claim is appropriate.
guidance: If a person skilled in the art, given common general knowledge and only the specification and the fully characterized antigen, would be enabled to produce the monoclonal antibody without inventive ingenuity or undue experimentation, enablement is satisfied.

name: Monoclonal antibody correct and full description factors
description: A specification must provide a correct and full description of a monoclonal antibody invention. Consider whether the antigen was fully characterized; if not, whether the applicant prepared and characterized the monoclonal antibody; whether a hybridoma producing the antibody was deposited in accordance with the Patent Rules on or before the filing date; and whether the scope of the antibody claim with respect to the antigen is appropriate.
guidance: Paragraph 27(3)(a) may be satisfied by describing the fully characterized antigen to which the monoclonal antibody specifically binds, but depending on facts, a disclosure of a representative antibody embodiment, deposit, or explicit sequences of binding regions may be required.

name: When detailed support is required for monoclonal antibody claims
description: Detailed support beyond a simple binding claim may be required where the applicant asserts functional properties beyond mere binding (agonist/antagonist/neutralizing activity), specificity for a particular epitope, remarkably high affinity, where the antigen is complex, or where there are indications antibodies to the class are difficult to raise or cross-reactivity/obviousness concerns.
guidance: Detailed support can take the form of a representative antibody embodiment, a biological deposit (e.g., hybridoma), or explicit disclosure of amino acid sequences of binding regions, epitopes, or binding pockets essential to function.

name: Patentability requirements specific to antibody inventions
description: In addition to enablement and description, a claimed monoclonal antibody must be novel, non-obvious, and useful under sections 28.2, 28.3 and section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: Novelty and inventive step may be supported by novel/ inventive antigen characterization; claims may be made more particular (and thus more likely novel/non-obvious) by reciting structure (nucleotide/amino acid sequences), reference to a deposited hybridoma, or a specific and supported binding activity such as higher-than-expected affinity.

name: Support for claims to nucleic acids or polypeptides relating to antibodies
description: Where an application claims nucleic acids or polypeptides relating to antibodies (e.g., light/heavy chains, variable regions, CDRs), the nucleic acids and polypeptides must be fully supported by the description.
guidance: Follow the general sequence disclosure rules (see chapter 23.05) to ensure adequate support for sequence-based claims.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) - Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
description: "A practitioner shall not ... engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation."
guidance: Applies where a practitioner affirmatively represents to a client (by invoice, email, or statement) that an application was prepared/filed when it was not, or otherwise misrepresents matter status (e.g., claiming a patent-pending number). OED and case law (In re Riley, In re Muhammad, In re Kang, Matter of Trey T. Meyer) support that false statements about filing/status and billing for unperformed services violate this rule.

name: Preamble and transitional phrase consideration
description: Preamble language (language before the transitional phrase) and the transitional term affect claim scope; 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate, and 'consisting of' is closed.
guidance: Interpret transitional terms according to case law (Genentech v. Chiron; Ex parte Davis; PPG Indus.). Absent clear specification language defining 'consisting essentially of', treat it as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior art search/102/103 purposes. If applicant asserts exclusion based on 'consisting essentially of', applicant bears burden to show additional elements would materially change basic/novel characteristics.

name: Consider the entire application to see how applicant provides support for each element/step
description: Before determining adequacy of written description, review claims and the entire specification (embodiments, figures, sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for claimed features.
guidance: Compare claim scope with disclosure scope from the viewpoint of one of ordinary skill in the art. Determine the field of the invention and the level of skill/knowledge in the art. See Rasmussen; Amgen v. Chugai.

name: Determine whether disclosure shows inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole
description: The examiner must determine whether the specification informs a skilled artisan that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
guidance: This is a factual, case-by-case inquiry; consider multiple factors (level of skill, partial structure, properties, function, method of making). See Purdue Pharma; Pfaff v. Wells; Vas-Cath.

name: Possession shown by detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas
description: A clear depiction in detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas may demonstrate possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Drawings alone may provide a written description (Vas-Cath; Wolfensperger). Generic formulae can indicate what a genus encompasses and be adequate in chemical cases (Eli Lilly). Drawings and formulae are appropriate means where visual representation fleshes out words.

name: Function-only disclosure is typically insufficient for composition claims
description: Describing a composition by its function alone typically will not suffice to describe the composition for written-description purposes.
guidance: Function-only disclosure may be merely a 'wish' or plan and not demonstrate possession (Eli Lilly; Fiers). Exceptions exist where a well-established structure-function correlation allows prediction of structure from function.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) limitations require corresponding structure/materials/acts in specification
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA 112 sixth paragraph), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts disclosed in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: Examiner must consider summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. A means-plus-function limitation is adequately described if (1) the written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to perform the function, or (2) it is clear that one skilled in the art would know what structure/materials/acts in the specification perform the function. See B. Braun; Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino. If a means-plus-function limitation is indefinite under 112(b), it also lacks adequate written description under 112(a). See In re Noll; MPEP § 2181.

name: Species vs genus: analyze scope relative to disclosure
description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species is analyzed as a species claim; a claim that encompasses multiple embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus claim.
guidance: See MPEP § 806.04(e). The disclosure required varies depending on whether the claim is to a single species or to a broader genus; follow the checklist for single-species claims.

name: Higher evidentiary requirement in emerging or unpredictable technologies
description: For inventions in emerging or unpredictable technologies, or those characterized by factors not reasonably predictable, more evidence is required to show possession; disclosure of method+function may not be sufficient to support a product claim.
guidance: Product-by-process claims: written description satisfied where process has actually been used to produce the product; may not be satisfied where it is unclear that the acts in the specification can be performed or that the product is produced. Partial-structure-only disclosures without further characterization may be insufficient (Fiers; Amgen).

name: Patents and specifications as prima facie evidence; defenses and notice requirement
description: In actions by a patentee for penalties, the patents or specifications shall be prima facie evidence that the patentee was the first and true inventor and that the same is truly specified; nevertheless the defendant may plead the general issue and give this Act, and any special matter (of which notice in writing shall have been given to the plaintiff or his attorney thirty days before the trial), in evidence tending to prove that the specification does not contain the whole truth concerning his invention or that it contains more than is necessary to produce the effect described.
guidance: Patents carry evidentiary weight as prima facie proof of priority and sufficiency, but defendants may file particularized defenses (with 30 days' written notice) alleging insufficiency, concealment, or overclaiming; if concealment or inclusion of unnecessary matter is intended to mislead or actually misleads so the claimed effect cannot be produced by specified means, verdict may favor the defendant.

name: Two-step Alice §101 framework
description: Apply the two-step framework: (1) determine whether the claim, as a whole, is directed to patent-ineligible subject matter (e.g., an abstract idea or law of nature); (2) if so, consider whether the claim contains an inventive concept sufficient to 'transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.'
guidance: Recognize that this framework contains underlying factual questions; courts will resolve these questions when evaluating eligibility. Use this framework as the baseline legal test when evaluating claims and drafting pleadings.

name: Avoid conclusory or boilerplate allegations
description: Allegations that are merely boilerplate or conclusory (e.g., attorney argument that the claims provide new computer functionality) are insufficient to survive a §101 motion.
guidance: Do not rely on attorney argument to create factual disputes. Courts have rejected boilerplate assertions that claims 'do not merely recite computers carrying out business practices' where such statements contradict the patent language or specification.

name: Claims should recite technological improvements (not generic computer use)
description: Claims should recite an improvement to the computer or technology itself and not merely use a computer or other conventional technology as a tool.
guidance: Draft claims to make inventive features evident in claim language — e.g., implementation of a particular machine or a particular way of programming software to achieve the invention — so that particular improvements can be clearly alleged in a complaint.

name: Draft specification to describe technological improvement
description: Describe in the specification how the invention is a technological improvement over the prior art.
guidance: While not strictly required if claims and complaint sufficiently allege improvements, a detailed specification may make it more difficult for defendants to prevail at the pleadings stage by providing support for nonabstract, inventive features (e.g., figures and tables).

name: Align complaint allegations with patent claims and specification
description: Allegations in the complaint must not be wholly divorced from the patent claims and the specification; they should align with the patent's plain language.
guidance: Attach the patent as an exhibit to the complaint so allegations can be directly supported by the specification (including figures/tables). Inconsistent allegations (e.g., claiming technical details not reflected in the claims/spec) risk dismissal with prejudice.

name: Assess whether claim limitations are routine or conventional
description: In high‑tech cases, courts will consider whether claim limitations, alone or in combination, demonstrate well‑understood, routine, or conventional activity, and whether the method is implemented with generic computing technology.
guidance: Draft claims and pleadings to show that limitations are not routine/conventional and to explain how the claimed application improves the capability of the system as a whole.

name: Show that claimed functions improve system capability
description: Demonstrate that a proposed new application or computer‑implemented function is an improvement to the capability of the system as a whole (not merely an abstract idea implemented on generic hardware).
guidance: When possible, describe how the invention improves performance, functionality, or other technological attributes of the computer/system, and capture those improvements in both claims and specification.

name: Avoid contradictions between complaint and patent/exhibits
description: Do not plead allegations that contradict the face of the patent, exhibits to the complaint, or matters subject to judicial notice.
guidance: Courts will ignore allegations that contradict the patent and may dismiss claims where the complaint's assertions are inconsistent with the patent's plain language; ensure consistency to avoid dismissal with prejudice after amendment opportunities.

name: Court guidance items that may bear on claim scope
description: A trial court may guide the jury on a number of other issues that bear on the scope of the claim, including: describing the role of design patent drafting conventions, such as broken lines; assessing and describing the effect of representations made during prosecution; and “distinguishing between those features of the claimed design that are ornamental and those that are purely functional.” (Egyptian Goddess).
guidance: When construing scope or instructing juries, courts may explain drafting conventions (e.g., broken lines indicate unclaimed environment), discuss prosecution history statements, and identify functional vs ornamental elements. Practitioners should address these topics in motions and jury-instruction drafts.

name: Two-level (threshold) analysis for infringement
description: Many district courts have utilized a two level analysis: a level-one or ‘threshold’ analysis to determine if comparison to the prior art is even necessary, and a second-level analysis that accounts for prior art in less obvious cases.
guidance: Level 1: ask whether the accused and claimed designs appear substantially similar (threshold). Level 2: if not plainly dissimilar, compare the claimed and accused designs alongside the prior art to determine whether an ordinary observer would still find them substantially the same. Courts disagree on specific tests (e.g., sliding-scale vs. observer-aware-of-prior-art approaches).

name: Portion practice: use of broken (dashed) lines and omission to limit claim scope
description: Use broken lines to show environment or portions not intended to form part of the claimed design; draw distinctive portions in solid lines. Alternatively, omit less-important portions or views from figures to focus the claim scope.
guidance: Broken lines effectively exclude elements from the claimed design (MPEP §1503.02; Egyptian Goddess noted role of broken lines). Omission of rear/bottom views can limit claimed scope to illustrated portions. These techniques change claim scope and can affect ordinary-observer analysis—examples include guitar-body/neck/headstock scenarios where broken vs solid lines alter infringement strength.

name: File multiple applications to claim different elements/levels of scope
description: File multiple design patent applications with varying degrees of coverage (detailed figures, broken lines, omitted features) to build a portfolio protecting one design concept at differing scopes.
guidance: Multiple applications increase cost but can strengthen protection and flexibility in enforcement by providing patents with varying claim breadths to counter design-arounds and capture different infringing variants.

name: Functionality and prosecution-history considerations may limit claim scope (district-court variance)
description: District courts differ on incorporating functionality and prosecution history into claim construction: some courts (e.g., Richardson v. Stanley Works) remove functional elements in claim construction, while others (e.g., Depaoli v. Daisy Mfg.) defer functionality/prosecution-history limitations until later (summary judgment or jury instructions).
guidance: Expect differing district-court approaches: in some jurisdictions the court may identify and exclude purely functional elements at claim-construction stage; in others the court will avoid detailed verbal constructions to prevent undue emphasis and address functionality later. Anticipate and plan briefing to address which approach the court should take and how to demonstrate prejudice if detailed verbal constructions are used.

name: Words per independent claim (claim length)
description: Fewer words per independent claim (shorter independent claims) are associated with higher likelihood of litigation and IPR petitions, suggesting broader claim scope.
guidance: Holding other factors constant, shorter independent claims are likely broader; this is used as a proxy for claim breadth in the study.

name: First-action allowance (allowed on first action)
description: Applications allowed on first action (without a rejection) are less likely to be involved in subsequent infringement litigation or IPR proceedings.
guidance: First-action allowances likely indicate clearer claims and less ambiguity/uncertainty, which reduces disputes.

name: Findings required for design-incentives/market-forces rationale (five findings)
description: When asserting that design incentives or market forces would have prompted predictable adaptation of prior art, Office personnel must articulate five findings.
guidance: The five required findings: (1) scope and content of the prior art included a similar or analogous device (method, or product); (2) there were design incentives or market forces which would have prompted adaptation of the known device (method, or product); (3) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art were encompassed in known variations or in a principle known in the prior art; (4) one of ordinary skill, in view of the identified design incentives or market forces, could have implemented the claimed variation and it would have been predictable to that artisan; and (5) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness. If any finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: Dann v. Johnston; Leapfrog; KSR; Ex parte Catan.

name: Conclusions that the claimed invention is within ordinary skill are insufficient without articulated reasoning
description: A mere statement that modifications would have been 'well within the ordinary skill of the art' is not sufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness absent objective reasons to combine.
guidance: Rejections must avoid conclusory statements and must include articulated reasoning with rational underpinning. Cases: Ex parte Levengood; KSR; In re Kahn. Provide factual/supporting explanation rather than generic assertions about skill level.

name: China: consider claims as a whole (Section 9.6)
description: For AI/big data applications, technical features, algorithms, business rules, and process steps should not be evaluated separately; the claim as a whole should be considered when assessing patentability.
guidance: Draft claims and specifications to show how all recited features work together; avoid relying on isolated analysis of algorithmic or business-rule elements divorced from their technical context.

name: China inventive-step guidance for algorithmic adjustments
description: If claim limitations differ from existing technology in terms of algorithm adjustments that solve a technical problem, the claims may possess an inventive step (e.g., adjusting a CNN to process variable image sizes to achieve a technical effect).
guidance: Emphasize algorithmic changes that achieve a technical effect or solve a technical problem rather than mere abstract or business-method improvements; provide examples and technical rationale tying algorithmic differences to technical effects.

name: Alice/Mayo two-part test application for AI (§101)
description: Apply the Alice/Mayo test: (1) determine if claims fall into statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition); (2A prong 1) ask whether the claims recite an abstract idea; (2A prong 2) consider if the claim is integrated into a practical application; (2B) determine whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the abstract idea.
guidance: When arguing eligibility for AI inventions, address each prong explicitly—show statutory category, explain why the claim is not an abstract idea or is integrated into a practical application, and identify additional elements (improvements, particular machines, transformations, unconventional steps) that amount to 'significantly more.'

name: Avoid functional claiming (risk under §101)
description: Claims described using functional language or broad 'black box' functional limitations have been held ineligible even with concrete elements (e.g., American Axle, Yu).
guidance: Avoid claims that merely recite high-level functionality without structure; include structural/architectural detail or specific steps to tie claimed functions to concrete implementations.

name: Claim AI-specific architecture or training elements
description: Reciting AI-specific architecture (e.g., CNN, RNN) or training elements can support patent eligibility because such elements are not 'generic computing environments' and can be integrated into a practical application.
guidance: Claim particular machine components (convolutional neural network, recurrent neural network, specific training stages/processes) and training processes to show non-conventionality; include architectural details in claims and specification where possible.

name: Rely on training-process claims (MPEP Example 39)
description: Claims reciting a method of training a neural network (specific staged training, datasets, transformations) are recognized in MPEP Example 39 as not reciting an abstract idea and can be patent-eligible.
guidance: Draft training claims with concrete staged processes, data transformations, and dataset construction details to align with MPEP examples and reduce §101 risk.

name: Problem/solution claim style to show technical improvement
description: Claims can avoid §101 rejections by reciting (1) a problem to be overcome, (2) a technical solution (often ML steps), and (3) the resulting improvement over prior art or improvement to computer/AI functionality.
guidance: Structure claims and specification to explicitly identify the problem, the technical steps/solution, and the measurable or concrete result; use problem/solution examples (e.g., converting non-standardized information to standardized format, generating a depth map to avoid obstacles) to demonstrate improvement.

name: List of AI-specific improvements to claim and describe
description: Examples of AI-specific improvements that support eligibility include improving predicted annotation accuracy, reducing size or layers of networks, improving inference accuracy, reducing required training data, enabling different kinds of training data, improving training speed/efficiency, enabling lifelong learning, reducing parameters, increasing speed/efficiency of operation/prediction, enabling hardware optimization.
guidance: When possible, claim and demonstrate one or more concrete AI-specific improvements in the specification and claims, and provide data/analysis showing the improvement relative to prior art.

name: Art unit selection and classification strategy
description: Because treatment of AI applications varies across USPTO art units, drafting to direct an application to an art unit more favorable to subject-matter eligibility (e.g., image processing/Class 382) can improve chances of allowance.
guidance: Use a title, claim preambles, and claim emphasis that clearly identify the technical field (e.g., image processing) and include independent claim language that aligns with the target art unit's subject matter.

name: Architecture description: three levels of abstraction
description: Describe AI architecture at three levels: (1) functional component (e.g., image classification neural network), (2) high-level architectural paradigm (CNN, RNN, feed-forward), and (3) technical details at layer/node/activation-function level (without needing to disclose every internal parameter).
guidance: Relate the problem to the chosen architecture, explain how the architecture performs claimed functions, and, where possible, weave the inventive concept into each abstraction level to meet §112 support.

name: Training description: three levels of abstraction
description: Describe training at three levels: (1) functional description of the trained network's purpose, (2) high-level training paradigm (supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement), and (3) fine details such as loss functions or policy models.
guidance: Provide enough training detail to show how the trained model is generated and why it performs the claimed functions—this supports enablement without necessarily disclosing exact parameter values.

name: Problem/solution disclosure requirements for §112
description: Provide a description of the technical problem, a description of the structure that performs each claimed function (including algorithms if software/AI), non-limiting definitions for AI-specific terms, and how the solution results in an improvement over existing systems.
guidance: Describe the field, give a generic device/task name, explain the problem without conceding unnecessary background, and clearly tie the structure/algorithm to the claimed improvement; ensure specification supports the claim language.

name: Drafting to withstand CAFC/PTAB challenges
description: To survive judicial review, claims and specifications should show concrete technical improvements and AI-specific elements/architecture; courts have denied early dismissal where plausible technical improvements are pled (e.g., LPHDR architecture improving computer performance).
guidance: Emphasize technical improvements in the specification and claims, provide factual/technical support for inventive effects, and avoid overly broad claims that risk preemption; use PTAB and district court examples (e.g., Ex parte Hannun, Singular Computing, Applied Predictive Techs.) to guide claim/pleading strategy.

name: Use specification examples and data to show improvement (PTAB Hannun lesson)
description: PTAB stressed the importance of the specification describing how a claimed invention provides an improvement to the technical field (e.g., demonstrating higher performance of a trained neural network versus traditional methods).
guidance: Include comparative statements, performance data, or concrete technical explanations in the specification demonstrating why the claimed approach improves the technical field to aid both examiner and judicial analyses.

name: Representing an organization — duties and disclosure when constituents violate law
description: When representing an organization, if a constituent's action or refusal to act is a violation of a legal obligation to the organization or a violation of law likely to result in substantial injury, the practitioner shall proceed as is reasonably necessary in the organization's best interest, refer the matter to higher authority, and, if the highest authority fails to address a clear violation that is reasonably certain to result in substantial injury, may reveal information relating to the representation to the extent reasonably necessary to prevent substantial injury (subject to exceptions).
guidance: Practitioner must refer the matter to higher authority (including highest authority able to act). Disclosure under this rule is permitted only if the practitioner reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent substantial injury and is subject to exception when the representation is to investigate an alleged violation or to defend the organization/constituent against a claim arising from the alleged violation. If discharged or if withdrawing under circumstances that permit action under these paragraphs, the practitioner must take steps reasonably necessary to assure the organization's highest authority is informed of the discharge or withdrawal. When dealing with constituents whose interests are adverse to the organization, the practitioner shall explain the identity of the client. Dual representation of organization constituents is allowed subject to § 11.107; required consent must be given by an appropriate official other than the individual represented or by shareholders.

name: Safekeeping client and third-party property
description: A practitioner shall hold client or third-person property separate from the practitioner's own property; funds must be kept in a separate account in the state where the practitioner's office is situated (or elsewhere with client/third-person consent). Complete records must be kept and preserved for five years after termination of the representation.
guidance: Other property must be identified and safeguarded. Practitioner may deposit own funds in a client trust account only to pay bank service charges and only in the amount necessary. Advance legal fees and expenses paid must be deposited into a client trust account and withdrawn only as fees are earned or expenses incurred. Upon receiving funds or property in which a client/third person has an interest, promptly notify the client/third person and promptly deliver any funds/property they are entitled to receive; upon request render a full accounting. When multiple persons claim interests in property, keep property separate until dispute resolved and promptly distribute undisputed portions.

name: Meritorious claims and contentions
description: A practitioner shall not bring or defend a proceeding, or assert or controvert an issue therein, unless there is a basis in law and fact that is not frivolous; this includes good-faith arguments for extension, modification, or reversal of existing law.
guidance: Practitioner must ensure claims and contentions have factual and legal support and may argue for changes in law in good faith.

name: Trial publicity restrictions and narrow exceptions
description: A practitioner who participates in litigation shall not make extrajudicial statements that the practitioner knows or reasonably should know will be disseminated and will have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing an adjudicative proceeding.
guidance: Permitted statements include identification of claim/offense/defense and persons involved (except when prohibited), information in a public record, that an investigation is in progress, scheduling/results of steps in litigation, requests for assistance obtaining evidence, and warnings of danger when there is reason to believe substantial harm may occur. Practitioner may make limited statements reasonably believed necessary to protect client from substantial undue prejudicial effect of recent publicity not initiated by practitioner or client. No practitioner associated in a firm/agency with a practitioner subject to the prohibition may make a prohibited statement.

name: Communications concerning services — specific compensation and certification rules
description: A practitioner may communicate regarding services through any medium but shall not compensate a person for recommending the practitioner's services except for enumerated exceptions (pay reasonable advertising costs, pay usual charges of legal service plan/referral service, pay for law practice purchase per § 11.117, non-exclusive reciprocal referral agreements with client informed, give nominal appreciation gifts). A practitioner shall not state or imply certification as a specialist unless certified by an approved or accredited organization and the certifying organization's name is disclosed.
guidance: Reciprocal referral agreements must be non-exclusive and clients must be informed of the existence and nature of the agreement. Nominal gifts are allowed if not intended or expected as compensation for recommendations. Certification claims must be truthful and identify certifying body when allowed.

name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (abstract idea grouping)
description: Includes fundamental economic principles or practices (e.g., hedging, insurance, mitigating risk); commercial or legal interactions (contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing, sales activities); business relations; managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions).
guidance: Examples from case law: hedging, offer-based price optimization, creating contractual relationships, marketing/sales processes, and organizational/management methods. If a claim limitation recites these concepts per se, treat it as an abstract idea. Improvements to how such activities are performed (e.g., technological improvements) may render a claim eligible at step one if the claim integrates the idea into a practical application or improves computer/technology functionality.

name: Claims not reciting enumerated abstract-idea groupings should generally not be treated as abstract ideas
description: Claims that do not recite matter that falls within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas, except in rare circumstances.
guidance: If an examiner believes a limitation outside enumerated groupings nonetheless constitutes an abstract idea, follow the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure (see Section III.C). Use the enumerated groupings in Section I as the primary reference instead of prior Quick Reference Sheets.

name: Step 1: Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
description: Determine whether the claimed subject matter falls within one of the four statutory categories identified by 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: This check is unchanged by the 2019 guidance. Examiners may use the existing streamlined analyses (Pathway A) where patent eligibility is self-evident. Passing Step 1 does not end patentability analysis—claims must still satisfy 102, 103, and 112, etc.

name: Revised Step 2A: Prong One — Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
description: Prong One evaluates whether the claim recites a judicial exception: a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (as grouped in Section I).
guidance: If the claim recites an exception, proceed to Prong Two. If not, claim is eligible at Prong One and analysis concludes (unless rare circumstances). Use the Section I groupings to determine whether a claimed concept is an abstract idea rather than comparing to prior Quick Reference Sheets or a case-by-case list. For laws of nature and natural phenomena, continue to follow MPEP 2106.04(b) and (c).

name: Revised Step 2A: Prong Two — Is the recited judicial exception integrated into a practical application?
description: Prong Two evaluates whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application of that exception.
guidance: A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception such that the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception. If integrated, the claim is not 'directed to' the judicial exception and is eligible at Prong Two (concluding analysis). If not integrated, the claim is 'directed to' the exception and proceeds to Step 2B. Examples of integration: improvements to computer functioning or other technology/technological field (cases: Enfish, McRO, Core Wireless, BASCOM, DDR Holdings).

name: Step 2B: Inventive-concept inquiry (does the claim provide 'significantly more'?)
description: If a claim is determined to be directed to a judicial exception under revised Step 2A, evaluate whether the additional elements individually or in combination provide an inventive concept — i.e., whether they amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: Consider whether additional elements: (a) add a specific limitation or combination not well-understood, routine, conventional in the field (indicative of an inventive concept), or (b) simply append well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level (indicative of no inventive concept). A determination that an element is well-understood, routine, conventional must be supported by factual findings (see Berkheimer memorandum). Reevaluate any elements previously considered 'insignificant extra-solution activity' when performing Step 2B because they may be unconventional in combination (examples: data-gathering steps that are performed unconventionally). If the additional elements amount to significantly more, the claim is eligible; otherwise reject for lack of subject-matter eligibility.

name: Treatment of claim limitations not falling in enumerated groupings: 'Tentative abstract idea' procedure
description: In rare circumstances, if an examiner believes a claim limitation not in Section I should be treated as an abstract idea (a 'tentative abstract idea'), follow prescribed procedure.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application; if not integrated, evaluate additional elements for inventive concept under Step 2B. If the examiner concludes the claim is ineligible based on treating a non-enumerated limitation as an abstract idea, the Technology Center Director must approve the rejection and a justification must be recorded in the file. Similarly, PTAB panels that treat a non-enumerated limitation as an abstract idea should seek PTAB leadership clearance.

name: Reevaluation of earlier 'insignificant' findings during Step 2B
description: Examiners should reevaluate conclusions made in Prong Two (Step 2A) about elements being insignificant extra-solution activity when performing Step 2B.
guidance: An element judged insignificant in Step 2A may, upon reevaluation, be found unconventional or unconventional in combination and thus constitute an inventive concept at Step 2B (example: unconventional data-gathering steps may render a claim eligible at Step 2B even if not integrated at Step 2A).

name: Avoid relitigation of validity during damages ('specific contribution over the prior art')
description: The phrase “specific contribution over the prior art” appears designed to allow de facto relitigation of claim construction and validity issues during the damages phase; validity questions (why the patent was allowed, novelty, nonobviousness) should not be relitigated at damages.
guidance: Issues of novelty/nonobviousness are validity issues and should be resolved in their proper phase (and if standards need modification, Congress should amend 102, 103, and 112—not section 284). Allowing relitigation overlays a second set of validity standards at damages and undermines bifurcated trial structure.

name: Prohibit revival of 'gist of the patent' tests that broaden claim scope
description: Tests like the “gist of the patent” (used historically under doctrine of equivalents) were discarded because they tended to unduly broaden patent scope and allow plaintiffs to assert rights beyond the claims.
guidance: Legislation should not reintroduce vague, overarching tests (e.g., 'gist' or 'nub') that permit plaintiffs to reduce claims to an amorphous core and thereby claim rights outside the actual claim language.

name: Limit discovery and make estoppel rules certain in second-window proceedings
description: If second-window proceedings are permitted, they should generally serve as a complete substitute for at least some phase of litigation, include limited discovery, and have clearer estoppel rules than the current 'could have raised' test.
guidance: Estoppel should not be so liberal as to encourage sequential gaming (raising only some prior-art issues, staying litigation, then later raising others). Consider requiring defendants who use the second window to raise all claims of a particular type identified by a reasonable search request to a commercial search firm.

name: Interlocutory appeals limited to sufficient-record cases and subject to appellate discretion
description: Interlocutory appeals should be allowed only if the district court finds there is a sufficient evidentiary record and that an appeal would save judicial resources; the Federal Circuit should retain limited discretion to refuse such appeals.
guidance: If a district court certifies an interlocutory appeal on a manifestly inadequate record, the Federal Circuit should be permitted to reject the certification and refuse the appeal when the district court’s predicate findings are clearly erroneous to avoid premature, possibly incorrect final claim construction rulings.

name: Action when Board affirms some claims and reverses others
description: If the Board affirms a rejection against independent claim(s) and reverses rejections against dependent claim(s) thereby leaving other claim(s) allowed, the examiner should either convert the dependent claim into independent form by examiner’s amendment and cancel the affirmed independent claim(s) and issue the application with the resulting claims, or set a ONE MONTH time limit for appellant to rewrite the dependent claim(s) in independent form (no extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) permitted). If no timely reply is received, cancel the affirmed independent claim(s) and any dependent claims not rewritten, and issue on the allowed claim(s) only.
guidance: Two explicit options (A or B). If option B used, NO EXTENSIONS OF TIME UNDER 37 CFR 1.136(a) WILL BE GRANTED. Use form paragraph language (¶12.119.*) to notify applicant. If uncorrected formal matters remain that cannot be handled without correspondence, take appropriate action on those formal matters but otherwise close prosecution.

name: Period for seeking court review has lapsed (form ¶12.120)
description: When the period under 37 CFR 1.304 for seeking court review has expired and appellant took no further action, the proceedings as to rejected claims are terminated; the application will be passed to issue on allowed claims provided formal matters are promptly corrected.
guidance: Applicant must correct formal matters within a shortened statutory period set to expire ONE MONTH or THIRTY DAYS, whichever is longer, from the mailing date to avoid ABANDONMENT. Extensions of time may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136. Use ¶12.120 to notify applicant and list the formal matters (bracket 3).

name: Claims require action when affirmance-in-part brings claims up on the merits
description: If the Board's partially affirming decision reverses a rejection that brings certain claims up for action on the merits (e.g., generic claims or nonelected species), the examiner will take up the application or reexamination for appropriate action on the matters thus brought up.
guidance: The application/proceeding remains closed to further prosecution except as to the specific matters brought up by the Board’s reversal. Handle only those matters; do not open general prosecution.

name: Procedure when Board affirms examiner rejection but enters new ground under 41.50(b) – appellant proceeds before examiner
description: If the Board affirms the examiner’s rejection but also enters a new ground under 37 CFR 41.50(b) and the appellant elects to proceed before the examiner with regard to the new rejection, the Board’s affirmance will be treated as nonfinal and no rehearing of the affirmance need be filed at that time.
guidance: Prosecution before the examiner of the 41.50(b) rejection can incidentally overcome the affirmed rejection even though that affirmed rejection is not open to further prosecution. If application becomes allowed during limited prosecution, do not return it to the Board. If not overcome, applicant may file a second appeal limited to the 41.50(b) rejection (may not include the affirmed rejection). If prosecution of the 41.50(b) claims terminates before the examiner without allowance/abandonment, return the file to the Board so the original affirmance can be made final. Similar rules apply in ex parte reexamination proceedings.

name: Petitions under 37 CFR 1.198 decided by Technology Center Director: acceptance categories
description: Petitions to reopen or reconsider prosecution after a Board decision (with no court action) are decided by the Technology Center Director (MPEP §1002.02(c)). The Director will ordinarily entertain petitions only in these categories: (A) Board decision suggests claim limitation or cure would lead to allowability; (B) Board decision indicates record lacks evidence of specified character and such evidence exists and can be offered; (C) Board decision is based on a practice, rule, law, or precedent which has since been rescinded, repealed, or overruled.
guidance: Such petitions are exceptional and ordinarily not entertained after the Director’s brief has been filed in a 35 U.S.C. 141 review or after trial in a 35 U.S.C. 145 case. If granted in a 141 appeal, steps will be taken to request remand so proposed amendments/evidence are entered of record.

name: Dismissal of appeal for failure to file brief within 37 CFR 41.37 time
description: If no brief is filed within the time prescribed by 37 CFR 41.37, the appeal stands dismissed by operation of the rule. PTOL-461 notifying appellant that the appeal stands dismissed is not an action and does not start any period for reply.
guidance: If no claims stand allowed, the application is considered abandoned on the date the brief was due. If claims stand allowed, failure to file the brief and consequent dismissal is treated as a withdrawal of the appeal for non-allowed claims and the application should be passed to issue. Do not dismiss until the extended period (up to five months under 37 CFR 1.136(a)) to file the brief has expired, unless appellant specifically withdraws the appeal as to rejected claims.

name: Cross‑proceeding invalidation rate comparison (IPR vs EPR vs inter partes reexamination)
description: Compare all-claims invalidation rates across different USPTO post-grant proceedings to benchmark PTAB performance.
guidance: Cited figures: average all-claims invalidation for Ex Parte Reexamination (EPR) ≈ 14%; for inter partes reexamination ≈ 34%; for IPRs ≈ 65–70%. Use caution: USPTO reports EPR data cumulatively back to 1981 and there are reporting errors, so exact EPR figures may be imprecise. The large disparity (IPR much higher) is the puzzle the article analyzes.

name: Institution threshold — reasonable likelihood of prevailing
description: For institution the petitioner must show a reasonable likelihood that it would prevail in demonstrating unpatentability (e.g., obviousness) of the challenged claims.
guidance: The Board evaluates the record at the institution stage on whether Petitioner 'sufficiently shows for the purposes of institution' a reasonable likelihood of success. Language used: 'sufficiently shows for the purposes of institution' and 'there is a reasonable likelihood that Petitioner will prevail'. This is the standard applied to decide whether to institute review on asserted grounds.

name: Obviousness — teachings and motivation to combine references
description: To show obviousness, Petitioner must demonstrate that the prior art references teach or suggest the claimed limitations and that a person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would have had a motivation or reason to combine those references to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Support can include expert testimony and specific citations to the references (paragraphs, figures). The asserted combination should yield predictable results. Courts/Board recognize that a course of action may have simultaneous advantages and disadvantages, and disadvantages do not necessarily obviate motivation to combine (Medichem).

name: Mapping prior-art structures to claimed elements (single-structure mapping)
description: When mapping structures in a prior-art reference to claimed elements, a petitioner must support the mapping; Patent Owner may argue that a single structure cannot satisfy two distinct claim elements.
guidance: Becton, Dickinson established that separately recited claim elements ordinarily indicate separate components; but Google v. EcoFactor clarified that this is a rebuttable presumption — separately listed limitations may but do not always require separate physical structures. The intrinsic record (specification/claims) can rebut the presumption if it permits a single structure to satisfy multiple claim limitations. Provide intrinsic support or expert testimony if arguing a single prior-art structure meets multiple limitations.

name: Claim construction and reliance on the intrinsic record
description: The scope and required structural features of claim limitations are determined by the intrinsic record (claim language, specification, figures) and may limit whether prior-art structures read on the claims.
guidance: If the patent's specification defines or narrows a term (e.g., 'first connector' requiring only 'an electrically conductive terminal'), the Board will interpret claims accordingly. Petitioners should show that the intrinsic record does not preclude their mapping; Patent Owners may rely on figures and specification language to require distinct structural features.

name: Spatial/positional claim-limitation interpretation (e.g., 'on one side of the body')
description: Spatial claim language (such as requiring a power socket and connector 'on one side of the body' and a second connector 'on another side') must be interpreted with reference to the patent's disclosure and figures; asserted prior art must be shown to teach the same spatial arrangement.
guidance: Use patent figures, specification text, and prior claim-construction positions (e.g., district court constructions) to determine whether a reference discloses the required spatial relationships. Disputes over whether a prior-art connector is on the 'same side' may hinge on how the term 'side' or orientation is used in the intrinsic record and cited prior art.

name: Requirement to show that a combination cures deficiencies
description: When combining multiple references, the petitioner must show the combination supplies teachings missing from one reference such that the combination, as a whole, teaches the claim limitation(s).
guidance: Demonstrate how a second (or further) reference provides the particular structure or positioning lacking in the primary reference and why a PHOSITA would apply that teaching to the primary reference. Cite explicit structural teachings (figures, paragraphs) and expert rationale for the combination.

name: Permissibility of relying on common design choices
description: Board may accept as a basis for modifications claims that certain changes (e.g., splitting signals between connectors or moving connectors to different edges) are matters of simple design choice available to a PHOSITA.
guidance: Support with expert testimony and citations to references showing the design choice is common or routine in the art. Show that such a modification would not materially affect operation and would yield predictable results.

name: Use of prior litigation claim-construction positions
description: Claim-construction positions taken by parties in district court litigation (e.g., how 'on one side of the body' was defined) may be cited in IPR to support interpretations of claim scope.
guidance: Board may consider those positions but will ultimately construe claims based on the intrinsic record and applicable law. Parties should cite and explain how prior constructions align with or differ from the intrinsic disclosure.

name: Board institution scope rule (SAS/37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a))
description: When the Board institutes review, it authorizes the review to proceed on all of the challenged claims and on all grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim.
guidance: Cite SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu and 37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a). If institution is granted on some claims/grounds, institution necessarily extends to all challenged claims and grounds in the petition.

name: Preamble teaching and limiting effect (doctrine of claim preamble)
description: If the petitioner demonstrates the prior art teaches the claim preamble, the Board need not resolve at institution whether the preamble is a limiting claim element.
guidance: Cite Nidec: when preamble is shown to be taught by the prior art, institution can proceed without determining if the preamble is limiting. If preamble is in dispute, show that the preamble is taught by the references or rely on intrinsic record for limitation analysis.

name: Interpretation of figures/annotations — avoid impermissible cross-device mappings
description: Annotated figures are useful to show correspondence between prior art and claimed structure, but care must be taken not to impermissibly attribute elements of one device/fan in a figure to different devices or to mis-map which element belongs to which claimed unit.
guidance: When using annotated multi-unit drawings (e.g., chains of fans), explicitly explain the mapping and ensure the mapping aligns with the claim language (e.g., which connector belongs to which fan body). Patent Owner arguments often focus on alleged mis-mapping across adjacent devices; address such objections with clear annotation and explanation.

name: Finland — Disclosure requirements in application
description: The person applying for a patent must deliver to the Government an exact description of his invention, with all essential details and the mode of carrying it into effect, and also the necessary plans and drawings, and models, if deemed necessary, not keeping back anything requisite to be known. The inventor must also state in what respects his invention is new, or whether it is an improvement upon an invention already used; the novelty of the invention or improvement must be specified in the claims.
guidance: Requires full and honest disclosure including how to carry the invention into effect; novelty must be specifically identified in claims.

name: France — Application formalities, language and single-object restriction
description: Persons desirous of obtaining a patent must apply by petition to the Minister and give a description, accompanied by drawings when needful. The petition must be in the French language, and must be restricted to a single principal object, with necessary details and proposed applications; it must mention the duration desired and give a title.
guidance: Strict formal requirements including language, single-claimlike principal object, and specifications for title and duration.

name: Hawaii — Application materials, examination and caveat priority
description: An Act of August 29, 1884 regulates granting of patents; Minister may issue patents up to ten years upon delivery of a full specification and in case of a machine full drawings and, if required, a complete model. Where the invention is a composition of matter, specimens sufficient for experiment must be furnished. The law also gives the inventor power to file a caveat, which is kept secret and gives priority for one year. If upon examination by the Commissioner of Patents he considers that claimant is justly entitled and invention sufficiently useful and important, the Minister will issue the patent.
guidance: Combines formal disclosure (specification/drawings/models/specimens), substantive Commissioner examination for utility/importance, and a caveat system granting one-year priority.

name: Effect of claiming a particular form or element
description: If the patentee describes and claims a particular form or element, and that form alone is capable of embodying the invention, the patent covers only that geometrical form; if the form is not copied, the invention is not used.
guidance: Where a specification insists on a particular component (e.g., a 'crank'), the court must determine whether the defendant's substitute (e.g., an eccentric axis with a collar) is the same thing in principle or merely a variation; relative terms may have reference to particular pieces of machinery and the specification's particularity affects the infringement inquiry (see Morgan v. Seaward discussion).

name: Similarity of appearance/structure as presumptive evidence of same process
description: Similarity in appearance and structure will not of itself always establish infringement where the patent is for a process; but similarity of structure of two things is presumptive evidence of their being made in the same way.
guidance: Where the patent covers a manufactured article but the claim is a process, courts infer that similar-appearing products were made by the same process only by drawing inferences from the evidence; similarity is presumptive, not conclusive (Lord Ellenborough rule cited).

name: Covered Business Method (CBM) scope
description: CBM: same as PGR, but must be a 'covered business method' patent — claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service — and does not include patents for 'technological inventions'.
guidance: CBM petitions must assert the patent is a covered business method. A technological invention is excluded: whether claimed subject matter as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious over prior art, and solves a technical problem using a technical solution. Emphasize financial-product nexus and absence of technological invention when filing CBM.

name: Estoppel effects
description: Estoppel for civil actions and ITC proceedings precludes petitioner, any real party in interest, or privy from later challenging the same patent claim. IPR/PGR: any ground 'raised or reasonably could have raised' during review that resulted in final written decision. CBM: any ground 'raised' during review that resulted in final written decision.
guidance: Understand the broader IPR/PGR estoppel (including grounds that reasonably could have been raised) versus CBM's narrower estoppel. Craft petitions and settlement strategies with estoppel consequences in mind.

name: Petition drafting strategy — scope and depth
description: Better to provide detailed analysis for limited number of challenges, rather than identify large number of challenges for which little analysis is provided.
guidance: Focus on a smaller set of well-developed grounds with sound, claim-by-claim legal analysis and pinpoint citations to the evidentiary record rather than numerous thinly-supported grounds.

name: Support and citation standards in petitions
description: Support conclusions with: sound, complete legal analysis per claim per ground; pinpoint citations to evidentiary record.
guidance: Every legal assertion should be tied to record evidence and explained claim-by-claim. Avoid sweeping assertions without specific citations.

name: Claim construction standard (BRI)
description: Standard: broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification of the patent in which claim appears. The Board will construe claim terms even if the parties do not.
guidance: Proposed constructions should be justified with evidence; most cases require more construction than a mere restatement of the BRI standard. Anticipate the Board performing constructions and prepare supporting evidence and arguments.

name: Claim charts — purpose and format
description: Purpose of claim charts is to summarize the evidence, not the argument. Claim charts support narrative analysis; they do not replace it. Use two-column format. Provide pinpoint references to the evidence.
guidance: Use claim charts as a concise evidence map that directly supports the narrative analysis; do not rely on charts alone. Follow two-column format and ensure precise citations to exhibits and record locations.

name: Expert declarations — content and weight
description: Provide underlying objective facts to support testimony; unsupported testimony is entitled to little or no weight (37 C.F.R. 42.65(a); see IPR2013-00022, Paper 43 denying petition). Avoid merely 'expertizing' claim charts and analysis.
guidance: Craft declarations to add objective factual support (e.g., experiments, data, methodology) rather than conclusory expert opinions reciting argument already in claim charts; focus on demonstrative tutorials where helpful.

name: Patent Owner preliminary response strategy
description: Patentability is not decided at institution stage. Focus arguments on dispositive issues: standing (statutory bar, RPI/privy issues); reference is not prior art; prior art lacks a material limitation or teaches away; unreasonable claim construction. Arguments not raised in preliminary response are not waived.
guidance: Use the preliminary response to address jurisdictional and threshold deficiencies and to show why the petition fails on dispositive grounds; preserve other arguments for later stages (they are not waived if omitted).

name: Practical drafting tip — target limited, supported challenges
description: Better to provide detailed analysis for limited number of challenges, rather than identify large number of challenges for which little analysis is provided. Claim charts and expert declarations should support, not substitute for, narrative legal analysis.
guidance: Emphasize depth over breadth: develop claim-specific narratives, supported by properly prepared charts, declarations, and pinpoint citations to record evidence.

name: Notice of Allowability (PTOL-37)
description: Notice of Allowability - a USPTO form (PTOL-37) is mailed to you if the patent examiner determines that all pending claims in the application are allowable (eligible to receive a patent).
guidance: The notice identifies the allowable claims and the required fees to be paid before a patent is issued.

name: Substantial New Question of Patentability (SNQ) — basic test
description: The presence or absence of 'a substantial new question of patentability' determines whether reexamination is ordered; the term is not defined in the statute and is developed case-by-case.
guidance: If the prior art patents and printed publications raise a substantial question of patentability of at least one claim, an SNQ is present unless the same question has already been decided by (A) a final holding of invalidity after all appeals, or (B) by the Office in a previous examination or pending/concluded reexamination. The Director's determination under 35 U.S.C. 312(c) is final.

name: Second or subsequent request requirement
description: A second or subsequent request made while an earlier reexamination is pending may provide information raising an SNQ for new/amended claims, but to be granted it must independently provide an SNQ different from that raised in the pending reexamination for the claims in effect at the time of determination.
guidance: The decision is based on the claims in effect at the time (37 CFR 1.923). If no 'different' SNQ is provided for the existing claims, the subsequent request must be denied. Once a different SNQ is established for current claims, information directed to proposed new/amended claims in the pending reexam may also be considered to permit examination of the entire patent package.

name: Prior adverse Office decisions on same art
description: A prior decision adverse to patentability of a claim by the Office based on prior art patents/printed publications would usually mean an SNQ is present.
guidance: Example: a reissue application abandoned after rejection without disclaiming the patent claim could support an SNQ.

name: Effect of federal court decisions on SNQ
description: Federal court decisions affect SNQ as follows: (A) a final court decision of validity does not necessarily preclude an SNQ; (B) a non-final holding of invalidity/unenforceability is not controlling; (C) a final holding of invalidity or unenforceability after all appeals is controlling and precludes an SNQ for the claims finally held invalid.
guidance: The Office may accord deference to factual findings by courts but determines SNQ independently. See Ethicon v. Quigg and related discussion.

name: Claims considered — claims in effect at determination
description: The claims of the patent in effect at the time of determination (37 CFR 1.923) are the basis for deciding whether an SNQ is present.
guidance: Reexamination determination generally limited to review of the claims for which reexamination was requested. 35 U.S.C. 311(b)(2) requires the requester to set forth pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested; failure to apply art to certain claims generally means requester is not statutorily entitled to reexamination of those claims. The Office may, at its discretion, reexamine claims not requested or initiate reexam on its own.

name: Required content of decision granting reexamination
description: If the Director finds an SNQ affecting a claim, the determination shall include an order for inter partes reexamination and the examiner's decision granting the request must (A) identify all claims and issues, (B) identify the patents and/or printed publications relied upon, and (C) provide a brief statement of the rationale supporting each new question.
guidance: Examiner must identify at least one SNQ and explain how the cited art raises that question. References relied on should be cited on proper PTO forms and copies supplied only where not previously provided.

name: Decision elements to 'point out' for each SNQ (A–F)
description: For each SNQ identified, the decision should point out specific elements (A–F).
guidance: A) The prior art patents/printed publications which add some new teaching as to at least one claim; B) What that new teaching is; C) The claims that the new teaching is directed to; D) That the new teaching was not previously considered nor addressed in prior examination or a final court holding; E) That the new teaching is such that a reasonable examiner would consider it important in deciding to allow the claim; and F) Where raised or where it is unclear that a reference predates the patent claims, explain why the reference is deemed available against the claims.

name: Petition to vacate reexamination order — limited grounds
