description: A 37 CFR 1.181 petition may be filed to vacate an ultra vires reexamination order; substantive determinations to institute reexamination are not otherwise subject to petition or review.
guidance: Appropriate circumstances under 37 CFR 1.181(a)(3) include: (A) order not based on prior art patents/printed publications; (B) reexamination prohibited under 37 CFR 1.907; (C) all claims held invalid by final decision of a Federal Court after appeals; (D) reexamination ordered for wrong patent; (E) order based on duplicate copy of the request; (F) order based wholly on the same question of patentability previously considered in an earlier concluded Office examination. When a 1.181 petition is filed, the third party requester may file a single opposition within two weeks of service; courtesy phone call to CRU SPE recommended; opposition should be faxed when possible. The third party requester may file only a single submission in opposition.

name: Cannot claim an abstract art or principle in the large — claims must be confined
description: A claim that purports to cover an art or principle in the abstract (for example, claiming the art of cutting ice by any non-human power) is unmaintainable; claims must be confined to particular methods, machinery, or modes disclosed.
guidance: A too-broad functional/omnibus claim (covering all means to an end) is invalid; a timely disclaimer may sometimes salvage narrower aspects. Example: Wyeth v. Stone (cutting ice claim invalid).

name: Two broad classes of patentable cases: new application of known agents vs discovery/application of new agents
description: One class covers new applications of known agents/things that change the series of processes or produce a new result; the other covers discovery and application of new agents or things that produce a new effect or result.
guidance: Use this classification when analyzing whether a claimed subject-matter is patentable; examples include use of electricity for telegraphy or application of light for photography (may fall in either class depending on facts). (§82)

name: New effect vs new occasion: only new effect supports patentability
description: When a known thing is used, determine whether the effect produced is itself entirely new, or whether only the occasion/use is new; only a genuinely new effect (not merely a new occasion) supports patentability.
guidance: If only the occasion is new and the effect is analogous to prior uses, the claim is likely a double use and invalid; if the effect is novel (no known analogous uses), it may be patentable. (§88)

name: Claims must be tied to described machinery/mode; overbroad functional claiming is invalid
description: A specification that describes a particular machine or mode supports a patent for that specific structure or mode; claiming a mere function detached from machinery or claiming all possible modes to achieve a function is insufficient and may render the claim void.
guidance: Example: Blanchard v. Sprague and Story's analysis — patent claims should identify the particular machine or mode; claiming only a function in the abstract is inadequate. A patentee should describe how the invention is to be constructed and operated to define scope. (§85 note)

name: Applicant preparation for the interview
description: Applicant should prepare a detailed agenda that clearly states the objective in advance, explain the inventive concept and any differences to distinguish patentability, and discuss how the inventive concept is captured in the claims.
guidance: If applicable, applicant should propose a response or an amendment to the claims; providing a focused agenda and proposed claim language improves efficiency and the likelihood of resolving issues.

name: Examiner preparation for the interview
description: Examiner should review the proposed agenda prior to the interview and be prepared to explain how the applied prior art is interpreted and how the art reads on the claim limitations.
guidance: Identify areas of agreement and allowable subject matter for a focused meeting; identify additional resources for effective discourse; strive to resolve differences during the interview.

name: PTO regulations identifying materials eligible for immunity
description: Proposed section 123(b) authorizes PTO to issue regulations identifying material submitted in an attempt to comply with the search-and-patentability program that shall receive file-wrapper immunity.
guidance: Regulations should encourage applicants who might fear that aborted or failed attempts would create a record later used in litigation to limit claim scope. Such regulatory identification helps assure participants that even an unsuccessful attempt will not be used against them.

name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A)
description: A streamlined eligibility analysis may be used when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
guidance: The streamlined (Pathway A) result must be the same as the full analysis; it is not a way to avoid an ineligibility finding. If there is doubt whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for the exception itself, perform the full Alice/Mayo analysis. The record may simply reflect eligibility by absence of a §101 rejection or include clarifying remarks. If viewed as a whole the claim's eligibility is self-evident, the claim is eligible at Pathway A.

name: Eligibility is self-evident (criteria for using Pathway A)
description: Claims that clearly do not seek to tie up a judicial exception such that others cannot practice it, and thus need not proceed through the full analysis.
guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes that recite meaningful limitations (e.g., robotic arm assembly with control system using mathematical relationships), artificial hip prosthesis coated with naturally occurring mineral, or claims with merely ancillary nature-based components (cellphone with gold contact). If claims are a close call, conduct full analysis. Claims that do not qualify under Step 2B are not suitable for streamlined analysis.

name: When making a rejection, identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A)
description: The rejection must point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth an exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, product of nature).
guidance: For abstract ideas, identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it corresponds to concepts courts have identified as abstract (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)); citing a supportive court decision is best practice. For laws of nature/natural phenomena, identify the law/phenomenon as recited and provide a reasoned rationale. For product of nature, identify the product and explain why it does not have markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart. Sample explanations are provided (e.g., claim reciting sorting information by X corresponds to abstract ideas in Digitech/Content Extraction; claim reciting correlation of X is a law of nature because it describes a natural bodily consequence). Avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match.

name: When making a rejection, explain why additional claim elements do not result in significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B)
description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the exception and explain why they do not add 'significantly more' to the exception, addressing elements individually and in combination.
guidance: Explain why additional elements, taken individually and as a combination, fail to amount to significantly more. Note that a new combination of well-known steps can be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr); therefore carefully consider whether the combination meaningfully limits the judicial exception. When an examiner concludes elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection should explain why courts or those in the field would so recognize them. See MPEP § 2106.05 for a listing of considerations courts have found to qualify or not qualify as significantly more.

name: Provide reasoned rationale when concluding elements are well-understood, routine, conventional
description: If examiner concludes particular claim elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in the relevant field, the rejection must include an explanation supporting that conclusion.
guidance: The rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the field would recognize, the additional elements as well-understood, routine, conventional. Provide a reasoned explanation (not conclusory) to support the prima facie finding that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more.

name: Identify and apply product-of-nature/markedly-different-characteristics analysis
description: When a claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify that exception and explain why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart and provide a reasoned rationale showing there is no marked difference in structure, function, or other properties as supported by the record. Sample language: 'X is a nature-based product ... there is no indication in the record that isolation of X has resulted in a marked difference ... X is a product of nature exception.' See MPEP § 2106.04(b)/(c) for details.

name: Eligibility outcome (eligible or ineligible) and scope of finding
description: Indicate whether the claims were eligible or ineligible; note that a finding applies to all claims in the patent/application unless otherwise noted.
guidance: Where the decision distinguishes particular claims (e.g., 'claims 1 & 7-8' or 'claims 2 & 7 eligible'), annotate those specifics. This field signals whether, and to what extent, the decision found claims patent-eligible or not.

name: Priority document and translation request (Rule 66.7)
description: If the Authority needs a copy of an application the priority of which is claimed and the International Bureau already has it, the Bureau furnishes a copy to the Authority on request. If the applicant failed to provide the priority document under Rule 17.1, the international preliminary report may be established as if priority had not been claimed, but elected Offices may not later disregard priority without giving the applicant a reasonable opportunity to furnish it.
guidance: Where the priority document is in a language other than the language(s) indicated for the Authority and the Authority considers validity of the priority claim relevant for novelty/inventive_step/industrial_applicability, the Authority may invite the applicant to furnish a translation in that language. The applicant must comply within two months; otherwise the report may be established as if priority had not been claimed.

name: Authority may comment on lack of clarity or inadequate support (Article 34(4)(a)(ii), Rule 66.2(a)(i))
description: The Authority may notify that the description, the claims or the drawings are so unclear, or the claims are so inadequately supported by the description, that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty, inventive_step or industrial_applicability.
guidance: This mirrors procedures used in the international search; the written opinion will explain the reasons.

name: Authority may accompany report with unfavorable observations on clarity/support (Rule 66.2(a)(v))
description: The international preliminary report may be accompanied by unfavorable observations on the clarity of the claims, the description and the drawings, or on whether the claims are fully supported by the description.

name: Procedure for effecting amendments before the Authority (Rules 11.14,46.5,55.3,66.8,70.2(c-bis))
description: The applicant must submit a replacement sheet for every sheet which, due to an amendment, differs from the sheet previously filed. The amendment must be submitted with an accompanying letter explaining the difference and preferably the reasons, and must indicate the basis for the amendment in the application as originally filed. For claim amendments, a complete set of claims in replacement must be submitted.
guidance: For deletions, minor alterations or additions, changes may be made on a copy of the relevant sheet provided clarity and direct reproducibility are not affected. No replacement sheet is required if an entire sheet is cancelled (a letter suffices). Amendments and accompanying letters must be in the language of publication (or of the translation on which the examination is based); translations are required where amendments filed in another language are to be taken into account. No fee is payable for Article 34(2)(b) amendments. Failure to furnish required accompanying letter may result in the Authority not taking the amendment into account.

name: Mention of inventor as such in patent (Section 28 / Chapter XIV provisions)
description: If the inventor desires his name to be mentioned in a patent he may apply; Controller if satisfied will cause mention in complete specification and register.
guidance: Request period: 2 months after advertisement of acceptance of complete specification, extendable by one month. Requests before grant made on Form 8; claims by persons not the applicant must be accompanied by a statement setting out circumstances. Controller not entertain request if applicant wrongly obtained invention from actual inventor who could succeed in opposition under Section 25(1)(a). Oppositions handled per rules 58–63. If Controller allows, mention in prescribed form (rule 70) and register. Applications to remove or correct inventor mention follow same procedure with opportunity to be heard and evidence.

name: Restoration of lapsed patents (Section 60) — conditions for restoration
description: When a patent has ceased to have effect because of non-payment of renewal fees, it may be restored provided application is made without undue delay and within 18 months from date of cessation, and failure to pay was unintentional.
guidance: Application must be on Form 15 with supporting evidence; any patent of addition to be restored should be specified (separate Form 15 for each main patent; no fee for patent of addition). Applicant must be patentee or legal representative; assignee may apply only when assignment is registered. If patentee failed to register change of name before cessation, must first correct register; identity proof required if name changed after cessation. The application must include a statement fully setting out circumstances leading to non-payment supported by recent evidence; evidence may cover several patents and must support claim of unintentional failure and no undue delay. Controller may call further evidence. Deliberate election not to pay fee under erroneous supposition is fatal; financial inconvenience is not ground (destitution may be considered). Negligence of agent may be sufficient if proved. If no prima facie case, applicant notified and may be refused unless requests hearing within one month.

name: Assignee patents where inventor employed and paid for another's inventive faculty
description: If the patentee employed and paid for the inventive faculty of another, the patentee may claim and hold a patent for the invention not as the inventor but as the assignee of the inventor.
guidance: This category of cases concerns assignments and is distinguishable from determining who the actual inventor is; assignment law and employment arrangements govern whether the employer or payor holds rights as assignee.

name: Directed-to inquiry: abstract idea vs technological solution
description: Determine whether the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea (or other judicial exception) or to a technological solution to a technological problem (a specific device, improvement, or concrete solution).
guidance: Courts contrast claims that are 'directed to an abstract idea' with claims directed to 'a purportedly revolutionary technological solution to a technological problem' or to a 'specific device' or 'allegedly improved' technological tool. Examples: WYSIWYG webpage editor held technological solution; roof-model creation through correlating data points held not abstract; radar-alert claims held directed to improving radar detectors by reducing false alerts; videoconferencing claims held directed to a specific device/switch.

name: Inventive concept (Alice step two)
description: After identifying an abstract idea or natural law, determine whether the claims contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: An inventive concept may exist where the claim recites a specific, novel implementation or improvement over the prior art (e.g., a specific solution to a problem, nonconventional steps, or particular limitations). Conversely, absence of an inventive concept is found where claims merely recite conventional, routine, well-understood activities or only instruct to apply a natural relationship in a routine manner (examples: feedback-based message distribution lacked inventive concept).

name: Specificity of treatment claims (dosage/population) supports eligibility
description: Treatment claims that recite specific dosages, administration ranges, and specific patient populations can be 'directed to' a new way of using a drug rather than to a mere natural relationship, supporting eligibility.
guidance: Vanda: claims reciting specific doses for a genotype and explaining how dosage correlates with QTc risk were held directed to a method of treatment rather than merely a natural relationship. Pain-treatment and antipsychotic examples: claims that specify extended-release formulations or dosage steps for a specific patient group found eligible.

name: Transforming a natural discovery into an improved process
description: Claims that take a natural discovery and employ it to create a new, improved, and useful process or technique can be patent-eligible.
guidance: Rapid Litigation/CellzDirect: inventors discovered cells' survival characteristics and then 'employed their natural discovery to create a new and improved way' of preserving hepatocytes, claiming more than the natural phenomenon itself; the improvement and utility supported eligibility.

name: Specific technical improvement / solution to prior art problems
description: Claims that recite a specific technical means for overcoming a problem in the prior art are indicative of an inventive concept and support eligibility.
guidance: Courts cite improvements such as novel sequencing-template methods for nanopore sequencing, improved mobile handset geo-location overcoming GPS receiver limitations, base-station selection requiring new indices to avoid call interruption, and novel methods of applying multiple energies concurrently to change material properties. The specification's explanation of benefits over prior art can bolster the inventive-concept finding.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity undermines inventive concept
description: If claimed elements are shown to be well-understood, routine, and conventional at the time of the invention, they do not supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Courts evaluate factual record to determine whether elements were conventional; if so, this disfavors eligibility. Example: judge dissent arguing claimed temperature-detection elements were long known and conventional. Berkhimer/Aatrix emphasize underlying factual disputes about conventionality.

name: Abstract idea categories: organizing, collecting, analyzing, reporting, and fundamental economic practices
description: Claims that essentially perform abstract activities—organizing data, collecting/analyzing/reporting results, or traditional business practices—are likely to be characterized as abstract ideas unless tied to a specific technical improvement.
guidance: Cases: blood-sample analysis claims were characterized as 'collecting, analyzing, and reporting results' (abstract) but saved by a specific novel implementation; other data-processing claims deemed ineligible when merely organizing human behavior.

name: Claims rooted in computer technology to solve a computer-specific problem
description: If the claim addresses a problem specific to computer networks/technology and the solution is necessarily rooted in computer technology, courts may find an inventive concept.
guidance: Examples: claims describing solutions to problems arising in computer networks (improved data extraction/mapping from resumes, systems that necessarily require digital implementation) have survived §101 challenges when tied to technical improvements in computing.

name: Claim construction often required before resolving §101
description: Courts frequently defer a definitive §101 ruling until after claim construction where claim meaning affects whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea or contains an inventive concept.
guidance: District courts repeatedly held that claim construction is necessary because §101 analysis can hinge on claim term meanings, representation of dependent claims by a representative claim, and factual disputes that cannot be resolved at the pleadings stage.

name: Claims describing concrete technological concepts (e.g., display screen, applet) may avoid being labeled abstract
description: When the purported abstract idea is described with concrete technological components in the specification/claims, courts may be less willing to treat the claim as an abstract idea.
guidance: Targeted-advertising example: the specification incorporated a display screen and an applet—'two seemingly concrete concepts'—undermining defendant's argument that the claims were directed to an abstract idea.

name: Specification-discussed benefits and nonconventionality can support inventive concept
description: Explicit statements in the specification about benefits, nonconventional methods, or advantages over prior art can help demonstrate that claims contain an inventive concept.
guidance: Examples: arterial thermometer claims noted 'transform[ing] the underlying natural laws into inventive methods and useful devices' with record evidence of nonobvious combination; ultrashort pulsed lasers claims relied on specification describing improved functionality for particular purposes.

name: Claims that recite novel and useful structural limitations
description: Structural or compositional limitations that are novel and useful (e.g., specific layered lamination) can weigh in favor of eligibility.
guidance: Example: tissue graft claim where amnion and chorion layers being 'directly laminated to each other' was novel and useful and supported denial of dismissal on §101 grounds.

name: Claims improving a device's functionality as a technological tool
description: Claims that improve a device's operation or accuracy (making it a better technological tool) can be treated as patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Examples: heart-rate monitor improvement, radar detector improvements by reducing false alerts, and improved methods for generating an intraoral model were treated as technological improvements supporting eligibility findings.

name: Showing that claimed computer functions were not previously well-known preserves eligibility
description: If defendants cannot show that the claimed computer functions were well-understood, routine, or conventional in the industry, courts may find that the claims could contain an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: denial of judgment where defendants failed to provide evidence that use of persistent mainstreams/substreams were previously known; lack of such evidence supported survival of claim.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 can be made when prior art product appears identical but is silent as to an inherent characteristic
description: Where applicant claims a composition in terms of a function, property or characteristic and the composition of the prior art is the same as that of the claim but the function is not explicitly disclosed, the examiner may make a rejection under both 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.
guidance: There is nothing inconsistent in concurrent rejections for obviousness and anticipation. This rationale applies to product, apparatus, and process claims recited in terms of function/property/characteristic. Cited case: In re Best.

name: Burden shifts to applicant after examiner establishes inherency for substantially identical prior-art product
description: Once a reference teaching a product appearing to be substantially identical is made the basis of a rejection, and the examiner presents evidence or reasoning to show inherency, the burden of production shifts to the applicant to show the prior art does not possess the characteristics relied upon.
guidance: The PTO can require applicant to prove that prior art products do not necessarily or inherently possess the claimed characteristics; burden similar to product-by-process contexts. Cited cases/examples: In re Best, In re Fitzgerald (applicant needed objective evidence comparing shrinkage rates), Schreiber (applicant declaration failed because it lacked necessary specifics). See MPEP § 2113 for product-by-process discussion.

name: Product and apparatus claims: substantially identical structure/composition presumes claimed properties/functions are inherent
description: When the claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure or composition, or are produced by identical or substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of either anticipation or obviousness has been established.
guidance: When the PTO shows a sound basis for believing products are the same, applicant has the burden of showing they are not. Cases: In re Best, Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner, In re Ludtke, Northam Warren Corp. v. D. F. Newfield. Examiner should rely on evidence of substantial identity; applicant can rebut with evidence showing prior art products do not necessarily possess the characteristics of the claimed product.

name: Composition claims: identical chemical structure implies identical properties
description: "Products of identical chemical composition can not have mutually exclusive properties." If the prior art teaches the identical chemical structure, the properties applicant discloses/claims are necessarily present.
guidance: Virtual identity of monomers and procedures can support a prima facie case of lack of novelty (In re Spada). Applicant must provide evidence of nonobvious or distinguishing properties to rebut.

name: Printed matter that is nonfunctional does not distinguish a claimed product from otherwise identical prior art
description: Where the only difference between a prior art product and a claimed product is printed matter that is not functionally related to the product, the printed matter will not distinguish the claimed product from the prior art.
guidance: Critical question: whether there exists a new and unobvious functional relationship between the printed matter and the substrate. Cases/examples: In re Ngai (kit with different instructions still anticipated), In re Gulack, In re Miller (writing showing how to 'half' a recipe was functional), In re Seid, In re Xiao, In re Bryan. Extension: instruction limitations added to known methods are treated similarly (King Pharmaceuticals v. Eon Labs; In re Kao).

name: Process claims: prior art device anticipates a claimed process if device would necessarily perform the method during normal operation
description: If a prior art device, in its normal and usual operation, would necessarily perform the method claimed, then the method claimed will be considered anticipated by the prior art device.
guidance: When the prior art device is the same as a device described in the specification for carrying out the claimed method, it can be assumed the device will inherently perform the claimed process. Examples/cases: In re King (coated substrate inherently performs claimed absorption/reflection process), In re Best (cooling step inherently performed), Ex parte Novitski, Ex parte Novitski and others where applicants failed to introduce comparative evidence to rebut.

name: Process-of-use claims: new and nonobvious uses of old structures/compositions may be patentable, but claims directed to a result/property may be anticipated
description: Discovery of a new use for an old structure based on unknown properties might be patentable as a process of using; however, when the claim recites using an old composition or structure and the 'use' is directed to a result or property of that composition/structure, then the claim is anticipated.
guidance: Cases: In re Hack (new use possibly patentable), In re May (claims to a method of achieving nonaddictive analgesia were anticipated because prior art taught same compounds for analgesia), In re Tomlinson (result of mixing was not enough to avoid anticipation). Applicants must show unexpected properties or nonobviousness to prevail on use claims directed to properties/results.

name: Product-by-process claims: product patentability is based on the product itself, not the recited process
description: "Even though product-by-process claims are limited by and defined by the process, determination of patentability is based on the product itself. If the product in the product-by-process claim is the same as or obvious from a product of the prior art, the claim is unpatentable even though the prior product was made by a different process."
guidance: Product identity or obviousness from prior art products defeats product-by-process claims even if made by different processes (In re Thorpe, Amgen v. F. Hoffmann-La Roche, Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma). However, in infringement analysis, a product-by-process claim is infringed only by a product made by the recited process. Consider the structure implied by the process steps when assessing patentability (In re Garnero, In re Nordt Dev. Co.).

name: Inherency and functional limitations in apparatus claims: examiner must explain inherency of functional limitations
description: If an examiner concludes that a functional limitation is an inherent characteristic of the prior art, the examiner should explain that the prior art structure inherently possesses the functionally defined limitations of the claimed apparatus.
guidance: When inherency of function is asserted, burden shifts to applicant to establish that the prior art does not possess the characteristic relied on. Cases: In re Schreiber (examiner justified in concluding inherent function based on structural similarity), Bettcher Industries v. Bunzl USA, In re Swinehart.

name: Manner of operating a device does not differentiate an apparatus claim from the prior art
description: "[A]pparatus claims cover what a device is, not what a device does." A recitation of the manner in which an apparatus is intended to be employed does not differentiate the claimed apparatus if the prior art teaches all structural limitations.
guidance: Operational or use-oriented preambles are immaterial to the structure; Ex parte Masham example (submersion amount immaterial). Case: Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Bausch & Lomb Inc.

name: A prior art device can perform all functions recited in an apparatus claim and still not anticipate if there is any structural difference
description: Even if the prior art device performs all claimed functions, the prior art cannot anticipate the claim if there is any structural difference required by the claim.
guidance: Means-plus-function limitations are met by structures equivalent to those in the specification. Cases: In re Donaldson, In re Robertson (claim construed to require three fastening elements; reference with two elements did not disclose a separate third element). Examiner should analyze structural elements, not solely functional equivalence.

name: Controls for applicant, application, and examiner characteristics
description: Control for applicant characteristics (ln employees at filing/first-action, ln(1+sales), employment growth, sales growth), application characteristics (ln # independent claims), and examiner characteristics (ln examiner experience, examiner grade indicators GS-9–GS-15) to account for potential quality-based assignment.
guidance: Columns 2–4 investigate quality-based assignment using applicant/application characteristics. Columns 5–6 investigate assignment based on examiner characteristics, including proxies for experience and seniority. These additional controls are included in alternative first-stage specifications and (in Internet Appendix) in second stage as robustness.

name: Argument requirement (content and citations)
description: Arguments with respect to each ground of rejection and the basis therefor, including citations of statutes, regulations, authorities and parts of the Record relied on.
guidance: Arguments shall explain why the examiner erred as to each ground of rejection contested by appellant. A statement which merely points out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument for patentability. See Ex parte Frye and In re Jung for examples. 37 CFR 41.37(c)(1)(iv) emphasizes inclusion of all arguments and authorities in the brief; otherwise they will be refused consideration by the Board for the present appeal.

name: Separate heading per ground of rejection
description: Each ground of rejection must be argued under a separate heading that clearly identifies the ground of rejection being contested.
guidance: For grounds applying to two or more claims, claims may be argued separately, as a group, or as a subgroup. When grouped, the Board may select a single claim and decide the appeal as to the group based on that claim alone. Failure to separately argue claims that appellant has grouped together constitutes a waiver of any argument that the Board must consider patentability of any grouped claim separately. Under each heading identifying the ground being contested, any claim(s) argued separately or as a subgroup shall be placed under a separate subheading that identifies the claim(s) by number.

name: Entry and treatment of amendments after notice of appeal but before brief
description: Amendments filed after the date of filing an appeal and prior to filing a brief may be admitted as provided in 37 CFR 1.116.
guidance: A new amendment must be submitted in a separate paper. Entry of an amendment in an application on appeal is not a matter of right and is governed by 37 CFR 41.33. Amendments filed after the filing of a notice of appeal but prior to a brief may be admitted only to (A) cancel claims (not affecting scope of other pending claims), (B) comply with form requirements expressly set forth in a previous action, (C) present rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal, or (D) amend the specification or claims upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why necessary and not earlier presented (see 37 CFR 41.33(a)). If examiner denies entry, use form PTOL-303 to notify applicant.

name: Amendments permitted after filing brief
description: Amendments filed on or after the date of filing a brief may be admitted only in limited circumstances.
guidance: Per 37 CFR 41.33(b), admitted amendments after filing a brief may be: (1) to cancel claims where cancellation does not affect scope of other pending claims; or (2) to rewrite dependent claims into independent form. 37 CFR 41.37(c)(2) provides that a brief shall not include any non-admitted amendment; any amendment filed at same time as brief must be submitted in a separate paper. Amendments filed after jurisdiction passes to the Board are not considered prior to expiration of time set in 37 CFR 90.3 unless remanded by the Board.

name: Rewriting dependent claims into independent form (what it includes)
description: Rewriting dependent claims into independent form as permitted under 37 CFR 41.33(b)(2) is defined.
guidance: Includes: (A) rewriting a dependent claim in independent form by adding thereto the limitations of the parent claim(s); and (B) rewriting an independent claim to incorporate all subject matter of a dependent claim, canceling the dependent claim and changing dependencies of claims that depended from the now-canceled dependent claim to the amended independent claim.

name: New grounds of rejection procedure and approval
description: A new ground of rejection is permitted in an examiner’s answer but must be approved and signed by the Director (or designee) and properly designated as 'NEW GROUNDS OF REJECTION'.
guidance: For each new ground, a complete explanation supporting the rejection must be provided with a proper reference to the applicable statute, prior art references relied upon, and claim numbers. Approval authority is delegated to Technology Center Directors or designees; the answer must include signature of TC Director/designee to indicate approval.

name: Office action clarity and specificity
description: When making a rejection, the Office action must provide an explanation as to why the claim is ineligible, which must be sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice of the reasons for ineligibility and enable the applicant to effectively respond.
guidance: The worksheet emphasizes that the written rejection must clearly identify why the claim is ineligible and provide sufficient notice so applicant can respond effectively. If the examiner maintains a rejection, the action should explain the identification of the abstract idea and comparison to court-identified abstract ideas.

name: Step 2A: Has a judicial exception been identified?
description: Determine whether the rejection identifies a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature) that the claim is alleged to recite.
guidance: The examiner must explicitly state what the judicial exception is (example given: 'the abstract idea of advancing funds based on future retirement payments').

name: Step 2A: Does the rejection point to words of the claim that recite the judicial exception?
description: The rejection should point to the specific claim language that sets forth or describes the judicial exception.
guidance: Worksheet checkbox: examiners should identify the claim words (example listing steps such as storing an account for a beneficiary, designating a benefit provider, periodically disbursing a portion of retirement payments, authorizing provider to provide benefit based on present value). This linkage must be in the action.

name: Step 2A: Is there an explanation of why those words are a judicial exception?
description: The action must explain why the identified claim language constitutes a judicial exception, e.g., by showing correspondence to concepts courts have found to be abstract.
guidance: Provide a reasoned rationale identifying the concept recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered an abstract idea, for example by comparing to concepts identified as abstract in case law (Alice, Bilski, Fort Properties). The worksheet notes courts treat eligibility as a question of law and do not rely on publications as evidence for abstractness.

name: Step 2B: Are any additional elements identified?
description: Identify any additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception (e.g., memory, processor, network interface, controller, electronic funds transfer, kiosk components).
guidance: List all additional elements claimed so that their role can be analyzed individually and in combination with the exception. Examples in the worksheet include generic computer components and kiosk elements (interactive display, network connector, smart card dispenser).

name: Generic computer elements performing generic functions do not supply 'significantly more'
description: Recitation of generic computer components or programming a computer to perform abstract steps is insufficient to make a claim patent eligible.
guidance: Cites guidance that a claim requiring no more than a generic computer to perform generic computer functions that are well-understood, routine and conventional does not qualify as 'significantly more' (2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance; Supreme Court decisions Alice and Bilski). The fact that a claim requires a computer and is not a pure mental process is not dispositive.

name: Machine-or-Transformation test is not determinative
description: The M-or-T test can be an important clue but is not a stand-alone test for eligibility.
guidance: Even if a claim requires computer implementation or passes M-or-T, it still must pass the Alice/Mayo two-part framework. The worksheet explains that machine components that amount to applying an idea with a computer do not necessarily impart eligibility.

name: Examiner's burden: provide a reasoned rationale (courts treat eligibility as law)
description: To establish that a claim is directed to an abstract idea, the examiner must provide a reasoned rationale identifying the claimed concept and explaining why it is an abstract idea.
guidance: Courts consider eligibility a question of law and do not rely on documentary evidence to find an idea is abstract; instead examiners should compare the recited concept to case-law-identified abstract ideas and explain the comparison (the worksheet uses the example of comparing to Alice, Bilski, Fort Properties).

name: Consideration of elements in combination may supply 'significantly more'
description: Evaluate whether additional limitations, when considered in combination with the claim as a whole, provide meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the abstract idea to a technological environment and thus amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: Worksheet example: Claim 2 (kiosk + system) was found persuasive because the kiosk elements combined with the funds-dispersal system represented a departure from routine and conventional sequence and provided meaningful limitations; the examiner should withdraw the rejection for such claims and provide clarifying remarks.

name: Extra-solution activity identification
description: Recognize when a claimed element is extra-solution activity (i.e., not adding a technical contribution), such as physical mechanisms performing ordinary distribution tasks.
guidance: Worksheet labels the smart card dispenser as 'extra-solution activity' in the hypothetical; such elements may not overcome an abstract-idea rejection unless their integration provides meaningful improvement.

name: Abstract — language and prohibited phrasing
description: The abstract should be clear and concise, avoid legal phraseology commonly used in claims, and should not repeat information given in the title.
guidance: Avoid use of words/phrases that can be implied (e.g., “The disclosure concerns,” etc.). Avoid claim words like “means” and “said.” The abstract should describe the disclosure sufficiently to help readers judge whether to consult the full patent. (See ¶ 6.16 and Examiner Note references to form paragraph 6.14.)

name: Brief Summary of the Invention — content and tone
description: A brief summary of the invention indicating its nature and substance, which may include a statement of the object of the invention, should precede the detailed description and be commensurate with the invention as claimed.
guidance: The summary should be directed to the specific invention being claimed, not generalities that apply to many patents. It should describe the exact nature, operation, and purpose in clear, concise sentences or paragraphs, and be consistent with the subject matter of the claims. Stereotyped general statements may be canceled as surplusage. The brief summary aids public understanding and future searches. (See 37 CFR 1.73 and MPEP § 608.01(d).)

name: Photographs — when acceptable and quality standards
description: Photographs (including photocopies) are not ordinarily permitted but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.
guidance: Acceptable examples include electrophoresis gels, blots, cell cultures, histological sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, TLC plates, crystalline structures, and ornamental effects in design patents. Examiner may require a drawing if the subject admits illustration by a drawing. Photographs must be of sufficient quality that all details are reproducible in the printed patent. Color photographs follow color-drawing conditions. (See 37 CFR 1.84(b).)

name: Reference characters and illustrations — proper application and limits
description: Reference characters must be properly applied; no single reference character should be used for two different parts or for a part and its modification. Every feature specified in the claims must be illustrated, but there should be no superfluous illustrations.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.84(p). Improper use of reference characters (e.g., not enclosed in parentheses in claims) can be objected to (form paragraph 7.29.02). Reference characters in claims should be enclosed within parentheses to avoid confusion and are considered to have no effect on claim scope. (See MPEP § 608.01(g) and related form paragraphs.)

name: Description must provide support/antecedent basis for claim terms
description: The description is a dictionary for the claims and should provide clear support or antecedent basis for all terms used in the claims.
guidance: Terms and phrases used in claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so the meaning of terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description. See 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and related MPEP sections (§ 608.01(i), § 608.01(o), § 1302.01).

name: Claims — statutory requirement and general function
description: The specification must conclude with a claim particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention or discovery (35 U.S.C. 112).
guidance: Claims define the protection sought and are an important part of the application. See MPEP § 608.01(i).

name: Claims — conformity and support (meaning ascertainable)
description: Claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification and the terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1). Also see §§ 1.141–1.146 for claiming different inventions in one application. If the nature of the case admits (e.g., improvement), claim drafting order and phrasing guidance applies (see next rubric).

name: Claims — recommended form for improvement-type inventions
description: Where applicable, an independent claim for an improvement should contain: (1) a preamble comprising a general description of conventional or known elements/steps; (2) a phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises'; and (3) those elements/steps/relationships which constitute the new or improved portion.
guidance: This combination-claim form is adapted to improvement-type inventions; the preamble is considered to positively include all elements recited therein as part of the claimed combination. Use this form where the nature of the case admits. (See 37 CFR 1.75(e).)

name: Claims — numbering, order, and placement
description: Claims shall be numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals; the least restrictive claim should be presented as claim number 1; all dependent claims should be grouped with the claim(s) to which they refer to the extent practicable.
guidance: Claims must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page and may not contain any other parts of the application on that sheet. Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each should be separated by line indentation. The original numbering must be preserved throughout prosecution; when claims are added they must be numbered consecutively after the highest numbered claim previously presented. At allowance the examiner may renumber claims as necessary. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 6.17, 6.18.01) to notify applicant of misplacement or misnumbering. (See 37 CFR 1.126, 1.75 and related MPEP sections.)

name: Form of claims — required formatting conventions
description: While there is no set statutory form for claims, office practice insists each claim be the object of a sentence starting with 'I (or we) claim,' 'The invention claimed is' (or equivalent). Each claim begins with a capital letter and ends with a period; periods may not be used elsewhere in the claims except for abbreviations.
guidance: Where plural indentations are needed they may be used to segregate subcombinations or related steps. Reference characters may be used in claims if enclosed in parentheses and are to have no effect on claim scope. Applicants are encouraged to include claims varying from the broadest to the most detailed. Claims should be arranged in order of scope and grouped by species or product/process as appropriate to facilitate classification and examination. (See MPEP § 608.01(m).)

name: Claims — common form objections and informalities
description: Claims may be objected to for minor informalities such as spelling errors, inconsistent terminology, reference characters not enclosed in parentheses, or crowded line spacing.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.29.01 to point out minor informalities; if the informalities render the claims indefinite use form paragraph 7.34.01 to reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. Use paragraph 7.29.02 for reference characters not enclosed in parentheses. Use paragraph 7.29.03 to object to crowded lines and require substitute claims one-and-one-half or double spaced. Amendments to claims must comply with 37 CFR 1.121(c).

name: Dependent claims — multiple dependent claim limitations and objections
description: A multiple dependent claim is a dependent claim which refers back in the alternative to more than one preceding independent or dependent claim; multiple dependent claims must be in alternative form, not cumulative, and may not serve as the basis for another multiple dependent claim.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 112 authorizes multiple dependent claims (filed on or after Jan 24, 1978) as long as they are in alternative form (e.g., 'claims 3 or 4'). A multiple dependent claim may refer in the alternative to only one set of claims and may not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claim. Improper multiple dependent claims should be objected to using form paragraph 7.45, and such claims may not be further treated on the merits. Fee and counting consequences also apply as noted in multiple-dependent-claims rubric. (See MPEP § 608.01(n).)

name: Materiality statement for environment/energy petitions
description: If the application disclosure is not clear on its face that the claimed invention materially enhances the quality of the environment or materially contributes to the conservation of energy, the petition must be accompanied by a statement explaining how the materiality standard is met.
guidance: Also revised to indicate that no fee is required for a petition under 37 CFR 1.102 based on the reason that the invention materially contributes to countering terrorism.

name: Double patenting for joint research agreement inventions (CREATE Act)
description: Incorporated discussion of double patenting between non-commonly owned inventions resulting from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as amended by the CREATE Act.
guidance: Revised charts overviewing treatment of conflicting claims; added information regarding terminal disclaimers where conflicting applications resulted from joint research agreements; discussed timing of double patenting rejections when a reference relied upon in a 103(a) rejection may be disqualified under 103(c).

name: Rejoinder practice and criteria
description: Rewritten to set forth general information pertaining to reconsideration of the propriety of a restriction requirement and rejoinder of certain previously nonelected inventions upon the determination that (1) all claims directed to the elected invention are in condition for allowance, and (2) claims to the previously nonelected invention depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim.
guidance: If any claims are rejoined, the restriction requirement between the elected invention and rejoined invention(s) must be withdrawn. Rejoinder between product inventions and between process inventions discussed; rejoinder of processes requiring an allowable product only if all claims to the elected product invention are allowable and all process claims subject to rejoinder depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable product claim.

name: Cancellation of nonelected claims before allowance
description: Where an application is in condition for allowance but for the presence of claims drawn to invention(s) nonelected without traverse, the claims drawn to the nonelected invention(s) may be canceled by examiner's amendment unless those claims are eligible for rejoinder.
guidance: Examiner should determine if any allowable claims are linking or generic, or if any nonelected invention is eligible for rejoinder, before canceling claims drawn to the nonelected invention(s).

name: Linking claims and rejoinder between linked inventions
description: Clarified definition of 'linking claim' and explained that linking claims and the inventions they link together are usually either all directed to products or all directed to processes; provided examples and limitations of linking claims for rejoinder.
guidance: Provided reference to rejoinder sections for product or process inventions and clarified that rejoinder applies to claims which require all the limitations of an allowable claim.

name: Reissue application filing and amendment practice
description: Revisions indicate when a petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim under 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3) is required in a reissue application; a reissue application can be granted a filing date without the basic filing fee, search fee, or examination fee; physical surrender of the original patent is no longer required.
guidance: Requirement for a copy of each U.S. patent or publication listed in an IDS eliminated unless required; broadened claims may be presented after the two-year period even though different; inventor consent requirements for deleting inventors clarified; forms updated (PTO/SB/50, PTO/SB/51, PTO/SB/52, PTO/SB/55 deleted where unnecessary).

name: Point A: If a claim includes limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind, it is not a mental process
description: Claims do not recite mental processes when they include limitations that humans cannot practically perform mentally (e.g., specialized technical steps that exceed human capability).
guidance: Cited examples where claims were not mental processes: detecting suspicious activity using network monitors and analyzing network packets (SRI Int’l v. Cisco); GPS calculations for absolute position/time involving pseudoranges (SiRF Tech.); specific multi-step data encryption methods (Synopsys); rendering halftone images pixel-by-pixel by comparing to a blue noise mask (Research Corp. Techs.). Examiners should recognize when claimed steps require technical processing or apparatus beyond mental performance.

name: Point B: Claims that encompass a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
description: If a claim reads on a human performing the claimed steps mentally, or mentally with a simple physical aid (pen and paper, slide rule), the claim falls within the mental processes group and thus is an abstract idea.
guidance: The guidance explains that use of a physical aid does not negate the mental nature of the limitation; it merely accounts for memory/capacity variation. Cited authorities include Benson, Synopsys, CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card numbers could be done by writing a list), Flook (computations by pencil and paper), University of Florida Research Foundation v. GE (specification describing flowsheets/patient charts), and Symantec (screening messages could be performed by a human). Examiners should consider whether claim language "reads on" a person performing the steps mentally or with simple aids.

name: Point C: Claims that require a computer may still recite a mental process
description: A claim can recite a mental process even if the claim is framed as being performed on a computer; implementation on generic computer hardware does not automatically make it non-abstract.
guidance: The guidance cites Benson (algorithm carried out in existing computers is still an abstract idea) and Mortgage Grader (concept could be performed by humans without a computer). Examiners are instructed to consider the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification to determine whether the claimed invention is merely a concept that can be performed mentally and is simply claimed as performed on a generic computer, in a computer environment, or using a computer as a tool. If so, treat it as reciting a mental process/abstract idea.

name: Guidance on reviewing the specification for computer-implemented claims
description: When evaluating computer-implemented claims for mental-process abstract ideas, examiners should review the specification to determine whether the applicant describes the concept as performed in the human mind or merely claims it on generic computer hardware.
guidance: Examiners should look for specification language that shows the claimed invention is described as a human-concept (e.g., cognitive actions) merely implemented on a computer. If the specification indicates the invention is essentially a mental process performed using generic computing, that supports treating the claim as an abstract idea. The guidance also notes examiners should consider whether the computer is performing functions that cannot practically be done mentally (see Point A) versus merely being a tool.

name: Subpoint 1: Performing a mental process on a generic computer is an abstract idea
description: If the claimed steps are mental/cognitive actions that have historically been performed by humans, performing them on a generic computer does not remove their abstract nature.
guidance: Examples: Voter Verified (voting, verifying, submitting votes are "human cognitive actions" performed for hundreds of years but claimed on a computer) and Versata (pricing determination implemented on general purpose computer hardware). The guidance reiterates that claiming longstanding human activities on generic computers supports a finding of an abstract idea.

name: Mental processes can appear in product claims as well as process claims
description: The categorization of 'mental processes' applies to the type of abstract idea recited and is not limited to process claims; product (e.g., system, computer-readable media) claims can also recite mental-process-type abstract ideas.
guidance: The guidance cites Versata as an example where product claims (computer systems, computer-readable media) were identified as reciting mental-process-type abstract ideas. Examiners should therefore apply the mental-process analysis across claim categories.

name: Claim chart structure (split claims into elements in tabular form)
description: A target patent claim is split into individual claim elements and represented in a tabular form.
guidance: Each claim element should be interpreted and evidence of use or prior art mapped correspondingly; evidences can include a patent, a product, or any published information. Claim charts are alternatively termed claims tables, infringement contentions (ICs), invalidity contentions, preliminary infringement contentions (PICs) depending on requirements.

name: Interpretation of claim elements
description: Each of the claim elements are interpreted individually to understand scope and limitations.
guidance: Reasonable claim construction principles should be applied when interpreting elements so that mapping to accused product features is meaningful and defensible.

name: Evidence mapping to claim elements
description: Map evidences of use or prior art directly to the corresponding claim elements in the chart.
guidance: Use concrete sources (e.g., patents, products, published information) and cite technical resources to support each mapped element; ensure traceability from claim language to factual evidence.

name: Exhaustive product search to identify potential infringers
description: Conduct an exhaustive product search to narrow down a list of potentially infringing products/services.
guidance: Search broadly across markets and suppliers to capture all candidate accused products before detailed mapping; this is a front-end step of the claim chart report.

name: Extensive technical research for evidence gathering
description: Perform extensive research to garner evidence from varied technical resources.
guidance: Consult data sheets, product manuals, technical articles, and other technical documentation to collect support for mapping claim elements to accused products/features.

name: Wide analysis of claim elements and limitations
description: Analyze each patent claim element and its limitations comprehensively.
guidance: Consider not only literal elements but also dependent claims and limitations; identify ambiguities and potential constructions that affect scope.

name: Detailed mapping onto accused product features using reasonable claim construction
description: Map the patent claims onto the features of the accused product on the basis of reasonable claim construction.
guidance: Ensure the mapping shows how each claim limitation is present (or absent) in the accused product, using a defensible construction standard to support infringement or non-infringement positions.

name: Provide a factual opinion on infringement
description: Deliver an opinion on infringement supported by facts and findings from the comparison chart.
guidance: The opinion should be grounded in the mapped evidence and explain how the evidence supports (or does not support) each claim element being met by the accused product.

name: Use claim charts to scrutinize claim scope to identify covered products/services
description: Scrutinize the claims of a patent to identify the products and services covered by them.
guidance: Systematically compare claim language to market offerings to determine the universe of potentially covered products and services.

name: Use claim charts to evaluate patent validity
description: Examine the claim elements of a patent to assess the validity of the patent.
guidance: Mapping can reveal prior art or inconsistencies relevant to invalidity contentions; claim charts may be used as invalidity contentions when supporting challenges to validity.

name: Support litigation tasks: narrow issues and advance discovery
description: Assist the court or parties' infringement contentions involved in litigation to narrow down the case so they can focus and advance discovery.
guidance: Well-prepared claim charts help identify the precise disputed elements and factual questions, enabling targeted discovery and more efficient case management.

name: Gather facts to support or rebut Doctrine of Equivalence (DOE) arguments
description: Help the parties in finding the facts to support the argument against (or for) the Doctrine of Equivalence.
guidance: Use mapping and technical evidence to show whether an accused product that does not literally meet a claim element nevertheless performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to yield substantially the same result, or to refute such a claim.

name: Interpretation of force majeure terms (‘force or violence of the elements’)
description: Contract language allowing time extensions for 'freshets, ice, or other force or violence of the elements' should be construed to mean forces like those specified; a loss (e.g., dredge lost by fire not from lightning) may not qualify; contractor must show inability to replace the dredge to claim excusal.
guidance: C. 12598, May 18, 1908 — general words following specific instances are limited to similar cases; mere non-negligent loss does not automatically excuse performance absent inability to mitigate.

name: Earlier-Filed Patent Application (Pre-AIA) (102(e))
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim[s] ___ ... are invalid because the invention[s] ... were described in [U.S./international PCT published patent application or patent] filed by another before [§ 102(e) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date].
guidance: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application or international PCT application published in English that designates the U.S., or a U.S. patent, filed by another person before that invention was invented by the patentee. If date of invention is disputed, instruct jury on how to determine date of invention. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(e)(1) and (2) (pre-AIA) and cases.

name: Earlier-Filed Patent Application (AIA) (102(a)(2))
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim[s] ___ ... are invalid because the claimed invention[s] were described in [published patent document/application/patent] by another inventor that was effectively filed before [§ 102(a) (AIA) Cutoff Date] and deemed published in the United States.
guidance: Invalid if described in a published U.S. patent application, issued U.S. patent, or published international PCT application that designates the U.S., filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. Practice note: if factual issues exist about whether disclosure was obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor, publicly disclosed earlier by the inventor/joint inventor/another who obtained the subject matter from them, or whether the subject matter was commonly owned or subject to assignment obligations, the jury should be instructed on exceptions under §§ 102(b)(2) and (c). Determine the effective filing date per 35 U.S.C. § 102(d). Citations: 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(a)(2), (b)(2), (c), & (d); 35 U.S.C. § 374.

name: Obviousness—General Standard (Graham Factors)
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ... are invalid because the claimed invention(s) would have been 'obvious.' A claimed invention is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art ... as of the Cutoff Date. Unlike anticipation, obviousness may be shown by considering one or more items of prior art.
guidance: Avoid hindsight: do not use knowledge of the patent as a road map, and do not consider what is known today. Put yourself in the place of a POSITA as of the Cutoff Date. The following factors must be evaluated for each claim: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) additional considerations (secondary considerations). Each factor must be evaluated (order flexible) and the defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. Obviousness is a mixed question of fact and law; consider roles of court and jury and risk of waiver by failing to move for JMOL. Citations: Graham v. John Deere; KSR; Microsoft v. i4i; relevant Fed. Cir. authorities.

name: Differences Between the Claimed Invention and the Prior Art (Second Factor)
description: Analyze whether there are any relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the view of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date. Determine the impact of such differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole.
guidance: Do not require precise teaching in the prior art; you may consider inferences and creative steps a POSITA would have employed. If claimed invention combined known elements and the combination yielded predictable results to a POSITA at the time, that favors obviousness. If combination yielded unexpected results or the prior art teaches away from combining elements, that favors nonobviousness. Consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine references (from prior art, background knowledge, market demand, or common sense) and whether there would have been a reasonable expectation of success. Inherency: may supply an element if it is the natural result of explicit disclosures and not shown by probabilities/possibilities; inherency must be based on the natural result and is limited in obviousness analysis. Tailor inherency instruction to evidence and give only if properly raised and supported. Citations: KSR; Graham; Arendi; PAR Pharm.; inherency cases.

name: Secondary Considerations / Other Considerations (Fourth Factor)
description: Consider secondary considerations which may help determine whether the invention would have been obvious. No single consideration is dispositive; consider obviousness or nonobviousness of the invention as a whole.
guidance: Only provide instructions on particular secondary considerations if relevant and supported by evidence and admissible (court determines admissibility and nexus). Examples include: commercial success due to the merits of the claimed invention (not advertising/promotion), long-felt but unsolved need satisfied by the invention, others tried and failed to solve the problem, others copied the invention, the invention achieved unexpectedly superior results, praise or surprise by others (including defendant), acceptance of licenses because of the merits. Patentee bears burden of proving nexus between consideration and the invention. Consider these factors along with all other evidence. Citations: Graham; U.S. v. Adams; relevant Fed. Cir. authorities.

name: Date Damages Begin / Notice and Marking (Alternate Rules)
description: 10.1.1 Alternate A: if parties stipulate, the start date for damages is the stipulated date. 10.1.2 Alternate B: if disputed, the date damages begin is the date Plaintiff first notified Defendant of its claim for patent infringement.
guidance: Two ways to give notice: (1) Public notice by marking substantially all products that include the patented invention with the patent number (or 'Patent'/'Pat' and a freely accessible Internet address tying product to patent), including licensees who use the patented invention—marking must be substantially all products in a consistent and continuous manner. Public marking is effective even if defendant did not see it. (2) Direct notice: specifically notify defendant of alleged infringement; effective as of the date defendant received notice. Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that defendant was put on notice as of the date alleged. If Plaintiff did not provide effective notice prior to filing suit, consequences follow (instruction continues beyond chunk).

name: Means-plus-function treatment avoided by sufficient structure recitation
description: Limitation in patent claim reciting 'internal steel baffles extending inwardly from steel shell walls' recited sufficient structure to avoid means-plus-function treatment. 35 U.S.C.A. §112, par. 6.
guidance: If a claim identifies particular structure (here 'internal steel baffles') rather than using a pure functional placeholder, §112, para. 6 (means-plus-function) does not apply. The absence of the word 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption that §112, para. 6 does not apply. Means-plus-function applies only to purely functional limitations that do not provide the structure performing the function.

name: Claims define the invention and right to exclude
description: It is a bedrock principle of patent law that 'claims of patent define invention to which patentee is entitled the right to exclude.'
guidance: Claims are the primary measure of the patentee's rights; courts must look to the claim language to determine what the applicant regarded as the invention. Do not rewrite claims to include elements not in their plain import except according to established claim-construction tools.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning to person of skill
description: Words of patent claim are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning, i.e., meaning that term would have to person of ordinary skill in the art in question on effective filing date of patent application.
guidance: Interpret claim terms as a person of ordinary skill in the art would at the time of the invention; this objective baseline governs claim interpretation unless patentee's lexicography or disavowal dictates otherwise.

name: Contextual reading by person of ordinary skill
description: Person of ordinary skill in the art, through whose eyes patent claim is construed, is deemed to read claim term not only in context of particular claim in which disputed term appears, but in context of entire patent, including specification.
guidance: Claim terms must be read in the full context of the patent (claims, specification) to capture how a skilled artisan would understand them.

name: Consistent usage across claims illuminates meaning
description: Because claim terms are normally used consistently throughout patent, usage of term in one claim can often illuminate meaning of same term in other claims.
guidance: Compare usage of a term across the claims; definitions or nuance in one claim can inform interpretation in others.

name: Dependent claim presumption
description: Presence of dependent patent claim that adds particular limitation gives rise to presumption that limitation in question is not present in independent claim.
guidance: When a dependent claim narrows an independent claim by adding a limitation, presume that limitation was not intended to be included in the independent claim absent contrary evidence.

name: Claims read in view of the specification
description: Patent claims must be read in view of specification, of which they are part.
guidance: The specification is part of the intrinsic evidence and must be consulted when construing claim language; claims are not interpreted in isolation.

name: Specification as single best guide
description: Patent specification is always highly relevant to claim construction analysis; it is single best guide to meaning of disputed term, and is usually dispositive.
guidance: Give primary weight to the specification when interpreting claim terms; where the specification clearly indicates a meaning, that guidance will often control.

name: Inventor's lexicography controls when present
description: When patent specification reveals special definition given to claim term by patentee that differs from meaning it would otherwise possess, inventor’s lexicography governs.
guidance: If the patentee explicitly defines a term in the specification, adopt that meaning even if it departs from the term's ordinary meaning.

name: Disavowal limits claim scope
description: Where patent specification reveals intentional disclaimer, or disavowal, of claim scope by inventor, such revealed intention is dispositive.
guidance: A clear and unambiguous disavowal or disclaimer in the specification or prosecution history will limit claim scope accordingly.

name: Prosecution history as intrinsic evidence
description: 'Prosecution history' consists of complete record of proceedings before Patent and Trademark Office and includes prior art cited during examination of patent.
guidance: Use prosecution history to understand how the inventor and PTO interpreted terms and whether the inventor limited claims during prosecution; treat it as part of the intrinsic record.

name: Prosecution history informs claim meaning by showing patentee's understanding
description: Prosecution history can often inform meaning of patent claim language by demonstrating how inventor understood invention and whether inventor limited invention in course of prosecution, making claim scope narrower than it would otherwise be.
guidance: Examine arguments, amendments, and cited art in prosecution history for evidence of limiting statements or disclaimers.

name: Extrinsic evidence secondary to intrinsic record
description: Although extrinsic evidence can shed useful light on relevant art, it is less significant than intrinsic record in determining legally operative meaning of patent claim language.
guidance: Prioritize intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history); use extrinsic evidence only to aid understanding, not to override intrinsic evidence.

name: Reject conclusory unsupported expert assertions
description: Conclusory, unsupported assertions by experts as to definition of patent claim term are not useful to construing court.
guidance: Admit expert evidence when well-founded; disregard unsupported or conclusory opinions that lack record support.

name: Discount expert testimony that conflicts with intrinsic evidence
description: Court, when construing patent, should discount any expert testimony that is clearly at odds with claim construction mandated by claims themselves, written description, and prosecution history.
guidance: Intrinsic evidence (claims/specification/prosecution) controls; extrinsic expert opinions conflicting with it carry little weight.

name: Extrinsic evidence must be considered in context of intrinsic evidence
description: Extrinsic evidence may be useful to construing court, but it is unlikely to result in reliable interpretation of patent claim scope unless considered in context of intrinsic evidence.
guidance: Do not interpret extrinsic evidence in isolation; always test it against the intrinsic record.

name: Court may use extrinsic evidence in its discretion to educate itself
description: It is permissible for patent-construing court, in its sound discretion, to admit and use extrinsic evidence; such evidence can help educate court regarding field of invention and can help court determine what person of ordinary skill in the art would understand claim terms to mean.
guidance: Admit extrinsic materials (textbooks, treatises, expert reports) when they genuinely illuminate the field and the skilled artisan's understanding.

name: Dictionaries useful but focus on skilled artisan's understanding
description: Although dictionaries or comparable sources are often useful to assist in understanding commonly understood meaning of patent claim terms, construing court’s focus remains on understanding how person of ordinary skill in the art would understand claim terms.
guidance: Give dictionaries weight only insofar as they reflect the skilled artisan's understanding at the relevant time; do not substitute them for intrinsic evidence.

name: No required formula or sequence for claim construction
description: There is no magic formula or catechism for conducting patent claim construction; court is not barred from considering any particular sources or required to analyze sources in any specific sequence, so long as those sources are not used to contradict claim meaning that is unambiguous in light of intrinsic evidence.
guidance: Flexibility is permitted in the order and sources consulted for claim construction, but intrinsic evidence governs when it is unambiguous.

name: Claims should not be limited to preferred embodiment absent clear intent
