description: Internal steel 'baffles,' called for in patent for vandalism-resistant wall panels, were not limited to non-perpendicular, projectile-deflecting structures disclosed in preferred embodiment; specification did not require that internal structures always be capable of performing that function.
guidance: Do not import limitations from the preferred embodiment into claim scope unless the specification or prosecution history clearly requires such limitation (lexicography or disavowal).

name: Objectives stated in specification do not automatically limit claims
description: Fact that patent asserts that invention achieves several objectives does not require that each claim be construed as limited to structures that are capable of achieving all those objectives.
guidance: Avoid reading every stated objective of the invention as a claim limitation; only adopt limitations when supported by the intrinsic record.

name: Limiting construction to preserve validity is a last resort
description: Application of patent construction maxim, that claims should be so construed, if possible, as to sustain their validity, is limited to cases in which court concludes, after applying all available tools of claim construction, that claim is still ambiguous.
guidance: Only when, after exhausting intrinsic-and-appropriate-extrinsic analysis, a claim remains ambiguous may a court consider a construction that favors validity; do not construe claims to save validity when intrinsic evidence is clear.

name: Absence of the word 'means' creates rebuttable presumption against §112, para. 6
description: The absence of the term 'means' in a claim limitation creates a rebuttable presumption that §112, paragraph 6 (means-plus-function) does not apply.
guidance: Start with the presumption that §112, para. 6 is inapplicable when 'means' is not used; the presumption can be rebutted by showing that the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure.

name: Means-plus-function applies only to purely functional limitations
description: Means-plus-function claiming applies only to purely functional limitations that do not provide the structure that performs the recited function.
guidance: If the claim language supplies structure (even if the structure has functional connotations), do not treat it as a means-plus-function limitation; compare to case law examples (e.g., 'compressed spring' vs general 'means').

name: Contested view—underlying factual findings deserve deference (Rule 52(a))
description: Subsidiary factual determinations underlying claim construction (e.g., level of ordinary skill, state of the art, meaning of terms to skilled artisan) are inherently factual and should be reviewed for clear error under Rule 52(a), rather than de novo.
guidance: This is a position articulated in the opinion's discussion of standards of review: district court factfinding (expert disputes, technical background) typically merits deference; appellate courts should accept district courts' factual findings unless clearly erroneous. Note: this view reflects disagreement among judges and represents the argument for deference to trial-court factfinding.

name: Claim recites a mental process (abstract idea)
description: Claims that can be performed mentally (e.g., by a human using pen and paper) qualify as mental processes and thus may be abstract ideas.
guidance: Courts have found that claimed steps that can be performed by humans mentally (e.g., listing transactions, computations by pencil and paper) are mental processes (see CyberSource, Flook, Univ. of Florida Research Foundation v. GE, Symantec). Examiners should look to the specification and consider whether claimed steps are performable mentally; if so, treat them as an abstract idea in the eligibility analysis.

name: Both product and process claims may recite mental processes
description: Product claims (e.g., computer systems, computer-readable media) as well as process claims can recite mental processes and thus be directed to abstract ideas.
guidance: Examiners should recognize that claims to systems, media, or methods can all be 'directed to' the same abstract mental concepts. Examples of product claims reciting mental processes include application program interfaces for extracting/processing information, computer systems for anonymous loan shopping, computer-readable media containing fraud-detection instructions, and post-office systems for email (cases: Content Extraction, Mortgage Grader, CyberSource, Symantec, Voter Verified, Electric Power Group, Versata).

name: Tentative abstract ideas — examiner procedure
description: A 'tentative abstract idea' is a claim limitation that an examiner believes should be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas; this requires a defined examiner procedure.
guidance: Apply the subject matter eligibility framework: if the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application, the claim is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If not integrated (Step 2A: YES), proceed to Step 2B: if the claim as a whole provides an inventive concept (Step 2B: YES) it's eligible at Pathway C. If no inventive concept (Step 2B: NO), bring the application to the Technology Center (TC) director — a Step 2B rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director and use form paragraph 7.05.017 with TC Director's signature. The TC Director will notify Patents Management so the public can be informed. Interviews with the examiner are permitted and may advance prosecution; examiner may withdraw or maintain rejections without TC Director interview. Examiner cannot issue a Step 2B rejection for a tentative abstract idea without TC Director approval.

name: Claims describing natural abilities/processes are not automatically laws of nature
description: Not every claim that describes a natural ability, quality, or process necessarily recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon; eligibility depends on claim focus.
guidance: Examples where claims were eligible: process steps of fractionating, recovering, cryopreserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect) were eligible because they were not focused on merely observing/detecting hepatocyte ability to survive freeze-thaw. Similarly, methods of treating cancer (effect of chemotherapy) or treating headaches with aspirin are not laws of nature. Such claims are eligible at Prong One unless they recite another exception requiring further analysis. Manufacturing processes focused on producing a new compound likewise are not directed to components' abilities.

name: Products of nature — definition and scope
description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, courts may treat it as a 'product of nature' exception; products of nature include naturally occurring products and synthetically created products that lack markedly different characteristics.
guidance: Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), primers (Ambry), cloned animals (Roslin), bacterial mixtures (Funk Bros.). Step 2A uses 'law of nature' and 'natural phenomenon' as inclusive of 'products of nature.' Non-naturally occurring products are not automatically eligible merely because of human intervention; the key is whether they possess markedly different characteristics from naturally occurring counterparts (Ambry, Roslin, Chakrabarty).

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (purpose)
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis identifies whether a nature-based product limitation is a product-of-nature exception by comparing claimed product characteristics to those found in nature.
guidance: This analysis is part of Step 2A Prong One. If the claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart, the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (NO) at Pathway B unless another exception is present. If it does not have markedly different characteristics, then the claim recites a product of nature and requires further Prong Two analysis (and Step 2B if needed). Case law: Chakrabarty (claimed bacterium had markedly different characteristics and was eligible) and Roslin (claimed sheep lacked markedly different characteristics and was product of nature).

name: Effect of markedly different characteristics result
description: Consequences for eligibility depending on whether the nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics.
guidance: If the nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics, the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (NO) at Pathway B unless the claim recites another exception. For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, showing a markedly different characteristic means no further analysis is necessary for eligibility (i.e., Step 2B is unnecessary). If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, it recites a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.

name: Best practices when claim recites a nature-based product with broad BRI
description: When a claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) encompasses both eligible and ineligible embodiments, examiners should take certain actions to assist prosecution.
guidance: If a claim recites a nature-based product that, under BRI, may encompass embodiments that lack markedly different characteristics, it is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or that are otherwise eligible. For nature-based product limitations that clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception, consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis in MPEP § 2106.06 is appropriate (no need to conduct a markedly different characteristics analysis).

name: Nature-based product limitations that are naturally occurring — no analysis needed
description: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, the markedly different characteristics analysis is unnecessary because the limitation is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and falls under the product-of-nature exception.
guidance: Examiners should recognize that a claim element that is inherently naturally occurring does not require further markedly different characteristics comparison; it is treated as a product-of-nature exception and proceeds to Prong Two/Step 2B analysis as applicable.

name: IPR institution standard (reasonable likelihood)
description: PTAB evaluates the IPR petition and any preliminary response to determine whether the challenger has established a reasonable likelihood that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable.
guidance: If reasonable likelihood is met for at least one challenged claim, the PTAB will institute trial as to all grounds in the petition (even if some grounds have deficiencies). Institution decision is typically issued within three months after patent owner preliminary response or when due. If instituted, Board issues a scheduling order to complete the proceeding within the statutory 12‑month deadline (subject to joinders/extensions).

name: PGR institution standard
description: To secure institution of a PGR, a petitioner must either show that it is more likely than not that at least one claim of the challenged patent is unpatentable, or raise a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents or applications.
guidance: The 'more likely than not' standard is higher than the IPR reasonable‑likelihood standard; alternatively, emphasize novel legal questions of broader importance to obtain institution.

name: Ex parte reexamination scope and features
description: Ex parte reexamination may be requested to challenge novelty or nonobviousness based on printed publications and patents only; other types of prior art (such as product prior art) cannot be raised.
guidance: Requests can be filed anytime after grant and up to six years after expiration (case‑by‑case variations possible). Third‑party involvement largely ceases after filing; requests can be anonymous; no estoppel applies to requester; patent owner may amend/add claims during reexam, potentially strengthening patent. USPTO decides if submitted prior art raises a substantial new question of patentability (SNQ). No statutory time limit but USPTO may conduct with 'special dispatch.' Weigh anonymity and no‑estoppel advantage against risk that patent owner can improve the patent.

name: Reissue requirements and bases
description: A reissue application may be filed by a patent owner to correct an error in a patent; reissue is proper where the patent is 'wholly inoperative or partly inoperative or invalid' as a result of the error.
guidance: Common bases: claims too narrow or too broad (broadening reissue must be filed within two years of issuance), disclosure inaccuracies, foreign priority errors, incorrect references to co‑pending applications. Use reissue to strengthen patents prior to litigation or correct substantive drafting errors.

name: Third‑party preissuance submission requirements
description: Third‑party preissuance submissions permit third parties to submit patents, published patent applications, and other printed publications with a concise description of the asserted relevance of each submitted item.
guidance: Submissions must be timely: before mailing of notice of allowance and before the later of six months from publication or mailing of a first office action rejecting any claim. Use to oppose competitor applications early; be mindful that submissions can cause examiners to incorporate prior art and narrow claim scope.

name: Derivation petition requirements
description: To initiate a derivation proceeding, a petitioner must file its own patent application and a petition within one year of publication of a pending application or one year of issuance of a patent (whichever is earlier) that claims the same or substantially the same invention.
guidance: The petition must state with particularity the basis for finding (1) that an individual named in the earlier‑filed application derived the invention from an individual named in the petition, and (2) that the earlier application was filed without authorization. A petition is insufficient unless supported by substantial evidence including at least one affidavit detailing corroborated communications and lack of authorization. PTAB may correct inventor naming, refuse earlier claims, or cancel involved patent claims. Use derivation when inventorship/ownership is disputed.

name: Patent interference standing and phases (pre‑AIA)
description: Interferences determine which party was first to invent for claims with effective filing dates before March 16, 2013; only an applicant with a pending application containing allowable claims toward the same or substantially the same invention has standing (examiners can also declare interferences sua sponte).
guidance: Proceeding has two stages: preliminary phase allowing broad validity challenges (limited discovery like expert depositions) and priority phase to establish earliest conception/reduction to practice (includes exchange of confidential invention records). Interference is useful where litigation is the alternative for ownership disputes.

name: Burdens of persuasion for motions to amend (USPTO rule)
description: Under USPTO final rules, a patent owner bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that a motion to amend complies with statutory and regulatory requirements; a petitioner bears the burden of persuasion, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.
guidance: This codifies post‑Aqua Products practice (petitioner bears unpatentability burden). Board may, 'in the interests of justice,' exercise discretion to grant or deny a motion to amend for reasons supported by readily identifiable and persuasive evidence of record, but such evidence is limited to related‑proceeding evidence or judicially noticeable district court evidence in most cases. Patent owners should prepare motions to amend and supporting evidence accordingly; petitioners should prepare robust opposition evidence.

name: Motion to amend practice and preliminary guidance (revised MTA timeline)
description: Motion to amend practice has evolved to include option of filing an initial motion to amend, receiving preliminary guidance from the Board, and then filing a revised motion to amend addressing the Board's preliminary guidance (PO may indicate whether it requests preliminary guidance).
guidance: Revised MTA timeline alters scheduling if a revised motion to amend (rMTA) is filed: Board adjusts schedule. Use preliminary guidance to refine substitute claims and supporting arguments; be mindful of sequencing and timing (deadlines for oppositions, replies, sur‑replies).

name: Unitary structure rule (entire profits when claim covers unitary structure)
description: When the claim infringed covers a unitary structure which is made and sold by the defendant without addition or change, the plaintiff is entitled to recover the entire profits.
guidance: Important modification: if the real invention lies in a single element (an improvement) and the defendant's unitary article includes many non-infringing elements that can be apportioned, full profits may not be recoverable. Rule informed by Patent Office practice requiring a claim to include a completely operative combination.

name: Conditions for entry of an amendment after final rejection
description: An amendment filed after final rejection but before an appeal brief may be entered upon or after filing of an appeal provided certain conditions are met.
guidance: Entry permitted if (A) total effect is to cancel claims or comply with a formal requirement previously set forth, or present rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal; or (B) for an amendment touching the merits, the patent owner provides a showing of good and sufficient reasons why the amendment is necessary and was not earlier presented. The first proposed amendment after final action will be given sufficient consideration to determine patentability or reduction/simplification of appeal issues. Unless entered in entirety, examiner will briefly explain reasons for not entering; identify new issues requiring search and explain why; notify if portions would be entered if filed separately. Any second or subsequent amendment after final will be considered only to the extent it removes issues for appeal or puts a claim in obvious patentable condition.

name: Failure to timely file appeal brief or fee
description: Failure to file the brief and/or the appeal brief fee within the permissible time will result in dismissal of the appeal.
guidance: Form PTOL-468 is used to notify dismissal. Reexamination prosecution is terminated and an NIRC will subsequently be issued indicating status of claims at time of appeal.

name: Requirements for the appeal brief content and form
description: A fee per 37 CFR 41.20(b)(2) is required for filing the appeal brief. 37 CFR 41.37 requires the appellant to file a brief of authorities and arguments relied on, including a summary of claimed subject matter which must refer to the specification by page and line number, to drawings by reference characters, and a copy of the claims involved.
guidance: Only one copy of the appeal brief is required. Where a third party requester filed the reexamination request, a copy of the brief must be served on that requester. In merged proceedings, one original copy of the brief should be provided for each reexamination proceeding and reissue application in the merged proceeding, and served on any third party requesters. The copy of claims should be double spaced, start on a new page, and include all underlining and bracketing reflecting changes; new claims added should be completely underlined (departure from MPEP §1205.02 for applications).

name: Duty of disclosure — information material to patentability (37 CFR 1.555)
description: Each individual associated with the patent owner in a reexamination proceeding has a duty of candor and good faith to disclose to the Office all information known to that individual to be material to patentability in the reexamination proceeding. Duty applies to patent owner, each attorney/agent representing the owner, and every other individual substantively involved on behalf of the patent owner, and continues with respect to each claim pending until cancelled.
guidance: Information is material when it is not cumulative and (1) it is a patent or printed publication that establishes, by itself or in combination, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) it refutes or is inconsistent with a position the patent owner takes in opposing an unpatentability argument or asserting patentability. Prima facie defined as compelling conclusion of unpatentability under preponderance standard using broadest reasonable construction. IDS should be filed (preferably via 37 CFR 1.98) within two months of order for reexamination or as soon thereafter as possible. An IDS filed as a separate paper must be limited to listing the information disclosed and explanation of relevance; discussion of patentability in a separate IDS is improper (discussion may be included if filed as part of 1.530 statement). Responsibility for compliance rests on the designated individuals; Office will not evaluate compliance in the proceeding. Fraud or intentional misconduct results in noncompliance. Such issues raised during proceeding will be noted as unresolved under 1.552(c).

name: Written description and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same; and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor.
guidance: Draft a thorough specification that describes the invention, how to make and use it, and the best mode. Include variations and permutations; avoid relying solely on functional descriptions. Drawings help expand disclosure. Avoid describing only what is claimed — provide concrete structure/steps/materials.

name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (definiteness)
description: The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention (statutory requirement).
guidance: Under Nautilus, claims must, in view of the specification and prosecution history, inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty. Strive for clarity while recognizing absolute precision is unattainable.

name: Definiteness standard (Nautilus reasonable certainty)
description: A patent is invalid for indefiniteness if its claims, read in light of the specification and prosecution history, fail to inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention (Nautilus v. Biosig).
guidance: Aim for clarity and objective boundaries in claim language; provide definitions or examples in the specification to remove ambiguity. Recognize courts require reasonable certainty, not absolute precision.

name: PTO/Federal Circuit approach to indefiniteness (Packard / McAward)
description: The PTO/Board may continue to apply the Packard approach: a claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear; claims required to be cast in clear, not ambiguous, terms.
guidance: Even after Nautilus, expect examiners to flag words or phrases with unclear meaning. Address ambiguities proactively in the specification and prosecution record.

name: Failing to comply with the written description requirement (common rejection)
description: A common §112 rejection is failure to comply with the written description requirement — i.e., the specification does not adequately show the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Ensure the specification describes the claimed subject matter with detail and examples. Describe alternatives, variations, and permutations. Use drawings and explicit embodiments to show possession.

name: Antecedent basis for claim terms
description: Claim terms must have proper antecedent basis in the specification; lack of antecedent basis can trigger §112 objections.
guidance: Proofread claims/specification to ensure each claim term that requires antecedent basis has an earlier-introduced antecedent phrase in the disclosure. Tools can check for missing antecedents.

name: Proper dependent and multiple dependent claim form (112(c)-(e))
description: Claims may be written in dependent or multiple dependent form where permitted; dependent claims must reference a previous claim and specify further limitations; multiple dependent claims have special rules (alternative references only, cannot serve as basis for another multiple dependent claim).
guidance: Follow statutory/formal rules for dependent and multiple dependent claims to avoid form rejections. Review MPEP 2181 et seq. and 35 U.S.C. 112(c)-(e).

name: Vague and indefinite claim language (avoidance)
description: Avoid language that is vague, ambiguous, or lacks objective boundaries because it can render claims indefinite under §112(b).
guidance: Replace subjective terms of degree with measurable limits or provide explicit examples/standards in the specification. If a subjective term is used, support with specific and unequivocal examples to provide a POSA with clear notice (see DDR).

name: Functional claiming and need for corresponding structure (112(f) risk)
description: Expressing an element as a means or step for performing a specified function without reciting structure/material/acts invokes §112(f), which construes the claim to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: If you use functional language, ensure the specification discloses corresponding structure/material/acts (including alternatives/variations) to support the breadth of the functional claim. Otherwise, the claim may be limited to the disclosed structure or be indefinite.

name: List of non-structural terms that may invoke §112(f)
description: Non-structural terms that may invoke means-plus-function treatment include 'mechanism for', 'module for', 'device for', 'unit for', 'component for', 'element for', 'member for', 'apparatus for', 'machine for', and 'system for' (not exhaustive).
guidance: Avoid using these generic/nonce terms as claim headings unless you provide clear structural meaning in the specification. Be particularly cautious with terms like 'module', 'mechanism', 'device', 'element', 'member', 'assembly'.

name: Nonce terms and adjectives (avoid adjective + nonce term)
description: Using an adjective combined with a nonce term (e.g., 'moving device', 'pivoting mechanism', 'light-capturing element') may still invoke M+F if the adjective merely describes the function. Adjectives that connote function raise risk.
guidance: If the adjective is the claimed function, the term may be treated as functional. Ensure the name for the limitation connotes concrete structure to a POSA or provide explicit structural disclosure.

name: Software-specific drafting to avoid 112(f) and indefiniteness
description: For software claims, describe sub-steps and algorithms that perform the claimed function (describe 100% of the algorithms where claimed) rather than only stating the function. Avoid claiming 'processor configured to' or 'processor programmed to' without structural detail.
guidance: Describe how software steps or structural components interconnect; use computer-readable-medium (CRM) claims and systems claims; include some structure (e.g., circuitry) to reduce risk of M+F; if M+F rejection issued, consider traversing the rejection when appropriate.

name: Means-plus-function strategic use (pros/cons)
description: Means-plus-function claiming can capture many permutations of disclosed means and broaden claim reach if the specification discloses alternatives and variations, but should not be the primary claim type and should be used sparingly.
guidance: Use a few M+F claims as 'seasoning' — they can be powerful if the spec contains deep and broad disclosure of corresponding structures. Avoid filing applications consisting only of M+F claims.

name: Alice / subject-matter eligibility risk from functional claiming
description: Functional 'wish list' claims that fail to disclose underlying structure/material/acts can be both indefinite under §112 and abstract under Alice (ineligible subject matter) for lacking a technological solution to a technological problem.
guidance: Define a technological solution to a technological problem in the specification and claims; avoid purely functional claiming that could be characterized as abstract.

name: Explain functionality but provide concrete structure/steps
description: While explaining functionality is necessary, function cannot substitute for concrete and tangible description; how a device is used generally won't distinguish over prior art.
guidance: Provide structural details, material descriptions, acts, and stepwise algorithms where needed; use claim language in specification examples to tie structure to claims.

name: Negative limitations (permitted if supported)
description: Negative claim limitations are not inherently ambiguous; they are adequately supported when the specification describes a reason to exclude the relevant limitation (e.g., 'wherein the composition contains no sucralfate').
guidance: Provide supporting disclosure that explains why an exclusion exists or describe alternative features without characterizing advantages/disadvantages. No heightened written-description requirement solely because a limitation is negative.

name: Numerical ranges and amount limitations (definiteness traps)
description: Open-ended numerical ranges (e.g., 'at least 20% sodium') can be ambiguous, especially when dependent claims' ingredient amounts sum to exclude the range. 'Up to' includes zero; phrases like 'an effective amount' depend on whether POSA can determine values from disclosure.
guidance: Carefully analyze range language and dependent claim interplay to ensure clear boundaries; provide measurement standards/examples when needed.

name: Business-method / commercial language caution ('profanity' list)
description: Avoid claim language that reads like pure business/economic terms (e.g., price, cost, bid, auction, financial, bank, account, buy, sell, commerce, insurance, negotiation, trade, stock, exchange, money, invoice, discount, coupon, advertise).
guidance: Business-oriented terms can invite subject-matter eligibility scrutiny under Alice; prefer technical/technological framing and concrete implementation details.

name: Proofreading, foreign translation, and definitions in the specification (examiner perspective)
description: Examiners emphasize proofreading claims/specification to avoid small errors; add specific definitions for terms with alternative dictionary meanings; correct foreign translations before filing.
guidance: Double-check for typographical errors, inconsistent labeling, and ambiguous wording. Define terms in the specification when dictionary provides multiple meanings; ensure translations are accurate to avoid examiner time spent deciphering.

name: Use automated checking and OA-response tools to improve quality
description: Tools (e.g., LexisNexis PatentOptimizer) can check claims for antecedent basis, lack of support, terminology issues, multiple-claim set problems, part-number consistency, and can auto-generate OA response shells.
guidance: Leverage software to identify potential §112 problems pre-filing (missing antecedents, possible functional/indefinite terms, profanity/business terms), streamline Office Action analysis, and reduce non-compliant or non-responsive amendments.

name: Seventh defence (claim not in original application) requires claim construction and proof — answer only
description: The seventh defence involves whether the letters patent claim something not indicated or described in the specification or drawings of the original application; the question what letters patent claim is a question of law for the court and to decide it the original application must be introduced as evidence. Therefore the defence cannot be raised by plea, demurrer, or motion to dismiss and is properly set up only in the answer (except where complainant takes the initiative).
guidance: Because resolution requires claim construction and comparison with the original application, it must be litigated with evidence in an answer; complainant may bear burden where he raised the issue.

name: When reissue about to issue: delay determination and base reexamination on reissue claims
description: If a reissue is expected to issue before the three-month determination for a reexamination request, the reexamination determination should normally be delayed until after granting of the reissue patent and then made based on the reissue patent claims.
guidance: If reexamination is ordered, it will be on the reissue patent claims; the reexamination starting point must be presented as a 'clean copy' of the reissue claims (bracketed words from the reissue patent do not appear in the clean copy).

name: Rejection for non-identical claims if housekeeping amendment not timely
description: If a required housekeeping amendment to make claims identical in each file is not timely submitted, any claim that does not contain identical text in all merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as indefinite.
guidance: Such a rejection is because the claim would fail to particularly point out the invention due to inconsistent texts across files.

name: Post-dissolution handling of grounds of rejection
description: When merger is dissolved and reexamination continues, any grounds of rejection not applicable under reexamination should be withdrawn and any new grounds applicable under reexamination should be made (e.g., grounds based on improper broadened claims).
guidance: Examiner should note any questions remaining that cannot be considered under reexamination pursuant to 37 CFR 1.552(c).

name: Treatment of federal court decisions known at determination time
description: If a federal court decision on the patent is known to the examiner when the determination on the reexamination request is made, that decision does not automatically preclude a finding of a substantial new question (SNQ) because the Office uses different standards of proof and claim interpretation than courts.
guidance: Non-final court holdings are not controlling; final holdings of invalidity or unenforceability (after all appeals) are controlling and mean no SNQ exists for the claims held invalid/unenforceable. Examiner determinations after a court decision must be reviewed by CRU SPRS to ensure conformity with Office litigation policy (see MPEP § 2240).

name: Handling court decisions that issue after reexamination ordered
description: If a federal court decision issues after an ex parte reexamination is ordered (or the Office becomes aware of such a decision), the order to reexamine will be reviewed to see if an SNQ still exists; if no SNQ exists, the reexamination will be terminated.
guidance: Non-final federal court decisions have no binding effect on reexamination. A final court holding of invalidity/unenforceability is binding—claims held invalid/unenforceable are withdrawn from reexamination; if all claims are finally held invalid the reexamination is vacated or terminated. Use form paragraph 22.20 to note claims held invalid by court.

name: Recognition of identicalness for trade-promotion applications without extra evidence
description: Where identicalness cannot be determined just based on the documents about the request of expedited examination, an examiner can recognize the request of expedited examination without requiring submission of additional evidential examination as long as there is a high possibility that the application directly related to trade promotion and the claimed invention are the same and no particular grounds to doubt such possibility exist.
guidance: Used when available documents make it highly likely the trade-promotion application and claimed invention are the same; examiner may accept without further proof if no special grounds to doubt exist.

name: Venture business — addition after filing: no retroactive eligibility (except narrow exceptions)
description: To be eligible on the ground of venture business, the applicant shall be a venture business when filing an initial application. Adding a venture business after filing does not make the application eligible for expedited examination.
guidance: Exception: where the venture business practices the claimed invention with the right to get a patent transferred from the original applicant (and similar situations for innovation businesses or other certified types), the examiner may confirm and recognize eligibility.

name: Relevance determination for certified companies (venture/innovation/component/material/etc.)
description: Applications filed by certified companies are entitled to expedited examination only when relevance between the claimed invention (or utility model) and the business type of the certified company is confirmed. Normally relevance is confirmed when the business type (from registration certificate or announcement) is the same as all or part of the industrial field of the claimed invention.
guidance: Examiner uses registration certificates or announcement websites to compare industrial field; where relevance cannot be confirmed, order correction and request further explanation or documents.

name: Companies with outstanding employee invention compensation system — relevance determination
description: If the business type of such a company is not relevant to the claimed invention, the request shall not be eligible. Relevance is determined based on evidential documents (business registration, etc.); where relevance cannot be identified, examiner shall order correction.
guidance: Same verification steps as other certified‑company categories.

name: National quality authentication projects — verification vs. presumptive acceptance
description: Where it is unclear that the claimed invention is the direct outcome of the certification project, examiner may order the requester to verify correlation. However, where the claimed invention is likely related to the direct outcome and there are no special grounds, examiner may recognize eligibility without further investigation.
guidance: Examiner exercises discretion to accept where likelihood is high and no contrary grounds exist; otherwise require verification documents.

name: Practiced or to be practiced by applicant — subject categories
description: An application is deemed to have its claimed invention being practiced or to be practiced by the applicant where it falls under items such as: filed by a parts&materials‑specialized certified company for related inventions, or an invention awarded in an open contest/competition hosted by government where the invention is financially supported by the government for commercialization or patent filing.
guidance: Certain certified company statuses or government‑supported awards can trigger this ground; check certification and financial support evidence.

name: Subject of practicing: who qualifies as practicing
description: Applicant should practice or be practicing the invention. Even if the practicing entity is not an applicant, if the practicing entity engages in an agreement to practice the claimed invention with the applicant, the practicing is eligible for expedited examination.
guidance: Evidence of agreements between applicant and third‑party practitioner supports eligibility.

name: Determination: explanation and evidential documents required
description: A requester shall explain that the claimed invention is being practiced (or prepared to be practiced) as a business in a written explanation and submit evidential documents. Examiner shall conduct expedited examination when submitted explanation and evidential documents confirm practicing or preparation to practice as a business.
guidance: If documents and explanation are sufficient (see list), examiner recognizes practicing; otherwise order correction.

name: Determination of identicalness between invention being practiced and claimed invention
description: For requests based on practicing (or preparation to practice), the invention being practiced and the claimed invention shall be identical. Requester must prove identicalness. Examiner determines identicalness based on articles, photographs, or other evidential documents and the written explanation; if identicalness cannot be confirmed, order correction of the request.
guidance: Provide clear side‑by‑side evidence (photos, specs, manuals) matching claimed features to the practiced product/process.

name: Recognition: component & material technology development business — automatic acceptance and evidentiary rules
description: A request on an application filed by a company confirmed as a component & material technology development business shall be accepted as the invention being practiced or prepared to be practiced as a business without submission of the usual evidential documents. Relevancy between such businesses and the claimed invention shall be determined based on proving documents enclosed in the expedited request form and, if necessary, by referring to the Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology database.
guidance: Joint filings where one applicant is such a confirmed company are accepted (subject to name and timing rules similar to other certified statuses). Original copy of the confirmation is evidential; copies acceptable if identical. Examiner may require supplements if relevancy cannot be checked.

name: Handling Procedures for Product-by-process Claims
description: Handling Procedures for Examinations involving Product-by-process Claims.
guidance: Specific page referenced for procedures applicable to examinations of product-by-process claims (link from JPO page).

name: Unity of Invention (Patent Act Article 37)
description: Unity of Invention (Patent Act Article 37).
guidance: Criteria for determining whether claims form a single general inventive concept; includes reference material on unity (Part II, Chapter 3).

name: Mathematical methods, business methods, computer programs per se and algorithms not patentable (Section 3(k))
description: Mathematical methods, business methods, computer programmes per se and algorithms are not considered patentable inventions.
guidance: Details: mathematical methods are acts of mental faculty and not patentable; business methods (commerce-related activities) are excluded even if implemented with internet/technical features if in substance they are business methods; computer programme products stored on a medium (program per se) are not allowable. However, claims not directed at computer programme per se could be patentable if other conditions met. For method claims involving computer programmes to be patentable they must clearly recite limiting hardware integers enabling the program to function; programs that work on general-purpose computers typically fail. Algorithm claims that merely express general principles (allowing different programs) are not patentable. Computer programs coupled to hardware that enable hardware to perform a function may be allowable if all patentability conditions are met.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure — claims must define scope properly
description: The claims should define the scope of the invention properly.
guidance: Claims are examined to ensure they are clear, supported by description, and delimit the monopoly sought.

name: Unity of invention — single inventive concept
description: The claims of a specification shall relate to a single inventive concept; where multiple inventive concepts are present examiner will report plurality and application may be divided.
guidance: Determination of linkage to form single general inventive concept is without regard to claim drafting format (separate claims or alternatives). Division can be required to cure plurality. Examples illustrate when product/process/apparatus claims may be considered a single invention.

name: Unity of invention — process and apparatus linkage
description: Unity between process and apparatus requires that the apparatus or means have been specifically designed for carrying out the process, or at least a step of the process.
guidance: Independent claims of different categories may nonetheless relate to single inventive concept (e.g., product and specially adapted manufacturing process; process and apparatus specifically designed for it). Examples 1–8 provided (product/process/mould/locking system/broadcasting system/spray bottle/drug and related claims).

name: Council proposition 9 — prompt reservation survey to enable locating
description: Request that the reservation be surveyed as soon as possible to enable Indians to locate during the coming summer.
guidance: Emphasize urgency to allow Indians to build fences and locate claims (stakes of old survey decayed), and recommend immediate completion of surveys.

name: Presumption of identity between re-issue and original
description: The invention claimed in a re-issue is presumed to be identical with that attempted to be patented in the original until the contrary appears.
guidance: This presumption is strong and rebuttable only by strong and controlling evidence (usually a comparison of the two specifications and related papers). Cases cited (e.g., Spaeth v. Barney) treat the Commissioner's allowance as prima facie evidence that re-issue is lawful, and the presumption in favor of validity and identity is substantial.

name: Inspection of original drawings and models permissible and often decisive
description: The original drawings and model filed may be examined to determine the identity of the re-issue with the original; a feature absent from the specification/drawings may be found in the model.
guidance: If a feature is claimed in the re-issue but not in the drawings/specification, inspection of the original model can determine whether the feature was present; where model is not produced it may be presumed to contain the feature unless rebutted. Dilapidated models may be aided by evidence of their primitive condition if consistent with drawings/description.

name: Delay in seeking re-issue affects construction (long delay disfavors broadening)
description: If a re-issue broadening the claims is granted after a significant delay (e.g., four and a half years), courts will construe it as covering the same matter as the original rather than allowing broadened scope.
guidance: Long delay may be evidence that the patentee sought to enlarge rights; courts are reluctant to allow materially broader scope after long intervening periods (see Albany Steam Trap Co. v. Felthonsen).

name: Fundamental written description inquiry (possession)
description: The fundamental factual inquiry is whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
guidance: This is a question of fact determined case-by-case. Examiner should consider whether the disclosure shows applicant had possession of the claimed subject matter at filing (e.g., Vas-Cath, AbbVie/Janssen).

name: Examiner methodology and burden (prima facie case)
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description is present; the examiner has the initial burden, after a thorough reading and evaluation, of presenting evidence or reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize the written description as providing adequate support.
guidance: To make a prima facie case the examiner must identify claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why the disclosure fails (e.g., Hyatt v. Dudas). If made, burden shifts to applicant to point out support or amend claims. A simple explicit statement may sometimes suffice for amended claims (see MPEP §2163.04).

name: For amended or newly added claims show support in original disclosure
description: Applicant should show support in the original disclosure for the new or amended claims; if applicant points out where/ how the originally filed disclosure supports the amendment(s) the examiner must then present reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize such support.
guidance: A simple statement such as 'applicant has not pointed out where the new claim is supported' may be sufficient where support is not apparent. See Hyatt v. Dudas and MPEP §§714.02, 2163.04, 2163.06.

name: Claim construction and whole-claim analysis
description: Each claim must be separately analyzed and given a reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; the entire claim (preamble, transitional phrase, body) must be considered in assessing written description support.
guidance: Claim construction is essential to the written description analysis; preamble language and transitional terms (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') affect scope and must be evaluated (see Genentech, PPG, Pac-Tec).

name: Do not import limitations from specification into claims
description: Limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification.
guidance: The absence of definitions or details of well-established terms or procedures should not be the basis for a written description rejection, but examiners must avoid reading specification-only limitations into claim scope (see Bell Comm., Corning Glass Works).

name: Review entire application for support (embodiments, figures, sequence listings)
description: Before determining adequacy of written description, examiner should review claims and entire specification including specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings to understand how applicant provides support for claimed features.
guidance: Information well known in the art need not be described in detail, but sufficient information must be provided to show possession of the invention. Consider field of invention and level of ordinary skill.

name: Possession may be shown by reduction to practice or detailed disclosure
description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice, detailed drawings, or structural chemical formulas that permit a person skilled in the art to recognize applicant had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Reduction to practice (constructing an embodiment or performing a process with all claim limitations) is strong evidence, but not always necessary. Drawings alone can provide sufficient written description in appropriate cases (Vas-Cath, Wolfensperger).

name: Possession may be shown by identifying characteristics
description: An adequate written description may be shown by disclosure of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics (e.g., partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with structure) so a skilled artisan recognizes possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: For biotechnology, function-plus-minimal-structure can suffice when there is a well-established correlation between structure and function. Examples include sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length; deposits may support biological material claims (37 CFR).

name: Function-only disclosure generally insufficient
description: Describing a composition or molecule by its function alone typically will not suffice to describe the composition adequately unless a well-established correlation between function and structure exists.
guidance: Function-only descriptions are 'little more than a wish' without enabling identification of the claimed subject matter (see Eli Lilly, Fiers, Amgen). For antibodies/biomolecules, claims defined only by binding affinity to an inadequately described antigen may fail (Noelle v. Lederman, Centocor).

name: Means‑(or step‑)plus‑function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) support requirement
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof; the written description must adequately link particular structure/materials/acts to perform the claimed function or be clear such structures are known to skilled artisans.
guidance: Examiners must consider the specification, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Mere assertion that skilled artisans would know the structures is insufficient; lack of corresponding structure may render the claim both indefinite under 112(b) and lacking written description under 112(a).

name: Species versus genus analysis and appropriate disclosure level
description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species is treated accordingly; a claim encompassing multiple embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus. The required description level varies with the invention's nature and the state of knowledge in the art.
guidance: For single-species claims, examiner should determine (A) whether application describes an actual reduction to practice, (B) whether drawings or structural formulas show completeness, or (C) whether identifying characteristics suffice. For genera, more disclosure may be needed depending on predictability of the art.

name: Checklist for single-embodiment/species claims
description: If claim is drawn to a single embodiment/species, determine: (A) whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, whether drawings/structural formulas sufficiently show invention as whole; (C) if not, whether identifying characteristics are sufficiently detailed to show possession.
guidance: If complete structure (or acts) is disclosed, written description satisfied. If not, consider whether other identifying characteristics (structure-function correlation, partial structure, methods of making) would lead a skilled artisan to conclude possession.

name: Correlation between skill level and required specificity
description: There is often an inverse correlation between the level of skill/knowledge in the art and the specificity of disclosure necessary to satisfy written description; more mature arts may require less detail, unpredictable arts require more.
guidance: In mature technologies, written description questions should not be raised for claims present in the original application even if the specification discloses only a method of making the invention and the function of the invention.

name: When to reject for lack of written description versus enablement or indefiniteness
description: A claim omitting matter disclosed as essential in the specification may be subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description), 112(b) (indefiniteness), or pre-AIA equivalents; rejection under 112(b) cannot stand where the specification satisfies 112(a) for means-plus-function recitations not challenged.
guidance: If a means‑plus‑function claim lacks corresponding structure the claim may be indefinite under 112(b) and also lack adequate written description under 112(a). Examiners should consider interplay between these grounds and treat each limitation accordingly (see In re Noll, Aristocrat, Atmel).

name: Standard for instituting reexamination (SNQ versus RLP)
description: For requests filed prior to September 16, 2011, institution is based on whether a 'substantial new question of patentability' (SNQ) is raised; for requests filed beginning September 16, 2011 and ending September 15, 2012, institution is based on whether there is a 'reasonable likelihood that the requester will prevail' (RLP) with respect to at least one challenged claim.
guidance: The examiner must identify at least one SNQ/RLP and explain how the cited prior art (patents and/or printed publications) establish that SNQ/RLP. The determination is made on the claims in effect at the time of determination (37 CFR 1.923). The examiner's substantive decision to institute is not subject to petition or judicial review except in very limited 'ultra vires' circumstances.

name: Prior art considered for institution
description: The determination whether an SNQ/RLP exists can be based upon any prior art patents or printed publications, not limited to the references relied upon in the request (35 U.S.C. 312(a)).
guidance: If it is not clear a patent/printed publication predates the patent claims, the examiner must discuss why the reference is deemed available as prior art. References relied upon by the examiner should be cited on PTO‑892 unless already listed on equivalent requester forms (PTO/SB/08A/08B/42). Only supply copies of references where not already supplied to the patent owner and requester.

name: Decision language and example usage (form paragraphs and sample decisions)
description: Specific sample language and form paragraphs are provided for decisions granting (¶ 26.01) and denying (¶ 26.02) inter partes reexamination, including tailored language for SNQ vs RLP timeframes.
guidance: Examiner should use provided sample text as appropriate (e.g., 'A substantial new question of patentability affecting claim [1] ... is raised' or 'The present request ... establishes a reasonable likelihood that requester will prevail with respect to claim [1]'). Examples illustrate how to explain why particular references do or do not raise SNQs/RLPs and which claims will be reexamined.

name: Lay-witness testimony must not opine on obviousness or underlying technical questions
description: Testimony from a lay witness that expresses an opinion that a claimed modification 'would be obvious' or otherwise reaches the ultimate obviousness conclusion is inadmissible if it addresses the central legal and technical question of obviousness.
guidance: Examples of improper lay testimony include answers like 'Yes, I did' to 'Did you think modifying the Cornette system to support two circuits to be obvious?' and similar statements about what would be obvious. Such testimony is 'in the clear purview of experts' and therefore improper from lay witnesses.

name: Scope of technical questions reserved for experts
description: Underlying technical questions related to obviousness that require expert qualifications include: the nature of the claimed invention; the scope and content of the prior art; differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and the motivation of a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine references.
guidance: Unqualified witnesses may not testify as to these underlying technical matters or the ultimate conclusions derived from them. Admission of such testimony is improper under controlling precedent (Sundance) and Fed. R. Evid. 702.

name: Do_not_claim_effects_that_cannot_be_produced
description: The patentee should inform the enquirer of the exact nature of the manufacture invented; if the article described has not the qualities, or the machine produce not the results set forth in the specification, the grant is invalid.
guidance: Ensure claimed properties and results are accurate and demonstrably producible by the disclosed methods; overstatements of capability risk invalidation (examples: Winter's multiple promised outputs).

name: Do_not_claim_more_than_the_invention (improvements)
description: The grant must not be more extensive than the invention; where the patent is for an improvement or addition, the inventor cannot monopolize the whole subject; the specification is incorrect if it contains description of more than the improvement unless it particularly distinguishes the new from the old parts.
guidance: When patenting an improvement, clearly identify and limit claims to new elements or combinations; distinguish old/background components so as not to claim pre-existing subject matter (cases: Williams v. Brodie; Macfarlane v. Price).

name: Claim_only_new_combinations_or_new_conformation
description: If the novelty consists in a new conformation or in new combinations of known parts, the patentee may claim the composition if the combination from the beginning is his invention; but if earlier combinations existed up to a point and the patentee only added beyond that, claiming the whole machine may be bad.
guidance: Carefully analyze prior combinations and claim only the genuinely novel structural configuration or added combinations. Courts will examine whether the patentee's contribution is merely an improvement of an existing engine or a wholly new machine (case: Brown/Boville/Jessop discussions).

name: Do_not_include_more_old_material_without_designation
description: Every old part which is essential and material in producing the intended effect will be considered as claimed if it is not designated as old; material old elements should be designated to avoid improper claiming.
guidance: When incorporating old elements into a specification, explicitly identify them as pre-existing to avoid being deemed to claim them as new; failure to mark them may expand claim scope improperly and invalidate the specification.

name: Excluded subject matter from utility model protection
description: The following shall not be considered objects of a utility model: (a) discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods; (b) esthetic creations; (c) schemes, rules or methods in performing mental acts, for playing games or in doing business, or computer programs; and (d) presentations of information. The provisions do not exclude protection as a utility model except where protection is requested for the above elements considered as such.
guidance: Enumerates exclusions (similar to patent exclusions), while clarifying only the listed items are excluded if claimed as such.

name: Formal requirements for filing an application for registration of a utility model
description: The application shall be filed with the Organization or the Ministry responsible and the application file shall contain: (a) an application addressed to the Director-General; (b) proof of payment of requisite fees; (c) an unstamped, private power of attorney if represented by an agent; and (d) a sealed envelope containing: (i) a specification stating by what configuration, arrangement or mechanism the utility model may be useful to the intended purpose, set out clearly and completely so that a person having ordinary knowledge and skill in the art could carry out the model; (ii) the drawings and photographs necessary or useful for understanding the specification; (iii) a descriptive abstract summarizing the contents of the specification; (iv) the claim or claims defining the scope of protection sought, which shall not exceed the contents of the specification; and (v) sufficient indications regarding the best manner of carrying out the invention known to the inventor on the filing date and, where priority is claimed, the priority date of the application.
guidance: Comprehensive checklist of required formal documents and substantive sufficiency of specification, claims, drawings and best mode information; claims must be supported by specification; application must include payment and (if applicable) power of attorney.

name: Contents of the registration
description: The international registration shall contain: (i) all the data contained in the international application (except certain priority claims), (ii) any reproduction of the industrial design, (iii) the date of the international registration, (iv) the number of the international registration, (v) the relevant class of the International Classification as determined by the IB.
guidance: See Hague Rule 15(2).

name: Additional mandatory contents required by certain Contracting Parties (Article 5(2))
description: Any Contracting Party whose Office is an Examining Office and whose law requires certain elements for a filing date may notify the Director General; the elements include: (i) indications concerning the identity of the creator; (ii) a brief description of the reproduction or of the characteristic features; (iii) a claim.
guidance: Where the international application contains the designation of a Contracting Party that has made such a notification, the application shall also contain, in the prescribed manner, the element(s) that were the subject of that notification. See Article 5(2) and Rule 11.

name: Optional contents and permitted additions
description: The international application may optionally contain: two or more industrial designs (subject to conditions), a request for deferment or immediate publication, optional inclusion of elements of Article 5(2)(b), representative name and address, priority claims under Paris Convention, declarations concerning exhibitions, requests for deferred publication, and statements identifying information known to applicant material to eligibility.
guidance: See Article 5(4)–(5) and Rule 7(5). Optional inclusion of elements may be strategic (e.g., include description or creator even if not required by designated CP).

name: Hague Administrative Instructions — permitted matters and required formats
description: Permitted matters include: (a) a DAS code accompanying a priority claim; (b) indication/claim and certificate of economic status for reduced fees; (c) a Declaration Concerning Exception to Lack of Novelty in prescribed wording and indication of designs concerned (with optional accompanying documentation); (d) statements in formats established by the IB for certain Rule 7(5)(g) statements.
guidance: See Hague Administrative Instructions Section 408. Follow prescribed wording and formats for declarations and supporting documentation when invoked.

name: US-specific required contents when the United States is designated
description: An international design application that designates the United States shall contain or be accompanied by: (1) a claim; (2) indications concerning the identity of the creator (inventor) in accordance with Rule 11(1); and (3) the inventor's oath or declaration.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.1021(d). Presentation of inventor identification and related information in the international application prior to international registration will be considered to satisfy certain oath/declaration requirements (see §§ 1.63 and 1.64 references).

name: Description must indicate the invention and avoid unnecessary information
description: The invention for which patent protection is sought in the patent claims must be indicated in the description; the description must not contain any information that is obviously not necessary for explaining the invention (section 34 (3) number 4 Patent Act and section 10 Patent Ordinance).
guidance: The description and drawings are used to interpret the claims (section 14 Patent Act). If agreement on claim wording is reached, the applicant must align the description with the valid claims and comply with Patent Ordinance requirements. To simplify, literal quotation of claim parts in the description may be replaced by references to those claim parts.

name: Structure and content of decisions
description: Decisions contain a caption (parties and representatives), an operative part (tenor) separated from the reasons, and a statement of reasons consisting of facts of the case and the reasons for the decision.
guidance: Facts should briefly describe essential content of claims and means of attack/defence, emphasizing motions submitted. Reasons should summarise the factual and legal considerations underpinning the decision.

name: Level of ordinary skill — designer perspective
description: Obviousness must be assessed from the viewpoint of a 'designer having ordinary skill in the art' to which the subject matter pertains; courts have described this as the perspective of the 'designer of ... articles of the types presented.'
guidance: When articulating obviousness, frame what would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the specific article type claimed (see In re Nalbandian, In re Carter).

name: Form paragraph usage for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections
description: Standardized form paragraphs are provided for rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (single or multiple references), for repeating rejections, final rejections, and rationale language focusing on overall appearance.
guidance: Use specified form paragraphs (¶¶ 15.18, 15.19, 15.67–15.40 series) and insert appropriate bracketed information (reference IDs, reasons). Emphasize that unobviousness must be in overall appearance rather than minute details.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112: drawings are incorporated into the claim
description: The drawing in a design application is incorporated into the claim by use of the claim language 'as shown'; the drawing disclosure can be supplemented by narrative description and is incorporated by 'as shown and described.'
guidance: Understand that claim scope is defined by what is shown in full lines in the drawings plus any written description. The title does not define scope; it merely identifies the article.

name: Enablement and scope — limit to surfaces shown in full lines
description: The scope of a claimed design is limited to those surfaces or portions of the article shown in the drawing in full lines in combination with any additional written description in the specification.
guidance: Do not rely on the title to define scope. It is prima facie evidence that omitted surfaces form no part of the claimed design. If visible surfaces are omitted, applicants should add statements clarifying that omitted surfaces form no part of the claimed design.

name: Only visible surfaces at point of sale/use must be disclosed
description: Only those surfaces of the article that are visible at the point of sale or during use must be disclosed to meet enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112 for design patents; the drawing should illustrate the design as it will appear to purchasers and users.
guidance: Hidden or non-claimed surfaces need not be described. If visible surfaces that are flat and unornamented are considered part of the design, include special description in the specification.

name: Inconsistencies among views — nonenabling disclosure
description: When inconsistencies among the drawing views are so great that the overall appearance of the design is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as nonenabling.
guidance: Otherwise inconsistencies should be objected to and corrected by applicant. Use form paragraph ¶ 15.20.01 for nonenabling rejection.

name: Suggestion to submit enlarged sketches/photographs to overcome enablement rejection
description: Examiners may suggest that applicant submit large, clear sketches or photographs showing unclear areas so the examiner can determine if the claim may be clarified without adding new matter.
guidance: Use ¶ 15.20.02 to request specific illustrations; identify unclear areas in the bracketed text.

name: New matter prohibition — amendments must have antecedent basis
description: New matter is subject matter with no antecedent basis in the original specification, drawings or claim. An amendment to a claim without antecedent basis introduces new matter and must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Amendments changing configuration (including removal of three-dimensional surface treatment integral to configuration) introduce prohibited new matter (37 CFR 1.121(a)(6)). Superimposed surface-treatment removals may be permitted only if the underlying configuration was clearly disclosed originally.

name: Permissible and impermissible amendments examples
description: Permissible: preliminary amendment filed with application and identified in the oath/declaration; inclusion of a disclaimer in the original filing. Impermissible: amendment to the claim without antecedent basis that changes the configuration or surface appearance by adding previously undisclosed matter.
guidance: Before entering post‑filing amendments, assess whether the change departs from original configuration or introduces new matter; use case examples (In re Berkman, In re Salmon, In re Daniels) for guidance.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph — definiteness standard
description: Defects in claim language give rise to a rejection under the second paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112. Definiteness must be analyzed in light of the prior art and application disclosure as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Phrases such as 'or similar article' or 'or the like' have been held indefinite (Ex parte Pappas), though such language in a title directed to environment may not always merit rejection. Evaluate definiteness on facts and circumstances.

name: Indefiniteness when title fails to specify a known article of manufacture
description: The claim should be rejected as indefinite when the designation of the design (title and drawings) is such that it cannot be determined what article of manufacture is being claimed (e.g., a design claimed as a 'widget' that does not identify a known article).
guidance: Use ¶ 15.22.03 when the title and disclosure do not inherently identify the article; attempts to clarify title may introduce new matter.

name: Preserve ability to bring improvement inventions and incentives to disclose
description: Terminal disclaimer practice is intended 'to be able to bring [] improvement inventions within the protection of the patent system, at the same time giving an incentive for their disclosure.'
guidance: The proposed rules will discourage filings in the U.S. patent system that include improvements, continuations, or claims clarifying scope (e.g., genus claims relative to species claims). Being required to file a terminal disclaimer under the proposed regime will practically eliminate the ability to enforce such claims, hampering innovation and reducing public disclosure.

name: Do not conflict with 35 U.S.C. §282's presumption of independent claim validity
description: 35 U.S.C. §282 states each claim of a patent shall be presumed valid independently of the validity of other claims. The proposed rule would make patent claims unenforceable whenever a single claim in the terminally disclaimed patent is found invalid, contradicting that statutory presumption.
guidance: Notes the semantic distinction between 'unenforceability' and 'invalidity' is immaterial if the practical result is a 'useless patent.' The rule should not convert the invalidity of one claim into a blanket removal of enforceability for other independently valid claims.

name: Avoid rules that enable infringers and weaken enforcement
description: The proposed rule makes it more difficult to enforce patent rights against infringers and thus seeks to make U.S. patents and use of the U.S. patent system less valuable to innovators. It lacks a good policy basis as it tilts enforcement in favor of infringers who can prove invalidity of a single claim.
guidance: Cites real‑world counterfeiting harms (e.g., CBP seizures) and argues that making narrower claims unenforceable because of broader claim invalidity will materially assist infringers and undermine innovators' ability to combat counterfeiters.

name: Protect valid narrower claims from being nullified by invalid broader claims or clerical errors
description: Invalidity of a broader claim in a parent patent should not render a narrower claim in a child patent unenforceable; similarly, a typographic mistake rendering a claim invalid under 35 U.S.C. §112 should not render a corrected claim in a child patent unenforceable.
guidance: Offers concrete examples of harms the proposed rule would cause—providing 'promising opportunities' for would‑be infringers to evade liability—and argues rules should avoid creating such exploitation vectors.

name: Direct tying via terminal disclaimer
description: A terminal disclaimer filed in X(P) or X(A) identifying W(P) or W(A) as a reference patent or application directly ties X(P) to W(P).
guidance: Example language and visual: W ← X. If a terminal disclaimer in X names W as the reference, X(P) is tied to W(P). Consequence: tying can affect enforceability when a claim of the reference patent is finally held unpatentable or invalid (see enforcement agreement requirement).

name: Indirect (transitive) tying via chains of terminal disclaimers
description: Terminal disclaimers can create indirect ties through multiple intermediate patents/applications (e.g., W ← X ← Y ← Z), such that Z(P) is indirectly tied to W(P) even if intermediates are abandoned or pending.
guidance: If patents are tied directly or indirectly by one or more terminal disclaimers and the terminal disclaimers contain the proposed agreement, the enforcement of downstream patents may be affected if any claim in the tied chain is finally held unpatentable or invalid over prior art. The preamble gives chain examples and consequences (e.g., if a claim of W(P) is held unpatentable, then Y(P), X(P), and Z(P) may not be enforceable depending on tying and the agreement).

name: Unidirectionality of tying (no automatic mutual tie)
description: Tying by a terminal disclaimer is directional: multiple patents can each disclaim to the same reference patent but not be tied to each other (e.g., X → Y ← Z means X tied to Y and Z tied to Y, but X is not tied to Z).
guidance: Consequences are limited by directionality: if a claim in the central reference (Y) is invalidated and the disclaimers contain the proposed agreement, X(P) and Z(P) may not be enforced; but invalidation of a claim in X(P) or Z(P) does not affect the other patents unless tying exists in that direction.

name: Required enforceability agreement in terminal disclaimers (proposed)
description: Proposed § 1.321(c)(3) and (d)(3) would require that a terminal disclaimer filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting include an agreement by the disclaimant that the patent in which the terminal disclaimer is filed, or any patent granted on the subject application, will be enforceable only if the patent is not tied and has never been tied directly or indirectly to a patent by one or more terminal disclaimers filed to obviate nonstatutory double patenting in which: (1) any claim has been finally held unpatentable or invalid under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 in a Federal court in a civil action or at the USPTO, and all appeal rights have been exhausted; or (2) a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 to that claim has been made.
guidance: This is the core new enforcement limitation: a subject patent with the required agreement is enforceable only if it was never tied (directly or indirectly) to a patent that has had claims finally invalidated under anticipation/obviousness or where a statutory disclaimer was filed after a 102/103 challenge.
