The preamble provides multiple examples showing how this enforceability limitation applies in chains of tied patents.

name: Options to obviate nonstatutory double patenting without filing a terminal disclaimer with the proposed agreement
description: An applicant facing a nonstatutory double patenting rejection may: (1) combine the conflicting claims into a single application; (2) cancel or amend any conflicting claims in the application or in the other application containing the conflicting claims; (3) argue that rejected claims are patentably distinct from the claims of the reference patent or application; or (4) file a reissue application of the patent whose claims formed the basis of the nonstatutory double patenting to add canceled conflicting claims from the application into the reissue application, provided the added claims do not introduce new matter.
guidance: These are presented as practical alternatives for applicants/patent owners concerned about the proposed agreement. The preamble also notes an alternative of separating patentably distinct claims into another application and filing a terminal disclaimer (with the agreement) only in the application with indistinct claims.

name: Alternative splitting approach for patentably distinct claims
description: An applicant may separate the patentably distinct claims into another application and file a terminal disclaimer with the proposed agreement in the application with the indistinct claims.
guidance: This allows applicants to avoid tying unrelated/patentably distinct claims to the enforcement-limiting agreement by moving distinct claims to a separate application that does not receive the terminal disclaimer containing the proposed agreement.

name: Withdrawal of a terminal disclaimer before patent issuance (petition under 37 CFR 1.182)
description: If the applicant amends the claims after filing the terminal disclaimer such that the claims no longer conflict with the claims in the reference patent or application, the applicant may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to withdraw the terminal disclaimer prior to the issuance of the application to avoid the effect of the proposed agreement on patentably distinct claims.
guidance: After patent grant, a recorded terminal disclaimer will not be withdrawn (see MPEP 1490, subsection VIII). This is a procedural avenue to escape the enforcement limitation if conflict is resolved before grant.

name: Spanish grounds for cessation/voidance
description: The patent is declared to be void — 1. When the time is elapsed. 2. When the party does not apply for it within three months from the time he presented his petition. 3. When the patent has not been put in force for a year and a day after the date thereof. 4. When the patentee abandons his right by not using it for a year and a day. 5. When the subject has been used in any part of the kingdom, or described in printed books, or in engravings, pictures, models, plans, or descriptions, contained in the Royal Conservatory of Arts; or when the subject has been used in a foreign country and the patentee has presented it as new and of his own invention.
guidance: Lists temporal, use, and novelty-related grounds that invalidate Spanish patents; publication or prior use domestically or abroad (if claimed as new) defeats validity.

name: Claims — Recognition and Support by Description
description: Claims must be supported by and be recognizable from the description; claims must not claim matter not disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Includes 'claims supported by description of invention' — examiners assess whether claims are adequately disclosed and justified by the specification; cross-reference to added-matter/amendment rules.

name: Claims — Clear and Concise Statement of Invention
description: Claims must be clear, concise and define the matter for which protection is sought.
guidance: Guidance on drafting for clarity, avoiding ambiguous terminology, properly defining technical features and boundaries of the claimed subject-matter.

name: Claims — Matters Necessary for Specification of Invention
description: Certain matters are deemed necessary to specify an invention within claims (e.g., essential technical features).
guidance: Examiner instructions on what technical details are considered necessary to include in the claims to properly specify the invention.

name: Claims — Claim Drafting Requirements
description: Formal and substantive requirements for claim drafting (dependent/independent claims, numbering, antecedent basis, allowable amendments).
guidance: Practical drafting rules, examples of acceptable claim formats, and cautionary notes regarding improper amendments and added matter.

name: Inventive Step — Computer-related inventions (specific guidance)
description: Special considerations when assessing inventive step for computer-related inventions: evaluate closest prior art, problems to be solved (software-implementation/computerization), ordinary skill in the art, and ordinary creative activity.
guidance:
Key points and examples from the guidelines:
- Reasoning should consider the closest prior art, well-known or commonly used art, and common general knowledge.
- Examiner evaluates whether claimed invention is selection of optimal material, mere design modification, mere aggregation, or whether closest prior art discloses a motivation/causal teaching to reach the claimed invention.
- Combining methods from different fields or applying methods to other fields is usually within ordinary creative activity unless technical difficulty (teaching-away) exists or special circumstances (remarkably advantageous effects) are shown.
- Problems to be solved (e.g., 'improve decision level using AI' or 'easier input via GUI') are considered as of filing.
- A person skilled in the art is expected to have common general knowledge of both the applied field and computer technology; may be regarded as a group rather than a single person.
- Examples of ordinary creativity include: applying techniques to other fields (file retrieval -> medical retrieval), adding commonly known means or equivalents, implementing hardware functions in software, systematizing human transactions using routine analysis/design methods, reproducing known events in virtual space, and design modifications based on known facts/customs.
- Effects such as faster processing, handling more data, reduced errors, or uniform results are general effects often resulting from computerization and are not usually unforeseeable; inventive step assessment takes these into account.
- Notes: commercial success can be evidence of inventive step if causally linked to claimed features; mere differences in data contents often do not confer novelty; recording a program/data on a storage medium or claiming a medium that merely transmits information are generally insufficient for inventive step/novelty.

name: Amendment of Specification, Claims or Drawings — Overview
description: General provisions governing amendments including Article 47, purpose of amendment, requirements, and amendment periods.
guidance: Specifies when voluntary amendments or amendments in response to rejections are allowed, timing limits and procedural steps.

name: Examination Criteria by Technology (technology-specific requirements)
description: Technology-specific requirements and examination guidance for particular fields (biotech, pharmaceutical & cosmetics, food, functional drinking water, chemical compounds, alloy, polymers, textile, architectural design, computer-related inventions, etc.).
guidance: Each technology chapter provides specific requirements for description and claims, patentability considerations, examples and special rules (e.g., sequences in biotech, data for food, unit conversions in textile, software/systemization guidance in computer-related inventions).

name: Substantive basis for domestic priority claim
description: A domestic priority claim can be made based on the invention disclosed in the specification or drawings originally attached to the prior-filed application; inventions disclosed outside the claims can serve as the basis.
guidance: It is not required that the invention be present in the claims of the prior-filed application; any invention disclosed in the original spec/drawings qualifies as basis matter for retroactive filing date for that invention.

name: Effect of domestic priority on retroactive filing date (scope of retroactivity)
description: For an invention identical with the one disclosed in the specification or drawings of the prior-filed application that forms the basis of the priority claim, the later-filed application is deemed to have been filed at the time of filing the prior-filed application for specified statutory provisions (e.g., novelty, inventive step, exceptions to public disclosure, first-to-file rules).
guidance: The guidance lists specific Patent Act provisions for which the retroactive date applies: Article 29(1),(2) (novelty, inventive step), main sentence of Article 29(3) (enlarged concept of novelty), Article 30(1) (exception to public disclosure), Article 36(1)-(3) (first-to-file), Article 96(1)(3), Article 98, Article 103, Article 105(1),(2), Article 129, Article 136(5) (trial for a correction). Exclude inventions not disclosed in the prior-filed spec/drawings; those are examined from the later filing date.

name: Requirements for an application to be added to domestic priority claim (Article 55(1) conditions)
description: An application that can be added must meet these requirements: (i) prior-filed app filed within one year prior to the later-filed filing date; (ii) prior-filed app is not a divisional or converted application; (iii) prior-filed app has not been invalidated/withdrawn/abandoned and a decision to grant is not final; (iv) applicant of prior-filed is identical to applicant of later-filed; (v) items related to the priority claim are written clearly enough to specify the priority claim.
guidance: Timing for determination: requirement (i) is assessed at the time of filing the later-filed application; requirements (iii) and (iv) are assessed at the time of amending or adding the priority claim. The law treats claims based on theoretical, another person's, or unspecified applications as inherently invalid.

name: Scope of permissible amendments to domestic priority claim
description: Within one year and four months from the filing date of the prior-filed application the applicant may wholly or partially withdraw priority claims in multiple priority claims, correct clerical errors, or add priority claims; after that period, amendments are limited to clerical errors only.
guidance: Priority claims cannot be withdrawn once 1y3m have elapsed since the prior-filed filing date. For multiple priority claims, whether 1y3m elapsed is determined from the earliest filing dates of each relevant prior-filed application. To change a withdrawn priority and add another, an amendment copy with all amended features suffices — no separate written withdrawal notice is needed.

name: Formality exam for international applications entering national phase
description: When an international patent application claiming priority based on a domestic application or an international application designating only Korea enters the national phase, the examiner must determine whether the prior-filed application is pending at the time of formality examination since such priority claim is deemed domestic.
guidance: If the prior-filed application has been invalidated/withdrawn/abandoned or a decision to grant has become final and binding at the filing date of the international application, the examiner shall request the applicant to amend; failure to correct leads to invalidation of the priority claim.

name: Substantive examination when domestic priority claim invalidated
description: If the domestic priority claim is invalidated due to irregularities, the examiner shall examine the application based on its actual (later-filed) filing date rather than applying retroactive dates to determine patentability.
guidance: When a domestic priority claim is invalidated, the prior-filed application is not deemed to have been withdrawn; examiners must be careful in applying Article 36 (first-to-file) accordingly.

name: Substantive examination applying retroactive dates by invention
description: When the domestic priority claim is valid, the examiner shall consider retroactive date calculations by invention: inventions disclosed in the prior-filed application's original specification/drawings are examined as if filed on the prior-filed date; inventions not disclosed are examined from the filing date of the later-filed application.
guidance: This parallels Treaty priority practice: retroactivity is applied on an invention-by-invention basis, not wholesale for the entire application content.

name: Use current subject matter eligibility guidance (MPEP §2106)
description: Examiners should assess patent eligibility in view of the current subject matter eligibility guidance, which has been integrated into the MPEP (particularly MPEP §2106).
guidance: See MPEP §2106.04(a)(1) for abstract ideas and MPEP §2106.06(b) for improvements to computer functionality. The Office's guidance maps to the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2A and Step 2B). Follow the integrated MPEP guidance when analyzing claims for §101 issues.

name: Software inventions can be eligible when they make non-abstract improvements to computer technology
description: Software-based innovations can make "non-abstract improvements to computer technology" and be deemed patent-eligible subject matter at the first step of the Alice/Mayo analysis (Step 2A in the Office's guidance).
guidance: Claims directed to improvements in computer functionality may be found not to be directed to an abstract idea. Use decisions such as Enfish, McRO, Finjan, and Core Wireless as examples where software claims were held eligible because they improved computer technology rather than claiming an abstract idea.

name: Claims directed to an abstract idea require an inventive concept to be eligible (MPEP §2106.05)
description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it must include an 'inventive concept' to transform the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter (see MPEP §2106.05).
guidance: Precedential Federal Circuit cases have found claims ineligible as directed to abstract ideas without inventive concept (e.g., Inventor Holdings; Two-Way Media; Smart Systems Innovations; Secured Mail Solutions). When a claim's substance maps to those abstract-idea holdings, evaluate whether additional claim elements contribute an inventive concept beyond the abstract idea.

name: Evaluate whether claims recite specific steps that accomplish a result improving computer functionality
description: Claims that recite specific steps producing a technical result that realizes an improvement in computer functionality are more likely to be patent eligible (e.g., Finjan).
guidance: In Finjan, the method 'scans an application program, generates a security profile identifying any potentially suspicious code in the program, and links the security profile to the application program' — the court found these specific steps effected an improvement (protecting against unknown viruses and obfuscated code) compared to traditional virus scanning. Look for claim language that details how the improvement is achieved and what technical problem is solved.

name: Determine whether claimed GUI or interface features constitute an improvement to electronic device functionality
description: Graphical user interface claims may be eligible when directed to an improved user interface for electronic devices rather than an abstract idea (e.g., Core Wireless).
guidance: Core Wireless' claims (displaying an application summary of each application on the main menu while applications are in an unlaunched state) were held eligible because the claims contained precise language delimiting the type of data to be displayed and how to display it, resulting in increased efficiency. Examine claim precision about data types, display behavior, and how the interface improves device operation or user efficiency.

name: Compare claimed improvements to precedent (Enfish, McRO, Thales, Visual Memory, Finjan)
description: Use existing Federal Circuit decisions that found eligibility for improved systems as comparators when determining if a software claim is directed to an improvement in computer functionality rather than an abstract idea.
guidance: The memorandum explicitly compares eligible GUI and software-improvement claims to Enfish, Thales, Visual Memory, and Finjan. Use factual and claim-scope parallels to inform whether a claimed invention aligns with these precedents.

name: Recognize common abstract-idea fact patterns that have been held ineligible
description: Be aware of abstract-idea subject matter categories and fact patterns that the Federal Circuit has recently found ineligible, such as local processing of payments for remote purchases, monitoring/delivery/accumulation of information, collection/storage/recognition of financial-transaction data for mass transit, and using markings on mail to communicate information.
guidance: The memorandum cites specific cases as examples: Inventor Holdings (local processing of payments), Two‑Way Media (sending/directing/monitoring/accumulating information), Smart Systems Innovations (collection/storage/recognition of transaction data), Secured Mail Solutions (marking affixed to mail object). If claim substance maps to these types of abstract-idea holdings without additional inventive concept, treat as likely ineligible.

name: Special Case procedure (Trade Marks)
description: Conflicting claims to a Trade Mark may be determined by a special case.
guidance: Parties may submit a special case; the Comptroller may submit or require parties to submit; the Comptroller may settle the case. Form of request and fees are prescribed. (Ref: 99, 282.)

name: Title in Specification
description: Title required in a specification; the title should reflect the object of the invention.
guidance: Title not to be wider than the rest of the specification and may narrow down the claim. Examiner to report on title. (Refs: 3–5.)

name: Who may be plaintiff / complainant in a patent action
description: Who may be a plaintiff or complainant in a patent action, including issues about assignees, executors, administrators, licensees, owners-in-common, and nominal plaintiffs.
guidance: Rules on standing, assignment of accrued claims, who may sue in their own name, and limitations on nominal plaintiffs (e.g., licensees cannot be purely nominal plaintiffs).

name: Causes of action involving multiple IP rights
description: Causes of action based on a plurality of patents or on both terms of an extended patent, or on a patent and a trade-mark.
guidance: How claims may be pleaded and litigated when multiple patents or mixed intellectual-property rights are involved.

name: Patent statutes: administrative and substantive provisions
description: Appendix listing many patent statutes and statutory sections: establishment of Patent Office; officers and employees; printing of specifications and drawings; requisites of specification and claim; what inventions are patentable; drawings; specimens; model; oath; examination and issuing patents; limitation on time to complete application; patents to assignees; renewal for failure to pay fees; assignment; marking requirements and penalties for false marking; filing/effect of caveats; notice of rejection of claim; interferences; affidavits, depositions, subpoenas, witness fees; appeals from examiners; reissue; disclaimer; suits for infringement; power of courts to grant injunctions; extensions; fees and mode of payment.
guidance: Catalog of statutory authorities and procedural/administrative rules that govern patent procurement, maintenance, enforcement, and remedies; each referenced section corresponds to a statutory topic discussed in the treatise.

name: Burden of proof for internet disclosure (claimant bears burden)
description: The person who states that a specific piece of information was disclosed on the Internet should have the burden of proof.
guidance: Hungarian Group and Israeli report indicate the party asserting existence of the internet disclosure must prove it; practice may vary by jurisdiction and case.

name: Archives are desirable/necessary for internet evidence
description: Archives are desirable (or necessary) for providing evidence for disclosures on the internet.
guidance: Archival records help prove content and timing of internet disclosures; several national reports endorse use of archives to support evidentiary claims.

name: Three-step comparison test for anticipation (India)
description: Guideline: (1) construe the prior document as at its publication date excluding hindsight; (2) compare each prior document separately with the patentee's claim; (3) ask whether the prior document discloses the same invention such that a skilled worker would inevitably produce it when following its clear and unmistakable directions.
guidance: This is an explicit method suggested by the Indian Group for assessing whether a prior document anticipates a claim (practical-utility/equivalence focus).

name: Errors in disclosed information can invalidate patents
description: Erroneous statements in a specification amounting to a false suggestion may invalidate the patent, even if the error would be noticed by a skilled workman.
guidance: If a specification asserts that multiple processes/machine combinations produce a claimed result but one is wholly ineffectual, the patent may be invalid despite obviousness of the error to a skilled worker.

name: Effect of transitional phrase on claim scope
description: Transitional phrases connect the preamble to the body of a claim and determine whether the claim is open, closed, or hybrid in scope.
guidance: Recognize that choice of transitional phrase directly controls whether additional, unrecited elements/steps are excluded (closed), allowed (open), or conditionally excluded (hybrid). Use the appropriate transition to reflect the intended breadth of coverage. Examples: 'comprising' = open; 'consisting of' = closed; 'consisting essentially of' = hybrid.

name: Comprising (open-ended)
description: 'Comprising' is an open-ended term allowing for additional steps or components; shorthand for 'including the following elements but not excluding others.' The word 'comprising' transitioning from the preamble to the body signals that the entire claim is presumptively open-ended.
guidance: Use when the drafter intends to cover the recited elements plus any additional, unrecited elements/steps. Equivalent open-ended terms include 'including,' 'containing,' and 'characterized by.' Infringement analysis and prior art searching should treat claims with 'comprising' as permitting additional features beyond those recited.

name: Consisting of (closed)
description: 'Consisting of' is closed and excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim.
guidance: Use to narrowly limit claim scope to the exact listed elements/steps (with the allowance of permissible impurities and conventional adjuncts). A claim 'consisting of' listed elements infringes only when those exact elements are present. Avoid if broader coverage is desired.

name: Consisting essentially of (hybrid)
description: 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground: it limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention.
guidance: Primarily used in chemical and metallurgical composition inventions to exclude additional unspecified ingredients that would affect basic and novel characteristics. Use when intending to exclude materials that alter key properties but allow others that do not materially affect them. Be aware that the precise meaning depends on what the specification or claims identify as the 'basic and novel characteristics.'

name: Treatment of 'consisting essentially of' in examination vs. litigation
description: How 'consisting essentially of' is interpreted differs between patent examination (prior-art searching) and litigation (claim construction).
guidance: For examination/prior-art purposes, 'consisting essentially of' will be construed as equivalent to 'comprising' absent a clear indication in the specification or claims of what the basic and novel characteristics are—meaning examiners may consider broader prior art. In litigation, courts construe the phrase during claim construction based on intrinsic evidence (specification, prosecution history) to define what materially affects the invention's basic and novel characteristics.

name: Composed of (typically closed)
description: 'Composed of' is typically treated as closed (similar to 'consisting of').
guidance: Use cautiously when a narrow, exclusive claim is intended. Confirm that 'composed of' will exclude unrecited elements or materials unless the specification indicates otherwise.

name: Selected from the group consisting of (Markush; closed)
description: 'Selected from the group consisting of' is a Markush-type expression and is treated as closed.
guidance: Use for claiming an element selected from a closed group of alternatives (Markush claim format). This construction excludes alternatives not listed in the group; proper drafting of the group members is critical to capture intended scope.

name: Evidentiary bases that can establish prima facie lack of ornamentality
description: Examples of proper evidentiary basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 that a claim is lacking in ornamentality include: (A) common knowledge in the art; (B) the appearance of the design itself; (C) the specification of a related utility patent; or (D) information provided in the specification.
guidance: Rejections for lack of ornamentality must be supported by evidence; do not make such rejections in the absence of evidence.

name: Affidavit/declaration showing ornamentality (visible in end use)
description: To overcome a §171 rejection for an article visible in end use, an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 may be submitted from the applicant or a company representative explaining specifically and in depth which features or areas of the claimed design were created with concern for enhancing saleable value or a concern primarily for the aesthetic appearance of the article.
guidance: Cite Gorham Manufacturing Co. v. White and provide detailed statements of motivating factors. Attorney argument alone insufficient.

name: Advertisements and commercial materials as rebuttal evidence
description: Advertisements which emphasize the ornamentality of the article embodying the claimed design may be submitted as evidence to rebut a §171 rejection.
guidance: See Berry Sterling Corp. v. Pescor Plastics Inc. Provide clear, specific indication in the advertisement that the appearance is ornamental (mere inclusion in catalogs/trade shows is insufficient absent specificity).

name: Alternative designs evidence when functionality is asserted
description: When the rejection asserts the design is purely dictated by functional considerations, evidence may be presented showing possible alternative designs which could have served the same function, indicating the claimed appearance was not purely dictated by function.
guidance: Cite L.A. Gear Inc. v. Thom McAn Shoe Co. Provide examples of feasible alternative ornamental designs that perform same function.

name: Evaluation of submitted evidence: look at design as a whole and influence of features
description: The examiner must evaluate evidence submitted by the applicant in light of the design as a whole to decide if the claim is primarily ornamental. The determination is not based on the size or amount of the features identified as ornamental but on their influence on the overall appearance of the design.
guidance: Focus on overall appearance; small size of an ornamental feature does not preclude it being determinative. Use cited cases and MPEP guidance for balancing.

name: Requirement that design was created 'for the purpose of ornamenting'
description: To overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171, applicant must provide evidence that he or she created the design claimed for the 'purpose of ornamenting'.
guidance: Cite In re Carletti. Use appropriate evidence concerning visibility and intent; mere display at trade shows/catalog inclusion is insufficient unless the material gives clear and specific indication of ornamentality (see Ex parte Webb, Berry Sterling).

name: Claim scope limited to the article of manufacture recited in the claim
description: A design claim is limited to the article of manufacture identified in the claim; it does not broadly cover a design in the abstract.
guidance: Cite In re SurgiSil: ensure the claim language and figures support the article of manufacture as claimed; do not treat a design as covering other articles not recited.

name: Functional/hidden features cannot be used to support patentability absent ornamentality showing
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102, features of the design that are functional and/or hidden during end use may not be relied upon to support patentability unless the ornamentality standard under §171 is also met.
guidance: Cite In re Cornwall, Jones v. Progress Ind., Black & Decker v. Pittway, In re Zonenstein. If applicant wishes to rely on such features, they must meet the ornamentality evidence standard described in MPEP §1504.01(c).

name: Foreign design registrations, priority, and pre-AIA 102(d) use
description: Registration of a design abroad is considered equivalent to patenting for priority purposes under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) prior art purposes; U.S. design application must be made within 6 months of foreign filing to claim priority and avoid statutory bars.
guidance: Use the provided country table for dates usable in 102(d) rejections; rejections under pre-AIA 102(d) should only be made when the examiner knows the foreign registration/patent actually issued before the U.S. filing date based on a foreign application filed more than six months prior. If the grant is not evident, include the specified statement in the first action.

name: Alloy composition claims must sum to 100%
description: A claim directed to alloy should set forth the invention so that composition range of each component in alloy should be added up to be 100%. Regardless of whether the claim is stated as a close claim (“consisting of”) or an open claim (“comprising”), the total sum of composition range should not be over or under 100%.
guidance: If one component is given as a relative ratio based on another component the composition ratio is deemed clear. Do not specify only main component while omitting additive components — structure/phase/application/property may vary with additives. Example: a copper alloy claim whose minimum of Cu plus maximums of others sums to less than 100% is unclear and not accepted. Also, list components and recite composition ranges exactly (see Part IX Ch.7).

name: Claims shall recite matters necessary to specify the invention (Article 42(6))
description: Claims must recite such matters regarded necessary to specify what is sought for patent protection as structures, methods, functions and materials or combination thereof.
guidance: Where appropriate, an invention may be defined by effect or operation method rather than physical structure; if an invention can be clearly specified this is permitted at applicant's choice. The provision itself is not a basis for rejection/invalidity — examiners must not reject or invalidate based solely on this provision.

name: Multiple-claims system: claims determine protection scope
description: The law prescribes how claims included in a specification must be drafted so they serve to determine the scope of protection of the claimed invention; the Korean Patent Act adopts a system of multiple claims.
guidance: Article 5 of the Enforcement Decree prescribes requirements for claim drafting under the multiple-claims system. Claims should be drafted to clearly define protection and follow statutory form and numbering rules.

name: Dependent claim concept: narrowing or adding limitations
description: Dependent claims are those that narrow or add further limitations to specify an independent claim (specifying by adding technical elements or narrowing a generic concept to a species).
guidance: If a claim narrows or adds to another claim in content but does not formally refer to it, it is not a dependent claim. Conversely, a claim that formally refers to an independent claim but does not narrow/add limitations (e.g., substituting A with B) is likewise not a dependent claim. Note Article 5(1) allows claims that substantiate independent claims by narrowing/adding to be presented as dependent, but they may also be presented as independent — it's not mandatory to use dependent form.

name: Independent-claim presentation and permitted references (Article 5(1))
description: Independent claims shall be presented without referring to other claims in the form of standing alone. However, independent claims can refer to other claims within the scope in which the invention can be clearly understood to avoid redundant description.
guidance: Permitted examples: 'A product of ... manufactured by the method of claim 0', 'A method of manufacturing a product of claim 0 by ...', etc. Claims that decrease elements or substitute subject matter of referred claims are treated as independent (not dependent). The provision is non-binding for rejection — examiners should not rely solely on it to reject.

name: Proper number of claims according to nature of the invention (Article 5(2))
description: Claims shall be presented in a proper number according to the nature of the invention; this is distinct from unity issues.
guidance: Improper cases include: (i) two or more inventions of different categories recited in one claim (e.g., chemical compound and a contact lens using it), (ii) two or more subject matters included in one claim, (iii) redundant identical claims (identical wording or merely different expressions with identical meaning), (iv) multiple claims technically referred to many times within a single claim (referring to many claims inside one claim) which may cause confusion. Examples provided.

name: Alternative numbering when referring to multiple claims (Article 5(5))
description: Where a claim refers to two or more claims, the claims referred to shall be numbered alternatively.
guidance: Allowed phrasings and their semantics are illustrated: 'in claim 1 or claim 2', 'in any of claims 1 to 3', 'in claim 1, claim 2 or claim 3', 'in any of claims 1 to 7 and claims 9-11', etc. The guide explains how 'any of' and conjunctions ('and'/'or') affect limitation and alternative listing recognition.

name: Claim referred-to must precede referring claim (Article 5(7))
description: A claim referred to by another claim should precede the other claim in numbering to facilitate interpretation.
guidance: If a claim refers to itself or refers to a later-numbered claim, an examiner shall notify a ground for rejection citing violation of Article 42(8) and Article 5(7) or cite indefiniteness under Article 42(4)(ii).

name: Presentation: each claim on a new line and sequential numbering (Article 5(8))
description: Each claim shall be presented in a new line and the claims shall be numbered in sequence.
guidance: To clearly define configuration even within a single claim, a claim can be presented in several lines — e.g., multi-step method claims listing steps (A),(B),(C),(D) are acceptable.

name: Deferral of submission of claims (system and deadlines)
description: An applicant may file a specification without including claims (deferral system) but must submit claims by set deadlines (the time limit for submission of claims), otherwise the application is deemed withdrawn.
guidance: Purpose: allow speedy filing and time to prepare claims. Claims must be submitted by three months after notification of intention of a request for examination or by 1 year 2 months (1 year 6 months for apps filed before Dec 31, 2014) from the priority date. If not submitted by deadlines the application is deemed withdrawn the day after deadline. If an application without claims requests examination, examiner should give opportunity for explanation and return it. Such applications are not laid open for publication. Special rules allow claim submission windows for divisional/converted applications filed after Jan 1, 2015 (claims until 30 days from filing). Whether deferral applied is determined by presence/absence of 'Patent Claims' identification symbols in Annexed Form no.15 — if present, deferral is not deemed employed even if claim text blank or contains only punctuation.

name: Unity of invention: general test (Article 45 and Art.6 Enforcement Decree)
description: A patent application shall be filed for each invention, but may be filed for a group of inventions linked so as to form a single general inventive concept. Requirements: (1) claimed inventions shall be technologically correlated; (2) claimed inventions shall have the same or corresponding technological features — these technological features are the improved features over the prior art.
guidance: The 'special technical features' concept is used to determine unity; these need not be identical but must be same or corresponding (e.g., different means to provide same function). They must involve novelty and inventive step over relevant prior art. Unity is determined considering the invention as a whole and by comparing to prior art; in some cases unity can be assessed a priori, in others after prior art search.

name: Procedure for determining unity of invention
description: Unity is determined by selecting a first invention, specifying its special technical features (improvements over prior art), selecting a second invention and its special technical features, and checking whether those features are the same or corresponding; if so, they form a single general inventive concept.
guidance: The first invention (main invention) is chosen independent of claim order. Repeat the process for other claims; the first technical group and inventions forming it are selected as subject to examination. Examination of patentability (novelty, inventive step, etc.) for the invention subject to examination proceeds. If lack of unity is notified, examiner must specify that the concerned inventions do not share the same or corresponding special technical features characterizing the first technical group. Lack of unity is a ground for rejection (to allow amendment/divisional filing) but not a ground for invalidation; examiners need not require amendment where examination can be completed without additional search (e.g., where all claims are unpatentable based on searched prior art).

name: Examples and edge cases for unity determination
description: Various examples illustrate when unity is or is not met: dependent claims that include independent claim's special technical features satisfy unity; generic/species, combination/sub-combination, corresponding features (e.g., timebase expander vs compressor) can meet unity; claims reciting unrelated special technical features do not have unity between them; claims where features are not single (A, B, and A+B) meet unity between A and A+B and between B and A+B but not between A and B.
guidance: Use examples to identify common features or corresponding features. When common features are later shown not to be improvements over prior art, unity may be lost a posteriori. Examiner should consider these examples when applying the rule.

name: Alice two-part framework
description: The Section 101 framework has two parts: (1) determine if the claim at issue is directed toward an abstract idea; and (2) examine the elements of the claim to determine whether it contains an “inventive concept” sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: This is the central test to apply to software patents post-Alice. The article notes the framework was adapted from Mayo and will be the locus of much future argumentation; practitioners should structure analyses around these two steps.

name: Directed-to-abstract-idea inquiry
description: Determine if the claim covers an abstract idea (e.g., a fundamental economic practice, a mathematical algorithm, or other longstanding conceptual practice).
guidance: Use recent lodestar cases (Bilski, Alice) as data points: Alice described intermediated settlement as a ‘fundamental economic practice long prevalent in our system of commerce.' Anti-patterns include claims that are too broad, cover well-known practices, or are drafted comprehensively without meaningful limitations. Examples: Bilski (hedging risk), Alice (intermediated settlement), and cases like Ultramercial likely fail this step post-Alice because of high-level, generalized claim language.

name: Inventive-concept (additional inventive concept) requirement
description: Examine the elements of the claim to determine whether there is an additional inventive concept sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: This second step asks whether the claimed implementation adds something significantly more than the abstract idea itself. The article observes this can hinge on novel hardware elements or non-conventional uses of technology (see Ancora’s BIOS example). Be aware that courts may treat this similarly to novelty/non-obviousness, creating overlap with other patentability doctrines.

name: Claim breadth and presence of meaningful limitations
description: Claims that are too broad, that cover well-known practices comprehensively, or that lack meaningful limitations are suspect for being abstract and therefore ineligible.
guidance: Illustrated by Bilski (claims drawn to the vast bulk of hedging activity) and Alice (claims covering all third-party intermediaries). Draft claims to include concrete, limiting features rather than sweeping functional language to avoid this anti-pattern.

name: Level-of-abstraction in claim drafting
description: The level at which the claim is drafted (highly generalized versus detailed and specific) affects whether a claim is seen as abstract.
guidance: Claims drafted at a high level (general steps) are vulnerable — Ultramercial’s view-for-content claims were criticized for generality. Where possible, draft claims to recite concrete, technical steps, limitations, or implementation details to reduce the risk of being categorized as abstract.

name: Practical litigational implications and unpredictability
description: The Alice framework is ‘brief yet baroquely obscure’ and will produce substantial argumentation and case-by-case uncertainty in future litigation.
guidance: Counsel should anticipate extensive disputes about where a claim falls under the two-step test and prepare multiple lines of argument (e.g., focusing on concrete technical improvements, distinguishing prior cases, or emphasizing non-generic implementations). The article implies strategic claim drafting and litigation posture must account for this unpredictability.

name: Substantive contents required of a public use petition
description: The petition must be submitted in writing, must specifically identify the application to which it is directed by application number or serial number and filing date, and should include a listing of all affidavits or declarations and exhibits relied on. The petition must contain a sufficient description of the subject matter alleged to have been in 'public use' or 'on sale', including any necessary photographs, drawings, diagrams, exhibits, or flowcharts to enable the examiner to compare the claimed subject matter to the alleged public use/on-sale subject matter.
guidance: The petition and accompanying papers must either (A) reflect that a copy has been served upon the applicant or applicant's attorney/agent, or (B) be filed in duplicate if service is not possible.

name: OPLA referral and examiner determination: prima facie showing standard
description: After OPLA's formal review, the examiner determines whether the petition establishes a prima facie showing that the invention was in public use or on sale more than one year before the filing date so as to create a statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) alone or in combination with 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: A prima facie case is established if the facts asserted in affidavits/declarations, as supported by exhibits, would, if later proved true by testimony, result in the statutory bar. The examiner must: (1) identify exactly what was in public use or on sale; (2) determine whether it was in use or on sale in this country more than one year before the effective filing date; and (3) determine whether the pending claims 'read' on or are obvious over the alleged public use/on-sale matter. The examiner should compare all pending claims with the matter alleged to have been in use or on sale, not just claims identified by petitioner.

name: Burden of proof in IPR (preponderance of the evidence)
description: In an [inter partes review], the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable. The burden of proof is on the Petitioner to show that the challenged claims are unpatentable; that burden never shifts to the patentee.
guidance: Petition must identify with particularity the supporting evidence per 35 U.S.C. §312(a)(3). The standard of proof for unpatentability in IPR is preponderance of the evidence (35 U.S.C. §316(e); applicable case law cited).

name: Claim construction standard (Phillips / §282(b) standard)
description: The Board applies the same claim construction standard used to construe claim terms in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b). Under that standard, claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
guidance: Look principally to intrinsic evidence (claim language, written description, prosecution history). Extrinsic evidence is less significant in determining legally operative meaning (Phillips; DePuy Spine; C.R. Bard).

name: Intrinsic evidence primary; extrinsic less significant
description: In determining the meaning of the disputed claim limitation, we look principally to the intrinsic evidence of record, examining the claim language itself, the written description, and the prosecution history, if in evidence. Extrinsic evidence is 'less significant than the intrinsic record' in determining claim meaning.
guidance: Give greatest weight to intrinsic sources; use extrinsic (expert testimony, dictionaries) only to assist, not to contradict intrinsic record.

name: Definition from specification controls when claim term is defined
description: Because the term 'fixed dose' is defined by the Specification and is not disputed by the parties, we determine that this term requires no further construction.
guidance: If specification expressly defines a claim term, adopt that definition (here: 'fixed dose' = dosage administered without regard to patient weight or BSA, not mg/kg or mg/m2).

name: Functional claim language can be limiting
description: Functional language is limiting upon an apparatus claim when the functional language informs the structural requirements of the claimed device. e.g., we interpret the claim phrase 'delivers to a patient' as a functional limitation requiring that the claimed device be capable of containing and delivering the dose.
guidance: Do not automatically treat functional language as mere intended use; analyze whether the language imposes structural capability requirements (K-2 Corp. cited). But avoid importing additional limitations beyond the claim language.

name: Do not import method-of-treatment or unwritten limitations into device claims
description: We decline to adopt Patent Owner’s construction that would require the device to 'safely and effectively deliver' the amount of drug to patients with IL-6-mediated disorders, because to do so would impermissibly extend the scope of the claims beyond their language.
guidance: Only read into the claim what the claim language and intrinsic evidence support; avoid adding substantive limitations that relate to patient condition or efficacy unless expressly recited.

name: Meaning of 'delivers to a patient' in this case
description: We construe the claim phrase 'delivers to a patient' as a functional limitation of the claims that requires that the claimed device be capable of subcutaneously delivering the dose contained within it to a person.
guidance: This construction does not limit 'patient' to persons with a particular disease nor require demonstrable safe/effective treatment outcomes; it requires capability to deliver subcutaneously.

name: Interpretation of 'contains and delivers' / single-device delivery not required
description: The claim language does not require that the fixed dose be administered in a single injection; the claims require only that the device be capable of containing and delivering the fixed dose. The term 'dose' is temporal ('to be taken at one time') and need not imply a single injection.
guidance: Do not construe 'contains and delivers' to mandate single-injection delivery absent specific claim or clear intrinsic support.

name: Anticipation standard (single reference, express or inherent)
description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference. A reference can anticipate even if it 'does not expressly spell out' all limitations, if a POSA reading it would 'at once envisage' the claimed arrangement or combination.
guidance: Assess whether a single prior-art reference discloses all claim elements either explicitly or inherently; inherent disclosure must necessarily be present in the reference.

name: Obviousness (Graham factors) and burden for obviousness
description: A patent claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a POSA. Resolve obviousness using factual determinations: (1) scope and content of prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: Petitioner must show obviousness by a preponderance of the evidence; use KSR and related precedent to inform analysis.

name: Efficacy or safety not required for apparatus claims
description: Independent claims directed to an article of manufacture (a device) are not limited by any requirement for a showing of the efficacy or safety of administering the drug; the claims are apparatus claims and whether the dose delivered is efficacious is immaterial to the apparatus claim's scope.
guidance: Do not require clinical efficacy data for anticipation/obviousness of device claims unless efficacy or safety is expressly recited in the claim language.

name: Intrinsic evidence over prosecut ion history and specification (avoid overreaching)
description: Do not impermissibly extend the scope of the claims through claim construction beyond the language of the claims. For example, requiring that the patient be in need of treatment or importing consideration of immunogenicity/comfort absent claim language is improper.
guidance: Limit construction to what is supported by claim language and intrinsic record; prosecution history may inform meaning but cannot add new substantive claim limitations without clear support.

name: Definition — "claimed invention" (35 U.S.C. 100(j))
description: The term “claimed invention” is defined as the subject matter defined by a claim in a patent or an application for a patent.
guidance: Used throughout AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 analysis as the unit assessed against prior art and exceptions; applies on a claim-by-claim basis when determining effective filing date and prior art effect.

name: Definition — "effective filing date" (35 U.S.C. 100(i)(1))
description: The “effective filing date” for a claimed invention is the earlier of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest provisional, nonprovisional, international (PCT), or foreign patent application to which the patent or application is entitled to benefit or priority as to such claimed invention.
guidance: Determination of prior art availability and applicability of AIA vs pre-AIA law turns on the effective filing date. Effective filing date is determined claim-by-claim and depends on satisfaction of support/112 requirements in earlier applications. See specific rules for continuation/divisional, CIP, provisional benefit (119(e)), and foreign priority.

name: Prior art patent-document category under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)
description: A claimed invention is not patentable if it was described in a U.S. patent, a U.S. patent application publication, or an application for patent deemed published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) that names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: WIPO publications of PCT applications that designate the United States are treated as U.S. patent application publications for prior-art purposes regardless of international filing/publication language or whether the PCT application enters U.S. national stage. A U.S. patent document’s prior-art date is its effective filing date as determined under 35 U.S.C. 102(d).

name: AIA one-year grace period — exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)
description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor; or (B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter from the inventor or joint inventor.
guidance: This effectively provides a one-year grace period after an inventor-originated disclosure during which a patent application may be filed and not be barred by that disclosure. The one-year period is measured from the filing date of the earliest application to which benefit/priority is properly claimed and which supports the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The end date is extended to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or federal holiday (35 U.S.C. 21(b)).

name: Measurement of the one-year grace period (AIA)
description: The one-year grace period in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) is measured from the filing date of any U.S. or foreign patent application to which the patent or application is entitled to benefit or priority as to such invention, provided the earlier application supports the claimed invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Differs from pre-AIA grace period measurement (which measured from earliest U.S. filing date); applies irrespective of whether the earlier application was filed in the U.S. or abroad. See MPEP §§ 2153.01(a), 2153.02 for additional guidance.

name: Common-ownership exception (102(b)(2)(C)) — scope and limits
description: A disclosure in a U.S. patent document is not prior art under 102(a)(2) if the disclosed subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Replaces pre-AIA 103(c) limited exception and applies to prior patents/published applications of co-workers/collaborators for both novelty (102) and nonobviousness (103) purposes when the conditions are met. It does not remove a disclosure as prior art under 102(a)(1); a coworker disclosure that is publicly available remains prior art under 102(a)(1) unless it fits a 102(b)(1) exception.

name: Joint research agreement deemed common ownership (102(c))
description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person for 102(b)(2)(C) purposes if: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application for patent discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: Requires a written contract/grant/cooperative agreement and satisfies the deemed-common-ownership condition only when all three predicate conditions are met; see 35 U.S.C. 100(h) definition of joint research agreement.

name: "Described" for anticipation under 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) — elements and enablement
description: For a prior art document to ‘describe’ a claimed invention such that it anticipates under 102, it must disclose “each and every element of the claimed invention” either explicitly or inherently, with the elements arranged or combined as in the claim, and a person of ordinary skill in the art must have been enabled to make the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: The description requirement for anticipation is distinct from the written-description/enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A prior art reference need not satisfy the 112(a) "how to use" requirement and can anticipate even if it does not disclose a use or reduce the invention to practice. Case law cited: In re Gleave; Eli Lilly; Net MoneyIN; In re Bond; Impax Labs; In re LeGrice; In re Donohue; In re Schoenwald; Schering Corp.

name: Printed publication may be evidence of earlier public use/sale
description: A printed publication that does not have a sufficiently early publication date to qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) may nonetheless be competent evidence of a previous public use, sale activity, or other availability of the claimed invention to the public where the public use or sale does have a sufficiently early date to qualify as prior art.
guidance: Office may rely on non-patent literature as supporting evidence for earlier public activities (see In re Epstein and MPEP § 2133.03(b)). Examiners should consider such evidentiary uses when publication date itself is insufficient.

name: Later factual references can be used for certain universal facts
description: In some circumstances, factual references need not antedate the filing date to be cited to show universal facts (characteristics/properties of a material, scientific truism) that are relevant to rejection.
guidance: Later publications can be cited to show evidence such as that undue experimentation would have been required (In re Corneil), that a parameter was or was not critical (In re Rainer), that a specification statement was inaccurate (In re Marzocchi), that an invention was inoperative or lacked utility (In re Langer), or that a claim was indefinite (In re Glass). However, later references impermissibly cannot be used to determine enablement or written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (In re Koller). Such references may also be used to show level of ordinary skill (Ex parte Erlich).

name: Drawings can be used as prior art if they show all claimed structural features
description: Drawings and pictures can anticipate claims if they clearly show the structure which is claimed; the picture must show all claimed structural features and how they are put together.
guidance: Origin of drawing is immaterial; drawings in design patents or utility patents can anticipate or make obvious claims. Features unintended or unexplained in the specification may still be relied upon if reasonably disclosed to one of ordinary skill (In re Mraz; In re Aslanian; Jockmus v. Leviton). Proportions in drawings not to scale are not evidence of actual proportions if the reference does not disclose scale (Hockerson-Halberstadt; In re Wright). Evaluate drawings for what they reasonably disclose and suggest.

name: Scope of a patent-reference's disclosure when used as a 'patent' (not a 'publication')
description: When a patent document is applied as a patent (rather than as a publication), the examiner may rely on any information in the specification germane to the claimed subject matter, not just what is in the patent claims.
guidance: Unclaimed details in the specification may be relied upon even if the patent is secret (Ex parte Ovist; In re Kathawala). The phrase 'invention ... patented' in pre-AIA 102 subsections has been interpreted to include all disclosed aspects of the invention. In re Fuge is not inconsistent—at least the claim scope embraces everything in the claim.

name: Provisional application filing date rule (post-Dec 18, 2013)
description: A provisional application filed on or after December 18, 2013 will be given a filing date as of the date a specification, with or without claims, is received in the Office.
guidance: Provisional applications filed prior to December 18, 2013 are dated under pre-PLT (AIA) 37 CFR 1.53(c) (written description and any necessary drawings). Amendments (other than those required to make the provisional comply with regulations) are not permitted after the provisional filing date.

name: Conversion from provisional to nonprovisional (37 CFR 1.53(c)(3)) — requirements and patent-term impact
description: A provisional application may be converted to a nonprovisional and accorded the original provisional filing date, but the request must be accompanied by the fee in 37 CFR 1.17(i) and an amendment including at least one claim as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (unless the provisional already contains such a claim). The nonprovisional must include filing/search/exam fees and possible surcharge.
guidance: Conversion will not refund provisional fees and can adversely affect patent term (the patent term will be measured from at least the provisional filing date). Applicants should consider claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) instead of conversion to avoid adverse patent term and be less expensive. Requests to convert must be filed prior to abandonment of the provisional or expiration of 12 months after the provisional filing date.

name: OPAP review for applications filed without all pages of specification
description: OPAP reviews application papers to determine whether all pages of specification are present. If an application filed without all pages nonetheless contains something that can be construed as a written description (and required figures/claims where applicable), OPAP will send a Notice of Omitted Items indicating a filing date was accorded but pages are lacking.
guidance: If the application contains nothing that can be construed as a written description, OPAP will mail a Notice of Incomplete Application indicating no filing date is granted (lack of 35 U.S.C. 112).

name: If application not entitled to filing date — applicant options
description: If OPAP mails a 'Notice of Incomplete Application' (no filing date), applicant may (A) file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) with fee and evidence asserting missing specification was submitted or that deposited papers contain adequate written description, (B) submit the omitted specification including at least one claim (if required) and accept the date of such submission as the filing date, or (C) submit an amendment under 37 CFR 1.57(b) in a nonprovisional application (if specification is completely contained in prior-filed application) accompanied by a petition under 1.53(e).
guidance: Two-month periods are extendable under 37 CFR 1.136; petitions must include sufficient evidence (37 CFR 1.181(b)).

name: Subject matter categories where drawings usually not necessary
description: The USPTO practice treats applications with at least one process/method claim or certain composition applications as not usually requiring drawings. Examples where drawings usually not considered necessary include coated articles/products, articles made from a particular material or composition, laminated structures (unless significant structure), and articles where the sole distinguishing feature is presence of a particular material.
guidance: If an application directed to such subject matter does describe drawing figures in the specification but was filed without drawings, it will be treated as filed without all drawing figures referred to in the specification (MPEP § 601.01(g)), provided the application contains something that can be construed as a written description.

name: No liability for incidental destruction of personal property during legitimate military operations; statutory limitations may bar claims
description: For injuries to or destruction of personal property incidental to legitimate military operations in war the Government is not responsible; certain statutes (e.g., acts of Feb. 21, 1867) specially inhibited settlement of such claims arising during the Civil War and similar limitations may apply.
guidance: R.55, 328, Jan. 20, 1888 and related decisions. Examples include cotton destroyed by explosion during possession of Mobile, AL (1865) and damage from naval bombardment.

name: Civil War 'loyal citizens' claims jurisdictional limits; relief requires express legislation
description: Claims for property taken from loyal citizens for use of the Union army during the Civil War were cognizable by the Southern Claims Commission but largely excluded from the Court of Claims; many such claims are barred by statute of limitations and the only relief available now is by express congressional legislation.
guidance: P.61, 468, Oct. 3, 1893; G.2764, Nov. 27, 1896. Highlights jurisdictional/temporal barriers to redress.

name: No Government liability for counsel fees or related expenses in court-martial matters and certain witness expenses
description: Claims against the United States by an attorney for services rendered as counsel for an accused officer in a court-martial trial are without merit as against the United States; likewise, no provision of law supports payment of time, cost, and expenses incurred by a claimant in traveling to collect fees due a civilian witness before a court-martial.
guidance: P.32,165, May 2, 1899; C.1807, Nov. 2, 1895. Distinguishes individual legal expenses from Government obligations.

name: Inventor Allows Another To Use the Invention Without Restriction or Obligation of Secrecy = Public Use
description: “Public use of a claimed invention under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) occurs when the inventor allows another person to use the invention without limitation, restriction or obligation of secrecy to the inventor.” (In re Smith)
guidance: Presence/absence of confidentiality agreement is one factor; must consider time, place, and circumstances showing amount of control inventor retained. Example: sale of seeds to growers and lack of confidentiality rose to public use/on-sale; hidden use without secrecy obligations may be public (Egbert).

name: On-Sale Bar: Definite Sale or Offer More Than One Year Before Filing That Anticipates or Renders Obvious
description: “An impermissible sale has occurred if there was a definite sale, or offer of sale, more than 1 year before the effective filing date of the U.S. application and the subject matter of the sale, or offer to sell, fully anticipated the claimed invention or would have rendered the claimed invention obvious…” (Ferag AG v. Quipp).
guidance: Apply Pfaff two-prong test: (1) product must be subject of a commercial offer for sale not primarily experimental; (2) invention must be ready for patenting. Use traditional contract law (UCC) to determine whether a commercial offer for sale occurred.

name: The Invention Must Be 'Ready for Patenting' (Pfaff Two-Prong: Offer + Readiness)
description: Pfaff test: (1) the product must be the subject of a commercial offer for sale; (2) the invention must be ready for patenting (either reduced to practice or described in drawings/other descriptions sufficiently specific to enable POSITA).
guidance: Ready for patenting can be demonstrated by reduction to practice before the critical date or by sufficiently specific drawings/specifications enabling a person skilled in the art. Inventions embodied in products that inherently possess each claimed limitation satisfy 'ready for patenting' even if parties did not know details (Pfaff; Weatherchem; Abbott).

name: Invention Need Not Be Ready for Commercial Marketing to Be 'Ready for Patenting'
description: The invention need not be ready for satisfactory commercial marketing for sale to bar a patent; readiness for patenting is a lower threshold.
guidance: Focus on technical readiness (enablement/embodiment of claimed limitations) rather than commercial marketability (Atlantic Thermoplastics).

name: Usage re: proving diligence when depository fails supports relief applications
description: When an authorized depository becomes insolvent, a disbursing officer should file and prove his claim in bankruptcy and prosecute collection; reasonable diligence in such legal measures supports any future application for discharge from liability.
guidance: R. 35, 365 May 7, 1874 — practical guidance for post-loss conduct to seek relief.

name: Required formal contents of petition
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.292 must be in writing, specifically identify the application (by application number or serial number and filing date), and should include a listing of all affidavits/declarations and exhibits relied on.
guidance: The petition must contain a sufficient description of the subject matter alleged to have been in 'public use' or 'on sale', including necessary photographs, drawings, diagrams, exhibits, or flowcharts, to enable the examiner to compare the claimed subject matter to the alleged public use/on-sale subject matter. The petition and accompanying papers must either (A) reflect that a copy has been served on the applicant or applicant’s attorney/agent, or (B) be filed in duplicate if service is not possible. Recommended identifying information (if known) to place on the petition includes: name of applicant(s); application number; confirmation number; filing date; title of invention; Technology Center art unit number; name of examiner; current status and location of application; and 'ATTENTION:' followed by the Office area to which the petition is directed. Petition should be clearly identified as 'PETITION UNDER 37 CFR 1.292.'

name: Examiner determination of prima facie case
description: The examiner determines whether the facts asserted in the affidavits/declarations and supported by exhibits establish a prima facie case that public use or sale in this country more than one year before the effective filing date would result in a statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) alone or in combination with 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: To make this determination the examiner must identify exactly what was in public use or on sale, whether it occurred in this country more than one year before the effective filing date, and whether the pending claims 'read' on or are obvious over what has been shown to be in public use or on sale. The examiner should compare all pending claims with the matter alleged to have been in use or on sale, not just claims identified by petitioner. If the examiner finds a prima facie case, he/she forwards a memorandum to the OPLA staff member summarizing alleged facts, comparing at least one claim with the alleged device, and other pertinent facts to aid the preliminary hearing.

name: Content requirements when petition alleges obviousness
description: When a petition alleges that the claims are obvious over subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale, the petition should include prior art or other information relied on and explain how the prior art or other information, in combination with the subject matter alleged to be in public use/on sale, renders the claims obvious.
guidance: The examiner is not expected to perform a prior art search in evaluating the petition. However, if the examiner is aware of prior art or other information which, in the examiner's opinion, renders the claims obvious over the subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale, the examiner may determine that a prima facie case is made out even if the petition only alleged anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(b).

name: Duty to disclose material information regardless of confidentiality
description: Inventors and others covered by 37 CFR 1.56(c) and 1.555 have a duty to disclose to the Office information they are aware of which is material to patentability, regardless of its classification as trade secret, proprietary, or subject to protective order.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.56(b) defines information as material to patentability when it is not cumulative and (1) it establishes, by itself or in combination with other information, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) it refutes or is inconsistent with a position the applicant takes in opposing an argument of unpatentability relied on by the Office or asserting patentability. A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under a preponderance of the evidence standard, giving each claim term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, before considering contrary evidence.

name: Classification of specifics or structural parts
description: If structural or functional specifics or parts are used only for a certain apparatus, classify the claimed invention into the place for that apparatus.
guidance: If such specifics or parts can be used for more than two apparatuses, classify into the place for the specifics/parts; if no place exists for them, classify in place for the relevant apparatus.

name: Classification for Markush-type compounds
description: For Markush-type chemical compounds generally defined in a chemical formula, classify the general chemical formula individually if it has few relevant places (for example, less than 5).
guidance: If specified compounds are things per se in the claims (composition), outputs from claimed processes, or derivatives, classify the compounds in each relevant place. 'Specified' includes being designated by formula/title, inferred from specific reactants, identified by physical properties, or described with detailed manufacturing examples.

name: Pro Se: Narrative/Indefinite Claims (35 U.S.C. 112, 2nd para.)
description: Claim [1] rejected as failing to define the invention in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph because the claim(s) are narrative in form and replete with indefinite and functional or operational language.
guidance: Structure must be clearly and positively specified, organized and correlated to present a complete operative device. Claims must be in one-sentence form only. Examiner should note format of claims in cited patents as examples.

name: Omnibus Claim (Failure to Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite in that it fails to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language; this claim is an omnibus type claim.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02. Use this paragraph to reject an 'omnibus' type claim; no further explanation is necessary. Example omnibus claim: 'A device substantially as shown and described.' See MPEP § 1302.04(b) for cancellation guidance.

name: Trademark or Trade Name as a Limitation
description: Claim [1] contains the trademark/trade name [2]; where a trademark or trade name is used in a claim as a limitation to identify or describe a particular material or product, the claim does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
guidance: Trademark identifies source of goods, not the goods themselves, so scope is uncertain. Insert the trademark and specify the material/product identified/ described by it (bracket instructions). Cite Ex parte Simpson. Explain why the identification/description is indefinite.

name: Duplicate Claims (substantial duplicates)
description: When two claims in an application are duplicates, or are so close in content that they both cover the same thing despite slight wording differences, examiner may object under 37 CFR 1.75 as being a substantial duplicate of an allowed claim.
guidance: Form paragraphs 7.05.05 (warning) and 7.05.06 (objection) may be used where duplicate claims are present. After allowing one claim it is proper to object to another that is a substantial duplicate. See MPEP § 706.03(k).

name: New Matter Prohibition (35 U.S.C. 132)
description: No amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention. Adding subject matter not disclosed in the original application (including adding specific percentages/compounds after a broader disclosure or omitting a step from a method) can constitute new matter.
guidance: In amended cases examiner must be alert to detect new matter. Use 35 U.S.C. 132 as basis for objection to amendments to the abstract, specification, or drawings attempting to add new disclosure. If subject matter capable of illustration is originally claimed but not shown in drawing, require applicant to add it to drawings (see MPEP § 608.01(l)). If new matter is added to claims, use form paragraph 7.31.01 (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph rejection) rather than 7.28.

name: Objection to New Matter Added to Specification (Form 7.28)
description: The amendment filed [1] is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 because it introduces new matter into the disclosure. The added material which is not supported by the original disclosure is as follows: [2].
guidance: Applicant is required to cancel the new matter in reply. Do not use this paragraph in reissue applications (use form paragraph 14.22.01). In bracket 2 identify new matter by page/line numbers and/or drawing figures and provide explanation addressing any applicant statements that the matter was described as filed; include unresolved questions raising doubt as to possession at filing. If new matter affects claims, also make a 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph rejection (form 7.31.01). Treat the new matter as part of the claimed subject matter for purposes of other rejections.

name: After Interference or Public Use Proceeding
description: The outcome of an interference or a public use proceeding may be the basis of a rejection of claims in a pending application.
guidance: For rejections following an interference, see MPEP § 2363.03. Public use proceeding outcomes may provide grounds (see 37 CFR 1.292 and case law such as In re Kaslow). Notify the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences upon termination of relevant proceedings to resume prosecution or interference as appropriate.

name: Res Judicata as Ground for Rejection
