description: Res judicata may constitute a proper ground for rejection where the earlier decision was by the Board of Appeals or a reviewing court and no opportunity for further court review exists.
guidance: Use sparingly — courts have restricted res judicata rejections. Ordinarily also make rejection based on prior art, especially in continuing applications. The MPEP lists cases where res judicata rejections were sustained and cases where they were reversed; analyze claim differences, new evidence, and scope carefully.

name: Rejection of Previously Allowed Claims — Procedure
description: A claim noted as allowable shall thereafter be rejected only after the proposed rejection has been submitted to the primary examiner for consideration of all the facts and approval of the proposed action.
guidance: Give full faith and credit to previous examiner's search and action unless clear error or new prior art. Examiner should not take an entirely new approach or make a new search merely hoping to find something. Use Form Paragraph 7.50 when withdrawing allowability; actions that withdraw allowability require Primary Examiner signature.

name: Further explanation of the "markedly different characteristics" analysis
description: (Public comment theme) Requests for further explanation of the markedly different characteristics analysis.
guidance: The Update responds with additional discussion and examples addressing how to analyze whether claimed subject matter possesses markedly different characteristics from a judicial exception (e.g., laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas), informing examiner determinations under the eligibility framework.

name: Comptroller may refuse registration where conflicting claims exist
description: Where several persons claim to be registered as proprietor of the same trade mark the comptroller may refuse to register any of them until their rights have been determined according to law, and may require or himself submit the claimants to the Court.
guidance: Conflicting claims are generally submitted to the High Court by special case (Trade Marks Rules). If parties cannot agree the comptroller may settle the special case on payment of the prescribed fee (see Forms T).

name: Inventiveness depends on whether prior art points to the invention
description: The issue of inventiveness depends on whether there is any pointer in the prior art which points to the invention or not.
guidance: If the prior art 'clearly points away' from obtaining the claimed invention, then even if a PSA following prior art instructions arrived at the invention, that does not necessarily make it obvious. Conversely, absence of any teaching/pointer towards the technical measure weighs in favour of inventive step.

name: Requirements for treating prior art teachings as motivation
description: TBA decisions show that absence in the prior art of a teaching towards a technical measure and absence of documentary evidence in support of common general knowledge do not support that PSA would have considered that technical measure.
guidance: Examiners should require an explicit hint, teaching, or documentary support that would motivate the PSA to modify the prior art in the claimed manner; mere availability of different types of solutions in other fields is insufficient without a demonstrated link or motivation.

name: 3-prong analysis for presuming invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph
description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, if it meets the 3-prong analysis set forth in MPEP 2181, subsection I.: (1) The claim limitation must use the phrase “means for” or “step for”; (2) The phrase “means for” or “step for” recited in the claim must be modified by functional language; and (3) The phrase “means for” or “step for” recited in the claim must not be modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function.
guidance: Use this 3-prong test as the starting presumption. If the claim meets all three prongs, treat it as a means/step-plus-function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. See MPEP 2181 for examples and further analysis.

name: Unclear whether limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph (phrase used but sufficiency of recited structure unclear)
description: When the phrase “means for” or “step for” is used and the claim is modified by some structure, material, or acts, it may be unclear whether the recited structure, material, or acts are sufficient for performing the claimed function and thus whether 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph applies.
guidance: If unclear to one of ordinary skill in the art whether the recited structure/material/acts are sufficient to perform the claimed function, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph may be appropriate. Examiners may use form paragraph ¶ 7.34.16. Require applicant to amend the claim to clarify whether it should be treated as means-plus-function (e.g., delete or modify “means for”/“step for”) or otherwise clarify sufficiency.

name: Unclear whether limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph (phrase not used)
description: If the claim limitation does not include the phrase “means for” or “step for”, it will not be presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. However, if the limitation is written as a function to be performed and does not recite sufficient structure, material, or acts, 112, sixth paragraph might apply; if it is unclear whether it does, a 112, second paragraph rejection may be appropriate.
guidance: If unclear whether the limitation invokes 112, sixth paragraph, examiner may require applicant to either (a) amend the claim to include the phrase “means for” or “step for” in accordance with the 3-prong analysis, or (b) show that the limitation lacks sufficient structure and thus should be treated as function-only. Examiners may use form paragraph ¶ 7.34.17 and must precede it with form paragraphs 7.30.02 and 7.34.01.

name: No disclosure or insufficient disclosure of corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification
description: Once a limitation is determined to be a means (or step) plus function limitation invoking 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, the written description must disclose the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function (as viewed by one skilled in the art). A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is appropriate if there is no disclosure or insufficient disclosure.
guidance: Review the specification (including drawings, figures, tables, sequence listings) to identify corresponding structure; disclosure only by incorporation-by-reference is insufficient. A bare statement that known techniques can be used is insufficient. Examiners may use form paragraph ¶ 7.34.18. Applicant may be required to (a) amend the claim to avoid means-plus-function, or (b) amend the written description to expressly recite the corresponding structure/material/acts without introducing new matter, or (c) state on the record where the corresponding structure is implicitly disclosed (with reference to 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP 2181/608.01(o)).

name: Computer-implemented means-plus-function claims require disclosure of an algorithm (corresponding structure)
description: For computer-implemented means-plus-function limitations, the corresponding structure must be more than a general purpose computer or microprocessor; it must include the algorithm that transforms the general purpose computer into a special-purpose computer that performs the function.
guidance: The written description must disclose the algorithm (may be expressed as math, prose, flow chart, etc.). Mere reference to a general purpose computer with appropriate programming or merely reciting 'software' without detail is insufficient. A 112, second paragraph rejection is appropriate if no corresponding algorithm is disclosed. See cited Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Aristocrat, WMS, Finisar) and MPEP 2181 for examples.

name: Check for written description and enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph when structure is insufficient
description: If there is no or insufficient disclosure of the corresponding structure, examiner should determine whether the written description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph are met for the claim as construed (including the full scope of corresponding structure and equivalents).
guidance: To satisfy written description, the specification must describe the invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession. For enablement, the specification must enable the full scope claimed; if more than routine experimentation would be required (e.g., to generate a missing program/algorithm), an enablement rejection under 112, first paragraph may be warranted. Use MPEP 2164.06(c), 2181, and cited cases for guidance and examples (e.g., mechanical vs electronic sensors).

name: Failure to clearly link or associate disclosed structure/material/acts to the claimed function
description: The structure disclosed in the written description qualifies as the corresponding structure only if the specification or prosecution history clearly links or associates that structure to the function recited in the means-plus-function limitation. If one of ordinary skill cannot identify what structure performs the claimed function, a 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph rejection is appropriate.
guidance: Examiners may use form paragraph ¶ 7.34.19. Applicant may be required to (a) amend the claim to avoid means-plus-function treatment, (b) amend the written description to clearly link the structure to the function without new matter, or (c) state on the record where the corresponding structure is set forth. The 'clear link' requirement is the quid pro quo for employing 112, sixth paragraph.

name: Implicit or inherent disclosure: acceptable only if one skilled in the art can identify corresponding structure; require clarification
description: In rare circumstances where the specification implicitly (rather than expressly) sets forth the structure/material/acts that perform the claimed function, 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph may be satisfied if one skilled in the art can identify that structure. However, the record must be clarified.
guidance: When disclosure is only implicit/inherent, the examiner should require applicant to either (a) amend the written description to expressly recite the corresponding structure/material/acts and clearly link them to the claimed function (without new matter), or (b) state on the record what the corresponding structure/material/acts are. Examiners may use form paragraph ¶ 7.34.20 and may alternatively state on the record what structure is implicitly set forth. Cite 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP 608.01(o).

name: Procedural/form paragraph usage and examiner notes
description: When issuing 112, second paragraph rejections in these contexts, examiners should use the provided form paragraphs (¶ 7.34.16–¶ 7.34.20) and follow the specified bracketed insertion and preceding-paragraph requirements.
guidance: Each form paragraph contains bracketed fields to recite the claim element and explain the deficiency; form paragraphs ¶ 7.34.16–¶ 7.34.19 must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.30.02 and 7.34.01. Examiners should follow the Examiner Notes in each form paragraph (e.g., what to include in each bracket) and cite relevant MPEP sections and case law where appropriate.

name: Alice step one — directed to ineligible concept
description: At step one, determine whether a patent claim is "directed to" a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea. (Alice, 573 U.S. at 217; Mayo, 566 U.S. at 70–73.)
guidance: If the claim is directed to one of these exceptions, proceed to step two. In software cases, the inquiry often asks whether the claims focus on specific asserted improvements in computer capabilities or instead on an abstract process for which computers are invoked merely as a tool (TecSec).

name: Software-specific step-one rubric — specific computer improvement vs abstract idea
description: In software cases, ask whether the claims "focus on specific asserted improvements in computer capabilities or instead on a process or system that qualifies [as] an abstract idea for which computers are invoked merely as a tool." (TecSec, Inc. v. Adobe Inc., 978 F.3d 1278, 1293.)
guidance: Merely improving a user's experience while using a computer application is not, without more, sufficient to render claims patent-eligible (Customedia). Claims that recite generic presentation/selection/organization of information without a technical improvement will be treated as abstract.

name: Result-oriented / functional claim language is insufficient
description: "A claim that merely describes an 'effect or result dissociated from any method by which [it] is accomplished' is usually 'not directed to patent-eligible subject matter.'" (Apple v. Ameranth, Inc., quoting Internet Pats. Corp. v. Active Network.)
guidance: Claims that use high-level functional verbs (presenting, receiving, selecting, synchronizing, applying, matching, determining, displaying, rearranging) without explaining how to accomplish those tasks are likely to be considered abstract. The specification should explain how to achieve the claimed result in a non-abstract way.

name: Mere automation of manual processes using generic computers is insufficient
description: Automating a pre-existing manual procedure on a generic computer does not constitute a patentable improvement in computer technology (Credit Acceptance; Univ. of Fla. Rsch. Found.).
guidance: If the claimed method could be performed by hand (e.g., with paper overlays, colored pencils, transparent sheets), then merely automating it on a computer is an Alice-type abstract idea. The claim must recite a technical solution beyond 'do it on a computer.'

name: Generic computer components and conventional activity do not supply inventive concept
description: Claims that add only generic computer components or recite conventional, well-understood computer activities fail to provide an inventive concept (BASCOM; Apple; BSG Tech).
guidance: Courts treat additions such as 'information handling system', 'computer program product', or generic synchronization as insufficient unless the claim provides a specific technical solution, tailored software, or particular programming that improves computer functioning.

name: Plausible and specific factual allegations required to survive Rule 12
description: On a Rule 12 motion, courts accept the facts alleged in the complaint as true, but the patentee must present plausible, specific factual allegations that aspects of the claims are inventive in order to defeat a motion to dismiss (Aatrix; Cellspin).
guidance: Conclusory allegations of inventiveness, divorced from the claims or specification, are insufficient. Examples of adequate allegations: specific descriptions of unconventional hardware/software structures or novel data-transmittance that are discussed in the specification and complaint (Cellspin).

name: Limitations known in prior art cannot supply inventive concept
description: A claim limitation that is acknowledged as known in the prior art cannot be relied on as an inventive concept (e.g., 'user determined shape' was known in the prior art for map-selection).
guidance: When the specification or prosecution history admits the limitation was known, that limitation cannot convert an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter at step two.

name: Insignificant post-solution activity does not confer eligibility
description: Claim elements that are merely post-solution activity (e.g., a synchronization step stated without instruction) are insignificant if they add nothing more than conventional computer implementation (Apple, Two-Way Media context).
guidance: Courts will disregard such limitations if the claim provides no technical details on how to implement the post-solution activity beyond using generic components.

name: Claims must improve the functioning of the computer itself or disclose specific technical implementation
description: To be patent-eligible, claims should recite an improvement in computer functioning (make it operate more efficiently, solve a technological problem) or provide specific programming/tailored software/meaningful implementation guidance (Enfish/Core Wireless/Intell. Ventures contrast).
guidance: Merely organizing information to help a user process it more quickly does not necessarily improve computer functionality. The specification should repeatedly emphasize the technical problem and how the claim elements solve it.

name: Problem specificity — is the problem specific to computing?
description: Ask whether the problem the claim addresses is specific to computing environments (e.g., limitations of small screens, interaction constraints) or whether the problem also existed in the non-computer (paper) world.
guidance: If the problem and the claimed solution are essentially the same as long-standing manual techniques (cartography, paper layering), that favors a finding of abstractness; if the specification shows solutions particular to computers or devices (as in Core Wireless), that supports eligibility.

name: Core Wireless exception — specific, repeated specification emphasis on computer improvement
description: Claims directed to particular or specific implementations of presenting information on electronic devices that are repeatedly emphasized by the specification as improving device functioning (e.g., solving navigation on small screens) can be patent-eligible (Core Wireless).
guidance: To benefit from Core Wireless, the specification must 'clearly indicate' that the claims are directed to an improvement in the functioning of computers or device-specific problems; mere broad claims about layering or display without device-specific technical detail will not suffice.

name: Responding to §101: Three key strategies
description: When responding to a Section 101 rejection, pursue one or more of three strategies: (1) argue the claim does not recite a judicial exception; (2) argue the claim is integrated into a practical application; (3) argue additional elements (or their combination) add significantly more than conventional solutions.
guidance: These strategies map to steps 2–4 of the eligibility test. Prepare arguments tailored to each prong and support them with specification detail and claim amendments as needed.

name: Prepare for the four-step subject-matter-eligibility test
description: Anticipate and prepare arguments for steps: (1) statutory category; (2) whether claims recite an abstract idea; (3) whether the claim is integrated into a practical application; (4) whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more'.
guidance: Remember examiners must go through all steps (unless rejected at step 1). Structure claim and specification content to address each step explicitly.

name: Avoid language reciting a mental process or show impracticality for human mind
description: Mental process rejections are common for AI claims; avoid claim language that sounds like mental processes or demonstrate that limitations cannot practically be performed mentally.
guidance: Change verbs like 'predict' to 'compute' or add architecture-specific elements that cannot be performed mentally (e.g., 'performing a convolution on an image', 'generating an embedding vector'). Explicitly describe computational complexity (e.g., training takes a month on a supercomputer) and state steps are 'impractical' to perform in the human mind. Note: 'impractical' is distinct from merely 'inconvenient' or 'faster with a computer'—convenience/speed alone will not save a claim.

name: Amend claim language to add architecture-specific elements
description: Overcome mental-process and abstract-idea concerns by reciting specific architectural elements or concrete computational steps.
guidance: Recite details such as particular layer types (self-attention layers, U-nets), specific activation functions, or concrete operations (convolutions, embedding generation) rather than generic terms ('ML model', 'neural network') to show the claim is not merely a mental process or abstract concept.

name: Describe computational complexity in the specification
description: Document in the specification that claimed elements are computationally intensive or complex to demonstrate impracticality of human performance and support eligibility.
guidance: Examples: claim steps that take substantial compute (e.g., month-long training on a supercomputer) or that are 'computationally intensive/complex' as described in the specification will support arguments against mental process rejections and show technical character.

name: Avoid invoking 'methods of organizing human behavior' language
description: Claims that explicitly recite activities in the enumerated sub-categories (fundamental economic practices, commercial/legal interactions, managing personal behavior/relationships) are vulnerable to this abstract-idea grouping.
guidance: Where possible, draft claims to focus on processes performed directly by the AI model (computing vectors, transforming text/images) rather than the ultimate human-facing objective (e.g., creating a legal agreement). Avoid terms like 'contract document' when not necessary, since such language can invite a legal-interaction characterization.

name: Avoid explicitly reciting mathematical formulas; claim descriptive technical specifics instead
description: Mathematical concept rejections are less common but risky if claims recite formulas; claims need not recite algorithms or formulas to be eligible.
guidance: For training claims, recite elements of a loss function descriptively rather than the exact formula. For inferencing claims, claim specifics of input data, the transformation to the data, specifics of output data, and data-preparation steps rather than mathematical operations. For model architecture claims, recite particular types of layers and their functions without reciting low-level mathematical operations (dot products, summations) where possible.

name: Claim specific structures rather than generic computer components
description: Claims stating use of 'a processor' and 'memory' or generic 'ML model' will likely draw §101 rejections under step 3 (2A Prong 2) for relying on generic computer components.
guidance: Recite more specific architectural elements (specific layer types, sensor inputs, data structures) and describe corresponding implementation details in the specification to avoid being considered 'generic computer components.'

name: Include improvements to computer/ML functioning and technical transformations
description: Limitations that show an improvement to the functioning of a computer or ML model, or that effect a transformation of a particular article to a different state, support arguments that claims are integrated into a practical application or amount to 'significantly more.'
guidance: Examples of persuasive limitations: improve functioning of a computer or ML model; implement judicial exception with a particular machine; include elements that perform claimed steps concretely; effect a transformation of a particular thing (e.g., transform images/documents/audio). Tie the improvement directly to the technical problem.

name: Apply the judicial exception in a meaningful, technology-specific way
description: Merely linking an abstract idea to a technological environment is insufficient; claims should include technical elements that meaningfully link the judicial exception to the technology.
guidance: Cite sensor-specific data, environment-unique outputs, architectural or procedural steps that are specific to the technological environment. Show how ordered tokens/embeddings or other ML specifics are rooted in the technical domain.

name: Incorporate unconventional mathematical techniques where appropriate
description: Unconventional mathematical techniques can be relevant additional elements in the §101 2B analysis when they are part of a novel combination.
guidance: Even if mathematical in nature, include and emphasize unconventional mathematical/algorithmic steps in the specification and claims, and explain how they contribute to a technological improvement when combined with other elements.

name: Draft training claims with sufficient specificity
description: Training claims that are drafted at a high level of generality are increasingly being rejected under §101; training claims should be detailed to demonstrate technical improvement and avoid abstract-idea characterization.
guidance: Model training claims should include specifics about data transformations, stages of training, structure of training sets, particular model architectures, and concrete improvements in model functioning or computing. Use the same considerations used for other AI claims to show practical application and technical improvement.

name: Written-description requirement (§112(a)): disclose computer and algorithm details
description: For computer-implemented functional claims, the specification should disclose the computer and the algorithm (necessary steps and/or flowcharts) that perform the claimed function.
guidance: Provide an identification of the structure performing each claimed function, a description of an algorithm (finite sequence of steps, flowcharts), details of structural elements used to perform the function, and descriptions of how exceptions are handled. Use the three recommended levels of architecture/training description to support enablement and written description arguments.

name: Enablement perspective: consider the PHOSITA standard in a fast-moving field
description: Section 112 requirements should be evaluated from the perspective of a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA), which may differ from the inventors' expertise in fast-moving AI fields.
guidance: Differentiate between what an ordinary practitioner in AI would understand and the inventors' specialized knowledge; include sufficient disclosure to bring PHOSITA to the claimed invention without undue experimentation.

name: Definiteness (§112(b)) and avoid means-plus-function pitfalls (§112(f))
description: Particularity and definiteness require proper antecedent basis and avoiding generic functional claim language that could be construed as means-plus-function without corresponding structure in the specification.
guidance: Avoid informalities like missing antecedent basis. For every claimed function, identify structure performing it and include corresponding structural/algorithmic disclosure to prevent the claim being interpreted under §112(f).

name: Avoid 'black box' descriptions; disclose implementation details
description: Describing computer parts or ML components as 'black boxes' risks findings that the disclosure is insufficient and that claimed elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional.
guidance: Provide detailed disclosure of computer hardware, functional requirements, and detailed flow charts or routines for performing claimed steps. Lack of detail can lead to PTAB or Examiner conclusions that details are conventional and thus not 'significantly more.'

name: Specificity matters: claim-level detail can distinguish eligible from ineligible examples
description: The level of specificity in claim limitations often determines eligibility: detailed technical steps are more likely to be seen as non-abstract than high-level 'collecting/analyzing/displaying' recitations.
guidance: Use the MPEP examples as guidance: claims detailing GPS pseudo-range calculations, network packet analysis, specific encryption methods, or pixel-wise halftoning are examples of claims that do not recite mental processes/mathematical concepts, whereas broad data-collection/analysis/display claims are problematic. Emphasize concrete data structures and manipulations.

name: Scope and limits of Article 128(4) presuming infringer's profit
description: Article 128(4) presumes the infringer's profit as the patentee's damage for patent infringement claims, but it does not presume occurrence of damage in all cases and is not applied where no damage occurred.
guidance: Sufficient proof for application can be a concern or probability of damage due to competitive business relations; the right holder's working of the patent is not required. If there has been no business activity using a registered trademark or product mark, the competitive relationship and thus damages may not be admitted.

name: Terms of degree must be understandable in light of the specification
description: Even if the specification uses the same term of degree as the claim, a rejection is proper if the scope of the term is not understood when read in light of the specification.
guidance: If the scope is unclear, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 112, second paragraph). Broadening modifiers are common drafting tools but do not excuse unclear scope (see In re Wiggins). Examiners should ensure the metes and bounds are discernible from the intrinsic record.

name: Use of 'about' and other approximations must be evaluated in context
description: The range encompassed by the term 'about' (and similar approximations) must be determined by considering the context in the specification and claims.
guidance: Contextual factors and available measurement techniques matter (e.g., W.L. Gore holding 'exceeding about 10% per second' definite because it was measurable). However, 'at least about' can be indefinite in presence of close prior art and no guidance from spec or prosecution (Amgen). Examiners should look for intrinsic or extrinsic indicators of the intended tolerance.

name: Use of 'substantially' is broad but can be definite with guidance
description: 'Substantially' is a broad term often used with other terms to describe characteristics; it can be definite if the specification contains guidelines that allow a POSITA to understand the meaning.
guidance: Case law (In re Nehrenberg, In re Mattison, Andrew Corp. v. Gabriel Electronics) shows claims with 'substantially' were held definite where the disclosure provided an objective basis. Examiners should look for such guidelines in the intrinsic record.

name: Addition of 'type' to otherwise definite expressions may render them indefinite
description: Adding the word 'type' (e.g., 'Friedel-Crafts catalyst type', 'ZSM-5-type') can extend scope and make the claim indefinite if it is unclear what 'type' is intended to convey.
guidance: Cases (Ex parte Copenhaver; Ex parte Attig) demonstrate that 'type' can create ambiguity, especially when dependent claims include species not clearly within the genus. Examiners should evaluate whether the term 'type' creates unclear boundaries.

name: Subjective terms require objective standards in the specification
description: If a claim uses a subjective term, the examiner must determine whether the specification supplies an objective standard for measuring scope; without such an objective standard, the claim may be indefinite.
guidance: Claims depending solely on unrestrained subjective opinions (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing' in Datamize) are indefinite. Applicants may overcome rejections by amending to remove the subjective term or by providing evidence/guidance showing how a POSITA would ascertain the term's meaning. Note: providing mere examples may not always satisfy the requirement (DDR Holdings).

name: Specific numerical ranges generally do not raise definiteness issues
description: The recitation of specific numerical ranges in a claim generally does not raise an issue of indefiniteness.
guidance: However, context matters—see additional rules for mixing ranges, open-ended ranges, and 'effective amount' limitations. Examiners should still confirm that the ranges have discernible boundaries.

name: Narrow and broader ranges in the same claim may render the claim indefinite
description: Including both a narrow range and a broader range within a single claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries are not discernible.
guidance: Examples like 'a temperature between 45 and 78 °C, preferably between 50 and 60 °C' have been held indefinite when placed in a single claim. Preferential or example-based narrower ranges belong in the specification, a dependent claim, or a separate independent claim. Dependent claims setting narrower ranges than their parent are acceptable (e.g., 70-150 ohms and dependent 70-100 ohms).

name: Open-ended numerical ranges should be carefully analyzed
description: Open-ended ranges (e.g., 'at least 20%') can create ambiguities depending on how they interact with other claim recitations, composition bases, or dependent claim language.
guidance: Examine whether other claim language inadvertently excludes the open-ended component (e.g., percentages adding to 100%). Court decisions (In re Kroekel, In re Kirsch) show claims may be held definite even if theoretically impossible combinations are included. Terms like 'up to' can include zero (In re Mochel); 'not more than 70% by weight' may read on dry material (Ex parte Khusid).

name: 'Effective amount' may or may not be indefinite depending on disclosure
description: Whether 'an effective amount' is definite turns on whether a person skilled in the art could determine specific values from the disclosure.
guidance: If the specification provides guidance or examples enabling POSITA to determine effective values and the amount is not critical, the phrase may be definite (In re Mattison; In re Halleck). It can be indefinite if the claim fails to state the function to be achieved or more than one effect is implied (In re Fredericksen).

name: Exemplary claim language ('for example', 'such as') can create ambiguity
description: Using language that purports to list examples or preferences in claims may lead to confusion about whether the examples are limiting, and thus may render the claim indefinite in some cases.
guidance: The mere use of 'such as' or 'for example' does not automatically make a claim indefinite, but examples exist where such phrasing was held indefinite (see listed historical Ex parte cases). Examiners should analyze whether the example language makes the intended scope unclear. See MPEP § 2173.02 for when a 112(b) rejection is appropriate.

name: Lack of antecedent basis can render a claim indefinite
description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear due to lack of antecedent basis (e.g., referencing 'said lever' when no lever was previously recited).
guidance: Assess antecdent basis (In re Packard). However, lack of explicit antecedent basis does not always make a claim indefinite if the scope is reasonably ascertainable by POSITA (Ex parte Porter). Inherent characteristics can provide antecedent basis (Bose v. JBL). Examiners should suggest corrections for antecedent problems where appropriate.

name: Terms in the claim body not recited in the preamble are not per se indefinite
description: Omission of elements from the claim preamble does not automatically render a claim indefinite; the totality of claim limitations and their interaction determine definiteness.
guidance: Consider the whole claim to ascertain the inventor's contribution and whether the claim apprises POSITA of its scope. See In re Larsen where an omitted preamble element did not make the claim indefinite.

name: Reference to limitations in another claim is acceptable if not confusing
description: Using a preceding claim to define a limitation (e.g., 'The product produced by the method of claim 1') is acceptable and not necessarily indefinite.
guidance: Such references are proper unless the format of the reference results in confusion. Examiners should also check compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (pre-AIA 112, fourth paragraph) when examining dependent claims (see MPEP § 608.01(n), subsection III).

name: Functional limitations are permissible but must convey clear scope
description: Functional claim language (defining a feature by what it does rather than by what it is) is not inherently improper; 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph) permits means-plus-function claiming, and functional language may be used outside that format.
guidance: Evaluate functional limitations for what they fairly convey to POSITA in context. Functional language that pairs structure with function (e.g., conical spout that 'allow[s] several kernels' as in In re Schreiber) may be acceptable. Purely result-oriented or problem-statement functional language can be indefinite because it fails to limit scope and may encompass all means of achieving the result (Halliburton; Ariad; Hyatt). Unlimited functional claims may also raise written description/enablement issues (35 U.S.C. 112(a)). Be mindful of the difference between general descriptive terms and means-plus-function treatment (Phillips v. AWH; K-2 Corp.).

name: Identify what applicant invented
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim.
guidance: The take away should focus on the invention (e.g., 'a mixture of texiol and water'). Use this identification to inform the subsequent SME analysis and inventive-concept evaluation; it helps relate additional elements to what applicant actually invented.

name: Identify nature-based limitation(s) and closest naturally occurring counterpart
description: (a) Identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe a nature-based product; (b) identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state for comparison.
guidance: Examples: (a) 'the claimed mixture of texiol and water'; (b) 'the naturally occurring texiol-water mixture in the sap of the Texas mint plant.' Judicial exceptions need not be old or long-prevalent.

name: Compare claimed limitation to counterpart for 'markedly different characteristics'
description: Compare the claimed nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether it exhibits markedly different characteristics.
guidance: If the claimed product exhibits markedly different characteristics, it is not a product-of-nature exception. If it lacks markedly different characteristics (e.g., components retain the same structure, function, and properties), then the limitation is a product-of-nature exception and you must proceed to Step 2B. Record the reasoning (choose (i) or (ii) and explain). Examples: retention of sweetness/bitter aftertaste indicates no marked difference; altered organoleptic property (neutralization of bitter aftertaste by Compound N) may indicate a marked difference.

name: If directed to other exceptions, identify exception limitations and explain why
description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon, identify the limitation(s) that recite the exception and explain why the recited subject matter is an exception.
guidance: Provide the limitation(s) and articulate the reasons (e.g., it recites a mathematical relationship, fundamental economic practice, natural principle, etc.). Use court-case discussions and the abstract-idea chart in the July 2015 Update for guidance.

name: Step 2B — identify additional elements beyond the exception
description: Determine whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the identified judicial exception(s).
guidance: If the claim is a product of nature comprising a combination of components that do not occur together in nature as claimed, treat each component as an additional element to the others for purposes of this inquiry. If there are no additional elements, conclude the SME analysis with a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015) and consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be suggested to applicant to render a claim eligible.

name: Evaluate significance of additional elements — search for an 'inventive concept'
description: Consider identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to 'significantly more' than the exception(s) (i.e., contains an inventive concept).
guidance: Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending routine activities at high generality); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extra-solution activity like mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations amounting to more than generally linking use of the exception to a particular technological environment. Also note: not adding the words 'apply it' or equivalent phraseology and not merely using a generic computer are negative factors.

name: Decide eligibility based on inventive-concept evaluation
description: If any additional elements, individually or in combination, amount to significantly more than the exception(s), conclude the claim is eligible; if not, conclude the claim is ineligible under §101.
guidance: If eligible, continue examination under other patentability requirements and optionally clarify reasoning in Office action. If ineligible, make a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015) and identify any elements in the disclosure that could be added to claims to attempt to achieve eligibility (e.g., adding 1-2% of Compound N to the sweetener). Examples and case law (e.g., Funk Brothers, Myriad, Roslin) are provided to illustrate outcomes and reasoning.

name: Streamlined analysis option
description: When eligibility is self-evident and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an exception such that others cannot practice it, use a streamlined analysis and conclude SME analysis without a full write-up.
guidance: Refer to February 2015 Training Slides for examples of when streamlined analysis is appropriate. If using assumptions (e.g., assuming an amendment yields a statutory category), make those assumptions clear in the record.

name: Office action / record-keeping guidance and sample rejection language
description: Guidance on documenting SME conclusions in Office actions, including sample rejection language and form-paragraph references.
guidance: Sample rejection language provided (e.g., 'Claim X is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception ... without significantly more'). Use Form Paragraphs 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.015 as appropriate. Clarify reasoning in the record where helpful (e.g., explain why claim is directed to a nature-based product or why additional elements do/don't provide significantly more).

name: Exceptions to 1.116(b) showing for after-final amendments
description: Some after-final amendments need not be supported by the 1.116(b) showing.
guidance: Specifically, an amendment that merely cancels claims, adopts examiner's suggestions, removes issues for appeal, or in some other way requires only a cursory review by the examiner can be entered without the substantive 1.116(b) showing.

name: First proposed amendment after final to be given full consideration
description: The first proposed amendment after final action in a reexamination proceeding will be given sufficient consideration to determine whether it places all the claims in condition where they are patentable and/or whether the issues on appeal are reduced or simplified.
guidance: If the proposed amendment is not entered in its entirety, the examiner will briefly explain reasons for not entering it. If the claims as amended present a new issue requiring further consideration or search, the examiner should identify the new issue and briefly explain why a new search or consideration is necessary. The patent owner should be notified if certain portions of the amendment would be entered if filed separately.

name: Second and subsequent after-final amendments limited in consideration
description: Any second or subsequent amendment after final will be considered only to the extent that it removes issues for appeal or puts a claim in an obvious patentable condition.
guidance: This limits serial after-final amendment practice to filings that directly simplify or resolve appealable issues or make claims patentable without reopening broad prosecution.

name: Filing language and translation requirement
description: The patent application can be filed in any language but a French translation is required within two months following receipt of a Communication issued by the French Patent Office (INPI) shortly after the filing date.
guidance: Applications must be filed in docx format via the INPI e-procedure. It is possible to obtain a filing date even if no claims are filed (applicant invited to file claims within 2 months from receipt of a communication). No power of attorney is needed to authorize the attorney filing the application.

name: Formalities examination (what is checked)
description: A formal examination is carried out by INPI before a prior art search to check compliance with formal requirements (e.g. adequate support for the claims in the specification).
guidance: Formal examination also determines whether claims are clear, cover only one invention, and whether the claimed invention is patentable subject matter. French patentable subject matter follows the EPC: programs for computers as such and business methods are not patentable.

name: Search procedure and preliminary search report
description: Search results are issued as a 'preliminary search report' with written opinion, having the same structure as a European or PCT search report.
guidance: For first filings (no priority), the EPO often conducts the search as subcontractor and the extended preliminary search report is usually sent within ~9 months. When priority is claimed, INPI uses a two-step procedure (information on prior art then preliminary search report).

name: Acceleration of examination (fast-track) conditions
description: Acceleration requests are possible (since December 2015) and shall be made within 10 months from filing and include a request for early publication (if not already published). No official fee is due.
guidance: To be accepted the application must be in condition for rapid examination: claims must be clear enough for a complete preliminary search report. Requesting an extension of a time limit for responding to an office action risks cancellation of accelerated proceedings. INPI endeavours to complete examination within 20 months but exceptions apply (objections, third-party observations).

name: Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) availability and requirements
description: PPH is available under a pilot program with the JPO (Japanese priority or PCT to Japanese national phase); PPH request is available as long as substantial examination of the French application has not started.
guidance: No official fee; INPI recommends filing the PPH request within 12 months from filing. Required elements include: (1) claim correspondence table or statement claims are identical; (2) copies of relevant JPO office actions; (3) translations of such office actions; (4) copies of claims determined patentable by JPO; (5) translations of those claims; (6) copies of references cited by JPO if non-patent literature. If admissible, examination is expedited.

name: Post-grant limitation procedure and acceptance criteria
description: The owner of a French national patent (or the French part of a European patent) can request limitation at INPI; in Court-challenged validity cases, limitation may be requested and Court proceedings will be stayed until INPI decides.
guidance: Limitation must amend at least one claim to limit its scope; amendment may find basis in the claims or description. INPI criteria: whether the claims are indeed limited and whether the amendments find clear basis in the patent. Patentee need not provide reasons for limitation.

name: Examples of amendments under 37 CFR 1.312
description: Examples of 'amendments' by applicant after allowance which must comply with 37 CFR 1.312: (A) an amendment to the specification, (B) a change in the drawings, (C) an amendment to the claims, (D) a change in the inventorship, (E) the submission of prior art, (F) a request to correct the spelling of an inventor's name (37 CFR 1.48(f)), (G) a request to change the order of the names of the inventors (37 CFR 1.48(f)), etc.
guidance: These amendments must also comply with other applicable requirements (e.g., amendments to specification, drawings, or claims must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 in addition to 1.312; submission of prior art must comply with 1.97 and 1.98 in addition to 1.312).

name: Primary examiner authority after Notice of Allowance
description: After the Notice of Allowance is mailed, the application is technically no longer under the jurisdiction of the primary examiner, but the primary examiner can make examiner's amendments and has authority to enter amendments submitted after Notice of Allowance that embody merely the correction of formal matters in the specification or drawing, or formal matters in a claim without changing the scope thereof, or the cancellation of claims, without forwarding to the supervisory patent examiner for approval.
guidance: Amendments other than those which merely correct formal matters or cancel claims require approval by the supervisory patent examiner. The TC Director sets policy on trivial informalities that seldom affect disclosure clarity or claim-defining clarity.

name: Requirements for remarks accompanying substantive amendments
description: For amendments affecting the disclosure, the scope of any claim, or that add a claim, the remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state the reasons on which reliance is placed to show: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: The requirements of 37 CFR 1.111(c) with respect to pointing out the patentable novelty of any claim sought to be added or amended apply in the case of an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312, as in ordinary amendments.

name: Examiner annotation and forwarding for substantive amendments
description: When an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 affects the disclosure of the specification, adds claims, or changes the scope of any claim, the examiner must annotate the amendment with 'OK' (recommended for entry), 'Enter In Part' (only part recommended), or 'Do Not Enter' (none recommended), and forward the recommendation to the supervisory patent examiner for consideration and approval.
guidance: If favorably considered, it is entered and a Response to Rule 312 Communication (PTO-271) is prepared; primary examiner indicates recommendation by stamping and signing PTO-271; use form paragraphs 7.85 (entered), 7.87 (not entered), or 7.86 (entered in part) as appropriate.

name: Amendments ordinarily denied entry — drawings alleged to contain new matter
description: Amendments to the drawing held by the examiner to contain new matter are not entered until the question of new matter is settled.
guidance: This practice does not apply to amendments to the specification and claims (which are handled under new matter rules elsewhere, see MPEP § 608.04 et seq.).

name: Amendments ordinarily denied entry — noncompliance with 37 CFR 1.121
description: An amendment including changes to the specification/claims which is not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 (e.g., one which does not include replacement paragraphs or claim listings) is ordinarily denied entry.
guidance: See MPEP § 714 for examples and procedures for non-compliant amendments.

name: List of amendments entered in part — substitute specification with other acceptable matter
description: An 'amendment' presenting an unacceptable substitute specification along with amendatory matter (e.g., amendments to claims or new claims) should be entered in part: the substitute specification should be denied entry and so marked, while the rest of the paper should be entered.
guidance: Entry-in-part avoids confusing the record; substitute specifications filed after notice of allowance are not a matter of right. See 37 CFR 1.125 and MPEP § 608.01(q).

name: 37 CFR 1.131 purpose — swearing behind references
description: 37 CFR 1.131 permits submission of an appropriate oath or declaration to establish invention of the subject matter of a rejected claim prior to the effective date of the reference or activity on which the rejection is based, or to disqualify a commonly owned patent or published application as prior art (e.g., by terminal disclaimer plus declaration under 1.131(c)).
guidance: This is used to 'swear behind' certain references and withdraw the rejection (the rejection is withdrawn, not the reference). See MPEP § 715 for scope and limitations.

name: Situations where 1.131 affidavits/declarations are inappropriate — current 102 or statutory bar
description: An affidavit or declaration under 1.131(a) is not appropriate where: (A) the application is subject to current 35 U.S.C. 102 and the affidavit is not directed to evidence used in a rejection based on pre‑AIA 102(g); (B) the reference publication date is more than 1 year prior to the effective filing date of the claimed invention (statutory bar under pre‑AIA 102(b)); (C) the reference U.S. patent or application publication claims interfering subject matter as defined in 37 CFR 41.203(a); (D) the reference is a foreign patent for the same invention to the applicant (or legal representatives/assigns) issued prior to the domestic filing date on an application filed more than 12 months prior to the domestic filing date (pre‑AIA 102(d)).
guidance: In some common‑ownership situations where claims are not identical but not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer plus an affidavit under 1.131(c) may be used to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection; see MPEP § 718.

name: Alice two-step §101 analysis (directed-to/abstract-idea step)
description: Determine whether the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea by considering 'the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art.' Claims that focus on receipt and display of market information and use of that information to place orders are directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: The court analyzes the claimed advance (not merely individual claim elements) and compares to precedent (e.g., Enfish, IBG II/III). A claimed combination of receipt and display of information, even in a particular arrangement, can be an abstract idea if it amounts to 'graphing bids and offers to assist a trader to make an order.' Focus on whether the claim improves computer functionality or merely uses generic computers to automate manual processes (the latter is abstract).

name: Alice step two — inventive-concept requirement
description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea, determine whether the claim adds 'something significantly more'—an inventive concept—beyond the abstract idea.
guidance: The abstract idea itself cannot supply the inventive concept. Courts look at claim elements 'individually and as an ordered combination.' Mere conventional activities (e.g., receiving market information, displaying indicators along a price axis, use of preexisting computers/displays) do not supply an inventive concept. An improvement must be to computer functionality (not merely better presentation of information).

name: Evaluate claims by their asserted limitations (claims measure the invention)
description: Each claim element is material to defining the scope of the patent; infringement and eligibility are assessed with respect to each asserted claim as a separate entity.
guidance: Patentee's rights extend only to the claimed combination of elements. Courts construe claims (including prosecution history) to determine scope (e.g., how 'static price axis' is construed can alter the analysis).

name: Apportionment requirement in reasonable-royalty damages
description: A reasonable royalty must be apportioned to reflect the value attributable to the claimed invention; royalties cannot include value for unclaimed upgrades or features.
guidance: When assessing whether to include foreign-made copies or later-upgraded CRMs in royalty bases, courts consider whether incremental value is attributable to the claimed invention; experts must provide a concrete apportionment tied to claimed elements.

name: Rule 702 exclusion reinforces requirement to tie damages theory to infringement as claimed
description: Expert theories that do not focus on the infringement defined by the asserted claims (e.g., failing to start from making a claimed CRM or practicing the claimed method) are legally insufficient and subject to exclusion under Rule 702.
guidance: Courts will not 'rewrite' an expert's theory to make it conform to the claims; experts and counsel must structure their damages theories to begin from infringing acts that the law recognizes for the asserted claim types.

name: Non-statutory product examples (Step 1 anti-patterns)
description: Examples of claims that do not fall within the statutory categories: information/data per se; computer program per se (software per se) when claimed without structural recitations; transitory propagating electrical/electromagnetic signals (signals per se); subject matter expressly prohibited (e.g., humans per se).
guidance: These serve as concrete non-statutory examples when evaluating whether a product claim has physical/tangible form. Even if created by human effort, an intangible collection of information or code detached from a medium is not a statutory product.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) must be established first
description: Before analyzing eligibility, establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole.
guidance: BRI sets claim boundaries and influences whether the claim falls within statutory categories or encompasses judicial exceptions. Claim construction can change the result (see Mentor Graphics, Enfish, Synopsys examples). See MPEP §2111 for details.

name: BRI covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments => Step 1 failure
description: If the BRI of the claim covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1 (not to a statutory category).
guidance: When this occurs, a §101 rejection is appropriate; examiners should point out the BRI and recommend amendments narrowing the claim to statutory embodiments where possible (best practice). Example: machine‑readable medium that can cover carrier waves (non-stat.) and memory (stat.). Use form paragraphs 7.05/7.05.01 per MPEP §2106.07(a)(1).

name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2 overview)
description: If the claim passes Step 1, apply the Alice/Mayo two-part test: Step 2A — determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon); Step 2B — if so, determine whether additional claim elements individually or as an ordered combination amount to significantly more than the exception (i.e., an 'inventive concept').
guidance: The two‑part test is the controlling framework. The flowchart organizes analysis into Pathways A (self-evident eligibility), B (not directed to judicial exception), and C (directed to exception but amounts to significantly more).

name: Step 2A — Identify judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena)
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon (judicial exceptions).
guidance: Abstract ideas include mathematical formulas, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, etc. Use the MPEP discussion and listed groupings/examples. Claims directed to nothing more than these exceptions are not patent eligible absent 'integration' or 'significantly more.'

name: Evaluating improvements in the functioning of a computer or other technology (Step 2A/2B indicia)
description: Consider whether the claim improves the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field, which supports eligibility.
guidance: Courts (e.g., Enfish, McRO) found claims eligible where the claim language tied the exception to unconventional technical solutions or rules that improved existing technological processes. Such improvements can show the claim is not directed to an abstract idea or that it provides 'significantly more.'

name: Step 2B — 'Amounting to significantly more' / inventive concept
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, evaluate whether additional elements individually or in combination add 'significantly more' than the exception (the 'inventive concept').
guidance: Search for meaningful limitations beyond the exception: unconventional technical features, particular machine or transformation, or other improvements to technology. The second part is the 'search for an inventive concept' as described in Alice and Mayo.

name: Particular machine indicator (Step 2B)
description: A claim element that ties the exception to a particular machine may indicate 'significantly more.'
guidance: The machine-or-transformation test is a relevant clue but not a separate test; reliance on a generic computer or special-purpose computer is insufficient by itself. The claimed machine must meaningfully limit the exception.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity is insufficient (Step 2B negative indicator)
description: Reciting well-understood, routine, conventional steps or components that are known in the art does not make a claim that is directed to a judicial exception eligible.
guidance: If additional elements are merely generic or conventional implementation of the exception, they do not supply the required 'significantly more.' See MPEP §2106.05(d) and related case law.

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception and insignificant extra-solution activity are insufficient
description: Claim limitations that are nothing more than instructions to apply an abstract idea, or that add insignificant extra-solution activity, do not make the claim eligible.
guidance: Examples include steps like 'apply the formula' or adding conventional post‑solution activity (e.g., data gathering, storing) that do not add a meaningful inventive concept. See MPEP §2106.05(f) and §2106.05(g).

name: Field-of-use and technological environment limitations are not sufficient by themselves
description: Simply limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or technological environment (e.g., the Internet) does not render the claim eligible.
guidance: Claims cannot be made non-abstract merely by restricting their application to a particular technological field or environment. See cited cases (Intellectual Ventures, TLI Communications).

name: Pathways B and C definitions
description: Pathway B: claim falls within a statutory category and is not directed to a judicial exception (Step2A:NO) — eligible. Pathway C: claim falls within a statutory category, is directed to a judicial exception (Step2A:YES), but recites additional elements that amount to significantly more (Step2B:YES) — eligible.
guidance: If a claim does not qualify under any pathway (A, B, or C), it is ineligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: Do not evaluate eligibility based on 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' or on utility
description: Eligibility should not be judged based on whether the claim recites a 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' or on the utility of the claimed invention.
guidance: Earlier tests (e.g., State Street 'useful, concrete, and tangible result') have been superseded. Utility under §101 is not the test for subject-matter eligibility; other statutes (35 U.S.C. 112, 102, 103) address those concerns.

name: Interplay with other statutory requirements (102, 103, 112)
description: Passage of the §101 eligibility threshold does not obviate examination under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description/enablement/claim definiteness), 102 (novelty), and 103 (non-obviousness); examiners must perform complete examination under all applicable statutes.
guidance: §101 is a threshold inquiry. Even if a claim is eligible under §101, it still must satisfy other conditions and requirements of the Patent Act.

name: Claim interpretation can affect both Step 1 and Alice/Mayo analysis
description: How claim terms are construed (under BRI and specification) can change whether a claim is statutory or directed to an exception, and whether additional elements provide significantly more.
guidance: Examples: Mentor Graphics (machine-readable medium scope), Synopsys (mental steps), Enfish and McRO (technical improvements). Use specification and claim language consistently when construing claims.

name: Streamlined vs. full analysis best practice
description: If eligibility is self-evident, streamlined analysis may be used; if uncertain, examiners should conduct the full two-part Alice/Mayo analysis to ensure consistent and correct results.
guidance: Claims that could be eligible under Pathway A but are unclear should be fully analyzed under Steps 2A/2B; this promotes consistency and reduces risk of error.

name: Functional claim language
description: Functional terms in claims (e.g., 'spongy', 'porous', 'transparent to infrared rays', 'fragile gel') must be examined to determine whether they provide sufficient particularity and distinctness under § 112, ¶2.
guidance: Functional language can be indefinite when it defines a claim only by what it does rather than what it is (United Carbon; Halliburton). Courts look to the intrinsic record (specification, figures, prosecution history) to find objective meaning or standards; if the intrinsic evidence provides a guideline or examples so a person of ordinary skill can determine scope, the term may be definite (In re Swinehart; Enzo Biochem). If the term leaves unresolved how to measure the required degree of a functional property (e.g., how 'fragile' a gel must be), it is indefinite (Halliburton). See MPEP 2173.05(g).

name: Relative terminology: terms of degree and subjective terms
description: Words of degree and apparently subjective descriptors (e.g., 'essentially free of', 'substantially equal to', 'so dimensioned', 'substantial absence of slug flow', 'aesthetically pleasing', 'readily installed') raise definiteness issues under § 112, ¶2.
guidance: Such terms are not automatically indefinite. The court evaluates whether the specification supplies a standard or examples that enable a person of ordinary skill to measure the claimed degree (In re Marosi; Seattle Box; Orthokinetics; Exxon; Hearing Components). Purely subjective terms lacking an objective anchor (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing' without a workable objective standard) are indefinite (Datamize). Where the specification, figures, or intrinsic evidence provide a standard (e.g., 'requires no tools', figures showing examples, relationship to reactor efficiency), the term may be definite (Hearing Components; Young v. Lumenis; Exxon). See MPEP 2173.05(b).

name: Numerical ranges and measurement methods
description: Claims reciting numerical ranges or amounts must be interpretable by a person of ordinary skill in light of the specification and must not leave ambiguity as to how the numbers are measured.
guidance: If different accepted sample-preparation or measurement methods produce materially different values (so that the claimed numerical limitation could vary depending on method), the intrinsic record must specify or at least clearly point to acceptable measurement methods. Failure to specify acceptable measurement/sample-preparation methods when necessary can render a claim indefinite (Honeywell v. ITC). See MPEP 2173.05(c).

name: Breadth alone does not equal indefiniteness
description: A claim that is broad in scope is not automatically indefinite under § 112, ¶2 provided it sufficiently notifies the public of the claim's scope.
guidance: Claims to broad genera or formulae with many possible combinations can be definite if the intrinsic evidence enables the public to determine whether a given embodiment falls within the claims (Ultimax Cement). The standard is whether the claim sufficiently notifies the public of the patentee's right to exclude. See MPEP 2173.04.

name: Whether non-structural claim terms invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112, ¶6 (means-plus-function)
description: Claim limitations expressed using terms other than 'means for' (e.g., 'mechanism', 'member', 'element', 'circuit', 'detector', 'assembly') may nonetheless be treated as means-plus-function under § 112, ¶6 if they do not recite sufficient structure.
guidance: The analysis considers whether the term connotes sufficiently definite structure to one skilled in the art. If not, the limitation may be interpreted under ¶6 and limited to the corresponding structure disclosed in the specification and equivalents. The 2011 Supplementary Guidelines provide factors and case examples to determine when these alternative terms invoke ¶6. See Section II and MPEP § 2181.

name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'mechanism'
description: Use of the term 'mechanism' in a claim can invoke means-plus-function treatment when the claim fails to recite structure for performing the function.
guidance: Courts examine whether 'mechanism' in context connotes sufficient structure. If not, the claim limitation may be governed by § 112, ¶6 and limited to the structures disclosed for performing the function (Greenberg v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery and related examples in Section II.A).

name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'element'
description: A claim reciting an 'element' may invoke means-plus-function analysis when the 'element' is defined only by function and lacks structural definition.
guidance: Assess whether the term 'element' in context imparts sufficient structure. If not, limit the claim to the disclosed structure that performs the function under § 112, ¶6 (Section II.C examples).

name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'assembly'
description: The word 'assembly' can be a generic placeholder; if it lacks structural definition it may invoke § 112, ¶6.
guidance: Examine whether 'assembly' is presented with structural detail; absent such detail, constrain the claim to disclosed structure performing the function (Section II.F examples).

name: Interplay of §112, ¶6 (means-plus-function) and §112, ¶2 (indefiniteness)
description: Some claim limitations may both invoke ¶6 (as means-plus-function) and raise indefiniteness concerns under ¶2; examiners must evaluate both.
guidance: The Guidelines use case examples to show when a limitation should be treated under ¶6 and then evaluated for definiteness under ¶2 (III.A: examples where indefiniteness rejection is appropriate) and when treatment under ¶6 does not render the claim indefinite (III.B: examples where rejection not appropriate). Consider whether an objective standard or disclosed corresponding structure resolves any vagueness.

name: Enablement for claimed scope (§112, ¶1)
description: Claims must be enabled across their full scope; if a claim is broad enough to cover multiple embodiments (e.g., video games and movies), the specification must enable the full scope.
guidance: A claim that covers multiple distinct embodiments must enable each embodiment; lacking enabling disclosure for a claimed embodiment (e.g., how to integrate user images into movies) may render the claim invalid for lack of enablement (Atari v. North American Philips; example in Section IV.B and '825 patent analysis). See doctrine discussed in Section IV.B.

name: Written description support for claims limited to a subset of disclosed problems/solutions
description: Whether a claim that addresses only one of several problems disclosed (or only one of several disclosed solutions) is supported by the written description under §112, ¶1.
guidance: A specification that discloses multiple problems and multiple solutions need not have every claim address every disclosed problem/solution. A claim limited to one disclosed solution or one problem is supported if the specification conveys possession of the invention recited in that claim (Revolution Eyewear; Crown Packaging). The key is whether the disclosure shows the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention.

name: Single-means-type claims and the enablement requirement
description: Claims drafted as a single means-plus-function limitation without reciting a combination (a 'single means' claim) raise enablement and §112 issues.
guidance: A 'single-means' claim (a claim whose body is only a means-plus-function limitation and additional language merely describes the means) does not satisfy §112, ¶1 because it would embrace all conceivable structures for performing the function while the specification discloses only specific structures. Such claims are subject to rejection for lack of enablement (In re Hyatt; discussion in MPEP §§ 2164.08(a), 2181 V).

name: Use of intrinsic evidence (specification, dependent claims, prosecution history) as objective anchors
description: Intrinsic evidence can supply objective standards or examples that make otherwise vague claim language definite.
guidance: Courts rely on dependent claims, specification examples, declared suitable structures, figures, and prosecution statements to construe terms lacking numerical precision (Enzo Biochem—dependent claim specified a particular linkage group; specification provided suitable examples and measurement techniques such as thermal denaturation profiles). Examiners should look to these intrinsic sources before finding indefiniteness.

name: Preamble, prosecution history, and claim scope
description: Preamble language and statements made during prosecution may limit or clarify claim scope and affect definiteness.
guidance: Statements distinguishing prior art or characterizing the invention during prosecution (or limiting language in the preamble) can render ambiguous terms definite by showing the applicant's intended meaning (Halliburton: preamble and prosecution distinguished 'fragile gel' to limit scope). Consider prosecution history and claim context when construing terms.

name: Overlapping applications by same applicant or same assignee
description: In general, examiners should not consider ex parte questions which are pending before the Office in inter partes proceedings involving the same applicant when at least one application/patent of the same applicant involved in interference/derivation/inter partes proceedings contains claims that overlap with claims of the application under examination.
guidance: When such a situation arises, the examiner should consult with the Technology Center Quality Assurance Specialist to determine appropriate course of action.

name: Claims — general rules and amendment procedures
description: General rules for claims in the IA: initial drafting, numbering, amendments under Articles 19 and 34, and annotations required by RO.
guidance: References: Art. 6 Rule 6; Art. 28 Rule 52; Art. 41 Rule 78; Art. 19 Rule 46; Art. 34 Rule 66.4/66.8; A.I. 205; 37 CFR 1.436.

name: Headings and arrangement of contents/elements of IA
description: Required arrangement and headings for parts of the IA (request, description, claims, drawings) and numbering conventions (three sets for request/description/drawings).
guidance: See Art. 5 Rule 5, Rule 11, A.I. 207, A.I. 307 and physical requirements under Rule 11 and 37 CFR 1.433/1.431.

name: Linking claims / rejoinder practice
description: Linking claims are claims which, if allowable, would require rejoinder of otherwise divisible inventions (e.g., genus claims linking species claims; subcombination claims linking plural combinations).
guidance: Linking claims must be examined with and are considered part of the elected invention. If an allowable linking claim exists, the restriction requirement between linked inventions must be withdrawn and any nonelected claims that depend from or require all the limitations of the allowable linking claim must be rejoined and fully examined. Canceled nonelected claims may be reinstated by amendment upon allowance of the linking claim; examiners must notify applicant of this right. Be mindful of provisional double-patenting issues for continuation/divisional claims and use the appropriate form paragraphs (see MPEP § 821.04 and form ¶ 8.12).

name: Election of species — examiner content requirements
description: Where restriction between species is appropriate the examiner should send a letter including only a restriction requirement or place a telephone requirement to restrict; identify generic claims or indicate none; clearly identify each (preferably exemplary) disclosed species to which claims are to be restricted; provide reasons why the species are independent or distinct; require applicant to elect a single disclosed species under 35 U.S.C. 121 and advise as to requisites of a complete reply and rights under 37 CFR 1.141.
guidance: Species are preferably identified by figures or examples; if not, state mechanical means, particular material, or other distinguishing characteristic. If species cannot be conveniently identified, group claims by species. Form paragraphs 8.01/8.02 and related templates should be used.

name: Reply content and completeness to a restriction requirement
description: A reply to a restriction requirement should include a proper election along with a listing of all claims readable thereon, including any claims subsequently added. An argument that a claim is allowable or that all claims are generic is considered non-responsive unless accompanied by an election.
guidance: A complete reply must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the examiner’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection per 37 CFR 1.111(b); replies must appear to be bona fide attempts to advance the application. If the reply fails to point out errors, the election will be treated as without traverse.

name: Indicate exactly how the application is to be restricted — clear demarcation
description: The examiner must provide a clear and detailed record of the restriction requirement to provide a clear demarcation between restricted inventions so that it can be determined whether inventions claimed in a continuing application are consonant with the restriction requirement.
guidance: Mention the particular claim limitations and the reasons why such limitations support restricting claims to a particular disclosed species. Read all claims to determine what each covers and note the invention to which they are drawn.

name: Clarity of claim language (PSIA standard)
description: The meaning of the terms of a claim must be clear for a Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA) from the wording of the claim alone. Clarity must be analysed in light of the application disclosure, teachings of the prior art, and the claim interpretation a PSIA would give at the time the invention was made.
