If a PSIA can determine the boundaries of the claimed invention with a reasonable degree of certainty, the claim complies with clarity.
guidance: Consider claim wording together with specification and prior art. Breadth alone does not imply lack of clarity. Raise an objection when a PSIA cannot determine boundaries with reasonable certainty (PCT ISPE GL refs).

name: Independent claims must specify essential features
description: An independent claim should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention, except insofar as such features are implied by the generic terms used.
guidance: Example: a claim to a 'bicycle' need not mention 'wheels'. Ensure essential technical features are present or clearly implied.

name: Clarity applies to individual claims and the claim set
description: The requirement that the claims should be clear applies both to individual claims and to the set of claims as a whole, irrespective of product, process or product-by-process claims.
guidance: Assess clarity both for each claim and for how claims interact as a set; inconsistencies among claims can create clarity issues.

name: Process claims producing a product must necessarily result in that product
description: If a claim relates to a process for producing the product of the invention, the process as claimed should be one which, when carried out in a manner which would seem reasonable to a PSIA, necessarily results in that particular product; otherwise there is internal inconsistency and lack of clarity.
guidance: Check that recited process steps, when reasonably performed, produce the claimed product. If not, object for inconsistency/lack of clarity.

name: Claims defining modified known products must identify modifications
description: In the case of a product claim where the product is of a well-known kind and the invention lies in modifying it, it is sufficient if the claim clearly identifies the product and specifies what is modified and in what way.
guidance: Ensure clear identification of the base product and clear specification of the modification (similar considerations apply to apparatus claims).

name: Terms of degree require disclosed measurement standards
description: If a term of degree (e.g., 'thin') appears in a claim, the examiner should determine whether the PSIA would be apprised of the meaning either by disclosure of a standard for measuring that degree in the description or in view of the prior art and state of the art.
guidance: If no standard is provided and PSIA would not know the meaning, raise an objection; provide concrete measuring conditions/numerical limits in description where needed.

name: Expressions like 'preferably' generally non-limiting
description: Expressions like 'preferably', 'for example', 'such as' or 'more particularly' should generally be regarded as having no limiting effect on the scope of a claim; the feature following such an expression should be regarded as optional.
guidance: Be cautious when applicants try to rely on such expressions to limit claims; consider them non-limiting unless the description explicitly states otherwise.

name: Applicant cannot rely on unclear terms to distinguish from prior art
description: An applicant cannot rely on an unclear or ambiguous term to distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art. It may be appropriate to invite the applicant to define or remove the term without extending subject-matter beyond the content as filed.
guidance: If applicant uses vagueness to evade prior art, require definition or amendment supported by the original disclosure.

name: Result-to-be-achieved type claims allowed only if verifiable and achievable
description: No objection should be raised if the invention can only be defined in result terms, so long as the result is one which can be achieved without undue experimentation and can be directly and positively verified by tests or procedures adequately specified in the description.
guidance: Require concrete verification methods in the description. Example distinction: vague 'low roughness' vs numerically defined roughness accepted.

name: Claims defining relationship to non-claimed second product require caution
description: Where a claim seeks to define an invention by reference to features of the use or relationship to a second product not part of the claimed invention, lack of clarity can result unless the claim sets forth a clear definition of the individual product being claimed or is directed to a combination of the two products.
guidance: Consider substituting wording (e.g., 'connectable' instead of 'connected') or recast as combination claims (e.g., 'engine with a cylinder head').

name: Trademarks and trade names generally lack clarity
description: Trademarks and similar expressions that characterise commercial origin rather than properties of goods relevant to the invention are usually considered to lack clarity.
guidance: Invite applicant to remove trademarks from claims unless unavoidable or generally recognised with precise meaning.

name: Disclaimers and negative limitations (limitations in claims)
description: A claim may be limited by a disclaimer or negative limitation (e.g., 'composition free of water'). Negative limitation is not ambiguous per se, but renders a claim unclear when it attempts to claim by excluding what applicant did not invent rather than reciting what was invented.
guidance: Negative limitations are acceptable where each recited limitation is clear or where alternative elements are positively recited in the description and can be excluded. The mere absence of a positive recitation is not a basis for exclusion.

name: Alternatives in a single claim allowed if not obscure and unity met
description: A claim may refer to alternatives provided the number and presentation of alternatives in a single claim does not make the claim obscure or difficult to construe and provided the claim meets the requirements of unity.
guidance: Ensure alternatives are presented clearly and do not cause interpretive ambiguity; consider limiting number of alternatives in one claim.

name: Multiple dependent claims — formatting and grouping
description: Multiple dependent claims (dependent on more than one other claim) are allowed in the AMS. They include all limitations contained in the claims to which they relate. Dependent claims should be grouped together practically to enable association of related claims.
guidance: Two alternative office practices: (1) require multiple dependent claim to refer only alternatively and prevent multiple dependent claims forming basis for other multiple dependent claims; or (2) allow reference alternatively or cumulatively and allow multiple dependent claims to be basis for other multiple dependent claims. Group dependent claims for readability and easy construction.

name: Use of ranges in claims — anticipation and selection inventions
description: Use of ranges in claims is explicitly allowed in certain AMS. A specific example in prior art within a claimed range anticipates the range. If a prior-art range overlaps/touches claimed range, novelty depends on case-specific factors; a narrow selected range may be novel if it is not merely an obvious carrying out of prior teaching and shows unexpected results.
guidance: Anticipation requires prior-art disclosure with sufficient specificity. Consider whether the claimed narrow range yields unexpected results (supporting novelty/inventive step) and examine overlap/touching ranges on a case-by-case basis.

name: Imprecise terms and transitional phrases guidance
description: Claims with vague/equivocal wording that leave reader in doubt should be objected for lack of clarity. 'Comprising' is open-ended and allowed; 'consisting of' is closed-ended and allowed; 'characterised by' is allowed in two-part claims. Terms like 'about', 'approximately', 'somewhat' are usually not allowed as they make claims unclear.
guidance: Prefer clear transitional phrases appropriate to intent. Discourage vague qualifiers unless context/description makes them unambiguous.

name: Types of claims allowed — product, process, product-by-process, use
description: Product, process and product-by-process claims are allowed in all AMS, and use claims are allowed in most AMS. All applications should contain one or more independent main claims directed to essential features, with reasonable dependent claims claiming specific forms of the invention.
guidance: Recognise two basic kinds of claim: product (physical entity) and activity (process/use). Permit reasonable dependent claims even if dependent claim features could be inventions themselves.

name: Amendment of claims requires corresponding amendment of description
description: Amendment of a claim should be supported by the description and be clear and concise in order to meet the requirement of clarity; amendment of a claim may require amending the description.
guidance: When applicants amend claims, ensure description is amended as needed to maintain consistency and clarity (PCT ISPE GL cross-reference).

name: Applicant responsibility for sufficiency and method details for parameters
description: It is the applicant's responsibility to supply a description meeting disclosure requirements. If claims define invention in terms of parameters, the application must include a clear description of methods used to determine parameter values unless PSIA would know which method to use or unless all methods yield the same result.
guidance: If methods for measuring parameters are non-obvious or not known to PSIA, require explicit description of measurement procedures in the specification.

name: Insufficiency cannot be cured by post‑filing additions
description: If examiner considers disclosure insufficient, the deficiency cannot be cured after filing by adding further examples or features that introduce subject‑matter extending beyond the content as filed. Remedy may be to restrict claims to embodiments sufficiently described and delete other embodiments.
guidance: Advise applicants to rely only on what is supported by the filing; corrective amendments should not add new matter.

name: Factors in determining undue experimentation
description: Factors to be considered in determining whether undue experimentation is needed include: (i) breadth of the claims; (ii) nature of the invention; (iii) general knowledge of PSIA; (iv) level of predictability in the art; (v) amount of direction provided in the application (including references to prior art); and (vi) amount of experimentation required to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the disclosure.
guidance: Use these factors case-by-case to assess whether disclosure enables practice without undue effort. Refer to PCT ISPE GL 5.48-5.51 for more detail.

name: Formatting and claim-tree visualization to improve accessibility
description: Macro-level formatting (e.g., claim trees, separating claim features) and micro-level highlighting (nominal terms with references) can increase accessibility without modifying factual content.
guidance: Generate claim dependency graphs and segment claims into preamble/transitional/body to visualize relationships and reduce cognitive load for non-experts; derive discourse references via POS, phrase boundaries, and discourse rules.

name: Patent writing—legal and linguistic precision, clarity, and formal requirements
description: Patent writing must produce formal, unambiguous, precise language that adheres to legal requirements for grants; automated patent-text generation is difficult because of these constraints.
guidance: Assess generated patent sections (claims, descriptions, abstracts) for legal compliance, clarity, precision, and completeness; failures may harm grant prospects or lead to litigation vulnerabilities.

name: Conditioning source selection for patent writing—description-based more promising
description: Title- and abstract-based generation are poorly conditioned (titles are short and abstracts often intentionally vague), whereas description-based claim generation is more promising because descriptions contain detailed embodiments.
guidance: Prefer conditioning generation models on rich description content rather than titles/abstracts; when using abstracts/titles, be aware of limited specificity and the need for substantial downstream revision.

name: LLM-generated claims/specifications require substantial human revision
description: LLMs can improve claim completeness and clarity after fine-tuning, but generated claims often need comprehensive revisions to pass rigorous patent scrutiny; LLMs can introduce ineffective edits that deviate from intended revisions.
guidance: Treat LLM outputs as drafts requiring expert attorney/agent edits; consider fine-tuning and post-editing pipelines as part of real-world drafting workflows.

name: Third-party cancellation application requirements
description: Where application to cancel is made by a third party, the entry on LOR may be cancelled if the Registrar is satisfied that the proprietor was and is so precluded. The application shall be supported by a statement setting out fully the nature of the claimant’s interest and the facts relied upon.
guidance: The Formalities officer will review against listed requirements (see Rule 73(1)/Section 54 subsections) and invite clarification within 2 months if deficiencies arise.

name: Admissions in the specification or prosecution can be relied on as prior art
description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission which can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify as prior art under the statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: See Riverwood Int’l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co., Constant v. Advanced Micro-Devices, and MPEP §2129. Where the admitted prior art anticipates the claim but does not qualify as prior art under any paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102, the claim may nonetheless be rejected as being anticipated by the admitted prior art without citing to 35 U.S.C. 102.

name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty) and 103 (obviousness)
description: For anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention either explicitly or impliedly; any feature not directly taught must be inherently present. For a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference teachings must be modified in a way which would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
guidance: Keep the legal distinction in mind when formulating rejections; see MPEP §§2131–2146 for guidance on patentability determinations under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.

name: Deciding whether to apply 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e)
description: Once an examiner finds a printed publication or patent that discloses the claimed invention, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be made under 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e) by determining the effective filing date of the application and comparing it with the date of the reference.
guidance: Refer to MPEP §706.02 for methods of determining effective filing date and comparison; determining the correct subsection affects statutory bar and available responses.

name: Rules for international applications and 35 U.S.C. 102(e) dates
description: Under revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e), an international filing date which is on or after November 29, 2000 is a United States filing date for prior art purposes if the international application (a) designated the United States, and (b) was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in the English language. If those three conditions are met, the international filing date (or an earlier U.S. filing date properly claimed) may be the prior art date for the reference under 102(e).
guidance: International applications filed prior to November 29, 2000 are subject to the pre-AIPA version of 102(e) and may not reach back via international filing dates; publications of international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000 do not have a 102(e) date (but may be prior art under 102(a) or (b)). See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) and 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/374 descriptions for details and exceptions.

name: Methods to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by: (A) persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78(a) (by amending the specification or filing an application data sheet) and establishing the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112 enablement/written description; or (D) perfecting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) by complying with 37 CFR 1.78(a).
guidance: Once a benefit claim under 119(e) is perfected, the rejection must be reconsidered to determine whether the prior art still qualifies under 102(b) or instead qualifies under 102(a). See MPEP §706.02.

name: Methods to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinction; (B) amending claims; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing prior invention if the reference is not a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claiming the same patentable invention; (E) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); or (F) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 (with required enablement/written description).
guidance: When the claims of the reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication and the application are directed to the same invention or are obvious variants, a 1.131 affidavit is not an acceptable method of overcoming the rejection; examiner must determine whether double patenting or an interference is appropriate. See MPEP §715, §716.10, §804, and Chapter 2300 for interferences.

name: Guidelines / flow for determining the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for a potential reference
description: I. Determine the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for each potential reference by following: (A) the potential reference must be a U.S. patent, a U.S. application publication (35 U.S.C.122(b)), or a WIPO publication of an international application under PCT Article 21(2); (B) determine if the potential reference resulted from, or claimed the benefit of, an international application; (C) if it did, determine whether the international application meets three conditions (filed on/after Nov 29, 2000; designated the U.S.; published under PCT Art.21(2) in English) — if so the international filing date is a U.S. filing date for 102(e) purposes; if not, follow subrules (C)(2)-(4) for various situations; (D) foreign application filing dates claimed in publications/patents may not be used as 102(e) dates for prior art purposes.
guidance: Detailed steps: (A) if reference did not result from or claim benefit of an international application, its 102(e) date is its earliest effective U.S. filing date (consider proper benefit claims 119(e)/120 and 112 support). (C)(1)-(4) and (D) enumerate how to treat international applications filed before/after Nov 29, 2000, publications, U.S. patents issued from internationals, and earlier filing dates properly claimed. See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) for flowcharts, examples and nine illustrative examples covering common factual situations.

name: Use of examples to determine prior art dates under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
description: Nine examples are presented to illustrate the prior art dates of U.S. and WIPO publications of patent applications and U.S. patents under 35 U.S.C. 102(e); the examples cover common factual situations encountered when determining the 102(e) date of a reference.
guidance: Examiners should consult these examples and timelines to understand histories of references (e.g., U.S. application publications, patents, priority claims, international applications) and to determine applicable prior art dates when applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e). See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) and accompanying flow charts.

name: Make prior art search the first step
description: A patent prior art search is the single most important first step an inventor can take to see if their idea has a real shot at becoming a patent.
guidance: Don't 'jump into the patent process' without a thorough prior art search — it can reveal roadblocks early and save time and legal fees. Treat the search as the foundation of your IP strategy that affects claim drafting and examiner negotiation.

name: Efficiently triage and read patent documents (drawings → abstract → specification → claims)
description: You don't need to read every word; start with figures for visual similarity, then read the abstract, scan the detailed description, and finally analyze the claims.
guidance: This staged approach lets you quickly discard irrelevant documents and focus detailed attention only on the references that appear relevant.

name: Dissect claims element-by-element to check for anticipation
description: The claims are the legally enforceable core; compare each claim of a prior art document, element-by-element, against the elements of your invention.
guidance: If a prior art claim discloses every element of one of your proposed claims, that claim is anticipated (novelty destroyed). Perform detailed, feature-by-feature comparisons.

name: Use a consistent checklist for analyzing each reference
description: Follow a structured process for each flagged reference: initial review, detailed comparison, claim dissection, obviousness check, and date verification.
guidance: Document why a reference was disqualified or kept. A consistent checklist ensures thoroughness and prevents emotional or ad-hoc decisions.

name: Turn search analysis into strategy (pivot, design-around, proceed, or consider alternatives)
description: Use your findings not just as a yes/no on patentability but as a strategic roadmap: abandon/pivot on 'knockout' references, design around close references, proceed if only distant art exists, or consider trade secrets/first-to-market if field is crowded.
guidance: Document how findings affect claim drafting, patent valuation, and commercial/IP strategy. The analysis informs whether to modify the invention, pursue protection, or adopt a non-patent strategy.

name: Presumption: 'means' or 'step' invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term "means" or "step" and includes functional language.
guidance: The presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure, material or acts necessary to perform the recited function (see TriMed v. Stryker). If the examiner determines that 'means' or 'step' is used but the second or third prong is not met, the Office action must explain why the limitation using 'means' or 'step' is not being treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f). Examiners should expressly state in the Office action when 112(f) is being applied.

name: Three-prong analysis to determine 112(f) applicability
description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation only if it meets this 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the term 'means' or 'step' or a generic placeholder (a substitute for 'means'); (B) the term is modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or similar); and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: The three prongs are cumulative. Functional linking words include 'for', 'so that', 'configured to', etc. If unclear whether a limitation falls within 112(f), the examiner should evaluate all prongs and state the conclusion. Applicants can rebut by showing sufficient structure or amending the claim to avoid 112(f).

name: Rebuttable presumption when 'means'/'step' not present
description: A claim limitation that does not use the term 'means' or 'step' triggers the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply.
guidance: Examiners should nonetheless consider whether the presumption is overcome (e.g., where a generic placeholder is used or the term 'fails to recite sufficiently definite structure' or else 'recites function without reciting sufficient structure' as in Williamson). Case law (Phillips, CCS Fitness, Personalized Media, Williamson) guides this inquiry.

name: Substitute/generic placeholder standard (Williamson)
description: A substitute term acts as a generic placeholder when it would not be recognized by one of ordinary skill in the art as being sufficiently definite structure for performing the claimed function; the standard is whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure.
guidance: Williamson and related cases explain that words like 'module' may be treated as non-structural. If POSA would not understand the term as the name of structure, 112(f) may apply even without the word 'means'.

name: Sufficient structure/material/acts excludes 112(f)
description: If the claim term is modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function, 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply.
guidance: Examples where structure precluded 112(f): 'baffle' with structure recited; 'positioning means for moving' where the claim provided list of structures; 'perforation means for tearing' where perforation structure is described. Conversely, sometimes similar terms have been held to invoke 112(f) (e.g., 'spring means'). Examiners should analyze whether claim recites definite structure for performing the function.

name: Element-by-element applicability
description: Whether 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies must be decided on an element-by-element basis; each claim must be independently reviewed even where similar language appears in other claims.
guidance: Not all words in a means-/step-plus-function clause are limited to the disclosed embodiment and equivalents because 112(f) applies only to the interpretation of the means/step that performs the recited function. Claims that are textually similar must be reviewed independently (O.I. Corp., IMS Technology).

name: Corresponding structure must be disclosed in specification
description: The corresponding structure (or material or acts) of a means-/step-plus-function limitation must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure will perform the recited function.
guidance: Disclosure may be explicit, implicit/inherent, or in drawings if clear to POSA (Atmel, Dossel, Vas-Cath). A bare statement that known techniques can be used does not disclose structure for means-plus-function (Biomedino). The disclosure obligation ties to 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b): means-plus-function claiming limits claim scope to disclosed structure and equivalents, and failure to disclose adequate structure can render the claim indefinite or fail the written-description requirement.

name: Computer-implemented means-plus-function: algorithm disclosure
description: For a computer-implemented 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitation, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: When disclosed structure is a computer programmed to carry out an algorithm, the corresponding structure is that special-purpose computer programmed with the disclosed algorithm, not a general-purpose computer (NetMoneyIN, In re Aoyama, WMS Gaming). Examiners should look for an algorithm in the specification; absence may make the claim indefinite.

name: Consequences of inadequate corresponding structure
description: If there is no disclosure of structure, material, or acts for performing the recited function, the claim fails to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefinite) and may also fail written-description/enablement requirements (112(a)/(b)).
guidance: Cases (Biomedino, Cardiac Pacemakers, Budde) illustrate that absence of disclosed corresponding structure can render means-plus-function claims indefinite or otherwise noncompliant. Examiners should consider whether the specification provides adequate structure, whether by text, drawings, or clear implication to POSA. Applicants may argue, amend, or supply clarifying disclosure where procedurally available.

name: Office action and applicant response procedures
description: The examiner must expressly state application of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) in the Office action when applicable, and must explain reasons when a 'means'/'step' term is not treated under 112(f).
guidance: In response to an Office action finding 112(f) invoked, applicant may (1) present a sufficient showing that the claim limitation recites sufficient structure to avoid 112(f), or (2) amend the claim limitation to avoid 112(f) (e.g., by reciting sufficient structure). If applicant disagrees with an examiner's interpretation, applicant may present arguments and amend to clarify whether 112(f) applies.

name: Fact-specific nature and no absolutes
description: There are no absolute rules or fixed lists of words that always result in or always avoid 35 U.S.C. 112(f); every case turns on its own facts.
guidance: Examiners must carefully consider claim language in light of the specification and commonly accepted meaning in the technological art. Examples given are fact-specific and should not be applied as per se rules (Signtech, Seal-Flex, Mas-Hamilton, etc.).

name: Government and professional fees during prosecution
description: There are specific government fees for special procedures during the prosecution of an application (e.g., accelerated examination upon payment of a fee; extension of a time limit under certain conditions including payment). Most jurisdictions assess an issue fee to bring a patent into force and most charge some sort of maintenance fee to keep a patent in force.
guidance: Professional fees may be significant at substantive examination because the drafter reviews prior art cited by the examiner and amends claims to overcome objections. Filing, searching and examination fees should generally be paid at filing; missing fees may incur surcharges or notices to submit fees. Consider the number and type of claims and small-entity status which can reduce government fees.

name: U.S. nonprovisional and provisional application content requirements (USPTO)
description: In the United States, a nonprovisional patent application must include claims, an abstract, a description, an oath or declaration and, in most cases, drawings. A provisional application need not include claims and is primarily used to establish a priority date. Applications must be in English or accompanied by an English translation and a statement that the translation is accurate.
guidance: File a utility patent application transmittal form to identify the contents; use a fee transmittal to calculate fees and payment method. Small entity assertions halve certain government fees. An application data sheet should contain bibliographic data. Oath/declaration must be in a language the inventor understands; translations and accuracy statements required if not in English.

name: Transmittal and fee forms and small-entity/fee-payment practice (USPTO)
description: A utility patent application transmittal form should be filed with every patent application to inform the USPTO what papers are being filed. A fee transmittal form may be used to calculate prescribed filing fees and indicate the method of payment. The amount payable depends on number/type of claims and small-entity status.
guidance: Filing, searching and examination fees should be paid at filing; if not, applicant will be notified and asked to submit fees within a given period and surcharges may apply for late payment. Be mindful of whether mailing date or office action date determines time limits.

name: PCT international phase structure and core documents
description: The PCT procedure consists of an international phase (including filing, international search and report, publication, optional supplementary search, optional international preliminary examination) and a later national phase. An international application must contain a request, a description, one or more claims, drawings where necessary, and an abstract.
guidance: Request form is available in all PCT publication languages and ePCT is available for online filing. The ISR and a preliminary nonbinding written opinion are issued by the ISA; if not withdrawn within 18 months the application and ISR are published.

name: Office actions represent the government’s official position
description: An office action (official action/examination report) may address virtually any aspect of the application (title, abstract length, etc.), with most important parts touching on patentability of pending claims.
guidance: Respond promptly; failure to respond can impair rights. Understand the examiner’s cited prior art and the basis for enablement, novelty and inventive-step objections.

name: Types of examination rejections and appropriate rebuttals
description: Examiners may issue enablement rejections (description insufficient), anticipation (prior art reads on claim), or obviousness (combination of prior art plus motivation to combine).
guidance: Rebut by showing where description discloses subject matter, argue that alleged missing matter was known in prior art, argue examiner misunderstood prior art or the invention, argue lack of motivation to combine references, or amend claims to avoid cited art.

name: Client involvement and strategic choices when amending claims
description: Drafter should explain draft response options to the client; amendments narrowing claims might overcome prior art but may render protection less useful because competitors can design around narrower claims. The client often best knows which additional claim element meets business needs.
guidance: Give client opportunity to make choices regarding amendments; consider business objectives when narrowing or changing claim scope.

name: Principle prohibiting addition of new matter in amendments
description: Universal rule in most jurisdictions: no new matter (new subject matter) beyond that originally disclosed as of the filing date may be added to claims, description or drawings (except to remedy obvious mistakes such as typographic errors).
guidance: This rule balances inventor/applicant interests and third-party predictability. Draft a complete disclosure prior to filing; if broad claims are not supported by original disclosure, later addition of new embodiments to justify breadth is not permitted. See Module VI for more on amending claims.

name: Determining original disclosure and permissible post-filing changes
description: Examiners generally raise no objection to amendments that introduce further information regarding prior art, straightforwardly clarify obscure expressions, or resolve inconsistencies. However, most jurisdictions prohibit introduction of new matter into the description, drawings or claims after filing.
guidance: When amending, ensure added content is directly and unambiguously derivable from the application as filed. Clarifications and correcting inconsistencies are usually acceptable; substantive new embodiments or features not present in the original filing are not.

name: Intrinsic evidence is most persuasive
description: The most persuasive type of evidence regarding a claim’s meaning is intrinsic evidence, which includes the patent claims, the patent specification, and the patent’s prosecution history.
guidance: The patent specification may, for instance, include special definitions given to words that later appear in the claim — such intrinsic sources control if they make the meaning apparent.

name: Each party must present evidence supporting its proposed construction
description: During the Markman hearing, each party presents evidence about what it believes to be the correct interpretation of the claim language.
guidance: Parties should marshal intrinsic and permissible extrinsic materials to support their proposed constructions and respond to opposing arguments.

name: Claim construction impacts infringement and validity outcomes
description: A judge’s narrow interpretation of a claim word or phrase may weaken an inventor’s ability to pursue claims of patent infringement; conversely, a broad interpretation can make the claim vulnerable to invalidation on grounds of obviousness or anticipation.
guidance: Counsel should consider the strategic tradeoffs of proposed constructions because the court’s construction can change both infringement exposure and invalidity risk.

name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof for invalidity
description: A patent shall be presumed valid and the burden of establishing invalidity of a patent or any claim rests on the party asserting such invalidity. (35 U.S.C. § 282(a)).
guidance: General statements of invalidity (including indefiniteness) proceed under the presumption of validity. The opinion cites Sonix: 'Indefiniteness must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.' For specific showings (e.g., whether a particular phrase invokes §112, ¶6), the court references case law (Zeroclick) holding the party invoking that argument must carry the applicable burden (the opinion states the government has the burden of proving by a preponderance that 'code for' invokes §112, ¶6). Be explicit about which burden/standard applies to each asserted defect.

name: Indefiniteness standard — reasonable certainty to a skilled artisan
description: A patent claim is indefinite under §112, ¶2 if it fails to 'apprise a skilled artisan of the scope of the claimed invention with reasonable certainty.' (Nautilus).
guidance: When assessing indefiniteness, interpret claim language in light of the specification and prosecution history. Only 'reasonable certainty' is required; courts should determine whether a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would be reasonably certain of the claim's scope. If claims, read in light of the specification and prosecution history, fail to inform PHOSITA with reasonable certainty, find indefiniteness.

name: Use intrinsic evidence; do not construe claims in a vacuum
description: Claim language is interpreted in light of all intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history); claim terms are 'not construed in a vacuum.' (DeMarini; Phillips).
guidance: Resolve ambiguities by reference to intrinsic record before turning to extrinsic evidence. Consider prior claim constructions in the case. Use the specification and prosecution history to inform meaning, but avoid importing limitations from embodiments without clear patentee intent.

name: Do not import preferred embodiments into the claims absent express disavowal
description: Embodiments in the specification are not to be read into the claims unless the patentee has expressly limited the claim to the embodiment. (Playtex; Karlin).
guidance: Even where a preferred embodiment shows particular structure or limitations, the court should not limit claim scope to that embodiment unless the patentee manifested an intent to limit. A party cannot create indefiniteness merely by pointing to a preferred embodiment and asking the court to read those details into the claim.

name: Antecedent basis requirement (definite if PHOSITA can reasonably ascertain antecedent)
description: A dependent claim phrasing like 'the [term]' must have antecedent basis in the independent claim; absence of explicit antecedent basis is not fatal if the scope is reasonably ascertainable by PHOSITA. (Energizer).
guidance: When multiple potential antecedents exist, resolve which antecedent PHOSITA would understand the dependent limitation to reference by reading the claims in context and against the specification. The court used this approach in deciding that 'the step of receiving' referred to the 'receiving a series of numerical values having tags...' clause rather than a macro-receiving clause because of language similarity and the specification.

name: Means-plus-function framework under §112, ¶6
description: A patentee may express an element as 'a means or step for performing a specified function' and, if so, the claim covers 'the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.' Presence of the word 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption of §112, ¶6 invocation, but the essential inquiry is whether the claim term names structure to PHOSITA. (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶6; Williamson).
guidance: Determine whether a claim term invokes §112, ¶6 by asking whether the words of the claim would be understood by PHOSITA as the name of structure. If §112, ¶6 applies, identify the corresponding structure in the specification (or equivalents); if no corresponding structure is disclosed, the claim is indefinite.

name: Sufficient structure requirement for means-plus-function limitations
description: A claim limitation is not §112, ¶6 if the limitation recites sufficient structure; 'sufficient structure is recited if the claim term is used in common parlance or by persons of skill in the pertinent art to designate structure, even if the term covers a broad class of structures and even if the term identifies the structures by their function.' (Skky quoting TecSec).
guidance: Assess whether the claim term itself or known conventions would identify structure to PHOSITA. If the claim term (or its usage in the art) names structure, §112, ¶6 does not apply; if not, look to the specification for corresponding structure (including algorithmic detail for software).

name: Algorithmic disclosure requirement for software means-plus-function claims
description: For software-implemented functions claimed in means-plus-function format, the specification must disclose an algorithm (or other structure) corresponding to the claimed function to avoid indefiniteness.
guidance: When a software limitation is treated as means-plus-function, identify algorithmic description(s) in the specification that map to the claimed function. If the specification contains algorithmic flowcharts, block diagrams with operations, or other specific disclosure enabling a PHOSITA to perform the function, the limitation may be definite; absence of such algorithmic structure supports a finding of indefiniteness (the court found Terms 3 and 4 supported by algorithmic disclosure but Terms 5–7 lacked disclosed structure).

name: Incorporation of well-established general knowledge in the art
description: The incorporation of general knowledge 'sufficiently well established in the art and referenced in the patent' can render a claim definite. (Presidio).
guidance: If the specification references concepts or structures that are well established in the art, courts may rely on that background knowledge to resolve claim scope and avoid indefiniteness, provided such general knowledge is properly referenced or relied upon in the intrinsic record.

name: When claim terms do not invoke §112, ¶6, apply plain and ordinary meaning consistent with intrinsic record
description: If a disputed limitation is not governed by §112, ¶6 and is not indefinite, it is given its plain and ordinary meaning as understood by PHOSITA, consistent with prior claim constructions in the case. (Nautilus; Phillips).
guidance: Adopt plain-and-ordinary-meaning constructions unless the intrinsic record requires a different construction. The court applied this to terms where it found no §112, ¶6 invocation (e.g., many 'code for' terms) and resolved antecedent-basis disputes by plain reading and specification context.

name: Substantive scope of what must be disclosed
description: You must disclose each reference that either anticipates or puts into question the inventive step (unobviousness) of the claimed invention.
guidance: The duty is defined by the claims as filed or as later amended. Sources include search reports on counterpart applications (e.g., PCT ISR), prior patent activity by the same applicant, and prior patents by the same inventors.

name: Adequate written description / Demonstration of possession
description: The patentee must disclose sufficient information to demonstrate that the inventor had possession of the invention at the time of filing.
guidance: The written description requirement ensures the public receives adequate disclosure in exchange for patent rights. See MPEP 2163 et seq. for guidance on the standard for compliance, support for claimed subject matter, typical circumstances where issues arise, burden on examiner, and relationship to claim scope and new matter.

name: Enablement — disclosure enabling one skilled in the art to make and use the invention
description: The specification must disclose sufficient information to enable those skilled in the art to make and use the invention.
guidance: Enablement is evaluated with respect to the quantity and quality of information needed as of the filing date and may involve analysis of undue experimentation, working/prophetic examples, predictability of the art, and whether the specification is enabling across the full scope of the claims (see MPEP 2164 and subparts).

name: Minimum quality and quantity of disclosure required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) sets forth the minimum requirements for the quality and quantity of information that must be contained in a patent application to justify the grant of a patent.
guidance: This principle frames both written description and enablement analyses: the disclosure must be sufficiently informative in both quality and quantity to justify excluding the public from practicing the claimed invention during the patent term. The MPEP delineates tests and factors (see 2163–2166) to determine whether the minimum has been met.

name: Consequences of failing the disclosure requirements
description: Failure to fully comply with the disclosure requirements (written description, enablement, best mode) could result in the denial of a patent, or in a holding of invalidity of an issued patent.
guidance: Examiners should apply the written description and enablement standards during prosecution; applicants should ensure their specification supports claim scope, enables practice across claimed scope, and discloses the best mode known. The MPEP provides procedural and substantive guidance on rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and related remedies (see sections 2166, 2164.05, 2165.03, etc.).

name: No amendment as of right after Notice of Allowance (37 CFR 1.312 general rule)
description: No amendment may be made as a matter of right in an application after the mailing of the notice of allowance; any amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 must be filed before or with payment of the issue fee and may be entered on recommendation of the primary examiner approved by the Director.
guidance: Amendments after allowance broadly include changes to spec, drawings, claims, inventorship, submission of prior art, petitions to correct spelling/order of inventors, etc. An amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 must be filed on or before date the issue fee is paid, except as required by Office of Patent Publication (PUBS).

name: 37 CFR 1.312 compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 and approval authority
description: An amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 must comply with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.121; Director has delegated approval of recommendations under 37 CFR 1.312 to supervisory patent examiners (SPEs).
guidance: Primary examiner may make examiner's amendments and enter corrections of formal matters, claim cancellations, or formal claim changes without forwarding to SPE; other amendments that change scope require SPE approval. Supplemental reissue oath/declaration is treated as an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 for reissue.

name: Required remarks accompanying amendments affecting disclosure/scope/claims
description: For amendments affecting the disclosure, scope of any claim, or adding a claim, the remarks must fully and clearly state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: The requirements of 37 CFR 1.111(c) with respect to pointing out the patentable novelty of any claim sought to be added or amended apply to amendments under 37 CFR 1.312 as in ordinary amendments. See MPEP §§ 713.04 and 713.10 regarding interviews.

name: Processing and handling of amendments under 37 CFR 1.312
description: Amendments under 37 CFR 1.312 that affect disclosure, add claims, or change claim scope are sent by OIPE to Publishing Division which forwards to the Technology Center; IFW applications use OIPE Central Scanning and IFW procedures.
guidance: Upon receipt TC promptly processes and a designated technical support staff forwards to the examiner via SPE. Examiner indicates 'Enter — 312', 'Do Not Enter' or 'Enter In Part' in red ink on amendment. If favorably considered, it's entered and PTO-271 (Response to Rule 312 Communication) is prepared and signed by primary examiner (or SPE if required). If adverse, reasons for nonentry are typed on PTO-271. The file, drawing, and unmailed notices are forwarded to SPE for consideration, approval and mailing. IFW-specific scanning and document coding procedures apply.

name: Entry of amendments embodying only formal corrections
description: Amendments that embody merely the correction of formal matters in the specification, formal changes in a claim without changing scope, or cancellation of claims may be entered without SPE prior approval.
guidance: The examiner indicates approval of such amendments by writing 'Enter Formal Matters Only' thereon. Such amendments do not require submission to the SPE prior to entry. If disapproved in whole or part they require SPE signature. IFW processing guidance: print first page, write 'Enter' and scan with appropriate code.

name: Entry-in-part of 37 CFR 1.312 amendments (when appropriate)
description: General rule: an amendment should not be entered in part; however, when strict observance would cause harm, acceptable portions should be entered and unacceptable portions denied entry.
guidance: Examples: (A) substitute specification unacceptable but other amendments acceptable — enter the rest and deny substitute spec; (B) 1.312 amendments partially approved are entered only as to approved part; (C) after Ex Parte Quayle, amendments curing only formal defect may be entered but new claims are not a right; (D) amendments accompanying a motion granted in part are entered to the extent motion granted. Examiner writes 'Enter' in red ink and initials opposite enterable portions. Applicant should be advised which changes were entered. Entry-in-part not recommended unless full additional fee (if any) accompanies the amendment.

name: List of amendment types ordinarily denied entry
description: The following types of amendments are ordinarily denied entry: (A) presenting an unpatentable claim or a claim requiring a new search or raising a new issue in an application whose prosecution before the primary examiner has been closed; (B) substitute specification that does not comply with 37 CFR 1.125; (C) a patent claim suggested by the examiner and not presented within the time limit unless Director authorizes; (D) copied patent claims may be refused entry under certain conditions; (E) unsigned or improperly signed amendments or signed by suspended/excluded attorney/agent; (F) amendments filed after expiration of statutory period or set time period for reply; (G) amendments so worded they cannot be entered with certain accuracy; (H) amendment canceling all claims and presenting no substitute claims; (I) amendments in an application no longer within examiner’s jurisdiction except on Director approval; (J) drawings held by examiner to contain new matter not entered until question settled; (K) amendatory paper containing objectionable remarks under 37 CFR 1.3; (L) amendments not in permanent ink or on easily erasable paper; (M) amendments presenting more claims than paid for without fees; (N) amendment canceling all claims drawn to elected invention and presenting only nonelected invention claims (nonresponsive); (O) amendments not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121; (P) preliminary amendments that unduly interfere with preparation of first Office action (37 CFR 1.115(b)); (Q) supplemental replies not filed during suspension period under 37 CFR 1.103(a) or (c).
guidance: While amendments within these categories should not be entered at filing, a subsequent showing by applicant may lead to entry. See referenced MPEP sections for details and exceptions (e.g., copied patent claims, IFW, reissue oaths).

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) prior-art exception (inventor/joint-inventor public disclosure)
description: The exception in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) focuses on the 'subject matter' that had been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor (or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor).
guidance: No requirement that the mode of prior disclosure by the inventor (or another who obtained the subject matter) be the same as the mode of disclosure of the intervening U.S. patent document; no requirement of verbatim/ipsissimis verbis disclosure. The exception applies only to subject matter in the intervening U.S. patent document that was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor (or someone who obtained it from them) before the date the subject matter relied upon was effectively filed. Example: if inventor publicly disclosed elements A, B, and C, and intervening reference discloses A, B, C, and D, then only element D is available as prior art under 102(a)(2). Species/genus examples: prior disclosure of a species can except a later-disclosed genus; prior disclosure of a genus does not except a later-disclosed species. Determination of applicability of the 102(b)(2)(B) exception is about the subject matter of the intervening document, not a comparison to 'the claimed invention.'

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) prior-art exception (common ownership / obligation of assignment)
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) excepts subject matter disclosed in a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO published document from constituting prior art under 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, 'were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.'
guidance: If conditions are met, a U.S. patent document that might otherwise qualify as prior art under 102(a)(2) is not available as prior art under either 102 or 103. This differs from pre-AIA 103(c). The 102(b)(2)(C) exception does not apply to disclosures that qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) (disclosures made before the effective filing date). Even if a document is not prior art under 102/103 due to 102(b)(2)(C), it may still be used for double patenting rejections or to show state of the art for enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a)). Office rules (37 CFR 1.104(c)(4)/(5)) address commonly owned or joint research agreement subject matter.

name: Limitations on usefulness of 102(b)(2)(C) (double patenting and 102(a)(1) exclusions)
description: The AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) exception does not remove a U.S. patent document as a basis for a double patenting rejection, and does not apply to disclosures that are prior art under 102(a)(1).
guidance: A document excepted from 102/103 by 102(b)(2)(C) may still be cited for double patenting (statutory or non-statutory/obviousness-type) or to indicate state of the art when making a lack of enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). If the publication or issue date is before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, it may be prior art under 102(a)(1) regardless of common ownership or assignment obligations.

name: Mechanics of invoking 102(b)(2)(C) — statements and evidence
description: A clear and conspicuous statement by the applicant (or the applicant's representative of record) that the claimed invention and the subject matter disclosed in the U.S. patent document were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date will be sufficient to establish that the 102(b)(2)(C) exception applies.
guidance: Applicant may present supporting evidence (e.g., assignment documents) but is not required to do so. The Office will not request corroborating evidence absent independent evidence raising doubt as to the veracity of the statement. Treated analogously to statements under pre-AIA 103(c).

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) joint research agreement exception (common ownership via JRA)
description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person for 102(b)(2)(C) purposes if: (1) the subject matter was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application for patent discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: A 'joint research agreement' is defined as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention (35 U.S.C. 100(h)). To invoke JRA-based common ownership, applicant or representative must provide a statement asserting the three statutory conditions; supporting evidence may be presented but is not required, and the Office will not request corroboration absent independent evidence raising doubt. If the issue or publication date of the cited document is before the effective filing date, 102(a)(1) may still apply regardless of the JRA.

name: Improper naming of inventors — requirements, consequences, and remedies
description: Patent laws require naming the actual inventor(s) of the claimed subject matter (35 U.S.C. 115(a)); the Office presumes the named inventors are the actual inventors.
guidance: If an application names a person who is not the actual inventor, the situation should be handled in a derivation proceeding under 35 U.S.C. 135, by correction of inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48, or through a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115, as appropriate. Where incorrect inventorship is present, applicant should submit a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48. In rare situations where it is clear the application does not name the correct inventorship and no correction request has been filed, Office personnel should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115. Use Form Paragraph 7.04.02.aia and related form paragraphs as instructed for such rejections, and include explanation of supporting evidence in bracketed text of the form paragraph.

name: Consulting extrinsic evidence in claim construction
description: Guidance to include discussion and citation to Phillips v. AWH Corp. (415 F.3d 1303) regarding consulting extrinsic evidence in claim construction.
guidance: Updated citations and discussions emphasize proper role of extrinsic evidence in claim meaning determinations; see added discussion in relevant subsections and cross references (e.g., Corephotonics/Apple citations).

name: Claim term meaning provided by the specification
description: Where previously the phrase 'special definition' was used, the manual replaces it with 'meaning provided by the specification.'
guidance: Examiners should look to the specification for the meaning of claim terms and treat any specification‑provided meaning as authoritative for claim construction unless other governing law requires otherwise.

name: Each reference used as basis for obviousness must be prior art and analogous to the claimed invention
description: Each reference 'to be applied as the basis for an obviousness rejection' must qualify as prior art and must also be analogous art 'to the claimed invention.'
guidance: Explicit clarity added to subsection II.A.1; ensure each cited reference meets both prior art status and analogy requirements before combining.

name: Fact‑findings must state a rationale supporting obviousness (KSR requirement)
description: Fact‑findings should state a rationale, as required by KSR, that supports a conclusion that the claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Updated subsection II.A.5 and added supporting citations (KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex) — examiners must articulate a reasoned rationale for the combination beyond naked conclusions.

name: Enablement: quantity of experimentation (post‑Amgen/Sanofi guidance)
description: Updated to incorporate 'Guidelines for Assessing Enablement' in view of the Supreme Court decision in Amgen Inc. v. Sanofi; subsection title updated to 'Quantity of Experimentation.'
guidance: Added citations and quotations from Amgen v. Sanofi and related Federal Circuit decisions; examiners should apply the updated enablement guidelines when assessing whether the specification enables the full scope of the claims.

name: Objective standard for measuring scope of subjective claim terms
description: Examiner should determine whether the specification supplies some objective standard for measuring the scope of a subjective term used in the claim.
guidance: Subsection IV clarified this duty; where subjective terms are used, examiners should look for objective measures in the specification to fix claim scope (and cite In re Kiely and Clearone v. Shure decisions as guidance).

name: Determining inventive step based on an uncertain prior document
description: How to determine inventive step of an invention based on a proposed prior document.
guidance: If a prior document asserts facts that are uncertain (e.g., efficacy claims), it may be difficult for PHOSITA to conclude effects from that document alone; uncertain statements should not be accepted as solid factual basis to combine with other art to deny inventive step.

name: Considering technological development trends in inventiveness
description: Whether to consider technological development when determining inventiveness.
guidance: Evidence showing trends of development (or absence of developments) in a field over time can prove that PHOSITA could not easily conceive a claimed feature; such trends support that an inventive step exists if the claimed solution was not foreseeable.

name: Novelty for inventions limiting purity of a known substance
description: Whether novelty is denied for an invention that merely limits the purity of a publicly known substance.
guidance: If the claimed purity cannot be obtained using published refinement technology and the patent discloses achieving that purity, the purity limitation may not be considered well-known or commonly used; novelty may therefore not be denied by prior art that lacks such achievable purity.

name: When a manufacturing process is necessary for identifying a product invention
description: A product invention case which describes the manufacturing process deems the process necessary to identify the structure and nature of the final product.
guidance: If a product claim includes a limitation 'manufactured by the method in Claim X' where method features (e.g., solvents, one-step impregnation) result in structural/compositional differences of the final product (e.g., no residual solvent), those manufacturing features become necessary elements for identifying the product and must be considered when abstracting similarities/differences.

name: Reasonable expectation of success standard for cancer-treatment use claims
description: Use of 'reasonable expectation of success' as a criterion to determine inventive step for cancer treatment usage inventions.
guidance: Given the special nature of cancer treatment development, inventive step for a cancer-treatment use is denied only when PHOSITA would have had a reasonable expectation of success of discovering the treatment from prior art, not merely a possibility.

name: Inventive step criteria for method-of-administration limitations
description: Criteria for determining inventive step when claims limit method of administration of a pharmaceutical.
guidance: If method-of-administration limitations do not produce significant beneficial effects beyond what is expected in the state of the art, and are within the range of what PHOSITA would expect, the limitation belongs to the public domain and inventive step is denied.

name: Adding pharmacological mechanism to medical use claims (correction)
description: Whether to allow correction that adds pharmacological mechanism in a medical-usage invention (Negative).
guidance: If the medical usage is already clearly specified (e.g., 'treatment use for human allergic conjunctivitis'), adding a pharmacological mechanism that does not narrow the claimed medical use is unnecessary; such addition may not qualify as correcting misrepresentation or clarifying an unclear description, and claims need not be changed because of the added mechanism.

name: Scope of revocation when correction inseparable from claims
description: In trials on invalidation where a petition for correction is raised, the scope of revocation of the administrative trial due to inseparability of the correction (Revoked in entirety).
guidance: If a petition for correction affects Claim 1 and subordinate claims depend on Claim 1, the correction covers subordinate claims as well; acceptance of invalidation for the main corrected claim may require revocation of the administrative decision in its entirety.

name: U.S. Counsel Requirement (Rule)
description: Final rule (effective Aug 3, 2019) requiring applicants, registrants, or parties to proceedings whose domicile or principal place of business is outside the U.S. to be represented by an attorney who is an active member in good standing of the bar of the highest court of a U.S. state.
guidance: Purpose: deter unauthorized representation, ensure proper signatures/averments/use claims, and enable enforcement of statutory/regulatory requirements. TPAC supported and commended issuance; Examination Guides provided implementation clarification.

name: Finality after appellate mandate (MPEP §1216.01)
description: Once this court has affirmed the rejection of a patent application's claims, the 'proceedings in the case are considered terminated on the issue date of the . . . mandate.'
guidance: An affirmative appellate mandate generally renders the Board's decision final for agency purposes; requests to reopen or reconsider are therefore treated as requests to reopen a final decision rather than continuation of active proceedings.

name: Change in law rarely constitutes extraordinary circumstances; limited exception when prior precedent precluded objection
description: Intervening developments in the law by themselves rarely constitute the extraordinary circumstances required for Rule 60(b)(6) relief; forfeiture may be set aside due to change in law only in the limited circumstance in which controlling precedent precluded the district court from adopting an objection before the Supreme Court issued its decision.
guidance: Per Gonzalez, Agostini, and Micron, a mere change in law (e.g., Arthrex) does not automatically excuse a party's delay unless earlier controlling precedent prevented raising the claim; Odyssey's situation did not meet that narrow exception.

name: Claim construction standard — Phillips when patent will expire before final decision
description: For patents that will expire prior to issuance of a final written decision by the Office, the Office proposes to apply a Phillips-type standard during the proceeding.
guidance: Such patents essentially lack viable opportunity to amend claims in an AIA proceeding; parties may be able to determine before filing which construction will apply. The Office invites comments on procedures (e.g., whether petitioners must brief both standards or whether briefing after filing but before patent owner preliminary response should be entertained).

name: Institution standard for inter partes review (IPR)
description: Inter partes review shall not be instituted for a ground of unpatentability unless the Board decides that the petition supporting the ground would demonstrate that there is a reasonable likelihood that at least one of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable. (§ 42.108(c))
guidance: In deciding institution, the Board will take into account a patent owner preliminary response where filed, but supporting evidence concerning disputed material facts will be viewed in the light most favorable to the petitioner. If patent owner submits supporting evidence, petitioner may seek leave to file a reply under § 42.24(c).

name: Institution standard for post-grant review (PGR)
description: Post-grant review shall not be instituted for a ground of unpatentability unless the Board decides that the petition supporting the ground would, if unrebutted, demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable. (§ 42.208(c))
guidance: Like IPR, the Board will consider a patent owner preliminary response but will view supporting evidence concerning disputed material facts in the light most favorable to the petitioner when deciding whether to institute. Petitioner may seek leave to reply if patent owner files evidence.

name: Motions to amend — statutory and substantive limits
description: Motions to amend may cancel a challenged claim or propose a reasonable number of substitute claims, and by statute must not enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new matter; the Rules include a rebuttable presumption that only one substitute claim is needed to replace each challenged claim. (37 CFR 42.221(a)(3); discussion of 35 U.S.C. 316(d)/326(d))
guidance: Patent owners are encouraged to submit a single substitute claim per cancelled claim for efficiency, but may propose more if need shown. Motions to amend cannot be entered like prosecution amendments; the Board does not perform a prior art search for amendments. The Office requires motions to show written description support and that substitute claims are narrower than replaced claims.

name: Meaning of 'prior art of record' and 'prior art known to the patent owner' for motions to amend
description: The term 'prior art of record' refers to: (a) any material art in the prosecution history of the patent; (b) any material art of record in the current proceeding, including art asserted in grounds on which the Board did not institute review; and (c) any material art of record in any other proceeding before the Office involving the patent. 'Prior art known to the patent owner' means material prior art that Patent Owner makes of record in the current proceeding pursuant to its duty of candor. (MasterImage clarification)
guidance: Patent owners must address these categories when making their prima facie case for substitute claim patentability; failure to make these showings can allow petitioner to shift burden of production back to challenge patentability.

name: Duty of candor; Rule 11-type representations and certifications
description: By presenting to the Board a petition, response, written motion, or other paper, an attorney, registered practitioner, or unrepresented party certifies that, to the best of the person’s knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances: (1) it is not presented for any improper purpose; (2) the claims, defenses, and other legal contentions are warranted by existing law or a non-frivolous argument to change law; (3) factual contentions have evidentiary support; and (4) denials of factual contentions are warranted on the evidence. (§ 42.11(c))
guidance: This is coupled with sanctions authority if violations occur; these representations do not apply to disclosures and discovery requests/responses/objections (§ 42.11(e)).

name: Ability to cure minor defects in motions to amend (discretionary)
description: If the Board deems it appropriate, the Board may allow a patent owner to cure minor defects in a motion to amend upon request (e.g., failure to construe a claim term or provide written description support).
guidance: Given time constraints, further exchanges of briefing may be incompatible with the schedule. Patent owners aware of defects should seek authorization from the Board to revise motions as soon as possible. The Board may allow cure but may limit additional briefing.

name: Patent owner estoppel under 37 CFR 42.73(d)(3)
description: Under § 42.73(d)(3), a patent applicant or owner is precluded from taking action inconsistent with an adverse judgment, including obtaining in any patent (1) a claim that is not patentably distinct from a finally refused or canceled claim; or (2) an amendment of a specification or of a drawing that was denied during the trial proceeding, except this provision does not apply to an application or patent that has a different written description.
guidance: The rule does not categorically bar obtaining all claims that could have been filed in response to a ground of unpatentability; it bars claims not patentably distinct from finally refused/cancelled claims. Parties may seek a panel conference to cancel claims before final decision; asserting conceded claims in litigation may give rise to sanctions or disciplinary investigation.

name: Application of known measures in an obvious way — incomplete teaching (a)(i)
description: If a prior document’s teaching is incomplete and at least one of the possible ways of supplying the missing claimed feature would naturally or readily occur to the skilled person, the invention lacks inventive step.
guidance: Example: prior disclosure of a lightweight structure but omission of 'aluminum' where aluminum would naturally occur to try as a material.

name: New use requiring non-routine overcoming of technical difficulties (b)(ii)
description: A new use of a known device or material that requires overcoming technical difficulties not resolvable by routine techniques involves an inventive step, provided the means for overcoming them are defined in the claim.
guidance: Example: adapting a device known in one field to another field where specific, non-obvious measures are required to make it work and those measures are claimed.

name: Secondary considerations/technical value as evidence of inventive step
description: Factors such as fulfilling a long-felt need, overcoming a scientific prejudice, prior failed attempts by others, unexpected results, and particular commercial success are relevant secondary considerations in assessing inventive step.
guidance: These factors are supportive evidence and should be weighed; a convincing link between the claimed features and the secondary consideration strengthens the case for inventive step.

name: Commercial success as qualified evidence
description: Commercial success alone does not indicate inventive step, but immediate commercial success coupled with a long-felt want and shown to derive from the technical features of the claimed invention may be relevant.
guidance: Ensure success is attributable to the technical merits (not marketing) and is commensurate with the claim scope before treating it as supporting inventive step.

name: Problem–solution approach — establish objective technical problem (Step 2)
description: Formulate the objective technical problem by studying the claimed invention, the closest prior art, and the differences in features; the problem is the aim/task of adapting the closest prior art to provide the technical effects the claimed invention provides.
guidance: The objective problem may differ from the applicant’s stated problem, should be based on objectively established facts (including discovered prior art), interpreted broadly, and if multiple technical effects exist each part/aspect should be considered in turn.

name: Problem–solution approach — assess obviousness from closest prior art (Step 3)
description: Determine whether the prior art as a whole would have prompted the skilled person, faced with the objective technical problem, to modify/adapt the closest prior art and thereby arrive at the claimed invention — the prior art must prompt (would), not merely permit (could).
guidance: Consider whether the prior art provides a teaching or suggestion that would have led the skilled person to make the specific modifications with a reasonable expectation of success.

name: Methodology for assessing industrial applicability
description: Assess industrial applicability by (i) determining what the applicant has claimed, and (ii) determining whether a person skilled in the art would recognize the claimed invention to have industrial applicability.
guidance: In most cases industrial applicability is self-evident and no detailed description is required; where claims imply impossible operation, notify the applicant.

name: Inventions contrary to well-established physical laws lack applicability
description: If any product or process is alleged to operate in a manner clearly contrary to well-established physical laws and thus cannot be carried out by a skilled person, the claim lacks industrial applicability and applicant should be notified.
guidance: Example: perpetual motion machines are not industrially applicable even if described.

name: Utility test — specific utility requirement
description: Utility may be considered as requiring that the invention have a utility that is specific (particular): the application must indicate a specific use or application rather than a general statement of possible usefulness.
guidance: General statements (e.g., 'useful biological properties') are insufficient. For biological/genetic claims, identifying specific targets or activities is necessary to show specific utility.

name: Three-part alternative test for industrial applicability (A14.01[2])
description: Some Authorities apply a three-part test: (1) the application indicates how the invention is capable of exploitation in industry (intended function/specific use); (2) the application discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for it to be carried out by a skilled person (or such information exists in prior public sources); (3) it must actually be possible while carrying out the claim to realize the indicated special purpose.
guidance: All three requirements must be met as of the priority date. Lack of any one (e.g., missing specific use, insufficient disclosure, or impossibility to realize purpose) undermines industrial applicability.

name: Special purpose requirement for industrial applicability
