description: The special purpose (specific use) is typically apparent from the claim or the nature of the invention; for computers the purpose is clear, but for novel chemical compounds or production processes a specific use must usually be indicated.
guidance: If no specific use is given for a chemical compound, the invention may fail the industrial applicability requirement unless other evidence shows practical use.

name: Verification of possibility to realize the special purpose (technical correctness)
description: Verification under requirement (3) checks the technical correctness of the invention as defined in each claim; successful verification means carrying out the claim yields an embodiment capable of the indicated special purpose.
guidance: Even if the disclosure enables carrying out the invention, impossibility to achieve the indicated special purpose (e.g., perpetuum mobile) means requirement (3) fails; findings about particular performance metrics (e.g., exact efficiency) are for sufficiency of description, not industrial applicability.

name: Alice step two — inventive concept / 'significantly more'
description: To survive Alice step two, a claim must recite elements or combinations that transform the nature of the claim beyond routine, conventional, or well-known elements, i.e., something 'significantly more' than the abstract idea.
guidance: Courts require specific, discrete implementations and will reject conclusory allegations of inventiveness that do not tie to claim text or specification. Use of conventional technologies (e.g., GPS on phones) generally does not supply an inventive concept. (AI Visualize; Beteiro; IBM v. Zillow.)

name: Computer-technology improvement requirement
description: For software/computer claims, the claimed advance must be an improvement in computer technologies themselves (a technological improvement) rather than mere use of computers as tools to implement an abstract idea.
guidance: Claims that merely create virtual views, manipulate data, or perform longstanding economic activities via generic computing are likely ineligible. Emphasize specific technological means (e.g., parallel video streams with bandwidth-saving transfer) when arguing eligibility. (AI Visualize; Beteiro; Contour IP v. GoPro.)

name: Problem with result-focused functional language
description: Claims that recite result-focused functional language without specifics on how the results are achieved are likely to be characterized as abstract ideas.
guidance: Include concrete mechanisms or specific steps/implementations in the specification and claims; avoid broad 'do X to achieve Y' recitations without structural/technical detail. (Beteiro.)

name: Avoiding impermissibly high-level claim characterization
description: Courts will reject treating claims at an overbroad, high level of generality when determining subject-matter eligibility; correct characterization focuses on the specific technological means claimed.
guidance: Draft claims and argue construction to show concrete technological improvements rather than sweeping goals. (Contour IP v. GoPro.)

name: Printed matter doctrine — content vs communication
description: Printed matter doctrine applies to 'matter claimed for what it communicates' (the content or information), not to mere communication mechanisms.
guidance: A claim involving communication is not excluded simply because it sends or receives data; the doctrine only bars patentability when the claimed matter is the communicated content itself. Program-code limitations that are silent as to content may not be barred. (IOENGINE v. Ingenico.)

name: Definiteness — claim limitations are conditions, not options
description: Claim limitations recite conditions that must be met; two limitations are not contradictory merely because one lists options that the other narrows, so long as both requirements can be met simultaneously.
guidance: Indefiniteness requires true contradiction; courts will not automatically find indefiniteness because of dependent/independent claim placement. (Maxell v. Amperex.)

name: Definiteness — need for measurement method when techniques diverge
description: A claim term that requires a quantitative measurement (e.g., particle size) is indefinite if the specification does not indicate which conventional measurement technique should be used and different conventional techniques produce meaningfully different results.
guidance: Provide measurement methodology or clear specification guidance when numerical ranges are claimed; absence of reliable evidence that techniques differ may defeat an indefiniteness challenge. (Janssen v. Teva.)

name: Functionally claimed structural elements — permissible functional construction
description: Functional claim limitations may be construed functionally rather than by rigid physical boundaries; functional constructions can differ in their physical manifestation across different claims without creating indefiniteness.
guidance: Courts will perform claim-by-claim constructions and may accept functional constructions that do not specify exact physical dimensions if the functional boundaries are sufficiently informing. (Vascular Solutions v. Medtronic.)

name: Written description — broad range can support narrower subrange
description: A broadly disclosed range in the specification can provide written-description support for a narrower claimed subrange where it would be clear to a skilled artisan that the subrange describes the same invention, especially in predictable arts and where endpoints are disclosed.
guidance: Ensure specification discloses endpoints or overlapping ranges and indicate predictability of the technology to support later-claimed subranges. (Rai Strategic Holdings v. Philip Morris.)

name: Printed matter and program-code limitations
description: Where claims recite program code or information, the printed matter doctrine only applies if the claim is directed to the content the matter communicates; a claim silent as to the contents of code may avoid the doctrine.
guidance: Draft claims to claim technical functionality or structure rather than pure informational content to avoid printed matter issues. (IOENGINE v. Ingenico.)

name: Design-patent obviousness — Graham-based framework (overruling Rosen-Durling)
description: Obviousness for design patents should follow a Graham-type analysis: consider (1) scope and content of the prior art (analogous art), (2) differences between the claimed design and the prior art (visual appearance from ordinary designer perspective), and (3) the level of ordinary skill (a designer of ordinary skill).
guidance: Assess whether ordinary designers would have been motivated to modify prior art to create the same overall visual appearance; secondary considerations remain relevant. This replaces the rigid Rosen-Durling two-step test. (LKQ v. GM en banc.)

name: Design patents — analogous art scope
description: At minimum, 'analogous art' includes prior art from the same field of endeavor as the article of manufacture claimed; other art may be analogous depending on context.
guidance: Broaden prior-art consideration appropriately in design cases while focusing on visual comparison from a designer's perspective. (LKQ v. GM.)

name: Two-step eligibility test
description: There are two criteria for subject matter eligibility and both must be satisfied: (1) the claimed invention must be directed to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter); and (2) the claim must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas).
guidance: Use the two-step analysis (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: judicial exception/practical application). If a claim fails Step 1 it is not eligible, but if the disclosure suggests amendment to reach a statutory category, still conduct Step 2. Evaluate the claim as a whole under the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification.

name: Four categories of statutory subject matter
description: The four patent-eligible categories are: (i) Process — an act or series of acts or steps; (ii) Machine — a concrete thing consisting of parts or devices; (iii) Manufacture — an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving them new forms/qualities/properties; (iv) Composition of matter — compositions of two or more substances or composite articles.
guidance: Apply court definitions (e.g., Gottschalk v. Benson; Burr v. Duryee; Chakrabarty) to determine whether the claim is directed to one of these categories. If clearly not within any of the four categories, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101, but still consider whether amendment could place the claim within a statutory category.

name: Non-statutory examples (claims not directed to a statutory category)
description: Non-limiting examples of claims not directed to one of the statutory categories include: transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., propagating electrical/electromagnetic signal per se), naturally occurring organisms, a human per se, legal contractual agreements, games defined as sets of rules, computer programs per se, companies, and mere arrangements of printed matter.
guidance: Cite relevant precedent (In re Nuijten; Chakrabarty; AIA sec.33; In re Ferguson; Gottschalk v. Benson; In re Miller). Use these examples to identify claims that are not statutory; consider whether claim language or breadth would encompass such non-statutory embodiments.

name: Claims covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (in light of the specification and PHOSITA) encompasses both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces non-eligible subject matter and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Example: a 'machine readable medium' claim that can be a compact disc (statutory) or a carrier wave (transitory, non-statutory) should be rejected when the claim as a whole encompasses non-statutory forms. Consider amendments to remove non-statutory breadth.

name: Judicial exceptions to the four categories
description: Judicially recognized exceptions to §101 include laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas; these are not patentable per se.
guidance: Cite Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Le Roy v. Tatham, Funk Bros., Benson, Flook, Diehr. Determine if the claim wholly embraces one of these exceptions; if so, it is not eligible unless limited to a particular practical application.

name: Practical application requirement
description: A claim that recites judicially excepted subject matter may still be eligible if it is limited to a particular practical application of that exception (i.e., how the exception is applied in a real-world product or process), rather than claiming the exception itself.
guidance: Evaluate the claim as a whole to see if it recites a tangible/practical application and does not preempt substantially all uses of the exception. Practical application is demonstrated by limitations showing real-world use or structure (see Ultramercial, Diehr).

name: Practical application for products (machines, manufactures, compositions)
description: Product claims (machines, manufactures, compositions) that are non-naturally occurring tangible embodiments and embody a particular practical application are typically evidence of eligibility.
guidance: Tangible structural limitations in product claims often make practical application self-evident. Examples: a cup as a tangible application of containing liquid; a magnetic door latch as an application of magnetism. Conversely, product claims that lack tangible limitations and thus encompass the underlying concept are impermissible. After establishing a practical application, evaluate preemption and other patentability issues (102/103/112).

name: Machine-or-transformation test as an investigative tool
description: The machine-or-transformation test remains a useful and important clue for determining whether some claimed processes are statutory: (1) tied to a particular machine/apparatus, or (2) transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
guidance: The test is not the sole test; consider additional factors from Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent. A claim satisfying the test weighs toward eligibility but failing it does not automatically mean ineligibility; consider totality of evidence.

name: Factors — machine/apparatus involvement
description: When a method recites a machine or apparatus, consider: the particularity vs generality of the claimed machine elements; whether the machine implements the steps (integral use) vs merely being an object on which the method operates; and whether the machine's involvement imposes meaningful limits or is only extrasolution/field-of-use.
guidance: For computer-implemented processes, a programmed general-purpose computer can be sufficiently particular if the claim conveys programming that creates a special-purpose computer (Alappat). However, merely adding a 'computer-aided' limitation without specifying how the computer aids or its significance is insufficient (DealerTrack). Extrasolution activity (e.g., mere data-gathering) typically weighs against eligibility (Cybersource, In re Grams, In re Meyer).

name: Factors — application of a law of nature
description: Even absent a particular machine or transformation, a claim that applies a law of nature in a practical way may represent patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Refer to Diehr and Bilski: determine if the claim embodies a practical application of the law of nature rather than claiming the law itself. Consider whether limitations tie the application to real-world use and avoid preempting the law.

name: Field-of-use and insignificant extra-solution activity
description: Field-of-use limitations (e.g., 'for use with a machine') and insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., generic data gathering) do not impose meaningful limits on claim scope and generally do not render an otherwise abstract claim statutory.
guidance: A field-of-use is merely descriptive of environment and not a meaningful boundary (Bilski; Parker v. Flook). Insignificant activities that are not central to the inventive purpose should be discounted when assessing practical application.

name: Evaluation of preemption
description: Once a practical application is established, assess whether the claim nonetheless impermissibly preempts substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception; claims that do so are not patent-eligible.
guidance: Limited occurrence of preemption must be evaluated. If a claim only covers a particular practical application and does not preempt substantially all uses, it is more likely eligible; if it covers substantially all applications, reject under §101. Use case law and claim scope analysis to assess preemption.

name: AIA Sec. 33(a) — prohibition on human organisms
description: Pursuant to the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act (AIA) sec. 33(a): 'Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.'
guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention as a whole encompasses a human organism, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and AIA sec. 33(a), indicating the claim is directed to a human organism and is nonstatutory. Form paragraph 7.04.01 may be used. Also continue to examine other issues pertinent to patentability (102, 103, 112) as applicable.

name: Whether the claim 'recites' a judicial exception (Step 2A, Prong One)
description: Evaluate whether the claim "recites" (i.e., sets forth or describes) a judicial exception such as a mathematical concept, mental process, or law of nature (MPEP 2106.04).
guidance: Identify specific limitations that align with at least one judicial exception. Examples from text: (b)-(e) recite mathematical concepts; partitioning embeddings may be a mental process. Use the claim language itself to determine whether the exception is set forth in the claim.

name: Grouping of judicial exceptions and mapping claim limitations
description: Map claim limitations to the judicial-exception groupings: mathematical concepts, mental processes, laws of nature, and certain types of organizing human activity.
guidance: Concrete examples: k-means clustering, binary masking, arithmetic weighting and summing -> mathematical concepts; comparing a PRS to a top-quartile threshold -> mental process; the relationship between genotype and phenotype -> law of nature. Note that items may fall under multiple groupings; pick at least one for analysis.

name: Consider limitations together where possible (avoid over-parsing)
description: When possible, consider claim limitations together as a single abstract idea rather than parsing the claim into multiple separate exceptions (MPEP 2106.04 II.B).
guidance: If steps (b)-(e) all fall within the mathematical-concepts grouping, analyze them together as a single abstract idea for Step 2A, Prong One. Do not artificially split limitations into multiple exceptions unless clearly distinct.

name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A, Prong Two)
description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application by (1) identifying any additional elements beyond the exception, and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination (MPEP 2106.04(d)).
guidance: Look for elements that meaningfully limit the claim or reflect a technical improvement. Compare additional elements (e.g., synthesis into time-domain waveforms, specific conversions, use of ASR to obtain transcripts) against the abstract idea to determine whether the claim as a whole is directed to a practical application.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity / post-solution activity
description: Post-solution activities or nominal steps that merely transmit or store data, or otherwise occur after the solution, are insignificant additions that do not integrate the judicial exception (MPEP 2106.05(g)).
guidance: Example: "transmitting the mixed speech signal x' for storage to a remote location" is a post-solution step that "does not meaningfully limit the claim." Label such elements as insignificant extra-solution activity and do not treat them as integrating the abstract idea.

name: Mere instructions to 'apply it' / use of a computer as a tool (MPEP 2106.05(f))
description: A recited computer or ML model that only amounts to instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (i.e., "apply it") does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: When reviewing generic recitations (e.g., "a DNN trained for source separation" with no structural detail), consider: (1) whether the claim recites only the idea/solution or outcome; (2) whether it invokes computers/machinery merely as a tool; and (3) the particularity or generality of the application. Generic ML recitations without specifics are likely mere implementation instructions.

name: Generic field-of-use or technological-environment linking is insufficient (MPEP 2106.05(h))
description: Confining the use of an abstract idea to a particular technological environment by general linking (e.g., "use a DNN") does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: A broad recital that ties the abstract idea to a field of use or technology without specifying how the technology is specifically used to solve a technical problem should be treated as an attempt to claim an abstract idea in a technological field rather than a meaningful integration.

name: Technical improvement to computer or other technology integrates the exception (MPEP 2106.05(a))
description: If the claim reflects a concrete technical improvement to computer technology or another technology, or otherwise solves a technical problem using specific features described in the disclosure, the claim integrates the abstract idea into a practical application.
guidance: Example: converting masked clusters into separate speech waveforms and generating a mixed speech signal that excludes an undesired source was treated as reflecting an improvement in speech-separation technology and thus integrates the abstract idea. Look for claim features that mirror the improvements described in the specification.

name: Non-mental, non-abstract physical/technical transformations are not judicial exceptions
description: Claim steps that require physical or technical transformations beyond what can be practically performed in the human mind are not mental-process abstract ideas (e.g., synthesizing waveforms, converting clusters to time-domain signals, ASR-generated transcripts).
guidance: If an element cannot be practically performed mentally and is not merely a mathematical concept described in text (e.g., no formula), treat it as a non-judicial-exception element that can help integrate the abstract idea into a practical application.

name: Mathematical concepts require specific formulae/relationships; mere variables may not suffice
description: A claim recites a mathematical concept when it sets forth mathematical operations/formulae/relationships (e.g., k-means clustering, arithmetic weighting). Merely reciting variables or naming an operation without mathematical detail may not itself be a mathematical concept recitation.
guidance: Example: "stitching" could involve a mathematical overlap-add method, but if the claim recites no details (no formulae, no calculations), the combining step may be considered merely based on a mathematical concept rather than reciting a mathematical concept. Examine whether explicit formulae or calculational steps are claimed.

name: Treatment of recitations that fall under multiple exceptions
description: When a limitation can be characterized under multiple judicial-exception categories, the examiner may identify it under at least one exception and proceed (MPEP 2106.04 I & II.B), but should be careful not to artificially fragment the claim into multiple separate exceptions.
guidance: Example: a weighted PRS limitation may be a mathematical calculation, a mental process, and involve a law of nature; it suffices to peg it to at least one grouping for further analysis, while considering the limitations together where appropriate.

name: Eligibility decision-flow labeling and outcomes (Step 2A results)
description: Record and report the Step 2A determinations (Prong One: does the claim recite an exception? Prong Two: does the claim integrate the exception into a practical application?). The combination of prong outcomes determines whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception.
guidance: If Prong One identifies an abstract idea (YES) but Prong Two finds the claim integrates that idea into a practical application (YES), then the claim is not "directed to" the judicial exception and is eligible. If Prong Two is NO, the claim is directed to an abstract idea and further analysis under the inventive-concept framework may be required.

name: Required contents of the appeal brief — status of claims (37 CFR 1.192(c)(3))
description: A statement of the status of all claims (pending, cancelled, allowed, rejected, etc.) and identification of the claims on appeal.
guidance: This avoids confusion as to which claims are on appeal and their precise wording, especially if amendments were made after final rejection. Each appealed claim must be identified.

name: Required contents of the appeal brief — summary of the invention (37 CFR 1.192(c)(5))
description: A concise explanation of the invention defined in the claims involved in the appeal, referring to the specification by page and line and to drawings by reference characters.
guidance: Preferably 'read' the appealed claims on the specification and drawings; page/line references help the Board quickly locate claimed subject matter in the record.

name: Argument specifics for 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the argument must specify the errors in the rejection and how the first paragraph of 112 is complied with, including how the specification and drawings describe the subject matter, enable one skilled in the art to make and use it, and set forth the best mode.
guidance: Cite pages/lines of the specification and drawings as appropriate; explain how each of the statutory requirements is satisfied for the rejected claims.

name: Argument specifics for 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the argument shall specify the errors in the rejection and how the claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention.
guidance: Explain claim language and why it meets the definiteness requirement; point out errors in examiner’s claim interpretation where appropriate.

name: Argument specifics for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the argument must specify the errors in the rejection and why the rejected claims are patentable under 102, including any specific claim limitations not described in the prior art relied upon.
guidance: Identify specific limitations absent from the cited reference; a general statement that not all limitations are in a single reference is insufficient without pointing out which limitations are missing.

name: Argument specifics for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the argument shall specify the errors and, where appropriate, identify claim limitations not described in the applied prior art and explain how such limitations render the claimed subject matter unobvious.
guidance: If the rejection is based on a combination of references, explain why the references, taken as a whole, do not suggest the claimed subject matter and, if appropriate, why features disclosed in one reference may not properly be combined with features disclosed in another. Mere assertion that limitations aren't in a single reference is inadequate.

name: Appendix requirement
description: An appendix containing a copy of the claims involved in the appeal must be included with the brief (37 CFR 1.192(c)(9)).
guidance: Include exact claim wording to avoid confusion as to the claims on appeal; aids the Board and examiner in review.

name: Office procedure following Federal Circuit decision
description: After the Federal Circuit issues its mandate, the mandate is entered in the application/reexamination/interference file and the file is returned to the appropriate USPTO official for further proceedings consistent with the mandate.
guidance: If all claims remain rejected, proceedings are considered terminated as of mandate date. If some claims are allowed, the file is processed for issuance on allowed claims and any remaining formal matters are handled. Remand, reopening, and examiner actions must follow agency policy and may require written approval for reopening after court decision.

name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify abstract idea and mapping
description: (a) Identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that you believe recites an abstract idea, and (b) determine whether the identified limitation(s) falls within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in the 2019 PEG.
guidance: Examiner should pinpoint claim limitations that potentially recite an abstract idea and then map those limitations to the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts; mental processes; certain methods of organizing human activity).

name: Mental process determination under broadest reasonable interpretation
description: A claim limitation that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in the human mind (or could practically be performed in the human mind) is a mental process.
guidance: The mere nominal recitation of generic computer components (e.g., 'by the network appliance') does not necessarily remove the limitation from the mental processes grouping if the rest of the claim could be performed mentally. Example: 'comparing ... to a predefined threshold' may cover a user comparing values mentally and thus is a mental process.

name: Mathematical concept requires explicit recitation
description: If a claim includes limitations that may be based upon mathematical relationships, formulas, or calculations, but those mathematical relationships/formulas/calculations are not explicitly recited in the claim, then the claim does not recite a mathematical concept for purposes of Step 2A Prong One.
guidance: Do not treat implicit or underlying math as a recited mathematical concept unless the claim explicitly recites mathematical formulas/relationships/calculations. (Example: digital simulation claim included math-based activity but did not explicitly recite a mathematical concept and thus was not treated as such.)

name: Evaluate claim elements both individually and as a whole
description: Elements that individually are mere pre- or post-solution activity may, in combination, yield a specific improvement and integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Assess whether the combination of elements recites a specific manner of achieving a technological improvement (e.g., targeted data collection to avoid excess network traffic and enable analysis). If the claim as a whole is directed to a particular improvement in computer-related technology or other field, it may be eligible despite component limitations being abstract when considered alone.

name: Drafting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (examination/practice guidance)
description: When rejecting a claim as lacking subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101, the rejection should: identify the abstract idea recited in the claim and include a reference to the appropriate enumerated grouping of abstract ideas; identify the additional elements and explain why they do not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application; and explain why the additional elements do not provide an inventive concept.
guidance: Use the 2019 PEG analysis structure in rejection wording. The training notes that new form paragraphs have been created for use with the 2019 PEG and that sample rejections are available on the microsite.

name: Outcome labeling guidance (Yes/No determinations)
description: For each Step/Prong the examiner records an outcome (e.g., 'Step 1 = Yes', 'Step 2A = No', 'Step 2B = No') and an eligibility conclusion (claim is eligible or ineligible).
guidance: Use explicit determinations for each stage. Examples: 'Step 2A = Yes. The claim is directed to the abstract idea.' or 'Step 2B = No, the claim does not provide an inventive concept. The claim is ineligible.' These labels clarify the analysis path and final conclusion.

name: Petition fees for reexamination proceedings
description: A petition in an ex parte reexamination proceeding must be accompanied by the fee set forth in § 1.20(c)(6), except for specific listed petition types (e.g., extension of response period under paragraph (c), petitions under paragraph (e) to accept delayed response, petitions under § 1.78 to accept unintentionally delayed benefit claim, and petitions under § 1.530(l) for correction of inventorship).
guidance: Check § 1.20(c)(6) and enumerated exceptions before filing a petition.

name: Copies required for submitted references (37 CFR 1.98(a)(2))
description: 37 CFR 1.98(a)(2) requires a legible copy of: (1) each foreign patent; (2) each publication or that portion which caused it to be listed, other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office; (3) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims, and any drawing of the application, or that portion of the application which caused it to be listed; (4) all other information or that portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: Failure to supply the required legible copies can limit consideration; parties should submit only the portion that caused listing when appropriate.

name: Scope of reexamination — patents/printed publications and 35 U.S.C.112
description: 37 CFR 1.552(a): Claims in an ex parte reexamination proceeding will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted in the reexamination proceeding, on the basis of the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Reexamination focuses on patents and printed publications; 35 U.S.C. 112 issues are limited to new/amendatory subject matter.

name: Claims may not enlarge scope of patent
description: 37 CFR 1.552(b): Claims in an ex parte reexamination proceeding will not be permitted to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent.
guidance: Any new or amended claims are examined to ensure that the scope of the original patent claims is not enlarged (see 35 U.S.C. 305).

name: Use of patent-owner statements to construe claims after order
description: 37 CFR 1.552(d): Any statement of the patent owner and any accompanying information submitted pursuant to § 1.501(a)(2) which is of record in the patent being reexamined may be used after a reexamination proceeding has been ordered to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim when applying patents or printed publications.
guidance: Patent-owner statements cannot be used at the initial order stage to establish a substantial new question but can be used in examination to determine claim meaning.

name: Admissions used only in combination with patents/printed publications
description: An admission, per se, may not be the basis for establishing a substantial new question of patentability, but an admission by the patent owner of record in the file or in a court record may be utilized in combination with a patent or printed publication.
guidance: Written statements submitted pursuant to 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) if relied upon in the request must be explained per 37 CFR 1.510(b)(2) showing how each patent owner claim scope statement is used to determine proper meaning of a claim in connection with prior art applied to that claim; admissions can be used in examination to interpret or modify prior art; third parties may not submit admissions made outside the file or court record.

name: Claim interpretation rule in reexamination
description: During reexamination, claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification and limitations in the specification are not read into the claims (In re Yamamoto).
guidance: For expired patents, claim construction pursuant to Phillips (ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill at time of invention) should be applied since expired claims are not subject to amendment. The statutory presumption of validity (35 U.S.C. 282) has no application in reexamination.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 issues limited to new/amendatory matter
description: Where new claims are presented or where any part of the disclosure is amended, the claims in the reexamination proceeding are to be examined for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112. Consideration of 35 U.S.C. 112 issues should, however, be limited to the amendatory (e.g., new language) matter.
guidance: A term in an original patent claim cannot be examined as too broad in a new or amended claim unless the amendatory matter creates the issue. Rewriting a dependent claim as independent cannot be examined under 112 unless the rewriting raises a new question (e.g., lack of antecedent). See MPEP § 2163 et seq.

name: Prohibition on adding new matter
description: 35 U.S.C. 305 provides for examination under 35 U.S.C. 132, which prohibits the introduction of new matter into the disclosure. Thus, the question of new matter should be considered in a reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Where new matter is added to the claims or affects claim limitations, the claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for failing to meet the written description requirement.

name: Amendment of the specification may raise 112 issues
description: Where the specification is amended in a reexamination proceeding, the examiner should make certain that the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 are met. An amendment to the specification can redefine the scope of the terms in a claim such that the claim is no longer clear or is not supported by the specification.
guidance: An amendment to the specification can result in failure of the claims to comply with 35 U.S.C. 112 even where the claims are not amended in any respect.

name: Claims must not enlarge scope of patent (restatement)
description: Claims in the proceeding must not enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent.
guidance: Consistent with 37 CFR 1.552(b) and 35 U.S.C. 305; ensure any new/amended claim is not broader than original.

name: Scope of burden when adding a claim — proving patentability
description: Obligation to 'prove patentability' when adding a claim is generally limited to showing compliance with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(1), except where the party reasonably has actual notice of other patentability problems.
guidance: Actual notice typically comes from prior rejections in the prosecution history or a substantive motion by the opposing party; opponents should explain issues in opposition rather than merely pointing them out; movants should explain lack of notice in their reply if appropriate.

name: Claim charts: form and page limits
description: Claim charts help illustrate a claim's meaning in comparison to prior art, other claims, or a specification; no specific form is required and the rules set no page limits.
guidance: Each party has incentive to produce clear claim charts; absence of a mandated form allows flexibility and tailoring to the point to be illustrated.

name: Estoppel from adverse judgment on patentability
description: A party that loses on patentability for an involved claim receives an adverse judgment and is estopped with respect to patentability of that claim's subject matter (§ 41.127(a)); priority is effectively a question of unpatentability under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1).
guidance: One never 'prevails' on priority in an absolute sense—priority determinations are framed as losses on the issue.

name: Construction of counts: plain language primary, claims/specs may inform
description: § 41.200(b) provides that the count defines the interfering subject matter and its primary meaning is based on the plain language of the count; corresponding claims and involved specifications can set bounds on what the count reasonably means.
guidance: Since § 41.200(b) permits reference to the specification in interpreting claims, specifications can indirectly influence the broadest reasonable construction of the count via the claim defining the count.

name: Threshold issues: 35 U.S.C. 135(b) bar and written description
description: 35 U.S.C. 135(b) bar and written description issues are designated as threshold issues, particularly narrowed to provoked interferences to address perceived abuses (e.g., copying claims to provoke interferences).
guidance: Written description as a threshold issue prevents applicants from provoking interferences to obtain inter partes challenges; the threshold list is inclusive, and other issues (e.g., enablement) may be treated as threshold in future adjudication.

name: Patentable subject matter under §101
description: "This part of U.S. law describes what is patent-eligible: 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof'. If the invention falls under one of several excluding categories, however, including a 'naturally occurring article' (a defined term in the law), then it is not patent eligible."
guidance: Use §101 as the threshold inquiry for subject-matter eligibility. Identify whether the claimed subject falls within the statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and then determine if it is excluded as a product of nature or other non-eligible category. The Myriad decision applies §101 to genetic material claims.

name: Purified-and-isolated doctrine (historical standard)
description: USPTO and courts historically allowed patents on molecules when 'isolated from their natural state and purified' (e.g., aspirin, adrenaline, vitamin B12, prostaglandins). Quoted USPTO guideline: 'Like other chemical compounds, DNA molecules are eligible for patents when isolated from their natural state and purified or when synthesized in a laboratory from chemical starting materials.'
guidance: This older doctrine supported claims to isolated natural molecules; Myriad effectively narrowed or rejected its application to naturally occurring DNA sequences. When evaluating older claims or prior PTO practice, consider that purified-and-isolated reasoning may no longer control post-Myriad for genomic sequences.

name: Markedly different test (Diamond v. Chakrabarty)
description: The Chakrabarty test asks whether the claimed subject is 'markedly different' from products found in nature (used in Federal Circuit reasoning to support patent eligibility of isolated DNA).
guidance: Courts may use a 'markedly different' analysis to ask whether the claimed composition possesses characteristics that make it significantly different from a natural counterpart. Applying Myriad, chemical/structural differences that make a molecule non-naturally occurring (e.g., cDNA, engineered organisms) support eligibility, but informational identity to a natural sequence may counsel against eligibility.

name: Method/diagnostic claims as abstract mental processes (Bilski/Mayo)
description: The District Court and Federal Circuit found that comparisons of DNA sequences were 'abstract mental processes' (In re Bilski) and therefore not patent eligible; the Court noted method claims that 'involve well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers' add nothing inventive.
guidance: Diagnostic or analysis method claims that essentially claim mental steps (e.g., comparing sequences, thinking about correlations) without a concrete, transformative step are vulnerable to §101 invalidation. Evaluate whether the claimed method effects a real-world transformation or merely recites an abstract practice or mental process.

name: Scope distinction: composition of matter versus information
description: The Federal Circuit treated gene claims as directed toward 'compositions of matter' rather than toward information, but the Supreme Court emphasized that genes and the information they encode are not patent eligible under §101 simply because they have been isolated.
guidance: When drafting or evaluating claims, distinguish whether the claim is to a physical, human-made composition (more likely eligible) or to information/content (less likely eligible). Claims that are essentially to informational content (sequence as information) are more vulnerable under Myriad.

name: Patentability of applications of knowledge about genes
description: The Court noted: 'This case does not involve patents on new applications of knowledge about the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes... Many of [Myriad's] unchallenged claims are limited to such applications.'
guidance: Claims that apply knowledge of a gene to new, specific, technological uses (diagnostic tools with inventive steps, therapeutics, engineered alterations) may be patentable even if the underlying natural sequence is not. Focus claims on concrete applications or methods that add inventive contributions.

name: Drug screening claims — mixed treatment in precedent
description: The Federal Circuit found drug screening assay claims patentable, and the Supreme Court's decision did not broadly invalidate drug screening claims; prior to Myriad, drug screening claims were 'not seriously questioned.'
guidance: Drug-screening/assay claims that describe concrete experimental steps and applications are more likely to be treated as patent-eligible than claims that merely state a principle or observational correlation. Assess claim drafting to emphasize practical experimental implementations and inventive features.

name: Inventorship overlap requirement (same inventor or common joint inventor)
description: An application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 must name the inventor or at least one joint inventor named in the previously filed application or provisional application.
guidance: If inventorship differs, correction may be required (see MPEP §§ 201.06, 602.01(c), 1412.04). Even with proper inventorship overlap, the later-filed application must still meet written description support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) to be entitled to the earlier date (see MPEP § 211.05).

name: Reference to the prior-filed application must be made and identified
description: A later-filed application claiming benefit must contain, or be amended to contain, a reference to each prior-filed application identifying it by provisional application number (series code and serial number) or by application number/international application number and filing date as appropriate.
guidance: If the later-filed application is a nonprovisional application, the reference must be included in an Application Data Sheet (ADS) per 37 CFR 1.76(b)(5). For pre-September 16, 2012 nonprovisionals, the first sentence(s) of the specification following the title satisfied the requirement. For international/national stage matters, include the proper international numbers and filing dates. Cross-references to other related applications may be made when appropriate, but do not include cross-references in the ADS to applications for which benefit is not claimed. See 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3), (d)(2) and MPEP § 211.01.

name: Types and entitlement of prior-filed nonprovisional/international applications for 120/121/365(c)/386(c)
description: To claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), each prior-filed application must name the inventor (or a joint inventor) named in the later-filed application and must be an application entitled to a filing date as an international application, international design application, or a nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) that meets the filing-date rules and fee requirements.
guidance: Specifically: (i) an international application entitled to a filing date per PCT Article 11 and designating the U.S.; (ii) an international design application entitled to a filing date per 37 CFR 1.1023; or (iii) a nonprovisional under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) with entitlement to a filing date per 37 CFR 1.53(b)/(d) and payment of the basic fee per 37 CFR 1.16 during pendency. See 37 CFR 1.78(d)(1) and MPEP § 211.01(d).

name: Reference must identify relationship (continuation/divisional/CIP) and continued prosecution application as specific reference
description: References to prior-filed nonprovisional/international applications claiming benefit under 120/121/etc. must identify the application number (series and serial), international application number and filing date, or international registration number and filing date, and must identify the relationship of the applications (i.e., whether the later-filed application is a continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part).
guidance: A request for a continued prosecution application under 37 CFR 1.53(d) is the specific reference required by 35 U.S.C. 120 to the prior-filed application. The identification of an application by application number is the identification of every application assigned that number necessary for a specific reference required by 35 U.S.C. 120. See 37 CFR 1.78(d)(2)-(4) and MPEP § 211.01.

name: Specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail (possession standard)
description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession is required but possession alone does not cure lack of written description. Compliance is a fact‑based inquiry varying with the nature of the invention. (Cited cases: Moba, Vas‑Cath, Enzo Biochem.)

name: Ways to show possession (descriptive means)
description: An applicant shows possession by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means such as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas.
guidance: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice, by showing that the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings or structural chemical formulas showing the invention was complete), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Cited: Lockwood; Pfaff; Amgen.)

name: Biological material deposits do not substitute for written description
description: A deposit of biological material (in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.) may satisfy written description for a claimed material but is not a substitute for a written description of the claimed invention.
guidance: The written description of the deposited material needs to be as complete as possible because examination proceeds solely on the basis of the written description. Deposits made after filing may support sequence corrections only if applicant files a conforming 37 CFR 1.804 statement. (Cited: Enzo Biochem; In re Lundak; 54 Fed. Reg. final rule.)

name: Presumption of adequate written description for original claims (but not absolute)
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the PTO has the initial burden of presenting reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as describing the claimed invention.
guidance: Even original claims may raise written description issues if an aspect of the claimed invention is not described with sufficient particularity (e.g., claims embracing additional structures beyond a disclosed sequence). Examine specification and drawings to assess support for originally filed claims. (Cited: In re Wertheim.)

name: Genus/species and breadth support (genus disclosure may not support all species)
description: A generic or 'laundry list' disclosure does not necessarily provide written description support for every species within a genus unless the disclosure reasonably leads those skilled in the art to the particular species.
guidance: The ordinary artisan must be able to 'envisage' the claimed product arising from the disclosed process; mere listing of possible moieties may be insufficient. Cases: Fujikawa; In re Ruschig; Purdue Pharma. Use caution when claiming broad ranges or subgenera without specific support.

name: New or amended claims must be supported by the original disclosure (no new matter)
description: The prohibition against introducing new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251) prevents adding information beyond originally filed subject matter; new or amended claims that introduce elements or limitations not supported by the original disclosure violate the written description requirement.
guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent; no in haec verba requirement. Amendments correcting obvious errors may be permissible if the ordinary artisan would recognize the error and appropriate correction. For sequence corrections, deposits and 37 CFR 1.804 statements can affect permissibility. (Cited: In re Rasmussen; In re Lukach; In re Smith; In re Oda; Cubist v. Hospira.)

name: Omission of an element described as essential raises written description issues
description: A claim that omits matter the applicant describes as essential or critical in the specification may fail the written description requirement.
guidance: Where specification statements make clear that a particular (narrow) understanding is essential, broader claims omitting that element may be invalid. Such omissions may also raise enablement or definiteness problems. (Cited: PIN/NIP v. Platte Chem.; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo.)

name: Examiner must make a prima facie case identifying unsupported claim limitations
description: To establish a prima facie case of lack of written description, the examiner must identify the claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure.
guidance: Example: Hyatt v. Dudas — examiner explained lack of adequate description of a claimed combination despite individual elements being listed. Once the examiner makes a prima facie case, the burden shifts to applicant to point out support or amend. For newly added/amended claims, a simple statement noting lack of apparent support for a given limitation may suffice to start the examination discussion. (Cited: Hyatt; Stored Value Solutions.)

name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers (claim construction component)
description: Claim construction is essential: each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
guidance: Consider the entire claim including preamble language and the transitional phrase ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of'). Guidance on open/closed claim language and when 'consisting essentially of' may be treated as 'comprising' for prior art purposes. Evaluate whether preamble language is structural or limiting (Pac‑Tec; Bell Communications Research; Corning).

name: Evaluate sufficiency of recited structures, acts, or functions; do not import limitations from the specification into claims
description: The examiner should evaluate whether sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim; limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification.
guidance: Absence of definitions or details for well‑established terms or procedures should not alone justify a written description rejection. Consider weight of preamble and whether claim limitations provide clear scope. (Cited: Lockwood; Bell Communications Research.)

name: Review entire application to understand how applicant provides support for claimed subject matter
description: Assess support by reviewing the whole application: specification, drawings, originally filed claims, examples, and any deposits or cross‑references.
guidance: Support for originally filed claims may be found in any portion of the specification or drawings. Examiner should also consider whether corrections, incorporations by reference, or inherent disclosures provide support; examination is fact‑specific and depends on the level of ordinary skill and predictability of the art.

name: Applicant obligations when amending claims — point out original support
description: When applicant amends claims, applicant should specifically point out where and/or how the original disclosure supports the amendment(s).
guidance: If applicant points to support and the examiner finds the disclosure does not reasonably convey possession, the examiner must present reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize such support. A simple statement pointing out lack of apparent support for a limitation may be sufficient to trigger further explanation by the examiner. (Cited: MPEP §§ 2163.04, 714.02.)

name: Written description inquiry is fact‑based and depends on the nature of the invention
description: Whether the written description requirement is met is a question of fact determined case‑by‑case and will 'necessarily vary depending on the nature of the invention claimed.'
guidance: Examiners should consider predictability of the art, level of ordinary skill, examples and working embodiments, and whether the disclosure imparts sufficient knowledge to those skilled in the art about the claimed subject matter. (Cited: Enzo Biochem; In re Smith; In re Wertheim.)

name: Preliminary information search and patentability evaluation by accredited organizations
description: The Draft introduces the opportunity for Rospatent to create conditions for preliminary information search and evaluating patentability of the claimed technical solution by the Russian scientific and educational organizations accredited by Rospatent with competencies in specific areas of knowledge.
guidance: Accreditation of such organizations will be free of charge. The preliminary information search service will be provided to applicants on a voluntary basis and is intended to improve examination procedures and the quality of incoming applications.

name: If novelty is in use/process, claims should be drafted to claim the use, not the old apparatus
description: If the particular apparatus or combination is not new and the novelty consists in the use that forms a new process or develops a new property, it is an error to describe and claim the invention in a way that makes it necessary to construe the patent as a claim for a new machine or agent.
guidance: Court constructions can convert a poorly-drafted claim into a broad claim (e.g., 'iron frame') covering more than intended and lead to invalidity. Draft claims to reflect the inventive feature (the novel use or process) to avoid misconstruction.

name: Care in stating the invention is critical to avoid misinterpretation and invalidity
description: Courts stress the necessity of great care in the statement of what constitutes the invention because misdescription can force a court to construe the patent in an unintended way, leading to invalidity if the purportedly claimed subject is not novel.
guidance: Illustration: a broad claim for 'iron frame' was construed to cover any iron frame for a ship, leading to failure. The treatise repeatedly warns patentees to claim the inventive feature (use/process/property) rather than an old machine or material.

name: Duty to inform client of significant PTO correspondence (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8))
description: A practitioner must inform a client when the practitioner receives correspondence from PTO that could have a significant impact on a pending matter and a reasonable practitioner would believe the client should be notified.
guidance: “Inform” is narrower than mere “notify.” It requires providing the client with the important correspondence (e.g., copies) and a full and accurate explanation of the document's contents, ramifications, deadlines (e.g., non-extendable two-month appeal deadline), and available options. Examples of failures: sending an email that mentions an office action without attaching it, misstating whether claims were allowed or only potentially allowable, failing to mention deadlines or need to rewrite claims. Inadequate explanation that leaves the client with an erroneous impression that no action is needed violates § 10.23(c)(8).

name: Making a false statement of law or fact (37 C.F.R. § 10.85(a)(5))
description: Prohibits making a false statement of law or fact in PTO proceedings; contains a knowledge element (the practitioner must know the statement is false).
guidance: Allegations under § 10.85(a)(5) require proof the practitioner knowingly made false statements. If practitioner lacked actual knowledge of the falsity, the claim fails.

name: "About"
description: In determining the range encompassed by the term “about”, one must consider the context of the term as it is used in the specification and claims of the application.
guidance: Analyze surrounding disclosure and prosecution history to determine what range "about" covers; note cases (Ortho-McNeil Pharm. v. Caraco; W.L. Gore v. Garlock) where "about" was definite (e.g., measurable with a stopwatch) and cases (Amgen v. Chugai) where "at least about" was indefinite because neither specification nor prior art indicated the covered range.

name: "Similar" / "Similar structure"
description: Use of the word “similar” (e.g., “nozzle for high-pressure cleaning units or similar apparatus”) can render a claim indefinite if it is not clear what applicant intended to cover by “similar.”
guidance: If "similar" appears, determine whether the specification or prosecution history clarifies the meaning; absent clarification, examples show claims invalid (Ex parte Kristensen; Ex parte Pappas).

name: "Substantially"
description: The term “substantially” is a broad term often used with another term to describe a characteristic of the claimed invention; it may be definite when read in view of general guidelines in the specification.
guidance: Evaluate whether the specification provides general guidelines or examples so that a person of ordinary skill would know what is meant (e.g., “substantially equal” held definite in Andrew Corp. v. Gabriel Electronics).

name: "Type"
description: The addition of the word “type” to an otherwise definite expression (e.g., “ZSM-5-type aluminosilicate zeolites”) can extend scope and render the claim indefinite if it is unclear what “type” was intended to convey.
guidance: Check whether the dependent claims or specification place the recited "type" within the genus; unclear use of "type" has been held indefinite (Ex parte Copenhaver; Ex parte Attig).

name: Narrow and broader numerical ranges in the same claim
description: Use of a narrow numerical range that falls within a broader range in the same claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries of the claim are not discernible (e.g., including examples/preferences in a single claim).
guidance: If unclear whether the narrower range is a limitation, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. Examples: “a temperature of between 45 and 78 degrees Celsius, preferably between 50 and 60 degrees Celsius” or “a predetermined quantity, for example, the maximum capacity.” Dependent claims may properly set narrower ranges without indefiniteness.

name: "Effective amount"
description: The phrase “an effective amount” may or may not be indefinite; the proper test is whether one skilled in the art could determine specific values for the amount based on the disclosure.
guidance: Look for disclosure (examples/guidelines) enabling determination of effective amounts (In re Mattison; In re Halleck). If the claim does not state the function to be achieved or multiple effects are implied, the phrase may be indefinite (In re Fredericksen). Recent cases accept "effective amount" when read in light of supporting disclosure and absence of prior-art uncertainty (Ex parte Skuballa).

name: Exemplary claim language ("for example", "such as")
description: Description of examples or preferences is properly set forth in the specification rather than the claims. If stated in the claims, examples and preferences may lead to confusion over the intended scope of a claim.
guidance: Where it is not clear whether an example is limiting, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. Provided examples held indefinite include: (A) “R is halogen, for example, chlorine”; (B) “material such as rock wool or asbestos”; (C) “lighter hydrocarbons, such, for example, as the vapors or gas produced”; (D) “normal operating conditions such as while in the container of a proportioner.” These are fact-specific and not per se rules.

name: Claim term with no antecedent basis in the disclosure is not necessarily indefinite
description: The mere fact that a term used in the claim has no antecedent basis in the specification does not necessarily mean it is indefinite; words in the claim need not match the specification exactly so long as the claim defines the invention with reasonable clarity.
guidance: Assess whether the claim, read as a whole, apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope; if so, it meets the notice function even without literal antecedent wording (In re Larsen example).

name: Claim body reciting additional elements not per se indefinite
description: A claim is not per se indefinite if the body of the claim recites additional elements which do not appear in the preamble; consider the totality of limitations to ascertain scope.
guidance: Examine the entire claim in context; courts have reversed rejections where the totality of limitations apprised skilled artisans of the scope (In re Larsen).

name: Factors for examining functional language
description: When a claim limitation employs functional language, the examiner’s determination of whether the limitation is sufficiently definite will be highly dependent on context (disclosure and knowledge of a person of ordinary skill).
guidance: Consider facts such as whether the limitation sets definite boundaries or merely describes a problem/result (Halliburton Energy Servs.), whether structural characteristics are adequately defined (General Elec.; United Carbon), and whether the specification provides general guidelines and examples (In re Marosi). Use these as non-exclusive points for analysis.

name: Alternative limitations — Markush groups
description: A “Markush” claim recites a list of alternatively useable species (commonly “selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C”). Markush claims are permissible if they present no uncertainty about scope.
guidance: Ensure members of a Markush group belong to a recognized physical/chemical or art-recognized class, or at least share a common property responsible for their function. A Markush group may be indefinite if so expansive that skilled artisans cannot determine the metes and bounds. Double inclusion is not per se problematic; evaluate facts in each case. See MPEP §§ 803, 608.01(p), 715.03.

name: Specification must not be more extensive than the invention (no over-claiming)
description: The grant must not be more extensive than the invention; the specification will be incorrect if it contains a description of more than the improvement or addition, unless it particularly distinguishes the new from the old parts.
guidance: A patentee cannot monopolize the whole subject when his patent is only for an improvement. Examples include chairs and lever cases where a specification that encompassed prior art rendered the patent invalid.

name: Particularize new parts and distinguish old parts in improvements
description: When the patent is for an improvement, the inventor may either describe the whole machine and particularize the addition, or describe the whole and point out which parts are old; but the new parts must be accurately distinguished.
guidance: There are several acceptable ways to draft an improvement's specification: (1) describe whole and particularize the addition; (2) describe whole and point out old/not material parts; (3) describe the improvement and how applied to old parts; (4) describe whole and refer to former patent. The choice depends on intelligibility and avoiding over-claiming.

name: When claiming combinations of known parts
description: If a combination of substances, materials, or machine parts in common use previously applied for same or different purposes is claimed, the specification may set out the whole as the invention provided it clearly expresses that it is the new combination only.
guidance: Nothing more than the invention must be claimed. Every old part which is essential and material in producing the intended effect will be considered as claimed if not designated as old.

name: Describe only the new combinations when adding to existing combinations
description: If the invention consists of a new set of combinations added to a manufacture composed of combinations, the specification should only describe the new combinations which have been invented and how they are to be added to the old ones.
guidance: Avoid claiming antecedent combinations not invented by the patentee; if a prior combination existed up to a given point and the inventor's contribution is only subsequent combinations, the specification must not claim the whole earlier combination as his invention.

name: Use of prior/expired patents in combination claims
description: If the combination consists of the subjects of several expired patents (or bought ones), a description of the method by which they were combined, with a reference to the several specifications, will be sufficient to sustain the patent.
guidance: Reciting and referring to enrolled prior patents is acceptable because they are matter of public record; careful explanation of the method of combination is required.

name: Method/principle claims require the same rigour as tangible means
description: If a method is the subject of a patent (in practice the tangible means carrying the method into effect), the description must be very accurate and so clear and evident that no experiments are necessary to learn and put it in practice as beneficially as the patentee enjoys it.
guidance: Specifications of methods are governed by the same rules as machines, improvements, or combinations — precise, enabling disclosure without need for inventive effort.

name: Do not claim multiple competent means if only one works
description: If the patentee represents several things as competent to produce a specific effect when only one will answer, that is bad.
guidance: Be careful not to assert several equivalent means as workable if only one is operative; such misrepresentation can invalidate the patent.

name: A. Claim limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind do not recite a mental process
description: If a claim contains limitations that the human mind is not equipped to perform practically, it does not recite a mental process.
guidance: Examiners should find these claims outside the mental-process grouping. Case examples: SRI Int’l v. Cisco (network monitors/analyzing network packets—human mind not equipped); SiRF (GPS pseudorange calculations); Synopsys (specific data encryption method requiring several-step data manipulation); Research Corp. Techs. (halftone rendering involving computer data structures). Contrasting examples of claims that do recite mental processes include: Electric Power Group (collecting, analyzing, displaying data at high level of generality), University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry (comparing BRCA sequences in any way), Classen (collecting and comparing known info), In re Brown (identifying head shape/applying hair designs). Examiner takeaway: focus on whether the limitation can be practically performed mentally (not merely theoretically).

name: B. Claim limitations that encompass human performance mentally (with or without physical aids) recite a mental process
description: If a claim recites a limitation that a human could practically perform mentally, even aided by pen and paper or similar physical aids, the limitation falls within the mental processes grouping and is an abstract idea.
guidance: Physical aids (pen/paper, slide rule) do not negate the mental nature of a limitation; they only account for memory/capacity differences. Examples: Benson (algorithm convertible to mental calculation); CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card numbers could be done by writing down transactions); Synopsys (translating logic description to hardware description could be done mentally/with pencil and paper); Flook (computations by pencil and paper); University of Florida Rsch Found. v. GE (reliance on specification to determine mental performability). Examiner takeaway: consult the specification and claim detail to see if claimed steps are simply mental operations (even with simple physical aids).

name: C.2 Performing a mental process in a computer environment
description: Performing a mental-process-type concept within a computer environment can still be an abstract idea if the claim steps are analogous to human cognitive actions.
guidance: Case examples: Symantec (electronic post office receiving, screening, distributing email analogous to human mail decisions); FairWarning (detecting misuse via rule-based analysis analogous to human fraud detection questions). Examiner takeaway: compare claimed rules/analysis to analogous human questions/actions described in the specification and case law.

name: C.3 Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
description: Using a computer merely as a tool to perform what is otherwise a mental concept renders the claim a mental process.
guidance: Case examples: Mortgage Grader (grading/comparing loan packages—concept of anonymous loan shopping could be done without a computer); Berkheimer (parsing and comparing data recited at a high level of generality—computer merely used as a tool). Examiner takeaway: determine whether computer implementation is essential or merely a tool for performing an otherwise mental concept.

name: D. Both product and process claims may recite a mental process
description: Both product claims (systems, computer-readable media) and process claims can be directed to mental processes and thus to abstract ideas.
guidance: Examples of product claims reciting mental processes: Content Extraction (API for extracting/processing info from hard-copy documents), Mortgage Grader (system enabling anonymous loan shopping), CyberSource (computer-readable medium for detecting fraud), Symantec (electronic post office), Voter Verified (self-verifying voting system), Electric Power Group (real-time monitoring system), Versata (computer readable media implementing price determination). Process claim examples discussed in earlier subsections (Flook, Benson, Berkheimer, Synopsys, Ambry Genetics). Examiner takeaway: do not assume product (apparatus/media) claims are immune—analyze claim substance and generality.

name: Tentative Abstract Ideas (procedure)
description: A 'tentative abstract idea' is a claim limitation that an examiner believes should be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, methods of organizing human activity, mental processes).
guidance: Procedure: evaluate under the subject matter eligibility framework—(1) If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application, the claim is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible (Pathway B). (2) If it does not integrate into a practical application, it is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis at Step 2B; if the claim as a whole provides an inventive concept at Step 2B, it is eligible (Pathway C). (3) If the claim does not provide an inventive concept at Step 2B, bring the application to the attention of the Technology Center (TC) director; a rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval recorded in the file), and a justification must be provided for treating the limitation as an abstract idea. The TC Director will authorize use of form paragraph 7.05.017 and include signature; public notification may follow. Interview guidance: examiner may conduct interview to advance prosecution; interview with TC Director is not required to withdraw/maintain rejection once TC Director has given initial approval.

name: Element-by-element mapping
description: For any claimed rejection or allowance, perform an element-by-element mapping between claim limitations and the selected prior art references (or specification for intrinsic reasoning).
guidance: Required for OA-RO and OA-RS outputs; examples provided in generated OA snippets showing detailed mapping for claims 1–30. This mapping must precede or accompany rejections/allowances.

name: Scope Lock (Scope_Lock)
description: All technical content and legal reasoning must be grounded only in the provided inputs (claims, provided references, prosecution history) and PHOSITA common sense where specified.
guidance: Explicit 'Scope Lock' requirement: do not invent external facts, inventions, or references; acknowledge claim amendments and identify new matter violations if present.

name: USPTO-style structure and headings
description: Output must follow a realistic USPTO-style Office Action structure using plain-text headings: DETAILED ACTION, OPENING STATEMENT, CLAIM REJECTIONS - 35 U.S.C. 101, CLAIM REJECTIONS - 35 U.S.C. 102, CLAIM REJECTIONS - 35 U.S.C. 103, CLAIM REJECTIONS - 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/(b), DOUBLE PATENTING, CONCLUSION, etc.
guidance: Prompt enumerates required sections; include only applicable sections and adhere to formal USPTO headings and organization.

name: Decide disposition explicitly (Allowed or Rejected) and avoid bias
description: For each claim set, explicitly decide whether claims should be Allowed or Rejected based strictly on claim language and technical reasoning; do not assume rejection merely because you are an examiner.
guidance: Prompt item 'Disposition (No Bias)': base decision strictly on claim language and reasoning. If no rejection applies, explain why allowance is warranted.

name: Identify new matter violations
description: When claims are amended, explicitly determine whether amendments introduce new matter (new subject matter not supported by the original disclosure).
guidance: Included in OA re-examination tasks: 'ensure the final report acknowledges claim amendments, identifies any new matter violations, and presents updated rejections.'

name: Avoid templated/formal language that masks lack of technical mapping (anti-pattern)
description: Avoid relying on templated legal discourse to camouflage insufficient technical claim-to-art analysis.
guidance: Case study findings: models often adopt templated legal language that reduces complex technical distinctions to superficial similarities — this is a failure mode to avoid.

name: Rebuttal expectations: targeted responses and refined claims
description: Rebuttals should provide amendment text, targeted arguments against specific rejections (e.g., §102), and refined claims where appropriate.
guidance: Example rebuttal outputs include Amendment and Remarks sections, point-by-point responses to statutory rejections, and concluding refined claims. Rebuttals should meaningfully counter the examiner's evidence-first mapping.

name: Balance scope, cost and legal requirements
description: When drafting a set of claims, you must carefully consider and strike a balance between the scope of protection sought, the likely cost of that protection and the need to meet requirements under the applicable law.
guidance: Professional tips note that drafters should ensure clients have an appropriate number of claims and recognize when the costs of additional claims (excess claim fees, annuity fees, etc.) tip towards diminishing returns. Consider fee structures (e.g., USPTO extra fees, EPO limits) when deciding claim breadth and count.

name: Vary claim breadth as insurance against prior art
description: Varying the breadth of claims can offer insurance against arguments that a patent is invalid based on the prior art – claims of varying scope help to defend the inventor against instances of prior art not known at filing or discovered during litigation.
guidance: Draft a combination of broad and narrow claims: first draft the broadest independent claim then dependent claims covering narrower ranges. Use dependent claims as fallback positions if the broad claim is anticipated or rendered obvious by later-found prior art.

name: Independent claim must specify essential features and technical-effect features
description: An independent claim should typically specify the essential features needed to define the invention. Where patentability depends on a technical effect, the claims should typically be drafted so as to include all of the technical features of the invention that are essential for the technical effect.
