guidance: Claims must be clear and directed to the heart of the invention. Generic terms may imply common features (e.g., ‘bicycle’ implies wheels) but where specific technical effects are relied upon, explicitly include the technical features that produce that effect to meet clarity/enablement standards.

name: Clarity and internal consistency of process vs product claims
description: If a claim is directed to a process for producing a product X, the process claimed should be such that, when carried out in a manner reasonable to a person skilled in the art, it necessarily leads to product X as its end result; otherwise, there is an internal inconsistency and therefore a lack of clarity in the claim.
guidance: Ensure process claims are drafted so the skilled person would obtain the claimed product; similarly, product claims should clearly identify modifications from known products. Internal inconsistency is an clarity objection risk.

name: Definition and format of dependent claims
description: A dependent claim is one that 'depends from' another claim – signaled by identifying a parent claim (e.g., “The apparatus of Claim 1, further comprising…”). By referring to another claim, the dependent claim includes everything from the parent claim plus whatever is newly recited in the dependent claim itself.
guidance: Dependent claims make the claim set more concise by avoiding repetition. Typical wording includes “The apparatus of Claim 1…”, “according to Claim 1”, “as in Claim 1”. Dependent claims commonly start with the definite article “The” though practices vary. They must refer back to at least one previous claim and cannot refer forward.

name: Dependent claims always narrower than the claim they depend from
description: Dependent claims are always narrower than the claim from which they depend; a dependent claim may only narrow the scope of the claim to which it refers not broaden it.
guidance: Anti-pattern: dependent claim that subtracts an element (e.g., 'wherein the light is not attached to the pencil') is improper. Dependent claims cannot extend scope; they can only add limitations or select embodiments to narrow scope. Infringement consequences: a product lacking added feature may infringe the independent claim but not the dependent one.

name: Three basic ways dependent claims narrow parent claims
description: Immediately after the reference to another claim, a dependent claim states at least one additional feature that is not present in that other claim by: (i) adding at least one new element (further comprising E); (ii) selecting at least one element from a broader element (wherein E is E1) or further characterizing an element; or (iii) a combination of (i) and (ii).
guidance: Use these formats deliberately to capture narrower fallback positions (examples: adding a light, specifying that the light is an LED, or both). Ensure each dependent claim contains at least one additional limiting feature.

name: Grouping and arrangement of dependent claims for readability
description: Dependent claims should be grouped together in the most appropriate way possible. The arrangement must enable a ready reckoning and construction of the association of related claims and their meaning.
guidance: Organize dependent claims so related limitations and dependency chains are clear (claim trees). Good arrangement aids prosecution, amendment and later interpretation; poor grouping increases examination and litigation complexity.

name: Dependent claims as fallback strategy and amendment practice
description: Patent drafters commonly prepare a combination of broad and narrow claims as fallback positions. If an examiner finds prior art denying patentability to a broad independent claim, narrower dependent claims may still be allowable. A dependent claim can be rewritten to become independent by specifically reciting all limitations of the former parent claim.
guidance: Example procedure: cancel rejected independent claim and rewrite an allowable dependent claim as a new independent claim (reciting all limitations). When amending, use appropriate amendment format (show deletions/insertions) and ensure amendments do not introduce new matter; check jurisdictional amendment rules (Module IX referenced).

name: Multiple dependent claims: format and meaning
description: Multiple dependent claims refer to more than one claim in the alternative (e.g., 'the apparatus of Claim 1 or Claim 2'). Such a claim depends from either Claim 1 or Claim 2 but not both, and the body must narrow the claim from which it depends.
guidance: Multiple dependent claims cover alternative bases; they reduce the countable number of claims in some systems. Ensure the wording indicates alternatives (accepted variants listed). Remember legal effects: an accused apparatus must meet one of the alternatives to infringe.

name: Pros and cons of multiple dependent claims (fee and amendment considerations)
description: Multiple dependency format usually reduces the countable number of claims, which can influence a client's decision because of cost structures. In the United States, multiple dependent claims trigger extra claim fees and are uncommon; at the EPO they may save fees because of counting rules. Multiple dependent claims can also make justifying amendments easier in some jurisdictions.
guidance: Choose multiple dependency when it provides fee or amendment advantages for the jurisdictions of interest. Consider that multiple dependent claims may complicate reading and amendment in jurisdictions that disallow certain formats; check local practice on multiple-multiple dependents.

name: Multiple-multiple dependent claims: jurisdictional permissibility and caution
description: Multiple-multiple dependent claims (claims that depend in multiple-dependent format from other multiple-dependent claims) are permissible in some jurisdictions (EPO, Japan) and not in others (US, Korea). Excessive use risks producing claims that combine many referred features and become difficult to comprehend.
guidance: Avoid unnecessary multiple-multiple dependencies; they complicate the application and can reduce clarity. Use sparingly and only when jurisdictional rules and strategic benefits justify them.

name: Wording that creates cumulative/impermissible references is not allowed
description: Wording that would cause the claims to become cumulative is not permitted, for example 'according to Claims 1 and 2', 'according to Claims 1–3', 'as in Claims 1, 2 and/or 3', etc.
guidance: Craft multiple references in the alternative (e.g., 'Claims 1 or 2' or 'any one of Claims 1–3') rather than conjunctive language that could be treated as cumulative/impermissible. Be mindful of EPO selection concerns when combining characteristics across claims unless specifically disclosed.

name: Definitional references for computer-implemented and cross-type claims
description: A definitional reference to another claim is frequently used for computer-implemented inventions: e.g., a method Claim 1 recites steps (i)–(x); a data-processing apparatus claim may read 'means for carrying out the method as defined in Claim 1'; a computer program product claim may read 'instructions which, when executed, cause the computer to carry out the method as defined in Claim 1.'
guidance: Use definitional references to obtain comprehensive protection across claim types (method, apparatus, program product, storage medium). Ensure such cross-reference structure is permissible in target jurisdictions and that the referenced claim supports the definition.

name: EPO-specific rule: product patentability can imply process novelty when process inevitably produces product
description: In some jurisdictions, such as the EPO, if a claimed process results in a product defined by a product claim and if the product claim is patentable, no separate examination for the novelty and nonobviousness of the process claim is necessary, provided all features of the product inevitably result from the claimed process.
guidance: Where applicable, this principle can simplify prosecution for process claims tied to patentable products. Do not assume cross-implication in jurisdictions without this doctrine; verify local practice.

name: Dependent claims can support broader interpretation of independent claims (specification support/enablement concern)
description: Dependent claims can be used to support a broader interpretation of independent claims. For example, an independent Claim 1 reciting 'a box' and dependent Claim 2 reciting 'wherein the box is wooden' can make it clearer that Claim 1 includes boxes of any material; however, an opponent may argue lack of support in the specification for nonwooden boxes.
guidance: While dependent claims may help argue that the independent claim covers broader embodiments, drafters should ensure the specification supports such breadth and consider enablement; reliance on examiner’s prior consideration of enablement may be part of the patentee’s argument.

name: Markush claims and dependent claims narrowing Markush groups
description: Where an independent Claim 1 is a Markush claim, a typical dependent claim may define a narrower subset of the Markush group (e.g., specifying R1 is methyl). Dependent claims can further narrow successive selections from a Markush group.
guidance: When specific combinations of selections are commercially important, consider dependent or multiple dependent formats that explicitly claim those combinations to avoid selection objections (particularly at the EPO). Multiple dependent claims can permit covering combinations without enumerating many single dependent claims.

name: Use of set theory/claim trees to visualize scopes and dependencies
description: Claims can be usefully represented as sets (Venn diagrams) to illustrate the logical relationships between independent and dependent claims and between a claim and its embodiments. A claim marks the boundaries (scope) of technical subject matter in peripheral claiming systems.
guidance: Use claim trees and set diagrams to plan claim scope, dependencies and to visualize overlaps, subsets and dependency chains. This helps detect missing combinations (e.g., specific A1+B3 combination not claimed) and to plan dependent claim placements.

name: Jurisdictional limits on number and categories of independent claims and fee consequences
description: Some jurisdictions require that the number of independent claims be limited to one in each category (e.g., one independent product claim and one independent process claim within one application at the EPO), discouraging filing many independent claims. The USPTO charges fees for each additional independent claim beyond an initial three.
guidance: Plan claim drafting to conform to jurisdictional limits and fee structures. Consider exceptions allowed by a jurisdiction (examples given for EPO), and weigh whether multiple dependent formatting or grouping can reduce fees or comply with limits.

name: Graham factual inquiries — Scope and content of the prior art
description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art is a basic factual inquiry in the Graham framework for obviousness.
guidance: Office personnel must first obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading the specification (including claims) and give the claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. Once scope is determined, determine what to search for and where to search. See MPEP §904 and §2111.

name: Graham factual inquiries — Differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
description: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
guidance: Office personnel must explain why the differences would or would not render the claim nonobvious; the mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness.

name: Claim construction — Broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Claims must be given the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification' when determining the scope of the claimed invention for obviousness purposes.
guidance: Read the specification (including embodiments and disclosure) to understand what has been invented; see Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111 for guidance.

name: Obviousness analysis must consider all claim limitations
description: All claim limitations must be considered when making an obviousness determination.
guidance: Do not ignore any limitation; explain how each limitation is taught, suggested, or would have been combined or otherwise rendered predictable to the person of ordinary skill.

name: Defects in letters-patent and amendments
description: DEFECTS — mode of removing from existing arts is a new art; defects in letters-patent not curable by strained interpretation; amendment provisions.
guidance: Addresses which defects in a patent or specification can be cured by amendment or interpretation and which are incurable; cross-references include Ambiguity, Amendment, Claim, Construction, Description, Errors, Letters-Patent, Re-issues, Substance and Form.

name: Describing without claiming leads to abandonment
description: DESCRIBING AND NOT CLAIMING — when describing and not claiming, may constitute abandonment.
guidance: Describing an invention in the specification but failing to claim it can lead to abandonment (but not necessarily ipso facto abandonment in all circumstances); relates to re-issues and public abandonment doctrines.

name: Description and claim both essential
description: DESCRIPTION AND CLAIM — both essential to patent; distinct; how written; must correspond; claim controls; contradictory matter may void both; claim cannot be enlarged by description.
guidance: Detailed requirements and rules: the specification and the claims are both essential and distinct; they must correspond and be consistent; a claim controls construction; contradictory description and claim may be void; description cannot be used to enlarge the claim. Cross-references: Ambiguity, Application for Patent, Claim, Drawings, Re-issues, Specification.

name: Disclaimer as method of amending/correcting patents
description: DISCLAIMER — object and character; a mode of amending a defective patent; distinction between disclaimer and re-issue; may cure excessive claims; may relinquish claimed method; cannot enlarge scope; must be filed without unreasonable delay; estoppel effects.
guidance: Twofold purpose: to amend defective patents and to save otherwise lost suits. Statutory/regulatory constraints exist; disclaimer amends only excessive claims and cannot correct certain substantive mistakes; must be timely and without fraud; effects limited territorially and to interests of disclaimant; becomes part of original specification and leaves patent as if originally issued in amended form; may estop parties. Cross-references: Amendment, Re-issues, Claims, Estoppel, Patent Office practice.

name: Drawings for Patent Office
description: DRAWINGS — when required; necessity/sufficiency determined by Commissioner; must correspond with specification; cannot supply place of written description; must be clear and full to supply place of model; must show every feature claimed.
guidance: Drawings may show invention where specification fails but cannot replace a written description; imperfect drawings can create fatal ambiguity; need not be working drawings; signature and requisites vary by class of invention; drawings generally cannot be amended in the Office; may be withdrawn after filing; not evidence of reduction to practice.

name: Elements of combination — identity and claim effect
description: ELEMENTS OF COMBINATION — defined; distinct from the combination as inventions; an unnecessary part is not an element unless so claimed; elements described and claimed make them essential.
guidance: Elements of a combination are distinct units; once claimed they become essential whether actually essential or not; unclaimed elements are conceded old; joinder with claims for combinations and subcombinations; re-issue considerations; use of less than all elements may not be infringement.

name: Two-step inquiry for anticipation and obviousness
description: "[B]oth anticipation under §102 and obviousness under §103 are two-step inquiries. The first step in both analyses is a proper construction of the claims ... The second step in the analyses requires a comparison of the properly construed claim to the prior art." (Medichem v. Rolabo cited)
guidance: Claim construction must be performed before comparing claim scope to the prior art; errors in either step can determine the outcome.

name: Claims interpreted as broadly as their terms reasonably allow
description: Claims must be interpreted as broadly as their terms reasonably allow. (In re Zletz, 893 F.2d 319, 321)
guidance: The Board follows the principle that claim terms are given their ordinary meaning unless the specification fixes a special definition.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill
description: "The words of a claim 'are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning.' ... The 'ordinary and customary meaning of a claim term is the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art ... as of the effective filing date." (Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
guidance: Unless the specification discloses a special definition, the common meaning is used in claim construction and in comparing to prior art.

name: In re Nuijten: consider statutory classes for signals
description: In the analysis of In re Nuijten, the Federal Circuit considers the four statutory classes for a signal, and bases determination of statutory subject matter on that basis.
guidance: When claims involve transitory signals or similar matter, consider the statutory class analysis from Nuijten in assessing §101 issues.

name: Combination of software components embodied on a computer-readable medium can be statutory (In re Lowry)
description: The combination of software components embodied upon a computer readable medium has been found statutory under the teachings of In re Lowry, 32 F.3d 1579 (Fed. Cir., 1994).
guidance: This precedent supports the view that a claimed combination of modules on a medium may satisfy §101 where the claims recite tangible embodiment.

name: Examiner must present a prima facie case; applicant may rebut
description: The record supports the following findings ... The Examiner has presented a prima facie case for the rejections of Appellant's claims under 35 U.S.C. §§101 and 103. ... On appeal to the Board, an applicant can overcome a rejection by showing insufficient evidence of prima facie obviousness or by rebutting the prima facie case with evidence of secondary indicia of nonobviousness. (Kahn; Rouffet cited)
guidance: If the Examiner presents a prima facie case, the applicant must present evidence or arguments (including secondary considerations) to rebut that case.

name: Naming/labeling functional modules does not negate obviousness
description: The naming of a module by certain nomenclature, for example 'configuration file processing module', does not render the module structurally or functionally unobvious.
guidance: Merely reciting module names or labels in claims is insufficient to show nonobviousness if the underlying functionality is taught or obvious in the prior art.

name: Common-meaning of technical terms can be relied upon absent special definition
description: We find the common meaning of the word, absent any special and express definition in the Specification, to be suggested by Shaughnessy. (See Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
guidance: Examiners and the Board may apply the ordinary technical meaning of claim terms unless the specification supplies a special definition; do not rely on idiosyncratic gloss without specification support.

name: Format and content of the requirement (identify rule and basis)
description: The requirement must clearly indicate that it is being made under 37 CFR 1.105, state the basis for the requirement, and specify the information being required.
guidance: Requirements should specify particular art areas and particular claimed subject matter to avoid overbroad requests; indicate the form the required information is expected to take (citations/copies, identification of collections, answers to questions, etc.). Preferably prepared as a separate document (though the rule permits inclusion within an Office action).

name: Form paragraph 7.120 — Names of Products or Services Incorporating Disclosed Prior Art
description: Require names of any products or services incorporating the disclosed prior art, with bracket specifying attributes of prior art approximating the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126; use bracket to narrow focus of reply.

name: Limitation on use of Patentability Reports — when not proper
description: PR practice is not obligatory and should be used only where it will save total examiner time or improve action quality due to specialized knowledge; PR is not proper where claims are related as manufacturing process and product, product and process that merely makes the product, or combination distinguished solely by characteristics of a subcombination.
guidance: Where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ only in scope, PR prosecution is never proper. PR permitted only with Director approval where it demonstrably saves total examiner time.

name: Entry of court decisions and litigation papers
description: The Solicitor’s Office will process notices required by 35 U.S.C. 290 and will accept copies of notices of suits, other proceedings involving the patent, and decisions from litigations for placement in the patent file.
guidance: Acceptable items include final court decisions, decisions to vacate or remand, and decisions as to the merits of patent claims. Non‑merit decisions (venue, discovery dates, sanctions) will not be entered and will be expunged. Papers that provide party arguments (e.g., memoranda in support of summary judgment) will not be entered unless they have entry rights in the reexamination proceeding; such material must be submitted via the rule‑provided vehicle. If the volume is excessive, the Office may return/expunge/discard all or part of the submission. Submissions must be bare notice without additional comment or argument; highlighting or underlining goes beyond bare notice.

name: 37 CFR 1.510(b) required elements of a request
description: Any request for ex parte reexamination must include: (1) a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability; (2) identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested with a detailed explanation of pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to each claim; (3) a copy of every patent or printed publication relied upon, with English translations of necessary parts of non‑English documents; (4) a copy of the entire patent (front face, drawings, specification/claims) in double column format and any disclaimer/certificates; (5) a certification that a copy of the request filed by a non‑owner was served on the patent owner (name/address indicated).
guidance: Form PTO/SB/57 is encouraged as a transmittal. A requester must list cited prior art in a comprehensive manner (37 CFR 1.98 listing). Copies must be plainly written on only one side of the paper. See MPEP §2214–§2219 for detailed guidance on each element.

name: Explanation and application requirement for each SNQ and proposed ground
description: For each identified substantial new question of patentability and each proposed ground of rejection, the request must explain how the cited documents are applied to meet or teach the patent claim limitations to establish the SNQ or proposed ground.
guidance: The request must apply all of the cited prior art to the claims for which reexamination is requested. The requester may also point out how claims distinguish over cited prior art if appropriate (patent owner may do so).

name: Document copy and format requirements
description: Copies of every cited patent or printed publication and a copy of the entire patent sought to be reexamined must be supplied; non‑English documents must have translations of the necessary parts.
guidance: The patent copy should reproduce the printed patent (front page, abstract, drawings, specification, claims) in double column format, on only one side of each sheet. Include any disclaimer, certificate of correction, or reexamination certificate issued in the patent.

name: Scope limitation on claim enlargement
description: The scope of a claim cannot be enlarged by amendment in an ex parte reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Amendments must not broaden claim scope; reexamination is focused on re‑evaluating patentability under SNQs.

name: Benefit claims and effective filing date determination
description: In determining a pre‑AIA 102(e) date, consider benefit claims to earlier‑filed U.S. provisional, nonprovisional, and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), and 386(c) only if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the earlier application's disclosure (and any intermediate applications).
guidance: A benefit claim to a U.S. patent issuing from an earlier‑filed international application (with international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000) may only result in an effective U.S. filing date as of the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1),(2) and (4) were fulfilled. Do NOT consider benefit claims to U.S. applications filed before an international application that has an international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)‑(d), 365(a) or (b), or 386(a) or (b).

name: Provisional application support requirement for benefit
description: A reference (U.S. patent, published U.S. patent application, or WIPO publication) is entitled to the benefit of the filing date of a provisional application only if at least one of the claims in the reference is supported by the written description of the provisional application in compliance with pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph or 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: See Dynamic Drinkware v. National Graphics and Amgen v. Sanofi for case law on provisional support; ensure claim support in the provisional before attributing its filing date to the reference.

name: Use of form paragraphs and paragraph precedence
description: Certain rejections must be preceded by specific form paragraphs before applying a 102(e) rejection paragraph.
guidance: Examples: ¶7.15.02.fti/7.15.03.fti must be preceded by 7.12.fti or 7.12.01.fti; patent application publications may only be used if preceded by 7.12.fti; for applications with filing date on/after Mar.16,2013 claiming priority/benefit to pre‑Mar.16,2013 filings, paragraph 7.06 must precede. Insert appropriate wording in brackets per instructions (e.g., --assignee--, --applicant--, or --joint inventor--).

name: Rejection for applicant not being the inventor (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f))
description: Claims may be rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) where the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.19.fti must be preceded by paragraphs 7.07.fti and 7.13.fti or 7.103. Insert explanation of supporting evidence establishing that the applicant was not the inventor (see MPEP §2137).

name: Graham factual inquiries to resolve obviousness
description: Obviousness is a legal conclusion based on underlying factual inquiries: (A) scope and content of the prior art; (B) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
guidance: Include objective evidence (secondary considerations) such as commercial success, long‑felt need, failure of others, unexpected results when present; weight is case‑by‑case. These factors control any obviousness analysis.

name: Determining scope and content of the prior art (search guidance)
description: Obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading specification and claims (give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification). The search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed.
guidance: Follow general search guidelines in MPEP §904‑§904.03. Prior art may be in the applicant's field or reasonably pertinent (analogous art). Searches should prefer references that provide teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine if such exist.

name: Ascertaining differences between claim and prior art
description: Interpret claim language and consider both the invention and prior art as a whole to ascertain differences.
guidance: See MPEP §2111 for claim interpretation and MPEP §2141.02 for considering invention and prior art as a whole.

name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence and secondary considerations
description: Office personnel must consider all timely rebuttal evidence, including secondary considerations such as commercial success, long‑felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results, when reevaluating an obviousness determination.
guidance: Applicants may submit evidence to rebut factual findings; Office personnel should articulate factual findings that support the rationale relied upon. Examples of rebuttal arguments include demonstrating technological difficulties that would have prevented one of ordinary skill from combining claimed elements by known methods.

name: State whether a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: USPTO directs examiners to 'state more consistently whether a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f)'.
guidance: Examiners should explicitly indicate in their analysis whether a given claim limitation is governed by 112(f) (means-plus-function or step-plus-function treatment) rather than leaving that determination implicit.

name: Provide detailed evaluation of adequacy of supporting disclosure
description: Examiners should 'provide a more detailed evaluation of the adequacy of the supporting disclosure.'
guidance: When a limitation is treated under 112(f), the examiner must evaluate whether the specification discloses corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function and must discuss equivalents; this evaluation should be clear and detailed so applicants and courts understand the basis for the determination.

name: Recognize benefits of drafting limitations that comply with 112(f)
description: ‘Drafting claims with limitations that comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) can be beneficial to applicants by allowing them to recite a function in a claim and rely on the specification for the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the function and equivalents…’
guidance: Means/step-plus drafting can serve as shorthand to point to a more robust description in the specification and to capture equivalents, but this must be balanced against risks (see other criteria).

name: Include sufficient structural support in the specification for means/generic placeholders
description: If terms such as 'means for' are used, 'the corresponding specification should include sufficient structural support.'
guidance: Patent drafters should ensure the specification identifies the structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function (and preferably their equivalents) so that reliance on 112(f) is supported; lack of such support can trigger rejections or invalidity challenges.

name: Avoid or carefully draft non-structural terms that could be construed as generic placeholders
description: An increase in Examiner interpretations of claim elements under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) 'most likely will occur based on the use of non-structural terms' and 'if there is a possibility that a term could be construed to be a “generic placeholder... for performing a claimed function”' practitioners should act accordingly.
guidance: When using non-structural wording, anticipate 112(f) treatment; either rephrase to include structure or ensure the specification supplies clear structure/acts to avoid unintended means/step-plus-function treatment.

name: Ensure the specification’s description does not unduly limit the generic placeholder
description: Practitioners should 'assess that such description, while sufficient, does not unduly limit the alleged “generic placeholder.”'
guidance: Draft structural support broadly enough to preserve intended claim scope; explanatory examples or multiple embodiments may help avoid unintentionally narrowing the claimed generic term to only the disclosed structure.

name: Watch for claim language formats that may invoke 112(f) (e.g., 'for' or 'configured to')
description: ‘As always, consideration should be given to description of terms in claims followed by “for” or “configured to,” for example.’
guidance: Terms followed by 'for' or 'configured to' can be treated as functional language triggering 112(f). Drafters should consider whether to recast such language to include structural detail or to ensure specification support is present.

name: Understand risks from failing to include structural support or recognize potential 112(f) interpretations
description: ‘Failing to recognize these potential interpretations, as well as failing to include at least some structural support, could lead to enhanced risks of arguments of indefiniteness, lack of enablement, or lack of written description support in an application or granted patent.’
guidance: Be aware that inadequate structure or unexpected 112(f) treatment can expose claims to multiple challenges — indefiniteness, lack of enablement, and insufficient written description — and plan drafting and prosecution strategy to mitigate these risks.

name: Anticipation (anticipating prior art)
description: For a claim to be invalid for lack of novelty (anticipation), the alleged infringer must show by clear and convincing evidence that all claim requirements were present in a single previous device, method, printed publication or patent.
guidance: The prior art reference need not use the same words as the claim, but must disclose all claim limitations, either expressly or inherently/impliedly to a person of ordinary skill in the art, so that that person could make and use the claimed invention from that one reference.

name: Inventorship requirement
description: A patent is invalid if it does not name all and only the actual inventors. To be an inventor one must make a significant contribution to the conception of at least one claim, measured against the scope of the full invention.
guidance: Merely explaining well-known concepts or carrying out instructions (experimentation) does not make one an inventor. Co-inventors need not contribute equally or to every claim and may be joint inventors without physically working together, but must have some open line of communication during or around the inventive effort. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 256 and various Federal Circuit cases.

name: Inequitable conduct — duty and elements
description: An applicant has a duty of candor and good faith to the PTO. Inequitable conduct occurs when a person involved in prosecution withholds material information or submits materially false information with intent to deceive the Examiner, rendering any resulting patent unenforceable.
guidance: Burden: alleged infringer must prove by clear and convincing evidence both materiality and intent to deceive. Materiality: information is material if the PTO would not have allowed the claim had it been aware; a false statement is material if it convinces the PTO to allow a claim it would not have otherwise. Affirmative egregious misconduct (e.g., filing an unmistakably false affidavit) is material. Intent: must be shown by direct evidence or inferred only if it is the single most reasonable inference; negligence, oversight, or gross negligence is insufficient. Materiality and intent are separate issues; both must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

name: Damages — general principles
description: If infringement of a valid claim is found, damages must adequately compensate the patent holder (not punish) and put the patent holder in approximately the position it would have been absent infringement. Patent holder bears the burden to establish damages by a preponderance of the evidence and must prove them with reasonable certainty (not mere speculation).
guidance: Different types of damages include lost profits and reasonable royalties. Damages must be tied to the intrinsic value of the patented feature (no recovery for remote or speculative consequences). Where damages cannot be ascertained precisely, doubts are resolved against the alleged infringer if the inability is due to the infringer’s own poor recordkeeping. If the patent holder committed to RAND licensing, damages must be consistent with RAND obligations. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 284 and numerous Federal Circuit cases.

name: Evaluate claims for subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101
description: USPTO guidance explains how USPTO personnel, including patent examiners and PTAB administrative patent judges, should evaluate claims for patent subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: The USPTO's current eligibility guidance is found in Section 2103 through 2106.07 of the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP). Apply that guidance when deciding whether claims recite patent-eligible subject matter under the governing law.

name: Use illustrative Examples (Examples 1–49) to inform fact-specific SME analyses
description: Sets of example claim analyses (Examples 1–49) are provided as teaching tools to assist understanding of how the USPTO applies its eligibility guidance in particular fact-specific situations.
guidance: The Examples illustrate exemplary SME analyses across a range of technologies. Analyses issued prior to the current guidance (Examples 1–36) still provide useful illustrations; all claims indicated as eligible in these examples remain eligible under current guidance. See the index of examples for relevance under current guidance.

name: Apply the 2024 AI SME Update for AI-related subject matter
description: The 2024 Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance Update, including guidance specific to artificial intelligence, is part of current USPTO guidance (effective July 17, 2024).
guidance: When evaluating claims involving AI or machine learning, incorporate the AI-specific aspects of the 2024 update (e.g., Examples 47–49 and accompanying explanations) as they reflect current USPTO practice.

name: Language requirements for application elements
description: Any element of the international application, other than the description and claims, must be in an admitted language.
guidance: If elements are not in an admitted language (Article 3(4)(i), Rule 12.1, Rule 26.3ter(a)), the receiving Office may invite correction. Some Offices have incompatibilities with Rule 26.3ter(a); where incompatible, all elements must comply with Rule 12.1 before an international filing date can be accorded (see Annex C).

name: Applicant comments on earlier search results
description: Where an international application claims priority to an earlier application that was searched by the same Office acting as ISA, some ISAs will consider applicant comments on earlier search results when carrying out the international search.
guidance: Applicants wishing that comments be considered should submit them to the receiving Office with the international application (typically by checking Box No. IX, sub‑box 'Other' and indicating 'Informal comments on earlier search results'). Such informal comments will be transmitted to the ISA and IB and will be published on PATENTSCOPE. Check Annex D for which ISAs offer this service (paragraph 7.002A).

name: Purpose and basis of the international search
description: The purpose of the international search is to discover relevant prior art — everything made available to the public by written disclosure — that can help determine novelty, inventive step (obviousness), and prior public availability before the international filing date.
guidance: The international search is made on the basis of the claims, with due regard to the description and drawings. Results are set out in the international search report (Article 15(4), Rule 33).

name: Requirements for merged proceedings (identical claims and filings)
description: Where merger is ordered, the decision should include a requirement that the patent owner maintain identical claims in both files and require that responses/comments be a single response/comment paper addressed to both files, filed in duplicate and signed for entry in both files.
guidance: If claims are not identical at the time of merger, the patent owner is given one month to provide an amendment to make the claims the same in each file (a 'housekeeping' amendment). The housekeeping amendment must not address any issue of patentability. Failure to timely submit identical amendments may result in rejection of any non-identical claim under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as indefinite.

name: Claims define scope of a patent
description: The scope of a patent is defined by its 'claims.' Examiners evaluate whether the invention described in the claims meets statutory patentability requirements.
guidance: Claim drafting determines exclusionary reach; examination focuses on the claims rather than broader specification.

name: Continuation practice and limits
description: U.S. applicants can file continuation applications repeatedly, with no limit, enabling patentees to pursue broader claims over time.
guidance: Continuations allow strategic hedging but also encourage applicants to file early and then seek broader scope later; reform proposals include limiting continuation practice to prevent abuse.

name: Doctrine of equivalents and scope expansion limits
description: The doctrine of equivalents can permit patentees to expand a patent's reach beyond literal claim language; courts have been moving to place limits on this doctrine.
guidance: Limiting the doctrine reduces post-grant expansion of scope and litigation uncertainty.

name: Cannot claim beyond method described
description: A patentee 'could not claim beyond the method actually described' in the specification.
guidance: Example: Bovill's ventilation-vanes patent did not cover Pimm's fan-in-centre method; each inventor entitled to protection only in respect of the method disclosed in their respective specifications.

name: Bound to the precise claim language (literal construction)
description: A patentee is bound to the claim as described; if the specification confines the claim to a particular form, the patentee cannot assert a broader combination than that described.
guidance: Example: plaintiff who claimed only the combination 'with a catch-plate as described' was held bound to that limited claim; defendant not using a catch-plate did not infringe (Boyd v. Horrocks).

name: Claim-construction dilemma: wide reading vs narrow reading
description: If the patentee's claim is read widely so as to cover the alleged infringement it may be anticipated; if read narrowly to avoid anticipation there may be no infringement.
guidance: Defendants often force patentees into this dilemma: broad claim risks invalidity for anticipation; narrow claim risks no infringement. Cases cited: Stevens v. Keating, Dowernes v. Falcon Works, Gosnell v. Bishop, Hutchison v. Patullo.

name: Subordinate parts not protected unless expressly claimed and patentable
description: Subordinate parts and minor combinations will not be protected unless they are expressly claimed, and when claimed must be new, useful, and patentable.
guidance: A patentee must make it plain in the specification that he intends protection for subordinate integers; absent express claim and patentability of the part itself, protection for parts is limited.

name: Manufacture/export of parts of a combination may infringe if part is new and claimed
description: When a patent is for a new combination made of old parts, manufacture of separate parts and exportation may be infringement if the part so made is new and is claimed as new.
guidance: Goucher v. Clayton held that making and exporting a part abroad could be an infringement where the part was new and claimed in the patent.

name: Chemical equivalents and the date-of-knowledge test
description: Use of a chemical equivalent may amount to infringement if either the specification covers equivalents or the equivalent was known to be such at the date of the patent; if an equivalent was not known at the patent date and the patentee claimed a specific substance, later equivalents may not infringe.
guidance: Heath v. Unwin: House of Lords held no infringement where defendant used component parts that produced carburet during operation but the patentee had claimed a specific metallic carburet and equivalents were not known at the patent date. Court examines whether patentee limited claim to particular substance and whether equivalents were known.

name: Specific-material claim limits scope; different materials may avoid infringement
description: Where the specification confines the claim to a particular material or mode of use, the use of a different material/process may not be infringement unless the judge/jury find them to be equivalents.
guidance: Examples: Talbot v. Laroche (collodion process vs. gallic-acid-prepared paper) — jury asked whether collodion use was the same; verdict found no infringement. The court asks whether the substitute is 'the same' or a 'chemical equivalent'.

name: Petition specificity requirement (identify claims, grounds, evidence)
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 312(a)(3)/322(a)(3) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.22(a)(2)/42.204(b)(4), the petition must identify in writing and with particularity each claim challenged, the grounds for the challenge to each claim, and the evidence supporting the grounds; where grounds are based on prior art, the petition must specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art.
guidance: The Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where a party fails to state relevance or to identify specific portions of evidence supporting the challenge (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104(b)(5), 42.204(b)(5)). Provide a full statement of the reasons for relief requested, including detailed explanation of the significance of the evidence, material facts, and governing law, rules, and precedent.

name: Horizontal redundancy — multiple references as interchangeable alternatives
description: Horizontal redundancy occurs when a plurality of prior art references are presented as distinct alternatives that each provide essentially the same teaching for the same claim limitation without explaining why one reference better satisfies the limitation than another.
guidance: If references are not identical, the petition must explain why each reference is preferable in some respect; otherwise the references will be collectively viewed as horizontally redundant and not entitled to consideration.

name: Board will resolve vagueness and ambiguity against petitioner
description: In evaluating petitions the Board will address only the basis, rationale, and reasoning put forth by the petitioner and will resolve vagueness and ambiguity in the petition against the petitioner.
guidance: Avoid vague or ambiguous explanations of how references are combined or how claim elements map to prior art; unclear reasoning will result in denial of grounds prior to institution (see CBM2012-00003, notice 8).

name: Motion to enlarge petition page limits (interests of justice standard)
description: Rule 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)(2) allows motions to waive petition page limits, but petitioner must show in the motion how a waiver is 'in the interests of justice.'
guidance: To succeed, petitioner must meaningfully explain why limitations of the challenged claims could not be addressed within the standard page limit (e.g., why claim complexity requires more pages), show that additional references are not cumulative, and provide concrete examples of content that cannot fit within the page limit. Historically, such motions are rarely granted.

name: Claim chart usage and single-spacing exception
description: Claim charts may be single spaced and may be used to provide the element-by-element showing of where claim elements are found in prior art (per 37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(2)(iii)).
guidance: Claim charts should be limited to the permitted element-by-element showings; placing full argumentative text in claim charts to avoid double-spacing is improper and may be rejected.

name: The European Patent Application (Part F)
description: Part F — The European Patent Application (content requirements for the application other than claims, abstract checklist, units, sufficiency, claims, unity, priority).
guidance: Part heading; detailed substantive drafting standards are in the chapters.

name: Claims (Article 84 and formal requirements)
description: Claims (Art. 84 and formal requirements) (Part F, Chapter IV).
guidance: Form, clarity, support and formal requirements for claims under Article 84.

name: Claim construction is a matter of law for the court (Markman)
description: In a case tried to a jury, the court has the power and obligation to construe as a matter of law the meaning of language used in the patent claim; construction of a patent claim is a matter of law exclusively for the court.
guidance: Cites Markman v. Westview Instruments and the Supreme Court affirmance: courts, not juries, interpret the legal meaning of claim language.

name: Give words their ordinary and customary meaning (Phillips)
description: The words of a claim 'are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning,' i.e., the meaning a term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art after reviewing the intrinsic record at the time of the invention.
guidance: In many cases ordinary meaning is readily apparent; in others, terms with a particular meaning in the art require examination of intrinsic evidence (specification, prosecution history).

name: O2 Micro rule — court must resolve actual disputes about claim scope
description: ‘When the parties raise an actual dispute regarding the proper scope of these claims, the court, not the jury, must resolve that dispute.’
guidance: If parties present a dispute as to meaning or whether a term allows exceptions, the ordinary meaning may not resolve it and the court must determine claim scope for use in infringement determination.

name: A determination that a term 'needs no construction' may be inadequate
description: A determination that a claim term 'needs no construction' or has the 'plain and ordinary meaning' may be inadequate when a term has more than one 'ordinary' meaning or when reliance on a term's 'ordinary' meaning does not resolve the parties' dispute.
guidance: Courts should avoid simply leaving ambiguous or multi-meaning terms to the jury; if the ordinary meaning doesn't resolve the dispute, perform claim construction.

name: Court not required to construe every limitation
description: District courts are not (and should not be) required to construe every limitation present in a patent's asserted claims; claim construction is a matter of resolution of disputed meanings and technical scope to clarify what the patentee covered.
guidance: Reserve construction for limitations that are actually disputed or necessary to clarify scope for the factfinder; avoid unnecessary constructions.

name: Do not construe when dispute is factual application rather than legal scope
description: If the parties merely have a factual—not legal—dispute as to a claim term (e.g., whether accused products fall within a construed meaning or whether prior art meets a limitation), that is for the jury (or factfinder) and not for claim construction.
guidance: Frame disputes appropriately: factual disputes about application should be presented as such to avoid O2 Micro invocation.

name: Plain and ordinary meaning acceptable when no dispute as to scope
description: Courts are not required to construe terms beyond their plain and ordinary meaning if there is no dispute as to scope or if a narrower proposed construction is rejected in favor of plain and ordinary meaning.
guidance: Examples: when experts' testimony shows the term was not fundamentally in dispute; when proposed constructions improperly read limitations into the claims.

name: Over-reliance on 'plain and ordinary meaning' can be litigation misconduct
description: A party's blanket reliance on plain and ordinary meaning for all claim terms and failure to engage in the claim construction process in good faith can support a finding of litigation misconduct.
guidance: Ensure parties meaningfully participate in claim construction and do not submit incomplete or misleading extrinsic evidence while claiming no construction is necessary.

name: O2 Micro applies at various stages and forums (motions, pleadings, PTAB, IPRs, reexams)
description: O2 Micro's duty to resolve actual disputes regarding claim scope applies at the motion to dismiss stage, in Article I tribunals (PTAB/IPRs), and in ex parte reexamination contexts—not only at Markman hearings or Article III final judgments.
guidance: Practitioners should consider claim-construction disputes early, as they may be outcome-determinative at pleading or administrative stages.

name: Waiver if O2 Micro challenges not timely brought
description: O2 Micro challenges are waived if not timely brought—parties cannot create a new claim construction dispute after close of the jury trial or on appeal if they failed to present proposed constructions at or prior to trial/Markman.
guidance: Raise construction positions at Markman or otherwise clearly and timely in pretrial proceedings; late-first-time appeals of constructions are routinely rejected as waived.

name: Appellate remedies for O2 Micro errors vary based on prejudice and record
description: If a district court fails to resolve an actual claim-scope dispute, remedies range from vacatur and remand for new proceedings to reversal of the verdict; remand is not always required if the error is harmless and the verdict is supported under the proper construction.
guidance: Whether to remand depends on whether the jury could have reasonably applied the proper construction and whether prejudice resulted from the court's failure to construe.

name: Strategic framing: present disputes as legal or factual depending on desired outcome
description: Practitioners should frame their arguments to the court in the light that best advances their position: to obtain a court construction under O2 Micro, argue the matter is a legal dispute of claim meaning/scope; to keep an issue for the jury, emphasize it is factual application.
guidance: Careful advocacy can determine whether an issue is decided by judge (claim construction) or jury (application). Avoid over-reliance on 'no construction' positions.

name: Know the O2 Micro landscape and judicial variability
description: Practitioners should be aware of varying Federal Circuit viewpoints—some judges are more reluctant to find claim-scope disputes—and account for differing approaches when arguing disputes.
guidance: Anticipate that some judges (per dissents) may treat expert disagreements over 'plain and ordinary meaning' as factual and resist converting them into legal disputes; tailor arguments accordingly.

name: Linking claims prevent restriction if allowable
description: Linking claims are claims which, if allowable, would require rejoinder of otherwise divisible inventions and thus prevent restriction between those inventions.
guidance: Common linking claims include genus claims linking species claims and subcombination claims linking plural combinations. If a linking claim is allowable, the restriction between linked inventions must be withdrawn; nonelected claims that depend from or require all limitations of an allowable linking claim must be rejoined and fully examined. If restriction is predicated upon nonallowability of linking claims, applicant may retain nonelected claims.

name: Treatment of linking claims (examination and rejoinder)
description: Linking claims must be examined with and are considered part of the elected invention. When all claims directed to the elected invention are allowable, should any linking claim be allowable the restriction must be withdrawn and appropriate rejoinder conducted.
guidance: Upon indication of allowability of linking claims, cancelations may be reinstated by amendment and will be examined in accordance with 37 CFR 1.104; amendments before final rejection or allowance are entered as a matter of right; later amendments governed by 37 CFR 1.116 and 1.312. Warning: claims in continuations/divisionals that are anticipated by or include all limitations of an allowable linking claim may be subject to provisional statutory and/or nonstatutory double patenting rejections over the instant application's claims. When a restriction is withdrawn, 35 U.S.C. 121 provisions no longer apply.

name: Election of species: identify generic claims and species; require election under 35 U.S.C.121
description: Where restriction between species is appropriate, the examiner should identify generic claims (or state none present), clearly identify each disclosed species to which claims are to be restricted, and require applicant to elect a single disclosed species under 35 U.S.C. 121.
guidance: Species are preferably identified by figures or examples; if absent, state mechanical means, particular material, or other distinguishing characteristic. If species cannot be conveniently identified, group claims by species. Provide reasons why the species are independent or distinct. Advise applicant of requisites of a complete reply and of rights under 37 CFR 1.141. A reply should include a proper election and listing of all claims readable thereon; arguments that a claim is allowable or that all claims are generic are non-responsive unless accompanied by an election.

name: Contents and completeness of restriction requirement letter (outline A–E)
description: Restriction requirement letters must provide a clear, detailed record demarcating restricted inventions and include specified sections (statement of requirement/statute, identification/grouping of claims, descriptions, classification, disposition of ungrouped claims, reasons for independence/distinctness, reasons for insisting on restriction, and summary).
guidance: Outline: (A) Statement of requirement and that it is under 35 U.S.C. 121; (1) identify groups; (2) list claims in each group; (3) short description of subject matter for each group and type (product/process/subcombination); (4) classify each group. (B) Account for claims not grouped (linking, other ungrouped claims, disposition). (C) Allegation of independence/distinctness with facts and demonstration (subcombination vs combination, process vs apparatus, etc.). (D) Provide reasons for insisting upon restriction (see separate items). (E) Summary statement covering independence/distinctness and reasons, advising as to reply required, and indicating effects of allowance/cancellation of linking/evidence/product claims. Use appropriate form paragraphs (8.14–8.20.02; 8.01/8.02 for species).

name: Telephone restriction practice procedures
description: If an examiner determines restriction should be made, formulate a draft indicating linking/generic claims, telephone the attorney/agent to request an oral election (with or without traverse) after they have time to consider, and arrange a follow-up call—generally within 3 working days.
guidance: Do not use telephone where requirement is complex, applicant is pro se, or election won't be made by phone. If attorney/agent objects to oral election or fails to respond, mail a restriction letter referencing the unsuccessful call. When an oral election is made, incorporate into Office action a formal restriction requirement including the election date, attorney/agent name, and a complete record of the telephone interview, followed by a complete action on the elected invention as claimed. Use form paragraphs 8.23/8.23.01 as appropriate.

name: Election and reply requirements; traverses
description: A reply must respond to each point raised by the examiner and may include a traverse or compliance. A traverse is a statement of reasons why applicant believes the restriction is in error and must be complete per 37 CFR 1.111(b). Applicant must make a provisional election even when traversing.
guidance: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the reply must be reduced to writing, distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors, and reply to every ground of objection/rejection. A mere broad allegation that the requirement is in error does not comply; failure to distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors results in the election being treated as an election without traverse. To preserve right of petition (37 CFR 1.144), the applicant must traverse; to reserve right to petition election must be made with traverse. Use form paragraph 8.22 in Office actions containing restriction requirements to inform applicant that reply must include (i) an election and (ii) identification of claims encompassing the elected invention. If traversing on patentable distinctness grounds, submit evidence or identify evidence on record showing obvious variants or clearly admit that case.

name: Make restriction requirement complete and clearly demarcated
description: The examiner must provide a clear and detailed record of the restriction requirement to permit determination whether claims in a continuing application are consonant with the restriction and subject to double patenting prohibitions; particular claim limitations and reasons supporting restriction should be mentioned.
guidance: Read all claims to determine what they cover. Identify separate inventions by grouping claims with short descriptions of total extent of invention claimed in each group, specifying type or relationship (process, subcombination, product, etc.), and indicate classification or separate status (class/subclass). While every claim should be accounted for, omission or misgrouping will not affect a proper final requirement if correct disposition is otherwise clear. Generic/linking claims should not be associated with any one of the linked inventions since they are examined with the elected invention.

name: Claim correspondence presumption
description: For determining priority and derivation, all claims of a party corresponding to the count are presumed to stand or fall together.
guidance: To challenge this presumption, a party must file a timely substantive motion to have a corresponding claim designated as not corresponding to the count. No presumption based on claim correspondence exists for other grounds of unpatentability.

name: Content and permissible subjects of substantive motions in an interference
description: In an interference, substantive motions must: (1) raise a threshold issue; (2) seek to change the scope of the definition of the interfering subject matter or the correspondence of claims to the count; (3) seek to change the benefit accorded for the count; or (4) seek judgment on derivation or on priority.
guidance: Motions must provide a showing, supported with appropriate evidence, such that, if unrebutted, it would justify the relief sought; the burden of proof is on the movant.

name: Sanctions: initiation, motion procedure, and limits
description: If the Board determines that representations to the Board (e.g., certification under § 11.18(b)(2)) have been violated, it may impose an appropriate sanction. A motion for sanctions must be made separately, describe the specific conduct, be authorized by the Board under § 42.20 prior to filing, and the moving party must serve the other party at least 21 days prior to seeking authorization.
guidance: A motion for sanctions must not be filed if the challenged paper/claim/defense is withdrawn or corrected within 21 days after service (or other time set by Board). Board may award reasonable expenses, including attorney’s fees, for the motion if warranted. On its own initiative, the Board may order a show-cause and impose sanctions; sanctions must be limited to what suffices to deter repetition and consistent with § 42.12. An order imposing a sanction must describe the sanctioned conduct and explain the basis.

name: Fees required for filing petitions and related requests
description: Specific fees are due when filing petitions for inter partes review, post-grant review, covered business method review, derivation proceedings, and for certain other requests (e.g., making a settlement agreement available, pro hac vice appearance fee, Director review).
guidance: Fees are set by rule (examples include request and post-institution fees for IPR and PGR; additional per-claim fees for claims over 20; derivation petition fee; fee for counsel not registered to appear pro hac vice; fee for Director review). (The rule text lists the amounts and the circumstances under which each fee is required.)

name: Materials the competent authority may consider when deciding rectification (Rules 91.1(d)–(e))
description: For mistakes in description/claims/drawings (and corrections/amendments) the competent authority shall only take into account the contents of the description, claims, drawings and, where applicable, the correction or amendment. For mistakes in the request part or documents referred to in (b)(iv), the authority shall only take into account the international application itself and any documents submitted with the request/correction/document, any available priority document, and other documents in the authority's international application file at the applicable date.
guidance: Priority documents cannot be used to support obvious mistake corrections to description/claims/drawings. The scope of materials the authority may look at is limited depending on the type of document containing the mistake.

name: Non-rectifiable mistakes under Rule 91.1(g)
description: A mistake shall not be rectifiable if: (i) the mistake lies in the omission of one or more entire elements of the international application referred to in Article 3(2) or one or more entire sheets; (ii) the mistake is in the abstract; (iii) the mistake is in an amendment under Article 19 (unless IPEA competent); or (iv) the mistake is in a priority claim or in a notice correcting/adding a priority claim where rectification would cause a change in the priority date.
guidance: These exclusions prevent using Rule 91 to add omitted whole elements or to alter priority-determining matters; other Rules (e.g., Rules 20.4, 20.5, 26 bis, 38.3) are not affected by this paragraph.

name: Content of the written opinion of the ISA (PCT Rule 43 bis)
description: The written opinion shall state whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step (to be non-obvious), and to be industrially applicable; and whether the international application complies with the Treaty and Regulations in so far as checked by the ISA. It may also include observations on clarity of claims, description and drawings, and whether claims are fully supported by the description.
guidance: The written opinion is an initial, non-binding technical/legal assessment that informs applicants and (if demanded) the IPEA; it may invite a written reply and amendments where appropriate. It also contains notification relevant to making a demand for international preliminary examination.

name: Relevant prior art for the international search (PCT Rule 33)
description: Relevant prior art consists of everything made available to the public anywhere in the world by means of written disclosure (including drawings and other illustrations) and capable of assisting in determining novelty and inventive step, provided the making available occurred prior to the international filing date. Written disclosures that refer to non-written means (oral, use, exhibition) shall be mentioned separately with the date. Published applications or patents whose publication date is same as or later than, but whose filing date or claimed priority date is earlier than, the international filing date, shall be specially mentioned.
guidance: ISAs must search broadly across written disclosures prior to the filing date and flag disclosures that involve or refer to other means of public availability; certain documents with later publication but earlier filing/priority merit special mention.

name: Determine invention and apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
description: Before performing the eligibility steps, an examiner should determine what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
guidance: See MPEP § 2111 for information on BRI. It is a best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment if the BRI encompasses non-statutory embodiments so that the claim may be narrowed to statutory embodiments.

name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 (Step 1: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Examiner should point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to those embodiments that fall within a statutory category. Example: machine-readable media whose BRI encompasses non-statutory transitory signals (e.g., carrier waves) should be rejected.

name: Step 2A is a two-prong inquiry (Prong One and Prong Two)
description: Step 2A consists of Prong One: determine whether the claim recites (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon; and Prong Two: determine whether the recited judicial exception is integrated into a practical application by additional claim elements.
guidance: Both prongs together answer whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception. If Prong One is negative (no recitation), the claim is eligible at Pathway B. If Prong One is affirmative, analyze Prong Two to see if the claim integrates the exception into a practical application (if so, Step 2A: NO; if not, Step 2A: YES and proceed to Step 2B).

name: Prong One: Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
description: Prong One asks whether a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea is set forth or described in the claim. 'Set forth' and 'described' indicate two ways an exception can be recited in a claim.
guidance: Examiners should (1) identify the specific claim limitation(s) they believe recite an exception and (2) determine whether those limitations fall within at least one judicial-exception grouping. Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception from those that merely 'involve' one (example: Diehr/Mayo claims that explicitly state a formula versus Alice-style claims that describe a concept). Example: a claim reciting 'elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' sets forth a law of nature and thus recites an exception, while a teeter-totter claim that is based on the principle of a lever merely involves an exception and does not recite it.

name: Prong Two: Do additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application?
description: Prong Two asks whether the claim's additional elements integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application. If they do, the claim is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO); if they do not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires Step 2B analysis.
guidance: Mere inclusion of a judicial exception (e.g., a mathematical formula) means the claim 'recites' an exception under Prong One, but does not automatically mean the claim is 'directed to' that exception. The additional elements must 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception (Alice). If there are no additional elements or if the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the exception into a practical application.

name: Additional elements must transform the claim; adding another exception is insufficient
description: To be eligible, additional claim elements must transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception; merely adding elements that are themselves judicial exceptions (or adding one abstract idea to another) is insufficient.
guidance: Cases such as RecogniCorp (adding one abstract idea to another) and Genetic Technologies (eligibility cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature itself) illustrate that stacking exceptions or having only the exception(s) present will not satisfy eligibility. If no sufficient additional elements exist, recommend amendment where possible.

name: Handling claims reciting multiple judicial exceptions
description: A claim may recite multiple judicial exceptions (e.g., two abstract ideas, or an abstract idea plus a law of nature). Examiners should apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of the number of exceptions.
guidance: Unless clearly distinct, care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions—consider treating limitations together as a single abstract idea for Prong Two and Step 2B. If exceptions are distinct (e.g., one limitation describes a law of nature and another recites an abstract idea), the examiner may select one exception for efficiency; if integrating that selected exception into a practical application or showing 'significantly more' is successful, the claim should be considered eligible. If neither selected nor other exceptions are integrated or shown to be 'significantly more,' the claim is ineligible.

name: Best practice: recommend amendments to resolve eligibility
description: When a claim fails Step 1 or when it appears a claim could be amended to resolve eligibility issues, the examiner should recommend an amendment.
guidance: If possible, suggest claim amendments that narrow scope to statutory embodiments or add elements that integrate a judicial exception into a practical application. When making a Step 1 rejection, use the appropriate form paragraphs and advise applicant of the BRI and possible amendments (see MPEP § 2106.07 and related guidance).

name: Customer-suit situations and stays
description: Stays of co-pending litigation against customers (customers of the accused technology) are commonly granted when resolution of a supplier/provider suit will resolve liability as to the customer.
guidance: Based on cases like Katz and Codex, courts sometimes prefer staying customer suits because resolving liability with respect to the supplier may resolve or narrow claims against the customer. Such situations are often treated differently from other co-pendency scenarios.

name: Three-factor test applied to stays pending AIA reviews (IPR/CBM/PGR)
description: Most courts continue to evaluate stay motions according to the three-factor test: (1) undue prejudice to the nonmoving party; (2) whether a stay will simplify issues and trial; (3) whether discovery is complete and a trial date is set.
guidance: The inquiry is based on the totality of the circumstances and is not limited to these three factors. Because the PTAB has up to six months to decide whether to institute review and the scope is unknown until institution, many courts are reluctant to grant stays based solely on filing a petition. Courts consider timing, likelihood of institution, and whether PTAB review would resolve the claims before the court; if not, courts may seek stipulations to streamline litigation instead of staying.

name: Effect of PTAB proceedings on litigation strategy and stay likelihood
description: The AIA-established PTAB procedures (IPR, PGR, CBM) are faster and lower-cost, with high institution and invalidation rates, prompting increased petitions and a higher rate of district-court stays pending PTAB review.
guidance: Statistics through early 2015 showed high institution rates (~80%) and meaningful claim cancellation rates; district courts have stayed litigation pending IPR in a large percentage of cases (rates vary by district and judge). Courts consider potential for PTAB to narrow or cancel claims when evaluating stay motions.

name: Rule 11 presuit investigation standard for filing patent infringement pleadings
description: Rule 11 requires that a party filing a complaint has sufficiently investigated to form a good-faith basis for its claims. A patentee must exercise reasonable diligence to ascertain infringement before filing, including investigation into claim interpretation.
guidance: Patentees are not required to assess validity pre-filing due to patent presumption of validity. The level of inquiry varies by context; where an accused product is readily obtainable, courts expect examination or reasonable explanation for not obtaining a sample. If a patent owner cannot fully investigate (e.g., secret method), Rule 11 permits identifying in pleadings contentions that 'will likely have evidentiary support after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery' (Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(3)). Failure to investigate (e.g., not obtaining or reverse-engineering an available device) can support unreasonable conduct findings.

name: Subject-matter jurisdiction for patent cases
description: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1338(a), federal district courts have exclusive original jurisdiction of 'any civil action arising under any Act of Congress relating to patents.' Whether a claim arises under patent law is determined from the well-pleaded complaint.
guidance: Cases that require resolution of substantive patent law issues (even in state-law causes of action like malpractice) can arise under federal patent law. The determination is made solely on the basis of the complaint, not counterclaims.

name: Markman Hearing (judge-led claim construction)
description: Markman Hearing: judges have responsibility for determining disputes over terms and claims (originating from Markman v. Westview). Timing is discretionary (no set rule from CAFC or Supreme Court); it is left to the district judge's discretion.
guidance: Typical practice (Judge Sleet): schedule at or near close of fact discovery, before expert reports are due and before close of expert discovery; oral argument is interactive (not like appellate argument); judges may attempt to steer parties toward agreement during the hearing.

name: Intrinsic vs. Extrinsic Evidence Hierarchy
description: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification/written description, prosecution history) is to be given the highest value in claim construction (per Philips); extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, technical manuals, expert declarations/testimony) is secondary and not exclusive.
guidance: Many judges confine discussion to the intrinsic record; extrinsic evidence can be useful (e.g., dictionaries), but judges often avoid expert testimony/declarations as litigation-driven. There are no absolute rules—courts weigh usefulness and may exclude extrinsic evidence depending on context.
