name: Two-stage procedure (first stage: claim construction/infringement; second stage: damages)
description: Some systems (e.g., Japan) operate a two-stage process where the court first resolves infringement/claim-construction issues and only if infringement is found proceeds to damages.
guidance: This front-loaded approach permits early termination if no infringement is found and promotes efficiency; when infringement is likely, courts disclose opinion and ask parties to submit damages evidence for the second stage.

name: Relationship of Claim Construction to Bifurcated Systems
description: Claim construction is generally the first step regardless of whether a jurisdiction uses a bifurcated system (separate courts for validity and infringement) or unitary proceedings.
guidance: Even in bifurcated systems, claim construction must be understood first to focus later infringement or validity analysis; where courts differ, later courts should give reasons if they depart from prior determinations.

name: Consistency of Claim Construction Criteria between Validity and Infringement
description: Whether the same interpretive criteria apply in validity and infringement decisions varies: some jurisdictions/practices apply the same criteria; others historically applied more restrictive constructions in infringement to avoid overbroad protection.
guidance: Examples: Korea nominally applies same criteria but Supreme Court guidance allows restrictive constructions in infringement when literal construction is 'clearly unreasonable'; Japan's Kilby decision and later case law trend toward using the same interpretation for both validity and infringement.

name: Functional Claims: contrasting standards (patent office vs. courts)
description: Patent offices (e.g., SIPO) and patent reexamination bodies may interpret function-defined features broadly ('embracing all the means capable of performing the function'), while courts typically construe functional features narrowly based on specific embodiments in the description/drawings or equivalents.
guidance: SIPO/Patent Office guidelines prefer avoiding functional features in product claims unless necessary; function-based claim language is permissible only if supported by description, experimentally verifiable, and not so broad as to include means that cannot solve the technical problem. Courts may limit functional claims to the embodiments disclosed.

name: Permissibility / Support Requirement for Functional Definitions
description: A claim element defined purely by function is permissible only if the function is supported by the description and the person skilled in the art can understand how to implement it; unsupported pure-functional definitions are not allowed.
guidance: If embodiments show a particular way of implementing the function, a skilled person may not assume other alternatives exist; examiners/courts will reject function claims that increase speculative alternatives or include means incapable of solving the problem.

name: Claim Construction: question of law vs. mixed question (fact/law)
description: Claim construction is often treated as a question of law, but subsidiary fact-finding (e.g., about facts necessary to construe terms, or the perspective/knowledge of the person skilled in the art) may occur and be reviewed for clear error (per Teva).
guidance: Different jurisdictions/levels treat this differently: CAFC historically treated it as law with de novo review; Teva requires clear-error review for factual findings made by district courts. Judges may therefore engage in some fact-finding but expect appellate review standards to differ for pure law vs. factual subsidiary findings.

name: Court's use of 'person skilled in the art' and need for factual evidence
description: Interpreting what a claim means may require assessing the perspective/abilities of a person skilled in the art (a legal 'dummy'); this may necessitate factual inquiry to determine education, skills, and knowledge of that hypothetical person.
guidance: Factual aspects can 'sneak in' through this lens; courts may take evidence (dictionaries, expert descriptions) to determine the skilled person's approach, but still frame the ultimate decision as legal construction.

name: Patent Case Management Special Rules (front-loading and timetables)
description: Some jurisdictions/districts have special patent case management rules or guidelines (e.g., Northern District of California, District of New Jersey, certain Chinese provisions); others (e.g., Delaware district courts) rely on robust Rule 16 case-management orders rather than formal patent-specific rules.
guidance: Where present, guidelines set expectations for submission timing (e.g., claimant's arguments/evidence by first preparation date, defendant's counters by second date) and seek rapid resolution (e.g., IP High Court aiming to conclude appeals in 7–8 months). In jurisdictions without formal rules, judges use scheduling conferences, pre-trial proceedings, and designation-of-pleading-date orders to front-load and manage patent cases.

name: Order for preparation / mandatory pre-submission of terms and technology slides
description: Courts may issue preparation orders requiring parties to submit terms/phrases to be construed, technology explanations (slides), and desired claim terms before the first trial/hearing date.
guidance: These orders facilitate focused early claim construction and limit surprise; failure to comply with such orders may lead to exclusion of late materials absent good cause.

name: Prohibition on amended/new claims enlarging scope (35 U.S.C. 305)
description: “No proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim of the patent will be permitted in a reexamination proceeding....” A claim presented in a reexamination “enlarges the scope” where the claim is broader than each and every claim of the patent.
guidance: A claim is broader if it contains within its scope any conceivable product or process which would not have infringed the original patent. A claim is broadened if it is broader in any one respect, even though it may be narrower in other respects. Examiner Note: The claim limitations which are considered to broaden the scope should be identified and explained in bracket 2. See MPEP § 2258.

name: Scope limitation to 'live' claims and requester’s obligation (35 U.S.C. 302)
description: Reexamination is generally limited to review of the 'live' claims (existing claims not held invalid by a final decision) for which reexamination has been requested.
guidance: The request must set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested (35 U.S.C. 302; 37 CFR 1.510(b)). If requester fails to apply the art to certain claims, requester is not statutorily entitled to reexamination of such claims. The Office may, in its sole discretion, reexamine claims for which reexamination was not requested (35 U.S.C. 303(a)), or initiate reexamination on its own initiative of non-requested claims.

name: Requirement to state non-patent/non-publication grounds from prior decisions (37 CFR 1.552(c))
description: For reexaminations ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304 where grounds are set forth in a prior Office or federal court decision that are not based on patents or printed publications, the examiner’s Office action should clearly state that the claims have not been examined as to those non-patent/non-publication grounds.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.552(c) and In re Knight, 217 USPQ 294 (Comm’r Pat. 1982). The Office action should explicitly note which grounds were not examined.

name: Restriction practice not permitted in reexamination
description: Restriction requirements cannot be made in a reexamination proceeding because no statutory basis exists for restriction in a reexamination.
guidance: Addition of claims to a 'separate and distinct' invention would be considered an enlargement of scope. See Ex parte Wikdahl, 10 USPQ2d 1546 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1989) and MPEP § 1412.03.

name: Ancillary amendments permitted to correct necessary patentability incidents
description: Matters ancillary to reexamination that are necessary and incident to patentability will be considered; amendments may be made to correct e.g., inadvertent failure to claim foreign priority or continuing status.
guidance: Amendments to the specification may be allowed when necessary to overcome a reference applied against a claim, such as correcting priority or continuity information.

name: Procedures to determine compliance with Portola Packaging (steps a–e)
description: Office personnel must follow a procedural checklist when deciding whether prosecution of an ongoing reexamination ordered prior to Nov 2, 2002 must be terminated to comply with Portola Packaging.
guidance: (a) Ascertain order date; (b) determine for prior related proceedings what prior art was (i) relied upon to reject any claim or (ii) cited and discussed; (c) base rejections at least in part on prior art that in prior proceedings was neither relied upon nor cited+discussed; (d) withdraw rejections based only on prior art previously relied upon or cited+discussed; (e) terminate prosecution where only remaining rejections are entirely based on such prior art. Director may search for new art under 35 U.S.C. 303 prior to termination.

name: Requirements when submitting a new foreign priority claim (items for on/after vs before Sept 16, 2012)
description: When claiming foreign priority for the first time during reexamination, specific items must be filed in the application file that matured into the patent and a notifying letter placed in the reexamination file. Requirements differ by the filing date of the underlying application (on/after vs before Sept 16, 2012).
guidance: For applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012, required items in the application file include: (a) grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.55(e); (b) application data sheet (37 CFR 1.76(b)(6)) identifying the foreign application; (c) certified copy of the foreign application (unless exception applies); (d) petition fee (37 CFR 1.17(m)); (e) statement that the entire delay was unintentional; and in the reexamination file (f) a separate letter notifying the Office that items (a)-(e) were or are being concurrently filed. For applications filed before Sept 16, 2012, similar requirements apply but alternatives for identifying the foreign application (ADS or oath/declaration) are permitted per 37 CFR 1.55(n). See MPEP § 214.02 for further guidance.

name: Claiming domestic benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 during reexamination (petition under 37 CFR 1.78(e))
description: A patent owner may correct failure to adequately claim domestic benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 by filing a grantable petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim under 37 CFR 1.78(e) in the file of the application that matured into the patent, with a notifying letter placed in the reexamination file.
guidance: The petition and required attachments (except certain specification amendments for pre-Sept 16, 2012 nonprovisional applications) must be filed in the application file which matured into the patent. The procedures and required items vary depending on whether the application that matured into the patent was filed on/after or before Sept 16, 2012; a letter must notify the reexamination file that the petition and attachments are being concurrently filed. See subsections II.A.1 and II.A.2 in MPEP § 2258.02 for itemized requirements.

name: Known-in-art can still be unconventional/non-routine
description: An additional element (or combination of additional elements) that is known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine.
guidance: Novelty/obviousness inquiries are 'fully apart' from eligibility; claims may improve conventional functionality even if anticipated by prior art (e.g., Enfish). Examine whether claimed features provide benefits/technical improvements (flexibility, speed, reduced memory, etc.) that render them non-conventional.

name: Computer functions courts have recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
description: The courts have recognized certain computer functions as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner (e.g., at a high level of generality) or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples include: receiving or transmitting data over a network (using Internet to gather data), performing repetitive calculations, electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining shadow accounts), storing and retrieving information in memory, electronically scanning/extracting data (OCR), and web browser back/forward button functionality. However, not all computer functions are conventional; generic recitation of computer components may be insufficient, whereas non-generic combinations or technical improvements can be significantly more (see DDR Holdings, Amdocs, BASCOM, McRO).

name: Laboratory techniques courts have recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
description: In the life sciences, certain laboratory techniques have been recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional activity when claimed in a merely generic manner or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples include: determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means, using PCR to amplify/detect DNA, detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample, immunizing a patient, analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants, freezing and thawing cells, amplifying/sequencing nucleic acids, and hybridizing a gene probe. Generic recitation of these techniques may not render a claim significantly more.

name: Other activities courts have recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
description: Courts have found other ordinary activities to be well-understood, routine, or conventional when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples include recording a customer's order, shuffling/dealing a standard deck of cards, restricting access by requiring viewing an advertisement, presenting offers and gathering statistics, determining an estimated outcome and setting a price, and arranging/sorting information to determine prices. Analyze these activities in context and relative to other Step 2B considerations.

name: Other meaningful limitations must add meaningful limitations beyond mere linking
description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Meaningful limitations are those that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception or integrate the exception into a practical application. Considerations in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(d) may qualify as meaningful limitations. Examples: Diehr (Arrhenius equation integrated into rubber-molding process) and Classen (analysis step plus immunization step integrated into specific application). Mere implementation via computers or routine data-gathering generally does not meaningfully limit an abstract idea (see Alice, OIP Technologies). Evaluate elements individually and in combination; treatment/prophylaxis limitations overlap with Step 2A Prong Two.

name: Conditions for treating an international filing date as a U.S. filing date for §102(e)
description: An international filing date (for an international application) is treated as a U.S. filing date for §102(e) prior art purposes only if: (1) the international application was filed on or after November 29, 2000; (2) it designated the United States; and (3) it was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in the English language.
guidance: Publication under PCT Article 21(2) can result from early publication request or after the 18-month period. If these three conditions are met, the international filing date (or an earlier effective U.S. filing date properly claimed) can be the §102(e) prior art date for WIPO publications, U.S. application publications, and patents derived from the IA.

name: International applications filed before November 29, 2000 are excluded from §102(e) bridging
description: International filing dates prior to November 29, 2000 may not be relied upon as §102(e) prior art dates. Patents deriving from such international applications have §102(e) dates determined under pre-AIPA §102(e). WIPO or U.S. publications of international applications filed before that date have no §102(e) effect.
guidance: For patents that resulted from international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000, the §102(e) date is the earlier of the date of compliance with §371(c)(1),(2) and (4) or the filing date of the later-filed U.S. application that claimed the benefit. Publications of such IAs do not have §102(e) dates and may only be applied under §102(a) or (b) as of their publication dates.

name: Examination step 1: determine effective filing date(s) of the application under examination
description: Before applying prior art rules, determine the effective filing date(s) of the application being examined (including any proper priority/benefit claims).
guidance: See MPEP sections 706.02, 1893.03(b)/(c), 1895 and 1895.01 as revised by this notice for procedures on establishing effective filing dates.

name: Examination step 4: determine the appropriate §102(e) date for each potential reference
description: Determine the correct §102(e) prior art date for each potential reference by following specific subrules addressing the type and origin of the reference and any priority/benefit claims.
guidance: Key subrules: (a) The potential reference must be a U.S. patent, a U.S. application publication (35 U.S.C. §122(b)), or a WIPO publication under PCT Art.21(2) to be applied under §102(e). (b) If the reference did not result from nor claim benefit of an IA, its §102(e) date is its earliest effective U.S. filing date, considering proper claims under §§119(e) or 120. (c) If the reference resulted from or claimed benefit of an IA, determine whether the IA satisfies: (i) filed on/after Nov 29, 2000; (ii) designated the U.S.; and (iii) published in English under PCT Art.21(2) — if so, the international filing date is a U.S. filing date and may be used as the §102(e) date (and can reach back to earlier filed U.S. or international applications if those earlier applications meet the same conditions). If the IA was filed on/after Nov 29, 2000 but did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English, do not treat the IA filing date as a U.S. filing date; apply the reference under §102(a)/(b) as of publication or under §102(e) as of a later U.S. filing date. If the IA was filed prior to Nov 29, 2000, apply pre-AIPA §102(e) rules: for patents use the earlier of completion of §371(c)(1),(2) and (4) or the filing date of the later-filed U.S. application claiming benefit; for U.S. application publications and WIPO publications of such IAs, never apply under §102(e) (only §102(a)/(b) as of publication). (d) Foreign filing dates claimed via §§119(a)-(d) or 365(a) (including international filing dates claimed as foreign priority) may not be used as §102(e) dates.

name: Foreign priority/foreign filing dates are not §102(e) dates
description: Foreign applications’ filing dates claimed via 35 U.S.C. §§119(a)-(d) or 365(a) may not be used as §102(e) dates for prior art purposes.
guidance: This includes international filing dates claimed as foreign priority dates under §365(a); the §102(e) date of a U.S. publication or patent remains determined by applicable U.S. filing/IA rules rather than foreign priority dates.

name: Consideration of §103(c) common-assignee (ownership) exclusions
description: If a §102(e) reference is used in an obviousness rejection under §103(a), ascertain whether the claimed invention and the reference were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the invention was made, which may exclude the reference under §103(c).
guidance: A clear statement of entitlement to the prior art exclusion by applicant(s) or a registered practitioner is sufficient evidence to establish the exclusion. However, a double patenting rejection based on the §102(e) reference could still be applied if appropriate. See MPEP 706.02(l) for more detail.

name: Required content of answer to complaint
description: The answer shall include a statement of the facts that constitute the grounds of defense and shall specifically admit or deny each allegation set forth in the complaint; must not deny a material allegation known to be true or claim lack of information when respondent possesses it; must state affirmatively special matters of defense and any intent to raise a disability as a mitigating factor, specifying the defense or disability, its nexus to the misconduct, and the reason it provides a defense or mitigation.
guidance: Failure to specify special matters or disability in the answer precludes reliance on them later, absent hearing officer's good-cause allowance for late filing. See § 11.36(c).

name: Relevant date for prior art (PCT Rule 64.1(b))
description: Defines the 'relevant date' for considering prior art for international preliminary examination as set out in PCT Rule 64.1(b).
guidance: Includes: (i) generally the international filing date of the international application under international preliminary examination (subject to (ii) and (iii)); (ii) if the application claims priority and the international filing date is within the priority period, the filing date of the earlier application (unless the IPEA considers the priority claim invalid); (iii) if the international filing date is later than the expiry of the priority period but within two months of that date and the application claims priority of an earlier application, the filing date of the earlier application (unless the IPEA considers the priority claim invalid for reasons other than the late filing). Parallel subparagraphs (B) and (C) reiterate these points. Examiners must apply these provisions when determining the relevant date for novelty and inventive step.

name: Consideration of claimed priority date validity
description: When a document was published between a claimed priority date and the international filing date, the examiner must decide whether the claimed priority date is valid for determining the relevant date.
guidance: For international applications filed on/after April 1, 2007, a priority date should not be considered invalid merely because the international application was filed within two months after the priority period expired. If there is insufficient time for the examiner to make a proper determination (e.g., need to issue a timely written opinion), the relevant date for the written opinion will be based on the claimed priority date. See WIPO Chapter 11 guidance. If the priority claim cannot be decided timely, treat the claimed priority date as the relevant date for the written opinion.

name: Novelty assessment (PCT Article 33(2))
description: A claimed invention is considered novel if it is not anticipated by the prior art as defined in the Regulations (PCT Article 33(2)).
guidance: This definition applies for international preliminary examination and mutatis mutandis to the ISA written opinion (see PCT Rule 43 bis.1(b)). Explanations in the report should clearly point to the criterion of novelty where applicable.

name: Industrial applicability assessment (PCT Article 33(4))
description: A claimed invention is industrially applicable if, according to its nature, it can be made or used in any kind of industry (broad sense, as in Paris Convention).
guidance: This definition is applied for the international preliminary examination and in the written opinion. Explanations in the report should indicate whether the criterion of industrial applicability is met for each claim examined.

name: Content and form of the International Preliminary Examination Report (PCT Article 35 and Admin Instructions Section 604)
description: The report must be established within prescribed time and form and must not state whether the claimed invention is patentable under national law; for each examined claim it should state whether the claim appears to satisfy novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability, with citations and explanations.
guidance: Explanations must clearly point to which of the three criteria any cited document is applicable and describe with reference to cited documents the reasons supporting conclusions. Explanations should be concise and preferably short sentences. If Article 34(4)(a) situations exist, the report must state that opinion and reasons and not contain the paragraph (2) statements. The report is established on Form PCT/IPEA/409.

name: Top-up search requirement and scope
description: Before preparing the Chapter II report, the IPEA should conduct a top-up search to identify prior art that became available after the international search report and that could affect examination (intermediate prior art).
guidance: A top-up search is distinct from an 'additional search' and is intended to find recently available prior art (e.g., applications published on/after the filing or valid priority date but with earlier filing/priority dates). Top-up searches should be performed in all Chapter II examinations except in rare circumstances (e.g., subject matter not examinable, application so unclear no meaningful opinion can be formed, or no international search for certain claims). When lack of unity applies to only part of claimed subject matter, the top-up search should be restricted to parts subject to Chapter II examination. If International Search Report documents already show novelty-destroying references and no amendments/comments were filed, a top-up search may serve no useful purpose.

name: Top-up search handling when lack of unity or unclear basis for amendments
description: If claims lack unity, or an Article 34 amendment has no locatable basis or no explanatory letter was filed, the scope of the top-up search is limited accordingly.
guidance: If claims lack unity, examiner issues invitation to pay further fees and performs top-up search only on inventions for which fees were paid. If Article 34 amendment has no basis, the top-up search may be limited to the scope of claims forming the basis for the report.

name: Form PCT/IPEA/409 completion guidance — Box I (Basis of report and amendments)
description: Instructions for completing Box No. I (itemizing basis of report, listing substitute sheets, sequence listing information, and indicating amendments going beyond original disclosure or rectifications).
guidance: Examiner must indicate whether report is based on the international application in the language filed or on translations/amendments; list substitute/rectified/incorporated-by-reference sheets as originally filed where appropriate; indicate if any amendments resulted in cancellation of pages/claims/sheets/figures/sequence listing; point out in item 4 any amendments considered to go beyond original disclosure and explain determination (new matter disregarded for report but other non-new-matter amendments considered); mark item 5 if report takes into account rectification of obvious mistake (Rule 91); mark item 6 whether top-up searches were carried out and provide dates and whether additional relevant documents were discovered (documents used to support negative statements cited in Box V; certain documents cited in Box VI).

name: Form PCT/IPEA/409 completion guidance — Box II (Priority)
description: Box II is used to inform the applicant if the report is established as if the priority claim had not been made and to state reasons.
guidance: Report may be established as if priority not made where: (A) IPEA requested but was not furnished a copy of the earlier application (PCT Rule 66.7(a)); (B) applicant failed to timely comply with an invitation to furnish a translation of the earlier application (Rule 66.7(b)); (C) priority claim found invalid or all claims directed to inventions not described/enabled by earlier application (Rule 64.1). If only certain claims are affected, specify which claims.

name: Form PCT/IPEA/409 completion guidance — Box III (Non-establishment of opinion)
description: Box III indicates when a reasoned opinion on novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability has not been established for some or all claims and requires specification of reasons.
guidance: Examiner must specify that the report was not established because: (A) subject matter does not require international preliminary examination; (B) description, claims or drawings so unclear that no meaningful opinion could be formed; (C) claims are so inadequately supported by the description that no meaningful opinion could be formed; (D) no international search report has been established for the claims; (E) examiner concluded the application did not comply with unity of invention but decided not to issue an invitation to restrict claims or pay additional fees. If examining less than all claims, indicate which parts were/were not the subject of examination. If lack of meaningful opinion stems from sequence listing non-compliance with WIPO ST.26 or late furnishing fee unpaid, indicate reason.

name: Form PCT/IPEA/409 completion guidance — Box V (Reasoned statement and citations)
description: Box V contains the reasoned statement under Article 35(2) regarding novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability and the citations/explanations supporting those statements.
guidance: The report should state, in relation to each examined claim, whether the claim appears to satisfy the criteria and should cite documents believed to support the conclusions with concise explanations pointing to the criteria to which cited documents are applicable and reasons for the IPEA's conclusions.

name: Example: pointing to a different portion of the claim to maintain a 'new matter' 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection constitutes a new ground
description: If the examiner’s answer identifies a different feature or aspect of the rejected claim as constituting 'new matter' (e.g., relying on a numerical limitation not previously alleged), the rejection should be designated as a new ground.
guidance: In re Waymouth: Board affirmed on a wholly different basis than the examiner (different alleged new matter), which required a new ground designation because it necessitated different responses by appellants.

name: Invalidation upon Patent Holder request – procedural constraints
description: Patent invalidation on the grounds of a Patent Holder's request is carried out upon a written request filed to the Minister. Invalidation of partial claim is adjusted without expanding scope. Invalidation is not carried out if the Licensee does not provide written approval appended to the request. Decision is communicated in writing to Patent Holder/Proxy and Licensee/Proxy, recorded and published, and takes effect from date of Minister decision. (Article 131(1)-(6))

name: Scope-limited invalidation
description: If a lawsuit regards only one or several claims or parts of claims, invalidation is granted only with respect to those claims or parts for which invalidation is sued. (Article 133)

name: Effective date and modification after partial invalidation
description: Unless decided otherwise by Commercial Court, an invalid Patent is entirely or partially invalid from the date the order for invalidation is final and binding. If partial claim invalidation occurs, amended claim is modified without expanding scope. (Article 138(1)-(2))

name: Grant procedure and implication of performing requested acts (EP.19)
description: Prior to the decision to grant the European patent the applicant receives a communication containing the text in which the Examining Division intends to grant and an invitation to pay the grant and printing fees and to supply translations of the claims in the two other official languages of the EPO.
guidance: Performance of these acts implies approval of the text. The communication may also include an invitation to pay additional claims fees.

name: Translation of claims on grant (EP.21)
description: Within the same period for payment of the grant fee the claims must be translated into the two official languages of the EPO which are not the language of proceedings.
guidance: See paragraphs EP.02 and EP.19 for language rules.

name: Restoration of priority (EP.28)
description: If the international application was filed more than 12 months from the filing date of the earlier application whose priority is claimed, the applicant may file or resubmit a request for restoration of priority under PCT Rule 49ter.2.
guidance: Requirements include: the filing date is within two months from the date on which the priority period expired; the failure to claim priority occurred despite all due care; the request is filed within one month from the date the European phase expired for entry (or within one month from receipt of a request for early processing); the fee for restoration is paid within the same time limit; and the request is accompanied by a statement of reasons and preferably supporting evidence.

name: Fees schedule and payment rules (Annex EP.I and Rules Relating to Fees)
description: A detailed schedule of fees applies (filing fees for online and non‑online filings; additional fees for pages in excess of 35; divisional application fees by generation; designation, extension and validation fees; claims fees for the 16th/51st claims; search fee distinctions; examination fee differences; renewal fees per year; fees for further processing, late furnishing of sequence listings, grant/printing/publication; fees for re‑establishment and appeals).
guidance: Fees are payable in euro by payment or transfer to a bank account held by the Office (Article 5). The President may allow other payment methods. Every payment must indicate the name of the person making the payment and contain necessary particulars to enable the Office to establish immediately the purpose of the payment (Article 6). Amounts and conditions are listed in Annex EP.I and in the Schedule of fees and expenses of the EPO; see Guidance for the payment of fees and expenses for current values.

name: Reasonable inquiry requirement supporting factual assertions
description: A practitioner who presents any paper to the USPTO certifies that the practitioner has conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances that supports the factual assertions set forth in the paper. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iii).
guidance: Failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry (e.g., not verifying specimens of use or other factual claims) can be cited as professional misconduct and grounds for discipline.

name: Patent Quality Index (6 components)
description: Quality index 6 – six components: forward citations (as above), patent family size, (corrected) number of claims, generality index, plus number of backward citations and the grant lag index.
guidance: Includes measures of cited prior art and examination duration to broaden the quality measure; components normalised by cohort and equally weighted. OECD notes correlation between 4‑component and 6‑component indices declines over time (partly due to truncation affecting grant lag).

name: Indicators dataset structure and variable definitions
description: OECD will make indicators available upon request as tables linked to PATSTAT appln_id; two main tables: 'indicators' (patent document level with non‑normalised indicators) and 'cohorts' (cohort statistics by filing year × technology field).
guidance: Key variables listed include appln_id, filing year, tech_field (Schmoch taxonomy), patent_scope, family_size, grant_lag, bwd_cits, npl_cits, claims, fw d_cits5/fw d_cits7 and XY variants, generality, originality, radicalness, renewal (life duration), quality_index_4, quality_index_6, and others. Note on many_field: when a patent maps to multiple technology fields, the field with majority IPC codes is kept (ties resolved randomly); many_field=1 flags patents allocated to other fields.

name: Statement of precise relief requested for each challenged claim
description: Provide a statement of the precise relief requested for each claim challenged.
guidance: For each claim the petition challenges, state plainly what you ask the Board to do (e.g., cancel claim 1 entirely, limit claim language, or find claim unpatentable). This overarching statement frames the subsequent detailed showings.

name: Identification of the claim (b)(1)
description: Identify the claim (i.e., specify which patent claims are being challenged).
guidance: List claim numbers clearly and unambiguously so the Board and patent owner know exactly which claims are at issue. Where multiple claims are challenged, identify each separately.

name: Specific statutory grounds and relied-upon patents/printed publications (b)(2)
description: State the specific statutory grounds under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 on which the challenge to the claim is based and the patents or printed publications relied upon for each ground.
guidance: For each challenged claim, tie the challenge to either anticipation (102) or obviousness (103) and identify the exact prior art references (patents or printed publications) relied upon for that ground. Be explicit which reference supports which ground for which claim.

name: Claim construction and 35 U.S.C. 112(f) identification (b)(3)
description: Explain how the challenged claim is to be construed. Where the claim contains a means-plus-function or step-plus-function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the construction must identify the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function.
guidance: Provide proposed constructions of claim terms/limitations relied on in the challenge. If asserting 112(f) limitations, explicitly point to the portions of the specification that disclose corresponding structure/material/acts. Make constructions clear because the unpatentability analysis depends on them.

name: Showing how the construed claim is unpatentable and element-by-element mapping (b)(4)
description: Explain how the construed claim is unpatentable under the statutory grounds identified in paragraph (b)(2). The petition must specify where each element of the claim is found in the prior art patents or printed publications relied upon.
guidance: Provide an element-by-element comparison mapping each claim limitation (as construed) to specific disclosures in the prior art references (or explain combination/reasoning for 103). Make the linkage explicit rather than conclusory to allow the Board to assess the merits.

name: SEP declaration databases are imperfect starting points
description: SEP declaration databases are meant to document fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (FRAND) obligations and are not maintained to provide an accurate landscape of verified SEPs.
guidance: Declaration practices vary by filer and SSO: some companies declare after careful claim mapping, others declare broadly or using blanket declarations; declarations are often filed while patents are pending and standards still evolve, so many declared patents may ultimately be non-essential or declarations may be incomplete. Use declaration databases as the best publicly available starting point but treat results cautiously.

name: Blanket declarations provide no disclosure of SEP magnitude
description: Some SSOs (e.g., IEEE, ITU) permit 'blanket declarations' where companies do not declare specific patent numbers.
guidance: Blanket practices mean no transparency about how many or which patents a company claims as potentially essential; these databases cannot be used to infer magnitude of SEP ownership without further investigation.

name: Strategically align R&D, standards development, and patent prosecution teams
description: Cross-departmental coordination is required to ensure inventions disclosed by R&D are protected, brought into standards, and prosecuted as SEPs.
guidance: The process: R&D invention → decision by patent board to file → preserve priority (e.g., provisional filing) → standards developers introduce the solution as a contribution → patent prosecution team aligns claim language to the evolving standard and verifies novelty/prior art. Organizational alignment increases chances of filing valid and essential SEPs.

name: Align and amend patent claims during prosecution to map to the latest standard version
description: Because standards change iteratively, claim language should be adapted during prosecution to correspond to the final standard implementation.
guidance: Claim amendments can be used up until grant to ensure the granted patent can be charted to the latest standard version—while also ensuring claims remain novel over prior art. Patent prosecution teams must monitor standard evolution and update claims accordingly.

name: Title: Must Indicate Subject-Matter and Avoid Certain Faults
description: The title is the short statement setting forth in very general terms the object of the invention and must sufficiently indicate the subject-matter; avoid language which lays the title open to charges of being 'too large, uncertain, inapplicable, inexplicable, inconsistent, vague, ambiguous, and at variance with the specification.'
guidance: Examiners/Comptroller may require amendment of an insufficient title; a deceptive title weighs heavily against the patentee (Cook v. Pearce). Examples of bad titles: overstating results or applicability (e.g., claiming multiple new notes from a single improvement when only one is new). Good titles: 'Improvements in the manufacture of plated articles' even where only a single improvement is disclosed. Always frame an unobjectionable title initially to avoid delay. Title and specification must be read together: an ambiguous title may be clarified by the specification (Neilson v. Harford).

name: Provisional Specification: Required Content and Purpose
description: A provisional specification must describe the nature of the invention, be accompanied by drawings if required, commence with the title, and should fairly describe the nature of the invention — its principal and essential features — without necessarily describing the modes of carrying it into effect.
guidance: Statutory references: Patents Act s.5 and s.6 and Patents Rules. The provisional specification 'ought not to comprise more than one invention' (sect.88). Its office is to afford means for securing the identity of the invention at the time of application and when finally specified; it is not intended to be a complete description enabling the workman of ordinary skill to make it. Judges' statements: it must describe generally and fairly the nature of the invention 'in its rough state.' Ensure key features intended to be claimed later are foreshadowed in the provisional.

name: Complete Specification: Particular Description and Enabling Requirement
description: The complete specification must 'particularly describe and ascertain the nature of the invention, and in what manner it is to be performed', must commence with the title and end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed, and be accompanied by drawings if required.
guidance: The complete specification is the instrument by which the public are acquainted with the inventor's secret and must describe it clearly and fully to enable others to work the invention. It greatly affects the security of a patentee's privileges; ambiguity, obscurity, or defects in the complete specification jeopardize enforcement. If filed at application it deprives the inventor of later improvement opportunities and may bar foreign patents unless covered by the Convention. Timing: if not filed at application it must be left within nine months (Comptroller may extend). Fees differ depending on timing of filing (see Manual).

name: Restriction on Introducing New Matter into Complete Specification
description: It is not allowable to vary the invention in any important respect when the complete specification is in preparation, or to introduce new matter into that instrument; the provisional specification should foreshadow the parts to be claimed in the complete specification.
guidance: Provisional spec's office is to establish identity; the complete spec must not go beyond the invention as disclosed in the provisional in any important way. Judges' statements emphasize that the provisional describes identity not entirety; when preparing the complete, ensure consistency and do not introduce new essential matter not supported by the provisional (if a provisional was filed).

name: Incorporation of third-party materials (claim charts)
description: Where the request for reexamination includes material such as a claim chart to explain a proposed rejection, the examiner may cut and paste the claim chart (or other material) to incorporate it within the body of the Office action.
guidance: If incorporating third-party material, carefully review it to ensure that any items incorporated in a statement of rejection 'clearly and completely address the patentability of the claims.' Do not blindly adopt wording — confirm completeness and clarity.

name: Panel review conference before issuing Office action
description: After an examiner has determined that the reexamination proceeding is ready for an Office action, the examiner will formulate a draft preliminary Office action and inform the CRU SPE or TC QAS of intent to issue it. The CRU SPE/TC QAS will convene a panel review conference, and the conference members will review the patentability of the claim(s) pursuant to MPEP § 2671.03.
guidance: If the conference confirms the examiner’s preliminary decision to reject and/or allow the claims, the proposed Office action shall be issued and signed by the examiner with two other conferees initialing. If not confirmed, the examiner must reevaluate and issue an appropriate action.

name: Adopt or explain rejections and provide statutory basis and reasoning
description: Office actions must set forth rejections with statutory citations (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 103) and explain the factual/technical reasoning (e.g., how references combine to render claims unpatentable). Proposed third-party rejections may be adopted essentially as proposed where appropriate.
guidance: Provide clear explanation of how prior art references teach claim limitations and why combination would have been obvious; expressly note when a rejection was proposed by a third party and whether adopted or rejected, with reasoning.

name: Treatment of dependent claims when base claim rejected/canceled
description: If an unamended base patent claim has been rejected or canceled, any claim which is directly or indirectly dependent thereon should be indicated as patentable if it is otherwise patentable. No requirement should be made for rewriting the dependent claim in independent form.
guidance: Do not reject or object to dependent claims solely because their base claim was canceled, except in specified situations: if a new base claim has been canceled, a dependent claim depending thereon should be rejected as indefinite; if an amended/new base claim is rejected, dependent claims should be objected to if otherwise patentable and require rewriting in independent form.

name: Patent owner reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111)
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the patent owner must reply to the Office action. The reply must be reduced to writing which 'distinctly and specifically points out the supposed errors in the examiner’s action' and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action. The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references.
guidance: Replies must be a bona fide attempt to advance the proceeding. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specific argument is insufficient.

name: Supplemental replies — limited entry as matter of right
description: A supplemental reply that is supplemental to a reply in compliance with § 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except if clearly limited to specified categories (cancellation of claims; adoption of examiner suggestions; placement in condition for allowance; reply to Office requirement made after first reply; correction of informalities; simplification of issues for appeal).
guidance: Supplemental replies will be entered only when they fall within the enumerated categories or if filed within a period where Office action is suspended under § 1.103(a) or (c). Plan initial replies accordingly to avoid reliance on supplemental entry.

name: Application size fee calculation
description: The application size fee for a national stage application (37 CFR 1.492(j)) is determined on the basis of the international application as published by WIPO pursuant to PCT Article 21.
guidance: Calculation is based on number of sheets of specification (description, claims, abstract, and, if present, a sequence listing in PDF) and drawings in the published international application, without regard to publication language. Certain sheets (Article 19 amendments/statement, international search report, additional bibliographic sheets other than the cover sheet with the abstract) are not counted. Article 34 amendments or preliminary amendments are not taken into account.

name: Pre‑AIA (pre‑Sept 16, 2012) oath/declaration rules and changes of inventive entity
description: For international filing dates before September 16, 2012, pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.497 applies: an oath/declaration must be executed in accordance with 1.66 or 1.68, identify the specification, identify each inventor and country of citizenship, and state belief that the named inventor(s) are original and first inventor(s).
guidance: If an oath/declaration filed pursuant to pre‑AIA 1.497 names an inventive entity different from that in the international application, applicant must submit statements from added/deleted inventors that any error occurred without deceptive intent, pay processing fee (1.17(i)), provide assignee consent if needed, and possibly file a new oath/declaration. The Office may require other information; changes to inventorship effected under PCT Rule 92bis or corrections to priority claims may require new oaths or ADSs.

name: Priority claim eligibility
description: An applicant in Japan may claim priority based upon a patent application filed in any other country that is a signatory of the Paris Convention or the TRIPS agreement.
guidance: When claiming priority provide priority right date and country and priority application number. For PCT national entry, the firm will obtain claims and specification from the PCT publication if published in English; inform the firm of the PCT application number (and publication number for confirmation).

name: Required application contents
description: A Japanese application may be filed with a copy of the specification in English or Japanese, drawings where necessary, and the following information: name and address of inventor(s), name and address of assignee(s), priority right date and country, and priority application number (if assigned).
guidance: Provide complete information at filing to enable priority claims and prosecution; additional PCT-specific handling described above.

name: Specification sufficiency (enablement)
description: The detailed explanation of the invention must describe the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Typical format recommended: industrial field of application; prior art; problems the invention is to solve; means of solving the problems; embodiments of the invention; effects of the invention. Include as much information as possible because the JPO is very strict about introduction of new matter and rarely allows new claims unless the language is specifically recited in the body of the specification.

name: Claim drafting and number of claims
description: There is no limit on the number of claims, but each claim beyond the first requires additional official fees for substantive examination and maintenance.
guidance: Because of additional fees Japanese patents tend to average fewer claims. Nevertheless, include claims drafted to maximize licensing fees and potential damage awards; include specific claims covering the most profitable uses.

name: New matter prohibition and strictness
description: The JPO will not allow applicants to introduce new matter into the application during prosecution; the definition of new matter is very strict in Japanese practice.
guidance: Unless specific parallel wording exists in the specification as first filed, it is difficult to add such wording to claims. If the wording can be shown as clearly inferred in the original specification it may sometimes be possible. Include repetitious text using varied terms and expressions in the original specification to provide multiple avenues for future claim amendments. Consider this when drafting PCT applications intended for Japan.

name: Enablement and inventive step strictness / intermediate concept strategy
description: Enablement and inventive step requirements are stricter in Japan than in the US; using an intermediate concept that is narrower than US claims but broader than specific examples helps in obtaining broader Japanese patents.
guidance: Such descriptions can be added by filing a domestic priority application similar to a US CIP if filed within one year from the US first priority date. Examples (How, When, What) illustrate drafting intermediate concepts: (1) choose A -> How to choose A; (2) renew -> When to renew; (3) status -> What status.

name: Grounds for examiner rejection
description: The Office Action may cite grounds for rejection including: new matter introduced by amendment; applicant is resident of non-reciprocal country; non-statutory subject matter; lack of novelty; lack of inventive step; applicant was not first to file; claimed invention disclosed in a prior application later published; invention contravenes public order/morality/health; application not filed by all joint owners; patent granted contrary to treaty provisions; insufficient description (enablement); allowed claims not supported, clear, concise, and in accordance with patent rules; unity of invention not satisfied; translation issues when English filing followed by Japanese translation; applicant not inventor/no right to obtain a patent.
guidance: Amendments in response to a final rejection are limited in scope. The Office Action will list a deadline, usually three months for foreign applicants, within which a response can be filed; a single three-month extension may be automatically obtained. If the examiner remains unconvinced, a second final rejection will be issued.

name: Invalidity trial process and grounds
description: Any third party having a commercial interest adversely affected by a patent may initiate an invalidity trial before the JPO appeal board; these trials are common in Japan.
guidance: Grounds are similar to examiner rejection but some grounds (claims conforming with patent rules and unity) are not available. Additional bases include loss of foreign priority or treaty benefits and failures in corrections meeting statutory requirements. The patent owner may narrow claims through amendment to avoid invalidation; invalidity appeals can delay related infringement litigation and may last two years or more.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents criteria (Tsubakimoto precedent)
description: An accused product may be regarded as equivalent to a claimed invention even if a specific claim element is missing when: (1) the element is not an essential feature of the claimed invention; (2) the claimed invention achieved the object and effect even after the element is replaced with a feature in the accused product; (3) the replacement would have been obvious when the accused product was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art; (4) the accused product was not identical to or obvious from the prior art; and (5) the accused product does not correspond to one intentionally excluded from the claim during prosecution.
guidance: This five-factor test stems from the Supreme Court decision in Tsubakimoto Seiki v Tei Eichi Kei (1998) and guides DOE analysis in Japan.

name: Inter Parte case types (listed)
description: Inter Parte Cases include: Trial for Invalidation; Offensive Claim Scope Confirmation Trial; Defensive Claim Scope Confirmation Trial; Trial to Establish a Non-Exclusive License; Trial for Correction; Trial for Invalidation of Correction.
guidance: These are trials between interested parties (or between an interested party and the patentee). Specific eligibility constraints for some of these types are described in other entries (e.g., who may demand invalidation or confirmation trials).

name: Claim scope confirmation trials — who may demand
description: A Trial for Confirmation of the Scope of the Patent Right (offensive or defensive claim-scope confirmation) may be demanded by the Patentee or by an interested party.
guidance: Both 'offensive' (patentee seeks affirmation of scope against others) and 'defensive' (third party seeks confirmation re: alleged infringement) confirmation trials are listed under Inter Parte cases and share the same eligibility rule.

name: Who may bring suits against KIPT rulings / who may be defendants
description: Suits of dissatisfaction against the rulings, etc. of the KIPT may be brought by the parties concerned, interveners, or parties whose intervention was rejected despite their petition for intervention in a parent trial or its re-trial.
guidance: In a suit in the Patent Court the Commissioner of the KIPO is named as a defendant in principle. However, a suit against the ruling in an invalidation trial, a claim scope confirmation trial or a trial to establish a non-exclusive license requires that its counterpart (i.e., winner of the parent trial) be named as the defendant.

name: Original patent requirement (35 U.S.C. § 251)
description: Reissue claims must be directed to "the invention disclosed in the original patent." A reissue that changes the scope of the original patent must still claim the same invention as shown on the face of the original instrument.
guidance: Compare the original specification and claims to the reissue claims; the reissue must "fully describe[] and claim[] the very invention intended to be secured by the original patent" (U.S. Indus. Chem.). If the reissue claims cover a different invention than that disclosed originally, they fail § 251.

name: Integral/necessary element cannot be omitted
description: If the original specification treats a particular element as an integral, necessary, or sole means for performing a claimed function, omitting that element in reissue claims renders those claims invalid under § 251.
guidance: Look for language that describes an element as the only disclosed mechanism to perform a function (e.g., the specification here discloses "a plurality of magnets" as the only structure for removably securing the grill). Omission of such an element is analogous to omission of 'water' in U.S. Industrial Chemicals or 'plurality of arbors' in Forum and will invalidate broadened reissue claims.

name: Mere suggestion or cursory mention is insufficient
description: A reissue claim is not supported merely because the original specification 'suggested' or 'indicated' the claimed subject matter; cursory mentions do not satisfy § 251.
guidance: Antares and U.S. Indus. Chem. teach that the original specification must 'explicitly and unequivocally' describe the reissue invention; a passing reference or brief suggestion of an alternative is not enough to permit broadening on reissue.

name: Broadening to undisclosed alternatives to an essential feature fails
description: Reissue claims that broaden a limitation to cover alternatives that were not disclosed, where that limitation appeared essential in the original disclosure, do not satisfy the original patent requirement.
guidance: If the original disclosure presents a particular feature (e.g., magnets) as the means for achieving a function, reissue claims cannot generically recite the function without that feature unless the original explicitly and unequivocally disclosed the alternatives.

name: Functional-role analysis (distinguish essential vs superficial features)
description: Determine whether the omitted limitation played a described functional role or was merely a superficial/configurational detail; omission may be permissible if the limitation had no functional importance in the original disclosure.
guidance: Use Peters as guidance: omissions of features that had no described functional significance (e.g., tapered shape with no functional importance) may be acceptable. Conversely, if the limitation is tied to the claimed function, omission is likely invalid.

name: Written description/§112(a) is distinct from §251 original-patent requirement
description: Satisfaction of the written description requirement does not automatically satisfy the original patent requirement of § 251; the § 251 inquiry is an independent limit on reissue broadening.
guidance: Revolution Eyewear's result was tied to written-description analysis; courts (e.g., Antares) caution that proving written description support is not the same as proving the reissue claims are directed to the invention disclosed in the original patent.

name: Single-embodiment disclosure increases risk of invalid broadening
description: When the original patent describes only a single embodiment characterized by particular structural elements, reissue claims that broaden beyond that embodiment are likely to fail § 251.
guidance: If the specification contains only one example and no disclosure of alternatives or optionality (as with the single-embodiment 'plurality of magnets' here), broadened reissue claims that omit that embodiment-specific element will likely be invalid.

name: Standard of review for § 251 Board decisions
description: The Board's assessment of whether reissue claims satisfy § 251 is a question of law reviewed de novo, with underlying factual findings reviewed for substantial evidence.
guidance: Apply de novo review to legal conclusions about whether the reissue claims are directed to the original invention, while treating factual findings (e.g., what the specification discloses to POSITA) under the substantial-evidence standard (Forum US, Inc. v. Flow Valve, LLC).

name: Practical indicator: sole disclosed mechanism for performing a function
description: A practical flag that reissue broadening will fail is when the original specification discloses only one mechanism to accomplish a claimed function (e.g., only magnets are disclosed to removably secure the grill).
guidance: If the specification repeatedly and definitionaly ties the function to that single mechanism (quotes: 'A flattened bottom side ... is removably securable to the plurality of magnets'), this supports a conclusion that the mechanism is essential and cannot be omitted in reissue claims.

name: 37 CFR 1.129 — scope of permissible submissions
description: A 'submission' under 37 CFR 1.129(a) includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims or drawings, and a new substantive argument or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: Submissions can be IDS, amendments, or new arguments/evidence, but any amendment entered as result of payment of the fee may not introduce new matter into the disclosure (35 U.S.C. 132).

name: Definition of 'submission' for RCE (content requirement)
description: A 'submission' for RCE purposes includes, but is not limited to, an IDS, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability. If a reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111.
guidance: Appeal briefs or reply briefs will not be considered submissions under 1.114(d), although arguments from those briefs may be incorporated by reference.

name: Permitted content of 35 U.S.C. 301 / 37 CFR 1.501 submissions
description: Submissions are limited to: prior art consisting of patents or printed publications, and/or statements of the patent owner filed in a proceeding before a Federal court or the Office in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim.
guidance: Submissions must be directed only to patents, printed publications, and/or patent owner written claim scope statements and additional information. Submissions containing issues not so directed (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 112 objections, public use allegations, or commentary on patent owner conduct) should not be entered and should be returned, discarded, or closed (see MPEP §2206).

name: Explanation of pertinence and manner of applying prior art
description: A submission must include an explanation in writing of the pertinence and manner of applying any prior art or written statement to at least one claim of the patent (37 CFR 1.501(b)(1) / 35 U.S.C. 301(b)).
guidance: The explanation should, for at least one claim, set forth how each item cited shows or teaches at least one limitation of the claim (examples provided in MPEP). If filed by the patent owner, the submission may include an explanation of how the claims differ from the submitted prior art or written statements.

name: Specific identification requirements for written-statement submissions
description: Submissions of patent-owner written statements (37 CFR 1.501(a)(2)/(a)(3)) must identify: (i) the forum and proceeding where the statement was filed; (ii) the specific papers and portions containing the statements; and (iii) how each statement is one in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim of the patent.
guidance: Identification of portions may be satisfied by citing documents and specific pages. The requirement prevents submission of mere restatements by other parties; submitters should include information about the status and relationship of the proceeding to the patent. Accompanying documents from the proceeding that address the written statement must be included (35 U.S.C. 301(c)).

name: What constitutes a 'proper' submission for entry
description: A proper 37 CFR 1.501 submission is limited to patents, printed publications, and/or patent owner written claim scope statements and additional information and includes the requisite citation description (explanation of pertinence and manner of application) and proof of service (if by a third party).
guidance: If any of these elements are missing (improper content, missing explanation, missing proof of service), the submission will not be entered and will be handled as described (returned, discarded, or closed), with notification to submitter/patent owner in many cases.

name: Prohibition on inclusion of non-patent-reference issues
description: A submission cannot include any issue not directed to patents, printed publications, or patent owner written claim scope statements and additional information. For example, statements about violations of 35 U.S.C. 112, public use, or the conduct of the patent owner are not permitted and submissions containing such issues should not be entered.
guidance: Submissions also should not include argument/discussion of references previously treated in the prosecution of the patent or in prior reexamination proceedings; if such extraneous issues are present, the submission should be returned/discarded/closed.

name: Reexamination certificate format, numbering, and content
description: The ex parte reexamination certificate number is the patent number followed by a two-character kind-code suffix (first letter B for pre-2001, C for on/after Jan 2, 2001; second letter identifies number of reexamination). Certificates identify which claims are confirmed, canceled, disclaimed, or not examined, and print amended/new claims (new claims in italics; amended claims with italics and bracketing).
guidance: Certificates also list bibliographic information, representative claim text, any changes to specification/drawings, prior court decisions, and, if ordered under 35 U.S.C. 257, indicate that reexamination was ordered under that section. See MPEP §2290-§2293 for further formatting rules.

name: Intervening rights effect of amended/new claims after reexamination
description: Any proposed amended or new claim determined to be patentable and incorporated into a patent following reexamination will have the same effect as specified in 35 U.S.C. 252 for reissued patents regarding intervening rights for prior makers, users, purchasers, or importers (35 U.S.C. 307(b)).
guidance: The intervening-rights situation parallels reissue; case law such as Fortel Corp. v. Phone-Mate and Kaufman Co. v. Lantech, Inc. is relevant.

name: Reexamination of a reexamination: basis for consideration
description: A reexamination request filed on a patent for which a reexamination certificate has already issued is considered based on the claims in the patent as modified by the previously issued reexamination certificate (not the original claims).
guidance: When a 'reexamination of a reexamination' is received, the CRU prints the issued reexamination certificate and makes it of record in the new file as a preliminary amendment; examiners decide issues based on the certificate-modified claims and specification.

name: Drafting of claims and description (form/content guidance)
description: There are specific guidance and requirements for drafting the claims and the description (including headings and how formulae should be presented).
guidance: References: Drafting of claims 5.112-5.113, drafting of description 5.094-5.099, headings for description (5.094), representation of chemical/mathematical formulae (5.107-5.108, 5.135).

name: 37 CFR 1.175(f)(1) — when a copy of inventor’s oath/declaration satisfies requirement
description: A continuing reissue application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) may satisfy the inventor’s oath/declaration requirement by a copy of the inventor’s oath/declaration from the earlier-filed reissue application provided that: (i) the inventor (or each joint inventor) executed an inventor’s oath/declaration for the earlier-filed reissue application (except as provided in § 1.64); (ii) the continuing reissue application does not seek to enlarge the scope of the claims of the original patent; or (iii) the application for the original patent was filed under § 1.46 by the assignee of the entire interest.
guidance: Examiners should verify each subcondition. If any condition is not met, the copy does not satisfy the requirement and a new oath/declaration is required. See also the interplay with 37 CFR 1.175(f)(2) regarding identification of errors relied upon for reissue.

name: Assignee consent copy acceptability in continuation reissue applications
description: A continuation reissue application filed with a copy of the assignee consent from the parent reissue application and a newly executed reissue oath/declaration generally: the copy of the assignee consent from the parent is not acceptable unless the continuation corrects an error for which consent was made.
guidance: Submission of a new oath/declaration is indicative of correction of a different error. Under such circumstances, OPAP will accord a filing date, and the examiner should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 251 and require a new consent. See MPEP § 1410.02. Examiners should compare the consent and the error statements to determine coverage.

name: Double patenting considerations for parent/continuation reissues
description: Where the parent reissue application issues before examination of the continuation, or where parent and continuation are examined together, the continuation’s claims should be reviewed for double patenting over the parent; a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection should be made as to any overlapping claims.
guidance: Consider terminal disclaimer to obviate a nonstatutory double patenting rejection; a terminal disclaimer ensures common ownership under 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3) or common enforcement under 37 CFR 1.321(d)(3) for the remainder of the unexpired term. See MPEP § 804 - § 804.05 and In re Berg/In re Graff guidance.

name: Amendments in reissue applications must comply with 37 CFR 1.173 and 1.121
description: Any amendment to the description and claims in reissue applications must be made in accordance with 37 CFR 1.173; amendments may be made by incorporation into the specification upon filing (with markings per paragraph (d)) or by a separate amendment paper complying with the specified format.
guidance: If made by amendment paper, the paper must direct specified changes and include full texts where required. The exception for examiner’s amendments under 37 CFR 1.121(g) does not apply in reissue applications. Use form paragraph 14.20.01 to advise applicants of proper manner.

name: Specification amendments — full paragraph submission and location identification
description: Changes to the specification (other than the claims, certain tables/listings, or drawings) must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph, including markings, and the precise point in the specification where the added/rewritten paragraph is located must be identified. An entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presenting the text.
guidance: All newly added paragraphs must be submitted completely underlined each time they are re-submitted; bracketing/underlining is always relative to the original patent text, not relative to prior amendment versions.

name: Claims amendment presentation and support requirement
description: An amendment paper must include the entire text of each claim being changed and each claim being added; for each claim changed, a parenthetical such as 'amended' should follow the claim number. A claim canceled may be canceled by a statement. Each amendment must be accompanied by the status (pending or canceled) of all patent claims and all added claims as of the date of the amendment, and an explanation of the support in the disclosure for the claim changes.
guidance: Failure to supply claim status or an explanation of support will generally result in a notification that the amendment before final rejection is not completely responsive (see 37 CFR 1.135(c)); an amendment after final rejection will not be entered. New claims added must be presented completely underlined.

name: Amendment may not enlarge scope or introduce new matter
description: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.173(a), no amendment in a reissue application may enlarge the scope of the claims unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent. Further, the amendment may not introduce new matter.
guidance: Examiners should verify time limits for enlarging claim scope (see MPEP § 1412.03) and check for new matter in the amendment; improper enlargements or new matter require appropriate rejection or requirement for correction.

name: Limit scope of 35 U.S.C. 112 examination to amendatory matter
description: Where new claims are presented or any part of the disclosure is amended, the claims of the reexamination proceeding are to be examined for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, but consideration of 112 issues should be limited to the amendatory (e.g., new language) matter.
guidance: A claim amended or new that contains a limitation not found in the original patent claim should be considered for 35 U.S.C. 112 compliance only with respect to that limitation. A term in an original claim cannot be examined as too broad in a new or amended claim unless the amendatory matter creates the issue. If a dependent claim is rewritten as an independent claim in reexamination, that independent claim cannot be examined as to 35 U.S.C. 112 unless the rewriting raises a new question (e.g., lack of antecedent). See MPEP §2163 - §2173.05(v) for extensive guidance.

name: New matter prohibition under 35 U.S.C. 132
description: 35 U.S.C. 305 provides for examination under 35 U.S.C. 132, which prohibits the introduction of new matter into the disclosure. The question of new matter should be considered in a reexamination proceeding.
guidance: If new matter is added to claims or affects claim limitations, the claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for failing the written description requirement. See MPEP §2163.06 regarding relationship between written description and new matter prohibition.

name: Claims in proceeding must not enlarge scope of the patent (35 U.S.C. 305)
description: When new or amended claims are presented or any part of the disclosure is amended, the claims of the reexamination proceeding should be examined under 35 U.S.C. 305 to determine whether they enlarge the scope of the original claims. 'No proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim of the patent will be permitted in a reexamination proceeding.'
guidance: A presented claim enlarges the scope where it is broader than each and every claim of the patent. A claim is broader if it contains within its scope any conceivable product or process that would not have infringed the original patent. A claim is broadened if broader in any one respect even if narrower in others. Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 305 should be made (Form paragraph 22.11). Identify claim limitations considered to broaden scope and explain in bracket 2 per MPEP §2258.

name: Identify and explain limitations that broaden claim scope
description: The claim limitations considered to broaden the scope should be identified and explained in bracket 2 of the Office action (see MPEP §2258).
guidance: Use form paragraph 22.11 and in bracket 2 insert the claim limitations considered broadening; provide explanation/mapping for why those limitations broaden compared to the patent claims.

name: Handling patents subject to prior Office or court decision
description: Where some of the patent claims have been the subject of a prior Office or court decision, special handling is required; claims not subject to reexamination because of prior adjudication should be identified.
guidance: See MPEP §2242. For 'live' claims dependent on claims not subject to reexamination, see MPEP §2260.01. If grounds are set forth in a prior Office or Federal Court decision which are not based on patents or printed publications, the examiner's Office action should clearly state those grounds have not been examined as they are not based on patents/printed publications (see 37 CFR 1.552(c)).

name: Reexamination generally limited to 'live' claims requested
description: The Office’s determination in the order for reexamination and examination stage will generally be limited solely to review of the 'live' claims (existing claims not held invalid by a final decision) for which reexamination has been requested.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 302 requires the request to set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested. If requester fails to apply art to certain claims, requester is not statutorily entitled to reexamination of those claims.
