The Office may, at its sole discretion, reexamine claims not requested or initiate reexamination on its own (35 U.S.C. 303(a)). If prior art discovered during reexamination raises SNQ as to non-requested claims, such claims may be added at the Office's discretion.

name: Ancillary amendments permitted if incident to patentability
description: There are matters ancillary to reexamination necessary and incident to patentability which will be considered; amendments may be made to the specification to correct certain failures when necessary to overcome a reference.
guidance: Examples include correcting an inadvertent failure to claim foreign priority or the continuing status relative to a parent application if necessary to overcome a reference.

name: Use of affidavits in reexamination
description: Affidavits under 37 CFR 1.131 and 1.132 may be utilized in a reexamination proceeding, with limitations.
guidance: An affidavit under 37 CFR 1.131 may not be used to 'swear back' of a reference patent if the reference patent is claiming the 'same invention' as the patent undergoing reexamination. In such situations, use affidavit under 37 CFR 1.130 or consider raising the issue via an interference or an appropriate reissue application (see MPEP §718 and §1449.02).

name: Reexamination requests on patents after reissue
description: Where a request for reexamination is filed on a patent after it has been reissued, reexamination will be denied because the patent on which the request is based has been surrendered.
guidance: If reexamination of the reissued patent is desired, a new request based on the specification and claims of the reissue patent must be filed. Any amendment made by the patent owner to accompany the initial reexamination request or later prosecution should treat the changes made by the granted reissue patent as the text of the patent (all bracketing/underlining should be with respect to the reissue changes). See MPEP §2285 if reissue issues after filing of a request.

name: Check file history for previously cited/considered art ('old art') before rejection
description: In the examining stage of reexamination, the examiner will consider whether claims are subject to rejection based on art; before making such a rejection the examiner should check the patent's file history to ascertain whether the art was previously cited/considered in an earlier concluded Office examination (referred to as 'old art').
guidance: The term 'old art' coined in In re Hiniker. If the rejection will be based on combination of old art and new art, the rejection is proper (Hiniker). If old art provides the sole basis, different rules apply depending on whether reexamination was ordered on or after Nov 2, 2002 (see next criteria).

name: Reexaminations ordered prior to Nov 2, 2002 — Portola Packaging constraints
description: For reexaminations ordered prior to Nov 2, 2002, old art generally cannot be used as the sole basis for a rejection (subject to exceptions) per In re Portola Packaging; implement Portola-based procedures for ongoing reexaminations.
guidance: If prior art was previously relied upon to reject a claim in a concluded prior related Office proceeding, the Office will not conduct reexamination based only on such prior art. If prior art was cited and its relevance to patentability actually discussed on the record in a prior related proceeding, reexamination based only on such prior art is precluded. Generalized 'state of the art' citations do not preclude reexamination. Procedures when determining termination for Portola: (a) ascertain order date, (b) determine what prior art was relied upon or cited & discussed in prior related proceedings, (c) base rejections at least in part on art not previously relied upon or discussed, (d) withdraw rejections based only on such previously relied-upon/discussed art, (e) terminate prosecution where only remaining rejections are based on such art. Director may search for new art before terminating.

name: Procedures for unusual fact patterns involving old art
description: Cases with unusual fact patterns (e.g., prior art cited but the examiner did not appreciate issues raised) should be brought to CRU or TC Director for determination.
guidance: Unusual fact patterns may include situations where a textbook was cited but only select information was discussed; if request relies on other information in the textbook that actually teaches the claims, it may be appropriate to rely on that other information to order/conduct reexamination. A request that merely provides a new interpretation of a previously relied-upon reference does not create an SNQ.

name: Specification components and embodiment disclosure
description: Provisional and nonprovisional components include abstract, drawings (if necessary), and description. Must describe completely a specific embodiment of the process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter or improvement.
guidance: Ensure the specification contains at least one complete, specific embodiment of the invention (including drawings/examples where necessary) so that claimed subject matter is supported and enabled.

name: Provisional application requirements
description: Provisional: automatically abandoned after one year period; no claims required; written disclosure must meet same requirements as nonprovisional.
guidance: A provisional filing must still adequately describe and enable the invention; plan for continuity to retain benefit of provisional filing date.

name: Continuity / priority benefit
description: Continuity is key to retaining the benefit of the filing date of the earlier-filed provisional application.
guidance: When relying on provisional priority, ensure subject matter in the provisional supports all claim elements you expect to claim in the nonprovisional to preserve the earlier filing date.

name: Specification must define and support claimed subject matter
description: If it is recited in the claims, then it absolutely needs to be described, enabled, and defined by the instant specification. The description should provide clear support for all terms used in the claims so that their meaning may be ascertainable by reference to the description.
guidance: Draft specification so every claim term has support and explanation; do not claim elements that lack support in the specification.

name: Claim term interpretation and applicant lexicography
description: Applicants may serve as their own 'lexicographer.' Claim terms must be given their 'plain meaning,' unless it is inconsistent with the specification. Broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification.
guidance: If you intend a special definition, define terms explicitly in the specification. Otherwise rely on plain meaning but be aware the office applies the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.

name: Identify invention type and component relationships
description: Before drafting claims consider: What is the invention? Tangible: composition, apparatus, machine. Method: making, doing, or using. If tangible, what are the pieces that compose the invention and how do they interrelate? Multiple inventions or multiple versions?
guidance: Use this brainstorming to determine claim categories (apparatus, composition, method) and how to structure independent and dependent claims to cover variations.

name: Claim strategy: breadth, variety, and claims budget
description: What are the goals? Obtain the broadest, valid claim(s) possible; obtain claims with a variety of type and scope; not just at filing but during prosecution; consider a claims budget (fees for excess claims).
guidance: Plan claim scope and types (independent/dependent, method/apparatus/composition) strategically; account for fees (example: micro-entity: independent claims in excess of 3 = $120/claim; each claim in excess of 20 = $25/claim) and prosecution changes.

name: Clear claim construction practices
description: Draft claims early to decide terms; ensure terms are used consistently and captured in the specification; determine which terms need more detailed definition or clarity; description is also provided as drawings and examples; be wary of indefinite language (terms of degree, 'exemplary' language, etc.); ensure that the claims are 'commensurate in scope'; look to U.S. patents as examples.
guidance: Use consistent terminology between claims and specification, avoid vague terms of degree, and provide definitions or examples for ambiguous terms to reduce indefiniteness risks.

name: Legal claim requirements: definiteness and dependency rules
description: A nonprovisional patent application must have at least one claim which particularly points out and distinctly defines the invention. Claims are written in independent or dependent form. A dependent claim necessarily incorporates by reference all of the limitations of the claim to which it refers. A dependent claim must refer to a preceding claim and must further limit the claimed invention.
guidance: Ensure at least one definite independent claim and that dependent claims properly refer to and further limit antecedent claims (do not leave dependent claims indefinite or improperly referenced).

name: Balance claim scope (not too specific vs not too general)
description: Claims that are too specific may make the invention not valuable; claims that are too general may be not patentable.
guidance: Aim for the broadest claim likely to be allowable, with dependent claims or alternative independent claims to capture narrower fallback positions.

name: Claim structure: preamble guidance
description: Every claim contains a preamble (e.g., 'A shovel…' for independent; 'The shovel of claim 1…' for dependent). Carefully consider the language recited in the preamble — effect is determined case-by-case; the preamble is read in the context of the entire claim; recitation may be structural or an intended use/purpose.
guidance: Draft preambles deliberately: choosing e.g., 'A topically-applied composition …' vs 'An ocular composition …' may affect scope and interpretation; consider whether the preamble introduces a structural limitation or only states intended use.

name: Transitional phrase selection
description: Transitional phrases set forth the scope of the claimed invention. The two most commonly used are 'comprising' (open) and 'consisting of' (closed). 'Comprising' is open-ended and understood as 'including, but not limited to'; 'consisting of' is closed-ended and limits claim elements to those recited. Claims may use both phrases repeatedly.
guidance: Choose transitional phrase to control whether unrecited elements are excluded ('consisting of') or allowed ('comprising'); use mixed transitions for hybrid scope where appropriate.

name: Claim body requirements
description: The body must clearly set forth elements, steps, and/or relationships which are considered to be the claimed invention. Terms/phrases used in the claims must have antecedent basis in the specification. Supported terms/phrases must be described/defined in the specification so their meaning may be ascertained by reference. Limitations should conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification.
guidance: List all necessary structural/functional elements and their relationships; ensure each limitation has support and enabling disclosure in the specification.

name: Antecedent basis and internal referencing
description: Antecedent basis is referencing within a claim and between claims. Must be first preceded by the indefinite article 'a' or 'an,' or by terminology like 'at least one…,' 'a plurality of…'. Subsequent references should be preceded by the definite article 'the' or 'said' (e.g., 'the at least one…,' 'the plurality of…'). Subsequent references to limitations can occur in both independent and dependent claims. Additional common cue words: 'wherein' or 'whereby.'
guidance: Provide clear antecedent basis for every element to avoid ambiguity (first introduce with 'a' or 'an' or 'at least one,' then refer back with 'the' or 'said').

name: Iterative drafting and claim clarity (examples)
description: Iteratively refine claim phrasing and structure to remove grammatical/structural issues (e.g., merge elements, add 'wherein' clauses, avoid stray commas) so the claim reads clearly as a single sentence and the relationships between elements are explicit.
guidance: Use iterative edits to simplify claim sentence structure, make dependencies explicit, and ensure the claim remains a single grammatically-complete sentence that properly limits invention scope.

name: Dependent claim drafting and examples
description: Dependent claim examples show that dependent claims must refer to claim 1 (e.g., 'The transdermal patch according to claim 1, wherein...') and add further limitations (e.g., separating layer is between matrix and adhesive layer).
guidance: When drafting dependent claims, make sure they properly incorporate all limitations of the referenced claim and add further limiting features; use dependent claims to capture fallback positions and particular embodiments.

name: Analyze claim for 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 compliance
description: Analyze the claim for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 in accordance with current guidance, which is unaffected by this provision.
guidance: Perform applicability checks for subject matter eligibility and specification/claim requirements (written description, enablement, definiteness) per existing USPTO guidance before applying tax-strategy-specific rules.

name: Identify tax strategy claim limitations
description: Identify any limitations relating to a tax strategy, as defined above (note the listed exclusions).
guidance: Determine whether claim limitations pertain to tax strategies, especially those suitable for use with tax-favored structures (employee benefit plans, tax-exempt organizations, or other entities requiring particular structure/operation to obtain tax consequences). See MPEP § 2124.01 for details.

name: Tax strategy limitations treated as within prior art for 35 U.S.C. 102/103
description: Evaluate the claim in view of the prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, treating any limitations relating to a tax strategy as being within the prior art, and not as a patentable difference between the claim and the prior art.
guidance: Do not accord patentable weight to tax-strategy limitations when assessing novelty/obviousness; analogous to the treatment of printed matter limitations (see MPEP § 2112.01).

name: Use form paragraph 7.06.01 for tax strategy limitations
description: Form paragraph 7.06.01 may be used to indicate claim limitation(s) interpreted as a tax strategy.
guidance: Form text: 'Claim limitation "[1]" has been interpreted as a strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability ("tax strategy") pursuant to Section 14 of the Leahy‑Smith America Invents Act. Accordingly, this claim limitation is being treated as being within the prior art and is insufficient to differentiate the invention of claim [2] from the prior art.' Examiner Note: recite the limitation in bracket 1, insert claim number(s) in bracket 2; see MPEP § 2124.01 for more information.

name: Computer-implemented methods: give weight to technical features, not tax strategy
description: A computer-implemented method that is deemed novel and non-obvious would not be affected by this provision even if used for a tax purpose. However, a prior art computer-implemented method would not become non-obvious by implementing a novel and non-obvious tax strategy.
guidance: Software-related inventions under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103: claim limitations directed solely to enabling individuals to file income tax returns or assist with managing finances should be given patentable weight, except that claim limitations directed to a tax strategy should not be given patentable weight.

name: Drawings/pictures can anticipate if they clearly show claimed structure
description: Drawings and pictures can anticipate claims if they clearly show the structure which is claimed.
guidance: The picture must show all the claimed structural features and how they are put together. The origin of the drawing is immaterial. Evaluate drawings for what they reasonably disclose and suggest to one of ordinary skill in the art. See In re Mraz; Jockmus v. Leviton; In re Aslanian.

name: When a patent is used as a 'patent' (not a 'publication'), examiner may rely on specification details
description: When the patented document is used as a patent and not as a publication, the examiner may use any information provided in the specification which relates to the subject matter of the patented claims when making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre‑AIA 102(a), (b) or (d).
guidance: Unclaimed details in the specification can be relied upon if they relate to the patented claims; courts treat 'invention ... patented' broadly to include disclosed aspects. See Ex parte Ovist; In re Kathawala; In re Fuge discussion.

name: Controller power to direct insertion/deletion of reference to another patent (S.19; Rules 32,33)
description: The Controller has the power to direct the insertion (in the specification) of the reference to another patent which could be infringed in the event of performing the invention of the application, and also for the deletion of such reference from there on request from the applicant, when the said referred patent ceases, or revoked or relevant conflicting claim is deleted from the other patent.
guidance: Controller may require specification to reference potentially infringed patents; applicant may request deletion when conflicting patent ceases or is revoked; Rules 32/33 govern procedure.

name: Amendment of application and specification — leave, form and fees (S.57; Rule 81(1))
description: The applicant or patentee may amend the application, complete specification or any document related thereto after taking leave for amendment in Form13. If the amendment is requested before grant the fee is Rs.500 (natural) and Rs.2000 (others); after grant fees are higher (Rs.1000/Rs.4000). For mere changes of name/address etc. the fee is Rs.200 and Rs.800 respectively.
guidance: The application should state the nature of proposed amendment (usually highlighted in red) and give full particulars of the reason. Priority date of a claim may be amended (S.57(5)). Proof required for change of name.

name: Substantive amendment restriction — no added matter or expanded claim scope (S.59(1))
description: Amendment can be allowed only if it is by way of disclaimer, correction or explanation for incorporation of actual fact. Amendment should not be allowed if the specification as amended claims or describes matter not in substance disclosed or shown before the amendment or the amended claims do not fall wholly within the scope of a claim of the specification before the amendment (S.59(1)).
guidance: No introduction of new matter or enlargement of claim scope beyond original disclosure; amended pages must be filed in duplicate with duly cancelled originals.

name: Pre-grant opposition — grounds (S.25(1) clauses a–k)
description: Where an application has been published but not granted, any person may within 6 months from publication represent opposition on specific statutory grounds: wrongful obtaining; prior publication before priority date; prior claim in another Indian complete specification; prior public knowledge/use in India; obviousness/lack of inventive step; subject-matter not an invention or not patentable; insufficient/unclear description; failure to disclose or false information under section 8; convention application timing breach; incorrect or missing source/geographical origin of biological material; anticipation by traditional/indigenous knowledge — but on no other ground.
guidance: Grounds are exhaustive (including substantive requirements like novelty, inventive step, industrial application and statutory exclusions). Controller will hear if requested and dispose per rules.

name: Statutory classification: 'Machine'
description: A machine as subject of a patent must be a particular construction of mechanism containing the improved method of producing an old effect or a method of producing a new effect; it is a function embodied in particular mechanism whose mode of operation and structure are pointed out.
guidance: The term 'machine' includes new combinations of machines and new organizations of mechanism for a single purpose. A machine patent may cover a new machine even if constituent machines are old, so long as the combination or organization is new. Example: telescope combining convex and concave glasses. What constitutes a claim for a combination only versus parts of a machine is a question of construction on the patent and specification.

name: Combination patents: scope and limits
description: When the invention consists of a new combination of existing machinery, the thing patented is the combination; the separate machines are not the patented thing unless the patent also claims them.
guidance: If a patent claims only the combination, using any of the machines separately (without the whole combination) is not infringement. Conversely, where a patent covers several distinct and independent improvements in the same machine taken in the aggregate, the patent will protect each improvement. Whether the patent is for the combination only or includes specified improvements affects remedies and infringement analysis.

name: Claims for whole machine vs specific improvements: scope and potential invalidity
description: If a patentee claims the whole of a machine as his invention while only parts or certain improvements are actually his invention, the patent may be void for exceeding the invention; conversely, where the whole machine is substantially new, piracy of a part may still be actionable.
guidance: Where a patent is for several distinct improvements which are clearly specified, piracy of any one improvement may violate the patentee's right. Where a patent is for a new combination only, unless that combination is substantially violated, the patentee has no remedy for use of separate parts. Courts examine whether the patent's terms exceed the patentee's true invention.

name: Classification choice determined by principal characteristics
description: The proper statutory class (art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) for a patent claim depends on the invention's principal characteristics and objects: whether application of a principle, particular machinery, or a new article/result is the core of the invention.
guidance: If application of a principle is central and machinery incidental, classify as 'art'. If machinery/structure is chief, classify as 'machine'. If the article/result produced is new, classify as 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter' as appropriate. The principal characteristic controls classification and thus framing of claims.

name: Meaning of 'claims the drug' for Orange Book listing
description: A patent "claims the drug for which the applicant submitted the application" when the patent "particularly points out and distinctly claims" the drug as the invention (35 U.S.C. §112(b)); it is not satisfied merely because an NDA product would infringe a patent claim.
guidance: The court rejects equating ‘‘claims’’ with ‘‘reads on’’ or mere infringement. To decide whether a patent claims the drug, analyze the patent document (claims and specification) to see whether the inventor defined the invention as the drug or drug constituent at issue. Examples/authority: 35 U.S.C. §112(b); Phillips v. AWH; Hoechst‑Roussel; the opinion contrasts claiming (internal document-based inquiry) with infringement (external-product-based inquiry).

name: Listing requires both 'claims the drug' and that infringement could reasonably be asserted
description: The listing provision includes two distinct statutory requirements: (1) that the patent "claims the drug for which the applicant submitted the application" and (2) that "a claim of patent infringement could reasonably be asserted" (21 U.S.C. §355(b)(1)(A)(viii) and related provisions).
guidance: Treat these as separate conditions; interpreting them as coterminous would render statutory language redundant. Evidence of (possible) infringement alone does not satisfy the separate statutory requirement that the patent claims the drug. The court relies on textualist canons to give effect to both elements (citing Reiter v. Sonotone and Nat’l Assn of Mfrs. v. Dep’t of Defense).

name: Patent must claim at least the active ingredient to be listable
description: To be listed in the Orange Book, a patent must claim an invention that contains at least the active ingredient identified in the NDA; patents claiming only device components or other non‑active parts of the approved product do not meet the listing requirement.
guidance: This rule follows from the FDCA statutory scheme and FDA approval practices: drug approval centrally focuses on the active ingredient; ANDA applicants must have the same active ingredient (21 U.S.C. §355(j)(2)(A)(ii)); cases cited include Sandoz and Ipsen. Policy rationale: the active ingredient is what makes a product approvable as a drug; listing a patent that does not claim the active ingredient would assert patents outside the scope Congress intended for Orange Book listing. Practical anti‑pattern: attempting to list patents that claim only dose counters, canisters, or other device parts of an NDA product is improper under this standard.

name: Distinction between claiming (claim construction) and infringement (literal + doctrine of equivalents)
description: Claiming focuses on what the patent document (claims and specification) particularly and distinctly claims (inquiry guided by Phillips), while infringement asks whether a particular accused product contains each claim limitation (literal infringement) or is equivalent (doctrine of equivalents) under 35 U.S.C. §271(a).
guidance: When assessing listability, use claim‑construction principles (intrinsic evidence, prosecution history, extrinsic evidence per Phillips) to determine what the patent claims. Recognize that infringement doctrines (literal reading vs. equivalents) are separate theories; infringement can be shown in ways that do not change what the patent actually claims. Examples: Allen Eng’g on literal infringement; Warner‑Jenkinson and Wilson Sporting Goods on doctrine of equivalents; Hoechst‑Roussel and Apotex discussed to distinguish the inquiries.

name: Claims are defined by the patent document and specification (35 U.S.C. §112 and Federal Circuit precedent)
description: A patent claim is a numbered paragraph that particularly points out and distinctly claims the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention (35 U.S.C. §112(b)), and the specification must describe and enable that invention (35 U.S.C. §112(a)).
guidance: Determination of whether a patent 'claims' a drug requires reading the claims together with the specification to define the invention the patentee sought to protect. The court cites Phillips, Merrill v. Yeomans, and the statutory enabling/written description mandates to support this inquiry. Practical implication: a claim that focuses on a device component need not enable or describe the whole NDA product (e.g., a steering wheel claim need not describe the entire car).

name: Combination‑product designation and NDA approval do not automatically make device components listable as the 'drug'
description: Even if the FDA approves a combination product via an NDA (because the primary mode of action is that of a drug), that administrative designation does not convert device components into listable "drug" inventions unless the patent claims the active ingredient or invention that made the product approvable as a drug.
guidance: Under 21 U.S.C. §353(g), the FDA uses primary mode of action to determine which center/approval pathway applies. But statutory and regulatory treatment of combination products does not alter the Orange Book’s statutory requirement that a patent claim the drug (i.e., the active ingredient). The court rejects Teva’s argument that combination‑product FDA processing means patents to device parts are listable. Cite to SMDA and Genus Med. for context.

name: Use of statutory interpretation canons in listing disputes (avoid redundancy; give words effect)
description: When interpreting listing/delisting provisions, courts must give effect to each statutory term and avoid interpretations that render statutory language meaningless or redundant.
guidance: The opinion applies canons (Reiter; Nat’l Assn. of Mfrs.) to reject interpretations that collapse distinct statutory requirements (e.g., 'claims' vs 'infringement'). Practitioners should craft arguments that respect separate statutory elements and explain how proposed readings fit the FDCA/Hatch‑Waxman scheme as a coherent whole.

name: Standard of evidence for asserted utility
description: The character and amount of evidence needed to support an asserted utility will vary depending on what is claimed and whether the asserted utility appears to contravene established principles and beliefs. An applicant does not have to provide evidence 'beyond a reasonable doubt' or establish utility as a matter of statistical certainty.
guidance: Evidence will be sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill in the art to conclude that the asserted utility is more likely than not true. (Cited cases: Ex parte Ferguson; In re Gazave; In re Irons; Nelson v. Bowler.)

name: Treatment of specific disease conditions — credibility varies
description: Claims directed to treating or curing diseases with no previously successful treatments warrant careful review; credibility of asserted utility may be more difficult when current scientific understanding suggests the task is impossible.
guidance: Lack of known cure is not automatically a basis to find lack of utility. An assertion of usefulness for treating a symptom may be credible with modest evidence, whereas an assertion of 'curing' the disease may require significantly greater evidentiary support. Expert affidavits indicating reasonable expectation of success, supported by sound reasoning, usually should be sufficient to establish credibility. (Cited cases: In re Jolles; In re Buting; In re Sichert; citations to FDA regulations 21 CFR 312.80-88.)

name: Joint inventorship — scope and requirements
description: When an invention is made by two or more persons jointly, they shall apply for patent jointly and each make the required oath; joint inventors may not have worked together or at the same time, may have different types or amounts of contribution, and need not have contributed to every claim.
guidance: A 'quantum of collaboration or connection' is required — e.g., collaboration, working under common direction, one inventor seeing a report and building on it, or hearing another's suggestion. Contribution to at least one claim suffices for joint inventorship. The contributor of a disclosed means for a means-plus-function element can be a joint inventor as to that claim. (Cited authorities: 35 U.S.C. 116; Kimberly-Clark Corp. v. Procter & Gamble; Ethicon Inc. v. United States Surgical Corp.)

name: Inventorship for continuing applications claiming 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit
description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application; the earlier application must disclose the named inventor's invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: So long as at least one inventor is common and other requirements are met, the Office will permit a 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit claim without additional submissions. Examiners must check the earlier application to determine common inventorship and compliance with 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78; benefit may be permitted without examining the earlier application for disclosure/support unless necessary (e.g., intervening reference).

name: Claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation (BROI) in light of the specification
description: During patent examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, as would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: The PTO determines claim scope not solely on claim language but by giving claims their broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1)). Examiners use BROI during prosecution to establish a clear record of applicant intent; courts interpret claims differently in infringement/validity proceedings with a fully developed record. (Cited cases: Phillips v. AWH Corp.; In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr.; In re Suitco Surface; In re Morris.)

name: 35 U.S.C. 255 Criteria for Certificate of Correction (In re Arnott)
description: Two separate statutory requirements must be met before a certificate of correction for an applicant's mistake may issue: (1) the nature/type of the mistake must be clerical, typographical, or a mistake of minor character; and (2) the proposed correction must not involve changes which would constitute new matter or require reexamination.
guidance: If the above is not satisfied, reissue must be used. Usually, any mistake affecting claim scope must be corrected by reissue. A mistake is not 'minor' if the requested change would materially affect the scope or meaning of the patent. See MPEP § 1412.04 for correction of inventorship via certificate of correction or reissue.

name: Use of certificate of correction to amend priority claims (35 U.S.C. 119(e) and 120) — conditions
description: Under certain conditions, a certificate of correction can be used to correct or add references to prior copending applications for 35 U.S.C. 120 and 119(e) priority or to correct incorrect references pursuant to 37 CFR 1.78(a)(2) and (a)(4).
guidance: For non-365(c) cases: (A) for 120 priority, all requirements in 37 CFR 1.78(a)(1) must have been met in the application which became the patent to be corrected; (B) for 119(e) priority, requirements in 1.78(a)(3) must have been met in the application which became the patent; (C) the prior copending application to be added via the certificate must be identified elsewhere in the application papers (not just first sentence of spec); and (D) it must be clear from the record of the patent and parent application(s) that priority is appropriate. For international-application-based 120/365(c) priority there are analogous conditions plus a requirement to submit documentation showing designation of states and other info. If these conditions are not satisfied, file reissue.

name: Statutory disclaimer requirements (35 U.S.C. 253; 37 CFR 1.321) - content and signature
description: A statutory disclaimer to be recorded must be in writing, signed by the patentee or an attorney/agent of record, identify the patent and the complete claim(s) or term being disclaimed (partial-claim disclaimers will be refused), state present extent of patentee's ownership interest, and be accompanied by the fee in § 1.20(d).
guidance: A disclaimer filed in an application must be signed by the proper party depending on assignment status (applicant, applicant+assignee if part interest, assignee if entire interest, or attorney/agent). A disclaimer filed in a patent or reexamination must be signed by the patentee (assignee or inventors as appropriate) or attorney/agent of record. Signature need not be original; copies/facsimiles are acceptable per 37 CFR 1.4(d)(2).

name: Terminal disclaimer specifics and limits (37 CFR 1.321(c) and practice in pending applications)
description: A terminal disclaimer (disclaiming all or part of the term) may be filed to overcome double patenting. In pending applications, a terminal disclaimer must be of a terminal portion of the term of the entire patent to be granted (cannot be directed to particular claim(s)); the statute does not provide for conditional disclaimers; the disclaimer should identify the disclaimant and their interest and specify the effective date.
guidance: When filed to obviate a judicially created double patenting rejection, terminal disclaimers must also include provisions that any patent granted shall be enforceable only while commonly owned with the application/patent which formed the basis for the rejection. In pending applications, paralegals process terminal disclaimers: determine compliance with statute/regulations, notify examiner re acceptability, record acceptable disclaimers, and provide data for printing. The paralegal marks the file (green label, stamp, endorsement, PALM entry) and completes a Terminal Disclaimer Informal Memo to notify examiner of informalities; the examiner should inform applicant in next Office action and initial/date the memo.

name: Definiteness requirement (Nautilus reasonable-certainty standard)
description: Section 112 requires that 'a patent’s claims, viewed in light of the specification and prosecution history, inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.' The court must ensure claims do not create an 'innovation-discouraging "zone of uncertainty."' (citing Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc.).
guidance: Assess whether a skilled artisan, in view of the intrinsic record, can determine claim scope with reasonable certainty. Look for a 'zone of uncertainty' that would make the claim invalid; if the intrinsic evidence provides reasonable certainty, the claim is not indefinite.

name: Claim-construction sources and hierarchy (Phillips)
description: Interpret claims by looking to the claim language, the specification, the prosecution history, and, where relevant, extrinsic evidence. 'The prosecution history, in particular, may be critical in interpreting disputed claim terms.' (Phillips v. AWH Corp. and Personalized Media communications citation).
guidance: Begin with claim language; consult specification for context; use prosecution history to resolve ambiguities; use extrinsic evidence only when relevant and subordinate to intrinsic record.

name: Prosecution-history amendments can define/limit claim scope
description: An amendment made to overcome a prior-art rejection can be used to construe disputed claim language. The circumstances of an amendment that overcame a prior-art rejection can provide sufficient clarity to construe a limitation. (Citing example where amendment distinguishing Hirshberg informed the meaning of 'only one option').
guidance: When a claim was amended to overcome a reference, interpret the amended language in light of the rationale for the amendment. Such amendments may limit the number of permissible constructions if they were made to avoid prior art.

name: Cannot establish indefiniteness merely by identifying multiple plausible interpretations
description: A party cannot show indefiniteness by 'merely identify[ing] different ways one could interpret' a claim term; otherwise nearly every term could be found indefinite. (Citing ClearOne, Nevro).
guidance: To prove indefiniteness the challenger must show that, after considering the intrinsic record, reasonable certainty is lacking. If the intrinsic evidence resolves among competing interpretations, indefiniteness is not established.

name: Intrinsic record controls; embodiments inform but do not necessarily limit
description: The specification’s embodiments help interpret claim scope but do not automatically limit claims to those embodiments. The intrinsic record—claims, specification, prosecution history—resolves meanings; reliance on one embodiment alone does not necessarily restrict claims.
guidance: Use embodiments to illuminate meaning, but avoid importing unnecessary limitations from a preferred embodiment into the claim unless the intrinsic record requires it.

name: Standard of review for indefiniteness
description: The ultimate legal conclusion of indefiniteness and any determinations based on intrinsic evidence are reviewed de novo; underlying factual determinations are reviewed for clear error. (Cox Commc’ns, Inc. v. Sprint Commc’n Co.).
guidance: On appeal, accept district court’s factual findings unless clearly erroneous; review claim-construction and indefiniteness conclusions anew.

name: How to construe 'wherein the representation consists of only one option for activating the function'
description: Interpreted (on this record) as 'wherein the representation consists of only one option for what function to activate at a given time (where a given time means the currently active application).' The 'option' limits how many functions can be activated from a given representation to one, though that single function can change depending on the active application.
guidance: Determine whether the limitation was added to distinguish prior art (e.g., Hirshberg's multifunction keys). Treat 'option' as referring to number of functions activatable from a representation (not the gesture itself). Consider specification language (e.g., claim 2 and embodiments) and prosecution statements that overcame the prior-art rejection.

name: Treatment of isolated or inconsistent prosecution/litigation statements
description: Isolated or contextless statements (e.g., post-allowance remarks or snippets from IPRs/litigation) do not necessarily change a claim construction or render a claim indefinite. The intrinsic record must be read as a whole; a 'bare statement made after allowance' is insufficient to override the rest of the prosecution history and specification. (Citing Univ. of Mass. v. L’Oréal and Sequoia Tech. v. Dell).
guidance: Weigh inconsistent or imprecise statements in the full context of prosecution and specification. Do not elevate isolated remarks above the broader intrinsic record that indicates meaning.

name: Evaluating terms susceptible to plain-and-ordinary-meaning construction ('gliding . . . away')
description: A term may be given its plain and ordinary meaning so long as that meaning, read in the context of the claim and intrinsic record, provides reasonable certainty and excludes clearly distinguishable operations (here, the court endorsed a plain-and-ordinary-meaning construction of 'gliding . . . away' with the caveat it 'did not include dragging, flicking, or a drag and drop operation').
guidance: If plain and ordinary meaning, together with intrinsic evidence and prosecution history, imparts reasonable certainty to a skilled artisan, that construction is acceptable. Compare prior decisions (e.g., companion Google v. Neonode) for consistency.

name: Using amendments to distinguish prior art and thereby narrow claim scope
description: When a claim amendment is made expressly 'in distinction' to a prior-art reference, that amendment can be understood to limit claim scope in the way necessary to avoid the reference (e.g., adding 'only one option' to distinguish Hirshberg’s multifunction keys).
guidance: Treat narrowing amendments as evidence the patentee surrendered certain claim scope during prosecution; incorporate that surrendered meaning into claim construction where appropriate to preserve consistency with prosecution history.

name: Primacy of claim language
description: The claim language is the best evidence of what ideas it is trying to convey.
guidance: The Article emphasizes that claim language should be treated as primary evidence of meaning; to say one must know the idea before understanding language is a conceptual error. (See text: "claim language is the best evidence of what ideas it is trying to convey.")

name: Claim construction should consider multiple documentary sources
description: Claim construction routinely considers the claim structure, the specification, the prosecution history, dictionaries, and expert testimony.
guidance: Markman and subsequent cases direct courts to consult these sources in construing claim terms; the Article lists these five categories explicitly as the traditional sources for interpretation.

name: Use of dictionaries in claim interpretation
description: Some precedents favor consulting dictionaries to determine ordinary meaning of claim terms.
guidance: Tex. Digital Sys. v. Telegenix is noted as favoring dictionaries; Phillips en banc questioned whether primary reliance should be on dictionaries or on patentee's use in the specification. The Article also cites criticisms of over-reliance on dictionaries.

name: Role of expert testimony and extrinsic evidence
description: Expert testimony and other extrinsic evidence can be used to explicate claim terms, particularly technical ones.
guidance: Some commentators (e.g., Nard) favor expert testimony; there is disagreement about the extent to which trial courts should receive and rely on such evidence versus treating construction as purely legal.

name: Inherent indeterminacy of claim language
description: Patent claim language may be inherently indeterminate; the nature of language makes it impossible to capture the full essence of an invention solely in claim text.
guidance: Cited authorities (Burk & Lemley, Lee, Liivak) argue that claim text often cannot yield a single determinate boundary; this supports the view that courts inevitably must shape boundaries when words are underdetermined.

name: Textualism vs anti-textualism (methodological approaches)
description: Competing interpretive philosophies: textualism (focus on claim text/plain meaning) versus anti-textualism (focus on the patentee's invention, functional scope, or policy outcomes).
guidance: The Article discusses these camps at length, noting labels like 'hypertextualism' (claim-centered) and 'pragmatic textualism' or invention-centered approaches; it emphasizes that the debate underlies claim-construction disputes.

name: When Phillips yields no clear answer, policy may inform construction
description: Substantive and policy considerations should come into play only when traditional claim construction does not yield a clear answer.
guidance: Proposed by commentators like Lee and some others: reserve non-textual/policy factors for gap-filling after ordinary interpretive tools are exhausted to avoid 'redrafting' claims while still addressing underdeterminate cases.

name: Doctrine of equivalents as narrow exception
description: The doctrine of equivalents allows a court to deem an unclaimed product to be infringing if the difference is 'insubstantial.'
guidance: The doctrine is described as a narrow exception to the rule that claims define the bounds of the monopoly; cases like Warner-Jenkinson and commentary about its waning application are cited.

name: Claims define the invention / claims as measure of the grant
description: Patent claims afford the measure of the grant to the patentee and define the invention's boundaries.
guidance: Foundational cases (e.g., Merrill, Milcor Steel) and treatises emphasize that it is the claims that determine what the patent excludes others from doing; this principle underpins textualist approaches.

name: Appellate standard of review for claim construction (de novo v. deference)
description: Whether claim construction is reviewed de novo on appeal or given deference to trial-court factual findings is contested: Cybor held de novo review, while others argue for deference to trial courts on factual predicates.
guidance: The Article recounts Cybor's en banc holding for de novo review and opposing views that favor deference (e.g., calls for 'something approaching' deference for factual predicates or clear-error review for fact findings).

name: Trial court's role in evaluating extrinsic evidence
description: Trial courts are positioned to gauge the relevance and need for additional evidence to explicate claim terms, including taking evidence at trial.
guidance: Eastman Kodak v. Goodyear is cited for the proposition that trial judges are best situated to assess the need for extrinsic evidence, in tension with Cybor's legal-question approach.

name: Tradeoff: broader claim language increases invalidity risk
description: Broad claim language may favor patentees by covering more, but it also increases the likelihood that the claim will be invalidated.
guidance: The Article notes the practical tradeoff: broader claims can be powerful if valid, but their breadth raises vulnerability to invalidity challenges.

name: Anti-pattern: considering dictionaries before the specification
description: Criticism exists of practices that place dictionary definitions ahead of the specification when construing claims.
guidance: Ben Hattenbach and others criticize 'process of considering dictionaries before specifications' as problematic; Phillips en banc asked parties to address whether dictionaries or patentee's usage in spec should be primary.

name: Claim construction may decide the case
description: To decide what the claims legally mean is often functionally to decide the patent case.
guidance: Authorities such as Wang Labs. and Markman (and quoted commentary) observe that claim-meaning determinations frequently determine infringement and validity outcomes.

name: Invention-centered (pragmatic) vs claim-centered framing of patent scope
description: Some commentators favor construing claims narrowly 'in light of the actual invention' (invention-centered) rather than relying solely on the claim text (claim-centered).
guidance: Burk & Lemley, Liivak, Nard, and others are discussed: invention-centered approaches conceptualize the invention functionally, potentially permitting courts to construe claims to reflect the actual invention rather than isolated words.

name: Circumstances where written description issues arise - amendment affecting a claim
description: An amendment to the claims or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed. An amendment to the specification may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim.
guidance: When claims are amended or new claims added, examiners must check that the as-filed disclosure supports the change (see In re Wright). Be mindful that specification amendments (e.g., changing a term definition) can affect claim scope.

name: Circumstances where written description issues arise - reliance on filing date of parent application (35 U.S.C. 120)
description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier U.S. application only if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph in the earlier application.
guidance: When claiming priority to a parent U.S. application under 35 U.S.C. 120, ensure the earlier application provides written description support for the subject matter in question (see Tronzo v. Biomet; In re Scheiber).

name: Circumstances where written description issues arise - reliance on foreign/provisional priority (35 U.S.C. 119)
description: Claims are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or provisional filing date only if the corresponding foreign or provisional application supports the claims as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Examiners must verify that the foreign/provisional priority document supplies the requisite written description support for the claimed subject matter (see In re Ziegler; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Gosteli).

name: Circumstances where written description issues arise - support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference
description: In an interference, the claim corresponding to a count must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph; earlier applications relied upon must meet the 112 requirement for the subject matter of the count.
guidance: A broad generic disclosure to a class may be insufficient for a specific compound; when benefit of an earlier-filed application is sought in interference, confirm the earlier app meets the 112 written description standard (Fields v. Conover; Hyatt v. Boone).

name: Statement of rejection requirements for lack of written description
description: When rejecting a claim, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which support the lack of written description conclusion: (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure as filed.
guidance: Provide specific findings and reasoning (MPEP §2163.04). A general allegation is not enough; a simple statement pointing out where support is absent may suffice for new/amended claims where support is not apparent. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments that can be supported, mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter (see Rasmussen).

name: Changes to scope of claims - general support requirement
description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: When claims are broadened, narrowed, or otherwise altered (including numerical ranges or terminology changes), verify that each limitation finds support in the as-filed specification/drawings/claims (see MPEP §2163).

name: Broadening claim - omission of a limitation (removing an essential feature)
description: Omission of a limitation can raise an issue whether the inventor had possession of the broader invention; a claim that omits an element which the applicant describes as an essential or critical feature does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: If the specification indicates a feature is 'essential' or 'the only possible location' (or similar), removing it may render the claim unsupported (Gentry Gallery; Tronzo; In re Wilder). Compare cases where a limitation was not described as critical and broadening was allowed (In re Peters).

name: Broadening claim - genus supported by species (addition of generic claim)
description: A claimed genus may be supported by a sufficient description of a representative number of species; when substantial variation exists, describe a sufficient variety of species. Disclosure of only one species supports a genus only if it indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.
guidance: Assess predictability and evidence that other species are operable. Single-species disclosures may suffice in predictable arts or when the disclosure indicates broader invention; otherwise, one species often won't support a genus (Enzo Biochem; In re Curtis; In re Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe).

name: Quality of patent drafting (claim scope)
description: A well drafted patent will cover several embodiments of a product and its key features or components, including their use in different/unrelated products rather than being limited to a single product.
guidance: Claims should not unnecessarily limit scope to only the immediate product; claim construction choices affect ability to license or enforce. Patent drafter should understand client needs to guide claim drafting and additional claim limitations during prosecution.

name: Design-around analysis
description: Determining the scope of claim coverage of patents to assess how a competitor might design around them.
guidance: Requires detailed review of claims, prior art cited during prosecution, and prosecution history (to find damaging admissions). Consider claim construction rules (ordinary/plain meaning, interpretation in light of description and prosecution history), means-plus-function treatment, and jurisdictional differences. Result often communicated in an attorney opinion.

name: Prosecution history estoppel and careful office responses
description: Statements made during prosecution can surrender claim coverage and limit later enforcement (doctrine of equivalents implications).
guidance: Responses to office actions need to be carefully worded and concise to avoid creating estoppel or limiting claim scope that may hamper enforcement; prosecution history should be checked during design-around analysis.

name: Doctrine of equivalents considerations
description: Some countries recognize infringement under the doctrine of equivalents, where substantially similar components used in a substantially similar manner may infringe even if literal claim elements are not met.
guidance: Whether doctrine applies can affect damages and infringement analysis; interplay with prosecution history estoppel is important and complex.

name: Patent drafter role boundaries and client guidance
description: Patent drafters should help clients create enabling environments, infrastructure and selection processes for patenting, but should not themselves create inventions or drive client patenting decisions.
guidance: Drafters can assist with invention disclosure forms, docketing, training, and advising on selection, but must avoid conflicts of interest (e.g., inventing for the client) and ensure they understand client business needs to guide claim drafting appropriately.

name: Amendment of Amendments
description: When a replacement paragraph or section to the specification is to be amended, it should be wholly rewritten and the original insertion canceled, so that no interlineations or deletions shall appear in the clause as finally presented.
guidance: Matter canceled by amendment can be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the canceled matter as a new insertion. A claim canceled by amendment (deleted in its entirety) may be reinstated only by a subsequent amendment presenting the claim as a new claim with a new claim number.

name: Situations Where 37 CFR 1.131 Is Inappropriate — Statutory Bars and Other Limits
description: A 1.131 affidavit/declaration is not appropriate where: (A) the reference publication date is more than 1 year prior (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)); (B) the reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claims the same patentable invention; (C) the reference is a foreign patent for the same invention to applicant issued prior to the domestic filing date on an application filed more than 12 months prior (35 U.S.C. 102(d)); (D) the effective filing date of applicant's parent application or an international convention proved filing date is prior to the effective date of the reference (affidavit unnecessary); (E) where the reference is a prior U.S. patent to the same entity (double patenting); (F) where the reference is disclosure of a prior U.S. patent to the same party not copending (dedication); (G) where applicant has clearly admitted on the record that subject matter relied on in the reference is prior art; (H) where the subject matter is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f); (I) where subject matter is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(g); (J) where subject matter corresponds to a lost count in an interference that is prior art under 102(g) or barred by interference estoppel.
guidance: Cite to relevant cases (e.g., In re Hellsund, In re Garfinkel, In re Blout, In re Lopresti, In re Bass) and MPEP sections (e.g., § 715.05, § 201.11–201.15, § 2138.01–.02). 1.131 is designed to overcome non-statutory-bar references (102(a), 102(e) in some cases) but not the listed inapplicable categories.

name: Effective Date of References — U.S. Patents and Publications
description: When a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO publication is used as a reference, its effective date as prior art is determined under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and related MPEP sections. If the portion relied on was introduced by amendment and constitutes new matter, the date to be overcome is the date of amendment.
guidance: The effective date of a domestic patent when used as a reference is not the foreign filing date; where the reference claims benefit of an earlier filed application, effective filing date is determined under 35 U.S.C. 102(e). See MPEP §§ 706.02(a), 2136–2136.03.

name: Form Paragraphs 7.57–7.64 for Examiner Responses to 37 CFR 1.131 Submissions
description: Form paragraphs 7.57–7.64 provide standard examiner language to indicate whether a submitted affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is effective or ineffective and the grounds for insufficiency. Paragraphs include headings and bracketed placeholders for insertion of specifics.
guidance: Specifics: 7.57 (heading 'Ineffective—Heading') must precede most others; 7.58 ('Ineffective, Claiming Same Invention'); 7.59 ('Ineffective, Insufficient Evidence of Reduction to Practice Before Reference Date'); 7.60 ('Ineffective, Reference Is a Statutory Bar'); 7.61 ('Ineffective, Insufficient Evidence of Conception'); 7.62 ('Ineffective, Diligence Lacking'); 7.63 ('Ineffective, Insufficient Evidence of Actual Reduction to Practice'); 7.64 ('Effective To Overcome Reference'). Examiner Notes prescribe bracket insertions and required precedences.

name: Form Paragraph 7.57 — Requirements and Precedence
description: Form paragraph 7.57 ('Affidavit or Declaration Under 37 CFR 1.131: Ineffective—Heading') must be followed by one or more of form paragraphs 7.58–7.63 or by a paragraph setting forth the basis for insufficiency (e.g., failure to establish acts performed in this country, or scope not commensurate with claims).
guidance: When used to respond to a submission, 7.57 should usually precede other specific form paragraphs; bracket fields indicate 'affidavit' or 'declaration' and other specifics.

name: General Rule as to Generic Claims and Exceptions for Unpredictable Arts
description: A reference or activity applied against generic claims may (in most cases) be antedated by an affidavit/declaration showing completion of only a single species within the genus prior to the effective date of the reference or activity (assuming no statutory bar or a patent/application publication claiming the same invention). In unpredictable arts, however, special practice is required: the affidavit must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to support a generic claim.
guidance: Cited authorities: Ex parte Biesecker; In re Fong; In re Defano. See MPEP § 715.03 for practice in unpredictable arts.

name: Bring an Invention Disclosure, Not a Marketing Doc
description: A useful invention disclosure has: (1) the technical problem in operational terms, (2) the closest known prior solution and why it falls short, (3) the new solution explained as if to a competent engineer who has not seen it, (4) at least one alternative way to implement the new solution, and (5) the result data if you have any. Marketing language ("disrupts," "revolutionary," "best-in-class") is filler.
guidance: Provide concrete technical details rather than marketing claims. Include the operational problem and the closest prior art plus shortcomings, a clear engineer-level explanation of your solution, implementation alternatives, and any experimental or result data. Avoid vague, promotional phrasing.

name: Whiteboards Are Better Than Slides
description: When you meet with the attorney, sketch on a whiteboard. Slides force you to commit to one architecture; whiteboards let you say 'or alternatively...' which is exactly what your attorney needs to write a broad spec.
guidance: Use sketching to show multiple architectures and alternatives instead of polished slide decks. Emphasize alternative flows/implementations verbally and visually so the attorney can capture breadth and fallback options for claims; avoid presenting only a single committed design.

name: Identify the 'Inventive Concept' in One Sentence
description: If you cannot finish the sentence 'The new thing is that ____,' you do not yet have an invention you can claim. The blank should be filled with a mechanism, not a goal.
guidance: Distill the invention into a single-sentence mechanism statement to test claimability. Ensure the sentence describes how something is done (a mechanism), not merely what outcome is achieved or a marketing goal. Use this as a gate before investing in drafting.

name: Variants Matter More Than the Best Mode
description: The single best version of your invention is what your competitors will design around. Your attorney needs to know the worse versions, the ugly hacks, the alternative materials. Each one becomes a fallback claim.
guidance: Document multiple implementations, degraded or cheaper variants, and hacked/ugly solutions. Provide alternative materials and less-preferred embodiments so the attorney can draft broader and multiple fallback claims to prevent easy design-arounds.

name: Generality of claim is not necessarily fatal if it is within the stated object and benefit
description: "This generality of claim, that is, for all modes of applying the principle to the purpose specified, according to or within a general statement of the object to be attained...is no objection to the patent."
guidance: If the patent fairly states the object and the use to be made of the agent, and the application or use can be carried out in a variety of ways, the broad wording may reflect the comprehensiveness and be upheld (Lord Justice in Neilson's case).

name: A claim that separates the principle from the means and is overly sweeping is void
description: Claims that amount to an abstraction (i.e., claiming the use of a motive power for a result without specifying means) are void — the seminal example is the invalidation of Morse's broad eighth claim.
guidance: Court rejected a claim that would grant exclusive right to all ways of printing at a distance by galvanic current because it would 'stop the progress of invention.' Validity depends on construing the claim with the specification: if the specification supplies the appropriate apparatus/conditions, a narrower construction may save the claim; otherwise it is too broad.

name: Novelty may lie in the application rather than in the means themselves
description: The novelty of the conception may consist in the discovery and application ... by which a new product in the arts or manufactures is the effect; the means or machinery are material only so far as they effect the identity of the application.
guidance: Courts recognize that the inventive merit often lies in the original conception (application of a principle) rather than mere mechanical contrivances; hence a patent can be supported by the new application even if many parts are old, provided the claimed application produces a previously unknown practical result.

name: Use by state monopoly holders and related takeover/compulsory measures (Article 88)
description: When a patent concerns subjects in the field of activity of state economic enterprises with monopolistic goods/services, allowing the monopoly right holder to use the invention depends on the patentee’s permission. The monopoly right holder may claim permission or the patentee may ask the monopoly holder to take over the patent; price is to be agreed or determined by court if parties fail to agree.
guidance: Monopoly holders are obligated to use inventions that provide considerable economic benefits and significant technical progress in their sector. If monopoly arises after grant, the patentee may claim the monopoly holder also take over the business/facility using the invention; court determines price if no agreement. If the invention cannot be used due to a legal monopoly, annual patent fees need not be paid.

name: Claims determine extent of protection; use of description and drawings in interpretation (Article 89(1))
description: The extent of protection provided by the patent application or the patent itself shall be determined by claims. The description and drawings shall be used in interpreting the claims.

name: Limits on claim interpretation and prohibition on impermissible extension (Article 89(2))
description: Claims shall not be interpreted strictly by literal word meaning, but when determining extent of protection claims must not be extended to cover ideas thought of by the inventor but not claimed, nor to cover features expected to arise merely by interpreting the description/drawings beyond the claims.
guidance: Claims should not be broadened to capture unclaimed subject matter implied by description beyond what a skilled person would reasonably derive as claimed.

name: Effect of published claims and retroactivity limits (Article 89(4))
description: Protection provided by the application is determined by the published claims of the application until the patent is granted. The situation of the patent when granted or after objection/invalidity procedures shall determine retroactive protection, provided the protection scope is not extended.

name: Doctrine of equivalents considered in scope (Article 89(5))
description: Factors equivalent to those mentioned in the claims at the time of alleged infringement are also considered in determining protection. An element is equivalent if it functions in the same way, meets the same functional requirements, and leads to the same conclusion.

name: Applicant/patentee statements and samples in claim interpretation (Article 89(6)‑(7))
description: During procedures determining claim extent, applicant or patentee’s statements shall be considered. If the patent includes samples, claims shall not be limited to such samples; products or methods should not be excluded merely because additional features are not present in samples or samples do not cover all specified objectives/features.

name: Required documents for patent application and confirming application date (Article 90(1)‑(3))
description: A patent application must include: (a) application form; (b) description explaining the invention; (c) claims; (ç) the drawings referred in description/claims; (d) abstract; (e) payment information. The application date is confirmed when the request for granting a patent, applicant identity/contact, and a description (in Turkish or permitted languages) or a referral to a previous application are submitted.
guidance: Description, claims, abstract and drawings may be submitted in Turkish or in the language of a Paris Convention/WTO party or reciprocity countries; further procedural rules by regulation.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure and biological material deposit rules (Article 92(1)‑(3))
description: The invention must be explained by a person skilled in the art in a very clear and complete way that enables practical application using the drawings, description and claims. If the invention involves biological material not publicly available and not definable sufficiently by a skilled person, the invention is considered sufficiently explained on condition the material is deposited/entrusted.
guidance: If entrusted biological material later becomes unavailable, re‑entrustment in accordance with the Budapest Treaty and submission of the deposit certificate copy within four months is required to maintain uninterrupted deposit. Requirements regarding entrusted biological material are set by regulation.

name: Basis of claims, clarity and not exceeding description (Article 92(4)‑(5))
description: The basis of the claims shall be the description; claims must define the subject to be protected, be clear and concise, and must not go beyond the invention as defined in the description.
guidance: The abstract is for providing technical information only and must not be used to determine extent of protection.

name: Priority right entitlement and scope (Article 93)
description: A person who filed an application for the same invention in any Paris Convention or WTO party country may claim priority in Turkey within 12 months of the first filing. Exhibitions recognized under the Paris Convention may also give priority within 12 months of presentation.
guidance: National equivalents, bilateral/multilateral agreements or Code provisions may extend entitlement; the priority date has effect for certain articles (e.g., Article 83 and Article 109). The date of a national application filed in due form is treated as the application date regardless of outcome.

name: Claiming priority: time limits and scope (Article 94)
description: Priority must be claimed (with fee) together with the application or within two months of the application date; supporting documents must be submitted within three months of application date. Multiple priority claims allowed; priority covers only subject matter included in the earlier application(s).
guidance: Priority may nevertheless cover specific invention features not present in the later claims if clearly disclosed in the original priority application as a whole. Detailed procedures by regulation.

name: Search request timing, preparation and reasons for not preparing search report (Article 96)
description: Applicant must request a search (and pay the fee) with the application or within 12 months from the application date; failing that, the application is considered withdrawn. If the application is consistent with formal conditions, the search report is prepared, the applicant notified and the report published. If the subject falls under Article 82(2)&(3) or unclear description/claims prevent preparation, no search report is prepared and the applicant is asked to submit objections or make changes within three months; failure results in refusal.
guidance: Council of Ministers authorized to reduce the 12‑month period by half; procedures by regulation.

name: Discoverability of first use information
description: Information concerning a party's first use of its involved mark is discoverable.
guidance: Dates, locations, and identifying information about first use are pertinent to priority claims; case citations show scope of discovery required.

name: Adjustment grounds under the Patent Term Guarantee Act — failure to take actions (§ 1.702(a))
description: An original patent (other than design) may be adjusted if issuance was delayed due to the failure of the Office to take specified actions within set timeframes, specifically: (1) mail at least one notification under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance under 35 U.S.C. 151 not later than 14 months after filing or national stage commencement; (2) respond to a reply under 35 U.S.C. 132 or to an appeal under 35 U.S.C. 134 not later than 4 months after filing/taking; (3) act on an application not later than 4 months after a PTAB or Federal court decision where at least one allowable claim remains; or (4) issue a patent not later than 4 months after issue fee payment and all requirements satisfied.
guidance: These grounds are subject to the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 154(b) and the subpart. (Editor notes indicate applicability to patents granted on or after certain dates.)

name: Period of adjustment calculation for § 1.702(a) (§ 1.703(a))
description: The period of adjustment under § 1.702(a) is the sum of the following non-overlapping periods (1) days from the day after 14 months after filing/national stage to mailing of either an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance under 35 U.S.C. 151 (whichever first); (2) days from day after 4 months after filing a reply under § 1.111 to mailing of action/notice of allowance; (3) days from day after 4 months after filing a reply in compliance with § 1.113(c) to mailing of action/notice of allowance; (4) days from day after 4 months after filing an appeal brief in compliance with § 41.37 to mailing of any examiner's answer under § 41.39, action under 35 U.S.C. 132, or notice of allowance; (5) days from day after 4 months after final PTAB or Federal court decision where at least one allowable claim remains to mailing of action/notice of allowance; and (6) days from day after 4 months after issue fee paid & requirements satisfied to patent issue.
guidance: Each listed interval is counted only to the extent it is non-overlapping with other counted periods; the definition uses 'day after' and specific triggering mailings/actions to determine interval endpoints. Editor notes specify applicability dates for some subparagraphs.

name: Evidence of proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom supports nonobviousness
description: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom in the art may be evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: Example: In re Hedges — process claimed at temperatures above accepted optimum indicated contrary-to-accepted-wisdom and supported nonobviousness. Consider whether claimed approach runs counter to known teachings suggesting a different course.

name: Known disadvantages in prior art may support nonobviousness
description: Known disadvantages in old devices which would naturally discourage search for new inventions may be taken into account when determining obviousness.
guidance: Consider whether prior art contains discouraging teachings or recognized disadvantages that would have deterred a skilled artisan from pursuing the claimed invention (citing United States v. Adams).

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) joint research agreement disqualification
description: Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g) shall not preclude patentability under 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, as demonstrated by three conditions.
guidance: Three requirements to disqualify commonly-assigned prior art (joint research agreement disqualification): (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. Applies only to prior art under 102(e),(f),(g) relied upon in a rejection under 103; does not disqualify prior art relied on for anticipation under 102. Be mindful of statutory amendments and effective dates (1999 AIPA, 2004 CREATE Act) when assessing applicability in reexamination and pending applications.

name: Written description for computer-implemented functional claim limitations
description: For computer-implemented inventions claimed functionally, the specification must disclose both sufficient hardware and sufficient software (algorithms/steps) so that one skilled in the art reasonably concludes the inventor possessed the claimed invention.
guidance: If the specification discloses the computer type and the necessary steps/algorithms (e.g., in sufficient detail to program a microprocessor), written description may be satisfied (In re Hayes). Conversely, purely functional recitation without disclosure of how the function is achieved (hardware plus algorithm/steps/flowcharts) may support a 112, para. 1 rejection. Examiners should determine whether the spec discloses the computer and the algorithm (necessary steps/flowcharts) to perform the claimed function in sufficient detail for a person skilled in the art to program the computer to perform those steps.

name: Scope of claims must be commensurate with the scope of enablement
description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of enablement provided by the specification.
guidance: A specification that enables only a subset of claim scope cannot support broader claims. Example: Sitrick where specification enabled integration into video games but not movies; claims covering both were not enabled.
