Ensure applicants provide sufficient teachings for all media/embodiments covered by claims.

name: Do not rely on general skill in the art to supply novel enabling details
description: While known information in the art may be omitted from the specification, an applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information necessary to enable the novel aspects of the claimed invention.
guidance: The specification must supply the novel aspects; omission of minor details may be acceptable, but where no disclosure of specific starting materials or process conditions exists for the novel aspect, enablement may fail (citing Genentech, ALZA, Auto. Techs.).

name: Do not rely on specific software operating systems or platforms
description: Think of TUX design innovations as platform agnostic; do not rely on a single OS or platform as the basis for protecting UX IP.
guidance: Although utility patents or platform-specific claims may be part of strategy, treating TUX as platform-independent improves robustness of protection (users care about what happens at the glass more than underlying OS).

name: Abstract placement on separate sheet
description: A brief abstract of the technical disclosure in the specification must commence on a separate sheet, preferably following the claims, under the heading "Abstract" or "Abstract of the Disclosure." The sheet or sheets presenting the abstract may not include other parts of the application or other material.
guidance: 37 C.F.R. 1.72; Form paragraph 6.16.01 notes the requirement and that it applies to amendments as well as the initial filing. The abstract for a national stage 35 U.S.C. 371 application may appear on the PCT publication front page. Examiner should require a new abstract if it does not commence on a separate sheet.

name: Avoid claim/legal phraseology and implied phrases
description: The form and legal phraseology often used in patent claims, such as "means" and "said," should be avoided. The abstract should avoid using phrases which can be implied, such as, "This disclosure concerns," "The disclosure defined by this invention," "This disclosure describes," etc.
guidance: Use plain, clear technical language rather than claim-style or boilerplate introductory phrases that add no substantive information.

name: Prohibited expressions category: irrelevant matter
description: Material that is 'obviously irrelevant or unnecessary' is prohibited under Rule 9.1(iv).
guidance: Irrelevant matter includes content having no bearing on the invention or its background prior art. Matter may be obviously irrelevant in the original description or may become so during proceedings (e.g., after claim limitation). Receiving Office, ISA, Authority for supplementary search or International Bureau handle removals; applicant should be informed of category applied.

name: Claims: three core requirements
description: Claims must (i) 'define the matter for which protection is sought', (ii) 'be clear and concise', and (iii) 'be fully supported by the description' (paragraph 5.02).
guidance: These are central criteria used to assess claim form/content, novelty and inventive step. Examiner should check all three when searching and examining.

name: Claims must be in terms of technical features
description: Claims must be drafted in terms of the 'technical features of the invention' (Rule 6.3(a)).
guidance: Do not include statements about commercial advantages or other non-technical matters; statements of purpose are allowed if they assist in defining the invention. Functional limitations are acceptable where a skilled person can provide means performing the function without inventive skill or such means are fully disclosed. Evaluate functional limitations for what they fairly convey to a skilled person in context. 'Use' claims (technical application) are permissible.

name: Two-part (preamble/characterizing) claim form whenever appropriate
description: Rule 6.3(b) defines a two-part form 'whenever appropriate' — first part indicates designation and prior art features, second part (characterizing portion) states the technical features added to the prior art (paragraphs 5.05–5.06).
guidance: Use two-part form to show which features are prior art and which are novel, but only when appropriate. If search reveals features in the second part already known in combination with first-part features, examiner may invite transferring them to the first part. If applicant chooses different but not incorrect division, examiner should generally not pursue the matter further because manner of claiming is for national laws. Invite adoption of two-part form when invention is a distinct improvement in an old combination; but where inappropriate (e.g., combinations of equal-status elements, modification of chemical process, complex interrelated systems, new chemical compounds not in a known class), other forms may be preferable.

name: Grouping of inventions and independent claims — single inventive concept
description: Determination whether a group of inventions is so linked as to form a single general inventive concept is made without regard to whether they are claimed separately or as alternatives (Rule 13.3) (paragraph 5.14).
guidance: Examiner should object to unnecessary independent claim proliferation but may accept two or more independent claims in the same category if a unifying inventive concept exists and claims satisfy Article 6 'concise' requirement. Consider practical factors (e.g., separable sale items, different phase arrangements, multiple manufacturing processes).

name: Independent and dependent claims: essentials and scope
description: Applications contain one or more independent main claims directed to essential features; dependent claims concern specific forms and must include all features of at least one independent claim (paragraph 5.15).
guidance: Dependent claims should be broad in meaning to cover more specific definitions or embodiments. Subject to Rule 13.1, reasonable number of dependent claims allowed even if features of dependent claim could be inventions themselves.

name: Dependent claims must refer to and include limitations of referenced claims
description: Any dependent claim must include a reference to the claim from which it depends and be construed as including all limitations contained in that antecedent claim (Rule 6.4(a),(c)) (paragraphs 5.16–5.17).
guidance: Multiple dependent claims include all limitations of the particular claim in relation to which they are considered. Dependent claims should be grouped to enable association of related claims and to avoid obscurity; examiner should invite amendments if arrangement causes obscurity.

name: Cross-category claim references are not dependent claims
description: A claim may refer to another claim even if not a dependent claim as defined in Rule 6.4 (for example, 'Apparatus for carrying out the process of Claim 1' or 'Process for the manufacture of the product of Claim 1') (paragraph 5.19).
guidance: Such references create functional or relational links between claims of different categories but do not carry the full limitations of dependent-claim structure; handle accordingly.

name: Interpretation: ordinary meaning to person skilled in the art
description: Claims should be read giving the words the ordinary meaning and scope which would be attributed by a person skilled in the relevant art, unless the description gives words a special meaning by explicit definition or otherwise (Article 6, paragraph 5.20).
guidance: Interpretation for search and examination purposes should be consistent. See appendix for further guidance on interpretation. Use description-defined meanings only where clearly indicated.

name: Effect of preamble on claim evaluation
description: The effect of the preamble on evaluation for search/examination should be determined case-by-case. Statements reciting purpose or intended use must be evaluated to determine whether they result in structural or process-step differences that limit the claim (paragraph 5.22).
guidance: In two-part claims the preamble is regarded as a limitation. Apparatus claimed 'for' a purpose means apparatus suitable for that purpose; if prior art apparatus is inherently capable of the purpose, the preamble may not limit novelty. Similarly for product-for-use claims, suitability for use is relevant to novelty evaluation.

name: Open, closed and 'consisting essentially of' transitional phrases
description: The type of transition phrase used (e.g., 'consisting of', 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of') determines the subject matter to be searched and scope (paragraph 5.24).
guidance: (a) 'Consisting of' generally construed as closed — excludes additional elements; (b) 'Comprising' is open — includes additional elements; (c) 'Consisting essentially of' is intermediate — limits scope to specified materials/steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)'. For search/examination, absent clear indication of the 'basic and novel characteristics' in description/claims, 'consisting essentially of' will be construed as open ('comprising'). Some Authorities may vary in treating 'consisting of' vs 'consisting essentially of'.

name: Product and apparatus limitations in process claims must be considered
description: Product and apparatus limitations appearing in process claims must be taken into account for search and examination purposes (paragraph 5.28).
guidance: Include consideration of product/apparatus features when assessing novelty/inventive step of a process claim; see effect of preamble guidance (paragraph 5.22).

name: Objection to vague general statements expanding protection
description: General statements implying protection may be expanded vaguely (e.g., to cover the 'spirit' of the invention) should be objected to as not complying with Article 6 (paragraph 5.30).
guidance: If claims directed to combinations only, statements implying protection for individual features/sub-combinations should be objected to. Require precise scope.

name: Clarity requirement for claims individually and as a whole
description: Claims must be clear individually and collectively; clarity is of utmost importance for formulating opinions on novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability (Article 6, paragraphs 5.31–5.33).
guidance: Terms should be understandable to a person skilled in the art from the claim wording alone where possible. Analyze clarity in light of application disclosure, prior art teachings, and skilled person's interpretation at time of invention. Breadth does not equal lack of clarity. Independent claims should specify essential features needed to define the invention, except insofar as implied by generic terms (e.g., 'bicycle' implies wheels). For process claims producing a product, the process must reasonably lead to that product when carried out by a skilled person.

name: Clarity of relative/degree terms and invitation to define
description: Claims should not use vague relative terms (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong') unless the term has a well-recognized meaning in the art; for degree terms, examiner should determine whether skilled person would be apprised of meaning by disclosure or prior art (paragraph 5.34).
guidance: If ambiguous, invite applicant to define or excise the term if possible without extending subject matter beyond filed disclosure. Applicant cannot rely on an unclear term to distinguish from prior art.

name: Avoid defining invention solely by result unless enabled
description: Claims that define invention or a feature by a result to be achieved should generally be objected to for lack of clarity, unless result-based definition is the only possible way and the description includes adequate directions enabling routine determination of required parameters without undue experimentation (paragraph 5.35).
guidance: Do not object if result can be achieved without undue experimentation and directions/tests are adequately specified. Example: ashtray extinguishing cigarette by shape/dimensions—relative dimensions may be defined by reference to result if description includes routine test procedures to determine required dimensions.

name: Jepson-Format Claims Imply Admission of Preamble Subject Matter
description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the preamble subject matter is prior art (37 CFR 1.75(e); MPEP §608.01(m)).
guidance: This implied admission can be overcome if applicant gives a credible reason for Jepson format (e.g., to avoid double patenting) or where the preamble actually describes applicant's own work. Case examples: In re Fout; In re Ehrreich; Reading & Bates.

name: Anticipation Requires Every Claim Element to Be Taught (Expressly or Inherently)
description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference.
guidance: Elements must be arranged as required by the claim, though identical terminology is not required (not an ipsissimis verbis test). A claim covering several alternative structures is anticipated if any one structure within the claim scope is known in the prior art. Case citations: Verdegaal Bros.; Brown v. 3M; Richardson v. Suzuki; In re Bond.

name: Using Extra References to Show the Primary Reference Is Enabled
description: An additional reference may be relied upon to show that the primary reference provides an "enabled disclosure" (i.e., that the public had sufficient information to make/use the invention).
guidance: Case examples: In re Samour; In re Donohue—when a publication disclosed the claimed structure and other patents showed methods of making the class, the publications taught all elements and patents supported enablement/documentation of public possession.

name: Reference That Clearly Names Claimed Species Anticipates the Species
description: When a reference clearly names the claimed species, that reference anticipates the species claim regardless of how many other species are named.
guidance: Example: Ex parte A (Merck Index analogy)—a specific compound listed among many is still 'described' for purposes of 35 U.S.C. §102(a). In re Sivaramakrishnan offers similar principle for additives named among many.

name: Nonprovisional filing date requirements
description: The filing date of a nonprovisional application is the date on which a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 containing a description pursuant to § 1.71 and at least one claim pursuant to § 1.75, and any drawing required by § 1.81(a) are filed in the Patent and Trademark Office. No new matter may be introduced into an application after its filing date.
guidance: A continuing application (continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part) may be filed under conditions in 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c) and § 1.78(c) and (d).

name: Interim copy allowance
description: An 'Interim Copy' of the original foreign application, labeled as such and including specification, drawings, and claims, filed with a separate cover sheet identifying the foreign application and stating it is a true copy, filed within the specified time limits, will be considered to satisfy the certified copy requirement provided a certified copy is filed later within the period specified in paragraph (g)(1).
guidance: Interim copy must be filed within the later of multiple time limits (e.g., 16 months from prior foreign filing or four months from US filing/national stage start).

name: Materiality standard for duty of disclosure
description: Information is material to patentability when it is not cumulative to information already of record and (1) it establishes, by itself or in combination, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) it refutes or is inconsistent with a position the applicant takes in opposing an argument of unpatentability relied on by the Office or asserting an argument of patentability.
guidance: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of the evidence standard, giving each term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, before considering contrary evidence submitted to attempt to establish patentability.

name: Content: convey basic idea and background; avoid claims/scope
description: Your abstract should effectively convey to readers the basic idea and background behind your invention. The more technical aspects are covered in more detail in the application itself, so there is no need to include claims or scope in the abstract.
guidance: If there is relevant prior art, mention the improved aspects of prior art without comparing your invention to the prior art. Focus on the invention's essence and background rather than legal claim language or exhaustive detail.

name: Claim wording requirement for U.S. designation (Article 5(2)(a) / Rule 11(3))
description: An international design application designating the United States must contain a claim, and the specific wording of the claim shall be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article as shown, or as shown and described.
guidance: See 37 C.F.R. 1.1021(d) and MPEP § 2909 subsection IV. The formal claim wording requirement is a U.S. declaration under Article 5(2)(a) and Rule 11(3).

name: Priority claims inclusion
description: The international registration includes any priority claim where the earlier filing is not more than six months prior to the international filing date.
guidance: Priority documents and related requirements for designated Contracting Parties may be triggered by publication or other dates; applicants should consult WIPO Hague Member Profiles for specific countries' requirements for priority documents.

name: Final Disposition Compliance Rate
description: A measure of the propriety of the final disposition of individual applications; i.e., allowance or final rejection. The compliance rate is the percentage of reviewed applications in which no deficiency is found with respect to the Office’s final determination concerning the patentability of the claims.
guidance: Sampling performed by OPQA via random sampling of actions that either allow or finally reject an application. Deficiencies are determined by a clear error standard: a clear error in allowance is an unreasonable failure to make a rejection for one or more reasons provided in the patent laws; a clear error in a final rejection is the making of an unreasonable rejection, objection, or other requirement. If any clear error is found in the reviewed action setting forth the final disposition, that action is non-compliant. Allowance compliance reviews occur after notice of allowance is mailed but prior to grant and focus on whether any allowed claims are unpatentable (e.g., omitted rejections, improper treatment of claims). Final rejection reviews consider whether the final rejection was premature, whether rejections that should have been made were omitted, whether rejections unnecessarily block advancement of prosecution, and whether objections could have been resolved via interview. When clear errors are found, corrective actions include rescinding the notice of allowance or correction in subsequent prosecution; aggregate results inform Corps-wide/Tech Center training.

name: Complete FAOM (Complete First Action On the Merits) Review
description: A detailed, claim-by-claim measure of the degree to which the first action on the merits in an application conforms with USPTO best practices, performed by random sampling of first Office actions on the merits.
guidance: This review analyzes the Office's action on a claim-by-claim basis and assigns points to measured factors proportional to their estimated impact on examination. Best practices (based on USPTO experience and stakeholder input) include proactive use of interviews, propriety of all rejections, requirements (including restriction requirements), objections, and compliance with statutes, the MPEP, and compact prosecution principles. For factors addressing propriety of rejections and indications of allowable subject matter, each claim is addressed and points given based on percentage of claims without an improper or omitted rejection. Attachment 1 lists many specific factors measured across Complete FAOM, In-Process, and Final Disposition reviews (e.g., omitted rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§102/103/112/101/double patenting; reasonableness and clarity of rejections under statutory grounds; interviews properly of record and substantive; handling of sequence compliance, restriction issues, priority claims; evaluation of applicant papers filed prior to examination; consideration of search reports from other offices; early/correct indication of allowable subject matter; actions providing correct suggestions to overcome rejections). When clear errors are found, Notices of Allowance may be rescinded and corrective actions taken; results used for targeted training.

name: Internal Quality Survey
description: Quarterly quantitative surveys of patent staff (examiners, SPEs) measuring examiner perceptions and experiences relevant to examination quality; used as a component of the composite metric.
guidance: Internal survey asks examiners to rate (numeric scales) experiences over the prior quarter on topics such as satisfaction with tools (search tools, OACS, e-Red Folder, eDAN), access to and effectiveness of training (technical, legal, automation, professional development), and evaluation of applicant/agent contributions (clarity/completeness of specification, clarity of claims, manageability and drafting of claims, IDS materiality, translations, drawings). It also gauges examiners’ views of external interactions (clarity and thoroughness of applicant responses, preparedness for interviews) and overall ability to provide high-quality examination. A sample internal questionnaire (Attachment 4) and scoring conventions are provided; results are used to identify systemic issues and guide training and process improvements.

name: Clear Error Standard for Deficiencies
description: A cross-metric standard defining what constitutes a 'deficiency' or 'clear error' in an examiner action used in Final Disposition and In-Process compliance metrics.
guidance: A 'clear error' in allowance is an unreasonable failure to make a rejection of a claim for reasons provided in the patent laws. A 'clear error' in a rejection/objection/other requirement is the making of an unreasonable rejection, objection, or other requirement. Differences between SPE preferred action and examiner action are treated as differences of opinion and not clear errors so long as the examiner's action is reasonable. Deficiencies are counted where clear errors result in unnecessary resource expenditure (multiple non-final actions, RCEs, notices of appeal, additional applicant responses). Examples of non-counted errors: inappropriate §112 rejection that also properly rejects under §102/§103; inappropriate statutory subsection cited but still prior art under another subsection.

name: Rule 12(c) standard for judgment on the pleadings
description: In ruling on a Rule 12(c) motion the court must accept as true all well-pleaded allegations in the non-movant’s pleadings and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-movant; judgment under Rule 12(c) is appropriate only where 'the movant clearly establishes that no material issue of fact remains to be resolved and that [the movant] is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.'
guidance: For patent §101 motions, eligibility can be resolved on the pleadings when there are no factual allegations that, when taken as true, prevent deciding the eligibility question as a matter of law (see Data Engine Techs. LLC v. Google). Courts should therefore examine whether factual disputes (e.g., about whether claim features are conventional) preclude resolution at the pleadings stage.

name: Statutory scope of patentable subject matter (35 U.S.C. § 101) and enumerated exceptions
description: Section 101 permits patents for any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (or improvements thereof). The Supreme Court recognizes three exceptions: laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas.
guidance: Claims that are directed to any one of these three categories are 'directed to' ineligible subject matter and must be tested under the Alice/Mayo framework; these exceptions are considered basic tools beyond patent protection.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework overview
description: Courts use a two-step framework: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea); (2) if so, search for an 'inventive concept' that transforms the ineligible concept into 'significantly more.'
guidance: If at step one the claims are not directed to an ineligible concept, the inquiry ends and §101 is satisfied; if directed to an ineligible concept, the court proceeds to step two to determine whether the claim elements (alone or in combination) supply an inventive concept.

name: Step One — consider claims in their entirety and focus on claimed advance
description: At step one, 'the claims are considered in their entirety to ascertain whether their character as a whole is directed to excluded subject matter' — the inquiry looks to the 'focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine what the claim is really directed to.
guidance: Courts must be careful not to oversimplify the claims or describe them at an improperly high level of abstraction; it is insufficient to merely identify a patent-ineligible concept underlying the claim — the court must determine whether that concept is what the claim is 'directed to' (see Enfish, McRO, Rapid Litigation Management).

name: Step Two — inventive concept inquiry
description: At step two the court examines claim elements and their combination to determine whether they transform the ineligible concept into something 'significantly more' — i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent on the ineligible concept itself.
guidance: An inventive concept requires more than performance of 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional activities previously known to the industry.' An inventive concept can arise from a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces. Whether elements (or their combination) are well-understood, routine, or conventional is a question of fact (Berkheimer) and may preclude resolution at the pleadings stage.

name: Comparative precedent analysis
description: Courts often compare the claims at issue to claims considered in the body of §101 decisions to determine whether they are analogous to previously held eligible or ineligible claims.
guidance: Identify the most analogous Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Enfish, McRO, Interval Licensing, Amdocs) and explain similarities and differences in focus, claimed advance, and claim detail; overreliance on superficial similarities may mischaracterize claims.

name: Avoid treating claims as mere results — look for specific steps achieving the result
description: Claims that 'recite more than a mere result' — i.e., that 'recite specific steps . . . that accomplish the desired result' — are less likely to be treated as directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Analyze whether the claim language provides concrete steps, structures, or limitations that accomplish the asserted technological improvement (e.g., synchronous and secure updating between processes in Mach-derived systems) rather than merely reciting the end result or high-level goal (citing Finjan).

name: Condition for examination (37 CFR 1.704(f))
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when the application includes a specification, including at least one claim and an abstract (§ 1.72(b)), and has papers in compliance with § 1.52, drawings (if any) in compliance with § 1.84, any English translation required by § 1.52(d) or § 1.57(a), a sequence listing in compliance with § 1.821 through § 1.825 (if applicable), the inventor’s oath or declaration or an application data sheet containing the information specified in § 1.63(b), the basic filing fee (§ 1.16(a) or § 1.16(c)), the search fee (§ 1.16(k) or § 1.16(m)), the examination fee (§ 1.16(o) or § 1.16(q)), any certified copy of the previously filed application required by § 1.57(a), and any application size fee required by the Office under § 1.16(s).
guidance: For international applications entering the national stage, analogous national-stage documents and fees (including search and examination fees per § 1.492) are required. Papers/drawings/sequence listings corrected prior to the mailing date of either an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance under 35 U.S.C. 151 are considered in compliance for purposes of this paragraph.

name: 37 CFR 1.703(a)(5) — 4-month period after final decision by Board or court
description: The number of days, if any, in the period beginning on the day after the date that is four months after the date of a final decision by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board or by a Federal court in an appeal under 35 U.S.C. 141 or a civil action under 35 U.S.C. 145 or 146 where at least one allowable claim remains in the application and ending on the date of mailing of either an action under 35 U.S.C. 132 or a notice of allowance under 35 U.S.C. 151, whichever occurs first.
guidance: ‘Allowable claims remain in the application’ means at least one pending claim that is not withdrawn and is not subject to a rejection/objection; the MPEP gives specific examples (A-C) illustrating when claims count. A Board decision is a qualifying 'decision' only if it sustains or reverses rejections or, in limited circumstances, a remand may be deemed a decision (see remand guidance). A Board decision containing a new ground of rejection under § 41.50(b) is not a 'final decision' for purposes of 1.703(a)(5).

name: Meaning of 'final decision' for purposes of 1.703(a)(5)
description: The phrase 'final decision' means: (1) the decision is the last decision in the review by the Board (or by a federal court); and (2) the decision does not require further action by the applicant to avoid termination of proceedings as to the rejected claims.
guidance: A Board decision containing a new ground of rejection under § 41.50(b) requires action by the applicant and therefore is not a 'final decision' for 1.703(a)(5). A Board decision reversing all rejections on appeal can be 'final' for 1.703(a)(5) even if judicial review remains possible.

name: 37 CFR 1.705(b) — PTA reconsideration application requirements and timing
description: Any request for reconsideration of the patent term adjustment indicated on the patent must be by way of an application for patent term adjustment filed no later than two months from the date the patent was granted (this two-month period may be extended under § 1.136(a)). The application must be accompanied by: (1) the fee set forth in § 1.18(e); and (2) a statement of the facts specifying the correct PTA and the basis or bases under § 1.702, the relevant dates as specified in §§ 1.703(a)–(e) and the adjustment as specified in § 1.703(f), whether the patent is subject to a terminal disclaimer and its expiration, and (iv) either circumstances during prosecution constituting a failure to engage in reasonable efforts under § 1.704 or that there were no such circumstances.
guidance: Applications for reconsideration must itemize the factual bases and dates underlying the claimed PTA; failure to provide required information or fee may be fatal. The two-month window is extendable under general extension rules.

name: Control variables for application characteristics
description: Control variables for the characteristics of the earliest U.S. utility patent application of a family include indicators for applications that claim priority to provisional applications, PCT applications or foreign applications, an indicator for applications filed by small entities, and the natural logarithms of the number of independent claims, the number of words per independent claim, and the number of inventors.
guidance: These controls capture observable application complexity, scope, and applicant size and are included in most specifications to adjust for covariate differences between SEPs and controls.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (Article 83)
description: Sufficiency of disclosure: the application must disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art (Article 83).
guidance: Part F gives instructions to examiners on assessing whether the disclosure is enabling across the claimed scope.

name: Clarity (Article 84)
description: Clarity: claims must be clear and concise and supported by the description (Article 84).
guidance: Guidance in Part F describes how to evaluate claim wording, clarity issues and support by the description.

name: Defense — Invalidity for failure to comply with section 112 (with best-mode exception)
description: Invalidity of the patent or any claim in suit for failure to comply with any requirement of section 112, except that the failure to disclose the best mode shall not be a basis on which any claim of a patent may be canceled or held invalid or otherwise unenforceable.
guidance: Section 112-related defects (e.g., lack of written description, lack of enablement, indefiniteness) are recognized invalidity defenses, but the specific 'best mode' failure is expressly not a basis for invalidating or cancelling a claim under this statute.

name: Notice requirement for asserting invalidity or noninfringement
description: In an action involving the validity or infringement of a patent the party asserting invalidity or noninfringement shall give notice in the pleadings or otherwise in writing to the adverse party at least thirty days before the trial, of the country, number, date, and name of the patentee of any patent, the title, date, and page numbers of any publication to be relied upon as anticipation of the patent in suit or ... as showing the state of the art, and the name and address of any person who may be relied upon as the prior inventor or as having prior knowledge of or as having previously used or offered for sale the invention of the patent in suit.
guidance: Specific pre-trial disclosure requirement: provide identifying information for patents, publications, and persons relied upon. If such notice is not given, proof of those matters may not be admitted at trial except on terms the court requires. Applies except in actions in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (per statutory text).

name: What is a Patent Case?
description: A case with one or more claims involving patent infringement, invalidity, or unenforceability brought under 35 USC § 271. False marking, inventorship, or contract cases are not included in the patent case type.
guidance: This definition determines which dockets are included in the dataset and analysis; exclude false-marking, inventorship, and contract matters from the 'patent case' category.

name: Patent Case Tags / Filtering
description: Lex Machina uses machine learning and natural language processing to create case tags that identify certain claims in a case and enable filtering (e.g., general patent cases, patent cases excluding high-volume plaintiffs, ANDA cases, PTAB cases, patent appellate cases).
guidance: Apply tags to enable apples-to-apples comparisons. Users can further apply custom tags in their research; filters materially affect trends (e.g., HVP exclusion).

name: Timing: Time-to-Event Metrics & Boxplots
description: Timing analytics to key milestones (median and distributional measures). Examples reported: median time to summary judgment = 814 days; median time to trial = 1,091 days; median time to termination = 205 days (for all patent cases terminated 2021–2023, excluding ANDA cases).
guidance: Present distributions via box plots (median, interquartile range, whiskers); emphasize variability (e.g., wide range to trial). Use judge-level and claim-level filters to refine forecasting and budgeting. See 'Understanding Box Plots' for interpretation rules.

name: Case Resolutions (resolution taxonomy)
description: Categorization of how cases terminate: likely settlement, procedural resolution (dismissal, contested dismissal, consolidation, stay, transfers, MDL), claimant wins and claim defendant wins by resolution type (default judgment, consent judgment, judgment on the pleadings, summary judgment, trial, JMOL), class action settlements, and open/no resolution.
guidance: Report counts and percentages for each resolution type. Note that the majority of district court patent cases in 2021–2023 resolved by likely settlement or procedural grounds (~91% combined); substantive claimant wins outnumber defendant wins when only substantive terminations are considered, but claim defendants prevail more often at summary judgment.

name: Findings by Judgment Event
description: Track patent-specific findings at litigation events (judgment on the pleadings, summary judgment/claim construction, trial): Infringement, No Infringement, Invalidity, No Invalidity, Unenforceability, No Unenforceability, and counts by event.
guidance: Count findings at each stage (a case can have findings at multiple stages). Report where findings most frequently occur (e.g., courts found Infringement most often overall—many at default; No Infringement was most common at summary judgment and trial). Use these patterns to assess likelihood of success at different litigation stages.

name: Patent Invalidity Reasons (taxonomy)
description: Specific statutory and doctrinal grounds for invalidity tracked: Subject Matter (101), Anticipation/Novelty (102), Obviousness (103), Definiteness (112), Enablement (112), Written Description (112), Improper Design Patent (171), Defective Correction / Obviousness-Type Double Patenting / other codes, and 'No Invalidity Reason Specified.'
guidance: Report counts by judgment event and note common loci (e.g., 101/subject-matter invalidity is frequently found at judgment on the pleadings; indefiniteness often appears at claim construction). Provide these breakdowns to inform motion practice and claim-drafting strategies.

name: Step-one inquiry for computer-technology claims
description: Ask whether the claims focus on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology or are instead directed to a result or effect that itself is the abstract idea and merely invoke generic processes and machinery.
guidance: Claims that simply claim a result or effect (e.g., content transfer) using generic components are more likely abstract. (McRO; Ancora; Universal Secure Registry.)

name: Requirement of claim/specification specificity
description: Claims/specification must describe how the elements recited in the claims refer to technological features functioning together to improve technology in a specific way.
guidance: A general recitation of processors/instructions/devices or placement in generic devices without explanation of how they effect a technical improvement is insufficient. (Packet Intel. LLC v. NetScout.)

name: Sequence or ordering of conventional steps alone is insufficient
description: A claim that merely requires a specific ordering of transmissions/receipts or a sequence of conventional authentication steps, without explaining how that ordering is a nonconventional technical solution, does not supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Result-oriented claims that do not provide limiting detail confining the claim to a particular solution are abstract. Compare Affinity Labs (abstract) to Bascom (specific location of filtering tool as inventive).

name: What counts as a sufficient inventive concept (exemplar features)
description: Claims that identify specific technical solutions or improvements — e.g., varying how check data is generated by modifying permutations, storing records in particular modifiable non-volatile memory for verification, object-oriented key managers, adding data fields to reduce latency, or hardware-based RFID serial-number data structures — have been found to supply inventive concepts.
guidance: Cited favorable examples: Koninklijke KPN (modifying permutation), Ancora (storing license record in particular BIOS area), TecSec (object-oriented key manager), Uniloc (additional data field to reduce latency), Adasa (hardware-based RFID structure). These demonstrate the specificity required to transform a claim from claiming only a result to claiming a way of achieving it.

name: Treatment of multiple dependent claims for NIRC and certificate
description: How additions, deletions, and changes to multiple dependent claims are characterized for purposes of the Notice of Intent to Issue Ex Parte Reexamination Certificate (NIRC) and the Examiner’s checklist.
guidance: Addition of a claim of the multiple dependency is viewed as adding a new claim (designated 'new' in the NIRC) because new subject matter/protection is provided (example: claim 2/8 designated new). Deletion of a claim of the multiple dependency is viewed as canceling the deleted claim (designated 'canceled' in the NIRC). A claim whose text or scope changes (e.g., range expanded) is designated as 'amended.' For the Examiner’s checklist (Form PTO-1516), however, the addition or deletion of a claim of the multiple dependency is viewed simply as amending the claim because of the way claims are printed on the certificate; thus such claims are designated as 'amended' on the checklist and printed in their amended form on the certificate. Provide concrete examples (claims 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 in the guidance) to reflect these conventions.

name: Reasons for patentability and/or confirmation
description: Requirement to provide reasons explaining why claims found patentable or confirmed are patentable over cited patents/printed publications.
guidance: Reasons for patentability must be provided unless all claims are canceled in the proceeding. Check Box 2 of PTOL-469 and attach a statement (may use form PTOL-476 or preferred form paragraph 22.16) indicating why the claims found patentable are clearly patentable over the cited patents/printed publications; this may be done in a manner similar to reasons for allowance in an application and may refer to record portions that establish patentability. Any 'Comments on Statement of Reasons for Patentability and/or Confirmation' received from the patent owner will be placed in the reexamination file without comment and may be considered if timely submitted to avoid processing delays.

name: Ex parte reexamination reminders — scope and substantive examination requirement
description: All patent claims for which a substantial new question of patentability (SNQ) has been found must have been examined before the case is forwarded.
guidance: Ensure every claim identified with an SNQ has been properly examined in accordance with MPEP § 2243 prior to forwarding the case for issuance of certificate or other final actions.

name: Ex parte reexamination reminders — issue fee and expired-patent limitations
description: No issue fee is charged in reexamination; claims cannot be amended or new claims added after patent expiration.
guidance: There is no issue fee in reexamination (see MPEP § 2233). Patent claims may not be amended nor new claims added after expiration of the patent (see MPEP § 2250). If the patent has expired, all amendments and claims added during the proceeding must be withdrawn and presently rejected/objected-to claims canceled by examiner’s amendment.

name: Ex parte reexamination reminders — no enlargement of claim scope
description: An amended or new claim may not enlarge the scope of the patent claims.
guidance: Ensure amendments and new claims do not broaden claim scope. See MPEP § 2250.

name: Contents and effects of ex parte reexamination certificate
description: Legal and substantive effects and required contents of the reexamination certificate.
guidance: Per 35 U.S.C. 307 and 37 CFR 1.570, the certificate will: (A) cancel any patent claims determined unpatentable; (B) confirm any patent claims determined patentable; (C) incorporate into the patent any amended or new claims determined patentable; (D) make any approved changes in the description; (E) include any statutory or terminal disclaimer filed by the patent owner; (F) identify unamended claims held invalid on final holding by another forum; (G) identify any patent claims not reexamined; (H) be mailed on its date to the patent owner (and a copy to the requester); and (I) identify patent claims dependent on amended claims determined patentable. If certificate cancels all claims, no further Office proceedings on that patent or related reissue/reexamination requests will be conducted (with rare exceptions allowing petition under 37 CFR 1.183).

name: Intervening rights resulting from reexamination certificates
description: Effect of newly incorporated amended or new claims on intervening rights of third parties who acted prior to certificate issuance.
guidance: Per 35 U.S.C. 307(b), any proposed amended or new claim determined patentable and incorporated into a patent by certificate will have the same effect as specified in 35 U.S.C. 252 for reissued patents regarding rights of persons who made, purchased, used, imported, or substantially prepared for the thing patented prior to issuance of the certificate. See cited cases for precedent (Fortel, Kaufman, etc.).

name: Processing a reexamination of a reexamination
description: How to handle a reexamination request filed on a patent already subject to a reexamination certificate or on which a prior reexamination certificate has issued.
guidance: Consider the request based on the patent claims as modified by the previously issued reexamination certificate, not the original claims. When the new reexamination is first received by CRU, support staff must incorporate certificate changes into the reexamination specification before forwarding to the examiner. Examiner should verify the certificate changes entry and base the order/denial decision on the certificate-modified claims/specification. If a first reexamination certificate will issue within ~3 months of filing a second request, proceedings normally will not be merged; the second request will be considered based on the claims as indicated in the issued certificate if the certificate issues before decision on the second request. Include copy of the reexamination certificate as attachment to the order/denial decision for third-party requesters.

name: Notice of certificate issuance in Official Gazette
description: What the Official Gazette notice for an ex parte reexamination certificate must include and emphasize.
guidance: The Official Gazette notice will include bibliographic information, an indication of the status of each claim after conclusion, and publication of a representative claim with any specification/drawing changes indicated. The notice will clearly indicate that it is a certificate for a concluded ex parte reexamination proceeding as opposed to an inter partes proceeding.

name: Request for corrected publication—material mistake standard (37 CFR 1.221(b))
description: The Office will grant a request for a corrected or revised patent application publication only when the Office makes a material mistake which is apparent from Office records. A request for a corrected publication under 37 CFR 1.221(b) must be filed within two months from the date of the patent application publication (this period is not extendable) and must identify the Office’s material mistake in the publication.
guidance: A material mistake is one that affects the public’s ability to appreciate the technical disclosure or determine the scope of provisional rights. Examples include omission of claims that were included in the originally-filed specification and not canceled by a preliminary amendment; omission of part of the specification that provides support for the published claims; omission of originally-filed drawings; omission of a timely submitted benefit claim in specified contexts. The request should include a listing of alleged material errors, marked-up copies of relevant pages, and an indication of where in the specification as filed the relevant text appears. If the period has expired or the mistake is caused by the applicants, applicants should request republication under 37 CFR 1.221(a) instead.

name: Non-material mistakes (not grounds for corrected publication)
description: Applicants should not file requests for corrected publication that include no material error made by the Office. Errors in the correspondence address, assignment information or missing assignment information, minor typographical errors, missing section headings, a failure to include an amendment, or similar matters are not material mistakes.
guidance: Examples given: publication did not include assignment information; publication shows the wrong assignee or a misspelled assignee name; publication did not include a benefit or priority claim to a prior application due to applicant’s failure to timely file or properly submit the reference; publication did not include claims or changes submitted in an amendment; typographical errors that do not affect interpretation of published claims. Filing corrected-publication requests for non-material errors is discouraged; incorrect requests may result in a patent term adjustment reduction where Office made only non-material errors.

name: Redacted publication eligibility and timing (35 U.S.C. 122(b)(2)(B)(v) and 37 CFR 1.217)
description: If an applicant has filed applications in one or more foreign countries and such foreign-filed applications or their descriptions are less extensive than the U.S. application, the applicant may submit a redacted copy of the U.S. application eliminating any part or description not also contained in the corresponding foreign applications. The Director may only publish the redacted copy unless the redacted copy is not received within 16 months after the earliest effective filing date for which a benefit is sought.
guidance: The provisions of 35 U.S.C. 154(d) shall not apply to a claim if the description published in the redacted application does not enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter of the claim. The redacted copy must be submitted in compliance with EFS requirements; the title must correspond to the application title at time of submission.

name: Outcomes by claim challenged
description: Claim-level outcome statistics for challenged claims within proceedings (e.g., whether claims were found unpatentable, patentable, or not decided).
guidance: Claim-level outcomes are reported (counts by outcome category) for FY22; joined cases and the specifics of claim-level treatment follow the same exclusion rules where noted.

name: Terminal disclaimer condition for certain pre-1995 applications (applicant received notice)
description: In any design application, any utility application filed before June 8, 1995, and any plant application filed before June 8, 1995, if applicant receives a notice of abandonment, any petition to withdraw the holding of abandonment not filed within two months of the mail date of the notice will not (absent extraordinary circumstances) be treated on its merits unless accompanied by a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(a) and required fee.
guidance: The period to be disclaimed is the terminal part of the term of any patent granted on the application (or on any utility/plant application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)) equivalent to the period between (A) the date two months after the mail date of the notice of abandonment and (B) the filing date of a grantable petition to withdraw the holding of abandonment. Use PTO/SB/62 for terminal disclaimer.

name: Intentional delay is not unintentional — enumerated examples
description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action is not 'unintentional' (e.g., applicant deliberately permits abandonment because claims considered unpatentable; to defer fees; to defer prosecution costs; or lack of commercial value).
guidance: Examples listed: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable over cited references; (B) applicant considers allowed/patentable claims insufficient breadth to justify expense; (C) applicant does not consider patent of sufficient value; (D) applicant does not consider patent worth maintaining; (E) applicant seeks to defer fees/prosecution expenses. A later change of mind does not render a prior deliberate abandonment 'unintentional.'

name: Full scope enablement (§ 112(a))
description: The specification must enable the full scope of the claimed invention — the patentee must enable the invention 'as broadly as it is claimed' so the public receives the 'full benefit' after expiration; claims cannot lawfully cover more than what is invented and described.
guidance: Grounded in historical statutes and Supreme Court precedent (Patent Act of 1790; O'Reilly v. Morse; Universal Oil; Evans v. Eaton). The brief explains that full scope enablement enforces the patent 'quid pro quo' (monopoly in exchange for disclosure) and prevents patentees from claiming beyond their disclosure. A claim that 'vastly outstrips' the specification is non‑enabled. Case examples: O'Reilly v. Morse; Consol. Elec. Light Co. v. McKeesport Light Co.; Halliburton Oil.

name: Quantity of experimentation necessary
description: One must assess how much experimentation a person of ordinary skill would need to perform to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention; excessive experimentation (i.e., 'substantial time and effort') indicates non‑enablement.
guidance: This is Wands factor #1. If each undisclosed embodiment would require case‑by‑case testing (especially in unpredictable arts), the claim fails. The brief emphasizes that when 'substantial time and effort' would be required to determine whether members of a claimed genus have the claimed function, enablement is lacking. Cases: In re Wands; In re Fisher; Incandescent Lamp; MagSil.

name: Amount of direction or guidance in the specification
description: Evaluate whether the specification provides sufficient direction/roadmap such that skilled artisans can make and use the full breadth of the claim without undue experimentation.
guidance: This is Wands factor #2. Guidance can 'cure' unpredictability (e.g., clear principles, general rules, 'roadmaps'). But conclusory or narrow guidance that only yields a small subset of embodiments is insufficient. The brief stresses the need for non‑conclusory evidence that the spec's roadmap predictably generates the full claimed scope (district/federal record must show this).

name: Presence or absence of working examples
description: Consider whether the specification includes working examples (and how many) and whether those examples, taken together with other disclosure, enable the full claimed genus.
guidance: This is Wands factor #3. Single working example may be insufficient in unpredictable arts; courts have invalidated claims where only one example exists but the claim sweeps many undisclosed members (Incandescent Lamp, Béné, Corona Cord, Holland Furniture). Working examples are weighed with other factors; mere presence does not guarantee enablement across a broad genus.

name: Nature of the invention (predictability vs unpredictability)
description: The inherent predictability of the technology field affects enablement: predictable arts (mechanical/electrical) require less disclosure to enable a genus; unpredictable arts (chemistry, biologicals) require more disclosure.
guidance: This is Wands factor #4 and ties to factor #7. The brief repeatedly emphasizes that unpredictability increases the experimentation burden and reduces the degree to which a single disclosure can be extrapolated to a broad claim. Courts compare mechanical/electrical arts to chemical/biotech when weighing enablement (In re Fisher; O'Reilly; Béné).

name: Totality / fact‑intensive balancing of Wands factors
description: Enablement is determined by a flexible, totality‑of‑the‑circumstances evaluation of the Wands factors; no single factor is dispositive or mandatory.
guidance: The brief emphasizes that the Wands factors are 'illustrative, not mandatory,' and must be weighed together. See In re Wands and subsequent Federal Circuit decisions cited (Amgen v. Chugai; Idenix; Enzo; Wyeth & Cordis). The district court's factual findings (predictability, claim breadth, experimentation) are reviewed for clear error.

name: Whether the specification provides a 'general quality' or common principle enabling extrapolation
description: Assess whether the specification identifies a general characteristic or principle (a 'general quality') that plausibly permits skilled artisans to predict which undisclosed members of the genus will have the claimed function.
guidance: If the patentee demonstrates a 'general quality' or mechanism running through the genus, a single example may suffice; absent that, courts have required more disclosure. Cases: Incandescent Lamp (no general quality across fibrous materials), Corona Cord Tire, Béné. The brief highlights that demonstration of such a unifying quality converts an unpredictable result into predictable extrapolation.

name: Evidence that the patent's 'roadmap' predictably generates the full claim scope
description: Evaluate whether the patentee submitted non‑conclusory, objective evidence that following the patent's described methods will predictably produce embodiments covering the full claim scope (not just a small subset).
guidance: The brief contrasts 'produces claimed antibodies every time' (insufficient if it yields only a subset) with the stronger showing that the roadmap 'could produce all antibodies within the claims'. Courts reject conclusory claims lacking non‑conclusory proof that the roadmap reaches full scope (district court and Federal Circuit findings in Amgen).

name: Reasonable correlation between claim scope and scope of enablement / 'make and use' across full breadth
description: The claim scope must bear a reasonable correlation to the scope of enablement — the disclosure must enable one of ordinary skill to 'make and use' the invention across the full breadth of the claim.
guidance: Paraphrases established formulations (In re Fisher: single embodiment provides broad enablement only in predictable arts; In re Vaeck; LizardTech). The brief cites AK Steel: the specification must enable as broadly as claimed; absence of such correlation supports invalidity under § 112(a).

name: Functional claiming: propensity for overbreadth and policy weight
description: When claims are drafted functionally (defining a genus by what it does rather than by what it is), they are especially prone to overbreadth and thus attract heightened enablement scrutiny.
guidance: The brief cites historical and policy authorities (Halliburton Oil; Fiers; Lemley, Collins) explaining that functional claims can preempt future innovation and create litigation/market harms, especially in software/high‑tech. Therefore courts should apply 'high hurdles' for enablement of functional genus claims and use § 112(a) to police overclaiming. The brief notes administrative responses (USPTO training, White House Task Force) recommending scrutiny of functional limitations.

name: Reliance on scientific theory
description: An obviousness rationale may rely on logic and sound scientific principle, but when an examiner relies on a scientific theory the existence and meaning of that theory must be provided and supported by evidence.
guidance: Unsupported chemical or technical theories are inadequate to establish prima facie obviousness (see In re Grose and related cases). If relying on theory, provide evidentiary support showing the theory applies to the claimed subject matter.

name: When official notice without documentary evidence is permissible
description: Official notice without documentary evidence is permissible only where the facts asserted to be well-known or common knowledge are capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration as being well-known.
guidance: Examples where notice was appropriate: matters of obvious/common practice (In re Ahlert), basic facts readily verifiable or supported by references of record. In a first Office action it may be reasonable to take notice of dependent claim limitations that are old and well known expedients, provided they are of notorious character and merely 'fill in the gaps.'

name: Finality of next Office action when relying on common knowledge
description: Determine whether the next Office action should be made final when common-knowledge findings are involved: if a newly added reference only supports a prior common-knowledge finding and does not introduce a new issue, the Office action may be made final; otherwise it should not be made final.
guidance: If no claim amendments are made, examiner must not rely on other teachings of the newly cited reference when making the action final. If the newly cited reference introduces a new ground or issues not necessitated by applicant’s amendment, the action should not be final. See MPEP §706.07(a).

name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious when function not desired
description: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if the function of the element is not desired in the claimed context.
guidance: Examples include deleting components whose function is unnecessary for the claimed environment; courts have affirmed rejections where omission was an obvious expedient (Ex parte Wu; In re Larson; In re Kuhle).

name: Changes in shape are usually obvious absent persuasive evidence
description: Configuration or shape that is a matter of choice is obvious unless persuasive evidence shows the specific configuration is significant.
guidance: Courts have found claimed configurations to be obvious when they are routine design choices (In re Dailey), unless the configuration imparts a functional difference.

name: Purifying an old product does not automatically render it nonobvious
description: Pure forms of known products may be patentable, but mere purity by itself does not render the product nonobvious; consider whether prior art suggests the claimed form/structure or methods to obtain it.
guidance: Free-flowing vs. crystalline forms, purification to homogeneity, and product-by-process claims require analysis of whether prior art suggested the form or how to obtain it; purity improvements without structural or functional difference usually do not confer patentability (In re Bergstrom; In re Cofer; Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma). See MPEP §2113 and Ex parte Stern.

name: Obviousness of overlapping, approaching, or similar ranges/amounts/proportions
description: If the claimed ranges 'overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art' or are merely close to prior art ranges, a prima facie case of obviousness exists.
guidance: Overlapping ranges, or ranges close enough that one skilled in the art would expect similar properties, support prima facie obviousness (In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff; In re Geisler; Titanium Metals Corp. of America v. Banner; Warner-Jenkinson; In re Aller). See MPEP §2131.03 for related case law.

name: Developing search strategy techniques
description: Examiners begin by reading the specification and claims to understand the invention and then develop a list of relevant search terms and a field of search in the classification system.
guidance: Perform an initial search using classification and a combination of classification and text; review and modify results to fully search the invention and claimed subject matter. May search NPL databases or contact STIC for specialized NPL assistance. See MPEP chapter 904 and USPTO search guidelines.

name: Anticipation — disclosure of every claim limitation
description: In an anticipation analysis, the dispositive question is whether a skilled artisan would 'reasonably understand or infer' from a prior art reference that every claim limitation is disclosed in that single reference.
guidance: Expert testimony may shed light on what a skilled artisan would reasonably understand or infer from a prior art reference (Acoustic Tech., Inc. v. Itron Networked Sols., Inc.). Anticipation requires that every limitation is disclosed 'arranged as in the claim' (Net MoneyIN, Inc. v. VeriSign, Inc.). Inherency can establish anticipation when the missing limitation is necessarily present or would be recognized by the POSA.

name: Enablement of prior art disclosures
description: A prior-art reference need not have actually made or tested a nucleotide sequence (or other embodiment) if the reference discloses it and making it would have been well within the skill of one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Enablement is satisfied if the disclosure allows a POSA to make the claimed subject matter without undue experimentation. Routine matters (e.g., converting protein sequence to nucleotide sequence) support enablement (In re Wallach; Bristol-Myers Squibb v. Ben Venue Labs.). Citations and statements in the prior art that established 'well known genetic engineering techniques' can show enablement.

name: Nexus requirement between objective evidence and claimed invention
description: A patentee must establish a legally and factually sufficient connection (nexus) between the objective evidence and the merits of the claimed invention for the objective indicia to be given weight.
guidance: A presumption of nexus arises when the patentee shows the asserted objective evidence is tied to a specific product that 'embodies the claimed features, and is coextensive with them' (Fox Factory; Polaris). If nexus is not presumed, the patentee may still prove nexus by showing the evidence is the direct result of the unique characteristics of the claimed invention (In re Huang). Evidence directed to a feature already in the prior art (not novel in the claim) lacks nexus.

name: Coextensiveness/commensurate-in-scope standard for presumption of nexus
description: A presumption of nexus is appropriate only when the marketed product embodies the claimed features and is coextensive (i.e., the product is essentially the claimed invention; unclaimed features are insignificant).
guidance: Coextensive means the product is the invention disclosed and claimed; unclaimed features must amount to nothing more than insignificant additions (Campbell Soup; Fox Factory; Zaxcom discussion). If a product includes significant differences (e.g., specific capsid, promoter), presumption may not apply and nexus may be weak or absent.

name: Inherency in anticipation and obviousness
description: A limitation may be inherently disclosed by a reference when a skilled artisan would necessarily recognize that limitation from the disclosure.
guidance: Example from record: because Stafford discloses administering an AAV vector to patients, a POSA would recognize the vector would necessarily be administered in a pharmaceutical composition, so claim reciting 'pharmaceutical composition comprising the vector' can be inherently disclosed. Expert testimony can support inherency findings.

name: Do not import intended-use or functional limitations into product claims
description: Product claims should not be limited by asserted intended uses or by reading functional limitations into the claim when those limitations are not recited.
guidance: Patent Owner's attempt to import functional limitations (e.g., 'vector is used to introduce a nucleic acid into a cell for expression') into a product claim was rejected. For product claims lacking functional language, the evaluation focuses on structural limitations disclosed in the prior art, not on the patentee's asserted purpose.

name: Motivation to combine prior art references
description: To establish obviousness over multiple references, a party must show that a POSA would have been motivated to combine the references to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Motivation may be supported by express teachings, industry context (e.g., use of AAV vectors in hemophilia gene therapy), or known advantages (e.g., improved activity of a variant). The Board examines whether prior art and contemporaneous knowledge would have provided the rationale to modify or combine teachings with a reasonable expectation of success.

name: Objective indicia insufficient if directed to features already in the prior art
description: Objective evidence (praise, copying, unexpected results) directed to a feature that was already known in the prior art does not establish nonobviousness of the claimed invention as a whole.
guidance: Example: praise directed to FIX-R338L itself (which Stafford disclosed) cannot establish nexus for claims covering AAV-FIX-R338L combinations. The Board will discount objective indicia that are attributable to previously known elements.

name: Basic application formal-content requirements on filing
description: A proper Request for Prioritized Examination requires that the application include a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 including claim(s) and any required drawings, and either an executed inventor's oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.63 or 1.64 for each inventor, or a signed ADS providing each inventor's legal name, mailing address, and residence (if not residing at the mailing address).
guidance: Failure to submit these required items on the date of filing will cause the request to be dismissed. If an ADS with the required inventor information is present on filing, the inventor's oath or declaration need not be submitted on filing. For guidance on inventor's oaths/declarations and substitute statements, see referenced USPTO examples and 37 CFR provisions. Applications must be in condition for examination (see MPEP 708.02 VIII.C) before a request will be acted upon.

name: Eligibility by application type and filing date
description: Original nonprovisional utility and plant patent applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), filed on or after September 26, 2011, are eligible for prioritized examination (Track One), provided they meet claim limits and other requirements.
guidance: Also, original nonprovisional utility and plant applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111, or having entered the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371, in which a proper RCE has been filed or is concurrently being filed, are eligible for prioritized examination under the RCE pathway (subject to RCE-specific timing and conditions). The effective date of Track One for new applications is September 26, 2011.

name: Effect of pre-examination notices and informalities
description: A pre-examination notice identifying missing items or informalities will delay a decision on a pending Request for Prioritized Examination until after applicant files a complete and timely reply; such notices do not automatically cause dismissal (unless required items are missing).
guidance: Requests for prioritized examination are acted upon once the application meets all formal requirements such that it is ready for examination (MPEP 708.02 VIII.C). Informalities like noncompliant paper formatting, language issues, or excess claims notices may delay the decision but not necessarily dismiss the request; however, missing required items (specification, claims, required fees, oath/declaration or ADS) on the filing date will cause dismissal.

name: Request (application form) contents
description: The request explicitly states that an applicant seeks patent protection and is signed by the applicant or its representative. The request form will generally contain: the title of the invention; the name and address of the applicant and their representative; an indication of the inventor; and information relating to the priority claim, such as the application number and filing date of the earlier application on which the priority is based.
guidance: Each patent office provides a specific request form; all priority information should be included in the patent application, whether on the request form or in an application data sheet. In the United States, related applications may be described under “CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATION.”

name: Description: sufficiency and completeness
description: The description discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely to the extent that a person skilled in the art will be able to carry out the claimed invention.
guidance: To improve readability, the description usually contains sections: title, technical field, background art, summary of the invention, brief explanation of the drawings, and detailed disclosure by way of examples (embodiments). Examples/embodiments often play an important role in meeting the support requirement and the enablement requirement.

name: Claims define scope and determine patentability
description: The claims define the scope of exclusive patent protection in terms of the technical features of the invention; they are the legally operative part of a patent application and whether an invention meets patentability requirements is determined on the basis of the claims.
guidance: Claims must be clear and concise, as well as fully supported by the description. The claims are typically the first portion examined by interested parties and examiners; therefore clarity is of the utmost importance.

name: Abstract: concise searchable summary
description: The abstract is a summary (a digest) of the invention limited to a certain number of words; it typically includes key features recited in the claims.
guidance: The abstract primarily aids patent searches and gives an overview to readers of patent documents.

name: Invention vs embodiment vs claims
description: An invention is a construct inside the mind of the inventor; an embodiment is a physical form of the invention; the claims must protect at least an embodiment of the invention but the best claims protect the invention itself.
guidance: Claims do not define the invention but are a written approximation; patent drafters should aim to claim the invention broadly (not just specific embodiments) so others cannot practice the inventive concept without infringing.

name: Support requirement: claims must be supported by the description
description: Claims must be supported by the description; terminology used in claims should track through the description consistently and every claim must be adequately supported in the description.
guidance: A claim not supported by the description can be thrown out. In jurisdictions with strict support (e.g., EPO), the description must specifically include at least one embodiment that explicitly demonstrates the claimed combination.

name: Claim breadth strategy (broad and narrow claims)
description: Patent drafters should aim at a broad set of claims that covers various aspects of the invention at various levels of detail while also including narrower claims as fallbacks.
guidance: Because prior art is unpredictable, include a range of claims from broad to narrow; narrower claims can survive if broad claims are invalidated. Drafting strategy complexity is acknowledged and further treated in Module VI.

name: Claim format conventions (sentence, tense, punctuation, numbering)
description: A patent claim is traditionally written as a single sentence and in the present tense. Each claim begins with a capital letter and ends with a period. Claims are numbered consecutively and all claims appear in a separate 'Claims' section clearly separated from other parts of the application.
guidance: Periods are usually not used elsewhere except in abbreviations; semicolons separate clauses/phrases; many offices accept or require line indentation for elements. Follow punctuation conventions (comma between preamble and transitional phrase; colon before body; elements separated by semicolons with penultimate element followed by '; and').

name: Parts of a claim: preamble, transitional phrase, body
description: A patent claim is generally in three parts – the preamble (identifies category), the transitional phrase (open or closed), and the body (recites elements and relationships).
guidance: Ensure each part is chosen carefully: the preamble's breadth affects scope, transitional phrase choice (open vs closed) impacts inclusivity, and the body must interrelate elements rather than merely list them.

name: Preamble breadth and drafting considerations
description: The preamble identifies the category of the invention (apparatus, method, composition, etc.) and may include premodifiers/postmodifiers; more adjectives or complements narrow the scope.
guidance: Choose the preamble at the right level of breadth; broader preambles may invite unity/divisional objections; preamble weight in litigation varies by jurisdiction—assess whether preamble 'breathes life' into the claim.

name: Body of claim must interrelate elements (not mere list)
description: The body recites the elements and explains how they exist in relationship to one another; a claim cannot be merely a list of parts.
guidance: Connect elements logically (e.g., 'a top configured to be supported by at least one leg'). Many patent offices will reject claims that are simple unconnected lists of parts.

name: Peripheral claiming doctrine and drafting implication
description: Most countries follow a 'peripheral claiming' doctrine in which the claims establish the outer limits of patent protection; thus drafting claims to set the limits of protection sought is critical.
guidance: Unless filing in a jurisdiction that allows 'central claiming', draft claims to define the outer limits of protection. Consider how claim wording will be interpreted by examiners and courts.

name: Punctuation and grammatical detail are substantive
description: Many patent offices stipulate requirements for punctuation and formatting; claims are frequently more extensively punctuated than grammatically required.
guidance: Use commas, colons, semi-colons and line indentation as appropriate to make the claim's intended structure clear. Failure to attend to punctuation/grammar may lead to rejections even for substantively sound claims.

name: Markush claims not allowable
description: Art. 30 states that claims must specify the subject matter for which patent protection is sought; they must be stated clearly and concisely and be fully substantiated by the description. Markush claims are not allowable in Ecuador.

name: Claims clarity and substantiation
description: Claims shall specify the subject matter for which patent protection is sought; must be clear, concise and fully substantiated by the description.
guidance: Claims may be independent or dependent; multiple dependent claims allowed (referring to two or more previous claims). For method/process claims, the inventive step should be well defined and characterized.

name: Application formalities and sufficiency of disclosure
description: With the application the applicant must submit title/name of invention, description, a summary, one or more claims, necessary plans and drawings; when biological material is involved, a deposit. The description must be sufficiently clear and complete to allow a person skilled in the art to execute it.
