guidance: Also require payment voucher of fees (article 280 of new Ecuadorian IP Law).

name: Claim amendments restriction
description: Applicant may request modification of the application at any time during registration, but the modification may not involve extending the scope of protection beyond the use indicated in the initial application; correction of material errors allowed.
guidance: Claims can be amended when answering official actions or third-party oppositions.

name: Markedly different (Chakrabarty) test for modified natural products
description: A modified natural substance may be patent-eligible if it is 'markedly different' from its natural predecessor in characteristics and identity.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed subject has distinctive chemical structure/identity and new properties or utilities not present in nature (Chakrabarty). If the modification creates a new substance with new characteristics and significant utility, it supports eligibility. Compare with Funk Brothers where mere discovery without alteration was insufficient.

name: Preemption inquiry / 'significantly more' (Mayo)
description: Determine whether the claim (method or composition) would have the practical effect of preempting all uses of an underlying natural law or product; a claim must amount to 'significantly more' than the natural law/product itself.
guidance: Ask whether granting the patent would 'tie up' future use of the natural substance or law. For method claims, require additional elements sufficient so the patent in practice is more than a patent on the natural law. For compositions, if isolation/changes are just prerequisites to use, treating them as inventions risks preemption and thus invalidity.

name: Structural / chemical-difference assessment
description: Consider whether the claimed composition has meaningful chemical or structural differences from the natural product (e.g., whether the isolated portion 'ever exists as a separate molecule in the body').
guidance: Assess physical changes such as bond-breaking, contiguity of sequence, or other structural transformations. Substantial structural change that yields a different chemical identity supports eligibility; trivial or incidental changes attendant to isolation do not.

name: Utility comparison as a factor
description: Compare the utility of the claimed (isolated or modified) molecule to the native, naturally occurring molecule; greater or new utility can support eligibility in some views.
guidance: Judge Moore's concurrence suggested isolated DNA could be eligible only if it had greater utility than native DNA (e.g., short sequences used as primers/probes). Usefulness that is merely a consequence of having removed the molecule from its environment (as opposed to new functional properties) is weaker support for eligibility.

name: cDNA-specific test: synthesized and not occurring in nature
description: cDNA molecules, being synthesized to contain contiguous exon sequences and lacking introns, generally do not occur in nature and thus are human-made inventions eligible under §101.
guidance: Because creation of cDNA requires synthesis from mRNA and significant manipulation, cDNA is treated as an artificial DNA molecule with different sequence/structure and utility. cDNA patents do not risk preempting the use of native genomic DNA in the same way isolated genomic DNA claims might.

name: Handling of obviously informal or insufficient disclosures
description: If impractical to give a complete action on the merits due to informal/insufficient disclosure, follow specific procedure: reasonable search as far as disclosure permits; point out informalities; require specification be revised to idiomatic English/US practice; reject claims that fail to define invention under 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: If disclosure incomprehensible so as to preclude reasonable search, state no search made. Use attachments to point out informalities (see MPEP §707.07(a)). Blanket rejection of informal claims usually sufficient. Treat multiple obviously informal claims as a single claim for fee/examination purposes. Applicants are urged to submit preliminary amendment (preferably within 3 months) correcting obvious informalities; such preliminary amendments must exclude new matter.

name: Search obligations and treatment of previous examiner's search
description: After reading the specification and claims, examiner searches the prior art; the invention should be thoroughly understood before searching. When assigned after previous actions, give full faith and credit to previous examiner's search/action unless clear error or knowledge of other prior art.
guidance: Do not reorient case or take entirely new approach merely to hope of finding something. See MPEP §904–904.03 for searching practice. Informal or imperfectly understood cases still receive a search to avoid piecemeal prosecution.

name: Authority to require information (37 CFR 1.105) — scope
description: In examining or treating a matter in a pending or abandoned application (or patent, reexamination), the examiner may require submission from individuals identified under 37 CFR 1.56(c) or an assignee such information as may be reasonably necessary to properly examine or treat the matter.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.105 permits requiring e.g., commercial databases known to inventors, whether a prior art search was made and what was searched, copies of non-patent literature/published applications/patents related to the claimed invention or used to draft the application or used in the invention process, identification of improvements, identification of any use of the claimed invention known to inventors at filing, etc. Where assignee asserts right to prosecute, such requirements may apply to assignee. A reply that required information is unknown/not readily available will be accepted as complete.

name: Criteria for 'information reasonably necessary' (reasonable necessity)
description: A requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 may be made only when the examiner has a reasonable basis for requiring information that would aid examination or treatment; scope should be narrowly defined and focused to minimize burden.
guidance: Typical need is for finding prior art or resolving issues from search/analysis. Requirement is not a substitute for examiner performing a search per MPEP §704.01 and §§904–904.03. Reasonable necessity is generally met where: (A) claimed subject matter cannot be adequately searched by class/keyword among patents and typical non-patent literature sources; or (B) the application file or lack of relevant prior art found justifies asking applicant if they have relevant information. Provide narrow, specifically focused requests and state the basis for requiring information.

name: Examples of information that may be reasonably required (non-exhaustive)
description: Specific examples listed in MPEP §704.11(a) of information that may be reasonably required under 37 CFR 1.105.
guidance: Examples include: name/citation of any particularly relevant indexed journal or treatise; trade names of goods/services embodying the claimed subject matter; citations/dates/copies of advertising/promotional literature; citations/copies of journal articles describing goods/services embodying claimed subject matter; trade names/providers of competing goods/services; written descriptions/analyses prepared by inventors/assignees of competitive goods/services; identification of pending/abandoned applications by the inventors or assignee disclosing similar subject matter not identified in current application; reply to a protest under 37 CFR 1.291; explanation of technical material in a publication (e.g., inventor's publication); identification of changes in reformatted continuing applications; mark-up for CIPs showing added subject matter; comments on Federal Circuit decisions on point; publication date of undated document mentioned by applicant; comments raising question of derivation under 35 U.S.C. 102(f). These are illustrative, not exhaustive.

name: Expungement of information or copies of papers (37 CFR 1.59) — general rule
description: Information in an application will not be expunged and returned except as provided in 37 CFR 1.59(b); information forming part of the original disclosure (specification, claims, drawings, preliminary amendment in oath/declaration) will not be expunged.
guidance: A petition under 37 CFR 1.59(b) with the fee under 37 CFR 1.17(h) must be filed to request expungement of information not part of the original disclosure. The petition must establish to Commissioner's satisfaction that return is appropriate. See MPEP §724 for factors and procedures.

name: Printed publication / anticipation — enabling disclosure
description: A printed publication (including an issued patent or a published patent application as of its publication date) is a printed publication as prior art only if the disclosure of the claimed invention in the printed publication is complete enough to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to use the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: In determining whether the disclosure is enabling, consider what would have been within the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date, and you may consider evidence that sheds light on the knowledge such a person would have had.

name: Prior patent (pre-AIA) as invalidating prior art
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was patented in the United States or a foreign country by another before the patentee invented it (or, where applicable, more than one year before the patentee filed the U.S. patent application).
guidance: If there is a factual dispute about the date of invention or priority date, the jury should be instructed on how to determine the date of invention; otherwise the Court should instruct the jury as to the Cutoff Date.

name: Graham factor 2 — differences between claimed invention and prior art
description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the viewpoint of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date; determine the impact of those differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole.
guidance: Consider inferences and creative steps a POSA would employ. Combination of known elements yielding predictable results favors obviousness; unexpected or unpredictable results, or references teaching away, favor nonobviousness. A claim is not obvious merely because each element was independently known. If inherency is alleged to supply a missing element, it may be used only if the element is the natural result of the explicit prior art combination and not established by mere probabilities or possibilities.

name: Graham factor 4 — secondary considerations / other considerations
description: Consider objective indicia that may indicate obviousness or nonobviousness; no single factor is dispositive and must be considered with all evidence.
guidance: Relevant considerations include: commercial success due to the merits of the claimed invention (not marketing), long-felt but unsolved need, failure of others to solve the problem, copying by others, unexpectedly superior results, praise or surprise by others, acceptance of licenses because of the merits. These factors are material only if there is a nexus between the consideration and the invention; the court determines admissibility and sufficiency of nexus before instructing the jury.

name: Damages — general standards
description: If claims are found infringed and not invalid, the jury must determine damages adequate to compensate the plaintiff for the infringement; plaintiff must prove each element of damages by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Damages aim to put the plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in absent the infringement. The award cannot be punitive or include interest, and cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. The jury should consider damages only if it finds at least one asserted claim both not invalid and infringed.

name: Date damages begin — stipulated or disputed start date
description: When calculating damages, the start date for the damages period may be stipulated by the parties or determined by the jury if disputed.
guidance: Alternate A: if parties agree, use stipulated date. Alternate B: if disputed, the date the plaintiff first notified the defendant of its claim for patent infringement is the start date; the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant was put on notice as of the alleged date. (Methods of notice are enumerated in the full instruction.)

name: Difference between double patenting and prior art (35 U.S.C. 102/103) rejections
description: Double patenting rejections must rely on comparison with the claims in an issued or to-be-issued patent, whereas 102(e)/103(a) rejections rely on what the reference patent discloses (claimed or unclaimed).
guidance: A terminal disclaimer cannot be used to obviate a 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection. For commonly owned references, consider 35 U.S.C. 103(c) disqualification; examiners should be aware of differences in available bases (claims vs disclosure) when framing rejections.

name: Terminal disclaimer cannot obviate statutory double patenting
description: A terminal disclaimer is not effective to overcome a statutory type double patenting rejection.
guidance: Statutory double patenting must be overcome by claim amendments to remove coextensiveness, canceling conflicting claims, or canceling all but one of the conflicting pending applications' claims. 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits are inappropriate for statutory double patenting.

name: Limitations on 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits for double patenting
description: Use of a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is inappropriate to overcome a double patenting rejection when the claims of the application and patent are 'directed to substantially the same invention' or where there is lack of 'patentable distinctness.'
guidance: Case law (In re Dunn; Knell v. Muller; In re Ward; In re Teague; In re Hidy) supports that 1.131 cannot substitute for a terminal disclaimer or eliminate double patenting where claims are essentially the same.

name: Situations where 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition does not apply (A–G)
description: Specific exceptions include: (A) applicant voluntarily filed multiple applications without a restriction requirement; (B) claims not consonant with restriction requirement due to material changes; (C) restriction was written subject to nonallowance of generic/linking claims and such claims later allowed (requiring withdrawal); (D) restriction made only in an international application by ISR/IPEA; (E) restriction withdrawn by examiner before patent issues; (F) claims of second app. drawn to the 'same invention' as the first; (G) certain product/process restriction-withdrawal situations.
guidance: In each instance examine whether the divisional claims were formally entered and restricted/removed in the earlier application and whether the examiner's restriction line was maintained (consonance). Case law cited: Geneva Pharms., Symbol, Gerber, Studiengesellschaft Kohle, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Ziegler.

name: Avoiding statutory double patenting (practical measures)
description: Statutory double patenting can be avoided by amending conflicting claims so they are not coextensive, canceling conflicting claims in pending applications, or canceling claims in all but one pending application.
guidance: Terminal disclaimers are ineffective against statutory double patenting; 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits are inappropriate. Cited cases include In re Dunn, Knell v. Muller, In re Ward, In re Teague, In re Hidy.

name: Requirements and form of a terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321)
description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all claims of a patent; requirements are set out in 37 CFR 1.321 and sample forms/guidance in MPEP §1490.
guidance: A terminal disclaimer must operate with respect to all claims in the patent (cannot disclaim only specified claims). For commonly owned conflicting claims, the disclaimer must include a provision that the patent is enforceable only while commonly owned (37 CFR 1.321(c)). 37 CFR 1.321(d) sets requirements where the invention resulted from a joint research agreement.

name: Terminal disclaimer requirements for continuing applications filed on/after June 8, 1995
description: For continuing utility or plant applications filed on or after June 8, 1995 (20-year term rules of 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2)), a terminal disclaimer is required to overcome nonstatutory double patenting rejections because patents may have differing term expirations and patent term extension considerations under 35 U.S.C. 154(b).
guidance: Terminal disclaimers must include common-ownership enforceability provisions (37 CFR 1.321(c)(3)) and follow 1.321(d) rules for joint research agreements to avoid harassment by multiple parties with patents claiming patentably indistinct inventions.

name: Definition of a submission for RCE (what counts)
description: A submission as used in this section includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: If reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of § 1.111. A request for suspension of action, an appeal brief or a reply brief (or related papers) will not be considered a submission under this section, but a submission may incorporate by reference arguments in a previously filed appeal or reply brief.

name: Paris Convention – right of priority (procedural rule)
description: A principle enabling an IP applicant to claim priority of an earlier application filed up to 12 months previously for patents (and utility models).
guidance: This convention underpins the priority mechanism used to construct patent families and to determine priority dates when assessing novelty and inventive step.

name: Art Relied Upon for Drafting Claimed Subject Matter (Form Para 7.117)
description: Provide the title, citation and copy of each publication that was relied on to draft the claimed subject matter and a concise explanation of the reliance placed on that publication in distinguishing the claimed subject matter from the prior art.
guidance: If claims are expressed as means or steps plus function, provide specific page and line numbers within the disclosure describing the claimed structure and acts. In bracket 1, insert a description of the most important inventive elements. Examiner Note: must be preceded by form paragraph 7.105 and followed by form paragraphs 7.122–7.126 as appropriate. Only documents actually relied on (not merely believed relevant) are required.

name: Names of Products or Services Incorporating Disclosed Prior Art (Form Para 7.120)
description: Provide the names of any products or services that have incorporated the disclosed prior art.
guidance: Examiner Note: must be preceded by 7.105 and followed by 7.122–7.126 as appropriate. In bracket 1, specify the attributes of the prior art that most closely approximate the claimed subject matter to narrow the focus of the reply.

name: Details of Improvement Over the Prior Art (Form Para 7.121)
description: State the specific improvements of the subject matter in claims [1] over the disclosed prior art and indicate the specific elements in the claimed subject matter that provide those improvements.
guidance: This form paragraph should appear at the end of the requirement for information, as appropriate. Preceded by and followed by form paragraphs as noted in Examiner Notes.

name: Goal and Timing for Rejection Articulation (MPEP §706 intro)
description: After understanding the claimed invention and performing a prior art search, the examiner should determine whether claims define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention that is clearly described, and clearly articulate any rejection early in prosecution so applicant can reply and provide evidence of patentability.
guidance: Where information reasonably necessary for examination should be required under 37 CFR 1.105, such requirement should generally be made either prior to or with the first Office action on the merits and should follow MPEP §704.10 et seq. Examiner should not overlook role in allowing claims which properly define the invention.

name: Rejection Content and Best References (37 CFR 1.104 / MPEP §706(c))
description: If invention is not patentable, claims (or unpatentable claims) will be rejected. In rejecting claims for lack of novelty or obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command, designate the particular part relied on when reference is complex, clearly explain pertinence, and specify each rejected claim.
guidance: Examiner may rely on admissions by applicant or facts within his/her knowledge. Includes rules on treating subject matter as commonly owned for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) and 103(c) (statements to that effect, joint research agreements, disclosure of parties). See moved sections for detailed guidance (MPEP §§2120, 2132–2156, 2142, etc.).

name: Uniform Application of Patentability Standard
description: Standards of patentability (patent eligible, useful, novel, nonobvious, enabled, and clearly described under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103 and 112) must be the same throughout the Office; 'picture' claims are not alone justification for allowance.
guidance: An application should not be allowed unless issues pertinent to patentability have been raised and resolved in examination and prosecution. The standard applied is 'preponderance of the evidence' — reject if, in view of prior art and record evidence, it is more likely than not the claim is unpatentable.

name: Handling Claims Otherwise Allowable But Defective in Form (MPEP §706.01 II)
description: When patentable subject matter is disclosed and claims are intended to be directed to such subject matter but cannot be allowed due to defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection but should be constructive and offer a definite suggestion for correction.
guidance: Example: dependency on a rejected claim where dependent claim is otherwise allowable (see MPEP §608.01(n)).

name: Patentable Subject Matter Disclosed but Not Claimed (MPEP §706.01 III)
description: If the examiner is satisfied that patentable subject matter has been disclosed and the record indicates applicant intends to claim it, the examiner may note in the Office action that certain aspects/features have not been claimed and that properly claimed such claims may be favorably considered.
guidance: This is a constructive practice to inform applicant of potentially allowable claim scope.

name: Rejection on Prior Art — Language and Frequency (MPEP §706.02)
description: The most frequent ground of rejection is unpatentability in view of the prior art (lack of novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102 or obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103). Language used in rejecting claims should be unequivocal.
guidance: For detailed guidance on choosing best art, reliance on abstracts/foreign language documents, distinction between 102 and 103, and related material see the referenced MPEP sections (e.g., §§2120, 2132–2156).

name: Original-patent requirement (35 U.S.C. § 251)
description: The Director may grant a reissue patent “for the invention disclosed in the original patent.” Reissue claims must satisfy the original-patent requirement.
guidance: Courts require that the invention claimed on reissue be more than merely suggested or indicated by the original specification; the specification of the original patent "must clearly and unequivocally disclose the newly claimed invention as a separate invention." (Antares, Forum). The reissue claim must be for the "exact embodiment claimed on reissue [that is] expressly disclosed in the specification." If the exact embodiment is missing from the original specification, the reissue claim is invalid under § 251.

name: Express-disclosure vs. inference standard
description: To satisfy the original-patent requirement, disclosure must appear on the face of the original patent; inferences that a person of ordinary skill would draw are insufficient.
guidance: Testimony about what a skilled artisan would understand from the specification (i.e., that the specification 'encompasses' the claimed subject matter) cannot substitute for an express disclosure. The focus is on what is apparent "from the face of the instrument," not on post-hoc expert inferences. Relying on broad embodiments to show express disclosure of a narrower, unexpressed embodiment is too lenient under precedent (Industrial Chemicals, Forum, Antares).

name: Corbin/Industrial Chemicals "more than merely suggested" principle
description: Reissue claims cannot be based on subject matter that is merely suggested or indicated in the original patent; it must appear that the subject matter was intended to be covered by the original patent.
guidance: Quoting Corbin and Industrial Chemicals: new and broader claims must not be merely suggested; they must constitute parts or portions of the invention intended or sought to be covered by the original patent. Courts applying § 251 continue to apply this principle when assessing whether the reissue covers the same invention disclosed originally.

name: Standard of proof for invalidity
description: Invalidity of reissue claims (under § 251) must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: The district court concluded Google had not proven invalidity under § 251 by clear and convincing evidence; appellate review considers whether that burden was met under applicable precedent.

name: Exact-embodiment requirement (expressness and specificity)
description: The specification must expressly disclose the exact embodiment claimed on reissue; a general or broader disclosure that merely "encompasses" the narrower claimed embodiment is not enough.
guidance: The court explained that a skilled artisan might well infer the claimed embodiment from a broader disclosure (and expert testimony supported that), but precedent requires an express disclosure of the exact embodiment. The opinion emphasizes that expressness means the embodiment containing the precise claimed features (e.g., two web browser processes) appears in the original specification.

name: Illustrative inference gaps (application example)
description: When mapping a claimed reissue embodiment to an original specification, multiple specific inferences may be required; if those inferences are necessary rather than the embodiment being expressly described, § 251 is not satisfied.
guidance: As an example, the court identified three inferences a skilled artisan would need to draw from the original specification to arrive at the reissue claims in this case: (1) that an "interactive network process" includes web browsing, (2) that "interactive network process status data" includes website data, and (3) that a web browser process could be executed on the processor identified (P1). Requiring such inferential leaps shows the absence of an express disclosure and thus failure to meet § 251.

name: Claims are the starting point for patentability assessment
description: The claims are the starting point and the basis for assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC.
guidance: When assessing novelty, inventive step and other patentability requirements, begin from the claim language itself as the primary reference. The claim text establishes the matter for which protection is sought and provides the baseline for evaluation, even though other sources (description/drawings) will be consulted.

name: Article 69(1) EPC (and its Protocol) concerns patent effects/infringement, not patentability
description: Article 69 EPC is found under 'Effects of the European patent and the European patent application' and in particular pertains to infringement and should therefore not be construed as a definitive basis for assessing patentability under Articles 52 to 57 EPC.
guidance: Practitioners should not rely on Article 69 or its Protocol as the legal basis for claim interpretation when assessing patentability in pre‑grant examinations or opposition procedures, because those provisions are directed at defining protection scope for infringement matters.

name: Article 84 EPC is a formal/technical provision and not itself a definitive basis for patentability
description: Article 84 EPC is found under 'Filing and requirements' and thus, having a formal and technical nature, also does not provide a definitive basis for patentability.
guidance: While Article 84 requires claims to be clear, concise and supported by the description, it should not be treated as the sole or controlling legal basis for interpreting claims in patentability assessments (even though case law has sometimes applied it that way).

name: Claims must be clear, concise and supported by the description (Article 84 substantive requirement)
description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.
guidance: Despite the Enlarged Board's position that Article 84 is formally categorised, the substantive requirement remains relevant for drafting: ensure claims are clear and supported by the description. Previously some EPO practice emphasised that claims should be clear 'in their own right', but G1/24 requires consulting description regardless of apparent clarity.

name: Definitions in the description are relevant but do not automatically override claim wording; discrepancy rules unresolved
description: A definition or similar information on a term used in the claims which is explicitly given in the description may be consulted, but the Decision does not require that the description define, or overrule, the interpretation of the claims; there is no explicit teaching in the event of a discrepancy between the claims and description.
guidance: When the description contains an explicit definition (e.g., industry vs. specification-specific meaning), that definition must be considered in interpretation, but G1/24 stops short of saying the description always controls. Practitioners should be cautious: the Decision leaves open how to resolve direct conflicts between claim wording and descriptive definitions (illustrated by the 'gathered sheet' issue in T439/22).

name: Decision raises unresolved practical issues regarding 'boilerplate' and unclaimed embodiments
description: While G1/24 confirms always consulting the description, it does not address — and in fact raises further questions for — the extent to which the description must conform with the claims, for example as regards 'boilerplate' language and unclaimed embodiments.
guidance: Drafters should take care with broad or boilerplate disclosure and unclaimed embodiments because consulting the description could expand claim interpretation; however, the exact limits (when such disclosure will be read into claims or be disregarded) remain uncertain and will require further case law.

name: Dependent-claim construction
description: Any dependent claim shall be construed as including all the limitations contained in the claim to which it refers or, if the dependent claim is a multiple dependent claim, all the limitations contained in the particular claim in relation to which it is considered.
guidance: Dependent claims add the limitations of the claims they refer to; multiple-dependent claims incorporate the limitations of the particular claim being considered.

name: Grouping dependent claims
description: All dependent claims referring back to a single previous claim, and all dependent claims referring back to several previous claims, shall be grouped together to the extent and in the most practical way possible.
guidance: Arrange dependent claims logically and practically so related dependent claims appear together for clarity and processing efficiency.

name: Abstract: required contents
description: The abstract shall consist of a summary of the disclosure as contained in the description, the claims, and any drawings; the summary shall indicate the technical field, allow clear understanding of the technical problem, the gist of the solution through the invention, and the principal use or uses of the invention. Where applicable, include the chemical formula which best characterizes the invention.
guidance: Abstract must summarize disclosure across description/claims/drawings and highlight field, problem, solution gist, principal uses; include representative chemical formula if relevant.

name: Abstract: prohibited content
description: The abstract shall not contain statements on the alleged merits or value of the claimed invention or on its speculative application.
guidance: Do not use promotional or speculative language in the abstract; keep it factual and technical.

name: Direct reproduction and consistency of presentation
description: All elements of the international application (request, description, claims, drawings, abstract) shall be so presented as to admit of direct reproduction by photography, electrostatic processes, photo offset, and microfilming, in any number of copies.
guidance: Format documents to be reproducible by common reprographic techniques; avoid features that impede reproduction.

name: Terminology and signs consistency
description: The terminology and the signs shall be consistent throughout the international application.
guidance: Use consistent terms and reference signs across description, claims, and drawings to avoid confusion.

name: Each element on a new sheet; connection of sheets
description: Each element (request, description, claims, drawings, abstract) shall commence on a new sheet. All sheets shall be so connected that they can be easily turned when consulted, and easily separated and joined again if separated for reproduction purposes.
guidance: Start each major part on its own sheet and bind/arrange sheets for easy consultation and reproduction.

name: Writing/typing of text matter: format and size
description: The request, description, claims and the abstract shall be typed or printed. Only graphic symbols/formulae and certain characters in Chinese/Japanese may be handwritten when necessary. Typing shall be 1½‑spaced. All text matter shall be in characters the capital letters of which are not less than 0.28 cm high and in a dark, indelible color; request text may use characters with capital letters not less than 0.21 cm high. Paragraphs (c) and (d) do not apply to Chinese or Japanese texts.
guidance: Use clear, legible typed/printed text at minimum size; maintain 1.5 line spacing; check special provisions for request and Asian scripts.

name: Determination of unity independent of manner of claiming
description: The determination whether a group of inventions is so linked as to form a single general inventive concept shall be made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim.
guidance: Unity assessment focuses on technical relationship, not claim drafting strategy.

name: Dependent claims: reasonable number allowed
description: Subject to Rule 13.1, it shall be permitted to include in the same international application a reasonable number of dependent claims, claiming specific forms of the invention claimed in an independent claim, even where the features of any dependent claim could be considered as constituting in themselves an invention.
guidance: You may include a reasonable number of dependent claims to cover specific embodiments; check national limits in designated States.

name: Specification limits BRI when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies
description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim element (also commonly referred to as a claim limitation) is limited by the description in the specification when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, is invoked.
guidance: When a limitation is interpreted under 112(f), the claim element is not given unconstrained BRI but is limited to the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification (and equivalents).

name: Three‑prong test for 112(f) interpretation
description: As explained in MPEP 2181, subsection I, claim limitations that meet the following three‑prong test will be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph:
guidance: (A) the claim limitation uses the term “means” or “step” or a term used as a substitute for “means” that is a generic placeholder (nonce or non‑structural term) for performing the claimed function; (B) the term is modified by functional language (typically linked by “for”, e.g., “means for”, or phrases like “configured to” or “so that”); and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function. If all three prongs are met, interpret under 112(f).

name: Presumption from use of 'means' or 'step'
description: Use of the word “means” (or “step”) in a claim with functional language creates a rebuttable presumption that the claim limitation is to be treated in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
guidance: The presumption can be rebutted when the claim limitation recites sufficient structure, material, or acts to entirely perform the recited function.

name: Presumption from absence of 'means' or 'step'
description: Absence of the word “means” (or “step”) in a claim creates a rebuttable presumption that the claim limitation is not to be treated in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
guidance: That presumption is rebuttable when the claim limitation recites function without reciting sufficient structure, material, or acts to entirely perform the recited function (i.e., a generic placeholder coupled with functional language can still trigger 112(f)).

name: Effect of interpreting a limitation under 112(f)
description: Because this/these claim limitation(s) is/are being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, it/they is/are being interpreted to cover the corresponding structure described in the specification as performing the claimed function, and equivalents thereof.
guidance: When 112(f) applies, the claim is limited to the corresponding structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification (and their equivalents) — examiners should state the identified corresponding structure in the Office action.

name: Identification and grouping of multiple §112(f) limitations
description: When multiple §112(f) limitations need explanation, they can be handled in a single paragraph.
guidance: Use FP 7.30.06 to list multiple limitations (e.g., “Such claim limitation(s) is/are: a device for cutting in claim 4; a mechanism for rotating the device around the fork in claim 4.”). Examiners may format insertions as a list or chart and may provide a single explanation regarding repeated use of certain generic placeholders. Dependent claims can be added when using FP 7.30.06.

name: Applicant options to avoid or change 112(f) interpretation
description: If applicant does not intend to have this/these limitation(s) interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, applicant may: (1) amend the claim limitation(s) to avoid it/them being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (e.g., by reciting sufficient structure to perform the claimed function); or (2) present a sufficient showing that the claim limitation(s) recite(s) sufficient structure to perform the claimed function so as to avoid it/them being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
guidance: Advise applicants of the two remediation paths: amendment to add structure, or evidentiary/argument showing that sufficient structure already exists in the claim/specification.

name: 'Means' reciting sufficient structure is not treated under 112(f)
description: This application includes one or more claim limitations that use the word “means” or “step” but are nonetheless not being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph because the claim limitation(s) recite(s) sufficient structure, materials, or acts to entirely perform the recited function. Such claim limitation(s) is/are: a knife blade means for cutting in claim 6.
guidance: Because these limitations are not being interpreted under 112(f), they are not being interpreted to cover only the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents. If applicant intends 112(f) treatment, applicant may amend to remove the structure or present a showing that the recited structure is insufficient.

name: Rule 919: Amendment of the Disclosure (No New Matter)
description: No deletion or addition shall broaden the disclosure of an application to include new matter after the filing date. All amendments made after filing must conform to at least one of the parts (description, claims, drawings) as of the filing date. Matter not found in the original disclosure cannot be added even if supported by a supplemental oath and must be the subject of a separate application.

name: Rule 920: Amendment of Claims
description: Claims may be amended by canceling particular claims, by presenting new claims, or by amending the language of particular claims (such amended claims are treated as new claims). Applicant must point out how new or amended claims avoid any reference or ground of refusal of record pertinent to them and indicate which part of the original disclosure constitutes the basis of the amendments.
guidance: To facilitate examination, indicate in the response which part of the original disclosure is the basis of the amendments.

name: Rule 925: Substitute Description
description: If the number or nature of amendments makes consideration or paper arrangement difficult, the Examiner may require the entire description, claims, or part thereof to be rewritten. A substitute description will ordinarily not be accepted unless required by the Examiner and may be required within two months from grant prior to publication of the patent.
guidance: Examiners may order substitute description where necessary for clarity/printing; generally only upon Examiner's requirement.

name: Rule 1100: Annual Fees (due timing and payment rules)
description: First annual fee is due on expiration of four years from date application is published, and on each subsequent anniversary. Payment for annual fee and claims in excess of five must be made in full and may be made within three months before due date. Obligation to pay terminates if application withdrawn, forfeited, refused, or cancelled.
guidance: Claims-in-excess fees payable; annual payments may be made up to 3 months before due date.

name: Rule 1206: Surrender of Patent (voluntary cancellation)
description: Owner of patent, with written sworn and verified consent of all persons having recorded grants/licenses/other rights, may surrender patent or any claim(s) for cancellation and voluntary surrender. Petition must be in writing, sworn, verified and authenticated if executed abroad.
guidance: All recorded rights-holders must consent in writing and verification; petition formalities required.

name: Rule 1209: Changes in Patent (scope and limits)
description: Owner may request Office to make changes in the patent to: (a) limit extent of protection through deletion of claim(s); (b) correct obvious mistakes or clerical errors; (c) correct mistakes or errors other than clerical made in good faith. Where change would broaden protection, no request may be made after two years from grant and change shall not affect rights of any third party who relied on published patent.
guidance: Limitations on broadening changes (two-year window); ensure third-party rights not affected.

name: Transformation prong applied to biological/medical claims
description: Transformative steps that change a physical object or the human body (e.g., administering a drug) can satisfy the transformation prong of the machine-or-transformation test.
guidance: In Prometheus the Federal Circuit held that (1) administering a drug transforms the human body, and (2) determining metabolite levels via chemical assays transforms tissue samples — both counted as transformative. Courts assess whether the claimed steps are merely data-gathering or are integral, transformative steps in the treatment or process.

name: Preemption / tailored-to-particular-application inquiry
description: Determine whether a claim is tailored narrowly enough to encompass only a particular application of a fundamental principle rather than to pre-empt the principle itself; claims that 'entirely preempt' a natural phenomenon or abstract idea are invalid.
guidance: Judge Lourie characterized the central issue as whether claims would 'entirely preempt' use of a natural correlation (Gottschalk v. Benson and Parker v. Flook). Prometheus's claims were evaluated for whether they preempted all uses of the recited correlations between metabolite levels and drug efficacy; the panel concluded they did not because they covered particular applications with transformative steps.

name: Mental processes / 'determine and infer' claims exclusion
description: Claims that consist primarily of mental processes (determining a fact and inferring a conclusion) can fall within the unpatentable 'mental processes' or 'abstract idea' exclusions.
guidance: Prometheus-type claims often involve: (1) determining a measurable biomarker for an individual and (2) making an inference about health or treatment from that value. Courts assess whether the inference is merely a mental step or whether the claim integrates the determination/inference into a patent-eligible, transformative method.

name: Integral versus incidental data-gathering
description: When evaluating transformative steps, courts distinguish between steps that are merely incidental data-gathering and steps that are integral to the claimed application or treatment.
guidance: The Federal Circuit in Prometheus held that measuring metabolites and administering drugs were integral and not merely incidental, supporting patent eligibility. If a step is only passive data collection, it is less likely to render the claim patent-eligible under transformation-focused analyses.

name: Minimalist (threshold) approach to § 101 exclusions (Judge Rader's view)
description: Patentable subject matter exclusions should be treated as a threshold test that does not override the broad statutory categories unless the disqualifying characteristic 'exhibit[s] itself so manifestly' as to override the Patent Act's framework.
guidance: Under this approach, courts should avoid excluding inventions at the § 101 threshold unless a claim so clearly embodies an abstract idea that it would override statutory eligibility. Inventions with specific applications or technological improvements are less likely to be excluded as abstract under this test (see Research Corp. Techs., Ultramercial, and Judge Rader's views in Classen).

name: Statutory patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101
description: "This part of U.S. law describes what is patent-eligible: 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof'. If the invention falls under one of several excluding categories, however, including a 'naturally occurring article' (a defined term in the law), then it is not patent eligible."
guidance: Use §101 as the threshold inquiry for eligibility; if claimed subject matter is a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter it is prima facie eligible, but the statute and case law exclude natural phenomena, laws of nature, and abstract ideas. Determine whether the claim falls into an excluding category before proceeding to other patentability inquiries.

name: Inventive contribution requirement for product-of-nature-like compositions
description: Judge Bryson (dissent below) applied Mayo-like reasoning to compositions: in cases where the claimed composition is nearly identical to a product of nature, ask whether the applicant has made an 'inventive' contribution beyond merely incidental changes; mere breaking of covalent bonds or routine isolation is insufficient.
guidance: When a composition claim is substantially the same as a natural product, courts will require evidence of inventive modifications or functional differences beyond routine manipulation to reach patent eligibility.

name: Patentability of drug-screening assays versus other claims
description: The Federal Circuit found assays to find drugs to treat cancer patentable and stated that drug screening claims were not seriously questioned prior to the case; the Supreme Court's focus on isolated DNA did not categorically foreclose drug-screening claims.
guidance: Evaluate drug-screening or screening assay claims on their own factual and claim limitations — they may be patentable if they do not claim only natural laws or abstract processes and include inventive, practical applications or transformations.

name: Scope distinction: compositions vs information/applications
description: The CAFC considered valid gene claims as directed toward 'compositions of matter' rather than toward information; the Supreme Court emphasized that it did not consider patents on new applications of knowledge about genes (applications might be patentable).
guidance: Differentiate between claims to physical compositions (molecules, engineered DNA) and claims to informational content or applications (diagnostic uses, methods). Applications or inventive uses of genetic information may be treated differently from claims that merely recite natural information.

name: Routine, well-understood, conventional steps do not confer patentability
description: The Court noted Myriad's processes used to isolate DNA 'were well understood, widely used, and fairly uniform' and thus were not at issue; similar language from Mayo emphasizes that conventional steps cannot supply the inventive concept needed for patent eligibility.
guidance: When assessing claims, identify whether claimed steps are merely routine laboratory work; if so these steps generally cannot transform a claim involving natural phenomena into patentable subject matter.

name: Number of patent claims (claim count)
description: More claims signal broader scope strategy, greater prosecution investment, and more careful claim drafting; higher claim counts correlate (weakly) with quality.
guidance: Use claim count as a scope proxy. Prefer independent claim counts where possible because correlation with quality is stronger than total claim count. Interpret high claim counts as suggestive of higher quality but not definitive — combine with other indicators.

name: Backward citations (technological lineage)
description: Backward citations indicate technological context: many backward citations may signal cumulative improvement patents; few backward citations may signal pioneering inventions or weak prior-art search. On their own, backward citations give a mixed quality signal.
guidance: Use backward citations to characterize whether a patent builds on existing art or is more original. Do not rely on backward citations alone — combine with forward citations, claims, and family size to resolve ambiguity (e.g., few backward citations + high forwards → pioneering). Consider diversity of backward citations across art units as a positive originality signal.

name: Top- and bottom-quartile composite classification
description: Patents in the top quartile of the composite score are deemed high quality with confidence; patents in the bottom quartile are deemed low quality with confidence; middle quartiles are ambiguous.
guidance: Use quartile cutoffs on the composite to classify patents into high/medium/low quality bands. For middle-quartile patents, seek additional evidence (litigation, prosecution depth, examiner identity) before strong claims about quality.

name: Treatment of first-to-file rule when prior-filed application contains new matter beyond foreign-language specification
description: Where an invention claimed in a prior-filed application includes new matter beyond the foreign language specification, the claimed invention cannot be relied on in issuing a rejection under Article 36(1)-(3) of the Patent Act. New matter introduced in a prior-filed application claim cannot be a bar to a later application.
guidance: The same rule applies to foreign language applications to conform to the first-to-file principle.

name: Basic concept: treating foreign-language applications as regular domestic applications
description: A foreign language application is considered a regular domestic application; divisional, converted, or applications with domestic priority claims shall be permitted accordingly.
guidance: Filing-date effects for division/conversion/priority are normally evaluated on the basis of the foreign language specification, not Korean translations; however, because foreign-language specifications often coincide with Korean translations, the examiner may depend on Korean translations in determining retroactive filing date when appropriate.

name: Evaluating domestic priority claims when prior-filed application is foreign-language
description: If Korean translations of a prior-filed foreign-language application have been filed, effects of a domestic priority claim shall be evaluated by comparing the Korean translations of the prior-filed application and the specification and drawings of the application claiming domestic priority.
guidance: If Korean translations of the prior-filed application are not yet filed at the time the domestic-priority‑claiming application is filed, compare the original specification and drawings of the prior-filed application with those of the application claiming domestic priority. In other cases, compare the prior-filed spec/drawings and the foreign-language application claiming domestic priority.

name: Procedure of filing a divisional application — formality and required statements
description: A divisional application shall be filed by attaching the specification and necessary documents to a written patent application in the prescribed Form; the divisional must state its purport and indicate the parent patent application which forms the basis of division.
guidance: If the parent application is not indicated, the divisional will not be recognized as legitimate. Amendments changing the indicated parent after filing are not accepted except for obvious errors. Applicants normally should amend the parent to differentiate claims, but if divisional inventions are disclosed only in description or drawings, amending the parent is not required. Claims for disclosure exceptions or priority must be stated and evidential documents submitted within prescribed periods (e.g., 30 days for disclosure exception, three months for priority). Applicants may rely on evidential documents already submitted for the parent if they state the purport of using the parent documents; otherwise the examiner will request amendment for missing formalities.

name: Interviews before first Office action
description: An interview for the discussion of the patentability of a pending application will not occur before the first Office action, unless the application is a continuing or substitute application or the examiner determines that such an interview would advance prosecution of the application.
guidance: For interviews before the first official action in non-continuing applications, the examiner may require the applicant to provide a paper including state of the art and up to three closest references with explanation of how the broadest claim distinguishes over them (see 37 CFR 1.133(a)).

name: PTOL-413 Interview Summary contents and handling
description: Examiners must complete an Interview Summary form PTOL-413 for each interview where a matter of substance has been discussed ... The PTOL-413 form provides for recordation of: (A) application number; (B) name of applicant; (C) name of examiner; (D) date of interview; (E) type of interview; (F) participants; (G) whether an exhibit was shown; (H) claims discussed; (I) specific prior art discussed; (J) whether an agreement was reached and description; (K) signature of examiner; (L) names of other USPTO personnel present.
guidance: PTOL-413 should be given a paper number, placed in right-hand portion of file, listed on Contents list; duplicate copy given to applicant in personal interviews or mailed/faxed for telephonic/video/email interviews.

name: Minimum items for complete interview record
description: The complete and proper recordation ... should include at least the following applicable items: (A) brief description of any exhibit shown; (B) identification of the claims discussed; (C) identification of specific prior art discussed; (D) identification of principal proposed amendments of a substantive nature discussed; (E) the general thrust of the principal arguments of the applicant and the examiner; (F) general indication of any other pertinent matters discussed; (G) if appropriate, the general results or outcome of the interview; (H) in electronic mail case, a paper copy of the e-mail contents placed in the file.
guidance: Identification of arguments need not be lengthy—general nature or thrust sufficient. Interview Summary alone is not complete unless supplemented to include these items.

name: Eligibility for extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a)
description: Extensions of time with the payment of a fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136 are possible in reply to most Office actions of the examiner.
guidance: Exceptions include: (A) all extensions in a reexamination proceeding (see 37 CFR 1.550(c) and MPEP § 2265); (B) all extensions during an interference proceeding (but not preparatory to an interference where a claim is suggested for interference); (C) those specific situations where an Office action states that the provisions of 37 CFR 1.136(a) are not applicable (e.g., reply to a notice of allowability, in reissue applications associated with litigation, or where an application in allowable condition has nonelected claims and time is set to cancel such claims); and (D) those limited instances where applicant is given a specified time limit to take certain actions.

name: Affidavit/Declaration Ineffective Because Reference Is a Statutory Bar (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)) (¶7.60.fti)
description: The [1] reference is a statutory bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) and thus cannot be overcome by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a).
guidance: The affidavit/declaration filed on [2] has been considered but is ineffective to overcome the [3] reference. This paragraph must be followed by one or more of form paragraphs 7.58.fti to 7.63.fti or a paragraph setting forth proper basis for the insufficiency (e.g., failure to establish acts performed in this country or that scope of the declaration is not commensurate with the claims).

name: Affidavit/Declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 Effective To Withdraw Rejection (¶7.65)
description: The [1] under 37 CFR 1.132 filed [2] is sufficient to overcome the rejection of claim [3] based upon [4].
guidance: In bracket 1 insert either --affidavit-- or --declaration--. In bracket 2 insert filing date. In bracket 3 insert affected claim(s). In bracket 4 indicate the statutory grounds for the rejection addressed (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 112(a), 35 U.S.C. 101, 35 U.S.C. 103, etc.). If insufficient, set forth reasons (untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane; showing not commensurate in scope) and include detailed explanation. Use any of form paragraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 as appropriate.

name: Affidavit/Declaration Insufficient - Refers Only to Invention, Not to Claims (¶7.66.03)
description: The submission refers only to the system described in another application and not to the individual claims, so objective evidence is not commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66. Provide full explanation if appropriate.

name: AIA-specific: Affidavit/Declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 Effective to Disqualify via 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (¶7.67.aia)
description: The [1] under 37 CFR 1.130 [2] filed on [3] is sufficient to overcome the rejection of claim [4] based on [5].
guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66. Provide full explanation when appropriate. (Note: used in AIA-examined cases where 35 U.S.C. 102/103 as amended is applicable—follow bracket instructions for inserting affida vit/declaration type, subsection, filing date, claims, references, and explanation of reliance on exception provisions of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) or 102(b)(2).)

name: AIA-specific: Affidavit/Declaration Ineffective to Disqualify via 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (¶7.68.aia)
description: The [1] under 37 CFR 1.130 [2] filed on [3] is insufficient to overcome the rejection of claim [4] based upon [5] because [6].
guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.66 where required. In bracket 6 insert explanation of how the affidavit/declaration fails to provide evidence of reliance on an exception provision of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) or 102(b)(2). Use appropriate bracket insertions as instructed.

name: Updated Accelerated Examination Support Document Required for Claim Amendments Not Encompassed (¶7.70.AE)
description: For any claim amendments (including new claims) not encompassed by previously filed preexamination search and AE support documents, applicant must provide updated preexamination search and AE support documents that encompass the amended/new claims at the time of filing the amendment.
guidance: Failure to provide such documents at time of amendment filing will cause the amendment to be treated as not fully responsive and not entered. Include this paragraph (and 7.71.AE) in every Office action other than allowance for AE applications filed on/after Aug 25, 2006 or granted special status under 37 CFR 1.102(c)(2) or (d). Do not use for special status under 1.102(c)(1) (health/age) or PPH.

name: Amendment Under 37 CFR 1.312 Entered (¶7.85)
description: The amendment filed on [1] under 37 CFR 1.312 has been entered.
guidance: Use for amendments under 1.312 that do not affect scope of claims (may be signed by primary examiner) and for amendments being entered under 1.312 which do affect scope of claims (requires signature of supervisory patent examiner). See MPEP § 714.16.

name: Bona Fide, Non-Responsive Amendments (¶7.95)
description: The reply filed on [1] is not fully responsive because of omission(s) or matter(s): [2]. Since the reply appears bona fide, applicant is given TWO (2) MONTHS to correct to avoid abandonment. Proposed amendment filed under 37 CFR 1.132 has not been entered: [2].
guidance: Extensions may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136(a). Reasons for non-entry should be specified in bracket 2 (e.g., 'The amendment changes the scope of the claims').

name: Known work in one field may prompt predictable variations
description: To reject a claim based on known work being adapted from the same or a different field, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate findings (1)–(5).
guidance: Office personnel must articulate: (1) that the scope and content of the prior art included a similar or analogous device/method/product; (2) that design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation of the known device; (3) that the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art were encompassed in known variations or a principle known in the prior art; (4) that one of ordinary skill, in view of identified design incentives/market forces, could have implemented the claimed variation and it would have been predictable to that person; and (5) any additional Graham findings necessary to explain obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness conclusion. Examples and case law (Dann, Leapfrog, KSR, Ex parte Catan) illustrate applying this rationale, including considerations of marketplace incentives and predictable benefits of adaptation (e.g., decreased size, increased reliability, reduced cost).

name: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art (T/S/M)
description: To reject a claim on the ground that references teach or motivate modification/combination to arrive at the claimed invention, examiners must resolve the Graham inquiries and articulate specific findings.
guidance: Office personnel must find: (1) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (explicit or implicit) in the references or in knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill to modify or combine; (2) a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) any additional Graham-based findings needed. The T/S/M test is flexible — explicit suggestion is not required; motivation may be implicit, found in the nature of the problem, or technology-independent (e.g., desire for improvements like cheaper, stronger, smaller, more efficient). Case law (DyStar, In re Kahn) supports implicit motivations and requires articulated reasoning to avoid hindsight. If any finding cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used.

name: Disclosure of desirable alternatives does not necessarily teach away
description: The mere disclosure of multiple alternatives in the prior art does not amount to teaching away from any of those alternatives unless the prior art criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution.
guidance: An applicant's argument that the prior art 'teaches away' because it discloses a more desirable alternative is insufficient unless the prior art specifically discourages the claimed alternative. Cite In re Fulton and related case law. The Board/courts may find that the prior art as a whole still suggests desirability of the claimed combination even if not shown as the preferred alternative. See examples (shoe sole orientation, enzymatic hydrolysis reaction times).

name: Conclusions must be supported by articulated reasoning (no mere conclusory statements)
description: A bare statement that a claimed invention is within the capabilities of one of ordinary skill is insufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness; there must be articulated reasoning with rational underpinning.
guidance: Examiners cannot rely on conclusory statements; must identify objective reasons to combine references. Cite Ex parte Levengood, KSR quoting In re Kahn. Provide factual bases and avoid hindsight reasoning.

name: Proposed modification cannot change the principle of operation
description: If the proposed combination or modification would change the basic principle under which the primary reference was designed to operate, the references do not supply sufficient teachings to render the claims prima facie obvious.
guidance: Determine whether combining references requires substantial reconstruction/re-design or a change in the fundamental principle (In re Ratti). If the claim's principle of operation is different, a prima facie obviousness rejection is improper.

name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered
description: A claim limitation considered indefinite cannot be disregarded; if a claim has more than one interpretation and at least one renders the claim unpatentable over the prior art, reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: If multiple reasonable interpretations exist and one makes the claim unpatentable, the examiner should reject for indefiniteness and should also reject over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders it unpatentable. Cite Ex parte Ionescu; compare In re Wilson and In re Steele regarding reliance on speculative assumptions about claim meaning.

name: Limitations lacking support in the original specification must be considered
description: Limitations in a claim that do not find support in the original specification (new matter) still must be considered in obviousness determinations and given weight.
guidance: Do not ignore negative or other limitations absent from the original specification when assessing obviousness (Ex parte Grasselli). Even if a limitation was not in the original disclosure, it limits claim scope and must be considered. Failure to consider such limitations in an obviousness rejection is error.

name: Computer program listing submission thresholds and placement
description: A computer program listing contained on three hundred printout lines or less may be submitted either as drawings, as part of the written specification, as an ASCII text file on a read-only optical disc, or as an ASCII text file via the USPTO patent electronic filing system. A computer program listing contained on 301 printout lines or more must be submitted as an ASCII plain text file on a read-only optical disc or submitted via the USPTO patent electronic filing system. A listing of over 60 lines and not more than 300 lines, if submitted as part of the specification, must be positioned at the end of the specification and before the claims.
guidance: Form paragraphs 6.64.01 and 6.64.02 are to be used to notify applicants. If >300 lines included in the descriptive portion of specification (filed on/after Sept 8, 2000), require conversion to a Computer Program Listing Appendix (text file via EFS or read-only optical disc) and insert appropriate reference at beginning of specification. For >60 and ≤300 lines included as printout, either incorporate as text file via EFS/disc or place the listing after detailed description but before claims. See 37 CFR 1.96 and MPEP § 608.05(a).

name: Information Disclosure Statement required contents and certifications
description: An IDS must state either a heading that clearly indicates the list is an information disclosure statement and include legible copies of: (i) each foreign patent; (ii) each publication or the portion causing it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office); (iii) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including claims and any drawing or the portion causing the listing; and (iv) all other information or the portion that caused it to be listed. The statement must also include one of two certifications: (1) that each item was first cited in a communication from a foreign patent office in a counterpart foreign application not more than three months prior to filing the IDS; or (2) that no item was cited in a foreign patent office communication and, to the knowledge of the signer after reasonable inquiry, no item was known to any individual designated in § 1.56(c) more than three months prior to filing the IDS.
guidance: The IDS must be complete and include the specified legible copies and appropriate certification. Use the correct heading and ensure the signer has made reasonable inquiry as required by § 1.98(e)(2). If items were cited by a foreign office within three months, use the corresponding certification option. Attach required copies and ensure procedural compliance to have the IDS considered.

name: Enablement requirement (make and use without undue experimentation)
description: The specification must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention across its full scope without resorting to undue experimentation (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
guidance: Enablement serves the dual function of ensuring adequate disclosure and preventing claims broader than the disclosed invention. Broad claim language is used at the peril of losing any claim that cannot be enabled across its full scope. The amount of required experimentation must be reasonable; no exact numerical standard exists and courts analyze facts case-by-case (see Wands, Telectronics, MagSil, Amgen).

name: Quantity/quality of experimentation (time, expense, difficulty)
description: Assess the quantity of experimentation needed (number of assays/examples, time, and expense) to practice the claimed invention; excessive time/cost/difficulty may indicate undue experimentation.
guidance: Time and difficulty are relevant but not determinative if merely routine. Examiners should consider whether assays are routine or highly difficult. Example: Telectronics — $50,000 and 6–12 months standing alone failed to show undue experimentation. Example: Amgen — necessity to screen millions of antibodies supported lack of enablement. Quantity of examples is only one factor in the overall analysis (In re Wands).

name: Missing information — identify what is missing and why
description: When enablement doubts arise because information is missing about essential claim elements or relationships, the examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and explain why that information is needed for enablement.
guidance: Examiners must present a factual analysis showing what is missing and why a skilled artisan could not develop it without undue experimentation. Specific citation: MPEP 2164.06(a) Examples of Enablement Issues-Missing Information.

name: Scope of claims must be commensurate with disclosure
description: Claims asserting broad applicability must be supported by a disclosure commensurate in scope and detail; claims broader than the teaching may be non-enabling.
guidance: Courts have invalidated claims where specification disclosed narrow examples but claims covered broad genera (e.g., Enzo Biochem — antisense technology disclosed for limited genes but claimed broadly; In re Wright, Goodman, Vaeck). Examiner should evaluate unpredictability of the technology and the amount of direction and working examples versus claim breadth.

name: Complex components need construction and performance details
description: An adequate disclosure of a device may require details of how complex components are constructed and perform the desired function; generic naming and overall function may be insufficient.
guidance: If complex elements known to perform broadly recited functions in different systems must be adapted for applicant's particular system, the specification should describe such adaptability or else risk non-enablement (In re Scarbrough). Examiners should look for whether an unreasonable amount of work would be required to arrive at detailed relationships claimed.

name: Biological materials and deposits (microorganisms) — availability via deposit
description: When living biological products (e.g., microorganisms) are critical elements, availability may be satisfied by deposit in a public depository; deposit must be made prior to issue (but not necessarily prior to filing).
guidance: In re Argoudelis accepted public depository availability to meet written description and enablement. Examine scope considerations: depositing specific strains may not enable an entire claimed species (Ex parte Jackson). See MPEP §§ 2402–2411.03 and § 2411.01 for deposit rules and deposit-related rejections.

name: Biotech/drug unpredictability — extra scrutiny when technology unpredictable
description: In unpredictable fields (e.g., genetics, vaccines, protein expression), the amount of disclosure and working examples required to enable broad claims is higher; unpredictable behavior supports findings of non-enablement for broad claims.
guidance: Examples: Enzo Biochem (antisense technology unpredictable), In re Wright (vaccine claims for all retroviruses not enabled), In re Goodman and In re Vaeck (expression in different classes of organisms). Examiner should consider the state of knowledge at filing and inventor failures in the record.

name: Computer-programming disclosures — present factual basis to question adequacy
description: To challenge enablement in computer-related inventions, the examiner must present a factual analysis showing a person skilled in the relevant technologies would not be able to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Recognize that POSITA may encompass knowledge in both computer programming and the application domain. Examiner should focus on whether the specification discloses programmed steps, algorithms, or procedures necessary to produce the claimed function. Mere high-level descriptions or flowcharts may be insufficient depending on complexity (see MPEP 2164.06(c)).

name: Program listings, flowcharts, and algorithms — level of detail required
description: Challenging a computer disclosure is reasonable when the specification fails to include the programmed steps, algorithms, or procedures that the computer must perform to produce the claimed function.
guidance: These can be described in any understandable way (e.g., detailed flowcharts delineating the sequence of operations). As complexity and generality increase, a bare flowchart becomes more likely to require more than routine experimentation to implement. If no program is disclosed and more than routine work is needed, examiner has reasonable basis to reject (In re Brown, White Consol. Indus.).

name: Effect of inadvertent overclaiming
description: Whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention, a patentee has in his specification claimed materially more than that of which he was the first inventor, his patent shall be valid for whatever is justly his own; and every such patentee ... may maintain a suit ... for the infringement of such part, if it is a material and substantial part of the thing patented, and is definitely distinguishable from the parts claimed without right.
guidance: If claim(s) cover more than the patentee's invention due to innocent error, the statute preserves rights in the true invention but only to the material/substantial and definitely distinguishable part. The patentee must take appropriate steps (disclaimer) to avoid statutory consequences; otherwise limitations apply (see costs/unreasonable delay).

name: Requirement to enter disclaimer to recover costs
description: In every such case, in which a judgment or decree shall be rendered for the plaintiff, no costs shall be recovered, unless the proper disclaimer was entered in the Patent Office, before the commencement of the suit.
guidance: A plaintiff who later proves some claims invalid/overbroad cannot obtain costs unless the proper disclaimer was filed at the Patent Office before suit began. This is strict and applies even if the delay in filing the disclaimer was not unreasonable in some cases.

name: Formalities of a disclaimer
description: Any such patentee ... may, on payment of the fee required by law, make disclaimer of such parts of the subject-matter of the patent, as he shall not choose to longer claim, stating therein the extent of his interest in such patent. Such disclaimer shall be in writing, attested by one or more witnesses, and recorded in the Patent Office, and shall thereafter be considered a part of the original specification to the extent of the interest possessed by the disclaimant and by those claiming under him after the record thereof.
guidance: Disclaimers must be written, witnessed, recorded, and state the disclaimant's interest; once recorded they are treated as part of the specification to the stated extent.
