If the disclaimant is the original patentee and the disclaimer is silent on transfers, it fairly implies full ownership.

name: Disclaimer cannot create a new ground not in the patent
description: But a disclaimer cannot confine a claim to ground which does not appear in the patent to constitute an invention; even where that ground is narrower than that which was originally claimed in the patent.
guidance: A disclaimer cannot be used to reformulate or invent a new basis of patentability that is not supported by the original patent; it can only carve away matter from what was claimed or clarify boundaries that appear in the patent.

name: When a disclaimer must leave a material distinguishable part
description: The statute provides that a disclaimer, to be effective, must leave claimed by the patent, at least one definitely distinguishable and material part of the original subject of the patent.
guidance: A disclaimer cannot eliminate all meaningful scope; it must preserve at least one material and definitely distinguishable part of the original subject-matter (commonly done by disclaiming some claims while leaving independent ones untouched).

name: Disclaiming parts within a single claim (phrasing with 'or' or 'with or without')
description: For example, where two or more claims in substance, are combined in one claim in form, by the use of the words 'with or without' or by use of the word 'or' alone, a disclaimer may be made to expunge one of those inventions from that claim, without disturbing any other.
guidance: Where a single claim in form covers alternative inventions, the patentee can disclaim one alternative to narrow the claim without disturbing others — i.e., disaggregate alternatives phrased in the claim language.

name: Disclaim generic claim while preserving specific claim
description: And where a patent contains a proper specific claim, and also a generic claim which covers not only the subject of the specific claim, but also covers other matter which requires to be disclaimed, that result can be accomplished by a disclaimer of the generic claim, without any injury resulting to the specific claim, from that disclaimer.
guidance: Disclaiming a broad/generic claim is an appropriate way to excise overbroad scope while leaving narrower, specific claims intact.

name: Use disclaimer to confine claim construction to boundaries of prior art
description: And where an invention is limited by the prior art, in some particular in which the patent states that it is not limited, that statement may be removed by a disclaimer, so as to confine the construction of the claim of the patent, to the boundaries to which the invention is limited by the prior art.
guidance: A disclaimer can remove statements in the patent that falsely assert non-limitation, thereby aligning claim construction with the true limits imposed by prior art.

name: Cannot disclaim surplus parts of combination and then accuse others of infringement
description: Where the invention of a patentee consisted in a combination of less than all of the parts specified in a combination claim in his patent, he cannot disclaim the surplus parts, and afterward hold as infringers, those who make, use or sell the other parts alone, ... because that operation would broaden the patent instead of narrowing it.
guidance: Disclaimers must not be used to impermissibly broaden claim scope by shedding elements and then asserting the remaining elements as infringed; that would defeat the statutory purpose of narrowing, not broadening, monopoly.

name: Construction of patent after disclaimer
description: The construction of a patent, after a disclaimer has been properly entered, must be the same that it would have been if the matter so disclaimed had never been claimed. The mere fact of disclaimer is no evidence that the matter disclaimed is a part of the prior art. And where a disclaimer disclaims a particular thing specifically, that thing cannot afterward be covered by the patent as being an equivalent of another thing which was not disclaimed.
guidance: Courts must construe the disclaimed patent as if the disclaimed matter had never been claimed; disclaimers do not operate as admissions that matter is prior art and bar later claims that the disclaimed thing is an equivalent.

name: Judicial practice varies on whether decree should await disclaimer
description: Where a District Court, before any disclaimer has been filed, decides that a part of the claims ... are valid, and have been infringed ... while another part are void ... and ought therefore to be disclaimed. Ought the judge ... to enter a decree for an injunction and an account on the valid claims, and allow the complainant to disclaim the others ...; or should he decline to enter any decree till the complainant shall have filed a disclaimer? The second of these courses has been the practice in the first circuit, in the sixth, and prior to Page Machine Co. v. Dow, in the second; other circuits have taken different approaches.
guidance: Circuit courts differ: some require the complainant to file a disclaimer before a decree; others allow decrees on valid claims and permit the complainant to disclaim later. Practitioners should be aware of circuit-specific practice and plan accordingly.

name: Particularity or generality of machine or apparatus elements
description: Assess the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (particular) versus generically recited (any and all machines).
guidance: A machine recited with particular structural details (e.g., specific antenna shape/length/angles in Mackay Radio or a Fourdrinier machine with specific components/arrangement in Eibel) is more likely to provide significantly more. A general-purpose computer that applies an exception by conventional computer functions does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial, TLI). Mere recitation of concrete/tangible components is not necessarily an inventive concept. When applicants assert a 'specially programmed' computer, evaluate whether the claimed elements add significantly more than the judicial exception.

name: Whether machine involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation
description: Evaluate whether the machine's involvement meaningfully limits the claim or merely contributes nominally (e.g., data gathering, field-of-use restriction).
guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly (such as mere data gathering or stating the Internet as a source) will not provide significantly more (Bilski, CyberSource, Parker v. Flook). If the machine's recitation only imposes a field-of-use limitation or is extra-solution activity, treat it as not favoring eligibility. See MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for additional guidance on insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations.

name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation
description: Assess whether the claimed transformation meaningfully limits execution of the method versus being nominal or peripheral.
guidance: If the transformation contributes only nominally or is merely a field-of-use limitation, it will not provide significantly more (Mayo example: administering a drug was deemed only a field-of-use limitation and not significantly more). See MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for further discussion. Consider whether the transformation meaningfully confines the claim.

name: Requirement to adapt the description to amended claims (Article 84 EPC)
description: The EPO considers Article 84 EPC to provide a legal basis requiring that inconsistencies between the claims and the description be removed so that the description is consistent with the claims 'not only in some part but throughout'.
guidance: This requirement is justified as ensuring legal certainty for national post-grant proceedings (Article 69 EPC). Expectation is that the requirement to adapt the description to amended claims will persist; applicants should therefore align description and claims across the whole specification.

name: Definition of 'inconsistency' between description and claims
description: An inconsistency is something that could throw doubt on the subject-matter for which protection is sought, thus making the claims unclear or unsupported.
guidance: Use this test to decide whether a passage in the description must be amended or marked; the focus is on whether the passage could create doubt for the skilled person about what is protected.

name: Description passages that suggest unclaimed ways to carry out the invention
description: Parts of the description that give the skilled person the impression that they disclose ways to carry out the invention, but are not encompassed by the wording of the claims, are considered inconsistent with the claims.
guidance: Such passages should be deleted or appropriately marked as not falling within the scope of the amended claims.

name: Presence of an alternative to a claimed feature with broader or different meaning
description: An inconsistency arises when an alternative to a claimed feature is present in the description with a broader or different meaning than the claim.
guidance: The description must be amended to remove or mark the broader/different alternative so that it does not cast doubt on the claim scope.

name: Feature in an embodiment demonstrably incompatible with an independent claim
description: If a feature shown in an embodiment is demonstrably incompatible with the wording of an independent claim, that embodiment is inconsistent with the claim.
guidance: Inconsistent embodiments should be deleted or marked; examiners may point to the incompatibility when raising objections.

name: Describing a mandatory feature as optional in the description
description: The description must be amended to remove terms that refer to a mandatory feature of an independent claim as being optional.
guidance: If an examiner alleges this inconsistency, they should provide an example passage in the description showing the mandatory feature described as optional; applicants should amend the text to remove the optional wording or mark it as not relating to the claimed subject-matter.

name: What is not an inconsistency: embodiments with extra features still encompassed by independent claims
description: An embodiment in the description comprising further features not present in the claims but encompassed by the subject-matter of an independent claim is not considered inconsistent.
guidance: Do not delete/mark embodiments simply because they include additional (narrower) features; they remain consistent if they fall within the claim scope.

name: Examiner obligation to provide at least one example before refusing for inconsistency
description: Before refusing an application due to an inconsistency between the description and the claims, examiners must provide at least one example of such an inconsistency.
guidance: This is an evidentiary requirement: examiners should cite specific passages. If they assert that a mandatory feature is described as optional, they should provide the exact passage illustrating that inconsistency.

name: Generic disclaimers without specific reference are not allowed
description: Generic disclaimers (e.g., statements such as 'embodiments not falling under the scope of the appended claims are to be considered merely as examples suitable for understanding the invention') introduced at the beginning of the description without indicating which parts of the description they specifically refer to are not allowed.
guidance: Any marking or disclaimer must be specific as to which embodiments or passages are excluded; blanket disclaimers at the front of the description are insufficient to resolve inconsistencies.

name: Claim-like clauses: requirement to delete or amend claim-like language
description: Claim-like clauses are clauses in the description which, despite not being labelled as a claim, appear as such; claim-like clauses must be deleted or amended to avoid claim-like language.
guidance: Care should be taken when drafting the description to avoid clauses that read like claims. However, there is some case-law nuance: T1444/20 found certain claim-like clauses could not be mistaken for claims and did not affect claim clarity, and the Guidelines may be inconsistent on whether such clauses always must be removed.

name: Case-law divergence: clarity of claims may negate need for description amendments (T1989/18 and T1444/20)
description: Some Boards (T1989/18, T1444/20) have held that description amendments are unnecessary if the claims are clear in and of themselves; the need to amend the description depends on case facts and whether the description actually casts doubt on the claim scope.
guidance: Applicants can argue that clear claims stand alone and do not require description amendment, but recent EPO practice (and T1024/18) tends toward requiring removal of inconsistencies; the law is in flux and may be subject to further referral or guidance.

name: Process vs. principle distinction (laws of nature)
description: A patent for a process is a patent for the described combined use of all the laws of nature utilized by that process; a patent for a principle is a patent for one only of the laws of nature used.
guidance: If a patent claims a principle (a single law of nature) it would be broader than a process patent because it would cover all processes aiming at the same result that use that law, regardless of combination. Granting patents for principles would suppress subsequent invention. Illustrations: Harley, Whitney, Tilghman, and Bell claimed combined uses (processes) and were sustained; Morse's eighth claim was construed to cover the use of electric current alone (a principle) and was overthrown. Proper drafting to claim the combined and methodical use of laws avoids this problem.

name: Theory-only inventions may be patentable (if later proven)
description: An invention that resides in a theory without reduction to practice at the time the patent was granted may be sustained if the theory afterward proves correct, or when the correctness is self-evident.
guidance: Supports claims based on theoretical discoveries where later validation or self-evidence shows the theory to be correct; courts have sustained such patents (e.g., Telephone Cases).

name: Avoid misappropriation of rights
description: Prevent misappropriation (unauthorized claiming) of rights to results of intellectual activity created under state R&D contracts.
guidance: Audits recorded misappropriation cases; proper documentation, registration and contractual clarity reduce risk.

name: Actual reduction to practice evidences completeness
description: A specification may describe an actual reduction to practice by showing that the inventor constructed an embodiment or performed a process that met all the limitations of the claim and determined that the invention would work for its intended purpose.
guidance: Cases: Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder v. L'Oreal; Mahurkar — reduction to physical embodiment including all claim limitations is required for reduction to practice; for biological materials, a deposit per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. (esp. 1.804, 1.809) can demonstrate an actual reduction to practice.

name: Drawings or structural chemical formulas can show possession
description: Disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed can show inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole (drawings alone may provide a 'written description').
guidance: Examples: Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger; Autogiro. In chemical claims, generic formulae usually indicate what the generic claims encompass (Eli Lilly). Use drawings where visual representation can 'flesh out' words.

name: Identifying characteristics may demonstrate possession
description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics (complete or partial structure, other physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics with a known/disclosed correlation between function and structure, or combinations thereof) may show possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Factors include partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with structure-function correlation, and method of making. Cases: Enzo Biochem; Written Description Guidelines. In biotech, sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length are examples.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) support requirement
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), the corresponding structure, materials, or acts must be described in the specification and interpreted to cover their equivalents; written description must adequately link described structure/materials/acts to the recited function.
guidance: Examiners must consider original disclosure across summary, detailed description, claims, abstract, and drawings. Two adequate-description paths: (1) written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to perform function, or (2) clear from facts that skilled artisan would know what structure/materials/acts perform the function (Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino). If insufficient corresponding structure -> rejection under 112(b)/(second paragraph) and also 112(a)/(first paragraph). See MPEP §2181 and related guidance.

name: Different analysis for claims to a single species vs a genus
description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species is analyzed as a species claim; a claim encompassing two or more embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus claim.
guidance: See MPEP §806.04(e). The written description showing required differs for species vs genus (see subsequent specific steps).

name: Species claim evaluation steps (i)(A)-(C)
description: (A) Determine whether application describes an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention. (B) If not, determine whether invention is complete as evidenced by reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed. (C) If not, determine whether specification sets forth distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficiently detailed to show possession.
guidance: If complete structure disclosed -> written description satisfied for that species and rejection should not be made. If not, evaluate other identifying characteristics and whether disclosure is 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms' to show possession (35 U.S.C. 112(a)). Cases: Fields v. Conover; In re Wilder.

name: Determine whether complete structure or acts are disclosed for species
description: Determine whether the application as filed describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole; a complete structure typically satisfies the written description requirement.
guidance: Complete structural disclosure meets 35 U.S.C. 112(a). If not disclosed, look for other identifying characteristics (see i(2)).

name: Unpredictable arts require more evidence to show possession
description: For inventions in unpredictable arts or emerging technologies, more evidence is required to show possession; disclosure of method+function may not be sufficient to support product-by-process claims.
guidance: Examples: Amgen, Fiers — conception not achieved for complex genes until reduction to practice/actual isolation; disclosure that fails to enable recognition of structure or method to obtain it may be mere wish.

name: Genus claim written description requirements
description: A claimed genus may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure/physical properties or functional characteristics coupled with a known/disclosed correlation) sufficient to show inventor was in possession of the claimed genus.
guidance: Cite Eli Lilly; Juno Therapeutics: specification must lead skilled artisan to understand inventor possessed entire claimed scope; Ariad purpose: prevent claims from overreaching disclosure.

name: Representative number of species must reflect genus variation
description: A 'representative number of species' means the species adequately described are representative of the entire genus; when substantial variation exists, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation.
guidance: AbbVie: disclosing only one structurally similar species may not be representative. Conversely, in some circumstances one species may support a genus if disclosure indicates invention of species sufficient to constitute the genus (Enzo Biochem; Rasmussen; In re Herschler). Consider whether disclosure provides blaze marks or other means to identify which species would possess claimed attributes.

name: Specification cannot always support expansive claim language from one embodiment
description: A specification that clearly describes one embodiment does not necessarily support broad/generic claim language unless skilled artisan would understand inventor possessed the broader claimed invention.
guidance: LizardTech: disclose only particular method may not support generic claims; Tronzo: species in parent may not support genus in child when specification taught against other species.

name: Examiner initial burden and applicant responsibility for amended/new claims
description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims; when filing an amendment an applicant should show support in the original disclosure for new or amended claims.
guidance: Cite Wertheim; MPEP §§714.02 and 2163.06: applicant should specifically point out support for amendments. Cases: Hyatt v. Boone; In re Wright; In re Robins.

name: Each claim limitation must be supported in originally filed disclosure for priority/benefit
description: To comply with written description or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365/386, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: If explicit limitation is not present, show that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation. Inherency must be proven clearly, not by possibilities. Cases: In re Robertson; Kennecott; Yeda Research; Regents of Univ. of Minnesota v. Gilead.

name: Claims must include all elements described as essential
description: Each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential.
guidance: If an element described as essential is not claimed, new/amended claims lacking such support must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or priority/benefit denied. Cases: Johnson Worldwide; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo.

name: Consequences when disclosure lacks support for claim limitations
description: If the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element described as essential is not claimed, a new or amended claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (lack of adequate written description), or priority/benefit must be denied.
guidance: Apply this when examiner or applicant cannot show express/implicit/inherent support; follow rejection protocols in Office actions.

name: Patentable subject matter — non-natural composition limitations
description: Claim limitations such as “dosage of omega-6 and omega-3”, “casings providing controlled delivery”, and “intermixtures [of lipids] in defined ratios” are not products of nature and render the claimed compositions structurally distinct on their face.
guidance: Page argues these limitations impart functional structure and materially change properties of lipids versus natural counterparts (e.g., oils/nuts/seeds). Cites Myriad and Chakrabarty as controlling precedent that products of nature are ineligible but structural/functional alterations can make compositions patentable. Examples: Claim 65 (dosage + casings + intermixture) and Claims 102, 107, 109, 128 asserted to be structurally distinct. The petition faults the panel for accepting that the claims are products of nature despite acknowledging these limitations elsewhere (Op10–12).

name: Examiner burden — show natural counterpart exists
description: The Examiner must provide evidence that a natural counterpart exists for the claimed composition; an admission that no natural counterpart appears to exist weighs against a product-of-nature finding.
guidance: Appellant cites Examiner admission: 'Relative to the compositions of Claims 102, 107, and 119, there does not appear to be a naturally occurring counterpart to all of these elements present together in the claimed combination' (Appx7776). The petition contends the panel overlooked that admission when affirming ineligibility under §101. Use prosecution record and examiner statements to check burden.

name: Intermixture as structural limitation
description: The term 'intermixture' can be construed as a structural limitation; product claims comprising intermixtures are patentable when the structure is unknown, complex, or expected to have distinct properties.
guidance: Cites Garnero and Abbott: intermixture is capable of construction as structural. The petition argues that mixtures of lipids from different sources necessarily change physical/chemical properties and thus are not mere natural products. Where structure is complex or not fully known, courts should treat 'intermixture' as structural rather than disregarding it under §101.

name: Printed matter/functional instructions combined with product may be patentable
description: A claim that combines printed matter (instructions/serving) with a product is patentable if the printed matter has a functional relationship to the product; such combinations are properly evaluated under §§102 and 103, not necessarily as products of nature under §101.
guidance: Cites Miller and Gulack: printed matter having a functional relationship to the subject matter can render a claim patentable. The petition argues that WebOOil/WebWOil references include serving instructions that functionally relate to the oil and therefore that combination should not be treated as a product of nature. Also notes that cited oils are themselves patented (U.S. Patent 7,620,531), supporting that they are not natural products in the §101 sense.

name: De novo review of legal determinations; broadest reasonable interpretation in examination
description: On review, the Board's legal determinations (including claim construction and eligibility questions) are reviewed de novo; during examination pending claims receive their broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: Cites In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech Ctr., 367 F.3d 1359. Petition stresses the panel failed to perform de novo review on claim construction and prior art interpretation, and improperly deferred to PTAB factual findings where legal interpretation was required. Use this standard to evaluate whether the court applied correct review scope.

name: Anticipation (§102) requires clear and enabling disclosure; 'may' or equivocal language insufficient
description: A prior-art reference must necessarily disclose and enable the claimed elements (e.g., specific dosage, ratios, steady delivery); equivocal statements ('may') or non-enabling examples do not establish anticipation.
guidance: Petition contends Mark and other references use permissive language and do not enable claimed dosages/steady delivery; PHOSITA testimony on record says Mark does not enable dosage. The petition argues that the Board improperly treated such references as anticipatory despite lack of necessary enabling disclosure. Use this when evaluating whether prior art truly teaches claimed ranges and functions.

name: Specification and prosecution history may make claim terms limiting
description: If the specification repeatedly emphasizes certain elements (e.g., dosage tables, examples) or prosecution statements/PHOSITA testimony construe terms in a limiting way, those claim elements should be treated as limiting and cannot be excised in eligibility or anticipation analyses.
guidance: Appellant points to specification tables and ~20 examples (Appx82–97) specifying dosages by age/gender and prosecution record where inventor/PHOSITA defined 'dosage' and 'casings providing controlled delivery.' The petition criticizes the Board for claiming these elements are non-limiting despite the specification and prosecution history.

name: Anticipation by composition: showing prior-art compositions contain the claimed components/ratios suffices when enabling
description: If a prior-art composition (e.g., nutrient analyses or patent disclosing oils) expressly contains the components and ratios recited in the claim and is enabling for the claimed use/dosage, that can support anticipation.
guidance: Board relied on Mark, Olive Nutrient Analysis, and Walnut Nutrient Analysis to find claims anticipated because they purportedly disclose omega-6/omega-3 ratios and serving sizes within claimed dosage limits. Petition disputes the enablement and operability of those disclosures and points to PHOSITA testimony to the contrary. Distinguish factual enablement and legal sufficiency when applying this criterion.

name: Patent specification required elements
description: A patent specification generally contains background and overview of the invention, a description of the invention and embodiments, claims, figures (where helpful), and an abstract and title; may include gene sequences or computer code depending on subject matter.
guidance: Offices set formal rules on structure, paper size, font, layout, section ordering and headings. Because descriptions cannot generally be modified once filed (with narrow exceptions), careful preparation is important.

name: Claims define scope and claim drafting constraints
description: The claims of a patent specification define the scope of protection; they describe the invention in a specific legal style, setting out essential features to clearly define what would infringe.
guidance: Claims often include independent (broad) and dependent (narrower) claims and are frequently amended during prosecution. In the U.S., claims can be amended after grant but cannot be broadened beyond what was originally disclosed; claim broadening after grant is restricted (no broadening more than two years after issue).

name: Formal requirements for obtaining a filing date under the PLT
description: For PLT Contracting Parties, an office must accord a filing date upon compliance with three simple formal requirements: (1) an indication that the elements received are intended to be an application for a patent for an invention; (2) indications allowing identification/contact of the applicant; (3) a part which appears to be a description of the invention.
guidance: A Contracting Party cannot require claims or a filing fee as part of the filing date requirement. These are absolute minimums for a filing date under the Patent Law Treaty.

name: Search and search report purpose
description: After filing a search is carried out to reveal prior art relevant to the claimed subject‑matter; a search report is generally published with the application.
guidance: Search reports help applicants decide whether to pursue prosecution or abandon, and inform the public/competitors about the likely scope of protection. In some jurisdictions search and examination are combined and no separate search report is issued.

name: Required elements of a PCT (international) application
description: An international (PCT) application must contain the following elements: request, description, claim or claims, one or more drawings (where necessary), and abstract.
guidance: WIPO coordinates centralised filing formalities, international searches by ISAs, publication, and preliminary examinations by IPEAs. The PCT preserves national phase options and delays national prosecution.

name: Filing date and inability to add subject matter afterwards
description: Since no subject matter can be added to an application after the filing date (subject to narrow exceptions), it is important that an application disclose all material relevant to the invention at the time of filing.
guidance: Failure to include material at filing may preclude later claiming of that matter; strategic decisions (e.g., provisional filings vs full) affect what can later be relied upon.

name: Step 2B inventive concept inquiry
description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
guidance: Examiners should answer by first identifying any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), then evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)). This evaluation is made with respect to the Supreme Court considerations introduced in MPEP § 2106 (and discussed in detail in subsections (a) through (h)). The evaluation is not a weighing test; it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to applicant's invention and whether the additional elements encompass an inventive concept. If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more than the exception (Step 2B: NO) it is not eligible; if it does (Step 2B: YES) it is eligible (Pathway C) and the eligibility analysis is complete.

name: Identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
description: Examiners must identify whether there are any elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate those elements both individually and as an ordered combination.
guidance: Consider whether each additional element by itself is well-understood, routine, conventional activity or a generic implementation, and whether a combination of elements produces a non-conventional, non-generic arrangement that amounts to significantly more. Courts have emphasized that the inventive concept inquiry requires more than recognizing that each claim element, by itself, was known in the art.

name: Consult the specification and use broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Evaluation of what the applicant has invented should be made by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with a reasonable interpretation (BRI).
guidance: Consult the specification to determine how elements are described (e.g., whether elements are described as well-known generic components or as providing technical details/solutions). Use MPEP § 2111 for claim construction. The specification can show whether a technical problem and an unconventional technical solution are disclosed (examples: McRO vs Affinity Labs).

name: Improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology (improvement consideration)
description: Consider whether the claim purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology or technical field (i.e., a technological solution to a technological problem).
guidance: This consideration may be evaluated at Step 2A or Step 2B. The claim focus must be examined under BRI to determine whether the invention purports to improve technology. The specification should provide a technical explanation showing how to implement the invention so a person of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The claim itself must reflect the improvement (not merely the specification). Avoid oversimplifying claims; evaluate the claim as an ordered combination.

name: Computer-functionality improvement criteria
description: For computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities or instead merely uses computers as a tool.
guidance: A claim that improves how a computer stores, retrieves, or processes data, or provides a specific implementation in software/architecture, may show an improvement (see Enfish, BASCOM, DDR, Amdocs, Visual Memory examples). Method claims must be limited to computer implementation to qualify; if the entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology. Courts have listed examples of improvements (e.g., modified Internet hyperlink protocol, inventive distribution of functionality in a network, specialized memory systems, specific GUIs, particular server structures) and examples that are insufficient (e.g., mere automation, using a general-purpose computer, mere speedups due to generic hardware).

name: Improvements to other technology or technical field
description: Claims showing improvements in non-computer technologies or broader technical fields may demonstrate eligibility when they describe particular ways to solve technical problems.
guidance: Courts have found eligibility where claims recite specific methods, devices, or configurations that improve a technological process (examples: Diamond v. Diehr thermocouple modification to rubber molding, particular telephone/server combinations, improved downloading for streaming, improved data compression, measurement devices generating new data, inertial sensor configurations, improved preservation processes). Claims must recite details on how a computer or other technology aids the method; merely adding generic components is insufficient.

name: Whether the machine implements the method steps (integral use)
description: Determine if the machine plays an integral role in achieving the claimed method steps rather than merely serving as an object on which the method operates.
guidance: Integral use of a machine to achieve performance of a method may provide significantly more; if the machine merely serves as a medium or obvious mechanism to permit a solution to be achieved more quickly, it generally will not. (See CyberSource and Versata examples.)

name: Extra-solution activity and field-of-use limits
description: Consider whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation that imposes no meaningful limits on the claim.
guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method (e.g., mere data-gathering from a source, or restricting use to a field of use) will not provide significantly more. Courts have held that data-gathering steps and nominal Internet sourcing do not make a claim statutory.

name: Claim-by-claim analysis; dependent claims may differ
description: Examine each claim for eligibility separately based on the particular elements recited therein; do not treat all claims in an application as automatically standing or falling together.
guidance: One claim may be ineligible while a dependent claim that adds additional elements that amount to significantly more may be eligible. If a claim clearly recites multiple discrete exceptions, an examiner may select one exception to analyze for examination efficiency, but if the selected-exception analysis finds significantly more, treat the claim as eligible.

name: Application size fee: thresholds, exclusions, and counting rules
description: The application size fee (37 CFR 1.16(s)) applies to any application whose specification (including claims) and drawings exceed 100 sheets of paper. The fee applies for each additional 50 sheets or fraction thereof over 100 sheets.
guidance: Excludes ASCII/plain text or XML sequence listings or computer program listing appendix submitted on read-only optical disc or via EFS as applicable (see 37 CFR 1.52(f)). Preliminary amendments present on filing date are part of original disclosure and are counted. Office does not recommend filing substitute specifications or multiple sets of drawings. For content on read-only optical disc, each three kilobytes of content is counted as a sheet (37 CFR 1.52(f)(1)). For EFS submissions, paper-equivalent is considered 75% of rendered sheets for computing the fee; sequence listings/program listings in ASCII/XML as associated files may be excluded; PDF/TIFF listings are not excluded.

name: Dependent claim form correctness and remedies
description: For purposes of determining fees, a claim will be treated as dependent if it contains reference to one or more other claims. Any claim in dependent form that is not a proper dependent claim (e.g., does not include every limitation of the claim on which it depends) will be required to be canceled as not being a proper dependent claim; cancellation of further claims depending on such a claim will likewise be required.
guidance: Applicant may amend claims to place them in proper dependent form, or redraft them as independent claims upon payment of any necessary additional fee.

name: Option 2 — Modified PCT 'unity of invention' standard
description: The current PCT 'unity of invention' standard, modified to require that any purported special technical/common feature comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, would be applied to all US applications. Applicants would be given the option of concurrent examination of multiple inventions that lack unity of invention for an additional fee.
guidance: Unity exists only when there is a technical relationship among the claimed inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding 'special technical features' that define a contribution which each invention makes over the prior art. Whether a technical feature makes a 'contribution' should be considered with respect to prior art and 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (support/enablement). If the examiner can demonstrate lack of support for the main claim, there is no technical relationship. Applicants may be invited to identify a reference claim to determine relationships in applications with many inventions. Feedback: implementation/examination under Option 2 considered more difficult than Option 1 but less difficult than Options 3 or 4.

name: Definition — 'Distinct' inventions
description: The term 'distinct' means two or more subjects as disclosed are related (e.g., combination and part/subcombination, process and apparatus for its practice, process and product made) but are capable of separate manufacture, use, or sale as claimed, and are patentable (novel and unobvious) over each other.
guidance: They may each be unpatentable over the prior art yet still be 'distinct' relative to each other for restriction purposes.

name: Examiner use of a reference claim for determining relationship among claims
description: In applications with many inventions, applicant will be invited to identify a reference claim for determination of the relationship of remaining claims (i.e., whether they contain 'the same or corresponding special technical/common feature(s)').
guidance: Reference-claim procedure used where necessary (particularly in chemical and biotechnology applications) to determine relatedness among many inventions; see Development of Restriction Standard Options for the Study.

name: Partial search vs assessing 35 U.S.C. §112 when lack of unity arises
description: Whether to perform only a 'partial search' when examination of entire scope of claims is unduly burdensome due to non-prior-art issues, or to assess adequacy of disclosure and industrial applicability (35 U.S.C. §112 issues) in addition to prior art when determining whether claimed common feature makes a contribution over the prior art.
guidance: Some international authorities make 'partial search' declarations in such circumstances; the USPTO historically does not. Public comments expressed mixed support for partial search and less support to look to §112 issues in making lack of unity determinations, though some organizations favored considering non-prior art issues.

name: Whether to adopt EPO (central claiming) practices (one independent claim per category and emphasis on independent claims)
description: Question whether USPTO should study adopting EPO claim treatment practice (normally allowing only one independent claim per category of invention and emphasizing search/examination of independent claims), and whether to modify examination of dependent claims and consider changes to presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. 282.
guidance: Public comments showed no consensus and generally strong objection to moving to EPO-style claim drafting/search/treatment. Consideration must account for differences in US practice (USPTO searches/examines every claim and every limitation).

name: Practice on examining first claimed invention vs applicant election (PCT-style)
description: Whether to adopt the PCT practice of examining the first claimed invention when lack of unity is held, or to allow applicant opportunity to elect an invention to be examined (or examine first claimed product vs first claimed invention).
guidance: Public comments generally encouraged retaining oral elections and some limited support for examining the first claimed invention if applicant fails to orally elect; preference to keep current practice of written requirement if oral election not possible.

name: Use of RCE authority to permit post-prosecution submission/examination of additional inventions
description: Use 35 U.S.C. 132(b) authority to permit applicants to pay an RCE fee and submit or rejoin claims to additional inventions after prosecution closed on first invention, provided submitted claims depend from or include features of allowed claims that make a contribution over the prior art.
guidance: Such an option would allow continued examination under a Unity standard without statutory change; questions include whether to limit availability to published applications and how to set RCE fee relative to current fee structure. Public comments generally expressed strong opposition, possibly due to misunderstanding of the scope.

name: Use of continued examination to permit requests to continue examination of withdrawn claims
description: Permit requests that the USPTO continue examination of claims withdrawn from consideration by requiring applicants to request continued examination, pay a fee for treatment of one additional invention, and present claims drawn only to that additional invention (available in addition to filing a divisional).
guidance: Public comments expressed mixed support for this proposed procedure. Considerations include how to offset loss in issue and maintenance fee collections.

name: Public/user impacts — practitioner strategy and claim drafting consequences
description: A revised restriction standard will require practitioners to become familiar with new filing and prosecution strategies; options to pay for immediate examination of additional inventions would affect whether practitioners request immediate examination or wait and file divisionals.
guidance: Decisions must be made prior to search and examination and therefore with limited patentability information. Claim drafting styles may need reconsideration; e.g., inclusion of purported same or corresponding special technical/common feature in independent claims may prove valuable under Option 2.

name: Alice two-step test (Mayo/Alice framework)
description: A two-step inquiry used to determine whether a claimed invention is directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
guidance: Step 1: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon. If not, the claim is patent-eligible and analysis ends. If yes, proceed to Step 2. Step 2: Determine whether the claim includes an 'inventive concept' — elements individually or in combination that transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter (must be 'significantly more').

name: Step 1 — Directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon
description: The court or examiner first determines whether the claims are directed to one of the judicially recognized exceptions to patentability: abstract ideas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena.
guidance: If the claim is not directed to a judicial exception, it is patent-eligible and the inquiry ends. If it is, proceed to the inventive-concept inquiry. Courts evaluate this on a claim-by-claim basis; look to claim focus and the problem the claim addresses.

name: Step 2 — Inventive concept requirement ('significantly more')
description: Even if a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it may be patent-eligible if it contains elements (alone or ordered combination) that constitute an inventive concept sufficient to transform the abstract idea into an application.
guidance: Inventive concept cannot be satisfied by mere recitation of generic computer components, conventional steps, or well-understood activity. The inventive concept can be a specific technical improvement, unconventional combination, solution to a technical problem, or non-generic implementation.

name: USPTO abstract-idea category: Certain methods of organizing human activity
description: Fundamental economic practices, commercial interactions, managing personal behavior, legal obligations (e.g., hedging risk, intermediated settlement, advertising methods, contractual relationships).
guidance: Business-method-type claims often fall into this category and are vulnerable under Step 1 unless tied to a specific technological implementation that meaningfully integrates the exception into a practical application.

name: USPTO abstract-idea category: Mental processes
description: Concepts performed in the human mind, including observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion (e.g., comparing data, categorizing information, forming a diagnosis based on observed symptoms).
guidance: Claims that can be performed mentally or with pen and paper are likely abstract ideas; to survive, the claim should show a technological application or specific machine implementation that adds 'significantly more.'

name: What does NOT constitute an inventive concept (negative indicators)
description: Examples of claim features that courts and examiners have held are insufficient to supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Includes: generic computer implementation (performing the idea on a generic computer); conventional steps or routine processes; mere 'apply it on a computer' language; field-of-use limitations without more; insignificant extra-solution activity such as routine data gathering or post-solution activity. Example: 'a method of hedging risk using a computer' fails because the computer is merely a tool.

name: Specific technical improvements (positive inventive-concept indicator)
description: Claimed features that improve computer functionality, network performance, data security, or system efficiency are strong evidence of an inventive concept.
guidance: Emphasize how the invention changes the way computers operate or solves a computer-technology-specific problem (e.g., reduced latency via dynamic partitioning of queries). Case example: Enfish (self-referential database improved computer functionality).

name: Limitations that solve a technical problem (positive inventive-concept indicator)
description: Claim features specifically tailored to address a technological challenge (e.g., preserving website look-and-feel while displaying third-party content) support eligibility.
guidance: Tie claim language to the technical problem solved rather than the business objective. DDR Holdings is an example where the claimed solution was 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' and thus patent-eligible.

name: Non-generic implementations and particular machines/tools
description: Limitations reciting particular machines, hardware structures, or non-generic implementations that go beyond general-purpose computing.
guidance: Claims that name specific machine architectures, sensor arrangements, protocols, or transformations are harder to dismiss as merely implementing an abstract idea on generic hardware.

name: Software and computer-implemented inventions: focus on technical contribution
description: Software patents face steep scrutiny; claims that simply automate manual processes, organize data, or perform calculations on generic hardware are highly vulnerable under Alice.
guidance: To survive, software claims should be drafted to claim improvements in computer functionality (memory management, processing speed, security, novel user interfaces) and include technical detail in the claim and specification. Enfish and McRO illustrate software wins when technical improvements are claimed.

name: Business methods and fintech: typically vulnerable
description: Business method patents (pricing, transactions, account management, etc.) are frequently rejected as abstract ideas.
guidance: Business-method claims generally must be tied to a specific technological implementation that solves a technical problem to survive. Purely economic practice claims are unlikely to be allowable after Alice and Bilski.

name: Strategy — Frame the invention as a technical improvement
description: When drafting claims, present the invention as solving a specific technical problem or improving technology rather than as a business outcome.
guidance: Use claim language and specification examples that articulate the technical problem, the technical solution, and measurable technical benefits (e.g., reduced latency, improved throughput). Good vs bad claim examples are provided in the guide.

name: Strategy — Include specific technical limitations in claims
description: Avoid generic terms; specify architectures, memory structures, data flows, protocols, or other technical details in claim limitations.
guidance: The more concrete and specific the limitations (rather than 'a processor' or 'a network'), the less likely an examiner or court will treat the claim as a mere abstract idea executed on generic hardware.

name: Strategy — Demonstrate unconventional combinations in the specification
description: Emphasize how claimed element combinations are non-routine and deliver unexpected results.
guidance: Provide disclosure explaining why the combination is different from prior art, how it works, and why it achieves results prior systems could not; support arguments with examples, test data, or declarations where possible.

name: Strategy — Use dependent claims to add implementation detail
description: Draft narrower dependent claims that recite specific implementations, architectures, or parameters to preserve protection if broader independent claims are vulnerable.
guidance: Dependent claims can survive even when broader claims are invalidated; include multiple tiers of specificity in the filing to maximize value and fallback positions.

name: Strategy — Build a strong specification supporting technical achievements
description: The specification should explain the technical problem, prior shortcomings, how the invention solves the problem, and any unexpected results or performance improvements.
guidance: Examiners and courts look to the specification to assess whether claim elements are conventional. Provide concrete examples, implementation details, test results, and explanation of how the claimed features produce technical benefits.

name: USPTO 2019 Revised Guidance — Step 2A Prong One (recitation of judicial exception)
description: Under the USPTO's 2019 guidance, the examiner first determines whether the claim recites a judicial exception (abstract idea/law/natural phenomenon) using the enumerated groupings.
guidance: If the claim does not fall into the enumerated categories, the examiner should not make a §101 rejection. This step formalizes Step 1 and emphasizes use of the USPTO's groupings.

name: USPTO 2019 Revised Guidance — Step 2A Prong Two (practical application/integration)
description: If the claim recites a judicial exception, the examiner evaluates whether the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Practical application examples include improvements to computer or technology functionality, application with a particular machine, transformation of an article to a different state, or other meaningful limitations beyond linking the exception to a technological environment. If integrated, the claim is patent-eligible and analysis ends.

name: USPTO 2019 Revised Guidance — Step 2B (inventive concept evaluation)
description: If the claim does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application under Step 2A, the examiner considers whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more' than the exception itself.
guidance: Examiner must assess whether the additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional; after Berkheimer, factual support is required for assertions of conventionality.

name: Examiner burden after Berkheimer (factual support requirement)
description: Following Berkheimer v. HP, an examiner asserting that claim elements are conventional must provide factual support (references, affidavits, or official notice) rather than conclusory assertions.
guidance: Applicants can challenge unsupported examiner assertions and demand factual evidence. Use declarations or technical evidence to show non-conventionality where possible.

name: Effective responses to a §101/Alice rejection
description: Tactics to overcome examiner rejections under §101/Alice during prosecution.
guidance: Include arguing the claim is not directed to an abstract idea (show it's a specific technological improvement), demonstrating practical application (integration into a machine or transformation), showing unconventional elements with evidence (declarations, prior-art distinctions), amending claims to add technical limitations, and challenging the examiner to meet their burden on conventionality per Berkheimer.

name: Consequences and limits of §101 invalidation
description: If a claim is invalidated under §101, that claim is unenforceable; widespread invalidation can render an entire patent worthless and often cannot be cured by amendment.
guidance: Because §101 invalidity attacks the fundamental concept, narrower claim amendment may not salvage eligibility. This underscores the importance of claiming technical contributions and building a strong specification at the drafting stage.

name: PATENT AT ISSUE
description: Instruction identifying the specific patent(s) asserted in the case and the claims in controversy.
guidance: Tells jurors which patent(s) and claim(s) they must consider; may include reference to patent numbers and claim language.

name: CLAIM INTERPRETATION
description: Instruction regarding how to interpret claim language (the meaning of claim terms) using intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) and extrinsic evidence as appropriate.
guidance: Directs jurors that definitions given in the instructions control and explains that some terms may have special meaning in the patent's context; references case law (e.g., Phillips/Markman).

name: SECTION 112, PARAGRAPH 6 (MEANS-PLUS-FUNCTION)
description: Instruction on treatment of claim elements governed by 35 U.S.C. § 112, ¶ 6 (means-plus-function claim limitations), including how to identify corresponding structure in the specification.
guidance: Explains that for such limitations, the claim covers the corresponding structure described in the specification and equivalents, and instructs jurors on how to apply that rule.

name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT BY 'LITERAL INFRINGEMENT'
description: Instruction that literal infringement occurs when the accused product or method contains every requirement (limitation) of a claim exactly as claimed.
guidance: If even one limitation is missing or different, there is no literal infringement of that claim; jury instructed to compare claim limitations to the accused device/method.

name: LITERAL INFRINGEMENT OF SECTION 112, PARAGRAPH 6 CLAIM REQUIREMENTS
description: Instruction addressing literal infringement for means-plus-function limitations: requires that the accused device include the structure in the specification corresponding to the claimed function (or an equivalent).
guidance: Explains how to determine whether accused device performs the claimed function using the disclosed structure.

name: DIRECT INFRINGEMENT 'UNDER THE DOCTRINE OF EQUIVALENTS'
description: Instruction that infringement can be found if the accused product/method performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result as the claimed limitation, even if not literally identical.
guidance: Provides jury guidance on applying the doctrine of equivalents and highlights the tests and boundaries.

name: LIMITATIONS ON DOCTRINE OF EQUIVALENTS
description: Instruction describing limits on the doctrine of equivalents (e.g., prosecution history estoppel, particularized tests), and that it cannot be used to cover subject matter surrendered during prosecution.
guidance: Explains circumstances where DOE is barred or narrowed by prior claim amendments or disclaimers.

name: BEST MODE
description: Instruction explaining the best mode requirement: if inventor knew a best mode of carrying out the invention at filing, it must be disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Describes legal consequences and how jurors should assess claims that best mode was not disclosed.

name: LOST PROFITS—CAPACITY
description: Subcriterion: the patentee must demonstrate it had the capacity (or could have had) to make and sell the lost units during the damages period.
guidance: Explains evidence that supports or undermines capacity claims (factory capacity, supply chain, ramp-up feasibility).

name: GLOSSARY—TERMS CONTROLLING JURY DELIBERATIONS
description: Glossary definitions of technical and legal terms (e.g., abstract, embodiment, enablement, claim, limitation, prior art, specification) that must be followed and control deliberations.
guidance: Provides short definitions to ensure jurors use consistent meanings; instructs that glossary and instruction definitions control over other characterizations.

name: Return / non-acceptance of illegitimate application documents (Enforcement Rules Article 11)
description: KIPO shall not deem certain application documents legitimate (and will return them) where they fall under specified subparagraphs, including form violations, unclear application type, missing name or applicant code, not written in Korean, missing specification, missing claims when amendment period elapsed, submission by person without domicile/place of business in Korea (except patent administrator), submissions not within designated period, requests for extension for non-extendable periods, requests submitted after certain expiries, documents submitted after termination of proceeding, submissions by persons not entitled, unclear/invalid annexed documents (specific annex forms), or electronic submissions not using KIPO software or in an unprocessable form.
guidance: Lists many concrete grounds (numbered 1–13-2 in the Enforcement Rules excerpt) and notes fees/processing implications; KIPO will return or not accept such documents except where special provisions apply.

name: Transitional after-final practice eligibility under 37 CFR 1.129(a)
description: An applicant in an application (other than reissue or design) pending for at least two years as of June 8, 1995 (taking into account references to earlier-filed applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 and 365(c)) is entitled to have a first submission entered and considered on the merits after a final rejection if the first submission and the fee in § 1.17(r) are filed prior to the filing of an appeal brief and prior to abandonment.
guidance: Finality is automatically withdrawn upon timely filing of the submission and payment of the fee. Applicant may have up to two submissions under 37 CFR 1.129(a) if conditions met. The transitional practice is only available to applications filed on or before June 8, 1995 and is not available for reissue, design applications, or reexamination proceedings. A 'submission' includes IDS, amendments to specification/claims/drawings, new substantive arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability. See MPEP § 706.07(g)(a) and related notes.

name: Request for Continued Examination (RCE) practice and eligibility (37 CFR 1.114)
description: If prosecution in an application is closed, an applicant may request continued examination by filing a submission and the fee set forth in § 1.17(e) prior to the earliest of: (1) payment of the issue fee (unless petition under § 1.313 granted); (2) abandonment; or (3) filing of a notice of appeal to the CAFC or commencement of civil action under 35 U.S.C. 145 or 146 (unless appeal/civil action is terminated).
guidance: Definitions: 'Prosecution is closed' means application is under appeal, last Office action is final (§ 1.113), notice of allowance (§ 1.311), or action that otherwise closes prosecution. A 'submission' includes IDS, amendments to written description/claims/drawings, new arguments, or new evidence; if reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, submission must meet reply requirements of § 1.111. Timely filed submission and fee will withdraw finality and the submission will be entered and considered. Filing an RCE after appeal but prior to decision treats it as request to withdraw appeal and reopen prosecution. An appeal brief or reply brief will not be considered a submission under this section. The provisions do not apply to provisional applications; certain pre-June 8, 1995 utility/plant or international applications; design patents; or patents under reexamination. See 37 CFR 1.114(a)-(e) and MPEP § 706.07(h).

name: Pre-filing/interviews under 37 CFR 1.312 (interviews after allowance)
description: After an application is sent to issue it is technically no longer under the primary examiner's jurisdiction (37 CFR 1.312); an interview involving detailed consideration of claims sought to be entered and discussion of prior art for determining allowability should not be given.
guidance: Requests for interviews on cases where a notice of allowance has been mailed should be granted only with specific approval of the Technology Center Director upon a written showing of extraordinary circumstances.

name: Amendment by instruction to delete/replace/add paragraph (specification amendments)
description: To amend the specification (other than claims), submit an instruction which unambiguously identifies the location to delete one or more paragraphs, replace a deleted paragraph with replacement paragraph(s), or add paragraph(s); include replacement/added paragraph(s) in clean form.
guidance: A separate marked-up version of any replacement paragraph(s) must accompany the amendment on pages separate from the clean replacement, showing all changes relative to the previous version (brackets for deletions, underlining for additions, or equivalent). A marked-up version is not required for a newly added paragraph or a deleted paragraph.

name: Amendment by substitute specification
description: The specification (other than claims) may be amended by submitting an instruction to replace the specification, a substitute specification in compliance with § 1.125(b), and a separate marked-up version showing all changes relative to the previous version.
guidance: Substitute specifications require compliance with § 1.125(b); marked-up version aids examiner review.

name: Preliminary amendment timing and status (37 CFR 1.115)
description: A preliminary amendment is received on or before the mail date of the first Office action under 37 CFR 1.104 (37 CFR 1.115(a)). A preliminary amendment not filed along with the original application does not enjoy the status of part of the original disclosure except in specific limited circumstances (e.g., certain 1.53(b) filings without oath).
guidance: Preliminary amendments should accompany the application or be filed after the application has its application number and filing date. An amendment canceling claims to reduce filing fee should be filed with the application. A preliminary amendment may be disapproved by the Commissioner if it unduly interferes with the preparation of an Office action (37 CFR 1.115(b)). If non-compliant with 1.121, the LIE will send a Notice of Non-Compliant Amendment with a 30-day/one-month time limit and no extensions; failure to comply results in examination without entry of the preliminary amendment.

name: Amendments must be fully responsive to a non-final Office action (37 CFR 1.111)
description: If the Office action after the first examination is adverse in any respect, the applicant must reply and request reconsideration or further examination. To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, the reply must be reduced to writing which distinctly and specifically points out the supposed errors in the examiner's action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. The reply must appear throughout to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specifically pointing out how the claims patentably distinguish them from the references does not comply.

name: Formal vs merits matters and completeness of reply
description: Where reply to a requirement is necessary to further consideration of the claims, or where allowable subject matter has been indicated, a complete reply must either comply with formal requirements or specifically traverse each one not complied with.
guidance: Drawing and specification corrections, presentation of a new oath, etc., are generally formal matters. The line between formal matters and merits is not sharp; examiners may insist on formal corrections prior to indicating allowable subject matter.

name: Marked-up & clean-version requirement for post-March-1-2001 amendments
description: After March 1, 2001, all amendments to the specification, including the claims, must be made by replacement paragraph/section/claim in clean form (without underlining/bracketing) and accompanied by a marked-up version showing changes relative to the immediate previous version.
guidance: This practice eliminates the need for Office handwriting/red ink and hard-to-scan markings. The marked-up version is an aid to the examiner. 'Previous version' means the version of record in the application as originally filed or from a previously entered amendment.

name: Second or subsequent supplemental reply entry/disapproval factors
description: A second (or subsequent) supplemental reply will be entered unless disapproved by the Commissioner. A second (or subsequent) supplemental reply may be disapproved if it unduly interferes with an Office action being prepared in response to the previous reply.
guidance: Factors considered in disapproving include: (i) the state of preparation of an Office action responsive to the previous reply as of the date of receipt of the supplemental reply; and (ii) the nature of any changes to the specification or claims that would result from entry of the supplemental reply.

name: 35 U.S.C. 305 — Claim enlarges scope (ex parte reexamination)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 305 as enlarging the scope of the claim(s) of the patent being reexamined. In 35 U.S.C. 305, it is stated that '[n]o proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of a claim of the patent will be permitted in a reexamination proceeding....'
guidance: A claim 'enlarges the scope' where the claim is broader than any claim of the patent. A claim is broader if it contains within its scope any conceivable product or process which would not have infringed the original patent; broadened if broader in any one respect even though narrower in others. Examiner should identify limitations considered to broaden scope and explain (see MPEP § 2258).

name: Amendments proposed must follow 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j) and 1.52
description: Any proposed amendment to the specification and/or claims in this reexamination proceeding must comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j), must be formally presented pursuant to 37 CFR 1.52(a) and (b), and must contain any fees required by 37 CFR 1.20(c).
guidance: Paragraph may be used in order granting reexamination and/or first Office action to advise patent owner of proper manner of making amendments in reexamination.

name: Claim added/amended but failure to provide claim chart showing written description (interference)
description: Claim [1] has been added or amended in a communication filed on [2] to provoke an interference. Applicant failed to provide a claim chart showing the written description for each claim in the applicant’s specification.
guidance: See 37 CFR 41.202(a)(5) and MPEP § 2304.02(d). Use form paragraph 23.06.05.

name: 35 U.S.C. 314(a) — Claim enlarges scope (inter partes)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 314(a) as enlarging the scope of the claims of the patent being reexamined. 35 U.S.C. 314(a) states that 'no proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of the claims of the patent shall be permitted' in an inter partes reexamination proceeding.
guidance: A claim is broadened if broader in any one respect even though narrower in others. Examiner should identify and explain limitations considered to broaden scope (see MPEP § 2658).

name: Right of Appeal Notice (RAN) — final decision and appeal rules
description: This is a RIGHT OF APPEAL NOTICE (RAN). The decision in this Office action as to the patentability or unpatentability of any original patent claim, any proposed amended claim and any new claim in this proceeding is a FINAL DECISION.
guidance: No amendment can be made in response to the RAN (37 CFR 1.953(c)). No affidavit or other evidence may be submitted after the RAN except as provided by 37 CFR 1.981 or 41.77(b)(1). Each party has thirty days or one month (whichever longer) to file a notice of appeal; cross-appeal rules (14 days after service) apply. Appeals must identify claims appealed and be signed by appropriate party/attorney. Failure to file timely notice of appeal/cross-appeal results in loss of right to appeal; if no party files timely appeal, reexamination prosecution is terminated and Director will issue and publish certificate under 37 CFR 1.997.

name: Definition of a design / distinction from utility
description: A design is the visual ornamental characteristics of an article of manufacture; it is distinct from utility patents which protect functional aspects.
guidance: When evaluating or drafting, focus on appearance/ornamentation rather than function. Functional features that are incidental to ornamentation may not be claimed as design; if the feature's existence is solely a byproduct of function and not intentionally ornamental, a lack-of-ornamentality rejection may apply.

name: Required application elements for design patents
description: Design patent applications consist principally of drawings, drawing descriptions, and a single claim; a brief narrative/specification is optional.
guidance: Ensure the file contains the required elements: high-quality drawings (or photographs when permitted), a claim pointing to the drawing(s), and any necessary drawing descriptions. Although a prose description is optional, drawings are the heart of a design patent and must fully disclose the claimed design.

name: Drawing specifications and visual presentation standards
description: Standards for the content and presentation of drawings that disclose the design (use of solid vs. broken lines, clarity, completeness).
guidance: Solid lines define the claimed design; broken (dotted) lines show unclaimed environmental structure. Broken lines may be used to show visible environmental structure but may not be used to show hidden planes. Drawings must be clear and adequate to fully disclose the claimed ornamental features; follow MPEP detail on views, shading, and reproduction quality.

name: Ornamentality requirement / lack of ornamentality rejection
description: Design must be ornamental — lack of ornamentality is a basis for rejection.
guidance: Ornamentation must have been made for the purpose of being decorative; ornament that is merely a byproduct of a functional design element may be unprotectable. Examiners may reject designs under 'lack of ornamentality' if the claimed appearance is dictated solely by function.

name: Non-obviousness (inventive step) for designs
description: Design patentability requires that the claimed design not be obvious to a designer of ordinary skill (in the applicable design field) in view of the prior art.
guidance: Apply design-specific obviousness principles (focusing on overall visual impression and the relevant body of design prior art). Consideration of analogous art is important: compare to designs of the same or similar articles rather than functional fields.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112 considerations for design patents
description: Written description/definiteness requirements as applied to design patents (i.e., the drawings and claim must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112).
guidance: For designs, the drawings serve as the disclosure that must satisfy 112; the claim must point to the drawings and be definite in what is claimed. Ensure the drawings and any description together reasonably convey the claimed ornamental features.

name: Priority and benefit claims
description: Rules and requirements for claiming priority/benefit to earlier applications in design patent prosecution.
guidance: Follow MPEP guidance when asserting benefit/priority under relevant statutes/treaties; ensure proper referencing of earlier-filed U.S. or foreign applications and that the earlier disclosure supports the claimed design.

name: Essential inquiry: element-by-element equivalence
description: The “essential inquiry” is whether “the accused product or process contain[s] elements identical or equivalent to each claimed element of the patented invention.”
guidance: Equivalence must be analyzed limitation-by-limitation; DOE is like literal infringement in that it is a question of fact. (Warner-Jenkinson Co., Inc. v. Hilton Davis Chem. Co., 520 U.S. 17, 40 (1997); Crown Packaging Tech., Inc. v. Rexam Beverage Can Co., 599 F.3d 1308, 1312 (Fed. Cir. 2009)).

name: Equivalence tests (function-way-result and insubstantial differences)
description: Equivalence is determined by either (1) the “function-way-result” test or (2) the “insubstantial differences” test.
guidance: Under the function-way-result test, the accused product infringes if, on a limitation-by-limitation basis, it “performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way with substantially the same result.” The insubstantial differences test mandates that an element in the accused device is equivalent to a claim limitation if the only differences between the two are insubstantial. (Warner-Jenkinson; Crown Packaging; Honeywell Int’l, Inc. v. Hamilton Sundstrand Corp., 370 F.3d 1131, 1139 (Fed. Cir. 2004)).

name: DOE may apply to numeric-range claim limitations (insubstantially different accused values)
