description: The mere existence of a numerical value or range in a claim, absent more limiting language in the intrinsic record, does not preclude application of the DOE; the key question is whether the accused product has a value that is “insubstantially different” from the claimed range.
guidance: Adams Respiratory: DOE applied where accused AUC was 3493.38 vs claimed “at least 3500” — court vacated summary judgment of no infringement and held DOE can cover specific numeric limits unless intrinsic record indicates otherwise. Look to intrinsic record for limiting language; ask whether accused value is insubstantially different from claimed threshold.

name: DOE cannot be applied if it would vitiate a claim limitation (all-elements rule)
description: Application of the DOE is barred where asserting equivalence would “entirely vitiate a particular claim element.”
guidance: The all-elements rule prevents recasting claims such that the claimed limitation is effectively eliminated. Trading Technologies affirmed that where specification and prosecution history show a claim forbids a feature (e.g., all automatic re-centering), allowing DOE to cover that feature would defeat the invention’s core advantage and thus is barred. Evaluate whether the alleged equivalence would erase the claim element's meaning.

name: Prosecution history estoppel limits DOE when surrendered scope is clear
description: A narrowing amendment (or related prosecution statement) that surrenders claim scope can estop the patentee from asserting DOE for the surrendered subject matter when the scope surrendered is clear.
guidance: Intervet: an amendment substantially related to patentability estopped the patentee from arguing equivalence for ORFs that were distinguished from prior art; but the estoppel may be limited to the specific subject matter surrendered. Analyze the reason for amendment and its relation to the alleged equivalent under Festo and Warner-Jenkinson.

name: Amendment-related estoppel is limited — only certain arguments are foreclosed
description: A narrowing amendment may estop the patentee from particular equivalence arguments but does not necessarily bar all DOE theories; scope of estoppel depends on what was surrendered.
guidance: Intervet example: amendment estopped arguments that ORFs present in PCV-1 were equivalent, but did not estop claims that a pathogenic porcine viral sequence with >99% nucleotide homology to a representative strain was equivalent. Identify precisely what scope was surrendered during prosecution.

name: Tangential relation / tangentiality exception to prosecution history estoppel
description: If the rationale underlying the narrowing amendment bears no more than a tangential relation to the equivalent in question, the amendment cannot reasonably be viewed as surrendering that equivalent.
guidance: Funai Electric: where a limitation was rejected for obviousness, but the nature of the insulating material was not a factor in allowance of other claims, cancelled claims did not surrender access to equivalency for that insulating-material aspect. Examine whether the prosecution rationale directly relates to the accused equivalent or is merely tangential.

name: Prosecution disclaimer through distinguishing prior art requires clear and unmistakable disavowal
description: Statements made during prosecution that distinguish prior art can result in disclaimer of claim scope, but only when the prosecution statements amount to a clear and unmistakable disavowal of claim scope.
guidance: Lazare Kaplan and Omega Eng’g: courts look for explicit, unmistakable statements of disavowal. Spine Solutions: distinguishing prior art by asserting that two anchors did not disclose a single anchor was treated as a clear disclaimer, producing estoppel. Carefully evaluate prosecution arguments and their clarity in limiting claim scope.

name: Claim construction and intrinsic record govern whether DOE may expand literal claim scope
description: The intrinsic record — specification, claim language, and prosecution history — controls claim construction and whether DOE can be applied without vitiating literal limitations.
guidance: Trading Technologies: specification and prosecution statements that the invention addressed moving price axes with a manual re-centering feature informed construction and precluded DOE on automatic re-centering. Note that use of “comprising” does not automatically permit importing unrecited features; intrinsic evidence can limit otherwise broad claim language.

name: Equivalence is a question of fact and must be supported by evidence on a limitation-by-limitation basis
description: Like literal infringement, infringement under the DOE is a question of fact and requires evidence addressing each claim limitation.
guidance: Cases vacating judgments of no DOE infringement often turned on insufficient evidence to prove equivalence limitation-by-limitation. Ensure trial evidence or expert proof addresses function/way/result or insubstantiality for each claimed element (Crown Packaging; Warner-Jenkinson).

name: Ensnarement of the prior art limits DOE
description: DOE is limited where application of equivalence would ensnare the prior art — i.e., extend the claim to cover what was already known.
guidance: Warner-Jenkinson and related cases identify ensnarement as a legal limitation on DOE; when considering equivalence, assess whether the proposed equivalent would improperly cover prior art and thereby be barred.

name: Decision where amended claim identical to previously-notified rejected claim
description: Where the amended claim is identical to the other claim to which a ground of rejection was notified, a decision to reject shall be made.
guidance: If an amended claim duplicates claim language that previously had a ground of rejection notified, treat the amended claim as not overcoming the notified ground and prepare a decision to reject rather than a non-final notice. (See examples where newly added claim identical to an earlier-notified indefinite claim results in a decision to reject.)

name: Non-final rejection: when to issue
description: An examiner may issue 'non-final rejection' regardless of voluntary amendments if it is issued for the first time since the start of examination; where an unamended portion of the specification includes a ground for rejection; or when the ground for rejection is due to the description/claims before amendment rather than being necessitated by amendments.
guidance: Specific points: (1) Issue non-final even if voluntary amendments exist when it's the first notice in examination; (2) If unamended specification portions include grounds, issue non-final; (3) If grounds after amendment are attributable to pre-amendment deficiencies, issue non-final; (4) Grounds arising for reasons other than amendments (e.g., change in foreigner's capacity) are non-final; (5) In ex-officio re-examination or remanded applications, certain grounds that might otherwise be 'necessitated by amendment' may be issued as non-final to avoid unfairly limiting applicants. Examples illustrate amended claim becoming examinable for novelty/inventive step but still treated as non-final when ground existed prior to amendment.

name: Final rejection necessitated by amendment: when to issue
description: Where the ground for rejection arises from amendments made in response to a previously-notified rejection, the examiner shall issue the final rejection necessitated by the amendment. Amendments in response to a prior notice are a prerequisite; final rejection can only be issued when a written amendment has been submitted and a new ground for rejection incurred in that amendment.
guidance: Typical examples: (1) Amendments add new matter or exceed permissible scope of division/conversion; (2) Claim amendments cause grounds regarding novelty or inventive step that did not exist prior to amendment (unless the amended invention is the same as another claim never notified); (3) Newly added claims or claims changed equivalent to new claims that contain novelty/inventive step grounds (unless identical to an uninvolved claim); (4) After amendment, claim becomes examinable for novelty/inventive step due to removal of clarity issues or addition of new matter. Examples show adding element D creating a new need to rely on prior art including D, thereby producing a final rejection necessitated by amendment.

name: Written notice structure and required parts
description: A written notice of grounds for rejection (Examination Report) shall include: 'Claims to be Examined', 'Relevant Provisions regarding Grounds for Rejection', 'Patentable Claims', and 'Specific Grounds for Rejection'. Matters not forming grounds but useful for applicant response may be included in 'Considerations of Amendment'.
guidance: Each part has specific content expectations (see separate rubric entries). The notice should enable the applicant to respond effectively by providing claim numbers, legal provisions, per-claim grounds, and helpful considerations for amendment. Avoid mixing up materials that are intended only as considerations vs actual grounds—if intending to use considerations as grounds, notify again as grounds.

name: Claims to be Examined content
description: 'Claims to be Examined' shall stipulate the number(s) of claims to be examined as of the date when the written notice is prepared.
guidance: Clearly list claim numbers included in the current examination scope so applicants know exactly which claims are under scrutiny in this report.

name: Relevant Provisions regarding Grounds for Rejection content
description: 'Relevant Provisions regarding Grounds for Rejection' specifies claims containing grounds for rejection and the relevant provisions of the Act. If the ground is not directly related to claims, the matters containing the ground for rejection are stated here.
guidance: When an amendment adds new matter or exceeds scope for divisional/converted applications, state that the newly added matters or those falling outside scope are grounds for rejection and cite the statutory provision (e.g., Article numbers).

name: Specific Grounds for Rejection: per-claim specificity and prior-art comparison
description: 'Specific Grounds for Rejection' stipulates specific reasons for notified grounds, and examiners shall specifically state grounds for each claim, identifying which parts of prior art are used and how they compare to claimed features.
guidance: Guidance includes: (i) state grounds per claim (or group claims with practically same grounds); (ii) when comparing to prior art, indicate which parts of reference correspond to claimed features; (iii) if multiple prior art references used, select and describe the closest prior art, state differences between claim and closest reference, and explain how other references supplement those differences considering common general knowledge; (iv) examiner may specify prior art and present assessment regarding inventive step in terms applicants can understand; (v) state grounds for independent and dependent claims separately; dependent claims' grounds generally include all grounds cited in claims they depend on.

name: Use of component comparison table
description: Where necessary for comparing claims and prior art, prepare a component comparison table showing relations between distinguishing technical components of the claimed invention and corresponding features of the prior art reference, including where corresponding features are written in the cited document.
guidance: The table may include the claim element, the corresponding element in each prior art reference, and locations (page/drawing). Examiner may add judgments about differences within or below the table. Examples provided show mapping of A, B, C elements to prior-art counterparts and narrative assessment of obviousness or combination of references.

name: Considerations of Amendment content and limitation
description: 'Considerations of Amendment' states matters not grounds for rejection but useful for applicant response (e.g., examiner opinions on description, reasons for not listing certain claims as patentable, considerations for amendments).
guidance: These are advisory and intended to help applicants respond. If examiner later intends to rely on this content as a ground, the examiner must re-notify it as a formal ground for rejection.

name: Preparation of written decision to reject: structure
description: A written decision to reject is prepared similarly to the written notice of grounds, except 'a matter notified for the ground for rejection' is replaced with 'a matter where the ground for rejection is not overcome'.
guidance: Sections include 'Claims to be Examined', 'Relevant Provisions for Matters Where Grounds for Rejection Not Overcome', 'Patentable Claims', 'Grounds for Decision to Reject', and 'Considerations in Amendment Submission'. If no written argument or amendment was submitted, examiner may not separately state 'Examination Results' and 'Rationale for Decision to Reject'. Newly added claims identical to previously-notified rejected claims may be included among matters where grounds are not overcome.

name: Attention to citing claims when cited claim has ground (Article 42(4) situation)
description: Where a claim cites another claim that has a ground for rejection under Article 42(4), the examiner must pay special attention to whether the citing claim still has such a ground. If so, state that the citing claim has the same ground for patent rejection as the cited claim. If the cited claim only violates manner of describing claims (Article 42(8)), then state only the cited claim has that ground.
guidance: Explicitly analyze whether dependence transmits the ground for rejection; state conclusions clearly in the notice to avoid applicant confusion.

name: Handling multiple groups of inventions and unity-of-invention objections
description: When examining applications with two or more groups of inventions, the examiner normally considers patentability for inventions in at least one group. When pointing out a violation of unity of invention, indicate claims in another group rather than the group already evaluated for patentability. Include claims without grounds under 'Patentable Claims' among evaluated groups; if novelty/inventive step rejections exist, notify those grounds together with unity objections for the other groups.
guidance: If necessary to notify lack of unity first for efficiency, state in 'Considerations of Amendment' that patentability tests were not performed for the unexamined group and do not include those claims in 'Patentable Claims'. This clarifies scope and prevents misleading applicants about which claims were fully examined.

name: Disclosure of prior art documents: citation requirement and standard
description: When preparing grounds for rejection related to a claim's technical subject matter, the examiner shall cite supporting documents for the rationale. Disclosure methods for information on prior art documents shall comply with WIPO Standard ST.14.
guidance: Always cite supporting prior art documents; follow WIPO ST.14 for disclosure methods not detailed here. Provide sufficient bibliographic detail so applicants can locate and understand the cited references.

name: Ethical/framing concern: protection racket characterization
description: “Ultimately, its business still boils down to a protection racket. An enlightened one, perhaps, but still a protection racket."
guidance: Consider ethical and reputational implications of paying recurring fees to avoid claims—whether the service is defensive insurance or functionally similar to extortion. This may influence corporate policy and public perception.

name: Step 2B: Do additional elements amount to an inventive concept?
description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
guidance: Answer by first identifying whether any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) are recited beyond the judicial exception(s), then evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)). Use the Supreme Court considerations introduced in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h). This evaluation is not a weighing test — it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant’s invention and whether the additional elements encompass an inventive concept.

name: Carry over findings from Step 2A Prong Two
description: Examiners should carry over identification of the additional element(s) in the claim from Step 2A Prong Two and carry over conclusions from Step 2A Prong Two on considerations discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(c),(e),(f),(h).
guidance: Re-evaluate any additional element or combination previously considered to be 'insignificant extra-solution activity' under MPEP § 2106.05(g), because a new finding that an element is unconventional or more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity may change the Step 2B determination. Also evaluate whether elements are other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or simply append such activities at a high level of generality per MPEP § 2106.05(d).

name: Outcome determination at Step 2B (Pathway C or rejection)
description: If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more than the exception itself (no inventive concept), the claim is not eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101; if the claim as a whole does amount to significantly more than the exception (there is an inventive concept), the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C.
guidance: Step 2B concludes the eligibility analysis. Use the flowchart in MPEP § 2106, subsection III to determine whether to issue an ineligibility rejection (see MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections).

name: Consider whether the claim improves computer functioning or other technology
description: In determining patent eligibility, examiners should consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.'
guidance: This consideration is the search for a technological solution to a technological problem. It should be evaluated at Step 2A Prong Two and at Step 2B (and in streamlined analysis where appropriate). Relevant precedents include Alice, DDR Holdings, Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Amdocs, and others. Improvements may support finding an inventive concept; mere use of a computer as a tool typically does not.

name: Specification must provide a technical explanation of the asserted improvement
description: If it is asserted that the invention improves upon conventional functioning of a computer or other technology, a technical explanation as to how to implement the invention should be present in the specification.
guidance: The disclosure must provide sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly recite the improvement, but the improvement must be apparent to a person of ordinary skill. Conclusory assertions of improvement without necessary detail are insufficient (see McRO v. Affinity Labs contrast).

name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement; evaluate claim as a whole
description: After the examiner has determined the specification discloses an improvement, the claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement.
guidance: The claim must include components or steps that provide the improvement described in the specification. The claim does not need to recite the improvement in 'thereby' language; the full scope under the broadest reasonable interpretation should be considered. Evaluate the claim 'as an ordered combination' and avoid oversimplifying the claims by ignoring specific requirements of individual steps (see Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec, McRO).

name: Improvement can be provided by additional elements alone or combined with the judicial exception
description: The judicial exception alone cannot provide the improvement; the improvement can be provided by one or more additional elements or by additional elements in combination with the recited judicial exception.
guidance: Analyze the claim as a whole to determine whether the additional elements (alone or in combination with the exception) supply the inventive concept (references: Diamond v. Diehr; Finjan v. Blue Coat).

name: Distinguish true computer-functionality improvements from mere use of computers
description: For computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities or instead invokes computers merely as a tool.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed invention provides a specific implementation or technical solution (e.g., data structure, distributed architecture, particular server structure) rather than generic post-hoc recitation of computers. Relevant cases and example categories that courts have found may show improvement include Enfish, DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Research Corp. Techs., Amdocs v. Openet, Visual Memory v. NVIDIA, TLI Communications, Apple v. Ameranth, Finjan, Core Wireless, Data Engine Techs., Ancora Tech. The examiner should assess whether the claim covers a particular solution to a problem rather than merely the idea of a solution.

name: Examples that may not show improvement in computer-functionality
description: Certain claim characteristics the courts have indicated may be insufficient to show improvement in computer-functionality.
guidance: Examples include: (i) generating menus with functionally claimed features (Ameranth); (ii) accelerating processing only by relying on general-purpose computer speed (FairWarning); (iii) mere automation of manual processes using a generic computer (Credit Acceptance; LendingTree non-precedential); (iv) recording/transmitting/archiving digital images using conventional tech without technical detail (TLI Communications); (v) affixing a barcode without technical details of generation/processing (Secured Mail Solutions); (vi) mere instructions to display two sets of information without how to achieve it (Interval Licensing); (vii) improving information stored by a database without improving database functionality (BSG Tech v. BuySeasons); (viii) arranging GUI information to assist traders without technical improvement (Trading Technologies).

name: Method claims must require computer implementation to show computer improvement
description: In order for a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation; a claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally cannot be said to improve computer technology.
guidance: If the claimed process can be practiced verbally or mentally, or all steps can be performed mentally by a skilled artisan, it does not improve computer technology (see Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics; RecogniCorp v. Nintendo).

name: Required petition content
description: The petition for CBM review must include an identification of the real parties in interest, the claims being challenged along with explanations of grounds of unpatentability for those claims, copies of evidence relied upon and an explanation of the relevance of that evidence, along with payment of a fee.
guidance: Complete and well-supported petitions should identify parties, pinpoint claims, articulate grounds, submit supporting evidence with relevance explanations, and include required fees to avoid procedural defects.

name: Institution standard (likelihood of unpatentability)
description: Upon review of a requesting petition and any preliminary response by the patent owner, the PTAB will determine whether it is more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable.
guidance: This 'more likely than not' standard is the threshold for instituting a full CBM review; petitions should be drafted to meet that evidentiary showing.

name: Issue narrowing and notice of grounds at institution
description: The PTAB may narrow issues at this time, and will provide a decision detailing the grounds of unpatentability that will be of issue in the proceeding.
guidance: The institution decision identifies which grounds/claims proceed to trial; expect potential limiting of issues and tailor subsequent strategy accordingly.

name: Step 1: Statutory category (machine/process/etc.)
description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (e.g., process, machine). The examples check Step 1 first (e.g., the claim is a process or a machine) and record Step 1: Yes when satisfied.
guidance: Verify claim recites a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition). This is the threshold procedural check before determining whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception.

name: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea)?
description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (e.g., fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, or mental processes). Example: fraud prevention by verifying a customer's identity is characterized as a long‑prevalent business practice and thus an abstract idea.
guidance: Point to the language of the claim that describes the abstract concept (e.g., obtaining and comparing customer information, inventory management, data collection and storage). Compare claim concept to ideas courts have previously found abstract (e.g., intermediated settlement, risk hedging, content extraction).

name: Step 2B: Does the claim recite 'significantly more' (an inventive concept)?
description: After identifying an abstract idea, analyze whether any element or combination of elements transforms the claim into a patent-eligible application by providing significantly more than the abstract idea (an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Consider additional limitations individually and in combination. Identify whether the limitations are conventional/generic or whether they represent a specific, non‑conventional and non‑generic implementation that improves a technical field (citing Diehr, Bascom, DDR as positive examples).

name: Insignificant pre‑solution activity / mere data gathering
description: Claim steps that are high-level data gathering (e.g., obtaining customer-specific information from a bank card) may be considered insignificant pre-solution activity and not contribute to an inventive concept.
guidance: Label obvious data-collection steps as mere inputs necessary to use the abstract idea rather than technical improvements. Such steps, when recited at a high level, usually do not transform the claim into eligible subject matter.

name: Non‑conventional combination or sequence can provide an inventive concept
description: A combination of conventional elements may provide significantly more if the combination operates in a non‑conventional and non‑generic way to solve a technical problem (e.g., sequence of ATM random code, mobile-device generated encrypted-image, ATM decryption/analysis to prevent skimmed card fraud).
guidance: Assess whether the claimed combination sets up a specific sequence of events or a particular technical implementation that addresses unique problems and differs from routine/conventional sequences (Bascom/DDR style reasoning). If so, treat the combination as a practical implementation that can supply 'significantly more' (Step 2B: Yes).

name: Claims focused on specific improvements in computer functionality (Enfish) may be eligible
description: Claims that are directed to a specific improvement in how a computer operates or a technological improvement in computer functionality can be patent-eligible, even if implemented on a computer.
guidance: Distinguish claims that improve computer functionality (Enfish) from claims that merely use computers as tools. If the claim's focus is a technological improvement in computer behavior, that can weigh in favor of eligibility.

name: Drafting/docketing practice: clarify reasons for eligibility or ineligibility in the record
description: Although an examiner is not required to provide an explanation of eligibility, the record is enhanced if clarifying remarks are provided to point to the reason for eligibility or to explain why additional limitations are conventional when rejecting.
guidance: If a claim is eligible, point to the combination of elements used in the non‑conventional implementation. If rejecting, identify the abstract idea and explain why additional limitations are conventional or generic (e.g., why a processor or memory performs only routine functions).

name: Claim interpretation: give broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification
description: For recently filed applications under examination, claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Use plain meaning of claim terms unless the specification provides special definitions. This interpretive standard affects whether limitations are read narrowly enough to supply an inventive concept.

name: Compare to precedent when characterizing abstractness or inventive concept
description: Use Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedents (e.g., Alice, CyberSource, Diehr, Bascom, Enfish, Electric Power, DDR, Content Extraction, TLI Communications, Digitech) to determine whether a claim's idea is similar to concepts previously found abstract or whether limitations are analogous to prior eligible claims.
guidance: Explicitly state which case(s) the claim is similar to and why (e.g., similarity to CyberSource for obtaining/comparing intangible data for fraud detection). Use precedential analogies to justify Step 2A or Step 2B conclusions.

name: Inventory-management and imaging claims: evaluate as data-collection/recognition concepts
description: Claims that recite capturing images, extracting features (character and contour), forming feature vectors, classifying, tracking across overlapping cameras, reconstructing 3‑D coordinates, and updating inventory records are analyzed as concepts of data collection/recognition and may be directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: When such claims merely use generic cameras, models, and processors for recognition/tracking without a specific technical improvement in imaging/computer vision, treat them as abstract (Step 2A) and evaluate additional limitations for conventionality. Show why memory/processor recitations are generic and do not supply an inventive concept unless they amount to a specific technological improvement.

name: Scope of appeal (from which determinations appeal must be taken)
description: An appeal or cross appeal must be taken from all the rejections of the claims in a Right of Appeal Notice which the patent owner proposes to contest or from all the determinations favorable to patentability (including any final determination not to make a proposed rejection) in a RAN which a requester proposes to contest.
guidance: A requester appealing an allowance must identify each previously proposed rejection it intends to contest — merely appealing the allowance is insufficient. Questions unrelated to merits may be required to be settled before an appeal is decided.

name: Appellant's brief required contents (37 CFR 41.67(c))
description: The appellant’s brief must contain, under appropriate headings and in order: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals/interferences/trials; (iii) Status of claims; (iv) Status of amendments; (v) Summary of claimed subject matter (concise explanation referring to specification columns/lines and drawings; identify means-plus-function elements per 35 U.S.C.112(f) with corresponding structure/material/acts); (vi) Issues to be reviewed on appeal; (vii) Argument (contentions on each issue with citations); (viii) Claims appendix; (ix) Evidence appendix; (x) Related proceedings appendix; (xi) Certificate of service.
guidance: Each item must be present and complete. For (v), for dependent claims argued separately, identify means/step-plus-function items and corresponding disclosure with page/line and drawing references. The evidence appendix must contain only evidence entered into the record (no reference to unentered evidence). A brief shall not include any new or non-admitted amendment/affidavit/evidence.

name: Prohibition on including new or non-admitted amendments or evidence in briefs
description: An appellant’s or respondent’s brief shall not include any new or non-admitted (non-entered) amendment, or any new or non-admitted affidavit or other evidence (37 CFR 41.67(c)(2) and 41.68(b)(2)).
guidance: See 37 CFR 41.63 and 1.116 for the narrow circumstances under which amendments or affidavits/evidence filed after filing an appeal may be admitted (e.g., cancellation of claims that do not affect scope; reopening prosecution under 41.77(b)(1)).

name: Procedure and consequences when brief is non-compliant
description: If a filed brief does not comply with 37 CFR 41.67(a) and (c), appellant will be notified of reasons and given a non-extendable one-month period to file an amended brief. Failure to correct defects results in dismissal of the appeal; if an appellant brief is late, respondent brief will be placed in file but marked 'not entered' and not considered.
guidance: Where all parties who filed appeals fail to timely file an appellant brief and fee within the time allowed, the reexamination proceeding is terminated by NIRC and a certificate is issued indicating claim status at time of appeal.

name: Argument presentation and waiver rules
description: Argument must present the appellant’s contentions on each issue with citation of statutes, regulations, authorities, and parts of the record. Each issue must be treated under a separate heading. If the patent owner groups multiple claims under a ground rather than arguing them separately, the Board may select a single claim from the group to decide the appeal; failure to separately argue grouped claims constitutes waiver of separate patentability arguments.
guidance: A statement merely pointing out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument. Arguments or authorities not included in the brief (or in permitted respondent/rebuttal briefs) will be refused consideration unless good cause is shown. Oral argument will not cure deficiencies in the brief.

name: Respondent brief limitations and required contents (37 CFR 41.68)
description: A respondent’s brief must be limited to issues raised in the appellant brief to which the respondent brief is directed. It must be signed, accompanied by the requisite fee, and contain under appropriate headings: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals/interferences/trials; (iii) Status of claims (accept or dispute appellant’s statement specifying errors with particularity if disputed); (iv) Status of amendments (accept/dispute); (v) Summary of claimed subject matter (accept/dispute); (vi) Issues to be reviewed on appeal (accept/dispute; may include counter-statement); (vii) Argument (accept/dispute appellant contentions with citations); (viii) Evidence appendix; (ix) Related proceedings appendix; (x) Certificate of service.
guidance: A requester’s respondent brief may not address any brief of any other requester. A respondent brief shall not include any new or non-admitted amendment, affidavit, or other evidence.

name: Admission of amendments, affidavits, declarations, or exhibits after appeal filing (37 CFR 41.63)
description: Amendments filed after filing an appeal that cancel claims may be admitted where such cancellation does not affect the scope of any other pending claim. All other amendments filed after filing an appeal will not be admitted except as permitted where patent owner reopens prosecution under 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1). Affidavits or other evidence filed after filing an appeal will not be admitted except as permitted where prosecution is reopened under 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1).
guidance: If the examiner desires an amendment or evidence during appeal stage, the examiner must reopen prosecution, accept the amendment/evidence for entry, permit timely comment by third-party requester, and then issue a new Action Closing Prosecution (ACP) (see MPEP §2673.01).

name: Effect of failing to file timely appeal-related papers
description: Where a party fails to file a timely notice of appeal or cross appeal, that party may no longer file an appellant brief to appeal a claim determination adverse to that party. If all parties who filed an appeal fail to timely file an appellant brief and fee, the reexamination proceeding is terminated and an NIRC is issued.
guidance: Ignoring or acquiescing in any rejection or determination (including correctable formal matters) will invite dismissal of the appeal as to the appropriate party. Prosecution is considered terminated as of the date of dismissal of all appeals.

name: ROUGE-1 (R-1)
description: ROUGE-1 — unigram overlap metric (Lin, 2004).
guidance: Measures surface-level overlap (recall/precision/F1) of single tokens between generated and reference claims; reported as R-1 in experiments.

name: LLM-as-a-judge: technical precision
description: Technical Precision: 'Does the candidate claim provide precise definitions and clear characterizations of technical features, compared to the referenced claim?' (Table 12).
guidance: Scored 1–10. Evaluators judge whether wording is technically precise (measure/thresholds not numeric) and aligns with reference specificity and tolerances.

name: LLM-as-a-judge: specificity
description: Specificity: 'Does the candidate claim explicitly describe technical features in concrete detail rather than using overly abstract or generalized language, compared to the referenced claim?' (Table 12).
guidance: Scored 1–10. Penalize vague/generalized language; reward concrete, reference-aligned descriptions of components/features.

name: LLM-as-a-judge: clarity
description: Clarity: 'Is the candidate claim logically coherent, unambiguous, and clearly understandable, compared to the referenced claim?' (Table 12).
guidance: Scored 1–10. Measures logical coherence and unambiguity; noted that GPT-4o achieved the highest clarity in experiments despite sometimes omitting key elements.

name: LLM-as-a-judge: dependency structure
description: Dependency Structure: 'Does the candidate claim exhibit correct hierarchical dependency relationships, compared to the referenced claim?' (Table 12).
guidance: Scored 1–10. Evaluates correct use of independent/dependent claim relationships and references (e.g., proper referring language and hierarchy).

name: LLM-as-a-judge: legal terminology
description: Legal Terminology: 'Does the candidate claim correctly and professionally use patent-standard legal terms and expressions, compared to the referenced claim?' (Table 12).
guidance: Scored 1–10. Judges professional/legal term usage (e.g., 'characterised in that', 'comprising') and adherence to jurisdictional drafting conventions (EPO vs USPTO).

name: LLM-as-a-judge: scope of protection
description: Scope of Protection: 'Does the candidate claim achieve an appropriate scope of protection, compared to the referenced claim?' (Table 12).
guidance: Scored 1–10. Measures whether claim wording yields an appropriate (not overly narrow or overly broad) coverage relative to the reference; considers legal drafting conventions across jurisdictions.

name: Difficult-subset classification (ROUGE-L threshold)
description: Difficult subset creation: a patent is 'easy' if at least one sentence in the description has an ROUGE-L score above 0.6 with the first claim; otherwise it is classified as 'difficult'.
guidance: Threshold ROUGE-L > 0.6 chosen because models generally struggle to exceed ROUGE-L 0.6 in prior work. Used to separate samples amenable to near-verbatim extraction from those requiring true generation/abstraction.

name: Dataset source/version preference: granted (B-kind) EPO patents and retention rules
description: Keep granted versions (B codes) from the EPO when available; the EPD dataset contains granted patents directly sourced from the EPO to ensure high-quality, legally validated claims. If no related application is provided, keep the granted version. Remove patent files if required fields are missing.
guidance: Rationale: granted claims are finalized and legally approved (avoid canceled/application-stage claims). Data processing: retrieve via OPS XML, require presence of required fields, convert to structured JSON; samples missing required fields are discarded.

name: Qualitative anti-patterns and desirable outputs for generated claims
description: Qualitative criteria gleaned from analysis: desirable outputs retain key technical features (e.g., 'rechargeable', 'manually activate'), reduce redundancy, align structure and scope with gold claims; anti-patterns include omission of key technical details, redundancy across dependent claims, and introduction of extraneous features not present in the gold claim.
guidance: Use qualitative comparison with gold claims to assess model behavior; examples and analyses provided in Section 5.3 and Appendix Table 12 illustrate common errors (omissions, redundancy, added features) and improvements after fine-tuning on EPD.

name: §101 Patent-Eligible Subject Matter for Chemical Compounds
description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 101, a composition of matter patent covers any novel combination of chemical elements or compounds with a definite structural identity, and the composition must be non-naturally occurring or modified to confer markedly different characteristics from its natural form.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed composition is 'made by man' (Diamond v. Chakrabarty) and not a product of nature (Mayo v. Prometheus; Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics). Natural laws and naturally occurring substances are ineligible; laboratory-created modifications (e.g., cDNA) may be eligible. Practitioners should perform a fact-intensive analysis of structural distinctiveness to assess § 101 risk during prosecution and post-grant challenges.

name: Myriad cDNA Distinction and Biological Composition Claiming
description: Myriad established that naturally occurring DNA sequences are products of nature ineligible under § 101 while preserving eligibility for complementary DNA (cDNA) because it is a laboratory-created molecule lacking non-coding intron sequences.
guidance: For gene therapies and nucleic acid therapeutics, structure claims should focus on engineered molecules (e.g., cDNA or otherwise modified sequences) rather than naturally occurring sequences. Biotech patent counsel should evaluate whether a proposed biological composition achieves the structural distinctiveness required to survive USPTO examination and post-grant validity challenges.

name: Written Description Requirement (§112(a))
description: The specification must demonstrate the inventor possessed the full scope of the claimed invention at filing; disclosure of representative species and structural features common to the genus is required as an independent obligation from enablement (Ariad).
guidance: When drafting genus or broad composition claims, ensure the specification includes representative examples and identifies structural features shared across the claimed members. Broad claims that extend beyond supported examples risk invalidation for lack of written description. Counsel should align claim breadth to the specification's exemplified embodiments from the outset.

name: Enablement Requirement (§112) for Broad Genus Claims
description: Enablement requires that the specification teach how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; failure to enable the full claimed scope can invalidate broad biological and pharmaceutical composition claims (e.g., Amgen Inc. v. Sanofi).
guidance: Assess whether practicing the full breadth of claims would require substantial additional experimentation. If so, narrow claims or add exemplar embodiments and technical guidance to satisfy enablement. Work with prosecution specialists to match claim scope to the disclosure and experimental support.

name: Markush Group Drafting Criteria
description: Markush claim drafting allows a closed-list phrasing (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of') to define a class of chemical substituents so a single claim can cover multiple structural variants of a chemical compound.
guidance: Members of a Markush group must share a single structural feature essential to the activity of all compounds in the group. Draft Markush groups with structural coherence and ensure the specification provides adequate support (representative species) for the listed members; overly broad Markush groups that include variants not exemplified may face written description and enablement challenges.

name: Balancing Markush Breadth with Specification Support
description: Practitioners must balance the breadth of the defined Markush group against supporting examples because extending to variants not exemplified may trigger Written Description challenges.
guidance: Limit Markush lists to structurally coherent choices and provide representative examples across the chemical space. Consider dependent claims and exemplar embodiments to shore up support for broader independent Markush claims.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents and Prosecution History Estoppel in Markush Context
description: The Doctrine of Equivalents interacts with Markush boundaries because prosecution history estoppel may bar equivalents for variants deliberately excluded from the closed list during examination.
guidance: Be mindful during claim amendments and argument that narrowing a Markush list can create estoppel that limits later equivalence arguments. Preserve arguments and record where possible to avoid unintended estoppel consequences.

name: Hatch-Waxman ANDA Litigation Considerations
description: In ANDA litigation, a generic manufacturer will often challenge pharmaceutical composition patents under §§ 101, 102, 103, and 112 while contesting claim scope via Markman proceedings; bioequivalence data from FDA approval can be used to argue the generic product falls within the literal scope or that a claim is anticipated.
guidance: Patent holders should prepare for simultaneous multi-issue invalidity attacks and claim construction disputes. Retain counsel experienced in both chemistry and pharmaceutical litigation and coordinate patent strategy with regulatory and bioequivalence evidence considerations.

name: Prior Art Search and Chemical Space Mapping for Claim Drafting
description: A robust prosecution strategy begins with a prior art search mapping the relevant chemical space to determine the minimum structural differentiation required for novelty and non-obviousness.
guidance: Use comprehensive prior art and chemical space analysis to set the baseline for how broadly to claim structures. Identify distinguishing structural features that confer patentability and craft claims around those minimum differentiators.

name: Claim Drafting Practices for Portfolio Protection
description: Independent claims should be drafted at the broadest structurally supportable scope using Markush formats while dependent claims should anchor preferred embodiments with the strongest experimental support; continuation applications can build a layered claim portfolio as data develops.
guidance: Draft broad independent claims that are adequately supported and follow with narrower dependent claims backed by experimental data to preserve fallback positions. Use continuations strategically to pursue multiple claim scopes as development and data evolve. Consider patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. § 156 to compensate for regulatory delays.

name: PTAB IPR Defense Strategies for Composition Patents
description: When challenged via inter partes review before the PTAB, effective defenses include filing a preliminary response challenging the petitioner's claim construction before institution, and submitting expert declarations contextualizing the composition's structural novelty within the relevant scientific field.
guidance: Prepare expert evidence early, challenge claim constructions at the institution stage, and consider claim amendments under 37 C.F.R. § 42.121 to add structural limitations that distinguish asserted prior art. Evaluate licensing or settlement options to preserve commercial exclusivity when claims narrow during PTAB proceedings.

name: Use of Claim Amendments under 37 C.F.R. § 42.121
description: Claim amendments during PTAB proceedings can add structural limitations distinguishing the composition from asserted prior art.
guidance: Assess whether proposed amendments will preserve patentable scope and commercial value; amendments can avoid institution or defeat grounds but may narrow enforceable rights. Coordinate technical expert input to craft defensible amendment language that maps to the specification.

name: Coordinated Lifecycle Strategy (Prosecution, Freedom-to-Operate, PTAB Readiness)
description: Strategic prosecution and enforcement requires coordinating claim drafting, prosecution history management, freedom-to-operate analysis, and PTAB litigation readiness into a unified lifecycle strategy to protect long-term exclusivity.
guidance: Anticipate litigation risks during initial drafting—failures to foresee challenges can permanently narrow commercially valuable scope. Integrate freedom-to-operate analyses, prosecution choices, and PTAB/ANDA defense planning when building and maintaining a composition-of-matter portfolio.

name: Specific elements that may mislead the public
description: The public may be misled by advertising or promotional activities, particularly with respect to: the manufacturing process of a product; the suitability of a product or service for a given purpose; the quality, quantity or other characteristic of a product or service; the geographical origin of a product or service; the conditions under which a product or service is proposed or supplied; and the price of a product or service or its method of calculation.
guidance: Enumerates typical factual claims that, if false or misleading, can constitute unfair competition.

name: Application contents — mandatory documents
description: The file shall contain: (a) an application for registration addressed to the Director-General bearing applicant’s name, address, nationality and habitual residence where different; (b) document proving payment of required fees; (c) a short and precise description of the layout design with sufficient information on how best to exploit it known to the creator on the date of deposit and priority date if claimed; (d) powers of applicant’s agent where appropriate, a copy or drawing of the layout design together with information defining the electronic function intended; applicant may omit manufacturing-method parts if submitted parts suffice for identification; (e) date of first commercial exploitation anywhere in world or statement exploitation not begun; and (f) particulars establishing entitlement to protection under Article 4.
guidance: Both formal and technical information required; applicant may omit manufacturing method detail provided identification is still possible; proof of fee payment is mandatory (see Article 11).

name: Examination of applications limited to formal requirements
description: The Organization shall examine each application to determine whether it complies with the requirements of Articles 2 and 10 above, without carrying out an examination of originality, of the applicant’s right to protection or of the correctness of the statements made in the application.
guidance: No substantive examination of originality or entitlement—Organization performs formal/admissibility check only; substantive disputes handled via opposition, claim, or court actions.

name: Statutory basis for reissue (35 U.S.C. §251) — grounds required
description: The error must cause the patent to be 'deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid, by reason of: (1) a defective specification or drawing, OR (2) by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than he had a right to claim in the patent.'
guidance: Reissue is available only where the error fits within these statutory categories (defective disclosure or incorrect scope of claim rights).

name: Claims are too narrow or too broad
description: One common reason to file reissue is that the claims in the issued patent are too narrow or too broad.
guidance: Broadening reissues are time-limited (see two-year window); narrowing reissues can be used to correct overbroad claims at any time during the patent term.

name: Failure to claim or incorrectly claimed foreign priority
description: Failure to claim, or incorrectly claiming, foreign priority in the issued patent is a common reason for reissue.
guidance: Use reissue to correct priority/priority-chain errors that affect entitlement dates or claim scope when attributable to applicant error.

name: Distinction: Certificate of Correction vs Reissue
description: Certificate of Correction fixes non-substantive errors (typos, minor); Reissue is for substantive errors. Certificates do not change scope and are low cost; reissue can change scope and requires full re-examination and is more expensive.
guidance: Use certificate of correction for PTO or applicant clerical errors that do not affect scope or validity; use reissue for substantive corrections that may alter claim scope or validity and require new examination.

name: Scope changes allowed in reissue (versus certificate)
description: Reissue allows scope changes (broadening or narrowing); Certificate of Correction does not allow scope changes.
guidance: Because reissue may change claim scope, it triggers full re-examination and strategic/legal consequences (e.g., intervening rights, recapture).

name: Two-year window for broadening reissue
description: A broadening reissue application must be applied for within 2 years from the grant of the original patent.
guidance: If seeking broader claims, the two-year limit is jurisdictional; missing it prevents filing a broadening reissue (narrowing reissue remains available thereafter).

name: Timing for narrowing reissue
description: Narrowing reissue can occur at any time during the patent term.
guidance: There is no two-year limitation for narrowing reissues; they can be filed throughout the patent term to correct overbroad claims or other narrowing corrections.

name: Intervening rights limiting remedies
description: Defendants who used the broadened scope before reissue may have intervening rights that limit the patentee's remedies.
guidance: When broadening claims via reissue, consider that parties who practiced the claimed invention between original grant and reissue may obtain limiting rights that reduce available relief for infringement.

name: Strategic considerations and risks of filing reissue
description: Reissue creates risk that other claims will be invalidated; all claims, not just amended ones, are subject to re-examination; public access to file makes reissue strategy visible to competitors; often used to expand claim scope to capture infringers not previously covered; consider if continuation application or reexamination is a better alternative.
guidance: Balance potential benefits of correcting or broadening claims against risks: full re-exam, exposure of strategy, possible loss of claim coverage, intervening rights, and expense. Evaluate alternatives (continuation, ex parte reexamination, etc.) before filing.

name: Two-column chart structure
description: In each, typically, there are two columns: the left column contains the language of the patent claim under analysis, separated into the successive limitations (e.g., elements or steps, integers, parts) of the claim; the right column contains the information relating to the claim element at its left.
guidance: Use a table with the claim broken into discrete limitations on the left and corresponding evidence/analysis on the right. This structure is described as a 'convenient and effective means for analyzing and presenting information regarding a patent claim.'

name: Break claim into successive limitations / integers
description: Break down the claim into suitable integers (i.e. separate parts) in order to explain a case on infringement with reference to specific elements of the alleged infringing product or process.
guidance: The UK IPEC Guide and MPEP examples recommend parsing the claim into discrete limitations so each can be addressed individually in the chart; necessary when explaining infringement or invalidity to a court or examiner.

name: Infringement chart: map each limitation to accused product/process (all elements test)
description: An infringement chart that allegedly shows how the product or process accused of infringement contains each claim element, thereby satisfying the all elements test for infringement.
guidance: Typically prepared by the plaintiff/patent owner. For each claim limitation show the corresponding part/feature/step in the accused device or process (and cite evidence, figures, or testimony) so that every limitation is accounted for.

name: Chart of references (invalidity): map limitations to prior art passages
description: A chart of references (such earlier patents and magazine articles) that allegedly show the invalidity of the patent because of anticipation or obviousness.
guidance: Typically prepared by the defendant/accused infringer. For each claim limitation, identify and quote passages from prior art that teach that limitation; use precise citations (e.g., patent column/line and figure) and split quotations to correspond to specific limitations when appropriate (as in the MPEP example).

name: Claim interpretation chart: cite specification/technical literature for meanings
description: A claim interpretation chart that shows, for each claim element, passages in the patent specification or in technical literature that show the proper meaning or interpretation that should be given to the language of the claim.
guidance: Either party may prepare this chart. For disputed claim terms, collect intrinsic (specification, prosecution history) and extrinsic (technical literature, dictionaries) support and place the relevant citations next to the claim limitation to support the proposed construction.

name: Patent-eligibility (Alice) / abstract-idea mapping charts
description: Claim charts may also be used to support an argument that a patent claims ineligible subject matter, such as a law of nature or a conventional business practice. In the right column, the steps or elements of a well known business concept or a way of organizing human activity are listed.
guidance: Use the chart to demonstrate that each claimed step corresponds to routine human activity or a well-known business practice (often illustrating 'do it with a computer' recitation). Courts (e.g., in Alice and Walker Digital v. Google) have used such charts to show claims are directed to abstract ideas and thus ineligible absent an inventive implementation.

name: Include diagrams / figures to show the accused device contains recited elements
description: These charts often contain diagrams of the relevant elements, to show that the device contains the element as recited in the claim.
guidance: Where possible, annotate or reference figures/diagrams of the accused product or prior art to visually tie claim limitations to physical structures or drawings. Courts and practitioner examples commonly include figures and callouts.

name: Precision of quotations and citations (split quotations per limitation)
description: Parse quotations as carefully as needed; split the corresponding quotation into parts corresponding to each limitation.
guidance: The MPEP example demonstrates splitting a prior-art quotation into parts aligned with claim limitations and providing precise citations (e.g., 'col. 6, lines 2–3; Figure 3'). Precise citation and alignment prevents overbroad or ambiguous mappings and aids examiners/courts.

name: Comprehensiveness: cover every claim element and corresponding evidence
description: Charts should address each claim limitation so a court/examiner can determine whether every claim element is present in the accused product/process or taught by prior art.
guidance: Failure to map even one limitation can undermine an infringement or invalidity argument. The Walker Digital example shows courts scrutinize whether every step/limitation is performed or taught when assessing invalidity or preemption concerns.

name: Select chart type for purpose and forum; list of common variants
description: There are three principal types of claim chart (chart of references/invalidity, infringement chart, claim interpretation chart) and other variants: initial or preliminary infringement contentions (PICs); domestic industry (DI) charts for ITC importation actions; expert claim charts; 'parts list' charts used as demonstrative exhibits; claim charts for licensing/settlement negotiations; and design patent charts.
guidance: Choose the chart variant that matches your objective (e.g., infringement proof, invalidity showing, claim construction support, ITC DI requirement, demonstrative use in trial, licensing discussion). Different forums (district court, ITC, PTO) may have specific content or formatting expectations.

name: Berkheimer memorandum requirement for factual findings on conventionality
description: USPTO April 2018 Berkheimer memorandum changed examiner instructions by requiring examiners to make a factual determination as to whether claim elements were common, well-understood, routine, or conventional.
guidance: Prior to the memorandum, examiners were not required to support such conclusions with factual evidence. The memorandum's requirement to record factual determinations is treated as a policy change that can affect the rate of Section 101 rejections and inter-examiner variability; the report measures its empirical impact.

name: 2019 PEG grouping of abstract ideas and 'practical application' guidance
description: The USPTO's January 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (2019 PEG) clarified legal distinctions: abstract ideas are grouped as mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes; a claim that recites an abstract idea is not 'directed to' the abstract idea if the claim as a whole integrates the abstract idea into a practical application.
guidance: The 2019 PEG is treated as a structured clarification intended to reduce interpretive latitude and improve consistency. The report measures the PEG's effect on reducing first-office-action Section 101 rejections and examiner-level uncertainty (finding substantial decreases after its issuance). The report also points readers to USPTO training and materials on implementing the 2019 PEG.

name: Application language, decision language and translation obligations
description: A national patent application may be filed in Finnish, Swedish or English. PRH issues decisions in Finnish, Swedish or English. The choice of application language and decision language determines which translations must be supplied to PRH during processing.
guidance: If filed in Finnish or Swedish, the decision language is the corresponding language and pending claims/abstract must be translated into the other national language before publication. If filed in English and applicant requests decisions in English, translations of the claims and abstract into Finnish or Swedish must be supplied before publication; the claims translation is a condition for provisional protection (PatL 60 § 1 mom.). If the applicant does not want English proceedings, a full translation into Finnish or Swedish must be provided.

name: Basic document (perusasiakirja) and limits on amendments
description: The 'basic document' is the specification (with drawings) and the claims as they were included in the application on the filing date (in Finnish, Swedish or English as applicable). A patent application must not be amended so as to seek protection for subject‑matter that was not evident from the basic document as filed.
guidance: For PCT national phase continuations and nationalised EPs there are special rules defining which documents count as the basic document (PatL 13 §; PatA 21 §; PatL 31 § and PatM references). Any amendment adding matter beyond the basic document is disallowed; changes are treated per chapter H.3.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement in the specification
description: The specification must describe the invention clearly and completely so that a person skilled in the art can understand the principle and carry out the invention without undue experimentation. The description must contain at least one sufficient example or embodiment enabling the invention across the claimed scope.
guidance: Repetition of the invention must not rely on luck; the skilled person must be able to reach the same result by following the disclosure. Unnecessary details that belong to common general knowledge should not be included. For broad claim scope, the description must include enough exemplifying embodiments to reasonably cover the claimed scope (PatA 17 §; PatM 4 §). For general structural formulae defining compound groups, the specification must include sufficiently diverse examples to enable preparation of members not explicitly exemplified.

name: Specification structure and required content
description: The specification must begin with a short, matter‑of‑fact title and comprise a general part and a particular part. The general part must state the field of the invention, the prior art known to the applicant (including patent publications and literature per WIPO ST.14) and what the invention achieves over the prior art, linking to the claims. The particular part explains the invention in detail, preferably using embodiments and referring to drawings.
guidance: Do not use fictitious names; trademarks are allowed only in exceptional cases and must be identified as trademarks (use ® for Finnish registered marks). If drawings are included, provide a list of all figures as an introduction to the particular part; text and drawings must be separate. Tables, chemical and mathematical formulae may be included in the text. Special requirements for biological materials and sequence listings are set out in chapter B.9.

name: Claims must be clear, precise, concise and intelligible
description: Inventions must be presented in the claims in a manner that is understandable, clear, precise and concise. This requirement applies to individual claims (independent and dependent) and to the claim set as a whole. Claims determine the scope of protection; therefore concepts used should be, where possible, understandable by a skilled person from the claim language alone.
guidance: Ambiguity in claim category or wording undermines the claimed scope. The claim wording should, if possible, define the category (product, device, method, use) and the technical features unambiguously (PatL 8 §).

name: Independent claims must include all essential features
description: Independent claims must present all essential features of the invention. A feature is essential if, from the specification, it is evident that the solution would not work in the asserted way without that feature. Implicit features known to be part of the general concept need not be recited explicitly (e.g., a car claim implicitly includes wheels).
guidance: Do not include merely wishful or optional features; essentiality is assessed by reference to the specification and how the invention functions.

name: Functional/effect‑defined claim limitations
description: Claims defined solely by the intended effect or result (functional/effect‑based) are generally not allowed. A claim using such definitions must make it clear how the intended effect is achieved and the means must be verifiable by a skilled person without inventive effort across the full claimed scope.
guidance: In rare special circumstances an effect‑based definition can be allowed if the specification and common general knowledge enable the skilled person to achieve the effect without inventive activity or undue experimentation across the scope (PatM guidance).

name: Negative limitations (disclaimers)
description: Negative claim limitations (disclaimers) which exclude parts of the otherwise defined scope are permitted in certain circumstances, primarily when the invention cannot be defined clearly and concisely by positive features or positive features would unreasonably limit the claim scope.
guidance: A disclaimer may be present in the original claim or added later (see amendment rules, H.3.2.5). Use disclaimers only when necessary to achieve clarity or appropriate scope.

name: Claim categories and how to formulate them
description: A claimed invention should, where possible, fall into product, apparatus/device, method or use categories. Products/devices are normally defined by composition or structural details; methods by steps or operations and, if necessary, devices and products used; uses by the specific purpose for which a product or method is used (PatM 14–17 §§).
guidance: Choose the claim category that best reflects the technical contribution. Where product properties cannot otherwise be stated, product‑by‑process claim formats are acceptable for chemical products (product-by-process) but should be used properly with appropriate supporting disclosure.

name: Product‑by‑process claims and chemical product guidance
description: For products (especially chemical products) which are hard to define other than by their process of manufacture, product‑by‑process formulation is acceptable and may be accompanied by parameters to further define the product.
guidance: When using product‑by‑process claims, ensure the specification supports the product as distinct and provides sufficient disclosure of its preparation and properties (PatM 14 §).

name: Use of trademarks and standards in claims
description: Trademarks are generally not used in claims because trademark meaning may change during the patent life. Internationally known trademarks may be used if their meaning is precise (examples: 'caterpillar belt', 'teflon', 'bluetooth'). If a standard is referred to, it must be sufficiently identified (publication date/version) and its use must not be merely wishful; the standard reference should define features precisely.
guidance: If a standard reference is to be part of a claim, identify the standard precisely. If the standard citation is wishful rather than defining, it will not normally be accepted as a limiting feature for inventive step (PatM guidance).

name: Relative and approximate terms and parameters in claims
description: Relative terms ('thin', 'strong', 'wide') are imprecise and not acceptable unless they constitute a known definition in the field. Approximate terms ('about', 'essentially', 'approximately') may be accepted depending on context; precision depends on whether their use prevents clear distinction from prior art. Parameters used in claims must be commonly used or their definition must be given in the claim.
guidance: Avoid vague relative terms unless the technical field provides a standard meaning; if approximate terms are used, ensure the context provides adequate precision so the claim remains distinguishable.

name: Claim drafting formalities and prohibition of non‑technical matter
description: Each patent claim must contain only one invention; claims must not include irrelevant or non‑technical information (for example, mentions of commercial advantage). Claims should include, where applicable, reference signs corresponding to the drawings (preferably in parentheses) but must be intelligible without them. Generic references like 'as described' are not accepted except in limited circumstances.
guidance: Claims may exceptionally refer directly to drawings' diagrams; chemical and mathematical formulae are allowed in claims but not drawings; tables may be included in claims only if clearly necessary for the invention (PatA 14 §; PatM 22–23 §).

name: Multiple independent claims within the same group — conditions
description: Multiple independent claims in the same group (e.g., multiple independent product claims) are permitted only if: (1) the inventions are based on the same inventive concept; (2) they are technically closely related; and (3) it is evidently difficult to define the inventions sufficiently precisely, for example because of alternative embodiments that share common features.
guidance: These criteria (PatM 19 §) must all be met to legitimately include several independent claims in the same category without raising unity objections.

name: Two‑part (preamble + characterising portion) claim format
description: A claim should, where appropriate, be drafted in two parts: (1) a preamble indicating the title and prior art and (2) a characterising portion that specifies the novel and inventive features, typically introduced by wording like 'characterised in that' or 'known characterised by'.
guidance: Two‑part format is recommended whenever a clear distinction between known features and distinguishing features exists; exceptions and alternative single‑part formulations are allowed where two‑part form is artificial or misleading (PatA 14 §; PatM 12 §). The claim is assessed as a whole regardless of the partition.

name: Medical use claim drafting and 'for use' requirement
description: First medical use claims (new therapeutic use of known substance) may be given product protection by phrasing as 'Substance X for use as a medicament' or 'Substance X for use in therapy/diagnostics/surgery'. Second (and further) medical uses are allowed by appropriate 'for use' formulations such as 'Substance X for use in the treatment of disease Y'. Dependent claims must also contain 'for use'.
guidance: Claims phrased merely as 'use of X as a medicament' or similar are treated as method-of-treatment claims and may not be allowable under PatL 1 § 3rd paragraph; use the 'for use' wording to obtain product-type protection for medical uses (PatL 2 § 4–5 mom.; PatM 15 §). Acceptable claim examples are provided in the guidance (English examples also shown).

name: Abstract: length, content and purpose
description: The abstract is a short summary of the invention as disclosed in the specification, claims and drawings, intended to provide quick technical information. It must be no longer than 150 words, be based on the basic document, include the title and describe the technical problem and the main principle of the solution in easily understandable form. Chemical applications should include the chemical formula that best characterises the invention. The abstract must not contain statements of advantage or value.
guidance: The abstract should enable readers to decide whether to consult the application/publication in full. If drawings are present, the applicant selects (or PRH may choose) a figure to publish with the abstract; reference numbers for illustrated features included in the abstract should be in parentheses. The applicant prepares the abstract and must file a translation in the other language in time before publication (PatA 18 §; PatM 26–27 §).

name: Formatting and layout requirements for specification, claims and abstract
description: For paper filings (and electronic filings intended for equivalent printing), the specification, claims and abstract must be prepared in black on white A4 paper (or equivalent electronic format) in a single column with 1.5 line spacing. Font size must ensure capitals are at least 0.28 cm high (e.g., Times New Roman 12). Margins: left 2.5–4 cm, top 2–4 cm, right and bottom 2–3 cm. Text must be even, crisp and legible.
guidance: Pages of the specification and claims must be numbered consecutively starting from the beginning of the specification using Arabic numerals; numbers should be centered at least 2 cm from the top. Every fifth line of the specification and claims should be numbered at least 2.5 cm from the left margin (PatM 31 § guidance). Electronic filings must be formatted so printed output meets these requirements.

name: Summary of the disclosure (technical field, problem, solution, uses)
description: The abstract shall consist of a summary of the disclosure as contained in the description, the claims, and any drawings; the summary shall indicate the technical field to which the invention pertains and shall be drafted in a way which allows the clear understanding of the technical problem, the gist of the solution of that problem through the invention, and the principal use or uses of the invention.
guidance: This is the core content requirement under PCT Rule 8; emphasize what is new in the art, clearly state the technical problem, summarize how the invention solves it, and list principal uses so that a reader can understand whether to consult the full application.

name: Prohibited content: no claims of merit or speculative applications
description: The abstract shall not contain statements on the alleged merits or value of the claimed invention or on its speculative application.
guidance: Do not include promotional language, statements of superiority, speculation about future uses, or other assertions of value. Also avoid superfluous language and legal phraseology (see related entry). Prohibited items defined in PCT Rule 9 must not appear in the abstract.

name: Reference copy requirements under 37 CFR 1.98
description: 37 CFR 1.98(a)(2) requires a legible copy of: (1) each foreign patent; (2) each publication or that portion which caused it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office); (3) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims and any drawing of the application, or that portion which caused it to be listed; and (4) all other information or that portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: Do not submit copies of copending reexamination proceedings/applications (these may be mistaken for new requests); instead provide the application/proceeding number and status. The exception in 37 CFR 1.98(d)(1) does not apply to reexamination proceedings (no 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit).

name: Differences for reexamination ordered under 35 U.S.C. 257 (supplemental examination leading to ex parte reexamination)
description: 37 CFR 1.625(d) provides that any ex parte reexamination ordered under 35 U.S.C. 257 will be conducted in accordance with §§ 1.530–1.570 except that: (1) the patent owner will not have the right to file a statement pursuant to § 1.530 nor will the order set a time period for such a statement; (2) reexamination of any claim may be conducted on the basis of any item of information in § 1.605 and is not limited to patents and printed publications; (3) issues in addition to those raised by patents/printed publications and added/deleted subject matter may be considered and resolved; and (4) information material to patentability will be defined by § 1.56(b), notwithstanding § 1.555(b).
