guidance: Reexamination ordered under 35 U.S.C. 257 may therefore involve broader types of information (e.g., sales invoices, audio/video transcripts) and any ground of patentability (e.g., subject matter eligibility, anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement, indefiniteness, double-patenting).

name: Reexamination under 35 U.S.C. 304: prior art limits, double patenting, and 35 U.S.C. 112 treatment
description: A reexamination proceeding ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304 provides a complete reexamination of the patent claims on the basis of prior art patents and printed publications. Double patenting issues may also be considered. Issues relating to 35 U.S.C. 112 are addressed only with respect to new claims or amendatory subject matter in the specification, claims or drawings. Any new or amended claims are examined to ensure the scope of the original patent claims is not enlarged (35 U.S.C. 305).
guidance: Double patenting may be considered both as a basis for ordering reexamination under 35 U.S.C. 304 and during subsequent examination on the merits; the examiner should determine whether double patenting raises a substantial new question of patentability and whether a double patenting rejection is appropriate during examination.

name: Applicable prior art regime (first-inventor-to-file vs first-to-invent) and effective date effects
description: The prior art regime under which the application for the patent was examined (first-inventor-to-file or first-to-invent) will generally be applied in reexamination. If an amended or new claim has an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, reexamination will be conducted under the first-inventor-to-file regime. If a benefit claim to a prior application with filing date before March 16, 2013 is made during reexamination, reexamination may be conducted under the first-to-invent regime only if the written description of the prior application provides adequate written support under 35 U.S.C. 112 for (1) all patent claims, (2) all claims presented at any time during prosecution of the application that matured into the patent, and (3) all claims presented at any time during prosecution of any application to which the benefit was sought.
guidance: Prior art rejections under first-inventor-to-file are based on 35 U.S.C. 102 as in effect on/after March 16, 2013; under first-to-invent, rejections may be based on provisions of 35 U.S.C. 102 in effect prior to March 16, 2013 (including subsections (a), (b), (d), (e), (g) as applicable).

name: Intervening patents or printed publications as prior art
description: Rejections may be made in reexamination proceedings based on intervening patents or printed publications where the patent claims under reexamination are entitled only to the filing date of the patent and are not supported by an earlier foreign or United States patent application whose filing date is claimed.
guidance: Intervening patents/printed publications are available as prior art under precedent (e.g., In re Ruscetta, In re van Langenhoven). Examiner should determine entitlement to earlier filing dates (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 120 benefits) to assess whether intervening art is applicable.

name: Use of admissions by the patent owner in reexamination
description: An admission per se may not be the basis for establishing a substantial new question of patentability at the order stage (consideration under 35 U.S.C. 303 is limited to patents and printed publications). However, an admission by the patent owner of record in the file or in a court record may be utilized in combination with a patent or printed publication. After reexamination has been ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304, the examination on the merits is dictated by 35 U.S.C. 305 and admissions may be used to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim when applying prior art.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 301(a)(2)/37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) permit submissions of patent owner statements filed in court or Office proceedings; if relied upon in a request, the requester must explain how the statement is used to determine claim meaning per 37 CFR 1.510(b)(2). Admissions in the record are to be considered in reexamination (may be used to interpret/modify prior art). Third parties may not submit patent owner admissions made outside the file or court record for order-stage consideration. Reexaminations ordered under 35 U.S.C. 257 may involve an admission by the patent owner without combination.

name: Claim interpretation rules and treatment in reexamination
description: During reexamination ordered under 35 U.S.C. 304 and under 35 U.S.C. 257, claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification (In re Yamamoto). Where there is related litigation and a federal court has made a judicial interpretation of a disputed claim term, the examiner should acknowledge the judicial interpretation and assess whether it is consistent with the broadest reasonable construction; if adopting a different construction the examiner should supply reasoning. For expired patents, claim construction pursuant to Phillips should be applied. The statutory presumption of validity (35 U.S.C. 282) has no application in reexamination.
guidance: When disclosure is amended, 35 U.S.C. 112 issues should be limited to amendatory matter; a limitation in an original patent claim that appears in a newly presented claim cannot be examined under 35 U.S.C. 112 unless the amendatory matter creates a new issue. Examiners should supply reasoning when differing from judicial constructions and may perform 35 U.S.C. 112 priority/written-description analyses where appropriate (see In re NTP).

name: Filing paths and time limits
description: Two paths: (A) national phase entry of a PCT patent application within 31 months from earliest priority date (or PCT filing date if no priority); (B) direct/convention filing claiming priority from one or more patent applications or utility models filed within the previous 12 months (no extension).
guidance: For PCT national phase: German translations of PCT specification and any Art.19/34 amendments are required at filing and cannot be filed after the 31-month limit. If filed before PCT publication, Forms PCT/RO/101 and PCT/RO/105 must be submitted on filing.

name: Document language and completeness on filing
description: The German Utility Model specification (description, claims, figures) must be filed in German and all required documents (including pdf copy of each priority application for convention filings) must be submitted together on filing.
guidance: For national phase PCT entries, if priority documents were provided to WIPO no priority documents need be filed with GlobalIPCo; if convention filing, upload either the as-filed application (preferably with filing receipt page 1) or a certified copy. DPMA does not accept published copies of priority documents.

name: Priority and partial priority principle
description: A German Utility Model may claim priority from one or more patent applications or utility models filed during the previous 12 months; the content of the German specification need not be strictly identical and partial priority applies — priority valid only for content disclosed in the priority application; added content has filing-date time rank.

name: Required uploads for PCT national phase
description: Upload three separate pdf files for German translations of the description, claims and drawings of the original PCT specification; ensure number of claims in the German translation is identical to the number in the original PCT specification and all drawings are included.
guidance: If filing before PCT publication, also upload Forms PCT/RO/101 and PCT/RO/105. If those forms or original PCT spec are unavailable, filing may proceed but DPMA processing and application number issuance will be delayed.

name: Claims: use of reference numbers and renumbering on deletion
description: Reference numbers are permitted in claims. If a claim is deleted all subsequent claims must be renumbered and antecedent references adjusted accordingly.

name: Amendments on filing and new matter prohibition
description: For national phase PCT entries amended documents may be submitted on filing (e.g., to remove method claims, correct errors, delete figures) by uploading clean sheets; for convention filings amended German version may be uploaded in clean form relative to priority. It is not allowed to add new matter not disclosed in the original PCT (e.g., new figures), but corrections to figures (e.g., reference numbers) are allowed.
guidance: Do not upload tracked change versions. New claims may be added only if supported by the original PCT description/claims (fair basis). Amended documents must be complete (upload all pages even if only one sentence changed).

name: Statutory definitions (inventor, joint inventor, joint research agreement, effective filing date, claimed invention)
description: Provides definitions used throughout the Act: 'inventor' means the individual (or individuals for joint invention) who invented or discovered the subject matter; 'joint inventor'/'coinventor' means any one of the individuals who invented or discovered the subject matter of a joint invention; 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention; 'effective filing date' defined by actual filing date or the earliest application to which priority/benefit is claimed under sections 119, 365(a)/(b), 120, 121, or 365(c); 'claimed invention' means the subject matter defined by a claim in a patent or application.
guidance: These statutory definitions control how later sections (e.g., prior art, derivation, common ownership) are applied. Effective filing date rules include benefit/priority claims and reissue determinations (e.g., application for reissue deemed to have claim contained in original patent).

name: §102 — Conditions for patentability; novelty (prior art bars)
description: A person is entitled to a patent unless: (1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date; or (2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published/ deemed published under §122(b), that names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: This is the fundamental novelty / prior-art exclusion. 'Otherwise available to the public' covers broad disclosure modes. Clause (2) addresses prior-filed patents/applications naming another inventor (intervening patents/applications). Later subsections (b)-(d) provide statutory exceptions and rules about effective filing dates.

name: §102(c) — Common ownership rule under joint research agreements
description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed owned by the same person (for purposes of §102(b)(2)(C)) if: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: Preserves CREATE-act style common-ownership protections for collaborative research when the statutory conditions (including disclosure of parties) are met.

name: §102(d) — Effective filing date rules for patents and published applications as prior art
description: For determining whether a patent or application is prior art under §102(a)(2), the patent or application shall be considered to have been effectively filed as of its actual filing date, or if entitled to priority/benefit under §§119/365/120/121/365(c), as of the filing date of the earliest such application that describes the subject matter.
guidance: This specifies how priority/benefit claims change the effective filing date of earlier patents/applications for prior-art determinations—important when evaluating intervening patents/applications.

name: §103 — Conditions for patentability; non-obviousness
description: A patent may not be obtained if differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
guidance: Standard statutory non-obviousness test anchored to a hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA). The Act clarifies that how the inventor arrived at the invention is not determinative of patentability.

name: §291 — Derived patents (civil relief for derivation)
description: The owner of a patent may have relief by civil action against the owner of another patent that claims the same invention and has an earlier effective filing date if the invention claimed in such other patent was derived from the inventor of the invention claimed in the complaining patent. An action may be filed only before the end of the one-year period beginning on the date of issuance of the first patent containing a claim to the allegedly derived invention and naming the individual alleged to have derived such invention.
guidance: Creates a civil remedy for derivation and imposes a strict one-year filing limitation tied to issuance of the first patent naming the alleged derived inventor.

name: §135 — Derivation proceedings (PTAB institution and petition requirements)
description: An applicant may file a petition to institute a derivation proceeding in the Office. The petition must set forth with particularity the basis for finding that an inventor named in an earlier application derived the claimed invention from an inventor named in the petitioner's application and, without authorization, the earlier application was filed. Any such petition may be filed only within the one-year period beginning on the date of the first publication of a claim to the same or substantially the same invention, shall be made under oath, and shall be supported by substantial evidence. The Director may institute a derivation proceeding; the Director's institution decision is final and nonappealable.
guidance: High pleading standard ('with particularity') plus evidentiary support and strict time windows; institution is discretionary but final as to institution.

name: PTAB conduct and remedies in derivation proceedings
description: In a derivation proceeding, the Patent Trial and Appeal Board shall determine whether an inventor named in the earlier application derived the claimed invention from the petitioner and, without authorization, the earlier application was filed. The Board may correct inventor naming, defer action for certain periods (e.g., 3-month delay after Director issues a patent including the claimed invention), stay proceedings pending other chapter 30/31/32 proceedings, and final adverse Board decisions constitute final refusal or cancellation of claims. Parties may settle by written statement (subject to Board review) and may choose arbitration under specified conditions.
guidance: Provides procedural mechanisms (deferral, stay, settlement, arbitration) and strong remedies (cancellation/correction) for proven derivation; requires regulations prescribing standards and evidence rules.

name: Effective date and applicability of first-inventor-to-file regime
description: Except as otherwise provided, the amendments converting the U.S. to 'first-inventor-to-file' take effect upon expiration of the 18-month period beginning on enactment and apply to applications/patents that contain claims with effective filing dates on or after that effective date or specific references under §§120, 121, or 365(c) to patents/applications containing such claims.
guidance: Transitional rules specify which prior-law provisions continue to apply in particular cases and provide phased applicability tied to effective filing dates and priority references.

name: §33 — Limitation on issuance of patents (human organism exclusion)
description: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.
guidance: Absolute statutory bar on claims directed to or encompassing human organisms; applies to applications pending on or filed on or after enactment and does not affect patents issued on earlier applications to which the subsection does not apply.

name: Derivation-related time and evidence standards (institution, deferral, stays, settlements, arbitration)
description: Derivation petitions must be supported by substantial evidence and filed within statutory windows; the Director's institution decision is final and nonappealable; PTAB may defer or stay actions (including waiting 3 months after the Director issues a patent containing the claimed invention), may accept settlements (subject to consistency with record), and parties may elect arbitration under Title 9 rules with notice to Director.
guidance: Emphasizes tight timeframes, evidentiary thresholds, finality of institution, and multiple procedural mechanisms to resolve derivation disputes while coordinating with parallel proceedings.

name: Direct infringement requirement (single-entity rule)
description: Direct patent infringement requires that a single party make, use, sell, offer to sell, or import a device that contains all the limitations of a patent claim, or perform a method that contains all the limitations of a patent claim; intent is irrelevant and the statute creates strict liability.
guidance: The single-entity rule can be satisfied by a party acting personally or vicariously (direction or control/agency). To establish direction or control, every step must be attributable to the controlling party; merely providing instructions or cooperating at arm's length is insufficient. Contracts must obligate the third party to perform the claimed method steps to show direction or control.

name: Akamai/McKesson holding on inducement liability
description: The Federal Circuit (en banc) held that liability for induced infringement under §271(b) may be found even if the steps of a patented method are divided among multiple parties — it is not necessary to prove that all steps were committed by a single entity.
guidance: The court focused on §271(b)’s text and policy, distinguishing it from §271(a). This means inducement liability can be asserted when an actor causes or induces others to collectively perform the claimed steps, so long as the elements of inducement (including knowledge/willful blindness) and performance of steps are established.

name: Proof elements for inducement under Akamai (McKesson fact pattern)
description: Per the Federal Circuit’s guidance in McKesson, Epic can be liable for inducing infringement if it can be shown that: (1) Epic knew of McKesson’s patent; (2) Epic induced the performance of the steps of the method claimed; and (3) those steps were in fact performed.
guidance: McKesson reflects a scenario where the defendant induced multiple third parties to collectively perform the method but itself did not perform any steps. Emphasizes the centrality of knowledge and proof that induced acts took place.

name: Prefer system/product claims where appropriate
description: Where technology permits, draft system or apparatus claims instead of method claims because recent cases treat system claims differently and a party may infringe a claimed system by merely using the system and obtaining benefit from it (ability to place the system as a whole into service).
guidance: System claims can avoid divided-infringement problems because infringement may be found without physical control/possession of every element. Assess whether system claim forms better capture the commercial actor you expect to target.

name: Draft method claims to prevent steps from occurring outside the United States
description: Patent prosecutors should draft method claims to prevent steps from occurring outside the United States since a method claim is infringed only if all steps are performed inside the U.S.
guidance: Where feasible, include claim language that requires acts to occur in the United States or recite steps in a manner that makes non-U.S. performance less likely; this can limit divided-infringement exposure and avoid territorial gaps.

name: Eliminate or rephrase steps performed by separate actors (claim drafting technique)
description: Where a second entity performs certain steps, consider eliminating those steps from the claim or drafting around them (for example, claim 'transmitting the data to a receiver' and omit a recitation of 'receiving the data').
guidance: Alternatively, draft multiple independent claims directed separately to each potential actor (one claim for the end user, another for the provider), to preserve direct-infringement options and avoid reliance on inducement theories.

name: Draft claims to capture actions of several unconnected actors (when useful)
description: Drafting method claims to incorporate the actions of several unconnected actors may satisfy inducement standards and help capture practices involving distributed responsibilities (e.g., diagnostics, cloud services).
guidance: Such claims can facilitate enforcement under inducement after Akamai, but require careful attention to proving knowledge and actual performance of steps by the multiple actors.

name: Burden on patentee to prove inducement elements (including intent)
description: Patentees pursuing inducement theories must prove both that the inducer displayed the requisite level of intent (knowledge or willful blindness) and that all steps of the claimed method were performed (even if by multiple actors).
guidance: Because inducement requires a mental state, fact issues about knowledge/willful blindness are likely to be disputed—gather direct evidence of knowledge, communications encouraging actions, marketing materials, or circumstantial evidence of deliberate avoidance of patent-related information.

name: Claim construction strategy shifts
description: Claim construction may be used strategically: patentees may seek constructions that attribute method steps to a single actor, while accused infringers may argue constructions that attribute steps to different actors.
guidance: Choice of claim construction can materially affect whether direct infringement is found; tailor claim construction arguments to support either direct-infringement or divided-infringement defenses as appropriate.

name: Ambiguous or nebulous claims defence (specification deceptive)
description: "Where a specification, by ambiguity and a needless multiplication of nebulous claims, is calculated to deceive and mislead the public, the patent is void."
guidance: This defence may be made by demurrer because validity against it is a question of construction of the letters patent themselves, though a special plea is probably the best means of interposing it; less meritorious necessity for special pleading than for other defences which assail validity.

name: Sixteenth defence — broadened reissue (timing and comparison with original)
description: Defence based on the relation between the original and the reissue: comparison of claims/contents and the particular length of time between original and application for reissue which may be fatal to a broadened reissue.
guidance: Plaintiff suing on a reissue need not introduce the original in evidence; defendant must prove contents of the original. The materiality of time lapse is a variable, circumstance-dependent question of fact; special plea is proper to notify plaintiff what must be met at trial.

name: March-in procedural rights and appeals (§203(b))
description: Determinations under §203 are not subject to the Contract Disputes Act; administrative appeals procedures shall be established by regulation (per §206); adversely affected parties may file a petition in the U.S. Claims Court within 60 days to review the agency determination on the record; in cases under §203(a)(1) and (3), the agency’s determination is held in abeyance pending exhaustion of appeals or petitions.
guidance: Specifies distinct appeal routes (administrative regs and Claims Court) and temporary stays for certain march-in determinations.

name: Exclusion for educational awards (§212)
description: No scholarship, fellowship, training grant, or other funding agreement made primarily to an awardee for educational purposes will contain any provision giving the Federal agency any rights to inventions made by the awardee.
guidance: Specifically excludes typical educational awards from agency claims to invention rights.

name: Scope rule re: inventions made in performance (§401.1)
description: These regulations apply to inventions "conceived or first actually reduced to practice in performance" of the project; inventions arising from separate, non-government-sponsored projects that fall outside the planned/committed activities and do not diminish performance generally are not subject to the regulations; challenges by agencies to contractor claims that an invention is not a subject invention are appealable (§401.11(d)).
guidance: Explains the boundary between government-subject inventions and independent or closely related non-government projects; disputes are subject to appeal.

name: National fast-track / expedited examination programmes (Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore)
description: Malaysia, Thailand and Singapore provide domestic fast track programmes for expediting examination and grant of patents with specific caps, technical-field restrictions, and conditions.
guidance: Common conditions include: applicant must indicate reason for expedited examination; caps on number of applications per month and per entity; field restrictions (e.g., medical/public health in Thailand pilot); limits on number of claims (e.g., Thailand: 10 claims); deadlines for responding to adverse S&E reports (e.g., 3 weeks in Malaysia/Thailand). Expected grant timetables (e.g., Singapore: less than 12 months from filing; Thailand: up to 12 months for invention patent and 6 months for petty patent).

name: Grounds for opposition
description: Pre-grant and post-grant oppositions may be filed on grounds that: (1) the claimed invention is not patentable, (2) lacks novelty, (3) lacks inventive step, (4) lacks industrial applicability. Some countries also consider lack of disclosure/support, incorrect amendments, and applicant eligibility as grounds.
guidance: Grounds vary by AMS; oppositions must identify grounds and typically include supporting evidence (e.g., prior art documents).

name: Definition of 'invention' for patentability
description: 'Invention' means that which is specified in the claim(s) of a patent; in most AMS an invention is defined as a solution to a technical problem that has a technical effect and can be a product, process, or product-by-process. Improvements of known products/processes may also be inventions.
guidance: If subject matter does not comply with the legal definition of 'invention' or is clearly not an invention, the application will be rejected and other grounds need not be examined. The term 'improvement' does not require superiority over prior art; an alternative providing similar effects may suffice.

name: Computer programs 'as such' excluded; technical effect required
description: Computer programs (sequences of executable instructions) are abstract and devoid of technical character and are excluded 'as such'. However, inventions implemented by a computer program that produce a 'technical effect' beyond normal physical interactions may be patentable.
guidance: Normal physical effects (circulation of currents) are insufficient. Examples of technical effects: controlling anti-lock braking, determining emissions, compressing video, restoring distorted images, encrypting communications, security measures protecting boot integrity. Claims must include all technical features essential for the technical effect; product, process and use claims may be allowable where technical character exists.

name: Four-step approach for assessing computer program related claims
description: One approach: (1) properly construe the claim; (2) identify the actual contribution made by the invention (examiner not bound by applicant's assertion); (3) determine whether the actual contribution falls solely within excluded subject matter 'as such'; (4) determine whether the contribution is actually technical in nature ('technical contribution').
guidance: If the contribution has technical character, proceed to examine novelty and inventive step. There is no single fixed AMS-wide criterion; examiners should apply these steps objectively.

name: Computer-implemented inventions and claim forms
description: A computer-implemented invention covers claims involving computers/networks/programmable apparatus where at least one feature is implemented by a computer program. A computer program and a corresponding computer-implemented method are distinct: the former is a sequence of executable instructions; the latter is a method actually performed on a computer.
guidance: Claims directed to a computer-implemented method cannot be objected to on the ground of being non-patentable subject matter because methods involving technical means have technical character; drafting should ensure technical features are included.

name: Drafting requirement for computer program claims
description: Because patentability of computer programs depends on technical effect, claims must be drafted to include all technical features essential for the technical effect.
guidance: Where patentability is admitted, product, process and use claims would generally be allowable. The presence of a programmable apparatus or other technical means in the claim may avoid exclusion but is not always determinative (Singapore exception).

name: Order of sources for claim construction
description: The proper analytical sequence is: (1) claim language itself, (2) remaining intrinsic evidence (specification and prosecution history), and (3) extrinsic evidence only in limited circumstances.
guidance: The article cites the 'black letter law' and Vitronics: 'the court should consider first the claim language, then the remaining intrinsic evidence, and, thereafter, in limited circumstances, extrinsic evidence.' District courts should rely primarily on the intrinsic record and use extrinsic sources sparingly and only when needed to understand technology or resolve residual ambiguity.

name: Extrinsic evidence is relevant but secondary
description: Extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, treatises, expert testimony, encyclopedias) may assist but is inherently less reliable than intrinsic evidence and must be used cautiously and secondarily.
guidance: Phillips states extrinsic evidence 'can help the district court better understand the underlying technology,' but courts must 'keep in mind the flaws inherent in each type of evidence and assess that evidence accordingly.' Use extrinsic evidence to illuminate technology or when intrinsic evidence is unclear, not as a primary source to define claim terms.

name: Five reasons why extrinsic evidence is less reliable
description: Phillips enumerates five inherent flaws that make extrinsic evidence less reliable than intrinsic evidence.
guidance: The five reasons listed: (1) extrinsic sources are not part of the patent created during prosecution to explain claim scope; (2) external publications may not be written for persons of skill in the art and may not reflect their understanding; (3) extrinsic expert reports/testimony are generated for litigation and can be biased (especially if not subject to cross-examination); (4) the universe of extrinsic evidence is 'unbounded,' allowing cherry-picking; (5) undue reliance risks changing claim meaning from the public record, undermining the public notice function of patents. Courts should weigh extrinsic evidence with these flaws in mind.

name: Role of dictionaries (Texas Digital context)
description: Dictionaries and general-purpose sources are not to be treated as the primary source for claim meaning; their use is subordinate to the intrinsic record and must be reconciled with the specification and prosecution history.
guidance: Phillips criticized Texas Digital's approach that elevated dictionary definitions, noting that dictionaries are 'at least two steps removed from the ultimate inquiry' and 'may not reflect the ordinary meaning in the relevant art at the relevant time.' If dictionaries yield multiple definitions, courts may consult the specification to determine which definition fits the patent context. District courts should be cautious in applying dictionary definitions and consider technical vs. general-purpose dictionaries accordingly.

name: Avoid importing specification embodiments into claims unless clear
description: Courts should not read preferred embodiments or examples from the specification into the claim scope absent a clear indication the patentee intended such a limitation (e.g., explicit lexicography or clear disclaimer).
guidance: Phillips acknowledges the concern of reading specification language into claims and rejects a methodology (from Texas Digital) designed mainly to avoid that problem by privileging dictionaries. The correct approach is to consult the specification as a primary source but to avoid treating specific embodiments as limiting unless the specification demonstrates a clear intent to limit (patentee acted as own lexicographer or explicitly disclaimed scope).

name: Claim differentiation presumption
description: The presence of dependent claims that add particular limitations gives rise to a presumption that those limitations are not present in the independent claim.
guidance: Phillips emphasizes context across claims: 'the context in which a term is used in the asserted claim can often illuminate the meaning of the same term in other claims' and dependent-claim limitations imply the independent claim lacks that limitation (illustrated by the 'steel baffles' example). Use claim differentiation as an interpretive tool within the intrinsic evidence.

name: Construing to preserve validity (limited application)
description: There remains a limited doctrine that ambiguous claim language may be construed to preserve validity, but it is of 'limited utility' and not a routine part of claim construction.
guidance: Phillips retained the maxim that claims will be construed to preserve validity, but the court warned it has 'not applied that principle broadly' and 'certainly not endorsed a regime in which validity analysis is a regular complement of claim construction.' Most amici argued validity should not drive claim construction except perhaps where two equally appropriate interpretations exist and one would render the claim invalid. In Phillips the doctrine was discussed in dicta and is to be applied narrowly.

name: Public notice function of claims
description: Claim construction must respect the public notice function of patent claims; constructions should not rewrite claims in ways that undermine public notice.
guidance: Phillips emphasizes that undue reliance on extrinsic evidence or reading in limitations from the specification risks undermining the patent's public notice role. Courts should interpret claims based on the public record (claims, spec, prosecution) to preserve predictability and notice to the public.

name: Deference to district court claim constructions (unresolved)
description: The en banc Phillips court declined to decide whether the Federal Circuit should afford any deference to district court claim construction rulings, leaving Cybor (de novo review) intact.
guidance: Phillips 'decided not to address' whether any deference should be accorded to trial court constructions. Many amici urged reversal of Cybor and adoption of clear-error review for underlying factual findings; the court left the question open, so the legal standard of no deference (per Cybor) remained unchanged pending future adjudication. Practitioners should therefore expect appellate review to remain governed by existing precedent until the Federal Circuit or Supreme Court rules otherwise.

name: Patentee bound by patent language as construed by courts
description: The protection afforded by a patent is limited and defined by the language it employs for describing and claiming the invention, as that language is interpreted by the courts.
guidance: If the patent language fails to cover the actual invention (too much or too little), the patentee may be defeated in securing rights; claiming more than invention may be treated as fraud on the public; claiming too little or incorrect description may be fraudulent concealment.

name: Disclaimer: purposes, statutory distinction, and effect
description: Disclaimer serves two purposes: (a) as a method of amending a defective patent (Sec. 4917) and (b) as a method by which a plaintiff in an infringement suit may avoid the defence that his original patent claimed more than his invention and still recover damages (Sec. 4922).
guidance: These provisions are distinct and have different scopes. A disclaimer is an abandonment of an apparent right, may be filed by any owner of the whole or a sectional interest, and as modified by the disclaimer the original patent is thereafter construed in cases where the disclaimant's rights are involved. A disclaimer does not admit the patent is void.

name: Excessive claim: definition and methods of ascertainment
description: A claim is excessive when it claims any material and substantial thing beyond the scope of the real invention of the patentee or beyond what he has described in specification, drawings, or model.
guidance: Immaterial or unessential features are not regarded as covered. To ascertain excess compare claims to descriptions on the face of the patent and investigate identity of invention by foreign patents, actual use (discarded features), or other evidence showing features were known at date of invention. If excess is separable it may be disclaimed; if not separable the whole claim is void and re-issue is required.

name: Excessive claim amendable by disclaimer only if mistake without fraud
description: An excessive claim can be amended by disclaimer only when the error arose through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention.
guidance: The law requires utmost good faith and reasonable diligence in drafting claims; a patentee who willfully inserts or persists in unlawful claims is not aided by disclaimer and risks rejection of the patent.

name: Core rules limiting amending power (inexorable rules)
description: Three rules cannot be affected by the amending power: (1) the invention must have existed at the issue of the original patent (clearly perceived as well as conceived and fully reduced to practice); (2) the original application must have attempted to describe and claim every attribute the inventor desired to bring within the monopoly; (3) the monopoly created by the patent must be commensurate with the invention the inventor then endeavored to protect.
guidance: These rules preclude introducing into an amended patent any patentable matter not clearly in the inventor's mind or not reduced to practice at the original issue; they distinguish amended patents from new original patents and preserve public rights.

name: Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means/step‑plus‑function)
description: Determine whether a claim limitation is a means‑ (or step‑) plus‑function limitation invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph). If it is unclear whether the limitation falls within the scope of 112(f), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA second paragraph) may be appropriate.
guidance: If ambiguous whether the claim language invokes 112(f), treat ambiguity as a potential basis for indefiniteness rejection under 112(b). Example: claims using 'means' or 'step' typically invoke 112(f) but context can negate invocation; examiner should make a determination and, if unclear, consider 112(b) rejection.

name: Specification must disclose corresponding structure/material/acts
description: A means‑plus‑function limitation must have its corresponding structure (or material or acts) disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure will perform the recited function.
guidance: Disclosure can be explicit in text or in drawings/figures. The test is whether one of ordinary skill would understand the specification itself to disclose the structure that performs the recited function (Atmel; Dossel). If no such disclosure exists, the claim fails 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA second paragraph).

name: Computer‑implemented means‑plus‑function requires disclosure of an algorithm
description: When the disclosed structure is a computer programmed to carry out an algorithm, the corresponding structure is the special purpose computer as programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm; the specification must disclose the algorithm for performing the claimed function.
guidance: A general purpose computer alone is not sufficient for a specific computer‑implemented function; the specification must disclose an algorithm (e.g., prose, math formula, flowchart, source code or other adequate description) that transforms a general purpose processor into the special purpose computer (Aoyama; WMS; Aristocrat; Noah).

name: General purpose computer is sufficient only for general computing functions
description: A general purpose computer may be adequate corresponding structure when the recited function is a general computing function (e.g., 'means for storing data'), but for claiming a specific function a general purpose computer without an algorithm is insufficient.
guidance: If the claimed functions (e.g., 'processing,' 'receiving,' 'storing') are truly coextensive with a general purpose processor's structure, additional algorithm disclosure may not be required (Katz example). Otherwise, require algorithm disclosure.

name: Algorithm disclosure must be sufficient to perform the entire claimed function
description: If an algorithm is disclosed, its sufficiency is judged by whether one of ordinary skill in the art would understand it to define the structure and enable performance of the entire claimed function; an algorithm that supports only part of the function is inadequate.
guidance: If the algorithm covers some but not all functional components, treat the specification as if no algorithm were disclosed and consider a 112(b) rejection. Importing off‑the‑shelf software or asserting that skilled artisans could fill gaps does not cure an inadequate algorithm (Noah; Finisar).

name: Mode of implementation limits claim scope (hardware vs software)
description: By using means‑plus‑function language an applicant limits the claim to the disclosed structure/implementation (e.g., hardware or hardware+software) and equivalents; the examiner should not construe the limitation to cover pure software implementation if the spec discloses hardware or hardware+software structure.
guidance: If no corresponding structure is disclosed (only software per se without algorithm), the limitation should be deemed indefinite and rejected under 112(b). Claims must be read as a whole: a claim with a means limitation lacking structural support is not necessarily directed to software per se unless other claim limitations also point that way.

name: Supporting disclosure must clearly link/associate structure to claimed function
description: The written description or prosecution history must clearly link or associate the disclosed structure, material, or acts to the function recited in the means‑ (or step‑) plus‑function limitation for that disclosure to qualify as the corresponding structure.
guidance: This 'clear link' requirement is the quid pro quo for using means‑plus‑function claiming. If one of ordinary skill cannot identify what in the specification performs the claimed function, a 112(b) rejection is appropriate (B. Braun; Medical Instrumentation & Diagnostics).

name: Examiner procedure: determine function and then identify corresponding structure in spec
description: Once a limitation is determined to be means‑plus‑function invoking 112(f), the examiner must determine the claimed function and review the written description (including drawings, figures, tables, sequence listings) to identify corresponding structure, material, or acts disclosed in the original specification.
guidance: The corresponding structure must be disclosed in the application itself; structures present only in incorporated‑by‑reference material or prior art are not valid corresponding structures (Pressure Prods.; Atmel). Review disclosure from the viewpoint of a person skilled in the art (Tech. Licensing; Med. Instrumentation).

name: When rejection under 112(b) is appropriate (enumerated situations)
description: A rejection under 112(b) (pre‑AIA second paragraph) may be appropriate: (1) when it is unclear whether a claim limitation invokes 112(f); (2) when 112(f) is invoked and there is no disclosure or insufficient disclosure of corresponding structure/material/acts; and/or (3) when 112(f) is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link/associate the disclosed structure/material/acts to the claimed function.
guidance: If the examiner cannot identify corresponding structure/material/acts, make a 112(b) rejection. The MPEP lists these three distinct circumstances as triggers for a 112(b) rejection.

name: Specific disclosure in specific terms satisfies 112(b) and 112(f)
description: If the corresponding structure/material/acts are described in the specification in specific terms (e.g., an emitter‑coupled voltage comparator), are linked to the claimed function and one skilled in the art could identify them as adequate to perform the recited function, then 112(b) and 112(f) requirements are satisfied.
guidance: Concrete, specific structural descriptions linked to the function (Atmel example) satisfy definiteness — no need to import additional material.

name: Means‑plus‑function claims must also meet 112(a) (written description/enablement)
description: A means‑plus‑function limitation found indefinite for lacking corresponding structure may also lack adequate written description and/or enablement under 112(a); the specification must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention, especially for genus/functionally defined claims which must be supported by species sufficient to justify the genus (Ariad).
guidance: When assessing 112(a) support consider original disclosure in summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Genus claims defined by function require evidence of species to support the breadth claimed.

name: Do not import unrecited functional or unnecessary structural limitations from the specification into claims
description: Functional limitations not recited in the claim, or structural limitations from the written description that are unnecessary to perform the claimed function, cannot be imported into the claim.
guidance: Claims must be construed to cover the disclosed corresponding structure and its equivalents, but examiners/applicants should not read extra functional or structural limitations from the spec into the claim (Welker Bearing; Wenger).

name: Description must not contradict allowable claims (Guidelines H-V 2.7; F-IV 4.3(iii))
description: The Guidelines for Examination require substantial amendments such that the description does not contradict the allowable claims (H-V, 2.7 and F-IV, 4.3(iii)).
guidance: Applicants are expected to align the description with the scope of allowable claims; the Guidance is an EPO-specific practice and may require deletion or clarification of description passages that conflict with the claims.

name: Delete or disclaim subject-matter not covered by the claims
description: Applicants are required either to delete subject matter no longer covered by the claims or explicitly state that the offending subject matter does not fall under the scope of the invention.
guidance: Practical considerations: applicants are often reluctant to remove or disclaim description material because amendments can affect claim interpretation (e.g., doctrine of equivalents), and because of the time and cost involved in extensive description edits.

name: Claims shall be clear, concise and supported by the description (Article 84 EPC)
description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.
guidance: This is the statutory basis cited by the Board in T 1024/18 for requiring descriptions to be consistent with claims. The support requirement is treated as a separate limb (support distinct from clarity and conciseness).

name: 'Supported by the description' requires support by the whole description (T 1024/18)
description: "'supported by the description' is a distinct requirement to clarity and means 'supported by the whole description'" (Board reasoning in T 1024/18).
guidance: According to T 1024/18, it is not sufficient that a single passage supports the claims if other portions of the description give a different or contradictory meaning; the entire description must be consistent with the claims.

name: Claims should be clear from their wording alone (Guidelines F-IV 4.2)
description: "Each claim must be read giving the words the meaning and scope which they normally have in the relevant art" and the Guidelines "require the claim to be amended whereby the meaning is clear from the wording of the claim alone" (F-IV, 4.2).
guidance: This guideline supports the idea that claims need not rely on the description for clarity. There is a tension between this principle and the view that the whole description must support the claims.

name: Alternate (contrary) interpretation: support limited to basis for claimed subject-matter (T 1989/18)
description: T 1989/18 held that Art. 84 EPC requires the claims to be supported by the description only to the extent that the claims should not include subject matter that does not have basis in the description; additional subject matter in the description that does not appear in the claims is not prohibited.
guidance: This represents a less onerous approach — inconsistencies in the description that do not undermine the claims' clarity/support (in the sense of added matter) need not be removed. The Board in T 1024/18 expressly disagreed with this view.

name: Disparity between description and claims can make claim scope unclear (Article 69 EPC / interpretative role of description)
description: There is an argument that the description should be used to interpret the claims (Article 69 EPC), and thus that a disparity between the description and the claims may make the scope of the claims unclear.
guidance: This supports the rationale for requiring alignment: if the description conflicts with claims, readers (or courts) might be uncertain about claim scope. However, EPO Guidelines elsewhere emphasize claim wording as primary for clarity.

name: Identity criterion for alloy inventions (novelty)
description: Identity of an alloy invention is determined by whether each element of the alloy is identical and whether its composition range, structure, and utility (property or use) are identical.
guidance: Note: For alloy inventions, utility that limits a specific composition or structure should be construed as specifying the alloy. For manufacturing-method claims, identity requires considering identity of both the alloy and the manufacturing process.

name: Method to determine identity — same composition & structure
description: If claimed and prior-art alloys have identical composition and structure, they are substantially identical even if perceived properties or uses differ.
guidance: Even if the prior art does not explicitly disclose a use, the composition and structure appropriate to that use may already be present; differences that are merely differences in stated use do not establish novelty. (See cited case law examples.)

name: Method to determine identity — composition identical but structure depends on manufacture
description: If alloy compositions are identical but structure depends on manufacturing method, identity must consider whether the same manufacturing method is applied; same composition plus same method => substantially identical.
guidance: Structure of an alloy commonly changes with manufacturing; where prior art and claim share both composition and manufacturing method, inventions are substantially identical.

name: Inventive-step rule — mere composition-range changes or substitutions are not sufficient
description: When comparing to a known alloy with the same base, an alloy differing only by (i) a different composition range, (ii) an additional alloying element, or (iii) substitution by another alloying element does not involve inventive step unless the claimed alloy shows significantly improved utility.
guidance: Illustration: If known alloy has 3–8% A, claimed 1–2% or 9–15% A (same objective/property) corresponds to (i); adding 0.05–0.5% B corresponds to (ii); substituting one element by another with known equivalent effect corresponds to (iii). Such differences are typically obvious absent significant improvement in utility. Case law and notes show overlap/impurities often negate novelty/inventiveness.

name: Inventive-step rule — different structure or utility may support inventiveness
description: If an alloy has a different structure or utility (e.g., different properties arising from manufacturing) compared to prior art, that difference may support inventive step; but if structure/utility is similar when composition and manufacturing method are similar, no inventive step.
guidance: Because structure depends on manufacturing, overlapping composition ranges can correspond to identical utility unless manufacturing conditions meaningfully differ. Claims asserting structural differences must provide evidence (effects/tests) showing practical, non-trivial difference.

name: Description requirement for polymeric compounds — sufficiency and specificity
description: A particular polymeric compound must be described with specific explanation sufficient to support the polymer defined in the claims.
guidance: In principle, specify the polymer by structure via: repeating units; arrangement of repeating units (homo, random, block, graft, head-to-tail coupling, etc.); molecular weight; local molecular properties (branching, substituents, double bonds, cross-linking, terminal groups); and stereospecificity (atactic, isotactic, syndiotactic). If complete specification is impossible, clearly specify main components and relevant structural requirements.

name: Requirement to disclose manufacturing methods (polymers) — at least one or more
description: To enable a skilled person to synthesize the claimed polymeric compound, describe at least more than one manufacturing method with essential matters such as source materials, manufacturing conditions, and, if necessary, manufacturing devices.
guidance: Examples and specific numerical values and operating conditions should be provided so the skilled person can carry out the process without undue experimentation.

name: If claim defines a use of a polymer, provide examples proving applicability
description: When a use of a polymeric compound is defined in the claim, the description must specifically describe at least one example proving that the claimed polymer is applicable for that use.
guidance: Practical demonstration in the specification supports utility and claim support.

name: Claims — polymers and polymer compositions (definitional principle)
description: Claims for polymeric compounds should particularly define the polymer sought for protection, preferably by structure; if structure is insufficient, add basic properties or manufacturing method. For manufacturing-method claims, define the three essential elements and their technical relationship. For polymer compositions, components and mixing ratio should be clearly defined; if function/use limitation is claimed, define that function/use in addition to components.
guidance: Functional claim language (e.g., 'composition having a function of XX') is appropriate when component limits alone do not distinguish the invention from other compositions lacking the function; otherwise component limits suffice.

name: Textile description requirements — chemical fibers
description: For inventions relating to chemical fibers characterized by material properties, applicants must specifically state technical means including source material, structural characteristics of the fiber, process conditions (spinning, drawing, post-treatment) to accomplish the claimed characteristics.
guidance: If a skilled person would need excessive repeated testing or trial-and-error due to lack of clear description of means, the description is insufficient for enablement.

name: Textile description requirements — textile structures (fabric/knit)
description: For inventions relating to textile structure, where the structure is not a basic structure readily recognizable to a skilled person, applicants must specifically state complete characteristics of the structure including repeating unit and manufacturing methods in the description and drawings.
guidance: Detailed structural and manufacturing disclosures are required to enable reproduction and to delimit the claimed subject matter.

name: Inventive-step consideration — parameter-based claims
description: If a claim specifies a new parameter for man-made fiber, it is necessary to compare the manufacturing method and material properties (e.g., strength) with prior art to determine inventive step.
guidance: If prior art discloses process variables that determine the parameter and values convert into the claimed parameter range, the parameter may be obvious. Examples show parameters that merely describe inherent properties are not patentable when predictable from prior art.

name: Claims specifying spinning/manufacturing method — claim scope construction
description: When construing claims relating to fiber material specified by a spinning/manufacturing method, the claim should not be limited to embodiments in the description but should include the whole span of properties producible by the claimed method.
guidance: If examples and comparative examples show meaningful differences in technical characteristics attributable to the method, novelty and inventive step may be recognized; but claim breadth should reflect the full range of properties the method can produce.

name: Effect from limited/minute shape differences — need for data
description: Minute shape differences of components (ring, traveler, metal card clothing, knitting needle, etc.) may greatly influence results; the examiner must consider the effect of small shape changes and, where doubtful, require test data or certified test results.
guidance: When effect is uncertain, objective evidence (tests, certified results) should be used to support claimed effects of shape differences.

name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the administration of the patent system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
description: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO patent process includes, inter alia, not conducting reasonable inquiry before claiming micro entity status, failing to have reasonable corroboration procedures, presenting incorrect certifications, claiming micro entity status when no longer entitled at the time of issue fee payment, and failing to notify the USPTO of loss of status and pay the correct fee.
guidance: Similar factual failures can be characterized as prejudicial conduct under § 11.804(d) and may support discipline.

name: Best-practice intake and verification procedures (recommended questionnaire items)
description: Implement an intake questionnaire (in an appropriate language) asking inventors/applicants to: voluntarily list all previous US patent applications in which they have been named as inventors; answer questions pertaining to inventorship under MPEP § 2109; provide information/questions on patentability and on-sale bar issues under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102; receive information and questions to help decide which entity status to claim (MPEP § 2550); be warned about potential damages from falsely claiming small or micro entity status (Unleashing American Innovators Act of 2022); sign the questionnaire with a handwritten signature; and be informed about ongoing duty to disclose material information to patentability under 37 C.F.R. § 1.56.
guidance: The Final Order describes these specific questionnaire items as effective measures KA adopted to corroborate entity status and reduce errors.

name: Technical problem/technical solution emphasis
description: Include description of technical problem/solution, focusing on making sure the problem is portrayed as a technical problem.
guidance: Practice tip: The specification bolsters eligibility when it explains the technological problem being solved (e.g., network vulnerabilities) and describes the technological solution. Quote/recite technical harms or network-specific issues in the spec to show the claims are rooted in computer technology rather than abstract ideas.

name: Claims must recite technical limitations improving computer functionality
description: Claims should be directed to improvements in existing computer functionality (e.g., improving functioning of computer systems, networks, GUIs, memory architectures) rather than mere abstract ideas or generic computer use.
guidance: Examples: object-oriented key manager and label use that improve network security (TecSec); plurality of network monitors that analyze specific types of data and integrate reports to identify intruders (SRI); specific graphical user interface structures that improve speed, accuracy, and usability (Trading Techs). Cast the invention as 'an improvement to the capability of the system as a whole.'

name: Support improvements with specification details and benefits
description: Provide specification-level technical details and explain benefits that flow from the claimed improvement (how and why the improvement works).
guidance: If drafting, include and explain benefits and technical details in the specification; if in prosecution, try to identify and emphasize specifics in the record to 'hang your hat on.' Courts look to the specification to decide whether claims are directed to a technological improvement (Visual Memory; Univ. of Florida).

name: Avoid claims that are merely human cognitive actions or mental processes
description: Do not draft method claims whose steps can be performed as human cognitive actions or otherwise amount to mental processes or fundamental human activities.
guidance: The Federal Circuit treats claims drawn to activities like voting/verifying as abstract if they correspond to longstanding human activities (Voter Verified). To avoid this, include steps or limitations that cannot be performed purely mentally and/or are tied to specific technical implementations.

name: Draft system claims that do not merely mirror method claims and include non-standard components
description: Where possible, include system claims with components that are not simply 'standard components' and that are supported in the specification as being specially configured or non-generic.
guidance: Practice tip: system claims that merely restate method steps with generic computers/printers/etc. are insufficient (Voter Verified). Include and support in the spec components that can be shown to be more than standard off-the-shelf hardware.

name: Frame the prior-art problem as technological and claim a specific technological solution
description: Cast the problem in the prior art in terms of technology and ensure claims recite a specific implementation that solves that technological problem.
guidance: The Federal Circuit favored claims that addressed specific technology problems (e.g., prior GUI deficiencies) and recited specific structured solutions. Emphasize lack of pre-electronic analog or that solution is specific to software/computer context (Trading Techs).

name: Use specific structured claim elements (not just 'displaying' or generic data handling)
description: Claims that require a specific, structured element paired with prescribed functionality (e.g., a structured GUI with fixed axes and moving indicators) are more likely to avoid abstraction than claims that merely claim displaying or manipulating data.
guidance: Ensure claims recite structure and specific interaction between structure and function, rather than high-level data presentation. Show how the structure resolves identified prior-art problems.

name: Provide technical explanation of functional elements (avoid purely functional language)
description: Do not rely on bare functional recitations (e.g., 'drivers' or other elements described only functionally) without explaining how those elements operate.
guidance: The court criticized claims where drivers or other elements were recited only functionally without detail. If operation of elements is explained in the specification, it may help eligibility (Univ. of Florida).

name: Emphasize technical distinctions over the prior art in both claims and specification
description: Ensure the specification and claims highlight any technical distinctions over prior art and that such distinctions are reflected in claim language.
guidance: Practice guidance: focus on ensuring the specification describes a technical distinction over the prior art that is reflected in the claims (TecSec). Use the specification to show how claimed features differ and improve over known technology.

name: Recitation of multiple, specific categories/limitations can strengthen technical character
description: Listing multiple specific categories, data types, or categories of monitored data in the claim may help demonstrate a technical solution rather than an abstract idea.
guidance: Example: SRI's claim listed multiple categories of network traffic data and an integration step; the recitation of multiple categories and integration may have supported eligibility. Consider including concrete categories and how they are processed.

name: When dealing with user-interface inventions emphasize improved functionality unique to the UI
description: For GUI-related inventions, claim the specific UI structure and functionality that directly solve prior UI problems (speed, accuracy, usability) rather than claiming generic UI actions.
guidance: Show that the UI has no pre-electronic analog and that the claimed structure imparts functionality to the system as a whole. Use concrete UI structure+behavior to demonstrate technical improvement (Trading Techs; IBG/Liu guidance).

name: Dynamic fee calculation inputs
description: Fees are dynamically generated based on values entered: entity status (Regular, Small, or Micro), number of pages in the specification, total dependent claims, total independent claims, and whether multiple dependent claims are being filed.
guidance: Micro entity applicants must provide certification (PTO/SB/15A and PTO/SB/15B); check boxes for other items such as petitions filed as part of the application.

name: Step 2A: Identify Judicial Exception
description: Assess whether the claim recites a judicial exception (for example, an Abstract Idea or a Product of Nature) or contains no judicial exception ('None' or 'n/a').
guidance: The Step 2A 'Exception' column classifies each example as Abstract Idea, Product of Nature, None, n/a, Streamlined (Particular Machine), Streamlined (Product of Nature), or similar labels. This determination (that a claim recites a judicial exception vs. not) directs whether to proceed to the MDC analysis and Step 2B. Use the example mappings to quickly locate situations pertinent to a claimed exception.

name: Step 2A: MDC Analysis (characteristics evaluated)
description: When a judicial exception is identified, perform the MDC (Meaningful Distinction/Characteristics) analysis to characterize the exception by attributes such as function/activity, chemical/physical property, structure or form, phenotype, or by whether it is tied to a particular machine/streamlined form.
guidance: The Step 2A 'MDC Analysis' column records the characteristics discussed for each example, e.g., function/activity; chem/phys property; structure or form; phenotype; particular machine; streamlined (Particular Machine) or Streamlined (Product of Nature). Use these characterizations to evaluate whether the claim elements are merely descriptive of a judicial exception or instead present a claim-specific manifestation (e.g., a particular machine, a structured composition, or a transformed composition).

name: Statement of substantial new question of patentability
description: A request must include ‘a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability based on prior patents and printed publications.’
guidance: The request should clearly and in detail set forth what the requester considers the substantial new question(s) of patentability to be in view of prior patents and printed publications, and should show how they are substantially different from questions raised in the prior examination (35 U.S.C. 304; 37 CFR 1.510(b)(1)). If a substantial new question is found as to one claim, all claims will be reexamined (see MPEP §2242).

name: Treatment of requests filed by patent owner including proposed amendments
description: A patent owner may include a proposed amendment with a request under 37 CFR 1.510(e), but any such amendment must comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j). The determination whether to institute reexamination is made on the claims in effect at the time of the request (without proposed amendments).
guidance: If the patent owner proposes to add claims, excess claim fees (37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (c)(4)) may apply. If reexamination is granted, subsequent prosecution will be on the basis of amended claims as presented during the proceeding.

name: Commissioner's examination and issuance standard
description: On filing and payment of fees the Commissioner shall examine the alleged new invention or discovery; if it appears the claimant is justly entitled and the invention is sufficiently useful and important, the Commissioner shall issue a patent.
guidance: Issuance depends on just entitlement and being sufficiently useful and important, as determined by the Commissioner. (Section 4893)

name: Reissue for defective/insufficient specification or inadvertent overclaiming
description: When any patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of defective or insufficient specification, or because the patentee claimed more than he had the right to claim, if the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent or deceptive intention, the Commissioner shall, on surrender of the patent and payment of duty, cause a new patent with corrected specification to be issued to the patentee (or successors) for the unexpired term.
guidance: Reissue allowed only for inadvertent mistakes without fraud; surrender and payment required; reissue specifications subject to revision/restriction like original applications. (Section 4916)

name: Disclaimer procedure for claimed parts not owned
description: When a patentee, through inadvertence, has claimed more than he was the original inventor of, his patent shall be valid for the part truly and justly his own (if material or substantial); the patentee may, on payment of the fee, make a disclaimer of such parts not chosen to claim, in writing attested by witnesses, and recorded in the Patent-Office; the disclaimer shall thereafter be considered part of the original specification to the extent of the interest claimed.
guidance: Disclaimer must be written, witnessed, recorded; affects extent of rights and is part of record; does not affect pending actions except as to unreasonable delay in filing it. (Section 4917)

name: Suit for infringement of bona fide part when overclaiming
description: Whenever, through inadvertence and without willful default, a patentee has claimed more than he was the original inventor of, the patentee (and executors/assigns) may maintain suit at law or in equity for infringement of any part that was bona fide his own, if it is a material and substantial part and definitely distinguishable from parts claimed without right.
guidance: Plaintiff may recover for bona fide part despite overclaiming, but no costs shall be recovered unless proper disclaimer entered at Patent-Office before suit commencement; benefits lost if patentee unreasonably neglected or delayed entering disclaimer. (Section 4922)

name: Predictors used in propensity score model
description: Predictors include continuation history, small entity status, claims of foreign priority, claimed parent type (relationship to earlier U.S. app), number of all claims at filing, number of 3-year forward citations, year of issue, interactions between year and 3-year citations, and technology categories (Hall, Jaffe, Trachtenberg).
guidance: These characteristics are mostly known at filing and are chosen to control for pre-examination correlates of litigation; include interaction terms to allow citation impact to vary by grant year.

name: Cost versus outcome comparison
description: A pro se applicant pays only USPTO fees (~$400–$1,600 for a small entity through allowance, plus issue and maintenance fees) while represented applicants may pay roughly $10,000–$25,000 in attorney fees.
guidance: Do the arithmetic against expected outcomes: many pro se cases go abandoned, and many that issue have narrow or defective claims that cannot be enforced. Low upfront cost can be false economy if enforceability or continuation options are lost.

name: Claims drafting quality (avoid lay-English pitfalls)
description: Common error: "Claims drafted in lay English that fail antecedent basis or use ambiguous terms."
guidance: Draft claims with proper antecedent basis, precise claim terminology, and consistent use of defined terms. Avoid colloquial phrasing and ambiguity that can cause indefiniteness rejections or limit enforceability.

name: Provisional application disclosure sufficiency
description: Common error: "provisional disclosures too thin to support later claims."
guidance: If using a provisional, include a robust disclosure (figures, multiple embodiments, ranges, alternatives) so the provisional actually supports the scope you later want to claim. Thin provisionals intended only to 'get the date' often fail to support later claim scope.

name: Office action response mistakes
description: Common error: "office action responses that argue without amending or amend without supporting the amendment in the spec."
guidance: When responding to office actions, choose appropriate strategy: amend claims when necessary and ensure amendments are supported by the specification; if arguing, present clear legal/technical bases. Don't merely argue without corresponding amendments when the record requires them, nor amend to new matter not supported by the spec.

name: Filing continuations to preserve future scope
description: Common error: "failure to file continuations before issuance, foreclosing future scope."
guidance: Plan prosecution to preserve continuation options when needed. Missing the opportunity to file continuations before issuance can permanently foreclose pursuing broader or different claim scopes later.

name: When pro se might make sense
description: Situations listed: (1) You are a registered patent agent or attorney already; (2) the invention is simple and the claims are narrow on purpose (e.g., a defensive publication might be more appropriate); (3) you are using the application as a learning exercise and do not need enforceability; (4) you intend to use it as a marker for a 'patent pending' status while you raise money for a real attorney.
guidance: Only consider pro se if you clearly accept the tradeoffs (reduced enforcement likelihood, greater procedural risk) and your objective matches one of the listed situations. For defensive or educational purposes, pro se can be reasonable; for enforceable commercial protection, prefer counsel.

name: Hybrid approach: pay for high-value tasks
description: Common middle path: pay an attorney for (a) a prior art search, (b) drafting the independent claims, (c) drafting the technical figures, then file the rest pro se.
guidance: This approach captures most drafting value at a lower cost (roughly $5,000–$8,000 vs. $20,000) while retaining some cost savings. Use counsel for tasks where practitioner experience materially affects outcome (search, claim drafting, figures/spec support for amendments).

name: Provisional-then-hire-counsel trap (write provisional as final spec)
description: Trap: "Filing a thin provisional pro se to 'get the date,' planning to retain counsel later for the non-provisional, often backfires."
guidance: If you cannot afford counsel for the provisional, write the provisional 'as if it were a final spec' — include figures, multiple embodiments, ranges, and alternatives. That preserves priority support for later claims and avoids losing substantive rights when counsel is retained later.

name: Avoid introducing useless ingredients or steps
description: If the specification inserts ingredients or steps which are unnecessary to produce the claimed effect, and the patentee never used them, the patent may be avoided.
guidance: Examples: Arkwright (extra parts introduced but not necessary); Turner's patent where extra ingredients were listed that did not produce the desired effect — insertion of unnecessary details can render the patent void because it fails to put the public in possession of the invention.

name: Burden when patentee improves after issuance
description: If a patentee employs an improved mode of working different from the specification, he may bear the burden of showing the improvement was made after issuing of the patent; otherwise it may be presumed he withheld the best mode.
guidance: Contrastingly, if a patentee claims as his invention a part that turns out useless but did not describe it as essential, that may not vitiate the patent. The facts determine whether a later improvement undermines the specification's sufficiency.

name: When improvement is the invention, confine claim to the improvement
description: The description of an improvement, when the improvement is the real subject-matter of the patent, should clearly show that the improvement only is claimed by the patentee.
guidance: If a machine substantially existed before and the patentee makes an improvement, the patent should not comprehend the whole machine in its improved state but should be confined to the improvement, even if the addition produces the same effects better or creates new combinations.

name: Recite prior use when claiming an improvement
