description: If the invention is an improvement but nothing is said of previous use, the patent may be construed as a claim of an entire and original discovery; accordingly there is a necessity for reciting what had formerly been done and describing the different mode as the improvement claimed.
guidance: Failure to qualify an improvement with a recital of prior art or prior use may render the claim broader than intended and risk invalidity (illustrated by Brooks v. Bicknell and cases concerning lime applied to iron).

name: Statutory requirement to explain principle and several modes
description: In case of any machine, the patentee shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle, and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his own invention.
guidance: By 'principle' is meant the peculiar structure and mode of operation; the statute presumes the patentee should point out all modes of applying the principle which he claims to cover, whether preferred or mere formal variations.

name: Avoid claiming an abstract principle or mere function
description: A patentee cannot appropriate a mere abstract principle, law of nature, or function by stating it without giving a practical application — the discovery of a principle alone is not an invention in patent-law sense.
guidance: If the principle is applied to any special purpose producing a practical result, the patent may be good. The specification must apply the principle to matter organized to produce a practical result; otherwise it will be treated as claiming an unpatentable abstract principle (see Barrett v. Hall; Househill Co. v. Neilson).

name: Describe a practical mode of carrying the principle into effect
description: It is essential that the specification describe some practical mode of carrying the principle into effect; the subject-matter becomes patentable when it is the mode of carrying the principle into effect rather than the principle itself.
guidance: Once a practical mode is described, on infringement the jury decides whether another mode is a colorable imitation of the patentee's mode. Examples where specification was sustained only when construed as claiming the specific machinery described.

name: Do not claim all possible means of achieving the effect (overbroad universal claims are void)
description: A claim that asserts the art of producing an effect by any means (e.g., 'to cut ice of a uniform size by means of an apparatus worked by any other power than human') is an overbroad claim to an abstract principle and is utterly void.
guidance: Claims must identify practical means or specific apparatus; overbroad 'by any means' claims will be struck down (example: Wyeth v. Stone). Courts will construe to the specific machinery or mode actually described when possible.

name: Claim construction — courts will treat vague functional claims as specific machinery if possible
description: When a specification appears to claim a function in the abstract, courts will, if possible, construe the claim as limited to the particular machinery or combination specially described.
guidance: Illustrations: claims framed as 'communication of motion ... which is produced as follows' were sustained only as claims to the specific machinery so described; broad functional drafting would otherwise be void.

name: Generic computer components insufficient
description: Reciting generic computer hardware, field-of-use limitations, servers/clients, GUIs, or 'parallel processing' without claiming anything different from existing systems does not render claims patent eligible.
guidance: Multiple decisions state that mere inclusion of a 'processor,' 'receiver,' server/client, or conventional architecture is inadequate; claim must specify an improvement other than generic computer implementation.

name: Read claims as a whole
description: The eligibility inquiry requires that the claims be read 'as a whole' rather than dissected into individual elements in isolation.
guidance: Cited explicitly in Data Engine Techs. 'The eligibility inquiry requires that the claims be read as a whole.' This affects both step one (directed to) and step two (inventive concept) analyses.

name: Conventionality / well-understood, routine, previously known
description: If claim limitations are well-understood, routine, and previously known to the industry, they do not supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Courts repeatedly reject assertions of inventive concept where the steps are 'conventional,' 'functional in nature,' or 'merely conventional steps that are well-understood, routine, and previously known to the industry.'

name: Claims that merely implement human practices on computers
description: Claims that simply recite longstanding human practices (e.g., budgeting, cataloging, upselling, auctions, business transactions, teaching) as implemented on a computer are directed to abstract ideas and lack inventive concept.
guidance: Many district court holdings treat computerized implementations of traditional human/commercial practices as abstract—e.g., loyalty award conversion, mortgage paydown strategies, auctions, broadcasting content, crowdfunding, etc.

name: Preemption concern and overly broad claim scope
description: Claims that could 'foreclose fields of research beyond the actual invention' or broadly preempt concrete applications of an idea weigh against eligibility.
guidance: Amdocs and other cases warn that overly general claims reciting conventional operations in broad terms risk invalidation because they could preempt too much ground.

name: Claim language that 'simply instructs the practitioner to implement the abstract idea on a generic computer' is invalid
description: Claims that effectively tell a practitioner to perform an abstract idea using a generic computer are insufficient to pass Alice step two.
guidance: E.g., diet behavior modification system and others were invalidated for doing no more than instructing implementation of an abstract idea on a generic computer.

name: Specific technical improvements vs. information-processing improvements
description: Claims that effect a specific technical improvement in how computers operate are more likely eligible than claims that merely improve abstract information-processing or presentation.
guidance: Data Engine's 'flip through' spreadsheet navigation produced a finding of non-abstract because it improved computer functionality; by contrast, claims that merely 'present the graphic user interface as merely a generic computer component' failed.

name: Claims that 'identify and store' or 'create base and new versions and determine changes' are routine
description: Claims that recite routine data-keeping steps (creating base version, creating new version, determining changes) are likely directed to an abstract idea and lack inventive concept.
guidance: Data Engine and other cases found such spreadsheet-tracking/record-keeping claims ineligible because they recited generic, routine steps.

name: Expert/specialized terminology does not overcome genericity absent specifics
description: Using specialized-sounding words or invoking 'technology used to improve communications' is insufficient without claim limitations describing how the technology is different from conventional practice.
guidance: Courts have rejected 'conclusory legal assertions' and expert declarations that merely assert advantages or novelty without tying limitations to specific technological improvements.

name: Specification must convey possession to skilled artisan
description: To satisfy the written description requirement, a patent specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Cite Moba v. Diamond Automation, Vas-Cath. This is the central substantive standard; the inquiry is fact-based and depends on nature of the invention (Enzo Biochem).

name: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas
description: An applicant shows possession of the claimed invention by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using such descriptive means as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession may also be shown by actual reduction to practice or by showing invention was 'ready for patenting' (drawings, structural or chemical formulas). Cite Lockwood; Pfaff; Amgen v. Chugai.

name: Original claims presumed to have adequate written description, subject to examiner's prima facie showing
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; examiner has initial burden to present evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure describes the claimed invention.
guidance: Cite In re Wertheim. Examiner may make a prima facie case by pointing out unsupported claim limitations and explaining why the disclosure does not show possession (Hyatt v. Dudas example).

name: Preamble and transitional phrase weighting in support analysis
description: The preamble language and transitional terms affect claim scope and the support required in the specification; 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate, and 'consisting of' is closed.
guidance: If applicant relies on a narrower meaning, applicant bears burden to show why; for prior-art purposes 'consisting essentially of' may be treated as 'comprising' absent clear specification language (PPG Industries).

name: Combination limitations must be supported as a combination
description: Even if individual elements are described, the specification must adequately describe the claimed particular combination of elements to show possession of that combination.
guidance: Examiner should explicitly point out lack of description of combination (Hyatt v. Dudas). Stored Value Solutions example (three authorization codes) shows each code may be described individually but not their combination.

name: New or amended claims cannot introduce new matter; must be supported in original disclosure
description: New or amended claim limitations that introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement (and the proscription against new matter).
guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent. Correction of obvious errors may be permissible if a person skilled in the art would recognize and correct the error (In re Oda). See MPEP §§ 2163.06–.07 for details.

name: Omission of an essential or critical feature undermines possession
description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential or critical to the invention as described in the specification may fail written description because the inventor did not convey possession of the broader claim.
guidance: Cite Gentry Gallery, PIN/NIP, Tronzo v. Biomet. If specification describes a feature as 'the only possible location' or 'essential', omitting it can be fatal.

name: Functional-only descriptions of biomolecule/genetic sequences are generally insufficient
description: A biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic, without any known or disclosed correlation between that function and the structure, normally is not a sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes.
guidance: Functional descriptions that lack structural correlation (e.g., claiming sequence by function alone) typically fail; see In re Bell, In re Deuel and related discussion. See MPEP §2106 for subject matter eligibility guidance.

name: Deposits of biological materials can help but do not substitute for written description
description: A deposit of biological material may satisfy written description with respect to a claimed material, but a deposit is not a substitute for a written description of the claimed invention; the written description of the deposited material must be as complete as possible.
guidance: Cite Enzo Biochem; 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; Final Rule discussion. Deposits made after filing generally cannot support additions or corrections to the filed disclosure; see MPEP and 37 CFR 1.804 conditions for corrections.

name: Examiner methodology — identify unsupported claim limitations and explain reasons
description: After a thorough reading of the application, the examiner must point out the claim limitations that are not adequately supported and explain reasons why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure to make a prima facie case.
guidance: Examiner need not present factual evidence but must make clear why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as describing the claimed invention (Hyatt v. Dudas). If examiner establishes prima facie, burden shifts to applicant to point to support or amend.

name: Applicant's procedural burden when amending claims
description: When applicant amends claims, applicant should point out where and how the originally filed disclosure supports the amendment; if applicant does so but disclosure still does not reasonably convey possession, examiner must explain why.
guidance: Cite MPEP §§ 2163.04–2163.06 and Hyatt. A simple statement by examiner identifying unsupported limitation(s) may be sufficient in some cases.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (general consideration)
description: Determine whether additional element(s) are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the industry; this consideration is evaluated in Step 2B of the eligibility analysis and, if present at a high level, does not favor eligibility.
guidance: If the additional element is a specific limitation that is unconventional/non-routine and confines the claim to a particular useful application, it favors eligibility. If the additional element is no more than well-known, routine, conventional activity recited at a high level, it generally does not amount to significantly more. Examples: DDR Holdings (additional elements favored eligibility because they modified conventional Internet protocol behavior); Mayo (measuring metabolite levels was routine and thus not inventive).

name: Life-science/laboratory techniques recognized as well-understood/routine/conventional (examples)
description: Courts have recognized certain lab techniques as well‑understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically or as insignificant extra‑solution activity.
guidance: Examples: (i) determining biomarker levels in blood by any means; (ii) using PCR to amplify/detect DNA; (iii) detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample; (iv) immunizing a patient; (v) analyzing DNA sequence or allelic variants; (vi) freezing and thawing cells; (vii) amplifying and sequencing nucleic acids; (viii) hybridizing a gene probe. Generic recitation of these techniques may not add significantly more.

name: Other activities courts have found routine/conventional (examples)
description: Other non-technical activities have been recognized by courts as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed at a high level or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples: recording a customer's order; shuffling/dealing a standard deck of cards; restricting public access by requiring viewing an advertisement; presenting offers and gathering statistics; determining estimated outcomes and setting price; arranging hierarchies, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing info and determining price. These generic activities alone typically do not render a claim significantly more.

name: Multiple independent claim sets / dependency groups
description: Include multiple independent claim sets directed to different aspects of the invention (e.g., apparatus, a key element, method), producing multiple dependency groups within the same application.
guidance: Example: draft an apparatus claim, a claim focusing on the novel element (lead–gold zapper), method claims for the element, and perhaps a process claim for the overall purpose. You can also create alternative independent claim sets by incorporating dependent features to focus on different points of novelty. Only pursue alternative claim sets when each truly represents independent novelty of commercial significance or when prior art is unclear.

name: Draft dependent claims from removed/altered elements
description: When broadening a claim, retain eliminated or altered elements as dependent claims to provide fallback positions.
guidance: Look back over edits made while seeking the broadest claim and add dependent claims from elements removed. Not every removed element is worth keeping, but the full set of dependent claims should draw from removed/altered elements to preserve fallback options.

name: Check inventor's envisioned scope before broadening
description: Before drafting the broadest possible claims, verify whether the inventor envisioned a viable, narrower scope for the invention.
guidance: If the inventor insists the invention is specific (e.g., a car with three wheels), draft narrow claims aligned with the inventor's expectations. If the inventor sees adaptability or you foresee adaptation by infringers, draft broader claims to cover such variants. The drafter can help the client recognize the invention's potential.

name: Conciseness / avoid undue repetition
description: Claims may be required by some jurisdictions to be 'concise' both individually and in the aggregate; unnecessary repetition should be avoided.
guidance: Avoid undue repetition of wording between claims by using dependent claim form. Be mindful examiners may object to multiple trivial claims; the reasonable number of claims depends on each case. Where jurisdictions impose limits on claim numbers, recognize those administrative limits and advise the client accordingly.

name: Clarity and careful word choice
description: Words used in claims must capture the invention in specific form and variants; wording must be chosen so the meaning and scope are clear to the person skilled in the art.
guidance: Imagine yourself as a potential infringer and draft to cover likely workarounds. Avoid ambiguity that would lead to unintended interpretations by examiners or courts. Use plain language where it suffices and draft terminology to cover the intended scope.

name: Define unfamiliar or alternative term meanings
description: If terms are unfamiliar or used in an unfamiliar way, define them in the description and ensure the meaning is clear in the claims.
guidance: Definitions may depart from literal meanings but should not depart from established meanings in the art. Ensure definitions provided are appropriate for the circumstances and that claims remain self-contained (understandable without reference to the description, although the description may guide interpretation).

name: Same element – same term – same numeral
description: Use the same term and the same reference numeral consistently for a single element throughout the application.
guidance: If several synonymous terms exist, cite all synonyms on first mention and confirm which will be used consistently. Define abbreviations in full on first instance and then use the same abbreviation thereafter. Because claims must be self-contained, establish consistency if abbreviations appear in claims.

name: Care with prepositions like 'in'
description: Using 'in' (and similar prepositions) to define relationships can make it unclear whether protection is sought for a subunit or the whole unit.
guidance: Prefer drafting claims to a 'unit with (or comprising) a subunit' or to the 'subunit as such, specifying its purpose' (e.g., 'cylinder head for a four-stroke engine'). Consider whether 'in' unnecessarily limits scope before using it.

name: Identify and address apparently essential features
description: If a feature in the description appears essential to performance but is not claimed, examiners may object; conversely independent claims may include apparently inessential features.
guidance: The drafter should ensure essential features are claimed or the description adjusted. The examiner flags claims that are 'too broad' but will not generally advise when claims are unduly narrow—it's the drafter's duty to seek broad protection.

name: Support requirement: description must support claims
description: There must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim; the description and drawings must support the claims.
guidance: Support does not mean identical wording, but claims are typically not interpreted broader than the description and drawings. Anticipate narrower elements you may later need by embedding support in the description at the outset. Examples: don't claim applicability to all plant seedlings if description applies to one; restrict claims if evidence lacking for broader generalization.

name: Jurisdictional variations on clarity/support
description: Practice on clarity and support varies by jurisdiction (e.g., US, EPO, Japan) and affects claim drafting.
guidance: US: indefiniteness often objected when lack of antecedent basis exists. EPC: independent claims must recite essential technical features and the description must disclose problem-solution-effect; excessive claims or lack of reference signs can cause objections. Japan: product-by-process claims may be unclear unless structural/characteristic elements cannot be used. For therapeutic functional claims, provide testable criteria or experimental tests so skilled person can recognize scope.

name: KISS: brevity, plain language, short sentences
description: Draft patent applications with clarity and brevity—use plain language, short sentences, and avoid redundant expressions.
guidance: Compare verbose drafts with revised concise versions. Keep claims and description readable without unnecessary verbosity. This aids examination and enforcement.

name: Draft for variations and alternative embodiments
description: Constantly consider variations (embodiments) of the invention and include alternative embodiments that perform the same function to broaden protection.
guidance: Imagine potential infringer workarounds and include those variants in the description and claims. Example: draft claims for 'pencil', 'crayon', then broader 'writing implement'. Be mindful of client budget when drafting many alternatives.

name: Avoid unnecessary limitations; remove inessential elements
description: Review claims to delete unnecessary limitations and arrive at the invention's essence to achieve the broadest appropriate claim.
guidance: One technique: draft a single extended claim listing reasonable elements for an embodiment, then eliminate inessential elements. Supplement that broad claim with sets of claims of different scope that reintroduce some elements. Avoid omnibus claims that simply refer to the description or drawings, except in rare, justified cases (peculiar shapes or chemical features definable only by graphs).

name: Use multiple claim types where appropriate
description: If the invention can be claimed in different statutory forms (e.g., method, apparatus, product), claim it in multiple forms to maximize protection.
guidance: Draft system/apparatus claims and corresponding method claims where feasible (example: Internet search system and a method for performing an Internet search). Different claim types capture different infringing activities and can provide broader coverage.

name: Claims must overcome known prior art
description: Prepare claims that distinguish and overcome any prior art the drafter or applicant knows about.
guidance: Claims should be drafted with the prior art landscape in mind so that novelty and inventive step can be established. Anticipate examiner objections and prepare fallback claim language supported by the description.

name: Do not claim things without support / avoid over-claiming
description: A patent drafter must not claim subject matter they cannot show falls within the invention; claims beyond support risk invalidity or objection.
guidance: The support requirement protects the public and the applicant. If variants are reasonably expected to have the properties ascribed in the description, they may be claimed; otherwise restrict claims or provide evidence. Examples provided: restrict plant seedling claims to disclosed species; restrict resin claims to thermoplastics if only thermoplastics are disclosed; include additives where described if they are essential to the claimed property.

name: Machine-or-transformation test is not the sole test
description: Although useful and important, the machine-or-transformation test has never been the exclusive test for § 101 patentability.
guidance: Benson rejects treating the test as the only pathway to process patentability. Courts should consider claims 'as a whole' and not rigidly exclude processes that do not literally transform an article or recite a particular machine. The Federal Circuit erred where it treated the test as the exclusive standard.

name: Business methods are not patentable 'processes' under §101
description: A series of steps for conducting business—i.e., business methods—are not, in themselves, 'processes' within the meaning of § 101 and historically were not considered patentable.
guidance: Supported by historical evidence from English and early American practice, treatises, and Supreme Court reasoning; courts should be cautious about treating business organization, management techniques, or methods of conducting commerce as patentable subject matter. Examples/anti-patterns: patents directed merely to business organization or financial techniques (without more) are properly excluded. The State Street decision and later developments are discussed as departures or limited decisions addressing machines/software claims rather than pure business methods.

name: Use of a generic computer does not make an abstract idea patent-eligible
description: Merely requiring generic computer implementation of an abstract idea fails to transform that abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
guidance: From Alice: a computer-implemented scheme for intermediated settlement was held drawn to an abstract idea; generic computer implementation added nothing inventive. Anti-pattern: drafting claims that tack on a 'computer' or 'server' without adding a specific improvement in computer technology will not save an otherwise abstract claim.

name: Consider claims 'as a whole' when evaluating §101
description: A process claim meets § 101 when, considered as a whole, it performs a function the patent laws were designed to protect (for example, transforming or reducing an article to a different state or thing).
guidance: Courts should not dissect claims into insubstantial post-solution activity; holistic analysis (Diehr) can show that a claim embodies patentable subject matter even if some elements are abstract when isolated. Conversely, holistic analysis can reveal when the claim is essentially an abstract idea.

name: Risk of vagueness and breadth for business method patents
description: Business method patents tend to be broad, intangible, and potentially vague, making it costly and time-consuming to search, negotiate licenses, and avoid infringement.
guidance: Because clarity is essential to promote progress, patents that claim intangible, widely-applicable steps can impose high informational and transaction costs on industry and may enable bullying litigation even when ultimately invalid. Anti-pattern: granting broad, high-level patents that cover 'big ideas' near the top of the knowledge pyramid.

name: Novelty, nonobviousness, and written-description requirements cannot alone confine §101
description: The requirements of novelty, nonobviousness, and particular description (e.g., § 112) cannot be relied upon to rescue § 101 from overbroad or absurd results; they do not substitute for proper subject-matter limits.
guidance: Even if a claim is novel or nonobvious, it might still be an improper subject for a patent if it falls into excluded categories (abstract idea, law of nature). Historical examples show many human activities could be novel yet inappropriate for patent monopolies.

name: Claims: scope, completeness, and construction
description: Claim is 'the life of' the patent; claim completeness affects patent value and scope.
guidance: Claims must be complete; excessive claims may render a patent defective. Claim language determines scope; courts construe patents liberally to sustain validity if possible. In combination claims, all claimed elements are essential. Value to patentee depends on completeness of claims; clerical errors and name errors have specific effects; claim identity must be preserved through amendments.

name: Patent Office examination and duties
description: Functions, duties, powers, and limitations of the Patent Office and Commissioner.
guidance: The Patent Office exists to secure correct and lawful letters-patent and has duty to see that claims are correct; rules of practice are statutory and the Commissioner has power to make rules. The Office cannot decide title questions, cannot repeal letters-patent, and has limited jurisdiction (e.g., no jurisdiction over abandoned patents). Proceedings in the Office are presumed regular; evidence and motions have specific procedures; appeals and new trials within the Office have defined rules.

name: Means-plus-function claiming ('means'/'mechanism')
description: Use of 'means', 'mechanism', and similar words in claims when proper.
guidance: Words like 'means' and 'mechanism' are permissible in claims when appropriate; there are rules about their use (e.g., in claims for combinations) and their consequences for claim scope and interpretation.

name: Combination claims and essential elements
description: Claims for combinations make all claimed elements essential; relationship to improvements and prior patents.
guidance: A patent for a combination treats claimed elements as essential; improvements cannot claim what is already covered by a prior patent's original. A patent for part(s) of a previously patented whole may be valid while a combination of previously patented elements cannot claim those elements anew.

name: Patent as contract and nature of patent privilege
description: PATENT as a contract between inventor and the public; PATENT PRIVILEGE defined as a lawful monopoly.
guidance: Patent privilege is a derogation of common right and is measured by the claim. It is a contract granting a lawful monopoly for a limited period in exchange for disclosure. The nature, scope, and justification (public policy, reward, stimulus) of patent privilege are doctrinally significant; rights are created at issue of letters-patent and governed by statutes and Constitution.

name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) — use and limits
description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
guidance: Key points: The streamlined analysis may be used for efficiency but should not be used when there is doubt as to whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for a judicial exception — then the full Alice/Mayo test should be conducted. The results of the streamlined analysis will always be the same as the full analysis; it is not a way to avoid a finding of ineligibility that would occur under the full test. If eligibility is self-evident when viewed as a whole (e.g., clear improvement to technology/computer functionality), the claim is eligible at Pathway A. In practice, use of Pathway A may be reflected by absence of an eligibility rejection or clarifying remarks in the record.

name: Eligibility is self-evident — when to apply
description: A streamlined eligibility analysis can be used for a claim that may or may not recite a judicial exception but, when viewed as a whole, clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it.
guidance: Illustrative situations: claims to complex manufactured industrial products or processes that recite meaningful limitations along with a judicial exception (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system using mathematical relationships), nature-based products that clearly do not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (e.g., artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral), and claims that merely include ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with an electrical contact made of gold). If a claim is a 'close call' on whether it improves technology or computer functionality, perform full eligibility analysis (see BASCOM example).

name: Clear improvement to technology or to computer functionality
description: Some improvements to technology or to computer functionality are not abstract when appropriately claimed, and thus claims to such improvements do not always need to undergo the full eligibility analysis.
guidance: Case guidance: Enfish (self‑referential table for a computer database held eligible), McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial expression animation found eligible as an improvement). If claims clearly improve computer-related technology or other technologies/technological processes, eligibility may be self-evident (Pathway A) or they may be found not directed to an abstract idea at Step 2A (Pathway B). When the claims present a close call (e.g., BASCOM), proceed to the full Alice/Mayo analysis.

name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and the record as a whole
description: Eligibility rejections must be based on failure to comply with the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent. Examiners should review the record as a whole before reaching a conclusion.
guidance: Examination should consider the specification, claims, prosecution history, and relevant case law precedent or prior art. Examination of eligibility should be claim‑by‑claim because dependent claims may add limitations that change eligibility. Examination guidance, training, and examples do not themselves serve as a basis for a rejection. Examiners must set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility when concluding a claim is more likely than not ineligible, explaining why clearly and specifically so applicant can respond.

name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify the judicial exception recited in the claim
description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception.
guidance: When the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception, explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why the described subject matter is a judicial exception. For abstract ideas, identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it falls within the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2). See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information relevant to Step 2A.

name: Step 2B — Explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more (inventive concept)
description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: If the examiner concludes certain claim elements recite well‑understood, routine, conventional activities in the relevant field, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III. See MPEP §§ 2106.05 et seq. for guidance on searching for an inventive concept and applying Step 2B.

name: Formulating an Office action rejection — required content and adequacy
description: When making a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, the Office action must provide an explanation as to why each claim is unpatentable that is sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice and enable effective response.
guidance: The rejection should provide an explanation for each part of the Step 2 analysis (Prong One, Prong Two, and Step 2B) and specifically point to claim elements and explain the reasons for the examiner's conclusions. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for details. Under the prima facie concept, the initial burden is on the examiner to explain ineligibility clearly and specifically.

name: Compact prosecution and consideration of other patentability requirements
description: Regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under each of the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and issues of utility, inventorship, double patenting).
guidance: Examiners should state all non‑cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action. Thus, include all applicable rejections (e.g., anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement, utility, inventorship, double patenting) even if a 101 rejection is also made.

name: Reject clear non-statutory claims at Step 1
description: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) (Step 1: NO), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating the claim is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05 and 7.05.01) and MPEP §706.03(a). However, if the specification suggests the claim could be amended to be statutory, proceed to analyze such an amended claim's eligibility and recommend amendment as a best practice.

name: Identify judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena)
description: Claims that are directed to nothing more than abstract ideas (e.g., mathematical algorithms), laws of nature, and natural phenomena are not eligible for patent protection.
guidance: Courts have described these exceptions with various overlapping terms (physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied concepts). There are no bright lines between exception types; it is sufficient for analysis to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. See MPEP §2106.04(a)/(b) for detailed discussions.

name: Step 2A core inquiry — does the claim recite a judicial exception?
description: Step 2A asks whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea. A claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception when such an exception is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim language.
guidance: ‘Recite’ covers different ways an exception can appear: it can be explicitly set forth (e.g., Diehr’s mathematical equation in a claim step), included in a wherein clause (Mayo), or described conceptually (Alice described intermediated settlement without using the exact words). Treat the claim as a whole when performing Step 2A. If Step 2A: NO (not directed to an exception), the claim is eligible at Pathway B. If Step 2A: YES, proceed to Step 2B to determine whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception itself.

name: Distinguish reciting an exception from merely involving one
description: Examiners must distinguish claims that recite an exception (which require further eligibility analysis) from claims that merely involve an exception (which are eligible and do not require further analysis).
guidance: Example reciting an exception: 'A machine comprising elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' (recites law of nature -> Step 2A: YES). Example merely involving an exception: a teeter-totter claim that is based on the law of the lever but does not recite the natural principle (-> Step 2A: NO). Evaluate the claim as a whole and focus on whether the exception is actually set forth in claim language.

name: Do not improperly parse or split a recited exception
description: Unless distinct, examiners should not parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions; related concepts (e.g., manipulation of information through a series of mental steps) should be considered a single abstract idea for analysis.
guidance: However, if a claim does recite multiple distinct exceptions (even if related), it is directed to at least one judicial exception and requires Step 2B analysis. See RecogniCorp v. Nintendo for an example where multiple abstract ideas were treated as a single abstract idea and subjected to Step 2B.

name: How to identify abstract ideas (two-step approach)
description: To determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea, examiners should (1) identify the claimed concept (the specific claim limitation(s) believed to be an abstract idea), and (2) compare that concept to concepts previously identified as abstract ideas by the courts.
guidance: If the claimed concept is similar to concepts previously identified as abstract ideas, it is reasonable to conclude the concept is an abstract idea (Step 2A: YES), requiring Step 2B analysis. If it is not similar and no basis exists to treat it as an abstract idea, the claim is not directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B unless another exception is recited.

name: What does NOT qualify as an improvement to computer functionality
description: Mere automation of manual processes, performance improvements that arise solely from using a general-purpose computer, claims that can be performed without a computer, or claims that merely implement an idea on generic components do not show an improvement in computer functionality.
guidance: Examples/cases: Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics (method performable mentally; not an improvement in a computer), FairWarning IP v. Iatric Systems and Credit Acceptance v. Westlake (mere automation or speed by generic computers insufficient), Affinity Labs and TLI Communications (claims using conventional implementation on generic components insufficient). Examiners should look for more than conventional implementation on generic machinery to find an improvement.

name: Resolve improvement question early where possible
description: Examiners are encouraged to resolve whether a claim reflects an improvement to computer-related technology as early as possible in the eligibility analysis (Step 2A or even Pathway A).
guidance: A clear improvement (e.g., Enfish) could justify finding eligibility at Pathway A under a streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea. If the improvement is not clear enough for Step 2A, it may still contribute to the Step 2B analysis. Examiners should evaluate specification and claim together under the BRI to determine whether an improvement is present.

name: Window of vulnerability / eligibility for IPR
description: IPRs: all patents are eligible and there is no general deadline for filing an IPR. However, if the patent has at least one AIA claim, the Petitioner must wait to file until the later of nine months after issuance (or re-issuance) or termination of any PGR on the patent.
guidance: If the Petitioner has been served with a complaint for patent infringement, a strict one-year deadline to file a petition applies (35 U.S.C. §315(b)).

name: Types of attacks permitted
description: IPR: the only attacks a Petitioner can make are anticipation (35 U.S.C. §102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103) based upon patents and printed publications. PGR: in addition to anticipation and obviousness, a Petitioner can attack based on lack of written description (35 U.S.C. §112), indefiniteness (35 U.S.C. §112), lack of enablement (35 U.S.C. §112), and eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101).
guidance: Under certain circumstances the PTAB may address eligibility of proposed amended claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 (see Uniloc2017LLC v. Hulu LLC precedent).

name: Institution thresholds and burdens
description: For an IPR to be instituted, the Petition must demonstrate a reasonable likelihood that the Petitioner will prevail as to at least one challenged claim (may encompass a 50/50 chance). For a PGR to be instituted, the Petition must demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (greater than 50% chance).
guidance: The burden of proof in IPRs and PGRs is 'preponderance of the evidence' (lighter burden) whereas in district court and ITC it is 'clear and convincing' (heavier burden).

name: Petition formal and substantive requirements
description: A Petition is a written document that may only attack one patent and must set forth the grounds for standing, the claim(s) attacked, the statutory grounds for the attack, how the claims are to be construed, and how/why the construed claim is unpatentable.
guidance: Petitions must identify real parties-in-interest, related matters, lead and back-up counsel, and service information, and are typically supported by one or more expert declarations and exhibits. Petitions have word limits: 14,000 words for IPRs and 18,700 words for PGRs.

name: Motions to amend: availability and burdens
description: Patent Owners have the option to propose substitute claims (generally on a claim-for-claim basis), but Motions to Amend are rarely granted.
guidance: Rules (amended Jan 2021): Patent Owner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the motion to amend complies' with statutory/regulatory requirements; Petitioner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.' The Board may exercise discretion to grant or deny a motion to amend only for reasons 'supported by readily identifiable and persuasive evidence of record.'

name: Estoppel effects on district court proceedings
description: If an IPR or PGR results in a Final Written Decision, a Petitioner (or real party in interest or privy of the Petitioner) may not assert in district court or in the ITC that any claim 'is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised' during the IPR or PGR (35 U.S.C. §§315(e)(2), 325(e)(2)).
guidance: Because PTAB now institutes on 'all challenged claims, all grounds' basis, instituted trials can have broad estoppel effects. If trial is not instituted, those grounds may be raised in district court.

name: Petition word limits and single-patent requirement
description: Petitions have word limits (14,000 words for IPRs and 18,700 words for PGRs) and may only attack one patent.
guidance: Adhere to word limits and single-patent restriction; supporting declarations and exhibits are typical and must be tailored to the claimed grounds.

name: Amendment (glossary)
description: A patent applicant’s change to one or more claims or to the specification either in response to an office action taken by a Patent Examiner or independently by the patent applicant during the patent application examination process.

name: Claim (glossary)
description: Each claim of a patent is a concise, formal definition of an invention and appears at the end of the specification in a separately numbered paragraph. In concept, a patent claim marks the boundaries of the patent ... Claims may be independent or dependent. An independent claim stands alone. A dependent claim does not stand alone and refers to one or more other claims, incorporating whatever the other referenced claim or claims say.

name: Continuation-In-Part (C-I-P) Application (glossary)
description: A patent application filed during the application process of an earlier application which repeats some or all of the earlier application and adds matter not disclosed in the earlier application to support the addition of new patent claims.

name: Elements (glossary)
description: The required parts of a device or the required steps of a method. A device or method infringes a patent if it contains each and every requirement of a patent claim.

name: Examination (glossary)
description: Procedure before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office whereby a Patent Examiner reviews the filed patent application to determine if the claimed invention is patentable.

name: Limitation / Requirement (glossary)
description: A required part of an invention set forth in a patent claim. The word 'limitation' is often used interchangeably with the word 'requirement.'

name: Patent (glossary)
description: A patent is an exclusive right granted by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to an inventor to prevent others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling an invention within the United States, or from importing it into the United States, during the term of the patent. The patent has three parts: a specification, drawings and claims. The patent is granted after examination of a patent application and the examination record is called the prosecution history.

name: Reexamination (glossary)
description: A process in which a patent is reexamined by the PTO to determine whether one or more claims are patentable with respect to submitted prior art (prior patents or printed publications). 'Ex parte' reexamination is initiated by the patent holder or a third party but does not include further participation by any third party. 'Inter partes' reexamination is initiated by a third party who continues to participate.

name: Specification (glossary)
description: A required part of a patent application and an issued patent; it is a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using the claimed invention.

name: Contributory Infringement (jury elements)
description: Has Patent Holder proven that it is more likely than not: (i) that Direct Infringer infringed claim 1; (ii) that Alleged Infringer supplied an important component of the infringing part of the product; (iii) that the component was not a common component suitable for non-infringing use; and (iv) that Alleged Infringer supplied the component with knowledge of the patent and knowledge that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing manner?

name: Inducing Infringement (jury elements)
description: Has Patent Holder proven that it is more likely than not: (i) that Direct Infringer infringed claim 1; (ii) that Alleged Infringer took action that actually induced that infringement by Direct Infringer; and (iii) that Alleged Infringer was aware of the patent and believed that its actions would encourage infringement of a valid patent, or alternatively that it was willfully blind as to whether its actions would encourage infringement of the patent?

name: Written Description Requirement (jury question)
description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that the specification of the Patent Holder’s patent does not contain an adequate written description of the claimed invention?

name: Enablement Requirement (jury question)
description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that the specification of the Patent Holder’s patent does not contain a description of the claimed invention that is sufficiently full and clear to enable persons of ordinary skill in the field to make and use the invention?

name: Anticipation (jury question and checklist)
description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that claim 1 was 'anticipated' (i.e., not new)? If yes, check applicable reasons such as prior public knowledge/use in the U.S. before conception, patented or printed publication anywhere before conception, made by someone else in the U.S. before conception and not abandoned/kept secret, described in another issued U.S. patent or published U.S. application based on an earlier application, or named inventor learned of the claimed invention from someone else/was not first inventor.
guidance: Provide only the specific factual disputes to the jury; the verdict form should list only reasons applicable.

name: Obviousness (Graham factors and jury role alternatives)
description: Jury may be asked to answer preliminary factual questions to assist the court on obviousness: (a) level of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention; (b) scope and content of the prior art; (c) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (d) secondary considerations/factors indicating nonobviousness (commercial success, long-felt need, unsuccessful attempts by others, copying, unexpected/superior results, acceptance by others/licensing, independent invention by others, other factors). Two alternatives are provided: (1) jury decides only the underlying factual issues and the court makes the ultimate legal conclusion on obviousness; or (2) jury answers the factual issues and may give an advisory verdict on the ultimate question of obviousness (but the ultimate judgment is a legal determination for the court).
guidance: Verdict form should require jury's findings on each factual issue so the trial judge may make the final determination; only the disputed factual matters should be presented.

name: Number and type of views
description: Drawings should contain as many figures as necessary to adequately show the claimed invention; views may be plan, elevation, section, perspective, detail or exploded views.
guidance: One figure should not be placed upon or within the outline of another. Use the simplest set of views compatible with fully and unambiguously defining the object (see paragraphs 5.136–5.138).

name: Abstract content: general
description: The abstract should summarise the disclosure as contained in the description, claims and any drawings and indicate the technical field (Rule 8.1(a)).
guidance: Draft to allow a clear understanding of the technical problem, the gist of the solution, and principal uses. Where applicable include the chemical formula that best characterizes the invention. Abstract should be primarily related to what is new in the art. See WIPO Standard ST.12/A for more detail.

name: Abstract must not contain statements of merits or speculative applications
description: The abstract must not contain statements on the alleged merits or value of the claimed invention or on its speculative application (Rule 8.1(c)).
guidance: Keep abstract factual and technical, avoid promotional or speculative language.

name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)
description: An inter partes review may not be instituted unless the information presented in the Petition and any preliminary response shows that 'there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.'
guidance: This is a preliminary standard (not a final determination). If instituted, the Board must address all grounds of unpatentability raised in the petition (see SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu and AC Techs. S.A. v. Amazon.com, Inc.). Institution requires a showing of reasonable likelihood for at least one challenged claim on the current record.

name: Obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) (Graham/KSR)
description: Section 103(a) forbids issuance of a patent when 'the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious' to a person having ordinary skill in the art. The obviousness inquiry involves underlying factual determinations including: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and when presented, (4) objective evidence of non‑obviousness.
guidance: Apply Graham factors and KSR precedent. Evaluate combination teachings (e.g., Wu + Doherty) in light of what a POSITA would find routine or predictable, and include consideration of any objective indicia if presented.

name: Determination of the level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
description: Factors for determining a POSITA include the types of problems encountered in the art, the sophistication of the technology, and the educational level of active workers in the field. One or more factors may predominate. Education and experience can be substitutable.
guidance: The Board adopts a POSITA definition consistent with the record (e.g., petitioner’s expert declaration). Use the POSITA to interpret claim terms and to assess obviousness.

name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/district-court-type; 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
description: In IPRs, the Board interprets claim language using the district-court-type standard described in Phillips: claim terms have their ordinary and customary meaning to a POSITA at the time of invention, in light of the claim language, the specification, and the prosecution history.
guidance: Rely on intrinsic evidence first (claims, spec, prosecution history). Parties may propose constructions but Board need only construe disputed terms as necessary to resolve institution/trial issues.

name: Limit constructions to terms 'in controversy' and 'to the extent necessary' (Nidec/Vivid)
description: The Board (and courts) need only construe terms that are in controversy, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy.
guidance: Avoid unnecessary claim construction at institution; construe additional terms later if needed for trial.

name: Preliminary-record sufficiency and the role of the Institution Decision
description: An Institution Decision assesses the petition on the current preliminary record and determines whether there is a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one claim; it is not a final decision on patentability.
guidance: The Board's institution determination is based on the petition, preliminary response, and associated evidence/declarations. Institution triggers the trial timeline but does not resolve ultimate patentability.

name: Specific example of claim-meaning guidance (interpretation of 'change a predetermined advertisement insertion point')
description: For purposes of this proceeding, the limitation 'change a predetermined advertisement insertion point ... in response to receiving a user input to update a current play position to a new play position' at least includes skipping over a predetermined ad insertion point to ultimately arrive at a different ad insertion point in response to the user activity.
guidance: Interpret claims in light of the specification and prosecution history but do not limit claims to a single example; the Board explained that the specification contemplates placing ad blocks between tracks or immediately before resuming play after a user-directed skip, and that limitation 1.e includes skipping over an insertion point to a different insertion point.

name: Restrictions on amendments and evidence after RAN and after filing an appeal
description: 37 CFR 1.116(d)(1) states that no amendment other than canceling claims (where such cancellation does not affect scope of other pending claims) can be made after the RAN in an inter partes reexamination except as provided by 37 CFR 1.981 or 41.77(b)(1). 37 CFR 1.116(f) bars affidavits or other evidence after the RAN except as provided. After filing an appeal (37 CFR 41.63), only certain canceling amendments and limited other submissions may be admitted under narrow reopening provisions.
guidance: An amendment filed after the RAN will not be entered absent a grantable 1.183 petition. After the date of filing an appeal, amendments canceling claims may be admitted (37 CFR 41.63(a)) where cancellation does not affect scope of other pending claims; other amendments and affidavits/declarations/exhibits filed after appeal generally will not be admitted except as permitted by reopening prosecution under 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1).

name: Appeal timing, notice of appeal content, and procedural requirements (37 CFR 41.61 and related)
description: Upon issuance of a RAN, the owner and requester have one month or thirty days (whichever is longer) to file a notice of appeal to the Board; the notice must identify the appealed claim(s), be signed by the party or authorized representative, and be accompanied by the fee. Time periods for filing notice of appeal or cross appeal may not be extended.
guidance: An appeal must be taken from all the rejections (for owner) or all determinations favorable to patentability (for requester) which the appealing party proposes to contest. If a notice of appeal or cross appeal is timely filed but defective, appellant will be notified of reasons for non-compliance and given a non-extendable time to file an amended notice; failure to correct will result in dismissal. If notice of appeal filed before RAN, it will be placed in the file but not considered. Forms (e.g., PTOL-2067) should be used for notifications of defects.

name: Third-party requester estoppel (35 U.S.C. 315(c))
description: A third-party requester whose inter partes reexamination request results in an order under section 313 is estopped from asserting in later civil actions the invalidity of any claim finally determined to be valid and patentable on any ground which the requester raised or could have raised during the reexamination.
guidance: This estoppel does not prevent assertion of invalidity based on newly discovered prior art unavailable to the requester and the Office at the time of the reexamination proceedings. Examiners and deciding officials should be mindful of this when considering petitions and decisions.

name: Art (category)
description: The term 'art' has been defined broadly as the application of knowledge to effect a desired result; alternatively defined more narrowly as 'an act or series of acts performed by some physical agent upon some physical object and producing in such object some change either of character or of condition.'
guidance: Courts have offered both broad and narrower constructions; context and purposive interpretation will determine whether a claimed practice qualifies as an 'art.'

name: Claims should include key compounds and structural derivatives
description: In the pharmaceutical industry, claims should include key compounds and all structural derivatives that are likely to have the same effects.
guidance: This is achieved by using Markush structures that describe a common core scaffold plus variable R groups to capture structural derivatives for broad protection.

name: Use Markush structures to describe series of compounds
description: Markush structures describe a series of chemical compounds having a common core structure and variable substituents called R groups.
guidance: When drafting composition claims, represent a set of analogs as a scaffold with defined R groups to capture related compounds in a single claim.

name: Ensure novelty by searching prior art using Markush queries
description: To ensure the novelty of a new composition patent, one needs to make sure that no compound in the claims is taken by prior arts. Performing a structure search using the Markush structure as input is the most efficient method.
guidance: Use large chemical patent databases (example given: SureChEMBL) to perform Markush-based structure searches rather than only exact-structure searches; incorporate these searches into claim-drafting workflow to avoid claiming known compounds.

name: Maximize patent coverage by adding new R-group variations
description: The next step in drafting compositional patent claims is to maximize patent coverage. Adding variations beyond the current Markush structure relies on the experience of patent attorneys.
guidance: Automated systems should not only recapitulate observed substituents but also propose common/likely R-group variations (from curated libraries) to broaden claim scope and reduce dependence on manual attorney extension.

name: Define common substituent groups and categorize with SMARTS
description: Identify common groups along with their text terms from patent claims (e.g., hydroxyl, cyano, halo, alkyl, aryl, heteroaryl) and generate SMARTS notations for detecting them.
guidance: Categorize R groups into a set of categories (the paper used 57 categories, including composite categories such as alkyl–aryl) to enable automated detection and textual description generation of substituents.

name: Generate textual R-group descriptions from distal-to-attachment ordering
description: If the R group comprises several common groups, the text term describing the R group should be generated from the most distant common group moving to the ones near the attachment point.
guidance: This ordering rule yields more consistent and chemically meaningful textual definitions for complex substituents when producing claim text.

name: If R-group matches library substituent, expand same-position variations
description: For R groups attached to a carbon chain or ring in the scaffold, if the R group structure exactly matches any of the common substituents on the corresponding main structure in our library, the rest of the common substituents will be added to the same ring or carbon chain.
guidance: This is the algorithmic rule used to expand local variation sets within the Markush representation to increase claim breadth by adding substituents that commonly occur at the same position in similar scaffolds.

name: Output formatting for claims
description: The chemical scheme of the Markush structure is shown after the first sentence of the claims, and the definition of the R groups follows. Results can be downloaded in MS Word format (.docx).
guidance: Present the visual Markush scheme immediately in the claim text and follow with explicit R-group definitions so the generated claims are readable and ready for human editing and inclusion in patent drafts.

name: Use R-group libraries from approved drugs to increase coverage
description: R groups from approved drugs (e.g., DrugBank extraction) can be used to broaden the set of candidate R substituents for claim expansion; example: 364 different R groups from approved drugs compared to the 269-group library.
guidance: Comparative analysis (paper example: 84.8% of R groups from approved drugs covered by library) can be used to evaluate and justify the library coverage and motivate adding more sources to improve expansion quality.

name: Treat generated claims as first draft and checklist; require human review
description: The resulting claim can serve as a first draft to reduce human labor and as a checklist while drafting claims to avoid omitting common R-group variations that should be covered and protected.
guidance: Automated outputs are intended to assist patent attorneys and scientists; final claim language and legal scope decisions must be reviewed and adjusted by experienced practitioners.

name: Privacy and data-retention practices for a public claim-drafting server
description: Input files are deleted immediately after computation at the end of the session; output files are removed within 12 hours; the server does not generate or retain any log file so user IP addresses are not traceable via the server.
guidance: For web-based claim-drafting tools, state clear data-retention and privacy behaviors to reassure users (especially when working with confidential proprietary compounds).

name: Disclaimers (Act of March 3, 1837 §§7 & 9) — when and how they operate
description: When a patentee, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, has claimed more than he was the original inventor of, and some material and substantial part truly and justly belongs to him, he (or his successors) may make a written disclaimer of such parts, stating the extent of his interest; the disclaimer must be attested by witnesses, recorded in the Patent Office on payment of ten dollars, and will be considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest.
guidance: A disclaimer filed before suit may permit the plaintiff to recover costs on proving infringement of the undisclaimed part; a disclaimer filed during a suit will not afford benefit in that suit (per Reed v. Cutter). Unreasonable neglect or delay in filing a disclaimer may prevent its benefits and constitute a defense to suits.

name: Partial validity where specification embraces more than inventor's contribution
description: Where a specification embraces more than that of which the patentee was the first inventor, the patent shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention as shall be truly and bona fide his own, provided it is a material and substantial part and definitely distinguishable from other parts claimed without right.
guidance: The patentee may maintain suit for infringement of the bona fide part, but will not be entitled to recover costs unless he had entered a disclaimer at the Patent Office prior to commencing suit; unreasonable delay in entering the disclaimer may bar its benefits.

name: Sufficiency of prior patent specifications — mere hints insufficient
description: Where the defense is a prior patent specification, it is not sufficient that the earlier specification contain a mere hint of the process or invention claimed in the subsequent patent; the prior specification must contain more than a hint — a substantial representation.
guidance: English authorities and the House of Lords hold that incomplete prior specifications that only suggest an invention do not defeat a later patent for that invention.

name: Number of RCEs filed (response to examiner pushback)
description: How many Requests for Continued Examination (RCEs) were filed — more RCEs indicate greater examiner pushback during prosecution.
guidance: Use RCE count as an indicator of how much negotiation/narrowing occurred; a higher number suggests more difficulty obtaining allowance and potentially weaker original claims.

name: Prohibition on amendments that enlarge or materially vary claimed invention (s.18(8))
description: No amendment shall be allowed that would make the specification, as amended, claim an invention substantially larger than or substantially different from the invention claimed by the specification as it stood before amendment.
guidance: This is a central statutory limit. Comptroller and law officers must ensure amendments do not extend scope; where question is doubtful, amendment may be allowed 'at the patentee's peril.' Cases: Math and Frost, Lake's Patent, Van Gelders Patent.

name: Enumerated grounds of opposition to amendments
description: Typical grounds: the proposed amendment will introduce disconformity between provisional and complete specification; the scope of the invention will be enlarged; the amended specification will claim an invention substantially different from the original; the invention will be made the same as one described in a prior specification.
guidance: Opponents should identify which statutory or equitable harm arises; narrowing amendments (restriction) are generally not valid grounds if the narrower invention remains covered by the original specification (cases cited: Cochrane, Ashworth, Nordenfelt).

name: Conditions under Act of 1883 and 1888 practice (limiting retrospective effect)
description: Under 1883/1888 practice the law officer sometimes imposed conditions that no action should be brought in respect of infringements prior to a given date (e.g., Jan 1, 1884) to confine scope of retrospective relief; special circumstances may still induce conditions exempting past infringement claims.
guidance: Typical terms include barring claims for past infringements, barring amended specification from being receivable in evidence in pending actions, and allocation of costs. Cases: Hearson's, Westinghouse, Allen's, Ashworth's.

name: Duty of decision-makers to prevent scope extension; permitting doubtful amendments at patentee's peril
description: It is part of the duty of the Comptroller and the law officers, when hearing applications for leave to amend, to see that the proposed amendment does not extend the scope of the patent or alter the claims so that the invention would become substantially larger or different; when the question is doubtful, the amendment ought to be allowed at the patentee's peril.
guidance: If clearly extending scope the amendment must be disallowed (Math and Frost); if doubtful, allowance is possible but risky (Lake's Patent). Challenges can be made in court if the amendment contravenes s.18(8).

name: Limits on altering claims and severing claims by disclaimer
description: A disclaimer may sever and reject claims to subordinate parts where specification claims both a general combination and subordinate parts, but a specification cannot be altered to claim a combination or parts if they were not previously claimed; cannot strike out an entire claim and insert another claim to a subordinate part if original contained a distinct specific claim.
guidance: Disclaimers can narrow but not introduce new claim scope; ensure sufficient matter remains to support the patent (Gaulard & Gibbs, United Horseshoe).

name: Cutting down broad method claims to a particular method
description: If there is a claim to all methods of effecting a certain result, it may be cut down by disclaimer to the particular method described in the specification.
guidance: Use disclaimer to restrict overbroad method claims to the described embodiment where appropriate (Ashworth's Patent).

name: Drawings constitute part of the specification and may supplement description
description: When the nature of the case admits of drawings, the statute directs the patentee to accompany his specification with a drawing or drawings and written references; the object is both to distinguish the thing patented and to explain the mode of constructing it. Drawings annexed constitute part of the specification and may be used to explain or help out an otherwise imperfect description.
guidance: A specification may be partly in writing and partly in drawing; if words and drawings together enable a skilful mechanic to perform the work and show the invention claimed, the specification is sufficient. Written references to drawings are not always necessary if the combination of drawing and text yields understanding.

name: Must state at least one method which will succeed
description: A specification must state at least one method which will succeed.
guidance: Claiming a class of means without providing a successful method is insufficient. If a generic term covers many species but only one species actually works, the specification is bad as misleading the public. Example: claiming 'fossil salt' when only 'sal gem' will succeed.

name: Cannot claim an entire class if some members will not answer
description: If a whole class of substances is stated as suitable and any one of them will not answer, the specification is bad as misleading the public.
guidance: All substances that will answer need not be enumerated, but the public must not be misled by a generic claim that includes non-working members. If a generally known substance contains foreign matter injurious to use, patentee must show a known easy method of removing it, or the specification is insufficient.

name: Disclaimer for inadvertent overbroad claims and its procedural effects
description: Whenever a patentee has, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, made his specification or claim too broad, claiming more than that of which he was the original inventor, he may make disclaimers of such parts of the thing patented as he does not claim to hold; disclaimers must be in writing, attested, recorded in the patent office on payment of a fee and become part of the original specification to the extent of the interest disclaimed.
guidance: Different statutory provisions operate differently: one disclaimer (7th section of Act of 1837) applies to suits pending when filed; another (9th section) applies to suits brought after filing and preserves validity for bona fide parts the patentee truly owns. Filing timing and whether all parties (e.g., assignees) join affect legal consequences; failure to file timely disclaimers can bar costs or equitable relief. Example: Wyeth v. Stone discussion of procedural effects and limitations.

name: Provisional application as a priority strategy
description: Filing a provisional application establishes an early government‑recognized filing date and gives the filer one year to file a non‑provisional application that claims that priority.
guidance: Advantages noted: inexpensive for small entities (example $110 fee), provides clear objective date and reduces potential for fraud/backdating, similar function to an inventor’s notebook but with government date. Caveats: provisional applications still must meet legal standards (adequate disclosure) and obtaining competent patent counsel can be the major expense; provisional inadequacy can jeopardize later protection, so provisionals are not a cost‑free panacea.

name: Limits on relying on assertions about advisors’ confidential sales data
description: An expert’s claim that advisors had access to licensees’ confidential sales data (and used that to compute lump sums) cannot be accepted absent record evidence those advisors actually had such access and performed such calculations.
guidance: If there is no record evidence that advisors accessed sales data or performed calculations, district courts can exclude testimony asserting reliance on such advisors. Arguments relying on supposed but unproven advisor analyses amount to unsupported assertions.

name: Expert must actually rely on the evidence it cites in support
description: Rule 702 requires the expert’s relied-upon facts or data to be the basis for the testimony; courts examine whether the expert actually used or relied upon the record evidence claimed.
guidance: An expert cannot be saved by alternative record evidence that the expert did not rely upon in forming the opinion; admissibility turns on the expert’s actual basis, as reflected in the report/testimony. If the expert used certain data only as an after-the-fact 'check' (or did not use it at all), courts evaluate whether that reliance suffices.

name: Purpose of a bidder's guaranty
description: The purpose of a bidder's guaranty is to furnish sufficient security that the bidder will, if his bid is accepted, enter into contract as prescribed; the direct object is to enable the Government to collect the difference between the bidder's bid and the amount the Government would have to pay someone else if the bidder should not enter into contract.
guidance: Prepare the guaranty to be as formal and legally sufficient as a contractor's bond so it can serve as the basis of a legal claim by suit if necessary.

name: Definition of 'cancellation petitioner'
description: “The term ‘cancellation petitioner’ means the real party in interest requesting cancellation of any claim of a patent under chapter 32 of this title and the privies of the real party in interest.”
guidance: Identifies who may be treated as the petitioner in post-grant cancellation proceedings—the real party in interest and its privies.

name: Interlocutory appeals of claim construction in patent cases
description: Adds interlocutory appealability: “(3) of an appeal from an interlocutory order or decree determining construction of claims in a civil action for patent infringement under section 271 of title 35. Application for an appeal under paragraph (3) shall be made to the court within 10 days after entry of the order or decree.
