The district court shall have discretion whether to approve the application and, if so, whether to stay proceedings in the district court during pendency of the appeal.”
guidance: Creates expedited interlocutory appeal path for claim construction orders, with a 10-day application window and district court discretion to permit the appeal and stay proceedings.

name: Inequitable conduct — defined remedies and referral for misconduct
description: “Upon a finding of inequitable conduct, the court shall balance the equities to determine which of the following remedies to impose: (A) Denying equitable relief to the patent holder and limiting the remedy for infringement to damages. (B) Holding the claims-in-suit, or the claims in which inequitable conduct occurred, unenforceable. (C) Holding the patent unenforceable. (D) Holding the claims of a related patent unenforceable. ... if there is evidence that the conduct can be attributable to a person or persons authorized to practice before the Office, the court shall refer the matter to the Office for appropriate disciplinary action under section 32, and shall order the parties to preserve and make available to the Office any materials that may be relevant to the determination under section 32.”
guidance: Provides a non-exhaustive list of possible equitable remedies and mandates referral to PTO disciplinary process when attorney/practitioner misconduct is implicated.

name: Cancellation petitions — required showing and evidence
description: “for each claim sought to be canceled, the petition sets forth in writing the basis for cancellation and provides the evidence in support thereof, including copies of patents and printed publications, or written testimony of a witness attested to under oath or declaration by the witness, or any other information that the Director may require by regulation.”
guidance: Prescribes the substance of a cancellation petition: written basis and evidentiary support (documents, testimony under oath, or other Director-required information); later notes Director should consider that discovery must be in the interests of justice.

name: Prima facie finding standard for materiality
description: “A prima facie finding of unpatentability under this section is shown if a reasonable examiner, based on a preponderance of the evidence, would conclude that the claim is unpatentable based on the information misrepresented or not disclosed, when that information is considered alone or in conjunction with other information or record. In determining whether there is a prima facie finding of unpatentability, each term in the claim shall be given its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and rebuttal evidence shall not be considered.”
guidance: Specifies the evaluative lens for materiality: preponderance standard, broadest reasonable claim construction, and exclusion of rebuttal evidence when determining prima facie unpatentability for materiality purposes.

name: Filing date entitlement
description: The filing date of the provisional or nonprovisional application is the date of receipt in the Office of the application which includes a specification containing description pursuant to 37 CFR 1.71 and at least one claim (for nonprovisional applications) and any drawings required by 37 CFR 1.81(a).
guidance: If any required items are missing, applicant will be notified to file them and the filing date will be the date of receipt of the missing part(s). If documents purporting to be a specification are so informal and incoherent that they would clearly not constitute a specification as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 37 CFR 1.71, the application will not be accorded a filing date until corrections are made; the filing date will then be the date corrections were made. Petitions to review a refusal to grant a filing date are by way of petition with applicable fee (37 CFR 1.17(f)); petitioner should provide arguments/evidence that items were not missing or that a filing date should be assigned regardless.

name: Informal application definition and treatment
description: An application is informal if typed on both sides of the paper, or is not permanent, legible, or reproducible. If such informalities are timely corrected, the application is given the filing date on which the original informal papers were filed.
guidance: OPAP accords a filing date (as of the Office Date stamp) to application papers including a specification containing a description and at least one claim (for certain nonprovisional categories prior to March 18, 2013 and design applications) and a drawing, even if informal because they do not comply with rules/notices. OPAP will send a Notice (e.g., Notice to File Corrected Application Papers) requiring correction; failure to correct within the specified time results in abandonment.

name: Order of application of insufficient payment — nonprovisional applications
description: When a payment submitted for fees due on filing in a nonprovisional application is insufficient and applicant has not specified application of the payment, the Office will apply the payment in the following order until expended: (1) basic filing fee (37 CFR 1.16(a),(b),(c),(e)); (2) non-electronic filing fee (1.16(t)); (3) non-DOCX fee (1.16(u)); (4) application size fee (1.16(s)); (5) late filing surcharge (1.16(f)); (6) processing fee for application filed in language other than English (1.17(i)); (7) search fee (1.16(k),(l),(m),(n)); (8) examination fee (1.16(o),(p),(q),(r)); (9) excess claims fee (1.16(h),(i),(j)).
guidance: The intent is to apply payments in a consistent order when the payor has not specified fee application. See MPEP § 607 for related guidance.

name: Step 1: Statutory Category (Is the claim to a statutory class?)
description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim falls within any statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). See MPEP 2106.03.
guidance: If the claim recites at least one step or act (e.g., calculating a ratio, administering a drug), it can be a process. If it recites a combination of concrete devices (memory, processor, reader) it can be a machine. (Example: 'The claim recites at least one step or act, including calculating a ratio. Thus, the claim is to a process...')

name: Step 2A Prong One: Does the claim 'recite' a judicial exception?
description: Determine whether the claim sets forth or describes a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, product of nature). A claim 'recites' an exception when the exception is set forth or described in the claim. See MPEP 2106.04(II) and October 2019 Update.
guidance: Identify specific claim limitations that align with exception categories; multiple exceptions may be present in a single limitation. It is sufficient to identify that a limitation aligns with at least one judicial exception to proceed to further analysis.

name: Law of Nature / Product of Nature exceptions
description: Claims that recite natural relationships (e.g., a correlation between biomarkers and a disease), naturally occurring products, or products found in nature may implicate law of nature or product of nature exceptions.
guidance: Where a claim describes a naturally occurring relationship (e.g., ratio of C11 to C13 indicates non-responder phenotype) treat as a law of nature; where it claims nature-based products evaluate under product-of-nature analysis (markedly different characteristics).

name: Particular Treatment or Prophylaxis consideration (integration prong)
description: A treatment or prophylaxis that is particular to an identified patient phenotype can integrate an exception into a practical application (i.e., a claim using an exception to identify patients and then administering a particular treatment is not 'directed to' the exception).
guidance: If claim requires administering a specific therapeutic agent or a treatment particular to the identified phenotype (e.g., non-steroidal agent, rapamycin, plasmapheresis), that limitation can have more than a nominal relationship to the judicial exception and support eligibility (see Vanda, Endo). The treatment limitation must meaningfully limit the abstract idea (not be wholly generic).

name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity (negative indicator)
description: Extra activities that are conventional, insignificant, or do no meaningful work beyond the exception do not integrate the exception.
guidance: Data-gathering steps, mere use of generic computer components, or other routine activities recited at a high level of generality are often insignificant extra-solution activity and do not make claim eligible under 2A Prong Two.

name: Field-of-Use and Technological Environment limitations (token limitation)
description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use (e.g., livestock management, commodities markets) is typically a token or mere recitation of field and does not make a claim patent eligible.
guidance: Cite Bilski: merely identifying the participants or field does little more than describe how the abstract idea could be used; treat such limitations skeptically as they often do not meaningfully limit the exception.

name: Step 2B: 'Inventive Concept' — Does the claim add 'significantly more' than the exception?
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception after Step 2A, evaluate whether any additional elements, individually or in combination, add something significantly more than the judicial exception (an 'inventive concept'). See MPEP 2106.05.
guidance: Consider whether additional elements are more than conventional or routine; mere instructions to apply an exception or nominal post-solution activity cannot satisfy 2B. If no inventive concept is present, claim is ineligible.

name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional (WURC) Activity (Step 2B consideration)
description: Assess whether additional claim elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional; if they are, they cannot supply an inventive concept under Step 2B.
guidance: WURC analysis is excluded from Step 2A Prong Two but is applicable in Step 2B. For example, if administering a conventional therapy is routine in the field, that fact is relevant to whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception under 2B.

name: Claim Interpretation: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
description: Claim terms are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as interpreted by a person of ordinary skill in the art (MPEP 2111).
guidance: Use BRI when determining what the claim 'recites' for eligibility analysis. The BRI may encompass multiple embodiments and can affect whether limitations are considered meaningful or nominal.

name: Wherein Clauses and Functional Language carry patentable weight
description: Limitations found in wherein clauses or recited functionally are not automatically disregarded; they can impose patentable weight if the specification supports them.
guidance: Do not ignore 'wherein' clauses — they may limit claim scope (e.g., specifying rapamycin or a non-steroidal agent). Examine written description support (MPEP 2163) for genus/functionally claimed limitations.

name: Preamble and Intended Use (when preamble limits claim)
description: A preamble does not limit a claim unless it positively adds a limitation or is necessary to give meaning to claim body.
guidance: If the preamble only indicates an intended use (e.g., 'for use in monitoring the health of dairy livestock'), it generally does not add limitations absent positive limiting language.

name: Contingent Limitations and Multi-Embodiment Coverage
description: Contingent limitations (conditional steps) can cause claims to encompass multiple alternative embodiments under BRI; prior art need only teach one embodiment to anticipate.
guidance: When a claim contains contingent actions (if A do X, if B do Y), the claim's BRI may include three or more embodiments. Examiners should be aware that anticipation can be established by references disclosing any single encompassed embodiment (see MPEP 2111.04(II)).

name: Use of Generic Computer/Processor does not negate a mental-process abstract idea
description: Reciting a processor or generic computer components that carry out mental processes or calculations does not necessarily avoid the abstract-idea exception; the computer may be treated as a tool automating human mental steps.
guidance: If the claim merely uses the computer to perform what humans can do mentally or is recited at a high level of generality using generic components, treat it as automating an abstract idea unless the claim recites a technological improvement in the computer itself or a particular machine implementation.

name: Identifying the Exception in a Rejection (practice note)
description: A rejection should identify the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations constitute an abstract idea, law of nature, or product of nature.
guidance: Explain how the limitation aligns with an exception (e.g., limitation (a) recites a mathematical calculation) and then explain why additional elements fail to integrate the exception or provide an inventive concept. Include citations to MPEP sections and relevant case law (Mayo, Vanda, Endo, Bilski, etc.).

name: Practice note: Consider all statutory requirements during examination (written description, novelty, obviousness)
description: Even if a claim is analyzed for eligibility under §101, examiners should also evaluate each claim for compliance with other statutory requirements (definiteness, written description, novelty, non-obviousness).
guidance: Example: a functionally claimed genus ('non-steroidal agent capable of treating NAS-3') may raise written description support issues (MPEP 2163). Also consider applicant-admitted statements as prior art (MPEP 2129(I)).

name: Examples Are Illustrative and Fact-Specific (use with 2019 PEG)
description: The Office's examples are hypothetical, illustrating claim analysis under the 2019 PEG and Issue Spotting Chart; different fact patterns may yield different eligibility outcomes.
guidance: Do not require a claim to mirror an example to be eligible; interpret examples based on their fact patterns and apply the 2019 PEG guidance to the claim at hand. Use broadest reasonable interpretation and cite appropriate MPEP and case law references when applying the examples.

name: Affidavit/Declaration required for evidence traversing rejections
description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection or objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
guidance: An affidavit is a written statement under oath before an authorized official; 37 CFR 1.68 permits a declaration instead of an affidavit. Declarations must include an acknowledgment referencing 18 U.S.C. 1001 and must state which statements are from the declarant’s own knowledge and which are on information and belief. Publications may be evidence if probative and properly submitted. All affidavits/declarations not falling under other specific rules are treated under this rule.

name: Use of form paragraphs 7.65 and 7.66 for Office actions
description: Form paragraph 7.65 should be used where an affidavit/declaration is effective to withdraw a rejection; form paragraph 7.66 where it is insufficient.
guidance: Form paragraphs include bracketed fields to be filled (type affidavit/declaration; filing date; affected claims; rejection overcome or not overcome with statutory grounds). When 7.66 is used, examiners must follow with detailed reasons for insufficiency (e.g., untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane; not commensurate in scope with claims) and may append subparagraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 as appropriate.

name: Reasons for insufficiency — ¶7.66.03: Refers only to invention, not to claims
description: Affidavit refers only to the system described in the application and not to the individual claims.
guidance: Such declarations fail to show objective evidence commensurate in scope with the claims. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and a full explanation provided if appropriate.

name: Consideration of comparative data in the specification
description: Examiners must consider comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention when reaching a conclusion on obviousness.
guidance: Comparative data can be probative of unexpected results; lack of such objective data does not, by itself, weigh in favor of obviousness, but failure to rebut a prima facie case is dispositive.

name: Probative value: objective evidence must be supported by proof
description: Objective evidence (unexpected results, commercial success, solution of long‑felt need, inoperability of prior art, invention before date of reference, allegations of derivation) must be factually supported by an appropriate affidavit or declaration to be probative.
guidance: Case law requires factual evidence (e.g., experimental data) for claims of unexpected results; conclusory assertions without tests/comparisons are insufficient.

name: Allegations of unexpected results (716.02)
description: Any differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may yield some differences in properties; the issue is whether the properties differ to such an extent that the difference is truly unexpected.
guidance: Guidance includes that unexpectedness must be shown (In re Merck & Co. example), the burden is on applicant to prove unexpected results, evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention, comparison should be with the closest prior art, and claimed advantages may be disclosed or inherent. See MPEP § 716.02(a)–(f) for detailed subpoints on burden, commensurateness, comparison, and weighing expected vs unexpected results.

name: Commercial success (716.03) — commensurateness and derivation
description: Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention and must be shown to be derived from the claimed invention to be probative of nonobviousness.
guidance: Examiners should look for evidence that sales/success are attributable to claimed features rather than other factors. If commercial success is due to an element known in the prior art, no nexus exists.

name: Long‑felt need and failure of others (716.04)
description: Evidence that the claimed invention satisfied a long‑felt need or that others failed to solve the problem may be probative of nonobviousness when properly supported and shown to relate to the claimed invention.
guidance: Applicant must show others were working on problem and could not solve it despite knowledge of prior art; mere assertion is insufficient.

name: Skepticism of experts (716.05)
description: Evidence showing skepticism of experts regarding the claimed invention can be an objective indicium of nonobviousness when tied to the claimed invention.
guidance: Must be supported by factual evidence and show nexus to claimed features; weight depends on factual support and context.

name: Copying (716.06)
description: Evidence that others copied the invention can be objective evidence of nonobviousness if it is shown that copying was of the claimed invention and not of prior‑art features.
guidance: Demonstrate that the copying was motivated by the novel aspects of the claimed invention and include evidence linking the copied features to the claim scope.

name: Inoperability of references (716.07)
description: Evidence showing inoperability of prior art references may rebut a rejection if supported by factual proof.
guidance: Must include factual tests or data demonstrating that the prior art would not operate as claimed; conclusory assertions insufficient.

name: Utility and operability of applicant’s disclosure (716.08)
description: Evidence that the applicant’s disclosure is useful and operable may support patentability where properly supported.
guidance: Must be supported by factual evidence; demonstrate that the claimed invention achieves the asserted utility and is operable across the claimed scope as required.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (716.09)
description: Affidavits/declarations may be evaluated for whether they disclose sufficient facts and documentary evidence to support their assertions relative to the claims.
guidance: Examiners should assess whether the showing is commensurate in scope with the claims and whether documentary evidence corroborates assertions (including inventorship/derivation issues).

name: Proportional scope of discovery (Rule 26(b))
description: Limit discovery to nonprivileged matter relevant to any claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case, considering factors including amount in controversy.
guidance: Discuss scope, nature, and amount of relief at first conference and compare to other patent cases to set a baseline; be open to revising proportionality as case develops.

name: Initial case-management conference technology summary
description: Ask for an informal description of the technology and a brief statement/summary of claims and defenses by each party including identity of accused products and whether asserted liability is direct or indirect.
guidance: Also ask about third parties for discovery, scope of accused products relative to defendant's business, scope of patented technology relative to patentee's business, and whether parties are competitors.

name: Scheduling claim construction and dispositive motions
description: Determine timing of summary judgment relative to claim construction; set schedules for exchanges of claim terms, proposed constructions, and supporting evidence; discuss tutorials and logistics.
guidance: Decide whether summary judgment should be timetabled first/second track; require explanation of significance of claim terms, limit number of terms, encourage tutorials (by counsel or experts) and use of visual aids.

name: Limit and prioritize claim terms and patents for trial
description: Discuss number of patents and claims that would be tried, ways of winnowing, limits on number of claim terms submitted for construction, and require parties to rank disputed terms by significance.
guidance: Require explanations of term significance (effect on infringement/validity) to focus claim construction and trial preparation on dispositive issues.

name: Assess summary judgment issues tied to claim construction
description: Discuss whether any summary judgment issues depend on claim construction or could be resolved with little/no discovery, including disputes about accused product structure/function, territorial issues, or purely legal claims/defenses.
guidance: Consider first-track and second-track summary judgment schedules where appropriate and limits on number/pages of motions.

name: In re Wands enablement factors
description: Factors to determine sufficiency of §112 enablement (from In re Wands) include: the level of skill in the art, the breadth of the claims, the nature of the invention, the state of the prior art, the level of predictability, the amount of direction and guidance provided, the presence or absence of working examples, and the quantity of experimentation required.
guidance: Apply these factors when drafting and prosecuting plant utility applications: narrower claims, clearer working examples and more guidance reduce the risk of enablement/undue-experimentation rejections. The analysis is fact-specific.

name: Form and recordation of patents; term and title requirement
description: All patents ... shall be issued in the name of the United States, under the seal of said office, signed by the Secretary of State and countersigned by the commissioner, and shall be recorded ... Every such patent shall contain a short description or title of the invention ... correctly indicating its nature and design, and in its terms grant ... for a term not exceeding fourteen years, the full and exclusive right and liberty of making, using, and vending ... referring to the specifications for particulars, a copy of which shall be annexed ... specifying what the patentee claims as his invention or discovery.
guidance: Patents must have a short accurate title, refer to annexed specifications and claims, be signed/recorded, and grant exclusive rights for a statutory term (≤14 years under this act).

name: Machine-specific disclosure: explain principle and modes
description: In case of any machine, he shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ... by which it may be distinguished from other inventions; and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his own invention.
guidance: For machines, applicant must disclose the operating principle and alternative modes and must particularly point out the claimed parts or combinations (precise claiming).

name: Requiring renewed oath if persisting after objection
description: But if the applicant ... shall persist in his claims for a patent, with or without any alteration in his specification, he shall be required to make oath or affirmation anew.
guidance: When persisting in application after notification of defects or prior art, applicant must reaffirm oath.

name: Board of examiners on appeal from commissioner
description: If the specification and claim shall not have been so modified as, in the opinion of the commissioner, shall entitle the applicant to a patent, he may, on appeal ... have the decision of a board of examiners, to be composed of three disinterested persons, one of whom at least to be selected ... for his knowledge and skill in the particular art ... who shall be under oath ... Said board shall be furnished with a certificate ... stating the particular grounds of his objection ... the board ... may reverse the decision of the commissioner, either in whole or in part, and their opinion being certified to the commissioner, he shall be governed thereby ...
guidance: Appeal mechanism: three disinterested examiners (one with relevant art skill) hear appeals; fee $25 to treasury; examiners compensated (up to $10 each). Board gives notice and considers evidence.

name: Caveat filing to preserve claim while maturing invention
description: Any person ... who shall have invented ... and shall desire further time to mature the same, may, on paying ... twenty dollars, file in the Patent Office a caveat, setting forth the design and purpose thereof, and its principal and distinguishing characteristics, and praying protection of his right till he shall have matured his invention; ... filed in the confidential archives ... And if application shall be made by any other person within one year ... for a patent with which it may in any respect interfere, it shall be the duty of the commissioner to deposit the description, specifications, drawings, and model, in the confidential archives of the office, and to give notice by mail to the person filing the caveat, who shall, within three months ... file his description, specifications, drawings, and model; and if ... the specifications of claim interfere ... like proceedings may be had as in the case of interfering applications.
guidance: Caveat preserves rights while maturing; $20 fee credited toward later application; triggers notice and short window (3 months) to file full application upon interfering application.

name: Reissue for defect or inadvertent overclaiming (non-fraudulent)
description: Whenever any patent ... shall be inoperative, or invalid, by reason of a defective or insufficient description or specification, or by reason of the patentee claiming ... more than he had a right to claim as new; if the error has arisen by inadvertency, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention, it shall be lawful for the commissioner, upon the surrender to him of such patent, and the payment of the further duty of fifteen dollars, to cause a new patent to be issued to the said inventor, for the same invention, for the residue of the period then unexpired ... in accordance with the patentee's corrected description and specification.
guidance: Reissue available to correct inadvertent defects or overclaims (non-fraudulent) on surrender and $15 fee; reissue has retroactive legal effect for subsequent causes of action as though corrected originally.

name: Court discretion where specification claims more than inventor had right to claim
description: Whenever the plaintiff shall fail to sustain his action on the ground that in his specification of claim is embraced more than that of which he was the first inventor, if it shall appear that the defendant had used or violated any part of the invention justly and truly specified and claimed as new, it shall be in the power of the court to adjudge and award as to costs, as may appear to be just and equitable.
guidance: Court can tailor costs/awards equitably when plaintiff over-claimed but defendant infringed actual, properly claimed parts.

name: Merits of a priority claim
description: The merits of a priority claim are not determined by the Office unless required for patentability reasons (Chapter 200).
guidance: Clarified that entitlement to a foreign filing date based on disclosure is not determined unless necessary for patentability; staff may not automatically adjudicate merits absent such need.

name: Small and micro entity status requirements
description: Clarifications to requirements for claiming small or micro entity status (Chapter 500).
guidance: Updated criteria for determining micro-entity status (including institution-of-higher-education basis limitations) and the situations that do not constitute a license under 37 CFR 1.27(a)(1); guidance on application filing limits for micro-entity status.

name: Double patenting analysis and patent-term considerations
description: Updated double patenting guidance to include consideration of the patent term filing date and analysis when prior art is excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) or disqualified under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (Chapter 800).
guidance: Clarified telephone restriction practice, added form paragraph 8.23.03, clarified that only inventions claimed in a divisional may potentially be subject to prohibition under 35 U.S.C. 121, and guidance for claims added after an office action.

name: Design claim scope and disclosure sufficiency
description: Design claims are limited to the article of manufacture identified in the claim and do not cover designs in the abstract; when a single plan or planar-view may be sufficient to comply with 35 U.S.C. 112 (Chapter 1500).
guidance: Added court decision guidance and clarified when a single planar view or plan may suffice for a design claim under 112; updated form paragraphs and emphasis that claims must identify the article of manufacture.

name: Written description, enablement, definiteness, and means-plus-function guidance
description: Incorporation of court decisions clarifying prior art availability, written description, enablement, definiteness, means-or-step-plus-function limitations, and claim interpretation during prosecution (Chapter 2100).
guidance: Added case law citations and clarifying discussion on how examiners should apply these doctrines during prosecution, including anticipation in genus-species contexts.

name: Evaluate the claims as a whole in Step 2A
description: When determining whether a claim is "directed to" a judicial exception, the claims must be evaluated as a whole, including any arguably conventional steps (e.g., genotyping and treatment steps).
guidance: The Federal Circuit evaluated the claims as a whole when determining that the claim was not "directed to" the recited natural relationship between genotype and QTc prolongation. Cases cited include Finjan and Core Wireless. Examiners should not isolate individual claim elements when doing the Step 2A 'directed to' analysis; include conventional steps in the overall assessment.

name: Distinguish treatment-purpose steps from data-gathering/diagnostic steps
description: Determine whether claimed steps (e.g., administering a drug) are performed to apply a natural relationship (treatment) or to gather data about the relationship (diagnosis); this distinction affects whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception.
guidance: The memo contrasts Vanda with Mayo: in Mayo the administering step was performed to gather data and was ancillary to the diagnostic focus, so the claim as a whole was directed to a natural law; in Vanda the administering step required a treating doctor to administer the drug to treat disease, which supports finding the claim directed to an application. Examiners should assess the purpose/context of steps when classifying claims.

name: Conventionality/unconventionality of steps is not required for Step 2A eligibility
description: It is not necessary for 'method of treatment' claims that practically apply natural relationships to include nonroutine or unconventional steps in order to be considered patent eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 in the Step 2A 'directed to' inquiry.
guidance: The Federal Circuit did not consider whether the treatment steps were routine or conventional when making its 'directed to' determination in Vanda. Thus, absence of non-routine steps does not alone make a method-of-treatment claim ineligible at Step 2A; non-routine analysis is part of Step 2B, which may be unnecessary if Step 2A is satisfied.

name: If claim is eligible under Step 2A, do not perform Step 2B
description: If, after evaluating the claim as a whole in Step 2A, the claim is determined not to be 'directed to' a judicial exception, there is no need to conduct the Step 2B (inventive concept) analysis.
guidance: Because the claim in Vanda was determined eligible in the Step 2A 'directed to' part of the test, the Federal Circuit did not perform a Step 2B analysis. Examiners should stop the Alice/Mayo framework once Step 2A resolves eligibility in favor of the claim.

name: Claims should 'confine their reach to particular applications' to be treated as applications rather than judicial exceptions
description: A claim that confines its reach to a particular application (rather than broadly claiming a natural relationship) is more likely to be treated as an application of that relationship and thus not 'directed to' the judicial exception.
guidance: The memo references the Supreme Court's distinction that method-of-treatment claims 'confine their reach to particular applications' and thus are not implicated by Mayo/Myriad. Examiners should consider whether claim scope limits the claim to a practical application (e.g., a treatment regimen tied to a particular patient genotype) when performing the Step 2A analysis.

name: Disclosure requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) for benefit claims
description: The prior-filed application must disclose the claimed invention of the later-filed application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description and enablement) for a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c).
guidance: The disclosure must provide adequate support and enablement to permit one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Example: New Railhead — where a provisional lacked explicit support for an 'angled' limitation, the later patent was not entitled to the provisional date. If the prior disclosure is insufficient, the later-filed claim is not entitled to the earlier filing date.

name: Translation and accuracy statement requirement for non‑English provisionals
description: If the prior-filed provisional application was filed in a language other than English and both an English-language translation and a statement that the translation is accurate were not previously filed in the provisional, applicant will be notified and given a period to file them in the provisional application.
guidance: If notice is mailed in a pending nonprovisional application, a timely reply must include either confirmation that the translation and statement were filed in the provisional, or an amendment or Supplemental ADS withdrawing the benefit claim, or the nonprovisional application will be abandoned. The translation and statement may be filed in the provisional even if it has become abandoned.

name: Copendency requirement for nonprovisional benefit claims (35 U.S.C.120/121/365(c))
description: When claiming the benefit of a prior nonprovisional under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c), the later-filed application must be copending with the prior application (filed before patenting, abandonment, or termination of proceedings in the prior application).
guidance: Copendency is satisfied if the later-filed application is filed on the same date the prior issues or before the patent issues. If proceedings in the prior application are terminated (e.g., mandate issued after affirmance), the later application must have been filed before that termination to be copending. If not copending, the later-filed application is not entitled to the benefit and prior art is judged from its actual filing date.

name: Form paragraphs and examiner procedural guidance for benefit-claim defects
description: Use form paragraphs (e.g., 2.09, 2.10, 2.10.01, 2.38–2.40) to notify applicant when claims are not entitled to an earlier filing date due to lack of support/enablement or presence of new matter, and to instruct on required corrections.
guidance: ¶2.10: Disclosure of prior-filed application does not provide support for claimed subject matter; ¶2.10.01: continuation/divisional contains new matter and must be changed to CIP. Follow examiner notes in each form paragraph (insert prior application number, explain lack of support, list claims not entitled to benefit, etc.).

name: Amendment document format requirements
description: From 1 Apr 2017, both marked-up amendments and clean copies of the amended sheets are required. From 1 Dec 2019, if amendments have been made to claims, a marked-up and clean copy of the full set of claims have to be submitted together with the request. The amendments or corrections should be reflected similarly in both the clean and marked-up copies. The request for amendments to specification should set out the reasons for making amendments and any evidence in support thereof should also be submitted.
guidance: Follow Chapter 5.1.12 for accepted format of marked-up copies. Reasons and evidence must accompany amendment requests.

name: Examples where Examiner may initiate informal communication
description: Examples: a) where subject matter relates to an emerging technology and the Examiner finds the applicant’s explanation would benefit prosecution; b) when application is ready for grant except for minor clarity issues in pending claims; c) when no substantive progress after several iterations and an interview may help close prosecution gap.
guidance: Informal communications are aimed at efficiency and may lead to invitations to amend or interviews to expedite resolution.

name: PPH request formal requirements (IPOS Formalities review checklist)
description: Formalities officer will review: a) PPH is selected on PF11/PF12 form; b) IPOS application and application forming basis of PPH request are corresponding applications or related sharing the same earliest date (for CNIPA/SAIP special filing-order rules apply); c) all office actions of the relied-upon application are submitted; d) list of allowable/patentable claims submitted, with at least one claim determined allowable/patentable by the other IP Office; e) for GPPH, if documents are available in other office’s Dossier Access System they need not be submitted (English translation submitted if not in English; VET not required); f) all claims in IPOS application must sufficiently correspond to one or more claims found allowable/patentable by the other IP Office and a claims correspondence table is submitted; g) cited documents referred to in the results may be submitted (not mandatory unless requested) and English translations may be requested if not in English.
guidance: Document completeness and claims correspondence are key to PPH acceptance.

name: Use of multiple related applications for PPH
description: The applicant may rely on the search and examination results of more than one related application (OFF/OEE) for PPH/GPPH. All relevant documents and multiple sets of claim correspondence tables are required to be furnished accordingly.
guidance: Where multiple earlier examinations are used, provide clear mapping and all supporting documents.

name: ASPEC request procedures and document requirements
description: ASPEC request may be submitted at any time before the final decision of grant or refusal via the e-ASPEC platform. When received, Formalities officer will review: a) ASPEC option selected or written notice submitted; b) Search and Examination result or Written Opinion of corresponding application submitted; c) list of claims referred to in the results submitted, with at least one claim determined allowable/patentable; d) all claims in IPOS application must sufficiently correspond to one or more claims found allowable/patentable by the first IP Office; e) English translation of documents submitted if not in English, with translation verified by a translator or by the patent agent before IPOS, if requested; f) optional supporting documents may include claim correspondence table, list of prior art with English translations, cited documents, and written opinion with translations if not relying on written opinion.
guidance: Verification of translations may be required; provide claim mapping and supporting prior art where possible.

name: Construction of means-plus-function language
description: When interpreting means-plus-function language in a claim, such language is construed to include only the structure, material, or acts (and equivalents of the structure, material, or acts) that are described in the patent’s specification as the means for performing the claimed function.
guidance: Only the structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification (and their equivalents) are within the scope of a means-plus-function limitation. Extrinsic evidence may be used to help construe claim language but not to vary claim terms. See In re Donaldson Co. and 35 U.S.C. § 112, ¶ 6.

name: Limitations on the doctrine of equivalents (range and prosecution-history estoppel)
description: Two major limitations: (1) the range of equivalents depends on the nature of the invention (pioneer inventions get broader range; crowded-field inventions narrower), and (2) prosecution-history estoppel can bar reliance on equivalents for subject matter surrendered during prosecution.
guidance: To test if prior art restricts equivalents, craft a hypothetical claim that would literally read on the accused product and determine if that hypothetical claim would have been patentable. If not patentable, DOE is not proper. Prosecution-history estoppel arises from what the applicant gave up to obtain allowance; only amendments critical to allowance create estoppel. Not all amendments create estoppel—amendments not critical to allowance typically do not.

name: Claims of noninfringement — common defenses
description: Examples of evidence/arguments an alleged infringer can introduce to show acts do not constitute infringement.
guidance: Typical defenses include: (1) properly interpreted claims do not read on the accused product/process; (2) the defendant acts within the scope of a license; (3) the defendant has an implied license; (4) the use is experimental and completely noncommercial; (5) the defendant acts within scope of 35 U.S.C. § 271(e)(1) (safe harbor); (6) entitlement to the reverse doctrine of equivalents; (7) patent owner barred from DOE by prosecution-history estoppel; (8) use on foreign vessel/aircraft/vehicle temporarily in U.S. fulfilling §272 requirements.

name: Claims of invalidity — proving a patent is invalid
description: An alleged infringer can avoid liability by proving the asserted patent is invalid; a duly issued patent is presumed valid and invalidity must be shown by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Two routes to establish invalidity: (1) show the invention fails one or more conditions of patentability (e.g., novelty, nonobviousness, utility), or (2) show the inventor failed to satisfy one or more patentability requirements (e.g., written description, enablement, formalities). Also, failure to obtain required PTO permissions (e.g., foreign filing license) is a non-substantive PTO defect that can render a patent invalid. See 35 U.S.C.A. § 282 (presumption of validity).

name: Inequitable conduct before the PTO (unclean hands)
description: The defense that the applicant engaged in inequitable conduct during prosecution (e.g., submitting false/misleading information or failing to disclose material information) which renders the asserted patent unenforceable.
guidance: Inequitable conduct requires proof by clear and convincing evidence that the conduct was both material and intended to mislead the PTO. Materiality and intent are factual issues: threshold levels must be met before the court balances actual materiality and intent and decides inequity. Materiality: substantial likelihood a reasonable examiner would consider the information important. Intent may be inferred from circumstantial evidence; gross negligence alone is insufficient. A high level of materiality plus clear proof of knowledge makes it difficult for patentee to show subjective good faith. If proven, all claims of the asserted patent are unenforceable.

name: Examination of computer-generated interfaces and icons (GUI/icon guidance)
description: Supplemental Guidance for Examination of Design Patent Applications Related to Computer-Generated Interfaces and Icons — Part 1: Overview of the Notice [FY 2026 - Q2]
guidance: Guidance specific to examination of GUI and icon designs, likely addressing how to treat screenshots, dynamic aspects, broken views vs. claimed views, and what constitutes the claimed ornamental design for computer-generated interfaces and icons.

name: Application of relevant Federal court decisions (Maatita, Curver, Surgisil)
description: Federal Court Decisions: Maatita, Curver and Surgisil [FY 2023 - Q1]
guidance: Materials summarizing and explaining how specific Federal Circuit decisions affect design patent examination practice; used to teach examiners how to apply case law to examination issues (e.g., claim scope, infringement/anticipation/obviousness analysis influences).

name: Examination and search of unity
description: Unity of invention is examined both in search and examination procedures; lack of unity may be determined a priori (before starting the search) in evident cases or a posteriori after taking into account the prior art.
guidance: Example: Claims: 1) Compound X; 2) Process of manufacturing X; 3) Use of X. If Compound X is unknown from the prior art it is the special feature and unity is satisfied. If Compound X is known from the prior art, it cannot be the special feature contributing over the prior art and there is no unity between claims 2 and 3; an objection of lack of unity should be raised.

name: Divisional claims must not duplicate parent claims
description: The claims of a divisional Eurasian application shall not contain inventions identical to the inventions for which legal protection is requested in the parent Eurasian application, except in the case of limitation of the parent application in accordance with Rule 4 where unity was violated.
guidance: This prohibits claiming the same subject-matter with the same scope in the divisional as in the parent, unless the parent has been limited under Rule 4; examiners will check for identity of claimed scope.

name: Requirements for divisional to enjoy parent's filing/priority date
description: The divisional application is entitled to the filing date and priority date of the parent only if: (i) it is filed only in relation to subject-matter disclosed in the parent application and which does not go beyond the content of the parent application; and (ii) the divisional does not claim an invention identical (with respect to claimed scope) to the invention contained in claims of the parent application or the Eurasian patent granted on its basis.
guidance: If the filed divisional does not comply with these requirements the applicant is notified to submit claims consistent with Rule 49(6) within two months; failure to do so will result in the divisional being deemed withdrawn, although further processing and restoration of rights are provided for in such a case.

name: Practical example illustrating unity determination
description: Example given: Claim 1: Compound X. Claim 2: Process of manufacturing compound X. Claim 3: Use of compound X.
guidance: If compound X is unknown from the prior art it is the special feature contributing over the prior art and unity across claims 1–3 is satisfied. If compound X is known from the prior art it cannot be considered a special feature and there is no unity between claims 2 and 3; an objection of lack of unity should be raised.

name: Actions when Board sustains examiner in whole/part — no claims allowed
description: When no claims stand allowed after Board decision and the period for seeking court review expires, proceedings are terminated; a Notice of Abandonment should be prepared and mailed. If provisional or double patenting rejections exist, applicant may file a terminal disclaimer prior to the expiration to attempt to overcome the rejection.
guidance: Dependent claims objected to as allowable except for dependency are treated as rejected unless rewritten in independent form within the period for seeking review. Examiner options when dependent claim(s) become allowable only after reversal of independent claims: (1) Convert dependent claim(s) into independent form by examiner’s amendment, cancel affirmed claims, and issue; or (2) set a 2-month time limit for applicant to rewrite dependent claim(s) in independent form (extensions under 1.136 available). Use provided form paragraphs (e.g., ¶12.291).

name: Treatment of non-elected claims and provisional double patenting after Board reversal
description: When a decision reverses rejections of generic claims in an application containing non-elected species, pending claims drawn to non-elected species must be acted upon (consider rejoinder) unless the examiner reopens prosecution and determines the election remains appropriate.
guidance: If a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection was not reached by the Board and the reference application has issued as a patent, the provisional rejection should be reissued as a non-provisional rejection and a terminal disclaimer required. If the reference application was abandoned or never matured and the provisional DPT rejection is the only remaining rejection, the examiner should withdraw the provisional rejection. See MPEP § 804.

name: Reopening prosecution after final Board decision (RCE and 1.198 petitions)
description: Prosecution before the primary examiner will not be reopened after a final Board decision except under 37 CFR 1.114 (RCE), 37 CFR 41.50 with Director authority, or by petition under 37 CFR 1.198 with Director approval.
guidance: An amendment filed with an RCE (and the appropriate fee) will be entered and prosecution reopened; if an amendment obviously places the application in condition for allowance, examiner should recommend entry even without an RCE, with supervisory concurrence. If an amendment cannot be entered, the examiner must notify appellant of the reason; the refusal must not be arbitrary or capricious. Use form ¶12.298 when refusing entry. Petitions under 1.198 to reopen are decided by the TC Director and are ordinarily granted only in limited categories (A) decision suggests claims could be made allowable by adding disclosed limitation/curing defect, (B) decision indicates missing evidence that exists and can be offered, or (C) decision based on a rule/practice/law/judicial precedent since rescinded/repealed/overruled.

name: Clarity — avoidably obscure or ambiguous language renders a patent invalid
description: A patent is invalid if it relies on 'language which, when fairly read, is avoidably obscure or ambiguous.'
guidance: This principle appears in Natural Colour Kinematograph and related case law. Examiners should ensure claims and specifications are clear and not avoidably obscure; ambiguous language will be viewed in the context of the whole specification.

name: Product produced by a method may be obvious (double‑patenting/double protection risk)
description: A method for preparing a product would usually be considered to render the product it produces obvious, potentially creating an appearance of double‑patenting if claims to product and method appear in different applications.
guidance: When drafting and examining claims, consider the relationship between method and product claims to avoid double‑patenting issues. The manual warns of the usual treatment that method steps leading to a product can make the product claim obvious in light of the method claim.

name: Patent eligibility risk under 35 U.S.C. §101 and Alice
description: Beauregard claims may be at risk of invalidation under §101, especially after Alice, which held that a claim merely reciting an abstract idea is not patentable.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea and whether it includes a sufficient inventive concept. The Supreme Court's skepticism about software patentability (Alice) means Beauregard claims require careful drafting to survive eligibility challenges.

name: Broader protection (advantage)
description: By focusing on the overall functionality, Beauregard claims can provide broader protection than claims that focus solely on individual hardware components.
guidance: Broader protection can make it harder for infringers to avoid liability by making minor modifications to products. Use Beauregard claims when broader coverage of software functionality is strategically important.

name: Clarity and precision (advantage)
description: Beauregard claims can often be more precise and easier to understand than claims that solely focus on hardware components.
guidance: Clear, precise claim language can make it easier to determine whether a product infringes. Draft claims to clearly define the encoded instructions and their functionality.

name: Flexibility (advantage)
description: Beauregard claims can be adapted to cover a wide range of inventions, from simple software applications to complex hardware systems.
guidance: They are versatile and can be tailored to different types of software-related inventions, but drafting should reflect the intended scope and implementation details.

name: Enhanced enforcement (advantage)
description: Beauregard claims can be easier to enforce in court, as they can more clearly define the scope of the invention and make it easier to prove infringement.
guidance: Clear product-oriented claim language (e.g., medium with encoded instructions) may simplify infringement analyses compared to certain process claims, but enforcement still depends on proving the claim elements.

name: Limited scope (disadvantage)
description: Beauregard claims are often limited in scope because they focus on specific steps or processes.
guidance: Such focus can make it difficult to protect broader concepts or inventions; consider complementing Beauregard claims with other claim types if broader coverage is desired.

name: Complexity of drafting and understanding (disadvantage)
description: Beauregard claims can be complex to draft and understand, especially for those not familiar with patent law.
guidance: Complexity can increase the cost and time required to obtain a patent. Ensure skilled counsel drafts the claims to balance clarity, scope, and eligibility.

name: Patent eligibility challenges specifically under the Alice test (disadvantage)
description: Beauregard claims may face patent eligibility challenges, particularly under the Alice test which requires claims be directed to patent-eligible subject matter and have sufficient inventive concept.
guidance: When drafting, emphasize how the claim is more than an abstract idea (e.g., tie to technological improvements or concrete implementation details) to reduce Alice risk.

name: Difficulty in enforcement due to proving steps/sequence
description: Enforcing Beauregard claims can be challenging because it may require proving that the infringer has performed all of the claimed steps in the exact sequence specified.
guidance: Consider how infringement will be proven in practice; if proof of exact step sequence is difficult, weigh alternative claim strategies or drafting approaches that avoid rigid step sequencing.

name: Risk of claim narrowing during prosecution or litigation
description: If a Beauregard claim is overly broad, it may be narrowed during prosecution or in litigation, which can limit its effectiveness.
guidance: Draft with care to avoid overbroad language that invites narrowing; consider fallback claim sets and claim amendments that preserve value.

name: Consideration of storage medium (tangible vs intangible)
description: Beauregard claims have historically been used for programs stored on tangible media but can also be used for programs stored on intangible media like the internet.
guidance: The choice of medium affects claim drafting and potential eligibility/enforcement issues; be explicit about the medium when beneficial, but recognize that claiming intangible distribution/storage may raise additional challenges.

name: Recommendation to consult experienced patent attorney
description: If you are considering filing a patent application for a computer program, you should consult with an experienced patent attorney to discuss whether a Beauregard claim is appropriate.
guidance: An attorney can help weigh benefits and drawbacks, advise on drafting to mitigate eligibility and enforcement risks, and recommend complementary claim types or prosecution strategies.

name: Applicant's Admissions of Prior Art (AAPA)
description: Statements made by applicant that certain information was 'prior art' (may appear in the background, drawings, or remarks) which are admissions that that work is available as prior art against applicant's claims.
guidance: See MPEP 2129 and MPEP 706.02 III. When material is labeled/ described as 'prior art', the examiner must determine whether the subject matter identified is applicant's own work or the work of another; admissions can be used even if the material wouldn't otherwise qualify under statutory categories.

name: Anticipation / Lack of Novelty (35 U.S.C. 102)
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102, prior art is used to establish lack of novelty, commonly referred to as 'anticipation' — when a single prior art reference teaches each and every element of a claim, either expressly or inherently.
guidance: A claim lacks novelty when it is anticipated by a single reference. Examiner must identify that each claim element is disclosed in the single reference (expressly or inherently).

name: Obviousness Legal Standard (35 U.S.C. 103)
description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA); patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
guidance: This is a legal conclusion based on underlying factual inquiries; apply the Graham factors and relevant case law (e.g., KSR) when determining obviousness.

name: Claims Must Be Viewed as a Whole
description: In determining differences between prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious—not whether individual differences would have been obvious in isolation.
guidance: Do not dissect the claim into parts for the obviousness inquiry; consider the claimed combination and reference Stratoflex v. Aeroquip for authority.

name: Graham v. John Deere — Core Obviousness Inquiries
description: The Graham inquiries: (1) Scope and content of the prior art; (2) Differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) Level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art at the time of the invention; (4) Does any objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations) exist?
guidance: Use these four factual inquiries as the framework for analyzing obviousness; support conclusions with articulated reasoning and evidence.

name: Claim Interpretation Standard
description: Claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: This interpretation determines the examiner's search scope. See In re Abbott Diabetes Care Inc., 104 USPQ2d 1337 (Fed. Cir. 2012) for guidance; structural similarity between prior art and invention is not required if similar utility exists.

name: Establishing a Prima Facie Case of Obviousness
description: The key to supporting any 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is clear articulation of the rationale or reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious; mere conclusory statements are not adequate. A prima facie case requires a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: If proposed modifications would render the invention inoperable or change its principle of operation, a prima facie case cannot be established. Cite In re Kahn and KSR guidance (In re Kahn, 78 USPQ2d 1329).

name: Teaching Away and Unexpected (Non‑Predictable) Results
description: A claimed combination may be nonobvious where the prior art teaches away from the claimed combination and the combination yields more than predictable results (e.g., Crocs — foam strap contacting foam base produced unexpected comfort/result).
guidance: Even if elements are individually known, teaching away or unpredictable synergistic results can support nonobviousness. Use factual findings about predictability and prior art attitudes.

name: Substituting One Known Element for Another (Predictable Variation)
description: A claim that is a simple substitution of one art‑recognized element for another (with well‑known, predictable function) is likely obvious (Agrizap example substituting resistive electrical switch for mechanical switch).
guidance: Consider whether the substitution was routine for PHOSITA and whether the substituted element's function was predictable; predictable, routine substitutions support obviousness.

name: Claims Define the Invention and Require Whole‑Claim Analysis
description: The claimed invention defines what applicant believes is the invention; claims must be considered as a whole and the analysis should include the problem being solved.
guidance: Avoid dissecting claims into isolated parts; analyze similarities/differences in structure and function relative to prior art and consider analogous vs non‑analogous art.

name: Difference Between Federal Courts and Patent Office Processes
description: Federal courts address infringement and validity and are not flexible (cannot amend patents); the Patent Office addresses patentability and prosecution is flexible (allowing give and take to determine appropriate claim scope), permits amendments by applicant, accepts rebuttal arguments, and considers secondary considerations.
guidance: Recognize procedural and remedial differences between court litigation and USPTO examination/prosecution contexts when framing rejections and responses.

name: Argue-only vs. Amend-and-Argue
description: Argue-only responses are allowed at substantially lower rates than amend-and-argue responses.
guidance: The difference is especially large for 103 (obviousness) rejections, where amendment is often necessary to overcome a multi-reference combination. Prefer amendment when the rejection hinges on combining multiple references or structural/claim-scope issues that an amendment can directly address.

name: Single-reference 102 rejections - argument often suffices
description: For 102 (anticipation) rejections, careful argument that the cited reference does not disclose every claim element can succeed without amendment.
guidance: Because anticipation is binary (the reference either does or does not disclose each element), a focused argument demonstrating a missing element can overcome a 102 rejection. Pull and analyze the exact cited passage; if it does not disclose an element, argue rather than amend.

name: 101 eligibility rejections - amendment often helps
description: For 101 rejections, adding technical-improvement language and concrete structural elements often helps even when arguing eligibility as filed.
guidance: Amendments that recite specific hardware tied to the claimed function move the needle. Consider adding concrete structural/technical limitations that show an improvement over abstract idea characterizations.

name: 112 rejections typically require amendment
description: 112 rejections (definiteness, written description, enablement) typically require amendment to resolve.
guidance: Pure argument that the claim is definite or that the specification supports the claim rarely succeeds without restructuring. Expect to amend claims or specification language (clarify terms, add embodiments, restructure claims) to overcome 112 grounds.

name: Examiner interview effect
description: Office action responses that are preceded by an examiner interview have substantially higher allowance rates than responses without an interview.
guidance: The interview effect is largest for complex cases with multiple rejections. Use interviews to clarify claim scope, understand examiner reasoning, and negotiate amendments or claim interpretations that will be persuasive in the written response.

name: Citing Federal Circuit cases selectively
description: Citing Federal Circuit cases for legal propositions (e.g., Phillips for claim construction, Williamson for 112(f)) is appropriate but should be selective.
guidance: One or two well-placed citations are better than a long string-cite of every relevant case. Use cases that directly and clearly support the legal proposition at issue rather than overloading the response with marginally relevant authorities.

name: Read and quote the examiner's cited passage
description: Always pull the examiner-cited passage and verify whether it actually discloses what the examiner claims.
guidance: A common pattern is the cited passage does not in fact disclose what the examiner says. If the passage fails to support the rejection, quote it back to the examiner in your response explaining why it does not teach the asserted limitation(s).

name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112)
description: A patent's specification must 'enable any person skilled in the art . . . to make and use' the patented invention.
guidance: The purpose is to ensure the public is told how to carry out the invention. The disclosure must be at least commensurate with the scope of the claims; when a range is claimed, there must be reasonable enablement of the scope of the range.

name: Challenger burden to prove lack of enablement
description: To prove that a claim is invalid for lack of enablement, a challenger must show by clear and convincing evidence that a person of ordinary skill in the art would not be able to practice the claimed invention without 'undue experimentation.'
guidance: This is a high evidentiary standard; after the challenger puts forward evidence that some experimentation is needed, the Wands factors provide the factual considerations a court weighs to determine whether experimentation is 'undue' or routine.

name: Wands Factor — amount of direction or guidance presented
description: One of the Wands factors is the amount of direction or guidance the specification provides to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Assess whether the specification's roadmap, examples, or protocols give sufficient guidance across the full scope of the claims (not merely for a narrow subset). Lack of meaningful guidance beyond examples weighs against enablement.

name: Wands Factor — presence or absence of working examples
description: One of the Wands factors is whether the specification includes working examples.
guidance: Working examples that cover only a narrow corner of a claimed genus may be insufficient; examples must be representative enough to support the full claimed breadth.

name: Wands Factor — predictability or unpredictability of the art
description: One of the Wands factors is how predictable the art is.
guidance: In unpredictable fields (e.g., translating sequence to structure or effect), courts more readily find that practicing the full claim scope requires undue experimentation. Evidence of unpredictability (expert testimony, admitted scientific limitations) is important.

name: Wands Factor — breadth of the claims
description: One of the Wands factors is the breadth of the claims.
guidance: Broad functional or genus claims raise the bar for enablement because the specification must enable the full scope; a narrow set of examples 'abide in a corner of the genus' and may not suffice for a broad claim.

name: Enablement must be commensurate with claim scope (range/genus guidance)
description: When a range is claimed, there must be reasonable enablement of the scope of the range; species/examples must meaningfully represent the claimed genus.
guidance: A specification does not need to describe every possible variant, but must provide enough to enable the full claimed range. If the disclosed embodiments occupy only a 'corner' of the claimed genus, enablement can fail.

name: Need for concrete identification of non-enabled embodiments
description: Wands analysis routinely involves concrete identification of at least some embodiment(s) asserted not to be enabled—including what particular products or processes are or may be within the claim.
guidance: Challengers should identify specific products/processes within the claim and explain how much experimentation a skilled artisan would need to make and use them; abstract assertions of breadth are insufficient.

name: Functional claim limitations increase enablement hurdles
description: Functional limitations (claims defined by what they do rather than precise structure) pose a high hurdle for enablement, especially when broad in functional diversity.
guidance: Undue experimentation can include the work needed to identify, among many structurally-eligible candidates, those that satisfy the required function (e.g., binding + blocking). Courts scrutinize functional genera closely for predictability and guidance.

name: Sufficiency of specification 'roadmap' and working examples
description: A specification's 'roadmap' and examples may provide guidance, but they must enable beyond the narrow scope of working examples to reach the full claim scope.
guidance: Even if a roadmap enables producing antibodies similar to working examples, without nonconclusory evidence that the roadmap predictably produces the full scope, a factfinder cannot reasonably find enablement for a broad claim.

name: Standard of review for enablement appeals
description: Whether a claim satisfies enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 is a question of law reviewed without deference, though it may be based on underlying factual findings reviewed for clear error.
guidance: Appellate courts independently review the legal conclusion of enablement, but accept district court factual findings unless clearly erroneous; parties should preserve and develop factual record on Wands factors.

name: Specification: clarity, fullness, and distinction
description: "The specification ... shall be so particular, and said models so exact, as not only to distinguish the invention or discovery from other things before known and used, but also to enable a workman or other person skilled in the art ... to make, construct, or use the same ..." (also phrased as "clearly, truly, and fully").
guidance: Requires written description and enablement: the specification must distinguish the claimed invention from prior known things and enable a skilled person to practice it; certified copies are admissible evidence.

name: Defendant's defenses to patent enforcement
description: Defendant may plead the general issue and give the act and any special matter (with 30 days' written notice) in evidence, e.g., that "the specification filed by the plaintiff does not contain the whole of the truth ... or that it contains more than is necessary ..." and if concealment or addition was intended or actually misled the public so the described effect cannot be produced by the means specified, verdict shall be for the defendant.
guidance: Permits invalidity defenses based on inadequate or deceptive specification, prior public use/description, surreptitious procurement, or claiming more than necessary; requires notice for special matters and can lead to patent being declared void and costs for defendant.

name: Photographs — black and white
description: Photographs, including photocopies of photographs, are not ordinarily permitted in utility and design patent applications, but will be accepted if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.
guidance: Acceptable examples include electrophoresis gels, blots (immunological, western, Southern, northern), autoradiographs, cell cultures, histological tissue sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, TLC plates, crystalline structures, and ornamental effects in design patents. If the subject can be illustrated by a drawing, the examiner may require a drawing instead. Photographs must be of sufficient quality so all details are reproducible in the printed patent. Photographs must be developed on paper meeting sheet-size (§1.84(f)) and margin (§1.84(g)) requirements.

name: Views — general requirement
description: The drawing must contain as many views as necessary to show the invention; views may be plan, elevation, section, or perspective, and detail views on larger scale may be used.
guidance: All views should be grouped together and arranged on the sheet(s) without wasting space, preferably upright, clearly separated from one another, and must not be included on sheets containing specifications, claims, or abstract. Views must not be connected by projection lines and must not contain center lines. Waveforms may be connected by dashed lines to show relative timing.

name: Commercial success must flow from specification-disclosed functions/advantages
description: To be pertinent to nonobviousness, commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success cannot be attributable to improvements or modifications made by others.
guidance: If commercial success derives from features not disclosed or inherent in the specification, it is not probative of nonobviousness. See In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure (enablement) and burden after prima facie
description: Once the examiner establishes a prima facie lack of enablement, the applicant bears the burden to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the disclosure as a guide.
guidance: Evidence to supplement a superficially deficient specification must show that missing information would have been known to one of ordinary skill (In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth). Affidavits cannot establish facts that the specification itself should recite (In re Buchner; In re Smyth).

name: Attribution affidavits/declarations to defeat prior art (37 CFR 1.132)
description: Under certain circumstances an affidavit or declaration may attribute an activity or reference to the applicant, thereby removing it as prior art, but specific showings under 37 CFR 1.132 are required.
guidance: When a reference discloses subject matter claimed in the application, applicant must provide satisfactory showing that the subject matter was derived from or originated with applicant (In re Katz). An uncontradicted unequivocal statement by the applicant may be accepted (In re DeBaun), but contrary evidence can defeat such a statement (Ex parte Kroger; In re Carreira).

name: Corrections to data on file wrapper / PALM bib‑data
description: If the examiner notices errors in data on the file wrapper or PALM bib‑data sheet, the examiner must correct per the application's series (08/ or earlier; 09/series; 10/ and above) by marking in red ink and forwarding to TC technical support for database correction and printing a new bib‑data sheet or label as appropriate.
guidance: Typical corrections include inventorship (37 CFR 1.48), filing date, prior U.S. application numbers, claims for priority/benefit (35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)). Distinguish 'residence' vs 'mailing address' and encourage Application Data Sheet (37 CFR 1.76) for residence changes to meet publication/printing timelines.

name: Quantitative experiments to determine operating parameters
description: He 'made the mixtures in all proportions... found by the experiments that when a current... forced up a tube 4/10 of an inch in diameter, the necessary current was 9 inches in a second to prevent its coming down that tube.'
guidance: Measure and record quantitative thresholds (diameter, velocity, mixture proportions) that define safe/working limits — use instruments, timed/measured trials, and numerical data to substantiate claims.

name: Prepare written specification and obtain a patent
description: 'This improved form of rail and chair was embodied in a patent... the specification of the same patent also described various important improvements in the locomotive itself.'
guidance: Draft a clear specification describing construction and claimed improvements (rails, chairs, locomotive features) and pursue formal patent protection; include practical details sufficient for reproduction and legal claims.

name: Maintain dated records, witnesses, and testimonials to support priority claims
description: Stephenson's dates of first/second/third lamp trials (21 Oct, 4 Nov, 30 Nov 1815), committee testimony (1835), public letters, and subscriptions/testimonials were used in the controversy over priority.
guidance: Keep dated experimental records, witness statements, and public demonstrations; deposit or publish contemporaneous accounts (letters, society presentations) to establish precedence in priority disputes.

name: Acknowledge prior observations and distinguish independent application
description: The text notes Tennant and Wollaston had observed the fact earlier; both Stephenson and Davy may have been independent, and priority claims were disputed.
guidance: Research prior art and publicly known observations; document how your contribution differs (application, construction, testing) from prior knowledge to support novelty and independent invention claims.

name: "Same invention" double patenting (35 U.S.C. 171)
description: A design-design statutory double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 prevents the issuance of a second patent for a design already patented. For this type to be proper, identical designs with identical scope must be twice claimed.
