guidance: This 'same invention' type cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer. Use form paragraph 15.23 (and 15.23.02 summary). Apply when the same design is being claimed twice (compare claims).

name: Design-utility "same invention" double patenting
description: A design-utility 'same invention' double patenting rejection is based on judicial doctrine (no statutory basis) when the same invention is claimed in a design and a utility patent.
guidance: The doctrine is applied as in In re Thorington. The 'same invention' type (statutory or nonstatutory) cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer (In re Swett). Use appropriate form paragraphs 15.24.07/15.24.08 where applicable.

name: Nonstatutory (obviousness-type) double patenting general rule
description: A nonstatutory double patenting rejection is based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the right to exclude. It applies where claims are directed to the same inventive concept with different appearances or differing scope which are patentably indistinct from each other.
guidance: May be overcome by submission of a terminal disclaimer (subject to ownership/common ownership conditions). Precede such rejections with form paragraph 15.24.06 (heading).

name: Prima facie case for obviousness-type double patenting (designs)
description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness-type double patenting: (A) the conflicting design claims must have overall appearances with basically the same design characteristics; and (B) the differences between the two designs must be insufficient to patentably distinguish one design from the other.
guidance: The claim in the reference must be considered as a whole (overall appearance), not by isolated elements. Differences may be considered patentably insufficient when they are de minimis or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the art. Perform the factual inquiries under Graham v. John Deere and then determine if results support a prima facie obviousness-type double patenting conclusion.

name: Obviousness-type double patenting when designs have differing scope (A–C test)
description: When designs have differing scope, a rejection is appropriate if: (A) the difference in scope is minor and patentably indistinct; (B) patent protection for the design, fully disclosed in and covered by the claim of the reference, would be extended by allowance of the later claim; and (C) no terminal disclaimer has been filed.
guidance: Consider combination vs subcombination (narrow vs broad claim). If the narrower claim is not fully disclosed in the broader reference, a nonstatutory double patenting rejection is inappropriate. Additional disclosure may be in title, descriptive statement, or broken-line drawing.

name: Comparison limitations between utility and design applications
description: Double patenting rejections are based on a comparison of claims; while there is a direct correlation between drawings and claim in a design application, no such correlation is necessary in a utility application or patent.
guidance: Any double patenting consideration between a utility application/patent and a design application cannot be based on the utility drawing disclosure alone. The examiner must be able to recreate the design claimed from the utility claims without reliance on the drawings. See Anchor Hocking Corp. v. Eyelet Specialty Co.

name: Right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) — certified copy/timing
description: No design patent application is entitled to right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) unless a claim therefor and a certified copy of the original foreign application, specification and drawings are filed in the USPTO before the issue fee is paid, or at such time during pendency as required by the Director (not earlier than six months after filing).
guidance: The certification must be made by the foreign patent office or proper authority and show dates. The Director may require translations and other information as necessary. See MPEP §15.02.

name: Identification of prior U.S. application(s) when claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: If applicant is entitled under 35 U.S.C. 120 to the benefit of an earlier U.S. filing date, the statement such as 'This is a division [continuation] of design Application No. ———, filed ———.' should appear in the first sentence(s) of the specification (or be included in an application data sheet per 37 CFR 1.76).
guidance: 37 CFR 1.78(a)(2) requires this; failure to timely submit such a reference is considered a waiver of benefit. Form paragraph 15.26 may be used to remind applicant and a suggested format is provided.

name: Disclosure requirement for entitlement to benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: Applicants are entitled to claim the benefit of earlier applications under 35 U.S.C. 120 only when the earlier application discloses the invention in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: In continuation and divisional applications, the examiner must determine whether conditions for priority under 120 have been met. If the claimed design in a continuation/divisional is not disclosed in the original application, the later application is not entitled to benefit and examiner should notify applicant with reasons, using form paragraphs 2.09/2.10 and require cancellation of the 'benefit' statement or submission of a supplemental ADS where appropriate.

name: C‑I‑P claiming benefit where parent claimed foreign priority — foreign status determination
description: Where a C‑I‑P claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 to an earlier U.S. application which in turn claims priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) to a foreign application, and the conditions of 120 are not met, the examiner must determine whether the foreign application has matured into a form of patent protection. If it has matured and would anticipate or render the CIP claim obvious, the foreign application qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172 and the CIP claim should be rejected under 102/103.
guidance: Use the charts in MPEP §1504.02 to determine the status of the foreign application. If status cannot be determined, use appropriate form paragraphs (15.75/15.75.01) to explain rejection or caution.

name: Practice for allegations of missing communications sent to the Office (external client claims delivered)
description: If a person alleges they submitted a communication to the Office but the item appears not to have been received by CIPO, the Office will consider an affidavit or statutory declaration with documentary evidence supporting reception.
guidance: Documentary evidence may include indications of reception or payment. If satisfied the Office received the item on a specified date, the Office will deem it received on that date. Re-submission of the documents will also be required.

name: Revised claim construction standard (Nov. 2018)
description: Revised claim construction standard used in AIA proceedings (Nov. 2018).
guidance: This is a change to the way claims are construed in AIA trials; practitioners should apply the November 2018 standard when drafting petitions, responses, and institution analyses.

name: 2019 revised patent subject matter eligibility guidance
description: 2019 revised patent subject matter eligibility guidance impacting ex parte appeals and AIA cases.
guidance: Changes to subject matter eligibility guidance affect both ex parte and AIA practice; practitioners should apply the revised guidance in claim drafting, petitioning, and appeal strategy.

name: RFC on discretion to institute AIA trials — institution considerations
description: Request for Comments (Oct. 2020) sought input on whether to promulgate rules with case-specific analyses for deciding whether to institute a trial for (1) petitions on claims previously challenged in another petition; (2) more than one petition filed at/about same time on same patent; (3) petitions on patents subject to U.S. district court or ITC proceedings; and (4) any other considerations regarding discretion to institute.
guidance: The RFC solicited stakeholder views on formalizing institution-discretion analyses. Practitioners should review the Executive Summary and comments (822 comments received) to understand stakeholder perspectives and possible future rulemaking affecting institution discretion.

name: Particular Machine (machine-or-transformation test as a clue)
description: When determining whether a claim recites significantly more than a judicial exception, consider whether the judicial exception is applied with, or by use of, a particular machine. The machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test is a useful clue and investigative tool but is not a stand-alone test for eligibility.
guidance: General points: All claims must be evaluated using the Alice/Mayo two-part test. A claim that passes Alice/Mayo is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test; a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes the M-or-T test. Examiners should consider other Step 2B factors (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use/technological environment) when deciding whether a recited machine provides significantly more. Relevant factors when determining whether a recited machine or apparatus provides significantly more include: I. The particularity or generality of the elements of the machine or apparatus — whether the machine can be specifically identified (not any and all machines). Example: Mackay Radio (specific antenna details) and Eibel Process (Fourdrinier machine arranged in a particular way). Note that a general purpose computer applying a judicial exception using conventional computer functions does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial v. Hulu). II. Whether the machine or apparatus implements the steps of the method — integral use of a machine to achieve performance may provide significantly more, whereas a machine that is merely an object on which the method operates generally does not (CyberSource v. Retail Decisions). If the machine only functions as an obvious mechanism to permit a solution to be achieved more quickly, it likely does not add significantly more (Versata v. SAP). III. Whether its involvement is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use — if the machine contributes only nominally or insignificantly (e.g., mere data-gathering or field-of-use limitations), it would not provide significantly more (Bilski; CyberSource). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f), 2106.05(g), and 2106.05(h) for additional related considerations, and MPEP § 2106.03 for the definition of 'machine.'

name: Particular Transformation (machine-or-transformation test clue)
description: Another consideration for determining whether a claim recites significantly more is whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing. Transformation and reduction of an article to a different state or thing is a clue to patentability for process claims that do not include particular machines.
guidance: General points: The transformation of an article is an important clue but not a stand-alone test; evaluate claims under Alice/Mayo. An 'article' includes a physical object or substance and must be particular (specifically identifiable). 'Transformation' means the article has changed to a different state or thing — usually more than mere use or change in location; a new/different function or use can be evidence of transformation. Purely mental processes are not considered an eligible transformation; for data, mere manipulation of basic mathematical constructs (the paradigmatic 'abstract idea') is not a transformation. Example of transformation: Tilghman v. Proctor (transforming fatty bodies into fat acids and glycerine); Diamond v. Diehr (transforming raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products). Where a transformation is recited, consider these factors in the 'significantly more' analysis: 1. The particularity or generality of the transformation — more particular transformations likely provide significantly more. 2. The degree to which the recited article is particular — transformations applied to generically recited articles or 'any and all' articles likely do not provide significantly more. 3. The nature of the transformation in terms of the type/extent of change — transformations resulting in different function or use are more likely to provide significantly more than mere relocation. 4. The nature of the article transformed — physical/tangible object/substance transformations are more likely to provide significantly more than transformations of intangible concepts. 5. Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use — if the transformation contributes only nominally or insignificantly (e.g., a data-gathering step or field-of-use limitation), it will likely not provide significantly more (Mayo example). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f), 2106.05(g), and 2106.05(h) for related considerations.

name: Enablement is separate from written description
description: Enablement (teach how to make and use) is a distinct requirement from the written description requirement.
guidance: The fact that an additional limitation lacks descriptive support in the original disclosure does not necessarily mean it is not enabled; enablement and written description must be analyzed with their separate and distinct criteria (Vas-Cath v. Mahurkar; see MPEP § 2161). When claimed subject matter appears only in the claims and not in the specification, object to the specification for lack of support (form paragraph 7.44) and analyze enablement separately.

name: Test of enablement — undue/unreasonable experimentation
description: The standard asks whether the experimentation needed to practice the invention is undue or unreasonable — if so, the claim is not enabled.
guidance: Rooted in Minerals Separation v. Hyde and interpreted via In re Wands and other cases. The test is whether one reasonably skilled in the art could make or use the invention from the disclosure plus what is known in the art without undue experimentation. Patent need not teach well-known art.

name: Wands factors (Undue experimentation factors)
description: Factors to assess whether necessary experimentation is reasonable or undue, as set out in In re Wands.
guidance: The Wands factors include, but are not limited to: (A) The breadth of the claims; (B) The nature of the invention; (C) The state of the prior art; (D) The level of one of ordinary skill; (E) The level of predictability in the art; (F) The amount of direction provided by the inventor; (G) The existence of working examples; and (H) The quantity of experimentation needed based on the disclosure. Examiners must consider all relevant factors and evidence — it is improper to rely on only one factor (In re Wands). See related MPEP subsections for deeper discussion of each factor.

name: None or one working example — evidentiary role
description: The absence of working examples, or presence of only a single working example, is not by itself dispositive of enablement.
guidance: A single working example can preclude a rejection that 'nothing is enabled' because that embodiment would be enabled; however, one example may not enable a claim that is broader than that example. Examiners must evaluate all facts and explain why extrapolation across the claimed scope is not justified (Amgen v. Sanofi; In re Borkowski).

name: Predictability of the art inversely relates to amount of required guidance
description: The more known and predictable the art, the less detailed the specification needs to be to enable one skilled in the art; conversely, nascent or unpredictable arts require more specific and useful teaching.
guidance: Assess enablement in light of the state of the art and predictability. Nascent technology must be enabled with specific and useful teaching because a person of ordinary skill has little independent knowledge (In re Fisher; Chiron v. Genentech). Predictability is measured by ability to extrapolate disclosed/known results to claimed invention.

name: Burden on the examiner under the enablement requirement
description: The examiner bears the initial burden to give reasons, supported by evidence, for a conclusion of lack of enablement (including lack of correlation for models).
guidance: Examiners must weigh evidence for and against enablement and explain why a person skilled in the art would not be able to make/use the full scope of the claims without undue experimentation. Rejections must state the factual basis and consider all Wands factors rather than rely on a single factor.

name: Determination of enablement based on evidence as a whole
description: Enablement is a question of law based on underlying factual findings; the determination must be made by weighing all relevant factual considerations and evidence together.
guidance: A conclusion of lack of enablement means that, considering all evidence on the Wands factors, the specification as filed would not have taught one skilled in the art to make and/or use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation (In re Wright; In re Vaeck; Amgen v. Sanofi).

name: Enablement must be to persons skilled in the art
description: The enablement requirement is satisfied if the disclosure enables 'one skilled in the pertinent art' to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Assessment involves factual findings about the level of ordinary skill, what was known in the art, and whether the specification provides sufficient direction for that skilled person (see MPEP § 2164.05(b)).

name: Enablement commensurate in scope with the claims (breadth principle)
description: The specification must enable the full scope of the claimed invention; broader claims require correspondingly broader enablement.
guidance: ‘The more one claims, the more one must enable’ (Amgen v. Sanofi). Examiners should consider whether representative examples and general qualities allow extrapolation to the entire claimed scope. See related subsections concerning single means claims, inoperative subject matter, and critical features not claimed (MPEP § 2164.08).

name: Burden on respondent for affirmative defenses (§11.49)
description: A respondent asserting any affirmative defense in a USPTO disciplinary proceeding bears the burden of proving that defense by clear and convincing evidence, per 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.
guidance: This aligns with the high evidentiary standard applied to the § 11.24(d) exceptions and requires robust proof for claims such as untimeliness, lack of jurisdiction, or challenges to the sufficiency of the state's discipline record.

name: Form and timing of submitting proposed amendments
description: A proposed amendment is made by filing a paper directing the proposed specified changes to the patent specification, including the claims, or to the drawings. An amendment paper may accompany a request by the patent owner under § 1.510(e), be part of a patent owner statement under paragraph (b) of § 1.530, or be submitted where permitted during prosecution under § 1.550(a) or § 1.937.
guidance: Amendment papers must follow the formal filing rules and can be submitted at specific permitted times in the reexamination process.

name: Specification amendments: full-paragraph requirement
description: Changes to the specification other than to the claims must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph including markings per paragraph (f), except that an entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presenting the text of the paragraph.
guidance: The precise point in the specification where an added or rewritten paragraph is located must be identified. This applies to paper or compact disc submissions (see §§ 1.96 and 1.825). See MPEP § 2250 for examples of proper claim amendment format.

name: Marking convention for showing changes
description: Any changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must include the following markings: (1) matter to be omitted must be enclosed in brackets; (2) matter to be added must be underlined.
guidance: Consistently use brackets for deletions and underlining for additions per § 1.530(f).

name: Amendment to disclosure may be required for correspondence
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: Be prepared to amend the disclosure to bring claims, specification, and drawings into substantial correspondence when requested.

name: Amendments made relative to the patent as of the request filing date
description: All amendments must be made relative to the patent specification, including the claims and drawings, which are in effect as of the date of filing the request for reexamination.
guidance: Reference the patent text as it existed on the request filing date when preparing amendments.

name: No enlargement of claim scope; no new matter; expired patent restrictions
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. Moreover, no amendment, other than cancellation of claims, will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after expiration of the patent.
guidance: Do not propose claim amendments that broaden scope or introduce subject matter not originally disclosed; after expiration only claim cancellations may be incorporated.

name: IFW reexamination amendment entry format (A–G)
description: For an IFW reexamination file, amendments are entered as follows: (A) amendment paper designated by consecutive letters (A, B, C, etc.); (B) each entry blocked by two lines and given successive numbers (A1, A2, ...); (C) copy of claims filed with the request and patent pages containing revised paragraphs printed from IFW file history; (D) a line drawn through any claim(s) or paragraph(s) amended with substituted copy indicated by amendment letter/number; (E) canceled claims/paragraphs part of the patent surrounded by brackets (not lined through); (F) marked up copy of claims filed with the request and patent pages scanned into IFW file history; (G) marked up amendment document scanned into IFW file history.
guidance: Follow IFW-specific formatting and scanning/entry procedures; claims must not be renumbered; numbering of claims added during reexamination must follow the highest numbered patent claim.

name: Director-initiated reexamination authority and criteria
description: Under 37 CFR 1.520 the Director may, at any time during the period of enforceability of a patent, determine whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised by patents or printed publications discovered by the Director or brought to his attention, and may initiate ex parte reexamination without a request and without fee; such orders are rare and only in compelling circumstances after review of all facts.
guidance: Authority to order reexamination at the Director's initiative is delegated to the Deputy Commissioner for Patent Examination Policy and others specified. If an employee becomes aware of unusual facts, forward a memorandum setting forth facts (including a proposed rejection of claims) with the patent file and prior art to OPLA through supervisory chain; include an electronic disk copy of the memorandum.

name: Director's statutory decision timeline and record (35 U.S.C. 303)
description: Within three months following filing of a request for reexamination under section 302 the Director will determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim is raised by the request, with or without consideration of other patents/printed publications. The determination is placed in the official file and a copy mailed to the owner of record and the requester.
guidance: The existence of an SNQ is not precluded by the cited reference having been previously considered by the Office.

name: Examiner determination timeline and appeal/petition rights (37 CFR 1.515)
description: Within three months following filing of an ex parte reexamination request, an examiner will consider the request and determine whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised by the request and prior art cited therein. Statements under § 1.501(a)(2) will not be considered by the examiner in making the determination. The determination is based on claims in effect at the time, becomes part of the official file, and is mailed to the patent owner and requester.
guidance: If no SNQ is found, a partial fee refund may be made under § 1.26(c). The requester may seek review by petition to the Director under § 1.181 within one month of mailing of the examiner’s determination; the petition must comply with § 1.181(b). If no timely petition is filed or if the petition affirms no SNQ, the determination is final and nonappealable.

name: Statements of ranges/proportions must be truthful and operative at extremes
description: When the patentee gives certain limits or proportions (e.g., ranges of alloy composition or mixture proportions), if particular specified extremes would not perform as claimed, that falsity may invalidate the patent.
guidance: Courts treat the accuracy of claimed ranges as a question of fact for the jury. If the patentee asserts that 'both of which extremes, and all intermediate proportions, will' produce a property, but evidence shows some extremes fail, the patent may be defeated (example: copper/zinc proportion disputes).

name: Compositions with approximate proportions can be sufficient
description: Descriptions stating approximate proportions (e.g., 'about from four ounces to a pound of sulphur to a pound of rubber') are sufficient if properly reduced to practice will produce the claimed article.
guidance: The inventive direction may be exhausted by giving the proportions and process; remaining work is that of a skilled workman. If, however, the described proportions fail to produce the article when properly practiced, then validity is a different question (may require experiment to determine optimum proportion).

name: Signatures and attestations required by statute
description: The statute requires a formal attestation: 'they must be signed by the inventor and by two witnesses.' (Act of 1870: 'the specification and claim shall be signed by the inventor, and attested by two witnesses').
guidance: Ensure proper execution and witness attestations; a copy of the drawings shall be attached to the patent as part of the specification. There is some historical ambiguity whether drawings must be separately signed, but current statutory language requires signature and attestation.

name: Suggested substitutions and equivalence are construed by specification proportions and are fact questions
description: When a specification suggests substitution of one component for another (e.g., 'naphtha' for 'kerosene') but prescribes proportions, the substitution is construed in light of those proportions; whether one compound is 'substantially the same' as another differing in proportions is a question of fact for the jury.
guidance: Claims using suggested substitutions will be interpreted according to the proportions expressly prescribed; expert evidence may be required to determine substantial equivalence (example: Tyler v. Boston, naphtha/kerosene proportions).

name: Mayo two-step framework (directed-to and inventive concept)
description: Step 1: determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea; Step 2: if so, consider whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: If the claim simply recites the law and adds conventional activity, it fails step 2. Courts apply precedent (Mayo, Diehr, Flook) to decide whether the additional elements integrate the law into a patent-eligible application or merely attempt to monopolize the law itself.

name: Transformation / machine-or-transformation indicia of eligibility
description: Implementation of a law/formula within a transformative process or via a specific machine (e.g., Diehr's rubber-molding process using the Arrhenius equation implemented by a computer controlling the press) supports patent eligibility.
guidance: While not a sole test, showing that a mathematical formula or natural law is integrated into a practical application (installation, continuous monitoring, automatic control) can demonstrate that the claim is 'significantly more' than the law itself.

name: Directed-to vs application distinction and the draftsman's-art warning
description: Courts caution against allowing patent eligibility to 'depend simply on the draftsman's art'—i.e., dressing an ineligible law in application language to claim it.
guidance: Flook, Alice, and related authorities warn that merely appending 'apply it' or adding conventional steps will not render a claim eligible. Examiners and courts will look beyond form to substance to determine whether the claim truly claims an application or merely the law itself.

name: AIA §33 prohibition on patents directed to human organisms
description: The America Invents Act §33 states: 'Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.'
guidance: This statutory limitation removes human organisms from patent eligibility; the PTO has advised applicants to include 'non-human' limitations where appropriate. The precise scope of 'human organism' can be a contested interpretive question.

name: PTO drafting guidance for claims touching human beings
description: PTO guidance: 'A claim directed to or including within its scope a human being will not be considered to be patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101' and suggests adding a 'non-human' limitation where needed.
guidance: This is administrative guidance for claim drafting to avoid a ground of rejection; negative limitations are a permissible drafting device. Administrative guidance does not change statutory text but affects examiner practice.

name: Software and business-method eligibility—'rooted in computer technology' criterion
description: For computer-implemented inventions, claims that are 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' to solve a problem specifically arising in computer networks or that provide an unconventional technological solution may be eligible (e.g., DDR Holdings, Bascom, Amdocs).
guidance: Courts distinguish between merely performing a conventional business practice on the Internet (likely abstract) and inventing a technical solution to Internet-centric problems (more likely to carry an inventive concept).

name: Conventionality fact-finding in eligibility determinations
description: Whether claim elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' in the relevant field is a factual inquiry that affects §101 outcomes (Mayo emphasized that routine lab steps cannot supply the inventive concept).
guidance: Evidence about common practice in the field, prior art, and technical conventionality can be determinative; examiners and courts will consider what was routine at the time of the claim.

name: Definition of a Markman hearing (Claim Construction Hearing)
description: A Markman hearing is a pre-trial hearing in a U.S. District Court during which a judge examines evidence from all parties on the appropriate meanings of relevant keywords used in a patent claim when patent infringement is alleged by a plaintiff. It is also known as a 'Claim Construction Hearing'.
guidance: This hearing is focused on construing claim language (what is and is not protected). The judge, not the jury, determines the meaning of claim terms for the case.

name: Importance of claim construction for infringement outcomes
description: Since the patent claims specify what constitutes and does not constitute protected intellectual property, claim construction is crucial in resolving patent disputes; the court determines patent infringement cases by interpreting the claims.
guidance: A favorable claim construction ruling can indicate likely case outcomes and often encourages settlement. The judge’s claim construction finding informs jury instructions and the jury then determines whether infringement occurred (including application of the doctrine of equivalents).

name: Judge vs. jury roles in patent trials
description: The judge decides how claims should be understood (claim construction) while the jury is the fact-finder that decides whether infringement actually occurred.
guidance: Although the Seventh Amendment protects the right to a jury trial, the Supreme Court (Markman) held that judges, experienced in interpreting written language, are better suited to define claim terms. The jury’s infringement decision must be informed by the judge’s claim construction.

name: Governing claim construction approach (Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
description: Phillips v. AWH Corp. (Federal Circuit, 2004) established the current method for construing patent claims. The correct claim construction cannot be determined using a predetermined process; instead, a set of criteria are applied to choose the right construction.
guidance: Later decisions have cited Phillips as foundational. The Phillips framework emphasizes intrinsic evidence, considers extrinsic evidence cautiously, and rejects rigid, single-step rules for construction.

name: Substantiating claim construction through documentation and evidence
description: Substantiate claim construction through critical review of specification, prosecution history, and expert evidence; draft opinions, notes, and documentation required to substantiate the scope/interpretation of claims and/or claim terms/elements and limitations.
guidance: Prepare detailed claim charts, mapping sheets, and technical analyses that align claim language to specification disclosures and prosecution history to justify proposed constructions.

name: Establishing expert credibility and preparing expert materials
description: Establish credibility and credentials of the testifying expert; provide technical tutorials and charts to help judges understand the claimed subject matter.
guidance: IIPRD-style support includes preparing technical tutorials, expert support for depositions, help with document requests, requests for admission, interrogatories, and other materials to build effective expert testimony and background.

name: Using claim charts to set up validity defenses and map prior art
description: Set up a validity defence through comprehensive claim charts demonstrating scope of each claim term/element/limitation and mapping with prior art reference(s).
guidance: Detailed claim charts help both invalidity and non-infringement strategies by showing where prior art reads on claimed limitations or where accused products fall outside claim scope.

name: Practical support activities for Markman proceedings
description: Provide assistance in preparing formal documents, technical disclosures, mapping sheets, deposition support, preparing document requests, preparing requests for admission, interrogatories, and other discovery-related activities.
guidance: Comprehensive pre-hearing preparation and supporting materials can simplify complex technical claims for the court and strengthen claim construction positions.

name: Claims should be clear and concise
description: Claims should be clear and concise and be supported by the description (Art. 84 EPC).
guidance: Clarity and conciseness are required to ensure that the scope of protection can be determined. The boards of appeal repeatedly emphasise clarity for legal certainty (e.g. T 337/95; T 586/97; T 437/98; T 728/98; T 1074/00; T 560/09; T 754/13; T 129/13).

name: Wording must satisfy Art.84 and Implementing Rule requirements considering invention's nature
description: The primary aim of the wording used in a claim must be to satisfy the requirements under Art. 84 and R.29(1) EPC 1973 (R.43(1) EPC), having regard to the particular nature of the invention, and the purpose of the claims (G 2/88).
guidance: Claim drafting must be tailored to the invention and the claims' purpose; literal/formal phrasing alone is not sufficient if it fails to meet Art.84/R.43 criteria. Consider both legal/formal requirements and the technical character of the invention when choosing wording.

name: Claims must enable the protection conferred to be determined (extent of protection)
description: The purpose of claims under the EPC is to enable the protection conferred by the patent or patent application to be determined (Art. 69 EPC), and thus the rights of the patent owner within the designated contracting states (Art. 64 EPC).
guidance: Claims should be drafted so third parties, courts and authorities can ascertain the extent of protection; the claim's wording determines scope and thus the rights conferred across contracting states.

name: Claims must be considered with regard to patentability requirements (Arts. 52–57 EPC)
description: The purpose of claims must be considered having regard to the patentability requirements of Art. 52 to 57 EPC.
guidance: Although Art.84 is a formal/content requirement, claims cannot be divorced from substantive patentability considerations: what is claimed must be coherent with novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, etc., when assessing scope and clarity.

name: Claims must provide legal certainty / public notice
description: Claims must be clear for the sake of legal certainty; the public should not be left in any doubt as to which subject-matter is covered and which is not.
guidance: Legal certainty is paramount where a monopoly affects public rights (see T 81/14). Claims serve as public notice; ambiguous claims undermine legal certainty and are objectionable.

name: Claims must allow the skilled person to establish demarcation of scope without undue burden
description: The skilled person should be able to establish the demarcation of the scope of the claim (i.e. its extent of protection) without undue burden (T 754/13).
guidance: Evaluate whether a person skilled in the art can, using the claim as drafted (and the description if necessary), determine whether a particular embodiment falls within the claim, without excessive analysis or interpretation.

name: Conclusive/common-sense assertions insufficient to prove motivation
description: Claims of obviousness cannot rest on conclusory testimony that elements are 'well-known' or on an assertion that combination is justified by 'common sense' without evidentiary support.
guidance: Generalized or conclusory expert testimony that elements were known or that a combination is 'common sense' is inadequate. The patentee/accuser must provide nonconclusory evidence showing why a POSA would combine the references.

name: Reasonable expectation of success in obviousness combinations
description: When combining references to show obviousness, a skilled artisan must have had a reasonable expectation of success in achieving the claimed invention.
guidance: In pharmaceutical/dosage cases, courts evaluate the combined message of prior art (e.g., teaching that an optimal dose may be higher) and whether that would lead a POSA to a dosage with a reasonable expectation of success. Evidence that prior art suggested higher dosing and available dosage increments can support obviousness.

name: Obviousness-type double patenting (OTDP) & patent term adjustments
description: OTDP prevents patentees from obtaining a second patent on a patentably indistinct invention to effectively extend the life of the first patent; the first‑filed, first‑issued patent in a family sets the maximum exclusivity period for claimed subject matter and variants.
guidance: Courts will consider whether continuing patents improperly extend rights beyond the first‑filed/first‑issued family's maximum exclusivity, including issues arising from patent term adjustments (PTA). Distinguish prior precedent where additional PTA in continuations was treated as extending term.

name: Claim construction: do not read limitations into claims absent support
description: Claims should not be construed to include limitations not present in the claim language unless the intrinsic record clearly compels it.
guidance: Example: claims reciting 'a psychiatric patient' were improperly read to require suitability for the 'general population.' Courts must base constructions on claim language and intrinsic evidence, avoiding importation of unclaimed limitations such as specific patient subgroups (e.g., 'mild renal impairment') unless clearly required.

name: Claim construction of numeric values and rounding
description: Numeric claim language (e.g., 'a pH of 13 or higher') can be ambiguous as to rounding and approximation, and may require extrinsic evidence to resolve whether conventional margins of error apply.
guidance: Where specification and prosecution history are inconclusive about whether a numeric value allows rounding (e.g., whether '13' means 12.5–13.4), courts may seek extrinsic evidence (textbook excerpts, expert testimony) to determine the proper construction.

name: Broad interpretation of 'based at least in part on' language
description: Phrases like 'based at least in part on' place no constraint on the manner in which inputs are used unless the specification imposes such a constraint; inputs need not be used distinctly from one another.
guidance: The broadest reasonable interpretation permits an input to be calculated from another claimed input. Absent intrinsic language limiting the manner of use, do not treat listed inputs as required to be independent components.

name: Specification statements describing 'the invention' can limit claims when uniform
description: When the specification uniformly refers to an aspect (e.g., pre-fetching) as part of 'this invention' or 'the method,' that description can inform a limiting claim construction.
guidance: Although references to 'the invention' are not always limiting, where the intrinsic evidence and prosecution history uniformly tie an embodiment (such as pre‑fetching advertising objects) to the invention, courts may construe the claims to include that aspect.

name: Claim construction on motion to dismiss — scope and need for fuller proceedings
description: District courts may perform claim construction on a motion to dismiss when based on intrinsic evidence alone, but some cases require fuller claim‑construction proceedings, extrinsic evidence, or expert testimony.
guidance: Where intrinsic evidence suggests multiple plausible constructions or the record is limited (e.g., interpretation of 'group' as 'one or more'), courts should recognize circumstances where dismissal‑stage construction is inappropriate and remand for more complete proceedings.

name: Doctrine of equivalents — particularized testimony and linking argument required
description: Proof under the doctrine of equivalents must include 'particularized testimony and linking argument' showing insubstantial differences between claimed elements and accused device features.
guidance: Experts or other evidence must identify specific elements in the accused product that correspond to claim limitations, explain how the function, way, and result are equivalent, and connect that analysis to the claim language. Generalized testimony is insufficient.

name: Doctrine of equivalents — means‑way‑result and insubstantial differences analyses
description: Under the means‑way‑result framework and the insubstantial differences approach, a patentee must show equivalence in function, way, and result, and explain why any differences are insubstantial in light of what the claim avoids.
guidance: Evidence should address each prong (function, way, result) with specifics. Demonstrations that the accused product performs the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result are required; unsupported generalizations fail.

name: Successful claim revisions overcome novelty objections
description: Revisions to patent drafts (claims/specification) that overcome examiner objections to novelty constitute successful edits.
guidance: The PatentEdits dataset contains 105K examples of successful revisions that overcome objections to novelty — these examples serve as targets for learnable models that predict what claims should change given prior art.

name: Sentence-level labeling of edits
description: Edits can be labeled sentence by sentence to indicate which sentences were changed and which remained, helping identify the parts of claims that were novel or required modification.
guidance: The authors design algorithms to label edits at the sentence level, enabling models to learn from fine-grained supervision about how claim language evolves in response to prior art.

name: Invention Information Definition and Determination
description: Invention information is technical information in the total disclosure of a patent document that represents an addition to the state of the art; it is determined in the context of the state of the art using guidance provided by the claims with due regard to the description and drawings.
guidance: The meaning of 'addition to the state of the art' is novel and unobvious subject matter specifically disclosed and not part of prior art; selection rules for classification symbols are the same for invention and additional information.

name: General Chemical Formulae Classification Procedure — Step 1 (Fully Identified Compounds)
description: When chemical compounds are specified using a general formula (large genus or Markush-type claims), classification should be given to all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious if they are (i) specifically claimed as such or in a composition, (ii) products of a claimed process, or (iii) derivatives of either of these.
guidance: A compound is 'fully identified' where: (a) the structure is given by exact chemical name or formula, or can be deduced from its preparation from specified reactants with at most one selected from a list of alternatives; and (b) the compound is characterised by a physical property (e.g., melting point), or its preparation is described in a worked example giving practical details. Compounds identified only by an empirical formula are not 'fully identified'. (Further steps continue beyond Step 1 in subsequent guidance.)

name: Foreign birth proof requirements for minority claims
description: Where applicant born abroad (e.g., Bermuda), evidence of age should include a transcript of the official parish or public register of births signed by the proper custodian and certified by the United States consul; baptismal transcript insufficient if birth register exists.
guidance: Case guidance (P. 43, 77, Sept., 1890).

name: Marriage or parent's foreign domicile can defeat minority discharge claim
description: An application by a parent for discharge of a minor soldier may be denied where the soldier had married (which in some jurisdictions is an emancipation) or where the parent/guardian is domiciled abroad (e.g., in France), viewed as having emancipated the child.
guidance: Citations: P. 53, 105, Apr., 1892; P. 62, 132, Oct., 1893. Marriage/emancipation law of local jurisdiction controls effect on parental rights.

name: Departmental practice warns parents of consequences when pressing minority claim
description: When parents apply for discharge on minority grounds they are informed the soldier is punishable for enlisting without their consent, and that if they press the matter charges will be prepared and the soldier charged; if convicted, penalties may include dishonorable discharge, forfeiture of pay, confinement, and later release to parents if sentence doesn't include dishonorable discharge.
guidance: Specific administrative practice cited with case references (C. 16379; 17964).

name: Limit number of restriction requirements and provide clear species groupings
description: Examiners should be limited in the number of restriction requirements issued; Applicant should in every instance be given clearly enumerated species and claims groupings to choose from; species restriction for each invention group should be provided with first restriction Office Action.
guidance: Reduce multiple restriction/ election practices that fragment prosecution; require clarity in species/group enumerations and include species restrictions at first restriction action.

name: Expand First Office Action Interview pilot and related practices
description: Expand PTO pilot program for first office action interviews: successfully leading to early allowances: Expand pilot to all art units; Identify situations where interview unsuccessful‐ improve interview process; Examiner production credit for interview; Examiners must be available for interviews (in person or by phone); Supervisors should participate when examiners lack signatory authority; Allow attorneys in firm to participate; Interviews should be collaborative: identify allowable subject matter and potential claim amendments; Agreements reached at interview should be honored: binding; All RCEs should have interview before first action within 30 days of RCE filing; Provide applicants with interview guidance/education; Monitor examiner performance regarding interview success.
guidance: Broaden and refine first-action interview pilots, ensure appropriate production credit to change examiner incentives, make interviews binding and collaborative, and monitor outcomes to measure efficacy.

name: Modify First Action Interview stage and credits to encourage early substantive engagement
description: Refocus the First Action Interview pilot to a stage prior to the examiners search and preliminary opinion might be more beneficial, assuming appropriate credit could be given. Such a pilot would allow applicant to inform the examiner on the invention and applicant’s view of the scope of the claims prior to the examiner searching and examining the invention.
guidance: Consider giving production credit for substantive advancement rather than merely issuing an action; early-stage interviews before search could improve focus and reduce later rework.

name: Provide differentiated examination options by application complexity
description: Explore different examination procedures for applications of differing complexity; Applicants could choose a fast track option providing expedited prosecution with commensurate scope of protection.
guidance: Allow applicants to opt into examination tracks based on complexity (references cited, claim scope/number), with corresponding count/time allocations.

name: Consider allowing multiple dependent claims aligned with other offices
description: Consider allowing use of multiple dependent claims that are in alignment with other patent offices, such as the European Patent Office.
guidance: Adopt multiple-dependent-claim practices to reduce the number of claims examined while preserving broad coverage options.

name: Require substantive rebuttal by examiner for after-final amendments/responses
description: If a response after final is entered (usually because it includes no claim amendments or new evidence), the Examiner usually just goes through the motions. At a minimum, the Examiner should be required to provide specific rebuttal of an applicant's arguments on the merits if an amendment is entered.
guidance: Demand specific, substantive examiner explanations for rejecting after-final arguments or amendments rather than perfunctory statements.

name: Comprehensive and clear reasons for allowance (MPEP 1302.14 compliance)
description: Examiner’s statement of reasons for allowance should be comprehensive and clear. Reasons for allowance should not introduce unsupported claim limitations or broadening language not of record.
guidance: When allowing claims, examiners must identify how claim elements distinguish over prior art, priority dates for claim elements in continuations/CIPs, interpretive statements (preamble/functional language), and identify file-history estoppel (amendments/arguments forming basis for allowance). Continue to review allowances for correctness.

name: Identify priority date and prosecution interpretations in allowance
description: Identify priority date for each claim element in continuing and continuation in part applications; Examiner should state the interpretation given in prosecution to claim preamble and any field of use or functional terminology.
guidance: Explicitly record prosecution positions and priority support to provide clarity to the public and reduce later disputes over claim scope.

name: Patent limited to the actual invention; cannot claim whole machine for a mere improvement
description: When a patentee adds a mere improvement to an existing machine, a patent cannot be for the whole machine but only for the improvement; the scope of the patent is limited to the patentee's actual invention or new combinations.
guidance: If separate stages/effects were previously produced by separate machines or known combinations, simply combining them does not sustain a patent for the entire combined machine (Whittemore v. Cutter, watch/steam-engine analogies).

name: Cannot patent an effect only; must claim a mode or peculiar manner of producing it
description: No patent can be obtained for an effect alone (e.g., admeasurement of time, expansive operations of steam); patents are for a new mode or new application of machinery to produce an effect.
guidance: A claim framed as for an effect without specifying the mode/operation will be invalid; courts look for the modus operandi or peculiar device described in the specification/claims.

name: Prior analogous structures may defeat novelty unless differences are radical
description: When prior art shows striking analogies, a patent may still be valid if the differences between the prior structure and the claimed invention are not merely mechanical but radical in character.
guidance: Court may rely on scientific expert testimony to determine whether differences are 'radical' (Blandy v. Griffith bed-plate: continuous shell + lateral attachment vs earlier frames).

name: Claims must be construed to the essence of the invention as described
description: Courts construe patent claims to embrace the specific elements described in the specification; the essence of the invention is determined by construction of the claim and the specification.
guidance: Example: in the portable steam-engine case the court construed the claim to three elements (hollow continuous bed-plate between boiler and engine; cast flanges on upper and outer side; attachment of operative parts to those flanges) and held the essence to be the bed-plate construction and lateral attachment.

name: Delay in applying not barred by statute; abandonment is the decisive issue
description: The statute does not limit any time in which the inventor must apply for a patent; delay is unimportant unless it amounts to evidence of abandonment of the claim. If there be any limit of the time of application, it must be a reasonable limit, and that is proper matter for the consideration of a jury.
guidance: Commissioner should not refuse patents for mere delay absent statutory grounds; issues of intent and abandonment are typically for a jury and determined under reasonable-time standards.

name: No finality when new rejection on prior art not of record affects amended claims that introduced expected limitations
description: A second or any subsequent action ... should not be made final if it includes a rejection, on prior art not of record, of any claim amended to include limitations which should reasonably have been expected to be claimed.
guidance: When an applicant amends claims to supply an omitted element or limitation that would reasonably be expected, the examiner should not make the next action final if the examiner introduces a new rejection based on prior art not of record.

name: Examiner caution when applicant does not point out patentable novelty after amendment
description: In the consideration of claims in an amended case where no attempt is made to point out the patentable novelty, the examiner should be on guard not to allow such claims. The claims may be finally rejected if, in the opinion of the examiner, they are clearly open to rejection on grounds of record.
guidance: If applicant amends claims but fails to identify the patentable distinction, the examiner should scrutinize carefully and may finally reject claims clearly open to rejection under the record.

name: When final rejection may be withdrawn for new facts/reasons or to apply new ground
description: The examiner may withdraw the rejection of finally rejected claims. If new facts or reasons are presented such as to convince the examiner that the previously rejected claims are in fact allowable ... the final rejection should be withdrawn. Although it is permissible to withdraw a final rejection for the purpose of entering a new ground of rejection, this practice is to be limited to situations where a new reference either fully meets at least one claim or meets it except for differences which are shown to be completely obvious.
guidance: Withdraw finality if convincing new information shows allowability, or if a new reference fully meets a claim or clearly renders it obvious. Do not withdraw finality merely to apply subsidiary, cumulative, or marginally better references.

name: Legislative changes should be general and not single‑company bailouts
description: The bill's clarifications (e.g., on filing deadlines, prior user rights) are presented as codifications of court rulings or general rules applying 'to all companies in the country equally' rather than special favors to individual firms.
guidance: Used to rebut claims the provisions are earmarks; sponsors emphasize broad applicability and equal treatment as a normative standard for acceptable legislative reform.

name: Patent Examiner Performance Standards (examination criteria)
description: Patent examiners review applications to determine whether the claimed invention is eligible for patent protection, useful, adequately disclosed, and clearly defined; they compare claims to technical information to determine novelty and non-obviousness.
guidance: Examiners also respond to appeal briefs, prepare PCT preliminary examination reports, and participate in policy development, education, and international cooperation; quality and timeliness metrics track examiner performance.

name: Three-prong test for applying 112(f)
description: 112(f) is applied when a claim limitation satisfies all three criteria (Prong A, Prong B, and Prong C).
guidance: Examiners must determine that (A) a generic placeholder or 'means/step' term is used, (B) the term is tied to a recited function (functional language), and (C) the limitation lacks sufficient structure; 112(f) only applies when all three prongs are met.

name: Prong (A): Generic placeholder or 'means'/'step'
description: The claim uses 'means,' 'step,' or a generic substitute term (e.g., 'module,' 'mechanism,' 'device') that functions as a nonce word without inherent structural meaning.
guidance: Ask whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure. Generic placeholders that do not connote structure trigger this prong.

name: Prong (B): Functional language
description: The term is connected to a recited function, typically expressed by words like 'for,' 'configured to,' or similar language that states what the element accomplishes rather than how it accomplishes it.
guidance: Identify whether the claim element describes a function (what) rather than structural means (how). Functional linking language commonly signals Prong B.

name: Prong (C): Lack of sufficient structure
description: The limitation contains no adequate structural details for performing the claimed function; if sufficient structure is present, the presumption that 112(f) applies is rebutted.
guidance: Determine whether the claim recites specific structural modifiers or technical details recognizable to practitioners. Presence of such structure rebuts the presumption of 112(f).

name: Presumptions about use of 'means' and 'step'
description: Claims using 'means' or 'step' presume 112(f) applies; claims without these terms presume 112(f) does not apply unless generic placeholders with functional language overcome the presumption.
guidance: Apply the statutory presumptions: explicit 'means'/'step' language triggers a presumption in favor of means-plus-function treatment; absence of those words starts with a presumption against 112(f) but can be overcome by evidence that the term is a generic placeholder.

name: How to invoke 112(f) when drafting claims
description: To invoke means-plus-function treatment, use 'means' or generic placeholder terms combined with functional language and avoid providing sufficient structural detail.
guidance: Drafters intentionally seeking means-plus-function scope can use nonce words like 'means for' or 'module for' and describe only the function, withholding specific structure in the claim language.

name: How to avoid 112(f) when drafting claims
description: To avoid means-plus-function treatment, include specific structural modifiers, add technical details recognizable to practitioners, and demonstrate the term has a 'sufficiently definite' structural meaning.
guidance: Prefer concrete structural names (e.g., 'detent mechanism' rather than 'mechanism') and include technical detail in the claim so the term will be understood as structure rather than a generic placeholder.

name: Scope limitation of means-plus-function claims
description: Means-plus-function claim limitations receive a narrower interpretation—limited to the structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: When 112(f) applies, construe the claim element to the corresponding structure (or acts/algorithm) disclosed in the specification and its equivalents; do not read broader functional scope than the disclosure supports.

name: Corresponding structure requirement in the specification
description: The specification must identify actual hardware, software, or acts that perform the recited function for the limitation to be sustained under 112(f).
guidance: Examiners should look for explicit disclosure of structure that performs the claimed function; vague or missing structural disclosure will render the claim indefinite or unsupported.

name: Clear association (linkage) requirement
description: The written description must 'clearly link or associate' the disclosed structure to the claimed function.
guidance: It is not enough to have structure and functions disclosed separately; the specification must explicitly associate the disclosed structure with the recited function so that a POSITA would understand the correspondence.

name: Algorithm disclosure requirement for software-implemented functions
description: For computer-implemented means-plus-function limitations, the specification must disclose an explicit algorithm; a general-purpose processor alone is insufficient unless the recited function is coextensive with basic processor operations.
guidance: Disclose steps, flowcharts, pseudo-code, or other algorithmic detail corresponding to the claimed function. Merely identifying a processor or saying standard programming can be used is inadequate unless the function is simply receiving/storing/processing data and thus coextensive with processor capabilities.

name: Incorporated references cannot alone supply corresponding structure
description: Structure cannot come solely from incorporated-by-reference materials without explicit support in the specification itself.
guidance: If the applicant intends to rely on incorporated references for structure, ensure the specification provides sufficient direct disclosure or explicit incorporation that ties the structure to the claimed function; otherwise examiners may require further support.

name: Multiple functions require disclosure for each function
description: If an element in the claim recites multiple functions, the specification must disclose corresponding structure for each recited function.
guidance: Examiners should verify that for every function attributed to the claimed element there is disclosed structure (or algorithm) corresponding to that function; failure to do so may render portions of the limitation unsupported.

name: Prior-art method-of-making relevance
description: Presence or absence of a prior art suggestion of a method of making a claimed compound may be relevant in determining prima facie obviousness.
guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making a claimed compound at the relevant time, it may not be legally concluded that the compound itself is in the possession of the public; absence of a known or obvious process for making the claimed compounds overcomes a presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity. See In re Maloney; In re Hoeksema; In re Payne. Examiners should consider whether prior art methods would have provided those skilled in the art a means to make the claimed compound.

name: Prior-art utility or intermediate-status
description: If prior art compounds have no specific or significant utility, or are disclosed only as intermediates, structurally similar claimed compounds may not be prima facie obvious over the prior art.
guidance: When reference compounds lack meaningful utility or are merely synthetic intermediates, one of ordinary skill would not have reason to make or investigate related compounds; see In re Stemniski, In re Albrecht, In re Lalu. Examiners should assess whether the prior art provides a motivation to make the claimed compounds.

name: Unexpected results as rebuttal evidence
description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties.
guidance: Unexpected results must be supported by objective evidence (not mere argument or speculation). Comparative data, declarations, or experimental results that demonstrate an unexpected property or large improvement over prior art can rebut obviousness (e.g., In re Papesch; In re Wiechert). Unsupported assertions (e.g., unsupported expert testimony of unusually low immune response) are insufficient (In re Mayne).

name: Nexus and commensurateness requirement
description: To be accorded substantial weight, objective evidence of nonobviousness must have a nexus to the claimed invention and be commensurate in scope with the claim.
guidance: Applicant bears the burden of establishing nexus; a presumption of nexus requires the product embody the invention and be coextensive with the claims (Volvo Penta; Fox Factory v. SRAM). Evidence not commensurate in scope or relating to products not covered by the claims is not probative (GPAC; Paulsen; Kulling; Grasselli). MPEP §716.01(b) provides further nexus guidance.

name: Enabling disclosure / public possession requirement
description: A conclusion of obviousness requires that the reference(s) relied upon, together with the knowledge of a person skilled in the art, be enabling in that it put the public in possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: If prior art references (plus ordinary skill) would not have enabled making the claimed compound, that undercuts a prima facie obviousness rejection (In re Hoeksema; In re Le Grice; Ashland Oil v. Delta Resins; In re Grose). Examiners should assess enablement when relying on structural similarity or other prior art teachings.

name: Extrapolation from narrow data / exemplary showings
description: Evidence of unexpected results for a single member or a narrow portion of a claimed genus or range may be sufficient to rebut a prima facie case if a skilled artisan could ascertain a trend to reasonably extend the probative value to the claim scope.
guidance: An exemplary showing can suffice (In re Clemens; In re Chupp) but may be insufficient in other circumstances (In re Greenfield; In re Lindner; Grasselli) where different species are not interchangeable or where no adequate basis exists to conclude other claimed compounds would behave similarly. Each case must be evaluated on its totality.

name: Commercial success evidentiary specifics
description: Evidence of commercial success may rebut obviousness but must be supported by hard evidence and be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention.
guidance: The PTO lacks means to independently gather such evidence in ex parte prosecution and thus relies on applicant to provide objective proof (sales figures, licensing data). Evidence concerning products not covered by the claims or not commensurate in scope is not probative (Ex parte Remark; In re Huang; GPAC; Paulsen; Kulling). Examiners should evaluate validity of claimed nexus and scope correspondence (Fox Factory; Volvo Penta).

name: Timing for determining relevant prior art (AIA vs pre‑AIA)
description: The relevant time for assessing prior art and obviousness differs depending on whether the application is examined under AIA or pre‑AIA law.
guidance: For AIA or first-inventor-to-file applications the relevant time is 'before the effective filing date of the claimed invention'; for pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 the relevant time is 'at the time of the invention.' Many cited cases involve pre‑AIA law but principles may apply with appropriate temporal adjustments. See MPEP §2145 and §2150 et seq.

name: License to make — what it confers and implied extensions
description: A license to make confers the right to construct the article described and claimed; if conferred alone it gives no right to use or sell the article unless such rights are necessary for the licensee to obtain benefit, in which case they may be implied.
guidance: Original wording: 'A license to make confers upon the licensee the right to construct the article ... If conferred alone, it gives the licensee no right to use or sell the article when constructed.' Courts will imply use or sale where necessary to give the license practical value (Steam Cutter Co. v. Sheldon).

name: Settlement compromises that allow mutual enjoyment operate as licenses
description: A compromise of litigated claims in which each party abandons rights to restrain the other, or an agreement allowing each part to do what he pleases, is treated as a license.
guidance: Original wording: 'A compromise of litigated claims ... are other forms which this mode of conveyance may assume, and which are equally valid with licenses of greater definiteness ...' Case: Troy Iron & Nail Factory v. Coming; settlements allowing mutual use are licenses.

name: Delivery and escrow of written license — proof required
description: Where a written license is found in the hands of the licensee but claimed to have been delivered as an escrow, the person alleging escrow must prove it; constructive possession does not prove delivery.
guidance: Original wording: 'That where a written license is found in the hands of the licensee, a person who claims that it was delivered as an escrow must prove it.' Case: Mellon v. Delaware, Lackawanna, & Western R.R. Co.

name: Solicitor General four-factor test for identifying the article-of-manufacture
description: Four factors proposed to determine the article-of-manufacture: (1) compare scope of the patented design as shown in the drawings; (2) determine how prominently that design features in the accused article; (3) determine whether there are other conceptually distinct innovations or components in the article not part of or associated with the patent design; (4) compare the physical relationship between the patented design and the rest of the article.
guidance: These factors are intended to guide courts in deciding whether the relevant article is the whole product or a component; they look to claim/drawing scope, prominence to consumers, conceptual distinctness of other parts, and physical unity/separability of the patented design.

name: Reasonable likelihood standard for institution (35 U.S.C. § 314(a))
description: The Board may institute review only upon a determination that 'there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least [one] of the claims challenged in the petition.'
guidance: This is the statutory threshold the Board applies at institution. The Decision explains that, applying that standard to the preliminary record (e.g., uncontested mapping of claim limitations to a prior-art disclosure), the Board may institute review. Institution requires showing a reasonable likelihood as to at least one challenged claim; once met, the Board will institute on the petition's challenges (see SAS/PGS discussion).

name: Claim construction standard (plain and ordinary meaning / Phillips)
description: Claim terms are construed 'in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent' (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Phillips v. AWH).
guidance: Terms are generally given their plain and ordinary meaning within the context of the specification. The Board will expressly construe disputed terms only as necessary to resolve the controversy; if no express construction is necessary to resolve institution issues, the Board may decline to provide one.

name: Anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102) — mapping limitations with particularity
description: A reference anticipates a claim when it discloses each limitation of the challenged claim. Petitioner should map with particularity every limitation to disclosures in the reference (e.g., claim charts identifying where each limitation is disclosed).
guidance: The Decision cites Petitioner's detailed claim charts mapping each claim limitation to the '888 Publication' (including Example 4 disclosing a 20 nm coating) as sufficient on the preliminary record, particularly where Patent Owner does not meaningfully contest the mapping. Anticipation requires that every claim limitation is found in the single prior-art reference.

name: Written-description requirement for priority (Ariad test and related caselaw)
description: To claim an earlier priority date, the specification of the earlier application must 'reasonably convey[] to those skilled in the art that the inventors had possession of the claimed subject matter' (Ariad). The level of detail required varies with the nature/scope of the claims and predictability of the art.
guidance: Apply the 'four corners' inquiry (Ariad). Consider whether a broad disclosed range supports a narrower claimed range (RAI Strategic Holdings and Wertheim): ask whether the broad described range 'pertains to a different invention than the narrower (and subsumed) claimed range' and whether the disclosed range 'behaves any differently than the claimed range.' In unpredictable arts (e.g., chemical), higher detail is required. Absence of explicit endpoints and prosecution statements may weigh against priority.

name: Effect of prosecution statements and prosecution history on written-description/priority
description: Statements made by the applicant/examiner during prosecution (e.g., distinguishing a prior-art coating of 35 nm from a claimed 30 nm) can bear on whether an earlier application conveys possession of the claimed range.
guidance: The Decision treats applicant statements to the Examiner (e.g., that '35 nm is not close enough' to 30 nm) as evidence that the broader range may not support the narrower claimed range and as supporting a preliminary finding against earlier priority. Whether prosecution-history estoppel applies is a separate issue; the Board may consider such statements in the written-description/priority inquiry.

name: Consideration of unpredictability of the art
description: When the claimed subject matter lies in an unpredictable field (e.g., chemical arts), a higher level of disclosure/detail is required to satisfy written-description and enablement.
guidance: The Decision notes that 'the claimed invention is within the unpredictable chemical arts' and that unpredictability supports a preliminary finding that the prior application lacks sufficient detail to establish possession of the narrower claimed ranges.

name: Requirement to map claim limitations with particularity (claim charts and evidence)
description: Petitioner should support anticipation/obviousness arguments with detailed mapping (claim charts) showing where each claim limitation is found/disclosed in the asserted reference(s).
guidance: The Decision relies on Petitioner's claim charts that 'map with particularity every limitation of the challenged claims to disclosures in the '888 Publication.' Where Patent Owner does not contest such mapping on the preliminary record, the Board may treat the mapping as sufficient for institution.

name: Step 2A 'directed to' analysis must examine the claim's focus/essence
description: The 'directed to' analysis of a process claim requires more than 'merely identify[ing] a patent‑ineligible concept underlying the claim' and instead requires an analysis of whether 'the end result of the process, the essence of the whole, was a patent‑ineligible concept.'
guidance: When applying Step 2A, assess the claim as a whole to determine its focus (the end result/essence). Do not stop at identifying an underlying natural phenomenon; determine whether the claimed end result itself is an observation/detection (ineligible) or a process producing a practical outcome (may be eligible). Example: the cryopreservation claims were focused on a process producing multi‑cryopreserved viable hepatocytes and thus were not directed to a judicial exception.

name: Process claims reciting methods of producing things or treating disease are often not 'directed to' a judicial exception when focused on achieving a desired outcome
description: Claims focused on a process for achieving a desired outcome (for example, methods of producing preparations or treating disease) are generally not directed to a judicial exception merely because they involve a natural phenomenon.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim's recited process steps meaningfully apply the natural law to produce a practical result (e.g., fractionating, recovering, and cryopreserving to make a preparation of multi‑cryopreserved viable hepatocytes). If so, Step 2A may support eligibility, as with 'thousands of other claims that recite methods of producing things or methods of treating disease.'

name: Step 2B — inventive concept requires more than routine or conventional steps
description: Even if a claim is directed to a natural phenomenon under Step 2A, it must recite an 'inventive concept' under Step 2B; routine, well‑understood, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers does not supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Use factual findings about whether the additional claim steps (e.g., amplifying and detecting) are routine and conventional.
