Example: in Sequenom the amplifying and detecting steps were held routine/conventional and thus insufficient to transform the natural phenomenon into patent‑eligible subject matter.

name: Follow USPTO subject matter eligibility guidance and consult subject matter experts as needed
description: Life sciences method claims should continue to be treated in accordance with the USPTO's subject matter eligibility guidance (most recently updated in May 2016).
guidance: Refer questions to Technology Center subject matter experts or your SPE when guidance or case law application is unclear.

name: Basis for examination in the European phase
description: Examination of the application in the European phase will be based on either A, B1 or C (see GL/EPO F‑V, 13.1(iii)). For the claims relating to inventions B2, B3 and D, an invitation under Rule 164(2) EPC will be issued in accordance with GL/EPO F‑V, 13.1(iv).
guidance: Indicates which ISR/WO‑ISA designations determine the scope of later European examination and when Rule 164(2) invitations are used for certain inventions.

name: Treatment of medical/therapeutic/diagnostic claims
description: Claims directed to medical treatment which would fall under the exceptions to patentability under Art. 53(c) EPC should, in principle, also be exempted from international search. Depending on claim wording (various types a–k), some claims may be searched and examined (e.g., 'compound X for use as a medicament' vs 'method of treatment using X') and the WO‑ISA should add a remark that novelty and inventive step have been assessed according to EPO practice.
guidance: Follow EPO practice and the table of claim types: certain use/Swiss‑type/composition claims are searchable with an EPO practice remark; method‑of‑treatment claims are generally excluded.

name: Meaning of 'no meaningful search' and its limited application
description: The term 'meaningful search' should be read to include a search that within reason is complete enough to determine whether the claimed invention complies with the substantive requirements, i.e. novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, and/or sufficiency, support and clarity. A finding of 'no meaningful search' should be limited to exceptional situations in which no search at all is possible for a particular claim, for example where the description, the claims or the drawings are totally unclear.
guidance: Examiner discretion: attempt to search any parts that can be sufficiently understood; do not use 'reasons of economy' to justify incomplete searches.

name: Examples where meaningful search may be impossible
description: Non‑limiting examples: (i) claims lacking support/insufficient disclosure (broad speculative claims supported only by limited disclosure), (ii) claims lacking conciseness (so many claims or possibilities that determining protection sought is unduly burdensome), (iii) claims lacking clarity (parameters that render comparison with prior art impossible).
guidance: In such cases, restrict search to worked examples or narrower disclosed invention where appropriate; consider informal clarification before restricting search.

name: Use of informal clarification prior to issuing incomplete ISR/no search
description: Where the description, claims or drawings fail to comply with a requirement to such an extent that no meaningful search can be made, the examiner may informally contact the applicant to clarify specific aspects of the application before the search is carried out. Informal clarification may take the form of a telephone consultation (minutes must be written) or a written request (Form PCT/ISA/207) sent by fax. A short time limit (normally two weeks) can be given.
guidance: Highly recommended to invite informal clarification before issuing incomplete ISR or no search; telephone may be preferable given short PCT time limits.

name: Content and indication of restrictions in ISR and WO‑ISA
description: A restriction of the search will not always be indicated in the ISR; often the extent of the search and reasons for restriction will only be indicated in the WO‑ISA. The opinion given is normally restricted to what has actually been searched. If only some claims/parts can be searched and no likely fallback exists, a precise indication of what has been searched with full reasoning must be entered into both the ISR and WO‑ISA and an opinion on novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability of the searched subject‑matter must be given. If a searchable fallback exists the ISR will be filled as for a complete search for those claims and the WO‑ISA must indicate what was searched and why.
guidance: Be explicit about what was searched and why; add full reasoning in WO‑ISA and ISR when applicable; opinions limited to searched subject‑matter.

name: Combination of incomplete search and lack of unity
description: The requirements of unity of invention and Art. 17(2)(a)(ii) (no meaningful search) are separate requirements. However, it is possible that an application both violates clarity/disclosure/support/conciseness to such an extent that a meaningful search cannot be carried out, and lacks unity. In that case, the examiner can combine an incomplete search and a finding of non‑unity. The applicant should not be invited to pay additional fees for subject‑matter which will later not be searched under Art. 17(2)(a)(ii). Typically, a non‑unity objection could be made first and then an incomplete search applied to the searched invention. However, if the complexity lies in lack of clarity, the search will be restricted first, and the non‑unity objection applied to the clear parts of the claimed subject‑matter.
guidance: Do not invite fees for subject‑matter that will be excluded from search; sequence the objections appropriately depending on whether clarity or unity drives complexity.

name: Multiple independent claims per category not per se reason for incomplete search
description: Multiple independent claims in one category are per se not a reason for an incomplete search. Generally, an opinion must be given on all searched claims. Only one independent claim in each category needs to be treated in detail; short comments would normally suffice for further independent claims.
guidance: Provide opinions on all searched claims; use concise treatment for multiple independent claims; consider clarity/conciseness objections under Box VIII of WO‑ISA where appropriate.

name: Assignee is charged with notice and bound by facts discoverable from prior owners
description: An assignee under certain forms of conveyance is put upon inquiry and is chargeable with notice of facts that he might have discovered by inquiring of prior owners or persons claiming rights under the patent; every one who derives title through such an assignment is presumed to have the same knowledge imputed to the original assignee.
guidance: Language such as 'right, title and interest' may be sufficient to put an assignee on inquiry (cases: Hamilton v. Kingsbury). Recording and supplemental assignments may be construed together; assignee should investigate prior conveyances and claims to avoid taking subject to undisclosed interests.

name: Enlarged concept of novelty for international applications (pre-2015 filing-date rule)
description: Where another application and the concerned application were all filed before December 31, 2014 (or another application filed before Dec 31, 2014 but concerned filed after Jan 1, 2015): an international application filed in a foreign language relied upon as 'another application' is considered to be laid open at the time of international publication; the scope of inventions of the 'another application' is limited to the inventions described in the specification, claims or drawings of both the international application as of the international filing date and its translation.
guidance: Where an international application claiming domestic priority is filed in a foreign language, the scope of inventions of the prior-filed application considered laid open or registered is limited to inventions described in the original specification or drawings of the prior-filed application that form the basis of the priority claim, out of inventions described both in the international application and its translation.

name: Enlarged concept of novelty for international applications (post-2015 filing-date rule)
description: Where another application and the concerned application were all filed after January 1, 2015: an international application filed in a foreign language is considered laid open at time of international publication, but the scope of inventions of the 'another application' is limited to the inventions described in the description, claims or drawings of the international application as filed.
guidance: Where an international application claiming domestic priority is filed in a foreign language, the scope of inventions of the prior-filed application considered laid open is limited to inventions described in the original specification or drawings of the prior-filed application which form the basis of the priority claim, out of those submitted as of the filing date of the international application.

name: Amendment scope for international applications filed before Dec 31, 2014
description: The specification or drawings of an international application filed in a foreign language can be amended within the scope of the matters described in the translations of the specification, claims, or drawings (limited to description parts on drawings) of the international application as of the international filing date.

name: Exception: lack of clarity -> limited notice without prior art search
description: Where contents of a claimed invention cannot be comprehended due to lack of clarity in the description, an examiner shall notify only the ground for rejection in violations of Article 42(3), (4) without conducting prior art search or assessing patentability requirements regarding novelty and inventive step.
guidance: However if the lack of clarity is insignificant so understanding is possible, the examiner shall conduct prior art search and review requirements within his/her comprehension and then notify all grounds discovered together.

name: Exception: certain decisive defects notified without patentability judgement
description: Where it is certain that a claim has newly added matter, or where it is not certain whether there is a ground pursuant to Article 32 (e.g., contravene public order), or where it is clear that a claimed invention does not constitute a statutory subject matter or is not industrially applicable, an examiner shall notify those grounds for rejection without judging other requirements for patentability such as novelty or inventive step.

name: Inventive step rejection must describe difference from closest prior art
description: When notifying rejection for lack of inventive step, an examiner shall clearly describe the difference between the invention recited in the claims and the closest prior art reference.
guidance: Exception: the examiner may not need to describe the difference where lack of novelty and lack of inventive step are notified together — then follow novelty assessment method for the novelty part, and inventive step notice may rely on logic that a person skilled in the art could easily make the invention from the prior art.

name: Decision to reject based on other claims (identical or adding limitations)
description: Where an amendment makes a claim identical (or substantially identical) to another previously-rejected claim, a decision to reject the amended claim can be made on the basis of the ground notified to the other claim. Where an amendment adds limitations of another claim but the amended claim still fails to overcome a ground notified to the other claim based on the same provision, a decision to reject can be made because an opportunity for submission of written arguments has been sufficiently provided.
guidance: If a new combination of references is required to reject the amended claim, a new ground is necessitated and, depending on stage, a second office action should be made or refusal to enter the amendment and proceed with original claim.

name: Determination whether applicant had opportunity to submit written arguments
description: When the examiner intends to make a decision to reject based on reasons different from the ground previously notified to the claim concerned, he should carefully review whether an opportunity for submission of written arguments has been supplied to the applicant before making a decision to reject.
guidance: Examples show erroneous changes of references or claim scope may necessitate issuing a non-final rejection instead of a decision to reject; if prior erroneous notice caused the need for a new combination of references, examiner should refuse to enter the amendment rather than making a decision to reject.

name: Determining opportunity regarding deficiencies in description (indefiniteness changes)
description: Even though a ground of rejection is identical, if a term or phrase found indefinite in the claim is changed by amendment (so applicant could not reasonably know to respond), an opportunity for submission of written arguments is not considered to have been substantially provided, and a decision to reject cannot be made without special circumstances.
guidance: Only where the amended claim fails to overcome the previously-notified ground and the concerned claim language substantially coincides can a decision to reject be made. New claims created by amendment that did not have previously-notified grounds ordinarily require providing an opportunity to submit written arguments.

name: Public use (AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)) — availability to the public
description: Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1), public use is limited to those uses that are available to the public — the provision has the same substantive scope with respect to uses by either the inventor or a third party as public uses under pre-AIA law.
guidance: Once an examiner becomes aware of a potentially public use, the examiner should require the applicant to provide information showing that the use did not make the claimed process accessible to the public.

name: On sale — commercial sale or offer for sale (Pfaff test)
description: On-sale activity will bar patentability if the claimed invention was: (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale, not primarily for experimental purposes; and (2) ready for patenting (Pfaff v. Wells Electronics).
guidance: Contract law and commercial law principles apply to determine whether a commercial sale or offer for sale occurred. The enablement inquiry is not applicable to whether a claimed invention is 'on sale' under pre-AIA 102(b). See MPEP § 2133.03(b). Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) the phrase 'on sale' is treated as having the same meaning. The sale/offfer need not occur in the United States under AIA, and secret commercial activity can be an on-sale bar (see MPEP discussion and Helsinn for confidential sales).

name: Procedure: Determining whether to apply 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2)
description: For an examiner: first consider whether the reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1); next determine if any exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) apply. Separately, consider whether the reference qualifies under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and then whether any exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) apply.
guidance: Patents, printed publications, public use, on sale, and other availability qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) if the reference predates the effective filing date. For 102(a)(2), U.S. patents and published applications (or WIPO publications designating the U.S.) are prior art if their effectively filed date is before the claimed invention's effective filing date; the concept of 'effectively filed' is controlled by 35 U.S.C. 102(d) and MPEP § 2154. Disclosures in a potential reference within the one-year grace period may be excepted under 102(b)(1) (see MPEP §§ 2153.01, 2153.02).

name: Overcoming a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection — available responses
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) can be overcome by a number of procedural and substantive paths in addition to arguing patentable distinctions or amending claims.
guidance: (A) Submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the 37 CFR 1.78 time period by providing the required reference to a prior application in a corrected ADS and establishing that the prior application satisfies enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a), or filing a grantable petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim. (B) Submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78 with required ADS corrections and establishing enablement/written description, or filing a petition for delayed acceptance. (C) Submitting a priority claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) within 37 CFR 1.55 and establishing the prior foreign application satisfies enablement/written description and is perfected by certified priority document and translation where necessary. (D) Filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130: (a) attribution affidavits under 1.130(a) to except a disclosure as made by the inventor/joint inventor or by one who obtained subject matter from them; (b) prior public disclosure affidavits under 1.130(b) to except an intervening disclosure if the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor (or one who obtained it from them) before the intervening disclosure or before the effective filing/effective filing of the reference. (E) Establishing common ownership or evidence of a Joint Research Agreement to overcome a 102(a)(2) rejection by entitlement to the 102(b)(2)(C) exception. Note: these remedies may also be used to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) prior art.

name: Form paragraphs for AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections and usage rules
description: Specific form paragraphs (¶ 7.06, ¶ 7.07.aia, ¶ 7.08.aia, ¶ 7.12.aia, ¶ 7.14.aia) are provided for making rejections under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and related statutory bases.
guidance: Examples and examiner notes: ¶ 7.06 (Notice re prior art available under both pre-AIA and AIA) must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013 that claims priority/benefit to an application filed before March 16, 2013; use only once per Office action. ¶ 7.07.aia (Statement of Statutory Basis) quotes 35 U.S.C. 102; statute need only be re-cited in first actions on the merits and final rejections. ¶ 7.08.aia for 102(a)(1) must be used where applicable and must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia. ¶ 7.12.aia for 102(a)(2) must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia and may be preceded by 7.08.aia; use only if the reference is a qualifying U.S. patent, U.S. application publication under 122(b), or WIPO publication with an earlier effectively filed date. ¶ 7.14.aia addresses pre-AIA 102(g) priority of invention language. Form paragraphs 7.07.aia, 7.08.aia, 7.12.aia and 7.14.aia are to be used ONLY ONCE in a given Office action.

name: Effective filing date considerations for 102(a)(2) (35 U.S.C. 102(d))
description: For purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2), U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and international patent applications published under PCT are prior art if the effectively filed date of the disclosure is before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Even if the issue or publication date is not before the effective filing date, the reference may qualify under 102(a)(2) if it was 'effectively filed' earlier. 35 U.S.C. 102(d) sets forth the criteria to determine when subject matter described in such documents was 'effectively filed'; see MPEP § 2154 for details.

name: Petition content requirements
description: Petitioner must identify: each claim that it is challenging; the basis for the challenge (known as the 'grounds'); the evidence that supports each ground.
guidance: These requirements are grounded in 35 U.S.C. §§ 311, 312(a)(3) and are essential for the PTAB to evaluate institution.

name: Standard for initiating review — IPR
description: IPR: 'a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail' with respect to at least one challenged claim.
guidance: This is a lower institution threshold than 'more likely than not' and applies specifically to IPRs.

name: Motion to amend claims
description: Patent owner may amend its claims during the trial phase to narrow the scope of the claims.
guidance: In some cases, the Board may cancel original claims but conclude that amended claims can be obtained. Additional guidance is in the Office Patent Trial Practice Guide and related notices (e.g., pilot program on Motions to Amend).

name: Final written decision and consequences
description: PTAB will issue a final written decision for all trials that are instituted, unless there is a termination (settlement). PTAB will rule on the patentability of each claim — uphold or find a claim unpatentable.
guidance: If PTAB finds claims to be unpatentable, it will order cancellation of those claims, meaning those claims will not be enforceable anymore. Source: 35 U.S.C. § 318.

name: Purpose of patent drawings
description: Drawings function to aid understanding of an invention and contribute to correct disclosure of the invention.
guidance: Embodiments of mechanical inventions may be easier to explain as drawings than by lengthy description; scientific data are intended to demonstrate plausibility or support claims but may not serve the same purpose or naturally conform to technical-illustration style requirements.

name: General Plastic Factor 5: petitioner’s explanation for delay
description: Whether the petitioner provides adequate explanation for the time elapsed between the filings of multiple petitions directed to the same claims of the same patent.
guidance: A persuasive, adequate explanation for delay (e.g., newly discovered art, reliance on pending institution decisions) can mitigate concerns and weigh against discretionary denial. Lack of explanation supports denial.

name: Plant patent claim and scope (one claim / one plant/genome; rights under 35 U.S.C. § 163)
description: A plant patent has only one claim and protects one plant or genome.
guidance: A plant patent holder has exclusive rights to prevent others from asexually reproducing the plant, and from using, offering for sale, or selling the patented plant or its parts, or from importing the patented plant, or any parts thereof. (35 U.S.C. § 163).

name: No new matter allowed in CPA; substitute specification rules
description: No amendment in a CPA may introduce new matter. Any new specification filed with a CPA request will not be considered part of the original application papers but will be treated as a substitute specification under 37 CFR 1.125; substitute specifications must comply with 1.125(b) (including statement that substitute contains no new matter).
guidance: Substitute specifications containing new matter will be denied entry. Preliminary amendments (other than substitute spec) ordinarily entered; however, any new matter entered will be required to be canceled pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 132 and any claim relying on such new matter will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. Applicant may petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to remove substitute spec or preliminary amendment from the CPA file to be treated as a separate application (with filing date equal to CPA filing date), but will not get filing fee refund for a proper CPA.

name: Fees, oath/declaration, and original disclosure for CPAs
description: Under 37 CFR 1.53(d), the specification, claims, drawings, and any amendments entered in the prior nonprovisional application are used in the CPA. A new basic filing fee, search fee, and examination fee are required (35 U.S.C. 41 and 37 CFR 1.16). The previously filed oath/declaration in the prior application will be considered the oath or declaration of the CPA (CPA cannot contain new matter).
guidance: Note: no search/exam fees were required for CPAs filed before Dec 8, 2004 (historical exception). Any subject matter added by amendment in the parent app which is new matter in the parent is also new matter in the CPA.

name: Composition Claims - The Core Asset
description: For a pharmaceutical, the composition-of-matter claim is the keystone. It typically claims a chemical compound or class of compounds.
guidance: Drafting choices include claiming the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) by structure, by name, by Markush group, or as a salt/polymorph. Composition claims are the primary defensive and exclusionary asset for a drug.

name: Markush Groupings
description: A Markush claim recites a closed group of alternatives ("R1 is selected from the group consisting of methyl, ethyl, propyl"). Markush is the standard format for genus claims in chemistry.
guidance: The group must be sufficiently disclosed to support written description; broad groups need representative species. Ensure adequate disclosure of representative members and avoid overbroad Markush lists without supporting examples.

name: Method of Treatment Claims
description: Claiming methods of treating disease (e.g., "A method of treating disease X comprising administering compound Y to a patient in need thereof").
guidance: File method-of-treatment claims in addition to composition claims because they reach pharmacy infringement and inducement liability against marketing. Use clear claim language (patient in need thereof, dosing/context) and include supporting data where possible.

name: Polymorph and Crystal Form Claims
description: Claim novel crystalline/polymorphic forms (e.g., Form I, Form II) which can affect bioavailability.
guidance: Polymorphs can be claimed by powder XRD pattern, melting point, FTIR characteristic peaks. These claims can support Orange Book listings and are commonly implicated in Hatch-Waxman litigation. Provide analytical characterization data to define and support the claimed form.

name: Salt Forms
description: Different pharmaceutically acceptable salts of the same active compound can be separately patentable if novel and non-obvious.
guidance: Salt selection patents are common follow-ons; demonstrate novelty/non-obviousness and provide supporting data (e.g., improved properties). Consider claiming salts explicitly and include examples.

name: Dosing Regimen Claims
description: Claims to specific dosing regimens, e.g., "administering compound Y at a dose of Z mg per day in a 28-day cycle."
guidance: Dosing/regimen claims are often patented separately and can provide a second wave of protection after composition patents expire. Draft clearly defined regimen parameters (dose, schedule, duration) and support with pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic or clinical data.

name: Combination Therapy Claims
description: Claims directed to administering two or more compounds together ("A method comprising administering compound A and compound B").
guidance: Useful when the combination shows synergy or improved tolerability. Provide evidence of synergistic effect or unexpected benefits to strengthen non-obviousness and enablement arguments.

name: Hatch-Waxman and Orange Book
description: Considerations for listing patents in the FDA's Orange Book and Hatch-Waxman litigation implications.
guidance: Patents covering an FDA-approved drug must be listed in the Orange Book; listed patents trigger the 30-month stay in Hatch-Waxman litigation. Listing decisions affect drafting choices: composition and formulation patents are listable; pure method-of-manufacture patents are not. Draft claims with awareness of whether they will be listable and the strategic consequences.

name: No lack-of-unity objection between a genuine dependent claim and its independent claim
description: A real dependent claim that contains all features of the independent claim shall not be objected for lack of unity with the independent claim, even if the dependent claim adds another invention.
guidance: Examples: dependent claim that narrows temperature range of a claimed process — even if the temperature range itself could be inventive, no unity objection is raised. However, if a claim appears dependent in form but omits features (thus is actually independent), unity must be examined under independent-claim rules.

name: Treatment when dependent-appearing claim is actually independent
description: If a claim that appears dependent does not contain all features of the independent claim (e.g. replaces feature C with D), it is actually an independent claim and unity should be examined as between independent claims of the same category.
guidance: Be alert to claims that are dependent in wording but lack essential features; treat such claims as independent for unity assessment.

name: Sufficient disclosure for chemical product inventions — identification requirement
description: The description shall describe identification of the chemical product: for compounds, indicate chemical name and structural formula (functional groups, stereochemistry) or molecular formula; provide property parameters (spectra, qualitative/quantitative data) sufficient for a skilled person to identify the compound.
guidance: For high molecular compounds, also disclose molecular weight and distribution, arrangement of repeating units, crystallinity, density, glass transition etc. If structure cannot fully identify the product, provide property parameters and/or manufacturing process to clearly identify the claimed product.

name: Specific mode for carrying out chemical inventions (embodiments requirement)
description: The description generally shall include embodiments and the number of embodiments depends on the extent of generalization in the claims; there must be a sufficient number of embodiments to show how to make and use the invention across the whole claimed scope.
guidance: Claims are judged on the initial description and claims only; embodiments or data submitted after filing are not considered in sufficiency assessment.

name: Claim drafting for compounds
description: A compound claim shall be characterized by the chemical name or the structural/molecular formula, using general nomenclature rather than trade or code names; the structure must be clear and unambiguous.
guidance: Avoid vague or ambiguous wording in compound claims.

name: Claim drafting for compositions — open-ended and close-ended modes
description: Composition claims may be presented in open-ended mode ('comprising', 'including', 'containing', 'essentially comprising', etc.) allowing unspecified additional components, or close-ended mode ('consisting of', 'be composed of', 'be balanced with', etc.) excluding other components (except normal impurities).
guidance: The chosen mode must be supported by the description. If nothing else is described in the description, an open-ended formulation is inappropriate. The mode used affects whether subsequent claims with added components are dependent or independent.

name: Definition of components and contents in composition claims
description: If the invention lies in component selection alone and a skilled person can determine contents from prior art/simple experiment, components alone may be defined; if the invention also depends on contents, both components and contents must be defined in the independent claim.
guidance: In fields like alloys, necessary components and their contents usually must be defined. Avoid ambiguous terms like 'about' or 'approximately' for content ranges; use numeric expressions (e.g., '0-X', '< X'). Total percentage contents must sum to 100% and content ranges must satisfy min/max constraints described in the guidelines.

name: Use of diagrams/formulae and qualitative descriptors in composition claims
description: Where relations among components are difficult to indicate by words or numbers, a formula or diagram may be used (with explanation in the description). Qualitative descriptions instead of numeric expressions are acceptable if clear and known in the art (e.g., 'catalytic amount').
guidance: Explain any diagram's specific meaning in the description.

name: Claims for chemical products not clearly characterizable by structure/composition
description: Where a chemical product cannot be clearly characterized by structure or composition alone, it is permitted to characterize the claim by physical/chemical parameter(s) and/or the manufacturing process, provided the parameters/process are clear enough to identify the product.
guidance: Only permitted under circumstances where other features cannot sufficiently characterize the product; parameters must be precise and supported by the description.

name: Claiming chemical processes — selectable feature types
description: A chemical process claim may be defined by procedure features (process steps and conditions like temperature, pressure, time, catalysts), substance features (components, structural/formula/property parameters of raw materials or products), or apparatus features (type of apparatus specially adapted or properties/functions of apparatus used).
guidance: Select the type(s) of features depending on subject matter, technical problem, and substance of the invention.

name: Determine inventive step for each claim
description: Where there are two or more claims, the examiner should determine the existence of an inventive step for each claim.
guidance: Assess inventive step claim-by-claim rather than treating a multi-claim application as a single unit.

name: Four-step inventive-step reasoning (JPO)
description: Examiner determines whether it is possible to reason that a skilled person would easily arrive at the claimed invention from the primary prior art by following steps (1)–(4): (1) determine possibility based on factors supporting non-existence (using secondary prior art or common general knowledge); (2) if impossible then inventive step exists; (3) if possible, comprehensively assess factors supporting existence; (4) if impossible then inventive step exists; if still possible, no inventive step.
guidance: Apply the sequence precisely: first attempt to show lack of inventive step using motivating factors; if that succeeds, then check whether positive/obstructive factors change the conclusion. The process is iterative and requires weighing both sets of factors.

name: Motivation for applying secondary prior art to primary prior art
description: If combining secondary prior art (B) with primary prior art (A) yields the claimed invention, the motivation to attempt that combination is a factor supporting non-existence of inventive step.
guidance: Determine motivation by comprehensively considering the following points of view: (1) relation of technical fields, (2) similarity of problems to be solved, (3) similarity of operations or functions, (4) suggestions shown in the content of prior art. It is not sufficient to rely on only one point of view; consider them together.

name: Similarity of problems to be solved (motivation subfactor)
description: Similarity between the problems addressed by primary and secondary prior art supports motivation to combine them where those problems would be obvious or easily conceived by the skilled person at the filing date.
guidance: Assess similarity based on the state of the art at filing; include cases where the claimed invention's problem isn't recognizable (e.g., trial-and-error inventions) — still consider differing reasoning processes.

name: Mere aggregation of prior art
description: Mere aggregation means each claimed element is well-known and their functions/operations are not related to each other; such aggregation is a factor supporting non-existence of inventive step.
guidance: If the claimed invention is simply a juxtaposition of independent known elements with no functional interaction or synergy, it lacks inventive step. Also consider implications of aggregation present within the primary prior art.

name: Advantageous effects (factor supporting existence)
description: Advantageous effects over the prior art (particular effects given by the claimed invention that are advantageous over prior art) are factors supporting the existence of an inventive step.
guidance: Examiner should take into account effects understood from description, claims and drawings. Identify effects that are attributable to distinguishing features and that impart an advantage over cited art.

name: Problem-and-solution approach (EPO) — Stage 3: could–would (would vs could)
description: Determine whether prior art as a whole would have prompted the skilled person, faced with the objective technical problem, to modify/adapt the closest prior art to arrive at the claimed invention; 'would' (motivating teaching) is required, not just 'could'.
guidance: Apply the ordered questions: (i) Would the skilled person take D2 into account when starting from D1? (consider common general knowledge and incentives), (ii) Could the skilled person find a solution from D2? (level of understanding), (iii) Can the solution from D2 be applied to D1? (technical hurdles, whether more than routine testing is required). If all answers are yes, obviousness is established; a no in any question supports inventive step.

name: Combination vs juxtaposition/aggregation (synergy requirement)
description: A claimed combination of features must be considered as a whole; when features functionally interact to produce a combined technical effect greater than the sum, it's a true combination; if not, it's a mere aggregation and can be shown obvious by showing individual features were known.
guidance: Look for synergistic functional interaction producing a combined technical effect. If absent, the aggregation rationale suffices for an obviousness finding (EPO case law: T 389/86, T 204/06).

name: Recognition/discovery of a new problem as potential inventive contribution
description: Discovery of a problem not previously recognized can itself be a contribution that supports patentability, even if the claimed solution appears non-progressive in retrospect.
guidance: If recognition of the problem is an important contribution to the patent achievement, the invention may have inventive step (caveat: introduction of a new problem that merely removes a use deficiency may not confer inventive step).

name: USPTO MPEP examples of obviousness (prima facie case) — combining known elements for predictable results
description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results supports a prima facie obviousness rejection.
guidance: Rejection requires: multiple prior arts include each claimed element; a skilled person could have combined them by known methods; a skilled person would have recognized the results as predictable; and separated elements perform the same function.

name: USPTO MPEP example — teaching/suggestion/motivation
description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led a skilled person to modify or combine references supports obviousness.
guidance: Demonstrate that prior art provided a motivation or suggestion that would lead to the claimed combination or modification.

name: Common procedural elements for inventive-step analysis
description: Common steps across jurisdictions: (i) Identification of the claimed invention; (ii) Identification of the primary prior art; (iii) Lifting commonalities and differences between claimed invention and primary prior art; (iv) Analysis of the ease of overcoming such differences.
guidance: Operationalize by examining whether elements exist in secondary prior art to relieve differences and whether negative or positive elements affect combining primary and secondary prior art.

name: Burden of particularized allegation for combination (proposal)
description: To reject inventive step a petitioner must present reasonable and sufficient logic detailing the process of arriving at the invention from prior art; petitioner should allege a primary prior art and explain in detail how other references combine to produce the invention.
guidance: This combats hindsight by requiring claimants of obviousness to define the primary prior art and the specific combination path so examiners/courts can evaluate obstructive factors and allow patentees to rebut with factual details.

name: Principle 3 — Limit preservation, disclosure, and discovery to relevant and necessary data
description: Preservation, disclosure, and discovery of Protected Data should be limited in scope to that which is relevant and necessary to support any party’s claim or defense in order to minimize conflicts of law and impact on the Data Subject.
guidance: Overarching requirement to minimize intrusion into Protected Data; anticipates use of narrowing techniques and proportionality analyses to reduce cross-border conflict and privacy impacts.

name: Scope of discovery under Fed. R. Civ. P. (relevance, proportionality, burden)
description: Discovery must be relevant to a party’s claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case; it should not be cumulative or duplicative and should be sought from the most convenient, least burdensome, and least expensive source.
guidance: Cites Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) and 26(b)(2)(C); courts must consider importance of issues, amount in controversy, parties’ access to information, resources, and whether burden outweighs benefit.

name: § 325(d) discretion — same or substantially same art/arguments
description: "[W]hether the petition presents to the Office the same or substantially the same art previously presented to the Office," or "whether the petition presents to the Office the same or substantially the same arguments previously presented to the Office."
guidance: Two-part framework: (1) Determine whether petition presents the same/substantially same art or arguments as presented during prosecution; (2) If so, deny review unless the petitioner shows the Office erred "in a manner material to the patentability of challenged claims." Examples of material error include misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of relevant prior art impacting patentability or an error of law (e.g., misconstruing a claim term) where the construction impacts patentability. (Cases: Advanced Bionics; Puma; Oticon.)

name: Material error standard for overcoming § 325(d)
description: Petitioner must show that the examiner materially erred "in a manner material to the patentability of challenged claims."
guidance: Examples: misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of relevant prior art that impact patentability; an error of law such as misconstruing a claim term where the construction impacts patentability. If petitioner fails to explain "how or why the Examiner erred," denial is appropriate (see Puma).

name: Section 101 may be considered for proposed substitute/amended claims in IPR
description: When a patent owner files a motion to amend proposing substitute claims during an IPR, the PTAB may consider grounds of unpatentability (including § 101) that could not have been raised in the initial IPR petition.
guidance: Statutory context: patent owner may propose substitute claims but they "may not enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter." The PTAB will evaluate patentability of new claims under § 101, § 112, etc., and issue a final written decision under § 318(a) "with respect to the patentability of ... any new claim added under [§ 316(d)]." Practitioners should expect § 101 challenges to be raised against motions to amend and should substantively respond to such arguments; failure to do so risks denial of the motion by preponderance of the evidence (see Uniloc v. Hulu). Also consider estoppel implications: § 315(e)(2) may bar grounds that were raised or reasonably could have been raised during the IPR from later being asserted in district court.

name: Nature of patent-expert testimony (partisan role)
description: A patent-expert is not a judge; he is commonly partisan and his testimony is expected to support the claims of the litigant who presents him. His opinion is received in evidence only in connection with the reasons on which it is based, and is to be accepted or rejected by the jury according to their own view of its fallacy or truth.
guidance: Do not ascribe judicial functions to the patent-expert or demand freedom from partisanship. The expert's relation to the jury is like counsel to the court: pointing out facts and applying them in support of claims. Their statements of fact and opinions are to be weighed like those of other witnesses; their opinions are followed when, in the judgment of the jury, they are supported by the facts from which they are deduced.

name: Admissibility and use of caveats, disclaimers, applications, and correspondence
description: Caveats, disclaimers, the patent application, and correspondence with the Patent Office may be admitted for limited purposes: to prove the claimant's ideas at a date, to show abandonment, or to define the nature/scope/meaning of the claimed invention.
guidance: A caveat may be offered to prove the inventor's claims at the date of transmission to the Patent Office (but not perfection). A disclaimer (signed/filed) is admissible on abandonment or scope-limiting issues. Application materials and Patent Office correspondence may be produced as declarations accompanying an act and to define what the inventor meant by his claims.

name: Nexus Requirement Definition
description: Nexus designates a factually and legally sufficient connection between the evidence of commercial success and the claimed invention so that the evidence is of probative value in the nonobviousness determination.
guidance: Determination of nexus should follow MPEP §§716.01(b) and 2145 and case law (Demaco). Applicant must show that the claimed features are responsible for success; mere embodiment of invention in a commercially successful article is insufficient without nexus evidence.

name: Commercial Success Must Be Commensurate in Scope With Claims
description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (including commercial success) must be commensurate in scope with the claims; success must be due to claimed features and not unclaimed features.
guidance: If commercial success relates to narrower features (e.g., dependent claim features) but the asserted claims are broader, the success may not be commensurate and thus not probative (In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies v. Manbeck). See MPEP §§716.01(b) and 2145.

name: Affidavit Language Attributing Success Insufficient
description: An affidavit or declaration merely attributing commercial success to a product 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' does not establish nexus.
guidance: Such generic language does not show the sold product corresponds to the claimed invention or that the success is attributable to the claimed features (Ex parte Standish). More specific corroborating evidence is required.

name: Commercial Success Must Flow From Functions/Advantages Disclosed or Inherent in Specification
description: To be pertinent to nonobviousness, commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification; success should not be due to improvements by others.
guidance: Success deriving from a unique combination of unclaimed ingredients or later-modified embodiments may not show nonobviousness of the claimed invention (In re Vamco; Merck & Cie v. Gnosis). Ensure linkage between disclosed/inherent advantages and market success.

name: Design Cases: Nexus Especially Difficult
description: In design patent cases, establishing nexus between commercial success and the claimed design is especially difficult; success must be clearly attributable to the design and not to brand recognition or improved performance.
guidance: Design success must be shown to arise from the design itself (Litton Systems v. Whirlpool). Be cautious attributing sales to a design when other factors could explain success.

name: Utility/Enablement Burden-Shifting and Affidavit Limitations
description: Once examiner establishes a prima facie lack of enablement, applicant must present persuasive arguments, supported by suitable proofs where necessary, that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention from the disclosure; affidavits/declarations cannot establish facts the specification should have recited.
guidance: Affidavits offering expert construction of non-described elements are generally insufficient (In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth; In re Buchner). Affidavits purporting only to explain or interpret a disclosure are usually not considered unless they explain underlying factual bases and are evaluated case-by-case (In re Oppenauer; Glaser v. Strickland). See MPEP §§2164-2164.08(c), 2107.02, 2107-2107.03 for related guidance.

name: Allegation of grant of letters-patent (second averment)
description: The plaintiff must allege and describe the application for a patent, its allowance by the Patent Office, and the issue of letters-patent, specifying the nature of the invention it purports to protect and making profert of the patent.
guidance: Compliance with preliminary Patent Office requirements need not be stated (presumed from the grant). Claims and specifications need not be set out at length (though may be). Indicate patent by date and number; if reissued, trace original and intermediate re-issues. The declaration must set out the attestation and delivery of the patent or it may be demurred to.

name: Allegation of infringement (fourth averment)
description: The plaintiff must allege that the defendant has infringed the patent by making, using, or selling the invention described, without authority from the owner.
guidance: This violation must be stated as broadly as the right claimed in the patent so it clearly appears the defendant's acts relate to the precise invention protected. No special phraseology is necessary—assertions such as 'in imitation of the patent' or that the defendant 'constructed, used, and vended' to others have been held sufficient. Repeated acts may be alleged together.

name: Formal requisites of the declaration
description: The declaration must put the defendant in possession of the facts on which the plaintiff's claim is based and must leave open to the defendant every legal defense he has a right to make.
guidance: Courts do not severely scrutinize language or logical coherence if the declaration accomplishes its purpose. Omissions of material facts that could have been proved under the pleadings and which the jury must have found are cured by verdict. Nominal damages are implied from infringement; a declaration that contains needed allegations to support evidence and leaves legal defenses open will be tolerated.

name: Pleas in bar and classification of defenses on the merits
description: A plea in bar takes the form of the general issue, the general issue with notice of special matters, or a special plea; defenses should be classified relative to which averment they attack.
guidance: Defenses attacking the first averment (inventive act) include lack of inventive act, prior performance by others in the country, non-patentable subject-matter, lack of novelty, lack of utility, and abandonment/public use. The treatise details that the first averment is true only when seven facts concur (inventive act, performed by patentee/assignor, preceded others, within patentable classes, legally new, practically useful, not abandoned). The second averment (grant) requires nine facts (issued by government, issued in mode provided by law, subject-matter patentable on face, specification free from fraudulent assertion or concealment, description without ambiguity, claims not broader than invention or cured by disclaimer, claims free from ambiguity, patent not surrendered, patent not repealed). Other defenses noted include fraudulent specification, ambiguity in claims, surrender or reissue issues, estoppel, and prior public use or sale greater than statutory bars.

name: Proof of difference for fiber inventions specified by manufacturing method
description: If the invention specified by a spinning method proves its difference with the prior art through an example and a comparative example considering technical characteristics which assign a suitable property of matter to undrawn fiber formed immediately after spinning by heat treatment and drawing, the invention may be considered to be novel and to involve inventive step.
guidance: Use concrete examples and comparative examples that consider the technical characteristics (properties) imparted by the method to the product immediately after processing; such empirical comparisons can support novelty and inventive step for method-specified fiber claims.

name: Claim construction breadth for method-specified fiber materials
description: In construing a claim relating to fiber material specified with a spinning method, the claim should not be construed to be limited by an embodiment presented in the description but should be construed to include a whole span of property of fiber material which is possible to produce according to the method specified.
guidance: Interpret claims to cover the full range of properties producible by the claimed method rather than being restricted to specific embodiments shown in the description.

name: Determination of effect from minute/limited shape changes
description: Minute different shape of a component (e.g., ring, traveler, metallic card clothing, knitting needle) may greatly influence the result; it is necessary to consider the effect from any difference between the shapes.
guidance: When small shape differences are claimed, assess their technical effect. If effect is doubtful or difficult to be sure of, require test data or certified test results to establish the effect.

name: State function of spaces in architectural design claims and description
description: An invention on architectural design is made by combining space(s) with function(s). It is necessary to state function of the space in claim(s) and the description of the invention, and where it is not easy to recognize the functional effect from only the function of the space, interaction among functions of unit spaces should be additionally stated in the description.
guidance: Claims and specifications for architectural designs must clearly identify the functions of unit spaces; when function alone isn't sufficient to show the invention, describe interactions among unit-space functions to complete the disclosure.

name: When claiming shape/structure also disclose functions and interactions
description: In architectural design, inventions can be stated by directly stating shape and structure (specifying the space) or by combination of interactive elements of spaces. Where shape and structure are directly stated, function of space and interaction among the functions should also be stated in the specification.
guidance: Don't rely solely on drawings or morphological descriptions; include functional explanations and interaction details in the specification even when the claim is structural.

name: Clarify category of claimed architectural invention (product vs method)
description: Claims must clearly specify whether the invention is directed to a product (e.g., an apartment), a method for constructing an apartment, or a method for designing an apartment, because unclear category leads to ambiguous subject matter.
guidance: Draft claims to explicitly reflect the intended statutory category of protection; avoid language that mixes product and method unintentionally.

name: Architectural design subject-matter eligibility requires functions/interactions tied to products
description: Invention of architectural design corresponds to product and method; unique characteristics include specification by division/combination of space and effects made by interaction among functions given to the space. Therefore, unless function is clearly recognized by unit space or products forming unit space, the function should be specified and interactions detailed to complete the invention.
guidance: Claims must relate the functional concept to concrete products/structures; functions alone are not the invention — claim a product that has the functions and interactions needed to realize the technical concept.

name: Claim construction for novelty/inventive step must include function (architectural)
description: To determine inventive step of an architectural design invention, it is not allowed to construe claims by excluding the function; one must consider the function of the invention and its effect based on the function of space.
guidance: Avoid construing structural claims purely as placement/combination of spaces without their claimed functions; excluding functions can render claims unreasonably broad and anticipate by structurally-similar prior art with different purposes.

name: Permissible claim categories for computer-related inventions
description: A computer-related invention can be claimed as (1) a method by specifying a series of steps, (2) a product by specifying multiple functions performed thereby, (3) a computer-readable-program-recording medium having program code recorded thereon to install/execute/distribute the program, (4) a computer-readable medium having data recorded thereon when the data structure determines operations, and (5) a computer program recorded in a medium combined with hardware to accomplish a specific task.
guidance: Claims must be drafted to fall into statutory categories; claims to 'computer program not recorded in a medium' (a program per se) are not allowed. Use concrete language such as 'program recorded on a medium' or 'program makes the computer operate as ...' to avoid indefiniteness.

name: Avoid ambiguous claim language like 'using a computer' (indefiniteness)
description: Expressions such as 'using a computer, comprising the steps of' can be indefinite because they permit multiple constructions (e.g., human-operated steps using a computer tool vs. an information-processing method by software).
guidance: Specify who/what performs each step (human vs computer/software) or rephrase to clearly indicate that the steps are performed by a computer program or by a human operating a computer.

name: Program vs functional means clarity in medium claims
description: A program per se does not function as a 'means'. Claims should state that the program 'makes the computer operate as' the functional means rather than treating the program itself as the means.
guidance: Draft claims to attribute functions to the computer when run with the program (e.g., 'program recorded on a medium, the program makes the computer operate as X'), which yields definite claims.

name: Define uncommon technical terms; undefined terms cause indefiniteness
description: If a term (e.g., 'the right-brain inference rule') is not defined in the description nor part of common general knowledge as of the filing, the claimed invention is unclear and indefinite.
guidance: Provide definitions or sufficient description for uncommon technical terms, abbreviations, symbols, etc., so the skilled person can understand the technical meaning.

name: Specify technical relationships among claim elements
description: Claims that merely state elements (e.g., 'an information transmission medium transmitting a certain computer program') without showing technical relationships between elements cannot technically define a product invention and are unclear.
guidance: Include how elements interact or are arranged technically (structure, timing, causation) so that the claimed combination constitutes a technical invention.

name: Clarify category for program signals/output/product distinctions
description: Categories such as program signals, program signal sequence, program product, and program output must be clearly identified to determine the category of the invention.
guidance: Avoid vague labels; explicitly claim as product/method/medium and describe how the claimed subject matter fits the statutory category.

name: Avoid vague scope-limiting terms (e.g., 'high speed')
description: Use of comparative or qualitative terms like 'high speed' without objective comparison criteria makes the scope of the claimed invention unclear.
guidance: Either remove vague qualifiers or quantify them (e.g., specific throughput, latency) or rephrase to describe structural/functional features that yield the claimed performance.

name: Claims reciting only results without means are unclear
description: A claim reciting only a result to be accomplished (e.g., a computer to predict down-burst) without concrete processing contents or means may be indefinite; unless the skilled person can introduce specific matter from the claim statement and common general knowledge, the scope is unclear.
guidance: Where function-only claims are used, ensure that either the skilled person can implement the function from the claim and common general knowledge, or include concrete means/procedures in the claim or description to make the invention definite.

name: Standards for when function-defined claims are acceptable
description: Determine clarity of function-defined claims as follows: (①) if a person skilled in the art may introduce specific matter(s) with the function based on general knowledge, the scope is clear; (②) if not, scope is generally unclear; (③) exceptions where specification/drawings properly define the invention only by function or connection between function and level of technology is easily understood, scope may be clear; (④)-(⑤) special notes about parameter/manufacture-method claims and when novelty/infringement assessment becomes difficult.
guidance: Apply these tests when assessing functional claims; if the function cannot be linked to concrete embodiments or common knowledge, require amendment/clarification.

name: Examples of enablement violations (abstract functional statements)
description: Violations include: (1) use of uncommon terms without definition; (2) abstract statements of steps/functions without disclosure on implementation so claimed invention cannot be carried out (e.g., business methods or game rules without computer implementation details; GUI steps without implementation); (3) hardware/software explained only by functional block diagrams or general flow charts insufficient to understand structure; (4) functional claims with embodiments explained only by flowcharts where relationship is unclear.
guidance: Provide concrete implementation details (algorithms, structure, modules, program listings with explanations) showing how functions are realized in hardware/software to meet enablement.

name: Patentability assessment applies to claimed invention as defined by claim language
description: Patentability requirements are applied to 'claimed inventions' and the claimed invention is defined on the basis of claim language, interpreted in light of the specification, drawings, and common general knowledge as of filing.
guidance: Claims are the primary basis for patentability evaluation; carefully interpret claim terms in context of the specification when assessing novelty, inventive step and eligibility.

name: Procedure for assessing subject-matter eligibility (computer-related)
description: Step (1) Understand the claimed invention based on claim language. (2) If information processing by software is concretely implemented by using hardware in the claimed invention (i.e., software and hardware cooperatively working to implement operations depending on use), the claimed invention constitutes statutory subject matter. (3) If not concretely implemented by hardware, it does not constitute statutory subject matter.
guidance: Apply this three-step test when evaluating computer-related claims. Example: a computer that 'prepares a summary' may be non-statutory if the processing means are not shown to be cooperatively implemented with hardware.

name: Specificity of claimed invention versus abstract concept
description: Patents should cover a specific invention or application, not broad concepts (e.g., Samuel Morse's electromagnetic waves example). Granting patents on concepts lets owners monopolize basic ideas rather than concrete implementations.
guidance: The Supreme Court historically limited patents to particular inventions; the PTO's trend toward patenting concepts is presented as an anti-pattern that should be corrected by courts or statute.

name: Claim breadth and granularity (snippets vs whole genes; broad vs narrow claims)
description: Filing many patents on small snippets or drafting overly broad claims expands monopoly scope and increases administrative burden and harms downstream research and development.
guidance: Careful claim drafting and limiting claim breadth to genuine inventive contributions helps prevent overbroad monopolies and reduces negative effects on innovation and testing.

name: Inappropriateness of trivial/non-innovative patents
description: Patents granted on trivial, non-innovative, or clearly social/obvious activities (e.g., comb-over, sports moves, certain tax shelters) represent overreach that can unduly affect daily life.
guidance: Patents should be reserved for true technical innovations with demonstrated utility and non-obviousness; administrative and judicial scrutiny should filter out trivial claims.

name: What is PPH and how does it help me?
description: The Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) is a framework in which an application whose claims have been determined to be patentable by an Office of Earlier Examination (OEE) is eligible to go through an accelerated examination in an Office of Later Examination (OLE) with a simple procedure upon an applicant’s request.
guidance: PPH uses search/examination-related information of the OEE to (1) deliver lower prosecution costs, (2) support efficient worldwide patent rights, and (3) reduce search/examination burden and improve examination quality among major patent offices.

name: How is sufficient correspondence between claims determined?
description: A claim sufficiently corresponds when it is of the same or similar scope as an allowable claim in the related OEE application. A claim that is narrower than an allowable OEE claim will also sufficiently correspond if presented as a claim dependent upon a claim that is of the same or similar scope to an allowable OEE claim.
guidance: See Questions 28–29 and 34–35 for category and amendment constraints and acceptable dependent-to-independent conversions.

name: Can 'use' claims be rewritten as 'method' claims when filing a PPH request?
description: No. Presenting a 'method' claim where the OEE allowed a 'use' claim introduces a different claim category and is not considered to sufficiently correspond. The scopes of 'use' and 'method' claims usually differ significantly.

name: Incorporating a narrower dependent claim into the independent claim during U.S. prosecution
description: If the narrower dependent claim is indicated as being allowable if written in independent form, you may rewrite the allowable dependent claim in independent form.
guidance: This addresses whether dependent-to-independent conversion is permissible when dependent claim was indicated allowable.

name: Will an amendment to an independent claim meet sufficient correspondence if it adds a limitation?
description: Yes, but only if the added limitation was previously presented in a dependent claim that is indicated as having allowable subject matter but was objected to only because it was dependent on a rejected base claim.

name: Distinctness of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) requirements
description: The requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) (or the first and second paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112) are separate and distinct.
guidance: If a description or the enabling disclosure of a specification is not commensurate in scope with the subject matter encompassed by a claim, that fact alone does not render the claim imprecise or indefinite or otherwise not in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph); rather, the claim is based on an insufficient disclosure (35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA first paragraph) and should be rejected on that ground. (See opening paragraph and In re Borkowski, 422 F.2d 904, 164 USPQ 642 (CCPA 1970).)

name: Enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
description: The specification's enabling disclosure must be commensurate in scope with the subject matter encompassed by the claim; the specification must teach how to make and use the full scope claimed.
guidance: Where the disclosure is narrower than the claim scope, the claim is based on an insufficient disclosure and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Example: In re Mayhew — the only disclosed mode involved use of a cooling zone at a particular location; claims failing to specify the cooling step or location were held not to be supported by an enabling disclosure (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).

name: Written description/support for claimed subject matter (35 U.S.C. 112(a) first paragraph)
description: The claims must be described in the application as filed; the specification must provide support for the claimed subject matter (written description).
guidance: If a claim (or an amended claim) recites subject matter that was not described in the application as filed, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as directed to subject matter not described in the specification as filed may be appropriate. Example: In re Simon — claims to a subcombination A+B+C were not described where the original application was directed to A+B+C+D+E, and the court concluded the subcombination claims were not described (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).

name: Omission of critical or essential features may render claims unsupported
description: If the specification discloses that a particular feature or element is critical or essential to the practice of the invention, failure to recite or include that feature or element in the claims may provide a basis for rejection for lack of support or enablement.
guidance: Where the specification indicates a feature is essential, claims omitting that feature can be rejected as not supported by an enabling disclosure. (Cited authority: In re Mayhew, 527 F.2d 1229, 188 USPQ 356 (CCPA 1976).)

name: Insufficiency of disclosure (112(a)) should not be conflated with indefiniteness (112(b))
description: An insufficient disclosure (specification not commensurate with claim scope or lacking necessary descriptive/enablement support) is a ground for rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a), not for a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) rejection.
guidance: The examiner should frame rejections based on the proper statutory provision: lack of adequate disclosure/support -> 112(a); particularity/definiteness issues -> 112(b). The MPEP cites In re Borkowski to underscore that insufficient disclosure alone does not make a claim indefinite under 112(b) but warrants rejection under 112(a).

name: Definiteness / claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b))
description: The requirement that claims 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention' under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) is a separate requirement from the written description/enablement obligations of 112(a).
guidance: Because 112(b) is distinct from 112(a), an examiner should not substitute a 112(b) indefiniteness rejection for an appropriate 112(a) rejection when the problem is lack of descriptive or enabling support. The page emphasizes treating these requirements separately when evaluating claims.

name: Deprivation of due process (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(i))
description: The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.
guidance: Respondent must demonstrate the lack of notice/opportunity to be heard by clear and convincing evidence. Challenges to the originating jurisdiction's rules or procedures are generally waived if the respondent knowingly and voluntarily consented to discipline (e.g., via guilty plea or consent judgment). The Office will reject due-process claims that were waived by a respondent's voluntary stipulation to facts and agreement to the sanction.

name: Argument that practitioner was not publicly disciplined (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(iv))
description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
guidance: If the respondent can show that the alleged discipline was not in fact publicly imposed, that may prevent imposition of reciprocal discipline; the claim must be supported by clear and convincing evidence of the absence of public discipline.

name: Directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A)
description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception such as a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea.
guidance: Example language: 'The claim is then analyzed to determine if the claim is directed to a judicial exception.' Use case-law analogies (e.g., organizing human behavior, collecting/recognizing/storing data, mathematical correlations) to identify abstract ideas.

name: No exception recited -> eligibility
description: If the claim does not recite any judicial exception, that alone may be sufficient for eligibility.
guidance: As noted: 'It is important to point out as well that there is no apparent exception recited in the claim, which alone would be sufficient for eligibility.' Examiners may note this in an Office action or reasons for allowance.

name: Claim 'directed to' vs merely 'involving' an abstract idea
description: Distinguish whether a claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (ending eligibility analysis) or only 'involves' it (may still be eligible under Step 2A if claim is an improvement in computer-related technology).
guidance: Example: Enfish and BASCOM discussions — if a claim is 'directed to' a non-abstract improvement (e.g., an improvement in computer functionality), the Step 2A inquiry may end with eligibility. The Federal Circuit described some claims as a 'close call' and examiners should consider whether the claim is clearly an Internet-centric problem or a computer-technology improvement.

name: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the exception (the inventive concept inquiry).
guidance: Example language: 'Under Step 2B, the claim as a whole is analyzed to determine whether any element, or combination of elements, is sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.' Consider both individual elements and the ordered combination.

name: Unconventional/non-generic combination can supply inventive concept
description: An unconventional and non-generic combination of known elements can supply the inventive concept that makes the claim 'significantly more' than the abstract idea.
guidance: Example language: 'Here, an inventive concept can be found in the unconventional and non-generic combination of known elements, and more specifically “the installation of a filtering tool at a specific location, remote from the end-users, with customizable filtering features specific to each end-user”.' Evaluate whether the ordered combination yields an improvement in technology.

name: Technology-based solution / improvement to technology
description: Claims that provide a technology-based solution that improves the functioning of a computer or other technology — and that overcome prior-art problems — are more likely to be eligible.
guidance: Example language: 'The claimed arrangement of elements in the system results in an improvement in the technology of filtering content on the Internet' and 'a “technology-based solution” of filtering content on the Internet that overcomes the problems in the prior art'. Use specification and factual record to show how the claimed arrangement solves technical problems.

name: Compare to relevant case law to identify abstract idea vs improvement
description: Use comparisons to Federal Circuit and Supreme Court decisions (e.g., Enfish, BASCOM, DDR, OIP, Content Extraction, Intellectual Ventures I, Ultramercial, Accenture) to determine whether the claim is abstract or a technological improvement.
guidance: The guidance provides detailed case-law contrasts (e.g., claims that are 'simply the generic automation of traditional techniques' are not technology-based solutions). A case-law comparison can be informative but is not mandatory during examination.

name: Mapping claim focus to known abstract-idea categories
description: Identify whether the focus of the claim maps to abstract-idea categories (e.g., methods of organizing human behavior, collecting/recognizing/storing data, mathematical correlations).
guidance: Example language: 'Filtering content is ... a “method of organizing human behavior” that is similar to other concepts that have been identified as abstract by the courts.' Use analogies to prior abstract-idea holdings to support Step 2A conclusions.

name: Specific meaningful limitations implementing the abstract idea
description: Additional claim elements that are specific, meaningful, and implement the abstract idea in a particular way can supply the inventive concept and render the claim eligible.
guidance: Example from ATM hypotheticals: claims that 'generate a random code and transmit it to a mobile communication device ... read an image ... decrypt code data ... and control access to the keypad' were found to have specific meaningful limitations and thus were eligible (Claims 2 and 3), whereas a generic recitation of steps (Claim 1) was ineligible.

name: If the record warrants, add explanatory remarks in Office action or reasons for allowance
description: Examiners may add remarks to an Office action or reasons for allowance to clarify why a claim is not directed to a judicial exception or why it is eligible.
guidance: Example language: 'If the examiner believes that the record would benefit from clarification, remarks could be added to an Office action or reasons for allowance, indicating that the claim is not directed to any judicial exception.' This is a procedural suggestion for examiners to document positions.

name: Novelty of selected numerical sub-ranges (selection inventions)
description: A claimed invention may be novel by selecting a narrower sub-range of numerical values within a broader known range, provided the selected sub-range has not been explicitly mentioned in the prior art.
guidance: The selected sub-range should be narrow and sufficiently specific from the known broader range and ideally illustrated by examples. Whether a prior art reference anticipates a range depends on whether the claimed subject matter is disclosed with sufficient specificity in that prior art; interpretation of 'sufficient specificity' depends on the facts of the case.

name: Close-but-non-overlapping ranges may be novel (criteria for 'close')
