description: Prior art which teaches a value or range very close to, but not overlapping or touching, the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range and the claim is novel (though inventive step must still be considered).
guidance: Viet Nam sets out three criteria for when a 'close' claimed numerical range still meets novelty: (a) the claimed numerical range is sufficiently far removed from any specific number disclosed; (b) the claimed range is narrow compared to the specific number disclosed; (c) the claimed range provides an effect that makes the claimed subject matter 'special' (e.g., unexpected effect).

name: Selection invention and unexpected results as novelty/inventive step support
description: Where a claim is directed to a narrow range and the prior art discloses only a broad range, the narrow selection may be novel if not merely one way of carrying out the prior teaching, especially when there is evidence (e.g., unexpected results) that the advantageous effect occurs only within the claimed narrow range.
guidance: Unexpected results may support novelty (selection invention) and may also render the claims unobvious (inventive step). Assessment depends on the specific facts and evidence showing the special effect.

name: Definition of 'invention' for patentability purposes
description: An 'invention' is what is specified in the claim(s): commonly a solution to a technical problem that produces a technical effect; can be a product, process, or product-by-process; improvements of known products/processes can also be inventions.
guidance: The term 'improvement' does not necessarily require superior technical effect; the problem might be seeking an alternative providing the same or similar effects (e.g., cost-effectiveness).

name: Problem-solution approach for assessing inventive step
description: A three-step method: (i) determine the closest prior art; (ii) establish the objective technical problem to be solved; (iii) consider whether the claimed invention, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, would have been obvious to the PSIA.
guidance: Closest prior art is the single reference most promising as a starting point—preferably same field/use and having the most features in common. Objective technical problem is formulated by comparing claimed invention and closest prior art and may be reformulated based on objectively established facts and evidence in the proceedings. Partial or multiple technical problems (where distinguishing features yield different technical effects) should be handled part-by-part. The examiner must ask whether there was any teaching that would have 'prompted' the PSIA to modify the closest prior art to arrive at the claimed invention with a reasonable likelihood of success.

name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework — Step 1: directed to patent-ineligible concept
description: First determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
guidance: Courts must 'identif[y] the abstract idea represented in the claim' and decide if the claim at its core embraces an ineligible building block (as applied in Alice and prior cases).

name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework — Step 2: inventive concept / 'significantly more'
description: If the claims are directed to an ineligible concept, analyze claim elements individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether they add an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Ask whether the additions are 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself' (Mayo language).

name: Generic computer implementation does not confer eligibility
description: The mere introduction or recitation of a computer into the claims, when that implementation is purely conventional or generic, does not alter the Alice/Mayo analysis or render an abstract idea patent-eligible.
guidance: The Court warned that 'wholly generic computer implementation is not generally the sort of "additional feature" that provides any "practical assurance"' the claim is more than drafting to monopolize the abstract idea. Electronic recordkeeping and other basic computer functions typically will not suffice.

name: Diehr exception — improvement to technological process can be eligible
description: Claims that employ a mathematical formula or abstract concept as part of a computer-implemented process may be eligible where the additional claim steps transform the process into an inventive application by solving a technological problem or improving conventional industry practice.
guidance: Diehr is distinguished from Benson/Flook/Alice: in Diehr a thermocouple measurement plus computer recalculation produced a technological improvement not previously obtainable, and that enabled eligibility.

name: Claims to fundamental economic practices are abstract ideas
description: Claims directed to fundamental economic practices long prevalent in commerce (e.g., intermediated settlement) are treated as abstract ideas and thus fall within the Section 101 exceptions.
guidance: Alice held that intermediated settlement was a 'building block' of the modern economy and therefore an abstract idea beyond Section 101's scope.

name: Hardware recitations must provide meaningful limitations beyond generic functions
description: Reciting 'specific hardware' or functional components (e.g., data processing system, communications controller, data storage unit) is not enough if those elements are purely functional and generic.
guidance: System and Beauregard (computer-readable medium) claims that merely tie a method to conventional hardware 'offer[] a meaningful limitation beyond generally linking the use of the [method] to a particular technological environment' only if the hardware contributes more than generic implementation.

name: Electronic recordkeeping/basic computer functions are not inventive
description: Claim steps that effectively recite 'electronic recordkeeping' or other of the most basic functions of a computer generally will not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Alice described electronic recordkeeping as one of the most basic computer functions and treated such recitations as insufficient under step two.

name: Proof that invention is a tangible, hardware-based implementation (not just data)
description: Courts may require evidence that the claimed invention is directed to a tangible, hardware-based implementation rather than merely the underlying data or abstract manipulation of information.
guidance: Showing concrete hardware effects or an improvement in computer functionality helps distinguish eligible inventions from claims to data or abstract ideas.

name: Demonstrate improvement on known procedures or previously unattainable solutions
description: An inquiry will consider whether the method or system improves upon a known procedure by providing a solution to a problem that had not previously been achieved (or could not be achieved) without the invention.
guidance: Showing a specific technological improvement or new capability can support finding an 'inventive concept' under step two and distinguish the claim from mere automation of prior practices.

name: Employee invention compensation rights and overview
description: An employee invention is an invention made by an employee in connection with their duties falling within scope of the employer’s business; an employer is automatically entitled to a free nonexclusive license, and where the employer succeeds rights or gets an exclusive license, the employee is entitled to fair compensation under the Invention Promotion Act.
guidance: Compensation provisions intersect civil law, labor law and patent law and are compulsory provisions to protect employees. Defenses to compensation claims include statute of limitations (10 years) and prior amounts paid that should be deducted.

name: Scope and limitations of permanent injunctions
description: Scope involves (a) claim for an injunction (court often issues default injunction to prohibit infringing practices), (b) claim for disposal of infringing products (must accompany injunction and be clearly specified), and (c) other measures necessary to prevent infringement (must be balanced to avoid excessive burden).
guidance: If patented invention is part/component of defendant’s product, issues arise whether injunction covers whole product and whether destruction of whole product can be claimed. Courts may issue injunctions only against infringing parts and order destruction of manufacturing equipment. Example injunction language is provided for guidance.

name: Statutory basis and elements for damages claims
description: Article 128(1) allows a patentee or exclusive licensee to claim compensation for damages caused by a person who has willfully or negligently infringed the patent or exclusive license; damages claims generally follow tort principles, requiring proof of (i) plaintiff is patentee; (ii) infringer willfully or negligently infringed; (iii) infringement unlawful; (iv) infringer capable of liability; (v) patentee suffered damages; (vi) proximate causation.
guidance: Patent infringement is presumed negligent under the Patent Act. The 2019 amendment allows courts to enhance damages up to three times actual damages if infringement is willful. Claimant must identify alleged infringer; actions based on unjust enrichment have a 10-year limitation; general damages actions must be filed within 3 years from awareness or within 10 years from date of infringement, whichever earlier.

name: Impermissible sale/on-sale bar
description: An impermissible sale has occurred if there was a definite sale, or offer to sell, more than 1 year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention and the subject matter of the sale, or offer to sell, fully anticipated the claimed invention or would have rendered the claimed invention obvious by its addition to the prior art.
guidance: Cites Ferag AG v. Quipp and Pfaff: on‑sale bar triggered when (1) subject of a commercial offer for sale not primarily for experimental purposes and (2) ready for patenting. Traditional contract law and UCC principles apply to determine whether a commercial offer for sale has occurred.

name: Ready for patenting — two routes
description: 'Ready for patenting' may be satisfied either by (a) proof of reduction to practice before the critical date, or (b) proof that prior to the critical date the inventor had prepared drawings or other descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention.
guidance: Pfaff; Invitrogen; examples where detailed drawings/specs allowed manufacture of claimed product. Readiness is applied in both on‑sale and public‑use contexts.

name: Inherent possession of claim limitations in offered product
description: If a product offered for sale inherently possesses each limitation of the claims, then the invention is on sale, whether or not parties recognized the claimed characteristics.
guidance: Abbott Labs v. Geneva Pharmaceuticals; STX LLC v. Brine Inc. — subjective unknown qualities cannot avoid the on‑sale bar.

name: Commercial activity must legitimately advance development
description: The commercial activity (sale/use) must legitimately advance the experimental development of the invention toward completion; otherwise it counts as commercial exploitation.
guidance: Where examiner finds prima facie sale/offer, applicant rarely meets burden to show experimentation unless clear and convincing necessity for the experimentation is established. See Sunoco Partners Marketing & Terminals LP v. U.S. Venture — testing at third party location and ability to test earlier undermined experimental claim.

name: Intent — requirement for objective evidence of experimental purpose
description: When sales occur in an ordinary commercial environment and goods are placed outside inventor's control, a secretly held subjective intent to 'experiment' is unavailing without objective evidence; under such circumstances the customer must, at a minimum, be made aware of the intended experimental purpose.
guidance: Assess whether objective evidence supports claimed experimental intent; mere subjective assertions are insufficient when transaction is commercial in nature.

name: Notice of subsequent interfering applications to caveator
description: Whenever an application for a patent for the same invention is filed by a rival, either simultaneously with the caveat or during its life, and the invention described is found by the Office to be patentable and to correspond apparently with that specified in the caveat, proceedings on the application are suspended, the application (specification, drawings, model) is deposited in secret archives, and the caveator is notified to file his application so rival claims may be determined.
guidance: If notified, the caveator must present his application within three months from the expiration of the normal mail transmission time from Washington; if both applications claim the same invention an interference will be declared and heard. Maintain readiness to file promptly upon notice.

name: Form and completeness of application (writing, language, contents)
description: An application and all communications with the Office must be in writing, correctly, legibly, and clearly written; the Commissioner may require them to be printed at party's cost. The application must be in English, addressed to the Commissioner, and include a petition, an oath, and a specification or Description and Claim; in certain cases it must be accompanied by drawings and a model or specimen. No application can be accepted for examination until complete in all its parts.
guidance: Prepare complete, legible, English-language filings with petition, oath, specification and claims, and any required drawings/models; unsigned, blank, altered, or partly filled applications may be stricken if irregularity discovered before grant.

name: Computer involvement must be particular and detailed
description: To show that the involvement of a computer assists in improving the technology, the claims must recite the details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method.
guidance: Merely adding generic computer components to perform the method is not sufficient. A claim must include more than mere instructions to perform the method on a generic component or machinery to qualify as an improvement to an existing technology. If applicant adds a generic computer or asserts the computer is 'specially programmed', the examiner should determine whether the added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more than the judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for mere-instructions guidance and case citations (Alice, In re Alappat, TLI, Eon, etc.).

name: Particularity or generality of machine elements
description: Evaluate the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (not any and all machines).
guidance: A machine recited with particular structure or detailed elements (e.g., specific antenna shapes/lengths, Fourdrinier machine structure) is more likely to integrate an exception into a practical application. By contrast, a general purpose computer that applies an exception using conventional functions does not qualify as a particular machine. Mere recitation of concrete/tangible components is insufficient if they are conventional. See Mackay Radio & Tel. Co. v. RCA, Eibel Process, Ultramercial v. Hulu, TLI, Eon, Alappat, Bilski citations in MPEP § 2106.05(b)(I).

name: Machine involvement must not be extra-solution activity or mere field-of-use
description: Assess the extent to which the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on the claim versus contributing only nominally/insignificantly (e.g., data gathering or field-of-use limitations).
guidance: Use of a machine that merely contributes nominally (e.g., as a source of data or a field-of-use limitation) will not integrate a judicial exception or provide significantly more. Examiners should apply the insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations (MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h)) and review cases such as Bilski, Parker v. Flook, and CyberSource for guidance. Example: describing the Internet as a data source does not make fraud-detection steps tied to a particular machine. See MPEP § 2106.05(b)(III).

name: Evaluate related considerations: mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use
description: Examiners should evaluate whether claim elements amount to mere instructions to apply a judicial exception, represent insignificant extra-solution activity, or merely impose a field-of-use, as these considerations affect whether a claim integrates an exception or recites significantly more.
guidance: Mere instructions to apply an exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(f)) or insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP § 2106.05(g)) typically do not confer eligibility. Field-of-use limitations that do not meaningfully limit execution of claimed steps likewise fail to provide significantly more (see Mayo and related discussion). These considerations are helpful when assessing particular machine/particular transformation/well-understood conventional activity questions.

name: Compare relative danger of reexamination vs litigation
description: Rather than blanket counsel that 'reexaminations are dangerous,' ask 'how much more dangerous is reexamination than trying to invalidate those same patent claims in patent litigation?' and whether known dangers can be reduced.
guidance: Make a thorough, balanced consideration of pros and cons, taking into account case-specific facts, potential downstream effects on litigation, and ways to mitigate reexamination risks.

name: Consider differences in claim construction and presumption of validity
description: USPTO construes claims 'as broadly as possible consistent with the specification' in reexamination and does not afford claims a presumption of validity (unlike courts under 35 U.S.C. §282); in reexamination it may be easier to demonstrate unpatentability over prior art.
guidance: Factor the more expansive PTO claim construction and absence of presumption of validity into forum choice and into how you frame prior-art arguments.

name: Risk of creating limiting prosecution history statements (estoppel)
description: Prosecution-history statements by the patent owner's attorneys to obtain re-allowance (including 'confirming' patentability) may create or greatly strengthen a third party's non-infringement argument or prosecution-history estoppel.
guidance: Weigh whether statements necessary to secure confirmation will limit claim scope in litigation; coordinate reexamination strategy with experienced trial counsel to avoid inadvertent estoppel.

name: Limited judicial/petition review of SNQ ordering (grounds to vacate narrow)
description: There is no right to have the examiner's determination that a 'substantial new question' (SNQ) exists reviewed by petition or immediate appeal except in narrow circumstances (e.g., reexam not based on patents/printed publications, wrong patent, duplicate request, or claims finally held invalid by a court).
guidance: If a patent owner files a petition to vacate an ultra vires reexamination order, a third-party can oppose; challenges must be timely and are limited in scope.

name: Use reexamination to correct inventorship and minor specification/claim errors
description: If you are the patent owner, seize reexamination opportunities to address inventorship problems and to clean up minor specification and claim errors (so long as you do not broaden claims).
guidance: Coordinate any corrections with counsel to ensure they do not broaden claim scope or create other adverse consequences; reexamination may be a safer time to make certain filings than during litigation.

name: Effect on claim scope, past damages, and intervening rights
description: Claims narrowed by reexamination will not be enforceable for past infringement before the reexamination certificate issued and are subject to intervening rights; however, patentees may obtain allowance of narrowed claims for future enforceability.
guidance: Consider how claim changes will affect past and future liability and damages; reexamination outcomes can have mixed enforcement consequences.

name: U.S. Patent Training Academy curricula and topics
description: Two patent examiner training programs exist: an Intellectual Property Experienced Examiner Training and an entry-level two-phased 12-month new examiner program. Curricula include USPC and CPC classification, searching (classification, text), claim interpretation, advanced text searching, writing an effective examiner’s answer, appeal procedure and practice, technology-specific introductions, automation training (specialized applications and multiple search systems), and life skills training.
guidance: Provide specialized automation classes, multiple search systems training (STN, Dialog), and include appeal procedure practice (Appeal Conference and Pre-Conference). Ensure experienced and entry-level curricula cover overlapping legal/procedural and technical competencies.

name: Jepson claim format (37 CFR § 1.75(e))
description: A Jepson claim has a specific format: (1) a preamble comprising a general description of all the elements or steps of the claimed combination which are conventional or known, (2) a phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises,' and (3) those elements, steps and/or relationships which constitute that portion of the claimed combination which the applicant considers as the new or improved portion.
guidance: Use the three-part structure: (i) preamble identifying conventional/known features, (ii) specific transitional phrase indicating the improvement, and (iii) recitation of the new or improved aspects. (Verbatim text from 37 CFR § 1.75(e) as cited.)

name: Written description requirement applies to the entire Jepson claim (including the preamble)
description: A Jepson claim preamble requires written description; the inventor must provide written description sufficient for the claim's totality, which necessarily includes the preamble.
guidance: Federal Circuit: 'The invention [of a Jepson claim] is not only the claimed improvement, but the claimed improvement as applied to the prior art, so the inventor must provide written description sufficient to show possession of the claimed improvement to what was known in the prior art.' Also: 'While a Jepson claim is directed to the improvement it makes to the prior art, the claim is a singular thing and cannot be separated; its totality is what must have written description support...' — thus do not assume the preamble can escape §112 analysis.

name: Inventor must show possession of the claimed improvement as applied to the prior art
description: Possession must be shown not just of the improvement in the abstract but of the improvement as applied to what was known in the prior art; you cannot avoid written description by asserting portions are 'well-known.'
guidance: Court admonition: 'A patentee cannot be permitted to use a Jepson claim to avoid the requirement that she be in possession of the claimed invention simply by asserting something is well-known in the art.' If relying on assertedly known prior-art features, provide specification support or evidence that those features were indeed well-known.

name: Written description sufficiency for a claimed genus (antibodies) — need species disclosure or proof of well-known genus
description: When claiming a genus of antibodies (various specificities/epitopes), disclosing only a single antibody species may be insufficient to satisfy the written description requirement for the broader genus.
guidance: In Xencor the specification disclosed only one anti-C5 antibody (5G1.1), which the USPTO found insufficient given the 'various specificities and epitopes' of the genus. To support a genus claim, disclose representative species or otherwise show that the genus was known/would be understood by an ordinary artisan to be within the inventor's possession.

name: Means-plus-function claiming under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f)
description: An element may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without reciting structure, material, or acts; such a claim is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: Statutory text (35 U.S.C. § 112(f)) and MPEP § 2181 govern interpretation: during examination the means-plus-function clause is interpreted as reciting 'the structure, material or act described in the specification as performing the entire claimed function and equivalents.' Ensure the specification discloses corresponding structure (e.g., the actual antibody species) if using means-plus-function language.

name: Functional claiming / genus support under Ariad (species sufficiency requirement)
description: When claims use functional language to define the boundaries of a claimed genus, the specification must show that the inventor has invented species sufficient to support a claim to the functionally‑defined genus.
guidance: Citing Ariad (en banc), MPEP § 2181 notes that functional/genus claims require adequate species disclosure. Courts may require multiple representative species or other disclosure demonstrating reduction to practice across the claimed scope; otherwise the claim risks failing written description even if framed functionally or as means-plus-function.

name: USPTO practice: examiners treat Jepson preambles as part of the invention and may invalidate claims for lack of written description
description: The USPTO's position is that Jepson claim preambles are part of the invention and thus require written description; the USPTO in Xencor invalidated claims for lack of written description in the preamble ('method of treating' clause).
guidance: Be prepared to defend Jepson-format claims on the merits (specification support for preamble and improvement) rather than relying solely on formal claim labeling; appeals may fail if specification lacks species or other support.

name: Practical caution on 'clever' claim drafting
description: While judges criticize attempts to use clever claim drafting to avoid statutory requirements, practitioners often try different drafting approaches because claim scope can hinge on precise wording.
guidance: Do not assume a particular claim label (Jepson, means-plus-function) will circumvent written description or other statutory requirements; draft with sufficient specification support for the claimed scope. As Judge Rich noted: 'the name of the game is the claims.'

name: Judicial determination of claim meaning (Markman principle)
description: Claim interpretation is a question of law for the court: a judge (not a jury) determines the meaning of disputed claim terms in a patent.
guidance: Cites Markman v. Westview Instruments, 517 U.S. 370 (1996). Emphasizes that because claim construction affects the scope of legal rights it is properly within the court's purview.

name: Start with ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill (Phillips rule)
description: The starting point for interpreting claim language is its ordinary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art, in light of the patent specification.
guidance: Cites Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc). Courts should read claim terms in the context of the entire patent, not in isolation.

name: Intrinsic evidence hierarchy
description: Intrinsic evidence — claim language, the specification, and the prosecution history — is the most authoritative source in claim construction and is preferred over extrinsic evidence.
guidance: Judges must first look to the intrinsic evidence. The claim language is the starting point; the specification serves as the 'dictionary' of the patent; and the prosecution history can illuminate intended scope and disclaimers.

name: Prosecution history's role and limits
description: The prosecution history (communications between applicant and examiner) can further illuminate intended claim scope and may establish disclaimers or limitations affecting interpretation.
guidance: Parties should analyze amendments and arguments made during prosecution; narrowing amendments can support a more limited interpretation for defendants.

name: Use of expert testimony to show POSITA understanding
description: Expert testimony can demonstrate how a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand particular claim terms based on technical context.
guidance: Experts are commonly used but may be deposed and cross-examined; their factual contributions may be reviewed for clear error on appeal per Teva. Ensure expert opinions are consistent with the intrinsic record.

name: Defendant strategy: seek narrower constructions and highlight prosecution history
description: Defendants typically seek narrower claim constructions to avoid infringement and should analyze prosecution history and any narrowing amendments or disclaimers.
guidance: Highlight ambiguities or inconsistencies between claim language and specification to support non-infringement or invalidity. Prepare to vigorously cross-examine plaintiff experts.

name: Limit the number of disputed claim terms
description: Parties should limit their selection to the most material disputed claim terms (suggested 5 to 10) to streamline the process and focus on issues most likely to affect case outcome.
guidance: Overloading the court with excessive disputes can dilute persuasive focus and lead to inefficient proceedings. Strategic claim selection enhances clarity and improves chances of favorable construction.

name: Initial disclosures and local rules compliance
description: Initial disclosures are governed by local rules and often require patentees to serve detailed disclosures (asserted claims, accused products/systems, relevant priority dates) early in the case.
guidance: Example: Northern District of California requires disclosures within ~45 days of the initial case management conference. Follow district-specific patent local rules to avoid procedural sanctions or surprises.

name: Claim construction briefing requirements
description: Each party must submit detailed written arguments supporting proposed claim interpretations, typically citing intrinsic evidence and may include extrinsic evidence like technical dictionaries or expert declarations.
guidance: Briefs often attach expert declarations; experts may be deposed or permitted to testify. Thorough citation to the specification, claims, and prosecution history is essential.

name: Court issues a written claim construction order with rationale
description: The court will issue a written claim construction order setting forth interpretation of each disputed term and explaining the rationale, citing evidence and legal standards.
guidance: Timing varies: orders may be issued early, after some discovery, or rarely during/after trial. A clear written ruling helps frame summary judgment, trial strategy, and potential appeals.

name: Appellate standard of review (Teva hybrid standard)
description: While claim construction remains a question of law reviewed de novo on appeal, factual findings underlying constructions (e.g., reliance on expert evidence) are reviewed for clear error.
guidance: Cites Teva Pharmaceuticals USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 574 U.S. 318 (2015). Preserve a robust factual record at district court because factual determinations receive deference on appeal.

name: Impact of claim construction on summary judgment, trial, and settlement
description: A favorable claim construction can lead directly to infringement or non-infringement on summary judgment, narrow trial issues, drive settlement, and informs jury instructions.
guidance: Parties should consider how constructions affect downstream proceedings and settlement incentives; claim construction often triggers settlement discussions.

name: Parallel administrative proceedings (PTAB/IPR/PGR) and claim construction
description: Post-grant proceedings before the PTAB (IPR/PGR) and ITC matters lack formal Markman hearings but still involve claim interpretation; PTAB and PTO routinely construe disputed terms and their constructions can influence parallel litigation.
guidance: Although evidentiary rules differ, intrinsic evidence remains important in PTAB proceedings; expert declarations are commonly used. Be mindful that PTAB constructions may diverge from district court rulings.

name: Special issues for business method patents and eligibility concerns
description: Business method patents often face heightened risk under 35 U.S.C. §§101 and 112; effective construction in these cases is critical to avoid characterizing the invention as an abstract idea or lacking written description/definiteness.
guidance: PTAB historically interpreted such claims narrowly to avoid eligibility/enablement issues. Although the CBM program is no longer in place, business method patents remain vulnerable in court and IPRs.

name: Coordination of claim construction across forums and with jury instructions
description: Align proposed claim constructions with eventual jury instructions and be mindful of how a district court’s construction may affect appeals, IPRs, and ITC proceedings.
guidance: Consistency helps ensure the jury receives a clear, legally sound framework. Consider cross-forum strategy early, since constructions may influence multiple concurrent proceedings.

name: Eligibility Step 1: statutory category
description: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter?
guidance: Evaluation should be made after determining what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). In the flowchart (MPEP § 2106, subsection III) Step 1 determines whether the claim as a whole falls within one or more statutory categories (Step 1: YES) or does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO).

name: BRI and mixed statutory/non-statutory embodiments
description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 (Step 1: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. It is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, that would narrow the claim to those embodiments that fall within a statutory category.

name: Non-statutory transitory signals example (machine-readable media)
description: Even when a product has a physical or tangible form, it may not fall within a statutory category; a transitory signal does not possess concrete structure that would qualify as a device or part under machine, a manufacture, or a composition of matter.
guidance: Example: machine readable media BRI can encompass propagating electrical or electromagnetic signals. A claim to a computer readable medium that can be a compact disc or a carrier wave covers a non-statutory embodiment and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. See In re Nuijten and Mentor Graphics v. EVE-USA for examples. If a claim is clearly not within the four categories (Step 1: NO), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made; use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)(1)). If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, proceed to analyze the amended claim and recommend amendment where possible.

name: Alice/Mayo framework required (Steps 2A and 2B)
description: After Step 1, claims that fall within a statutory category must be analyzed under the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B) to determine whether they are directed to a judicial exception and, if so, whether they amount to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Preemption concerns are inherent in and resolved by the Alice/Mayo framework. The absence of complete preemption does not by itself make a claim eligible; conversely, a preemptive claim may be ineligible. Use the Alice/Mayo test to evaluate eligibility.

name: Step 2A two-prong inquiry (Prong One)
description: Prong One asks: does the claim recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon?
guidance: Examiners should identify the specific claim limitation(s) that the examiner believes may recite an exception and determine whether those limitations fall within a judicial exception. Distinguish between a claim that 'recites' an exception and one that merely 'involves' an exception. Example: a claim stating 'elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' sets forth a law of nature (recites an exception); a teeter-totter claim merely involves the law of the lever and does not recite the exception.

name: Step 2A two-prong inquiry (Prong Two)
description: Prong Two asks: do additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application?
guidance: If additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, then the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If they do not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis at Step 2B. Mere recitation of an exception triggers Prong One, but integration into a practical application is determined under Prong Two. Additional elements that are merely another judicial exception or do nothing more than recite conventional or generic implementation are insufficient to integrate the exception.

name: Transformation requirement (Alice: 'transform the nature of the claim')
description: For a claim reciting a judicial exception to be eligible, the additional elements must 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception (either at Prong Two or in Step 2B).
guidance: If there are no additional elements beyond the judicial exception, the claim cannot be eligible. After making the appropriate rejection for lack of eligibility, recommend amendment if possible to resolve eligibility of the claim.

name: How to determine if limitation recites an abstract idea
description: Determine (1) the specific claim limitation(s) the examiner believes recite an abstract idea, and (2) whether those limitations fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
guidance: If the limitation falls within a grouping, it is reasonable to conclude the claim recites an abstract idea and requires Prong Two analysis. If the limitation does not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea (barring rare circumstances discussed in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)).

name: Distinguish 'recite' vs 'involve' an exception
description: Claims that 'set forth' or 'describe' an exception recite it and require further eligibility analysis; claims that merely 'involve' an exception may be eligible and not require further eligibility analysis.
guidance: The terms 'set forth' and 'described' indicate two ways an exception can be recited. Examiners should carefully distinguish recitation from mere involvement to avoid improperly treating eligible claims as directed to judicial exceptions. See examples such as Diehr and Mayo (set forth) vs teeter-totter (involves).

name: Mere aggregation/addition of exceptions is insufficient
description: Adding one abstract idea to another, or having additional elements that merely recite another judicial exception, does not render the claim non-abstract or eligible.
guidance: Cited cases: RecogniCorp v. Nintendo (adding math to encoding/decoding insufficient); Genetic Techs. v. Merial (eligibility cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature itself). Examiners should find such claims require further analysis and not treat aggregation as a workaround to eligibility.

name: Software and business-method claims not categorically excluded
description: Software and business methods are not automatically abstract ideas or categorically outside §101's scope; the presence of an underlying mathematical calculation or relationship does not by itself doom the claim to abstraction.
guidance: Use precedent (e.g., Bilski, Thales Visionix, McRO, Enfish) to evaluate whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea or is a patent-eligible application. Examine the claim as a whole under the Alice/Mayo framework.

name: Best practice to recommend amendment where appropriate
description: When a claim fails Step 1 or lacks additional elements beyond an exception, it is a best practice for the examiner to recommend an amendment that would resolve eligibility of the claim, if possible.
guidance: If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category or to integrate the exception into a practical application, proceed with examining such an amended claim and suggest amendments on the record.

name: Particular Treatment and Prophylaxis integration (Step 2A Prong Two)
description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; one way to demonstrate such integration is when the additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Claims that use the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis meaningfully limit the claim by going beyond generally linking the exception to a technological environment and thus are eligible at Step 2A. See Vanda (method of treating patients where dosing depended on genotype) as an example of eligibility. Examples of treatment/prophylaxis include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, immunization steps that lower disease risk (Classen). The limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid to a patient'); mere intended use, prescribing without actual use, or field-of-use language (e.g., 'pharmaceutical composition', 'feed dispenser operable to dispense') do not integrate the exception.

name: Affirmative recitation requirement for treatment/prophylaxis limitations
description: To qualify under the treatment/prophylaxis consideration, the claim must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Positive examples: steps like 'administering amazonic acid to a patient' or 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient' are affirmative. Non-positive examples that fail to integrate the exception include mere intended uses ('prescribing a topical steroid' — does not require actual use) or labels/field-of-use statements ('pharmaceutical composition', 'feed dispenser operable to dispense a mineral supplement').

name: Search for an inventive concept (Step 2B)
description: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature (or natural phenomenon or abstract idea) itself; it is furnished by additional element(s) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception that ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
guidance: The search for an inventive concept asks what else is in the claims beyond the exception. Courts and MPEP instruct that an inventive concept must be an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception. See Alice, Genetic Technologies, RecogniCorp. The presence of additional elements must be evaluated to determine whether they constitute significantly more than the judicial exception.

name: Consideration: Adding specific limitations or unconventional arrangements
description: Adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: BASCOM — a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known components (installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable filtering features) constituted significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

name: Limitations that are insufficient to constitute significantly more
description: Certain types of additions to a claim have been found to be insufficient to qualify as an inventive concept.
guidance: Examples identified by the courts include: (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality (generic computer functions); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity (mere data gathering) (CyberSource); and (iv) generally linking the abstract idea to a particular technological environment or field-of-use (Bilski, Parker v. Flook). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f)-(h).

name: Tangibility/physicality of additional elements is not determinative
description: Mere physical or tangible implementation of an exception is not, by itself, an inventive concept; conversely, non-physical or intangible elements are not automatically disqualifying.
guidance: The fact that a computer is a tangible machine is 'beside the point' if the claimed computer performs only conventional, generic functions (Alice). Physical steps alone (e.g., DNA amplification/analysis) do not necessarily provide sufficient inventive concept (Genetic Technologies). Conversely, improvements not defined by reference to physical components can still be eligible (Enfish; McRO — intangible result that improved technological process). Consider the substance and how elements operate together, not mere physicality.

name: How courts apply the second-part analysis in practice
description: Courts identify additional claim elements, evaluate them individually for whether they are well-understood/routine/conventional, and then evaluate them as an ordered combination to determine if the combination yields significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Alice: Court identified additional elements (computer functions/hardware), found each was well-understood/routine/conventional, and determined that the ordered combination added nothing significantly more. BASCOM: district court recognized additional elements as generic when viewed individually, but the Federal Circuit emphasized the need to assess the combination, which produced an inventive concept in that arrangement. Use these steps as a template for Step 2B analysis (identify additional elements, analyze individually, analyze in combination).

name: Claims quality: independent/dependent structure, hierarchical organization, and comprehensive coverage
description: Claims should include robust independent claims defining system and method, dependent claims elaborating specific features, and a well-organized hierarchical structure ensuring clear coverage of technical aspects.
guidance: High-quality claims provide legal robustness and technical applicability (e.g., cover regenerative braking, load balancing, mode transitions); omissions of detailed scenarios weaken legal defensibility as shown in case study.

name: Jurisdictional compliance and adaptability
description: Generated patent text must comply with jurisdictional variations in patent laws and drafting conventions (claim structure, count restrictions, procedural norms).
guidance: Because training data were primarily USPTO patents, evaluation should check for regional legal requirements (EPO, JPO, CNIPA, etc.); authors recommend retrieval-augmented generation, jurisdiction-specific prompts, and cross-jurisdictional datasets to ensure compliance.

name: Specification Lexicography Beats Claim Construction Surprises
description: The Federal Circuit repeatedly defers to explicit definitions in the specification.
guidance: Drafting implication: For any claim term whose ordinary meaning may not capture your intended scope, define it explicitly. Use clear definitional language such as 'As used herein, X means Y.' Relying on explicit spec lexicography reduces the risk of unexpected claim constructions.

name: Disclaimers Must Be Clear and Unmistakable
description: Statements in the specification or during prosecution can disclaim claim scope only if they are clear and unmistakable; vague characterizations of prior art are usually not disclaimers.
guidance: Examples of disclaimers: statements like 'the invention requires X' or 'in contrast to prior art Y, the invention does not include Y' can operate as disclaimers. Drafting implication: avoid language that could be read as an explicit disclaimer of claim scope; be cautious in characterizing prior art or describing preferred embodiments so as not to unintentionally narrow claims.

name: Method Claims Need Single-Actor Architecture
description: Direct infringement of a method claim by multiple actors requires proof of direction or control or a joint enterprise (Akamai line of cases).
guidance: Drafting implication: where possible, draft method claims so that a single actor performs all steps. If multiple actors are unavoidable, structure the claims or the specification to show one party directing/controlling the others (e.g., through instruction, contractual relationship, or agent/principal language) to support liability for divided performance.

name: Functional Language Without Structure Triggers 112(f)
description: Claim terms like 'module configured to,' 'mechanism for,' 'system that performs' without structural anchoring may be construed as means-plus-function under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (Williamson).
guidance: Drafting implication: Use concrete structural terminology (processor, circuit, memory, sensor, database, etc.) and supply corresponding structure in the specification to avoid §112(f) treatment. When using functional phrasing, provide clear structural examples or algorithms in the spec as corresponding structure.

name: Eligibility Survives With Concrete Technical Improvement
description: Post-Alice, claims are more likely patent-eligible when they recite specific technical mechanisms tied to a concrete improvement in computer functioning (cases such as Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory).
guidance: Drafting implication: For software-related inventions, anchor the specification and claims in a specific technical improvement (e.g., reduced latency, improved memory utilization, a novel data structure, enhanced signal processing), rather than framing the invention as merely solving a business problem or performing generic computer tasks.

name: Written Description for Genus Claims
description: For genus claims in unpredictable arts (e.g., biotechnology, chemistry), Amgen v. Sanofi and Ariad require disclosure of representative species and a unifying structure or common feature to satisfy written description.
guidance: Drafting implication: Disclose multiple representative species and identify the common structural or functional features that unify the genus. Provide examples, experimental results, or other evidence showing possession of the claimed genus across embodiments to support broad claims in unpredictable fields.

name: Negative Limitations Need Spec Support
description: Negative claim limitations (for example, 'wherein the device is free of X') require explicit specification support that the excluded feature is or may be omitted (Santarus v. Par).
guidance: Drafting implication: If you intend to claim the absence of a feature, explicitly state in the specification that the feature can be omitted and describe embodiments or rationale for excluding it; do not rely on mere silence or implication to support negative limitations.

name: Range Claims Need Range Disclosure
description: Claimed ranges should be supported by specification disclosure of the range or at least the endpoints (In re Wertheim and progeny).
guidance: Drafting implication: Disclose multiple ranges and endpoints in the specification, and provide examples or data where appropriate to support claimed numerical ranges. Consider describing preferred sub-ranges and how endpoints were chosen to reduce indefiniteness or lack-of-support issues.

name: Weight and character of a prior adjudication as foundation
description: An adjudication in another case must result from a regular hearing in equity or trial at law to furnish a suitable foundation for an injunction; interlocutory decrees may be as effective as final decrees for this purpose.
guidance: Equity adjudications raise a stronger presumption than law trials. Prior adjudication of one claim may support an injunction as to a narrower claim specifying the same invention, but a prior adjudication of an original patent cannot be used to support injunctions for new claims in a reissue.

name: Inventive step / Obviousness assessment
description: Determine whether the invention involves an inventive step by comparing the claimed invention with cited prior art and common general technical knowledge to see if a person skilled in the art could easily derive the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Identify distinguishing features, assess whether substitution/combination with known techniques would be obvious, consider whether expected effects are predictable, and look for obstructive factors; conclude 'involves an inventive step' when differences are non-obvious and produce significant unexpected technical effects.

name: Identify differences between claim and cited art
description: The first step is to identify the point(s) of difference (distinguishing features) between the claimed invention and the cited document(s).
guidance: Explicitly list differing claim elements (e.g., neural network vs regression model; inclusion of certain input variables); base subsequent assessment on these identified differences.

name: Determination of the technical problem actually solved
description: Clarify the technical problem that the invention actually solves as a basis for inventive-step analysis.
guidance: Frame the problem in technical terms (e.g., improving inference accuracy in semantic search) and use it to evaluate whether prior art would have motivated the claimed solution.

name: Combination of cited documents plus common knowledge to show obviousness
description: An invention may be considered obvious if the combination of prior documents and common general technical knowledge would lead a skilled person to the claimed solution.
guidance: Explicitly demonstrate how each element of the claim is disclosed or suggested by the combination; show that no obstructive factor exists and that the expected effect would have been foreseen.

name: Implementation by software/hardware cooperation as evidence of technical subject matter
description: Showing that a claimed method establishes a mathematical model and is implemented concretely by cooperating software and hardware supports finding that it is a technical invention.
guidance: Demonstrate concrete implementation details (software using hardware resources) rather than mere abstract algorithms to support patentable technical character.

name: Principles for Scriptural and Patristic argumentation
description: Scriptural passages must be interpreted in context (e.g., Romans IX is obscure and not an unambiguous locus classicus for absolute predestination); Patristic evidence is mixed (Greek Fathers favor hypothetical predestination; Augustine is contested and claimed by both sides).
guidance: Doctrinal claims about predestination should not press ambiguous texts beyond their context, and must weigh Patristic testimony critically; neither Scripture nor Tradition yields conclusive proof for all disputed theories, so balanced exposition is required.

name: Use of post-published data in inventive step assessment
description: Post-published data (data not present in the application as filed) can be taken into account in the assessment of inventive step only if the skilled person, having common general knowledge and based on the application as originally filed, can derive that the effect is encompassed by the technical teaching and embodied by the same originally disclosed invention.
guidance: Guidelines updated (Part E-IV, 4.1; Part G-VII, 5.2; Part G-VII, 11) to reflect G 2/21. The EBA confirmed post-published data may be considered, but further practical guidance is limited and applicants will have to rely on later case law for clarification. Practitioners should ensure the application as filed plausibly and directly supports the claimed technical effect such that post-published data only confirms what is already derivable from the original disclosure.

name: Sufficiency requirements for AI/ML inventions — disclosure of training-data characteristics
description: Generally there is no need to disclose a specific training dataset itself, but if the technical effect relied upon depends on particular characteristics of a training dataset, those characteristics required to reproduce the technical effect must be disclosed unless the skilled person can determine them without undue burden using common general knowledge.
guidance: Part G-II, 3.3.1 updated. For AI/ML inventions, assess whether claimed technical effects hinge on dataset-specific features; if so, include sufficient detail about those characteristics in the disclosure or provide a path for the skilled person to reproduce the effect without undue burden.

name: Panel review: composition and scope
description: A panel review is conducted at each stage of the examiner's examination in an ex parte reexamination proceeding (except for notices of informality or incomplete response), to review the examiner's preliminary decision to reject and/or allow claims.
guidance: Panel make-up: three or more members including a manager, the examiner in charge, and a third member selected by the manager; conferees should be primary examiners knowledgeable in the technology or experienced in reexamination practice. The majority of conferees should not have been involved in the original examination. An 'original' examiner should only be chosen as a conferee if they are the most knowledgeable or there is a specific justifiable reason.

name: Standards for entry of amendments after final rejection
description: An amendment filed after final rejection and prior to the appeal brief requires a showing under 37 CFR 1.116(b) if it touches the merits of the patent under reexamination; certain limited amendments may be entered without such a showing.
guidance: Amendments that merely cancel claims, adopt examiner's suggestions, remove issues for appeal, or otherwise require only a cursory review by the examiner may be excepted. The first proposed amendment after final action will be given sufficient consideration to determine whether it places all claims in patentable condition or reduces/simplifies issues on appeal. If a proposed amendment is not entered in its entirety, the examiner will briefly explain reasons for not entering it (e.g., it presents a new issue requiring further search). The patent owner should be notified if parts of an amendment would be entered if submitted separately.

name: Requirements and formatting for the appeal brief in reexamination
description: Appeal briefs must comply with 37 CFR 41.37 and applicable MPEP instructions: include authorities and arguments, a summary of claimed subject matter with references to specification pages/lines and drawings, copies of the claims involved, and required fees.
guidance: A fee as set in 37 CFR 41.20(b)(2) is required for the first filing of an appeal brief. Only one copy of the brief is required. The copy of the claims should be double spaced and start on a new page; claims on appeal in reexamination must include all underlining and bracketing required by 37 CFR 1.530(f) to reflect changes during prosecution. Any new claims added during reexamination should be completely underlined (departure from MPEP § 1205.02 for applications). The brief should indicate the art unit and reexamination control number. Briefs must be responsive to every ground of rejection; a reply brief, if filed, shall be entered, but amendments/affidavits/evidence remain subject to 37 CFR 1.116 and 41.33. The Board expects briefs to fully state the appellant's position so no search of the record is required to determine that position.

name: Handling of defective appeal briefs and the division of responsibilities between Board and examiner
description: Since May 25, 2010, the Board has sole responsibility for determining compliance of appeal briefs with 37 CFR 41.37 and will complete that determination before forwarding the brief to the examiner; examiners are no longer to hold briefs defective.
guidance: If the Board determines a brief is non-compliant, the Board will notify appellant to file a corrected brief within the time set to avoid dismissal. Examiners should report serious defects that prevent drafting an examiner's answer to the Director of CRU, who will communicate with the Board if appropriate. Once the Board accepts a brief as compliant, it will not later be held defective by CRU or the examiner. Examiners are not required to determine whether fewer than all rejected claims are identified as appealed; the examiner should treat all pending rejected claims as being on appeal and maintain rejections unless overcome. A distinction is drawn between lack of any argument (which may justify summary sustainment of the rejection) and arguments that carry no conviction (which lead to a decision on the merits). Appellant must traverse every ground of rejection presented for review; oral argument will not remedy failure to traverse a ground.

name: Patent-eligibility under Section 101 (Mayo/Alice test)
description: The Court applied the patent-eligibility test described in Mayo v. Prometheus (2012) and concluded that: (1) Alice’s patent claims are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas; and (2) implementing those ideas on a computer was not sufficient to transform them into patent-eligible inventions.
guidance: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea it is ineligible for patent protection under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Review claim scope to determine whether it is 'directed to' an abstract idea and whether any additional elements transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter under Mayo/Alice.

name: Do not rely on mere computer implementation to make an abstract idea patentable
description: Implementing abstract ideas 'on a computer' is not sufficient to transform them into patent-eligible inventions.
guidance: Avoid drafting claims that simply add generic computer functions to conventional abstract concepts. The Alice decision invalidated patents that attempted to gain protection over abstract ideas merely by adding a computer to perform generic computer functions.

name: Claims must recite more than routine or conventional activity (avoid 'egregious' abstract-software claims)
description: The invalidated patents in Alice were commonly regarded as relatively egregious examples of trying to use the patent system to gain protection over abstract ideas merely by adding a computer to perform generic computer functions.
guidance: Emphasize specific, non-abstract technical improvements, inventive concept, or concrete practical applications in claims and specification rather than high-level business concepts or routine data-processing steps. Use claim language that shows how the invention improves computer/technical operation where possible.

name: Business methods and software can still be patentable if they meet the Supreme Court's test
description: Post-Alice, it is still possible to obtain a patent on business methods (or, more broadly, software), provided that the claimed invention meets the Supreme Court’s patent-eligibility test.
guidance: When evaluating or drafting software/business-method inventions, apply the Mayo/Alice framework to demonstrate that claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter — e.g., show an inventive concept or technical solution beyond an abstract idea plus generic computer implementation.

name: Consult USPTO post-Alice examiner guidance
description: In response to Alice, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has issued additional guidelines to its patent examiners (link provided).
guidance: Review the USPTO guidance (http://www.uspto.gov/patents/announce/alice_pec_25jun2014.pdf) to understand how examiners are instructed to apply the Alice/Mayo framework in practice and to align claim drafting and prosecution strategy with examiner expectations.

name: Consider alternative IP protection such as copyright for software
description: Intellectual property owners may continue to rely on copyright law to protect, license and enforce similar business methods so long as the underlying software code contains sufficient copyrightable expression.
guidance: If patent protection is unlikely (e.g., claims deemed abstract), evaluate whether the implementation's source code, user interface, or expressive elements qualify for copyright protection and whether licensing, trade secret, or other strategies are appropriate.

name: Consistent application of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a)
description: Section 112 applies to all industries and inventions; USPTO trains examiners to apply Section 112 to all industries and does not instruct examiners to apply §112(a) more rigorously for some industries than others.
guidance: There is more judicial precedent applying §112(a) in life sciences than computer technologies; to ensure consistency USPTO delivered targeted §112 training in FY2019 in areas perceived as treated less rigorously and is exploring additional guidance and training to raise examiner awareness on proper application of §112(a). The USPTO also issued January 2019 guidance addressing written description and enablement issues under §112(a), especially for computer-implemented functional claims that recite only a solution or outcome without reciting how the solution is accomplished. The USPTO will monitor effects of guidance and consider additional guidance if needed.

name: Allocation of examination time tailored to application attributes
description: Examination time is adjusted and should be tailored to specific attributes of an application so examiners have adequate time to apply patent statutes.
guidance: Since October 2019, examiners receive additional time based on attributes including overall number of claims, length of the specification, and number of pages in any filed information disclosure statements; examiners with least time also received increases. USPTO plans further time increases and an updated automatic assignment process (classification 'picture' and examiner workload/experience) to match applications to the examiner best suited to examine them. USPTO will continue to monitor examining time to ensure appropriateness and that pendency goals are met.

name: Rigorous application of Sections 102 and 103 (novelty/obviousness)
description: Examiners should properly interpret claim scope, perform high-quality prior art searches, evaluate and analyze relevant prior art, apply it to claims when appropriate, and clearly convey patentability determinations in office actions.
guidance: USPTO provides training on claim interpretation; principles of §§112, 102, 103; legal argument analysis; proper prior art searching techniques; and discipline-specific databases including non-patent literature. Additional initiatives include more examination time, improved workload assignments, enhanced prior-art resources, and more comprehensive patent quality reviews.

name: Clarity of office actions
description: Office actions should be clear in articulating statutory rejections, meanings of claim terms or claim scope, and reasons for allowances so rejections are understandable.
guidance: USPTO updated its office action review form to measure multiple components of clarity and will use the updated form to capture not only non-compliance but also specific reasons (correctness or clarity concerns). The new performance appraisal plan provides a roadmap emphasizing clarity; OPQA reviewers now also provide positive recognition for best practices in correctness and clarity.

name: Performance Appraisal Plan (PAP) emphasizing search, compact prosecution, and clarity
description: Examiners' performance ratings will be partly based on exemplary practices that demonstrate comprehensive searching, compact prosecution, and clarity in the written record.
guidance: Exemplary activities for comprehensive search include: searching the inventive concept as defined at the time of first action on the merits; citing prior art pertinent to significant though unclaimed features or the state of the art; and providing brief descriptions in office actions for relevant prior art cited but not applied. For compact prosecution and clarity, exemplary activities include providing annotations showing where claim limitations are met by prior art, providing proper reasons for allowance, and suggesting ways for applicants to overcome rejections. The new PAP was planned for implementation in FY2021 and includes more detail (pages 7–8 of PAP).

name: Patent Quality Team activities and examiner training programs
description: Dedicated quality teams and programs should drive continuous improvement through training, assessment, and recognition of best practices.
guidance: The Patent Quality Team has engaged in examiner training (entry-level and refresher), guidance on subject-matter eligibility, restriction practice, interviews, §112 and claim interpretation, examiner trainer development, NPL search training, peer search collaboration pilot, Patent Examiner Technical Training Program (PETTP), Site Experience Education (SEE), STEPP, virtual instructor-led trainings (VILT), patent quality chats, semi-annual Patent Quality Surveys, a customer experience team, updating the master review form (MRF), an accolades program, PTAB Case Study on AIA trials, and the OPQA search feedback pilot. USPTO will continue integrating Office of Patent Quality work with the broader Patents organization.

name: Use of Global Dossier and international work-sharing to improve efficiency and examination quality
description: Leverage file histories and search/results from other major IP offices to create a more complete patent record and improve examination quality and efficiency.
guidance: Global Dossier provides single-point access to related applications across IP5 offices; Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) enables fast-track examination where claims are allowed by another office; Collaborative Search Pilot (CSP) provides multi-office search results early in examination; PCT Collaborative Search & Examination (PCT CS&E) allows IP5 collaboration to produce an ISR and written opinion with contributions from participating offices.

name: Burden allocation and examiner assistance in AIA motions to amend
description: Rulemaking to allocate burdens of persuasion on motions to amend in AIA trials, with the Board evaluating statutory/regulatory requirements and whether petitioners have shown unpatentability.
guidance: USPTO issued an NPRM allocating burdens to petitioners based on Federal Circuit decisions and public comments; Board may exercise discretion to reach determinations when appropriate. Under pilot programs, if a petitioner ceases participation, the Board may solicit examiner assistance to prepare advisory reports addressing patentability of proposed substitute claims based on prior art provided or found by the examiner.

name: Field-of-use / technological-environment limitations generally insufficient
description: Limitations that merely specify a technological environment or field of use (e.g., execution on a generic computer, use within a telephone network or the Internet, data related to a particular domain like the power grid, or implementing budgeting/advertising on the Internet) do not meaningfully limit an abstract idea and therefore typically do not render the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Provide an explanation in a rejection why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim. Examples: Flook (industry-limited math), FairWarning v. Iatric (computer execution), Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec (telephone/Internet), Electric Power Group (power-grid data), Genetic Techs. Ltd. v. Merial (informing doctors to apply law of nature), Ultramercial (advertising on Internet), buySAFE v. Google (computer/network use). Note: courts often use “technological environment” and “field of use” interchangeably. Consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP §2106.05(g)).

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) for self-evident eligibility
description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., the claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality), but the result must be the same as the full Alice/Mayo analysis.
guidance: Only use when eligibility is clear; if there is doubt whether the claim seeks coverage of a judicial exception, perform the full analysis. The streamlined analysis is not a way to avoid findings of ineligibility. The record may simply reflect eligibility by absence of a 101 rejection or by clarifying remarks.

name: Eligibility is self-evident (Pathway A) — criteria and examples
description: Claims that, when viewed as a whole, clearly do not tie up any judicial exception or clearly improve technology/computer functionality may be eligible without a full analysis.
guidance: Examples include a complex manufactured industrial product or process with meaningful limitations, a robotic arm assembly with control system using mathematical relationships (not attempting to tie up the math), or a product that includes incidental nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with gold contact). Such claims do not require a markedly different characteristics analysis for product-of-nature issues.

name: Clear improvement to technology/computer functionality avoids full analysis
description: Claims that are directed to clear improvements to computer-related technology or functionality (i.e., not abstract when appropriately claimed) may avoid full Alice/Mayo analysis and be found eligible.
guidance: Cite Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization/animation) as examples. If a claim is a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM filtering content), perform the full analysis. It may be reasonable for an examiner to find such claims eligible at Pathway A or at Step 2A/2B depending on facts.

name: Base eligibility rejections on substantive law and precedent; explain prima facie case
description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent and must set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility so the applicant has sufficient notice and can effectively respond.
guidance: Review the substantive law in MPEP §§2106.03–2106.06. The examiner's initial burden is to clearly and specifically explain why a claim is ineligible. Even if relying on training or examples, those do not themselves constitute the legal basis for a rejection—cite substantive precedent and reasoned rationale.

name: Evaluate eligibility on a claim-by-claim basis and review the entire record
description: Determine eligibility for each claim separately by reviewing the specification, claims, prosecution history, and relevant case law or prior art before concluding whether the claimed invention is patent eligible.
guidance: Dependent claims may be eligible even if an independent claim is ineligible (they may add limitations that integrate the exception). Conversely, dependent claims can be ineligible if they add judicial exceptions without integrating them. Consider each claim on its own merits.

name: Identify additional claim elements and explain why they do not integrate the exception or add significantly more (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B)
description: After identifying the judicial exception, the rejection must identify claim features/limitations beyond the exception and explain why these additional elements, individually and in combination, do not integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.
guidance: Address elements both individually and as a combination. Remember that a new combination of known steps may be patent eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Explain the rationale supporting the conclusion so the applicant can respond. See MPEP §2106.05 for detailed considerations.

name: Support assertions that elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (Step 2B) with specified evidence
description: If asserting that particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, or conventional in the relevant field (a Step 2B factual finding), the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one or more of the prescribed evidentiary bases.
guidance: Permitted supports: (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or a prosecution statement showing the element is well-understood/routine/conventional; (B) citation to one or more court decisions that note the conventional nature of the element(s) (ensure claim language and level of generality match); (C) citation to a publication (book, manual, review article) demonstrating the element is well-known and in common use. A specification's silence alone is insufficient to establish conventionality.

name: Generic computer components/functions at high level often insufficient to add 'significantly more'
description: Claim limitations that recite generic computer components performing generic computer functions at a high level (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) typically do not meaningfully limit an abstract idea and thus do not add significantly more.
guidance: Explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim. However, courts have found combinations of generic components to perform non-generic functions and thereby be significantly more (DDR Holdings). See MPEP §§2106.05(f) and 2106.05(d) for more on generic computing functions and well-understood/routine elements.

name: Address insignificant extra-solution activity and Flook/Parker restrictions
description: Extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) or limitations that only generally link the judicial exception to a technological environment are often 'insignificant' and do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Explain why the extra-solution activity or field-of-use limitation does not integrate the exception or add significantly more. Examples: adding storing data to a process of computing a mathematical area; limiting a mathematical formula to particular industries (Flook). See MPEP §§2106.05(g) and 2106.05(h).

name: When issuing a rejection, suggest claim amendments from the specification when appropriate
