description: If a rejection is made, it is best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and identify those elements in the Office action.
guidance: Identify specific specification elements and suggest them as ways to overcome the rejection, thereby clarifying possible paths for applicant amendment.

name: Compact prosecution: perform and state complete examination under other patentability statutes
description: Regardless of a 35 U.S.C. §101 rejection, examiners should perform a complete examination of every claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting, and non-statutory double patenting) and state all non-cumulative reasons for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
guidance: State all non-cumulative rejections and bases in the first Office action to support compact prosecution and provide the applicant with a complete picture of patentability issues.

name: No attempt in original bars inclusion in re-issue
description: If no attempt was made to secure the invention by the original patent, it cannot be embraced in a re-issue.
guidance: Where the original specification/drawings/model show no effort to claim an invention, the re-issue cannot legitimately expand to cover that matter (cases: Hoskin v. Fisher, Marsh v. Seymour referenced).

name: Re-issue cannot claim a different or broader invention
description: A re-issue cannot claim either another invention or a broader invention than the one attempted to be described and claimed in the original patent.
guidance: Claims in a re-issue that enlarge the invention beyond what was attempted in the original are invalid; compare original and re-issue instruments to determine scope.

name: Original specification/drawings/model are primary test
description: The original specification, as illustrated by the model or drawings if any, and as interpreted by proper explanation and examination, must bear upon its face sufficient evidence of the alleged endeavor to describe and claim.
guidance: The Office and courts rely primarily on the original patent instruments to determine what the inventor attempted to claim; extrinsic assertions are subordinate.

name: If original description is complete, extrinsic inquiry unnecessary
description: Where the description of the original patent is complete and accurate, and the fault resides only in an obscure, too restricted, or excessive claim, the original description becomes the standard and exterior evidence or examination of the actual invention is unnecessary.
guidance: In such cases the Patent Office/courts should judge and correct claim imperfections by reference to the original specification/drawings/model alone.

name: Apply Graham factual inquiries and make appropriate factual findings
description: Determination of obviousness is dependent on the facts of each case and requires appropriate factual findings as explained in MPEP § 2141 and § 2143 (i.e., scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims, level of ordinary skill, and secondary considerations).
guidance: Office personnel must make factual findings necessary to explain a conclusion of obviousness and analyze those findings to link them to the legal conclusion. If factual findings required by the Graham inquiries cannot be made, the chosen rationale cannot support obviousness.

name: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
description: To reject a claim on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate (1)–(4):
guidance: (1) a finding that the prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element in combination performs the same function as separately; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that the combination's results were predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot be used. Example: Anderson’s-Black Rock shows combining known elements yielding predictable results; counterexample Adams shows that predictable results requirement is essential and that teaching away can render combination nonobvious.

name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results
description: If a known device is ready for improvement, applying a known technique to it such that the results are predictable can support obviousness.
guidance: Must show the device was 'ready for improvement' and that applying the technique would predictably produce the claimed results. Provide factual findings linking prior art to the claimed invention.

name: Predictability requirement and effect of teaching away
description: Combining known prior art elements is insufficient to render a claimed invention obvious if the results would not have been predictable to one of ordinary skill; prior art that teaches away from a combination increases likelihood of nonobviousness.
guidance: Example: United States v. Adams — although elements were known, prior art taught away and successful combination was nonobvious. Examiners must identify and evaluate any teachings away and cannot ignore teachings that would have deterred combination.

name: Element-granularity choice (coarse vs. fine)
description: The claim construer’s choice of element granularity (coarse parsing into few multi-word elements vs. fine parsing into many single-word/short-phrase elements) decisively affects claim scope: coarse parsing yields broader doctrine-of-equivalents reach and broader literal scope; fine parsing yields narrower literal scope and more opportunities to defeat equivalence.
guidance: There is no neutral or correct granularity; the choice depends on the construer’s purposes. Drafting is strategic: broad elements increase DOE reach but raise indefiniteness and 112(f) risks; narrow elements reduce DOE reach but support defensible literal scope.

name: Explicit element boundaries
description: Are the element boundaries marked explicitly (commas, structural separators, 'comprising' introduction)?
guidance: Use punctuation and structural markers in claim language to make element boundaries explicit. Clear boundaries reduce claim-construction uncertainty and limit unexpected parsing variations during Markman.

name: Specification vocabulary maps to claim elements
description: Does the specification consistently use vocabulary that maps to claim elements?
guidance: Consistent, element-defining vocabulary in the specification supports a predictable mapping from claim language to disclosed structure/function. Inconsistent or varied terminology invites divergent constructions.

name: Working/examples illustrating each element
description: Are there working examples illustrating each claim element?
guidance: Provide examples in the specification that demonstrate and instantiate claimed elements; examples help courts identify element boundaries and support desired granularity in claim construction.

name: Dependent claims reinforce independent claim parsing
description: Are dependent claims structured to reinforce (not contradict) the independent claim's element parsing?
guidance: Draft dependent claims so they clarify and narrow elements in ways consistent with the independent claim’s element boundaries; avoid dependent claims that imply alternate parsing or combine/disaggregate elements in conflicting ways.

name: Use of bracketed/numbered limitations
description: Use of bracketed/numbered limitations in claim language to increase notice-quality.
guidance: Bracketed or numbered limitations make element boundaries visually and structurally clear, aiding notice to competitors and promoting predictable claim construction.

name: Defined claim terms for novel or coined vocabulary
description: Are novel or coined claim terms expressly defined in the specification?
guidance: Defining novel or coined terms in the specification reduces ambiguity and prevents later parties from pressing conflicting constructions that alter element granularity or scope.

name: Operative element-definition test (five-point checklist)
description: A five-question operative test to assess element-definition quality: (1) Are element boundaries marked explicitly? (2) Does the specification consistently use vocabulary mapping to claim elements? (3) Are there working examples illustrating each element? (4) Does the prosecution history reflect a consistent element granularity? (5) Are dependent claims structured to reinforce the independent claim's element parsing?
guidance: Patents passing all five tests have predictable claim construction; failing them increases Markman risk. Use this checklist to evaluate issued patents or to guide drafting and prosecution.

name: Summarization: conciseness and informativeness tailored to audience
description: Patent summarization aims to create concise and informative summaries of patent documents that extract the most important information (e.g., claims, background, detailed descriptions) and paraphrase in more accessible language depending on the target audience (examiners, researchers, engineers, legal professionals).
guidance: Summaries should condense key aspects while remaining informative for the intended reader; choose level of technicality according to audience needs. Ensure essential legal/technical content (claims and their scope) is represented rather than only generic overview.

name: Extractive summarization: preservation of original wording and context
description: Extractive methods select key phrases or sentences verbatim from the patent text to retain the most significant and representative parts without altering wording.
guidance: Pros: simpler implementation and preserves original terminology and precise legal phrasing. Cons/anti-patterns: can be disjointed and lack coherence; may fail when crucial information is implicit (not explicitly stated); can inherit the incomprehensibility of terse claim language.

name: Formatting-based simplification: claim trees and feature segmentation
description: Formatting methods improve accessibility by structuring claims into trees (dependencies), splitting claims into features, and visually representing which features are added by each claim; within-claim segmentation into preamble, transitional phrase, and body is recommended.
guidance: Use explicit claim references and linguistic analysis to build dependency graphs; segment claims into preamble/transitional/body to clarify structure. Visualizations (claim trees, feature highlighting) increase readability without modifying original texts.

name: Patent writing: legal precision, specificity, and section-aware generation
description: Automated patent writing involves generating sections (title, abstract, claims, description) while meeting linguistic, technical, and legal complexities—language must be formal, unambiguous, precise, and adhere to office requirements.
guidance: Avoid relying solely on titles or abstracts for claim generation (titles are too short; abstracts are often generic). Prefer description-based generation for claim drafting because descriptions contain detailed embodiments. Always plan for human revision to meet examination standards.

name: Evaluation criteria for generated patent text: completeness, clarity, logical linkage
description: Quality of generated patent claims/text should be judged on completeness of claimed features, conceptual clarity, and logical linkage between description and claims.
guidance: Fine-tuning models can improve completeness and clarity, but outputs typically require comprehensive human revision to pass legal scrutiny. Include checks for consistency with disclosed embodiments and formal claim structure.

name: Evaluation metrics for patent text generation: domain-specific metrics required
description: Existing general-purpose text evaluation metrics may be inappropriate for patent texts because patents have specific legal and linguistic requirements.
guidance: Develop and adopt evaluation metrics that measure legal fidelity, terminological accuracy, claim completeness, and non-misleading paraphrase rather than relying solely on BLEU/ROUGE-type measures.

name: Requirement to front-load evidence and tie challenges to specific claims
description: Elevated institution thresholds require challengers to 'front load' their case and tie challenges to particular validity arguments against particular claims to prevent expansion of issues after institution.
guidance: This prevents 'mushrooming' of challenges into additional arguments or other claims after review is instituted.

name: Factors USPTO will consider in joinder timing and allowance
description: When deciding whether and when to allow joinder, the USPTO will consider: differences in accused products/processes; breadth or unusualness of claim scope alleged (especially if alleged later); claim-construction rulings substantially different from the first petition’s interpretation; large numbers of patents or claims at issue; consent of the patent owner; court requests; requests by first petitioner for termination; and offers to pay the patent owner’s costs.
guidance: The Office intends to encourage early requests for joinder and discourage late requests; time limits for joinder are set pursuant to statutory provisions (e.g., 35 U.S.C. §316(a)(5)).

name: Special authority required for certain acts (limits of general POA)
description: A representative (except a patent administrator of an overseas resident) cannot perform certain acts unless given special authority: converting/abandonment/withdrawal of an application, abandonment of a patent right, withdrawal of a patent application, withdrawal of request or Domestic Priority under Article 55(1), petition for trial or designation of subagent under Article 132(3), and related special acts.
guidance: Wording ‘all matters regarding the application’ does not include these special authorities by default. The special authority must be expressly stated (examples shown for priority claims and prior application identification).

name: Invalidity (definition)
description: If a patent or any of its claims do not comply with prerequisites in 35 U.S.C., the patent or its claims are invalid.
guidance: PTAB does not presume validity; petitioner bears a lower burden (preponderance) than in district court (clear and convincing). See Standard of Proof entries.

name: Obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103 and Graham factors)
description: A patent may not issue if claimed invention differences from prior art make the claimed invention obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art. Courts consider Graham factors when determining Obviousness.

name: Ordinary and Customary Meaning / Plain Meaning (claim construction)
description: Claim terms are given the meaning they would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, based on the entire record (intrinsic and extrinsic evidence).
guidance: Includes patent claims, specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence like dictionaries and expert reports.

name: Patent Prosecution (definition)
description: Process of applying for a patent: drafting, filing, communicating with PTO examiner, and potentially amending claims to establish patentability.
guidance: Distinct from patent litigation and PTAB Proceedings, which occur after prosecution and issuance.

name: Petition, Content of (statutory and regulatory requirements)
description: Statutory: (1) identify all Real Parties-in-Interest, (2) identify all challenged claims and all Grounds of Invalidity, (3) provide copies of Evidence relied upon, and (4) pay filing fee. 35 U.S.C. § 312.
guidance: Regulatory: (1) identify grounds for standing, (2) propose Claim Construction for each challenged claim, (3) specifically explain Grounds of Invalidity, and (4) specifically explain relevance of Evidence relied upon. 37 C.F.R. § 42.22(a)(2). IPR petitions must also set forth grounds for standing and provide precise identification of relief requested for each challenged claim and supporting exhibits. 37 C.F.R. § 42.104.

name: Petition Formatting (font, margins, spacing, page size)
description: Submissions must use page size 8.5 x 11 inches except exhibits requiring larger size. Markings must be black or equivalent high-contrast; fonts must be proportional 14-point or monospaced no more than 4 characters/cm; double spacing used except certain items; margins at least 2.5 cm (1 inch). 37 C.F.R. § 42.6.
guidance: See specific exemptions for claim charts, headings, tables of contents, tables of authorities, indices, signature blocks and certificates of service.

name: Post-Grant Review (PGR) scope and timing
description: PTAB Proceeding to request cancelling claims on Grounds including Novelty, Obviousness, Written Description, Enablement, Indefiniteness and Patentable Subject Matter. All prior art available including Prior Sale and Prior Use.
guidance: Petition for PGR not instituted if Petitioner previously filed declaratory judgment challenging patent validity. PGR only for first-to-file patents within nine months after issuance. 35 U.S.C. § 321(b); 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.201-42.204.

name: Primary and Secondary References (for combining prior art)
description: Primary Reference: discloses many claim elements and may be combined with Secondary Reference(s) to show Obviousness. Secondary Reference(s): disclose other claim elements to be combined with Primary Reference.
guidance: Use when alleging combination grounds; see Motivation to Combine guidance to avoid hindsight.

name: Priority (effective filing date)
description: Date on which inventor established a right to patent — generally effective filing date; in multijurisdictional filings, applicant may claim priority within 12 months under WIPO conventions.
guidance: Affects novelty and prior art determinations.

name: Secondary Reference (prior art combination)
description: Reference(s) that disclose other claim elements to be combined with a Primary Reference to show Obviousness.
guidance: Identifies role of multiple references in combination arguments.

name: Substitute Claim (requirements for motion to amend)
description: Claim proposed by Patent Owner to replace original claims via Motion to Amend; may propose one Substitute Claim per original claim intended to be amended and must be traceable to an original patent claim at issue.
guidance: Substitute Claims considered only if original replaced claim is determined unpatentable or cancelled. Proposed substitute may only narrow claim and cannot broaden it. Patent Owner must show proposed new claims are patentable at least over prior art known to Patent Owner. 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.121, 42.221.

name: Technological Invention (CBM eligibility exception)
description: A patent is not eligible for CBM review if it claims subject matter that as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious and solves a technical problem using a technical solution.
guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.301; see Transitional Program for Covered Business Method Patents definitions.

name: Institution decision when copending reexamination/reissue exists
description: Whether to institute an AIA trial when the same claims are at issue in a copending reexamination or reissue proceeding.
guidance: The Office will continue to determine institution on a case-by-case basis and will not automatically delay proceedings in favor of a copending reexamination/reissue absent facts/circumstances warranting delay. Relevant facts include whether claims challenged by the petitioner were amended in the copending proceeding, the advanced stage of the reexamination (e.g., reexamination certificate issued), or other circumstances showing duplication or inefficiency. Examples of denials where copending reexamination/amendments were dispositive include Intromedic Co. Ltd. v. Given Imaging Ltd., IPR2015–00579, and Juniper Networks, Inc. v. Linex Techs., Inc., IPR2014–00595. The Office does not propose rule changes to enumerate specific stay/denial circumstances.

name: Factors for consolidation of copending reexamination/reissue with AIA trial
description: Factors the Board should consider when deciding whether to consolidate an AIA trial with a copending reexamination or reissue.
guidance: The Office and commenters identified multiple relevant factors (not exhaustive): (1) type of additional proceeding; (2) time between filing dates of initial and additional proceedings; (3) stage of the initial proceeding; (4) duration of additional proceeding; (5) scope of each proceeding; (6) whether third-party filers are the same or different; (7) relation between third-party filer and filer of initial proceeding; (8) number of total proceedings filed against the patent; (9) whether the additional proceeding is a reexamination (ex parte reexamination generally should not be transferred to PTAB due to loss of patent owner procedures); (10) whether district court litigation is stayed pending reexamination; (11) whether validity of claims is on appeal to the Federal Circuit; (12) express interests of the parties; (13) issues raised in different proceedings; (14) ability of the Board to reach a timely conclusion in any proceeding; and (15) cost/resource savings from consolidation. The Office will weigh these and other factors on a case-by-case basis and will not adopt a bright-line rule requiring consolidation.

name: Standards for extending the one-year statutory period
description: Circumstances constituting 'good cause' to extend the one-year period for the Board to issue a final determination in an AIA trial.
guidance: The Office will continue to strive to complete trials within the one-year statutory period and will not adopt a specific enumerated list of good-cause circumstances into the rules. Instead, extensions will be decided on the facts of each case. The Office will, however, revise the Practice Guide to provide examples of instances where extensions may be warranted (not an exclusive list). Commenters suggested appropriate circumstances including: need for comparative tests; delay attributable to the non-requesting party; existence of later-filed AIA proceedings on the same patent; additional discovery (e.g., on secondary considerations or real party-in-interest); time needed to consider amended claims; unexpected unavailability of an irreplaceable participant; complexity arising from multiple proceedings, many parties, complicated discovery, consolidated/joined trials, or particularly complex inventions. The Office retains discretion to deny extensions to preserve the one-year benefit.

name: Hearing logistics: recesses, panel attendance, and facilities
description: Practical expectations for hearings, including availability of recesses, panel member attendance, and hearing-room access.
guidance: Requests for a recess during oral argument (e.g., to confer with an expert over claim construction issues) will be evaluated case-by-case by the panel. The Office generally ensures that panel members assigned to a particular case are present at the session when that case is heard and encourages participation across multi-session related hearings, though scheduling conflicts may occasionally occur. Hearing rooms are opened to the parties and public 30 minutes before scheduled start times. The Office plans upgrades to enable hearings in regional offices.

name: Rationale rejecting petition page limit tied solely to number of claims or excess claim fees
description: Whether petition page limits should be determined by the number of claims challenged or tied to excess claim fees.
guidance: The Office did not adopt proposals to set petition page limits solely based on the number of claims challenged nor to provide automatic page extensions tied to excess claim fees. The Office concluded that number-of-claims alone does not provide sufficient flexibility for a petition to present the precise relief requested and the detailed reasons supporting it.

name: Application information required in ADS
description: Application information includes the title of the invention, a suggested classification by class and subclass, the Technology Center to which the subject matter is assigned, the total number of drawing sheets, a suggested drawing figure for publication (in a nonprovisional application), any docket number assigned to the application, and the type of application (e.g., utility, plant, design, reissue, provisional).
guidance: Suggested classification and Technology Center information should be supplied for provisional applications whether or not claims are present, and should be based upon the disclosure if claims are absent. The Office may not use suggested classification/figure for publication but may use the ADS-provided data for front page continuity data when not present in the specification.

name: Domestic priority (benefit) information content
description: Domestic priority information includes the application number, the filing date, the status (including patent number if available), and relationship of each application for which a benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c).
guidance: Providing this information in the ADS constitutes the specific reference required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and need not otherwise be made part of the specification. No continuity data will be included in the first sentence(s) of the specification if applicant does not provide it there. Pre-AIA, this does not apply to provisional applications.

name: PLT/PCT forms can substitute for ADS for certain items
description: 37 CFR 1.76(f) and (g) provide that requirements for presentation of priority/benefit claims, references to previously filed applications, and the name of the applicant in an ADS will be satisfied by presentation of such information in Patent Law Treaty Model International Request Forms or the PCT Request Form in certain contexts.
guidance: Specifically: (1) presentation of priority/benefit claim in PLT Model International Request Form satisfies § 1.55/1.78; (2) reference to previously filed application in PLT form satisfies § 1.57(a); (3) name of applicant in PLT/PCT forms satisfies § 1.46. For national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371, the PCT Request Form contained in the international application or presence of the claim on the front page of publication may satisfy ADS requirements, but submissions during the national stage may require an ADS to add/correct information. If a PCT Request Form is submitted in an application under 35 U.S.C. 111, it must be accompanied by a clear indication that treatment as a §111 application is desired.

name: Antibody disclosure must show possession in structural terms
description: The specification must describe an antibody in structural terms sufficient to show possession (e.g., deposit of a hybridoma or description of antibody structure in drawings or chemical formula).
guidance: Absence of a deposit or structural description means the specification does not provide an actual reduction to practice of antibodies to other species; merely asserting binding activity is insufficient. (Applied in Example 13/14 where disclosure of murine antibody did not support claims to human/non-murine antibodies.)

name: An adequate antigen description can support antibodies but only if antigen is described
description: An adequate description of an antigen may be accepted as sufficient to put an inventor in possession of antibodies against the antigen, but only when the antigen itself is adequately described.
guidance: If the specification does not provide a description of the antigen (e.g., human Protein X), then relying on antigen-description principles fails. See Example 13: antigen-based justification does not rescue claims when human Protein X is not described.

name: Disclosure must provide correlation between species variants to support cross-species claims
description: To support claims covering a protein (or antibodies thereto) from multiple species, the specification must disclose correlations (structural features or properties) between the disclosed species (e.g., murine) and other species (e.g., human or non-murine) that would allow recognition of other members of the genus.
guidance: If no correlation is shown and properties are unpredictable across species, disclosure of one species is insufficient to support a claim to a genus encompassing other species (Examples 14 and 15).

name: Functional-only disclosure is insufficient without structural/physical/chemical detail
description: A disclosure that describes an entity only functionally (e.g., 'human Protein X' by function) without providing its physical or chemical properties, structural features, or sequence does not satisfy written description for claims to that entity.
guidance: Functional identification without structural correlation leaves the claim directed to an unknown identified only by reference to another unknown; examiner should conclude failure of written description (Example 13 conclusion).

name: Method-of-making requirement when antigen/unavailable material is needed
description: The specification must describe a method of making the claimed antibody that can be performed without first having the target antigen (e.g., human Protein X) when the claim seeks antibodies to that antigen.
guidance: If the only disclosed method requires possession of the specific antigen, the applicant has not shown possession of antibodies to un-disclosed antigens (Examples 13/14).

name: Representative number of species or common structural features required for genus claims
description: For genus claims (claims that encompass many species), the specification must either provide a representative number of species within the genus or disclose common structural features that distinguish the genus and allow identification of other members.
guidance: A single described species will only support a genus claim if it is representative of the genus by sharing common distinguishing features; otherwise the specification fails written description for the full scope of the genus (Example 15 and Claim 1 analysis).

name: Predictability in the art affects written description sufficiency
description: The level of predictability known in the art (e.g., genetic code predictability) can permit broader claims: where predictable correlations exist, disclosure of one form may allow those skilled in the art to envisage other structural embodiments.
guidance: Example: disclosure of an amino acid sequence (SEQ ID NO:2) plus knowledge of the genetic code allows one skilled in the art to envisage nucleic acid sequences encoding that protein, supporting written description for claims to nucleic acids encoding the protein (Examples 15, Claims 2–4).

name: Complete sequence disclosure supports claims to nucleic acids encoding disclosed proteins
description: Providing the full nucleic acid sequence (SEQ ID NO:1) and correlating it to the amino acid sequence (SEQ ID NO:2) supports possession of that sequence and predictable variants that encode the same protein.
guidance: When the specification includes a complete sequence and a method of isolating similar sequences, and the art provides predictable correlations (genetic code), the written description requirement is satisfied for claims to that sequence and to sequences encoding the disclosed protein (Examples 15 Claims 3–4).

name: Process claims supported when novelty resides in process steps and predictability is high
description: If the novelty of a claim resides in specific process steps (e.g., complexing nucleic acid with a defined compound and specified incubation conditions) and practicing the process does not require unknown structural variants, the specification can satisfy written description for the method claim.
guidance: Example 16: disclosure of compound X, a working example (transformation of mitochondria in mouse cells), and predictable applicability to other nucleic acids/cells supports written description for a method claim even though component sequences are not all disclosed. Note: enablement issues are separate and should also be considered.

name: Screening assay claims acceptable for methods but may not support product claims
description: A disclosed screening method for identifying compounds (detailed steps) can satisfy written description for a method of identifying compounds, but does not by itself provide written description of the compounds identified by that method.
guidance: Example 17: Claim 2 (screening method) satisfied written description because the steps are disclosed and are followable. Claim 3 (compound identified by the method) failed because no structural description of the compound was provided (reach-through claim problem).

name: Functionally claimed compounds require structural or property disclosure
description: Claims that define compounds solely by their function (e.g., 'a compound that selectively inhibits POPKIN-2') require the specification to disclose complete structure, partial structures, or physical/chemical properties, or a correlation between target and inhibitor structure, to satisfy written description.
guidance: Without such disclosure (no known selective inhibitors and no correlation), one skilled in the art cannot visualize the claimed compounds and written description fails (Example 17 Claim 1 and Claim 3 conclusions).

name: Generic claim language ('comprising') broadens scope and raises representation requirement
description: Use of open transitional language like 'comprising' yields genus claims that allow unspecified additional members; the specification must demonstrate possession of the genus across that broader scope.
guidance: Examiners should begin with narrower dependent claims (subgenera) to evaluate whether the broader genus claim is supported. If subgenera are described and representative, genus may be supported; otherwise genus fails (Examples 15 analysis of claims 1–5).

name: Actual reduction to practice or deposit can support possession of species
description: An actual reduction to practice (e.g., working example demonstrating the species) or deposit (e.g., hybridoma) provides strong support that the inventor possessed that species at filing.
guidance: Where a working example shows the species (e.g., SEQ ID NO:1 cDNA or antibody produced), related subclaims directed to that species satisfy written description (Examples 15 Claim 4; antibody examples).

name: Written description and enablement are distinct inquiries
description: Satisfaction of the written description requirement (showing possession) is a separate inquiry from enablement (whether the disclosure teaches how to make and use the full scope).
guidance: Even when written description is satisfied (e.g., Example 16 method claim), the specification may still raise enablement concerns that should be addressed separately during examination (practice note in Example 16).

name: Burden to submit evidence when claiming diligence
description: A party arguing it acted diligently must submit evidence to support that claim.
guidance: Absent documentary or testimonial evidence demonstrating prompt and reasonable effort, assertions of diligence are insufficient. (Citing Turner, 1991 Comm'l. Pat. LEXIS 5.)

name: Nature-based product analysis — select closest natural counterpart
description: For claims reciting nature-based products, compare the claimed nature-based product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics.
guidance: Choose the appropriate natural counterpart (e.g., the virus from which a live attenuated virus was derived; for mixtures, either components or naturally occurring combinations such as soil). The chosen counterpart affects the marked-differences comparison. Guidance includes examples where the closest counterpart may be a single component or a naturally occurring combination (e.g., water/aluminum phosphate in soil).

name: Markedly different characteristics criterion (nature-based products)
description: A claimed nature-based product must have 'markedly different characteristics' from its natural counterpart (structural, functional, or other characteristics) to avoid being a 'product of nature' exception.
guidance: Look for structural changes (e.g., mutation in nucleotide sequence) or functional/physical changes (e.g., loss of virulence, inability to replicate, changed immunogenicity, semi-solid form) that are not found in nature. Structural differences that produce functional changes are dispositive in many examples (e.g., live attenuated virus with a non-natural mutation). If no marked difference exists for at least one embodiment within the BRI, the limitation may be a 'product of nature' exception.

name: Mixtures and combinations — evaluate whether combination changes properties
description: When a claim recites a mixture of naturally occurring components, analyze whether combining them changes the structure, function, or other properties of the components in a marked way.
guidance: If the components do not occur together in nature, compare the claimed mixture to the individual components; absence of structural/functional change supports finding an exception (e.g., peptide + water where peptide retains natural structure and water retains natural properties). Conversely, an emulsion or a synergistic functional improvement (e.g., increased immunogenicity with adjuvant) can be a marked difference. Cite Funk Brothers as illustrative of mixtures that remain ineligible when each component retains the same effect it always had.

name: Step 2A/2B procedural flow
description: Use the two-step (Step 2A, Step 2B) analysis after Step 1: Step 2A asks whether the claim is directed to an exception (and applies markedly-different analysis for nature-based products); if directed to an exception, Step 2B asks whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the exception.
guidance: If analysis at Step 2A shows the claim is not directed to an exception, do not perform Step 2B. If Step 2A shows the claim is directed to an exception, then proceed to Step 2B to evaluate 'significantly more' (e.g., whether recited additional elements are particular and unconventional).

name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' (additional elements) inquiry
description: After identifying that a claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any additional element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Consider whether the additional elements are particular, unconventional, and provide meaningful limitations beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Particular devices or unconventional combinations (e.g., a coated microneedle array used for vaccine delivery) can supply 'significantly more.' Conversely, high-level recitations or routine carriers may not.

name: Additional elements must be more than mere instruction to 'apply' the exception
description: An additional element that merely instructs to apply the judicial exception using well-understood, routine, conventional activity does not make the claim 'significantly more.'
guidance: Assess whether the element confines the exception to a particular useful application (e.g., an unconventional device) or whether it just tells practitioners to use a conventional tool/procedure. Example anti-pattern: reciting 'administer and detect' with conventional techniques or generic sequencing steps at a high level.

name: Synergy or changed functional property as evidence of marked difference
description: A claimed combination that yields a changed or synergistic functional property (e.g., significantly increased immunogenicity) can be a marked difference from natural counterparts.
guidance: Document experimental or disclosed evidence that the combination’s immunogenicity (or other functional measure) is materially different from the sum of components. Example: Peptide F + aluminum adjuvant producing 80% seroprotection vs components alone.

name: Particular, unconventional devices or manufactures can supply 'significantly more'
description: Recitation of a specific, unconventional device or manufacture that is not routine in the field can confine an exception to a particular useful application and thereby contribute to eligibility.
guidance: Examples: a coated microneedle array for transcutaneous vaccine delivery was treated as an unconventional delivery device that yields 'significantly more' when combined with a peptide that is a product of nature. Evaluate whether the device was routine/conventional for the claimed use at filing.

name: Process-focused claims may avoid product-of-nature analysis
description: When a claim as a whole is focused on a process or method (e.g., detecting hybridization, sequencing), it may not be necessary to perform the markedly-different characteristics analysis on recited nature-based products.
guidance: If the claim recites process steps that are not themselves judicial exceptions (e.g., amplifying with Cool-Melt PCR and sequencing), analyze the claim as a process; if the claim as a whole is not directed to an exception, it is eligible without product analysis. Note: dependent claims that incorporate an abstract idea may still require Step 2B analysis for unconventional additional steps.

name: Streamlined analysis — eligibility may be self-evident
description: In some cases, eligibility is self-evident from the claim as a whole (e.g., mechanical arrangement improving a machine) so a full Step 2A/2B analysis is unnecessary.
guidance: Use a streamlined analysis where the claim clearly provides meaningful limitations and improvements (e.g., Fourdrinier machine arrangement using gravity to improve speed without tying up a law of nature). Document reasoning in remarks or reasons for allowance as appropriate.

name: Examiner practice guidance — record-keeping and citation
description: If the record would benefit from clarification, examiners should add remarks to an Office action or reasons for allowance explaining the eligibility analysis and may cite analogous court decisions to support positions.
guidance: Rejections should identify the exception(s) and explain why claimed nature-based products lack markedly different characteristics, and why combinations or additional elements do or do not amount to significantly more. Practice examples include citing Myriad, Funk Brothers, Mayo, Alice, and other relevant cases for analogy.

name: Patent strength and scope
description: Broad patents with strong legal protection often command higher royalties.
guidance: Assess enforceability, claim breadth, prosecution history, and freedom-to-operate; stronger IP rights justify premium royalty rates and more favorable license terms.

name: Grounds of rejection: general requirement
description: For each ground of rejection applicable to the appealed claims, an explanation of the ground of rejection, or reference to a final rejection or other single prior action for a clear exposition of the rejection.
guidance: Explain each ground or refer to a single prior Office action which sets forth the rejection and comply with the specific paragraph requirements for 35 U.S.C. 112, 102, 103, and others.

name: Grounds of rejection – 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the examiner’s answer (or single prior action) shall explain how the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 is not complied with.
guidance: Include, as appropriate, how the specification/drawings (i) do not describe the subject matter defined by each rejected claim, (ii) would not enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter without undue experimentation, and (iii) do not set forth the best mode contemplated by the appellant.

name: Grounds of rejection – 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the examiner’s answer (or single prior action) shall explain why the rejected claims are anticipated or not patentable under 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: Point out where all of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims are found in the prior art relied upon in the rejection.

name: Grounds of rejection – 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) explanation
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner’s answer (or single prior action) shall: (i) state the ground of rejection and point out where each of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims is found in the prior art relied upon; (ii) identify any difference between the rejected claims and the prior art relied on; and (iii) explain how and why the claimed subject matter is rendered unpatentable over the prior art.
guidance: If the rejection is based upon a combination of references, the answer (or single prior action) shall explain the rationale for making the combination.

name: Feature-by-feature comparison when claim-to-prior-art correspondence unclear
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 where there are questions as to how claim limitations correspond to features in the prior art, the examiner shall compare at least one of the rejected claims feature by feature with the prior art relied on in the rejection.
guidance: The comparison shall align the language of the claim side-by-side with a reference to the specific page, line number, drawing reference number, and quotation from the prior art, as appropriate.

name: Form paragraphs and cover sheet use
description: Use specified form paragraphs (e.g., ¶12.49 Examiner’s Answer Cover Sheet, ¶12.50 Heading For Examiner’s Answer, and follow-on form paragraphs) to structure the examiner’s answer and include required bracketed insertions (dates, claim numbers, paper numbers, names).
guidance: Follow Examiner Notes for proper insertion and sequencing of form paragraphs; e.g., form ¶12.50.01 Real Party in Interest, ¶12.51 Status of Claims, etc.

name: Primary reference suitability
description: A piece of prior art may serve as the primary reference only if its design characteristics are 'basically the same as the claimed design' and major modification would not be required to make the reference look like the claimed design.
guidance: Cites In re Rosen and In re Harvey. Example: the Triumph bit could serve as the primary reference because it is 'almost identical' to Figure 2 of the ’575 patent except for the shaft shape; the difference (cylindrical vs hexagonal shaft with narrow groove) did not require major modification. If major modification would be required, the reference cannot be the primary reference.

name: Use of secondary references — motivation to combine required
description: Secondary references may be presented to show that a primary reference and the secondary reference together make the claimed design obvious, but there must be some suggestion in the prior art to modify the basic design with features from the secondary references.
guidance: Cites In re Borden and L.A. Gear v. Thom McAn. The court found that the ’157 patent provided an express motivation to combine because it taught that a hexagonal shaft with a narrow groove could be placed on 'any other such tool' including drill bits, thereby furnishing a motivation to combine that teaching with the Triumph bit.

name: Long-felt need as evidence of nonobviousness — substantive requirement
description: Evidence of a 'long-felt need' can support nonobviousness only if it meaningfully demonstrates that the claimed solution satisfied a persistent unmet need, not merely that the claimed design is new.
guidance: The court criticizes equating a 'new design in an old art field' with long-felt need: if novelty alone established long-felt need, the doctrine would be meaningless. Testimony that reduced hexagonal shafts had 'been around forever' while the exact configuration was new does not demonstrate long-felt need.

name: Allegations of copying require supporting evidence (timing/awareness)
description: Claims that an accused party copied a patented design require evidence that the accused party was aware of the patent/design and copied it; mere similarity is insufficient.
guidance: Example: Kouvato alleged Old Jore copied the ’575 patent, but the record showed Old Jore was designing and selling the accused bit at least five months before anyone there knew of the ’575 patent, undermining any copying inference.

name: Definition and benefits of PPH
description: The Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) is a framework in which an application whose claims have been determined to be patentable by an Office of Earlier Examination (OEE) is eligible to go through an accelerated examination in an Office of Later Examination (OLE) with a simple procedure upon an applicant’s request.
guidance: PPH exploits search/examination information of the OEE to (1) deliver lower prosecution costs, (2) support applicants in obtaining stable patent rights efficiently worldwide, and (3) reduce search/examination burden and improve examination quality in major patent offices.

name: Claim correspondence and amendment rules for 'sufficiently correspond'
description: US claims will be considered to sufficiently correspond with the claims allowed by the OEE if the US claims are of the same or similar scope or the US claims are narrower in scope than the allowed claims; the additional limitation that makes the US claims narrower must be presented in dependent form.
guidance: If the narrower dependent claim is indicated as being allowable if written in independent form, you may rewrite the allowable dependent claim in independent form. An independent claim rejected by the US examiner may be amended to include a limitation previously presented in a dependent claim indicated as having allowable subject matter; such an amendment can meet the sufficient correspondence requirement only if that limitation was previously presented in a dependent claim indicated as allowable but objected to only because it depended on a rejected claim.

name: Entire profit recovery when patented feature gives entire efficiency/salability
description: Where the entire efficiency and salability of an invention depend on the patented feature the patentee is entitled to recover all the profits.
guidance: If the patented element is what makes the product valuable, the patentee may claim all defendant profits. (See McDonald v. Whitney (1889).)

name: Re-issue cannot enlarge claims unless clear inadvertent mistake in wording
description: A re-issue cannot enlarge Claims unless there has been a clear mistake inadvertently committed in wording them.
guidance: Broadening requires proof of inadvertent clerical/wording error, not mere desire to expand scope. (See Huber v. N. O. Nelson Mfg. Co. (1889).)

name: Cannot enlarge a claim by omitting an element previously claimed as essential
description: A re-issue cannot enlarge a Claim by omitting an element previously claimed as essential.
guidance: Removing an essential element to broaden scope is impermissible. (See Matthews v. Iron Clad Mfg. Co. (1888).)

name: Patentee aware of Office-imposed limitations cannot later claim inadvertence
description: A patentee taking his patent with full knowledge of the limitations imposed by the Patent Office and the consequent imperfection of his Claims, cannot set up inadvertence, etc., as a ground for a re-issue.
guidance: Actual knowledge of limitations negates later assertions of inadvertence. (See Ex parte Page (1888).)

name: Specific conditions denying retroactive filing date for division
description: Enumerated situations where a divisional shall NOT take the parent's filing date and instead be deemed filed on its actual filing date.
guidance: Listed conditions include: (①) divisional corresponds to 'another application' under Article 29(3) or to a patent application under Utility Model Act Article 4(3); (②) applicant seeks application of proviso Article 30(1)(1) and must state purport and submit evidential documents; (③) claiming priority under the Treaty—must state purport, country, and date of first filing; (④) claiming domestic priority—must state purport and prior-filed application in the patent application.

name: Examination of divisional scope based on filing date (time-dependent rules)
description: Examinations on the scope of a divisional application shall be conducted based on the filing date, but the applicable procedure differs depending on whether the parent was filed before Sept 30, 2006 or on/after Oct 1, 2006.
guidance: If parent filed before Sept 30, 2006 and divisional claims an invention not described in parent, the examiner issues a preliminary notice for inadmissible division and may examine based on actual divisional filing date if division not accepted; published patent gazette of parent can be used as prior art. If parent filed on/after Oct 1, 2006, examiner shall notify grounds for rejection and decide to reject if not remedied. If non-described inventions are deleted by amendment during examination, examiner shall examine based on parent's filing date.

name: Priority-claim and reference-date rules for nested divisional chains
description: A divisional application may claim priority under the Treaty or domestic priority; reference dates to determine patentability for particular inventions in a chain depend on the filing dates of the relevant prior-filed application that disclosed that invention.
guidance: Example: a divisional based on an application that itself claimed various earlier filings will retain the filing date of its immediate parent for inventions disclosed therein, but the reference date for each invention is the filing date of the prior-filed application that first disclosed that invention. Article 36(2) applies when the same invention is described in both parent and divisional.

name: Special handling when parent has decision to grant (post-29 July 2015)
description: When examining a divisional from a parent which received a certified copy of a decision to grant on or after 29 July 2015, examiners should note special conditions.
guidance: If applicant did not request a trial for correction when filing a divisional for an invention disclosed only in the description or for inventions recited in parent's claims, examiners should check whether divisional claimed inventions are identical to those of parent and inform applicant of conflicting application when sending a rejection. If applicant divides part of an invention described in the granted parent while requesting trial for correction, examination of the divisional should be deferred until trial concludes.

name: Avoiding a Double Patenting Rejection
description: Practices and filing/claim strategies to avoid nonstatutory double patenting rejections (e.g., terminal disclaimers, claim amendments, divisional practice).

name: Claims Limited to Species
description: Treatment of claims that are limited to particular species and their relationship to broader generic claims.

name: Patent as prima facie evidence of validity
description: A patent, regular on its face, is prima facie evidence of all the facts essential to its own validity.
guidance: Specifies that the patent, until contradicted, proves the invention resulted from an inventive act; that the patentee or assignor was first and true inventor; that the subject-matter is patentable, new, and useful; not abandoned; lawfully issued to the proper patentee; if a re-issue, that it corresponds with the original; if an extension, that legal requirements were obeyed; that the invention described differs essentially from prior patents; that the specification is without fraud and ambiguity; that the claims are not excessive and clearly define the actual invention; and that the patent has not been surrendered or repealed. This prima facie proof can be overcome only by clear evidence removing all reasonable doubt. The weight of the presumption is increased by re-issue, success in interference proceedings, extension, and long/continuous public recognition (long admitted validity).

name: Court's interpretation limits admissible evidence about invention
description: A patent covers the invention(s) which the court, in construing its provisions, decides it describes and claims; evidence inconsistent with that construction is inadmissible.
guidance: Parties and jury must proceed on the court's construction; evidence offered under any other view is inadmissible and a verdict based on it is contrary to law. The court may use testimony, expert evidence, and Patent Office papers connected with the patent or known to the inventor at application date to explain terms or ascertain essential characteristics, but the interpretation must be based on the patent as it stands and cannot be limited or extended by extraneous evidence. Patents offered by defendant to defeat a plaintiff's patent cannot be made admissible by extraneous evidence. File-wrapper and contents are not admissible to limit the construction of the patent (file-wrapper cannot be used to narrow claim scope).

name: Exclusion of evidence by estoppel
description: Evidence otherwise admissible may be excluded if the witness or party is estopped by prior record or conduct from asserting contrary facts.
guidance: A party cannot deny the truth of documents or assertions by which he induced another to act. Examples: a patentee cannot assert patent is worthless or abandoned against his assignee; a disclaimer prevents claiming the disclaimed part was embraced in the invention; admissions in the application or specification estop patentee from denying validity; an assignor cannot testify against his assignee to defeat title. Estoppel rests on preventing a party from deceiving another by subsequent contradiction of induced beliefs.

name: Use of models, rejected applications, and foreign documents to show circumstances
description: Models, rejected applications of third persons, and earlier foreign provisional specifications may be used to show the circumstances of the invention and the state of the art.
guidance: Such items are admissible in connection with evidence that the patentee knew of them to give construction to the patent. An earlier provisional specification (e.g., English) may show the state of the art and thus negative invention; models and rejected applications may narrow the field of invention and limit inquiry. However, these items cannot be used to vary or enlarge the claims by extraneous evidence.

name: Two‑part Alice/Mayo framework (Steps 2A and 2B)
description: Apply the Supreme Court’s two‑part framework as Steps 2A and 2B: Step 2A—determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea); Step 2B—if so, determine whether the claim as a whole contains additional elements that amount to 'significantly more' than the exception.
guidance: Use case law comparisons to identify exceptions in Step 2A; use the 'significantly more' inquiry in Step 2B to evaluate whether additional elements (individually and in combination) render the claim eligible. The framework already incorporates preemption concerns; follow the flowchart in the 2014 IEG and this Update.

name: Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis in Step 2A
description: For claims reciting nature‑based products, determine whether the recited product has 'markedly different characteristics' from what occurs in nature; if so, the claim is not directed to a 'product of nature' and may qualify as eligible at Step 2A.
guidance: MDC is retained in Step 2A to provide (1) early eligibility for many claims, (2) an additional pathway to eligibility for product‑of‑nature exceptions, and (3) consistency across technologies. Examples (e.g., Chakrabarty, Myriad/cDNA, and Examples such as NBP‑2 pomelo juice) illustrate application. Do not move MDC to Step 2B.

name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination (Step 2B)
description: In Step 2B, examiners must consider all additional claim elements both individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Even if an element is generic (e.g., a generic computer component) and does not amount to significantly more on its own, it may do so in combination with other elements. Use examples (AI‑3, AI‑4, 21, 25) to see how combinations of generic components can perform non‑generic functions.

name: Identifying abstract ideas by comparison to case law
description: Because courts have not provided a single definition of 'abstract idea,' examiners should identify abstract ideas by comparing the claimed concept to concepts already held to be abstract in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions.
guidance: Associate claimed concepts with judicial descriptors derived from case law to avoid overbroad identification; ensure a claimed concept is not labeled abstract unless similar to at least one concept the courts have identified as an abstract idea. Newly discovered concepts can still be judicial exceptions.

name: Examples of computer functions considered well‑understood, routine, and conventional
description: Courts have recognized certain generic computer functions as well‑understood, routine, and conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner.
guidance: Listed examples include: performing repetitive calculations; receiving, processing, and storing data; electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (OCR); electronic recordkeeping; automating mental tasks; receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., Internet). Use these as benchmarks in Step 2B to determine whether additional elements are merely routine.

name: Prima facie case requirements for eligibility rejections
description: An examiner meets the initial burden (prima facie case) by clearly articulating why a claim is not eligible: identify the judicial exception recited and why it is considered an exception, identify any additional elements, and explain why those elements do not amount to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: The rationale may rely on general knowledge in the art, case law precedent, applicant disclosure, or evidence. Training worksheets and sample rejections (Examples 5‑8) illustrate how to satisfy this burden. After the examiner meets the initial burden, the burden shifts to the applicant.

name: Streamlined analysis for clearly non‑preemptive/self‑evident claims
description: A streamlined analysis is available for claims that clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it (i.e., claims with self‑evident eligibility).
guidance: The streamlined analysis yields the same result as the full Steps 2A/2B analysis for claims suitable for it. It is not a way to avoid the results of the full analysis; claims that require a full Step 2B significantly‑more inquiry are not suitable for the streamlined path. Examples 26 and 27 illustrate claims eligible under the streamlined analysis; Example 24 is not suitable.

name: Distinguish generic computer implementation from invention that is 'significantly more'
description: A claim that merely instructs to 'apply' an abstract idea on a computer or recites a computer performing generic functions is not sufficient to render an abstract idea eligible; conversely, claims in which generic computer components in combination perform non‑generic functions can be 'significantly more.'
guidance: Use case law and examples to determine whether the computer implementation is merely generic (e.g., Examples 7, 22, 24) or amounts to significantly more (e.g., Examples 3, 23, 25; DDR Holdings example discussed in case law). Analyze the claim as a whole and consider combinations of elements.

name: Original claim not sufficiently described (written description defects)
description: An original claim may lack written description support when (1) the claim defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved; or (2) a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence that the genus is contemplated.
guidance: The mere appearance of claim language in the specification ('ipsis verbis') does not necessarily satisfy the written description requirement. Examiner should consider whether one skilled in the art can recognize from the specification that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention (Ariad; Enzo Biochem).

name: Indefiniteness rejection for means‑ (or step‑) plus‑function limitations
description: A claim limitation expressed in means‑ or step‑plus‑function language 'shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof' (35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph).
guidance: If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function, the limitation is indefinite because the applicant has failed to 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA para. 2) (In re Donaldson). Such a limitation also may lack adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) because an unbounded functional limitation would cover all ways of performing a function and indicate insufficient disclosure. See MPEP § 2181 for further guidance.

name: Suggesting amendments when rejecting for lack of written description
description: When appropriate, examiners should suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application's written description, while being mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter.
guidance: Suggested amendments should stay within the original disclosure and not introduce new matter; see Rasmussen for guidance on permissible amendments.

name: Changes to scope of claims after filing (general written description principle)
description: Failure to meet the written description requirement commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow claim breadth, alter numerical ranges, or use language not synonymous with terminology in the original disclosure.
guidance: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and to be entitled to an earlier priority or filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure. See MPEP § 2163 for examination guidelines.

name: Broadening claim — addition of a generic claim (genus supported by species)
description: A claimed genus may be supported by a sufficient description of a representative number of species; a single species may support a genus only if the disclosure 'indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the gen[us]'.
guidance: When there is substantial variation within the genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation. Disclosure of only one species is inadequate when ordinary artisans could not predict operability of other species. However, in some situations one species may suffice (Enzo Biochem; In re Curtis; In re Rasmussen). Consider unpredictability in the art and whether specification teaches against other species (AbbVie; Tronzo; In re Gosteli).

name: Range limitations — changing numerical ranges
description: Analysis of changing numerical range limitations must account for which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
guidance: Claims with open‑ended limits (e.g., 'at least 35%') that read on embodiments outside disclosed ranges may fail written description, whereas narrower ranges bounded within disclosed ranges may be acceptable (In re Wertheim; Purdue Pharma; Union Oil v. Atl. Richfield). Consider whether the specification shows the inventors considered particular ratios or ranges as part of their invention.

name: Claimed subject matter disclosed only in claims (antecedent/disclosure issues)
description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if an original claim discloses material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Form paragraph 7.44 may be used where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification (In re Benno).

name: Description requirements for Markush-type claims (Article 42(3))
description: In the case where a claim of a medicinal invention is described as a Markush-type claim, even if some components of the selective elements thereof are not described as specific embodiments in the specification, if a person of ordinary skill in the art would not have had any difficulty in understanding and practicing the effect of the invention from the description of the specification and such effect can also be fully expected, such claim cannot be deemed to violate the description requirements of Article 42(3) of the Patent Act.
guidance: Focus on whether a person skilled in the art can understand and practice the invention's effect from the specification despite lack of explicit embodiments. The test is practical understandability and expectation of effect, not strict enumeration of every Markush member as specific embodiments.

name: Public domain technology defense limitation
description: The principle of public domain technology applies when the invention subject to confirmation merely consists of known technology or could have easily been practiced from known technology by a person of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: However, if the invention subject to confirmation includes all constitutional elements of a claim of the patented invention and thus literally infringes, the public domain technology principle is not applied. Use this as a restriction against expanding patent scope via doctrine of equivalents.

name: Claim scope is not necessarily limited by drawings
description: A claim's scope should not be limited to what is shown in the drawings merely because a particular embodiment in the drawings (e.g., 'formed of one frame') appears that way; drawings may illustrate embodiments but do not automatically limit claim language.
guidance: Interpret claims by overall consideration of claim language, specification text (e.g., 'Constitution and Function of Invention'), and drawings. Determine whether drawing descriptions define a limitation or merely illustrate one way of implementing a feature. Example: 'bridge top face installing unit' interpreted by function (surface-contacting to support load) rather than being limited to a single-frame, curved structure shown in drawings.

name: Doctrine of equivalents / All Elements Rule applied flexibly
description: In assessing equivalence between claim elements and accused or compared features, the 'All Elements Rule' may be applied flexibly in light of the essential technical idea and the theory of solving the problem in the patent.
guidance: Consider factors including: (a) whether the inventions share the same theory of solving the problem (same essential technical idea); (b) possibility and easiness of substitution/modification by a person of ordinary skill in the art; (c) whether the difference affects function or effect (substantial functional equivalence); and (d) whether a difference is merely an additional limitation in a dependent claim rather than part of the essential technical idea. Use overall consideration of specification and publicly known technology at filing date.

name: Same theory of solving the problem (equivalence factor)
description: Determine whether the subject patent and the compared invention embody the same essential technical idea or theory of solving the problem addressed by the patent.
guidance: Review the specification's statement of objectives and unique solving means; if both inventions implement the same core solution (e.g., separating parts to facilitate manufacture and replacement), differences in non-essential features may still be equivalent. Distinguish essential technical ideas from additional dependent-claim matters.

name: Functional effect comparison (equivalence factor)
description: Evaluate whether differing structural features produce the same substantial functional effects claimed by the patent (e.g., reinforcement in multiple directions vs only one direction).
guidance: If the accused device lacks the claimed functional advantages (e.g., only strengthens panel in one direction rather than both), it may not be within the equivalent scope. The presence or absence of the improved functional effect can be decisive.

name: Prosecution history estoppel (doctrine applicability)
description: If the patentee obtained the patent by limiting claim language during prosecution (e.g., limiting a feature's height), prosecution history estoppel can preclude the patentee from later claiming scope intentionally excluded during prosecution.
guidance: Examine prosecution file history to see what claim scope was surrendered. If the patentee narrowed a claim to obtain allowance, under estoppel the patentee may be barred from recapturing the surrendered scope (e.g., feature heights lower than amended claim).

name: Contents of order when granting Ex Parte Reexamination
description: If SNQ exists, the determination will include an order for ex parte reexamination of the patent; the examiner must identify at least one SNQ and explain how the prior art raises such a question with respect to at least one claim.
guidance: The prior notice in the Official Gazette is constructive notice and reexamination will proceed. No rejection of a claim should be included in the order, but all issues identified in the request should be addressed. See 37 CFR 1.525 and MPEP § 2246.

name: Identification of issues required in the Order
description: For each SNQ identified, the decision should state the prior art adding new teaching, what the new teaching is, the claims the new teaching is directed to, that the teaching was not previously considered nor addressed in prior examination or final court holding, that a reasonable examiner would consider it important, and when priority is raised explain why the prior art is available against patent claims.
guidance: These elements must be explicitly stated so the scope and basis of the reexamination are clear. See MPEP § 2246 and § 2646 for ex parte and inter partes respectively.

name: Denying a reexamination request – required explanation
description: If no new question of patentability is raised, reexamination is denied and the decision must indicate for each prior art reference why the citation is cumulative, not available against the claims, or not important to a reasonable examiner in determining patentability.
guidance: Requester has one month after the determination denying the request to file a petition under applicable CFR sections for review; a petition decision affirming denial is final and non-appealable. If no petition is filed the reexamination is terminated. (MPEP § 2247, § 2647)

name: Patent Owner’s Statement timing and acknowledgment
description: If ex parte reexamination is ordered, the decision will set a period of two months in which patent owner may file a statement or amendment of claims (optional). Except as provided, no premature statement/response will be acknowledged in the determination of the request.
guidance: There is a pilot for waiver of Patent Owner’s Statement in Ex Parte Reexamination; Office may consider making permanent. See 35 U.S.C. § 304 and 37 CFR § 1.510(e).

name: Form and content of Examiner’s First Action on the Merits (FAOM) in Ex Parte
description: The examiner’s FAOM should be so complete that the second Office action can properly be a final action; it should respond to the substance of each argument raised by the patent owner and requester and, if one or more claims are considered allowable, indicate why the claim(s) are clearly patentable.
guidance: Follow MPEP § 2271 and § 1302.14 for reasons for allowance and detailed explanations. The FAOM should develop issues to enable compact prosecution.

name: Scope of Ex Parte Reexamination
description: Reexamination provides a complete reexamination of the patent claims on the basis of prior art patents and printed publications; 35 U.S.C. § 112 issues are not raised for original (unamended) patent claims; new or amended claims may be considered for § 112 issues; claims may not be broader than those of the original patent.
guidance: See 37 CFR § 1.552 & MPEP § 2258. Claims cannot be broadened (35 U.S.C. § 305).

name: Initial Office Action practice (Inter Partes)
description: Initial Office action usually accompanies the order for inter partes reexamination; if all claims are found patentable in the first action, examiner will issue an Action Closing Prosecution (ACP); where one or more claims are rejected, a non-final action is mailed.
guidance: Inter partes uses specific forms and form paragraphs; both patent owner and requester are sent copies. See 37 CFR § 1.935 and MPEP § 2660.

name: Patent Owner response requirements (Inter Partes)
description: If an Office action is adverse in any respect, patent owner must reply and request reconsideration or further examination; the response must distinctly and specifically point out each supposed error in examiner’s action (general allegations inadequate).
guidance: Patent owner normally given two months to respond. Amendments must comply with 37 CFR §§ 1.530(d)-(k), 1.941, and 1.943. Supplemental responses are not entered as a matter of right except in specified limited circumstances (e.g., cancellation of claims, adoption of examiner suggestions, placement in condition for allowance, correction of informalities). See MPEP § 2666.

name: Patent Owner amendments formal requirements
description: Amendments to the specification, claims, and drawings must follow 37 C.F.R. § 1.530 and MPEP instructions: entire text of added/rewritten specification paragraphs, entire text of each claim with parenthetical ("amended", "new"), markings per 1.530(f); drawings as sketches showing changes.
guidance: Claims cannot be broadened (35 U.S.C. §§ 305 and 314); no new matter may be introduced (35 U.S.C. §§ 112 and 132); no amendment other than cancellation will be incorporated after expiration; amendments not effective until reexamination certificate issues.

name: Language and document language requirement
description: The office’s official language is English; the title, abstract, claims, description, and drawings of the invention must be in English.
guidance: No translations are required to be submitted in any of the designated States. A copy of the priority document must be provided with an English translation if necessary.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents (DOE) — purpose
description: The doctrine of equivalents protects patent holders by preventing others from making immaterial changes to an invention while keeping its fundamental elements so as to avoid liability for infringement.
