guidance: Cited authority: Graver Tank & Mfg. Co. v. Linde Air Prods. Co., 339 U.S. 605, 608 (1950). DOE is balanced against the public's right to rely on the patent's publicly available claim language.

name: Foreseeability test (Supreme Court) — central inquiry for estoppel
description: When an amendment is made, courts look to whether a broader claim description was foreseeable at the time of amendment—if the equivalent at issue was disclosed in the field, a broader claim was foreseeable and estoppel is presumed.
guidance: If a broader claim was foreseeable and the applicant did not draft it, the presumption is that the applicant chose not to pursue it, supporting application of PHE to bar DOE. Cited: Festo Corp. v. Shoketsu Kinzoku Kogyo Kabushiki Co., 535 U.S. 722, 740.

name: Office Action / §112 clarification amendments — risk of surrendering equivalents
description: Amendments made in response to Office Actions requesting clarification (e.g., under 35 U.S.C. §112) that narrow claims can surrender claim elements and their equivalents, potentially producing estoppel depending on whether the amendment was required or foreseeable alternatives existed.
guidance: Example from Festo: an examiner's §112 request led to a narrowing amendment; the courts treated that narrowing as surrendering equivalents because broader language was foreseeable and not pursued. Whether an examiner 'required' the change versus merely requesting clarification matters.

name: Interviews before first Office action — limits and applicant material requirements
description: A request for an interview prior to the first Office action is ordinarily granted in continuing or substitute applications; in other applications, an interview before the first Office action is encouraged only if examiner determines it would advance prosecution.
guidance: The examiner may require the applicant requesting such an interview to provide a paper including a general statement of the state of the art, identification of no more than three references believed to be the closest prior art, and an explanation of how the broadest claim distinguishes over such references.

name: Items required in a complete and proper interview summary
description: Complete recordation should include at least: (A) brief description of nature of any exhibit or demonstration; (B) identification of claims discussed; (C) identification of specific prior art discussed; (D) identification of principal proposed amendments; (E) general thrust of principal arguments of applicant and examiner; (F) general indication of any other pertinent matters; (G) general results or outcome of the interview; (H) for email interviews, a copy of the contents exchanged must be placed in the file.
guidance: Identification of arguments need not be lengthy; sufficient if general nature or thrust can be understood in context of file. Applicant may fully describe arguments they deem persuasive.

name: Assignments of rights to recover past damages must expressly include right of action
description: Assignments purporting to transfer claims for past infringements must expressly include the right of action; the mere assignment of the patent does not necessarily transfer the right to sue for past infringements.
guidance: Courts require express language transferring the right to damages for past infringements. Assignments of such claims are subject to all equities existing between the assignor and alleged infringer; notice to defendant of transfer is necessary to avoid protecting bona fide payments to record plaintiff. Cases: Hamilton v. Rollins, Emerson v. Hubbard, Kaolatype Engraving Co. v. Hoke.

name: Assignment of patent does not automatically transfer right to past-claim actions
description: The mere assignment of the patent does not transfer the right to sue for past infringements unless the assignment expressly includes claims for past damages; courts have held such transfers must be clearly expressed.
guidance: Several cases hold an assignment by an administrator does not cover past claims; severing past-claim rights from the patent may be impermissible contrary to statutes. Examples: Kaolatype Engraving Co. v. Hoke; Gordon v. Anthony.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning of claim terms
description: Claim construction determines 'the ordinary and customary meaning' of a disputed claim term, which 'is the meaning that the term would have to a person of ordinary skill in the art in question at the time of the invention, i.e., as of the effective filing date of the patent application.'
guidance: Interpret claim terms from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the effective filing date; timing matters (means of the term at filing date).

name: Specification is highly relevant and primary basis
description: The specification is 'always highly relevant' in claim construction and is usually dispositive.
guidance: Use the specification as the primary basis for construing ambiguous claim language, but be careful not to import limitations from the specification into the claim ('limitation should not be read from the specification into the claim').

name: Intrinsic evidence hierarchy and weight
description: Intrinsic evidence consists of the claims, the specification, and the patent prosecution history record. Intrinsic evidence should be given great weight in construing claims.
guidance: Give greatest weight to intrinsic evidence (claims and specification), with prosecution history as part of intrinsic record to be considered.

name: Prosecution history is intrinsic but less useful
description: The court can consider the prosecution history as intrinsic evidence, but since the prosecution history shows the intermediate steps of negotiation with the PTO, rather than the final product of those negotiations, it is less useful than the claims and specification.
guidance: Treat prosecution history as informative but subordinate to claims/specification because it reflects bargaining positions and amendments during examination.

name: Extrinsic evidence is less significant and less reliable
description: Courts may also consider extrinsic evidence, such as dictionaries, treatises, and the testimony of inventors and experts. The Federal Circuit, however, regards such evidence as 'less significant than the intrinsic record in determining the legally operative meaning of claim language.' Extrinsic evidence is also 'less reliable than the patent and its prosecution history in determining how to read claim terms.'
guidance: Extrinsic sources can be consulted to inform how a person of ordinary skill would understand technology or terms, but give them less weight than intrinsic evidence; use dictionaries/treatises/experts cautiously.

name: Practical importance of precise claim language
description: Claim construction is critical ... These claims delineate the inventor's exclusive rights, necessitating a thorough examination within the context of the entire patent document.
guidance: Precise drafting and careful reliance on specification and prosecution history influence enforcement and litigation outcomes; claim construction can determine whether a patent is infringed or valid, so align claim drafting and litigation strategy with these rules.

name: Refusal to enter amendment
description: Refusal to enter amendment within 30 days from the filing of an appeal shall fall under: (①) Where the amendment does not comply with requirements for amendment under Article 47(2)-(3) of the Patent Act; ② Where new grounds for rejection are deemed to be arisen from the amendment (‘deletion of claim(s)’ excluded among amendments according to Article 47(3), subparagraph 1-4).
guidance: If grounds for rejection previously notified are not overcome by the amendment within 30 days from filing of an appeal, but no new reasons arise from the amendment, the amendment shall be accepted but the original decision stands. If prior grounds are not overcome AND new grounds arise from the amendment, the amendment shall be refused to be entered and review proceeds based on the specification before the amendment.

name: Evaluation for amendment requirements (Article 47(3))
description: Assessment of whether an amendment satisfies the requirements under Article 47(3) shall be performed by comparing the amendment with the specification or drawings of the relevant prior amendment (e.g., amendment II).
guidance: Specifically, whether the scope of claims is narrowed shall be determined by comparing corresponding claims between the earlier amendment (e.g., amendment II) and the later amendment (e.g., amendment III or IV).

name: Determination whether claim scope is narrowed
description: Whether the scope of claims is narrowed is determined by comparing corresponding claims between the prior amendment and the new amendment (e.g., amendment II vs amendment III/IV).
guidance: Used to evaluate compliance with Article 47(3) when amendments are filed during appeal/review; governs whether the amendment is permissible as narrowing rather than broadening.

name: Limitations on triggers for ex-officio re-examination
description: Ex-officio re-examination is not permitted where the obvious ground for rejection is: (i) improper description of background art; (ii) claim(s) improperly formulated; or (iii) beyond unity of invention.
guidance: These categories are expressly excluded from ex-officio re-examination even if a problem is obvious.

name: Positive examination — examiner may suggest amendments
description: An examiner may suggest amendments when notifying grounds for rejection so that an applicant can rapidly obtain a patent with a reasonable scope of protection.
guidance: Suggestions aim to accelerate allowance with reasonable claim scope; examiner should indicate related grounds for rejection when suggesting amendments (use 'Advices on Amendment' section).

name: Target application suitability for suggested amendments
description: An examiner can suggest amendments for an application meeting the following requirements: ① the invention should be understandable; ② sufficient prior art search is made (except where lack of description prevents search); ③ the claimed invention has a technical feature distinguished from prior art.
guidance: To maximize effect, focus suggestions on proper scope rather than fixing lack of description. Amendments should be suggested simply and clearly; more detailed suggestions for applicants without representatives.

name: How to suggest amendments for novelty and inventive step
description: Examiner may suggest amendments in cases: ① where dependent claims are allowable, suggest adding a technical element from allowable dependent claims to the claim needing amendment while explaining the reason; ② where no claim is allowable but the description discloses a technical element distinguishing from prior art, suggest adding that element; ③ where a dependent claim is allowable but description discloses a technical element that yields a more reasonable scope, examiner may suggest that element (and may suggest both options).
guidance: Explain the reason/technical effect when suggesting elements. If selecting elements from multiple elements in a dependent claim or description, point to paragraphs/drawings evidencing the element and the technical effect. In some cases, indicate elements rather than full redrafting to avoid excessive claim drafting by the examiner.

name: How to suggest amendments for indefinite claims
description: Amendments may be suggested to overcome rejection for indefinite claims (e.g., delete vague term like 'high-speed' or replace with 'speed ranging from ㅇㅇ to ㅇㅇ' as described in the description).
guidance: Use specific numerical ranges or clear definitions from the description to remove indefiniteness; cite the paragraph in the description from which the specific wording is taken.

name: Avoid suggesting amendment to already patentable claims
description: It is inappropriate to suggest amendment to claims that are already patentable (i.e., avoid proposing to add elements from patentable claims into other claims in a way that undermines granted patentable subject-matter).
guidance: Example: do not suggest adding a structure that is currently patentable as-is into another claim if that would be counterproductive; avoid undermining claim strategy by unnecessary incorporation.

name: Avoid excessively narrowing the claim scope
description: Do not suggest amendments that excessively narrow the scope of patent claims (e.g., combining multiple claims or adding many descriptive elements leading to undue narrowing).
guidance: Examples show suggestions that over-limit claims are inappropriate; examiner should balance overcoming rejection with retaining reasonable protection scope.

name: Avoid causing new grounds for rejection by suggestion
description: Examiner should avoid suggesting amendments that could introduce ambiguity or relationships that create new grounds for rejection (e.g., adding an element that makes the relation between parts ambiguous).
guidance: If adding an element to a claim could cause ambiguity leading to new rejections, suggest adding it to an intermediate dependent claim rather than directly to the independent claim.

name: Prohibition on suggesting new matter or broadening at final-rejection stage
description: It is not appropriate to suggest introduction of new matter or broadening a claim when notifying the grounds for final rejection necessitated by amendment.
guidance: When issuing a final rejection necessitated by amendment, suggestions must not propose adding new subject-matter or enlarging claim scope beyond what was present in the relevant baseline (original filing or prior amendment as applicable).

name: Mechanistic inference about neurotransmission (GABA-A and mGluR5)
description: Interpretation of strain differences and drug effects in terms of underlying neurotransmitter systems: results suggest differences are mediated at least in part by GABA-A and mGluR5 transmission.
guidance: Combine behavioural, endocrine, and c-Fos data to support mechanistic claims about neurotransmitter systems. Use converging evidence (behaviour + hormonal + neural activation patterns) to justify conclusions about receptor-mediated transmission.

name: Definition of inventive step
description: If an invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art, the invention does not have an inventive step (Article 29(2) of the Patent Act).
guidance: The term is not defined in the Act, but the guideline states that an invention that 'could have been easily made' by a skilled person lacks inventive step. The examiner must decide whether the claimed invention could have been easily made alone or by combining prior art references; if so, inventive step is denied.

name: General principles of determining inventive step
description: Determine whether the claimed invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art from prior art references (alone or combined). If so, the invention lacks inventive step.
guidance: Apply the determination to each claim separately; novelty determination should come first (distinct from inventive-step determination). Examiners may notify applicants of novelty and inventive-step grounds together, but the analyses are distinct. For claims with multiple inventions/Markush groups, the examiner must precisely point out which invention is rejected and why.

name: Examiner's holistic method of determining inventive step
description: Examiners should consider the overall state of the art a skilled person would consider at filing, and thoroughly consider the invention's purpose, technical configuration, advantageous effects, and applicant arguments, focusing on the difficulty of the claimed technical configuration.
guidance: Determination should comprehensively weigh purpose/effectiveness and focus on whether the claimed configuration would have been difficult to arrive at for a skilled person.

name: Procedure for determining inventive step (stepwise)
description: 1) Specify the claimed invention; 2) Specify scope/content of prior art references from the viewpoint of a skilled person; 3) Choose the closest prior art and compare as a whole; 4) Determine whether the claimed invention could have been easily made in view of prior art or common general knowledge.
guidance: Specifying claimed invention and prior art scope uses the same methods as novelty determination. The combined elements of an invention should be compared as a whole (not separated) to corresponding elements in prior art.

name: Selection of prior art reference (relevant technical field)
description: As a principle, the prior art used for comparison should be selected from the same technical field or a reasonably relevant technical field to the problem, effect, and use of the claimed invention.
guidance: The 'same technical field' usually refers to the industrial field of application but can also be inferred from effects/functions of claim elements. A prior art from a different field can be used if it might be applied across fields or would be used by an applicant in solving the technical problem; examiner should consider relevance, closeness of problems, and similarity of function/work/operation. Examples (container cap vs. eruption closure; umbrella vs. parasol) illustrate relevance-based selection.

name: Close similarity of function, work, or operation
description: A close similarity in function, work, or operation between claimed invention and prior art (or between prior art references) supports a finding that a skilled person would arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: If functions/operations match, applying a component from one reference to another may be obvious (example: transferring a filtering part structure from automobile filter to home filter).

name: Consideration of advantageous effects to support inventive step
description: If matters defining a claimed invention achieve effects advantageous over prior art, those effects are considered to support inventive step.
guidance: Remarkable advantageous effects not foreseeable by a skilled person from the state of the art can justify granting inventive step even if combination seems straightforward. Particularly important for selection inventions and chemical inventions where effects are hard to predict. Examiner may consider applicant's arguments and experimental evidence only if effects are inferable from description/drawings or supported by evidence; unsupported assertions should not be considered. Case law references (Supreme Court decisions) illustrate when effects can overcome obviousness.

name: Definition of Earliest Benefit Date (EBD)
description: The EBD is the earliest filing date for which benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), and 37 CFR 1.78(d).
guidance: EBD is determined application-by-application. The EBD cannot be the filing date of a foreign application or the filing date of a provisional application to which benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e). For utility and plant applications, the EBD is also the 'patent term filing date' (the date from which the 20-year patent term is calculated under 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2)). See Fee Rule citations for further discussion.

name: Processing when insufficient or incorrect CAF payment
description: When the appropriate § 1.17(w) fee is not paid or authorized for charge to a deposit account, the USPTO will not enter benefit claims that require that fee; benefit claims not requiring the fee may still be entered.
guidance: The Filing Receipt will reflect only the benefit claims that were entered. Non-entry of specific benefit claims can change the application’s EBD (see Examples 16 and 17). Applicants should monitor Filing Receipts and correct by presenting the claim with the applicable fee if needed.

name: Art-recognized suitability for intended purpose supports obviousness
description: Selection of a known material based on its suitability for its intended use can support a prima facie obviousness determination.
guidance: Example: choice of a solvent with particular vapor pressure characteristics for printing ink (Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp.). When prior art teaches desired properties and a separate reference teaches specific materials having those properties, combining those teachings may render a claim obvious.

name: Graham factors to establish a prima facie case of obviousness
description: To make out a case of obviousness, examiners must apply the Supreme Court's Graham factors: (A) scope and content of the prior art; (B) differences between the prior art and the claims; (C) level of ordinary skill in the art; (D) evaluation of secondary considerations.
guidance: If a prima facie case is made, burden shifts to applicant to rebut. Use the Graham framework to organize fact-finding and ensure a rationale (see KSR). See In re Bell, Rijckaert, Oetiker for burden and analysis discussions.

name: When prior art is a genus, make findings on structure, properties, predictability, and number of species
description: For a prior-art genus, examiners should find: (A) the structure of the disclosed genus and any expressly described species; (B) any physical/chemical properties and utilities disclosed and limitations/problems; (C) predictability of the technology; (D) number of species encompassed, considering all variables.
guidance: These findings help determine whether the genus teaches or suggests the claimed species; document specifics about disclosed species and claimed species comparisons when relying on a genus reference.

name: Ascertain differences between the closest disclosed prior-art species and the claimed species
description: Identify the closest disclosed species/subgenus in the prior art and explicitly compare similarities and differences in structure, properties, and utilities to the claimed species.
guidance: The obviousness inquiry focuses on whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious (Stratoflex). Document why the chosen prior-art species is the closest and what the relevant differences are.

name: Consider whether one of ordinary skill would have had a reason to select the claimed species
description: After evaluating the Graham factors, determine whether there was a motivation or reason for a skilled artisan to select the claimed species/subgenus from the disclosed genus.
guidance: This is the key issue in genus-species cases—document teachings or suggestions in the prior art that would have motivated selection and explain how they lead to a prima facie case (Kulling; Panduit).

name: Consider any other relevant teaching (totality of the evidence)
description: Beyond enumerated categories, consider all relevant prior-art teachings that might support selection of the claimed species or subgenus.
guidance: The listed categories (size, express teachings, structural similarity, properties, predictability) are common but not exhaustive—document any unusual or additional teachings that bear on motivation or suggestion.

name: True homologous or isomeric relationship is not controlling
description: Prior art need not be a true homolog or isomer to render a claimed compound prima facie obvious; non-homologous but closely similar structures can suffice.
guidance: Cases (In re Payne; In re Mayne; In re Merck; In re Dillon) show that structural and property similarity—rather than formal homolog/isomer labels—can support obviousness. Conversely, biological/genetic analogies may differ (In re Bell; In re Deuel).

name: Presence or absence of a prior-art method for making the claimed compound is relevant
description: Whether the prior art discloses or makes obvious a method of making the claimed compound can affect the obviousness analysis for product claims.
guidance: Absence of a known or obvious method for making the compound at the relevant time may rebut a presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity (In re Maloney; In re Hoeksema). Consider whether methodology taught in the prior art would have enabled making the claimed compounds.

name: Presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity is overcome if no reasonable expectation of similar properties
description: The presumption that structural similarity renders a species obvious is rebutted where there is no reasonable expectation that the prior-art structures would share the claimed properties.
guidance: Document evidence showing unpredictability or lack of expectation of similar properties; without reasonable expectation of success, structural similarity alone will not sustain a prima facie obviousness rejection.

name: Conditions and evidentiary showing required for patent extension (value and inadequate remuneration)
description: An inventor is entitled to an extension only when the recompense received during the original term is not commensurate with the benefit conferred; the value of the invention must be demonstrated by experience or by the nature of the process or instrument and not rest in conjecture or mere assertions.
guidance: Burden: applicant must prove practical value in the arts and actual profit (or lack thereof) derived; improvements made since issuance cannot be the sole basis for value claimed; sufficiency of remuneration already obtained is a question of fact for each case. Practical negatives: patents in little demand or gone out of use will not be extended; evidence such as a contract to purchase for a substantial sum may demonstrate value. Cases/Ex parte decisions cited: Ex parte Lockwood; Ex parte Marston; Ex parte Roots; Ex parte Slemmons; Ex parte Behr.

name: Contents and bibliographic information in oath/declaration
description: The inventor’s oath or declaration must include certain inventor bibliographic information, name each inventor or joint inventor and, except as otherwise provided, be signed by each inventor, and identify the application to which it is directed.
guidance: See MPEP § 602.08(a)-(c) for details specific to inventor bibliographic information, required signature and name, and identification of the application. Unless included in an application data sheet (ADS), oaths and declarations must reference any foreign application for which priority is claimed (application number, country/office, and filing date).

name: 37 CFR 1.48(a) — Requirements for nonprovisional correction requests
description: A request to correct or change inventorship once inventorship has been established must include (1) an application data sheet (ADS) identifying each inventor by legal name and (2) the processing fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(i).
guidance: Inventorship is established upon the first submission of an ADS or an inventor’s oath/declaration. The ADS submitted with a 1.48(a) request must identify information being changed using underlining for insertions and strike-through or brackets for removals (per 37 CFR 1.76(c)(2)). 1.48(a) enables correction where improper inventorship was set forth or where prosecution leads to adding/deleting inventors (e.g., claims added or canceled).

name: Requirement to recite foreign priority applications
description: Unless included in an ADS, oaths and declarations must reference any foreign application for patent (or inventor’s certificate) for which priority is claimed, including foreign application number, country/office, and filing date of each foreign application to which priority is claimed.
guidance: See pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.63(c)(2) and MPEP § 602.03 for additional information. The applicant is required to recite all foreign applications filed prior to the application on which priority is claimed.

name: Review the entire application to assess support for claimed elements
description: Prior to determining whether the disclosure satisfies the written description requirement for the claimed subject matter, the examiner should review the claims and the entire specification, including the specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings, to understand how applicant provides support for the various features of the claimed invention.
guidance: Consider how applicant provides support for each element/step; an element may be critical where those skilled in the art would require it to determine possession. The review should determine the field of the invention and the level of skill/knowledge in the art, since these affect the specificity required. Rely on the specification (summary, detailed description), original claims, abstract, drawings, and sequence listings when appropriate.

name: Possession may be shown by reduction to practice, detailed drawings, or identifying characteristics
description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention. Possession may also be shown by a clear depiction of the invention in detailed drawings or in structural chemical formulas which permit a person skilled in the art to clearly recognize that applicant had possession of the claimed invention. An adequate written description may be shown by any description of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics so long as a person skilled in the art would recognize that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Examples: constructed embodiments or performed processes that meet all claim limitations (reduction to practice); detailed drawings; structural chemical formulas; deposits of biological materials per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. Identifying characteristics for biomolecules include sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length, restriction maps, etc. Functional descriptions coupled with known correlations between function and structure can suffice in some arts; function alone is inadequate where no such correlation exists. Case law examples cited (Pfaff, Cooper, Vas‑Cath, Eli Lilly, Enzo Biochem, Falkner, Capon).

name: Written description requirement for chemical and molecular inventions (precision required)
description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention requires a precise definition, such as by structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties, and not merely a wish or plan for obtaining the chemical invention claimed.
guidance: Merely describing assays or screening methods without disclosing the actual compounds that achieve the claimed result is insufficient. For biological macromolecules, while examples are not always necessary, adequate characterization or identifying information (structure, sequence, deposit) is often required to show possession. Case examples: Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle; Noelle v. Lederman; Falkner v. Inglis; Capon v. Eshhar.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre-AIA 112, para. 6) written description test
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6, it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.'
guidance: Adequacy under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112, para. 1 for a means-/step-plus-function limitation is satisfied if: (1) the written description adequately links or associates adequately described particular structure, material, or acts to the function recited; or (2) it is clear based on the facts of the application that one skilled in the art would have known what structure, material, or acts perform the function. Consider the original disclosure in the summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Note: a rejection under 112(a)/para. 2 cannot stand where there is adequate description in the specification regarding means-plus-function recitations that are not challenged for being unclear.

name: Species (single embodiment) vs genus claim analysis and checklist
description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment or species is analyzed as a claim drawn to a single embodiment or species; a claim that encompasses two or more embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus. For each claim drawn to a single embodiment/species, determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice, a reduction to drawings/structural formulas, or sufficiently detailed identifying characteristics.
guidance: Follow the stepwise checklist: (A) Determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention. (B) If not, determine whether the invention is complete as evidenced by reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed to show possession. (C) If not, determine whether the invention has been set forth in terms of distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficiently detailed to show possession. Then (1) ask whether the application describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole — if yes, written description satisfied; (2) if not, determine whether other relevant identifying characteristics (e.g., function coupled with known correlation to structure) would allow a skilled artisan to recognize possession. Disclosure of function alone, without correlation, is insufficient; compare arts where software or microprocessor disclosures may be adequate versus unpredictable biological arts where more detail is required.

name: Effect of maturity and predictability of the art on required disclosure
description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with the scientific and technological knowledge already in existence. There is generally an inverse correlation between the level of skill/knowledge in the art and the specificity of disclosure necessary to satisfy the written description requirement.
guidance: In mature technologies where knowledge/skill is high, written description questions should rarely be raised for originally filed claims even if the specification discloses only a method and function (example: microprocessors). In emerging, unpredictable, or less predictable technologies, more evidence/detail is required to show possession (examples: biological molecules where unpredictability demands structural detail rather than mere functional description). Use prior art to gauge maturity of the field.

name: Do not base rejections on lack of detail for well-known information; applicant's burden when invoking limiting language
description: Information which is well known in the art need not be described in detail in the specification. Conversely, if an applicant contends that additional steps/materials in the prior art are excluded by a recitation like 'consisting essentially of,' the applicant has the burden of showing that the introduction of additional steps/components would materially change the characteristics of applicant’s invention.
guidance: Assess what is conventional or well known in the art (citing Hybritech and related cases). Where applicant uses intermediate claim language ('consisting essentially of'), absent clear specification of what materially changes the invention, treat it as open for prior art purposes. Applicant must provide evidence/specification detail to justify narrower construction.

name: Balance public notice and fair scope of protection
description: Claim construction should balance the public notice function of patents with the competing policy of a fair scope of protection for patentees.
guidance: Interpretations should facilitate equitable treatment of patentees and the public and produce predictability; courts should ensure patentees 'understand, and correctly describe, just what he has invented, and for what he claims a patent' (Merrill v. Yeomans).

name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence (Vitronics)
description: Intrinsic evidence of record — the claims, specification, prosecution history and cited prior art — is the primary source for claim meaning and should be given primacy over extrinsic evidence.
guidance: The specification is 'usually dispositive; it is the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term.' Rely on intrinsic evidence first to preserve doctrines of patent law and settled expectations (Vitronics).

name: Extrinsic evidence only to resolve remaining ambiguity
description: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, treatises, dictionaries) may be used only when intrinsic evidence leaves ambiguity and may not be used to contradict intrinsic evidence or vary the scope of the claims.
guidance: If intrinsic evidence provides sufficient clarity, reliance on extrinsic evidence is improper; extrinsic evidence may 'help the court come to the proper understanding of the claim term' but cannot trump intrinsic sources (Vitronics).

name: Interpret terms from perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art
description: Claims must be construed from the viewpoint of one of ordinary skill in the art; judges should attempt to replicate that perspective.
guidance: Use extrinsic evidence when necessary to ascertain the level of ordinary skill and the art-recognized meaning of technical terms; for non-technical words a dictionary may be unnecessary (Brookhill-Wilk; Microsoft).

name: Characterize whether a specification feature is exemplary or essential
description: In deciding whether to import a specification feature into a claim, determine if a person of ordinary skill would view the feature as merely exemplary or essential to the invention's character.
guidance: If the specification 'as a whole suggests that the very character of the invention requires the limitation be a part of every embodiment,' then importing may be appropriate; if merely exemplary or used only for best mode, do not import (Alloc; Sumace Roots; SciMed; Wang Labs; Toro).

name: Use claim differentiation only as an aid when ambiguity persists
description: Claim differentiation (not reading a limitation into a claim that appears in another claim) is a proper secondary tool where intrinsic/extrinsic evidence fail to yield a single clear definition.
guidance: Apply claim differentiation sparingly to avoid overshadowing the express intentions of the draftsman; reserved for when review of intrinsic/extrinsic evidence fails to produce a single meaning (SRI Int'l; Hormone Research).

name: Constrict interpretation to preserve validity when multiple reasonable meanings exist
description: When several reasonable interpretations exist and one would render the claim invalid, construe claims, where practicable, to preserve validity consistent with 35 U.S.C. § 282.
guidance: This doctrine is limited: the preserving-construction must be practicable, based on sound claim-construction principles, and must not revise or ignore explicit claim language (Liebel-Flarsheim; Generation II).

name: Consider prosecution history and USPTO context
description: Prosecution history and the manner in which the USPTO examined/understood the claims are relevant intrinsic considerations.
guidance: Because the USPTO gives claims their 'broadest reasonable interpretation' during prosecution, courts should consult intrinsic evidence (specification, cited prior art, prosecution arguments) to avoid interpretations at odds with the USPTO's understanding (In re Morris; In re American Academy of Sciences).

name: Treat the patent as a fully integrated written instrument
description: A patent should be read as an integrated whole; terms must be defined in a way that comports with the instrument as a whole.
guidance: Claim construction is a 'necessarily sophisticated analysis of the whole [patent] document' and a term's meaning must align with the document in its entirety (Markman).

name: Effect of prior art disclosure on novelty and inventive step
description: A prior art disclosure can be adverse to patentability. For novelty, generally all elements of the claimed invention must be disclosed in a single document; for inventive step (obviousness), several pieces of prior art may be combined to demonstrate non‑obviousness.
guidance: Novelty: require that a single prior document disclose all claim elements. Inventive step: multiple prior art items may be relied upon and combined. National examples: Brazil, Bulgaria and Canada all distinguish novelty (single-document) from inventive step (combination permitted).

name: Novelty test (single‑publication/enablement requirement)
description: For novelty, a single prior publication must disclose the subject‑matter of the claim so clearly that a skilled person could produce the claimed invention without exercise of inventive skill.
guidance: Canadian articulation (Beloit / Free World Trust): the prior publication must contain so clear a direction that a skilled person reading and following it would in every case and without possibility of error be led to the claimed invention.

name: Patentably distinct embodiments cannot be included in same design application
description: Embodiments that are patentably distinct from one another do not constitute a single inventive concept and thus may not be included in the same design application. Multiple embodiments of a single inventive concept may be included only if they are patentably indistinct. (Cites: In re Rubinfield; In re Platner.)
guidance: If embodiments have overall appearances that are not basically the same, or if differences are not minor/patentably indistinct or are not shown to be obvious over analogous prior art, they must be treated as distinct. Designs covering segregable, patentably distinct parts require separate patents; combination vs subcombination subject matter, if patentably distinct, must be supported by separate claims. Examiner should group obvious variations together as a single inventive concept; otherwise restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121.

name: Statutory (“same invention”) double patenting (35 U.S.C. 171) standard
description: A statutory same-invention double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 applies where identical designs with identical scope are claimed twice (design-design).
guidance: This rejection prevents issuance of a second patent for a design already patented. A terminal disclaimer may not be used to overcome a 'same invention' type double patenting rejection. Use form paragraph 15.23.02 following such rejections.

name: Nonstatutory double patenting — overall appearance comparison rule
description: To determine nonstatutory double patenting, the examiner must compare the overall appearance of the claimed design in the application with the overall appearance of the claimed design in the conflicting application or patent; the claim must be considered as a whole rather than by isolated elements.
guidance: Unlike anticipation/obviousness where elements may be considered individually, the nonstatutory double patenting analysis focuses on overall design characteristics. If overall appearances are basically the same and differences are insufficient to patentably distinguish (de minimis or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill), nonstatutory double patenting may be appropriate. See MPEP §804 (II.B).

name: Three-part test for nonstatutory double patenting when scope differs
description: When designs have differing scope, a nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate if: (A) the difference in scope is minor and patentably indistinct; (B) allowance of the later claim would extend patent protection fully disclosed/covered by the earlier claim; and (C) no terminal disclaimer has been filed.
guidance: This often arises between a combination (narrow claim) and a subcombination/element (broad claim). Examiner must determine whether the narrower subject matter is fully disclosed and covered by the broader claim of the reference. If the broader claim does not disclose the narrower claim, NSDP rejection is inappropriate.

name: One-way vs two-way distinctness determinations
description: Design-design nonstatutory double patenting rejections do not always have to be made in both conflicting applications; if the rejection is only appropriate in one direction, it is proper to reject only one application. However, design-utility situations require a two-way distinctness determination for the rejection to be proper.
guidance: Examiners should follow criteria in MPEP §804 II.B.4 and II.B.5 to decide whether one-way or two-way determinations are needed. Consider common inventorship, common applicant, or ownership and whether claims create a one-way rather than mutual indistinctness.

name: Claim scope measures (ICC and ICL) for claim-breadth control
description: Use independent claim count (ICC) and shortest independent claim length (ICL) from the Patent Claims Research Dataset to capture claim scope (breadth) for each application.
guidance: Include ICC and ICL as application-level co-variates in regression specifications to control for claim scope when estimating effects on §101 rejections. These variables are available for public data; not always available in proprietary dataset.

name: Abstractness of application language
description: A text-based measure of abstract language in patent claims derived from PGPub or granted patent claim text (USPTO bulk XML), computed per application.
guidance: Include abstractness as a covariate and as an interaction term with treatment indicators to test whether Alice had differential effects for more abstractly worded applications. Abstractness variables rely on public-text sources and thus are not available for the proprietary dataset used in certain analyses.

name: Inclusion of application- and cell-level co-variates for non-random assignment
description: Control for multiple patent characteristics to mitigate omitted-variable bias: claim-scope measures (ICC, ICL), abstractness, average number of independent claims, average word count in claims, average examiner variance, number of examiners, number of applications, average applications per examiner, and variance in abstractness.
guidance: Select co-variates appropriate to dataset (some abstractness/claim scope measures unavailable in proprietary data). Averaged or variance measures are used in technology-half-year models. These covariates address potential confounders related to both assignment to treatment group and outcome variation.

name: Specific disclosure vs generic claim principle
description: A specific disclosure does take away the novelty of a generic claim embracing that disclosure, whereas a generic disclosure does not normally take away the novelty of any specific example falling within that disclosure.
guidance: Examples given: a disclosure of copper takes away the novelty of 'metal' as a generic concept, but a generic disclosure (e.g., of a general teaching) normally does not deprive a specific embodiment of novelty. Case law and Guidelines support this distinction (see decisions T 651/91, T 776/07).

name: Legal fiction of Article 54(4) and (5) EPC — new medical/therapeutic uses
description: Article 54(4) and (5) EPC acknowledge the notional novelty of substances or compositions even when they are as such already comprised in the state of the art, provided they are claimed for a new use in a method which Article 53(c) EPC excludes as such from patent protection.
guidance: This allows, for example, first medical use claims to be treated as novel and to receive broad protection covering any use in a medical method even if only one specific use is disclosed (see case law T 128/82, T 36/83 and G 2/08). This principle complements Article 53(c)'s exclusion of medical methods from patentability of methods (not products).

name: Restriction of search for clarity problems
description: If the complexity lies in lack of clarity, the search will be restricted first, and the non-unity objection applied to the clear parts of the claimed subject-matter.
guidance: An invitation to pay additional fees may remark on clarity problems related to further inventions. The EPO as ISA may ask the applicant to clarify the subject-matter to be searched using the procedure in GL/PCT-EPO B-VIII, 3.3–3.4.

name: Types of limitations of scope of the search report
description: Possible limitations include: (i) a declaration issued instead of the search report (Art.17(2)(a)); (ii) an incomplete search report (Art.17(2)(b)); (iii) a partial international search report due to lack of unity (Art.17(3)(a) and Rule 13); (iv) an incomplete search report due to missing sequence listings (GL/PCT-EPO B-VIII, 3.2).
guidance: The ISR must indicate whether the subject of the search was restricted and which claims have or have not been searched. The reasons for no search should be indicated in the declaration. In some cases the extent/reasons for restriction may be indicated only in the WO-ISA rather than the ISR.

name: Relationship between cited documents and claims; identification of relevant passages
description: The search report and accompanying documentation should set out the relationship between documents cited and the claims, and identify the relevant passages in prior art documents.
guidance: Ensure clear mapping from cited documents to specific claims and specify the passages relied upon (see GL/ISPE references).

name: Scope of the written opinion (WO-ISA)
description: The WO-ISA gives a preliminary and non-binding opinion on whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step and to be industrially applicable. When appropriate, it also addresses added subject-matter, unity, insufficient disclosure and clarity or support issues, as well as formal defects.
guidance: Findings must be consistent with document categories in the search report and with other issues raised (e.g., lack of unity or limitation of the search). If there are no defects the WO-ISA should state reasons why the application is considered to fulfil the requirements.

name: Reasoned objections for novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability
description: A full explanation of the conclusions reached should always be given for all searched claims, regardless of whether the conclusion is positive or negative. The opinion given in the WO-ISA is restricted to what has actually been searched and this should be made clear.
guidance: Normally only one independent claim in each category is treated in detail; for negative conclusions regarding further independent claims and dependent claims comments may be shorter, but full explanation should be given for searched claims.

name: Clarity, conciseness, support and formal defects reporting
description: Major clarity, conciseness or support issues will be mentioned under Box VIII unless they make a meaningful search impossible (in which case treated under Section III). Formal defects and minor clarity issues are dealt with under Boxes VII and VIII respectively.
guidance: If the application is severely deficient and claims will need drastic redrafting, it is not necessary to make objections about minor clarity or formal issues.

name: WO-ISA in relation to lack of unity and restricted searches
description: In cases of lack of unity where more than one invention has been searched, for each invention searched one independent claim in each category must be treated in detail. When the search was restricted, the WO-ISA opinion is normally restricted to what has actually been searched and must be consistent with the restrictions.
guidance: See GL/PCT-EPO B-VII and B-VIII for further detail on unity and restriction handling; arguments and objections must align with the declared scope of the search.

name: Basis and scope of the Supplementary International Search (SIS)
description: The SIS is always made on the claims as originally filed (or a translation) and at the EPO the scope of a SIS is the same as for any other international search carried out by the EPO and is not limited to documentation in a specific language.
guidance: If the main ISA ISR is available it will be taken into account; the SISA will not automatically adopt limitations made by the main ISA but will assess appropriateness case-by-case under EPO practice.

name: Structural variables to include
description: Include CPC classification (Class A,B,C,...), USPTO-generated AI patent measure, industry flags (ICT, biotechnology, high tech) defined via EU classification, number of CPC classes, ln(number of claims), research-institution assignee flag, and Fama-French 12 industry classification. For application prediction, include natural log of market capitalization (nearest quarter prior to publication, inflation-adjusted).
guidance: These structural/contextual variables provide critical context for textual embeddings and should be combined with the embedding vector in the feature matrix; omit variables not available in processed PatentView application data when necessary.

name: Acknowledge data limitations on rejection intensity
description: The data capture the incidence of any obviousness rejection but do not reveal the full force (e.g., whether it covers one claim or many, how easy it is to overcome).
guidance: Use relative-share measures and multiple robustness checks rather than relying on raw counts; explicitly note the limitation when interpreting results.

name: Attack the prima facie case procedural defects (preferable to simple rebuttal)
description: Tip 2: Attacking the prima facie case rather than rebutting may help the resultant possibility of avoiding amending claims and prosecution history estoppel.
guidance: Focus on showing the examiner failed to meet the initial burden (e.g., conclusory reasoning, incomplete Graham analysis) so you avoid creating a record that limits future claim scope.

name: Full Graham analysis is required (all four Graham factors)
description: Obviousness depends on the Graham factual inquiries: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) evaluation of any relevant secondary considerations. All four must be analyzed (KSR; MPEP §2141).
guidance: Challenge any faulty or incomplete Graham analysis; insist examiner address each factor and articulate factual findings supporting any legal conclusion of obviousness.

name: Recognition of problem is not recognition of solution
description: Recognition of a need or problem in the art does not render the particular solution obvious; the prior art must suggest the particular cure or solution, not merely the problem (Cardiac Pacemakers).
guidance: Distinguish general motivation to solve a problem from motivation to create the claimed specific solution; demand explanation of how prior art suggested the claimed approach.

name: Prior art teaches away (evidence of discouragement is strong evidence of nonobviousness)
description: A reference teaches away when it suggests that developments from its disclosures are unlikely to produce the applicant's objective; mere disclosure of alternatives or unfavorable description is usually insufficient—there must be clear discouragement (In re Gurley; In re Fulton; Syntex v. Apotex).
guidance: Show explicit discouragement in the references or prosecution history that would have led artisans away from the claimed approach; be mindful that teaching-away is typically a high bar.

name: Interview the examiner/case to demonstrate cited reference does not teach modification/combination
description: Tip 14: Use interviews and the cited reference's file history and statement of reasons for allowance to show the cited reference does not teach or motivate the claimed modification/combination.
guidance: Conduct interviews to present arguments about specific gaps in the reference, show how none of the reference's examples reach the claimed substitution, and obtain a clear record (Reasons for Allowance) if the examiner accepts.

name: Submit objective indicia of nonobviousness and establish nexus/commensurability
description: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) include: (1) showing criticality or unexpected results; (2) resolution of a long-felt need; (3) failure of others; (4) commercial success; (5) industry acquiescence/licensing; (6) copying by others; (7) disbelief and acclaim by experts; (8) admissions of nonobviousness by an adversary; (9) near-simultaneous invention. A nexus between the indicia and the claimed invention must be shown and evidence must be commensurate in scope with claims (MPEP §716; Demaco; Allergan).
guidance: Provide documentary evidence linking the indicia to the claimed features (sales data, licensing, expert statements, comparative tests). Ensure nexus and scope alignment; unsupported assertions will be disregarded.

name: Use comparative testing to show unexpected results (strict evidentiary rules)
description: Comparative test data showing unexpectedly improved properties can rebut a prima facie case. Requirements: compare to the closest prior art disclosure (closest species), tests must be commensurate in scope with claims, results must be actually unexpected (differ in kind, not just degree), and ideally agree testing scope with examiner beforehand (MPEP §716.02).
guidance: Before testing, interview the examiner to agree on what testing would be persuasive; test against the closest disclosure and document methods/data fully; be aware that testing only one species may suffice only if supported by rationale that other species would be equivalently affected.

name: Rule of liberal construction in favor of the patentee
description: A liberal construction is given to the patent when its terms are so interpreted as to sustain the patent and cause it to protect the actual invention; doubtful points must be resolved so as to support the patentee's claims.
guidance: Apply legitimate meanings to words/phrases that make the claim/description correspond to the essential characteristics of the true invention; courts recognize claims/descriptions may be unskilfully drawn and should be read liberally to secure the actual invention. (See §736 and multiple cited cases.)

name: Claims construed by their own language; clear claims control
description: Claims must be construed by the language which is employed; when a claim is clear and explicit its language controls and need not be aided by other parts.
guidance: Do not rely on what might have been employed; treat clear claims as definitive. Only when claims are ambiguous should the specification and other parts be consulted. (See §737, §742.)

name: Construction must not be elastic or ambiguous
description: The rule of liberal construction does not permit interpretations that render claims elastic or ambiguous; interpretation aims to make the indefinite exact and the doubtful plain.
guidance: Use interpretative power to remove, not create, ambiguities; do not erect or destroy limitations arbitrarily. (See §738.)

name: Claims cannot be enlarged by construction beyond explicit description
description: A patent is not to be enlarged by construction beyond what is explicitly described and claimed; limited claims are not to be expanded into general ones by implication.
guidance: Do not cover matter intentionally omitted or later inventions by construing claims broadly; if the patent does not cover something the patentee intended, the remedy is amendment, not construction. (See §737–§739.)

name: Specification and drawings used to construe claims when claims ambiguous
description: When claims are obscure or capable of different constructions, the whole description, drawings, model, oath, and title should be considered as exponents and interpreters of the claims.
guidance: Use the specification as the inventor's own interpreter of claim meaning and essential qualities; be mindful that no descriptive portion controls others and that the specification should be read to learn what the patentees meant to claim. (See §742.)

name: Patentee entitled to protection for all forms of his invention unless he restricted himself
description: A patentee is entitled to such a construction as will enable the patent to protect all forms of his invention, even if he described but one, unless the claims restrict him to certain forms.
guidance: Give effect to the manifest design and essential attributes of the invention to protect other forms that embody the same inventive principle, subject to the literal terms and any clear restrictions in the claims. (See §740.)

name: Use of prosecution history and inventor's pre-grant statements
description: The position assumed before the Patent Office — application, claims asserted, amendments, disclaimers, objections answered or avoided — are proper matters for examination in construing the patent.
guidance: Examine correspondence, file history, and concessions made to the Patent Office; a patentee cannot later insist the patent covers matter he was compelled to abandon. Rejected applications and amendments may limit scope. Post-issue statements by the inventor have little weight. (See §741.)

name: Entire patent construed together as an indivisible instrument
description: In ascertaining the purpose of the patent, the entire patent must be construed together and effect given to all its parts (claims, specification, drawings, model, oath, title) as members of a single instrument.
guidance: When claims are ambiguous, look through the whole patent to ascertain what is claimed; no one descriptive part may unilaterally control others. (See §742 and multiple case citations.)

name: Details and peculiarities are not essential unless claimed or described as such
description: Peculiarities of shape or arrangement, or mere details recommended in the description, are not to be construed as essential features of the invention unless the description or claim suggests them.
guidance: Do not construe non-essential details as distinct limitations to save a claim; only features expressly or clearly indicated as essential should limit claim scope. (See §738.)

name: Claims for special arrangements limited to those special parts and arrangement
description: A claim that is for the special arrangement of parts must be construed to cover only the special parts and special arrangement described.
guidance: Do not treat a claim to a particular arrangement as a broad claim to the general idea; construction must respect the specificity of such claims. (See §739.)

name: Patents are construed in view of human knowledge — not as intending impossibilities
description: The specification will be construed in view of the state of human knowledge and not as intending the impossible; the description is limited by what appears new in the art at the invention date.
guidance: Avoid construing disclosures as claiming more than what contemporary knowledge made possible; restrict claims consistent with the art's capabilities at that time. (See §740.)

name: No construction can supply what the inventor deliberately omitted or was denied in prosecution
description: Claims may not be construed to cover matter the patentee intentionally omitted or was forced to abandon in the Patent Office; acquiescence in rejection restricts later claim breadth.
guidance: The records of the Patent Office (applications, rejections, amendments) may be examined, and an assignee cannot expand scope to cover matter excluded by claim allowance/rejection. (See §741–§742.)

name: POP discretionary joinder under 35 U.S.C. § 315(c)
description: Standards for whether the Board will allow a petitioner to be joined to a proceeding in which it is already a party and whether new issues may be joined into an existing proceeding under § 315(c).
guidance: § 315(c) provides discretion to allow same-party joinder and joinder of new issues; the existence of a time bar under § 315(b) is one factor among several. The Board will exercise discretion only in limited circumstances—where fairness requires it and to avoid undue prejudice. Exemplary factors to consider: actions taken by patent owner in co-pending litigation (e.g., late addition of newly asserted claims); conduct of the parties; the stage and schedule of an existing inter partes review; non-exclusive factors from General Plastic Industrial Co., Ltd. v. Canon Kabushiki Kaisha (factors supporting exercise of discretion to deny institution under § 314(a)).

name: Motion to Amend (MTA) requirements and guidance (Lectrosonics)
description: Substantive and procedural requirements the Board expects when a patent owner files a motion to amend during an AIA trial.
guidance: Guidance includes: allowance for contingent motions to amend; the burden of persuasion the Office applies when considering patentability of substitute claims; requirement that a patent owner propose a reasonable number of substitute claims; requirement that the amendment respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial; attention to the scope of the proposed substitute claims; requirement that a patent owner provide a claim listing with its motion to amend; default page limits that apply to motion to amend briefing; and the duty of candor. (This guidance reflects statutory/regulatory requirements as interpreted in Lectrosonics v. Zaxcom.)

name: Scope of grounds considered for substitute claims (§311(b) v. §316(d))
description: Limits on petitioners and the Board with respect to grounds of unpatentability for existing claims and for substitute claims proposed in an MTA.
guidance: § 311(b) limits a petitioner to requesting cancellation of existing claims only under §§ 102 and 103. However, § 316(d) does not prevent the Board from considering other grounds of unpatentability (e.g., § 101) with respect to substitute claims not yet part of the patent; petitioners may raise, and the Board may consider, such other grounds for substitute claims.

name: Denial of institution for inefficient use of resources (§314(a) / SAS considerations)
description: When the Board may deny institution of a petition because proceeding would be an inefficient use of Board resources.
guidance: Panel may evaluate challenges and determine whether, in the interests of efficient administration of the Office and the integrity of the patent system (see 35 U.S.C. § 316(b)), the entire petition should be denied under § 314(a) when petitioner demonstrates a reasonable likelihood of prevailing only for a limited subset of claims or grounds. Examples: institution denied where only two dependent claims out of 20 had a reasonable likelihood of prevailing; institution on all claims/grounds based on arguments directed to only two claims/one ground is inefficient.

name: Motion to lift a stay after a Final Written Decision (FWD)
description: Standards the Board applies when a patent owner moves to lift a stay of a parallel proceeding after a Final Written Decision issues.
guidance: If PO files a motion to lift a stay after a FWD, the Board typically will lift the stay absent reasons not to do so. The Board typically will lift a stay if PO proposes amendments in a reissue or reexamination in a meaningful way not previously considered by the Office. Meaningful amendments include narrowing the scope of claims considered in the AIA proceeding or otherwise attempting to resolve issues identified in the FWD.

name: Reexamination procedures and interaction with appeals
description: How ex parte reexamination proceedings proceed and interact with Federal Circuit appeals on the same patent.
guidance: Unlike reissue, POs cannot abandon ex parte reexamination once started; reexaminations proceed with special dispatch to completion (35 U.S.C. § 305). After the Office lifts a stay (or determines a stay is not appropriate), reexamination typically will continue to completion notwithstanding a Federal Circuit appeal of a FWD on the same patent. If the Office identifies allowable subject matter or determines claims unpatentable, it typically will issue a NIRC and reexamination certificate even if a related Federal Circuit appeal is ongoing—unless PO timely files a notice of appeal in the reexamination. To prevent a reexamination certificate from canceling original patent claims that are separately on appeal at the Federal Circuit, PO must timely file an appeal of any final rejection in reexamination to the Board.

name: Final written decision scope after revised MTA filing
description: What the Final Written Decision (FWD) will address when a revised motion to amend has been filed.
guidance: When a patent owner files a revised MTA, the Final Written Decision addresses only the substitute claims at issue in the latest filed MTA (i.e., the most recent set of proposed substitute claims).

name: Claim scope restriction requirement (Art.3 IX)
description: Claims filed at INPI must claim subject equal to or more restricted than the one considered patentable by the Office of Earlier Examination for the same family, prohibiting inclusion of subject the Office did not search or technically examine; differences due to translation are permitted.

name: Documents to attach to participation request (Art.4 V a–g)
description: Request must present, in the annex, specified documents: (a) copy of cover proving Article 3 VI definition; (b) copy proving Article 3 VII compliance; (c) copy proving Article 3 VIII compliance; (d) copy of non-patenting prior art cited in any technical examination report of the Office of Earlier Examination, or a statement that none were cited; (e) copy of the claim frame as approved by the Office of Earlier Examination; (f) modified patent application to comply with Article 3 IX or a statement that the application already complies; (g) table of correspondence of the claim frame (Annex I model) evidencing correlation between claims considered patentable and new claims presented to INPI, or a declaration that the new claims are mere translation of the partner office's claims.
guidance: §3: If attached documents are in languages other than Portuguese, English or Spanish, provide translation into one of those languages. §4: Presentation of documents issued by INPI is not required. The table of correspondence must follow Annex I model.

name: Elements/examples of procedural due-process protections
description: Specific protections showing due process: notice of charges, ability to respond to allegations, opportunity to testify at length in own defense, present witnesses and evidence, cross‑examine witnesses, be represented by counsel, and make arguments.
guidance: When assessing a due-process claim, the Director examines the record to confirm these procedural opportunities existed; documentary proof (e.g., notices, filings, hearing transcripts, counsel participation) is strong evidence that due process was afforded.

name: Provisional application conversion to nonprovisional: timing, fees, and effects
description: A provisional application may be converted to a nonprovisional application and accorded the original filing date of the provisional, but conversion will not entitle applicant to a refund of fees paid in the provisional. A request to convert must be accompanied by the fee in § 1.17(i) and an amendment including at least one claim as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112(b), unless the provisional already contains at least one such claim. The resulting nonprovisional must include filing/search/examination fees, the inventor's oath or declaration, and any surcharge required by § 1.16(f) if those items were not present on the provisional filing date. The request must be filed prior to abandonment of the provisional or expiration of 12 months after its filing date.
guidance: Conversion causes the patent term to be measured from at least the provisional filing date; applicants are cautioned that conversion (versus claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e)) may have adverse patent term impacts. No refund or fee credit applies from provisional to nonprovisional.

name: Filing date rules for nonprovisional and design applications (post-Dec 18, 2013)
description: Except for design applications, for applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) on or after December 18, 2013, the filing date of a nonprovisional application is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received by the Office. For a design application (except a CPA under 1.53(d)), the filing date is the date on which the specification as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, including at least one claim, and any required drawings are received.
guidance: These amendments implement PLTIA changes. Although minimal requirements may secure a filing date, applicants are advised that meeting minimal filing-date requirements is not a best practice; include claims and drawings where appropriate to ensure adequate disclosure and avoid loss of rights.

name: 37 CFR 1.53(d) CPA-specific requirements and filing deadline events
description: A CPA filed under 37 CFR 1.53(d) (a nonprovisional CPA filed on or after December 1, 1997) may be used only for continuation or divisional (not continuation-in-part) of a design application. The prior nonprovisional application must be complete as defined by 37 CFR 1.51(b) (except for the inventor’s oath/declaration in some cases) and contain an ADS indicating name, residence, and mailing address of each inventor. Any application filed under 1.53(d) must disclose and claim only subject matter disclosed in the prior nonprovisional application and must name as inventors the same or fewer inventors than in the prior application. Under 1.53(d), the filing date assigned is the date on which a request, on a separate paper, for an application under 1.53(d) is filed. An application under 1.53(d) must be filed before the earliest of: (A) payment of the issue fee on the prior application (unless a petition under 1.313(c) is granted); (B) abandonment of the prior application; or (C) termination of proceedings on the prior application.
guidance: CPAs have narrow eligibility (design-only, continuity constraints) and strict timing; ensure subject matter and inventor naming conform to the prior application and that the CPA request is timely filed before the enumerated triggering events.

name: Use of BRI to determine abstraction
description: Determine the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim in view of the specification to decide if the claim limitation falls within an enumerated grouping.
guidance: If at least one embodiment within the BRI of the limitation(s), when viewed in context of the claim as a whole, falls within an enumerated grouping, then the claim recites an abstract idea and requires further analysis at Step 2A Prong Two.

name: Do not rely on examples as basis for rejection
description: Claim concepts should not be compared to prior §101 examples to determine abstract idea status.
guidance: Compare claimed concepts to the enumerated groupings in the 2019 PEG instead. Examples may illustrate application of groupings for particular fact situations but should not be required models for applicants. Use new Examples 37–42 to understand 2019 PEG application; exercise caution with Examples 1–36.

name: Definition of 'integration into a practical application' (Step 2A Prong Two)
description: Integration requires additional element(s) (or combination) to apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception so the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception.
guidance: Identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements meaningfully limit the exception. This is a new analytical step not found in prior guidance.

name: Distinction between Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B
description: Step 2A Prong Two evaluates whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application but does not consider whether those elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity; Step 2B evaluates inventive concept including conventionality.
guidance: Because Prong Two omits the conventionality check, claims with conventional elements can nonetheless integrate an exception at Prong Two. Step 2B must be applied where appropriate to assess 'significantly more.'

name: Improvement-to-technology analysis at Step 2A
description: When considering whether a claim pertains to an improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology, analyze the improvement without reference to whether the elements are well-understood, routine, conventional.
guidance: Refer to MPEP 2106.04(a) and 2106.05(a) for discussion of improvements insofar as they do not contradict the 2019 PEG; the analysis focuses on whether the claim pertains to a technological improvement.

name: Step 2B (inventive concept / 'significantly more') requirements
description: Step 2B analysis (inventive concept) is unchanged and evaluates whether claimed elements add significantly more than the judicial exception, including assessing whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
guidance: When an examiner asserts that an element (or combination) is well-understood, routine, conventional activity, the examiner must support that assertion with evidence consistent with the Berkheimer memo (use one of memo options 1–4).

name: Reevaluation when Prong Two finds insignificant extra-solution activity
description: If Step 2A Prong Two concludes an additional element is insignificant extra-solution activity, the claim must be reevaluated under Step 2B.
guidance: If Step 2B finds the element unconventional or otherwise more than routine, that may indicate an inventive concept and render the claim eligible. Other Step 2B considerations may not need reevaluation if the answer will be the same.

name: Handling applications previously rejected under prior guidance
description: When next acting on applications with pre-2019 PEG §101 rejections, the examiner must analyze claims under the 2019 PEG and withdraw prior rejections where appropriate.
guidance: Withdraw prior §101 rejection if the examiner determines the claim does not recite a judicial exception, integrates the exception into a practical application, or provides an inventive concept. A §101 rejection may be made final only if the basic thrust of the rejection remains the same as in the previous Office action.

name: When a change constitutes a new ground of rejection
description: A new ground of rejection exists when a rejection relies upon new facts or a new rationale not previously raised to the applicant; certain changes do not constitute a new ground.
guidance: Not new grounds: maintaining that claim recites an abstract idea but changing explanation to refer to enumerated groupings; relying on same Step 2B considerations; changing form paragraphs. If basic thrust is changed, prosecution must be reopened and next action cannot be final.

name: Office action explanation requirement
description: When making a §101 rejection the Office action must provide an explanation why each claim is patent ineligible that is sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant notice and enable an effective response.
guidance: For abstract ideas, explain which specific limitation(s) correspond to an enumerated grouping or justify why a limitation is treated as an abstract idea if it does not fall within the enumerated groupings (rare and requires Director approval). Also explain why the claim does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.

name: Citing court decisions consistently with PEG
description: Examiners may cite court decisions to support identification of claimed subject matter as an abstract idea, but the identification must be consistent with the 2019 PEG and its enumerated groupings.
