guidance: Address applicant's arguments regarding specific cases similarly to how examiners address case-based arguments in other patentability grounds. Indicating the appropriate grouping(s) for a previously-identified abstract idea does not change the basic thrust of the rejection.

name: Use of word counts for key briefs
description: Adopt word counts (instead of page limits) for the petition, preliminary response, patent owner response, and petitioner's reply brief; retain page limits for other briefing.
guidance: Switching to word counts gains administrative efficiencies (petitions won’t be reviewed to determine whether claim charts contain argument), streamlines administrative review, and reduces non-compliant petitions requiring correction.

name: Determination of petition page/word limits (not tied solely to number of claims)
description: Petition length should not be determined solely by number of claims challenged nor by automatic extensions tied to excess claim fees.
guidance: Board declined to adopt claim-count-based limits because Rule 42.22(a) requires presentation of precise relief, significance of evidence, material facts, governing law, and substantive unpatentability discussion; word limits for inter partes review, CBM, and post-grant review are expected to be sufficient, with waiver available under 37 CFR 42.24(a)(2) in appropriate circumstances.

name: Scope of estoppel under 37 CFR 42.73(d)(3)
description: Estoppel precludes an applicant/owner from obtaining a claim that is not patentably distinct from a finally refused or canceled claim in an AIA review.
guidance: Office declined to change the rule; the rule appropriately prevents seeking claims not patentably distinct from finally refused/cancelled claims. Clarification that estoppel does not arise where an amendment is proposed but not granted was requested, but no rule change was proposed.

name: Treatment of prior claim constructions (issue preclusion not adopted)
description: Office will consider prior claim constructions from other proceedings but will not apply strict issue preclusion; claim construction will be decided case-by-case given different approaches and evidentiary records.
guidance: Because PTAB may follow a different claim construction approach than district courts and evidence may differ, strict issue preclusion is inappropriate in every case; determinations will depend on facts presented in the particular proceeding.

name: Prior commercial use defense (35 U.S.C. 273(a))
description: A person shall be entitled to a defense under section 282(b) with respect to subject matter consisting of a process or machine/manufacture/composition used in a manufacturing or other commercial process that would otherwise infringe, if such person, acting in good faith, commercially used the subject matter in the United States (internal commercial use or arm's length sale/transfer of a useful end result) and such commercial use occurred at least 1 year before the earlier of (A) the effective filing date of the claimed invention or (B) the date the invention was publicly disclosed qualifying for the exception under section 102(b).
guidance: Establishes elements of the prior commercial use defense: good faith, commercial use in the U.S., and timing at least one year before filing or qualifying disclosure.

name: Limitations on who may assert prior commercial use (personal defense and transfer restrictions) (35 U.S.C. 273(e)(1)-(3))
description: Defense may be asserted only by the person who performed or directed the commercial use, or by an entity that controls/is controlled by/under common control with such person; the right to assert the defense is not licensable or assignable except as an ancillary/subordinate part of a good-faith assignment or transfer of the entire enterprise or line of business; defense when acquired by assignment may only be asserted for uses at sites where subject matter was in use before the later of the effective filing date or date of assignment/transfer. Also, defense is not a general license but extends only to the specific subject matter established.
guidance: Defines personal nature of the defense, restrictions on assignment/licensing, site-limited scope, and that it is not a blanket license under all patent claims.

name: University exception to prior commercial use defense (35 U.S.C. 273(e)(5))
description: A person commercially using subject matter may not assert the defense if the claimed invention was, at the time made, owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to an institution of higher education or to a technology transfer organization whose primary purpose is commercialization of technologies developed by such institutions, except when activities required to reduce the invention to practice could not have been undertaken using funds provided by the Federal Government.
guidance: Limits defense for inventions tied to universities/technology transfer organizations, with narrow exception tied to federal funding constraints.

name: Damages award standard (35 U.S.C. 284)
description: Upon finding for the claimant the court shall award damages adequate to compensate for the infringement but in no event less than a reasonable royalty, together with interest and costs. The court may increase damages up to three times the amount found or assessed; increased damages do not apply to provisional rights under section 154(d). The court may receive expert testimony as an aid to determination of damages or reasonable royalty.
guidance: Establishes compensatory damages floor (reasonable royalty), discretionary treble damages for enhancement, and allowance for expert evidence.

name: Time limitation on damages (35 U.S.C. 286)
description: Except as otherwise provided by law, no recovery shall be had for any infringement committed more than six years prior to the filing of the complaint or counterclaim for infringement. Special rules apply for claims against the U.S. Government where a pre-suit period may not be counted.
guidance: Statute of limitations for monetary recovery limited to six years preceding filing; provides carve-outs for governmental claims and administrative claim periods.

name: Special remedies and good-faith disclosure requests for 271(g) importation claims (35 U.S.C. 287(b))
description: An infringer under section 271(g) shall be subject to damages and injunctions except as modified by this subsection: no remedies are available for a product in the possession of or in transit to the person liable before that person had notice; in determining remedies courts shall consider defendant's good faith with respect to a request for disclosure (a written request made before first importation/use/sale and before notice), responses to such requests, and need to restore exclusive rights. Evidence of good faith includes making a request, reasonable response time, and submission of response to manufacturer/supplier with request for written statement the process is not used. Failure to perform these acts is evidence of absence of good faith unless mitigating circumstances exist.
guidance: Provides a safe-harbor-like procedure for importers to request disclosure of process patents from manufacturers/suppliers and makes cooperative conduct evidence of good faith affecting remedies for 271(g) cases.

name: Cross-bill — permissible scope
description: Where the defendant, in an action in equity, is entitled to relief against the plaintiff, in some matter connected with the suit, he may file a cross-bill with his answer setting up his claims and praying for the relief required. A cross-bill cannot introduce new parties, or a new and independent controversy, but may be used for purposes of discovery or for the determination of any issue subordinate to that involved in the original bill.
guidance: Cross-bill must relate to matters in original bill; cannot create an independent cause of action or new parties without leave. It must aver all facts essential to sustain the defendant's right and disclose the relation between the remedy sought and the principal suit. Leave of court and due notice usually required.

name: Supplemental bill — when permissible and limitations
description: Whenever any action in equity becomes defective after the filing of the original bill, whether by a change of the persons interested in the subject-matter of the suit, or by the occurrence of events enlarging or diminishing the rights of the parties, or whenever the plaintiff discovers facts essential to the proper decision of the controversy concerning which he had no information at the commencement of the action, he may file a supplemental bill alleging the new matter and thereby making it a part of his original claim. A supplemental bill must not vary the character of the suit or the cause of action; and can be filed only by leave of the court, for sufficient reasons and upon proper notice to the defendant.
guidance: Use supplemental bills to add newly discovered parties, subsequent infringements, effects of patent extension, bankruptcy/assignee issues, etc. Must not change the character of suit; leave and notice required. Courts differ on reissue-pending-suit issues; can be waived by defendant's acquiescence.

name: Standards for allowing amendments (examples of permissive grounds)
description: The authority to permit amendments is conferred upon the court for the furtherance of justice, and to relieve the parties from the consequences of their unavoidable ignorance or mistake, and this authority may be exercised at any stage of the proceedings when its necessity becomes apparent. Thus where the evidence discloses that the description of the parties in the bill is incorrect, or that a different re-issue is in force from the one recited in the bill, or where the allegations of a bill brought by an assignee are broad enough to embrace, but do not specifically mention, claims for past infringements, or where the answer and the defendant's proof set up new matter in avoidance of his liability for the infringing acts, the plaintiff may amend the bill by the correction of the error, the enlargement of the insufficient allegation, or the insertion of new facts to meet the evidence and answer of the defendant.
guidance: Courts will allow amendments to cure mistakes disclosed by evidence (e.g., party description, re-issue number, add claims for past infringements, add missing prior user names) so pleadings conform to proof, unless other evidence shows plaintiff cannot be defeated.

name: Affidavit/declaration content counts
description: Affidavits/declarations containing opinion(s) or argument(s) about anticipation/obviousness or claim elements are treated as comments and counted against page limits.
guidance: Declarations limited to establishing facts (dates, comparative tests, data analysis) are excluded. Exhibits/drawings are not counted unless they themselves include argument; any pages containing argument are counted.

name: Defective amendments retained but not considered; enlarging/new matter handled specially (37 CFR 1.530(d)-(k))
description: Proposed amendments not complying with 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(k) will be retained in the file but not considered.
guidance: Exception: if the only defect is that the amendment enlarges the scope of the claims or introduces new matter, the amendment will be considered and a rejection will be made in the next Office action. New matter amendments to the disclosure must be canceled; claims with new matter rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112; drawing new matter ordinarily not entered. Amendment that enlarges claim scope will be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 314(a).

name: Consequences for failure to timely respond (37 CFR 1.957(b)/(c))
description: If the patent owner fails to file a timely and appropriate response to any Office action, the reexamination prosecution may be terminated or limited depending on whether any claims are allowable.
guidance: If no claims are allowable, prosecution terminated under 37 CFR 1.957(b) and certificate under 37 CFR 1.997 issued canceling all claims under reexamination. If at least one claim is allowable, proceeding continues but is limited to claims found allowable at time of failure (37 CFR 1.957(c)). Rejected claims terminated under 1.957(c) can be revived if delay was unintentional under 1.137.

name: Reconsideration and conferencing prior to action
description: After receipt of responses/comments, the examiner prepares for and participates in a conference (MPEP § 2671.03) and the proceeding is reviewed by SPRS/QAS before mailing action.
guidance: Examiner must handle any requested corrections/revisions expeditiously and return to SPRS/QAS within set time. Patent owner and requester will be notified of claims rejected/allowable and may respond in accordance with MPEP §§ 2671/2672. Examiner will consider amendments for 35 U.S.C. 112 or claim broadening issues.

name: Get professional help when needed
description: Find professional assistance—hire a patent attorney, use USPTO assistance, pro bono programs, or a law school clinic to help draft and file the application.
guidance: Patent attorneys typically have a science/engineering undergraduate degree and must pass the patent bar. Clinics can be good lower‑cost options supervised by USPTO‑approved professors. A lawyer is strongly recommended for drafting claims and formal parts.

name: Complete required application sections / cover sheet
description: Ensure the application includes all required parts: title, abstract, detailed description, claims, drawings, and any other required information in the correct order.
guidance: There are specific rules about each required part and the order in which they must appear (see MPEP §601). Have an attorney review the assembled application before filing.

name: Prepare a full specification (narrative)
description: Write a specification that describes the type of invention, prior iterations, the invention’s purpose, how it is assembled, and how it works; include claims and an abstract.
guidance: The specification must enable others to carry out the invention and disclose the best mode known at filing. The claims within the specification are often the most important and difficult part; professional counsel is recommended.

name: Draft clear independent and dependent claims
description: Claims should be written (often as sentence fragments) to succinctly describe the invention; independent claims state the broad invention, dependent claims refine or narrow them.
guidance: Example independent claim: 'A bag closure comprising a flat body of material having a lead‑in notch...'. Dependent claim example: 'The bag closure recited in claim one, where said bag closure is made of flexible plastic.' Sometimes dependent claims must be merged to form a new, narrower independent claim to obtain patentability.

name: Pay applicable fees and understand cost drivers
description: Pay filing, search, and examination fees and be aware additional fees may apply for extra pages, excess claims, translations, or late filings.
guidance: Costs vary by entity status (micro/small/large) and jurisdiction; U.S. filing may be a few thousand to ~$10,000; global filing can be $30k–$40k. Consult the USPTO fee schedule for specifics.

name: Expect examination delays and possible rejections
description: Patent examination can take years due to backlog. Applications may be rejected for lack of novelty, obviousness, or formal defects.
guidance: If rejected for novelty, consider narrowing claims. Objections may concern form; correct them. Do not continue commercialization if doing so would infringe an existing patent.

name: USPTO authority to sanction misconduct in USPTO proceedings
description: The AIA broadly shifts responsibility for sanctioning misconduct in USPTO proceedings from the federal courts to the USPTO itself (see Leahy‑Smith AIA secs. 6(a) §316(a)(6) and 6(d) §326(a)(6)).
guidance: Legislative materials (House report) state the Director 'may impose sanctions in the form of monetary fines (or payments to other parties) or restrictive orders relating to the proceedings, including dismissal of petitions or cancellation of claims.' The shift to USPTO adjudication of misconduct is emphasized.

name: Timing / one-year limitation (§273(a)(2))
description: The commercial use must have occurred at least one year before the earlier of (A) the effective filing date of the claimed invention; or (B) the date on which the claimed invention was disclosed to the public in a manner that qualified for the exception from prior art under section 102(b).
guidance: This ties the prior-user right to the §102(b) grace-period concept; the defendant must demonstrate the required commercial use timeline relative to filing or qualifying public disclosure.

name: Implied contract for reasonable compensation for use and occupancy
description: When lands are used as quartermaster and commissary depots under conditions indicating an understanding between proprietor and quartermaster that the lands were to be so used for a reasonable compensation, there is an implied contract for a reasonable compensation for the use and occupancy for that period.
guidance: Leases executed after the occupancy period may be treated as a liquidation of the claim for use and compensation. (C.16525, Nov.16,1904.)

name: Effect of leases made after the occupancy period
description: Leases for a period made out after the period of occupancy (ineffectual to create an actual term) may nevertheless be treated as a liquidation of the claim for use and compensation.
guidance: Use such post-period leases as evidence of agreed compensation for the earlier use. (C.16525, Nov.16,1904.)

name: Identify abstract idea as recited and justify grouping or use tentative procedure
description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim, and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).
guidance: Alternatively, provide justification for why a specific limitation(s) recited in the claim is being treated as an abstract idea if it does not fall within the groupings (use the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure). While not required, the explanation may include citing an appropriate court decision that supports the identification. Examiners should be familiar with any cited decision and avoid relying on language taken out of context or on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match. A sample explanation: 'The claim recites the step of comparing collected information to a predefined threshold, which is an act of evaluating information that can be practically performed in the human mind. Thus, this step is an abstract idea in the "mental process" grouping.'

name: Identify product of nature exception and explain lack of markedly different characteristics
description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as it is recited in the claim, and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: See MPEP § 2106.04(b) and § 2106.04(c) (markedly different characteristics analysis). Sample explanation: 'The claim recites X, which as explained in the specification was isolated from naturally occurring Y. X is a nature-based product, so it is compared to its closest naturally occurring counterpart (X in its natural state) to determine if it has markedly different characteristics. Because there is no indication in the record that isolation of X has resulted in a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties as compared to its counterpart, X is a product of nature exception.'

name: Identify additional claim elements and evaluate integration/amounting to significantly more (Step 2A Prong Two & Step 2B)
description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and explain why they do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application and do not add significantly more to the exception.
guidance: The explanation should address additional elements both individually and in combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. It is important to remember that a new combination of steps may be patent eligible even though all steps were individually known (Diamond v. Diehr). Thus, address combinations carefully because combined additional elements may meaningfully limit the judicial exception. A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on expertise in the art in the Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B inquiries. When making a rejection, explain the rationale so applicant can effectively respond. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 for considerations that qualify or do not qualify as integrating an exception or providing significantly more.

name: Support findings that elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (evidentiary requirement for Step 2B)
description: If the examiner concludes particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities (Step 2B), the rejection should support this conclusion in writing with a factual determination using one or more specified options.
guidance: Examiners should not assert that an additional element is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless they find and expressly support the rejection in writing with one or more of the following: (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or applicant's prosecution statements demonstrating the element is well-understood/routine/conventional; (B) citation to one or more court decisions noting the well-understood/routine/conventional nature (ensuring the claim limitations match the court's); (C) citation to a publication that demonstrates the element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field; or (D) a statement that the examiner is taking official notice of the well-understood/routine/conventional nature (used only when certain based on personal knowledge). See Subsection III and MPEP § 2106.05(d) for details.

name: No evidence required to identify a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One)
description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A Prong One, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale that identifies the judicial exception recited in the claim and explains why it is considered a judicial exception; there is no requirement to rely on evidence such as publications or affidavits.
guidance: Cite Federal Circuit decisions that characterize eligibility as a question of law (e.g., Rapid Litig. Mgmt., OIP Techs., DDR Holdings). Examples show courts identifying abstract ideas without relying on evidence. Thus, for Step 2A Prong One, a reasoned rationale is sufficient and evidence is not required.

name: Explain why generic computer components or generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Keep in mind courts have found computer-implemented processes to be significantly more than an abstract idea where generic components in combination perform non-generic functions (DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for generic computing functions that the courts have found to be mere instructions to implement a judicial exception on a computer, and MPEP § 2106.05(d) for information on well-understood/routine/conventional activities. Examples: merely using the Internet to gather data or storing data in a final step may be insignificant extra-solution activity that does not add a meaningful limitation.

name: Address insignificant extra-solution activity and mere field/technological environment limitations
description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering) or that generally link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Examples: adding a final step of storing data to a process that only recites computing a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation; employing well-known computer functions to execute an abstract idea, even when limiting to one environment, may be insufficient (Parker v. Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(g) and § 2106.05(h) for more information.

name: Best practice: consult specification to suggest claim amendments to overcome §101 rejection
description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and identify those elements in the Office action as a way to overcome the rejection.
guidance: If such elements exist in the specification, the examiner should identify and suggest them in the Office action.

name: Compact prosecution: perform complete examination under other patentability requirements and state non-cumulative reasons in first Office action
description: Under the principles of compact prosecution, regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under each of the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and utility, inventorship, double patenting, and non-statutory double patenting). Examiners should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
guidance: This requirement ensures a complete record and supports efficient prosecution.

name: Use of specified form paragraphs for §101 rejections and procedural ordering
description: Use designated form paragraphs (e.g., 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, 7.05.017) for rejections based on subject matter eligibility and nonstatutory rejections, and follow required ordering (e.g., 7.04.01 must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions and final rejections).
guidance: ¶ 7.04.01: Statement of statutory basis (35 U.S.C. 101) — must precede first use of 101. ¶ 7.05: Rejection heading only — must be preceded by 7.04.01 and followed by detailed explanation using other form paragraphs. ¶ 7.05.01: Rejection nonstatutory (not one of four statutory categories) — explain why not within process/machine/manufacture/composition. ¶ 7.05.016: Rejection directed to a judicial exception without significantly more — identify type of exception, how recited in claim, why not integrated, why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. For tentative abstract ideas, include ¶ 7.05.017 and TC Director signature. Follow examiner notes and bracket guidance when filling these paragraphs.

name: Evidentiary expectations for RFI/document production (privilege/logs)
description: When OED requests documents (e.g., contracts, compensation records, correspondence), assertions of confidentiality/privacy must be supported with redactions or a privilege log and explanation; blanket privacy claims are insufficient.
guidance: Respondent's failure to produce or adequately justify non-production weighed against her; proper responses require either production with appropriate redactions or a legal basis and log for withholding.

name: Recovery of goodwill and reputation claim specificity
description: When demanding restorative measures such as advertisements to reinstate goodwill or reputation in lieu of or in addition to damages, the plaintiff should specify in the complaint the specifics of such advertisements.
guidance: Specifics include contents, size, font size and so on.

name: Elements plaintiff must prove for employee invention compensation
description: To claim compensation the plaintiff should contend and prove: (i) that they invented the employee invention; (ii) that the defendant (employer) succeeded from the plaintiff the patent/utility model/design right (or rights to acquire them); (iii) that the employer earned sole and exclusive profits generated by the employee invention; and (iv) the scope of compensation for the employee invention.
guidance: Typical defenses include statute of limitations (10 years) or prior payments to the employee to be deducted.

name: Scope of permanent injunctions and related claims
description: Scope considerations include: what extent injunction covers whole product when patented invention is a part/component; claim for disposal of infringing products; and 'other measures necessary to prevent infringement.'
guidance: Claim for disposal must accompany a claim for injunction and specify products in an appendix. Courts have differed on whether injunction covers whole product or only infringing part; 'other measures' require balancing disadvantage to defendant versus disadvantage to patentee to avoid excessive burden. (Patent Act, art.126 and case law.)

name: Statute of limitations for damages claims
description: An action for damages must be filed within three years from the date the plaintiff became aware of the damages caused by the infringement or within 10 years from the date of the infringement, whichever is earlier.
guidance: An action for damages based on an infringer’s unjust enrichment may be filed within 10 years.

name: Elect to proceed before examiner after Board 1.196(b) new rejection
description: If the appellant elects to proceed before the examiner with regard to the new rejection, the Board’s affirmance will be treated as nonfinal, and no request for rehearing of the affirmance need be filed at that time.
guidance: Prosecution before examiner on the 1.196(b) rejection can incidentally overcome the affirmed rejection even though the affirmed rejection is not open to further prosecution. If the application becomes allowed or abandoned it should not be returned to the Board. If the 1.196(b) rejection is not overcome, the applicant may file a second appeal limited to the 1.196(b) rejection (may not include the affirmed rejection). If prosecution of claims rejected under 1.196(b) is terminated before the examiner, the file must be returned to the Board so the original affirmance can be made final.

name: Categories of petitions ordinarily grantable under 37 CFR 1.198 (Commissioner)
description: Commissioner will ordinarily grant petitions only in categories: (A) Board decision suggests rejection proper because claims omit a disclosed limitation or suffer a curable defect and decision reasonably suggests claims including the limitation or devoid of defect would be allowable; (B) Board decision asserts record lacks evidence of specified character, and it's reasonably suggestive that presenting such evidence would make claims allowable and such evidence exists and can be offered; (C) Board decision based on practice/rule/law/judicial precedent which since has been rescinded, repealed, or overruled.
guidance: Such petitions ordinarily will not be entertained after filing of Commissioner's brief in 35 U.S.C. 141 cases, or after trial in 35 U.S.C. 145 cases. If petition granted in a 141 appeal, steps taken to request court remand so proposals/amendments/evidence/arguments are entered of record; in 145 cases seek dismissal without prejudice to consideration of proposals.

name: Evaluation of evidence — credibility determinations and testimonial weight
description: The tribunal assesses witness credibility and weighs documentary and testimonial evidence in applying the clear-and-convincing standard. Direct testimony, deposition transcripts, and admitted exhibits form the record for findings of fact.
guidance: Credibility findings (e.g., finding a witness credible that she first contacted OED on a particular date) are central to resolving timing and fact disputes; lack of corroborating evidence weakens speculative claims.

name: Willfulness / intent to violate disciplinary rules
description: Willful misconduct — deliberate or intentional disregard of rules — aggravates discipline. A practitioner’s assertion that conduct was legally justified generally does not excuse willful violations when courts have warned the practitioner and they continued conduct.
guidance: Tribunal examines whether practitioner consciously intended the acts; even if the respondent claims a good-faith legal belief, repeated warnings and deliberate continuation support a finding of willfulness.

name: Petition defines the scope of IPR post-SAS
description: After SAS, 'the petitioner's contentions, not the Director's discretion, define the scope of the litigation all the way from institution through to conclusion.'
guidance: Because SAS rejected the Board's partial-institution practice, the IPR scope is defined by the petition's contentions. Thus, whether grounds/claims were 'instituted' is less determinative for estoppel than whether they were included in the petition and could have been considered under the petition-defined scope.

name: "Reasonably could have raised" standard
description: § 315(e)(2) bars later assertion of any ground that the petitioner 'raised or reasonably could have raised' during the IPR.
guidance: This language means that estoppel can reach beyond the specific grounds actually decided by the Board to include grounds that the petitioner could reasonably have asserted against claims included in its petition — particularly after SAS established that the petition, not partial institution, defines the litigation's scope.

name: Review standard for district-court procedural matters (abuse of discretion)
description: District-court decisions on procedural matters in patent cases, such as granting leave to amend claim selections, are reviewed for an abuse of discretion.
guidance: Courts give deference to district courts' case-management decisions (citing O2 Micro, Mayeaux, S&W Enterprises) and will reverse only for clear abuse of that discretion.

name: Good-cause requirement and timeliness for amending asserted claims
description: A party seeking to amend its asserted claim selection long after initial selection and after a prolonged stay must show 'good cause' to reopen selection; unexplained multi-year delay weighs against amendment.
guidance: Failure to request amendment during long stays or promptly after IPR conclusion, combined with minimal supporting justification, is a valid basis for the district court to deny leave to amend; courts 'generally refuse to reopen what has been decided previously.'

name: Petition inclusion of a claim can trigger estoppel even if Board did not address it
description: If a petitioner included a claim (and relevant grounds) in its IPR petition and the IPR otherwise resulted in a final written decision, the petition's inclusion of that claim and related references (e.g., Dezonno) can support estoppel even if the Board did not specifically decide that claim due to partial institution practices later invalidated by SAS.
guidance: Under SAS and Caltech, because the petition defines the scope, a petitioner who included a claim in its petition cannot avoid estoppel merely because the Board's partial-institution decision left that claim unaddressed — particularly where the petitioner could have sought a SAS remand and did not.

name: Understand PTAB decision labeling rules and their bias
description: A decision is labeled 'Reversed' only if every rejection on appeal is reversed; any affirmed rejection prevents that label. 'Affirmed' vs 'Affirmed-in-Part' depends on whether any claim is left free of rejections.
guidance: Because of this labeling, the USPTO statistics under-report reversals and over-report affirmances for individual rejections. Applicants should not rely on the single case-level label for inferences about treatment of specific rejection types.

name: Adjust expectations and tactics by statutory rejection type
description: Each statute has different observed reversal behavior: enablement (~60.9% reversed) is applicant-friendly; written description, anticipation, and indefiniteness are often reversed (~50%); obviousness (~40% reversed) and subject-matter eligibility (§101, ~24.7% reversed) are harder to overcome.
guidance: Applicants should weigh these empirical rates when deciding to appeal, prioritize arguments accordingly (e.g., give special attention to secondary independent claims and dependent claims in obviousness cases), and be cautious about pursuing §101 appeals absent strong grounds.

name: Benefits received by licensee bar challenge to validity in royalty suits
description: Although a patent may not be good for all it claims, a licensee having the benefit of it cannot take advantage of its invalidity in a suit for royalties.
guidance: Where licensee has had all the benefit of a valid patent (e.g., kept off competition, exploited the market), courts hold he is liable for royalties despite some invalidity of specific claims. Exceptions exist where eviction/destruction of patent occurs or prior patent owner's superior title is established (cases vary; see Bartlett v. Holbrook and related authorities).

name: Court of Claims jurisdiction and government use compensation
description: The Court of Claims has jurisdiction over contract claims of individuals against the United States, and is the proper forum to seek compensation when the Government has used a patented invention without consent; jurisdiction historically limited as to torts but the court may entertain implied-contract claims for compensation.
guidance: Principles: wrongful invasion by sovereign presumed to be under an implied contract to pay reasonable compensation; the U.S. may be liable for using the invention without license; officials cannot bind the U.S. by unauthorized contracts; damages measure may be the value of the invention to the government; Congress may direct references to determine compensation. See discussion of James v. Campbell, Palmer v. United States, Dahlgren, Hubbell, and other cases in §1258.

name: Eligibility requirements for requesting reexamination
description: Requirements: the application has not been invalidated, withdrawn or abandoned; has been rejected (excluding rejection after reexamination); has not requested an appeal trial against the decision to reject; and declares intention to request reexamination with amendment of the specification, drawings, or claims. 'Amendment' includes any amendment made in the specification.
guidance: The request for reexamination is made by submission of the amendment; formalities for reexamination requests follow amendment examination procedures.

name: Definite claims under 35 U.S.C. Section 112, second paragraph
description: Definite claims under 35 U.S.C. Section 112, second paragraph — (topic heading listed in the book's table of contents).
guidance: Table-of-contents entry only on this page; no further elaboration available on this metadata page.

name: An application of a natural law is not patentable if its steps are routine/conventional
description: An application of a natural law is not patentable if the steps used to apply the natural law involve well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers in the field.
guidance: When assessing claims, identify whether claimed steps merely recite known, conventional techniques. If so, they do not transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent-eligible invention. The Court applied this to the Prometheus claims (measuring metabolites, applying correlations, adjusting dosage).

name: Additional features that add nothing specific to the natural law do not make the claim patentable
description: Additional elements or steps that add nothing specific to laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas—beyond what is well-understood, routine, and conventional—do not render the claim patentable.
guidance: Evaluate whether extra claim language meaningfully integrates the natural principle into a practical application (i.e., adds 'significantly more'). Mere recitation of generic or conventional elements is an anti-pattern.

name: Must do more than state the law and add the words 'apply it' ('significantly more')
description: In order for an application of a natural law to be patentable, one must do more than simply state the law of nature while adding the words 'apply it.' The claimed invention must amount to 'significantly more' than the natural principle itself.
guidance: Search for transformative, inventive integration of the law into a specific, novel application rather than high-level or result-focused instructions. The absence of 'significantly more' supports ineligibility.

name: Conventional steps specified at a high level of generality cannot make a law patentable
description: Appending conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality, to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas cannot make those subjects patentable.
guidance: Assess whether claimed steps are described at a high level of generality and are routine. Examples/anti-patterns provided: 'administering' that merely identifies an interested class of users (doctors); 'determining' that allows measurement 'through whatever process the doctor wishes' where such methods are well known; a step that merely tells a practitioner to consider results when making decisions.

name: Limiting a formula/idea to a particular technological environment is not sufficient
description: A prohibition against patenting abstract ideas cannot be circumvented by attempting to limit the use of the formula to a particular technological environment.
guidance: Claims that merely place an abstract idea or law of nature into a field-specific context (e.g., targeting doctors treating a disease) without adding nonconventional, specific application elements should be treated as ineligible.

name: Relying solely on other statutory provisions (novelty/non-obviousness) to preserve eligibility is inadequate
description: The government's proposed approach—treating any step beyond a statement of a law of nature as potentially patentable and relying on novelty, non-obviousness, and disclosure requirements to police overbroad claims—would render the law-of-nature exception a dead letter and create greater legal uncertainty.
guidance: When evaluating claims, do not collapse §101 into later patentability inquiries; maintain a §101 inquiry to prevent undue monopolization of fundamental tools and to provide clearer legal boundaries.

name: Design patents protect appearance; utility patents protect function
description: Design patents protect appearance; utility patents protect function.
guidance: Use design patents to protect aesthetic aspects (appearance of a cellphone, tablet surfaces, bezels, etc.); use utility patents for functional/internal innovations. This distinction informs claim drafting, asserted rights, and defenses such as functionality-based invalidity arguments.

name: Dotted (broken) lines must be accompanied by a specification disclaimer
description: Broken (dotted) lines depict unclaimed subject matter, but an applicant is required to include a statement in the specification to make it clear if the applicant is disclaiming portions shown in dotted lines. 'Unclaimed subject matter must be described as forming no part of the claimed design or of a specified embodiment thereof.' (MPEP 1503.03 III, MPEP §1503.02).
guidance: Failure to include the written disclaimer can result in courts construing broken lines as part of the claimed design (see Bernardo Footwear v. Dillard's). If ambiguous, the drawing may be held indefinite under 35 U.S.C. §112 (In re Blum). When using dotted lines to disclaim background/environment or features, include explicit specification language clarifying the intent.

name: Surface shading conveys claim-limiting information about contour and material
description: Surface shading is used to show contour (plane, concave, convex, etc.) and oblique lines are required to depict transparent, translucent, highly polished, or reflective surfaces (MPEP 15.48 and 15.49). Shading in drawings can function as a claim limitation.
guidance: If intending to claim a flat glass front face (or a recessed/front contour), use appropriate surface shading (cross-hatching or oblique lines) in the drawings and disclose their meaning in the specification. Lack of shading where contour is relevant can create indefiniteness or allow invalidity challenges; conversely, shading that limits the claim can be used to distinguish prior art that lacks the limited surface characteristic.

name: Drawings are effectively the claim — drawing errors can be dispositive
description: In the world of design patents, because the drawings are effectively the claim, errors such as inconsistent use of solid vs. dotted lines (e.g., a user's left hand in solid lines) can prove costly.
guidance: Carefully proof drawings and specification statements. Small drafting errors or omissions may create unanticipated claim scope, indefiniteness, or vulnerabilities that litigants will exploit. Examiner amendments and prosecution history may mitigate some errors but the face of the issued drawing controls unless the record clearly disclaims otherwise.

name: Prosecution history is intrinsic evidence and can clarify drawing ambiguities
description: Prosecution history is deemed intrinsic evidence; statements made during prosecution (e.g., examiner amendments disclaiming dotted lines) can be used to interpret ambiguous drawings or disclaimers.
guidance: When faced with §112 or claim construction challenges based on drawings, review prosecution records for clarifying statements or examiner amendments. Relying on prosecution history can sometimes rescue an ambiguity on the face of the issued patent, but it's preferable to have clear specification language on the face of the patent.

name: Failure to disclose meaning of dotted lines or shading can render a claim indefinite under 35 U.S.C. §112
description: Dotted and broken lines may mean different things in different circumstances and 'in each case it must be made entirely clear what they do mean, else the claim is bad for indefiniteness under 35 USC 112.' (In re Blum).
guidance: To avoid §112 indefiniteness attacks, explicitly describe the meaning of broken lines and any shading in the specification. Do not rely on the prosecution history as the primary means for clarifying drawing intent whenever possible.

name: Functionality challenges must consider overall appearance, not dissected elements
description: When determining whether a design is primarily functional or ornamental, 'the claimed design is viewed in its entirety... the ultimate question is not the functional or decorative aspect of each separate feature, but the overall appearance of the article.' (L.A. Gear).
guidance: Defendants' 'divide-and-conquer' functionality arguments or 'masking tape' approaches (ignoring allegedly functional elements) are legally suspect. Focus on overall visual impression; alleged functions of individual features do not automatically render the claimed design invalid if alternative designs exist. Functionality arguments often raise factual disputes for the factfinder.

name: Claim construction: do not 'mask over' functional features without proper legal basis
description: Samsung's counsel attempted to argue functional aspects should be ignored in claim construction (citing Richardson), but such a 'masking tape' approach is flawed and has been rejected in some cases (Good Sportsman Marketing discussion).
guidance: When construing design claims, courts must be cautious about excising features deemed 'functional' absent clear precedent; improper excision could unsettle many design patents. Counsel should prepare to rebut requests to remove features from visual comparison and show existence of alternative designs.

name: Strategic use of multiple embodiments and dotted-line practice
description: Multiple embodiments and liberal dotted line practice can increase the effective scope of a single design patent by allowing a patentee to select an embodiment to match an accused product, but this practice also increases exposure to prior art and to doctrine that a single invalid embodiment can defeat the whole claim.
guidance: Use a combination strategy: file multiple-embodiment applications for broad coverage and separate stand-alone applications for particularly valuable embodiments to hedge risks. Consider costs (application, search, issue fees) versus commercial value when choosing prosecution strategy.

name: MPEP practice on broken lines and surface shading
description: MPEP guidance: MPEP 1503.03 III 'Broken Lines' (broken lines for environment/unclaimed subject matter must be described); MPEP 15.48 and 15.49 on 'Surface Shading' (use shading to show contour and depict transparent/reflective surfaces).
guidance: Follow MPEP drawing conventions to avoid rejections and indefiniteness issues. Use explicit specification statements required by MPEP when relying on broken lines; use appropriate surface shading conventions to indicate materials/contours that will limit the claim.

name: Temporal market context affects scope under the ordinary observer test
description: In initial years of a new product category, differences in later entrants' designs may need to be greater to avoid design patent infringement because 'the ordinary observer' in a nascent category may not yet be able to discriminate between designs—scope may be broadest the day a design patent issues and diminish over time as the ordinary observer develops greater discriminatory faculties.
guidance: Consider market maturation when evaluating enforcement prospects and when drafting claims/drawings. Early in a product category, design rights can be especially potent; long-term enforcement may become harder as consumer discernment increases.

name: Written description of the invention
description: The specification must include a written description of the invention.
guidance: Statutory wording: the specification 'shall contain a written description of the invention.' Case law (Ariad Pharm. v. Eli Lilly; Vas‑Cath v. Mahurkar; Vasudevan Software v. MicroStrategy; In re Barker) establishes that the written description requirement is distinct from enablement. Examples/notes: An invention may be described without the disclosure being enabling (e.g., a chemical compound disclosed without a method of making it). The presence of some discussion showing possession of claimed subject matter can create genuine issues of fact as to written description support (see Vasudevan Software example concerning 'disparate databases').

name: Cross-noting / Front page notation of prior U.S. applications (including provisionals)
description: The front page of a printed patent identifies all prior applications for which benefits are claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c) in continuation-in-part, continuation, divisional, substitute, and reissue applications; examiners should review identifying data to ensure accuracy and presence in the specification or application data sheet per 37 CFR 1.78(a).
guidance: Reference to a prior nonprovisional must include appropriate relationship (continuation, divisional, CIP). Preprinted PALM bib-data sheet entries should be checked and corrected if necessary; if applicant claims benefit to a provisional that itself claims priority to earlier apps, earlier apps should not be reflected on PALM because provisional is not entitled to priority of other applications.

name: Oath/declaration identification of foreign applications (37 CFR 1.63 & 1.76)
description: 37 CFR 1.63 requires that the oath or declaration must identify any foreign application for which a claim for priority is made pursuant to 37 CFR 1.55, specifying application number, country, day, month, and year, unless such information is supplied on an application data sheet in accordance with 37 CFR 1.76.
guidance: Ensure oath/declaration or ADS contains required foreign priority identifiers to support priority claims and proper front-page and file notation.

name: Effect of inventorship correction on benefit claims and intervening references
description: Grant or denial of a request under 37 CFR 1.48 may result in loss of inventorship overlap between a parent and continuing application and consequent inability to claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120; intervening references must be considered.
guidance: If a 1.48 request is denied in a final agency action, the examiner must determine whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g) is appropriate. If request was entered and dismissed for correctable defect, treating 102(f)/(g) may be premature. For allowed applications where issue fee paid prior to entry of 1.48 request, if request is dismissed/denied, application must be withdrawn from issue to permit correction; if granted, withdrawal is unnecessary.

name: Perspective views guidance
description: Include one or more perspective views to show the invention clearly.
guidance: Preferably keep one view per sheet; do not recommend more than two views per sheet for clarity. Avoid wasting sheets; maintain proper spacing between views. NOTE: Do not use the same sheets for both views and claims.

name: Nature of proceedings — action (trial) proceedings
description: Action proceedings: Where a dispute of fact exists or is likely to arise. Evidence is given by expert witnesses in the form of oral evidence; further evidence may be led by way of affidavit.
guidance: Witnesses are examined and cross-examined. Action proceedings commence by issuing summons supported by particulars of claim that set out essential claims and material facts relied upon.

name: Collation of evidence for IPR proceedings
description: Collation of evidence confirming validity of IPRs and proof of infringement is critical. Consider any expert evidence required and identify the person best suited to provide it.
guidance: Evidence should be compiled and retained systematically to support validity and infringement claims; consideration of who can provide credible expert testimony is essential when planning proceedings.

name: Specification: written description and enablement requirement
description: Before receiving a patent, the inventor shall file in the Patent Office a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making, constructing, compounding, and using it, 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which it appertains ... to make, construct, compound, and use the same.'
guidance: For machines, the inventor must explain the principle thereof and the best mode contemplated of applying that principle so as to distinguish it from other inventions; the specification must particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which is claimed as the invention; the specification and claim must be signed by the inventor and attested by two witnesses.

name: Death of inventor — executor/administrator rights
description: If a person having made a new invention dies before a patent is granted, the right to apply for and obtain the patent devolves on his executor or administrator in trust for heirs (or, if testate, in trust for devisees) on the same terms and conditions as if claimed by the deceased in his lifetime; the required oath/affirmation shall be varied so it can be made by such legal representatives.
guidance: Provides succession rules allowing legal representatives to pursue patent rights.

name: Commissioner rulemaking and printing powers
description: The Commissioner, subject to approval of the Secretary of the Interior, may from time to time establish rules and regulations (not inconsistent with law) for conduct of proceedings in the Patent Office; he may also print copies of specifications, drawings, claims of current issues, and copies of laws, decisions, rules and circulars necessary for public information.
guidance: Administrative delegation allows the Commissioner to manage procedures and public dissemination of patent materials.

name: Graham factual inquiries — differences between claimed invention and prior art
description: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art is a required factual inquiry.
guidance: Requires interpreting claim language (see MPEP §2111) and considering the invention and prior art as a whole (see MPEP §2141.02). The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness; explain why differences matter to obviousness.

name: Claim scope determined by broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification
description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
guidance: Cite Phillips v. AWH Corp. and MPEP §2111. Determination of claim scope informs what to search and what references can read on the claims.

name: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting claim language and considering whole
description: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and prior art requires interpreting the claim language and considering both invention and prior art as a whole.
guidance: Use MPEP §2111 and §2141.02; differences must be explained in context of claim construction and total disclosure.

name: Applicant's reply requirements under 37 C.F.R. 1.111(b)
description: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: Replies must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable. A traverse must include reasoned statements explaining why the examiner erred; mere conclusory assertions are inadequate.

name: Physical requirements of documents (Section 3(2)(a), AI 26)
description: Documents making up the application (request, description, claims, abstract, drawings) must meet the form requirements of AI 26(1–9) to enable reasonably uniform publication.
guidance: Formality Section responsible for ensuring requirements met; replacement documents and translations follow same form rules.

name: Biotechnology/chemistry disclosure sufficiency — definition of proteins and polypeptides
description: Proteins may be claimed by explicit amino acid sequence (SEQ ID NO) or by referring to derived proteins (substitution/deletion/addition) combined with functional definition, but derived proteins are permissible only if: I. the derived protein is exemplified in the description (e.g., examples); and II. the description states technical means for producing and verifying its function; otherwise disclosure is insufficient.
guidance: When sequence-based or function-based claim formats are used, the description must enable production and verification; alternative descriptors (function, physicochemical properties, origin, source, production process) may be used when sequence/function formats cannot be applied.

name: Biotech claim drafting — monoclonal antibodies and hybridomas
description: A claim directed to a monoclonal antibody may be defined by specifying the hybridoma which produces it (for example, 'a monoclonal antibody produced by a hybridoma having deposit no. xxx').
guidance: Deposit information (access number, depositary) is acceptable to identify biological material; defining antibodies solely by function/epitope requires support to establish novelty and inventive step.

name: Microorganism claim description requirements
description: A microorganism claim shall be described according to microbiological taxonomic denomination with Latin name in brackets when first mentioned; if deposited, the deposit institution abbreviation and access number should be indicated.
guidance: If a specific mutant strain is not described in the application, a claim for that mutant strain is not permissible; claims for 'derivative' are potentially indefinite and unclear about scope.

name: Novelty and inventive step standards in genetic engineering
description: Novelty and inventive step for genes, recombinant proteins, monoclonal antibodies, vectors, transformants, fused cells and microorganisms are assessed case-by-case: e.g., a gene is novel if its protein is novel; a recombinant protein identical in amino acid sequence to a known purified protein lacks novelty; inventive step generally lacking when claimed combinations are predictable from known components unless unexpected technical effects are shown; for microorganisms, new taxonomic characteristics or unexpected technical effects support inventive step.
guidance: Examiners must consider whether a person skilled in the art could readily derive the claimed subject-matter from prior art and whether unexpected technical effects are credibly disclosed or demonstrated.

name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) and 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
description: For anticipation under 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention either explicitly or impliedly; any feature not directly taught must be inherently present. For 103, the reference teachings may be modified to meet the claims and the modification must have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill.
guidance: Apply strict element‑by‑element comparison for 102 anticipation; for 103, evaluate what a POSITA would find obvious in view of the combined teachings of the prior art and common knowledge. See MPEP §§ 2131-2146, 2150-2159.04.

name: Determine correct statutory subsection and effective filing/reference dates for 102 rejections
description: In order to determine which paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 102 applies, the effective filing date of each claimed invention must be determined and compared with the date of the reference. The examiner must also determine the issue or publication date of the reference so that a proper comparison between the application and reference dates can be made.
guidance: Use MPEP §§ 2139.01, 2152.01 for effective filing date determination and MPEP §§ 2124, 2126, 2128‑2128.02, 2152.02‑2154.02(c) for reference date determination. Use form paragraphs 7.03.aia or 7.03.fti to indicate which prior art regime applies and follow MPEP § 2152.05 for choosing between 102(a)(1) and (a)(2).

name: Prior art presumed operable/enabling where it expressly anticipates or makes obvious
description: When the reference relied on expressly anticipates or makes obvious all of the elements of the claimed invention, the reference is presumed to be operable. Once such a reference is found, the burden is on applicant to rebut the presumption of operability.
guidance: Make a proper prima facie case of anticipation with adequate notice under § 132. Applicant may submit rebuttal evidence of non‑enablement. See In re Sasse and In re Antor Media Corp.; see MPEP § 716.07 for rebuttal/inquiry standards.

name: Efficacy/utility not required in prior art for anticipation
description: A reference must identically disclose the claimed compound, but no utility need be disclosed by the reference for it to be anticipatory; proof of efficacy is not required for a prior art reference to be enabling for purposes of anticipation.
guidance: Focus on whether the compound/structure and method of making are taught or inherent; utility omission does not preclude anticipation. See In re Schoenwald, Impax Labs. v. Aventis Pharm., and MPEP § 2122.

name: Plant genetics — enabling prior art requires ability to grow and reproduce the plant
description: When claims are drawn to plants, the reference, combined with knowledge in the prior art, must enable one of ordinary skill to reproduce the plant; possession via publication plus ability to obtain plant (e.g., seed sale) and asexual reproducibility may create a statutory bar.
guidance: Consider whether publication identifies the plant, whether foreign sales put POSITA in possession, and whether asexual reproduction is possible without undue experimentation. Distinguish cases where only picture was published vs where seeds were commercially available. See In re LeGrice, Ex parte Thomson, In re Elsner, and MPEP § 2152.02(d).

name: Apparatus and articles — pictures/drawings may be enabling
description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured and may be used to reject claims to the article, but the picture must show all the claimed structural features and how they are put together.
guidance: Use drawings as prior art where they disclose all structural elements and assembly (In re Bager). See MPEP § 2125 for drawings as prior art.

name: Requirements for establishing criminal patent infringement
description: For criminal patent infringement to be established, (i) a valid patent right should exist, (ii) the product or process practicing the patent right should be within the protective scope of the patent right, (iii) the alleged infringer’s practice of the patent right should be unlawful, (iv) the alleged infringer should have the ability to fulfill their legal responsibility, and (v) the alleged infringer should have intent.
guidance: Determining protective scope requires claim interpretation focusing on claim language (literal interpretation) while taking into account descriptions, drawings, and common technical knowledge at filing (principle of reference to the descriptions). A defendant’s product/process must include all claim elements to literally infringe, though infringement under the doctrine of equivalents can apply. Indirect infringement is treated as a preparatory act and generally not punishable in criminal law absent specific statutory provision.

name: Subject-matter must be a patentable invention
description: The application must claim a patentable invention: a concrete art, instrument, or process within the statutory classes that is new, useful, and not abandoned to the public.
guidance: Nothing less than a statutory patentable invention can be the subject of an application. The application must describe the invention and the manner and process of making/using it in full, clear, concise, and exact terms to enable a person skilled in the art to construct and use it. Drawings or a model must be provided when required by the Commissioner. See Ex parte Stair v. Farmer (1888).

name: Prior U.S. patent to rival or foreign patent by same inventor (when not a bar)
description: A patent issued to a rival inventor is not necessarily a bar to a later patent to the true inventor; a prior foreign patent does not always prevent issuance of a broader American patent.
guidance: Where the earlier U.S. patent was granted to one who was not the true original inventor, that patent does not bar the true inventor's later patent. A prior foreign patent may limit term or practice but does not automatically invalidate a U.S. patent or bar a broader claim. See Hibbard v. Richmond; Faore v. Bradley; Kendrick v. Emmons.

name: Subject-matter must not include matter already patented by the same inventor
description: An application that includes matter already patented in the U.S. by the same inventor (even together with new matter) is within the rule against double patenting; the application must distinguish the earlier invention and claim only the new invention.
guidance: An inventor who improves his own patented invention cannot obtain a patent for the entire improved invention covering previously patented elements — he may only claim the new development. It may be necessary to describe the earlier patent fully but the new application must clearly show it seeks patent only for the last invention.

name: Integral parts/combinations and option to separate patenting
description: Where a concrete invention is composed of parts each resulting from separate inventive acts, the inventor may choose to obtain separate patents for each part or one patent for the whole; but if the first patent clearly confers monopoly as to all, later patents for parts may be barred.
guidance: If the inventor's first application/patent attempted to claim all subordinate inventions and the government conferred an all-encompassing monopoly, no later application for those parts can be entertained; otherwise, separate patents may be possible. Distinguish unitary inventions (must be protected as whole) from composite inventions (parts separable).

name: Duty to return client files and effect proper transition upon termination
description: Upon termination of representation, the practitioner must provide complete copies of client files and otherwise effect an orderly transition; failing to return files is misconduct.
guidance: Here, respondent did not produce requested files despite a court order and claimed to have transmitted transition materials that the client never received; first production of some documents occurred only during litigation or disciplinary proceedings.

name: Requirement to produce credible, corroborated documentary evidence (avoid forged/altered documents)
description: Documents produced in defense or to corroborate actions must be authentic and corroborated; forged or doctored documents (or documents with metadata inconsistent with purported dates/senders) undermine credibility and support findings of misconduct.
guidance: OED engaged a digital forensics expert who found Outlook/PDF files had metadata showing creation dates inconsistent with claimed transmission dates and lacked essential metadata indicating they had been sent; an 'Acknowledgement Receipt' had fields missing or mismatched and appeared forged.

name: Distinguish objections vs rejections
description: Understand the difference between an objection (procedural/formality issues that must be corrected) and a rejection (substantive reasons the examiner will not approve the claimed invention).
guidance: The page explains that rejections relate to substantive issues (ineligible subject matter, lack of novelty, obviousness, indefiniteness) while objections concern formal aspects (e.g., missing description for drawing figures, non-sequential claims, incorrect dependencies, drawing line clarity). Treat them differently when planning your response.

name: Interview the patent examiner when appropriate
description: Schedule and prepare for a discussion with the examiner (often by telephone) to discuss claim rejections/objections and proposed amendments.
guidance: Prepare an agenda and list of discussion points, send the agenda and any proposed amendments before the meeting, use the interview to clarify misunderstandings, and record the examiner's interpretations. The article emphasizes using the interview to narrow issues and craft an efficient response.

name: Craft a structured, lawyer-worthy response
description: Organize the response with an Introduction, Point-by-Point Responses for each issue, and a Conclusion summarizing requests for advancement.
guidance: For each cited issue provide clear, concise responses backed by legal argument and evidence; include any claim amendments or clarifications. The page stresses systematic treatment of each item raised by the examiner to maximize chances of overcoming the refusal.

name: Contribution to a single claim suffices for inventorship
description: A joint inventor need not contribute to every claim of a patent; a contribution to one claim is sufficient to be a joint inventor of that claim.
guidance: Example: contributing a disclosed means for a means-plus-function claim element can make one a joint inventor as to that claim, unless the contributor only reduced to practice someone else's broader concept. Case: Ethicon Inc. v. United States Surgical Corp. There is no requirement that all inventors be joint inventors of the subject matter of any single claim.

name: Claims given Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during examination
description: During patent examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: The PTO construes claim scope not solely by claim language but by giving claims their broadest reasonable construction 'in light of the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.' This standard is applied by examiners during prosecution (distinct from how courts construe claims in litigation) to encourage applicant amendment and to establish a clear record. Relevant cases: Phillips v. AWH Corp.; In re American Academy of Science & Technology Center; In re Morris; In re Zletz.

name: Plain meaning under BRI: ordinary and customary meaning prevails
description: Under BRI, words of a claim must be given their plain (ordinary and customary) meaning unless that meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: Plain meaning is the meaning a person of ordinary skill in the art would give the term at the relevant time (effective filing date). Sources evidencing ordinary meaning include the claim language itself, the specification, drawings, and prior art; the specification is the best source. Cases include Phillips v. AWH Corp., Vitronics Corp. v. Conceptronic, and others. Example: simple English words are construed to mean exactly what they say absent contextual change (Chef America v. Lamb‑Weston).

name: Means‑plus‑function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) treatment
description: When an element is claimed under 112(f) (means‑/step‑plus‑function), the specification must be consulted to determine the structure, material, or acts corresponding to the function, and the element is construed as limited to that corresponding structure/material/acts and equivalents.
guidance: If claim language falls under 112(f), examiners must identify corresponding disclosure in the specification to construe the limitation. See In re Donaldson and MPEP §§ 2181‑2186 for details and examples.

name: Use of extrinsic evidence in claim interpretation
description: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries, treatises, etc.) may be consulted only when intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) does not offer sufficient clarity.
guidance: The specification is the best source; when intrinsic evidence clearly supports an interpretation, extrinsic evidence is unnecessary. However, if intrinsic evidence is ambiguous or insufficient (e.g., unclear numeric boundaries), extrinsic evidence may be necessary to determine meaning to a person skilled in the art at the relevant time. Cases: Phillips; Actelion; Teva v. Sandoz; Seabed Geosolutions.

name: Disavowal (disclaimer) of claim scope by applicant
description: An applicant may also rebut ordinary meaning by clearly and unmistakably disavowing or disclaiming the full scope of a claim term in the specification.
guidance: Disavowal requires clear and unmistakable statements in the specification; in some cases disavowal may be made by implication (e.g., consistent disparagement of alternatives and exclusion in every embodiment). If an examiner believes BRI is narrower due to implicit disavowal, the examiner should make the interpretation clear on the record. Cases: SciMed Life Systems; In re American Academy of Sci. Tech. Ctr.; In re Abbott Diabetes Care. Note: prosecution history estoppel applies differently after issuance.

name: Flowchart summary for claim term interpretation (non‑112(f))
description: Procedural steps examiners should follow to ascertain claim interpretation for terms not invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
guidance: Step 1: Determine whether the claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning to those of ordinary skill. If yes, check the specification for a special definition. If no special definition, apply the ordinary meaning. If the specification provides a special definition, use it and the Office action should acknowledge and identify it. If the term lacks an ordinary meaning, check the specification for a meaning; if none, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation as best understood and consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d).

name: Effect of the preamble on claim scope
description: Whether a preamble limits a claim is determined case-by-case based on the entire claim; a preamble limits the claim if it is necessary to give life, meaning, and vitality to the claim or if the claim as a whole suggests limitations.
guidance: There is no bright‑line test. Examiners should apply guideposts from case law (e.g., Catalina Marketing; Bell Communications; Pitney Bowes; Jansen) and consider whether the preamble recites limitations or is required to provide purpose/context that affects scope. Review facts of each case to decide whether the preamble limits the claim.

name: Scope of practice in patent matters (examples)
description: Practice in patent matters includes preparing/prosecuting patent applications, consulting in contemplation of filing, drafting specifications or claims, drafting amendments/replies requiring written argument, appeals to the PTAB, interference/derivation/reexamination proceedings, and other patent proceedings.
guidance: Registration authorizes performance of services reasonably necessary and incident to preparation and prosecution of patent applications or proceedings in which the practitioner is authorized to participate (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1)).

name: Alternate IV (FAR) — Research Performed Solely by Universities
description: Alternate IV is to be used in contracts for basic or applied research to be performed solely by universities/colleges. It provides blanket permission for universities to claim copyright without limitation in any data first produced in performance. When asserting copyright under Alternate IV, universities must acknowledge government sponsorship (including contract number).
guidance: Alternate IV is critical for universities wishing to assert copyright in contract-generated data; it cannot be used when the contract purpose is development of software for public distribution, and contracting-officer permission is required if non-university parties are performing work. Ensure Alternate IV is included where appropriate.

name: Government License Even if Copyright Is Perfected
description: Perfecting a copyright claim in data first produced and delivered to the government still obligates the contractor to provide the federal government a paid-up, nonexclusive, irrevocable worldwide license to reproduce, prepare derivative works, distribute copies to the public, and perform/display publicly, by or on behalf of the government.
guidance: Even with copyright, universities must recognize and plan for the government's broad license; for software, if copyright is perfected the government may not have the right to distribute copies to the public (contrast with other data).

name: Mandatory initial disclosures — Option 1 (FRCP-style)
description: Option 1 (modeled after Fed. R. Civ.
