P. 26(a)(1)(A)) requires disclosure of: (1) the name and, if known, contact information of each individual likely to have discoverable information and the subjects of that information (unless solely for impeachment); and (2) a copy or description by category and location of all documents, ESI, and tangible things in the disclosing party's possession, custody, or control that may be used to support its claims or defenses (unless solely for impeachment).
guidance: These disclosures permit automatic discovery upon institution and must be filed as exhibits to enable discovery related to them.

name: Minimum procedural compliance for petition filing
description: To obtain a filing date a petition must meet minimum statutory standards (e.g., § 42.106; 35 U.S.C. 312(a)) — a complete petition must be filed with the required fee and include a certificate of service for the petition, fee, and evidence relied upon.
guidance: For IPR, the petitioner must certify the patent is eligible for IPR and that the petitioner is not barred/estopped, identify challenged claims, and state the specific basis for the challenge (§ 42.104). Similar petition requirements exist for PGR (§ 42.204), CBM (§ 42.304), and derivation (§ 42.404).

name: Covered business method (CBM) demonstration and examples
description: A CBM petitioner must demonstrate the patent is a covered business method patent (§ 42.304(a)); covered business method patents claim methods or apparatus for data processing or operations used in practice/administration/management of financial product/service, excluding technological inventions.
guidance: Examples of techniques that typically do not render a patent a technological invention: mere recitation of known technologies (hardware/network/software), reciting use of known prior art technology to accomplish a process, or combining prior art structures to achieve predictable results. Example CBM patents: methods for hedging risk in commodities trading; methods for verifying credit card transactions. Example non-CBM (technological) patents: novel hedging machine; novel credit card reader.

name: Claim charts usage
description: Claim charts are optional but may help explain how a claim maps to a reference, specification, or another claim; they can streamline identification of key claim features and comparison to evidence.
guidance: Claim charts submitted as part of a petition/motion/prelim response/response/opposition/reply count toward applicable page limits; claim charts need not be double-spaced to reduce page count. Claim charts from other proceedings submitted as exhibits do not count toward page limits.

name: Patent owner preliminary response timing and content
description: For IPR, PGR, and CBM proceedings, a patent owner may file a preliminary response no later than three months after the grant of a filing date (§§ 42.107(b), 42.207(b)). The preliminary response may present evidence other than new testimonial evidence to demonstrate that no review should be instituted; new testimonial evidence may be permitted where in the interests of justice.
guidance: Potential arguments include: petitioner is statutorily barred; asserted references are not prior art; prior art lacks material limitation in all independent claims; prior art teaches away; petitioner's claim interpretation is unreasonable; for 101 grounds in PGR, provide brief explanation of patent eligibility. Patent owner may elect to waive the preliminary response to expedite proceeding without adverse inference; statutory disclaimer of challenged claims may terminate or narrow proceedings.

name: Statutory institution thresholds by proceeding
description: Different statutory thresholds apply for institution: (a) IPR — Director may not institute unless petition and any response show a reasonable likelihood the petitioner would prevail on at least one challenged claim (35 U.S.C. 314(a)); (b) PGR — Director may not institute unless petition (if unrebutted) would demonstrate it is more likely than not (>50%) that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. 324(a)); PGR may also be satisfied by a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents (35 U.S.C. 324(b)); (c) CBM — transitional CBM treated as PGR with additional standing requirement (suit/charge of infringement) and exclusion for technological inventions; (d) Derivation — petition must state with particularity basis for derivation, be filed within one year of first publication of the earlier applicant's claim, be made under oath, and be supported by substantial evidence (35 U.S.C. 135(a)).
guidance: Standards vary in stringency (PGR >50% vs IPR reasonable likelihood). CBM has statutory standing limitation. Derivation requires particularized and timely factual showing.

name: Considerations in instituting a review (325(d), timeliness, complexity)
description: When deciding institution, the Board considers whether the petitioner satisfied the statutory standard and may take into account whether the same or substantially the same prior art/arguments were previously presented to the Office under 35 U.S.C. 325(d). The Board may decline to institute where it could not complete the proceeding timely or where complexity (many claims/references or need for extensive foreign witness testimony) would prevent timely completion.
guidance: The Board exercises discretion to manage docket and ensure trials can be completed within statutory timeframes; petitions seeking overly broad or unmanageable reviews may be denied on administrative grounds.

name: Content and scope of institution decision
description: If the Board institutes a trial, it will streamline issues by authorizing trial only on challenged claims and grounds that meet threshold standards, identifying grounds on a claim-by-claim basis; any claim/issue not included is not part of the trial.
guidance: If no trial is instituted, the decision will typically contain a short statement why standards were not met. The Board's determination whether to institute is final and nonappealable (35 U.S.C. 314(d), 325(d), 324(e); § 42.71(c)).

name: Purpose of re-issue (defects of statement only)
description: "The sole office of a re-issue is to correct faults of statement in the description and claim of the original patent."
guidance: Re-issue is a remedy for mistakes in specification drafting (to relieve inventor from lack of skill in drawing specification and to prevent the public from taking undue advantage). It is intended to make the patent 'better' by correcting statement defects, allowing repeated re-issues until language corresponds exactly with the actual invention intended to be protected. It is not intended to remedy mistakes in an inventor's choice or judgment as to what to attempt to cover.

name: Re-issue must be for the same invention as the original patent
description: "A re-issue must be for the same invention as the original patent, and cannot be expanded to cover intervening inventions."
guidance: A re-issue cannot lawfully embrace subject-matter the patentee did not endeavor to describe and claim in the original specification. Courts will construe re-issue claims narrowly; where a re-issued patent 'will bear no construction which confines its subject-matter to this invention,' its claims are invalid. The inventor seeking to capture a distinct or broader invention must file a new application.

name: Re-issue cannot introduce a different principle or other forms not within original limits
description: "The re-issue cannot introduce a different principle though it were known to the patentee when he obtained the original patent" and "where the original patent accurately defines the invention, a re-issue cannot embrace antecedent improvements not within the limits of the original patent."
guidance: Even if the patentee knew other principles or forms at the time of the original patent, the re-issue may not be used to claim a different underlying principle or other forms of the invention beyond the original's defined limits. Where original patent covers but one form of an invention, re-issue cannot be used to cover other forms.

name: Re-issue cannot correct errors of judgment as to what to claim
description: "An error in judgment as to what the patent shall cover, or in conclusions of fact, is no ground for a re-issue" and "an error in judgment as to the nature of the invention cannot be corrected by re-issue."
guidance: Mistakes that are matters of selection, strategy, or substantive judgment about claim scope are not remediable by re-issue. Courts distinguish inadvertent omission from deliberate choice or mistaken judgment; the latter cannot be fixed by re-issuing the same patent.

name: Re-issue available for inadvertence, accident, or mistake in statement
description: A re-issue is permissible to correct inadvertence, accident, or mistake in the original specification so as to protect "just what he invented" — i.e., to state clearly and accurately what the inventor actually made and intended to claim.
guidance: To obtain re-issue on this basis, the patentee must show that he honestly attempted to describe and claim the invention in the original application but failed through inadvertence, accident, or mistake. Re-issue thus can remedy defects of statement so that the patent describes the invention the inventor actually made and attempted to protect. Courts will require good faith and evidence of the original attempt; cases emphasize jealousy against any attempt to enlarge scope beyond the original.

name: Four-step conception/practice test for what belongs to original invention
description: The treatise sets out four steps an inventor must have taken to be entitled to patent subject-matter: (1) conceive an idea of means and reduce it to practice; (2) perceive essential character with sufficient completeness for reproduction; (3) determine to patent entire invention or separable parts and apply; (4) incorporate in the application a specification that attempts to describe/claim that which he intends to secure.
guidance: Only subject-matter that the inventor had actually invented, comprehended, selected as the subject-matter of his patent, and attempted to describe and claim in the original specification (even if imperfectly) can be embraced by re-issue. Possibilities or undeveloped aspects perceived but not reduced to practice or claimed do not form part of the original invention for re-issue purposes; later developments require new patents.

name: Test for whether suggested/indicated matters in drawings/models/specification are part of original invention
description: Matters 'suggested or indicated' in the original specification, drawings, or Patent Office model are not automatically part of the invention intended to be covered; they may be included in re-issue only if a comparison of the two patents shows the original intended to embrace them.
guidance: Courts will compare the original and re-issued patents: only if the original patent (specification, drawings, or model) fairly embraced the things now claimed will the re-issue be deemed to cover them. Merely being suggested or indicated is insufficient unless it is apparent that the original intended to secure them.

name: Re-issue cannot appropriate inventions for which original patent rights have expired or are limited by foreign patents
description: A re-issue cannot claim matter for which the original has expired or which is limited in effect by foreign patents; to cover matters excluded by such limitations would be impermissible.
guidance: If parts of the invention were covered by expired foreign patents or excluded by the reasons for limitation, the re-issue cannot revive or appropriate them. Similarly, one cannot expand a claim by re-issue so as to cover subject-matter the original patent no longer had rights to.

name: Scope determination is by construction against enlargement; courts presume Patent Office acted properly
description: To determine the limits of the invention originally attempted, the Patent Office and courts must construe the original patent; courts are logically and legally compelled to presume the Patent Office performed its duty, and courts will regard attempts to enlarge scope by re-issue with 'jealousy and disfavor.'
guidance: When scope is ambiguous, the courts construe re-issue narrowly and assume the original application defined the invention intended to be secured. Decisions emphasize that re-issue should be confined to curing defects of description/claims and not used to appropriate other inventors' subsequent achievements; any claimed enlargement will be scrutinized and likely invalidated.

name: Re-issue may correct term/clerical errors and make claims conformable to rights
description: Re-issue may correct clerical or statement errors (e.g., fixing the term of a patent so as to conform to a foreign patent previously granted) and may modify claims to make them more conformable to the patentee's exact rights.
guidance: Courts recognize narrow corrective uses of re-issue such as clarifying specification, correcting term errors, or altering claim form to conform to what the patentee actually invented, provided no new matter or broader invention is introduced. Examples include re-stating a patent to include what was plainly the subject but not fully secured due to misstatement of principles.

name: Best Mode Requirement (separate from enablement)
description: The best mode provision of 35 U.S.C. 112 is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement; if the applicant knew of a specific mode thought to be the best way to carry out the invention, the applicant has an obligation to disclose that information.
guidance: Cites In re Newton and Spectra‑Physics v. Coherent. The enablement requirement places the subject matter of the claims in the possession of the public generally; best mode requires disclosure of specific instrumentalities or techniques recognized by the applicant as the best way of carrying out the invention.

name: Two Separate Requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph
description: The statute sets forth two separate requirements: (A) claims must set forth the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention (subjective); (B) claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter to be protected (objective/definiteness).
guidance: The examiner should determine whether a rejection under 112(b) is based on indefiniteness or on failure to claim what the inventor regards as the invention; see In re Zletz and Ex parte Ionescu.

name: Claims Must Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim (Definiteness Purpose)
description: The primary purpose of definiteness is to ensure the scope of the claims is clear so the public is informed of the boundaries of what constitutes infringement; secondary purpose is to provide a clear measure of what applicants regard as the invention for patentability and 112(a) analysis.
guidance: Claims that do not meet this standard must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph. Rejections must clearly identify the language causing indefiniteness and thoroughly explain the reasoning.

name: Applicants Are Their Own Lexicographers
description: Applicants may define terms in the claims in whatever terms they choose, provided any special meaning assigned to a term is clearly set forth in the specification.
guidance: Functional language, alternative expressions, negative limitations, etc., are permissible if the special meaning is clearly set forth in the specification. Applicant may not add a special definition or disavowal after the filing date, but may point out a definition contained in the specification as filed.

name: Determine Whether Each Claim Limitation Invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means‑plus‑function)
description: Examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA sixth paragraph); if so, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181 for detailed means‑plus‑function analysis. This affects claim construction and scope during examination.

name: Determining Whether Claim Language is Definite (Threshold Requirements)
description: The examiner's focus is whether the claim meets statutory threshold requirements of clarity and precision; a claim is indefinite if, given its BRI, a person of ordinary skill would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation.
guidance: Analyze claim terms in view of (A) the application disclosure, (B) prior art teachings, and (C) the understanding of a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time. Do not conflate breadth with indefiniteness: broad claims can be definite if boundaries are clear. Cite Packard, Zletz, Nautilus.

name: Claims Under Examination vs Patented Claims (Court Standard)
description: Claims are construed differently during examination than in court; the PTO uses BRI during prosecution, while courts apply Nautilus's 'reasonable certainty' standard to issued patents.
guidance: Examiners should apply BRI to facilitate narrowing/amending during prosecution; applicants can amend claims during prosecution to ensure clarity. Persistent ambiguity after a well‑grounded rejection justifies a §112(b) rejection (Packard).

name: Unclaimed Essential Matter
description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential to the invention as described in the specification may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as not enabling; failure to interrelate essential elements may be rejected under 112(b) for failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
guidance: Essential matter may include missing elements, steps, or necessary structural cooperative relationships. Case citations: In re Mayhew, In re Venezia, In re Collier. Note precedents holding interdependency not always required (Ex parte Nolden, Ex parte Huber).

name: Improvements in the functioning of a computer or other technology
description: An additional element (or combination) may integrate the exception into a practical application if it demonstrates an improvement in the functioning of a computer or an improvement to another technology or technical field.
guidance: Examine the specification to determine if it discloses sufficient detail so that a person of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The claim must reflect components/steps that provide the improvement (though it need not literally state 'thereby increasing X'). This 'improvements' analysis at Step 2A does not consider whether the elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional. See cited cases (Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Finjan, SRI Int'l) for examples.

name: Implementing the exception with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
description: Use of a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim can integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Evaluate whether the machine/manufacture is integral (not merely a generic computer) and whether claim limitations reflect specific machine-related features; see MPEP §2106.05(b) for detailed analysis and relevant case law.

name: Effecting a particular transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing
description: An additional element that effects a transformation/reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing may integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Assess whether the claimed steps transform an article in a meaningful way (particular transformation test) as discussed in MPEP §2106.05(c) and relevant precedent.

name: Applying the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond mere linking to a technological environment
description: If the additional elements apply or use the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment or field of use, the claim as a whole may integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: This is a catch-all consideration for meaningful limitations that impose more than a generic field-of-use limitation; see MPEP §2106.05(e) for examples and case analyses.

name: Specificity of claim limitations matters (but is not standalone)
description: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluating considerations (e.g., particular machine, particular transformation, or whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception), but 'a specific way of achieving a result' is not by itself a stand-alone consideration.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim provides specifics that reflect meaningful limitations and how those specifics affect the integration analysis. Lack of specific disclosure (e.g., Parker v. Flook) can indicate limitations are insignificant post-solution activity.

name: Two-step evaluation procedure for Prong Two
description: Evaluate integration into a practical application by (1) identifying any additional elements beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using the listed considerations.
guidance: Not all considerations will apply to every claim and the analysis is not a weighing test; evaluate the significance of additional elements relative to the invention, how limitations interact, and assess each claim on its own (dependent claims may be eligible even if an independent claim is not). See MPEP §§2106.04(d) and 2106.05 subsections for detail.

name: Specification and claim coherence for demonstrating improvement
description: To show an improvement to technology, the specification should provide sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement, and the claim must reflect the components/steps that provide that improvement.
guidance: A conclusory assertion of improvement without substantive detail is insufficient. The claim need not explicitly state the improvement (e.g., 'thereby increasing bandwidth') but must include the elements that produce it. This supports finding integration under the improvements consideration.

name: Use of case-law examples to inform analysis
description: Apply and compare relevant Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Mayo, Alice, Enfish, McRO, Finjan, Vanda, Solutran, BASCOM, Roslin) to determine whether claimed additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Use examples to identify whether limitations produced meaningful technological benefits (e.g., improved computer functionality, safer treatment regimens) or were mere field-of-use or post-solution activity. The MPEP provides detailed application of these cases for guidance.

name: Comparison to other acceleration options
description: How Track One compares to other USPTO acceleration programs.
guidance: Summary table: Track One (~$4,200) requires <30 claims and disallows extensions with ~12-month timeline; Accelerated Examination (low fee) requires a pre-examination search and statement; PPH relies on allowable claims in another office; Petition to Make Special requires specific reasons (e.g., age/health); First Action Interview Pilot accelerates first action if interview occurs within 60 days of FAOM. Use these differences to choose the appropriate acceleration path.

name: Claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought
description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall define the matter for which protection is sought in terms of the technical features of the invention (Rule 43(1) EPC).
guidance: This is the core requirement of Art. 84 — claims must delineate what is to be protected by reference to technical features. The page emphasises that claims must identify the technical features necessary for definition and that the EPO assesses claims for their role in defining the claimed subject‑matter.

name: Use of the two‑part form where appropriate (Rule 43(1)(a) and (b))
description: Where appropriate, claims shall contain (a) a statement indicating the designation of the subject‑matter and the technical features necessary for definition that form part of the prior art, and (b) a characterising portion beginning with 'characterised in that' or 'characterised by' specifying the technical features for which protection is sought (Rule 43(1)).
guidance: The two‑part form is required 'wherever appropriate' (Guidelines F IV 2.2). It is particularly intended to let the skilled person see which features are part of the prior art versus the characterising features. However, the two‑part form need not be used if it would give a distorted or misleading picture of the invention or the prior art (Guidelines F IV 2.3). Applicants can and should argue against a two‑part form request if the indication of prior art in the description already makes the relevant division sufficiently clear (Guidelines F IV 2.3.2).

name: Claims shall be clear to the person skilled in the art from the wording alone
description: Claims must be clear to the person skilled in the art from the wording of the claim alone (Art. 84 EPC).
guidance: Relative or similar terms such as 'thin', 'wide', 'strong' are potentially unclear unless their meaning is clear from the whole disclosure (Guidelines F IV 4.6.1). Terms like 'upper', 'lower', 'higher' should be avoided or replaced by 'first'/'second' with an explicit relative clause. Vague qualifiers such as 'approximately', 'substantially', 'about' should be avoided unless defined in the description. The Guidelines require that the claim wording itself enable the skilled person to understand the claimed subject matter.

name: Avoid vague qualifiers and relative descriptors (define them in the description if used)
description: Terms that are relative, context‑dependent or indefinite (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'upper', 'approximately', 'substantially') can render claims unclear unless their meaning is made clear in the disclosure.
guidance: If such terms are used, the applicant should provide clear definitions or contextual explanations in the description. For positional descriptors, prefer numbering (first/second) plus a relative clause. For quantitative imprecision words, include a concrete definition or range in the description to avoid clarity objections.

name: Functional/result‑oriented claiming allowed only in narrow circumstances (T 68/85)
description: Claiming by the result to be achieved (functional claiming) may be problematic but may be allowed if the invention cannot otherwise be defined more precisely without unduly restricting scope and if the result is directly and positively verifiable by tests or procedures adequately specified in the description or known to the skilled person and which do not require undue experimentation (T 68/85).
guidance: Use result‑oriented claim language only when necessary and ensure the description provides adequate, testable procedures or recognizes known tests so the claimed result can be directly verified. Otherwise, the EPO may object for lack of clarity.

name: Claims shall be concise (avoid unnecessary multiplicity, repetition, and alternatives)
description: Claims shall be concise. Conciseness is used by the EPO to justify reducing the number of claims and to object to multiple independent claims in the same category, use of alternatives within a claim, and repetition in dependent claims (Guidelines F IV 5).
guidance: What is a reasonable number of claims depends on the facts and circumstances; the presentation must not make it unduly burdensome to determine the matter for which protection is sought (T 79/91 and T 246/91). The EPO prefers fewer claims (and there are financial implications for more than 15 claims). Applicants should avoid unnecessary repeated wording in dependent claims, multiple overlapping independent claims in one category, and gratuitous alternatives that inflate claim count.

name: Claims must be supported by the description; remove or explicitly mark inconsistent disclosure (T 1808/06)
description: The claims shall be supported by the description. Any disclosure in the description and/or drawings inconsistent with the amended subject‑matter should normally be excised. Embodiments in the description which are no longer covered by the independent claims must be deleted unless they can reasonably be considered useful for highlighting specific aspects of the amended subject‑matter; in that case it must be prominently stated that the embodiment is not covered by the claims (T 1808/06).
guidance: The 2021 Guidelines (F‑IV 4.3(iii)) cross‑reference T 1808/06 and make clear that generic statements such as 'embodiments not falling under the scope of the appended claims are to be considered merely as examples' are insufficient. Merely relabeling 'invention' as 'disclosure' or 'embodiment' as 'example' is also insufficient. Applicants must explicitly specify which parts of the description are no longer covered, or delete them. Examiners are now obliged to be more stringent in assessing this requirement.

name: Examiner must address prior responses in subsequent Office actions
description: Subsequent to the first Office action, the examiner must be careful to additionally address all patent owner responses to previous actions.
guidance: If the examiner concludes in any Office action that one or more of the claims are patentable over the cited patents or printed publications, the examiner should indicate why the claim(s) is clearly patentable in a manner similar to that used to indicate reasons for allowance (MPEP § 1302.14). If the record is clear why the claim(s) is/are clearly patentable, the examiner may refer to the particular portions of the record which clearly establish the patentability of the claim(s).

name: Use of patent owner statements (37 CFR 1.501(a)(2))
description: If any statement of the patent owner submitted pursuant to 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) is relied upon in the detailed explanation, requester must have explained how that statement is being used to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim in connection with prior art applied to that claim.
guidance: That explanation will be considered by the Office, when drafting the Office action, in determining the scope of the claims of the patent which are subject to reexamination.

name: When an AI-related invention is a 'technical solution' (CNIPA specifics)
description: An AI-related claim counts as a technical solution if: the data processed have exact technical meanings in a technical field and execution of the algorithm directly reflects solving a technical problem under the laws of nature; or the algorithm has specific technical associations with internal computer structure and solves technical problems improving hardware computing efficiency or execution effects; or the solution mines internal associations in big data in a specific application field to improve reliability/accuracy.
guidance: Concrete technical effects include reducing data storage/transmission, improving hardware processing speed, or improving reliability/accuracy of big-data analysis (e.g., classification, clustering, regression, neural networks). See CNIPA Guidelines Section 6.1.2, Chapter 9, Part II.

name: JPO approach for determining statutory 'invention' (two-step style)
description: The JPO assesses whether an AI-related invention constitutes a statutory 'invention' by examining whether the claimed subject-matter expresses information processing based on software/hardware cooperation or is otherwise the creation of technical ideas utilizing laws of nature.
guidance: If it is recognized that a specific information processor or operation method is constructed through cooperation of software and hardware resources, eligibility can be recognized without separately determining whether the intended use is technical. Conversely, if hardware resources that enable information processing for each function are not specifically identified, the JPO may find the claim does not constitute an invention even if it mentions a 'computer'. See the JPO's multi-step process (Step 1/Step 2 referenced).

name: Novelty/inventive_step — JPO method
description: The JPO considers claims as a whole (including features not characterized as technical) and selects the most suitable prior art ('primary prior art'), then determines whether a person skilled in the art would easily arrive at the claimed invention by four-step reasoning (see Chapter II.C).
guidance: The JPO does not divide claimed features into 'technical' and 'algorithmic' when assessing inventive step; all claimed features are considered in the 'claims as a whole' approach.

name: Novelty/inventive_step — CNIPA method
description: The CNIPA evaluates whether the invention has prominent substantive features and represents notable progress vs prior art, usually following three steps: (1) determine the closest prior art; (2) determine distinguishing features and the technical problem actually solved; (3) determine whether the claimed invention is obvious to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: When evaluating notable progress, main consideration is whether the invention produces advantageous technical effects. Examiner considerations include motivation to apply other prior art, advantageous effect, and whether there is a technical barrier.

name: Enablement requirement — JPO (Article 36(4)(i))
description: The statement (description) shall be clear and sufficient to enable a person ordinarily skilled in the art to work the invention. The JPO determines for each claim whether the skilled person who intends to carry out the claimed invention can understand how to carry it out based on the description, drawings, and common general technical knowledge at filing.
guidance: A flagged non-enablement situation: a claim to a generic concept where only embodiments of part of the encompassed specific concepts are described such that only those specific concepts can be carried out, and there is a well-founded reason to find other specific concepts are not enabled based on the description plus common general knowledge. Methods of experimentation and analysis may be part of common general technical knowledge.

name: Types that satisfy enablement/sufficiency of disclosure
description: Both offices tend to find enablement/sufficiency where: correlations among multiple types of training data are presumable by common general knowledge; the description contains explanatory/statistical information supporting correlations; or performance evaluation of an actual AI model supports the presence of such correlations.
guidance: Examples: Case C-1 (presumable correlation), Claim 2 in Case C-2 (statistical support), Claim 2 in Case C-3 (performance evaluation).

name: Types that do not satisfy enablement/sufficiency of disclosure
description: Examples of non-enablement include: where the description does not support correlations claimed among training data and such correlations cannot be inferred from common general knowledge (JPO cases); claims relying on AI estimates without verification on actual products when such substitution is not common general knowledge; CNIPA: concrete technical solution without experimental evidence when the solution can only be established upon experimental confirmation.
guidance: Specific examples: Claim 1 in Case C-2 and Claim 1 in Case C-3 (JPO non-enable); Case C-4 where description needs experimental evidence (CNIPA).

name: Claims supported by the description — JPO (support requirement Article 36(6)(i))
description: A claimed invention shall be disclosed in the description. If the claimed invention exceeds 'the extent of disclosure in the description to which a person skilled in the art would recognize that a problem to be solved would actually be solved', the claims fail the support requirement.
guidance: Enablement and support are different purposes; violation of one does not necessarily imply violation of the other. However, in AI-related cases, where enablement fails (see types above), it is likely the support requirement will also fail because the claim exceeds the scope described as enableable.

name: Claims supported by the description — CNIPA (Article 26.4)
description: Claims shall be supported by the description and shall define the extent of patent protection sought clearly and concisely. The technical solution in each claim shall be one that a person skilled in the art can reach directly or by generalization from the sufficiently disclosed contents in the description and shall not go beyond the scope of the contents disclosed.
guidance: In CNIPA practice, whether claims are supported is generally considered only when the description discloses the invention sufficiently; if the description is insufficient, the issue of claim support may not be separately considered (see Case C-4).

name: Generalization in claims — CNIPA caution
description: For claims generalized in generic terms, examiners shall examine whether the generalization can be supported by the description. Where generalization includes content speculated by the applicant and the effect is difficult to determine or evaluate beforehand, the generalization is regarded as going beyond the contents disclosed.
guidance: If the generalization leads a skilled person to reasonably doubt that one or more specific options included in the generic term can solve the technical problem and achieve the same technical effects, the claim is not supported by the description (examples: Claim 1 in Case C-2, Claim 1 in Case C-3).

name: Eligibility of claims pertaining to data — JPO stance
description: The JPO does not treat 'data' per se as equivalent to a program; what is acceptable is 'data with a structure that has similar properties to a computer program', i.e., data that prescribe the processing performed by the computer ('structured data').
guidance: If structured data is recognized as equivalent to a program, it may be evaluated under the 'idea based on the standpoint of software' and more likely qualify as an invention. If data are characterized only by informational content, eligibility is not satisfied. A 'data structure' is an acceptable claim format regardless of storage medium.

name: Eligibility of claims pertaining to data — CNIPA stance
description: In CNIPA practice, a claim titled 'data' that only involves the training data itself (specific numerical values/feature values) and contains no technical features is a method of presenting information (rules/methods for mental activities) and is not patentable.
guidance: If, however, the claim's features include technical features (technical means applying laws of nature producing technical effects), then the claim is a technical solution under Article 2.2 CPL and may be patentable. Thus, the presence of technical features in data-related claims is determinative.

name: Clarity of categories — JPO (data/program/model labeling)
description: Article 2(3) JPA includes computer programs in the term 'product'. If description/drawings and common general technical knowledge make clear the claimed invention is a 'program' even if labeled differently (module/library/neural network/model), it will be handled as a 'program' (invention of a product).
guidance: Structured data/data structure with features similar to programs (they define computer processing by their structure) are recognized as 'equivalent to computer programs' and handled as product claims. See JPHB Annex B guidance.

name: Clarity of categories — CNIPA (titles do not determine category)
description: In CNIPA practice, titles like 'data', 'computer program', and 'model' do not by themselves indicate whether the claims are product or process claims; therefore such claims may not comply with the clarity requirement under Article 26.4 CPL.
guidance: Applicants should make clear in the description and claims whether the subject-matter is intended as a product claim, process claim, or other category to satisfy clarity.

name: Chemical alteration (severing bonds) not dispositive
description: Breaking covalent bonds to isolate a DNA segment is a chemical alteration, but that alone is not dispositive of patent eligibility when claims are framed by informational content.
guidance: Federal Circuit judges disagreed on weight to give chemical cleavage; the Court emphasizes that claims focusing on genetic information rather than chemical composition are not saved by mere severing of bonds. Claims expressed in chemical-composition terms could raise a different inquiry.

name: Claim drafting matters: information-focused claims vs chemical-composition claims
description: Whether claims are expressed in terms of chemical composition/chemical changes or in terms of genetic/informational content affects the §101 inquiry.
guidance: If a claim relies on creation of a unique molecule (chemical composition) or on inventive chemical changes, eligibility analysis may differ; claims directed to information encoded by genes are more likely to be treated as products of nature.

name: Method claims and new applications are distinct and may be patentable
description: Method claims or patents on new applications of knowledge about genes are not implicated by this decision and could be patent eligible.
guidance: This case does not involve method claims or claims directed to new applications of BRCA knowledge; where an inventive method or a new application exists, §101 analysis may support patentability even if the underlying natural product is unpatentable.

name: Easy design-around (limitation of patents)
description: Competitors can often invent around patent claims, reducing patent effectiveness.
guidance: Assess the feasibility and cost of design-arounds when evaluating potential claim scope; narrower or easily worked-around claims are lower strategic quality.

name: Invalidation risk (limitation of patents)
description: Patents may be held invalid in litigation, undermining their protective value.
guidance: Factor litigation/validity uncertainty into patent-quality assessments; claims that are legally fragile are lower strategic quality even if technically descriptive.

name: Quality marker: robust composition-of-matter claims (pharma/chemical)
description: In high-patent-dependence industries, strong composition-of-matter claims are a hallmark of high-quality patents.
guidance: Draft claims that clearly cover core chemical or molecular entities to maximize exclusionary power; robustness against design-arounds is key.

name: Quality marker: method-of-treatment / method-of-use claims (pharma/chemical)
description: Method-of-treatment/use claims are important quality features for pharmaceutical and related patents.
guidance: Include therapeutic use claims where appropriate to broaden protection; ensure statutory/ethical considerations are addressed in claim drafting.

name: Quality marker: manufacturing process claims with detailed conditions (pharma/chemical)
description: For process claims in pharma/chemicals, detailed process conditions and parameters strengthen patent quality.
guidance: When filing process claims, disclose specific, practically meaningful steps/conditions that improve enforceability and reduce design-around options.

name: Quality marker: continuation strategy preserving commercial coverage
description: Using continuations/continuation-in-part strategies to maintain or extend claim coverage is a feature of high-quality patent portfolios in some industries.
guidance: Plan prosecution strategies (continuations, divisional filings) to adapt claim scope to emerging commercialization and to preserve freedom to assert.

name: Low-patent-dependence marker: defensive portfolio depth
description: Defensive breadth (many patents) rather than single-patent strength is a quality marker where patents are secondary.
guidance: Build portfolios that deter litigation or enable mutual assurance rather than relying on isolated, strong claims.

name: Process patent quality marker: detection-friendly process steps
description: Process patents are higher quality when process steps produce observable features in the product that enable infringement detection.
guidance: If process steps leave observable signatures in end products, process claims are more enforceable; seek to tie process steps to detectable outcomes.

name: Process patent quality marker: narrow conditions enabling detection
description: Narrowly defined process conditions that are detectable make process patents more valuable.
guidance: Draft process claims with measurable, enforceable parameters rather than broad, hard-to-prove steps.

name: Specification statutory requisites (Act of July 4, 1836, §6)
description: Before receiving a patent the inventor must deliver a written description of the invention or discovery, and of the manner and process of making, constructing, using and compounding the same, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which it appertains ...; and in case of any machine, he shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ...; and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.
guidance: Include an enabling disclosure sufficient for a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention; avoid unnecessary prolixity; for machines explain the principle and contemplated modes of application; expressly point out what is claimed.

name: Specification is part of the patent and controls its construction
description: Under U.S. practice the specification is drawn up and filed before the patent and a copy is annexed and referred to in the patent; the patent and the specification are to be construed together to ascertain the subject-matter of the invention, and the specification may control or limit the generality of the terms of the patent.
guidance: Draft the specification with awareness that its language and drawings will be read with the patent itself and may restrict broad claim language; don't rely on the patent text alone—the specification and drawings will be used in construction.

name: Court's role in construing patents
description: It is the province of the court to determine what is intended to be patented and whether the patent is valid in law; whether the invention is described with reasonable certainty is a question of law for the court upon construction of the patent terms.
guidance: Anticipate judicial construction issues: the court will resolve legal questions of claim scope and sufficiency of the written description/enablement; draft to minimize ambiguity that could generate adverse legal rulings.

name: Short title/description requirement (Act of 1836, §5)
description: Every patent shall contain a short description or title of the invention or discovery, correctly indicating its nature and design, and referring to the specification for particulars, a copy of which shall be annexed to the patent specifying what the patentee claims as his invention or discovery.
guidance: Provide a concise, accurate title that reflects the invention and points readers to the full specification for details; ensure claims are clearly identified in the annexed specification.

name: Schumer-Kyl institution threshold: 'more likely than not' standard
description: Under the Schumer-Kyl provision, the PTO will only institute a post-grant review if it determines it is more likely than not that a claim of the patent is invalid.
guidance: This is a higher threshold than current reexamination practice; practical effect: patents without a serious challenge are unlikely to be subject to the proceeding. The proceeding has limited practical effect where courts have already upheld validity.

name: 35 U.S.C. §112(a) enablement requirement
description: Inventors must describe their invention in 'full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to… make and use the same' (35 USC 112(a)).
guidance: This statutory requirement is the baseline for enablement analysis; the disclosure must be sufficient such that a person of ordinary skill can make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. MPEP 2164 attempts to summarize controlling decisions.

name: Wands factor (A): Breadth of the claims
description: The breadth of the claims is a factor in determining undue experimentation and enablement.
guidance: Broader claims are more problematic for enablement because they increase vulnerability to lack-of-enablement rejections. Practical drafting tip: consider having narrower claims as a backstop to reduce enablement risk.

name: Practical drafting tactics to reduce enablement risk
description: Tactical measures a drafter can take to lower the chance of a §112(a) not-enabled rejection by leveraging the Wands factors they can control.
guidance: Key takeaways from the page: (1) Draft narrower claims as a backstop because broad claims increase risk; (2) Provide as much direction as feasible (protocols, parameters, stepwise instructions); (3) Include multiple working examples where possible; (4) Add tips and optimization guidance to reduce the amount/quantity of experimentation needed; (5) Pay special attention to unpredictable arts (biotech, chemistry, AI) where courts scrutinize enablement more closely. The page also notes that factors B–E are largely uncontrollable, so focus effort on A, F, G, and H.

name: Entries in 'SEARCH NOTES' box — required formats and types of entries
description: Entries made in the 'SEARCH NOTES' box are intended to complete the application file record of areas and/or documents considered by the examiner in their search. The examiner will record specific types of information in the 'SEARCH NOTES' box, each entry dated and initialed.
guidance: Required entries include (A) annotations indicating how a classification search was limited; (B) notation 'See search history printout(s)' for text searches where no classification search was performed (and include the printout); (C) searches within the IPC; (D) searches performed by STIC (record 'See search history printout(s)' and date); (E) consultations with other examiners (record class/subclass and '(consulted)', may include name and art unit); (F) searches in electronic journals/books (include printouts/history); (G) searches in other media/databases (record unique identification, query, location/form e.g., CD-ROM); (H) Internet searches — print the first page and any subsequent pages with webpages reviewed, ensure search engine name, search logic and date are present or write them on the printout, indicate all webpages reviewed; (I) nonelectronic searches of print materials — record titles/terms/periods/volumes/pages as appropriate (examples provided); (J) review of art cited in parent/original patent files — record application/patent number followed by 'refs. checked' and note exceptions; (K) review of documents cited in related PTAB trials where claims DO NOT have similar scope — record trial number and U.S. Patent on trial and date reviewed; (L) review of documents cited in related PTAB trials where claims DO HAVE similar scope — record trial number, document reviewed, U.S. Patent on trial and date reviewed. Use examples/formats provided in MPEP for each type. All entries should be dated and initialed.

name: Interference search history requirements
description: When an application is in condition for allowance, an interference search must be made by using the most efficient and effective manner based on the claimed subject matter in the broadest claim (e.g., text search, classified search, or combination). Examiners are reminded that continuation-in-part applications may contain claims entitled to different effective filing dates and each effective filing date should be considered when performing the interference search.
guidance: If the application contains a claim directed to a nucleotide or peptide sequence, request STIC to perform an interference search of the sequence. Record completion of the interference search in the 'INTERFERENCE SEARCH' section of the 'Search Notes' form and identify the manner in which it was limited (if any). Make of record a printout showing only the database(s) searched, the query(ies) used (if any), and the date the interference search was performed. Do not place result printouts of the interference search in the application file.

name: Issue Not Within Scope of Inter Partes Reexamination (form paragraph 26.03)
description: It is noted that an issue not within the scope of reexamination proceedings has been raised. The issue will not be considered in a reexamination proceeding. 37 CFR 1.906(c).
guidance: Use form paragraph 26.03; in the bracket identify the issues. Advise patentee it may be desirable to consider filing a reissue application if claims may be partially or wholly inoperative or invalid. Such issues (e.g., public use, on-sale, conduct, abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 102(c)) should not be raised independently by the examiner; if independently discovered by the examiner but not raised by patent owner or third party requester, they will not be noted by the examiner (37 CFR 1.906(c)).

name: Panel review conference required before Office actions (general rule)
description: A panel review will be conducted at each stage of the examiner’s examination in an inter partes reexamination proceeding, other than for actions such as notices of informality or incomplete response.
guidance: Panel reviews examiner’s preliminary decision to reject and/or allow claims prior to issuance of each Office action. Matters outside examiner jurisdiction (petitions, extensions, support staff notices) are excluded from panel review.

name: ACP issuance criteria
description: An ACP shall set forth all rejections and determinations not to make a proposed rejection, and the grounds therefor. An ACP will not usually close prosecution if it includes a new ground of rejection not previously addressed by the patent owner, unless the new ground was necessitated by an amendment.
guidance: Although an ACP has attributes similar to a 'final rejection,' it is not a final action and cannot be appealed until a RAN is issued. Before an ACP, a clear issue should be developed. When all claims are found patentable in the first action, the examiner should issue an ACP. The criteria for issuing an ACP is analogous to MPEP § 706.07(a) for making a rejection final.

name: Presumption against redundancy in claim drafting/interpretation
description: When a patent contains multiple claims (some broad, some narrow), assume each claim is intended to have a distinct meaning and purpose rather than being redundant.
guidance: Apply this presumption to preserve the separate scopes of broader and narrower claims. Examples provided: (1) Software — a broad 'system for managing digital media files' should not be limited to systems that categorize by AI when a narrower claim expressly recites AI categorization; (2) Pharmaceutical — a broad 'chemical compound for treating inflammation' should not be read as limited to salicylic-acid derivatives when a narrower claim names that derivative; (3) Manufacturing — a broad 'method for producing lightweight composite materials' should not be construed to only cover a UV-curing-at-specific-wavelength process when a dependent claim specifies that process. Anti-pattern: construing a broad claim so narrowly that a dependent claim becomes pointless or superfluous.

name: Trademark application declaration factual assertions
description: Declarations in trademark applications (use-based under 15 U.S.C. § 1051(a)) contain specific factual assertions to which § 11.18 certifications apply: signatory believes applicant is owner; mark is in use in commerce as of filing date for listed goods/services; specimen shows the mark as used on or in connection with the goods/services as of filing date; facts recited are accurate to the best of the signatory's knowledge and belief.
guidance: These factual assertions are made under penalty of perjury; knowingly false statements subject to criminal penalty. Presenters must have a reasonable inquiry supporting these factual claims.

name: United States Patents — scope and purpose
description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention within the United States or importing it into the United States; claims are the numbered sentences that define the scope of the patent owner’s exclusive rights.
guidance: Explains patent application contents (specification, claims), role of Patent Examiner, the concept of prior art, and prosecution history (file wrapper); intended as background instruction to jurors.

name: Presumption of validity and standard of proof for invalidity
description: A patent is presumed to be valid because it was granted by the PTO; that presumption may be overcome only by clear and convincing evidence that a challenged claim is invalid.
guidance: Practice Note: consider substituting 'clear and convincing' with language such as 'highly probable' to aid juror understanding; clarifies relation to other evidentiary standards (preponderance of the evidence and beyond a reasonable doubt).

name: Claim construction — general principle (use same meaning for infringement and invalidity)
description: Each claim must be considered individually, and the jury must use the same claim meaning for both infringement and invalidity determinations.
guidance: Explicit instruction to avoid different meanings across issues; ties claim construction to §§112 and controlling case law.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. §112(f)) claim construction
description: When a claim element is in the form of a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, the claim is construed to cover the structure, material, or acts described in the specification that perform the recited function and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Judge determines the recited function and corresponding structure in the specification; Instruction 2.2 should be given when means-plus-function limitations are at issue to avoid jury confusion; cites Mettler-Toledo, JVW, Utah Med., Valmont.

name: Literal infringement — all claim elements
description: A claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every element (or method step) of that claim.
guidance: Literal infringement must be determined claim-by-claim; absence of any claim element defeats literal infringement for that claim.

name: Doctrine of equivalents — insubstantial differences
description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents only if the accused product/method contains an equivalent component or step for each claimed element that is not literally present; an equivalent is one that is only insubstantially different and performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result.
guidance: Requires a factual determination by the jury by a preponderance of the evidence; includes limitations such as prosecution history estoppel and subject matter dedicated to the public (see separate rubrics).

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — prosecution history estoppel
description: Prosecution history estoppel can bar assertion of equivalents for claim scope surrendered during prosecution.
guidance: Explains prosecution history/file wrapper and that estoppel is a limitation on DOE; practice notes and citations highlight how estoppel operates as a bar or limit.

name: Joint infringement / divided infringement
description: Rules and jury instructions govern situations where multiple actors together perform all claim elements; specific standards address when one party can be held responsible for combined actions of multiple parties.
guidance: Instructional guidance to distinguish direct joint infringement issues and ensure jury understands legal tests (text references joint infringement instruction sections).

name: Prior art — definitions (pre-AIA and AIA)
description: Prior art is technical information existing before the relevant cutoff date; under pre-AIA law different subsections of §102 have different cutoff dates, while under the AIA the Cutoff Date is the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Practice Note: refer to 'Cutoff Date' language; may require separate instructions if different asserted claims have different cutoff dates.

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA)
description: The level of ordinary skill in the art is defined by reference to education, experience, and training generally possessed by workers in the area at the relevant time (pre-AIA: time of invention; AIA: before effective filing date).
guidance: PHOSITA is a factual construct used for obviousness, enablement, written description, and claim interpretation; jury may need instruction to determine that level.

name: Anticipation (novelty) — generally
description: A claim is anticipated if a single prior-art reference or prior act discloses each and every element of the claimed invention such that the claimed invention is not new.
guidance: Anticipation is addressed through prior public knowledge, prior public use, printed publication, prior patent, and prior U.S. application; separate pre-AIA and AIA formulations appear in instructions.

name: Obviousness — Graham factors and analysis
description: Obviousness is determined using the Graham framework: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) secondary considerations (objective indicia) such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and copying.
guidance: Model instructions explain combining references, reasons to combine, and secondary considerations; cites controlling case law and distinguishes legal and factual questions for the jury.

name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims
description: Invalidity must be considered claim-by-claim; dependent claims incorporate all limitations of the claims from which they depend and can be invalid independent of or in light of their parent claims.
guidance: Instructions explain how jurors should approach dependent-claim invalidity relative to independent claims.

name: Use of bracketed template language — customizing instructions
description: Model instructions use bracketed terms (e.g., [the Plaintiff], [the Defendant], [claims in dispute], [abbreviated patent number], [[product] [method]]) to facilitate tailorability to case-specific facts.
guidance: Guides users to find-and-replace bracketed terms and to select among bracketed options to reflect whether the case involves products, methods, means-plus-function terms, AIA vs pre-AIA issues, etc.

name: Construction of claims with reference to the whole specification
description: You must always construe a claim with reference to the whole context of a specification. Every claim in every patent must be read and construed with reference to the specification, and not as if the claim was an isolated sentence having no connection with or reference to what precedes it.
guidance: Court authorities cited (Plimpton v. Spiller; Edison & Swan v. Woodhouse; Kaye v. Chubb). Read claims in light of specification to determine scope; do not treat claims in isolation.

name: Ambiguous claim: prefer construction that does not enlarge monopoly
description: If a claim can be read in two senses, one of which would make the patentee appear to claim something which was well known and in common use, the construction should be such as not to enlarge the patentee's monopoly beyond what he is entitled to.
guidance: Cases: Cropper v. Smith; Westinghouse v. Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Co.; Tindal in Haworth v. Hardcastle. Even if one construction makes claim practically repetitive of prior art, it will not invalidate patent provided it does not seek to enlarge monopoly.

name: Permitted statutory grounds of opposition (three grounds)
description: An opponent is restricted to three grounds: (i) that the applicant had obtained the invention from him, or from a person of whom he is the legal representative; (ii) that the invention had been patented in this country on an application of prior date; or (iii) that the complete specification describes or claims an invention other than that described in the provisional specification, and that such other invention forms the subject of an application made by the opponent in the interval between the leaving of the provisional and the leaving of the complete specification.
guidance: These are the exclusive statutory grounds (Act of 1883, amended 1888). The third ground was substituted by s.4 Patents Act 1888.

name: Second statutory ground: prior patent in this country — standing and particulars
description: The opponent must be a person who has a real interest in the prior patent, or the originator of the invention sought to be patented. Manufacturing under a prior patent is not necessarily sufficient; alleging intention to work is insufficient. A prior patent described but not claimed is not 'patented in this country'; provisional protection alone cannot be cited against applicant; however, a complete specification accepted at the Office (even if patent not issued) entitles the party to be heard.
guidance: Cases: Heath & Frost's Patent; Glossop's Patent; MacEvoy's Patent; Bailey's Patent; Paterson's Patent; L'Oiseau d'Pierrard. Provide title/number/date when relying on a prior patent.

name: If claim covered by earlier patent, applicant ordered to strike it out or insert disclaimer
description: Where it is clear that a claim is covered by an earlier patent the applicant will be ordered to strike it out. An applicant is frequently required to state in his specification that he is aware of a given patent and that he does not claim anything which is described and claimed in the specification under it; disclaimers are sometimes ordered.
guidance: Reference to an earlier specification must not put a construction on the later one. Cases: Hall & Hall; Webster; Grenfell & others.

name: Rival applications — joint grants, partitioning, and trusteeship
description: When two contending applicants claim to be independent contemporaneous discoverers, the law officer usually refuses to allow the grant to issue to either separately but offers it to the two jointly. Where one applicant is entitled to part and the other to another part, warrants may be issued to both limiting specifications accordingly; patents have been ordered to be vested in trustees for the benefit of both.
guidance: Examples: Craig and Macfarlane; Evans & Cutting; cases where Lord Chancellor ordered different allocations or trusteeship.

name: Core patent validity requirements (novelty, utility, intelligible specification, proper claiming)
description: Patent instructions: first, the invention must be novel; secondly, it must be useful; thirdly, the specification must be intelligible; additionally, the specification must not attempt to cover more than the patentee is strictly entitled to claim.
guidance: Utility and intelligibility are typically matters for the jury as facts, while whether a specification overclaims (attempts to cover too much) is a question of law. A specification that claims more than the patentee is entitled to renders the patent ineffectual even to the extent of fair entitlement. Patents for new combinations or methods must clearly confine the claim to the new combination or application and not claim original invention of materials already known.

name: Entitlement to damages limited until acceptance of complete specification
description: A patentee under this section will not be allowed to recover damages for infringements happening prior to the date of the actual acceptance of his complete specification in this country.
guidance: Even where priority is claimed from a foreign application, recovery of damages in the UK is measured from the date of actual acceptance of the complete specification in the UK, not from the foreign filing date.

name: Court constructs written instruments (specifications and claims)
description: The construction (legal meaning) of a specification or claim, as a written instrument, belongs to the court; the court must determine, upon the whole instrument, what the claim actually covers and whether the patent is valid in point of law.
guidance: The jury must take the construction of the patent (as to extent of claim) from the court and apply it to determine novelty. If the specification is ambiguous such that meaning cannot be ascertained, the law may declare it insufficient for uncertainty.

name: Patentee may forfeit protection by improper claim wording
description: A patentee who actually invented a useful machine or process may still lose the patent (in whole or in part) if the claim is so clumsily drawn as to comprise matters of which the patentee is not the inventor.
guidance: Jury findings as to who invented what do not save a patent whose claim on its face covers things beyond the patentee's invention; the court must pronounce such a patent invalid to the extent it claims more than the inventor's actual invention.

name: Utility: legal vs factual components
description: The question of utility has two aspects: (1) whether the subject-matter is injurious or against public policy (not a patentable subject) — this is a question of law for the court; (2) whether the means asserted to achieve an innocuous object actually will succeed in practice — this depends on evidence and is a question of fact for the jury.
guidance: It is enough for validity that an invention is capable of some use; total failure of an essential claimed element renders the patent invalid as a factual matter. The degree or extent of usefulness is immaterial if the invention is capable of some use.

name: Use the descriptive parts of the specification to construe the claim
description: Resort may be had to the descriptive parts of the specification (preamble, body, summing up) to ascertain what the patentee has said he has invented; the court should, if possible and without violating principle, construe the claim so as to include the actual invention previously set forth (ut res magis valeat quam pereat).
guidance: Examine the whole instrument together unless the summary explicitly excludes part of the description. The real invention is an auxiliary to the construction of the language employed.

name: Where descriptive terms leave doubt, look to evidence of the state of the art and actual invention
description: If the precise extent of the invention is uncertain from the description alone (but not so ambiguous as to be void), the court must attend to evidence showing what is new or old, the state of the art, and whether the patentee discovered the underlying principle or only a particular form of application.
guidance: Determine whether patentee claimed a general application of a principle (entitling broader claims) or only a particular form; this inquiry involves assessing substance and essence of the invention from evidence.

name: Judge may receive and use evidence of actual invention when construing the claim
description: In the course of trial the judge should inform himself from the evidence about the state of the art and the surrounding circumstances bearing on the meaning of the claim; if the material facts are not in doubt, construction will be given absolutely, but if evidence requires findings by the jury, the court's construction may be conditional.
guidance: The judge 'must gather as he goes along' — observe which facts are controverted — and apply the appropriate legal construction either absolutely or conditionally depending on whether factual determinations remain.

name: Presumption that patentee does not intend to claim known matter
description: A patentee is to be presumed not to intend to claim things which he must know to be in use; a specification should be read, consistently with fair import of language, so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery or invention and not to include matter known before.
guidance: The previous existence, familiarity, and constant use of something mentioned in the specification are elements in deciding whether the patentee intended to claim it as his own invention.

name: Sufficient detail to show possession
description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas. A showing of possession alone does not cure lack of written description. Case examples: Moba v. Diamond Automation; Vas-Cath; Enzo Biochem.

name: Possession shown by describing all claim limitations
description: An applicant shows possession of the claimed invention by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using such descriptive means as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession may be demonstrated by actual reduction to practice, or by showing invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen v. Chugai).

name: Biological material deposits are corroborative but not substitute
description: A reference in the specification to a deposit may satisfy written description with respect to a claimed material, but such a deposit is not a substitute for the written description of the claimed invention.
guidance: The written description of deposited material needs to be as complete as possible because examination proceeds on written disclosure. Deposits made after filing cannot be relied upon to support additions or corrections except under narrow regulatory conditions (37 CFR 1.801 et seq.).

name: Original claims presumed adequate but may lack particularity
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; however, the claimed invention as a whole may not be adequately described if an essential or critical feature is not described with sufficient particularity.
guidance: Examiner initially bears burden to present reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as supporting the claims (In re Wertheim). Example: claim 'A gene comprising SEQ ID NO:1' may implicitly include promoters or regulatory elements that are not described.

name: Functional claim language insufficient for some biomolecules
description: A biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic, without any known or disclosed correlation between that function and the structure of the sequence, normally is not a sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes.
guidance: Describing method of obtaining a claimed sequence without structural identification is typically insufficient. Compare software disclosure (functions may suffice where writing code is within skill of the art). See In re Bell, In re Deuel, Fonar.

name: New or amended claims must be supported by original disclosure
description: New or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations that are not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement (and may constitute improper new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 251).
guidance: Support for new limitations may be express, implicit, or inherent. Applicant may amend specification to include claimed subject matter present in original claims. Correction of obvious typographical errors is allowed when one skilled in the art would recognize and correct the error. See In re Rasmussen; In re Benno; In re Oda; MPEP §§2163.06-07.

name: Omission of an essential limitation can invalidate broader claims
description: Omission of a limitation can raise an issue whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits matter disclosed as essential or critical in the specification may fail the written description requirement.
guidance: Examples: claims broadened by removing location of a control means where specification stated location was 'the only possible location' (Gentry Gallery); omitting an element applicant described as essential may also lead to enablement or indefiniteness rejections.

name: Examiner initial burden to make a prima facie case
description: There is a presumption of adequate written description, so the examiner has the initial burden, after thorough reading and evaluation, of presenting evidence or reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize that the written description supports the claims.
guidance: To make a prima facie case the examiner need not present factual evidence but must point out claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why. Hyatt v. Dudas: examiner listed each element of unsupported combination, shifting burden to applicant to show support or amend.

name: Applicant must identify support for amendments
description: When applicant amends claims, applicant should show support in the original disclosure for the new or amended claims; applicant should specifically point out where the originally filed disclosure supports the amendment(s).
guidance: If applicant points out support and examiner still finds disclosure does not reasonably convey possession, examiner has the initial burden of explaining why persons skilled in the art would not recognize support. (MPEP §2163.04; Hyatt).

name: Evaluate sufficiency of recited structures, acts, or functions
description: The examiner should evaluate if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given to the preamble.
guidance: Even if individual elements are described, lack of adequate description of their particular combination can support a prima facie lack of written description (Hyatt). Preamble may be structural limitation depending on application. See Bell Communications; Corning Glass Works.

name: Transitional phrase treatment and impact
description: Transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') affect claim scope; 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate and may be construed as 'comprising' for prior art purposes absent clear specification limiting what would materially affect the invention.
guidance: Applicant bears burden to show that inclusion of additional components would materially change characteristics. See Genentech; PPG Indus.; AK Steel; MPEP §2111.03.

name: Combination claims require disclosure of combination, not just parts
description: A claim to a particular combination of elements requires that the written description adequately describe that particular combination, not merely the individual elements in isolation.
