guidance: Examiner should point out if the claimed combination is not adequately described; applicant must then identify where the combination is supported or amend. (Hyatt; Stored Value Solutions example where three authorization codes were essential claim limitations).

name: Written description support for priority/benefit claims and interferences
description: Adequate written description issues arise when determining whether a claimed invention is entitled to the benefit of an earlier priority or effective filing date, or whether the specification provides support for claims corresponding to an interference count.
guidance: Evaluate original disclosure for support of subject matter for priority under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 365, 386 and for interference counts; see cited case law (New Railhead; Tronzo; Fiers; In re Ziegler; Martin v. Mayer; Fields v. Conover).

name: Practical examiner methodology — read, analyze, and point out deficiencies
description: Office personnel should thoroughly read and evaluate the content of the application and, where appropriate, present reasons or evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize support for the claims; point out unsupported claim limitations and explain deficiencies to make a prima facie case.
guidance: Examiner practices include: analyze each claim separately, construe claims broadly reasonable in light of specification, list unsupported limitations, reference relevant MPEP sections and case law, and consider enablement/other statutory requirements in tandem before completing office action that includes a written description rejection.

name: Scope of claim (preamble, transitional language) must be supported
description: The claim as a whole, including preamble language and transitional phrase, must be sufficiently supported to satisfy the written description requirement.
guidance: Preamble language may be structural and part of invention depending on entire disclosure; examiner should determine how much weight preamble receives by reviewing whole application. See Pac-Tec; Corning Glass Works; MPEP §2111.

name: You cannot patent a principle alone
description: The law says you cannot take out a patent for a principle, that is, for a barren principle; a mere idea or principle alone cannot support a patent and, if the principle alone be the foundation of the patent, the patent must be void ab initio.
guidance: Examples: the general principle or effect of steam was known before Watt; if only the principle is claimed, the patent is invalid. A principle must be clothed with form (an embodiment) to be patentable.

name: Broad claims ('every shape' or 'from whatever source') risk claiming a principle
description: If a claim is so framed as to claim every shape or every source of a property (e.g., 'elasticity to backs of cards from whatever source derived'), it amounts to a claim for a principle and is improper.
guidance: Neilson & Walton examples: claiming 'every shape' equates to claiming the principle itself. The inventor must claim some specific mode of doing it; otherwise the claim may be treated as claiming the principle and be invalid.

name: Method- or mode-only claims insufficient without practical effect
description: It is impossible to support a patent for a method only without having carried it into effect and produced some new substance; the mere application or mode of using a thing is not sufficient ground unless realized in practice.
guidance: Court commentary: claiming a method without showing carrying into effect (and producing something concrete) will not support patentability. The 'method' must result in or be embodied in a manufacture or operative apparatus.

name: Anticipation standard (35 U.S.C. §102)
description: A claim is anticipated if “each and every limitation is found either expressly or inherently in a single prior art reference.” (Sanofi–Synthelabo v. Apotex).
guidance: Anticipation may be established by showing that all elements arranged as specified in a claim are disclosed within the four corners of a reference, either expressly or inherently, in a manner enabling a POSITA to practice an embodiment without undue experimentation (ClearValue).

name: Obviousness standard (35 U.S.C. §103 and KSR/Graham framework)
description: A claim is unpatentable under §103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Apply Graham factual inquiries: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claims and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness when in evidence. KSR v. Teleflex governs the legal standard; underlying factual determinations drive the obviousness conclusion.

name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/district-court-type; 37 C.F.R. §42.100(b))
description: In IPRs, claim language is interpreted using the district-court-type standard (Phillips): claim terms get their ordinary and customary meaning to a POSITA at the time of invention, in light of claim language, specification, and prosecution history; extrinsic evidence may be useful but is considered in context of intrinsic evidence.
guidance: The Board construes only those claim terms that are in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Realtime Data v. Iancu). If no disputed construction is needed to resolve the grounds at the preliminary stage, the Board may decline explicit construction.

name: Priority-date and chain-of-applications requirement for priority
description: To claim an earlier priority date from parent applications (including provisionals and continuations), the patent must demonstrate entitlement via the priority chain and written description support in the parent/priority applications.
guidance: If entitled to an earlier priority date, asserted prior art filed after that date may not qualify as prior art. The Board analyzes the chain (provisional → pre-CIP → post-CIP → later applications) and evaluates whether new limitations were present in earlier filings.

name: 37 C.F.R. §1.57(d) — essential material cannot be incorporated from a provisional
description: Material that is 'essential' (necessary to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention, per 37 C.F.R. §1.57(d)(2)) may be incorporated by reference only via a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication; a U.S. provisional application is not a qualifying source.
guidance: If the subject matter relied upon for written description is 'essential' and was omitted from parent applications, incorporation by reference to a provisional is ineffective under §1.57(d). Thus omitted essential material disclosed only in a provisional generally cannot be used to support priority.

name: Interpreting specification examples and figures conservatively when assessing written description
description: Disclosure of exemplary injection points or examples in a specification (e.g., 'before, after, or within the boiler') may not support broader claim scope such as adding promoter to coal vs. adding to flue gas — the Board examines what the examples actually disclose rather than inferring broader coverage.
guidance: A passage describing injection of a 'promoted sorbent' at multiple points does not necessarily disclose separate steps of (1) adding a promoter to coal/combustion chamber and (2) separately injecting sorbent downstream. The Board will compare the exact wording, figures, and context and will not accept mere obvious variations as satisfying written description.

name: Anticipation/enablement nexus — four-corners disclosure must enable practice
description: For anticipation, the single reference must disclose all claim limitations within its four corners and in a way that enables a POSITA to practice an embodiment of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Even if every limitation appears to be described, the disclosure must be enabling; mere theoretical or model descriptions that do not show how to practice the claimed invention may be insufficient for anticipation.

name: Standards for willful infringement and notice specificity
description: The bill deals with willful infringement and creates clearer standards by requiring greater specificity in notice letters alleging infringement.
guidance: Requiring specific notice letters and clearer willfulness standards is intended to reduce opportunistic claims of willfulness and provide fairer bases for enhanced damages; also tied to requiring courts to include in the record information about how they calculate damages.

name: Research-tool: claims narrowly tailored to specific tool
description: Claims should be appropriately narrow to the specific tool (assays, reagents, methods) rather than sweeping generically over methods or entire classes of tools.
guidance: Avoid genus claims that cover broad classes of research methods; specificity prevents bottlenecks and preserves downstream research.

name: Research-tool: disclosure sufficient for researchers to use without reverse-engineering
description: Patent disclosure should be complete enough that other researchers can practice the claimed tool without having to reverse-engineer it.
guidance: Enablement for the research community is a quality marker; inadequate disclosure that forces practical secrecy reduces patent quality in the science context.

name: Research-tool defect — genus claims over broad classes
description: Genus claims that sweep across broad classes of research methods or tools are a quality defect for research-related patents.
guidance: Such claims create bottlenecks and risk stifling downstream research; they are specifically problematic even if they survive formal validity tests.

name: Biotechnology: specific sequence claims with disclosed function
description: Biotech patents should claim specific sequences and disclose the function associated with those sequences.
guidance: Functional specificity (sequence + function) avoids overbreadth; functional genus claims invite enablement and eligibility challenges (e.g., Amgen-related concerns).

name: Biotechnology: method claims tied to specific applications
description: Method claims in biotech should be tied to concrete, specific applications rather than generic uses of a material.
guidance: Application-tied method claims reduce preemption of future research and downstream uses.

name: Biotechnology: disclosure enabling routine practice by skilled researchers
description: The disclosure should enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention as claimed without undue experimentation.
guidance: Enablement in biotech is a strong quality marker; lack of routine-practice disclosure is a defect (referenced in Amgen enablement debates).

name: Biotechnology defect — functional genus claims
description: Claims that define inventions purely by function (without adequate structural or sequence disclosure) are a quality defect in biotech patents.
guidance: Functional genus claims are vulnerable to enablement/validity challenges and tend to overreach, impeding research.

name: Biotechnology defect — broad gene-fragment patents lacking disclosed utility
description: Patents that claim broad gene fragments or sequences without disclosing a specific, practical utility are quality-deficient.
guidance: Utility disclosure is essential; claims lacking it risk preempting research without offering clear public benefit.

name: Basic-science: application-specific claims rather than claims to scientific principles
description: Patents on scientific discoveries should claim a specific application or implementation rather than the underlying scientific principle.
guidance: Claims to applications preserve the scientific principle for the public domain while protecting a concrete use.

name: Basic-science: claim specific implementations, not discovery itself
description: A quality basic-science patent protects concrete implementations of a discovery rather than claiming the discovery in the abstract.
guidance: This reduces the risk of preempting future research that builds on the scientific finding.

name: Basic-science defect — claims preempting all uses of a natural correlation
description: Claims that effectively preempt all uses of a natural correlation or law (Mayo-type concerns) are a quality defect.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim scope monopolizes a natural phenomenon rather than protecting a specific application.

name: Basic-science defect — overly broad claims capturing underlying scientific principle
description: Claims so broad they capture the underlying scientific principle are a quality defect because they preempt further research.
guidance: Broad functional or principle-capturing claims should be narrowed to specific, practical applications.

name: Experimental-use exemption: pure research use should not infringe
description: A robust experimental-use exemption is desirable so that pure (non-commercial) scientific research does not constitute infringement.
guidance: Recognizing such an exemption reduces the need for research-oriented narrow claims/licensing arrangements; doctrinal lines between pure and commercial research are contested.

name: Applicant should anticipate doctrinal landscape (experimental-use assumption)
description: Patent applicants should draft claims with an awareness of whether experimental-use exemptions are robust or weak, because that assumption affects desirable claim scope.
guidance: Quality requires anticipating how courts and policy will treat experimental research; strategic drafting and disclosure can mitigate harmful overbreadth.

name: Bayh–Dole: tie claims to specific commercial application disclosed at filing
description: For university or federally funded inventions, high-quality patents have claims tied to a specific commercial application disclosed at filing.
guidance: Avoid patenting fundamental research without an articulated application; tying claims to applications aligns with public-funding expectations.

name: Operative quality test — claim scope matching disclosed applications
description: Does the claim scope match the disclosed application(s), or does it extend beyond them?
guidance: Claims extending materially beyond disclosed applications signal overbreadth and reduced patent quality.

name: Operative quality test — preemption of scientific phenomena vs specific application
description: Does the patent preempt the underlying scientific phenomenon, or does it claim a specific application?
guidance: Patents that preempt a phenomenon are poor-quality from a science-progress perspective; prefer application-limited claims.

name: Identification of an 'abstract idea'
description: Claims that recite fundamental economic practices or methods of organizing human activity (e.g., intermediated settlement, hedging) or basic algorithms/mathematical concepts can be 'abstract ideas' and therefore patent-ineligible under § 101.
guidance: Compare claimed concept to prior Supreme Court examples (e.g., Benson, Flook, Bilski, Diehr). If the claim depicts a building-block activity long prevalent in commerce (e.g., 'intermediated settlement'), treat it as an abstract idea.

name: Preemption concern as the core §101 rationale
description: The exclusion for laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas is driven by a concern about pre-emption—monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work that would impede innovation.
guidance: When evaluating eligibility, assess whether the claim would 'disproportionately tie up' the underlying building-block idea; claims that risk broad preemption are suspect.

name: Functional/generic hardware claiming does not confer eligibility
description: System claims that recite 'specific hardware' only in purely functional and generic terms (e.g., 'data processing system,' 'communications controller,' 'data storage unit') do not add a meaningful limitation beyond implementation via computers and therefore do not make an abstract idea patent-eligible.
guidance: Evaluate whether recited hardware offers a meaningful limitation beyond generally linking the method to a technological environment. If nearly any computer could perform the recited functions, the hardware is likely conventional and not an inventive concept.

name: Inventive concept must be more than conventional activity
description: At Mayo step two, additional features must 'add a specific limitation or combination of limitations that are not well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field,' indicating an inventive concept; merely appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level of generality is indicative that an inventive concept is not present.
guidance: Assess each additional element for novelty and whether it meaningfully limits the claim beyond the abstract idea. The PTO guidance explicitly frames this as the dividing test for 'inventive concept.'

name: PTO Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (2019) — practical application prong
description: The PTO added a prong to the first step of the Mayo test: if the claim recites a judicial exception and is 'integrated into a practical application,' then it is patent-eligible and the PTO does not proceed to Mayo step two.
guidance: Under the guidance, determine whether the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application; if so, eligibility is established at step 1. Otherwise, proceed to evaluate whether additional elements supply an inventive concept (see the two bullet tests). Empirical evidence indicates the 2019 guidance lowered initial rejections and decreased examiner variability in 'Alice-affected' areas.

name: Three PTO-drawn categories of 'abstract ideas'
description: The PTO distilled 'abstract ideas' into three groups: (1) Mathematical concepts (relationships, formulas, calculations); (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity (fundamental economic principles/practices, commercial/legal interactions, managing personal behavior/relationships); (3) Mental processes (observations, evaluations, judgments).
guidance: When analyzing claims, map claimed subject matter to one of these three groups as part of determining whether a judicial exception is present.

name: Business method and internet-centric claims — factual/claim-specific inquiry
description: Not all software- or Internet-related claims are ineligible. A claim that merely recites a business practice performed on the Internet (or routine Internet use) is likely abstract, whereas claims that are 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' to overcome a problem specifically arising in computer networks may have an 'inventive concept' sufficient for eligibility (e.g., DDR Holdings).
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed solution addresses a technical problem particular to computer networks or whether it merely applies a pre-Internet business practice on the Internet. Courts (and the PTO) examine prior cases to find analogous reasoning when a universal definition of 'abstract idea' is elusive.

name: Case-law comparative methodology for defining 'abstract idea'
description: Because a single universal definition of 'abstract idea' is difficult, courts examine earlier cases with similar descriptive natures—what prior cases were about and how they were decided—to determine whether a claim is an abstract idea.
guidance: Use analogies to Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedents (Benson, Flook, Diehr, Bilski, Alice, Ultramercial, DDR Holdings, Amdocs) to situate the claim and predict eligibility outcomes rather than relying on a single testable definition.

name: Correction of inventorship procedures
description: When a request to add or delete inventors under 37 CFR 1.48 is granted, the change should be noted in red ink in the left margin of the original oath or declaration (paper files) and appropriate database and file-wrapper corrections made.
guidance: For IFW/09/ or later series applications, TC technical support or OPAP will update PALM database and print new bib-data sheet. Include an 'Application Division Data Base Routing Slip' brief explanation when forwarding to OPAP. Applicants must correct inventorship pursuant to 37 CFR 1.48 when amendments to claims change inventorship.

name: Partial fee-shifting detail recording
description: Record whether fee awards were partial and, if so, for which portion (e.g., certain claims, certain time periods, specific expenses).
guidance: Purpose: investigate whether judges exercise new Octane discretion via new forms of partial awards. Tabulate types of partial awards (only certain claims; only after discovery; only certain expenses; etc.).

name: Lack of inventive concept — routine and conventional steps insufficient
description: Even if a claim is directed to a natural law or abstract idea, it must include an 'inventive concept'—something more than well-understood, routine, and conventional activity—to be eligible.
guidance: Courts have repeatedly held that recited amplification/detection steps, use of PCR, taking routine measurements (e.g., forehead temperature), administering known drugs, or applying conventional clinical techniques do not supply an inventive concept. Examples: Ariosa (cffDNA detection steps were routine), Cleveland Clinic (detection and comparison were conventional), Esoterix (routine techniques), temporal artery thermometer (measuring forehead temperature not inventive).

name: Naturally occurring compositions (genes, primers) are ineligible unless structurally or functionally altered
description: Claims directed to nucleotide sequences, primers, or other naturally occurring biological materials are ineligible when they are indistinguishable from naturally occurring counterparts, unless the material has been altered or modified so it no longer exists in nature.
guidance: BRCA1/BRCA2 and related decisions hold that primers indistinguishable from natural nucleotide sequences are not patent-eligible; however, the court noted that primers altered by investigator-induced mutations or chemical modifications (so they cannot be isolated directly from naturally occurring DNA) may be patent-eligible.

name: Improvement to computer functionality or specific technical solution can render claims eligible
description: Claims that are 'necessarily rooted in computer technology' to overcome a problem specifically arising in computer networks or that recite a specific technical improvement to the way computers operate are not directed to an abstract idea and can be eligible.
guidance: Enfish (self-referential table improving database function), DDR Holdings (composite web pages solving a computer-network problem), McRO (automating lip synchronization with limited rules), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system) are examples where courts found claims directed to specific technological improvements and therefore eligible. The specification's teaching that the claim provides a technological improvement is important.

name: Merely adding a generic computer does not confer eligibility
description: Claims that add only the generic use of a computer to an abstract idea typically lack an inventive concept and remain ineligible.
guidance: District courts repeatedly rejected claims where the only addition to an abstract idea was implementation on a generic computer (e.g., vertigo management claims, certain data-processing claims). Courts look for a specific, non-generic computer-based improvement rather than mere automation of an abstract task.

name: Claim elements in an 'ordered combination' can supply an inventive concept
description: An inventive concept may arise from the specific ordered combination of claim elements, even if individual elements are conventional.
guidance: McRO and BASCOM illustrate that the combination of features—installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable filtering for each user (BASCOM), or particular limited rules for animation (McRO)—can provide the required inventive concept. Courts evaluate claims as a whole.

name: Claims addressing a specific, identified technological problem and providing unconventional solutions are favorable to eligibility
description: Claims that resolve a specifically identified technical problem with an unconventional solution that provides advantages over prior art are more likely to be found eligible.
guidance: Amdocs (correlating network accounting records), Trading Technologies (structured interface and graphical user functionality resolving a prior-art problem), and other cases emphasize that unconventional solutions to technical problems support eligibility even if the claimed subject matter touches abstract ideas.

name: Claims that organize human behavior or long-standing practices are abstract ideas
description: Claims that simply recite longstanding human practices or methods of organizing human activity are treated as abstract ideas and are likely ineligible absent additional inventive concept.
guidance: McRO described certain claimed content-filtering and organization tasks as akin to long-standing human methods; Data Engine and other decisions treated organizing and parsing data or tracking human activities as abstract when implemented generically.

name: Eligibility analysis requires reading claims as a whole and considering the specification
description: Courts emphasize reading claim language in context — as a whole — and considering the specification to determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea and whether it supplies an inventive concept.
guidance: Data Engine, Enfish, and other cases stress the importance of claim-as-a-whole analysis and that the specification may teach how claimed features produce a technological improvement, which can affect the §101 outcome.

name: Patent eligibility may present underlying factual questions
description: Although eligibility is ultimately a question of law, there may be factual disputes (e.g., whether claimed elements were conventional) that preclude resolution on a Rule 12 or summary judgment where those facts are contested.
guidance: Data Engine Technologies held that district courts erred by concluding there were no underlying factual questions for the §101 inquiry; remand was necessary where questions of fact existed about whether claims provided an inventive concept.

name: Procedural/evidentiary posture matters — absence of claim construction or expert evidence can doom §101 defenses
description: Courts have granted early dismissal where patentees failed to provide proposed claim constructions or expert testimony necessary to show that claim terms or claimed techniques were not routine or conventional.
guidance: Cleveland Clinic and other decisions denied arguments that eligibility challenges were premature when the patentee provided no proposed constructions or expert evidence to rebut assertions that steps were routine/conventional.

name: Claims to specific machines or physical configurations can avoid being abstract
description: Claims reciting a particular machine, sensor configuration, or physical arrangement that specify how raw data are processed or used may not be considered abstract ideas.
guidance: Thales Visionix (inertial tracking system specifying configuration and method of using sensors), certain 'machine' claims denied being abstract because they recited concrete configurations and methods that improved functioning over prior art.

name: Written description — distinguish old from new
description: The statute requires the patentee to give 'a written description of his invention or discovery.' This involves the necessity ... of distinguishing between what is old and what is new. He is required to point out in what his invention or discovery consists; and if he includes in his description what has been invented before, without showing that he does not claim to have invented that, his patent will be broader than his invention, and therefore void.
guidance: The specification must identify the novel subject-matter and, where prior art is used, clearly indicate that such portions are not claimed. Failure to distinguish may render the patent broader than the inventor's actual invention and invalidate it.

name: Claims are indivisible — if any claimed subject is old, patent may be void
description: Whatever appears to be covered by the claim of the patentee, as his own invention, must be taken as part of the claim, for courts of law are not at liberty to reject any part of the claim; and therefore if it turns out that anything claimed is not new, the patent is void, however small or unimportant such asserted invention may be.
guidance: Drafters must avoid claiming things that include prior art. Courts will not excise invalid portions of a claim — the presence of any non-novel claimed element can void the whole claim.

name: Construction to be co-extensive with actual discovery
description: A specification should be so construed, as, consistently with the fair import of language, will make the claim co-extensive with the actual discovery. So that, a patentee, unless his language necessarily imports a claim of things in use, will be presumed not to intend to claim things which he must know to be in use.
guidance: Interpretation should, if possible, align claim scope with what the inventor actually discovered; ambiguous language will be construed against a claim that would appropriate known, in-use items.

name: State distinctly what is claimed
description: The object of the distinction between what is new and what is old is to show distinctly what the patentee claims as his invention ... The patentee is not confined to any precise form of words. The more usual form is to state affirmatively what the patentee claims as new, and if he makes use of anything old, to state negatively that he does not claim that thing.
guidance: The specification should clearly and unambiguously set out the subject-matter claimed. Affirmative statements of new features plus explicit disclaimers of known elements are common and effective.

name: Do not appropriate prior art; identify old/immaterial parts
description: The patentee must not only claim neither more nor less than his own invention, but he must not appear even unintentionally to appropriate to himself any part which is old, or has been used in other manufactures. Those parts that are old and immaterial, or are not of the essence of the invention, should either not be mentioned, or should be named only to be designated as old.
guidance: When including known elements in the specification, either omit unnecessary prior-art details or expressly label them as old to avoid implying novelty in those parts. Describing irrelevant known parts as essential risks a construction against the patentee.

name: When improving a machine, set out prior art and then disclaim it
description: In describing an improvement of a machine ... the former machine ... should be set forth in the patent sufficiently to make known ... what it is that the patentee engrafts his improvement upon; he should then disclaim the invention of the thing thus referred to or described, and state distinctly his improvement as the thing which he claims to have invented.
guidance: For improvements, explain the existing machine enough to show the context, but explicitly disclaim prior parts and then clearly describe the particular improvement being claimed to avoid overclaiming.

name: Generic claims must be enabled across the claimed class
description: If it be stated that a whole class of substances may be used to produce a given effect, when, in fact, only one is capable of being so used, an ambiguity is at once produced, and the public are misled; but, if the patentee states the substances which he makes use of himself, and there are still other substances which will produce the effect, and he claims them by a generic description ... his claim will not be void for ambiguity, or too broad ... provided the combination is new in respect to all the substances thus referred to.
guidance: Broad/generic claims to a class are permissible only if the specification either (a) actually enables the class, or (b) the inventor discloses the exemplars he uses and the claim is honestly supported by novelty across the class. Otherwise claiming an inoperative class element is ambiguous.

name: Claiming substitutes and multiple modes — allowed if disclosed and new
description: The patent act ... does not limit the inventor to one single mode, or one single set of ingredients, to carry into effect his invention. He may claim as many modes, as he pleases, provided always, that the claim is limited to such, as he has invented, and as are substantially new.
guidance: You may claim alternative structures, substitutes, or multiple modes of performing the invention, but only to the extent those alternatives are actually within what you have invented and are novel. The patentee should describe the modes he contemplates as best, although he need not enumerate every conceivable formal variation.

name: Claim construction is for the court; enablement is for the fact-finder
description: The question whether the specification discloses what the invention is, is a question for the court on construction of the patent; while the question whether it sufficiently describes the mode of carrying the invention into practice, is a question for the jury.
guidance: Legal interpretation of claims is judicial; factual questions about whether a skilled person can practice the invention from the disclosure are matters of fact (historically jury). Drafting should thus both aim for clear claim language and factual sufficiency.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / sufficiency commensurate with the claims
description: The description must disclose the invention sufficiently to allow the person skilled in the art to carry it out, commensurate with the scope of the claims.
guidance: Examiner to assess whether disclosure supports the full breadth of the claims; includes consideration of best mode, possibility of realizing special purpose, clear and complete disclosure and whether amendments introduce added subject-matter.

name: Form and content of claims
description: Claims must conform to formal requirements for form and content, including categories, independent/dependent claims, clarity, conciseness and support by the description.
guidance: Guidance covers claim categories, drafting of independent/dependent claims, interpretation principles, limitations on number/conciseness, and examples (means-plus-function, product-by-process, use claims, preamble, open/closed claims).

name: Clarity of claims (including relative terms and other terms)
description: Claims must be clear; relative terms and other ambiguous terms must be interpreted and clarified where necessary.
guidance: Examiner is directed on interpreting unclear terms, when to object, and how lack of clarity may be expressed in written opinion or IPER; includes standardized clauses and inviting applicant to correct or amend.

name: Support in description / clear and complete disclosure of claimed invention
description: Claims must be supported by the description; there must be a clear and complete disclosure of the claimed invention.
guidance: Assess whether claims go beyond or are inconsistent with the description; guidance on detecting added subject-matter and on recommending amendments to restore support.

name: Interpretation of claims for search and examination purposes
description: Examiners are instructed how to interpret claims (including special formats) to determine novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability.
guidance: Includes directions to adopt particular constructions to make the examiner’s conclusions understandable to designated/elected offices while noting that those offices are not bound to the interpretation.

name: Priority: right to priority, determining and claiming priority dates
description: Rules and practice for the right to priority, how to determine priority dates and how priority claims should be made and checked.
guidance: Examiner guidance on documents casting doubt on priority, correcting priority claims, and relevant dates for search and examination purposes.

name: Extent of search and preliminary examination in special situations
description: Guidance on how far the search and examination should extend in particular situations (e.g., unclear claims, excluded matter, non-prior-art issues).
guidance: Includes examples where a search is possible with indication in the written opinion, exceptional situations where no search is possible, and handling cases like perpetual motion, sequence listings, and non-written disclosures.

name: Unity of invention determination
description: How to determine whether unity of invention exists (single general inventive concept) and handling of multiple inventions in one application.
guidance: Extensive illustrations (examples 1–43) for combinations of claim categories, Markush practice, intermediate/final products, complementary forms, alternative forms, dependent claims diverging from inventive concept; procedures for invitations to pay additional fees, search of additional inventions, protests, and a posteriori lack of unity.

name: Novelty assessment (meaning and methodology)
description: Principles for assessing novelty, including inherent/implicit disclosure, interpretation of claims, combining documents, generic vs specific disclosures and ranges.
guidance: Examiner methodology and examples on determining novelty and dealing with issues like inherent disclosure and combining teachings from multiple sources.

name: Inventive step / non-obviousness assessment
description: Principles and considerations for determining inventive step: what is 'obvious', the person skilled in the art, combining teachings, assessing contribution against prior art and problem-solution approach.
guidance: Includes discussion of ex post facto analysis, technical value, long-felt need, commercial success, treatment of dependent claims, examples and appendices on problem-solution approach and single-document situations.

name: Assessing industrial applicability during search/examination
description: How to judge whether the invention is industrially applicable including methodologies and examples.
guidance: Covers special considerations for utility claims (specific, substantial, credible), dates for requirement satisfaction, and when lack of industrial applicability should be raised.

name: Objective and scope of the international search
description: The objective is to identify relevant earlier disclosures; scope includes minimum documentation and possibly more depending on the claims and field.
guidance: Guidance on examiner responsibilities, basis of the search, orientation and subject of search, analysis of claims, treatment of inventions for which no fees paid, full coverage vs speculative claims and dependent claims.

name: Selection and citation of prior art in ISR (identifying most relevant portions)
description: Criteria for selecting citations and indicating the most relevant portions of cited documents in the International Search Report.
guidance: Guidance on citation categories (particularly relevant documents, documents defining state of the art, intermediate documents, documents relating to theory/principle, potentially conflicting patent docs), relationship between documents and claims, and marking of quotations or relevant passages.

name: Supplementary international search procedure and scope
description: Procedure for requesting and conducting supplementary international searches, their basis, and which claims may be excluded from supplementary search.
guidance: Covers requesting supplementary searches, start and withdrawal of request, basis of supplementary search (e.g., language/geographical coverage), claims excluded from supplementary search, and filing/copy transmission practices.

name: Dealing with major objections first in written opinions/IPER
description: When issuing opinions/reports, major objections (e.g., excluded subject matter, lack of unity, lack of novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability) should be addressed first.
guidance: Includes separate treatment where no international search was made for some or all claims, how to structure the report and use standard clauses to make the report maximally useful for national/regional phases.

name: Handling cases where no meaningful search is possible or declaration of non-establishment
description: Guidance on situations where a meaningful search cannot be carried out for all or some claims and procedures for declaring non-establishment of an ISR.
guidance: Examples include excluded subject matter, unclear claims, perpetual motion, or where Authority lacks equipment (e.g., computer program search). Includes how to record and communicate such non-establishment in Box III of written opinion/IPER.

name: Inventive step (Art. 56)
description: Inventive step (non-obviousness) is required under Art. 56.
guidance: Part G sets out how to apply problem-solution approaches and other methods to determine whether claimed subject-matter involves an inventive step.

name: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art (must articulate)
description: To reject a claim based on combining or modifying prior art, Office personnel must find (1) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (explicit or implicit) in the references themselves or in knowledge available to one of ordinary skill to modify/combine, (2) a reasonable expectation of success, and (3) whatever additional Graham factual findings are necessary to explain obviousness for the facts of the case.
guidance: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate the three findings. Motivation can be explicit or implicit (e.g., market forces, design incentives, interrelated teachings, known problems). If any of the findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used to support an obviousness conclusion. See cited case law (DyStar, KSR, Plantronics, Perfect Web).

name: Proposed modification must not change the principle of operation
description: If the suggested modification or combination would change the basic principle under which the primary reference was designed to operate, the references do not render the claim prima facie obvious.
guidance: Determine whether the combination would require substantial reconstruction or redesign and a change in the underlying operating principle (see In re Ratti). If so, that argues against obviousness.

name: Reasonable expectation of success is required for obviousness
description: Where there is a reason to modify or combine the prior art to achieve the claimed invention, a claim may be rejected as prima facie obvious only if there also was a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.
guidance: Reasonable expectation does not require conclusive proof of efficacy; it requires at least some degree of predictability. Prior art that teaches enabling methods, or shows similar compounds/processes with predictable results, can support reasonable expectation. See In re Merck, Blanc, Acorda, Hoffmann-La Roche and related cases.

name: Types of claim language that may raise limiting-effect questions
description: Certain claim language may raise questions as to its limiting effect (non-exhaustive): preambles; clauses like 'adapted to', 'adapted for', 'wherein', 'whereby'; contingent limitations; printed matter; functional language associated with a claim term.
guidance: Analyze each such term in context to determine whether it is a true limitation. See cited MPEP subsections for guidance on interpreting these constructions.

name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered and not ignored
description: A claim limitation considered indefinite cannot be disregarded; if a claim is susceptible to interpretations, at least one of which renders it unpatentable, the examiner should reject for indefiniteness and also reject over the prior art under the interpretation that renders it applicable.
guidance: Do not base a prior art rejection on speculative claim meaning. Avoid piecemeal review by making both indefiniteness and prior art rejections when appropriate. Cite Ex parte Ionescu, In re Wilson, and In re Steele for limits on speculation.

name: Principles governing the right of priority under PCT
description: PCT does not change Paris Convention Article 4 provisions; priority claims under PCT are treated in line with Paris Convention and TRIPS obligations. The priority claim is important for computing PCT time limits. Validity is not determined during the international phase.
guidance: A priority claim will be considered not made for PCT purposes if the earlier application wasn't filed in a Paris Convention country or WTO member, if filed more than two months after expiration of priority period (subject to corrections), or if required details are missing. Corrections may be possible per specified paragraphs.

name: How to file a request for restoration of the right of priority and its requirements
description: The request can be filed via the request form (Box VI) which includes an option, via ePCT, or separately by letter to the receiving Office. For success the following must be met: (a) the international application must contain a priority claim and must have been filed within two months from expiry of the priority period (or the claim added within that time); (b) the request must state reasons for failure to timely file (submitted as a separate document); (c) any applicable fee for restoration must be paid before the two-month time limit (fee payment period may be extended up to two months); (d) if required, declaration/evidence in support of reasons should be furnished with the request or upon invitation by the receiving Office.
guidance: In multiple priority claims, clarify which priority claim restoration is requested for. Annex C indicates which receiving Offices require a fee and what restoration criteria they apply. See Rules 26bis.1, 26bis.3 and related paragraphs (5.062–5.064).

name: Sequence disclosed in spec/drawings/claims but not in XML (¶ 24.23.26)
description: The application contains sequence disclosures under definitions in 37 CFR 1.831(a)/(b) but fails to comply with 37 CFR 1.831-1.834 (i.e., sequences present in specification, drawings or claims are not included in the Sequence Listing XML).
guidance: Required response — Applicant must provide: a replacement 'Sequence Listing XML' part of the disclosure (per item 1 or 2), a statement identifying the location of all additions/deletions/replacements in the XML per 37 CFR 1.835(b)(3), a statement indicating support for the amendment per 37 CFR 1.835(b)(4), a statement that the XML includes no new matter per 37 CFR 1.835(b)(5), and a substitute specification in compliance with 37 CFR 1.52, 1.121(b)(3), and 1.125 inserting the required incorporation by reference paragraph as required by 37 CFR 1.835(b)(2) (marked-up and clean versions plus statement no new matter). Examiner Notes: use only where compliance not required for examination or lack arose during prosecution; must be preceded by 24.17.26; examiner should identify sequences missing from the XML that were found in claims/drawings/specification; may be followed by deficiency paragraphs.

name: Amendment missing statement of support (¶ 24.26.26)
description: The 'Sequence Listing XML' has not been entered into the application because the required statement of support for the 'Sequence Listing XML' in the application as filed, in accordance with 37 CFR 1.835(a)(3) or 1.835(a)(4), is missing.
guidance: Required response - Applicant must submit a proper statement that indicates the basis for the 'Sequence Listing XML,' with specific references to particular parts of the application as originally filed (specification, claims, drawings) for added, deleted and/or modified sequence data. Examiner Notes: use only where compliance not required for examination or lack arose during prosecution; must be preceded by 24.17.26; may be followed by deficiency paragraphs.

name: Euro‑PCT corrected international filing date (Rule 20.5bis PCT)
description: For Euro‑PCT applications where an element was subsequently corrected under Rule 20.5bis PCT during the international phase and the international filing date was not postponed, the EPO will consider as filing date only the date on which the complete correct documents were filed.
guidance: Because this affects priority claims and prior art, the applicant will be given the opportunity (within 2 months after request) to file a written statement to choose either (a) continue with the original international filing date and base examination on the originally filed (partially erroneous) documents, or (b) accept the date when correct documents were filed as the filing date and recognize those as the original application documents. The applicant may also proactively make this request within the 31‑month period to avoid delays. See Section C‑III.1.3.

name: Adaptation of the description to amended claims (Article 84 EPC)
description: Where part of the subject‑matter of the description and/or drawings is not covered by the claims, the description must be adapted to the claims to avoid inconsistencies between claims and description.
guidance: Embodiments in the description no longer covered by the independent claims must be deleted (e.g., alternatives no longer covered) unless they can reasonably be considered useful for highlighting specific aspects of the amended claims; if retained, it must be prominently stated that the embodiment is not covered by the claims (T 1808/06). Claim‑like clauses must be deleted or amended prior to grant, particularly if inconsistent with claimed subject‑matter or merely repeat the claimed subject‑matter in a very literal manner (considered 'an irrelevant and unnecessary reduplication' not fulfilling Rule 48(1)(c)). See Sections F‑IV.4.3 and F‑IV.4.4.

name: Examination criteria for antibody claims
description: New antibody‑focused examination practice addresses admissible structural/functional antibody definitions in claims and the basis for examining inventive step in this field.
guidance: Key points: a structural antibody definition must reference at least all six CDR regions; broader structural definitions must be supported by experimental evidence. If an antibody is defined by target antigen/epitope, the antigen/epitope must be referenced without open‑ended formulations (e.g., broad sequence identity ranges or 'comprising'); negative features (antigens/epitopes not bound) are possible. If solely functional features are used and prior art discloses an antibody binding the identical antigen, the burden of proof of novelty lies with the applicant. Product‑by‑process definitions are possible if the general requirements are met, but claims relying on immunization methods with non‑100% identical sequences of the alleged antigen may fail Article 84 EPC. See Section G‑II.5.6.

name: Patentability standards (novelty, non-obviousness/inventive step, industrial applicability)
description: Core substantive standards used by offices when examining claims: novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness), and industrial applicability (utility).
guidance: These are the legal/technical criteria applied during substantive examination to determine whether claims are patentable; mentioned as the standards offices assess claims against when processing applications.

name: Provide reproducible dataset extraction (SQL) instead of preprocessed dumps
description: We prepared a new dataset based on the CPC with more than three millions US patents. We deem SQL statements as a better way than sharing conventional datasets for two reasons: (1) Separation of concerns... (2) Clarity and flexibility.
guidance: Publish data-extraction queries (e.g., BigQuery SQL) that select claims and aggregate CPC codes rather than sharing a preprocessed static dataset, so others can re-create or adapt the dataset and preprocessing criteria.

name: Physicality/tangibility is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B
description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not, by itself, a relevant consideration in Step 2B and does not guarantee eligibility.
guidance: The Supreme Court explained that a computer's physical existence is 'beside the point' — physical implementation alone cannot convert an ineligible abstract idea into a patent-eligible application (Alice Corp.). Likewise, physical steps (e.g., DNA amplification) do not automatically provide an inventive concept (Genetic Technologies Ltd. v. Merial LLC). Conversely, non-physical elements likewise may not doom claims (Enfish; McRO).

name: Step 2B procedure: identify additional elements and evaluate individually and in combination
description: Examiners must identify any additional elements beyond the judicial exception(s) and evaluate those additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more).
guidance: This evaluation should reference the Supreme Court's relevant considerations as discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h). The test is not a weighing test — it is important to evaluate significance relative to what the applicant has invented (consult entire disclosure and apply broadest reasonable interpretation). Considerations may overlap; not all will be relevant to every claim. Claims should be examined separately (one claim might be ineligible while a dependent claim is eligible). If a claim clearly recites multiple discrete exceptions, an examiner may select one and conduct the analysis for that selected exception for efficiency.

name: Claim-as-a-whole requirement: claim must amount to significantly more to be eligible (Pathway C)
description: For a claim to be eligible under Step 2B, the claim as a whole must amount to significantly more than the judicial exception; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more, it is eligible at Pathway C and the eligibility analysis is complete. If there are no meaningful limitations that transform the exception into a patent-eligible application, the claim is not eligible and should be rejected (see MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating rejections).

name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology/technical field can show an inventive concept
description: Consider whether the claim purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology or technical field — such an improvement may demonstrate an inventive concept and support eligibility.
guidance: This is the search for a technological solution to a technological problem (Alice; DDR Holdings; Amdocs). Examiners may evaluate improvement considerations at Step 2A or Step 2B. To show an improvement, the specification should provide a technical explanation sufficient for a person of ordinary skill to recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement (discuss technical problem, unconventional technical solution, or technical improvements over the prior art). After consulting the specification, the claim must itself reflect the improvement (consider full scope under BRI and evaluate the claim as a whole as an ordered combination without oversimplifying).

name: Improvement to computer functionality: distinguishing true computer improvements from mere computer implementation
description: In computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities (a true technical improvement) or merely invokes a computer as a tool to perform conventional or abstract processes.
guidance: Courts have recognized improvements where the specification and claim focus on improving how computers store/retrieve data, distribute functionality, render images, reduce congestion, provide particular memory system structures, specific transmission techniques, server structures, or particular software designs (Enfish; BASCOM; Research Corp.; Amdocs; Visual Memory; TLI; Apple v. Ameranth). Conversely, claims whose entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, or that merely automate manual processes using generic computers, are not improvements (Synopsys; RecogniCorp; FairWarning; Return Mail; Credit Acceptance; LendingTree; TLI). Examples that may show improvement: modification of hyperlink protocol (DDR), inventive distribution of network functionality (BASCOM), halftone rendering (Research Corp.), unconventional distributed network arch. (Amdocs), configurable memory (Visual Memory), technical details for image transmission (TLI), particular server structure for storing organized digital images (TLI), particular software/menu programming (Apple). Examples that may not suffice include menu generation (Ameranth), mere speed increases from general-purpose computers (FairWarning), using a computer to perform an abstract idea (Return Mail), mere automation of manual processes (Credit Acceptance; LendingTree), and conventional digital image handling (TLI).

name: Improvement to non-computer technologies may also demonstrate eligibility
description: Improvements in other technologies or technical fields (beyond pure computer-functionality improvements) can demonstrate patent eligibility when the claim describes a particular way to solve a technical problem or an improvement in an existing technological process.
guidance: Examples the courts have indicated may be sufficient include: computerized methods of operating industrial machinery (Diamond v. Diehr), new telephone/server combinations (TLI), advances in downloading/streaming (Affinity Labs), improved digital compression methods (DDR/Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec), virus screening incorporated into the Internet (Symantec), measurement devices generating new data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom), and particular sensor configurations and their methods of use (Thales Visionix). The claim and specification should convey the particular technical solution rather than merely the idea of a solution or outcome.

name: Inventive concept may arise from non-conventional, non-generic arrangement of elements (consider combination)
description: Even if individual additional elements are known and conventional, their non-conventional and non-generic arrangement as claimed may together supply an inventive concept.
guidance: BASCOM illustrates that a remote filtering tool installed at a specific location with customizable features for each end user — an arrangement of known components — yielded an inventive concept when considered as an ordered combination. Thus examiners must consider both individual elements and their combination; inventive concept can be found in the claimed arrangement.

name: Certificate after final decision
description: If the PTAB issues a final written decision and the time for appeal has expired or any appeal has terminated, the Director shall issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined to be unpatentable, confirming any claim determined to be patentable, and incorporating in the patent by operation of the certificate any new or amended claim determined to be patentable.
guidance: Certificate effects claim cancellation/confirmation and incorporates new/amended claims into the patent.

name: Changed institution standard (inter partes reexamination context)
description: Language changed from 'a substantial new question of patentability' to requiring that 'the information presented in the request shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the requester would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the request.'
guidance: Alters the threshold demonstrating whether a petition warrants institution (higher specificity about likely success on at least one claim).

name: Scope of post-grant review grounds
description: A petitioner in a post-grant review may request to cancel as unpatentable one or more claims of a patent on any ground that could be raised under paragraph (2) or (3) of section 282(b) (relating to invalidity of the patent or any claim).
guidance: Post-grant review is broad in scope and can encompass many traditional invalidity grounds.

name: Petition formal requirements
description: A petition for post-grant review will be considered only if: (1) accompanied by payment of the Director-established fee; (2) identifies all real parties in interest; (3) identifies, in writing and with particularity, each claim challenged, the grounds on which the challenge is based, and the evidence supporting the grounds, including copies of patents/printed publications and affidavits/declarations if relying on other factual evidence or expert opinions; (4) provides other information as the Director may require; and (5) provides copies of required documents to the patent owner or its representative.
guidance: Emphasizes particularity, evidentiary support, disclosure of real parties, fee payment, and service on patent owner.

name: Limitation on post-grant review of reissue patents
description: A post-grant review may not be instituted if the petition requests cancellation of a claim in a reissue patent that is identical to or narrower than a claim in the original patent, and the time limitations in section 321(c) would bar filing a petition for the original patent.
guidance: Prevents circumvention of the 9-month filing window via reissue patents that narrow/duplicate original claims.

name: Motion to amend standards and public disclosure of amendment-supporting information
description: Regulations shall set forth standards and procedures for allowing the patent owner to move to amend the patent to cancel a challenged claim or propose a reasonable number of substitute claims, and ensure that any information submitted by the patent owner in support of any amendment entered is made available to the public as part of the prosecution history of the patent.
guidance: Allows limited amendment while preserving public record of amendment-supporting materials.

name: Patent owner amendment options during review
description: During a post-grant review the patent owner may file one motion to amend the patent to: (A) cancel any challenged claim; and/or (B) for each challenged claim, propose a reasonable number of substitute claims.
guidance: Additional motions may be permitted jointly to materially advance settlement or for good cause; however, amendments may not enlarge scope or introduce new matter.

name: Prohibition on enlarging scope or introducing new matter in amendments
description: An amendment under the amendment provision may not enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter.
guidance: Ensures amendments are narrowing/clarifying, not broadening or adding new subject matter.

name: Right to submit citations of prior art and owner written statements
description: Any person at any time may cite to the Office patents or printed publications believed to have a bearing on patentability of any claim of a particular patent, or statements of the patent owner filed in a proceeding before a Federal court or the Office in which the patent owner took a position on claim scope.
guidance: Provides public ability to bring relevant prior art and owner statements to the Office's attention.

name: Limitations on use of submitted written statements
description: A written statement submitted pursuant to the owner-statement rule and additional information shall not be considered by the Office for any purpose other than to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim in a proceeding ordered or instituted pursuant to specified sections; if subject to a protective order, such information shall be redacted to exclude information subject to that order.
guidance: Restricts the Office's use of such materials to claim construction in specific proceedings and protects protected material.

name: Finality considerations when adding references to support prior common-knowledge finding
description: If the examiner adds a reference after applicant’s rebuttal only to provide documentary evidence for a prior common-knowledge finding and it does not create a new issue, the Office action may be made final.
guidance: If the newly cited reference introduces a new issue or a new ground of rejection not necessitated by applicant’s amendment, the rejection may not be made final. If no claim amendments, examiner must not rely on other teachings in the reference if making final (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if function is not desired
description: Omission of an element (and its function) is obvious where the function attributed to that element is not desired or required.
guidance: Examples: Ex parte Wu (omit polybasic acid salts when their function is unnecessary in certain environments); In re Larson; In re Kuhle. Examiner should assess whether the omitted element serves a function that would be desired in the claimed context.

name: Omission of element with retention of function indicates nonobviousness
description: If an element is omitted but its function is retained by other claimed structure, that omission is an indicium of nonobviousness.
guidance: Cite In re Edge: elimination of a layer while retaining its function (erasable metal layer obscuring print) supported nonobviousness. Examiners should determine whether the function remains and whether prior art taught such retention.

name: Making devices portable/integral/separable/adjustable/continuous is not per se inventive
description: Claiming a device as portable, integral, separable, adjustable, or continuous is not sufficient by itself to patentably distinguish over the prior art unless new or unexpected results arise.
guidance: Cite In re Lindberg (portable not sufficient), In re Larson (making integral), and other examples. Examiner should evaluate whether these structural/functional modifications produce unexpected results or advantages beyond routine expedients.

name: Timing requirement for common ownership/joint research agreement
description: The common ownership or joint research agreement must be shown to exist at the time the later invention was made. A statement of present common ownership is not sufficient. The joint research agreement must be in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made.
guidance: An invention is 'made' when conception is complete (citing Mergenthaler v. Scudder; In re Tansel) and must also meet the Pfaff readiness-for-patenting standard (e.g., drawings or descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention). The JRA may be in effect prior to the CREATE Act effective date and does not need to be in effect on or before the prior art date of the reference sought to be disqualified.

name: Definition of a Joint Research Agreement (103(c)(3))
description: 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3) defines a 'joint research agreement' as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention, that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made.
guidance: The claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA. A JRA limited to activities for a different, distinct invention does not qualify to disqualify the later reference.

name: Examiner procedure when reference is not shown disqualified under 103(c)
description: If the application file being examined has not established that the reference is disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the examiner will assume the reference is not disqualified and proceed accordingly.
guidance: Specifically the examiner will: (A) assume the reference is not disqualified; (B) examine the application on all grounds other than any conflict between the reference patent(s) or application(s) arising from a possible 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on 102(e),(f),(g); (C) consider applicability of any references under 103 based on 102(e),(f),(g), including provisional rejections under 102(e)/103; (D) apply the best references against the claimed invention by rejections under 102 and 103, including 102(e)/103 rejections, until the reference is disqualified under 103(c). The examiner should anticipate that a 102(e)/103 reference may be disqualified under 103(c).

name: Treatment of commonly owned applications of different inventive entities (double patenting)
description: Commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting, even if the later filed application claims 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit to the earlier application. The CREATE Act amendment may cause double patenting rejections between applications not owned by the same party by treating the subject matter disqualified under 103(c) as if commonly owned.
guidance: Double patenting rejections can be overcome in certain circumstances by disclaiming, pursuant to 37 CFR 1.321, the terminal portion of the later patent's term and including a provision that the patent shall be enforceable only for and during the period the patent is commonly owned with the application or patent which formed the basis for the rejection. For a double patenting rejection based on a non-commonly owned patent treated as commonly owned pursuant to the CREATE Act, the double patenting rejection may be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer in accordance with 37 CFR 1.321(d). See MPEP § 804 and § 804.02.

name: Form paragraph use and examiner notes for 103(a) rejections
description: The MPEP provides specific form paragraphs (¶ 7.20, 7.20.01, 7.20.02, 7.20.04, 7.20.05, 7.21, 7.21.01, 7.21.02, etc.) that should be used in making appropriate rejections and communications concerning 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and related 103(c) issues.
guidance: Follow the examiner notes for when each paragraph is required (e.g., ¶7.20 is required in first actions on the merits employing 103(a) and final rejections; ¶7.20.02 must be used in all applications with joint inventors unless claims are clearly restricted). Use ¶7.20.04 when applicant attempted to disqualify a reference via common ownership but failed to provide a conspicuous statement. Use ¶7.20.05 when attempt to use JRA provisions fails to meet statutory/rule requirements. Precede certain paragraphs with 7.20 or 7.103 per instructions.

name: Use of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date rules (AIPA / pre-AIPA distinctions)
description: When a rejection relies upon prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), examiners must use 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as amended by the American Inventors Protection Act (AIPA) to determine the reference's prior art date, unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from an international application with an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000 (pre-AIPA).
guidance: Use pre-AIPA 102(e) only if the reference is a U.S. patent issued from an international application filed prior to November 29, 2000 or a continuing application claiming benefit to such an international application. See Examiner Notes for form paragraphs 7.12 and 7.12.01 for assistance in determining the 102(e) date.

name: Presumption of common ownership for joint inventors (¶ 7.20.02)
description: When an application currently names joint inventors, the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were made absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and invention dates of each claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was made so the examiner can consider applicability of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art under 103(a). This paragraph must be used in all applications with joint inventors unless claims are clearly restricted to only one claimed invention.

name: Commissioner notice and re-examination on rejection
description: Whenever, on examination, any claim for a patent is rejected for any reason the commissioner is required to notify the applicant thereof, giving him briefly the reasons for such rejection, together with such information and references as may be useful in judging of the propriety of renewing his application or of altering his specification.
guidance: If the applicant, after receiving such notice, persists in his claim for a patent with or without altering his specifications, the commissioner is required to order a re-examination of the case.

name: Grounds and statutory conditions for surrender and reissue
description: Whenever any patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective or insufficient specification, or by reason of the patentee claiming more than he had a right to claim as new, if the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent or deceptive intention, the commissioner shall, on surrender of the patent and payment of the duty required by law, cause a new patent to be issued to the patentee for the unexpired part of the term.
guidance: The surrender of the old patent takes effect upon the issue of the amended patent; the commissioner may, in his discretion, issue several patents for distinct and separate parts of the thing patented upon demand and payment of the required fee for each reissue.

name: Purpose and legitimate use of reissue; anti-patterns
description: The object of surrender and reissue is to enable patentees to remedy accidental mistakes in description or claim; reissue is not intended as a vehicle to expand and equivocal claims or to enlarge coverage beyond the original invention.
guidance: Courts have pointedly condemned the practice of surrendering valid patents and obtaining reissues for the purpose of inserting expanded claims; such conduct may indicate fraudulent intent and is disfavored (see Burr v. Duryee).

name: Permissible scope of amendments to claims and specifications
description: Whether the defect be in the description or the claim, the patentee may surrender his patent and by an amended specification cure the defect; the patentee may restrict or enlarge his claim so as to give it validity and effectuate his invention, but cannot claim a substantially new and different invention.
guidance: For machine patents the model or drawings may only be amended by each other; if there is no model or drawing, the commissioner may permit amendments only upon satisfactory proof that the omitted matter was part of the original invention.

name: Acceptance despite non-compliance if explanation is clear
description: Even if the request fails to comply with one of the above-identified requirements, the request may be accepted if it is readily understood from the explanation provided in the request as to how the cited patents or printed publications are applied to all claims which requester considers to merit reexamination.
guidance: A non-compliant request can still be granted a filing date if the submitted explanation clearly shows how the cited art applies to the claims at issue; this is a limited exception and depends on whether the explanation makes the application of the cited art readily understood.

name: Copy of the patent for which reexamination is requested
description: Requesters are required under 37 CFR 1.510(b)(4) to include a copy of the patent for which reexamination is requested, to serve as the specification for the reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Provide a full printed copy (double column format including front page) so the abstract, drawings, specification, and claims are present. Include copies of any disclaimer, certificate of correction, or prior reexamination certificate, and any relevant Federal Court decisions, complaints, or interference decisions so a complete patent history is before the Office.

name: Entry and format of amendments in reexamination proceedings
description: Any proposed amendment to the description and claims in patents involved in reexamination proceedings must be made in accordance with 37 CFR 1.530 (and manner of making amendments per 37 CFR 1.121). A proposed amendment is made by filing a paper directing that proposed specified changes be made to the patent specification, including the claims, or to the drawings.
guidance: Amendments may be submitted as accompaniment to a patent owner’s request (37 CFR 1.510(e)), as part of a patent owner statement under 1.530(b), or when permitted during prosecution under 1.550(a) or 1.937. Follow the procedural formatting and signature requirements in 1.121 and 1.530; see MPEP § 2250 and § 2234 for details.

name: Response options for juristic entities asserting 'no fixed physical address'
description: Permissible responses for a juristic applicant/registrant that claims it has no fixed physical address.
guidance: A juristic entity may (1) provide a new acceptable domicile address (e.g., obtained principal place of business) or (2) provide the full name, title, and acceptable domicile address of an individual with legal authority to bind the entity (e.g., an officer or partner). The name/title/address may be included in the Domicile Address field so the domicile address is masked from public view; only information in that field is masked. Examiners may presume the person directs and controls the entity if the title clearly indicates legal authority to bind the entity.

name: If no amendments: pay grant and printing fees and file claim translations within 4 months
description: If no amendments to the Druckexemplar are necessary, grant and printing fees must be paid within a 4-month period and translations of the claims into the other two official EPO languages must be filed by the same deadline.
guidance: Claims fees may also be due if the number of claims has increased during examination. Ensure correct payments and translations are filed to progress to grant.

name: Derivation proceedings must be fair, reliable, and based on a solid record
description: Derivation proceedings are a new process by which a party can defeat an earlier-filed patent application by showing that the invention in the earlier application was derived from the party’s invention or concept. The bill requires a party to support a petition for derivation by 'substantial evidence' to initiate a proceeding.
guidance: Design derivation proceedings to balance access for true inventors with protection against speculative claims. Require rules for exchange of relevant information and evidence, permit rebuttal evidence, and ensure the Patent Office can decide on a complete evidentiary record. Anti-pattern: a petition-stage threshold so high that legitimate derivation claims (especially where inventor lacks direct documentary evidence) cannot be heard; or conversely, too low a threshold that invites frivolous proceedings.

name: Require PTO rules for exchange of relevant information in derivation
description: Amendment would require the PTO to provide rules for the exchange of relevant information by both parties, including requiring parties to provide sufficient evidence to prove and rebut a claim of derivation.
