guidance: Procedural rules should enable both sides to develop the factual record (discovery/exchange tailored to administrative setting) so the PTO can make informed determinations. Consider special evidentiary contexts (e.g., disclosures to intermediaries or venture capitalists) where direct documentary proof may be limited; allow mechanisms to link disclosures and downstream filings. Anti-pattern: leaving evidence exchange undeveloped, resulting in unfair outcomes or incomplete records.

name: Priority documentation and indication of priority validity
description: If waiting to obtain the priority document and/or the translation an appropriate comment should be made under the heading 'Additional observations, if necessary:' in Box No. II. If a copy of the priority document and/or the translation is not available because of non-compliance by the applicant with Rule 17.1 ... any written opinion ... may be established as if the priority had not been claimed and this is indicated in the report. Where the right to priority is invalid, item 2 of Box No. II ... must be completed. 'Additional observations' in item 3 of Box No. II relate to Priority considerations only and not to clarity, descriptive support, defects or any other consideration relevant to Box No. VIII.
guidance: Include reasons for which a priority claim was considered invalid, or indicate that the priority claim had been checked and was considered valid; place remarks under Box II 'Additional observations' only for priority matters.

name: Clarity or support preventing formation of meaningful opinion
description: Where the description, the claims, or the drawings are so unclear, or the claims are so inadequately supported by the description that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability, the examination may be restricted to claims or parts of claims that are sufficiently clear and supported to enable an opinion.
guidance: Mark the appropriate check box(es) in Box No. III and include observations on lack of clarity/support to explain the limitation of examination. Issues of clarity and descriptive support should, as appropriate, be raised separately at Box No. VIII.

name: Nucleotide and/or amino acid sequence listings compliance
description: A failure to furnish a nucleotide and/or amino acid sequence listing complying with the standard provided for in Annex C of the Administrative Instructions and in an accepted language may preclude any meaningful preliminary examination from being carried out.
guidance: Make a meaningful search or examination to the extent possible; if some or all claims cannot be examined for this reason, note the reasons in the final check boxes of Box No. III and provide details in the Supplemental Box if necessary. See Chapters 15 and 18 for further discussion.

name: Reasoned statement on novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability (Box V)
description: A statement as to whether the claims appear to satisfy the criteria of novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness) and industrial applicability is made in item 1 of Box No. V for each claim to be examined (YES or NO). Each such statement must be accompanied by relevant citations, explanations and observations in item 2 of Box No. V. A statement on all three criteria should be made, and the examiner should always cite documents believed to support any negative statement.
guidance: Citations must follow WIPO Standard ST.14. Explanations should clearly indicate, with reference to the cited documents, the reasons supporting the conclusions and identify particularly relevant passages (page/column/lines). For patent documents in another language, indicate corresponding part of an English family member if available. For non-written disclosures, describe the most relevant elements and give spatial/temporal references (e.g., timestamps). See Chapters 12–14 for further guidance on each consideration.

name: Observations on clarity and support (Box VIII)
description: If there are significant and pertinent issues as to the clarity of the claims, the description and the drawings, or whether the claims are fully supported by the description, observations should be made in Box No. VIII. The examiner should list relevant claim numbers and indicate reasons for lack of clarity and/or support.
guidance: Decide whether to include observations based on their significance for further processing. Observations need not be included where likely amendments to overcome other objections would also resolve clarity/support issues; but where a positive statement on patentability for all claims is given, raise significant clarity/support matters. Cross-reference paragraphs 5.31–5.58 and 17.09.

name: Invitation to correct or amend and time limits for reply
description: The written opinion of the International Searching Authority includes notification that if the applicant demands international preliminary examination he is invited to file observations, correct formal deficiencies and submit amendments before the expiration of the time limit for filing the demand. Any written opinion established by the International Preliminary Examining Authority must fix a time limit for reply that is reasonable under the circumstances (normally two months, not shorter than one month, and at least two months after the international search report was transmitted; should not be more than three months after the opinion date).
guidance: Failure to reply to the invitation may cause the international preliminary examination report to be established with a negative determination in relation to certain claims. Set time limits carefully and ensure applicant is properly notified.

name: Circumstances for partial or no written opinion
description: There may be cases when the Authority is not required to perform an international preliminary examination covering the whole application, or it is more efficient to defer some matters. These include: only inventions which have been searched need be subject to international preliminary examination; subject matter on which the Authority is not required to carry out examination; claims lack unity; fundamental objections (e.g., clear lack of novelty) or where amendments add matter beyond the original disclosure.
guidance: Indicate the scope limitation in the opinion and use the appropriate Box III/IV checkboxes or explanations. See Rule 66.1(e) and Article 34(4)(b).

name: Dealing with major/fundamental objections first
description: If fundamental objections arise (including introduced by amendment), it may be more appropriate to deal with these objections before making a detailed examination; e.g., if claims need recasting, avoid raising subsidiary clarity objections which will be moot.
guidance: At the first written opinion stage seek to make the maximum impact to provide a useful international preliminary report on patentability and to bring proceedings to a conclusion without undue delay to meet time limits if examination is demanded.

name: Parallel proceeding strategy (pursue inter partes reviews)
description: We pursue parallel inter partes reviews (IPR) of the asserted patents to take advantage of more favorable standards in determining invalidity and to force the patent holder into taking positions that also compromise infringement.
guidance: A recommended tactical criterion: coordinate IPRs with ITC litigation to leverage different invalidity standards and to extract concessions or positions from the patent owner that can aid the ITC defense or undermine infringement claims.

name: Indicator importance varies by technology field
description: Relative importance (weights/signal rates) of indicators differs by field: forward citations ~48% weight in drugs, claims much more important in most other fields; family size generally small but larger role in computers.
guidance: Report field-specific weights and signal rates and tailor index construction to technology area; dropping a field-critical indicator (e.g., claims in non-drug fields) greatly reduces information content.

name: Consistent application of patentability requirements
description: The same standard of patentability applied in the examination of claims must be the same throughout the Office. All requirements for patentability (e.g., novelty, usefulness and unobviousness, as provided in 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, and 103) must be met before a claim is allowed.
guidance: The mere fact that a claim recites in detail all of the features of an invention (i.e., is a “picture” claim) is never, in itself, justification for the allowance of such a claim.

name: Constructive handling of defects in form or omission of a limitation
description: When an application discloses patentable subject matter but claims in their present form cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection.
guidance: The examiner's action should be constructive in nature and when possible should offer a definite suggestion for correction.

name: Determining which subsection of 35 U.S.C. 102 applies (102(a),(b),(e))
description: Once a printed publication or patent is found to disclose the claimed invention, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be made under 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e) by determining the effective filing date of the application and comparing with the date of the reference.
guidance: Determine the issue/publication date of the reference (including rules for weekend/holiday cutoff and that a magazine is effective as of the date it reached the addressee). If the publication/issue date is more than 1 year prior to effective filing date, 102(b) applies. If too recent for 102(b), consider 102(e): the reference must be a U.S. patent (or SIR) with a filing date earlier than the application's effective filing date and have a different inventive entity. If 102(e) does not apply, consider 102(a) where the reference has a publication date earlier and is not applicant's own work.

name: Overcoming a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection (printed publication or patent more than 1 year prior)
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by: (A) persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish; or (C) perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 by amending the specification to specifically reference a prior application in accordance with 37 CFR 1.78(a).

name: Overcoming a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinction; (B) amending claims; (C) filing a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit/declaration (showing the reference invention is not by 'another'); (D) filing a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration showing prior invention if the reference is not a U.S. patent (subject to limitations); (E) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); (F) perfecting priority under 119(e) or 120 by amending the specification per 37 CFR 1.78(a).
guidance: When the claims of the reference and the application are directed to the same invention or are obvious variants, a 1.131 affidavit is not acceptable; consider double patenting or interference. If common assignee/inventor exists, a double patenting rejection must be made. If no common assignee/inventor and 102(e) is the only possible rejection, consider whether an interference should be declared.

name: Overcoming a 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(a) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinction; (B) amending claims; (C) filing a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration; (D) filing a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit/declaration showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (E) perfecting foreign priority under 119(a)-(d); (F) perfecting priority under 119(e) or 120 by amending the specification per 37 CFR 1.78(a).

name: Language for rejections should be unequivocal
description: The language to be used in rejecting claims should be unequivocal.
guidance: See MPEP § 707.07(d) for guidance. Rejections should clearly identify the statutory basis and the prior art parts relied upon to support the rejection.

name: Board of examiners review on request (sec. 7)
description: If the specification and claim have not been so modified as, in the opinion of the Commissioner, shall entitle the applicant to a patent, the applicant may, on appeal and upon written request, have the decision of a board of examiners who may reverse the Commissioner's decision.
guidance: This provides an internal administrative review step where the Commissioner objects to the claim/specification as not properly modified to sustain a patent.

name: Expedited Cancellation Pilot Program evaluation metrics
description: Assess expedited cancellation proceedings by measuring claims distribution and default judgment rates (e.g., abandonment included in 34% of proceedings; likelihood of confusion 27%; default judgment rates: 44% overall, 49% when nonuse/abandonment included, 60% when abandonment only).
guidance: Use pilot analysis to confirm cancellation proceedings' utility for clearing unused/abandoned marks and to inform future procedures (including preparations for TMA).

name: Standard of review: legal vs factual
description: We review the Board’s legal decisions de novo and its factual determinations for substantial evidence.
guidance: Claim construction and obviousness are treated as questions of law that depend on underlying factual findings, so courts review legal aspects de novo but underlying factual findings for substantial evidence (citing Teva; In re Brandt).

name: Anticipation requirement
description: Anticipation is a question of fact, and a finding of anticipation requires that every limitation of the claim is present in a single prior art reference.
guidance: The Board must identify each claim limitation in a single prior reference (citing Ericsson).

name: Obviousness: sufficiency when prior art sometimes meets claim
description: Combinations of prior art that sometimes meet the claim elements are sufficient to show obviousness.
guidance: It is enough that the combination would sometimes perform all the method steps (citing Unwired Planet and Hewlett‑Packard v. Mustek). Example: a prior-art system that would determine a claimed element 'some of the time' can teach that aspect of the claim.

name: No addition of unwritten claim limitations
description: It is incorrect for the Board to read unwritten limitations into claims.
guidance: The Board may not import extra requirements that are not recited in the claim; courts will reverse where the Board imposes an unrecited limitation (citing In re Zletz). Example in opinion: Board's implicit requirement of user 'interaction' with a delivered 'list of goods' was an unwritten limitation not present in the claim language.

name: Intrinsic evidence controls claim scope (specification can define terms)
description: Claim terms are interpreted in light of the specification; if the specification expressly defines a term (e.g., 'object' may include intangible items), that meaning can be used.
guidance: Mapping a claim term to prior-art elements must be consistent with the patent specification; the opinion points out the specification explicitly stating that 'object' may be intangible (e.g., electronic music file), supporting mapping content promoted by a billboard to the claimed 'object.'

name: Consistency in construing related claims
description: Claims that share limitations should be construed consistently; dependent claims should not be given more stringent, unwritten requirements than their independent claim counterpart absent justification.
guidance: The Board construed claim 1 without requiring user 'interaction,' yet applied an 'interaction' requirement to dependent claims 37 and 43—an inconsistent and improper added limitation leading to reversal in the opinion.

name: Speculation is insufficient to meet prior-art disclosure
description: Board conclusions that rely on speculation (e.g., that advertised products 'may be' in store vs. out of stock) are insufficient to show that prior art discloses a claim limitation.
guidance: Factual findings must be grounded in evidence, not conjecture; where the Board labels an asserted mapping as 'speculation,' that rationale is inadequate to deny a finding of disclosure.

name: Remand when Board fails to analyze subsequent limitations
description: When the Board fails to analyze subsequent claim limitations (or otherwise errs such that not all limitations were considered), the proper remedy is vacatur and remand for the Board to consider the remaining limitations.
guidance: If the Board applied an incorrect legal standard or omitted analysis of later limitations, the Federal Circuit vacates and remands (opinion vacated Board's decision on claim 25 and dependent claims and remanded to consider subsequent limitations).

name: Alice § 101 two-step test
description: Determining patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 requires a two-step inquiry: (1) decide whether the claims are directed to a traditional patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas) (Alice Step One); and (2) if so, ask whether the remaining elements, alone or in combination, supply an "inventive concept" that "transforms the nature of the claim" into a patent-eligible application (Alice Step Two).
guidance: Cite Alice, 573 U.S. 208, 217-218. Use Mayo/Alice lineage: if claims merely require a generic computer to perform generic functions, they fail Step Two. Include the Mayo language about "well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the industry."

name: Alice Step Two — presence of an inventive concept
description: Ask whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, provide an inventive concept sufficient to transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application. Claims cannot survive Step Two if they recite only "well-understood, routine, conventional activities" or generic computer functions.
guidance: An alleged inventive feature must be part of the claims (not only in the specification). Unclaimed or merely described features (e.g., a 'layered architecture' in the specification but not claimed) cannot be relied on to supply an inventive concept. Cite Berkheimer where factual disputes about whether elements are "well-understood, routine, conventional" may preclude summary judgment.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activities test
description: To defeat Step Two, a court asks whether the claimed additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional activities previously known in the industry (Mayo/Alice language).
guidance: If resolution of whether elements are routine is fact-dependent (per Berkheimer), summary judgment may be inappropriate; conversely, if the record and claim language show only generic functionality, summary judgment is proper. Use factual record only when necessary.

name: Claim construction and reliance on unclaimed/specification-only features
description: An inventive-concept argument must be grounded in claim language or a correct claim construction; relying on features present only in the specification (unclaimed features) is improper to establish patentability.
guidance: If a party wants to limit or supply an inventive feature (e.g., 'layered architecture'), it should propose that limitation during claim construction; courts will not import unclaimed features post hoc to save claims under § 101.

name: Scope of Section 337 / Covered Causes of Action
description: Section 337 'broadly declares unlawful unfair methods of competition and unfair acts in the importation and/or sale of imported articles.' The majority of Section 337 investigations have focused on patent, unregistered trademark, or trade secret claims, and the ITC has accepted jurisdiction over registered trademarks, trade dress, false designation of origin, trademark dilution, copyright (including DMCA), mask work infringement, misappropriation of trade secrets, and various business torts and unfair competition allegations.
guidance: Section 337 was originally a 'catch all' statute but has evolved into an IP enforcement statute. Certain acts (e.g., dumping, unlawful subsidies) are not within Section 337. The Commission looks to general principles/precedents and may consider defenses such as the §271(e)(1) safe harbor where applicable.

name: Appeals to the Federal Circuit — Markman de novo and limits of preclusive effect
description: Appeals from Commission decisions go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which applies Markman claim construction de novo and can vacate and remand Commission rulings on infringement issues. Commission findings are not binding interpretations of patent law and generally do not have res judicata or collateral estoppel effect in federal courts for patent validity/infringement.
guidance: Trademark adjudications may receive greater preclusive effect. Parties should anticipate Federal Circuit review and possible de novo claim construction in appeals from ITC determinations.

name: Pleading and evidentiary standard for patent coverage allegations
description: A patent-related complaint must support the allegation that the accused imported item or foreign manufacturing process is covered by the asserted patent — i.e., there must be adequate detail showing how the accused products/practices fall within the patent claims.
guidance: Notice pleading is insufficient; preparing a Section 337 complaint typically requires more resources than a district-court complaint. Include claim charts, exhibits, and factual support showing literal infringement or doctrine-of-equivalents theories as appropriate.

name: Disposition of IPR petitions completed to date (outcome categories)
description: Outcomes for all IPR petitions filed to date that have reached a final disposition, including totals for Trials Not Instituted, Trials Instituted, Petitions Denied, Terminations Before Institution Decision (broken into settled, dismissed, request for adverse judgment), Terminations After Institution Decision (settled, dismissed, request for adverse judgment), Trials Completed (Reached Final Written Decision), and counts/percentages for Trials with all instituted claims unpatentable / some instituted claims unpatentable / no instituted claims unpatentable.
guidance: Shown as a 'stepping stone' visual with numeric breakdowns and percentages (example totals: 3672 total petitions; 1771 trials not instituted; 1901 trials instituted; 1214 trials completed; breakdowns of outcomes with percent of total petitions and percent of trials instituted). '*Data current as of: 9/30/2016.'

name: Disposition of CBM petitions completed to date (outcome categories)
description: Outcomes for all CBM petitions filed to date that have reached a final disposition, including Trials Not Instituted, Trials Instituted, Petitions Denied, Terminations Before Institution Decision (settled, dismissed), Terminations After Institution Decision (settled, dismissed, request for adverse judgment), Trials Completed (Reached Final Written Decision), and counts/percentages for trials with all/some/no instituted claims unpatentable.
guidance: Shown as a 'stepping stone' visual with numeric breakdowns (example totals: 391 total petitions; 176 trials not instituted; 215 trials instituted; 143 trials completed; percentages provided for outcomes). '*Data current as of: 9/30/2016.'

name: IPR petitions claims-level termination breakdown (claims available → challenged → instituted → final outcomes)
description: Claims flow visualization for IPR petitions showing total number of claims available to be challenged, claims challenged vs not challenged, claims on which trial was instituted vs not instituted, and final outcomes: claims found unpatentable in final written decision, claims cancelled/disclaimed by patent owner, claims remaining patentable (not subject to final written decision), and claims found patentable by PTAB.
guidance: Presented as four cylinders with numeric counts (examples: Total claims available within 3672 petitions; Claims challenged: 56233; Claims instituted: 25626; Claims found unpatentable by PTAB in final written decision: 13140; Claims cancelled or disclaimed: 2220; Claims found patentable by PTAB in final written decision: 3519; Claims remaining patentable (not subject to final written decision): 6747). Note: 'Completed' petitions include terminations (before or after a decision on institution) due to settlement, request for adverse judgment, or dismissal; final written decisions; and decisions denying institution. '*Data current as of: 9/30/2016.'

name: CBM petitions claims-level termination breakdown (claims available → challenged → instituted → final outcomes)
description: Claims flow visualization for CBM petitions showing total number of claims available to be challenged, claims challenged vs not challenged, claims on which trial was instituted vs not instituted, and final outcomes: claims found unpatentable in final written decision, claims cancelled/disclaimed by patent owner, claims remaining patentable (not subject to final written decision), and claims found patentable by PTAB.
guidance: Displayed as four cylinders with numeric counts (examples: Total claims available within 391 petitions: 13832; Claims challenged: 7424; Claims instituted: 3374; Claims found unpatentable by PTAB in final written decision: 2031; Claims cancelled or disclaimed: 301; Claims found patentable by PTAB: 73; Claims remaining patentable (not subject to final written decision): 969). Note repeats the definition of 'Completed' petitions. '*Data current as of: 9/30/2016.'

name: Substantive engagement with 35 U.S.C. §112 issues
description: Whether the examiner raises and develops written-description, enablement, and definiteness (§112) issues, not just 102/103 (novelty/obviousness) rejections.
guidance: Time-constrained examiners may avoid detailed §112 analysis; substantive §112 examination (claim construction, support, enablement questions) is evidence of thorough review.

name: First-action allowance of broad claims
description: Allowance on first office action, particularly of broad genus or method claims, without prior substantive rejections.
guidance: First-action allowances—especially for broad claims—are a quality red flag associated with reduced examiner time. Treat such allowances as weaker evidence of a reliable grant unless countervailing indicators are present.

name: Lower counts of substantive 102/103/112 rejections
description: Fewer substantive rejections under novelty (102), obviousness (103), or §112 grounds per application.
guidance: Declining counts of substantive rejections per application can reflect less rigorous examination. Contrast rejection frequency with expected norms for the technology area and claim scope.

name: Downstream litigation frequency per patent
description: Number of suits or other enforcement actions per patent after grant.
guidance: Time-pressured grants were associated with more downstream litigation per patent. Elevated litigation frequency can reflect both low-quality patents that invite challenges and poor claim clarity from cursory examination.

name: Inappropriate use: Reference claims the same patentable invention (U.S. patent or application publication)
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is not appropriate where the reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claims the same patentable invention.
guidance: See MPEP § 715.05 for "same patentable invention" and MPEP Chapter 2300. Where reference patent and application/patent under reexamination are commonly owned and inventions are not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103. See MPEP § 718.

name: Effective date rule: U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and international application publications
description: U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and WIPO publications of international applications are available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) against all patent applications and patents under reexamination; the effective date of a domestic patent when used as a reference is the effective U.S. filing date, not the foreign filing date.
guidance: When entitled to claim benefit of an earlier filed application, effective filing date is determined under 35 U.S.C. 102(e). See MPEP § 706.02(a), § 706.02(f)(1), § 2136–§ 2136.03. Note: effective date of domestic patent is not the foreign filing date (In re Hilmer).

name: Form paragraph 7.57: Affidavit or Declaration Under 37 CFR 1.131: Ineffective - Heading
description: ¶ 7.57  The [1] filed on [2] under 37 CFR 1.131 has been considered but is ineffective to overcome the [3] reference.
guidance: Examiner Note: bracket 1 insert --affidavit-- or --declaration--; must be followed by one or more of form paragraphs 7.58–7.63 or a paragraph setting forth proper basis for insufficiency (e.g., failure to establish acts performed in this country, or scope not commensurate with scope of claims).

name: Activities applied against the claims: how to overcome
description: A rejection based on an activity showing the claimed invention was used or known prior to the filing date may be overcome by an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 establishing a date of invention prior to the activity date, or by a specific affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the activity was performed by the applicant(s).

name: Genus-species practice where predictability is in question
description: Where predictability is in question, the 1.131 affidavit/declaration must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to furnish support for a generic claim; showing one species may not ordinarily withdraw rejection if reference discloses another species not antedated.
guidance: Test: whether facts in the affidavit would persuade one skilled in the art that the applicant possessed enough of the invention to justify the claimed genus. In unpredictable arts, prior completion of one or a few species is generally not sufficient; number required depends on size and predictability of genus (e.g., small genus like halogens may require 2–3 species, large genus many). Cited cases: In re Shokal, In re Mantell, In re Rainer, In re DeFano, In re Clarke, In re Schaub.

name: Essence or substance of the invention
description: The application of a law, property, or quality of matter to a subject by particular means for a particular end 'constitutes the essence and substance of the invention' and is what the patentee has invented.
guidance: What the patentee actually invented (the essence) cannot be taken from him without violating the principles of property in invention; this essence is the primary measure when construing claims and determining scope.

name: Two-part test for whether old matter is included in a claim
description: In determining whether the patentee has included in his claim something not new, ascertain (1) whether he makes use of anything not new, and (2) whether that thing, according to the fair import of his language, is represented to be part of the invention claimed.
guidance: The first is an evidentiary question (is the thing old?), the second is a question of construction (does the claim language include it?). If the public is misled, the patent ought not to stand; but construction should be fair to reach just import.

name: Presumption in doubtful cases: construe in favor of the patentee
description: If, after applying rules of construction, doubt remains whether the claim is broader than the invention, the patentee is to be presumed to have intended to claim no more than he actually invented.
guidance: Fraud is not to be presumed; the maxim ut res magis valeat quam pereat guides courts to support a claim if it can be done without violating principle. This presumption operates only in doubtful cases and not where a claim is manifestly too broad.

name: Constrictive construction to make claim coextensive with actual invention
description: The specification should be construed so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual invention, if this can be done consistently with legal principle.
guidance: This rule helps preserve the patent for the real invention (patent may remain valid pro tanto) but will not save claims that clearly attempt to appropriate more than was invented.

name: Construction balancing: protect public from misleading claims vs. protect inventor
description: If the public has been misled by a claim (e.g., patentee represents he invented something that existed before), the patent ought not to stand; yet courts should not adopt constructions that destroy a patent lightly.
guidance: Apply fair construction to reach the just import; where no doubt exists that the claim is manifestly broader than the invention, the patent may be invalidated; otherwise prefer an interpretation that preserves the real invention.

name: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101
description: Claimed subject matter must fall within one of the four categories recited in 35 U.S.C. 101: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
guidance: If claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, natural phenomenon, law of nature), explain why it is a judicial exception and whether the claim is directed to a practical application of that exception (e.g., requires physical transformation or produces a useful, concrete, and tangible result). Also explain if the claim would impermissibly preempt all substantial practical applications of the exception.

name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101) — Utility Lacking
description: The claimed invention lacks patentable utility.
guidance: Examiner must provide explanation of lack of utility (see MPEP §§ 706.03(a) and 2105-2107.03). Use form paragraph for this rejection and identify facts supporting absence of a credible/specific/substantial utility.

name: Utility must be specific/substantial/credible or well-established
description: Claims must be supported by either an asserted utility that is specific and substantial (or credible) or by a well-established utility.
guidance: Use Format A when there is no asserted utility or asserted utility is not specific and substantial; Format B when utility must be characterized as 'credible'; Format C when multiple utilities exist with varying sufficiency — address each utility. When lacking, also make a 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph (enablement) rejection as appropriate.

name: Written description deficiency (claim contains subject matter not described)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for failing to comply with the written description requirement because the claim contains subject matter not described in the specification so as to reasonably convey possession to one skilled in the art.
guidance: Identify by page/line and/or figure the subject matter not properly described and explain the position, including any unanswered examiner questions that raise doubt about possession at filing. This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 (or 7.103).

name: Scope of enablement must be commensurate with claims
description: When the specification is enabling for some embodiments but the claims are broader, the claims may be rejected because the specification does not provide enablement commensurate in scope with the claims.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.31.03 when scope of claims exceeds scope of enabling disclosure. Identify the enabling portions of the specification and the claim aspects that are not enabled; explain using In re Wands factors and cite MPEP §§ 2164.01(a) and 2164.04.

name: Essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement)
description: Reject when a feature considered critical or essential by applicant to practice the claimed invention is omitted from the claims and the disclosure does not enable practice without it.
guidance: Recite the omitted subject matter and give rationale for considering it critical or essential, citing applicant statements/arguments/drawings/etc. that demonstrate applicant viewed the feature as essential. Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01.

name: Indefiniteness — failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim
description: Claim rejected as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
guidance: Identify particular term(s) or limitation(s) rendering claim indefinite and explain why. If claim scope can be determined by one of ordinary skill, a rejection is not appropriate. Precede with form paragraph 7.30.02 (or 7.103).

name: Claim term used inconsistently with accepted meaning
description: When applicant acts as their own lexicographer to give a claim term a meaning contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term and set forth the uncommon definition to put one skilled in the art on notice.
guidance: Identify the term, the meaning assigned in the claim, and the accepted meaning, with support for the accepted meaning (textbook/dictionary). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Relative term / term of degree renders claim indefinite
description: A relative term (term of degree) that is not defined by the claim or the specification and for which no standard for ascertaining the requisite degree is provided renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: Explain which parameter/quantity/limitation is made indefinite by the term and how the specification fails to provide a standard. Precede with form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Broad range and narrow range in same claim renders claim indefinite
description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation that falls within the broad range (in the same claim) is considered indefinite because it raises doubt whether the narrower language is exemplary or required.
guidance: Insert the broader and narrower ranges and locations in the claim; modify to fit other instances of indefiniteness. Precede with form paragraph 7.34.01. See Ex parte Wu and MPEP § 2173.05(c).

name: Use claims must recite steps — mere 'use' may be indefinite/improper
description: A claim that provides for the use of something but does not set forth any steps involved in the method/process is unclear what method/process is intended and is indefinite; a mere recitation of a use may also be an improper process claim under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Insert what is being used and, if applicable, reference related claims. This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01. See MPEP § 2173.05(q) and cited cases for examples.

name: Claims are literal translations — narrative/grammatical defects
description: Claims appearing to be literal translations into English from a foreign document that are narrative and replete with grammatical/idiomatic errors are generally indefinite and fail to conform to U.S. practice.
guidance: Use this form paragraph (preceded by 7.34.01) to describe failure to conform to claim drafting norms and indicate need for correction.

name: Indefinite claim language: 'for example', 'such as', 'or the like'
description: Phrases like 'for example', 'such as', or 'or the like' render claims indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following those phrases are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: Use the specific form paragraph for the offending phrase (7.34.08 for 'for example', 7.34.10 for 'such as', 7.34.09 for 'or the like'). These must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01 and reference MPEP § 2173.05(d).

name: Means-plus-function modifier lacks specified function (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph)
description: Where 'means' is used but the word(s) preceding 'means' do not convey a function, it is impossible to determine equivalents as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, and the claim is indefinite.
guidance: Ensure words preceding 'means' convey a function (e.g., 'latch means' conveys 'latching'). If not, the claim is indefinite. Precede with form paragraph 7.34.01 and cite Ex parte Klumb.

name: Essential elements omitted from claims
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph for omitting essential elements such that the claim is incomplete.
guidance: Recite the omitted elements and give rationale for considering them critical or essential. Precede with form paragraph 7.30.02.

name: Essential structural cooperative relationships omitted
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph when essential cooperative structural relationships among elements are omitted, creating a gap between necessary structural connections.
guidance: Recite omitted structural cooperative relationships and explain why they are critical. Precede with form paragraph 7.30.02. See MPEP § 2172.01.

name: Pro se claim drafting deficiencies
description: Pro se claims may be narrative, indefinite, and contain functional/operational language; device structure must be clearly and positively specified and claims must be in one-sentence form.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.34.15 for pro se applicants and note the format of claims in cited patents as examples. Precede with form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103.

name: Omnibus claim — 'substantially as shown and described' is indefinite
description: An omnibus-style claim (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') is indefinite for failing to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.35 for omnibus claims; this must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02. No further explanation is necessary for such a rejection; see MPEP § 1302.04(b) for cancellation upon allowance.

name: Trademark or trade name used as claim limitation is indefinite
description: A trademark or trade name used in a claim to identify or describe a material/product does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph because a trademark identifies source, not the goods, making claim scope uncertain.
guidance: Insert the trademark/trade name and what it is used to identify/describe; specify the material/product and explain why identification/description is indefinite. Precede with form paragraph 7.30.02 and cite Ex parte Simpson.

name: New matter prohibited (35 U.S.C. 132(a)) — objection to added material
description: No amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention. Adding subject matter not disclosed in the original application (including specific percentages/compounds after a broader disclosure or omission of a step) is new matter.
guidance: Object to new matter using form paragraph 7.28, identify added material by page/line or figure, provide explanation and unresolved questions, and require cancellation of the new matter in reply. If new matter affects claims, make corresponding 35 U.S.C. 112 first-paragraph rejections.

name: Foreign filing without license — abandonment and statutory consequences
description: Filing an application in a foreign country prior to six months after filing in the United States without authorization may constitute abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 182 and related statutes, and may result in forfeiture of claims against the United States.
guidance: Applicants subject to orders under section 181 must obtain a license to file abroad; the Commissioner may treat unauthorized foreign filing as abandonment as of the time of violation. Licenses may be granted retroactively in narrow circumstances (error without deceptive intent and non-disclosing of section 181 subject matter).

name: Search scope
description: The search process involves a worldwide search for all materials and information which are relevant to the subject of the invention.
guidance: Search is intended to identify relevant prior art. If application relates to two or more inventions not forming a single inventive concept, the examination/search may be restricted to the first invention specified in the claims and applicant will be notified.

name: Supplementary examination grounds
description: For supplementary examination, the Patent Examiner will only review the following grounds – support, relatedness of claims, morality, methods of medical treatment or diagnosis, double patenting, and no added matter.
guidance: From 30 Oct 2017, the Examiner will also determine whether the invention defined in each claim constitutes an invention; if not patentable subject matter, Examiner will state full reasons in a written opinion.

name: Recommendation to keep inventions confidential
description: Despite Singapore grace period provisions, individuals and businesses are strongly encouraged to keep inventions confidential until filing because not all jurisdictions have a broad grace period and third parties can still claim prior user rights.
guidance: This is practical legal advice to preserve rights internationally (Chapter 6.1.24).

name: Additional checks for Request for Search & Examination (Patents Form 11)
description: For Form 11, checks include: i) the number of claims indicated on the form should tally with the latest number of claims on record; ii) the 'ISR/IPRP established by IPOS' option is correctly indicated; iii) if applicant indicates a disclosure within 12 months prior to filing, the criteria and required documents (Chapters 6.1.18–6.1.24) are met.
guidance: These are specific formalities to ensure correct fee, discount and grace period handling.

name: Form and content requirements for responses / Patents Form 13A
description: A response to written opinion/invitation to amend must be submitted with Patents Form 13A. The response may include written submissions and/or an application to amend the specification with amendments indicated as per Chapter 5.1.12. From 1 Apr 2017, both marked-up amendments and clean copies are required for online submission. From 1 Dec 2019, if amendments/corrections have been made to claims, a marked-up copy and a clean copy of the full set of claims must be submitted. The request for amendment should set out reasons for amendments and any supporting evidence.
guidance: Marked-up and clean copies should be attached as correct document types; amendments must be based on latest specification on record. Failure to follow format may lead to disregarded responses (Chapters 6.3.10–6.3.11).

name: Examination review request requirements (Patents Form 12B)
description: To request an examination review (Form 12B) the applicant must file within 2 months of the Notice of Intention to Refuse. The applicant may submit written submissions in response to the Examiner's opinion (mandatory) and/or amendments to specification (optional). From 30 Oct 2017, applicants may include proposed amendments with Form 12B instead of filing Patents Form 13 separately. From 1 Apr 2017 both marked-up and clean copies of amended sheets are required; from 1 Dec 2019, if claims amended, marked-up and clean copies of full set of claims must be submitted.
guidance: The request should set out reasons for amendments and include supporting evidence where appropriate; attachments must be of correct document type (Chapters 6.4.1–6.4.4).

name: Single-invention requirement (restriction/election)
description: If the examiner determines the application contains more than one invention, the first Examiner's Action will list the inventions and include either a 'restriction requirement' (inventions clearly different) or an 'election of species requirement' (related inventions with a generic claim).
guidance: Applicant must choose one invention for prosecution; non-elected inventions under a restriction require divisional applications to pursue them; nonelected claims under an election may be rejoined if a generic claim is allowed.

name: Prior-art search and documentation
description: After determining the application is examinable and single-invention, the examiner conducts a search for prior art relevant to the claimed subject matter and notes the classes/subclasses searched on the file wrapper. Documents found are called 'references.'
guidance: Search may be conducted in the examiner's private materials, the examining group's restricted library, or the PTO Scientific Library. The quality and thoroughness of the search depend on the examiner's searching skill, allotted time, and completeness of libraries searched.

name: Types of substantive Examiner actions
description: The first substantive Examiner's Action can allow claims, reject claims, object to claims, object to the specification, or withdraw claims not elected for prosecution.
guidance: Rejections commonly arise under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 (anticipation) and 103 (obviousness) and under §112 for indefiniteness; specification objections include nonenablement under §112 ('enablement' — must describe invention in full, clear terms enabling one skilled in the art).

name: Permissible responses and evidentiary submissions
description: Applicants may respond to rejections and objections by amendment of the claims, by argument, or by a combination; responses may include affidavits as to nonobviousness or to establish invention prior to some reference.
guidance: If claims are amended to overcome prior art, supporting the amended claim must be consistent with the original disclosure; affidavits can be used where appropriate to challenge prior art dates or obviousness.

name: Prohibition on introducing 'new matter'
description: In amending the application, particularly the specification, the applicant may not introduce 'new matter'—subject matter that was not in the application as filed.
guidance: Amending the specification to support an originally filed claim is acceptable; adding material not supported by the original disclosure to support an amendment is prohibited and can render the amendment impermissible (see In re Rasmussen, In re Winkhaus). Corrections of grammar or language (e.g., to non-idiomatic English) are generally permissible without introducing new matter.

name: Enablement standard for specification (§112)
description: The specification must describe the invention 'in such full, clear, concise and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains . . . to make and use' it; otherwise, the specification may be objected to as nonenabling and claims directed to nonenabled subject matter are rejected.
guidance: Nonenablement objections may preclude amending the specification to add support without introducing new matter; enablement is a substantive requirement.

name: Definitions and priority effects of continuation, continuation-in-part, divisional
description: Continuation: same specification as parent, claims may differ, entitled to parent's filing date for subject matter contained in it. Continuation-in-part: shares some subject matter with parent and also adds new matter; entitled to parent's filing date only for common subject matter and to its own filing date for new matter. Divisional: a continuing application based on a parent with same specification but different claims (often due to restriction/election); entitled to parent's filing date for all purposes and protected from being used as prior art when division was made because of an examiner's requirement.
guidance: Voluntary divisions that are actually continuations are not protected from prior-art effects of a patent issued on the earlier application; continuation-in-part may be filed to include new matter (e.g., improvements) as long as parent is still pending.

name: Interference declaration and standards (first-to-invent)
description: If two or more applications claim the same subject matter, the examiner can declare an interference (or the applicant can provoke one). An interference determines which party was first to make the invention. 'Invention' for interference includes conception and reduction to practice (actual or constructive).
guidance: Activities relied upon to establish invention must occur in the United States, a NAFTA country, or a GATT/WTO member; where one party conceived first but reduced to practice later, diligence between conception and reduction to practice may determine priority (35 U.S.C. § 102(g)).

name: Disclaimers, dedications, and terminal disclaimers
description: A patent owner may disclaim or dedicate to the public the entire term of an entire patent, the entire term of any complete claim, or the terminal part of the term of the entire patent. Terminal disclaimers may be used to avoid 'double patenting' and cause patents to expire on the same day.
guidance: Disclaimers require payment of a fee set by regulation, publication in the Official Gazette, and printed copies for attachment to patents; terminal disclaimers are effective only for obviousness-type double patenting (35 U.S.C. § 253; 37 C.F.R. § 1.321).

name: Knowledge Fine-Tuning (KFT) workflow
description: A workflow that enhances LLM performance in concepts and patents generation by incorporating knowledge injection pre-training (KPT), domain-specific supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).
guidance: KFT combines structured knowledge and original text: (1) Knowledge Injection (transform structured triples into text and inject during pre-training), (2) SFT with domain-specific datasets (fine-tune on patent drafting dialogues), and (3) RLHF (align outputs with human knowledge recognition). The paper claims KFT significantly improves downstream patent-writing performance compared to traditional PT + SFT + RLHF.

name: Knowledge learning (Supervised Fine-Tuning, SFT)
description: Align model outputs to specific patent drafting tasks by training on a dialogue dataset Q of (q, a) pairs to reduce differences between outputs and ground-truth labels.
guidance: SFT loss LSFT(χ) = E(q,a)∈Q[log πχ(a|q)]. The SFT dialogue dataset in the paper contains 60,000 Q–A pairs for drafting patent titles, abstracts, and claims.

name: SFT dialogue dataset requirements
description: Dialogues for supervised fine-tuning should reflect patent drafting scenarios (titles, abstracts, claims).
guidance: The paper's SFT dataset contains 60,000 question–answer pairs derived from USPTO patent texts; dataset design should capture drafting tasks to teach the model how to use injected knowledge in context.

name: Patent writing benchmark (task sampling and prompt design)
description: A benchmark specifically evaluating LLMs' ability to write patentable concept texts: 1,000 instances sampled from all eight IPC categories using a designed prompt (Appendix C).
guidance: Evaluates title/abstract/claim generation quality across diverse fields; ensures sampling across IPC for coverage of industry domains.

name: Utility (industrial applicability)
description: Microbe or microbiological processes must have a specific function and used for manufacturing particular products.
guidance: Claims must show a specific, practical application (e.g., production of antibiotics, enzymes, vaccines, biofuels). The Mashelkar committee and TRIPS-consistent standards require demonstrable industrial application.

name: Characterization and storage requirements for microbial patent submissions
description: Microorganisms are determined via phenotypical characterization, 16S rRNA analysis, MALDI-TOF analysis, etc., and should be stored (e.g., lyophilized) for preservation before patenting.
guidance: The article recommends specific laboratory characterizations (phenotype, 16S rRNA, MALDI-TOF) to support claims and to emphasize secure storage and deposit prior to patent examination; these practical evidentiary elements aid examination and reproducibility.

name: Examples of circumstances disfavouring a due care determination
description: Circumstances that may favour a determination that due care was not taken include: lack of financing claimed by patentee; human error due to increased workload, lost file, poor organization; lack of knowledge of the Patent Act/Rules; absence from the office because deadline fell on planned vacation or medical appointment.
guidance: Routine organizational mistakes, financial inability, or ignorance of the law are less likely to meet the due care standard.

name: Disclaimer purpose and nature
description: Disclaimer is a mechanism whereby a patentee may, at any time during the life of a patent, amend a patent to claim less than that which was claimed in the original patent (subsection 48(1) of the Patent Act). It is used where the patentee has, by mistake/accident/inadvertence and without wilful intent to defraud, made a specification 'too broad'. A disclaimer is a renunciation of subject-matter and a clear and unequivocal statement that the original patent claims are too broad.
guidance: A disclaimer need not be limited to whole claims; part of a claim may be disclaimed provided the disclaimer does not extend the scope of that or dependent claims.

name: Formal requirements for filing a disclaimer
description: To file a disclaimer, Form 2 of Schedule 1 of the Patent Rules must be completed and filed with the Patent Office along with the appropriate fee (subsection 48(2) of the Patent Act and section 120 of the Patent Rules). In completing Form 2, the patentee must follow the precise form of subsections 3(1) and 3(2) specifying the subject-matter disclaimed.
guidance: The specific wording in Form 2 must be followed; language in Form 2 cannot be used to reformulate or redefine the invention disclosed and claimed.

name: Roles of Patent Office and Courts regarding disclaimers
description: The filing of a disclaimer does not involve examination of the subject-matter by the Patent Office. The Office only ensures the disclaimer is filed in the prescribed form and manner and that the fee is paid. The Commissioner has no discretion to refuse to record it if proper. The onus is on the patentee to show the disclaimer satisfies subsection 48(1) of the Patent Act.
guidance: Validity depends on: patentee's state of mind at time of specification preparation; good faith; timeliness; whether disclaimer broadens scope; whether it recasts invention or adds new combination. If courts find disclaimer invalid, disclaimed claims revert, but pre-disclaimer claims may be invalid for overbroad admission.

name: Effects of a disclaimer on proceedings and claim scope
description: Disclaimers do not normally affect any court action pending at the time they are made (subsection 48(4)). Following a disclaimer, the remaining claims are deemed to be valid for the matter not disclaimed. The disclaimer is unconditional; the existing claims of the patent are the claims as amended by virtue of the disclaimer.
guidance: A timely valid disclaimer can save an otherwise overbroad claim from finding of invalidity, but it is a renunciation of subject-matter and final in effect.

name: Purpose and scope of re-examination
description: The purpose of re-examination is to provide a relatively summary and inexpensive alternative to impeachment by litigation, or an opportunity for a patentee to have the Patent Office reconsider the claims of an issued patent. Re-examination is limited to issues arising from the prior art supplied by the requesting party and is generally less comprehensive than a court action.
guidance: Re-examination is administrative and generally ex parte; the board cannot test credibility via cross-examination; determinations reviewed by courts on a reasonableness standard.

name: First stage — substantial new question (SNQ) threshold and timing
description: Within three months of establishment, the re-examination board must determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim of the patent is raised by the request (subsection 48.2(2)). To raise a SNQ the request must present an issue relating to validity not previously considered during prosecution or other prior proceedings, and not so closely related to a previously considered issue as to be not 'substantial' and 'new'.
guidance: SNQ often raised by prior art not on original record; the same prior art can raise a SNQ if applied differently. Absence of evidence of how an examiner considered prior art means the board will not presume it was considered in the same manner as alleged in the request.

name: Second stage procedures, amendment rules, and timelines
description: The second stage begins upon a patentee reply or expiration of three months from notification. The re-examination proceeds on the SNQ; the patentee may propose any amendment to the patent (including description/drawings). Amended or new claims must be numbered consecutively beginning with the next claim number (section 123). No amendment or new claim shall enlarge the scope of a claim of the patent (subsection 48.3(2)); at minimum any proposed claim must include all features of the broadest independent claim.
guidance: Exchanges may include oral or written submissions; oral submissions can be in person, teleconference, or videoconference. The second stage must be completed within twelve months (subsection 48.3(3)).

name: Completion of re-examination — outcomes and effect
description: Upon completion of the second stage, the re-examination board will issue a certificate of re-examination delivered by registered mail. The certificate may: cancel any claim determined unpatentable; confirm any claim determined patentable; or incorporate any proposed amended or new claim determined patentable. Accompanying the certificate will be a decision letter explaining reasons and a registration certificate indicating the re-examination certificate is registered against the patent.
guidance: Cancellation removes scope of protection but does not necessarily remove text from dependent claims; amendments incorporated will be noted. A new cover page is generated to indicate re-examination. Board determinations are functionally equivalent to a Commissioner decision under section 40 and are reviewed on a reasonableness standard.

name: Requesting priority — where to make request and required information
description: The request for priority must be made in the petition of the pending application or in another document other than the specification or drawings of the pending application. For each previously regularly filed application (a priority application), subsection 28.4(1) of the Patent Act and 73(1) of the Patent Rules require: the filing date; the name of the country or office of filing; and the number of the previously regularly filed application.
guidance: Do not bury priority claims in the specification or drawings; provide filing date, country/office and application number for each priority application to be safe.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure
description: The requirement and test that the application disclose the invention sufficiently for a skilled person to carry it out.
guidance: Benchmarks for adequacy of disclosure, examples of insufficient disclosure, and interplay with claim scope and post‑filed data.

name: Unity of invention (application content)
description: Requirements and tests for unity of invention as applied to the content of the application (claims and description).
guidance: Explains legal criteria to determine whether claims form a single inventive concept and how to handle multiple inventions (divisional, partial search).

name: Patentable subject matter general rule
description: Patentable subject matter must be concrete, rather than an abstract idea, and laws of nature, products of nature, and natural phenomena are not patentable.
guidance: This is the baseline legal standard for subject-matter eligibility: focus on whether the claimed subject is a human-made concrete invention versus an ineligible natural law/product/phenomenon. Apply when analyzing biotech claims to determine whether they cross the statutory/constitutional boundary for patents.

name: cDNA can be patentable (human alteration doctrine)
description: Complementary DNA, cDNA, was determined to be patentable material because humans alter the gene by removing introns—non-coding regions of DNA—from the DNA sequence.
guidance: Distinguish claims to cDNA (which reflect human-directed modification of natural sequences) from claims to native genomic DNA. The presence of meaningful human alteration may support subject-matter eligibility; analyze the nature and extent of the alteration.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (core Step 2A test for nature-based products)
description: For a nature-based product, analyze whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' from any naturally occurring counterpart(s) in their natural state (structural, functional, or other properties).
guidance: If the claimed product has such marked differences, it is not a 'product of nature' exception (Step 2A: NO) and may be eligible; if not, it is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires Step 2B analysis. Examples explain comparing combinations to individual components when no natural counterpart to the combination exists.

name: Compare combination claims to natural counterparts appropriately
description: When a claimed product is a combination of multiple natural components, compare the claimed combination to naturally occurring counterpart(s): if the combination as claimed does not occur in nature, compare to the individual components in their natural states.
guidance: If the combination exhibits properties (e.g., explosiveness, slower spoiling, synergistic fermentation) that are markedly different from the components individually, those properties support eligibility (examples: gunpowder, pomelo juice with preservative, yogurt starter culture).

name: Claims that encompass both natural and non-natural embodiments are problematic
description: If a claim covers embodiments that are identical to naturally occurring material as well as embodiments that are altered, the claim may fail the 'markedly different characteristics' test because it includes natural forms.
guidance: Examples: a broad claim to 'amazonic acid' that includes both natural and purified forms is ineligible because some embodiments are identical to nature; narrowing to only structurally/phenotypically distinct forms can render claim eligible.

name: Mixtures where components are unchanged vs mixtures that change components
description: If components in a claimed mixture remain unchanged (e.g., separate bacteria in a kit), the claim may be directed to a product of nature; if mixing produces changed characteristics (synergy, new properties), it may show marked difference.
guidance: Examples: a kit containing separate bacterial species is ineligible because they are not combined; a starter culture where mixing produces lower-fat yogurt or faster fermentation is eligible because the mixture has different functional properties.

name: Additional elements can provide 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), evaluate whether additional elements, alone or in combination, add 'significantly more' to transform the claim into eligible subject matter (Step 2B).
guidance: Elements that improve technology or add meaningful limitations (e.g., cores enveloped by polymeric layer producing colon release and improved bioavailability; scaffold + cells improving tissue regeneration) can supply 'significantly more'. Generic, well-understood, routine elements (e.g., generic containers) typically do not.

name: Generic, well-understood, routine, conventional elements do not add 'significantly more'
description: Features that are well-understood, routine, and conventional in the relevant field—especially when recited at a high level of generality—do not transform an ineligible claim into eligible subject matter under Step 2B.
guidance: Example: recitation of a generic container to hold cells is routine and does not add significantly more; thus a claim to a cell population 'in a container' remained directed to an exception and ineligible.

name: Structural uniqueness that prevents preemption supports eligibility
description: A claimed molecule or product that is structurally unique and does not preempt others from using the natural product supports eligibility because it does not tie up the natural product's future uses.
guidance: Examples: 5-methyl amazonic acid is a unique molecule distinct from amazonic acid and therefore not a 'product of nature' exception; distinct molecules that do not prevent others from using the natural product are favorable.

name: Changes in genetic information/sequence or percent-identity claims
description: Modifications to nucleic acid sequences (substitution modifications) or claims limited to sequences with specified percent identity (e.g., ≥90% identity to SEQ ID NO: 1) can indicate structural/genetic differences sufficient for eligibility analysis.
guidance: Examples include modified Gene W sequences with substitutions; silent changes may or may not affect characteristics, but percent-identity limitations and sequence-based limitations can narrow claims away from natural sequences.

name: If claimed combination does not exist in nature, possibility of rare natural occurrence does not bar eligibility
description: The mere theoretical possibility that a similar composition might arise rarely in nature does not render a composition nonpatentable; the examiner should determine whether the particular mixture exists in nature.
guidance: Cites Myriad: possibility of rare natural occurrence does not defeat eligibility if claim is otherwise markedly different; unless examiner can show the particular mixture exists in nature, eligibility can stand.

name: Definitions and claim language may limit scope to avoid encompassing natural forms
description: Explicit definitions in the specification (e.g., defining 'purified Antibiotic L' to mean only tetrahedral crystal form or specific glycan) can limit the claim scope to non-natural embodiments and support eligibility.
guidance: Use of clear claim limitations/definitions that exclude naturally occurring forms (e.g., crystal form, glycan type, percent identity, phenotype markers) helps avoid covering natural counterparts and supports Step 2A: NO.

name: Mixtures that produce new inter-component interactions can be markedly different
description: When components interact in the claimed mixture to produce new behaviors (e.g., altered growth rates, new host-range infectivity, synergistic fermentation), those emergent properties can constitute marked differences from natural counterparts.
guidance: Examples: certain Rhizobium strains when mixed infect additional plant species; mixed pacemaker cell populations interact to change growth rates enabling tissue regeneration; these emergent interactions support eligibility.

name: Claims limited to particular useful applications may amount to 'significantly more'
description: Limiting a claim to a particular useful application of a nature-based product—where the combination does more than generally link exceptions together—can provide 'significantly more' and render the claim eligible.
guidance: Example: pacemaker cells plus scaffold facilitating faster tissue regeneration is tied to a specific application and was found to add significantly more (Step 2B: YES).

name: Scope of claim must be considered under broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Claims are analyzed under their broadest reasonable interpretation for eligibility purposes; if under that interpretation the claim encompasses natural forms it may be ineligible.
guidance: Examples repeatedly apply broadest reasonable interpretation when determining whether claims cover natural embodiments (e.g., Antibiotic L claim covering both natural and modified forms was ineligible).

name: Use of well-understood conventional materials or steps at high generality will not rescue a claim
description: Reciting conventional component(s) (e.g., 'natural polymeric material', 'container', common preservatives) at a high level of generality typically will not add significantly more to an exception.
guidance: Example: a generic 'container' for cells was insufficient to pass Step 2B; conversely, a specifically recited scaffold that improved outcomes could suffice.

name: Evaluate claim as a whole when determining whether to apply the nature-product analysis
description: For some process or method claims, analyze the claim as a whole to determine whether it is focused on the nature-based product per se or on a practical application/assembly such that the nature-product exception analysis is unnecessary.
guidance: Examples: firework assembly claims and methods of treatment were analyzed as focused on assemblies/applications, so marked-difference analysis was not required to conclude ineligibility/eligibility.

name: Delay is not per se fatal; abandonment is the key
description: The statute does not limit the time to apply for a patent; delay is unimportant unless it amounts to evidence of abandonment of the claim.
guidance: Delay, lapse of time, or taking long to apply does not automatically forfeit rights unless there is intervening public use or other evidence of abandonment or dedication to the public. Determination of intent behind delay and whether delay constituted abandonment is a question of fact for a jury.

name: General Plastic factor: explanation for elapsed time between filings
description: Whether the petitioner provides adequate explanation for the time elapsed between the filings of multiple petitions directed to the same claims of the same patent.
guidance: An adequate, specific explanation can mitigate concerns about serial petitions; vague or no explanation increases risk of denial.

name: Delivery of particulars in infringement actions: timing and scope
description: (1) 'In an action for infringement the plaintiff must deliver with his statement of claim particulars of the breaches complained of.' (2) 'The defendant must deliver with his statement of defence particulars of any objections on which he relies.' (3) If disputing validity, particulars must state on what grounds and, for want of novelty, the time and place of the previous publication or user.
guidance: No evidence at hearing shall be admitted in proof of any alleged infringement or objection of which particulars were not delivered except by leave. Particulars may be amended by leave. On taxation of costs, regard shall be had to particulars delivered; costs for particulars require Court/judge certificate they were proven or were reasonable and proper.

name: Statutory foundation for right to amend applications
description: The real foundation of the right to amend applications is found in Section 4888 of the Revised Statutes (and analogous provisions in earlier Acts): before an inventor receives a patent he shall file a full, clear, and exact written description, and (since 1836) shall particularly point out and claim the part or combination he claims as his invention.
guidance: Statute implies these things can be done prior to issuance and thus supports amendment rights; details of permissible amendments are determined by court decisions and Patent Office rules.

name: No new or amended claim unless for the 'same invention'
description: The general rule is that no amended or new claim can be allowed unless it is for the 'same invention' as the original application.
guidance: The phrase 'same invention' is not strictly limited to what was actually claimed originally; claims may be broadened while applications are pending if supported by the original specification and drawings. Cases (e.g., Hobbs v. Beach) explain permissible breadth.

name: Drawings may be amended to conform to specification
description: A drawing may be amended in the light of the specification, even to the extent of inserting in it the distinguishing characteristic of the invention when that was accidentally omitted from the original drawing.
guidance: Judge decisions permit correction of accidental omissions where the original specification suggests the final claims; see caveats/qualifications in cited cases (e.g., Kirchberger qualification).

name: Duty to amend specification and drawings to correct inaccuracies and secure correspondence
description: An applicant must amend his specification and drawings whenever such amendment is required to correct inaccuracy or unnecessary prolixity therein, or to secure correspondence between the claims and the other parts of the specification and the drawings.
guidance: Patent Office Rule 71; applicant also must supply amended drawings that conform to Patent Office standards of artistic excellence under rules 49–55 when originals do not conform.

name: Situations where 1.136(a) extensions are not available
description: Extensions of time with the payment of a fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) are not available in: (A) reexamination proceedings (ex parte and inter partes exceptions noted), (B) all extensions during an interference proceeding (but not preparatory to an interference where a claim is suggested), (C) specific situations where an Office action states 1.136(a) is not applicable (e.g., reply to a notice of allowability, reissue apps associated with litigation, application in allowable condition with nonelected claims and time set to cancel such claims), and (D) limited instances where applicant is given a specified time limit to take certain actions.
guidance: See relevant MPEP sections and CFR citations for details.

name: Pharmaceutical quality markers
description: For pharmaceuticals, patent quality is critically important; commercial value flows almost entirely through patent protection.
guidance: Key markers: compound claims with structural specificity; composition and method-of-treatment claim layering; robust IDS preventing later inequitable conduct; clear scope amenable to ANDA/Hatch-Waxman litigation. Drafting/prosecution should prioritize litigation-readiness, continuation strategy (e.g., salts/polymorphs/formulations), and international family coverage in major jurisdictions.

name: Chemical industry quality markers
description: In chemicals, patents matter especially for product chemistry but less for process chemistry.
guidance: Key markers: product claims with structural support; process claims tied to specific operating conditions; preserve cross-licensing potential through clear claim scope. Allocate drafting effort toward robust support for product claims and clarity that facilitates licensing negotiations.

name: Operative quality markers for high-patent-dependence industries
description: In industries where patents are central to appropriation, patent quality directly determines commercial outcomes.
guidance: Expect to invest in robust drafting and prosecution, maintain litigation-readiness, execute continuation strategies to preserve commercial coverage, and ensure claims and specification support likely enforcement scenarios. Quality is measured by enforceability, scope clarity, and strategic claim families.

name: Industry-calibrated drafting — pharmaceutical drafting practices
description: Pharmaceutical drafting should include single-compound claims with broad structural support, distinct method-of-treatment claims, salt/polymorph/formulation continuation strategies, and an international family in major jurisdictions.
