guidance: Structure applications to support both product and method claims, include exemplified embodiments for polymorphs and formulations, and plan prosecution to enable Hatch-Waxman/ANDA enforcement paths. Robust disclosure and prior-art handling (IDS) are essential to avoid later inequitable-conduct challenges.

name: Industry-calibrated drafting — mechanical drafting practices
description: Mechanical drafting should provide means-plus-function clarity, multiple embodiment disclosure, and dependent-claim layering to resist design-around.
guidance: Disclose alternative embodiments and implementation details to support claim breadth; use dependent claims to create graduated protection that complicates design-arounds while recognizing that blocking claims are less central in mechanical industries than in pharmaceuticals.

name: Rejoining all previously withdrawn process claims (use form paragraph 8.43)
description: Claim [1] directed to an allowable product. Pursuant to the procedures set forth in MPEP § 821.04(b), claim [2], directed to the process of making or using an allowable product, previously withdrawn from consideration as a result of a restriction requirement, [3] hereby rejoined and fully examined for patentability under 37 CFR 1.104.
guidance: All claims directed to a nonelected process invention must require all the limitations of an allowable product claim for that process invention to be rejoined (MPEP § 821.04(b)). Because all claims previously withdrawn under 37 CFR 1.142 have been rejoined, the restriction requirement is withdrawn and, once withdrawn, the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 121 are no longer applicable (In re Ziegler). Applicants are to be advised that continuation/divisional claims anticipated by or including all limitations of an allowable claim may be subject to provisional statutory and/or nonstatutory double patenting rejections. Examiner bracket-insert instructions specify claim numbers, dates, group numbers, and appropriate singular/plural forms.

name: Rejoinder when LESS THAN ALL previously withdrawn claims are rejoined (use form paragraph 8.42)
description: If LESS THAN ALL previously withdrawn process claims are being rejoined, then form paragraph 8.42 should be used instead of this form paragraph.
guidance: All claims directed to a nonelected process invention must require all the limitations of an allowable product claim for that process invention to be rejoined (MPEP § 821.04(b)). Use 8.42 when not all previously withdrawn claims are being rejoined; follow bracket insertion instructions for claim identification and appropriate verb forms.

name: Elected invention allowable; rejoin all previously withdrawn claims when nonelected not canceled (use 8.45)
description: Claim [1] allowable. Claim [2], previously withdrawn from consideration as a result of a restriction requirement, [3] all the limitations of an allowable claim. Pursuant to the procedures set forth in MPEP § 821.04(a), the restriction requirement [4] inventions [5], as set forth in the Office action mailed on [6], is hereby withdrawn and claim [7] hereby rejoined and fully examined for patentability under 37 CFR 1.104.
guidance: Use form paragraph 8.45 whenever ALL previously withdrawn claims depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim and wherein the non-elected claims have NOT been canceled. Use other form paragraphs (8.46–8.50) as appropriate where non-elected claims have been canceled or the restriction is withdrawn only in part. Include the double patenting advisory and the 35 U.S.C. 121 inapplicability notice.

name: Elected invention allowable; nonelected claims canceled; other issues remain (use 8.46)
description: Claim [1] allowable. The restriction requirement [2] inventions [4], has been [3] reconsidered in view of the allowability of claims to the elected invention pursuant to MPEP § 821.04(a). The restriction requirement is hereby withdrawn as to any claim that requires all the limitations of an allowable claim. ... Claim [7], which required all the limitations of an allowable claim, previously withdrawn from consideration as a result of the restriction requirement, [8] canceled by applicant in the reply filed on [9]. The canceled, nonelected claim(s) may be reinstated by applicant if submitted in a timely filed amendment in reply to this action. Upon entry of the amendment, such amended claim(s) will be examined for patentability under 37 CFR 1.104.
guidance: This paragraph applies where non-elected claims requiring all limitations HAVE BEEN canceled. Canceled nonelected claims can be reinstated by timely amendment in reply; upon entry they will be examined under 37 CFR 1.104. If no issues remain and application is otherwise ready for allowance, use form paragraph 8.47 or 8.47.01 instead. Include double patenting advisory and 35 U.S.C.121 notice. Bracket instructions specify wording and dates.

name: Elected invention allowable; nonelected claims canceled; before final rejection; no outstanding issues (use 8.47)
description: Claim [1] allowable. The restriction requirement [2] inventions [3], as set forth in the Office action mailed on [4], has been reconsidered in view of the allowability of claims to the elected invention pursuant to MPEP § 821.04(a). The restriction requirement is hereby withdrawn as to any claim that requires all the limitations of an allowable claim. ... The canceled, nonelected claim(s) may be reinstated by applicant if submitted in an amendment, limited to the addition of such claim(s), filed within a time period of TWO MONTHS from the mailing date of this letter. Upon entry of the amendment, such amended claim(s) will be examined for patentability under 37 CFR 1.104. If NO such amendment is submitted within the set time period, the application will be passed to issue. PROSECUTION ON THE MERITS IS OTHERWISE CLOSED.
guidance: Use only when there are no outstanding issues remaining and with only a PTO-90C cover sheet. Applicable when restriction requirement was between related product or process inventions and application has not been finally rejected. Includes two-month limited window for reinstatement of canceled nonelected claims by amendment limited to adding such claims; otherwise application proceeds to issue.

name: Elected invention allowable; nonelected claims canceled; after final rejection; no outstanding issues (use 8.47.01)
description: Claim [1] allowable. The restriction requirement [2] inventions [3], as set forth in the Office action mailed on [4], has been reconsidered in view of the allowability of claims to the elected invention pursuant to MPEP § 821.04(a). The restriction requirement is hereby withdrawn as to any claim that requires all the limitations of an allowable claim. Specifically, the restriction requirement of [5] is [6]. In view of the withdrawal of the restriction requirement as set forth above, applicant(s) are advised ...
guidance: This paragraph is applicable where a restriction requirement was made between related product inventions or related process inventions and the application has been finally rejected. Use 8.47 before final rejection. Same double patenting and 35 U.S.C.121 advisories apply. Use bracket insertion instructions as specified.

name: Elected invention allowable; claims stand withdrawn as not in required form (use 8.49)
description: Claim [1] allowable. The restriction requirement [2], as set forth in the Office action mailed on [3], has been reconsidered in view of the allowability of claims to the elected invention pursuant to MPEP § 821.04(a). The restriction requirement is hereby withdrawn as to any claim that requires all the limitations of an allowable claim. Specifically, the restriction requirement of [4] is [5]. Claim [6], directed to [7] withdrawn from further consideration because [8] require all the limitations of an allowable generic linking claim as required by 37 CFR 1.141.
guidance: This form paragraph applies where a restriction was made between related product or process inventions and nonelected claims are withdrawn for not being in required form per 37 CFR 1.141. Use 8.50 when some claims are no longer withdrawn. Include 35 U.S.C.121 and double patenting advisories. Bracket instructions identify which inventions and dates.

name: Elected invention allowable; some claims no longer withdrawn (use 8.50)
description: Claim [1] allowable. The restriction requirement [2], as set forth in the Office action mailed on [3], has been reconsidered in view of the allowability of claims to the elected invention pursuant to MPEP § 821.04(a). The restriction requirement is hereby withdrawn as to any claim that requires all the limitations of an allowable claim. Specifically, the restriction requirement of [4] is [5]. Claim [6], directed to [7] no longer withdrawn from consideration because the claim(s) requires all the limitations of an allowable claim. However, claim [8], directed to [9] withdrawn from consideration because [10] require all the limitations of an allowable claim.
guidance: Applicable where some, but not all, nonelected claims require all the limitations of an allowable claim. If all claims are in proper form, use 8.45, 8.46, or 8.47 as appropriate. Includes bracket insertion instructions and double patenting/35 U.S.C.121 advisories.

name: Advisory on double patenting when restriction requirement withdrawn
description: Applicant(s) are advised that if any claim presented in a continuation or divisional application is anticipated by, or includes all the limitations of, a claim that is allowable in the present application, such claim may be subject to provisional statutory and/or nonstatutory double patenting rejections over the claims of the instant application.
guidance: This caution is repeated in many form paragraphs where the restriction requirement is withdrawn. Examiners must include this advisory to notify applicants of potential double patenting issues arising from rejoined/allowable claims.

name: Appeal dismissed — allowed claims but formal matters remaining (form paragraph 12.209)
description: In view of applicant’s failure to file a brief within the time prescribed by 37 CFR 41.37(a), the appeal stands dismissed and the proceedings as to the rejected claims are considered terminated. This application will be passed to issue on allowed claim [1] provided the following formal matters are corrected. Prosecution is otherwise closed. Applicant is required to make the necessary corrections within a shortened statutory period set to expire TWO MONTHS from the mailing date of this letter to avoid ABANDONMENT of the application.
guidance: Use when the notice of appeal was filed on or after January 23, 2012 and formal matters cannot be handled by examiner’s amendment (see MPEP § 1215.04). Insert description of formal matters to be corrected. Claims indicated as containing allowable subject matter but objected to as dependent upon a rejected claim are to be considered rejected (MPEP § 1215.04).

name: Completeness of examiner's action (limited exceptions)
description: The examiner’s action will be complete as to all matters, except that in appropriate circumstances, such as misjoinder of invention, fundamental defects in the application, and the like, the action of the examiner may be limited to such matters before further action is made. However, matters of form need not be raised by the examiner until a claim is found allowable.
guidance: Limit scope of action only for specified circumstances (misjoinder, fundamental defects). Do not require raising form objections until claim allowability stage.

name: Rejection – general rule
description: If the invention is not considered patentable, or not considered patentable as claimed, the claims, or those considered unpatentable will be rejected.
guidance: Clearly identify which claims are rejected and on what basis (novelty, obviousness, statutory bars, etc.).

name: Explanation of pertinence and specificity for rejections
description: The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.
guidance: When relevance isn't obvious, provide an explanation linking reference disclosure to claim limitations; specify which claims are affected.

name: Reliance on admissions and examiner knowledge
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant ... as to any matter affecting patentability and, insofar as rejections in applications are concerned, may also rely upon facts within his or her knowledge pursuant to paragraph (d)(2) of this section.
guidance: Admit reliance on applicant statements where appropriate. When relying on facts within personal knowledge, follow affidavit/support procedures (see separate rubric).

name: Preclusion by statutory invention registration
description: The claims in any original application naming an inventor will be rejected as being precluded by a waiver in a published statutory invention registration naming that inventor if the same subject matter is claimed ...
guidance: Where a published statutory invention registration exists naming an inventor, determine whether it precludes claims in the application or reissue and reject if so; cite specifics of the preclusion criteria.

name: Reasons for allowance must be recordable and commentable
description: If the examiner believes that the record of the prosecution as a whole does not make clear his or her reasons for allowing a claim or claims, the examiner may set forth such reasoning. The reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims ... or be the subject of a separate communication to the applicant or patent owner. The applicant or patent owner may file a statement commenting on the reasons for allowance within such time as may be specified by the examiner.
guidance: Document reasons for allowance on the record; allow opportunity for applicant comment; failure to respond does not imply anything.

name: For 103 rejections explain combination/modification reasoning
description: For rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, the way in which a reference is modified or plural references are combined should be set out.
guidance: Explicitly explain the rationale for combining or modifying references to make the claimed invention obvious; map claim limitations to reference teachings.

name: Patent term and priority-date search considerations
description: Examiners should search all applications based on the actual U.S. filing date of the application rather than on the filing date of any parent U.S. application for which priority under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c) is claimed. Examiners should cite of interest all material prior art having an effective filing date after the filing date of the U.S. parent application but before the actual filing date of the application being examined.
guidance: Be aware of 20-year term measured from earliest claimed priority and adjust searches to reflect actual filing dates; cite intervening-material prior art as relevant.

name: Claim Directed to Product-By-Process or Product and Process
description: Claims may permissively reference more than one statutory class. A product-by-process claim (product defined by process) is proper; by contrast a single claim claiming both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite.
guidance: I. PRODUCT‑BY‑PROCESS: Product claims defined in terms of process are proper if clearly directed to the product (cases: Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma; In re Luck; In re Pilkington; In re Steppan). Applicants may present claims of varying scope even if product must be described product‑by‑process. II. PRODUCT AND PROCESS IN THE SAME CLAIM: A claim that recites a product and actions by users (method steps) may be indefinite (e.g., In re Katz). If additional limitations focus on system capabilities (not user actions), claim may be definite (Mastermine Software v. Microsoft).

name: "Use" Claims
description: Claims that attempt to claim a process without setting forth steps (mere 'use' claims) generally raise indefiniteness issues under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and may fail 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Example: a claim reciting a 'process for using X to isolate Y' held indefinite for reciting only a use without active steps (Ex parte Erlich). 'Use' claims that do not purport to be a statutory class fail 101 (In re Moreton). It may be appropriate to reject under both 101 and 112(b) if facts support both. However, some claims reciting 'utilizing' have been held not indefinite (Ex parte Porter). When rejecting, use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05.01, 7.34.01) as indicated.

name: Omnibus Claim
description: An omnibus claim (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph) as indefinite.
guidance: Such claims fail to point out what is included or excluded. Use form paragraph 7.35 to effect rejection; see Ex parte Fressola for history and explanation.

name: Reference to Figures or Tables
description: Claims should, where possible, be complete in themselves; incorporation by reference to a figure or table is permitted only in exceptional circumstances where there is no practical way to define the invention in words.
guidance: Incorporation by reference is a 'necessity' doctrine, not for applicant convenience (Ex parte Fressola). Reference characters may be used in claims alongside recitation of elements; generally their presence/absence does not affect claim scope. See MPEP § 608.01(m) for treatment of reference characters.

name: Chemical Formula
description: Chemical structures in claims should not be considered indefinite nor speculative in the absence of evidence that the assigned formula is in error.
guidance: Absence of corroborating spectroscopic or other data is not a basis for indefiniteness (Ex parte Morton; Ex parte Sobin). A chemical compound claim is not indefinite merely because structure is partial or not presented (In re Fisher). Compounds can be claimed by adequate names, combinations of physical/chemical characteristics, or by process of making without raising indefiniteness.

name: Trademarks or Trade Names in a Claim
description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper, but the claim should be carefully analyzed to determine how the mark or name is used.
guidance: Trademarks identify source and do not define goods; using a trademark as a limitation to describe a material/product fails 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (Ex parte Simpson). If applicant substitutes a generic term in response, examiner should determine whether sufficient support exists in the application for that generic term (see MPEP § 2163 II.A.3(b)). If a mark's presence causes confusion as to claim scope, reject under 112(b). Case example: Eli Lilly & Co. v. Apotex discussed handling of trade name 'ALIMTA'.

name: Mere Function of Machine
description: Process/method claims should not be rejected solely on the ground that they define the inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus.
guidance: In re Tarczy‑Hornoch: a process claim otherwise patentable should not be rejected merely because the application discloses an apparatus that will inherently carry out the recited steps. Do not use inherent machine function as sole basis for 112(b) rejection of process claims.

name: Practice Compact Prosecution: Interpret the Claim and Apply Art with Explanation
description: Under compact prosecution, examiners should identify all applicable grounds of rejection in the first Office action and clearly articulate any rejection early so applicant can reply completely.
guidance: Examiner should review each claim for compliance with all statutory requirements (37 CFR 1.104(a)(1)). When a claim term renders the claim indefinite, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and also make rejection(s) over prior art (35 U.S.C. 102/103) based on examiner's interpretation — state on the record how the term is being interpreted. Reject each claim on all valid grounds available to avoid piecemeal examination (see MPEP § 707.07(g)).

name: Practice Compact Prosecution: Prior Art Rejection of Claim Rejected as Indefinite
description: All words in a claim must be considered when judging patentability against prior art; indefinite terms do not automatically make a claim obvious over the prior art.
guidance: Two approaches: (1) If uncertainty is not great and at least one interpretation renders the claim unpatentable, enter both an indefiniteness rejection under 112(b) and a prior art rejection based on the interpretation that makes it unpatentable (identify how claim is being interpreted); (2) If confusion is great, do not reject on prior art (avoid speculation per In re Steele). The first approach is recommended to avoid piecemeal examination and to help applicant redraft.

name: Relationship Between the Requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b)
description: The requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enabling) and 112(b) (indefiniteness) are separate and distinct.
guidance: If the specification is not commensurate in scope with the claim, that indicates insufficient disclosure under 112(a) (not necessarily indefiniteness under 112(b)). If the specification shows a feature is critical/essential and claim fails to recite it, a 112(a) rejection may be appropriate (In re Mayhew). If claim is amended to include subject matter not described in the application as filed, a 112(a) new matter rejection may be appropriate (In re Simon, In re Panagrossi).

name: ¶ 7.34.01 Rejection, Failure To Particularly Point out and Distinctly Claim (Indefinite)
description: Form paragraph for rejecting claim(s) under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Insert appropriate claim numbers and check dependent claims for same reason. Follow with applicable sub‑form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.10, 7.34.23–7.34.24, or provide a full explanation identifying particular indefinite terms/limitations. If person skilled in the art can determine scope, do not use this rejection. See MPEP §§ 2171–2174 for guidance; form paragraph 7.34.15 for pro se applicants.

name: ¶ 7.35 Rejection, Failure To Particularly Point out and Distinctly Claim - Omnibus Claim
description: Form paragraph for rejecting an omnibus type claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite because it fails to point out what is included/excluded.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Use this paragraph to reject 'omnibus' claims; no further explanation necessary. Example omnibus claim: 'A device substantially as shown and described.'

name: Obvious‑to‑try rationale for obviousness
description: Where the prior art makes a finite number of identified, predictable solutions available and a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in trying those options, the fact that an invention was 'obvious to try' may show the invention was obvious under § 103 (KSR).
guidance: KSR: 'A person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options within his or her technical grasp. If this leads to the anticipated success, it is likely that product [was] not of innovation but of ordinary skill and common sense.' But the admonition that 'obvious to try' is not the standard has been directed at cases where (1) one would vary many parameters or try numerous possible choices with no indication which parameters are critical or which choices are likely to be successful, or (2) the prior art gives only general guidance about a promising field of experimentation and not specific direction as to how to achieve the claimed invention (see In re O'Farrell). Examiners should apply 'obvious to try' only where the situation meets KSR's predictable/finite/reasonable expectation of success criteria; avoid relying on it where the prior art suggests broad exploration or numerous blind trials.

name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) common‑ownership/joint research disqualification
description: Under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (as amended 1999/2004/CREATE Act), subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art under certain pre‑AIA 102 subsections shall not preclude patentability if the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment at the time the claimed invention was made, with a joint research agreement exception when three conditions are met.
guidance: CREATE Act conditions: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. Applicability depends on filing/grant dates (see text): changes apply to patents granted on/after Dec 10, 2004 that are subject to pre‑AIA 102. For reexamination or other procedural situations, examiners must check which version applies (see MPEP § 706.02(l)(1) and related guidance). Note: pre‑AIA 103(c) only disqualifies certain categories of prior art—examiners must ensure statutory prerequisites are met before invoking the disqualification.

name: Determine whether an application is governed by pre‑AIA or AIA 102/103
description: Whether pre‑AIA or AIA versions of 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 apply depends on the application's filing history and effective filing dates (March 16, 2013 is the AIA effective date).
guidance: Applications filed before March 16, 2013 remain governed by pre‑AIA 102/103 even if an RCE or national stage entry is filed after that date; adding new matter on/after March 16, 2013 does not change status. Applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 are AIA applications unless they never contained a claim with an effective filing date on/after that date as defined in 35 U.S.C. 100(i). Examiners should consult MPEP §§ 2131–2138 and § 2159 et seq. to determine which statutory scheme applies to a given application or claim; partial or mixed filing histories may require per‑claim analysis.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) prior art categories
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) provides that a person is not entitled to a patent if the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: The categories of prior art for 102(a)(1) include issued patents, published applications, non‑patent printed publications, and evidence of public use or sale. A printed publication that lacks an early enough date to qualify itself may still serve as evidence of an earlier public use or sale. Examiners must use the appropriate documentary or factual evidence to support a 102(a)(1) rejection and identify dates and facts that establish public availability before the effective filing date.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) one‑year grace period exceptions to (a)(1)
description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art under 102(a)(1) if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor, or (B) the subject matter had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor or someone who obtained it from the inventor.
guidance: The one‑year grace period is measured from the filing date of the earliest U.S. or foreign patent application to which a proper benefit or priority claim is asserted and that supports the claimed invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a). This differs from pre‑AIA 102(b), where the measurement was from the filing date of the earliest U.S. application. Examiners must evaluate whether the disclosure falls within the inventor‑originated exceptions and compute the grace period from the correct filing date.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) exceptions to (a)(2), including ownership exception (102(b)(2)(C))
description: A disclosure is not prior art under 102(a)(2) if (A) the subject matter was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor, (B) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor or one who obtained it from the inventor before the 102(a)(2) effective filing date, or (C) the disclosed subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: 102(b)(2)(C) replaces the pre‑AIA 103(c) common‑ownership exception but applies only to prior art under 102(a)(2) (U.S. patent documents), not to 102(a)(1) disclosures (patents, publications, public uses, sales). Examiners must determine whether the ownership/assignment condition is satisfied as of the relevant effective dates and recognize that some disclosures by co‑workers/collaborators may still be prior art under 102(a)(1) unless within a 102(b)(1) exception.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103: timing and scope of obviousness inquiry
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 states that a patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: The AIA shifts the temporal focus of the obviousness inquiry to before the effective filing date (rather than time of invention under pre‑AIA law). The provision tracks pre‑AIA 103(a) in substance and clarifies patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made. Pre‑AIA 103(c) provisions have been replaced by AIA 102(b)(2)(C) and (c); other pre‑AIA exceptions (e.g., 103(b) biotech‑related) were eliminated. Examiners should apply Graham factors and KSR rationales with the effective filing date as the temporal anchor.

name: Examiner's duty to state reasons and provide supporting information
description: The Office bears the initial burden of explaining why statutory or regulatory requirements have not been met when a claim is rejected; whenever a claim is rejected or an objection made, the Office shall notify the applicant, state the reasons, and provide information and references useful to the applicant.
guidance: This duty remains unchanged under the AIA. See 35 U.S.C. 132, 37 C.F.R. 1.104(c) and MPEP § 706. Examiners must articulate the factual and legal basis for rejections (e.g., why references are combinable, why a reference qualifies as prior art, computation of effective dates, how teachings of references apply) and supply references or information that assist applicants in assessing the propriety of continuing prosecution.

name: No amendment may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C.132 / 37 CFR 1.121)
description: No amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of an application; matter not present on the filing date in the specification, claims, or drawings that is added after filing is usually new matter.
guidance: If new matter is introduced, the amendment should be objected to under 35 U.S.C.132 and the new matter must be canceled in reply to the Office action. If new matter has been entered into claims or affects the scope of claims, reject claims under 35 U.S.C.112(a) (pre-AIA 112 first paragraph). Replacement drawings containing new matter should not be entered; identify new matter by page/line numbers and explain the examiner's position.

name: Apply the Graham factors to design patents
description: The traditional four Graham factors (scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claimed invention, the level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations) apply to design‑patent obviousness.
guidance: Court evaluated design patent obviousness by applying these factors in design context (e.g., Whitman Saddle). The Federal Circuit reaffirmed these factors and described how they map to design issues (see other rubric entries for specific mappings).

name: Scope and content of prior art: analogous art requirement
description: Prior art considered in the Graham first factor should be limited to 'analogous art' — typically art in the same field of endeavor as the claimed design's article of manufacture, but it need not be literally in the same field if it is nevertheless analogous.
guidance: The court stated '[t]he primary reference will typically be in the same field of endeavor as the claimed ornamental design’s article of manufacture, but it need not be, so long as it is analogous art.' The opinion left open precise tests for analogy; USPTO guidance instructs examiners to consider analogous art when assessing prior art scope.

name: Assess differences by their effect on overall visual impression
description: When comparing prior art and the claimed design, courts should evaluate differences based on how they affect the overall visual appearance, rather than using a binary 'basically the same' test.
guidance: Board in LKQ found that differences between certain visual features affected overall visual impression. Under LKQ, differences must be analyzed to determine their impact on the overall impression from the viewpoint of an ordinary designer/observer.

name: Ordinary designer / ordinary observer perspective
description: The claim should be assessed through the viewpoint of an ordinary designer (in determining obviousness) or ordinary observer (in anticipation/infringement/visual similarity inquiries), i.e., a person of ordinary skill in the pertinent design art.
guidance: The court explained that in design contexts the level of skill should be the 'ordinary designer in the field' and quoted the Gorham 'ordinary observer' standard ('if in the eye of an ordinary observer...') used to determine substantial similarity and deception. Whitman Saddle and LKQ applied these concepts.

name: Permissible use of primary and secondary references (analogous, not 'so related')
description: Primary and secondary references can both be considered even if they are not 'so related' to each other; they must simply be analogous to the claimed design.
guidance: Unlike Durling (which required secondary references to be 'so related' to a primary reference), LKQ allows combination of references that are each analogous to the claimed design — broadening the scope of prior art that can be combined to show obviousness.

name: Utility requirement (specific, substantial, credible)
description: A claimed invention must be useful; the utility must be specific, substantial, and credible.
guidance: See MPEP §2107 for a detailed discussion of utility. Utility is distinct from eligibility under §101 (i.e., utility is not the test for patent-eligible subject matter), but it is a separate statutory requirement that must be satisfied.

name: Human organisms excluded from patentability
description: Claims directed to or encompassing a human organism are nonstatutory and cannot be patented pursuant to AIA sec. 33(a).
guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim as a whole encompasses a human organism, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and AIA sec. 33(a) indicating the claim is directed to a human organism and therefore nonstatutory. Use form paragraph 7.04.03 and continue to examine other patentability issues (35 U.S.C. 102/103/112) as applicable.

name: Step 1 — Four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
description: Determine whether the claim as a whole is directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. For product categories (machine, manufacture, composition) the subject matter generally must have a physical or tangible form.
guidance: Definitions and examples: 'process' = series of acts or steps; 'machine' = concrete thing consisting of parts or combination of devices; 'manufacture' = tangible article given new form/quality/property by human activity; 'composition of matter' = combination of two or more substances. See MPEP §2106.03 for citations and examples. It is sufficient if the claim falls into at least one category; it need not be assigned a single 'correct' category.

name: Non-statutory examples for Step 1
description: Certain claimed subject matter does not fall within the four statutory categories (and so fails Step 1), including information/data per se, a computer program per se (software per se) claimed as a product without structural recitations, transitory signal transmissions (carrier waves), and subject matter expressly prohibited (e.g., humans per se).
guidance: Non-limiting examples: data per se; software per se when claimed as a product without structure; signals per se (propagating electrical/electromagnetic signals); transitory carrier waves. Use Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Digitech, Nuijten, Mentor Graphics) when assessing whether a claim covers non-statutory embodiments.

name: BRI must be established before eligibility analysis
description: Determine the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim as a whole prior to evaluating eligibility; the BRI sets claim boundaries and affects whether the claim covers statutory or non-statutory subject matter and whether it is directed to a judicial exception.
guidance: Evaluating eligibility under the BRI prevents the outcome from depending on the drafter's art. Claim interpretation can affect both Step 1 (e.g., whether a medium encompasses non-statutory carrier waves) and Step 2 (e.g., whether claim limitations require computer implementation, or amount to an improvement in technology). See MPEP §2111 for BRI guidance and cases such as Mentor Graphics, Enfish, Synopsys, McRO, and Amdocs for examples of how construction affects eligibility.

name: Step 2 — Alice/Mayo two-part test (determine judicial exception and inventive concept)
description: Apply the Alice/Mayo framework: Step 2A — determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon); Step 2B — if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements (individually or in combination) that amount to significantly more than the exception (i.e., an 'inventive concept' or practical application).
guidance: The Alice/Mayo test (Mayo/Alice) is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility under Step 2. If claims are directed to an exception, search for an 'inventive concept' beyond the judicial exception. The machine-or-transformation test and other superseded tests (e.g., 'useful, concrete and tangible result' or 'special purpose computer') may be considered as clues but are not separate tests for eligibility. See MPEP §§2106.04 and 2106.05 for detailed guidance and Supreme Court/Federal Circuit precedent (Alice, Mayo, Bilski, Diehr, etc.).

name: Eligibility flowchart — Pathways A, B, and C
description: Use the eligibility flowchart: Pathway A (streamlined analysis) — claims that fall within a statutory category and whose eligibility is self-evident; Pathway B — claims that fall within a statutory category and are not directed to a judicial exception (no Step 2B required); Pathway C — claims that fall within a statutory category, are directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A YES), but recite additional elements that amount to significantly more (Step 2B YES).
guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis (Pathway A) applies, conduct the full eligibility analysis. If a claim is not eligible under any pathway, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. Regardless of a 101 rejection, continue complete examination under 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, and 112 as appropriate.

name: BRI covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments requires rejection
description: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-eligible subject matter and fails Step 1 (should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101).
guidance: When this occurs, best practice is to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment that narrows the claim to statutory embodiments if possible. Example: claims to 'machine-readable medium' that encompass both RAM (statutory) and carrier waves (non-statutory) should be rejected and applicant advised to amend.

name: Specification section headings and format
description: Specification section headings should appear in uppercase and without underlining or bold type; if no text follows a section heading, use the phrase 'Not Applicable'.
guidance: Section headings should be in upper case and plain formatting. If an application data sheet is used, duplicate data need not be repeated elsewhere except where specific older rules apply (e.g., citizenship for applications filed before Sept 16, 2012). The most recent compliant ADS controls certain priority/benefit claim information for applications filed on or after Sept 16, 2012.

name: Background of the Invention content
description: The Background should set forth the field of the invention and a description of the related art (including information disclosed under 37 CFR 1.97 and 1.98). It should describe the state of the prior art and, where applicable, indicate problems in the prior art which are solved by the applicant’s invention.
guidance: Field of the Invention may paraphrase applicable CPC definitions and be directed to the subject matter of the claimed invention. Description of Related Art should include references to specific related art where appropriate and point out problems solved by the invention. See MPEP §§ 608.01(a), (p), and § 707.05(b).

name: Brief summary of the invention
description: A brief summary indicating its nature and substance should precede the detailed description; the summary should be commensurate with the invention as claimed and describe the nature, operation, and purpose in clear, concise sentences or paragraphs.
guidance: Summary should be directed to the specific invention being claimed (not mere generalities), may point out advantages or how it solves problems indicated in the Background, and should be consistent with the subject matter of the claims. The summary is distinct from the abstract and should aid future searches and understanding of the patent.

name: Claims formatting and placement
description: The claim or claims must commence on a separate sheet or electronic page; where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step should be separated by a line indentation. There may be plural indentations to further segregate subcombinations or related steps.
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.75 and MPEP § 608.01(m). Claims must be clearly presented and start on a separate page; proper indentation helps segregate elements/subcombinations and aids clarity.

name: Abstract content specifics
description: The patent abstract should be a concise statement of the technical disclosure and should include that which is new in the art to which the invention pertains; it should not refer to purported merits or speculative applications or compare the invention with the prior art.
guidance: If the patent is basic in nature the abstract may be directed to the entire disclosure; for improvements it should include the technical disclosure of the improvement. Where applicable, include: (1) machine/apparatus—organization and operation; (2) article—method of making; (3) chemical compound—identity and use; (4) mixture—ingredients; (5) process—the steps. Extensive mechanical/design details should not be included. In chemical cases, give general nature and use and exemplify species if illustrative. The abstract should be narrative and generally a single paragraph of 50–150 words (preferably) and not exceed 15 lines. Avoid legal phraseology and claim-style terminology such as 'means' and 'said', and avoid repeating the title or using implied phrases like 'This disclosure concerns'.

name: Abstract language and format requirements
description: The abstract must commence on a separate sheet (preferably following the claims), be in narrative form, generally limited to a single paragraph within 50–150 words, and should not include other parts of the application.
guidance: Use heading 'Abstract' or 'Abstract of the Disclosure'. If the abstract does not commence on a separate sheet, require a new abstract on a separate sheet (form paragraph 6.16.01). The abstract should describe the disclosure sufficiently to assist readers in deciding whether to consult the full patent text. Examiner may require correction in first Office action or at earliest point noted; replies are treated under 37 CFR 1.111(b).

name: Drawings and photographs standards (black & white, color, photographs)
description: Black and white drawings are normally required (India ink or equivalent). Color drawings are permitted in design applications and, on rare occasions, in utility applications if color is the only practical medium; photographs are not ordinarily permitted but allowed if they are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.
guidance: Color drawings in utility applications require a petition with fee (§ 1.17(h)), submission of specified sets of color drawings, and insertion of specific language in the brief description of drawings stating that the file contains color drawings and that copies with color drawings will be provided upon request and fee. Color drawings must be reproducible in black and white in the printed patent and are not permitted in international applications (PCT Rule 11.13). Photographs (black & white or color) are acceptable for certain subject matter (e.g., electrophoresis gels, blots, cell cultures, histological sections, animals, plants, in vivo imaging, TLC plates, crystalline structures, ornamental effects) and must be of sufficient quality so all details are reproducible in the printed patent. If the subject admits illustration by a drawing, the examiner may require a drawing instead of a photograph. See 37 CFR 1.84 and relevant MPEP paragraphs.

name: Illegitimacy criterion 5-2 — Specification without claims after amendment period
description: Where a specification which does not include the claims is attached to a patent application filed by the lawful holder of a right and the amendment period of the specification under Article 42(2)(ii) has already elapsed.
guidance: If claims are missing and the amendment period has passed, the filing is illegitimate.

name: Illegitimacy criterion 15 — Request for examination attached to specification without claims
description: Where a patent applicant has submitted a request for examination on a patent application attached with a specification which does not include the claims.
guidance: A request for examination with a specification lacking claims is illegitimate.

name: When to limit action on a claim to a particular issue
description: Some situations exist where examination of an application appears best accomplished by limiting action on the claim thereof to a particular issue.
guidance: Situations include: (A) application too informal for complete action on the merits (MPEP § 702.01); (B) undue multiplicity of claims with no successful telephone election (MPEP § 2173.05(n)); (C) misjoinder of inventions with no successful telephone election (MPEP § 803, § 810, § 812.01); (D) disclosure directed to perpetual motion (Ex parte Payne). For perpetual motion cases, cite best prior art and point out pertinency without specifically applying it to the claims. Conversely, rejections based on res judicata, no prima facie showing for reissue, new matter, or inoperativeness (not involving perpetual motion) should be accompanied by rejection on all other available grounds.

name: State when claims are allowable (general principle)
description: When patentable subject matter is disclosed and apparent from claims/arguments, examiners should indicate when claims are allowable or suggest allowable claim language.
guidance: For pro se applicants, draft one or more claims and indicate they would be allowed if incorporated. Examiner actions should be constructive — offer definite suggestions for correction for form defects or omitted limitations and consider suggesting an interview to reach agreement on allowable claims.

name: Allowable except as to form — constructive suggestions
description: If application discloses patentable subject matter but claims cannot be allowed due to formal defects or omitted limitation, do not stop at a bare objection or rejection.
guidance: Offer definite suggestions for correction; indicate aspects/features not claimed that could be claimed for favorable consideration; suggest interviews when useful. If a claim is otherwise allowable but depends on a canceled or rejected claim, state it would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.

name: Form paragraph use for specific 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections
description: Use specific form paragraphs when dependent or independent claims are rejected solely under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and would be allowable if amended.
guidance: ¶ 7.43.01 for independent/ dependent claims rejected under 112 second paragraph; ¶ 7.43.02 for dependent claims that would be allowable if rewritten to include base claim limitations. Examiner notes specify when to use each paragraph.

name: Questioning results and examples — standard for rejection
description: The results of tests and examples should not normally be questioned unless there is a reasonable basis; if questioned, reject appropriate claims as based on insufficient disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Applicant must reply by providing actual test/example results or relevant arguments supporting predicted results. Care must be taken that no new matter is entered into the application. See MPEP § 2161–§ 2164.08(c) for written description and enablement discussion.

name: 15.10.15 Notice re prior art available under both pre-AIA and AIA
description: Notice that if the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
guidance: Examiner Note: In bracket 1, identify the reference applied against the claimed design. For applications with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013, that claim priority to, or the benefit of, an application filed before March 16, 2013, this form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 15.10.15 (i.e., this paragraph often precedes or accompanies other paragraphs to notify of dual‑status prior art).

name: 15.15.02.aia 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) Provisional rejection - design disclosed in another application with common inventor and/or assignee
description: The claim is provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [1] which has a common [2] with the instant application. Because the copending application names another inventor and has an earlier effective filing date, it would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if published under 122(b) or patented. This provisional rejection is based upon a presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application.
guidance: This provisional rejection might be overcome by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the design in the reference was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor of this application (not prior art under 102(b)(2)(A)); (2) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing certified priority document satisfying 35 U.S.C. 112(a); (3) perfecting the benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 by filing an application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 with specific reference per 1.78 and establishing enablement/description under 112(a); (4) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B); or (5) providing a statement under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) that subject matter and claimed invention were owned by same person or subject to assignment/joint research agreement. This rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Examiner Notes: Used to provisionally reject over copending application (utility or design) with earlier filing date that discloses the claimed invention; copending application must have either common assignee or at least one common inventor. In bracket 2 insert 'inventor' or 'assignee'. For certain priority situations precede with paragraphs 15.10.aia and 15.10.15.

name: 15.15.02.fti Provisional Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection - design disclosed but not claimed in another application with common inventor and/or assignee
description: The claim is provisionally rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by copending Application No. [1] which has a common [2] with the instant application. Based upon the different inventive entity and the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), if published under 122(b) or patented.
guidance: Suggested ways to overcome: (A) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the design in the reference was derived from the designer of this application (thus not 'by another'); (B) showing a date of invention for the instant application prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the reference under 37 CFR 1.131(a); (C) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing certified priority document meeting 112(a) requirements; (D) perfecting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 per 37 CFR 1.78 and establishing enablement/description. Administrative notes: If application filed before Sept 16, 2012 include specific reference in first sentences of specification or in ADS; if on/after Sept16,2012 include in ADS. Use pre‑AIA 102(e) as amended by AIPA to determine reference's prior art date unless reference is US patent issued from int'l app with filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000; otherwise use pre‑AIPA 102(e). Examiner Notes: In bracket 2 insert inventor or assignee. For certain priority situations precede with paragraph 15.10.15.

name: 15.15.04.aia 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) rejection - design disclosed in a patent
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by patent [1]. Because the patent names another inventor and has an earlier effective filing date, it constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2).
guidance: This rejection might be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that disclosure in the reference was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor of this application (not prior art under 102(b)(2)(A)); (2) perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing certified priority documents meeting 112(a); (3) perfecting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 via ADS per 37 CFR 1.76 and 1.78; (4) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of prior public disclosure under 102(b)(2)(B); or (5) providing statement under 102(b)(2)(C) of common ownership/assignment/joint research. This rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Examiner Note: Use when claimed design is disclosed in the drawings of an earlier‑filed design or utility patent; insert patent number in bracket 1. For certain priority situations precede with 15.10.aia and 15.10.15.

name: 15.15.04.fti Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection - design disclosed but not claimed in a patent
description: The claim is rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 as being anticipated by patent [1]. Based upon the different inventive entity and the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the reference, it constitutes prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: Since the design claimed in the present application is not the same invention claimed in patent [2], suggested ways to overcome include: (A) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the design in the reference was derived from the designer of this application and is thus not 'by another'; (B) showing a date of invention for the instant application prior to the reference under 37 CFR 1.131(a); (C) perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119; or (D) perfecting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 and establishing enablement/description. If application filed before Sept 16, 2012 include specific reference in spec or ADS; if filed on/after Sept 16, 2012 include in ADS. This rejection may not be overcome by filing a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). Examiner Note: Use when claimed design is disclosed in drawings of earlier‑filed design or utility patent but not claimed therein.

name: 15.16.fti Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) Rejection
description: The claim is rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 because applicant did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented.
guidance: Use where factual showing supports that the named applicant is not the actual inventor. (No additional bracket instructions in the excerpt.)

name: 15.17.aia Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) Rejection
description: The claim is rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 because, before the applicant’s invention thereof, the invention was made in this country by another who had not abandoned, suppressed or concealed it.
guidance: A rejection based on this statutory basis can be made in an application or patent that is examined under the first‑to‑file provisions of the AIA if it also contains or contained at any time (1) a claim to an invention having an effective filing date as defined in 35 U.S.C. 100(i) that is before March 16, 2013, or (2) a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) to any patent or application that contains or contained at any time such a claim. Examiner Note: For applications with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013 that claim priority to, or the benefit of, an application filed before March 16, 2013, this form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraphs 15.10.aia and 15.10.15.

name: 15.19.02.aia Preface 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)/103 rejection - Different inventors, common assignee, obvious designs, no evidence of common ownership not later than effective filing date of claimed design
description: The claim is directed to a design not patentably distinct from the design of commonly assigned [1]. Specifically, the claimed design is different from the one in [2] in that [3]. These differences are considered obvious and do not patentably distinguish the overall appearance of the claimed design over the design in [4]. The commonly assigned [5] names another inventor and was effectively filed before the present application and thus qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2).
guidance: This rejection might be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the design in the reference was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor (not prior art under 102(b)(2)(A)); (2) perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119; (3) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 via ADS and 1.78; (4) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure under 102(b)(2)(B); or (5) providing a statement under 102(b)(2)(C) that the designs were owned by the same person or subject to assignment/joint research agreement as of the effective filing date. Examiner Notes: An obviousness double patenting rejection may also be included. In brackets insert 'patent' and number, or 'copending application' and serial number as appropriate. In bracket 3 identify differences. This paragraph should only be used ONCE in an Office action and for certain priority situations precede with 15.10.aia and 15.10.15.

name: 15.19.02.fti Preface pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection - Different inventors, common assignee, obvious designs, no evidence of common ownership at time later design was made
description: The claim is directed to a design not patentably distinct from the design of commonly assigned [1]. Specifically, the claimed design is different from the one in [2] in that [3]. These differences are considered obvious and do not patentably distinguish the overall appearance of the claimed design over the design in [4]. The commonly assigned [5] has a different inventive entity and therefore qualifies as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) and forms the basis for rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) if the conflicting design claims were not commonly owned at the time the design in this application was made.
guidance: Applicant/assignee/attorney can resolve by stating that conflicting designs were commonly owned at the time the design in this application was made, or the assignee can name the prior inventor of the conflicting subject matter. A showing of common ownership at the relevant time will overcome a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) based upon the commonly assigned case as a reference under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or 102(g), or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) for apps filed on/after Nov 29, 1999. Examiner Notes: Use when commonly assigned but no indication of common assignment at time invention was made. If conflicting claim is in a patent with earlier US filing date, make 102(e)/103(a) rejection. If in commonly assigned copending application with earlier filing date, provisionally reject under pre‑AIA 102(e)/103(a). An obviousness double patenting rejection may also be included. Insert patent/copending application numbers in brackets and identify differences in bracket 3. This paragraph should only be used ONCE in an Office action. For determining reference's pre‑AIA or pre‑AIPA 102(e) date follow guidance in paragraphs 7.12.fti / 7.12.01.fti.

name: 15.19.03.fti Provisional Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection - design disclosed but not claimed in another application with common inventor and/or assignee
description: The claim is provisionally rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over copending Application No. [1] which has a common [2] with the instant application. Based upon the different inventive entity and the earlier effective U.S. filing date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if published under 122(b) or patented. This provisional rejection is based upon a presumption of future publication or patenting of the conflicting application.
guidance: Since the design claimed in the present application is not the same invention claimed in the [4] application, this provisional rejection may be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the design in the reference was derived from the designer of this application and is thus not 'by another,' or by a showing of a date of invention for the instant application prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the reference under 37 CFR 1.131(a). For applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999, this rejection might also be overcome by showing that the subject matter of the reference and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. Alternatively, merging the two applications into a single continuation‑in‑part and abandoning the separate parent applications may overcome the rejection. Examiner Notes: In brackets insert serial number of copending application and inventor/assignee. Provide explanation of obviousness/differences in bracket 3 and follow explanation with form paragraphs 15.70.fti and 15.67 or 15.68 as applicable. Use pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as amended by AIPA to determine reference's prior art date unless special exceptions apply. For certain priority situations precede with 15.10.15.

name: Activities applied against claims: antedating uses/knowledge
description: A rejection based on an activity showing that the claimed invention was used or known prior to the filing date may be overcome by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 establishing a date of invention prior to the date of the activity.
guidance: Alternatively, applicant(s) may file a specific affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the activity was performed by the applicant(s). Statutory bars are exceptions.

name: General rule as to generic claims (species antedates genus)
description: A reference or activity applied against generic claims may (in most cases) be antedated as to such claims by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing completion of the invention of only a single species, within the genus, prior to the effective date of the reference or activity.
guidance: See Ex parte Biesecker and cases. Distinguish unpredictable arts (see MPEP § 715.03) where species may not support genus antedating.

name: Genus-species and predictability considerations
description: When generic claims are rejected on a reference disclosing a species not antedated by the affidavit, the affidavit will not ordinarily be withdrawn unless applicant establishes possession of the generic invention prior to the effective date; the affidavit must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to support a generic claim.
guidance: If reference discloses several species of a claimed genus, applicant must show prior completion of all species shown in the reference to overcome directly under 1.131. Indirect antedating possible by showing other species made that make the reference species obvious. Tests consider predictability and size of genus (e.g., halogens example). Cases: In re Plumb, In re Schaub, In re Shokal.

name: Permissible exhibits and how to support affidavit
description: Exhibits that may accompany an affidavit include sketches, blueprints, photographs, reproductions of notebook entries, models, supporting statements by witnesses, testimony in an interference, and disclosure documents; each exhibit relied upon should be specifically referred to in the affidavit or declaration in terms of what it is relied upon to show.
guidance: Exhibits and models must comply with 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into an application file. An accompanying exhibit need not support all claimed limitations provided missing limitations are supported by the declaration itself. See Ex parte Ovshinsky.

name: Inventive concept / additional features must provide practical assurance
description: Additional features beyond the natural law must provide 'practical assurance' that the claim amounts to a genuine application of the law rather than an attempt to monopolize it.
guidance: The Court requires an 'inventive concept' — elements or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent in practice is significantly more than a patent upon the natural law itself. The presence of such features distinguishes claims like Diehr (where integration of steps into a whole rendered the claim patent-eligible) from claims like Flook or Benson.

name: Preemption concern: claims must not tie up the use of a law of nature
description: A patent should not preempt the entire use of a natural law or otherwise 'tie up' future research and applications of that law beyond what the inventor discovered.
guidance: The Court repeatedly stresses concern that allowing patents that effectively grant monopolies over laws of nature would inhibit future innovation. Cases referenced include Morse, Benson, and Bilski. Even narrow natural laws can unduly foreclose later refinements or alternative implementations; preemption is a central policy consideration under §101.

name: Consider the claim as a whole but test whether added steps integrate the law meaningfully
description: Claims should be considered as a whole, but consideration must determine whether the non-law elements integrate the law into an inventive application rather than merely append conventional steps.
guidance: Diehr teaches considering the claim as a whole (and found patent eligibility where the additional steps integrated the equation meaningfully). Mayo clarifies that even when looked at as a whole, if the additional steps are conventional and add nothing significant, the claim remains ineligible. The analysis compares integration (Diehr) versus mere statement+application (Flook, Benson).

name: Claims that merely identify the relevant audience are inadequate
description: An 'administering' step or other element that only identifies who will be interested in or use the law (e.g., doctors) does not contribute to patent eligibility.
guidance: Mayo points out that calling out the relevant practitioners or beneficiaries (e.g., doctors who use a drug) is merely picking out a pre-existing audience and cannot supply the inventive concept required under §101.

name: Post-solution activity specified at a high level of generality is insufficient
description: Post-solution or implementation activity drafted at a high level of generality (covering any way to perform the activity) will not convert a law of nature into a patentable process.
guidance: The Court criticized claims that instruct practitioners to perform measuring or other steps 'through whatever process the doctor wishes to use' or otherwise claim implementation in general terms. Such broad, high-level claiming risks capturing later-discovered methods and inhibits future innovation.

name: §101 inquiry is distinct from §§102, 103, 112; cannot be displaced by novelty/obviousness/enablement
description: The §101 patent-eligibility inquiry is a separate gatekeeping inquiry and should not be replaced by later statutory inquiries into novelty (§102), non-obviousness (§103), or written-description/enablement (§112).
guidance: The Government argued that novelty or obviousness could filter out undeserving claims, but the Court rejected turning §101 into an empty formality. Relying solely on §§102/103/112 would undermine the law-of-nature exclusion and create legal uncertainty; §101 must be applied independently.

name: Specification required six parts
description: The specification properly consists of six parts: (1) the preamble, (2) a general statement of the nature and object of the invention, (3) a brief description of the drawings, if any, (4) a detailed description of the invention, (5) the claim or claims, and (6) the signature of the applicant.
guidance: Prior witness requirements were removed (1915 amendment); each part has particular functions and must be present to form a proper specification.

name: General statement must avoid limiting particulars
description: Every general statement of the nature and object of the invention should be free from any particularity or limitation which, if imported by implication into one or more of the claims, might reduce the area covered by the patent to territory more narrow than the state of the prior art required.
guidance: Draft the general statement broadly to avoid inadvertently narrowing claim scope by implication.

name: Definition of Anticipation (35 U.S.C. §102 rejection)
description: A 35 USC 102 rejection ("anticipation rejection") occurs when the USPTO examiner determines that the invention is not novel because all elements of the claimed invention are disclosed in a single prior art reference.
guidance: Anticipation is lack of novelty; it requires that every claim element is disclosed by the single prior art reference. This sets the fundamental standard for evaluating novelty rejections.

name: Single Reference Rule
description: To reject a claim as anticipated, the disclosure must teach every element required by the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation. Anticipation requires all elements in a claim to be found in a single piece of prior art.
guidance: Examiner/practitioner must verify that a single reference, by itself, discloses every claim limitation (no combination of references permitted for anticipation). Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim when comparing to prior art.

name: Elements Required for Valid Anticipation
description: For a valid 102 anticipation rejection: 1) All elements of the claimed invention found in a single prior art reference; 2) Prior art must disclose the identical invention 'arranged as in the claim'; 3) Prior art reference must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the invention.
guidance: All three elements are required: identity of elements, arrangement as claimed, and enablement. Failure of any of these defeats an anticipation rejection. 'Arranged as in the claim' emphasizes that the prior art must disclose the claimed combination/organization, not merely isolated elements.

name: Examiner Requirements When Asserting a 102 Rejection
description: Examiners cite the most relevant prior art reference. The rejection should identify each claim limitation, map each to specific portions of the prior art, and be specific about where each element is disclosed (column/line, paragraph, figure number).
guidance: Proper 102 rejections must be specific and show clear mappings from claim limitations to particular disclosure locations in the reference. Vague citations or failure to identify where limitations are disclosed is a defect in the rejection.

name: Strategic Responses to a 102 Rejection
description: Principal responses include: 1) Argue claim language distinguishing from prior art; 2) Argue absence of element (not all elements disclosed); 3) Argue lack of enablement (reference doesn't enable practice); 4) Antedate the reference (swear behind under pre-AIA); 5) Invoke grace period (post-AIA inventor disclosures); 6) Amend claims to add limitations not in prior art.
guidance: Select responses based on factual record: parse claim interpretation arguments, identify missing elements or enablement defects, rely on statutory grace/antedating where available, or amend claims to recite features absent from the cited reference. Use evidence (declarations, dates, publications) to support arguments.

name: Chapter 600 - Parts, Form, and Content of Application
description: Requirements for the parts, format, and substantive content of patent applications (specification, claims, drawings, abstract).
guidance: Details statutory and rule-based content requirements (e.g., 35 U.S.C. §112-related items), formatting rules, claim requirements, and examples of acceptable/defective filings.

name: Chapter 1500 - Design Patents
description: Substantive and procedural guidance specific to design patent applications and their prosecution.
guidance: Covers claim/drawing requirements unique to design patents and prosecution differences from utility patents.

name: Chapter 1600 - Plant Patents
description: Guidance for preparation, examination, and issuance of plant patents.
guidance: Describes requirements particular to asexual reproduction, specimen deposit, and claim drafting for plant patents.

name: Scope of patent design rights and examples of non-infringement
description: Patent design owner's rights are applicable only within the boundaries of the drawings, title, claims, and brief description of the design patent.
guidance: Material/properties/utilization/benefits from features not within the rights are not allowed to be exploited. Examples listed as non-infringement include: private use with no commercial interest; research and experiments that do not conflict with owner’s benefits; prior use in good faith; temporary/emergency entry by equipment of ship vessels; and use after receiving consent from the owner.

name: Seed Agent — patent claim analysis
description: The 'Seed Agent' employs fine tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) to analyze patent claims and map their technological capabilities.
guidance: Use fine-tuned LLMs to parse and semantically characterize patent claims, producing capability representations ('Seeds') for downstream matching to market needs.

name: Exclude value contributed by non-patented elements and other non-inventive factors
description: Instructions should clearly exclude value contributed by factors other than the claimed invention (technical components not claimed, manufacturing process, product marketing, brand recognition, conventional elements).
guidance: Tell jurors to ignore benefits of conventional elements or benefits obtainable via noninfringing alternatives when determining the patent's market value.

name: Priority Period definition
description: The term 'priority period' in relation to a priority claim means 12 months from the filing date of the earlier application whose priority is claimed; the day of filing of the earlier application is not included.
guidance: Rule 2.4 sets the standard 12‑month Paris Convention priority period and cross-references Rule 80.5 as applicable.

name: Check list contents on the Request (Rule 3.3)
description: The request shall contain a list indicating: (i) total number of sheets constituting the international application and number of sheets of each element (request, description, claims, drawings, abstract, sequence listing part if any); (ii) where applicable, that the application is accompanied by a power of attorney, copy of general power, priority document, sequence listing in electronic form, payment document or other specified documents; (iii) number of the figure applicant suggests to accompany the abstract (applicant may suggest more than one figure in exceptional cases).
guidance: If applicant fails to complete the checklist, the receiving Office should make necessary indications except it shall not indicate the figure number for abstract; checklist particulars for printouts are prescribed by Administrative Instructions.

name: Mandatory and optional contents of the Request; Signature (Rule 4.1)
description: The Request shall contain: (a) mandatory contents — a petition, the title of the invention, indications concerning the applicant and the agent, and indications concerning the inventor where required by national law; (b) where applicable — a priority claim, indications relating to an earlier search, a reference to a parent application or parent patent, an indication of applicant's choice of competent International Searching Authority; (c) may contain — certain other indications (e.g., inventor where not required, requests to transmit priority document, declarations under Rule 4.17, statement under Rule 4.18, request for restoration of priority); the Request shall be signed.
guidance: Rule 4.1 enumerates mandatory elements that must appear in the Request and lists optional/allowed items; signature by applicant(s) is required (see Rule 4.15).

name: Declarations for national requirements (Rule 4.17)
description: The Request may, for national law purposes in designated States, contain one or more declarations worded as prescribed by Administrative Instructions, including (i) identity of the inventor, (ii) applicant’s entitlement as at the international filing date to apply for and be granted a patent, (iii) applicant’s entitlement to claim priority, (iv) declaration of inventorship as in Rule 51 bis.1(a)(iv) (signed per Admin Instr.), and (v) declaration as to non‑prejudicial disclosures or exceptions to lack of novelty.
guidance: These declarations are optional in the Request but when provided must follow the prescribed wording in Administrative Instructions to satisfy national requirements.

name: Statement of incorporation by reference (Rule 4.18)
