description: Where the international application claims priority and an element or part of the application is completely contained in the earlier application but not otherwise contained in the international application, the Request may contain a statement that that element or part is incorporated by reference in the international application for purposes of Rule 20.6, subject to confirmation under Rule 20.6; such a statement, if not in the Request on the filing date, may be added only if it was otherwise contained in or submitted with the international application on that date.
guidance: Incorporation by reference is narrowly permitted and subject to confirmation procedures to ensure the material is in fact present in the earlier application.

name: Manner of the Description (Rule 5.1)
description: The description shall first state the title as in the Request and shall: (i) specify the technical field; (ii) indicate the background art useful for understanding/searching/examining the invention and preferably cite documents reflecting such art; (iii) disclose the invention, as claimed, in terms that the technical problem and its solution can be understood and state advantageous effects with reference to background art; (iv) briefly describe figures in the drawings; (v) set forth at least the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention, in terms of examples where appropriate with reference to drawings (unless national law of designated State does not require best mode); (vi) explicitly indicate how the invention is capable of industrial exploitation and how it can be made and used (industry in broadest sense). The manner and order should be followed except when a different order results in better understanding; each part should preferably be preceded by an appropriate heading as suggested in Administrative Instructions.
guidance: Rule 5.1 provides the structure and minimum content for a description to meet sufficiency / disclosure expectations across national Offices; best mode requirement is subject to national law variations.

name: References to other parts of the application in claims (Rule 6.2)
description: Claims shall not, except where absolutely necessary, rely in respect of technical features on references to the description or drawings (e.g., 'as described in part ...' or 'as illustrated in figure ...'); where drawings exist, technical features in claims should preferably be followed by reference signs placed between parentheses, which may be removed by designated Offices for publication.
guidance: Claims should be self-contained and define technical features in claim language rather than by cross-reference; use reference signs only to facilitate understanding.

name: Manner of claiming (two‑part/form/characterizing portion) (Rule 6.3)
description: The matter for which protection is sought shall be defined in terms of technical features. Whenever appropriate, claims shall contain: (i) a statement indicating those technical features which are necessary for the definition but which, in combination, are part of the prior art; and (ii) a characterizing portion—preceded by words such as 'characterized in that', 'characterized by', 'wherein the improvement comprises', or similar—stating concisely the technical features which, in combination with the features under (i), it is desired to protect. Where national law does not require such manner, failure to use it has no effect if the claim used satisfies national law.
guidance: Two-part claim form is preferred where appropriate (particularly for inventions building on prior art); wording for the characterizing portion should be concise and standardized to clarify the novel features.

name: Dependent claims format and grouping (Rule 6.4)
description: A dependent claim includes all features of one or more other claims and shall do so by a reference (preferably at the beginning) to the other claim(s) and then state additional features. A multiple dependent claim referring to more than one other claim shall refer to such claims in the alternative only; multiple dependent claims shall not serve as basis for another multiple dependent claim. Dependent claims shall be construed as including all limitations of the claim to which they refer. All dependent claims referring back to a single previous claim and those referring back to several previous claims shall be grouped together to the extent practical. If national law of the Office acting as ISA does not allow a different drafting of multiple dependent claims, failure to use the provided manner may result in an indication under Article 17(2)(b) in the international search report; failure to use the said manner has no effect in a designated State if the used manner satisfies that national law.
guidance: Dependent claims must be properly referenced and grouped; multiple dependent claims have specific format constraints and may trigger an Article 17 indication if non‑conforming to the ISA's national practice.

name: Abstract contents and form (Rule 8.1)
description: The abstract shall consist of: (i) a summary of the disclosure as contained in the description, claims, and drawings indicating the technical field and drafted to allow clear understanding of the technical problem, gist of the solution, and principal uses; (ii) where applicable, the chemical formula which best characterizes the invention among formulas contained in the application.
guidance: Abstract must summarize the invention clearly to allow quick technical assessment; include a representative chemical formula when relevant.

name: Abstract concision and prohibition on merit statements (Rules 8.1(b)–(c))
description: The abstract shall be as concise as the disclosure permits (preferably 50 to 150 words if in English or translated into English). The abstract shall not contain statements on the alleged merits or value of the claimed invention or on its speculative application.
guidance: Keep abstracts short (50–150 words preferred) and factual—no promotional or speculative language.

name: Claims (scope and drafting tradeoffs)
description: The claims circumscribe the legal bounds of the invention and are generally written using specialized terms.
guidance: Claims should describe essential elements, first broadly and then more narrowly. Narrow claims are easier to obtain but may be easier to design around. To determine if a product falls within a claim, compare the product to each element of the claim — all elements must be present. Patent prosecution centers on debate over claim breadth/narrowness.

name: Claims determine inventorship
description: The patent application claims determine who is and who is not an inventor.
guidance: Claims define the invention from a legal viewpoint and thus guide inventorship determinations.

name: Inventorship criteria
description: An inventor is a person who conceives of an original and non-obvious idea which can be described clearly — the invention.
guidance: A person who contributed a basic idea that resulted in development of the claimed invention is an inventor. A person who contributed only labor or routine supervision but not to the inventive concept is not an inventor (e.g., a technician simply translating an idea into a physical embodiment). Extraneous ideas that do not contribute directly to the claimed invention do not make someone an inventor. Joint inventors have joint rights. Do not confuse inventorship with scientific authorship — criteria differ.

name: Prosecution timing, responses, and amendment options
description: Patent prosecution is an iterative process with the PTO often issuing rejections that must be answered within set timeframes.
guidance: An Examiner will usually reject all or some claims in a first Office Action. The attorney will ask you to comment and may need additional information. There is a three-month response window to the Examiner (extendable month-by-month for three months by paying extra fees). The attorney may prepare amendments to modify claim scope or argue against the Examiner. If rejections become final, options include filing a divisional application, a continuation-in-part (CIP), a continuation, or appealing to the PTO Board of Appeals.

name: Costs and licensing input in prosecution decisions
description: The cost of prosecution and likelihood of getting commercially useful claims influence prosecutorial decisions.
guidance: OTL considers cost and commercial usefulness when determining prosecution strategy; if licensed, the licensee typically has input into whether and how to pursue patenting.

name: Definition of submission for RCE (37 CFR 1.114(c))
description: A 'submission' includes, but is not limited to, an information disclosure statement, an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: If reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111. Previously filed amendments after final (entered or unentered) or arguments from appeal briefs may satisfy the submission requirement where responsive within 37 CFR 1.111.

name: Specification as primary guide
description: The specification is 'the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term' and 'acts as a dictionary when it expressly defines terms used in the claims or when it defines terms by implication.'
guidance: Consult the specification in every case; give it primary weight in determining claim term meaning. Do not treat dictionary definitions as dispositive if they conflict with meanings ascertainable from the patent documents.

name: Ordinary meaning in context of entire patent
description: The 'ordinary meaning' of a claim term is its meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art after reading the entire patent.
guidance: Interpret claim terms based on how a POSITA would understand them in the context of the claims, specification, and prosecution history—not based on an abstract dictionary definition divorced from context.

name: Intrinsic evidence priority (claims, specification, prosecution history)
description: Intrinsic evidence (the claims, specification, and prosecution history) is the primary source for claim construction and should be the main focus at the outset.
guidance: Start by examining how the patentee used the term in the claims, specification, and prosecution history. This approach reduces the risk of adopting an unduly expansive construction derived from extrinsic sources.

name: Risks of excessive reliance on dictionaries
description: Heavy reliance on dictionaries focuses inquiry on abstract meanings rather than on claim meaning within patent context and may transform a claim term's meaning to its abstract dictionary meaning.
guidance: Avoid starting with broad dictionary definitions and then narrowing; general dictionaries collect many uses (common to obscure), which can lead to overbroad constructions inconsistent with the patentee's disclosure.

name: Specification may define terms implicitly
description: The specification may define claim terms by implication even when guidance is not provided in explicit definitional format.
guidance: Look for implicit definitions and usages in the specification; the absence of an explicit 'defined as' phrase does not preclude the specification from defining a term.

name: Avoid importing limitations from specification into claims
description: Courts must avoid reading limitations from the specification into the claims; there is a fine line between construing a claim in light of the specification and importing limitations.
guidance: Distinguish between exemplary embodiments used to teach/enable and limitations that should be read into the claims. Focus on whether a POSITA would understand the specification to restrict the claim scope to the embodiments.

name: Purpose of specification (teach, enable, best mode)
description: The specification's purposes are to teach and enable those of skill in the art to make and use the invention and to provide a best mode.
guidance: Keep these purposes in mind when interpreting whether embodiments are illustrative or limiting; examples often illustrate how to practice the invention rather than define claim boundaries.

name: Claim differentiation (dependent claims inform scope)
description: A dependent claim’s inclusion of a specific limitation makes it likely the independent claim does not contain that limitation (to avoid redundancy).
guidance: Use the presence of narrower limitations in dependent claims as evidence that the broader independent claim was intended to be broader; do not read limitations into independent claims that would render dependent claims redundant.

name: Multiple objectives in specification do not narrowly limit claims
description: A patent stating several objectives does not require that each claim be construed as limited to structures capable of achieving all objectives.
guidance: If the specification lists multiple purposes or advantages for an element, do not construe the claim to require that the element perform every listed purpose unless the claim language or specification clearly so requires.

name: Doctrine of construing to preserve validity is limited
description: Claims may be construed to preserve validity only where, after applying all claim construction tools, the claim remains ambiguous and it is reasonable to infer the PTO would not have issued an invalid patent.
guidance: Do not routinely factor validity into claim construction; only apply this maxim when (1) ambiguity remains after full construction, (2) the proposed construction is practicable and based on sound principles, and (3) it does not revise or ignore explicit claim language.

name: Dictionaries cannot overcome art-specific intrinsic evidence
description: A general-usage dictionary cannot overcome art-specific evidence of the meaning of a claim term.
guidance: When intrinsic (art-specific) evidence indicates a particular meaning, that meaning controls over generic dictionary definitions; judges should not let dictionary editor preferences determine claim scope.

name: Safekeeping client property and funds; accurate billing (37 C.F.R. §11.115)
description: Practitioner must safeguard client funds/property and must prepare accurate fee calculations and invoices; overcharging or misallocating client funds violates the rule.
guidance: Specific misconduct: invoice (Aug 5, 2010) showing improper charges ($770 for excess independent claims and $2,288 for total claims — overcharge about $3,058); billing for more claims than filed; accepting client payment but not remitting USPTO fees; charging for a trademark filing that was never filed. The Order notes restitution (goods provided) as mitigation for returning over-charged expenses and fees.

name: Problem-and-solution approach (three-step method)
description: Assess inventive step by (1) identifying the closest prior art and differences between the invention and that art; (2) determining the technical effect(s) of the differences and defining the objective technical problem; and (3) examining whether the claimed solution to that problem is obvious to the skilled person in view of the state of the art.
guidance: Used predominantly by EPO Examining Divisions, Opposition Divisions and Boards of Appeal as an objective way of deciding inventive step (see T 24/81 and subsequent case law).

name: Determining distinguishing features and technical effect
description: Identify the feature(s) distinguishing the claimed subject‑matter from the closest prior art and determine the technical effect(s) produced by those distinguishing features.
guidance: The objective technical problem (task) is then framed as how to adapt or modify the closest prior art to obtain the identified technical effect(s). Any alleged technical effect must be proved or at least be 'plausibly solved' at the filing date to rely on it.

name: Technical effect must be credibly obtained across claim scope
description: An alleged technical effect relied upon to define the objective technical problem must be credibly obtained throughout the whole range covered by the claims.
guidance: If the effect is not credibly achieved across the claimed scope, it cannot be taken into account when defining the objective technical problem or when assessing inventive step (see case law references such as T 1214/09, T 0960/15).

name: Evidence requirement for alleged advantages or technical effects
description: Alleged advantages or technical effects referred to by the applicant/proprietor must be supported by sufficient evidence; mere assertion without support cannot be relied upon in determining the underlying problem and assessing inventive step.
guidance: If evidence is lacking, the problem must be reformulated. Providing experimental data in the application is not strictly required if the technical problem is at least plausibly solved at filing, but unsupported claims of advantage are insufficient.

name: Signed statement to establish common ownership (content & form)
description: An applicant or patent owner may establish common ownership by submitting a clear, conspicuous, signed statement (signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b)) that the application and the subject matter disclosed in the reference were, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, owned by or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person(s) or organization(s).
guidance: The statement should be clear and conspicuous (e.g., on a separate paper or separate labeled section) so the examiner notices it. Example wording provided in the MPEP is sufficient. The statement may be made by the applicant/patent owner or their representative and is ordinarily sufficient because of the applicant’s paramount obligation of candor and good faith.

name: Joint research agreement (JRA) invocation requirements
description: To invoke the JRA provisions (35 U.S.C. 102(c)) for the 102(b)(2)(C) exception, the applicant/patent owner must provide a statement that (1) the subject matter and the claimed invention were developed or made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement (within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 100(h) and 37 CFR 1.9(e)); (2) the agreement was in effect on or before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; and (3) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
guidance: The statement should be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)). The statement must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). If the names of the parties to the JRA are not in the application, the application must be amended to include them (see 37 CFR 1.71(g)(1)). The applicant may but is not required to file additional evidence supporting the existence of the JRA.

name: Terminal disclaimer / entry refusal and effect on prosecution
description: An amendment under 37 CFR 1.71(g) submitted to overcome a rejection based on a U.S. patent (available only under 102(a)(2)) may be refused entry by the examiner if not accompanied by an appropriate terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(d), because the amendment may necessitate reopening prosecution (e.g., entry of a double patenting rejection).
guidance: If the examiner withdraws the rejection upon entry of the amendment, the examiner may need to issue a new double patenting rejection based on the excepted subject matter; such an Office action can be made final provided no other new ground of rejection not necessitated by the amendment or an IDS during the 37 CFR 1.97(c) period is introduced. The Office action may be final even if the claims were not amended.

name: Court defines legal questions; jury decides factual questions
description: The court defines legal attributes (e.g., construction of the patent, doctrine of estoppel, statute of limitations), while the jury determines factual matters (e.g., execution and authenticity of instruments, identity of parties, whether the accused device is the same as the claimed invention, whether acts constitute infringement, and computation of damages).
guidance: The court instructs on legal doctrines and the scope of claims; the jury applies those doctrines to the evidence. Either tribunal assuming the powers of the other on important matters is ground for error unless the parties have waived objection by treating the question as decided by that authority during trial.

name: Writ of error to Supreme Court — scope and requirements
description: A writ of error lies to the Supreme Court from the judgment of a circuit court in any action at law for infringement; it is a matter of right and amount involved is immaterial if the error relates to a principle or rule of patent law.
guidance: Requirements: the judgment must be final; errors of law alone are reviewable and must appear on the record with exceptions duly taken; writ must issue within two years after entry of final judgment except where disability extends time; the entire record must be sent and matters claimed as error properly assigned or they will not be noticed. The Supreme Court may reverse, modify, or affirm and may award damages for delay.

name: General rule on costs in patent infringement suits
description: As a general rule, the party who recovers judgment in an action at law for infringement also recovers costs.
guidance: Statutory provisions cited. However, important exceptions apply (see related metrics): disclaimers of excessive claims, abandonment of claims at trial, re-issue complications, suits solely for vindication, apportionment when multiple patents/claims involved, nominal damages, and conduct of parties may alter taxation of costs. Specifics include: (a) costs denied where excessive claim is cured by disclaimer pending suit or where certain claims abandoned at trial; (b) disclaimer filed without necessity or after verdict may allow costs; (c) nominal damages usually carry costs; (d) where plaintiff recovers on one of several claims and others are invalid and not disclaimed, costs may be denied or apportioned; (e) where suit is for judicial interpretation or vindication and defendant is not guilty of wilful wrong, costs may be denied against defendant.

name: Patent document element requirements
description: Patent documents normally include publication information, title, bibliometric information (applicants, inventors, assignees, examiners, attorneys), patent classification codes, citations, abstract, drawings, background, detailed description, and claims.
guidance: These sections are canonical inputs/targets for many patent NLP tasks — e.g., use claims for scope, description for long-context analysis, drawings when relevant; treat each element according to its typical function in patent processing.

name: Claims formal/structural requirements
description: Each claim is a single sentence which describes the invention in specific features that make the invention novel and not obvious; claims define the legal scope of the patent.
guidance: Claims require extreme precision and consistent terminology; generation tasks must respect single-sentence structure and legal scope semantics to be defensible and useful.

name: Text generation evaluation (human and automated)
description: Human evaluation (accuracy, fluency, coherence, relevance) is gold standard; automated metrics include BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore; a keystroke-based evaluation measures saved keystrokes for autoregressive completion (proposed for claims).
guidance: Use automated metrics for fast comparisons but complement with human evaluation for legal/precision-sensitive outputs; keystroke metrics are useful for productivity-focused evaluations.

name: Fee payment timing and fee-setting factors
description: The Director must set fees to be paid by the person requesting review; the fee must accompany the petition on filing.
guidance: Under 35 U.S.C. 311(a)/321(a) the Director may establish multiple fees based on the aggregate costs of performing the reviews and the complexity of the review. The Office adopted the number of claims for which review is requested as an administrable factor affecting fee amount. Alternatives considered and rejected include: (i) charging by number of grounds (difficult/contentious to determine), (ii) charging by pages of argument (difficult to administer/distinguish argument vs evidence), (iii) charging fees at multiple steps in the process (would hamper timely completion and conflict with 35 U.S.C. 312/322), and (iv) setting reduced fees for small/micro entities or refunds if a review is not instituted (statutory limitations under 35 U.S.C. 41(d)(2)(a), 42(h)(1), 42(d) limit reductions/refunds).

name: Weight of unsubstantiated applicant assertions about internet reliability
description: If an applicant refutes the publication date of an internet disclosure with no reasoning or merely with generic statements about the reliability of internet disclosures, this argument will be given minimal weight and is therefore unlikely to sway the examiner’s opinion.
guidance: Applicants must provide specific reasons/evidence; generic claims of unreliability are insufficient.

name: Effective date: filing date or priority date per claim
description: The 'date of filing' is to be interpreted as meaning the date of priority in appropriate cases. Different claims or alternatives in one claim may have different effective dates (filing or one of the claimed priority dates). The question of novelty must be considered against each claim (or part of a claim).
guidance: If all state-of-the-art matter was public before the earliest priority document, no allocation of effective dates is necessary. Late-filed missing parts get the date of filing of those elements unless fully contained in the priority document.

name: Inclusion of earlier published applications in state of the art
description: Other applications filed or validly claiming a priority date earlier than — but published on or after — the filing or valid date of priority of the application being examined, form part of the state of the art for novelty (but not inventive step). 'Content' includes description, drawings and claims, including explicit disclaimers (except for disclaimers for unworkable embodiments), references to other documents and prior art explicitly described.
guidance: The 'content' does not include any priority document (which serves only to determine priority validity). Whether a published application is a conflicting application depends on filing date and publication date and whether priority claims were valid at publication.

name: Implicit features and well-known equivalents in novelty
description: A document takes away the novelty of any claimed subject-matter derivable directly and unambiguously from that document including features implicit to a person skilled in the art. However, it is not correct to interpret the teaching document as embracing well-known equivalents not disclosed; that is a matter of obviousness.
guidance: Assess whether subject-matter is 'derivable directly and unambiguously' from the document; implicit but inevitable consequences can destroy novelty.

name: Generic disclosure vs specific examples in novelty
description: A generic disclosure does not usually take away the novelty of any specific example within that disclosure, but a specific disclosure does take away the novelty of a generic claim embracing that disclosure.
guidance: Example: disclosure of copper takes away novelty of 'metal' as a generic concept but not the novelty of other metals; disclosure of rivets takes away novelty of 'fastening means' as a generic concept but not other fastening types.

name: Examination of novelty: disregard of non-distinctive use characteristics
description: In determining novelty, the examiner should remember that, particularly for claims directed to a physical entity, non-distinctive characteristics of a particular intended use should be disregarded.
guidance: Example: a claim to substance X 'for use as a catalyst' not novel over same substance known as a dye unless the use implies a particular form distinguishing it from the known form. For first medical use, a claim to a known compound for a particular purpose based on a technical effect is interpreted as including that technical effect as a functional technical feature and is not objectionable under Section 3(10)(b) provided the feature was not previously made available to the public.

name: Novelty of selected sub-ranges (three criteria)
description: A sub-range selected from a broader known numerical range is considered novel if: (a) the selected sub-range is narrow compared to the known range; (b) it is sufficiently far removed from any specific examples disclosed in the prior art and from the end-points of the known range; and (c) the selected range is not an arbitrary specimen of the prior art but another invention (purposive selection, new technical teaching).
guidance: An effect occurring only in the claimed sub-range cannot by itself confer novelty, but may confirm criterion (c). 'Narrow' and 'sufficiently far removed' are decided case-by-case.

name: Novelty assessment for overlapping ranges and chemical formulae
description: For overlapping ranges (numerical or chemical), novelty is destroyed by an explicitly mentioned end-point, intermediate values or specific examples in the overlap. For overlapping chemical formulae, novelty is acknowledged if the claimed subject-matter is distinguished in the overlap by a new technical element (e.g., a specifically selected residue not individualized in the prior art).
guidance: Consider the whole content of the prior art document and whether the skilled person would seriously contemplate applying the prior teaching in the range of overlap; apply the sub-range criteria analogously.

name: Obviousness test and temporal scope of knowledge
description: The question is whether, before the filing/priority date valid for the claim, having regard to the art known at the time, it would have been obvious to the person skilled in the art to arrive at something within the claim. 'Obvious' means something not going beyond normal technological progress and not involving skill beyond that expected of the skilled person.
guidance: In considering inventive step, construe any published document in the light of knowledge up to and including the day before the filing/priority date and regard all knowledge generally available to the skilled person up to that day.

name: Problem-and-solution approach for inventive step
description: To assess inventive step in an objective and predictable manner, the problem-and-solution approach should be applied (deviation should be exceptional). The approach has three main stages: (i) determining the closest prior art, (ii) establishing the objective technical problem to be solved, and (iii) considering whether the claimed invention, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, would have been obvious to the skilled person.
guidance: Follow the three-stage problem-and-solution framework to ensure predictable, objective inventive-step assessments.

name: Selection of the closest prior art
description: The closest prior art is that single reference disclosing the combination of features which constitutes the most promising starting point for an obvious development leading to the invention. It should be directed to a similar purpose/effect or at least belong to the same or a closely related technical field.
guidance: In practice, the closest prior art corresponds to a similar use and requires the minimum structural and functional modifications to arrive at the claimed invention. Assess from the skilled person's point of view as of the day before filing/priority date. Take account of what the applicant acknowledges as known unless applicant corrects it.

name: Required contents of utility model application (Rule 1403 list)
description: The application shall contain: (a) request for registration; (b) description (title, technical field, background, summary, brief description of drawings, detailed description); (c) claims; (d) drawings if necessary; (e) abstract; (f) payment of required fees at filing; (g) appointment of agent/representative if applicant not a Philippine resident.
guidance: All listed elements are required for a proper filing.

name: Summary of the utility model (Rule 1403.4)
description: Summary must disclose the utility model as claimed, explaining the technical problem and its technical solution, and state differences versus background art in terms of advantages and benefits.

name: Detailed description requirements (Rule 1403.6)
description: Detailed description must completely specify the manner of making and using the utility model to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to understand and practice it; set forth the precise and exact utility model as claimed; distinguish it from relevant prior art; and indicate the technical problem solved.
guidance: Provisions for detailed description in Part 4 Rules 405-409 of Patent Regulations apply mutatis mutandis.

name: Abstract requirements and length (Rule 1403.7)
description: Abstract must be on a separate sheet with heading and title, consist of a concise summary of disclosure contained in description, claims, and drawings preferably not more than 150 words, drafted to clearly convey technical problem, gist of solution, and principal use(s).
guidance: Abstract serves merely as technical information; preferably disclose scope to serve as efficient search basis.

name: Claim drafting requirements (Rule 1403.9)
description: Claims must define the subject matter sought, be clear and concise, and fully supported by the description. For improvements, claims should specifically point out and distinctly claim the improvement with a preamble indicating necessary prior art features.
guidance: Claim requirements in Part 4 Rules 416(a),(c),(d),(e) and 417 apply mutatis mutandis.

name: Filing date requisites for utility model (Rule 1406)
description: Filing date is the date Office received these elements in English or Filipino: (a) request indicating utility model registration; (b) abstract; (c) description; (d) at least one claim; (e) drawings if necessary; (f) payment of required fees at filing; (g) appointment of agent if applicant not Philippines resident.

name: Unity of utility model (Rule 1409)
description: Only one independent genus or generic claim permissible in a utility model application; specific variations may be claimed in a reasonable number of dependent claims provided they fall under a single statutory class and single general innovative concept and within scope of generic claim.

name: Claim form and limit for industrial designs (Rule 1506.4)
description: Claim shall be in formal terms of the ornamental design for the article, using phrases like '(specifying name) substantially as shown and described' or '(specifying name) substantially as shown'. More than one claim is neither required nor permitted.

name: Amendment of the Claims, the Description, the Drawings and the Abstract
description: Conditions and procedures for amending claims, specification, drawings and abstract during prosecution (heading: 'Amendment of the Claims, the Description, the Drawings and the Abstract').

name: Four-step test for excluded subject matter / technical character
description: One approach consists in applying the following four steps: 1. Properly construe the claim; 2. Identify the actual contribution made by the invention; 3. Determine whether the actual contribution falls solely within the excluded subject matter or not 'as such'; and 4. Determine whether the actual or alleged contribution is actually technical in nature ('Technical contribution').
guidance: If it passes the test for having technical character, the examiner then proceeds to the examination of other substantive aspects, such as novelty and inventive step. The examiner must objectively investigate the contribution actually made and is not bound to accept the contribution claimed by the applicant.

name: Plants, animals and 'essentially biological processes' exclusion
description: Plant and animal varieties are excluded from patentability in AMS, but transgenic plants and genetically modified animals (except in some jurisdictions) and methods of making them may be patentable.
guidance: Whether a process is 'essentially biological' depends on degree of technical intervention by man; significant technical intervention that determines/controls the result means the process is not excluded. Product claims for plant/animal varieties cannot be allowed even if produced by microbiological process.

name: Evaluation criteria for unity of invention
description: The examiner assesses unity by determining whether two or more inventions in the claims have the same or corresponding special technical features determined from the claims, description, drawings and common general knowledge as of the filing date.
guidance: 'Same' or 'corresponding' means special technical features achieve the same technical effect or solve the same technical problem; correspondence may be in alternative solutions or interrelated features (e.g., interaction between plug and socket). If inventions share such a feature they fulfill unity requirements; examples provided (spring vs rubber block both achieving resilience).

name: No lack of unity between independent claim and its dependent claims/juxtaposition
description: Lack of unity does not arise if one claim contains a number of individual features which merely present a juxtaposition and do not present a technical interrelationship; by definition no lack of unity exists between an independent claim and its dependent claims.
guidance: Objection for lack of unity should not be raised on narrow, literal or academic grounds; there should be a broad, practical consideration of interdependence in relation to the state of the art, and benefit of doubt afforded to the applicant.

name: Actions and remedies when lack of unity is found (appeal/options)
description: If examiner determines application lacks unity, they inform applicant and describe inventions not deemed subject of examination and reasons; claimed subject-matter is divided into separate inventions/groups.
guidance: Applicant should be given five options: appeal against examiner's decision or file counter statement at patent office; amend the claims; delete the claims said to be directed to other invention(s); file divisional application(s); abandon/withdraw the application. Appeal rights and procedures vary by AMS; in some countries certain rejections cannot be appealed but counter-arguments may be submitted.

name: Requirement: clarity and conciseness of abstract, claims, description, drawings
description: All AMS require the abstract, claims, description, and drawings, if any, of a patent application to be clear and concise. If unclear such that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability, examination may be restricted to claims/parts sufficiently clear.
guidance: Where an opinion cannot be established on a claim the examiner may issue an objection for lack of clarity. Issues of clarity should be raised separately from novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability. The clarity of claims is of utmost importance in formulating an opinion on novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability.

name: PCT claim requirements
description: The PCT Guidelines require that the claims must: (i) 'define the matter for which protection is sought'; (ii) 'be clear and concise'; and (iii) 'be fully supported by the description.'
guidance: Requirement that claims be clear applies to individual claims and to the claims as a whole.

name: Form and content of claims (technical features; two-part form; reliance on description)
description: Claims must be drafted in terms of the 'technical features of the invention.' The two-part form should be used 'whenever appropriate.' The claims must not, with respect to technical features, rely on references to the description or drawings 'except where absolutely necessary.'
guidance: Claims and description may contain chemical or mathematical formulae but not drawings. Any claim may contain tables 'if the subject matter of the claim makes the use of tables desirable' — examiners should not object to convenient use of tables.

name: Kinds of claims; independent and dependent claims
description: Two basic kinds of claim: claims to a physical entity (product, apparatus) and claims to an activity (process, use). All applications will contain one or more independent main claims directed to essential features of the invention. Dependent claims concern specific forms and must include essential features of at least one independent claim.
guidance: PCT ISPE GL sections apply mutatis mutandis; see other sections for product-by-process, means-plus-function, product/apparatus limitations in process claims, and inconsistencies between claims and description.

name: Interpretation of claims (PSIA standard and transition phrases)
description: Claims should be read giving words the ordinary meaning and scope as attributed by a person skilled in the relevant art (PSIA), unless description explicitly gives special meaning. A claim to a substance/composition for a particular use should be construed as meaning a substance/composition suitable for the stated use.
guidance: In evaluating novelty/inventive step, examiner should consider transition phrase used ('consisting of', 'comprising', 'characterized by', 'consisting essentially of') as it affects subject-matter to be searched. Means-plus-function claims, product-by-process claims, and product/apparatus limitations in process claims have specific guidance (PCT ISPE GL references).

name: Conditions for claim clarity (PSIA can determine boundaries; breadth vs clarity)
description: The meaning of terms of a claim must be clear for a PSIA from the claim wording alone. Clarity must be analysed in light of application disclosure, teachings of prior art, and PSIA interpretation at time of invention. If PSIA can determine boundaries with reasonable degree of certainty, claim complies.
guidance: Breadth is not equivalent to lack of clarity. Independent claims should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention, except insofar as implied by generic terms. The clarity requirement applies to individual claims and the set of claims irrespective of claim type.

name: Process claims producing a product; internal consistency
description: If a claim relates to a process for producing the product of the invention, the process as claimed should be one which, when carried out in a manner reasonable to a PSIA, necessarily results in that particular product; otherwise there is internal inconsistency and lack of clarity.
guidance: For product claims where invention lies in modifying a well-known product, it suffices that the claim clearly identifies the product and specifies what is modified and how. Similar considerations apply to apparatus claims.

name: Terms likely to cause lack of clarity
description: The following terms, when used in claims/descriptions, may be regarded as ambiguous, inadequate, unclear or too broad and lead to lack of clarity: indefinite/relative words (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong'); terms of approximation (e.g., 'about', 'approximately'); ambiguous adverbs/expressions ('preferably', 'more preferably', 'in particular', 'substantially', 'mostly', 'similarly', 'for example', 'such as'); references ('as described in part ...'); trademarks/trade names/proper names; multiple outcomes (e.g., 'and/or').
guidance: More generally, any vague or equivocal wording leaving doubt as to the scope of a feature should be objected to for lack of clarity.

name: Contractor appeals of exception determinations (§401.4)
description: A contractor has the right to administrative review of a determination to use an exception (§401.3(a)(1)–(4)) if it believes the determination is contrary to chapter policies or an abuse of discretion. The appeal procedure and timelines are specified in §401.4.
guidance: Key procedures/timelines: • Contractor must give written notice within 30 working days of receiving the determination (or longer if agency regulation permits). • Appeal decided by agency head or designee above originator. • If genuine dispute over material facts, fact-finding is to be undertaken (informal as practicable; opportunities to appear with counsel, submit evidence, witnesses; transcribed record available at cost unless waived). • Fact-finding should be completed within 45 working days of agency receipt of written notice. • Agency decision based on facts found and arguments; after fact-finding the decision due within 30 working days, or within 45 working days if no fact-finding. • Contractor may petition U.S. Claims Court within 60 days after determination.

name: Corresponding structure/material/acts requirement
description: A means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must have corresponding structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification that perform the recited function; where the specification discloses such corresponding structure the claim may be definite under 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
guidance: If one skilled in the art would recognize the structure for performing the function (e.g., a general/special purpose computer for performing complex computations), the disclosure may suffice. If not, applicant must amend the specification to include the relevant portions of any incorporated-by-reference material that correspond to the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation (37 CFR 1.57(c)(3)). Applicant should include only the relevant portions, not entire referenced documents. See In re Mott; Intel; Atmel; B. Braun; Medical Instrumentation & Diagnostic Corp. examples.

name: Amend specification when corresponding structure not identifiable
description: If one skilled in the art would not be able to identify the structure, material or acts from the specification to perform the recited function, the applicant will be required to amend the specification to contain the material incorporated by reference, including a clear link or associated structure, material or acts to the function recited in the claim.
guidance: Do not require inserting entire referenced document; include only relevant portions corresponding to the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation. See 37 CFR 1.57(c)(3) and Atmel guidance.

name: Means-plus-function limitations must be analyzed for written description/enablement
description: A means- (or step-) plus-function limitation that is indefinite for lack of disclosed corresponding structure may also lack adequate written description and/or enablement to support the full scope of the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph).
guidance: Functional genus claims must show the applicant invented species sufficient to support the claimed functionally-defined genus; otherwise written description/enablement rejections may be appropriate. See Ariad (en banc) discussion.

name: Consider all parts of the original disclosure for 112(a) support
description: When assessing whether 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) support exists for a limitation, the examiner must consider the original disclosure in the summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, drawings, and other original application material.
guidance: Cited authorities: In re Mott; In re Anderson; Hill-Rom v. Kinetic Concepts; In re Armbruster; Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger. Drawings and abstracts can supply support.

name: Claims that cannot invoke 112(f) are not limited to disclosed structure
description: If a claim element cannot properly invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), it is not limited to the structure, material or act disclosed in the specification that performs the claimed function and will cover all means of performing the claimed function.
guidance: Single means claims that therefore cover every conceivable means for achieving the stated result risk non-enablement and can be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). See In re Hyatt.

name: Interpret multiple functional limitations as separate elements
description: When a claim recites multiple functions (common in computer-implemented inventions), each separately recited function should be interpreted as a separate element subject to treatment under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) if appropriate.
guidance: A generic placeholder (e.g., 'system configured to: extract...; compare...') does not avoid invoking 112(f); treat each function as a separate section 112(f) limitation as appropriate. Example demonstrates breaking 'system configured to' into two separate limitations.

name: Single means claim identification and risk
description: A single means claim recites a means-plus-function limitation as the only limitation of a claim; 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies only to 'an element in a claim for a combination' so single means claims may fail to be treated as a combination and risk non-enablement or overbreadth.
guidance: Hyatt held single means claims covering every conceivable means are nonenabling for the claimed scope. Examiner should identify when a claim is a 'single means' claim and consider 112(a) rejection.

name: Ensure prosecution record clearly states 112(f) interpretation
description: When an examiner interprets a claim limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the Office action should specify that the examiner has done so and explain reasons; if non-standard terms (other than 'means'/'step') are treated as invoking 112(f), the reasons should be clearly stated.
guidance: Office action can state that a claim limitation is functional language coupled to a generic placeholder (e.g., 'module for') that does not connote structure and therefore invokes 112(f). If corresponding structure is determined, the Office action may specify it. Establish rebuttable presumptions on the record and explain any rebuttals.

name: Presumptions regarding use/absence of 'means' or 'step'
description: Two rebuttable presumptions: (1) Using 'means' or 'step' creates a presumption the claim element is to be treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f); (2) Absence of 'means' or 'step' creates a presumption the element is not to be treated under 112(f).
guidance: The first presumption is rebutted when 'means'/'step' is not modified by function or when the function is recited with sufficient structure/material within the claim. The second is rebutted when the claim element recites function but fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or material. See MPEP § 706.03 for form paragraphs.

name: Attempt to identify corresponding structure to facilitate prior art search
description: If the corresponding structure for the claimed function is not clearly identifiable in the specification, the Office action should nevertheless attempt to identify the structure most closely associated with the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation to facilitate a prior art search.
guidance: This is especially important where multiple disclosed implementations might support the limitation and there may be confusion about which implementation is relied upon. See subsection II.B.

name: When allowing a claim treated under 112(f), indicate it in reasons for allowance
description: If allowing a claim that was treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the examiner should indicate that the claim was interpreted under 112(f) or pre-AIA sixth paragraph in the reasons for allowance, and clarify the associated structure if not previously made of record.
guidance: This provides public notice of the claim construction used by the examiner during prosecution.

name: Prior art application to means-plus-function requires identical function and equivalence analysis
description: Application of a prior art reference to a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation requires that the prior art element perform the identical function specified in the claim, and the examiner bears the initial burden of showing the prior art structure or step is the same as or equivalent to the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification.
guidance: If prior art teaches identity of function only, examiner must show a 'sound basis for believing' the prior art structure/acts could perform the claimed function (In re Spada). See MPEP § 2114 for inherency standards.

name: Two-step claim construction for means-plus-function
description: Constructing a means-plus-function limitation involves two steps: (1) define the particular function of the claim limitation (the functional boundaries contained in the claim language), and (2) look to the specification/prosecution history for the corresponding structure that performs that function and is clearly linked or associated to it.
guidance: Cases: Budde; Cardiac Pacemakers; Golight; B. Braun; Elekta. The corresponding structure must be clearly linked/associated in spec or prosecution history.

name: Prima facie case of equivalence – examiner burden and required explanation
description: If the examiner finds (A) the prior art element performs the claimed function, (B) is not excluded by any explicit definition in the specification for an equivalent, and (C) is an equivalent of the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation, the examiner should provide an explanation and rationale in the Office action for why the prior art element is an equivalent.
guidance: If a prima facie case of equivalence is made, the examiner should explain why and identify supporting factors/case law (e.g., In re Bond).

name: If nonequivalence not shown, examiner must still consider obviousness
description: Even where applicant shows that a prior art element is not equivalent to the structure/material/acts described in the specification, the examiner must still perform a 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) analysis to determine if the claimed means- (or step-) plus-function is obvious from the prior art.
guidance: A finding of nonequivalence prevents anticipation but does not prevent an obviousness rejection. Examiner may apply 102/103 rejections where appropriate, and may rely on alternative grounds when prior art elements differ but together render the claim obvious.

name: Specification can narrow or broaden scope of equivalents
description: Whether a means-plus-function limitation is limited to particular structures/materials/acts or covers any and all structures performing the claimed function depends on how the specification treats equivalents: the spec may limit the claim to disclosed embodiments or allow coverage of equivalents.
guidance: If only one embodiment is described, corresponding structure may be limited to that embodiment and equivalents (NOMOS); conversely, allowing equivalents too broadly can render the claim so broad as to encompass any means for performing the function (In re Meyer; In re Abele; In re Walter). Examiner must interpret scope case-by-case.

name: Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) consistent with the specification
description: During examination a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: BRI reduces the chance an issued claim will be interpreted more broadly than justified; focus is what is reasonable from the perspective of one of ordinary skill. Plain meaning is used unless inconsistent with the specification. Sources for meaning include claim words, specification, drawings, and prior art, but the specification is the best source. Applicant may be their own lexicographer if a special meaning is clearly set forth in the specification. See cited Federal Circuit precedent (Yamamoto, Zletz, Buszard).

name: Plain meaning of claim terms (ordinary and customary meaning)
description: Words of the claim must be given their plain meaning — the ordinary and customary meaning given by those of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention — unless inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: Ordinary use may be evidenced by the claims, specification, drawings, and prior art. The specification serving as a glossary gives greatest clarity. A presumption of plain meaning may be rebutted by a clear and intentional special definition in the specification as filed.

name: Determine whether each claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA 112 sixth paragraph)
description: Examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means‑plus‑function) or pre‑AIA sixth paragraph.
guidance: If a limitation invokes 112(f)/sixth paragraph, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof. See MPEP § 2181 and In re Donaldson and related authorities for more on means/step‑plus‑function analysis.

name: Definiteness standard: skilled artisan must understand what is claimed in light of the specification
description: A decision on indefiniteness requires determining whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.
guidance: During prosecution, applicants have the opportunity and duty to amend ambiguous claims. If, under BRI and in view of the specification, a person of ordinary skill would read a claim with more than one reasonable interpretation, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected. Examiners should analyze claim terms from the perspective of those skilled in the relevant art.

name: Claims during examination are construed differently than issued claims in court
description: The Office construes claims during examination by applying the BRI consistent with the specification; courts construe patented claims differently, using the prosecution record and without BRI.
guidance: Patented claims in court are not given BRI and must inform those skilled in the art of scope with reasonable certainty (Nautilus). The PTO applies a lower threshold for ambiguity during prosecution because claims can be amended to sharpen clarity; this may result in a lower threshold for indefiniteness than in court. Examiners should therefore apply BRI to identify ambiguities that can be corrected during prosecution.

name: Consider the claim as a whole and interaction of limitations
description: In reviewing claims for compliance with 112(b), the examiner must consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope.
guidance: The totality of limitations and their interactions must be considered to ascertain the inventor’s contribution and whether the claim serves its notice function (see Larsen). Do not read limitations into claims from preferred embodiments absent a clear disclaimer.

name: Office action must provide sufficient explanation to permit a meaningful applicant response
description: Because an indefiniteness rejection requires applicant to explain why the language is not indefinite or to amend the claim, the Office action should provide enough information for the applicant to prepare a meaningful response.
guidance: Point out the specific term or phrase, explain in detail why it renders the metes and bounds unclear, and, when practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness issues may be resolved. Failure to adequately respond to a prima facie case may allow the examiner to make the rejection final. See MPEP § 707.07(d).

name: Examiners encouraged to suggest claim language but not insist on preferences
description: Examiners may suggest claim language to improve clarity or precision, but should not insist on examiner’s own linguistic preferences if applicant's language satisfies statutory requirement.
guidance: Allow latitude in the manner of expression so long as 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is satisfied. Suggest improvements but do not force a particular phrasing when alternate phrasing meets the requirement.

name: Applicants may resolve indefiniteness by amending claims or providing persuasive explanation/evidence
description: In response to an indefiniteness rejection, the applicant may amend the claim or provide a persuasive explanation (with evidence as necessary) that a person of ordinary skill would not consider the language unclear.
guidance: In some cases the applicant may need to provide a separate definition (e.g., art‑recognized dictionary) to show how the ordinarily‑skilled artisan would understand the claim language. If the examiner is persuaded, the examiner should indicate the previous rejection is withdrawn and explain what prompted the change (referencing applicant’s remarks where appropriate) to clarify the prosecution record.

name: No per se rules; indefiniteness examples are fact specific
description: Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections for indefiniteness; examples set forth in MPEP are fact specific and should not be applied as per se rules.
guidance: MPEP § 2173.05 lists numerous rationales that may support an indefiniteness rejection (e.g., functional claim limitations, relative terminology/terms of degree, lack of antecedent basis). Use the facts of the case to support the rejection; do not adopt blanket categorical rules.

name: When more information is necessary, consider a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105
description: If the examiner determines more information is necessary to ascertain the meaning of a claim term, a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 may be appropriate.
guidance: See MPEP § 704.10 regarding requirements for information. Use procedural tools when needed to clarify claim meaning rather than defaulting to a rejection without giving applicant opportunity to supply information.

name: Indefiniteness arises if claim, under BRI, has more than one reasonable interpretation
description: If the language of a claim, given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, is such that a person of ordinary skill in the relevant art would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is appropriate.
guidance: Examiners should distinguish between breadth (acceptable) and ambiguity (not acceptable). Provide a clear rationale showing the multiple reasonable interpretations and why that creates uncertainty about the metes and bounds of the claimed subject matter.

name: Determination of whether a 'product' is protected by the patent (claims test / Teva clarification)
description: Case law (C-322/10 and C-422/10) indicated that the 'product' needs to be 'specified [or identified] in the wording of the claims'. The Teva decision (2018) clarified that for a product composed of several active ingredients, Article 3(a) requires that 'even if the combination of active ingredients ... is not expressly mentioned in the claims of the basic patent, those claims relate necessarily and specifically to that combination.'
guidance: Whether a product is 'protected by a patent' is a key, often controversial factual/legal inquiry—analysis of claim scope and whether claims necessarily and specifically relate to the product (including combinations) is required.

name: Citing a deleted claim (antecedent corrections)
description: Where a deleted claim is cited and only one antecedent claim exists, the citation may be amended ex‑officio to point to the remaining antecedent (examples provided converting references to the correct antecedent).
guidance: Adjust antecedent citations to the obvious remaining claim when citation would otherwise cite a deleted claim.

name: Citing claims where some cited claims were deleted
description: Where claims that have not been deleted are cited in combination with deleted claims, citations may be amended ex‑officio to remove references to deleted claims (example: 'claim 1 or claim 2' where claim 2 is deleted → 'claim 1').
guidance: Make citation language coherent and reflect only existing claims.

name: Where dependent claim subject matter differs from citing claim
description: If a dependent claim's subject matter differs from that of the claiming (antecedent) claim, the dependent language may be amended ex‑officio to restore consistent claim dependency (example converting a method dependency incorrectly referring to an apparatus into an apparatus dependency).
guidance: Ensure dependent claims properly refer to compatible claim types (e.g., apparatus vs method).

name: Obvious wrong claim citation (correct target claim)
description: Where it is obvious that a particular claim was cited incorrectly, examiner may correct to the obvious cited claim (example changing which claim is cited when context makes intent clear).
guidance: Only when the intended citation is obvious from the disclosure may it be fixed.

name: Cited claims not indicated as alternatives (correct conjunctions)
description: Correct non‑alternative citations to alternative form (examples: 'according to claims 1 and 2' → 'according to claim 1 or 2'; other corrections to indicate alternative claims properly).
guidance: Use precise alternative language (or, any one of) when claims are meant as alternatives.

name: Do not change claim scope by ex-officio amendment
description: Care should be taken that the scope of the claims should not be changed by ex‑officio amendment; if there is any possibility that terms may be construed differently, ex‑officio amendment should not be made.
guidance: When in doubt about claim scope effects, refrain from ex‑officio changes.

name: Principle: do not amend if applicant's intention is unclear
description: Even if obviously wrong, if the applicant’s intention is not clearly understood from specification and written arguments, ex‑officio amendment is not permitted (example: ambiguous antecedent claim among plural antecedents).
guidance: Require clear evidence of applicant intent before correcting ambiguous matters.

name: Contents of preliminary examination interview
description: Any matter can be discussed: applicant explains technical content and differences with prior art; examiner explains results of preliminary review on patentability and deficiencies; parties discuss how to amend claims to resolve grounds for rejection and secure appropriate scope.
guidance: Interview aims to facilitate amendment and understanding; avoid using interview as venue for matters outside scope (progress queries etc.).

name: Specific requirements to decide preliminary examination
description: Requirements include: (①) application having high level of difficulty; (②) application decided for expedited examination (including PPH cases where examiner decides to expedite); (③) request filed within timing limits; (④) proper interview participants (applicant, agent, inventor, authorized person); (⑤) desired interview dates within 3–6 weeks; (⑥) absence of inappropriate reasons (e.g., too broad claim scope for interview).
guidance: All requirements should be satisfied, but examiner may suggest corrections or accept ex‑officio if possible after consultation.

name: Examiner preparation for interview
description: Before interview, examiner shall read the claimed invention, review patentability requirements and specification deficiencies comprehensively to an extent comparable to substantive examination, prepare documents, prior art search results, Minutes and Additional paper for the minutes.
guidance: State preview results in minutes to explain to applicant; ensure examiner is ready to explain grounds and suggestions clearly.

name: Definitions (Invention, Alleged Invention, Meaning of a Document etc.)
description: Authoritative definitions used during examination to interpret claims and cited documents (section 5.6.1.3).
guidance: Guides construction of terms such as 'invention' and 'document' when assessing patentability.

name: Omnibus Claims – References to the Description or Drawings
description: Treatment and validity of omnibus claims that refer to the description or drawings (section 5.6.3.3).
guidance: Examines the acceptability and limits of omnibus-style claim drafting.

name: Determining Novelty
description: Approach to assessing novelty of claimed subject-matter (section 5.6.5.1).
guidance: Includes consideration of whole-of-contents objections and examples.

name: Inventive Step Issues Specific to Chemical Compositions
description: Particular considerations for inventive step when chemical compositions or related claims are involved (section 5.6.6.6).
guidance: Examples specific to chemistry and how tests may be applied differently.

name: Claims are Clear and Succinct
description: Requirement that claims be clear and succinct as part of s40 and claim construction (section 5.6.7.1).
guidance: Examiner must object where claims are ambiguous, vague, or overly prolix.

name: Support for the Claims – s40(3)
description: Requirement that the specification provides support for the claims under s40(3) (section 5.6.7.3).
guidance: Guides examiners in determining whether claim scope is fairly based on the description.

name: Difference Between 'Clear and Complete Disclosure' and 'Support'
description: Distinction between enablement (clear and complete disclosure) and claim support/fair basis (section 5.6.7.4).
guidance: Explains different legal questions and tests for these two requirements.

name: Each cited publication must indicate relevant parts and claim linkage
description: Kunkin julkaisun kohdalla eritellään myös ne julkaisun kohdat, jotka ovat relevantteja patentoitavuuden arvioinnin kannalta. Viitejulkaisut esitetään WIPOn standardin ST.14 mukaisesti. Alkuperäinen julkaisu esitetään aina kun mahdollista, minkä lisäksi voidaan esittää tiivistelmä tai alkuperäisen julkaisun käännös.
guidance: For each cited document state the claim number(s) it relates to and list the specific passages or figures that are relevant. Provide original source where possible; if not available present abstract or translation; include category code(s) and mark family relations (&) when applicable.

name: Novelty assessment: publications compared individually
description: Kutakin julkaisua verrataan yksitellen tutkittavaan hakemukseen. Erillisiä julkaisuja ei uutuuden arvioinnissa käsitellä yhdessä, ellei julkaisu eksplisiittisesti viittaa toiseen julkaisuun ja tuo sen opetukset esiin julkaisunsa julkaisupäivänä.
guidance: A claim lacks novelty only if all features recited (as read as a whole, combining preamble and characterising portion) are disclosed in a single document either explicitly or implicitly. Do not combine distinct documents to attack novelty except when one document explicitly incorporates or refers to another and that other was publicly available at that time.

name: Novelty requires technical features to be present
description: Vaatimukselta puuttuu uutuus, ellei ainakin yksi sen tunnetusta tekniikasta erottavista piirteistä ole tekninen. Tekninen piirre on sellainen piirre, joka patenttivaatimuksen kontekstissa määrittää teknistä ratkaisua tekniseen ongelmaan. Teknisen piirteen mahdollinen osallistuminen teknisen ongelman ratkaisuun voidaan vaihtoehtoisesti käsitellä arvioitaessa olennaisen eron olemassaoloa.
guidance: When assessing novelty, determine whether each distinguishing feature is ‘technical’ in the claim context and whether it is disclosed explicitly or can be unambiguously and certainly implied by the prior publication. Non-technical features do not normally negate novelty in themselves.

name: Reasons for leaving claims unsearched
description: Tutkimusraportin liitteissä ilmoitetaan patenttilain 1 §:n, 8 §:n ja/tai 10 §:n nojalla tutkimatta jätettyjen patenttivaatimusten numerot ja yksilöity perustelu tutkimatta jättämiseen. Tutkimatta jättämisen syitä voivat olla: vaatimukset eivät ole hyväksyttävissä patenttilain 1 §:n nojalla; vaatimukset ovat liian laajat, epäselvät tai monimutkaiset (PatL 8 §); vaatimukset ovat epäyhtenäiset (PatL 10 §).
guidance: When claims are left unsearched, the report must identify exactly which claims were not searched and provide statutory reasons. These grounds include unpatentable subject-matter, lack of clarity/overbreadth/complexity, or lack of unity between claims.

name: Claim construction: ordinary meaning in light of the specification and prosecution history
description: Interpret claim terms by looking to their ordinary meaning in light of the specification and prosecution history (Phillips v. AWH Corp.).
guidance: The Board may construe claims sua sponte when a dispute arises, provided it gives the parties notice and an opportunity to respond. Do not import limitations into claims that are not present in the claim language; consider specification and prosecution history to avoid constructions that exclude disclosed examples.

name: Do not import unclaimed limitations absent support
description: Claims should not be construed to add limitations that are simply not there; the claim language controls and the specification cannot be used to import limitations absent a clear basis.
guidance: Even if dependent claims or specification discuss a display relationship, the plain claim language controls. Rejection of constructions that would exclude examples disclosed in the specification is improper (see Verizon Servs. Corp. v. Vonage).

name: Petition particularity and claim-by-claim proof (37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4); 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3))
description: An IPR petition must identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim and must address claim limitations with sufficient specificity.
guidance: Petitioners cannot 'lump' together claims without addressing limitations unique to a challenged claim. The petitioner bears the burden to present a clear argument; the Board should not be required to 'decode' the petition to locate arguments. Failure to address a unique limitation may render the petition deficient as to that claim.

name: Abuse-of-discretion standard for Board application of its regulations
description: Board decisions applying its own procedural regulations (e.g., deciding a petition is deficient under 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4)) are reviewed for abuse of discretion.
guidance: An abuse of discretion may be found if the Board's decision rests on a legally erroneous interpretation of claim language or misapplies its regulations; but deference is given to the Board's procedural judgments otherwise.

name: Forfeiture of arguments not presented to the Board
description: Arguments not raised to the Board are forfeited on appeal and generally may not be considered for the first time in the appellate proceedings.
guidance: Post-hoc attempts on appeal to raise additional arguments or to remedy petition defects will be rejected (Netflix; Intell. Bio-Sys. / Illumina guidance). Petitioners should present all claim-specific arguments before the Board.

name: Presumption that different claim terms connote different meanings (but not absolute)
description: There is a general presumption that the use of different terms or phrases in separate claims denotes different meanings.
guidance: This presumption is rebuttable: different terms may be construed to cover the same subject matter where the context shows the patentee used different words to express similar concepts (Edwards Lifesciences; Nystrom; Ohio Willow Wood). The patentee must explain how an additional limitation changes the invalidity analysis.

name: When slightly different claim language does not create a new invalidity issue
description: Where claims 'use slightly different language to describe substantially the same invention,' the mere use of different words does not create a new issue of invalidity.
guidance: Courts will treat substantially similar claim limitations as the same for invalidity analysis unless the patentee shows the additional words materially change the claim scope or analysis (Innova/Pure Water, Soverain Software).

name: Motivation-to-combine and reliance on prior-art teachings
description: A petitioner must show why an ordinarily skilled artisan would be motivated to combine the teachings of the prior art references to reach the claimed invention.
guidance: Such motivation can be supported by express teachings in the references or expert testimony tying the references together; the petition should explain how combination addresses claim limitations (e.g., using Geva to supply intensity teachings in combination with Bird/Ishii).

name: Prosecution-history amendments do not automatically import additional limitations
description: An amendment made during prosecution (e.g., adding a limitation such as 'outside the input area') does not necessarily establish relationships (such as coextensiveness with a display) unless the prosecution history clearly supports such a narrowing.
guidance: Claims must be interpreted primarily from their language; prosecution history is relevant but courts will not read into claims limitations that the amendment record does not demonstrate.

name: Petition incorporation-by-reference limits
description: Incorporation by reference to other parts of the petition is permissible but does not relieve the petitioner of the obligation to present a clear, claim-specific showing.
guidance: Even if a petitioner incorporates arguments made elsewhere in the petition, any limitation unique to a claim must still be addressed in a way that the Board can readily identify; mere placement of the claim in a grouped discussion is insufficient if the unique limitation is not substantively argued.

name: Fallacies of Generalization (inductive fallacies from correct facts)
description: Cases where the facts are correct but the generalization drawn from them is not warranted by those facts.
guidance: Avoid overgeneralization; assess whether the available instances legitimately support the breadth of the claimed general proposition.

name: Substantial New Question of Patentability (SNQ) — threshold
description: The presence or absence of 'a substantial new question of patentability' determines whether or not reexamination is ordered. If prior art patents and printed publications raise a substantial question of patentability of at least one claim, then a substantial new question of patentability is present, unless the same question has already been decided by a final holding of invalidity or by the Office in a previous examination or pending reexamination.
guidance: SNQ is not defined in the statute and is developed case-by-case. A prior art patent or printed publication raises an SNQ where there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable examiner would consider it important in deciding patentability. It is not necessary that a 'prima facie' case of unpatentability exist; SNQ may exist even if the examiner would not necessarily reject the claim as anticipated or obvious based on the art.

name: Decision should identify and explain at least one SNQ when granting request
description: If a request is granted, the examiner’s decision must conclude that an SNQ has been raised by identifying all claims/issues, the patents/printed publications relied on, and providing a brief statement of the rationale supporting each new question.
guidance: The examiner must identify at least one SNQ and explain how the cited patents/publications raise such a question. The decision should indicate, insofar as possible, the examiner's initial position on issues identified in the request so that the patent owner can respond.
