In simple cases the examiner may adopt the requester’s reasons. Prior art relied on should be listed on appropriate PTO forms and copies supplied only where not previously supplied. For each SNQ the decision should point out: (A) which prior art adds new teaching as to at least one claim; (B) what that new teaching is; (C) the claims directed to; (D) that the new teaching was not previously considered/addressed in prior examination or final court holding; (F) where relevant, why the reference is available as prior art (date/availability discussion). The decision should not decide claim patentability — only whether SNQ exists.

name: Second or subsequent request for reexamination (multiple requests policy)
description: A second or subsequent request for reexamination should be denied if it raises the same question of patentability as that raised in the pending reexamination proceedings.
guidance: However, a second/subsequent request may raise an SNQ with respect to any new or amended claim proposed under 37 CFR 1.530(d) in the pending reexamination, to permit examination of the entire patent package. Prevents parties from waiting until a certificate issues to challenge amended claims and prevents patent owners from nominally amending all claims to preclude subsequent requests. In aggravated situations, after grant of a second/subsequent request, if it appears the filing was for purposes of harassment and a 37 CFR 1.182 petition by the patent owner is granted, prosecution on the second/subsequent reexamination may be suspended. The second/subsequent request should be determined on its own merits without reference to the pending reexamination.

name: Petition to vacate an order granting reexamination (limitations)
description: A substantive determination to institute reexamination based on an SNQ is not subject to judicial review until a final agency decision in the reexamination proceeding. There is no right to petition or request reconsideration of the SNQ finding after reexamination is granted, except in limited circumstances under 37 CFR 1.181.
guidance: A 37 CFR 1.181 petition may be filed to vacate an ultra vires reexamination order (e.g., order not based on patents/printed publications). Appropriate circumstances to vacate under 1.181(a)(3) include: (A) reexamination order not based on patents/printed publications; (B) all claims of the patent were held invalid by final federal decision after appeals; (C) reexamination ordered for wrong patent; (D) ordered based on duplicate copy of the request; (E) order based wholly on the same question of patentability raised by prior art previously considered in an earlier concluded Office examination. When such a petition is filed by a third party, the third-party requester may file a single submission in opposition, generally within two weeks of service to ensure consideration.

name: Scope of Reference’s Disclosure Which Can Be Used to Reject Claims When the Reference Is a 'Patent' but Not a 'Publication'
description: 2126.02-Scope of Reference’s Disclosure Which Can Be Used to Reject Claims When the Reference Is a “Patent” but Not a “Publication”

name: All Claim Limitations Must Be Considered (obviousness)
description: 2143.03-All Claim Limitations Must Be Considered

name: How to Make and Use the Claimed Invention (enablement)
description: 2164.01(b)-How to Make the Claimed Invention; 2164.01(c)-How to Use the Claimed Invention

name: Two Separate Requirements for Claims Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness)
description: 2171-Two Separate Requirements for Claims Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, Second Paragraph

name: Interpreting the Claims; Determining Whether Claim Language is Definite; Correspondence Between Specification and Claims
description: 2173.01-2173.03 (Interpreting the Claims; Determining Whether Claim Language is Definite; Correspondence Between Specification and Claims)

name: Specific Topics Related to Issues Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b): new terminology, ranges, antecedent basis, functional limitations, alternatives, negative limitations, etc.
description: 2173.05-Specific Topics Related to Issues Under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, Second Paragraph (subitems a through v listing many claim-drafting/definiteness topics)

name: Practice Compact Prosecution (claim drafting/examiner procedure)
description: 2173.06-Practice Compact Prosecution

name: Eligibility is Self-Evident — Examples
description: Examples of claims whose eligibility may be self-evident and thus suitable for streamlined analysis.
guidance: Examples: a complex manufactured industrial product/process with meaningful limitations (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with control system using mathematical relationships); an artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral that does not attempt to tie up the mineral; products with ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with gold contact, plastic chair with wood trim). Such claims do not require full analysis to determine they are not attempting to tie up a judicial exception.

name: Formulating and Supporting Rejections — General Requirements
description: Eligibility rejections must be based on substantive law under 35 U.S.C. §101 as interpreted by judicial precedent; examiners must review the record as a whole and make claim-by-claim evaluations. The rejection must set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility that is clear and specific.
guidance: Examiners should review specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, and any relevant prior art. Each claim should be considered separately because dependent claims may add limitations that change the eligibility outcome. The initial burden is on the examiner to explain why a claim is ineligible so the applicant can respond. If the examiner determines it is more likely than not that the claim fails eligibility criteria, formulate an appropriate rejection under Step 1 and/or Step 2B. See MPEP §§2106.03–2106.06 for substantive law, and MPEP §2106.07(a) for drafting rejections.

name: Step 1 Rejection Requirement (Statutory Categories)
description: When an examiner determines a claim does not fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO), the rejection must explain why the claim does not fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention.
guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation tied to the statutory categories; see MPEP §2106.03 for discussion and guidance on Step 1 analysis.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — Evaluate Integration into a Practical Application
description: For Prong Two, the rejection should identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: The examiner must explain that either 1) there are no additional elements in the claim, or 2) the claim as a whole, looking at additional elements individually and in combination, does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements even if they represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

name: Step 2B — Explain Why Additional Elements Do Not Provide 'Significantly More' (Inventive Concept)
description: The rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: When the examiner concludes certain claim elements recite well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III (i.e., provide appropriate factual or evidentiary support). The explanation should cover both individual elements and their combination and be sufficiently clear and specific to enable applicant response. See MPEP §2106.05 et seq. and MPEP §2106.07(a).

name: Reservation land usability and resource constraints
description: Surveyed acreage and the portion usable for farming (e.g., '102,118.19 acres included; of that balance, 7,448 acres, all but 2,000 is rough and mountainous; 2,500 lie in this valley and about 1,200 cultivated'); timber resources often inaccessible.
guidance: Provide acreage breakdowns, explain geographic limitations (mountainous, rocky, swamp claims), note inaccessibility of timber for lumber manufacture due to lack of roads and cost, and implications for economic viability.

name: Abstract
description: Abstract is a short summary.
guidance: Useful for a quick high-level understanding, but not authoritative for determining claim scope.

name: Representative drawing
description: On the front page is a representative drawing, selected by the examiner.
guidance: The title, abstract, and front page drawing together provide a simple summary but are not the source for determining what the patent actually covers; always consult claims and full disclosure for scope.

name: Drawings (presence, types, and reference numbers)
description: Patents generally include at least one drawing, which are provided to help understand the invention. There may be multiple views, an exploded view to show the individual elements, and drawings of one or more components.
guidance: Drawings are an important part of the disclosure; good disclosures include as many drawings as needed to demonstrate the invention. Each element is distinguished with a reference number which is described in the description—use drawings to understand embodiment structure and element mapping to claims.

name: Description sections (background, summary, list of drawings, detailed description)
description: The description follows and can be quite lengthy. It is usually broken into sections, and those sections vary between authorities. Usually there is a background section, summary of the invention, list of drawings, and detailed description.
guidance: Background often provides general context but little about the invention; focus on the summary and detailed description for embodiments, alternatives, and implementation details that inform claim interpretation and enablement analyses.

name: Reference-number naming / element descriptions
description: The drawings are listed and described, and the little reference numbers that point to each element are named and described in the description.
guidance: Use the mapping between reference numbers and element names to tie drawings to written embodiments and to trace element definitions relevant to claim terms.

name: Claims (scope definition)
description: The claims set forth and define the scope of the exclusive rights – what the patent covers.
guidance: Claims are the authoritative source of legal scope; use claim language for freedom-to-operate, infringement, and scope mapping rather than relying on title/abstract/drawings alone.

name: Caveat: front-page summary not authoritative for scope
description: The title, abstract, and front page drawing together provide a simple summary of the invention, but are not the source for determining what the patent actually covers.
guidance: Always rely on claim language (and supporting description) for determining coverage; use front-page elements only for quick triage and initial understanding.

name: Examiner disclosure on lack of novelty
description: If the ground of the rejection be the absence of novelty in the subject-matter of the application, the examiner must disclose to the applicant all his own information on the subject, citing the best references at his command.
guidance: When references are prior patents, designate each by date and number, patentee's name, and class of the invention; when prior publication, give title, date, page/plate, and place of publication or where a copy may be procured; when the reference is a fact within the knowledge of the examiner or Office, provide as precise data as nature admits and support by affidavit. Explain pertinence of the reference if not obvious, and particularly specify the anticipated Claim relied on.

name: Claims amended in substance are treated as new (date and filing consequences)
description: Claims amended in matters of substance are to be treated as new claims; when an amendment requiring a new oath is filed, the date of the application is changed to that of the new oath and is thereafter regarded as the true date of the amended application.
guidance: This can affect priority, intervening rights, and whether the amendment can antedate cited references; careful drafting and timely oath are critical.

name: Separate applications cannot qualify or support each other
description: Two distinct applications cannot qualify or support each other; each application is regarded as that of an independent inventor and is in no manner affected by any other.
guidance: A later application by the same inventor describing the same invention but claiming it more precisely is not an amendment of the earlier application; the earlier stands unaffected and may be amended independently.

name: Applicant must point out patentable novelty when offering amendment to overcome rejection
description: In offering an amendment to remove grounds of rejection the applicant must point out all the patentable novelty he thinks the case presents in view of the state of the art, and must show how his amendment avoids such references or objections.
guidance: If the examiner produces new references the applicant must address them; arguments should map claim elements to avoid cited art.

name: Prosecution history estoppel and disclaimer considerations
description: Issues and considerations arising from prosecution history estoppel and disclaimer that can affect claim scope and enforcement.

name: Means-plus-function or step-plus-function claims under 35 U.S.C. Section 112, sixth paragraph
description: Treatment and requirements for means-plus-function (or step-plus-function) claim elements under 35 U.S.C. §112, sixth paragraph, including necessary disclosure of structure/acts/ materials corresponding to the claimed function.

name: Completeness of disclosure (support/enablement)
description: Applications should provide sufficient description, examples, and details so the invention can be carried out by a person skilled in the art.
guidance: While explicit '§112' style language is not visible in this chunk, the document emphasizes descriptive completeness (claims supported by specification); lack of enablement or missing essential information can be grounds for rejection.

name: Pleading specificity for conspiracy claims (Twombly/Iqbal)
description: A plaintiff must allege the necessary specifics of a conspiracy claim — i.e., 'who, did what, to whom (or with whom), where, and when.'
guidance: General allegations of 'agreements with RPX, joint defense agreements, NPE insurance, common counsel, meetings, phone calls, emails, and discussions' were held insufficient under Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly. Complaints must identify concrete facts showing the existence of an agreement and each defendant's role; boilerplate or conclusory descriptions will not survive a motion to dismiss.

name: Plead facts supporting a group boycott theory (vs. individual disputes)
description: To state a group boycott claim, plaintiffs must plead how the alleged harm resulted from a concerted group boycott rather than from individual business disputes or tactical negotiation conduct.
guidance: The court rejected allegations that could be explained as 'individual business disputes.' Plaintiffs should plead facts showing coordinated refusal to deal or collective concerted action causing anticompetitive effects, not merely parallel or independent conduct arising from licensing negotiations.

name: Formal deficiencies (enumerated types)
description: Formal deficiencies that may be objected to include: incomplete request or deviation from power of attorney; doubts about whether patent is requested for applicant or company; in multiple applicants cases lacking authorised service person or missing signatures; missing parts of application (claims, description, drawings, abstract); incomplete or missing power of attorney; unclear/uncise title; missing or incomplete designation of inventor.
guidance: These deficiencies may be raised in the examination as to obvious deficiencies if they are evident from the documents. Specific remedies and time limits should be given.

name: Deficiencies of the patent claims and description (grave deficiencies only)
description: Only grave deficiencies regarding contents and structure of patent claims and description are to be notified during examination as to obvious deficiencies; grave deficiencies are those that risk misleading the public at first publication.
guidance: Assessment should be made on the basis of the facts submitted and examiner's technical knowledge without using external material or full substantive searches; novelty and inventive step are not examined at this stage.

name: State of the art (section 3 of the Patent Act)
description: Determine the relevant prior art that defines novelty and inventive step comparisons.
guidance: Search and identify prior art documents (patent and non-patent) relevant to claimed subject matter; non-patent literature handling noted in public inspection section.

name: Inventive step (section 4 of the Patent Act)
description: Examine whether the claimed invention involves an inventive step relative to the state of the art.
guidance: Apply relevant case law and technical assessment; for program-related inventions only technical features contributing to a solution of a specific technical problem count toward inventive step (see three-stage approach).

name: Patent claims and patent category (drafting and categorisation)
description: Examine claims for clarity, support by the description, proper categorisation (e.g., device, method), and allowable scope.
guidance: Claims must meet statutory requirements; mark up for clarity and consistency with description; grave deficiencies only objected during obvious-deficiencies stage, but substantive claim defects addressed in substantive examination.

name: Preparation of the grant of the patent applied for — filing and editing of documents
description: Procedures for filing documents ready for grant and editing official documents prior to grant (e.g., finalising description, claims, drawings).
guidance: Ensure hand-over of corrected, printable documents; prepare the specification for publication and grant according to formatting, language, and content rules.

name: Exceptions to patentability for program-related inventions (section 1(3),(4))
description: Evaluate whether claimed subject-matter is excluded as mathematical method, method for doing business, or presentation of information, and whether claimed instructions solve a specific technical problem.
guidance: Non-technical instructions that merely collect/store/analyse data are relevant only to the extent they influence a technical solution. Visual/presentation features that account for human perception may contribute to solving a technical problem.

name: Principle, method, or process must be carried into practice by tangible means
description: A principle, method, or process must be carried into practice by tangible means; courts construe broad claims to abstract principles as limited to the mechanical means described.
guidance: Judicial decisions (e.g. construction of Jones's suspension claim) limit claims to the way the principle is 'carried into effect by the mechanical means before described.' Legislative clarity is desirable. Mere statement of a principle without practical means may not be patentable.

name: Different patents for same principle allowed if mechanical means differ
description: Several persons may have several patents founded on the same principle, if they use different mechanical contrivances to effect the object.
guidance: Hullett v. Hague: same objective (evaporation at low temperature) achieved using the same general idea (heated/forced air) but by different apparatus (perforated coil vs other means) — courts treated the patents as distinct because the means were different. Drafters should claim and describe the specific apparatus/means.

name: Claim drafting caution — do not claim an unconstrained universal principle
description: Where a specification's language appears to claim a principle in the abstract, courts may construe it as a claim only to the principle as carried into effect by the described mechanical means.
guidance: Practical effect: draft claims to practical embodiments and avoid overbroad language that purports to monopolize an abstract principle; courts will narrow interpretation to described means, and competing inventors may obtain patents for alternative means achieving the same principle.

name: Bracket insertion requirements in form paragraphs
description: In specified form paragraphs, examiner must insert appropriate bracketed items (e.g., in bracket 3, insert --assignee--, --applicant--, or --joint inventor--; in bracket 1 insert claim numbers; in bracket 2 insert application number; in bracket 4 insert explanation of obviousness).
guidance: Follow the specific bracket instructions for each form paragraph (numeration varies by paragraph); see corresponding Examiner Notes for examples and where to draw explanations (e.g., MPEP §2144 for obviousness explanations).

name: Nonstatutory double patenting rejection when not patentably distinct
description: Any claims in the instant application that are directed to subject matter that is not patentably distinct from an invention claimed in the reference should be rejected (or provisionally rejected if the reference has not yet issued as a patent) on the grounds of nonstatutory double patenting using form paragraph 8.33 and at least one of form paragraphs 8.34 - 8.39.
guidance: If the claimed invention is not patentably distinct, make appropriate nonstatutory double patenting rejections and consider requirements for terminal disclaimers or other remedies.

name: §121 protection when restriction requirement in parent application
description: When a claimed invention that was the subject of a restriction requirement is presented in a divisional application, a nonstatutory double patenting rejection cannot be applied to that claimed invention unless the restriction requirement was withdrawn.
guidance: Section 121 shields those withdrawn claims in a later divisional application against rejection over a patent that issues from the original application; if the restriction requirement does not clearly set forth the line of demarcation, consonance may be lacking and §121 protection may not apply. See Geneva Pharmaceuticals, Applied Materials, Symbol Technologies.

name: Consonance requirement for §121 protection
description: Section 121 shields claims against a double patenting challenge if consonance exists between the divided groups of claims and an earlier restriction requirement. If a restriction requirement does not clearly set forth the line of demarcation, then challenged claims could not satisfy the consonance requirement.
guidance: Examiner must assess whether the line of demarcation of the original restriction was maintained; loss of consonance can permit double patenting, but double patenting does not automatically follow if claims are patentably distinct or §121 requirements are otherwise met.

name: Impact of Patent Term Extension (PTE) under 35 U.S.C. 156 on double patenting
description: Nonstatutory double patenting does not invalidate any patent term extension (PTE) granted under 35 U.S.C. 156, if the claims are otherwise valid under its pre‑PTE expiration date.
guidance: Per Novartis AG v. Ezra Ventures LLC, a PTE pursuant to §156 is valid so long as the extended patent is otherwise valid without the extension; courts will not let a judge‑made doctrine cut off a statutorily authorized time extension.

name: General principles for determination of distinctness/independence (§806)
description: (A) Where inventions are independent (no disclosed relation), restriction to one is ordinarily proper. (B) Where inventions are related as disclosed but are distinct as claimed, restriction may be proper. (C) Where inventions are related as disclosed but are not distinct as claimed, restriction is never proper. (D) A reasonable number of species may be claimed when there is an allowable claim generic thereto.
guidance: These summarize the core tests for restriction practice; see MPEP §§806.04–806.06 and §802.01 for criteria for patentably distinct inventions.

name: Compare claimed subject matter to determine distinctness (§806.01)
description: In passing upon questions of double patenting and restriction, it is the claimed subject matter that is considered and such claimed subject matter must be compared in order to determine the question of distinctness or independence.
guidance: A provisional election of a single species may be required where only generic claims are presented and the generic claims encompass a multiplicity of species making an unduly extensive and burdensome search necessary. See MPEP §803.02 and §808.01(a).

name: Single embodiment / same essential features — no restriction (§806.03)
description: Where the claims of an application define the same essential characteristics of a single disclosed embodiment of an invention, restriction therebetween should never be required because the claims are different definitions of the same disclosed subject matter.
guidance: If such claims are voluntarily presented in different applications having common inventor/assignee (no Office restriction), see MPEP §804–§804.02 for treatment; do not require restriction among claims that are merely alternative breadth definitions of the same embodiment.

name: Genus and species restriction rules (§806.04)
description: Where an application includes claims directed to different embodiments or species that could fall within the scope of a generic claim, restriction between the species may be proper if the species are independent or distinct. 37 CFR 1.141 provides that an allowable generic claim may link a reasonable number of species embraced thereby.
guidance: Apply election of species practice (37 CFR 1.146) in first action on applications with a generic claim and multiple patentably distinct species; if more than a reasonable number of species present, examiner may require restriction to not more than a reasonable number before taking further action.

name: Definition and effect of a generic claim (§806.04(d))
description: A generic claim should read on each species; in general, a generic claim should require no material element additional to those required by the species claims, and each species claim must require all the limitations of the generic claim.
guidance: Once a generic claim is allowable, species claims that require all limitations of the generic claim will ordinarily be allowable over the prior art; when species claims do not require all limitations, see MPEP §821.04(a) for further practice.

name: Claims limited to species — terminology and relationship to generic claims (§806.04(e))
description: Claims are definitions or descriptions of inventions; claims themselves are never species. A claim may be limited to a single disclosed embodiment (specific species claim) or encompass two or more embodiments (generic/genus claim). Species refer to different embodiments and may be independent or related.
guidance: Evaluate whether species are independent or related when deciding restriction or double patenting issues; see §806.04 and §806.04(b).

name: Restriction between mutually exclusive species (§806.04(f))
description: A requirement for restriction to a single species may be proper if the species are mutually exclusive: claims to different species are mutually exclusive if one claim recites limitations disclosed for a first species but not a second, and vice versa — i.e., the claims must not overlap in scope.
guidance: Establish non‑overlapping scope (no claim reads on the other) before requiring restriction between species.

name: Species must be patentably distinct from each other (§806.04(h))
description: In making a requirement for restriction in an application claiming plural species, the examiner should group together species considered clearly unpatentable over each other. If generic claims are allowable, applicant may claim additional species as provided by 37 CFR 1.141. If species are voluntarily presented in a different application (no election by Office), closely investigate for double patenting.
guidance: If divisional claims arise consonant with an election to a species, 35 U.S.C. 121 may prohibit double patenting rejections; otherwise applicant may overcome rejections by terminal disclaimer (In re Goodman, In re Braithwaite).

name: Generic claim filed after issuance of species claims — double patenting risk (§806.04(i))
description: If a generic claim is presented in a separate application after the issuance of a patent claiming one or more species within the scope of the generic claim, the Office may reject the generic claim on the grounds of nonstatutory double patenting when the patent and application have at least one common inventor and/or are commonly assigned/owned (or subject to joint research agreement).
guidance: Applicant may overcome such a rejection by filing a terminal disclaimer. See MPEP §804 and cited case law (In re Goodman, In re Braithwaite).

name: Combination vs subcombination distinctness criteria (two‑way test) (§806.05(c))
description: To support a requirement for restriction between combination and subcombination inventions, both two‑way distinctness and reasons for insisting on restriction are necessary — i.e., there would be a serious search burden (separate classification/status/field of search) and/or a serious examination burden (non‑prior art issues relevant to one invention but not the other).
guidance: Inventions are distinct if (A) the combination as claimed does not require the particulars of the subcombination for patentability (novelty/unobviousness), and (B) the subcombination can be shown to have utility either by itself or in another materially different combination. Provide evidence (classification, utility, claim scope) to support distinctness. See examples I (subcombination essential — no restriction) and II (subcombination not essential — restriction proper if other reasons exist).

name: Use of form paragraph 8.15 for combination‑subcombination restriction
description: ¶ 8.15 Combination‑Subcombination — Inventions [1] and [2] are related as combination and subcombination. Inventions in this relationship are distinct if it can be shown that (1) the combination as claimed does not require the particulars of the subcombination as claimed for patentability, and (2) that the subcombination has utility by itself or in other combinations (MPEP §806.05(c)).
guidance: In bracket 3 specify the limitations of the claimed subcombination not required by the claimed combination or evidence supporting the conclusion; in bracket 4 suggest separate utility. Conclude restriction requirement with form paragraph 8.21. If applicant elects a subcombination that is later found allowable, examine dependent claims per 37 CFR 1.104 and be alert to provisional double patenting rejections over the instant application.

name: Section-aware document representation (section selection)
description: Patent documents have multiple sections (title, abstract, description, claims); different sections contain different information useful to different tasks.
guidance: For classification/retrieval/generation, select or weight relevant sections (e.g., claims for classification) or design multi-section models (MSABERT, multi-input architectures). Ignoring section structure or using only full-text naively can reduce performance and increase computational cost.

name: Patent quality indicators as evaluation targets
description: Commonly used measures for patent quality/value include forward citations, backward citations, number of claims, grant lag, patent family size, remaining lifetime, maintenance period, and investor reaction; composite indices such as OECD indices are also used.
guidance: These indicators are used as prediction targets in patent-quality models (regression/classification). However, their relation to actual monetary value is ambiguous; forward citations are most directly associated with value but weighting of indices is unclear. Researchers should state which proxy they use and justify it.

name: Lack of universally accepted gold-standard for patent value
description: There is no universally accepted 'gold standard' metric for patent quality/value.
guidance: Because of metric ambiguity, experiments should report multiple indicators, discuss limitations, and avoid claiming definitive monetary valuation solely from citation-based proxies.

name: Human-in-the-loop and expert feedback (RLHF) for legal robustness
description: Human oversight and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with patent experts (attorneys/reviewers) are necessary to align generated patent outputs with drafting goals (novelty, clarity, consistency with prior art).
guidance: Design reward functions that encode drafting preferences (e.g., favourable claim length, inclusion of limiting terms). Use structured expert ratings on novelty, clarity, and consistency to train or fine-tune models; report the human evaluation protocol.

name: Designing reward functions for claim drafting
description: Custom reward functions (for RLHF) can be constructed to prefer claim attributes (e.g., claim length up to a defined length, inclusion of limiting terms) that improve chances of patent approval.
guidance: Explicitly describe reward components and their rationale. Rewarding limiting terms and appropriate length can help reduce overbroad or vague claims, but trade-offs with completeness must be considered.

name: Modeling dependency between patent parts for generation
description: Patent generation benefits from modeling dependencies among parts (e.g., using abstract/claims to generate specification or using claim+drawing to produce specification).
guidance: Generative tasks can be formulated as part-to-part generation (Claim → Specification, Claim+Drawing → Specification). Use appropriate conditioning inputs and multimodal encoders when images are involved.

name: Contractual terms imposed by deposit application
description: Legal/contractual obligations the depositor accepts by completing the collection's application form.
guidance: Common obligations recited include: supply all information requested, pay requisite fees, indemnify the collection against claims (except negligence), not withdraw deposit during required storage period, authorize the collection to supply samples per patent procedure, and replace microorganism at depositor's expense if collection cannot furnish samples. Specific wording: BEA application constitutes a contract and lists these obligations; CECT application is a contract under which depositor undertakes to supply information, pay fees, indemnify, not withdraw, and authorize supply; IMI application form CC PF1 constitutes a contract binding similar obligations.

name: Definition and legal status of the Volunteer Army
description: The term 'Volunteer Army' comprehensively denotes a temporary military organization which the Government employs and maintains in time of war or public danger, comprising persons who engage directly with the United States, conscripts, and State militia called into U.S. service by the President.
guidance: Volunteers raised directly by the United States are usually termed 'volunteers'; the President cannot raise or maintain volunteers at will without express authority of Congress; the legal status of persons claiming to be volunteers depends on whether an act of Congress authorized their raising and employment at the time. (C. 1301, May, 1895; C. 1377, May, 1895; others.)

name: Patent Value and Scope
description: The intrinsic value and scope of the patent — foundational/broad patents command higher royalties; niche patents less.
guidance: Assess claims breadth, applicability across industries, and potential to drive market adoption. Example: a broadly applicable drug-delivery patent justifies higher rates than a narrow niche invention.

name: Obviously Informal Cases — examiner procedure
description: When an application is impractical for complete action on the merits due to informal or insufficient disclosure, follow a limited procedure: make a reasonable search (unless disclosure is incomprehensible); point out informalities and drawing deficiencies; require specification revision to idiomatic English and U.S. patent practice; reject informal claims under 35 U.S.C. 112 (blanket rejection usually sufficient).
guidance: Attempt to point out specific points of informality. Treat a number of obviously informal claims as a single claim for fee and examination purposes. Applicants are urged to submit a preliminary amendment (preferably within 3 months) correcting informalities; preliminary amendments must not add new matter. Use form paragraph 7.01 or 7.02 when a proper search cannot be made due to unconventional terminology or incomprehensible disclosure.

name: Search — examiner must search prior art (MPEP § 704.01)
description: After reading the specification and claims, the examiner searches the prior art. The invention should be thoroughly understood before a search is undertaken. Informal cases also receive a search to avoid piecemeal prosecution.
guidance: Give full faith and credit to prior examiner’s search/action unless clear error or knowledge of other prior art exists; generally do not reorient the approach merely to attempt to find something new. See MPEP Chapter 900 (esp. §§ 904–904.03) for search procedures.

name: Examples of Information Reasonably Required (illustrative list)
description: Specific examples of information that may be reasonably required include: name/citation of particularly relevant indexed journal or treatise; trade name of goods/services embodying claimed subject matter; citations/dates/copies of advertising/promotional literature; journal articles describing goods/services; trade names/providers of competing goods/services; written descriptions/analyses prepared by inventors or assignees; identification of pending/abandoned applications by inventor/assignee disclosing similar subject matter; replies to protests; explanation of technical material in a publication; identification of changes made in reformatted continuing applications; CIP mark-ups showing added subject matter; comments on new Federal Circuit decisions; publication date of undated documents; information bearing on derivation (35 U.S.C. 102(f)); and other art or factual information pertinent to patentability.
guidance: This list is illustrative, not exhaustive. A requirement for such information is justified when necessary to find prior art or resolve issues arising from the examiner’s search or analysis. The examiner must still perform a search per MPEP § 704.01; a requirement for information is not a substitute for the examiner’s search.

name: Interrogatories or Stipulations that may be required
description: An examiner may require interrogatories or stipulations seeking applicant’s factual knowledge about matters such as: common technical features among claims; admissions that certain claim groups lack common technical features; support in the disclosure for means- or steps-plus-function claim limitations; identification of portions of the disclosure that provide written description and enablement for specific claim elements; meanings of claim terms or which prior art teachings would be covered by claim limitations; which claim portions correspond to any admitted prior art; specific utility provided by claimed subject matter on a claim-by-claim basis; whether a dependent claim element is known in the prior art; support for added limitations in an amended claim; facts related to public use or sale situations.
guidance: Interrogatories/stipulations should seek factual information, and may be required in a focused manner when reasonably necessary. Responses may be accepted as complete if applicant states information is unknown or not readily available.

name: Rejections Under 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 101, 112 and Related Form Paragraphs
description: Guidance for making rejections under sections 102 (novelty), 103 (obviousness), 101 (statutory subject matter), and 112 (written description and claim definiteness), including contrasts with objections, printed publications or patents, provisional rejections, and various subparts and form paragraphs for use in rejections.
guidance: Detailed subsections (e.g., 706.02 through 706.07) provide specific handling for each statutory basis, including examination guidelines for references under 102(e), provisional rejections when reference is copending, rejections under 102(f)/(g)/(d)/(c), form paragraphs for 102 rejections, contents of a 103 rejection, provisional rejections combining 102(e)/103, biotechnology process applications (35 U.S.C. 103(b)), rejections not based on prior art, rejections after allowance, final rejections and their proper timing, and treatment of duplicate claims, new matter, disclaimers, reissue, res judicata, etc. Use the appropriate form paragraphs and follow procedural rules for final rejections, withdrawals, RCE practice, and after-final practice.

name: Examiner’s Letter or Action — completeness and clarity requirements
description: The examiner’s Office action must be complete and clear: indicate all outstanding requirements, complete action on formal matters, use proper language in rejecting claims, answer all material traversed, avoid piecemeal examination, notify of inaccuracies in amendments, mention each claim in each action, state when claims are allowable, number paragraphs, comment on examples, and ensure reviewing and initialing by assistant examiner and signing by authorized examiner.
guidance: Follow internal procedures for entry, dating, mailing returned office action. Use appropriate form paragraphs (MPEP § 707 et seq.). Ensure draftsman requirements and that examiner notes and citations are complete. See detailed subsections for use of form paragraphs and examiner notes.

name: Affidavits/Declarations Traversing Rejections — Objective Evidence of Nonobviousness
description: Affidavits or declarations (37 CFR 1.132) that traverse rejections must address generally applicable criteria: objective evidence of nonobviousness, nexus requirement and evidence, probative value and weighing of objective evidence, unexpected results, comparison with closest prior art, advantages disclosed or inherent, and proper affidavit/declaration form.
guidance: Objective evidence must show unexpected results commensurate in scope with the claimed invention; burden lies with applicant to provide probative evidence and nexus where needed. Examiner weighs expected vs. alleged unexpected results and considers commercial success, long-felt need, copying, skepticism of experts, and inoperability of references. See MPEP §§ 716–716.03 and subparts for evaluation details.

name: Commercial Success and Other Secondary Considerations
description: Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention and derived from the claimed invention. Secondary considerations include long-felt need and failure of others, skepticism of experts, copying, and attribution.
guidance: When evaluating commercial success, examiner considers whether success is due to claimed invention, scope alignment, market evidence, and other factors indicating nexus between claimed features and success. Treat as part of overall nonobviousness analysis (see MPEP § 716.03 and following).

name: File Wrapper Contents and Organization; Public Use Proceedings
description: Papers in the file wrapper must be organized: arrangement of papers, prints, data entered, changes of inventor name or title, classification during examination, index of claims, field of search, foreign filing dates, related applications, public use proceedings, preliminary handling, examiner determination of prima facie showing, preliminary hearings, public use proceeding testimony, and final decision.
guidance: Maintain completeness of the patent file wrapper and follow record-keeping instructions. Public use proceedings and testimony require special handling. See MPEP § 724 and related sections.

name: Petition to Expunge Information or Copy of Papers in Application File (37 CFR 1.59)
description: Information in an application will not be expunged except as provided. Information forming part of the original disclosure (specification, claims, drawings, preliminary amendments specifically incorporated in an executed oath/declaration) will not be expunged. An applicant may request expungement (37 CFR 1.59(b)) for information other than original disclosure by petition and fee, establishing to the Director that expungement is appropriate.
guidance: Expungement of material originally submitted under MPEP § 724.02 or in an IDS is appropriate if petitioner complies with conditions (items A–E in MPEP § 724.05) and examiner or appropriate official determines information is not material to a reasonable examiner's decision of patentability. If unintentionally submitted, petition may request return rather than transfer. Petitions requiring waiver of 1.59(a) must be filed under 37 CFR 1.183 and directed to Office of Petitions. Decisions often held in abeyance until allowance, Ex parte Quayle action, or abandonment; use form paragraphs (7.204–7.213, 7.205–7.213) to grant/dismiss and to explain deficiencies (lack of fee, failure to show trade secret/proprietary/unintentional submission, failure to commit to retain expunged material, unclear identification of material, not submitted by or on behalf of original submitter, etc.).

name: Patent may be void in whole or in part even if invention is new
description: A patent may be void, although the invention be new, either altogether or for something in particular.
guidance: It is possible for novelty to exist but for other legal defects (e.g., monopoly, insufficient specification) to render the patent void as to some claims or entirely.

name: Specification must be sufficiently correct and complete
description: A patent is invalid when the specification is not sufficiently correct.
guidance: Insufficiency of specification (failure to describe/enable what is claimed) is a standalone ground to destroy the patent; the patentee must be prepared to defend sufficiency in scire facias.

name: Board termination if patent owner fails to act
description: If the patent owner does not exercise either permitted option (rehearing or requesting reopening), then the Board may terminate the appeal as to the newly rejected claim(s).
guidance: If the patent owner files a submission under 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1) or (2) that is denied entry by the Board, then the Board may terminate the appeal as to the newly rejected claim(s), designate the decision as to any remaining claims as a final decision, and permit a request for rehearing for the affirmed claims within one month from the date of notice of termination.

name: Third-party comments under 37 CFR 41.77(c)
description: The third party requester may once file comments on the patent owner’s submission under 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1) within one month of the date of service of the request to reopen prosecution. The one-month time period cannot be extended.
guidance: Comments must be limited to issues concerning the new ground(s) of rejection raised by the Board or the patent owner’s response; may include new evidence and arguments if limited to supporting the new grounds (including evidence directed to amended/new claims if necessitated). Comments addressing issues not raised by the new grounds will be refused entry. If the third party is not an appellant or cross-appellant, comments may still be filed only with payment of the appeal and appeal brief fees per 37 CFR 41.20.

name: Advantageous effects considered to support inventive step
description: If an effect achieved by matters defining a claimed invention is advantageous in comparison with an effect of a prior art reference, it is taken into consideration as a fact to affirmatively support its inventive step.
guidance: If an advantageous effect compared to the prior art is so remarkable that it could not have been foreseen by a person skilled in the art from the state of the art, inventive step may not be denied (Supreme Court decision examples). Conversely, inventions made by collecting/improving publicly known arts are not considered inventive except where: it is difficult to collate the arts and achieve a new advantageous effect beyond what was expected; or a new technical method is added.

name: Qualitatively different or quantitatively prominent effects
description: Even if a claimed invention appears easily made by combining prior art references at first glance, an inventive step can be acknowledged if the claimed invention has an advantageous effect that is qualitatively different or quantitatively prominent compared with those of the prior art references, and the effect could not have been foreseen by a person skilled in the art from the state of the art.
guidance: Particularly important for selection inventions and chemical inventions where product effect is hard to predict from structure. Example: mixing chemical compounds in a certain ratio that yields unexpected results can support inventive step (Supreme Court decision cited).

name: Numerical limitation inventions
description: Inventions with indispensible elements expressed by numerical values. Experimentally selecting an optimal numerical range from publicly known art is normally considered ordinary creativity and inventive step is generally denied.
guidance: A claimed invention involves inventive step if it has a more advantageous effect within the limited numerical range than the prior art; the advantageous effect should be remarkably improved across the whole range. Criteria for 'critical significance' include: (1) required regarding any part of the numerical range if the invention is in line with prior art; (2) not required if two inventions solve different problems and have qualitatively different effects even if configurations differ only by numerical limitation. For recognition: (a) remarkable change in effect across the boundary, (b) technical meaning of limitation described in the specification, (c) embodiments or supplemental materials proving upper/lower limits are critical, and (d) objective confirmation generally via experimental results covering the whole range. Examples illustrate when a numerical limitation is technically meaningless or when improved quality/economy supports inventive step.

name: Parameter invention criteria
description: A parameter invention creates a certain (nonstandard) parameter, parameterizes it mathematically using correlations among parameters, and employs it as part of essential claim elements.
guidance: Determine inventive step after defining the subject matter from the specification/drawings/common knowledge. Consider functions/characteristics caused by the parameter; do not compare claimed invention to prior art without accounting for functions/characteristics. If parameter is merely a different expression or confirmation of intrinsic features and the cause-effect link to advantageous effect is weak, inventive step is denied. If the parameter invention is effectively a numerical limitation, apply numerical-limitation criteria. Examiner may notify applicant of concrete grounds for rejection and propose solutions when reasonable doubt exists; if the parameter is standard/common, the special criteria do not apply. Examples and possible examiner actions (notify, describe grounds concretely, propose solutions) are given.

name: Product-by-process claims: product interpreted by properties/structure
description: A product claim expressed by its manufacturing process must have the manufacturing process construed as a limitation defining the structure and properties of the final product; the subject matter sought is the final product, not the process or apparatus.
guidance: Novelty and inventive step are determined by comparing the product (with structure/properties defined by claim limitations) to publicly known products. If the manufacturing process affects product structure/properties, inventive step is determined for the product having those properties. If process affects only efficiency/yield and not product properties, inventive step is determined solely on the final product ignoring the process. Where structure/properties are hard to infer from the process, examiner shall define scope using the whole specification (including experimental data/embodiments/drawings) and may issue a rejection. If prior art discloses the same/similar manufacturing process, the examiner may infer same product and reject for lack of inventive step. Several examples (pharmaceutical extraction steps; belt coupling device; polarizing film) illustrate application.

name: Combination invention: whole-claim assessment
description: A combination invention gathers technical features disclosed in prior art as a whole to solve a technical problem; the claim should be considered as a whole and inventive step should not be negated merely because each claim element is known from prior art.
guidance: When determining inventive step, assess difficulty in forming structurally combined elements as a whole (problem-solution approach) and consider unique effects of the invention as a whole.

name: Synergistic effect vs aggregation (juxtaposition)
description: If a combination invention achieves an effect by functional interaction between technical features that is different from or greater than the sum of individual effects (synergistic effect), inventive step may be recognized; if the claim is merely a juxtaposition or aggregation of known features without meaningful interaction, inventive step may be denied.
guidance: Assess whether modification/substitution leads to structural difficulties or yields effects greater than the summed effects of prior art. Examples: combinations that merely substitute known parts without added functional advantage are treated as aggregation and are obvious.

name: Synthesis principle and other factors in obviousness
description: In principle, determination of inventive step synthesizes the objective, technical configuration, and functional effect of the claimed invention; but other factors may also be taken into account and the examiner should not readily deny inventive step without considering applicant arguments.
guidance: Other factors include: (i) prior art teaching away the claimed invention may prevent denying inventive step (but mere description of prior art as inferior does not necessarily teach away), (ii) commercial success, favorable industry comments, or long-unimplemented demand may be secondary evidence indicative of inventive step but alone are insufficient and must be tied to technical features disclosed in the specification.

name: Reduction to Practice / Ready for Patenting
description: An invention is reduced to practice when it has been (1) constructed or performed within the scope of the patent claims; and (2) determined that it works for its intended purpose. The claimed invention is ready for patenting when there is reason to believe it would work for its intended purpose.
guidance: Used repeatedly (e.g., in on‑sale bar and conception analyses). Ready for patenting can be shown either by reduction to practice or by drawings/descriptions sufficient to allow a person of ordinary skill in the art to make or use the invention. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) and multiple Federal Circuit cases (e.g., Cooper v. Goldfarb).

name: On‑Sale Bar (35 U.S.C. §102(b))
description: A patent claim is invalid if more than one year before the filing date an embodiment of the claimed invention was both (1) subject to a commercial offer for sale in the United States; and (2) ready for patenting.
guidance:
Definition of commercial 'offer for sale': made if another party could make a binding contract by simply accepting the offer; embodiment must have been actually sold or offered for sale (no actual sale required). Essential question is whether there was an attempt to obtain commercial benefit. The invention must have been conceived before any offer can exist. Ready for patenting is defined by reduction to practice or sufficient drawings/descriptions. See Pfaff v. Wells Electronics and cited authorities. If a factual issue on date of invention exists, jury instructions on determining invention date should be given.

Examples/Notes: the instruction emphasizes conception and readiness; citations include Pfaff, August Tech, and others.

name: Printed Publication (anticipation / prior art)
description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was described in a printed publication either before it was invented or more than one year prior to the U.S. filing date. A printed publication must have been maintained in some tangible form (e.g., printed pages, microfilm, internet publication) and sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter.
guidance: Accessibility: 'publicly accessible' means distributed or made available so that persons interested and ordinarily skilled exercising reasonable diligence can locate it; not necessary to be available to every member of the public. An issued patent or published patent application is a printed publication. The printed publication's disclosure must be enabling — complete enough to enable one of ordinary skill to use the invention without undue experimentation; jurors should consider what would have been within the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) and numerous cases (In re NTP, Orion IP v. Hyundai, etc.).

name: Prior Invention by Another (35 U.S.C. §102(a),(g))
description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the United States before it was invented by the patentee (and that prior inventor did not abandon, suppress, or conceal the invention). The defendant must show it is highly probable that before the patentee, the third party reduced to practice a product or method that included all claim elements, or that the third party first conceived and exercised reasonable diligence to reduce to practice.
guidance: The prior device must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would recognize it would work for its intended purpose. If the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed, it does not anticipate; abandonment/suppression requires active concealment or unreasonable delay in making the invention public. It is not necessary that the patentee had knowledge of the prior invention. Case citations provided (Teva v. AstraZeneca, Monsanto v. Mycogen, etc.). Note: further instructions required where priority is submitted to the jury (conception dates and reduction to practice comparisons, diligence issues).

name: Prior Patent (anticipation)
description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was patented in the United States or a foreign country before it was invented by the patentee or more than one year before the patentee filed a U.S. application.
guidance: If date of invention is disputed, the jury should be instructed on determining that date. Cited authorities include 35 U.S.C. §102(a)-(b) and cases such as Adv. Display Sys. v. Kent State Univ.

name: Prior U.S. Application / Published U.S. Patent Application (35 U.S.C. §§102(e))
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application or U.S. patent filed by another person before the invention was made by the patentee.
guidance: If invention date is a factual issue, instruct jury on how to determine it. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §§102(e)(1)-(2); In re Giacomini, Sun Studs, In re Wertheim.

name: Obviousness — Factor 2: Differences Between the Claimed Invention and the Prior Art
description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the viewpoint of a POSITA at the time of invention; determine the impact of those differences on obviousness of the invention as a whole, not merely a portion.
guidance: Do not require precise teaching in the prior art; consider inferences and creative steps a POSITA would have employed. If combination of known elements yielded predictable results, that supports obviousness; unexpected results or 'teaching away' support nonobviousness. A claim is not proved obvious merely by showing each element was independently known; consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine elements (from prior art, background knowledge, market demand, or common sense). Conduct separate analysis for each claim. Citations: KSR, Abbott Labs., Graham, Stratoflex, Medtronic.

name: Materiality in Inequitable Conduct (non‑disclosure cases)
description: Information is material if 'but for' the individual's failure to disclose or misrepresentation, the Patent and Trademark Office would not have allowed one or more claims of the patent. In other words, it is more likely than not that the PTO would not have allowed one or more claims if it had been aware of the withheld/true information.
guidance: To decide whether the PTO would not have allowed a claim, use the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim(s) under consideration and apply the 'more likely than not' standard (how the PTO would have evaluated it). This is the materiality prong of inequitable conduct in non‑disclosure cases. (Further instructions continue beyond the excerpt.) Citations: Therasense and related precedent.

name: Housekeeping amendment must not address patentability
description: Housekeeping amendments filed solely to make claims identical in merged files must not address any issue of patentability.
guidance: Such housekeeping amendments may be accomplished by amending either or both proceedings, but must be limited to harmonizing text. If not timely submitted, any claim not identical across merged files should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 2, as indefinite.

name: Title and abstract changes in reexamination
description: Normally the title will not need to be changed during reexamination; if change is necessary, notify patent owner to provide an amendment changing the title early. If all claims are found patentable and a NIRC is or will be mailed, the examiner may change the title only by examiner’s amendment; merely initialing a change is not permitted.
guidance: An examiner’s amendment can be made to change the abstract when narrowing amendments have changed the focus of the invention (e.g., claim made more specific and abstract no longer reflects specific limitation).

name: Selection of claim(s) and drawing figure for publication
description: A representative claim and an appropriate drawing figure are to be indicated for publication in the Official Gazette; the broadest claim should be selected.
guidance: Examiners should ordinarily designate one claim on each invention; in regular prosecution up to five may be designated for publication when multiple inventions exist, but in reexamination the examiner must select only one claim.

name: Statutory disclaimer scope and limitation
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 253(a) an owner may disclaim a complete claim or claims of a patent (statutory disclaimer).
guidance: A statutory disclaimer relinquishes legal rights to one or more complete claims of an issued patent but is not a vehicle for adding or amending claims; there is no provision in the statute or rules to add or amend claims via a statutory disclaimer. If patent is involved in interference or PTAB trial, see 37 CFR 41.127(a) and 42.80. A patent owner cannot avoid double patenting by disclaiming the earlier patent (Eli Lilly v. Barr).

name: Terminal disclaimer restrictions — no disclaimers of individual claims or conditional disclaimers
description: A terminal disclaimer must be of a terminal portion of the term of the entire patent to be granted; a disclaimer of a terminal portion of the term of an individual claim or individual claims will not be accepted, and the statute does not provide for conditional disclaimers.
guidance: Disclaimers contingent on PTA determinations, litigation outcomes, allowance of certain claims, or petitions are improper and cannot be accepted.

name: Multiple copending applications and terminal disclaimer coverage
description: When two or more copending applications share overlapping inventive entities or ownership and would raise double patenting issues, provisional NSDP rejections should be made and maintained until obviated.
guidance: If three applications contain conflicting claims such that provisional NSDP rejections exist in each based on the other two, it is not sufficient to file a terminal disclaimer in only one application; an appropriate terminal disclaimer must be filed in at least two of the applications (and sometimes in all three) to require common ownership or enforcement for all applications.

name: Carrying over of terminal disclaimers to continuing proceedings and reexaminations/reissues
description: A terminal disclaimer filed in a parent application normally has no effect on a continuing application claiming benefit of the parent, except it carries over to a Continued Prosecution Application (CPA) that retains the same application number; terminal disclaimers filed during prosecution continue to operate in reexamination and reissue.
guidance: If applicant does not want a terminal disclaimer to carry over to a CPA, a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 with required fee may be filed requesting the disclaimer not be carried over. Filing an RCE does not create a new application and the terminal disclaimer continues to operate. For reissue applications, a copy of an originally filed and approved terminal disclaimer need not be filed; the disclaimer will be effective for the reissue patent even if the front page of the reissue patent does not indicate it.

name: Infringement — identity with the patented invention
description: On infringement, the question is whether the thing made or used by the defendant is, in the sense of the patent law, identical with the invention of the patentee; this is akin to the novelty/identity inquiry.
guidance: Principles of evidence applicable to determining whether two things are identical (as for novelty) apply to infringement. Analyze whether defendant's thing embodies the same invention as claimed.

name: Public use petition content and identification requirements
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.292 must be submitted in writing, must specifically identify the application to which the petition is directed by application number or serial number and filing date, and should include a listing of all affidavits or declarations and exhibits relied on. The petition must contain a sufficient description of the subject matter alleged to have been in 'public use' or 'on sale,' including any necessary photographs, drawings, diagrams, exhibits, or flowcharts, to enable the examiner to compare the claimed subject matter to the subject matter alleged to have been in 'public use' or 'on sale.' In addition, the petition and any accompanying papers must either (A) reflect that a copy has been served upon the applicant or applicant’s attorney/agent of record; or (B) be filed with the Office in duplicate in the event service is not possible.
guidance: Include a 'Certificate of Service' when served; include as much identifying information as possible (recommended list includes applicant name, application number, confirmation number, filing date, title of invention, Technology Center art unit number, examiner name, current status/location of application, and 'ATTENTION:' area). Clearly identify the filing as 'PETITION UNDER 37 CFR 1.292' and label exhibits to avoid separation.

name: Restricted application considerations in public use petitions
description: If the petition alleges that subject matter covering both elected claims and nonelected claims is a statutory bar, only that part of the petition drawn to subject matter of the elected claims will be considered. However, if a public use proceeding is ultimately instituted, it will not necessarily be limited to the subject matter of the elected claims but may include the nonelected subject matter. Any evidence adduced on the nonelected subject matter may be used in any subsequently-filed application claiming subject matter without the requirement of a new fee (37 CFR 1.17(j)).
guidance: Be aware that initial consideration focuses on elected claims but instituted proceedings can include broader matter, and evidence may be reused in later applications without another fee.

name: INJUNCTION variable definition
description: Binary variable [INJUNCTION] indicating whether a permanent injunction was granted for at least one claim of the patent(s)-in-suit.
guidance: Treat outcome as granted/denied at the decision level (binary) — study notes limitation that timing, duration, or scope of injunctions are not considered.

name: Patent of Addition: expiry and independence
description: A patent of addition expires along with the main patent unless it is made independent according to the provisions in S.54.
guidance: The Complete Specification for a patent of addition must include specific reference to the number of the main patent or its application and a definite statement that the invention comprises an improvement in, or a modification of, the invention claimed in the specification of the main patent.

name: Divisional application rules
description: When an application claims more than one invention the applicant may, on request or to meet an official objection, divide the application and file two or more applications (divisional applications).
guidance: Priority date for divisional applications is the same as the parent (ante-dating). The complete specification of a divisional must not include matter not in substance disclosed in the first application and must reference the parent application in the body of the specification.

name: Form 2 and first-page formalities
description: Provisional/complete specification must be submitted in Form 2. The first page should contain the title, name/address/nationality of each applicant, and a preamble to the description.
guidance: Complete description should start from the second page followed by date and signature. Claims follow the description and an abstract should be included on the next page after the date and signature. Drawings, if any, can be attached thereafter.

name: Provisional specification: nature and required content
description: A provisional specification is not a rough draft; it is a permanent independent document that should contain the title and description and start with the prescribed preamble.
guidance: Claims need not be included. After the preamble set forth the object of the invention, a statement of the principle or discovery underlying the invention, and a general statement of the actual invention. Include as much information as available; description should be adequate to identify the invention.

name: Object of the invention (problem & solution)
description: Specification should clearly bring out the necessity of the invention by stating the technical problems associated with existing technology and the solution provided by the invention.
guidance: Use clear object statements: 'The principal object of this invention is ...', 'Another object ...', etc., and show obvious differences between claimed invention and prior art.

name: Claims define boundaries and must be precise
description: Claims define the boundaries of the protection sought; what is not claimed is open to public use even if disclosed in the description.
guidance: Claims' object is to show concisely and accurately how much of what is described is sought to be protected. Each claim is evaluated on its own merit; one claim being objected does not invalidate others.

name: Claims: single invention or linked group and basis in specification
description: Claims shall relate to a single invention or a group of inventions linked so as to form a single inventive concept; they must be clear, succinct and fairly based on the matter disclosed in the specification (S.10(5)).
guidance: Ensure claims are fairly based on disclosure; terms used in claims must appear in or be clearly inferred from the description.

name: Product claims should not be mere property listings
description: A product claimed merely by stating its properties (e.g., a lubricating oil defined only by specific gravity and boiling point) does not properly define the invention.
guidance: Claims should identify structural or compositional features that define the invention, not only properties.

name: Claims referencing description/back-references
description: Claims that merely refer back to the description (e.g., 'as described' or 'the invention described in the specification') are not sufficiently definitive unless the description explicitly states the characteristic features of the invention.
guidance: Ensure the description contains explicit statements of the features relied upon by such referential claims.

name: Include modifications and variations
description: An account of modifications and variations which fall within the scope of the claim may be included in the description.
guidance: Mention alternative embodiments and optional features to widen effective protection and guide interpretation.

name: Claims: number, drafting order, and fees
description: There is no restriction on the number of claims, but claims beyond 10 are chargeable. Good drafting typically begins with broad claims and proceeds to narrower claims.
guidance: Use broad principal claims and narrower dependent claims specifying more details; multiple claims with varying scopes provide layered protection. Prefer one-sentence claims.

name: Claims should be specific, not vague or speculative
description: A claim must be specific, not vague, ambiguous, speculative or hypothetical; avoid subjective terms like 'thin', 'strong', 'a major part', 'such as', 'when required', 'any'.
guidance: Each claim should be complete, covering the inventive feature and enough surrounding elements to put the invention in context; terms must be found in or inferred from the description.

name: Claim structure: introductory phrase, body, and linking words
description: A claim usually consists of an introductory phrase (category/purpose), the body (legal description), and a linking part joining the two.
guidance: Common linking words/phrases include 'which comprises', 'including', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'. Example claim structure is provided for guidance.

name: Independent and dependent claims: roles and grouping
description: The principal (first) claim should clearly define essential novel features of the preferred embodiment; subsidiary claims (dependent) claim alternative embodiments, optional features or linked inventions.
guidance: Dependent claims should be grouped with their independent claims. Independent claims may define alternate embodiments or inventions linked to principal claim (product/process/apparatus unity).

name: Omnibus claim use
description: An omnibus claim (e.g., 'An apparatus substantially as hereinabove described') may be added as the last claim to get integral protection only if a 'statement of invention' is incorporated in the specification.
guidance: One or two application claims can precede the omnibus claim.

name: Examples for assessing claim clarity (vagueness, syntax, functional claiming)
description: Illustrative negative examples: (1) 'near-amorphous' is vague and unclear; (2) ambiguous syntax in specifying materials leads to multiple readings; (3) claiming by result (e.g., 'adapted to operate at temperatures down to 200 K') defines the object to be achieved rather than technical features.
guidance: Use these examples to judge claim clarity: avoid vague adjectives, resolve syntactic ambiguity, and claim technical features rather than desired results where concrete features can be stated.

name: Ready for patenting — reduction to practice or enabling description
description: Under Pfaff, 'ready for patenting' may be satisfied either by reduction to practice before the critical date or by prior drawings/descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention.
guidance: Evaluate (a) whether invention was actually reduced to practice (testing under working conditions showing practical utility), or (b) whether drawings/specifications before critical date contained each claim element and enabled practice (Pfaff; Weatherchem; Vanmoor; Abbott Labs. examples).

name: Consideration of multiple dependent claim limitations
description: Director Vidal explains that the Board must consider each separately incorporated claim limitation in determining patentability of multiple dependent claims and, here, patentability of one of the independent claims incorporated by reference in multiple dependent claims renders those multiple dependent claims patentable as well.
guidance: Precedential decision on rehearing (Nested Bean, Inc. v. Big Beings Pty Ltd., IPR2020-01234, Paper 42). When evaluating multiple dependent claims, the Board must assess the patentability impact of each incorporated limitation individually; patentability of an incorporated independent claim can render the multiple dependent claims patentable.

name: Differing testimony cannot establish definiteness
description: The Board denied a Motion to Amend where Patent Owner’s own witnesses gave differing meanings to a term in the substitute claims (different but overlapping values for 'high pressure').
guidance: Halliburton Energy Services, Inc. v. US Well Services, LLC, IPR2021-01316, Paper 44: Inconsistent or differing expert/witness testimony about claim term meanings undermines a showing of definiteness; harmonized, consistent testimony is necessary to support definiteness of amended claims.

name: Specified time limits (non‑statutory) and their consequences
description: Certain actions may be given a specified time (often <30 days) which is not a shortened statutory period under 35 U.S.C. 133, and failure to timely take the specific action results in a consequence other than abandonment of the entire application.
guidance: Examples: (A) Petition under 37 CFR 1.14(e) for public access — applicant usually given ~3 weeks to state objections; failure to reply results in decision on petition without applicant's objections (MPEP § 103). (B) IDS that omits part of 37 CFR 1.98 content — examiner may set 1‑month time to complete IDS; failure results in noncompliant material placed in file but not considered (MPEP § 609). (C) When application is allowable but contains traverse of a restriction requirement — applicant may be given 1 month to cancel non‑elected claims; failure treated as authorization to cancel and application passed to issue (37 CFR 1.141 and 1.144; MPEP § 809.02(c), § 821.01).
