(Suggested claims for interference must be presented within not less than one month; failure treated as disclaimer — see MPEP § 2305.02).

name: Two different periods running — how to determine controlling date
description: When two different periods for reply are running (one regular statutory period from an earlier unanswered rejection and another limited period set in a subsequent Office action), the running of the first period is not suspended by an ex parte limited time action. In cases where claims are copied from a patent and rejected, the date of the last unanswered Office action on the claims other than the copied patent claims is the controlling date of the statutory period.
guidance: Do not assume a later limited time action suspends earlier statutory periods; compute control dates per MPEP examples (see Ex parte Milton).

name: Consider the claimed invention as a whole
description: In determining the differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: Interpret the claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art references as a whole; do not focus improperly on isolated structural differences (see Stratoflex, Schenck v. Nortron, In re Hirao).

name: Include disclosed inherent properties in the 'as a whole' analysis (inherency)
description: In delineating the invention as a whole, look not only to the subject matter literally recited in the claim but also to those properties inherent in the subject matter and disclosed in the specification.
guidance: Consider inherent properties when they are disclosed in the specification (In re Antonie). Note that after KSR, a known result-effective variable may motivate experimentation but is not alone determinative; do not predicate obviousness on features not known at the relevant time (see In re Rijckaert and MPEP §2112).

name: Improvement in existing technology
description: Consideration of whether the claimed invention provides an improvement in existing technology; an improvement in technology (e.g., improving computers or a technical process) supports eligibility, whereas an improvement in an abstract idea itself does not.
guidance: This consideration applies across technologies (computer-implemented, life sciences, etc.). Examples of sufficient improvements include McRO (specific rules improving animation automation) and Rapid Litigation Management (preserving hepatocytes). An improvement that merely enhances an abstract idea or business process without improving technology is insufficient (e.g., Trading Technologies where UI simply provided more information). To be persuasive, claims should show how they improve the technological process rather than claiming only the idea or outcome. See list of court-recognized examples (particular computerized methods, new telephone/server combinations, improved compression methods, GUIs that improve accuracy, improved biological preservation methods).

name: Requirement to recite how a computer aids the method
description: To show that the involvement of a computer assists in improving technology, the claims must recite details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent to which the computer aids the method, or the significance of a computer to the performance of the method.
guidance: Merely adding generic computer components or generic instructions to perform a method on a computer is not sufficient. The claim must include more than mere instructions to perform the method on generic machinery to qualify as an improvement to an existing technology. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for additional guidance about mere instructions to apply an exception.

name: Particular machine consideration (M-or-T as a clue)
description: Whether the judicial exception is applied with or by use of a particular machine is an important clue for eligibility, but it is not a stand-alone test; all claims must still be evaluated under the Alice/Mayo two-part test.
guidance: The machine-or-transformation test is a useful investigative tool but satisfying (or failing) it alone does not determine eligibility. If a claim passes Alice/Mayo it is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test; if it fails Alice/Mayo it is ineligible even if it passes M-or-T. Examiners should also consider related analyses (mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use) and consult MPEP §2106.03 for definition of 'machine'.

name: Degree to which the recited article is particular
description: Determine whether the article being transformed is specifically identified or is generic/recited broadly (transformations limited to particular articles are more persuasive).
guidance: A transformation applied to a generically recited article or to 'any and all articles' is less likely to provide significantly more than the judicial exception. Specific identification of the article or limiting the claim to particular articles tends to favor eligibility.

name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
description: Evaluate whether the recited transformation meaningfully limits the claimed method or whether it is merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation.
guidance: A transformation that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to claim execution (e.g., merely administering a drug that the Supreme Court viewed as a field-of-use limitation in Mayo) will not provide significantly more than the judicial exception. See Mayo and discussion in MPEP §§ 2106.05(g) & (h).

name: Nullity of certain employment contract conditions
description: Any condition in a contract of employment which requires an employee to assign to his employer an invention made by him otherwise than within the course and scope of his employment; or restricts the right of an employee in an invention made by him more than one year after termination of the contract of employment, shall be null and void.
guidance: Protects employee inventors from overbroad assignment clauses and prolonged post‑employment restrictions; statutory limits on employer contractual claims to employee inventions.

name: Grounds for revocation of a patent (exhaustive list in section)
description: Any person may apply for revocation on specified grounds only: (a) patentee not entitled under section 27 to apply; (b) grant was in fraud of applicant's rights; (c) invention not patentable under section 25; (d) invention as illustrated/exemplified in the complete specification cannot be performed or does not lead to results/advantages set out; (e) complete specification does not sufficiently illustrate/describe/ascertain/exemplify the invention and manner of performance to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it out; (f) the claims of the complete specification are not clear or not fairly based on matter disclosed; (g) prescribed declaration contains a false material statement which patentee knew to be false at time of making; (h) application should have been refused under section 36; (i) complete specification claims a microbiological process/product and provisions of section 32(6) have not been complied with.
guidance: The statute enumerates substantive validity/formal grounds for revocation, including entitlement, fraud, patentability, sufficiency of disclosure, clarity and support of claims, and false declarations. Procedure requires service and lodging in prescribed manner; commissioner decides whether to revoke or uphold and may allow amendments consistent with section 51(6)/(7); commissioner may take into account patentee conduct re specification framing for costs.

name: Commissioner’s powers when patent revocation is sought
description: On an application for revocation the commissioner shall decide whether the patent shall be revoked or whether and, if so, subject to what amendments of the specification or claims the patent shall be upheld; the commissioner shall not allow any amendment in conflict with section 51(6) or (7) and may take patentee conduct into consideration in awarding costs.
guidance: Commissioner has remedial power to conditionally uphold patents by permitting amendments; must respect statutory limits on allowable amendments and may penalize irresponsible drafting in costs.

name: Relief when specification is partially valid (amendments and relief)
description: If in infringement proceedings the commissioner finds some claims valid and others invalid, he may postpone any order on the counterclaim to enable patentee to amend the specification pursuant to conditions the commissioner imposes. After amendment, the commissioner may grant relief in respect of any claim previously found valid and infringed, subject to orders as to costs and date from which damages shall be calculated; the commissioner may consider patentee conduct in inserting or permitting invalid claims.
guidance: Statute provides a remedial pathway to correct defective claims and still permit recovery for valid claims, while allowing commissioner to impose equitable conditions and costs based on conduct.

name: Certification of validity and cost consequences
description: If in proceedings a claim in a complete specification is found valid the commissioner or court may certify to that effect. If in subsequent proceedings the validity of that claim is unsuccessfully attacked, that party shall, unless otherwise directed, pay to the other party his full costs, charges and expenses as between patent agent/attorney and client so far as that claim is concerned.
guidance: Certification creates a procedural/evidentiary benefit and potential cost penalty for unsuccessful re‑attacks on a claim previously certified as valid, shifting commercial risk to re‑litigant.

name: Be proactive in rebuttal options to obviousness rejections
description: When an examiner finds the claimed invention motivated to combine prior art references, the examiner will reject the pending claim for obviousness. The patent drafter can rebut such a rejection by: arguing the examiner has misunderstood cited prior art; arguing the examiner has misunderstood the applicant’s invention/pending claims; arguing the lack of inventive step cannot be asserted by combining the cited references; and/or amending the pending claims so they recite an invention not disclosed in or obvious from the cited prior art references.
guidance: The patent drafter must not be a passive actor. Counsel the client on rebuttal options and point to additional evidence that suggests allowance. Prepare arguments and, where appropriate, claim amendments to overcome cited references.

name: No new matter: amendments must not introduce subject matter beyond original disclosure
description: A universal rule in most jurisdictions is that no new matter (new subject matter) beyond that originally disclosed as of the filing date may be added (except to remedy obvious mistakes, such as typographic errors). The same rule applies in principle to both the claims and the description and drawings.
guidance: The restriction balances inventors’ rights and third-party predictability; therefore drafting a complete disclosure prior to filing is of paramount importance. If broad claims are not fully supported by the filed disclosure, you cannot add new embodiments later to justify breadth. Examiners generally allow clarifying language, prior art references, or resolving inconsistencies, but substantial additions risk being regarded as new matter.

name: Jurisdictional variation on what constitutes new matter (EPO standard)
description: While many jurisdictions share common principles regarding permissible amendments, there are variations. In Europe, matters that are not 'directly and unambiguously derivable by those skilled in the art from the original disclosure' are assumed to be new matters that cannot be introduced after filing.
guidance: Because EPO practice is strict, patent drafters often use extensive multiple dependent claims and explain all possible combinations of elements and features in the description as filed to maximize allowable amendment flexibility.

name: When amending claims, check unity, consistency and support
description: When amending the claims substantially and limiting their scope, examiners may pay particular attention to: (i) Do the amended claims satisfy the requirement of unity of invention? (ii) Will the amended claims be seriously inconsistent with the description, meaning that the description requires corresponding amendment? (iii) Conversely, are all amended claims supported by the description as filed?
guidance: Before filing claim amendments, evaluate these three questions. If the description does require amendment to avoid serious inconsistency, address that. Ensure support for all claim amendments in the originally filed disclosure.

name: Modifying the stated problem/effect must be supported by the original disclosure
description: Upon receipt of an office action raising lack of inventive step, a drafter may seek to restrict claims and revise the stated problem to emphasize a particular effect obtainable by the restricted invention that the cited prior art does not achieve. Such modification of the 'problem to be solved' is permissible only if that emphasized effect is supported by the original disclosure.
guidance: Only emphasize effects that are deducible from the application as filed; otherwise the change may amount to new matter or unsupported amendments.

name: Negative limitations and disclaimers raise new matter issues
description: Amending claims by introducing a negative limitation (e.g., 'excluding X' or 'without performing Y') can raise issues of new matter if the excluded subject matter lacks support in the application as filed. For example, excluding a particular species not supported when only a genus was disclosed may introduce new matter.
guidance: Some jurisdictions permit certain disclaimers (e.g., to overcome accidental anticipation or to exclude nonpatentable subject matter), but this varies. Approach negative limitations through the lens of new matter and check jurisdictional rules carefully.

name: Broadening claims during prosecution is limited and jurisdiction-dependent
description: In many jurisdictions, broadening the claim by removing claimed features is permissible during prosecution as long as no new matter is introduced. In Japan, amendment to claim a broader concept or to remove claimed features is not allowed unless such amendments do not add any new technical significance. In some jurisdictions (EPO, China), it is impermissible to delete from an independent claim a feature the application consistently presented as 'essential'.
guidance: Avoid characterizing features in the description as 'essential' or 'indispensable' unless needed, because that may prevent later deletion or broadening. Know national limits on broadening amendments.

name: Adding new claims during prosecution allowed only if no new matter and subject to national rules
description: In many jurisdictions, adding a new claim during prosecution is not prohibited provided no new matter is introduced. Some jurisdictions, however, have special rules limiting addition of claims after certain procedural events.
guidance: Japan: after receiving the first office action, amendments that change the special technical feature are prohibited; after final office action, additions are limited to deletion, narrowing, correction, or clarification. United States: substantial amendments after final are limited to (i) deletion of a claim; (ii) amendments as requested or suggested by the examiner; or (iii) amendments that raise no new issue. Plan claim additions with jurisdictional constraints in mind.

name: Examiners may conduct supplemental searches after claim amendments
description: If the examiner considers it necessary, they may conduct a supplemental search for pertinent prior art, particularly where the applicant amended the claims, taking into account the prior art cited in the first office action.
guidance: Amendments may trigger further prior art discovery and additional office actions if the examiner remains unconvinced. Claims are often assessed under a 'broadest reasonable interpretation' in view of the prior art.

name: Use interviews with examiners strategically and document them
description: Many patent offices allow patent drafters and inventors to speak with the patent examiner about the pending application (an interview). Because official business will be discussed, both parties may be required to submit complete and accurate written descriptions of the interview; these records typically become part of the file history.
guidance: Prepare thoroughly: review the office action and prior art, be ready to explain in clear, concise and persuasive language why the claims are patentable, prepare possible claim amendments to share, and consider bringing the inventor (where permitted) after pre-counseling. Note: examiners typically do not conduct interviews before issuing the first office action.

name: Divisional, continuation and continuation-in-part applications: definitions and strategic uses
description: A divisional application is 'divided' from a parent application and claims only part of the invention set out in the parent; it may retain the parent’s filing and priority dates. In the United States, a continuation application discloses and claims only subject matter disclosed in a parent application and retains the parent’s filing date. A continuation-in-part repeats substantial portions of the parent and adds matter not disclosed in the parent; parts disclosed in the parent get parent's priority date, added matter gets CIP's filing date.
guidance: Use divisionals to pursue withdrawn claims (e.g., after restriction requirements), continuations to pursue variants of claims while keeping parent filing date, and CIPs to claim improvements developed after filing but be aware of priority date limitations for added matter.

name: Opposition proceedings: pre-grant and post-grant challenges and practitioner role
description: Third parties may challenge a patent grant before a court or through administrative opposition mechanisms. In pre-grant opposition, the office publishes claims for public opposition; opposers must argue convincingly (e.g., that the examiner missed key prior art). Applicants may rebut; opposition may be heard by the examiner or a special panel, and outcomes can be appealed.
guidance: Be aware some parties strategically use oppositions to delay or narrow competitors’ patents. Patent drafters typically prepare opposition documents and should counsel clients that a notice of intended grant does not ensure immediate issuance without further delay.

name: Prepare a complete disclosure at filing as paramount
description: Drafting a complete disclosure of the invention prior to filing is of paramount importance because later amendments are constrained by what was originally disclosed and third-party predictability concerns.
guidance: Include sufficient detail, embodiments, and combinations so that future claim narrowing or selections are supported. Anticipate possible examiner rejections and provide material that could support later allowable claim sets.

name: Examples of what constitutes intentional delay (not unintentional)
description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action by the applicant is not 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b).
guidance: Examples of deliberate courses of action that preclude a finding of unintentional delay include: (A) applicant does not consider the claims patentable over outstanding references; (B) applicant considers allowed/ patentable claims not broad enough to justify expense; (C) applicant considers any patent not worth the expense; (D) applicant does not wish to maintain interest in obtaining the patent; (E) applicant seeks to defer patent fees and prosecution expenses. A later change of mind or change in circumstances does not render a prior deliberate abandonment 'unintentional.'

name: Prosecution beyond procedural compliance (creative, proactive approaches)
description: We don’t just go through the motions of patent prosecution. By thinking outside of the box, we stress creative and proactive approaches to accelerating and improving prosecution results.
guidance: Assess whether counsel offers proactive strategies (e.g., creative claim drafting, tactical filings, accelerated prosecution techniques) rather than merely responding to office actions. Examples: participation in pilot programs, examiner meetings.

name: Technical and scientific depth of attorneys
description: Our attorneys have strong technical and scientific backgrounds that enable us to deeply understand the details of our clients’ technologies, which allow us to craft an individualized patent strategy for each client. Many have doctoral, medical, or masters degrees, and many have years of industry experience prior to becoming an attorney.
guidance: Measure the technical credentials and industry experience of prosecution attorneys as a factor in their ability to understand inventions, draft claims, and interact with examiners and clients. Specialized degrees and prior industry work are cited as important.

name: Individualized patent strategy for each client
description: Strong technical understanding allows us to craft an individualized patent strategy for each client.
guidance: Look for evidence of tailored strategies (rather than cookie-cutter filing), e.g., claims and filing pathways that reflect client business objectives and technology specifics.

name: Creating patents that support stronger litigation outcomes
description: These hybrid teams are able to create stronger patents in the patent office that lead to better litigation results as well as greater insight into defending against patent lawsuits.
guidance: Assess the firm's emphasis on drafting and prosecution choices that anticipate litigation (e.g., claim breadth vs. enforceability, evidence preservation). Look for stated benefits linking prosecution decisions to courtroom performance.

name: Diligence for acquisitions and portfolio management tied to exits
description: Conduct diligence associated with acquisitions, and create prosecution portfolio management strategies tailored around individual exit plans.
guidance: Measure experience doing IP due diligence for M&A, and ability to shape prosecution and portfolio structure to maximize exit value (e.g., claim scope, geographic coverage, term management).

name: Petition scope defines litigation
description: “The petitioner’s contentions . . . define the scope of the litigation all the way from institution through to conclusion.”
guidance: If the Board deems a claim unpatentable on a ground absent from the petition, that can be error. Courts examine whether the Board's final written decision stayed within the grounds and arguments actually presented in the petition (examples: SAS Inst., Koninklijke Philips).

name: Anticipation is a question of fact from the skilled artisan perspective
description: “What a prior art reference discloses is a question of fact.” and “Anticipation is an inquiry viewed from the perspective of one skilled in the art.”
guidance: Whether a reference anticipates a claim limitation depends on what a skilled artisan would understand from the reference (Mettler-Toledo, Wasica). The Federal Circuit will defer to substantial-evidence-supported factual findings about disclosure.

name: Claim construction — 'protected resources' (Board's adopted definition)
description: Board's construction: “[A]n application, an object, a document, a page, a file, executable code, or other computational resource, communication-type resource, etc., identified by a Uniform Resource Locator (URL), or more generally, a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), that can only be accessed by an authenticated and/or authorized user.”
guidance: This specific construction was used to assess whether a prior-art reference disclosed ‘protected resources’; the construction can be outcome-determinative for anticipation/obviousness analyses.

name: Precision in claim-to-prior-art mapping for corresponding circumstances
description: To show a claim limitation is taught by a prior art reference, the prior art must disclose the limitation in the same circumstance recited by the claim (e.g., requesting user attributes from the first system 'in response to a determination' that the second system lacks sufficient information).
guidance: Two claims that are textually similar can be differently patentable depending on the exact actor and circumstance claimed (example: sending a request to the first system vs. sending to the fourth system); the Board must find the prior art discloses the same temporal/causal circumstance.

name: Use of court decisions to support conventionality
description: Examiners should be careful to ensure the claim limitations before the examiner are the same as those found to be well-understood, routine, conventional by the courts.
guidance: The additional elements under examination should be recited in the same manner (same high level of generality) as in those court decisions; similarity is not enough. Court decisions do not imply that all computer functions are conventional or that a generic computer performing generic functions is necessarily ineligible. See DDR Holdings and MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more.

name: ¶ 7.05.016 — Nonstatutory (Directed to a Judicial Exception without Inventive Concept)
description: Form paragraph to explain that the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more and to identify and explain the exception and why additional elements fail to amount to significantly more.
guidance: Populate brackets: (1) identify whether claim directed to law of nature, natural phenomenon (including product of nature), or abstract idea; (2) identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain why it is an exception (e.g., map to abstract idea groupings in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)); (3) explain why the combination of additional elements fails to integrate the exception into a practical application; (4) identify additional elements and explain why, separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more (inventive concept). Provide examples (e.g., generic computer elements merely implement idea on a computer; data-gathering steps are extra-solution activity; placing a product of nature in a test tube is nominal).

name: Burden and options for applicant responding to eligibility rejection
description: After examiner identifies why a claim is directed to an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to either amend the claim, present persuasive arguments, and/or submit evidence (per MPEP § 716.01 and 37 CFR 1.132).
guidance: Applicant may: (i) amend claims to add/modify elements so claim amounts to significantly more or integrates into a practical application; (ii) present persuasive arguments why rejection is in error; (iii) submit evidence traversing rejection. Examiner must carefully consider all arguments and evidence and, if claims amended, determine broadest reasonable interpretation and repeat eligibility analysis.

name: Examiner rebuttal and explanation where rejection maintained
description: If applicant properly challenges the examiner's findings but the examiner maintains the rejection, a rebuttal must be provided in the next Office action.
guidance: Appropriate rebuttal examples: (1) explain why the abstract idea identified is similar to the concept in a cited case if applicant's challenge to tentative abstract idea not persuasive; (2) if applicant rebuts assertion of conventionality, reevaluate and consider providing supporting evidence or affidavit/declaration (37 CFR 1.104(d)(2)) if official notice was taken; (3) where applicant amends to add generic computer/components claiming 'specially programmed' machine, analyze whether elements integrate exception—mere addition of generic computer is insufficient (see Alice); (4) if applicant argues lack of preemption/specificity, reconsider Step 2A (is claim improvement to computer or other technology?) and then Step 2B to evaluate inventive concept in combination.

name: Utility examination — initial steps
description: Office personnel shall read the claims and the supporting written description to determine what the applicant has claimed, noting any specific embodiments, and ensure the claims define statutory subject matter.
guidance: If at any time it is readily apparent that the claimed invention has a well-established utility, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility. Ensure claims are process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvement thereof.

name: When to reject for lack of utility and associated 112(a) rejection
description: If no assertion of specific and substantial utility made by applicant is credible, and the claimed invention does not have a readily apparent well-established utility, reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112 first paragraph) for failing to teach how to use the invention.
guidance: Rejecting under both statutes shifts burden to applicant to: (i) explicitly identify a specific and substantial utility; and (ii) provide evidence that one of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that the identified specific and substantial utility was well-established at filing. Examiner should ensure adequate nexus between submitted evidence and properties of the claimed subject matter as disclosed in the application as filed.

name: Documentation and evidence for utility rejections
description: Any rejection based on lack of utility should include a detailed explanation why the claimed invention has no specific and substantial credible utility and, whenever possible, documentary evidence to support the factual basis for the prima facie showing.
guidance: Documentary evidence can include scientific/technical journals, treatises, books, or U.S./foreign patents. If documentary evidence is unavailable, the examiner should explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions. The examiner must evaluate all relevant evidence of record when considering applicant responses.

name: Dismissal because no brief was filed
description: If no brief is filed within the time prescribed by 37 CFR 41.37, the appeal stands dismissed by operation of the rule.
guidance: Do not dismiss until any available extension to file the brief has expired (e.g., up to 5 months of extension under 37 CFR 1.136(a)), unless appellant specifically withdraws the appeal as to rejected claims. Applications with no allowed claims will be abandoned. Claims indicated as allowable except for dependency from rejected claims are to be treated as if they were rejected. If an amendment obviously places the application in condition for allowance (with supervisory concurrence per MPEP § 1002.02(d)), the primary examiner may recommend entry of the amendment. Examiner should follow the provided examples (A–D) about canceling rejected claims and issuing application on allowed claims, or holding the application abandoned where appropriate. If formal matters remain, the examiner may handle them by examiner's amendment (MPEP § 1302.04) or use form paragraph 12.209 to require corrections within a shortened statutory period; prosecution is otherwise closed except as to such formal matters.

name: Form paragraph 12.209 — Appeal Dismissed; allowed claims with formal matters remaining
description: Template/form paragraph to notify applicant that the appeal stands dismissed, that allowed claim(s) will be passed to issue provided certain formal matters are corrected, and to set a shortened statutory period for correction.
guidance: Use when formal matters cannot be handled by examiner's amendment. Insert mailing date and describe formal matters to be corrected in bracket 2. Require corrections within TWO (2) MONTHS to avoid abandonment; extensions under 37 CFR 1.136 may be granted but cannot extend reply beyond statutory maximum SIX MONTHS (35 U.S.C. 133). Include Examiner Notes: use only if notice of appeal filed on/after Jan 23, 2012; form-specific bracket instructions; reminder that claims allowable except for dependency are considered rejected (see MPEP § 1215.04).

name: Treatment of claims 'allowable except for dependency' (dependent-claim rule)
description: Claims indicated as containing allowable subject matter but objected to as being dependent upon a rejected claim are to be considered as if they were rejected.
guidance: This rule is reiterated in multiple dismissal/issuance contexts: dependent claims objected as allowable because of dependency are treated as rejected for purposes of abandonment/dismissal and for determining whether any claims remain allowable. Examiners should follow MPEP § 1215.04 when deciding whether to cancel, convert, or hold the application abandoned due to such dependent-claim situations.

name: Office procedure following decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (mandate entry)
description: After the Federal Circuit decides an appeal, the court issues a certified copy of its decision (the 'mandate') which is entered in the file; the date the mandate was issued marks the conclusion of the appeal (termination of proceedings per 35 U.S.C. 120).
guidance: Actions depend on whether all claims were rejected, some claims allowed, remand required, or prosecution reopened: - All claims rejected: proceedings considered terminated on mandate issue date; application ordinarily not open to amendment or revival by USPTO (send notice of abandonment unless mandate indicates further action). - Some claims allowed: proceedings terminated only as to claims still rejected; dependent claims previously objected as allowable because of dependency are treated as rejected. Examiner should either (1) convert dependent claims to independent form by examiner's amendment, cancel claims in which rejection was affirmed, and issue application; or (2) set a 2-month time limit for appellant to rewrite dependent claims in independent form (extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) available). If no timely reply, application is abandoned. If formal matters remain, examiner should promptly handle them (examiner's amendment or setting a 2-month shortened statutory period). Examiner should set forth reasons for allowance, referring to and incorporating appellate brief and court decision (see MPEP § 1302.14).

name: Test for whether reissue claims are for the same invention
description: The entire disclosure, not just the claim(s), is considered in determining what the patentee objectively intended as his or her invention. The proper test is an essentially factual inquiry confined to the objective intent manifested by the original patent.
guidance: Claims presented in a reissue application are considered to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 251 that the claims be 'for the invention disclosed in the original patent' where: (A) the claims presented in the reissue application are described in the original patent specification and enabled such that 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph is satisfied; and (B) nothing in the original patent specification indicates an intent not to claim the subject matter of the claims presented in the reissue application. Some disclosure (description and enablement) in the original patent should evidence that applicant intended to claim or considered the material now claimed to be his or her invention.

name: Two-step test for recapture
description: First determine whether and in what aspect the reissue claims are broader than the patent claims. Second, determine whether the broader aspects relate to surrendered subject matter by reviewing prosecution history for arguments/changes made to overcome prior art rejections.
guidance: Broadening includes omission of a limitation. To determine surrender look to prosecution history (arguments, claim amendments) made in effort to overcome rejections (see Mentor, Clement, Ball). Each omitted or broadened limitation must be reviewed for relation to surrendered subject matter.

name: Examiner review for presence of broadening
description: In every reissue application, the examiner must first review each claim for the presence of broadening, as compared with the scope of the claims of the patent to be reissued.
guidance: A reissue claim is broadened where some limitation of the patent claims is no longer required in the reissue claim. If a claim is in fact broadened, the examiner must next determine whether the broader aspects relate to previously surrendered subject matter. Identify omitted/broadened limitations and analyze each limitation of the patent claims omitted or broadened in the reissue claim.

name: Criteria for determining surrendered subject matter
description: If the limitation now being omitted or broadened was originally presented/argued/stated in the original application to make the claims allowable over a rejection or objection, the omitted limitation relates to subject matter previously surrendered.
guidance: Review original application prosecution history (rejections and applicant's arguments). An amendment added to obviate a rejection can establish surrender even without explicit argument. Examiner must look for specific, limitation-directed statements rather than boilerplate statements about claims generally.

name: Boilerplate arguments insufficient to show surrender
description: General statements regarding the claims as a whole (e.g., 'the limitations of claims 1-7 distinguish the claims from the teachings of the prior art') are not sufficient by themselves to establish surrender and recapture.
guidance: The argument that the claim limitation defined over the rejection must have been specific as to the limitation; a general 'boiler plate' sentence will not be sufficient to establish surrender.

name: Argument alone may effect surrender
description: Surrender of claimed subject matter may occur by arguments made during the prosecution of the original patent application even where there was no claim change.
guidance: Following Hester, examiners should review prosecution history for persuasive applicant arguments that limit claim scope; argument-only surrender must be considered when deciding recapture rejections.

name: Recapture rule bars reclaiming previously cancelled subject matter
description: The recapture rule bars the patentee from acquiring through reissue claims that are, in all aspects, of the same scope as, or are broader in scope than, those claims canceled from the original application to obtain a patent.
guidance: If reissue claims are as broad as or broader than canceled original-application claims in aspects germane to prior art rejections, recapture applies (Ball Corp. and related cases).

name: Reissue claims narrower in all aspects permitted (timing for certain broadenings)
description: The patentee is free to acquire, through reissue, claims that are narrower in scope in all aspects than claims canceled from the original application to obtain a patent.
guidance: If the reissue claims are narrower than the canceled claims but broader than the issued patent claims, reissue must be sought within 2 years after the grant of the original patent. See MPEP § 1412.03 for broadening claims timing rules.

name: Mixed broader and narrower aspects — avoid recapture if unrelated
description: Reissue claims that are broader in certain aspects and narrower in others vis-à-vis claims canceled from the original application may avoid the effect of the recapture rule if the claims are broader in a way that does not attempt to reclaim what was surrendered earlier.
guidance: If the broadening aspect relates to surrendered subject matter, determine whether any newly added narrowing limitation modifies the claim such that scope no longer results in recapture. If narrowing limits the claim to avoid recapture, explain reasons of record why no recapture exists; if not, reject for recapture.

name: Reissue to take advantage of 35 U.S.C. 103(b)
description: A patentee may file a reissue application to permit consideration of process claims which qualify for 35 U.S.C. 103(b) treatment if the patent is entitled to the benefit and the omission was an error without deceptive intent.
guidance: Addition of process claims will generally be considered a broadening of the invention and must be applied for within two years of the grant of the original patent. See Ex Parte Wikdahl and MPEP § 1412.03.

name: Reissue for 'article' claims (computer-readable medium) — timing and broadening
description: A patentee may file a reissue application to permit consideration of article of manufacture claims which are functional descriptive material stored on a computer-readable medium, where these article claims correspond to the patented process or machine claims; the error must have been without deceptive intent.
guidance: The addition of these 'article' claims will generally be considered a broadening of the invention and must be applied for within two years of the grant of the original patent. See Ex Parte Wikdahl and MPEP § 1412.03.

name: Form-and-examiner requirements when rejecting for recapture (¶14.17)
description: Reissue claims which recapture surrendered subject matter should be rejected using form paragraph 14.17.
guidance: Examiner Note: explain specifics of why recapture exists, including identification of the omitted/broadened claim limitations that provide the 'broadening aspect' and where in the original application the narrowed claim scope was presented/argued to obviate a rejection/objection. See MPEP § 1412.02.

name: Meaning of 'broadened reissue claim'
description: A broadened reissue claim is a claim which enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent, i.e., a claim which is greater in scope than each and every claim of the original patent. A claim of a reissue application enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent if it is broader in at least one respect, even though it may be narrower in other respects.
guidance: A claim is broadened if it contains within its scope any conceivable product or process which would not have infringed the original patent claims. If any amended or newly added claim reads on something the original claims do not, it is broadened (Tillotson, In re Ruth, In re Rogoff).

name: Addition of combination claims vs subcombination claims
description: The addition of combination claims in a reissue application where only subcombination claims were present in the original patent could be a broadening of the invention.
guidance: Analyze whether the added combination claim contains every limitation of the subcombination of any claim of the original patent. If the combination contains every limitation of the subcombination, infringement of the combination results in infringement of the subcombination and broadening may not exist; otherwise broadening exists.

name: Consideration of 35 U.S.C. 271(g) (broadening-indirect infringement)
description: Adding a limitation to process claims (e.g., converting a claim to an intermediate into a claim to a final product) can provide an element of broadening because it may allow invocation of 35 U.S.C. 271(g) (liability for importation of products made by a patented process).
guidance: Examiners should be careful in chemical/process cases to check for this unique type of broadening: even an added step that appears narrowing may broaden practical protection by creating new infringers under 271(g).

name: Dependent claim enlarged but not a broadened reissue claim
description: A claim that is broadened in a reissue as compared to its scope in the patent is not a broadened reissue claim if it is narrower than, or equal in scope to, any other claim which appears in the patent.
guidance: Example: dependent claim 2 may be broadened via reissue but if independent claim 1 is not broadened (and claim 2 must contain all limitations of claim 1), claim 2 is not a broadened reissue claim.

name: When broadened claims may be presented — timing and intent requirements
description: A broadened claim can be presented within two years from the grant of the original patent in a reissue application. A broadened claim can also be presented after two years if a broadening was indicated in the reissue application (or a parent reissue) within two years.
guidance: A reissue application filed on the 2-year anniversary date is timely. Cases: In re Graff, In re Fotland (oath/declaration indicating desire to seek broadened claims within two years required), In re Bennett (correction of declaration execution), In re Doll (timely indication in oath allows subsequent broadening). Examiners should check for improper presentation of broadened claims filed outside the two-year period.

name: Reissue oath/declaration content and signature rules for inventorship correction
description: The reissue oath or declaration must state that the applicant believes the original patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid through error in inventorship and that such error arose without deceptive intention; it must comply with 37 CFR 1.175 and 1.63.
guidance: If the reissue does not seek to enlarge claims, the reissue oath may be made and sworn to by the assignee of the entire interest (37 CFR 1.172). If a reissue to correct inventorship also changes claims to enlarge scope, inventors' signatures are required; if an inventor refuses, a petition under 37 CFR 1.47 may be used. Petitions under 1.48 or 1.324 should not be used in a reissue application; if filed, they should be dismissed and fees refunded, and material considered under 1.175 if compliant.

name: Content requirement of reissue oath/declaration (general)
description: The reissue oath or declaration, in addition to complying with § 1.63, must state that the applicant believes the original patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than the patentee had the right to claim, stating at least one error relied upon as the basis for reissue.
guidance: This is a statutory and regulatory content requirement for a reissue filing under 37 CFR 1.175; the applicant must identify at least one error being relied upon.

name: Selective prosecution defense standard
description: To prevail on selective prosecution, a respondent must show (1) he was singled out while similarly situated violators were not pursued, and (2) the OED Director pursued action invidiously or in bad faith (based on impermissible considerations such as race, religion, or to prevent exercise of constitutional rights).
guidance: Evidence of mere selectivity, without proof of invidious or bad-faith motivation, cannot sustain a selective-prosecution claim (citing Smithfield, Hendrickson). The nonmoving party must produce specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial.

name: Prosecution bar (scope and effect)
description: Absent written consent from the Producing Party, any individual who receives access to 'HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – ATTORNEYS' EYES ONLY' [Optional: or 'HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – SOURCE CODE'] information shall not be involved in the prosecution of patents or patent applications relating to [insert subject matter ...], including without limitation the patents asserted in this action and any patent or application claiming priority to or otherwise related to the patents asserted in this action, before any foreign or domestic agency, including the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
guidance: For purposes of this paragraph, 'prosecution' includes directly or indirectly drafting, amending, advising, or otherwise affecting the scope or maintenance of patent claims. 'Prosecution' does not include representing a party challenging a patent before a domestic or foreign agency (e.g., reissue protest, ex parte reexamination or inter partes reexamination). The Prosecution Bar begins when access is first received and ends two (2) years after final termination of the action (unless alternative language is used).

name: Definitions and designation procedures for Confidential and Highly Confidential
description: Definitions: 'Confidential' information is information concerning business operations, processes, and technical and development information ... disclosure of which is likely to harm competitive position. 'Highly Confidential' information is trade secrets and plans more sensitive or strategic than Confidential information, the disclosure of which is likely to significantly harm competitive position. Designation: designate by clearly marking on its face as 'CONFIDENTIAL' or 'HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL'; deposition designations may be made on the record or in writing within 14 days after receipt of the transcript.
guidance: A failure to designate does not constitute forfeiture of a claim of confidentiality as to other materials. A designating person may withdraw a designation by written notification. If a party disputes a designation, it must notify the producer in writing identifying specific documents and propose a new designation; parties must meet and confer; unless producer moves to maintain the designation within 14 days, the proposed new designation will be applied. The producer bears the burden to prove the designation.

name: Statutory one-year grace for novelty (paragraph 28.2(1)(a))
description: Paragraph 28.2(1)(a) of the Canadian Patent Act: the claimed invention in the Canadian patent application must not have been disclosed more than one year before the filing date by the applicant, or by a person who obtained knowledge, directly or indirectly, from the applicant, in such a manner that the subject-matter became available to the public in Canada or elsewhere.
guidance: Key points: (a) the provision creates a one-year grace period for disclosures made by the applicant (or those who obtained knowledge from the applicant); (b) the one-year period runs from the Canadian filing date (not the priority date); (c) for PCT national phase entries, the Canadian filing date is deemed to be the PCT international filing date. Practitioners should note the precise statutory wording when assessing whether a disclosure falls within the grace window.

name: AIA (U.S.) changes and cross-border filing strategies
description: The AIA introduces changes to U.S. §102 including a one-year grace period with no geographic restrictions and no limitation to forms of disclosure; however, under the AIA the U.S. grace period is calculated back from the priority date, not the U.S. filing date.
guidance: Filing strategies arising from the difference: (a) file in Canada within one year of the public disclosure (required by Canadian law) and then file the corresponding U.S. application a year later claiming priority back to the Canadian application — this can delay the start of U.S. patent term; (b) consider accelerated examination in Canada and use favorable Canadian allowance to leverage the Patent Prosecution Highway in the U.S. Practitioners should account for the different reference dates (Canadian filing date vs U.S. priority date) when docketing cross-border filings.

name: Construction of specification
description: Specification to be construed according to ordinary meaning; with reference to state of knowledge when it was prepared; benevolent construction; both words and drawings looked at; prior specifications as showing anticipation; evidence to explain technical terms; patentee's evidence as to meaning of specification inadmissible; claims, construction of, with reference to whole context; when two meanings possible; construed as merely appendant.
guidance: Interpretation relies on ordinary meaning and the contemporaneous state of knowledge; read specification as a whole (words + drawings); courts may adopt a benevolent construction; prior specifications can show anticipation; technical terms may be explained by evidence but the patentee's own testimony on meaning is inadmissible; claims are construed in context and, where ambiguous, may be treated as appendant.

name: Requisites for letters patent to be valid
description: Letters patent must show that the invention possesses utility, display novelty, show some measure of ingenuity, that the patentee is the true and first inventor (unless communicated from abroad), and that the specification be sufficient.
guidance: A valid patent requires utility (usefulness), novelty (newness), inventive contribution above triviality, correct ownership/entitlement, and a sufficient specification (complete specification describing and claiming the invention).

name: Sufficiency of specification / disclosure
description: Complete specification must describe the invention sufficiently; question whether specification describes material with sufficient accuracy is for the court; complete specification should disclose improvements (in complicated machines point them out distinctly); if complete specification describes or claims invention other than that in provisional it is a ground of opposition.
guidance: Specifications must enable the skilled reader to practise the invention; divergence between provisional and complete specifications can be a basis for opposition; courts decide sufficiency and identity with prior specifications.

name: Claims construction
description: Construction of claims with reference to whole context; where two meanings possible, principles for construction; claims may be construed as merely appendant.
guidance: Claims are read in light of specification and drawings; ambiguities resolved by reference to specification and the state of knowledge; some claims may be interpreted narrowly as appendant or limited to embodiments described.

name: Opposition to grant of patent — grounds and procedure
description: Oppositions must be given within prescribed time (notice within two months of advertisement of acceptance) and state grounds; evidence in opposition by statutory declarations; onus of proof lies on opponent; comptroller may hear parties and may allow amendment in notice of opposition; grounds of opposition are limited (1) applicant obtained invention from opponent or legal representative, (2) invention already patented in this country on a prior application date, (3) complete specification describes or claims an invention other than that in the provisional and such other invention is subject of opponent's application.
guidance: Opposition practice is formal: timely notice, stated grounds, statutory-declaration evidence, possible amendment, hearing before Comptroller, limited grounds, and rules regulate proceedings; in cases of doubt patent may be granted.

name: Extension of letters patent — evidence and accounts required
description: Petitioner should produce all material facts; accounts must be full, clear, unreserved and properly proved; what profits must be shown and what deductions may be made are specified; deductions claimed should appear in petition or accounts.
guidance: Financial proof is central to extension petitions: full account of profits derived from the patent, with proper proof and disclosure of claimed deductions; failure to present adequate accounts may defeat extension.

name: Opposition grounds — three main grounds
description: Grounds of opposition to grant: (1) applicant obtained invention from opponent or from person of whom he is legal representative; (2) invention patented in this country on application of prior date; (3) complete specification describes or claims invention other than that in provisional and such other invention is subject of opponent's application.
guidance: Opponents must have standing/interest; oppositions may be founded even on expired prior patents; disclaiming clauses may be required; procedural rules (timing, statutory declarations) are strict.

name: Particulars of breaches and objections in infringement actions
description: Particulars of breaches and of objections must be delivered in actions for infringement (and may be required in actions for threats); particulars may be amended; insufficient particulars may be ordered to be made more specific; evidence outside particulars not admitted except by leave.
guidance: Claimants must plead and particularise alleged infringing acts and objections; failure to particularise can limit admissible evidence at trial and can attract costs.

name: Performance/error rate threshold as a basis for marginal/unacceptable rating
description: Performance ratings in the 'patentability' quality element turn on measured error rates; the decision notes that an oral warning was issued when an examiner's error rate was 18% (unacceptable) and that to achieve at least a marginal rating an error rate must not exceed a specified maximum (the decision references 'requiring an error rate not to exceed 7%').
guidance: High error rates (examples in the record: 18%, 20%) justify marginal/unacceptable patentability ratings. An applicant's admission of exceeding the maximum error rate undermines claims for waiver. The Director will not disregard such error-rate-based ratings merely because the absolute number of allowances was low.

name: Duty to investigate entitlement to small entity status
description: Applicants need to do a complete and thorough investigation of all facts and circumstances before determining and asserting entitlement to small entity status; where entitlement is uncertain it should not be claimed.
guidance: Investigation should include consulting co-inventors about assignments/licensing and, for business concerns, review of size standards in 13 CFR 121.801–121.805. Costs of investigation may outweigh benefits; the person asserting should be in a position to know the facts and must be able to unequivocally self-certify.

name: First proposed amendment after final — examiner consideration and explanation
description: The first proposed amendment after final action in a reexamination proceeding will be given sufficient consideration to determine whether it places all the claims in condition where they are patentable and/or whether the issues on appeal are reduced or simplified.
guidance: Unless the proposed amendment is entered in its entirety, the examiner will briefly explain the reasons for not entering a proposed amendment (e.g., if the claims as amended present a new issue requiring further consideration or search, the new issue should be identified and a brief explanation provided). Patent owner should be notified if portions of the amendment would be entered if submitted separately.

name: Appeal brief content and formatting (37 CFR 41.37)
description: Appellant shall file a brief of the authorities and arguments relied on to maintain the appeal, including a summary of claimed subject matter which must refer to the specification by page and line number, and to the drawing, if any, by reference characters, and a copy of the claims involved.
guidance: Only one copy of the appeal brief is required. In reexamination, copy of claims on appeal must include all underlining and bracketing as required by 37 CFR 1.530(f) to reflect changes made during reexamination. Any new claims added in reexamination should be completely underlined. Where a third-party requester exists, a copy of the brief must be served on that requester. The brief and all appeal papers should indicate the art unit and reexamination control number.

name: Dismissal for failure to timely file notice of appeal or fee
description: If the patent owner does not timely file a notice of appeal and/or the appropriate appeal fee, the patent owner will be notified that the appeal is dismissed.
guidance: Form PTOL-468 may be used to notify the patent owner that the appeal is dismissed. The reexamination prosecution is then terminated and a NIRC will subsequently be issued indicating the status of the claims at the time of final rejection.

name: Specification must enable the full scope of the invention
description: “The specification must enable the full scope of the invention as defined by its claims.” (Slip op. at 13.)
guidance: If a patent claims an entire class of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class. The Court emphasized: “the more a party claims, the broader the monopoly it demands, the more it must enable.” This principle applies across technology areas (telegraphs, glues, antibodies).

name: Genus claims require more than a few narrow working examples
description: Claims to a broad genus cannot be supported solely by a small number of working examples purporting to fall within that genus.
guidance: In Amgen, claiming millions of antibodies while disclosing only 26 sequences was held insufficient. A specification must provide adequate guidance beyond narrow examples to enable the full claimed class; reliance solely on a small representative set is an inadequate basis for a broad monopoly.

name: A few examples may suffice only if a general quality running through the class is disclosed
description: “It may suffice to give an example (or a few examples) if the specification also discloses ‘some general quality . . . running through’ the class that gives it ‘a peculiar fitness for the particular purpose.’” (Slip op. at 13.)
guidance: Courts will accept limited examples when the specification identifies a unifying property or 'general quality' across the claimed class that enables practitioners to recognize or make other members of the class without undue experimentation.

name: Cannot force 'painstaking experimentation' to make the invention
description: Forcing a scientist to engage in 'painstaking experimentation' to see what works is not enablement; it is more like providing 'a hunting license.' (Slip op. at 18.)
guidance: If the path from disclosure to practicing the full claimed scope requires extensive, unpredictable trial-and-error, courts are likely to find lack of enablement. The boundary between reasonable and 'painstaking' experimentation is evaluated case-by-case.

name: Enablement depends on the state of the art and the nature of the invention
description: What counts as adequate disclosure and a reasonable degree of experimentation 'will depend on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.'
guidance: Assessment requires technical judgment about whether, given the contemporaneous state of knowledge, the specification provides sufficient guidance to make and use the claimed scope without undue effort. If success is an 'uncertain prospect given the state of the art,' enablement is less likely to be satisfied.

name: Courts may decide enablement as a matter of law where no reasonable factfinder could find adequacy
description: The Federal Circuit held that 'no reasonable factfinder could conclude' Amgen provided adequate guidance beyond the 26 working examples, leading to a decision as a matter of law that the claims are not enabled.
guidance: Enablement can be resolved at summary judgment or on the pleadings if the record shows that even taking evidence in the light most favorable, the specification cannot support the claimed scope. Practitioners should be aware of the risk of early termination of claims on enablement grounds.

name: Specification need not disclose every embodiment
description: Section 112 does not require that the specification describe how to make and use every single embodiment within a claimed class; examples can be sufficient in appropriate circumstances.
guidance: This is a limiting principle to balance the 'full scope' rule: courts will consider whether the examples plus disclosed general principles are enough to enable the rest without undue experimentation.

name: Appeal process
description: An appeal can be filed against decisions taken by the Trilateral Offices; applicants can appeal decisions to reject an application or revoke a patent, opponents can appeal decisions to maintain a patent.
guidance: Procedure: examining department first studies arguments and may revise decision; if not, case goes to a Board of Appeal which may decide or refer back. JPO specifics: appeal examiners examine supplementary reasons; if amendments to description/claims/drawings were made within 30 days from filing date of an appeal against refusal, the examiner re-examines the amendment before forwarding to appeal examiners.

name: Determination of unity not affected by manner of claiming
description: The determination whether a group of inventions is so linked as to form a single general inventive concept shall be made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim. (PCT Rule 13.3)
guidance: Unity analysis looks to substance, not claim drafting form; alternatives within one claim can still present lack of unity if they are distinct embodiments without a unifying inventive concept.

name: Dependent claims permitted despite potentially being separate inventions
description: It is permitted to include in the same international application a reasonable number of dependent claims claiming specific forms of the invention claimed in an independent claim, even where the features of any dependent claim could be considered as constituting in themselves an invention. (PCT Rule 13.4)
guidance: Dependent claims that add specific features may be retained with the independent claim if the independent claim itself satisfies unity; the presence of potentially patentable dependent claims does not by itself create lack of unity.

name: 37 CFR combinations of categories that confer unity
description: An international or national-stage application containing claims to different categories will be considered to have unity if the claims are drawn to one of the following combinations: (1) product and process specially adapted for the manufacture of said product; (2) product and process of use of said product; (3) product, process specially adapted for manufacture, and use; (4) process and apparatus/means specifically designed for carrying out the process; (5) product, process specially adapted for manufacture, and apparatus/means for carrying out the process. (37 CFR 1.475(b))
guidance: These specific category-combination permutations are treated as having unity provided the required relationships (e.g., 'specially adapted', 'specifically designed') exist in the claimed subject matter.

name: Unity determination: a priori vs a posteriori and practical approach
description: Lack of unity may be evident a priori (before considering prior art) or a posteriori (after considering prior art). Examiners should avoid raising or maintaining lack of unity on a narrow, literal, or academic approach and should apply a broad, practical assessment of interdependence in relation to the state of the art, giving the benefit of any doubt to the applicant.
guidance: Use practical analysis rather than overly technical/legalistic parsing; consider examples (e.g., independent claims to A+X, A+Y, X+Y lack unity a priori; A+X and A+Y have unity a priori unless A is shown to be known in which case lack of unity may arise a posteriori).

name: Genus/species and combination/subcombination guidance
description: Genus claims that avoid the prior art are acceptable provided the genus is directed only to alternatives of a similar nature; combination/subcombination situations similarly cause no objection if subcombination claim avoids prior art and the combination claim includes all features of the subcombination.
guidance: To determine 'similar nature' for genus/species situations, apply the Markush / subsection III.B principles; examine whether alternatives are of similar technical character and share the unifying features.

name: Markush practice criteria (alternatives of similar nature)
description: For Markush groupings (single claim defining alternatives), the requirement of technical interrelationship and same/corresponding special technical features is met when the alternatives are of a similar nature. For chemical compounds, this is satisfied when (A) all alternatives have a common property or activity, and (B) either (1) a significant structural element is shared by all alternatives or (2) all alternatives belong to a recognized class of chemical compounds in the art. (subsection III.B)
guidance: Assess common property/activity and whether a common structural element is structurally significant given prior art, or whether members belong to a recognized class with expected similar behavior. If at least one Markush alternative is not novel, unity should be reconsidered by the examiner.

name: Required parts of a nonprovisional utility application
description: A nonprovisional utility patent application must include a specification (including a description and at least one claim), drawings when necessary, an oath or declaration, and the prescribed filing, search, and examination fees.
guidance: Specification, claims and abstract constitute the 'complete specification.' Other items (sequence listings, large tables, computer listings) included when applicable. Claims must begin on a new page.

name: Patent Center and electronic filing format (DOCX) requirements and surcharges
description: Patent Center accepts electronic documents formatted in DOCX and allows the complete specification (description, claims, abstract) to be filed in one DOCX file. Beginning January 17, 2024, the description, claims, and abstract must be filed in DOCX format to avoid a non-DOCX surcharge.
guidance: Non-DOCX surcharge is $430 (reduced for small/micro entities). Other application documents (drawings, hand-signed declarations) may be scanned as PDF. Fee per 37 CFR § 1.16(u) applies when written description, claims, and/or abstract do not conform to DOCX requirements. Applicants used to filing PDF specifications must switch to DOCX for nonprovisional filings on/after Jan 17, 2024.

name: Document formatting: page size, margins, spacing, font and numbering
description: Each document must have a top margin of at least 2 cm (3/4 inch), a left margin of at least 2.5 cm (1 inch), right and bottom margins of at least 2 cm (3/4 inch). DOCX document size should be 8.5x11 inches or A4. The specification must have lines 1.5 or double-spaced in a single column; text must be a nonscript font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier), preferably font size 12. Pages must be numbered consecutively starting with page one (centrally located above or below text).
guidance: These formatting requirements apply to the specification (description, claims, abstract). It is desirable to indent paragraphs and number paragraphs (e.g., [0001], [0002], etc.). Failure to meet format requirements can trigger surcharges or nonconforming status.

name: Order and minimum elements of a complete application
description: A complete nonprovisional utility patent application should contain elements arranged in the following order: Utility Patent Application Transmittal Form or Transmittal Letter; Appropriate Fees; Application Data Sheet (ADS); Specification (description, at least one claim, abstract); Drawings (when necessary); Executed Oath or Declaration; Nucleotide and Amino Acid Sequence Listing (if necessary); Large Tables or Computer Listings (if necessary).
guidance: Descriptions of each element are provided in the guide. Omitting required elements can result in 'Notice of Incomplete Application' and loss of filing date in certain circumstances.

name: Application size fee and excess claims fees
description: For electronic filings, an application size fee is due if total number of specification and drawing pages exceeds 133; for paper filings, size fee due if pages exceed 100. Excess claim fees are due if there are more than three independent claims or more than 20 total claims.
guidance: Fees are subject to change; consult current fee schedule. Paper filings also incur the non-electronic filing fee referenced above.

name: Fee discounts based on Small Entity and Micro Entity status
description: Small entity status under 37 CFR § 1.27(a) reduces most patent fees by 60 percent; micro entity status under 37 CFR § 1.29(a) or (d) reduces fees by 80 percent.
guidance: Applicants must determine appropriateness before asserting status and paying reduced fees. Small entity may be indicated by checking a box on the transmittal form; micro entity requires specific certification forms (PTO/SB/15A or PTO/SB/15B) and detailed certifications. Recommendation: use USPTO micro entity certification forms when claiming micro entity status.

name: Application Data Sheet (ADS) submission and timing
description: Submission of an ADS should be routine and is required in certain instances. For applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012, any domestic benefit claim(s) and any foreign priority claim(s) must be made in an ADS within four months from filing or 16 months from the filing date of the prior application, whichever is later.
guidance: Form PTO/AIA/14 is the USPTO's ADS form. See 37 CFR § 1.76 and MPEP § 601.05. Corrected ADS must include underlined text for insertions and strike-through or brackets for deletions. Certain changes cannot be made by corrected ADS alone (e.g., named inventors, correspondence address, foreign priority/domestic benefit information) and must comply with specific CFR provisions.

name: Specification: written description, enablement, best mode and claim placement
description: The specification must include a written description of the invention and the manner and process of making and using the invention that concludes with the claims. The specification must be in clear, full, concise, and exact terms to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention. The best mode contemplated by the inventor must be set forth. Claims must begin on a new page.
guidance: For inventions involving computer programming, program listings may be submitted per 37 CFR § 1.96(b) and (c). Except for reissue or reexamination, pages of the specification (including claims and abstract) must be numbered consecutively starting with 1. It is desirable to indent paragraphs and to number them (e.g., [0001]). MPEP references provided for more info.

name: Detailed description requirements and enablement standard
description: The Detailed Description must explain the invention and the process of making and using the invention in full, clear, concise, and exact terms, distinguish the invention from prior art, and describe completely the claimed subject matter or improvement. It must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the invention without extensive experimentation. Each element in the drawings should be mentioned in the description. The best mode must be disclosed.
guidance: For improvements, confine description to the specific improvement and cooperating parts necessary. See MPEP § 608.01(g). New matter cannot be added after filing.

name: Claims: form, content, numbering, dependent claims rules
description: Claims must 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the subject matter regarded as the invention. A nonprovisional application must contain at least one claim. Claims must begin on a separate physical sheet or page and, if multiple, be numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals. Dependent claims may refer back to and limit another claim; dependent claims should be grouped with the claims they refer to. Multiple dependent claims must refer to other claims 'in the alternative' only. Each claim should be a single sentence; elements or steps should be separated by line indentation.
guidance: Claims define scope of patent protection. The number and type of claims affect fee calculation (excess claims fees). Proper claim drafting and grouping is important for examination and fee purposes.

name: Form and content detail requirements when mailing with postcard
description: When submitting a postcard with a mailed patent application, the detailed listing should include title and number of pages of each USPTO form; number of pages of specification (excluding claims); number of claims and claim pages; number of drawing figures and sheets; whether an oath/declaration is included and its page count; types and numbers of other documents and page counts; payment amount and method.
guidance: Postcard must itemize each component precisely; failure to itemize may cause postcard not to serve as evidence for missing items. The USPTO will stamp the postcard with receipt date and application number before returning it.

name: Prosecution history estoppel (general rule)
description: Claims must be interpreted in light of the proceedings before the Patent and Trademark Office (PTO); when a patentee originally claimed subject matter but narrowed the claim in response to a rejection, he may not argue that the surrendered territory comprised an unforeseen equivalent.
guidance: A rejection indicates the examiner did not believe the original claim could be patented; by amending rather than appealing, the patentee is taken to concede the patent as issued does not reach as far as the original claim. Estoppel prevents recapturing surrendered subject matter in infringement suits.

name: Kinds of amendments that may give rise to estoppel
description: Prosecution history estoppel may apply to any claim amendment made to satisfy the Patent Act's requirements, not only amendments made to avoid the prior art.
guidance: Amendments made to satisfy §§101-103 (utility, novelty, nonobviousness) or §112 (describe, enable, best mode) can give rise to estoppel. The Court rejects limiting estoppel only to amendments made to avoid prior art; purpose for amendment is relevant only insofar as it affects whether the amendment narrowed the claim's scope.

name: Presumption and burden regarding amendment purpose
description: Where no explanation for an amendment's purpose is established, courts should presume the amendment had a substantial reason related to patentability and that prosecution history estoppel applies.
guidance: Warner-Jenkinson placed the initial burden on the patentee to show an amendment was not for a patentability-related reason. Festo holds the patentee should bear the burden of showing the amendment does not surrender the particular equivalent in question. When the court cannot determine purpose, presume the patentee surrendered the territory between original and amended claim.

name: Start with literal claim language in claim interpretation
description: Interpretation of a patent begins with its literal claims; the prosecution history is relevant to construing those claims and identifying what was surrendered.
guidance: When a patentee narrows a claim, courts may presume the amended text was composed with awareness of the estoppel rule, and that the territory surrendered is not an equivalent; nonetheless, rebuttal may be shown as above. The literal claim is the starting point for analysis.

name: §112 disclosure requirements as a foundation for amendments
description: To enable the patent holder to know what he owns and the public what he does not, the inventor must describe his work in 'full, clear, concise, and exact terms' under 35 U.S.C. §112; the application must describe, enable, and set forth the best mode.
