guidance: Amendments made to satisfy §112 (e.g., clarifying ambiguous terms, translation fixes, rewriting claims) may be cosmetic and not narrow scope, but if necessary and narrowing they can give rise to estoppel. Failure to meet §112 can lead to invalidity.

name: Interference search requirement (when app is in condition for allowance)
description: When an application is in condition for allowance, an interference search must be performed by text searching the 'US-PGPUB' database in EAST or WEST directed to the comprehensive inventive features in the broadest claim.
guidance: If claims involve nucleotide or peptide sequences, request STIC to perform a sequence interference search. Make a printout of the database(s) searched, the query(ies) used, and the date of the search of record in the application file; do NOT place the search results in the application file. The search must extend beyond the application's class/subclass to all relevant classes and Technology Centers (see MPEP § 1302.08).

name: Sorting claims / consolidating interfering claims
description: If an applicant has several related applications with interfering claims intermixed with non-interfering claims, the examiner should consider consolidating interfering claims into a single application or restricting an application to non-interfering claims so examination can proceed for non-interfering claims without interference delay.
guidance: Interfering claims are 'conflicting claims' under 37 CFR 1.78(b); the examiner may require consolidation into any applicant disclosure that supports the claims (35 U.S.C. 132(a)). Alternatively require restriction so applicant can file a divisional for non-interfering claims (35 U.S.C. 121). Do not consolidate a claim into an application lacking 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph support for that claim.

name: Applicant requirement to identify all interfering claims, propose counts, and show correspondence (37 CFR 41.202(a)(2))
description: The suggestion must identify all claims the applicant believes interfere, propose one or more counts, and show how the claims correspond to one or more counts.
guidance: A count is a description of the interfering subject matter used by the Board to determine what evidence may prove priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1). The applicant must identify at least one patentable claim from every application or patent that interferes for each count.

name: Claim added/amended to provoke interference must include written-description claim chart (37 CFR 41.202(a)(5))
description: If a claim has been added or amended to provoke an interference, the applicant must provide a claim chart showing the written description for each claim in the applicant's specification.
guidance: Because added or amended claims copied from an opponent may lack equivalent written description support in the applicant's disclosure, such claims are subject to heightened scrutiny early in the interference (see 'Threshold issue' under 37 CFR 41.201). Use Form Paragraph 23.06.05 where appropriate.

name: Charts for claimed constructive reductions-to-practice (37 CFR 41.202(a)(6))
description: For each constructive reduction-to-practice for which the applicant wishes to be accorded benefit, provide a chart showing where the disclosure provides a constructive reduction-to-practice within the scope of the interfering subject matter.
guidance: A description in an application that would have anticipated the subject matter of a count is a constructive reduction-to-practice. One disclosed embodiment can suffice. For benefit chains under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/121/365 the anticipating disclosure must be continuously disclosed through the entire benefit chain or no benefit is accorded.

name: If suggestion used instead of 37 CFR 1.130–1.132 declaration, check 35 U.S.C. 102(a)/102(e) rejections
description: If an applicant files a suggestion under 37 CFR 41.202(a) instead of a declaration under 37 CFR 1.130–1.132, and an application claim is subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(e), the examiner must verify that the applicant's showing, taken at face value, is sufficient to overcome the rejection.
guidance: If the examiner determines the showing is insufficient, examination is not complete (37 CFR 41.102), the rejection should be maintained, and the suggestion should not be referred to the Board.

name: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 135(b) (one-year bar and substantially same subject matter)
description: If an application claim interferes with a patent claim and the applicant added the claim more than one year after the patent's issuance, or the application was filed more than one year after issuance (but the patent is not a statutory bar), an interference will not be declared unless at least one of the claims present in the application or its parent prior to expiration of the one-year period was for 'substantially the same subject matter' as at least one patent claim (35 U.S.C. 135(b)).
guidance: The test is not obviousness but whether all material limitations of the interfering claim necessarily occur in the prior claim (focus on different material limitations). If none of the prior claims meets the 'substantially the same subject matter' test, reject the interfering claim under 35 U.S.C. 135(b) (see In re McGrew). Use form paragraphs 23.14/23.14.01 where appropriate.

name: Adequate written description for interfering claims
description: An applicant is not entitled to an interference simply because it wants one; the interfering claim must be allowable, particularly with respect to the written description supporting the interfering claim.
guidance: Claims added or amended to provoke an interference are subject to heightened scrutiny for written description adequacy early in the interference (see 37 CFR 41.201 'Threshold issue'). Better practice is to add or amend to a fully supported claim and explain equivalence rather than literally copy an opponent's claim.

name: Principles guiding requiring applicant to add a claim (A–E)
description: Guiding principles include: (A) generally do not suggest interference if examination is not otherwise complete; (B) required claim must not encompass prior art or be barred; (C) application must provide adequate 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph support for the required claim; (D) do not require a claim when applicant expressly states the commonly described subject matter is not the applicant's invention; (E) do not require a claim based on a claim from a published application unless that published application's claim has been allowed.
guidance: Use these principles and examples (e.g., prior art, time-bar under 135(b), applicant disclaimers) to exercise discretion. The examiner may withdraw the requirement if persuaded by applicant's reasons.

name: Requirement to show priority and sufficiency standards (37 CFR 41.202(d) and (e))
description: When an application has an earliest constructive reduction-to-practice later than the apparent earliest constructive reduction-to-practice of a competing published application with allowed claims or patent, the applicant must make a priority showing under 37 CFR 41.202(d)(1). A showing is not sufficient unless it would, if unrebutted, support a determination of priority in favor of the party making the showing.
guidance: When testimony or production necessary to show priority is not available without authorization, the showing must include any necessary interrogatory/request/admission/deposition requests and a detailed proffer of the expected responses and an explanation of relevance. If the applicant fails to show priority, the Board may still declare an interference to place the applicant under an order to show cause; new evidence admission is limited to showings of good cause.

name: Avoid explicit 'means for' language
description: 35 USC 112(f) says that a claim element expressed as a 'means for' performing a function is construed to cover only the corresponding structure described in the spec, plus equivalents.
guidance: In practice, this narrows the claim dramatically and makes invalidation under 112(b) (indefiniteness) easier when the spec lacks structure. As a drafting rule, avoid using 'means for' unless you intentionally want the claim limited to structures disclosed in the specification.

name: Watch for the Williamson Trap — functional language without 'means'
description: After Williamson v. Citrix (Fed. Cir. 2015), courts apply 112(f) even without the magic word 'means,' whenever a claim term is a 'nonce word' that does not connote sufficient structure.
guidance: Terms held to invoke 112(f) include 'module,' 'mechanism,' 'element,' 'device for,' 'unit configured to.' Audit claim terms that are generic or 'nonce' and avoid presenting functional recitations without structural context.

name: Deliberately invoke 112(f) when a narrow, spec-tied claim is desired
description: Sometimes you actually want narrow construction tied to your spec - for example, when the prior art is so close that any broader reading reads on it.
guidance: In those cases, deliberately use 'means for' and put one or more clear corresponding structures in the spec. Use 112(f) as a strategic narrowing tool when appropriate.

name: Specification must disclose corresponding structure and link it to the claimed function
description: If you do invoke 112(f), the spec must clearly disclose the corresponding structure and link it to the claimed function.
guidance: For software functions, the Federal Circuit (Aristocrat, WMS Gaming) requires an algorithm — flowchart, pseudocode, or prose — not just 'a general-purpose computer.' Merely reciting a generic computer without an algorithmic disclosure risks indefiniteness or overly narrow construction.

name: Audit claims before filing for nonce words and 112(f) risks
description: Read every independent claim looking for nonce words. Each one is a 112(f) risk.
guidance: Either replace nonce/functional words with structural language or, if the functional/means-plus-function reading is intentional, ensure the specification has clear corresponding structure (and algorithms for software) to support the claim construction.

name: Claim amendments during prosecution
description: Voluntary claim amendments are possible at any time during prosecution and, in any case, before a final decision granting the patent is issued.
guidance: Amendments cannot extend the original scope of the invention and must find support in the specification. If the patent is rejected, claims can be further amended by filing a Reconsideration Action.

name: Scope of exclusionary rights (patent infringement)
description: If the patent protects a product, the patent owner can prevent third parties from importing, using, manufacturing, offering for sale or selling the product without consent. For method patents, the owner can prevent third parties from using the method or performing acts involving products obtained directly through the protected method.
guidance: A patent will be infringed if any of its claims read on an allegedly infringing product or process.

name: Antitrust considerations when enforcing patents
description: Patent rights are not absolute and are limited to the scope of the claims as granted; unduly broad interpretation could be interpreted as abuse of IP rights.
guidance: If a patent holder has a dominant market position, sham litigation based on patents could be taken as an abuse of dominant position. There is limited judicial/antitrust authority precedent in Colombia on this point.

name: Employee inventions / ownership and remuneration (Article 10)
description: Inventions made by a worker in the course of contract/employment where the object is the performance of inventive activity belong to the employer; worker may be entitled to additional remuneration if contribution and importance exceed contract terms; employer may claim ownership when invention connected to professional activity and influenced by company knowledge/means (must exercise option within 90 days); workers entitled to fair economic compensation; inventions filed within one (1) year after leaving employment are considered developed during the contract.
guidance: Specifies when employer ownership applies, rights to extra compensation, option exercise period (90 days), and prohibition of advance waiver by worker (null and void). (Article 10 a–f).

name: Claims determine scope of patent rights (Article 11 & 22)
description: The first of the approved claims determines the right conferred and defines/demarcates scope; claims shall define the subject matter, be clear and concise, be based on the description without exceeding it; first claim refers to main subject matter and the remainder are subordinate.
guidance: Claims interpreted with description, drawings, plans, or biological deposit where applicable. Claims must not extend beyond description (Article 11, 22).

name: Filing requirements and formalities for priority (Articles 12–15, 18)
description: An application filed with the National Patent Administration must include characteristics and data as Law/regulations indicate; a patent may be applied for by inventor/successors/representative; priority date is date of first application abroad if within one (1) year; priority must be claimed at filing and may require priority document and Spanish translation; several inventors — right belongs to earliest filing (first-to-file). Filing date requires: declaration of application, applicant identity, description and one or more claims (even if not formally compliant).
guidance: Priority partial if Argentine application is broader than foreign one; reciprocity required in country of first application; Administration may request priority document during substantive examination.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / best mode / enablement (Article 20)
description: The invention must be described with sufficient clarity and completeness for an average skilled person to carry it out; must include clear account of best known method and materials; methods/processes described shall be directly applicable in production; for microorganisms, deposit and access requirements apply.
guidance: Includes requirement of deposit for strains in authorized institution and public access conditions after publication; description is used to interpret claims and must enable reproduction by skilled person.

name: Utility model requisites and application content (Articles 55–57)
description: Essential requisites: inventions under Title III must be new and industrial in nature. Application must include title, description of single main instance of new configuration or arrangement and explanation of causal relationship to functional improvement sufficient for skilled person to reproduce, claims, and necessary drawings. After filing and substantive exam fee payment, Administration examines compliance and publishes if approved; 30-day post-publication objection window; failure to pay substantive exam fee within three (3) months from filing = abandonment.
guidance: Utility model objections must be reasoned and based on lack/insufficiency of legal requisites; examination and publication process similar to patents but quicker and with different time limits.

name: Form paragraph 7.22.fti (Further in View Of) usage
description: Claim [1] rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2] as applied to claim [3] above, and further in view of [4].
guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21.fti. An explanation of the rejection must follow this form paragraph (see MPEP § 2144). If the rejection relies on prior art under pre-AIA 102(e), determine the reference’s 102(e) date using the AIPA rules unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued from an international application with an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000 (see MPEP § 2146 guidance and Examiner Notes for 7.12.fti and 7.12.01.fti).

name: Test for Obviousness (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a))
description: The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows: 1) Determining the scope and contents of the prior art. 2) Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue. 3) Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. 4) Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: Use this four-factor test to frame obviousness analyses and as a response to arguments about applicability of the factors. Provide factual findings that map to these inquiries when making or explaining an obviousness rejection (see MPEP § 2144).

name: Form paragraph 7.27.fti for alternative 102/103 rejection
description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102([2]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over [3].
guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended to substitute for making a single appropriate rejection under 102 or 103 when practicable. Appropriate uses include: (a) disputed claim interpretation where one interpretation supports 102 and another supports 103; (b) where reference discloses all limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine inherent properties; (c) genus/species issues; (d) product-by-process equivalence issues; (e) means-plus-function equivalence or obvious variant uncertainty; (f) overlapping ranges without explicit example. If claim interpretation renders claim indefinite, consider 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection. Bracket instructions: insert claim numbers, paragraph letters, and references per Examiner Notes. A full explanation must follow. Precede this paragraph with the listed form paragraphs (7.07.fti, relevant 7.08–7.14.fti, 7.20.fti or 7.103) and for certain filings include 7.06 where applicable (see MPEP for details).

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) definitions of prior art
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) provides that a person is not entitled to a patent if the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) provides that a person is not entitled to a patent if the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under 35 U.S.C. 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b), in which the patent or application names another inventor, and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Office personnel must note the unchanged introductory phrase '[a] person shall be entitled to a patent unless', preserving the Office's initial burden to explain rejections. The categories of prior art documents and activities are set forth in 102(a)(1) (documents and public activities) and 102(a)(2) (U.S. patent documents). Use appropriate documentary evidence (issued patents, published applications, non-patent literature) or evidence of public use/sale to support rejections; printed publications can sometimes be used as evidence of prior public use or sale when their own date is not sufficiently early (see In re Epstein and MPEP § 2133.03(b)).

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) one-year grace period exceptions
description: A disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date of a claimed invention shall not be prior art under 102(a)(1) if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor; or (B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
guidance: This creates a one-year grace period measured from the filing date of the earliest U.S. or foreign patent application to which a proper benefit/priority is asserted and that supports the claimed invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Under pre-AIA 102(b) the one-year grace period was measured from the earliest U.S. filing date; under AIA it is measured from the earliest application to which benefit is properly claimed.

name: Treatment of WIPO/PCT publications and U.S. patent documents under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)
description: A WIPO publication of a PCT international application that designates the United States is an application for patent deemed published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) for purposes of AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2). Thus, WIPO published PCT applications that designate the U.S., U.S. patents, or U.S. patent application publications that name another inventor and were effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention are prior art under AIA 102(a)(2).
guidance: WIPO publications of PCT applications are treated as U.S. patent application publications for prior art purposes regardless of international filing date, language, or whether the PCT entered the U.S. national stage. Under pre-AIA 102(e) different rules applied (e.g., PCT filing date thresholds and language/publishing considerations).

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) definition of 'effectively filed' for U.S. patent documents
description: A U.S. patent document is considered to have been effectively filed for prior art effect under 102(a)(2) as of the earlier of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or the application for patent; or (2) if the patent or application is entitled to claim the benefit of, or priority to, an earlier U.S. provisional, nonprovisional, international (PCT), or foreign patent application, the filing date of the earliest such application that describes the subject matter of the claimed invention.
guidance: Measure the prior art effect of U.S. patent documents from the effective filing date (earliest application to which benefit/priority is claimed that describes the relied-upon subject matter), regardless of whether that earliest application is a U.S. provisional/nonprovisional, international (PCT), or foreign application. Use AIA 102(d) to determine whether a U.S. patent document predates a claimed invention's effective filing date.

name: Common ownership/joint research agreement exception (AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c))
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 100(h) 'joint research agreement' is a written contract/grant/cooperative agreement between two or more persons or entities for experimental/developmental/research work in the field of the claimed invention. 35 U.S.C. 102(c) provides that subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to assignment to the same person in applying 102(b)(2)(C) if: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: Use the three-part test to determine whether the common ownership exception applies. The exception operates to treat disclosures made pursuant to the joint research agreement as commonly owned for the purposes of 102(b)(2)(C), potentially removing certain disclosures as prior art under 102(a)(2).

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness standard and temporal focus
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 provides that a patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art. The temporal focus for the obviousness inquiry is before the effective filing date of the claimed invention rather than at the time of invention.
guidance: This tracks pre-AIA 103(a) substantively but shifts the temporal benchmark to effective filing date. The provisions of pre-AIA 103(c) have been replaced with AIA 102(b)(2)(C) and (c); biochemical/process-specific 103(b) provisions have been eliminated. Ensure obviousness analyses use the effective filing date as the temporal reference and account for any changed exceptions under the AIA.

name: Office burden and requirements when making rejections (35 U.S.C. 132 and related MPEP guidance)
description: The AIA preserves the requirement that whenever a claim for a patent is rejected or an objection or requirement is made, the Office shall notify the applicant and state the reasons for such rejection, objection, or requirement, and provide such information and references as may be useful to the applicant in judging the propriety of continuing the prosecution of the application (see 35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.104(c) and MPEP § 706).
guidance: Office personnel must identify and explain the statutory/regulatory basis of rejections, include references and factual findings supporting the rejection, and provide sufficient information for the applicant to respond meaningfully.

name: Effective filing date of the claimed invention (AIA 35 U.S.C. 100(i) and MPEP § 2152.01)
description: The AIA defines 'effective filing date' for a claimed invention as the earlier of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent or application is entitled to a right of priority or the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386 (see 35 U.S.C. 100(i)(1)).
guidance: In examining AIA 102 issues, the effective filing date is generally the actual U.S. filing date unless specific situations apply (continuation/divisional/national stage/priority/benefit per 35 U.S.C. 120, 365(c), 386(c), etc.). The MPEP lists situations (A)-(D) that can cause the effective filing date to be earlier; e.g., (A) if the application is a continuation or divisional and requirements of 35 U.S.C. 120, 365(c), or 386(c) are satisfied, the effective filing date is the earliest filing date in the line. Follow MPEP § 2152.01 for detailed determination steps.

name: AIA prevents antedating/'swearing behind' certain prior art disclosures
description: Under the AIA the date of invention is not relevant for determining prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102; it is no longer possible to antedate or 'swear behind' certain prior art disclosures by showing that the applicant invented the claimed invention prior to the effective date of the prior art disclosure (e.g., via 37 CFR 1.131).
guidance: Do not rely on invention date evidence to overcome disclosures that are prior art under AIA 102(a); focus analyses on effective filing dates, documented prior disclosures, and applicable exceptions (102(b)). Where applicable, consider derivation proceedings or correction of inventorship for disputes about who was the actual inventor.

name: Mark in Color, Color Claims and Standard Characters
description: How to claim color(s) in an international application and how standard character marks are treated.
guidance: Guidance on indicating which parts of the mark are in color, how to claim color(s) (including when basic mark is B/W), and implications for reproduction and scope of protection; discusses marks consisting exclusively of color or combinations of colors.

name: Claim structure and punctuation
description: A claim should have a preamble, a transitional phrase, and a body made of elements typically separated by semicolons, with the penultimate element followed by "; and," and the last element ending with a full stop. In some countries each element or combination of elements is separated by line indentation.
guidance: Model: Preamble, transitional phrase: – – – Element (#1); Element (#2); and Element (#3). Example: 'An apparatus, comprising: a plurality of printed pages; a binding configured to hold the printed pages together; and a cover attached to the binding.' Follow local practice on indentation (e.g., US often requires indentation; other countries accept but do not require it).

name: Special claim words and transitional phrases
description: Words and phrases such as 'comprising', 'wherein', 'whereby', 'such that', 'so as to', and 'configured to' carry particular meanings in claims and must be used with an understanding of their legal interpretation.
guidance: 'Comprising' is open-ended (typically), 'wherein' often introduces a function/operation/result that flows from previously recited structure and should be used where the result necessarily follows. The drafter must know how courts in target jurisdictions interpret these words and choose phrasing appropriate to the protection sought.

name: Requirement for multiple elements (avoid single-element overbreadth)
description: Many patent offices require claims to recite at least two elements; a single-element claim may be impossibly broad and read on unrelated items.
guidance: Compare a claim 'A computer, comprising: a processor.' (too broad) with a claim that recites processor, memory, and bus (appropriately structured). Ensure the claim provides sufficient structure/limitations to avoid being unacceptably broad.

name: Two-part (Jepson/improvement) claims
description: A two-part claim sets out the most relevant known prior art in the preamble and characterizes the improvement in the body, connected by a transitional phrase (e.g., 'characterized by', 'characterized in that', or 'wherein the improvement comprises').
guidance: Pros: clearly highlights the inventive contribution over the prior art and is preferred in some offices (e.g., EPO). Cons: it constitutes an admission that the preamble part was known, which may be undesirable. Use when invention is a distinct improvement on an old combination; avoid when it would give a misleading picture (e.g., combination of known integers of equal status, modifications of a known chemical process, complex interrelated systems, or new chemical compounds). Consider drafting standard-format claims first and adopting two-part format if required by examiner or advantageous for filings limited to jurisdictions that prefer it.

name: Alternative elements and Markush groups
description: Claims may include alternative elements, but ordinary 'or' expressions can lack clarity. Markush claim style ('selected from the group consisting of X, Y and Z') is commonly used (especially in chemical claims) to claim alternatives.
guidance: If an inclusive 'or' is meant, use 'and/or', 'at least one selected from', or equivalent language. If multiple members can be selected simultaneously, explicitly state 'and combinations thereof'. Markush groups must not be ambiguous and should be used cautiously: if one alternative is anticipated in the prior art, the whole Markush claim can lack novelty. Consider claiming members in separate dependent claims where appropriate. Markush useful in chemical claims; in other fields prefer a generic term where possible.

name: Specification support for functional/means claims
description: Means-plus-function claims typically require adequate description in the specification of specific structures that perform the recited functions; otherwise the claims risk narrow construction or rejection.
guidance: Provide clear disclosure of the structures (e.g., list example structures like 'tapes, adhesives, rivets') that perform the function. Avoid failing to identify which structures perform which functions and avoid reciting unnecessary structures that could invite narrow interpretation. If all elements are purely functional without structure, risk rejection as a mere desideratum (a desired result without how it is achieved).

name: Claim sets strategy (independent and dependent claims)
description: A typical claim set contains one or more independent claims and multiple dependent claims; at least one independent claim must define the essential features needed to meet patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step).
guidance: Draft a broad independent claim to capture the broadest protection and multiple dependent claims of narrower scope as fallbacks. Balance the number and breadth of claims against filing/examination/maintenance fees and administrative limits (some offices charge per-claim fees or limit independent claims per category). Vary claim breadth to provide insurance against later-found prior art.

name: Number and breadth of claims—costs and administrative limits
description: Patent laws rarely set an upper claim limit, but many offices impose fees for excess claims or limit independent claims per category (e.g., EPO), so drafters must weigh costs against protection gained.
guidance: Consider office-specific counting rules (some count only numbered claims; USPTO charges for multiple dependent claims even if not separately numbered). Over-proliferation of claims increases fees and complexity; choose a reasonable number proportional to the invention's complexity and client's budget.

name: Independent claim content: essential features and clarity
description: Independent claims should specify the essential features that define the invention and any features necessary for the technical effect; claims must be clear and directed to the heart of the invention.
guidance: If the invention's patentability rests on a technical effect, include the features essential to achieve it. For product claims of a known kind modified in specified ways, clearly identify the known product and the modifications. For process claims, ensure the process reasonably leads to the claimed product to avoid internal inconsistency and clarity problems.

name: Dependent claim form, scope and drafting effect
description: A dependent claim 'depends from' another claim, includes all features of the parent claim even if not explicitly repeated, and narrows the scope relative to its parent; dependent claims are shorter and serve to define specific embodiments.
guidance: Format dependencies by referencing the parent claim (e.g., 'The apparatus of Claim 1, further comprising: ...'). Be aware that dependent claims are narrower than the independent claim. Use dependent claims to claim preferred embodiments and to provide fallbacks if broad claims are attacked by prior art. Examples in the manual show how dependent claims incorporate parent text and further limitations.

name: Dependent claims as fallback protection
description: Dependent claims serve as fallback positions: if a broad independent claim is rejected (e.g., by prior art), narrower dependent claims may still be allowable and provide practical protection.
guidance: Draft dependent claims covering narrower ranges, particular configurations, or preferred features that might survive if the broad claim is invalidated. Use dependent claims strategically to preserve commercially important claim scope while managing prosecution risk.

name: Clarity and conciseness requirement
description: Claims must be clear and concise as a matter of law; excessive, ambiguous, or convoluted claim drafting can lead to objections or rejections.
guidance: Avoid unclear parenthetical expressions, ambiguous alternatives, or overly lengthy two-part claims where inappropriate. Keep the number of dependent claims reasonable to avoid undue complication. Draft as if claims must be understandable without reference to drawings (claims are not to incorporate drawings).

name: Avoid claiming mere desideratum
description: Claims that define all elements only functionally without disclosure of how to achieve them risk being rejected as claiming a mere desideratum (a desired result without specifying how it is achieved).
guidance: Ensure the specification provides sufficient detail and structure for any functional limitations. If all claim elements are functional, include supporting structural disclosure to avoid objections for lack of clarity or sufficiency.

name: Record of disciplinary proceeding considered in future matters (aggravating/rebuttal use)
description: The record of this disciplinary proceeding, including this Final Order, shall be considered 1) when addressing any further complaint or evidence of the same or similar misconduct ... and/or 2) in any future disciplinary proceeding a) as an aggravating factor to be taken into consideration in determining any discipline to be imposed and/or b) to rebut any statement or representation by or on Respondent's behalf.
guidance: Disciplinary records are persistent and may be used against a practitioner in subsequent matters as aggravation or to rebut claims; practitioners should be aware of long-term consequences.

name: Remedial best practices: use of checklists and additional training
description: Respondent has created and currently uses a two-page checklist of USPTO requirements when drafting and reviewing patent applications as one means of ensuring compliance with MPEP requirements; he attended relevant CLE and a Practicing Law Institute seminar.
guidance: As part of remediation or best practice, practitioners should adopt drafting/review checklists, obtain targeted training in claim drafting/prosecution, and proactively correct errors to reduce risk of future discipline.

name: Definition and requirements of a terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321)
description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner (in whole or in part) of a patent or a patent to be granted that is used to disclaim or dedicate a portion of the entire term of all the claims of a patent. The requirements for a terminal disclaimer are set forth in 37 CFR 1.321.
guidance: Sample forms of a terminal disclaimer and guidance as to filing and treatment are provided in MPEP § 1490. See 37 CFR 1.321 for specific filing content and formal requirements.

name: Enforceability provision required in terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321(c)(3))
description: A terminal disclaimer for commonly owned conflicting claims must include a provision that any patent granted on that application shall be enforceable only for and during such period that said patent is commonly owned with the application or patent which formed the basis for the rejection.
guidance: Ensure the disclaimer explicitly limits enforceability to the common ownership period to satisfy 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3).

name: Terminal disclaimer requirements where invention resulted from joint research agreement (37 CFR 1.321(d))
description: 37 CFR 1.321(d) sets forth the requirements for a terminal disclaimer where the claimed invention resulted from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
guidance: When the claimed invention results from a joint research agreement, use the terminal disclaimer provisions at 37 CFR 1.321(d) and include the parties to the agreement as appropriate per statute and regulations.

name: Terminal disclaimer required to overcome nonstatutory double patenting even after 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2) change
description: A terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321 is required in an application to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection, even if the application was filed on or after June 8, 1995 and claims the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) of the filing date of the patent or application which forms the basis for the rejection.
guidance: Cite MPEP section or Official Gazette notice (1202 O.G. 112 (Sept. 30, 1997)) when applicants argue a terminal disclaimer should not be required due to 20-year term rules; terminal disclaimer still required because of patent term extension issues under 35 U.S.C. 154(b) and the enforceability-limiting provision in 37 CFR 1.321(c)(3).

name: When double patenting rejection applies (commonly owned different inventive entities)
description: Claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting to prevent an organization from obtaining two or more patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter.
guidance: Use case law (e.g., In re Zickendraht; In re Christensen) to support that claims must be patentably distinct; mere form/content differences are insufficient.

name: Double patenting for non-commonly owned inventions under joint research agreements (35 U.S.C. 103(c))
description: Non-commonly owned applications that claim inventions resulting from activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement may be subject to double patenting treatment under the CREATE Act amendment to 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
guidance: Apply 35 U.S.C. 103(c) to permit treating certain non-commonly owned inventions as if commonly owned for obviousness/double-patenting purposes when statutory conditions are met.

name: Common ownership criteria (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1) requirements)
description: Applications or patents are 'commonly owned' pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(1) if they were wholly or entirely owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) at the time the claimed invention was made. Two inventions of different inventive entities come within the common ownership provisions when: (A) the later invention is not anticipated by the earlier invention under 35 U.S.C. 102; (B) the earlier invention qualifies as prior art for obviousness only under subsections (f) or (g) of 35 U.S.C. 102, or under 102(e) for certain dates; and (C) the inventions were, at the time the later invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: See MPEP § 706.02(l)(2) for detailed common ownership definition and date-specific considerations for 102(e).

name: Joint research agreement criteria (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) requirements)
description: Two inventions come within the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) when: (A) the later invention is not anticipated by the earlier invention under 35 U.S.C. 102; (B) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (C) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (D) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
guidance: A 'joint research agreement' is defined by 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3) as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.

name: Use of form paragraph 8.27 (Different Inventors, Common Assignee, Same Invention)
description: ¶ 8.27: Claim [1] directed to the same invention as that of claim [2] of commonly assigned [3]. The issue of priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and possibly 35 U.S.C. 102(f) of this single invention must be resolved.
guidance: Use when the claims listed are for the same invention (not merely obvious variants). The assignee is required to state which entity is the prior inventor. A terminal disclaimer has no effect in this situation since the basis is priority under 102(f)/(g). Insert appropriate data in brackets; see examiner notes for prerequisites and related form paragraphs.

name: Provisional rejection practice for copending applications (7.21.01 and 7.15.01)
description: ¶ 7.21.01: Claim provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over copending application having a common assignee or at least one common inventor. ¶ 7.15.01: Claim provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as anticipated by copending application with common assignee or inventor.
guidance: These provisional rejections are based on the presumption the copending application will be published or patented. They may be overcome by showings under 37 CFR 1.132 (derivation) or 37 CFR 1.131 (date of invention) or by showing the copending application is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). A terminal disclaimer cannot overcome certain provisional 102(e) rejections (see In re Bartfeld). Use appropriate form paragraphs when claims conflict or would be obvious over copending disclosures.

name: Damages—Generally
description: If you find that the accused [device/method] infringes any of the claims and those claims are not invalid, you must determine the amount of damages to be awarded. The Plaintiff must prove each element of its damages—including the amount—by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Damages must be adequate to compensate the Plaintiff for the infringement and put the Plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in absent the infringement. The damage award cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. You may not add anything to the amount of damages to punish an accused infringer or to set an example, nor add anything for interest. Instruction on damages does not imply court preference for outcome; consider damages only if you find valid, infringed claims.

name: Date Damages Begin—Proof of Notice (marking or direct notice)
description: The start date for damages is either a stipulated date or, if disputed, the date the Plaintiff first notified the Defendant of its claim for patent infringement.
guidance: Plaintiff can prove public notice by marking substantially all products that include the patented invention with the patent number (or marking with a free internet address linking product to patent). Licensees who use the invention must also mark substantially all their products. Alternatively, Plaintiff may directly notify Defendant with a specific charge; the notice-based damages period starts from the date Defendant received notice. If Plaintiff failed to provide effective public marking and did not properly provide direct notice before filing suit, damages are recoverable only from the lawsuit filing date. Plaintiff bears burden to prove notice by a preponderance.

name: Entire Market Value Rule (narrow exception)
description: Generally royalties should be based on the smallest salable unit that practices the patent and is closely related to the claimed invention; the entire market value rule is a narrow exception permitting damages based on the whole product only if the patented feature drives demand for the entire product or substantially creates the product's value.
guidance: If the smallest salable unit is multi-component with non-infringing features unrelated to the patented feature, damages must be limited to portion of value attributable to patented technology. To use entire-product revenue, Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that the patented feature 'substantially creates the value of the product' or drives customer demand.

name: Initial disclosures — Option 1 (Rule 26(a)(1)(A)-style)
description: Option 1 (modeled after Rule 26(a)(1)(A)) requires disclosure of: (1) name and, if known, address and telephone of each individual likely to have discoverable information and the subjects of that information (unless solely for impeachment); and (2) a copy or description by category and location of all documents, ESI, and tangible things in the disclosing party's possession, custody, or control that may be used to support claims or defenses (unless solely for impeachment).
guidance: These disclosures enable immediate discovery upon institution; file disclosures as exhibits to permit related discovery.

name: Expert testimony — admissibility, qualification, and content requirements
description: Expert testimony may be submitted with the petition, preliminary response, and at other stages as ordered. Expert testimony is generally permitted where the expert’s specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact. Experts must be qualified by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education (Fed. R. Evid. 702). Expert testimony is presented as an affidavit or declaration. The testimony must be based on sufficient facts and data (Fed. R. Evid. 702(b)), be the product of reliable principles and methods (702(c)), and reliably apply those principles to the facts (702(d)). 37 C.F.R. § 42.65(a).
guidance: Absence of an advanced degree does not preclude qualification if experience suffices. Expert testimony that does not disclose underlying facts or data may be entitled to little or no weight. Experts may explain technology, level of skill, prior art teachings, reasons to combine references, reasonable expectation of success, and weigh objective indicia of nonobviousness. Expert testimony cannot substitute for disclosure in a prior art reference or supply missing claim elements; it can explain patents/printed publications but not provide the missing disclosure itself.

name: Word count and page limits — specific limits and certification
description: Word and page limits apply: 14,000 words for IPR and derivation petitions, 18,700 words for PGR petitions (37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)). Motions (other than motions to amend) are limited to 15 pages; motions to amend limited to 25 pages. Patent owner preliminary responses and responses to petitions are subject to same word limits as the petition. Replies and oppositions have specific limits: replies to patent owner responses to petitions limited to 5,600 words; replies to oppositions to motions to amend limited to 12 pages; replies to all other oppositions limited to 5 pages. Sur-replies, if authorized, are subject to same limits. 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(d) requires that any paper with type-volume limits include a certification stating the number of words.
guidance: Exemptions to word count include table of contents, table of authorities, mandatory notices, certificate of service, or appendix of exhibits or claim listing (but not grounds for standing). Parties may rely on their word-processing software for certification. Abusive tactics to circumvent word counts can lead to briefs not being considered; Board generally accepts certifications unless obvious abuse—raise violations promptly and attempt to remedy before approaching the Board.

name: Petition minimum procedural compliance and filing requirements
description: To obtain a filing date, the petition must meet certain minimum standards (see 37 C.F.R. § 42.106 and 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)). For IPR a complete petition must be filed with the required fee, certificate of service for petition/fee/evidence, a certification that the patent is eligible for IPR and the petitioner is not barred or estopped, and identification of claims being challenged and specific basis for challenge (37 C.F.R. § 42.104). Similar petition requirements apply to PGR and derivation.
guidance: Ensure all statutory and regulatory filing requirements are met to obtain a proper filing date and avoid procedural defects.

name: Positive first office determination
description: There must be at least one corresponding earlier application at a participating office where at least one claim has been found patentable/allowable (a completed examination or PCT search that yielded an allowable claim addressing novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability).
guidance: The OEE work product can be a notice of allowance, a positive office action, or a favorable PCT work product. The PPH request relies on that positive determination; without it you are not eligible.

name: Claim correspondence
description: The claims of the second application must 'sufficiently correspond' to the allowed claims from the first application—generally identical to or narrower in scope than the OEE's allowed claims.
guidance: You typically must amend OLE claims to match allowed OEE claims. New dependent claims that add limitations are usually acceptable (they’re narrower). Wholly new claims or omission of critical features break correspondence. Most offices require a claims correspondence table mapping each OLE claim to one or more allowed OEE claims.

name: Formal documentation required for a PPH request
description: A complete PPH request normally includes a filled request form, copies of the OEE work product showing allowed claims, translations if required, copies of prior art cited by the OEE examiner, a claims correspondence table, and identification of any PCT work product for PCT‑PPH cases.
guidance: Each office has specific forms (e.g., USPTO SB/20GLBL, EPO Form 1009). Ensure translations when documents are not in the OLE’s official language and provide prior art lists as requested.

name: Common rejection reasons for PPH requests
description: PPH requests are frequently refused for missing or incorrect translations, incomplete claim correspondence, examination already started, incorrect forms or formalities, and unclear priority linkage.
guidance: If a PPH request is found defective, some offices allow correction—monitor the request status and correct deficiencies promptly. Ensure correct signing, up‑to‑date forms, and clear claim mapping to avoid denial.

name: Strategic trade‑offs: potential to lock in narrowed claim scope
description: Using PPH to present already‑narrowed claims across jurisdictions can foreclose the opportunity to obtain broader claims in other offices where different prior art or standards might have allowed broader protection.
guidance: Evaluate whether time savings are worth narrowing claim scope. Strategies include using PPH only in critical markets, pursuing broader claims in other jurisdictions through normal prosecution, or obtaining an early PPH allowance and keeping a continuation/divisional pending to pursue broader claims later.

name: Strategic coordination benefits (harmonization and enforcement planning)
description: PPH enables applicants to harmonize claim scope across countries, simplifying licensing, fundraising due diligence, and multi‑jurisdiction enforcement planning when claims are consistent.
guidance: Coordinated claims make licensing and litigation strategy more straightforward. However, harmonization depends on substantive outcomes in each office—consistent grants strengthen validity arguments but do not guarantee litigation success.

name: Claims define scope / notice function
description: In a patent or patent application, the claims define in technical terms the extent, i.e. the scope, of the protection conferred by a patent, or the protection sought in a patent application. This is termed as the 'notice function' of a patent claim—to warn others of what they must not do if they are to avoid infringement liability.
guidance: Claims are paramount in prosecution and litigation. See MPEP §2173 ('Claims Must Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim the Invention'). The claims should be precise and clear enough to give the public notice of what is claimed (Nautilus v. Biosig discussion).

name: Requirement of at least one claim in application
description: In most modern patent laws, patent applications must have at least one claim, which are critical defining elements of the patent and the primary subject of examination.
guidance: Some laws permit obtaining a date of filing without any claim; however, generally prepare at least one claim for filing because claims are the principal subject of examination.

name: EPC requirement: claims expressed in terms of technical features
description: Under the European Patent Convention (EPC), a claim must define the matter for which the protection is sought in terms of technical features.
guidance: Technical features can be structural (e.g., a nail, a rivet) or functional (e.g., fastening means). See EPC Article 84 and EPO Guidelines: claims should be formulated around technical features.

name: Claim parts (preamble, transitional phrase, limitations, purpose clause)
description: A claim may include: a preamble that recites the class of the invention; a 'transitional' phrase that characterizes the elements that follow; a set of 'limitations' that together describe the invention; and optionally, a purpose clause that further describes the operation or goal of the invention.
guidance: Preamble may or may not limit claim scope. Limitations should describe interacting/cooperating elements. Purpose clauses (wherein/whereby/thereby) typically limit scope.

name: Transitional phrase selection and effect on scope ('comprising' vs 'consisting of' etc.)
description: Transitional phrases such as 'comprising', 'containing' and 'including' are open (inclusive) and mean 'having at least the following elements'; 'consisting of' and 'consisting essentially of' are more limiting (exclusive).
guidance: In the US, 'consisting of' excludes additional limitations, while 'consisting essentially of' excludes additional limitations that would 'materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention. Choice of transitional phrase materially affects claim scope.

name: Limitations should describe interacting/cooperating elements (combination vs aggregation)
description: The set of limitations should be described as though they interact or cooperate to achieve the desired result; a combination requires joint operation, while an aggregation is merely adding separate contributions.
guidance: Draft limitations to show mutuality of action (cooperation) when claiming a combination; avoid wording that suggests mere aggregation unless intended (see case law discussing combination vs aggregation).

name: Purpose/wherein/whereby clauses limit scope
description: Optional purpose clauses (e.g., 'wherein', 'whereby', 'thereby') further describe the overall operation or goal and typically limit the scope of the claim.
guidance: Use purpose clauses when you want to tie a structural or functional limitation to an intended effect; be aware these clauses can be treated as limiting during claim construction (see In re Roemer, Griffin v. Bertina).

name: Independent and dependent claims (structure and strategic use)
description: Independent claims stand on their own; dependent claims refer to earlier claims, assume all their limitations, and add restrictions. Each dependent claim is, by law, narrower than the claim upon which it depends.
guidance: Dependent claims clarify/broaden understanding of terms in the independent claim (doctrine of claim differentiation presumption). Use dependent claims as fall-back positions and to claim preferred embodiments. Dependent claims can survive if an independent claim is invalid.

name: Multiple dependent claims: reference rules and fee/counting consequences
description: Multiple dependent claims reference more than one other claim and must reference specific claims and do so in the alternative; rules for these are specific and, in some jurisdictions (e.g., U.S.), multiple dependent claims are counted for filing/fee purposes according to the number of claims they reference.
guidance: Draft multiple dependent claims carefully (correct alternative phrasing). Be mindful of excess-claim fees at the USPTO; multiple dependent claims are common in Europe but costly in the U.S.

name: Claim interpretation / construction principles (objective, context-sensitive)
description: Construction is not concerned with the author's subjective intent but with what a reasonable person to whom the utterance was addressed would have understood the author to mean; meaning depends on words, context, audience, and background knowledge.
guidance: Interpret claims in light of the specification, prosecution history, and ordinary meaning. Context and background are crucial; dictionaries/grammars and case law inform interpretation.

name: Inventor may act as lexicographer (definitions in specification control)
description: In U.S. patent practice, inventors may 'act as their own lexicographer' by giving common words or phrases specific meanings in the specification that differ from normal definitions.
guidance: If you define terms in the specification, those definitions can control claim construction; ensure definitions are clear and consistently used.

name: Claim construction standards: BRI (exam) vs Phillips (litigation) and USPTO change
description: Historically the USPTO used the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification' (BRI) during examination, while U.S. courts used a narrower standard (Phillips). On November 13, 2018 the USPTO switched to the Phillips standard for AIA proceedings.
guidance: Be aware which construction standard will apply (examination vs litigation vs AIA/PTAB) as it affects claim wording strategy and how broad or narrow claims will be read.

name: Definiteness / clarity requirement
description: A patent claim must be precise and clear enough to give the public clear notice of what is claimed; tolerating imprecision that renders a claim 'insolubly ambiguous' would undermine the public-notice function.
guidance: Draft claims to satisfy definiteness requirements (see Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc.). Avoid ambiguous terms or provide clear definitions in the specification.

name: Embodiments language and prosecution consequences
description: Phrases like 'in one embodiment', 'in a preferred embodiment', or similar are used in the description to introduce particular implementations; these embodiments may or may not each be claimed specifically.
guidance: Be cautious: examiners may treat variations presented as separate inventions requiring individual examination. Use embodiment language strategically to disclose alternatives while preserving claim scope.

name: Doctrine of equivalents and scope expansion risks
description: The doctrine of equivalents can be used to expand the effective scope of claims beyond literal wording, but its application has created unpredictability; jurisdictions have constrained it (e.g., Warner-Jenkinson).
guidance: Relying on doctrine of equivalents is uncertain; draft clear literal claim coverage and consider fallback dependent claims rather than relying solely on equitable doctrines.

name: EPC vs US differences in dependency across categories
description: Under the European Patent Convention, when a claim in one category (e.g., process) depends on a claim from a different category (e.g., product), it is not considered a dependent claim but an independent claim; under U.S. law this is still counted as a dependent claim.
guidance: Be mindful of jurisdiction-specific formal rules when drafting cross-category claims and when counting/formatting dependent claims for filing and prosecution.

name: Drafting consideration: balance breadth with novelty/non-obviousness risk
description: It is more valuable to obtain claims that include the minimal set of limitations that differentiate an invention over the prior art; however, fewer limitations increase the risk of the claim covering prior art and being rejected for obviousness or lack of novelty.
guidance: Strategically draft claims to be as broad as possible while including necessary novel limitations; use dependent claims and multiple claim scopes to manage risk.

name: Search based on actual filing date and citing post‑parent art
description: Examiners should search all applications based on the actual U.S. filing date of the application rather than on the filing date of any parent U.S. application for which benefit/priority is claimed. Examiners should cite of interest all material prior art having an effective filing date after the filing date of the U.S. parent application but before the actual filing date of the application being examined.
guidance: Due to 20‑year patent term rules, searches must use the actual filing date; identify and cite intervening art filed after the parent but before the child application's actual filing date.

name: Mayo/Alice two-step test (courts)
description: The two-step Mayo/Alice analysis: Step One — determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (judicial exceptions: law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step Two — if Step One is satisfied, consider the elements of each claim individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application; Step Two searches for an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to 'significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.'
guidance: Courts apply only these two steps. Courts have rarely found inventive concepts at Step Two, so Step One typically controls the inquiry. Citations: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank; Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus Laboratories.

name: USPTO MPEP §2106 Alice framework (Step 2A / Step 2B)
description: MPEP §2106 implements the Alice analysis as Step 2A (which corresponds to courts' Step One) and Step 2B (which corresponds to courts' Step Two), but subdivides Step 2A into two prongs (Prong One and Prong Two).
guidance: Flow: Step 2A Prong One — determine whether the claim recites a patent-ineligible concept; if yes, Step 2A Prong Two — determine whether additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application; if not integrated at Prong Two, proceed to Step 2B to determine whether the additional elements amount to significantly more than the ineligible concept.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — integration into a 'practical application'
description: At Prong Two of Step 2A, examiners determine whether claims that recite a judicial exception nonetheless recite additional elements that 'integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.' If the exception is integrated into a practical application, the claim is deemed not directed to a judicial exception.
guidance: The MPEP/2019 Guidance instructs that examiners should evaluate integration into a practical application and, if integrated, may deem claims patent-eligible without proceeding to Step 2B. Prong Two thus incorporates aspects of what courts treat as the Step Two inventive-concept inquiry into Step One analysis.

name: How examiners evaluate 'integration into a practical application' (2019 Guidance)
description: Examiners evaluate integration by: (a) identifying any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (b) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application, using one or more of the considerations laid out by the Supreme Court and the Federal Circuit.
guidance: The 2019 Guidance specifically instructs that 'revised Step 2A specifically excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.' Examiners should give weight to all additional elements, whether or not they are conventional, when evaluating whether a judicial exception has been integrated into a practical application.

name: Step 2B — inventive concept and conventionality analysis
description: Step 2B corresponds to the court's Step Two: determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to 'significantly more than' the ineligible concept itself. Analysis at Step 2B includes consideration of whether additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities.
guidance: If Prong Two of Step 2A does not establish integration into a practical application, examiners move to Step 2B to analyze inventive concept and conventionality. The 2019 Guidance reserves conventionality analysis for Step 2B.

name: Streamlined eligibility (MPEP §2106.06(b)) — improvement to technology/computer functionality
description: The USPTO allows a 'streamlined eligibility' analysis when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident, e.g., because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality.
guidance: If a claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality, an examiner may find it qualifies as eligible subject matter under §101 without further analysis. This offers a path for quicker allowance where improvements to technology are clear from the claim.

name: MPEP: transformation may be found at Prong Two or Step 2B
description: The MPEP states that for 'a claim reciting a judicial exception to be eligible, the additional elements (if any) in the claim must “transform the nature of the claim” into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception, either at Prong Two or in Step 2B.'
guidance: Thus, integration into a practical application (Prong Two) or an inventive-concept finding at Step 2B can both suffice to make a claim patent-eligible under the USPTO framework.

name: USPTO 2024 AI Guidance — reiteration of Step 2A Prong Two approach
description: The 2024 Guidance for AI inventions 'doubled down' on asking 'whether the claimed invention as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application,' and reiterates that 'at Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the exception is not integrated into a practical application or that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more than the exception unless the examiner asserts that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in Step 2B.'
guidance: The updated guidance applies specifically to AI-related claims but underscores the same structural difference: examiners may find integration at Prong Two and need not require evidence unless conventionality is asserted at Step 2B.

name: District court practice and non-deference to PTO §101 determinations
description: District courts apply the two-step Alice test and have in some cases declined to give weight or deference to the Patent Office's determinations that claims 'integrate' an abstract idea into a practical application. Courts may not expressly use the 'integration into a practical application' language in Step One and instead treat practical-application arguments as part of Step Two inventive-concept analysis.
guidance: Example: Aviation Capital Partners v. SH Advisors — claims allowed by an examiner under 'integrated practical application' were treated as abstract by a district court, which stated it gave 'no weight to the Patent Office’s overall determination that the patent was eligible.' The Federal Circuit and district courts are not bound by USPTO guidance; case law controls.

name: Prosecution strategies to bridge USPTO–court divergence
description: Applicants facing §101 rejections may consider strategies that account for both MPEP/USPTO guidance and how district courts approach Alice, including creating a record that additional elements are not routine and conventional and pursuing claims of varying scope within the same patent family.
guidance: Suggested actions: provide analysis beyond USPTO Step 2A Prong Two (e.g., record evidence or arguments that additional elements are not well-understood, routine, conventional); claim drafting to include multiple claim scopes; create a prosecution record useful in later litigation. These strategies may help claims withstand rigorous §101 scrutiny in district court.

name: Language style
description: Language style evaluates how closely the language and word choice of the specification matches the style a human would use when writing a description of an invention. The disclosure should be dry and factual, avoiding excessive promotional or advocating language. It should not directly reference the claims (for example, by saying “as given in claim 1”) and should avoid "patent profanity," which are overly specific words like "crucial" or "critical" when describing the invention.
guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = pervasive issues (excessive advocacy, patent profanity, frequent claim references). 3 = mix of inappropriate and acceptable language with substantial portions in suitable legal tone. 5 = almost entirely in proper style: dry, factual, minimal issues. Minimal advocating language is acceptable. Avoid direct claim references and avoid words that unnecessarily limit scope (e.g., "crucial", "critical"). Also format disclosure as paragraphs (no markdown headers/lists) since patent disclosure should be a series of paragraphs.

name: Elaboration
description: Elaboration assesses how well the specification expands on the content of the claims. Good disclosure should not simply repeat the claim language but should explain and elaborate on the key technical concepts contained in the claims to help the reader better understand the scope of invention.
guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = specification simply restates the claims with little or no additional detail. 3 = some elaboration present but much of the disclosure closely mirrors claim content. 5 = thorough elaboration on all key technical concepts needed to adequately understand the invention. Retrieval/external-context steps are important to encourage elaboration rather than rote repetition.

name: Factual accuracy
description: Factual accuracy evaluates how accurate the content in the disclosure is. All of the content should be factual without hallucinations. The disclosure should also not contain any references to nonexistent figures, claims, other sections not present in the patent specification.
guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = frequent inaccuracies including false/misleading statements and references to nonexistent elements. 3 = occasional issues but majority accurate and consistent with claims. 5 = entirely accurate with no hallucinated content or invalid references. Particular failure modes to watch for: hallucinated figures, incorrect mapping of technical concepts (e.g., mixing domain senses), and including irrelevant retrieved information that misstates invention context.

name: Coverage of claims
description: Coverage of claims evaluates whether or not there is any content missing in the disclosure. All of the claims should be addressed in the disclosure without any important information omitted.
guidance: Scored 1–5. 1 = specification covers few or none of the claims with significant omissions. 3 = partial coverage (approximately half of claim content addressed). 5 = fully incorporates all information from the claims with no important elements missing. Assess whether every claim element is discussed/explained in the disclosure.

name: Five-category 1–5 annotation scheme
description: Structural evaluation framework: disclosures are assessed across five categories (Language style, Elaboration, Diversity, Factual accuracy, Coverage of claims), each rated on a scale from one to five.
guidance: Annotators should apply the provided definitions and example anchors (1 = poor, 3 = mixed/partial, 5 = excellent) consistently across documents. Use expert judgement to interpret borderline cases; annotators in the study were patent attorneys and inter-annotator agreement metrics (Kendall's Tau, weighted Cohen's kappa) were used to quantify consistency.

name: Patent profanity (automatic keyword metric)
description: Approximation of language quality by checking for the presence of problematic patent-specific terms and direct claim references ("patent profanity").
guidance: Lower counts are better (↓). Implement via keyword matching on a curated list provided by patent experts: e.g., "crucial", "critical", "prior art", "necessary aspect", "necessary component". Also detect the literal pattern of the word "claim" followed by an integer to flag direct claim references. Penalize documents with many flagged instances because such terms can unnecessarily limit claim scope or indicate advocating language.

name: Patent application publication basis and allowable amendments
description: The patent application publication shall be based upon the specification and drawings deposited on the filing date, as well as the application data sheet and/or inventor’s oath or declaration; the publication may also be based on substitute specifications or certain amendments (other than abstract or claims) and amendments to the abstract, claims (complete claim listing), and drawings if submitted in sufficient time to be entered into the file wrapper before technical preparations (generally begin 4 months prior to projected publication) have begun. National-stage applications may include international-stage amendments.
guidance: Applicants seeking to have amendments reflected in publication must submit them early enough — technical preparations usually start ~4 months before publication — or supply a compliant EFS copy per § 1.215(c).

name: Selection, coordination, arrangement, and modification can create human authorship
description: A human may claim copyright for the resulting work where they select, coordinate, arrange, or modify AI-generated material in a sufficiently creative way to meet the originality standard (Feist).
guidance: Office found compilation protection where images and human-authored text were selected and arranged creatively (Zarya of the Dawn example). Modifying AI-generated output (editing, adapting, enhancing) may contribute new authorship assessed like editorial changes to pre-existing works. Tools (e.g., Midjourney’s Vary Region/Remix, OpenAI Canvas) can enable users to exert such control. However, whether modifications meet Feist is case-by-case.

name: Minimum creativity threshold / de minimis selection rule
description: Selection, coordination, or arrangement must clear a minimal creativity threshold; the selection of only two or three elements is generally insufficient for copyright protection.
guidance: Refer to COMPENDIUM (THIRD) § 312.2 and legislative history noting compilations with relatively few elements typically do not qualify (selection is necessarily de minimis). This limits registration claims where only a very small number of AI elements are chosen.

name: Scope of protection for human contributions in AI-generated outputs
description: Copyright protection for works containing human inputs and AI-generated elements extends only to the human-contributed material (perceptible human expression) and to the human author’s selection, coordination, and arrangement — not to AI-generated elements standing alone.
guidance: Analogous to derivative works: protection covers material added by the later human author and does not affect the public domain status of pre-existing material. Office registrations have annotated claims to limit protection to unaltered human-authored elements when necessary.

name: Simple substitution rationale — required findings
description: To reject a claim based on substitution of one known element for another, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate specific findings.
guidance: Articulate: (1) that the prior art contained a device differing from the claimed device only by substitution of components; (2) that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) that a person of ordinary skill could have made the substitution and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary in the case. If any of these findings cannot be made, this substitution rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples: In re Fout (substituting distillation for aqueous extraction), Agrizap (substituting resistive switch for mechanical switch).

name: Analogous art / pertinence across fields
description: A reference from a different field may be analogous art if it is reasonably pertinent to the problem to be solved by the claimed invention.
guidance: When determining whether a reference is applicable, consider the problem addressed rather than superficially limiting by field labels. A reference is analogous if it addresses a similar problem or is within the same field of endeavor; it need not be narrowly focused on the exact type of device.
