Example: ICON — folding bed art was analogous to folding treadmill because both addressed retaining/stabilizing a folding mechanism.

name: Secondary considerations (objective evidence) and nexus
description: Evidence such as failure by others, copying, skepticism by experts, praise, commercial success, long-felt need, and unexpected results are secondary considerations that may support nonobviousness but require a nexus to the claimed invention.
guidance: Evaluate whether the proffered objective evidence is commensurate with and tied to the full scope of the claims. Lack of coextensiveness between the evidence and the claimed invention reduces its weight. Examples: Muniauction (secondary considerations lacked nexus), Procter & Gamble (unexpected results and long-felt need weighed in favor of nonobviousness). Consider timing: long-felt need is assessed as of the filing date, not market date.

name: Lead compound analysis in chemical obviousness
description: In chemical cases, obviousness based on structural similarity often involves identifying a 'lead compound' and a reason to select and modify it to arrive at the claimed compound.
guidance: Office personnel should identify some motivation that would have led one of ordinary skill to select and modify a known compound (the 'lead compound') in a particular way. The requisite motivation can come from many sources and need not be explicit in the art. Structural similarity that creates a reasonable expectation of similar properties may suffice. Examples: Aventis (need not require explicit teaching to purify stereoisomer), Eisai (no reason to modify lead compound because modification would have destroyed advantageous property).

name: Use of known technique to improve similar devices — required findings
description: To reject a claim based on applying a known technique to improve similar devices, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate specific findings.
guidance: Articulate: (1) the prior art contained a 'base' device that the claimed invention improves; (2) the prior art contained a 'comparable' device that had been improved in the same way; (3) one of ordinary skill could have applied the known improvement to the base device and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary. If any finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. The rationale is that the enhancement method is part of ordinary capabilities of skilled artisans. If application of the technique would have been beyond skill, it is not obvious (KSR). Example: In re Nilssen (applying known overload protection techniques).

name: Clarity and conciseness
description: The abstract should be clear and as concise as the disclosure permits.
guidance: Generally the abstract should not exceed 250 words and preferably be in the range of 50 to 150 words. It may contain chemical or mathematical formulae and tables. Avoid phrases that can be implied (e.g., “This disclosure concerns”, “This invention relates to”) and avoid legal claim-style phraseology often used in claims (e.g., 'said', 'means'). Draft wording with any authority-specific requirements (e.g., inclusion of drawings) in mind.

name: Change of applicants or registrants procedure
description: If court decides applicants/registrants fail to satisfy requirements or Office finds so ex officio or a declaration of amendment is submitted, this is published; within three months other parties meeting Article 36 may file requests to amend application/registration records. If no suitable request submitted, rights terminate and cancellation is published. In case of multiple requests, Office accepts most appropriate one per implementing regulation. Agreements between parties who meet conditions may lead to amendment upon submission of documents and fees. Changes in name/address/characteristics of firm or registrant title shall be recorded and published.
guidance: There is a statutory process to replace registrants; publication and three‑month windows apply; Office discretion and implementing regulation procedures govern selection among claims.

name: Scope of rights: prohibited acts under GI protection
description: Registrants and entitled users may demand prevention of: (a) direct or indirect commercial use of the GI or emblem to benefit from its reputation for products that do not satisfy registered product properties; (b) misleading use or imitation of the GI on products not meeting registered properties or similar enough to be associated with it, even with qualifiers like 'style', 'type', 'method', 'as produced in'; (c) use of false or misleading statements about origin and natural/essential qualities on packaging, promotional or any written material; (ç) deceptive use of the emblem of registered GI.
guidance: The prohibition covers exploitation of reputation, imitation and misleading origin claims, including translations and qualifying terms.

name: Inventor's certificate priority-claim affidavit/declaration
description: When claiming priority to an application for an inventor's certificate (in countries granting both inventor's certificates and patents) under 35 U.S.C. 119(d), the applicant must include an affidavit or declaration.
guidance: The affidavit/declaration must specifically state that, upon investigation, the declarant is satisfied that, to the best of their knowledge, the applicant had the option when filing the inventor's certificate application to file either a patent application or an inventor's certificate application as to the subject matter of the identified claim(s) forming the basis for the priority claim.

name: Priority claim acceptable forms for applications filed before September 16, 2012
description: For applications filed prior to September 16, 2012, the priority claim need not be in any special form and may be made by a person authorized to sign correspondence under 37 CFR 1.33(b).
guidance: No special language is required; any expression reasonably interpreted as claiming the benefit of the foreign application is accepted. For such pre-2012 applications the priority claim must appear in the oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.63 or in an application data sheet (37 CFR 1.55(n)).

name: Identification requirements for the foreign application
description: A priority claim must identify the foreign application for which priority is claimed by specifying the application number, country (or intellectual property authority), and the day, month, and year of its filing.
guidance: This information is required for original applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a). For international applications entering the national stage or for international design applications, follow the specific MPEP/PCT/Hague instructions referenced.

name: Recognized-country requirement for claiming priority
description: The foreign application must have been filed in a foreign country that affords similar privileges to U.S. applicants or nationals, typically a country recognized via PCT, Paris Convention, or WTO membership.
guidance: See the MPEP list of recognized countries and WIPO/WTO resources for current status. If a claimed foreign filing was in a country not on the list, an examiner should contact the Office of Policy and International Affairs to determine any status changes. The right of priority is based on the country of foreign filing, not applicant citizenship.

name: Same inventor / at least one common joint inventor requirement
description: To claim priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a), the foreign application must have been filed by the same applicant as the U.S. applicant, or by applicant's legal representatives or assigns; interpreted to mean the U.S. and foreign applications must name the same inventor or have at least one joint inventor in common.
guidance: An application where inventorship does not overlap (e.g., sole inventor A abroad and sole inventor B in the U.S.) cannot claim priority even if owned by the same party. Joint inventors may each properly claim benefit to their respective foreign-filed applications. See MPEP §§ 602.xx for correction of inventorship and relevant CFR sections (1.45, 1.48, 1.78).

name: Same-invention requirement for priority claim
description: The foreign application must be for the same invention as the U.S. application to serve as the basis for a priority claim.
guidance: If a later foreign application discloses additional subject matter, a U.S. claim specifically limited to that additional disclosure may be entitled to the date of the later foreign application for that subject matter. See relevant MPEP sections for examples and treatment.

name: Certified copy and translation filing requirement during pendency (37 CFR 1.55(g))
description: The claim for priority and the certified copy of the foreign application (and translation if required) must be filed within the pendency of the U.S. application, unless filed with an appropriate petition (e.g., under paragraphs (e) or (f)) or a petition with fee and showing of good and sufficient cause for delay.
guidance: If the claim for priority or the certified copy is filed after the issue fee is paid, the patent will not include the priority claim unless corrected by a certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323. See MPEP §§ 215.02 et seq. for specifics for applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 and §215.03 for prior filings. Priority claims and certified copies must in any event be filed during pendency and before grant.

name: PCT/national-stage timing and procedures for priority claims
description: For applications entering the U.S. national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371 from an international (PCT) application, the priority claim and the certified copy of the foreign application must be filed within the time limits set forth in the PCT Articles and Regulations.
guidance: Follow PCT deadlines for national-stage entry; in the U.S. it is permissible but not required to present the claim in an application data sheet when entering national stage. See 37 CFR 1.55(d)(2) and related MPEP sections for specifics.

name: Incorporation by reference and inadvertent omission protections (37 CFR 1.57(b))
description: For applications filed on or after September 21, 2004, a priority claim present on the filing date is considered to incorporate by reference the prior-filed foreign priority application as to inadvertently omitted material, subject to 37 CFR 1.57(b) conditions.
guidance: This provides a safeguard when portions of the specification/drawings were inadvertently omitted from the U.S. application, or to permit correction of translation errors when the foreign priority application is in a non‑English language. Applicants are encouraged to provide an explicit incorporation-by-reference statement to the prior foreign application if they do not wish to rely on inadvertent-omission procedures. See MPEP §§ 201.06(c), 217, and §601.01(a) subsection III for additional guidance.

name: Derwent Registry numbers for common compounds
description: In 1981 a list of ~2100 commonly mentioned compounds/elements was assigned Registry numbers. A patent is indexed with a Registry number when it mentions a Registry compound as a significant compound or non-metallic element in the claims or examples (insignificant mentions such as generic solvents are excluded).
guidance: Use Registry numbers to improve retrieval of frequently-occurring compounds; consult the CPI Registry Compounds User Guide for lists and synonyms.

name: Measures of patent scope change
description: Two measures of patent scope change from published application to granted patent: (i) change in the number of independent claims (Marco et al., 2019), and (ii) change in the length of the first independent claim (Kuhn and Thompson, 2019).
guidance: These measures are used to test whether claim narrowing/expansion is correlated with continuation filing, via linear probability models controlling for filing year, issue year, art unit, and examiner.

name: Interpretation criterion for continuations' purpose
description: Interpret continuation filings in light of whether they respond to rejections or are used to obtain additional claims after allowance.
guidance: Results suggesting higher continuation probability after notice of allowance and modest relationship with rejections support the conclusion that continuations are primarily used to add new claims after allowance rather than to respond to rejections or claim narrowing.

name: Reporting of descriptive statistics and sample construction details
description: Provide detailed summary statistics (means, SD, quartiles) for variables such as CON, CONs, PostStandard × SEP, SEP indicator, age, number of independent claims, words per independent claim, number of inventors, provisional/PCT flags, small entity, foreign priority, and leniency (grant rate).
guidance: Clear definition of units (application-quarter), sample period (filed on or after November 29, 2000), and matching/membership rules is required to interpret results and replicate analyses.

name: Definition of 'condition for examination' per 37 CFR 1.704(f)
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when it includes: a specification including at least one claim and an abstract (37 CFR 1.72(b)); papers in compliance with 37 CFR 1.52; drawings in compliance with 37 CFR 1.84; any required English translation (37 CFR 1.52(d) or 1.57(a)); a sequence listing in compliance with 37 CFR 1.821–1.825 (if applicable); the inventor's oath or declaration or application data sheet with information specified in 37 CFR 1.63(b); the basic filing fee (1.16(a)/(c)); the search fee (1.16(k)/(m)); the examination fee (1.16(o)/(q)); any certified copy required by 1.57(a); and any application size fee required under 1.16(s).
guidance: International applications entering the national stage have parallel requirements (e.g., 1.492 series fees). Papers/drawings/sequence listings corrected by a reply before the first action or notice of allowance are considered compliant as of the filing date of the latest correcting reply.

name: Date and numeric field qualifiers and numeric operators
description: Date fields searchable as year-month-day (PD=YYYY-MM-DD); can specify specific date, before/after/inclusive, ranges; use numeric operators <, >, <=, >=, = for numeric fields (e.g., NCL>=5).
guidance: Use Link (L) operator to specify a date with a specific patent authority/country (e.g., /PN US L 2002). Single numeric fields include family member counts, number of claims, number of drawings. Presence flags: CT=YES, UAB=YES.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 314 "reasonable likelihood" standard for institution
description: Institution of an inter partes review is authorized by statute when 'the information presented in the petition . . . and any response . . . shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.'
guidance: See 35 U.S.C. § 314 and 37 C.F.R. § 42.4. This is the statutory threshold the Board uses to determine whether to institute on the merits (separate from the Board's discretionary authorities).

name: Becton, Dickinson factor (e): whether petitioner pointed out Examiner error
description: (e) whether Petitioner has pointed out sufficiently how the Examiner erred in its evaluation of the asserted prior art;
guidance: A petitioner must point to specific, material Examiner errors to overcome a § 325(d)-based discretionary denial. Generalized claims of failure are insufficient.

name: Claim construction standard (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Phillips)
description: Claims are construed 'in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' Only those claim terms in controversy need to be construed, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy.
guidance: Apply Phillips v. AWH. If the record does not present claim term disputes, the Board may adopt plain-and-ordinary meaning and proceed without express construction.

name: Fintiv factor 3 — investment in parallel proceeding
description: Investment in the parallel proceeding by the court and the parties (how far advanced is the other forum?).
guidance: Significant investments (completed discovery, completed claim construction, evidentiary hearings, post-hearing briefing) in the parallel proceeding support discretionary denial to avoid duplication.

name: Omission of an element when the element's function is not desired
description: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if the function of the element is not desired.
guidance: If a prior art reference teaches an element for a particular function but the claimed use/environment does not require that function (e.g., no freshwater environment), omitting that element may be an obvious modification. (Cases: Ex parte Wu; In re Larson; In re Kuhle.)

name: Omission of an element with retention of the element's function indicates nonobviousness
description: Omission of an element and retention of its function is an indicium of nonobviousness.
guidance: Where the claimed invention removes a prior-art element but preserves the element's function by another means (e.g., eliminating an intermediate layer but retaining its protective function through a different layer), that fact supports nonobviousness. (Case: In re Edge.)

name: Making a device portable does not alone confer patentability
description: Fact that a claimed device is portable or movable is not sufficient by itself to patentably distinguish over an otherwise old device unless there are new or unexpected results.
guidance: Portability must produce some non-obvious functional advantage or unexpected result to overcome obviousness. (Case: In re Lindberg.)

name: Overlapping, approaching, or similar ranges/amounts/proportions give rise to prima facie obviousness
description: When claimed ranges overlap or lie inside prior art ranges (or are merely close), a prima facie case of obviousness exists.
guidance: Overlapping endpoints, numerically close values, or ranges disclosed across multiple references can establish a prima facie case unless applicant shows criticality or unexpected results. Considerations include whether the prior art range is so broad as to be a genus, and whether the prior art teaches a preference leading away from the claimed species. (Cases: In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff; In re Geisler; Titanium Metals v. Banner; In re Peterson; others.) See MPEP § 2131.03 and §§ 2144.x references.

name: Rejections based on routine optimization must include an articulated rationale
description: To properly support a rejection based on routine optimization, the examiner must make findings of relevant facts and present underpinning reasoning in sufficient detail explaining why it would have been routine to arrive at the claimed invention and why a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: A conclusory assertion of 'common sense' or 'intuitive' is insufficient; the articulated rationale should explain the motivation and reasonable expectation of success (see In re Stepan; In re Van Os; Arendi v. Apple). 'Obvious to try' can be a valid rationale post-KSR when there is a design need/market demand and a finite number of predictable solutions, but prior to relying on 'obvious to try' the parameter must be recognized as a result-effective variable in some contexts (see In re Antonie; KSR).

name: Purpose and Benefits of the Proceeding
description: High‑level description of what each proceeding is intended to accomplish and its practical advantages/limitations.
guidance: IPR: "Canceling one or more claims in less time, and at a lower cost, than district court, with minimal discovery."; PGR: "Canceling or compelling narrowing amendment of one or more claims in relatively slow, low cost ex parte forum with no advocacy by requester after initial request, no discovery, low standard of review, and broad claim interpretation."; Ex Parte Reexamination (XPR): "Canceling or adding one or more claims by right (narrower at any time before patent expires, or broader if filed within two years of issuance) in relatively slow, low cost ex parte forum with no discovery, low standard of review, and broad claim interpretation."; Reissue: (similar to XPR—canceling or adding claims by right); Supplemental Examination: "Curing possible defects relating to inequitable conduct in relatively slow, low cost ex parte forum with no discovery, lower standard of review and broader claim interpretation."; District Courts: "Invalidating one or more claims; finding of unenforceability; finding of infringement or non‑infringement; obtaining injunction and damages for infringement."; ITC: "Invalidating one or more claims; finding of unenforceability; obtaining exclusion order."

name: Qualification of Patent
description: Which patents are eligible for the forum (timing or claim date limitations).
guidance: IPR/PGR/Ex Parte Reexamination/Reissue/Supplemental Examination/District Courts/ITC: "Any patent."; Note: IPR/PGR apply only to patents having at least one claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013 (AIA cut‑off).

name: When the Challenge Can Be Filed
description: Timing restrictions for filing a challenge in each forum.
guidance: IPR: "For pre‑AIA patents, any time; for AIA patents (having at least one claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013), on or after 9 months after issuance or reissuance, or termination of PGR."; PGR: "Within 9 months of issuance or reissuance for patents having at least one claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013."; Ex Parte Reexamination: "Any time during enforceability of the patent (up to 6 years after lapse or expiration)."; Reissue: "Any time before patent expires."; Supplemental Examination: "Anytime during enforceability of the patent (up to 6 years after lapse or expiration)."; District Courts: "Any time before six years after expiration of the patent or six years after last infringing conduct."; ITC: "Any time before patent expires."

name: Discovery
description: Scope and availability of discovery in each forum.
guidance: IPR: "Yes, automatic deposition of witnesses submitting declarations or affidavits, automatic discovery of contradictory evidence; additional discovery by motion as necessary in the 'interests of justice'."; PGR: "Yes, automatic deposition of witnesses submitting declarations or affidavits, automatic discovery of contradictory evidence; additional discovery by motion upon showing of 'good cause' and limited to evidence directly related to factual assertion of other party (broader than IPR)."; Ex Parte Reexamination/Reissue/Supplemental Examination: "No (ex parte forums have no discovery)."; District Courts: "Yes, broad and can involve any non‑privileged material that is 'relevant to any party’s claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case'."; ITC: "Yes, broad, but governed by ITC Rules of Practice and Procedure (19 C.F.R. §§ 210.1 et seq.) and Ground Rules specified by presiding Administrative Law Judge."

name: Specification must fully explain the principle and the several modes
description: The specification must 'fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.'
guidance: The 'principle' means the peculiar structure and mode of operation or the character by which the invention may be distinguished. The patentee should state not only the preferred device or construction but also the other modes of applying the principle he intends to claim; however, he need not enter into minute descriptions of every variation — it is sufficient to indicate what variations of application he claims beyond the preferred embodiments.

name: Do not claim an abstract principle; show a practical application
description: A patentee cannot appropriate a mere abstract principle, idea, or function; the specification must give the discovery a practical application to some useful purpose by its incorporation with matter so as to produce a practical result.
guidance: If the invention is only stated as an abstract philosophical principle or law of nature, it is not patentable. But if the principle is applied to a special purpose so as to effectuate a practical and previously unknown result, the patent can be valid. (Illustrated by the Househill/Neilson discussion: a general principle stated plus an application to a special purpose becomes a 'practical invention'.)

name: Claims must recite the means/apparatus, not merely a result
description: A claim that is effectively a claim for a result or function without identifying the means by which it is produced will not be sustained; the claim must be for the means or apparatus by which the result is produced.
guidance: Example: a claim to the use of proper chemicals to precipitate metal from a solution, by putting such chemicals into any proper vessel, was held too general and vague and therefore invalid. Claims should identify the operative means/structure.

name: For machines, patent the machine (embodiment), not a bare mode or idea
description: Where the invention falls within 'machines', the patent must be for the machine itself and not for a 'mode of operation,' 'principle,' 'idea,' or other abstraction.
guidance: Claims framed as the specific machine or its organization (mode of operation embodied in particular structure) will be sustained, whereas claims sweeping all possible modes of operation are void. Court examples show courts construing such patents as for the described machine when the specification points to a particular structure.

name: Combination claims cover the specific combination, not all modes of combining
description: A claim for a combination of several devices is a claim for that combination as described, and is not a valid claim for any and all modes of combining such devices.
guidance: Courts will sustain a claim only as to the particular combination or the machine specially described; they will not permit a combination claim to function as a universal claim to any mode achieving the result.

name: Claims referring back to the specification ('substantially as described') are construed in light of the spec
description: A claim containing words referring back to the specifications (e.g., 'substantially as described' or 'substantially as set forth') must be construed in connection with the specification and may be held valid when so construed.
guidance: Where a claim immediately follows the descriptive part of the specification, courts will read the claim in the context of that description rather than isolate the claim language.

name: A claim broader than its specification is invalid
description: If a claim 'stands outside' or extends beyond the specification — i.e., the claim's broad terms are not supported by the specification — the claim is invalid.
guidance: Famous example: the broad eighth claim in O'Reilly v. Morse, which claimed the use of electromagnetic force to print characters 'at any distance' beyond the specification, was held invalid. Claims cannot derive substance from bare broad terms unsupported by the spec.

name: Courts must construe the specification to determine whether the claim is for a patentable subject
description: Determining what the patentee's claim is requires construing the description in the specification to see whether it discloses a patentable subject (a particular organization of matter/machine) or merely a function/abstract principle.
guidance: The real invention may be patentable, but if claimed as an abstract principle or function, courts will declare it not patentable; the specification's form of description can change a claim from impermissible abstraction into a patentable applied invention if it shows the application to a special purpose.

name: Scope of appeal – which rejections are appealed (§41.31(c) / §41.61(d))
description: An appeal must be taken from the rejection of all claims under rejection which the applicant or owner proposes to contest; similarly, an appeal/cross appeal must be taken from all rejections or determinations favorable to patentability which the party proposes to contest.
guidance: Questions not affecting the merits may be required to be settled before appeal considered.

name: Amendments after filing a brief (§41.33(b)-(c))
description: Amendments filed on or after the date of filing a brief may be admitted only to cancel claims (when cancellation does not affect scope of other pending claims) or to rewrite dependent claims into independent form; all other amendments filed after filing an appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by specified sections (§§41.39(b)(1), 41.50(a)(2)(i), 41.50(b)(1), 41.50(c)).
guidance: Non-permitted amendments are excluded; limited exceptions permit admission in connection with certain Board orders or remands.

name: Required contents and order of an appeal brief (§41.37(c)(1) / §41.67(c)(1))
description: A brief must contain under appropriate headings and in the indicated order: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals and interferences (with copies of decisions in an appendix); (iii) Status of claims and identification of claims appealed; (iv) Status of amendments after final rejection; (v) Summary of claimed subject matter with specification and drawing references and identification of means-plus-function/step-plus-function elements with corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification; (vi) Grounds of rejection to be reviewed on appeal; (vii) Argument treating each ground/issue under separate headings with legal/record citations; (viii) Claims appendix; (ix) Evidence appendix (copies of evidence entered by examiner and where entered in the record); (x) Related proceedings appendix (copies of decisions).
guidance: Appellants unrepresented by registered practitioners need only substantially comply with many of the items. For inter partes, similar content rules and specific references to columns/lines in the specification apply. Reference to unentered evidence is not permitted.

name: Means-plus-function and step-plus-function identification (§41.37(c)(1)(v) / §41.67(c)(1)(v))
description: For each independent claim and each dependent claim argued separately, every means-plus-function and step-plus-function must be identified and the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification must be set forth with specification (page/line or column/line) and drawing references.
guidance: Precise citation to the specification and drawings is required to show corresponding structure for 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph matters.

name: Argument format and waiver for grouped claims (§41.37(c)(1)(vii) / §41.67(c)(1)(vii))
description: Arguments must address each ground/issue and be supported by citations; each ground/issue must be under a separate heading. When multiple claims subject to the same ground are argued as a group, the Board may select a single claim to decide for the group; failure to separately argue grouped claims constitutes a waiver of separate patentability arguments.
guidance: A statement merely pointing out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument for separate patentability. Claims argued separately or as a group must be placed under subheadings identifying the claim numbers.

name: Amendment in conformity with Board opinion (§41.50(c))
description: The Board may include an explicit statement of how a claim may be amended to overcome a specific rejection; appellant has the right to amend in conformity therewith, and such an amendment will overcome the specific rejection.
guidance: An examiner may reject the so-amended claim provided the rejection constitutes a new ground of rejection.

name: Inter partes: amendments and evidence after appeal (§41.63)
description: In inter partes appeals, amendments filed after filing an appeal that cancel claims may be admitted where cancellation does not affect scope of other pending claims; all other amendments filed after appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by §41.77(b)(1). Affidavits or other evidence filed after appeal will not be admitted except as permitted by reopening prosecution under §41.77(b)(1).
guidance: Inter partes appeals have stricter post-appeal amendment/evidence rules; consult §41.77(b)(1) for permitted circumstances.

name: Inter partes appellant's brief content and formalities (§41.67)
description: An inter partes appellant's brief must be signed by the appellant or authorized attorney/agent, accompanied by the requisite fee (§41.20(b)(2)), and contain (under headings and order) real party in interest; related appeals/interferences (with decisions in an appendix); status of claims (owner must identify rejected claims appealed; requester must identify claims with determinations favorable to patentability being appealed); status of amendments; summary of claimed subject matter with column/line references and means/step-plus-function identification like ex parte; issues to be reviewed; argument with separate headings; claims appendix; evidence appendix (copies of evidence entered and statements where entered).
guidance: Third-party requester cannot propose a new ground of rejection unless withdrawn by the examiner during prosecution and the requester hasn't had opportunity to propose it; arguments/authorities not included in permitted briefs will be refused unless good cause is shown.

name: Clarity of claims (general)
description: A claim complies with clarity if a person skilled in the art can determine the boundaries of the claimed invention with a reasonable degree of certainty; breadth is not automatically lack of clarity.
guidance: If the scope of the subject matter embraced by the claims is clear and the applicant has not indicated a different intended scope, the claims are clear. Independent claims should specify all essential features except those implied by generic terms (e.g., 'bicycle' need not mention wheels).

name: Claims defining by result to be achieved (result-type claims)
description: Claims that attempt to define an invention or feature by a result to be achieved should generally be objected to for lack of clarity.
guidance: No objection if the invention can only be defined that way and the result is achievable without undue experimentation, e.g., verified by tests or procedures adequately specified in the description and involving nothing more than routine trial and error. Example: ashtray defined by a resulting automatic extinguishing effect is acceptable if description enables routine tests to determine dimensions.

name: Claims referencing features of use or a second product
description: Defining an apparatus/product by reference to the use relationship to a second product (not part of the claim) can cause lack of clarity.
guidance: Such claims must either clearly define the individual product (e.g., 'connectable' instead of 'connected') or be directed to a combination (e.g., 'engine comprising a cylinder head'). It may be permissible to define dimensions of first product by general reference to the shape/dimensions of a second related product where reasonable.

name: Clarity of trademarks and similar expressions
description: Trademarks characterize commercial origin rather than technical properties; they should generally be removed from claims unless unavoidable.
guidance: They may be allowed exceptionally if generally recognized as having a precise meaning. Examiner should invite removal where trademarks introduce ambiguity.

name: Non-limiting effect of expressions of preference
description: Expressions such as 'preferably', 'for example', 'such as', 'more particularly' should be treated as non-limiting and not to restrict claim scope.
guidance: Features following such expressions should be regarded as optional and not limit the claim unless otherwise clearly stated.

name: Conciseness of claims (entirety and individual claims)
description: Claims must be concise both as a set and individually; undue repetition or an undue multiplicity of trivial claims may fail the conciseness requirement.
guidance: Undue multiplicity or duplicative claims that confuse rather than clarify may be objected to. Individual claims containing long recitations or unimportant details making scope indefinite may be objectionable. See Appendix for divergent authority practices on conciseness.

name: Support in description (Article 6)
description: Claims shall be fully supported by the description; there must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and the scope must not be broader than justified by description and drawings.
guidance: As a general rule, claims are supported unless there are well-founded reasons to believe a skilled person could not extend the teaching to the whole claimed field using routine methods. Vague assertions with no technical content provide no basis. When raising lack-of-support, reasons should, where possible, be supported by a published document.

name: Sufficiency commensurate with the claims (generalisation limits)
description: Permissible extent of generalization from particular examples depends on the prior art and whether it is reasonable to predict that all variants covered by the claims have the ascribed properties or uses.
guidance: Appropriate claim is not so broad as to go beyond the invention nor so narrow as to deprive applicant of a just reward. Obvious modifications and equivalents described should not be questioned. Examiner may invite applicant to establish that invention applies to whole claimed field or to restrict claim.

name: Relationship of claims to disclosure (consistency and missing essential elements)
description: Claims must be fully supported by description/drawings showing applicant claimed subject matter recognized and described on filing date; claims inconsistent with disclosure or missing essential elements fail the requirement.
guidance: If essential element for function/operation is missing from claim, it's not commensurate with description. Examples: functional property relying on an undisclosed additive; contradictions between claims and description. Claims covering speculative, unexplored possibilities may be objectionable.

name: Functional claim support and means equivalents
description: A claim may define a feature in terms of its function even where only one example is given if a skilled person would appreciate other means for same function.
guidance: If description gives impression the function is to be carried out in a particular way with no hint of alternatives, a claim embracing other means may not comply with support. Mere vague statements that alternatives 'may' be adopted may be insufficient.

name: Characterization of chemical compounds by parameters (support)
description: Characterization solely by parameters may be appropriate when supported by relevant identifying characteristics showing applicant recognized and described the claimed invention at the time of filing (partial structure, properties, function/structure correlations, etc.).
guidance: Sufficient relevant identifying characteristics are required to evidence recognition of the invention on filing date.

name: Independence of sufficiency and support determinations
description: Compliance with sufficiency (Article 5) and support for claims (Article 6) are determined independently; a claim may fail one or both requirements.
guidance: A claim too broad to be supported may also render disclosure insufficient to enable the whole claimed scope; both objections can apply.

name: Interpretation of claims when description provides special definitions (divergent practices)
description: Authorities diverge on whether special definitions in the description should be used for claim interpretation or whether the claim should be amended to make meaning clear from claim wording alone.
guidance: Alternative practices: (1) use the description's special definition for interpreting the claim (do not limit claims to examples); take into account description, drawings and general knowledge if wording needs interpretation; or (2) require amendment so meaning is clear from claim alone and read claim attempting to make technical sense even departing from strict literal wording.

name: Product-by-process claims practices (divergent approaches)
description: Authorities have divergent practices regarding product-by-process claims: (1) construe as a claim to the product per se possessing characteristics derived from the manufacturing process; patentability does not depend on method of production (product not novel merely because made by new process), or (2) construe as relating to and anticipated only by a product actually produced by the recited process.
guidance: Either alternative guideline may be relied upon by an International Authority as appropriate.

name: Conciseness divergent practice detail (A5.42[1] and [2])
description: Divergent practices on conciseness: (1) claims may be objected to as unduly multiplied or duplicative when repetitious and confusing; (2) number of claims must be considered relative to nature/scope of invention; undue repetition or multiplicity of trivial claims rendering it burdensome may violate conciseness.
guidance: Whether number of claims is reasonable depends on facts/circumstances; presentation should not obscure protection sought. Number of alternatives within a single claim should not make it unduly burdensome to determine subject matter.

name: First application and withdrawn/abandoned first application exception
description: Normally the earlier application must be the first application filed for the invention, but a subsequent application can be considered the first for priority if the first was withdrawn/abandoned/refused without public inspection and without outstanding rights and had not served as a basis for claiming priority.
guidance: Examiner will not normally examine this unless clear evidence exists of an earlier application, but may invite applicant to satisfy the examiner that no rights remained outstanding where priority is important due to intervening prior art.

name: Multiple priorities and allocation of priority dates
description: An international application may claim priority from more than one earlier application even from different countries; each element of the application gets the priority date of the earliest priority application which discloses it.
guidance: If different embodiments A and B were disclosed in different earlier applications, each embodiment is accorded its respective priority date. A combination of features disclosed only separately in different priorities is not entitled to earlier priority and will have the international filing date unless an explicit reference allows combination.

name: Determining entitlement to priority (specificity and disclosure test)
description: To be entitled to the priority date, the subject matter of the claim must be explicitly or inherently disclosed in the priority document, including features implicit to a skilled person; the test is the same as for Article 34(2)(b) amendments.
guidance: Disclosure must be specific; mere broad or implied references are insufficient though exact correspondence is not required—there must be, in substance, disclosure of all important elements. Implicit disclosures (e.g., general concept of 'releasable fastening' disclosed by examples of nut-and-bolt, spring catch etc.) can suffice.

name: Statutory obviousness standard (35 U.S.C. 103)
description: A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed under section 102, if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made. Subsections (b)-(c) provide special biotech/process/ownership/joint-research provisions; an obviousness rejection is grounded in the statutory language and appropriate prior art categories (e.g., 102(a),(b),(e)).

name: Scope and content of prior art — claim interpretation and broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art after first understanding the invention disclosed and claimed by reading the specification and claims; claims must be given the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
guidance: Once claim scope is determined, determine what to search for and where. Search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed (see MPEP §904).

name: Ascertaining differences between claim and prior art (claim interpretation)
description: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting the claim language and considering the invention and prior art as a whole.
guidance: See MPEP §2111 for claim interpretation guidance; comparisons should be holistic, identifying which claim limitations remain unshown or how they differ from the prior art.

name: Rationales to support an obviousness rejection (exemplary list)
description: A non-exhaustive list of rationales that may support obviousness: (A) combining prior-art elements by known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of known elements to obtain predictable results; (C) using a known technique to improve similar devices; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement; (E) 'obvious to try' — choosing from a finite set of predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) variations prompted by known work in another field when predictable; (G) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references.
guidance: List is illustrative, not exhaustive. Examiners must articulate why a chosen rationale applies and how it makes the claim obvious; see MPEP §§2143–2144 for examples and additional guidance.

name: Applicant's reply obligations (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection; replies must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable.
guidance: A traverse disputing factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining the alleged error; mere statements that a prima facie case is not established or unsupported claims of misuse of common knowledge are substantively inadequate and may lead to final rejection (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — evidence and burden for common ownership/joint research
description: An applicant seeking benefits of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) has the burden of establishing that subject matter which qualifies as prior art only under 102(e),(f),(g) and the claimed invention were, when the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person (or were within a qualifying joint research agreement).
guidance: For joint research benefits applicant must show (A) invention made by/on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) for requirements.

name: Analogous art requirement for applied references
description: To be proper for use in an obviousness rejection, a reference must be analogous prior art: either (1) from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field).
guidance: Examiners must determine what constitutes analogous prior art when analyzing obviousness (see In re Bigio). The Supreme Court's KSR decision confirms that cross-field references may be analogous when variations would be predictable to one of ordinary skill.

name: Manner of amending the specification (§ 1.121(b))
description: Amendments to the specification, other than the claims, must be made by adding, deleting, or replacing a paragraph; by replacing a section; or by providing a substitute specification, in the manner specified in this section.
guidance: Instructions must unambiguously identify location(s). Replacement or added text must show changes relative to the prior version: added subject matter underlined; deleted matter shown by strike-through (or double brackets for five or fewer characters); deleted subject matter may be indicated within double brackets if strike-through not easily perceived. Full text of replacement paragraphs or added paragraphs required. Previously deleted paragraph/section may be reinstated only by subsequent amendment adding it back. Once a paragraph/section is amended in a first amendment document, it must not be represented in a subsequent amendment document unless amended again or a substitute specification is provided.

name: Amendment by replacement section or substitute specification (§ 1.121(b)(2)-(3); § 1.125)
description: If sections contain headings, amendments may be made by deleting and replacing a section with a replacement section showing all changes. The specification may also be amended by submitting an instruction to replace the specification and a substitute specification in compliance with §§ 1.125(b) and (c).
guidance: A substitute specification may be required if papers are illegible or too changed to consider; subject to § 1.312, a substitute (excluding claims) may be filed up to payment of the issue fee if accompanied by a statement that it includes no new matter. Substitute specifications must include markings showing all changes relative to the immediate prior version and be accompanied by a clean version. Substitute specifications are not permitted in reissue applications or reexamination proceedings.

name: Disclosure consistency and prohibition on new matter (§ 1.121(e)-(f))
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings. No amendment may introduce new matter into the disclosure of an application.
guidance: Office may require amendments to ensure consistency. Introducing any new matter is prohibited and will not be permitted.

name: Exception for examiner's amendments (§ 1.121(g))
description: Changes to the specification, including the claims, made by the Office in an examiner's amendment may be made by specific instructions to insert or delete subject matter set forth in the examiner's amendment by identifying the precise point in the specification or the claim(s) where the insertion or deletion is to be made.
guidance: Compliance with paragraphs (b)(1), (b)(2), or (c) of this section is not required for examiner's amendments executed by such specific instructions.

name: Amendment document organization (§ 1.121(h))
description: Each section of an amendment document (e.g., amendment to the claims, amendment to the specification, replacement drawings, and remarks) must begin on a separate sheet.
guidance: Ensure separate sheets for different amendment sections; claim listing must commence on a separate sheet and sheets containing claim text shall not contain other parts of the amendment.

name: Transitional limited examination after final rejection (§ 1.129(a))
description: An applicant in an application (other than reissue or design) pending at least two years as of June 8, 1995 is entitled to have a first submission entered and considered on the merits after final rejection if the first submission and the fee in § 1.17(r) are filed prior to filing an appeal brief and prior to abandonment; the finality of the final rejection is automatically withdrawn upon timely filing of the submission and payment of the fee.
guidance: Applicant entitled to a second submission under similar conditions; any submission filed after the fee has been paid twice will be treated under § 1.116. 'Submission' includes IDS, amendment to written description/claims/drawings, and new substantive argument or evidence in support of patentability.

name: Affidavit or declaration of attribution or prior public disclosure under the AIA (§ 1.130)
description: When any claim is rejected, the applicant or patent owner may submit an affidavit or declaration to disqualify a disclosure as prior art by establishing that the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor, or the subject matter was obtained from the inventor or joint inventor.
guidance: For prior public disclosure affidavits: identify the subject matter and provide the date of public disclosure; if printed publication, include copy; if not printed, describe with sufficient detail and particularity to determine what was disclosed. Not available if the disclosure is more than one year before the effective filing date. If the rejection is based on a U.S. patent/application publication naming another inventor and derivation is claimed, a derivation petition may be required.

name: Claims (Article 84 EPC)
description: Legal requirement: Claims and clarity under Article 84 EPC.
guidance: Case law covers when clarity may be examined in opposition (only to the extent an amendment introduces non-compliance) and issues of claim interpretation when assessing patentability.

name: No substantive distinction between method and use claims; allowability of second medical indications (G 1/83 et al.)
description: Headnote: 'No substantive distinction between method claims and use claims, allowability of second medical indications' (G 1/83, G 5/83, G 6/83).
guidance: Establishes that second medical use claims are allowable under the EPC framework; published headnotes available in official languages.

name: Scope of examination limited to extent of opposition; dependent claims may be examined if prima facie in doubt (G 9/91)
description: The power of an Opposition Division or a Board of Appeal to examine and decide on maintenance depends upon the extent to which the patent is opposed (Rule 55(c)/now Rule 76(2)(c)). Claims dependent on an independent claim falling in opposition may be examined if their validity is prima facie in doubt on available information.
guidance: If an opponent deliberately limits the scope of opposition, other subject-matter is not strictly 'opposed' though Boards may examine dependent claims where prima facie doubts arise.

name: Plant-variety claims and Article 53(b) EPC exclusions (G 1/98)
description: Headnote: (I) A claim wherein specific plant varieties are not individually claimed is not excluded from patentability under Article 53(b) EPC even though it may embrace plant varieties. (II) When examining a process claim for production of a plant variety, Article 64(2) EPC is not to be taken into consideration. (III) Exception to patentability in Article 53(b) applies to plant varieties irrespective of production method; plant varieties containing genes introduced by recombinant technology are excluded.
guidance: Clarifies interplay between plant variety exclusions and claim scope; important for biotech patentability assessment.

name: Diagnostic methods exclusion under Article 53(c) EPC — claim features determining exclusion (G 1/04)
description: Diagnostic methods practised on the human or animal body are prohibited from patentability by Article 53(c) EPC if the subject‑matter includes: (i) diagnostic reasoning representing the deductive decision phase as a purely intellectual exercise, (ii) preceding constitutive steps for making the diagnosis, and (iii) specific interactions with the body among these preceding steps which are technical.
guidance: Explains which claim features bring a claimed diagnostic method within statutory exclusion and which steps may be considered technical.

name: Undisclosed disclaimer that removes an embodiment is not allowable unless remaining claim directly and unambiguously disclosed (G 2/10)
description: An amendment introducing a disclaimer that disclaims subject‑matter that was (positively) disclosed as an embodiment in the application as filed is not allowable under Article 123(2) EPC 'if the subject‑matter remaining in the claim after the introduction of the disclaimer is not, explicitly or implicitly, directly and unambiguously disclosed to the skilled person using common general knowledge, in the application as filed.'
guidance: Limits disclaimers that remove disclosed embodiments; requires that the post-disclaimer claim be directly and unambiguously derivable from the original filing.

name: Clarity (Article 84) only examinable in opposition to the extent an amendment introduces non-compliance (G 3/14)
description: In considering whether a patent as amended meets Article 84 EPC for the purposes of Article 101(3) EPC, the claims of the patent may be examined for compliance with Article 84 only when, and then only to the extent that, the amendment introduces non-compliance.
guidance: Limits when clarity can be used as a ground to refuse maintenance of patent after amendment in opposition.

name: Partial priority entitlement for generic 'OR' claims (G 1/15)
description: Under the EPC, entitlement to partial priority may not be refused for a claim encompassing alternative subject-matter by virtue of generic expressions or otherwise (generic 'OR'‑claim) provided that said alternative subject‑matter has been disclosed in the priority document directly, implicitly, unambiguously and in an enabling manner; no other substantive conditions apply.
guidance: Clarifies entitlement to partial priority when a claim covers multiple alternatives and some alternatives have priority support.

name: Third party under Article 115 has no right to oral hearing on re-entry request; no suspensive effect; venue for oral proceedings (G 2/19)
description: (1) A third party under Article 115 EPC who has lodged an appeal against grant has no right to an oral hearing before a Board of Appeal about their request to order re-entry into examination to remedy unclear claims (Article 84). Furthermore, such an appeal has no suspensive effect. (2) Oral proceedings before Boards of Appeal may be held in Haar without infringing Articles 113(1) and 116(1) EPC.
guidance: Clarifies procedural rights of third parties and permissible venues for oral proceedings.

name: Claims are the starting point; description and drawings must always be consulted when assessing patentability (G 1/24, from 2025)
description: 'The claims are the starting point and the basis for assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC. The description and drawings shall always be consulted to interpret the claims when assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC, and not only if the person skilled in the art finds a claim to be unclear or ambiguous when read in isolation.'
guidance: Affirms interpretive principle that description/drawings are always part of claim interpretation for patentability assessment, not merely for resolving ambiguity.

name: Permissibility of supplemental examiner's answer / new issues in reply brief
description: An examiner may file a supplemental examiner's answer unless the reply brief raises new issues; examples of new issues include arguing nonanalogous art or different claim limitations in a reply brief that were not raised in the principal brief.
guidance: Examples: (1) Brief argues that element 4 of reference B cannot be combined with A; reply brief argues B is nonanalogous art (new issue). (2) Brief argues pump means not taught; reply argues retaining means not taught (new issue). An appellant who disagrees with an examiner's decision that a supplemental examiner's answer is permitted may petition under Rule 181.

name: Scope of Board decision: affirm, reverse, remand
description: The Board, in reviewing adverse examiner decisions, may affirm or reverse the decision of the examiner in whole or in part on the grounds and claims specified by the examiner; affirmance of a rejection on any grounds specified constitutes general affirmance of the examiner's decision on that claim except as to reversed grounds, and the Board may remand an application to the examiner.

name: Board may suggest amendments and appellant's right to amend in conformity
description: The Board's opinion may include an explicit statement how a claim could be amended to overcome a specific rejection; when the Board includes such a statement appellant has the right to amend in conformity therewith, which would overcome that specific rejection.
guidance: An examiner may still reject a claim so-amended if the rejection constitutes a new ground of rejection.

name: Definitions and filing certificate requirement
description: Key terms for subpart C proceedings: 'proceeding' shorthand for inter partes reexamination proceeding; 'owner', 'requester', 'appellant', 'respondent' defined; 'filing' requires any document filed to include a certificate indicating service to all other parties as required by Rule 903.
guidance: If more than one party appeals or cross-appeals, each is an appellant with respect to the claims directed by their appeal; no requester may be a respondent to another requester's appellant brief.

name: Prohibition on post-appeal amendments and evidence
description: Amendments submitted after the date the proceeding has been appealed are prohibited except for amendments permitted by § 41.77(b)(1) and amendments canceling claims where such cancellation does not affect the scope of any other pending claim. Affidavits and other evidence submitted after appeal are likewise prohibited except as permitted by § 41.77(b)(1).
guidance: This replaces prior practice permitting such evidence on a showing of good and sufficient reasons; the Office expects prosecution to occur before the examiner prior to an appeal being filed.

name: Concise explanation of subject matter of independent claims with specification and drawing references
description: For each independent claim involved in the appeal and each dependent claim argued separately, a concise explanation of the subject matter defined in the claim is required and shall refer to the specification by page and line number and to the drawings, if any, by reference characters.
guidance: For each independent claim and each dependent claim argued separately, every means-plus-function and step-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph) must be identified and the structure, material, or acts described in the specification as corresponding to each claimed function be set forth with reference to the specification by page and line number and to the drawing by reference characters.

name: Concise statement listing each issue presented for review
description: A concise statement is required listing each issue presented for review (example: 'claims 1 to 10 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by U.S. Patent No. X').
guidance: This is § 41.67(c)(1)(vi) and intended to provide clear, compact presentation of issues for the Board.

name: Refusal to consider arguments or authorities not included in brief without good cause
description: Any arguments or authorities not included in a brief permitted in the section or filed pursuant to §§ 41.68 and 41.71 will be refused consideration by the Board unless good cause is shown; a separate heading is required for each ground of rejection instead of prior grouping of claims.
guidance: This enforces clear organization and completeness in briefs; good cause exceptions exist but are limited.

name: Identification of patent interferences as contested cases and interpretation of copied claims
description: Patent interferences are specifically identified as contested cases under subpart D; practice continues of looking at the applicant's specification (not the source specification) to determine the meaning of a copied claim.

name: Definitions specific to patent interferences
description: Definitions include 'accorded benefit' (application providing proper constructive reduction to practice), 'constructive reduction to practice', 'count' redefined to emphasize relationship to admissible proofs of priority under § 102(g), 'involved claim' consistent with other definitions, 'senior party' focusing on earliest constructive reduction to practice, and 'threshold issue' defined to include no interference-in-fact, the bar under 35 U.S.C. 135(b), and lack of written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(1).
guidance: These definitions clarify priority, standing, and which issues can bar participation in an interference; threshold issues are limited to motions from a party with a patent or published application against a party with an involved application.

name: Requirements and practice for provoking an interference
description: Applicants provoking an interference must follow requirements (adding a claim to provoke an interference, special requirements when copying claims from patents) and may be subject to summary proceedings if unable to show they would prevail on priority.
guidance: Section 41.202(d) provides bases for summary proceedings; showings under § 41.202(e) must by themselves, if unrebutted, warrant determination of priority in favor of the applicant.

name: Standard for declaring an interference
description: The standard for declaring a patent interference is a two-way unpatentability test to determine whether claimed inventions interfere; an administrative patent judge declares the interference and may redeclare it sua sponte or in response to motions; parties may suggest that an APJ declare or redeclare an interference to accommodate files.

name: Definition of a design (subject matter of a design patent)
description: In a design patent application, the subject matter which is claimed is the design embodied in or applied to an article of manufacture (or portion thereof) and not the article itself.
guidance: Design consists of the visual characteristics embodied in or applied to an article — configuration, surface ornamentation, or combination. A design is inseparable from the article to which it is applied, must be a definite, preconceived thing capable of reproduction, and cannot be a design in the abstract. Case citations (e.g., In re SurgiSil; Curver Luxembourg) emphasize that a design claim is limited to the article identified in the claim.

name: Elements of a design patent application (37 CFR 1.154)
description: A design patent application has essentially the elements required of a utility patent application; a drawing is an essential element and a claim in a specific form is necessary.
guidance: Suggested order of elements: design application transmittal form; fee transmittal form; application data sheet (§ 1.76); specification; drawings or photographs; inventor's oath or declaration (§ 1.153(b)). The specification should include: preamble (name, title, brief description of nature and intended use), cross-reference to related applications, statement regarding federally sponsored research, description of the figure(s) of the drawing, feature description, and a single claim. See 37 CFR 1.154 for arrangement and MPEP ¶15.05 for framing the specification.

name: Specification content — general rule and permissible statements
description: No description other than brief reference to the drawing is ordinarily required; however certain types of statements are permissible in the specification.
guidance: Permissible statements include: (1) description of appearance of portions not illustrated (must be in original filing); (2) disclaimers of portions not shown as forming no part of claimed design (as originally filed for antecedent basis); (3) statement indicating purpose of broken lines (e.g., environmental structure or boundaries not part of design); (4) description of nature and intended use if not in preamble; (5) 'characteristic features' statement describing a feature considered novel or nonobvious (37 CFR 1.71(c)). The USPTO may telephone applicants at docketing to resolve nature/intended use to facilitate classification and proper search. Any added description must not introduce new matter.

name: Characteristic feature statement cautions
description: A 'characteristic features' statement describing a particular feature of novelty or nonobviousness may be included but does not serve as the basis for determining patentability.
guidance: Recommended phrasing: 'The characteristic feature of the design resides in [description].' Inclusion may later limit the claim. Patentability of a design is determined by comparison of the overall appearance with the prior art (e.g., In re Rosen; In re Leslie). The examiner will not suggest a characteristic feature statement and it is optional for applicant.

name: Drawing requirements for design applications (37 CFR 1.152; §1.84)
description: The design must be represented by a drawing that complies with § 1.84 and must contain a sufficient number of views to constitute a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design.
guidance: Use appropriate and adequate surface shading to show character or contour. Solid black surface shading is not permitted except to represent the color black or color contrast. Broken lines may show visible environmental structure but not hidden planes or surfaces not visible through opaque materials. Alternate positions of a component illustrated by full and broken lines in the same view are not permitted. Photographs and ink drawings may not be combined as formal drawings; photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must be limited to the claimed design and not disclose environmental structure. Drawings/photographs must be clear and complete; inconsistencies among views should be objected to and, if so severe that overall appearance is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b).

name: Claim form and content for design patents (37 CFR 1.153)
description: A design patent application may include only a single claim, normally in formal terms to 'The ornamental design for (the article) as shown' or 'as shown and described.'
guidance: The claim should be consistent in terminology with the title. 'And described' is added when the specification includes a proper descriptive statement. Full lines in drawings show the claimed design; broken lines serve specific purposes (e.g., environment, boundaries, stitching) and may not be used to indicate immaterial portions. The design is unitary; all portions contribute to the appearance and are material.

name: Broken lines usage in drawings and claims
description: Broken lines may be used for certain illustrative purposes but may not be used to identify portions of the claimed design which are immaterial or unimportant.
guidance: Broken lines are permitted to illustrate environmental structure, boundaries, stitching, and fold lines, but are not permitted to show hidden planes or alternate positions in the same view. They cannot be used to disclaim solid-line claimed portions as 'immaterial.' Improper use may lead to objections or rejections.

name: Design patent and trademark overlap; trademark use in applications
description: A design patent and a trademark may be obtained on the same subject matter, but certain uses of trademarks in design applications are restricted.
guidance: Derogatory use of a trademark in a design application is prohibited and will result in rejection of the claim under 35 U.S.C. 171 as offensive subject matter. It is improper to use a trademark alone or coupled with 'type' in the title (e.g., 'Band-Aid type Bandage') — examiners must object and require deletion. If a trademark appears in the drawing disclosure, the specification must include a statement preceding the claim identifying the trademark material forming part of the claimed design and the name of the owner of the trademark (use form paragraph 15.76).

name: Translation of the priority document
description: A designated Office may require a translation of the priority document only where validity of the priority claim is relevant to patentability determination or to determine whether an incorporated element/part is completely contained in the priority document.
guidance: If part of description/claims/drawings was incorporated by reference, the Office may require an indication where the part is contained in the translation of the priority document.

name: Opportunity to respond to intended refusal of restoration
description: If the designated Office intends to refuse the request for restoration of the priority claim, it must notify the applicant of its intention and give the applicant an opportunity to make observations within a reasonable time specified in the notification.
guidance: The notification may be sent together with an invitation to file declarations or other evidence; applicants should use the opportunity to present supporting facts.

name: Amendment of the international application in the national phase
description: Applicants are guaranteed an opportunity to amend claims, description and drawings before any designated Office in the national phase; designated and elected Offices must permit such amendments for at least one month from the time the applicant enters the national phase.
guidance: Many Offices permit amendments at any time during national examination. Where examination must be specifically requested, requests to amend may only be made after entry into the national phase. National Chapters provide further indications and any exceptional time limits under Rules 52.1 and 78.

name: Correction of obvious mistakes (rectification)
description: Obvious mistakes in the description, claims and drawings may normally be corrected before the designated Office; correction can be presented as an amendment provided the scope of the international application as originally filed is not broadened.
guidance: Designated and elected Offices must generally process the international application 'as rectified' unless they already started processing before notification of rectification. An Office may disregard an authorized rectification if it finds it would not have authorized it; however, it must give the applicant an opportunity to make observations before disregarding. Conditions for rectification depend on national law and practice.

name: Federal Government use license exceptions
description: Certain government-use licenses or rights do not preclude claiming small entity status where specific statutory or Executive Order-based conditions are met.
guidance: Examples include: rights determinations under Executive Order 10096 (§501.6), Federal agency action under 15 U.S.C. 3710d(a) allowing employee-inventor to retain title, retention under 35 U.S.C. 202(d) where the license is equivalent to 202(c)(4), funding agreements under 35 U.S.C. 202(c)(4) if the invention was made solely by employees of the small business/nonprofit or if the agency assigns/license rights as described, and CRADA-related provisions under 15 U.S.C. 3710a(b)(2)/(b)(3)(D) provided the lab has waived/assigned government ownership rights. Regardless of exception applicability, no refund under § 1.28(a) is available for any patent fee paid by the Government.

name: Reexamination statutory scope and availability (any person, any time on published prior art)
description: '[A]ny person at any time may file a request for reexamination by the [PTO] of any claim of a patent on the basis of any prior art' that was published. (35 U.S.C. Sec. 302).
guidance: Reexamination may confirm patentable claims or cancel unpatentable claims; the process is intended to increase the reliability of the PTO’s action by reexamining patents thought 'doubtful.' Cites In re Etter.

name: No constitutional bar from Article III/Seventh Amendment to administrative reexamination
description: There is no conflict between Section 6 and other parts of the Constitution such as Article III and the Seventh Amendment; investment of regulatory/validity functions in an administrative agency is consistent with precedent.
guidance: Cites cases rejecting claims that PTO reexamination 'overrules' Article III court determinations (In re Swanson, Patlex, Joy Technologies). Emphasizes differing proceedings and evidentiary standards.

name: Medal of Honor — award must be based on official War Department records
description: Under the act of April 23, 1904, award of the Medal of Honor must appear from 'official records' in the War Department; an oral recommendation is not an official record and cannot form the basis of an award.
guidance: The 1904 act removes the time element in making a recommendation but requires documentary 'official records'; absence of such records is fatal to extra-statutory claims. Establishing extra-statutory time limits in executive regulation is inadvisable (G.17810; G.16305; G.19139).

name: Claims excluded from supplementary international search — general categories
description: In addition to limitation of the supplementary international search due to a lack of unity of invention, the supplementary search may exclude: (i) any claims which would not be the subject of international search by the Authority carrying out the supplementary search, whether for reasons of clarity, subject matter or failure to provide, after a warning and opportunity to comply, a sequence listing in an appropriate form and language; (ii) where the international search report or a declaration under Article 17(2)(a) has been established before the start of the supplementary search, any claims which were not the subject of the international search; (iii) certain claims, in accordance with a limitation or condition specified in the agreement between the Authority and the International Bureau under Article 16(3)(b) (in particular limitations to the effect that supplementary international searches will not extend to any claim beyond a certain number of claims).
guidance: When exclusions (i) or (ii) mean that no supplementary international search report will be established, the Authority so declares and promptly notifies the applicant and the IB using Form PCT/SISA/502. If some claims are excluded but a report is established, the limitations are indicated in Box No. II of the supplementary international search report (Form PCT/SISA/501).

name: Unity of invention — scope and absence of extra-fee opportunity
description: Unlike the case for the main international search, no opportunity is offered to pay additional fees in case it is found that the international application lacks unity of invention. Rather, the supplementary international search report is immediately established on those parts of the international application which relate to the main invention (normally the invention first mentioned in the claims).
guidance: Examiner should consider factors in determining unity and main invention (see next metric entries). The examiner’s opinion on unity and consequent scope should be reported on the supplementary report similarly to the main search.

name: Factors to consider when determining unity of invention for supplementary search
