description: In determining whether there is unity of invention and what is considered to be the main invention the examiner should: (i) take due account of any opinion on unity of invention included in the documents indicated in items (vi) and (vii) of paragraph 15.79; (ii) consider an applicant’s specification under Rule 45bis.1(d) to limit the supplementary search to one of the inventions; (iii) where the invention first claimed would not be searched for any reason, consider the first searchable invention instead; (iv) if other inventions are easily searched, it may be appropriate to include those inventions within the scope of the supplementary search report.
guidance: Although not bound by ISA views, the supplementary examiner should give due account to them; if applicant specified a wish to limit and examiner agrees and relevant claims not excluded, focus on that invention.

name: Use of continuation sheets and which sheets are published
description: The printed international search report Form (PCT/ISA/210) contains two main sheets and six optional continuation sheets for necessary information: 'continuation of first sheet (1)', '(2)', '(3)'; 'continuation of second sheet'; 'patent family annex'; and 'extra sheet'. Specific continuation sheets have defined uses (e.g., continuation of first sheet (1) for sequence listing indications; (2) for unsearchable claims and/or lack of unity; (3) for abstract). Not all continuation sheets apply to supplementary or international-type searches.
guidance: Only the 'second sheet', 'continuation of second sheet' (if any), 'continuation of first sheet (2)' (if any), and 'extra sheet' (if any), and any patent family sheet will be subject of international publication; the 'first sheet' and some continuations contain information already on front page and are not published. Supplementary international search report is not included in the published international application, but the complete document is made available to the public, with English translation where appropriate.

name: Cases where no or limited search report is established — subject-matter exclusions
description: No International Searching Authority is required to search or examine an international application to the extent that its subject matter is: (i) scientific and mathematical theories, (ii) plant or animal varieties or essentially biological processes for production of plants and animals (other than microbiological processes and products thereof), (iii) schemes, rules or methods of doing business, performing purely mental acts or playing games, (iv) methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy, as well as diagnostic methods, (v) mere presentations of information, (vi) computer programs to the extent that the ISA is not equipped to search prior art concerning such programs.
guidance: Chapter 9 deals with these exclusions in detail as well as other situations (lack of clarity) where it may not be possible to establish a meaningful search in respect of some or all claims; supplementary international search reports may also exclude claims which were not the subject of the main international search.

name: Omnibus claims and reporting of breaches
description: Claims which rely, in respect of the technical features of the invention, on references to the description or drawings ('omnibus claims') are searched and reported upon if they can be given a definite construction. However, in the written opinion and for international preliminary examination, any breach of Rule 6.2(a) (no reference to the description or drawings except when absolutely necessary) may be reported in Box No. VII of the opinion or report.
guidance: If the national law of the Office acting as ISA permits multiple dependent claims non-compliant with Rule 6.4(a), such claims are included in the international search and no indication is made under item 3 of Box No. II.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification
description: During examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification (i.e., construed as broadly as their terms reasonably allow, taking into account the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art).
guidance: BRI reduces the chance that an issued claim will later be interpreted more broadly than justified; applicants can amend claims during prosecution, so the PTO applies BRI rather than the narrower claim construction used in infringement suits. Case law examples: Phillips, In re American Academy of Sci. Tech. Ctr., In re Yamamoto, In re Zletz, In re Morris. Ensure interpretation remains reasonable and consistent with how skilled artisans would understand the claim in light of the specification.

name: Claim words given plain meaning unless inconsistent with specification
description: Under BRI, claim terms are given their ordinary and customary (plain) meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, unless that meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: Ordinary and customary meaning is evidenced by claim language, specification, drawings, prior art, and the best source is the specification (which can serve as a glossary). If the specification conflicts with the plain meaning, the specification controls. Example: Chef America v. Lamb‑Weston (ordinary English words construed as written).

name: Sources to determine ordinary and customary meaning
description: The ordinary and customary meaning of a claim term may be evidenced by the words of the claims, the specification, drawings, prosecution history, prior art, and extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, technical treatises, expert testimony).
guidance: When extrinsic sources give multiple definitions, consult the intrinsic record to select the meaning most consistent with the applicant's use. Dictionaries and other references must be compared against the context in the specification. Case examples: Phillips, Ferguson Beauregard/Logic Controls, Renishaw, Vitronics, Brookhill‑Wilk, Rexnord, Toro.

name: Applicant-as-lexicographer (special definitions by applicant)
description: An applicant may act as his/her own lexicographer and define a term differently from its ordinary meaning, but must do so with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision in the specification so that one of ordinary skill in the art is put on notice.
guidance: Explicit definitions in the specification control claim interpretation. Implicit definitions by consistent usage in the specification may also define terms. The special meaning must be sufficiently clear to justify departure from common usage. Case examples: In re Paulsen, Multiform Desiccants, Merck v. Teva (failure to clearly redefine 'about'). See MPEP § 2173.05(a).

name: Effect of preamble determined case-by-case
description: Whether preamble language limits claim scope depends on the entire record; there is no single litmus test—preamble may be limiting when it supplies essential structure/steps or gives 'life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim, but non-limiting when it merely states purpose or intended use and the claim body is structurally complete.
guidance: If preamble language recites structural limitations, it should be treated as part of the claimed invention (Corning Glass Works, Pac‑Tec, In re Stencel). If the preamble only states purpose and deletion does not affect claim structure, it is generally not limiting (Pitney Bowes, Rowe v. Dror). Evaluate whether the preamble was relied upon during prosecution to distinguish prior art—clear reliance can transform the preamble into a limitation (Catalina, Metabolite Labs.). Use prosecution history and specification to determine whether the preamble provides context or a limiting feature.

name: Preamble statements that limit structure vs. statements of purpose/intended use
description: Preamble terminology that limits the structure of the claimed invention functions as a claim limitation; preamble recitations of purpose or intended use generally do not limit the claim unless they result in a structural/manipulative difference or were relied upon during prosecution.
guidance: Analyze whether the body of the claim intrinsically sets forth all limitations; if so, the preamble likely is non-limiting. If the preamble supplies essential characterizing structure or the prosecution history shows reliance on the preamble to distinguish prior art, treat it as limiting. Case examples: Corning, Pitney Bowes, Jansen, In re Otto, In re Cruciferous Sprout Litig., Poly‑America, Intirtool.

name: Transitional phrases define openness/closedness of claim scope
description: Transitional phrases such as 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', and 'consisting of' affect whether additional, unrecited elements or steps are excluded; determination is fact-specific.
guidance: 'Comprising' (including/containing/characterized by) is presumptively open-ended and allows additional elements or steps (e.g., method claims using 'comprising' are open). 'Consisting of' and 'consisting essentially of' signal more closed scope; 'group consisting of' often indicates a closed Markush group. Case examples: Mars v. H.J. Heinz, Invitrogen v. Biocrest, Genentech v. Chiron, Gillette v. Energizer, In re Baxter.

name: When claim terms are ambiguous, consult the specification for the inventor's meaning
description: If a claim term is ambiguous, the specification should be consulted to determine the meaning ascribed to that term by the inventor; the specification may define ambiguous terms or point away from improper meanings.
guidance: Use the specification to clarify ambiguous terms rather than importing extraneous limitations. Case examples: In re Weiss (look to specification-defined meaning for 'preselected level of force'), Renishaw (disqualifying improper dictionary meanings inconsistent with intrinsic record), Rapoport v. Dement (distinguishing treatment vs. secondary symptoms).

name: Means/step-plus-function claim elements require specification for corresponding structure
description: When an element is claimed using means-plus-function or step-plus-function language (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph), the specification must be consulted to determine the structure, material, or acts corresponding to the claimed function.
guidance: Determine the corresponding structure disclosed in the specification that performs the recited function; failure to identify adequate corresponding structure can affect statutory subject matter/definiteness. Case example: In re Donaldson; see MPEP §§ 2181–2186 and § 2173.05(a).

name: Language requirement for carrying out international preliminary examination
description: Where neither the language of filing nor the language of publication is accepted by the IPEA, the applicant must furnish with the demand a translation of the international application into a language accepted by the IPEA and which is a language of publication. The translation must include elements referred to in Article 11(1)(iii)(d) or (e) and any relevant parts of description, claims or drawings considered to be contained under Rule 20.6(b).
guidance: If translation already furnished to the ISA and IPEA is part of same office, that translation may be used unless applicant furnishes another. IB will translate the ISA written opinion into English on request, to be forwarded within two months.

name: The Enablement Requirement [R-2]
description: The specification must describe how to make and how to use the invention as defined by the claims so that one skilled in the art can make and use the claimed invention.
guidance: Purpose is to ensure the invention is communicated to the public in a meaningful way. The requirement does not demand teaching a commercially viable or perfected embodiment absent a claim limitation to that effect. Enablement is separate and distinct from the written description requirement and must be analyzed under its own criteria.

name: Test of Enablement / Undue Experimentation Standard [R-5]
description: Enablement is tested by whether one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention from the disclosure and the knowledge in the art without undue experimentation.
guidance: Standard derived from Mineral Separation v. Hyde and In re Wands. The question is whether necessary experimentation to practice the invention would be undue or unreasonable; some experimentation may be acceptable if not undue. A patent need not teach what is well known in the art.

name: Factor (A): The breadth of the claims
description: Breadth of the claims is a key factor in determining whether the disclosure enables the full claim scope.
guidance: Wide claim breadth may require more detailed disclosure; enablement must be commensurate with claim scope. See MPEP § 2164.08 for further discussion.

name: Factor (G): The existence of working examples
description: Whether the specification includes working (actual) examples or prophetic examples, and how those examples relate to the claim scope.
guidance: Working examples are persuasive, particularly in unpredictable arts, but are not required. Absence of working examples is a factor to consider but never alone dispositive. See MPEP § 2164.02.

name: Working Example (working vs. prophetic)
description: Examples in a specification may be based on actual work (working) or predicted outcomes (prophetic); the presence or absence of examples is not dispositive for enablement but is a factor.
guidance: An applicant need not reduce the invention to practice before filing. Lack of a working example is considered more strongly in unpredictable arts. A single working example can preclude a rejection that nothing is enabled, but may not alone establish enablement across broad claim scope.

name: None or One Working Example — limits on rejections
description: The absence of working examples should not be the sole reason for a non-enablement rejection; conversely, a single working example is often enough to preclude a blanket non-enablement rejection.
guidance: Presence of one working example should not automatically be interpreted as enabling the full breadth of claims without analyzing other factors; examiner must explain why extrapolation from the example would or would not be expected.

name: Working Examples and a Claimed Genus
description: For genus claims, representative examples plus a statement applicable to the genus may be sufficient to enable the genus as a whole if one skilled in the art would expect use across the genus without undue experimentation.
guidance: Proof of enablement may be required for un exemplified members only where the examiner advances adequate reasons to show a person skilled in the art could not use the genus as a whole without undue experimentation.

name: Burden on the Examiner Under the Enablement Requirement [R-1]
description: Before rejecting for non-enablement, the examiner must construe the claims and establish a reasonable basis to question enablement, giving specific reasons and evidence.
guidance: Examiner must select and state definitions for ambiguous terms, explain why the disclosure is doubted, and back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning (In re Marzocchi, In re Bowen). The first Office action should present the best case with all relevant reasons and evidence, and examiners should identify limitations that would render claims enabled where appropriate.

name: Whether a 'wherein' clause limits a means-plus-function term
description: A 'wherein' clause narrows a recited function only if it substantively limits the term, rather than merely stating the result of the limitations in the claim (Lockheed). If the clause affects the manner of performing the function (e.g., requires identification using semantic tags or differing characteristics), it limits the function.
guidance: Distinguish clauses that 'merely state a result' (Lockheed example: a 'whereby' clause stating a byproduct) from clauses that change how the function is performed (the opinion finds the Term 7 'wherein' clause limits 'identifying' because it prescribes identification by 'computer-readable semantic tags' and differing characteristics). BBA Nonwovens shows contrasting treatment where post-positional language described a result and thus did not limit the function.

name: Katz exception / whether a general-purpose computer can perform the function
description: A means-plus-function claim need not disclose algorithmic structure if the claimed functionality is coextensive with a general-purpose computer (the Katz exception). Determine whether the recited function is 'coextensive' with a microprocessor or general-purpose computer or instead requires specialized programming.
guidance: Use EON (quoting Katz) as authority: if additional elements (e.g., semantic tags, different characteristics) make the function more than simple identification/readout, the Katz exception likely does not apply and algorithmic structure must be disclosed. The court found Term 7 was not coextensive with a general-purpose computer because it required specialized identifying functionality.

name: Requirement to disclose an algorithmic structure for means-plus-function terms
description: When a means-plus-function limitation is not covered by Katz, the specification must disclose an algorithm (sufficient structure) to perform the claimed function; otherwise the claim is indefinite.
guidance: Cite Noah Sys., EON, and Finisar: the specification must provide enough detail — not mere high-level 'accessing' or locating — to 'clearly link[] or associate[]' structure to the claimed function. Bare software references or black-box 'readers' without algorithmic steps are insufficient.

name: Indefiniteness standard for means-plus-function clauses
description: A means-plus-function clause is indefinite if a person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would be unable to recognize the structure in the specification and associate it with the corresponding function in the claim.
guidance: Noah Sys. articulated this standard. Even if some structures are named (e.g., 'reader'), the specification must disclose the structure's algorithmic steps or sufficient detail so a PHOSITA can associate that structure with the claimed function; otherwise find indefinite.

name: Presumption against means-plus-function when 'means' is absent
description: If a claim does not use the word 'means', there is a rebuttable presumption that § 112, ¶ 6 does not apply; the patentee enjoys this presumption unless the challenger proves otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence (Zeroclick, Williamson).
guidance: In practice, terms like 'code for' create a presumption that § 112, ¶ 6 does not apply. The challenger (e.g., government/accuser) must present intrinsic/extrinsic evidence to overcome the presumption by showing that the term fails to connote definite structure to a PHOSITA.

name: How to rebut the presumption (what evidence overcomes it)
description: To overcome the presumption, show that the non-'means' term (e.g., 'code for', 'logic to') is a nonce or functional black box that does not connote sufficiently definite structure to a PHOSITA (Egenera, Dyfan).
guidance: Courts examine intrinsic evidence (claim language, specification, prosecution history) and extrinsic evidence (expert declarations). The challenger must show by preponderance that the term is just a general category name (e.g., 'logic' or 'code') and lacks structural disclosure such that § 112, ¶ 6 should apply.

name: Look beyond boilerplate words like 'code' to the functional language of the claim
description: Evaluate the entirety of the limitation — not just the presence of 'code' or 'application' — to determine whether the claim connotes sufficiently definite structure (Dyfan).
guidance: If the functional description reveals particular conventional structures or algorithms a PHOSITA would recognize, § 112, ¶ 6 may not apply even when 'code for' appears. Conversely, purely functional recitations without structural detail support a means-plus-function treatment.

name: Claim differentiation and comparative claim drafting considerations
description: Differences in wording across related claims or patents (e.g., explicit 'means' usage in one patent vs 'code for' in another) can inform but do not control the § 112, ¶ 6 inquiry; the question remains one of law for the court.
guidance: The court noted claim differentiation can counsel that 'code for' is not means-plus-function, but a party cannot circumvent the legal test by asserting intent; the presumption is rebuttable and the court decides based on evidence (Howmedica, Karlin).

name: Three-question framework for analyzing a potentially means-plus-function claim
description: When assessing a term, the court considers: (1) whether the function is limited by a 'wherein' clause (Lockheed); (2) whether a general-purpose computer can perform the function (Katz/EON); and (3) if not, whether the specification discloses sufficient structure/algorithm (Noah Sys/Finisar).
guidance: Apply these sequentially: if the 'wherein' clause limits the function and the function is not coextensive with a general-purpose computer, require sufficient structural disclosure; absence of such disclosure renders the term indefinite.

name: Referencing sequences in description, claims, or drawings
description: Where the description or claims discuss a sequence that is set forth in the 'Sequence Listing,' reference must be made to the sequence by use of the sequence identifier (preceded by 'SEQ ID NO:' or the like) in the text of the description or claims, even if the sequence is also embedded in the text; when in drawings, use the sequence identifier either in the drawing or in the Brief Description where correlation is clear.
guidance: Sequence identifiers must match those assigned in the Sequence Listing (§ 1.823(a)(5)).

name: Deeming provisions for pending interferences and reexaminations (§6(f)(2)(B), §7(e))
description: For pending interferences, the Director may deem the PTAB to be the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences and conduct any further proceedings; similar authority for pending inter partes reexaminations; language deems references to derivation proceedings to extend to interferences commenced before repeal.
guidance: Designed to provide continuity for proceedings that began under the prior statutory scheme; ensures claims of pending matters are processed consistently during transition to new procedures.

name: Prior-user rights (35 U.S.C. §273, AIA §5)
description: Creates a broadened prior-user defense applicable to all utility patents: can be asserted for any process or for any product used in a manufacturing or other commercial process; to prevail, the defendant must show commercial use of the subject matter at least one year before the earlier of either the effective filing date of the claimed invention or a public disclosure that qualifies for the §102(b) grace period; defense applies only against patents issued on or after September 16, 2011; defense cannot be asserted against inventions made by a university.
guidance: House and Senate proponents argued the defense prevents incentive to offshore manufacturing and addresses policing difficulties for process patents; legislative history notes changes through floor amendments (e.g., elimination of reduction-to-practice requirement and clarification of who may assert the defense—'performed or directed the performance'). The Committee Report contained limited discussion and some elements changed after the report (so practitioners should read statutory text and floor remarks).

name: Labels like 'isolated', 'recombinant', 'synthetic' do not add patent-eligibility weight
description: Words such as 'isolated', 'recombinant', and 'synthetic' add no weight to the patent eligibility analysis.
guidance: Merely reciting such terms without substantive structural or marked functional changes will not make a claim patent-eligible under the USPTO standard.

name: Method-of-use claims require a practical, specific, significant application
description: A method of using natural products should involve a practical, specific, and significant application so the claimed method would not foreclose others from using the same natural product in other ways.
guidance: Claims that merely recite (i) a general instruction to use the natural product; (ii) well-understood, purely conventional, or routine steps; or (iii) steps that anyone must use to apply the product are insufficient. Example: 'administer amazonic acid' may fail, whereas specifying a regimen/dosage (10–20 days at 0.76–1.25 teaspoons daily) could satisfy the requirement.

name: Product-by-process claim limits and requirements
description: 'Product-by-process' claims define a product by the process used to make it (e.g., 'product X obtained by process Y') and are accepted only when the product cannot otherwise be adequately defined.
guidance: In the U.S., patentability of a product-by-process claim is determined by the product itself regardless of the process; the process is considered only if it implies distinctive structural characteristics. If the product is identical or similar to known products, applicants bear the burden to show novelty/non-obviousness. Enforcement: such claims typically only cover products produced by the recited process, so an accused product made by a different process may not infringe.

name: Sufficient disclosure: written description and enablement requirements
description: Applications must sufficiently describe the invention so that one skilled in the art would recognize and be enabled to practice the invention; generic claims cannot be broader than what is enabled/disclosed.
guidance: A claim to a general formula is not patentable if only a few species are disclosed—claims may be limited to explicitly described species. Disclose as many substitutions, modifications, and parameters (e.g., temperature, pH, reagents) as reasonably possible to support broader claim scope.

name: Claim-drafting strategy: focus and scope
description: Claims should be drafted within a reasonable scope and be of sufficient significance so they do not appear to be a general application of the natural products.
guidance: Avoid overbroad claims that simply claim the natural product; instead claim derivatives, modified structures, formulations, specific dosages/regimens, manufacturing processes, and particular applications to increase likelihood of eligibility and enforceability.

name: Practical advice: include multiple claim types and detailed characterizations
description: Include all features and available information that may characterize the products in the application and draft separate claims directed to the manufacturing process and the product-by-process for broader protection.
guidance: Researchers are highly advised to include detailed descriptions of individual embodiments and combinations, and to draft both product and process claims to expand protection and mitigate risks of invalidation or narrow enforcement.

name: Applicant burden when claimed product resembles known products
description: If the claimed product is identical to or similar to a known product, the applicant bears the burden of proving novelty and non-obviousness to overcome prior art.
guidance: This is particularly important for product-by-process claims since U.S. law evaluates the product itself for novelty; patentees should be prepared to demonstrate distinguishing structural or marked functional characteristics.

name: Privilege/logging requirement when withholding documents
description: A party withholding responsive documents on the basis of privilege must expressly make the claim and describe the nature of the documents, communications, or tangible things not produced or disclosed in a manner that, without revealing privileged information, will enable other parties to assess the claim (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5)).
guidance: The most common way to particularize privilege/protection is a privilege log identifying each withheld document, the nature of the privilege/protection claimed, names of communicants, date/place, and general subject matter. See advisory committee notes and case law for log content guidance.

name: Types of after-final amendments that may be entered
description: The types of after final amendments that may be entered are: (1) to cancel claims or comply with any requirement of form expressly set forth in a previous action; (2) to present rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal; and (3) an amendment touching the merits upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why the amendment is necessary and was not earlier presented.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.116(b)(1),(2),(3) and MPEP 714.13(II). Note: If an examiner can readily determine a proposed amendment will place the application in condition for allowance, the final amendment may be entered.

name: Treatment of after-final amendment filed with or after appeal brief
description: An after final amendment filed before the appeal brief is treated under 37 CFR 1.116. An amendment filed with or after the appeal brief is treated under 37 CFR 41.33(b) and may only be entered to cancel claims (without affecting scope of other claims) or rewrite dependent claims into independent form.
guidance: 37 CFR 41.33(b) restricts the types of post-brief amendments that may be entered for appeals.

name: Purpose and uses of examiner's amendments
description: Examiner's amendments are typically used to cancel or amend claims, and to make formal corrections to the application, including the drawings and the specification.
guidance: Must be signed by a primary examiner and authorized by applicant in a formal interview (personal or telephone). If examiner amends drawings, applicant must provide replacement drawings reflecting changes. MPEP 1302.

name: RCE submission requirement — what must be included
description: Must include a reply to the final rejection that meets the reply requirements of 37 CFR 1.111 (e.g., an amendment filed with the RCE or a previously-filed after final amendment). Mere request for RCE and payment of the fee is not sufficient.
guidance: Submission can be an amendment to the specification/claims/drawings, new arguments, new evidence in support of patentability, or an IDS in an application subject to a notice of allowance (but not where last action is a final rejection or Ex parte Quayle).

name: AFCP 2.0 — eligibility and application limits
description: Application must: have an outstanding final rejection; have been filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) or 371(c); have a request for AFCP 2.0; amend at least one independent claim that does not broaden the scope of that claim in any aspect.
guidance: Only one AFCP 2.0 request may be filed in response to an outstanding final rejection. Include a statement that applicant is willing and available to participate in an examiner-initiated interview concerning the response.

name: AFCP 2.0 — incomplete or disqualifying submissions
description: If submission is incomplete or request is improper, examiner should process the after final submission under 37 CFR 1.116 (pre-pilot practice). If request qualifies, examiner determines whether additional search/consideration would be required and is possible within AFCP 2.0 time allotment.
guidance: Factors (not exhaustive) that might require more time: claims added, complexity of amendment, at least one added claim directed to a different invention (possible restriction), prior after final interviews or traditional after final submissions.

name: P4 Analgesic/anaesthetic/antiinflammatory/CNS structure
description: Subset P4 contains analgesic/local anaesthetic (P41 with P411–P412), antiinflammatory (P42 with P420–P423), immunological (P43 with P430–P434), CNS depressants/tranquillisers (P44 with P440–P448), CNS stimulant (P45 with P450–P453). Many P4 codes include historical M5 applicability notes.
guidance: Assign the most specific P4 subcode based on disclosed therapeutic/activity claims and take into account pre-1981 steroid coding exceptions.

name: R05 Timed-release formulations
description: R05 includes timed-release formulation subcodes R051 (delayed release) and R052 (sustained release). Note: R051 and R052 are not searchable for general-use chemicals (Chemdoc - Section E) prior to 1981.
guidance: Use R051/R052 for novel timed-release claims and account for searchability limitations in pre-1981 Chemdoc records.

name: Deliberate course of action is not an unintentional delay (enumerated examples)
description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action by the applicant cannot be considered 'unintentional' under 37 CFR 1.137.
guidance: Examples of deliberate choices that render delay intentional include: (A) applicant does not consider the claims patentable over outstanding references; (B) applicant does not consider allowed/patentable claims broad enough to justify expense; (C) applicant does not consider any patent sufficiently valuable to justify expense of obtaining a patent; (D) applicant does not consider any patent sufficiently valuable to maintain interest in obtaining it; (E) applicant remains interested but seeks to defer patent fees and prosecution expenses. A later change of mind does not render the earlier deliberate decision unintentional (see In re Maldague).

name: Two-component best mode analysis
description: A proper best mode analysis has two components: (A) Determine whether, at the time the application was filed, the inventor knew of a mode of practicing the claimed invention that the inventor considered to be better than any other (a subjective inquiry). (B) If (A) is true, compare what was known with what was disclosed — is the disclosure adequate to enable one skilled in the art to practice the best mode (an objective inquiry).
guidance: Only if the first (subjective) inquiry is answered affirmatively should the examiner analyze the second (objective) inquiry. A best mode rejection is proper only when (A) is affirmative and (B) is negative with reasons supporting nonenabling specification with respect to the best mode.

name: Rejection for lack of written description — form paragraph 7.31.01
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... as failing to comply with the written description requirement: the claim contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Examiner must identify the subject matter not properly described (page/line/drawings) and provide an explanation including any unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to possession.

name: Rejection for lack of enablement — form paragraph 7.31.02
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... as failing to comply with the enablement requirement: the claim contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. If problem is scope, use 7.31.03. In the explanation identify claimed subject matter not enabling and apply the Wands factors (In re Wands) as appropriate. Include any unresolved examiner questions relevant to enablement.

name: Scope of enablement / commensurate scope rejection — form paragraph 7.31.03
description: Claim [1] rejected ... because the specification, while being enabling for [2], does not reasonably provide enablement for [3]; the specification does not enable a person skilled in the art to [make/use] the invention commensurate in scope with these claims.
guidance: Use when specification enables some embodiments but the claims are broader than the enabled disclosure. Identify the enabled subject matter and specific aspects of the claims not enabled; state whether the deficiency is make/use or both.

name: Best mode requirement rejection — form paragraph 7.31.04
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... because the best mode contemplated by the inventor ... has not been disclosed. Evidence of concealment of the best mode is based upon [2].
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Insert specific basis for holding best mode concealed (e.g., disclosure quality effectively results in concealment). Use rarely; explain why the disclosure is so poor as to amount to concealment.

name: Scope of enablement of a 'single means' claim — form paragraph 7.31.05
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... because the claim purports to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph) but fails to recite a combination of elements as required and thus cannot rely on the specification to provide the structure, material or acts to support the claimed function; the claim covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated function while the specification discloses at most only those means known to the inventor.
guidance: Use only when the claim recites a single element in means-plus-function format. This situation should be rare. Precede with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103.

name: Essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement) — form paragraph 7.33.01 / related guidance
description: Claim [1] rejected ... as based on a disclosure which is not enabling: the disclosure does not enable one of ordinary skill in the art to practice the invention without [2], which is/are critical or essential to the practice of the invention but not included in the claim(s).
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite omitted subject matter and in bracket 3 give rationale for considering it critical/essential. Examiner shall cite statement/argument/date/drawing or other evidence showing applicant considered the feature essential.

name: Two separate requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 2nd paragraph)
description: Two separate requirements: (A) the claims must set forth the subject matter that the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention; and (B) the claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter to be protected (definiteness).
guidance: The first requirement is subjective (dependent on inventor's view); the second is objective (evaluated for definiteness by a person of ordinary skill in the art). Examiners should determine whether rejection is for indefiniteness or for failure to claim what the inventor regards as the invention.

name: Evidence to the contrary for what inventor regards as the invention
description: A rejection based on failure to satisfy the requirement that claims set forth what the inventor regards as the invention is appropriate only where the inventor has stated, somewhere other than in the application as filed, that the invention is something different from what is defined by the claims.
guidance: Evidence of contrary inventor view may be found in contentions or admissions in briefs, remarks, or affidavits (37 CFR 1.132). The content of the specification is not used as evidence that claim scope is inconsistent with what the inventor regards as the invention.

name: Unclaimed essential matter — multi-section rejection guidance
description: Omitted matter described as essential in the specification may support rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement or written description) or under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness or failure to claim inventor-regarded invention), depending on facts.
guidance: Essential matter may include missing elements, steps, or necessary structural cooperative relationships. If claim omits matter necessary to practice the invention, follow MPEP §§ 2163 and 2164 guidance. Features described as preferred or illustrative are not necessarily critical or essential.

name: Claim interpretation principle — applicants as their own lexicographers
description: Applicants may define in the claims what the inventor regards as the invention in whatever terms they choose so long as any special meaning assigned to a term is clearly set forth in the specification.
guidance: Applicants may use functional language, alternative expressions, negative limitations, etc. A claim may not be rejected solely because of the type of language used to define subject matter. Where a special definition is used, it must be clearly in the specification as filed.

name: Plain meaning, specification as glossary, and limits on importing embodiments
description: Under BRI, words of the claim must be given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. The best source for determining meaning is the specification; however, limitations drawn solely from the preferred embodiment should not be imported absent clear disclaimer.
guidance: If an Office action used plain meaning and applicant claims a special definition, the applicant must point to where the specification as filed provides a clear and intentional special definition. An applicant may not add special definitions or disavowal after filing; may only point to what was in the specification as filed.

name: Determine whether claim limitations invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph)
description: For each claim limitation, determine whether it invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre-AIA sixth paragraph (means-plus-function treatment).
guidance: If a limitation invokes 112(f), evaluate whether the claim recites sufficient structure/elements or improperly attempts to rely on the specification to supply structure for a broad function-only claim; use 7.31.05 guidance when a single means element is present.

name: 111(a)_application_with_benefit_to_prior_US_app_acquires_earlier_filing_date_for_102(e)
description: For 35 U.S.C. 111(a) applications that claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a prior U.S. provisional application or under 35 U.S.C. 120 to a prior nonprovisional application, the prior art dates under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) are the earlier filing date.
guidance: This is true assuming the earlier-filed application has proper support for the subject matter as required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120. (See Example 2.)

name: consider_proper_benefit_claims_under_specific_statutes
description: When considering earlier filing dates for 102(e), consider benefit claims properly made under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to U.S. provisional applications, 35 U.S.C. 120 to U.S. nonprovisional applications, and 35 U.S.C. 365(c) involving international applications.
guidance: Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) when determining 102(e) dates. Ensure the benefit claims are properly made and that earlier applications provide adequate support (see 112, first paragraph).

name: IA_published_in_non-English_language_after_Nov29_2000_has_no_102(e)_date
description: All references (WIPO publication, U.S. application publication, U.S. patent) of an international application that was filed on or after November 29, 2000 but was not published in English under PCT Article 21(2) have no 35 U.S.C. 102(e) prior art date.
guidance: Such references may be applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) as of their publication dates, but never under 35 U.S.C. 102(e). If a later-filed U.S. nonprovisional application claimed the benefit of the IA, the 102(e) date of the patent or publication of the later-filed U.S. application would be the actual filing date of the later-filed U.S. application. (See Example 5.)

name: continuation_of_IA_rules_follow_IA_original_filing_and_publication_language
description: When a U.S. 35 U.S.C. 111(a) application is a continuation of an IA, determine the IA’s filing date and whether the IA designated the U.S. and was published in English to decide the 102(e) date.
guidance: If the IA was filed on or after Nov. 29, 2000 and published in English and designated the U.S., then the WIPO publication, the U.S. application publication, and the U.S. patent of (or claiming benefit of) that IA have the 102(e) prior art date of the international filing date or earlier effective U.S. filing date. If the IA was not published in English, no 102(e) date is given for the IA publication and the U.S. publication/patent get the actual U.S. filing date of the continuation. (See Examples 7–9 and Additional Benefit Claims sections.)

name: provisional_102(e)_rejection_when_copending_app_has_common_inventor_or_common_assignee
description: If (1) at least one common inventor exists between the applications or the applications are commonly assigned and (2) the effective filing dates are different, then a provisional rejection of the later-filed application under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) should be made.
guidance: The provisional rejection is appropriate where, if the earlier-filed application is published or becomes a patent it would constitute actual prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102. Use form paragraph 7.15.01. The provisional rejection can be overcome in the same manner as a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (see MPEP §706.02(b)), or by abandoning the applications and filing a new application containing the subject matter of both. The rejection might be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of this application (i.e., not “by another”), or by an appropriate showing under 37 CFR 1.131. This rejection may not be overcome by the filing of a terminal disclaimer (In re Bartfeld). If claims would have been obvious over the other copending application, use form paragraph 7.21.01. If conflicts exist, also consider provisional double patenting rejections using form paragraphs 8.30 and 8.32. If evidence shows 102(f) or (g) issues, make appropriate rejections (7.13/7.14).

name: subject_matter_must_satisfy_35_U.S.C._112_first_paragraph_for_earlier_date
description: The subject matter used in a rejection must be disclosed in the earlier-filed application in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, in order for that subject matter to be entitled to the earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: When applying an earlier filing date (e.g., benefit to an earlier U.S. application or IA), verify that the earlier application’s disclosure provides proper written description and enablement for the claimed subject matter to establish entitlement to the earlier date.

name: flowchart_decision_nodes_and_output_actions_for_102(e)_dates
description: Use the provided flowcharts (Chart I and Chart II) to determine 35 U.S.C. 102(e) dates: key decision nodes include whether the reference is an IA after national stage entry, whether IA was filed on/after Nov. 29, 2000, whether the IA designated the U.S., and whether the WIPO publication was in English.
guidance: Flowchart outputs: (a) For patent and U.S. application publication where IA meets Nov. 29, 2000 + designation + English publication: §102(e) date = international filing date or earlier effective U.S. filing date (Form Para 7.12); (b) If IA does not meet those criteria: no §102(e) date and reference is prior art under §102(a) or (b) as of publication/grant date (Form Para 7.08/7.09); (c) For patents based on IA filed prior to Nov. 29, 2000, §102(e) date is the §371(c)(1),(2) and (4) date (Form Para 7.12.01); (d) For U.S. application publications of certain continuations, §102(e) date may be the actual U.S. filing date of the U.S. application that claimed benefit to the IA (Form Para 7.12). The flowcharts also reiterate: consider benefits properly made under §§119(e),120,365(c); do NOT consider foreign priority claims.

name: Use and evaluation of large language models (LLMs)
description: LLMs are promising for patent analysis and generation tasks but have been under-evaluated specifically on patent-related tasks.
guidance: Because patents feature formal language, dense technical content, and legal implications, LLMs could identify nuanced patterns for classification, novelty prediction, and assist in drafting claims or descriptions. Rigorous evaluation on patent-specific tasks is needed.

name: Precision and legal formality in generated patent text
description: Patent documents require a specific style: formal, unambiguous language and precise, accurate, and clear descriptions and claims to satisfy legal requirements.
guidance: Lack of precision/range/clarity hampers examination, risks a small scope, and may provide leverage for litigation. Generation systems must aim for legal adequacy, not just naturalness or fluency.

name: Complete specification components
description: A complete specification is made up of Description, Claims, Abstract and Drawings (if any).
guidance: These parts form the document on which a patent, if granted, is based. Each part must start on a new page. Ensure all components are present and consistent with one another before filing.

name: Title of the Invention
description: The title must indicate clearly and concisely the subject matter of the invention.
guidance: Use short, direct titles (e.g., 'A TOOTHBRUSH'). Ensure consistency between the title and the independent claim preamble (function/purpose).

name: Definition and use of embodiments
description: Embodiments are different variations of the same inventive concept, used to maximize the scope of protection claimed in the patent.
guidance: Describe multiple embodiments to cover variations. Use dependent claims to capture particular embodiments and examples to illustrate scope and operation.

name: Claims determine scope and must meet core requirements
description: Claims determine the scope of the monopoly. Claims must define the subject matter to be protected, be clear and concise, and be fully supported by the description.
guidance: Ensure each claim's technical features have been described earlier. Avoid ambiguity: the meaning should be clear to a person skilled in the art from the wording of the claim alone. Consistency between description and claims is vital to avoid unclarity or lack of support.

name: Claims drafted in technical terms (no commercial matter)
description: Claims must be drafted in terms of the technical features of the invention; claims should not contain statements relating to commercial advantages or other non-technical matters.
guidance: Statements of purpose are allowed if they assist in defining the invention. Always prefer technical feature wording and ensure support in the description for each claimed feature.

name: Independent claim requirements
description: An independent claim represents the broadest claim, stands alone (does not refer to any preceding claim) and must include all essential technical features of the invention.
guidance: Include all elements indispensable for providing the effect and solving the technical problem. Draft so the claim recites enough features that the invention can work.

name: Dependent claim requirements
description: A dependent claim depends on another claim, must reference the depended claim at the beginning, contains all features of the independent claim plus further features, and may only narrow the scope.
guidance: Draft dependent claims to describe particular embodiments and further limitations. They must not broaden the scope of the claim they depend upon.

name: Number of claims and fees
description: Additional fees will be imposed for the number of claims exceeding 10 (fees escalate with claim count).
guidance: Be aware of per-claim fee schedule (e.g., specific RM amounts for claim ranges). For utility innovation applications only one claim is allowed. Plan claim drafting with fee implications in mind.

name: Formality requirement: part separation
description: Each part of the specification (Description, Claims, Abstract, Drawings) shall start on a new page.
guidance: Ensure clear page breaks and headings for each part so examiners and filing systems can process the application correctly.

name: Practical drafting sequence advice
description: It is advisable to start with drafting the claims first then followed by other subcomponents of the specification.
guidance: Claims define the invention's scope; writing claims first helps ensure consistency across the Summary, Detailed Description, Abstract and Drawings and avoids unsupported claim features.

name: Construction of patent claims is a question of law for the court
description: The construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court.
guidance: The Seventh Amendment does not require a jury to decide the meaning of disputed claim terms; judges should construe claims as a legal determination. The Court expressly affirms that judges — not juries — determine claim meaning.

name: Distinct allocation: claim construction (law) vs. infringement (fact)
description: Patent litigation has two elements: (1) construing the patent (a question of law for the court) and (2) determining whether infringement occurred (a question of fact for the jury).
guidance: Courts decide the legal scope of claims; juries decide whether the accused product or process falls within that scope. Trial procedure should reflect this division.

name: Claims define scope and must 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the invention
description: A claim 'particularly poin[t] out and distinctly clai[m] the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention' and 'defin[e] the scope of a patent grant.' Claims cover processes, machines, manufactures, compositions, or designs, not merely functions or scientific explanations.
guidance: When drafting or construing claims, focus on their role in delimiting patent rights and informing the public of what is and is not claimed; avoid claiming mere results or abstract functions.

name: Interpret claim terms in light of the specification and the patent as a whole
description: A claim term must be defined in a way that comports with the instrument as a whole; claim construction requires interpreting the claim in the context of the specification and entire patent document.
guidance: Judges should perform a holistic analysis of the patent to ensure internal coherence; isolated dictionary meanings may be inadequate if inconsistent with the specification or claim structure.

name: Functional consideration: judges are better suited to construe technical patent claims
description: Because construction of written instruments is a judicial function and patent claims are often highly technical, judges, by training and discipline, are more likely than juries to give a proper interpretation that preserves internal coherence.
guidance: Deference to judges reduces the risk of inconsistent or unschooled interpretations; judges are better positioned to assess how expert testimony fits the whole patent.

name: Uniformity and public notice require judicial claim construction
description: Allocating claim construction to courts promotes uniformity and certainty in patent scope, which is necessary for protecting patentees, encouraging inventive activity, and informing the public what is dedicated to the public domain.
guidance: Judicial construction supports stare decisis and inter- and intrajurisdictional consistency (and undergirds the purpose of the Federal Circuit). Jury determinations of claim meaning would undermine that uniformity.

name: Claims lacked clear 18th-century antecedent; use specification-construction practice as closest analogue
description: Because modern claims did not exist in 18th-century patent practice, the closest antecedent is construction of specifications, and historical reports show judges — not juries — construed specifications.
guidance: When using historical analogy, treat specification-construction practice as the most relevant antecedent for resolving who should construe modern claims.

name: Services expended to save a vessel have priority over Government's summary remedy; use admiralty proceedings to determine priorities
description: When services and expenses were incurred in raising and repairing a vessel that had been swung free from a channel, such expenses should be regarded as having priority over the Government's claim under the statute for swinging her free; rather than resorting to the summary remedy that gives entire proceeds to Government, admiralty proceedings should be used to enforce liens and determine priorities.
guidance: Analogy to 'bottomry bonds' priority; if owners decline vessel (elect to abandon) summary remedy may apply; if vessel sold in admiralty in foreign jurisdiction and proceeds insufficient to satisfy Government claim after payment of superior liens the Department should not retain further contract price though interest may not be payable (C. 28032, Jan. 10 & Mar. 23, 1911; Oct. 30, 1911). (VII C2).

name: When Congress appropriates specific sums for improvements executive must proceed to execute work without questioning expediency or delaying over title claims
description: Where Congress makes an appropriation in general terms for improving a river, the executive officer charged with the improvement must proceed with the work under the appropriation without entertaining questions as to expediency of the expenditure or delaying to raise or consider claims of title to land affected by the improvement.

name: Review the Entire Application to Understand Support for Claimed Invention
description: Before determining written description sufficiency, review claims and the entire specification (including embodiments, figures, sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for claim features.
guidance: Determine field of invention and level of skill in the art. For some arts there is an inverse correlation between skill level and specificity required. Information well known in the art need not be described in detail. See Rasmussen; Amgen v. Chugai; Wang Labs.; Hybritech.

name: Written Description Requirement: Applicant Must Show Possession of the Claimed Invention
description: There must be sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at filing.
guidance: This is a factual, case-by-case inquiry. The description must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention with all its limitations. See Purdue Pharma; Pfaff v. Wells; Lockwood.

name: Means- (or Step-) Plus-Function Limitations (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre-AIA §112, para.6) Must Have Corresponding Structure/Materials/Acts in Specification
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA para. 6), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts disclosed in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.'
guidance: The written description must adequately link particular structure/materials/acts to perform the recited function, or make it clear one skilled in the art would know the corresponding structure. Reliance on a skilled artisan's ability to implement is insufficient without disclosure. See B. Braun; Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino. A 112(b) indefiniteness rejection for lack of corresponding structure often requires a simultaneous 112(a) written description rejection. See In re Noll; MPEP § 2181; Supplemental Examination Guidelines (65 Fed. Reg. 38510).

name: Species vs Genus Analysis (Single Embodiment/Species vs Genus Claims)
description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment or species is analyzed as a species; a claim encompassing two or more embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus.
guidance: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment/species: (A) determine whether application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed to show possession; (C) if not, determine whether invention is described with distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficiently detailed to show possession. Then (1) does the application describe the complete structure or acts of the process? If yes, written description satisfied; (2) if not, are there other relevant identifying characteristics (function+structure correlation) sufficient to demonstrate possession? See MPEP § 806.04(e) and cases cited (Fields v. Conover; others).

name: Factors to Consider in Determining Written Description Sufficiency
description: Whether specification shows applicant was in possession is a factual determination considering multiple factors.
guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (esp. with known structure-function correlation), method of making the claimed invention. Also rely on patents/printed publications to assess maturity of the art. See Eli Lilly; Capon v. Eshhar.

name: Technological Maturity and Predictability Affect Required Disclosure
description: In mature, predictable arts, less detailed disclosure may be sufficient; in emerging or unpredictable technologies, more evidence is required to show possession.
guidance: In mature technologies with high skill/knowledge, written description questions are less likely for originally filed claims even if specification shows only method of making and function. In unpredictable/emerging fields, disclosure of only method+function may not support a product claim (except product-by-process if process actually used to produce the product). Partial structure without further characterization may be insufficient. See Amgen; Fiers v. Revel; discussion of product-by-process.

name: Disclosure Must Distinguish the Claimed Invention from Other Materials
description: The specification must provide identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and lead a skilled artisan to conclude applicant was in possession of the claimed species.
guidance: Disclosure of any combination of identifying characteristics (structure, properties, function with correlation, method of making) that allows distinction can be sufficient. See Eli Lilly; Lockwood; cases on biochemical identifiers and enzymatic properties.

name: Rejection Guidance: Adequate Description Precludes 112(a) Rejection
description: If a complete structure is disclosed for a species/embodiment, the written description requirement is satisfied and a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) must not be made for lack of written description.
guidance: If the specification discloses complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole, do not make 112(a) rejection. See Fields v. Conover and accompanying MPEP instructions.

name: 112(f) workshop with technology-specific examples
description: In-Progress: 35 U.S.C. §112(f) Workshop — follow-up to the CBT training earlier in the year; driven by technology-specific examples including instructions on how to use the new form paragraphs to establish claim interpretation.
guidance: Workshops should use concrete technology examples to show how to apply form paragraphs to claim interpretation.

name: Training on novelty (35 U.S.C. §102)
description: Under development for delivery later this fiscal year: 35 U.S.C. §102.
guidance: Develop modules that clarify novelty analyses and application to claim language.

name: Written description training emphasizing new matter (35 U.S.C. §112(a))
description: Under development: 35 U.S.C. §112(a) Written Description - The emphasis will be on new matter.
guidance: Focus training on identifying new matter and ensuring claims/specification satisfy written description requirements.

name: STEPP Day 1 — first-read examination and claim interpretation
description: Day 1: Role of an examiner and the steps an examiner would take when reading an application for the first time; claim interpretation and 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 are emphasized.
guidance: Emphasize initial application review steps and core patentability/definiteness principles on Day 1.

name: STEPP Day 2 — search planning and mapping prior art (102/103)
description: Day 2: Use of information gathered during Day 1 to plan a search and conduct a search; mapping of prior art to claims using 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.
guidance: Teach practical search strategies and how to map prior art references to claim limitations for novelty and obviousness analyses.

name: Virtual instructor-led (VILT) Hops courses and topics
description: New for FY18 is a virtual instructor-led training (VILT) Hops courses — one or more topics related to examination practice and procedure. Upcoming topics include Claim Interpretation - Product by Process; Functional Language Workshop - Claim interpretation and Definiteness Under 35 U.S.C. §112(b); Inherency, 35 U.S.C. §102/103 Rejections, and Official Notice.
guidance: Use VILT to deliver focused topical modules; choose topics that address common interpretation and rejection issues.

name: UPC competence (scope of actions)
description: The UPC has competence for infringement actions, declarations of non-infringement, revocation actions, and related counterclaims concerning patents that fall within its jurisdiction; this includes all forms of relief and protective and/or preventative measures.
guidance: The UPC also has competence to deal with claims arising from decisions of the EPO relating to its function as granting/administrative body for UPs. The UPC does not have competence for contractual disputes relating to patent licences or ownership (those remain with national courts).

name: Principles of claim interpretation at the UPC
description: The UPC Court of Appeal has held that the description and drawings must always be used as explanatory aids for claim interpretation, not only to resolve ambiguities — only after examination of the description and drawings does the scope of the claims become apparent.
guidance: No statutory test for infringement by equivalence in the UPCA, but first-instance cases have applied tests based on national practices; Gillette/Formstein defenses and equivalents issues have arisen and UPC panels have considered national doctrines in their reasoning.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure standard
description: UPC sufficiency approach appears similar to EPO practice: the patent must disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art over the whole scope of the claims.
guidance: If the patent fails this test the UPC may revoke the patent (case examples exist).

name: Novelty assessment principle
description: Novelty in the UPC is assessed in line with EPO practice: decisive is whether the subject-matter of the claim with all its features is directly and unambiguously disclosed in the prior art citation.
guidance: Second medical use claims are purpose-limited and patentable provided the specific use is novel and inventive.

name: Article 6 — The Claims
description: Article 6 The Claims
guidance: TOC only. Full article provides requirements for claims (form, number, clarity, support) used to define the scope of protection.

name: Possession test / objective standard
description: "Does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed."
guidance: The disclosure must "convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, he or she was in possession of the invention, and that the invention, in that context, is whatever is now claimed." (Vas‑Cath). Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, actual reduction to practice, or by showing the invention was "ready for patenting." (Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen).

name: Support for claims to a species
description: For each claim drawn to a species, the specification must provide sufficient disclosure (e.g., reduction to practice, drawings, identifying characteristics) to show possession of that species.
guidance: Disclosure of a method of making plus function may be insufficient in unpredictable arts; where the process has actually produced the product, written description for product‑by‑process claims is clearly satisfied. Conception that lacks structural specificity (e.g., defining a gene only by a principal biological property) is inadequate. (See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen; Burroughs Wellcome).

name: Support for claims to a genus
description: A claimed genus may be supported by (i) sufficient description of a representative number of species (including actual reduction to practice or drawings), (ii) disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure or physical/chemical properties), (iii) functional characteristics coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure, or (iv) a combination of such identifying characteristics.
guidance: When there is substantial variation within a genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation. In unpredictable arts, one species often will not support a broadly claimed genus without a demonstrated structure‑function correlation (AbbVie; Enzo Biochem; In re Curtis).

name: Structure‑function correlation as support for genus
description: A reasonable structure‑function correlation disclosed by the inventor or known in the art can support a functionally defined genus.
guidance: Such correlations may be established in the specification or be known in the art at filing; where established, they can permit broader genus claims even if only limited species are disclosed. Lack of correlation in unpredictable arts undermines genus support (AbbVie).

name: Each claim limitation must be supported in the originally filed disclosure
description: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (and to be entitled to an earlier filing/priority date), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: When an explicit limitation is not present in the written description, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone). Inherency requires that the missing matter is necessarily present and recognized by skilled artisans, not mere possibilities (In re Robertson).

name: Claims must recite elements described as essential
description: Each claim must include all elements which the applicant has described as essential or critical in the specification.
guidance: Omitting an element described as essential can render a claim unsupported and require rejection. Courts have invalidated claims broadened by omitting elements the specification treated as critical. (Johnson Worldwide; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo).

name: Requirements for a written description rejection statement
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express factual findings that (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue and (B) establish a prima facie case with reasons why a person skilled in the art would not have recognized possession of the claimed invention in view of the filed disclosure.
guidance: A simple statement identifying where support is not apparent may suffice for new/amended claims, but broad conclusory statements are inadequate. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supported by the original disclosure, mindful of the prohibition on adding new matter. (MPEP §2163.04(I)).

name: Indefiniteness of means‑/step‑plus‑function limitations due to insufficient corresponding structure
description: A means‑(or step‑) plus‑function claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA sixth paragraph) must be supported by corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification that perform the claimed function; otherwise the limitation is indefinite and lacks adequate written description.
guidance: Failure to disclose sufficient corresponding structure renders the limitation indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (second paragraph) and also fails the written description requirement because it covers all ways of performing the function and indicates lack of possession. (In re Donaldson; see MPEP §2181).

name: Amendments that change claim scope require support
description: Changes to claim scope after filing (broadening or narrowing, altering numerical ranges, or using terminology not synonymous with original disclosure) commonly raise written description issues and each resulting claim limitation must be supported by the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: Omission of a limitation can suggest lack of possession of a broader invention, particularly where the specification described the omitted element as the only possible location or essential. Examples: Gentry Gallery, Tronzo, In re Wilder. When appropriate, suggest supported amendments but avoid adding new matter.

name: When relying on benefit/priority/parent filing dates
description: To claim the benefit of an earlier U.S. or foreign filing date (35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 365, 386), the subject matter of the claim must be described in the earlier application in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA first paragraph).
guidance: The examiner initially must present evidence/reasoning why the earlier disclosure does not support the later claim. Applicant should specifically point out original support for amendments. Cases: Tronzo; In re Scheiber; In re Gosteli.

name: Original claims may still lack written description
description: An original claim may lack written description support if it defines the invention in purely functional language without sufficient identification of how the function is performed, or if a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure describes only a narrow species with no evidence the genus was contemplated.
guidance: Even if claim language appears verbatim in the specification, indistinct or mere words may not satisfy the requirement; the specification must describe the claimed invention so one skilled in the art can recognize what is claimed (Enzo Biochem; Ariad en banc).

name: 37 CFR 1.111 supplemental replies limitation
description: A reply supplemental to a reply that is in compliance with 37 CFR 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except when clearly limited to specific categories.
guidance: The Office may enter a supplemental reply if it is clearly limited to: (A) Cancellation of claim(s); (B) Adoption of examiner suggestion(s); (C) Placement of the application in condition for allowance; (D) Reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply was filed; (E) Correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors); or (F) Simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply will be entered if filed within the period during which action is suspended under 37 CFR 1.103(a) or (c). The list is not exhaustive and examiner discretion may allow other supplemental replies; non-compliant amendments under 37 CFR 1.121 will not be entered.

name: Claims added without pointing out patentable novelty should not be allowed
description: In amended cases where no attempt is made to point out the patentable novelty, the claims should not be allowed.
guidance: An amendment failing to point out the patentable novelty that applicant believes the claims present may be held not fully responsive and a time period set to furnish a proper reply if statutory period has expired or nearly so. If claims as amended are clearly open to rejection on the record, a final rejection should generally be made.

name: Checklist for amended applications (items to inspect)
description: All amended applications forwarded to the examiner should be inspected at once to determine signature, filing within statutory period, full responsiveness and compliance with 37 CFR 1.121, whether changes warrant transfer, special status, interference-related copied claims, traversal of restriction requirement, use of permanent ink, cited references, terminal disclaimer, or added security matter.
guidance: References to specific MPEP sections: signature (§ 714.01(a)), statutory period (§ 710 - § 710.05), responsiveness (§ 714.03 and § 714.04), transfer (§ 903.08(d)), special (§ 708.01), interference issues (Chapter 2300), restriction traversal (§ 818.03(a)), permanent ink (§ 714.07), cited references (§ 707.05(b) and § 1302.12), terminal disclaimer (§ 804.02, § 804.03, § 1490), security (§ 115).

name: Limitations on applicant rights after final rejection
description: Once a final rejection that is not premature has been entered, applicant no longer has any right to unrestricted further prosecution; applicant cannot as a matter of right amend finally rejected claims, add new claims after a final rejection (see 37 CFR 1.116) or reinstate previously canceled claims.
guidance: Further examination may be obtained via RCE (1.114) or CPA (1.53(d)) where applicable; amendments that merely cancel claims, adopt examiner suggestions, remove issues for appeal, or otherwise require only cursory review are exceptions. The U.S. PTO does not recognize 'conditional' authorizations to charge an appeal fee; any conditional authorization to charge an appeal fee will be treated as unconditional payment.

name: Rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness (KSR list)
description: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include: (A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way; (D) Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'Obvious to try' – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; (G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: See MPEP §2143 for discussion and examples illustrating use of these rationales to support an obviousness finding; examiners must articulate factual findings supporting the chosen rationale(s) rather than rely on conclusory statements (citing KSR, 550 U.S. at 418).

name: Applicant's reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action; the reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references.
guidance: If an applicant disagrees with factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred substantively; mere assertions that the Office failed to establish a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence are not substantively adequate under 37 CFR 1.111(b). Examiners may repeat the rejection and make the next Office action final if the traverse is ineffective (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden and evidence to show benefits apply
