description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants the benefits of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) must establish that subject matter (only qualifying as prior art under subsections (e), (f) or (g) of pre-AIA §102) used in a §103 rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: To avail joint research agreement benefits, the applicant bears the burden to show (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) the invention resulted from activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) for requirements to establish common ownership/JRA. Historical limitations apply for certain filing/grant dates.

name: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103 it must be analogous prior art
description: A reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection. A reference is analogous if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field).
guidance: In assessing 'reasonably pertinent,' the reference must 'logically have commended itself to an inventor's attention' (In re Icon Health & Fitness) and examiners should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification. To support analogy, it may be appropriate to state the examiner's understanding of the problem and factual reasons why the prior art is pertinent. See In re Bigio, In re Klein, and In re Clay for related case law.

name: Consider similarities and differences in structure and function when assessing analogy
description: Similarities and differences in structure and function between the prior art and the claimed invention carry greater weight than classification or cross-references when determining whether art is analogous.
guidance: Patent Office classifications and search notes are evidence but structural/functional comparisons are more persuasive (citing In re Ellis). Examiners should emphasize structure/function parallels in rationale for relying on a reference.

name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider the claimed invention 'as a whole'
description: In determining differences between the prior art and the claims at issue under 35 U.S.C. 103, the question is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: Interpret claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art references as a whole. Do not isolate single differences if the combination of elements as a whole provides nonobvious features (citing Stratoflex, In re Hirao).

name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'—respect 'as a whole' requirement
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' of an invention disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Avoid restricting analysis to a single perceived advantage or concept while ignoring express claim limitations; case law (e.g., W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb) shows courts reverse when the 'gist' approach disregards claim limitations or treats claims as though they read differently than allowed.

name: Clear articulation of reasons for obviousness rejection
description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning (KSR citing In re Kahn). Office personnel must make explicit the analysis supporting a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection and articulate findings of fact that support the rationale relied upon.

name: Use of known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products
description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way may support obviousness.
guidance: Demonstrate that the technique is known in the relevant art and would have been applied in a predictable manner to the claimed device/product/method.

name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results may support obviousness.
guidance: Show why the device was 'ready for improvement' and that applying the known technique would predictably achieve the claimed result.

name: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) supporting combination/modification
description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention may support obviousness.
guidance: Although KSR cautioned against rigid TSM application, TSM remains a valid rationale. If TSM suffices, the examiner should use it; otherwise consider other rationales. Provide articulated factual basis for any asserted motivation to combine or modify.

name: Applicant reply must distinctly and specifically point out errors
description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable. A mere statement that a prima facie case was not established or unsupported assertions about common knowledge are not substantively adequate; traverse must include reasoned statement explaining why the examiner erred.

name: Rebuttal evidence examples to show nonobviousness for combinations
description: Applicants may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that: (A) one of ordinary skill in the art could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., due to technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each element performs separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
guidance: If such evidence is presented, examiners should reconsider initial obviousness conclusions in view of the entire record and articulate how findings support continued rejections or why they do not.

name: Evidence required to show 35 U.S.C. 103(c) applies (common ownership/joint research)
description: An applicant seeking benefits of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) must establish that subject matter which only qualifies as prior art under subsection (e), (f) or (g) and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: For joint research agreement benefits (applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004), applicant must show: (A) invention made by/on behalf of parties to an agreement effective on or before invention date; (B) invention made as result of activities within scope of the agreement; and (C) patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) and related case law (Ex parte Yoshino, In re Bartfeld).

name: Reference must be analogous art to be relied on under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: In order for a reference to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous art if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor. 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering his problem. Examiners should consider the problem as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support analogy determinations (Bigio, Icon Health, In re Klein).

name: Weight similarities and differences in structure and function for analogy
description: While classifications are some evidence, similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions carry far greater weight in determining analogy.
guidance: Examiners should emphasize structural and functional overlap between references and claimed inventions when assessing whether references are analogous art (In re Ellis).

name: Consider the claimed invention as a whole when assessing differences
description: In determining the differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: Interpret claim language and consider both the invention and prior art references as a whole (see MPEP §§2111-2116.01 and relevant case law such as Stratoflex and In re Hirao). Avoid focusing solely on an isolated difference if other claim limitations or admitted unobvious steps exist.

name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' (anti-pattern)
description: Distilling the invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' of an invention disregards the 'as a whole' requirement and is improper.
guidance: Avoid restricting consideration to a narrow conceptualization that excludes express claim limitations; ensure all claim limitations are considered rather than treating the claim as if it read differently (see W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb examples).

name: Contingencies appropriation cannot supplement specific appropriations
description: The appropriation for contingencies of the Army is to meet necessary and appropriate expenses in connection with the Army 'not otherwise provided for,' and therefore is not available to supplement a specific appropriation for furnishing certain supplies or rendering certain services.
guidance: If a specific appropriation (e.g., repairs to a named building) is insufficient, the contingencies appropriation should not be used to cover the deficiency. Presenting claims should follow procedures for deficiency acts rather than charging contingencies.

name: Top declarers — Who is leading the 5G SEP race?
description: Chart showing overall declaration numbers so users can get a glance at which companies are leading in declared 5G SEPs.
guidance: Use one-click and advanced filters when viewing overall declaration status to adjust scope (e.g., 5G landscape filter). This is useful for quickly assessing leadership in declaration counts; be mindful that declaration counts alone may not reflect portfolio relevance or claim validity.

name: Prepare effective U.S. utility patent applications
description: Students will learn how to prepare effective U.S. utility patent applications (classes 1-6). As part of this, each student will draft patent claims and then a complete patent application.
guidance: Emphasis on drafting both claims and a complete application; practical exercises occur in classes 1–6. (No further examples/anti-patterns provided on page.)

name: At least one claim required
description: A non-provisional utility patent application must have at least one claim.
guidance: Claims define the scope of the invention and what aspects are legally protected and enforceable.

name: Claim formatting and presentation
description: Start claims on a separate sheet with the heading 'claim listing' or 'claims'; each claim must begin with a capital letter and end with a period; periods may not be used elsewhere in the claims except for abbreviations; where there are several claims, they shall be numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals.
guidance: Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step of the claim should be separated by a line indentation.

name: Independent vs dependent claim form
description: Claims may be written in independent or dependent form. An independent claim is a stand alone claim that contains all the subject matter necessary to define the invention. A dependent claim refers to a previous claim and specifies a further limitation of the subject matter claimed.
guidance: Dependent claims must have proper antecedent basis and should specify a further limitation; use correct dependent transitions (e.g., 'The device of claim 1, wherein...').

name: Particularity and distinctness of claims
description: A claim(s) shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor regards as his invention or discovery.
guidance: Claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the specification and the terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description.

name: Claims must conform to specification/support requirement
description: The claim or claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the specification; claim terms and phrases must find clear support in the description.
guidance: Ensure claim terms have support in the written description so that their meaning is ascertainable by reference to the specification (avoid unsupported claim terms).

name: Statutory categories for claimed subject matter
description: The claimed invention must be to one of four categories: method/process claims, machine/apparatus, article of manufacture/device, or composition of matter.
guidance: Method/process claims: directed to series of acts/steps for performing desired functions. Machine/apparatus: directed to elements or components comprising the apparatus. Article of manufacture/device: directed to structure and functional components of a device or manufactured article. Composition of matter: directed to compositions/mixtures (may include chemical formulas or ingredient lists).

name: Pre-claim invention review
description: Before writing claims, answer: What is the invention? What are the pieces and parts that make up the invention? How do the pieces and parts relate to one another? Do you have more than one invention? Product: apparatus, machine, composition. Method: making or using. Are there multiple versions of each invention?
guidance: Use these questions to identify fundamental elements, relationships, and whether multiple inventions/versions exist.

name: Preamble considerations (limiting vs non-limiting)
description: A claim usually begins with a preamble (introductory phrase). The claim preamble must be read in the context of the entire claim: terminology in the preamble that limits the structure or is intrinsically linked to the body is given patentable weight; terminology that merely recites purpose or intended use and does not add structure is not considered a limitation.
guidance: Example: 'A device…' (does not add structure) vs 'A device to be worn by a user…' (adds structure and limits scope).

name: Transition phrase choice and meaning
description: A claim usually includes a transition phrase. Common transitions: 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', and 'consisting of.'
guidance: 'Comprising' is open-ended (includes but not limited to recited elements) and is generally most commonly used. 'Consisting of' is closed-ended and excludes additional unrecited elements. 'Consisting essentially of' limits scope to specified materials/steps and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s); it is a middle ground. Absent clear indication in the specification of what the basic and novel characteristics are, 'consisting essentially of' may be construed as equivalent to 'comprising'. Avoid non-standard transitional phrases (may raise interpretation questions).

name: Body of the claim: limitations and interrelationships
description: The body follows the transitional phrase and recites the limitations (structure/elements or acts/steps) in clear, full, and concise terms necessary to define the invention.
guidance: The body should not merely be a list of components or steps; it should recite how the essential elements are interrelated. For composition claims, include chemical formula or list of ingredients where appropriate. Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step should end with a semicolon.

name: Dependent claim drafting and transitions
description: When adding a component in a dependent claim use 'further comprising' and explain how it is connected; when further describing something already introduced use 'wherein.'
guidance: Notice dependent transitions. Ensure each dependent claim has antecedent basis and includes all limitations of the claim from which it depends as a further limitation. (See 35 U.S.C. 112(d), MPEP 608.01(n)). Avoid referring back to only a portion of another claim in a dependent claim.

name: Focus on the inventive concept
description: Identify the features that set the invention apart from prior inventions; identify fundamental elements and omit unnecessary elements unless needed to distinguish over prior art.
guidance: Select broad terms and identify their relationships carefully; remove unnecessary claim limitations to maximize appropriate scope.

name: Outline-based drafting and alignment with specification
description: Consider drafting an outline of the invention first and then claims based on terms used in the specification.
guidance: Think about the legal protection desired and tailor claims accordingly; look at claims in patents issued in your field of technology; review and reconcile both specification and claims, making necessary additions and corrections so claim terms find support in the specification.

name: Avoid inconsistent terminology
description: Avoid the use of terms inconsistently between the claims and/or specification (e.g., visor, visor member, visor section, removable visor portion).
guidance: Use consistent terms throughout specification and claims to prevent ambiguity and indefiniteness.

name: Avoid 'removing' or 'replacing' elements in dependent claims
description: Do not 'remove' or 'replace' elements from another claim within a dependent claim (e.g., 'The vehicle of claim 1 where the removable top portion is non-removable').
guidance: Dependent claims must add limitations, not contradict or improperly amend the claim they depend from.

name: Avoid non-limiting/optional language that fails to limit
description: Do not use language that merely suggests or makes optional and, thus, does not limit the claim.
guidance: Ensure claim language actually imposes the intended limitation rather than merely suggesting it.

name: Avoid purely functional language without structure
description: Do not use functional language that is unconnected to the structure or steps that perform the function.
guidance: Claims should recite structure or steps corresponding to claimed functions; purely functional recitations can be problematic.

name: Avoid unsupported terms, trademarks, and tradenames
description: Do not use terms in the claim that are unsupported by the specification; do not use trademarks or tradenames in the claims.
guidance: Use generic terms (e.g., 'hook and loop fastener' instead of Velcro.®) and ensure all claim terms have support in the specification.

name: Claim construction sources
description: Claim construction is based on the patent claims, specification, prosecution history, and, in some cases, on extrinsic evidence to reconstruct what patent claim terms would have meant to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) is primary; extrinsic evidence (including inventor testimony) is typically given less weight but can illuminate context, background, and prosecution events. Courts should consider which sources are necessary to meaningfully construe terms and avoid abstract constructions that do not affect outcome.

name: Weight and use of inventor testimony and expert evidence
description: An inventor’s testimony is typically seen as extrinsic evidence and given less weight, particularly when self-serving; Teva expanded the use of expert declarations and testimony in claim construction.
guidance: Because Teva allows greater use of expert evidence on subsidiary factual determinations, courts should ask early whether parties intend to rely on expert testimony and its substance. Courts may allow expert tutorials and reserve the option to take expert evidence if factual disputes arise; consider methods like the 'hot tub' to have opposing experts address each other to clarify disputed issues and credibility.

name: Permitting fact discovery prior to claim construction
description: Permitting fact discovery in advance of claim construction helps focus claims and defenses because knowledge of accused product structure and relevant prior art often determines which claim terms need construction.
guidance: Pre-claim-construction discovery is common and often mandated by local patent rules (e.g., early disclosures of infringement and invalidity contentions). Courts should discuss potential limits or phasing to avoid wasteful discovery on issues unrelated to claim construction (e.g., damages, equitable defenses, willfulness) when a claim-construction ruling could be dispositive.

name: Fact discovery after claim construction
description: As a result of a court’s claim-construction order, issues often arise which justify additional fact discovery.
guidance: Most courts set fact discovery to proceed for a period after the ruling. Inventor depositions for Markman purposes are sometimes initially limited to claim-construction topics, with broader depositions allowed after the Markman process completes.

name: Timing of expert discovery relative to claim construction
description: Expert reports on infringement, invalidity, and damages are central; technical experts opine based on the meaning of claim terms as determined by (or anticipated from) the court’s claim-construction order. For this reason, claim construction should precede expert reports and depositions.
guidance: Many courts schedule expert discovery and depositions to begin after claim construction. Other courts set expert discovery before claim construction but require experts to write reports in the alternative relative to each side’s proposed constructions. Courts should structure expert scheduling to reflect whether claim scope will materially affect expert analyses (including damages).

name: Claim construction before summary judgment (or combined with it)
description: Claim construction is a critical predicate to the most common summary judgment motions; most courts complete claim construction first, before allowing dispositive motions, on the theory parties need a definitive statement of claim scope.
guidance: Some courts combine claim construction with summary judgment (especially motions that turn primarily on claim construction) to increase efficiency; others require explanation of the significance of competing constructions and limit later alternative theories. Courts should account for burden of drafting summary-judgment motions under multiple potential constructions and consider appellate ripeness concerns (Federal Circuit views on developing factual record).

name: Use of early, limited claim construction to encourage settlement
description: Early, separate claim construction (sometimes limited to a subset of case-dispositive terms) can facilitate settlement by recalibrating parties’ assessments of exposure.
guidance: Courts may schedule settlement conferences shortly after a claim-construction order. Use this procedure only where a party persuasively shows the case largely turns on a discrete issue; otherwise there is potential for strategic abuse by defendants or tactical resistance by plaintiffs seeking nuisance-value leverage.

name: Preliminary claim construction for preliminary injunctions
description: Preliminary injunction motions in patent cases typically require a court to construe claim terms on an accelerated schedule.
guidance: Preliminary constructions are less informed (less discovery) and are not binding; courts may later reconsider and revise constructions applied during preliminary-injunction decisions as more detailed briefing/record is developed.

name: Disclosure of joint-infringement roles in contentions
description: Where joint direct infringement is alleged, a patentee must describe 'the role of each such party in the direct infringement' in infringement contentions under many local patent rules.
guidance: Districts with such requirements include N.D. Cal., D. Idaho, N.D. Ill., Maryland, E.D. Mo., D. Nev., and others. Clear mapping of accused actors to claim elements is expected.

name: Optional local-rule practices (summary judgment, oral-advice summaries, damages, licenses, bifurcation)
description: Less common PLR provisions include requiring summary judgment motions as part of claim-construction, producing written summaries of oral advice when waiver of privilege is alleged, requiring damages disclosures after Markman, producing license agreements, and district variation in bifurcation practice.
guidance: Examples: D. Utah LPR 6.2 (SJ as part of claim construction); S.D. Cal. P.L.R. 3.7(b) (produce summary of oral advice if waiver); S.D. Ind. CMP (damages statement within 30 days after Markman); S.D. Tex. P.R. 3-2(a)(4) (produce license agreements); S.D. Ohio always bifurcates willfulness, N.D. Ga. disfavors liability/damages bifurcation, W.D.N.C. suggests considering bifurcation. Courts should consider these tools to manage case scope and costs.

name: Formal requirements of the notice of opposition (Art. 99(1), Rule 76)
description: The notice of opposition must meet Art. 99(1) and Rule 76 and, per Rule 76(2)(c), contain a statement of the extent to which the patent is opposed, the grounds relied on, and an indication of the facts and evidence presented in support.
guidance: Specify whether the entire patent, particular claims, or embodiments are opposed; identify which grounds under Art. 100 are invoked (at least one ground must be cited, even implicitly); the 'indication' must substantiate the attacks so proprietor and division can understand and respond without undue burden.

name: Amendments by proprietor during opposition (Rule 80; Arts. 52–57, 84, 123)
description: The proprietor may amend claims but only to address grounds for opposition (Rule 80). Amendments must comply with EPC substantive requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability Arts.52–57), clarity (Art.84), and must not add matter (Art.123(2)) or extend scope (Art.123(3)).
guidance: Amendments cannot be used to 'tidy up and improve the disclosure' (T 127/85). Ensure any amendment is clearly limited to addressing the specific objections raised and stays within original disclosure.

name: Request for central limitation or revocation by proprietor (Arts. 105a–105c)
description: Proprietor‑initiated central administrative procedure (introduced with EPC 2000) to request limitation or revocation at any time after grant. Pending opposition proceedings take precedence (Art.105a(2)). The procedure is ex parte, designed for rapid processing (<2 months), and the limitation/revocation takes effect ex tunc (Art.68).
guidance: Request must include amended claims limited in scope; the EPO will not examine patentability of the resulting limited patent in this procedure. This procedure avoids non‑permitted 'self‑opposition' (G 9/93).

name: Petition for compulsory licence — required contents
description: A petition to the Board of Trade for an order upon a patentee to grant a licence shall show clearly the nature of the petitioner's interest, and the ground or grounds upon which he claims to be entitled to relief, and shall state in detail the circumstances of the case, the terms upon which he asks that an order may be made, and the purport of such order.
guidance: State the petitioner’s interest, factual circumstances, grounds under section 22 (or applicable provision), and proposed licence terms clearly and in detail. Use Form H/I as guidance.

name: Form Al/A2: Applications communicated from abroad / priority claims
description: Forms Al/A2 for inventions communicated from abroad or under international/colonial arrangements require declaration of communicant, statements that the invention is not in use in the UK, and may include priority details and lists of foreign applications and dates.
guidance: Provide full details of communicant and foreign filing dates; follow priority claim wording and attach supporting documents where relevant.

name: Form C: Complete Specification format, claims phrasing and signature
description: Complete Specification (Form C) to be furnished in duplicate (one unstamped); must contain full description 'in what manner the same is to be performed', and must end with a distinct statement of claim(s) in the form: 'Having now particularly described and ascertained the nature of my said Invention, and in what manner the same is to be performed, I declare that what I claim is: ' followed by the features of novelty claimed. Continuation on foolscap (one side only), two-inch left margin; signed by applicant or agent on last sheet with date.
guidance: Ensure full descriptive disclosure and clear, distinct claims in the required wording; comply with paper/format/signature rules.

name: Form L: Request to enter name upon the Register of Patents — content & proof
description: Form L requires the claimant to state name, full address, description, the nature of the claim to the patent, particulars of supporting documents (dates, parties), and to transmit the accompanying examined copy of the document as proof. For matters of record, a certified or official copy may be left in lieu of attested copy.
guidance: Attach examined copies/certified copies as appropriate when requesting register entry under assignment/transmission claims.

name: Items that must be present upon filing
description: To be considered for Track One, the application must include upon filing: a Request for Prioritized Examination; a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 including at least one claim; any required drawings; either an executed inventor's oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.63/1.64 for each inventor, or a signed ADS that provides each inventor's legal name, mailing address, and residence (if different); and the required fees.
guidance: All these items must be present on filing (or effectively present via same-day follow-on submission) to meet the 'present upon filing' requirement of 37 CFR 1.102(e)(1).

name: Events that terminate or suspend Track One special status
description: Track One special status remains until one of the following occurs: applicant files a petition for extension of time for filing a reply; applicant files an amendment that causes the application to contain >4 independent claims, >30 total claims, or a multiple dependent claim; applicant files an RCE; applicant files a notice of appeal; applicant files a request for suspension of action; a notice of allowance is mailed; a final Office action is mailed; the application is abandoned; or examination is completed as defined in 37 CFR 41.102.
guidance: Any of these events will terminate special status; specific procedural effects and MPEP references apply.

name: Pre-examination notices delay decision (but not dismissal)
description: A pre-examination notice identifying missing items or informalities will delay a decision on a Track One request until applicant files a complete and timely reply to the notice.
guidance: Common causes: papers not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.52, missing English-language specification, missing excess claims fees. Pre-examination notices generally define a period for reply. Any request for an extension of time to reply to such a notice will cause the application to be ineligible for further Track One treatment.

name: Effect of preliminary amendment
description: A preliminary amendment filed in an application that included a Track One request will not result in dismissal of the request, or termination of special status if already granted, so long as the preliminary amendment does not cause the application to contain more than four independent claims, more than thirty total claims, or a multiple dependent claim.
guidance: Amendments that do not violate claim limits are tolerated and will not negate Track One status.

name: Definition of continuation application
description: A continuation application seeks protection for new claims based on the invention disclosed in a prior 'parent' application, using the parent's priority date to assess novelty and obviousness.
guidance: Explains that continuations allow applicants to add new claims while retaining the parent's priority date; used to delay claim drafting and to tailor claims later. Example: a continuation contains new claims on the invention disclosed in its parent application and benefits from the original priority date.

name: Enablement / written description support requirement
description: Each claim in a continuation must be supported by the disclosure in its parent; specifically, the parent application must provide enough information for a 'person having ordinary skill in the art' (PHOSITA) to make and use the claimed invention (the 'enablement' requirement: 35 U.S.C. §112(a)).
guidance: Limitation on late claiming: claims in continuations cannot introduce subject matter not enabled by the original disclosure. Anti-pattern: drafting continuation claims that lack adequate support in the parent risks invalidation for lack of enablement/written description.

name: Timing/window to file continuations
description: Applicants can file a continuation at any time during the pendency of a parent application or during the pendency of that parent's previous children; chains of continuations can be used to seek new claims many years after the original disclosure (subject to the parent's priority/term).
guidance: Allows very long lags between priority date and claim drafting (e.g., 99th percentile lag up to 15 years for certain filings). Important for assessing 'late claiming' relative to observable events (e.g., standard publication).

name: Costs of filing continuations
description: Each continuation costs roughly $6,500 to prosecute; attorney fees commonly range from $3,000 to $6,000 and USPTO fees about $2,000.
guidance: Cost is a practical limitation and factor in applicants' strategic choices to file continuations or abandon low-value claims.

name: Functions/legitimate uses of continuations
description: Continuations are used to delay claim drafting to better understand the invention, to abandon low-value claims, to lock-in gains during negotiation with an examiner (allowing some claims to issue while continuing to pursue others), to amend claims in response to changes in patent law, and to draft claims that cover new uses of an invention that emerge after the priority date (if supported).
guidance: Enumerates pro-social and strategic reasons for continuations; evaluators should consider the stated purpose when assessing welfare implications.

name: Continuation-in-part, divisional, and reissue distinctions
description: Continuation-in-part (CIP) claims new subject matter not entitled to earlier priority; divisionals respond to restriction requirements; reissuance allows correction and (if within 2 years) enlargement of scope but requires surrender of the original patent and is relatively rare.
guidance: These alternative mechanisms each have distinct priority/subject-matter and procedural consequences and should be treated differently when evaluating prosecution strategy or measuring 'late claiming'.

name: Restriction on reissuance enlargement
description: Reissuance allows the patent owner to correct mistakes and to enlarge the scope of claims if filed within two years of the original grant date, but requires surrender of the original patent and is relatively rare.
guidance: Limits practical use of reissue to enlarge claims beyond a narrow window; contrasts with continuations which can be used over longer periods.

name: PHOSITA forecasting / notice standard
description: In principle, a PHOSITA should be able to forecast every claim that emerges from a parent application; in practice, vague or opaque written descriptions make forecasting difficult, causing notice failures (Menell & Meurer, 2013).
guidance: Assessment of whether continuations harm notice should consider the technical quality and specificity of the parent disclosure; anti-pattern: relying on overly vague descriptions that hinder PHOSITA forecasting.

name: Potential harms: notice failures, holdup, patent thickets
description: Continuations can create ambiguity about the scope of patent rights (notice failures), contribute to patent thickets that increase costs for entrants, and enable holdup where claims drafted late read on already-commercialized technology.
guidance: When evaluating social welfare effects or policy responses, weigh these harms against potential benefits (e.g., encouraging early disclosure and higher-value claim drafting).

name: Potential benefits: encouraging early disclosure and conserving USPTO resources
description: Continuations provide applicants an option to delay claim drafting, which can encourage early invention disclosure (by allowing early filing) and help the USPTO conserve resources by avoiding examination of low-value claims that can be abandoned later.
guidance: Policy evaluation should consider whether these benefits outweigh the harms in particular sectors or application clusters (e.g., startups vs. incumbent licensors).

name: Use of continuations to tailor claims to post-disclosure technology ('late claiming')
description: Applicants may use continuations to draft claims that cover products and technologies developed after the original invention is disclosed — a practice termed 'late claiming'.
guidance: Empirical indicators of late claiming include filing of continuations after an observable industry milestone (e.g., SSO standard publication) and increased textual similarity of continuation claims to later-published technology. Anti-pattern: drafting claims explicitly to cover known competitor products without adequate original disclosure.

name: Non-statutory double patenting rejection as an examination signal
description: A non-statutory double patenting rejection issued by an examiner signals that applicants are seeking to expand the scope of claims in a parent application (and may indicate strategic late claiming).
guidance: Use examination outcome datasets (Office Action Research Dataset) to detect such rejections as empirical evidence of scope-expanding continuation practice.

name: Examiner leniency as a moderating factor
description: The effect of standard publication on continuation filings is larger when patent examiners are more lenient (i.e., when examiners are more likely to allow broader claims).
guidance: When evaluating or modeling continuation behavior, control for examiner-specific tendencies as they influence issuance probabilities and applicants' strategic incentives.

name: Provisional and PCT as alternative delay mechanisms
description: A provisional patent application establishes priority and provides up to one year to file a non-provisional with specific claims; PCT international applications allow applicants to amend claims for up to ~30 months.
guidance: These alternatives provide shorter delay windows than continuations but are relevant when assessing an applicant's overall strategy for delaying claim drafting.

name: Litigation association as suggestive evidence of effectiveness
description: Continuation filings (especially post-standard continuations) are positively correlated with involvement in U.S. district court litigation among SEPs.
guidance: While courts ultimately determine infringement, higher litigation incidence is suggestive that some late-claimed continuations target enforceable subject matter; use litigation datasets (e.g., Lex Machina) as part of evaluation.

name: Suggesting an interference — applicant requirements
description: An applicant may suggest an interference. The suggestion must: (1) provide sufficient information to identify the application or patent, (2) identify all claims the applicant believes interfere, propose one or more counts, and show how the claims correspond to one or more counts, (3) for each count provide a claim chart comparing at least one claim of each party corresponding to the count and show why the claims interfere, (4) explain in detail why the applicant will prevail on priority, (5) if a claim has been added or amended to provoke the interference provide a claim chart showing the written description for each such claim, and (6) for each constructive reduction to practice for which the applicant wishes to be accorded benefit provide a chart showing where the disclosure provides a constructive reduction to practice within the scope of the interfering subject matter.
guidance: A suggestion to declare an interference must be supported with claim charts, priority analysis, written-description charts for provocative claims, and benefit charts for constructive reductions to practice.

name: Requirement to show priority when earlier benefit exists
description: When an applicant's earliest constructive reduction to practice is later than the apparent earliest constructive reduction to practice for a patent or published application claiming interfering subject matter, the applicant must show why it would prevail on priority. If the applicant fails to show priority, an administrative patent judge may nevertheless declare an interference to place the applicant under an order to show cause why judgment should not be entered; new evidence in support of priority will not be admitted except on a showing of good cause.
guidance: Applicants facing earlier-accorded benefit must proactively demonstrate entitlement to priority and prepare good-cause showings for any late evidence.

name: Presumptions — priority and evidentiary standard
description: Parties are presumed to have invented interfering subject matter in the order of the dates of their accorded benefit for each count. If two parties are accorded the same earliest date, neither is entitled to a presumption. Priority may be proved by a preponderance of the evidence except a party must prove priority by clear and convincing evidence if the date of its earliest constructive reduction to practice is after the issue date of an involved patent or the publication date under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) of an involved application or patent.
guidance: Accorded benefit dates drive presumptions; higher clear-and-convincing standard applies when the claimed earliest date is after involved patent issue or application publication.

name: Content and sufficiency of substantive motions in interferences
description: In an interference, substantive motions must: (1) raise a threshold issue, (2) seek to change the scope of the definition of the interfering subject matter or the correspondence of claims to the count, (3) seek to change the benefit accorded for the count, or (4) seek judgment on derivation or on priority. To be sufficient, a motion must provide a showing, supported with appropriate evidence, such that, if unrebutted, it would justify the relief sought. The burden of proof is on the movant. A party moving to add or amend a claim must show the claim is patentable; a party moving to add or amend a count must show the count is patentable over prior art.
guidance: Substantive motions must be focused on specified interference issues and include unrebutted-supporting evidence and patentability showings when adding claims or counts.

name: Filing date requirements for an international filing date (PCT Article 11 / 37 CFR 1.431)
description: An international application shall contain a Request, a description, one or more claims, an abstract, and one or more drawings (where required). The Receiving Office shall accord an international filing date provided that at the time of receipt: (i) at least one applicant is a United States resident or national (for U.S. RO), (ii) the application is in the prescribed language (English), and (iii) the application contains at least: an indication that it is an international application, designation of at least one Contracting State, the name of the applicant, a part which on its face appears to be a description, and a part which on its face appears to be a claim or claims.
guidance: Payment of international filing, transmittal, and search fees may be made in full at filing or within one month; if fees are not paid within one month and prior to notice of deficiency, applicant will be given a one-month non-extendable time to pay deficient fees plus a late payment fee. If required payments to cover fees and late payment fee are not timely made, the Receiving Office will declare the international application withdrawn under PCT Article 14(3)(a). The international filing date is the earliest date on which the PCT Article 11(1) requirements were satisfied; if not satisfied at initial receipt, the RO will invite the applicant to correct defects.

name: Claims must define protection sought in technical terms (Rule 7(1))
description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought in terms of the technical features of the invention; they shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description. The number of claims shall be reasonable, and where several, numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals.
guidance: Claims should balance completeness and concision; 'reasonable' depends on nature of the invention.

name: Two-part claim structure where appropriate (Rule 7(1)(a)-(b))
description: Where appropriate, claims shall contain (a) a statement indicating technical features necessary for definition but which, in combination, are part of the prior art; and (b) a characterizing portion—preceded by words such as 'characterized in that', 'characterized by', 'wherein the improvement comprises'—stating concisely the technical features which with (a) are desired to be protected.
guidance: Use of standard transitional/characterizing language recommended for clarity of novel contribution.

name: Claims must not rely on references to description or drawings (Rule 7(2))
description: Claims shall not, except where absolutely necessary, rely, in respect of technical features, on references to the description or drawings; in particular avoid references such as 'as described in part ...' or 'as illustrated in figure ...'.
guidance: Claims should be self-contained; reliance on description/drawings weakens claim clarity and may be objected to.

name: Dependent claim formalities and multiple dependent claims (Rule 7(4)(a)-(c))
description: A dependent claim including all features of one or more other claims shall do so by a reference (if possible at the beginning) to the other claim(s) and then state the additional features. Multiple dependent claims must refer to the claims in the alternative only and shall not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claims. Claims shall be grouped logically.
guidance: Dependent-claim structure must be clear; multiple-dependence restricted to alternative references and cannot chain multiple-dependent claims.

name: Partial search/examination and divisional remedy for lack of unity (Rule 7(5)(b))
description: If the Office considers the application lacks unity, it shall draw up a partial search/examination report on the invention first mentioned in the claims, inform applicant that search/examination opinion covers only that subject-matter, invite limitation to that invention, and advise that remaining inventions can be filed as divisional applications.
guidance: Applicant may file divisionals to pursue non-first inventions; expect partial coverage in search/exam reports.

name: Unity determination independent of claim format (Rule 7(6))
description: Determination whether a group of inventions is so linked as to form a single general inventive concept shall be made without regard to whether the inventions are claimed in separate claims or as alternatives within a single claim.

name: Use of reference signs in claims (Rule 7(8))
description: Where drawings include reference signs, technical features in the claims shall preferably be followed by such reference signs in parentheses if intelligibility is increased; these reference signs shall not be construed as limiting the claim.
guidance: Reference numerals may aid clarity but are non-limiting.

name: Contents of declaration of priority (Rule 8(1))
description: A declaration claiming priority shall indicate: (i) the date of the earlier application; (ii) the number of the earlier application (subject to Rule 8(2)); (iii) the name of the State in which the earlier application was filed or, for regional/international applications, the State(s) for which it was filed; (iv) where regional/international, the office with which it was filed.
guidance: Declaration should identify earlier filing precisely to claim Paris Convention priority.

name: Documents to support priority claim (Rule 8(5)-(6))
description: Applicant shall, within 3 months from filing of the application containing the declaration, furnish a certified copy of the earlier application; if in a language other than English, furnish an English translation within 6 months.
guidance: Failure to comply means declaration is disregarded (Rule 8(7)).

name: Modification of examination timeline: expedited and delayed options (Rule 18(7)(a)-(d))
description: Applicant may request preferential substantive examination with a modified timeframe: (a) Expedited/Accelerated Examination to have decision within a period specified in Administrative Instructions, subject to: single invention or applicant agrees examining division considers only first identified invention; applicant undertakes to respond immediately to clarifications; application being withdrawn and then reinstated before conclusion of examination; and a search report based on acceptable minimum documentation on claims of same or narrower scope is availed. (b) Delayed commencement of substantive examination up to 1 year beyond Rule 18(1)(a) provided a request for substantive examination has been lodged in time, a written explanation satisfactory to Director General submitted, and application not deemed withdrawn due to non-payment of annuities. (c) Office will acknowledge requests and direct applicant to remit fees or confirm concurrence if relates to green technologies or indicate impossibility with reasons. (d) Requests not considered made unless prescribed fees paid.
guidance: Conditions for expedited/delayed handling are strict (single invention, immediate responses, supporting search reports, fees); green technology may receive special confirmation per Administrative Instructions.

name: Patent dance timelines and exchange obligations
description: If the biosimilar applicant provides its BLA to the RPS, the RPS has 60 days to provide a list of patents it wants to assert and indicate which it would license (42 U.S.C. 262(l)(3)(A)). The biosimilar applicant then has 60 days to provide its own patent list and either detailed statements with factual and legal bases for invalidity/unenforceability/non‑infringement or a statement that it does not intend to market before patent expiry (42 U.S.C. 262(l)(3)(B)). The RPS has 60 days to reply with its detailed statements (42 U.S.C. 262(l)(3)(C)).
guidance: These timed disclosures mirror claim/exchange narrowing meant to focus first‑wave litigation; the statutes specify exact day counts for each step.

name: Patent document structural elements
description: Patent documents normally include publication information, title, bibliometric information (applicants, inventors, assignees, examiners, attorneys), classification codes, citations/prior art, abstract, background, detailed description, claims, and drawings.
guidance: Each section has a distinct role: abstracts are brief and generic; descriptions contain comprehensive embodiments and are information-rich; claims define the legal scope; drawings support but do not replace text. For NLP tasks, segmentation into these sections is a common preprocessing step.

name: Long context handling
description: Patent descriptions are often very long (average description token counts can exceed 11,000 tokens), exceeding many LLMs' context windows.
guidance: For analysis and generation, models must handle long-range dependencies; use long-context LLMs, sparse/structured attention (e.g., BigBird, Longformer), or segmentation strategies. Avoid relying solely on titles/abstracts—the description and claims contain crucial details.

name: Dataset curation and preprocessing requirements
description: Preprocessing typically involves segmenting patents into sections (abstract, claims, description), rectifying irregularities (missing fields, encoding/format issues), and assembling task-specific labeled sets.
guidance: Patent offices provide raw bulk data but not always pre-processed structured datasets. Curated datasets (e.g., HUPD, BigPatent, DeepPatent) reduce effort. Researchers must handle paywalls, access restrictions, and decide on silver vs gold labeling approaches for tasks like simplification.

name: Task taxonomy for patent NLP
description: Patent-related tasks are grouped into analysis (subject classification, retrieval, information extraction, novelty/granting/litigation prediction, valuation, forecasting, innovation recommendation) and generation (summarization, translation, simplification, patent writing).
guidance: Define task-specific datasets, baselines, and metrics. Note differences between tasks that use short text portions (title/abstract) and those that require full descriptions or claims; tailor model architectures and evaluation accordingly.

name: Patent owner’s statement timing and content (37 CFR 1.530)
description: Except as provided in §1.510(e), no statement or other response by the patent owner shall be filed prior to determinations under §1.515 or §1.520; the order for ex parte reexamination will set a period of not less than two months from the date of the order within which the patent owner may file a statement on the new question of patentability, including any proposed amendments.
guidance: Any statement must clearly point out why the subject matter as claimed is not anticipated or rendered obvious by the prior art patents or printed publications, either alone or in any reasonable combinations. A copy of the statement must be served on the requester (unless requester is the patent owner). If proof of service is omitted, CRU should contact patent owner to correct; absence of service after the two‑month period may render the statement inappropriate and it may be denied consideration.

name: Amendments in reexamination proceedings (37 CFR 1.121(j) and 1.530(d))
description: Any proposed amendment to the description and claims in patents involved in reexamination proceedings must be made in accordance with §1.530. An amendment paper must direct specified changes to the patent specification, including claims, or to the drawings, and may accompany a patent owner request or statement or be filed during prosecution where permitted.
guidance: Specification changes: submit entire text of added/rewritten paragraph with markings per paragraph (f), or delete an entire paragraph by a deletion statement identifying the precise location. Claims: include entire text of each claim being changed and of each new claim; follow claim number with a parenthetical 'amended,' 'twice amended,' etc.; changed and added claims must include markings per paragraph (f), or cancel a claim by a canceling statement. Drawings: submit a sketch showing proposed changes in red for examiner approval; upon approval file new sheets in compliance with §1.84, identify amended figures as 'Amended' and new figures as 'New'; canceled figures bracketed and identified as 'Canceled.'

name: Marking conventions for amendments (brackets/underlining) and claim numbering
description: Changes relative to the patent being reexamined which are made to the specification, including the claims, must include: deletions enclosed in brackets and additions underlined. Patent claims may not be renumbered; numbering of any claims added in reexamination must follow the number of the highest numbered patent claim.
guidance: Use consistent markings per paragraph (f). Preserve numbering sequence; do not renumber existing claims.

name: Limitations on amendments (no new matter / no enlargement / expiration)
description: No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. No amendment, other than cancellation of claims, will be incorporated into the patent by a certificate issued after the expiration of the patent.
guidance: Amendments must be relative to the patent specification in effect as of the filing date of the request for reexamination. Proposed amendments are treated as entered in Office actions but are not effective until the reexamination certificate is issued and published.

name: Office may require amendment of disclosure to secure correspondence
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: Where the Office finds inconsistencies or inaccuracies, require amendment to ensure the specification supports the claims and drawings.

name: Integration of a Judicial Exception Into a Practical Application
description: A claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application when the claim as a whole applies, relies on, or uses the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.
guidance: If the claim integrates the exception into a practical application, it is not "directed to" the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B, ending the eligibility analysis. If it does not, the claim is "directed to" the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis under Step 2B (to determine whether it amounts to an inventive concept). The evaluation uses the considerations listed in the MPEP; the list is not exclusive.

name: Improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology (Improvements consideration)
description: A claim that demonstrates an improvement in the functioning of a computer or an improvement to another technology or technical field can integrate the judicial exception into a practical application and thus not be "directed to" the exception.
guidance: Evaluate the specification to see if it provides sufficient detail that a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly state the improvement but must describe it so it would be apparent to POSITA; conclusory bare assertions of improvement are insufficient. The claim must reflect the disclosed improvement by including the components or steps that provide it (the claim need not contain the literal word "thereby increasing..." etc.). Step 2A Prong Two evaluates improvement without regard to whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional. Examples cited: Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip-synchronization), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system), Finjan (virus scanning improvements), SRI Int’l v. Cisco (network monitors/packet analysis). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for more detail.

name: Applying or using the exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis (Treatment/prophylaxis consideration)
description: Claims that apply or use a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition can integrate the exception into a practical application and be eligible at Step 2A.
guidance: This consideration covers limitations that treat or prevent disease or medical conditions (e.g., acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery). The key is that the steps use the natural law/exception to safely or effectively treat the patient, rather than merely gathering diagnostic data. Vanda v. West-Ward distinguishes claims that administer therapy as part of treatment (eligible at Step 2A) from claims where administration is ancillary to diagnostics as in Mayo. See MPEP § 2106.04(d)(2) and cited case law for application.

name: Implementing the exception with or using it in conjunction with a particular machine or manufacture (Particular machine/manufacture consideration)
description: A claim that implements a judicial exception with, or uses the exception in conjunction with, a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim may integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim limitations tie the exception to a particular machine or manufacture in a way that meaningfully limits the exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(b)). Mere recitation of a general-purpose computer without more is likely insufficient (see non-integrating considerations). Specificity of how the machine is used can be relevant.

name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing (Particular transformation consideration)
description: A claim that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed steps or elements change an article in a meaningful way (see MPEP § 2106.05(c)). The transformation must be more than nominal or insignificant; how the limitation interacts with the judicial exception is important.

name: Applying or using the exception in some other meaningful way beyond linking to a technological environment
description: If the additional elements apply or use the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, the claim as a whole may integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: This is a catch-all 'other meaningful limitations' consideration (see MPEP § 2106.05(e)). The limitation must be more than a general field-of-use or technological environment tie and must meaningfully limit the judicial exception so the claim is not just an attempt to monopolize the exception. The Office provides examples in MPEP § 2106.05(e).

name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity is insufficient
description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Evaluate whether the extra activity is meaningful or merely post-solution activity. If it is ancillary, conventional, or merely incidental, it will not render the claim eligible (see MPEP § 2106.05(g) and Parker v. Flook example where lack of specifics led to finding additional elements insignificant).

name: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant to certain considerations
description: Although a specific way of achieving a result is not by itself a stand-alone consideration, the specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluating the use of a particular machine, particular transformation, and whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception.
guidance: Lack of disclosure of how to perform claimed steps or missing specifics can indicate that additional elements are insignificant post-solution activity (Parker v. Flook). Examine whether the claim and specification provide sufficient detail to show the claimed limitations actually effect the purported integration.

name: If no additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception, integration fails
description: If the claim contains no additional claim elements besides the judicial exception, or if the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: The Prong Two analysis considers the claim as a whole; the absence of meaningful additional limitations means the claim is directed to the judicial exception. Examiners should consider how any additional limitations interact with the exception rather than evaluating them in isolation.

name: Evaluate specification and claims to ensure claim reflects disclosed improvement
description: When asserting an improvement to technology as the basis for integration, the specification should provide sufficient details so POSITA would recognize the improvement, and the claim must include components/steps that provide that improvement.
guidance: An asserted improvement stated only in conclusory language in the specification is insufficient. The claim does not need to recite the improvement in a particular phrase but must recite the structural or functional components that embody the improvement. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) and cited cases.

name: Selling factor — grave injustice
description: The respondent may avoid reciprocal discipline by showing that imposition of the same discipline by the USPTO would result in a grave injustice.
guidance: Grave injustice analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct (i.e., whether the sanction is so ill-fitted that imposing it would be fundamentally unfair). Evidence that the state already considered mitigating factors (e.g., illness) weighs against a grave injustice claim. The respondent must prove grave injustice by clear and convincing evidence; cited cases illustrate that sanctions within the state’s usual range are not a grave injustice.

name: Consideration of state mitigation in grave-injustice claims
description: Mitigating factors considered by the state (e.g., physical or mental illness) are part of the state record and generally undercut claims that reciprocal discipline would be a grave injustice.
guidance: If the state proceeding already considered and accounted for mitigation in setting the sanction, claiming that such mitigation warrants avoiding identical discipline before the USPTO is unlikely to succeed unless new, clear-and-convincing evidence shows otherwise.

name: Types of conduct supporting discipline (examples of misconduct)
description: Specific ethical violations alleged/found in the underlying state proceeding that support discipline (fees, termination, meritorious claims, respect for rights, misconduct prejudicial to administration of justice).
guidance: The Arizona decision identified violations of ER 1.5 (Fees), ER 1.16 (Termination of Representation), ER 3.1 (Meritorious Claims and Contentions), ER 4.4 (Respect for the Rights of Others), and ER 8.4(d) (Misconduct Prejudicial to the Administration of Justice). The Final Order summarizes factual examples: failing to promptly return a client's file and inappropriate billing practices (including billing time to 'wait and see' if opposing counsel filed documents). Such factual findings in the state record support imposition of reciprocal discipline absent successful Selling challenges.

name: Start with the claims, then work backwards
description: Draft claim 1 first, decide which elements are truly essential, then write the specification to support every word in that claim. If a term appears in a claim but is not anchored in the spec, you have a 112(b) problem waiting to happen.
guidance: The claims define what you actually own — structure the entire application around them. Identify essential claim elements before drafting the spec and ensure each claim term is expressly supported in the specification to avoid written‑description/claim‑support issues (the author cites a potential 112(b) problem).

name: Your independent claim is probably too narrow
description: First-timers reflexively describe their commercial product, producing claims with many non‑load‑bearing elements. Strip each independent claim down to the minimum combination that distinguishes over the closest prior art.
guidance: Audit each claim limitation and remove anything unnecessary (e.g., 'wherein the user clicks a button' is likely an unnecessary limitation). Focus independent claims on the minimal distinguishing features versus closest prior art to preserve breadth.

name: Use multiple independent claims of different scope
description: Do not file with just one independent claim. File three or four: one broad, one of moderate scope, and one narrow but commercially aligned.
guidance: Claim diversity is a prosecution/post‑grant hedge: if the broad claim is killed, narrower claims may survive. Structure claim sets to include varied scopes (broad, medium, narrow) tailored to both legal strength and commercial value.

name: Describe three embodiments, not one
description: Even if you only built one prototype, describe (a) the prototype, (b) a more general version with components swapped for functional equivalents, and (c) a degenerate or simplified version.
guidance: Providing multiple embodiments makes later claim breadth and claim construction easier. Include functional equivalents and simplified/degenerate examples to guard against overly narrow interpretations and to support claim amendments or continuations.

name: Avoid 'Patent Profanity'
description: Words like 'essential,' 'critical,' 'must,' 'always,' 'the invention is,' and 'the present invention requires' are landmines. Courts read these as disclaimers of scope.
guidance: Prefer non‑absolute phrasing such as 'in some embodiments,' 'may include,' or 'one example.' Avoid absolute terms that can be construed as limiting or disclaiming claim scope.

name: Draw the figures yourself first
description: You will discover gaps in your own understanding when you try to label every reference number. Aim for one figure per concept. Block diagrams beat photographs for clarity.
guidance: Sketching figures forces precision about structures and relationships; use clear block diagrams rather than photos when possible. Ensure each figure supports the described embodiments and claim elements with reference numerals.

name: Disclose more than you want to claim
description: Disclosure is cheap; you cannot add new matter later. If you have alternative materials, alternative orderings, alternative ranges — put them in the spec even if you do not currently claim them.
guidance: Include alternatives, variations, and ranges in the specification to preserve options for continuations and claim amendments. Over‑disclose to create 'fodder for continuations' and to avoid losing rights later.

name: Get a real search done before filing
description: Not a Google search. A real prior art search by a professional searcher costs $500–$2,000 and routinely surfaces the closest art.
guidance: Invest in a professional prior art search before drafting to identify the closest references and shape claim strategy appropriately. Knowing the closest art up front can save years of wasted prosecution on claims that read on older references.

name: Step 2A: directed to a judicial exception
description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).
guidance: Mathematical relationships and algorithms (e.g., specific formulas) have been characterized as abstract ideas or laws of nature by the courts (citations: Mackay Radio, Flook, etc.). Point to the claim elements (e.g., generating/scaling steps, formulas) that recite the exception.

name: Step 2B: additional limitations must amount to 'significantly more'
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, amount to significantly more than the exception (Step 2B: YES/NO).
guidance: Consider each additional element alone and the claim elements as an ordered combination. Generic computer implementation or merely adding conventional activities ordinarily does not amount to significantly more; a specific application that improves technology or effects a transformation can.

name: Preamble limiting effect — 'life, meaning and vitality'
description: Determine whether the preamble gives 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim such that it limits the claim scope (if so, treat preamble limitations as claim limitations).
guidance: If the preamble only states purpose or field of use it does not limit the claim. See MPEP 2111.02 for guidance on when preamble language is limiting.

name: Limiting use to a particular technological environment is insufficient
description: Simply restricting the abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., graphical user interface) is not typically enough to make the claim significantly more.
guidance: Courts have found that merely limiting the use of an abstract idea to a particular technological environment (see Flook) does not supply significantly more absent meaningful limitations that realize a technological improvement.

name: Improvement to computer or other technical field can show significantly more
description: Claim limitations that describe a specific application which improves computer functionality or another technical field can amount to significantly more and confer eligibility.
guidance: Examples: reciting features that improve the computer's basic ability to display information and interact with the user (scaling and relocating text in overlapping windows) or software that controls a device to improve a specific technological process (precision rubber molding) can be eligible because they 'improve another technical field' or 'improve the functioning of the basic display function of the computer itself.'

name: Data gathering and post-solution activity do not add significantly more
description: Mere collection of data (e.g., determining a process variable) or post-solution activity (e.g., adjusting an alarm) typically are not sufficient to make a claim significantly more than an abstract idea.
guidance: Claims that only add data gathering or post-solution activity to a formula or algorithm fail Step 2B absent further meaningful integration into a technical process.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity fails to add significantly more
description: Additional elements that are 'well-understood, routine and conventional' do not individually confer eligibility.
guidance: When claim limitations are routine computer functions or conventional activities, the examiner should treat them as not contributing 'significantly more' unless the combination or specific implementation yields a technical improvement.

name: Conduct Step 2B for each abstract idea when multiple are present
description: If a claim recites multiple judicial exceptions (e.g., a mathematical relationship and mental steps), the Step 2B analysis must be conducted for each abstract idea separately until ineligibility is shown for one or eligibility is shown for all.
guidance: Analyze each abstract-idea thread individually and determine whether additional limitations address that particular exception.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation affects eligibility analysis
description: Claims are analyzed under their broadest reasonable interpretation; if that interpretation covers performance by hand as well as by computer, that fact bears on the abstract-idea analysis.
guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation covers manual performance of claimed steps, that may support a finding that the claim recites abstract ideas performable mentally or by humans.

name: Use of 'non-transitory' language to avoid signal coverage
description: Including 'non-transitory' in claims can ensure the claim does not encompass transitory signals and helps place a claim in a statutory category (manufacture/article).
guidance: Example: 'A non-transitory computer readable medium' ensures the claim is directed to an article, not a signal.

name: Physical transformation or improvement in a technical field supports eligibility
description: Claims that effect a transformation of a physical article or improve a technical field (e.g., transforming uncured rubber into cured product) can amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.
guidance: Physical transformation of an article to a different state or thing, or integration of an abstract idea into a process that improves a technological field, are strong indicators of eligibility.

name: How to frame a rejection or allowance regarding exceptions
description: When making a rejection, identify the judicial exception by pointing to the claim elements that recite it and explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. When allowing/clearing, add remarks or reasons for allowance explaining that although the claim recites an exception, the additional limitations—individually or as an ordered combination—demonstrate meaningful improvements.
guidance: A rejection should (1) point to the exception (e.g., the formula/mental steps), (2) explain why the preamble does or does not limit the claim, and (3) explain why the additional claim elements fail Step 2B (e.g., mere data gathering, field-of-use, generic computer functions). If eligible, the Office action or reasons for allowance may note that the claim recites the exception but is eligible due to meaningful limitations.

name: Grouping of Claims; Separate Patentability Statement (37 CFR 1.192(c)(7))
description: For each ground of rejection that applies to a group of two or more claims, appellant must state whether the claims 'stand or fall together' or state they do not and provide reasons.
guidance: If appellant considers claims in a group to be separately patentable, 37 CFR 1.192(c)(7) requires (A) a statement that the claims do not stand or fall together and (B) presentation of reasons why the claims are separately patentable in the argument section (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)). Merely pointing out differences in claim scope is not sufficient. Absence of the statement and reasons is a concession that the ground, if sustained as to one claim, applies to all; the Board will normally select the broadest claim in the group for decision.

name: Argument Content for 35 U.S.C. 112, First Paragraph (enablement/written description/best mode)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the brief must contain an argument specifying the errors in the rejection and how the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 is complied with.
guidance: Argument should address: (a) description of the subject matter defined by each rejected claim; (b) how a person skilled in the art can make and use the claimed subject matter (enablement); and (c) the best mode contemplated by the inventor, where applicable. Use specifics from the specification and drawings as required.

name: Argument Content for 35 U.S.C. 112, Second Paragraph (definiteness)
