description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the brief must contain an argument specifying the errors in the rejection and how the claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter.
guidance: Provide claim-specific explanation identifying why the examiner's assertion of lack of definiteness is erroneous and how each claim limitation is adequately claimed.

name: Argument Content for 35 U.S.C. 102 Rejections (anticipation)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the brief must specify the errors in the rejection and why the rejected claims are patentable under 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: Include any specific claim limitations that are not described in the prior art relied upon in the rejection and explain clearly how those limitations are absent from the cited reference(s). Identify the claim(s) for which no argument was specified when applicable.

name: Argument Content for 35 U.S.C. 103 Rejections (obviousness)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the brief must specify the errors in the rejection and, if appropriate, the specific limitations in the rejected claims not described in the prior art, and an explanation how such limitations render the claimed subject matter unobvious.
guidance: If the rejection is based on a combination of references, explain why the references, taken as a whole, do not suggest the claimed subject matter and, as appropriate, why features disclosed in one reference may not be properly combined with another. A general statement that all limitations are not described in a single reference is insufficient.

name: Argument Content for Other Rejections (37 CFR 1.192(c)(8)(v))
description: For any rejection not falling under the 112/102/103 subparagraphs, the argument should specify particular claim limitations, if appropriate, or other reasons which cause the rejection to be in error.
guidance: For example, for a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection (nonstatutory subject matter) it may be unnecessary to specify particular claim limitations; instead explain why the claims are statutory (see Ex parte Hibberd example).

name: Statement of Status of Claims and Identification of Appealed Claims (37 CFR 1.192(c)(3))
description: The brief must contain a statement of the status of all the claims, pending or canceled, and identify the claims appealed.
guidance: Failure to include the claim status and identify appealed claims is a defect and should be specifically indicated in the examiner's notification.

name: Examiner's Answer Requirements and Timing (37 CFR 1.193)
description: The primary examiner may furnish a written answer including necessary explanation of the invention, references, and grounds of rejection; the examiner should furnish the answer within 2 months after receipt of the brief.
guidance: The answer should contain a response to allegations/arguments in the brief, call attention to errors in appellant's copy of the claims, and clearly state any withdrawn rejections. The answer must not include a new ground of rejection (unless prosecution is reopened). Examiners should treat affidavits/declarations/exhibits filed with or after the notice of appeal in accordance with 37 CFR 1.195; if such evidence was refused entry, the examiner should not comment on it in the answer.

name: Support requirement / written description requirement
description: Claims must be supported by the description (written description in the U.S.): there must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and the scope of the claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
guidance: A claim is regarded as supported unless a person skilled in the art would be unable, on the basis of the application as filed, to extend the teaching of the description to the whole of the field claimed. U.S. written description: describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that a person skilled in the art reasonably concludes the inventor had possession at filing.

name: Clarity requirement / definiteness requirement
description: Claims must be clear and concise and distinctly define the subject matter of the invention; vague or indefinite terms are not acceptable.
guidance: In most jurisdictions words in a claim get their normal meaning in the relevant art; where appropriate, a drafter may give a word a special defined meaning in the description. Description and drawings may be considered when interpreting claims. See Module VI, section 3 for practical aspects of drafting clear and concise claims.

name: Inventive step (nonobviousness)
description: The invention must involve an inventive step (nonobviousness) beyond the prior art; for determining lack of inventive step, prior art references may be combined to show obviousness.
guidance: Inventive step is distinct from novelty: novelty looks at single references, while inventive step may involve combining references and considering whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art.

name: Description structure and content
description: The description discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for a person skilled in the art to carry out the claimed invention and usually contains several sections.
guidance: Typical elements: (i) title of the invention; (ii) technical field; (iii) background art; (iv) summary of the invention outlining full scope and how problem is solved; (v) brief explanation of the drawings; (vi) detailed disclosure of embodiments with reference to drawings. Embodiments help meet support and enablement requirements.

name: Claims define legal scope
description: Claims define the scope of exclusive patent protection in terms of technical features; they are the legally operative part of the application and patentability is determined on the basis of the claims.
guidance: Claims must be clear, concise and fully supported by the description. Claims are typically drafted in a particular format (example provided). Drafters commonly prepare claims first as they drive the content of the description.

name: Drawings
description: Drawings provide visual support and facilitate understanding of the claimed invention; they may include figures, tables, flow charts and diagrams.
guidance: A representative drawing is often placed on the front page of a published patent document. Use drawings where necessary to understand and exemplify embodiments.

name: Provisional application as a filing strategy
description: A provisional patent application discloses the invention but does not require claims; it serves as a placeholder and expires one year after filing and can preserve a priority date if a subsequent regular application is filed within one year.
guidance: Provisional filings can rescue situations where an imminent bar date prevents preparation of a full application in time. Draft the best provisional possible within time constraints; ensure adequate disclosure to support later claims.

name: Identifying patentable inventions (core inventive concept)
description: Patent drafters must focus on patentable aspects within disclosure; inventors may conflate discoveries/products with patentable claimable inventions; the drafter often must articulate the inventive concept.
guidance: Explore the problem solved in light of prior art to craft essential claim elements. Ask about possible alternatives and embodiments to broaden claim scope. Use examples and follow-up questioning to distinguish inventive features from nonpatentable details.

name: Understanding invention: essential vs non-essential elements
description: Drafter should understand invention well enough to define it by the fewest possible elements—know what elements are essential and what need not be recited to obtain the broadest allowable claims.
guidance: Confirm uncertain details with inventors or experts, seek alternative embodiments, and ensure the description discloses working embodiments. The drafter may assist inventors in considering broader applications and alternatives to strengthen disclosure and claim breadth.

name: Claims-first drafting practice
description: Patent drafters ordinarily prepare the claims first because the claims are the heart of a patent and will partly dictate the content of the description.
guidance: Use the claims to decide what to include in the description and embodiments. Ensure claims are drafted to be as broad as justified by the disclosure while meeting clarity, support and enablement requirements.

name: Burden after prima facie lack of enablement
description: Once the examiner establishes a prima facie case of lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the burden shifts to the applicant to present persuasive arguments, supported by suitable proofs where necessary, that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the disclosure as a guide.
guidance: Applicant evidence must show enablement or that missing information was known to those of ordinary skill (In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth).

name: Inventorship designation and lack of presumption from authorship
description: Designation of authorship in a published article or inventorship in a patent or application publication does not create a presumption that the named author/inventor is the inventor of subject matter disclosed but not claimed so as to justify a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(f).
guidance: Inventorship inquiries may still be appropriate to clarify ambiguities; applicants must provide satisfactory showings to rebut rejections (In re Katz).

name: 37 CFR 1.130(a) conditions to disqualify commonly owned U.S. patent/app as prior art
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 on a U.S. patent or patent application publication that is not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b), and the claimed inventions are not identical but not patentably distinct and are owned by the same party, the applicant/owner may disqualify that patent or publication by submitting: (1) a terminal disclaimer under § 1.321(c); and (2) an oath or declaration stating current common ownership and that the inventor named in the application/patent is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104.
guidance: The declaration may be signed by inventor(s), attorney/agent of record, or assignee(s). Ensure requirements of §1.321(c) and 35 U.S.C. 104 are met.

name: Double patenting rejections and terminal disclaimer remedy (37 CFR 1.130(b))
description: When an application or patent under reexamination claims an invention not patentably distinct from an invention claimed in a commonly owned patent, a double patenting rejection will be made; a judicially-created double patenting rejection may be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer under § 1.321(c).
guidance: See MPEP § 804.02 and related guidance on double patenting and terminal disclaimers.

name: Correcting data on the file wrapper label/bib-data
description: If the examiner notices an error in data originally entered on the file wrapper or PALM bib-data sheet, make the correction in red ink and forward the application to TC technical support for correction of the PALM database and printing/placement of updated sheets or labels, with series-dependent procedures for 08/09/10-series applications.
guidance: Common corrections include inventorship changes (37 CFR 1.48), filing date, prior U.S. application number errors, and benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c). Assignment name/address corrections go to Assignment Division.

name: Office personnel not to express opinion on validity, patentability, expiration, or enforceability
description: Every employee of the USPTO shall refuse to express to any person any opinion as to the validity or invalidity of, or the patentability or unpatentability of any claim in any U.S. patent or the expiration date of any patent, except to the extent necessary to carry out specified Office functions.
guidance: Exceptions (A–H) where opinions/determinations may be given: (A) examination of a non-reissue patent application where expiration date necessary for examination; (B) examination of a reissue application of the patent; (C) supplemental examination or reexamination proceedings; (D) interference or derivation proceeding involving the patent; (E) patent term adjustment/extension under 35 U.S.C. 154/156 where determination of expiration date necessary; (F) notification that a patent has expired for failure to pay maintenance fee; (G) consideration of a request under the regulations (e.g., a petition) where patent term determination is necessary or ancillary; (H) inter partes or post-grant review. Employees may provide general factual information about patent term calculation (e.g., design patent term rules) but should refuse to determine or opine on a specific patent's expiration date except as provided above. Employees must refuse inquiries that could indicate a patent should not have issued; accepting private payments (bounties) for prior-art searching or accepting payments from outside sources for prior art search activities may lead to disciplinary action. Examiners should not suggest a field of search if the invention has been patented. Employees who examined an application should not discuss whether a particular reference was considered or whether a claim would have been allowed over that reference; the file must speak for itself. Definitions in 37 CFR 104.1 and exceptions in 37 CFR 104.21 apply.

name: Restrictions on current and former Office employees regarding patents (35 U.S.C. 4 and 37 CFR 11.10)
description: Officers and employees of the USPTO may not apply for a patent or acquire any patent or interest in a patent during their appointment and for one year thereafter; post-employment practice before the Office is restricted under 37 CFR 11.10.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 4 bars applying for patents or acquiring rights during employment and for one year after; any patents applied for thereafter cannot claim priority earlier than one year after termination. 37 CFR 11.10 requires post-employment undertakings by former Office employees: they must agree not to knowingly act as agent/attorney for others before the Office in connection with any patent or application they participated in personally and substantially as an Office employee, and not to act within two years after termination as agent/attorney before the Office in connection with any particular patent/application if such matter was pending under their official responsibility within one year prior to termination. By virtue of conflict-of-interest statutes (e.g., 18 U.S.C. 203, 205) and OGE regulations, former employees remain barred from prosecuting or aiding prosecution of patent/trademark applications where conflicts exist. An Office employee named as inventor will be presumed incapable of executing an inventor's oath/declaration under 35 U.S.C. 4; for applications filed on or after Sept 16, 2012, a substitute statement under 37 CFR 1.64 may be filed in lieu of the employee's oath/declaration without contacting the current employee.

name: Official Gazette publication content and browsing features
description: The Official Gazette (OG) is published electronically weekly in two sections (Patents and Trademarks) and provides listings and browsing functionality for issued patents and trademarks.
guidance: The Electronic Official Gazette — Patents (eOG:P) reports reexamination certificates, reissues, plant, utility, and design patents issued and statutory invention registrations. Browse features: (A) Browse by CPC or USPC to access patents by classification; (B) Classification of Patents page linking to patents within CPC classes and USPC class ranges; (C) Browse Granted Patents page to access patents by number or type and links to certificates from reexaminations/supplemental examinations/administrative trials; (D) Index of Patentees (alphabetical/cumulative); (E) Geographical Index of Inventors; (F) Notices page linking to weekly USPTO Notices. For each patent the OG may provide: (A) patent number; (B) title of invention; (C) inventor(s) name, city, state/country; (D) assignee info; (E) applicant info; (F) filing date and application number; (G) reissue cross-reference; (H) U.S. benefit application data; (I) PCT/international design application data; (J) foreign priority data; (K) publication number and date; (L) international classification; (M) CPC classification; (N) U.S. class/subclass (for design/plant); (O) number of claims; (P) selected drawing figure; (Q) a claim or claims.

name: 803.02-Election of Species Requirements – Markush Claims
description: Restriction/election practice specifically as it applies to species requirements and Markush claims.

name: 803.04-Nucleotide Sequences
description: Restriction and unity issues specific to nucleotide sequence claims.

name: 806-Determination of Distinctness or Independence of Claimed Inventions
description: Criteria and procedures for determining whether claimed inventions are distinct or independent for restriction purposes.

name: 806.01-Compare Claimed Subject Matter
description: Guidance that determination of distinctness/independence involves comparing the claimed subject matter.

name: 806.05(i)-Product, Process of Making, and Process of Using
description: Assessment when claims cover product, process of making, and process of using—how distinctness is determined among these.

name: 808.01-Reasons for Holding of Independence or Distinctness
description: Specific reasons that support a finding of independence or distinctness between claimed inventions.

name: 818.01(d)-Traverse of Restriction Requirement With Linking Claims
description: Specifics on traversing a restriction requirement that involves linking claims.

name: Claims for combinations — scope and limitations
description: Rules concerning claims directed to combinations: what a claim for a combination covers and limits on coverage
guidance: Index guidance: Claim for (524,525). Key points: does not cover its elements; cannot cover elements already patented; elements not claimed are regarded as old; elements claimed thereby become essential; claims not withdrawn by disclaimer; not declared unessential by the courts; regarded as material by inventor so held against transferees; covers the exact union of the exact elements; joinder of subcombinations and elements; what acts infringe; use of less than all elements (references 888,928); defenses must apply to entire combination (1026 n.3); anticipated when (282ii.8); not anticipated by prior use of elements (318 n.1). Also relates to identity of arts, omission/alteration of essential steps, and distinctions for machines vs manufactures.

name: Construction (claim interpretation) — general rules
description: Construction of patents (claims and specification) — how words are applied to subject matter and how patents are interpreted by courts
guidance: Index entries: Construction defined as part of inventive act; measures the monopoly; may be made by court or jury; often treated as matter of law; liberal in favor of patentee; cannot depart from or cure defects in language; must tend to clear definition of the invention; not alternative to render claim elastic or ambiguous; should be consistent with real nature of the invention if possible; actual character of invention may be shown; names given to inventions construed by persons skilled in the art; entire patent construed together; description construed with other parts of specification; claims govern when clear; description used if claims ambiguous; general words limited by nature of invention; extrinsic evidence (parol) admissible in certain circumstances; expert evidence may aid; construction is liberal on questions of joinder; later patents not construed to cover earlier if avoidable; arrangement of words unimportant; words mean what applicant intended; words take meaning they had at date of invention; general limited and special extended when necessary; construed by correspondence with Patent Office; ambiguous language may be rejected as surplusage; pioneer patents broadly construed; re-issue construed by original; construction applied to combinations, improvements, joint inventions, etc. Also: make all claimed elements material; construction for principle, function, effect; aid of drawings and model; words and special phrases (e.g., 'substantially as described', 'generic') treated specially.

name: Composition — definition, unity, and patentability
description: Composition defined; essential attributes and how composition differs from its elements and mode of intermixture
guidance: Index entries: Composition defined 192; essential attributes 195; composition is a true combination (193), distinct from elements and mode of intermixture (194); character determined by analysis (801); intermixture of ingredients (192); no special substance or mode of intermixture essential (194); unit and unity destroyed by additions/omissions (196); identity of composition determined by identity of ingredients, combination, and properties. Additional rules: identical however produced (197); natural vs artificial (197); equivalents governed by special rule; improvement in composition; removal of defects; reducible to practice in many forms and all covered by patent (199); not patentable until reduced to practice (198). Description and claim guidance: description in patent (500); claim for composition (532) covers only equivalent ingredients (514), requires neither model nor drawing (549), joinder with ingredients/process/apparatus (476); infringement rules applicable (1928).

name: Court powers and jurisdiction in patent cases
description: Courts' powers to interpret, review, and adjudicate patent rights; jurisdictional rules for federal and state courts
guidance: Index entries: courts interpret patents and may refuse evidence to aid; can decide sufficiency of claim as matter of law; ambiguity usually for jury; Supreme Court construction is final; courts may declare patent void if description insufficient on its face. Federal courts have exclusive jurisdiction over cases arising under Patent Law to secure uniformity; jurisdiction conferred to Circuit and Supreme Court issues; State court jurisdiction limited/affected; court powers regarding appeals, mandamus, and finality of Patent Office decisions discussed. See related topics: Court of Claims, federal/state jurisdictional distinctions, remedies, contempt.

name: Damages for infringement — measure and limitations
description: Rules for measuring damages in actions at law and in equity for patent infringement
guidance: Index summary: Damages in actions at law (1049-1071); implied from infringement; not synonymous with profits; liberal doctrine in American law; assessed irrespective of parties' financial condition; remote/consequential damages generally not allowable; nominal damages occasions; burden of proof on plaintiff; plaintiff's evidence liberally construed; license fee as measure in some cases; measure depends on plaintiff's mode of exploiting invention (use/sale); defendant's profits may guide measurement; value at date of infringement relevant; special rules for improvements, partial infringement, making-only cases; interest, trebling, counsel fees considerations (treble in court discretion; counsel fees sometimes covered). Also allocation among co-owners, proof requirements, and limits (cannot exceed amount claimed in declaration).

name: Litigation phase/variety breakdown (standard cost slices)
description: For litigation (e.g., Patent Infringement, All Varieties) costs are reported by the following varieties: Initial case management; Inclusive of discovery, motions, and claim construction; Inclusive of pretrial, trial, post-trial, and appeal (when applicable); Cost of mediation.
guidance: Report costs separately for each of these discrete phases/varieties to enable stage-by-stage comparison; these are the primary slices used in the AIPLA tables.

name: Prong Two — additional elements must transform judicial exception
description: For a claim reciting a judicial exception to be eligible, the additional elements (if any) in the claim must "transform the nature of the claim" into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception, Alice Corp., 573 U.S. at 217, either at Prong Two or in Step 2B. If there are no additional elements in the claim, then it cannot be eligible.
guidance: If a judicial exception is the only thing recited, or the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. After making the appropriate rejection, it is a best practice for the examiner to recommend an amendment, if possible, that would resolve eligibility of the claim (see MPEP §2106.07 for formulating such a rejection).

name: Step 2A Prong One — identification procedure
description: Determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
guidance: If the identified limitations fall within at least one grouping, the claim is reasonably concluded to recite an abstract idea and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two. If the identified limitations do not fall within any grouping, it is reasonable to find that the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the abstract idea exception inquiry concludes (eligible at Pathway B) unless the claim recites another judicial exception (law of nature or natural phenomenon).

name: Groupings may overlap — identify all applicable groupings
description: The abstract idea groupings are not mutually exclusive; some claim limitations may fall within more than one grouping or sub-grouping.
guidance: Examiners should identify at least one abstract idea grouping, but preferably identify all groupings to the extent possible if a claim limitation is determined to fall within multiple groupings, and then proceed with the Step 2A Prong Two analysis. Example: a formula that could be performed in the human mind may fall within both the mathematical concepts and mental processes groupings.

name: Mathematical concepts grouping (general)
description: The mathematical concepts grouping is defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have identified various kinds of mathematical concepts as abstract ideas (e.g., Benson, Flook, Diehr, Bilski). When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, examiners should consider whether the claim actually recites the mathematical concept or merely limitations that are based on or involve a mathematical concept. A limitation merely based on or involving a mathematical concept (e.g., using math to implement a particular configuration) may not fall in the grouping if the mathematical concept itself is not recited in the claim. Note that mathematical concepts need not be expressed in symbols — words operating on data can serve the same purpose as formulas.

name: Determining prior art available in reissue examination (AIA vs pre-AIA considerations)
description: Available prior art for examination of a reissue application is generally the same as that under which the original application was examined, but in some cases the reissue may be subject to different prior art (AIA vs pre-AIA) depending on the effective filing date of claims in the reissue application.
guidance: If any claim in the reissue application has an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 (first-inventor-to-file) apply to the patent application containing such claim; applications filed before that date are governed by pre-AIA 102/103. Example: benefit claims and effective filing dates can make the entire reissue application subject to AIA provisions or to pre-AIA 102(g). See MPEP §§ 2150 et seq., 2159, and related discussion for how to determine which prior art/statute applies. Also see Grant v. Raymond: reissue claims are treated as if presented in the original patent for effective filing date purposes.

name: Treatment of federal court decisions affecting SNQ
description: A final court decision of claim validity in view of the same or different prior art does not necessarily mean no SNQ is present; the Office's determination is made independently. A nonfinal holding of invalidity or unenforceability will not be controlling. A final holding of invalidity or unenforceability after all appeals is controlling on the Office and an SNQ would not be present as to those claims.
guidance: Office may accord deference to district court factual findings but is not bound by court rulings on validity for SNQ determinations; see Ethicon v. Quigg for authority.

name: Claims considered are those in effect at time of determination
description: The claims of the patent in effect at the time of the determination will be the basis for deciding whether an SNQ is present (37 CFR 1.515(a)).
guidance: Examiner’s determination generally limited to claims for which reexamination was requested. If requester fails to apply art to certain claims as required by 35 U.S.C. 302 and 37 CFR 1.510(b), those claims generally will not be reexamined. The Office may nevertheless reexamine other claims at its discretion and may initiate reexamination on its own initiative (35 U.S.C. 303(a)).

name: Decision granting reexamination—required content
description: If a request for reexamination is granted, the examiner’s decision granting the request will conclude that an SNQ has been raised by (A) identifying all claims and issues, (B) identifying the patents and/or printed publications relied on, and (C) providing a brief statement of the rationale supporting each new question.
guidance: Examiner must identify at least one SNQ and explain how the prior art raises it. Examiner should indicate initial positions on issues identified (without rejecting claims) so patent owner and requester can comment. Prior art relied on should be listed on proper PTO forms (PTO-892, PTO/SB/08A/08B, PTO/SB/42 or equivalent) and copies supplied only if not previously provided.

name: Required particulars to show for each substantial new question (A–F)
description: For each SNQ identified, the decision should point out: (A) the prior art patents and printed publications which add some new teaching as to at least one claim; (B) what that new teaching is; (C) the claims that the new teaching is directed to; (D) that the new teaching was not previously considered nor addressed in the prior examination of the patent or a final holding of invalidity by the Federal Courts; (E) that the new teaching is such that a reasonable examiner would consider the new teaching to be important in deciding to allow the claim being considered; and (F) where the question is raised or where it is not clear that a reference pre-dates the patent claims, a discussion why the reference is deemed available against the patent claims.
guidance: These six points must be explicitly addressed in the decision; see MPEP § 2247.01 for examples. Item (F) requires providing reasons for availability/antedating when dates are unclear.

name: Do not decide patentability in the decision on the request
description: In the decision on the request, the examiner will not decide, and no statement should be made as to, whether the claims are rejected over the patents and printed publications. The examiner only decides whether there is an SNQ to grant the request to order reexamination.
guidance: Avoid language that implies claims are rejected; limit the decision to whether an SNQ exists. Provide initial positions on issues only to solicit comments.

name: Timing and statement/reply periods when reexamination ordered
description: When reexamination is ordered, the patent owner will be given a reasonable period, not less than two months from the date a copy of the determination is mailed or given, within which to file a statement on the question, including any amendment and new claims. If the patent owner files a statement, the requester may file a reply within two months of service.
guidance: Decision must set forth the time periods for filing statements and replies. Note special dispatch rules and extension limitations (see separate entry on extensions).

name: Petition under 37 CFR 1.181 to vacate ultra vires reexamination orders—acceptable grounds
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.181 may be filed to vacate an ultra vires reexamination order, e.g., where the order is not based on prior art patents or printed publications; all claims were held invalid by final Federal Court decision; reexamination ordered for the wrong patent; reexamination ordered based on a duplicate copy of the request; or the order is based wholly on the same question of patentability raised by prior art previously considered in an earlier concluded Office examination.
guidance: Substantive Director determinations to institute reexamination are not subject to review by courts until a final agency decision; 1.181 petitions are limited to ultra vires circumstances. See In re Recreative Technologies for relevant precedent.

name: Examples should reflect correct application of criteria (illustrative precedent)
description: Examples (e.g., MPEP § 2247.01) show how to articulate an SNQ: identify claims, state which references raise or do not raise SNQ, explain why (e.g., a teaching not present in prosecution and likely important to a reasonable examiner), and state which claims will or will not be reexamined.
guidance: Use example language and structure when drafting decisions (grant or denial) to ensure required elements (claim identification, reference identification, teaching explanation, availability issues, and practical effect on which claims are reexamined) are present and clear.

name: Conclude declaration with value, breach, and damages
description: The declaration should conclude by averring the value of the patent right, the breach by the defendant, and the damages sustained by the plaintiff.
guidance: (§267) These allegations support claims for relief and damages.

name: Clear articulation of reasons for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
guidance: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness (KSR quoting In re Kahn). The analysis supporting a rejection should be made explicit. See MPEP § 2143 for further discussion.

name: Applicant’s reply must distinctly and specifically point out errors (37 CFR 1.111(b))
description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A blanket assertion is insufficient; address each ground with specific distinctions.

name: Applicant rebuttal: inability to combine elements by known methods
description: Applicant may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that one of ordinary skill in the art could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., due to technological difficulties).
guidance: Provide specific factual evidence (experiments, declarations) showing technological barriers or incompatibilities that would have prevented combination by known methods.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden to establish common ownership or joint research
description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants the benefits of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) must establish that the subject matter used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, or that joint research conditions are met.
guidance: To establish joint research provisions, applicant must show: (A) the invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the invention was made; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. See MPEP §§ 2146.01–.02 and Ex parte Yoshino.

name: Reference must be analogous art to be relied upon under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: In order for a reference to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art.
guidance: A reference is analogous art if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). To support a determination of reasonable pertinence, the examiner may include a statement of understanding of the problem and factual reasons why the prior art would have commended itself to an inventor. Consider the specification's reflection of the problem when assessing applicant arguments about nonanalogous art (Bigio, ICON Health, Klein).

name: Claimed invention must be considered as a whole in difference analysis
description: In determining differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: Do not focus solely on isolated differences; analyze the invention as a whole, including how disparate elements interact to produce an overall effect. Case examples (Stratoflex, Hirao) illustrate that admitted unobvious components can render the whole nonobvious.

name: Do not distill invention to a ‘gist’ or ‘thrust’ in place of whole analysis
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Avoid narrowing the claim focus to a single advantage or feature that ignores express claim limitations; ensure the full claim scope and limitations are considered (W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy).

name: Contributory infringement
description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for contributory infringement of a claim if [patent holder] proves by a preponderance of the evidence:
guidance: Elements (must prove each by a preponderance): (1) [alleged infringer] sells, offers to sell, or imports within the United States a component of a product, or apparatus for use in a process, during the time the [ ] patent is in force; (2) the component or apparatus has no substantial, noninfringing use; (3) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) [alleged infringer] is aware of the [ ] patent and knows that the [products or processes] for which the [component or apparatus] has no other substantial use may be covered by a claim of the [ ] patent or may satisfy a claim of the [ ] patent under the doctrine of equivalents; and (5) that use directly infringes the claim. Proof standard: preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(c); Aro Mfg. Co. v. Convertible Top Replacement Co., Ricoh v. Quanta, Alloc, Mentor H/S, Hewlett-Packard v. Bausch & Lomb, Preemption Devices v. Minn. Mining & Mfg., etc.

name: §271(f)(1) — infringement by supplying components from the U.S. for combination abroad (active inducement)
description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for §271(f)(1) infringement if patentee proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) [alleged infringer] supplies [or causes to be supplied] components from the United States to a place outside the United States, which make up all or a substantial portion of the invention of any one of the claims; (2) [alleged infringer] takes action intentionally to cause another to assemble the components outside the United States; (3) [alleged infringer] knows of the [ ] patent, and knows that the encouraged acts constitute infringement of that patent; and (4) the encouraged acts would constitute direct infringement if carried out in the United States.
guidance: If the defendant believed the acts encouraged would not constitute infringement if carried out in the United States, the defendant cannot be liable for inducement. Mere awareness that the alleged direct infringer itself infringes or awareness of the acts is insufficient — must find that defendant specifically intended for the other to infringe. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(1); cases include Cardiac Pacemakers, Microsoft v. AT&T, Liquid Dynamics, Pellegrini, NTP v. RIM, Union Carbide, Waymark. Committee comment: instruction omits 'willful blindness' standard (Global-Tech) for simplicity; include when patentee proceeds on that theory.

name: §271(f)(2) — contributory foreign infringement
description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for §271(f)(2) infringement if [patent holder] proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) [alleged infringer] supplies, or causes a component to be supplied, from the United States to a place outside the United States; (2) the only substantial use for the component is in a product that would infringe if the combination had occurred in the United States; (3) [alleged infringer] is aware of the [ ] patent and knows that the [component or apparatus] has no other substantial use and may be covered by a claim [literally or under the doctrine of equivalents]; and (4) intends for the component to be used in a product that would directly infringe the claim if used in the United States.
guidance: Elements must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f); relevant Federal Circuit decisions cited in the instruction.

name: §271(g) — infringement by import/sale/use of product made abroad by patented process
description: [Alleged infringer] is liable for direct infringement if [patent holder] proves by a preponderance that [alleged infringer], without authorization, imports, offers to sell, sells, or uses within the United States a product which was made outside of the United States by a process that, if performed in the United States, would infringe the claim literally or under the doctrine of equivalents.
guidance: Exception: if the product has been materially changed by an additional process or has become a trivial and nonessential component of another product, there is no infringement. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(g); Bayer AG v. Housey, Ajinomoto v. Archer-Daniels-Midland.

name: Direct infringement when one or more system components are located outside the United States
description: When some (but not all) elements of a claimed system are located outside the United States, [patent holder] must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the control of the system was exercised and the benefit of the system was enjoyed in the United States for infringement to occur within the United States.
guidance: Direct infringement requires that the accused system include every element recited in the claim; to find infringement in the U.S. the place where the system is put into service must be where control is exercised and beneficial use obtained. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(a); NTP, Inc. v. Research in Motion, Ltd.

name: Direct infringement by combined acts of multiple parties (joint enterprise or direction/control)
description: Direct infringement occurs where all steps of a claimed method are performed by or attributable to a single party. If more than one party is involved, infringement may exist only if the acts of one are attributable to the other because they formed a joint enterprise or one party directed or controlled the other's performance.
guidance: To establish infringement by multiple parties, patentee must prove by a preponderance: (1) all steps were performed in the United States; and (2) acts of party B are attributable to party A either because (a) A and B formed a joint enterprise, or (b) A directed or controlled B's acts. Elements to prove a joint enterprise (patentee must prove all four): (1) agreement (express or implied) between parties; (2) shared common purpose; (3) each had a financial interest in that purpose; and (4) each had an equal right of control. To prove direction/control: show B performed claim steps to receive a benefit from A and that A established how or when the steps were performed. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 271(a); Limelight Networks v. Akamai.

name: Invalidity—burden of proof
description: To prove that any claim of a patent is invalid, [alleged infringer] must persuade you by clear and convincing evidence, i.e., you must be left with a clear conviction that the claim is invalid.
guidance: Patents are presumed valid under 35 U.S.C. § 282; invalidity may be asserted under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112, or 251. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 282; Microsoft Corp. v. i4i; Schumer v. Lab. Computer Sys.; Buildex; Hybritech.

name: Prior art (effective filing date before March 16, 2013) and anticipation definition
description: Prior art may include items publicly known, used, on sale, or printed publications or patents that disclose the claimed invention or elements. To be prior art, the item must have been made, known, used, published, or patented either before the invention was made or [insert date if undisputed] or more than one year before the filing date. For anticipation, [alleged infringer] must show by clear and convincing evidence that all the requirements of the claim were present in a single previous device or method known, used, or described in a single printed publication or patent.
guidance: Prior art exclusions: a publication that describes the inventor’s own work is not prior art if published less than one year before the date of invention. For anticipation, the prior reference need not use the same words, but must disclose all claim limitations expressly or inherently such that a person skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 102 (pre-AIA); relevant Federal Circuit authorities cited in the instruction.

name: Invention date / conception and reduction to practice (when in dispute)
description: If invention date is disputed, the jury must determine the date of invention (conception and/or reduction to practice) for the claimed invention or alleged prior art. Conception is the formation in the mind of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention; reduction to practice occurs when constructed/used/tested sufficiently to show it will work or when a patent application is filed.
guidance: Diligence: conception is effective only if followed by diligence in reducing to practice; diligence means working continuously though not necessarily every day. Conception may be evidenced by drawings, disclosure to another, or other evidence beyond the inventor's testimony. Reduction to practice may be shown by prototype or by a filed patent application. Authorities and examples provided in instruction.

name: Anticipation and loss of right to patent — specific non-novelty grounds
description: Ways a patentee can lose rights or a claim can be not new (patentee must be convinced by clear and convincing evidence):
guidance: Enumerated items (choose applicable ones): (1) invention known to or used by others in the U.S. before the date of invention; (2) already patented or described in a printed publication anywhere before the date of invention; (3) patentee lost rights if claim was patented or described in a printed publication more than a year before effective filing date; (4) publicly used, sold, or offered for sale in the U.S. more than one year before the effective filing date; (5) abandonment; (6) foreign patenting or earlier foreign filing more than one year before U.S. filing; (7) described in a published patent application by another in the U.S. before date of invention; (8) described in a patent granted on an application filed by another before the relevant date; (9) patentee did not himself invent the invention; (10) another made the invention in the U.S. before patentee and did not abandon, suppress, or conceal it. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)-(g) and multiple Federal Circuit decisions cited.

name: Prior art (effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013 — AIA rules)
description: For patents with effective filing dates on or after March 16, 2013, prior art may include: (1) items publicly known or used, on sale, or otherwise made available to the public before the filing date; (2) publications made available to the public before the filing date; and (3) patents and published patent applications naming another inventor filed before the filing date.
guidance: Excluded from prior art: an item/publication that is the inventor’s own work or obtained from the inventor unless made public more than one year before filing; a patent or application that discloses the inventor's own work or was obtained from/owned by the same person. Anticipation standard (single reference must disclose all claim limitations expressly or inherently so that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention) still applies. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1)-(2); 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)-(2).

name: Infirmity of proof defense (scope and limits)
description: To invoke infirmity of proof, the respondent must show such an infirmity of proof establishing the charges that accepting the state's conclusion would be inconsistent with the USPTO's duty.
guidance: Deference is given to trier-of-fact credibility determinations; mere disagreement about credibility, factual findings, or legal conclusions does not establish infirmity. Documentary or evidentiary challenges must be developed; failing to appeal state findings in the state system undercuts later infirmity claims.

name: Improver three-question framework (UK)
description: The English Patents Court framed equivalency analysis as a three-question inquiry; the first two are factual background and the third is an exception that can limit claim interpretation to the literal meaning of the claim's words.
guidance: Justice Hoffmann viewed the third question as 'a question to be asked in all cases of infringement by equivalence' and emphasized that the first two questions merely provide background against which the third should be asked. The third question can, in certain circumstances, force the court to limit the scope of the claim to the strict literal meaning of the claim's words (and thus defeat a claim of equivalence). In Epilady, the third question led to a literalist result despite factual answers to the first two favoring equivalence.

name: German two-question test (Epilady)
description: The German court asked (1) whether the accused device has the identical effect of the claimed means (i.e., is it an equivalent), and (2) whether that equivalent would have been an obvious equivalent to a person skilled in the art when the patent was issued.
guidance: The court used the patent claim to determine the patent's 'teaching' and required that each essential feature in the claim be embodied by the accused device either literally or by equivalence. The second question requires assessing, prospectively at the time of grant, whether a skilled person, using professional knowledge and orienting to the meaning of the claims, would be able to detect the modified means as an identical-in-effect solution to the underlying problem. The German approach was described as aligning with Article 69(1) EPC and the Protocol.

name: Seven-feature claim-teaching analysis (Epilady claim 1)
description: When determining the patent's 'teaching' the court identified seven essential features from claim 1 that must be embodied (literally or by equivalence): (1) hand-held portable housing; (2) motor means in housing; (3) helical spring comprising plurality of adjacent windings; (4) windings arranged to be driven in rotational sliding motion relative to skin; (5) spring includes an arcuate hair-engaging portion (a. arcuate, b. convex side where windings are spread apart, c. concave side where windings are pressed together); (6) rotational motion produces continuous motion of windings from spread apart to pressed together for engagement and plucking of hair; (7) surface velocity of windings relative to skin greatly exceeds surface velocity of housing.
guidance: To establish infringement the accused product must embody each of these features exactly or in equivalent form. The German court found features 1 and 2 literal and 3–7 satisfied by equivalents (rubber rod considered a replacement means equivalent to coil spring). This shows a feature-by-feature assessment requirement.

name: Every claim limitation must be present or a substantial equivalent
description: To establish infringement, every limitation set forth in a claim must be found in the accused product or process exactly or by a substantial equivalent.
guidance: Cited authority (e.g., Johnston v. IVAC) and applied in both German and U.S. contexts; reinforces element-by-element analysis rather than holistic comparison of the invention as a whole.

name: U.S. function-way-result (three-prong) test
description: Under U.S. law, the doctrine of equivalents permits finding infringement if the accused device performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain substantially the same result.
guidance: All three prongs (function, way, result) must be met for equivalence of a claim element. The doctrine focuses on each claim element individually; therefore the patentee must show the presence of every essential element or its substantial equivalent. Example analysis: helical spring vs. rubber rod — function and result met clearly; 'way' requires mechanistic comparison (arcuate deformation causing openings, rotation producing gripping and plucking). A federal court would likely find the 'way' substantially the same in that example.

name: Doctrine focuses on claim elements, not invention as a whole
description: Equivalency analysis is performed element-by-element; the doctrine does not focus on the invention as a whole.
guidance: A finding of infringement requires the patentee to show the presence of every essential element or its substantial equivalent in the accused device; thus courts analyze each limitation separately under equivalents tests.

name: Identical-in-effect requirement (German formulation)
description: The German court required that the accused means be 'identical in effect' to the claimed means to be considered an equivalent.
guidance: The court stated it 'had no doubt the rubber rod was an equivalent based on the fact that the rubber rod "is identical in effect to a device making use of the wording of claim 1 of the patent in suit."' This places emphasis on functional/operational identity as a threshold for equivalence under German approach.

name: Prosecution history estoppel (file-wrapper estoppel)
description: Coverage surrendered during prosecution with the patent office cannot be recaptured through equivalence.
guidance: Prosecution history estoppel prevents a patentee from broadening claim scope via equivalents to reclaim subject matter given up during examination. Determining what was given up may require reviewing the prosecution history (not undertaken in the article for Improver).

name: Specification and equivalents-clause can limit claim construction
description: A patent's specification and any 'equivalents' clause may nonetheless constrain claim scope if a skilled reader would interpret the patentee as confining the claim to the literal meaning of a term.
guidance: Example: Dr. Laming's testimony that the Improver specification referred only to 'helical spring' and lacked language suggesting alternatives; Justice Hoffmann accepted that a skilled reader would interpret 'helical spring' literally despite an equivalents clause referencing 'other specific forms' and asking readers to look to appended claims. Thus specification detail and how alternatives are (not) signaled can defeat a broad generic construction.

name: Mechanistic 'way' analysis — use of examples to determine 'way' prong
description: Determining the 'way' prong involves detailed mechanistic description of how the claimed element operates (e.g., how arcuate form and rotational motion produce gaps, grip hairs, and pluck them).
guidance: The article models this analysis by describing how both the helical spring and the rubber rod deform when held arcuately, how gaps open/close on convex/concave sides, and how rotation causes hairs to enter gaps and be plucked; this type of technical comparison supports a finding that the 'way' is substantially the same.

name: EPC/Protocol alignment as interpretive constraint
description: Courts may frame equivalence analyses to align with Article 69(1) of the EPC and the Protocol on interpretation, influencing national approaches to claim scope and equivalents.
guidance: The German court explicitly stated its inquiry was intended to align German patent law with Article 69(1) EPC and the Protocol. Different understandings of the Protocol by national courts (UK vs Germany) produce divergent scopes of protection and pose harmonization challenges; WIPO's draft Patent Harmonization Treaty (Article 21) seeks to define equivalence consistent with EPC Protocol concepts.

name: Anticipation by specific example within a claimed range
description: Anticipation is considered when prior art teaches a specific example within a claimed range.
guidance: If a prior art disclosure expressly teaches a specific embodiment whose values fall within the claimed numerical range (and meets other claim limitations), that embodiment anticipates the claim (see MPEP §2131.03).

name: Anticipation by overlapping ranges with sufficient specificity
description: Prior art that teaches a range overlapping the claimed range anticipates if it is determined that claimed range is disclosed with sufficient specificity.
guidance: MPEP §2131.03: overlapping or touching ranges anticipate only if the prior art discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity.' Examiner must perform a fact-dependent analysis of specificity rather than mechanically equating overlap with anticipation.

name: Genus-species rule: species may anticipate a genus
description: Disclosure of a Species Anticipates a Claim to a Genus.
guidance: Case law (In re Slayter; In re Gosteli; Ex parte A) supports that a species disclosed in the prior art can anticipate a generic claim; the number of species disclosed and whether a species is preferred are immaterial.

name: Genus-species specifics — 'clearly envisaged' standard
description: A genus claim may be anticipated by a prior species-reference if the species would be 'at once envisage[d]' by one skilled in the art given the total circumstances.
guidance: In re Petering: courts consider overall circumstances (limited number of variations, substituent preferences, unchanging parent nucleus, etc.) and may treat a prior disclosure as describing each permutation 'as fully as if' each were specifically drawn or named.

name: Factors for sufficient specificity analysis (size, overlap, variable nature, criticality)
description: Factors to consider in a sufficient specificity analysis: size of the ranges; extent of overlap; nature of the variables (e.g., predictable or unpredictable); criticality of claimed range relative to prior art range.
guidance: Use these factors to determine whether an overlapping/broad prior-art range discloses the claimed range with sufficient specificity to anticipate.

name: Factors regarding criticality of the claimed range
description: Consider whether the reference establishes the same or different functions/properties within the prior art range relative to the claimed range; whether data points are equivalent; whether different criteria apply at different points; and whether the prior art range is so limited the claimed species can be readily envisaged.
guidance: These questions probe whether the claimed (often narrower) range is 'critical' and thus not simply anticipated by a broader prior-art range (see MPEP §2131.03 II).

name: Sufficient specificity is fact-dependent; narrow claims within broad references need other facts considered
description: "What constitutes a 'sufficient specificity' is fact dependent. If the claims are directed to a narrow range, and the reference teaches a broader range, other facts of the case, must be considered."
guidance: Do not automatically treat a broad prior-art range as anticipating a narrow claimed range; evaluate the totality of evidence (examples, enablement, criticality, predictability). (MPEP §2131.03 II)

name: Unexpected results may defeat anticipation/obviousness for narrow ranges
description: If the prior art disclosure does not disclose a claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' to anticipate a claimed invention, any evidence of unexpected results within the narrow range may render the claims unobvious.
guidance: Unexpected results shown for the narrower range can rebut a prima facie case and support patentability even when a broader range exists in the prior art.

name: Anticipation requires more than disclosure of a range when endpoints or specific embodiments are not disclosed
description: Disclosure of a broad range in a reference is not the same as disclosure of each specific point or endpoint in that range; mere overlap is not always sufficient for anticipation.
guidance: Atofina v. Great Lakes: a slight overlap did not disclose the claimed temperature range with sufficient specificity because the prior art disclosed only a range (not the endpoints or specific embodiment) and evidence showed the claimed range was critical.

name: Encompassed prior-art ranges can support anticipation or obviousness depending on deviation and criticality
description: If a prior art range entirely encompasses a claimed narrower range, courts may find anticipation/obviousness when the encompassed range 'entirely encompasses, AND does not significantly deviate from, [the] claimed ranges.'
guidance: Perricone/Pereira example: when the prior-art range entirely encompassed the claimed ranges and did not significantly deviate, anticipation was found; but criticality or differences can change the outcome.

name: Obviousness: overlapping or encompassing prior-art ranges create prima facie case
description: Obviousness is considered when prior art teaches ranges that overlap or encompass a claimed range, or touch a claimed range at one end point.
guidance: MPEP §2144.05 and cases (In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff) establish that overlap/encompassment supports a prima facie obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. §103.

name: Non-overlapping but close ranges can support prima facie obviousness
description: A prima facie case of obviousness exists where the claimed ranges and prior-art ranges do not overlap but are close enough that one skilled in the art would have expected them to have the same properties.
guidance: Evaluate whether the proximity of ranges would have led a person of ordinary skill to expect similar behavior across the ranges (citing In re Geisler, In re Woodruff, Titanium Metals, In re Malagari).

name: When prior art's generic range is overly broad, selecting a narrow species may be nonobvious
description: If the reference’s disclosed generic range is so broad as to encompass a very large number of possible distinct compositions, this might present a situation analogous to the nonobviousness of a claimed species.
guidance: A very broad genus in the prior art may not render every narrow species obvious — consider the number of distinct compositions and whether the species would have been 'clearly envisaged.' (See In re Peterson discussion and related cases.)

name: Written description/new matter standard for ranges (35 U.S.C. §112(a))
description: The test for written description compliance is whether the disclosure of the application as originally filed reasonably conveys to the artisan that the inventor had possession at that time of the later claimed subject matter.
guidance: Compliance is a question of fact determined case-by-case; the required level of detail varies with the nature/scope of the claims and the complexity/predictability of the technology (Vas-Cath; Ariad).

name: Factors for determining whether original disclosure conveys a later-claimed range
description: Consider (1) explicit/implicit disclosure of a generic range encompassing the new range; (2) specific/preferred/exemplified embodiments relating to the new range; (3) explicit/implicit disclosure that particular ranges are part of the inventor's invention; (4) disclosure of direction/guidance for obtaining ranges; (5) complexity/unpredictability of the invention; (6) evidence that the new range is a different invention.
guidance: Use these factors to assess whether an amendment to add or narrow a range adds new matter under §112(a). Presence of examples, preferred embodiments, or explicit guidance supports written-description sufficiency.

name: Literal endpoint support not always required for new endpoints
description: Literal support for a newly claimed endpoint is not required; the original disclosure may still reasonably convey possession of the later-claimed endpoint.
guidance: Example: Ex parte Jackson and In re Wertheim — specific examples at certain values may support a broader (or shifted) claimed range if persons skilled in the art would regard the claimed range as part of the invention; do not let form triumph over substance.

name: Examiner approach to §112(a) rejections with amended ranges (practical examples)
description: If an applicant narrows a claim to a sub-range and presents evidence of unexpected results unique to that sub-range, do not necessarily maintain a §103 rejection; instead, consider making a §112(a) new matter rejection if the narrower range lacks written-description support.
guidance: Slides' examples: (1) amendment without literal support to 62.5-100 ppm — likely no §112(a) rejection absent reason to doubt that the broader disclosure describes the narrower range; (2) amendment to 40-50 ppm with a declaration of unexpected results — drop the §103 rejection (prima facie case overcome) and make a §112(a) rejection because applicant is asserting the narrower range is a different invention.

name: Range limitation is a genus limitation; prior-art embodiments within claimed range will anticipate
description: A range limitation is a genus limitation. Embodiments disclosed in the prior art that fall within the claimed range (and meet all other claim limitations) will anticipate the claim.
guidance: When only ranges are disclosed in the prior art, the disclosed ranges must be considered to determine whether they anticipate the claimed range; overlapping ranges also raise obviousness issues; evidence of criticality impacts both anticipation and obviousness.

name: Enable the full scope of the claims
description: If a patent "claims an entire class of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the patent's specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class."
guidance: Claims 'measure the invention.' The specification must enable the full scope of what the claims define — the broader the claim (e.g., an entire genus defined by function), the more that must be enabled. Illustrative precedents: Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture. If the claimed class includes embodiments the specification does not teach, the claim may be invalid.

name: Examples may suffice only if a general quality running through the class is disclosed
description: A specification may give one or a few examples and still enable a claimed class if it also discloses "some general quality ... running through" the class that gives it "a peculiar fitness for the particular purpose."
guidance: Incandescent Lamp shows that a few working examples can enable a broader genus when the inventor identifies a common characteristic that reliably guides others to make other embodiments. Absent such a disclosed common quality, examples alone are often insufficient.

name: Reasonable experimentation tolerated; undue experimentation is not
description: A specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation to make and use a claimed invention; what is reasonable depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.
guidance: Cases like Wood and Minerals Separation recognize that some adaptation/testing by a skilled artisan is acceptable. The key is whether the required experimentation is reasonable in light of the field, or instead amounts to undue experimentation that fails to constitute enablement.

name: Functional-descriptive claiming (describing inputs by function) can defeat enablement
description: Describing key inputs or class members only by their 'use or function' rather than their physical or chemical characteristics can leave artisans unable to make or use the invention without 'elaborate experimentation.'
guidance: Holland Furniture / Perkins Glue: where the specification described a 'starch ingredient' by function, claim was invalid for lack of enablement because practitioners would have to experiment extensively to find suitable materials. Guidance: when functionally defined elements are central, disclose structural/chemical/physical characteristics or other enabling criteria.

name: Trial-and-error research assignments are not enablement
description: Methods that merely instruct practitioners to 'try a large set' of candidates or to perform general trial-and-error screening (the opinion calls Amgen's "roadmap" and "conservative substitution" examples) do not enable a claimed genus.
guidance: The Court rejects 'roadmap' approaches that amount to telling skilled artisans to engage in random or extensive trial-and-error (likened to a 'hunting license' or a combination-lock analogy). If the only disclosed way to reach claimed embodiments is open-ended trial-and-error, the specification fails enablement. Anti-pattern: instructions that amount to 'make lots of candidates and test them' without principled selection criteria.

name: The more one claims, the more one must enable
description: "The more one claims, the more one must enable." Broad claims demanding monopoly over wide classes require correspondingly comprehensive enabling disclosure.
guidance: This principle flows from matching claim scope to disclosure. Claim-drafting and specification drafting should anticipate that expanding claim breadth increases the disclosure burden. Practical rule: when seeking genus/functionally-defined claims, provide either many representative embodiments plus a disclosed unifying trait or sufficiently detailed methods to reliably make and use the genus.

name: Enablement assessment focuses on quality of disclosure, not merely cumulative time/effort
description: Enablement is not measured only by the cumulative time and effort it would take to make every embodiment within a claim; courts ask whether the disclosure gives adequate guidance beyond trial-and-error.
guidance: The Federal Circuit's consideration of how much effort is required is not dispositive; what matters is whether the specification provides adequate guidance to avoid undue experimentation. Even if making every embodiment would take long cumulative time, a specification can still be enabling if it provides reliable, instructive guidance.

name: Predictability of the art affects what disclosure suffices
description: The state of the underlying science (predictable vs unpredictable technology) matters: in unpredictable fields (e.g., antibody sequence→structure/function mappings), broader claims require more detailed disclosure because substitutions can produce unpredictable results.
guidance: In antibody/biotech contexts where a single amino-acid change can unpredictably alter function and where sequence-to-structure translation remains imperfectly understood, enabling a broad genus by generic methods (conservative substitution, roadmap) is less likely to succeed. Drafters should tailor disclosure to the predictability of the technology and provide structural detail, robust representative examples, or mechanistic principles where possible.

name: Claims must be matched by particularity when necessary to avoid overbroad monopoly
description: A patent cannot claim more than it enables; claiming broadly without particularized disclosure 'would extend the monopoly beyond the invention.'
guidance: Precedents warn against claiming entire 'kingdoms' of subject matter (telegraphic means, all fibrous materials, all starch glues that work) when the specification does not teach how to make and use them. Practical implication: limit claim scope or expand disclosure (characteristics, representative embodiments, enabling methods) to justify genus claims.

name: Specifying Claimed Invention
description: Rules and guidance on how the claimed invention should be specified for examination purposes (Section 1).
guidance: See PDF for criteria used to determine what the claims encompass and how to interpret them.

name: Handling Procedures for Examinations involving Product-by-process Claims
description: Specific handling and examination procedures for product-by-process claims.
guidance: Separate linked page provides detailed treatment for product-by-process claim examination.

name: 28 U.S.C. §1498(c) and foreign-activity jurisdictional boundary
description: Section 1498(c) provides that patent claims against the United States do not extend to 'any claim arising in a foreign country.'
guidance: § 1498(c) does not apply where the alleged infringing activities took place within the United States. Allegations that accused products were manufactured in the United States (even if later used abroad) can be sufficient to establish the court's jurisdiction (Zoltek). The court draws reasonable inferences in plaintiff's favor if jurisdictional facts are not challenged.

name: Preclusion from prior litigation as a jurisdictional/merits issue
description: Claims may be precluded if previously litigated and dismissed with prejudice against the same accused products or actors.
guidance: Whether preclusion applies depends on factual allegations showing the accused products were manufactured/sold by the same entity previously sued. Bare assertions by a defendant are insufficient on a motion to dismiss; the court presumes undisputed facts in plaintiff’s favor and requires more specific evidence or allegations to find preclusion.

name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework for patent-eligible subject matter
description: First, determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas). If so, second, determine whether the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, supply an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: The inquiry looks to the 'focus' or character of the claim as a whole (Elec. Power Grp.; Enfish). If directed to an ineligible concept, the court asks whether additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (Alice; Mayo).

name: 'Directed to' / focus-of-the-claim inquiry
description: The court must consider the asserted patent claims 'in their entirety to ascertain whether their character as a whole is directed to excluded subject matter.'
guidance: The court asks what the patent asserts to be the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art to determine whether the claim’s character as a whole is directed to an ineligible concept (ChargePoint; Simio). Look to claim language, specification disclosures, and what the patent describes as its advance.

name: Inventive concept standard (step two of Alice)
description: An 'inventive concept' is an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a claim on the ineligible concept itself.
guidance: The inventive concept must be more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously known to the industry (Affinity Labs; Mayo). Implementation of a known technique with particular devices in a specific combination can be inventive if plausibly alleged (Cellspin). If the only inventive concept is the application of an abstract idea using conventional techniques, the claim remains ineligible (BSG Tech).

name: When §101 can be decided on a motion to dismiss
description: Patent eligibility under §101 is a question of law that may involve underlying questions of fact; the court may determine eligibility on a motion to dismiss only when there are no factual allegations that, taken as true, prevent resolving the eligibility question as a matter of law.
guidance: If factual issues material to §101 exist, the court cannot resolve eligibility at the 12(b)(6) stage (Berkheimer; Aatrix; Simio). Conversely, where the 'character as a whole' of the claims is clear from the pleadings and patent documents, the court may rule as a matter of law (e.g., CardioNet, Univ. of Fla. examples).

name: Pleading requirement for alleging an inventive concept
description: To survive a motion to dismiss, a plaintiff must plead plausible and specific factual allegations that aspects of the claim are inventive rather than merely label techniques as inventive.
guidance: Boilerplate conclusory assertions or labels are insufficient. Plaintiff should identify specific technical improvements or non-conventional combinations and allege facts suggesting these techniques had not been implemented in a similar way (Cellspin). Specificity about how claimed elements improve technological functioning supports survival of a motion to dismiss.

name: Requirement for common ownership at time invention was made
description: The requirement for common ownership at the time the claimed invention was made is intended to preclude obtaining ownership of subject matter after the claimed invention was made in order to disqualify that subject matter as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
guidance: Common ownership must exist at the time the claimed invention was made; ownership obtained after that time does not disqualify the subject matter as prior art. Determine common ownership based on the facts of the particular case.

name: Pre-Appeal Review panel composition and possible outcomes
description: A designated panel (including at least a supervisor and the examiner of record) will review the request and may (A) determine the application remains under appeal, (B) reopen prosecution, (C) allow the application on existing claims, or (D) dismiss the request for noncompliance.
guidance: Panel has authority to reopen prosecution and may propose a corrective amendment. Applicant is not allowed to attend the review and no interviews are granted prior to issuance of the pre-appeal decision. Filing certain subsequent papers (appeal brief, RCE, after-final amendment, affidavit/evidence, or express abandonment) prior to panel decision terminates the panel review.

name: Interviews after notice of appeal — permitted and restricted situations
