description: One interview after final rejection is normally permitted (time from mailing of final rejection through filing of appeal brief). No interviews are allowed from filing of a pre-appeal request through issuance of that decision; generally no interviews after an appeal brief is filed; interviews after Examiner’s Answer but prior to forwarding fee are usually not permitted except in unusual circumstances.
guidance: Requests for interviews after Board jurisdiction should be granted only with specific approval of the Technology Center Director upon a showing in writing of extraordinary circumstances justifying a remand. Unusual circumstances may include wanting to cancel all appealed claims to proceed to allowance or where the examiner is convinced some previously rejected claims are in condition for allowance.

name: Office procedure following Federal Circuit decision (mandate effects)
description: When the Federal Circuit issues its mandate, the certified decision is entered in the file and marks termination of the appeal; Office action depends on whether all claims remain rejected, some claims allowed, remand required, or reopening of prosecution is necessary.
guidance: If all claims remain rejected, proceedings terminate and application is ordinarily abandoned; if some claims allowed, examiner may convert dependent claims to independent form or set a two-month period for applicant to rewrite dependent claims in independent form. Any Office action proposing to reopen prosecution after a court decision must be forwarded for written approval.

name: Claim construction is a matter of law (Markman)
description: Claim construction is a question of law to be determined by the court rather than the jury; judges are particularly well-suited to interpret patent claims as legal documents.
guidance: Apply judicial interpretation principles (as with contracts or other legal instruments); Markman reaffirmed that judges, not juries, determine the meaning of claim terms. Consider historical precedent (Winans) and Markman II reasoning when framing the analysis.

name: Extrinsic evidence only when intrinsic ambiguous; cannot contradict intrinsic
description: Extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, treatises, expert testimony, etc.) may be consulted only if the meaning of a disputed claim term remains ambiguous after consultation of all intrinsic evidence, and extrinsic evidence must not be used to contradict intrinsic evidence.
guidance: Resort to extrinsic sources only after intrinsic sources fail to resolve ambiguity; never use extrinsic evidence to contradict a meaning established by the patent documents (claims, specification, prosecution history).

name: Hierarchy of claim construction sources (Phillips list)
description: Six articulated sources of evidence, in order of importance: (1) the claims themselves; (2) the written specification; (3) the file (prosecution) history; (4) technical dictionaries and learned treatises; (5) general dictionaries; and (6) expert testimony.
guidance: Treat the first three as intrinsic and the last three as extrinsic. Use technical dictionaries/treatises before general dictionaries. Expert testimony is lowest-ranked extrinsic evidence and should be treated skeptically, primarily for background rather than construing claim meaning.

name: Distinguish using dictionaries for background versus defining terms
description: It is permissible to use dictionaries or treatises to understand the underlying technology, but not to rely on them to construe claim term meaning if that meaning is established by the intrinsic record.
guidance: Use extrinsic sources to supply technological context or background; avoid substituting a dictionary definition for an intrinsic, document-based meaning.

name: Skeptical and limited use of expert testimony
description: Expert testimony may provide background information about a technology but should not be a major factor in claim construction because such testimony is generated for litigation and is less objective.
guidance: Limit experts to explaining technology/terminology to aid the court; do not allow expert testimony to override intrinsic evidence. Treat expert testimony as least reliable among extrinsic sources.

name: Don't import limitations from the specification into the claims
description: Courts must avoid reading limitations from specific or preferred embodiments in the specification into the ordinary claim scope (i.e., not every embodiment limitation should narrow the claims).
guidance: Recognize the tension between reading the specification as a guide and improperly restricting claims to preferred embodiments; the inquiry is whether the specification clearly limits the term or merely discloses an embodiment. Use claim language and claim differentiation to avoid inadvertent importation of limitations.

name: Claim differentiation canon
description: Differences between independent and dependent claims are indicative: when a dependent claim adds a limitation (e.g., 'disposed at angles for deflecting projectiles') the absence of that limitation in the independent claim suggests the independent claim is not so limited.
guidance: Use claim differentiation as a canon to infer that independent claims do not include limitations appearing only in dependent claims, unless intrinsic evidence shows otherwise.

name: Interpret claim terms in context and consistently across claims
description: A court must construe terms by considering the entire claim (and other claims in the patent), ensuring consistent use of the same terms in different claims.
guidance: Examine asserted and non-asserted claims because non-asserted claims can help establish the meaning of terms. Interpret terms in the context of claim as a whole and in light of the specification.

name: Prosecution history as evidentiary guide with limitations
description: Prosecution history may be consulted to show how the PTO and applicant understood the patent, but it often lacks the clarity of the final specification and thus is less valuable.
guidance: Use prosecution history to identify explicit disclaimers or arguments made to the PTO that affect claim scope, but treat it as an incomplete, negotiated record—less dispositive than the specification.

name: When phrase/combination lacks dictionary guidance, rely on intrinsic or indefiniteness
description: For combinations or phrases not found in dictionaries (e.g., 'lever for deforming a grommet'), intrinsic evidence (the specification/§112 support) is dispositive; absent sufficient intrinsic support the claim may be indefinite.
guidance: If the specification provides enough information to understand a phrase, use it; if not, consider §112 indefiniteness; do not rely on piecemeal dictionary parsing of component words when the phrase as a whole is what matters.

name: Use of canons of claim construction without clear prioritization
description: There are numerous canons (roughly ten) used in construing claims (e.g., claim differentiation, ejusdem generis, etc.), but Phillips did not clarify how these canons fit into the intrinsic/extrinsic hierarchy or how to prioritize them.
guidance: Apply canons cautiously and in conjunction with the intrinsic record; recognize the uncertainty and that failure to clarify canon application contributes to high reversal rates.

name: Public notice function should guide methodology
description: The ultimate objective of claim construction methodology is to serve the patent system's public notice function—ensuring competitors can ascertain claim scope from public, accessible records.
guidance: Favor intrinsic evidence and publicly accessible technical treatises/dictionaries contemporaneous with filing over litigation-generated or post-filing extrinsic materials to maximize notice and predictability.

name: Required contents of utility model application
description: The application file shall contain: (a) an application addressed to the Director-General; (b) proof of payment of requisite fees; (c) an unstamped private power of attorney if represented by an agent; (d) a sealed envelope containing: (i) a specification stating configuration/arrangement/mechanism set out clearly and completely so a person skilled in the art could carry out the model; (ii) necessary drawings/photographs; (iii) a descriptive abstract summarizing the specification; (iv) the claim(s) defining the scope of protection sought, not exceeding contents of the specification; (v) sufficient indications regarding best manner of carrying out the invention known to the inventor on the filing date (and priority date if claimed).
guidance: All listed parts are mandatory; claims must not exceed the specification; the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention.

name: Filing date requirements — documents needed at filing
description: The Organization shall grant as the filing date the date of receipt of the application drafted in one of its working languages, provided that at the time of filing the application contains: (a) an express or implicit indication that grant of a certificate is sought; (b) information to establish the identity of the applicant; (c) a part which, prima facie, purports to be the description of an invention and one or more claims; and (d) proof of payment of the prescribed fees.
guidance: These minimal elements must be present at filing to secure a filing date; language of filing must be one of the Organization's working languages.

name: Publication requirements and timeline for applications
description: For each application the Organization shall publish: application number, filing date, applicant name and address, inventor name/address (unless inventor requested omission), agent name/address, statement of any priority(ies), priority date/country/number, title, abstract, date and number of international application (if any), and international patent classification symbols; the Organization shall also publish the specification, any claims and drawings (if applicable). The application shall be published within 18 months of filing or priority date (save for international applications).
guidance: Publication is comprehensive and generally occurs at 18 months; certain items may be omitted for international applications as specified.

name: Opposition grounds and procedure
description: Any interested party may oppose issuance of a certificate by sending within three months of the publication a written statement setting out reasons based on infringement of Articles 1,2,3,4 and 8 of this Annex, or of a prior registered right of the opposing party. The Organization sends the opposition to the applicant who may reply within three months (renewable once). The Organization may hear parties; if opposition is well-founded it may re-examine certain claims or terminate examination for all claims (or continue if groundless).
guidance: Strict three-month window for filing opposition; reply windows and possible hearing; outcomes include re-examination or termination of examination depending on grounds.

name: Examination criteria and research report requirements
description: An examination shall be conducted for all applications to establish: (a) the invention is not excluded under Article 4; (b) any claims are consistent with Article 11(2)(d)(iv) (claims not exceeding specification); and (c) provisions of Article 12 (unity) are met. A research report shall ascertain: whether at filing an earlier application for the same invention with older priority was in process of being granted; and whether the invention is new and industrially applicable. For PCT international applications the Organization may rely on PCT search and preliminary examination reports.
guidance: Examination covers formal exclusions, claim consistency, unity, novelty and industrial applicability; international search/exam reports may be used for PCT cases.

name: Publication requirements for granted utility model certificates
description: The Organization shall publish for each granted utility model: certificate number; filing number of application; filing date; applicant name and address; creator name and address (unless omitted by request); agent name/address; indication of any priorities; priority date/country/earlier application number; grant date; title; abstract; and international classification symbols. Implementing regulations determine procedures for publishing the model, drawings, claims and abstract.
guidance: Publication of granted registrations is thorough and controlled by implementing regulations for format and procedure.

name: Waiver of Claim or Requirement in Brief
description: An applicant may waive a claim or requirement in a brief, thereby removing it from the issues on appeal.
guidance: TBMP §1203.02(g) addresses waiver in briefs — when applicant expressly abandons a claim or requirement in its brief, the Board will not consider it. Properly indicating waiver can affect scope of appeal and possible remand consequences.

name: Inventive step analysis (four-step test)
description: KIPO uses a test similar to other jurisdictions: 1) Determine the closest cited art; 2) Identify differences; 3) Examine whether differences could be easily made by combining cited prior art; 4) Consider effects achieved by the invention.
guidance: Apply these sequential steps to assess whether the claimed differences over the closest prior art would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art, taking into account the technical effects produced by the invention.

name: AI / Fourth Industrial Revolution technology guidance
description: KIPO announced Patent Examination Guidelines for key technology areas related to the Fourth Industrial Revolution, including machine learning based artificial intelligence, on January 18, 2021.
guidance: There are specialized examination guidelines and examples addressing AI/ML and related emerging technologies; examiners and applicants should consult these sector-specific provisions when evaluating AI-related claims.

name: International harmonization and use of IP5-derived standards/examples
description: KIPO established 39 examination standards based on a comparative study of the IP5 offices (Korea, US, Europe, Japan, China) and increased the number of application examples to 50 to help examiners better understand the standards.
guidance: Examiners are expected to apply harmonized standards informed by IP5 practice and use the expanded set of concrete application examples to promote consistent examination. Applicants can use those examples to understand claim drafting and prosecution expectations.

name: GDIPIM / MIPIM module mapping to QE papers
description: Specific GDIPIM/MIPIM modules correspond to QE papers and satisfy the module-based pre-requisite: IPM527 – Patent Claims and IPM529 – Patent Applications → Paper A; IPM525 – Patent Office Action → Paper B; IPM531 – Patent Infringement and Validity → Paper C; IPM523 – Patent Practice in Singapore → Paper D.
guidance: Overview table provided so candidates know which module(s) they must pass to enrol for each QE paper. The page also notes these modules may be taken as CET courses to prepare for QE.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — Undescribed broken lines (Form paragraph 29.21)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite where the reproductions include broken lines that are not described in the specification and the scope of the claimed design cannot be determined.
guidance: Applicant may overcome the rejection by inserting a statement immediately preceding the claim (provided it does not introduce new matter) such as: 'The broken line showing of [structure] is for the purpose of illustrating [portions of the article/environmental structure] and forms no part of the claimed design.' Examiner instructions provide bracketed insertion points for figure numbers, structure name, and whether 'portions of the article' or 'environmental structure.' Use this form paragraph in international design applications with undescribed broken lines.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — Undescribed broken lines as boundary (Form paragraph 29.23)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite where the reproductions include undescribed broken lines serving as a boundary and the scope of the claimed design cannot be determined.
guidance: Applicant may overcome the rejection by inserting a statement immediately preceding the claim (provided it does not introduce new matter) such as: 'The [type] broken line(s) define the bounds of the claimed design and form no part thereof.' Examiner Note indicates bracketed fields: figure numbers and type of broken line (e.g., dashed, dot-dash). Use when broken lines function as boundary lines.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — Unclear use of coloring (Form paragraph 29.25)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite where the reproductions include coloring that is not described in the specification and the scope of the claimed design cannot be determined.
guidance: If the coloring identifies matter for which protection is not sought, applicant may overcome the rejection by inserting a statement immediately preceding the claim (provided it does not introduce new matter) such as: 'The portion of the design shown in the color [color] is for the purpose of illustrating [portions of the article/environmental structure] and forms no part of the claimed design.' Examiner Note: insert figure numbers and identify the color indicating excluded matter.

name: Suggestion to overcome rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) by converting undescribed portions to broken lines or coloring (Form paragraph 29.27)
description: Applicant may indicate that protection is not sought for those portions of the reproductions considered indefinite and nonenabling by amending the reproductions to color those portions or convert them to broken lines, and amending the specification to include a statement that such portions form no part of the claimed design.
guidance: Amendments must not introduce new matter (see 35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121). Use this form paragraph only in an international design application. Insert the title of the article into the bracketed field.

name: Acceptance of delayed priority claim (petition) — required contents
description: A delayed priority claim not presented within the required time is considered waived unless accepted under the petition provisions; acceptance requires a petition with specific materials.
guidance: A petition to accept a delayed claim must be accompanied by: (1) the priority claim in an ADS identifying the foreign application; (2) a certified copy of the foreign application unless previously submitted or an exception applies; (3) the petition fee (§ 1.17(m)); and (4) a statement that the entire delay was unintentional. The Director may request additional information.

name: Benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 386(c) — entitlement to benefit of prior national or international design filing
description: An international design application designating the United States shall be entitled to the benefit of the filing date of a prior national application, prior international application as defined in section 351(c) designating the United States, or a prior international design application designating the United States; similarly, a national application shall be entitled to the benefit of a prior international design application designating the United States.
guidance: If any claim for the benefit of an earlier filing date is based on a prior international application which designated but did not originate in the United States, the Director may require filing of a certified copy of such application together with an English translation if it was filed in another language.

name: Practical two-step assessment procedure (recommended steps)
description: Determine whether an applicant may rely on PPE by: first identifying the technical teaching of the claimed invention in light of the application and common general knowledge; then considering whether the content of the PPE (the technical effect relied upon) is encompassed by that technical teaching and embodied by the same originally disclosed invention.
guidance: If the PPE effect is encompassed and embodied by the original technical teaching, it 'does not change the nature of the claimed invention' and may be used to support inventive step. If not, it should be excluded from the inventive-step assessment.

name: Common bases for filing reissue
description: The most common bases are: (A) the claims are too narrow or too broad; (B) the disclosure contains inaccuracies; (C) applicant failed to or incorrectly claimed foreign priority; and (D) applicant failed to make reference to or incorrectly referenced prior copending applications.
guidance: Each of these may support a reissue when they cause the patent to be partly or wholly inoperative/invalid under 35 U.S.C. 251.

name: No new matter in reissue
description: No new matter shall be introduced into the application for reissue; the reissue must be 'for the invention disclosed in the original patent.'
guidance: Reissue specification must contain the entire specification (including claims) and drawings of the patent as a copy of the printed patent; amendments are permitted only under the reissue amendment procedures and must preserve columnar format or be submitted as separate amendment papers with required markings (37 CFR 1.173).

name: Broadening reissue two‑year rule
description: No reissued patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent (35 U.S.C. 251(d)).
guidance: If filed within two years, diligence is presumed and examiners should not inquire why applicant failed to file earlier. Filing on the two‑year anniversary counts as within two years. See MPEP § 1412.03 for practice on broadening reissues.

name: Scope-of-claims error: omission of narrower claims allowed
description: Omission of a narrower claim from a patent can render a patent partly inoperative, permitting addition of narrower claims by reissue without narrowing preexisting patent claims.
guidance: A reissue applicant can retain broad independent claims while adding new dependent (narrower) claims. However, failure to timely file a divisional after a restriction requirement is not considered an error correctable by reissue (see MPEP § 1412.01).

name: Effect of reissue on patent term
description: Reissue is for the unexpired part of the term of the original patent; reissue cannot extend the patent term. Deleting an earlier-obtained benefit claim (35 U.S.C. 120) via reissue will not lengthen the patent term.
guidance: If a reissue declaration indicates the correction is to extend term, examiner should point out statutory limits. Specific examiner actions differ if the deletion of benefit claim is the only error identified versus one of multiple errors (detailed handling described in § 1405 subsections A and B).

name: Content and form of a reissue application (37 CFR 1.171, 1.173)
description: A reissue application must contain the same parts required for an original patent application and must furnish the entire specification, including the claims, and the drawings of the patent (copy of the printed patent in double column format), and comply with reissue rules; no new matter allowed.
guidance: A reissue oath/declaration complying with 37 CFR 1.63 and 1.175 is required. If the patent is assigned, a consent of assignee and evidence of ownership required; if unassigned, applicant should affirm patent is not assigned. Amendments at filing may be made by physically inserting changes into printed patent columns with markings or by separate amendment paper per 37 CFR 1.173(b). Retyped specifications allowed only with a grantable petition (37 CFR 1.183) when changes are extensive and reading is error-prone. Preliminary amendment cancelling all original claims without presenting new claims is inappropriate.

name: Filing date and missing parts in reissue application (37 CFR 1.53(f))
description: A reissue application can be accorded a filing date without an oath/declaration or without basic filing/search/examination fees being present; OPAP will accord a filing date and issue a missing parts notice providing time to supply missing parts and pay surcharges.
guidance: Applicants given period to provide missing documents; surcharge under 37 CFR 1.16(f) applies when filing incomplete. Note that 37 CFR 1.53(b) filing-without-claims provision does not apply to reissue applications because 37 CFR 1.173(a)(1) requires the entire specification including claims.

name: Prohibition on claim enlargement
description: No proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope of the claims of the patent shall be permitted in an inter partes reexamination proceeding (35 U.S.C. 314(a)).
guidance: A claim presented enlarges the scope where it is broader than each and every claim of the patent; a claim broadened in any one respect is considered broadening. Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 314(a) should use form paragraph 26.03.01 and identify the broadened limitations (see MPEP § 1412.03 for guidance).

name: Scope of reexamination (patents/printed publications and 35 U.S.C.112)
description: Claims in an inter partes reexamination proceeding will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted in the reexamination proceeding, on the basis of the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112. Issues other than these will not be resolved in an inter partes reexamination proceeding (37 CFR 1.906).
guidance: If parties raise issues outside these bounds, the examiner should note their existence in the next Office action and may suggest filing a reissue application to resolve them.

name: Reference copy requirements (37 CFR 1.98(a)(2))
description: 37 CFR 1.98(a)(2) requires a legible copy of: (1) each foreign patent; (2) each publication or the portion which caused it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and US patent application publications unless required); (3) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including the claims and any drawing or the portion causing it to be listed; (4) all other information or that portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: Failure to provide required copies can limit examiner consideration; for references not scanned into IFW, the patent record's commentary is the full extent of consideration unless parties supply copies.

name: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description/enablement)
description: Where new or amended claims are presented or any part of the disclosure is amended, the claims in the reexamination proceeding are to be examined for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: MPEP § 2258 discussion of 112 in ex parte reexamination applies analogously; the Office may perform a 35 U.S.C. 112 written description priority analysis during reexamination (see In re NTP, Inc.).

name: Specification amendments must not enlarge claim scope
description: When the specification is amended in a reexamination proceeding, examiners should ensure that the amendment does not enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent. An amendment can enlarge claim scope by redefining claim term scope even if the claims themselves are unchanged.
guidance: Carefully evaluate how specification changes affect claim term meanings and scope; treat such changes as potential broadening under 35 U.S.C. 314(a).

name: Procedure for rejecting broadened claims
description: Any claim which enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 314(a). Form paragraph 26.03.01 is to be employed in making the rejection and the claim limitations considered to broaden the scope should be identified and explained.
guidance: Include bracketed explanation identifying the limitations that broaden scope and reference MPEP § 2658 and § 1412.03 for guidance on what constitutes broadening.

name: Effect of prior adjudication (res judicata/collateral estoppel)
description: Claims finally held valid by a federal court after all appeals will be withdrawn from consideration and not reexamined during a reexamination proceeding. Res judicata based on a court holding in an infringement proceeding is not applicable in reexamination because the Office was not a party to the litigation.
guidance: If prior decisions involve grounds not based on patents or printed publications, the examiner's Office action should clearly state that the claims have not been examined as to those grounds.

name: Requester specificity requirement (37 CFR 1.915(b))
description: A requester must 'set forth the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested' as required by 37 CFR 1.915(b). If a request fails to do so, that claim will generally not be reexamined.
guidance: Requests lacking the required claim‑by‑claim articulation may result in claims being left unexamined; ensure the requester applies art to each claim requested for reexamination.

name: Restriction practice not applicable in reexamination
description: Restriction requirements cannot be made in a reexamination proceeding since no statutory basis exists for restriction in a reexamination.
guidance: Adding claims directed to a 'separate and distinct' invention would be considered an enlargement of scope and is prohibited in reexamination (see Ex parte Wikdahl and MPEP § 1412.03).

name: Ancillary amendments permitted
description: Amendments necessary and incident to patentability may be considered in reexamination. For example, amendments to correct an inadvertent failure to claim foreign priority or to reflect continuing status relative to a parent application if necessary to overcome a reference.
guidance: Permitted ancillary amendments should be narrowly tailored to correct factual/legal defects relevant to patentability and not to broaden claim scope.

name: Affidavit use and limitations
description: Affidavits under 37 CFR 1.131(a) and 1.132 may be utilized in a reexamination proceeding. However, an affidavit under 1.131(a) may not be used to 'swear behind' a reference patent if the reference patent is claiming the same invention as the patent undergoing reexamination.
guidance: If appropriate, use 1.131(c) affidavits or consider a reissue application for issues related to swearing behind references that are patents claiming the same invention (see MPEP § 718 and § 1449.02).

name: Reexamination requests on reissued patents
description: A request for reexamination filed on a patent after it has been reissued will be denied because the patent on which the request is based has been surrendered; to reexamine a reissued patent a new request must be filed based on the reissue patent's specification and claims.
guidance: Any amendment by the patent owner during reexamination should treat the changes made by the granted reissue patent as the text of the patent (including bracketing/underlining conventions). See MPEP § 2686.03 for timing issues.

name: Examiner duties and content of the first Office action
description: On taking up a patent in a reexamination proceeding, the examiner shall make a thorough study and investigation of the available prior art and make the examination complete as to applicable statutes/rules and patentability. The examiner must notify parties of the action and state reasons for any adverse action in an Office action, citing useful information or references.
guidance: When rejecting claims for lack of novelty or obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references available, designate the particular part relied on when complex, clearly explain pertinence, and specify each rejected claim. Examiner may rely on admissions by the patent owner or requester and on facts within knowledge as allowed.

name: Use of subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/(f)/(g) and 103(c) joint-research exception
description: Subject matter developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) may be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103 unless the entire rights to the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned or subject to an obligation of assignment at the relevant time. To overcome a 103 rejection under 103(c)(2), the applicant must provide a statement concerning a joint research agreement and that the claimed invention resulted from activities within its scope.
guidance: The 'joint research agreement' exception requires (A) agreement in effect on or before the date invention was made, (B) invention made as a result of activities within the agreement's scope, and (C) the application discloses/ is amended to disclose the parties' names.

name: Disclosure requirement in Rule 42 EPC (description must disclose technical problem and solution)
description: Rule 42(1)(c) EPC: the description shall disclose the invention, as claimed, in such terms that the technical problem, even if not expressly stated as such, and its solution can be understood, and state any advantageous effects of the invention with reference to the background art.
guidance: This is a disclosure/description requirement (ensuring the application explains the technical problem and solution) and not a definition of inventive step. Ensure applications disclose the problem and advantageous effects relative to the prior art, but remember this does not replace the Article 56 obviousness test.

name: Claims define the invention/scope
description: The claims define the invention that the patentee is entitled to exclude others from practicing; the written description does not itself delimit the right to exclude — that is the function and purpose of claims.
guidance: Start with the claims: "The claims define the invention that the patentee is entitled to exclude others from practicing." See Markman. Use claim language as the primary datum for scope determination.

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art provides context
description: The claim term is to be understood as a skilled artisan would understand it, which provides an objective baseline for interpretation.
guidance: The skilled artisan is deemed to read the claim term in the context of the particular claim, the entire patent (including specification), and the prosecution history. Use that composite perspective as the starting point.

name: Context: consider claim, entire patent, prosecution history
description: Read the disputed term in the context of the particular claim, the entire patent (including the specification), and the prosecution history.
guidance: Context sources include the claim's surrounding words, other claims (both asserted and unasserted), the specification, and the prosecution history. Differences among claims (claim differentiation) are a useful guide.

name: Specification governs special definitions and disclaimers
description: A special definition in the specification for a claim term (including implied definitions) will govern; an intentional disclaimer or disavowal in the specification is dispositive of claim scope.
guidance: Patentees acting as their own lexicographers can define terms; if the specification reveals clear disavowal, that limits claim scope. Look for explicit definitions or language of manifest exclusion or restriction.

name: Sequence of evidence consultation is flexible
description: There is no required sequence for consulting sources (claims, specification, prosecution history, dictionaries, experts); courts are not barred from consulting any particular source or required to analyze sources in a specific order.
guidance: A judge might start with a dictionary or technical treatise to get background, then read the patent to determine how the patentee used the term. More important is the weight attached to sources, not order.

name: Means-plus-function (§112, para. 6) rule application
description: Means-plus-function rules apply only to purely functional claim limitations that do not recite the structure performing the recited function; if the claim recites structure, the means-plus-function rule does not apply.
guidance: If a claim recites physical structure (e.g., "baffles") rather than a bare functional recital, treat it as structural and construe its proper meaning rather than invoking §112(6).

name: Claim differentiation as a guide
description: Differences among claims (particularly dependent claims that add limitations) can be valuable in understanding whether a limitation is inherent in an independent claim; the presence of a dependent claim adding a limitation raises a presumption that the independent claim lacks that limitation.
guidance: Examine dependent claims: if a dependent claim explicitly adds a feature, it is evidence that the independent claim did not already contain that feature.

name: Specification must enable all claims but embodiments do not necessarily limit every claim
description: The specification must teach and enable all the claims, but descriptions of particular embodiments or objectives (e.g., deflecting projectiles) do not automatically restrict all claims to those objectives unless the claim language or specification clearly requires it.
guidance: Use specification to enable claim scope; do not import limitations from preferred embodiments into claim scope absent clear intent to limit. Example: description of baffles deflecting projectiles enables dependent claims that claim that function but does not limit all claims to that function.

name: A claim need not achieve every objective stated in the specification
description: The fact the patent asserts several objectives does not require each claim be construed as limited to structures capable of achieving all those objectives.
guidance: Distinguish between embodiments/advertised advantages and the actual claim language; do not construe independent claims to require capabilities only recited in some embodiments or dependent claims.

name: Construing to preserve validity is limited
description: Courts have recognized that claims may be construed to preserve validity, but that maxim is applied narrowly — only when, after applying all available claim construction tools, the claim remains ambiguous.
guidance: Do not make validity-preserving constructions routine; apply only as a last resort when ambiguity persists.

name: Construction should "stay true" to claim language and align with specification
description: The correct construction is the one that stays true to the claim language and most naturally aligns with the patent's description of the invention.
guidance: Aim for the construction that best matches the ordinary meaning to the skilled artisan while being consistent with the patent's specification and prosecution history.

name: Subjective inventor testimony is of limited weight
description: Subjective inventor testimony about what was intended to be claimed is heavily discounted.
guidance: Rely on objective intrinsic evidence and credible extrinsic support about the skilled artisan's understanding rather than on inventor's post hoc assertions of intent.

name: Provide evidence to establish key factual predicates
description: Evidence establishing who is a person of ordinary skill and how that person would understand claim terms is central to claim construction, but must be consistent with the patent document.
guidance: When asserting a particular construction, supply contemporaneous technical definitions, treatises, or credible expert analysis tied to the intrinsic record to show how a skilled artisan would read the patent.

name: Federal Circuit review and standard of law
description: Claim construction is treated as a legal question subject to plenary review by the Federal Circuit (per en banc Phillips), though some judges dissent that factual aspects may warrant deference.
guidance: Anticipate that claim constructions may be reviewed de novo at the appellate level; ensure the record explains interpretive choices and factual predicates clearly.

name: Case-specific extraction of requirements from claim language
description: Courts should extract explicit requirements from the claim language itself (e.g., in the Phillips case the claim language imposed three clear requirements on 'baffles': made of steel; part of load-bearing means; pointed inward from the walls).
guidance: When construing a term, list explicit limitations present in the claim text rather than importing unclaimed features from embodiments; use the claim wording to identify discrete requirements.

name: Protection measures for legitimate holder filing (procedural requirements)
description: A legitimate holder seeking protection under Articles 34/35 must file an application in Annexed Form No. 14 to the Commissioner of KIPO, attached with a specification, abstract or drawings, evidential document of the legitimate holder of right, and representation document if applicable.
guidance: Specifies the form and documentary evidence to claim protection; required attachments mirror normal application contents plus evidence of entitlement.

name: Scope requirement for retroactivity of legitimate-holder application
description: For the scope of the invention of the legitimate-holder application to be deemed legitimate, the invention disclosed in the description and drawings and the claimed invention must be included in the scope of the invention of the application filed by the unentitled person. If the legitimate-holder application includes inventions not disclosed in the unentitled person's application, the retroactive filing date has no effect for those out-of-scope inventions.
guidance: Retroactivity only applies to subject matter that was disclosed in the earlier unentitled filing; new matter in the legitimate-holder filing receives no retroactive priority.

name: Abstract use limitation (Article 43)
description: The abstract shall be used only for technical information and shall not be used to define the scope of the invention for which patent protection is sought.
guidance: Abstract is informational only and cannot alter claim scope or be used to interpret limits of protection.

name: Application cover sheet content and other indicia
description: The application cover sheet includes applicant name/domicile (or juristic person details), representative/agent details and designated patent attorney if applicable, title of the invention (which must be brief and identical with the specification), name/domicile of inventor, applicant code, priority claim, claim on grace period disclosure exception, and request for examination indication.
guidance: Title should be concise and must match specification; cover sheet must indicate procedural flags (priority, grace period claim, request for examination) to ensure proper processing.

name: Claim construction: ordinary meaning and context
description: Claim terms should receive their ordinary meaning based on interpretation of the entire claim in context, not by isolating a single element.
guidance: The Court cautioned that 'it is not always appropriate to break down a phrase and give it an interpretation that is merely the sum of its parts.' Use intrinsic evidence to interpret terms in context.

name: Obviousness: combination disclosures can support obviousness
description: A claim limitation disclosed only by combining references can still render the claim obvious if a POSITA would have been motivated to combine and there is substantial evidence that combining would yield the claimed limitation.
guidance: Court emphasized POSITA's 'knowledge, creativity, and common sense' in combining teachings; the fact that only the combination discloses the limitation does not defeat obviousness.

name: Board should not ordinarily find substitute claims unpatentable on sua sponte grounds
description: Proposed substitute claims should rarely be found unpatentable by the Board on sua sponte grounds; the record must 'readily and persuasively establish' unpatentability for such sua sponte action.
guidance: POP reversed a sua sponte finding where record did not convincingly support that substitute claims were unpatentable for same reasons as original claims.

name: Industry skepticism is a secondary consideration in obviousness and must be invention-specific
description: Evidence of general industry skepticism about a field does not necessarily defeat motivation to combine; any skepticism must be specific to the claimed invention and combination, not generic to the field.
guidance: Vague or generic testimony that a field was skeptical is insufficient; remand may be required for Board to weigh specific evidence.

name: Product-by-process limitations give no patentable weight if they do not change structure
description: A 'cast in one piece' (product-by-process) limitation imparts no patentable weight if it is not shown to impart a structural difference from products not cast in one piece.
guidance: Claims construed as product-by-process limitations may fail to distinguish over prior art if no structural difference is demonstrated.

name: Patent eligibility §101: claims directed to abstract mental processes are ineligible
description: Claims directed to abstract processes that essentially perform steps in the human mind (e.g., determining Social Security Disability Insurance benefits via a computer network framed as an abstract idea) are patent-ineligible under §101.
guidance: Board applied abstract-idea analysis and found essential steps were performed in the human mind; §101 rejections under Alice/Mayo framework supported.

name: Responsibility for leaving boats in way of sailing vessels
description: Every vessel anchored, who may have its long boat or boat astern, and, seeing another vessel under sail, neglects to haul them up out of the way, not only will forfeit the right to claim in case of average, but will even be responsible for that which such negligence may occasion.
guidance: Police of the Port Article 7: keep boats clear of navigable paths; failure forfeits claim and creates liability.

name: Four statutory categories (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: The four categories are processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter. Processes define 'actions' (a series of steps); the latter three define physical or tangible 'things' or 'products.'
guidance: When determining whether a claim falls in one of these categories, verify that the invention is claimed in a physical or tangible form for machines/manufactures/compositions. Non-limiting non-statutory examples include data per se, computer program per se (product-type claims without structural recitations), transitory signals, and subject matter expressly prohibited (e.g., humans per se).

name: Establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of claim as a whole
description: It is essential that the BRI of the claim be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility; the BRI sets the boundaries of coverage sought and influences whether the claim seeks to cover non-statutory subject matter or is directed to a judicial exception.
guidance: Claim interpretation affects both Step 1 (statutory category) and Step 2 (Alice/Mayo). Examples: Mentor Graphics (BRI covered non-statutory carrier waves) and Synopsys/Enfish (claim construction affected whether claims were considered mental steps or technological improvements). If BRI covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim may fail Step 1.

name: Flowchart pathways A, B, and C (streamlined/standard analyses)
description: Pathway A: Claims that fall within a statutory category and whose eligibility is self-evident may be found eligible using a streamlined analysis. Pathway B: Claims that fall within a statutory category and are not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) are eligible at Pathway B. Pathway C: Claims that fall within a statutory category, are directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), and recite additional elements that amount to significantly more (Step 2B: YES) are eligible at Pathway C.
guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis is appropriate, the examiner is encouraged to conduct a full eligibility analysis. Claims not eligible under any pathway should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: BRI covering statutory and non-statutory embodiments — consequences and remediation
description: If the BRI of a claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter, fails Step 1, and should be rejected.
guidance: Best practice: point out the BRI and recommend an amendment narrowing the claim to statutory embodiments if possible. Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05, 7.05.01) when making a §101 rejection for lack of statutory subject matter.

name: Abstract ideas: groupings and examples
description: Abstract ideas include certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, mathematical concepts/formulas, and other concepts courts have identified as abstract.
guidance: MPEP provides example lists and 'tentative abstract ideas' to guide examiners. Determine whether claimed steps are mere mental steps, mathematical formulas, or other abstract groupings; consider whether claim limitations meaningfully integrate the idea into a practical application.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (product-of-nature)
description: A product of nature is patent-ineligible unless the claimed subject matter has 'markedly different characteristics' from the naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: Assess structure, function, and properties compared to naturally occurring form. If the claimed subject matter exhibits markedly different characteristics due to human modification, it may not be a product of nature and may pass Step 2A consideration.

name: Eligibility Step 2B: whether the claim amounts to significantly more (inventive concept)
description: Step 2B evaluates whether additional claim elements, individually or in combination, provide 'significantly more' than the judicial exception — i.e., an inventive concept that transforms the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Factors/considerations include: (a) improvements to the functioning of a computer or other technology, (b) particular machine, (c) particular transformation, (d) well-understood, routine, conventional activity (negative factor), (e) other meaningful limitations, (f) mere instructions to apply an exception (negative), (g) insignificant extra-solution activity (negative), and (h) field of use or technological environment. Evaluate whether claimed limitations are conventional or amount to a technical contribution.

name: Streamlined analysis (2106.06): eligibility is self-evident or clear technology improvement
description: When eligibility is self-evident or the claim demonstrates a clear improvement to technology or computer functionality, a streamlined analysis (Pathway A) may be appropriate.
guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis is appropriate, conduct the full two-part Alice/Mayo analysis. Claims that would be eligible under Pathway A but subjected to Steps 2A/2B should ultimately be found eligible at Pathway B or C if appropriate.

name: Do not rely on superseded or incorrect tests or utility as the eligibility metric
description: The MPEP emphasizes that certain prior tests are superseded or should not be used as the basis for eligibility determinations.
guidance: Do not evaluate eligibility based on whether the claim recites a 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' (State Street/Alappat era test) or on 'utility' (utility is not the test for §101). The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue but not a separate test. The 'special purpose computer' rationale (In re Alappat) has been superseded by Bilski and Alice.

name: §101 is a threshold inquiry; use §102, §103, §112 and other provisions as tools
description: Examiners are reminded that 35 U.S.C. 101 is only a threshold test; other statutes (35 U.S.C. 112, 35 U.S.C. 102, 35 U.S.C. 103) provide additional tools to ensure claimed inventions meet conditions for patentability.
guidance: Even if a claim is eligible under §101, it must still be novel, nonobvious, and meet written-description/enablement requirements. Conversely, a §101 rejection does not obviate examining other statutory requirements during prosecution.

name: Overall practical-application/integration test (summary)
description: Process claims having a natural principle as a limiting element or step should be evaluated by determining whether the claim includes additional elements/steps or a combination of elements/steps that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that the natural principle is practically applied, and are sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself.
guidance: If the claim as a whole satisfies this inquiry the claim is directed to patent-eligible subject matter; if not, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 as non-statutory subject matter.

name: Inquiry 2 — Does the claim focus on a natural principle?
description: Does the claim focus on use of a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or naturally occurring relation or correlation (collectively referred to as a natural principle)? (Is the natural principle a limiting feature of the claim?)
guidance: A natural principle is the handiwork of nature and occurs without the hand of man (examples: disinfecting property of sunlight; relation between blood glucose and diabetes). If the natural principle is not a limitation of the claim, this natural-principle analysis is not required (but consider abstract-idea analysis per MPEP §2106).

name: Inquiry 3 — Practical application/integration and 'significantly more'
description: Does the claim include additional elements/steps or a combination of elements/steps that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that the natural principle is practically applied, and are sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself? (Is it more than a law of nature plus the general instruction to simply 'apply it'?)
guidance: Additional elements or steps must relate to the natural principle in a significant way to impose a meaningful limit on claim scope; a bare statement of a natural correlation or adding only insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., recording a diagnosis on a chart) is insufficient. The claim must not effectively monopolize the natural principle or cover every substantial practical application of it.

name: Claim construction — determine what applicant invented and broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Review the entire specification and claims to determine what applicant believes he or she invented. Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claims when read in light of the specification and from the view of one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Claim analysis begins by identifying and evaluating each claim limitation and then considering the claim as a whole. It is improper to dissect a claimed invention into discrete elements and then evaluate the elements in isolation. Use the same interpretation to evaluate compliance with statutory requirements (see MPEP §§2111, 2173 et seq.).

name: Integration requirement — at least one additional element must practically apply the natural principle
description: There must be at least one additional element or step that applies, relies on or uses the natural principle so that the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself; not every recited element must integrate the principle.
guidance: Elements or steps that do not integrate the natural principle and are merely appended to it are not sufficient; the additional steps must meaningfully relate to the principle (e.g., change how it is implemented or confine it to a particular practical application).

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity insufficient
description: Elements or steps that are mere extra-solution activity unrelated to the correlation or principle (e.g., recording a diagnosis on a chart) do not make the claim eligible.
guidance: A claim that merely adds routine administrative or data-recording steps to a natural correlation will fail Inquiry 3 because those steps do not integrate the natural principle into a practical application.

name: Avoiding preemption — additional elements must meaningfully limit scope
description: The additional elements or steps must narrow the scope of the claim such that others are not foreclosed from using the natural principle for future innovation; the claim must not cover every substantial practical application of the natural principle.
guidance: Elements that are well-understood, purely conventional, routine, or that merely limit field-of-use are insufficient. A claim that adds something that confines its reach to particular patent-eligible applications (e.g., a new drug) may be eligible even if the natural principle is present.

name: Machine-or-Transformation (M-or-T) factors are relevant but not dispositive
description: The weighing factors used previously (including the Machine-or-Transformation test) are useful tools for assisting in the evaluation, but satisfying the M-or-T factors does not ensure eligibility if those features do not integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention.
guidance: A particular machine or transformation recited in more than general terms may help show integration, but merely reciting a machine generically or a tangential transformation (e.g., only a change in position) may not. The machine/transformation should be described so as to show how it implements the natural principle.

name: Claims covering known and unknown uses or performable without apparatus are suspect
description: A claim that covers known and unknown uses of a natural principle and can be performed through any existing or future-devised machinery, or even without any apparatus, would lack features that are sufficient for eligibility.
guidance: Such broad claims risk preempting the natural principle; eligibility favors claims with limiting, specific, practicable implementation details.

name: A particular machine/transformation described in detail may show integration
description: A particular machine or transformation recited in more than general terms may be sufficient to limit the application to a particular implementation such that the claim does not cover every substantial practical application of a natural principle.
guidance: Describing details of machine parts or how a transformation implements the natural principle (e.g., how parts of an internal combustion engine apply combustion to produce energy) helps show integration; nominal or incidental use of a machine does not.

name: Absence of machine-or-transformation indicates likely disembodied claim
description: Complete absence of a machine-or-transformation in a claim signals the likelihood that the claim is directed to a natural principle and has not been instantiated (e.g., is disembodied or can be performed entirely in one’s mind).
guidance: Lack of any machinery or transformation often suggests the claim merely recites an abstract or natural principle without concrete application.

name: Making a rejection — required explanatory elements
description: When making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 for failing Inquiry 3, identify the natural principle, identify that the claim is effectively directed to the natural principle itself, and explain the reason(s) that the additional claim features or combination of features fail to integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention or fail to be sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself.
guidance: Provide an analysis of how the claim passes Inquiries 1 and 2 but fails Inquiry 3, and explain why the additional steps are insufficient (e.g., they are routine, conventional, generic, or merely appending extra-solution activity). The guidance includes a sample rejection template and a sample claim analysis.

name: Eligibility is distinct from patentability (other statutory requirements)
description: A claim that is deemed eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101 is not necessarily patentable; it must also comply with other statutory and non-statutory considerations for patentability such as utility, double patenting, novelty (35 U.S.C. 102), obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103), and written description/definiteness (35 U.S.C. 112).
guidance: Examiner analyses under 101 should not conflate eligibility with other patentability conditions; follow other MPEP sections as appropriate for those determinations.

name: Purpose and style of communications
description: Communications in the examination procedure serve to prepare the grant or the refusal of the patent and must be drafted in a clear and neutral style.
guidance: The number of communications is determined by the obligation to inquire into the facts, to grant the right to be heard and by particular circumstances in the individual case. The applicant should be invited to revise the description only after patentable claims have been submitted or proposed by the examining section.

name: Communications must propose positive claim amendments
description: A communication should not only state those aspects which are an obstacle to grant, but also provide positive proposals for amending the claims.
guidance: This should clearly show the applicant whether and to what extent the examining section considers the subject matter of the application to be patentable.

name: Preparation and conduct of hearings
description: In preparation for hearings, the examining section and the applicant must be familiar with the matter and case file; issues not previously considered should be indicated in the summons.
guidance: If hearing took place before a change of examining section, repeat only if new section has serious reasons. At the beginning of hearing the applicant/representative must identify himself. A non-lawyer representative must produce power of attorney. The examining section should first outline controversial issues and may submit proposals. If agreement reached on patentability, wording of claims and structure of description should be laid down.

name: Definiteness of claim language (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Definiteness must be analyzed not in a vacuum but in light of the teachings of the prior art and of the particular application disclosure as it would be interpreted by one possessing ordinary skill in the pertinent art (In re Moore). Claims may appear indefinite when read in a vacuum but may be definite upon reading of the application disclosure or prior art teachings; conversely an otherwise definite claim in a vacuum may be uncertain when read in light of the disclosure and prior art. See MPEP § 2173.05(b).

name: Use of broadening phrases (e.g., 'or the like', 'or similar article') may render claims indefinite
description: Use of phrases in the claim such as 'or similar article,' 'or the like,' or equivalent terminology has been held to be indefinite.
guidance: Ex parte Pappas (23 USPQ2d 1636) is cited. However, the use of such broadening language in the title when directed to the environment of the article embodying the design should not be the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (see MPEP § 1503.01). Examiner form paragraphs and examiner notes provide bracketed text for inserting the objectionable phrase when preparing rejections or examiner amendments.

name: Cancellation of indefinite phrase as remedy
description: Cancellation of the objectionable phrase in the claim and each occurrence of the title throughout the papers, except the oath or declaration, will overcome the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
guidance: Form paragraph ¶ 15.69.01 (Remove Indefinite Language by Examiner's Amendment) is used to record cancellation by examiner after authorization (e.g., telephone interview). Bracketed placeholders in form paragraphs indicate where to insert the objectionable phrase (e.g., --or the like--).

name: Title must identify a known article of manufacture
description: A claim is indefinite when the title fails to identify an article of manufacture and the drawing disclosure does not inherently identify the article in which the design is embodied; the drawing disclosure referenced by 'as shown' is incorporated into the claim.
guidance: Clarifying the title by specifying the article in which the design is embodied may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121). If the title is too ambiguous for proper examination under 37 CFR 1.104, applicant must be required to explain the nature and intended use of the article in a separate paper (not inserted into the specification). See MPEP § 1503.01.

name: Relationship and overlap between 35 U.S.C. 112 first and second paragraphs in design practice
description: While requirements of the first and second paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 112 are separate and distinct, the relationship between them is not always easily distinguishable in design patent practice because the drawing disclosure (equivalent to written description) is incorporated into the claim by use of 'as shown.'
guidance: A rejection under both paragraphs should be made when the drawing disclosure and the claim disagree, conflict, or are inconsistent (other than in scope), and confusion exists as to whether the claimed design is sufficiently disclosed in the enabling teachings of the drawings. Example: claim directed to a chair while drawing discloses a table — reject under both paragraphs for nonenabling disclosure and indefiniteness. When amendment to drawings introduces new matter, it may give rise to a 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph rejection (35 U.S.C. 132).

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and/or second paragraphs) — use and content
description: The claim may be rejected as not described in full, clear, concise and exact terms to enable one skilled in the art to make and use the invention (first paragraph) and/or for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (second paragraph).
guidance: Separate rejections under the first and/or second paragraph are preferred; this combined paragraph should be used only when uncertainty exists as to whether the claimed invention is sufficiently described or whether the claim language is indefinite. A full explanation should be provided with such a rejection. If a design claim would otherwise be patentable but for the presence of any 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection(s), Form Paragraph 15.58.01 may be used to indicate the design is patentable over the references cited pending resolution of the 112 issue(s).

name: Restriction practice in design applications (35 U.S.C. 121) — general principle
description: A design patent application may only have a single claim and thus must be limited to a single invention; the examiner will require restriction in each design application which contains more than one invention.
guidance: Restriction may be required under 35 U.S.C. 121 if subject matter disclosed in the drawings is either independent or distinct and able to support separate design patents. If embodiments are patentably indistinct and can be covered by a single claim, a rejection of one embodiment over the prior art will apply equally to other embodiments. See relevant case law (e.g., Ex parte Appeal No. 315-40).

name: Combination/subcombination (difference in scope) — when separate protection is required
description: A design claim covers the entire design as a whole, but may cover embodiments of different scope (combination vs subcombination/element) within a single application only if the designs are not patentably distinct.
guidance: If embodiments directed to combinations vs subcombinations are patentably distinct, the designs are considered separate inventions requiring separate claims. Design protection does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts; separate patents are needed to protect segregable parts. Case law: In re Rubinfield; Blumcraft v. Ladd; In re Kelly; Ex parte Sanford; Ex parte Heckman.

name: Understand the invention and determine claim scope
description: An examiner should understand the invention based on the claims and the specification; an examiner cannot search effectively without understanding the inventive concept or scope of the claims.
guidance: Take notes on key concepts and/or diagram the claims. Check for claim interpretation issues: determine the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification and ensure proper weight is given to claim limitations.

name: Complete and thorough search (MPEP guidance)
description: A complete and thorough search enables an examiner to get the most pertinent art as early as possible; a text search alone is rarely sufficient and should be combined with other criteria (e.g., classification).
guidance: Prioritize areas most likely to yield relevant prior art. A proper field of search normally includes the classification locations where the claimed subject matter would be properly classified at the time of classification or grant (MPEP 904.02 and 904.02(a)).

name: When to start searching
description: Begin searching when the examiner understands the invention and the claim limitations and the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification.
guidance: Do not undertake a search until the inventive concept and claim scope are clear enough to craft an effective search strategy.

name: When to stop searching
description: Stop searching after completely executing the search strategy, after searching for all claimed limitations and potential reasonably expected limitations, and after assessing whether the art can be easily overcome.
guidance: Consider whether 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) & 102(b)(2) exceptions (same applicant) apply. Evaluate whether the art reads on the inventive concept (not just the words of the claims).

name: Decision to make a rejection
description: Before making a rejection, determine whether it is applied under the proper statute (35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112), whether it is legally and technically proper, whether it will clarify the record, and whether an examiner’s amendment would place the claims in condition for allowance.
guidance: Reject only when statute and facts support it, it helps clarify record issues, and after considering the impact of potential examiner amendments.

name: Allowance decision criteria
description: To determine if a claim is allowable, ensure all relevant searches are completed, ensure no claim limitations are characterized in the specification as known or conventional, compare reasons for allowance against the strongest rejection, and consult supervisor/trainer as needed.
guidance: Allowance should be based on thorough search and legal analysis; consultation is recommended when in doubt.

name: Formation of an Office action — statutory checks
description: When forming an Office action, examine whether the claimed invention meets statutory requirements: 35 U.S.C. 101, support in specification per 35 U.S.C. 112(a), definiteness per 35 U.S.C. 112(b), novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102, and non-obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: Each statutory point should be expressly considered and addressed in the Office action where relevant; failures must be explained with factual and legal support.

name: Scope of review (grounds and subject matter)
description: Inter partes review is a trial proceeding ... to review the patentability of one or more claims in a patent only on a ground that could be raised under §§ 102 or 103.
guidance: The proceeding is limited to patentability challenges under 35 U.S.C. §§102 (novelty) and 103 (obviousness); other statutory grounds are not available in IPR. The review is of one or more claims (not other patent issues).

name: Institution standard
description: An inter partes review may be instituted upon a showing that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one claim challenged.
guidance: The Board uses the 'reasonable likelihood' standard (i.e., reasonable likelihood to prevail on at least one challenged claim) when deciding whether to institute IPR. Petition drafting should therefore focus on demonstrating that likelihood for at least one claim.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 prior art and exceptions guidance
description: Clarified 'effective filing date' by adding 'of a claimed invention.' Clarified that potential references 'within the one-year grace period' are excepted as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A) and (B). Revised text to better align with statutory text of 35 U.S.C. 102 (e.g., using 'except' rather than 'disqualify'). Added guidance that the subject matter of the prior disclosure relied upon must be the same 'subject matter' as the inventor-originated disclosure for exceptions to apply. Added statements that 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(A)/(B)/(C) exceptions may apply without grace-period limitation in some contexts.
guidance: Defines 'inventor-originated disclosure' (disclosure by an inventor or joint inventor, or another who obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor). Clarifies when affidavits or declarations may be used to except a disclosure, includes illustrative examples (1–4) based on First Inventor to File Declarations training material, and explains effects on double patenting rejections when exceptions apply.

name: Working and prophetic examples
description: Added that claims should be drafted in a manner that assists readers in differentiating between actual working and prophetic examples. Added new subsection IV to provide guidance on prophetic examples and added 'in art areas having a high degree of uncertainty (i.e. the unpredictable arts)' and guidance on the applicable evidentiary standard.
guidance: Stated that evaluation of prophetic examples is 'based on a preponderance of evidence standard.' Added citations and discussions (e.g., Pac. Biosciences of Cal., Inc. v. Oxford Nanopore Techs.) and cross-references; guidance advises drafting claims to clearly distinguish working examples from prophetic ones.

name: Enablement and undue experimentation timing
description: Clarified that the relevant time for undue experimentation to enable the full scope of the claims is before the effective filing date (discussion referencing Amgen Inc. v. Sanofi and other cases). Changed wording throughout to use 'relevant time' instead of 'time of the invention' or 'date of invention.'
guidance: Added case citations and discussion about undue experimentation and enablement, stressed that the relevant time is the effective filing date (pre-AIA/AIA differences noted), and included cross-references to related MPEP sections.

name: Claim construction during prosecution (broadest reasonable interpretation)
description: Revised text to make it clear that during prosecution the Office construes claims by giving them their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: Corrected citations (e.g., Nautilus) and clarified that BRI applies during prosecution; includes cross-references to 35 U.S.C. 112(b) guidance and related sections on claim definiteness and rejections under 112.

name: Judicial Exceptions (Step 2A)
description: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas; laws of nature and natural phenomena; and products of nature.
guidance: Under the Step 2A analysis, determine whether the claim recites or is directed to a judicial exception. If so, proceed to prong two (integration into a practical application).

name: Markedly Different Characteristics Test
description: Evaluate whether claims possess characteristics that are 'markedly different' from naturally occurring items.
guidance: For claims involving natural products, examine whether the claimed subject matter exhibits markedly different characteristics (structure, function, or other properties) relative to the natural product. If markedly different, the claim may be patent eligible.

name: Integration into Practical Application (Step 2A Prong Two)
description: Claims must show integration of judicial exceptions into a practical, real-world application rather than mere recitation of the exception.
guidance: Assess whether additional claim limitations integrate the exception into a practical application (e.g., by applying the exception in a specific technological environment or improving a technological process). Mere field-of-use or generic computer implementation is insufficient.

name: Novelty / Anticipation — Post-AIA Standards (35 U.S.C. § 102)
description: A claimed invention is anticipated if patented, described in a printed publication, or otherwise publicly available before the effective filing date, or by certain earlier-filed U.S. patent documents naming another inventor.
guidance: Examine prior art disclosures to determine whether a single reference discloses every claim limitation. Consider effective filing dates, priority claims, and whether the reference is enabling. Anticipation requires a clear, enabling disclosure of the claimed subject matter.

name: Non-Obviousness — Prima Facie Obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103)
description: A prima facie case of obviousness requires: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) a motivation to combine references; and (5) a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: Use the Graham framework to evaluate obviousness. The examiner must articulate how the references, knowledge, and reasoning lead to a conclusion of obviousness, addressing each Graham factor.

name: Written Description Requirement (§ 112(a))
description: Claims must find adequate support within the specification demonstrating that the inventor possessed the full scope of the claimed invention.
guidance: Evaluate whether the specification describes the claimed invention in sufficient detail to show possession of the claimed subject matter across its full scope. Mere recitation of claim language without adequate descriptive support can fail this requirement.

name: Enablement Requirement (§ 112(a))
description: The specification must enable persons skilled in the art to 'make and use' the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Assess whether the disclosure provides sufficient teaching to allow skilled artisans to practice the claimed invention across the full scope without undue experimentation. Consider the predictability of the art and the amount of experimentation required.

name: Clarity / Definiteness Requirement (§ 112(b))
description: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention; claim language that lacks ordinary meaning or clarity is indefinite.
guidance: Reject claims when terms are ambiguous, lack antecedent basis, or otherwise fail to inform a skilled artisan of the scope with reasonable certainty. Applicants may respond by narrowing claim scope, adding antecedent basis, or supplying structural limitations.

name: Common Indefiniteness Issues
