description: Representative problems include functional limitations without structure, relative terminology lacking clarity, antecedent basis failures, and aggregated limitations without meaningful relationships.
guidance: When examining for indefiniteness, look for unsupported functional language, undefined relative terms (e.g., 'substantially', 'about' without context), missing antecedent references, and claim element aggregations that do not indicate how elements interact. Require amendments or clarifying disclosure as appropriate.

name: §101 Eligibility — Examiner Rejection Standard and Applicant Responses
description: Ground: §101 Eligibility. Burden: Prima facie rejection using claim analysis. Applicant Response: Demonstrate integration into practical application or add 'significantly more' limitations.
guidance: Examiners should identify why a claim is directed to a judicial exception and provide analysis; applicants can respond by amending claims to include technological improvements, demonstrating practical application, or arguing the claims already include 'significantly more.'

name: §102 Anticipation — Examiner Rejection Standard and Applicant Responses
description: Ground: §102 Anticipation. Burden: Single reference disclosure or admission. Applicant Response: Antedate reference, show the reference is non-enabling, or claim narrow distinctions.
guidance: Examiners must point to the single reference elements that anticipate every claim limitation. Applicants may submit affidavits/declarations to antedate or argue non-enablement of the reference, or amend claims to distinguish the reference.

name: §103 Obviousness — Examiner Rejection Standard and Applicant Responses
description: Ground: §103 Obviousness. Burden: Motivation + reasonable expectation of success. Applicant Response: Present secondary considerations, unpredictability, or argue narrow claim scope to overcome obviousness.
guidance: Examiners should articulate the reasoning and evidence supporting a motivation to combine and expectation of success. Applicants can rebut with objective indicia of non-obviousness (e.g., unexpected results) or demonstrate that the combination would have been unpredictable.

name: §112 Definiteness — Examiner Rejection Standard and Applicant Responses
description: Ground: §112 Definiteness. Burden: Terms lack ordinary meaning. Applicant Response: Narrow scope, add antecedent basis, or provide structural limitations.
guidance: When issuing a §112 rejection, identify the specific terms or claim language that are indefinite and explain why. Applicants should amend claims or provide explanations/definitions in the specification to clarify claim scope.

name: Formulating Rejections — Identification and Reasoning
description: Examiners must clearly identify which limitation(s) trigger a rejection and provide reasoning connecting evidence to conclusions.
guidance: Rejections should map claim limitations to prior art or explain how claim language implicates a judicial exception. Provide factual findings and step-by-step reasoning so applicants can understand and respond effectively.

name: Streamlined Analysis (§ 2106.06)
description: Eligibility may be self-evident for clearly patentable subject matter; detailed analysis may be waived.
guidance: For claims that are clearly directed to patent-eligible subject matter, examiners can apply a streamlined analysis and need not perform the full stepwise eligibility framework. Document when and why streamlined analysis is appropriate.

name: Claim Interpretation Standard — Broadest Reasonable Interpretation
description: During prosecution, claim terms are given their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification.
guidance: Interpret claim language with plain meaning consistent with the specification as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art. Apply broadest reasonable interpretation when construing claim terms for examination purposes.

name: The Specification Is the Foundation
description: Every claim term, every amendment, every continuation depends on the specification.
guidance: A weak spec cannot be patched later because new matter cannot be added. Invest in the specification at the outset because such investment pays dividends across the patent lifecycle (prosecution, claim amendments, continuations, litigation).

name: The Three Disclosure Requirements (35 U.S.C. §112(a))
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) imposes three disclosure requirements: written description (showing possession), enablement (showing the POSITA can make and use), and best mode (now non‑defensive but still required).
guidance: All three requirements must be satisfied for every claim term. Draft the specification to meet written description, enablement, and best mode for each claimed element and reasonable variations.

name: Written Description - Show You Had It
description: The spec must show that the inventor was in possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.
guidance: For genus claims in unpredictable arts, disclose representative species and unifying structural features to demonstrate possession (citing Ariad Pharmaceuticals v. Eli Lilly). Ensure the specification supports the full scope of what is claimed.

name: Enablement - Show How to Make and Use
description: The spec must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) to make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Use the Wands factors (In re Wands) to assess enablement: nature of the invention, state of the prior art, predictability of the art, breadth of the claims, presence of working examples, quantity of experimentation needed, guidance provided by the spec, and level of ordinary skill. Include sufficient working examples and procedural detail when unpredictability or claim breadth raises undue experimentation concerns.

name: Define Terms Affirmatively
description: If a claim term has a meaning specific to the application, define it explicitly in the specification (e.g., 'As used herein, X means Y').
guidance: Express definitions in the spec are respected by courts (Phillips v. AWH). Use clear, affirmative definitions to control claim construction and avoid ambiguous or shifting meanings.

name: Multiple Embodiments
description: Disclose multiple embodiments of the invention to support claim breadth and provide fallbacks during prosecution.
guidance: At minimum disclose three embodiments: the simplest embodiment, the prototype (working example), and a commercially‑relevant variant. More embodiments help support broader claim construction and provide alternatives if certain embodiments are later narrowed or invalidated.

name: Background Section - Brief and Neutral
description: Keep the background section short and neutral, focused on technical context.
guidance: Long backgrounds can invite admissions and disclaimers about the prior art. Avoid characterizing prior art in ways that create negative admissions or limit claim scope; state only the necessary technical context.

name: Summary Section - Mirror the Claims
description: The Brief Summary should track the independent claims at a high level.
guidance: Avoid summarizing the invention in ways that go beyond what is claimed. Use the summary to reflect claim scope without introducing new, broader embodiments not supported by the claims.

name: Drawings As Anchors
description: Use drawings as anchors for the written description and walk the specification through figures figure by figure.
guidance: Each reference number should be defined in the text and shown in the corresponding figure. Maintain a tight spec‑figure correspondence to aid examiner understanding and support claim construction.

name: Length and Conciseness
description: Modern utility patent specifications typically run 30–100 pages, but length alone is not a virtue.
guidance: Aim for the shortest specification that fully discloses every claim term and reasonable variations. Prioritize useful disclosure over verbosity—provide sufficient detail but avoid unnecessary text that could invite problematic admissions or confusion.

name: Use of solid and broken lines
description: Solid lines are used for claimed features; broken lines are used for unclaimed environment (in design patents) or hidden features.
guidance: Apply solid vs. broken lines consistently and according to whether the element is claimed. Misuse leads to ambiguity and potential rejection, especially in design practice.

name: Merging/combining copending ex parte reexamination proceedings (37 CFR 1.565(c))
description: If ex parte reexamination is ordered while a prior ex parte reexamination is pending and prosecution in the prior proceeding has not been terminated, the ex parte reexamination proceedings will be consolidated and result in issuance of a single certificate.
guidance: Decision whether to combine is made by the Technology Center (TC) Director (may delegate to TC SPRE). No decision to combine should be made until reexamination is actually ordered in the later-filed request. If merged, prosecution continues at the most advanced point possible for the first proceeding; a single combined examiner's action will be prepared listing both control numbers. When merged, files are maintained as separate complete files but require identical claims or the patent owner given 1 month to amend to make claims identical. If claims are not identical after that period, non-identical claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as indefinite.

name: Requirements for merged proceeding filings and claims
description: When proceedings are merged the decision should require that the patent owner maintain identical claims in both files, and responses and other papers must consist of a single response filed in duplicate, each signed and containing identifying data for both files for entry in both files.
guidance: If the merger decision requires an amendment to make claims identical and the patent owner fails to timely submit it, any claim not identical in all merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as indefinite. Clerical and printing procedures (e.g., action cover form, PALM printer, PTOL-465 transmission form) must follow merged-file process. If multiple requests (>2) are filed, extend guidelines accordingly.

name: Action in interference following reexamination certificate issuance
description: If one or more claims of a patent involved in an interference are canceled or amended by issuance and publication of a reexamination certificate, the Board must be promptly notified and the patent owner must notify the administrative patent judge upon issuance and publication of the certificate.
guidance: After the certificate issues, the examiner and Board should review the certificate to determine if changes affect interference status; if so, propose or adjust interference accordingly per MPEP Chapter 2300.

name: Requirements for precise exceptions to master's reports
description: Exceptions to a master's report must be aimed with precision at the alleged errors and supported with references to the particular evidence or master's statements relied upon.
guidance: Defendant or complainant affirmative exceptions must cite particular evidence; negative exceptions challenging admissibility should specify evidence objected to when possible, or require the master to make a special statement in his final report of the evidence that convinced him if the exceptor claims there was none.

name: Abstract idea / judicial exceptions (Alice-era constraints)
description: Claims that describe abstract concepts (e.g., mathematical algorithms or mental processes) or that are "capable of being executed by 'an ordinary mental process', 'within the human mind', or 'by an individual using pen and paper'" have been routinely treated as ineligible unless they demonstrate a distinct technological advancement.
guidance: Following Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank, courts apply heightened scrutiny to software- and AI-related claims. If a claim merely recites an abstract idea or mental process (even if tied to a computer), it risks invalidation absent an 'inventive concept' that transforms the idea into patent-eligible subject matter. Examples of anti-patterns: framing routine human reasoning or basic data manipulation as a patentable computer-implemented invention.

name: Claims that merely apply an abstract idea using standard computer components are ineligible
description: Claims that implement an abstract idea by invoking a generic or conventional computer/system without adding a technical improvement are treated as attempts to monopolize the abstract idea and are thus ineligible (as in Blue Spike, LLC v. Google Inc.).
guidance: When drafting or evaluating claims, avoid relying solely on conventional computer implementation language (e.g., 'using a computer', 'executed by a processor') as that will not supply the inventive concept required under Alice; instead, identify and claim the specific nonconventional technological feature or improvement.

name: Practical impact of post-2014 jurisprudence on AI/software patenting
description: Changes introduced to criteria for patentable subject matter in 2014 (Alice decision) have made the path to patenting AI and software technologies significantly more rigorous.
guidance: This heightened standard affects strategy: applicants and advisers must consider §101 risk early, craft claims that highlight technological solutions and improvements, and be prepared to address eligibility challenges. The article notes broader concerns about how these tightened standards may impede innovation and the need for careful legal and policy analysis.

name: Computer program listing location in specification (>60 lines)
description: Any listing having more than 60 lines of code that is submitted as part of the specification must be positioned at the end of the description but before the claims.
guidance: Large listings in the specification must appear after the description and before the claims; amendments to such listings must be made by substitute sheet.

name: Disclosure consistency with drawings
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.
guidance: Maintain alignment between claims, specification text, and drawings; Office may require amendments to achieve substantial correspondence.

name: Design photographs vs ink drawings
description: Photographs and ink drawings are not permitted in one application. Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings in design patent applications must not disclose environmental structures but must be limited to the design claimed for the article.
guidance: Choose either photographs or ink drawings in a single design application; if using photographs, limit the image to the claimed design and avoid showing environmental or extraneous structures.

name: Plant drawings: supplemental close-ups when scale insufficient
description: Where flowers, foliage, fruit, etc. of the claimed plant are not depicted in sufficient scale in a whole plant drawing or view, this view should be supplemented with a close-up view of specific parts.
guidance: Provide magnified views for small but distinctive parts so detail remains visible even after possible 50% reproduction reduction.

name: Plant drawing examples of required supplemental views
description: Examples: Ornamental flowering plants — views at bud, early bloom, and late bloom; Fruit/nut bearing plants — views depicted at different attitudes, with fruit split in different directions to show details and coloration.
guidance: Follow botanical practice in showing relevant developmental stages and internal structures (e.g., seeds, stone, flesh coloration) where these are needed to claim distinctiveness.

name: Number of drawing views limited to minimum necessary (plant)
description: The number of drawing views (and sheets) in plant patent applications should be limited to the minimum number necessary to adequately depict the distinctive botanical characteristics of the claimed patent which are capable of being visually represented.
guidance: Provide only the views needed to disclose the plant clearly; the Office examines drawings for content, detail, scale, and color fidelity, and informal/single copies will delay prosecution.

name: Reissue application drawing requirements
description: An application for reissue must contain the entire specification, including the claims, and the drawings of the patent. No new matter shall be introduced into the application.
guidance: Submit clean copies of each drawing sheet of the printed patent when filing a reissue; if changes are to be made, follow the redline sketch/approval/new-drawings process.

name: Specification language must be 'full, clear, concise, and exact' / reasonable certainty in claims
description: Statutory standard: the Description must be in terms 'full, clear, concise, and exact.' What is claimed as new should appear with reasonable certainty on the face of the patent, either expressly or by necessary implication.
guidance: Claims/specification should not leave the scope of the invention to minute inferences or conjecture. The patent must show with reasonable certainty what the patentee claims as new; otherwise the public cannot know the exclusive right. Reasonable certainty is judged against what the specification states and what a person skilled in the art would understand from it.

name: Specification must be read in context and interpreted for skilled reader
description: The language of the specification is to be considered in connection with its context: clauses together, drawings, model, petition, oath, and other application parts; read as if the invention were present and the reader skilled in the art.
guidance: Interpretation should give effect to the specification as a whole and give the skilled reader the modifications and understandings that such a reader would supply. Claims and descriptions are to be construed in light of accompanying materials and the perspective of the ordinary artisan, not by isolated literalism or by the patentee's private understanding.

name: Substantive strength of the litigating position
description: A party’s substantive strength on the merits (both law and facts) is relevant to exceptionality; extremely weak positions can support fees.
guidance: Even given the presumption of patent validity, a patent or claim that is 'demonstrably weak on its face' can justify fee awards. Specific untenable positions taken after a motion to dismiss (e.g., relying on arguments that case law rejects) weigh against the patentee.

name: 'Demonstrably weak on its face' patent criterion
description: A patent may be described as 'demonstrably weak on its face' such that no reasonable litigant could have expected success on the merits.
guidance: Court will consider the content of the claims and legal precedent (e.g., abstractness under § 101) and may find the patent weak despite issuance and the presumption of validity if positions advanced are untenable under controlling law.

name: Apparent material error by the Office standard
description: To overcome a §325(d) denial, a petitioner may demonstrate an 'apparent error in the examiner’s findings' that is 'material to the patentability of the challenged claims.'
guidance: Director relied on prior Board findings (e.g., that Nishida discloses 'simultaneously knitting a textile element with a surrounding textile structure') to conclude the examiner’s error was apparent and material. Showing prior authoritative findings that the same reference discloses claim limitations supports a conclusion of material examiner error (citing IPR2016-00922, Ex. 1017, 25–26; IPR2024-00460, Ex. 1069, 23–24; and IPR2024-00460 Paper 30 at 29–30).

name: Petitioner’s burden to carry under the Board’s §325(d) framework
description: A petitioner bears the burden to carry its arguments under the Board’s §325(d) framework — demonstrating examiner error and materiality sufficient to overcome denial of institution based on prior art previously considered by the Office.
guidance: Arguments should (1) identify the particular error (misapprehension/overlook), (2) tie that error to claim limitations and patentability, and (3) use supporting evidence such as prior IPR findings or petition exhibits. Failure to meet this burden supports denial (the Decision initially found Petitioner failed to carry this burden, but Director disagreed as to Nishida).

name: Persuasiveness of additional prior art grounds
description: Separate grounds relying on other references (e.g., Günther, Orei) must be persuasive on their own merits; unpersuasive arguments will not justify institution.
guidance: The Director expressly found Petitioner’s additional arguments as to Günther and Orei 'unpersuasive' (DR Request 5–9, 12–15), indicating that mere citation of references without adequate explanatory linkage to claim limitations and materiality will fail. Present clear claim-charting, reasoning, and evidence for each reference relied upon.

name: A: Claims that cannot practically be performed in the human mind are not 'mental processes'
description: If the claim limitations cannot practically be performed in the human mind (i.e., humans are not equipped to perform them), the claim does not recite a mental process.
guidance: Examples of non-mental claims: calculating absolute GPS position and time using pseudoranges (SiRF Tech.); detecting suspicious network activity by using network monitors and analyzing packets (SRI Int'l); specific multi-step data encryption methods requiring complex data manipulation (Synopsys); rendering a halftone image by pixel-by-pixel comparison against a blue noise mask (Research Corp. Techs.). Examiners should identify whether the claimed operations are beyond human mental or pen-and-paper capabilities when deciding they are not 'mental processes.'

name: B: Claims encompassing a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
description: If a claim can practically be performed wholly in a human mind, or by a human with a simple physical aid (e.g., pen and paper, slide rule), it falls within the mental processes grouping and is an abstract idea.
guidance: Use cases: Benson (binary-coded decimal to binary conversion could be done mentally), CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card transactions could be done by writing down transactions), Synopsys (translating a functional description into a hardware description reads on an individual performing the steps mentally or with pencil and paper). The use of simple physical aids does not negate the mental nature of the limitation; examiners should consider specification disclosures that show steps are performable by humans with simple aids.

name: C: Claims that require a computer may still recite a mental process
description: A claim that is implemented on a computer can nonetheless be an abstract idea if the underlying concept could be performed mentally (or is a human cognitive action).
guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Benson, Mortgage Grader) show that computer implementation alone does not save an otherwise-mental concept. Examiners should review the specification and the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim to determine whether the applicant merely claims a concept performed on a generic computer, in a computer environment, or uses a computer as a tool. Examples: Voter Verified (voting, verifying, and submitting votes are human cognitive actions); Versata (pricing implemented on general purpose hardware). If the claim is just a human-performed concept on a generic computer, treat it as a mental-process abstract idea.

name: Evaluate claims using broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification
description: When deciding whether a computer-implemented claim recites a mental process, examiners should use the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in view of the specification to see whether the claimed invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind or merely implemented on generic computer hardware.
guidance: Specifically, determine if the specification describes the claimed invention as: 1) a concept performed in the human mind, and the applicant merely claims it performed on a generic computer; 2) a concept performed in a computer environment; or 3) a concept where a computer is merely a tool to perform the concept. In such scenarios, the claim is considered to recite a mental process. The examination should consider specification descriptions of mental/pen-and-paper methodologies, flowsheets, or charts that indicate human-performable steps.

name: Product and process claims can both recite mental-process abstract ideas
description: The 'mental processes' label refers to the type of abstract idea, not the statutory claim category; both product (e.g., systems, computer-readable media) and process claims may be directed to mental processes.
guidance: Courts have identified product claims (e.g., computer systems, media) as reciting mental processes when the claimed functions read on human-performable mental steps (Versata; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec; Mortgage Grader). Examiners should therefore not assume that claim drafting as a system or medium avoids the mental-process classification; analyze the substantive claimed steps and whether they are human mental work or equivalent.

name: Case resolution categorization and rates
description: Classify case terminations into resolution types (likely settlement, procedural outcomes, claimant win, claim defendant win) and track proportions over time.
guidance: For cases terminating 2009-2016: 74.6% settled, 15.3% procedural outcomes, 6.1% claimant wins, 4.0% claim defendant wins. For 2016 terminations alone: 76.7% settled, 13.8% procedural, 5.5% claimant win, 4.0% claim defendant win. Use resolution mix to inform settlement likelihood and expected end-state distribution.

name: International registration date and U.S. filing date relationship
description: The date of international registration is the later of the international filing date or the date a required element under Article 5(2) is received by the IB; the filing date of an international design application in the United States is the date of international registration (35 U.S.C. 384).
guidance: An Article 5(2) element is required when a designated Contracting Party has declared that its national law requires identification of the creator, a brief description of the reproduction/features, and/or a claim. The United States has made an Article 5(2) declaration requiring a claim.

name: Claiming benefit to an international design application from a nonprovisional U.S. application
description: A nonprovisional application may claim benefit to an international design application designating the United States in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 120, provided the international design application is entitled to a filing date under 37 CFR 1.1023 and the specific reference identifies the relationship per 37 CFR 1.78(d).
guidance: Identify the international application by U.S. application number or international registration number and filing date as required.

name: Identicalness of composition between patented substance and approved substance
description: For an invention subject to patent term extension by approval, the approved substance must have the same composition as the substance recited in the claims (for substance inventions) or as the matter manufactured by the claimed method (for method inventions).
guidance: If compositions are not identical, the examiner shall deem it a ground for rejection under Article 91(1). (i) Where the claimed subject matter is a substance invention, compare the claimed substance and the approved substance. (ii) Where the claimed subject matter is a manufacturing-method invention, compare the substance manufactured by the disclosed method with the approved substance; manufacturing methods themselves need not be compared.

name: Treatment of written arguments and timing/eligibility of amendments
description: After a notice of ground for rejection, an applicant may submit written arguments or amendments; the examiner must consider submitted arguments and re-examine amended matters when amendments are accepted.
guidance: A written argument shall be submitted within the designated period; even if submitted late (after period) or before notice, the examiner shall take the argument into consideration rather than returning it. An amendment can be presented before delivery of a copy of the decision to grant registration of extension, but after notice of grounds for rejection amendments are only allowed within the argument period. Matters eligible for amendment under Article 90(6) include: (①) indication of claims for registration of extension, ② the period for extension request, ③ the content of approval/registration under Article 89, ④ the ground for extension specified in Ordinance of the Ministry). Amendments are severely restricted: clerical-error-type corrections may be allowed; amendments to add co-owners, change applicant where not legitimate, or amend after termination of proceedings are not acknowledged. If an amendment is not legitimate, examiner shall deliver a preliminary notice for inadmissible amendment and proceed accordingly. When an amendment is recognized legitimate, the amended application is examined as if submitted at the initial filing time.

name: Definition of 'period delayed due to an applicant' (Enforcement Decree Article 7(2))
description: 'The period delayed due to an applicant' for purposes of Article 92-2 is expressly defined to include many specific patent-proceeding, litigation, and administrative-appeal periods when delay is attributable to the applicant.
guidance: Included periods (selected list as enumerated): (1) In patent-related proceedings pending before KIPO or the Trial & Appeal Board: (a) period from ordering appointment/replacement of an agent to appointment, (b) extended periods at applicant's request, (c) postponed dates for patent-related proceedings at applicant's request, (d) period from cessation of a cause not attributable to applicant to completion, (e) suspension/interruptions under Articles 20/23(2)/78(1)/164(1), (f) periods to report consultation results under Article 36(6), (g) period until specification amended as required under Article 42(5), (h) periods ordered for amendment under Articles 46/141(1)/203(2), (i) period from making to withdrawing a priority claim under Article 56, (j) delayed determination of expedited examination under Article 10, (k) period while applicant responds to grounds for rejection under Article 63(1) (with exceptions), (l) periods related to payment/exemption of patent fees after receipt of certified copy of decision to grant, (m) period from service of certified copy of decision to reject to request for reexamination, (n) period when request for examination/reexamination is made after cause not attributable to applicant ceases under Article 67-3(1), (o) suspension period where motions for disqualification/recusal are unresolved under Articles 149/150/152/153, (p) period for examination/preservation of evidence requested by applicants under Article 157 when such process concludes it is unnecessary, (q) periods when review on merits is resumed after closing upon applicants' request, (r) period from awareness of grounds for retrial to filing retrial, (s) periods when presiding judge grants additional period under Article 186(5), (t) periods of delayed service of documents or service by publication due to applicant. (2) In litigation concerning trial decisions or court decisions: specified stay/suspension periods, delays due to motions for disqualification/recusal, court-ordered corrections, appointment of special representatives, resumed trials due to applicant, hearing postponements caused by applicant, extensions/grants of additional periods at applicant request, and other service delays attributable to applicant. (3) In administrative appeal or litigation on administrative dispositions: analogous periods where delay is attributable to the appellant/applicant, including Commission-ordered corrections, deadlines for supplemental briefs, postponed hearing dates at applicant request, and service delays.  (The enforcement decree lists many subitems in detail; examiners should apply the full enumerated list when determining applicant-caused delay reductions.)

name: Use of foreign patents/specifications as prior art
description: Foreign patents or specifications that were published or issued may be available as references under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and 102(b); a foreign patent or published specification that claims the priority of a U.S. application (or of an application in another country) may supply an earlier printed publication date or earlier effective date.
guidance: Check whether a foreign document claims priority to a U.S. or other earlier application; if so, the earlier application/patent/publication may make the foreign document effective earlier. Example: a British specification claiming priority to a Belgian application may have an earlier effective date because Belgian patents issue soon after filing. Also note countries that publish applications 18 months after filing — such publications may provide an 18-month printed-publication date useful as prior art.

name: Check foreign patent family members for earlier publications
description: When a foreign patent family member is located, determine whether any related family member was published or issued at an earlier date that could be used as the reference date.
guidance: Related family members are often printed at different stages (e.g., published application then issued patent). The top-listed document within a related group in the table is the one 'published' first. Examiners must verify that the earlier related document contains the subject matter necessary for the rejection because disclosures are usually identical but can sometimes differ in claims or minor specification details.

name: Minimum and commonly used INID elements for patents (selected list)
description: Specific INID codes identify bibliographic elements for patents (e.g., identification, number, document kind, filing dates, priority data, publication/making-available dates, classification, title, abstract, references, parties, and PCT/SPC related data).
guidance: Selected codes and uses from the manual (based on WIPO ST.9): (10) identification of the patent document; (11) number; (12) plain language designation of kind of document; (13) kind of document code (ST.16); (15) patent correction information; (19) WIPO ST.3 code identifying the office; (20) data concerning the application; (21)-(23) application numbers and filing dates; (24) date from which rights have effect; (25)-(26) original and published language codes; (30)-(34) priority data and country/office codes; (40)-(48) dates of making available to the public (various forms such as viewing, printing, grant, corrected docs); (50)-(58) technical information including IPC, national classification, title (54), list of prior art (56), abstract/claim (57), field of search (58); (60)-(68) references to related domestic/procedural documents (continuations, reissues, substitutions, etc.); (70)-(76) identification of parties (applicant, inventor, grantee, agent); (80)-(97) PCT/SPC/other convention related data such as designated states, PCT filing/publication data, SPC expiry (94), SPC product name (95), etc. Notes in the manual provide usage specifics (e.g., (41)-(47) are minimum for patent documents).

name: Extinguish pre-emption/clouds on title to enable partition and improvement
description: Clouds on title (e.g., Ogden Land Company pre-emption claim) prevent partition of lands in severalty and paralyze industry and improvement.
guidance: Recommendation: use of annuity funds or other means to extinguish such claims to remove barriers to partition and economic development.

name: Basic requirements to enter national phase in India
description: Requirements and formalities to enter the Indian national phase from a PCT international application.
guidance: PCT national phase application is a convention application under Section 135; file within 31 months from priority date or international application date (whichever earlier). Pay prescribed national fees and file a duly verified translation of the basic application if not filed/published in Hindi or English. The title, description, drawings, abstract and claims as filed with the international application are taken as the complete specification; at time of national phase filing no other amendment shall be allowed to the complete specification as filed in the international application. Amendments made before ISA/IPEA may be taken as amendments before the Patent Office if applicant so desires. Change in applicant name after international filing may be effected by filing Form 6 and/or Form 13. If PCT/IB/304 (priority document) is available on WIPO website, IPO will not require submission; if not available, Office may request it. If applicant fails to comply with priority document requirement after invitation, priority claim may be disregarded. All other formalities required for ordinary patent application apply. Processing of national phase application will not commence before expiry of 31 months, unless applicant files an express request in Form 18 for early processing.

name: Search by the Examiner — databases and recordkeeping
description: Examiners conduct searches across national and international patent and non-patent literature and must record details of the search.
guidance: Databases include Indian Patent Database, EPO, WIPO, USPTO, JPO, TKDL, and PCT minimum required databases (STN, QPAT, QWEB, DELPHION) and non-patent literature including technical/scientific journals. Examiner records: international classification; search strategy adopted; keywords used; language of search; databases consulted; list of search statements; final findings; limitations on search (e.g., unclear claims, multiplicity); and analysis indicating similarities with citations.

name: Determination of inventive step — analysis approach
description: For inventive step determination, examiner relies on all or any prior art revealed during search to decide if prior art teaches the claimed invention; invention considered as a whole.
guidance: Publications existing on priority date are considered. It is insufficient to deem a claim obvious just because individual parts are known separately — the claim must be assessed as a whole. Mere verification of previous predictions without substantial technical/economic advancement means lack of inventive step. For establishing obviousness, citing a mosaic of prior arts is permissible provided such prior art is enabling.

name: Industrial applicability (usefulness) requirement
description: An invention must be capable of industrial application — capable of being made or used in an industry — to be patentable.
guidance: Examiner shall assess if claimed invention is capable of use in any industry or made using an industrial process. Typically industrial applicability is self-evident; if not, mere suggestion is insufficient. A specific utility should be indicated in the specification supported by the disclosure. For example, indicating a compound may be useful in treating 'unspecified disorders' or having 'useful biological' properties is insufficient — specific usefulness must be specified.

name: Undue experimentation factors (Wands factors)
description: There are many factors to be considered when determining whether necessary experimentation is 'undue.' These factors include, but are not limited to: (A) the breadth of the claims; (B) the nature of the invention; (C) the state of the prior art; (D) the level of one of ordinary skill; (E) the level of predictability in the art; (F) the amount of direction provided by the inventor; (G) the existence of working examples; and (H) the quantity of experimentation needed to make or use the invention based on the content of the disclosure.
guidance: Do not rely on a single factor to conclude nonenablement; weigh all factors and the evidence as a whole. Examiner must consider all evidence related to each factor and base any conclusion of nonenablement on the record as a whole. (Cites: In re Wands.)

name: Claim breadth vs enablement
description: A specification must teach how to make and/or use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; if it does not, enablement is lacking for the full scope.
guidance: When making an enablement rejection, explain why the scope of protection sought is not adequately enabled and provide specific findings of fact (e.g., missing information about essential parts or relationships). Identify information missing and why one skilled in the art could not supply it without undue experimentation. References should be supplied if possible to support a prima facie case. (See MPEP § 2164.06(a), In re Marzocchi.)

name: How to use the claimed invention (utility/use limitations)
description: If a statement of utility contains a connotation of how to use, or standard modes of administration are known and contemplated, 35 U.S.C. 112 is satisfied for 'how to use.'
guidance: Dosage or method need not be specified if one skilled in the art could obtain such information without undue experimentation based on knowledge of similar compounds. If claim is limited by a particular use, evaluate enablement based on that limitation. If claim is not limited by a use, any enabled use reasonably correlating with the entire scope is sufficient to preclude a nonenablement rejection. If multiple uses are disclosed, an enablement rejection must explain why the specification fails to enable each disclosed use. (Cites: In re Johnson; In re Hitchings; In re Brana; In re Vaeck.)

name: Working examples (presence and weight)
description: Compliance with enablement does not hinge on disclosure of examples; examples may be 'working' (based on actual work) or 'prophetic.' The specification need not contain an example if the invention is otherwise disclosed enablingly.
guidance: Lack of working examples is a factor to consider, especially in unpredictable/undeveloped arts, but absence should never be the sole reason for rejecting on enablement grounds. A single working example can preclude a rejection that nothing is enabled, but presence of only one example is not by itself a reason to reject claims as broader than the enabling disclosure. Examiner must evaluate whether extrapolation from the one example across the claim scope is reasonable and explain why not if rejecting. (Cites: Gould v. Quigg; In re Borkowski; In re Wands.)

name: Correlation of in vitro / in vivo examples
description: An in vitro or in vivo animal model example in the specification constitutes a 'working example' only if it 'correlates' with the disclosed or claimed method of use.
guidance: If the art recognizes a model as correlating to a specific condition, it should be accepted unless examiner has evidence it does not correlate. Examiner carries initial burden to give reasons for lack of correlation and must weigh evidence for and against correlation; rigorous exact correlation is not required. (Cites: In re Brana; Cross v. Iizuka.)

name: Predictability of the art (relationship to required disclosure)
description: The amount of guidance needed to enable the invention is inversely related to knowledge in the prior art and predictability in the art: the more predictable the art, the less explicit information needed in the specification.
guidance: Nascent or unpredictable technologies require more specific and useful teaching. In unpredictable arts (e.g., many chemical and physiological activities), disclosure of a single species usually does not support broad genus claims; in predictable arts (mechanical, electrical), a single embodiment may provide broad enablement. (Cites: In re Fisher; In re Vickers; In re Soll; Chiron v. Genentech.)

name: Burden on the examiner to support nonenablement
description: Before enabling analysis, examiner must construe the claims. The examiner has the initial burden to establish a reasonable basis to question the enablement provided for the claimed invention and must provide a reasonable explanation why the scope is not adequately enabled.
guidance: Examiner must set forth claim meanings when terms are ambiguous. To make a rejection, the examiner must explain why the examiner doubts the truth/accuracy of any supporting disclosure and back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning. Minimal requirement per In re Bowen: give reasons explaining uncertainty. Specific technical reasons are always required. Examiner should not base determination on one factor alone and must consider all evidence related to Wands factors. (Cites: Genentech v. Wellcome; In re Wright; In re Marzocchi; In re Bowen; In re Wands.)

name: Determination of enablement based on the evidence as a whole (applicant rebuttal)
description: Once examiner establishes a reasonable basis to question enablement, the burden falls on applicant to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs showing one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the application as a guide.
guidance: Applicant may submit affidavits/declarations (37 CFR 1.132) or cite references. Declarations are evidence whose weight depends on supporting factual detail; conclusory expert statements are insufficient. Examiner must compare conditions in post-filing declarations with the disclosure to ensure commensurate scope. Examiner must weigh all evidence (specification, applicant's new evidence, references/evidence in rejection) and decide based on the weight of the record, not personal opinion. (Cites: In re Brandstadter; In re Buchner; In re Alton; Scott v. Finney.)

name: Claim construction prior to enablement analysis
description: Before any enablement analysis, the examiner must construe the claims and, for ambiguous terms, select the definition intended for examination and explicitly set forth the meaning and scope in an Office action.
guidance: Claim construction sets the scope against which enablement is judged. For terms not well-known or having multiple meanings, the examiner's stated construction guides the enablement analysis and the rejection. (Cites: Genentech v. Wellcome.)

name: Compact prosecution / best-first Office action practice
description: In accordance with compact prosecution, if an enablement rejection is appropriate the first Office action on the merits should present the best case with all relevant reasons, issues, and evidence.
guidance: Provide the best rejection early so applicant can rebut; identify limitations that would render claims enabled and communicate enabled, allowable subject matter to applicant as early as possible. This helps allow subsequent Office actions to be final if applicant fails to rebut. Avoid expanding arguments in later Office actions unnecessarily. (Policy guidance in MPEP.)

name: Hierarchy of evidence: laws from experimentum crucis outrank testimonial/perceptual evidence
description: A law established by critical experiments (experimentum crucis) and repeated tests (excluding observer error) has such strength that any alleged single occurrence contradicting it (without counteracting cause) should be disbelieved unless evidence overturning the law is equivalent in strength.
guidance: If an antecedent A has been repeatedly shown to produce effect B, then an assertion that A occurred without B (and no counteracting cause) must be rejected unless evidence comparable to that which established the law is produced. Testimonial or perceptual claims are only approximate generalizations and are weaker.

name: Requirement to explain how pleaded patents disclose elements or negative novelty
description: In some courts (Northern District of Ohio) a bill of particulars will be required of the defendant setting forth in what respects each of the patents pleaded in the answer discloses any of the elements or combinations of elements described in the patent in suit, and in what respect they negative the novelty and invention of the device shown and described in the complainant's letters patent.
guidance: This operates to force mapping of prior patents to claim elements; tensions exist between this requirement and the traditional function of pleadings.

name: Use and scope of specific interrogatories under Equity Rule 58
description: Specific interrogatories have been retained as a separate procedure: the defendant may use interrogatories to sustain his defence as the plaintiff formerly could to sustain his bill; interrogatories permit discovery of facts and documents material to the support or defence of the cause.
guidance: Interrogatories are directed to facts/documents material to the party's own claims/defences and are not intended to enable a party to discover the evidence or witnesses the opponent will use solely to establish the opponent's case.

name: Interrogatories limited to facts/material documents supporting own claim or defence
description: Under the present rules, interrogatories are intended to allow discovery only of such facts and documents as will sustain the claims of the party filing the interrogatories (or his defence), not to ascertain matters relating exclusively to the opponent's title or ground of defence.
guidance: Courts reject interrogatories that would force a party to disclose his 'case' or matters having no relation to the interrogating party's ground of action or defence.

name: 35 U.S.C. 101 statutory baseline
description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
guidance: Use the statutory language as the baseline for patentable subject matter. Claims must be considered against this statutory text when determining eligibility under §101.

name: Abstract idea — Mental Processes grouping
description: If a claim limitation, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in the mind but for the recitation of generic computer components, then it falls within the 'Mental Processes' grouping of abstract ideas.
guidance: Evaluate whether the limitation (e.g., 'determining the amount of use of each icon' or 'ranking the icons based on the determined amount of use') could be performed manually or mentally. Examples: without 'by a processor', 'determining' could encompass a user manually calculating usage; 'ranking' could encompass a user thinking which icons are most used. If so, treat the limitation as an abstract idea in the Mental Processes category.

name: Broadest reasonable interpretation for mental-process analysis
description: Claim elements should be given their broadest reasonable interpretation to determine whether, absent the recitation of generic computer components, they cover activity that can be performed in the human mind.
guidance: Strip away generic computer-language (e.g., 'by a processor') when testing whether the recited step could reasonably be performed mentally. If the limitation still reads as a mental step, it supports classification as an abstract idea.

name: Integration into a practical application (significantly more test)
description: Determine whether the judicial exception (abstract idea) is integrated into a practical application; additional claim elements must do more than nominally recite generic technology and must impose meaningful limits on practicing the exception.
guidance: A claim that only adds a generic computer performing the abstract idea at a high level does not integrate the exception into a practical application. Look for elements that provide a technical solution, improve computer functionality, or impose concrete limits on how the abstract idea is applied. If additional elements 'amount to no more than mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component,' they do not supply 'significantly more.'

name: Generic computer components recited at a high level are insufficient
description: Reciting a processor (or other generic computer components) at a high level of generality, performing generic computer functions, amounts to mere instructions to apply the abstract idea using a generic computer and does not supply an inventive concept.
guidance: When a claim's only additional element is 'using a processor' to perform abstract-idea steps (e.g., ranking and determining), that high-level recitation 'does not impose any meaningful limits' and therefore cannot transform the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter. Examiners should reject claims that add only such generic computer implementation.

name: Mere instructions to apply the exception cannot provide an inventive concept
description: The presence of mere instructions to apply an abstract idea using a generic computer component cannot provide an inventive concept sufficient for patent eligibility.
guidance: Assess whether any claimed element contributes something more than conventional or generic implementation. If the claimed additional elements simply tell a practitioner to implement the abstract idea on a computer without more, they fail to supply the required 'significantly more.'

name: The invention (identify inventive concept / claim)
description: Identify the inventive concept of the claim in question or, if that cannot readily be done, construe it.
guidance: Determining 'what is the invention as claimed' is a prerequisite for obviousness. For each claim in issue determine the inventive concept; where the claim is a bare chemical formula or otherwise does not reveal inventiveness, it is acceptable to read the specification to determine the inventive concept (e.g., selection patents). For New Act patents consider s.28.3 requirements when assessing obviousness of the subject-matter defined by a claim.

name: Windsurfing four-step approach
description: A four-step methodology to structure the obviousness inquiry: (1)(a) identify the person skilled in the art; (1)(b) identify their common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept of the claim or construe it; (3) identify differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept; (4) consider whether those differences would have been obvious to the skilled person.
guidance: The Supreme Court of Canada endorsed the Windsurfing approach as a useful tool but not a mandatory, rigid test. Failure to explicitly follow the structure does not by itself amount to an error of law. The approach should be applied expansively and flexibly, taking into account any secondary considerations that prove instructive.

name: Inventive concept may require looking to the specification (selection patents special rule)
description: Where the claim language does not reveal inventiveness (e.g., bare formulas), it may be necessary to read the specification to determine the inventive concept, particularly for selection patents.
guidance: Sanofi accepted that the inventive concept can be found in the specification when claims are insufficient to reveal it. This can resurrect considerations akin to 'spirit of the invention' for the purpose of identifying inventive concept, but claim construction principles still delimit the monopoly; for New Act patents, s.28.3 frames obviousness with regard to prior disclosures.

name: Step 1: Statutory requirements and four categories of invention
description: Step 1: Statutory requirements and four categories of invention (posted September 24, 2015).
guidance: Determine whether the claimed subject matter satisfies statutory requirements and falls into one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). This is the initial statutory-category inquiry before applying judicial-exception analysis.

name: Steps 2A and 2B: Guidance overview
description: Guidance overview and steps 2A and 2B (computer based training & slides).
guidance: Step 2A: determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon). Step 2B: if a judicial exception is present, evaluate whether the additional claim elements amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (e.g., provide inventive concept). Use the two-step framework in the USPTO guidance to structure eligibility analysis.

name: Step 2A: Revised examination procedures (2019 PEG)
description: Step 2A: Revised examination procedures in view of the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (2019 PEG).
guidance: Apply the 2019 PEG procedures for identifying whether claims recite judicial exceptions and how to characterize those exceptions. The training focuses on how examiners should perform Step 2A under the revised procedures.

name: Evaluate Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Activity
description: Subject Matter Eligibility: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Activity (posted May 7, 2018).
guidance: Assess whether additional claim elements reflect activity that is well-understood, routine, and conventional to a skilled artisan at the time of the invention. If so, those elements may not supply the required 'significantly more' to render the claim patent eligible.

name: Use of analysis worksheets and answer keys for hypothetical claims
description: Hypothetical application, exemplary office action and applicant responsive remarks, and worksheets; worksheet answer keys; analysis worksheets for hypothetical claims 1 and 2.
guidance: Adopt structured worksheets to record Step 1/2A/2B analyses for specific claims. The training provides blank worksheets and answer keys to standardize reasoning and ensure all relevant factors are considered.

name: Domain-specific evaluation: life sciences (life-sciences workshops)
description: Life Sciences Workshop I materials (June 2016), for use with life sciences examples 28–33 (slides, handout, blank worksheet, worksheet answer keys).
guidance: Use life-sciences-specific examples and training to evaluate claims in biotech/medical fields, focusing on issues unique to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and diagnostic or therapeutic method claims under the eligibility framework.

name: Indicating determined state of the art per claim
description: For each claim that does not only contain commonly known facts, the determined state of the art has to be indicated.
guidance: The documents indicated by the applicant or registered proprietor shall be taken into consideration by the competent examining section; if needed, the applicant/registered proprietor shall be requested to provide the documents.

name: Selecting prior art for broad main claims
description: If, due to the broadness of the main claim, the state of the art to be cited is too broad, the state of the art shall be selected which comes closest to the subject matter of the invention taking into account restricting features of the dependent claims.
guidance: Description and drawings shall be considered for claim interpretation when selecting closest prior art.

name: Handling deficiencies preventing search
description: If a search on the subject matter or parts of it cannot be carried out due to deficiencies in the documents filed, this shall be included in the search report indicating the respective claims and giving the reasons why the search was not carried out.
guidance: State clearly which claims were affected and why; do not perform ungrounded examination-like assessments.

name: Search report — results with claim references (C)
description: The determined state of the art with reference to the respective numbers of the claims, if applicable, with explanations and references to relevant passages and drawings, shall be listed (table if necessary). No reference to claims shall be made in case of state of the art which cannot be attributed to any of the claims.
guidance: Publications are to be cited according to the two-letter country code pursuant to WIPO ST.3; include numbers and kind codes.

name: Subject matter not searched — notice and prohibition of examination-like statements (E)
description: If subject matter of claims under section 2 is not protectable or a search cannot be carried out for other reasons, a notice stating this and the reasons shall be included in the search report. Further references suggesting an examination-like assessment of the subject matter are not allowed.
guidance: Clearly indicate which claim items were not searched and why; avoid making patentability judgments.

name: Excess claims fees when adding claims
description: Applicant must pay excess claims fees for each claim that is in excess of 3 in independent form or in excess of 20 total claims; fees for a proper multiple dependent claim are calculated based on the number of claims to which it refers and a separate fee is required in each application containing a proper multiple dependent claim.
guidance: When adding new claims that increase the number beyond previously paid-for claims (after accounting for canceled claims), the required excess claims fees must be paid before the examiner considers the new claim. Nonelected claims withdrawn from consideration after a restriction requirement are included in fee determination unless canceled. See MPEP § 607 and 37 CFR 1.75(c).

name: Recommendation to file multiple claim breadths early
description: Applicants are encouraged to include, at filing or no later than the first reply, claims varying from the broadest to which they believe they are entitled to the most detailed claims they are willing to accept to alleviate prosecution difficulties after final rejection.
guidance: Providing a claim set with varying breadths reduces need for after-final amendments and simplifies prosecution.

name: Notification when proposed amendment not entered
description: If a proposed amendment does not place the case in better form for appeal nor in condition for allowance, applicant should be promptly informed (whenever possible within the statutory period); refusal to enter should not be arbitrary and should give sufficient consideration. Specific deficiencies need not always be discussed, but new matter must be identified and reasons concisely expressed.
guidance: Illustrative reasons for nonentry include: (A) amended claims would not avoid rejections; (B) amendment raises new matter; (C) amendment presents new issues requiring further consideration or search; (D) addition of claims without canceling finally rejected claims does not place case in better condition for appeal.

name: Scope and requirements for amendments after allowance (37 CFR 1.312)
description: Amendments after allowance include changes to specification, drawings, claims, inventorship, submission of prior art, correction of inventor name spelling/order, etc., and must comply with 37 CFR 1.312 and other applicable requirements (e.g., 1.121, 1.97, 1.98). An amendment under 1.312 must be filed on or before payment of the issue fee (except where required by Office of Data Management).
guidance: Primary examiners may enter amendments correcting merely formal matters without forwarding for supervisory approval; amendments affecting disclosure or claim scope or adding claims require supervisory approval. Entry may be recommended if amendment (A) is needed for proper disclosure or protection and (B) requires no substantial additional work by the Office.

name: Required statements accompanying amendments after allowance
description: For amendments affecting disclosure, scope of any claim, or adding a claim under 37 CFR 1.312, the remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: The requirements of 37 CFR 1.111(c) with respect to pointing out patentable novelty apply; see MPEP §§ 713.04 and 713.10 for interview guidance.

name: Purpose and limits of reissue
description: The jurisdiction to allow reissues exists solely to enable an inventor to correct a defective patent, not to extend an existing patent to new inventions or to cover inventions intentionally omitted from the original patent.
guidance: Claims of the reissue must be confined to inventions not advertently excluded from the original claims. A reissue that covers new matter must be cured by disclaimer or fails; if reissue claims matter disclosed but not claimed originally, the question of intentional exclusion and reasonable delay in seeking amendment arises.

name: Thirteenth defence: excessive claims and cure by disclaimer
description: Claim asserted to be excessive (covers more than the actual invention) and not cured by disclaimer within a reasonable time.
guidance: The court construes claims as a matter of law and instructs the jury on the nature of the invention; the jury determines if the claim includes more than the actual invention. Patent is prima facie evidence of correctness of the claim; defendant must prove the essential characteristics of the true invention showing the claim covers more. If disclaimer is filed promptly upon discovery the excess may be cured; plaintiff bears burden to show disclaimer filed without unreasonable delay or that reasonable time has not elapsed since discovery. An inventor is not chargeable with notice of excess until judicial interpretation, unless excess is evident on its face.

name: Fourteenth defence: ambiguity of claim (claim construction)
description: Claim is ambiguous when the court cannot ascertain from it what the patentee intended to protect; ambiguity is a question of law for the court.
guidance: Allowance by the Patent Office is prima facie that claims are not ambiguous, but courts will construe them and may consider extrinsic evidence (experts, persons in the art, Patent Office papers) at judicial discretion to render technical phraseology intelligible. When a claim depends on facts, the jury may be required to find those facts and then apply the court's construction.

name: Disclosure requirements for AI-related inventions (F-III-3; G-II-3.3.1)
description: AI inventions require supporting data and examples similar to biotech: mathematical methods and training datasets must be disclosed in sufficient detail to reproduce the technical effect over the whole range claimed; otherwise the disclosure may amount to an invitation to a research programme.
guidance: Guidelines quote: "Occasionally applications are filed in which there is a fundamental insufficiency... another example can be found in the field of artificial intelligence if the mathematical methods and the training datasets are disclosed in insufficient detail to reproduce the technical effect over the whole range claimed. Such a lack of detail may result in a disclosure that is more like an invitation to a research programme" (F-III-3). Also: "The technical effect that a machine learning algorithm achieves may be readily apparent or established by explanations, mathematical proof, experimental data or the like. While mere allegations are not enough, comprehensive proof is not required, either. If the technical effect is dependent on particular characteristics of the training dataset used, those characteristics that are required to reproduce the technical effect must be disclosed unless the skilled person can determine them without undue burden using common general knowledge. However, in general, there is no need to disclose the specific training dataset itself" (G-II-3.3.1). Practical takeaways: provide sufficient methodological detail and dataset-relevant characteristics; allegations alone insufficient; full dataset usually not required.

name: Antibodies — claiming genus by antigen/epitope; sufficiency and burden of proof (G-II-6.2)
description: At the EPO it is possible to claim a genus of antibodies according to their target antigen or epitope; the Guidelines clarify conditions when such claims are permitted, including sufficiency requirements and the burden of proof with respect to prior art antibodies.
guidance: Updates reflect Boards of Appeal case law. The Guidelines provide further clarification on sufficiency and on who bears the burden to show lack of novelty/obviousness based on prior-art antibodies. Note that specific guidance relating to defining antibodies by epitope has been removed (i.e., less prescriptive guidance on epitope-based definitions). Practitioners should ensure sufficiency across claimed genus and be prepared to address prior‑art antibody comparisons and proof burdens.

name: Adaptation of the description when claims are amended (D-V-5)
description: The description of the patent may be examined for compliance with Art. 84 only when, and then only to the extent that, an amendment of the patent introduces non-compliance with Art. 84; inconsistencies between description and claims resulting from amendments during opposition proceedings and casting doubt on the subject-matter for which protection is sought must be avoided.
guidance: Quote from Guidelines: "the description of the patent may be examined for compliance with the requirements of Art. 84 only when, and then only to the extent that, an amendment of the patent introduces non-compliance with Art. 84. In particular, inconsistencies between the description and the claims resulting from amendments during opposition proceedings and casting doubt on the subject‑matter for which protection is sought must be avoided" (D‑V‑5). Context: controversy exists over requiring applicants to amend descriptions to align with allowed claims; a referral on the legality of forcing such amendments is pending. Practically, when claims are amended during opposition applicants should check and, where necessary, adapt the description to avoid inconsistencies that cause doubt about the scope.

name: Basis of the international preliminary examination report (Rule 70.2)
description: Sets the basis on which the report shall be issued: (a) if claims have been amended, the report issues on claims as amended; (b) if established as if priority had not been claimed under Rule 66.7(a) or (b), the report shall so indicate; (c) if any amendment goes beyond disclosure in the application as filed the report shall be established as if such amendment had not been made and shall indicate reasons; (c‑bis) where replacement sheets lack required letter indicating basis for amendment, report may be established as if amendment had not been made and shall indicate that; (d) if claims concern inventions without an international search report, the report shall so indicate; (e) if rectification of an obvious mistake is taken into account under Rule 66.1 the report shall so indicate (and if not taken into account pursuant to Rule 66.4bis the report shall indicate this if possible or IB shall be notified); (f) the report shall indicate the date on which a top‑up search under Rule 66.1ter was made or state that no top‑up search was made.
guidance: Contains multiple specific procedural markers the Authority must state in the report (amendment status, priority handling, beyond‑disclosure findings, rectifications, top‑up search).

name: Two-stage patent classification workflow (CPC + claim indicators)
description: The USPTO currently classifies patents using a two-stage process: first assign a set of Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) symbols to each patent; second determine the subset of CPC symbols ('claim indicators') associated with claim scope.
guidance: AI systems for classification should reflect this two-stage workflow; the USPTO has deployed ML to assign claim indicators and is augmenting models to assign full CPC sets, typically trained on annotated USPTO patent data.

name: Use curated, annotated USPTO corpora to train practical IP tools
description: The USPTO and commercial developers have used publicly-available USPTO data to train AI models that provide capabilities to IP software products (e.g., claim-indicator assignment, portfolio intelligence).
guidance: For production tools aimed at practitioners, train models on annotated USPTO data and validate on use-cases such as examiner search augmentation, claim scope identification, and portfolio analytics.

name: Purpose and legal effect of publication
description: Publication of a patent application in the official journal/gazette (paper or electronic) serves to make the application prior art, enable public monitoring and filings of observations/oppositions/revocations, and, in some AMS, triggers provisional protection and liability for damages from the publication date.
guidance: Generally, pending applications do not create infringement liability, but certain AMS provide provisional protection and claim to damages from publication—see national provisions (Paragraph 3.9).

name: Contents of patent gazette/bulletin publication
description: Publication must include title, description, claims, most representative drawings filed (if any), any sequence listing filed at filing date, late-filed missing parts (if not withdrawn and not introducing new matter), applicant name/address, inventor(s), patent agent (if any), priority application number/date (if any).
guidance: Amendments that introduced new matter outside the disclosure as filed are not included in publication. Specific contents published vary by AMS and are detailed in CSR Annexes.

name: Amendment of claims of published applications (pre-grant)
description: Amending claims of a published patent application before grant is normal but amendments must not introduce subject-matter extending beyond the initial application's disclosure and must not create clarity issues or other objections.
guidance: An amendment is unallowable if the overall content change is not directly and unambiguously derivable by the person skilled in the art. Obvious clarifications in context may be permitted. A request to limit an already allowable claim, or to improve clarity, is normally allowed. Substantial claim limitation raises special considerations: unity of invention and alignment between description and claims. Re-publication after amendment is not generally required (except Viet Nam); Singapore posts amendments to the dossier.

name: Substantive examination purpose and scope (overview)
description: Substantive examination involves prior art search and assessment of patentability: novelty, inventive step, industrial application, excluded subject-matter, sufficiency (enablement), clarity of claims, unity of invention, and that amendments do not go beyond original disclosure.
guidance: If objections are raised, examiners invite applicants to amend and/or explain; if objections are overcome a patent is granted, otherwise refused. Most AMS conduct search and examination directly; some outsource search/examination to other capable offices.

name: Modified examination relying on foreign granted patents
description: Some AMS allow replacement of part or all of national search/examination by evidence that equivalent work has been done by a recognised foreign patent office (e.g., amendment to match granted specification and evidence of grant).
guidance: The specification must be amended to be substantially the same as the specification and claims of the granted counterpart and evidence of the granted patent filed; the local examiner will then examine the application.

name: Scope of substantive examination — patentable subject matter
description: Examination includes determination of whether claimed subject-matter is excluded from patentable subject matter (e.g., abstract theories, discoveries, methods of treatment).
guidance: Assessments of excluded subject-matter are complex and are typically handled during substantive examination by examiners experienced in patentability conditions; see Chapter 5 for details.

name: Scope of substantive examination — clarity of invention (claims)
description: Clarity of the application, especially the claims, is vital; meaning of claim terms should be clear to the person skilled in the art from the claim wording alone.
guidance: Clarity affects assessment of novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability; see Chapter 7 for details.

name: Scope of substantive examination — inventive step (non-obviousness)
description: The claimed invention must involve an inventive step; it must not be obvious to a person skilled in the art with regard to prior art on the effective filing/priority date.
guidance: Inventive step analysis is jurisdiction-dependent; see Chapter 11 for methodology and examples.

name: Options for expediting substantive examination (PPH and regional programmes)
description: Applicants may accelerate examination via Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) bilateral programmes, regional PPH (ASPEC) programmes, PCT-ASPEC, and national/bilateral acceleration schemes.
guidance: Under PPH, if corresponding claims are found patentable by an earlier office, applicants may request accelerated examination at the later office which can use prior work product. Regional ASPEC programmes and national fast-track schemes (Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore) have specific eligibility criteria, caps, fees, tech-field restrictions and procedural conditions (e.g., applicant reasons, claim caps, entity caps). National programmes may impose additional conditions, response deadlines, and expected grant timelines (examples provided for Thailand, Singapore).

name: Specified time limits for particular actions (not shortened statutory periods)
description: The examiner may specify a time for applicant to take some action where failure results in a consequence other than abandonment. Specified time limits can be less than the 30-day statutory minimum and are used in situations such as: (A) petition under 37 CFR 1.14(a) for access — usually 3 weeks to state objections; (B) completion of an IDS where part omitted — 1-month time limit; (C) cancelling claims to nonelected invention or petitioning restriction — e.g., 2 months; (D) requiring an added claim to provoke an interference — period not less than one month.
guidance: Failure to timely comply with a specified time limit generally will not result in abandonment but will have specific consequences (e.g., Office will decide petition without applicant input, noncomplying IDS information will be placed in file but not considered, cancellation treated as authorization). Specified time limits should be used where failure will not produce abandonment; if the failure could result in abandonment, a time period should be set that is not subject to extensions under 37 CFR 1.136 when appropriate.

name: Exceptions to availability of 37 CFR 1.136(a) extensions
