description: Extensions with payment of a fee under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are not available in certain situations, including: (A) all extensions in a reexamination proceeding; (B) all extensions during an interference proceeding (but not preparatory to an interference where a claim is suggested); (C) situations where an Office action states 1.136(a) is not applicable (e.g., reply to notice of allowability, reissue applications associated with litigation, or where nonelected claims/time set to cancel such claims); (D) limited instances where applicant is given a specified time limit to take certain actions.
guidance: Cross-reference applicable CFR sections and MPEP chapters (ex parte reexamination, inter partes reexamination, interferences) to determine whether (a) is applicable. If (a) is not available, consider (b) or other remedies.

name: Defenses to patent infringement
description: Available defenses include showing patent invalidity on grounds that the invention is not new or patentable, insufficient disclosure, or contrary to public order/morality; prior user defense; government-authorized use.
guidance: Good faith is not a defense unless claiming prior user status under Sections 73 or 159 or when specific damages provisions apply (Sections 76, 156, 216).

name: Costs of enforcement and fee recovery
description: Costs depend on the type of action elected by the IPR holder; for ordinary civil actions for damages, the IPR holder pays necessary filing fees, which depend on the amount of damages claimed.
guidance: No single fixed schedule provided here; other court rules and fee schedules determine exact costs. Recovery of costs may depend on the forum and claims for litigation expenses/damages.

name: CREATE Act / Joint Research Agreement (JRA) statement requirements (37 CFR 1.104(c)(4))
description: To invoke prior art disqualification under the CREATE Act, applicant must submit a statement that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3), that the JRA was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
guidance: The statement should be on or begin on a separate sheet, must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)), and must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). In addition to amending the specification to disclose the names of the JRA parties, the required statement must be submitted to properly invoke disqualification.

name: JRA timing and scope requirements for disqualification
description: To disqualify a reference under the JRA provisions of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the joint research agreement must be in effect on or before the date the later invention was made, and the claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
guidance: Examples: (1) JRA in effect before invention and invention arises from JRA activities—disqualification possible; (2) JRA effective after invention date—cannot invoke JRA disqualification; (3) JRA limited to unrelated activities (e.g., covers invention Y but not X)—cannot invoke JRA disqualification. Ownership of inventions by separate parties does not, by itself, prevent invoking 103(c) if other requirements met.

name: Form paragraph 7.20.02 — Joint inventors; common ownership presumed
description: When an application currently names joint inventors, the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time the inventions were made absent evidence to the contrary.
guidance: Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and invention dates for claims not commonly owned so the examiner can consider applicability of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential 102(e),(f) or (g) prior art under 103(a). This paragraph must be used in all applications with joint inventors (unless claims are clearly restricted to only one claimed invention).

name: Form paragraph 7.21 — Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (general)
description: Use to reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over cited art.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.20 or 7.103. An explanation applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow. If the rejection relies on prior art under 102(e), follow AIPA rules to determine the reference’s prior art date (with exceptions noted). If the rejection is a provisional 103(a) rejection based on a copending application, use paragraph 7.21.01 instead. If the applicability of the rejection prevents disqualification under 103(c), follow with 7.20.01.

name: Form paragraph 7.21.01 — Provisional 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection (common assignee or at least one common inventor)
description: Used to provisionally reject claims not patentably distinct from a copending application having an earlier U.S. filing date and either a common assignee or at least one common inventor; the copending application would constitute prior art under 102(e) if published or patented.
guidance: This provisional rejection may be overcome by (1) a 37 CFR 1.132 showing of derivation, (2) a 37 CFR 1.131 showing of a date of invention prior to the copending application’s effective U.S. filing date, or (3) showing that the copending application is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Do not use 7.21.01 where the copending application is disqualified under 103(c) as of Dec 10, 2004. Use AIPA rules to determine 102(e) dates where applicable.

name: Form paragraph 7.22 — 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection, further in view of
description: Used to reject a claim under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over a primary reference as applied to another claim and further in view of an additional reference.
guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21. An explanation applying the Graham v. Deere test must follow. If relying on 102(e) prior art, use AIPA rules to determine the prior art date where applicable.

name: When to use a combined 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) rejection (¶ 7.27) and illustrative circumstances
description: Paragraph 7.27 may be used to reject a claim under 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) or alternatively under 103(a) as obvious. It is not intended for common use as a substitute for making the appropriate single rejection; a single rejection under 102 or 103(a) should be made whenever possible.
guidance: Circumstances where 7.27 may be used include: (a) disputed claim interpretation where one interpretation yields 102 and another 103, (b) reference discloses all limitations except a property/function and examiner cannot determine inherent possession, (c) genus teaches a small genus placing the claimed species in the public, (d) product-by-process where product appears same despite different process, (e) means-plus-function uncertainty whether referenced element is equivalent or obvious variant, and (f) overlapping ranges where reference lacks a specific example in claimed range. A full explanation must follow the paragraph; if claim interpretation renders claims indefinite, consider a 112 rejection.

name: Claim limitation relating to a tax strategy deemed within the prior art (¶ 7.06)
description: A claim limitation interpreted as a strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability ('tax strategy') is deemed to be within the prior art pursuant to Section 14 of the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act.
guidance: When a limitation is so interpreted, recite the limitation in bracket 1 and the affected claim numbers in bracket 2; see USPTO memorandum 'Tax Strategies Are Deemed To Be Within the Prior Art' (Sept. 20, 2011) for more information.

name: Determination of Novelty (general rule)
description: The examiner shall determine novelty by judging whether the claimed invention falls under inventions categorized in Article 29(1) subparagraphs (1) to (2). If it falls under those categories, the invention is not novel; otherwise it is novel.
guidance: Claims must describe the subject matter for which protection is sought (Article 42(4)). Identicalness of invention is determined by identicalness of matters described in the claims. Each claim is judged separately when there are multiple claims in an application.

name: General Principle of Defining the Claimed Invention (claim language clear)
description: When the claim language is clear, defining the claimed invention should be made as recited in the claim. Terminology in claims is interpreted with the general meaning and scope generally accepted in the technical field, except where a specific meaning is explicitly defined in the description.
guidance: Interpretation should be objective and reasonable considering ordinary skill at filing. Avoid limiting a clear claim by reference to description/drawings unless the claim itself requires it.

name: Avoiding Undue Limitation by Description or Drawings
description: Where claim description is clear, an examiner should avoid limited interpretation just by referencing the description of the invention or drawings. Matters not described in the claims but only in the description/drawings should be considered as not recited in the claims.
guidance: An examiner should not examine claims by applying subject matters not described in the claims. Examples: (i) 'cream' in claims should not be limited to a specific embodiment in description; (ii) 'thin film type probe' claim should not be limited to a specific pattern shown in the embodiment; (iii) rotation direction shown in drawings does not limit claim if not claimed.

name: Identification of a judicial exception at Step 2A
description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale that identifies the judicial exception recited in the claim and explains why it is considered a judicial exception.
guidance: There is no requirement for the examiner to rely on evidence, such as publications, to find that a claim is directed to a judicial exception. Examiners may cite relevant case law where courts identified similar exceptions (e.g., Affinity Labs, OIP, Content Extraction).

name: Evidence not required for Step 2B findings but may be used
description: At Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the claim does not recite significantly more than the judicial exception (e.g., that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities).
guidance: If available, sources of evidence can support assertions or rebut applicant arguments. Examples: specification statements that elements are conventional, manuals/handbooks showing conventional computer components/functions, patents describing background conventional components, and court decisions. Ensure case-law facts comport with application facts before citing.

name: Burden shifts to applicant after examiner identifies judicial exception
description: After examiners identify and explain the reasons why a claim is directed to an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to either amend the claim or make a showing why the claim is eligible for patent protection.
guidance: Applicant may amend claims (add/modify elements) and/or present persuasive arguments or evidence. Examiners must carefully consider all applicant arguments and evidence rebutting the eligibility rejection and, if claims are amended, determine the amended claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and redo the eligibility analysis.

name: When to withdraw the rejection
description: If applicant's amendment(s) and/or argument(s) persuasively establish that the claim is not directed to a judicial exception or is directed to significantly more than a judicial exception, the rejection should be withdrawn.
guidance: Applicant can argue that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more when additional elements are considered both individually and in combination. Examiners must consider both individual and combined effects of added elements.

name: What may qualify as 'significantly more' individually
description: An additional element individually may be enough to qualify as 'significantly more' if it meaningfully limits the judicial exception.
guidance: Examples include: it improves another technology or technical field; it improves the functioning of a computer itself; it adds well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field; or it adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application. (Note: examiners should be mindful that well-understood/routine/conventional additions ordinarily will not supply 'significantly more' unless they meaningfully limit the exception.)

name: Combination of generic elements can produce 'significantly more'
description: Even if an element does not amount to significantly more on its own (e.g., because it is merely a generic computer component performing generic functions), it can still amount to significantly more when considered in combination with other claim elements.
guidance: Generic computer components that individually perform generic functions (e.g., CPU performing calculations, clock producing time data) in combination may perform functions that are not generic computer functions and therefore amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.

name: Handling applicant challenges to identification of an abstract idea based on case law
description: If applicant challenges the identification of an abstract idea that was based on a court case and the challenge is not persuasive, the examiner should explain why the abstract idea identified in the claim is similar to the concept in the cited case.
guidance: If the original rejection did not identify a Supreme Court or Federal Circuit decision where a similar abstract idea was found and applicant challenges the identification, the examiner needs to point to such a case and explain why the claim's abstract idea corresponds to that in the case. Adding citation to support the original rationale is not a new ground unless the basic thrust of the rejection changes.

name: Claims amended to add generic computer or 'specially programmed' computer
description: If applicant amends a claim to add a generic computer or generic computer components and asserts that the claim recites significantly more because the generic computer is 'specially programmed' or is a 'particular machine', the examiner should evaluate whether the added elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Merely adding a generic computer, generic computer components, or a programmed computer to perform generic computer functions does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection (see Alice and related cases). Examine the actual added functionality and whether it meaningfully limits the exception or is merely conventional.

name: Consideration of preemption arguments
description: If applicant argues that the claim is specific and does not preempt all applications of the exception, the examiner should reconsider Step 2A (is the claim directed to an improvement to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology?) and, if still directed to an exception, reconsider Step 2B (do additional elements amount to an inventive concept?).
guidance: Although preemption is not a standalone test for eligibility, it remains the underlying concern driving the two-part framework from Alice and Mayo. Reconsider both steps with an eye to whether claim scope meaningfully limits the exception and avoids preemption.

name: Clarifying the record when claims are eligible
description: When the claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record to explain the basis for eligibility or to identify the portion of the specification that describes the claimed improvement.
guidance: Clarifying remarks can be made at any point during prosecution, including with a notice of allowance. Examples include noting the specification portion describing the improvement and claim elements producing that improvement, or explaining the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of a claim to assist applicant in responding to rejections (e.g., BRI of a computer-readable-medium claim may cover a carrier wave).

name: Initial claim and specification review for utility
description: Read the claims and the supporting written description to determine what the applicant has claimed, noting any specific embodiments, and ensure the claims define statutory subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvement).
guidance: If at any time it becomes readily apparent that the claimed invention has a well-established utility, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility. A well-established utility exists if (i) a person of ordinary skill in the art would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on the invention's characteristics, and (ii) the utility is specific, substantial, and credible.

name: Assessment of asserted specific and substantial utility
description: Review the claims and supporting description to determine if the applicant has asserted any specific and substantial utility that is credible for the claimed invention.
guidance: If applicant has asserted a credible specific and substantial utility, do not reject for lack of utility. Credibility is assessed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in view of the disclosure and any other evidence of record (e.g., test data, declarations, patents, publications). Applicant need only provide one credible assertion for each claimed invention.

name: Rejecting when no credible specific/substantial utility or no well-established utility
description: If no assertion of specific and substantial utility is credible, and the invention does not have a readily apparent well-established utility, reject the claim(s) under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and also reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112) for failing to teach how to use the invention.
guidance: The 112 rejection imposed in conjunction with the 101 rejection should incorporate by reference the grounds of the 101 rejection. These rejections shift the burden to the applicant to (i) explicitly identify a specific and substantial utility, and (ii) provide evidence that a POSITA would have recognized that the identified utility was well-established at the time of filing. Ensure an adequate nexus between evidence and properties of the claimed subject matter as disclosed in the application as filed.

name: Content of a utility rejection (prima facie showing)
description: Any rejection based on lack of utility should include a detailed explanation why the claimed invention has no specific and substantial credible utility.
guidance: Whenever possible, provide documentary evidence (scientific/technical journals, treatises, patents) to support factual basis for the prima facie showing. If documentary evidence is not available, specifically explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions. The prima facie showing must: (i) clearly set forth reasoning used; (ii) provide support for factual findings; and (iii) evaluate all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art.

name: Applicant's burden to rebut a prima facie utility rejection
description: Once a proper prima facie showing of no specific and substantial credible utility has been established, the applicant bears the burden of rebutting it.
guidance: Applicant may rebut by amending claims, providing reasoning/arguments, or submitting evidence (declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, patents, printed publications). Examiners should review original disclosure, evidence relied upon, claim amendments, and any new reasoning/evidence, and must recognize, fully consider, and respond to each substantive element of the applicant's response. If rebuttal is satisfactory, withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and the corresponding 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection.

name: Specific utility standard
description: A 'specific utility' is specific to the subject matter claimed and provides a well-defined and particular benefit to the public.
guidance: Distinguish specific uses from general utility statements. Examples of insufficient specificity: indicating a compound may be useful in treating unspecified disorders, describing a polynucleotide merely as a 'gene probe' without a specific DNA target, or general diagnostic utility without identifying the condition. Assertions that reasonably correlate a disclosed biological activity to a disease condition can be sufficient.

name: Substantial utility standard
description: 'Substantial utility' requires the asserted use to show a significant and presently available benefit to the public; utilities that require further research to identify or confirm a real-world context are not substantial.
guidance: Examples that are not substantial utilities include: basic research into properties/mechanisms, methods to treat unspecified diseases, assays that identify materials having no specific/substantial utility, methods of making materials that lack utility, and claims to intermediate products intended for making a final product that lacks utility. Do not require that products/services be currently available to the public; any reasonable use that provides a public benefit is acceptable.

name: Treatment of applications filed without drawings when something can be construed as a written description
description: A nonprovisional application (filed prior to Dec. 18, 2013) or design application having at least one claim, or a provisional application having some disclosure, directed to subject matter usually not requiring drawings, filed without drawings but containing something that can be construed as a written description, will be processed (i.e., accorded a filing date) so long as there is something that can be construed as a written description.
guidance: If the Technology Center determines drawings are necessary under 35 U.S.C. 113, the filing date issue will be reconsidered and the application may be returned to OPAP for mailing of a 'Notice of Incomplete Application.'

name: Limitations on enlarging purchase price after lump-sum acquisition or recovering for acreage shortage
description: Where part of a tract was purchased for a lump consideration described as containing '150 acres, more or less' and later more acreage was found, the Secretary could not legally add to the purchase price to procure the addition (this would amount to satisfying a claim). Where lands were purchased in gross and a later survey showed shortage of acreage, absent fraud the United States could not recover for the shortfall.
guidance: Citations: C. 9469 (Jan. 3, 1901); C. 24464 (Sept. 5 and 23, 1911). Practical implication: lump-sum purchases generally stand; buy-by-acre agreements differ.

name: Adverse possession/prescription does not run against the sovereign; statutes of limitation not binding on U.S.
description: It is well settled that adverse possession cannot give title as against the Government; while the United States may avail itself of statutes of limitation, it is not bound thereby. Thus long continued occupancy by private parties gives them no title against U.S.
guidance: Citations: C. 1069 (Mar. 13, 1895); C. 9003 (Oct. 3, 1900); authorities cited (Lindsey v. Miller, Jordan v. Barrett, etc.). Practical effect: claims by prescription against government lands generally fail.

name: Explain benefits of the invention over the prior art
description: Clearly illustrate the benefits of the claimed technology compared to the prior art in patent applications and specifications.
guidance: The Federal Circuit found that explaining the benefits of the invention helps get past motions to dismiss even if it may not ensure Section 101 validity. Judges look to the specification for information showing why patents are different from the prior art; there is a 'heightened standard' in practice. Drafting applications to explain advantages and improvements is recommended.

name: Plead plausible, factual allegations of inventive concepts in complaints
description: Include plausible and factual allegations in complaints that the claims recite inventive concepts or improvements over the prior art.
guidance: The Federal Circuit reversed a dismissal because the complaint contained plausible factual allegations that claims included inventive concepts. Well-pleaded allegations of an inventive concept can be enough to survive a motion to dismiss under Section 101.

name: Anticipate and rebut defendants' Section 101 arguments
description: Proactively anticipate common defendant arguments (e.g., that innovations are not inventive because only standard computer elements are claimed) and rebut them in pleadings and briefs.
guidance: Counsel can cite this case to counter claims that purported inventions lack inventiveness because they use standard computing equipment. Anticipatory arguments and tailored explanations of improvements can blunt such defenses.

name: Burden of Proof for Invalidity (clear and convincing)
description: [The Defendant] must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
guidance: Claims of an issued patent may be found invalid, but the defendant bears the heightened burden of clear and convincing evidence for each asserted claim. This burden never changes regardless of whether the Patent Examiner considered the reference. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i and related guidance.)

name: Prior Art Defined (AIA)
description: Prior art includes: anything that was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public anywhere in the world before the effective filing date of claim(s) ___; and anything that was described in a patent, or in an application for patent published or deemed published, in which the patent or application names another inventor and was filed before the effective filing date of claim(s) ___.
guidance: Identify items contended as prior art. Use the effective filing date of the claims when determining AIA prior art. (Statutory cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102 as amended by the AIA; 35 U.S.C. § 100(i); Helsinn v. Teva.)

name: Exceptions to Prior Art (AIA limited exceptions)
description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art if: A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or person who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from such inventor; or B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from such inventor. Additional exceptions: disclosure obtained from inventor; subject matter and claimed invention owned by same person or subject to same obligation of assignment.
guidance: If factual issues (e.g., whether public availability results from a disclosure within one year by inventor or derived from inventor, or ownership/assignment questions) exist, instruct the jury on these specific exceptions under § 102(b) and (c) as needed.

name: Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art (POSITA) Standard
description: Invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the [time of the invention/effective filing date].
guidance: Use this POSITA perspective when evaluating anticipation, obviousness, enablement, and what a prior reference would have conveyed to one of ordinary skill. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 103; KSR.)

name: Prior Public Use (pre-AIA) — definition and readiness for patenting
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid because the invention defined in that claim(s) was publicly used by others in the United States before [Cutoff Date]. An invention was publicly used in the U.S. if an embodiment was both: (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the United States, and (2) ready for patenting.
guidance: Factors relevant to determining public use include nature of the public activity, public access, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation, and circumstances of testing/experimentation. To be ready for patenting, the invention must be reduced to practice or the inventor must have prepared drawings/descriptions enabling a POSITA to make or use it. Reduction to practice requires constructing an embodiment or performing a process and determining that it works for its intended purpose. (Cites: pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(a),(b); Pfaff; cases.)

name: Prior Public Use (AIA) — worldwide public use / commercial exploitation
description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid because the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before [effective filing date]. An invention was in public use if the claimed invention was accessible to the public or commercially exploited anywhere in the world.
guidance: Public use is use by the inventor or by a person not under secrecy obligations; absence of affirmative steps to conceal is evidence of public use. Commercial exploitation (e.g., selling a product made using an invention or promoting a product embodying an invention) can be public use even if specifics kept secret. To be a public use the invention also must have been ready for patenting (reduced to practice or enabling drawings). (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) (AIA).)

name: Statement of Claim — Patent infringement (form)
description: Model Statement of Claim in an action for infringement of a patent.
guidance: Must identify the defendant's infringement of the plaintiff's Patent No., grant term and grant date, state plaintiff was first inventor, claim injunction to restrain further infringement and a sum for damages, deliver particulars of breaches, and specify place of trial. (Form based on Rules of the Supreme Court, 1883.)

name: Particulars and Notice of Breaches (attachment to claim)
description: Details to accompany Statement of Claim setting out particulars and notice of breaches as required by statute.
guidance: Should state that defendants have at divers times between certain dates infringed the patent by manufacture, sale, or use or imitation of the invention/ specification; if precise days/amounts unknown, advise plaintiffs will claim full compensation when ascertained and may claim an account and payment of all profits and an injunction against repetition and continuance of infringements.

name: Particulars and Notice of Objections (attachment to defence)
description: Particulars of objections the defendant will rely on at trial, delivered with the Statement of Defence.
guidance: Enumerated objections include: no infringement; plaintiff not first inventor; invention not new; not proper subject of letters patent; patent for a principle only (not a manner of new manufacture); claim is a principle of applying old contrivances to new objects; invention not useful; specification fails to describe/ascertain nature or manner of performance; invention does not produce described effects; specification not enabling to a person of reasonable skill; some alternative methods described are impracticable; omission of necessary steps/processes; specification fails to distinguish claimed from admitted-old matters; invention generally known prior to grant; prior use; prior publication in UK; prior manufacture and sale by others. The form may cite specific publications, dates, and reliance upon whole specification.

name: Notice re prior art available under both pre‑AIA and AIA (¶ 15.10.15)
description: When the determination of whether an application is subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 is incorrect, correction of statutory basis will not be a new ground of rejection if prior art and rationale would be the same under either status.
guidance: Must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013 that claims priority to, or the benefit of, an application filed before March 16, 2013. Use only once in an Office action.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) Rejection (AIA) - Anticipation by another's patent/application (¶ 15.15.aia)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by a patent or an application published or deemed published under section 122(b) that names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
guidance: Identify the reference in the bracket. For claims with priority to earlier filings, precede with 15.10.aia and 15.10.15. This rejection may be overcome by specific showings (e.g., derivation, priority/benefit claims, prior public disclosure, common ownership statements).

name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) Rejection - Not invented by applicant (¶ 15.16.fti)
description: The claim is rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 because applicant did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented.
guidance: State the basis supporting conclusion that applicant is not the inventor in the bracketed explanation.

name: 35 U.S.C. 102(g) Rejection - Prior invention by another (¶ 15.17.aia / ¶ 15.17.fti)
description: The claim is rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (g) because, before the applicant’s invention thereof, the invention was made in this country by another who had not abandoned, suppressed or concealed it. (AIA form notes similar contexts where pre‑AIA claims are present.)
guidance: If application claims or previously contained claims with effective filing dates before March 16, 2013, precede with appropriate form paragraphs (15.10.aia or 15.10.fti and 15.10.15). Explain supporting evidence in bracketed text.

name: Identical claim: common assignee — priority/identical-invention issue (¶ 15.24.05.fti)
description: When a claim is directed to the same invention as that of the claim of a commonly assigned copending application, the issue of priority under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g) must be resolved, and the assignee is required to state which entity is the prior inventor of the conflicting subject matter.
guidance: A terminal disclaimer has no effect on this priority‑of‑invention refusal. Failure to state the prior inventor will result in holding the application abandoned. Include this paragraph after the form paragraph setting forth the 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection.

name: Provisional pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection — design disclosed but not claimed in copending application (¶ 15.15.02.fti)
description: Provisionally reject under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) when a copending application (with common inventor/assignee) discloses the claimed design but does not claim it, based on a presumption of future publication or patenting.
guidance: Suggest possible ways to overcome: (A) show under 37 CFR 1.132 that the design was derived from the designer of this application; (B) show a date of invention prior to the reference under 37 CFR 1.131(a); (C) perfect priority under 35 U.S.C. 119; or (D) perfect benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 with specific reference filings complying with 37 CFR 1.78 and enablement/description requirements. Terminal disclaimer cannot overcome (In re Bartfeld). Also follow guidance for determining the proper 102(e) date (AIPA/pre‑AIPA nuances).

name: Nonobviousness evaluation — Graham factual inquiries applied to design patents (§ 1504.03 introductory)
description: The basic factual inquiries from Graham v. John Deere (1966) apply to design patent nonobviousness: (A) determine scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertain differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (C) resolve the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (D) evaluate any objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations).
guidance: Use these four inquiries to gather facts. After fact‑finding, determine whether a prima facie case of obviousness exists by checking whether all claim limitations are taught or suggested by the prior art and whether the overall appearance would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill.

name: Differences between prior art and claimed design — identify all differences and address de minimis distinctions (§ 1504.03 B)
description: All differences between the claimed design and the closest prior art reference should be identified in any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103. Mere existence of differences is not alone sufficient for patentability.
guidance: If any differences are considered de minimis or inconsequential from a design viewpoint, the rejection should state that. Cite relevant case law (e.g., In re Lamb) when explaining why differences do or do not support patentability.

name: Prima facie obviousness for design claims — overall appearance and claim limitation teaching
description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness for a design claim, the overall appearance of the design must be considered and all claim limitations must be taught or suggested by the prior art. The proper standard is whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill with the claimed type of article.
guidance: After applying the Graham inquiries and considering analogous arts and secondary considerations, determine whether the combined prior art would cause a designer of ordinary skill to arrive at the claimed overall appearance. If so, a prima facie case of obviousness is established.

name: Evidentiary Support and Burden of Proof
description: Claims in a request for reconsideration must be supported by evidence and authority; unsupported allegations will not overcome unrebutted record evidence.
guidance: When challenging factual findings (e.g., sufficiency of bank funds, issuance of debit/credit cards, calculation of fees), the appellant must submit corroborating documents (bank statements, correspondence) and show why such evidence was not available earlier. Unrebutted hearing evidence will control unless credible new proof is provided.

name: Product of nature rejection requirement
description: When rejecting a claim as a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as it is recited in the claim (i.e., set forth or described) and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: Explain the comparison to the closest naturally occurring counterpart (e.g., isolated X vs X in natural state). Cite MPEP § 2106.04(b) (products of nature) and MPEP § 2106.04(c) (markedly different characteristics analysis). Provide a sample explanation demonstrating identification of recited exception and rationale (structure, function, properties).

name: Explain why additional claim elements do not add significantly more (Step 2B)
description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and explain why they do not add significantly more to the exception.
guidance: Address additional elements both individually and as a combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. Note that a new combination may be patent eligible even though each step was known individually (Diamond v. Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05 for considerations courts have found to qualify or not as 'significantly more.'

name: Rejection only when readily apparent to examiner expertise
description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise in the art in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to claiming significantly more than the recited judicial exception.
guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why additional elements provide an inventive concept by meaningfully limiting the judicial exception.

name: Explain conventionality with reasoned rationale
description: When concluding particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection should explain why courts or those in the relevant field would recognize those claim limitations as such.
guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation supporting the conclusion that the element is well-understood, routine, conventional. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) for more on well-understood, routine, conventional activities and elements; consider citing examples or sources when appropriate.

name: Generic computer components/functionality guidance
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: MPEP § 2106.05(d) lists computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood/routine when claimed generically. Do not assume all computer functions are conventional; assess whether generic components in combination perform non-generic functions (DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more on generic computing functions as mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer.

name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use linking
description: Claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, storing data) or merely link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment/field of use generally do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Provide examples (storing data after computing a mathematical relationship does not add meaningful limitation; limiting to particular industry insufficient per Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(g) for insignificant extra-solution activity and § 2106.05(h) for field-of-use linking.

name: Best practice: suggest claim elements to overcome rejection
description: When making a rejection, it is best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and identify those elements in the Office action as suggested ways to overcome the rejection.
guidance: If specification discloses elements that would make the claim significantly more, point them out to applicant as potential narrowing/amendment options.

name: Evidentiary standard for identifying judicial exceptions (Step 2A)
description: When performing Step 2A, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered a judicial exception; there is no requirement to rely on external evidence to find a claim is directed to a judicial exception.
guidance: Courts typically treat eligibility as a question of law and often identify exceptions by comparing claimed subject matter to precedent without requiring evidence (cases cited: Rapid Litig. Mgmt., OIP Techs., Content Extraction).

name: Evidentiary standard for Step 2B (significantly more)
description: At Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the claim does not recite significantly more than the judicial exception (e.g., that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities).
guidance: However, if available, sources of evidence can be provided to support the assertion or to rebut applicant arguments. The specification's statements that elements are conventional may be used. Other evidence could include manuals, handbooks, prior patents, or court decisions describing conventionality or state of the art.

name: Evaluating applicant's response to §101 rejection
description: After issuing a §101 rejection, examiners must carefully consider all applicant arguments and evidence rebutting the subject matter eligibility rejection; if the applicant amends, determine the amended claim’s broadest reasonable interpretation and re-perform the eligibility analysis.
guidance: If amendments/arguments persuasively establish eligibility, withdraw the rejection. Applicant may amend or present persuasive arguments/evidence in good faith. Consider combination of elements and whether individual or combined elements amount to significantly more.

name: What counts as 'significantly more' (examples of qualifying limitations)
description: An additional element may qualify as 'significantly more' if it meaningfully limits the judicial exception, e.g., it improves another technology or technical field, improves functioning of a computer itself, adds a specific limitation beyond well-understood routine activity, or adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application.
guidance: Even if an element is generic individually, it can amount to significantly more when combined with other elements. Generic components in combination may perform non-generic functions and thus be eligible.

name: Required rebuttal when maintaining rejection after applicant challenge
description: If applicant properly challenges the examiner's findings but the examiner deems it appropriate to maintain the rejection, a rebuttal must be provided in the next Office action.
guidance: Appropriate responses include: (1) explaining why the abstract idea identified in the claim is similar to a concept in a cited case (and cite a supporting case if one was not previously cited), (2) reevaluating if applicant provides evidence that additional elements are not well-understood/routine and considering providing evidence if maintaining the rejection, (3) analyzing whether adding a generic computer or 'specially programmed' computer supplies significantly more (mere addition is insufficient), (4) reconsidering Step 2A/2B if applicant argues claim specificity or lack of preemption, including whether claim improves computer functioning or technical field.

name: Clarifying the record when claims are eligible or when issuing rejections
description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record describing which specification portions support the claimed improvement and which claim elements produce that improvement; clarifying remarks may also be useful to explain the rationale for a rejection (e.g., explain the BRI).
guidance: Clarifying remarks can be made during prosecution or at notice of allowance. Example: explaining that the BRI of a computer-readable-medium claim covers a carrier wave and suggesting narrowing amendments to overcome a §101 rejection.

name: Patent subject matter eligibility (Section 101) analysis
description: Analysis of whether claimed inventions satisfy Section 101 subject matter eligibility; the page attributes improved analysis to the USPTO's January 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (2019 PEG).
guidance: The 2019 PEG is presented as the framework that 'greatly improved the analysis' of Section 101 determinations across technologies affected by Alice. Use the 2019 PEG's approach when assessing eligibility (as reflected in the USPTO's conclusions).

name: APA §553 procedural requirements control substantive rulemaking
description: The APA §553 sets procedures (notice-and-comment) agencies must follow for rulemaking, and interpretive rules/statements of policy are generally exempt.
guidance: If a PTO statement qualifies as a substantive (legislative) rule, it must comply with §553's notice-and-comment procedures unless a narrow statutory exception applies. Failure to follow §553 can invalidate substantive rules; agencies sometimes claim 'good cause' to avoid notice-and-comment when impracticable or contrary to public interest.

name: Possession (written description) standard
description: The specification must show that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention; the fundamental factual inquiry is whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
guidance: Objective standard formulations include: 'does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed' and Vas-Cath's requirement that the applicant convey with reasonable clarity that he or she was in possession of the invention. Possession may be shown using words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, reduction to practice, or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics.

name: Variation by nature/scope of invention and art maturity
description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technological knowledge already in existence; in mature arts less evidence is required while in emerging or unpredictable technologies more evidence is required.
guidance: In most mature technologies, written description should not be raised for claims present when originally filed even if only a method and function are disclosed. For unpredictable arts, disclosure of only a method and function may not support a product claim; more specific characterization or corroborating evidence is required.

name: Product-by-process claims and process disclosure
description: Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, the written description requirement for a product-by-process claim is clearly satisfied; however, the requirement may not be satisfied where it is not clear that the acts set forth in the specification can be performed, or that the product is produced by that process.
guidance: If the specification does not establish that the disclosed process produces the claimed product (or is operable), the written description for the product may be inadequate. Examiners should evaluate whether the process was actually used/reported and whether operability is evident.

name: Partial structure disclosure insufficiency
description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization of the product may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: For complex chemical/biological inventions, conception requires ability to define and distinguish the compound (structure, method of preparation, properties). Merely stating a principal biological property (e.g., 'encodes human erythropoietin') without enabling specificity is often insufficient.

name: Structure-function correlation as basis for genus support
description: A specification may support a genus by establishing a reasonable structure-function correlation, either by the inventor's disclosure or by what was known in the art at the time of filing.
guidance: Such correlations allow description of a representative genus without enumerating every species. Examiners should assess whether the specification provides correlation or whether it is known in the art; absent such correlation, broader genus claims may be unsupported.

name: Representative disclosure does not require per-species support
description: Description of a representative number of species does not require specificity sufficient to provide individual support for each species in the genus; e.g., in molecular biology, disclosure of an amino acid sequence can support nucleic acid genus claims because the genetic code is widely known.
guidance: Assess whether the technical knowledge (like the genetic code) makes certain direct derivations routine; where common scientific knowledge bridges descriptions, broader claims can be supported without explicit per-species disclosure.

name: Each claim limitation must be supported in original disclosure
description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: When an explicit limitation in a claim is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood that the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone). Examiners should evaluate express, implicit, and inherent support.

name: Examiner initial burden in written description rejections
description: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless or until the examiner presents sufficient evidence or reasoning to rebut the presumption; the examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure the claimed invention.
guidance: The examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting lack of written description and should not rely on conclusory allegations. See Wertheim; the examiner's role is to establish a reasonable basis for challenge.

name: Required express findings when rejecting for lack of written description
description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description the examiner's findings should: (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the original disclosure.
guidance: A general allegation such as 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. Findings should be factual and tied to the disclosure and the knowledge in the art.

name: Prohibition on adding new matter and treatment of amendments
description: If a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed, involving a departure from, addition to, or deletion from the disclosure, the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or deny priority/benefit as appropriate.
guidance: While the analysis for new matter and written description is similar, the procedural treatment differs. Applicant should specifically point out support for amendments and examiners should be mindful of new matter rules (MPEP § 714.02, § 2163.06).

name: Essential/critical elements must be claimed
description: Each claim must include all elements which the applicant has described as essential; if an element described as essential is not claimed, the claim may be rejected as lacking adequate written description.
guidance: Cases like Johnson Worldwide and Gentry Gallery illustrate that omission of described essential elements can undermine claim support; examiners should identify such essential elements from the disclosure.

name: Original claims and functional language risks
description: An original claim may lack written description support when (1) it defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved, or (2) a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence the genus is contemplated.
guidance: Even if claim language appears verbatim in the specification, mere indistinct words do not necessarily satisfy the requirement. Courts (e.g., Ariad) caution that appearance of language alone is not dispositive; the disclosure must enable recognition of possession.

name: Definition of 'applicant' and submission of statements
description: The term 'applicant' includes each of several persons claiming to be registered proprietor of the same trade mark; Comptroller may require any such person to submit a written statement within notified time or attend and make oral explanations as Comptroller requires.
guidance: Used in Rules 17–19 context regarding hearings and statements; helps Comptroller adjudicate competing claims.

name: Conflicting claims resolution — special case or Court submission
description: Where several persons claim registration of same trade mark and Comptroller refuses registration until rights are determined, the manner of submission to Court shall (unless Court orders otherwise) be by a special case filed and proceeded with like any other special case; the special case may be settled by Comptroller on payment of prescribed fees.
guidance: Fees for settling special case (e.g., 2s) set out in First Schedule; Form S for request. Comptroller may settle where parties agree or differ.

name: No implied warranty of validity; fraud exception
description: No warranty of validity is implied in any assignment of a patent right.
guidance: If the assignor knows the patent to be invalid when making the assignment he is guilty of fraud and the assignee may have relief; if both parties are equally innocent, the loss falls on the owner of the patent. An assignee generally may not defend against a suit for the purchase price by claiming patent invalidity; an assignment of an invalid patent is nevertheless sufficient consideration to support a promissory note where there is neither warranty nor fraud.

name: Trademark application date rule
description: Application date is the filing date in Malaysia.
guidance: The application date of a trademark in Malaysia is its filing date, regardless of any Paris Convention priority claimed; priority date is used only for determining precedence during examination.

name: Scope of design protection (visual appearance and single appearance)
description: Limitations on what is protected and how many appearances may be claimed.
guidance: Protection is for the external visual appearance of the article as a whole. Not possible to protect more than a single external visual appearance; patent-type claims/descriptions attempting to claim multiple appearances are impermissible. Cannot register part of an article unless that part is normally made and sold separately.

name: Statement of novelty requirements
description: Content and form guidance for the statement of novelty in design applications.
guidance: Applicants must include a statement of novelty, typically 'the novelty resides in the features of shape and configuration of the article as shown in the representations' or analogous wording for pattern/ornament. If highlighting a particular feature, indicate it (e.g., 'as shown in solid line'). Avoid patent-type claims or descriptions; registrations are generally for whole articles but novelty residing in part may be reflected in the statement.

name: Voluntary notification (recording with MyIPO)
description: Optional recording of copyright claims and requirements for notification.
guidance: Under Copyright (Voluntary Notification) Regulations 2012 and Section 26A, author/owner/assignee/licensee (or representative for non-residents) may notify Copyright Controller and deposit a copy of eligible work for recording in Register. Notification requires particulars of owner/author, statutory declaration of locus standi, a copy of the work, date/place of first publication, prescribed fee; translations required if not in national language or English. Controller does not verify claims; accuracy depends on applicant. Submitted copy must be clear and durable; hard or electronic copies permitted. Registered notification certificate (for fee) is prima facie evidence in Malaysian courts.

name: Duty to investigate before asserting small entity status
description: Applicants must do a complete and thorough investigation of all facts and circumstances before making a determination of actual entitlement to small entity status (37 CFR 1.27(f)). Where entitlement is uncertain, it should not be claimed.
guidance: Investigations should include review of whether a business is a 'small business concern' under section 3 of the Small Business Act and relevant SBA size standards (13 CFR 121.801–121.805). If rights have been assigned/licensed or are shared with other entities, review each related entity. For multiple inventors, check with co-inventors before one asserts status. The person asserting has a duty to investigate and self-certify unequivocally. The USPTO will not provide advisory opinions as to qualification.

name: Conciseness, number of claims
description: Where it is found that the claims lack conciseness under Art. 6, it may be appropriate for the examiner to first invite the applicant to provide informal clarification before the search is carried out.
guidance: See ISPE Guidelines 5.42; EPO applies option GL/ISPE A5.42. If independent claims of the same category result in lack of clarity and conciseness (see GL/PCT‑EPO F‑IV, 3.2), an objection may arise under Rule 6.

name: Support in the description
description: Claims must be supported by the description; dependent claims must find adequate support in the disclosure.
guidance: See ISPE Guidelines 5.43. If claims lack support under Art. 6, examiner may invite informal clarification before search (GL/PCT‑EPO B‑VIII, 3.3–3.6). The examiner applies the same criteria as in EPO Guidelines (mutatis mutandis).

name: Objection of lack of support (Art. 6)
description: If a broad claim is not supported over its whole breadth, the onus of demonstrating full support lies with the applicant once examiner sets out a reasoned case.
guidance: See GL/PCT‑EPO F‑IV, 6.3 and ISPE Guidelines 5.53. Examiner should set out reasons; applicant must show support or provide amendments/arguments. Informal clarification may be sought before search.

name: Definition in terms of function
description: Claims defined in functional terms must be assessed for support and sufficiency.
guidance: See ISPE Guidelines 5.56 and GL/PCT‑EPO F‑IV, 2.1 and 4.10 for how functional definitions affect support/clarity.

name: Support for dependent claims
description: Dependent claims must be supported by the description according to the same criteria as applied in EPO examination.
guidance: See GL/PCT‑EPO F‑IV, 6.6 and ISPE guidance referenced for specifics.

name: Evaluation of essential features
description: Use examples in the EPO Guidelines Annex to determine whether a claim contains all essential features of the invention; same criteria apply under PCT.
guidance: The examiner applies the Annex examples mutatis mutandis when assessing essential features under the PCT.

name: Unity of invention (one general inventive concept)
description: The international application must relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept.
guidance: See Art. 17(3)(a) and Rule 13.1. Lack of clarity of claims alone is not sufficient for lack of unity. Claims in different categories or multiple independent claims are not per se lack of unity if substantive criteria (Rules 13.1–13.3) are met.

name: Impact of claim sequence on unity
description: Normally sequence of claims should not impact unity determination, but it affects which invention is considered the 'first invention' mentioned in the claims.
guidance: See GL/PCT‑EPO F‑V, 8.2; the identified 'first invention' influences search/examination scope.

name: Special technical features
description: Identification of special technical features is part of unity assessment and search practice.
guidance: See ISPE Guidelines 10.01 and 10.12–10.16 and Rule 13.2 for determining features that link claimed inventions.

name: Markush grouping and unity
description: For Markush claims, a 'significant structural element' need not be novel per se but must distinguish claimed compounds in relation to the common property/activity; if at least one alternative is not novel, unity should be reconsidered.
guidance: See ISPE Guidelines 10.17. If a compound within the Markush group is known in combination with the property, that may indicate lack of unity for the remaining alternatives.

name: Determination of the invention first mentioned in the claims
description: Rules for deciding which invention is 'first mentioned' in the claims are applied as in the EPO Guidelines.
guidance: See GL/PCT‑EPO F‑V, 8.2 and GL/PCT‑EPO B‑VII, 2.

name: Dependent claims and unity
description: Consideration of dependent claims in relation to unity follows ISPE Guidelines 10.06–10.08.
guidance: Dependent claims may affect unity and search scope; see referenced ISPE provisions.

name: Subsequent application considered as first application (limitations)
description: Some applications cannot be recognised as a 'first application' for priority purposes (e.g., US continuation or continuation‑in‑part where subject‑matter was already disclosed in original US application).
guidance: Examples include US 'con' and 'cip' forms and national applications claiming priority from national utility models; specific formal statements and declarations are required in US con/cip cases. See ISPE Guidelines 6.04.

name: Determining priority dates / Examining validity of a right to priority
description: Examination of whether a claimed priority is valid and whether the same invention is present between filings.
guidance: See ISPE Guidelines 6.06–6.09 for tests on identity of invention and GL/PCT‑EPO references regarding disclaimers and their effect on identity of invention under Art. 8.

name: Examination practice for excluded subject‑matter
description: Exclusions from patentability apply only to the extent the application relates to excluded subject‑matter as such; the claim must be considered as a whole to decide technical character.
guidance: See GL/PCT‑EPO G‑II and ISPE Guidelines 9.02–9.15; the EPO's discretion under Agreement with WIPO determines search/examination on excluded matter.

name: Prior art — general definition and scope
description: Prior art consists of everything made available to the public anywhere in the world by written disclosure (including drawings) capable of assisting determination of novelty/inventive step if made available before the international filing date (or priority date where validly claimed).
guidance: See Art. 33(2), Rules 33.1 and 64.1 and ISPE Guidelines 11.01 and 11.12. No geographic or language restrictions; no age limit on prior art documents.

name: Enabling disclosures (prior art)
description: The principles for determining whether prior documents are enabling and thus anticipate claimed subject matter follow EPO Guidelines mutatis mutandis.
guidance: See GL/PCT‑EPO G‑IV, 2 and ISPE guidance for enabling disclosure tests.

name: Utility
description: Whether the claimed invention has a specific, substantial, and credible utility.
guidance: Listed alongside other §112-related inquiries (Section III.B.3); treated as case-specific and thus fact-laden in the Article's survey of validity doctrines.

name: Nonobviousness (Graham framework)
description: Assessment of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 using Graham factors: scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claims, level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations.
guidance: Nonobviousness is discussed as paradigmatic of mixed/law-based-on-facts issues: underlying Graham inquiries are factual (prior art, level of skill, motivation to combine, expectation of success, secondary considerations) while the ultimate legal determination of obviousness has been variously characterized; the Article argues it should be treated as a mixed question and typically reviewed deferentially.

name: Role of claim construction
description: Interpreting claim scope (claim construction) as a procedural and substantive step that affects both infringement and validity analyses.
guidance: Markman teaches that claim construction is for the judge; the Article suggests using claim construction to reduce jury trials and to permit judges to decide patentability more effectively, thereby streamlining litigation.

name: Fintiv Factor 3 — investment in the parallel proceeding by the court and parties
description: Assessment of how much time, effort, and resources the district court and parties have invested in the parallel litigation.
guidance: High investment by the court/parties supports discretionary denial. This factor encompasses things like completed claim construction proceedings, substantial discovery, or other pretrial investment. Petitioner conduct (e.g., timing of filing) is relevant to this factor.

name: Enablement standard for broadly claimed antibody compositions (Wands factors)
description: Enablement requires sufficient disclosure to enable the full scope of claimed subject matter; in the antibody context, broad functional claims face high enablement hurdles under Wands factors.
guidance: Broad claims with functional language that cover many antibodies require more than a handful of exemplars; courts may find lack of enablement where identifying claimed embodiments would require undue experimentation, trial-and-error, or de novo screening (see Amgen v. Sanofi). Counsel should analyze predictability of the art and the number/sufficiency of exemplars.

name: Analogous art (field of endeavor / same problem / structural similarity)
description: A reference is analogous art if it is within the field of the inventor's endeavor or if it is reasonably pertinent to the particular problem the inventor was trying to solve; structural similarity or common problems across fields can render art analogous.
guidance: Apply the field-of-endeavor test and the problem-solved test. Consider whether a person of ordinary skill would look to the other art for solutions (examples: toothbrush references to a hair brush claim; fastener/hinge art to pen holding means; clutch art to braking materials). Use case law examples from mechanical, electrical, and design arts to determine analogousness.

name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole'
description: In determining differences between prior art and claims under 35 U.S.C. 103, the claimed invention must be considered as an integrated whole, not by focusing solely on isolated differences.
guidance: Interpret claim language and view both the invention and referenced art as wholes. Do not improperly limit analysis to a single structural difference if the overall invention yields a new result or insight (see Stratoflex, Schenck examples).

name: Do not distill an invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'
description: Reducing an invention to a broad gist or single advantage ignores statutory requirement to analyze the invention as a whole and may lead to improper obviousness findings.
guidance: Respect all express claim limitations; avoid treating the advantage or one characteristic as the entire invention (cases: W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb).

name: Requirements for using the 'combine prior art elements' rationale
description: To reject under the rationale that prior art elements could be combined by known methods to yield predictable results, specific factual findings are required.
guidance: Office personnel must articulate: (1) prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in one reference); (2) one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element would perform the same function; (3) one of ordinary skill would have recognized the combination's results as predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-fact findings necessary in the particular case. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness.

name: Limitations on amendments in inter partes reexamination
description: No amendment other than canceling claims (where cancellation does not affect scope of other pending claims) may be made in an inter partes reexamination proceeding after the right of appeal notice under § 1.953, except as provided in § 1.981 or § 41.77(b)(1).
guidance: Similar restrictions apply to affidavits/evidence after final in inter partes reexamination. See MPEP § 714.12 and related CFR sections.

name: Claim drafting advice to avoid after-final difficulties
description: Applicants are encouraged to include at filing or no later than the first reply claims varying from the broadest believed allowable to the most detailed they are willing to accept.
guidance: Including a range of claim scope early may alleviate difficulties in prosecution after final rejection.

name: Entry not a matter of right after final; permissible replies limited
description: Applicant cannot, as a matter of right, amend any finally rejected claims, add new claims after a final rejection (see 37 CFR 1.116) or reinstate previously canceled claims. A reply under 37 CFR 1.113 is limited to: (A) an amendment complying with 37 CFR 1.116; (B) a Notice of Appeal (and appeal fee); or (C) a request for continued examination (RCE) filed under 37 CFR 1.114 with a submission and fee.
guidance: RCE practice under 1.114 does not apply to utility or plant applications filed before June 8, 1995 and design applications. Continued prosecution by CPA applies only to design applications (with limitations).

name: Criteria and reasons for nonentry of after-final amendments
description: Refusal to enter a proposed amendment should not be arbitrary. The proposed amendment should be given sufficient consideration to determine whether claims are in condition for allowance and/or whether issues on appeal are simplified. If the amendment raises new matter or new issues requiring further consideration/search, the examiner should identify and explain concisely why entry is refused.
guidance: Examples of adequate concise reasons for nonentry include: (A) amended claims would not avoid rejections and thus not place the case in condition for allowance or better for appeal; (B) amended claims would raise the issue of new matter; (C) amended claims present new issues requiring further consideration/search; (D) amendment presents additional claims without canceling any finally rejected claims so not placing application in better condition for appeal. Examiner need not always discuss specific deficiencies unless new matter is raised.

name: Scope of 'amendment' under 37 CFR 1.312
description: The term 'amendment' broadly encompasses any change in the file record after allowance, including amendments to the specification, drawings, claims; changes in inventorship; submission of prior art; petitions to correct spelling or change order of inventors, etc.
guidance: An amendment under 1.312 must comply with 37 CFR 1.121 and be filed on or before the date the issue fee is paid (except where required by Office of Data Management). The supervisory patent examiner approves recommendations under 1.312. Supplemental reissue oaths/declarations are treated as amendments under 1.312; supplemental oaths/declarations (non-reissue) are not.

name: Requirements for amendments under 1.312 that affect claims or disclosure
description: For amendments affecting disclosure, scope of any claim, or adding a claim under 1.312, the remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: The requirements of 37 CFR 1.111(c) with respect to pointing out patentable novelty of any claim sought to be added or amended apply to 1.312 amendments as in ordinary amendments. See MPEP §§ 713.04, 713.10 and 714.16.

name: Routing/processing of 1.312 amendments affecting disclosure after allowance
description: Amendments under 37 CFR 1.312 affecting the disclosure, adding claims, or changing claim scope are sent by OPAP to Publishing Division which forwards the proposed amendment, file, and drawing (if any) to the Technology Center which allowed the application; for IFW applications OPAP Central Scanning scans and messages Data Management and the TC.
guidance: Hand-delivered amendments under 1.312 are no longer accepted in the TC (unless required by Office of Data Management) and must be delivered to the Customer Window. If the application has been reclassified to another TC after allowance, the proposed amendment and file are transmitted to that TC.

name: Permissible claim amendments after certain rejections
description: Amendments to the claims made pursuant to Article 47(1)2 and 3 may be made only in cases such as: (1) narrowing claims by restricting/deleting/adding limitations; (2) correcting clerical errors; (3) clarifying ambiguous descriptions; (4) reinstating prior claims under narrow circumstances.
guidance: Claims cannot be broadened beyond original disclosure in these amendment periods except as specifically allowed; reinstatement is limited to restoring previously presented claims under defined situations.

name: Scope of permissible amendment varies by amendment period
description: The scope of permissible amendment to specification or drawings differs depending on amendment periods: voluntary amendment period (before start of examination) and period for arguments in reply to non-final rejection allow no addition of new matter; periods for arguments in response to rejection necessitated by amendment and on request for reexamination further restrict permitted amendments to narrowing claims and clarifying errors, etc., and still prohibit new matter.
guidance: Different remedies and sanctions apply depending on when an illegitimate amendment is made; see handling table (grounds for rejection, decision to refuse entry, invalidation grounds etc.).

name: Narrowing from genus to species can be new matter
description: Where an amendment narrows a claim from a genus to a species, unless the species is supported by the original specification/drawings or unless a skilled person would readily recognize the species from the genus, the amendment is viewed as introduction of new matter.
guidance: Examples: adding a specific material (e.g., 'ABS') is new matter unless originally disclosed or obvious; substituting 'sensor' with 'proximity sensor' may be supported if a skilled person would intuitively associate them.

name: Broadening from species to genus can be new matter
description: Where an amendment broadens a claim from a species to a genus, if the genus includes other species that may have different functions or effects, the amendment shall constitute introduction of new matter. Deleting limitations described as essential is new matter; deleting arbitrary non-essential limitations may be permitted.
guidance: Examples: broadening geometric detail of a connector leading to changed electrical contact is new matter; deleting an identifying code communication step from traffic-control method may or may not be permitted depending on whether the problems can still be addressed.

name: Medium must contain program instructions
description: The medium must contain program instructions or other software-related content.
guidance: Draft claims to recite that the storage medium 'contains program instructions' (or equivalent) so the claim ties the intangible functionality to content residing on a tangible medium.

name: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. § 112 (definiteness and specification support)
description: The claim must be written in a way that complies with 35 U.S.C. § 112, including being definite and supported by the specification.
guidance: Ensure claims are definite and that the specification provides written description and enablement support for claimed elements; avoid claim language that lacks specification support.

name: Patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and the Alice two-step test
