description: Beauregard claims must survive §101 analysis: determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea and, if so, whether it contains an inventive concept sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
guidance: When drafting, consider the Alice framework early—emphasize tangible aspects, technical improvements, or inventive concepts in the claim/specification to reduce the risk of being characterized as an abstract idea.

name: Use specific language to define scope
description: Use specific language to define the scope of the invention.
guidance: Prefer precise claim terms over vague or overly broad phrasing; clearly describe the tangible medium, the instructions, and any structural/functional relationships to limit ambiguity and strengthen §112/claim-construction positions.

name: Include dependent claims for added definition and protection
description: Consider using dependent claims to further define the invention and provide additional protection.
guidance: Draft dependent claims that add concrete limitations, alternative embodiments, and fallback positions to preserve claim scope through prosecution or litigation.

name: Conduct thorough prior art searches
description: Conduct thorough prior art searches to identify potential issues.
guidance: Search for prior art that could affect novelty, obviousness, or claim-eligibility; use the results to tailor claim scope and draft supporting specification content.

name: Draft claims that are specific, clear, and concise
description: Draft claims that are specific, clear, and concise.
guidance: Clarity and concision aid examiner understanding, reduce §112 risks, and strengthen enforcement—avoid unnecessary functional/formal obfuscation.

name: Ensure the specification provides adequate support
description: Ensure the specification provides adequate support for the claims.
guidance: Include examples, embodiments, and detailed descriptions of how the program instructions operate on the medium to satisfy written description and enablement requirements.

name: Avoid common pitfalls in Beauregard claim drafting
description: Common pitfalls to avoid: using overly broad or vague language; failing to comply with 35 U.S.C. § 112; not providing adequate support in the specification; ignoring prior art and potential validity issues.
guidance: Proactively prevent these mistakes by using precise claim language, robust specification disclosure, and careful prior-art-based claim drafting.

name: Emphasize claim language and specification support in litigation
description: Emphasize the specific language used in the claim to define the scope of the invention and highlight the support provided in the specification for the claim.
guidance: Use claim-construction briefs and specification citations to show that claim elements are concrete and supported, countering §112 and §101 attacks.

name: Infringement requires meeting each claim element
description: To succeed in a patent infringement case, the patent owner must demonstrate that the accused product or process meets each element of the Beauregard claim.
guidance: Prepare element-by-element infringement analyses, claim charts, and factual evidence showing the accused product contains the claimed medium/content or equivalent.

name: Stay informed of evolving case law and its impact
description: Recent court decisions continue to shape Beauregard claims; stay informed about developments (e.g., In re Beauregard, State Street, Bilski, Alice, Vanda) and their implications for §101 and claim drafting.
guidance: Monitor jurisprudence and adapt drafting and litigation strategies accordingly—cite favorable precedent and distinguish adverse decisions when possible.

name: Rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) — common assignee/applicant/joint inventor
description: Claims rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over a reference that has a common assignee, common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118), or at least one common joint inventor and which constitutes prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) by virtue of an earlier effective U.S. filing date.
guidance: This rejection might be overcome by: (1) a 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation of the reference's subject matter from this application's inventor; (2) showing an earlier date of invention under 37 CFR 1.131(a); or (3) an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) that current ownership is common and that the named inventor is the prior inventor under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 104 plus a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c). Also consider disqualification under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Follow MPEP §§706.02(l)(1)-(3). Fill bracket placeholders: claim numbers, prior art reference, and which common relationship (assignee/applicant/joint inventor).

name: Rejection — 35 U.S.C. 103, 'further in view of' (combination of references)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as unpatentable over a primary reference as applied to another claim and further in view of an additional reference.
guidance: For AIA applications (filed on/after March 16, 2013), use only when claims are examined under AIA 102/103 and must be preceded by form paragraph 7.03.aia and 7.21.aia. An explanation of the rejection must follow (see MPEP §2144). For pre-AIA use form paragraph 7.22.fti and ensure proper determination of any 102(e) date per MPEP guidance.

name: Use of combined 35 U.S.C. 102/103 form paragraph (7.27) — when appropriate
description: Claim(s) rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102([paragraph]) as anticipated by or, alternatively, under 35 U.S.C. 103 as obvious over a cited reference.
guidance: This combined paragraph is NOT intended as a common substitute for making a single clear rejection under 102 or 103; use only in special circumstances such as: disputed claim interpretation leading to either 102 or 103; where the reference discloses all limitations except a property/function with uncertainty about inherent properties (In re Fitzgerald); genus/species issues (In re Schaumann); product-by-process concerns (In re Marosi); means-plus-function equivalence uncertainty; overlapping ranges without a specific example in reference. If used, must be preceded by specified form paragraphs (e.g., 7.07.aia, 7.08.aia, 7.12.aia) and must be followed by a full explanation of both anticipation and obviousness grounds. For priority claims predating March 16, 2013, precede with form paragraph 7.06.

name: Objection — New Matter Added to Specification (35 U.S.C. 132(a))
description: An amendment is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132(a) because it introduces new matter into the disclosure; the added material not supported by the original disclosure must be identified.
guidance: Applicant must cancel the new matter in reply. Do not use for reissue applications (use 14.22.01). In bracket 2 identify new matter by page/lines or figures and provide an explanation addressing any applicant statements claiming support. If new matter affects claims, also make a 35 U.S.C. 112(a) / first paragraph rejection (form paragraph 7.31.01). Include a full explanation following this paragraph.

name: Disclosure/Claims Objected to — Minor Informalities
description: The disclosure or claims are objected to because of minor informalities (spelling errors, inconsistent terminology, numbering issues, etc.).
guidance: Use to point out minor corrections required; cite specific informalities in bracket placeholders. See form paragraphs 6.28–6.31 for examples. If informalities render claims indefinite, use the appropriate 112 rejection (7.34.01). Precedence rules for form paragraphs apply (e.g., must be preceded by 7.07.fti and others as appropriate).

name: Claims Objected — Reference Characters Not Enclosed Within Parentheses
description: Claims objected to because reference characters corresponding to elements in the detailed description/drawings are not enclosed within parentheses.
guidance: Reference characters in claims should be enclosed in parentheses to avoid confusion with other numbers/characters. If lack of parentheses renders claim(s) indefinite, use form paragraph 7.34.01 (112(b)). Cite MPEP §608.01(m).

name: Statement of Statutory Basis — 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness/claiming)
description: Quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (second paragraph) requiring claims to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
guidance: Use in first actions on the merits and final rejections only (or use 7.103 otherwise). Use 7.30.02 only once per Office action. Follow with form paragraphs addressing particular deficiencies (7.34.xx).

name: Statement of Statutory Basis — 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / means-plus-function
description: Quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (sixth paragraph pre-AIA) regarding means or step-for claiming and construction to corresponding structure, material, or acts and equivalents.
guidance: Use only once per Office action when claim elements use 'means'/'step for' or otherwise invoke 112(f). Must be followed by form paragraph 7.30.04. The absence of the word 'means' raises a rebuttable presumption that 112(f) is not invoked; presence raises a presumption that it is invoked unless rebutted by clear claim structure.

name: Claim Interpretation — presumptions regarding 'means' / 'step for'
description: Claim elements using 'means' (or 'step for') are presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f); elements not using 'means' are presumed not to invoke 112(f). The presumption is rebuttable when claim language supplies sufficient structure/material/acts.
guidance: Use this paragraph only once in an Office action when appropriate. Provide explanation when presumptions are rebutted (e.g., 'means' used but definite structure recited, or no 'means' but lacking structure). May be followed by specific 112-related form paragraphs (7.34.11, 7.34.16, etc.).

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — Written Description (possession)
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (first paragraph) for failing the written description requirement: the claim contains subject matter not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor had possession.
guidance: Identify by reference (page/lines/figures) the missing support in bracket 2 and explain why the specification fails to convey possession; may precede form paragraph 7.30.03. Include any unresolved examiner questions and specific rationale.

name: Use of 'Means' (7.30.04) — rebuttable presumption guidance
description: Using the word 'means' (or 'step for') with functional language creates a rebuttable presumption that the element is to be treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f). The presumption is rebutted when the function is recited with sufficient structure, material, or acts within the claim itself to entirely perform the recited function.
guidance: This rejection must be preceded by 7.30.01 or 7.103. In bracket 2 identify any subject matter not properly described and explain why. Follow-up with appropriate 112(f)-related form paragraphs if necessary.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — Enablement
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) first paragraph for failing to enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention.
guidance: In bracket 2 identify the claimed subject matter not enabled (by page/line or figures) and explain why, referencing unresolved examiner questions that raise doubt as to enablement. Apply In re Wands factors and MPEP §§2164 et seq. Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — Best Mode Requirement
description: Claim rejected because the best mode contemplated by the inventor (or joint inventor) has not been disclosed, with evidence of concealment identified.
guidance: Use rarely. Must be preceded by 7.30.01 or 7.103. In bracket 2 insert the basis for holding that best mode has been concealed (e.g., poor disclosure quality). If the problem is one of claim scope rather than best mode, consider 7.31.03 instead. Follow MPEP §§2165–2165.04.

name: Rejection — Scope of Enablement (claims broader than enabled disclosure)
description: Claim rejected because the specification, while enabling for some subject matter, does not reasonably provide enablement for other claimed aspects; the claims are not commensurate in scope with the enabling disclosure.
guidance: Use when claim scope exceeds what the specification enables. Identify enabling portions (bracket 2), aspects not enabled (bracket 3), whether enablement to 'make'/'use'/'make and use' is lacking (bracket 4), and the claimed subject matter not enabled (bracket 5). Apply Wands factors and provide detailed explanation (MPEP §§2164.01(a), 2164.04). Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103.

name: Rejection 7.33.01 — Essential subject matter missing from claims (enablement)
description: Claim rejected because the disclosure does not enable one of ordinary skill to practice the invention without critical or essential subject matter that is omitted from the claims.
guidance: In bracket 2 recite the omitted subject matter; in bracket 3 provide rationale for considering it critical/essential. Cite statements, arguments, dates, drawings, or other evidence showing applicant considered the feature essential. Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — Indefiniteness (failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim)
description: Claim rejected as indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention.
guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Follow with one or more of form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.11 as applicable; if none apply, supply a full explanation identifying the term(s)/limitations rendering the claim indefinite and why, referencing MPEP §§2171–2174. For pro se applicants, consider 7.34.15.

name: Terminology used inconsistent with accepted meaning (claim term redefinition)
description: Where applicant acts as his/her own lexicographer to redefine a claim term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term and put one skilled in the art on notice of the uncommon definition; otherwise the term is indefinite.
guidance: Point out applicant's claimed meaning (bracket 3) and the accepted meaning supported by citations (bracket 4). Use only where the specification does not clearly redefine the term. Precede with 7.34.01. Provide supporting reference (textbook/dictionary) per MPEP §2173.05(a).

name: Relative term/term of degree rendering claim indefinite
description: A relative term (term of degree) in a claim renders the claim indefinite where the claim/specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree and one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of the scope.
guidance: Identify the relative term (bracket 1) and the claim (bracket 2); explain why no ascertainable standard exists (bracket 3). Precede with 7.34.01 and follow MPEP guidance on terms of degree and definiteness.

name: Treat patents as investment assets, not compliance documents
description: A patent is a financial asset. Drafting choices should be evaluated by their effect on the asset's value (licensing potential, enforcement potential, defensive value at acquisition). A patent that is 'filed' is not the goal; a patent that creates economic value is.
guidance: Evaluate every drafting decision by its impact on commercial value: will the claim scope enable licensing, enforcement, or add defensive/acquisition value? Avoid drafting solely to satisfy formalities or to 'file something' without regard to market relevance. Prioritize claims and specifications that support monetization and enforceability over procedural completion.

name: Investor's lens on claim scope (market-driven scope)
description: A patent's value is roughly proportional to the size of the market its claims cover. When choosing claim scope, ask: what is the market my broadest accurate claim reads on?
guidance: Quantify the market size your broadest credible claim would cover (e.g., $10M niche vs $1B mass market) and prioritize drafting/scopes that target larger markets when feasible. Balance accuracy and breadth: broader claims that are still accurate and defensible increase portfolio value. Use market knowledge to guide claim breadth choices.

name: Detectability drives enforceability
description: A claim that requires reverse-engineering an internal algorithm is hard to enforce. A claim that reads on observable user behavior, network traffic, or physical product features is enforceable without litigation discovery.
guidance: Make detectability a first-order drafting consideration: draft claims to read on observable artifacts (user actions, logs, network traffic, visible product features). Antipatterns: claims relying on hidden server-side behavior or internal-only steps that are difficult to prove in court. Prefer claim elements that can be proven with external evidence.

name: Claims as marketing for acquirers
description: When a startup is acquired, the acquirer's IP team reviews the portfolio. A portfolio with claims that obviously read on competitors' products, or that obviously cover the company's flagship product, signals quality. A portfolio with vague aspirational claims signals filed-and-forgotten quality.
guidance: Draft claims so they clearly map to real products and competitive landscapes; ensure the portfolio tells a coherent story about the company's tech and market position. Antipatterns: vague aspirational claims that don't clearly read on tangible implementations — these reduce perceived acquisition value.

name: Don't over-index on issuance
description: Issuance is a milestone, not the goal. A patent that issued with overly narrow claims because the applicant gave up early in prosecution is worth less than a pending application with broader claims still being negotiated.
guidance: Be willing to appeal, file RCEs, or abandon and refile when issuance would lock in unduly narrow claims. Treat prosecution as part of value-maximization, not merely a compliance box. Antipatterns: conceding overly narrow claim constructions simply to obtain issuance quickly.

name: Patent family architecture planning
description: A serious portfolio includes a parent, multiple continuations claiming different scopes, and foreign counterparts. Plan the family architecture at filing, not retroactively.
guidance: At the initial filing stage, map out desired claim-scope diversification via continuations and decide foreign filing strategy. Use continuations to pursue broader or narrower claim sets over time. Plan territorial coverage consistent with target markets and acquisition/licensing goals.

name: Discovery framework in TTAB inter partes proceedings
description: Discovery includes a discovery conference (topics: discovery planning, Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)), initial disclosures under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a), interrogatory requests, requests for production, depositions, requests for admission, and expert disclosures.
guidance: Board participates in the discovery conference; identify individuals likely to have discoverable information and documents supporting claims/defenses; discovery is subject to TTAB rules and timelines.

name: Abbreviated proceedings and dispositive motion standards (TTAB)
description: Motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim when facts alleged do not constitute grounds for relief. Motion for summary judgment when no genuine dispute of material fact exists and movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Accelerated Case Resolution (ACR) is similar to summary judgment but the Board may determine disputed facts.
guidance: Use these vehicles to resolve cases efficiently when appropriate factual disputes are absent or limited; ACR may produce quicker finality but involves tradeoffs.

name: Supervisory review requirement (minimum four written decisions/year)
description: Supervisors are required to conduct an in-depth review of a minimum of four written decisions per examiner each fiscal year as part of the performance appraisal process.
guidance: Although supervisors claim to review more, USPTO historically did not require documentation of which cases were reviewed. The minimum of four reviews versus an average examiner workload (about 73 final determinations/year) creates statistical limits on detecting poor performance.

name: Product of nature rejection explanation
description: The rejection should identify the exception as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim, and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart (the product 'in its natural state') and explain whether isolation resulted in a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties. See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for products of nature and § 2106.04(c) for the markedly different characteristics analysis. Sample explanation: specify that the claim recites X isolated from naturally occurring Y and explain why there is no indication of a marked difference.

name: Explain why additional elements do not add significantly more (Step 2B)
description: After identifying the judicial exception in the rejection, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and explain why they do not add significantly more to the exception.
guidance: Address the additional elements both individually and as a combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. Recognize that a new combination of known steps may nevertheless be patent eligible. Provide a reasoned rationale so the applicant can effectively respond. See MPEP § 2106.05 for considerations courts have found to qualify (or not) as significantly more.

name: Rejection only when readily apparent to examiner
description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise in the art in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to claiming significantly more than the recited judicial exception.
guidance: When appropriate, explain why the additional elements do provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. If maintaining a rejection, provide the underlying rationale in the record. See Diamond v. Diehr and MPEP § 2106.05.

name: Provide reasoned explanation for 'well-understood, routine, conventional' findings
description: When concluding that particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities (or elements) in the relevant field, the rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the relevant field would recognize, those claim limitations as such.
guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation that supports the conventionality conclusion (do not assert conventionality without rationale). See MPEP § 2106.05(d) for more information and examples of activities/elements courts have found to be well-understood, routine, conventional.

name: Address generic computer components and functions
description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2106.05(d) and § 2106.05(f) for lists/examples. Do not assume all computer functions are routine; courts have found some computer-implemented processes to be significantly more (e.g., DDR Holdings). Consider whether generic computer components in combination perform non-generic functions.

name: Identify insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations
description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, final storing step) or merely link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
guidance: Provide examples and precedent: e.g., storing data after computing area does not add a meaningful limitation; limiting a mathematical formula to a particular industry may be insufficient (Parker v. Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(g) and § 2106.05(h).

name: Suggest claim amendments to overcome rejection
description: It is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible, and, if so, identify those elements in the Office action and suggest them as a way to overcome the rejection.
guidance: When appropriate, point out specification passages and possible narrowing amendments that could supply meaningful limitations or improvements to the technology to traverse a §101 rejection.

name: Evidentiary standard for eligibility determinations
description: The courts consider the determination of whether a claim is eligible to be a question of law; therefore, courts generally do not require 'evidence' to identify a judicial exception and decide eligibility.
guidance: At Step 2A, a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception is sufficient; at Step 2B there is likewise no requirement for evidence to find lack of significantly more. However, when available, sources of evidence (e.g., specification admissions, manuals, patents, court decisions) may be provided to support assertions or rebut applicant arguments; care should be taken that cited case facts comport with the application. See cited Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Alice, Smith, Content Extraction) and MPEP guidance.

name: Use prior precedent to identify exceptions
description: When determining whether claimed subject matter is judicially-excepted, the Federal Circuit typically compares the claimed subject matter to subject matter identified as an exception in its prior precedent.
guidance: Examine earlier cases to see whether the claimed concept is similar to concepts previously held to be exceptions. Examples: Amdocs, In re Smith, Apple v. Ameranth, Versata.

name: Evaluate applicant's responses and amendments fully
description: After examiners identify and explain the reasons why a claim is directed to an exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend the claim or present persuasive arguments or evidence; examiners must carefully consider all of applicant's arguments and evidence rebutting the subject matter eligibility rejection.
guidance: If applicant amends, determine the amended claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and reperform the eligibility analysis. If applicant persuasively establishes eligibility, withdraw the rejection.

name: Considerations for what qualifies as 'significantly more'
description: An additional element may qualify as 'significantly more' if it meaningfully limits the judicial exception, for example by improving another technology or technical field, improving the functioning of a computer itself, adding a specific limitation beyond what is well-understood/routine/conventional, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application.
guidance: Even if an element does not amount to significantly more on its own, it can amount to significantly more when considered in combination with other elements. See MPEP § 2106.05(a), (e), (f).

name: Combination of elements may amount to significantly more
description: Even if claim elements individually are generic or conventional, their combination may enable functions that are not merely generic and therefore amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.
guidance: Provide rationale showing how the combination meaningfully limits the exception (e.g., generic computer components able in combination to perform non-generic functions). Cite DDR Holdings as an example where combination produced eligibility.

name: When relying on case law, explain correspondence and avoid new grounds
description: If applicant challenges the identification of an abstract idea that was based on a court case and the challenge is not persuasive, the examiner should explain why the abstract idea identified in the claim is similar to the concept in the cited case.
guidance: If the original rejection did not identify a Supreme Court or Federal Circuit decision, and applicant challenges the identification, the examiner must point to a case in which a similar abstract idea was identified and explain the correspondence to maintain the rejection. Citation to supporting case law is not a new ground unless there is a change to the basic thrust of the rejection. See MPEP § 706.07(a).

name: Handling 'specially programmed' or 'particular machine' amendments
description: If applicant amends a claim to add a generic computer or generic computer components and asserts that the claim recites significantly more because the generic computer is 'specially programmed' or is a 'particular machine', the examiner should analyze whether the added elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Merely adding a generic computer, generic computer components, or a programmed computer to perform generic computer functions does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection (see Alice and OIP Techs.). Examine whether the addition meaningfully limits the exception.

name: Consider preemption arguments—reconsider Steps 2A and 2B
description: If applicant argues that the claim is specific and does not preempt all applications of the exception, the examiner should reconsider Step 2A to determine whether the claim is directed to an improvement to the functioning of a computer or any other technology or technical field, and if still directed to an exception, reconsider Step 2B whether the additional elements in combination amount to an inventive concept.
guidance: Preemption is not a standalone test but remains an underlying concern driving the two-part framework from Alice and Mayo. Reevaluate both steps where applicant presents persuasive preemption arguments. See cited cases (Synopsys, Rapid Litigation, Ariosa).

name: Clarifying the record when claims are eligible or to assist applicant
description: When the claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record (e.g., reference the portion of the specification that describes the claimed improvement and note the claim elements that produce that improvement).
guidance: Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution and may be useful in explaining the rationale for a rejection as well. Explaining the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of a claim will assist applicant in understanding and responding; for example, note that a computer-readable-medium claim's BRI could cover a carrier wave and suggest narrowing amendments to overcome a rejection.

name: Unexpected utility can support inventiveness
description: In many cases, the ingenuity of an invention is related to its utility. This is particularly the case where some unexpected result is achieved through the subject-matter of the claim.
guidance: Examples: a known product/process modified to be useful for a new purpose or to provide an additional advantage; simplification that retains original utility. Unexpected result may support patentability where it shows inventive contribution rather than mere routine modification.

name: New use of a known thing requires novelty and unobviousness
description: Where the invention lies in discovering that a known thing has properties that make it useful for some new purpose, that mere discovery does not confer patentability on the known thing. The new use may be patented, however, if it is novel and unobvious.
guidance: "A patent for the mere new use of a known contrivance, without any additional ingenuity in overcoming fresh difficulties is bad and cannot be supported. If the new use involves no ingenuity, but is in manner and purpose analogous to the old use, although not quite the same, there is no invention." Applicants should show additional ingenuity or unexpectedness for new-use claims.

name: Claim date = filing date unless compliant priority claim valid
description: In accordance with subsection 28.1(1) of the Patent Act, the claim date is the filing date unless there is a compliant request for priority to a previously filed application filed within 12 months and the claimed subject-matter is disclosed in the priority document. Under subsection 28.1(2), where those criteria are satisfied, the claim date is the filing date of the priority document.
guidance: Each claim may have a different claim date in principle. Examiner will verify: (1) whether a compliant request for priority was submitted; (2) the filing date of the priority document to determine timeliness; and (3) the content of the priority document to determine whether the subject-matter of each claim was disclosed in that document. Generalized claims may not benefit from an earlier priority date if the priority document only discloses specific embodiments without support for the broader subject-matter.

name: Multiple priority documents — earliest filing date applies
description: Where an application claims priority from two or more prior regularly filed applications, subsection 28.4(4) provides that paragraph(s) shall be applied using the earliest filing date of the previously regularly filed applications.
guidance: This gives the earliest possible claim date for subject-matter claimed in the pending application based on content of the earliest corresponding priority document. Examiner must consider content of each priority document to determine which subject-matter benefits from which claim date.

name: U.S. continuation and continuation-in-part (CIP) priority rules
description: A United States continuation application has the same specification as an earlier application but contains claims directed to different subject-matter; no new matter is disclosed. A continuation-in-part discloses and claims additional subject-matter over the earlier application. If a Canadian application is filed within one year of a continuation-in-part, that CIP may serve as a priority document for any new matter not disclosed in the original U.S. application.
guidance: Where priority questions arise involving continuations/CIPs, it may be necessary to identify matter derived from the original U.S. application. Because a U.S. CIP does not identify new matter, applicants must submit certified copies of both the original and CIP whenever required. Example provided where priority was denied because original US application's filing date was more than 12 months before Canadian filing.

name: Grace period for applicant-originated disclosures
description: The Patent Act provides for a grace period before the filing date during which information that became publicly available due to a disclosure by the applicant, or by a person who obtained knowledge, directly or indirectly, from the applicant, is not considered during the assessment of novelty and inventiveness. The grace period is one year before the filing date (or between claim date and filing date if claim date is earlier).
guidance: Grace period covers oral and written disclosures. In assessing applicability, examiners typically consider shared authorship or same applicant in prior publications and domestic patent documents. Grace period applies when considering anticipation or obviousness, but not when assessing double-patenting. Applicants may provide evidence to support relationship between author of prior disclosure and applicant.

name: Verify content of priority documents (post-Oct 30, 2019)
description: For applications where the request for priority was made on or after October 30, 2019, the content of the priority document can be verified using the copy submitted or made available under subsection 74(1) of the Patent Rules. If examination commences before a copy is submitted, examination should proceed assuming claim date is the filing date until copy is available.
guidance: Examiner should obtain and inspect the submitted priority document to determine whether claimed subject-matter is disclosed. If necessary, request certified copies per Patent Rules where documents are missing or accuracy is in doubt.

name: Double-patenting doctrine — prohibits multiple patents for same invention
description: Double-patenting is the judicially recognised proscription against an applicant being granted more than one patent for a single invention. Jurisprudence recognises two branches: 'same invention' and 'obviousness' double-patenting. Underlying principle: a second patent cannot be justified unless the claims exhibit 'novelty or ingenuity' over the first patent.
guidance: Assessment is a specialised evaluation of anticipation and obviousness where the prior art is an earlier patent by the same applicant; only the claims of the earlier patent are considered. Claims are given purposive construction in light of the specification and common general knowledge on the claim date. Double-patenting applies to the 'same applicant' including legal representatives and applies if the application belonged to the same applicant at any time.

name: Overlap — identical operating embodiment bars grant
description: Overlap describes the situation in which an operating embodiment in a claim of an application being examined is identical to an operating embodiment in a claim in an existing patent. The embodiment in the existing patent therefore acts as a bar against the latter; granting that embodiment in two patents would result in double-patenting.
guidance: Overlap may involve only a small fraction of claim scope but still creates a defect. Removing the overlap (e.g., deleting duplicated subject-matter) will remove the double-patenting defect. Example: dependent claims that define A+B in both documents can cause overlap unless removed.

name: Greater disclosure required in unpredictable or emerging technologies
description: For inventions in emerging and unpredictable technologies, or for inventions characterized by factors not reasonably predictable, more evidence is required to show possession.
guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not be sufficient to support a product claim other than a product-by-process claim. Where process has actually been used to produce the product, written description for a product-by-process claim is satisfied; otherwise it may fail if it is not clear the acts can be performed or the product is produced. Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization may be insufficient. (See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen; Burroughs Wellcome.)

name: Tests for species claims (must meet at least one)
description: Any claim to a species that does not meet the test described under at least one of (a), (b), or (c) must be rejected as lacking adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
guidance: The referenced tests (a)-(c) include (A) proof by actual reduction to practice, (B) reduction to drawings, or (C) disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, properties, functional characteristics coupled with correlation) sufficient to show possession.

name: Written description support for genus claims
description: A claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with correlation) or a combination thereof.
guidance: The disclosure must be sufficient to show the applicant was in possession of the claimed genus. (See Eli Lilly, 119 F.3d at 1568.)

name: Representative number of species requirement
description: A 'representative number of species' means that the species which are adequately described are representative of the entire genus; when there is substantial variation within the genus, one must describe a sufficient variety of species to reflect that variation.
guidance: Disclosure of only one species supports a genus claim only if the disclosure 'indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the gen[us].' Courts caution that a patentee cannot necessarily claim a genus after describing only a limited number of species when unpredictability exists. (See Enzo Biochem; Noelle v. Lederman; In re Curtis; Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe.)

name: Specification cannot support broad claims by describing only one embodiment
description: A specification cannot always support expansive claim language merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed; the issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand applicant to have invented, and been in possession of, the invention as broadly claimed.
guidance: If the specification teaches only one particular method and there is no evidence that a more generic method was contemplated, broad claims can be invalid under 35 U.S.C. 112. (See LizardTech v. Earth Resource Mapping; Tronzo v. Biomet.)

name: Treatment of applicant reply
description: Upon reply by applicant, the examiner must again determine patentability of the claimed invention including whether written description is satisfied by reperforming the analysis in view of the whole record.
guidance: If the whole record demonstrates adequacy, do not repeat the rejection. If inadequacy remains, repeat the rejection, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal, and properly treat any further showings. Affidavits relevant to the written description must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed. (See In re Alton.)

name: Claims must include all elements applicant described as essential
description: Each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential; omission of an element described as essential may render a new or amended claim deficient under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
guidance: If the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element applicant described as essential is not claimed, the claim must be rejected or the claim for priority denied. (See Johnson Worldwide; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo v. Biomet.)

name: Objective standard for determining compliance
description: The essential question is whether the description clearly allows persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed; the disclosure must convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, the applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
guidance: Tests and formulations include the 'does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill...to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed' (In re Gosteli) and 'convey with reasonable clarity...that the inventor was in possession' (Vas-Cath). The test for sufficiency in a parent application is whether the disclosure 'reasonably conveys to the artisan that the inventor had possession at that time of the later claimed subject matter.' (See Ralston Purina; In re Kaslow.)

name: Ways to show possession
description: Possession may be shown in a variety of ways including description of an actual reduction to practice, by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession.
guidance: Examples: Pfaff v. Wells Elecs.; Regents of the Univ. of California v. Eli Lilly; Amgen v. Chugai. Descriptive means include words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention. (See Lockwood.)

name: Nonliteral description and amended claims
description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally in the specification to satisfy the written description requirement; however, if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed, the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
guidance: This conclusion leads to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (description requirement), or denial of the benefit of the filing date of a previously filed application, as appropriate.

name: Determine broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
description: determine the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim (remember to consider whether the claims invoke 112(f)).
guidance: Worksheet step 1. Interpret claims under their BRI and explicitly consider whether claim limitations invoke 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function). Example: determine whether terms like “capturing unit”, “analyzing unit”, etc. invoke 112(f).

name: Analyze written-description support in the provisional application
description: analyze whether each of the claim limitations has adequate written-description support in the provisional application.
guidance: Worksheet step 2. For each limitation, ask whether the provisional specification discloses structure/material/acts sufficient to show the inventor possessed the claimed invention. Example: generic 'units' in the provisional did NOT provide sufficient detail to show possession of software/algorithmic structure.

name: Analyze written-description support in the non‑provisional application
description: analyze whether each of the claim limitations has adequate written-description support in the non‑provisional application.
guidance: Worksheet step 3. Evaluate whether the non‑provisional disclosure provides corresponding structure, algorithms, or other disclosure adequate to support the claim scope; if structure is present (e.g., CPU + instructions + APIDQ), written description may be adequate.

name: Identify which features are unsupported
description: identify which features are unsupported if support is lacking.
guidance: Worksheet step 4. Specify which claim limitations lack adequate written-description support in either the provisional or non‑provisional disclosure and document them for potential rejections or applicant notification.

name: Three‑prong test for applying 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means‑plus‑function)
description: Apply 112(f) when claim limitations use terms that are a substitute for 'means' (generic placeholder), are modified by functional language, and are not modified by sufficiently definite structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed functions.
guidance: If 112(f) applies, the claim must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.' See MPEP 2181. Example: 'capturing unit', 'analyzing unit', 'determining unit', 'transmitting unit' invoked 112(f) in Original Claim 1.

name: Corresponding structure requirement for computer‑implemented functions
description: For computer‑implemented specialized functions, the structure corresponding to the function must include a general purpose computer or computer component along with the algorithms that the computer uses to perform each claimed specialized function.
guidance: A flowchart or bare functional statement is not enough; the specification must disclose sufficient algorithms/instructions. Discussion: 'the structure corresponding to the 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitations that are computer‑implemented specialized functions must include ... the algorithms that the computer uses.' If absent, limitation lacks written‑description support and may be indefinite under 112(b).

name: Written description standard — specification must show possession
description: The specification as filed must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: General rule cited (e.g., Transco). Restating a function in claim language without disclosing how it is performed may fail written description, especially for software when algorithms/steps are not explained in sufficient detail.

name: Claims must be commensurate in scope with disclosed support
description: Claims cannot be broader than what the specification supports; the scope of the claim must be reasonably commensurate with the disclosure.
guidance: Example: a claim reciting 'at least 90% accuracy' covers up to 100% accuracy; if the specification only supports up to 97%, the claim is broader than supported and should be rejected under 112(a).

name: Generic placeholders vs definite structure (term‑by‑term analysis)
description: Determine whether claim terms are generic placeholders invoking 112(f) or recite sufficiently definite structure that does not invoke 112(f).
guidance: Example: 'unit' used generically invoked 112(f) because it was a placeholder modified by function and lacked definite structure in the provisional; 'filter' was held to be sufficiently definite structure (one of ordinary skill would recognize 'filter' as structure) and did not invoke 112(f).

name: Flowchart/diagram disclosure may be insufficient without algorithms
description: A flowchart (e.g., Figure 2) does not necessarily provide a sufficient algorithm corresponding to claimed functions.
guidance: Even if a flowchart shows steps, absence of specific algorithms/implementation details can render corresponding structure insufficient for 112(f) support (not showing how to program the computer to perform specialized functions).

name: When to question entitlement to earlier filing date / benefit claims
description: Evaluate whether the later‑filed application is entitled to the benefit of the earlier filing date by checking whether the earlier application provides proper 112(a) support.
guidance: Triggering circumstances include intervening prior art, significantly broadened later‑filed claims, or when the earlier‑filed application appears substantially less than the later application. Best practice: ensure the benefit claim is proper.

name: Examiner actions when earlier application lacks 112(a) support
description: Notify applicant that the later application is not entitled to the earlier filing date and conduct a prior art search based on the actual filing date.
guidance: Sample examiner instructions: (1) Notify applicant that claims are not entitled to benefit because earlier disclosure fails 112(a); (2) Conduct prior art search based on actual filing date and use intervening references as appropriate until benefit is shown or corrected. Suggested form paragraphs: 2.09 and 2.10.

name: New matter prohibition when amending to recite specifics not in original disclosure
description: An amendment that introduces a specific embodiment or species that was not present in the original disclosure may constitute new matter.
guidance: Example: adding 'Gaussian high pass filter' by amendment to a dependent claim after filing was treated as introducing new matter and not supported by original disclosure.

name: Remedy for lack of written description: narrow claim to disclosed species
description: To remedy lack of written description for a broadly worded limitation, amend the claim to recite the disclosed species that is supported by the specification.
guidance: Workshop example: amend to recite the disclosed APIDQ histogram technique to bring claim scope into commensuration with specification support.

name: Original claims do not automatically provide written‑description support
description: Merely reproducing a claim limitation in the specification, or pointing to an original claim, does not satisfy the written‑description requirement unless the claim itself conveys enough information to show possession at filing.
guidance: Determination is case‑by‑case and technology‑dependent; pointing to an original claim rarely suffices unless the claim conveys sufficient detail to demonstrate possession.

name: Definiteness of relative terms like 'about' depends on context
description: Relative terms (e.g., 'about') are evaluated in context; they are not necessarily indefinite.
guidance: Assess definiteness in view of the specification, claim context, and state of the art. Example: 'about 95% accurate' did not render a claim indefinite given the relative precision available for measuring detection rates and MPEP 2173.05(B)(II).

name: Principles vs Patentable Application
description: An abstract principle or mere scientific discovery, disconnected from a mode of application, is not patentable; a claim for an abstract principle or for an abstract result apart from means is invalid.
guidance: A principle may be patented only insofar as it is embodied in or applied by particular means; claim for principle apart from means prevents subsequent invention and is invalid. The treatise outlines requisites when a principle may be claimed and limitations.

name: Extent of Principle / Scope of Claim
description: A patent (claim) cannot be more extensive than the invention; claims are construed together with the specification, and cannot cover what is merely well-known or an abstract principle.
guidance: Claims are construed liberally but limited to the disclosed invention; courts interpret claim scope in light of specification and prior art.

name: Claims: Purpose and Drafting
description: The claim's object is to ascertain what is claimed as new (not to aid the description); it must be clear, distinguish the new from the old, and not be broader than the invention.
guidance: Claims may be a means of clearly presenting subject-matter; while clumsy wording may sometimes cover both product and process, defective or imperfectly worded claims can defeat a patent.

name: Prior Patents / Prior Public Work
description: A prior patent or prior public work that contains a full and clear description can defeat a later patent; a mere hint is insufficient.
guidance: To defeat later claims, prior patents must themselves be full and clear. The treatise explains evidence required to show prior art anticipates.

name: Reissue and Amendment of Patents
description: Reissue is permitted to correct errors; new patent upon surrender presumed to be for same invention; reissue may be used to amend specification/claims under limits.
guidance: Reissue allowed when original patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of defective specification or claim; reissue cannot be used to enlarge claim scope improperly. Surrender and reissue effects discussed.

name: Abandonment and Intermediate Abandonment
description: Abandonment of an invention or intermediate abandonment can affect patent rights; a single subsequent abandoned use does not necessarily defeat patent but may in some cases.
guidance: Whether abandonment defeats patent depends on whether there was a complete invention prior to patentee's claim and the nature of the subsequent use.

name: Questions of Law vs Questions of Fact (Court and Jury Roles)
description: Distinguishes issues for the court (e.g., claim construction) from those for the jury (e.g., sufficiency under proper instructions, novelty in some contexts), and how judges should instruct juries.
guidance: Treatise provides guidance on dividing questions (construction of patent and specification for the court; factual determinations like public use and enablement for the jury) and appropriate instructions.

name: Rule on Claims for Useless Parts
description: Claiming a useless part is not fatal if the machine as a whole is useful; but claiming what patentee knows to be useless is fatal.
guidance: Court examines inventors' knowledge and the practical usefulness of claimed elements in context of entire invention.

name: Requirement that nonprovisional applications include a compliant oath/declaration (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.51(b)(2), 1.63)
description: Nonprovisional patent applications must include an oath or declaration by each inventor that complies with 37 C.F.R. § 1.63; the required § 1.63 oath/declaration must state that the person making it has reviewed and understands the contents of the application, including the claims, as amended by any amendment specifically referred to in the oath or declaration (see § 1.63(b)(2)).
guidance: An oath/declaration signed before the inventor has reviewed and understands the finished/complete application fails to satisfy § 1.63 and is contrary to patent prosecution rules; such noncompliance may cause harm to the client, the public, and the Office.

name: Prohibition on obtaining inventor oaths/declarations prior to inventor review of completed application
description: Practitioners must not have inventor-clients sign the § 1.63 oath/declaration before the client has had the opportunity to review the completed specification, drawings, and claims.
guidance: The practice of obtaining signatures prior to preparation/completion of the application is 'plainly contrary' to patent prosecution rules and the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility and is a basis for disciplinary action. Practitioners should offer clients the option to review the completed application before filing and signing the oath/declaration.

name: Purpose and scope of the 2024 AI SME Update
description: The 2024 AI SME Update will assist USPTO personnel and stakeholders in evaluating the subject matter eligibility (SME) of claims in patent applications and patents involving inventions related to Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology (AI inventions). The 2024 AI SME Update does not reflect any new USPTO practice or procedure and is meant to be consistent with existing USPTO guidance, as set forth in the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP), and supplements this guidance to provide further clarity on evaluating SME for AI inventions.
guidance: Effective July 17, 2024. The Update supplements (but does not change) existing MPEP SME guidance (sections 2103–2106.07(c)); it will be incorporated into the MPEP in due course. Office personnel are to follow this 2024 AI SME Update to the extent earlier guidance is inconsistent with it.

name: Determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea
description: One inquiry addressed by the new examples is whether a claim recites an abstract idea.
guidance: Examples 47–49 provide exemplary SME analyses under 35 U.S.C. § 101 of hypothetical claims to illustrate how to assess whether a claim recites an abstract idea. Use these examples as fact‑specific illustrations when evaluating similar claim issues.

name: Determine whether a claim integrates an abstract idea into a practical application
description: Another inquiry addressed by the new examples is whether a claim integrates the abstract idea into a practical application.
guidance: Examples 47–49 illustrate how to analyze whether claimed subject matter that involves an abstract idea is nonetheless integrated into a practical application under the USPTO’s SME framework. Apply the reasoning in the examples to factual situations involving AI inventions.

name: Support requirement for claims
description: You must always provide adequate support in the description for your client’s claims. You cannot add wholly new material in response to an examiner’s objections and should anticipate any narrower elements you may later need to add to the claims by embedding support in the description at the outset.
guidance: The admissible degree of generalization is judged by the examiner in light of the prior art and varies by technology field. A fair claim is neither so broad it goes beyond the invention nor so narrow as to deprive the applicant of a just reward. Applicants may cover obvious modifications, equivalents and uses if it is reasonable that the variants will have the properties or uses ascribed in the description. Examples: a process disclosed for one plant kind cannot validly be claimed for all plant seedlings without convincing evidence; claims for synthetic resin methods limited to thermoplastics if examples only show thermoplastics; omitting a disclosed additive from a broad composition claim can render the claim unsupported. Professional tip: embed support for foreseeable narrower claim elements in the description from the start.

name: Degree of generalization in claim drafting
description: The admissible degree of generalization claimed may vary depending on the field of technologies and related prior art; claims that open up a whole new field may be more extensively generalized than those that improve a well-known field.
guidance: Examiners judge generalization case-by-case. Broader protection generally requires more extensive disclosure; narrow protection may suffice with a single embodiment. Unnecessarily extensive disclosure is not prohibited but increases cost and public disclosure. Ensure reasonable evidence that claimed variants have the ascribed properties or uses.

name: Unity in Markush-type claims (chemical alternatives)
description: Where a single claim defines alternatives (a Markush group), unity exists if the alternatives are of a similar nature and can fairly be substituted for one another. Under the PCT for chemical alternatives: (A) all alternatives have a common property or activity, and (B) either (B.1) a common structure is present (significant structural element shared) or (B.2) alternatives belong to a recognized class of chemical compounds expected to behave the same way.
guidance: The 'significant structural element' may be a single component or a combination of linked components and must be essential to the common property/activity. If at least one alternative is not novel, re-evaluate unity. Unity may be apparent a priori or only a posteriori when prior art shows lack of novelty/inventive step.

name: Claim point of view (consistent point of view)
description: All limitations or elements set out in a single claim should have a consistent 'point of view' (e.g., all steps in a method claim must be performed by the same party).
guidance: Consistent point of view is important for identifying parties that could directly infringe. If inventive components are spread across parties, a single claim lacking a consistent point of view may make proving infringement difficult. Draft claims to enable direct infringement (or anticipate evidence for indirect infringement) and to facilitate enforcement/licensing. Examples: combined battery/flashlight claim that mixes parties may leave no single entity directly infringing; better to draft separate flashlight, battery, and connector claims.

name: Draft claims to facilitate enforcement and licensing (all-element rule awareness)
description: A claim should be set out so that imitation of the protected subject matter will be considered an act of direct infringement; at least one claim should read on embodiments made, used and sold by the client.
guidance: Direct infringement is often prerequisite to asserting contributory or induced infringement; product claims are generally easier to detect/prove than process claims. If claims do not read on the client's embodiment, the drafter may have misunderstood the invention or the client’s practice may have changed. Consequences include inability to mark products as patented and difficulties collecting lost profits damages. Use multiple claims targeted at different parties/parts when appropriate (e.g., client/server splitting).

name: Narrowing claims during prosecution
description: A claim may be narrowed by (i) adding new elements, (ii) adding a limitation to a previously recited element, and/or (iii) further defining how previously recited elements interoperate.
guidance: When adding a new element, it should further define an existing structure/functional element or be relational; the new element must be present in the description (impermissible to create new relationships not disclosed at filing). Consider alternative amendments and counsel the client about the impact on claim breadth and enforceability. Examples: adding a removable cap to a pencil claim; further defining a light's direction to narrow scope. More on amendments in Module IX.

name: Show amendments clearly during prosecution
description: Most patent offices require the drafter to clearly show any changes made to amend a claim during prosecution.
guidance: Depending on local rules, amendments may be submitted with editorial indications: bracketed notes like '[Amended]', strike-through for deletions and underlining for additions. Use these conventions to make the nature of amendments explicit.

name: Exclusions from patentability (subject-matter exceptions)
description: Most jurisdictions exclude certain subject matter from patent protection; lists and scope vary by country (e.g., judicial exceptions in the U.S.).
guidance: If claims are rejected on exclusions, redrafting may sometimes obtain protection (substance preserved, form changed). Software-related inventions may require particular wording to avoid exclusions. Biotechnology inventions require special care: some discoveries or exploitations may be unprotectable for reasons of public order/morality. Stay up to date with national/regional law developments and advise clients accordingly.

name: Requirement for industrial applicability
description: The description should indicate how the invention is capable of exploitation in industry where this is not self-evident; for sequences/partial gene sequences, the industrial application must be disclosed.
guidance: A mere nucleic acid sequence without indication of function is not patentable; if a sequence is used to produce a protein, specify which protein and its function. If a nucleotide sequence is not used to produce a protein, indicate a functional activity such as promoter activity. Recast claims if examiner finds lack of industrial applicability (e.g., device for dispensing fashion advice might be recast as an inventory device).

name: Reading on a patent claim ('all-elements rule')
description: For a claim to read on an accused product or process, every element of the claim must be present in the accused product or process.
guidance: Ensure at least one claim reads on the client’s own embodiments. If claims don't read on the client's embodiment, drafter misunderstanding or client changes may be the cause. Consequences include inability to mark products as patented and potentially reduced damages (lost profits harder to collect). See Module IV, section 1.3 for all-elements rule details.

name: Claim construction in the courts (interpretation principles)
description: Courts interpret claims by reading the claims and the description; if not clear, courts refer to the ordinary meaning to a person skilled in the art and may consult dictionaries, handbooks, treatises and expert testimony. In the U.S., courts begin with ordinary meaning then review description and prosecution history for special meanings.
guidance: Where a patent creates a new term or a term is ambiguous, define it in the description (the description can act as a glossary). Be extremely careful about potential ambiguities in the application and in prosecution responses because intrinsic evidence and prosecution history may be used to construe terms. Aim for a self-contained application understandable without external context.

name: Doctrine of equivalents (scope beyond literal words)
description: Some jurisdictions provide protection beyond the literal scope of claim words via the doctrine of equivalents, which may treat substituted features as infringing if they are equivalent in the invention’s context.
guidance: Doctrine of equivalents varies by jurisdiction and can be unpredictable. Example: a screw might be found equivalent to a nail for holding two widgets. Professional tip: draft claims as though doctrines of equivalents do not exist—give terms their ordinary and customary meaning to a person skilled in the art to maximize certainty.

name: Avoiding ambiguity; defining multiple-meaning terms
description: Words used in claims often have multiple dictionary meanings; courts will prefer the customary meaning in the specific art when relevant. If multiple meanings are possible and only one is meant, define the meaning in the description.
guidance: When construing claim terms, courts may examine intrinsic evidence (claims, description, drawings, prosecution file) to ascertain the meaning consistent with the drafter’s intent. Use definitions in the description, and be mindful that technical dictionaries and expert testimony may be consulted; avoid leaving terms ambiguous during prosecution.

name: Additional statements formatting and use
description: Additional statements (disclaimers, colors claimed, description of mark, stippling, claim of prior registrations, translation/transliteration, Section 2(f) claim, consent, supplemental register amendment, concurrent use claim, miscellaneous statement) will display in the "Additional Statement(s)" section; include only words that are in the mark or translations/transliterations in quotation marks.
guidance: Do not use this section for attachments where a specific section exists. Use the miscellaneous statement field to request deletion of a statement already of record. The Section 2(f) declaration will automatically appear where needed.

name: Standard character vs special form mark guidance
description: To indicate standard characters (no claim to font/style/size/color) or Special Form (stylized/design) or Sound Mark. If object to USPTO-generated image, use Special Form to attach your own image and claim standard characters if desired.
guidance: Appropriateness of claiming standard characters will be determined during examination.

name: Limits on amendments during opposition
description: Only amendments that respond directly to a ground of opposition are allowed. Added matter is not permitted; claim broadening is also not allowed, even if it would be necessary to address a ground of opposition.
guidance: Example: if a feature present in claim 1 is alleged to add matter, it cannot be deleted in response if doing so would broaden scope of the claim.

name: Inter Partes Review (IPR) institution and scope
description: IPR is a trial proceeding to challenge patentability of one or more claims under 35 U.S.C. § 102 and/or § 103 based only on patents or printed publications; almost any party except the patentee may file; timing: available after the later of nine months after patent issuance or after any pending PGR has ended.
guidance: A three-judge APJ panel determines whether there is a 'reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 claim challenged in the petition' (35 U.S.C. § 314(a)). If instituted, PTAB issues a final determination within one year (extendable for good cause by six months). Statutory estoppel: if a final decision is reached, the petitioner is estopped in district court/ITC from raising any ground it 'raised or reasonably could have raised' in the IPR, and the patent owner is estopped from prosecuting patentably indistinct claims (35 U.S.C. § 315(e); 37 C.F.R. § 42.73). Use these timing and estoppel rules when assessing whether to file or defend an IPR and when planning parallel district/ITC litigation or further prosecution.

name: Covered Business Method (CBM) review requirements and limits
description: CBM review is a PTAB trial to review patentability of claims in a 'covered business method' patent (claims to a method or apparatus related to a financial product or service, not a technological invention). Only a person accused of infringement may file a CBM petition; CBM can be filed before litigation or after complaint service, subject to other timing limits.
guidance: Institution standard: 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. § 324). CBM may be based on any ground of invalidity (§§ 101, 102, 103, 112). CBM is a transitional program (sunset on Sept. 16, 2020). If a final decision issues, the petitioner is estopped from raising in litigation any ground 'raised' in the CBM, and from raising in subsequent PTO proceedings any ground that 'reasonably could have been raised' in CBM; patent owner estopped from prosecuting patentably indistinct claims (AIA § 18; 37 C.F.R. § 42.73). These constraints affect whether to pursue CBM and how to structure litigation and prosecution strategies.

name: Post-Grant Review (PGR) institution and scope
description: PGR is a PTAB trial to review patentability of claims under a broad set of grounds (35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112) for patents issuing from first-inventor-to-file applications; a non-owner who has not previously filed a civil action challenging validity may file on or prior to nine months after issuance.
guidance: Institution standard: 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. § 321(b)). If instituted and not dismissed, PTAB issues a final determination within one year (extendable by six months). After institution, the petitioner is precluded from re-litigating in a civil action any issue it raised or reasonably could have raised in the PGR. Use the broader grounds and early filing window (within nine months) when evaluating the advisability and timing of a PGR petition vs. IPR.

name: Motion to amend during post-grant proceedings (statutory limit and constraints)
description: During IPR, CBM or PGR, the patent owner may file one motion to amend the patent (35 U.S.C. § 316(d)); substitute claims may not 'enlarge the scope' of the claims or 'introduce new subject matter' (37 C.F.R. § 42.121(a)(2)).
guidance: Requests to cancel claims are typically granted without substantive review; substitute-claim motions are generally decided only when the panel first determines the original claims are unpatentable (many motions are contingent on an unfavorable decision for original claims). The PTAB's Motion to Amend study (Apr. 30, 2016) shows motions to amend were decided on the merits in a small fraction of trials (118/1539, 8%), and of those decided on the merits only 5% were granted-in-part/ granted. Denial reasons included: anticipation/obviousness over art of record (35%), multiple statutory reasons (23%), lack of written description (8%), non-statutory subject matter (6%), claim enlargement (5%), unreasonable number of substitute claims (3%), indefiniteness (1%), and procedural failures such as failure to show substitute claims are patentable over 'the prior art in general' (19%). These high denial rates and common denial rationales should guide patent owners' decision whether to attempt amendment in PTAB proceedings vs. pursue other remedies.

name: Reissue application (statutory basis, scope, benefits, and risks)
description: A reissue application under 35 U.S.C. § 251 may be filed when a patent is 'through error, deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid' due to defective specification/drawing or claiming more/less than the patentee had a right to claim. Reissue can be used to pursue amended (often narrower) claims.
guidance: Advantages: patent owner may prosecute narrower claims to avoid estoppel and to present different arguments over prior art; may pursue broader claims if filed within two years of issuance (broadening reissue), and may file continuing reissue applications claiming priority to the first reissue. Risks: reissue requires surrender of the original patent and reopens prosecution — examiner may reject claims on new grounds; doctrine of intervening rights may limit damages for amended claims to the period after issuance of the reissued claim; third parties may file protests or later challenge the reissue via PGR, IPR, or CBM. Pendency: average reissue pendency decreased to ~2.3 years for reissued patents through Apr. 2016 (previously ~5 years). Weigh pendency, possible reexamination, intervening rights, and the possibility of additional challenges when choosing reissue.

name: Institution standards and timing comparisons
description: Different AIA proceedings apply different institution standards and timing rules and have similar one-year final-decision clocks (extendable six months).
guidance: IPR institution standard: 'reasonable likelihood' petitioner would prevail on at least one claim (35 U.S.C. § 314(a)). CBM and PGR institution standard: 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. §§ 321(b), 324). IPRs are available after the later of nine months post-issuance or after conclusion of any PGR; PGR must be filed within nine months of issuance for eligible patents. Final PTAB determinations are expected within one year of institution (extendable by six months for good cause). CBM is a transitional program with a sunset date (Sept. 16, 2020). Use these institution standards and timing windows when choosing the most appropriate challenge or defense strategy.

name: Practical statistics on post-grant proceedings and motions to amend (empirical context)
description: Empirical PTAB/PTO statistics show high rates of claim cancellation in completed post-grant proceedings and low success rates for motions to amend decided on the merits.
guidance: As of Sept. 30, 2016: 5,656 petitions filed (91% IPR, 8% CBM, 1% PGR). Of IPR petitions completed to date, 1,214 reached final written decisions and 85% cancelled all or some claims. Of CBM petitions completed to date, 143 reached final written decisions and 98% cancelled all or some claims. PTAB Motion to Amend Study (Apr. 30, 2016) reported the Board decided merits of substitute-claim motions in only 118 of 1539 completed AIA trials (8%); of those 118, motions were granted or granted-in-part in 6 trials (5%) and denied in 112 (95%). Reasons for denial (with percentages) are summarized in the MTA study (anticipation/obviousness 35%; multiple statutory reasons 23%; lack of written description 8%; non-statutory subject matter 6%; etc.). These data should inform realistic expectations about likelihood of preserving original claim scope or obtaining substitute claims via PTAB proceedings.

name: Comparative benefits and risks table for post-decision options
description: High-level comparison of standards, benefits, and risks for rehearing, appeal, reissue, supplemental examination, ex parte reexamination, and continuation applications, to guide option selection after claims are cancelled.
guidance: Rehearing: must identify misapprehensions, reviewed for abuse of discretion; advantage: may elicit additional rationale useful on appeal; risk: rarely granted and may bolster PTAB rationale. Appeal to Federal Circuit: de novo review of legal questions, substantial evidence for facts; advantage: potential reversal but historically low reversal rates; cost/time considerations. Reissue: full prosecution, can seek broader claims within two years (but surrender original patent); advantage: full examination and potential for broadened or alternative claims; risks: intervening rights, reopened prosecution, third-party protests, pendency. Supplemental examination: can immunize against unenforceability (if completed before certain litigation), broader submission scope than ex parte reexam; risk: exceptions if prior allegations exist. Ex parte reexamination: ex parte process with examiner, possibly quicker than reissue, may allow amendments without admitting error; risk: patents not presumed valid, intervening rights if claims amended. Continuation: maintain pending application to pursue patentably distinct claims informed by PTAB record; cost/time tradeoffs.
