Use the summarized benefits/risks to select one or more options to preserve rights post-cancellation, frequently combining strategies (e.g., appeal plus reissue or continuation) based on business objectives and timelines.

name: Pre-appeal readiness — focus on claims and finalized record
description: Appeals before the PTAB must focus on the claims, not the disclosed invention, and the record at the time the Appeal Brief is filed should be finalized.
guidance: Thoroughly review each claim (each independent claim) and the prosecution record to ensure the claims are of the correct scope and all evidence to be relied upon is properly entered and considered by the examiner. Opportunities to present additional evidence after filing a Notice of Appeal are limited.

name: Claim construction standard — broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification
description: The PTO applies the broadest reasonable meaning of claim words as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account guidance in the written description.
guidance: Because examiners and PTAB panels may construe claims broadly, practitioners must step back to determine how broad claims will be read under the BRI/consistent-with-spec standard (In re Morris). This affects what to argue and whether amendments are needed prior to appeal.

name: Appeal Brief — Summary of claimed subject matter (37 CFR § 41.37(c)(iii))
description: A concise summary for each independent claim involved in the appeal referring to the specification and drawings is required.
guidance: Provide claim chart tables tying claim elements to figures/paragraphs in the specification. For limitations that may be means/step-plus-function under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), separately identify and analyze them — burden is on appellant to identify such limitations. Avoid 'mystery' words; be able to point to where claim language appears in the specification to avoid new matter or lack of written description problems.

name: Ensure claim terms have antecedent/support in the specification; avoid new matter
description: The terms and phrases used in claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so meanings are ascertainable by reference to the description (37 CFR § 1.75(d)(1)).
guidance: When claims are amended to include language not explicitly in the original disclosure, make appropriate specification amendments concurrently (if needed) and explain how original disclosure provides written descriptive support. Adherence to this avoids new matter and written description rejections.

name: Appeal Brief — Argument section: claim-by-claim and refined advocacy (37 CFR § 41.37(c)(iv))
description: Arguments should be presented on a claim-by-claim basis, refined and expanded beyond prior prosecution responses; only arguments in the Appeal Brief will be considered by the Board.
guidance: Do not copy/paste the previous response. Use separate headings by ground of rejection and additional headings for different parts of your theory (e.g., failure to establish prima facie case, lack of suggestion/motivation, evidence of unexpected results). Avoid arguing by groups of claims — if claims are lumped, the panel will pick the most vulnerable claim as representative. Argue individual claims to maximize chances and patent term.

name: Oral hearing — when to request and how to conduct
description: Oral argument can help but must be carefully prepared and is limited to the briefing content.
guidance: Request hearings when complex facts or cutting-edge legal issues are present; avoid hearings where only a §103 rejection exists without richer issues. Prepare a list of technical terms for the transcriptionist; note that you are typically limited to 20 minutes (panels may be lenient). Limit arguments to those in the briefs; avoid introducing new arguments. Avoid computer presentations — provide concise briefing packages and copies of key passages to panel members. Be ready to be interrupted with questions about claim scope and prior art and preface answers that raise issues not before the Board to avoid creating new grounds of rejection. Consider whether an applicant/assignee representative should attend (weigh ability to explain tech vs. risk of admissions). Be mindful of remote panelists and accessibility (e.g., color blindness).

name: Post-decision practice — rehearing, RCE, PTA and new grounds
description: After the PTAB decision, examine what was affirmed/reversed, preserve PTA where possible, and pursue rehearing or reopening appropriately.
guidance: If decision reverses all rejections, proceed to allowance. If affirmed-in-part with at least one independent claim patentable, avoid filing an RCE (it may forfeit patent term adjustment); instead examiner should cancel affirmed claims and allow remaining claims. Compare panel reasoning to examiner's Answer to detect designated or undesignated new grounds of rejection. If you believe a new ground was made, raise it explicitly in a single request for rehearing (37 CFR § 41.52) and state arguments with particularity. If a new ground under 37 CFR § 41.50(b) is made, elect either to reopen prosecution or to request rehearing before the PTAB; you cannot pursue both.

name: Maximizing patent term — claim strategy in briefing
description: Careful claim-by-claim argumentation can maximize patent term adjustment (PTA).
guidance: Separately argue dependent claims that seem likely to win so an appellate reversal on at least one claim may lead to PTA. Know the statutory and regulatory provisions tying appellate reversals to PTA (35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(C)(iii); 37 CFR § 1.702(e)). Consider that certain remands may also result in PTA.

name: Single-invention requirement and election without traverse
description: The claims must be directed to a single invention. If the Office determines the claims are not obviously to a single invention, applicant must make an election without traverse as a prerequisite to special status; the petition must include a statement that applicant will agree to make such an election in a telephonic interview.
guidance: If applicant refuses to make an election without traverse, the application will not be further examined at that time and the petition will be denied. The telephone restriction practice will be followed if required.

name: Preexamination search statement requirements
description: At filing applicant must provide a statement that a preexamination search was conducted, listing the field of search by class and subclass, publication, Chemical Abstracts, foreign patents, etc., and for database searches include search logic or chemical structure/sequence used, name of files/databases and date.
guidance: The preexamination search must involve U.S. patents and patent application publications, foreign patent documents, and non-patent literature unless applicant justifies with reasonable certainty why elimination is permissible; it must be directed to the claimed invention and encompass all claim features under the broadest reasonable interpretation. A foreign patent office search report only satisfies this requirement if it meets these requirements. Statements must be made in good faith (see 37 CFR 1.56 and 10.18).

name: Scope coverage of preexamination search and consequences of uncovered amendments
description: The preexamination search must encompass the disclosed features that may be claimed. An amendment to the claims (including any new claim) that is not encompassed by the preexamination search or an updated accelerated examination support document will be treated as an improper reply and will not be entered.
guidance: Amendments that broaden the search field are improper replies. Applicants must provide an updated support document when submitting amendments that change claim scope.

name: Accelerated examination support document (content requirements)
description: Applicant must provide an accelerated examination support document including: (1) an IDS per 37 CFR 1.98 citing each reference deemed most closely related to the subject matter of each claim; (2) for each reference, identification of all claim limitations disclosed and where disclosed; (3) a detailed explanation of how each claim is patentable over the references with particularity required by 37 CFR 1.111(b) and (c); (4) a concise statement of the utility of the invention as defined in each independent claim; (5) a showing where each claim limitation finds support under the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 in the written description (and identification of corresponding structure/material/acts for means-plus-function elements under 112, para. 6, and in any priority applications); and (6) identification of any cited references that may be disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
guidance: The support document is detailed and must map claim limitations to prior art and to the specification. Failure to include or defects in the document can cause denial of the petition; applicants may be given a single opportunity to perfect certain defects within one month (no extensions).

name: Initial examiner action timing and pre-action conference
description: Once granted special status the application will be docketed and taken up expeditiously (e.g., within two weeks). The USPTO will not issue an Office action (other than notice of allowance) unless (A) an interview was conducted but did not result in allowance, or (B) there is a determination that an interview is unlikely to result in allowance. Prior to mailing any Office action rejecting the claims, the USPTO will conduct a conference to review the rejections set forth in the Office action.
guidance: If claims are not to a single invention, telephone restriction practice will be followed and applicant must make an election without traverse during telephonic interview. If examiner cannot reach applicant, claim 1 may be constructively elected.

name: Reply content limits (responsiveness) in accelerated examination
description: A reply to an Office action must be restricted to the rejections, objections, and requirements made. Any amendment that would (A) add claims resulting in more than three independent or more than twenty total claims, (B) present claims not encompassed by the preexamination search or an updated support document, or (C) present claims directed to a nonelected invention, will be treated as not fully responsive and will not be entered.
guidance: For any amendment not encompassed by the support document, applicant must file an updated support document at the time of filing the amendment. IDS filed with updates must comply with 37 CFR 1.97 and 1.98. Replies and other papers must be filed electronically via EFS-Web to be expeditiously processed.

name: Detailed conditions for examination (items to be present at filing)
description: At time of filing the application must include: (1) basic filing fee, search fee, and examination fee; (2) application size fee if applicable; (3) executed oath/declaration in compliance with 37 CFR 1.63; (4) specification with description and claims in compliance with 37 CFR 1.52/1.71/1.75; (5) title and abstract per 37 CFR 1.72; (6) drawings per 37 CFR 1.84; (7) electronic sequence listings/large tables/computer listings in ASCII via EFS if applicable; (8) foreign priority claim identified per 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) if applicable; (9) domestic benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, or 365(c) in compliance with 37 CFR 1.78 if applicable; (10) English translation and accuracy statement and processing fee under 37 CFR 1.17(i) if specification is non-English; (11) no preliminary amendments present on filing date; and (12) no petition under 37 CFR 1.47 for a non-signing inventor.
guidance: Design applications must also comply with 37 CFR 1.151-1.154. Petition to make special will be dismissed if the application omits an item or includes a paper that causes formality-review notices. Applicants should provide suggested classification to expedite processing.

name: DKPTO must have at least one allowable/patentable claim (eligibility 2)
description: The DKPTO application(s) relied upon must have at least one claim determined by DKPTO to be allowable/patentable.
guidance: Applicant must submit a copy of the allowable/patentable claims and an English translation with a statement that the translation is accurate if claims are not in English. If the DKPTO office action does not explicitly state a claim is allowable/patentable, the applicant must include a statement in the PPH request (or transmittal letter) that no rejection was made regarding that claim and thus it is deemed allowable/patentable by DKPTO.

name: Claims correspondence requirement (eligibility 3)
description: All claims in the U.S. application for which PPH participation is requested must sufficiently correspond to the allowable/patentable claims in the DKPTO application(s).
guidance: Sufficient correspondence is determined by whether, accounting for translation and claim format differences, claims are of the same or similar scope. Applicant must submit an English claims correspondence table indicating how each U.S. claim corresponds to the DKPTO allowable/patentable claims.

name: Explaining a lack of unity defect
description: A report identifying a lack of unity of invention should explain the basis for the conclusion so the applicant can decide whether and how to limit or divide their claims for further examination.
guidance: The explanation should identify what the examiner considers the distinct inventions to be and provide sufficient detail for the applicant to understand why the different inventions do not share a single general inventive concept. Where the defect is identified a posteriori, cite the prior art supporting this conclusion and explain the significance of each document. Wherever possible, relate the individual inventions to the claims in which they are defined so the applicant can group claims into sets viewed as sharing a single general inventive concept. Generally set out groups of claims considered to be directed to one invention only and indicate to which group each independent claim belongs. Unless explicitly indicated otherwise, dependent claims are presumed to belong to the group in which the claim they refer to is found. If lack of unity exists among alternatives within a single claim, separate inventions into groups where practical and relate dependent claims to the alternative they refer to. Note: using the term “invention” is for convenience and does not imply patentability.

name: When a lack of unity defect should be identified
description: A lack of unity of invention should generally be identified in the first report written in respect of the claims that lack unity.
guidance: Exceptions: if other defects (e.g., obviousness, ambiguity, lack of utility or support) bear on unity and the applicant’s response would be germane, the unity defect may be formally identified in a later report. A lack of unity can be introduced by amendments and may be identified regardless of prior examination length. If prior art suggests a posteriori lack of unity but some claims are anticipated/obvious, it may be preferable to not formally identify lack of unity until the prior art defect is addressed; the applicant may be informed informally. If applicant amends to avoid cited prior art but the amended claims lack unity, the examiner may identify the defect.

name: Referral to the Commissioner of Patents
description: If an applicant declines to limit claims after being notified of a lack of unity defect, the application may be forwarded to the Commissioner for determination, but referral must follow internal review.
guidance: To ensure efficiency and fairness, an examiner must first submit the application to a Unity Review Board (URB) for review. Possible URB outcomes: (a) unity exists → proceed with substantive exam of all claims; (b) lack of unity exists but further clarification needed → examiner issues further report; (c) lack of unity exists and was clearly communicated → application forwarded to Commissioner. If Commissioner directs limitation (under subsection 36(2.1)), a Notice of Direction is sent. If applicant’s response to the Notice is unsatisfactory, application may be forwarded to the Patent Appeal Board, and refusal will not happen without an opportunity to be heard (per subsection 86(13)). Examiners should expect referral after at least two reports identifying the defect.

name: Claims in different categories presumed to have unity (a priori)
description: Certain combinations of claim categories can generally be presumed to satisfy unity of invention when present in a single application.
guidance: Presumed category combinations: (a) a product and a process for making that product; (b) a product and a use of that product; (c) a product, a process for making it, and a use; (d) an apparatus and a process carried out on that apparatus. If 'process for making a product' is a 'process carried out on an apparatus,' apparatus claims can be included with product/process/use claims provided the product is inventive by virtue of properties arising from its being prepared using the apparatus. Claim breadth need not be similar to satisfy unity; unity may still exist if scopes differ. Examples illustrate grouping decisions and when claims lack unity a priori or may lack unity a posteriori when prior art is found.

name: Unity when the inventive linking feature is not claimed
description: Unity of invention may still exist a priori even if the claim language does not explicitly recite the common inventive linking feature.
guidance: In a priori assessment examiners should consider the description and common general knowledge before concluding lack of unity. Identify the claim with the fewest elements and check for common elements across independent claims. An applicant may respond to a lack of unity a priori by identifying features they consider the inventive elements common to all claims; the examiner may verify by searching on those elements. Examples show when a linking inventive concept is implicit in the description (and thus unity exists) versus when it is not.

name: Unity of invention and utility
description: The utility of claimed subject-matter (demonstrated or soundly predicted) can inform whether claims form a single invention or multiple inventions.
guidance: If all embodiments' utility can be soundly predicted using a single line of reasoning based on one set of facts, unity likely exists. If different parts require significantly different sound predictions to support utility, multiple inventions are likely present. A species that has a significantly different utility from the genus may be an aspect of the same invention (if it retains generic utility) or a separate invention (if it replaces the generic utility). Examples clarify when species may be treated as same invention or separate.

name: Markush groups and lists of alternatives
description: A Markush group must define alternatives that are technical equivalents performing the same function in substantially the same way; the skilled person should expect direct substitutability in operable embodiments.
guidance: Criteria for a valid Markush group: (a) each alternative shares a common property or activity and either (i) shares a common structure relevant to activity in the invention, or (ii) belongs to a class recognized in the art where members behave the same way in the invention context. If alternatives do not satisfy these and unity cannot be established by other claim elements, the shared structure or utility must be novel and inventive over prior art to provide unity. Where a list meets the requirements, unity will generally be acknowledged regardless of whether presented as a Markush group.

name: Intermediates and final products
description: An intermediate that is transformed to produce a final product may have unity of invention with the final product despite different inventive steps or utility.
guidance: Requirements: the intermediate must necessarily be useful for producing the final product; must share principal structural elements with the final product or introduce an essential structural element; must be a direct precursor to the final product (removed by only one or a few steps) and not a precursor to a known intermediate produced on the way to the final product. Different intermediates that introduce different structural parts will generally not share unity among each other. Chemical examples and detailed analyses illustrate when unity exists (e.g., open-ring precursors sharing core structures) and when certain uses of an intermediate may lack unity with final product claims and thus be appropriate for a divisional.

name: Multi-step methods of preparation
description: Claims to a single inventive transformative step and claims to larger methods that include that step can share unity; other individual steps that do not include the transformative step may not share unity with it.
guidance: The transformative step transforms a precursor into a product and typically shares unity with that product and possibly with certain precursors. Other steps or combinations that do not include the inventive transformative step do not share the general inventive concept and thus do not have unity with it. Products not meeting intermediate/final requirements likewise won't share unity. Example with steps A–E illustrates which combinations have unity based on where the inventive step occurs and how groups can be formed.

name: Effect of provisos on unity
description: A proviso (clause excluding matter from a claim) may make claimed subject-matter 'discontinuous' and could remove the general inventive concept, potentially causing lack of unity, but the effect depends on facts and reasons for the proviso.
guidance: Assess the reason for the proviso. If used to avoid prior art, determine whether the prior art merely discloses an embodiment within the claim or teaches the same inventive concept. If the latter, unity is likely absent a posteriori; if the former, unity may remain. Example: a genus claim with proviso excluding an earlier species still had unity when the earlier patent had not identified the structure-function relationship that is the inventive concept.

name: Examination of divisional applications
description: Examination of divisional applications is similar to regular applications but includes specific checks to ensure the divisional claim set is directed to a different invention and contains no new matter relative to the parent.
guidance: Compare the specification and drawings of the divisional to the parent to determine if claims are directed to a different invention and whether the divisional was filed with new matter. If claims are not directed to a different invention than the parent, the later application is not a proper divisional under section 36. If the divisional has a presentation date after October 30, 2019 and contains new matter relative to the parent, it is defective under section 91 or 155.7 of the Patent Rules. Amendments introducing new matter to a divisional invoke subsection 38.2(3.1) of the Patent Act or 155.6 of the Patent Rules (see referenced sections for details). Note: if filing of a divisional was directed by the Patent Office, double-patenting doctrine does not apply between the divisional and its parent/siblings.

name: Rule 25 — Divisional applications: timing, content and fees
description: A European divisional application may be filed at any time after receipt of the earlier European application provided it is filed within any period prescribed after the first communication from the Examining Division or is otherwise considered justified; or within two months following a limitation at invitation of the Examining Division if the earlier application failed Article 82. Description and drawings should, where possible, relate only to the matter for which protection is sought; if necessary they may include a cross-reference to another application. Filing, search and designation fees must be paid for each divisional within one month after filing. Designation fees may be paid up to the expiry of the period specified for the earlier application if that later expiry follows the one-month period.
guidance: Timing constraints for filing divisionals, expectation that divisional documents stay focused on claimed subject-matter (or cross-reference when overlap needed), and strict short deadlines for fees (one month) with limited deferral for designation fees tied to Article 79(2) periods.

name: Rule 26 — Contents of the request for grant
description: The request for grant must be filed on an EPO form and shall contain: (a) a petition for grant; (b) the title of the invention clearly and concisely stating the technical designation and excluding fancy names (if multiple claim categories this must be evident from the title); (c) name, address and nationality of applicant with format rules for natural and legal persons and adequate postal address (recommend telegraphic/telephone details); (d) representative's name and business address if appointed; (e) indication if application is a divisional and number of earlier application; (f) number of original European application where Article 61(1)(b) applies; (g) declaration claiming priority with date and country; (h) designation of Contracting State(s) for protection; (i) signature of applicant or representative; (j) list of accompanying documents indicating number of sheets of description, claims, drawings and abstract filed; (k) designation of inventor where applicant is inventor. If multiple applicants, request should preferably appoint one common representative.
guidance: Use the official EPO form; include all required identification, priority and procedural data and the list of submitted parts; adhere to naming/address formatting conventions; appoint a common representative if multiple applicants to simplify correspondence.

name: Rule 27 — Description: required content and order
description: The description shall: (a) state the title as in the request; (b) specify the technical field; (c) indicate background art useful for understanding the invention and preferably cite documents; (d) disclose the invention, as claimed, so that the technical problem and its solution can be understood and state advantageous effects with reference to background art; (e) briefly describe figures in drawings; (f) describe in detail at least one embodiment of the claimed invention using examples where appropriate and referring to drawings; (g) explicitly indicate industrial applicability where not obvious. The description shall be presented in the manner and order specified unless another order better serves understanding and economy of presentation.
guidance: Description must enable understanding of problem-solution and at least one practicable embodiment; include background and advantages; follow prescribed structure unless deviating improves clarity.

name: Rule 29 — Form and content of claims
description: Claims shall define the subject-matter sought in terms of technical features. Where appropriate, claims shall contain: (a) a statement indicating designation of the subject-matter and technical features necessary for definition but which are part of the prior art; (b) a characterising portion preceded by 'characterised in that' or 'characterised by' stating the technical features which in combination with (a) are desired to be protected. Subject to Article 82, multiple independent claims in the same category are permitted if appropriate. Claims stating essential features may be followed by claims to particular embodiments. Dependent claims including all features of another claim shall, if possible at the beginning, reference that claim and then state additional features. Dependent claims may refer to dependent claims. Dependent claims referring back to single or multiple previous claims should be grouped appropriately. Number of claims must be reasonable; claims numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals. Claims should not, except where absolutely necessary, rely on references to description or drawings (e.g., 'as described in part...'). Where drawings exist, reference signs may be used in claims (in parentheses) to increase intelligibility but are not limiting.
guidance: Draft claims in clear technical-feature language, use characterising clause format for distinguishing features, keep claim count reasonable, number consecutively, avoid reliance on description/drawings for essential features; dependent claims must reference and add features correctly; reference signs may be used but are non-limiting.

name: Rule 30 — Claims in different categories (combinations permitted)
description: Article 82 permits that the same application may include, e.g., in addition to an independent product claim an independent claim for a process specially adapted for manufacturing the product and an independent claim for a use of the product; or in addition to a process claim an independent claim for an apparatus or means specifically designed for carrying out the process; or combinations of product/process/apparatus claims as appropriate.
guidance: Permitted to claim related aspects (product, process, apparatus, use) in the same application where appropriate to cover the subject-matter comprehensively.

name: Rule 32 — Drawings: format and execution requirements
description: Sheets containing drawings: usable surface shall not exceed 26.2 cm x 17 cm; no frames round usable surface. Minimum margins specified (top 2.5 cm, left 2.5 cm, right 1.5 cm, bottom 1 cm). Drawings executed in durable black or blue uniformly thick well-defined lines without colourings. Cross-sections indicated by hatching that should not impede reading of reference signs and lines. Scale and execution such that photographic reproduction with linear reduction to two-thirds still distinguishes all details; if scale given, represent graphically. Numbers, letters and reference signs must be simple and clear; avoid brackets, circles or inverted commas with numbers/letters. Lines ordinarily drawn with drafting instruments. Elements of same figure in proportion unless difference needed for clarity. Height of numbers/letters not less than 0.32 cm; use Latin (and where customary Greek) alphabets. Same sheet may contain several figures; multi-sheet figures arranged so whole can be assembled without concealing parts; figures arranged without wasting space preferably upright and clearly separated; figures numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals independently of sheet numbering. Reference signs not mentioned in description/claims shall not appear in drawings and vice versa; same features must use same reference signs throughout. Drawings should not contain text matter except when absolutely indispensable a single word or words (e.g., 'water', 'steam', 'open', 'closed', 'section on AB') and catchwords for circuits/flow diagrams; such words must be replaceable by translations. Flow sheets and diagrams are considered drawings.
guidance: Strict physical and graphical standards to ensure reproducibility and legibility after reduction; limit textual labels; maintain consistent reference signs; follow margin and size rules; use drafting instruments and minimum lettering sizes.

name: Rule 33 — Abstract: content, length and purpose
description: Abstract must indicate the title of the invention and contain a concise summary of disclosure as in description, claims and drawings; indicate technical field, allow clear understanding of technical problem, gist of solution and principal use(s). Where applicable include the chemical formula that best characterises the invention. Abstract must not contain statements on alleged merits or speculative application. Preferably not more than 150 words. If drawings exist applicant should indicate figures suggested to accompany the abstract; EPO may publish other figures if considered better. Each main feature in abstract illustrated by a drawing should be followed by a reference sign in parentheses. The abstract shall be drafted to constitute an efficient instrument for searching in the technical field and to help decide whether to consult the full application.
guidance: Keep abstract concise (<=150 words preferred), factual and focused on problem/solution/uses; avoid promotional language; indicate suggested figure(s) and include reference signs for illustrated features; write abstract to aid searchers.

name: Rule 35 — Presentation and physical characteristics of application documents
description: Translations under Article 14(2) are included as documents making up the application. Documents shall be filed in three copies (except the request and certain Article 14(2) documents). Documents must admit direct reproduction by photography, electrostatic processes, photo-offset and micro-filming; sheets free from cracks, creases and folds; only one side used. Documents on A4 paper (29.7 x 21 cm) pliable, strong, white, smooth, matt and durable; each sheet used with short sides at top/bottom (upright) subject to Rule 32 exceptions. Each document (request, description, claims, drawings and abstract) shall commence on a new sheet; sheets connected so they can be turned over, separated and joined easily. Minimum and recommended maximum margins specified (top of first sheet 8 cm, top of other sheets 2 cm, left 2.5 cm, right 2 cm, bottom 2 cm; recommended maxima also given). Margins when submitted must be completely blank. All sheets shall be numbered in consecutive Arabic numerals at top middle but not in top margin. Lines of description and claims preferably numbered in sets of five on left side. Request, description, claims and abstract shall be typed or printed; only graphical symbols and chemical/mathematical formulae may be handwritten or drawn. Typing shall be 1.5 spaced; all text characters with capital letters not less than 0.21 cm high and in a dark indelible colour. Request, description, claims and abstract shall not contain drawings. Description and abstract may contain tables; claims may contain tables only if subject-matter makes tables desirable. Units expressed in metric system (or also expressed in metric if other units used); temperatures in Celsius (and also given in Celsius if other system used); densities and other physical values use metric/international practice. Terminology and signs shall be consistent throughout. Each sheet should be reasonably free from erasures and free from alterations, overwritings and interlineations unless authorised where authenticity not in question and reproduction not jeopardised.
guidance: Comply with detailed physical/formatting, paper, margin and typographical standards to ensure reproducibility; provide three copies; maintain consistent terminology and legibility standards; avoid drawings in textual parts; adhere to metric units and presentation conventions.

name: Rule 38 — Priority declaration and filing of priority documents
description: The declaration of priority must state the date of previous filing, the State in which it was made and indicate the file number. Date and State of previous filing must be stated on filing the European application; file number must be indicated before the end of the 16th month after the date of priority. Copy of the previous application required for claiming priority must be filed before the end of the 16th month after priority date, certified as an exact copy by the authority which received the previous application and accompanied by a certificate stating the date of filing of the previous application. Where translation of the previous application into one of the EPO official languages is required, the translation must be filed within 20 months after the date of priority. The particulars stated in the declaration of priority shall appear in the published European application and on the European patent specification.
guidance: Timely file certified copies and required translations of priority documents and ensure priority particulars are complete and entered within strict 16- and 20-month deadlines to preserve priority claims.

name: Rule 44 — Content of the European search report
description: The search report shall mention those documents available to the EPO at the time of drawing up the report which may be taken into consideration for novelty and inventive step. Each citation shall be referred to the claims to which it relates and, if necessary, the relevant parts identified (e.g., page/column/lines or diagrams). The report shall distinguish documents published before the date of priority claimed, between priority date and filing date, and on or after filing date. Any document referring to an oral disclosure, use or other non-written disclosure prior to filing shall be mentioned with an indication of date of publication, if any, and date of non-written disclosure. The search report shall be drawn up in the language of the proceedings and shall contain classification according to the international classification.
guidance: Search report must map citations to claims, classify by publication timing relative to priority/filing, record non-written disclosures with dates, be in proceedings language and include IPC classification.

name: Court retains exclusive duty to construe patent claim language
description: Claim construction is a question of law for the court to decide after considering evidence (including extrinsic evidence).
guidance: The court must pronounce claim meanings as a matter of law (often in jury instructions or in dispositive motions); courts may use expert affidavits or testimony prior to trial to aid construction (Markman framework).

name: Identify questions of law typically reserved for the court
description: Issues characterized as legal questions include enablement, indefinite claiming, claim construction, prosecution history estoppel, implied license, and repair vs. reconstruction.
guidance: These are generally for the court to decide as law (citations to Federal Circuit decisions provided).

name: Specified time limits (non-statutory) and their consequences
description: There are situations where the examiner specifies a time for the applicant to take an action and the failure to timely take that specified action results in consequences other than abandonment. Examples: (A) Petition for public access under 37 CFR 1.14(e): applicant usually given 3 weeks to state objections — failure results in PTO decision without applicant's objections; (B) Incomplete information disclosure statement: examiner may set a 1-month time limit to complete IDS — failure results in noncomplying info placed in file but not considered; (C) When application is otherwise allowable but contains traverse of restriction requirement: applicant may be given e.g., 1-month to cancel claims to nonelected invention — failure treated as authorization to cancel and application passed to issue; (D) Suggested claims for interference must be presented within at least one month or be treated as a disclaimer.
guidance: Specified time limits can be less than 30 days and do not cause abandonment if missed; instead they cause loss of rights in the specific matter (e.g., disclaimer, non-consideration of incomplete IDS contents). Examiners may set such limits where appropriate.

name: International filing date requirements (Article 11)
description: To obtain an international filing date the international application must satisfy Article 11 requirements (include a description, a claim, names at least one applicant who is a resident or national of a PCT Contracting State, be filed in a prescribed language, and designate at least one Contracting State).
guidance: The international filing date is used for timing international processing, transmittals, payment of fees, and publication. If no priority is claimed, the international filing date is treated as the priority date (PCT Article 2(xi)). See MPEP § 1810 for more detail.

name: Written Opinion of the ISA — substantive criteria
description: The written opinion indicates whether each claim appears to satisfy PCT Article 33 criteria of novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability, and may indicate defects in form or content (clarity, description support, drawings).
guidance: The written opinion (PCT Rule 43 bis) normally accompanies the ISR and may be considered the first written opinion of the IPEA. It may also note defects the ISA wishes to make on clarity and support of claims/description/drawings.

name: International publication timing and content
description: The International Bureau normally publishes the international application along with the search report and any amended claims at the expiration of 18 months from the priority date (PCT Article 21).
guidance: Publication includes a front page with bibliographical data, the abstract, and a figure of the drawing (PCT Rule 48). For applications filed on or after July 1, 2014, the written opinion of the ISA and applicant's informal comments are made public in their original language as of publication date. If published in a language other than English, the search report and abstract are also published in English.

name: International Preliminary Report on Patentability (IPRP) timing and scope
description: The IPEA establishes the international preliminary examination report (international preliminary report on patentability) presenting the examiner’s final position on whether each claim is novel, involves inventive step, and is industrially applicable by 28 months from the priority date.
guidance: A copy of the report is sent to the applicant and the International Bureau, which communicates it to elected Offices.

name: Differences between 35 U.S.C. 111(a) national applications and 35 U.S.C. 371 national-stage applications
description: There are differences in filing date determination, priority claim procedures and timing, unity of invention/restriction practice, and fee regimes between a U.S. national application under 111(a) and a national-stage application under 371.
guidance: Examples: filing date for 111(a) is when a specification is received (37 CFR 1.53(b)), whereas national-stage uses the international filing date; priority document submission rules differ (37 CFR 1.55(f)(1) vs 1.55(f)(2)); unity/restriction practice follows 37 CFR 1.141-1.146 for 111(a) but unity under 1.475/1.499 for national-stage; fees differ (37 CFR 1.16 vs 1.492).

name: Effect of claim narrowing on doctrine of equivalents
description: A narrowing amendment during patent prosecution does not necessarily result in a complete bar to the doctrine of equivalents; it raises a rebuttable presumption that the complete bar applies.
guidance: The Supreme Court rejected the Federal Circuit's 'absolute bar' rule and adopted a presumption-of-bar approach: narrowing amendments create a presumption that the patentee surrendered equivalents, but that presumption can be rebutted by the patentee. (See: 'The patentee should bear the burden of showing that the amendment does not surrender the particular equivalent in question.')

name: Burden on patentee to rebut presumption
description: The patentee bears the burden of showing that the amendment did not surrender the particular equivalent at issue.
guidance: To overcome the presumption, the patentee must demonstrate that, at the time of the amendment, one skilled in the art could not reasonably be expected to have drafted a claim that would have literally encompassed the alleged equivalent. The Court places on the patentee the responsibility to explain why the narrowed claim should still reach the accused equivalent.

name: Rebuttal factors (exceptions) to prosecution history estoppel
description: The presumption that an amendment surrenders equivalents may be rebutted if the patentee proves one of the following: (1) the equivalent was unforeseeable at the time of the amendment; (2) the rationale underlying the amendment bears no more than a tangential relation to the equivalent in question; or (3) there is some other reason suggesting the patentee could not reasonably be expected to have described the alleged equivalent when it narrowed the claim.
guidance: These three lines of inquiry provide concrete pathways for patentee proof. Courts will evaluate foreseeability of the equivalent, the relation between the amendment's rationale and the specific equivalent, and any other contextual reasons why the patentee could not have been expected to claim the equivalent when narrowing.

name: Original application literally covering the accused device defeats rebuttal
description: If the original application once embraced the purported equivalent but the patentee narrowed claims to obtain the patent or to protect validity, the patentee cannot assert that he lacked the words to describe the subject matter in question.
guidance: Where the original (pre-amendment) claim would have literally covered the accused device, courts will not allow the patentee to rebut the presumption; the rebuttal 'will fail' if the original application literally covered the accused device.

name: Doctrine of equivalents — purpose and scope
description: The doctrine of equivalents accommodates the difficulty of patent applicants to foresee every possible infringement and allows finding infringement where an accused action, though not literally within the claim, is nevertheless equivalent to the claimed invention.
guidance: This remedial doctrine balances literal claim scope against fair protection; its application must be considered in light of claim amendments and prosecution history so as not to expand claims beyond what was surrendered during prosecution.

name: Presumption of surrender when claims are narrowed during prosecution
description: A patent holder who narrows claims during prosecution is presumed to have surrendered any claim scope (equivalents) that was relinquished by that narrowing.
guidance: This presumption creates an evidentiary baseline in infringement litigation: unless rebutted by the patentee under the Festo exceptions, prosecution history estoppel will limit reliance on the doctrine of equivalents for the amended element.

name: Common procedural reasons for claim amendments
description: Claims are frequently amended during prosecution to respond to rejections under 35 U.S.C. §112 (e.g., failing to disclose how the invention operates), §102 (lack of novelty/anticipation), and §103 (obviousness/lack of inventive step).
guidance: Amendments made to overcome enablement, novelty, or inventive-step objections typically narrow claim scope to distinguish over prior art; such narrowing is the factual basis for applying the presumption of surrender under prosecution history estoppel.

name: Explain claim interpretation in Office actions
description: Clarity of claim terms in granted patents is improved when the interpretation of claim terms is explained in Office actions.
guidance: Early explanation of the Examiner’s interpretation will allow the Applicant to clarify the meaning of a term, amend the claim, and/or provide a more effective response to any rejections, thus leading to more efficient prosecution. The prosecution record will provide a map for the public to understand the boundaries of the patent protection and will inform the PTAB and courts as to what the Examiner and Applicant understood the claims to mean.

name: Give claim terms their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification
description: Claim terms are given their plain meaning unless it is inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: Claims must be interpreted in light of the specification without reading limitations from the specification into the claims. (See: MPEP 2111.01)

name: Use Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during examination
description: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) is always used to interpret claims under examination.
guidance: BRI does not mean broadest possible interpretation. The interpretation of a term must be consistent with the specification and how the term is commonly used in the art. (See: MPEP 2111)

name: Consider every word of a claim; ignore no limitation
description: Also, every word in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art.
guidance: No limitation, functional or otherwise, can be ignored. (See: MPEP 2143.03)

name: Definition and forms of product-by-process claims
description: A product-by-process claim is a claim where an article or at least one element of an article is claimed by reciting the process of making the article or the element of the article.
guidance: A product-by-process claim can be in either independent or dependent form. Claiming the article and then referring back to a previously presented claim reciting a method of making the article is an acceptable way to present a product-by-process claim. (See: MPEP 2173.05(f), MPEP 2113)

name: Patentability of product-by-process claims depends on the product's structure, not the method
description: Patentability of product-by-process claims is based on the product itself and does not depend on its method of production—only the structure implied by the steps.
guidance: Once a product appearing to be substantially identical is found and a 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejection made, the burden shifts to the Applicant to show an unobvious difference. The use of 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections for product-by-process claims has been approved by the courts.

name: Examination procedure for product-by-process claims
description: How to examine Product-by-Process Claims: (1) determine what structure is implied by the process step; (2) determine if the prior art reasonably appears to be identical with or only slightly different than the claimed product—if so, reject under 35 U.S.C. 102/103; (3) advise the Applicant that the claim is being construed as a product-by-process claim.
guidance: Follow MPEP guidance (see: MPEP 2113). Explain the construction and why process steps do or do not impart patentable weight.

name: Process steps only limit the claim to the extent they imply structure
description: Product-by-process limitations are NOT limited to the manipulations of the recited steps, only the structure implied by the steps.
guidance: Evaluate whether a recited process step imparts distinctive structural characteristics to the final product. If the step does not change the product's structure, it will not confer patentable weight.

name: Do not require prior art to disclose same process to reject
description: In order to anticipate or make a 102/103 rejection, a reference need not teach the claimed process if the product/structure in the reference appears identical or substantially similar to the claimed product.
guidance: If the product in the prior art appears identical/substantially identical, the burden shifts to the Applicant to present evidence that the claimed process imparts distinctive structural characteristics resulting in an unobvious difference.

name: Applicant must present factual evidence to overcome a product-by-process rejection
description: Applicant could overcome an anticipation rejection by providing evidence that the product-by-process limitation imparts a distinctive structural characteristic to the claimed product.
guidance: A statement or argument by counsel is not factual evidence. Evidence must be presented (e.g., data, comparative structure) showing that the process imparts distinctive structural characteristics. If convincing evidence is provided, the rejection must be withdrawn.

name: Examiner must state that claim is being construed as product-by-process
description: The Examiner should explain that the claim is a product-by-process claim and why the recited process steps are or are not given patentable weight.
guidance: Include this explanation in the Office action so the Applicant is informed and can respond appropriately; this practice aids efficient prosecution and creates clear public notice.

name: Process recitations that inherently confer structure may limit the claim
description: Some process recitations inherently confer certain structural properties/characteristics to the product (e.g., chain-stitching confers structural properties).
guidance: Where the process step inherently changes structure, that limitation can be limiting for patentability. Evaluate and require evidence as appropriate.

name: Use of 35 U.S.C. 102/103 against product-by-process claims is appropriate
description: If the product/structure of a prior art reference appears substantially identical to the claimed product, rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102/103 is proper even if the prior art uses a different process.
guidance: Court precedent supports applying 102/103 rejections to product-by-process claims; the key is whether the products are identical/substantially identical and whether the Applicant can show an unobvious structural difference imparted by the claimed process.

name: Examples guide application of principles to varied facts
description: Use case examples (materials essentially free of x metal, foam insoles 'not molded under heat or pressure,' dental appliance overlayer 'formed by fitting,' lost wax casting, chain-stitching textile, synthetic diamond layer formed by dry-chemical etching) to illustrate how to determine whether process recitations limit product-by-process claims.
guidance: Examples show: (a) where process steps do not change structure and rejection is appropriate; (b) where process steps may impart structural differences requiring evidence to overcome rejection; (c) that the Examiner should explain constructions and bases for rejections in Office actions. See cited MPEP sections for further guidance.

name: Situations that commonly cause abandonment (insufficiency or timing issues)
description: Abandonment may result when a reply is within the period but not fully responsive; copying claims from a patent when not suggested by the Office does not constitute a reply unless the Office relied solely on the patent; abandonment can result from withdrawal/failure to prosecute appeals, dismissal of appeals/court action without timely amendment, interference-related issues, improper RCE/CPA filings, or failure to pay issue/publication fees.
guidance: See MPEP sections cited for each situation (e.g., §710, §714, §1215, §706.07(h)). Specific examples: (A) copying claims from a patent doesn't save app unless last action based solely on the patent; (B)-(G) list appeal/interference/RCE/CPA/issue fee related abandonment examples. Improper RCE filings will not toll periods and may be treated as withdrawal of appeal or not prevent abandonment.

name: Utility vs. false suggestion / misleading specification
description: Inquiry whether some part of a thing claimed or described in a specification is useless to the intended effect is a question of whether the patent is void for a false suggestion or calculated to mislead the public.
guidance: Do not conflate the statutory usefulness requirement with isolated questions as to whether a claimed part is necessary to produce an effect — such issues probe the accuracy and honesty of the specification rather than statutory utility. (See §105 discussion.)

name: Classification: patent to one or more elements (Clifford's second class)
description: Second class embraces patents for one or more elements of a machine (but not the entire machine), e.g., a coulter of a plow or divider of a reaping-machine.
guidance: In such patents others may make, use, or vend the remainder of the machine and may employ the patented element only if it is not 'substantially different' from the claimed element. Infringement requires substantial similarity of the element. (See §111a, second class.)

name: Definition of a patentable combination
description: A combination in machinery is a new union of elemental parts not before brought together in that kind of machine, producing a method of operation differing from what had been done before in that kind of machine.
guidance: Elements of the combination may be new or old; successive action of elements that contributes to a practical result suffices (not necessary to act simultaneously). It is not requisite to include in the claim every part necessary to the machine's action, except as they enter into the mode of combining and arranging the elements. (See §111 and cited cases like Buck v. Hermance and Forbush v. Cook.)

name: Claim construction affects validity and scope
description: Whether claims are presented as claims for separate machines, as combinations, or both affects validity and what the patent covers.
guidance: Examples: Evans (claims separate machines and conjointly) created doubts as to regularity under general patent law; Wyeth v. Stone and Emerson v. Hogg show that claims for separate machines and combinations may be sustained when the devices relate to a common purpose. Drafting should make clear whether claim is for combination or for distinct machines, because that will determine infringement and potential invalidity for embracing more than one subject-matter.

name: Application contents — high-level items (statutory A–E / 37 CFR 1.740)
description: The application shall contain: (A) identity of the approved product and Federal statute under which regulatory review occurred; (B) identity of the patent and each claim which claims the approved product / method / manufacturing; (C) information to enable Director to determine eligibility and extension rights and to enable HHS/USDA to determine the extension period; (D) brief description of applicant activities during regulatory review period and significant dates; (E) such patent or other information as Director may require.
guidance: This is the statutory A–E list; 37 CFR 1.740 expands these into detailed formal requirements (see next items).

name: Complete identification of the approved product
description: Provide complete identification of the approved product by appropriate chemical and generic name, physical structure or characteristics to enable the Director to determine whether the patent claims the approved product or a method of using/manufacturing it.
guidance: Be specific enough for comparison to patent claims; include all identifying information useful to the Director.

name: Complete identification and copies of the patent
description: Provide complete identification of the patent (inventor name, patent number, issue date, expiration date) and a copy of the patent including entire specification (including claims) and drawings; include copies of any disclaimer, certificate of correction, maintenance-fee receipt, or reexamination certificate.
guidance: Expiration date should be expiration under law (35 U.S.C. 154) at time of filing, including any patent term adjustment under 154(b).

name: Claim listing and showing (limit of three claim explanations)
description: Provide a showing which lists each applicable patent claim and demonstrates the manner in which at least one such claim reads on: (i) the approved product (if product claims exist); (ii) the method of using the approved product (if method claims exist); and (iii) the method of manufacturing the approved product (if manufacturing claims exist). At most a showing explaining three claims is required, but every claim that claims the approved product/method/manufacture must be listed.
guidance: The showing should clearly explain how each listed claim reads on the approved product. For generic chemical structures, list variables/substituents corresponding to the approved product. For means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6 / 112(f)) claims, reference column/line numbers and drawing references and describe relevant equivalents.

name: Statement of relevant dates required by 35 U.S.C. 156(g)
description: Provide relevant dates and information so HHS or USDA can determine the regulatory review period, with product-specific required dates (e.g., IND effective date and number; NDA/PLA submission date and number; NDA approval date for human drugs; NADA dates for animal drugs; IDE/effective clinical investigation start dates for devices; dates for biologicals, food/color additives, etc.).
guidance: Include substantiation where available. If no regulatory event clearly reflects commencement of testing/approval phase, provide claimed dates and reasonable bases and any means of substantiation; e.g., for foreign clinical trials, state the date clinical investigation began and explain why that date is appropriate.

name: Statement of eligibility opinion and length claimed (calculation)
description: A statement that in the opinion of the applicant the patent is eligible for extension and a statement as to the length of extension claimed, including how the length of extension was determined and whether statutory limits (14-year limit of 35 U.S.C. 156(c)(3) or five-year limit of 156(g)(6)(A)) apply.
guidance: Show calculation and note applicable caps; MPEP provides examples and cautions.

name: Filing date establishment (37 CFR 1.741 — 'complete application')
description: The filing date is the date a complete application is received in the Office (or filed under 37 CFR 1.8/1.10 procedures). A 'complete application' must include identification of approved product, statutes, patent, claims, sufficient information to enable Director/HHS/USDA to determine eligibility/rights/length of regulatory review period, and brief description of marketing-applicant activities (see enumerated 1–6).
guidance: Requirements of 37 CFR 1.741 (statutory) must be satisfied within the 60-day filing period to establish the filing date. The distinction between 1.740 (formal requirements) and 1.741 (filing-date statutory requirements) is important: 1.740 items may be satisfied outside the 60-day period, but 1.741 items must be satisfied within it. The Office will consider an application meeting 1.741 satisfied even if further information may be desired before final determination.

name: Identify applicant's invention and establish BRI
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim based on plain meaning and the disclosure.
guidance: This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim. Example: for a vaccine claim, the BRI may be (i) a sufficient amount of Peptide F to produce an immunogenic response and (ii) a sufficient amount of carrier substances to make a carrier suitable for administration. Use plain-meaning analysis (e.g., what 'cream' means in the pharmaceutical arts) and identify embodiments encompassed by the BRI. If an examiner will assume an amendment to make a claim fall into a statutory category, make that assumption clear in the record.

name: Step 2A — is the claim directed to a judicial exception
description: Decide whether the claim is 'directed' to a product of nature, a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicially recognized exceptions).
guidance: A claim is 'directed' to a product of nature when it recites a nature-based product limitation that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart. Abstract ideas include fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, or mathematical relationships/formulae. Use case law charts and the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance for assistance. Choose A (no), B (yes but streamlined analysis appropriate), or C (yes — proceed to marked-difference analysis).

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (nature-based products)
description: If the claim recites a nature-based product limitation, identify the limitation(s), identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart(s), and compare to determine whether the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics compared to the counterpart in its natural state.
guidance: Complete parts (a) identify the limitation(s); (b) identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart(s) (e.g., components if the claimed mixture has no naturally occurring counterpart); (c) compare and choose (i) exhibits markedly different characteristics (eligible) or (ii) lacks markedly different characteristics (exception). Provide specific factual reasoning (e.g., changed form, physical properties, adherence, or changed functional property such as enhanced immunogenicity).

name: Types of characteristics considered for 'markedly different'
description: Non-limiting examples of characteristics the courts consider when determining marked difference.
guidance: Consider biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype, including functional and structural characteristics; and structure and form, whether chemical, genetic, or physical. Use these factors when comparing the claimed limitation to its natural counterpart.

name: Process-claim exception for marked-difference
description: Process claims are generally not subject to the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis for nature-based products, except in limited situations.
guidance: Only apply the marked-difference analysis to a process claim when the process claim is drafted so there is no difference in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple'). Otherwise, analyze product limitations only where appropriate.

name: Step 2B — additional elements / 'significantly more' inquiry
description: Determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception by identifying any additional elements beyond the exception and evaluating their significance.
guidance: A. Are there additional elements beyond the exception? If 'No', conclude SME analysis with a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). If 'Yes', list the additional elements and continue. Note: where a product claim comprises a combination of components that do not occur together in nature, each component should be considered as an additional element to the other components when determining whether the combination results in significantly more.

name: Significance / inventive concept considerations (reasons supporting significance)
description: Evaluate identified additional elements (individually and in combination) to determine whether they provide an 'inventive concept' such that the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic computer functions; not adding mere words 'apply it'); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well‑understood, routine and conventional in the field (do not append known routine activities at a high level); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations amounting to more than generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment. Use these factors and the provided anti‑patterns when drafting the examiner's reasoning.

name: Identify and suggest disclosure elements that could render a claim eligible
description: Search the disclosure for elements that could be added to the claim that may make it eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant.
guidance: Provide concrete examples where possible (e.g., the disclosed element of an 'immuno-effective amount of an aluminum salt adjuvant' might make a vaccine claim eligible — see claim 5 of Example 28). Record suggested amendments in the file where appropriate.

name: Procedural guidance: use of form paragraphs and sample rejection language
description: When concluding that a claim is ineligible, use specified form paragraphs and include clear sample rejection language.
guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (and 7.05.01 as applicable) available in Custom OACs. The worksheet provides sample §101 rejection language describing why the claim is directed to a judicial exception and why additional elements do not amount to significantly more; customize factual details to the claim under review.

name: Conclude SME analysis and proceed to other patentability requirements
description: If any elements (individually or combined) amount to significantly more than the exception, conclude the SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements.
guidance: If the SME analysis finds eligibility, document reasoning and proceed with novelty, nonobviousness, enablement, etc. If ineligible, make the §101 rejection and continue with other examinations as required; clarify the record with remarks where helpful (for example, explain how a claim recites a product-of-nature 'x' but with additional element 'y' amounts to significantly more).

name: Argument — primary purpose
description: Explain why the examiner’s decision to reject the pending claims is improper and should be reversed.
guidance: The argument section is where appellant shows the examiner erred; structure and clarity are critical.

name: Argument — preliminary steps
description: Before drafting argument, review the prosecution history, decide which rejections and which claims to address, and identify your strongest arguments.
guidance: Select and prioritize matters to address; do not assume unaddressed rejections can be raised later.

name: Argument — suggested format for grounds of rejection
description: Address each ground of rejection under a separate heading; identify the ground by claim number, statutory basis, and references (if any).
guidance: Example heading format: 'Whether claims 1-3 are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Reference A in view of Reference B.' Use clear headings for each ground.

name: Common arguments showing examiner error
description: Typical bases to show error include: examiner misunderstood or mischaracterized the claimed invention or the pending claims; examiner misunderstood the cited prior art; examiner misunderstood the law or legal basis for the rejection.
guidance: Use specific explanations tied to specification, claim language, prosecution history, and legal standards to rebut each misunderstanding.

name: Argument: misunderstood the invention
description: Explain that the examiner’s characterization or interpretation of the claim language is inconsistent with the specification.
guidance: Show what a person of ordinary skill would understand from the specification and identify specific portions that support your interpretation. Provide explicit contrasts with the examiner’s interpretation.

name: Argument: misunderstood the prior art
description: Explain why the examiner’s understanding of a prior art reference is incorrect—e.g., why the examiner erred in finding the reference discloses or suggests a claim element.
guidance: Cite the reference and explain why it does not disclose the recited element(s), identifying specific passages or lack thereof.

name: Design-patent claim scope: 'as shown' vs. 'as shown and described'
description: A patented design may be claimed 'as shown' or 'as shown and described.' Where claimed 'as shown and described,' the patent’s scope of protection is limited by both the drawings and the accompanying description.
guidance: The MPEP notes that 'the illustration in the drawing views is its own best description' but allows use of written description to identify appearance for portions not illustrated (MPEP §1503.01(II) and §1503.01(II)(A)(1)). When the specification explicitly describes a feature (e.g., stating oblique shading 'denote[s] transparency'), the description can narrow what otherwise ambiguous drawing conventions might indicate. Anti-pattern: relying solely on drawings where the specification expressly clarifies or limits meaning.

name: Claim construction: plain and ordinary meaning vs. art-specific meaning
description: Where a claim term is not disclaimed or specially defined in the specification, the jury must apply the plain and ordinary meaning of the term. If a party asserts an art-specific plain and ordinary meaning, it must be established with reliable extrinsic evidence.
guidance: Extrinsic evidence may be considered to establish an art-specific meaning but testimony at odds with the written patent record should be afforded no weight (Phillips). Conclusory expert testimony unsupported by objective sources (industry publications, dictionaries) is insufficient (Network Com., Wireless Agents). On remand, district court may determine whether an art-specific meaning exists, but the proponent must produce reliable extrinsic material.

name: Limits on extrinsic evidence in claim construction
description: Extrinsic evidence (including expert testimony) that conflicts with the patent's written record should be disregarded in claim construction.
guidance: Courts must start with intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history). Extrinsic evidence can inform meaning only when consistent with intrinsic evidence and supported by reliable sources. Anti-pattern: relying on expert assertions that contradict express statements in the specification.

name: Review standard for claim construction and factual findings
description: Claim construction based on intrinsic evidence is reviewed de novo; underlying factual findings based on extrinsic evidence are reviewed for clear error.
guidance: Apply Phillips and subsequent Federal Circuit precedent: interpret claim terms according to their ordinary and customary meaning to a POSA in the context of the entire patent. Where the district court resolves subsidiary facts from extrinsic evidence, appellate review accords clear-error deference.

name: Design patents protect ornamental/aesthetic features and have narrow scope
description: Design patents protect the ornamental or aesthetic features of a design (35 U.S.C. §171(a)) and are given narrow scope compared to utility patents.
guidance: Do not import functional interpretations into design-patent scope. When construing design claims, focus on drawings and accompanying description; be mindful that courts construe design patents narrowly (Top Brand; Carman Indus.).

name: Construction of structural claim terms using intrinsic evidence (example: 'frame')
description: Claim terms that are repeatedly and consistently described in the specification (e.g., a 'frame') may be construed narrowly to require a specific structural characteristic (e.g., a 'separate and distinct component').
guidance: If the specification 'repeatedly, consistently, and exclusively' refers to a component as separate (see In re Abbott Diabetes Care; Irdeto), the claims should be read to require that separation. Look to the specification's described functions (e.g., 'configured to removably receive the sign') and embodiments (frameless, replaceable lens) to inform construction. Anti-pattern: reading a broad literal scope when the specification consistently points to a narrower structural requirement.

name: Determining function for doctrine-of-equivalents analysis
description: The function of a claimed element for DOE can be established by the patent's disclosure; if the patent is silent, courts turn to the ordinarily skilled artisan to determine function.
guidance: When the specification explicitly teaches certain functions (e.g., removably receiving the sign so it can be serviced or customized), that intrinsic evidence can be dispositive in deciding whether the accused product performs the same function. If the accused device does not perform the patent-disclosed function, DOE infringement fails (Hill-Rom example).

name: Doctrine of equivalents test: insubstantial differences / function-way-result
description: DOE prevents avoiding infringement by changing only minor or insubstantial details. The function-way-result test asks whether the accused product 'performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result.'
guidance: Both parties may agree on the function-way-result articulation. For DOE to succeed, equivalence must be demonstrated as to each claimed element (Lockheed Martin) and supported by particularized testimony and a linking argument (VLSI Tech.). Anti-pattern: asserting equivalence based on general similarities without element-by-element particularized proof.

name: Requirement of particularized testimony and linking argument for DOE
description: A patentee must provide particularized testimony and linking argument showing how each claimed element is equivalent to the accused product's corresponding feature.
guidance: General or conclusory expert testimony that fails to tie the accused structure to the claimed element's disclosed function/way/result is insufficient. Courts require detailed, element-specific analysis (VLSI Tech.).

name: Standard and review for JMOL in patent trials
description: JMOL is appropriate if no reasonable, properly instructed jury could have found for the non-moving party on the issue; appellate review of the denial of JMOL is de novo.
guidance: In reviewing JMOL, the court must take the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving (prevailing at trial) party (Sundance). If undisputed evidence (including concession by patentee's expert) shows an element's function is not performed by the accused device, no reasonable jury could find equivalence and JMOL should be granted. Practical tip: develop record evidence that either establishes or refutes the claimed function; concessions by experts are dispositive.

name: Expert testimony cannot contradict the patent's written record; conclusory testimony insufficient
description: Expert testimony that is 'at odds with . . . the written record of the patent' should be afforded no weight, and conclusory testimony unsupported by reliable extrinsic material is insufficient for claim construction or equivalence findings.
guidance: Experts should support opinions with objective contemporaneous sources (industry publications, dictionaries, technical references). Absent reliable support, courts may disregard expert statements (Phillips; Network Com.; Wireless Agents). Anti-pattern: relying solely on an expert's ipse dixit to override clear intrinsic disclosure.

name: Bona fide reply requirement
description: The applicant’s or patent owner’s reply must appear throughout to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application or the reexamination proceeding to final action. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specifically pointing out how the language of the claims patentably distinguishes them from the references does not comply with the requirements of this section.
guidance: Responses must specifically point out patentable distinctions over applied references; boilerplate assertions of patentability are insufficient.

name: Amendment must point out patentable novelty
description: In amending in reply to a rejection of claims in an application or patent under reexamination, the applicant or patent owner must clearly point out the patentable novelty which he or she thinks the claims present in view of the state of the art disclosed by the references cited or the objections made.
