guidance: The applicant or patent owner must also show how the amendments avoid such references or objections.

name: Content of patent owner response to rejection
description: In response to any rejection, such response may include further statements and/or proposed amendments or new claims to place the patent in a condition where all claims, if amended as proposed, would be patentable.
guidance: Responses should aim to place claims in condition for allowance if possible; consider proposed claim amendments and supporting arguments.

name: Supplemental response entry conditions (37 CFR 1.111)
description: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.111(a)(2), a response that is supplemental to a response that is in compliance with 37 CFR 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right. The Office may enter a supplemental response if the supplemental response is clearly limited to specified categories.
guidance: Allowed supplemental response categories include: (A) cancellation of claim(s); (B) adoption of examiner suggestions; (C) placement of the proceeding in condition for Notice of Intent to Issue Reexamination Certificate (NIRC); (D) response to a requirement made after the first response was filed; (E) correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors); or (F) simplification of issues for appeal. Entry is subject to examiner cursory review and timing (must be entered before examiner considers prior response).

name: Unpersuasive Argument: Novelty Not Clearly Pointed Out (¶7.37.12)
description: Applicant’s arguments do not comply with 37 CFR 1.111(c) because they do not clearly point out the patentable novelty which he or she thinks the claims present in view of the state of the art disclosed by the references cited or the objections made, nor show how the amendments avoid such references or objections.
guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.37.

name: Avoidance of Piecemeal Examination (707.07(g))
description: Piecemeal examination should be avoided where possible; the examiner ordinarily should reject each claim on all valid grounds available, avoiding undue multiplication of references.
guidance: Major technical rejections (lack of proper disclosure, lack of enablement, serious indefiniteness, res judicata) should be applied where appropriate and stated with full development of reasons rather than by mere conclusion. Where prior art discloses the 'heart' of the invention, secondary rejections on minor technical grounds should ordinarily not be made. Certain technical rejections (e.g., negative limitations, indefiniteness) should not be made where the examiner is not aware of an improved mode of definition.

name: State When Claims Are Allowable (707.07(j))
description: When the application discloses patentable subject matter but claims cannot be allowed due to defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should be constructive and offer definite suggestions for correction and may indicate desirability of an interview.
guidance: If aspects of patentable invention are not claimed but appear in the disclosure, note that if properly claimed such claims may receive favorable consideration. If a claim is otherwise allowable but dependent on a canceled or rejected claim, state it would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.

name: Early Allowance of Claims
description: Where the examiner is satisfied that the prior art has been fully developed and some claims are clearly allowable, allowance of such claims should not be delayed.
guidance: Form paragraphs 7.43, 7.43.01, and 7.43.02 may be used to indicate allowable subject matter.

name: Allowable Subject Matter — 35 U.S.C. 112, Second Paragraph (¶7.43.01 & ¶7.43.02)
description: Claim [1] would be allowable if rewritten or amended to overcome the rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, set forth in this Office action.
guidance: Use ¶7.43.01 when noted independent or dependent claims are rejected solely on the basis of 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. Use ¶7.43.02 for dependent claims to include all limitations of the base claim and intervening claims. Examiner notes explain when each is appropriate.

name: Objection to Claims — Allowable Subject Matter / Numbering Paragraphs
description: If a claim is objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all limitations, state so; number paragraphs of the Office action consecutively to facilitate identification.
guidance: Good practice to number paragraphs consecutively for traceability in prosecution.

name: Petition To Make Special — Energy (VI)
description: The Office will accord 'special' status to applications for inventions which materially contribute to (A) discovery/development of energy resources or (B) more efficient utilization and conservation of energy resources.
guidance: Examples include fossil fuels, hydrogen fuel, nuclear, solar, or inventions reducing energy consumption. Petition must state which category is claimed; no fee if clear on face (37 CFR 1.102(c)). If not clear, petition must be accompanied by a statement explaining how materiality is met. Materiality cannot be speculative.

name: Unity (a priori): common property/activity plus significant structural element
description: A group of alternatives meets the requirement of unity of invention (a priori) if the alternatives have a common property or activity and share a significant structural element that is essential to the common property or activity.
guidance: Examples: SEQ ID NOs sharing an element that allows a probe to detect disease-specific mRNA; compounds sharing the iminothioether group linked to a six-atom ring and the same therapeutic use. Some Offices may regard such a claim as a Markush grouping when both requirements are met.

name: Markush grouping acceptability
description: A Markush-style claim (listing alternatives) can be acceptable when the alternatives share a common property/activity and either share a common structure or belong to a recognized class.
guidance: Catalyst example: (X) and (X+a) share a common component and catalytic activity so a Markush grouping is acceptable. Offices differ; some may still treat as a Markush grouping even for biological molecules.

name: Common source alone is insufficient for unity
description: Merely deriving claimed biological molecules from the same source (e.g., human liver) is not sufficient to meet unity requirements.
guidance: Polynucleotide example: SEQ ID NOs from the same cDNA library that are non-homologous and lack a disclosed common property do not satisfy unity. The sugar-phosphate backbone is not a 'significant structural element.'

name: Dependent claims that add substantial divergent features can cause lack of unity a posteriori
description: Dependent claims that introduce substantial features diverging from the inventive concept of the independent claim may be considered separate inventions if the independent claimed common matter is known.
guidance: Example: humidifier dependent claims 2 and 3 each define distinct inventive features (resistive wire + insulating layer vs. tubular support with wicking) that are not linked by a single inventive concept once common matter is known.

name: Complex/overlapping claim sets: identify special technical features and group accordingly
description: When claims overlap in features, examiners should identify the special technical feature(s) of each independent claim to determine whether a single general inventive concept links them; avoid narrow, literal, or academic reasoning.
guidance: Turbine blade/alloy example: independent claims directed to the blade shape and to alloy Z lack unity a priori if no special technical feature is common; but groupings may change depending on novelty/inventiveness findings (e.g., if blade is novel, unity exists between blade and dependent claim 2).

name: Approaches for selecting the 'first invention' in large-variable claims
description: When a broad formula with many variables lacks a readily ascertainable significant structural element, examiners may determine a 'first invention' by (a) considering the content of dependent claims, (b) taking the first-mentioned structure for each variable, or (c) selecting a broader first invention as some Authorities do.
guidance: Different Authorities may adopt different approaches; dependent claims limited to the first invention may be searched without additional fees; other combinations may be invited for additional search fees. Description and examples can guide selection of useful groupings.

name: Biological claims: 'isolated' term and Office practice
description: Some Authorities presume biological molecules are claimed in isolated form and do not require the explicit term 'isolated'; others require explicit wording.
guidance: Apply local/Authority-specific practice when assessing claims to polynucleotides, proteins, SNPs, fusion proteins, etc.

name: SNP and point-mutation claims: need disclosed common property or functional relationship
description: Claims listing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) or point mutations in a sequence lack unity if the mutations are uncharacterized and no common property or activity is disclosed; presence within the same prior-known sequence is insufficient.
guidance: Example: SNPs within SEQ ID NO:1 where SEQ ID NO:1 is prior art and no function is identified -> lack of unity. Groupings proposed: treat each SNP as separate invention.

name: Judicial Exception Categories
description: Determine whether the claim recites an Abstract Idea, Law of Nature, Product of Nature, multiple exceptions in the same claim, or no recited exception.
guidance: Each example is annotated with which judicial exception(s), if any, the claim is found to recite; this classification drives the Step 2A/2B eligibility pathway.

name: Step 2A Prong One: Generally
description: Step 2A prong one general inquiry: does the claim 'recite' a judicial exception (abstract idea, law/product of nature) under the general analysis?
guidance: For post‑June 2020 guidance, the rationale for why a recited concept is an abstract idea should point to one or more abstract idea groupings in MPEP 2106(a)(2). For laws/products of nature, the Step 2A Prong One analysis parallels MPEP 2106.04(II)(A)(1).

name: Step 2A Prong One: Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis
description: Perform an MDC analysis for nature-based product limitations to determine whether the claim limitation exhibits markedly different characteristics from naturally occurring counterparts.
guidance: MDC analysis is performed when the claim is focused on nature-based product (NBP) limitation(s) (with certain exceptions for process claims). The MDC evaluation considers chemical/physical properties, function/activity, phenotype, structure/form and other meaningful characteristics to decide if the NBP is markedly different.

name: When to Perform MDC Analysis
description: Rules for whether MDC analysis is required: e.g., when the claim is focused on NBP limitations; process claims generally exempt unless exception applies.
guidance: If the claim is focused on NBP limitation(s), perform MDC analysis. If a process claim is not focused on NBP limitations (per MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)(c)), do not perform MDC analysis. If an exception to the general rule applies, MDC should be performed for process claims that are focused on the NBP limitation(s).

name: Step 2A Prong Two: Exception Integrated Into a Practical Application
description: Assess whether the judicial exception is integrated into a practical application such that the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception itself.
guidance: Step 2A Prong Two asks whether elements of the claim apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception; examples identify factors (see considerations) that support integration into a practical application. For older examples (pre-June 2020), Prong Two analysis can sometimes be extrapolated from Step 2B (minus WURC consideration).

name: Step 2B: Generally (Inventive Concept Inquiry)
description: If Step 2A does not establish eligibility, analyze whether additional claim elements, individually or in combination, supply an 'inventive concept' that makes the claim eligible.
guidance: Step 2B examines whether the additional elements are more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity and whether they transform the nature of the claim into patent-eligible subject matter. The index flags when the claim is eligible at Step 2B because it provides an inventive concept.

name: Improvements to Functioning of a Computer or Other Technology
description: Consider whether the claim's additional elements improve the functioning of a computer or other technology as evidence that the claim integrates an exception or provides an inventive concept.
guidance: This consideration supports finding eligibility at Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B when the claimed elements materially improve technological operation, not merely use generic computer implementation.

name: Particular Treatment or Prophylaxis (Prong Two only)
description: For claims in the life sciences/medical space, evaluate whether the claim provides a particular treatment or prophylaxis as a factor for Prong Two.
guidance: A claim that applies a natural-law-based concept to a specific, concrete treatment or prophylactic regimen may integrate the exception into a practical application (Prong Two) supporting eligibility.

name: Particular Machine
description: Assess whether the claim is tied to a particular machine (beyond generic computer implementation) as a factor favoring eligibility.
guidance: Recitation of a specific machine or machine improvement that is integral to the claimed invention can support Step 2A Prong Two/Step 2B findings of eligibility.

name: Particular Transformation
description: Determine whether the claim effects a particular transformation of matter as a meaningful limitation supporting eligibility.
guidance: A meaningful physical transformation of subject matter may show integration of the exception or presence of an inventive concept, consistent with historical machine-or-transformation considerations.

name: No Additional Elements — No Prong Two or Step 2B Analysis
description: If there are no additional elements beyond the judicial exception, then Prong Two and Step 2B analyses are not applicable.
guidance: The index flags examples where claims recite only the exception, meaning no further analysis for integration or inventive concept is possible — such claims remain ineligible absent claim amendments.

name: MDC Characteristics Evaluated
description: Enumerate specific characteristics examined in MDC analysis: chemical or physical property, function or activity, phenotype, structure or form.
guidance: When performing MDC analysis for nature-based products, examiners evaluate these characteristics (and related properties) to determine whether the claimed product exhibits markedly different characteristics from what occurs in nature.

name: Patent owner amendment rights
description: The patent owner may submit one amendment with a reasonable number of substitute claims, and additional amendments either as agreed to by the parties for settlement, for good cause shown in post-grant review, or as prescribed in regulations by the Director in inter partes review.
guidance: Provides a right to amend claims but limits scope and further amendments subject to agreement, good cause, or regulation.

name: False marking reforms: qui tam and damages rules and safe harbors
description: Only the United States may sue for the qui tam penalty; a person who has suffered a competitive injury may bring a civil action in US district court for compensatory damages; persons liable under Sec. 292 are protected during a 3-year window beginning on the date the patent at issue expires; beyond the 3-year window, protection applies if marking is consistent with virtual marking provisions.
guidance: Narrows qui tam enforcement, preserves injured-party damages claims, and provides limited temporal safe harbors to reduce abusive false-marking litigation.

name: CBM definition (financial/business-method focus, excludes technological inventions)
description: Defines 'covered business method patent' as one that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, except that it does not include patents for technological inventions.
guidance: Narrows CBM scope to financial-service related inventions and excludes technological inventions to avoid overbroad application.

name: Task formulation: abstract from first claim
description: Generate the patent abstract given the first claim of the patent. The benchmark's main objective is generating abstract given the first claim.
guidance: The first claim is used as the input because it ‘defines the scope of protection’ and concisely summarizes the invention’s key elements; framework can be extended to other inputs/outputs.

name: Zero-shot prompting
description: Provide the model only a task description without any examples to test the model's generalization based on pretraining.
guidance: Example prompt: 'You are a patent expert. Given the following patent claim, write an informative abstract that captures the key invention, technical purpose, and functionality.' Measures baseline generalization ability.

name: Few-shot prompting
description: Include a small number of input-output examples to condition the model on desired output format and content.
guidance: Use three claim-abstract pairs as examples (chosen with varying lengths and performance levels: high, medium, low NLP scores) to improve coherence, structure, and adherence to domain-specific language.

name: Qualitative measure — abstract length (verbosity)
description: Compute abstract length (in tokens) to assess verbosity and structural compactness.
guidance: Longer abstracts may capture more detail but risk redundancy; generated abstracts were longer on average (e.g., GPT-4o > Llama3 > human) and correlate more strongly with claim length.

name: Consequences of non-disclosure / inequitable conduct (Therasense standard)
description: If a patent applicant, with deceptive intent, fails to submit material prior art known to the applicant, then any resulting patent may be declared unenforceable because of inequitable conduct (Therasense v. Becton Dickinson, Fed. Cir. 2011).
guidance: Therasense requires two elements for inequitable conduct: (1) Materiality — but-for materiality (the PTO would not have allowed the claim if it had known); and (2) Intent — the single most reasonable inference from the evidence must be intent to deceive. Non-disclosure with deceptive intent can render a patent unenforceable.

name: Non-litigation vagueness or statutory-interpretation claims insufficient absent state litigation
description: Claims that a state statute was vague or unclear (e.g., Cal. Civ. Code § 2944.7) do not defeat reciprocal discipline if the practitioner admitted the violation in the state record and did not prevail on such a challenge in the state proceeding.
guidance: Unrelated post-hoc evidence (e.g., news reports of sponsor misconduct) does not typically render a statute's plain language unclear for purposes of § 11.24 review.

name: Priority document and translation may be requested by IPEA
description: If the IPEA needs a copy of a claimed priority application and the IB already has it, the IB furnishes a copy on request; if applicant failed to provide the priority document under Rule 17.1 the IPRP may be established as if the priority had not been claimed.
guidance: No elected Office may later disregard the priority claim without giving the applicant opportunity to furnish the priority document within a reasonable time. If the priority document is in another language and IPEA considers validity of the claim relevant, the IPEA may invite a translation to be furnished within two months or the IPRP may be established as if the priority was not claimed.

name: Purpose of the international preliminary examination (substantive scope)
description: The purpose of the IPE is to formulate a preliminary and non‑binding opinion on whether the claimed invention appears (i) to be novel, (ii) to involve an inventive step (to be non‑obvious), and (iii) to be industrially applicable.
guidance: The IPRP gives a good indication of likely results in the national phase, although national laws differ in approach to these criteria.

name: Specification and patent-substantive requirements for validity and scope
description: The judge stated as law on patents: first, that the invention must be novel; secondly, that it must be useful; and thirdly, that the specification must be intelligible. Further, the specification must not attempt to cover more than that which is the proper subject of protection; if a patentee seeks by specification any more than he is strictly entitled to, his patent is rendered ineffectual to that extent.
guidance: For combinations or new methods using previously known materials, the specification must clearly state that protection is sought only for the new combination or application and not claim broader original invention; whether novelty, utility, intelligibility are factual matters for a jury, but overclaiming is a question of law.

name: Support by provisional for benefit/earlier date
description: A provisional application can provide the critical reference date under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) only if at least one claim of the reference patent, patent application publication, or international application publication is supported by the written description of the relied upon provisional application in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, or 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: See MPEP § 2136.03, subsection III and examples (e.g., examples 2, 4, and 7). Case citations: Amgen Inc. v. Sanofi; Dynamic Drinkware v. National Graphics. The provisional must describe the subject matter relied upon in the reference in compliance with the written description requirement to antedate the reference.

name: International application (IA) filed on/after Nov 29, 2000 — three-condition test
description: If an international application (IA) was filed on or after November 29, 2000, designated the United States, and was published under PCT Article 21(2) in English, then the international filing date is a U.S. filing date for prior art purposes under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
guidance: If the IA properly claims benefit to an earlier-filed U.S. or IA, apply the reference as of the earlier filing date provided 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c) and 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112 support requirements are met. If the IA claims benefit to a provisional, the provisional support rules (see above) apply.

name: Benefit of a nonprovisional U.S. parent under 35 U.S.C. 120
description: A U.S. patent or patent application publication that claims the benefit of an earlier U.S. nonprovisional application (continuation, divisional, CIP) will be accorded the earlier filing date for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) purposes only if the earlier-filed application properly supports the subject matter relied upon in the rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: If the earlier parent does not support the relied subject matter, the earlier filing date cannot be used to antedate the reference. See MPEP § 2136.04 and examples.

name: Entire disclosure of patent/publication may be relied on
description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the entire disclosure of a U.S. patent, a U.S. patent application publication, or an international application publication having an earlier effective U.S. filing date can be relied upon to reject the claims.
guidance: Sun Studs, Inc. v. ATA Equip. Leasing, Inc. (Fed. Cir. 1989) supports that any part of the issued/published disclosure may be used as prior art under 102(e). See MPEP § 2120.01 for related guidance.

name: Appropriation term 'citizen' means 'civilian' excluding military reward claims
description: Appropriations for payment of rewards for apprehension of deserters use 'citizen' synonymously with 'civilian' to distinguish civil persons from officers or enlisted men; thus meant to preclude officers/enlisted men from obtaining reward for apprehension without request.

name: Legible copies requirement (37 CFR 1.98(a)(2))
description: An IDS must include legible copies of: (A) each foreign patent; (B) each publication or the portion which caused it to be listed (other than U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications unless required by the Office); (C) for each cited pending unpublished U.S. application, the application specification including claims and drawings, or that portion which caused it to be listed (unless stored in IFW); and (D) all other information or that portion which caused it to be listed.
guidance: Copies of U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications are no longer required unless the Office requests them. A pending U.S. application copy requirement is waived if the cited pending application is stored in the USPTO’s Image File Wrapper (IFW) system. Applicants may cite only portions of a pending application (including claims) rather than the entire application.

name: Cumulative references handling (37 CFR 1.98(c))
description: When two or more patents or publications listed are substantively cumulative, a copy of one may be submitted without copies of the others if a statement is made that the others are cumulative.
guidance: The examiner will consider only the copy submitted and may cross out cumulative listings on form PTO/SB/08. However, case law (Semiconductor Energy Laboratory Co. v. Samsung) cautions that a withheld reference may still be highly material if it discloses a more complete combination of claimed elements even if other references are before the examiner.

name: IDS filed after payment of issue fee — not considered unless withdrawn from issue
description: Information disclosure statements filed after payment of the issue fee will not be considered but will be placed in the application file.
guidance: Applicants may withdraw the application from issue by petition under 37 CFR 1.313(c) and file a RCE or continuing application to have the information considered. The petition can be filed under different 1.313(c) subsections depending on the circumstances (e.g., unequivocal statement of unpatentability of claims over the information). Applicants are encouraged to call the Office of Petitions to determine timing feasibility.

name: Waiver for copies when cited pending U.S. application is stored in IFW
description: The requirement for a legible copy of the specification (including claims and drawings) of each cited pending U.S. application is sua sponte waived where the cited pending application is stored in the USPTO’s Image File Wrapper (IFW) system.
guidance: If the cited pending U.S. application is in IFW, no copy need be provided. A pending U.S. application identified only in the specification’s background rather than separately on an IDS listing is not part of an IDS submission and the 1.98(a)(2)(iii) supply requirement is not applicable.

name: When prior foreign office search report can satisfy concise explanation requirement
description: Where non-English information was cited in a foreign patent office search report or other action in a counterpart foreign application, the requirement for a concise explanation of relevance can be satisfied by submitting an English-language version of that search report or action indicating the degree/portion of relevance.
guidance: The English-language version may indicate which portion of the reference is relevant, to which claims, or an 'X', 'Y', or 'A' marking. A mere statement that a reference was cited in prosecution of a U.S. application (not relied on under 35 U.S.C. 120) does not satisfy the requirement.

name: Define key claim terms and argue claim construction under BRI
description: Define key claim terms.
guidance: Acknowledge when an issue turns on claim construction and provide an interpretation for the key claim terms with a basis for the interpretation under the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' standard. Demonstrate why the examiner's interpretation is not 'reasonable.'

name: Distinguish appealable issues from petitionable matters
description: Understand the difference between appealable and petitionable issues.
guidance: The Board reviews adverse decisions of examiners (i.e., claim rejections). The Board typically does not review matters within the examiner's discretion (i.e., objections to the figures or specification, restriction requirements, refusal to enter an amendment, etc.). These matters are decided by the Director on petition. See MPEP § 1002.

name: Use the Summary of Claimed Subject Matter effectively
description: Use Summary of Claimed Subject Matter to support your appeal.
guidance: The Board uses the Summary of Claimed Subject Matter portion of the appeal brief to understand the claimed invention and how the claim elements correspond to the drawing elements and the description in the specification. This section is particularly important when the claim recites elements in §112(f) (means-plus-function) format.

name: Limit reply briefs to responding to Examiner's Answer
description: Use reply briefs to respond to points raised in the Examiner's Answer.
guidance: Do not reiterate arguments presented in the appeal brief. Use the reply brief to reply to specific findings made, or positions taken, by the examiner in the answer, or to address intervening case law relevant to the issues on appeal. Do not raise new arguments in a reply brief that are not responsive to arguments made in the examiner's answer. Do not separately argue claims for the first time in a reply brief.

name: Doctrine of Claim Differentiation (core definition)
description: The doctrine of claim differentiation is a legal principle stating that each claim in a patent is presumed to have a different scope, especially when comparing an independent claim to its dependent claims.
guidance: Do not read a limitation from a narrower dependent claim into the broader independent claim as a matter of course; analyze each claim on its own terms to avoid improperly narrowing scope. The doctrine prevents redundancy and assumes inventors do not write different claims intending identical meanings.

name: The Presumption of Difference (starting point for construction)
description: When an independent claim and one or more dependent claims use different language, there is a starting presumption that they mean different things and have different scopes.
guidance: Use the presumption as the baseline in claim-construction/Markman analysis to argue for a broader interpretation of an independent claim. Example: if Claim 1 recites 'a chair' and Claim 2 recites 'the chair of Claim 1, wherein the chair has four legs', presume Claim 1 is not limited to four-legged chairs.

name: Rebuttable Nature of the Presumption
description: Claim differentiation is a strong but rebuttable presumption — it is not an absolute rule and can be overcome by intrinsic evidence showing a different intent.
guidance: Always search for intrinsic evidence that rebuts the presumption (explicit definitions, clear disavowals, or prosecution statements). If rebutted, courts may read limitations from dependent claims into independent ones.

name: Rebuttal by Explicit Specification Definitions (inventor as lexicographer)
description: If the specification clearly defines a claim term in a way that limits its meaning (e.g., 'a container always means an insulated container'), that explicit definition overrides the presumption of claim differentiation.
guidance: When arguing for narrowing or broadening, point to definitional language in the specification (phrases like 'the invention is...', 'all embodiments...', etc.). For drafters: avoid unintentionally definitive language if you do not intend to limit claim scope.

name: Rebuttal by Prosecution History (prosecution_history_estoppel)
description: Statements or amendments made during prosecution can estop a patentee from later arguing for a broader reading of a claim if the patentee narrowed claims to overcome rejections.
guidance: Obtain and scrutinize the complete USPTO file history. Look for arguments distinguishing prior art or limiting claim scope; such statements can rebut claim differentiation. For drafters/prosecutors: be careful in concessions to the examiner, as they may limit later litigation positions.

name: Statutory Foundation: 35 U.S.C. §112 and Dependent-claim Rule
description: Section 112 requires claims to 'particularly point out' the invention and §112(d) authorizes dependent claims and instructs that a dependent claim 'shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers and shall specify a further limitation.'
guidance: Use §112(d) as the statutory backbone for the logical corollary that a dependent claim adds limitations that the independent claim lacks. Cite it when explaining why dependent-claim limitations should not be imported into independent claims absent clear intrinsic evidence.

name: Practical Step 1: Identify Relevant Independent and Dependent Claims
description: Map out which claims are independent and which depend on which other claims; identify the specific limitations added by each dependent claim relative to the independent claim.
guidance: Create a clear dependency chart before arguing construction or infringement. This mapping establishes the factual basis for invoking the presumption of difference and identifying which limitations are at issue.

name: Practical Step 2: Establish the Initial Presumption in Claim Construction
description: Start claim construction with the presumption provided by claim differentiation that independent claims are not limited by dependent-claim limitations.
guidance: Frame your Markman arguments around the baseline presumption. Use it to secure a broader initial interpretation before searching for potentially rebutting evidence.

name: Practical Step 3: Scour the Specification for Definitions or Disavowals
description: Read the entire specification to determine whether the patentee acted as their own lexicographer or made statements that clearly define or limit claim terms.
guidance: Search for key phrases ('the invention is...', 'all embodiments...', 'must be', etc.). A single explicit definition can overcome claim differentiation. For drafters: avoid specification bloat and stray limiting language that could be used against you.

name: Practical Step 4: Analyze the Prosecution History Thoroughly
description: Obtain the USPTO file history and read every argument and amendment to see if the patentee limited claim scope to secure allowance, which would estop broader readings later.
guidance: Prosecution history is often dispositive. Look for arguments distinguishing prior art by invoking particular limitations; these arguments can rebut claim differentiation. For prosecutors: preserve flexibility and avoid clear narrowing statements when possible.

name: Limitations on the Doctrine (cannot rescue invalid claims / cannot override explicit text)
description: The doctrine cannot be used to save a claim that is otherwise invalid, nor can it override explicit definitions or disavowals in the patent text.
guidance: When defending or attacking validity, do not rely solely on claim differentiation to change an outcome that depends on novelty, obviousness, or statutory requirements. Cite Curtiss-Wright and similar cases to show the doctrine's limits.

name: Drafting Guidance: Use a Mix of Broad Independent and Narrow Dependent Claims
description: When drafting or prosecuting patents, include both broad independent claims and narrower dependent claims to leverage the doctrine from the outset and clearly stake out coverage ranges.
guidance: A well-structured claim set can preserve broad protection while providing fallbacks. However, be mindful that overly detailed specifications or unnecessary limiting language can create intrinsic evidence that rebuts the presumption.

name: Procedural and Strategic Roles of Actors (how each party uses the doctrine)
description: Different actors apply the doctrine differently: patentees use it to preserve broad claim scope, accused infringers use intrinsic evidence to rebut it, district judges apply it at Markman hearings, the Federal Circuit reviews for uniform application, and the USPTO uses it during prosecution.
guidance: Tailor arguments to actor perspectives: patentees emphasize the presumption and claim language; defendants emphasize specification/prosecution history; trial judges decide at Markman; appellate courts harmonize application. Recognize where in the process (district, CAFC, USPTO) the doctrine will play different roles.

name: Practical Caution: Specification Bloat and 21st-century Documents
description: Large, complex specifications (especially in software/biotech) can inadvertently contain stray sentences that courts may use to rebut claim differentiation and narrow claims.
guidance: Drafters should review long specifications to avoid unintended limiting language. Litigators should exploit (if defending) or guard against (if prosecuting) such passages when constructing arguments about whether the presumption is rebutted.

name: Use of Precedent: Key Cases to Support Arguments
description: Cite and rely on controlling cases—e.g., Phillips v. AWH (claim construction framework), Curtiss-Wright (limits of doctrine), and Seachange (example of rebuttal via specification)—to ground claim-differentiation arguments.
guidance: Use Phillips to emphasize primacy of claim language/specification; cite Curtiss-Wright to show the doctrine cannot save invalid claims or override explicit statements; use Seachange as an example of successful rebuttal via specification language.

name: Drawings must be readable and reproducible for publication
description: OPAP will accept drawings if they are readable and reproducible for publication purposes; drawings are either acceptable or not acceptable (the Office no longer distinguishes formal vs informal drawings).
guidance: Examiners should review drawings for disclosure of the claimed invention and for proper use of reference numerals. Objections to drawings in utility or plant applications will not be held in abeyance absent specific Office notification (37 CFR 1.85(a)). Corrections should be made promptly before allowance to avoid delays in issuance or reductions in term adjustment (37 CFR 1.704(c)(10)).

name: Drawings must show every claimed feature (complete illustration)
description: The drawing in a nonprovisional application must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims (37 CFR 1.83(a)).
guidance: Conventional features whose detailed illustration is not essential may be illustrated as graphical symbols or labeled representations (e.g., labeled rectangular boxes). Tables and sequence listings are not permitted in the drawings (except for applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 371). If the invention is an improvement on an old machine, when possible show the improved portion disconnected from the old structure in one or more views and also show just enough of the old structure in another view to show the connection (37 CFR 1.83(b)). Any structural detail of sufficient importance to be described should be shown in the drawing (Ex parte Good).

name: Claims reciting mental processes
description: Claims can recite a mental process even if they are claimed as being performed on a computer. A claimed step that can be performed mentally (e.g., with pen and paper) qualifies as a mental process and thus can be an abstract idea.
guidance: Examiners should look to the specification and case law (e.g., CyberSource; Flook; Univ. of Florida Research Foundation; Symantec) when determining whether claimed steps are mental processes. If steps can be performed mentally or with pen and paper, treat the limitation as a mental process (abstract idea). Examples given include listings of credit card transactions, computations that "can be made by pencil and paper calculations," and data analysis described as performed with "pen and paper methodologies".

name: Evaluate computer-implemented claims using the specification and BRI for mental processes
description: In evaluating whether a claim that requires a computer recites a mental process, examiners should carefully consider the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in light of the specification.
guidance: Review the specification to determine if the claimed invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind and applicant is merely claiming that concept performed (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. In such situations the claim is considered to recite a mental process. Case examples include Benson and Mortgage Grader.

name: Product and process claims can both recite mental processes
description: Both product claims (e.g., computer systems, computer-readable media) and process claims may recite mental processes and thus be directed to abstract ideas.
guidance: Examiners should not assume that only method claims recite mental processes. Examples include a computer-implemented system and method claiming anonymous loan shopping (Mortgage Grader), systems for detecting improper access (FairWarning), and inputting information from hard copy into a program (Content Extraction & Transmission). The term "mental processes" refers to a type of abstract idea, not the statutory category of claim.

name: Not every claim mentioning natural abilities is a law of nature
description: A claim describing a natural ability, quality, or process does not automatically recite a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
guidance: Examples: claims reciting process steps for fractionating, recovering, and cryopreserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect) were eligible because they were not focused on merely observing or detecting an ability. Similarly, a method of treating cancer with chemotherapy or treating headaches with aspirin is not considered a law of nature when focused on the treatment steps. Such claims are eligible at Prong One unless they recite another exception, in which case further analysis (Prong Two/Step 2B) is required.

name: Products of nature and broadly reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: Product of nature exceptions include both naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from their natural counterparts; BRI can encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments.
guidance: Examples: Myriad (isolated DNA) and Ambry Genetics (primers) were treated as products of nature. A synthetic product structurally identical to a natural counterpart remains a product of nature. Under BRI, a claim to a nature-based product (e.g., "cloned giraffe") may encompass embodiments with and without markedly different characteristics. If a claim recites a product of nature and is rejected for lacking an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO), examiners should point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments where possible to focus on embodiments that are not products of nature.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (purpose and outcomes)
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is used to determine whether a nature-based product limitation is a "product of nature" exception (part of Step 2A Prong One).
guidance: Guidance: - If the claim includes a nature-based product that has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart, the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless another exception is present. - If the claim is a single nature-based product (e.g., "a Lactobacillus bacterium") and markedly different characteristics are shown, no further eligibility analysis is necessary (Step 2B not required). - If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, then the claim recites a product of nature and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (and potentially Step 2B). Case law: Chakrabarty (bacterium with markedly different characteristics not a product of nature) and Roslin (cloned sheep lacked markedly different characteristics and was a product of nature).

name: Nature-based products (living organisms, synthetic products) require markedly different characteristics analysis
description: Non-naturally occurring products (including living organisms and synthetic products) are not automatically eligible simply because they were created by human ingenuity; eligibility depends on whether they possess markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart.
guidance: Examples: Roslin (cloned sheep treated as product of nature); Chakrabarty (bacterium with markedly different characteristics eligible). Examiners should evaluate whether the claimed nature-based product possesses markedly different characteristics; if not, treat as product of nature and continue eligibility analysis. For claims that nevertheless are directed to inventions that clearly do not tie up a judicial exception, consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis of MPEP § 2106.06 is appropriate.

name: Markush claim structure / format
description: Use a generic chemical formula identifying a core molecular structure and specify various substituents or chemical groups as possibilities at certain positions (i.e., claim a family of compounds rather than a single compound).
guidance: Example phrasing given: "A compound of the formula [Core Structure] wherein R1 is selected from the group consisting of [List of Substituents]." The claim should specify the core structure followed by a list of potential substituents that can occupy specific positions on this core.

name: Choice of claim-open vs claim-closed language ('comprising' vs 'consisting of')
description: Decide between open-ended and closed claim language to control scope: 'consisting of' limits the claim to only the listed elements; 'comprising' allows additional, unlisted elements.
guidance: Select wording strategically depending on desired breadth: use 'consisting of' for narrow/closed scope and 'comprising' to permit additional unlisted elements; the choice tailors claim scope to prosecution and enforcement goals.

name: Support in the specification (define substituents, give examples)
description: Provide definitions, examples, and supporting disclosure in the specification for substituents and listed groups to substantiate their inclusion in the Markush claim.
guidance: Each substituent in the Markush group should be well-defined; include examples or explicit definitions in the patent specification to support claim scope and to reduce the risk of challenges during examination or litigation.

name: Balance breadth and enforceability (strategic drafting)
description: Weigh the advantage of broad coverage (protecting multiple variations) against the drafting pitfalls that can make a claim vulnerable.
guidance: Markush claims offer a strategic advantage but can be a double-edged sword: broader coverage increases protection but may invite scrutiny or invalidation if not drafted precisely. Draft with attention to both commercial coverage needs and patentability/defensibility.

name: Superguide construction — use of 'or' to claim combinations
description: Use the SuperGuide approach: test whether the claim recites "OR" or "AND" when listing a series of elements. "At least one of A, B, or C" is interpreted to permit combinations of the elements; by contrast, "at least one of A, B, and C" is interpreted as requiring at least one A, at least one B, and at least one C.
guidance: Practical test: does your claim recite "OR" (combination-allowing) or "AND" (requires each element)? See SuperGuide Corp. v. DirecTV Enters., Inc., 358 F.3d 870 (Fed. Cir. 2004). To claim combinations straightforwardly, use wording like "at least one of A, B, or C."

name: Markush construction — default presumption of single-member selection
description: A Markush claim that recites "a member selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C" is presumed to permit the member to be one and only one of A, B, or C, and to exclude mixtures or combinations of A, B, and C.
guidance: Because Markush groupings are by nature closed and presume single-member selection, drafters should not expect a plain Markush recitation to cover combinations or mixtures without additional qualifying language. See Multilayer Stretch Cling Film Holdings, Inc. v. Berry Plastics Corp., 831 F.3d 1350, 1363 (Fed. Cir. 2016) and MPEP 2173.05(h).

name: To encompass combinations or mixtures in a Markush group, add qualifying language
description: If a claim is intended to encompass combinations or mixtures of the alternatives set forth in the Markush grouping, the claim may include qualifying language preceding the recited alternatives (such as "at least one member" selected from the group), or within the list of alternatives (such as "or mixtures thereof").
guidance: Example modifications: (1) "at least one X selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C" (to recite combinations); (2) "an X selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C, or mixtures thereof" (to recite mixtures). See MPEP 2173.05(h) (citing Abbott Labs v. Baxter Pharmaceutical Products, Inc., 334 F.3d 1274, 1281 (Fed. Cir. 2003)).

name: Proper Markush syntax — use the transitional phrase 'group consisting of' to close the group
description: A Markush grouping is a closed group of alternatives and requires the transitional phrase "group consisting of" rather than "group of," "comprising," or "including." Without "consisting," the phrase is presumptively open and the PTO will insist on adding "consisting of" to ensure a closed meaning.
guidance: Use the transition phrase "group consisting of" in Markush claims to avoid issues with open language. The PTO will typically insist on "consisting of" to close the group; failure to include it risks later §112(b) indefiniteness challenges. See Abbott Labs. v. Baxter Pharm. Prods., Inc., 334 F.3d 1274, 1280 (Fed. Cir. 2003) and Gillette Co. v. Energizer Holdings, Inc., 405 F.3d 1367, 1372 (Fed. Cir. 2005).

name: Risk of §112(b) indefiniteness and court review for improperly formed Markush syntax
description: Reciting a Markush claim without proper syntax (e.g., omitting "consisting of") raises the risk that the Patent Office might fail to spot the missing language and that the claim's definiteness under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) may later be reviewed by the courts.
guidance: Courts evaluate definiteness in light of the specification; while it is the PTO's job to ensure a claim is definite and that Markush expressions are used properly on examination, district courts reviewing indefiniteness assess the claim language and written description, not simply whether the PTO made a technical error. Take care in claim drafting and ensure specification support to mitigate later indefiniteness challenges. See Lexington Luminance LLC v. Amazon.com Inc., 601 F. App'x 963, 968 (Fed. Cir. 2015).

name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 324(a)
description: "Institution of a post-grant review is authorized by statute when 'the information presented in the petition . . . would demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable.'"
guidance: Apply the 'more likely than not' threshold on the basis of the Petition, Preliminary Response, and the evidence of record. Institution is discretionary but the statutory threshold must be met before instituting trial. Consider all presented grounds and evidence to determine whether Petitioner would likely prevail on at least one challenged claim.

name: Claim construction standard in post-grant review
description: In a post-grant review, claims are construed using the same claim construction standard as in civil actions under 35 U.S.C. 282(b): 'in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' (37 C.F.R. § 42.200(b))
guidance: If no party identifies terms requiring construction, the Board need not construe any term at institution. Construction follows intrinsic evidence (specification and prosecution history) and PHOSITA understanding.

name: Written description requirement (possession standard)
description: 'A specification that "reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date" has adequate written description.' (citing Novartus/Ariad)
guidance: Apply an objective inquiry into the four corners of the specification from the PHOSITA perspective. The written description inquiry asks whether the skilled reader would recognize that what is claimed corresponds to what was described. It is distinct from enablement (i.e., not about proof that the invention works). Examples: the Board may find a disclosure of a specific embodiment (e.g., magnetic quick-connect) can support claims to a broader 'quick release connector' if a PHOSITA would understand equivalent connectors were known.

name: Obviousness framework (Graham/KSR)
description: Apply Graham's four factual inquiries: (1) determine scope and content of the prior art; (2) ascertain differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) resolve the level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) consider objective evidence (secondary considerations) indicating obviousness or non-obviousness. KSR adds that combination of familiar elements per known methods is likely obvious when it yields predictable results.
guidance: Motivation-to-combine is flexible: any need or problem known in the field that is addressed by the patent can provide a reason for combining elements. Courts/Board may rely on inferences a POSITA would make; the combination need not be the best option, only a suitable option, and a reasonable expectation of success supports obviousness findings.

name: When a single disclosed example can support broader generic claims
description: Written description may be adequate even if the specification provides only a single working example, provided the skilled reader would understand the broader generic claim (i.e., the inventor's contribution is characterized sufficiently). Case law: Capon, Alcon, Reiffin.
guidance: The Board distinguishes written description from enablement: it's not necessary to demonstrate every permutation of a generic claim if the effect is sufficiently demonstrated to characterize a generic invention and a PHOSITA would recognize equivalents or known alternatives (e.g., multiple types of 'quick release connectors').

name: Date Damages Begin — Alternate B (disputed — marking and notice rules)
description: The date that the Plaintiff first notified the Defendant of its claim for patent infringement is the date for the start of damages. The Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the Defendant was put on notice as of the date alleged.
guidance: Plaintiff can give notice to the public by marking substantially all products with the patent number or marking plus an Internet address linking product to patent number, or by direct specific notice to the Defendant. Marking is effective even if defendant did not see it. If Plaintiff did not provide effective public marking and did not provide direct notice before suit, Plaintiff can recover damages only after filing date (subject to Practice Note: if no products were sold or only method claims asserted, plaintiff may recover up to six years before filing). Relevant statutes: 35 U.S.C. §§ 286, 287(a); cases cited.

name: Panduit Factor — Capacity (manufacturing and marketing ability)
description: Plaintiff must prove it had the manufacturing and marketing ability to supply the additional products/methods needed to make the sales it claims it lost, or that someone working with Plaintiff could have supplied them.
guidance: Also must prove ability to market and sell those additional outputs by a preponderance. Case citations: Wechsler; Fonar; Datascope; Gyromat.

name: Willful Infringement — Generally
description: If you find that it is more likely than not that the Defendant infringed a valid claim of the Plaintiff's patent, either literally or under the doctrine of equivalents, then you must also determine whether or not the Defendant's infringement was willful.
guidance: To show willful infringement the Plaintiff must prove [text continues beyond chunk]; instruction establishes that willfulness determination follows a finding of infringement of a valid claim. (Further elements and burdens are in subsequent instruction text.)

name: Benefit-of-doubt claim construction for patentee
description: The specification should be construed, where possible, so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual invention; in cases of doubt give the patentee the benefit of this presumption so the patent will remain good for the real invention.
guidance: Apply this rule only where consistent with principle; if there is no room for doubt and the claim is manifestly broader or narrower than the real invention, courts should not apply the presumption. Note that patents may remain valid pro tanto after the real invention is judicially ascertained.

name: Reduction-to-practice: no patents for mere abstract theories
description: A patent cannot be obtained for a mere philosophical or abstract theory; it must be a theory reduced to practice — an art actually put in practice, a machine substantially new in structure and mode of operation, or a manufacture/composition actually made and substantially different from what was known.
guidance: Ensure the claimed invention is a practical application, not an intellectual principle alone. For machines, emphasize new structure or mode of operation rather than mere change of form or proportions.

name: New mode of operation can support a patent even if effect is old
description: If the principles or peculiar device/manner of producing the given effect are new, although the effect itself is old, a patent may be claimed for the machine.
guidance: When many elements are known, test what is new in the mode of operation. Focus on the novel method by which known elements are combined to produce a result.

name: Statutory 'useful' interpreted narrowly: excludes frivolous or mischievous inventions
description: The statutory term 'useful' was construed to mean capable of use and not injurious to the public (i.e., excludes things absolutely frivolous or mischievous); it was not intended to establish general utility as the sole test of sufficiency.
guidance: Ensure claimed invention is at least practically usable and not contrary to public good; 'useful' does not alone prove inventive sufficiency.

name: If change produces no beneficial result, patent will not be supported
description: If the change is immaterial and productive of no beneficial result so that the end can be attained equally well without the supposed improvement, it will not support a patent.
guidance: Look for demonstrable advantages arising from the claimed change; absent real advantages, treat claim as invalid.

name: Treatment of claims by category (process, inoculum, organism)
description: Claim types can be treated differently: process claims and claims to an inoculum/composition were allowed by the examiner, whereas claims to the organism itself were initially rejected as non‑§101 subject-matter.
guidance: Drafters should note that claim drafting strategy matters: process and composition claims may avoid §101 rejections even where organism claims are contested, but organisms that are shown to be human-made/non-natural can also be patentable as held in Chakrabarty.

name: Review the detailed disclosure and specific embodiments to understand invention
description: Use the written description to determine the function of the invention and the features necessary to accomplish at least one asserted practical application.
guidance: The specification exemplifies the invention, explains how it relates to prior art, and the relative significance of various features. Examiners should correlate claim limitations to disclosure.

name: Identify and evaluate each claim limitation
description: Begin claim analysis by identifying and evaluating each claim limitation (steps for processes; structures/materials for products).
guidance: Correlate each claim limitation to all portions of the disclosure that describe the limitation. Do this regardless of means-/step-plus-function language to ensure correct interpretation in light of the specification.

name: Claims define rights; determine claim scope by broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: The subject matter of a properly construed claim is defined by the terms that limit the scope of the claim when given their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the supporting disclosure.
guidance: Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the disclosure. Grammar and plain meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art guide interpretation. Do not read positive limitations from the specification into a claim that does not impose them.

name: Types of claim language that may raise questions as to limiting effect
description: Certain language may or may not limit claim scope (preambles, 'adapted to'/'adapted for', 'wherein'/'whereby' clauses, contingent limitations, printed matter, terms with functional language).
guidance: Whether such language is limiting depends on the specific facts; see MPEP §§ 2111.02–2111.05 for more detail. Examples: a 'wherein' clause may be limiting if it gives meaning and purpose to manipulative steps.

name: Consider the claim as a whole; do not dissect into elements
description: Examiners may not dissect a claimed invention into discrete elements and evaluate elements in isolation; the claim as a whole must be considered.
guidance: A new combination of known steps or elements may be patentable even though constituents were known individually (Diamond v. Diehr).

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 (inventions patentable)
description: Assess whether the claimed invention meets the four interpreted requirements of 35 U.S.C. 101: (i) only one patent per invention (basis for double patenting), (ii) inventor(s) must be identified properly, (iii) claimed invention must be eligible subject matter and not a judicial exception (unless claim as a whole includes significantly more), and (iv) claimed invention must be useful.
guidance: Patent-eligibility threshold is distinct from novelty/nonobviousness/112 requirements; avoid focusing solely on 101 to the detriment of other statutes. See MPEP § 2106 for detailed guidance.

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness / claims particularly point out the invention)
description: Two distinct requirements: (A) claims set forth the subject matter applicants regard as the invention; (B) claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention with reasonable precision and particularity as interpreted in light of the disclosure.
guidance: An application is deficient under (A) when evidence shows applicant's statement of invention conflicts with claims. For (B), evaluate definiteness in light of the disclosure as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art.

name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — written description, enablement, best mode
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) contains three separate requirements: adequate written description, enablement (make and use without undue experimentation), and best mode (inventor possessed best mode and disclosed it).
guidance: Written description: specification must reasonably convey possession of claimed invention (see MPEP § 2163). Enablement: consider undue experimentation factors, predictability of the art, working examples, and that the specification must enable persons skilled in the art as of filing (see MPEP § 2164). Best mode: two‑prong inquiry — possession at filing and disclosure sufficient to practice it (see MPEP § 2165).

name: Means‑(or step‑) plus‑function limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: The scope of a limitation invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is defined by the corresponding structure, material, or acts set forth in the written description and equivalents thereof that perform the claimed function.
guidance: Examiners must correlate claim limitations to the specification and interpret means/step-plus-function limitations consistent with corresponding structures. Consider support, enablement, and definiteness issues when corresponding structure is not present; see MPEP §§ 2181–2186.

name: Enablement commensurate in scope with the claims; undue experimentation assessment
description: Specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation; complexity alone does not make experimentation undue.
guidance: Consider quantity of experimentation, working examples, predictability of the art, and other undue experimentation factors (see MPEP § 2164 and subsections). Determine enablement as of filing date and for persons skilled in the art.

name: Written description standard — possession of the claimed invention
description: Specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as of the date of invention.
guidance: Examine typical circumstances where written description issues arise, burden on examiner, relationship to new matter and claim scope changes. See MPEP § 2163 et seq.

name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty) and 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
description: Compare the claimed subject matter to prior art: if no differences exist, reject under 102 (anticipation); if differences exist, assess whether claim would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art (103).
guidance: Follow guidelines in MPEP §§ 2131–2146 (102) and §§ 2150–2159 (103). Establish a prima facie case considering scope/content of prior art, differences, level of ordinary skill, motivation to combine, reasonable expectation of success, and all claim limitations.

name: Correlate claim limitations to all portions of disclosure
description: Examiners should correlate each claim limitation to all portions of the disclosure that describe the claim limitation, to ensure correct claim interpretation in light of the specification.
guidance: Do this for all claim types, including means-/step-plus-function claims. This step prevents incorrect scope determinations and supports adequate written description/enablement analyses.

name: Search and consider unclaimed aspects when reasonable expectation of later claiming exists
description: Both claimed and unclaimed aspects of the invention described in the specification should be searched if there is a reasonable expectation that the unclaimed aspects may be later claimed.
guidance: A search must take into account structure/materials and their equivalents corresponding to means-/step-plus-function limitations in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f).

name: Do not unduly favor eligibility (§ 101) over other statutory analyses
description: While determining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 is important, examiners should avoid focusing on 101 to the detriment of analyzing compliance with 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, and 112.
guidance: Treat 101 as a threshold inquiry but ensure claims are evaluated for novelty, nonobviousness, and adequate description/definiteness as well.

name: Requirements for rejections based on means‑plus‑function lacking corresponding structure
description: If a means‑plus‑function limitation is not supported by corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification, consider rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement), 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description), 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness), and 35 U.S.C. 102/103 where appropriate.
guidance: Block diagrams without structure are acceptable if structure is conventional and determinable without undue experimentation. If specification is silent, applicant may be required to amend claims or provide evidence.

name: Assess nonequivalence after a prima facie case of equivalence
description: When examiner makes a prima facie case that a prior art element is equivalent to claimed structure in a means-/step‑plus‑function limitation, the burden shifts to applicant to show nonequivalence.
guidance: Applicant may rely on specification teachings, prior art teachings, or 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit evidence. Mere allegations are insufficient — examiner should weigh indicia and determine whether applicant met burden of proof.

name: Consider the doctrine of equivalents in prosecution context (but do not let it unduly influence 112(f) determinations)
description: Doctrine of equivalents applies in infringement actions; decisions involving it should be considered but should not unduly influence examination under 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 112(f) restricts broad literal claim language to equivalents of actual means shown in specification; consult doctrine of equivalents jurisprudence for context but rely on statutory and MPEP guidance.

name: Required papers for right of priority (35 U.S.C. 119(b) and MPEP §201.14(b))
description: To secure the right of priority, the applicant must (a) file a claim for the right and (b) file a certified copy of the original foreign application (or, for post-AIPA filings, identify the original foreign application by number, authority and date).
guidance: For original U.S. applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) (other than design) on/after Nov. 29, 2000, the claim must identify the foreign application (application number, country/authority, day, month, year) and any foreign application for same subject matter with an earlier filing date. The claim may be made in the oath/declaration, application data sheet, or transmittal letter; no special form or language is required.

name: Waiver of untimely claims and petition to accept unintentionally delayed claims (37 CFR 1.55(c))
description: Any claim for priority not presented within the time period provided is considered waived unless accepted under the provisions of paragraph (c). A late claim may be accepted if the identifying claim was unintentionally delayed and a petition to accept delayed claim is filed.
guidance: The petition must be accompanied by: (1) the claim for priority (unless previously submitted); (2) the surcharge in § 1.17(t); and (3) a statement that the entire delay was unintentional. The Director may require additional information to determine whether the delay was unintentional.

name: Filing a complete specification
description: Every person desirous of obtaining letters patent must file a complete specification in the office of the Registrar/Colonial Secretary (in duplicate where required).
guidance: The specification must clearly describe the invention and state clearly what is claimed as new; must be in writing and usually signed by the applicant or agent. Drawings are to be furnished where necessary; some jurisdictions require duplicate copies and permit inspection of specifications in public offices.

name: Specification sufficiency and particularity
description: Specifications must particularly describe and define the nature of the invention and the manner of performing it, distinguishing explicitly between what is old and what is new where necessary.
guidance: Insufficient or defective specifications may be amended; patents may be surrendered and new patents issued with amended specifications where description is insufficient or claims overbroad if errors arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake.

name: Court discretion to restrict or preserve valid parts
description: If a specification or claim is too wide causing plaintiff to fail generally but defendant is found to have infringed a properly specified part, the Court may discriminate and give judgment accordingly (i.e., preserve valid portions).
guidance: Courts may hold patent valid pro tanto for parts properly specified when overclaiming arose involuntarily.

name: PatentBench: Patent_Writing
description: Dataset to evaluate LLM ability to draft patent texts: drafting specifications from technical disclosures, rewriting/refining description sections, and supplementing claims. Instances constructed manually by annotators with LLM-assisted tools using patent specs in English or Chinese. Total 300 instances.
guidance: Assess practical drafting ability across different sections of patent specs; include human-constructed gold outputs to judge quality.

name: Reissue for defective or insufficient specification or overclaiming
description: Whenever a patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective or insufficient specification, or because the patentee claimed more than he had right to claim, if the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent or deceptive intention, the Commissioner shall, on surrender of the patent and payment of duty, cause a new patent (reissue) to be issued in accordance with the corrected specification.
guidance: Allows reissue to correct inadvertent errors; requires surrender and fee; reissued patent relates to unexpired term and can be split into several patents for distinct parts on demand with separate reissue fees.

name: Reissue limitations — no new matter, revision subject to original-application rules
description: No new matter shall be introduced into the specification in a reissue; specifications and claim in every such case shall be subject to revision and restriction in the same manner as original applications are. In case of machine patents the model or drawings may not be amended except each by the other; when there is neither model nor drawing, amendments may be made upon proof satisfactory to the Commissioner that such new matter or amendment was part of the original invention and omitted by inadvertence, accident, or mistake.
guidance: Prohibits introducing new subject-matter in reissues unless narrowly proven to have been part of original invention; subjects reissues to original-application scrutiny.

name: Partial validity and disclaimer procedure
description: Whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent intention a patentee has claimed more than he was original inventor of, his patent shall be valid for all that part which is truly and justly his own provided it is a material or substantial part; the patentee (or heirs/assigns) may, on payment of duty, make disclaimer of such parts not chosen to be claimed, stating extent of interest; the disclaimer shall be in writing, attested by witnesses, and recorded in the Patent Office and thereafter be considered part of the original specification to the extent of interest.
guidance: Allows curing overclaiming by recorded disclaimer; disclaimer is formal (writing, witnesses, recording) and becomes part of the record; does not affect pending actions except as to unreasonable neglect or delay.

name: Damages and enhancement in infringement decrees
description: Upon decree for infringement the claimant shall be entitled to recover, in addition to profits to be accounted for by the defendant, the damages the complainant has sustained thereby; the court shall assess the same and shall have the same powers to increase the damages in its discretion that are given to increase verdict damages; actions must be brought during the patent term or within six years after expiration.
guidance: Permits recovery of profits and actual damages, and discretionary enhancement up to statutory bounds; statute of limitations tied to patent term or six years post-expiration.

name: Claim drafting — object and requirements
description: The object of a claim is not to aid the description but to ascertain what is claimed as new; it must be a means of clearly presenting the subject-matter of the patent, must distinguish between the old and new, need not describe in detail what is old, and must not be for an abstract principle but for a principle embodied in a particular organism or machine.
guidance: Guides claim drafting: claims should define the novel scope, avoid abstract formulation, distinguish old from new, and be sufficiently concrete to identify the invention.

name: Ambiguity in description or claim is fatal
description: Ambiguity in the description of the invention is fatal; ambiguity of claim is distinguishable from want of clear and sufficient description and may be produced by introduction of things unnecessary or misuse of terms; ambiguous claims covering a whole class of subjects where only one answers are problematic.
guidance: Warns that unclear descriptions/claims can invalidate or defeat enforceability; avoid unnecessary elements and imprecise terms.

name: Statutory category — Process
description: A process is an act, or a series of acts or steps (a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result). See cases such as Gottschalk v. Benson and Bilski v. Kappos.
guidance: To be statutory under §101, a process claim must be directed to a particular practical application and not merely recite an abstract idea; see §100(b) and MPEP §2106.01 for processes involving laws of nature.

name: Statutory category — Machine
description: A machine is a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices; includes mechanical devices or combinations of devices to perform functions and produce effects.
guidance: Claims reciting a machine with tangible elements that work together in a defined combination will generally be within the machine category; however, mere recitation of a machine without tangible limitations under the broadest reasonable interpretation may fail to show a practical application of an exception.

name: Statutory category — Manufacture
description: A manufacture is an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations (regardless of whether by hand or machinery).
guidance: Claims to articles produced from materials that embody a tangible practical application fall within this category; tangible structural limitations are evidence of a particular practical application.

name: Non-statutory example embodiments
description: Certain things are non-statutory and not patent-eligible as claimed per se, e.g., transitory forms of signal transmission (a propagating electrical or electromagnetic signal per se), naturally occurring organisms, a human per se, a legal contractual agreement, a game defined as a set of rules, a computer program per se, a company, and a mere arrangement of printed matter.
guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim encompasses non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Examples and case citations (e.g., In re Nuijten, Chakrabarty, Gottschalk v. Benson, In re Miller) illustrate these categories.

name: Claim covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
