description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (in light of the specification and a person skilled in the art) covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1.
guidance: Reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 when claim scope includes non-statutory embodiments (e.g., a computer readable medium that can be a compact disc or a carrier wave). Consider whether amendment could limit the claim to statutory embodiments; nevertheless, still perform Step 2.

name: Judicial exceptions — identification and practical application
description: Judicially recognized exceptions to §101 include laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas (also described using terms like natural phenomena, scientific principles, systems depending on human intelligence alone, disembodied mathematical algorithms, mental processes). Claims wholly directed to these exceptions are not eligible unless limited to a particular practical application.
guidance: Consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it is merely directed to an exception or to a particular practical application (which may be eligible). Practical application relates to how the judicial exception is applied in a real-world product or process and whether the claim preempts substantially all uses of the exception.

name: Practical application criterion for product claims (machines, manufactures, compositions)
description: If the claimed product is within one of the product categories and does not recite a judicial exception, it is eligible. If a judicial exception is recited, determine if the exception has been practically applied in the product — tangible embodiments that embody a specific practical application support eligibility.
guidance: Tangible structural limitations (e.g., a cup, magnetic door latch) indicate practical application; claims that recite product-type language but lack tangible limitations under the broadest reasonable interpretation may be construed to wholly embrace a concept and be ineligible. After finding a practical application, evaluate preemption (does the claim cover substantially all practical applications of the exception?).

name: Practical application criterion for method/process claims
description: A process claim, to be statutory under §101, must be limited to a particular practical application; merely claiming an abstract idea or preempting substantially all uses of a law of nature or physical phenomenon is ineligible.
guidance: Use the machine-or-transformation test as a useful investigative tool (but not the sole test). Consider whether the claim recites structure or a transformative step and whether additional limitations are insignificant post-solution activity (field-of-use) or meaningless data-gathering.

name: Factors for abstract idea determination — machine/apparatus involvement
description: One factor to consider is whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus. For computer-implemented processes, a general purpose computer may be sufficiently particular when programmed to perform the claimed steps, effectively becoming a special-purpose computer.
guidance: Weigh: (a) particularity/generality of machine elements (is the machine specifically identified?), (b) whether the machine implements the method steps (integral use vs. mere object of operation), and (c) whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation. Mere recitation of 'the Internet' or general-purpose computer without how it aids the method is insufficient. Adding a 'computer-aided' limitation without showing significance to performance is insufficient.

name: Factors for abstract idea determination — transformation of an article
description: Another useful factor (from the machine-or-transformation test) is whether the claimed process transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
guidance: If the claim satisfies machine-or-transformation criteria (tied to a particular machine or transforms an article), it is less likely to be drawn to an abstract idea; but failure to satisfy these inquiries does not automatically render a claim abstract — consider all factors and the claim as a whole.

name: Weighting of multiple factors; field-of-use and extra-solution limits
description: Determine eligibility by weighing multiple relevant factors (machine implementation, transformation, practical application evidence). Field-of-use limitations do not impose meaningful claim boundaries, and insignificant 'extra-solution' activity (e.g., routine data gathering) does not save a claim.
guidance: Consider both factors favoring eligibility (e.g., satisfying machine-or-transformation or practical application evidence) and factors weighing against it. Do not base a conclusion solely on one factor while ignoring others; recognize that new factors may develop with emerging technologies.

name: Making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 for claims to laws of nature or natural correlations
description: When Inquiries indicate the claim does not amount to a patent-eligible practical application (fails Inquiry 3 / integration), the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as not being drawn to patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: When making the rejection, identify the natural principle, explain that the claim is effectively directed to the principle itself, and explain why additional features or their combination fail to integrate the principle into a practical application or fail to add significantly more than the principle itself. Provide a clear factual and legal basis (example rejection language and analysis are provided).

name: Evaluating and responding to a subject-matter-rejection — applicant actions that can overcome rejection
description: A proper response may include amendments that add steps/features (or amend existing ones) that integrate the natural principle into the process so the claim practically applies the principle, or persuasive arguments that existing steps add something significantly more and are not routine/conventional.
guidance: Amendments should add limitations that confine the application beyond mere high-level application (e.g., constructing a specific device that integrates a natural principle rather than merely applying it). Arguments that steps are unconventional or non-routine can be persuasive. Examples: adding a UV sanitizing device structure rather than simply exposing to sunlight; specifying a nonconventional testing technique rather than routine blood testing.

name: Obvious-to-try inappropriate when prior art gives only general guidance to explore a promising field
description: Obvious-to-try is improper where the obvious step would be to explore a new technology or general approach and the prior art provides only broad guidance without specific direction to the claimed invention.
guidance: This is the second Kubin/O'Farrell class. If prior art merely suggests exploring an area (but not specific, predictable avenues), that exploratory work is not sufficient to show obviousness.

name: Combining known references with routine methods can render claims obvious
description: If a prior art reference identifies an entity (e.g., a polypeptide) and routine, conventional methods would have been used to obtain the claimed invention (e.g., sequence and isolate nucleic acid), then a rejection may be proper.
guidance: Kubin illustrates that the presence of conventional techniques (Sambrook) combined with a disclosure of the target molecule in the prior art supported an obviousness finding. Examiners should document the routine nature of methods and the reasonable expectation of success when relying on such combinations.

name: Standing Order / authentication requirements for exhibits and scientific data
description: Standing Order §43 requires a party who is relying on scientific data to explain, through testimony of a witness, why the data is being relied upon, how the test is performed, how the data is used to determine a value, and other information; exhibits should be authenticated if they are to be considered evidence.
guidance: Failure to comply with these requirements (e.g., failing to authenticate or offer testimony explaining data) weighs against treating an exhibit as submitted evidence. Respondent's failure to comply with such requirements undermined any claim GX 2195 was a relied-on scientific exhibit.

name: Construction may rest on facts referred to as part of the description
description: Sometimes, the construction may rest on facts, which are so referred to as to make a part of the description and to govern it. If these facts are controverted, they are to be left to the jury. But if they are proved, or admitted, the court will take notice of them in giving a legal construction to the instrument.
guidance: Example: specification describing an improvement and referring to admitted facts (Davoll v. Brown / bow-flyer). If factual statements are incorporated into the description they can govern claim construction; if disputed they go to the jury, if proved the court will consider them in construing the instrument.

name: Patentee must describe invention with reasonable certainty
description: A patentee should describe, with reasonable certainty, his invention; the Act of Congress requires that he 'shall, particularly, specify and point the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention.'
guidance: Reasons: enable the public to know whether they violate the patent and, after expiry, to make the machines correctly; this statutory requirement informs both claim drafting and judicial scrutiny of sufficiency.

name: Evidence may affect construction but cannot be used to supply positive omissions
description: The plaintiff is always entitled to say that his specification requires the explanation of facts to determine the extent of his claim and the character of his invention; the court is to receive and watch the evidence, and to apply it to the construction, taking care that it be not allowed to go so far as to supply positive omissions, which would render the specification defective.
guidance: Limit: evidence can be used to explain terms of art or surrounding circumstances and thus affect claim meaning, but it must not be permitted to fill in essential omissions in the written specification that the statute requires.

name: Separate the court's legal construction role from the jury's factual role
description: The provinces of the court and the jury are distinct: the court determines the meaning of the specification (legal construction) after facts bearing on that meaning are ascertained; the jury determines factual questions such as whether the specification's directions are sufficient to enable practice.
guidance: Practical cautions: avoid letting the jury 'decide what the claim is' when they are tasked with intelligibility/practicability. Courts should separate the legal question of what the paper means from the factual question of whether it enables practice.

name: Infringement is a factual determination of substantial identity
description: The question of infringement is whether the invention of the defendant is substantially the same thing as that of the plaintiff. The identity of two things is a matter of fact, depending upon evidence; it is for the jury to determine, under proper instructions, whether the two things are the same or different.
guidance: Trial procedure: jury decides infringement as a factual inquiry under judicial guidance on claim scope and principles of identity/diversity in patent law (see cited authorities).

name: Effect on small and independent inventors
description: The transition “should help small and independent inventors” (as asserted by supporters) but opponents argue first-to-file would be “severely harmful to innovation, and especially burdensome on small inventors, startups, and small businesses.”
guidance: Evaluations must consider whether provisions (e.g., micro-entity fee reductions, specific protections) adequately protect startups and individual inventors. The Record contains both endorsements (claims that small firms will not be disadvantaged and that the bill was drafted with attention to universities and small inventors) and objections (fear of disadvantaging cash‑constrained inventors, race-to-file costs).

name: Improve patent quality and increase certainty
description: A transition to first-inventor-to-file is described as “necessary to fulfill the promises of higher quality patents and increased certainty” that are goals of the America Invents Act.
guidance: Policy evaluation should track whether changes (priority rule, post-grant procedures, etc.) actually yield higher-quality issued patents and more predictable property rights. Supporters cite fewer disputed priority claims and feasibility of post-grant review as mechanisms to achieve this.

name: PDP internal codes used for benefit relationships
description: When making a change to the domestic benefit claim, the Corrected ADS that will be generated will use internal PDP codes rather than the language that you use to specify the relationship. These codes on a Corrected Web-based ADS will be accepted.
guidance: Common codes include: Continuation – CON; Division of – DIV; Continuation in part of – CIP A; 371 of international – NST; Substitution of – SUB; Reissue of – REI; Claims benefit of provisional – PRO.

name: Specification requirements: accuracy, intelligibility, sufficiency, and distinct claims
description: The specification, that is the patentee's formal description of his invention, must be accurate, intelligible, and sufficient; it must point out distinctly what the patentee claims as his own; and must not claim anything that is not his own.
guidance: The text repeatedly stresses that the specification must describe how to carry the invention into effect (mode/embodiment) and must clearly delimit the patentee's monopoly; deficiencies in specification (vagueness, over-claiming) will jeopardize validity. See also guidance that one should consult an experienced practitioner rather than rely solely on books.

name: Must disclose a mode of carrying a principle into effect (embodiment requirement)
description: To be supported, a patent claiming the application of a principle must include an embodiment — a practical mode described in the specification for carrying the principle into effect.
guidance: Courts reject claims that amount to asserting 'every shape' or claiming a principle in the abstract. The specification must 'start with having invented some mode of carrying the principle into effect.' Example: Neilson's patent succeeded because he claimed a mode embodied in apparatus (an air-vessel) rather than a mere principle; conversely, claiming 'every shape' of vessel would be a claim to principle and invalid.

name: Claim scope and specificity: avoid claiming the 'principle' or every possible shape
description: A patentee must not claim the abstract principle or claim every shape/variation; claims must be specific to a mode or machine embodying the principle. If a claim is effectively for a principle (e.g., 'every shape of vessel'), it will be treated as a principle and not allowed.
guidance: Courts distinguish acceptable claims (specific mechanical embodiments or modes) from unacceptable sweeping claims. Example: Baron Alderson's comment in the Neilson case: 'Then I think that is a principle, if you claim every shape. If you claim a specific shape, ... then I can understand it.' Overbroad claiming is an anti-pattern that risks invalidity.

name: Distinction between defendant's profits and patentee's lost profits
description: Damages may be measured by either (a) profits the plaintiff derives from his own manufacture/sales, or (b) profits the infringer derived from the use of the invention; neither measure is universally controlling.
guidance: The measure of defendant's profits is not controlling where those profits do not correspond with the fair profits the patentee would have realized; juries may look to what the patentee would have made under the circumstances if left alone, but such a claim must be substantiated by clear and distinct evidence (Seymour v. McCormick).

name: When part of the claimed invention is not original (improvements)
description: Where part of an invention is not original (e.g., patent is for an improvement), that part cannot be mixed with original parts so that the jury may regard the whole as a unit when estimating damages.
guidance: Damages must reflect only the contribution of the patented improvement; the patentee cannot treat an old element as if it were newly patented to claim a larger recovery (Jones v. Moorehead).

name: Patentee's market-established license value fixes actual damage ceiling
description: Where the patentee has established the market value of his improvement as separate and distinct (e.g., by selling licenses at a set price), that license price fixes the average of his actual damage when the invention is used without his license.
guidance: If patentee claims more than established license value, he must substantiate by clear and distinct evidence to recover above that amount; jury instructions should reflect that established license values are controlling absent clear evidence to the contrary (Seymour v. McCormick).

name: Prior art limitation (patents and printed publications only)
description: Substantial new questions of patentability must be based on prior art patents or printed publications. Other matters (public use, on sale, conduct, compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, inventor- ship, 35 U.S.C. 101, fraud, etc.) will not be considered when making the determination on the request and should not be presented.
guidance: A prior art patent or printed publication cannot be used merely as evidence of alleged prior public use or on sale; it must be applied directly to claims under 35 U.S.C. 103 and/or an appropriate portion of 35 U.S.C. 102. Exceptions (e.g., double patenting or certain 102(g)(2) scenarios) are discussed in MPEP.

name: Statement applying prior art to each claim (35 U.S.C. 311(b)(2) / 37 CFR 1.915(b)(3))
description: The request must 'set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested' and include 'a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the patents and printed publications to every claim for which reexamination is requested.'
guidance: The prior art applied may only consist of patents or printed publications. The statement should, where appropriate, show that claims are only entitled to the patent's filing date and are not supported by earlier applications. For each claim, the requester must explain how the cited documents apply limitation-by-limitation; see also MPEP § 2614 sample request.

name: Explanation must be complete; use of claim charts recommended
description: The mere citation of new patents or printed publications without an explanation does not comply with 37 CFR 1.915(b)(3). Requester should present an explanation of how the cited patents or printed publications are applied to all claims which the requester considers to merit reexamination.
guidance: Ideally provide a detailed claim chart comparing, limitation by limitation, each claim with the relevant teachings of each reference. The explanation must not lump together proposed rejections or combinations. If the explanation is insufficient the Office will issue a 'Notice of Failure to Comply...' and requester may either (A) provide separate explanations for each identified deficiency or (B) withdraw the deficient document/combination/claim from the request.

name: For proposed obviousness rejections: provide a basis for combining references
description: For proposed obviousness rejections, requester must provide at least one basis for combining the cited references and a statement of why the claim(s) under reexamination would have been obvious over the proposed reference combination.
guidance: Preferably quote pertinent teachings in the references with specific citations (page/column/line and figure numbers). The explanation must not lump proposed combinations together; give specific articulation of how each reference contributes. Examples of acceptable and unacceptable language are provided (e.g., 'Claim 2 is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over Smith in view of Jones.' is appropriate; 'Claim 1 is unpatentable ... as being anticipated by, or in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over the Smith reference.' is inappropriate).

name: Proscribed and preferred wording/examples (anti-patterns and models)
description: The MPEP provides examples of inappropriate language that lumps grounds/alternatives and of appropriate precise formulations for rejections applied to specific claims.
guidance: Avoid language that combines alternatives or lumps multiple references/claims into one assertion. Use specific, separate statements such as 'Claim 1 is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by Smith.' or 'Claims 3-10 are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over Smith in view of Jones, and further in view of Cooper.'

name: Admissions (limitations on use)
description: An admission by the patent owner of record in the file or in a court record may be utilized in combination with a patent or printed publication for establishing a substantial new question of patentability. An admission, per se, may not be the basis for establishing a substantial new question.
guidance: Any admission used should be in the patent file or court record. Third parties may not submit admissions made outside the record unless entered into a court record; even then such admissions filed in reexamination will not be given weight as an admission for establishing a substantial new question or as a basis for rejecting claims. See MPEP § 2258 for post-order handling.

name: Treatment/prophylaxis must affirmatively recite an action
description: To qualify as a “treatment” or “prophylaxis” limitation the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition (e.g., “administering amazonic acid to a patient” or “administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient”).
guidance: If the limitation is merely an intended use or a field-of-use (e.g., “prescribing a topical steroid to a patient with eczema”) or merely indicates how a claimed product might be used (e.g., that a claimed product is a “pharmaceutical composition” or a dispenser “to dispense a mineral supplement”), it is not an affirmative treatment/prophylaxis limitation and cannot integrate a judicial exception under the treatment/prophylaxis consideration.

name: Inventive concept must be provided by elements beyond the judicial exception
description: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself; it must be furnished by an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception.
guidance: Do not conflate the search for an inventive concept with novelty/non-obviousness (§§102/103) or written-description/enablement (§112) inquiries—lack of novelty or obviousness is not determinative of §101 inventive-concept analysis. Consider case law distinguishing these inquiries (e.g., Mayo, Alice, RecogniCorp).

name: Effecting a transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing
description: A process that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can amount to significantly more.
guidance: Example: transforming raw uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded synthetic rubber products (Diehr). The transformation must be meaningful and tied to the claimed steps.

name: Adding specific, non-conventional limitations or unconventional arrangement of known elements
description: Adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (including a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known components) can supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: BASCOM — non-conventional arrangement of filtering components at a specific remote location with customizable features. The inventive concept may arise from the combination even if individual elements are known. Evaluate whether the claim recites such non-conventional arrangements or limitations (MPEP § 2106.05(d)).

name: Physicality/tangibility is not by itself decisive
description: The mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element (e.g., reciting a computer) is not a relevant consideration that by itself supplies an inventive concept.
guidance: A computer is a tangible machine, but reciting it does not guarantee eligibility if the claims only require generic computer functions. Conversely, the presence of a non-physical or intangible additional element does not automatically make a claim ineligible; what matters is whether the claim recites an improvement or inventive concept (see Alice, Enfish, McRO, Genetic Technologies).

name: Specification support and claim-reflection of improvements
description: If the applicant asserts that the invention improves conventional functioning, the specification must contain sufficient technical detail so a person of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement, and the claims must reflect the improvement described in the specification.
guidance: The specification need not state the improvement in formulaic terms, but conclusory assertions of improvement without detail are insufficient. After finding a disclosed improvement, examiners must ensure the claim itself includes components or steps that provide the improvement (claims should be considered under the broadest reasonable interpretation and evaluated as an ordered combination). Case examples: McRO (spec explained automation rules), Affinity Labs (spec failed to provide necessary detail).

name: Technical secondary factors (guidance)
description: Technical indicators include overcoming a scientific prejudice, teaching away, unexpected technical advance, and evidence of long-felt need or prior failed attempts.
guidance: Overcoming a scientific prejudice: examiners should hesitate to find lack of inventive step where the invention solves a long-standing technical problem or overcomes prejudice. Teaching away: if prior art would have led the PSIA away from the invention, that supports inventive step. Unexpected technical progress: must derive from the claimed subject-matter (characterising features) and be described precisely — vague assertions are insufficient. Foreseeable disadvantageous modification or arbitrary non-functional changes normally do not confer inventive step unless accompanied by unexpected advantage.

name: Commercial secondary factors (guidance)
description: Commercial or economic success may indicate inventive step but is not sufficient alone.
guidance: Commercial success is relevant only if examiner is satisfied the success derives from technical features of the claimed invention (not from marketing, selling techniques or advertising) and is commensurate in scope with the claimed invention. Coupled evidence of long-felt need strengthens the pointer.

name: Role and evidential requirement for advantageous effects
description: Advantageous effects can support inventive step only if they derive from the characterising features of the claim, not merely from description-only features.
guidance: Unexpected effect must be described precisely; vague statements (e.g., 'unexpectedly good pharmaceutical properties') cannot support inventive step. The effect must be tied to claimed features in combination with known features.

name: Requirement to disclose advantageous effects in the application
description: Some AMS require the description to specifically state advantageous effects of the claimed invention; others do not.
guidance: Any advantageous effects the applicant considers relevant should be stated, but not in a way that disparages prior products or misleads (e.g., ambiguous presentation implying prior art solved less than was the case).

name: Reality and evidential standard for advantageous effects
description: Paper or hypothetical examples of advantageous effects may be insufficient if contrary evidence exists; advantageous effects should be described via structural analysis, theoretical explanation or experiential data.
guidance: Examiners should seek concrete analysis linking structural features of the invention to the claimed advantageous effect; unsupported or purely speculative assertions are weak.

name: Secondary considerations indicating lack of inventive step
description: If an invention results from a foreseeable disadvantageous modification of the closest prior art, which the skilled person could predict and assess, and no unexpected technical advantage is present, then the claimed invention does not involve an inventive step.
guidance: Similar considerations apply where the invention is merely an arbitrary non-functional modification or an arbitrary choice from many possible solutions. See EPO Guidelines para 10.1 re: predictable disadvantage; non-functional modification; arbitrary choice.

name: Notice Required — Elements of a Proper DMCA Takedown Notice
description: A copyright owner’s notice of claimed infringement must contain specified elements to be effective.
guidance: Required: (1) physical/electronic signature on behalf of owner of exclusive right; (2) identification of copyrighted work claimed infringed; (3) identification of claimed infringing material and info reasonably sufficient to permit location; (4) contact info for complaining party; (5) statement of good faith belief that use is not authorized; (6) statement that info is accurate and complainant authorized to act. For caching exception, notice must also confirm removal from originating site or a court order.

name: Purpose of an interference proceeding
description: An interference is a proceeding instituted for the purpose of determining the priority of the inventive act between two or more parties who claim substantially the same patentable invention.
guidance: The proceeding is a contested, judicial-type proceeding within the Patent Office (the only contested case there) in which adverse parties have a right to be heard by evidence and argument; it results in a judgment awarding the patent to the lawful patentee (the one shown to be prior). See opening of §586–§587 for context.

name: Scope of Patent Office jurisdiction for interferences
description: An interference can be instituted only between two or more pending applications, or between a pending application and an unexpired patent.
guidance: The Patent Office has no authority to adjudicate conflicts between patents already granted (patentees must go to the courts). Forfeited and abandoned applications have no standing in the Patent Office as the basis of any claim and are not noticed in examination of other applications. The Office’s jurisdiction extends to applications only while actually pending before it (§588).

name: Conflict requirement — inventions must be substantially the same
description: An application does not conflict with another application, or an unexpired patent, unless the invention covered by each specification is substantially the same.
guidance: Similarity of name or appearance is immaterial. The relation between two interfering inventions must be identity, equivalence, specific difference, or generic difference. Applications for identical or equivalent inventions are for the same invention. Specifically different inventions are distinct unless a genus claim is involved and not disclaimed. The examiner must look to substance (subjects/things) not merely words. (See §589 and cited cases.)

name: Classification of relations between inventions (identity/equivalence/specific/generic)
description: Every invention occupies toward every other the relation either of identity or of equivalence or of specific difference or of generic difference.
guidance: In identity/equivalence the earlier is fatal to the later; in generic difference the earlier may not bar a specific later patent but may present obstacle to the later's generic claim; in specific difference there may still be interference if one party claims the genus and the other does not disclaim. Use this classification to determine whether an interference is appropriate (§589; Banks v. Snediker explanation).

name: Examiner must consider whole specification and potential claims
description: On an interference the Claims actually made are considered, but the examiner must have regard to the whole specification and to the Claims which might be made.
guidance: The examiner should consider not only the literal current claims but the specification and whether lawful amendments could incorporate claims that would create conflict. Under modern rules an interference is not to be declared until the conflict appears specifically in the Claims (rules changed from earlier practice). Examples and cases (Ex parte Wheeler, Drawbaugh v. Blake) illustrate when amendments and potential claims matter.

name: Substance-over-form: differences in name/appearance do not avoid interference
description: An interference may exist though the inventions have different names or different appearance; the subjects (things) matter, not the words.
guidance: Examples: designs may interfere with mechanical inventions if they claim the same subject-matter; different names or appearances do not prevent interference if the inventions are equivalent; double uses can interfere; a single claim in one application may interfere with several in another. Conversely, certain claims (e.g., carrying an invention into use in a specific way) may not interfere with a claim to the invention itself (Drawbaugh v. Blake examples).

name: Applications conflict when anything shown in one is claimed in the other
description: Applications conflict with each other (or with a patent) whenever anything that is shown in one is claimed in the other.
guidance: Even if one application lacks an element of a combination, it can still interfere with a broader combination claim (the lesser anticipates the larger). A claim that includes matter shown in a prior patent requires notification to the patentee. (See Bell v. Gray; Marvin v. Lillie.)

name: First procedural step — notice and exact statement of conflicting claims
description: The first step in an interference is to secure from the adverse parties an exact statement of their conflicting claims and give notice thereof to the applicants or applicant and patentee, as the case may be, and shall direct the primary examiner to proceed to determine the question of priority of invention.
guidance: An application should not automatically trigger an interference solely because it contains a claim embraced in an unexpired patent; ordinarily the application is rejected on reference to the patent. An interference is declared only when the applicant makes the required oath/averments. If the record conclusively establishes priority for one party, an interference should not be declared (to avoid frivolous proceedings). However, no prima facie showing on the record can prevent a later applicant from claiming an interference if he makes proper averments under oath (Ex parte Nagel).

name: Anticipation general rule
description: The prior art anticipates a patent claim when a single reference exhibits or discloses all limitations of the claim in the same arrangement or combination as the claim.
guidance: Anticipation turns on disclosure of every limitation arranged as claimed; novelty is denied when the claimed subject matter is already known or disclosed to the public. (General statement appearing throughout the newsletter.)

name: Anticipation by disclosure of components (combination must be immediately apparent)
description: When a prior reference lists components of an invention, anticipation of a claimed combination depends on whether the particular combination would be "immediately apparent to one of ordinary skill" given the number and type of categories/components disclosed.
guidance: Wrigley v. Cadbury: a reference that specifically discloses menthol as a flavoring agent and WS-23 as a cooling agent (each in amounts within claimed ranges) supported anticipation because one skilled in the art would view using both in a single product as envisioned. Contrast with Impax Labs where picking components from long lists and experimenting with amounts did not anticipate. Consider: number of categories, specificity of listings, whether components are identified as preferred/nonessential, and whether the art links components to the claimed use.

name: Genus vs species / narrow range vs broad range
description: Disclosure of a genus or a broad numerical range is not necessarily a disclosure of every species or every narrower subrange, but a broad numerical range may anticipate a narrower range under certain circumstances.
guidance: ClearValue v. Pearl River Polymers: a prior art disclosure of alkalinity up to 150 ppm anticipated a claimed ≤50 ppm limitation when there was no evidence the narrower range was 'critical' or that the claimed process worked differently within the broader range, and the prior art provided examples throughout the broader range. Atofina (distinguished) applied where the patentee had shown that the narrow range was critical to enabling the invention. When assessing range anticipation, look for evidence that the narrow range is critical or that the prior art enables the narrower portion of the range.

name: Enablement for anticipation (practice without undue experimentation)
description: To anticipate, the reference must disclose the invention and enable one of ordinary skill to practice an embodiment without undue experimentation.
guidance: If a reference enables practicing the claimed embodiment across the disclosed range (with examples), it may anticipate. Testimony that the prior art 'taught away' is relevant to obviousness but not to anticipation. Focus on whether the prior reference provides sufficient enabling disclosure.

name: Appreciation of patented features not required for prior invention
description: A prior inventor need not have appreciated that a particular feature was the reason for a result or have characterized the invention in the same words the patentee later uses in claims.
guidance: Teva: the defendants had made a stable formulation and need not have understood crospovidone was the stabilizer to show prior invention; 'the invention is not the language of the claim but the subject matter thereby defined.' Do not require contemporaneous recognition of patentable significance to prove prior making.

name: Inherent anticipation — necessity/inevitability requirement
description: A reference may anticipate inherently if all claim limitations are 'necessarily present, or inherent' in the reference even if not expressly stated; inherency requires that the missing characteristic inevitably flows from practicing the disclosed subject matter.
guidance: Montgomery: court found efficacy limitation inherent because administration of an RAS inhibitor to at-risk subjects inevitably treated or prevented stroke (court skeptical whether claims required efficacy but held inherency satisfied). Dissent (Lourie) emphasized that inherency requires inevitability and that an 'invitation to investigate' is not an inherent disclosure. Evaluate whether the allegedly inherent feature necessarily follows from the disclosure or is merely a possible/unproven result.

name: Functional claim limitations are not inherent from mere structural disclosures unless the structure necessarily performs the function
description: A prior structural disclosure does not inherently anticipate a claim recited in functional terms unless the prior structure necessarily performs the recited function.
guidance: Bettcher Indus. v. Bunzl: prior blades with chamfers did not necessarily have 'bearing surfaces' just because chamfers existed; defendant failed to show more than a possibility that chamfers could perform bearing function. Courts will not transform one disclosed structure into a different claimed structure based on hypothetical surrounding configurations not disclosed. Look for evidence that the structure in the reference necessarily produced the claimed function.

name: Impacts on access to technical information — improved patent disclosures
description: Some commenters asserted that the current jurisprudence has made technical information more readily available and reliable by incentivizing more detailed patent disclosures and marginally narrower claims.
guidance: Statements include that ‘Alice was a “forcing function”’ leading to more detail in claims and descriptions, resulting in higher-quality patents and better public disclosure that more fully supports the disclosure function of the patent system.

name: Consequences on prosecution behavior and disclosure (narrower claims, abandonment, flight of innovation)
description: The current jurisprudence is resulting in narrower claims; more frequent abandonment of applications; discouragement of disclosure of new innovations; and flight of innovation from the United States to other markets.
guidance: Stakeholders reported strategic behavior (e.g., filing separate applications to isolate more-eligible subject matter), reduced willingness to disclose inventions, and in some cases opting to seek protection only abroad or rely on non-disclosure to preserve competitive advantages.

name: Establish Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of the claim
description: Construe the claim in accordance with its broadest reasonable interpretation for the purposes of the eligibility analysis.
guidance: Use the BRI when identifying whether the claim recites an abstract idea and when determining the scope of additional elements.

name: Are there additional elements beyond the abstract idea? (Step 2B - A)
description: Determine whether the claim recites any elements (features/limitations/steps) beyond the abstract idea. Choose (1) No or (2) Yes.
guidance: If No (no other elements), conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with examination under other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). If Yes, list the additional elements and continue the analysis.

name: Evaluate significance of additional elements (search for an 'inventive concept')
description: The additional elements must show an 'inventive concept' — evaluate all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.
guidance: It is not important how the elements are characterized or how many considerations apply from the list — what matters is the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant's invention. Consider the applicant's invention (Section I) when evaluating significance.

name: Improves another technology or technical field
description: One possible indicator that additional elements provide significantly more is that they 'improve another technology or technical field.'
guidance: Demonstrate how the claimed elements produce a technological improvement beyond the abstract idea (examples in worksheet show improvements to digital image processing or GPS signal acquisition).

name: Effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
description: An element that effects a transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing supports eligibility.
guidance: Identify how the claim's steps transform or change a physical or tangible article or data representation in a meaningful way.

name: Adds a specific limitation beyond well‑understood, routine, and conventional activity
description: An additional element that adds a specific limitation other than what is well‑understood, routine, and conventional in the field can provide significantly more.
guidance: Avoid merely appending known industry activities at a high level of generality; show that the claim adds a novel and concrete limitation.

name: Generic computer components do not alone decide eligibility
description: Generic computer components in a claim (e.g., 'processor,' 'memory') alone do not by themselves confer or preclude eligibility.
guidance: Evaluate how the generic components function in combination with other claim elements to determine whether they amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.

name: Office action drafting and use of form paragraphs for §101 rejections
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more, make a §101 rejection and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 in Custom OACs.
guidance: Sample rejection wording is provided in the worksheet and should be used in the Office action. If elements could be added to render a claim eligible, identify them and consider suggesting amendments to the applicant in the Office action.

name: Conclude SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements
description: If the claim is eligible (i.e., amounts to significantly more) conclude the SME analysis and continue examination under each of the other patentability requirements; if not, make a §101 rejection and continue with examination.
guidance: If needed, clarify the record with remarks explaining why the claim is or is not eligible (e.g., 'the claim recites the abstract idea of X, but amounts to significantly more with additional element Y because ABC').

name: Consider suggesting claim amendments to applicant
description: If no additional elements are present that would render the claim eligible, identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to the claim to potentially make it eligible and consider suggesting them to the applicant.
guidance: Provide specific candidate elements from the disclosure in the Office action for applicant consideration.

name: Flowchart Question 1: Statutory category
description: Is the claim directed to one of the four statutory categories: a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter?
guidance: Using the claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), evaluate whether the claim falls within at least one statutory category before proceeding to judicial-exception analysis.

name: Flowchart Question 2: Judicial exception present?
description: Does the claim recite or involve judicial exception(s)? Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural principles, natural phenomena, and natural products.
guidance: If the claim recites or involves an abstract idea, use the appropriate MPEP guidance (e.g., MPEP 2106(II)) to analyze eligibility. If judicial exceptions are present, proceed to Question 3.

name: Flowchart Question 3: Significantly different?
description: Does the claim as a whole recite something significantly different than the judicial exception(s) it recites or involves?
guidance: If the claim as a whole recites something significantly different, the claim may be eligible; if not, reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. §101 as drawn to ineligible subject matter.

name: Two pathways to eligibility ('Significantly Different' standard)
description: The 'significantly different' standard reflects two Supreme Court pathways to eligibility for claims reciting judicial exceptions: (1) a marked difference from what exists in nature (Chakrabarty/Myriad pathway), or (2) the addition of significantly more to the judicial exception (Mayo pathway).
guidance: Both pathways are evaluated by weighing relevant factors; there are no bright-line categories. Consider both Group One (product/marked difference) and Group Two (elements adding significantly more) factors as applicable.

name: Group One: Marked Difference (product claims)
description: For product claims, eligibility can be shown by features demonstrating a marked difference from what exists in nature — specifically structural differences that are more than incidental or trivial.
guidance: Marked difference requires a structural difference from what exists in nature, and if that structural difference changes properties or characteristics of the product, eligibility is more likely. This inquiry focuses on the product's structure, not on how it was made or the effort required.

name: Factor a) Product recites non-naturally occurring, markedly different product (toward eligibility)
description: Product claim recites something that initially appears to be a natural product, but after analysis is determined to be non-naturally occurring and markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
guidance: This factor weighs toward eligibility under the 'marked difference' pathway (e.g., cDNA that is structurally different from genomic DNA, or a genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids).

name: Factor g) Product appears to be natural and not markedly different (against eligibility)
description: Product claim recites something that appears to be a natural product that is not markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
guidance: This factor weighs against eligibility (e.g., isolated genomic DNA where genetic information is unchanged, or a mere aggregation/mixture of naturally occurring bacteria).

name: Group Two: 'Adding Significantly More' (Mayo pathway)
description: Claims can be eligible if they recite elements or steps beyond the judicial exception(s) that add significantly more than the exception itself.
guidance: Guidance provides ten Group Two factors (b–f and h–l) to analyze whether additional claim elements/steps amount to 'significantly more.' Adding 'significantly more' can occur in multiple ways and requires careful fact-specific weighing.

name: Factor b) Elements impose meaningful limits on claim scope (toward eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that impose meaningful limits on the claim scope.
guidance: Meaningful limitations that narrow the claim beyond the exception weigh toward eligibility under the 'significantly more' pathway.

name: Factor c) Elements relate significantly to the judicial exception (toward eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that relate to the judicial exception(s) in a significant way, e.g., they are more than insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Elements that are integrally related to the exception and help implement or apply it in a concrete way support eligibility.

name: Factor d) Elements do more than general instructions to use/apply the exception (toward eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps that do more than describe the judicial exception(s) with general instructions to apply or use it.
guidance: Merely instructing how to apply the natural principle at a high level is insufficient; steps must add substantive limitations or unconventional features.

name: Factor e) Includes a particular machine or particular transformation (toward eligibility)
description: Claim includes a particular machine or a particular transformation which implements or integrates the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Recitation of a specific machine or a transformation that meaningfully integrates the exception can weigh in favor of eligibility.

name: Factor f) Adds a feature beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity (toward eligibility)
description: Claim adds a feature that is more than well-understood, purely conventional, or routine.
guidance: Elements that are inventive in combination or effect (not mere conventional steps) favor eligibility under the 'significantly more' pathway.

name: Factor h) Elements recited at a high level of generality (against eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps at a high level of generality.
guidance: High-level, generic recitations that do not meaningfully limit the claim weigh against eligibility.

name: Factor i) Elements must be used/taken by others to apply the judicial exception(s) (against eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps that must be used/taken by others to apply the judicial exception(s).
guidance: If the claim would effectively preempt others from practicing the natural principle because the elements are necessary to apply it, this factor weighs against eligibility.

name: Factor j) Elements are well-understood, purely conventional, or routine (against eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps that are well-understood, purely conventional, or routine.
guidance: Purely conventional features, absent additional inventive concept, weigh against eligibility (per Mayo).

name: Factor k) Elements are insignificant extra-solution activity, merely appended (against eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps that are insignificant extra-solution activity, e.g., merely appended to the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Activities that do no more than append conventional or ancillary steps to the exception do not make the claim patent eligible.

name: Factor l) Elements amount to nothing more than a mere field of use (against eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps that amount to nothing more than a mere field of use.
guidance: Stating that a natural principle/product is to be used in a particular field without more substantive limitations will weigh against eligibility.

name: Evaluate 'Significantly Different' by weighing factors
description: Determine whether the claim as a whole recites something significantly different than the judicial exception by weighing the listed factors (Group One and Group Two) and considering every relevant factor, related evidence, and the claim as a whole.
guidance: The examiner's analysis should carefully consider all relevant factors and evidence before concluding eligibility; factors may cut for or against eligibility and must be balanced on a case-by-case basis.

name: No bright line rules; avoid conclusory judgments based on particular words
description: The Guidance does not set forth bright line rules or per se categories of ineligible subject matter, and examiners should not make conclusory judgments based only on the recitation of particular words in the claim.
guidance: Words such as 'cDNA', 'composition', 'isolated', 'primer', 'purified', 'recombinant', and 'synthetic' may reflect 'hand of man' but are not necessarily determinative of eligibility; analyze substance over form (Myriad examples).

name: BRI & Example-specific guidance (gunpowder example)
description: When applying BRI, consider that a term may encompass multiple embodiments (some markedly different, some not). If the BRI includes a non-markedly different embodiment, the term is not considered markedly different.
guidance: Example: 'gunpowder' under BRI can include a simple mixture (not markedly different) and various processed powders (markedly different). The eligibility outcome depends on the claim language, specification, and whether the BRI includes non-markedly-different embodiments.

name: Examine cDNA and similar molecular claims case-by-case
description: A claim to a cDNA sequence may or may not be eligible depending on the nucleotide sequence; do not assume eligibility from the label 'cDNA'.
guidance: Examine whether the cDNA spans exon-exon junctions, whether the sequence differs from natural genomic sequence, and other structural attributes; make no assumptions about presence/absence of introns in the underlying gene without evidence.

name: Marked difference limited to product claims rationale
description: Marked difference analysis is applied mainly to product claims because it focuses on structural characteristics of products; process claims frequently recite multiple judicial exceptions and the marked-difference test is rarely determinative.
guidance: For process claims, focus on Group Two 'significantly more' factors and other applicable analyses (e.g., abstract idea or law of nature considerations).

name: Other claiming options when product is not structurally changed
description: If a natural product is not changed structurally, applicants may still claim eligible subject matter by combining the natural product with something else to make a markedly different combination or by adding steps/elements that add significantly more.
guidance: Examples include creating a manufacture comprising the natural product plus additional components, or claiming methods of using the natural product that include meaningful limitations beyond simple application of the natural product.

name: Jepson preamble must be supported by an adequate written description
description: The preamble of Jepson-style patent claims must be supported by an adequate written description.
guidance: As the Federal Circuit held in In re Xencor, the preamble in a Jepson claim requires an adequate written description even though there is an implied admission that most, if not all, of the preamble is known prior art. Practitioners cannot rely on placing information in the Jepson preamble to expand the specification's written description without actual support in the specification or extrinsic evidence.

name: Written description requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a)
description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), the specification of a patent must 'contain a written description of the invention.' The specification must describe an invention understandable to that skilled artisan and show that the inventor actually invented the invention claimed.
guidance: This is the baseline legal standard for written description inquiries cited in Xencor (and cases like Ariad). It governs whether the specification shows possession of the claimed invention and is applied to the claim as a whole.

name: The claimed invention is a singular totality; entire claim needs written description support
description: The claim is a singular thing and cannot be separated; its totality is what must have written description support, which necessarily includes support sufficient to lead an ordinary artisan to understand that the inventor did, indeed, possess what the patent contends was in the prior art.
guidance: When the Jepson format is used, the preamble defines the claimed invention and limits the scope of the claims. Therefore written description support must cover both the improvement and how that improvement applies to the prior-art recited in the preamble.

name: Applicant must establish that purportedly well-known prior art is actually well-known
description: The applicant must establish that what is claimed to be well-known in the prior art is, in fact, well-known in the prior art.
guidance: Implying something is 'well-known' in the Jepson preamble does not shift burden; the patentee must show (via the specification or extrinsic evidence) that the preamble's recited prior art was known to a person of ordinary skill.

name: Consideration of extrinsic evidence to show what a POSITA would know
description: A finder of fact conducting a written description inquiry for a Jepson claim may consider not only the disclosures in the patent itself, but also evidence outside the patent in order to understand what a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known.
guidance: Practitioners should consider and, where necessary, supply or rely on extrinsic evidence (prior art, textbooks, declarations) to demonstrate that the Jepson preamble material was known in the art or that the specification shows possession.

name: Heightened written description expectations in unpredictable arts (life sciences/chemistry)
description: Jepson-format risk is especially significant for the so-called unpredictable arts, such as the life sciences and chemistry, where the written description requirements are often more stringent.
guidance: In Xencor (antibody modifications), the Board and ARP criticized absence of specific disclosure: 'The Specification does not describe what patients with what diseases or conditions can be successfully treated with an anti-C5 antibody. Nor is there a single working example describing treatment of patients with a disease or condition with an anti-C5 antibody possessing the claimed Fc modifications.' This illustrates that therapeutic/biotech claims often need concrete examples or clear disclosure of indications/conditions to satisfy written description.

name: Limited appropriate uses for Jepson claims
description: Jepson-style claims may still prove beneficial in a few specific, limited circumstances, such as distinguishing one claimed invention from another or seeking to overcome/prevent a double patenting rejection.
guidance: Because the preamble is limiting and now requires written description support (post-Xencor), Jepson claims should be used sparingly and only where the practitioner is confident the specification or extrinsic evidence will support the preamble's assertions of what was 'conventional or known.'

name: Cannot expand written description scope by adding information to preamble
description: Xencor precludes the use of Jepson-style claims to expand the scope of the written description contained in the patent specification by simply including additional information in the preamble and, thereby, implicitly asserting that the new information is well-known in the art.
guidance: Drafting strategy: do not rely on the Jepson preamble as a shortcut to claim broader prior-art context unless the specification or external evidence independently supports that context; otherwise risk rejection for lack of written description.

name: Use of admissions as prior art evidence
description: Admissions by the patent owner as to any matter affecting patentability may be utilized to determine the scope and content of the prior art in conjunction with patents and printed publications in a prior art rejection.
guidance: The admission must stand on its own; information supplementing or further defining the admission would be improper. Admissions may reside in the patent file, be presented during reexamination, or be in litigation. A third party may not submit admissions of the patent owner made outside the record of the file or court record unless such admissions were entered into a court record; if entered into a court record and a copy filed, it could be admitted under MPEP § 2282 but would not be given weight as an admission for establishing an SNQ for reexamination or as a basis for rejecting claims. See Ex parte McGaughey, 6 USPQ2d 1334, 1337 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1988).

name: Copy of the printed patent required
description: Requesters must include a copy of the patent for which reexamination is requested (37 CFR 1.510(b)(4)), to serve as the specification for the reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Provide a full copy of the printed patent (double-column format preferred) including front page, abstract, drawings, specification, and claims. Include any disclaimer, certificate of correction, or reexamination certificate issued, and copies of any federal court decision, complaint in a pending civil action, interference or derivation decision to present a complete history.

name: Decision on request uses claims in effect at filing
description: The request should be decided on the wording of the patent claims in effect at that time (without any proposed amendments).
guidance: The decision on whether to grant reexamination is made as though any proposed amendments had not been presented. If reexamination is granted, later prosecution is on the basis of claims as amended.

name: Form and content requirements for entry of amendments (37 CFR 1.530(d))
description: Proposed amendments in reexamination must follow § 1.530(d): specification changes, claims changes, drawings changes, and formal requirements.
guidance: Specification (other than claims): submit entire text of any added or rewritten paragraph including markings (or delete an entire paragraph by statement deleting it); identify the precise point where addition/rewrite is located. Claims: include entire text of each claim being changed and each new claim proposed; parenthetical like 'amended' or 'twice amended' should follow claim number; include markings pursuant to paragraph (f); a claim may be canceled by a statement canceling it without presenting its text. Drawings: submit a sketch on separate paper showing proposed changes in red for examiner approval; upon approval, file new sheets in compliance with § 1.84; amended figures identified as 'Amended', added figures as 'New', canceled figures bracketed and identified as 'Canceled.' Formal requirements for other papers are in § 1.52. Status/support: supply status (pending/canceled) of all claims as of the date of amendment on separate pages and an explanation of support in the disclosure for the claim changes. (Changes shown by markings per paragraph (f) — text continues beyond chunk.)

name: Study inclusion and exclusion rules (Methodology and Scope)
description: The study 'covers all patent cases decided by the Federal Circuit in 2023, whether by precedential opinion, nonprecedential opinion or summary affirmance. It includes merits decisions and rulings on writ petitions, but it excludes denials of leave to appeal, dismissals for lack of finality, stipulated dismissals and remands, and dismissals for mootness.'
guidance: Includes appeals and writ petitions from district courts, the PTAB, the ITC, and the Court of Federal Claims, but only cases in which the Federal Circuit decided at least one patent law issue. If companion cases are resolved separately they are counted separately; if multiple appeals are decided in a single opinion they are counted as one decision. When an opinion is reissued after rehearing the reissued opinion is counted and the retracted opinion disregarded.

name: Equivalence principle for program and method/device claims
description: Principle: a claim directed to the computer program or program product should define a technical effect similar to that obtained by a corresponding method- or device-claim executed on computing equipment. (Finnish: "Periaatteena on se, että tietokoneohjelmaa itseään ... koskevassa patenttivaatimuksessa keksintö määritellään siten, että tietokoneella suoritettuna saa aikaan samanlaisen teknisen vaikutuksen kuin... menetelmä- tai laitevaatimuksen mukaisella keksinnöllä.")
guidance: If the scope of protection of the program claim cannot be determined merely by referring to method/device claims, the program claim must fully express the invention (see B.4.3.1).

name: No patentability by adding only conventional technical means
description: Adding technical limitations (e.g., known computing devices) to patent claims does not render non-patentable subject matter patentable if those limitations do not achieve technical effects beyond normal computer operation. (Finnish: "tavanomaisten tietojenkäsittelyvälineiden käyttö ei pelkästään riitä takaamaan patentoitavuutta...")
guidance: Examiner must assess whether claimed technical features produce more than routine physical effects (like electrical current) in order to support patentability.

name: Requirements for claims in distributed systems
description: For distributed systems, each unit/system may have corresponding method claims; the claim set must be unitary and satisfy novelty, inventive step and clarity for each unit. Interactions between units must be described so that all technical features appear from the claims. If method steps are performed in different units, it must be clear which unit performs which steps. (Finnish: "Eri yksiköiden väliset vuorovaikutukset tulee kuvata, jotta kaikki tekniset ominaispiirteet käyvät vaatimuksista ilmi... mitkä menetelmävaiheet kukin yksikkö suorittaa.")
guidance: Clarity requires specification of per-unit responsibilities; refer to EPO guidance (EPO GL F-IV, 3.9.3) for examples.

name: Drafting computer-program claims — necessary features only
description: In patent claims directed to computer programs, the invention must be defined by the particular features necessary to achieve the intended effect; claims must not include program listings. (Finnish: "Patenttivaatimuksessa keksintö on määriteltävä niiden erityispiirteiden avulla, jotka ovat välttämättömät tarkoitetun vaikutuksen aikaansaamiseksi. Vaatimukset eivät saa sisältää ohjelmalistausta.")
guidance: Claims should focus on technical-functional features rather than literal code; program listings belong in the description if needed.

name: Acceptability of program claims when method/device claims lack clarity
description: If program/device claims refer to method/device claims but the scope of protection is not unambiguously determinable by such reference, the program claim must fully disclose the invention in the claim language. (Finnish: "Jos hakemuksen menetelmä- tai laitevaatimukset ovat sellaiset, että haetun patenttisuojan laajuus ei käy yksiselitteisesti selville pelkästään viittaamalla niihin tietokoneohjelmaa koskevassa patenttivaatimuksessa, ... keksintö on ilmaistava patenttivaatimuksissa täydellisesti.")
guidance: Particular attention where method/device claims include features not realizable by software.

name: Diagnostic methods exclusion and definition
description: A diagnostic method comprises four main phases: (1) examination/data collection, (2) comparison of data to standards, (3) finding a significant deviation/symptom, and (4) reasoning to associate deviation with a clinical picture (diagnosis). A diagnostic method is excluded under PatL 1 §(3) only if the examination phase requires presence of the tested human or animal. (Finnish: list of four phases and exclusion condition.)
guidance: In vitro diagnostic methods (e.g., blood/urine analysis) are patentable. If a diagnostic claim lacks one of these phases, examiner may request inclusion to meet PatL 8 §(2) sufficiency/precision requirements. Methods producing only measurement data that do not enable treatment decisions may be patentable.

name: Formal notice triggers
description: PRH may issue a formal notice at various phases for formal defects such as insufficient clarity/precision of the invention (B.4.1), defects in abstract or figures, additional fee request when claim count exceeds paid number, or to request other offices' search results (PatL 74 § 3 mom.). (Finnish: examples given.)
guidance: Formal notices may be replaced by informal phone contact for minor issues. If applicant has amended to claim subject-matter not apparent at filing (PatL 13 § / PatA 19 §), PRH may object by formal notice.

name: Purpose and content of the first technical notice
description: The first technical notice's main purpose is to give the applicant a clear picture of the patentability of the invention so they can decide whether to continue prosecution in Finland and abroad. It describes the subject of the novelty search, the basis for the search, and for each examined claim addresses novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability. (Finnish: description of first technical notice.)
guidance: The notice should justify any limitations on the search and list prior art cited in novelty assessment. It should explain reasons for lack of inventive step typically using the problem-solution approach (E.4).

name: List of substantive defects leading to technical notice objections
description: If PRH considers that the application has deficiencies affecting patentability, the technical notice will state the deficiencies with reasons. Examples: (•) claim concerns non-patentable subject-matter (PatL 1/1a/1b); (•) claim lacks novelty and/or inventive step (PatL 2 §); (•) claims are indefinite (PatL 8 §); (•) claims are not supported by the description enabling skilled person (PatL 8 §); (•) application lacks unity (PatL 10 §); (•) patent sought for subject-matter not apparent in original application (PatL 13 §). (Finnish: bullet list from text.)
guidance: Technical notice should also explain which parts of the description/claims the novelty search covered and justify any limitations. It may also point out drafting or formatting issues (e.g., two-part claim form, translations).

name: Multiple technical notices policy
description: A second technical notice is issued if new relevant publications appear after the first notice, if the invention is patentable but claims cannot be accepted in current form, or if the invention remains unpatentable and applicant's response raises issues requiring PRH reply. Further technical notices beyond the second are rare and issued only for newly arisen obstacles or significant claim amendments. (Finnish: description.)
guidance: PRH aims in the first technical notice to give clear instructions so fewer further notices are needed. New third+ notices only for new grounds or substantial claim changes.

name: Approving (acceptance) notice conditions
description: When the invention is patentable based on the examination and the application is acceptable as-is or with minor corrections, PRH issues an approving notice informing the applicant how the patent will be granted and requesting confirmation that the applicant wants a patent in that form. A prerequisite is that claims are acceptable in substance and wording. (Finnish: description of hyväksyvä välipäätös.)
guidance: Approving notice may request translations of claims and abstract and permit minor corrections; substantial formal defects are handled in a separate formal notice. If claims are amended after an approving notice (e.g., due to a third-party observation), a second approving notice may be issued.

name: Restrictions after PatL 19 § notice (no broadening/division)
description: After PRH has given the PatL 19 § notice that the application can be accepted, claims may not be amended to broaden protection, nor may a new (divisional) application be created by splitting/parting the application (PatA 22 and 23 §§). The notice is given only when publishable documents are available. (Finnish: explanation.)
guidance: Purpose is to prevent changes that would unnecessarily prolong grant procedure. Applicants must pay publication fee within two months or the application lapses.

name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool
description: Assess whether computers/machinery are used only in their ordinary capacity (tools to perform an existing process) rather than improving computer/technical capabilities.
guidance: Using a computer to receive, store, or transmit data, or adding a general-purpose computer to an abstract idea, typically does not integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Case examples of tool-use: Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (cellular telephone), TLI Communications v. AV Auto (server & telephone unit). Contrasting examples where computer/technology improvement supported eligibility: McRO, Enfish (improvements to computer functioning/technology). See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a) for discussion of technological improvements.

name: Whether the limitation is significant (imposes meaningful limits on the claim)
description: Assess if the limitation imposes meaningful limits such that it is not merely nominal or tangential to the invention.
guidance: If a limitation meaningfully confines the claim, it may be significant. Examples found insignificant: restricting public access to media (Ultramercial), certain electronic menu features (Ameranth). This significance inquiry is relevant in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.

name: Only number/extension laws and universal causality justify impossibility claims
description: The only natural laws that can warrant asserting impossibility are (1) laws of number and extension (mathematical/structural constraints) and (2) the universal law of causality (no change if antecedents identical).
guidance: Distinguish when an impossibility claim is supported by formal/mathematical necessity or by strict causal determinism versus when it is merely empirical absence. Be explicit which category a purported impossibility falls into.

name: Avoid resolving radically different phenomena into a single element (illicit reductionism)
description: The attempt to reduce qualitatively distinct phenomena (e.g., sensation, colour, consciousness) to one fundamental element (motion, electricity, chemistry) is necessarily false when it pretends to eliminate the generic peculiarity of the phenomenon rather than merely identify conditions.
guidance: It's permissible to show physical conditions or necessary antecedents for a phenomenon, but not to claim that those conditions are a full explanation that removes the distinct nature of the phenomenon. Example: showing motions in the nervous system are conditions for sensation does not thereby explain the qualitative character ('the law of colour' remains distinct).

name: Beware post hoc and cum hoc causal fallacies
description: Do not infer causation merely from temporal succession (post hoc ergo propter hoc) or mere coexistence (cum hoc ergo propter hoc) of events without elimination of other antecedents or independent grounds for causation.
guidance: Causal claims need elimination of alternative antecedents and supportive evidence that the candidate cause has properties tending to produce the observed effect. Single instances of conjunction are weak verification; seek additional, independent support.

name: Be cautious of sweeping empirical generalizations about human society
description: Generalizations about human nature or social trends derived solely from a limited historical or cultural sample (e.g., assuming human nature is constant or that progress is universal) are empirical laws with narrow limits and may be false when causes differ across times/places.
guidance: When generalizing about society, identify and analyze the specific causes producing observed changes; do not assume a single summary law (e.g., 'progress of species') without causal investigation. Limit claims to adjacent cases unless causal relations are shown.

name: What did applicant invent? / Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
guidance: Use the specification to determine what applicant invented and record it in Section I. Every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited; use a separate worksheet for each claim. The worksheet use is optional but recommended. If needed, clarify claim interpretation in the Office action record (for example: the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim is not directed to an abstract idea or nature-based product).

name: Does the claimed invention fall within one of the four statutory categories (Step 1)
description: Determine whether the claimed invention is a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.
guidance: Choose A or B. If No (not one of the four categories), make a rejection as drawn to non-statutory subject matter and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record if a rejection is made under Step 2.
