If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and continue examination under the other patentability requirements.

name: Is the claim directed to a product of nature, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea (Step 2A)
description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (product of nature, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
guidance: A claim is 'directed' to a product of nature exception when the claim recites a nature-based product limitation that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. For other exceptions, it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. Refer to the Subject Matter Eligibility Quick Reference Sheet, 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance, July 2015 Update, and the court decisions chart for assistance. Choose A (no exception), B (streamlined analysis appropriate), or C (claim directed to an exception — proceed to further questions).

name: Product-of-nature: apply the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to nature-based product limitations
description: Apply the markedly different characteristics test only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim to determine whether the nature-based products are 'product of nature' exceptions.
guidance: Non-limiting examples of characteristics considered by the courts when determining whether there is a marked difference include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype, including functional and structural characteristics; and structure and form, whether chemical, genetic or physical. Note that a process claim is not subject to the markedly different analysis for nature-based products used in the process, except in the limited situation where a process claim is drafted such that there is no difference in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple.'). Apply the analysis limitation-by-limitation.

name: If claim directed to a nature-based product: identify limitation(s), closest naturally occurring counterpart, and compare
description: Identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe a nature-based product; identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state; compare to determine whether the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics.
guidance: Complete parts (a) (list the nature-based product limitations), (b) (identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart), and (c) (explain comparison and select (i) The nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics (and thus is not a product of nature exception) with reasons; or (ii) The nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics (and thus is a product of nature exception) with reasons). Proceed thereafter to analyze whether the claim is directed to another type of exception (Question 2) or to Step 2B if an exception is found.

name: Identify limitations that recite an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon and explain why
description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, and/or natural phenomenon, identify the claim limitation(s) that recite the exception and explain why the recited subject matter is an exception.
guidance: Record the limitation(s) and the reason(s) they are considered a judicial exception. Examples given: laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles or substances; abstract ideas include fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. Use the case law chart and 2014 Guidance for examples and alignment.

name: Are there any additional elements beyond the exception(s)? (Step 2B.A)
description: Identify whether the claim recites additional elements (features/limitations/steps) beyond the judicial exception(s) identified in Step 2A.
guidance: Note that if the claim is directed to a product of nature comprising a combination of component elements that do not occur together in nature as claimed, each component element should be considered as an additional element to the other components to determine whether their combination results in significantly more. Choose 1 (No additional elements — conclude SME analysis with §101 rejection) or 2 (Yes — list additional claim elements and continue). If no additional elements, make a §101 rejection and consider whether there are elements in the disclosure that could be added to make the claim eligible (identify and suggest them to applicant). Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015.

name: Evaluate significance of additional elements to determine 'significantly more' / 'inventive concept' (Step 2B.B)
description: Consider the identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception(s).
guidance: Search for an 'inventive concept' by considering whether the additional elements: improve another technology or technical field; improve the functioning of a computer itself; apply the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic computer functions; not merely 'apply it'); effect a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; add a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending routine activities at high-level); add unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); add meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment. Keep in mind what applicant invented (Section I) when evaluating significance.

name: Conclusion and Office action / sample rejection language
description: Conclude SME analysis based on whether additional elements amount to significantly more; prepare rejection or continue examination accordingly.
guidance: If any elements, individually or as a combination, amount to significantly more than the exception(s), conclude SME analysis and continue examination under each of the other patentability requirements; clarify the record as needed (e.g., explain why the claim with additional element 'y' amounts to significantly more than the product of nature 'x'). If no elements amount to significantly more, conclude the SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with examination under other patentability requirements. Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. The worksheet provides sample rejection wording: 'Claim __ is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Claim __ is directed to _____. The claim does not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because _____.' Also, identify and propose elements from the disclosure that could be added to the claim to attempt to make it eligible.

name: Fee deficiency procedure (PTOL-475)
description: If required excess claims fees are not paid with presentation of excess claims, a Notice of Defective Paper (PTOL-475) will be issued setting a one-month period to correct the fee deficiency.
guidance: An extension to correct the deficiency may be requested under 37 CFR 1.550(c). If unpaid within the time set, the reexamination will be terminated under 37 CFR 1.550(e) effecting abandonment per 37 CFR 1.20(c)(5).

name: Examiner consideration of properly filed submissions
description: Once reexamination is ordered, any submissions properly filed and served in accordance with 37 CFR 1.530 and 1.535 will be considered by the examiner when preparing the first Office action.
guidance: Examiner guidance for consideration of proposed amendments to specification/claims is in 37 CFR 1.530(d)-(j); for patent owner statements see 1.530(c); for requester reply see 1.535. New issues raised by requester within scope will be addressed in Office action.

name: Conduct of ex parte reexamination — general (35 U.S.C. 305; 37 CFR 1.550)
description: After filing periods expire, reexamination is conducted according to initial examination procedures (35 U.S.C. 132, 133) and results in issuance of a reexamination certificate under § 1.570. Patent owner may propose amendments or new claims to distinguish over cited prior art, but no proposed amendment or new claim that enlarges scope will be permitted.
guidance: Proceedings (including appeals) will be conducted with special dispatch. A full search will not routinely be made by examiner.

name: Scope of reexamination — limited bases (37 CFR 1.552(a)-(c))
description: Claims will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted, on the basis of 35 U.S.C. 112. Claims in reexamination will not be permitted to enlarge scope. Issues other than those indicated (patents/printed publications and 112 for added matter) will not be resolved in reexamination.
guidance: If such other issues are raised, examiner will note them in the next Office action and patent owner may consider reissue to have them resolved; new/amended claims are examined to ensure scope not broadened per 35 U.S.C. 305.

name: Intervening patents/printed publications
description: Rejections may be made based on intervening patents or printed publications where the claims under reexamination are entitled only to the patent's filing date and are not supported by an earlier application whose filing date is claimed (e.g., under 35 U.S.C. 120 situations).
guidance: Intervening patents/publications are treated as prior art per In re Ruscetta, In re van Langenhoven, and MPEP § 201.11.

name: Double patenting — consideration in reexamination
description: Double patenting is appropriate for consideration in reexamination both as a basis for ordering reexamination and during subsequent examination; examiner should determine whether double patenting raises a substantial new question and whether a double patenting rejection is appropriate during examination.
guidance: Double patenting may exist where the reexamined patent and another patent/application contain conflicting claims and (A) are filed by same inventive entity; (B) filed by different entities having a common inventor; (C) filed by a common assignee; and/or (D) result from joint research agreement activities as defined in 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3). Post-2004/date-specific conditions and terminal disclaimer remedies are addressed (use form paragraphs 14.23.01, 14.25–14.32 as appropriate).

name: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 for new/added matter
description: Where new claims are presented or where any part of the specification/claims/drawings is added or deleted in reexamination, those changes are examined for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: This ensures that added subject matter meets written description/enabling/definiteness requirements; see MPEP § 2270 for handling new matter.

name: Purpose of Discovery
description: Through disclosures and discovery devices a party may ascertain the facts underlying its adversary's case; discovery may lead to settlement, simplify issues, reveal basis for summary judgment or additional claims/defenses, and permit stipulations and preparation for trial.
guidance: Discovery enables proposing stipulations of fact, procedures for introducing evidence, narrowing issues, or pursuing Accelerated Case Resolution (ACR). Initial and expert disclosures are intended to obviate the need for traditional discovery to obtain 'basic information.'

name: Subjects to be Discussed at Discovery Conference
description: Parties must consider: (1) the nature and basis of their respective claims and defenses; (2) the possibility of settling or narrowing claims/defenses; (3) arrangements relating to disclosures, discovery and introduction of evidence at trial; and any topics listed in the institution order.
guidance: Discussion should include whether to seek mediation/arbitration, consideration of the Board's ACR process, whether to alter disclosure/discovery procedures or the Standard Protective Order, limitations on disclosures, stipulations of fact, and efficient options for introducing discovery-produced material at trial.

name: Initial Disclosures — Required Content
description: Per Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1): (i) the name and, if known, address and telephone of each individual likely to have discoverable information and the subjects of that information that the disclosing party may use to support its claims or defenses; (ii) a copy — or a description by category and location — of all documents, electronically stored information, and tangible things in the disclosing party's possession, custody, or control that it may use to support its claims or defenses.
guidance: Subsections (iii) and (iv) of Rule 26(a)(1)(A) do not apply to Board proceedings. Pertinent ESI must be identified. If a trial witness is identified, the subject matter the witness is likely to have discoverable information about must be provided, along with any known contact information. A party may either provide the location of identified documents or produce them; the Board encourages actual exchange of copies rather than mere identification of location.

name: Scope and Limitation of Initial Disclosures
description: A party is not obligated to disclose every witness, document, or thing that may have discoverable information; only those witnesses, documents, and things having discoverable information that the disclosing party may use to support its claims or defenses must be disclosed.
guidance: Initial disclosures are intended to prompt routine disclosure of basic information, not to substitute for comprehensive discovery. Discovery in Board proceedings should be more limited than in district court due to limited TTAB jurisdiction; parties may, with Board approval, stipulate to more expansive reciprocal disclosures to reduce formal discovery.

name: Ornamentality requirement for design patents
description: A design consists of the visual ornamental characteristics embodied in, or applied to, an article of manufacture. The subject matter may relate to the configuration or shape of an article, the surface ornamentation applied to an article, or the combination of configuration and surface ornamentation.
guidance: The claimed design must be ornamental in character; pure functionality negates design-patent eligibility. Consider whether the aspects claimed are visual/ornamental rather than dictated by utilitarian needs.

name: Test for ornamentality (primarily ornamental)
description: A design must be 'primarily ornamental' — the claimed design is viewed in its entirety and the overall appearance is evaluated to determine whether it is dictated by utilitarian purpose.
guidance: Courts commonly ask whether alternative designs could achieve the same function: if alternatives exist, the design is likely ornamental (and patentable); if no alternatives exist, the design is likely functional (and not patentable as a design). Always assess the overall visual impression rather than isolated features.

name: Claiming format (single claim for design patents)
description: Utility patents: multiple claims allowed. Design patents: single claim only — typically 'The ornamental design for [article] as shown and described.'
guidance: Draft the single design claim to encompass the exact visual elements shown in the drawings and description; do not attempt multiple independent claimed designs in one application.

name: Drawings requirement for design patents (critical)
description: Drawings must show all sides of the article (top, bottom, left, right, front, back, perspective). Surface lines define the design. Broken lines indicate an unclaimed environment; solid lines indicate the claimed design.
guidance: Because drawings are dominant in a design application, ensure completeness and clarity of all views. Insufficient drawings (not showing all views) are a common ground for rejection or objection; use solid vs broken lines correctly to delimit claim scope.

name: Specific USPTO Rules and regulatory provisions implicated by such conduct
description: The Final Order identifies violations of specific USPTO rules: 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a), 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(b)(5), 10.85(a)(2), 10.85(a)(3), 11.804(i), and 10.23(b)(6) in connection with filing claims, serving interrogatory responses, multiplying proceedings, and other conduct.
guidance: The Order ties particular acts to these rule citations (e.g., filing complaints while aware of false declarations; serving responses asserting actual reduction to practice; unreasonably multiplying proceedings). Practitioners should consult the text of these sections for the exact regulatory requirements and prohibitions.

name: Step 2A — Prong 1: Judicial Exception Recited?
description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (abstract idea), such as a mathematical concept/formula, a mental process, or a certain method of organizing human activity.
guidance: If the claim recites a judicial exception, proceed to Prong 2 to determine whether the exception is integrated into a practical application. Examples show identifying mental processes (e.g., calculating amount of use), mathematical formulas (e.g., modular arithmetic in cryptography), and methods of organizing human activity (e.g., managing interactions between people/medical record notifications).

name: Mental Processes Group
description: A claim limitation is a 'mental process' if, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, it covers performance in the human mind (or using pen and paper) rather than requiring something beyond mental performance.
guidance: Check whether the limitation could practically be performed in the mind except for a nominal recitation of a generic computer/processor. Mere insertion of 'by a processor' does not remove a step from the mental-process grouping (Example 37, 39, 40 analyses).

name: Mathematical Concepts
description: Claim limitations that explicitly recite a mathematical relationship, formula, or calculation are judicial exceptions (mathematical concepts).
guidance: If a mathematical formula is recited, evaluate whether the combination of additional elements uses the mathematical concepts in a specific manner that limits their use to a practical application (Example 41: modular arithmetic in cryptography integrated into securing network communications).

name: Methods of Organizing Human Activity
description: Claims that are methods of organizing human activity (e.g., fundamental economic concepts, managing interactions between people) are judicial exceptions.
guidance: Examples include methods that manage how people interact or share information (Example 42: transmission of notifications when medical records are updated is a method of managing interactions between people). If so, proceed to determine whether additional elements integrate the idea into a practical application.

name: Step 2A — Prong 2: Integration into a Practical Application
description: Assess whether the additional claim elements, individually and in combination, integrate the judicial exception into a practical application such that the claim is not directed to the exception.
guidance: Consider whether the claim as a whole provides a specific improvement (e.g., improved user interface, improved network monitoring) or otherwise applies the exception in a particularized way. If the additional elements amount to more than nominal/generic recitations and provide a specific technological improvement, the claim may be 'not directed to' the judicial exception (Examples 37, 40, 41, 42 analyses).

name: Specific Technical/Technological Improvement
description: A claim that recites a specific improvement to computer functionality or other technology (e.g., improved user interface, reduced network traffic, improved audio simulation fidelity) supports integration into a practical application.
guidance: Identify factual assertions of a specific improvement over prior systems (Example 37: improved GUI by automatically displaying most-used icons closer to start icon; Example 40: limiting NetFlow data collection to abnormal conditions reduces network burden; Example 38: simulating analog variances for improved audio quality). Such statements support finding the claim integrates the exception into a practical application.

name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity / Data Gathering
description: Claimed steps that amount to mere data gathering, receiving signals, or other pre-/post-solution activity are treated as insignificant extra-solution activity and generally do not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: Collecting or receiving data in a generic manner (e.g., collecting network statistics, receiving a plaintext signal) is often considered insignificant; such limitations should be re-examined at Step 2B to determine if they are well-understood, routine, and conventional (Examples 40, 41, 42).

name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Inquiry (2B Re-evaluation / Berkheimer Considerations)
description: Under Step 2B, decide whether claimed additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional activity; if so, they do not supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Background and evidence of conventionality matters. The guidance notes that an element considered insignificant extra-solution activity in 2A should be re-evaluated in 2B to determine conventionality (Example 40's collecting step determined to be well-understood, routine, conventional). Case law (e.g., Berkheimer) is invoked for this re-evaluation.

name: Integration vs. Inventive Concept Distinction
description: Step 2A Prong 2 examines integration of an exception into a practical application (i.e., whether claim as a whole is directed to the exception), while Step 2B examines whether additional elements supply an inventive concept (i.e., 'significantly more').
guidance: Even if an exception is integrated into a practical application at Step 2A (making the claim 'not directed to' an exception), Step 2B is not always applicable. Conversely, if Step 2A finds the claim directed to an exception, Step 2B asks whether the claim's additional elements supply significantly more (see Example 41 discussion and notes).

name: Explicit Recitation of Mathematical Formula vs. Use of Mathematics
description: A claim explicitly reciting a mathematical formula or calculation is treated as reciting a mathematical concept; however, use of math in service of a specific technological application can integrate the concept into a practical application.
guidance: If the mathematical formula is explicitly claimed (e.g., modular exponentiation in cryptographic encoding), analyze whether the claim applies the mathematics in a specific manner that secures communications or achieves a specific technological result (Example 41: cryptography math integrated into securing communication was treated as integrated and eligible).

name: Claims Must Also Meet Other Patentability Requirements
description: Subject-matter eligibility (Section 101) is only one requirement; all claims must ultimately be analyzed for compliance with every requirement for patentability, including 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 103, and 112.
guidance: The PEG examples explicitly note that the §101 analysis does not address novelty, non-obviousness, or written description/enablement, which must be considered separately.

name: Examples Are Illustrative and Fact-Specific
description: The examples are hypothetical, illustrative of claim analysis under the 2019 PEG, and should be interpreted based on the specific fact patterns set forth; different fact patterns may lead to different eligibility outcomes.
guidance: It is not necessary for a claim to mirror an example to be eligible; use the examples only as guidance and consider case-specific facts and claim wording.

name: Patent dance timeline and mandatory disclosures
description: The BPCIA patent dance is a (statutorily described) choreography with specific deadlines: Day 1–20 aBLA disclosure, Day 20–80 RPS patent list (and license offers), Day 80–140 applicant responses (claim‑by‑claim invalidity/ noninfringement contentions), Day 140–200 RPS contentions, Day 200–215 patent selection and Phase I lists, followed by Phase I litigation filing and Phase II 180‑day notice triggers.
guidance: Missing deadlines (e.g., omitting a patent from the RPS list) has serious consequences (e.g., pre‑commercial §271(e) assertion bar); draft claim‑by‑claim dance contentions carefully because they form the earliest iteration of PTAB arguments.

name: Choosing between IPR and PGR
description: IPR challenges only §102/§103 based on patents and printed publications and is available after the nine-month post-grant window (subject to a one‑year bar after service). PGR can challenge on any ground (including §101, §112 written description/enablement) but must be filed within nine months of grant and is only available for AIA (post‑March 16, 2013) patents.
guidance: Use PGR for biologic patents vulnerable to §112 written‑description/enablement attacks (prophetic claims); use IPR for older patents or when PGR window has closed; ensure continuous monitoring of grants to capture PGR windows.

name: Draft claim‑by‑claim contentions as early PTAB argument skeletons
description: Claim‑by‑claim invalidity/ non‑infringement statements in the patent dance are effectively the earliest form of the IPR petition arguments.
guidance: Draft dance contentions with the rigor of PTAB petitions to set favorable tones for later filings and avoid re‑work; include strong prior art support because these contentions influence settlement and PTAB strategy.

name: Proposed terminal disclaimer enforceability condition
description: The USPTO proposes that terminal disclaimers can overcome an obviousness‑type double patenting rejection only if the terminal disclaimer ties the subject application's enforceability to the reference application's validity.
guidance: Specifically, the proposed rule would require the terminal disclaimer to include an agreement that the subject patent is only enforceable so long as it is not tied “directly or indirectly” to a patent in which “any claim has been finally held unpatentable or invalid as anticipated or obvious by a Federal court in a civil action or by the USPTO, and all appeal rights have been exhausted; or a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on anticipation or obviousness to that claim has been made.” In practice this would make a terminally disclaimed patent unenforceable if the referenced patent has even a single claim found invalid for anticipation or obviousness (with appeals exhausted).

name: Existing common‑ownership requirement (37 C.F.R. § 1.321(c)(3))
description: Current regulation requires that a terminal disclaimer include a provision that the subject patent be enforceable only so long as it and the reference patent are commonly owned.
guidance: This anti‑harassment provision is intended to prevent different patentees from separately asserting patents with patentably indistinct claims against the same defendant. The proposed rule would add an additional validity‑tying condition on top of this common‑ownership requirement.

name: Obviousness‑type double patenting doctrine
description: Obviousness‑type double patenting is a judicially created doctrine that prohibits obtaining multiple patents with patentably indistinct claims.
guidance: Two main policy motivations: (1) prevent patent owners from extending the term of their monopoly by obtaining multiple patents with indistinct claims, and (2) prevent harassment where different patentees could separately assert substantially the same invention. Terminal disclaimers are a common mechanism to address this doctrine by aligning patent term or ownership conditions.

name: Applicant strategic responses to double patenting rejections
description: If the proposed rule is enacted, applicants should reconsider whether to file terminal disclaimers and may prefer alternative responses.
guidance: Recommended strategies include: traversing the double patenting rejection (arguing against it), amending claims to overcome the rejection rather than filing a terminal disclaimer, filing earlier family applications with relatively narrow claims, amending more aggressively in earlier applications and progressively broadening in continuation applications, and otherwise managing claim scope across a family to reduce the risk that later applications will be rendered unenforceable by broader earlier applications. The article notes applicants may more strongly consider these options because a terminal disclaimer could link enforceability to another patent’s ultimate invalidity.

name: USPTO policy rationale for proposed change
description: The USPTO says the proposal aims to reduce litigation costs caused by multiple related patents with very similar scope by tying validity/enforceability.
guidance: By making related patents’ enforceability interdependent, defendants and patentees could focus validity disputes on a single patent, potentially producing more focused claim construction hearings, lower litigation costs, and faster resolution. The article reports this as the USPTO's justification for the proposed rule.

name: Consider the claim as a whole under Step 2A; avoid oversimplification
description: Examiners should consider the claim as a whole under Step 2A of the USPTO's SME guidance, and should not overgeneralize the claim or simplify it into its 'gist' or core principles when identifying a concept as a judicial exception.
guidance: The McRO court cautioned that courts 'must be careful to avoid oversimplifying the claims' by looking at them generally and failing to account for the specific requirements of the claims. Examiners should account for the specific claim limitations rather than reducing claims to an overly broad characterization similar to previously-identified abstract ideas.

name: Claims directed to an improvement in computer-related technology may be eligible
description: A claim directed to an improvement in computer-related technology is not necessarily directed to an abstract idea and therefore may be patent eligible under Step 2A.
guidance: An 'improvement in computer-related technology' can include improvements beyond mere operation of a computer or network; it can be a set of 'rules' (mathematical relationships) that enable a computer to perform a function not previously performable by a computer. The McRO decision found claims eligible because they were directed to improving computer animation (automating tasks previously requiring human animators) rather than an abstract idea. Contrast decisions (e.g., Affinity Labs, Electric Power Group) where lack of detail as to how the improvement is achieved or mere presentation of results led to a finding of an abstract idea.

name: Indicators that a claim is directed to a computer-related improvement
description: Certain facts in the specification and claim language can indicate the claim is directed to an improvement in computer-related technology rather than an abstract idea.
guidance: Notable indicators include: (1) teaching in the specification about how the claimed invention improves a computer or other technology (McRO relied on such specification explanations); and (2) a claim that defines a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome (e.g., McRO's use of particular rules to set morph weights and transitions), as opposed to merely claiming the idea or outcome.

name: Do not treat use of a computer as mere automation of a known human process
description: A claim that merely uses a computer as a tool to perform an existing process is more likely to be an abstract idea; claims that improve computer-related technology by enabling new computer performance can be eligible.
guidance: McRO distinguished claims that improved the technological process (specific rules enabling automation) from cases like Alice where a computer was merely used as a tool. Examine whether the claimed invention allows computers to do something not previously performable or improves existing computer functionality.

name: Step 2B — evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination for an inventive concept
description: When a claim is determined to be directed to a judicial exception, examiners should apply Step 2B by determining whether the additional elements, alone or in combination, amount to 'significantly more' (an inventive concept).
guidance: BASCOM teaches that although additional elements may be generic individually, their non-conventional and non-generic arrangement can supply an inventive concept. Example: the installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable filtering features for each end user was found relevant to eligibility. Examiners must consider combinations of elements as well as individual elements when assessing 'significantly more.'

name: Use the Mayo/Alice framework (Steps 2A and 2B) to resolve preemption questions
description: Examiners should continue to use the MayolAlice framework (implemented as Steps 2A and 2B) to analyze whether claims preempt a judicial exception and to resolve any preemption arguments.
guidance: If an applicant argues that a claim does not preempt all applications of the exception, the examiner should: (a) reconsider in Step 2A whether the claim is directed to an improvement in computer-related technology or a specific way of achieving a desired outcome; and (b) if still directed to a judicial exception, reconsider in Step 2B whether the additional elements in combination are more than a non-conventional/non-generic arrangement of known, conventional elements. The memorandum notes that absence of preemption has been used in some decisions to support eligibility but not in others; use the structured framework rather than preemption alone.

name: Related‑company limitation on recovering another entity’s lost profits
description: A patentee generally may not claim, as its own damages, the lost profits of a related company.
guidance: Courts reject attempts by one corporate affiliate to claim the lost profits of another unless special proof supports aggregation. Edgewell’s attempt to recover EPC’s lost profits was deemed unpersuasive; courts cite precedent that bars claiming related companies’ lost profits absent additional justification.

name: Clarity of the Record Pilot
description: Identify best practices for enhancing clarity of specific aspects of the prosecution record—claim interpretation, reasons for allowance, and interview summaries—and explore the impact of implementing these best practices during examination.
guidance: Pilot seeks to create a complete, comprehensive record to give inventors and investors confidence and to avoid costly litigation. Findings may inform examiner guidance and training.

name: Structure-based vs function-based 'markedly different' inquiry
description: Two analytical approaches exist: (1) focus on chemical/structural differences created by human intervention (Judge Lourie), or (2) focus on new and distinct uses/functions the claimed subject enables (Judge Moore).
guidance: Different outcomes can follow depending on which approach is used: Lourie upheld claims based on chemical identity after isolation; Moore emphasized novel utility and uses rather than mere chemical change.

name: Isolated genomic DNA ineligibility (Myriad holding)
description: Isolated DNA molecules are not patent eligible because the chemical changes from isolation were not what the patent claims were 'articulated in terms of' or dependent upon.
guidance: The Court rejected deference to PTO practice and held that merely isolating native DNA did not produce patent-eligible subject matter when the claimed invention's utility derived from the natural sequence.

name: Perfection of foreign priority claims (37 CFR 1.55)
description: The foreign priority filing date must antedate the reference and be perfected. The filing date of the priority document is not perfected unless applicant has filed a certified priority document in the application (and an English language translation, if the document is not in English) (see 37 CFR 1.55).
guidance: If priority was not perfected by timely filing of the certified priority document/translation, survival of the earlier filing date may require filing a grantable petition to accept an unintentionally delayed priority claim under 37 CFR 1.55. See MPEP §§ 213-216 for more detail.

name: Submitting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 (37 CFR 1.78/1.76)
description: To claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 within the time periods set in 37 CFR 1.78: (a) for applications filed on or after September 16, 2012, file an application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 which contains a specific reference to a prior application in accordance with 37 CFR 1.78; or (b) for applications filed prior to September 16, 2012, amend the specification to contain a specific reference or file an ADS under 37 CFR 1.76 containing the specific reference.
guidance: Additionally, the applicant must establish that the prior application satisfies the enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (for applications filed on or after Sept. 16, 2012) or 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (for earlier filings), or file a grantable petition to accept an unintentionally delayed claim under 37 CFR 1.78.

name: Combination claims in a reference do not, by themselves, establish inventorship of individual elements or subcombinations
description: The existence of combination claims in a reference is not evidence that the inventor invented individual elements or subcombinations included in that combination if the elements/subcombinations are not separately claimed apart from the combination.
guidance: Declarations or affidavits that do not identify the specific species or separate claimed subcombination will be insufficient (see In re DeBaun; In re Facius; In re Mathews). Examiners should require evidence addressing the particular elements at issue.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) — requirement of correct inventorship
description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) bars issuance of a patent where an applicant did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented; correct inventorship of a claimed invention must be named in the application.
guidance: The examiner must presume applicants are the proper inventors unless there is evidence of record that another made the invention and that the applicants derived the invention. In an uncommon situation where it is clear the application does not name the correct inventive entity and there has been no request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48, the examiner should reject the claims under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) (see In re VerHoef; Pannu v. Iolab Corp.).

name: Definition and content of a submission
description: A 'submission' for RCE purposes may include an information disclosure statement (IDS), an amendment to the specification/claims/drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: If a reply to an Office action under 35 U.S.C. 132 is outstanding, the submission must meet the reply requirements of 37 C.F.R. 1.111. An appeal brief or reply brief alone is not a submission, but arguments in a previously filed appeal/reply brief may be incorporated by reference. Previously filed after-final amendments that were not entered may in some cases satisfy the submission requirement.

name: RCE after filing notice of appeal to Federal Circuit or civil action — general bar
description: The RCE procedure under 37 C.F.R. 1.114 is not available after filing a Notice of Appeal to the Federal Circuit or the commencement of a civil action in federal district court, unless that appeal/civil action is terminated and the application remains pending.
guidance: If an RCE is filed after court review, the examiner should bring the application to the attention of supervisory personnel or quality assurance to determine whether the RCE is proper. Termination of unsuccessful appeal/civil action generally results in abandonment unless allowed claims or the court’s mandate instructs further Office action (see MPEP § 1216.01).

name: Reservation boundaries and enlargement requests
description: State treaty-defined reservation boundaries, record Indian claims/disputes about boundaries, and recommend enlargement to include specific geographic resources (rivers, bends) for wood, water, and arable land.
guidance: Provide geographic detail and justification (e.g., need for wood and arable land) and discuss likely settlement moves by parts of the tribe.

name: Consider claims 'as a whole' (Diehr principle)
description: Under Diehr, claims 'must be considered as a whole' and courts should not 'dissect' claims into new and old elements and ignore the old elements in the eligibility analysis. (Diehr, 450 U.S. at 188.)
guidance: When applying § 101, evaluate the claimed invention in its entirety rather than breaking it into constituent steps and treating some as 'ineligible' and discarding them. The petition criticizes lower courts that analyze individual steps separately instead of the whole-claim perspective.

name: Technical-improvement test from Alice
description: In Alice, the Court said inventions that 'improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'effect an improvement in any other technology or technical field' should be patent-eligible. (Alice, 573 U.S. at 225.)
guidance: Claims that effect a technical improvement to computer functionality or another technical field should be treated as eligible; show how claimed features solve a problem specifically arising in the technical realm and materially improve functioning.

name: DDR test — 'necessarily rooted in computer technology'
description: DDR Holdings articulated that a computer invention is eligible if 'the claimed solution is necessarily rooted in computer technology in order to overcome a problem specifically arising in the realm of computer networks.' (DDR, 773 F.3d at 1255-59.)
guidance: Apply this test to ask whether the claimed solution inherently requires computer technology to solve a computer-specific problem (example: fusing website 'look and feel' with third-party content). The petition notes this test was an early Federal Circuit attempt to cabin eligibility for software claims.

name: Enfish test — 'specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities'
description: Enfish held that eligibility turns on whether 'the focus of the claims is on the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities … or, instead, on a process that qualifies as an 'abstract idea' for which computers are invoked merely as a tool.' (Enfish, 822 F.3d at 1335-36.)
guidance: Use this criterion to distinguish claims that improve computer capabilities (eligible) from those that merely use a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea (ineligible). The petition criticizes this distinction as subjective and panel-dependent in practice.

name: Correct identification of the 'abstract idea' (proper level of abstraction)
description: The 'abstract idea' must be defined at the correct level — neither too broad nor too narrow. The petition criticizes the Federal Circuit for (a) treating concrete computer steps as 'abstract' and (b) failing to recognize the key, technology-specific benefits (e.g., MD functions providing virtually unique identifiers).
guidance: When identifying the purported abstract idea, account for the invention's technical features and benefits (credit what the MD/hash provides) rather than collapsing claims to overly generalized analogies (e.g., library call numbers). Define the abstract idea consistent with Benson/Flook (e.g., the message-digest algorithm itself when that is the mathematical feature).

name: Do not 'read out' ineligible elements at Alice step two
description: It is improper, at step two, to read the elements deemed 'abstract ideas' out of the claim and search for an 'inventive concept' only among the remaining elements; claims must be considered as an 'ordered combination.'
guidance: Evaluate whether an 'inventive concept' exists by considering all claim elements in combination, including those that relate to the judicial exception. The petition identifies cases (e.g., BSG) where courts dissected claims and disregarded ineligible elements, resulting in erroneous invalidations.

name: Integration into specific technical operations ('significantly more')
description: A claim that integrates a mathematical computation into specific, useful computer operations that produce useful results recites 'significantly more' than the algorithm itself (Diehr analogy). Claims that merely claim the algorithm in the abstract are more likely ineligible.
guidance: Show that the mathematical/algorithmic element is tied to concrete implementation steps that effect a technological improvement (examples: using MD values to control authorization, to store/retrieve files, and to deduplicate files). Distinguish from claims that only add 'insignificant pre- or post-solution activity' (Flook).

name: Preemption consideration
description: A claim should not 'wholly preempt' the underlying algorithm; uses of the algorithm outside the specific claimed application should remain open (Flook concern).
guidance: Assess whether the claimed invention precludes all uses of the underlying mathematical tool. If the claim is limited to a specific application or technical environment, preemption concerns are reduced and eligibility support increases.

name: Need for objective, consistent standards (avoid panel-dependent subjectivity)
description: Eligibility jurisprudence should provide predictable, objective standards rather than 'panel-dependent' subjective distinctions that allow similar claims to be alternately held eligible or ineligible based on judicial composition.
guidance: Adopt clear, consistent tests (e.g., affirming 'claims as a whole' approach, clarifying what counts as 'technical improvement') to avoid inconsistent outcomes across panels and cases (examples of contradictory Federal Circuit outcomes are provided).

name: Claims control over Description
description: That where the Description and Claims disagree, the Claims control.
guidance: The claim language governs the patentee's exclusive right even if the description suggests otherwise; however parts shown in the Description to be essential should be understood even if not mentioned in the Claim (see Ex parte Richardson (1875)).

name: Parts shown essential in Description are understood
description: That parts shown in the Description to be essential to the invention must be understood, though not mentioned in the Claim.
guidance: If the specification shows certain parts as essential, they will be treated as such for claim interpretation even if omitted from claim language (Ex parte Richardson).

name: Drawings cannot replace written Description
description: That drawings cannot so far supply the place of a written Description that a Claim can be construed to cover matter shown only in the drawings.
guidance: Matter appearing only in drawings, without adequate written description, will not be treated as part of the claim scope (Gunn v. Savage (1887)).

name: Combinations must be claimed as inventions by themselves
description: A combination is the union of several elements under one co-operative law and must be claimed as an invention by itself, distinct from its elements and from their law of co-operation.
guidance: A combination cannot be adequately protected by claims directed only to individual elements, to all elements collectively under a different co-operative law, or to elements separately considered.

name: New arrangement must be specifically pointed out
description: If the real invention consists only in the new arrangement of an existing combination, the Claim must point out the new arrangement as the limit of its request for protection.
guidance: Failure to point out the special construction or arrangement that constitutes novelty renders the claim too broad (Terry Clock Co. v. New Haven Clock Co.).

name: Non-essential features should not be introduced into combination claims
description: Features not essential to the combination should not be introduced into the Claim.
guidance: Including non-essential elements makes them 'essential' for purposes of the patent and prevents the patentee later asserting they are unnecessary (Rapid Service Store R.R. Co. v. Taylor; Fay v. Cordesman).

name: Exclude unrelated portions of wider art
description: If the new combination forms merely a part of some art or instrument of wider scope, other portions should not be mentioned unless necessary; when necessary, they should be disclaimed.
guidance: Avoid claiming the connecting mechanism to a principal invention unless necessary and coupled with an appropriate disclaimer.

name: Claim invalid if it includes non-coacting element
description: That a Claim including an element not co-acting as part of the combination is invalid.
guidance: Elements that do not participate in the cooperative operation cannot properly be part of a combination claim (Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co.).

name: Combination claim covers only the precise combination claimed
description: A Claim for a combination covers the exact combination claimed and nothing more; it does not protect the elements, their mode of union, or their cooperative law separately considered.
guidance: It does not embrace other unions of the same elements with additional elements or different unions among subsets of those elements.

name: Comprehensive terms ('means','mechanism') are improper in combination claims
description: That 'means,' 'mechanism,' and similar comprehensive terms are not proper in Claims for combinations for the purpose of pointing out the invention.
guidance: Such broad catch-alls fail to identify the invention's inventive elements (Ex parte Paige; Ex parte Wilkin).

name: Words like 'substantially as described' are limiting
description: That a Claim for 'substantially as described' will be limited to the elements described as composing it.
guidance: Phrases of generality do not enlarge a claim beyond the elements and mode of union set forth in the Description (Hailes v. Van Wormer).

name: Omitted elements are excluded from the claimed combination
description: That elements omitted from the Claim are thereby excluded from the combination.
guidance: Unclaimed elements of a described combination are thereby typically conceded to be old as to that patent, though they may be reserved for later patents (Bowell v. Lindsay; Conover v. Roach).

name: Claim for combination can be joined with claims for elements/sub-combinations
description: The specification of a combination may contain several different Claims: besides the Claim for the combination as a whole, each of its elements and sub-combinations, if new and patentable, may also be claimed.
guidance: But claims for the same element performing different functions or for different combinations of the same elements cannot be inserted unless joinder rules permit (Pattee v. Moline Plow Co.; Ex parte Shepard).

name: Claims that make non-essential elements essential bind patentee
description: That a Claim including non-essential elements makes them essential, and the patentee cannot afterwards assert they are unnecessary.
guidance: Draft carefully: including extra elements in a claim may change scope irrevocably (Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co.; Boyer v. Schultz Belting Co.).

name: Claims for elements may be separately asserted though only useful in combination
description: That the elements, if new, may be separately claimed even though useless out of the combination.
guidance: Separate claims for new elements or sub-combinations are permitted when they are independently patentable (Stevens v. Pritchard; Henderson v. Cleveland Co-operative Stove Co.).

name: Different combinations of the same elements cannot be covered by one patent
description: Different combinations of the same elements (particularly when performing different functions) cannot be covered by a single patent.
guidance: You cannot claim multiple distinct combinations of the same components in one patent application (Ex parte Shepard; Ex parte Wheat).

name: Form flexibility of combination Claims
description: Any form of words may be employed in a Claim for a combination provided it accurately describes the real invention; enumerating elements and stating their method of combination is perfect but not always possible.
guidance: If inventor lacks full understanding of modes of union, it suffices that he combined elements and produced a new operative means and that language makes invention intelligible to public so they can practise it and perceive claim limits (§526b).

name: Means claims limited to particular arrangement, not to function
description: The means alone are claimed, and claimed only when specially arranged to produce a given result; this is far from claiming a function.
guidance: Claims directed to mere functions or results (without structural limitation) are improper; the specific means arranged to produce the effect must be described (Silsby v. Foote).

name: Process claims cover all ways of practicing the art if stated generally
description: An art covers all ways of practising it, and if its elements possess equivalents, a general Claim may cover it under every form; a specific Claim will cover the method as described.
guidance: A general process claim is broad; specific method claims protect particular implementations (Tilghman v. Proctor).

name: Machine must be claimed as a specific piece of mechanism
description: A machine must be claimed as a specific piece of mechanism, not as a mode of operation, a principle, an idea, a means of producing an effect, or an effect produced.
guidance: New machine parts must be clearly pointed out and claimed; unclaimed or un-invented parts should not be mentioned or must be disclaimed. 'Means of doing' phrasing is improper (Ex parte Bates; Hatch v. Moffitt).

name: In a machine patent, do not claim the mode of operation
description: That in a machine patent a Claim for the 'mode of operation' is void.
guidance: Claims should describe structural elements; asserting 'mode of operation' without structure will not sustain validity (Hatch v. Moffitt).

name: Manufacture must be claimed as a new product distinct from process
description: A manufacture must be claimed as a new product, apart from any Claim for the process of making it or for the purpose for which it is employed.
guidance: If product is new, enumerate essential qualities. If character depends on method of production, claim it only as produced by that specific process. 'Article of manufacture' has no special claim significance.

name: Claim for a manufacture should not set forth the process
description: That a Claim for the manufacture should not explain nor set forth the process by which it is made.
guidance: Claims for the product should focus on product qualities; process descriptions belong in the specification and separate process claims if appropriate (Ex parte Shalters; Ex parte Cobb).

name: Single composition requires single Claim and must enumerate ingredients
description: A single composition of matter requires only a single Claim, set forth by enumerating its elements and stating the mode of their union and the essential qualities of the resulting composition.
guidance: If the composition consists of well-known ingredients, the Claim should enumerate them; if proportions/mode not stated, those in the Description are presumed.

name: Composition claims cover only same use of same or equivalent ingredients
description: A Claim for a chemical composition covers only the same use of the same or equivalent chemical ingredients.
guidance: Claims to compositions are limited in scope to the uses and ingredient equivalents described (Goodyear v. Berry).

name: Design Claim must be specific and confined to ornamentation
description: A Claim for a design must be as distinct and specific as any other Claim and should mention nothing beyond the configuration or ornamentation constituting the invention.
guidance: Do not include qualities of the material or mechanical functions; Claims may be verbal descriptions or references to drawings and should contain 'as shown and described' to limit scope.

name: Improvement claims must distinguish new from old
description: An improvement is essentially distinct from the original art or instrument and a Claim for an improvement must define the improvement and fully and accurately distinguish it from the old invention.
guidance: Claims should confine themselves entirely to the characteristics of the improvement, embracing nothing not necessarily connected; if original features are mentioned they must be clearly not claimed as new (Ex parte McMurray; Whitemore v. Cutter).

name: Acquiescence limited by scope and notice of claimed invention (reissues/new claims)
description: Acquiescence in an original patent avails the plaintiff on a re-issue only for the same precise invention; a re-issue containing claims not in the original patent is treated as a new patent for purposes of acquiescence and public acceptance.
guidance: If the public had no notice of the new claim in the reissue, prior acquiescence in the original patent cannot be construed as acquiescence to the new claims. Cases: Irwin v. McRoberts; commentary on reissues.

name: Sources excluded from assessment of added matter
description: A first country application or a prior-filed application forming the basis of a priority claim shall not be used as the basis of assessment in addition of new matter; an abstract shall not be included in the specification or drawing(s) which forms the basis of assessment.
guidance: Do not treat priority applications or abstracts as part of the original disclosure when assessing new matter.

name: Narrowing claim from genus to species
description: Where an amendment narrows a claim from a genus to a species, it introduces new matter unless the species is supported by the original specification/drawings or one skilled in the art would readily recognize the species from the genus at the time of filing.
guidance: Example: changing 'transparent plastic plate' to 'transparent ABS plastic plate' introduces new matter unless ABS is disclosed or obvious to the skilled person. Example2: changing 'sensor detecting rotation' to 'proximity sensor' is allowable if a skilled person would intuitively associate the sensor with a proximity sensor.

name: Broadening claim from species to genus
description: Broadening a claim from a species to a genus constitutes introduction of new matter if the genus encompasses other species than the species disclosed in the original specification and those other species may have different functions/effects in addressing the problem.
guidance: Also, deleting limitations described as essential for solving a problem is introduction of new matter; deleting arbitrarily added limitations unrelated to solving the problem may be allowable. Examples: connector shape amendment and traffic-control method example showing when deletion is allowable.

name: Negative limitations (deleting elements)
description: Amendment to delete elements from the claims ('negative limitations') is permitted provided the deletion does not introduce any new technical matter not disclosed in the original specification.
guidance: Example: excluding humans from 'treatment methods for mammals' is permissible where the original disclosure indicates not directed only to particular animals.

name: Permissible categories of claim amendments under Article 47(3)
description: An amendment to claims in response to a rejection necessitated by a previous amendment or upon a request for reexamination shall be one of: narrowing of claims by restricting claims, correction of clerical errors, clarification of ambiguous descriptions, or deletion of new matter.
guidance: Article 47(3) requirements apply only to the amended claims; if an independent claim is amended, dependent claims referring to it are deemed amended.

name: How to determine correspondence to Article 47(3)
description: Whether an amendment corresponds to allowable cases shall be determined by comparing the claim under examination (upon notice of final rejection) with the claim having the same claim number; if a claim after amendment is clearly the same as the amended claim with a different number, assess by comparison with the claim of the different number.
guidance: Even a one-word amendment may be legitimate if it falls under the subparagraphs of Article 47(3); when one claim contains multiple inventions they are assessed individually.

name: Fairness note on partial vs whole-claim amendments
description: Determining whether an amendment meets requirements based on the amended term or phrase may raise fairness issues between an amendment of a whole claim (re-describing the invention) and an amendment to parts of the claim; Article 47(3) is not intended to substantially restrict amendment contents but to prevent examination difficulties caused by excessive amendments.
guidance: Examiner should be mindful of fairness and the statutory intent when applying Article 47(3).

name: Types of narrowing under Article 47(3)(i)
description: Restricting a claim includes internal restriction of the scope recited in the original claim, such as reduction of numerical range, change from genus to species, deletion of alternatively recited elements, and reduction of a referred claim from claims referring to multiple claims.
guidance: Reduction of numerical range means reducing within the original claim's range (simultaneous reduction and extension does not count as reduction). Deleting 'A or B' to remove one alternative is legitimate restriction.

name: Narrowing by adding technical features
description: The scope of an invention is narrowed by adding new technical features described in the description or claims (e.g., changing 'B attached to A' to 'B attached to A and then C attached to B').
guidance: Adding features that are supported by the original description is a legitimate narrowing amendment under 47(3).

name: Cases not falling under Article 47(3)(i)
description: An amendment that newly adds a claim or adds an invention to claims by adding alternative elements or adding a referred claim does not fall under Article 47(3)(i). Inevitable additions resulting from reorganization of claims are exempted.
guidance: Example given where reorganization of claim numbering leads to an unavoidable new claim.

name: Examples of amendments that go beyond the original scope
description: Examples include: change from species to genus; deletion of elements from a set; addition and deletion of elements in a set (changing elements present); broadening of numerical range; replacement of element (bolt to rivet); change of numerical range to a non-overlapping range.
guidance: These are explicitly listed as amendments that take claims beyond original scope and thereby are not allowable as mere 'restriction' under Article 47(3).

name: Clarification of ambiguous description
description: An ambiguous description is one whose meaning in context is not clear; includes unclear claim language, mismatch between a claim element and other descriptions, or claims technically unspecified and ambiguous despite clear claim language.
guidance: Redrafting the overall claim without substantial changes is deemed clarification under Article 47(3)(iii), unless other specific conditions exist.

name: Definition of 'new rejection necessitated by the amendment'
description: 'New rejection necessitated by the amendment' means a ground for rejection which did not exist prior to the amendment but newly arises due to the amendment (e.g., claim rendered indefinite or new lack of novelty/inventive step).
guidance: Rejection grounds present before the amendment but not notified are not considered 'new' for these purposes.

name: Cautions when making a decision to refuse to enter amendments
description: When an amendment contains multiple amended matters, all amended matters must be assessed individually; if any amended matter violates Article 47(2) or (3) or results in a new rejection (except deletion of claim), the whole amendment shall be refused to be entered. The unit of refusal is determined by submitted forms identifying subject matter.
guidance: When multiple amendments are filed during the response period, refusal is determined per amendment; for applications filed on/after July 1, 2013, earlier amendments are deemed withdrawn and assessment is based on the last-filed amendment. Also: when decisions have been revoked on appeal and remanded, the examiner is bound by the appeal's findings.

name: Collateral estoppel requires claims to be 'materially the same' and identity of issues
description: Collateral estoppel may bar asserting claims materially the same as those held unpatentable in IPR/reexamination if ordinary issue-preclusion elements are met; differences in claim limitations or differing claim construction standards can prevent estoppel.
guidance: Court denied estoppel for most asserted claims because they included additional limitations distinguishing them from PTAB-held claims; but where an asserted claim recited the same features as a PTAB-unpatentable claim, estoppel applied (XR Commc’ns v. D-Link).

name: Dependent claims can survive estoppel applied to parent independent claims
description: A plaintiff asserting dependent claims that add limitations to an independent claim held unpatentable in IPR may nevertheless be allowed to argue lack of the limitation in prior art because PTAB's lower standard may not preclude differing district-court outcomes for dependent claims.
guidance: Court denied motion to estop plaintiff from arguing that prior art lacked a limitation for dependent claims even though independent claims were held unpatentable in IPR (IOENGINE LLC v. PayPal).

name: Form paragraph bracket insertion instructions
description: In bracket 3, insert the number of the reference application. In bracket 4, insert a description of the subject matter being claimed which is covered in the reference application.
guidance: Follow the prescribed form paragraph formatting: include the reference application number and a clear description of the overlapping subject matter.

name: Terminal disclaimer guidance & earlier-filed determination
description: See MPEP §1490 for guidance regarding terminal disclaimers and withdrawal of nonstatutory double patenting rejections when these are the only rejections remaining. Note especially that priority or benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a) and (e) are not taken into account in determining which is the earlier-filed application for double patenting purposes.
guidance: Consult MPEP §1490 for form and treatment of terminal disclaimers; when determining earlier-filed application for double patenting, do not factor priority/benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)/(e).

name: Claim-to-claim comparison requirement for double patenting
description: A double patenting rejection must rely on a comparison with the claims in an issued patent or pending application, whereas an anticipation or obviousness rejection based on the same patent or application under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 relies on a comparison with what is disclosed (whether or not claimed) in the same issued patent or pending application.
guidance: For double patenting, analyze only the claim scope of the reference; for 102/103, analyze the full disclosure of the reference. Do not conflate the two analyses.

name: Pre-AIA 103(c) disqualification effects
description: For pre-AIA applications (certain filing/pending dates): a commonly assigned/owned patent or application may be disqualified as pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) prior art in a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection under 103(c).
guidance: If a reference is disqualified under pre-AIA 103(c), do not make or maintain 102(e)/103(a) rejections based on that disqualified prior art; nonetheless, the same reference may still support a double patenting rejection (claims-to-claims). See MPEP §2146 et seq.

name: Situations where 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition does not apply — withdrawal subject to allowance of linking claims (C)
description: The restriction requirement was withdrawn because the requirement was written in a manner which made it clear to applicant that the requirement was made subject to the non-allowance of generic or other linking claims and such generic or linking claims are subsequently allowed.
guidance: If the requirement was explicitly conditional and later the linking/generic claims are allowed, the original restriction effectively disappears and 121 protection may not apply in the same way; examine the withdrawal circumstances.

name: Terminal disclaimer procedural & legal effects
description: A terminal disclaimer is a statement filed by an owner that disclaims or dedicates a portion of the entire term of all the claims of a patent; filing a terminal disclaimer to obviate a nonstatutory double patenting rejection is not an admission of the propriety of the rejection.
guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.321 for formal requirements; a terminal disclaimer removes the double patenting rejection statutory effect but does not create a presumption on merits. Ensure any terminal disclaimer extends to continuations if intended; include unenforceability clause if ownership ceases as required.

name: Terminal disclaimer unenforceability provision and JRA-specific requirements
description: Terminal disclaimers that overcome nonstatutory double patenting must include provisions (per 37 CFR 1.321) that the patent shall be unenforceable if it ceases to be commonly owned with the referenced application/patent; 1.321(d) sets requirements where the claimed invention resulted from activities within a joint research agreement.
guidance: Ensure terminal disclaimers contain the enforceability clause and comply with special JRA rules in 1.321(d) when applicable; sample forms and further guidance are in MPEP §1490.

name: Limitations on use of 37 CFR 1.131 / 1.132 affidavits
description: The use of a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit in overcoming a statutory double patenting rejection or a double patenting rejection is inappropriate where the application is being rejected over a patent which claims the rejected invention; 37 CFR 1.132 may be used to show derivation in some circumstances.
guidance: Do not accept 1.131(a) affidavits as a substitute for addressing double patenting where claims are directed to substantially the same invention; consider 1.132 derivation showings where relevant and per MPEP §§715, 716.10, 718 guidance.

name: Distinctness definition under 35 U.S.C. 101 and effect on double patenting
description: 35 U.S.C. 101 prevents two patents from issuing on the same invention; 'same invention' means identical subject matter. Claims that differ (aside from minor wording differences) are not considered to be drawn to the same invention for double patenting purposes under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Use the statutory double patenting standard (identical subject matter) for 101 rejections; if claims are different though obvious variants, terminal disclaimers may be effective to overcome nonstatutory double patenting rejections.

name: Effect of disclaimer in reference patent on propriety of later rejection
description: A disclaimer filed in a reference patent that disclaims the earlier patentably indistinct claim(s) would have no impact on whether a nonstatutory double patenting rejection is proper in a patent that has, or an application for a patent that would have, a later expiration date.
guidance: Do not consider a disclaimer in a reference patent as automatically negating a double patenting rejection in a later application; evaluate claim overlap and terminal disclaimer requirements separately.

name: Reference claims may form basis for double patenting even if subject matter excepted as prior art
description: The claims of a reference excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) may still be the basis for a double patenting rejection, whether statutory or nonstatutory.
guidance: Even when disclosure is excepted from being prior art, perform a claims-to-claims analysis to determine whether the reference's claims create double patenting issues; do not assume exception eliminates double patenting concerns.

name: Novelty (absolute newness)
description: An invention is patentable only if it is novel; an invention lacks novelty if all of its essential features are disclosed in a single piece of prior art information forming part of the prior art base before the priority date (Sections 7(1) and 18(1)(b) of the Patents Act 1990 (Cth)).
guidance: Novelty is assessed claim-by-claim and focuses on what the claim requires, not the general idea. The prior art base is broad (any information publicly available anywhere by written publication, oral disclosure, use or other act). Establishing novelty often involves amending claims to more precisely define and distinguish the invention from known material.

name: Anticipation / 'reverse infringement' test
description: Novelty (anticipation) is assessed by asking whether carrying out what is disclosed in a prior art disclosure would necessarily fall within the scope of the claim (the 'reverse infringement' principle as in General Tire & Rubber Co v Firestone).
guidance: Anticipation requires more than resemblance or overlap; the prior art must disclose all essential features of the claim in a clear, unequivocal and complete manner. Case law (Nicaro Holdings v Martin Engineering; Asahi Kasei) emphasises reading the disclosure through the eyes of the person skilled in the art and whether the disclosure enables putting the invention into practice. Ambiguous, incomplete or requiring further invention disclosures do not necessarily destroy novelty.

name: Whole of contents novelty (earlier Australian filings)
description: Australian 'whole of contents' provision allows novelty to be objected to based on the information contained in earlier Australian patent applications, even if those earlier applications were not published at the relevant priority date.
guidance: This provision aims to prevent two patents for the same invention. It operates strictly for novelty (not for inventive step). When raised, detailed analysis and careful comparison of disclosures and claim scope is required, as minor differences can be decisive.

name: Cripps question / 'led as a matter of course' test
description: A guiding test for inventive step (from Aktiebolaget Hässle v Alphapharm): would a skilled person, faced with the problem the invention solves, have been 'led directly as a matter of course to try the claimed invention in the expectation that it might well produce a solution'?
guidance: This is not a hindsight 'obvious to try' test; it asks whether the path to the invention was straightforward and predictable. Demonstrating that the invention was not a predictable routine choice supports inventive step.

name: Claim drafting and disclosure management as strategic tools
description: Effective patent protection depends on disciplined disclosure management and precise claim drafting to navigate novelty and inventive step objections.
guidance: When faced with objections, amend and refine claims to distinguish over prior art, frame the technical problem and advantages clearly, and use evidence and secondary indicators where available. Seek professional advice to turn examination objections into opportunities to strengthen the application.

name: Distinction and interplay between novelty and inventive step
description: Novelty and inventive step are distinct but complementary legal gates: novelty asks whether the claimed subject-matter is absolutely new; inventive step asks whether it would have been obvious to the skilled person.
guidance: Failure on either ground is fatal to patentability. Legal strategy must address both: securing clear differences from single-piece disclosures for novelty, and demonstrating non-obviousness (including via combinations, skilled person analysis, Cripps question and secondary indicators) for inventive step.

name: Omitted Inventor and Correction of Errors in Inventorship
description: If through error a person is named as inventor or an inventor is omitted, the Director may permit the application to be amended accordingly under terms he prescribes (35 U.S.C. 116, pre‑AIA).
guidance: If a joint inventor refuses to join or cannot be reached after diligent effort, the other inventor(s) may file on behalf of both and the Director, on proof and after prescribed notice, may grant a patent subject to the omitted inventor's rights; the omitted inventor may later join. Applicants are responsible for correcting inventorship in compliance with 37 CFR 1.48 when claims are amended to change inventorship. 37 CFR 1.48 permits correction where the correct inventor(s) were disclosed in the application as filed.

name: Required elements of a proper RCE
description: A proper RCE must be accompanied by the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(e) and include a submission as required by 37 CFR 1.114. The submission may include an information disclosure statement (IDS), an amendment to the written description, claims, or drawings, new arguments, or new evidence in support of patentability.
guidance: For an RCE to be 'proper' the submission should be responsive (within meaning of 37 CFR 1.111) to the last outstanding Office action. If the submission is not fully responsive but is a bona fide attempt to provide a complete reply, the applicant should be notified of deficiencies and given a new time period to complete the reply (use form paragraph 7.42.08).

name: RCE filed after a Board decision but before further appeal or civil action — timeliness and limitations
description: An RCE filed after a PTAB decision but before filing a Notice of Appeal to the Federal Circuit or commencement of a civil action will withdraw finality and reopen prosecution if timely filed; generally the deadline to file a notice of appeal to the Federal Circuit is sixty-three (63) days after the final Board decision.
guidance: An RCE filed within the 63-day period and before filing of a notice of appeal is timely. Note the res judicata effect of a Board decision: a Board decision is the 'law of the case' and is controlling in that application and related applications. A submission containing arguments without amendment of rejected claims or a showing of facts will not be effective to remove new grounds of rejection entered by the Board.

name: RCE availability relative to Federal Circuit appeal or civil action
description: The procedure under 37 CFR 1.114 is not available in an application after the filing of a Notice of Appeal to the Federal Circuit or commencement of a civil action in federal district court, unless the appeal or civil action is terminated and the application is still pending.
