guidance: If an RCE is filed in an application that has undergone court review, the examiner should bring the application to a supervisory patent examiner or quality assurance specialist to determine propriety. Unless the application contains allowed claims (or the court's mandate indicates further action), the termination of an unsuccessful appeal or civil action results in abandonment of the application. See MPEP § 1216.01.

name: Forms and form paragraphs to be used for RCE notices and transmittals
description: Form PTO/SB/30, 'Request for Continued Examination (RCE) Transmittal,' may be used by applicant. The Office uses form paragraphs 7.42.05–7.42.16 for various notices regarding RCEs; the Notice of Improper Request for Continued Examination (RCE), Form PTO-2051, is used by technical support personnel to notify applicant that continued examination does not apply.
guidance: Use the specified form paragraphs according to the factual situation (e.g., 7.42.05 for RCE after payment of issue fee with petition granted; 7.42.06 after appeal but before Board decision where RCE is proper; 7.42.07 after Board decision; 7.42.10–7.42.14 for specific situations when appeal withdrawn and claims allowed/abandoned; 7.42.16 for improper RCE after Board decision). Use PTOL-90 where appropriate to preserve time for court review.

name: Revival petition fee
description: On filing each petition for the revival of an abandoned application, delayed payment of issuance fee, delayed response in reexamination, delayed maintenance payment, delayed submission of priority/benefit claim, or extension of the 12-month period for filing a subsequent application, $1,700.
guidance: The Director may refund any part of this fee in exceptional circumstances as determined by the Director.

name: Claim interpretation (broadest reasonable interpretation)
description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation, the terms of the claim are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art. MPEP 2111.
guidance: No limitations can be disregarded; a wherein clause still may have patentable weight. Use the specification to determine what the claim language encompasses when applying eligibility analyses (e.g., whether a functional wherein clause imposes structural limitation).

name: Process claims: general rule for nature-based product limitations
description: For a process claim, the general rule is that the claim is not subject to the markedly different analysis for nature-based products used in the process. MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)(C).
guidance: Exception exists where a process claim is drafted such that it is no different in substance than a product claim; only then might the markedly different analysis be applied. Otherwise, do not treat nature-based product limitations in process claims as automatically 'reciting' products of nature for eligibility analysis.

name: Particular-machine consideration (three-factor test)
description: Evaluate whether a recited machine is a 'particular machine' using the three factors set forth in MPEP 2106.05(b).
guidance: Factors include whether the machine is recited at a high level of generality or as a particular machine with specific components, and whether the machine is an integral part of the claim (more than a field-of-use or insignificant limitation). If it is a particular machine that applies or uses the exception in a meaningful way, it can integrate the exception into a practical application (example: delivery device with reservoir, valve, needle assembly).

name: Step 2B — Whether claim amounts to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited exception, i.e., whether any additional element, or combination of additional elements, adds an inventive concept to the claim. MPEP 2106.05.
guidance: Assess whether additional elements are sufficient to transform the claim into eligible subject matter. Mere instructions to apply an exception (e.g., a generic container or 'apply it') cannot provide an inventive concept. Cite MPEP 2106.05 and case law as appropriate.

name: Mixtures and multi-component nature-based products — resultant combination analysis
description: When the claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components, the markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied to the resultant nature-based combination rather than its component parts. MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)(A).
guidance: If the components do not occur together in nature and the claimed combination exhibits a changed functional property (e.g., changed glycemic control profile), the combination may have markedly different characteristics and therefore not be a product-of-nature exception. Compare the resultant mixture to its natural counterpart(s) or components as appropriate (examples: denveric acid + protamine resulting in different onset/ duration).

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception — anti-pattern
description: Mere instructions to apply an exception (for example, adding a generic 'container' or the words 'apply it') cannot provide an inventive concept and thus do not make a claim 'significantly more.'
guidance: When additional limitations are generic or amount to nothing more than 'apply it,' the claim fails Step 2B. Examiners should explain why a limitation is merely an instruction to apply the exception and may cite MPEP 2106.05(f) and relevant case law (e.g., Roslin, Myriad) in the rejection.

name: Practice note — compact prosecution and other statutory requirements
description: Although a claim may be eligible under subject-matter eligibility analysis, it may be unpatentable for other reasons; examiners should practice compact prosecution by examining each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application.
guidance: Evaluate prior art anticipation and obviousness (including applicant-admitted prior art), indefiniteness, written description, and whether functional genus claims are supported by correlation between structure and function. Cite MPEP 2129(I), 2173.05(g), 2163(II)(A)(3)(a) as relevant.

name: Practice note — Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) vs Full analysis (Pathway B)
description: For examination efficiency, examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident; if the claim is a 'close call,' perform a full analysis (Pathway B). MPEP 2106.06.
guidance: Examples of claims suitable for Pathway A include claims that clearly are not attempts to tie up a natural product (e.g., wearable delivery device with detailed components). If the eligibility outcome is not self-evident, perform the full Step 2A/2B analysis.

name: Rejection drafting guidance for nature-based product claims
description: A rejection should identify the exception by pointing to the nature-based product in the claim (e.g., denveric acid) and explain why it is a product-of-nature exception, and explain why the claim as a whole does not integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Explain the marked-difference comparison and why additional limitations are insufficient (e.g., generic container). If helpful, cite court decisions (e.g., Roslin, Myriad, Funk Brothers) and MPEP sections (e.g., 2106.05(f)) to support the reasoning.

name: Correctness and sufficiency of patentability determinations
description: When rejecting a claim, to meet the Office’s burden of establishing unpatentability, the patentability determination must be correct and must, at a minimum, (1) identify the claim and relevant statute, and (2) set forth sufficient evidence to put a person skilled in the art on notice as to why the claim is unpatentable so as to provide applicant with a fair opportunity to respond.
guidance: Sufficiency is considered in the context of the entire prosecution history, including examiner explanations. Correctness is evaluated based on whether determinations were reasonable (not reviewer hindsight or what the reviewer would have done).

name: 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection compliance — identify claim/statute and sufficiency
description: If a 102 rejection is made, determine whether all 35 USC 102 rejection(s) in the Office action are in compliance (Yes/No). Compliance requires properly identifying the claim(s), the statute (including subparagraphs) and being supported by sufficient evidence to support anticipation of the claim(s) by the applied disclosure.
guidance: Consult statutory compliance scenarios for assistance in determining compliance. If compliant, proceed to accolade/characteristics questions; if noncompliant, document details in following questions.

name: Check for alternate compliant prior art rejection when 102 noncompliant
description: For claims with a noncompliant 102 rejection, determine whether another compliant prior art rejection (either under 102 or 103) was applied to those claims.
guidance: If every claim listed as noncompliant under 102 also has another compliant prior art rejection, answer Yes; otherwise No. If Yes, indicate whether the compliant prior art rejection was applied under 102 and/or 103.

name: 102 noncompliance reason — failure to properly identify claims/statute
description: The rejection does not properly identify the rejected claim(s) and/or identify the correct statute/subparagraph.
guidance: Do NOT use this box when the reviewer concludes the reference fails to anticipate claims (that is lack of evidence — use the insufficient evidence box). Use this when the claim listing or statutory subparagraph applied is incorrect. Explain specifically how claims/statute identification is deficient; avoid rhetorical or personalized language.

name: 102 noncompliance reason — insufficient evidence to demonstrate anticipation under BRI
description: The rejection does not provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the disclosure teaches every element required by the claim under its Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI).
guidance: If this is checked, at least one of two subboxes must be checked: (1) no citation(s)/mapping to the prior art for the missing element(s), or (2) mapping provided but the relevant portion does not provide sufficient evidence to meet the limitation(s). For each claim and limitation identified, explain how the reference fails to meet the limitation and why the applied interpretation is inappropriate.

name: Mapping provided but relevant portions insufficient (102)
description: The rejection maps the limitation(s) to the prior art, but the relevant portion(s) do not provide sufficient evidence to meet the limitation(s).
guidance: Indicate which portions were mapped and why they are insufficient to support anticipation (technical/claim construction reasons).

name: Additional noncompliance/quality flags for 102 rejections
description: Check applicable issues contributing to noncompliance: (a) rejection included obviousness rationale; (b) improper reliance on features from different embodiments; (c) improper reliance on inherency; (d) non-compliance due to unreasonable claim interpretation; (e) part of a combined 102/103 rejection; (f) none of the above.
guidance: For each box checked, include an explanation in the corresponding comment box that supports the selection. Do not guess root causes.

name: Characteristics of 102 rejections — claim grouping and claim lumping
description: The rejection addresses substantially all claims individually and only groups together claims that are of substantially similar scope (limited claim lumping).
guidance: Check this when the rejection treats claims individually where necessary and groups only similar claims; avoids overbroad lumping that hides differences between claims.

name: Characteristics of 102 rejections — explains how/why limitations are met or equates terminology
description: The rejection goes beyond pinpointing where the limitations are taught by summarizing how/why the limitations are met by the prior art or reciting terminology from the prior art to equate with terminology from the claims.
guidance: If this is checked, the 'reasonably pinpoints' characteristic should also be checked. This indicates the rejection provides explanatory analysis, not merely mapping.

name: Characteristics of 102 rejections — statements of patentable weight
description: The rejection includes statements of patentable weight, particularly when patentable weight is not being given to intended use limitations, preambles, or claim language that suggests optional structure or steps.
guidance: Note when the examiner assigns patentable weight to elements that may not warrant it; document such interpretive choices.

name: Characteristics of 102 rejections — claim interpretation stated
description: The rejection sets forth a claim interpretation that points out how the examiner is interpreting the claim/term/phrase for purposes of the rejection (e.g., BRI, special definitions).
guidance: Check when the rejection explicitly states an interpretation; this helps reviewers assess reasonableness of the construction applied.

name: Characteristics of 102 rejections — includes suggestions to overcome rejections
description: The Office action included appropriate suggestions to overcome rejection(s) (not general 'FP' language or merely indicating claims with allowable subject matter).
guidance: Suggestions should be substantive and actionable rather than generic; note when included.

name: Prima facie case requirement for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
description: To support an obviousness conclusion, the rejection should articulate a prima facie case: findings of fact supported by sufficient evidence in the prior art; articulate how the prior art is to be modified to arrive at the claimed invention; provide a convincing line of reasoning taught by the prior art or provided by the examiner.
guidance: Reasoning/rationale should be taught by applied art or be provided by examiner and form a convincing line of reasoning as to why the artisan would have found the claimed invention obvious.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection compliance — identify claim/statute and sufficiency
description: If a 103 rejection is made, determine whether all 35 USC 103 rejection(s) in the Office action are in compliance (Yes/No). Compliance requires properly identifying the claim(s), the statute (including subparagraphs) and being supported by sufficient evidence to support the conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: Use statutory compliance standard and scenarios for guidance. If noncompliant, proceed to identify claims and reasons.

name: Check for alternate compliant prior art rejection when 103 noncompliant
description: For claims with a noncompliant 103 rejection, determine whether another compliant prior art rejection (either under 102 or 103) was applied to those claims.
guidance: If every claim listed as noncompliant under 103 also has another compliant prior art rejection, answer Yes; otherwise No. Indicate whether the compliant prior art rejection(s) was applied under 102 and/or 103.

name: 103 noncompliance reason — failure to properly identify claims/statute
description: The rejection does not properly identify the rejected claim(s) and/or identify the correct statute/subparagraph for the 103 rejection.
guidance: Use when claim listing or statute identification is incorrect; do not use if the issue is lack of evidentiary support (use the insufficient evidence box).

name: 112(f) three-prong analysis for invocation
description: As the reviewer, perform the three-prong analysis (MPEP 2181(I)) to determine whether any claim limitations invoke 112(f) (Yes/No).
guidance: Base this on the reviewer's independent application of the three-prong test; identify specific limitations invoking 112(f) in comments if not documented by the examiner.

name: Office action typographical/grammatical quality
description: Assess whether the Office action is generally free from typographical/grammatical errors (Yes/No).
guidance: Answer No if situations occur such as: rejection addresses a specific claim in the body but that claim not listed in the statement; a cancelled claim is included in the statement of rejection; AIA 103 references 'time the invention was made' instead of effective filing; substantive copy/paste errors; typographical errors in reference numbers or inventor names; references mentioned in body but not included in statement of rejection, etc. Provide examples in comments.

name: Proposed back-up prior art rejection
description: Determine whether the reviewer proposes any back-up prior art rejection(s) for claims that already have a compliant prior art rejection (Yes/No).
guidance: Use only in rare situations where a back-up rejection provides meaningful protection against easily-invoked exceptions; the back-up must be a complete rejection fully explained. Do not use to propose general additional rejections; if no compliant prior art rejection exists, raise as an omitted rejection instead.

name: Examiners' Step 2A Prong One identification procedure
description: Examiners should (1) identify the specific claim limitation(s) that the examiner believes recite an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated abstract-idea groupings.
guidance: If the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea at Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional claim elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (MPEP §2106.04(d)). If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the eligibility analysis at Step 2A Prong One ends (Pathway B), unless the claim recites another judicial exception (law of nature or natural phenomenon). Examiners should identify at least one grouping, and preferably all applicable groupings, if a limitation falls into multiple groupings.

name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting examples)
description: Certain claims do not recite an abstract idea even if they are based on or involve an abstract idea; such claims are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B).
guidance: Non-limiting hypothetical examples provided: i) a printer with belt, roller, printhead and ink cartridge; ii) a washing machine with tub, drive motor, controller, housing; iii) an earring sensor for blood glucose with memory; iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences via PCR and sequencing; v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer from remote memory; vi) a method of rearranging GUI icons based on usage metrics tracked via processor memory allocation; vii) a method of training a neural network with staged training sets and transformations. The Step 2A Prong One analysis requires a claim to 'recite' (set forth or describe) an abstract idea before proceeding to Prong Two; mere involvement or basis on an abstract idea is not sufficient to find the claim recites an abstract idea.

name: Handling claims that implicate multiple judicial-exception groupings
description: Claims can recite limitations that fall within more than one abstract-idea grouping or sub-grouping.
guidance: When claim limitations fall within multiple groupings, examiners should identify at least one grouping and preferably identify all applicable groupings before proceeding with the Step 2A Prong Two analysis. Example: performing mathematical calculations using a formula that could also be performed in the human mind may fall within both the 'mathematical concepts' and 'mental process' groupings.

name: Claims reciting other judicial exceptions (laws of nature/natural phenomena)
description: If a claim recites another judicial exception (e.g., a law of nature or a natural phenomenon), the examiner should consult the relevant MPEP sections for Step 2A analysis.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2106.04(b) and 2106.04(c) for guidance on claims that recite laws of nature or natural phenomena. The abstract-idea grouping analysis is specific to the abstract-idea judicial exception; other exceptions require their own analysis.

name: Treatment of federal court decisions known at time of determination
description: If a federal court decision on the merits of a patent is known to the examiner at the time the determination on the request for inter partes reexamination is made, the existence of a final court decision does not necessarily preclude a question of patentability because the Office uses different standards of proof and claim interpretation.
guidance: The Office may accord deference to factual findings made by the court, but the determination of whether a basis for reexamination exists will be made independently of the court’s decision. Non-final holdings of invalidity or unenforceability are not controlling; only a final holding after all appeals is controlling (see In re Zletz; In re Etter; In re Swanson).

name: Examiner's three-question test when requester was a party to litigation
description: When the examiner is aware that the third party requester was a party to previous federal court litigation as to the patent, the examiner must determine: (1) Was the federal court decision adverse to the third party requester as to at least one claim of the patent? (2) Was the federal court decision a final decision, after all appeals? (3) Is the issue being raised in the reexamination request the same issue as was raised in the federal court during the civil action, or an issue that the third party requester could have raised in the federal court during the civil action?
guidance: If (1)-(3) are all yes for one or more (but not all) claims, those claims will not be treated and the examiner’s action will point out the claims not treated and the reason why. If (1) or (3) is no for all claims, examination proceeds without discussion of these considerations. If (1) and (3) are yes but (2) is no for a claim, examination proceeds using guidance for non-party situations, but the examiner’s action will discuss considerations (1)-(3). If the examiner later learns the decision is final and all three are yes for all claims, notify SPRS who will contact OPLA for guidance.

name: Effect of a final holding of claim invalidity by a court
description: A final holding of claim invalidity or unenforceability (after all appeals) is controlling on the Office.
guidance: In such cases, a substantial new question of patentability or reasonable likelihood of prevailing would not be present as to the claims held invalid or unenforceable. Where all claims for which reexamination was requested are affected, the reexamination will be vacated/terminated by the CRU Director. Use form paragraph 26.80 at the beginning of the Office action for claims held invalid by the court.

name: Requirements for a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to terminate prosecution (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 315(c)/317)
description: A grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to terminate prosecution of claims under reexamination must provide evidence that the following requirements, which track pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 315(c), have been satisfied: 1. The third party requester was a party to the litigation; 2. The decision is final, i.e., after all appeals; 3. The court decided that the requester/party had not sustained its burden of proving the invalidity of any claim in suit, which claim is also under reexamination; and 4. The issue(s) raised in the reexamination proceeding are the same issue(s) that were raised or could have been raised by the requester in the civil action.
guidance: Evidence should include a copy of the district court decision, any jury verdict, any CAFC decision including any mandate, any dismissal of an appeal by the CAFC, any Supreme Court ruling on certiorari, and submission of a copy of the district court’s docket is recommended. For item (1) show requester named in court documents; for (2) show finality (mandate, dismissal, docket); for (3) show which claims were before the court (verdict form, docket, other court documents); for (4) show the issues are the same or could have been raised (compare invalidity contentions, jury forms, trial materials).

name: Treatment when requester was not a party to the litigation
description: The issuance of a final court decision upholding validity during an inter partes reexamination, where the person who filed the request was not a party to the litigation, will have no binding effect on the examination of the reexamination.
guidance: The Office is not bound by a court’s decision upholding validity because district courts and the Office use different standards of proof ('clear and convincing' in court vs 'preponderance' in the Office) and different claim interpretation approaches. Deference will ordinarily be accorded to factual findings where evidence is the same, but the Office need not reach the same conclusion and may reject claims upheld by the court if sufficient reasons are present (see Ethicon v. Quigg; In re Swanson; In re Baxter).

name: Injunction may issue under extension or reissue depending on original support
description: An injunction will issue under an extension if the original had been sustained and other supporting circumstances exist.
guidance: Court will consider whether original patent had been sustained, extended, or reissued and whether the reissue broadens claims; careful inquiry needed when reissues are involved.

name: A judgment is precedent only upon issues decided
description: A judgment is a precedent only upon the issues which it expressly, or by necessary implication, has determined.
guidance: If prior litigation did not decide the specific issue now raised (e.g., different claims, reissue claims, or different defenses), those matters remain open. Courts demand that the prior judgment either show on its face or be supported by testimony proving it decided the same issues.

name: Where prior judgment does not show which claims were held valid, scope remains open
description: If a former judgment does not show which claims of the patent were held valid, both the scope of the patent and the fact of infringement are open for inquiry.
guidance: Particularly where multiple claims or multiple patents were involved, a court on a motion for a preliminary injunction should require proof of which specific claim was adjudicated (Russell v. Place; Cobum v. Clark).

name: Legal/construction points may be treated as settled across parties
description: Certain matters relating to validity governed by rules of legal definition and construction — e.g., whether an invention results from inventive skill, class protected by statute, whether reissue claims are identical, formal sufficiency, and what the patent claims — once carefully decided may be regarded as permanently settled for future litigation.
guidance: Unlike fact-contingent issues, pure legal questions and constructions have broader precedential effect and will often be followed by other courts (Treatise discussion in §1179).

name: Courts require careful inquiry before using indefinite prior orders as basis for injunction
description: Preliminary injunctions should not be based on indefinite or perfunctory prior orders that may have ostensibly covered many claims; courts should require explicit showing of what claim was held valid.
guidance: A more searching inquiry is needed for preliminary injunctions than a mere perfunctory order possibly covering all claims; otherwise defendants may suffer destructive prejudice (Coburn v. Clark).

name: Missing sequence list — enablement rejection
description: Where an invention disclosed in claims cannot be easily practiced because the sequence list is not disclosed in the specification, an examiner shall notify a ground for rejection under Article 42(3)(i) of the Patent Act.
guidance: Failure to include a required sequence list that prevents enablement should lead to a rejection under Article 42(3)(i).

name: Non-technical subject matter exclusion and technical effect exception
description: If a claimed invention uses laws other than laws of nature (economic laws, mathematical methods, logics, cartography, mental activities), arbitrary arrangements, or mental activities, the claimed invention is not statutory. However, where data processing or methods are specifically executed using hardware or give useful, concrete and tangible results by increasing or controlling performance of technical tools, they may be deemed statutory.
guidance: Look for a technical device or technical effect (concrete/tangible result) to transform an otherwise non-statutory abstract method into statutory subject matter.

name: Animal-only limitation may render medical method applicable
description: Even if a method could be used for treatment of the human body, it is considered industrially applicable if the method is limited to be practiced on the animal body excluded from being practiced on a human body.
guidance: Claims explicitly limited to non-human animals can avoid medical-practice exclusion.

name: Substantive examination for patentability and sufficiency of description
description: The examination relates to the sufficiency of description and the patentability of the matter claimed, and requires a critical reading of the specification and a search through descriptions of prior inventions ... Such search is more or less extended according to the complexity of the invention and the antiquity of the art to which it pertains. It frequently requires, in single cases, the inspection of many hundred drawings and extended reading, occupying several days' time.
guidance: Examiners assess both sufficiency of disclosure and novelty/non-obviousness by searching domestic and foreign patents and printed publications; more complex or older arts demand deeper searches. About fifteen percent of completed applications are allowed without objection.

name: Claims must particularly and distinctly point out the invention
description: If upon examination it appears that the matter specified is patentable, and that it is well and sufficiently described, and that it is particularly and distinctly pointed out in the claim, the application is allowed.
guidance: Claims must clearly and distinctly define the invention; sufficiency of specification and claim clarity are prerequisites for allowance.

name: Graham framework for obviousness (§103)
description: Apply the Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art, and (4) secondary considerations (objective indicia) of nonobviousness.
guidance: The ultimate judgment of obviousness is a legal determination; courts should make explicit findings applying these factors and not rely on conclusory statements. The KSR Court reaffirmed that Graham remains the analytical starting point for §103.

name: Interrelated teachings, design incentives, market forces and background knowledge as reasons to combine
description: A court should look to interrelated teachings of multiple patents; effects of demands known to the design community or marketplace; and background knowledge possessed by a person of ordinary skill in the art to determine whether there was an apparent reason to combine known elements.
guidance: These sources can provide a reason to combine or modify prior art references even when no precise teaching specifically directs the claimed combination.

name: Narrow standard for "teaching away"
description: A reference teaches away only if, upon reading it, a person of ordinary skill would be discouraged from following the path set out in the reference or led in a direction divergent from the applicant's path.
guidance: A mere preference for one alternative does not necessarily teach away unless the reference criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed alternative; statements that a combination is 'less desirable' often do not teach away.

name: Reasonable expectation of success when combining references
description: When all claim limitations are found in multiple prior art references, an articulated showing should include that one of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in making the combination.
guidance: Reasonable expectation is a subsidiary requirement under the Graham framework; unpredictability in the art does not automatically preclude obviousness if a reasonable probability of success exists.

name: Summary judgment appropriate when obviousness is apparent
description: Summary judgment of obviousness is appropriate where the content of the prior art, the scope of the patent claim, and the level of ordinary skill in the art are not in material dispute, and the obviousness of the claim is apparent in light of these factors.
guidance: KSR affirmed that, in some cases, obviousness can be resolved as a matter of law when the record shows no material factual disputes relevant to obviousness.

name: Arguments applicants should develop to rebut obviousness
description: Applicants should be prepared to show, where factually supportable, that: (1) the level of skill in the art is low; (2) the prior art is non-analogous; (3) there is no viable reason to combine or modify prior art references; (4) the function of a claim element is not disclosed in the prior art; (5) the ordinarily skilled person lacked requisite knowledge to combine or modify the prior art; (6) the examiner's assertions of general principles are erroneous; (7) the prior art teaches away; (8) the claimed invention provides unpredictable, unexpected or surprising results; and (9) there are significant secondary considerations with a nexus to the claimed invention.
guidance: These enumerated defenses summarize the types of factual showings that may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness post-KSR; applicants may need more fully articulated rebuttals and increased use of inventor and expert declarations.

name: Consider carefully framing field of invention and background
description: Applicants may advantageously define the field of the invention narrowly and describe a long-standing problem unique to that field, or characterize the invention as discovery of a problem or counter to conventional wisdom, to support later nonobviousness arguments.
guidance: While including background has potential pitfalls for claim scope, factually supportable framing may help establish distinctions from the broader prior art.

name: Competitor strategies for attacking patents post-KSR
description: Competitors should consider arguing obviousness based on: (1) interrelated teachings of the prior art as a whole, needs or problems known in the field, design incentives or market forces, background/common knowledge and common sense; (2) it would have been obvious to try a claimed combination that was predictably successful; (3) the person of ordinary skill is creative and can fit teachings together without precise teachings; and (4) references expressing preferences do not necessarily teach away.
guidance: KSR expands the range of obviousness arguments available to challengers; competitors should assemble holistic prior-art narratives and consider summary judgment where factual disputes are minimal.

name: Means-plus-function claim per 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
description: The US Code, Title 35 § 112, says: '(f) Element in Claim for a Combination.— An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.'
guidance: A claim element drafted as a 'means for' performing a function is construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents — not all possible means of performing that function. This statutory text is the controlling rule for how such claim elements are interpreted and limited.

name: Limitation: coverage only of corresponding structure/material/acts
description: A patent can claim a 'means for' doing something, but this won't cover all means for doing that thing; it will only cover the specific means which is/are described in the rest of the patent.
guidance: Practical implication: functional claiming under §112(f) narrows claim scope to what the specification actually discloses as the corresponding structure (and equivalents). Drafters seeking broad coverage via purely functional language risk having the claim confined to disclosed embodiments.

name: Requirement to disclose corresponding structure (risk of indefiniteness/invalidity)
description: If the patent doesn't describe any means (i.e., no corresponding structure), then the patent can be found invalid.
guidance: Courts have repeatedly held that a patent is invalid as indefinite under Section 112(b) if a claimed 'means' has no particular corresponding structure disclosed in the specification. Reported examples include Function Media, LLC v. Google, Inc., 708 F.3d 1310, 1319 (Fed. Cir. 2013) and Blackboard, Inc. v. Desire2Learn Inc., 574 F.3d 1371, 1382-83 (Fed. Cir. 2009). Anti-pattern: drafting functional claims without describing the algorithms, structures, or acts that implement the function.

name: Application and risk of means-plus-function drafting in software patents
description: Patent drafters sometimes write software patents with claims to means of doing things, but they don't give the algorithms for exactly how to do that thing.
guidance: Such patents are sometimes easier to invalidate — in software contexts, failing to disclose algorithmic structure corresponding to claimed functions invites indefiniteness challenges. While drafters may use functional claiming to try to obtain broader patents, the lack of disclosed structure can make enforcement and validity more vulnerable in litigation.

name: Presumption against means-plus-function when 'means' not used
description: If the limitation does not use the term 'means,' it is subject to a rebuttable presumption that it is not in means-plus-function form. Williamson, 792 F.3d at 1348.
guidance: The presumption may be overcome if the challenger demonstrates that the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or else recites function without reciting sufficient structure for performing that function. Courts should explain application of the presumption but need not rely on extrinsic evidence to overcome it; intrinsic evidence alone may suffice.

name: Test for whether claim words connote structure (Williamson test)
description: Determine 'whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure.' Williamson, 792 F.3d at 1349.
guidance: Look to how a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand the term as a name for structure, using intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history). If the term is understood as the name of structure, § 112, ¶ 6 does not apply; if not, it may be means-plus-function.

name: No categorical rule for 'processor' — examine context
description: There is no categorical rule that 'processor' is or is not structural; whether 'processor' connotes structure depends on context and how it is used in the claim and specification.
guidance: If 'processor' is used generically as an equivalent to 'means' (a nonce word), or if the claim/specification does not describe how the processor interacts with other components to impart structure, the presumption against means-plus-function may be overcome. Conversely, conventional code or other structural disclosure could support a structural reading.

name: Functional/self-referential claiming is means-plus-function in essence
description: Claim language that describes only what a component does (e.g., 'configured to manage collaborative applications') without structural detail is self-referential and captures any structures that perform the function — the 'epitome of functional claiming.'
guidance: Such black-box functional descriptions (e.g., 'What manages the collaborative applications? The processor.') indicate lack of structure and support a means-plus-function construction because they sweep broadly to 'any and all structures that fulfill the function.'

name: Identify function and corresponding structure (§ 112, ¶ 6 step two)
description: Once a limitation is deemed means-plus-function, the court must (1) identify the claimed function and (2) identify the corresponding structure in the specification that performs that function, and clearly link that structure to the function. Williamson, 792 F.3d at 1351; Triton Tech. of Tex., LLC v. Nintendo of Am., Inc., 753 F.3d 1375, 1378 (Fed. Cir. 2014).
guidance: If the patentee fails to disclose adequate corresponding structure, the claim is indefinite. The specification must disclose structure (not merely restate the function) and must clearly link that structure to the claimed function.

name: Requirement of algorithm disclosure for special-purpose computer functions
description: For general-purpose computers or processors performing a claimed function, the specification must disclose an algorithm (a step-by-step procedure for accomplishing a given result) as corresponding structure; mere functional description or lists of data components are insufficient. Alfred E. Mann Found. for Sci. Res. v. Cochlear Corp., 841 F.3d 1334, 1342 (Fed. Cir. 2016).
guidance: Databases or lists of components that 'enable storage of data' do not constitute an algorithm. To prevent pure functional claiming, the spec should provide algorithmic detail or conventional code/structure that shows how the function is performed.

name: Specification must clearly link disclosed structure to claimed function
description: The specification must identify corresponding structure for performing the claimed function and clearly link that structure to the function; bare mention of components without showing how they perform the function is inadequate.
guidance: Court looks for a disclosure that connects structure (e.g., code, modules, algorithms, steps) to the specific claimed function. Mere examples or enabling storage/recording of data do not satisfy the linkage requirement.

name: Databases or lists of components are not necessarily structure
description: Describing databases that 'enable storing of data related to collaborative applications' is functional and does not necessarily describe structure for performing 'managing' functions.
guidance: A specification passage that only lists databases or components (e.g., 'databases 107, 108, 109 enabling...') without describing how those components carry out the claimed function will likely be insufficient as corresponding structure for §112 ¶6.

name: Superficial replacement of 'means' with functional language does not avoid § 112, ¶ 6
description: Replacing the term 'means' with other functional language (e.g., 'processor configured to...') does not avoid a means-plus-function construction if the amended claim still fails to recite corresponding structure.
guidance: Amendments during prosecution substituting 'a collaborative application management processor configured to manage collaborative applications' for 'means for management of collaborative applications' do not automatically confer structure; the patentee must recite structure.

name: Intrinsic evidence can suffice; extrinsic evidence not always required
description: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) can be informative and sufficient to determine whether disputed claim language recites sufficiently definite structure or was intended to invoke §112, ¶ 6; extrinsic evidence (expert testimony) is not always required. Dyfan, 28 F.4th at 1365, Diebold Nixdorf, Inc. v. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 899 F.3d 1291, 1299 (Fed. Cir. 2018).
guidance: Courts may construe limitations and find terms structural or functional based on intrinsic record alone; however, conventional code or expert testimony (when present) may support a structural reading in appropriate cases (e.g., Dyfan, Zeroclick).

name: Burden and quantum of proof for indefiniteness
description: The challenger seeking to invalidate a claim as indefinite for lack of corresponding structure bears the ultimate burden to show indefiniteness by clear and convincing evidence. Budde v. Harley-Davidson, Inc., 250 F.3d 1369, 1376–77; Intel Corp. v. VIA Techs., Inc., 319 F.3d 1357, 1365–66.
guidance: District courts evaluate the intrinsic record and any extrinsic evidence under the clear-and-convincing standard when determining whether the specification discloses adequate corresponding structure.

name: Consideration of how claimed component interacts with other components
description: A limitation that fails to describe how a claimed module interacts with other components (i.e., lacks interaction/structural detail) is less likely to be understood as structural and more likely to be treated as functional/means-plus-function. Williamson, 792 F.3d at 1351.
guidance: Look for claim/spec language that describes interactions or connections among components that would impart structural character; absence of such interactions supports finding of functional claiming.

name: Categories of patent-eligible subject matter (§101)
description: There are four categories of patent-eligible subject matter: processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter; these categories should be read broadly to encourage innovation.
guidance: Claims should be evaluated to determine whether they fall within one of these statutory categories (e.g., method patents, data processing systems, computer-readable media). Being in a statutory category is a necessary starting point but not alone dispositive because judicial exceptions may still apply.

name: Abstract ideas exception — core inquiry
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to an 'abstract idea' (e.g., fundamental truths, mathematical formulas, or fundamental economic concepts such as intermediated settlement or hedging).
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed subject matter is essentially a longstanding practice or fundamental economic principle (CLS's position) or instead claims a specific technical application beyond a preexisting fundamental truth (Alice's position). Look to precedent (e.g., Bilski) for examples of abstract economic concepts.

name: "Significantly more" / inventive concept requirement
description: Claims that involve a judicial exception (like an abstract idea) must add 'significantly more' than the exception itself (as articulated in Mayo) to be patent-eligible.
guidance: Ask whether the claim recites an inventive concept or additional elements that transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (e.g., Diamond v. Diehr: combination of steps plus a formula was eligible). Mere recital of an abstract idea plus routine steps is insufficient.

name: Specific, concrete configurations or non-conventional steps support eligibility
description: Claims that require a specific configuration of computer hardware or particular, concrete steps (e.g., creating two shadow accounts, a particular series of steps beyond simple computations) may demonstrate the 'significantly more' needed for eligibility.
guidance: Look for claim elements that meaningfully limit the scope in a technological way (novel hardware arrangement, novel sequence of steps producing a technical effect) rather than generic computer implementation; such specificity can distinguish from 'disembodied concept' claims.

name: Treatment of computer-readable media claims
description: Claims to computer-readable media containing program code are evaluated for §101 eligibility and can be found ineligible if they are directed at the same abstract concept as method/system claims.
guidance: Do not assume drafting as a media claim avoids §101 problems; analyze whether the media claim simply recites the abstract idea in software form without adding an inventive application.

name: Determining whether a claim 'recites a fundamental truth' or is reducible to a formula
description: A claim is more likely to be an abstract idea if it merely recites a fundamental truth or is reducible to a mathematical formula or preexisting principle.
guidance: Examine whether the claimed subject matter exists apart from human action or is a longstanding/prior commercial practice; if so, courts may find it falls within the abstract-ideas exception.

name: Role of precedent (Bilski, Mayo, Diehr) in eligibility analysis
description: Prior Supreme Court decisions provide tests and examples (Bilski: hedging as abstract idea; Mayo: 'significantly more'; Diehr: combinated process including formula was eligible) that guide §101 analysis.
guidance: Apply tests and analogies from these cases: compare claimed invention to prior holdings (is it like hedging or like Diehr's integrated process?) to determine whether the claim adds an inventive application beyond an abstract idea.

name: Need for clarity and consistent framework in applying the abstract-ideas exception
description: Lower courts currently face uncertainty applying the abstract ideas exception; commentators urge the Court to clarify standards or emphasize tests (e.g., method-and-means) to provide consistent guidance.
guidance: When analyzing claims, be explicit about which test is applied (abstract-idea identification, then whether the claim adds 'significantly more' or a method/means) and document how each claim element affects the analysis to reduce uncertainty.

name: Due-process particulars in disciplinary proceedings
description: The fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.
guidance: Specific due-process protections include reasonable notice of charges, ability to be represented by counsel, ability to present evidence, testify, cross-examine witnesses, make objections, and present argument. Attendance and active participation in hearings weigh strongly against a due-process claim.

name: Extent of protection determined by claims and interpreted by description/drawings
description: The extent of the protection conferred by an ARIPO patent or application shall be determined by the terms of the claims; the description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims.
guidance: Section 24. Claims are primary; description/drawings are interpretative aids.

name: Filing date determination
description: The filing date of an ARIPO patent application shall be the date on which the filing requirements, as provided under Section 31(1)(a) to (c) (request, description, one or more claims), are fulfilled.
guidance: Section 33. Meeting minimum requirements is essential to secure filing date.

name: Claims clarity and support requirement
description: A claim or claims shall, in a clear and concise manner, define the matter for which protection is sought and shall be supported by the description.
guidance: Section 36. Claims must be consistent with the description and not ambiguous.

name: Abstract role limitation
description: An abstract shall merely serve as a source of technical information and shall not be used for the purposes of interpreting the scope of the protection sought.
guidance: Section 37. Abstract is informational only, not interpretative for claim scope.

name: Claiming priority (declaration and documents)
description: An applicant intending to take advantage of priority must file a declaration of priority and any other document required in accordance with the Regulations; multiple priorities may be claimed and may apply to a single claim; the right of priority covers only elements included in the earlier application(s).
guidance: Section 39(1)-(5). Time limits running from priority run from the earliest priority date when multiple priorities are claimed.

name: Post-grant limitation / amendment of patents
description: An ARIPO patent may be limited by post-grant amendment at the request of the proprietor; request filed per Regulations and fee; any amendment to claims shall fall wholly within the scope of the claims before the amendment; re-examination and re-publication occur subject to fees.
guidance: Section 50(1)-(3). Post-grant amendments cannot broaden claim scope beyond original claims.

name: Utility model protection standards
description: ARIPO utility models shall be registered for inventions in all fields of technology provided they are new and susceptible of industrial application; certain patent provisions apply mutatis mutandis; no utility model where claimed subject matter already the subject of a patent or utility model registration based on a prior application.
guidance: Sections 59-61. Utility models have different substantive thresholds (inventive step may be omitted) and specific applicability is described in Section 60.

name: Primary and secondary purposes of definiteness
description: Primary purpose: ensure the scope of the claims is clear so the public is informed of the boundaries of infringement. Secondary purpose: provide a clear measure of what the inventor regards as the invention so patentability and written description can be assessed.
guidance: Examination should focus on these notice and measurement functions when evaluating claim language. Rejections should be tied to failure to meet these purposes.

name: Plain meaning and specification as best source
description: Under BRI, words of the claim must be given their plain (ordinary and customary) meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, with the specification being the best source for determining meaning.
guidance: The presumption of plain meaning can be rebutted only by a clear specification definition. Avoid importing limitations from preferred embodiments absent clear disclaimer. Applicant may not add a special definition after the filing date, though they may point to a special definition present in the specification as filed.

name: Determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-plus-function)
description: Examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph). If invoked, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: See MPEP § 2181 and In re Donaldson. When a limitation invokes 112(f), identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification during claim interpretation.

name: Different construction for claims in prosecution vs. in court
description: Claims under examination are construed under BRI by the Office, while patented claims in court are not given BRI and are interpreted based on a fully developed prosecution record (Nautilus standard of reasonable certainty applies in litigation).
guidance: Examiners should apply a lower threshold for ambiguity during prosecution to facilitate sharpening/clarifying claims; applicants have opportunity to amend during prosecution to ensure clarity prior to issuance.

name: Threshold requirements: clarity and precision (particularity and distinctness)
description: The examiner’s focus is whether the claim meets statutory threshold requirements of clarity and precision—claims must set out and circumscribe a particular subject matter with reasonable clarity and particularity.
guidance: Examiner should allow claims that define patentable subject matter with required particularity even if alternate phrasing exists. Examiners may suggest language improvements but should not insist on personal preferences if statutory requirements are met.

name: Totality of the evidence: analyze claim terms in light of specification, prior art, and POSITA understanding
description: Definiteness must be analyzed in light of (A) the content of the particular application disclosure, (B) teachings of the prior art, and (C) the claim interpretation that would be given by one of ordinary skill in the pertinent art at the relevant time.
guidance: Consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises POSITA of its scope and serves the notice function. A term’s commonly understood meaning may vary by art; analyze from the relevant-art perspective.

name: Indefiniteness: more than one reasonable interpretation under BRI
description: If the language of a claim, given its broadest reasonable interpretation, is such that a person of ordinary skill would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is appropriate.
guidance: Do not confuse breadth with indefiniteness: a broad but clearly defined claim is not indefinite. Example: a genus claim can be broad yet definite; a genus claim is indefinite if it is unclear which species are covered.

name: Office action must provide sufficient explanation for applicant to respond
description: The Office action must set forth the specific term or phrase that is indefinite and why the metes and bounds are unclear, and, when practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness may be resolved.
guidance: Because the rejection requires a response explaining why the language is definite or amending the claim, give enough information for a meaningful response; if applicant fails to adequately respond, the examiner may make the rejection final.

name: Provide claim interpretation in reasons for allowance when the prosecution record is unclear
description: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.104(e), if the prosecution record as a whole does not make clear the reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in reasons for allowance (and specify allowable subject matter).
guidance: Setting forth reasons for allowance improves the quality and reliability of issued patents but avoid placing unwarranted broad or narrow interpretations on the claims in doing so.

name: Attempt resolution through interview before rejecting when indefiniteness is sole issue
description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, examiners are encouraged to initiate an interview with the applicant to discuss claim interpretation, meaning of limitations, scope of preamble, means-plus-function issues, etc., prior to issuing a rejection.
guidance: Interviews can clarify issues and may eliminate need for rejection. The substance of any interview must be made of record (document why a term is or is not clear, whether it invokes 112(f), and any amendments discussed). See MPEP § 713.04 and 37 CFR 1.2.

name: Correspondence between specification and claims; antecedent basis and support (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1))
description: The specification should serve as a glossary to claim terms so meaning can be ascertained; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification per 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).
guidance: Glossaries are helpful. If the specification lacks needed support or antecedent basis, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require amendment to description or claims (without introducing new matter). See MPEP § 608.01(o) and § 2181 subsection IV.

name: Specification sufficiency presumption
description: The law presumes that every one who applies for a patent will embody his invention in specifications sufficiently definite to preserve as much of his discovery as he desires to protect by a patent.
guidance: If, from mistake, he has overlooked anything within the scope of his invention, he may surrender his patent on that ground and claim a new one in accordance with amended specifications; but relief will be denied unless brought within the statute, and not if omission resulted from culpable negligence or misconduct.

name: Re-issue cannot claim matter intentionally omitted or intentionally included
description: A re-issue cannot claim matter intentionally omitted from the original, nor can it be used to restore matter intentionally excluded from the original patent.
guidance: Matter deliberately embraced within or excluded from a patent cannot be reclaimed by amendment; the central difficulty is determining whether the original misstatement was deliberate or unintentional, using surrounding circumstances (face of patent, PTO records, inventor's conduct).

name: Intent to abandon shown by express disclaimer or conduct
description: A voluntary and intelligent disavowal (express disclaimer) in the original patent or during prosecution is conclusive evidence of intentional exclusion of matter from the patent.
guidance: A disclaimer in the specification or filed subsequently, or withdrawal of claims by amendment (to save application or escape interference), or acquiescence in examiner's rejection can indicate intentional abandonment; such matter generally cannot be reclaimed by re-issue.

name: Limitations imposed during prosecution are binding when accepted
description: Limitations and disclaimers imposed by the Patent Office which narrow the scope of the invention as described and claimed in the application are irrevocable admissions that such limitations are of the essence of the invention.
guidance: When a patentee accepts his patent containing such limitations, he is bound by them even if they were voluntary or enforced; third parties rely on these limitations. A disclaimer directed by the Commissioner in an application for a re-issue does not necessarily concede that the modification was not covered in the original patent (case-specific).

name: Re-issue addresses the application, not the invention
description: ‘Inadvertence, etc.’ exists in reference to the application, not the invention, and occurs only where the former does not describe and claim what the inventor intended to protect.
guidance: The test is whether the omission was from the application/specification/claims rather than a change in the inventor’s view of patentability or strategy; errors of opinion or judgment are not 'mistake or inadvertence'.

name: Unreasonable delay can bar re-issue
description: A re-issue that seeks to restore matter omitted from the original claims is barred unless the claims are amended by re-issue without unreasonable delay.
guidance: Less delay is allowable when narrowing claims than when expanding them, but unreasonable delay or intervening rights acquired by others can preclude re-issue. Cases: Ex parte Mathews; Ives v. Salant; examples shown where delay defeated relief.

name: Acceptance of patent containing narrower claims estops asserting broader invention
description: If a patentee accepts a patent containing limitations which narrow the scope of his invention, he is bound by those limitations and if he accepts a claim not covering his entire invention he abandons the residue.
guidance: Even if the limitation was enforced by PTO rather than voluntarily assumed, acceptance of the resulting patent may prevent later enlargement by re-issue. See Toepfer v. Goetz and related authorities.

name: Re-issue may reinstate claims omitted by misunderstanding of attorney if timely
description: A re-issue may embrace a claim shown in the original application and erased by a misunderstanding of the attorney, provided the re-issue is sought without unreasonable delay and other bars do not apply.
guidance: This is an exception: mistakes by counsel in drafting that are not attributable to the inventor personally may sometimes be corrected, but material matters generally require applicant's action; see Stutz v. Armstrong.

name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — determining when subject matter was 'effectively filed'
description: Under 102(d), a U.S. patent, application publication, or WIPO published application is prior art as of either its actual filing date or the filing date of a prior application to which a priority or benefit claim is made, provided that the prior-filed application 'describe[s] the subject matter' relied upon.
guidance: For 102(d) prior-art determinations the reference patent document need only meet the 'ministerial requirements' of 35 U.S.C. 119 and 120 (e.g., (1) containing a priority/benefit claim, (2) filed within the applicable period, (3) having a common inventor or same applicant). The prior-filed application must 'describe[] the subject matter' relied upon (Penumbra, Inc. v. RapidPulse, Inc.). 102(d) does not require the description to meet enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The AIA eliminated the Hilmer doctrine: if the U.S. patent document claims priority to earlier foreign/international applications that describe the subject matter, the U.S. document is effective as of the earliest such application filing date, regardless of where filed.

name: Provisional rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) based on copending U.S. applications
description: If an earlier-filed, copending, unpublished U.S. patent application discloses subject matter that would anticipate claims in a later-filed pending U.S. application with a different inventive entity, an examiner may determine whether a provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) can be made.
guidance: I. If copending applications have at least one common (joint) inventor, common applicant, or are commonly assigned, and publication/issuance of the first would qualify as 102(a)(2) prior art to the second, a provisional anticipation/obviousness rejection of the second may be made even though the first is unpublished or unissued. The provisional rejection can be overcome as any 102(a)(2) rejection can be (see MPEP §2152.06) or by abandoning and refiling a new application containing both subject matters. Use form paragraph 7.15.01.aia when making such a provisional rejection. II. If there is no common inventor/applicant/assignee and the earlier application was not published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b), maintain confidentiality and do not make a rejection relying on the earlier unpublished application; after the earlier application issues it may be used as a 102(a)(2) reference against the later application.

name: Article 84 EPC — Claims must define, be clear, concise, supported
description: "The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description." (Art. 84 EPC; Rule 43 EPC; Guidelines F-IV 4–6)
guidance: Claims must meet form and content requirements (Rule 43) and the Guidelines sections on clarity, conciseness and support (F‑IV,4; F‑IV,5; F‑IV,6). This is the primary legal requirement for claim drafting.

name: Clarity from the claim wording alone
description: The meaning of the terms of the claim should be clear for the person skilled in the art from the wording of the claim alone, without reference to the description.
guidance: Cited sources: T 2/80; GL F‑IV, 4.1 and 4.2. Examiner/expert should not have to rely on the description to make the claim intelligible.

name: Claims should be read to make technical sense (with good will) and be contradiction‑free
description: The claim should be read with an attempt to make technical sense out of it (with good will), and the claims must be free of contradiction.
guidance: Interpretive principle to give reasonable technical meaning where possible, but not at the expense of creating contradictions or ambiguity in claim terms.

name: Article 69 EPC and Protocol — interpretation limits
description: "The extent of the protection conferred... shall be determined by the claims. Nevertheless, the description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims." (Art.69(1) EPC)
guidance: Art.69 and its Protocol do not allow excluding what is literally covered by claim terms or reading limitations from the description into the claims to avoid novelty/inventive step objections. A claim must be clear on its own (GL F‑IV,4.2; T 223/05; T 681/01).

name: Avoidance of vague/relative terms unless well‑recognised in the art
description: Relative terms should not be used unless they have a well‑recognised meaning in the particular art and that is the intended meaning.
guidance: An unclear term cannot be allowed in a claim if the term is essential given the invention. Examples: 'substantially non‑polymerisable' (T 445/12 — clarity no) vs 'middle polyhedron' (T 610/13 — clarity yes because well‑recognised in mathematics).

name: Claims must include essential features underlying technical effect (Art.84 vs Art.56)
description: If features in a claim do not achieve the necessary technical effects underlying the solution of the objective technical problem, the claim may lack inventive step (Art.56) and/or lack clarity because it omits essential features (Art.84).
guidance: Guidance: GL F‑IV, 4.5.1. A claim that omits features presented in the description as essential may be unsupported even if it appears broad.

name: Sufficiency (Art.83) vs clarity (Art.84) — scope vs teaching
description: Art.83 is fulfilled if the application contains sufficient information to allow the person skilled in the art to perform the invention over the whole area claimed without undue burden; Art.84 is fulfilled if the skilled person can, from the application as filed, extend the particular teaching to the whole of the field claimed using routine methods.
guidance: References: GL F‑III,1 and GL F‑IV,6.3. Distinguishes the threshold for sufficiency (enablement) from the requirement that claim breadth be commensurate with the teaching in the description.

name: Art.83 and Art.84 can give rise to simultaneous objections
description: If the claim, over its whole range, extends to technical subject‑matter not made available to the skilled person by the application as filed, objections may be raised under both Art.83 and Art.84; both objections could be raised at the same time.
guidance: GL F‑IV,6.4. Examiners may raise both lack of sufficiency and lack of clarity/support when claim scope is not commensurate with the disclosed teaching.

name: Novelty (Art.54) vs clarity (Art.84) — broad claims problems
description: The broader a claim, the easier it is that the claim is not new (Art.54) or not supported by the description (Art.84). Very broad claims are normally both not new and not supported by the description.
guidance: An examiner will choose to raise a novelty or clarity objection depending on which is more efficient for concluding examination. Practical note on prosecution strategy and claim breadth.

name: Conciseness and compliance with Rule 43 (form and content of claims)
description: Claims must be concise (Guidelines F‑IV,5) and comply with the form and content requirements of Rule 43 EPC.
guidance: Conciseness is a separate formal/content requirement in addition to clarity and support; ensure claim wording avoids unnecessary verbosity and complies with prescribed claim structure.

name: Policy rationale — clarity reduces uncertainty and delimitation disputes
description: Clear claims reduce the 'area of uncertainty' between prior art, alleged infringing subject‑matter, and the invention — i.e., 'good fences make good neighbours.'
guidance: Practical justification for strict clarity/support standards: precise claim borders reduce borderline infringement issues and litigation/administrative uncertainty.

name: Adding inadvertently omitted material under 37 CFR 1.57(b)
description: 37 CFR 1.57(b) permits inadvertently omitted material to be added to the application by way of a later filed amendment if the inadvertently omitted portion of the specification or drawing(s) is completely contained in a prior-filed application (for which priority/benefit is claimed) even though there is no explicit incorporation by reference of the prior-filed application.
guidance: See MPEP §217 for discussion regarding 37 CFR 1.57(b). This provides a procedure (created by PLTIA implementation) to add omitted material when it is fully contained in a prior-filed application for which priority/benefit is claimed.

name: Definition of 'essential material' (37 CFR 1.57(d))
description: “Essential material” is material necessary to (1) provide a written description and enablement (35 U.S.C.112(a)), (2) describe the claimed invention in terms that particularly point out and distinctly claim it (35 U.S.C.112(b)), or (3) describe structure/material/acts corresponding to a claimed means or step (35 U.S.C.112(f)).
guidance: In any application that is to issue as a U.S. patent, essential material may only be incorporated by reference to a U.S. patent or patent application publication. Material meeting any of these statutory requirements is treated as essential and cannot properly be incorporated from improper sources.

name: Appropriate corrective avenues (no 1.183 petition; use revive/reissue where applicable)
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.183 to suspend the time period requirement in 37 CFR 1.57(h) is not appropriate. After abandonment applicant must file a petition to revive under 37 CFR 1.137; after issuance, corrections may require reissue. Correcting via certificate of correction is not appropriate because it may alter claim scope.
guidance: Corrections that would alter claim scope should be made via the reissue process. Reliance on 1.183 is unlikely to succeed; selection of the appropriate corrective mechanism is required depending on stage (abandonment, issuance).

name: Effect of applicant amendments that change essentiality of incorporated material (examples)
description: If applicant files an amendment (e.g., adding a limitation) that makes previously-incorporated material essential, an examiner may require the applicant to amend the specification to include that material and may make rejections under 35 U.S.C.112(a) if the material is not included. Correction must comply with 37 CFR 1.57(g) and timing rules; applicant may also file an RCE under 37 CFR 1.114 with appropriate fee and amend under 1.57(g).
guidance: Examples given: (1) examiner notices specification incorporated essential material from a foreign patent and requires amendment to add material; (2) applicant adds claim limitation supported only by foreign patent making the incorporated subject matter essential, leading to a 112(a) rejection in final Office action. If rejection results from applicant amendment, finality of action is proper.

name: Use of incorporation-by-reference statement at filing to safeguard benefit claims
description: An applicant may include a statement at the time of filing the later application incorporating by reference the prior application as a safeguard against omission of a portion of a prior application for which priority/benefit is claimed. The incorporation-by-reference statement must be filed at the time of filing the later-filed application to be effective.
guidance: An incorporation statement added after filing is not effective because no new matter may be added after filing (35 U.S.C.132(a)). Note: such a statement will not satisfy the specific reference requirement of 35 U.S.C.119(e) or 120 or 37 CFR 1.78. See MPEP §§201.06(c), 211 et seq., 213–216, and 217.

name: When the Office may require a substitute specification (37 CFR 1.125(a))
description: If the number or nature of the amendments or the legibility of the application papers renders it difficult to consider the application, or to arrange the papers for printing or copying, the Office may require the entire specification, including the claims, or any part thereof, be rewritten (37 CFR 1.125(a)).
guidance: Legibility includes ability to be photocopied/scanned for electronic reproduction. Form paragraph 6.28 may be used where the specification is in faulty English.

name: Voluntary substitute specification filing and limits (37 CFR 1.125(b))
description: Subject to §1.312, a substitute specification, excluding the claims, may be filed at any point up to payment of the issue fee if it is accompanied by a statement that the substitute specification includes no new matter.
guidance: A substitute specification voluntarily filed will be accepted if requirements of 1.125(b) are satisfied. A substitute specification is not permitted in a reissue application or in a reexamination proceeding (37 CFR 1.125(d)).

name: Formatting and marking requirements for substitute specifications (37 CFR 1.125(c))
description: A substitute specification submitted must be accompanied by markings showing all changes relative to the immediate prior version of the specification of record. Added subject matter must be shown by underlining; deleted matter by strike-through or double brackets as specified. An accompanying clean version must also be supplied. Paragraph numbering of the specification of record is not considered a change for marking purposes.
guidance: Paragraphs of any substitute specification (other than claims) should be individually numbered in Arabic numerals (e.g., [0001]) to permit replacement paragraphs under 37 CFR 1.121(b)(1). The substitute must be submitted in clean form without markings and with a marked-up copy showing changes.

name: Examiner duties and limitations regarding substitute specifications (no duty to detailed-compare)
description: There is no obligation on the examiner to make a detailed comparison between the old and new specifications to determine whether new matter has been added. If, however, an examiner becomes aware that new matter is present, an objection should be made.
guidance: A substitute specification which complies should normally be entered; if denied entry, form paragraph 6.28.02 may be used to notify applicant of reasons (e.g., missing no-new-matter statement, missing marked copy, filed in reissue, filed after payment of issue fee, containing claims). See MPEP §714.20 regarding entry of amendments.

name: Prior Art Search and Determination of Novelty, Inventive Step, etc.
description: Procedures for conducting prior art searches and the method for determining novelty and inventive step (patentability) of claimed subject matter.
guidance: Covers search strategies, how prior art is compared to claimed features, and stepwise determination of novelty and inventive step; see detailed section for examiner methodology.

name: Patent Act Article 36(5) (Requirements for Claims)
description: Reference to statutory/formal requirements for claims under Article 36(5) (format and content requirements).
guidance: See Claims chapter for specifics on required elements of claim statements and formal compliance.

name: Application cover sheet required contents (Article 42(1))
description: A patent application cover sheet must state: 1) the name and domicile of the patent applicant (if a corporation, its name and place of business); 2) the name and domicile or place of business of an agent if represented (if a patent firm, its name/place of business and the name of the designated patent attorney); 3) the title of the invention; 4) the name and domicile of the inventor.
guidance: The cover sheet shall be accompanied by a specification, necessary drawings, and an abstract. The cover sheet should also indicate applicant code, priority claim, claim on grace period disclosure exception and request for examination. The title on the cover sheet must be identical to that in the specification.

name: Abstract usage and limits (Article 42(2) / Article 43)
description: The abstract is to be used only for technical information and shall not be used to define the scope of the invention for which patent protection is sought.
