guidance: Abstracts facilitate searching and disclosure but cannot determine claim scope (Article 97). Matters disclosed only in an abstract do not constitute content of another application (Article 29(3)) and cannot be added to the specification by amendment. If an abstract is missing or deficient, the applicant will be requested to amend; continued deficiency may lead to invalidation of the application proceeding. Examiners should not cite Article 42(3) or (4) as grounds for rejection merely because an abstract is incorrect.

name: Specification must contain description and claims (Article 42(2))
description: A specification filed at the time of filing must contain the description of the invention and the claims; necessary drawings and an abstract should accompany it. Claims may be omitted at filing but must be submitted by the period specified under Article 42-2(2).
guidance: The specification serves both as the right-document (defines scope) and as a technical disclosure. Guidelines on preparing description and claims are set out in Chapters 3 and 4. The description must enable the invention and satisfy method/format rules.

name: Title of the invention: brevity, content and identity
description: The title of the invention shall be written briefly and concisely according to the subject matter of the invention and shall be identical in the cover sheet and the specification.
guidance: Avoid ambiguous or wordy titles (examples given). Do not include a person's name, trademark, product nickname, expressions indicating only abstract functions, or the word 'patent' (examples: 'Upgraded', 'Improved'). If claims cover multiple categories (product, process, device, use), use a concise encompassing title (example: 'Paper, manufacturing process and manufacturing device thereof'). The title should clearly indicate what is claimed (example guidance for automatic control device vs automatic temperature control device). If claims change by amendment, amend the title accordingly. If title is inappropriate, examiner will notify and may suggest a proper title; inappropriate title alone is not a ground for rejection, though an examiner may ex officio amend titles when granting a patent.

name: Drawings: when required and preparation standards
description: Drawings may be attached when necessary for explanation of the claimed invention and shall be prepared according to the guideline for drawings of Annexed Form No.17 of the Enforcement Rules.
guidance: Where drawings are difficult to prepare per Annexed Form No.17 (e.g., crystal structures, particle shapes, oscilloscope results) or pictures better describe an embodiment, pictures may replace drawings. Pictures must be clear enough for publication in the official gazette; grayscale or color may be accepted if unavoidable. Utility model registration applications must include drawings; absence leads to illegitimate application returned to applicant. Irrelevant drawings (e.g., drawings from another application) that give rise to a ground for rejection under Article 42(3)(i) must be noted by the examiner; if the drawing error does not affect practice of the invention it may be treated as reference only. Submitting new drawings as amendment can constitute addition of new matter—examiners must be cautious.

name: Enablement / clarity and detail requirement (Article 42(3)(i))
description: The description shall describe the invention with such clarity and in such detail that a person skilled in the art can easily practice the invention based on ordinary skill, the specification and drawings at the filing date.
guidance: 'A person skilled in the art' is defined as a technician with average understanding in the technical field. 'Easily practicing' means the skilled person fully understands and can reproduce the invention without adding special knowledge, undue trial and error, or repetitive experimentation. The invention to be enabled is the invention as recited in the claims; material disclosed only in the description but not in claims is not judged under Article 42(3)(i) for enablement of the claimed subject matter.

name: Enablement for method (process) inventions
description: Where claims recite a method invention, the description must contain clear and full explanation so a skilled person is enabled to use the method; the roles and sequences of each step specifying the process should be described together.
guidance: Full disclosure of the steps and their sequences is expected so that the method can be practiced without undue experimentation.

name: Enablement for manufacturing method inventions
description: For manufacturing method claims, the description must enable a skilled person to produce a product by the claimed manufacturing method; the manufacturing method itself and roles/sequences of each step must be fully described.
guidance: A manufacturing method generally consists of detailed steps dealing with raw materials—raw materials and a series of detailed steps must be fully described. The product manufactured by the method should be clearly described, except where the product is easily understood from raw materials or steps.

name: Medicinal (use) inventions: demonstration of effect
description: For chemical/medicinal use inventions, the effect of the invention should be disclosed in the description; medicinal inventions require medical data proving effect or a sufficiently detailed description replacing such data, except where the medical mechanism is clearly known at filing.
guidance: Because predictability/reproducibility may be low, experimental/clinical data are usually necessary to support that the medicine has the claimed medical effect.

name: Support of claims by description; genus/species and Markush issues (Article 42(4)(i))
description: Claims must be supported by the description such that the subject matter of the claims is disclosed in the description. If claims cover a generic invention (genus) but the description only discloses species embodiments and the genus cannot be clearly recognized, Article 42(4)(i) applies. Conversely, if claims recite species but the description discloses only the genus and the species is not clearly recognized, Article 42(4)(i) applies. Article 42(3) may apply when other embodiments within the claimed genus cannot be easily practiced.
guidance: Examples: (1) Extrusion molding claims broadly covering many materials but description only details edible plastics—examiner should notify rejection under Article 42(3) or 42(4)(i) as appropriate. (2) Claims reciting broad oxygen-absorbing compositions with precise numeric constituents while description only discloses a narrower embodiment—examiner should notify lack of support. Markush groups: if only some group members have embodiments and others lack embodiments enabling practice, examiner shall notify rejection under Article 42(3).

name: Term consistency between description and claims
description: If terms used in the description and the claims do not clearly match, an examiner shall notify a ground for rejection citing violation of Article 42(4)(i) since the invention recited in the claims is deemed not supported by the description.
guidance: Ensure consistent terminology between claims and specification; inconsistent terms can lead to rejection for lack of support.

name: Examination process for enablement and support (basic considerations and special cases)
description: Examiners assess enablement and support by considering the type of invention (product, method, manufacturing method) and special cases (chemical, medicinal, parameter inventions). Lack of sufficient manufacturing steps, experimental data, or disclosure for all claimed embodiments can lead to notices of rejection under Article 42(3) or 42(4)(i).
guidance: Examiners shall apply the criteria consistently to maintain examination efficiency. Examples and illustrations indicate how to apply Article 42(3) vs 42(4)(i) depending on whether the description lacks enablement or lacks support for the claimed scope.

name: Anticipation / prior publication comparison test
description: To determine anticipation, compare the earlier publication with the patentee’s claim as at the date of publication, having regard to surrounding circumstances and without hindsight. If the prior art so construed discloses the same product/process or contains 'clear and unmistakeable directions' to the invention, the claim is anticipated.
guidance: Interpret both the prior art and the patent claim as at their respective dates (no benefit of hindsight). Use the approach from General Tire & Rubber Co v Firestone (1972) as applied in Singapore. The comparison is document-by-document.

name: Direct Infringement—Knowledge of the Patent and Intent to Infringe Are Immaterial
description: [The Defendant] is liable for directly infringing [the Plaintiff]’s patent if you find that [the Plaintiff] has proven that it is more likely than not that [the Defendant] made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention defined in at least one claim of [the Plaintiff]’s patent during the term of the patent. A party can directly infringe a patent without knowing of the patent or without knowing that what the party is doing is patent infringement.
guidance: Standard: preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Cite 35 U.S.C. § 271(a) and supporting case law (Commil; Medtronic; Global-Tech; Warner-Jenkinson).

name: Infringement of “Comprising,” “Consisting of,” and “Consisting Essentially of” Claims
description: (Alternative 1: “comprising”) The word “comprising” means “including the following but not excluding others.” ... (Alternative 2: “consisting of”) The word “consisting of” means “including the following and excluding others.” ... (Alternative 3: “consisting essentially of”) means “including the following and possibly including unlisted [[components] [method steps]] that do not materially affect the invention.”
guidance: Explain how additional components/method steps affect literal infringement depending on claim open/closed language. Cite Shire Dev.; Multilayer Stretch; other Federal Circuit cases.

name: Limitations on the Doctrine of Equivalents—Prosecution History Estoppel
description: Prosecution history estoppel: if the patentee made a representation or argument, or amended a claim for reasons related to patentability, the presumption that equivalent subject matter has been surrendered may apply. I have determined, as a matter of law, that the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to certain elements of the asserted claims: [LIST ELEMENTS]. Consequently each of the elements above must be literally present within [the Defendant]’s [[product] [method]] for there to be infringement of the claim.
guidance: This instruction given only if the Court has determined prosecution history estoppel applies as a matter of law. Explain presumption and how it can be rebutted (Festo). Cite Festo; Warner-Jenkinson.

name: Limitations on the Doctrine of Equivalents—Subject Matter Dedicated to the Public
description: If the Court has determined that certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to the listed elements. Consequently each of the elements above must be literally present for there to be infringement of the claim.
guidance: Give only where court has determined dedication applies as a matter of law. Cite SanDisk; Pfizer; PSC Computer Prods.; Toro; Johnson & Johnston.

name: Actively Inducing Patent Infringement (Inducement)
description: To establish that [the Defendant] actively induced infringement, [the Plaintiff] must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (A) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement ... and (B) [the Defendant] actively induced these acts of infringement by [alleged direct infringer]. To prove active inducement, [the Plaintiff] must establish that it is more likely than not that: (1) [the Defendant] aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with the intent to cause acts ... that would constitute direct infringement; (2) [the Defendant] knew of the patent, or showed willful blindness to the existence of the patent, at that time; (3) [the Defendant] knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the [alleged direct infringer] would infringe at least one claim of the patent; and (4) [alleged direct infringer] infringed at least one patent claim.
guidance: Plaintiff must prove all four elements. Define willful blindness: subjective belief of high probability a patent existed and deliberate actions to avoid learning of the patent. Cite 35 U.S.C. §271(b) and cases (Commil; Limelight; Global-Tech; Takeda; Info-Hold; DSU; Metabolite; Ferguson; Hewlett-Packard). Practice note: clarify difference between joint infringement and inducement.

name: Infringement by Supply of All or a Substantial Portion of the Components to Another Country (§271(f)(1))
description: [Plaintiff] asserts that [Defendant] infringed by supplying all or a substantial portion of the components of the patented product from the United States to another country and actively inducing the assembly of those components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the United States. To show infringement under §271(f)(1), [Plaintiff] must prove more likely than not: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one claim; (2) [Defendant] supplied components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention; and (3) [Defendant] specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into an infringing product.
guidance: A 'substantial portion' requires a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment—the export of a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability. Practice note: §271(f)(1) does not apply to method claims. Cite 35 U.S.C. §271(f)(1); Life Techs.; Cardiac Pacemakers; Microsoft.

name: Infringement by Supply of Components Especially Made or Adapted (§271(f)(2))
description: Plaintiff asserts that Defendant infringed by supplying components of a claimed invention from the U.S. into a foreign country where the exported components were especially made or adapted for use in an invention covered by the patent and have no substantial non-infringing uses, and where Defendant knew the components were especially made or adapted and intended for the components to be combined in a way that would have infringed the patent if combined in the U.S. To show infringement under §271(f)(2) Plaintiff must prove: (1) Defendant actually supplied the components from the U.S. into a foreign country; (2) Defendant knew or should have known components were especially made/adapted for use in an infringing product; (3) components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) Defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually were combined abroad; intent to combine into an infringing product suffices. Cite 35 U.S.C. §271(f)(2); WesternGeco; Microsoft; Cardiac Pacemakers; Waymark; Rotec.

name: Summary of Invalidity Defense (Burden and Contentions)
description: [The Defendant] contends that the asserted claim(s) of the patent[s]-in-suit are invalid. [The Defendant] must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid. Claims of an issued patent may be found to be invalid. Thus, you must determine whether each of [the Plaintiff]’s claims is invalid. [The Defendant] contends that patent claims [insert claim numbers] are invalid for the following reasons: [Insert invalidity contentions]
guidance: Court will instruct in more detail on invalidity grounds. Note the heightened burden (clear and convincing) for proving invalidity of issued patent claims. Include specific invalidity contentions on the instruction/verdict form.

name: 0600 - 600 Parts, Form, and Content of Application
description: Requirements for the form and content of patent applications, including specification, claims, drawings, and required elements.
guidance: Sets standards for sufficiency of disclosure, claim format, margins, and other formal requirements.

name: 1500 - 1500 Design Patents
description: Rules and examination practice specific to design patent applications.
guidance: Covers drawing standards, claim scope, novelty and ornamentality issues unique to designs.

name: 1600 - 1600 Plant Patents
description: Guidance on plant patent practice and requirements for asexually reproduced plants.
guidance: Explains disclosure, claim requirements, and illustrations specific to plant patents.

name: Identify any judicial exception
description: Evaluate whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
guidance: Examine the claim elements to see if they recite an exception (e.g., mathematical relationship, product of nature). If an exception is recited, proceed to determine whether the claim is directed to that exception (Steps 2A/2B) or whether other limitations remove it from being 'directed to' the exception.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) for eligibility analysis
description: Interpret the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation when performing the eligibility analysis and when identifying closest natural counterparts for nature-based claims.
guidance: Use the BRI to identify embodiments encompassed by the claim (e.g., a vaccine claim's BRI may include a peptide mixed with water). The BRI affects whether a claim reads on a natural counterpart or a mere combination of natural products.

name: Markedly different characteristics (nature-based products)
description: For claims reciting nature-based products, compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine if it has markedly different characteristics (structural or functional).
guidance: If the claimed nature-based product exhibits marked differences from the natural counterpart (e.g., a nucleotide mutation in a live attenuated virus; formalin-induced chemical modification of a virus), it is not a 'product of nature' exception. Structural differences that produce functional changes support eligibility (Myriad and Chakrabarty analogies).

name: Mixtures and carriers: assess whether combination changes properties
description: When a claim recites a mixture of naturally occurring components, determine whether mixing changes the structure, function, or other properties of the components in a marked way.
guidance: A mere mixture (e.g., peptide + water) that does not alter the components' structure/function and is routine/conventional does not show markedly different characteristics and thus may be an ineligible 'product of nature' (compare Funk Brothers). Conversely, reciting a specific carrier form (e.g., cream/emulsion) that imposes structural/physical changes can confer eligibility.

name: Step 2A analysis (when applicable)
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether the claim as a whole is nonetheless not directed to the exception because it integrates the exception into a practical application or recites markedly different characteristics.
guidance: Claims that integrate a mathematical relationship into a technical control scheme (e.g., Arrhenius equation used to control press timing) or that recite nature-based products with markedly different characteristics can be resolved at Step 2A (NO to exception) without proceeding to full Step 2B analysis.

name: Step 2B: 'significantly more' inquiry
description: When a claim is determined to be directed to a judicial exception at Step 2A, analyze whether additional elements, or an ordered combination of elements, provide significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Look for meaningful limitations that limit the use of the exception and improve a technical field (e.g., ordered combination of sensors, specific control systems that improve rubber molding or engine technology). Generic or routine computer components used only to implement an abstract idea typically do not supply 'significantly more.'

name: Assess whether mathematical relationships are integrated into a technical improvement
description: For claims reciting mathematical relationships or calculations, evaluate whether the claim merely tells practitioners to use the formula in isolation or whether it integrates the mathematical concept into a technical process or device to improve technology.
guidance: Claims that merely instruct calculation/comparison are suspect; claims that use the mathematical relationship as part of a control system or specific apparatus that improves a technological process (e.g., initiating a signal to open a press when reaction time equivalence is reached) amount to 'significantly more' and are eligible.

name: Ordered combination and meaningful limitations
description: Consider whether additional claim limitations, when viewed in combination and as an ordered arrangement, provide meaningful limits on the use of any judicial exception and contribute to a technical improvement.
guidance: Even if individual elements are conventional or components of an exception, their particular ordered combination may demonstrate improved functioning in a technical field and thus render a claim eligible (examples: specific arrangements of sensors, processors, valves in engine/EGR control).

name: When to use streamlined analysis and when to document reasoning
description: If eligibility is self-evident (e.g., claim plainly amounts to significantly more or does not recite an exception), examiners may use a streamlined analysis without issuing a written rejection; however, remarks may be added to an Office action or reasons for allowance to clarify the basis.
guidance: Examples where streamlined analysis applies include claims that clearly recite a statutory category and meaningful technical limitations (internal combustion engine example, BIOS loading method). If record would benefit from clarification, add remarks that identify any recited exceptions and explain why the claim nonetheless provides meaningful limitations or improvements.

name: Practice-note: how to frame a rejection or allowance
description: If rejecting for lack of eligibility, an examiner should identify the specific exceptions in the claim and explain why the claimed subject matter lacks markedly different characteristics or why additional claim elements/combination do not amount to significantly more.
guidance: A proper rejection should point to the nature-based products or abstract ideas in the claim, explain comparison to natural counterparts, and state why combining components is routine, conventional, or fails to change properties in a marked way. Conversely, reasons for allowance may note that claimed limitations provide meaningful limitations and improve the technical field.

name: Functional vs. structural change consideration
description: Determine whether claimed changes are functional, structural, or both; structural changes that produce functional differences are persuasive for eligibility, and sometimes functional changes inseparable from structural changes will suffice.
guidance: Live attenuated virus example: nucleotide mutation (structural) resulted in reduced virulence (functional), supporting markedly different characteristics. In other cases functional changes alone may be sufficient if they are inseparable from an underlying structural change.

name: Particular/unconventional device analysis (Step 2B for nature-based claims)
description: For claims that are directed to nature-based products or exceptions, assess whether the claim recites a particular and unconventional device or implementation that amounts to significantly more.
guidance: Example: a vaccine delivery device comprising a coated microneedle array (an unconventional delivery device relative to syringes) may be eligible under Step 2B because the recited particular device can provide significantly more than the nature-based exception alone.

name: Essential Filing Requirements
description: Before submitting, pro se applicants need: Specification (detailed written description of the invention); Claims (defining the scope of protection sought); Drawings (when necessary for understanding); Abstract and title of the invention; Appropriate filing fees (varying by application type); Executed Oath or Declaration (establishing inventorship).
guidance: Ensure all listed parts are prepared and included at filing. Verify appropriate filing fees for the specific application type. Completeness and correct execution (e.g., oath/declaration) are common areas where pro se applicants make errors—review USPTO guidance before submitting.

name: Critical patentability requirements (utility patents)
description: For utility patents, inventions must be: New: Not identically disclosed in prior art. Non-obvious: Meaningfully different from existing technology. Useful: Accomplishes something with "specific, substantial, and credible" utility. Cannot be patented: Laws of nature, abstract ideas, mere ideas without complete description, or literary/artistic works.
guidance: When drafting the specification and claims, address novelty, non-obviousness, and the specific, substantial, and credible utility of the invention. Avoid claiming ineligible subject matter (laws of nature, abstract ideas, etc.) and ensure the disclosure is complete enough to support the claimed invention.

name: Pre-filing recommendation: conduct a prior art search
description: Conduct a prior art search to determine whether similar inventions already exist. The USPTO provides: Public Search Facility in Alexandria, Virginia; Patent and Trademark Resource Centers at libraries nationwide; Web-based tutorials and search strategy guides.
guidance: Use USPTO facilities and tutorials to perform searches before filing to assess novelty and patentability, refine claim scope, and reduce the likelihood of avoidable rejections. A prior art search is recommended to inform drafting and filing decisions.

name: Amendment process guidance for specifications, claims, and drawings
description: For specifications: Submit marked-up copies showing additions (underlined) and deletions (struck through), plus clean versions. For claims: Indicate status of each claim—Original, Currently amended, New, Canceled, etc. For drawings: Submit replacement sheets labeled clearly, explaining all changes in detail.
guidance: When amending, follow USPTO formatting and labeling conventions to clearly show changes and maintain clean copies. Properly categorize claim status to aid examiner review. Clearly explain drawing replacements to avoid confusion during prosecution.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (eligibility factual component)
description: Whether claimed elements are 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional activity' is a factual inquiry used in step two of the Alice test to assess the presence of an inventive concept.
guidance: The Federal Circuit has held this is a question of fact (e.g., Berkheimer), which can preclude early disposition if genuine disputes exist about conventionality; courts may consider extrinsic evidence about the state of the art.

name: Intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence and who decides
description: When only intrinsic evidence (patent claims, specification, prosecution history) is at issue, resolution is a judicial determination of law; when extrinsic evidence about the state of the art is relevant, factual issues may arise for the finder of fact.
guidance: Teva explains that intrinsic-only questions are legal and reviewed de novo; the article warns that Berkheimer sometimes treated specification statements as creating factual disputes even though intrinsic-only disputes are typically legal.

name: Need for clear articulation of reasons supporting obviousness (avoid conclusory statements)
description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
guidance: KSR and In re Kahn require that examiners set forth factual findings and a reasoned explanation avoiding conclusory generalizations. The key is clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.

name: Examples of rebuttal evidence that may show nonobviousness
description: Applicants may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that (A) one of ordinary skill in the art could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., due to technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each element performs separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
guidance: When applicant presents such evidence, examiners should reconsider the initial obviousness determination in view of the entire record and review all rejections and proposed rejections to confirm continued viability.

name: Minimum contents and timing of a filed application (UK)
description: The filed application must contain a request for the grant of a patent, a written description of the invention including any relevant diagrams (a specification), and either immediately or within 12 months of filing, a list of claims and an abstract.
guidance: Claims and abstract may be filed up to 12 months after initial filing; ensure specification adequately discloses the invention and accompanying diagrams. (Original wording: "The filed application must contain a request for the grant of a patent, a written description of the invention including any relevant diagrams, called a specification, and, either immediately or within 12 months of filing, a list of claims and an abstract.")

name: Minimum contents and timing of a filed application (European/EPO)
description: A European application must contain a request for the grant of a European patent, a written specification, a list of claims, and an abstract; applications may declare a priority date based on an earlier application.
guidance: Applications designating the UK should include the UK among designations. Formalities examination, search and publication follow if procedural and substantive requirements are met and fees are paid. (Original wording: "The filed application must contain a request for the grant of a European patent, a written specification, a list of claims, and an abstract. Provided the procedural and substantive requirements are met and the fees paid, the application will proceed to the formalities examination, publication and search phases.")

name: Electronic Document Citation (WIPO ST.14 Standard)
description: Follow WIPO ST.14 'Recommendation for the Inclusion of References Cited in Patent Documents' for electronic documents; format similar to paper documents with additional items where appropriate.
guidance: Include (A) medium type in [ ], (B) retrieval date in [retrieved on YYYY-MM-DD], (C) 'Retrieved from' source and address, (D) DOI or unique identifier if known, (E) ISBN/ISSN where necessary, (F) indicate format when multiple renderings exist, (G) paragraph/sentence/line numbers to locate cited material, (H) claim/figure/chemical/gene/program listing numbers, (I) specific headings when page/line not available, (J) specific passage words or pagination when available.

name: Federal jurisdiction when validity, title, or infringement are put in pleadings and enter judgment
description: The Federal courts obtain jurisdiction on the ground of the subject-matter only when validity, title, or infringement are put in issue by the pleadings and must enter into the judgment.
guidance: If the defendant's proofs require the court to examine conflicting patents or priority claims to determine the plaintiff's property right, the bill must be dismissed in state court because such matters are exclusively federal. (Cites Hovey v. Rubber Tip Pencil Co., Campbell v. James, Puetz v. Bransford, etc.) See §857 and §862.

name: Contract or tort actions concerning patented articles are generally not cases affecting the monopoly (state jurisdiction)
description: Breach of contract or torts to the patented article (breach of warranty, fraud, royalties, purchase-money claims, etc.) are wrongs at common law and ordinarily are to be redressed in state tribunals and do not, by themselves, form cases arising under the Patent Laws.
guidance: The existence and scope of the monopoly are determined by Patent Law and are not altered by private contracts; such contract/tort actions remain state matters unless diversity of citizenship confers federal jurisdiction or the patent's validity/title/infringement is actually put in issue. See §864, §869.

name: Patent rights defined
description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention within the United States or importing it into the United States.
guidance: Explain to jurors that patents are granted by the USPTO and the application/specification/claims framework; claims define the scope of exclusive rights.

name: Claims define scope and are the only part infringed
description: The purpose of the claims is to particularly point out what the applicant regards as the claimed invention and to define the scope of the patent owner’s exclusive rights.
guidance: Only the claims of the patent can be infringed; written description and drawings are not themselves infringed. Use the same claim meaning for both infringement and invalidity determinations.

name: Patentability standards considered by examiner
description: In examining a patent application, the Patent Examiner searches prior art and considers whether each claim defines an invention that is new, useful, and not obvious, whether the claims are directed to eligible subject matter, and whether the claims are definite, enabled, and adequately described.
guidance: Explain prosecution history and Office Actions to jurors; prior art and patentability are described in jury instructions where relevant.

name: Means-plus-function (§ 112 ¶ 6 / §112(f)) claim interpretation
description: When an element is expressed as a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, the element is construed under §112: it covers the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents, not every means that performs the recited function.
guidance: Instruction 2.2 should be given only if the case involves means-plus-function claims. Provide the recited function and the corresponding structure from the specification; instruct jurors to use that interpretation for infringement and validity.

name: Literal infringement requires every claim element
description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product or method includes each and every element (or method step) in that patent claim.
guidance: Jurors must determine literal infringement with respect to each asserted claim; absence of even one element means no literal infringement of that claim.

name: Limitations on DOE—prosecution history estoppel
description: Prosecution history estoppel can limit the application of the doctrine of equivalents where claim amendments or arguments in prosecution surrendered subject matter.
guidance: Instruct jurors about any relevant prosecution history estoppel and how it affects equivalence inquiries.

name: Joint infringement / divided performance
description: Claims may be directly infringed in circumstances involving multiple actors if one party exercises control or direction over the others or if the combined actions meet all claim limitations.
guidance: Provide jury guidance on when joint or divided performance can give rise to direct infringement; adapt instructions to the evidence and contentions in the case.

name: Infringement of means-plus-function or step-plus-function claims (literal and DOE)
description: Literal infringement of means-plus-function claims requires that the accused device perform the claimed function using the structure in the specification (or equivalent). DOE analysis for such claims must consider the statutory and precedential constraints.
guidance: Give the special instruction for means-plus-function elements as required, and explain how equivalents are evaluated given the claim construction.

name: Construction and meaning of transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of')
description: Clarify how transitional claim language affects claim scope (e.g., 'comprising' is inclusive; 'consisting of' is closed; 'consisting essentially of' permits unrecited elements that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristics).
guidance: Provide tailored instruction defining the transitional term(s) used in the asserted claims.

name: Indirect infringement—inducement and contributory infringement
description: A claim may be indirectly infringed if a defendant induces another to infringe or contributes to another's infringement (e.g., by supplying a component especially made for use in the invention).
guidance: Distinguish inducement from contributory infringement; instruct jurors on elements that must be proven for each form of indirect infringement under §271 and relevant case law.

name: Summary of invalidity defenses
description: Defendant contends that asserted claims are invalid or unenforceable; the jury must decide invalidity for each challenged claim.
guidance: Explain that invalidity can be based on anticipation, obviousness, lack of written description, lack of enablement, or statutory bars, among others, and that defendant bears burden by clear and convincing evidence.

name: Anticipation—prior public knowledge and printed publication
description: Anticipation requires that the claimed invention was known or described in the prior art (including prior public knowledge and printed publications) before the Cutoff Date.
guidance: Separate AIA and pre-AIA Cutoff Date rules; evaluate whether a reference qualifies as prior art and whether it discloses every element of the claim.

name: Obviousness—Graham factors / four-factor framework
description: Obviousness should be assessed using (1) the scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art, and (4) secondary considerations (other considerations).
guidance: Explain how to apply these factors and weigh them collectively; include examples of secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, and failure of others.

name: Willful infringement—standard
description: If infringement is found, the jury must determine whether the infringement was willful. Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant knew of the patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
guidance: Consider whether the defendant’s behavior was deliberate or intentional and assess all circumstances and the defendant’s knowledge at the time of the conduct. A mere knowledge of the patent, without deliberate or intentional infringement, is insufficient to prove willfulness.

name: Use of Practice Notes and bracketed terms
description: Practice Notes are provided as practical guidance but are not statements of law and are not intended to be included in jury instructions. Bracketed terms (e.g., [the Plaintiff], [claims in dispute]) are provided for find-and-replace customization.
guidance: Customize bracketed language to case facts; remove instructions or alternatives not applicable to the case (e.g., if doctrine of equivalents or certain defenses are not at issue).

name: Doctrine of Equivalents — limitation by Prosecution History Estoppel
description: Prosecution history estoppel is determined by the Court; only give the following instruction if the Court has determined estoppel applies as a matter of law. If estoppel applies, the patentee made a representation/argument or amended a claim for reasons related to patentability and has not rebutted the presumption that equivalent subject matter was surrendered.
guidance: If court has determined estoppel applies, list the specific claim elements (claim-by-claim) to which DOE cannot be applied. For those elements, each must be literally present in the accused product/method to find infringement; remaining elements may be judged under DOE. Cites Festo and Warner-Jenkinson.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents — limitation by Dedication to the Public
description: If the Court determines that certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those listed claim elements.
guidance: When dedication to the public is found as a matter of law, identify elements (claim-by-claim) excluded from DOE; those elements must be literally present for infringement. Remaining elements may be evaluated under DOE. Cites SanDisk, Pfizer, PSC Computer Prods., Toro, Johnson & Johnston.

name: Active Inducement to Infringe — prima facie elements
description: To establish active inducement, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/method steps accused infringe at least one claim), and (2) the defendant actively induced these acts of infringement by the alleged direct infringer.
guidance: If both joint infringement and inducement instructions are given, consider presenting them back-to-back to clarify differences and required evidence. Cites 35 U.S.C. §271(b) and cases including Commil, Limelight, Global-Tech.

name: Active Inducement — detailed elements (intent/knowledge/willful blindness/direct infringement)
description: To prove active inducement, plaintiff must establish by a preponderance that: (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with the intent to cause acts by the alleged direct infringer that would constitute direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent, or showed willful blindness to its existence at that time; (3) the defendant knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one patent claim.
guidance: Definition of willful blindness: (1) defendant subjectively believed there was a high probability a patent existed covering the accused product/method, and (2) defendant took deliberate actions to avoid learning of the patent. Plaintiff must prove all four elements by a preponderance.

name: Infringement under §271(f)(1) — supply of all or a substantial portion abroad
description: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(1), plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that: (1) the product, as intended to be assembled outside the U.S., included all elements of at least one claim; (2) the defendant supplied (or caused to be supplied) components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention of any one claim; and (3) the defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into a product that would infringe the patent if combined in the U.S.
guidance: A 'substantial portion' is a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment—export of a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability under §271(f)(1). Practice note: §271(f)(1) does not apply to method claims; cites Life Techs., Cardiac Pacemakers, Microsoft.

name: Infringement under §271(g) — import/sale/use of product made by patented process
description: To show infringement under Section 271(g), plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that: (1) defendant imported into the U.S. or, within the U.S., sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the patent; (2) the product was made between the issue date of the patent and expiration (or date of trial); and (3) defendant imported/sold/offered/used the product between the issue date and expiration (or date of trial).
guidance: Determine whether evidence establishes the product was 'made by' the claimed process. If product was materially changed by later processes, or is only a trivial/non-essential part of another product, find it was not 'made by' the claimed process. Infringement under §271(g) does not require a single entity to perform the patented process. Cites §271(g) and relevant cases.

name: Summary of Invalidity Defense — burden and scope
description: Defendant contends asserted claim(s) are invalid and must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
guidance: Jury should determine whether each of plaintiff's claims is invalid; identify defendant's specific invalidity contentions and instruct in detail on why defendant alleges invalidity for each asserted claim.

name: Invalidity of Independent and Dependent Claims — how to evaluate
description: There are independent claims (do not refer to other claims) and dependent claims (refer to at least one other claim). A dependent claim includes all elements recited in it and all elements of the claim to which it refers. You must evaluate invalidity for each asserted claim separately.
guidance: Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims that depend from it are not automatically invalid — decide validity claim-by-claim. However, if you find a dependent claim invalid, you must find the independent claim from which it depends also invalid. Provide examples and identify differences between specific independent/dependent claims. Cites Federal Circuit authority.

name: Anticipation — newness requirement and single-reference test
description: To prove anticipation, defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention is not new. To anticipate a claim, each element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim; you may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation.
guidance: Consider what a POSITA would have understood from the particular publication/patent/etc. If inherent anticipation is alleged, instruct on inherency: a missing element is inherently present if it necessarily results from the prior art reference; necessity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence. Evidence outside the reference (including testing) may be used to show inherency. Cites many Federal Circuit authorities and practice note on inherency.

name: Prior Public Use (pre-AIA) — public use and readiness for patenting
description: Defendant contends claims are invalid because the invention was publicly used by others in the U.S. before the relevant Cutoff Date or more than one year before the patentee filed. An invention was publicly used if an embodiment was both (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the U.S., and (2) ready for patenting.
guidance: Factors for public use: nature of activity, public access, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation (even if specifics kept secret), circumstances of testing/experimentation; absence of steps to conceal is evidence of public use. Secret use by a third party is not public unless public or employees had access. 'Ready for patenting' means reduced to practice or having drawings/descriptions enabling a POSITA to make/use the invention. Reduction to practice requires constructing an embodiment or performing the process and determining it would work for its intended purpose. Cites pre-AIA §102(a),(b) and numerous cases (Pfaff, Am. Seating, etc.).

name: Determine Whether Each Claim Limitation Invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, ¶6
description: As part of the claim interpretation analysis, examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, ¶ 6 (means-plus-function) or not.
guidance: If the claim limitation invokes 112, ¶ 6, the claim limitation must "be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof." See PART 1, section III.C for more information regarding the determination and means-plus-function claim limitations.

name: Definiteness under § 112, ¶ 2
description: A decision on whether a claim is indefinite requires determining whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.
guidance: Claim terms are typically given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; analyze claim terms in view of the specification from the perspective of those skilled in the relevant art.

name: Functional Claiming (when claim recites what it does rather than what it is)
description: A claim term is functional when it recites a feature 'by what it does rather than by what it is.' §112, ¶6 expressly authorizes a form of functional claiming (means-plus-function), and functional language can be used outside means-plus-function format (structure followed by function).
guidance: Functional language is permissible but may be indefinite if it fails to provide a clear-cut indication of scope (e.g., merely stating a problem to be solved or a result achieved) or if it encompasses all means/methods without reciting structure/material/steps. Such unlimited functional limitations may lack written description or enablement under §112, ¶1.

name: Factors for Determining Ambiguity of Functional Language
description: When a claim limitation employs functional language, the examiner’s determination of whether the limitation is sufficiently definite depends on context (specification disclosure and knowledge of a person of ordinary skill).
guidance: Consider (1) whether there is a clear-cut indication of the scope covered by the claim; (2) whether the language sets forth well-defined boundaries or only states a problem/result; and (3) whether one of ordinary skill in the art would know from the claim terms what structure or steps are encompassed. These are examples and not exhaustive.

name: Remedies for Ambiguous Functional Limitations During Prosecution
description: Applicant may resolve ambiguities of a functional limitation in multiple ways during prosecution.
guidance: Examples include: (1) using a quantitative metric (numeric limitation); (2) providing a formula and examples that meet and do not meet the limitation; (3) providing general guidelines and examples sufficient for a skilled person to determine when the limitation is satisfied; or (4) amending the claims to recite the particular structure that accomplishes the function.

name: Terms of Degree
description: When a term of degree is used in the claim, the examiner should determine whether the specification provides some standard for measuring that degree.
guidance: If the specification lacks a standard, determine whether one of ordinary skill could nevertheless ascertain the scope (e.g., recognized art standard, figures). The claim is not indefinite if the specification provides examples or teachings usable to measure the degree. An applicant may submit a 37 CFR 1.132 declaration showing examples and non-examples.

name: Markush Groups
description: A 'Markush' claim recites a list of alternatively useable species (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C'); such claims are not necessarily indefinite for breadth, but may be in certain circumstances.
guidance: A Markush group may be indefinite if so expansive that skilled persons cannot determine the metes and bounds due to inability to envision all members. Under compact prosecution, examiner should require election of species for search/examination and extend search to species that share a single structural similarity and common use when appropriate.

name: Improper Markush Grouping Doctrine
description: A Markush claim contains an 'improper Markush grouping' if the species do not share a 'single structural similarity' or a common use.
guidance: Single structural similarity means membership in the same recognized physical/chemical or art-recognized class; common use means disclosed in the specification or known to be functionally equivalent. Examiner should reject for improper grouping until applicant amends to include only species sharing the similarity/use or shows they do share it. Claim may be rejected under §112, ¶2 and/or improper grouping doctrine.

name: Dependent Claims Must Comply with § 112, ¶ 4
description: Dependent claims must contain a reference to a previous claim in the same application, specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed, and necessarily include all the limitations of the previous claim.
guidance: If a dependent claim omits an element from its base claim or fails to add a limitation, the examiner should reject the dependent claim under §112, ¶4 (unpatentable), rather than merely objecting as a form matter.

name: Correspondence Between Specification and Claims / Antecedent Basis (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1))
description: The specification should serve as a glossary to claim terms so examiners and the public can ascertain their meaning; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification.
guidance: Exact claim terms are not required if specification provides needed guidance via equivalent terms. Express definitions (glossaries) are encouraged as best practice. If needed support or antecedent basis is missing, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require amendment to description or claim amendments (without introducing new matter).

name: Internal Consistency Between Claim and Specification
description: A claim, although clear on its face, may be indefinite when a conflict or inconsistency between the claimed subject matter and the specification disclosure renders scope uncertain.
guidance: Examples include claim terms contradicted by specification definitions or examples; examiner should treat internally inconsistent claims as indefinite and explain why in Office action.

name: Presumption that 'means for' or 'step for' Invokes § 112, ¶ 6
description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke §112, ¶6 when it explicitly uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language.
guidance: That presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function.

name: Presumption that Absence of 'means for' or 'step for' Does Not Invoke § 112, ¶ 6
description: A claim limitation that does not use 'means for' or 'step for' triggers the rebuttable presumption that §112, ¶6 does not apply; this presumption is strong and not readily overcome.
guidance: It may be overcome if the claim uses a non-structural term that is a nonce word or verbal construct substituting for 'means for' and is associated with functional language, unless the term is understood by a skilled person to name structure.

name: Non-structural Terms That May Invoke §112, ¶6 and Structural Terms That Do Not
description: Examiners should determine whether a claim uses non-structural terms (which may invoke ¶6) or structural terms (which do not).
guidance: Non-structural examples that may invoke ¶6 include 'mechanism for,' 'module for,' 'device for,' 'unit for,' 'component for,' 'element for,' 'member for,' 'apparatus for,' 'machine for,' or 'system for' (list not exhaustive). Structural terms found not to invoke ¶6 include 'circuit for,' 'detent mechanism,' 'digital detector for,' 'reciprocating member,' 'connector assembly,' 'perforation,' 'sealingly connected joints,' and 'eyeglass hanger member.' A structural modifier preceding a non-structural term (e.g., 'detent mechanism') can avoid invocation of ¶6; a non-structural modifier does not.

name: Tests to Determine Whether a Word/Term/Phrase Denotes Structure
description: To determine whether a term coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners should check whether the specification and external evidence indicate structural meaning.
guidance: Check (1) whether the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill that the term denotes structure; (2) whether general or subject-matter dictionaries provide evidence the term is recognized as a noun denoting structure; and (3) whether the prior art provides evidence the term has an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.

name: Conditions Under Which Examiners Will Apply §112, ¶6
description: Examiners will apply §112, ¶6 to a claim limitation that meets certain conditions.
guidance: Apply ¶6 when (1) the claim uses 'means for'/'step for' or a non-structural term without a structural modifier; (2) the phrase or non-structural term is modified by functional language; and (3) the phrase or non-structural term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts to achieve the specified function. Note: this guideline modifies the 3-prong analysis in MPEP §2181.

name: Rejections Under §112, ¶2 When Examining Means-Plus-Function Limitations
description: Once a claim limitation is determined to be a means-plus-function limitation invoking §112, ¶6, the examiner should determine the claimed function and then review the written description to identify corresponding structure/material/acts.
guidance: The disclosure must be reviewed from the viewpoint of one skilled in the art to determine whether the written description discloses the corresponding structure/material/acts and clearly links them to the claimed function. Rejection under §112, ¶2 is appropriate if there is no disclosure or insufficient disclosure, or no clear link/association. A bare statement that known techniques can be used is insufficient. Examiner may require information under 37 CFR 1.105 to identify corresponding structure; failure to identify supports rejection.

name: Construction of Means-Plus-Function Limitations When Supported
description: If the written description sets forth the corresponding structure/material/acts in compliance with §112, ¶2, the claim limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Functional limitations not recited in the claim, or structural limitations in the specification that are unnecessary to perform the claimed function, cannot be imported into the claim.

name: Computer-Implemented Means-Plus-Function Limitations Require an Algorithm
description: For a computer-implemented means-plus-function claim invoking §112, ¶6, the corresponding structure must be more than simply a general purpose computer or microprocessor; it must include the algorithm needed to transform the general purpose computer to a special purpose computer.
guidance: An algorithm may be expressed as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flowchart, or other manner providing sufficient structure. Mere reference to a general purpose computer with appropriate programming, or simply reciting 'software,' 'logic,' 'code,' or undefined computer components is insufficient. If no corresponding algorithm is disclosed, §112, ¶2 rejection is appropriate.

name: Office Action Should Provide a Sufficient Explanation for Indefiniteness Rejection
description: The Office action must set forth the specific term or phrase that is indefinite and explain why the metes and bounds are unclear, providing enough information for the applicant to prepare a meaningful response.
guidance: Indicate the specific term, explain in detail why it renders claim scope unclear, and whenever practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness issues may be resolved to overcome the rejection. Claims receive their broadest reasonable interpretation during prosecution to facilitate sharpening and clarifying.

name: Scope of institution decision
description: Under the rules, the Board may authorize the review to proceed on all or some of the challenged claims and on all or some of the grounds of unpatentability asserted for each claim. (§§ 42.108(a) and 42.208(a))
guidance: The decision to institute can be claim-by-claim and ground-by-ground; the Board has discretion to limit proceedings to particular claims/grounds to streamline issues for consideration.

name: Statutory threshold for instituting review
description: Review will not be instituted unless the Board decides that the petition supporting the ground would demonstrate that there is a reasonable likelihood (for inter partes proceedings), or more likely than not (for post-grant proceedings), that at least one of the claims is unpatentable. (35 U.S.C. 314(a) and 324(a))
guidance: A 'reasonable likelihood' is a lower threshold than 'more likely than not.' Whether the petitioner meets the threshold must be considered case-by-case. The rules adopt the statutory thresholds rather than further defining them.

name: Consideration of timeliness and complexity in institution
description: The Office may take into account whether the review could be timely completed and may decline to institute where it could not complete the proceeding timely.
guidance: Examples where Board may decline: petitions seeking review of several hundred claims based on a thousand references, or where determination would require dozens of depositions of non-party witnesses in foreign countries requiring compelled testimony. The AIA requires consideration of the integrity of the patent system, efficient administration, and ability to complete proceedings timely (35 U.S.C. 316(b), 326(b)).

name: Deadline for first motion to amend
description: Unless a due date is provided in a Board order, a motion to amend must be filed no later than the filing of a patent owner response. (§§ 42.121(a)(1) and 42.221(a)(1))
guidance: The first motion to amend does not require Board authorization but does require the patent owner to 'confer with the Board' (e.g., a conference call to identify intent and number/scope of substitute claims).

name: Amendment substantive restrictions (no new matter, no enlargement, must respond to grounds)
description: Any motions to amend (including the first motion) may be denied where the amendment does not respond to a ground of unpatentability, seeks to enlarge the scope of the claims, or introduces new matter. Failure to comply with any requirement may result in denial. (§§ 42.121, 42.221)
guidance: Amendments should narrow claims and be responsive to grounds of unpatentability; amendments not meeting these requirements will be denied rather than entered and substantively rejected later.

name: Form and support requirements for proposed substitute claims
description: Amendments must clearly state 'original,' 'cancelled,' 'replaced by proposed substitute,' or 'proposed substitute for original claim X' and the motion must clearly describe the changes. Amendments should clearly state where the specification and any drawings disclose all the limitations in the proposed substitute claims and the patentably distinct features. (§ Part II, Item G of the Patent Trial Practice Guide referenced)
guidance: Acceptable substitute claim example: adds a patentably distinct feature to respond to a ground without adding new matter or enlarging scope. Conforming amendments may be presented. This aids the Board in assessing whether the amendment narrows claims and responds to grounds.

name: Procedure for presenting number/need for substitute claims (conference call and scheduling order)
description: The Board will enter a Scheduling Order concurrently with the decision to institute the review. An initial conference call will be held about one month from the date of institution to discuss intended motions and determine if scheduling adjustments are needed; during the call the patent owner identifies the number of substitute claims intended and reasons why more than one per claim is needed.
guidance: The Board may indicate whether the number of substitute claims seems reasonable based on reasons given. Patent owner is not required to identify a fully developed claim set at the call.

name: Amendments are not permitted in the patent owner’s preliminary response
description: A motion to amend the patent is not provided for until after the institution of a review. (35 U.S.C. 316(d)(1) and 326(d)(1))
guidance: Patent owner may discuss scope of intended substitute claims during the conference call, but formal claim amendments require filing a motion to amend after institution.

name: Claims lacking support / insufficient disclosure
description: Broad or speculative claims supported only by a limited disclosure may render a meaningful search over the whole claim impossible.
guidance: In such cases a meaningful search could be performed only on the narrower, disclosed invention (e.g., specific examples). A complete search may be de facto impossible or of no useful purpose if the claim's breadth makes it indefensible in subsequent prosecution.

name: Claims lacking conciseness
description: A claim set with so many claims or possibilities that it is unduly burdensome to determine the matter for which protection is sought can render a complete search impossible.
guidance: Where lack of conciseness makes the search de facto impossible or the claim set indefensible, the search may be restricted or not carried out in full.

name: Claims lacking clarity (parameters preventing comparison)
description: If the applicant defines the invention by parameters that prevent meaningful comparison with prior art (e.g., prior art uses different or no parameter), clarity is lacking and a meaningful search may be impossible.
guidance: Search may be restricted to worked examples or to how the desired parameter is obtained; the basic principle is clarity and openness about what has and has not been searched.

name: Purpose of the abstract
description: The application must contain an abstract whose purpose is to give brief technical information about the disclosure in the description, claims and drawings.
guidance: The examiner determines the definitive content; the abstract is for technical information only and must not be used to interpret the scope of protection sought. It should be drafted as an efficient instrument for searching in the technical field.

name: Utility patent eligibility (definition)
description: Utility patents may be granted to anyone who invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, article of manufacture (AofM), or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.
guidance: Provides the statutory subject-matter categories for utility patents and scope of what may be claimed; points users to the Patent Basics webpage for application and maintenance procedures.

name: Patent statutory compliance metric — 35 U.S.C. §112 (written description / claims / 112(f))
description: Percent measure evaluating statutory compliance on Section 112 (35 U.S.C. §112(a), (b), including (a)/(b) rejections related to 35 U.S.C. §112(f)).
guidance: Monitors written description, enablement, definiteness, and claim construction/means-plus-function compliance; FY2023 actual (94.4%, Exceeded).

name: Reissue applications and adding non-corresponding claims
description: The Board does not permit reissue applicants to add claims that would not correspond to a count (Winter v. Fujita).
guidance: Reissue applications are not subject to patent term adjustments; burden lies with the reissue applicant to comply with Winter, so an examiner need not require restriction of non-interfering claims. Practice under Winter may explain multiple reissue filings by an applicant who seeks to amend claims in response to an interference.

name: Avoid unnecessary suspensions; issue allowed claims
description: Suspensions should rarely, if ever, be used and applications with allowed claims should be issued to the greatest extent possible (because applicants may be eligible for patent term adjustments).
guidance: Examples: (1) An interference may not be declared between two patents — do not hold an allowable claim to issue simply to await interference. (2) If one application is complete and the other is not, the complete application should generally issue; suspensions must not be used to create ties between applications. If issuance as patent creates prior art, appropriate rejections should be made or a priority showing required (37 CFR 41.202(d)).

name: Interference search requirement when application in condition for allowance
description: When an application is in condition for allowance, an interference search must be made using the most efficient and effective means based on the claimed subject matter in the broadest claim (text search, classified search, or combination, of US-PGPUB database).
guidance: Consider each effective filing date (continuation-in-part issues) when searching. If claims involve nucleotide/amino acid sequences, request STIC to perform sequence interference search. Make the search of record (MPEP § 719.05 III). Search must be extended to all classes/subgroups necessary (not limited to classification of the application). Include applications under Secrecy Order when required; request inspection of paper files/prints/drawings via Licensing and Review when needed.

name: Sorting and consolidating claims to mitigate interference delay
description: If an applicant has related applications with interfering claims intermixed with non-interfering claims, the examiner should consider consolidating interfering claims into a single application or requiring restriction of an application to non-interfering claims so examination can proceed for non-interfering claims.
guidance: Interfering claims of applications with same assignee or inventive entity are 'patentably indistinct claims' under 37 CFR 1.78(f); the examiner may require consolidation into a single application that provides support. Alternatively require restriction in accordance with pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 121 and permit a divisional for non-interfering claims. Do not consolidate a claim into an application that lacks 35 U.S.C. 112(a) support.

name: Applicant suggestion formal requirements (37 CFR 41.202(a) checklist)
description: When an applicant suggests an interference, the suggestion must: (1) provide sufficient information to identify the other application/patent; (2) identify all claims the applicant believes interfere, propose one or more counts, and show claim-to-count correspondence; (3) for each count provide a claim chart comparing at least one claim of each party and show why they interfere under § 41.203(a); (4) explain in detail why applicant will prevail on priority; (5) if a claim was added/amended to provoke an interference provide a claim chart showing written description for each claim in the applicant’s specification; (6) for each constructive reduction to practice for which benefit is requested provide a chart showing where the disclosure provides that constructive reduction-to-practice.
guidance: Form paragraphs 23.06–23.06.06 may be used to acknowledge or indicate specific formal deficiencies. Examiner reviews for formal sufficiency but is generally not responsible for substantive adequacy of priority showings, though may offer observations to accompany referral to the Board (Form PTO-850).

name: Counts and requirement to identify patentable claims for each count
description: Applicant must identify at least one patentable claim from every application or patent that interferes for each proposed count; a count describes the interfering subject matter used by the Board to determine admissible priority evidence.
guidance: Examiner must confirm that (A) at least one patentable count is identified, (B) at least one patentable claim from each party is identified for each count, and (C) a claim chart comparing at least one set of claims for each count is provided. Examiner need not agree with applicant’s substantive position—role is to confirm interfering claims and formalities of 37 CFR 41.202 are met.

name: Compliance with pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b) (one‑year rule)
description: If a claim was added or an application filed more than one year after issuance/publication of the potentially interfering patent/application, an interference will not be declared unless at least one claim present prior to the one‑year cutoff is for 'substantially the same subject matter' as a claim of the patent/published application.
guidance: The determination uses a 'substantially the same' test based on presence/absence of different material limitations (not an obviousness test). If none of the pre‑cutoff claims meet the test, the interfering claim should be rejected under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b). Form paragraphs 23.14 and 23.14.01 may be used for rejections under 135(b)(1) and 135(b)(2).

name: Adequate written description requirement for interfering claims
description: An applicant is not entitled to an interference merely because the applicant requests one—the interfering claim must be allowable with respect to written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a); written description is satisfied if the application/priority application sufficiently describes the subject matter to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Written description does not necessarily require examples or an actual reduction-to-practice. Added or amended claims to provoke an interference receive heightened scrutiny; copied claims are construed in view of the originating specification when challenged. Written description unavailability can be a threshold issue in an interference.

name: Requirement to provide written-description claim chart for added/amended provocation claims
description: If a claim has been added or amended to provoke an interference, applicant must provide a claim chart showing the written description for each claim in the applicant's specification (37 CFR 41.202(a)(5)).
guidance: Form paragraph 23.06.05 addresses failure to provide such a chart. Failure to show written description support is a formal deficiency and a substantive threshold for entitlement to interference.

name: Patentee limitations on suggesting interference
description: A patentee cannot suggest an interference under 37 CFR 41.202 but may, to the extent permitted under 37 CFR 1.291, alert the examiner of an application claiming interfering subject matter.
guidance: A patentee may only suggest via becoming an applicant (e.g., by filing a reissue application) or by alerting the examiner under limited rules; see MPEP §§ 1134 and 1901 for guidance.

name: Guiding principles for examiner discretion in requiring a claim
description: Principles to guide whether an examiner should require an interfering claim: (A) generally do not suggest interference if examination is not otherwise completed; (B) the required claim must not encompass prior art or otherwise be barred; (C) the application must provide adequate support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for the required claim; (D) do not require a claim when applicant expressly states the commonly described subject matter is not the applicant’s invention; (E) a claim based on a claim from a published application should not be required unless that published claim has been allowed.
guidance: Given cost and complexity of interferences, the requirement should not be lightly made; consult with IPS before making the requirement. Examples illustrate when a requirement is inappropriate (e.g., patent is prior art, time-bar issues).

name: Whole-application review for allowance
description: Before allowance, the examiner must review the entire application to ensure it meets all formal and substantive (statutory) requirements and that claim language is enabled by and has adequate descriptive support in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: Neglect may lead to confusion as to scope. Ensure clear support/antecedent basis for terminology used in claims. Exact terms need not appear verbatim but substantial correspondence is required (37 CFR 1.121(e)). See cited case law (Eiselstein v. Frank; In re Wertheim) and MPEP §§ 608.01(o), 608.01(j), 608.01(n).

name: Antecedent basis and terminology consistency
description: There should be clear support or antecedent basis in the specification for terminology used in the claims; amending/adding terms not appearing in the specification can create uncertainty.
guidance: Check that claim terms track the specification; avoid introducing unsupported special definitions. See MPEP § 608.01(o).

name: Limits on examiner corrections to written record
description: Examiners may not make corrections/interlineations in the body of written portions of the specification or other papers except via examiner’s amendment approved by applicant, except for enumerated exceptions (A–F).
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.121. Exceptions include: (A) renumbering claims (37 CFR 1.126); (B) correcting erroneous citations on IDS; (C) correcting non-compliant 1.312 amendments whose entry would otherwise be recommended; (D) canceling non-elected claims (no traverse) not eligible for rejoinder; (E) amending title to correspond with claim when Office has established title; (F) amendment/cancellation of claims following PTAB decisions (MPEP §§ 1214, etc.).

name: Handling parent references for continuing applications
description: For continuing applications filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b), a parent-application reference in the first sentence of the specification is no longer required if the reference is in the Application Data Sheet; the examiner should not add such a reference without applicant approval.
guidance: Verify Applicant Data Sheet accuracy; applicant may delete benefit claim; petition under 37 CFR 1.78 may be required for unintentionally delayed benefit claims for certain filings. See MPEP § 211.04 and § 601.05.

name: Scope of examiner’s amendments for expediting allowance
description: 37 CFR 1.121(g) permits examiner’s amendments to make additions/deletions to the specification/claims without complying with certain 1.121(b)/(c) formalities to expedite prosecution and reduce cycle time.
guidance: Examiners may instruct technical staff to make precise changes. Examiner’s amendments can correct non-compliant applicant amendments that would otherwise place the application in condition for allowance (see MPEP § 714, II.E).

name: Examiner’s amendments by fax/email and attachments
description: A clean-version paragraph/claim or portions submitted by applicant via fax or email (requested by examiner) may be attached and relied upon as part of an examiner’s amendment, but the attachment must be marked “requested” to avoid patent term adjustment reductions.
guidance: Print and attach the email/fax to the examiner’s amendment; the paper copy should be entered in the file. Examiners are not required to retain electronic copies once printed. Email exceptions are limited to applicant-to-examiner emails complying with MPEP § 502.03.

name: Substantive changes to abstract/specification require applicant approval
description: No examiner’s amendment may make substantive changes to the written portions of the specification, including the abstract, without first obtaining applicant’s approval.
guidance: Because the abstract may affect claim interpretation, examiners should review and point out defects early. Case law supports that abstract can determine claim meaning (Pandrol USA; Hill-Rom).

name: Interference search before issue
description: When an application is in condition for allowance, an interference search must be made using the most efficient/effective manner based on the broadest claimed subject matter; consider all effective filing dates for CIPs and extend search beyond the application’s classification.
