guidance: Use text searches, classified searches, or combinations (e.g., US-PGPUB). For nucleotide/peptide claims, request STIC to perform sequence interference searches. Record the search in the file and extend search to all classes/subgroups used during examination. See MPEP §§ 2133.01, 2152.01, 719.05.

name: Selection of claim(s) and figure for Official Gazette printing
description: Select the broadest claim for printing; ordinarily designate one claim per invention (max five if multiple inventions). Do not select a dependent claim unless its independent claim is also printed. Select a single figure consistent with the printed claim that is not labeled 'prior art'; if none, indicate 'None'.
guidance: For reissue, select the broadest changed or additional reissue claim. Record renumbered patent claim numbers when designating print claims. For multiple claim selections separate numbers by commas; in multiple dependent selections include the entire claim chain for one embodiment.

name: Reasons for allowance — when and how to record
description: If the record does not make clear the examiner’s reasons for allowing claims, the examiner may set forth such reasoning (37 CFR 1.104(e)); reasons should be specific when record is not explicit.
guidance: Reasons for allowance are intended to improve quality/reliability of issued patents and help public/patentee evaluate scope. Include at least (1) the major difference in the claims not found in prior art of record and (2) reasons why that difference is considered patentable over the prior art (if not otherwise clear). Avoid stock, meaningless statements and avoid using reasons to improperly narrow claims by special definitions unsupported by the description. Reasons may be included in an Office action rejecting other claims or in a separate communication; applicant may comment. Be accurate and precise to avoid misinterpretation (see Festo, and MPEP guidance).

name: Three-prong analysis for § 112(f) invocation
description: Examiners are instructed to use a three-prong test to determine if a claim limitation invokes § 112(f): (1) the use of “means,” “step,” or a generic placeholder; (2) functional language associated with these terms; and (3) absence of sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: All three prongs must be considered when deciding whether §112(f) applies. The memorandum reiterates that this three-prong framework governs interpretation of means-plus-function and step-plus-function limitations. Clear recordation of the examiner's application of this test is important for prosecution and later challenges.

name: Presumption from use of 'means', 'step', or generic placeholders
description: The memo clarifies existing presumptions about the use of terms like “means” or “step” (or generic placeholders) in claims and their implications under §112(f).
guidance: Use of those words raises a presumption that §112(f) applies. That presumption can be overcome only by examining claim language and the common understanding in the relevant technological field (e.g., showing sufficient structure is recited). Examiners should carefully assess and record whether the presumption is rebutted.

name: Functional language associated with claim terms
description: A claim limitation uses functional language describing what the element does rather than reciting structure, material, or acts.
guidance: Whether language is functional should be evaluated in context. Functional recitation combined with means/step or generic placeholders supports invoking §112(f). The examiner should note how the functional language contributes to the determination and whether supporting disclosure supplies structure.

name: Absence of sufficient structure, material, or acts
description: A key prong is that the claim does not recite sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: If the claim itself recites sufficient structure (or equivalent concrete material/acts), §112(f) may not be invoked despite functional language or use of ‘means/step.’ Examiners must evaluate claim text and common knowledge in the art to determine sufficiency.

name: Adequacy of supporting disclosure under §§ 112(a) and (b)
description: For a §112(f) limitation, the adequacy of supporting disclosure must be evaluated under §§ 112(a) and (b), including assessment for definiteness, written description, and enablement.
guidance: When §112(f) applies, examiners must assess whether the specification provides the requisite structure, acts, or materials to support the claimed function and whether the disclosure satisfies definiteness, written description, and enablement requirements. Deficiencies in the specification can render the limitation indefinite or unsupported.

name: Clear linkage between functional claim language and disclosed structure/material/acts
description: Emphasize the necessity of clear linkage between the claim’s functional language and the structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification to support the claimed functions.
guidance: Patent drafters should ensure the specification ties functional claim elements to corresponding structure or algorithms (as applicable). Examiners should look for explicit connection in the specification; absent a clear linkage, the claim may be vulnerable under written description/enablement/definiteness analyses.

name: Requirement for algorithm disclosure in computer-implemented claims
description: Computer-implemented claims under §112(f) must disclose a specific algorithm for the claimed function to meet definiteness.
guidance: The algorithm may be expressed in any understandable terms — mathematical formula, prose, a flowchart, or other manner — so long as it provides sufficient structure. Drafters should include sufficiently specific algorithms; examiners will look for algorithmic disclosure to avoid indefiniteness in functional computer-implemented claim limitations.

name: Strategic drafting considerations for means-/step-plus-function limitations
description: Adding means-plus-function and step-plus-function claim limitations can provide strategic advantages but requires careful framing.
guidance: Practitioners should be attentive to how such limitations are drafted because they may affect claim scope and enforceability. Drafting may intentionally invoke or avoid §112(f) consequences; the specification should be prepared to supply adequate structure/algorithms if functional language is used.

name: Risk of narrower interpretation affecting patentability and infringement
description: §112(f) limitations may lead to a narrower interpretation of claims, influencing patentability and infringement analysis.
guidance: Because means/step limitations are limited to the structure/acts/materials disclosed and equivalents, claim scope can be narrower than comparable structural claim language. Applicants and practitioners should weigh this potential narrowing when deciding whether to use functional claim limitations.

name: Permissibility of describing claim elements as means/step without explicit supporting structure
description: The memorandum notes that claim drafters may describe an element in a claim as a means or step for performing a specified function without explicitly stating the supporting structure, material, or acts.
guidance: While permissible, doing so triggers the need for adequate supporting disclosure in the specification and careful consideration of the §112(f) consequences (see requirements for disclosure, algorithms for computer-implemented claims, and potential narrowing). Practitioners should ensure the specification supplies what will be required upon examination.

name: Maintain awareness of USPTO resources and standards
description: The memorandum reminds examiners and practitioners of resources available for examining claims under §112(f) and clarifies that it reinforces existing practices rather than introducing new legal standards.
guidance: Practitioners should stay informed about USPTO guidance and updates to ensure consistent prosecution strategy. Use USPTO resources and precedents when evaluating or drafting functional claim limitations.

name: Domestic priority claim — combination of earlier application subject-matter
description: For a domestic priority claim based on 2 or more earlier applications, when the invention of the priority claim is a combination of technical subject-matter separately stated in 2 or more first specification of earlier applications, or a combination of new technical subject-matter and those separately stated in 2 or more first specification of earlier applications, the invention of the priority claim shall be treated as an 'invention which is not stated in the first specification of earlier application'.
guidance: Treat such combination as not entitled to the earlier filing date for priority purposes; examiner must apply the rules for inventions not stated in earlier first specifications.

name: Non-retroactivity when earlier application itself claims priority
description: When the earlier application which forms a basis of the domestic priority claim claims priority based on another application filed beforehand, the effect of the priority claim shall not be recognized for the invention which is stated in both the first specification of the earlier application and another priority claim.
guidance: Examiner shall not conduct examination as of the earlier application's filing date for overlapping subject-matter; if prior art discovered prevents retroactive application, examiner must specify reason for non-retroactive application in the notice of grounds for rejection.

name: Treatment when earlier application and priority-app are identical and earlier app considered withdrawn
description: Where the inventions stated in the first specification or drawings attached to the application with domestic priority claim and those in the first specification of the earlier application are identical, the earlier application (deemed withdrawn when one year and three months has lapsed from the filing date) is regarded to be laid open at the time when the application with the priority claim is laid open or published in the patent gazette in applying Article 29(3).
guidance: Be aware of lay-open timing and withdrawal timing (1 year 3 months) when assessing prior art and novelty.

name: Requirements for application by a person entitled (lawful holder)
description: For an application to be recognized as by a lawful holder, these requirements shall be met: (①) unentitled person's application filed earlier than by lawful holder; (②) unentitled person's application is rejected or invalidated due to illegitimacy of applicant; (③) lawful holder files within thirty days from date of rejection or invalidation confirmation (with extra 'within two years from publication of registration' requirement in some invalidation cases); (④) scope of claimed invention in lawful holder's application falls within invention scope in application by unentitled person.
guidance: When lawful-holder form used, examiner shall study legitimacy before other grounds; if doubts on requirements ①, ③, ④, deliver notice that filing date shall not be retroactive; if ② not satisfied, defer examination.

name: Retroactive filing-date effect for lawful-holder applications
description: Where an application is recognized as legitimate by the lawful holder pursuant to Articles 34, 35, it is deemed to have been filed at the date when the unentitled person filed; thus judgments of patent requirements, period calculations, and related rules are determined as of that earlier date.
guidance: Third-party intervening filings between the unentitled filing and lawful-holder filing do not invalidate the lawful-holder's retroactive claim; third-party applications may be rejected based on lawful-holder's retroactive date.

name: Scope limitation for lawful-holder retroactivity
description: The scope of invention in an application by the lawful holder is limited to claimed inventions as well as those disclosed in the specification or drawings of the application by the unentitled person; inventions beyond that scope do not receive retroactive filing date.
guidance: If lawful-holder application includes inventions beyond the unentitled person's disclosure, those inventions are examined with the actual (non-retroactive) filing date.

name: International (PCT) application treated as ordinary domestic application on international filing date
description: An International Patent Application (PCT) is treated as an ordinary patent application filed on the international filing date; description, claims, and drawings submitted at international application are considered legitimate under Article 42(2).
guidance: Korean translation must be submitted per Article 201 or the international application filed in foreign language is deemed withdrawn.

name: PCT priority vs domestic priority distinctions
description: Where an international application enters domestic phase with Korean translation submitted, claiming priority under the PCT, this priority claim is treated as the priority claim under the Treaty. If the application serving as basis of the priority claim is a Korean application or an international app where Korea is the only designated State, the priority claim is considered domestic priority.
guidance: Determine whether a priority claim is Treaty-based or domestic based on identity/nature of the earlier application and designation.

name: Korean translation of PCT amendments — self-amendment treatment
description: Where Korean translation of written amendment regarding description or claims under PCT Articles 19 or 34 is submitted within the reference date, an examiner proceeds considering an international application to have been self-amended under Article 47 of the Patent Act.
guidance: Accept translations of PCT amendments submitted timely as part of domestic file history for amendment scope.

name: Scope of permissible amendments for international applications filed in foreign language
description: The scope of amendments to the specification of an international application filed in a foreign language is limited to the description, claims, or drawings (limited to explanatory parts in drawings) of its translation, or drawings (except explanatory parts) of the international application as of the international filing.
guidance: Do not permit amendments that introduce matter outside the translated materials or the original international application drawings.

name: Enumerated grounds for rejection (list of bases)
description: The grounds for rejection include: (①) claimed invention not patentable pursuant to Articles 25, 29, 32, 36(1),(3) or 44; ② no persons entitled to obtain a patent or subject to proviso of Article 33(1); ③ violation of treaty clauses; ④ requirements in Article 42(3),(4),(8) or Article 45 not satisfied; ⑤ amendment out of scope per Article 47(2); ⑥ divisional filed out of scope per Article 52(1); ⑦ converted application filed out of scope per Article 53(1)).
guidance: When issuing grounds, cite the specific statutory provisions and state grounds claim-by-claim.

name: Content and form of notice of grounds for rejection
description: When notifying grounds for rejection, the examiner shall stipulate the relevant provisions and indicate grounds on a claim-by-claim basis; statements should be definite, concise, and normal sentences.
guidance: Be specific: (i) for inventive step cite minimum necessary documents and specify parts relied upon; (ii) where alleging public knowledge/work, state specific facts; (iii) for detailed-description deficiency specify deficient parts and reasons.

name: Final notice of grounds for rejection — definition and examples
description: A final notice is issued where the ground for rejection incurs from amendments corresponding to a previously-issued notice of grounds for rejection; amendments according to prior notice are prerequisite. Examples: (1) amendments add new matter or exceed permissible division/conversion scope; (2) claim amendments cause novelty or inventive step issues; (3) newly generated/substantially changed claims contain novelty/inventive step grounds; (4) reexamination after amendment reveals novelty/inventive step grounds that were previously inexamnable.
guidance: Final notices are narrower in amendment scope allowed to applicant; see selection rules for when to issue final vs non-final.

name: Industrial applicability — third requirement (contrary to physical laws)
description: An invention fails the third industrial applicability requirement if it operates contrary to well-established physical laws; compliance with clear and complete disclosure (second requirement) is insufficient if the claimed subject-matter cannot be made to work for the special purpose indicated.
guidance: Technical errors not necessarily linked to basic laws of nature may still result in failure to meet the third requirement where they make the claimed subject-matter unusable for the special purpose. Examiner should object where the claimed subject-matter is not usable for the indicated purpose.

name: Examiner's view of acceptable amendments
description: Acceptable amendments include restriction of claim scope; amendments that improve clarity of the description; and desirable claim amendments that do not change subject-matter or scope.
guidance: An amended application must satisfy all other filing requirements. Examiners should consider whether claim amendments raise issues of unity, inconsistency with description, or lack of support.

name: Data/evidence submitted after the filing date (admissibility test)
description: Applicants may submit data or evidence after filing to address examiner objections; whether admitted depends on field and case but if support exists in original disclosure the examiner may consider it.
guidance: If the data/evidence provides a new teaching (e.g., a selection invention unsupported in the original filing), it is inadmissible. For example, claiming a specific compound by merely providing its advantages later is not allowable.

name: Broadening claims — pre-grant vs post-grant rule
description: There is no pre-grant restriction on broadening claims provided the amendment does not add matter beyond the disclosure as filed; post-grant amendments are further restricted — the scope of claims cannot be broadened post-grant.
guidance: If disclosure is broader than claims as filed, pre-grant amendments may bring claims in line with the specification. Post-grant broadening is disallowed in most AMS.

name: Lack of support — support between description and claims
description: If subject-matter is disclosed in a claim but not mentioned in the description, it is permissible to amend the description to include that subject-matter, but must ensure the amended description provides required support for the claims.
guidance: Contradictions/inconsistencies between claims and description must be resolved by amending either. Each claim limitation must be explicitly or inherently supported in the original disclosure. Negative limitations, exclusions or disclaimers must be examined for potential new matter.

name: Post-grant amendments — effect and tests
description: Post-grant amendments, once allowed, take effect and are deemed always to have had effect from the date of grant; the test for added subject-matter is the same as for pre-grant amendments, but scope of claims cannot be broadened post-grant.

name: ASPEC programme — purpose and non‑binding nature
description: ASPEC shares S&E results among nine participating AMS to allow applicants to obtain corresponding patents faster; participating offices may consider but are not obliged to follow findings from other offices.
guidance: ASPEC has enabled high allowance rates (reported ~95% for ASPEC-based examination as of Jan 2022). Since 15 June 2021 applicants can use a written opinion establishing at least one allowable claim to request ASPEC before a second AMS office without needing a final S&E report (except Thailand).

name: Recognition/validation eligibility (Singapore→Cambodia/Lao; EPO→Cambodia)
description: Recognition/validation schemes require conditions such as: applicant first granted patent in Singapore; Singaporean patent in force at filing; filing date on or after specified date (e.g., 11 Feb 2003); for EP→Cambodia, EP application filed on/after 1 Mar 2018 and validation request within three months of EPO grant with Khmer translation of title, abstract and claims.
guidance: Procedures are generally simple and inexpensive but include country-specific timing, translation and fee requirements.

name: ASPEC request eligibility and correspondence requirement
description: To qualify for ASPEC, a patent application filed at a 'second' AMS office must be a corresponding application of the 'first' AMS office and the ASPEC Request must be supported by that first office's S&E documents.
guidance: All claims filed in subsequent patent offices must correspond sufficiently to allowable/patentable claims referred to in the first IP Office's S&E documents. ASEAN Comparative Study Report (CSR) is recommended to assess compatibility of practices across AMS.

name: Government use when invention recorded/tested by government before priority date — royalty-free
description: Where an invention has, before the priority date of the relevant claim of the complete specification, been duly recorded in a document, or tested or tried, by or on behalf of the government or a government undertaking, otherwise than in consequence of the communication of the invention directly or indirectly by the patentee ..., any use of the invention by the Central Government or any person authorized in writing by it for the purposes of government may be made free of any royalty or other remuneration to the patentee.
guidance: Section 100(a) creates a royalty-free exception where government had independently recorded/tested the invention prior to priority.

name: Reference of disputes to High Court and High Court procedural powers (Section 103)
description: Any dispute as to the exercise by the Central Government or a person authorised by it of the powers conferred by section 100, or as to terms for the use of an invention for the purposes of government thereunder or as to the right of any person to receive any part of a payment ... or as to the amount of compensation payable for the acquisition of an invention ... may be referred to the High Court by either party to the dispute. In such proceedings the Central Government may petition by way of counter-claim for revocation of the patent on any ground upon which a patent may be revoked under section 64; and whether a patentee is or is not a party to the proceedings, put in issue the validity of the patent without petitioning for its revocation.
guidance: Section 103 grants the High Court broad jurisdiction and allows the Government to attack patent validity in disputes about use/compensation; confidentiality procedures and references to referees/commissioners/arbitrators are available.

name: Wrongful use of words 'Patent Office' (Section 121)
description: If any person uses on his place of business or any document issued by him which would reasonably lead to the belief that either his place of business is the Patent Office or is officially connected with the Patent Office, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term that may extend to 6 months, or with fine, or with both.
guidance: Protects public from misleading claims of official Patent Office status.

name: Mentioning inventor in patent — grounds, timing and procedure (Section 28)
description: If the Controller is satisfied, upon a request or claim made in accordance with the provisions of this section— (i) that the person in respect of or by whom the request or claim is made is the inventor of an invention in respect of which application for a patent has been made, or of a substantial part of that invention; and (ii) that the application for the patent is a direct consequence of his being the inventor, the Controller shall ... cause him to be mentioned as inventor in any patent granted ... Such a request or claim shall be accompanied by a statement setting out the circumstances. A request or claim shall be made before the grant of patent. The Controller shall give notice of the claim to every applicant for the patent (not being the claimant) and to any other person whom the Controller may consider to be interested and before deciding upon any such request or claim, the Controller shall, if required, hear the person in respect of or by whom the request or claim is made, and also any person to whom notice of the claim has been given. Where any person has been mentioned as inventor ... any other person who alleges that he ought not to have been so mentioned may at any time apply to the Controller for a certificate to that effect, and the Controller may, after hearing, if required, issue such a certificate and rectify the specification and the register accordingly. The procedure specified in rules 55A and 57 to 63 relating to filing of notice of opposition, written statement, reply statement, leaving evidence, hearing and cost shall, so far as may be, apply to the hearing of such a claim or application as they apply to the opposition proceedings subject to modification that reference to patentee shall be construed as the person making the claim or application.
guidance: Provides a full adversarial procedure for inventor-mention claims analogous to opposition proceedings; ensures right to be heard and rectification mechanisms.

name: Preemption of state-law rights by Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. §301)
description: The Copyright Act preempts state law protection of rights equivalent to the exclusive rights of the copyright owner.
guidance: State-law claims that require an extra element beyond copying may not be preempted; contract restrictions beyond copyrights can be enforceable (cases: ProCD, National Car Rental).

name: Improper Naming of Inventors
description: The patent laws require naming the actual inventor or joint inventors of the claimed subject matter; an application must include or be amended to include the name of the inventor for any invention claimed (35 U.S.C. 115(a)).
guidance: The Office presumes the named inventors are the actual inventors. Where an application names incorrect inventorship, applicant should submit a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48 (see MPEP § 602.01(c) et seq.). In rare situations where it is clear the application does not name the correct inventorship and no request to correct has been filed, Office personnel should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 115. Do not use pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) rejections if the application is subject to first inventor to file (FITF) AIA provisions; consult MPEP § 2159 et seq. and MPEP § 2137 for pre-AIA 102(f) information.

name: Nonobviousness Determination Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 103
description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 sets forth the nonobviousness requirement, with important differences from pre-AIA law: obviousness is determined as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention and requires consideration of 'the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.'
guidance: Use the effective filing date (not invention date) to determine obviousness for AIA-subject applications. The term 'claims' has long defined the invention; thus differences should be ascertained at the claim level (Graham factors). Continue to follow MPEP § 2141 et seq. and KSR guidance in formulating rationales to support conclusions of obviousness. Pre-AIA provisions like 103(b) and 103(c) differ and may be rare or replaced by AIA 102(b)(2)(C) and 102(c); consult MPEP § 2158 for distinctions.

name: Applicability of AIA vs Pre-AIA 102/103 (Determining Effective Filing Date Status)
description: The AIA changes to 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 apply only to applications (or claims) having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013; determining whether an application/claim is subject to AIA or pre-AIA provisions is critical.
guidance: An application is an 'AIA application' if it contains or ever contained a claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, or claims the benefit of an earlier application that ever contained such a claim. If even a single claim ever had such an effective filing date, AIA 102 and 103 apply to all claimed inventions in the application (even if claims with post-March 16, 2013 effective dates are later canceled). Applications filed before March 16, 2013 remain governed by pre-AIA law. Adding claims after March 16, 2013 that introduce new matter does not make a pre-March 16 application subject to AIA (35 U.S.C. 132(a) prohibits new matter). See MPEP §§ 2159-2159.03 for rules about transition applications and priority/benefit claims.

name: Treatment of Amendments That Contain New Matter
description: 35 U.S.C. 132(a) prohibits introduction of new matter into the disclosure; amendments believed to contain new matter must be treated to avoid improperly changing an application's applicable law status.
guidance: If an examiner discovers a new drawing contains new matter, do not enter the drawing (MPEP § 608.02). Amendments to the written description or claims involving new matter are ordinarily entered, but the new matter must be canceled from the written description and claims directed to new matter rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (MPEP § 608.04). This process is administrative to handle alleged new matter and disputes between applicant and examiner. An amendment that would add a claim directed to new matter does not make a pre-AIA application into an AIA application for purposes of determining AIA applicability.

name: Enablement for Computer-Implemented Functional Claim Limitations
description: To satisfy enablement for computer-implemented functional limitations, the specification must teach how to make and use the full scope of the claimed function without undue experimentation, considering the interrelationship of hardware and software.
guidance: Assess whether the disclosure of hardware and software reasonably conveys possession and enables the full scope claimed. Consider the Wands factors, the nature and predictability of the technology, the amount of direction provided, existence of working examples, and whether undue experimentation would be needed. If the specification does not disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts to perform the entire claimed function of a means-(or step-)plus-function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA second paragraph) must be made in addition to written description rejection (In re Donaldson). See MPEP §§ 2163-2163.07(b) and 2181.

name: Genus/Functional Claim Pitfall (Original Claims May Lack Written Description Support)
description: Original claims often fail written description when claim language is generic or functional (e.g., claiming a genus using functional language without describing sufficient species).
guidance: An adequate written description of a claimed genus requires more than a generic statement of the invention’s boundaries; the specification must demonstrate that the applicant invented species sufficient to support the functionally-defined genus. Cases such as Ariad, LizardTech, and Enzo Biochem illustrate that describing only one embodiment or restating desired results without describing how to achieve them may be insufficient. Examiners should look for support in the original disclosure that reasonably conveys possession of the claimed scope.

name: Means-Plus-Function / Step-Plus-Function Requirements (35 U.S.C. 112(f) / Pre-AIA Sixth Paragraph)
description: Claims with means- (or step-) plus-function limitations require sufficient disclosure of corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the claimed function; failing to provide this corresponding disclosure can lead to rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA second paragraph).
guidance: If the specification does not provide sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts for the full scope of a means- or step-plus-function limitation, the applicant has failed to 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention' as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Make a 112(b) rejection in addition to any written description rejection. See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181 for means/step-plus-function guidance.

name: Summary of claimed subject matter (optional for pro se)
description: Provide a concise explanation of the subject matter defined in each rejected independent claim, including references to supporting portions of the original-filed specification and drawings.
guidance: Include a short explanation of each independent claim with references to (1) supporting aspects of the original-filed specification by page/line or paragraph number and (2) drawings by reference numerals. Pro se applicants may omit this section, but it may help the Board understand issues. See MPEP § 1205.02(iii) and § 1205.02(v).

name: Argument organization and headings
description: Argue each ground of rejection under a separate heading identifying the ground (claim number(s), statutory basis, and applied reference(s)). Claims subject to the same ground may be argued individually, as a group, or in subgroups.
guidance: If the same argument applies to multiple claims, argue them as a group under a single heading rather than repeating. If different arguments apply to particular claims, use separate sub-headings for those claims. Use clear headings such as 'Whether claims 1–3 are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Iranpour in view of Stroud' and then discuss individual claims or subparts as needed. See MPEP § 1205(c)(1)(iv).

name: Types of persuasive errors to identify
description: When arguing a rejection is improper, you may show the examiner (1) misunderstood the invention or claims, (2) misunderstood the cited prior art, and/or (3) misunderstood or misapplied the law or legal basis for the rejection.
guidance: Support assertions with evidence (specification citations, dictionary definitions, case law). Explain specifically why the examiner’s interpretation is inconsistent with the specification or is overly broad/unreasonable. Provide examples and suggested wording to explain misinterpretation of claim terms or prior art teachings.

name: Use of annotated drawings and record evidence
description: Consider using annotated drawings to explain differences between the claimed invention and cited prior art, and direct attention to evidentiary items in the record.
guidance: Annotated drawings can make differences clearer for the PTAB. You may rely on affidavits or declarations in the record to support arguments, but such evidence must have been before the examiner during prosecution; otherwise it will not be considered by the PTAB. Examples given where declarations explain why references do or do not suggest combinations.

name: Improper hindsight and requirement for explicit reasoning to combine references
description: Argue that an examiner’s suggestion to combine references for obviousness must be supported by explicit reasoning and cannot be based on impermissible hindsight using the applicant’s disclosure as a blueprint.
guidance: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, the examiner must explain why a person of ordinary skill would have had an apparent reason to combine the references as proposed. The analysis must be explicit—not merely conclusory—and cannot rely on knowledge of the claimed invention (impermissible 'hindsight'). Provide example argument templates to challenge insufficient reasoning to combine.

name: Challenge examiner’s characterization of prior art and case citations
description: If the examiner has misinterpreted or mischaracterized a prior art reference, explain why the reference does not disclose or suggest the claim element; similarly, if cited case law does not support the examiner’s proposition, point out the error.
guidance: Explain specifically why the cited reference fails to disclose or suggest the claimed feature. If you know PTAB or federal court decisions that support your position, explain how those cases apply to your facts and require ruling in your favor. Examples provided for misapplied and supportive cases.

name: Conclusion section (optional summary and requested relief)
description: Optionally include a Conclusion summarizing overall positions and the particular decision requested (normally reversal of final rejection and allowance of pending claims).
guidance: If included, state clearly the decision requested (e.g., reversal and remand for allowance). Provide date and signature block in closing as shown in template.

name: Substitution with additional search results from authorized sources
description: Where additional search results related to the claimed invention exist (e.g., search results made with support of local IP centers), the results may be submitted instead of search processes and search results.
guidance: Even when substitute search results are submitted, the contrastive explanation shall still be disclosed in the application.

name: Definition of 'inappropriately disclosed' self-search results
description: Self-search results are inappropriately disclosed where any of the mandatory contents of disclosure are not disclosed, specifically ① search processes of prior arts and search results (more than four results), independent claims, or ② contrastive explanation is inappropriately disclosed.
guidance: However, an examiner's additional finding of prior arts that deny novelty or inventive step does not necessarily mean the self-search was inappropriately conducted.

name: Evidence required for third-party practicing ground (Article 4(1))
description: A person requesting expedited examination under Article 4(1) (third party's practicing of the invention under Article 61(1) of the Patent Act) shall specify the condition under which a third party practiced the claimed invention or utility model in a written explanation.
guidance: The written explanation must provide sufficient factual specification of the third party's practice to support the ground.

name: Consideration of unclaimed but obvious grounds
description: Determination is assessed based on the ground indicated in the explanation; eligibility cannot be determined on a ground the requester did not claim, but where an unclaimed ground is obvious or explained enough, it can be considered when determining eligibility.
guidance: If other grounds exist or become apparent, the person in charge may order complement before dismissal and consider newly-submitted grounds.

name: Handling changed grounds after complementation
description: If the ground for expedited examination is changed after a complementation order, the person in charge shall determine whether to conduct expedited examination based on the newly-submitted ground.
guidance: Example: requester first claims third-party practicing but fails to supplement evidence, then changes ground to being a venture company — if the claimed invention relates to that industry type, the new ground may justify expedited status.

name: Treatment of prior-filed applications claiming domestic priority
description: Where an application requested for expedited examination is confirmed to be a prior-filed application of an application claiming domestic priority before determination, the application is not eligible for expedited examination because the ground for urgent processing is not recognized.
guidance: An examiner shall order the requester to complement the request indicating expedited cannot be conducted because it is a prior-filed application; after the designated period, dismiss the request. If the priority claim is withdrawn before dismissal, deem the request valid. If an application becomes a prior-filed application after determination, the examiner shall withhold examination until the application is deemed withdrawn.

name: Transfer when application is 'best examinable' elsewhere
description: Where an application’s claims include a combination of limitations for plural disciplines, an SPE or primary examiner may request transfer to another discipline on the ground that the application is 'best examinable' in the other discipline.
guidance: The requesting SPE/examiner should cite art showing the limitations classifiable in his/her discipline; see MPEP § 903.08(e) for examples and further discussion.

name: Read claims in light of the disclosure; do not go behind the record
description: The claims and statement of invention are generally taken as they read; however, claims must be read in light of the disclosure (claimed disclosure). Any attempt to go behind the record and decide the case upon what is deemed the 'real invention' would introduce more errors than it would cure.
guidance: SPEs cannot possess specific knowledge of all art; such merit questions are for the examiners to determine and may be appealed.

name: Do not assign based on only a single element of a combination
description: Ordinarily, an application cannot be assigned to a class which includes one element or part only of several claimed in combination. The claim is treated in its entirety.
guidance: Assignment must consider full combination recited in claims.

name: Assignment of composition/alloy-only claims
description: Ordinarily, where all the claims of an application are for an article made of a specific composition or alloy with no other structure of the article recited, the application will be assigned to the composition or alloy class.
guidance: Treat composition-only claims as composition-class cases for assignment.

name: Scope of first search—should avoid need for second search
description: The first search should be such that the examiner need not ordinarily make a second search of the prior art, unless necessitated by amendments to the claims in the first reply.
guidance: First search should cover the invention as described and claimed, including inventive concepts toward which the claims appear directed; should not be extended merely to add immaterial variants.

name: Carefully analyze claim breadth; apply broadest reasonable interpretation
description: The breadth of the claims in the application should always be carefully noted; the examiner should be fully aware of what the claims do not call for as well as what they do require. During patent examination, the claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
guidance: See MPEP § 2111–§ 2116.01 and In re Morris for case law on claim interpretation.

name: Consider equivalents unless expressly excluded
description: All subject matter that is the equivalent of the subject matter as defined in the claim, even though specifically different from the definition in the claim, must be considered unless expressly excluded by the claimed subject matter.
guidance: See MPEP § 2181–§ 2184 for discussion of equivalents when claim employs means- or step-plus-function terminology.

name: Consider analogous arts
description: Consideration of analogous arts is required when determining what references are pertinent to a claim (904.01(c) heading indicates analogous arts discussion follows).
guidance: Examiners should apply the principle of analogous arts when searching for relevant prior art (full guidance in subsequent text).

name: Claim construction standard (de novo with clear-error for facts)
description: "Claim construction is a question of law and receives de novo review on appeal."
guidance: Underlying factual findings made during claim construction are reviewed for clear error. (Cites Markman; Nature Simulation Sys. Inc. v. Autodesk.) When construing terms courts should state and review both legal conclusions and any subsidiary factual findings.

name: Indefiniteness standard (Nautilus / §112)
description: "Claim indefiniteness is a legal conclusion, in implementation of 35 U.S.C. § 112." Claims must be "precise enough to afford clear notice of what is claimed, thereby 'appris[ing] the public of what is still open to them.'" (Nautilus).
guidance: Indefiniteness is judged from the viewpoint of a person of ordinary skill in the art; if claims fail to inform such a person with reasonable certainty as to the scope of the invention they are indefinite.

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) definition
description: The proper PHOSITA may be defined concretely for the case: here, either (1) a medical doctor who completed a coronary intervention training program and worked as an interventional cardiologist; or (2) a person with an undergraduate engineering degree and three years' experience designing medical devices (such as catheters).
guidance: Parties may agree or courts may adopt a factual definition of PHOSITA; advanced experience can substitute for education and vice versa. Claim definiteness and construction are evaluated from that PHOSITA's viewpoint.

name: Functional claim limitations are permissible
description: A limitation may be a functional limitation (e.g., the "substantially rigid portion/segment" as a portion that is "substantially rigid enough to achieve some function").
guidance: Defining a claim term by its function is not improper so long as the claim, specification, and knowledge of a PHOSITA give reasonable certainty as to scope. Functional constructions may avoid specifying exact physical boundaries.

name: Consistency of claim terms across claims and related patents
description: "A claim term should be construed consistently with its appearance in other places in the same claim or in other claims of the same patent." Where multiple patents derive from the same parent application, interpret terms consistently across asserted patents.
guidance: Consistency is required, but consistency can be achieved by a common (e.g., functional) construction that does not rigidly fix a boundary when the function-based definition is what informs PHOSITA of scope.

name: Claims need not be mutually exclusive; claim drafting can vary
description: Claims are not required to be totally consistent with other independent claims; "the art of claiming sometimes involves drafting claims in a variety of ways to encompass the disclosed subject matter."
guidance: A court should not declare claims indefinite merely because different claims define different boundaries or combinations of limitations; differing claim formulations can coexist so long as each informs PHOSITA of scope with reasonable certainty.

name: Claim-by-claim construction imperative
description: Courts should "conduct claim construction on a claim-by-claim basis," recognizing each independent claim is a different ordered combination of limitations.
guidance: Do not force a single, inflexible boundary of a term across all claims if the claim language leads to different boundaries; evaluate each claim's language and how it informs PHOSITA.

name: Role of specification and figures in claim scope
description: Figures and the specification inform claim scope but do not necessarily illustrate all embodiments (e.g., "Figure 4 doesn't illustrate all embodiments").
guidance: Do not treat a single drawing or embodiment as limiting; read claims in light of the specification and the knowledge of PHOSITA to determine what the claim reasonably conveys about scope.

name: How to measure boundaries of functional limitations
description: When a limitation is functional, the claims themselves (and their language) indicate to a person skilled in the field how to measure the boundary, claim-by-claim.
guidance: If a functional construction does not specify a precise boundary, that measurement question may be addressed in the infringement context rather than by invalidating the claim at the construction stage.

name: Use of court-appointed or party experts in construction (subsidiary factfinding)
description: District courts may appoint independent experts (or consider party experts) to propose constructions or make factual findings bearing on claim terms.
guidance: Subsidiary factual findings by experts are subject to clear-error review on appeal; courts should still ensure final legal claim constructions reflect the record and applicable law.

name: Compatibility with Tradition (Fathers and Councils)
description: The doctrine must accord with the teaching of the Fathers and Ecumenical Councils; patristic consensus (especially Eastern Fathers) is treated as a critical touchstone.
guidance: The page emphasizes unanimous patristic opposition to Calvinist determinations (with the one contested case of Augustine). Councils cited include the Second Council of Orange (condemning predestining some to evil) and the Tridentine Council (anathema against those who make grace restricted to the predestined). Use Fathers and Council declarations to evaluate theological claims.

name: Interpret scripture and patristic texts contextually; avoid simplistic literalism
description: Scriptural passages and patristic statements must be read in context and balanced with other texts and traditions; isolated readings that produce deterministic conclusions are suspect.
guidance: Example: Beza’s use of 1 Pet. II to claim persons are 'predestined not to believe' is criticized; other scriptures (Is. VIII, Matt. XXI) and patristic exegesis must be considered. The method of interpretation is itself a criterion for doctrinal soundness.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
description: "[a] practitioner shall not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice."
guidance: Typically includes conduct that negatively impacts the public's perception or efficacy of the courts or legal profession. Examples: failure to adequately or properly represent a client; tardiness or absence from trial; failure to appear on behalf of a client; failure to communicate with a client; failure to prosecute a claim; failure to inform a client of suspension. Case citations (Schroeder, Attorney Grievance Comm’n v. Rand, Brown) are used to support scope. The tribunal assesses repeated/pattern behavior (e.g., repeatedly ignoring court orders) as prejudicial.

name: Step 2B: identify and evaluate additional elements
description: Step 2B asks whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s). Examiners should identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and then evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)).
guidance: Evaluate additional elements with respect to Supreme Court-identified considerations discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h). Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or every claim. The evaluation is not a weighing test; it is important to assess the significance of additional elements relative to the invention and whether they encompass an inventive concept.

name: Outcome determination at Step 2B (Pathway C eligibility vs ineligibility)
description: If the claim as a whole does amount to significantly more than the exception (there is an inventive concept), the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C and the eligibility analysis is complete. If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more (no inventive concept), the claim is not patent-eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
guidance: Examine each claim for eligibility separately; similar claims in the same application should not automatically be judged to stand or fall together. For example, a dependent claim may be eligible even if the independent claim is not. See MPEP § 2106.07 for how to formulate an ineligibility rejection.

name: Improvement to functioning of a computer or other technology (improvement consideration)
description: Consider whether the claim purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology or technical field (i.e., whether it provides a technological solution to a technological problem).
guidance: If improvement to conventional computer functioning or other technology is asserted, the specification should provide a technical explanation sufficient for one of ordinary skill in the art to recognize the claimed invention as providing the improvement. Conclusory assertions in the specification are insufficient. An indication of improvement can include identification of a technical problem and details of an unconventional technical solution or identification of technical improvements over the prior art. After consulting the specification, the claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement.

name: Claim must reflect disclosed improvement and be evaluated as a whole
description: The claim must include the components or steps that provide the improvement described in the specification (though it need not explicitly state the improvement). The claim should be evaluated "as a whole" as an ordered combination without ignoring individual step requirements.
guidance: Consider the full scope of the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to determine if the claim reflects an improvement. Avoid oversimplifying claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for specific claim requirements. Improvements may be provided by one or more additional elements alone or in combination with the judicial exception (see Diamond v. Diehr and Finjan discussions).

name: Computer-functionality criterion: improves computer capabilities vs using computer as a tool
description: For computer-related inventions, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities (improvement in computer functionality) or merely uses computers as a tool to implement an abstract idea or process.
guidance: Cases where courts found improvements in computer functionality include specific data structures that change how data is stored/retrieved (Enfish), inventive distribution of network functionality (Bascom), particular ways of programming or structuring software, particular memory systems, technical details for transmission or image processing, improved user interfaces, and similar concrete technical solutions. The specification's disclosure of how to implement the improvement is important (technical details).

name: Limitation to computer implementation and mental-process exclusion
description: A method claim must be limited to computer implementation (under the BRI) in order to be an improvement to computer functionality; if the entire scope can be performed mentally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
guidance: Claims that cover embodiments performable without a computer (e.g., verbally or by phone) or that can be performed mentally fail the improvement-in-computer-functionality criterion (Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics; RecogniCorp v. Nintendo). Ensure the claim scope is not purely mental or performable without computer implementation.

name: Anti-patterns: examples insufficient to show computer-functionality improvement
description: Certain kinds of claim features have been held insufficient to demonstrate an improvement in computer functionality.
guidance: Examples courts have indicated may not be sufficient include: functionally claimed restaurant menus (Ameranth); speedups that arise solely from using a general-purpose computer (FairWarning); mere automation of manual processes using generic computers (Credit Acceptance, LendingTree non-precedential); recording/transmitting/archiving digital images with conventional tech absent technical details (TLI Communications); affixing a barcode without technical details (Secured Mail Solutions); instructions to display information without specifying how to achieve it (Interval Licensing); improving stored information rather than database functionality (BSG Tech); arranging GUI information to help humans process faster (Trading Technologies). Use these as anti-pattern guidance when assessing claimed improvements.

name: Binding nature of prior factual determinations by appellate courts
description: Where a question of fact in a patent case has been decided by a Circuit Court of Appeals, that decision is binding in District Courts of the same circuit when the evidence is substantially the same and will be followed in later suits even if the claim of invalidity was not urged on prior appeal.
guidance: Where the Supreme Court decided a question of fact, that decision is conclusive in subsequent patent cases so far as the evidence is substantially identical, but the evidence must be taken in the subsequent cases and cannot be imported from the higher court's record.

name: Reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111
description: If the Office action after the first examination is adverse, the applicant or patent owner must reply and request reconsideration or further examination, with or without amendment; the reply must be reduced to writing which distinctly and specifically points out the supposed errors and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specifics does not comply. Requests to hold form objections in abeyance may be made where appropriate. Replies must appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application or reexamination to final action.

name: Supplemental replies limitations (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2))
description: A supplemental reply that is supplemental to a reply in compliance with 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except where clearly limited to: (A) cancellation of claim(s); (B) adoption of examiner suggestion(s); (C) placement in condition for allowance/notice of intent to issue reexamination certificate; (D) reply to Office requirement made after the first reply; (E) correction of informalities (typographical errors); or (F) simplification of issues for appeal.
guidance: A supplemental reply filed during a period when action is suspended under § 1.103(a) or (c) will be entered. The examiner may enter a supplemental reply after a cursory review if it meets one or more of these conditions. Unentered supplemental replies will not be entered later when a response to a subsequent Office action is filed; their contents must be included in a proper subsequent response if they are to be considered.

name: Amendment content requirements (point out patentable novelty)
description: When amending in reply to a rejection, the applicant or patent owner must clearly point out the patentable novelty believed present in the claims in view of the art and must show how the amendments avoid such references or objections.
guidance: This requirement applies in both applications and reexamination proceedings; arguments and amendments should specifically address the cited references and objections.

name: Statutory Benefit/Claim Requirements for Divisional
description: The divisional application must claim the benefit of the prior nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 121 or 365(c).
guidance: See MPEP §201.11 for conditions to receive the benefit of the filing date of the prior application. To claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c) include a specific reference per 37 CFR 1.78(a) in the first sentence(s) of the specification or in an application data sheet.

name: Do Not Call a 119(e) Provisional-Benefit Application a 'Division'
description: An application claiming the benefits of a provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) should not be called a 'division' of the provisional application.
guidance: Patent term calculations differ: provisional-benefit application has patent term from its own filing date, whereas applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) may have term calculated from the earliest application date if properly claimed. Cite 35 U.S.C. 154(a)(2) and (a)(3).

name: 37 CFR 1.53(b) Filing Date Completeness Requirements
description: For a complete filing date under 37 CFR 1.53(b), an application must include a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. 112 (description pursuant to 37 CFR 1.71), at least one claim pursuant to 37 CFR 1.75, and any drawing required by 37 CFR 1.81(a).
guidance: Statutory filing fee and an oath/declaration are also required by 37 CFR 1.51(b) but may be filed after filing date upon payment of surcharge under 37 CFR 1.16(f). Continuation, divisional, and CIP may be filed under conditions specified in 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) and §1.78(a). See MPEP §201.11.

name: Specification and Drawings in Continuing/Divisional Applications
description: A continuation or divisional may be filed with (A) a new specification and drawings and a copy of the signed oath/declaration from the prior application provided the new specification/drawings do not contain new matter; or (B) new specification/drawings and a newly executed oath/declaration provided no new matter is added.
guidance: To claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c), include a reference per 37 CFR 1.78(a) in first sentence(s) or application data sheet. Applicants should file a new set of claims as the original claims of the continuing application rather than relying on a preliminary amendment to avoid publication issues.

name: Preliminary Amendments and Publication Risk
description: Filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) with a preliminary amendment that makes desired changes is NOT recommended because the changes may generally not be reflected in the patent application publication.
guidance: To ensure the published application contains the desired claims, file the continuation/divisional with a new specification containing only the desired set of claims or submit the specification with amended claims through EFS.

name: Incorporation by Reference of Prior Application (37 CFR 1.57)
description: An applicant may incorporate by reference the prior application by including an explicit statement in the continuation/divisional specification that the prior application(s) are 'hereby incorporated by reference.'
guidance: For applications filed on/after Sept 21, 2004, a claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 is considered an incorporation by reference as to inadvertently omitted material subject to 37 CFR 1.57(a). Explicit incorporation by reference in the specification permits addition of subject matter from the prior application without petition, provided the continuation/divisional is entitled to a filing date. Incorporation added after the filing date is ineffective (no new matter after filing). Mere reference without explicit incorporation is not incorporation for 35 U.S.C. 112 disclosure purposes (In re de Seversky).

name: Recommendations on Preparing Continuing/Divisional to Control Publication
description: To have an application publication of a continuation/divisional contain only the desired set of claims, it is strongly recommended the continuation/divisional be filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) with a new specification containing only the desired set of claims.
guidance: If filed with a copy of prior specification plus a preliminary amendment cancelling/amending/adding claims, publication may exclude the preliminary amendment unless the amended specification was also submitted through the Office’s Electronic Filing System (EFS). File preliminary amendments and IDSs early (preferably at filing) to avoid delay.

name: CPA — Benefit of Earlier Filing Date and Specific Reference Requirements
description: A request for a CPA is a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120 to every application assigned the application number identified in the request. Where an application claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of a chain of applications, the application must reference the first (earliest) application and every intermediate application.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.78(a)(2) explains that identification by application number is the specific reference required. In a chain of CPAs, references by application number constitute references to every CPA in the chain and the original non-continued prosecution application. For applications filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) seeking benefit of a CPA under 35 U.S.C. 120/121, a reference to the CPA by application number must appear in the first sentence(s) of the specification unless made in an application data sheet.

name: Expansive and flexible approach to obviousness
description: Assessing obviousness is based on an 'expansive and flexible approach' that 'need not seek out precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter of the challenged claim, for a court can take account of the inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill in the art would employ.' (KSR; Updated Guidance; MPEP §2141).
guidance: Consider market forces, design incentives, interrelated teachings of multiple patents, any need or problem known in the field at the time of invention, and the background knowledge, creativity, and common sense of a person of ordinary skill. Do not apply rigid rules that preclude common-sense inferences.

name: Motivation to combine (institution stage)
description: The motivation-to-combine inquiry asks whether a skilled artisan 'not only could have made but would have been motivated to make the combinations . . . of prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.' (Auris Health v. Intuitive Surgical; Belden).
guidance: At institution, the petitioner must demonstrate a sufficient motivation to combine references to show a reasonable likelihood of prevailing. Motivation may come from many sources (see guidance above) and need not be a precise teaching in the prior art.

name: Simultaneous invention as objective evidence
description: Simultaneous (near-simultaneous) invention may bear on obviousness by (1) showing the level of skill in the art and (2) constituting objective evidence that persons of ordinary skill understood the problem and a solution to that problem (Regents v. Broad; Ecolochem; Geo. M. Martin).
guidance: Consider independently made inventions and contemporaneous disclosures (including some post‑dating references) as persuasive evidence that the claimed invention was within ordinary skill; demonstrate timing (a comparatively short space of time) and independent development to bolster the inference.

name: Computer-implemented invention standard
description: Computer-implemented inventions may be patentable if the computer or other technical features defined in the claims are integral to the invention and constitute the actual contribution.
guidance: The technical features should interact with the claimed steps (e.g., servers, databases, user devices) to a material extent and in a manner that addresses a specific problem. Merely reciting a generic computer or standard OS to perform a pure business method will not render it an invention (see sections 8.6 and 8.7, IPOS Examination Guidelines).

name: Specification sufficiency (section 25)
description: Specification must disclose the invention clearly and completely so a person skilled in the art can perform it; application must include request for grant, specification, claims, any drawings referenced, and an abstract.
guidance: Statutory requirement: disclosure must be clear and complete; see rules 19, 21 and 22 and section 25 of the Patents Act.

name: Claims substantive requirements
description: Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought; be clear and concise; be supported by the description; and relate to one invention or a group of inventions linked as a single inventive concept.
guidance: Claims must not rely on references to the description or drawings unless necessary for understanding or clarity (section 25, rule 19).

name: Third‑party observations rules (section 32)
description: After publication and before issuance of search/exam report, third parties may file written observations on patentability, stating reasons and providing supporting documents.
guidance: Examiners consider only the documents submitted by the third party; reasoning should include accurate features mapping to claims and documentary support. Observations after establishment of search/exam report are placed on record but not forwarded to Examiner. Third‑party observations were formally introduced on 1 Oct 2021.

name: Re‑examination filing requirements and supporting evidence (rule 52A)
description: Request must be filed on Patents Form 36 with official fee (SGD900) and a statement identifying each ground relied on, explaining how each ground is satisfied, and including relevant documents (with translations and VETs where needed).
guidance: Statement should identify the claims affected and state full reasons for each claim. Prior art should be dated (when made available to public). Supporting documents need not be limited to prior art (e.g., evidence that priority claims are invalid). If prior art was previously considered by Examiner, it must be presented in a new light with material new argument or interpretation.

name: Re‑examination outcomes and remedies (sections 38A(11)–(14))
description: If re‑examination report contains unresolved objections, Registrar must order either unconditional revocation or conditional revocation (revocation unless specification amended under section 83 to Registrar's satisfaction). Conditional revocation allows proprietor a final opportunity to amend; failure to amend results in full revocation. Revocation takes effect from date of grant. Patentee may appeal to High Court.
guidance: Where conditional revocation arises, amendments typically involve limiting claims to those deemed valid. Appeal available to General Division of High Court (section 90(1)).

name: Integration into a practical application
description: The claim as a whole integrates the judicial exception into a practical application if it 'applies, relies on, or uses the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.' If so, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B.
guidance: Evaluate integration using the considerations listed in the MPEP subsection I (improvements, particular treatment/prophylaxis, particular machine/manufacture, particular transformation, other meaningful uses). If the claim integrates the exception into a practical application the eligibility analysis concludes at Step 2A. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 for detailed discussion and examples.

name: Applying the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond linking to a technological environment
description: Integration is also demonstrated when the judicial exception is applied or used in a meaningful way beyond generally linking the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use.
guidance: This is a catch-all for meaningful limitations that do not fit the other listed categories but still make the claim more than an attempt to monopolize the exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) for discussion and case law examples.

name: Merely reciting 'apply it' or implementing on a computer is insufficient
description: Merely reciting the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent), merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: This limitation is discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(f). Examiners should treat such recitations as non-meaningful additions that do not prevent the claim from being 'directed to' the judicial exception.

name: Generally linking to a technological environment or field of use is insufficient
description: Generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(h). Claims that simply state a field-of-use or technological context without meaningful limitations are still considered directed to the judicial exception.

name: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant
description: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluating considerations such as use of a particular machine, particular transformation, and whether the limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception.
guidance: If claims lack specifics (e.g., do not explain how to select parameters, how to perform steps, or how the steps effect the result), those limitations may be characterized as insignificant post-solution activity (see Parker v. Flook). Conversely, sufficiently specific limitations that show how the exception is used can support integration.

name: How to evaluate integration (procedure)
description: Examiners evaluate integration into a practical application by: (1) identifying whether there are any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using one or more of the listed considerations.
guidance: The evaluation applies equally to abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena/products of nature. Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim; the analysis is not a weighing test—what matters is the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant's invention and whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception. If the claim integrates the exception based on these considerations, the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit and the claim is eligible at Step 2A.

name: Evaluate each claim separately; dependent claims may differ
description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited therein; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application.
guidance: One claim may be ineligible while another dependent claim is eligible if the dependent claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more or that integrate the exception into a practical application.

name: Specification support required to recognize an improvement
description: To find that a claim demonstrates an improvement in technology, the specification should provide sufficient details such that a person of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing that improvement.
guidance: The specification need not use the word 'improvement' explicitly, but must disclose sufficient detail to make the improvement apparent; bare/conclusory assertions of improvement are insufficient. After establishing specification support, ensure the claim actually reflects the improvements described in the specification (claim limitations must embody the components/steps providing the improvement).

name: Examples and case-law illustrations
description: The MPEP provides numerous case examples illustrating Prong Two conclusions (e.g., Solutran, Finjan, Enfish, McRO, Vanda, BASCOM, Visual Memory, SRI).
guidance: Use these cases as guidance: Solutran (claims directed to abstract idea due to lacking technological improvement), Finjan (virus scanning found to improve computer functionality due to security profile steps), Vanda (treatment/prophylaxis eligible), Enfish/McRO/Visual Memory/SRI (examples of technological improvements). Apply factual distinctions and specification/claim analysis from cases to the facts of the application under examination.

name: Priority claim conditions
description: An applicant may claim priority on the basis of the first application if: (a) the first application filed in Vietnam or member country of treaty or country agreed with Vietnam; (b) the applicant is a national/resident or has establishment in Vietnam or that country; (c) the claim was clearly mentioned and a certified copy of the first application provided; (d) the application filed within treaty time limit.
guidance: Multiple priorities may be claimed for different earlier applications provided corresponding contents are indicated. A registration application enjoying priority bears the priority date identical with the first filing date.

name: Encourage individual claims, fencing, and cultivation of land
description: Promote settlement on separate farms and the fencing of individual claims; government should support reclamation and fencing (barbed-wire with cedar posts) to increase cultivated acres and yields.
guidance: Examples provided of reclaimed and fenced agency farm, acreage planted (wheat, oats, corn), yields and estimated profit; also note communal planting of three large fields by 180 Indians and common hay-making.

name: Reference itself must contain the subject matter relied on in the rejection
description: When a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or an international application publication is used to reject claims under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the disclosure relied on in the rejection must be present in the issued patent or application publication; subject matter not included cannot be relied on as of the reference's filing date.
guidance: Portions canceled in prosecution are not part of the patent/publication and cannot be relied on (Ex parte Stalego). Subject matter disclosed only in an abandoned, unpublished parent that was not carried into the child patent/publication may not be relied on (In re Klesper). For CIPs, subject matter in parent but not included in the CIP cannot be relied on as prior art of the CIP (In re Lund). When a patent claims benefit to a provisional, at least one claim of the patent must be supported by the provisional in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 to use the provisional filing date. See MPEP § 2136.03.

name: Foreign priority date cannot be used as the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) reference date
description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) is explicitly limited to certain references 'filed in the United States before the invention thereof by the applicant.' Foreign applications' filing dates claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119 or 365(a) cannot be used as pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) dates for prior art purposes.
guidance: Applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 102(e) rejection by proving entitlement to a U.S. priority date (35 U.S.C. 119) earlier than the reference's U.S. filing date; see In re Hilmer and MPEP § 216 for procedures considering applicant's right of priority. Certain PCT filings (meeting specific conditions) may be treated as U.S. filings—see MPEP § 2120.01 and related sections.

name: Benefit of provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) requires written description support
description: The critical reference date of a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or international application publication having prior art effect under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) may be the filing date of a relied-upon provisional application only if at least one claim of the reference is supported by the written description of the provisional application in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, or 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
