guidance: Dynamic Drinkware and Amgen v. Sanofi cited. The provisional must describe the subject matter relied upon in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112; see MPEP § 2136 examples for illustration. International applications that (1) were filed before Nov 29, 2000, (2) did not designate the U.S., or (3) were not published in English cannot be used to reach back via priority for pre-AIA 102(e) purposes.

name: Benefit of nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 120 requires support in the earlier-filed application
description: A U.S. patent or patent application publication that claims the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 (continuation, divisional, CIP) will be accorded the earlier filing date as its prior art date under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), provided the earlier-filed application properly supports the subject matter relied upon in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: If the earlier-filed application does not support the relied-upon subject matter, the earlier filing date cannot be used to antedate the reference. See MPEP § 2136 examples 2 and 5–9.

name: Ways to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection (A–F)
description: An applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection by: (A) persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing reference is not by 'another'; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing prior invention (when appropriate); (E) submitting and perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); and/or (F) submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and establishing the prior application satisfies enablement/written description requirements.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2132.01, 2133.02(a), 715–716, 2136.05(a) and (b) for procedural requirements and examples. Note: a terminal disclaimer does not overcome a pre-AIA 102(e) rejection. If the rejection is the only possible ground and there is no common assignee or inventor, the examiner must consider whether an interference should be declared (MPEP Chapter 2300).

name: Antedating a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) reference via 37 CFR 1.131 or priority/benefit claims
description: A pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection can be overcome by antedating the filing date of the reference by submitting an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 proving prior invention, or by establishing priority/benefit to an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119 or 120.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavits can prove invention prior to the reference's effective date, but are not acceptable if the claims of the reference and application are directed to the same invention or obvious variants—in such cases double patenting or interference may be appropriate. See MPEP §§ 715, 2136.05(a). Priority/benefit claims must be timely (see 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.78), and applicant must show the earlier application satisfies enablement and written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 112). Details differ for applications filed on/after vs prior to September 16, 2012 (use of corrected ADS, ADS or oath/declaration). Certified priority documents and translations may be required.

name: Affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 vs 1.132: appropriate uses and limitations
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) may overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by proving invention prior to the effective date of the reference. An affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 is used when the reference is inventor's or a joint inventor's own work (i.e., to show reference is not 'by another').
guidance: 1.131 is not appropriate if the reference describes an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work; in that case submit 1.132. A 1.131 cannot be used when claims are directed to the same invention or obvious variants—then consider double patenting or interference. A naked assertion of inventorship under 1.132 without context, explanation, or supporting evidence is insufficient (EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen). See MPEP §§ 715, 716, 2136.05(a)–(b) for required contents and permitted situations.

name: Establishing priority/benefit requirements and timing (37 CFR 1.55, 1.78; ADS/Oath differences)
description: To antedate a reference via priority (35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d)) or benefit (35 U.S.C. 119(e)/120) claims, applicant must submit the claim within the time periods set in 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 and establish that the prior foreign or prior U.S. application satisfies enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (for post-Sep 16, 2012) or pre-AIA 112 first paragraph (for earlier filings).
guidance: For applications filed on/after Sep 16, 2012, identify prior applications via a corrected application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76; for earlier applications identify in the oath/declaration or ADS per 37 CFR 1.63/1.76. The foreign priority filing date must antedate the reference and be perfected (certified priority document and English translation required if not in English). Grantable petitions exist for unintentionally delayed priority/benefit claims. See MPEP §§ 213–216 and 2136.05(a).

name: Misrepresentation as an act involving moral turpitude (Business & Professions Code § 6106)
description: Submitting a medical report not authored by the claimed doctor and representing that the report had been prepared by that doctor constitutes an act involving moral turpitude, dishonesty, or corruption in willful violation of Business and Professions Code section 6106.
guidance: The Notice summarizes the state-court stipulation that on December 21, 2009 the Respondent faxed a three-page medical report to the State Bar, misrepresenting the author; such factual misconduct supports ethical discipline.

name: Burden of proof — general rule in patent cases at law
description: Burden of proof in patent cases at law — how satisfied and allocation of burdens between parties
guidance: General index entry referencing many sub-issues (inventive skill, prior use, publication, utility, abandonment, first inventor, specification fraud, description ambiguity, excessive claims, surrendered/repealed patent, infringement voluntariness, foreign patent limits, estoppel, disclaimer timeliness, infringement, co-ownership/license status, damages, profits, title by assignee). See many specific sub-entries.

name: Burden as to specification fraud, ambiguity, excessive claims
description: Proof that specification is fraudulent, description ambiguous, or claims excessive
guidance: Entries: specification fraudulent 1034; description ambiguous 1036; claims excessive 1036; effect of failure to claim clearly described matter 890 n.5.

name: Combination patents: co-operation of elements and sub-combinations
description: Principles governing combination patents — co-operation of elements, whether making a part constitutes infringement, sub-combinations, combination equivalents
guidance: Entries: co-operation of elements in combination 155 n.1; combination-patent may be infringed by making an element to be united by others 924 n.1; combination-patent not infringed by use of a part 928; re-issue of combination patent may cover sub-combinations (Gill v. Wells, Christian v. Ramsey); measures to distinguish old and new in claims 525 n.2.

name: Re-issue rules and limitations
description: When re-issue is allowable and how it may alter claims
guidance: Re-issue allowable only where error arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake (Conklin, Coon v. Wilson); re-issue may enlarge claims 656; re-issue confined to matter attempted to be described/claimed in original 663; decision of Commissioner on re-issue as to fraud is final 715 n.1; courts' duty to sustain honest and correct re-issue 684.

name: Joinder of inventions and claim multiplicity
description: Rules about joinder of inventions in one patent/claiming multiple species vs generic claims; claims not to be unnecessarily multiplied
guidance: Entries: joinder of inventions and appropriate practices 469, 470 a.; joinder of generic and specific claims barred or regulated (Bwart, Ex parte); claims not to be unnecessarily multiplied 521 ft.; joinder of art and apparatus 478.

name: Judicial Exceptions: Abstract Ideas, Laws of Nature, Natural Phenomena
description: Courts have held that abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (including products of nature) are exceptions to patentable subject matter under §101 and are not patentable per se.
guidance: See Alice, Myriad, Benson, Flook, Diehr, Funk Bros., Chakrabarty. MPEP §2106.04 discusses these judicial exceptions and their scope; identifying whether a claim is 'directed to' one of these exceptions is the first part of the eligibility inquiry.

name: 2019 PEG Definition of 'Mathematical Concepts'
description: The 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance (PEG) defines 'mathematical concepts' as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
guidance: Use this definition when evaluating whether claim limitations recite an abstract idea under the 'mathematical concept' subclass of abstract ideas. The PEG and its incorporation into MPEP §2106.04(a) are authoritative examiner guidance.

name: Significantly More / Eligibility Step 2B (Inventive Concept)
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, the claim must be considered as a whole to determine whether it contains additional limitations that amount to 'significantly more' than the exception (an 'inventive concept') to render it patent eligible.
guidance: See MPEP §2106.05 and Alice. 'Significantly more' is a relative notion and has been the focus of much case law; courts look for limitations that transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application rather than a claim that pre-empts the underlying idea.

name: Practical Application / Useful, Concrete, and Tangible Result (Diehr Principle)
description: A mathematical formula or other abstract idea, when reduced to a practical application that produces a 'useful, concrete and tangible result', can render a claim patent eligible.
guidance: Diehr distinguished claims that merely claim a formula from those that apply it in a specific, practical way. Cases like State Street and Arrhythmia show that transforming data through a machine to produce a practical result can support eligibility. Evaluate whether the claimed application meaningfully limits the abstract idea.

name: Preemption Concern and 'Storehouse of Knowledge' Rationale
description: The courts have expressed concern that patents which preempt the use of fundamental tools of science and technology (the 'storehouse of knowledge') would improperly monopolize basic building blocks and are therefore disfavored.
guidance: Cases cited include Funk Bros., Le Roy, and O'Reilly v. Morse. Examiners and courts often analyze whether a claim would preempt all practical uses of a principle. Note: the document criticizes overbroad preemption reasoning when applied to novel, nonobvious discoveries that were not previously in the storehouse.

name: Basic Tools and Models Are Not Patentable Absent Application
description: Fundamental tools, models, and mathematical techniques (e.g., Fourier transform, linear algebra, numerical methods, Newton’s laws) are considered part of the basic tools of science and are not patentable on their own; patentability requires an application beyond the tool/model itself.
guidance: The MPEP and case law treat such items as in the abstract; examples in the text include Fourier transform, finite difference/element methods, Richards' equation, Newton's second law, Hooke's law, etc. To be eligible, a claim must apply these tools in a particularized, inventive manner rather than claim the tool itself.

name: Mathematical Algorithms as Abstract Ideas — Need Application
description: Mathematical algorithms, being akin to laws of nature or abstract ideas, are not patentable when recited alone; to be patentable they must be tied to a concrete application or implementation that confers 'something more.'
guidance: Cite Benson, Flook, Bilski, Gottschalk v. Benson, and related Federal Circuit decisions. The presence of routine or conventional steps implemented on a computer is typically insufficient; the claim must do more than recite an abstract algorithm and say 'apply it on a computer.'

name: Enhanced Disclosure Considerations for AI Inventions (Algorithms as Material)
description: Arguments exist for an enhanced disclosure standard for AI inventions, including disclosing algorithms, because algorithms are a key aspect of such inventions and AI concepts are often ill-defined.
guidance: Scholarly and policy literature (e.g., Ebrahim, Penn State Law Review; USPTO AI report) discuss whether algorithmic detail should be required in patent disclosures for AI-related claims. This is a procedural/quality consideration: better algorithm disclosure can affect enablement, written description (§112), and the practical assessment of what the claim actually covers for §101 purposes.

name: Preemption vs. Inventive Concept Tension (Alice and Post-Alice Analysis)
description: Post-Alice, courts ask whether remaining claim limitations contain an 'inventive concept' instead of relying solely on preemption analysis; Alice emphasizes looking for 'something more' in the claim that transforms an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Alice reiterated the test focusing on inventive concept. While preemption remains a policy concern underlying §101 doctrine, the modern test operationalizes eligibility through the 'directed to' and 'significantly more' framework; practitioners should frame arguments in these terms.

name: Administrative Requirements: Language and Contract (CChRGM - Chile)
description: Official languages of CChRGM are Spanish and English. Depositor must complete the application form (serves as contract) whereby the depositor undertakes to supply all requested information, pay required fees, compensate CChRGM for claims from altered/misleading/third-party information, decline to withdraw deposit during the required storage period, and authorize CChRGM to supply samples in accordance with Rule 11 of the Regulations under the Budapest Treaty.
guidance: Where an organism has been accepted for deposit, CChRGM shall notify the depositor and remind him of the contract terms.

name: Patent outcome aggregation rules (by patent)
description: To determine a net outcome for a patent in a FY, identify each patent that had a petition reach an outcome in the FY and consider the outcomes of all petitions ever challenging that patent as of the end of the FY.
guidance: If there is one petition or every petition had the same outcome, that is the patent outcome. If any petition had a FWD outcome, the patent outcome is FWD (even if the FWD happened in an earlier FY). If multiple petitions have a mixture of different outcome types (and none are FWD), the patent outcome is 'mixed outcomes'. For FWD categorization by patent, the net claim outcome of all claims challenged in all FWDs addressing that patent is considered; if a claim is ever found unpatentable, the claim is listed as unpatentable.

name: Misconduct finding: seeking to mislead a judge / act of moral turpitude
description: State Bar Court found Respondent sought to mislead a judge by knowingly making a false and misleading statement to a court in claiming not to have been served with the prior sanctions order, constituting an act of moral turpitude in violation of Business and Professions Code §§ 6068(d) and 6106.
guidance: Knowing misrepresentation to a tribunal (moral turpitude) is an aggravated basis for disciplinary action and supports disbarment/reciprocal discipline.

name: Surface treatment must be applied to or embodied in an article
description: The ornamental appearance of a design includes shape/configuration and any indicia, contrasting color or materials, graphic representations, or other ornamentation applied to the article ("surface treatment"). Surface treatment must be applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture; surface treatment, per se (i.e., not applied to or embodied in a specific article of manufacture), is not proper subject matter for a design patent under 35 U.S.C. 171.
guidance: Surface treatment must be shown with the article (in full lines or in broken lines if unclaimed) to meet statutory requirement (see MPEP § 1504.01). Surface treatment shown in drawings/photos is prima facie evidence it was considered part of the claimed design. An amendment cancelling two-dimensional surface treatment or reducing it to broken lines is permitted if the application shows possession of the basic design without the surface treatment at filing (In re Daniels). Removal of three-dimensional surface treatment that is integral to configuration (e.g., beading, grooves, ribs) will introduce prohibited new matter. See MPEP §§ 1504.01, 1504.04.

name: Color photographs/drawings treatment and lining for color
description: Color photographs and color drawings may be submitted only with a grantable petition; color may be shown in pen-and-ink drawings by lining surfaces using MPEP § 608.02 symbols.
guidance: If the formal drawing in an application is lined for color, insert the statement 'The drawing is lined for color.' in the specification to avoid confusion. Lining entire surfaces for color may interfere with clear showing of design contours (35 U.S.C. 112). Partial lining with a description that color extends across the entire surface is permitted; alternatively submit a separate view properly shaded to show contours but omitting color, identified as shown only for clarity. If color photographs/drawings are filed with the original application, color is considered an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design; omission of color later is permitted only if the application makes clear the applicant had possession of the basic design without color at filing (In re Daniels).

name: Photographs and ink drawings must not be combined
description: Photographs and ink drawings must not be combined in a formal submission of the visual disclosure of the claimed design in one application.
guidance: Introducing both photographs and ink drawings in the same design application creates a high probability of inconsistencies between corresponding elements and is therefore prohibited. Informal photographs/drawings may be filed to obtain a filing date, but formal submission rules still apply later.

name: Design claim form and single-claim limitation
description: A design patent application may include only a single claim. The claim should be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article (specifying name) 'as shown' or 'as shown and described' (37 CFR 1.153).
guidance: Description in the claim should be consistent with the title. If a special description of the design or modified forms is included in the specification, add 'and described' after 'shown'. The claimed design must be shown by solid lines; it is not permissible to show any portion of the claimed design in broken lines (broken lines indicate unclaimed elements). See MPEP § 1503.02 and In re Blum.

name: Novelty and unobviousness requirements for design claims
description: Ornamentality, novelty and unobviousness are necessary prerequisites to the grant of a design patent; inventive novelty or unobviousness resides in the ornamental shape/configuration of the article.
guidance: Novelty and unobviousness of a design claim should generally be determined by a search in the pertinent design classes and extended to mechanical classes of the same general type; consult catalogs and trade journals as well.

name: Ex parte Quayle action when patentable but formal matters remain
description: If the examiner determines the design claim is patentable under statutory requirements but formal matters need addressing, an Ex parte Quayle action is sent indicating allowability and listing necessary corrections.
guidance: Prosecution on the merits is closed under Quayle practice; shortened statutory reply period of two months applies. In pro se applications examiners should suggest hiring a registered patent attorney/agent or draftsperson and may include the 'Guide To Filing A Design Patent Application.'

name: Computer-generated icons must be embodied in an article of manufacture
description: Design applications for computer-generated icons must comply with the 'article of manufacture' requirement of 35 U.S.C. 171: a computer-generated icon alone (standing alone) is surface ornamentation and not proper subject matter; if shown on a computer screen, monitor, display panel, or portion thereof, the claim complies.
guidance: PTO personnel must: read entire disclosure to determine claimed design and embodiment; review drawings to determine whether a display or portion is shown and ensure sufficient views (37 CFR 1.152, 1.84); review title to ensure it describes the claimed article (bad titles: 'computer icon'/'icon'; good titles: 'computer screen with an icon', 'portion of a monitor displayed with a computer icon image'); review specification for a characteristic feature statement describing the icon embodied in a display. If drawing does not depict embodiment, reject under 35 U.S.C. 171. If disclosure suggests embodiment, suggest amendments to bring into compliance. Upon applicant reply, enter amendments and review all arguments and record; if applicant establishes by preponderance of evidence that the icon is embodied in a display, withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 171 rejection. See In re Strijland, In re Hruby, In re Oetiker guidance.

name: Designs comprising multiple articles or multiple parts embodied in a single article
description: While the claimed design must be embodied in an article of manufacture, it may encompass multiple articles or multiple parts within that article.
guidance: Multiple independent parts forming the claimed design may be disclosed with or without the article shown in broken lines. If the article is not disclosed in broken lines, the title must disclose the article in which the design is embodied and the association of claimed parts must be shown by a bracket. Title must clearly define the articles/parts as a single entity (e.g., set, pair, combination, unit, assembly). See MPEP §1503.01.

name: Ornamentality requirement and functional vs. ornamental analysis
description: An ornamental feature is one 'created for the purpose of ornamenting' and cannot be merely a by-product of functional/mechanical considerations. To be patentable, a design must be 'primarily ornamental.'
guidance: Determination of functionality vs. ornamentality views the claimed design in its entirety; the ultimate question concerns the overall appearance, not the function/decorative aspect of each separate feature. Consider the purposes of particular elements. Distinguish between functionality of the article and functionality of the particular design of article features. Evidence that significant decisions about assembly/market presentation were informed by ornamental considerations may establish ornamentality. Case law cited: In re Carletti; L.A. Gear v. Thom McAn; Power Controls v. Hybrinetics; Smith v. M & B.

name: Hidden-in-use as prima facie evidence of lack of ornamentality
description: Knowledge that the article would be hidden during its end use (based on examiner experience or application information) is prima facie evidence of lack of ornamentality of the claim.
guidance: Visibility during normal use is a guideline, not a statutory requirement. If a design is clearly intended to be noticed during sale but hidden in final use, a lack-of-ornamentality rejection may not be required absent additional persuasive evidence (e.g., utility patent). To establish lack of ornamentality from hidden use, the article must always be hidden in end use. Examples of intermittently hidden items (lingerie, garment hangers, tent pegs, inner soles) require case-by-case analysis.

name: Examiner's prima facie burden for rejections under 35 U.S.C. 171
description: To properly reject a claimed design under 35 U.S.C. 171 for lack of ornamentality, the examiner must make a prima facie showing and provide sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon.
guidance: Proper evidentiary bases include common knowledge in the art, the appearance of the design itself, a related utility patent specification, information in the application, or evidence the article is hidden in end use. When evidence is based on well-known art, the examiner should take official notice and state it (MPEP § 2144.03). Rejections must be supported by evidence and not made absent such evidence (In re Oetiker).

name: Inventor oath/declaration requirement (non-provisional)
description: The inventor, or each individual who is a joint inventor of a claimed invention, in an application for patent (other than a provisional application) must execute an oath or declaration directed to the application, except as provided for in pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.64.
guidance: When joint inventors execute separate oaths or declarations, each oath or declaration should make reference to the fact that the affiant is a joint inventor together with each of the other inventors indicating them by name (e.g., stating belief to be original, first, and joint inventor together with 'A' or 'A & B'). Forms PTO/SB/01 and PTO/SB/01A may be used for applications filed before September 16, 2012. See MPEP § 602.08 et seq. for details specific to required inventor bibliographic information and identification of the application.

name: Oath/declaration must reference foreign applications when priority is claimed
description: Unless included in an application data sheet, oaths and declarations must make reference to any foreign application for patent (or inventor’s certificate) for which priority is claimed and any foreign application filed prior to the filing date of an application on which priority is claimed.
guidance: The applicant must recite all foreign applications filed prior to the application on which priority is claimed, giving the foreign application number, name of country or office, and filing date of each foreign application to which priority is claimed. See MPEP § 602.03 for information pertaining to defective oaths or declarations.

name: Relief from prescribed time limits for international design applications (37 CFR 1.1051; 35 U.S.C. 387)
description: An applicant's failure to act within prescribed time limits in connection with requirements pertaining to an international design application may be excused as to the United States upon a showing satisfactory to the Director of unintentional delay and under such conditions (including payment of fee) as the Director may prescribe.
guidance: A grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.1051(a) must be accompanied by: (1) a copy of any IB invitation setting the prescribed time limit; (2) the required reply (unless previously filed); (3) the fee per § 1.17(m); (4) a certified copy of the originally filed international design application (or prior communication from IB) and translation if in another language; (5) a statement that the entire delay was unintentional (Director may require additional info); and (6) a terminal disclaimer (and fee per § 1.20(d)) dedicating to the public a terminal part of the patent term equivalent to the delay period and applying to continuing patents claiming priority under 35 U.S.C. 120,121,365(c),386(c). If petition is refused, request for reconsideration/review must be filed within two months (may be extended under § 1.136). The required reply for a grantable petition may be: (1) filing of a continuing application (and, if not internationally registered, a grantable petition under § 1.1023(b) to accord a filing date) or (2) a grantable petition under § 1.1052 where application was filed with the Office as an office of indirect filing.

name: Undue experimentation / Wands test
description: Enablement fails if a person of ordinary skill in the art would not be able to practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation (In re Wands formulation).
guidance: Evaluate whether the efforts required exceed what practitioners of the art are prepared to undertake in the regular course. If skilled artisans must exercise 'independent invention' or more than ordinary skill to create an operative embodiment, the experimentation is 'undue.' Consider the depth of information provided and whether following the patent's directions alone produces a practically operative invention.

name: Federal Circuit 'reach-the-full-scope' test for genus/functional claims
description: For genus claims with functional claim limitations, the Federal Circuit has looked to whether skilled artisans can 'reach the full scope of claimed embodiments'—i.e., cumulatively identify and make all or nearly all embodiments—without 'substantial time and effort.'
guidance: This criterion focuses on the number of possible candidates within the claim and the cumulative time/effort to generate and screen them. The page criticizes this as a departure from §112 text, noting it effectively makes enablement a numbers game and imposes a higher hurdle for genus claims. When applying, courts should identify what 'reach the full scope' means factually and whether there is evidence of actual, non-enabled embodiments rather than mere speculation about theoretical candidates.

name: Proof standard and presumption of validity
description: Invalidity (including lack of enablement) must be proved by clear and convincing evidence; patents enjoy a statutory presumption of validity. (35 U.S.C. §282(a); Microsoft v. i4i)
guidance: Challengers bear the burden of overcoming the presumption of validity. If no one identifies even one actual claimed embodiment that cannot be made by following the patent's disclosure, the presumption remains and invalidity has not been shown by clear and convincing evidence.

name: Historical/precedential approach to enablement (practice over centuries)
description: Longstanding practice from English and early American courts asks whether the specification describes the invention well enough that skilled tradespeople can reproduce it; courts historically did not measure enablement by how long it would take to exhaustively generate every embodiment.
guidance: Use historical precedents (Arkwright, Neilson, Carver, etc.) to resist tests that focus on exhaustive enumeration or cumulative time-to-exhaust. The relevant inquiry remains whether a competent worker, 'fairly following' the specification, can produce the claimed invention without inventive additions.

name: Rights conferred by the patent
description: Subject to the Annex, the patent confers on its owner the exclusive right to work the patented invention and the right to prohibit any person from working the patented invention.
guidance: Defines 'working' for product patents (manufacturing, importing, offering for sale, selling, using, and holding for those purposes) and for process patents (using the process and performing product-related acts for products directly obtained by the process). Owner may assign or transfer the patent, enter into contracts. The scope of protection is determined by the claims, with the description and drawings serving to interpret the claims. For process patents, protection encompasses products obtained by the process.

name: Filing formalities and contents of the application
description: A patent application shall be filed with the Organization or the Ministry responsible for industrial property. The application file shall contain: (a) a patent application addressed to the Director-General in sufficient copies; (b) proof of payment of filing and publication fees; (c) an unstamped private power of attorney if represented by an agent; and (d) a sealed envelope containing: (i) a specification set out clearly and completely so that a person having ordinary knowledge and skill in the art could carry it out; (ii) any necessary drawings; (iii) any claim(s) defining the scope of protection sought which shall not exceed the contents of the specification; (iv) a descriptive abstract; and (v) sufficient indications regarding the best manner of carrying out the invention known to the inventor on the filing date (and priority date, where applicable).
guidance: Emphasizes enablement/clear & complete disclosure, claims limited by specification, and requirement to disclose best-known mode/indications available at filing/priority date.

name: International (PCT) application procedures and secrecy
description: The Organization shall act as a receiving office for international (PCT) applications filed by persons with residence/headquarters in a Member State where priority is not claimed. Inventions the subject of international applications filed with the Organization may not be disclosed and freely worked unless authorization is granted by the Director-General. During that time, applications may not be made public nor certified copies issued without authorization.
guidance: Implementing regulations shall set the procedure including language, forwarding fees and agent conditions. Authorization to act as receiving office or to disclose may be granted by the Director-General and may be granted at any time. Paragraph (3) lists exceptions (e.g., applicant not resident in Member State, Organization acting on behalf of another national office, or a State designated as receiving office by the Washington Treaty assembly).

name: Publication of patent application
description: The Organization shall publish for each patent application: filing number; filing date; applicant's name and address; inventor's name/address (unless inventor requested not to be mentioned); agent name/address; indication of priorities; priority date/country/number; title; abstract; international application date/number if applicable; and international patent classification symbols. The Organization shall also publish the specifications, claim(s) and any drawings. Publication shall occur within 18 months of the filing date or priority date, save for international applications.
guidance: Standard bibliographic and substantive publication obligations; international applications handled separately.

name: If a patentee claims a method but the specification describes tangible matter, the grant is valid for that tangible subject
description: Where a patentee claims a 'method' but sets forth in the specification some new substance or machine, the real subject of the grant is that substance, machine, improvement or combination, and the grant is valid.
guidance: Practically inventors often avoid titling an invention by claiming a 'method' while describing tangible matter; courts will treat the patent as for the corporeal subject described. Nevertheless, to avoid doubt an inventor should take a patent for the improvement/substance itself.

name: Patents for improvements must be limited to the improvement (not claim the whole old machine)
description: A patentee who has an improvement should claim the improvement; claiming the whole old machine as new may render the grant invalid for requiring too much or for covering things already known.
guidance: Several judges criticized Watt's broad drafting; a patent for an addition is good but 'then it must be for the addition only, and not for the old machine too.' If claimed too broadly it may be void.

name: Double use of a thing known before not patentable unless subject is a distinct substance
description: A man cannot have a grant for the discovery of a double use of a thing known before; but a patent is not objectionable if its subject is founded on the same principle as another, provided the former is for a substance distinctly different from the latter.
guidance: Example and citation: Cutler case — if patentee had claimed a new instrument (distinct substance) rather than the principle, the patent might have been supported. Thus novelty in the corporeal article can suffice even if principle is old.

name: Statutory/examiner decision standard and timing (35 U.S.C. 312 / 37 CFR 1.923)
description: Not later than 3 months after filing of a request for inter partes reexamination, the Director (or examiner) must determine whether a 'substantial new question of patentability' is raised (for requests filed prior to September 16, 2011) or whether the request shows a 'reasonable likelihood that the requester would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged' (for requests filed between September 16, 2011 and September 15, 2012).
guidance: The determination is based on the claims in effect at the time, becomes part of the official file, is mailed to patent owner and requester, is final and non-appealable, and may result in a partial refund of the request fee if reexamination is not ordered (37 CFR 1.925). No input from the patent owner is considered prior to the determination. The decision's main object is granting or denying reexamination; ultimate patentability is decided later during the examination stage.

name: Scope of claims considered in decision and examination
description: The decision on the request should discuss all of the patent claims requested for reexamination; the Office's determination and reexamination will generally be limited to the claims for which reexamination was requested and the requester must set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim requested (35 U.S.C. 311(b)(2) and 37 CFR 1.915(b)).
guidance: If the requester fails to apply the art to certain claims, those claims are not statutorily entitled to reexamination and will generally not be reexamined. If a request fails to set forth pertinency and manner for any claim, a filing date will not be awarded to the request. The Office may, in its discretion, reexamine claims not requested or initiate reexamination on its own (35 U.S.C. 303(a)).

name: One-claim sufficiency for granting reexamination
description: It is only necessary to establish that a substantial new question of patentability or a reasonable likelihood that the requester will prevail exists as to one of the patent claims in order to grant reexamination.
guidance: No prima facie case of unpatentability need be found to grant an order for reexamination; the examination stage will determine ultimate patentability.

name: Effect of reissue on reexamination requests
description: Where a request for reexamination is filed on a patent after a reissue patent for that patent has already issued, reexamination will be denied because the patent on which the request is based has been surrendered.
guidance: If reexamination of the reissued patent is desired, a new request for reexamination, including and based on the specification and claims of the reissue patent, must be filed. If the reissue issues after the filing of a request for reexamination, see MPEP § 2686.03.

name: Definition of 'covered business method patent' — financial products/services
description: Section 18's covered business method patent definition encompasses patents that claim a 'financial product or service' and is intended to be broader than just traditional banking operations.
guidance: Legislative statements clarify that 'financial product or service' is not limited to banks but includes insurance, brokerages, mutual funds, annuities, and an array of financial companies outside traditional banking. Senators noted the provision targets patents describing steps used in everyday business applications in financial products and retail services. (Sen. Leahy, Sen. Schumer, Sen. Cantwell statements cited.)

name: 'Method or corresponding apparatus' covers many claim types
description: Section 18's phrase 'a method or corresponding apparatus' is meant to encompass any type of claim in a patent regardless of claim structure.
guidance: Sen. Schumer explained this phrase was intended to include method claims, system claims, apparatus claims, graphical user interface claims, data structure (Lowry) claims, and storage-media (Beauregard) claims. The point: clever drafting should not avoid PTO review—substance over form.

name: Different standards of proof and claim construction in PTO proceedings vs district courts
description: PTO proceedings apply a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard and give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, whereas district courts apply clear-and-convincing evidence and different claim-construction approaches.
guidance: Because the standard of proof is lower in PTO review, and because claim construction and issues considered differ between forums, the same evidence may lead to different outcomes in PTO proceedings versus district court litigation. This explains why previous court findings are not determinative for PTO review. (In re Swanson discussion.)

name: Effect on §288 and inequitable-conduct doctrine
description: Amendments to §288 (via AIA §20) provide that whenever a claim of a patent is invalid, an action may be maintained for infringement of a claim of the patent which may be valid—i.e., repeal of deceptive-intent bars should limit infectious invalidity caused by inequitable conduct.
guidance: Legislative history notes ambiguity because §288 speaks of a claim that is 'invalid', while inequitable conduct traditionally leads to 'unenforceability.' Historically, courts construed §288's 'without deceptive intention' requirement to bar enforcement if any claim was invalid by reason of fraud (Kearney & Trecker; Chromalloy). The repeal aims to protect otherwise untainted valid claims, but its precise scope and interaction with modern inequitable-conduct doctrine may be uncertain.

name: Strong Claims Have Two Properties
description: (1) They survive validity attacks (no anticipation, not obvious, definite, enabled, supported by written description). (2) They cover commercially valuable activity (the kinds of products competitors actually want to make).
guidance: A claim must satisfy patentability/validity requirements and also read on economically important competitor activity; both aspects are necessary for a "strong" claim.

name: Element Count - Fewer Is Generally Better
description: Each element is a hurdle the patentee must clear in proving infringement, and each is a target for invalidity attack. A claim with 5 elements is generally stronger than the same invention claimed with 12.
guidance: Minimize the number of elements where possible to reduce infringement proof burden and avenues for attack, but do not delete elements required to distinguish the prior art—those must remain.

name: Avoid Numerical Limits Unless They Distinguish
description: "Wherein the temperature is between 50 and 100 degrees Celsius" is a hard limit. If the prior art discloses 49 or 101, the limit was needed; if not, the limit was unnecessary scope-shrinking.
guidance: Only add numeric ranges/limits when they are necessary to overcome prior art; otherwise they unnecessarily narrow claim scope and weaken the claim.

name: Functional Language - Useful but Risky
description: "A processor configured to determine X" is functionally claimed. It is broader (covers any processor that determines X) but invokes 112(f) under Williamson if there is not enough surrounding structure.
guidance: Functional claim language can broaden scope but risks being limited to disclosed structure under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (per Williamson); pair functional language with concrete structural elements to reduce 112 risks.

name: Strong Spec Support for Each Element
description: Every claim element should have at least one paragraph of spec discussion explaining what it is, what it does, what alternatives exist, and how it interacts with neighboring elements.
guidance: Provide robust specification disclosure for each claim element—sparse support creates a §112 vulnerability (written description/enablement issues). Explain purpose, alternatives, and interactions in the spec.

name: Single-Actor Drafting
description: Method claims should describe a single entity performing every step. After Akamai v. Limelight (Fed. Cir. 2015), divided infringement requires either a directing/controlling relationship or joint enterprise.
guidance: Prefer single-actor claim formulations to avoid divided-infringement issues; if multi-actor steps are necessary, draft to capture directing/controlling relationships or joint-enterprise circumstances.

name: Robust to Construction Variation
description: The strongest claims read on the accused product under both broad and narrow constructions of the disputed terms. If your infringement read depends on a single favorable claim construction, you are betting the case on one issue.
guidance: Aim to draft claims that will cover the target product across plausible claim constructions—avoid reliance on a single, optimistic construction for infringement.

name: Claim Differentiation Within Family
description: Different claims in the same patent should differ on legally meaningful dimensions - different scope, different element types, different transitions - not trivial restatements.
guidance: Use dependent and alternative claims to cover materially different scope or embodiments; avoid wasted dependent claims that merely restate the independent claim without adding legal distinctions.

name: Continuation Discipline
description: Even the strongest claim does not future-proof a portfolio. Always have a continuation pending so new claims can be drafted as new infringers emerge or as new claim-construction trends develop.
guidance: Maintain continuations to adapt claim scope over time—file follow-on applications to pursue changed enforcement or claim-construction landscapes and to capture newly relevant competitors.

name: Nexus requirement between claimed invention and commercial success
description: Applicant asserting commercial success must establish a factually and legally sufficient connection (nexus) between the evidence of commercial success and the claimed invention.
guidance: Burden of proof rests on applicant to provide 'hard evidence' of commercial success and nexus in ex parte prosecution (In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen). The term 'nexus' designates a connection so the evidence is probative (Demaco Corp.).

name: Nexus is especially difficult to establish in design cases
description: In design patent or design-related claim contexts, evidence of commercial success must be clearly attributable to the design itself rather than brand recognition, improved performance, or other factors.
guidance: Demonstrate that consumers purchased for the design; mere market leadership or brand strength may undermine a nexus finding (Litton Systems v. Whirlpool).

name: Long-felt need and failure of others: existence and persistence required
description: To support nonobviousness, the claimed invention must satisfy a long‑felt need that was recognized, persistent, and not previously solved by others.
guidance: Need must be objective and recognized by those of ordinary skill; if a prior art product satisfied the need before applicant's invention, long-felt need is negated (In re Gershon; Newell Companies v. Kenney Mfg.). Evidence of prior unsuccessful attempts by others strengthens the factor (Orthopedic Equipment Co. v. All Orthopedic Appliances).

name: Copying is a secondary consideration but requires more than mere imitation
description: Evidence that competitors copied the invention may support nonobviousness, but more than mere copying is necessary; copying may be due to other motives.
guidance: Copying persuasive when an alleged infringer expended substantial effort over time and, after failing, copied the claimed invention (Dow Chem. Co. v. American Cyanamid). Not persuasive where copies are non‑identical or the competitor had not tried to develop its own solution (Pentec; Vandenberg; Panduit).

name: Limits on establishing prior invention dates in foreign countries
description: An applicant may not establish a date of invention in certain foreign countries for purposes of prior inventor claims earlier than specified treaty dates.
guidance: The phrase 'prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104' disallows establishing a date of invention in a foreign country other than a NAFTA or WTO member; and contains specific earliest dates for WTO/NAFTA countries (e.g., no earlier than Jan 1, 1996 for WTO country other than NAFTA; no earlier than Dec 8, 1993 for NAFTA country other than the U.S.).

name: Reference date determined on a claim-by-claim basis
description: The reference date for determining patentability is determined in principle on a claim-by-claim basis.
guidance: Examiners must evaluate each claimed invention separately when deciding which filing/priority date is the relevant reference date.

name: Priority not recognized when first-country application itself claims earlier priority
description: When the first-country application (that would serve as the basis) claims priority based on another earlier application, that first-country application shall not be regarded as the 'earliest application' for the invention described in both applications; the effect of the priority claim shall not be recognized for that invention.
guidance: Examination in this case shall not be retroactively conducted to the reference date and the examiner shall notify a specific reason for non-retroactive application.

name: Domestic priority: eligible claimant
description: A person eligible to claim domestic priority is an applicant of the prior-filed application. If the applicant of the prior-filed and later-filed applications are not the same, the examiner shall request amendments and invalidate the priority claim procedure if the deficiency is not cured.
guidance: The scope of amendment requests is limited to correction of obvious errors. The determination whether applicants are the same is made as of the time the domestic priority claim is filed (cover sheet or subsequent amendment).

name: Domestic priority: one-year time limit
description: The domestic priority claim must be made within one year from the filing date of the prior-filed application which forms the basis of the domestic priority claim.
guidance: If filed after the statutory period the examiner requests amendments and invalidates the priority claim procedure if the deficiency is not cured; scope of allowed amendments limited to obvious errors.

name: Reference date rules for domestic priority (identical / not stated / combinations)
description: For domestic priority claims the reference date is determined claim-by-claim: (i) identical inventions: reference date = filing date of the prior-filed application (earliest if multiple); (ii) inventions not stated in the prior-filed original specification: reference date = filing date of the domestic priority claim; (iii) combinations of matters from two or more prior-filed applications (or combining new matter) are treated as inventions not stated in the original specification.
guidance: If the prior-filed application itself claims priority to another application, the effect of the domestic priority claim is not recognized for inventions stated in both; examiner to specify reasons for non-retroactive application where applicable.

name: Application by a legitimate right holder: four requirements
description: To be recognized as an application by a legitimate right holder (Articles 34 and 35), the following must be met: (1) an application by an unentitled person was filed earlier than the legitimate holder's application; (2) the unentitled person's application is rejected or invalidated in trial on the ground it was not filed by the entitled person; (3) the legitimate holder's application is filed within thirty days from when the trial decision became conclusive and unappealable; and (4) the scope of the claimed invention in the legitimate holder's application falls within the disclosure of the unentitled person's application.
guidance: When filed with Form (xiv) or legitimacy argued in written argument during examination, the examiner shall study legitimacy before any other grounds for rejection.

name: Legitimate-right-holder scope limitation
description: The scope of invention in an application by the legitimate holder is limited to the claimed inventions and those disclosed in the specification or drawings of the unentitled person's application.
guidance: If the legitimate holder's application includes inventions beyond that disclosure (e.g., multiple inventions where only some fall within the disclosed scope), the filing date for those beyond-scope inventions shall not be retroactive in examination.

name: Effect of translation submission varies by filing date (pre-2015 vs post-2015)
description: Where the international application was filed before Dec 31, 2014, translations of description, claims, drawings and abstract submitted as of the filing date are considered as the specification/drawings under Article 42(2). Where filed after Jan 1, 2015, the description, claims and drawings submitted as of the filing date are considered to be the specification and drawings as originally filed pursuant to Article 42(2); abstract translation rules differ by language.
guidance: Different transitional rules apply depending on the international filing date; examiners should follow date-based rules when assessing original filing content.

name: Examiner attention to national-phase PCT details and priority treatment
description: When an international application enters the national phase with Korean translation submitted and claims priority under the PCT, the priority claim is treated as the priority claim under the Treaty. If the application serving as the priority basis is Korean or an international application where Korea is the only designated State, the priority claim is considered domestic.
guidance: When an international application serves as the basis of domestic priority and becomes 'another application' under Article 29(3), the application is considered laid open at international publication time, but the scope of inventions is limited to those described in the specification/claims/drawings as of the international filing date and as in the domestic priority claim.

name: Domestic priority where prior-filed app is international application
description: Where a prior-filed application that serves as a basis for domestic priority is an international application, inventions commonly stated in both the application with domestic priority claim and the international application (limited to specification/claims/drawings submitted at the international filing date) are considered filed at the international filing date.
guidance: Examiner should consider the international filing date as the effective date for commonly stated inventions in domestic priority analysis.

name: Korean translation of PCT Article 19/34 amendments considered voluntary amendment if timely
description: If Korean translation of written amendments regarding description or claims under PCT Articles 19 and 34 is submitted within the reference date, the examiner proceeds considering the international application to have been voluntarily amended according to Article 47 of the Patent Act.
guidance: Timely translation of PCT amendments affects the scope of what is treated as filed/ amended in national phase examination.

name: Parts of the patent document (cover page, abstract, drawings, specification, claims)
description: The patent document includes a cover page (grant date, patent number, inventor, filing date, cited references), an abstract, drawings illustrating the invention, a written description (specification), and numbered patent claims at the end that define the claimed invention.
guidance: Court/jury may be directed to these parts to understand the asserted patent; the specification includes the 'best way' believed by the inventor at filing and supports claim construction.

name: Judge's role in claim construction (meaning of claim terms)
description: The judge determines the correct construction or meaning of words in the patent claims; jurors must accept and apply those meanings in deciding infringement and invalidity.
guidance: Instruction to read and apply the words as the court has interpreted them; court may provide a glossary of patent and technical terms and add technical terms expected at trial.

name: Direct (literal) infringement — element-by-element comparison
description: To prove direct literal infringement the patent holder must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused product or method includes every requirement (element/step) of the asserted claim as the court has interpreted it.
guidance: If any requirement/step recited in the claim is omitted in the accused product/method, there is no literal infringement. No intent or knowledge is required for literal infringement.

name: Open-ended 'comprising' claims
description: 'Comprising' means 'including' or 'containing but not limited to' — a claim using 'comprising' is infringed if the accused product/method includes all recited requirements, even if it has additional items.
guidance: Example: a table 'comprising' tabletop, legs, glue is infringed by a table that also has wheels. Cites authorities that 'comprised of' has same open-ended meaning.

name: 'Consisting essentially of' claims
description: 'Consisting essentially of' means the claimed invention may include additional unlisted requirements provided those additions do not materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention as defined.
guidance: Claims with this language are infringed only if added elements do not materially affect the basic and novel features of the claimed invention.

name: Means-plus-function claims (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶6)
description: A 'means' (or step) claim element recites a means for performing a function rather than a structure; such claim elements cover the structure, material, or acts described in the specification for performing that function, and equivalents thereof.
guidance: To prove literal infringement of a means-plus-function element the patent holder must show (1) the accused device employs a structure/act identical or equivalent to the structure disclosed in the specification, and (2) that the structure in the accused device performs the identical function specified in the claim. Equivalence under §112 ¶6 requires insubstantial differences and is evaluated as of issuance; §112 ¶6 equivalence is not necessarily coextensive with doctrine of equivalents.

name: Inducing infringement — elements and intent
description: To prove inducement the patent holder must show by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) the alleged inducer actively encouraged or instructed another to use a product or perform a process in a way that infringes the patent claims; (2) the alleged inducer knew of the patent; (3) the alleged inducer knew or should have known that the encouragement would induce infringement; and (4) another person actually infringed the patent.
guidance: The patent holder must prove specific intent to induce infringement — knowing inducement of infringement, not merely knowing the acts that constitute infringement.

name: Willful infringement
description: Willful infringement may be found if the patent holder proves by clear and convincing evidence (or as instructed in a case-by-case manner) that the alleged infringer acted with reckless disregard of whether the claim was infringed or was invalid or unenforceable.
guidance: Jury's willfulness finding should not directly affect the damage award; judge will take willfulness into account for enhanced damages under governing law. Model verdict asks whether willfulness is 'highly probable' (clear and convincing).

name: Anticipation (novelty) — public use, prior publication, prior invention by others
description: A claim is anticipated (not new) if a single prior art reference or prior use/disclosure (in this country or published elsewhere) discloses all elements of the claim; anticipation can include public use, known use, or prior publication.
guidance: Anticipation must be proven by clear and convincing evidence; separate instructions address 'publicly used or known, or previously published' anticipation and anticipation by prior invention by someone else.

name: Obviousness (nonobviousness) — general standard
description: A claim is invalid as obvious if, considering the scope and content of the prior art, differences over the prior art, and the level of ordinary skill in the art, the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill at the time of invention.
guidance: Obviousness is typically proved by clear and convincing evidence; the instructions include breakdowns (scope/content of prior art, differences, level of ordinary skill) and alternative formulations. Jury should consider objective indicia where relevant.

name: Scope and content of the prior art / differences over prior art / level of ordinary skill
description: To assess obviousness jurors must (1) determine the scope and content of the prior art, (2) identify differences between the prior art and the claimed invention, and (3) determine the level of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: These factual inquiries feed into the legal conclusion of obviousness; evidence may include expert testimony, prior references, and industry practices.

name: Lost profits — Panduit factors (four elements)
description: To recover lost profits the patent holder must prove by a preponderance of the evidence: (1) demand for the patented product/method, (2) absence of acceptable non-infringing alternatives (or that the patentee lost sales due to infringement), (3) the patentee had manufacturing and marketing capacity to meet the infringing sales it claims, and (4) the amount of profit the patentee would have made but for the infringement.
guidance: If lost profits are not proven for particular infringing sales, the law requires awarding a reasonable royalty for those sales.

name: Prosecution history / file wrapper relevance (prosecution history estoppel)
description: The prosecution history (communications between applicant and PTO) is part of the public record and can affect claim interpretation and the availability of equivalents (prosecution history estoppel may bar some equivalents).
guidance: Issues of prosecution history estoppel are legal questions resolved by a judge rather than the jury; jury should be instructed about limitations on doctrine of equivalents where appropriate.

name: Claim interpretation (claim construction)
description: The same legal standard for claim construction applies in an IPR and in a district court case: 'in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.'
guidance: Claim construction positions taken during IPR proceedings may be used against a party in corresponding district court litigation; parties are encouraged to take consistent positions across proceedings. The PTAB will consider claim construction determinations and statements made in other proceedings and instructs parties to file relevant determinations as soon as available. Parties may propose constructions or state terms need no express construction.

name: Motions to amend (claim amendments during IPR)
description: A patent owner may file a motion to amend the patent after institution; the motion must clearly show changes and describe how disclosures in the original and priority applications support the proposed amended claims.
guidance: PTAB rule changes (Mar 15, 2019) allow requesting preliminary guidance on the motion's merits and filing a revised motion. The petitioner ordinarily bears the burden to show by a preponderance of the evidence that proposed amended claims are unpatentable. Petitioners may submit new evidence in response and raise additional grounds (e.g., subject matter eligibility). Patent owners should carefully consider whether to request preliminary guidance because negative feedback may provide a roadmap for petitioners.

name: Legal grounds and prior art considered
description: IPR challenges are limited to anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) based on patents and printed publications.
guidance: Anticipation means a single reference discloses all claim elements; obviousness means one or more references in combination disclose or suggest claim elements such that a person of skill would have modified or combined teachings to arrive at the claimed invention. Product-based prior art is not part of IPR prior art scope.

name: Burden of proof and standard vs. federal court
description: To prevail, an IPR petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence—a lower burden than the clear and convincing standard in district court.
guidance: This lower standard, combined with limited discovery and technically trained PTAB judges, generally makes challenging claims in IPRs easier and less costly than in federal court.

name: Claims: commencement and formatting
description: The claim or claims must commence on a separate sheet or electronic page (37 CFR 1.52(b)(3)). Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step of the claim should be separated by a line indentation; plural indentations may segregate subcombinations or related steps.
guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.75 and MPEP § 608.01(i)-(p) for claim form; ensure claims start on separate page and use indentations consistently for clarity of claim structure.

name: Abstract of the Disclosure: language and form
description: The abstract should be narrative, generally limited to a single paragraph on a separate sheet (preferably within 50–150 words). It should describe the disclosure sufficiently to assist readers in deciding whether to consult the full patent text.
guidance: Language should be clear and concise; do not repeat title information; avoid phrases that can be implied ('The disclosure concerns'); avoid legal phraseology and claim-like terms (e.g., 'means', 'said').

name: Title of Invention must be descriptive
description: The title of the invention must be clearly indicative of the invention to which the claims are directed. If the title is not descriptive, a new title is required.
guidance: If examiner suggests a change, use form paragraph 6.11.01 to propose suggested title (provide suggested title in bracket).

name: Substitute specification required by examiner — identify reason
description: A substitute specification [1] the claims is required pursuant to 37 CFR 1.125(a) because [2].
guidance: In the bracketed fields, identify the substitute specification's relation to claims and the specific reason(s) (e.g., language, format, new matter). Provide the required statement that the substitute contains no new matter.

name: Practice of double patenting rejections in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities
description: In view of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the Commissioner has reinstituted in appropriate circumstances the practice of rejecting claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities on the grounds of double patenting.
guidance: Such rejections can be overcome in appropriate circumstances by filing terminal disclaimers. This prevents improper extension of patent protection while permitting legitimate benefits to inventors/assignees. See MPEP § 804 for further guidance.

name: Double patenting rejection and how to overcome
description: Commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting, including in cases where later-filed application claims 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit to the earlier application.
guidance: Double patenting rejections prevent an organization from obtaining multiple patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter. They can be overcome in certain circumstances by disclaiming, pursuant to 37 CFR 1.321, the terminal portion of the term of the later patent and including a provision that the patent shall be enforceable only during the period of common ownership with the application/patent that formed the basis for the rejection. See MPEP §§ 804, 804.02.

name: Form paragraph 7.21 and related form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections (¶ 7.21, 7.21.01, 7.21.02, 7.22)
description: ¶ 7.21: Generic rejection form for claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over identified art; must be followed by an explanation applying the Graham v. Deere test. ¶ 7.21.01: Provisional rejection under 103(a) based on copending application with common assignee or at least one common inventor (anticipation if copending app later patents). ¶ 7.21.02: Rejection under 103(a) where applied reference has a common assignee or at least one common inventor, and ways to overcome. ¶ 7.22: Rejection under 103(a) 'further in view of' another reference.
guidance: Each paragraph has Examiner Notes specifying when to use, required follow-ups (e.g., Graham analysis), how to fill bracketed insertions (e.g., identify common assignee/inventor), and how such rejections may be overcome (37 CFR 1.131, 1.132, 1.130 plus terminal disclaimer for certain cases). Use 7.21.01 for provisional rejections where appropriate; do not use 7.21.01 for post-Nov 29, 1999 applications when common ownership is established per §706.02(l)(3).

name: Graham v. Deere test factors for obviousness
description: The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co. used to establish a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a): (1) Determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: An explanation applying the Graham test must follow form paragraphs that assert a 103(a) rejection. Paragraph 7.23 may be used in response to an argument invoking Graham v. Deere.

name: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) special rules for biotechnological processes
description: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) provides that, notwithstanding subsection (a), a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter novel under 102 and nonobvious under 103(a) shall be considered nonobvious if (1) claims to the process and composition are in the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date, and (2) the composition and the process at the time invented were owned by or subject to obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: Additional requirements: (A) patent on process must also contain claims to composition used or made by the process or, if composition is in another patent, patents must expire on same date; (B) definition of 'biotechnological process' enumerated (genetically altering organisms to express/inhibit sequences or express specific physiological characteristics; cell fusion procedures yielding cell lines expressing specific proteins; methods of using products produced by such processes); (C) timely election to proceed under 103(b) via petition under 37 CFR 1.182 must be made, normally no later than earlier of payment of issue fee or filing of an appeal brief; (D) for pending apps where issue fee paid prior to specific dates, timeliness may be satisfied by 37 CFR 1.312(b) conditions; (E) if patent issued without election due to error without deceptive intent, reissue may be filed to permit consideration of process claims qualifying for 103(b) treatment. See MPEP § 2116.01 and cited Federal Circuit decisions.

name: Statutory Compliance Standard — allowed claims
description: For an allowed claim, the Office action must: not omit a statutorily compliant rejection, clearly identify the claim, and set forth that the claim is allowable.
guidance: An allowance must affirmatively show that applicable rejections were considered and that the claim is properly identified and determined allowable.

name: Statutory Compliance Standard — rejected claims
description: For a rejected claim, the Office action must: clearly identify the claim, identify the relevant statute, and set forth sufficient evidence to put a person skilled in the art on notice as to why the claim is unpatentable to provide applicant with a fair opportunity to respond.
guidance: Rejections must include clear claim identification, statutory basis, and adequate reasoning/evidence so the applicant can meaningfully respond.

name: Return postcard itemization for filing receipt evidence
description: If a self-addressed postcard is submitted with a patent application for a receipt, the postcard should itemize all components of the application (applicant's name(s); title; number of pages of specification, claims, and drawing sheets; whether oath/declaration is included; list of additional forms; amount and manner of fee payment).
guidance: If the postcard does not itemize each component, it will not serve as evidence that any non-itemized component was received by the USPTO.

name: Same invention requirement for 102(d)
description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d), the 'invention... patented' in the foreign country must be the same as the invention sought to be patented in the U.S.; the foreign application must support the subject matter of the U.S. claims.
guidance: Claims need not be identical or in the same statutory class; if the foreign specification fully discloses the invention and thereby supports U.S. claiming options, 102(d) applies to disclosed aspects even if the foreign claims are narrower or different (In re Kathawala).

name: Provisional application benefit requires 112 support
description: A U.S. patent that claims benefit to a provisional application is usable as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) as of the provisional filing date only if at least one claim of the patent is supported by the provisional application's disclosure in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) and examples; inadequate provisional support prevents the provisional filing date from being the critical 102(e) date (see Dynamic Drinkware v. National Graphics).

name: Treatment of international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000
description: International applications filed prior to November 29, 2000 are subject to the pre-AIPA version of 102(e); various specific rules apply depending on whether the reference is a U.S. patent, U.S. application publication, or WIPO publication.
guidance: For example: (1) U.S. patents: apply 102(e) as of earlier of completion of 371(c) requirements or filing date of later U.S. application claiming the international app; (2) U.S. and WIPO publications: generally not applied as 102(e) as of publication date under the older statute but may be used under 102(a)/(b); (3) follow the three listed subrules in MPEP §2136.03(B).

name: Benefit of nonprovisional parent (35 U.S.C. 120) requires 112 support
description: A U.S. patent or application publication that claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 to an earlier nonprovisional (continuation/divisional/CIP) is accorded the earlier filing date as its 102(e) prior art date only if the earlier-filed application properly supports the subject matter relied upon in the rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112, first paragraph.
guidance: Subject matter not supported in the earlier application cannot be given the earlier date. See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) and examples 2 and 5–9.

name: 102/103 rejection appropriate when prior art product appears identical but silent on characteristic
description: Where applicant claims a composition in terms of a function, property, or characteristic and the composition of the prior art is the same as that of the claim but the function is not explicitly disclosed by the reference, the examiner may make a rejection under both 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (a 102/103 rejection).
guidance: There is nothing inconsistent in asserting anticipation under 102 and obviousness under 103 concurrently (In re Best). This applies to product, apparatus, and process claims claimed in terms of function/property/characteristic.

name: Product/apparatus claims: identical or substantially identical structure presumes properties/functions inherent
description: Where the claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure or composition, or are produced by identical or substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of either anticipation or obviousness has been established and claimed properties/functions are presumed inherent.
guidance: If the PTO shows a sound basis for believing the products are the same, applicant has burden to show they are not (In re Best; In re Spada; Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner). Applicant can rebut by showing the prior art product does not necessarily possess the claimed characteristics.

name: Composition claims: identical chemical structure implies same properties
description: Products of identical chemical composition cannot have mutually exclusive properties; if the prior art teaches the identical chemical structure, the properties applicant discloses and/or claims are necessarily present.
guidance: Virtual identity of monomers and procedures can support prima facie unpatentability for lack of novelty (In re Spada). Applicant must produce evidence to show a real difference in properties if asserted.

name: Nonfunctional printed matter does not distinguish product claims
description: Where the only difference between a prior art product and a claimed product is printed matter that is not functionally related to the product, the printed matter will not distinguish the claimed product from the prior art.
guidance: Critical inquiry is whether there exists any new and unobvious functional relationship between the printed matter and the substrate (In re Ngai; In re Gulack; In re Miller). Courts extend this to 'instruction limitations' in method claims—informational limitations that do not transform or depend on the method are non-functional (King Pharmaceuticals v. Eon Labs).

name: Process claims: prior art device anticipates a claimed process if device inherently carries out the process during normal operation
description: If a prior art device, in its normal and usual operation, would necessarily perform the method claimed, then the method claimed will be considered to be anticipated by the prior art device.
guidance: When the prior art device is the same as a device described in the specification for carrying out the claimed method, it can be assumed the device will inherently perform the claimed process. Applicant must present evidence (e.g., comparative data) to rebut (In re King; In re Best; Ex parte Novitski).

name: Process-of-use claims: new uses of old structures may be patentable, but claims directed to mere discovery of a property are anticipated
description: A discovery of a new use for an old structure may be patentable as a process of using; however, when the claim recites using an old composition/structure and the 'use' is directed to a result or property of that composition/structure, the claim is anticipated if the prior art already reads on that property.
