guidance: Finding a new property of an old compound does not necessarily create a patentable new use (In re Hack; In re May; In re Tomlinson). Distinguish true new uses from mere recognition of previously inherent properties.

name: Product-by-process claims judged on the product, not the process
description: Even though product-by-process claims are limited by the recited process, determination of patentability is based on the product itself; if the product is the same as or obvious from a prior art product, the claim is unpatentable even if the prior product was made by a different process.
guidance: Infringement analysis differs (infringement only by product made by recited process), but validity is determined by product identity (In re Thorpe; Amgen v. F. Hoffmann‑La Roche). Consider structure implied by process steps when assessing patentability (In re Garnero).

name: Use of 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections for product-by-process claims is acceptable
description: When the prior art discloses a product which reasonably appears to be identical with or only slightly different from a product claimed in a product-by-process claim, a rejection based alternatively on either section 102 or section 103 is fair and acceptable.
guidance: Office personnel must explain both anticipation and obviousness aspects of such rejections; practical limits on Office ability to physically compare many products support this approach (In re Brown).

name: Apparatus claims: inherency and functional limitations
description: If an examiner concludes that a functional limitation is an inherent characteristic of the prior art, the examiner should explain that the prior art structure inherently possesses the limitations of the claimed apparatus.
guidance: Burden shifts to applicant to show prior art does not possess the relied-on characteristic (In re Schreiber; Bettcher Industries v. Bunzl; In re Swinehart). See MPEP §§2173.05(g), 2181–2186 for means-plus-function guidance.

name: Manner of operating device does not differentiate apparatus claims from prior art
description: An apparatus claim covers what a device is, not what a device does; a recitation regarding intended use or manner of operation does not differentiate the claimed apparatus from prior art if the prior art teaches all the structural limitations.
guidance: Preamble use or specified intended employment is immaterial to structure-based rejections (Hewlett‑Packard Co. v. Bausch & Lomb; Ex parte Masham). Examiners should focus on structural limitations.

name: Structural differences can prevent anticipation even if prior art performs same functions
description: Even if the prior art device performs all the functions recited in the claim, the prior art cannot anticipate the claim if there is any structural difference.
guidance: Means‑plus‑function limitations are met by structures equivalent to corresponding structures in the specification; claims may require specific structural elements (In re Donaldson; In re Robertson). Examiner should analyze structural correspondence, not solely functional equivalence.

name: Functional claim language without structural limitation covers all devices capable of performing the function
description: Functional claim language that is not limited to a specific structure covers all devices that are capable of performing the recited function, affecting the scope of what is anticipated or obvious under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.
guidance: If a claim is functional-only (no structure), it may be read broadly to cover any device performing the function; examiners should consider whether the claim needs structural limitation or whether prior art devices inherently fall within such broad functional language. (Section introduces treatment for computer‑implemented functional claim limitations.)

name: Filing date entitlement for nonprovisional applications filed on or after Dec 18, 2013
description: Except for design applications, the filing date is the date on which a specification, with or without claims, is received by the Office.
guidance: Design applications (except CPA) require a specification including at least one claim and any required drawings to obtain a filing date. Although minimal formal requirements were reduced by PLTIA, applicants are advised that including claims on filing is a best practice to ensure disclosure satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(a).

name: Filing date entitlement for nonprovisional applications filed before Dec 18, 2013
description: For applications filed prior to Dec 18, 2013, a filing date is the date a specification containing a description (37 CFR 1.71), at least one claim (37 CFR 1.75), and any required drawings (37 CFR 1.81(a)) are filed.
guidance: Failure to meet these requirements will result in denial of a filing date; the filing date becomes the date when all requirements are met.

name: Continuation/divisional/continuation-in-part filing allocation
description: A continuing application may be filed as a continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) and 37 CFR 1.78(c) and (d); specific subparagraphs of 37 CFR 1.53 specify which type must be filed under which paragraph.
guidance: Continuation-in-part applications (which can disclose/claim subject matter not disclosed in the prior application) or any continuation/divisional that names an inventor not named in the prior application must be filed under paragraph (b). Continuations or divisionals that name the same or fewer inventors may be filed under paragraph (d) when appropriate (e.g., design CPA rules).

name: Completion of nonprovisional application missing fees/claims/oath (without correspondence address)
description: If the application has no correspondence address and is missing required fees, claims, or oath/declaration, applicant generally has a fixed short period from the filing date to supply missing parts (e.g., three months) to avoid abandonment.
guidance: Specific timeframes vary by rule and filing-date regime (e.g., some pre- and post-AIA rules described two months or three months). If applicant fails to correct within the time period or timely petition, proceedings will be terminated and fees refunded less handling fee per 37 CFR 1.21(n).

name: When PR practice is improper — same character claims
description: Where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ in scope only, prosecution by Patentability Report is never proper.
guidance: Do not use PR when claims share the same character irrespective of scope differences; PR suits cases of plural, distinct specialties only.

name: Examination process before rejecting claims
description: After the application has been read and the claimed invention understood, a prior art search for the claimed invention is made; with search results the application should be reviewed and analyzed in conjunction with the state of the prior art to determine whether the claims define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention that has been clearly described in the specification.
guidance: Goal is to clearly articulate any rejection early in prosecution so applicant can reply; examiner should review all evidence, including applicant arguments and responsive evidence, before issuing the next Office action. If information reasonably necessary should be required under 37 CFR 1.105, do so prior to or with the first Office action on the merits per MPEP § 704.10 et seq.

name: Standard for rejection — 37 CFR 1.104(c) (must reject unpatentable claims)
description: If the invention is not considered patentable, or not considered patentable as claimed, the claims, or those considered unpatentable will be rejected.
guidance: When rejecting for want of novelty or obviousness, cite the best references available; designate the particular part relied on when a reference is complex; clearly explain the pertinence of each reference if not apparent; specify each rejected claim.

name: Joint research agreement exception for 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2)
description: To overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection based on subject matter qualifying as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g), the applicant must provide a statement that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement.
guidance: The term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. Applicant must amend/disclose parties as required.

name: Defects in form or omission of a limitation — constructive action
description: When an application discloses patentable subject matter but the claims in their present form cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection of the claims.
guidance: Examiner’s action should be constructive and, when possible, offer a definite suggestion for correction rather than mere objection.

name: Reliance upon admitted prior art
description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission which can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify under statutory categories of 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: Admitted prior art can be used to reject claims even where it might not meet statutory categories; see MPEP § 2129 for admissions discussion.

name: Rejections corresponding to claims of a patent
description: When claims corresponding to claims of a patent are presented in an application, the examiner must determine whether the presented claims are unpatentable on any ground(s) (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, 112, double patenting).
guidance: If a ground of rejection would also be applicable to claims in the corresponding patent, any office action including the rejection must have approval of the Technology Center Director; follow MPEP § 1003 and related interference guidance.

name: When to consider 102(a), (b), or (e)
description: Once a printed publication or patent that discloses the claimed invention is found, the examiner should determine whether the rejection should be made under 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b), or (e) by comparing the effective filing date of the application with the date of the reference.
guidance: First consider 102(b) because it results in a statutory bar; if 102(b) does not apply due to timing, consider 102(e) and the inventive entity criteria; follow MPEP guidance on dating and reference qualification.

name: Enablement requirement (practicability)
description: If an embodiment related to the claims is deemed different from the embodiment disclosed in the description and the invention related to the claims cannot be practiced only with the embodiments disclosed in the description, an examiner shall notify a ground for rejection in violation of Article 42(3)(i) of the Patent Act.
guidance: When notifying enablement violations, the examiner shall specify the violation and the corresponding claims. For applications filed after Jan 1, 2015, enablement-type deficiencies may be proposed for amendment under Article 46 rather than immediate invalidation. If description meets Article 21(3) layout but is not detailed/clear enough to practice the claimed invention, notify under Article 42(3).

name: Claims supported by description (written support)
description: Claims shall be supported by the description of the invention (Article 42(4)(i)). An examiner shall determine support based on whether a person skilled in the art can figure out the subject matters corresponding to the claims from the description.
guidance: Determine support by whether the claimed subject matter departs from the scope a skilled person would grasp from the description, not by literal identity. If claims recite subject matter neither disclosed nor implied, or terms differ creating ambiguity, or claimed functional means lack corresponding specific configuration, notify lack of support. Examples include numerical limits not disclosed and claims directed to a motor type not disclosed in the description.

name: Industrial applicability disclosure
description: Where it is hard to determine whether the claimed invention is industrially applicable, the utilization method, manufacturing method, or method of industrial applicability shall be stated in the Industrial Applicability section.
guidance: If industrial applicability can be well inferred from other parts of the specification, additional description may not be necessary.

name: Foreign language and translation issues
description: Except for specifications written in a foreign language under Article 42(3)(i), where terms are not written in Korean so the description is unclear, an examiner shall give the applicant an opportunity to explain (Article 11(1)(iv)) and return the application; if only part is foreign but content is understandable, do not return—order amendment under Article 46.
guidance: For priority applications with translation errors, do not notify rejection solely for translation error; notify only when failure to meet description requirements is found in the priority-claiming specification. Examiners should examine thoroughly because amendments to correct translation may risk adding new matter or changing what is practiced.

name: Determination of invention and claim scope
description: The invention recited in the claims is what the applicant regards as their invention for which protection is sought; determination of the invention shall be made based on claim limitations in accordance with the applicant's will. Description and drawings are considered only when claims are indefinite or terms ambiguous.
guidance: Do not determine protection scope based on description disclosure beyond claim limitations. Abstract cannot be used to decide protection scope. Examiner should be mindful that improper claims may unfairly limit third-party rights or cause invalidation.

name: How examiner should notify grounds for rejection for description defects
description: When notifying grounds for rejection citing enablement and description method requirements, any violation shall be specified and notified; especially for enablement, the corresponding claims shall be specified.
guidance: For applications filed before Dec 31, 2014, violation of both enablement and description method could be a ground for rejection; for applications filed after Jan 1, 2015, examiners should notify under Article 42(3)(i) and propose amendment under Article 46. If description method requirement is violated but all claimed inventions can still be easily practiced, the description shall be deemed legitimate.

name: Expand exclusive jurisdiction to cover civil infringement motions and criminal cases
description: Pursue legislative changes so the court's exclusive jurisdiction includes appeals from motions such as preliminary injunctions and, in the long term, first-instance trials and appeals in criminal cases related to patent and other IP rights.
guidance: Including such matters under exclusive jurisdiction aims to enable prompt and consistent adjudication of main claims and motions, reduce inconsistency and delay arising from jurisdictional separation, and improve IP protection at an early stage.

name: Visual disclosure requirement (drawing or photograph)
description: Every design patent application must include either a drawing or a photograph of the claimed design; the drawing or photograph constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the claim.
guidance: As the drawing or photograph constitutes the whole disclosure, it is of utmost importance that the drawing or photograph be clear and complete, and that nothing regarding the design sought to be patented is left to conjecture. An insufficient drawing may be fatal to validity (35 U.S.C. 112(a)) and may negatively affect the effective filing date in a continuing application.

name: Sufficient number of views / adequate disclosure of appearance
description: Drawings or photographs should contain a sufficient number of views to disclose the complete appearance of the design claimed (may include front, rear, top, bottom and sides).
guidance: For inherently two-dimensional designs a single plan- or planar-view may suffice (see In re Maatita). Perspective views are suggested for three-dimensional designs and may obviate other views if surfaces are fully disclosed. Views that are merely duplicative or flat with no ornamentation may be omitted if the specification explicitly states so (e.g., mirror-image sides).

name: Broken lines: permitted uses and restrictions
description: Broken lines may be used to disclose environmental structure or to define the bounds of the claim, but not to indicate that portions of a design are unimportant or immaterial.
guidance: Unclaimed subject matter may be shown in broken lines for illustrating environment; such matter must be described as forming no part of the claimed design. Broken lines may not be used to show hidden planes and surfaces, nor to indicate that a portion is less important. When broken-line boundaries are added by amendment or continuation, they must comply with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Broken-line boundaries other than straight broken lines may constitute new matter (prohibited by 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121(f)).

name: Requirement to describe broken lines in specification
description: When broken lines are used, the specification must explicitly describe their purpose and whether they form part of the claimed design or are environment.
guidance: Suggested statement: '--The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design.--' This description should precede the claim in the specification so that the scope of the claim is clear, especially when different broken lines in the same application serve different purposes.

name: When broken-line environment obscures full-line disclosure
description: If superimposed broken lines showing environmental structure obscure the full-line disclosure of the claimed design, a separate figure showing the broken lines must be included in addition to the figures showing only claimed subject matter.
guidance: This avoids obscuring or confusing the visual disclosure of the claimed design and preserves enablement/definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b).

name: Alternate positions and combined media restrictions
description: Alternate positions illustrated by full and broken lines in the same view are not permitted. Photographs and ink drawings are not permitted to be combined as formal drawings in one application.
guidance: Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must not disclose environmental structure and must be limited to the design claimed for the article. Introducing both photographs and drawings in one application risks inconsistencies and is not allowed.

name: Photographs: when allowed and quality requirements
description: Photographs may be accepted in utility and design patent applications only if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.
guidance: If the photographs are not of sufficient quality so that all details are reproducible, objections will follow and no application will be issued until acceptable photographs are submitted and approved. Photographs used in lieu of ink drawings must be limited to the design claimed and must not disclose environmental structure (37 CFR 1.84(b)).

name: Sectional views: limited and potentially confusing
description: Sectional views presented solely to show internal construction or functional/mechanical features are unnecessary and may lead to confusion as to the scope of the claimed design; the examiner should object and require cancellation unless the sectional view is needed to clarify external contour.
guidance: Where a sectional view is added during prosecution, the examiner must determine whether there is antecedent basis in the original disclosure for material shown in hatching per 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) and MPEP § 608.02. Historical precedent (Ex parte Tucker; Ex parte Kohler; Ex parte Lohman) supports caution.

name: Claim form and single-claim rule for design patents
description: A design patent application may include only a single claim. The single claim should normally be in the formal terms: 'The ornamental design for (the article which embodies the design or to which it is applied) as shown.'
guidance: The description of the article in the claim should be consistent in terminology with the title of the invention. More than one claim is neither required nor permitted. When the specification includes an appropriate descriptive statement or modified forms, add 'and described' (i.e., 'as shown and described').

name: Use of 'as shown' vs 'as shown and described' in claim language
description: For proper form under 37 CFR 1.153 (or 1.1025 for international design applications), the claim should read either 'The ornamental design for [article] as shown' or '...as shown and described' when descriptive matter is included in the specification.
guidance: Form paragraph templates indicate how to amend claims: include 'I' or 'We' as appropriate, and ensure the title of the article is inserted consistently. Examiner notes instruct inserting '--must be--' or '--has been--' in bracketed amendment language when making examiner amendments.

name: Inconsistencies among views and effect on enablement/definiteness
description: When inconsistencies are found among the views, the examiner should object and request that the views be made consistent; if inconsistencies are of such magnitude that the overall appearance is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite.
guidance: See Ex parte Asano and Hadco Products precedent. If a reply overcomes a rejection, the examiner must indicate the rejection as withdrawn in the next Office action unless notice of allowability is being issued.

name: Novelty/nonobviousness search scope for designs
description: Novelty and nonobviousness of a design claim must generally be determined by a search in the pertinent design classes, and the search must be extended to mechanical classes encompassing inventions of the same general type.
guidance: Catalogs and trade journals as well as available foreign patent databases are also to be consulted. The inventive novelty or unobviousness resides in the ornamental shape/configuration or surface ornamentation applied to or embodied in the design.

name: Color submissions and later omission of color
description: If color photographs or color drawings are filed with the original application, color will be considered an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design; omission of color in later filed drawings may be permitted only if the application shows possession of the underlying configuration without color at filing.
guidance: See In re Daniels precedent: omission of color later is permitted where underlying configuration was apparent in the original filing. Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must not disclose environmental structure (37 CFR 1.152).

name: Written description requirement — general principle
description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1). This requirement is separate and distinct from enablement and implements the principle that a patent must describe the technology sought to be patented; it serves to demonstrate that the inventor was in possession of the claimed subject matter and to put the public in possession of what is claimed.
guidance: Policy objectives: convey that applicant invented the claimed subject matter and put the public in possession. Case law cited (e.g., Vas-Cath, Univ. of Rochester v. Searle, Capon v. Eshhar). Rejections are based on substantive law; Guidelines assist Office personnel but do not have force of law.

name: Possession standard — must show applicant had possession of claimed invention
description: To satisfy the written description requirement, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas; description of reduction to practice or evidence that invention was 'ready for patenting' (drawings, structural chemical formulas), or by distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. Cite Lockwood, Pfaff, Eli Lilly, Amgen v. Chugai.

name: Original claims presumption and limits
description: There is a strong presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed, but the presumption can fail if aspects of the claimed invention are not described with sufficient particularity (e.g., essential or critical features not disclosed).
guidance: Original-claim rejections should be rare; when an original claim requires an essential feature not described in spec and that feature is not conventional or known, the claim as a whole may not be adequately described (examples: gene claims where promoters, coding regions, regulatory elements may be implicitly included). Case citations: In re Wertheim, LizardTech, Eli Lilly, In re Bell/Deuel discussion.

name: Claim-by-claim analysis and broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; the examiner must determine what the claim as a whole covers (including preamble and transitional phrase).
guidance: Claim construction is essential. Consider preamble language, transitional phrases ('comprising' = open-ended; 'consisting essentially of' = middle ground), and include weight given to preamble and transitional terms. See In re Morris, Genentech v. Chiron, PPG v. Guardian, Pac-Tec v. Amerace.

name: Evaluate support for each element/limitation/step in claim
description: Review the entire application to understand how the applicant provides support for the claimed invention, including each element and/or step; an applicant shows possession by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations.
guidance: Examine specification, claims, figures, examples, and incorporated material for support. Determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim. Absence of definitions for well-established terms should not be the basis for rejection, but limitations may not be imported into claims from the specification. (See Lockwood, Bell Communications Research, Corning Glass Works.)

name: Applicant must show support for amendments; examiner initial burden for rejections
description: When claims are amended, applicant should specifically point out where the originally filed disclosure supports the amendments; the examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning why persons skilled in the art would not recognize support for the claim amendment.
guidance: See MPEP §§714.02, 2163.06, 2163.04. If applicant points out support and examiner finds disclosure does not reasonably convey possession, examiner must present reasoning. Rejection of original claims for lack of written description should be rare (Wertheim).

name: Omission of an element disclosed as essential can create written description problems
description: Omitting a limitation that the specification describes as an essential or critical feature may indicate the inventor did not possess a broader claimed invention, leading to lack of written description for the broader claim.
guidance: Examples: claims broadened by removing location or mixing elements where spec described a composition; if spec states a particular understanding is 'the only possible location' or essential, broader claim may be invalid for lack of written description. Cases: PIN/NIP v. Platte Chem., Gentry Gallery, Tronzo.

name: Functional-only descriptions (especially biomolecules) are often insufficient
description: A biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic, without a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure, normally is not a sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes, even when accompanied by a method of obtaining the claimed sequence.
guidance: Functional language that does not identify structural characteristics generally fails for written description (In re Bell, In re Deuel). By contrast, software functions may suffice in some circumstances where code is within skill of the art (Fonar v. GE — flow charts/source code not always required).

name: Deposits of biological materials — limited role and requirements
description: A deposit made in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may satisfy the written description requirement for claimed biological materials but is not a substitute for a written description; the written description of deposited material needs to be as complete as possible.
guidance: Deposits provide antecedent basis and aid verification but examination proceeds solely on the written description. Deposits made after filing cannot support additions or corrections to the original disclosure unless specific regulatory statements are filed (see 37 CFR 1.804). See Final Rule and In re Lundak guidance.

name: No in haec verba requirement; support may be express, implicit, or inherent
description: While literal wording is not required ('in haec verba' is not required), claim limitations added later must have support in the specification by express, implicit, or inherent disclosure and cannot introduce new matter.
guidance: Examples where genus/species interplay matters: a subgenus is not necessarily described by a genus plus an example species. Case law: In re Lukach, In re Smith. Corrections of obvious errors are allowed when recognizable by a skilled artisan (In re Oda).

name: Claim language and transitional phrase impact on scope and written description analysis
description: Transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') and preamble language affect claim scope and thus what must be supported in the specification; absent clear indication of basic and novel characteristics, 'consisting essentially of' may be construed as 'comprising' for prior art purposes.
guidance: Applicants bear burden to show that additional steps/materials would materially change invention when relying on 'consisting essentially of' language. Case citations: PPG v. Guardian, AK Steel, In re De Lajarte, Ex parte Davis.

name: Complete specification — sufficiency requirements
description: Complete specification must (1) be intelligible to ordinary workmen possessing some skill; (2) not omit a material part of a process nor contain misleading or ambiguous statements; (3) distinguish what is new from what is old (except universally known matters or parts not forming part of the invention); (4) disclose the most beneficial way of exercising the invention, referring to materials used including cheapest and specifying improvements; (5) not vary from the provisional specification; (6) end with a claim which must not exceed the title and ought to be limited to one invention.
guidance: Examiners report on preparedness and variance from provisional specification; reports are not conclusive; Comptroller may require amendment after hearing; claims exceeding title or multiple-invention issues give rise to specific procedures; omission or variance cases discussed in authorities.

name: Action for infringement — prerequisites, pleadings, and evidence limitations
description: An action for infringement cannot be brought until the Patent is granted and not for acts committed prior to publication of the complete specification (with limited exceptions). Trials are without jury unless leave granted; assessors may be called. Statements of claim must be accompanied by particulars of breaches and should state the part of the specification and parts of the accused machine alleged to infringe. No evidence is allowed of infringements not particularised unless by leave; particulars may be amended by leave.
guidance: Costs of actions tied to certification of reasonable proof; amendments of particulars/defences by leave only; account and damages remedies and elections; procedural forms and timing rules apply; courts may order inspection and call assessors.

name: Claims — structure and limits
description: Every complete specification must end with a claim. A claim must not exceed the title; claims should be limited to one invention in the complete specification (though multiple-invention claims on application have special procedures). A claim of more than one invention in specification is not ground to invalidate a patent at trial in some circumstances but is handled procedurally on application.
guidance: Comptroller and Examiners consider whether title indicates subject matter; rules exist for when multiple inventions appear and for rectifying or amending claims; changes to claims are subject to scrutiny and possible restriction.

name: Statutory authorization for functional claiming (35 U.S.C. §112(f))
description: An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Means-plus-function claiming is expressly authorized by statute; such claims are construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification and their equivalents. Functional claiming contrasts with claiming by structure in the claim body.

name: Indefiniteness determination standard for §112(f)
description: Whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.
guidance: Traditionally terms receive their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art. For means-plus-function claims the key is whether the specification supplies the structure such that POSITA would understand the claim. If no structure is in the specification, the disclosure cannot be saved by POSITA understanding.

name: Means-plus-function claims limited to corresponding structure in specification
description: Means-plus-function claims are valid only to the extent that the specification contains support for the structures that define the means; the claim is construed to the structure, material or acts described in the specification and their equivalents.
guidance: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a means-plus-function claim will be drawn to the structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents (see MPEP 2181).

name: Presumption when §112(f) is invoked: 'means for' or 'step for'
description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke §112(f) when it explicitly uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language.
guidance: That presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function. Examiners should look for structural content that would defeat the presumption.

name: Rebuttable presumption against §112(f) when 'means' wording absent
description: A claim limitation that does not use the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' will trigger a rebuttable presumption that §112(f) does not apply.
guidance: This presumption is strong and not readily overcome; the Federal Circuit rarely finds means-plus-function treatment without explicit 'means' language (see Apple Inc. v. Motorola, Inc., 757 F.3d 1286 (Fed. Cir. 2014)).

name: Substance-over-form approach (focus on whether claim words denote structure)
description: Determination cannot merely focus on presence or absence of the word 'means'; focus must be on 'whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure.'
guidance: Even terms using 'means' may avoid means treatment if they in substance recite structure (see Greenberg v. Ethicon; Williamson v. Citrix Online). Examiners and courts consider whether the term is understood to describe structure.

name: Three-factor check for whether a term denotes structure
description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject matter specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term has achieved recognition as a noun denoting structure; and (3) the prior art provides evidence that the term has an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
guidance: Use specification disclosure, dictionary evidence, and prior art recognition together to assess whether a term is structural for means treatment purposes.

name: Three-condition test examiners use to apply means treatment
description: Examiners will apply means treatment to a claim limitation that meets the following conditions: (1) The claim limitation uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' or a non-structural term that does not have a structural modifier; (2) the phrase/term recited in the claim is modified by functional language; and (3) the phrase/term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function.
guidance: All three conditions should be considered together when deciding to apply §112(f) treatment.

name: When to issue a §112(b) rejection regarding means-plus-function
description: A rejection under §112(b) may be appropriate when: (1) it is unclear whether a claim limitation invokes §112(f); (2) §112(f) is invoked and there is no disclosure or there is insufficient disclosure of structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function; and/or (3) §112(f) is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link or associate the disclosed structure, material, or acts to the claimed function.
guidance: Use §112(b) (indefiniteness) rejections to address unclear invocation, lack of corresponding structure, or failure to link structure to function. The preamble context may also warrant §112(b) if it's unclear whether it recites a means-plus-function limitation.

name: Preamble considerations for means-plus-function
description: When applicant uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' in the preamble, a rejection under §112(b) may be appropriate when it is unclear whether the preamble is reciting a means (or step) plus function limitation or whether the preamble is merely stating the intended use of the claimed invention.
guidance: When a structural or nonstructural term with the word 'for' appears in the preamble, the examiner should not automatically construe that phrase as reciting a means-plus-function limitation; consider context.

name: Examiner procedure after determining a limitation is means-plus-function
description: Once the examiner determines that a claim limitation is a means-plus-function limitation invoking §112(f), the examiner should determine the claimed function and then review the written description of the specification to determine whether the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function are disclosed.
guidance: Review disclosure from the perspective of one skilled in the art and require that the written description clearly link or associate the corresponding structure/material/acts to the claimed function. If the examiner cannot identify corresponding structure/material/acts, a §112(b) rejection should be made rendering the claim indefinite. If adequate, the claim is limited to disclosed corresponding structure and equivalents.

name: Outcomes when corresponding structure is missing or present
description: If the examiner cannot identify the corresponding structure, material, or acts, a rejection under §112(b) should be made, thus rendering the means-plus-function claim indefinite. If the written description sets forth the corresponding structure, material, or acts in compliance with §112(b), the claim limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: The practical effect: absence of identifiable corresponding structure results in indefiniteness; adequate disclosure limits claim scope to the disclosed structure/equivalents.

name: Drafting best practice: fullest disclosure early
description: File the most complete disclosure possible at the earliest date possible. Describe things generally and build to ever more specific embodiments and alternative descriptions, explaining all the variations and possibilities with as much detail as you possibly can.
guidance: This approach is essential if using means-plus-function claims. High quality patent drawings that show structures can be a highly effective way to avoid indefiniteness rejections.

name: Strategic guidance on using means-plus-function claims
description: Means-plus-function claiming can capture within the claims all of the various means disclosed in the application and can be a useful way to have claim scope reflect the disclosure, but they should not be the primary claims or the only claims filed.
guidance: Use means-plus-function claims sparingly (analogized as 'seasoning' — a little is OK, too much is poor). They can be a cost-effective way to claim permutations but should supplement, not replace, structural claims.

name: Special rules for software and computer-implemented inventions
description: The rules for means-plus-function claiming apply very differently with respect to software and computer implemented inventions.
guidance: Practitioners should consult the algorithm/software-specific case law ('The Algorithm Cases') when asserting or defending means-plus-function treatment for software-related claim limitations.

name: When an international-application-derived reference is pre-AIPA
description: If the copending reference is a national stage of an international application (35 U.S.C. 371) or a continuing application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) to an international application with an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000, apply pre-AIPA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (form paragraph 7.12.01).
guidance: Consult Examiner Notes for form paragraph 7.12.01 to determine the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date. A benefit claim to a U.S. patent of an earlier-filed international application with an international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000, may only result in an effective U.S. filing date as of the date the 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1),(2),(4) requirements were fulfilled.

name: Consideration of priority/benefit claims in determining 102(e) date
description: In determining the 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), U.S. nonprovisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 120 or 121, and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c) if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the earlier-filed application's disclosure.
guidance: Do NOT consider any priority/benefit claims to U.S. applications which are filed before an international application that has an international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a).

name: Overcoming 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejections
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) may be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the inventor of the instant application (not an invention 'by another'), or by an appropriate showing under 37 CFR 1.131 (date of invention).
guidance: Also consider a showing under 37 CFR 1.131 or other appropriate evidence. If evidence indicates derivation or earlier invention date, the rejection may be withdrawn. Examiner Notes: ensure supporting factual basis is of record when making or withdrawing such rejections.

name: General principles for determination of distinctness/independence
description: Distinctness/independence summarized: (A) where inventions are independent (no disclosed relation), restriction ordinarily proper; (B) where related as disclosed but distinct as claimed, restriction may be proper; (C) where related as disclosed but not distinct as claimed, restriction is never proper; (D) a reasonable number of species may be claimed where there is an allowable generic claim (37 CFR 1.141).
guidance: Where restriction is required by the Office, double patenting cannot be held — so ensure requirement is not made where related inventions as claimed are not distinct. See referenced MPEP sections for details (§806.06, §806.05-§806.05(j), §806.04).

name: Compare claimed matter (claimed subject matter controls)
description: In double patenting and restriction inquiries, it is the claimed subject matter that is considered and must be compared to determine distinctness or independence.
guidance: A provisional election of a single species may be required where only generic claims are presented and the generic claims recite so many species that an unduly extensive and burdensome search is necessary. See MPEP §803.02 and §808.01(a).

name: Genus and species election/restriction practice
description: When an application includes claims to different embodiments or species that could fall within the scope of a generic claim, restriction between species may be proper if the species are independent or distinct; 37 CFR 1.141 allows an allowable generic claim to link a reasonable number of species embraced thereby.
guidance: If an application contains claims to more than a reasonable number of species, the examiner may require restriction to not more than a reasonable number of species before taking further action (37 CFR 1.146). See MPEP §806.04(d) for definition of generic claim and §806.04(e) for claims that include species.

name: Definition and consequences of an allowable generic claim
description: A generic claim should require no material element additional to those required by the species claims, and each species claim must require all the limitations of the generic claim. Once a generic claim is allowable, species that require all limitations of the generic claim will ordinarily be allowable over the prior art.
guidance: If some species claims do not require all limitations of the generic claim, see MPEP §821.04(a) for handling. When a generic claim is allowable, rejoinder of species and examination of dependent claims follows 37 CFR 1.104 and MPEP §821.04.

name: Claims vs. species terminology
description: Claims are definitions or descriptions of inventions; claims themselves are never 'species.' A claim may be limited to a single disclosed embodiment (specific/species claim) or may encompass multiple embodiments (genus/generic claim).
guidance: Species always refer to different embodiments of the invention; species may be independent or related as disclosed.

name: Generic claim presented after issuance of species may raise OTDP
description: If a generic claim is presented after issuance of a patent claiming one or more species within the scope of the generic claim, the Office may reject the generic claim on the grounds of obviousness-type double patenting if there is at least one common inventor and the applications/patents are commonly assigned or within joint research agreement exceptions.
guidance: Applicant may overcome such a rejection by filing a terminal disclaimer. See cases cited (In re Goodman; In re Braithwaite) and MPEP §804.

name: Combination vs. subcombination distinctness criteria
description: To support a restriction between a combination and a subcombination, both two-way distinctness and reasons for insisting on restriction (e.g., serious search burden) are necessary. The inventions are distinct if: (A) the combination as claimed does not require the particulars of the subcombination as claimed for patentability, and (B) the subcombination can be shown to have utility either by itself or in another materially different combination.
guidance: Search-burden evidence (separate classification, status, or field of search) must exist to justify restriction. Examples and diagrams (ABsp, ABbr, Bsp) illustrate when restriction is proper or improper. Use form paragraph 8.15 where appropriate; provide specifics in brackets as instructed by the form paragraph's Examiner Note.

name: Plural combinations requiring common subcombination (linking claim practice)
description: When an application includes a single subcombination required by plural claimed combinations, the subcombination claim is a linking claim and will be examined with the elected combination; claimed plural combinations showing the subcombination's utility in more than one combination support linking.
guidance: List the linking subcombination in form paragraph 8.12. If elected combination is allowable, reconsider the propriety of restriction and rejoin claims requiring the subcombination as appropriate. See MPEP §809.03 and §821.04(a).

name: Subcombinations usable together: distinctness and restriction
description: Two or more claimed subcombinations disclosed as usable together in a single combination are usually restrictable when they do not overlap in scope and are not obvious variants and at least one subcombination is separately usable.
guidance: Restriction is proper only when there would be a serious burden if restriction were not required, evidenced by separate classification, status, or field of search. Examiner must show by example that one subcombination has utility other than in the disclosed combination. If applicant proves the suggested other use cannot be accomplished, the burden shifts to the examiner to document a viable alternative or withdraw the requirement. Use form paragraph 8.16 for restriction requirements between subcombinations.

name: Burden on examiner to suggest separate utility and rejoinder practice
description: The examiner has the burden to suggest an example of separate utility for subcombinations or subcombinations usable together; if applicant disproves the suggested utility, examiner must document an alternative viable use or withdraw the restriction requirement.
guidance: Upon determining that all claims directed to an elected combination invention are allowable, the examiner must reconsider the propriety of the restriction requirement and rejoin claims as required. If a subcombination is elected and found allowable, nonelected claims requiring all limitations of the allowable claim will be rejoined in accordance with MPEP §821.04.

name: Patentability requirements (substantive examination)
description: The substantive examination process usually consists of determining whether the claimed innovation is novel, non-obvious and industrially applicable.
guidance: Some offices perform only formal examination (e.g., South Africa) while others undertake both formal and substantive examination (e.g., Japan). The substantive test (novelty, inventive step/non-obviousness, industrial applicability) is the core of granting decisions and affects comparisons of outcomes across offices.

name: Examination of cited documents
description: Documents cited in the application should be examined if they are cited as the starting point of the invention, show the state of the art, are alternative solutions to the problem, or are necessary for a correct understanding of the application; citations that clearly relate only to details not directly relevant to the claimed invention may be disregarded.
guidance: Examine cited documents when they affect understanding or claim scope; disregard citations only when clearly irrelevant to the claimed invention.

name: Search statement (defining subject of search)
description: Examiner may prepare a written search statement defining the subject of their search as precisely as possible; claims may serve but might need generalisation to cover embodiments. Exclusion from search and lack of unity should be borne in mind.
guidance: Where unity lacking, examiner may search only the first invention or inventive concept; restrict search only in exceptional situations where necessary.

name: Search focus on documents affecting novelty, inventive step, and sufficiency
description: The examiner carries out the search directing attention to any prior art likely to have bearing on novelty or inventive step and is encouraged to cite prior art likely to assist in determining sufficiency of description and support.
guidance: Prioritize documents that affect novelty, inventive step, adequacy of support, and industrial applicability throughout the claimed field.

name: Determination of novelty and inventive step
description: The examiner determines whether the claimed invention meets the standards for novelty and inventive step.
guidance: Use identified prior art and legal tests to assess novelty and inventive step as separate requirements.

name: Contents required in a search report
description: The search report should include at least: list and details of prior arts identified, date of first publication/availability and weblink when available; scope of the patent search; databases used; classification (IPC); summary of the search; relevance of prior art(s) to the claim(s); comments or written opinion from the examiner on patentability.
guidance: Ensure search report documents key bibliographic details, relevance assessments, and examiner opinions to support downstream examination and applicant awareness.

name: Partial search / no-search options and limits
description: Options for a partial search and/or a 'no search' are available in some AMS. The aim is to issue search reports as complete as possible; no meaningful search should be limited to exceptional situations where no search is possible (e.g., totally unclear description/claims/drawings).
guidance: Meaningful search must be complete enough to determine novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, sufficiency, support and clarity; where parts are non-compliant but understandable, perform a search and account for non-compliance when determining extent.

name: Legal definition of novelty (PCT approach)
description: A claim is novel if it is not anticipated by prior art. PCT Guidelines: 'The invention, as defined by a claim, lacks novelty if every element or step is explicitly or inherently disclosed within the prior art including any features implicit to a person skilled in the art.'
guidance: Assess novelty by checking whether every claim element is explicitly or implicitly disclosed in a single prior-art reference.

name: Methodology for determining claimed-invention scope using PSIA
description: To determine whether an invention is new, the examiner shall compare the claimed invention to identified prior art through the lens of the Person Skilled In the Art (PSIA), applying successive steps: (i) evaluate elements of the claimed invention; (ii) determine if a prior art forms part of the state of the art; (iii) assess whether each and every element or step was explicitly or inherently disclosed in combination to a PSIA on the prior-art date.
guidance: Interpret claims using description and drawings as needed; if every element is disclosed, novelty is lacking.

name: Consideration of purpose/intended use in claim interpretation
description: In interpreting claims for novelty consideration, regard should be had to the purpose or intended use of the invention to determine whether the recited purpose results in a structural difference; non-distinctive characteristics of use should be disregarded.
guidance: Example: substance X claimed as catalyst not novel over same substance known as dye unless the use implies distinguishing form (e.g., additives); implied characteristics from intended use should be taken into account.

name: Enabling disclosure requirement in prior art
description: The prior art disclosure must enable a PSIA to carry out the claimed invention; a mere mention (e.g., name/formula of a compound) is not considered known unless the document and general knowledge enable its preparation or separation.
guidance: Treat non-enabling prior art as not destroying novelty though it may still be relied upon for inventive-step analysis; for patent documents enablement is ordinarily inferred, but for non-patent literature check enablement carefully.

name: Rules for anticipation of ranges
description: Guiding principles: (1) a specific example in prior art within a claimed range anticipates the range; (2) prior-art ranges touching/overlapping the claimed range may anticipate if disclosed with 'sufficient specificity' (case-by-case); (3) a narrow claimed range within a broader prior-art range may still be novel if selection is sufficiently specific and yields unexpected results; (4) prior art teaching values very close but not overlapping do not anticipate.
guidance: Interpret 'sufficient specificity' based on facts; consider examples and jurisdictional guidelines (Indonesia, Singapore, Viet Nam) and selection-invention doctrine when narrow ranges show special effects.

name: Election when multiple inventions (telephonic interview)
description: If it is determined that all the claims presented are not directed to a single invention, the telephone restriction practice set forth in MPEP § 812.01 will be followed. Applicant must make an election without traverse during the telephonic interview.
guidance: If applicant refuses to make an election without traverse or the examiner cannot reach the applicant after a reasonable effort, the examiner will treat the first claimed invention (the invention of claim 1) as constructively elected without traverse for examination.

name: Interview before issuing non-allowance Office action
description: The USPTO will not issue an Office action (other than a notice of allowance) unless either: (A) an interview was conducted but did not result in the application being placed in condition for allowance; or (B) there is a determination that an interview is unlikely to result in the application being placed in condition for allowance.
guidance: Prior to the mailing of any Office action rejecting the claims, the USPTO will conduct a conference to review the rejections set forth in the Office action.

name: Reply scope limitation
description: A reply to an Office action must be limited to the rejections, objections, and requirements made.
guidance: Any amendment that attempts to: (A) add claims resulting in >3 independent claims or >20 total claims pending; (B) present claims not encompassed by the preexamination search or an updated accelerated examination support document; or (C) present claims directed to a non-elected invention or an invention other than previously claimed, will be treated as not fully responsive and will not be entered.

name: Updated accelerated examination support document required for claim amendments
description: For any amendment to the claims (including any new claim) that is not encompassed by the preexamination search and accelerated examination support document, applicant is required to provide an updated accelerated examination support document that encompasses the amended or new claims at the time of filing the amendment.
guidance: Failure to provide such updated document at time of amendment will cause the amendment to be treated as not fully responsive and to not be entered. Any IDS filed with an updated accelerated examination support document must also comply with the requirements of 37 CFR 1.97 and 1.98.

name: Conditions for examination (items required at filing)
description: The application must be in condition for examination at the time of filing. This means the application must include specified items.
guidance: Required items include: (1) basic filing, search, and examination fees (37 CFR 1.16); (2) application size fee if >100 sheets (1.16(s)); (3) executed inventor’s oath/declaration (37 CFR 1.63/1.64); (4) specification compliant with 1.52 and description/claims per 1.71/1.75; (5) title and abstract per 1.72; (6) drawings per 1.84; (7) sequence listings/CRFs or XMLs and large tables per applicable CFR and filing-date-dependent rules; (8) foreign priority claim identified in the ADS; (9) domestic benefit claims compliant with 37 CFR 1.78 with specifics depending on filing date; (10) English translation and statement and processing fee if specification in non-English; (11) no preliminary amendments present on filing date; (12) no petition that would delay processing (examples provided). For design applications, comply with 37 CFR 1.151–1.154.

name: Scenario 1 — technical solution when AI processes data with precise technical meaning
description: A solution is a technical solution if the claim reflects that the object processed by the AI algorithm/model is data with a precise technical meaning in the technical field, and a person skilled in the art can see that executing the algorithm embodies use of laws of nature to solve a technical problem and obtains a technical effect.
guidance: Draft claims to tie input/output data to precise technical meanings and show how processing those data solves a technical problem (e.g., image recognition/classification). Show how steps of processing features are closely related to the technical problem and produce a corresponding technical effect.

name: Scenario 2 — technical solution when there is a specific technical connection between algorithm/model and internal computer structure
description: If the claim reflects a specific technical connection between the AI algorithm/model and the internal structure of the computer system that solves technical problems such as improving hardware computing efficiency, reducing storage/transmission, or improving processing speed, and obtains technical effects of improving internal performance of the computer system, the solution is a technical solution.
guidance: Specific technical association may be shown by adapting algorithms to hardware parameters (e.g., adjusting pruning granularity to memristor array size), optimizing system resource configuration, changing system architecture or parameters, or algorithmic adaptations constrained by hardware conditions. The Guidelines note that the hardware structure need not be physically changed; optimization of resource scheduling can suffice. Conversely, a negative example: claims that merely recite a conventional memory and processor storing instructions to run a neural-network training method (with no specific technical connection) do not constitute a technical solution.

name: Scenario 3 — technical solution when mining intrinsic correlations that conform to natural laws in specific application fields
description: When AI algorithms/models are used to mine intrinsic correlations in big data in a specific application field and those correlations conform to natural laws, thereby solving technical problems (e.g., improving reliability/accuracy of analysis) and producing technical effects, the claim constitutes a technical scheme.
guidance: Clarify in the claim/specification which indicators, parameters, etc. reflect the characteristics of the analyzed object and whether the intrinsic correlations between these inputs and model outputs conform to natural laws. Use examples (food safety knowledge graph with timestamps reflecting changing food properties) to show how the correlations follow natural law. By contrast, correlations governed only by economic or social laws (e.g., predicting an economic prosperity index) do not constitute use of natural laws and are not technical.

name: Adequate disclosure / sufficiency of description for AI inventions
description: The specification should clearly record the technical solution, describe in detail specific implementation methods, and fully disclose the technical content essential for understanding and realizing the invention so that a technician in the relevant field can implement it. AI 'black box' characteristics require sufficient information to achieve full disclosure.
guidance: Record and fully describe the parts that contribute over prior art. State beneficial effects objectively and provide evidence when necessary. Recommended practices by invention-type: for model training contributions, disclose the algorithms, specific steps, and training process; for model construction, disclose module structure, hierarchy, connections, functions, and demonstrated effects (experimental data if necessary); for applications in specific fields, clarify how the model combines with the scenario, how input/output data are set, and correlations between inputs and outputs. When issuing a disclosure insufficiency opinion, explain the reasons based on the original description and claims.

name: Inventiveness examination — when algorithmic features count toward inventive step
description: To include algorithmic features as part of the technical means in the inventiveness assessment, claims should show that the AI algorithms/models are applied to specific functions or application fields and solve specific technical problems so that algorithmic features and technical features functionally support each other.
guidance: If the algorithm/model in the application is prior art, consider the distance between technical fields, whether there is technical inspiration to apply it, difficulty of applying across fields, necessity to overcome technical difficulties, and whether unexpected technical effects arise. If application to a new field only changes the meaning of data (e.g., counting ships versus fruits) without changing processing methods, model training, or producing unexpected technical effects, the application is likely predictable and lacks inventiveness.

name: Steps without Acts
description: Method claim elements that recite only a function/’step’ without reciting the acts by which that function is performed can trigger §112(f) treatment (means/step-plus-function) and may be invalid if the specification fails to disclose acts sufficient to perform the function.
guidance: Statutory text: 35 U.S.C. §112(f) allows an element 'expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof' to be construed to cover corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification and equivalents. Judge Rader: 'underlying function' corresponds to what the element accomplishes; 'acts' correspond to how the function is accomplished. If a claim element recites only an underlying function without acts, §112, ¶6 may apply even absent express step-plus-function language. Practical approach: for each method step, ask whether it recites acts that perform the function or only the function/result; if only the latter, analyze the specification to see whether it discloses and links acts sufficient to perform the function. Examples/case citations: Seal-Flex (Rader concurrence), O.I. Corp. v. Tekmar, Dionex Softron (non-precedential) and related §101 decisions (Internet Patents Corp.).

name: Indefiniteness stemming from unclear application of §112(f)
description: When it is unclear whether claim language invokes §112(f), the scope of the claim is uncertain and that ambiguity can render the claim indefinite under §112(b).
guidance: Practical approach: if arguing that a limitation triggers §112(f), also argue alternatively that uncertainty as to whether §112(f) applies renders the limitation indefinite under §112(b). The USPTO/Examiner guidance (MPEP §2181 I) instructs examiners that if it's unclear whether a limitation falls within 112(f), a rejection under 112(b) may be appropriate. Emphasize that invoking or contesting §112(f) affects how broadly a limitation is interpreted and thus can be fertile ground for indefiniteness arguments.

name: Failure to Mitigate Damages
description: Patent owners, like plaintiffs in other torts, have a duty to mitigate damages; failure to take reasonable steps to avoid or minimize damages can reduce or preclude recovery.
guidance: Legal principle: patent infringement is a tort and is presumptively governed by common law tort damages principles (e.g., Staub v. Proctor Hospital). The victim/plaintiff has a duty to use reasonable means to avoid or minimize damages; failure to do so can limit recovery. Illustrative actions by patent owners that may constitute failure to mitigate include failure to mark patented products, 'lying in wait' while damages accrue, failing to take a clear or consistent position on claim scope, keeping a licensed supplier secret, or failing to offer a FRAND license when obligated. Case references: Faragher (background on mitigation principles), Bank of Stockton (example under state law). Practical approach: investigate patent owner conduct and plead/argue failure to mitigate as a defense to damages, presenting evidence of reasonable steps that could have reduced harm.

name: Expiring Patents Add to the Public Domain
description: Disclosures in expired (non-asserted) patents are in the public domain; accused features described in such expired patents may not be proprietary and can reduce or eliminate liability or damages.
guidance: Legal principle and cases: expired patents dedicate their disclosed inventions to the public (Bonito Boats; Scott Paper; Singer Mfg.); courts recognize that the public may use the invention and obvious or indistinct modifications (Gilead). Practical effects: identify expired patents that describe part or all of the claimed subject matter and assert that those disclosures are free for public use; even if not a complete defense, such public-domain disclosures may reduce damages by excluding value attributable to material in the public domain. Use apportionment principles (e.g., AstraZeneca v. Apotex on accounting for conventional vs. unconventional elements) to argue exclusion of public-domain-contributed value from damages.

name: Antedating generic claims by showing a single species
description: A reference or activity applied against generic claims may (in most cases) be antedated as to such claims by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing completion of the invention of only a single species, within the genus, before the prior art date of the reference or activity.
guidance: Exceptions where predictability is in question (unpredictable arts): see MPEP § 715.03. The affidavit must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to furnish support for a generic claim; where predictability is low, one or a few species may not suffice to infer generic applicability.

name: Species claim antedating rules
description: Where the claim under rejection recites a species and the reference or activity discloses the claimed species, the rejection can be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131(a) directly by showing prior completion of the claimed species or indirectly by a showing of prior completion of a different species coupled with a showing that the claimed species would have been an obvious modification of the species completed by the inventor.
guidance: Case examples: In re Spiller. Applicant may rely on prior completion of a different species if it would have rendered the claimed species obvious to a person of ordinary skill.

name: Limitations when reference is a U.S. patent or application publication claiming same invention
description: A 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit is ineffective to overcome a United States patent or patent application publication that claims the same invention as the application being examined (not only verbatim correspondence but also where there is no patentable distinction). If the reference claims the same invention and its publication date or issue date is within certain timeframes relative to the presentation of claims, remedies other than Rule 131 (e.g., interference under 37 CFR 41.202 or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b)) may apply.
guidance: If commonly owned patents/applications contain claims that are identical or not patentably distinct, the subject matter is 'interfering subject matter' (37 CFR 41.203(a)). Where the reference and application are commonly owned but not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) may be used to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection. Form paragraphs (¶ 23.14, ¶ 23.14.01) and MPEP Chapter 2300 and § 2159 provide additional instructions.

name: Claim construction principle for 'first' and 'second' modifiers
description: Modifiers such as 'first' and 'second' may simply distinguish between repeated instances of an element rather than denote spatial relationships.
guidance: The district court construed 'first' and 'second' as distinguishing repeated instances of an element and not as requiring a specific spatial location relative to the shaker's inlet; that construction was sustained as proper in light of the claim language and specification.

name: Use of extrinsic disclosures to satisfy claim limitations (degassing chamber)
description: A court may rely on related patent disclosures and technical reports to determine whether an accused system embodies a claim limitation (here, a 'degassing chamber' that separates air/vapor from drilling fluid).
guidance: The district court relied on FPUSA's own patent (the '959 patent) and a Technology Evaluation Report describing a vacuum line with a fluid or air separator to conclude the Vac Screen included a degassing chamber; the Federal Circuit found that determination not clearly erroneous.

name: Presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. §282
description: Issued patents are presumed valid under 35 U.S.C. §282; this presumption informs the preliminary-injunction inquiry.
guidance: The opinion states there is a statutory presumption that issued patents are valid and that the district court did not err in relying on that presumption when concluding the '288 patent claims were supported by the written description in the parent application.

name: Types of designs and modified forms (entire article, portion, surface ornamentation)
description: An ornamental design may be embodied in an entire article, only a portion of an article, or ornamentation applied to an article. If directed to surface ornamentation only, the article must be shown (typically in broken lines) and a statement explaining that broken lines form no part of the claimed design must be added to the specification.
guidance: Designs that are independent and distinct must be filed in separate applications; modified forms/embodiments of a single design concept may be filed together if not patentably distinct (examples: minimal configuration differences). Use broken lines or other techniques to graphically distinguish the article from the ornamentation and include required explanatory statements in the specification. See MPEP 1504.05.

name: Specification sections and order
description: The specification should include, where applicable and in order: preamble, cross-reference to related applications, statement regarding federally sponsored research, description of the figure(s) of the drawing, feature description, and a single claim.
guidance: Section headings in uppercase without underlining or bold should precede each section. Sample specifications and disclosure examples are provided in the guide. See 37 CFR 1.154 for arrangement guidance.

name: Formal claim language and incorporation of drawings
description: The single claim must identify the subject as the 'ornamental design' and indicate the article of manufacture and incorporate the drawings. Claim form: 'The ornamental design for (the article which embodies the design) as shown.' If descriptive statement included, add 'and described.' The article designation should match the title.
guidance: The claim must be in formal terms; see MPEP 1503.01(III) for more information. Accurate claim wording ties the scope to the drawings and any descriptive statements.

name: Drawings or photographs are the critical disclosure
description: Every design patent application must include a drawing or photograph of the claimed design. The drawings/photographs constitute the entire visual disclosure of the claim and must be clear and complete; nothing should be left to conjecture. They must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, and include sufficient views to completely disclose the appearance of the claim.
guidance: Poor or incomplete drawings may render the disclosure fatally defective and nonenable. It is recommended to use a professional draftsperson. Changing drawings after filing to add new matter is prohibited (35 U.S.C. 132; 35 U.S.C. 112(a)).

name: Color drawings and color photographs rules
description: Color drawings/photographs are permitted if filed according to 37 CFR § 1.84(a)(2) and § 1.84(b)(2). If color is included, one set of color drawings/photographs is required for e-filing or three sets if not e-filed, and the specification must include language noting color in the file.
guidance: If color is integral to the claimed design, omission of color later is permitted only if underlying configuration is clear. If color is not part of the claim, include the statement: 'The color shown on the claimed design forms no part thereof.' Petitions are no longer required for color; examples and required wording are in the guide.

name: Broken lines usage and requirements
description: Anything not part of the claimed design may be shown in broken lines (environment, bounds, article when claim is only surface ornamentation). Broken lines should not interfere with clear understanding and should be lighter than lines of the claimed design. Broken lines may not be used to show hidden planes/surfaces which cannot be seen through opaque materials.
guidance: When broken lines are used, the specification must explicitly identify their purpose so the scope of the claim is clear. If broken lines obscure the claimed design, provide an unobscured separate figure. See MPEP 1503.02(III). Include a statement when the article form shown in broken lines forms no part of the claimed design.

name: Transparent materials depiction
description: Oblique line shading must be used to show transparent or translucent surfaces (and highly polished/reflective surfaces). Elements visible behind transparent surfaces should be shown in light, full lines, not broken lines.
guidance: Correct depiction ensures clarity about what is part of the claimed design versus what is background or internal.

name: Article shown broken away guidance
description: A separation and bracket may be used in an enlarged view when full length of the article is shown in another view.
