Alternatively, when the article is consistently shown with a break, the claim is understood to be directed only to the portions shown between break lines; the specification must explain that appearance of portions between breaks forms no part of the claimed design.
guidance: Provide explicit description in specification to avoid ambiguity about scope when broken-away or truncated views are used.

name: Cross-sectional view limitations
description: Cross-sections may be used to clarify disclosure and minimize number of views, but sectional views presented to show strictly interior construction or functional/mechanical features are unnecessary and may confuse the scope of the claimed design.
guidance: Use sectional views only to clarify external appearance relevant to the design; avoid sections that suggest interior/functional claim scope.

name: Filing process, filing receipt and initial checks
description: When an application with at least a specification, a drawing and a claim is received, it is assigned an application number and filing date and a filing receipt is sent. Applicants should promptly check the filing receipt for accuracy (inventor names, benefit/priority claims recognized).
guidance: Follow suggested application formats to avoid defects; ensure accurate information to avoid problems later. Applications are generally examined in order of filing date.

name: Examination scope and possible actions by examiner
description: Examination checks formal requirements, whether the design can be understood from the drawing disclosure, and compares claimed subject matter with prior art. Examiner may reject claims if disclosure is incomplete/indefinite, or if prior art shows unpatentable subject matter; objections to form (e.g., drawing disclosure) may be made.
guidance: Office actions will detail objections/rejections and may suggest amendments; keep Office actions in applicant files and do not return them to the Office. See MPEP references for exam practice.

name: Three statutory conditions under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) to invoke joint research agreement exception
description: To establish that a joint research agreement makes the 102(b)(2)(C) exception applicable, three conditions must be satisfied: (1) subject matter disclosed must have been developed and claimed invention made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; (3) the application must disclose, or be amended to disclose, the names of the parties to the joint research agreement (35 U.S.C. 102(c)(1)-(3)).
guidance: A 'joint research agreement' is defined (35 U.S.C. 100(h)) as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. Joint research agreement subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) is treated under 37 CFR 1.104(c)(4)(ii).

name: Requirements and timing to establish common ownership
description: To invoke common ownership, the applicant or patent owner must provide a statement that the disclosure and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention. A statement of present common ownership is not sufficient.
guidance: The statement should be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)); it must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). The question of whether common ownership exists as of the effective filing date is determined on the facts of the case; moral or unenforceable obligations are insufficient. Because applicants/patent owners have the best knowledge and a duty of candor, their signed statement is sufficient unless the examiner has independent evidence raising material doubt.

name: Statement and amendment requirements for invoking joint research agreement under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) and 37 CFR 1.71(g)
description: To invoke the joint research agreement exception, the applicant or patent owner must provide a statement that the disclosure and claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement, that the agreement was in effect on or before the effective filing date, and that the claimed invention resulted from activities within the agreement's scope. The statement must be on or begin on a separate sheet and signed per 37 CFR 1.33(b).
guidance: If the names of the parties to the joint research agreement are not already in the application, the application must be amended to include the names in accordance with 37 CFR 1.71(g)(1). An amendment under 1.71(g)(1) may require the processing fee per 37 CFR 1.17(i) if not filed within specified timing windows (e.g., within three months of filing date, before first Office action on merits, etc.). If an amendment under 1.71(g) is filed after issue fee payment, the issued patent may not include names unless corrected by certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323. Such amendments remain subject to rules of practice (e.g., 37 CFR 1.116, 1.121, 1.312).

name: Effect of invoking common ownership or joint research agreement exception
description: Once common ownership or a qualifying joint research agreement is properly established, the subject matter disclosed in the reference may not be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 35 U.S.C. 103 against the claims of the application.
guidance: However, the reference could still be used as the basis for a double patenting rejection, if appropriate. Also, only the portion of the reference that is commonly owned or within the scope of the joint research agreement is excepted; other portions remain available as prior art.

name: Unimaginative skilled technician / 'man in the Clapman omnibus' test
description: Whether, in light of the state of the art and common general knowledge as at the claimed date of invention, the mythical skilled person would have 'come directly and without difficulty to the solution taught by the patent' (Hugessen J.A. wording).
guidance: Ask whether the claimed invention would have been plain to an unimaginative technician given prior art and common general knowledge. Emphasis on 'directly and without difficulty' — not whether someone could eventually have achieved it after extensive exploration.

name: Sanofi factor 1: 'more or less self-evident' / finite predictable solutions
description: Is it 'very plain' or 'more or less self-evident' that what is being tried ought to work? Are there a finite number of identified predictable solutions known to persons skilled in the art?
guidance: This language is a synonym for 'readily apparent' or 'predictable' — ask whether, at the relevant date, one could predict that the claimed solution would work. If success was predictable, the claim leans toward obviousness.

name: Sanofi factor 3: motive provided in the prior art
description: Is there a motive provided in the prior art to find the solution the patent addresses?
guidance: Evidence that prior art motivated skilled persons to pursue the claimed solution supports obviousness; absence of such motivation (or teaching away) supports non-obviousness. See chapter references on 'motivation: the climate of the invention.'

name: Effect of assignment/control-of-litigation provisions on standing
description: Contractual language granting an assignee the 'exclusive right and complete discretion to bring (or not to bring) infringement or unfair competition proceedings or any other legal proceeding' transfers the cause of action and thereby the standing to prosecute those claims to the assignee.
guidance: If the original plaintiff assigned its litigation rights (expressly relinquished the right to bring suits) before filing, the assignor lacks standing. When contracts grant exclusive litigation control to another entity, courts treat that as relinquishment of the right to sue unless the agreement indicates otherwise.

name: Reversion of litigation rights upon termination requires explicit language
description: Absent any language in the agreements indicating an intent to revert litigation rights upon termination, termination does not operate to revert those rights to the original parties; silence on reversion indicates no manifestation of intent to restore litigation rights.
guidance: When a party claims rights reverted after termination, the court looks for express contractual language providing for reversion. Termination provisions that address remedies, events upon termination, confidentiality, marketing, and performance do not imply reversion of assigned litigation rights unless stated.

name: Construal under 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
description: A claim limitation expressed in means-plus-function form 'shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure ... described in the specification and equivalents thereof.'
guidance: When a claim limitation is treated as means-plus-function under §112(f), the court or examiner will limit the claim to the structure disclosed in the specification that corresponds to the claimed function, and to equivalents of that structure. This construal can materially narrow claim scope.

name: Invocation condition: recitation of 'means' or 'step' or generic placeholder
description: The claim limitation recites the term 'means' (or 'step') or a generic placeholder (e.g., mechanism, module, device, unit, component, element, member, apparatus, machine, system).
guidance: Use of the word 'means' or similarly generic nouns/labels for an element is a trigger for §112(f). The page explicitly lists examples of generic placeholders to watch for: mechanism, module, device, unit, component, element, member, apparatus, machine, system.

name: Invocation condition: absence of sufficient structure/material/acts
description: The term is not modified by sufficient structure, material or acts for performing the function.
guidance: Even if a non-'means' term is used, §112(f) will be invoked when the claim lacks sufficient structural or physical detail (structure, materials, or specific acts) that perform the recited function.

name: Corresponding structure requirement — algorithm for computer-implemented functions
description: Once §112(f) is invoked, the specification must describe the 'structure' that corresponds to that function; for computer-implemented functions, 'the corresponding structure ... for a computer-implemented function is the algorithm disclosed in the specification.' (Aristocrat Tech. Aus. Pty Ltd v. Int’l Game Tech.)
guidance: The required corresponding structure is not satisfied by merely naming a generic computer or microprocessor. The specification must disclose an algorithm (or equivalent sufficient structural detail) that performs the claimed function; otherwise the claim lacks the necessary corresponding structure.

name: Consequence of failing to disclose corresponding structure (indefiniteness)
description: Failure to disclose the structure that performs the claimed function renders the claim invalid for indefiniteness.
guidance: If the specification does not provide sufficient corresponding structure (e.g., an algorithm for a software function), courts or examiners may find the claim indefinite under §112 and invalidate or reject it.

name: Drafting best practice: avoid generic placeholders
description: When drafting a claim, avoid the §112(f) trap by avoiding generic placeholders, e.g. 'a software module comprising software instructions.'
guidance: Do not rely on generic labels like 'module' or 'mechanism' without describing structure. Instead, explicitly describe the substeps, operations, data structures, or other structural features that implement the function so the claim element is tied to sufficient structure rather than pure function.

name: Drafting best practice: include algorithmic substeps or sufficient structure
description: Modify each element with applicable substeps in sufficient detail to accurately describe the algorithm.
guidance: To prevent §112(f) treatment, draft claim elements to recite concrete substeps, specific acts, or structural features that show how the function is performed (i.e., the algorithmic implementation), rather than only high-level functional language.

name: Litigation/vetting practice: look for §112(f) and algorithm disclosure
description: When litigating, look for the §112(f) issue and whether the specification explicitly describes an algorithm or some way to program a computer/processor to perform the recited function.
guidance: As a litigation or clearance strategy, examine claims for triggers (means/generic placeholders, purely functional language, lack of structure) and analyze the specification for corresponding algorithmic disclosure; these points may be used to narrow or invalidate claims or to defend against indefiniteness arguments.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration (MPEP §2106.05(d))
description: When making a determination whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
guidance: General guidance: this consideration overlaps with other Step 2B considerations (improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity) and examiners should analyze all relevant considerations together. Key points: (1) An additional element known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine; novelty/obviousness inquiries are separate from eligibility (e.g., Enfish). (2) A prior art search is not necessary to determine whether an element is well-understood, routine, conventional; examiners may rely on what courts or those in the art recognize and on the examiner's own expertise — only conclude an element is conventional if it can be readily concluded that it is widely prevalent or in common use. (3) Even if individual elements are conventional, their combination may be an inventive concept (e.g., Diamond v. Diehr; Rapid Litigation Mgmt.; BASCOM). The specification may indicate elements are well-known or conventional; courts may take judicial notice. A rejection under Step 2B should only be made if the examiner, based on expertise, can readily conclude the additional elements do not amount to significantly more. See also MPEP §2106.07(a). Examples of elements courts have recognized as well-understood/routine/conventional when recited generically: computer functions (receiving/transmitting data over a network; repetitive calculations; electronic recordkeeping; storing/retrieving in memory; OCR; browser navigation), life-science laboratory techniques (measuring biomarkers, PCR, detecting DNA/enzymes, immunization, DNA analysis/sequencing, freezing/thawing cells, hybridizing probes), and other activities (recording a customer order; shuffling/dealing cards; restricting access by requiring viewing an advertisement; identifying undeliverable mail; presenting offers and gathering statistics; determining estimated outcome and setting a price; arranging/sorting information). Caveat: listing examples does not mean all computer functions are conventional; generic computer components used only to implement an abstract idea may render a claim ineligible, but generic components in combination can sometimes perform non-generic functions (e.g., DDR Holdings).

name: Other meaningful limitations (MPEP §2106.05(e))
description: For a claim directed to a judicial exception to be patent-eligible, it must include additional features that ensure the claim applies the exception in a meaningful way (i.e., more than drafting to monopolize the exception); such additional features are "meaningful limitations."
guidance: The considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(d) (e.g., improvement, particular machine, particular transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional) are examples of meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr—additional physical steps applying a mathematical equation were meaningful because they limited the equation to a practical application; Classen—analysis plus an immunization step integrated results into a specific, tangible application; contrast Alice and OIP Technologies—recitation of a generic computer or routine data-gathering steps did not meaningfully limit the abstract idea. When evaluating meaningful limitations, consider additional elements both individually and in combination; combinations of otherwise-generic elements can amount to significantly more (Diamond, BASCOM). Examiners should, when appropriate, explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (MPEP §2106.05(f))
description: A claim element (or combination) that merely recites the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) or is nothing more than an instruction to implement an abstract idea/other exception (for example, on a generic computer) does not amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit authority (Mayo, Alice, Benson) show that merely adding a generic computer or generic implementation is insufficient. Examiners should avoid treating drafting choices as dispositive; instead analyze whether the additional elements do more than state the exception and add 'apply it.' Requiring more than mere instructions does not require narrow claims—some broad claims are eligible and some narrow claims are ineligible—so evaluate each claim on its merits and alongside other Step 2B considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional). For claim limitations that appear to be mere instructions to apply an exception, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection. Considerations examiners may use include: (1) Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., fails to recite details or mechanism for accomplishing the result). Result-oriented or functional claim language that effectively covers any solution is equivalent to 'apply it' (see Electric Power; Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One). Other cited cases illustrate where claimed steps were found to be mere instructions (Mayo, Alice, Benson) or where recitations merely linked the idea to a technological environment without meaningful limitation.

name: Scope of claim amendments cannot enlarge claim scope
description: The scope of a claim cannot be enlarged by amendment.
guidance: Any amendment by patent owner during reexamination must not broaden the claimed scope; this is a firm limitation on allowable claim changes.

name: Reexamination proceedings normally conclude with a reexamination certificate
description: If ordered, a reexamination proceeding will normally be conducted to its conclusion and the issuance of a reexamination certificate.
guidance: When prosecution of a reexamination proceeding is terminated, a reexamination certificate is issued which indicates the status of all claims following the reexamination (see MPEP §§2287–2288).

name: Required narrative form and clarity
description: The abstract should be written in narrative form with clear and concise language (MPEP 608.01(b)).
guidance: Write in plain narrative sentences rather than lists of claim elements; emphasize clarity and brevity.

name: Avoid paraphrasing an independent claim
description: There is a tendency to summarize the invention by simply paraphrasing an independent claim; such an approach can lead to an objectionable abstract.
guidance: Do not merely restate claim language; provide a concise descriptive statement that is not simply a claim paraphrase (paraphrasing may be acceptable in the Brief Summary but not the abstract).

name: Forbidden phrases and words
description: The abstract should omit certain introductory or claim-like phrases and words.
guidance: Specifically avoid: "This disclosure concerns", "The disclosure defined by this invention", "This disclosure describes", and avoid claim-limiting or functional terms such as "means" and the archaic claim word "said". Also avoid phrasing that reads as boilerplate introductions.

name: How to correct or amend the abstract depending on filing path
description: Correction procedures differ by filing route: if filing a new US application with a conventional Paris Convention priority claim, the abstract can be revised in the specification itself without showing markings; if entering the US national stage of a PCT application, a Preliminary Amendment with a marked-up version of the amended Abstract should be filed with the initial national stage filing.
guidance: Be proactive: correct an over-long or objectionable abstract upon initial filing to avoid an unnecessary Office Action; use the appropriate amendment route (spec revision for new US filings with Paris priority vs Preliminary Amendment with marked-up abstract for PCT national stage).

name: Reference discloses all claim limitations except a property or function (shift burden)
description: When a prior art reference discloses all limitations of a claim except a property or function and the examiner cannot determine whether the reference inherently possesses the claimed property/function, the examiner may have basis to shift the burden of proof to the applicant (see In re Fitzgerald).
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2112 - 2112.02. Examiner should explain why the burden is shifted and cite supporting authority; include full factual basis on the record.

name: Reference teaches a small genus placing a claimed species in the public possession
description: When a reference discloses a small genus that places a claimed species in the possession of the public, the species may be anticipated or obvious even if genus disclosure would not generally support anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102.
guidance: See In re Schaumann and MPEP §§ 2131.02 and 2144.08. Consider genus/species relationship and whether the species would have been obvious from the genus disclosure.

name: Reference discloses all claim limitations except a means-plus-function limitation (equivalence/variant uncertainty)
description: When a reference teaches all claim limitations except a means-plus-function limitation and the examiner is unsure whether the element disclosed in the reference is an equivalent of the claimed element (anticipatory) or whether it is an obvious variant, further analysis is required.
guidance: See MPEP §§ 2183 - 2184. Determine whether corresponding structure in the specification limits the claimed means-plus-function and whether prior art discloses that structure or an equivalent.

name: Overlapping claimed and prior-art ranges without specific example within claimed range
description: When the ranges disclosed in the reference and those claimed by the applicant overlap but the reference does not contain a specific example within the claimed range, the overlap may nevertheless support a rejection in appropriate circumstances.
guidance: See concurring opinion in Ex parte Lee and MPEP § 2131.03. Evaluate whether the overlap and teachings provide a sufficient basis for anticipation or obviousness; explain reasoning on the record.

name: If claim interpretation renders claim(s) indefinite, use 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection
description: If, upon claim interpretation, the claims are rendered indefinite, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness) may be appropriate.
guidance: Explain how claim language leads to indefiniteness and provide clear reasons on the record linking claim language to 112(b) grounds.

name: Amendments that add AIA-era claims can convert a pre-AIA application to an AIA application
description: If an application filed on or after March 16, 2013 is amended to contain a claim whose effective filing date is on or after March 16, 2013, the application becomes an AIA application — provided the new claim has support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) in the application.
guidance: The application remains AIA even if the newly added claim is subsequently canceled. Treat any new grounds of rejection necessitated by this change as new grounds for purposes of finality rules (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

name: Treatment of amendments that introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132(a))
description: 35 U.S.C. 132(a) prohibits introduction of new matter into the disclosure; if an amendment introduces new matter, the Office follows specific administrative procedures (e.g., new drawings not entered if found to contain new matter; amendments with new matter ordinarily entered but new matter canceled and claims directed to new matter rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)).
guidance: See MPEP §§ 608.02 and 608.04. This process is administrative and for resolving disputes over whether new matter was introduced; maintain clear record and explain rejections for claims presenting new matter.

name: Applicant statement required in transition applications (37 CFR 1.55 / 1.78)
description: For nonprovisional applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 that claim benefit/priority to an earlier application filed before March 16, 2013 and that contain or contained at any time a claimed invention having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, the applicant must provide a 37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78 statement to assist the Office in determining applicability of AIA vs pre-AIA statutes.
guidance: Applicant is not required to provide the statement if it was filed in an earlier transition application to which benefit is claimed. See 37 CFR 1.78(c)(6)(i) and MPEP § 2159.04.

name: Written description requirement is separate and distinct from enablement
description: Written description and enablement are distinct inquiries: written description shows the inventor possessed the claimed invention at filing, while enablement shows how to make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: Cite Ariad (en banc), Vas-Cath, Barker, and related cases. Examiners must assess written description and enablement independently and explain deficiencies separately on the record.

name: Written description: must convey possession of claimed subject matter (genus/species, breadth considerations)
description: To satisfy written description, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that a person of ordinary skill in the art would reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at filing. The sufficiency varies with the nature/scope of claims; genus claims require adequate species support depending on state of the art.
guidance: See Ariad, Hynix, LizardTech, Rivera and related cases. Consider whether generic/functional claim language is supported by the disclosure; generic statements alone may be insufficient. Provide factual explanation tying disclosure to claimed scope.

name: Computer-implemented functional claim limitations: written description must disclose computer, steps/algorithm, and/or corresponding structure
description: For computer-implemented functional claim limitations, the specification must disclose the computer and the necessary steps and/or algorithm (or other sufficient structure) that perform the claimed function so one skilled in the art can conclude inventor possessed the claimed invention.
guidance: Algorithm can be expressed as math formula, prose, flowchart, or other understandable terms. Simply restating the function is not necessarily sufficient. See Vasudevan Software, Finisar, Microsoft Computer Dictionary, and MPEP §§ 2163 - 2163.07(b), 2181 subsection IV. If insufficient, make 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 112 first paragraph rejection.

name: Means-plus-function limitations require disclosure of corresponding structure/materials/acts (112(f) / sixth paragraph)
description: If a claim invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means or step plus function), the specification must disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts to perform the entire claimed function. Failure to provide sufficient corresponding structure can also implicate 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness).
guidance: If corresponding structure is missing or insufficient, make a written description rejection under 112(a) and a 112(b) rejection for failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention. See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181.

name: Enablement requirement: must enable full scope of claimed invention without undue experimentation (Wands factors)
description: Enablement requires that the specification teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation. The In re Wands factors guide assessment: (1) claim breadth, (2) nature of the invention, (3) state of prior art, (4) level of skill, (5) predictability in the art, (6) amount of direction provided by inventor, (7) existence of working examples, (8) quantity of experimentation needed.
guidance: Weigh all Wands factors; do not treat enablement as single-fact determination. Cite In re Wands and MPEP §§ 2164 - 2164.08(c). If examiner has reasonable basis to question enablement, place burden on applicant to rebut with factual demonstration (In re Brown, In re Scarbrough, In re Doyle).

name: When claim language is functional but does not invoke 112(f), broad claim scope raises enablement concerns
description: If a claim recites the ability to perform a function without invoking 112(f) and does not limit to particular structure, it is typically construed broadly to cover any embodiments that perform the function; this broad scope raises concern whether the specification enables the full scope of the claim.
guidance: Evaluate whether disclosure enables all embodiments covered by the broad functional language. Applicants choosing broad functional claim language risk invalidity for lack of enablement. Cite In re Swinehart, AK Steel, In re Moore.

name: Examiner must establish reasonable basis for enablement rejections; applicant must rebut with evidence
description: Before sustaining an enablement rejection, USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning adequacy of disclosure to enable one of ordinary skill to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. After that, the applicant has the opportunity to rebut with factual evidence.
guidance: Cite In re Brown, In re Ghiron, In re Doyle, In re Scarbrough and MPEP guidance. Provide clear factual reasoning supporting the examiner's position and identify specific deficiencies.

name: Claims scope must be commensurate with enablement (claims no broader than enabled scope)
description: The scope of patent claims must be less than or equal to the scope of enablement provided by the specification; claims broader than enabled disclosure may be invalid for lack of enablement or written description.
guidance: Cite Sitrick, MagSil examples where overly broad claims were invalidated because specification could not enable the full claimed scope. Explain how claimed elements exceed disclosure and why undue experimentation would be required.

name: Co-authorship (overcoming reference by co-authored publication)
description: Where the applicant is one of the co-authors of a publication cited against his or her application, he or she may overcome the rejection by filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131. Alternatively, the applicant may overcome the rejection by filing a specific affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 establishing that the article is describing applicant’s own work. An affidavit or declaration by applicant alone indicating that applicant is the sole inventor and that the others were merely working under his or her direction is sufficient to remove the publication as a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(a).
guidance: Cites In re Katz. Use 1.132 when showing the article describes applicant’s own invention. An affidavit by applicant alone claiming sole inventorship and that others worked under direction can remove the publication as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a).

name: Activities applied against the claims (when non-statutory activities can be antedated)
description: Unless it is a statutory bar, a rejection based on an activity showing that the claimed invention was used or known prior to the filing date of the application may be overcome by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 establishing a date of invention prior to the date of the activity. Alternatively, the applicant(s) may overcome the rejection by filing a specific affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the activity was performed by the applicant(s).
guidance: Distinguish statutory bars (which cannot be antedated) from activities that can be antedated via 1.131 or shown to have been performed by applicant under 1.132.

name: Genus-species and predictability (when single-species showing is insufficient)
description: Where generic claims have been rejected on a reference or activity which discloses a species not antedated by the affidavit or declaration, the rejection will not ordinarily be withdrawn ... unless the applicant is able to establish that he or she was in possession of the generic invention prior to the effective date of the reference or activity. In other words, the affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to furnish support for a generic claim.
guidance: If predictability is in question (unpredictable arts), showing one or a few species generally not sufficient. The affidavit must provide an adequate basis for inferring generic applicability. Size of genus affects how many species may be needed (e.g., small genus may need fewer species demonstrated).

name: Species claim: overcoming when reference discloses the claimed species
description: Where the claim under rejection recites a species and the reference or activity discloses the claimed species, the rejection can be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131 directly by showing prior completion of the claimed species or indirectly by a showing of prior completion of a different species coupled with a showing that the claimed species would have been an obvious modification of the species completed by applicant.
guidance: Cites In re Spiller and related cases. Indirect antedating requires showing obviousness relationship between species.

name: U.S. patent or application publication claiming same invention (limitations on using 1.131)
description: When the reference is a noncommonly owned U.S. application or publication claiming the same invention as applicant and its publication date is less than 1 year prior to the presentation of claims to that invention in the application being examined, applicant’s remedy, if any, must be by way of 37 CFR 41.202 instead of 37 CFR 1.131. If the reference is a U.S. patent which claims the same invention as the application and its issue date is more than 1 year prior to the presentation of claims to that invention in the application, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(1) should be made.
guidance: If the reference is a U.S. application publication under 35 U.S.C. 122(b), or a WIPO publication claiming the same invention and its publication date is more than 1 year prior to presentation of claims, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(2) should be made only if the application being examined was filed after the publication date of the reference. Use form paragraphs 23.14/23.14.01 as appropriate. Note complexity when references are commonly owned or when interference practice applies.

name: Common ownership and terminal disclaimer/1.130 practice
description: Where the reference and the application (or patent under reexamination) are commonly owned, and the inventions defined by the claims ... are not identical but are not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or application publication not only where there is verbatim correspondence between claims but also where there is no patentable distinction between respective claims (various cases cited). If claims are identical or not patentably distinct, the application and patent are claiming the 'same patentable invention' and interference rules apply (37 CFR 41.203(a)). See MPEP §718 for terminal disclaimer practice.

name: Facts and documentary evidence required (must show facts, not conclusions)
description: The essential thing to be shown under 37 CFR 1.131 is priority of invention and this may be done by any satisfactory evidence of the fact. FACTS, not conclusions, must be alleged. Evidence in the form of exhibits may accompany the affidavit or declaration. Each exhibit relied upon should be specifically referred to in the affidavit or declaration, in terms of what it is relied upon to show.
guidance: Acceptable exhibits include: attached sketches; blueprints; photographs; reproductions of notebook entries; an accompanying model; supporting witness statements; testimony given in an interference; disclosure documents. Exhibits and models must comply with 37 CFR 1.91. A general allegation of prior completion is insufficient. Original exhibits or photocopies must accompany affidavit or absence satisfactorily explained per 1.131(b) (Donovan). Examiner must consider entire evidence package; an exhibit need not support all claim limitations if declaration supports missing ones. Vague/general descriptions of exhibits amount to mere pleading and are insufficient (In re Borkowski). Applicant must clearly explain which facts the exhibits establish and rely upon (In re Harry).

name: Statutory compliance standard for Office actions
description: When rejecting a claim, the Office’s patentability determination must be correct and must, at a minimum, identify the claim and relevant statute and set forth sufficient evidence to put a person skilled in the art on notice why the claim is unpatentable.
guidance: For an allowed claim, the Office action must not omit a statutorily compliant rejection. Correctness is considered through the lens of whether determinations were reasonable and not based on what the reviewer would have done in the first instance. Statutory compliance supports reliability and durability of issued patents.

name: Three-judge court requirement for Section 5 cases
description: Congress has required that certain voting-rights/preclearance cases be heard by a Three-Judge Court rather than a single judge; a single judge lacks authority to rule finally on the merits of those Section 5 claims when the statute requires a three-judge panel.
guidance: Argument that the trial judge erred in failing to convene a Three-Judge Court and in deciding the merits; cites precedent indicating that when approval provisions of the Voting Rights Act are implicated, a three-judge court must decide coverage questions (citing case law such as Saint Landry Parish School Bd. discussion).

name: Claims survive facial dismissal if pleadings state plausible facts (Rule 12(b)(6) standard)
description: On a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, the complaint must be construed in the plaintiff's favor, taking well-pleaded factual allegations as true; dismissal is improper if any set of facts could entitle plaintiff to relief.
guidance: Cites Conley v. Gibson, In re Longhorn Securities Litigation, U.S. v. Howell: courts must accept well-pleaded facts, draw reasonable inferences for plaintiffs, and disregard unsupported legal conclusions. Quotation: 'A complaint should not be dismissed for failure to state a claim unless it appears beyond doubt that the Plaintiff can prove no set of facts ... which would entitle him to relief.'

name: Standard for determining whether a federal claim is 'insubstantial'
description: A federal claim is 'unsubstantial' only if its soundness so clearly results from prior Supreme Court decisions as to foreclose any controversy (Goolsby/Goolsby-derived standard).
guidance: Cites Goolsby v. Osser and Pine Township Citizens Assoc. explanation: 'its soundness so clearly results from the previous decisions of this Court as to foreclose the subject and leave no room for the inference that the questions sought to be raised can be the subject of controversy.' Used to argue the federal questions here are substantial.

name: Claim construction — starting point and tools
description: Courts generally interpret claim terms by giving them their ordinary meaning to a person skilled in the art; only thereafter will courts consult the description and prosecution history to see whether terms were given different or special meanings. Particularly in the United States, courts increasingly use dictionaries when construing claims and interpret ordinary terms accordingly.
guidance: If claims and description do not clearly communicate a specific meaning, courts will refer to the general meaning to a skilled person. Technical dictionaries, encyclopedias, treatises and expert testimony may be used to establish field-specific meanings. Draft with awareness that courts begin from ordinary meaning and then look to intrinsic evidence.

name: Define new or ambiguous claim terms in the description
description: Where a patent application creates a new term, when several different meanings for a term are possible and only one is meant or when the meaning of a term may be ambiguous, it should sensibly be defined in the description section of the patent application.
guidance: The description can act as a glossary of special claim terminology. Aim for a self-contained application that can be understood without external context to avoid reliance on dictionaries or treatises in later construction.

name: Draft claims as if no doctrine of equivalents exists
description: Claims should be drafted literally, giving terms their ordinary and customary meaning to a person skilled in the relevant art, rather than relying on the doctrine of equivalents to provide protection.
guidance: Professional tip: to deter imitators or litigate effectively, draft claims as though equivalents do not exist. Avoid relying on uncertain equivalents regimes across jurisdictions.

name: Doctrine of equivalents — jurisdictional variability and prosecution history estoppel
description: The doctrine of equivalents provides legal protection beyond literal claim words in some jurisdictions, but its scope and standards vary significantly from country to country.
guidance: Patent drafters must learn the regime applicable in jurisdictions of interest, including whether communications during prosecution can foreclose application of the doctrine (prosecution history estoppel). Be careful in responses to office actions that might limit later arguments on equivalents.

name: Prepare claims before other parts of the application
description: Drafting first the broadest main claim(s) reciting the inventive features is an efficient way of formulating the essential inventive concept.
guidance: Avoid drafting the background art first (risk: too long/detailed). Drafting claims first helps identify what embodiments, examples and drawings are needed to support the claimed invention and prevents extraneous limiting elements.

name: Recommended order of drafting and iterative review
description: Suggested workflow: (i) draft broadest main claim(s); (ii) draft title, technical field, background and summary; (iii) draft brief description of figures, detailed description of embodiments and drawings; (iv) revisit and refine claims; (v) check drawings and description for support, consistency and appropriate disclosure of claim terms.
guidance: The application is rarely drafted strictly sequentially; drafting is iterative. Revisit claims after drafting description/drawings to spot unnecessary or inadequately supported claim elements and to narrow or add claims as needed to address prior art.

name: Title of invention — breadth and concision
description: The title should describe the subject matter of the invention broadly, yet concisely. Avoid being overly narrow so as not to unduly limit implied scope, but make the subject matter sufficiently indicated.
guidance: Many drafters adopt a broad title because the title may be published soon. Note jurisdictional preferences: e.g., in the United States 'title' is preferred to 'title of invention' to avoid narrowing claim interpretation.

name: Summary of invention — outline full scope and advantages but avoid absolutes
description: Summary should outline what has been invented, in its full scope, and explain how the inventor has overcome the background problem; often prepared by turning independent claims into paragraphs.
guidance: Include advantageous effects to support inventive step but avoid absolute expressions ('fully eliminated')—use relative expressions ('reduced', 'lower'). Do not produce a broad meta-summary that goes beyond the claims (risk: suggests additional prior art or incomplete disclosure). Check jurisdictional preferences for headings (e.g., use 'summary' rather than 'summary of invention' in the US).

name: Brief description of drawings — state what each figure represents and avoid limiting language
description: State what each drawing figure represents and how drawings relate to one another; define drawing types and visual perspectives and briefly note what each figure depicts.
guidance: Since drawings often illustrate embodiments rather than general principles, consider starting the brief description with a statement that drawings are illustrative of embodiments only and not of 'the invention' to avoid limiting claim interpretation.

name: Description of embodiments — provide enabling, reproducible disclosure
description: This section explains various embodiments/examples of the claimed invention; it expands the earlier sections and provides sufficient explanation that a person skilled in the art could reproduce, use and understand the invention.
guidance: Tie the description closely to drawings (use reference numerals). Ensure the disclosure is complete at filing because substantive amendment to add new technical matter is not permitted later. Provide sufficient detail so claims can be narrowed during prosecution to avoid prior art.

name: Ensure sufficiency of disclosure at filing — cannot add new matter
description: The description of embodiments cannot be substantively amended after the filing date to include new technical disclosure; the application must be sufficient and complete on filing day.
guidance: Draft the description to reflect inventor-provided material, enable reproduction by skilled persons, and provide depth to allow later claim narrowing if necessary. If insufficient, client may need a new application, risking loss of original filing date.

name: Terminology and consistency — tie abstract terms to embodiments and provide alternatives
description: If claims use an abstract term, the description should use the same term but tie it to specific embodiments and provide alternative examples (e.g., list a horn, siren, buzzer as possible 'warning devices').
guidance: Consistency across the application reduces ambiguity. Use plain technical language rather than jargon to aid understanding and translation. Providing alternative examples supports broader claim interpretation.

name: Use of the word 'invention' in the description — avoid unnecessary narrowing
description: Avoid phrases like 'the invention is …'; instead use 'an embodiment of the invention' or 'an exemplification of the invention' to preserve broad interpretation.
guidance: Stating 'the invention is X' may unnecessarily narrow claimed scope; framing as an embodiment helps ensure the description is read as illustrative.

name: Avoiding discussions that limit claims — condition contextual descriptions
description: When including drawings or context, condition discussions so they do not become limiting (i.e., part of the claim) and avoid language that would narrow claims unintentionally.
guidance: Be careful with language choices throughout the application because wording can have consequences in prosecution and litigation. Avoid descriptions that imply essentiality unless intended.

name: Avoid absolute words unless truly essential
description: Words such as 'must' or 'always' should be used only when they precisely and accurately indicate essential features of the claimed invention.
guidance: Absolute words can create unintended essential limitations. Professional tip: compile a list of absolute words to find and replace before finalizing the application.

name: Preferred/optional features — describe as such and recite advantages
description: Features in dependent claims should be described as preferred or optional embodiments; otherwise they may be regarded as essential features of the claimed invention.
guidance: Recite advantages of preferred features to support later amendments or opposition proceedings. Note: in the United States, practitioners often avoid discussing 'preferred' embodiments because case law disfavors finding infringement where accused products lack preferred features.

name: Who may bring a challenge
description: Which parties are eligible to initiate post‑grant reviews or related proceedings.
guidance: IPRs and PGRs in the U.S. are initiated by third parties (not the patent owner) and decided by the PTAB. EPO oppositions may be filed by any person within the first nine months; the EPO accepts straw‑man oppositions (subject to anti‑circumvention). Patentees can initiate limitation or revocation at the EPO/DPMA. German nullity (BPatG) actions can be filed by any entity but are often filed in response to infringement claims; intervenors/assumed infringers may be allowed (EPC art. 105). Who may bring a proceeding shapes access to review and strategic behavior (e.g., patentee‑initiated limitation requests).

name: Ability of the patentee to amend claims
description: Whether and under what conditions a patent owner may amend claims during post‑grant proceedings.
guidance: At the EPO the patentee has a right to amend when justified by at least one ground of opposition; amendments must be restricted to what is necessary to retain patentability and typically are filed within a set deadline (four months after opposition period). In German nullity proceedings patentees may amend but may not extend scope (Section 22(1) Patentgesetz). In U.S. IPRs patentees have a statutory right to move to amend or cancel challenged claims and propose substitute claims, but in practice motions to amend are rare and rarely fully granted (PTAB data through Sept. 30, 2017: 10% of trials included an MTA; 62% of those had motions decided; only ~4.2% fully granted). Amendment practice (and administrative willingness) materially affects the fairness and outcome of reviews.

name: Revocation and limitation (patentee‑initiated 'life of patent' options)
description: Procedures allowing patentees to limit or revoke their own patents during the life of the patent and the operational differences from oppositions.
guidance: EPO (introduced in EPC 2000): patentee can request limitation or revocation anytime; revocation requests are seldom used but are immediately granted if formalities and fee met; limitations are more common and can be filed without a stated reason, are ex parte (patentee deals only with examiner), and can be used strategically to tailor claim scope. DPMA requires justification for limitation. These procedures differ from opposition since third parties lack equivalent ex parte paths and may view them as unfair strategic tools.

name: Reference to another claim
description: Reference to limitations recited in another claim is not per se indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph; e.g., reference to 'the nozzle of claim 7' was held to comply.
guidance: While cross-referencing other claims is permissible, if the format of making reference to limitations recited in another claim results in confusion, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA second paragraph) is proper. See Ex parte Porter, 25 USPQ2d 1144 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1992).

name: Dependent claim compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(d)
description: When examining a dependent claim, the examiner should determine whether the claim complies with 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (pre-AIA fourth paragraph).
guidance: See MPEP § 608.01(n), subsection II for procedures and details on dependent claim treatment.

name: Functional limitations — general permissibility
description: Functional claim language (reciting a feature 'by what it does rather than by what it is') is not inherently wrong and may be employed; 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-/step-plus-function) expressly authorizes a form of functional claiming.
guidance: Functional language often involves reciting some structure followed by its function and may be permissible (e.g., conical spout that 'allow[ed] several kernels…to pass through'), but must be evaluated like any other limitation for what it fairly conveys to a person of ordinary skill in the art in context.

name: Functional limitations — when they are indefinite or unsupported
description: Functional language may fail to provide a clear-cut indication of scope when it merely describes a problem to be solved or a result achieved, or when it lacks particular structure/materials/steps that accomplish the function.
guidance: Unlimited functional claim limitations that extend to all means or methods of resolving a problem may be indefinite or lack written description/enablement support under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Courts cited: Swinehart, Halliburton, United Carbon, Ariad, Hyatt, Datamize. Examples: claiming a device as merely 'aesthetically pleasing' or reciting only a desired result without structure can be indefinite.

name: Factors to determine ambiguity of functional language
description: Consider whether (1) there is a clear-cut indication of the scope of subject matter covered by the claim; (2) the language sets forth well-defined boundaries of the invention or only states a problem/result; and (3) a person of ordinary skill would know from the claim terms what structure or steps are encompassed.
guidance: These factors are examples and not exhaustive; relevance may vary by art. The primary inquiry is whether the language leaves room for ambiguity or whether the boundaries are clear and precise.

name: Ways to resolve ambiguity of functional limitations
description: During prosecution, applicant may resolve ambiguities by e.g., using quantitative metrics, providing specification formulas/examples, providing general guidelines and examples, or amending claims to recite particular structure.
guidance: Examples: (1) numeric limitation as to a physical property; (2) specification providing a formula and examples that meet/do not meet the limitation (Oakley example); (3) general guidelines and examples sufficient to teach POSITA (Marosi example); (4) amend to recite particular structure that accomplishes the function.

name: Markush group (alternatives) — closed vs open grouping
description: A Markush grouping is a closed group of alternatives (selected from the group 'consisting of' the listed members). If a Markush grouping requires selection from an open list (e.g., 'comprising' or 'consisting essentially of'), the claim should generally be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite because it is unclear what other alternatives are intended.
guidance: See MPEP § 2117 and Supplementary Guidelines. If combinations/mixtures are intended, include qualifying language ('at least one member', 'or mixtures thereof'). Redundancy within the group does not necessarily render the claim indefinite (Eli Lilly v. Teva).

name: Markush groups — breadth is not automatically indefiniteness
description: A Markush claim may encompass many alternatives and breadth alone does not make a claim indefinite.
guidance: However, if the Markush group is so expansive that skilled artisans cannot determine the metes and bounds of the claimed invention (e.g., an enormous chemical space), a rejection for indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be appropriate. Evaluate case-by-case (In re Gardner example).

name: Product and process in same claim
description: A single claim that claims both an apparatus (product) and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Claims mixing statutory classes can create confusion as to when infringement occurs (Katz Interactive; IPXL Holdings). In contrast, claims that recite a product plus limitations focusing on system capabilities (not user actions) may be definite (Mastermine v. Microsoft).

name: 'Use' claims
description: Attempts to claim a process without setting forth any steps (mere 'use' recitation) generally raise indefiniteness issues under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and may also fail 35 U.S.C. 101 because 'use' alone is not a statutory class.
guidance: Examples: claims reciting only a use ('a process for using X to isolate Y') found indefinite (Ex parte Erlich). Use-claims that do not claim a statutory class may be rejected under 101 and/or 112. However, certain recited 'utilizing' steps were found not indefinite in particular contexts (Ex parte Porter). Examine whether steps are sufficiently recited and whether claim fits a statutory class.

name: (R) Clarification for means/steps-plus-function support
description: (R) Clarification of the correlation and identification of what structure, material, or acts set forth in the specification would be capable of carrying out a function recited in a means or steps plus function claim limitation.
guidance: If support for such claim limitations is not apparent and applicant cannot identify it, examiner may conclude lack of support and make rejections (e.g., under 35 U.S.C. 112). Applicant should be asked to point to specific spec/drawings pages/lines.

name: (S)(1) Common technical features among claims / admissions
description: (S)(1) Of the common technical features shared among all claims, or admission that certain groups of claims do not share any common technical features.
guidance: Used to determine claim grouping, unity, or claim correspondence for examination and restriction purposes.

name: (S)(2) Support for means/steps-plus-function claims (35 U.S.C. 112, ¶6)
description: (S)(2) About the support found in the disclosure for means or steps plus function claims (35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 6).
guidance: Interrogatory to identify where specification provides structure/acts corresponding to claimed functions.

name: (S)(3) Which portions provide written description and enablement for specific claim elements
description: (S)(3) Of precisely which portion(s) of the disclosure provide the written description and enablement support for specific claim element(s).
guidance: Applicant should point to exact pages/lines illustrating support for each claim element to address 112 concerns.

name: (S)(4) Meaning of claim limitations / scope of terms
description: (S)(4) Of the meaning of claim limitations or terms used in the claims, such as what teachings in the prior art would be covered by particular limitations or terms in a claim and which dictionary definitions would define a particular claim term, particularly where those terms are not used per se in the specification.
guidance: Used to clarify claim language and scope; applicant may be asked to identify dictionary definitions or prior art teachings that correspond to claim terms.

name: (S)(5) Which portions of each claim correspond to any admitted prior art
description: (S)(5) Of which portions of each claim correspond to any admitted prior art in the specification.
guidance: Helps isolate novel claim aspects and assess obviousness/anticipation relative to admitted prior art.

name: (S)(6) Specific utility provided by the claimed subject matter on a claim-by-claim basis
description: (S)(6) Of the specific utility provided by the claimed subject matter on a claim-by-claim basis.
guidance: Applicant should state what utility each claim provides to satisfy utility requirements.

name: (S)(7) Whether dependent claim element is known in prior art
description: (S)(7) As to whether a dependent claim element is known in the prior art based on the examiner having a reasonable basis for believing so.
guidance: Applicant may be required to confirm whether dependent elements are novel or anticipated by prior art.

name: (S)(8) Support for added limitations in an amended claim
description: (S)(8) Of support for added limitations in an amended claim.
guidance: When claims are amended, applicant may need to identify where new limitations are supported in the disclosure.

name: Format and content of the requirement (notice content)
description: The requirement must clearly indicate that a 1.105 requirement is being made, the basis for the requirement, and what information is being required. Requirements should specify the particular art area involved and the particular claimed subject matter within such art area, and indicate the form the required information is expected to take (citations/copies, identification of collections, answers to questions, etc.).
guidance: Prepare as a separate document (preferred) or attached to an Office action; state why the requirement was made and how the information is necessary to examination.

name: Form paragraphs and specific required-subject templates
description: A set of form paragraphs (7.105 – 7.127 etc.) should be used when preparing a requirement, with tailored templates for domains such as domain of search, level of skill, background description, products embodying the invention, art suggested as relevant, list of keywords, citations for searchable databases, copies of art referred to but not submitted, copies of inventor-authored publications, art relied upon for prior art description/development/drafting, names of products incorporating claimed invention or prior art, details of improvement over prior art, etc.
guidance: Use the specific form paragraph that matches the information sought; follow the examiner notes in each paragraph for how to populate bracketed fields and limitations on scope (many templates limit the requirement to documents actually relied on vs. merely relevant documents).

name: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception
description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
guidance: Identify whether claim elements recite abstract ideas such as organizing/comparing information, mathematical algorithms, mental processes, or laws of nature. Provide specific comparison to precedent (e.g., Cyberfone, SmartGene, Benson, Flook, Grams, etc.) when appropriate.

name: Step 2B: Significantly more analysis
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether additional elements individually or as an ordered combination amount to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Consider whether additional limitations provide meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the abstract idea to a technological environment. Evaluate both individual elements and the claimed ordered combination.

name: Field‑of‑use / technological environment limitations are insufficient
description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., the Internet, GUI) does not by itself make the claim significantly more.
guidance: Internet limitations are merely a field of use; merely linking the idea to the Internet or other environment does not transform an abstract idea into patent‑eligible subject matter (e.g., claims that simply use the Internet to implement an organizing/comparing idea remain ineligible).

name: Preamble and claim limitation effect (MPEP 2111.02)
description: Determine whether preamble language merely states purpose/field of use or actually limits claim scope; a non‑limiting preamble does not add 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim.
guidance: If the preamble only states purpose/field of use it ordinarily does not limit the claim; do not treat a non‑limiting preamble as an additional limitation in Step 2B (see example of GUI meal planning preamble).

name: Claims that improve computer technology or another technical field support eligibility
description: A claim that provides an improvement in computer technology or another technical field, or transforms matter, can be patent eligible.
guidance: Examples: GUI relocating obscured text that is necessarily rooted in computer technology; software that controls a rubber molding press to improve precision molding (transforms material/state); internal combustion engine control that improves engine technology. Improvements must be integrated and provide meaningful limitations, not mere field‑of‑use labels.

name: Mathematical algorithms and laws of nature require special care
description: Mathematical procedures and equations (e.g., scaling factor algorithms, Arrhenius equation) are likely abstract and require Step 2B scrutiny whether additional claimed elements amount to significantly more.
guidance: If the mathematical relationship is recited, determine whether additional elements integrate the math into a control scheme or otherwise improve technology (e.g., automated control of press), thereby providing significantly more.

name: Non‑transitory computer‑readable medium claims
description: Reciting 'non‑transitory' ensures the claim does not encompass transitory signals and asserts a manufacture category.
guidance: Use this language when the claim is for stored instructions; recognizing 'non‑transitory' helps clarify statutory category and exclude signal‑based subject matter.

name: Streamlined analysis for clearly eligible claims
description: If eligibility is self‑evident (e.g., claim clearly amounts to significantly more or is not directed to any exception), a streamlined analysis can be used and a written rejection need not be issued.
guidance: For claims like certain engine or BIOS examples where the claim as a whole clearly provides significant meaningful limitations, examiners may conclude eligibility without performing full Steps 2A/2B and may add clarifying remarks if desired.

name: Rejection content guidance
description: When issuing a rejection under §101, identify the judicial exception and explain why the claim recites it by pointing to specific claim steps; also explain why additional elements do not add significantly more.
guidance: Example language: point to filtering/generating/formatting steps as mental processes or to generating/scaling steps as mathematical algorithms; explain why transmission server/microprocessor/memory are only generic computer functions and do not impose meaningful limits.

name: Remarks for allowance / reasons for allowance guidance
description: When a claim is allowed but recites an exception in part, add remarks or reasons for allowance clarifying that while the claim recites an abstract idea or other exception, additional limitations amount to significantly more.
guidance: Include language identifying the abstract idea and indicating which additional limitations (as ordered combination) provide a technologically‑rooted solution or meaningful limits (e.g., activation via wireless device enabling later Internet connection).

name: Use of precedent to frame analyses
description: Apply and analogize to relevant court decisions (e.g., Cyberfone, SmartGene, DDR Holdings, Flook, Benson, Grams) to characterize the exception and the sufficiency of additional elements.
guidance: The examples repeatedly map claim features to prior judicial characterizations: organizing/comparing information (mental processes), mathematical conversions/algorithms (Benson/Flook), and technology‑rooted solutions (DDR Holdings). Use such analogies to support Step 2A/2B conclusions.

name: High‑level claim language construed broadly weakens the showing of significantly more
description: Elements recited at a high level of generality will be construed broadly as generic and thus less likely to supply meaningful limitations.
guidance: When the claim does not expressly recite how components perform unconventional functions, the examiner should construe them at the highest reasonable level of generality and treat them as generic (examples: 'user interface', 'database', 'transmission server').

name: Ordered combination vs individual element analysis
description: Evaluate additional claim elements both individually and as an ordered combination for whether they amount to significantly more.
guidance: Even if individual limitations are routine, their particular combination may be unconventional and solve a technical problem (compare ineligible Claim 1 vs eligible Claim 2 in the stock quote example). Document the reasoning for both perspectives.

name: Claims that transform matter or improve manufacturing processes are likely eligible
description: Processes or claims that transform a physical material or improve a manufacturing process can provide significantly more than judicial exceptions.
guidance: Illustrated by the precision rubber molding example: integrating a mathematical relationship into a control scheme that changes the state of material (curing rubber) and controls machinery can amount to significantly more.

name: When additional limitations merely automate human tasks, likely ineligible
description: Claims that merely automate tasks that can be performed mentally or by pen-and-paper (e.g., meal planning, selecting meals to meet goals) are typically directed to abstract ideas and lack significantly more.
guidance: Use examples where the core concept is a mental process or organizing/comparing data; if the claimed computerization only provides automation without unconventional steps, reject under §101.

name: Patent subject classification task definition
description: The automated subject classification task is a multi-label classification task. The aim is to predict patents’ specific categories or classes based on patent content, including title, abstract, and claims. Given inputs x = [w1, w2, ..., wn], the objective is to predict label y ∈ {y1, y2, ..., ym}; since patents may belong to multiple classes, sometimes more than one label needs predicting.
guidance: Crucial for organizing patent databases, facilitating patent searches, and assisting examiners in evaluating novelty. Use multi-label modelling approaches and consider inputs from title, abstract, claims (and potentially full descriptions) to capture class information.

name: Use of parts of patent documents for classification
description: Typical inputs for classification models are title, abstract, and claims; many studies focus on short texts (abstracts and claims).
guidance: Titles and abstracts are generic and may lack detailed information; the paper recommends future work to focus on full descriptions which contain more specific technical information. Consider which patent fields to include depending on task and model capacity.

name: Freedom-to-operate (FTO) search definition and core requirement
description: Freedom-to-operate search determines if a product/technology would be covered by active IP rights. It differs from prior-art novelty search by focusing on active patents/applications and whether independent claims cover the technology (claims with fewer features covering broader scope).
guidance: FTO requires detailed claim analysis and automated retrieval of targeted patent claims; design systems to retrieve and compare specific claim language to the technology's feature set. This is underexplored and recommended for future research.

name: Patent quality assessment dimensions
description: Quality assessment covers novelty prediction, granting prediction, litigation prediction, and patent valuation as measures reflecting patent quality and scope.
guidance: Novelty prediction helps pre-filing assessment; granting prediction models whether the office will grant an application (considering formal language/figures/documents); litigation prediction estimates odds of future litigation (ambiguous claims increase risk); valuation quantifies economic worth. Use appropriate labeled datasets and combine textual, metadata and procedural features.

name: Data collection ease and label availability for classification tasks
description: Because granted patents are assigned classification codes and contain referenced patents, researchers can collect and filter patents to formulate datasets without additional labeling for subject classification.
guidance: Exploit existing IPC/CPC labels for supervised training but be mindful of label granularity/hierarchy. Provide clear train/validation/test splits and document parts used (title, abstract, claims, full text).

name: Bifurcation and phased trials as a tool to aid juror comprehension
description: Consider bifurcating the trial (e.g., separating damages from liability, willfulness issues, or antitrust claims) or conducting multiple phases with the same jury to handle overlapping evidence and complexity.
guidance: Bifurcation is not barred by the Seventh Amendment. Courts have both granted and denied motions to bifurcate; separation of validity/infringement from willfulness/damages with a 60–90 day hiatus is a recommended approach in some situations. Downsides include creating a piecemeal trial and potentially detracting from seeing the case as a whole. Bifurcation is most appropriate when there is a clearly separable issue that would control the outcome.

name: Avoid secondary rejections when prior art discloses the 'heart' of the invention
description: In cases where there exists a sound rejection on the basis of prior art which discloses the “heart” of the invention (as distinguished from prior art which merely meets the terms of the claims), secondary rejections on minor technical grounds should ordinarily not be made.
guidance: Apply restraint: if principal prior art defeats the invention's core, do not add minor technical rejections. Recognize limits of language; certain technical rejections (e.g., negative limitations, indefiniteness) should not be made where the examiner, recognizing the limitations of the English language, is not aware of an improved mode of definition.

name: Limit action on claim to a particular issue in specified situations
description: Some situations exist where examination appears best accomplished by limiting action on the claim to a particular issue.
guidance: Situations include: (A) application too informal for complete action (see MPEP §702.01); (B) undue multiplicity of claims where telephone election request unsuccessful (see MPEP §2173.05(n)); (C) misjoinder of inventions with no successful election request (see MPEP §§803, 806.02, 812.01); (D) disclosure directed to perpetual motion—in such cases cite best prior art and its pertinency without specifically applying it to the claims.

name: Allowable except as to form — be constructive and suggest corrections
description: When an application discloses patentable subject matter but claims cannot be allowed because of defects in form or omission of a limitation, the examiner should not stop with a bare objection or rejection; the action should be constructive and offer a definite suggestion for correction.
guidance: If examiner is satisfied that patentable subject matter has been disclosed and applicant intends to claim it, note unclaimed aspects that may be given favorable consideration if properly claimed. Suggest possible desirability of an interview to accelerate agreement on allowable claims. If a claim is otherwise allowable but dependent on a canceled or rejected claim, state it would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.

name: Use of form paragraphs to indicate objection/allowable subject matter
description: Form paragraphs 7.43, 7.43.01, and 7.43.02 may be used to indicate allowable subject matter and to state specific conditions under which claims would be allowable.
guidance: Examples include ¶7.43 to note dependency upon rejected base claim but allowability if rewritten; 7.43.01/7.43.02 specific to 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph rejections. Use form paragraph 7.97 for allowance. Follow examiner notes: use paragraphs only where appropriate (e.g., 7.43.01 only when independent claims were rejected solely under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph).

name: Professional-conduct findings by the disciplining state authority
description: The Disciplinary Board of the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania found violations of Rules of Professional Conduct pertaining to: diligence; communication; safekeeping of property; meritorious claims and contentions; candor to the tribunal; committing a criminal act that reflects adversely on honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness; misconduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; and failing to respond to disciplinary counsel's request under the Disciplinary Rules.
guidance: These specific state-law findings served as the factual and ethical basis for the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's disbarment, which in turn supported the USPTO's reciprocal discipline under § 11.24. The Order summarizes the Board's findings in the Notice of Exclusion text.

name: Timely and appropriate response in inter partes reexamination
description: If the patent owner fails to file a timely and appropriate response in an inter partes reexamination proceeding, the prosecution in the reexamination proceeding will be a terminated prosecution and the Director will proceed to issue and publish a certificate concluding the reexamination proceeding under § 1.997 in accordance with the last action of the Office.
guidance: If claims are found patentable and the patent owner fails to file a timely and appropriate response to any Office action, further prosecution is limited to the claims found patentable at the time of the failure and to any claims added thereafter which do not expand the scope of those claims. If the action by the patent owner is a bona fide attempt and substantially complete but omits some matter inadvertently, an opportunity to explain and supply the omission may be given.

name: Merger of reissue application and inter partes reexamination
description: If a reissue application and an inter partes reexamination proceeding are pending concurrently on a patent, the Office may merge the proceedings or suspend one. Where merger is ordered, the merged proceeding will be conducted in accordance with §§ 1.171–1.179.
guidance: Patent owner must place and maintain the same claims in the reissue application and the inter partes reexamination during the merged proceeding. Third party requester participation is limited to issues within inter partes scope. Examiner actions and responses apply to both files. Any inter partes reexamination merged with a reissue application shall be concluded by the grant of the reissued patent.

name: Additional/optional contents and Contracting Party-specific mandatory elements
description: An international design application may contain two or more industrial designs subject to conditions; a request for deferment of publication or immediate publication; and other elements.
