Where designation of a Contracting Party requires certain elements, the application must include them (e.g., identity of creator, brief description of reproduction/characteristic features, a claim).
guidance: Other optional items include name/address of representative, priority claim, Paris Convention exhibition declaration, administrative instructions items, statements of material information, and proposed translations. The application must include elements specifically required by designated Contracting Parties under Article 5(2) and relevant Rules.

name: Claim wording for U.S. designation
description: The specific wording of the claim in an international design application designating the United States shall be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article (specifying name of article) as shown, or as shown and described. More than one claim is neither required nor permitted for purposes of the United States.
guidance: Use a single formal ornamental-design claim specifying the article name; do not include multiple claims for U.S. purposes.

name: Determine what is the invention
description: Determine what the invention is — the invention is defined in the claims.
guidance: The specification need not set forth details not relating to the essence of the invention. Unclaimed matter unrelated to the operation of the claimed invention does not trigger best mode. Case citations: In re Bosy; Northern Telecom v. Samsung; Eli Lilly v. Barr (failure to disclose unclaimed preferred mode for routine detail does not violate best mode).

name: Best mode is distinct from enablement
description: The best mode requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Enablement looks to placing the claimed subject matter in the possession of the public; best mode requires disclosure of the inventor's recognized best way of practicing the invention if such existed at filing. (In re Newton; Spectra-Physics v. Coherent.)

name: Two separate requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
description: The second paragraph contains two distinct requirements: (A) claims must set forth the subject matter applicants regard as their invention (subjective), and (B) claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the invention (objective/definiteness).
guidance: The first requirement depends on what applicants regard as their invention; the second is evaluated from perspective of one of ordinary skill to determine definiteness and clarity of scope.

name: Rejection for failure to claim what applicants regard as their invention
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is appropriate only where applicant has stated, outside the application as filed, that the invention is different from what is defined by the claims.
guidance: Evidence to the contrary may appear in briefs, remarks, or affidavits (e.g., Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark; In re Prater; In re Cormany). The specification itself is not used as evidence for this requirement (In re Ehrreich).

name: Unclaimed essential matter (112 first paragraph)
description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential to the invention as described in the specification may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as not enabling.
guidance: Essential matter may include missing elements, steps, or necessary structural cooperative relationships. See In re Mayhew and MPEP §2164.08(c).

name: Failure to interrelate essential elements (112 second paragraph)
description: A claim that fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined by applicants in the specification may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph for failure to point out and distinctly claim the invention.
guidance: However, not all lack of interdependency between elements defeats paragraph two compliance; elements may serve independent purposes. (In re Venezia; In re Collier; Ex parte Nolden; Ex parte Huber.)

name: Determine whether each claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph
description: As part of claim interpretation, determine whether a limitation invokes paragraph six (means-plus-function); if so, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: Paragraph six applies regardless of context (PTO examination or court proceedings). If means-plus-function is present, consult MPEP §2181(I) for determining corresponding structure and equivalents. (In re Donaldson Co.)

name: Determining whether claim language is definite during prosecution
description: Decide whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification; applicant has opportunity and duty to amend ambiguous claims.
guidance: During prosecution the Office uses BRI and a lower threshold of ambiguity than courts (no presumption of validity). Examiners should demand applicants resolve ambiguities so claims can be amended during prosecution rather than leaving issues for litigation. (Halliburton Energy Servs.; In re Morris; Ex parte Miyazaki.)

name: Different standard for claims under examination vs issued claims
description: Patented claims enjoy a presumption of validity and are not given BRI in courts; the PTO must construe pending claims under BRI without presumption, applying a lower threshold for ambiguity.
guidance: Because prosecution record is in development, applicants can explain or amend claims; the Office may reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph if, under BRI, the claim has more than one reasonable interpretation. Avoid conflating claim breadth with indefiniteness: broad is not necessarily indefinite if scope is clear.

name: Consider claim as a whole to serve notice function
description: In reviewing compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope and thus serves the notice function.
guidance: The totality of limitations and their interaction must be considered. Example: a preamble may be insufficient alone but the whole claim may still satisfy notice requirements. (Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark; In re Larsen.)

name: Undeclared claim terms not indefinite if meaning discernible
description: A claim term that is not used or defined in the specification is not indefinite if the meaning of the term is discernible to one skilled in the art.
guidance: If components of a compound term have well-recognized meanings, the reader can infer the compound meaning with reasonable confidence; thus lack of a definition in the specification does not automatically render a term indefinite. (Bancorp Services v. Hartford Life.)

name: Scope of the required translation
description: Translation must comprise the description (including title), the claims, and any text matter in the drawings, as originally filed and/or as amended; pages incorporated by reference must be included.
guidance: National Chapters list what must be translated for each Office. See paragraphs 4.010 and following for details on amended material.

name: Correction of obvious mistakes
description: Obvious mistakes in the description, claims and drawings may normally be corrected before the designated Office, presented as an amendment provided scope is not broadened.
guidance: Reference to Rule 91.3(f); check national practice for allowing such rectification.

name: Objections — merits vs. characteristics-based objections
description: Objections to discovery that go to the merits include relevance, overbreadth, vagueness, ambiguity, burdensomeness, or not reasonably calculated to lead to admissible evidence; objections based on privilege/confidentiality/work product concern characteristics of the information sought rather than the merits.
guidance: Merits objections can be forfeited by failure to timely respond. Privilege claims must be asserted expressly and described per Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5).

name: Requirement to reference CPA when seeking benefit in later-filed application
description: Where an applicant in an application filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) seeks to claim the benefit of a CPA under 35 U.S.C. 120 or 121, 37 CFR 1.78(d)(2) requires a reference to the CPA by application number in an application data sheet or (for apps filed before Sept 16, 2012) in the first sentence of the specification.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.78(d)(4) treats identification by application number as identification of every application assigned that application number; thus referencing a CPA in a chain will constitute reference to every CPA in that chain and the non-continued prosecution application.

name: Priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) carry over to CPA
description: Priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) made in a parent application will automatically carry over to a CPA.
guidance: Examiner should note that provisional-applicant-specific rules apply (provisionals are not entitled to benefit of other applications) and check bib-data sheet entries for accuracy.

name: Continuation-in-part (CIP) definition and filing constraints
description: A continuation-in-part application repeats some substantial portion or all of a prior-filed application and adds matter not disclosed in the prior application; a CIP must be filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b), must claim the benefit of the prior under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)/386(c), and CANNOT be filed as a CPA under 37 CFR 1.53(d).
guidance: An application claiming the benefit of a provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) should not be called a CIP of the provisional. The Office need not determine 35 U.S.C. 120/35 U.S.C. 112(a) entitlement unless the earlier filing date is relied upon in a proceeding before the Office. Use form paragraph 2.06 to inform applicants of possible CIP status.

name: Conditions for claiming benefit of earlier nonprovisional in alleged CIP
description: An alleged CIP should be permitted to claim the benefit of an earlier nonprovisional application if it complies with other requirements of 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78, such as: (A) same inventor or at least one common joint inventor; (B) filed before patenting, abandonment, or termination of proceedings on the first application; and (C) contains or is amended to contain a specific reference to the earlier filed application (ADS for apps on/after Sept 16, 2012; first sentence(s) or ADS for apps before that date).
guidance: See MPEP § 211 et seq. for more information. A petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim may be required in some circumstances.

name: Examiner duties re: notation of prior application data on bib-data sheet
description: Examiners must review identifying data of all prior applications for which benefits are claimed to ensure accuracy and that the data is provided in an ADS (for apps filed on/after Sept 16, 2012) or in the first sentence(s) of the specification or ADS (for apps filed before that date).
guidance: If prior application data errors exist, technical support staff can correct Patent Data Portal entries and republish bib-data sheets; applicant errors should be corrected via corrected or supplemental ADS or amendment. See MPEP §§ 601.05, 211.02(a). Inclusion of prior application information on the bib-data sheet does not automatically indicate entitlement to benefit; check MPEP §§ 213.01, 2136.03, 2154.01(b), and §306 for further guidance.

name: USPTO proposed terminal-disclaimer unenforceability agreement
description: A terminal disclaimer filed to overcome ODP will include an agreement that any patent granted on the subject application would be unenforceable if the patent is tied through a terminal disclaimer to another patent with a claim that has been held unpatentable or invalid under 35 USC §§ 102 or 103 and all appeal rights have been exhausted, or a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on anticipation or obviousness to that claim has been made.
guidance: The practical effect is that patents tied together via a terminal disclaimer "will fall together," allowing a challenger to potentially invalidate multiple patents by successfully challenging a single claim. The USPTO states this would reduce the cost barrier to challengers and discourage issuance of patents on trivial variations. Opponents counter that validity should be determined claim-by-claim, that claims are presumed valid under 35 U.S.C. § 282, and that prior art invalidating one claim may not invalidate another tied claim.

name: Obviousness-type double patenting (ODP) rejection criteria
description: An ODP rejection can be issued if the claims in the different patents or patent applications have the same inventive entity, at least one common inventor, or a common applicant, owner, or assignee.
guidance: ODP is nonstatutory double patenting that arises when claim variations between applications are essentially obvious variations of the same invention. Common responses to an ODP rejection include arguing against the rejection, amending claims, or filing a terminal disclaimer (a common practice). The citation references MPEP 804.

name: Current terminal-disclaimer conditions on patent term and ownership
description: Under a terminal disclaimer, the applicant agrees that the term of the patent with obvious claim variants will not expire after the expiration date of the patent over which the patent office issued the ODP, and that the patent will only be enforceable while both patents are commonly owned.
guidance: Applicants frequently file terminal disclaimers to reduce cost and expedite prosecution rather than litigate the merits of an ODP rejection. Often the related patents would expire at the same time regardless of the disclaimer, but differences can arise when one patent receives a patent term adjustment (PTA); see In re Cellect, LLC for interplay between terminal disclaimers and PTA (81 F.4th 1216 (Fed. Cir. 2023)).

name: Effect of terminal disclaimers on enforcement and validity challenges (current practice)
description: Although patents tied through a terminal disclaimer expire simultaneously, the patent owner can choose which patent to assert against an infringer, while the infringer or any third party who wishes to challenge the validity of claims subject to a terminal disclaimer must challenge each patent separately.
guidance: Under current practice, challengers face the high cost of separately invalidating each patent subject to a terminal disclaimer; the proposed rule is intended to change this by making tied patents unenforceable together if one is invalidated, reducing challengers' costs.

name: USPTO rationale for changing terminal-disclaimer practice
description: The USPTO views the high cost of separately challenging the validity of each patent with obvious variants as a bar to competition. In proposing the new rule, the USPTO desires to promote competition and innovation and reduce costs to patent challengers.
guidance: The USPTO argues the rule would allow a challenger to invalidate multiple patents by successfully challenging a single claim and would decrease the number of patents issued on trivial variations. Opponents argue that claims should be judged individually, that claims carry a presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. § 282, and that prior art invalidating one claim may not necessarily invalidate another tied claim.

name: Anticipated applicant prosecution and filing-strategy changes
description: If the proposed rule were adopted, applicants would need to approach terminal disclaimers differently and, generally, be more selective about what continuation applications they pursue, if those continuations are more vulnerable under the new rule.
guidance: Applicants may: choose to argue against ODP rejections or amend claims (increasing prosecution cost); pursue single applications with many more claims of different scope to avoid filing continuation applications; or increase filing of divisional applications. The memo notes these strategy shifts would likely raise prosecution costs for applicants.

name: Scope/triggering events for proposed unenforceability (appeals and statutory disclaimers)
description: The proposed unenforceability obligation in a terminal disclaimer is triggered when a tied patent claim has been held unpatentable or invalid under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 or 103 and all appeal rights have been exhausted, or when a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on anticipation or obviousness to that claim has been made.
guidance: This wording limits the proposed effect to final invalidity determinations (appeals exhausted) or to situations where an asserted claim has been statutorily disclaimed after a challenge; it does not state that mere institution of a challenge would trigger unenforceability.

name: Claim-by-claim patentability (no 'invention' or grouped-claims decision)
description: Patentability must be decided on a claim-by-claim basis. Merits decisions of the Board in ex parte appeals must determine the patentability of individual claims, not whether an 'invention' is patentable or a group of claims is patentable.
guidance: Arguments in the Appeal Brief are preferably directed to individual claims. If appellant groups claims as permitted, the Board will pick a single claim to decide the appeal as to that ground of rejection. Failure to separately argue grouped claims can constitute waiver of arguments of separate patentability (see discussion referencing In re McDaniel).

name: Clarification: 'separate' patentability (word addition)
description: Pointing out what a claim recites will not be considered an argument for 'separate' patentability of a claim; the word 'separate' was added to § 41.37(c)(1)(vii) and § 41.67(c)(1)(vii).
guidance: This clarifies that merely pointing out claim recitation is distinct from asserting that a claim is separately patentable on its own merits.

name: Scope of reply brief to a new ground (§ 41.39(b)(2))
description: A reply brief filed in response to a new ground of rejection in accordance with § 41.39(b)(2) only has to address the new ground of rejection.
guidance: Such a reply brief should include, each on a separate page: (1) Identification page; (2) Status of claims page(s); (3) Grounds of rejection to be reviewed on appeal page(s); (4) Argument page(s). Alternatively, a reply brief may be a substitute brief replacing the original brief by responding to both the new ground and all remaining grounds; in that case it must meet all § 41.37(c) requirements.

name: Unity of invention (single general inventive concept) — Rule 13.1
description: Claims must relate to a single general inventive concept; groups of inventions must be so linked as to form a single general inventive concept.
guidance: Determine whether claims share the same or corresponding special technical feature(s) (see Rule 13.2). Analyze the technical features and the problems they solve; if special technical features solve different problems and do not correspond, unity is lacking. Example analyses: identify the special technical feature(s) of each claim and the technical problem(s) they solve to assess technical relationship.

name: Selection of the main invention for search stages
description: The main invention will normally be the invention first mentioned in the claims, but the examiner should exercise discretion where the first-mentioned invention is not searchable or the applicant requests a different selection.
guidance: Examples include when the first-mentioned invention is unclear, excluded from search, or has been shown to be completely anticipated by the main international search; applicant requests to limit supplementary search to an invention other than the first mentioned should be respected (paragraph 10.86).

name: Relevant date for written opinion and international preliminary examination (Rule 64.1)
description: For written opinion and IPER purposes the relevant date is generally the international filing date, except where a valid earlier priority date applies (see Rule 64.1 and paragraph 11.04).
guidance: Where priority is claimed and within the priority period, the filing date of the earlier application may be the relevant date unless the priority claim is invalid. Examiner must consider documents published between claimed priority date and international filing date and may base written opinion on claimed priority date if insufficient time to determine priority validity (see paragraphs 6.17 and 17.29(b)).

name: Documents casting doubt on priority claim
description: Documents showing that a priority claim might not be justified should be mentioned in the ISR and explained in the written opinion.
guidance: No special search is normally made to determine priority validity unless a special reason exists (e.g., continuation-in-part, differing country of residence), but such documents should be reported and, if relevant, may justify some extension of the search (paragraph 11.06).

name: Integration of a natural principle into a practical application (Inquiry 3)
description: A claim that includes a natural principle must include additional claim features that integrate the principle into a patent-eligible practical application; the additional features must do more than merely recite the natural principle plus routine activity.
guidance: Additional limitations cannot merely limit the field of application (e.g., 'for use in catalytic conversion systems') if that still covers every substantial practical application of the principle. Features that are necessary for all practical applications of the principle (so that everyone practicing the principle must perform them) are insufficient. Use of observable and verifiable steps that show how the principle is employed helps narrow the claim. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr (claims integrating Arrhenius equation with machine and steps were eligible) vs. Mayo (claims reciting correlations plus routine steps were ineligible).

name: Machine-or-transformation showing integration
description: Reciting a particular machine or transformation can demonstrate integration of a natural principle by describing how specific parts implement the principle or how a transformation implements it.
guidance: A machine that concretely implements the method (e.g., parts of an internal combustion engine) or a transformation that changes the state or thing (not merely position) supports integration. By contrast, a machine or transformation that is merely nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related (data gathering/storage, incidental apparatus, a computer used only as a weight) does not show integration. Complete absence of such a machine-or-transformation signals a likely disembodied claim directed to a natural principle.

name: Mere statement of a general concept (natural principle) is insufficient
description: Claims that simply state a general concept or law of nature without tangible, specific implementation are directed to the principle itself and are not patent-eligible.
guidance: Tangible implementations with elements or steps recited with specificity (observable and verifiable steps rather than subjective or imperceptible steps) are required to avoid preemption of the principle. A general instruction to 'apply' the principle or to 'gather data' that merely informs an audience of a law of nature will not suffice.

name: Making a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection for claims failing integration (Inquiry 3)
description: When a claim fails Inquiry 3 (i.e., does not integrate a natural principle into a patent-eligible practical application), reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 as not drawn to patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: A proper rejection should: identify the natural principle; identify that the claim is effectively directed to the natural principle; and explain why the additional claim features or their combination, when considered as a whole, fail to integrate the principle into a practical application or fail to ensure the claim is 'significantly more' than the principle itself. Provide factual reasoning and, where possible, cite supporting authority or evidence.

name: Required content of a sample rejection (analysis & conclusion)
description: A rejection should walk through Inquiry 1-3 analysis: whether claim is a statutory category (process/machine/etc.), whether the claim includes a natural principle as a limitation, and whether additional features integrate the principle into a practical application.
guidance: Include an explicit analysis showing which Inquiries pass/fail and why (see sample insulin/insulin-testing claim). Conclude with a clear 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection statement and rationale that the claim covers every substantial practical application of the correlation or principle.

name: Evaluating and responding to 101 rejections (applicant rebuttal guidance)
description: A proper applicant response may amend claims to add steps/features that integrate the natural principle or provide persuasive arguments/evidence that the additional steps add significantly more than merely describing the principle.
guidance: Amendments should practically apply or make use of the principle such that the scope is narrowed beyond the principle plus routine activity. Evidence that the additional steps are not routine, well-known, or conventional can be persuasive (e.g., declarations or publications). Examiner must review amendments, new evidence, and reasoning and recognize/respond to each substantive element of the response.

name: Examination procedure for utility requirement (general steps)
description: Office personnel must: read the claims and supporting description; determine what is claimed and any specific embodiments; ensure claims define statutory subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition); and determine whether a well-established utility is readily apparent.
guidance: If a claimed invention has a well-established utility (one of ordinary skill would immediately appreciate the utility and it is specific, substantial, and credible), do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility. Otherwise, proceed to evaluate asserted utilities for specificity, substantiality, and credibility.

name: When to reject for lack of utility and corresponding 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph rejection
description: If no asserted specific and substantial credible utility is present and no well-established utility is apparent, reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for failure to teach how to use the invention.
guidance: The 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 rejections shift the burden to the applicant to (i) explicitly identify a specific and substantial utility and (ii) provide evidence that one skilled in the art would have recognized that utility as well-established at filing. Ensure an adequate nexus between submitted evidence and the properties of the claimed subject matter as originally disclosed.

name: Burden shift and applicant rebuttal
description: Once examiner makes a proper prima facie showing of lack of specific/substantial/credible utility, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut by amending claims, providing reasoning, or submitting evidence (declarations, patents, printed publications).
guidance: Examiners must review original disclosure, prior evidence, claim amendments, and any new reasoning or evidence submitted. Only maintain the rejection if the totality of the record continues to show lack of specific, substantial, and credible utility.

name: Definition and examples of 'specific utility'
description: Specific utility provides a well-defined and particular benefit to the public, tied to the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Examples of insufficient specificity: claiming a compound 'useful in treating unspecified disorders' or ESTs described only as general 'gene probes' without target. Contrast with disclosing a specific biological activity reasonably correlated to a disease condition — that may be sufficient.

name: Definition and examples of 'substantial utility'
description: Substantial utility denotes an immediate, well-defined, real-world benefit to the public; utilities that require further research to identify or confirm a real-world context are not substantial.
guidance: Examples of non-substantial utilities: (A) basic research on properties, (B) methods for treating unspecified diseases, (C) assays identifying materials that themselves lack specific/substantial utility, (D) methods of making a material that has no specific/substantial/credible utility, (E) claims to intermediate products used to make a final product that lacks specific/substantial utility.

name: Research tools and intermediate products — not per se excluded from utility
description: Inventions used in research settings (research tools, assays, instruments) can have specific and substantial utility if their disclosed use provides an immediate benefit; labels like 'research tool' are not determinative.
guidance: Distinguish inventions that identify a specific substantial utility in current form from those whose asserted utility requires further research. Examiner should focus on whether a claimed invention has a specific and substantial utility, not on the setting in which it will be used.

name: Rule 12(b)(6) pleading standard
description: When considering a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, the court must accept as true all factual allegations in the complaint and view them in the light most favorable to the plaintiff; dismissal is appropriate only if the complaint does not contain sufficient factual matter to state a claim plausible on its face (Iqbal/Twombly).
guidance: Court need not accept as true allegations that contradict matters properly subject to judicial notice or exhibits, such as the claims and patent specification (Secured Mail Solutions). Patent eligibility can be resolved at the pleading stage when no factual allegations prevent resolving the eligibility question as a matter of law (Aatrix Software).

name: Characterizing the claim 'directed to' focus
description: The court should identify whether the claim is truly focused on an abstract idea (or other ineligible matter) by reference to the claim language; the specification may help but must yield to the claim language in identifying the focus.
guidance: The claim language defines the breadth of the claim and thus the preemption concern; reliance on the specification cannot override what the claims actually claim (ChargePoint; Alice; Graver Tank).

name: Preemption concern as the basis for exceptions
description: The judicial exceptions to patentability are driven by the concern of preemption—preventing patenting that would monopolize basic tools of scientific and technological work.
guidance: Courts assess whether the claim would preempt all applications of the underlying idea; broad claims that effectively cover an entire field are problematic (Alice; Mayo; ChargePoint).

name: Conventional components do not supply inventive concept
description: Claims that merely add conventional elements or generic physical limitations (e.g., 'upper layer,' 'lower layer,' conventional processors) to an abstract idea fail to supply an inventive concept.
guidance: If the specification describes components as 'conventional' or 'generally available,' that supports a finding that the claim elements are routine and not inventive (numerous specification citations; TLI; Ariosa; Mayo).

name: Physical/apparatus claims can still be abstract
description: Claims to physical devices are not immune from §101 scrutiny; a claim reciting concrete, tangible components can nonetheless be directed to an abstract idea if those components merely provide a generic environment for the abstract idea.
guidance: Examples include apparatus claims found abstract where physical limitations simply describe a conventional environment (ChargePoint; TLI). Courts look to whether the asserted improvement is a specific technical improvement or merely the abstract idea implemented in a physical setting.

name: Enfish distinction (improvement vs. abstract idea)
description: A relevant inquiry is whether the claims are directed to an improvement in technology/functionality (which may be patent eligible) versus being directed to an abstract idea implemented with conventional components.
guidance: If a claim outlines a specific asserted improvement to computer (or other) functionality it may not be abstract (Enfish). By contrast, merely applying a sensor at the nanoscale without a technical improvement is not an 'Enfish' style inventive focus.

name: Claim construction not always required for §101
description: Claim construction is not an inviolable prerequisite to a §101 determination when eligibility is apparent from the face of the patent and complaint.
guidance: Genetic Technologies and other Federal Circuit authority permit §101 rulings without full claim construction where resolution can be made as a matter of law.

name: Specification can confirm conventionality
description: Statements in the specification that components or fabrication are 'conventional' or 'well-known' support the conclusion that claim elements are routine and do not supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Courts will point to specification language describing self-assembled monolayers, field-effect transistors, conventional semiconductor processes, conventional driver circuits, or conventional readout methods as evidence that the claimed elements are not inventive.

name: Futility of amendment / leave to amend standard
description: If the specification and claims make clear that the asserted claims are directed to an abstract idea and recite only conventional components, the plaintiff cannot amend to state a valid §101 claim and leave to amend may be denied as futile.
guidance: When the patent itself forecloses any non-abstract formulation of the claims, amendment is futile (citing Shane v. Fauver and the court's reasoning here).

name: Withdraw when USPTO determines former client's publication is material prior art
description: A practitioner must withdraw from representation where continued representation would violate the Rules — for instance, after the examiner determines that a former client's published application is material prior art to the new client's claims, the practitioner must withdraw if continuing would cause a Rules violation.
guidance: Failure to withdraw under those circumstances (here, continued prosecution of application C after the examiner deemed Company 1's publication material) was cited as a violation of § 11.116(a)(1).

name: Availability — Unpublished abandoned applications identified or relied upon (§ 1.14(a)(1)(iv))
description: The file contents of an unpublished, abandoned application may be made available to the public if the application is identified in a U.S. patent, statutory invention registration, U.S. patent application publication, an international publication of a PCT application under Article 21(2), or a publication of an international registration under Hague Agreement Article 10(3). A copy may also be made available if benefit of the abandoned application is claimed under specified statutes in an application that has issued or published. Copies provided upon written request and payment of the appropriate fee (§ 1.19(b)).
guidance: Identification requires providing specific application-identifying information (application number/serial number and filing date; first named inventor; title; filing date or other application-specific info) in the text of the identifying document; mere inclusion in a file paper is insufficient.

name: Access by participating foreign intellectual property offices (§ 1.14(h)(1)-(3))
description: Access to an application-as-filed may be provided to any foreign IP office participating in a bilateral or multilateral priority document exchange agreement if the application contains written authority granting such access. Written authority authorizes the Office to provide (i) a copy of the application-as-filed and its related bibliographic data; (ii) a copy of the application-as-filed of any application whose filing date is claimed by the application and its bibliographic data; and (iii) the date of filing of the written authorization under this paragraph.
guidance: Access is limited to participating foreign IP offices and requires written authority; the scope of provided materials is defined in subparagraphs.

name: Additional fee for DOCX nonconformity (§ 1.16(u))
description: Additional fee for any application filed on or after January 17, 2024 under 35 U.S.C. 111 for an original patent, except design, plant, or provisional applications, where the specification, claims, and/or abstract does not conform to the USPTO requirements for submission in DOCX format: By a micro entity $86.00; By a small entity $172.00; By other than a small or micro entity $430.00.
guidance: Fee applies when submission format requirements (DOCX) are not met; added to encourage conformity to electronic format standards.

name: Statutory baseline for patent eligibility (§101 and implicit exceptions)
description: Section 101 defines patent-eligible subject matter as any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any improvement thereof; the Supreme Court has explained there are 'implicit' exceptions: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas.
guidance: Use this statutory baseline as the starting point for inquiry; the Alice/Mayo framework is applied to determine whether a claim falls within an implicit exception.

name: Alice step one — determine whether claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept
description: At step one, 'determine whether the claims at issue are directed to one of those patent-ineligible concepts' (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas).
guidance: Focus on the 'focus' of the claim as written; consider the claim in light of the specification but do not import limitations from the specification into the claim language. Examples of ineligible focuses include abstract ideas such as data manipulation, mental processes, and longstanding human activities implemented on a computer.

name: Claims that merely organize, alter, or manipulate data are likely abstract
description: Claims that organize, alter, or manipulate data, without more, are patent ineligible (collecting precedents: Broadband iTV; Intell. Ventures; Elec. Power Grp.; Digitech).
guidance: If a claim primarily recites receiving, analyzing, storing, transforming, or displaying data—especially using generic computing components—and does not explain a technical way the improvement is achieved, treat it as directed to an abstract idea.

name: Functional/results-oriented claim language without details is insufficient
description: Claims framed entirely in functional, results-oriented terms (describing what is accomplished rather than how) are suspect and may be treated as abstract; the district court characterized the claims as 'functional and ends-oriented.'
guidance: Claims that merely recite high-level steps such as 'determining', 'acquiring', and 'adjusting' without describing how those steps are performed or what specific technical rules/operations accomplish them are vulnerable at step one and step two.

name: Claims must explain how the arrangement achieves a technological improvement
description: Merely using new data or parameters does not render a claim patent eligible unless the claims (not just the specification) 'explain how these arrangements actually result in the claimed improvement.'
guidance: To survive §101, claims should recite specific rules, algorithms, or constrained steps showing how the claimed elements produce a technological improvement (cf. McRo: claims 'limited to rules with specific characteristics'). General statements of improved result are not enough.

name: Do not import specification details into claim language during the §101 focus
description: While the claims are considered in light of the specification, courts 'avoid importing concepts from the specification into the claims' and the §101 inquiry must focus on the language of the asserted claims themselves.
guidance: When arguing patent eligibility, ensure the claim text itself embodies the claimed technical detail; relying solely on detailed disclosure in the specification (without claim language support) is improper to escape abstraction.

name: Alice step two — inventive concept (transforming claim into patent-eligible application)
description: At step two, 'consider the elements of each claim both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application.'
guidance: Look for an inventive concept beyond the abstract idea—e.g., non-generic computer implementation, concrete technical improvements, or specific rules/algorithms. Mere recitation of applying correction conditions or parameters without more will not qualify as an inventive concept (citing Broadband, BSG Tech).

name: Use of generic computers or using computers 'as a tool' does not supply an inventive concept
description: Claims that merely use generic computing components or 'merely use computers as a tool' to implement an abstract idea do not supply an inventive concept.
guidance: If the only novel aspect is automating a human activity using a conventional computer, the claim will likely fail §101 unless it recites specific computer improvements or unconventional configurations.

name: Representative-claim treatment is acceptable when claims are substantially similar
description: A court may treat a single claim as representative and dismiss all claims if the others are 'substantially similar and linked to the same abstract idea' (Content Extraction & Transmission).
guidance: When claims differ only by trivial variations (e.g., different labels for the same data types or slight refinements of the same functional steps), a representative-claim analysis is permissible; however, materially different claims require separate consideration.

name: Absence of inventive concept can be resolved from intrinsic record; factual disputes necessary only when present
description: The absence of an inventive concept does not necessarily entail subsidiary factual determinations; 'a patent itself may establish that the claims contain no inventive concept' (Berkheimer acknowledged).
guidance: If the claim language and specification on their face show no inventive concept, §101 can be decided as a matter of law. If the patentee points to genuine factual disputes about what the specification or claim elements mean, Berkheimer may require further factfinding.

name: Recitation of parameters without explaining what they are or how to manipulate them is inadequate
description: Reciting 'parameters' or 'correction conditions' without describing what those parameters are or how they should be manipulated does not turn an abstract data-manipulation concept into a patent-eligible invention (citing Hawk).
guidance: Claims should define the nature of parameters, their computation, mappings, or algorithms for manipulation; vague references to parameters or properties leave claims vulnerable under §101.

name: Reads On
description: A patent claim 'reads on' a device or method when each required part (requirement) of the claim is found in the device or method.
guidance: Terminology used when comparing accused products/methods to claim requirements to determine literal infringement.

name: Requirement (limitation) definition
description: A required part or step of an invention set forth in a patent claim; often used interchangeably with 'limitation.'
guidance: Clarifies vocabulary used throughout the instructions when referencing claim elements/limitations.

name: Royalty definition
description: A payment made to the owner of a patent by a nonowner in exchange for rights to make, use, or sell the claimed invention.
guidance: Glossary term relevant to damages instructions (appears elsewhere in the instructions).

name: Specification definition
description: A required part of a patent application and an issued patent; a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using the claimed invention.
guidance: Specifies the document that supports claims and discloses structure (important for means-plus-function analysis, written description/enablement issues).

name: Patent At Issue — court should show jury patent materials
description: The court should show the jury the specification, drawings and claims including the claims at issue.
guidance: Practical instruction to help jurors follow the evidence by making the patent documents available during trial.

name: Summary of Contentions — jury's role and issues
description: The court provides a summary of each party's positions; the jury must decide whether asserted claims have been infringed and whether those claims are invalid, and, if infringement and validity are found, determine money damages and willfulness.
guidance: Frames the central factual and legal questions for jurors and clarifies that invalidity is a defense to infringement; includes admonition to keep an open mind and that willfulness is a separate finding that should not affect the damage award directly.

name: Direct infringement — two-step process and claim-by-claim analysis
description: Deciding direct infringement involves (1) determining the meaning of the patent claim (claim construction) and (2) deciding whether the accused party has made, used, sold, offered for sale, or imported a product or method covered by a claim; each asserted claim must be considered individually.
guidance: Exception: dependent claims include all requirements of their independent claim plus additional requirements (if independent not infringed, dependent cannot be infringed; if independent infringed, still evaluate dependent's additional requirements). Jurors must compare the accused product to the claims, not to plaintiff's commercial product.

name: Literal infringement — every claim requirement present
description: A product or method literally infringes a claim if every requirement (limitation) of that claim is included in the product or method; if any requirement is missing, there is no literal infringement.
guidance: Explains claim transition language: 'comprising' = open claim (extras allowed); 'consisting of' = closed (no other parts/steps allowed); 'consisting essentially of' = partially closed (extras allowed unless they materially affect basic and novel properties). Also explains that missing claim elements supplied by others do not establish liability unless the accused directed or controlled the other party (direction/control test); system claims may allow liability when parts operate in different places or times (Centillion).

name: Rule against comparing accused product to plaintiff's commercial product
description: In deciding infringement, the jury may not compare the alleged infringer’s accused product or method to the patent holder’s commercial product or method; instead, the jury must compare the accused product or method to the claims of the patent.
guidance: Ensures jurors focus on claim language as the boundary of protection rather than comparisons between competing products.

name: Doctrine of Equivalents — equivalence test
description: If there is no literal infringement, the jury must decide whether the accused product/method infringes under the doctrine of equivalents by determining whether the accused parts/steps are identical or equivalent to the claim requirements.
guidance: A part/step is equivalent if persons of ordinary skill would think the differences were not substantial at the time of alleged infringement; one way to evaluate is the function-way-result test (performed substantially same function, in substantially same way, to achieve substantially same result). Known interchangeability at time of infringement may support equivalence but is not required. Doctrine cannot be used to cover subject matter that was in the prior art or would have been obvious, nor to recapture subject matter described but not claimed in the patent. Authorities: Warner-Jenkinson, Graver Tank, Festo, etc.

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents (prior art and described-but-not-claimed)
description: The doctrine of equivalents cannot be used to find infringement if the subject matter alleged to be equivalent was in the prior art or would have been obvious, or if it was described in the patent but not claimed (unless sufficiently specific that one of ordinary skill would understand it was present).
guidance: If accused product is shown to be in the prior art, burden shifts to the patent holder to prove the asserted equivalents were not in the prior art or would not have been obvious. Cites Festo and related cases regarding limits.

name: Means-Plus-Function claims — scope and literal infringement
description: A means-plus-function requirement covers only the specific structure disclosed in the patent specification for performing the claimed function and the equivalents of those specific structures, not all possible structures that could perform the function.
guidance: The court will identify the corresponding structure in the specification; to prove infringement the jury must find the accused product has structure that performs the claimed function (or equivalents). Example: 'means for processing data' is limited to structures disclosed in the spec and equivalents, not every possible data processing means.

name: Judge's claim interpretations do not indicate views on infringement/invalidity
description: The judge's interpretation of claim language should not be taken as an indication that the judge has a view regarding issues such as infringement and invalidity; those issues remain for the jury to decide.
guidance: To be read if claim constructions are handed out to jurors; reinforces neutrality of claim construction.

name: Technical Necessity
description: The patented invention must be required to implement mandatory portions of the standard. Optional features or alternative implementations generally don’t create essentiality.
guidance: Determine essentiality by verifying that practicing the standard necessarily infringes the claim limitations; optional features and alternative implementations typically do not create essentiality. This is a technical determination tied to mandatory portions of the spec.

name: Claim-Level Analysis
description: Essentiality exists at the claim level, not the patent level. Individual patents may contain both essential and non-essential claims.
guidance: Analyze each claim independently against the standard. Do not assume whole-patent essentiality; map each claim element to the standard to determine which claims (if any) are essential.

name: Conduct Pre-Contribution Patent Searches
description: Before proposing technical solutions to standards bodies, comprehensive prior art search helps identify existing inventions that might limit patentability or create essentiality conflicts.
guidance: Perform thorough prior art and patent landscape searches prior to submitting proposals to SDOs to reduce risk of later conflicts and to plan claim drafting around known art.

name: Conduct Independent Essentiality Analysis (for implementers and owners)
description: Never assume declared patents are actually essential. Systematic evaluation using specialized tools identifies over-declared patents and reduces royalty exposure.
guidance: Undertake claim-to-standard mapping, claim construction, and specification analysis using independent experts and tools (including AI-assisted tools) to quantify which declared claims truly read on implemented standards. Note statistic: only ~35–45% of declared SEPs typically withstand independent technical analysis.

name: Maintain Detailed Standardization Records
description: Document all standards contributions, including technical proposals, meeting minutes, and email correspondence. These records prove crucial in establishing contribution value during licensing negotiations or litigation.
guidance: Keep organized archives of all standardization activities and communications to support claims of inventive contribution, chronology, and intent; use these records in essentiality and valuation analyses.

name: Claim Construction and Claim-to-Standard Mapping (analysis process)
description: Essentiality checks begin with claim construction, followed by detailed standard specification analysis and systematic claim-to-standard mapping to determine whether each claim element is practiced by the standard.
guidance: Follow a rigorous, documented workflow: (1) legal claim construction, (2) identification of mandatory vs optional spec language, (3) element-by-element mapping of claim limitations to the standard, and (4) flagging claims for further technical expert review. This is the core analytical sequence for independent essentiality verification.

name: Use of AI in Essentiality Analysis
description: AI-powered NLP systems can analyze thousands of patent claims against voluminous standard specifications, identifying potential matches based on semantic understanding rather than simple keyword overlap.
guidance: Leverage AI tools to prioritize candidate claims for human review, recognize synonymous technical terms, and accelerate claim-to-standard mapping. Use AI outputs as triage and evidence-support tools, followed by domain-expert validation.

name: Claim-by-claim explanation of proposed combinations
description: The request must explain how each of the proposed combinations specifically applies to each claim that it is asserted against (i.e., claim-by-claim), explaining how each document (reference) identified for the combination is used.
guidance: Ideally provide an appropriately detailed claim chart that compares, limitation by limitation, each claim for which reexamination is requested with the relevant teachings of each reference cited in the request. See sample request in MPEP § 2214. Any failure to provide the required explanation for any document, combination, or claim will be identified in a Notice of Failure to Comply.

name: Basis for combining references for obviousness rejections
description: For proposed obviousness rejections, the requester must provide at least one basis for combining the cited references and a statement of why the claim(s) under reexamination would have been obvious over the proposed reference combination.
guidance: Preferably quote the pertinent teachings in the references, referencing each quote by page, column and line number and any relevant figure numbers. The explanation must not lump together proposed rejections or proposed combinations of references. Examples of appropriate and inappropriate language are provided to illustrate specificity (e.g., avoid 'Smith and/or Charles' or 'either Jones and Cooper or Harvey and Cooper'; use specific combinations tied to specific claims).

name: Avoid lumped/alternative language when asserting rejections
description: Do not use language that lumps together multiple possible rejections or ambiguous alternative combinations when asserting unpatentability.
guidance: Examples of inappropriate language include statements like 'anticipated by, or in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over the Smith reference' or 'Smith and/or Charles'. Appropriate language spells out the exact rejection and exact combination for a specific claim (e.g., 'Claim 2 is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over Smith in view of Jones').

name: Include a copy of the printed patent in the request
description: Requesters are required under 37 CFR 1.510(b)(4) to include a copy of the patent for which reexamination is requested to serve as the specification for the reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Provide a full copy of the printed patent (including front page) in double-column format so it can be used for the abstract, drawings, specification, and claims. Also include any disclaimer, certificate of correction, reexamination certificate, and copies of relevant Federal Court decisions, complaints, or interference decisions so the Office has a complete history.

name: Patent owner may include proposed amendments with request
description: Under 37 CFR 1.510(e), a patent owner may include a proposed amendment with his or her request, but any such amendment must comply with 37 CFR 1.530(d) through (j).
guidance: If an amendment adds claims, excess claims fees under 37 CFR 1.20(c)(3) and (c)(4) may apply. The request should be decided on the wording of the patent claims in effect at the time (without any proposed amendments); if reexamination is granted, subsequent prosecution is on the basis of claims as amended.

name: Reissue application must contain entire printed patent specification and claims (formatting)
description: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.173(a)(1) the application specification, including the claims, of the patent for which reissue is requested must be furnished in the form of a copy of the printed patent, in double column format, each page on only one side of a single sheet of paper. No new matter shall be introduced into the application.
guidance: Each page of the patent must appear on only one side of each individual page of the specification of the reissue application; a two-sided copy is not proper. If changes are so extensive that reading is extremely difficult and error-prone, a clean copy of the specification may be submitted if accompanied by a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.183 for waiver of 37 CFR 1.125(d) and 1.173(a)(1).

name: Amendment of claims at filing must include status and support
description: An amendment of the claims made at the time of filing of a reissue application must include a separate paper setting forth the status of all claims (i.e., pending or canceled), and an explanation of the support in the disclosure of the patent for the changes made to the claims.
guidance: Amendments at filing must comply with 37 CFR 1.173(b)-(e) and (g); see MPEP § 1453 for further guidance.

name: Include certificate of correction or disclaimer changes without markings
description: The applicant should include any changes, additions, or deletions that were made by a certificate of correction to the original patent grant in the reissue application without underlining or bracketing. Certificate of correction changes and disclaimer of claim(s) under 37 CFR 1.321(a) should be made without using underlining or brackets.
guidance: Because these are retroactively part of the original patent, they must appear in the printed reissue patent document as part of the original patent (not in italics or bracketed). If improperly submitted with underlining and brackets, the examiner will require correction — possibly requiring a replacement paragraph or a clean copy entered as a substitute specification with a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.183 for waiver of 1.125(d) and 1.173(a)(1).

name: New matter prohibited in reissue applications (35 U.S.C. 251)
description: New matter, i.e., matter not present in the patent sought to be reissued, is excluded from a reissue application in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 251. The claims in the reissue application must be for subject matter which the applicant had the right to claim in the original patent.
guidance: New matter may exist by omission of a feature or step in a method. If new matter has been added anywhere in the application for reissue, form paragraph 14.22.01 may be used. If the new matter is added to the claims or affects the claims, consider also a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. If new matter is added to the specification and does not affect the claims, consider an objection under 35 U.S.C. 132 using form paragraph 7.28. See MPEP §§ 2161-2163, 2166, and § 608.04(a) for guidance.

name: Form paragraph 14.22.01 for rejection under 35 U.S.C. 251 for new matter
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 251 as being based upon new matter added to the patent for which reissue is sought. The added material which is not supported by the prior patent is as follows: [2].
guidance: In bracket 2, fill in the applicable page and line numbers and provide an explanation of the position as appropriate. Consider also 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejections if the new matter affects claims.

name: Original patent requirement — same general invention (35 U.S.C. 251)
description: The reissue claims must be for the same invention as that disclosed as being the invention in the original patent. The entire disclosure, not just the claims, is considered in determining what the patentee objectively intended as the invention.
guidance: Case law (e.g., In re Amos, Antares Pharma, Forum US v. Flow Valve) establishes that the specification must clearly and unequivocally disclose the newly claimed invention as a separate invention if that is what is sought. Reissue claims may be rejected under § 251 if the original specification does not demonstrate to one skilled in the art that the patentee could have claimed the subject matter.

name: Examination checklist for original patent requirement (A–C)
description: Examiners should review whether (A) the claims presented are described in and enabled by the original patent specification such that 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph is satisfied; (B) nothing in the original patent specification indicates an intent not to claim the subject matter presented in the reissue application; and (C) the newly claimed invention is clearly and unequivocally disclosed in the specification as a separate invention with the claimed combination of features.
guidance: Examiners should discuss any possible rejection under 35 U.S.C. 251 based on failure to meet the original patent requirement with their TQAS or SPRS.

name: Overlooked aspects — claims to disclosed but never claimed embodiments
description: Claims to separate inventions/embodiments/species that were disclosed but never covered by the claims in the original prosecution are considered 'overlooked aspects' and are not subject to recapture because they were never surrendered.
guidance: To determine whether reissue claims are drawn to overlooked aspects, examiner must first determine if the claim meets the original patent requirement. If claims are drawn to overlooked aspects, the examiner should state which claims are drawn to overlooked aspects on the record. See examples and case law (e.g., Youman, Hester, Meyers) for application.

name: Recapture prohibition — cannot reclaim surrendered subject matter
description: A reissue will not be granted to 'recapture' claimed subject matter which was surrendered in an application to obtain the original patent. Whether a reissue patent violates the rule against recapture of surrendered subject matter in original prosecution is a question of law (see cited case law).
guidance: Claims to overlooked aspects are not part of recapture analysis. Examiner must perform recapture analysis when presented with broadened reissue claims and consider definitions and precedent (see MPEP § 1412.02 and cited Federal Circuit cases).

name: Definitions relevant to recapture analysis
description: Definitions: Broadening Claim — a reissue claim is 'broadened' where at least one limitation of the patent claims is either completely eliminated or is only presented in a broader way in the reissue claim relative to the broadest patented claim(s). Canceled Claim — a claim canceled from the original application to obtain the patent (including claims replaced by narrower claims). Original Application — includes the prosecution record of the application that issued as the patent and the patent family’s entire prosecution history.
guidance: These definitions inform whether a reissue claim is a broadened claim and whether recapture applies. Surrender may occur because of prosecution history of related applications; examine family history where relevant (see MBO Laboratories, In re McDonald).

name: Complete specification requirements (form and timing)
description: The complete specification must commence with the title, end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed, and must be left with the application (or within the permitted period, typically nine months).
guidance: Complete specifications are referred to examiners, may be required to be amended by the Comptroller, and if not left within due time the application may be deemed abandoned. The complete must be substantially the same as the provisional; developments within scope allowed but not material additions beyond the provisional.

name: Good faith and full disclosure
description: Good faith must be observed in the specification; full disclosure of the invention is required.
guidance: Patentee should fully disclose what he claims to have invented. Where invention was partly communicated from abroad, that should be distinguished. Failure to disclose (or misrepresentation) can be ground for revocation.

name: Claims — presence, clarity, and scope
description: Specifications must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed (claims). Claims should show clearly what is intended to be claimed; everything not claimed is impliedly disclaimed.
guidance: Claims are not intended to aid the description. If all parts are old, only the combination should be claimed; new parts and minor combinations must be expressly claimed. Claims must not cover too much; vague or speculative claims are to be avoided; a large number of claims is dangerous.

name: Interpretation / construction of specification and claims
description: Rules govern the construction of the specification and the interpretation of the claims — how courts and examiners construe the language.
guidance: Construction looks to description, title, and claims together; principles for claim construction and limits on interpretation are drawn from case law and statutory framework.

name: Infringement doctrines and scope of infringement
description: Standards for what constitutes infringement: e.g., where the principle is not new, invention of improvements is not a defence, combinations, chemical processes and products, dealing in articles made by infringing a patent, user infringement, liability of agents/carriers/foreign vessels/the Crown, and cases of non-infringement.
guidance: Intention of the infringer is not material. The manual explains tests for infringement, including construction of claims, equivalents, indirect infringement (dealing in), and special rules for chemical inventions and processes; many case examples illustrate these principles.

name: Entire diligence period must be accounted for by affirmative acts or acceptable excuses
description: The patentee must account for the entire period during which diligence is required by showing reasonably continuous diligence through affirmative acts or acceptable excuses; mere statements are insufficient and short unexplained lapses can be fatal.
guidance: Reasonably continuous (not necessarily continuous) diligence is required (Perfect Surgical Techniques v. Olympus). Unexplained inactivity (even 2 days in some cases) can defeat diligence claims (In re Mulder; Fitzgerald v. Arbib; In re Mulder). Evidence must be specific with dates/facts. Some excuses (vacation, illness) may be considered; lack of funding or personnel often are not acceptable (Griffith v. Kanamaru; Litchfield v. Eigen).

name: Work relied upon must be directly related to the reduction to practice
description: Activities used to show reasonable diligence must be directly related to reducing the specific subject matter of the count to practice; work on related inventions may sometimes be relied upon but only if it is sufficiently directed to attaining reduction of the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Cases: Naber v. Cricchi; Scott v. Koyama; In re Jolley; Ginos v. Nedelec (closely related inventions may be credited in some circumstances); Gunn v. Bosch (work on different inventions that merely fortuitously produce the actual reduction is not diligence). Preparation of foreign filings and related activities can count (Broos v. Barton; De Solms v. Schoenwald).

name: Pre‑AIA regime applicability (timing rule)
description: Any application filed before March 16, 2013 is governed by pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103; certain applications filed on or after March 16, 2013 that claim benefit to an earlier filing date may also be governed by pre‑AIA 102.
guidance: Requests for continued examination or national stage entry do not constitute filing of a new application; see MPEP §§2159 and 2150 et seq. for applicability determinations.

name: Effective filing date rules under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102
description: The effective filing date is normally the actual U.S. filing date unless: (A) the application is a continuation/divisional with 35 U.S.C. 120 satisfied (earliest date in chain), (B) a continuation‑in‑part—claims not supported by parent have the new filing date while fully supported claims have the parent's date, or (C) proper claim to 35 U.S.C. 119(e) provisional (claims fully supported by provisional have provisional filing date).
guidance: The effective filing date for an application that entered the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371 is the international filing date; the foreign priority document filing date itself is not the effective filing date for pre‑AIA 102 claims (though it may overcome certain references). See MPEP §§1893.03, 211.01(c), 1895.

name: When an international filing date counts as a U.S. filing date for 102(e)
description: An international filing date is a United States filing date for 35 U.S.C. 102(e) if the international application (1) was filed on or after November 29, 2000, (2) designated the United States, and (3) was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in the English language.
guidance: If all three conditions are met, the prior art date of a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) may be the international filing date or an earlier U.S. filing date for which priority or benefit is properly claimed. Publication under PCT Art. 21(2) may result from a request for early publication or after 18 months from the earliest claimed filing date.

name: General ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by: (A) Persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) Amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; or (C) Perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 within the applicable time periods by amending the specification or filing an application data sheet and establishing that the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph.
guidance: Follow the timing rules in 37 CFR 1.78(a) and MPEP §201.11 and §706.02. Priority/benefit perfection requires demonstrating enablement and written description support in the priority application.

name: General ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by: (A) Persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable; (B) Amending the claims; (C) Filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 that the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) Filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing prior invention if the reference is not a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claiming the same patentable invention; (E) Perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.55(a)(1); or (F) Perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 within the time periods in 37 CFR 1.78(a).
guidance: 37 CFR 1.131 is not acceptable if the claims of the reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication and the application are directed to the same invention or are obvious variants. In such cases consider double patenting rejections or interference procedures (MPEP §804 or Chapter 2300). Establish enablement and written description for any perfected priority claim per 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

name: 706.02(f)(1) Step (B): Reference resulting from or claiming benefit of an international application
description: Determine if the potential reference resulted from, or claimed the benefit of, an international application. If it did not, its 102(e) date is its earliest effective U.S. filing date, taking into account any proper benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120.
guidance: When the reference did not result from or claim benefit of an IA, consider any proper earlier U.S. benefit claims that would shift the earliest effective U.S. filing date for 102(e) purposes.

name: Examples illustrating determination of 102(e) prior art dates
description: Nine illustrative examples (Examples 1–9) show common factual situations for determining 35 U.S.C. 102(e) dates for references, covering 111(a) applications with and without priority/benefit claims, 111(a) with foreign priority claims, and various international application scenarios.
guidance: Use the examples to determine whether a reference’s 102(e)(1) (publication) or 102(e)(2) (patent) date is an international filing date, an earlier U.S. filing date, a later U.S. filing date, none, or the date of fulfillment of 371(c) requirements depending on the facts (e.g., filing dates, language of WIPO publication, designation of U.S.).

name: Automatic 30‑month stay of FDA approval upon timely suit
description: FDA approval to market the generic drug is automatically postponed for 30 months if the patent holder files suit within 45 days of ANDA notification, unless the patent expires or is judged to be invalid or not infringed before that time.
guidance: The 30‑month stay provides the patent holder time to litigate its infringement/validity claims in court before generic market entry; it can be shortened if the court decides the patent is invalid/not infringed or if the patent term expires during the stay.

name: PPH (Patent Prosecution Highway) — overview
description: The Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) accelerates examination of corresponding patent applications filed in participating IP offices. If at least one claim is found allowable by a first office, the applicant can request fast-track examination in a second office.
guidance: By leveraging existing expedited procedures, PPH enables quicker and more efficient patent decisions—at no additional cost. PPH is useful when there is at least one allowed claim in an Office of Earlier Examination (OEE) that can be used to request accelerated examination in the U.S. or another participating office.

name: Track One eligibility and filing requirements
description: Application must include a specification with no multiple-dependent claims, max 4 independent claims, and no more than 30 total claims. Include any required drawings. Must be filed via USPTO’s electronic filing system (EFS-Web or Patent Center).
guidance: These claim-count and formatting limits are preconditions for Track One prioritized examination; applications exceeding the limits may incur fees or be ineligible. Ensure required drawings are included and file through USPTO's accepted electronic systems to satisfy procedural requirements.

name: Track One fees and applicable additional fees
description: The fees required to be paid on a utility patent application upon filing a request for prioritized examination of that application are: Basic filing fee, Search fee, Examination fee, Publication fee, Prioritized examination processing fee, Prioritized examination fee.
guidance: The article lists the applicable statutory/regulatory fee citations (e.g., 37 CFR 1.16(a) basic filing fee; 1.16(k) search fee; 1.16(o) examination fee; 1.18(d) publication fee; 1.17(i) processing fee; 1.17(c) prioritized examination fee). Additional applicable fees may include: application size fee (37 CFR 1.16(s)) if specification and drawings exceed 100 sheets; excess independent claim fee (37 CFR 1.16(h)) if independent claims exceed three; excess claim fee (37 CFR 1.16(i)) if total claims exceed twenty; and, if requesting prioritized examination for an RCE, the RCE fee (37 CFR 1.17(e)). Confirm current fee amounts and rule citations on the USPTO fee schedule before filing.

name: Comparative tradeoffs when choosing between PPH and Track One
description: While both aim to accelerate examination, they differ in eligibility, cost, and process: PPH speeds up patent examination by using fast-track procedures across participating offices at no extra fee; Track One offers prioritized examination within 12 months for a fee, with fewer requirements than accelerated examination and no pre-examination search.
guidance: Consider eligibility (do you have an allowed claim in an OEE?), cost (PPH generally has no extra fee; Track One requires multiple fees), timing (Track One targets a final decision within 12 months), and prosecution strategy. The article cautions that Track One may pressure examiners to limit claims or reject applications quickly, whereas PPH leverages the examiner’s prior knowledge/allowance to support smoother prosecution. Choose based on whether fee-based speed or leveraging prior allowance and potentially smoother prosecution better fits your objectives.

name: Combination patents — use of different or fewer elements
description: For combination patents, use of different elements, fewer elements, a different grouping, or elements selected from several combinations is generally not an infringement of the claimed combination.
guidance: Substitution of newly discovered elements, adding elements, or using elements for new purposes raises nuanced questions; mere suggestion by the patented combination does not make a different combination an infringement.

name: Use of unclaimed elements and sub-combinations
description: Use of unclaimed elements or sub-combinations is not necessarily infringement; infringement is more likely where any claimed element is used or where an element invented by the patentee is used contrary to the claims.
guidance: Whether use of an unclaimed element infringes depends on claim scope and whether the element is a material part of the claimed invention.

name: Single-element patents and combination use
description: A patent on an element may be infringed by its use in a combination; conversely, a patent to a combination may give rise to infringement claims against makers of an element when intended for use in the patented combination.
guidance: Determination focuses on the role of the element in producing the claimed result and intent to induce combination.

name: Product-of-infringing-process rule limits
description: Use of a product made by an infringing art is not always itself infringement of the art patent (distinctions exist between product, process, and manufacture patents).
guidance: Whether use or sale of a product made by an infringing process infringes depends on the type of patent (art, machine, manufacture, composition, design) and claim scope.

name: Assignment and transfer of rights
description: Rights of action for infringement are assignable with the patent but require distinct words of conveyance; assignments can transfer claims including those of expired patents depending on wording and context.
guidance: Formal conveyancing language is required to transfer infringement causes of action; nuances exist for expired patents and transferred suits.

name: Interference proceedings purpose and scope
