description: Interferences in the Patent Office are contests over priority between pending applications or between pending applications and unexpired patents; priority is the sole question and proceedings deal with applications rather than applicants.
guidance: Interferences are instituted only where claims conflict (identical, equivalent, or one embracing another) and are governed by rules different from court litigation.

name: Interference procedure and preliminary statements
description: Interference proceedings require preliminary statements, notices to rival claimants, completion of specifications when conflict discovered, filing and amendment rules, and allowance for inspection of files and conflicting specifications.
guidance: Preliminary statements have formal requisites; failure to file can have serious effects (judgment for failure); amendments and disclaimers are treated specially.

name: Identity and equivalence in invention and claims
description: Identity and equivalence are assessed by identity of force, object, and mode of application; equivalence exists when the same means produce the same effect; whether inventions are identical or diverse is a fact question and claims govern determination.
guidance: Specific versus generic differences, differences in form, materials, arrangement, or use, and whether one embodiment can substitute for another are analyzed; claims control scope and equivalence analysis.

name: Termination of proceedings and abandonment when no claims allowed (37 CFR 1.197(c))
description: Proceedings are considered terminated by dismissal of an appeal or failure to timely file an appeal to the court or a civil action, except where claims stand allowed or further action by the examiner is required; if no claims stand allowed the application is abandoned.
guidance: The date of termination is the date the appeal is dismissed or the time for court action expires. The time for seeking review by the Federal Circuit or District of Columbia is the same (2 months) and when that time has passed without review, the examiner must take up the application. If proceedings terminate and no claims are allowed, stamp abandoned and send to abandoned files.

name: Treatment of dependent claims when parent claim rejected
description: If an independent claim is affirmed/rejected and dependent claims were objected to as allowable except for dependency, the examiner should either (1) convert the dependent claim into independent form by examiner's amendment, cancel all claims in which the rejection was affirmed, and issue the application; or (2) set a 1-month time limit for appellant to rewrite dependent claims in independent form.
guidance: Extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) will not be permitted for the 1-month period. If no timely reply is received, the examiner will cancel rejected and objected-to claims and issue the application with the allowed claims only. Suggested form language and examiner notes are provided in the MPEP.

name: Interpretation of purpose/functional language in claims
description: Where a claim contains wording indicating a purpose (e.g., "for re-melting galvanic layers"), determine whether that wording is to be treated as a mere statement of suitability for an outcome or as a functional/technical feature defining a step of the claimed method.
guidance: If the claim is directed to a process that comprises physical steps which result in a product, mentioning its purpose often implies mere suitability (the process need only be suitable to produce the intended outcome) and will not necessarily be treated as an actual method step. Conversely, when purpose wording clearly defines a function of the method (i.e., a functional feature concerning the re-melting of galvanic layers), it should be understood as defining one of the steps of the claimed method. This distinction affects anticipation by prior art: prior art disclosing the same method without indicating the particular product outcome may anticipate a claim that later recites that particular product when the purpose is only suitability.

name: General use claims (use claims)
description: Claims seeking protection for a particular purpose of using a product (a subtype of process claims), e.g., "the use of substance X as an insecticide."
guidance: In some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO for non-medical uses) such a use claim will be treated as equivalent to a process/method claim (e.g., "a process of killing insects using substance X"). Use claims are not universally accepted (the United States does not treat "use" as a statutory class of claim). When drafting, be mindful of how the claim should be interpreted in the target jurisdictions to avoid unintended product-claim or apparatus interpretations.

name: Medical indication claims (first/second medical uses and claim formats)
description: Claims directed to new medical uses of known products (first or subsequent medical indications), and the various permissible claim formats depending on jurisdiction.
guidance: Medical-use inventions require careful attention to national laws and practices as permissibility and scope vary. Common formats include: Swiss-type claims ("use of X in the manufacture of a medicament for the treatment of Y") — historically accepted at EPO (1985–2010) and in many countries; purpose-limited product claims ("substance X for use in the treatment of Y") — compulsory at EPO since 2011 and used in some national laws; plain use claims ("use of X for the treatment of Y") — accepted in some countries (Germany, Canada, Australia); "substance when used to treat" formulations; and method-of-treatment claims ("a method of treating a human having Y comprising administration of X") — accepted in the United States and Australia. Jurisdictional differences extend to patentability, claim format, infringement/enforcement (e.g., U.S. practitioners may be protected from liability and enforcement often focuses on manufacturers/distributors), and whether product claims covering known substances remain patentable when a new medical use is discovered. Professional tip: ensure the first application’s description supports selecting the most appropriate format(s) for jurisdictions of interest and consider including a combination of product, use and process claims (and preparation process claims) to maximize protection and mitigate invalidity risks.

name: Biotechnology claims and deposit requirements
description: Claims involving biological material where words alone may be insufficient to enable a person skilled in the art (e.g., seeds, microorganisms, DNA sequences).
guidance: When biological material cannot be fully described in words, access to the material (deposit) may be necessary to satisfy disclosure and statutory requirements. Many jurisdictions require or allow deposit systems; the Budapest Treaty facilitates international recognition of microorganism deposits with International Depositary Authorities (IDAs). Claims can reference deposited samples by accession numbers (example: 'A seed of cotton cultivar designated PHY 78 Acala, wherein a representative sample ... was deposited under ATCC Accession No. PTA-5666'). Ensure compliance with sequence listing and deposit rules in the target jurisdictions.

name: Computer-implemented invention claims and formats
description: Drafting guidance for inventions involving software, algorithms, data structures, computer-readable media and hardware implementations, considering the exclusion of abstract ideas/software 'as such' in many jurisdictions.
guidance: Many jurisdictions exclude abstract ideas, software per se, pure mental acts and business methods. Patent applications for computer-implemented inventions typically include product (apparatus/system), method and use claims. The first claim is frequently a method claim because algorithms represent dynamic behavior. Include product claims (e.g., a data-processing system) that refer back to method claims where allowed; where such referencing is not allowed, rephrase method steps as "means for ..." or concrete "a transmitter for sending ..." but note 'means' language (means-plus-function) may be narrowly interpreted in jurisdictions like the U.S. Specialized claim formats include computer-readable medium (Beauregard) claims (preambles like "A computer-readable storage medium storing instructions that when executed by a computer cause the computer to perform a method ...") and data-structure (Lowry) claims (claims to memory/data structures stored in memory). Choose formats with attention to target-jurisdiction practices and evolving case law. Professional tip: stay up to date as practices evolve with technology.

name: Claim scope balance: drafting broad and narrow claims
description: Draft a set of claims that ranges from the broadest to the narrowest to effectively capture the full scope of an invention’s novelty and to provide fallback positions during prosecution.
guidance: An ideal approach is to draft claims from broadest to narrowest. In practice, it can help to start with a narrow claim of the embodiment then gradually remove or generalize elements to reach the broadest claim. Use abstract/general terms (e.g., 'power source' instead of 'electric motor') where appropriate, but ensure at least one independent claim recites more than one element (in jurisdictions that require it). Keep dependent claims that reintroduce narrowed/omitted features to capture fallback positions. Consider drafting multiple independent claim sets (apparatus, element-focused, method, process) to cover different aspects of the invention; create alternative claim sets only when each truly represents independent novelty of commercial significance or when prior art is unclear. Always check the inventor’s intended commercial scope — if the inventor wants a narrow, specific scope, draft accordingly rather than overbroadly. The drafter should use removed elements as sources for dependent claims (e.g., dependent claims restoring earlier, narrower terms) and may split claim sets to focus on alternative points of novelty.

name: Markedly different characteristics (product of nature)
description: To be 'markedly different' a characteristic must be changed as compared to the naturally occurring counterpart and cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic or an incidental change; applicant must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart.
guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product of nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and the change came about or was produced by applicant’s efforts or influences, then the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic such that the claimed product is not a product of nature exception. Examples: Chakrabarty (genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and new hydrocarbon-degrading capacity deemed markedly different); Myriad (full-length cDNA with exon-only sequence deemed not a product of nature). Anti-examples: isolated genes (Myriad) and primers (Ambry) lacked sufficient marked difference because structural/function characteristics remained innate or incidental.

name: Step 2A Prong Two - integration into a practical application
description: After determining a claim recites a judicial exception in Step 2A Prong One, evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two).
guidance: If the claim as a whole integrates the judicial exception into a practical application, the claim is not 'directed to' the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible (Pathway B). If not, the claim is directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis under Step 2B (inventive concept). The analysis evaluates whether additional elements impose a meaningful limit on the judicial exception such that the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception.

name: Consideration: effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing
description: An additional element that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing supports integration into a practical application.
guidance: This is analogous to the 'particular machine' consideration and is discussed further in MPEP § 2106.05(c). The claimed transformation should be substantive and tied to the exception's application, not merely incidental or nominal.

name: Consideration: applying/using the exception in some other meaningful way beyond merely linking to technology or field of use
description: Applying or using the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment or field of use may integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: This is a catch-all for additional meaningful limitations that prevent the claim from being merely a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) for examples and discussion.

name: Specificity of achieving a result is not standalone but can inform other considerations
description: A specific way of achieving a result is not by itself a stand-alone consideration in Step 2A Prong Two, but specificity of limitations is relevant to evaluating particular machine use, particular transformation, and whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception.
guidance: Failure to explain specifics (e.g., how to select parameters, monitor processes, or implement steps) can suggest that additional elements are insignificant post-solution activity (Parker v. Flook). Thus examiners should consider whether the claim explains sufficient specifics of how the result is achieved when assessing whether limitations meaningfully integrate the exception.

name: Procedure: identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
description: Examiners evaluate integration into a practical application by (1) identifying whether there are any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using one or more of the considerations provided.
guidance: Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim; the analysis is not a weighing test. Examiners should evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and consider how the limitations interact when evaluating integration. Each claim must be examined separately; dependent claims may be eligible even if independent claims are not, if they recite additional elements that amount to significantly more or that integrate the exception into a practical application. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1)-(2) and 2106.05(a)-(h) for further detail and examples (e.g., Solutran, Finjan).

name: Definition and purpose of patents and claims
description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention within the United States or importing it into the United States. The specification should have a written description of the invention, how it works, and how to make and use it so as to enable others skilled in the art. The claims define the scope of the patent owner’s exclusive rights.
guidance: Provide jurors background on patent prosecution, Office Actions, and the prosecution history (file wrapper); clarify that only claims can be infringed, not the written description or drawings.

name: Burden and standard of proof for infringement (preponderance)
description: [The Plaintiff] must prove that [the Defendant] infringes one or more claims ... by a preponderance of the evidence.
guidance: Preponderance of the evidence is described as slightly greater than 50%; apply this standard to infringement and most other issues except invalidity (clear and convincing).

name: Presumption of validity and standard for invalidity (clear and convincing)
description: A patent is presumed to be valid. To overcome the presumption of validity, [the Defendant] must prove invalidity of each challenged claim by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Practice Note suggests substituting or explaining 'clear and convincing' as 'highly probable' to aid juror understanding; explains relationship between evidence standards (preponderance < clear-and-convincing < beyond a reasonable doubt).

name: Claim construction — judge provides meanings
description: It is the judge's job to provide to the jury the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted. Jurors must accept the meanings given and use them for both infringement and invalidity decisions.
guidance: For limitations not construed by the court, use the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. Cite relevant authority (Phillips, Teva).

name: Means-/step-plus-function claim construction (§ 112 ¶6 / §112(f))
description: Where a claim element is in the form of a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, the element is interpreted to cover only the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: Judge determines the recited function and corresponding structure/steps; Instruction 2.2 recommended where means/step language is used to avoid jury confusion; include statutory and case citations.

name: Literal infringement — each claim element present
description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the Defendant's product/method includes each and every element/method step in that patent claim.
guidance: If the accused product/method does not contain one or more elements/steps, it does not literally infringe that claim; determine literal infringement for each asserted claim.

name: Doctrine of equivalents — equivalence for missing elements
description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents only if there is an equivalent component/part/method step in the accused product/method for each element/method step of the patent claim that is not literally present.
guidance: Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that accused product contains equivalents for each missing element; practice notes discuss limits (e.g., prosecution history estoppel, dedication to the public).

name: Direct infringement — knowledge and intent immaterial
description: Direct infringement is established by acts that fall within the scope of the claims; knowledge of the patent and intent to infringe are immaterial to direct infringement.
guidance: Separate instructions exist for literal infringement, joint infringement, means-plus-function literal infringement, and infringement of dependent claims.

name: Infringement of means-plus-function or step-plus-function claims
description: Literal infringement of means-plus-function or step-plus-function claims requires that the accused device or process contain the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification or equivalents.
guidance: Use the court's construction of the means/step element (see Instruction 2.2); jurors must be instructed on corresponding structure or steps identified in the specification.

name: Claim language constructions for 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
description: Instructions include guidance on infringement analyses for claims using transitional or limitative claim language such as 'comprising of', 'consisting of', and 'consisting essentially of'.
guidance: Explain the legal effect of those transitional phrases on claim scope and infringement findings.

name: Obviousness — Graham factors (scope/content of prior art; differences; level of skill; secondary considerations)
description: Obviousness instructions cover: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) other considerations (secondary considerations).
guidance: Provide guidance on how these factors interact; include Practice Notes and case citations; instruct jury on determining person of ordinary skill in the art.

name: Person of ordinary skill in the art
description: Define the level of experience, education, or training generally possessed by those who work in the area of the invention (pre-AIA) or before the effective filing date (AIA).
guidance: Used for claim construction, obviousness, enablement, written description, and other analyses; instructions explain that the level may vary by claim/technology.

name: Written-description requirement (§ 112)
description: The written-description requirement ensures that the specification adequately describes the claimed invention.
guidance: Provide standards and jury guidance for determining whether specification shows possession of the claimed invention at the relevant time.

name: Willful infringement — totality of circumstances and knowledge/intention
description: If infringement is found, the jury must determine whether the infringement was willful. Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that Defendant knew of the patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
guidance: May consider whether conduct was deliberate or intentional; cannot find willfulness merely because Defendant knew of the patent; consider totality of circumstances at time of challenged conduct.

name: "consisting essentially of" transitional phrase
description: The transitional phrase “consisting essentially of” limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps “and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)” of the claimed invention.
guidance: Use case law (In re Herz, PPG Industries v. Guardian Industries, Atlas Powder, In re Janakirama-Rao, Water Technologies v. Calco) to interpret. It occupies a middle ground between “consisting of” (closed) and “comprising” (open). For purposes of searching/applying prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, absent a clear indication in the specification or claims of what the basic and novel characteristics are, “consisting essentially of” will be construed as equivalent to “comprising.” Applicants bear the burden of showing that additional steps or materials in the prior art are excluded by “consisting essentially of” language (In re De Lajarte). Specification statements defining what materially changes the invention (e.g., AK Steel specifying silicon content ≤ 0.5% and deleterious effects above that level) can provide basis to limit scope.

name: Transitional phrases generally (e.g., "having", "composed of")
description: Transitional phrases such as “having” must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether open or closed claim language is intended.
guidance: Interpretation depends on facts and the specification. Example: Lampi Corp. interpreted “having” as open terminology; Crystal Semiconductor noted “having” does not create a presumption that the claim body is open; Regents v. Eli Lilly shows ‘having’ can permit inclusion of other moieties in context. The phrase “composed of” has been interpreted like “consisting of” or “consisting essentially of” depending on the facts and specification (AFG Industries, In re Bertsch). Always read the transitional phrase with the specification and other evidence to decide scope.

name: "adapted to", "adapted for", "wherein", "whereby" clauses
description: Claim scope is not limited by claim language that suggests or makes optional but does not require steps to be performed, or by claim language that does not limit a claim to a particular structure. Examples of language that may raise limiting-effect questions include: (A) “adapted to” or “adapted for” clauses; (B) “wherein” clauses; and (C) “whereby” clauses.
guidance: Whether such clauses are limitations depends on case-specific facts. Use case law: Griffin v. Bertina (wherein clause limited process claim because it gave meaning/purpose to manipulative steps); In re Giannelli (an “adapted to” clause limited a machine claim where written description made clear a narrower meaning); Hoffer v. Microsoft (a “whereby” clause stating a condition material to patentability cannot be ignored). But courts may decline to give weight to a “whereby” clause that merely expresses an intended result of a positively recited process step (quoting Minton v. NASD). Read clauses in context of the specification and claim as a whole.

name: Contingent limitations — broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) differences for method vs system claims
description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a method (process) claim having contingent limitations requires only those steps that must be performed and does not include steps that are not required because the condition(s) precedent are not met. The broadest reasonable interpretation of a system (apparatus/product) claim having structure that performs a function which only needs to occur if a condition precedent is met requires structure for performing the function should the condition occur.
guidance: Apply the distinction illustrated in Ex parte Schulhauser (PTAB Apr. 28, 2016). For a method claim, if a claimed invention may be practiced without a condition occurring, then the contingent step is not required under BRI. For a system claim, the claimed structure must be present regardless of whether the condition occurs. Consequence: Examiner need not present obviousness evidence for method steps not required under BRI, but to render a system claim obvious the prior art must teach the structure that performs the contingent function along with other limitations. See also MPEP § 2143.03 for contingent claim limitations.

name: Printed matter analysis — threshold: is the limitation directed to printed matter?
description: A limitation is printed matter only if it claims the content of information. The first step of printed matter analysis is determining that the limitation in question is in fact directed toward printed matter.
guidance: Use In re DiStefano and related cases to determine whether the limitation claims content (printed matter). If not directed to printed matter, do not proceed to printed-matter-specific inquiry. If it is printed matter, proceed to determine functional/structural relationship to substrate. Note that printed matter analysis has been extended to method claims where instructional limitations are added to a known method (assess whether a new and nonobvious functional relationship exists).

name: Evidence against functional relationship (printed matter)
description: If a product merely serves as a support for printed matter, or the claim as a whole is directed toward conveying a message or meaning to a human reader independent of the supporting product, no functional relationship exists.
guidance: Examples include images on a hatband not arranged in sequence, a deck of cards with pictures (functions relate to game-play rather than structure), a measuring tape with wiring information unrelated to the tape's structure, or a kit with generic instructions not tied to that specific set of chemicals. See Gulack, In re Bryan, Ex parte Gwinn. Where printed matter and product do not depend upon each other, printed matter lacks functional relationship.

name: Machine-readable media — printed matter and functional relationship considerations
description: When determining the scope of a claim directed to a computer-readable medium containing certain programming, the examiner should look to the relationship between the programming and the intended computer system. Where the programming performs some function with respect to the computer, a functional relationship will be found. Where the claim as a whole is directed to conveying a message or meaning to a human reader independent of the intended computer system, and/or the medium merely serves as a support for information or data, no functional relationship exists.
guidance: Examples: A medium programmed with attribute data objects that facilitate retrieval/addition/removal of information establishes a functional relationship (citing Lowry). A memory stick storing batting averages or musical tracks merely supports information and is not functionally related to the computer. Additionally, a claim to a computer-readable medium storing instructions or executable code that recites an abstract idea must be evaluated for eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (see MPEP § 2106).

name: Assess improvements in patent quality beyond grant-rate changes (claim narrowing)
description: Greater examination time may improve issued patent quality in ways not solely captured by reduced grant rates—for example, helping examiners narrow claim scope of patents that would have issued and thereby reducing litigation risk.
guidance: Include qualitative measures of patent quality (claim breadth/narrowing) and consider how these qualitative changes affect litigation, enforcement, and innovation incentives in addition to changes in grant rates.

name: Copendency requirement for 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c) benefit
description: When a later-filed application is claiming the benefit of a prior-filed nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c), the later-filed application must be copending with the prior application or with an intermediate nonprovisional application similarly entitled to the benefit of the filing date of the prior application.
guidance: Copendency is satisfied if the later-filed application is filed before (A) patenting of the prior application; (B) abandonment of the prior application; or (C) termination of proceedings in the prior application. If the prior application issues as a patent, filing on the same date or before the patent issues is sufficient (applicants encouraged to file continuing applications no later than the date the issue fee is paid). If the prior application is abandoned, the later-filed application must be filed before abandonment. If not copending, the later-filed application is not entitled to the earlier filing date and prior art is determined from the later filing date.

name: Twelve-month filing rule for provisional benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e)
description: A nonprovisional application that directly claims the benefit of a provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) must be filed within 12 months after the filing date of the provisional application.
guidance: If the 12-month anniversary falls on a weekend or federal holiday in D.C., the nonprovisional may be filed on the next succeeding business day. If not filed within 12 months, an intermediate nonprovisional filed within 12 months that itself claims the provisional may preserve benefit, but that intermediate must be clearly identified. Failure to timely file directly claiming a provisional will render the direct claim improper.

name: Specific reference requirement (first sentence(s) or ADS) under 37 CFR 1.78
description: The later-filed application must contain a specific reference to the prior application appearing as the first sentence(s) of the specification following the title (preferably as a separate paragraph) and/or in an application data sheet (ADS).
guidance: If the specific reference is only in the ADS, the benefit claim information appears on the front page but not in the first sentence(s) of the specification. A reference submitted after filing cannot include an incorporation by reference of the prior application unless that incorporation was presented upon filing. If the reference is missing or improperly made, the Office may not recognize the benefit claim.

name: Identification of prior nonprovisional by application number and relationship
description: Benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, and 365(c) must identify the prior nonprovisional application by application number (or international application number and date) and indicate the relationship between the applications (continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part).
guidance: A statement must include both the application number and the relationship (e.g., “This application is a continuation of prior Application No. ---, filed ---.”). A claim that merely states "claims the benefit of Application No. ---" or omits the relationship does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78(a)(2)(i). The relationship terms are exclusive and must be specified for each application in a chain where multiple prior applications are involved.

name: Do not specify relationship for provisional claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e)
description: When claiming benefit to a prior provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), the relationship (continuation/divisional/CIP) is not required and should not be specified.
guidance: Applicants should not state that the nonprovisional is a "continuation" of a provisional or claim 120 benefit to a provisional; doing so may create ambiguity between claiming under 119(e) or 120 and may have adverse effects (e.g., on patent term).

name: Chain of benefit claims must specify relationship for each link
description: Where benefit to multiple prior nonprovisional applications is claimed through a chain (e.g., A -> B -> C), the reference must identify all prior applications and indicate the relationship (continuation, divisional, or continuation-in-part) between each nonprovisional application to establish copendency through the entire chain.
guidance: Statements that merely list application numbers without specifying the relationship for each link are improper. Each intermediate application must include appropriate references in its file to maintain the chain.

name: Contents and formatting of multiple benefit claims in specification
description: If claiming the benefit of multiple prior applications, the references may be in a continuous string of multiple sentences at the beginning of the specification; these must begin as the first sentence after the title and not be separated by any other sentence not making a benefit claim.
guidance: Any additional sentences including a benefit claim must immediately follow the first sentence and be contiguous; otherwise the claim may not be recognized.

name: Procedure when specific reference is not timely filed (petition & surcharge)
description: A benefit claim filed after the required time period may be accepted only if accompanied by a petition under 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3) (or (a)(6) where applicable), the surcharge under 37 CFR 1.17(t), and a statement that the entire delay was unintentional.
guidance: The petition must include the required reference (unless previously submitted). The Director may require additional information to determine whether the delay was unintentional. If the reference was previously recognized on the filing receipt despite not being in the first sentence(s) or ADS, petition/surcharge may not be required but applicant must still amend the specification or file an ADS to comply.

name: Effect of failing to be copending or to include proper reference
description: A later-filed application that is not copending, or that does not contain the specific reference as required, is not entitled to the benefit of the prior application's filing date; prior art against its claims is determined from the later application's filing date.
guidance: If the Office does not recognize a benefit claim because it lacks the required reference and the time for submitting it has expired, applicant must submit a petition and surcharge to accept an unintentionally delayed claim. The Office may not schedule publication based on an unrecognized earlier filing date.

name: Deletion of benefit claims and effects on patent term and prior art
description: Applicants may cancel their claim to priority by amending the specification or submitting a new ADS to delete references to prior applications; deletion may be used to avoid measuring patent term from an earlier date.
guidance: Examiners should consider whether deletion makes new prior art available. Deleting a benefit claim after final rejection/allowance is treated under 37 CFR 1.116/1.312 respectively. Cancellation may be considered an intentional waiver, and a later petition to accept an unintentionally delayed claim may be refused if benefit was intentionally cancelled.

name: Form paragraphs and examiner wording for improper benefit claims
description: Use form paragraphs (e.g., ¶2.09, ¶2.11, ¶2.11.01, ¶2.15, ¶2.16) to indicate improper or missing benefit claims and instruct applicants what to delete or insert.
guidance: Examples: ¶2.11 instructs deletion of a prior nonprovisional reference unless copendency can be established; ¶2.11.01 addresses failure to file within 12 months for provisional benefit. Examiner notes indicate bracket insertions (e.g., application number) and special-use rules (e.g., do not use certain paragraphs for 119(e) provisional claims).

name: Plan Markman hearing logistics
description: Plan for the Markman (claim construction) hearing, including scope of tutorial and whether to have live testimony from experts or other witnesses.
guidance: Early planning for tutorial and testimony informs claim-construction and summary-judgment readiness and can guide discovery scope and scheduling.

name: Manage multidefendant cases based on standards compliance
description: When multidefendant litigation is based on compliance with industry standards, recognize that discovery regarding functional specifications can often be fairly limited, but anticipate complicated SSO-related defenses and counterclaims (e.g., noncompliance with SSO policies, FRAND issues).
guidance: Such cases may implicate equitable, contract-based, and antitrust claims and defenses; confidentiality and damages concerns may counsel bifurcating damages from liability; identifying the standards-based nature at outset can significantly narrow fact discovery.

name: Manage customer/manufacturer multidefendant litigations
description: When plaintiffs sue manufacturers and their customers (OEMs, distributors), the court should consider staying claims against customer defendants pending resolution of manufacturer claims, and be mindful of third-party discovery and protective-order issues.
guidance: Customers are often superfluous; courts frequently stay customer suits or require customers to consent to be bound by judgments. Manufacturers may intervene or file declaratory-judgment actions; first-to-file and customer-suit-exception analyses (judicial efficiency) often determine outcomes.

name: Use early, targeted claim construction
description: Require parties to identify claim terms which, if construed, could dispose of a significant portion of the case and proceed to construe those terms on an expedited schedule (sometimes with shorter briefs and without expert discovery).
guidance: Some courts (e.g., E.D. Tex.) have used this to encourage early resolution when plaintiffs appear to seek nuisance settlements; expedited claim construction can prompt early settlements or dismissals.

name: Patentable subject matter (§101) is amenable to early resolution
description: Patent eligibility under § 101 (abstract ideas, laws of nature) can often be addressed early via motion to dismiss or summary judgment, especially for simple business methods or broad claims.
guidance: Complex inventions may require claim construction, background tutorials, and factual development; factual disputes over inventive application may implicate subsidiary factual determinations (Teva) and may warrant awaiting discovery/tutorial before deciding.

name: Extrajurisdictional/extraterritoriality issues can be resolved early
description: Claims based on extraterritorial conduct (e.g., §§ 271(f), 271(g), 271(b)) often involve ascertainable facts about a defendant’s contacts with the U.S. that could lead to early resolution.
guidance: Early fact-finding on contacts can narrow or dispose of claims alleging foreign conduct as infringement.

name: Early disposition of indirect infringement claims
description: Indirect infringement claims (and willfulness) require that the accused infringer knew of the asserted patents prior to litigation and are therefore susceptible to early determination.
guidance: In method-claim cases, indirect-infringement theories often depend on whether a single entity is responsible for all claimed steps (Limelight, Muniauction); absence of control/direction or multiple noninfringing uses can be fatal early on.

name: Re-recording patents and deposit of drawings (patents issued prior to Dec 15, 1836)
description: Any person in possession of a patent issued prior to Dec 15, 1836 (or recorded assignment) may, without charge, on presentation to the Commissioner, have the same recorded anew in the Patent Office together with descriptions, specifications of claim, and drawings; the Commissioner must transcribe or obtain authenticated copies.
guidance: Where a drawing was not originally annexed, a delineating drawing, verified by oath as required, may be transmitted and placed on file or copied. Clerks of U.S. judicial courts must transmit authenticated copies they hold when requested by the Commissioner.

name: Disclaimer procedure for overbroad claims
description: Whenever a patentee has inadvertently claimed more than he was the original inventor of, but some material/substantial part is truly his, he may disclaim such parts not claimed by virtue of the patent, stating extent of his interest; disclaimer must be in writing, attested, recorded on payment of $10.
guidance: Disclaimer becomes part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest and of those deriving under him after recordation. It does not affect pending actions except insofar as relates to unreasonable neglect or delay in filing.

name: Revision/restriction of claims for improvements and reissues
description: When application is made for addition of newly discovered improvement to an existing patent, or when a patent is returned for correction and reissue, the specification of claim shall be subject to revision and restriction in the same manner as original applications.
guidance: Commissioner shall not add improvement nor grant reissue until applicant enters disclaimer or alters specification in accordance with his decision; dissatisfied applicants have the same remedy and privileges as in original applications.

name: Effect of mistaken claims of originality and limits on recovery
description: If by mistake and without wilful default a patentee claimed to be original inventor of a material/substantial part of the thing patented of which he was not the first inventor, the patent shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention as is bona fide his own, provided it is material, substantial, and definitely distinguishable.
guidance: Such patentee (or successors) may sue for infringement of the part truly his; however, he shall not recover costs unless he entered a disclaimer at the Patent Office prior to commencement of suit. No benefits if he unreasonably neglected or delayed entering the disclaimer.

name: Claim architecture: three layers (preamble, transition, body)
description: Every well-drafted independent claim has three layers: (1) the preamble, which states what the claim is for; (2) the transition, which sets the scope ("comprising," "consisting of," "consisting essentially of"); and (3) the body, which lists the elements/limitations.
guidance: Design claims with clear separation of these layers so each performs its drafting function (preamble states purpose/context, transition sets openness, body recites elements/limitations).

name: Preamble limitingness
description: A preamble is generally not limiting unless it (a) breathes life and meaning into the claim, (b) provides antecedent basis for terms in the body, or (c) was relied upon during prosecution to distinguish prior art.
guidance: Treat every preamble as a potential limitation; avoid marketing language in the preamble. If the preamble supplies essential context or antecedent terms, it may be construed as limiting. Be cautious that statements made during prosecution relying on the preamble can create prosecution-history-based limitations.

name: Transition choice: openness of scope
description: "Comprising" is open: the claim covers anything containing the listed elements plus more. "Consisting of" is closed: only the listed elements. "Consisting essentially of" is semi-closed: listed elements plus things that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristics.
guidance: Default to "comprising" unless there is a tactical reason to limit scope (e.g., to exclude certain materials or steps). Choose transition deliberately to control claim breadth and exclusion of unrecited features.

name: Element order in the body
description: Elements should appear in an order that supports the function of the invention - typically the order in which they interact.
guidance: Reciting elements in the order they operate makes the claim easier to read and easier to argue. Avoid haphazard ordering that frustrates comprehension and prosecution/claim-construction arguments.

name: Antecedent basis hygiene
description: Each noun in a claim should be introduced with "a" or "an" once, then referred to with "the" or "said" thereafter.
guidance: Failure to provide proper antecedent basis (e.g., using "the widget" without first reciting "a widget") invites 35 U.S.C. §112(b)/indefiniteness rejections. Maintain consistent introduction and subsequent reference forms to avoid ambiguity.

name: Active voice verbs in method claims
description: Each step in a method claim should use an active verb: "applying," "determining," "transmitting," "decoding."
guidance: Avoid passive constructions (e.g., "the signal is received") because they make it ambiguous who performs the step and can create divided-infringement issues. Active verbs clarify the actor and reduce ambiguity.

name: Single-actor drafting for method claims
description: Method claims should be drafted so a single actor performs every step.
guidance: Because divided-infringement doctrines (e.g., Akamai v. Limelight) make proving infringement by multiple parties difficult, the easiest defense is to write claims so one entity performs all steps. Where multiple parties may be involved, consider drafting system/apparatus claims or including agent language to attribute acts to a single entity.

name: "Whereby" clause caution
description: "Whereby" clauses describe results. They are usually held to be non-limiting (Texas Instruments v. ITC).
guidance: Use "whereby" clauses sparingly. Do not rely on them to distinguish prior art—move substantive distinguishing material into affirmative claim limitations rather than a result-oriented "whereby" clause.

name: Length-of-claim heuristic
description: A claim that takes more than a single page in 12-point single-spaced text is almost always too narrow. A claim that takes less than 4 lines is almost always too broad to survive examination.
guidance: Aim for a claim of moderate length—neither extremely short nor excessively long. Use this heuristic as a quick check on likely prosecution survivability: target somewhere between 4 lines and one page in 12-pt single-spaced text.

name: International design applications – mandatory form DM/1 and required documents
description: Applicants filing international design applications through the USPTO must present the international design application on Form DM/1 (Application for International Registration) or any form having the same form and content as the official form; the DM/1 includes boxes for applicant, entitlement, creator, product ID, designations, priority claim, description, and other relevant information.
guidance: EFS-Web provides a specific selection path for 'International Design Application (Hague) for filing through the USPTO as an office of indirect filing.' Include the specified documents in new international design application submissions per the guidance.

name: Claims must be supported by the disclosure at filing
description: Limitations of claims can be modified based only on the disclosed invention at the time of filing.
guidance: Capture the invention using clear and consistent language throughout the disclosure so claim terms find antecedent basis in the specification.

name: Use clear and consistent language throughout the disclosure
description: Important to capture the invention using clear and consistent language throughout the disclosure.
guidance: Draft terminology deliberately (drafting claims first is recommended) to ensure terms used in claims are supported and consistently used in the specification and drawings.

name: Nonprovisional application characteristics
description: Nonprovisional applications are examined, require at least one claim, must meet written description/enablement requirements (35 U.S.C. §112), and are generally published 18 months from earliest filing date unless non-publication is requested.
guidance: Nonprovisional applications can result in an issued patent; follow formal filing requirements and prepare claims carefully.

name: Provisional application filing/legal requirements
description: A provisional filing must clearly indicate that a provisional application is being filed, include payment of the fee, a description enabling someone to make and use the invention, and drawings if necessary to understand the invention.
guidance: Use PTO/SB/16 (cover sheet) or otherwise make the provisional status clear; include sufficient disclosure to support later nonprovisional claims.

name: Nonprovisional filing package requirements
description: A nonprovisional utility patent application must include a specification (description and claim(s)), drawings when necessary, an oath or declaration, and prescribed filing, search, and examination fees.
guidance: Follow USPTO guidance/online resources and include all required components to avoid processing delays.

name: Specification purpose and basic requirements
description: The specification is the written description of the invention and how to make and use it; it must be in clear, full, concise, and exact terms to allow a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention and must include at least one specific embodiment and conclude with at least one claim (on a new page).
guidance: Ensure the specification gives practical instructions and includes at least one concrete embodiment (preferably the best mode known).

name: Specification page format
description: Specification, abstract and claims must be 1.5 or double-spaced in a single column, written on one side in portrait orientation, on 8.5x11 inch paper with margins (¾ inches all around except left margin at least 1 inch), pages numbered consecutively starting with page one, and use a nonscript font (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier), preferably 12 point.
guidance: Adhere to these formatting rules to meet USPTO filing standards and avoid processing issues.

name: Specification sections (required/typical)
description: Typical sections include Title of the Invention; Background; Brief Summary of the Invention; Brief Description of the Drawings; Detailed Description of the Invention; Claims (on a separate sheet); and Abstract (less than 150 words, one paragraph, on a separate sheet).
guidance: Organize the specification with these sections in mind; ensure the abstract and claims are on separate sheets as required.

name: Drawings content requirements
description: Drawings must show every feature of the invention claimed and contain as many views as necessary to show the invention; drawings are deemed acceptable/unacceptable based on readability and reproducibility.
guidance: Provide sufficient views and detail to allow clear understanding of the claimed features; unreadable drawings can be rejected.

name: Detailed description requirements
description: The detailed description should explain the invention and the process of making and using it in full, clear, concise and exact terms, focusing on structures, processes or compositions, and should refer to the figures explaining parts by reference numerals.
guidance: This is the most important part of the application; provide specific detail and link claim terms to clear embodiments and figures.

name: Provide clear support/antecedent basis for claim terms
description: The detailed description should provide clear support or antecedent basis for all terms used in the claims so the meaning of claim terms is ascertainable by reference to the description.
guidance: Draft claims first if helpful; use the claims as a checklist to ensure the description supports all claimed terms and limitations.

name: Specification DOs (recommended practices)
description: Describe the invention clearly to allow any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation; ensure each reference numeral is used for only one part and mentioned in the specification; provide at least one specific embodiment including the best known to you at filing; include a Brief Description of the Drawings that names each figure; provide proper antecedent basis for all claim terms; focus on technical features.
guidance: Follow these practices to strengthen compliance with written description and enablement requirements and to reduce prosecution issues.

name: Specification cautions (what to avoid)
description: Do not use trademarks in the title or to describe structure; Background need not state how the inventor conceived the invention; avoid claims of future commercial success (e.g., 'will sell and make millions'); do not include detailed discussion of the figures or refer to reference characters in the Brief Description of the Drawings; proofread for grammatical errors.
guidance: Avoid non-technical, promotional, or improperly placed content that may confuse the scope or sufficiency of disclosure.

name: Claim support rule: 'If it is in the claim, it must be in the specification'
description: Claims define the invention and what aspects are legally enforceable; they must conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification and claim terms must find clear support/antecedent basis in the description.
guidance: Ensure every claimed limitation has textual support in the specification to withstand written description challenges.

name: Form and formal requirements of claim(s)
description: Claims must start on a separate sheet with the heading 'Claim Listing', be 1.5 or double spaced, each claim be a single sentence (begin with a capital letter and end with a period), have numbering preserved throughout prosecution, and applicants may file up to 3 independent claims and 20 total claims before excess claim fees apply.
guidance: Follow formatting rules, observe claim count limitations to anticipate fees, and preserve original numbering during prosecution.

name: U.S. patent claim statutory requirements
description: A nonprovisional patent application must have at least one claim that particularly points out and distinctly defines the invention; claims may be written in independent or dependent form, and a dependent claim incorporates by reference all limitations of the claim to which it refers.
guidance: Write clear claims that distinctly point out the invention; use dependent claims to add limitations and fallback positions.

name: Questions to answer before drafting claims
description: Prior to writing claims, determine: What is the invention? What are the pieces and parts that make up the invention? How do the pieces and parts relate to one another? Do you have more than one invention (tangible vs method)? Are there multiple versions of each invention?
guidance: Use these questions to decompose the invention and plan claim scope and claim sets (apparatus, method, composition) appropriately.

name: Claim drafting strategy
description: Think strategically to obtain the broadest valid claim possible and claims with a variety of claim scope, not just at time of filing but during prosecution; consider whether some claims filed are likely to be patentable without amendment and the implications of provisional rights (35 U.S.C. §154(d)).
guidance: File a mix of broad and narrower claims to maximize protection and immediate enforceability; plan for prosecution amendments and provisional priority where applicable.

name: Identification of every claim and detailed explanation of pertinency (37 CFR 1.510(b)(2))
description: Identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested and a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to every claim.
guidance: For each patent owner statement submitted under 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2) that is relied upon, the request must explain how that statement is used to determine the proper meaning of a claim in connection with the prior art applied to that claim and how each relevant claim is being interpreted. The requester may point out how claims distinguish over cited prior art. The Office will consider these explanations during examination; at the order stage the Office will not consider patent owner claim scope statements referenced in the request (see 35 U.S.C. 301(d)).

name: Copies and submission format of the patent (single-sided, double-column spec)
description: The patent copy submitted should present the specification and claims in double-column format and all pages must be plainly written on one side of paper.
guidance: Drawing pages and front page should be presented as they appear in the printed patent. A two-sided copy is not proper. Include any disclaimers, certificates of correction, or reexamination certificates as part of the patent copy.

name: Entity status statements (small/micro/large) for fee determination
description: Different filing fees apply to large entities, small entities, and micro entities; a requester who claims small or micro entity status must affirmatively state eligibility.
guidance: A requester can assert small entity status by checking the appropriate box on the transmittal form (PTO/SB/57). Only a patent owner requester can establish micro entity status; a third‑party requester cannot claim micro entity status. See 37 CFR 1.27 and 1.29 and MPEP §§ 509.02–509.04 for details.

name: Commercial or legal interactions — legal obligations
description: Claims that are essentially legal obligations or legal tools (e.g., tax-free exchanges, regulatory/tax structures, hedging) can be abstract ideas as commercial/legal interactions.
guidance: Example: Fort Properties claimed aggregating real property and subjecting shares to a master agreement (tax-free exchanges) and was found to be an abstract concept. Other listed legal-obligation examples include hedging (Bilski), mitigating settlement risk (Alice/CLS), and arbitration (In re Comiskey).

name: Commercial or legal interactions — advertising/marketing/sales activities
description: Claims that recite advertising, marketing, or sales activities or behaviors may be abstract ideas under the commercial/legal interactions grouping.
guidance: Example: Ultramercial's eleven-step method for displaying an ad in exchange for access (using advertising as an exchange/currency) was held to recite an abstraction. Other examples: structuring a sales force or marketing company (In re Ferguson), algorithms determining optimal business visits (In re Maucorps), and offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs.).

name: Commercial or legal interactions — business relations
description: Claims describing business relations or interactions between commercial parties (e.g., customer/dealer/financing workflows or clearing-house relationships) can be abstract ideas.
guidance: Example: Credit Acceptance (processing a credit application and creating financing packages) was characterized as directed to the abstract idea of processing a financing application. Another example is Dealertrack (processing through a clearing-house between dealers and funding sources).

name: Mental processes — A: Limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind do not recite a mental process
description: If claim limitations cannot practically be performed in the human mind (the human mind is not equipped to perform them), the claim does not recite a mental process.
guidance: Examiners should identify when claimed operations require capabilities beyond human mental performance. Examples: GPS pseudorange calculations to compute absolute position/time (SiRF Tech.), detecting suspicious network activity via monitors/analyzing packets (SRI Int'l), specific multi-step data-encryption methods involving manipulation of data structures (Synopsys), and pixel-by-pixel halftone image rendering using masks (Research Corp.). These demonstrate practical impossibility of human mental performance and thus are not mental-process abstract ideas.

name: Mental processes — B: Claims that encompass a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
description: If a claim recites limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind—either purely mentally or with simple physical aids like pen and paper—it falls within the mental-process grouping (an abstract idea).
guidance: Use of physical aids (pen/paper/slide rule) does not negate the mental nature; it only accounts for differences in memory/capacity. Examples: constructing a map/listing of credit card transactions (CyberSource) could be done by writing down transactions; Benson and Flook noted computations by pencil-and-paper; Univ. of Florida v. GE relied on spec descriptions of pen-and-paper methodologies. Claims that 'read on' a human performing the steps mentally are abstract (see Synopsys, Symantec, Mortgage Grader).

name: Mental processes — C: Claims that require a computer may still recite a mental process
description: A claim that requires a computer can nonetheless be directed to a mental process if the claimed concept could be performed mentally or if the specification describes it as a human-performed concept merely implemented on a generic computer.
guidance: Examiners should analyze the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in view of the specification to determine whether the applicant is simply claiming a concept performed on a generic computer or using the computer as a tool. Precedents: Benson (algorithm performed mentally despite being implemented in a computer), Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping could be performed by humans). If the spec describes the concept as human cognitive actions or pen-and-paper methods, the claim may be an abstract mental process even though computer-implemented.

name: Mental processes — C.1: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
description: Performing a mental process on a generic computer does not necessarily render it patent-eligible; claims that are 'human cognitive actions' merely implemented on general-purpose hardware remain abstract.
guidance: Examples: Voter Verified (voting/verification steps described as human cognitive actions even when performed on a computer), Versata (determining a price implemented using general purpose computer hardware). Examiners should look to whether the specification characterizes the claimed steps as human cognitive tasks merely carried out on generic computing hardware.

name: Mental processes — D: Product and process claims may both recite mental processes; 'mental processes' refers to the type of abstract idea, not statutory claim category
description: Both product claims (systems, computer-readable media) and process claims can recite mental-process-type abstract ideas; the courts do not limit the mental-process grouping to process claims only.
guidance: The Federal Circuit has identified numerous product claims (e.g., system and computer-readable media claims in Versata) as reciting mental-process-type abstract ideas. Examiners must apply the mental-process analysis based on the concept recited, not on whether the claim is drafted as a product or a process.

name: Estoppel — patent applicant or owner
description: A patent applicant or owner is precluded from taking action inconsistent with an adverse judgment, including obtaining in any patent a claim that is not patentably distinct from a finally refused or canceled claim, or an amendment of a specification or drawing that was denied during the trial proceeding.
guidance: Provision does not apply to an application or patent that has a different written description. This preclusion applies when attempting to obtain inconsistent claim scope or amendments after an adverse trial judgment.

name: Certificate issuance after final written decision
description: After a final written decision in an IPR, PGR, or covered business method review and after appeal time has expired or appeals terminated, the Office will issue and publish a certificate canceling any claim finally determined to be unpatentable, confirming any claim determined to be patentable, and incorporating any new or amended claim determined to be patentable by operation of the certificate.
guidance: Certificate effects: formally updates the patent record to reflect trial outcomes; issuance occurs after appeal window or termination of appeals.

name: IPR/PGR — claim construction standard
description: In IPR and PGR proceedings, a claim shall be construed using the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. 282(b): ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history.
guidance: Any prior claim construction determination made in a civil action or ITC proceeding that is timely made of record in the IPR/PGR will be considered.

name: IPR — who may petition
description: A person who is not the owner of a patent may file a petition to institute an IPR unless: (a) before petition filing the petitioner (or RPI/privy) filed a civil action challenging the patent; (b) petition is filed more than one year after service of an infringement complaint; or (c) petitioner (or RPI/privy) is estopped from challenging the claims on the grounds identified in the petition.
guidance: Eligibility and timing are narrowly defined; estoppel and prior civil actions can bar IPR petitions.

name: Petition content — grounds for standing and identification of challenge
description: Petition must certify that the patent is available for review and petitioner is not barred/estopped, and must provide precise relief requested for each claim challenged, identifying: the claim; specific statutory grounds (35 U.S.C. 102/103 for IPR; 35 U.S.C. 282(b)(2) or (3) for PGR) and the patents/printed publications relied upon; how the claim is to be construed (including 112(f) means-plus-function specifics); how the construed claim is unpatentable (specify where each claim element is found in prior art or how it fails statute); and exhibit numbers and specific portions of evidence relied upon.
guidance: Petition must identify relevance and specific portions of evidence; Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where a party failed to state its relevance or identify specific portions. For 112(f) limitations, petitioner must identify spec portions describing corresponding structure/material/acts.

name: Preliminary response — patent owner preliminary response (IPR/PGR)
description: The patent owner may file a preliminary response limited to reasons why no review should be instituted under the applicable statutory section (35 U.S.C. 314 for IPR; 324 for PGR) and can include supporting evidence.
guidance: Preliminary response is subject to word count (§42.24); due no later than three months after notice granting filing date; patent owner may waive by election to expedite; preliminary response shall not include any amendment; patent owner may file statutory disclaimer under 35 U.S.C. 253(a) and disclaimed claims will not be instituted.

name: Motion to amend — scope limitations
description: Any motion to amend may be denied where: (i) the amendment does not respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial; or (ii) the amendment seeks to enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new subject matter.
guidance: Motions that go beyond addressing grounds raised in the trial or that broaden claim scope are vulnerable to denial.

name: Motion to amend — content requirements (support and claim listing)
description: Any motion to amend must include a claim listing (may be in an appendix) that shows changes clearly and must set forth: (1) the support in the original disclosure of the patent for each proposed substitute claim; and (2) the support in any earlier-filed disclosure for each claim for which earlier filing date benefit is sought.
guidance: Claim changes should be clearly shown. The motion must tie each substitute claim to specific disclosure support to satisfy written description/enablement and priority benefit requirements.

name: Motion to amend — determination standard when Board exercises discretion
description: Where the Board exercises discretion to raise a new ground in connection with a proposed substitute claim, the Board must determine unpatentability based on a preponderance of the evidence of record.
guidance: Board may request examination assistance; results of such assistance will be made of record and considered.

name: PGR — who may petition and timing
description: A person who is not the owner may file a petition for post-grant review unless before petition filing the petitioner filed a civil action challenging validity, or the petitioner (or RPI/privy) is estopped from challenging the claims on the grounds identified.
guidance: A post-grant review petition must be filed no later than nine months after the grant of a patent or issuance of a reissue patent. For reissue patents, PGR may not be requested for a claim identical to or narrower than the original patent claim unless the petition is filed within nine months after grant of the original patent.

name: PGR — petition content specifics (statutory grounds and evidence identification)
description: In addition to general requirements, a PGR petition must identify statutory grounds permitted under 35 U.S.C. 282(b)(2) or (3), explain claim construction (including 112(f) specifics), show how the construed claim is unpatentable (for prior art, specify where each element is found; for other grounds, identify the specific part of the claim failing to comply and explain how), and cite exhibit numbers and specific portions relied upon.
guidance: Board may exclude or give no weight to evidence where party failed to state its relevance or identify specific portions of evidence that support the challenge. Motions to correct clerical errors do not change filing date.

name: Claims — general requirements (definition, clarity, support)
description: The claim or claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. Claims shall be clear and concise. They shall be fully supported by the description.
guidance: These requirements are set forth in PCT Article 6 and PCT Rule 6 and echoed in 37 CFR 1.436. Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought and be fully supported by the description; the physical requirements for claims are the same as for the description (claims must commence on a new sheet).

name: Claims — manner of claiming (two-part form and characterizing portion)
description: The definition of the matter for which protection is sought shall be in terms of the technical features of the invention. Whenever appropriate, claims shall contain (i) a statement indicating those technical features necessary for the definition but which, in combination, are part of the prior art; and (ii) a characterizing portion—preceded by words such as 'characterized in that' or equivalent—stating concisely the technical features which, in combination with (i), it is desired to protect.
guidance: The claims must, whenever appropriate, be in two distinct parts: statement of prior art and the characterizing portion. Where national law of a designated State does not require this manner, failure to use it shall have no effect in that State provided the actual manner used satisfies national law.

name: Dependent claims — form, construction, and grouping
description: Any claim which includes all the features of one or more other claims (dependent claim) shall do so by a reference, if possible at the beginning, to the other claim(s) and shall then state the additional features claimed. Any multiple dependent claim shall refer to such claims in the alternative only and shall not serve as a basis for any other multiple dependent claim.
guidance: Any dependent claim shall be construed as including all limitations contained in the claim to which it refers. All dependent claims referring back to a single previous claim, and all dependent claims referring back to several previous claims, shall be grouped together to the extent and in the most practical way possible. Failure to conform to a particular manner used by an ISA may result in an indication under Article 17(2)(b) in the international search report, but has no effect in a designated State if national law is satisfied.

name: Abstract — content and required elements
description: The abstract shall consist of a summary of the disclosure as contained in the description, the claims, and any drawings; it shall indicate the technical field to which the invention pertains and be drafted to allow clear understanding of the technical problem, the gist of the solution, and the principal use or uses of the invention. Where applicable, include the chemical formula which best characterizes the invention.
guidance: Each main technical feature mentioned in the abstract and illustrated by a drawing shall be followed by a reference sign in parentheses. The abstract should be primarily related to what is new in the art to which the invention pertains; it shall be as concise as the disclosure permits (preferably 50 to 150 words in English).

name: Abstract — prohibited content and drafting guidance
description: The abstract shall not contain statements on the alleged merits or value of the claimed invention or on its speculative application. Phrases implicit (e.g., 'the invention relates to...') and legal phraseology (such as 'said' and 'means') should not be used.
guidance: The abstract must be drafted as a scanning tool to assist specialists in determining whether to consult the international application itself. Use concise, factual language; avoid superfluous language and prohibited items defined in PCT Rule 9.

name: Limit scope of post-grant review to avoid satellite issues
description: Post-grant review procedural scope should be circumscribed so it does not become a vehicle for collateral, costly disputes (e.g., best mode claims).
guidance: The Pence amendment is cited as clarifying that best mode cannot be raised in post-grant review. The underlying guidance is that post-grant review should focus on core patentability/validity issues rather than ancillary, subjective specification issues that generate separate litigation tracks.

name: Specific exemptions—national defense/foreign policy materials (k)(1) (§102.34(a))
description: Some USPTO systems contain material subject to exemption at 5 U.S.C. 552a(k)(1) relating to national defense and foreign policy.
guidance: Systems within this exemption are listed (COMMERCE/PAT-TM-6, -7, -8, -9). USPTO claims exemption of such materials wherever they appear; such materials are exempt from select subsections (e.g., 5 U.S.C. 552a(c)(3), (d), (e)(1), (e)(4)(G),(H),(I), and (f)) to protect materials required by Executive order to be kept secret in interest of national defense/foreign policy.

name: No current claim of exemptions under k(3),(4),(6),(7) (§102.34(c))
description: USPTO states it currently claims no exemption under 5 U.S.C. 552a(k)(3), (4), (6), and (7).
guidance: Statement of non-assertion—used to clarify scope of exemptions claimed.

name: Determination of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date (AIPA vs pre-AIPA)
description: Use 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as amended by the American Inventors Protection Act (AIPA) and subsequent amendments to determine the copending application's prior art date unless the copending reference is based on an international application with an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000 (in which case pre-AIPA 102(e) applies).
guidance: Apply AIPA rules for references filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) or national stages/WIPO publications of international applications with international filing dates on/after Nov 29, 2000 (form paragraph 7.12). Apply pre-AIPA 102(e) for U.S. patents issued from international applications filed prior to Nov 29, 2000 (form paragraph 7.12.01). See Examiner Notes for form paragraphs 7.12 and 7.12.01. Consider priority/benefit claims (119(e), 120, 121, 365(c)) only when subject matter is appropriately supported in the earlier application(s). Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a).

name: Overcoming 102(e)/103 rejections via derivation, inventorship, or terminal disclaimer
description: A 102(e) or 103(a) rejection based on a copending or earlier-filed reference may be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 (derivation), 37 CFR 1.131 (earlier date of invention), or by an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 plus a terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(c).
guidance: Use these procedural remedies where applicable; when claiming common ownership and prior inventorship, ensure compliance with rules for terminal disclaimers and 1.130 declarations.

name: Requirement to give provisional double patenting rejection when claims conflict
description: If the claims of the copending application conflict with the claims of the instant application, a provisional double patenting rejection should be given (use form paragraphs 8.30 and 8.32).
guidance: Also consider statutory/nonstatutory double patenting and whether terminal disclaimers or other remedies apply; coordinate rejections with other applicable grounds (e.g., 102/103).

name: General principles for determining distinctness or independence
description: (A) Where inventions are independent (no disclosed relation), restriction to one is ordinarily proper. (B) Where inventions are related as disclosed but distinct as claimed, restriction may be proper. (C) Where inventions are related as disclosed but not distinct as claimed, restriction is never proper. (D) A reasonable number of species may be claimed when there is an allowable generic claim.
guidance: Apply these general principles (see MPEP §806.06, §806.05, §806.04) when deciding restriction or double patenting issues; consult cited sections for specifics and examples.

name: Compare claimed matter for distinctness
description: In questions of double patenting and restriction, it is the claimed subject matter that is considered and such claimed subject matter must be compared to determine distinctness or independence.
guidance: Do not rely solely on disclosure; focus on claim scope. However, a provisional election of a single species may be required where generic claims recite so many species that an unduly extensive and burdensome search is necessary (see MPEP §803.02 and §808.01(a)).

name: Genus and species restriction criteria
