description: Where an application includes claims directed to different embodiments/species that could fall within the scope of a generic (genus) claim, restriction between the species may be proper if the species are independent or distinct. 37 CFR 1.141 provides that an allowable generic claim may link a reasonable number of species embraced thereby.
guidance: If application contains claims to more than a reasonable number of species, the examiner may require an election of species before taking further action. See MPEP §806.04 and 37 CFR 1.146 for election-of-species practice.

name: Definition of a generic claim
description: A generic claim should require no material element additional to those required by the species claims, and each of the species claims must require all the limitations of the generic claim.
guidance: Once a generic claim is allowable, species claims that require all limitations of the generic claim will ordinarily be allowable over the prior art; if some species do not require all limitations, follow MPEP §821.04(a).

name: Claims limited to species (species claims)
description: A claim's scope may be limited to a single disclosed embodiment (a species claim); claims themselves are definitions or descriptions of inventions and thus are not 'species' in and of themselves.
guidance: Species always refer to different embodiments; determine whether species are independent or related as disclosed (see MPEP §806.04 and §806.04(b)).

name: Generic claim presented after issuance of species — double patenting risk
description: If a generic claim is presented after issuance of a patent claiming one or more species within the scope of the generic claim, the Office may reject the generic claim on obviousness-type double patenting grounds when there is at least one common inventor/owner (or joint research agreement).
guidance: Applicant may overcome such rejection by filing a terminal disclaimer. See cited Federal Circuit authorities (e.g., In re Goodman) and MPEP §804.

name: Related inventions — principal distinctness test
description: Where two or more related inventions are claimed, determine whether the inventions as claimed are distinct; if they are distinct, restriction may be proper; if not distinct, restriction is never proper.
guidance: For inventions in different statutory categories, generally only one-way distinctness is needed to support restriction; some relationships (e.g., combination/subcombination, related products/processes) may require two-way distinctness (see MPEP §806.05(c) and §806.05(j)).

name: Combination and subcombination distinctness criteria
description: To support restriction between combination and subcombination inventions, both two-way distinctness and reasons for insisting on restriction are necessary (e.g., there would be a serious search burden evidenced by separate classification or field of search). The inventions are distinct if: (A) the combination as claimed does not require the particulars of the subcombination as claimed for patentability, and (B) the subcombination can be shown to have utility either by itself or in another materially different combination.
guidance: If the combination requires the details of the subcombination, inventions are not distinct and restriction must not be required. Use examples (ABsp/ABbr/Bsp diagrams) and form paragraphs (e.g., 8.15) when drafting restriction requirements. If combination claims are amended to require the subcombination particulars, maintainers should withdraw earlier restriction.

name: Subcombinations usable together — restriction criteria
description: Two or more claimed subcombinations disclosed as usable together in a single combination, and which can be shown to be separately usable, are usually restrictable when the subcombinations do not overlap in scope and are not obvious variants.
guidance: Support restriction by demonstrating two-way distinctness and a serious search burden (e.g., separate classification). Presence of claims to multiple subcombinations can be evidence that the details of one are not required for patentability of a combination. Upon allowance of an elected combination or subcombination, the examiner must reconsider and rejoin allowable claims in accordance with MPEP §821.04.

name: Novel combination versus mere improvement
description: If a combination of parts existed before up to a given point, and the inventor's contribution merely takes up at that point and adds further combinations, then if the subsequent combinations alone are his invention the former combinations give him no right; if he has only invented an improvement of the old engine his specification claiming the whole will be bad. If, however, he has invented a machine consisting of a perfectly new conformation of parts (though all parts were used before), he is entitled to a patent for a new machine.
guidance: Determine whether the invention is an improvement of an existing engine or a new engine by virtue of a new conformation of parts; if only an improvement, claiming the whole machine is objectionable and will render the specification bad. Jury/verdict implications illustrated by the Browne example.

name: Description sufficiency for methods and principles
description: A principle cannot be the object of a patent. A method merely as such is not a proper subject unless the patent is in fact granted for tangible means of carrying that method into practice. If a method is claimed, the description must be very accurate: so clear and evident that no experiments are necessary to learn it and to put it in practice as beneficially as the patentee enjoys it.
guidance: Treat descriptions of methods like descriptions of manufactures or machines: provide tangible means and such accuracy/detail that a skilled person needs no experimentation to practice the method.

name: Effect of claiming known matter and statutory disclaimer/remedy
description: It was a technical rule that if the inventor claims anything in the title or specification which is not new, the whole patent became void. The Act (5 & 6 William IV c.83) altered this: a grantee may enter a disclaimer of any part of the title or specification, stating the reason, or enter a memorandum of any alteration not extending the exclusive right; disclaimers or alterations, when filed and enrolled, are deemed part of the letters-patent/specification in all courts. Caveats may be entered against such disclaimers/alterations; the attorney-general/solicitor-general may require advertisement of the disclaimer. The entry of a disclaimer under this Act does not give a right of action for infringements committed previously to the disclaimer.
guidance: If non-new material is claimed, use statutory mechanisms (disclaimer/memorandum of alteration) rather than risking entire patent invalidation. Be aware of caveat rights, advertising requirements, and limitations of using disclaimers as retroactive cures for past infringements.

name: Caveat interference procedure and timelines
description: If another person applies for a patent within one year for an invention which may in any respect interfere with the caveat, the commissioner must deposit the application materials in confidential archives and give notice by mail to the caveat filer, who then has three months after notice to file description, specifications, drawings, and model; if specifications of claim interfere, like proceedings to interfering applications may follow.
guidance: Filing a caveat triggers a statutory notice/response procedure and can lead to interference proceedings; ensure timely filing of full materials upon notification.

name: Reissue/renewal for defective or insufficient specification
description: Whenever a patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective or insufficient description or specification, or by claiming more than the patentee had right to claim, and the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake without fraudulent intent, the commissioner may, upon surrender of the patent and payment of fifteen dollars, cause a new patent to be issued to the inventor for the residue of the unexpired term in accordance with the patentee's corrected description and specification. In case of death or assignment, the right vests in executors, administrators, or assignees. The reissued patent and corrected specification have the same effect in law as if originally filed in corrected form.
guidance: Use surrender-and-reissue to cure inadvertent defects or overbroad claims (non-fraudulent). Pay the statutory $15 and follow the statutory recording/annexing procedures. Reissue is a statutory remedy but commissioner review and revision of claims applies.

name: Commissioner's revision, restrictions, and applicant remedies on reissue/addition
description: Whenever application is made for an addition of a newly-discovered improvement or for re-issue, the specification of claim annexed shall be subject to revision and restriction in the same manner as original applications. The commissioner will not add the improvement or grant re-issue until the applicant has entered a disclaimer or altered his specification of claim in accordance with the commissioner's decision; the applicant, if dissatisfied, shall have the same remedy and privileges as in original applications.
guidance: Expect examination and possible requirement to disclaim or amend claims on reissue/annexation; administrative decision subject to statutory review remedies but commissioner has primary authority.

name: Effect and scope of a renewed patent
description: When a patent is renewed (reissued), it is granted for the unexpired term commencing from the date of the original patent which is surrendered, and consequently operates from the commencement of the original and will enure to the benefit of assignees who became such before the renewal. An inventor in a renewed patent may omit a part of his original invention and retain only what he deems fit to retain; a renewed patent claiming less than the original may nevertheless be valid.
guidance: Reissue dates back to the original grant for term computation and benefits prior assignees; patentees may narrow claims/omit parts in renewal without necessarily injuring their rights.

name: Disclaimers to cure overbroad claims
description: Specifications may be amended by filing a disclaimer whenever, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, the original claim was too broad, claiming more than that of which the patentee was the original or first inventor, provided some material and substantial part of the thing patented is justly and truly his own. Such a disclaimer may be filed in the patent office by the patentee, his administrator, executors, and assigns.
guidance: File statutory disclaimers to narrow overbroad claims (non-fraudulent situations) to preserve the valid portion of the patent; disclaimers can be entered by the patentee or successors.

name: Visual disclaimers and use of dotted lines
description: To claim protection for only part of a product, visual disclaimers can be used—commonly dotted lines or color shading indicate excluded parts; WIPO allows dotted lines or color shading as visual disclaimers.
guidance: Interpretation varies by jurisdiction: EU and Japan allow dotted lines to show context without claiming it; USPTO may treat such reference views as normal views (risking refusal). Dotted lines can be interpreted as part of the design (e.g., stitching) in EU practice. Alternatives include color shading, blurring, or boundary outlines. EUIPO does not accept verbal disclaimers; UKIPO does. Avoid ambiguous dotted lines (Apple v Samsung example).

name: Claim interpretation (broadest reasonable interpretation / BRI)
description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation, claim terms are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art; preambles do not necessarily add limitations; wherein/contingent clauses cannot be disregarded; system claims require the structure for performing a recited function to be present.
guidance: Use MPEP 2111. Consider the specification to construe terms (e.g., memory, display, processor are known classes of structures). Contingent limitations in system and process claims must be given weight (see MPEP 2111.04(II)). The same claim interpretation must be used across eligibility, definiteness, novelty, obviousness, written description analyses. Examples: wherein clauses carrying patentable weight; contingent step (d) producing multiple embodiments under the BRI—anticipation analysis need only target one embodiment.

name: Step 2B — Significantly more / inventive concept analysis
description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited judicial exception — i.e., whether any additional element or combination adds an inventive concept.
guidance: Re-evaluate elements previously deemed 'insignificant extra-solution activity' with regard to whether those elements are well-known or routine; if they are well-known, they cannot supply an inventive concept. Mere instructions to apply an exception on a computer (memory/display/processor) generally do not supply 'significantly more.' Use MPEP 2106.05 and relevant Federal Circuit case law (e.g., Credit Acceptance, Trading Technologies, FairWarning).

name: Role of generic computer components
description: Recitation of generic computer components (e.g., processor, memory, display) does not negate the mental nature of claim limitations when the computer is merely used as a tool to perform the mental process.
guidance: Generic computer hardware recited at a high level is often treated as 'mere instructions to apply the judicial exception on a computer' and does not improve computer functionality. Cite Alice, Credit Acceptance, and related MPEP discussion.

name: Field-of-use / token limitation does not make an abstract idea patent eligible
description: Limitations that merely link the claim to a particular field (e.g., livestock management) are token field-of-use restrictions and do not integrate an abstract idea into a practical application.
guidance: Analogy to Bilski: identifying participants or application area without technical improvement does not make the claim eligible (MPEP 2106.05(h)).

name: Automation of human mental processes is insufficient absent technical improvement
description: Automating mental processes using generic computer components, even if improving convenience or daily life, does not constitute an improvement to computer functionality or other technology and thus does not render the claim eligible.
guidance: Cite cases where improved speed or convenience from a general-purpose computer was insufficient (e.g., Credit Acceptance, Trading Technologies, FairWarning, Trading Technologies Int'l v. IBG). The claim must change the computer or other technology in a meaningful way.

name: Particular treatment or prophylaxis consideration
description: A claim invokes the 'particular treatment or prophylaxis' consideration only if it affirmatively recites an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: If the claim only detects a condition but does not affirmatively perform the treatment (e.g., does not actually dispense therapeutics), the treatment/prophylaxis consideration does not apply (see practice note referencing Ino Therapeutics). However, combining detection with automatic control of equipment to effect treatment may invoke the 'other meaningful limitation' consideration and support eligibility.

name: Practice note for drafting / issuing rejections
description: When issuing a rejection under the eligibility framework, identify the specific limitations that embody the judicial exception and explain why they are abstract; explain why the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.
guidance: Cite supportive court decisions where appropriate (e.g., CyberSource, University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics, Electric Power Group). Explain which elements are insignificant extra-solution activity and whether any element adds a meaningful limitation or inventive concept. Provide clear linkage to the claim language (e.g., point to limitations (a) and (b)).

name: Contingent claim limitations and embodiment breadth under BRI
description: Contingent limitations create alternative embodiments under the broadest reasonable interpretation; the claim may encompass multiple distinct embodiments and a prior art reference need only teach one embodiment to anticipate the claim.
guidance: See MPEP 2111.04(II). Example: a contingent step that routes animals in certain conditions creates embodiments where only one or both contingent actions occur; all such embodiments are encompassed by the claim under BRI and must be considered for novelty/anticipation.

name: Applicable periods and applications of these Guidelines
description: Specification of which versions of the Examination Guidelines apply to examinations and the effective dates (e.g., Guidelines effective on and after October 1, 2015; previous Guidelines remain effective for examinations on or before September 30, 2015).
guidance: Guidelines include revision history and special applicability rules (see linked page for product-by-process claims and patent term extension grandfathering).

name: Procedures of Examination
description: Detailed procedures to be followed during examination.
guidance: See Chapter 2 (Procedures of Examination) for sectioned procedures including specification of claimed invention, prior art search, notice of reasons for refusal, handling of written opinions/amendments, decisions, appeals, communications, etc.

name: Enablement Requirement (Patent Act Article 36(4)(i))
description: Description must enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention as claimed (enablement requirement).
guidance: See Part II Chapter 1 Section 1 for examples, required level of detail, and how enablement is assessed (PDF).

name: Support Requirement (Claims) (Patent Act Article 36(6)(i))
description: Claims must be supported by the description — claims should not claim subject-matter beyond what is described.
guidance: See Part II Chapter 2 Section 2 for tests of support, examples, and anti-patterns (PDF).

name: Clarity Requirement (Claims) (Patent Act Article 36(6)(ii))
description: Claims must be clear; ambiguous wording or indefinite terms that obscure the scope are objectionable.
guidance: See Part II Chapter 2 Section 3 for examples of unclear claim language and how examiners evaluate clarity (PDF).

name: Conciseness Requirement (Claims) (Patent Act Article 36(6)(iii))
description: Claims should be concise and not include unnecessary repetition or superfluous elements.
guidance: See Part II Chapter 2 Section 4 for guidance on claim drafting to meet conciseness requirements (PDF).

name: Ministerial Ordinance Requirement on Statement of Claims (Patent Act Article 36(6)(iv))
description: Formal requirements for the statement/format of claims as prescribed by ministerial ordinance.
guidance: See Part II Chapter 2 Section 5 for the specific ministerial ordinance requirements (PDF).

name: Parts, Form, and Content of Application
description: Requirements governing the required parts of an application (specification, claims, drawings, oath/decl.), formatting, and substantive content requirements.

name: Arrangement of the Sections of the Specification
description: The specification of a utility application should include the listed sections in order (a) TITLE OF THE INVENTION; (b) CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS; (c) STATEMENT REGARDING FEDERALLY SPONSORED RESEARCH OR DEVELOPMENT; (d) THE NAMES OF THE PARTIES TO A JOINT RESEARCH AGREEMENT; (e) INCORPORATION-BY-REFERENCE OF MATERIAL SUBMITTED ON A COMPACT DISC OR AS A TEXT FILE VIA EFS-WEB; (f) STATEMENT REGARDING PRIOR DISCLOSURES BY THE INVENTOR OR A JOINT INVENTOR; (g) BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION; (h) BRIEF SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION; (i) BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE SEVERAL VIEWS OF THE DRAWING(S); (j) DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION; (k) CLAIM OR CLAIMS (commencing on a separate sheet); (l) ABSTRACT OF THE DISCLOSURE (commencing on a separate sheet); (m) SEQUENCE LISTING.
guidance: Each lettered item should appear in upper case as a section heading; if no text follows a heading, state 'Not Applicable'. See 37 CFR 1.77(b). Claims and abstract must commence on separate sheets. See MPEP cross-references for design, plant, and reissue applications.

name: Detailed Description of the Invention (enablement and sufficiency)
description: Describe preferred embodiment(s) required by 37 CFR 1.71 in such particularity as to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation and to clearly convey enough information to show that applicant invented the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Description should be as short and specific as necessary. Conventional elements need not be described in detail unless not widely known. Where complexity warrants, refer to another patent or readily available publication. Reference characters must be properly applied (no single character used for two different parts). The description serves as a dictionary for the claims and must provide clear support or antecedent basis for all claim terms. See MPEP § 608.01(g) and cross-references.

name: Claims: Statutory Requirement and Structure
description: The specification must conclude with claims 'particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming' the subject matter inventor regards as the invention (35 U.S.C. 112). Claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the specification and claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description.
guidance: More than one claim permitted if they differ substantially and are not unduly multiplied. Dependent claims are permitted and must refer back; multiple dependent claims have special rules (refer only in the alternative, cannot be basis for another multiple dependent claim). For fee purposes, multiple dependent and dependent-from-multiple-dependent claims are treated by number of references. See 37 CFR 1.75 and MPEP § 608.01(i).

name: Claims: Form and Ordering for Improvements
description: Where applicable (e.g., improvement claims), an independent claim should contain in the following order: (1) a preamble comprising a general description of all elements/steps that are conventional or known; (2) a phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises'; (3) those elements/steps/relationships considered new or improved.
guidance: Suggested order to clarify which portions are known and which are claimed as improvement. See MPEP § 608.01(i)(e).

name: Claims: Commencement, Indentation and Separation
description: Claims must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page; where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step should be separated by a line indentation. There may be plural indentations to further segregate subcombinations or related steps.

name: Least Restrictive Claim as Claim 1 and Grouping of Dependent Claims
description: The least restrictive claim should be presented as claim number 1, and all dependent claims should be grouped together with the claim(s) to which they refer to the extent practicable.
guidance: Facilitates examination and clarity. See MPEP § 608.01(i)(g).

name: Abstract of the Disclosure: Language and Format
description: The abstract should be in narrative form and generally limited to a single paragraph preferably within the range of 50 to 150 words (preferably not exceeding 150 words). The abstract should not exceed 15 lines of text. Avoid claim legal phraseology (e.g., 'means', 'said') and avoid repeating information given in the title or using phrases that can be implied (e.g., 'This disclosure concerns').
guidance: Form paragraph 6.16.01 may be used if the abstract does not commence on a separate sheet. Examiners should check overlength abstracts for conciseness. Abstract is part of the specification for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 112 (In re Armbruster). See MPEP § 608.01(b)(C)-(D).

name: Drawings: Standards for Media, Color, and Photographs
description: Black-and-white drawings (India ink or equivalent) are normally required. Color drawings are permitted in design applications and rarely in utility applications upon petition and meeting conditions. Photographs are not ordinarily permitted but are acceptable if they are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention; color photographs follow color drawing rules.
guidance: Color drawings in utility apps require a petition with fee, one set via EFS-Web or three sets otherwise, and insertion of prescribed language in the brief description of the drawings. Color must be reproducible in black-and-white in printed patent. Photographs must be of sufficient quality so that all details are reproducible in the printed patent. See 37 CFR 1.84 and MPEP § 608.01(f).

name: Completeness of the Specification
description: For completeness of the specification, ensure all required sections, references to drawings, disclosure of best mode, and support for claim terms are present so that the specification provides adequate support for prosecution and establishment of disclosure.
guidance: See cross-references to MPEP §§ 608.01(p), 2161, 2162, 1302.01, 2111.01 and related guidance throughout the specification sections.

name: Benefit of earlier foreign filing; right of priority (35 U.S.C. 119)
description: An application filed in the U.S. by a person who previously regularly filed an application for the same invention in a foreign country (that affords similar privileges or is a WTO member) shall have the same effect as if filed on the date of the foreign filing if the U.S. application is filed within 12 months from the earliest foreign filing date. The Director may by regulation permit an additional 2 months if the delay was unintentional.
guidance: Substantial details and requirements: (b) a timely claim for priority identifying the foreign application number, authority/country, and filing date must be filed when required by the Director; failure to timely claim may be considered a waiver, but the Director may accept unintentionally delayed claims and may require a certified copy, translation, and other information; (c) right may be based on a subsequent foreign application under conditions (earlier application withdrawn/abandoned and not laid open); (d) inventors' certificates treated like patent applications for priority; (e) provisions for provisional applications (12‑month benefit to nonprovisional if filed within 12 months, must contain specific reference to provisional; Director may permit 2‑month unintentional delay; provisional reliance limited if required fee unpaid; timing rules for weekend/holiday falling on 12‑month day); (f) plant breeder rights in WTO/UPOV countries treated similarly; (g) definitions (WTO member, UPOV). Also includes amendment and certification requirements and potential fees (section 41(a)(7)).

name: Confidentiality and publication of applications (35 U.S.C. 122)
description: Applications shall be kept in confidence by the Office except as provided in subsection (b). Subject to paragraph (2), each application shall be published promptly after 18 months from the earliest filing date for which a benefit is sought; applicant may request earlier publication. No information concerning published patent applications shall be made available to the public except as the Director determines; Director's determination to release or not to release is final and nonreviewable.
guidance: Exceptions to publication: (b)(2)(A) application no longer pending; subject to secrecy order under section 181; a provisional application; or a design patent application. Nonpublication request (b)(2)(B)(i): applicant can request nonpublication upon filing certifying that no corresponding foreign/ international application that requires 18‑month publication will be filed; rescission allowed; if applicant later files abroad, they must notify Director within 45 days or application is regarded as abandoned. Redacted publication allowed when applicant has foreign filings with narrower descriptions; Director may publish redacted copy and section 154(d) doesn't apply to claims not enabled by redacted description. (d) National security: no publication if detrimental; Director to maintain secrecy under chapter 17.

name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103 (KSR/Graham framework)
description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. Apply the Graham factual inquiries (scope/content of prior art; differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; level of ordinary skill; objective indicia) and KSR’s flexible approach.
guidance: Must show more than separate references that each disclose separate limitations — there must be a motivation to combine and a reasonable expectation of success. Obviousness requires that a person of ordinary skill would have selected and combined prior art elements in the normal course of research to yield the claimed invention (Unigene Labs.). Consider objective indicia (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others) when available. The inquiry is expansive and flexible (KSR).

name: Graham factors / factual inquiries for obviousness
description: The obviousness inquiry is resolved based on underlying factual determinations: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others).
guidance: Address each factor; objective indicia can weigh against obviousness but must be tied to the merits of the claimed invention. The sequence of questions can vary, but the factors control the inquiry.

name: When to construe a term (Nidec/Vivid principle)
description: Terms need only be construed if they are in controversy and construction is necessary to resolve the controversy.
guidance: Avoid unnecessary claim construction; construe specific terms (e.g., 'treating a coagulopathy') when their meaning may affect the outcome.

name: Use of intrinsic evidence and specification admissions
description: Intrinsic evidence (specification, claims, prosecution history) is primary for claim construction and for assessing obviousness; admissions in the specification may be relied upon when assessing obviousness.
guidance: Cite and apply express definitions in the specification (e.g., definition of 'treat' in the patent). Admissions in the specification can support a person of ordinary skill’s expectations and may be used against the patentee (Koninklijke Philips).

name: Construction of 'treating a coagulopathy' (case-specific claim construction)
description: The patent expressly defines 'treat' or 'treatment' as 'the prophylaxis and/or therapy and/or cure of this pathology,' and states therapy includes 'partial or total alleviation of the disease symptoms.' The Board construed 'treating a coagulopathy' to include prophylaxis and/or therapy and/or cure, including partial alleviation of symptoms, for any duration of therapeutic efficacy.
guidance: Dependent claims (e.g., claim 16 reciting reduction/prevention of hemorrhages) can support a broader construction that encompasses partial symptom alleviation; absence of a duration requirement in the specification means duration is not required by the claim.

name: Written description requirement for § 112(a) and priority
description: To claim the filing date of an earlier application (§ 119(e), § 120), the earlier application must disclose the claimed invention in the manner provided by § 112(a). The hallmark of written description is disclosure: the specification must convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention (Ariad; Lockwood).
guidance: Written description requires more than what would render the invention obvious; it must show possession of the claimed subject matter as of the earlier filing date. General statements or desires are insufficient; concrete disclosure or examples are often necessary to support specific claim limitations.

name: Proof required to claim priority (procedural/documentary requirements)
description: To rely on earlier foreign or domestic applications for priority, applicants must present the earlier application disclosure in a manner that satisfies §112(a) and provide necessary documentary evidence (e.g., English translations where required).
guidance: Failure to provide English translations of earlier non-English applications during prosecution can undermine a priority claim; the record must show the earlier disclosure adequately supports the later-claimed limitations.

name: Written examples/data to support quantitative claim limitations
description: Claims reciting quantitative limitations (e.g., expression levels, dosing ranges) require earlier disclosures that reasonably convey possession of those numerical ranges or show how to achieve them; mere general statements without examples may be insufficient.
guidance: Absence of gene therapy examples or numerical data in earlier applications weighs against finding written description support for specific expression levels or dose ranges. Expert testimony may help, but cannot substitute for an earlier disclosure that conveys possession.

name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)
description: A claim is anticipated if a single prior art reference discloses every limitation of the claimed invention (as of the relevant priority date); prior art published before the effective date is §102 prior art.
guidance: Identify whether the prior reference (e.g., Monahan) is prior art based on effective date/priority; compare specific claim limitations to the single reference’s disclosure. Where priority date is disputed, resolution of priority affects whether a reference is §102 prior art.

name: Burden and standard of proof in PTAB IPR final decision
description: At final written decision, the petitioner must show unpatentability of the challenged claims by a preponderance of the evidence under 35 U.S.C. § 318(a).
guidance: The Board weighs the totality of evidence — prior art, specification disclosures, expert declarations, deposition testimony, and trial record — and issues a final determination addressing all claims challenged by the petitioner (SAS Inst.).

name: Determination of invention based on claim limitations (applicant’s will)
description: The determination of the invention for which patent protection is sought shall be made based on the limitations recited in each of the claims in accordance with the applicant’s will. The description or drawings shall be considered only when the claims are indefinite or the definition and meaning of technical terms are ambiguous. The abstract cannot be used to decide the protection scope of the invention.
guidance: Do not determine protection scope from the description beyond the claim limitations. Use the description/drawings only to resolve claim indefiniteness or ambiguity of technical terms; never use the abstract to set scope.

name: Unsupported: claim subject matter neither disclosed nor implied in description
description: A claim is not supported where the subject matters or limitations of the claims are neither disclosed nor implied in the description of the invention.
guidance: Examples: reciting specific numerical limitations not present in the description; reciting use of an ultrasonic motor when the description only discloses a direct current motor. Exception: if the description indicates other motors can be used and, based on ordinary skill, practicing with the alternative motor is possible, the claim may be supported.

name: Unsupported: ambiguous correspondence between claim terms and description terms
description: A claim is not supported where terms used in the claims are different from those used in the description so that correspondence is ambiguous.
guidance: If the mapping between claim terms and the description is unclear to a skilled person, support is lacking. Ensure consistent terminology or clear mappings in the description.

name: Unsupported: functional means/steps without disclosed specific configuration
description: Where the claims recite means or steps to perform particular functions but the specific configuration corresponding to such means or steps is not disclosed in the description, the claims lack support.
guidance: Claims that invoke functional language must be grounded by corresponding structural/configurational disclosure unless the functional language is otherwise made clear by the specification.

name: Unsupported: omitting indispensable features described as necessary to solve technical problem
description: Claims that do not recite features explained in the description as indispensable to solve the technical problem are not supported, because a skilled person cannot recognize the claimed invention from the description.
guidance: Example: description states a specific property (e.g., low water content cream) is required to achieve the effect, but the claim states only 'cream' without the property; the indispensable feature must be claimed or support is lacking.

name: Clear and concise statement of the invention required (Article 42(4)(ii))
description: Claims must set forth the claimed invention clearly and concisely so they can determine the scope of protection and enable assessment of patentability. This is judged by a person skilled in the art in light of the claims, description, drawings and the level of skill at filing.
guidance: Conciseness refers to claim language (not the breadth of the inventive idea). Do not rely on parts other than the claims to determine clarity and conciseness.

name: Not clear/concise: unclear claim language
description: A claim is unclear where its language is unclear. However, a mere clerical error that does not lead a skilled person to find the invention unclear (given description/drawings/skill level) is not deemed unclear.
guidance: If unclear wording can be resolved by the description or drawings so the invention is understandable by a skilled person, do not find violation. Otherwise, notify ground for rejection.

name: Not clear/concise: listing elements without relationships
description: Where each claim element is merely listed but the relationships between the elements are not recited, the invention is unclear.
guidance: Claims must specify how elements relate; avoid mere enumerations that leave the overall configuration ambiguous.

name: Not clear/concise: unclear category of claimed invention
description: Where the category (e.g., product vs method) to which the claimed invention belongs is unclear, the claim is not concise/clear.
guidance: As a principle, determine category based on terms/expressions used at the end of the claim; if difficult, deem ambiguous. For products, explain structure/function; for methods, explain steps. Clarify claim endings to indicate category.

name: Not clear/concise: overly lengthy or repetitive claim language
description: Claim language that is too lengthy, including repetition of the same matter, may render the subject matter unclear and not concise.
guidance: Avoid unnecessary repetition; craft succinct claim language specifying necessary limitations only.

name: Not clear/concise: unclear expressions or vague qualifiers
description: Use of expressions that make the configuration unclear (e.g., 'at one's will', 'if necessary', 'in particular', 'for example', 'and/or') or vague comparative/degree terms ('mainly', 'appropriate', 'about', 'approximately') or unclear negative limitations ('except for') can render claims unclear.
guidance: Where such expressions cause multiple contrasting inventions to be claimed or ambiguity (e.g., 'and/or'), examine whether description clarifies meaning; otherwise consider ground for rejection. For numerical limitations lacking explicit min/max ('more than', '0~10', dual ranges in one claim) ensure precise numeric bounds.

name: Not clear/concise: unclear subject of indication (reference antecedent issues)
description: Claims become unclear when the indicated subject (antecedent) is ambiguous (e.g., many gears recited and later references like 'said gear' don't specify which).
guidance: Use clear antecedent basis and unambiguous reference terms (or explicit reference numerals) so a skilled person can identify the referenced element.

name: Not clear/concise: same expression used for different functions without specification
description: When multiple technical terms of the same expression serving different functions are used in the claims without specifying different functions or indicating corresponding reference numerals, the invention is unclear.
guidance: Differentiate identical terms that play different roles (e.g., via reference numerals or explicit function labels) to avoid ambiguity.

name: Not clear/concise: inclusion of irrelevant non-technical matters
description: Claims that recite matters irrelevant to technical configuration (e.g., commercial benefits, regions/places of sale) render the invention unclear and not concise.
guidance: Exclude commercial/marketing information from claim language; focus on technical configuration.

name: Not clear/concise: defining by reference to description/drawings without reciting configuration
description: Claims defined solely by reference to the description or drawings without reciting the configuration may be unclear; however, reference is allowed where inevitable (e.g., alloys where special relations cannot be described only in words).
guidance: Use reference to drawings only when necessary and ensure the reference permits a skilled person to ascertain the claimed configuration.

name: Clerical errors: exceptions and examiner handling
description: Certain clerical errors are not deemed violations of Article 42(4)(ii) and should not be grounds for rejection: (i) 'said OOO' lacking antecedent but invention clear when read excluding 'said'; (ii) slight non-identical terms deemed corresponding by meaning; (iii) claims depending on deleted claims but still understandable when dependencies are adjusted.
guidance: When clerical errors are present and the invention is clearly understood, the examiner should make an ex officio amendment (if no other rejection grounds exist). If other rejection grounds exist, recommend amendment as 'Matters to be noted' when notifying rejection. If uncertain whether case falls under clerical error, notify ground for rejection to allow applicant response. If after response the claim clearly falls under clerical error, do not reject; make ex officio amendment.

name: Markush-type claim requirements (grouping of alternatives not indefinite)
description: A Markush-type claim selecting alternatives from a group does not render the claim indefinite if all inventions configured by selecting an alternative possess a similar property or function.
guidance: For chemical substances a Markush grouping is acceptable only if (①) all alternatives share a common property/vitality and (②) they share important chemical structure or belong to a group deemed one group in the pertinent art. The same principle may apply in other technical fields (machine, electricity).

name: Functional limitations: when permitted and examiner determination
description: Claims that include functional limitations reciting a function or effect are not allowed if the configuration is not deemed clear; functional claim language is permitted where (①) defining functionally is necessary because the technical idea cannot be set forth only by configuration (e.g., some biotech or computer-related inventions), or (②) the meaning of the functional limitation is clearly specified by the description or drawings.
guidance: The examiner must determine whether a skilled person can clearly understand the subject matter in light of the description/drawings and the level of skill at filing. If not clear, issue ground for rejection citing Article 42(4)(ii).

name: Product claims defined by manufacturing/process limitations
description: A product claim may define the product by the manufacturing method ('product manufactured by the method of...') and is not necessarily indefinite if the product's configuration or nature is clearly understood from the method limitation.
guidance: If the manufacturing method recited in a product claim is unclear even in light of the specification, drawings and ordinary skill at filing, notify rejection under Article 42(4)(ii). If the product's structure/nature cannot be understood from method limitation but the applicant must define by process due to circumstances or proves the process does not affect structure/nature, the examiner may consider the ground remedied and not reject.

name: Parameter inventions: when parameter claims are acceptable
description: Parameter inventions include parameters arbitrarily created by an applicant (not generally used in the art) or mathematical combinations of variables. Such inventions are generally not clear unless: (①) the technical meaning/definition of the parameter is clearly understood; (②) the inevitable reason for using the parameter is clearly shown; and (③) the relationship with the level of skill at filing is understood in light of the description/drawings and skill level.
guidance: To show the inevitable reason, include comparative examples satisfying and not satisfying the parameter, demonstrating relation between parameter and effect and solving the technical problem. Also include comparative examples for known materials or logical explanation so ordinary skill excludes known materials from the claimed invention. If the parameter's meaning/reason/skill relationship can be understood considering the level of skill at filing even if not explicit, do not deem unclear.

name: Composition ratio (%): numeric consistency requirements
description: For claims reciting composition ratios as percentages, certain numeric inconsistencies render the claimed configuration unclear: (①) sum of maximum ratios of all components under 100%; ② sum of minimum ratios of all components over 100%; ③ sum of max of one component and mins of others over 100%; ④ sum of min of one component and max of others under 100%.
guidance: Example: composition ranges that logically cannot sum to 100% make the invention unclear. For open claims using 'comprising', some percentage-sum problems may be acceptable because unspecified other components could make 100%.

name: Open 'comprising' claims can mitigate percentage-sum issues
description: In open claims ('comprising~') which may include unspecified other components, cases where sums would otherwise conflict with 100% (e.g., sum of maxima < 100% or sum of one min + others max <100%) may still be deemed clear because other components can bring total to 100%.
guidance: Consider claim phrasing ('comprising') when evaluating composition percentage consistency; do not automatically reject percentage-sum issues for open claims.

name: Use of parts by weight (phrasing) avoids percentage-sum requirement
description: When composition ratios are described as parts by weight, they do not need to satisfy the percentage-sum requirements applicable to percentages.
guidance: Parts by weight typically indicate relative amounts based on a reference component and allow conversion to relative ratios; such claims are generally considered clear even without a 100% sum check.

name: Alloy claims: composition ranges must sum to 100%
description: A claim directed to an alloy should set forth composition ranges so that the component ranges add up to 100%. Regardless of 'consisting of' or 'comprising', the total sum should not be over or under 100% for alloy claims.
guidance: Because alloy properties vary with additives, claims must not only list main components but also recite ranges for other additives as necessary. Example: an alloy claim whose component ranges cannot mathematically reach 100% is unclear and not accepted.

name: Claims should recite matters necessary to specify protection sought (Article 42(6))
description: Claims shall recite matters regarded necessary to specify what is sought for patent protection, such as structures, methods, functions, materials or combinations thereof. If an invention can be clearly specified, the applicant may choose how to set it forth.
guidance: This provision itself is not a ground for rejection or invalidation; examiners should not notify rejection based solely on this note.

name: Claim drafting requirements and multiple-claims system (Enforcement Decree Article 5)
description: The law prescribes how claims are drafted to ensure they determine the scope of protection. Korea adopts multiple claims where one or more claims directed to subject matters may be prepared.
guidance: Follow formal requirements for claim presentation and numbering to ensure clarity of scope per statutory drafting rules.

name: Discrimination criteria between independent and dependent claims
description: Dependent claims must narrow or add further limitations to specify an independent claim in terms of content of the invention. A claim that narrows or adds limitations but does not formally refer to the other claim(s) is not a dependent claim; conversely, a claim referring formally to an independent claim but not narrowing/adding limitations is not a dependent claim either.
guidance: Ensure dependent claims both (a) refer to another claim formally and (b) actually narrow or add limitations to that claim. Article 5(1) of the Enforcement Decree requires dependent claims to substantiate the independent claim by narrowing or adding limitations.

name: Enablement and definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112 (design claims)
description: A design patent is indefinite for § 112 purposes whenever its claim, read in light of the visual disclosure (whether it be a single drawing or multiple drawings), 'fail[s] to inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.' (In re Maatita, quoted).
guidance: Purpose is to give potential competitors (skilled in the art) notice of what design is claimed and what would infringe. Examiner should assess whether the disclosure (claim + visual disclosure) allows understanding the claimed design with reasonable certainty. Example: In re Maatita—court reversed PTAB and found the single plan view sufficient for that shoe-bottom design.

name: Ordinary observer perspective for assessing indefiniteness
description: In the design patent context, one skilled in the art would assess indefiniteness from the perspective of an ordinary observer. 'Thus, a design patent is indefinite under § 112 if one skilled in the art, viewing the design as would an ordinary observer, would not understand the scope of the design with reasonable certainty based on the claim and visual disclosure.' (In re Maatita, quoted).
guidance: When evaluating definiteness, consider how an ordinary observer (with skill in the art) would view the drawings and claim together. The test emphasizes notice to competitors and visual discernability rather than purely technical description.

name: Drawings/photographs should disclose complete appearance (MPEP 1503.02)
description: The drawings and photographs should contain a sufficient number of views to disclose the complete appearance of the design claimed. (MPEP 1503.02; cited in Maatita takeaways).
guidance: Some designs may be capable of being understood from a single, two-dimensional plan view (e.g., bath mat). There is no per se rule that a single plan view is insufficient; sufficiency depends on whether three-dimensional aspects are being claimed and whether the visual disclosure gives an ordinary observer reasonable certainty about scope.

name: Indicators that three-dimensional aspects are being claimed
description: The following application content may indicate that three-dimensional aspects are being claimed and therefore a single plan view may not be sufficient: (1) the article identified in the claim and shown in solid lines in the figures is inherently three-dimensional; (2) the application includes multiple figures showing the claimed design from various points of view; and/or (3) the application includes a figure(s) with surface shading to show the contour of 3D aspects.
guidance: These are exemplary considerations; they may not all apply in every situation, and there may be additional considerations. Use these factors to determine whether additional views or shading are necessary to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112.

name: No per se rule equating a single plan view with indefiniteness/non-enablement
description: There is no per se rule that a design claim will, or will not, always meet the enablement and definiteness requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 when the claimed design is visually disclosed using a single, two dimensional plan view.
guidance: Examiner must consider the nature of the article and other factors (e.g., inherent 3D nature, shading, additional views) rather than automatically rejecting single-view disclosures. Knowledge check explicitly: 'False. There is no per se rule equating a single plan view with indefiniteness and lack of enablement.'

name: Title of the application and claim language may define article of manufacture and limit claim scope
description: The title of the design identifies the article in which the design is embodied by the name generally known and used by the public and may contribute to defining the scope of the claim. Claim language can limit the scope where the article of manufacture is identified in the claim but not in the figures. (Curver Luxembourg v. Home Expressions; MPEP 1503.01(II)).
guidance: If the title/claim recites an article (e.g., 'Pattern for a chair'), the claimed design can be limited to that article even if similar surface ornamentation appears elsewhere. During examination, consider whether the title/claim constrains scope and whether the article is shown in figures.

name: Design is inseparable from the article of manufacture (design not a freestanding ornamentation)
description: A design is inseparable from the article to which it is applied, and cannot exist alone merely as a scheme of surface ornamentation. Design patents are granted only for a design applied to an article of manufacture, and not a design per se. (Curver cited).
guidance: When examining, treat the claimed design as embodied in the recited article. If the application fails to establish an article of manufacture in the figures or claim, consider rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112 (nonenable/indefinite) and/or 35 U.S.C. 171.

name: Claim scope limited to the recited and depicted article of manufacture (In re SurgiSil)
description: A design claim is limited to the article of manufacture identified in the claim; it does not broadly cover a design in the abstract. The claim identifies a lip implant; therefore the claim is limited to lip implants and does not cover other articles of manufacture. (In re SurgiSil, quoted).
guidance: Do not disregard the claim language when applying prior art in an anticipation rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102. The claimed article (as recited and depicted) defines the universe of potentially anticipating prior art.

name: Comparator rule for anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102: article-of-manufacture match required
description: When considering an anticipation rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, examiners should identify the article of manufacture recited in the claim language and depicted in the figure and compare it to the reference article of manufacture. The reference may only be used as prior art under § 102 if it is the same article (or reasonably can be considered the same article).
guidance: Decision tree: identify claimed article; compare to reference article; if YES (same article) reference may be appropriate prior art under § 102; if NO, reference cannot be used as prior art; if NOT SURE, consult design supervisors. Examples: cookie vs shoe deodorizer = NOT the same (no anticipation); syringe vs 'medical device' = 'medical device' can reasonably encompass syringe (anticipation possible); mop handle vs jump-rope handle = both are 'handle' (anticipation possible). Note: intended use does not necessarily limit the article (In re Zonenstein—patentability of design cannot be predicated on utility).

name: Consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 when article of manufacture not established
description: During examination, where the article of manufacture does not appear anywhere in the figures, examiners should consider whether to reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112 for being nonenabled and indefinite, and/or under 35 U.S.C. 171 for not establishing an article of manufacture. (Curver takeaways).
guidance: If the drawings only show a pattern or ornamentation without an identifiable article, determine whether the application sufficiently establishes an article of manufacture; if not, a § 171 rejection (or § 112 as applicable) may be appropriate.

name: Particular treatment or prophylaxis requirement
description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
guidance: Examples of positive limitations: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient' or 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient.' Anti-examples: intended-use language or field-of-use language (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid to a patient with eczema'—not positive because it does not require actual use; 'pharmaceutical composition' or 'feed dispenser is operable to dispense' are not affirmative). Examiners should ensure the limitation actually provides treatment/prophylaxis rather than merely indicating intended use.

name: Factor b — More-than-nominal relationship to the exception
description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s).
guidance: Example: a claim reciting a natural correlation between high blood glucose and ketoacidosis plus 'treating a patient ... with insulin'—insulin materially reduces the risk and thus is significantly related. Counterexample: treating with aspirin (not known to treat ketoacidosis)—only at best a nominal connection and does not integrate the law of nature into a practical application. Examiners may consult considerations such as 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and 'field of use' when analyzing relationship strength.

name: Inventive concept principle (Step 2B) — cannot be the judicial exception itself
description: An inventive concept 'cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature (or natural phenomenon or abstract idea) itself.' An inventive concept must be an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception that ensures the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: The 'search for an inventive concept' requires identifying claim elements beyond the exception and assessing whether they render the claim 'significantly more.' See Alice and related cases.

name: Relevant consideration v — Adding a specific limitation beyond routine/conventional activity
description: Adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: non-conventional arrangement of computer components for filtering Internet content (BASCOM). See MPEP §2106.05(d).

name: How courts conduct Step 2B analysis (procedural steps)
description: Courts identify additional elements in the claim, consider those additional elements individually (e.g., are they well-understood, routine, conventional?), and then consider them as an ordered combination to determine if the combination adds 'significantly more.'
guidance: Alice example: Court identified computer functions/hardware as additional elements, found them individually generic, and found their ordered combination added nothing. BASCOM example: district court identified elements individually as generic but should have considered whether the combination produced a non-conventional, inventive arrangement. Use this three-step approach when conducting the inventive-concept inquiry.

name: Rejection‑free (first‑action) allowances are suspect
description: First-action allowances—particularly by senior examiners—are quality red flags absent unusual circumstances (very narrow claims, well-developed art unit precedent).
guidance: Treat first-action grants skeptically unless there is independent evidence (e.g., extremely narrow claims, clear prior precedent) explaining the lack of pushback.

name: Injunctions and expiration disputes
description: Where the date of the expiration of the patent is in dispute the court will not limit the injunction, but the defendant can move for a dissolution when the date at which he claims the patent must expire has arrived.
guidance: Courts avoid prematurely narrowing injunctions when expiration is contested; defendants have remedy to seek dissolution at the proper time.

name: Use of separately claimed parts
description: To use a separately claimed part of the invention is a contempt.
guidance: Even partial practice of claimed elements (if separately claimed) can violate an injunction forbidding the invention; courts have held that using separately claimed parts may be punished as contempt.

name: Procedure prior to search: analysis and use of application content
description: Before searching, the examiner shall analyze technical subject-matter of the invention; searches should be based on the claimed invention but the examiner shall pay due regard to the description and drawings if necessary. When the application cites documents, the examiner shall review them to determine whether they provide a starting point, show technology status, explain alternative solutions, or aid understanding.
guidance: If cited documents are not directly related, they may be disregarded. If necessary documents cannot be acquired by common methods, examiner shall request submission from applicant and defer examination until submission.

name: Conditions under which search is not required or is limited
description: No special search effort is needed or search may be limited where: ① amendment includes new matter (Patent Act Art.47); ② the claimed invention is not patentable under Article 32; ③ the claimed invention is incomplete or not industrially applicable under Article 29; ④ claims lack unity (Article 45) such that they do not relate to one invention or a linked group forming single inventive concept; ⑤ the examiner is unable to understand the invention due to lack of written description.
guidance: Examiner shall notify applicant if a meaningful search is impossible for some/all claims. If lack of unity, examiner may first notify lack-of-unity grounds and await applicant response. If invention can be understood despite specification deficiencies, proceed with search within that understanding.

name: Time coverage of search and reference dates
description: Primary rule: search documents published before the filing date (or, for priority applications, before the priority date). Exceptions: in exceptional cases search may extend to documents published after filing date for purposes of applying Articles 29(3),(4) or 36. For applications with priority claims, the basic reference date for each claim is the filing date of the application, but if documents published between earliest priority date and filing date are found, examiner shall determine reference date for each claim between priority date and filing date and then decide which documents to cite.
guidance: Documents published after filing date may be used as supporting material to confirm incorrectness/incompleteness of underlying facts. When reference dates are clear per claim, examiner may set priority date per claim and search by claim.

name: Suspension of search
description: Examiner may suspend the search when prior art clearly demonstrates lack of novelty or inventive step for the entire claimed invention. Also, if completing the search would require substantial time/energy, examiner shall devise most effective method to conduct thorough search within available time/cost and may suspend search if rational judgment fails to discover effective prior arts.
guidance: Suspension is permitted when further search is unlikely to change outcome or is impracticable given resources.

name: General principles of search (equivalents, dependent claims, categories)
description: Search should consider prior art incorporating technical features equivalent to claimed features in light of the description; equivalents are not limited to explicitly described technical features. Examiner conducts prior art search for dependent claims that fall within identical classification as the independent claim; dependent claims are interpreted as restricted by features of claims they depend on. When independent claim patentability is not questioned, no need to further search dependent claims. If application contains claims of different categories, all must be included in search, though if product claim is clearly novel/non-obvious, no special effort to search related process/use claims is needed.
guidance: Examples provided (e.g., welding interpreted to include gluing/riveting unless welding is essential). Examiner may search inventions stated in description but not claimed if no excessive effort required and applicant might amend to include them.

name: Classification/annotation of cited prior art relevance (X, Y, A, O, P, E, T, L)
description: Related prior art in search reports can be classified by relevance: ① 'X' — alone destroys novelty or inventive step; ② 'Y' — destroys inventive step when combined with other documents; ③ 'A' — related but not X or Y; ④ 'O' — oral disclosure/use/exhibition; ⑤ 'P' — published between international filing date and priority date; ⑥ 'E' — filed before international filing date but published after it; ⑦ 'T' — discloses principle/theory or disclosed later than priority/filing date of international application; ⑧ 'L' — may throw doubt on a priority claim or negate claimed invention or determine other contents.
guidance: Examiners should annotate citation sheets and ER with X/Y (at least) to indicate relevance.

name: Understanding of the invention for examination
description: Examiner shall clearly understand claimed subject matter in light of the specification by considering the problems to be solved, means for solving the problems, what differentiates from the background art, and effects of the invention. Examination proceeds based on the specification as originally filed but should take into account amendments made by the applicant prior to notice of rejection. Claims should be construed within general scope and meaning of the technical field unless specifically defined in the description.
guidance: Refer to Part V for confirmation methods for amended specifications; be cautious about construing claim terms beyond their logical meaning.

name: Review of prior art documents during substantive examination
description: Examiner shall determine whether retrieved prior art provides grounds for rejection regarding novelty, inventive step, enlarged concept of novelty or first-to-file application. Publication date is critical — examiner shall review bibliography to ascertain whether publication date precedes filing/priority date. Examiner shall have clear understanding of technical issues disclosed in prior art and be careful not to acknowledge matters not disclosed or to over-interpret claims without logical grounds.
guidance: Detailed guidance on publication dates and enlarged concept of novelty appears in other sections (e.g., Chapter II of Part 2).

name: Priority claim under treaty: entitlement, timing, reference date rules, and evidential documents
description: Entitlement: priority under the treaty may be claimed by the applicant who filed in a Treaty State or legitimate successor; examiner may request evidential documents proving legitimacy. Timing: treaty priority must be claimed within 12 months from earliest filing date; if claimed after statutory period, examiner requests amendment and may invalidate if not cured. Reference dates: where invention is identical (including substantially identical) to first-country application, reference date is filing date of first-country application; for matter not described in first-country application, reference date is filing date of application claiming priority. For multiple priorities, earliest filing date of first-country applications applicable for common inventions; claim-by-claim determination of reference date is principle. Evidential documents for priority must be submitted within one year and four months from earliest filing date; failure to submit within statutory period causes loss of priority effect; post-period submission does not cure deficiency. Copies of description/drawings may be exempt if on-line exchange systems between countries are available.
guidance: If application in first country claims priority based on an earlier application, that first-country application may not be regarded as the 'earliest application' under Paris Convention for inventions described in both; examiner should specify reasons when applying non-retroactivity in notice of grounds. Examiner should not examine whether the first-country application is pending. When evidential documents are missing, examiner requests procedural amendment and may invalidate procedure if not amended.

name: Drawings required where necessary (MPEP § 608.02)
description: Drawings are required where necessary for the understanding of the subject matter to be patented (MPEP § 608.02).
guidance: Determine whether a drawing is necessary to understand the claimed invention; drawings often determine whether claims are fully supported under 35 U.S.C. § 112.

name: Multiple views for utility patents
description: Utility patent illustrations should include multiple views: perspective, top, side, cross-sectional.
guidance: Provide all views necessary to show claimed features clearly. Cross-sectional views must be labeled and drawn to show internal structure; include perspective and orthogonal views as needed for full understanding.

name: Use of broken lines
description: Use broken lines only to show unclaimed environment or alternate positions (utility); in design patents use broken lines to disclaim unclaimed subject matter.
guidance: Broken lines should not be used to depict claimed features. For design applications, use broken/dashed lines to show contextual or non-claimed elements; misuse can lead to confusion and rejection.

name: Design patent drawings are the entire disclosure
description: Unlike utility applications, design patent drawings are the entire disclosure.
guidance: Because drawings constitute the whole of the disclosure for design patents, they must completely and clearly show the claimed visual appearance — omissions or ambiguities cannot be corrected by a written description.

name: Surface shading for design patents to show contour
description: Use appropriate surface shading to show contour in design patent drawings.
guidance: Apply shading techniques consistently and conservatively to indicate three-dimensional shape; improper or inconsistent shading can mislead the scope of the claimed design.

name: Ensure drawings show every feature described in the claims
description: For utility patents, illustrations must show every feature described in the claims.
guidance: Map claim language to drawing elements during drafting to ensure each claimed limitation is depicted; failures lead to § 112 support issues and examiner objections.

name: No new matter: prohibition and examiner actions
description: No amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention (35 U.S.C. 132). When new matter is introduced into the specification, the amendment should be objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 (35 U.S.C. 251 if reissue) and a requirement made to cancel the new matter. The subject matter considered new must be clearly identified by the examiner.
guidance: If the new matter has been entered into the claims or affects their scope, the claims affected should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. The examiner’s holding of new matter may be petitionable or appealable (see MPEP § 608.04(c)). Use form paragraph 7.28 to object to new matter in the specification.

name: New matter examples and scope guidance
description: New matter includes addition of wholly unsupported subject matter, adding specific percentages or compounds after a broader original disclosure, or omission of a step from a method. Matter not present on the filing date that is added after filing is usually new matter.
guidance: See In re Wertheim and MPEP §§ 2163.05–2163.07 for guidance in determining whether added characteristics are inherent and hence not new matter. If subject matter capable of illustration is originally claimed but not shown in the drawing, the applicant is required to add it to the drawing (see MPEP § 608.01(l)). Replacement drawings containing new matter should not be entered.

name: Reviewability of examiner’s holding of new matter
description: Where the new matter is confined to amendments to the specification, review of the examiner’s requirement for cancellation is by way of petition. But where the alleged new matter is introduced into or affects the claims, thus necessitating their rejection on this ground, the question is appealable and should not be considered on petition.
guidance: See MPEP § 2163.06. If new matter affects claims, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) using form paragraph 7.31.01.

name: Arrangement and order of application elements (37 CFR 1.77)
description: The elements of the application, if applicable, should appear in the following order: (1) Utility application transmittal form; (2) Fee transmittal form; (3) Application data sheet; (4) Specification; (5) Drawings; (6) The inventor’s oath or declaration. The specification should include Title, Cross-reference to related applications, Statement regarding federally sponsored research, Names of parties to a joint research agreement, Reference to Sequence Listing/table/program listing on compact disc, Statement regarding prior disclosures, Background, Brief summary, Brief description of the drawings, Detailed description, Claims, Abstract, and Sequence Listing if on paper.
guidance: Text of specification sections should be preceded by a section heading in uppercase without underlining or bold type. See 37 CFR 1.77(b) and (c) for section order and formatting.

name: Requirements for description
description: Requirements for description are an explicit curriculum topic: what the description must contain to support claims.
guidance: Covered in classroom and on-the-job training; used to evaluate sufficiency of disclosure and written-description compliance during examination.

name: Claims define patent scope
description: The words of the claims define the scope of the patent owner’s exclusive rights during the life of the patent.
guidance: Only the claims of the patent can be infringed; neither the written description nor the drawings can be infringed. Each claim must be considered individually and the same claim meaning must be used for infringement and invalidity analyses.

name: Patent Examiner considerations for patentability
description: In examining a patent application, the Patent Examiner searches for prior art and considers whether each claim defines an invention that is new, useful, and not obvious, and whether claims are directed to eligible subject matter and are definite, enabled, and adequately described.
guidance: Explains the prosecution process and that prosecution history (file wrapper) may be relevant to claim interpretation and estoppel issues.

name: Prior art (AIA vs pre-AIA) / Cutoff Date
description: Prior art is technical information against which patentability is judged; definitions vary under the AIA and pre-AIA. Under the AIA, prior art is knowledge publicly available before the effective filing date; pre-AIA definitions vary by subsection (§§ 102(a),(b),(d),(e),(g)).
guidance: Practice Note: Model instructions refer to a 'Cutoff Date' which may differ by claim and pre-AIA subsection; juries may need instructions to determine differing Cutoff Dates and resulting pools of prior art.

name: Claim construction is the court’s role
description: It is the judge’s job to interpret the meaning of claim language; jurors must accept the court’s claim constructions and use them for both infringement and invalidity.
guidance: For limitations not expressly construed by the court, jurors should apply the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention (Teva/Phillips/Markman authority).

name: Plain and ordinary meaning / PHOSITA standard
description: For claim limitations not construed by the court, use the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art (level of experience, education, training in the field) at the relevant time (pre-AIA: time of invention; AIA: before effective filing date).
guidance: Model glossaries define 'ordinary skill in the art' differently for pre-AIA and AIA contexts. The jury may need guidance on establishing that skill level.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. § 112) construction
description: Means[[step]]-plus-function claim limitations are limited to the corresponding structure (or act/step) described in the specification and equivalents thereof; the court determines the recited function and corresponding structure.
guidance: Model language provides blanks for the recited function and corresponding structure; jurors must use the court's identification of corresponding structure when assessing infringement and validity of such limitations.

name: Prosecution history estoppel limits DOE
description: Prosecution history estoppel can limit application of the doctrine of equivalents where claim scope was narrowed or surrendered during prosecution.
guidance: See Practice Notes and cited cases; jury should be instructed on whether prosecution history estoppel applies in the case at hand.

name: Indirect infringement: inducement (active inducement)
description: Indirect infringement may occur if a defendant actively induces another to infringe a claim of the patent (induced infringement).
guidance: Model includes separate instructions (and Practice Notes) to distinguish induced infringement from contributory infringement and to lay out the elements the plaintiff must prove for inducement.

name: Anticipation (novelty) and related prior-art doctrines
