description: Anticipation requires that a single prior art reference (or earlier public disclosure) disclose every element of the claimed invention; the Model breaks out categories of prior art (prior public knowledge, public use, printed publication, prior patent, earlier-filed application, prior invention) and treats pre-AIA vs AIA distinctions.
guidance: Multiple subsections (e.g., Prior Public Knowledge, Prior Public Use, On-Sale Bar, Printed Publication, Prior Patent, Earlier-Filed Patent Application, Prior Invention) provide detailed elements and fact patterns the jury must consider when deciding anticipation.

name: Obviousness (Graham factors)
description: Obviousness is decided using the four Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) secondary considerations (other considerations).
guidance: Model provides instructions for each factor and emphasizes the need to consider them collectively; examples and case citations are provided.

name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND
description: For SEPs, juries must be instructed on the particulars of any FRAND commitment, established patent law principles, and only those Georgia‑Pacific factors relevant to the case; royalties must be apportioned to the incremental value of the claimed invention, not the standard as a whole.
guidance: Practice Note: Emphasizes apportionment and limitation on irrelevant Georgia‑Pacific factors; cites Federal Circuit precedent.

name: Claims content requirements for microorganisms and cell lines
description: Claims characterizing a microorganism strain should contain its species and generic name in Latin and the purpose of the strain; claims for a line of plant or animal cells should include their name and purpose.
guidance: Specified in Russian Administrative Regulation: 'The claims, characterizing a microorganism strain should contain its species and generic name in Latin, the purpose of the strain.' Provide Latin names and functional/purpose statements in claims when characterizing biological material.

name: Interpretation of product-by-function/characteristic claim language
description: When a claim specifies a product by its function, characteristic, etc., such an expression should, in principle, be construed as every product that has such function, characteristic, etc., except when it should be construed otherwise because the expression is specifically defined in the detailed description.
guidance: An examiner should not exclude the disclosed function/characteristic from the features of the invention when interpreting the claims. However, take into account common general technical knowledge at the time of filing — there are cases where a product described by function should not be construed as every product with that function (Example: 'means to selectively join plastic materials' should not apply to materials like magnetics which are difficult to join with plastic).

name: Interpretation of limitation of use (product specified by its use)
description: Where a claim specifies a product by its use (limitation of use), the claimed invention should be interpreted only as a product specially suitable for the use disclosed in the claim, taking into account the specification, drawings, and common general technical knowledge at filing.
guidance: Even if a product includes all technical characteristics described in the claims, do not regard it as the claimed product when it is not appropriate for the relevant use or needs conversion to be used (Example: 'crane hook with a shape of ~' should be construed differently from 'fishing hooks' with regard to structure). If a product with a limitation of use is not suitable for that use per specification/drawings/common knowledge, the limitation of use has no impact in specifying the claimed invention and does not affect novelty.

name: Construction of product-by-process claims
description: A product claim that defines a product by its manufacturing process should, in principle, be construed as defining the product per se; examiners should compare the claimed product itself with prior art when determining novelty and inventive step, unless there is a special reason in the claim description.
guidance: Special reasons to treat the product different from product-per-se should be accepted only in extremely exceptional cases (e.g., when it is greatly difficult to define the product in the ordinary way in the relevant technical field). If an identical product can be obtained by a different process, the claimed invention is not novel even if the applicant intended to limit the product to a specific process (e.g., 'Z obtained solely by process A' is still treated as the product per se). Example: a panel formed by a cutting process — if same panel exists, novelty lost despite process language.

name: Treatment of Jepson-type claims (preamble and body)
description: Even for Jepson-type claims dividing preamble and body, the invention should be specified as a whole including the preamble because claim type does not change technical scope.
guidance: Do not consider subject matter in the preamble publicly known merely because it appears there; whether preamble matters were publicly known is a factual question. The technical idea of the whole invention (including preamble) is the subject matter for patentability. The preamble can be construed as limiting field of invention, limiting applied product, or excluding scope of right — the body combined with preamble defines technical characteristics subject to protection.

name: Method of determining novelty (compare claim vs cited invention)
description: Determine novelty by comparing matters defining the claimed invention and matters disclosed in the cited invention and extracting differences; if no difference exists the claimed invention is not novel; if there is a difference it is novel.
guidance: 'Substantially identical' means no newly produced effect because the difference is caused by mere addition/conversion/deletion of well-known or commonly used art and does not practically affect the technical idea of the claimed invention.

name: Novelty rules for inventions with numerical limitations
description: For claims with numerical limitations, a claimed invention is regarded novel when it is not identical to the cited invention even when numerical limitation not considered; specific rules apply when comparing numerical ranges.
guidance: (1) If cited art lacks numerical limitation and the claim adds a new numerical limitation, the claim is regarded novel, unless the numerical value can be chosen by a person skilled in the art or is hinted by cited invention/common knowledge. (2) If claimed range is included in a cited range, novelty can still be acknowledged only by establishing criticality of the claimed range — requires detailed description of technical meaning, embodiments or supplemental materials proving criticality, and objective experimental confirmation across the range. (3) If the claimed range includes the cited range, novelty can be denied at once. (4) If ranges differ, novelty is generally acknowledged.

name: Novelty and examination of parameter inventions
description: A parameter invention creates a nonstandard parameter and uses it as an essential element; because parameters may not precisely define subject matter, determination of inventive step should follow after clarifying subject matter from description, drawings, and common knowledge.
guidance: Novelty is determined by interpreting the parameter as part of the claims, but novelty cannot be confirmed solely because the parameter is novel. Novelty is generally denied if the parameter merely experimentally identifies nature/characteristics of a publicly known product or is merely an expression change. If reasonable doubt exists about identity with cited invention, examiner may await applicant's written arguments or experimental certificates after notifying reason for refusal; examiner must concretely describe ground of reasonable doubt and may propose ways to overcome it. These rules do not apply if parameter is standard, commonly used, or easily understandable to a person skilled in the art.

name: Generic vs specific concept comparison for novelty
description: When claim and cited invention use generic or specific concepts, consider: (①) if claim is generic and cited is specific, the claim is not novel; (②) if claim is specific and cited generic, the claim has novelty unless the specific can be directly derived from the generic given common general knowledge.
guidance: Examples: 'metal' claimed vs 'Cu' cited => claimed invention not novel. Conversely, a specific material (silver) in a specific use may be non-novel if using that material in that use belongs to common general knowledge and can be conceived without undue difficulty.

name: Do not mix novelty with inventive step (no combining multiple cited inventions for novelty)
description: Novelty determination shall not be conducted by comparing a claimed invention with a combination of two or more cited inventions; combination of references relates to inventive step, not novelty.
guidance: Exceptions: when a cited invention itself cites a distinct publication providing required detail, that distinct publication can be regarded as a cited invention. When a dictionary and a reference are needed to interpret a term in a cited reference, both can be cited as supporting references.

name: Treatment of Markush-type / multiple-embodiment claims
description: For claims reciting multiple alternatives (Markush type), refusal may be notified on the ground that novelty and inventive step are lacking for each alternative invention with respect to a single prior art.
guidance: When a cited document contains more than two embodiments, do not determine novelty by combining two embodiments — combining embodiments concerns inventive step. Exceptional cases exist when one cited invention is obviously drawn from multiple embodiments in view of common general knowledge.

name: Use of applicant-admitted background technology
description: If an applicant admits background technology in the specification or written opinion, an examiner may determine novelty by citing that background technology.
guidance: Admitted background may be used as prior art for novelty determination claim-by-claim.

name: Distinction between disclosure by right-holder vs disclosure against intention
description: Different evidentiary and procedural requirements apply depending on whether the invention was disclosed by the person with right to file or disclosed against their intention; common requirements include filing within the grace period and case-by-case examination claim-by-claim.
guidance: If disclosure was by a non-successor (someone not entitled), Article 30 may not apply. Determination depends on clear intention to lay open at the time of disclosure. Types of disclosure and required documents differ between the two cases.

name: Condemnation of erroneous propositions denying necessity of charity or meritoriousness
description: Prop. Baii ... sensu est probabilis ... Prop. damnata: 'Probabile est, ne singulis quidem rigorose quinquenniis per se obligare praeceptum caritatis erga Deum.' and other condemned propositions (Baius, Quietism, etc.).
guidance: The treatise references specific condemned propositions (e.g., Baius, certain Jansenist or Quietist claims) to indicate doctrinal boundaries: positions denying the necessity of charity, denying meritoriousness of good works, or minimizing human cooperation are explicitly rejected.

name: Required marking/statement on applications approved for publication
description: When an application seeking concurrent registration is approved for publication, it is marked with a statement such as: 'SUBJECT TO CONCURRENT USE PROCEEDING WITH _____________. APPLICANT CLAIMS EXCLUSIVE RIGHT TO USE THE MARK IN THE AREA COMPRISING ______.'
guidance: Blanks are filled with involved application/registration numbers or names/addresses of parties and the area for which applicant seeks registration. Alternate templates apply when concurrent registration is based on prior Board determination or court decree (include proceeding/decree identifiers and prior involved application numbers).

name: Answer requirement, timing, and default consequences
description: There is no complaint; the Board's notice informs parties of the due date for an 'answer' (usually 40 days). Applicants/registrants whose application/registration is involved are not required to answer but may do so; other specified parties (e.g., common law users) must file answers or risk default. Failure to file an answer when required results in judgment entered against that party precluding it from claiming any right more extensive than that acknowledged by applicant in the concurrent use application(s).
guidance: Even where default judgment is entered against a party, the concurrent use applicant still bears the burden of proving entitlement to registration as against that party. Defaulting parties will not continue to receive all Board communications, but will be mailed a copy of the Board’s final decision and must be served with any proposed amendment narrowing rights.

name: Specific matters/defenses other parties may assert
description: Any other party may attempt to prove any ground or basis for refusal of registration that could be asserted against an unrestricted registration (e.g., bad faith junior user, failure to meet jurisdictional prior use date, unlawful use), or that applicant is entitled only to registration covering some of the area specified.
guidance: Board decisions and cases illustrate common grounds: overlapping advertising, expansion beyond claimed territories, insufficient proof of territorial limits; consent alone may be insufficient to show entitlement.

name: Content of prior art determined at the relevant time to avoid hindsight
description: The content of the prior art and the obviousness inquiry must be assessed at the relevant time (pre-AIA: 'at the time the invention was made'; AIA: 'before the effective filing date of the claimed invention') to avoid impermissible hindsight.
guidance: Rebuttal of hindsight-based arguments is discussed in MPEP § 2145, subsection X.A. Courts require the decisionmaker to 'cast the mind back' to the relevant time when the invention was made or before the effective filing date.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) common ownership / joint research agreement requirements
description: To rely on pre-AIA 103(c) (or to invoke its protections), the applicant has the burden of establishing that subject matter which only qualifies as prior art under subsections (e), (f) or (g) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: For applications pending on or after December 10, 2004, to rely on joint research provisions the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. See MPEP § 2146.02 for requirements to establish common ownership or a joint research agreement.

name: Examiner must determine analogy when analyzing obviousness
description: The examiner must determine whether a reference is analogous art to the claimed invention when analyzing the obviousness of the subject matter under examination.
guidance: When more than one prior art reference is used as the basis of an obviousness rejection, it is not required that the references be analogous art to each other. Explanations of the examiner's reasoning (e.g., why a reference is reasonably pertinent) may be appropriate.

name: Determining 'same field of endeavor' focuses on the reference's disclosure (embodiments, function, structure)
description: When applying the 'relevant field of endeavor' test, consider explanations of the invention’s subject matter in the patent application, including the embodiments, function, and structure of the claimed invention; the primary focus is on what the reference discloses.
guidance: Consider the disclosure 'in view of the reality of the circumstances' weighed from the vantage of common sense likely to be exerted by a POSITA. See Airbus and Bigio analyses.

name: Consider claimed invention 'as a whole' when comparing to prior art
description: In determining differences between prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether individual differences would have been obvious.
guidance: Interpret claim language and consider the invention and references as a whole. Avoid improperly focusing only on an isolated structural difference (see Stratoflex, Schenck examples). See MPEP § 2111 - § 2116.01 for claim interpretation guidance.

name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' (preserve 'as a whole' requirement)
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Avoid treating the invention as if claims read differently than they do by focusing on a single advantage or feature to the exclusion of other claim limitations (see W.L. Gore and Bausch & Lomb cases).

name: Test for enablement — determine claim scope and commensurate teaching
description: Two-step test: (1) determine the scope of the claimed invention; (2) ascertain whether the teachings in the specification are commensurate in scope so that one of skill in the art could practice the invention (over its full scope) without undue experimentation.
guidance: Both claim breadth and the amount of disclosure must be compared — claims may be restricted if the specification does not enable the full claimed scope.

name: Undue experimentation principle
description: The test is not whether any experimentation is necessary, but whether the necessary experimentation is undue.
guidance: Consider whether the experimentation required would be excessive such that the specification fails to enable the full claim scope (In re Angstadt).

name: Wands factor: quantity of experimentation needed
description: Estimate how much trial-and-error or empirical work a skilled artisan would need to perform to practice the full scope of the claims.
guidance: If the required experimentation is extensive and not guided by the specification or prior art, it may be undue. The quantity of experimentation is influenced by how well prior art and the disclosure complement each other.

name: No-limitation-of-use rule for product claims
description: When a product claim is not limited by a recited use, any enabled use that reasonably correlates with the entire scope of the claim is sufficient to preclude a lack-of-enablement rejection.
guidance: An in vitro disclosure that enables a product may be sufficient to enable a product claim that is not limited to in vitro use (Example B).

name: Intended-use limitation rule
description: When a compound/composition claim is limited by a particular intended use, enablement should be evaluated with respect to that claimed use.
guidance: If the claim recites a specific therapeutic use (e.g., gene therapy), the specification must enable the claimed use (see In re Vaeck).

name: Enablement continuum — higher bar for prevention/cure than treatment
description: Enablement requirements increase along a continuum (e.g., from treatment to cure and prevention) depending on the claimed therapeutic outcome.
guidance: Claims to prevention or cure may require more detailed disclosure (e.g., ability to identify who will develop the disease) than claims merely directed to treatment.

name: Guidance for prior-art-focused inquiry in Wands analysis
description: Look to prior art for teachings of similar compounds/vectors, roles in reducing target levels, disease etiologies (shared vs divergent), association strength between biomarker and disease, required levels causing disease, and predictability of disease development.
guidance: Prior art can supply essential enabling information; if prior art and the specification together enable the claim, applicant disclosure may be sufficient even if specification alone lacks detail.

name: Application of Wands factors to claim scope (example-driven mapping)
description: Apply Wands factors to determine enabled scope: e.g., a claim may only be enabled for in vitro embodiments, or treatment claims may be enabled only for diseases with a cause-effect nexus rather than mere association.
guidance: Use the factors to carve down claim scope when the specification/prior art do not enable the entire breadth; possible outcomes include partial enablement limited to certain environments or subpopulations.

name: Pay for a Real Search Before You Pay for Drafting
description: Multiple registered patent agents in this thread emphasized that the single highest-ROI step is a $1,000-$2,000 prior art search before drafting.
guidance: Knowing the closest art shapes claim scope, saves prosecution rounds, and prevents expensive surprises. Invest in a substantive prior-art search ($1k–$2k) to inform claim strategy rather than jumping straight to drafting.

name: Your First Idea Is Almost Never the Right Claim Scope
description: Inventors describe their commercial product. Practitioners pointed out that the broadest claim should describe a generalization of the product - the underlying mechanism that would also cover competitors' versions.
guidance: Avoid claiming only features unique to your current product; such claims are usually too narrow. Draft claims that capture the mechanism or broader inventive concept so competitors' variants are covered.

name: Avoid the Cheap Patent Mills
description: Several commenters warned about $5,000 fixed-fee patent services. The complaint pattern: thin specs, claims with obvious 112 problems, no continuation strategy, and applications that get one office action and abandon.
guidance: Beware fixed-fee/cheap providers that produce thin specifications and poor claim drafting. Real prosecution from filing through allowance typically costs $15,000–$30,000; cheap up-front fees often lead to abandonment and wasted priority.

name: Provisional Without Substance Is Worse Than Useless
description: A throwaway provisional gives you priority for nothing.
guidance: If the provisional disclosure is too thin, you may lose priority on the actual claims in the non-provisional. Ensure provisionals contain substantive disclosure sufficient to support later claims—don't file a 'placeholder' provisional.

name: If You Cannot Detect Infringement, You Cannot Enforce It
description: A claim that requires inspecting internal circuitry of a chip is hard to enforce. A claim that reads on observable user behavior or product packaging is easy to enforce.
guidance: Draft claims for detectability/enforceability: prefer claim language tied to observable behavior, outputs, or packaging rather than hidden/internal structure that would be impractical to inspect during infringement enforcement.

name: Ambiguity fatality threshold
description: If the inventor has left the invention 'wholly ambiguous and uncertain, so loosely defined, and so inaccurately expressed' that the court cannot, upon a fair interpretation of the words, gather what it is, the patent is void.
guidance: Courts will construe fairly and liberally; if fair interpretation reveals the nature and extent of the claim the patent may survive; ambiguity that prevents understanding by skilled persons is fatal. Ambiguity may sometimes be removed by considering oath or other application parts.

name: Generic specification may describe one species
description: A specification for a generic invention need describe but one species, though it may describe more.
guidance: Describing a representative species can be sufficient for a generic claim, but the description must enable the claimed scope; constructions illustrating generic claims may be described even if they are not themselves claimed.

name: Class-of-substances rule
description: The description of a class of substances as an element in the invention is not correct except when each substance in the class will serve the purpose.
guidance: If any substance in the claimed class will not answer the purpose, the patent is void as to that generic formulation (see Schneider v. Thill).

name: Composition inventions — ingredients, mixing, result
description: A composition of matter requires description of the ingredients, their mode of intermixture, and the resulting composition. Each ingredient must be completely and exactly described; nothing must be left to experiment as to their nature or number.
guidance: No substance should be specified as an ingredient unless essential; the inventor is bound by the ingredients he specifies and cannot later claim compositions lacking those essential elements.

name: Mode of use is not description of the thing used
description: A device is not portrayed by the delineation of its mode of use, nor is the use itself described unless a practical rule is given by following which the desired result can be obtained.
guidance: Describing only the manner of using an article without describing the article itself is insufficient; to claim a use, the specification must provide a practical rule enabling the use.

name: Patent/utility model/industrial design registration procedure
description: General procedural steps: filing application with required information (title, specification, claims, abstract, drawings), payment of filing/publication fees, IPOPHL initial/formality examination, search for prior art, publication (generally after 18 months for patents), (upon request) substantive examination, and grant upon meeting statutory/regulatory requirements and payment of fees.
guidance: Specifics vary by IP type (utility model similar but registration certificate granted rather than patent grant; industrial designs and layout-designs have formality and registrability checks and publication in IPOPHL E-Gazette).

name: Amendment and new matter restriction
description: An applicant may amend a patent application during examination; amendment shall not include new matter outside the scope of the disclosure contained in the application as filed.
guidance: If, after official action, applicant presents claims directed to an invention divisible from previously claimed invention, such claims if entered will be refused and applicant required to limit claims to the invention previously claimed.

name: Avoid method steps that are human cognitive actions/mental processes
description: Review your method claims to determine if they can include steps that cannot be performed as "human cognitive actions" or mental process steps; if possible, include system claims that do not mirror the process steps of the method claims, and include components that can be supported as not being "standard components".
guidance: Where method steps are plausibly performable mentally, amend claims to add non-mental limitations or add system/hardware claims that do not merely mirror the method steps. Support in the specification that method steps include limitations representing a specific application under the USPTO 2019 Examination Guidelines and an inventive concept that transforms the process into substantially more (so as to avoid Verified Voter-style §101 issues).

name: Integrate abstract mental processes into a practical application (Step 2A, prong 2)
description: Limitations that "integrate the abstract mental process into a practical application" — e.g., "laying layer over an image provides a 2-dimensional graphical interface including an image, by which a user can position a pointing and selecting device over the image and quickly and easily provide evaluation of the image in two criteria simultaneously by positioning an onscreen cursor."
guidance: Show that claim limitations provide a specific technological improvement over prior GUIs or other technology (immediate visual numerical feedback, image map with x/y coordinates, simultaneous update during user motion). If Step 2A prong 2 is met, the Board may not reach step 2B.

name: Do not draft claims that merely 'collect information, analyze it, and display certain results'
description: Claims that merely recite collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying results are likely recited as mental processes under Step 2A, prong 1 (example language: "collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying certain results" or "judgment of the user which pertains to [a] mental process").
guidance: If claims include such limitations, add additional limitations that tie the steps to a technological implementation (e.g., specific UI behavior, hardware actions) or otherwise transform the claim into a 'practical application.'

name: Tie claims to specific technical problems and technical-field concepts
description: Detail within claims tying the claims to specific problems or concepts in the given technical field can help survive §101 challenges.
guidance: Draft claim limitations that explicitly address the technical problem and recite the technical solution; include claim detail that ties the elements to that technical field (e.g., memory footprint/segmenting for PDF print jobs, vehicle transaction processing specifics).

name: Claim specific technological improvements to underlying technology
description: Claims that recite improvements to technology (e.g., "improved computer functionality," "improvement to the operation of the insulin pump," dynamic splitting of PDF print jobs) are more likely to be treated as integrated into a practical application.
guidance: Emphasize how the claimed features improve the underlying technology (reduced memory footprint, enabling vehicle transactions via dynamic UI, downloading pump configuration and delivering insulin). Support each asserted improvement in the specification.

name: Avoid reciting components in generic terms (show elements are non-conventional)
description: If the specification describes the computer and elements in generic terms, the PTAB concluded those components were conventional computer components under Alice Step 2.
guidance: Where possible, claim and describe components with specificity or unconventional functionality; provide specification support that components are not "well-understood, routine, conventional activities" to avoid Step 2B rejections.

name: Include claim limitations that cannot practically be performed mentally
description: If you can, explain in the specification or in a response to a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 why the claimed subject matter cannot practically be performed mentally.
guidance: Explicitly argue and provide factual/specification support showing that claimed processing, interactions, or hardware control steps require machine execution and are not amenable to being performed in the human mind or with pen-and-paper.

name: Use tangible device control or real-world effects to support practical application
description: Limitations such as "downloading the pump configuration file from the configuration device to an insulin pump; and delivering insulin, by the insulin pump" were found to integrate an abstract idea into a practical application because they improve device operation.
guidance: Include claim steps that cause physical or device-level effects (actuating pumps, controlling hardware, producing machine-readable ballots) and show in the specification how these steps improve operation or safety of the device/technology.

name: Be cautious with 'computer-readable medium' claims that broadly cover propagation signals
description: Claims directed to a computer readable medium which broadly recite a signal and as such is not one of the four categories of patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 can be rejected (e.g., propagation signal issue).
guidance: Avoid claiming computer-readable media in a manner that could be interpreted to cover signals or propagation ineligible subject matter; define storage mediums and exclude transitory signals where appropriate in view of §101 jurisprudence.

name: Draft a variety of differently scoped claims
description: A variety of differently scoped claims can provide options on appeal or challenge.
guidance: Include narrower and broader claim sets (method, system, apparatus, computer-readable medium with careful drafting) to preserve fallback positions during prosecution or appeal.

name: Apply the USPTO 2019 SME Guidance process when a judicial exception is recited
description: If a claim recites a judicial exception, determine whether additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A, prong 2) or whether the claim adds a specific limitation beyond the judicial exception or simply appends well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality.
guidance: Follow the two-prong Step 2A analysis: (1) identify whether the claim recites a judicial exception (mental process, mathematical concept, etc.); (2) evaluate whether additional claim elements integrate that exception into a practical application. If not integrated, proceed to Step 2B to evaluate inventive concept.

name: Characterize the claim 'as a whole' focusing on technical aspects and asserted improvements
description: The Board focused on the technical aspects of the claim and considering the claim as a whole (e.g., distinguishing sales/marketing behavior from a technical improvement in a print-server or search-engine use case).
guidance: When drafting/specifying, present the claim as a whole with emphasis on technical improvements and avoid framing the invention as merely a business method; explain how the combination of elements yields a technical benefit rooted in computer technology.

name: Add technology to business-method claims and use non-conventional terminology where useful
description: Add technology to your business method in order to have a chance to get it allowed. Use unconventional names, such a "proactive search engine" to make it harder to assert that the elements are conventional.
guidance: Introduce specific technological components or behavior that solve a technical problem; while naming alone is not sufficient, unconventional terminology combined with specification support can help distinguish claimed features from conventional systems.

name: Identify limitations that are indicative vs not indicative of 'integration into a practical application'
description: The PTAB summarizes USPTO 2019 SME Guidance for "limitations that are indicative of 'integration into a practical application' versus limitations that are not."
guidance: When analyzing or arguing eligibility, explicitly map claim limitations to the indicia in the USPTO guidance (e.g., particular machine, particular transformation, improvement to another technology, specific rules applied to a particular content) and show why each limitation is indicative of integration rather than being an abstract idea or insignificant post-solution activity.

name: Specification determines claim meaning
description: Claim terms get their ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art in light of the specification; the spec is the dictionary.
guidance: Federal Circuit decisions over the last decade have repeatedly turned on what the specification did or did not say (e.g., Phillips v. AWH (2005, en banc)). Treat the specification as the primary source for construing claim terms because courts will look to it when determining ordinary meaning.

name: Avoid singular framing of 'the invention'
description: When the spec says 'the present invention is X' or 'the invention requires Y,' courts may construe every claim as limited to X or Y.
guidance: Do not present features as universally required by 'the invention' because statements framed that way can be used to narrowly construe all claims. Example: SciMed v. Advanced Cardiovascular (Fed. Cir. 2001) where language describing a coaxial design led to excluding other designs such as dual-lumen.

name: Affirmatively define terms when useful (be your own lexicographer)
description: If you want a claim term to have a specific meaning, define it explicitly in the specification (e.g., 'As used herein, the term "X" means ...').
guidance: Courts respect express definitions provided in the spec. Use clear, affirmative definitions to control claim term meaning when appropriate.

name: Avoid definition by negative implication
description: Do not write 'in contrast to prior systems, which used Y, the present system uses X' because that can be read as disclaiming Y from the claim scope.
guidance: Describe what your system does without negatively contrasting it with prior art. Negative comparisons can be interpreted as an express exclusion of alternatives and narrow the claims.

name: Disclose ranges rather than single numeric values
description: If the prototype runs at 50 Hz, the spec should say 'between approximately 30 Hz and 100 Hz, e.g., 50 Hz.' Single values invite narrow construction; disclosed ranges support broader claims.
guidance: Provide ranges and examples rather than only a single data point to avoid implying that the invention is limited to that exact value.

name: Disclose multiple embodiments across different use cases
description: A specification that describes only one product is implicitly limited to that product; describing the invention in multiple fields and with multiple embodiments supports broader construction.
guidance: Include varied examples and embodiments (e.g., applying the invention to three different fields with three different embodiments) to demonstrate breadth and avoid limiting the claims to a single implementation.

name: Keep the background concise and factual; avoid disparaging prior art
description: Long background sections that disparage prior art create estoppel and admissions under 35 U.S.C. § 103. Avoid characterizing prior art as having 'drawbacks' or 'deficiencies' you have solved.
guidance: Keep the background short and factual. Overly negative descriptions of prior art can be quoted against you in litigation and used to limit claim scope or support obviousness findings.

name: Patent examination criteria
description: The Patent organization examines patent applications to determine whether the claimed invention is eligible for patent protection, useful, adequately disclosed, clearly defined, and evaluates the claimed invention in comparison to a large body of technological information to determine whether it is novel and non-obvious.
guidance: Examiners perform administrative review of newly filed applications, publish pending applications, issue patents to successful applicants, disseminate issued patents to the public, respond to appeal briefs, and prepare preliminary PCT examination reports. Evaluation is done against existing technological information (prior art) to assess novelty and non-obviousness.

name: Claim construction standard in inter partes review (IPR)
description: During inter partes review, a patent claim 'shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the patent in which it appears.'
guidance: The Supreme Court (Cuozzo) upheld the USPTO regulation adopting broadest reasonable interpretation for claim construction in IPRs. This standard governs how PTAB judges construe claims during AIA proceedings and provides certainty to parties and adjudicators.

name: Step 1: Apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) and exclude claims covering non-statutory embodiments
description: Evaluate Step 1 after determining what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: If the claim's BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable media that could be a carrier wave), the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1 (Step 1: NO). Examiners should point out the BRI, recommend an amendment where possible to narrow to statutory embodiments, and, if appropriate, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 using form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05, 7.05.01). If amendment could place the claim within a statutory category, proceed to analyze whether such an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C.

name: Three eligibility pathways (A, B, C) and when to use each
description: Use the flowchart to determine eligibility via Pathway A (streamlined/self-evident), Pathway B (Step 1 YES and Step 2A NO), or Pathway C (Step 1 YES, Step 2A YES, Step 2B YES).
guidance: Pathway A: claims that fall within a statutory category and whose eligibility is self-evident may be found eligible via a streamlined analysis (see MPEP §2106.06). Pathway B: claims that fall in a statutory category and are not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A NO) are eligible without Step 2B. Pathway C: claims that fall in a statutory category, are directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A YES), but recite additional elements (individually or in combination) that amount to significantly more than the exception (Step 2B YES) are eligible. If uncertain whether a streamlined analysis is appropriate, conduct the full eligibility analysis. If not eligible at any pathway, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.

name: Step 2A (Alice/Mayo Part 1): Whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature), or an abstract idea (judicial exceptions).
guidance: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena, products of nature, mathematical formulas, scientific principles, mental processes, and similar concepts. There are no bright lines between exceptions; many concepts can fall under multiple labels. The concern underlying these exceptions is preemption, but preemption is not a standalone test — the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B) resolves preemption questions. Evaluate Step 2A after construing claims under BRI and reviewing disclosure.

name: Step 2A Two-Prong Inquiry: Prong One — Recitation of a judicial exception
description: Prong One asks whether the claim 'recites' (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon.
guidance: Recitation can be explicit ('set forth', e.g., mathematical equation in Diehr or laws in Mayo) or implicit/descriptive (e.g., concept of intermediated settlement in Alice). Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception (require further analysis) from claims that merely 'involve' an exception (which may be eligible). Example: a claim stating 'operates in accordance with F=ma' recites a law of nature; a teeter-totter claim that does not state the physical law merely involves it and is not directed to an exception. See MPEP §2106.04(a)/(b)/(c) for detailed analyses of abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural phenomena, and products of nature.

name: Step 2A Two-Prong Inquiry: Prong Two — Integration into a practical application
description: Prong Two asks whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application of that exception.
guidance: If additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If additional elements do not integrate the exception, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis under Step 2B to determine whether it amounts to significantly more (an inventive concept). Mere recitation of the exception is insufficient; additional elements that are themselves judicial exceptions (or merely add another abstract idea) do not integrate the exception into a practical application.

name: Mere inclusion of an exception does not equate to being directed to it
description: A claim that recites a judicial exception (e.g., a mathematical formula) under Prong One may nevertheless not be 'directed to' that exception under Prong Two if the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Prong Two distinguishes claims that simply recite an exception from those directed to that exception. If there are no additional elements in the claim beyond the judicial exception, or if the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, the claim cannot be eligible. Examiners should recommend amendments where possible to resolve eligibility.

name: Examples and non-limiting illustrations of non-statutory subject matter
description: Claims to products without physical or tangible form do not fall within statutory categories and are therefore non-statutory.
guidance: Non-limiting examples include: information/data per se, computer program per se (software claimed as a product without structural recitations), transitory signal transmissions (signals per se), and paradigms/business models. The guidance cites Digitech (intangible device profile), Microsoft v. AT&T (software without medium), In re Ferguson (business model), and Nuijten/Mentor Graphics (transitory signals). Where a product lacks physical embodiment, it does not meet the statutory category requirements.

name: Use of form paragraphs and best practices when making 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections
description: If a claim is clearly not within the statutory categories (Step 1 NO), the examiner must reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and use specified form paragraphs; if the claim could be amended to become statutory, recommend amendment and continue analysis.
guidance: When rejecting for lack of statutory subject matter, use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 (see MPEP §2106.07(a)(1)). If the claim fails Step 1 but the disclosure suggests an amendable path to statutory subject matter, document that and proceed to determine whether an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C. It is a best practice to recommend amendments and explain the BRI that leads to the rejection.

name: Question 9 – Effects on patent litigation
description: Please explain how, in your experience, the status of patent eligibility jurisprudence in the United States has affected any litigation for patent infringement in the United States in which you have been involved as a party, as legal counsel, or as another participant (e.g., an expert witness).
guidance: For example, explain whether this jurisprudence has affected the cost or duration of such litigation, the ability to defend against claims of patent infringement, the certainty/uncertainty of litigation outcomes, or the likelihood of settlement. Provide concrete examples and supporting facts when possible.

name: Petition questions presented to the Supreme Court (as background)
description: The petitions presented the questions: (1) What is the appropriate standard for determining whether a claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept under step one of the Alice two-step framework? and (2) Is patent eligibility a question of law for the court or a question of fact for the jury?
guidance: These background legal questions frame the study; comments addressing standards for 'directed to' analyses or the law/fact allocation are responsive. Cite case examples or concrete litigation/prosecution effects if available.

name: Field of use / technological environment limitation is insufficient
description: Limitations that merely link the use of a judicial exception to a particular field of use or technological environment (i.e., 'limiting to the Internet', 'to cellular telephones', 'to power-grid data') do not by themselves amount to significantly more than the exception and cannot integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: The guidance gives many case examples (e.g., Parker v. Flook; Diamond v. Diehr contrast; Affinity Labs; Mayo; Bilski; FairWarning; Intellectual Ventures; Ultramercial; buySAFE) showing that token or incidental field‑of‑use/technology restrictions are insufficient. Examiners should treat the terms 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeably, consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity, and explain in the rejection why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)).

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A)
description: A streamlined analysis may be used when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (for example, because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
guidance: The streamlined (Pathway A) analysis must yield the same result as the full Alice/Mayo test; it is a tool for examination efficiency, not a way to avoid a finding that would result from full analysis. If there is doubt whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for a judicial exception, the full analysis (Alice/Mayo) should be conducted. The record may simply reflect eligibility by the absence of an eligibility rejection or a clarifying remark when Pathway A is used (see MPEP § 2106.06).

name: Eligibility is self-evident (use of streamlined pathway)
description: Claims that, when viewed as a whole, clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception and therefore have self-evident eligibility do not require a full Alice/Mayo analysis.
guidance: Examples include complex manufactured industrial products/processes with meaningful limitations (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system using mathematical relationships) or nature-based products that obviously do not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (e.g., an artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral). Such claims can be eligible under Pathway A. However, claims that would fail Step 2B of the full analysis are not suitable for streamlined analysis (see MPEP § 2106.06(a)).

name: Step 2A Prong One — identify the judicial exception and explain why
description: A rejection under Step 2A Prong One must identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited in the claim and explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).
guidance: If the claim 'describes' but does not 'expressly set forth' the judicial exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter the limitations describe and provide a reasoned rationale why it is a judicial exception. For abstract ideas, the rejection should identify how the recited concept fits within the groupings enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) (mathematical concepts, mental processes, methods of organizing human activity).

name: Step 2B — explain why additional elements do or do not amount to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
description: A Step 2B rejection must explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: When the examiner concludes that certain elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing using one of the four options specified in Subsection III (e.g., factual findings, citations, reasoning — see MPEP § 2106.07(a) for required support). The explanation must be sufficient to establish a prima facie case of ineligibility and provide applicant adequate notice to respond.

name: Support for Step 1 rejections (statutory category)
description: When a claim is determined not to fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO), the rejection must explain why the claim does not fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention.
guidance: Examiners should follow the discussion and standards in MPEP § 2106.03 when drafting Step 1 rejections, and provide clear, specific explanations in the Office action to enable effective applicant response.

name: Novelty strict identity test (equivalents)
description: A strict identity test is required in assessing novelty: a single prior art reference must disclose each and every element of a claimed invention to destroy novelty. Equivalents are considered only in assessing inventive step.
guidance: Do not rely on equivalents to defeat novelty; equivalents may be used when assessing obviousness/inventive step only.

name: Enabling disclosure particulars (including chemicals/pharmaceuticals)
description: Enabling disclosure must contain clear and detailed description of at least one way of doing the invention using working examples; sufficient and clear disclosure of technical features including manner/process of making, performing, and using the invention, leaving nothing to conjecture. For chemical substances and pharmaceutical subject matter, include representative embodiments/working examples, pharmacological test results (for pharmaceuticals), and claimed activity for all compounds.
guidance: For biotech/pharma, include experimental data and representative compounds/activities to satisfy enablement and support claims.

name: Required contents of the description
description: The description must include: (a) technical field; (b) background art useful for understanding and examination (preferably cite documents); (c) summary of the invention in terms such that the technical problem and solution and advantageous effects are understood; (d) brief description of figures; (e) detailed description pointing out novel/inventive features relative to prior art with reference signs; (f) examples describing at least one way of carrying out the invention (referring to drawings where appropriate); (g) explicit indication of industrial applicability when not obvious.
guidance: Descriptions should enable search and examination; tie claims to description and include examples and references to prior art where possible.

name: General requisites for drawings
description: Drawings must be signed by the applicant or attorney/agent name may appear, show every feature covered by claims, may consist of several views with consecutive numbering, and each figure must be briefly described.
guidance: Ensure drawings illustrate claimed features clearly and correspond with description and reference signs.

name: Claims requirements (form and support)
description: The application must conclude with a claim particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the part, improvement or combination regarded as the invention. Application may contain one or more independent claims in same category (product/process/apparatus/use) where appropriate. Each claim shall be clear, concise, and supported by the description. Dependent claims may further limit another claim; multiple dependent claims have special treatment.
guidance: Draft clear independent claims each defining a single inventive concept per category; ensure support in description and permissible dependent claim formats.

name: Substantial new question (SNQ) may be based on non-requested claims
description: The finding of 'a substantial new question of patentability' can be based upon a claim of the patent other than the ones for which reexamination was requested (35 U.S.C. 303(a)). The Office may also initiate a reexamination on its own initiative of a non-requested claim.
guidance: While the examiner will ordinarily concentrate on claims for which reexamination is requested, the examiner is not limited to those claims and can determine an SNQ as to other claims without necessarily finding an SNQ as to the requested claims.

name: Determination must be made on claims in effect at time of decision
description: The determination should be made on the claims in effect at the time the decision is made (37 CFR 1.515(a)).

name: Decision must identify claims/issues, references relied on, and provide rationale for each SNQ
description: If a request for reexamination is granted, the examiner's decision will conclude that a substantial new question of patentability has been raised by (A) identifying all claims and issues, (B) identifying the patents and/or printed publications relied on, and (C) providing a brief statement of the rationale supporting each new question.
guidance: The examiner must identify at least one SNQ and explain how the prior art patents and/or printed publications raise such a question. The examiner should indicate, insofar as possible, his or her initial position on all issues identified in the request (without rejecting claims) so comment may be received in the patent owner's statement and the requester's reply.

name: Specific points to address for each SNQ (A–F)
description: As to each substantial new question of patentability identified in the decision, the decision should point out: (A) the prior art patents and printed publications which add some new teaching as to at least one claim; (B) what that new teaching is; (C) the claims that the new teaching is directed to; (D) that the new teaching was not previously considered nor addressed in earlier concluded examination/review or final court holding of invalidity and was not raised in pending reexamination/supplemental examination; (E) that the new teaching is such that a reasonable examiner would consider it important in deciding to allow the claim being considered; and (F) where the question is raised, or where it is not clear that a patent or printed publication pre-dates the patent claims, a discussion as to why the patent or printed publication is deemed to be available against the patent claims.
guidance: See MPEP § 2247.01 for an example of a decision granting a request for reexamination. In simple cases, examiner may adopt the requester's reasons.

name: Time periods for patent owner and requester to file statements/replies
description: If the Director orders reexamination under 35 U.S.C. 304, the patent owner is given a reasonable period, not less than two months from the date a copy of the determination is given or mailed, within which he may file a statement on such question including any amendment and new claims. If the patent owner files such a statement, the requester may file and have considered a reply within two months from date of service.
guidance: The decision granting the request must set forth the time periods for the patent owner and requester to file their statement and any reply. Extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) will not be permitted in these proceedings because 1.136 applies only to 'an applicant'; extensions are provided for under 37 CFR 1.550(c).

name: Patent owner statement content and procedural rules
description: Any statement filed by the patent owner shall clearly point out why the subject matter as claimed is not anticipated or rendered obvious by the cited prior art patents or printed publications, either alone or in any reasonable combinations. A copy of the statement must be served by the patent owner on the requester (unless the request was filed by patent owner).
guidance: Except as provided in § 1.510(e), no statement or other response by the patent owner shall be filed prior to the determinations made in accordance with § 1.515 or § 1.520; premature statements will not be acknowledged or considered and will be returned/discarded/expunged. The patent owner's response to an Office action must point out supposed errors and reply to every ground of objection and rejection (37 CFR 1.111(b)).

name: Petition and review procedures for SNQ determinations and denials
description: A patent owner may challenge the correctness of a decision to grant order for ex parte reexamination on basis there is no SNQ by requesting reconsideration of the examiner's SNQ determination (e.g., in a patent owner's statement under 37 CFR 1.530 or response under 37 CFR 1.111). For denials under 35 U.S.C. 302, the requester may seek review by petition to the Director under § 1.181 within one month of mailing of the examiner's determination refusing reexamination (37 CFR 1.515(c)).
guidance: For ex parte reexamination ordered on or after June 25, 2010, patent owner may seek final agency decision from the Board on SNQ only if patent owner first requested reconsideration before the examiner and then sought Board review; in appeal brief present SNQ issue under separate heading and identify communication first requesting reconsideration. Petitions under 37 CFR 1.181 to vacate an order as 'ultra vires' are rare and will be granted only where USPTO acted in 'brazen defiance' of statutory authorization. Examples of 'appropriate circumstances' to vacate include (A) order not facially based on patents/printed publications, (B) all claims already invalidated by final court decision, (C) reexamination ordered for wrong patent, (D) ordered based on duplicate copy of request.

name: Rejection of theological/metaphysical certainty of personal justification without private revelation
description: Theologians (except rare exceptions) deny that anyone can be theologically or metaphysically certain of his justification without special/private revelation.
guidance: Reasons: (1) Scripture and Tradition do not support such claims, (2) lack of objective criteria outside private revelation, (3) Council of Trent censured assertions that one may be absolutely certain. Only in rare, divinely-revealed cases could theological certainty be mandated to the individual.

name: Alternative protection under utility patents (35 U.S.C. 101)
description: An asexually reproduced plant may alternatively be protected under 35 U.S.C. 101 (utility patent) provided the written description requirement can be satisfied; an application under 101 may claim the same asexually reproduced plant as under 161 and may include plant materials and processes involving plant materials.
guidance: Consider double patenting and obviousness-type double patenting rejections across 101 and 161 filings; filing a terminal disclaimer may be appropriate in some cases.

name: Plant patent term
description: A plant patent issuing from an application filed after June 7, 1995 has a term which expires 20 years after the filing date of the application, or any earlier filing date claimed under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c).
guidance: Calculate term from the effective filing date as with other patents; be mindful of priority claims that may affect term.

name: Single claim and form of claim (37 CFR 1.164)
description: The claim shall be in formal terms to the new and distinct variety of the specified plant as described and illustrated, and may also recite the principal distinguishing characteristics. More than one claim is not permitted.
guidance: Only one claim is necessary and permitted; method claims are improper in a plant patent. Example proper claim: 'A new and distinct variety of hybrid tea rose plant, substantially as illustrated and described herein.'

name: Required sections of the specification (37 CFR 1.163(c))
description: The specification should include, in order if applicable: (1) Title; (2) Cross-reference to related applications; (3) Statement regarding federally sponsored research; (4) Latin name of genus and species; (5) Variety denomination; (6) Background; (7) Brief summary; (8) Brief description of drawing; (9) Detailed botanical description; (10) A single claim; (11) Abstract of the disclosure.
guidance: Text sections should be preceded by upper-case headings. Latin name and variety denomination should be clearly stated (see form paragraph ¶16.05 for missing denomination).

name: Examination standards applicable to plant patents
description: Plant applications are subject to the same examination process as other national applications with respect to patentable subject matter, utility, novelty, obviousness, disclosure, and claim specificity (35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, and 112). The sole exception in applicability of these statutory provisions is set forth in 35 U.S.C. 162.
guidance: Prior art searches should include appropriate patent subclasses and patent/non-patent literature databases. Consider ARS or USDA input where appropriate.

name: Claim and title must be directed to the entire plant (not flower/fruit alone)
description: The claim language must be such that it is directed to the 'new and distinct variety of plant.' Under no circumstance should the claim be directed to a new variety of flower or fruit in contradistinction to the plant bearing the flower or the tree bearing the fruit. The title of the invention must relate to the entire plant and not to its flower or fruit (e.g., 'Apple Tree', 'Rose Plant').
guidance: Examiners may amend to insert words like 'tree' if necessary. Avoid claims/titles suggesting only fruit or flower are claimed. The specification should avoid unwarranted advertising or laudatory expressions and unnecessary statements about products made from fruit.

name: Identity determined by comparison or inspection
description: When the defendant acts under a separate patent the identity of the inventions is ascertained by comparing the claims of the patents; when the defendant acts without a patent, identity is best shown by actual inspection of the two inventions or of models exhibiting essential attributes, with or without expert explanation.
guidance: Inspection of inventions in actual use is desirable when practicable; designs often manifest identity to a careful observer. If inspection suffices, it is strong evidence; otherwise expert testimony may be used to explain characteristics.

name: Plaintiff limited to his patent's claims and descriptions
description: The plaintiff must abide by the claims and descriptions contained in his own patent, neither adding nor discarding anything to bring his invention into correspondence with that of the defendant.
guidance: Plaintiff's case cannot be expanded beyond the patent specification and claims to shoehorn the defendant's device into infringement.

name: Overlong term in patent limited to lawful period
description: If the term stated in the patent is greater than the seventeen years permitted by the statutes, it is incorrect on its face and the patent will be held valid only for the lawful period.
guidance: Courts will restrict an overstated term to the statutory maximum; claimant seeking to limit the term bears the burden of proof.

name: Limitation by prior foreign patent requires production and linkage
description: A defendant who claims the patent's term should be restricted because of a prior foreign patent must produce the foreign patent covering the invention, or a certified copy from the Patent Office, and establish by sufficient evidence the connection of the plaintiff or his assignor with its prior issue.
guidance: When the patentees' names are identical the outside evidence must show identity of persons; when different persons, relations (contracts, correspondence, co-operation, profit participation, etc.) must be shown to connect the foreign patent to the domestic patentee.

name: Written description requirement (Ariad test)
description: The written description requirement is met when the disclosure relied on for support 'reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.' Ariad Pharms., Inc. v. Eli Lilly & Co., 598 F.3d 1336, 1351 (Fed. Cir. 2010).
guidance: The level of detail required varies depending on the nature and scope of the claims and on the complexity and predictability of the relevant technology. The inquiry is objective and examines the 'four corners' of the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art. The inquiry is a question of fact.

name: Four-corners objective inquiry
description: Written description is determined by an 'objective inquiry into the four corners of the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art.'
guidance: Look only to the specification (and what it conveys to a POSITA) rather than extrinsic labels; evaluate whether the specification shows the inventor 'possessed' the claimed subject matter at filing.

name: Range-claim analysis: 'mere comparison of ranges is not enough'
description: When claims recite a narrower numerical range than the specification's disclosed range(s), it is not sufficient simply to compare ranges; the question is whether the claimed narrower range is part of the invention described in the specification.
guidance: If the broader described range pertains to a different invention than the narrower claimed range, the specification does not provide written description support. Precedents illustrating both outcomes include Wertheim (narrower range supported), Blaser (supported), Kolmes (supported), Baird (not supported), and Indivior (not supported).

name: Disclosure of endpoints and internal support for subranges
description: The specification need not literally recite the claimed subrange, but disclosure of the subrange endpoints or embodiments at or near the endpoints supports that the inventor possessed the claimed subrange.
guidance: Presence of endpoints expressly disclosed (e.g., specification discloses 'about 75% to about 125%' and 'about 85% to about 115%') and lack of inconsistent statements increases the likelihood a POSITA would understand the narrower claimed subrange to be part of the invention. Conversely, absence of endpoints or inconsistent/overbroad statements (e.g., 'any desired level') can weigh against support (see Indivior).

name: Effect of predictability and complexity of the art on required detail
description: The level of descriptive detail required to satisfy §112 varies with the predictability of the technology: predictable/electro-mechanical arts require less detail than unpredictable arts.
guidance: For predictable arts, a lower level of detail may be sufficient to show possession of claim limitations (e.g., simple dimensional/range limitations); for unpredictable arts, more precise exemplification or explanation is often required.

name: Assessing whether a claimed subrange is a different invention
description: Determine whether the claimed subrange results in a different invention (different operability, effectiveness, or other distinct property) than the broader disclosed range.
guidance: If the specification shows values outside the claimed subrange produce materially different results (e.g., Baird where values outside the claimed temperature range caused curling or brittleness) and provides no guidance toward the claimed range, that supports lack of written description for the subrange.

name: Obviousness review: divisions of responsibility and standards
description: The ultimate determination of obviousness is reviewed de novo, while the Board's underlying factual findings (e.g., scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and claims, level of ordinary skill, motivation to combine, and objective indicia) are reviewed for substantial evidence.
guidance: Appellate review asks whether a reasonable factfinder could have arrived at the agency's decision on the factual predicates; legal conclusion of obviousness is reviewed anew.

name: Types of evidence that can support motivation to combine
description: Evidence that can justify a motivation to combine includes prior-art statements inviting design choices or alterations, explicit advantages taught by a reference (e.g., manufacturability, size reduction, ability to achieve different heating profiles), and expert testimony credibly tying the prior-art teachings to the claimed combination.
guidance: A finding of motivation may rest on a combination of the references' teachings and expert opinions; the Board may credit testimony from either party's experts to support its factual findings. Courts will sustain the Board's conclusion if substantial evidence (including such testimony and the references' teachings) reasonably supports it.

name: Requirement to disclose corresponding structure for means-plus-function under 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: The recited “means” for performing the specified function shall be construed to cover the corresponding “structure or material” described in the specification and equivalents thereof; examiners must determine whether the written description discloses the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function.
guidance: If no corresponding structure is disclosed (e.g., the limitation is only supported by software without an algorithm and the computer/microprocessor programmed with the algorithm), the limitation should be deemed indefinite and rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph). See MPEP § 2163.03; determine claimed function then review the written description/drawings/figures/sequence listing for corresponding structure.

name: Algorithm disclosure requirement for computer-implemented means-plus-function claims
description: For computer-implemented means-plus-function limitations, the specification must explicitly disclose an algorithm (a sequence of steps) corresponding to the claimed function; merely reciting the function or outcome is insufficient.
guidance: An algorithm must be a sequence of steps; implicit or inherent disclosure of a class of algorithms is not sufficient and a ‘one-step’ pseudo‑algorithm is insufficient. Case law: Blackboard; Noah; Encyc. Brittanica v. Alpine; Biomedino; Atmel. Code fragments that only return error messages or do not explain how to perform an essential action are inadequate (Media Rights example).

name: Multiple claimed functions require disclosure of corresponding structure for each function
description: When a means-plus-function limitation performs multiple identifiable functions, the specification must disclose adequate corresponding structure/algorithm to perform all of the claimed functions.
guidance: If the specification discloses an algorithm that accomplishes only one of multiple functions, the disclosure is treated as if it disclosed no algorithm and the limitation is indefinite (see Noah, Williamson, Media Rights). Examiners should verify that structure/algorithms for each recited function are present.

name: Mode of implementation limits claim scope (hardware vs. software)
description: By choosing a means-plus-function limitation and invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the applicant limits that claim element to the disclosed structure (e.g., hardware or combination of hardware and software) and equivalents; examiners should not construe the limitation as covering pure software implementation unless the specification discloses corresponding structure for software.
guidance: If the limitation is only supported by software and there is no corresponding algorithm/structure disclosed, treat as indefinite under 112(b). Claims should be read as a whole to determine whether the claim as a whole is directed to software per se.

name: Clear linkage / association requirement between disclosed structure and claimed function
description: The structure disclosed in the written description is the corresponding structure only if the written description or the prosecution history clearly links or associates that structure to the function recited in the means/step-plus-function limitation.
guidance: This linkage is the quid pro quo for employing 112(f). If one of ordinary skill in the art cannot identify what structure, material, or acts disclosed performs the claimed function, a rejection under 112(b) is appropriate. See B. Braun; Medical Instrumentation & Diagnostics; Telcordia.

name: Three common situations warranting a 112(b) rejection for means-plus-function limitations
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph) may be appropriate when: (1) it is unclear whether a claim limitation invokes 112(f); (2) 112(f) is invoked and there is no or insufficient disclosure of structure/material/acts for the claimed function; and/or (3) 112(f) is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link or associate the disclosed structure/material/acts to the claimed function.
guidance: Examiners should apply the 3‑prong analysis and determine whether 112(f) applies, then whether disclosure and linkage are present. Ambiguous claim language may render the 3‑prong analysis inconclusive, warranting rejection. Applicant can rebut or amend during prosecution to clarify.

name: Examiner procedure for evaluating whether 112(f) applies and for identifying corresponding structure
description: Once a limitation is determined to invoke 112(f), the examiner should identify the claimed function and then review the written description (including drawings, figures, tables, sequence listings) to determine whether the corresponding structure/material/acts that perform the function are disclosed.
guidance: Review the claims, specification, and how a person of ordinary skill would understand the claims in view of the disclosure. If examiner cannot identify corresponding structure, make a rejection under 112(b) or require information under 37 CFR 1.105 to compel identification. See MPEP § 704.11(a) Example R and § 704.12 for replies to requirements for information.

name: Mere recitation of function insufficient for written description and enablement
description: Merely restating the function associated with a means-plus-function limitation in the specification, without more description of the means to accomplish it, is insufficient to provide corresponding structure for definiteness and will likely fail to satisfy written description and enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: Cases: Noah; Blackboard; Aristocrat. 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) requires terms in claims to find clear support or antecedent basis in the description. Distinguish between describing the outcome (insufficient) and describing the means/structure to achieve it (required).

name: Interplay: indefiniteness often signals lack of written description/enablement
description: A means-plus-function limitation found indefinite under 112(b) for failure to disclose sufficient corresponding structure (e.g., computer plus algorithm) will also likely lack adequate written description under 112(a) and may not be enabled for the full scope of the claim.
guidance: Examiners should consider both written description and enablement requirements when assessing means-plus-function limitations. See MPEP §§ 2163.03, 2161.01, and 2164.08. The enablement inquiry is separate from written description and examines whether one skilled in the art could make and use the full scope of the claimed invention.

name: Functional/structural material not recited in claim should not be imported unless necessary
description: Functional limitations not expressly recited in the claim, or structural limitations in the specification that are unnecessary to perform the claimed function, cannot be imported into the claim during claim construction under 112(f).
guidance: Do not read extraneous structural or functional limitations from the specification into the claim unless they are the corresponding structure necessary to perform the recited function. See Welker Bearing; Wenger Mfg.

name: Remedies and examiner actions when applicant does not identify corresponding structure
