description: If the examiner cannot identify corresponding structure/material/acts, the examiner should reject the claim under 112(b); the examiner may also issue a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 to require identification of the corresponding structure.
guidance: If a 1.105 requirement is made and applicant states they lack the information or fails to identify the corresponding structure, a 112(b) rejection should be made. Failure to reply to such requirements can result in abandonment. See MPEP § 704.11(a) Example R and § 704.12 on replies to requirements for information.

name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — diligence and promptness
description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
guidance: Violations include failing to pay required filing fees, failing to respond to Notices to File Missing Parts, failing to file required documents (e.g., Application Data Sheet, oath/declaration), failing to timely file applications claimed by the client, failing to obtain or correctly file client signatures on power of attorney forms, and otherwise allowing client matters to be abandoned. The decision lists numerous specific failures as examples of breaching § 11.103.

name: Correction of errors in filed documents
description: Linguistic errors, transcription errors and mistakes in any document filed with ARIPO may be corrected on request at any time, subject to limitations where third parties might be affected.
guidance: If error affects items third parties might rely on (e.g., priority claims), request for correction must be filed as soon as possible and at least in time to be incorporated in publication. Exception if mistake is apparent on face of published application. Corrections in description/claims/drawings must be obvious — immediately evident that nothing else could have been intended — and within what a skilled person would derive directly and unambiguously from the whole of the documents as filed. Not allowable to replace complete application documents with other documents applicant had intended to file with request for grant.

name: Invention information vs additional information
description: Two types of information in patent documents: 'invention information' (technical information in the total disclosure that represents an addition to the state of the art) and 'additional information' (non-trivial technical information which does not in itself represent an addition to the state of the art but might be useful for the searcher).
guidance: Invention information is determined in the context of the state of the art using guidance from the claims, with regard to description and drawings. The rules for selection of classification symbols are the same for both types of information (paragraphs 76–80).

name: Classification of general chemical formulae (Markush-type): three-step procedure
description: General formulae representing large sets of related chemical compounds cause classification problems; apply a three-step classifying procedure when general Markush-type formulae are used.
guidance: Step 1: Classify all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious when they are specifically claimed, products of a claimed process, or derivatives; a compound is 'fully identified' if structure is given by exact name/formula or deducible from preparation with not more than one alternative reactant and is characterised by a physical property or worked example. Step 2: If no 'fully identified' compounds are disclosed, classify only compounds with exact chemical name or developed formula and limit classification to a single or very small number of groups. Step 3: When only the general Markush formula is disclosed, classify in the most specific group(s) that cover all or most potential embodiments and limit classification to a single or very small number of groups (paragraph 100).

name: Duties under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 during suspension
description: Disciplined practitioners must comply with duties enumerated in § 11.58, which include, among other things, filing notices of withdrawal in each patent and trademark application pending before the USPTO and providing notices of the discipline to all State and Federal jurisdictions and to all clients.
guidance: To obtain nunc pro tunc recognition for time served, a respondent must show compliance with § 11.58. Failure to file withdrawals or to notify jurisdictions/clients is fatal to a nunc pro tunc claim. The USPTO enforces the express terms of § 11.24(f) in evaluating such claims.

name: Identify what applicant invented and claim construction (BRI)
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim based on plain meaning and specification.
guidance: This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim. The take away is what the invention is focused on (e.g., 'vaccine'). Establish BRI showing how terms are interpreted (example: BRI of 'inactivated Pigeon flu virus' = dead virus chemically modified by formalin so nucleic acids are chemically modified and cannot reproduce, in an amount to produce an immunogenic response). Use a separate worksheet for each claim; use Quick Reference Sheet/flowchart/form paragraphs as aids.

name: Step 1 — Statutory category determination (process/machine/manufacture/composition)
description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter).
guidance: Choose A (yes) to continue with the SME analysis. If B (no), make a rejection as drawn to non-statutory subject matter using Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 available in Custom OACs. If claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption and document the assumption clearly in the record; if no amendment is possible, end SME analysis and continue with examination of other patentability requirements.

name: Identify limitations reciting other exceptions (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon)
description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon, identify which limitation(s) recite the exception and explain why they are considered a judicial exception.
guidance: Provide the limitation(s) text and reasons why these are judicial exceptions (e.g., mathematical relationship, fundamental economic practice, naturally occurring principle), with supporting references to case law/chart. If no judicial exception found, conclude SME and continue with other examination.

name: Evaluate significance of additional elements (search for 'inventive concept')
description: Assess whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, result in the claim as a whole amounting to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (i.e., provide an inventive concept).
guidance: Consider the invention identified in Section I and how additional elements relate to it. The additional elements must show an 'inventive concept.' Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following (each is a potential basis): improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic computer functions; not mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; not adding words like 'apply it'); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending routine activities at a high level of generality); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment.

name: Combining component elements that do not occur together in nature
description: When a claimed product comprises a combination of component elements that do not occur together in nature, treat each component element as an additional element to the other components for determining whether their combination results in significantly more.
guidance: Evaluate whether the combination changes functional properties or structure in a marked way compared to individual natural components (example: peptide + aluminum adjuvant showing synergistic increased immunogenicity = markedly different characteristics; peptide + water mixture that leaves both components unchanged = not markedly different). Assess both individual contributions and their combination.

name: Outcome decisions and required actions (eligible vs. §101 rejection)
description: Conclude SME analysis based on the markedly-different and inventive-concept evaluations: If claim is not directed to any judicial exception or additional elements supply significantly more, conclude SME and continue examination of other patentability requirements; if not, make a §101 rejection.
guidance: If making a §101 rejection, use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (or 7.05 and 7.05.01 for Step 1 non-statutory rejections) in Custom OACs. Identify the exception(s) the claim is directed to, explain why the claim lacks additional elements sufficient to amount to significantly more, and optionally suggest claim amendments or disclosure elements that could render the claim eligible (provide examples from the disclosure). The worksheet includes sample rejection language to populate Office Actions.

name: Use of supporting materials and examples (case law and training materials)
description: Use the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance, July 2015 Update, Quick Reference Sheets, the Subject Matter Eligibility Court Decisions chart, case law examples (e.g., Chakrabarty, Myriad, Funk Brothers), and training slides to inform the analysis and identify judicial exceptions.
guidance: The worksheet suggests cross-referencing the Quick Reference Sheet (flowchart and form paragraphs), the July 2015 Update chart of abstract idea concepts, and the court decisions chart. Use example analyses (several Example 28 claims provided) to guide application of the markedly-different and significantly-more analyses and to craft Office Action language or amendment suggestions.

name: Documentation and remediation suggestions
description: Where appropriate, document interpretations and suggested claim amendments or disclosure elements in the record to clarify conclusions or offer applicant paths to eligibility.
guidance: If assuming an amendment to reach a statutory category, make the assumption clear in the record. When finding ineligibility, identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to claims to make them eligible (examples given: immuno-effective amount of an aluminum salt adjuvant). Provide suggested form-paragraph language and sample rejection text to populate Office Actions.

name: Determination of subject of prior art search (include working examples and reasonably expected amendments)
description: Examiners should take into consideration working examples of a claimed invention which are shown in the description as the subject of prior art searches. Also, elements which are reasonably expected to be recited in amended claims should be taken into account.
guidance: Inventions which may be excluded from the subject of prior art search include: inventions to which new technical matter is apparently added; subject matter which is apparently patent‑ineligible; or inventions which cannot be identified even when the description is taken into consideration. Even when a claimed invention may be excluded, if it is reasonably expected, taking into account a possible amendment, that the invention can overcome the exclusion, the examiner conducts prior art searches based on a virtually amended claim. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2)

name: Scope and strategy of prior art searches
description: Examiners should retrieve all prior arts relevant to claimed inventions and determine the scope of prior art searches based on their own knowledge and experience from the perspective of efficiency of the searches.
guidance: Examiners should first search the technical field most probable to retrieve relevant prior arts (usually that most relevant to working examples in the description), then gradually extend to less relevant fields if needed. Where examiners cannot retrieve enough prior arts for denying novelty or inventive step in the initially searched fields, and believe it probable to retrieve such prior arts from less relevant fields, they should extend the search. Examiners may stop searches when they have retrieved enough relevant prior arts, there is little expectation of retrieving more significantly relevant prior arts, or they have retrieved a document which denies novelty or inventive step based on the document itself. When prior art information is stated in the description, examiners should consider those cited prior arts before searching for other prior arts. When search/examination results by foreign Offices or outsourced searches are available, the examiner should consider those results. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2)

name: Comparison for novelty determination
description: Examiners specify the claimed invention and the prior art, and then compare both in determining novelty and an inventive step.
guidance: As a result of the comparison, they determine that the claimed invention lacks novelty when there is no difference between claimed elements and elements specifying prior art. When there is a difference, the claimed invention is novel. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2)

name: Assessment of inventive step
description: When a difference between the claimed invention and prior art exists, examiners determine whether there is an inventive step by considering factors in support of existence/nonexistence of an inventive step based on the contents of the prior arts.
guidance: With regard to reasons denying an inventive step, the examiner needs to clarify the differences between the claimed invention and elements specifying prior arts, and specifically describe the reason that a person skilled in the art would easily arrive at the claimed invention based on the prior art. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.2 & Sec.3)

name: Clarity and sufficiency of notice of reasons for refusal
description: Examiners should prepare notifications of reasons for refusal that are clear and sufficient so that applicants can easily understand and respond to the notices. Each reason should be accompanied with the claims concerned.
guidance: For inventive step refusals, examiners must clarify claim‑to‑prior‑art differences and explain why a person skilled in the art would arrive at the claimed invention. When notifying “final” reasons for refusal, examiners must explicitly indicate that the notice is “final” and the reason for such; otherwise the notice cannot be regarded as final. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.3)

name: Amendments allowed after final notice of reasons for refusal (limitations)
description: After the final notice of reasons for refusal, the applicant may amend the claims for limited purposes: deleting claims; restricting the scope of claimed inventions in a limited way; correcting errors; or clarifying ambiguous statements on which an objection that the statements are unclear was raised (Japanese Patent Act Art. 17bis(5)).
guidance: This restriction is provided for the efficiency of examinations and violating it does not constitute grounds for invalidation. In applying the provision, the examiner should ensure, giving due consideration to the objective thereof, that it should not be applied more strictly than necessary—especially when the examiner believes that the results of the examination already performed can be used effectively to complete the examination process promptly even if an amendment does not comply with the restriction. (GL Part IV, Chap.4)

name: Decision to grant or refuse (what must be described)
description: When deciding refusal, examiners need to determine whether the reasons notified are resolved or not, and whether the reasons notified are appropriate or not.
guidance: In the decision of refusal, all reasons which are not resolved should be described. Each reason should be clearly described and be accompanied with the claims concerned. Examiners should also describe their determinations on issues raised in written arguments. (GL Part I, Chap.2, Sec.5)

name: Factors for determining evidence of possession
description: Evidence of possession is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
guidance: Factors include the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude the applicant was in possession is sufficient (citing Eli Lilly).

name: Mature-technology exception for method/function disclosure
description: In most mature technologies, and where knowledge/skill in the art is high, a written description question should not be raised for claims present in the application when originally filed, even if the specification discloses only a method of making the invention and the function of the invention.
guidance: Example: microprocessor programming—disclosing a microprocessor capable of performing certain functions can be sufficient because one skilled in the art would know how to implement the necessary details (In re Hayes).

name: Greater specificity required in unpredictable/emerging arts
description: For inventions in emerging and unpredictable technologies, or for inventions characterized by factors not reasonably predictable, more evidence is required to show possession.
guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not support a product claim (except product-by-process where the process was actually used to produce the product). Reduction to practice may be the only clear evidence of possession in such fields (citing Fiers, Amgen, Burroughs Wellcome).

name: Partial structure disclosure may be insufficient
description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization of the product may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Example in molecular biology: conceiving a gene requires being able to define it to distinguish it from other materials (structure, method of preparation, physical/chemical properties); defining solely by a principal biological property (e.g., encoding EPO) is insufficient (Amgen).

name: Species claims must meet established tests
description: Any claim to a species that does not meet the test described under at least one of (a), (b), or (c) must be rejected as lacking adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
guidance: Although the specific (a)-(c) tests are referenced elsewhere in the guidance, the point is that a species claim must satisfy the applicable written-description test to avoid rejection.

name: Genus claim support options
description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties), or by functional characteristics coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure.
guidance: See Eli Lilly and related case law for when such approaches are adequate.

name: Specification cannot support expansive claims by describing only one embodiment
description: A specification cannot always support expansive claim language merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed; the issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand the applicant invented, and was in possession of, the invention as broadly claimed (LizardTech).
guidance: If only one particular method/embodiment is taught, there must be evidence that the specification contemplated more generic methods or broader subject matter.

name: Examiner initial burden when alleging lack of written description
description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
guidance: In making a rejection the examiner must set forth express findings of fact: (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supported by the application (see Rasmussen).

name: Applicant reply and re-evaluation requirement
description: Upon reply by applicant, the examiner must re-determine the patentability of the claimed invention, including whether the written description requirement is satisfied, by reperforming the analysis in view of the whole record.
guidance: If the whole record demonstrates that the written description requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If it still does not, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal and properly treat further showings; affidavits relevant to 112, para. 1 must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed if rejection is maintained (In re Alton).

name: Support requirement for new/amended claims and priority benefit
description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
guidance: When an explicit limitation in a claim is not present in the written description, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood that the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone).

name: Objective standard for written description compliance
description: The essential question is whether the description clearly allows persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed.
guidance: An applicant must convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, he or she was in possession of the invention as now claimed (Vas-Cath, In re Gosteli, Ralston Purina v. Far-Mar-Co.).

name: Non-literal description and amendments
description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally to satisfy the description requirement, but if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed (a departure/addition/deletion), the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
guidance: Such a conclusion will result in rejection under 35 U.S.C.112, first paragraph, or denial of the benefit of the filing date of a previously filed application, as appropriate.

name: Typical factual circumstances giving rise to written-description disputes
description: Written description issues most commonly arise in several circumstances: (I) amendments affecting a claim; (II) reliance on filing date of parent application under 35 U.S.C.120; (III) reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C.119; (IV) support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference.
guidance: Each circumstance raises the question whether the subject matter of the claim is supported in the application as filed; see cited cases (Wright; Tronzo; Scheiber; Ziegler; Fields v. Conover; Hyatt v. Boone).

name: Analyze claims under their broadest reasonable interpretation
description: Claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: All examples are analyzed based on the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim language; examine embodiments encompassed by the claim when determining whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception.

name: Step 1: Determine statutory category
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
guidance: If the claim is not within a statutory category, it is ineligible at Step 1; if it is, proceed to evaluate whether it is directed to a judicial exception.

name: Use the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis for nature-based products
description: For nature-based product claims (e.g., nucleic acids, antibodies, cells, bacteria), analyze whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart(s) in their natural state.
guidance: Consider structural and functional characteristics, whether differences arose from human manipulation, and whether claimed differences prevent improperly tying up natural products. If markedly different, the claim is not directed to a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: NO).

name: Assess structural characteristics vs. natural counterpart
description: Evaluate whether the claimed product has different structural characteristics (e.g., chemical bonds severed, altered nucleotide sequence, fused domains, engineered amino acid changes) compared to the natural counterpart.
guidance: Examples: isolated nucleic acid with identical sequence but severed bonds was considered different structurally but not markedly different; sequence substitutions, labels attached to create a single molecule, heterologous combinations, or engineered Fc domains can provide structural differences that rise to marked difference.

name: Assess functional characteristics vs. natural counterpart
description: Evaluate whether the claimed product exhibits different functional characteristics (e.g., encodes different protein, becomes fluorescent, altered cytotoxicity or serum half-life, changed phenotype, altered growth rate) compared to the natural counterpart.
guidance: Functional differences created by human manipulation (e.g., expression of a new marker, increased oxygen utilization, fluorescence) can contribute to a marked difference and support eligibility.

name: Sequence modifications can confer marked difference
description: Claims limited to nucleic acids having non-naturally occurring substitutions (sequence changes) can have structural differences sufficient to be markedly different from natural sequences.
guidance: A nucleic acid with changed nucleotide sequence may encode a different protein and thus be not a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: NO).

name: Claim breadth: if claim encompasses natural and non-natural embodiments, may be ineligible
description: If a single claim encompasses embodiments that are structurally/functionally identical to naturally occurring items as well as changed items, the claim as a whole may lack marked difference and be a product-of-nature exception.
guidance: Example: a broad claim to 'an antibody to Protein S' that embraces naturally occurring antibodies and engineered variants fails Step 2A because some embodiments are identical to nature.

name: Limiting claims to non-naturally occurring species (e.g., human antibodies to Protein S) can confer eligibility
description: Claims specifically limited to forms not found in nature (e.g., human antibodies to an antigen where no human antibodies naturally occur) can have markedly different characteristics.
guidance: If the claimed subject matter does not exist in nature, the structural differences support that the claim is not directed to a product-of-nature exception.

name: Limiting to specific sequences or CDRs supports eligibility unless shown to exist in nature
description: Claims reciting specific complementarity determining region (CDR) sequences or SEQ ID NOs are limited to concrete molecules and are eligible unless the examiner can show that the identical molecule exists in nature.
guidance: The mere possibility that nature might randomly create a similar molecule does not bar eligibility (Myriad).

name: Engineered domain/variant changes (e.g., variant Fc) can provide marked difference
description: Claims to antibodies with engineered variant Fc domains comprising amino acid modifications relative to wild-type Fc domain are structurally and functionally different from natural antibodies.
guidance: These modifications (changed cytotoxicity, serum half-life) can rise to the level of marked difference.

name: Population/mixture claims: emergent properties from combinations can be markedly different
description: Claims to populations or mixtures (e.g., cell populations with specific percentages or bacterial mixtures) should be analyzed for whether interactions among components give rise to properties not present in nature.
guidance: If the claimed ratio or mixture results in emergent biological properties (e.g., altered growth rates, synergistic fermentation, lower fat yogurt), those functional differences can be a marked difference.

name: Step 2B: Determine whether claim elements add 'significantly more'
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, add significantly more to the exception to transform it into eligible subject matter.
guidance: Consider whether claimed additional features are meaningful limitations beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity, or whether they confine the claim to a particular inventive application or improve the technology.

name: Generic, routine, and conventional limitations do not add 'significantly more'
description: Recitation of well-understood, routine, conventional items or high-level generic features (e.g., 'a container') typically does not provide significantly more.
guidance: If a container is claimed at a high level of generality and is routinely used in the art, it does not make a nature-based product claim eligible under Step 2B.

name: Combination that confines claim to a particular useful application or improves technology can add 'significantly more'
description: An element or combination that confines the claim to a particular useful application (e.g., pacemaker cells in a biocompatible scaffold that facilitates faster tissue regeneration) and improves the technology can supply significantly more than the exception.
guidance: Example: combining pacemaker cells with a particular scaffold to achieve a demonstrable technological improvement satisfied Step 2B (YES) and produced eligibility.

name: Do a streamlined analysis when claim clearly does not seek to tie up natural/mineral or abstract idea
description: If the claim is clearly focused on an assembly, manufacturing configuration, or application that does not seek to tie up a natural product or abstract concept, a full markedly-different or abstract-idea analysis may not be required.
guidance: Examples: a hip prosthesis assembly including hydroxyapatite (natural mineral) focuses on the assembly and does not require a full marked-difference analysis; a robotic arm claim using velocity relationships but not tying up the mathematical relationship may qualify without full analysis.

name: Conduct a detailed IP audit
description: Conduct a detailed IP audit to ensure all patent documentation is accurate and up-to-date.
guidance: Verify ownership, claim scope, maintenance status, and documentation completeness before negotiating. Accurate paperwork strengthens enforceability and bargaining power.

name: Articulate the patent's value with factual data
description: Approach negotiations armed with factual data about the patent’s value and potential so both parties understand and respect positions.
guidance: Use market analyses, revenue projections, and technical demonstrations to support claims. Effective communication underpinned by data is emphasized as essential to successful negotiations.

name: Statement of Statutory Basis, 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, Second Paragraph (¶ 7.30.02)
description: Quotation of the statutory text of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (and pre-AIA second paragraph): the specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor (or applicant pre-AIA) regards as the invention.
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) The statute need not be re‑cited in all Office actions — required in first actions on the merits and final rejections; where not cited use paragraph 7.103. (2) Paragraphs 7.30.01 and 7.30.02 are to be used ONLY ONCE in a given Office action.

name: Failure To Claim Inventor’s Invention (¶ 7.34)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA second paragraph) as failing to set forth the subject matter which the inventor/joint inventor (or applicant pre‑AIA) regards as the invention; evidence that the claim(s) fail to correspond in scope with that which the inventor regards as the invention can be found in a reply or other submission by the inventor/applicant.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. (2) Use only where inventor/applicant has stated (outside the application as filed) that the invention is different from what is defined in the claim(s). (3) In bracket 3 identify the submission and its filing date. (4) In bracket 4 set forth what the inventor/applicant stated. (5) In bracket 5 explain how that statement indicates an invention other than what is being claimed.

name: Failure To Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim (Indefinite) (¶ 7.34.01)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA second paragraph) as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter the inventor/applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. (2) Insert proper claim numbering/grammar; review dependent claims for same defect and add if necessary. (3) Follow this paragraph with one or more of form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.10 and/or 7.34.23–7.34.24 as applicable; if none appropriate, supply a full explanation identifying particular term(s)/limitation(s) rendering the claim indefinite and why. If one of ordinary skill can determine the scope, do not use this rejection. See MPEP §§2171–2174. See form paragraph 7.34.15 for pro se applicants.

name: Terminology Used Inconsistent with Accepted Meaning (¶ 7.34.02)
description: Where applicant acts as his/her own lexicographer to specifically define a claim term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the claim term and set forth the uncommon definition so as to put one reasonably skilled in the art on notice that the applicant intended to so redefine that claim term. The term '[1]' in claim [2] is used by the claim to mean '[3]' while the accepted meaning is '[4]'; the term is indefinite because the specification does not clearly redefine the term.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) In bracket 3, point out the applicant‑assigned meaning taking into account the entire disclosure. (2) In bracket 4, point out accepted meaning and support via textbook/dictionary citation; see MPEP §2173.05(a). (3) Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01. (4) Use only where the specification does not clearly redefine the claim term at issue.

name: Relative Term — Term of Degree Rendering Claim Indefinite (¶ 7.34.03)
description: The term '[1]' in claim [2] is a relative term (term of degree) which renders the claim indefinite because the term is not defined by the claim, the specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, and one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of the scope of the invention.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) In bracket 3 explain which parameter, quantity, or other limitation in the claim has been rendered indefinite by the term. (2) This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Broader Range/Limitation And Narrow Range/Limitation in Same Claim (¶ 7.34.04)
description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation that falls within the broad range or limitation (in the same claim) may be indefinite if the resulting claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the patent protection desired. Example: claim [1] recites the broad recitation [2] and also recites [3], the narrower statement; the claim(s) are indefinite because there is doubt whether the narrower language is merely exemplary or a required feature.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) In bracket 2 insert broader range/limitation and where it appears; in bracket 3 insert narrower and where it appears. This paragraph may be modified to fit other indefiniteness instances. (2) Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01. See MPEP §2173.05(c).

name: Lack of Antecedent Basis in the Claims (¶ 7.34.05)
description: Claim [1] recites the limitation [2] in [3]. There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim (e.g., 'said lever' or 'the lever' without prior introduction).
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) In bracket 2 insert the limitation lacking antecedent basis; (2) in bracket 3 identify where in the claim the limitation appears; (3) Use this form paragraph ONLY in aggravated situations where lack of antecedent basis makes scope indeterminate. It must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Claims Are a Literal Translation (¶ 7.34.07)
description: The claims are generally narrative and indefinite, failing to conform with current U.S. practice; they appear to be a literal translation into English from a foreign document and are replete with grammatical and idiomatic errors.
guidance: Examiner Note: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Indefinite Claim Language: 'For Example' (¶ 7.34.08)
description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase 'for example' renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitation(s) following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: See MPEP §2173.05(d). Examiner Note: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Indefinite Claim Language: 'Or The Like' (¶ 7.34.09)
description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase 'or the like' renders the claim(s) indefinite because the claim(s) include(s) elements not actually disclosed (those encompassed by 'or the like'), thereby rendering the scope of the claim(s) unascertainable.
guidance: See MPEP §2173.05(d). Examiner Note: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Indefinite Claim Language: 'Such As' (¶ 7.34.10)
description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase 'such as' renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
guidance: See MPEP §2173.05(d). Examiner Note: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

name: Essential Steps Omitted (¶ 7.34.12)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA) as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, such omission amounting to a gap between the steps. The omitted steps are: [2].
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. (2) In bracket 2, recite the steps omitted from the claims. (3) Give the rationale for considering the omitted steps critical/essential and explain basis for concluding inventor regards the omitted matter as essential. See MPEP §2172.01.

name: Essential Elements Omitted (¶ 7.34.13)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA) as being incomplete for omitting essential elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the elements. The omitted elements are: [2].
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. (2) In bracket 2, recite the elements omitted from the claims. (3) Give the rationale for considering the omitted elements critical/essential and explain basis for concluding inventor regards the omitted matter as essential. See MPEP §2172.01.

name: Essential Cooperative Relationships Omitted (¶ 7.34.14)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA) as being incomplete for omitting essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the necessary structural connections. The omitted structural cooperative relationships are: [2].
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. (2) In bracket 2, recite the omitted structural cooperative relationships of elements. (3) Give the rationale for considering these cooperative relationships critical/essential and explain basis for concluding inventor regards them as essential. See MPEP §2172.01.

name: Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 112, Pro Se (¶ 7.34.15)
description: Claim [1] rejected as failing to define the invention in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA second paragraph). The claim(s) are narrative in form and replete with indefinite language; the structure making up the device must be clearly and positively specified and organized to present a complete operative device. Claims must be in one sentence form only; note the format of claims in cited patents.
guidance: Use when applicant is pro se; provides guidance on required claim form and clarity for pro se filers. See form paragraph usage notes.

name: Failure To Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim — Omnibus Claim (¶ 7.35)
description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA) as being indefinite in that it fails to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language. This claim is an omnibus type claim.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. (2) Use this paragraph to reject an 'omnibus' type claim — no further explanation necessary. (3) Example of an omnibus claim: 'A device substantially as shown and described.' See form paragraph 7.34.01 for related procedural context.

name: Trademark or Trade Name as a Limitation in the Claim (¶ 7.35.01)
description: Claim [1] contains the trademark/trade name [2]. Where a trademark or trade name is used in a claim as a limitation to identify or describe a particular material or product, the claim does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA); the claim scope is uncertain since a trademark/trade name identifies a source of goods, not the goods themselves, and thus does not properly identify or describe the goods.
guidance: Examiner Notes: (1) In bracket 2, insert the trademark/trade name and where it is used in the claim. (2) In bracket 3, specify the material or product which is intended to be identified/ described by the trademark/trade name. Cite Ex parte Simpson, 218 USPQ 1020 (Bd. App. 1982). Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103 where applicable.

name: Reissued patents treated as new; scope and retroactivity limits
description: A re-issue is considered a new patent for determining infringement timing; acts performed before re-issue are not infringements of the re-issue.
guidance: However, whether a re-issue with broader claims reaches devices that did not infringe the original depends on how the original patent is measured (by description or claims) and relevant case law (Ives & Miller v. Hartford Spring & Axle Co.; Cammeyer v. Newton).

name: Permission to file a banned application overseas (scope and conditions)
description: Where the Korean government grants permission to file a patent application banned from filing overseas, the application may exceptionally be filed in foreign countries — currently restricted by agreement to filing in the United States of America only.
guidance: Conditions for issuing permission include: (1) the specification's content must be clear and specific to enable examination in the U.S.; (2) the right to claim damages caused by confidentiality in the U.S. must be waived (except for damages from unauthorized U.S. use/disclosure). To obtain permission, submit a written request (Annexed Form No.21) and follow consultation procedures with the Defense Acquisition Program Administration. Detailed administrative instructions and implementation procedures govern the process.

name: Eligible category: treaty-priority-basis pending abroad
description: A patent application which serves as a basis of a priority claim under treaties (limited to where a foreign application claiming priority is pending before a foreign patent office) is eligible.
guidance: This is limited to cases where the foreign office has a pending application claiming priority to the Korean application.

name: Necessity-of-urgent-processing standard and factors
description: Applications eligible by category are, in principle, deemed necessary for urgent processing (except those based on third-party practicing); to determine necessity, the determining officer considers: (i) relevance to national policies, (ii) protection of the applicant's interest, and (iii) whether urgent processing would make grant of a patent likely.
guidance: For factor (iii), submitting prior-art search results and an explanation of patentability supports the claim of necessity. Where prior-art searches are done by specialized institutes or under foreign-office agreements, the requester may omit detailed prior-art explanations because the institute's search suffices.

name: Required contents of a written RCE request
description: A properly filed RCE must include: the proper request form; payment of the proper fees; an information disclosure statement (IDS); and new justifications or supporting information for the patentability of the written description, claims, or drawings.
guidance: All listed elements are required for the PTO to continue processing the application; omission may prevent the RCE from taking effect.

name: Situations when an RCE is unnecessary
description: An RCE is unnecessary if the examiner suggested a particular claim would be allowed (you can submit an after-final response incorporating the suggested language), or if only minor claim restrictions are contemplated (consider AFCP). If the examiner will not enter an after-final response, they will issue an Advisory Action.
guidance: Before automatically filing an RCE, consider after-final responses, the After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP), and whether the intended changes truly require reopening prosecution and additional examiner search time.

name: Strategic guidance on when to file an RCE
description: File an RCE when you want to make additional claim revisions and/or arguments after a Final Office Action, particularly if your changes will require the examiner to perform more extensive prior-art searching. An examiner interview before filing can help determine necessity.
guidance: The page recommends an examiner interview as a diagnostic step to see whether an RCE is required and to understand the examiner’s view on whether the claims merit further time.

name: AFCP 2.0 eligibility and process notes
description: AFCP 2.0 can be requested following receipt of a final office action but is appropriate only if the examiner believes the claims are almost certain to be accepted; the applicant must request AFCP 2.0 during an examiner interview. If the examiner does not agree, an RCE must be filed.
guidance: AFCP 2.0 is a narrow pilot route to avoid an RCE when allowance is highly likely — it requires examiner concurrence obtained in an interview.

name: Claims that recite limitations directed to purported improvements may raise factual issues
description: Claims that include limitations reflecting purported improvements described in the specification (e.g., 'storing ... without substantial redundancy' resulting in improved system efficiency) can raise a genuine issue of material fact as to whether those limitations are more than well‑understood, routine, conventional activity.
guidance: When claims include limitations tied to concrete improvements described in the specification, examiners should consider whether the claim limitations are themselves unconventional in light of the factual-record support; such claims may preclude summary rejection on eligibility until fact‑finding is complete (as illustrated by Berkheimer's reversal of summary judgment for claims reciting such improvements).

name: Interfering subject matter (37 CFR 41.203)
description: An interference exists if the subject matter of a claim of one party would, if prior art, have anticipated or rendered obvious the subject matter of a claim of the opposing party and vice versa; 'same invention' means patentably indistinct inventions.
guidance: Apply familiar anticipation/obviousness principles; identical claim language does not guarantee same invention—construe claims in light of their own specifications. See multiple examples (Markush groups, genus/species, means-plus-function) illustrating how interference-in-fact is determined.

name: Count definition and scope
description: A count is the Board’s description of the interfering subject matter that sets the scope of admissible proofs on priority; where there is more than one count, each count must describe a patentably distinct invention.
guidance: Every count must have at least one corresponding claim for each party; counts define what proofs are admissible on priority issues.

name: Claim correspondence test (37 CFR 41.207(b)(2))
description: To determine whether a claim corresponds to a count, assume the subject matter of the count is prior art to the party; if the count would have anticipated or rendered the claim obvious, the claim corresponds to the count.
guidance: At least one corresponding claim required per party; a claim may correspond to multiple counts. Examples clarify genus/species and Markush situations where anticipation vs obviousness matters and may require showing of prior art to support obviousness.

name: Broadest reasonable construction (37 CFR 41.200(b))
description: A claim shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the application or patent in which it appears for interference purposes.
guidance: Interpret claim terms in context of the particular specification; means-plus-function limitations may produce different scopes depending on corresponding structure disclosed.

name: Interference search requirements (2304.01(a))
description: When an application is in condition for allowance, an interference search must be made by performing a text search of the 'US-PGPUB' database in EAST or WEST directed to the comprehensive inventive features in the broadest claim; sequence claims require STIC sequence search requests.
guidance: A printout of the databases searched, the queries used, and the date must be made of record in the application file; the search results must not be placed in the application file. If potential interfering subject matter is identified, review and follow Chapter 2300 guidance.

name: Obtaining control over involved files / assignment
description: Ordinarily, applications believed to interfere should be assigned to the same examiner. If applications are in different Technology Centers, reassign so both are in the TC where the commonly claimed invention would be classified.
guidance: After termination of interference, further transfer may be appropriate depending on outcome.

name: Restriction practice for interfering vs non-interfering claims
description: Restriction of interfering claims from non-interfering claims, or from unpatentable claims whose further prosecution would unduly delay initiation of the interference, can be appropriate under 35 U.S.C. 121; consult IPS when imposing such restrictions.
guidance: Applicants may instead cancel claims and refile in continuation applications; issuing non-interfering claims promptly is important to avoid unjustified delay given patent term adjustments.

name: Suspension of related examinations
description: Examination may continue in related cases, including benefit files; once related file examination is completed, consult IPS to determine further action. Suspension may be necessary if claims would be barred by a loss in the interference, but steps should be taken to minimize patent term adjustment effects.
guidance: Consider restriction of application to non-interfering claims so they can be issued and divert interfering claims to a divisional that can be suspended.

name: Added or amended claims during interference
description: An applicant may file a motion during the interference to add or amend a claim; a patentee may file a reissue application in support of such a motion. The paper adding/amending will be placed in the official record but not entered unless and to the extent authorized by the Board.
guidance: Examiner may only enter added/amended claims if authorized by the Board, and can still reject those claims during further prosecution.

name: Definitions relevant to interference practice (37 CFR 41.2/41.201)
description: Key defined terms include affidavit, Board, involved claim (claim designated as corresponding to the count), involved (Board declared subject of contested case), constructive reduction to practice, earliest constructive reduction to practice, senior/junior party, threshold issue, business day, and others.
guidance: Earliest constructive reduction to practice requires continuous disclosure through a chain of applications (35 U.S.C. 120/121 or timely 119/365 filings). Senior party entitled to presumption under §41.207(a)(1).

name: Intrinsic-record dismissal for eligibility (§101)
description: Patent eligibility can be dismissed at the pleading stage when the intrinsic record makes clear the claim is directed to an abstract idea or natural phenomenon and employs only conventional technology.
guidance: Provides case examples (BSG Tech; Cleveland Clinic; Chamberlain) where intrinsic evidence made ineligibility obvious. Contrasts with cases where factual allegations about unconventionality should be credited and the case permitted to proceed to discovery (Aatrix tension).

name: Anticipation (§102) pleading-stage rule when prior art is judicially noticeable
description: Anticipation can be resolved on the pleadings when all elements of the claim are plainly disclosed in a prior art document that is subject to judicial notice (e.g., a prior art patent), because that public record's veracity cannot be controverted.
guidance: But dismissal is inappropriate when claim construction or interpretation of the prior art is plausibly disputed; recasting anticipation as a mixed question clarifies that pleading-stage resolution is sometimes appropriate.

name: Indefiniteness (§112(b)) as mixed question and when resolvable on pleadings
description: Indefiniteness stems from §112(b) requiring claims to 'particularly point[] out and distinctly claim[]' the invention; a patent is indefinite if it 'fail[s] to inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.' Determining indefiniteness involves claim construction and thus is properly characterized as a mixed question of law and fact.
guidance: Indefiniteness can be decided at the pleading stage when the judge can confidently determine impermissible vagueness based on the intrinsic record (patent, specification, prosecution history). If extrinsic evidence is needed, decision should be postponed. Argues that judges, not juries, should decide indefiniteness.

name: Role of intrinsic versus extrinsic evidence in validity determinations
description: Intrinsic evidence (the patent specification, claims, prosecution history) can be evaluated as a matter of law and may suffice for early dismissal in clear cases; extrinsic evidence (prior art not judicially noticeable, expert testimony about a person of ordinary skill, etc.) raises factual disputes requiring further proceedings.
guidance: Examples: enablement/nonobviousness usually require extrinsic evidence and are harder to resolve on pleadings; eligibility, anticipation, and indefiniteness sometimes resolve on intrinsic record. Emphasizes when factual disputes exist, dismissal is inappropriate.

name: Purpose of the written description requirement
description: The written description requirement compels disclosure of the technologic knowledge upon which the patent is based and demonstrates that the patentee (inventor) was in possession of the invention that is claimed; it promotes the progress of the useful arts by ensuring adequate description in exchange for the right to exclude others.
guidance: Explains policy rationale for the requirement and anchors subsequent analysis — the specification must adequately describe the invention in return for the patent monopoly (Capon v. Eshhar and related authority).

name: Sufficiency standard — possession by one skilled in the art
description: To satisfy the written description requirement, a patent specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Compliance is a fact‑based inquiry that varies with the nature of the invention; cites cases such as Moba v. Diamond, Vas‑Cath, Enzo Biochem. The examiner must determine whether the disclosure conveys reasonable clarity that inventor was in possession as of the filing date.

name: Form of disclosure that can show possession
description: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention, including description of all claim limitations.
guidance: Lists multiple descriptive means and cites Lockwood; possession may be established by actual reduction to practice, drawings, structural chemical formulas, or distinguishing identifying characteristics.

name: Reduction to practice or "ready for patenting"
description: A showing of possession may be shown by an actual reduction to practice or by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas that show the invention was complete).
guidance: Examples and citations (Pfaff, Eli Lilly, Amgen). Reduction to practice may be shown by constructing an embodiment or performing a process that meets all claim limitations and shows it works for its intended purpose; testing may be required depending on the invention.

name: Deposits of biological materials as support (but not a substitute)
description: Reference to a deposit of biological material may satisfy the written description requirement for claimed biological materials, but a deposit is not a substitute for a written description; the written description of the deposited material should be as complete as possible.
guidance: Cites Enzo Biochem and the Deposit of Biological Materials rule (37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; 54 Fed. Reg. 34,864). Explains that deposits aid verification and infringement questions; deposits made after filing can support corrections only with required statements under 37 CFR 1.804.

name: Presumption of adequacy for original claims and examiner's initial burden
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the examiner has the initial burden, after a thorough reading, to present evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as providing adequate support.
guidance: Cites In re Wertheim. To make a prima facie case, the examiner must identify the specific claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure (Hyatt v. Dudas example). If applicant points to support, burden shifts back to examiner.

name: Original claims — essential/critical feature requirement
description: The claimed invention as a whole may not be adequately described if the claims require an essential or critical feature that is not adequately described in the specification and which is not conventional or known in the art.
guidance: Gives examples (e.g., gene claim including promoters or regulatory elements not described). If specification indicates a particular feature is essential, omitting it in a claim can render the claim unsupported (Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).

name: Mere obviousness is insufficient for written description
description: A description that merely renders the claimed invention obvious may not sufficiently describe the invention for purposes of the written description requirement.
guidance: Cites Eli Lilly and contrasts with situations where functional disclosure of software may be adequate due to skill in the art (Fonar). Examiner should not conflate obviousness with possession.

name: New or amended claims — prohibition on new matter and support requirement
description: New or amended claims must be supported by the original disclosure; the proscription against introduction of new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251) prevents adding subject matter beyond what was filed.
guidance: Cites In re Rasmussen and related cases. Newly added claims or limitations must be supported by express, implicit, or inherent disclosure. If original claims disclose material not elsewhere in the specification, applicant may amend the specification to include it (In re Benno), but the reverse is not permitted.

name: Omission of a limitation may indicate lack of possession of broader genus
description: Omission of a limitation in a claim can raise an issue whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; claims that omit matter described as essential in the specification do not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: Examples: PIN/NIP, Gentry Gallery, Johnson Worldwide, Tronzo. If the specification makes clear a narrow understanding is essential, broader claims may be unsupported.

name: Examiner methodology — read and analyze the specification first
description: Office personnel should thoroughly read and evaluate the entire content of the application when reviewing for compliance with the written description requirement, recognizing the presumption of adequacy and then presenting reasons to overcome it.
guidance: Describes that the examiner must identify unsupported limitations and explain deficiency; suggests what may constitute a sufficient examiner statement (e.g., 'applicant has not pointed out where the new (or amended) claim is supported'). Citations include MPEP § 2163.04 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers (claim construction)
description: Claim construction is essential: each claim must be separately analyzed and given a reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; the entire claim (including preamble and transitional phrase) must be considered.
guidance: Cites Katz, In re Morris, and other authorities. The examiner should determine the scope and meaning of the claim, including weight to give the preamble and meaning of transitional terms.

name: Transitional phrases and preamble treatment
description: Understand and apply the meaning of transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') and evaluate whether preamble language constitutes a structural limitation; the claim as a whole must be supported.
guidance: Explains 'comprising' is open‑ended; 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground and should be construed relative to the specification; applicant bears burden to show additional elements do not materially change basic and novel properties. Citations: Genentech v. Chiron, PPG, AK Steel, Janakirama‑Rao.

name: Sufficiency may be shown by drawings, formulae, or identifying characteristics
description: An adequate written description may be shown by detailed drawings, structural or generic chemical formulas, generic formulae for a genus, or other identifying characteristics that permit a skilled person to recognize inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Cites cases where drawings alone provided written description (Vas‑Cath, Wolfensperger) and discusses generic chemical formulae as normally adequate descriptions of claimed genera (Eli Lilly). The description need only detail what is new or not conventional.

name: Procedural standard for making a prima facie case and burden shifting
description: To make a prima facie case of inadequate written description, the examiner must identify unsupported claim limitations and explain why the claim is not supported; a clear explanation can shift the burden to applicant to point to support or amend claims.
guidance: Hyatt v. Dudas example: examiner explicitly explained why combination of elements lacked adequate support; for amended claims, a simple statement that applicant hasn't pointed out support may suffice where support is not apparent. See MPEP §§ 2163.04, 714.02, 2163.06.

name: Field-of-use / technological-environment limitations are insufficient
description: Examples of limitations that the courts have described as merely indicating a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception.
guidance: The guidance lists specific examples (i–x) such as limiting drug administration to a particular patient population (Mayo), identifying hedging participants as commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), narrowing a formula to wheels (Flook), specifying execution on a computer (FairWarning), limiting virus screening to telephone/Internet networks (Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec), limiting collecting/analyzing/displaying information to electric power grid data (Electric Power Group), informing doctors to apply a law of nature to detect polymorphisms (Genetic Techs.), implementing budgeting via a broad "communication medium" (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One), using advertising-as-currency on the Internet (Ultramercial), and requiring online/computer implementation for guaranteeing transactions (buySAFE). Examiners should treat "technological environment" and "field of use" interchangeably and consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP §2106.05(g)). For claim limitations that merely link an exception to a particular environment, explain in the rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.

name: Consider 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeable
description: Examiners should be aware that the courts often use the terms 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeably.
guidance: For purposes of the eligibility analysis, treat these terms interchangeably and consider overlap with Step 2B factors like insignificant extra-solution activity. Evaluate each claim on its own merits and the other Step 2B considerations before deciding.

name: Eligibility is self-evident when claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality
description: A claim that, when viewed as a whole, clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception and clearly improves technology or computer functionality may be eligible at Pathway A.
guidance: Examples: a robotic arm assembly with a control system operating using certain mathematical relationships; an artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral; products with merely ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with gold contact). Do not use streamlined analysis if the claim lacks self-evident eligibility or if it's a close call.

name: Clear improvement to technology/computer functionality can avoid full analysis
description: Claims directed to clear improvements to computer-related technology or functionality (or other technological processes) may avoid the full eligibility analysis (e.g., Enfish, McRO).
guidance: When claims are viewed as a whole and their eligibility is self-evident based on a clear improvement, no further analysis is needed. If claims present a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM), perform the full Alice/Mayo test.

name: Eligibility rejections must be based on substantive law and judicial precedent
description: Eligibility rejections must be based on failure to comply with 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent; training materials and examples do not themselves serve as the legal basis for a rejection.
guidance: Examiners may cite training materials or examples in support of an argument, but applicants should not be required to model claims after those examples to attain eligibility.

name: Review the record as a whole and evaluate claims individually
description: When evaluating a claimed invention for eligibility, examiners should review the record as a whole (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law or prior art) and make eligibility determinations claim-by-claim.
guidance: Dependent claims may be eligible even if an independent claim is ineligible because they may add limitations amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception. Consider each claim separately based on its particular elements.

name: Prima facie case requirement for §101 rejections
description: If it's more likely than not that a claim does not satisfy eligibility criteria, examiners should formulate an appropriate rejection that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility.
guidance: The initial burden is on the examiner to explain why a claim is ineligible clearly and specifically so the applicant has sufficient notice and can effectively respond. The rejection should provide clear and specific reasons for ineligibility.

name: Step 1 rejections must explain why claim is not within a statutory category
description: When concluding a claim does not fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO), the rejection should explain why the claim is not directed to one of the four statutory categories of invention.
guidance: See MPEP §706.03(a) for instructions on making such a rejection; provide sufficient clarity and specificity in the Office action.

name: Step 2A: identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim
description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites or describes the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea).
guidance: Identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it corresponds to concepts the courts have identified as abstract (see MPEP §2106.04(a)(2)). Citing appropriate court decisions that support the identification is a best practice; ensure the cited decision's facts reasonably tie to the present case. Avoid relying on non-precedential decisions unless facts match uniquely. Sample explanation provided: 'The claim recites the steps of sorting information by X, which is an abstract idea similar to concepts identified by the courts...'

name: Step 2A for laws of nature/natural phenomena/products of nature: identify and provide reasoned rationale
description: When the claim is determined to recite a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature, the rejection should identify that subject matter as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered such an exception.
guidance: Provide explanations for correlations (law of nature), naturally occurring phenomena, or why a product lacks markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart. Sample explanations illustrate comparing isolated products to natural counterparts and assessing marked differences in structure, function, or properties.

name: Step 2B: identify additional elements and explain why they do not amount to significantly more
description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the exception and explain why they, individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Address both individual elements and the combination; a new combination of known steps may be eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Provide a reasoned explanation—if elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, explain why courts or those in the field would recognize them as such.

name: Explain conventionality when relying on 'well-understood, routine, conventional' findings
description: When concluding certain claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or persons in the relevant field would recognize, those limitations as such.
guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation supporting that conclusion and, where available, use sources of evidence (specification statements, manuals, patents, case law) to support assertions. See MPEP §2106.05(d) for further information.

name: Generic computer components performing generic functions do not meaningfully limit a claim
description: Claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) may be explained as not meaningfully limiting the claim.
guidance: MPEP §2106.05(d) lists computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically. However, not all computer functions are necessarily conventional; courts have found eligible situations where generic components in combination perform non-generic functions (e.g., DDR Holdings). Explain why the claimed computer functions are generic and do not add significantly more.

name: Best practice: consult the specification to identify elements that could overcome a §101 rejection
description: If a rejection is made, examiners should consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to a claim to make it eligible and identify those elements in the Office action.
guidance: Suggesting claim amendments from the specification is a way to assist applicant in overcoming the rejection and clarifies how the claim could be made eligible.

name: Claim construction — use of extrinsic dictionaries and intrinsic evidence; forfeiture
description: Courts may construe technical terms (e.g., 'VoIP') by reference to industry-agreed plain and ordinary meaning and extrinsic technical dictionaries, but intrinsic evidence controls; failure to raise a proposed redefinition in district court may forfeit the argument on appeal.
guidance: District courts can rely on technical dictionaries and expert evidence to construe terms; a party that claims a patentee redefined a term must timely raise that argument below or risk forfeiture. Court may reject expert testimony inconsistent with documentary evidence.

name: Doctrine of equivalents — requirement for particularized testimony and linking argument
description: To prove infringement under the doctrine of equivalents, a patentee must present particularized expert testimony and linking argument tying specific elements of the accused product to claim limitations.
guidance: Generalized testimony about overall similarity is insufficient. Experts must (1) identify particular elements in the accused product that correspond to claim limitations and (2) provide a meaningful explanation under the function-way-result (or other) test explaining why those elements are equivalent. Failure to do so supports JMOL of non-infringement.

name: Insubstantial-differences formulation requires particularized proof
description: An 'insubstantial differences' theory of equivalence likewise requires particularized testimony and linking argument regarding the insubstantiality of the differences between claimed invention and the accused device/process.
guidance: Patentees must present an independent insubstantial-differences theory at trial with element-by-element linking; relying on general similarity testimony is insufficient.

name: Motions to amend in IPR — scope of permissible opposing arguments
description: The statutory limit that only grounds in the petition be considered does not apply in the same way to motions to amend; when a patent owner introduces new claims, the Board may consider arguments, including those based on references not in the original petition, to oppose the proposed substitute claims.
guidance: A time-barred or previously non-participating party (e.g., a joinder) may be permitted to oppose a revised motion to amend and rely on additional prior art to show the proposed claims would be unpatentable. Patent owners seeking to amend should be prepared to face broader opposition arguments.

name: Motivation-to-combine and substantial-evidence standard at PTAB
description: The Board may find proposed substitute claims unpatentable as obvious based on a motivation-to-combine supported by expert testimony (e.g., that a skilled artisan would look to a reference's method/algorithm to address a need), and the Federal Circuit reviews such findings for substantial evidence.
guidance: Board reliance on experts to establish what a skilled artisan would do is permissible; appellants must show lack of substantial evidence to overturn the PTAB. When challenging PTAB obviousness findings, courts expect a record-level engagement with the references and expert testimony.

name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR)
description: General rule: royalties should be based on the smallest salable unit that practices the patented invention and is closely related to the claimed invention; EMVR is a narrow exception.
guidance: If the smallest salable unit is a multi-component product with non-infringing components unrelated to the patented feature, damages must be based only on the portion of that unit’s value attributable to the patented technology. The EMVR permits using entire product revenues only if the patentee proves the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates the product's value. (Cites: Ericsson v. D-Link; VirnetX; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Lucent; Rite-Hite.)

name: Willful Infringement — General Standard
description: To find infringement willful, plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant knew of the plaintiff’s patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
guidance: Jury may consider whether the defendant’s behavior was deliberate or intentional, but cannot find willfulness solely because the defendant knew about the patent. Consider all circumstances and defendant’s knowledge at the time the conduct occurred. If infringement is willful, that determination should not affect the amount of the damages award. (Cites: Eko Brands; Halo.)

name: Petition particularity requirement
description: Inter partes review petitions must identify 'with particularity … the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim' (35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3)).
guidance: Petitions must point to concrete evidence for each alleged claim deficiency; general assertions without specific supporting evidence are insufficient.

name: Claim construction standard (Phillips)
