description: Claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; look principally to intrinsic evidence (claim language, written description, prosecution history).
guidance: Extrinsic evidence is less significant than intrinsic record in determining the legally operative meaning of claim language (Phillips v. AWH; DePuy Spine). Use specification and prosecution history first, then extrinsic evidence to aid understanding.

name: Weight of intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence
description: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) is primary; extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries) is less significant.
guidance: Rely on intrinsic record for claim meaning; use extrinsic evidence only to assist and not to contradict intrinsic evidence.

name: Specification-defined terms control
description: When the specification expressly defines a claim term (e.g., 'fixed dose' defined in the specification), that definition governs and the term requires no further construction.
guidance: If parties do not dispute a specification definition, the Board will adopt the specification definition as the meaning of the claim term.

name: Functional claim language may be limiting
description: Functional language in an apparatus claim can be limiting on claim scope (citing K-2 Corp.), rather than mere intended use, depending on the natural reading of the claim language.
guidance: Analyze whether the functional language informs structural requirements of the claimed device; if so, treat it as a limiting functional limitation rather than an unlimiting intended use.

name: Intended use vs structural limitation (In re Casey guidance)
description: A recited intended use of a device is not automatically given patentable weight (In re Casey), but functional language that imposes structural capability requirements may be limiting.
guidance: Do not import method-of-treatment limitations from claim language that recites intended use unless the language naturally requires structural or functional capability.

name: Construction of 'delivers to a patient' (functional limitation)
description: The phrase 'delivers to a patient' is construed as a functional limitation requiring that the claimed subcutaneous administration device be capable of containing and subcutaneously delivering the dose to a person.
guidance: Do not import additional limitations (e.g., limited to patients with a specific disease or requiring 'safe and effective' delivery) unless the claim language supports them.

name: Construction of 'contains and delivers … 162 mg fixed dose' (no single-injection requirement)
description: Claims reciting 'a subcutaneous administration device, which contains and delivers to a patient a 162 mg fixed dose' require the device to be capable of containing and delivering the 162 mg fixed dose subcutaneously but do not require that the dose be delivered in a single injection.
guidance: The plain claim language controls; the common meaning of 'dose' (e.g., 'taken at one time') does not necessarily mandate a single physical injection—multiple sequential injections delivering the total amount can be within scope unless the claim expressly restricts method of delivery.

name: Obviousness standard and Graham factors
description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 103, obviousness is determined by Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness.
guidance: Also consider whether there was a motivation to combine references and whether a POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of success; apply KSR guidance (including 'obvious to try' when there are a finite number of predictable solutions).

name: Apparatus claims are not limited by efficacy or safety
description: Device/apparatus claims directed to an article of manufacture are not necessarily limited by claims of efficacy or therapeutic effect (i.e., they need not recite safety/effectiveness that would be required for method-of-treatment claims).
guidance: Avoid importing efficacy/safety requirements into apparatus claims unless the claim language or specification clearly impose such limits.

name: Use of prosecution history in claim interpretation
description: Prosecution history (e.g., addition of claim language like 'contains') can inform claim meaning but cannot be used to import limitations beyond the claim language.
guidance: Examine amendments and statements during prosecution for how the patentee distinguished claims, but do not extend claim scope by reading in unrecited limitations from prosecution remarks.

name: Director authority to institute IPRs/PGRs
description: Effective October 20, 2025, the USPTO Director will decide whether to institute IPR and post-grant review (PGR) trials (in consultation with at least three PTAB judges). This replaces prior practice where merits panels of APJs made institution decisions.
guidance: Director will consider both discretionary denial and merits issues raised by the petition; may issue a 'summary notice' granting or denying institution; may issue fuller decisions for "novel or important factual or legal issues"; may refer institution decisions to one or more PTAB members for detailed treatment of issues (e.g., claim construction, priority analyses, real-party-in-interest determinations). Petitions referred to an APJ panel prior to Oct. 20, 2025, are unaffected.

name: Earlier 2024 Notice (withdrawn) on serial petitions and expanded briefing
description: The USPTO withdrew a 2024 Notice that would have given APJ merits panels discretion to decline to institute 'serial petitions' narrowly defined as petitions filed by the same party (or real party in interest) challenging the same claims, and that would have implemented expanded briefing for discretionary-denial issues.
guidance: The withdrawal signals a shift from an APJ-panel-centric approach to institution toward Director control; the 2024 Notice contained narrower, panel-discretion-focused proposals (including 325(d) considerations) that the new Proposed Rules supersede or replace.

name: Court-recognized examples of well-understood, routine, conventional computer functions
description: The courts have recognized certain computer functions as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner (e.g., at a high level of generality) or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples the courts have recognized include: (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (using the Internet to gather data; forwarding information); (ii) performing repetitive calculations (recomputing or readjusting values); (iii) electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining shadow accounts, updating activity logs); (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory; (v) electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (OCR); (vi) a web browser's back and forward button functionality. The listing is not exhaustive and does not imply all computer functions are conventional (see decisions like DDR Holdings, Amdocs, BASCOM for eligible computer-implemented claims). Courts have found claims ineligible where the claim as a whole amounts to generic computer functions used to implement an abstract idea; conversely, combinations that perform non-generic functions may be significantly more (DDR Holdings).

name: Court-recognized examples of well-understood, routine, conventional laboratory techniques (life sciences)
description: In the life science arts, certain laboratory techniques have been recognized by courts as well-understood, routine, conventional activity when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
guidance: Examples include: (i) determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means; (ii) using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA; (iii) detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample; (iv) immunizing a patient against a disease; (v) analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants; (vi) freezing and thawing cells; (vii) amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences; (viii) hybridizing a gene probe. These techniques, when recited generically, have been treated as conventional in decisions such as Mayo, Ariosa/Sequenom, Rapid Litig. Mgmt., Ambry Genetics, and related cases.

name: Meaningful limitations (Other Meaningful Limitations)
description: For a claim directed to a judicial exception to be patent-eligible, it must include additional features that ensure the claim applies the exception in a meaningful way — i.e., add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the exception to a particular technological environment.
guidance: The phrase 'meaningful limitations' describes additional elements that provide an inventive concept; considerations in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(d) are examples of meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr — steps applying a mathematical equation in a specific automated rubber-molding process were meaningful because they limited practical application; Classen — immunization step integrated analytical results into a specific tangible method. The claim should add limitations beyond mere implementation on a generic computer or mere linkage to a technological environment. Examiners must consider additional elements both individually and in combination; when appropriate, examiners may explain on the record why the additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

name: Assessment whether a claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (result-oriented claims)
description: One key indicator of a mere instruction to apply an exception is whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome, failing to recite details of how the solution is accomplished.
guidance: Result-oriented or highly functional claim language that covers any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished is equivalent to saying 'apply it' and typically does not provide significantly more. Courts have found such claims ineligible (Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or specific way to achieve an outcome may provide significantly more. Example: Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One — claims that were result-oriented and lacked details of how modifications were performed were held ineligible. Examiners should look for concrete, specific steps/mechanisms rather than mere high-level result language.

name: Who may file a notice of appeal
description: 35 U.S.C. 134 and 37 CFR 41.31: An applicant any of whose claims has been twice rejected may appeal to the Board by filing a notice of appeal accompanied by the fee; a patent owner in certain reexamination proceedings may also appeal under specified conditions.
guidance: The 'twice rejected' requirement need not be within the same application (e.g., rejections in parent and continuing applications count). Specific rules apply for ex parte reexamination depending on filing date. Time for filing and applicable fees are governed by 37 CFR and 35 U.S.C. 41.

name: Defective notice of appeal procedures
description: Notices of appeal are reviewed by the Patent Appeal Center; if defective the Office will notify the applicant of the non-compliance. A notice is defective if it was not timely filed or the notice of appeal fee was not timely filed, or if none of the applicant's claims had been twice rejected.
guidance: Communications indicating defects should be sent by the Patent Appeal Center (e.g., PTOL-461). If defects are identified after the notice is entered, examiner should contact the Patent Appeal Center to determine appropriate action.

name: Amendments filed with/after appeal and 37 CFR 1.116
description: An amendment filed after a final action with a notice of appeal may not be entered as a matter of right under 37 CFR 1.116; such an amendment may be admitted if it cancels claims or complies with explicit form requirements, or presents rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal, or amends the specification upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons.
guidance: When appellant files an amendment, notice of appeal and appeal brief on the same date after mailing of a final action, 37 CFR 1.116 applies; examiners should apply requirements for entry of such amendments.

name: Interviews after notice of appeal rules
description: Normally one interview after final rejection is permitted before an appeal brief is filed; no interviews are permitted after the appeal brief is filed except in unusual circumstances. Interviews after mailing of an examiner's answer and prior to payment of forwarding fee are generally not permitted and may confuse the record.
guidance: Requests for interviews on cases under Board jurisdiction require specific approval of the Technology Center Director upon a written showing of extraordinary circumstances justifying a remand. Unusual situations (e.g., appellant wishes to cancel all appealed claims) may permit interviews.

name: Appeal brief content — required headings and order
description: 37 CFR 41.37(c): The brief shall contain specified items under appropriate headings and in the order indicated (except certain items may be relaxed for unrepresented appellants), including: (i) Real party in interest; (ii) Related appeals/interferences/trials; (iii) Summary of claimed subject matter (concise explanation with specification references); (iv) Arguments for each rejection; and additional required sections per the rule.
guidance: For each rejected independent claim and for dependent claims argued separately, if the claim contains a means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) recitation, the concise explanation must identify the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification. Unrepresented appellants need only substantially comply with certain subsections.

name: Limited claim amendments allowed after final rejection
description: Allowed limited claim amendments after final rejection (subject to AFCP 2.0 requirements).
guidance: Amendments after final should be narrowly tailored (not broadening) and aimed at overcoming specific rejections or improving form for appeal; avoid broad changes that would be inappropriate in an after-final context.

name: Requirement — amendment to at least one independent claim (no broadening)
description: To qualify for AFCP 2.0: Include an amendment to at least one independent claim that does NOT broaden scope.
guidance: Any independent-claim amendment must be narrowing (or at least not broaden). Draft claim changes to clearly reduce scope or correct formal/clarifying language rather than expand claim scope; explicitly note narrowing effect in remarks.

name: Standard after-final practice — goal of amendments
description: Proposed amendments should place the application either in condition for allowance or in better form for appeal.
guidance: Draft after-final amendments with the narrow objective of securing allowance or improving the appellate record (e.g., clarifying claim scope, addressing examiner's key grounds). Avoid extensive rewriting that cannot be justified after final rejection.

name: Statutory ground for reissue (invalidation/inoperativeness due to inadvertence)
description: To be the subject of a reissue under the statutory law, a patent must be invalid, or at least inoperative, because that fault resulted from a defective or insufficient specification, or from the patentee claiming more than he had a right to claim as new — and that fault must have arisen from inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention.
guidance: This is the core meritorious ground (derived from Grant v. Raymond and later statutes). The statute's proviso that the fault be inadvertent/accidental/mistaken and non-fraudulent is imperative in all cases. (References: Acts of 1832/1836, section summaries in text.)

name: Meaning of 'defective' versus 'insufficient' (description/claims)
description: 'Defective' means 'bad' (e.g., obscure in parts though otherwise complete); 'insufficient' means 'lacking' (e.g., clear so far as it goes but omitting parts). A claim may be defective (liable to be misunderstood) or insufficient (clear but too narrow to cover the invention).
guidance: Distinguishing these meanings matters because the statute uses both words; they are not synonymous and point to different remedial approaches via reissue.

name: Reissues that do not add or broaden claims are safe and may be sought at any time
description: Invalidity or insufficiency arising from defective/insufficient description or defective claims, where that invalidity arose by inadvertence and without fraud, may be remedied by a reissue where the reissue does not add nor broaden any claim.
guidance: Such corrective reissues have not been held void in adjudicated cases; they improve public information and can be invoked at any time during the patent's life.

name: Claims are the operative parts; inoperativeness from omitted claimed inventions justifies reissue (broadened reissues)
description: If the descriptive part describes multiple allied inventions but the claims cover only one, the patent is operative as to the claimed invention but inoperative as to the others — that inoperativeness suffices to found a right to reissue. Reissues granted to cover such omitted aspects are called 'broadened reissues.'
guidance: Although not called out by name in early statutes, broadened reissues are authorized by general statutory terms and upheld by the Supreme Court in many cases. They allow claiming matter described but not claimed originally.

name: Remedy by disclaimer vs. remedy by reissue
description: If a patentee has claimed more than he had a right to claim, that fault has generally been curable by disclaimers since 1837; where the matter cannot be excised by disclaimer because it is blended with other matter, rewriting the specification and obtaining a narrower reissue may be the proper remedy.
guidance: Where possible, disclaimer is preferable because reissue involves loss of rights of action for infringements committed prior to reissue. Use reissue only when disclaimer cannot practically remove the offending subject-matter.

name: Source of inadvertence: acceptable origins vs. forbidden manipulations
description: Inadvertence/accident/mistake may be on the part of the patentee or the Patent Office. Examples of acceptable origins include mistake about the state of the art, inadvertent failure to make claims as extensive as invention, or erroneous decisions by the Commissioner (including in interferences).
guidance: Unacceptable situations: attempting to reclaim a previously canceled/rejected claim by reissue; making a new claim that, though narrower than a rejected claim, is broader in the same direction than the patent's claim; intentionally omitted claims; using reissue to narrow a disclaimer; or claiming only a machine's function previously done by hand. These scenarios do not satisfy the statutory inadvertence requirement.

name: Use of machine translations
description: An examiner may rely on a machine translation of a document in an unfamiliar non‑official language and should send it to the applicant; a translation must render the meaning in a familiar language.
guidance: Grammatical/syntactic errors that do not impede understanding do not prevent qualification as a translation. A general claim that machine translations 'cannot be trusted' is insufficient; the applicant bears the burden of adducing evidence (e.g., an improved translation) to show defects. If applicant substantiates objections, the examiner must take them into account similarly to disputes over publication date.

name: IPEA determinations when prior use is alleged
description: When the IPEA learns of an object or process used such that it may be prior art, it must determine (i) whether a written disclosure before the relevant date confirms the use; (ii) the date of alleged use; (iii) what exactly was used to determine degree of similarity with claimed subject‑matter; and (iv) all circumstances of use (place, form) to determine whether and to what extent it was made available to the public.
guidance: Factors such as demonstration details, delivery and sale can provide information on public availability. See GL/PCT‑EPO E‑II, ISPE 16.57 and PCT/AI section 801 for third‑party use.

name: Inaccessibility example: process not ascertainable
description: If it cannot be clearly ascertained by exhaustive examination by which process a known product was produced, then making available of a process (as prior art) may be refuted.
guidance: Shows importance of being able to demonstrate how an alleged use produced the claimed subject‑matter.

name: Implicit features and direct & unambiguous derivability
description: A document takes away novelty of any claimed subject‑matter derivable directly and unambiguously from that document, including features implicit to a person skilled in the art.
guidance: Example: disclosure of rubber where elastic properties are clearly used takes away novelty of use of an elastic material. Limitation to 'derivable directly and unambiguously' is important; well‑known equivalents not disclosed are a matter for inventive step, not novelty.

name: Generic disclosure vs specific examples
description: A generic disclosure does not usually take away novelty of a specific example within that disclosure, but a specific disclosure does take away the novelty of a generic claim embracing that disclosure.
guidance: Example: disclosure of copper takes away novelty of 'metal' as generic, but not novelty of metals other than copper; disclosure of one of rivets takes away novelty of 'fastening means' generic but not other specific fastenings.

name: Novelty of second non‑medical use claims
description: A claim to the use of a known compound for a particular non‑medical purpose based on a technical effect will be interpreted as including that technical effect as a functional technical feature; novelty of such use cannot be deduced from a new property of the produced product—the use may be novel only if the process of production is novel.
guidance: Use of a compound for production of a product is interpreted as a process claim; novelty requires novelty of the production process itself.

name: Novelty of 'reach‑through' claims
description: Claims that functionally define chemical compounds by their action on a biological target ('reach‑through' claims) may lack novelty because compounds falling within such a functional definition may already be known; applicant data sometimes demonstrates known compounds exert the action, establishing lack of novelty.
guidance: Functional definitions in terms of biological target do not necessarily confer novelty on compounds; applicant's own test results can establish that compounds meeting the functional definition are already in prior art.

name: Obviousness test for inventive step
description: Question: before the filing or priority date, having regard to the art known at the time, would it have been obvious to the person skilled in the art to arrive at something falling within the terms of the claim? If so, the claim lacks inventive step. 'Obvious' means following plainly or logically from prior art without exercise of skill beyond the skilled person's expected ability.
guidance: In considering inventive step, it is fair to construe any published document in light of knowledge up to the day before the relevant date and to have regard to all knowledge generally available to the skilled person up to that day. See GL/ISPE 13.11 and Rule 65.1.

name: Problem‑and‑solution approach (EPO standard)
description: The EPO's problem‑and‑solution approach comprises three stages: (i) determine the 'closest prior art'; (ii) establish the 'objective technical problem' to be solved; (iii) consider whether, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, the claimed invention would have been obvious to the skilled person.
guidance: Apply this approach consistently; EPO uses option A13.08.1 of the ISPE Appendix. The approach aims to render inventive‑step assessment more objective.

name: Controller-invoked requirement under Section 8(2) (documents relating to processing abroad)
description: At any time after an application is filed in India and till grant or refusal, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish details relating to the processing of the application in a country outside India, and the applicant shall furnish information available to him within such period as may be prescribed.
guidance: Typical documents requested under Section 8(2) include search and examination reports, office actions, notices of allowance, grant or refusal decisions, and granted/allowed claims. These must be provided in English where originally in a foreign language. The obligation under 8(2) arises on Controller request (not automatically).

name: Range limitations and numeric/subgenus support
description: When claims recite numerical ranges or subgenus limitations, the analysis must determine which ranges or subgeneric members a person of ordinary skill would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
guidance: Example: In re Wertheim — original disclosure of 25%-60% with examples of 36% and 50% did not support a new claim 'at least 35%' (because no upper limit), but 'between 35% and 60%' was acceptable. Case citations (Purdue Pharma, General Hosp. Corp., Union Oil) illustrate that overlap, discrete values, and whether the disclosure shows the inventors considered the claimed ratio as part of the invention are relevant.

name: Claimed subject matter disclosed only in claims
description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if an original claim discloses material not found in the remainder of the specification, the specification may be amended to include that claimed subject matter.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.44 where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification. This is an objection to the specification; enablement issues should be treated separately (see MPEP § 608.01(o) and § 2163.06).

name: None or one working example — sufficiency
description: A single working example in the specification can be sufficient to preclude a rejection that nothing is enabled, though rejections limiting enablement to particular scope may still be appropriate.
guidance: If other factors point toward enablement, absence of working examples alone will not render the invention non-enabled. However, an absence of working examples can be relevant when assessing whether the specification enables the full scope of the claims.

name: Rules for drawings and models in re-issue
description: New drawings must accompany the specification when the invention is susceptible of delineation and must conform in style, number and artistic perfection to regulations governing original drawings; new drawings may vary from the old only where the variation appears in the original model or relates to unimportant matter not affecting the invention claimed. Amendment of the model is limited to features found in the original drawings.
guidance: Great care should be exercised to exclude new matter if the original patent lacked drawings or model. Extraneous evidence about a model destroyed by fire or loss will generally not be received on a re-issue application. (Cited: Ex parte Gottstein; McWilliams.)

name: Examination on merits — applicable standards and timing
description: The specification annexed to a re-issue application is subject to the same formal corrections as an original. Examination on the merits inquires into patentability of the invention, identity with the invention attempted to be covered by the former patent, and the cause of the alleged error in the original.
guidance: Patentability (novelty, utility, abandonment, priority) is judged as on original applications and the relevant state of the art is that at the date of the original application. Repetition of exact original claims does not exempt them from examination. Abandonment may be shown by more than two years' public use/sale before the original application, omission to claim after clear description and unreasonable delay, or other conduct indicating dedication to the public. (Cited: Carroll v. Morse; Funck v. Doty.)

name: Identity test between re-issue claims and original disclosure
description: A re-issue invention is not identical to the original unless all essential characteristics of the invention claimed in the re-issue were described or attempted to be described in the original specification, drawings, or model as part of the patented invention.
guidance: In machine patents identity must appear by comparison of drawings and models (which can be amended only by each other). Where no drawings/models exist, extrinsic proof may be offered to establish identity. Examiners must be guided by statutes and judicial decisions, not personal discretion. Parol evidence is not admissible to enlarge the scope beyond the original disclosure. (Cited: Giant Powder Co. v. California Powder Works; Shaw v. Colwell Lead Co.)

name: Order of examination and effect of insufficient statement
description: The examiner must first determine the sufficiency of the statement accompanying a re-issue application; if the statement is insufficient the re-issue will not be examined on the merits, and the proceedings will terminate.
guidance: Claims of a re-issue application will not be examined on their merits in connection with the sufficiency question but in proper order once the statement is sufficient. An insufficient affidavit or conclusory statement (e.g., 'not fully valid and available') may render the re-issue void. (Cited: Ex parte Timken; Poage v. McGowan.)

name: Date, term, and legal effect of a re-issued patent
description: A re-issued patent bears the date of the original for all purposes except as the foundation of an action for infringement; when term is expressed in years the term runs from the grant of the original; all rights of parties claiming under the re-issue are held to have accrued when the original patent issued.
guidance: Surrender of the original patent extinguishes actions under it and abates suits pending at the date of re-issue; a re-issue only affects suits subsequently begun. When the original was limited by duration of a foreign patent, the re-issue is subject to same limitation. (Cited: Whitely v. Fisher; Jones v. Barker; United States Stamping Co. v. King.)

name: Two-condition test for denying entry of preliminary amendment
description: Entry of a preliminary amendment may be denied only if (1) the examiner has devoted a significant amount of time preparing an Office action before receipt, and (2) entry would require significant additional time to prepare the Office action.
guidance: The receipt date is the 37 CFR 1.6 receipt date. Examples satisfying condition (1): examiner has conducted prior art search or drafted an Office action. Examples satisfying condition (2): amendment amends claims, adds numerous new claims, changes specification to change scope of claims, introduces new matter, includes arguments, includes affidavits/declarations under 1.131/1.132, or includes evidence traversing rejections from parent application and would require another prior art search or extensive revision of Office action. This list is not exhaustive. SPE approval required before denying entry.

name: Form paragraph for denial due to undue interference (7.46)
description: Use form paragraph 7.46 to notify applicant when entry of a preliminary amendment is denied because it unduly interferes with preparation of the Office action.
guidance: Form paragraph requires bracketed insertions: [1] date Office received amendment (37 CFR 1.6 date), [2] state of preparation of Office action at receipt (e.g., 'claim analysis and prior art search of all pending claims' or 'drafting of Office action awaiting SPE approval'), [3] explanation of how entry would require significant additional time (e.g., 'conduct prior art search in another classification area' or 'revise the Office action extensively to address new issues and new claims'). Advises applicant to file a responsive reply under 1.111/1.113 to avoid abandonment and to resubmit amendment with a reply if not final.

name: Reply must be fully responsive and specific (37 CFR 1.111)
description: To be entitled to reconsideration or further examination, reply must be reduced to writing and must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the examiner's action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
guidance: Reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render claims (including newly presented claims) patentable over applied references. A general allegation that claims define a patentable invention without specifics does not comply. Applicant may request that objections not necessary to consideration of claims be held in abeyance. Replies must appear bona fide attempts to advance the application.

name: Amendments in reply must show patentable novelty and avoid references
description: When amending in reply to a rejection, the applicant must clearly point out the patentable novelty the claims present and show how the amendments avoid applied references or objections.
guidance: This applies to new claims as well; requirements of 37 CFR 1.111(b) must be complied with when presenting arguments in support of new claims and amendments. If lacking, an amendment may be held not fully responsive.

name: Types of claim amendments permitted (37 CFR 1.121(c))
description: Claims may be amended by canceling particular claims, presenting new claims, or rewriting particular claims as indicated in 37 CFR 1.121(c).
guidance: Requirements of 1.111(b) must be followed in presenting arguments supporting new claims and amendments. An amendment after a second or subsequent non-final action that increases the number of claims previously acted upon is not to be held not fully responsive for that reason alone (see 37 CFR 1.112).

name: Fee informality and excess claims fees (notification and payment)
description: When an amendment to a non-final Office action presents additional claims and there is an informality as to the fee, technical support staff notifies applicant; excess claims fees must be paid before examiner considers new claim.
guidance: Applicant required to pay excess claims fees for each claim beyond limits (in excess of 3 independent claims or in excess of 20 total claims). Fees for proper multiple dependent claims calculated per 37 CFR 1.75(c); separate fee required for each application containing a multiple dependent claim. Example provided illustrating calculation when claims cancelled and added.

name: Supplemental replies not entered as a matter of right (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2))
description: A reply supplemental to a reply in compliance with 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except in limited circumstances.
guidance: Supplemental reply may be entered if clearly limited to: (A) cancellation of claim(s); (B) adoption of examiner suggestion(s); (C) placement in condition for allowance; (D) reply to an Office requirement made after first reply; (E) correction of informalities (typographical errors); or (F) simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply filed during a period when action is suspended under 1.103(a) or (c) will be entered. Applicants encouraged to include a complete, fully responsive reply to prevent need for supplemental replies. Supplemental replies reduce accumulated patent term adjustment under 1.704(c)(8). If not approved for entry, examiner should notify applicant (form paragraph 7.147 available).

name: Claims presented without attempt to point out patentable novelty (not allowed)
description: Amended claims presented without attempt to point out the patentable novelty should not be allowed.
guidance: Such an amendment may be held not fully responsive and a time period set to furnish a proper reply if statutory period expired or nearly expired; however, if claims as amended are clearly open to rejection on record, a final rejection should generally be made.

name: Immediate inspection of amendments filed near end of period
description: Actions by applicant filed near the end of the period for reply should be inspected immediately on filing to determine whether they are completely responsive and to prevent abandonment.
guidance: Examiners should check: (A) amendment properly signed (see MPEP § 714.01(a)); (B) filed within statutory or shortened period or time limit (MPEP § 710 - § 710.05); (C) amendment fully responsive and complies with 37 CFR 1.121 (MPEP § 714); (D) whether changes warrant transfer (MPEP § 903.08(d)); (E) whether application is special (MPEP § 708.01); (F) if claims suggested for interference have been copied (Chapter 2300); (G) traversal of restriction requirement (MPEP § 818.03(a)); (H) use of nonpermanent ink (MPEP § 714.07); (I) whether applicant cited references (MPEP § 707.05(b) & § 1302.12); (J) if a terminal disclaimer filed (MPEP §§ 804.02, 804.03, 1490); (K) if any security-related matter added (MPEP § 115). If amendment crosses with action, prepare supplemental action specifying disregarded portions and that reply period runs from mailing of supplemental action.

name: Amendments after final action (37 CFR 1.116) — permissible types
description: After a final rejection or other final action but before appeal, amendments may be admitted in limited circumstances.
guidance: Permitted: (1) amendments canceling claims or complying with form requirements set forth in previous Office action; (2) amendments presenting rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal; (3) amendments touching the merits may be admitted upon showing good and sufficient reasons why necessary and not earlier presented. Admission or refusal to admit amendments after final does not relieve application from appeal condition or save from abandonment. Special rules apply for reexamination and inter partes reexamination regarding cancellation affecting scope of other pending claims (see details in 1.116(d)).

name: Purpose/benefits of PPH
description: The PPH enables an applicant who receives a positive ruling on patent claims from one participating office to request accelerated prosecution of corresponding claims in another participating office; it promotes processing efficiency by allowing the office of later examination (OLE) to reuse the search and examination results from the office of earlier examination (OEE), thereby reducing workload and duplication of effort.
guidance: Explains rationale for using PPH: obtain a patentability decision more quickly and leverage OEE work products. (Background/contextual guidance; not an eligibility requirement.)

name: Corresponding application must have at least one allowable/patentable claim
description: The corresponding application has at least one claim indicated by the OEE in its capacity as a national or regional Office, ISA, or IPEA to be allowable/patentable. A claim determined as novel, inventive, and industrially applicable by the ISA or IPEA has the meaning of allowable/patentable for the purposes of this program.
guidance: An explicit positive indication from the OEE (including PCT work products) that at least one claim is allowable/patentable is required to base the PPH request on.

name: All U.S. claims must sufficiently correspond to OEE allowable/patentable claims
description: All claims in the U.S. application for which participation is requested must sufficiently correspond to the allowable/patentable claims in the corresponding OEE application.
guidance: Defines 'sufficiently correspond': accounting for differences due to claim format requirements, the claim is of the same or similar scope as an allowable/patentable claim in the OEE. A narrower U.S. claim can sufficiently correspond if presented as dependent on a claim of same/similar scope. A claim that introduces a new/different category (e.g., product claims when OEE had only process claims) is not considered to sufficiently correspond. Example and explanation of narrower-scope claims and dependent-claim strategy are provided.

name: Consequences of improper RCE when application is under appeal
description: If an improper RCE is filed while the application is under appeal, withdrawal of the appeal results in either allowance or abandonment depending on the status of the claims: if no claim is allowed, the application is abandoned; if there is at least one allowed claim, the application should be passed to issue on the allowed claim(s). Claims allowable only by virtue of dependency upon rejected claims are treated as rejected.
guidance: Upon withdrawal, proceedings as to the rejected claims are considered terminated. See MPEP § 1215.01. Use form paragraphs (e.g., ¶ 7.42.10, 7.42.11, 7.42.13) tailored to whether claims are allowed and whether submissions/fees are missing.

name: Shortened statutory period to correct formal matters when passing to issue
description: If the application will be passed to issue on allowed claim(s) but formal matters are outstanding, applicant should be given a shortened statutory period of ONE MONTH or THIRTY DAYS, whichever is longer, to correct the formal matters.
guidance: Form paragraphs 7.42.12 and 7.42.14 describe this practice. Extensions of time may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136. Explain the specific formal matters to be corrected in the notice (bracketed text).

name: RCE unavailable after appeal to Federal Circuit or civil action unless terminated
description: 37 CFR 1.114 practice is not available after filing of a Notice of Appeal to the Federal Circuit or commencement of a civil action, unless the appeal or civil action is terminated and the application is still pending.
guidance: If an RCE is filed after court review, the examiner should bring the application to the attention of the supervisory patent examiner or special program examiner to determine whether the RCE is proper. Unless the application contains allowed claims (or the court’s mandate indicates further Office action), termination of an unsuccessful appeal or civil action results in abandonment (see MPEP § 1216.01).

name: Rejection citation standard (cite best references; identify parts relied on)
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command. When a reference is complex or shows or describes inventions other than that claimed, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable.
guidance: The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified. In exceptional or pro se cases, a more complete explanation may be needed.

name: Reliance on admissions and facts within examiner's knowledge
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant (or patent owner in reexamination proceedings), and may also rely upon facts within his or her knowledge.
guidance: When a rejection is based on facts within the personal knowledge of an Office employee, the data shall be as specific as possible and the reference must be supported, when called for by the applicant, by the affidavit of such employee; such affidavit shall be subject to contradiction or explanation by affidavits of the applicant and other persons.

name: Use of subject matter developed by another as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103
description: Subject matter developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) may be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103 against a claimed invention unless the entire rights to the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned by the same person or organization or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person or organization at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: An exception for joint research agreements applies if (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.

name: Reasons for allowance must be set forth when unclear
description: If the examiner believes that the record of prosecution as a whole does not make clear his or her reasons for allowing a claim or claims, the examiner may set forth such reasoning. The reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims or be the subject of a separate communication.
guidance: The applicant or patent owner may file a statement commenting on the reasons for allowance within a specified time. Failure by the examiner to respond to any such statement does not give rise to any implication.

name: Requirements for 35 U.S.C. 132 notifications and 103 explanations
description: Whenever, on examination, any claim for a patent is rejected, notification of the reasons for rejection and/or objection together with such information and references as may be useful in judging the propriety of continuing the prosecution (35 U.S.C. 132) should be given. For rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, the way in which a reference is modified or plural references are combined should be set out.
guidance: Include specific figures, pages, or paragraphs of references when necessary. In exceptional cases and in pro se cases where the inventor is unfamiliar with patent law and practice, a more complete explanation may be needed.

name: Consideration of existing federal court decisions at time of determination on request
description: When a Federal Court decision on the merits is known to the examiner at the time the determination on the ex parte reexamination request is made, the Office will follow guidelines recognizing that a court decision does not necessarily preclude a substantial new question (SNQ) of patentability; the Office makes an independent determination.
guidance: Because courts and the Office use different standards of proof and claim interpretation (e.g., clear-and-convincing in court vs. preponderance in the Office), a court decision is not controlling. Deference may be accorded to factual findings of the court where the evidence is the same, but the Office independently determines SNQ. Non-final holdings of invalidity or unenforceability are not controlling; a final holding of invalidity or unenforceability (after all appeals) is controlling on the Office such that those claims would not present an SNQ. Any determination made after a court decision must be reviewed by the CRU Supervisory Patent Reexamination Specialist (SPRS). See cases cited (e.g., In re Zletz, In re Etter, Ethicon v. Quigg, In re Swanson, Translogic, Trans Texas, Baxter) and MPEP § 2242.

name: Effect of subsequent federal court decisions on ongoing reexamination
description: If a Federal Court decision issues while a reexamination is pending (or the Office becomes aware of such decision), the order to reexamine is reviewed to determine if a substantial new question of patentability still exists. A non-final court decision has no binding effect. A final court decision upholding validity does not bind the Office (the Office may continue reexamination), but a final holding of invalidity or unenforceability after all appeals is binding and claims held invalid/unenforceable will be withdrawn from reexamination.
guidance: If no SNQ remains, the reexamination is terminated by the CRU or TC Director. If some claims were held invalid, use form paragraph 22.20 (Claims Held Invalid By Court, No Longer Being Reexamined) to state which claims are not being reexamined and why, with bracketed instructions for inserting specifics. If all claims being examined are finally held invalid/unenforceable, the reexamination will be vacated or terminated as appropriate.

name: Preparation of Notice of Intent to Issue Reexamination Certificate (NIRC) and requirements for reasons
description: Upon conclusion of the ex parte reexamination, the examiner must prepare a NIRC (form PTOL‑469) and, where claims are found patentable, provide reasons for each claim found patentable. The examiner must also prepare the reexamination file so the Office of Data Management can prepare and issue a certificate per 35 U.S.C. 307 and 37 CFR 1.570.
guidance: An examiner’s amendment may also be prepared where appropriate. After preparing the NIRC and attachments and completing the Examiner Checklist (PTOL‑1516), files are forwarded to CRU support staff for processing and eventual mailing/forwarding to OPLA and the Office of Data Management. Changing the patent title requires an examiner’s amendment; titles should be corrected early in prosecution. Amendments or papers filed after prosecution terminated require a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 to be considered.

name: Selection rules for claims to be printed on certificate/Official Gazette
description: When selecting representative claim(s) for printing on the certificate cover sheet and in the Official Gazette, the broadest claim should be selected. Examiners should ordinarily designate but one claim per invention (up to five where multiple inventions exist); in reexamination, the examiner must select only one claim for publication. A dependent claim should not be selected unless the independent claim it depends on is also printed. If a dependent patent claim is selected where the original independent patent claim has been canceled, the dependent claim may be printed while the independent is not.
guidance: When recording selection: write the claim number clearly in black ink; separate multiple claim numbers with commas; refer to claims by renumbered patent claim numbers rather than original application claim numbers. In reissue applications, select the broadest claim with changes or the broadest additional reissue claim for printing.

name: Examiner and clerk checklist items when preparing case for publication
description: Before publication of the certificate, the examiner must review the reexamination and patent files to ensure all appropriate parts are completed, including: IFW Search Notes (classes/subclasses searched), IFW jacket form (Litigation Review and Copending Office Proceedings boxes), Bibliographic Data Sheet correctness, Issue Classification IFW form (status and final claim numbers, international/U.S. classification), and designation of a representative claim for publication.
guidance: Complete Examiner Checklist (PTO‑1516) and forward to Office of Data Management. CRU support staff will complete Reexamination Clerk Checklist (PTO‑1517) and check for changes in title, inventor, assignee, continuing data, foreign priority, attorney address, and requester’s address; ensure proper entry in PALM. If patent owner requests attorneys' names printed on certificate, a separate paper explicitly requesting printing must be filed.

name: Procedure when all claims in the reexamination are canceled
description: If all live claims in the reexamination are to be canceled (e.g., patent owner failed to timely respond or Board affirmed all rejections and appeal windows expired), the examiner should telephone the patent owner to verify whether a timely filing was made. If none, the examiner proceeds to issue a NIRC terminating prosecution and attaches an examiner's amendment canceling all live claims and explaining why the claims are canceled.
guidance: Two example explanatory statements are provided (failure to timely respond; Board decision affirmed and no timely appeal). The telephone interview, if made, should be made of record. To physically cancel live claims, place brackets around claims on a printed copy of the claims from the file history and scan into IFW file history. Designate a canceled original patent claim for printing in the Official Gazette (Issue Classification IFW form). No panel is required when all claims are canceled.

name: Section 112: Disclosure (written description & enablement)
description: Claims may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. §112 for failing to adequately describe and enable the invention or for failing to clearly define what is claimed.
guidance: 112 rejections are more common in biotechnology and are not prior-art-based rejections; therefore not the core focus of prior-art usage analysis.

name: 37 CFR 1.130: disqualifying a commonly owned patent as prior art
description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 in view of a U.S. patent that is not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b), and the inventions in the application/patent and the patent are not identical but not patentably distinct, and are owned by the same party, the patent may be disqualified as prior art by submission of (1) a terminal disclaimer under § 1.321(c), and (2) an oath or declaration stating current common ownership and that the inventor named in the application/patent is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.130(a) applies only in situations described (A)-(C). The oath/declaration may be signed by the inventor(s), attorney of record, or assignee(s) of the entire interest. The inventor named must have invented the claimed subject matter before the actual date of invention of the reference patent claims.

name: Corrections to file wrapper data and routing
description: If an examiner notices an error in data on the file wrapper or PALM bib-data sheet, they should return the application to OIPE for correction or have technical support correct PALM data and print a new bib-data sheet for placement in the file wrapper.
guidance: Instances requiring correction include: inventorship changes (37 CFR 1.48), filing date corrections, prior U.S. application number errors (see § 202.02), and priority claim corrections under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c). Applications sent to OIPE should be accompanied by an OIPE Data Base Routing Slip explaining the correction.

name: 37 CFR 1.292 public use proceedings: petition threshold and hearing procedures
description: When a petition for institution of public use proceedings supported by affidavits/declarations makes a prima facie showing that an invention claimed was in public use or on sale more than one year before the filing date, a hearing may be had before the Commissioner to determine whether to institute public use proceedings. If instituted, testimony procedures under §§ 1.671–1.685 apply and the petitioner will be heard but will not be heard further in prosecution after decision.
guidance: A petition must be accompanied by the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(j), be served on the applicant in accordance with § 1.248 (or filed in duplicate if service impossible), and be submitted prior to mailing of a notice of allowance (§ 1.311). Duplicate copies should be submitted only when service is not possible despite diligent effort; bulky papers may be represented by a notice in the file with the papers available separately.

name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter to be protected
description: “the claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the subject matter to be protected by the patent grant.”
guidance: This is an objective requirement evaluated by whether the claim is definite — i.e., whether the scope of the claim is clear to a hypothetical person possessing the ordinary level of skill in the pertinent art. Failure to meet this requirement supports a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA second paragraph).

name: Definiteness standard: clarity to a person of ordinary skill in the art
description: Definiteness is judged by whether the scope of the claim is clear to a hypothetical person possessing the ordinary level of skill in the pertinent art.
guidance: When evaluating definiteness, the examiner should consider how clear the claim scope would be to PHOSITA. The second requirement is objective (not dependent on the inventor's views) and should be applied consistently to remove uncertainties of claim scope during examination.

name: Claims must be precise, clear, correct, and unambiguous
description: “Another essential purpose of patent examination is to determine whether or not the claims are precise, clear, correct, and unambiguous.”
guidance: Uncertainties of claim scope should be removed, as much as possible, during the examination process. Examiners should aim to resolve ambiguities through office actions and rejections where appropriate.

name: When issuing a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection, explain the basis (indefiniteness vs failure to claim inventor's invention)
description: “If a rejection is based on 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner should further explain whether the rejection is based on indefiniteness or on the failure to claim what the inventor or a joint invention regards as the invention.”
guidance: Procedural requirement for examiners: when making a rejection under 112(b)/pre-AIA second paragraph, state clearly whether the problem is that the claim is indefinite (objective deficiency) or fails to claim the inventor's subjective invention. Cite appropriate authority and factual basis (e.g., In re Zletz; Ex parte Ionescu) as needed.

name: Leveraging Legal Expertise
description: Work closely with patent attorneys and agents for legal guidance on search results, patentability, and application strategy.
guidance: Legal experts ensure searches support defensible claims and navigation of patent law nuances; involve them early for claim-drafting and prosecution planning.

name: Detailed Examination of Prior Art
description: Conduct in-depth analysis of identified patents and publications by examining claims, specifications, and drawings to understand scope and limitations.
guidance: Thorough review clarifies how existing documents compare to your invention and what must be distinguished in claims and specification.

name: Identifying Key Differences
description: Highlight and document the key differences between your invention and prior art to support novelty and non-obviousness arguments.
guidance: Clearly articulate distinctions in applications and filings; these differences are central to claim drafting and responding to examiner objections.

name: Text Mining and Natural Language Processing (NLP)
description: Apply text mining and NLP to analyze large volumes of patent text to identify patterns, keywords, and relevant concepts.
guidance: Use text-mining tools to surface frequently associated phrases and concepts; NLP can parse complex language and reveal contextual relevance across claims and descriptions.

name: Using NLP for Enhanced Analysis
description: Use NLP to parse legal/technical language, identify key terms, and understand relationships between concepts in patent documents.
guidance: NLP assists in claim/abstract parsing and semantic understanding; combine NLP outputs with human review for claim-differentiation and novelty assessment.

name: Analyzing Semantic Relationships
description: Study semantic relationships between patents to map how technologies are conceptually connected and uncover innovation pathways.
guidance: Semantic clustering can show interdisciplinary linkages and alternative solution spaces useful for drafting claims or identifying non-obvious improvements.

name: Use of patent owner statements in claim construction
description: Allows written statements of the patent owner regarding claim scope that have been filed in court or in the Office to be made part of the official file and to be considered in reexaminations and inter partes and post-grant reviews for purposes of claim construction.
guidance: Helps the Office understand and construe key claims and identify inconsistent statements where owners advocated broader scope in litigation than they urge in PTO proceedings.

name: Joinder of inter partes/post-grant reviews and Director factors
description: Sections 315(c) and 325(c) allow joinder of inter partes and post-grant reviews; Office anticipates joinder as of right for identical petitions but gives the Director discretion to allow or deny joinder.
guidance: Director may consider factors such as differences in accused products/processes, breadth/unusualness of claim scope, claim-construction differences, number of patents/claims at issue, consent of patent owner, court requests, offers to pay patent-owner costs, and whether joinder petitions present additional challenges that meet institution thresholds.

name: Extension of estoppel to real parties in interest and privies (privity rules)
description: Estoppels and other procedural limits are extended to real parties in interest and privies of the petitioner; privity is an equitable rule based on 'practical situation.'
guidance: Whether privity estoppel should extend to codefendants depends on fairness and whether patent owner has clearly and reliably identified asserted claims and constructions; Office may use joinder timing rules to mitigate unfairness.

name: Elimination of deceptive-intent requirements for certain corrections
description: Section 16 reinserts language eliminating various deceptive-intent requirements related to correcting the naming of inventors, obtaining retroactive foreign filing licenses, seeking reissue, or enforcing remaining valid claims if a claim is invalidated.
guidance: Moves the U.S. patent system away from subjective-intent inquiries toward a more objective, evidence-based system that is cheaper to litigate and easier to administer.

name: Definition and examples of material mistake
description: A material mistake is one that affects the public’s ability to appreciate the technical disclosure or determine the scope of provisional rights; errors in claims, filing date, or serious errors in written description or drawings necessary to support claims may be material.
guidance: Examples: (A) Publication omitted claims included in originally-filed specification and not canceled by preliminary amendment; (B) Publication omitted part of the specification providing support for published claims; (C) Publication omitted any of the drawings originally filed; (D) For apps filed on/after Sep 16, 2012, publication omitted the benefit claim to a prior-filed nonprovisional application where the specific reference was timely submitted in an ADS (for pre-Sep 16, 2012 similar rules apply re first sentences or ADS).

name: Non-material mistakes and appropriate corrective action
description: Errors that are not material (e.g., correspondence address, assignment information, minor typographical errors, missing section headings, choice of first-page figure, missing assignment information) should not be the subject of a corrected publication request under 1.221(b).
guidance: Applicants should not file requests for corrected publication for non-material errors. Examples include missing assignment information, wrong/misspelled assignee name, missing benefit/priority claim caused by applicant's filing, omission of claims or changes submitted in an amendment, typographical errors not affecting interpretation of published claims, or the first page figure differing from one suggested by applicant. Filing a corrected publication request for only non-material Office errors may result in a patent term adjustment reduction.

name: Substantive review: examiner's understanding and use of examiner interview
description: Is the examiner not understanding your claims and arguments? Would a conversation with the examiner help clear any confusion or misunderstanding?
guidance: Consider an examiner interview to clear up misunderstandings and to determine the examiner's openness to certain claim amendments before choosing after-final vs RCE. Interviews can reveal whether an examiner might entertain amendments without an RCE.

name: When an After‑Final response is appropriate
description: After-final responses are usually disfavored by examiners but a simple after-final response may work. For example, claim amendments to take allowable subject matter would be appropriate for an after-final response.
guidance: After-final responses are usually disfavored because the extra work required will typically dissuade an examiner from considering the merits. Use for narrow amendments (e.g., to capture allowable subject matter) or when you learn the examiner may entertain amendments (often determined via interview). Note: an Advisory Action may follow if examiner believes the after-final raises new issues.

name: When a continuing application (continuation/CIP) is appropriate
description: If your original specification does not provide sufficient support for certain elements you wish to claim, it may be advisable to file a continuation-in-part (CIP) to add the new subject matter. You might also consider filing a continuation application in addition to filing a FOA response (e.g., to pursue different claim scope such as method vs apparatus).
guidance: Keep in mind CIP new matter gets a later priority date. A continuation does not include new matter — description and drawings are the same; only the claims differ.

name: Abstract-idea groupings (2019 Guidance)
description: The 2019 Guidance enumerates groupings of abstract ideas and states: 'claims that do not recite matter that falls within these enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas.'
guidance: This transforms prior 'if' formulations (if a claim recites X then it's an abstract idea) into an 'only if' presumption—i.e., the guidance creates an exhaustiveness presumption that only matters within the three enumerated categories support rejections, except in 'rare circumstances' with Technology Center Director approval.

name: Practical-application analysis (Step 2A)
description: The 'practical application' inquiry determines whether a claim 'integrates the abstract idea into a practical application' and thus is not an abstract idea ineligible under § 101.
guidance: The 2019 Guidance reorders the analytic sequence by moving practical-application considerations into Step 2A (with two prongs) to promote early resolution; it also states that Step 2A 'specifically excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.' This reordering can materially affect outcomes.

name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Berkheimer issues)
description: Whether claim elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' is used to determine if additional elements add an 'inventive concept' beyond an abstract idea (a factual inquiry highlighted in the Berkheimer memo and related guidance).
guidance: This inquiry is typically considered in Step 2B under prior frameworks; Berkheimer and related USPTO memoranda treat these as factual questions that may preclude summary judgment and can affect whether a claim survives a § 101 rejection.

name: Written description requirement — purpose and separation from enablement
description: The first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 requires that the 'specification shall contain a written description of the invention * * *.' This requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
guidance: Policy objectives include: (1) clearly convey that the applicant has invented the subject matter claimed; (2) put the public in possession of what the applicant claims; and (3) describe the technology being patented. Case citations: Vas-Cath, Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle, Capon v. Eshhar.

name: How an applicant shows possession (descriptive means)
description: An applicant shows possession of the claimed invention by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means such as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession may be demonstrated by actual reduction to practice, showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. (Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen.)

name: Deposits of biological materials — limited role
description: Reference in the specification to a deposit of biological material made in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may satisfy the written description requirement with respect to a claimed material.
guidance: A deposit is not a substitute for written description; the written description of the deposited material needs to be as complete as possible because examination proceeds on the written disclosure. Deposits made after filing generally cannot support additions or corrections to the original disclosure; see 37 CFR 1.804 and MPEP guidance.

name: Original claims — essential/critical feature must be described
description: Even for original claims a lack of adequate written description may arise if an aspect or an essential/critical feature of the claimed invention has not been described with sufficient particularity so that one skilled in the art would recognize applicant had possession.
guidance: If a claim requires an essential feature not adequately described in the specification and that feature is not conventional or known in the art, the claimed invention as a whole may not be adequately described (example: 'A gene comprising SEQ ID NO:1' where promoters, enhancers, coding regions, etc., may be insufficiently described).

name: Genus/species disclosure — requirement to 'reasonably lead' to species
description: A broad or 'laundry list' disclosure of every possible moiety does not constitute a written description of every species in a genus because it would not 'reasonably lead' those skilled in the art to any particular species.
guidance: There must be sufficient disclosure to reasonably lead to the claimed species; generic disclosures do not necessarily support a claimed subgenus or species. Case examples: Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, Purdue Pharma.

name: Prohibition on new matter for new or amended claims
description: The proscription against the introduction of new matter in a patent application (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251) prevents adding information that goes beyond the subject matter originally filed.
guidance: New or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement. The original claims are part of the disclosure; applicants may amend the specification to include claimed subject matter if originally present (In re Benno). See MPEP §2163.06–.07.

name: Support for added claim limitations — express, implicit, or inherent
description: Newly added claim limitations must be supported in the specification through express, implicit, or inherent disclosure; an amendment to correct an obvious error may be permissible if one skilled in the art would recognize the error and the appropriate correction.
guidance: With sequence data, corrections for sequencing errors may be possible if the application included sequence information and referenced a deposit; deposits made after filing generally cannot support additions unless accompanied by a compliant 37 CFR 1.804 statement.

name: Omission of disclosed 'essential' limitation can defeat written description
description: Omission of a limitation that the specification describes as essential or critical to the invention may mean the inventor did not possess the broader claimed invention, and such a claim may fail the written description requirement.
guidance: If the specification makes clear that a particular narrow understanding of a claim term is an 'essential element' and variations are outside the inventor's stated purpose, omitting that element in a claim can render the claim unsupported (Gentry Gallery, Tronzo examples).

name: Examiner methodology — read and analyze the specification; examiner initial burden
description: Office personnel should read and evaluate the entire application; the examiner has the initial burden, after a thorough reading and evaluation, of presenting evidence or reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize that the written description provides support for the claims.
guidance: Applicant should point out support for any amendments; if the examiner finds disclosure does not reasonably convey possession, the examiner must present evidence or reasoning explaining why.

name: Review entire application to find support for each element/step
description: Prior to determining compliance, the examiner should review the claims and the entire specification including embodiments, figures, and sequence listings to understand how applicant provides support for the various features of the claimed invention.
guidance: Analyze whether an element is critical to show possession; determine the field of the invention and the level of skill in the art. Generally, the higher the skill/knowledge in the art, the less specificity required; well-known information need not be described.

name: Biomolecule-specific identifying characteristics
description: For some biomolecules, identifying characteristics that can demonstrate possession include a sequence, structure, binding affinity, binding specificity, molecular weight, and length.
guidance: Structural formulas and deposits are convenient methods, but other characteristics may suffice. Example: an antigen fully characterized by structure, formula, chemical name, physical properties, or deposit may provide adequate written description for an antibody claimed by binding affinity; conversely, an antibody claim defined by binding affinity to an inadequately described antigen fails (Noelle v. Lederman).

name: Assess disclosure-to-claim scope correlation from skilled artisan viewpoint
description: The examiner must compare the scope of the claim with the scope of the description from the standpoint of one of skill in the art at the filing date to determine whether applicant demonstrated possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: This includes determining whether the disclosure reasonably conveys possession of the invention as now claimed, taking into account field-specific knowledge and what is conventional in the art. The inquiry is case-by-case and factual (Vas-Cath; In re Smith).

name: Written Description Requirement — Purpose
description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention; this requirement is separate and distinct from enablement and serves to demonstrate that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention and to put the public in possession of what is claimed.
guidance: Explains policy objectives: convey that applicant invented the claimed subject matter, disclose technology upon which patent is based, and promote public knowledge. Cites cases (e.g., Capon v. Eshhar, Regents v. Eli Lilly) and stresses that the requirement implements the disclosure/possession principle.

name: Specification Must Show Possession to One Skilled in the Art
description: To satisfy the written description requirement, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas; examples include reduction to practice, drawings or structural chemical formulas, or identifying distinguishing characteristics. Written description is a fact-based inquiry that varies with the nature of the invention.

name: Possession Requires Description of All Claim Limitations
description: An applicant shows possession of the claimed invention by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means (words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas) that fully set forth the claimed invention.
guidance: Examiner should ensure the claimed invention as a whole is described; mere functional statements without structure or identifying characteristics may be insufficient.

name: Original Claims — Strong Presumption of Adequate Written Description
description: There is a strong presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the PTO has the initial burden of presenting reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize support for the claims.
guidance: Rejections of original claims for lack of written description should be rare. Nonetheless, even original claims can fail if an essential or critical feature of the claim is not described with sufficient particularity in the specification.

name: Evaluate Sufficiency of Structures, Acts, or Functions
description: Examiners should evaluate whether sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble.
guidance: Absence of detail for well-established terms should not automatically justify a written description rejection. Determine whether the claim recites enough to show possession to one skilled in the art.

name: Transition Phrase Effects on Scope and Support
description: Transitional phrases affect claim scope: 'comprising' is open-ended; 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground; 'consisting of' is closed.
guidance: For prior art searches and scope determination, if the specification does not define what is 'basic and novel' the middle ground phrase may be construed as open-ended. Applicant bears burden to show exclusion of additional elements where appropriate.

name: Original Claims Can Constitute Their Own Description
description: A satisfactory description may be in the claims or any other portion of the originally filed specification; original claims can serve as part of the disclosure.
guidance: Historical cases (In re Koller, In re Gardner) support that claims may provide descriptive content; however, quality and specificity of that description still matter.

name: Genus/Species Support Requirement
description: A generic disclosure of a genus or a 'laundry list' of possible moieties does not necessarily provide written description support for every species within that genus unless the disclosure reasonably leads skilled artisans to those species.
guidance: Cases (e.g., Fujikawa, In re Ruschig) illustrate that mere recitation of many possibilities without guidance to particular species can fail written description for particular claimed species or ranges.

name: Functional Descriptions of Biomolecules Usually Insufficient
description: A biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic, without any known or disclosed correlation between that function and the structure, normally is not sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes.
guidance: Functional claiming of sequences or products without structural identifying information will generally fail unless there is a known structure-function correlation or other identifying disclosure; compare software functional descriptions where function may be sufficient if coding is routine in the art.
