name: Omission of Limitation May Broaden Claims and Cause Lack of Possession
description: Omission of a limitation that the specification treated as essential or critical can render a claim broader than the disclosed invention and lead to lack of adequate written description.
guidance: Cites examples (e.g., Gentry Gallery, PIN/NIP) where claims broadened by removing an essential element were invalid for lacking written description support.

name: Incorporation by Reference Treated as Part of Application
description: Material properly incorporated by reference is considered part of the application as filed and may be used to support claimed subject matter as if the text were repeated in the application.
guidance: Refer to 37 CFR 1.57(a) and MPEP §608.01(p) for rules on incorporation by reference. Replacing incorporated material with the actual text is not new matter. Incorporation affects written description and 112(f) analyses per MPEP cross-references.

name: Burden on Examiner and Applicant Regarding Support for Amendments
description: Examiners have the initial burden, after reading the application, to present evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize that the disclosure provides support for the claims; applicants should specifically point out support for amendments.
guidance: If applicant points out support and the examiner disagrees, the examiner must present evidence or reasoning why the disclosure does not reasonably convey possession. See MPEP §714.02, §2163.04.

name: Claims That Omit Matter Described as Essential May Also Trigger Enablement/Definiteness Issues
description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential in the specification may be subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description), 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness), or as not enabling.
guidance: Where the specification makes clear a feature is essential or its location is the 'only possible' location, removing that feature may broaden the claim improperly; consider related MPEP sections (e.g., §2172, §2173).

name: Determination Is Fact‑Intensive and Case‑By‑Case
description: Compliance with the written description requirement is essentially a fact-based inquiry that necessarily varies depending on the nature of the invention claimed.
guidance: Examiner must weigh the specification disclosure, claim language, level of skill in the art, predictability, and relevant precedent to reach a written description determination.

name: Sufficient Detail for Software Best Mode vs Sequence Claims
description: For software, disclosure of functions may suffice for best mode/description because writing code is often within the skill of the art; for nucleotide/amino acid sequences, mere function may not identify the claimed sequence.
guidance: Cite Fonar v. GE (software functions acceptable in many cases) contrasted with sequence cases (In re Bell, In re Deuel) where structural identification is required. Evaluate according to skill level in art and predictability.

name: When Assessing Whether a Specification Provides Adequate Written Description, Consider Whether It Provides Identifying/Distinguishing Characteristics
description: A specification may show possession by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Examples include structural formulas, drawings, or specific descriptions rather than generic functional descriptions; one must define compounds or materials by characteristics that sufficiently distinguish them.

name: PTOL-413 Interview Summary form contents and handling
description: The Interview Summary form PTOL 413 shall be given an appropriate paper number, placed in the right hand portion of the file, and listed on the 'Contents' list on the file wrapper. In a personal interview, the duplicate copy is given to the applicant (or attorney or agent) at the conclusion of the interview; for telephonic, electronic mail, or video conference interviews the copy is mailed to the applicant's correspondence address either with or prior to the next official communication and may be faxed at conclusion.
guidance: PTOL-413 provides for recordation of: (A) application number; (B) name of applicant; (C) name of examiner; (D) date of interview; (E) type of interview (personal, telephonic, electronic mail, or video conference); (F) name of participant(s); (G) indication whether an exhibit was shown or demonstration conducted; (H) identification of the claims discussed; (I) identification of the specific prior art discussed; (J) indication whether an agreement was reached and description of its general nature (attachments allowed); (K) signature of the examiner who conducted the interview; (K) names of other PTO personnel present. If a complete record of the interview is incorporated in an examiner's amendment, completing PTOL-413 may not be necessary.

name: Complete and proper recordation of interview substance (minimum required items)
description: The Interview Summary form alone will not be considered complete and proper recordation unless it includes or is supplemented to include all applicable items concerning the substance of the interview.
guidance: The substance record should include at least applicable items: (A) brief description of nature of any exhibit shown or demonstration conducted; (B) identification of the claims discussed; (C) identification of specific prior art discussed; (D) identification of principal proposed substantive amendments discussed unless already on PTOL-413; (E) identification of the general thrust of the principal arguments of applicant and examiner (need not be verbatim or highly detailed—sufficient if the general nature or thrust can be understood in context); (F) general indication of any other pertinent matters discussed; (G) if appropriate, general results or outcome of the interview (unless already described on PTOL-413); (H) for interviews via electronic mail, a paper copy of the e-mail contents MUST be made and placed in the file as required by the Federal Records Act.

name: Replies/amendments must be fully responsive (37 CFR 1.111)
description: After an adverse Office action, to be entitled to reconsideration or further examination the applicant must reply in writing and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action, distinctly and specifically pointing out supposed errors.
guidance: Reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that claims define a patentable invention without specifics does not comply. In amending, applicant must clearly point out patentable novelty in view of references and show how amendments avoid such references. Support for amendments in the disclosure must be specifically pointed out (see MPEP § 2163.06). Formal matters vs merits line is not sharp; some formal corrections may touch merits and be insisted upon prior to indicating allowable subject matter. Claims may be amended by canceling, presenting new claims, or rewriting per 37 CFR 1.121. Replies must appear bona fide to advance the application to final action.

name: Immediate inspection checklist for amended applications
description: Amended applications filed near the end of the period for reply should be inspected immediately upon filing to determine completeness and to prevent abandonment.
guidance: When an amended application is put on the examiner's desk it should be inspected to determine: (D) if changes warrant transfer (MPEP § 903.08(d)); (E) if case is special (MPEP § 708.01); (F) if claims suggested to applicant for interference purposes have been copied; (G) if there is a traverse of a restriction requirement (MPEP § 818.03(a)); (H) if 'easily erasable' paper or other nonpermanent method of preparation has been used (MPEP § 714.07); (I) if references cited by applicant (MPEP § 707.05(b) and § 1302.12); (J) if a terminal disclaimer has been filed (MPEP § 508.01, § 804.02, § 804.03, § 1490); (K) if any matter involving security has been added (MPEP § 115).

name: Status of amendments filed before the first Office action
description: An amendment filed before the first Office action but not filed along with the original application does not enjoy the status of part of the original disclosure.
guidance: However, an application will be accorded a filing date based upon submission of a complete specification including claims and required drawings. If an application filed under 37 CFR 1.53(b) is filed without a signed oath/declaration and accompanied by an amendment, that amendment is considered part of the original disclosure; a subsequently filed oath/declaration must refer to both the application and the amendment. Any copy of the application as filed must include the amendment where certified copies for priority purposes are requested. Amendments should accompany the application or be filed after the application has received its application number and filing date (see MPEP § 502).

name: Definition of 'in condition for examination' (paragraph (f))
description: An application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) is in condition for examination when it includes: a specification with at least one claim and an abstract (§ 1.72(b)); papers in compliance with § 1.52; drawings (if any) in compliance with § 1.84; any required English translation (§ 1.52(d) or § 1.57(a)); a 'Sequence Listing' (if applicable) in compliance with §§ 1.821–1.825 or 'Sequence Listing XML' in compliance with §§ 1.831–1.835; an inventor's oath or declaration or an application data sheet containing the information in § 1.63(b); the basic filing fee (§ 1.16(a)/(c)), search fee (§ 1.16(k)/(m)), examination fee (§ 1.16(o)/(q)); any certified copy required by § 1.57(a); and any application size fee required by § 1.16(s).
guidance: For international applications entering the national stage, analogous requirements and fees under § 1.492 apply. Papers/drawings/sequence listings corrected by the latest reply filed prior to mailing of an action or notice are considered compliant as of that latest reply's filing date.

name: Eligibility for patent term extension due to regulatory review (§ 1.710 & § 1.720)
description: A patent is eligible for extension of the patent term if the patent claims a 'product' (as defined) either alone or in combination, or a method of using or manufacturing such a product, and meets all other conditions and requirements of the subpart. 'Product' definitions include: (1) active ingredient of a new human drug/antibiotic/human biological product (including salts/esters) alone or in combination; (2) active ingredient of a new animal drug or veterinary biological product (with manufacturing-method restrictions) including salts/esters; (3) any medical device, food additive, or color additive subject to regulation under the FD&C Act.
guidance: Eligibility requires both the claim scope to meet the product/method definitions and satisfaction of additional conditions in § 1.720 (see next entry). Historical amendments and applicability dates may affect particular patents.

name: 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (2014 IEG)
description: Guidance (Federal Register notice December 2014) to assist USPTO personnel when determining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 in view of Supreme Court decisions (Alice, Myriad, Mayo).
guidance: The 2014 IEG supplements earlier preliminary examination instructions, and it superseded the March 4, 2014 Procedure for Subject Matter Eligibility Analysis of Claims Reciting or Involving Laws of Nature/Natural Principles, Natural Phenomena, and/or Natural Products. It includes a quick reference sheet and example sets (nature-based product examples, abstract idea examples).

name: Subject matter eligibility examples (nature-based, abstract idea, life sciences, business methods, etc.)
description: Sets of hypothetical and claim-based examples illustrating how to perform subject matter eligibility analyses across technologies (e.g., nature-based product examples, abstract idea examples, life sciences examples, business method examples).
guidance: Examples provide exemplary subject matter eligibility analyses of hypothetical claims and claims drawn from case law to guide examiners on applying the eligibility framework in specific fact patterns (e.g., December 2016 business method examples; May 2016 life sciences examples; July 2015 and October 2019 example appendices).

name: Who may cite prior art or written statements (35 U.S.C. 301)
description: Any person at any time may cite to the Office prior art consisting of patents or printed publications or statements of the patent owner filed in a proceeding before a Federal court or the Office in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim of the patent.
guidance: “Any person” includes individuals, corporate or governmental entities, patentees, licensees, reexamination requesters, real parties in interest, persons without a real interest, and persons acting for real parties in interest. Examiners must not, on their own initiative, create and place submissions in patent files.

name: Content requirement: explanation of pertinence and manner of applying (35 U.S.C. 301 / 37 CFR 1.501)
description: A submission must include an explanation in writing of the pertinence and manner of applying any cited prior art or written statement to at least one claim of the patent for the submission to be entered into the patent file.
guidance: The explanation must, for at least one claim, set forth how each cited item shows or teaches at least one claim limitation. Submissions by patent owners may also explain how claims differ from the cited art or statements.

name: Section 301 written statements identification requirements
description: A submission of a patent-owner written statement must identify: (i) the forum and proceeding in which the patent owner filed each statement; (ii) the specific papers and portions that contain the statement; and (iii) how each statement is one in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim.
guidance: Identification can be aided by citing specific documents and page citations. Provide status of the proceeding and its relationship to the patent to assist the Office in readily identifying the statement.

name: Scope/limitation of permissible submission content
description: Submissions under 37 CFR 1.501 are limited to patents, printed publications, patent owner written claim scope statements, accompanying information, and an explanation of pertinency and manner of applying them.
guidance: Submissions must not include issues not directed to patents/printed publications/written claim scope statements — e.g., allegations under 35 U.S.C. 112, public use, conduct of the patent owner, or argument about prosecution history or references previously treated in prosecution/reexamination. If submission contains unauthorized content it should not be entered (return, discard, or close).

name: Copies and translations to be submitted
description: Copies of all cited prior-art patents or printed publications and any necessary English translations should be included so that the value of the citations can be readily determined.
guidance: Copies of section 301 written statements and accompanying information must be submitted (redacted if subject to a protective order) to allow easy inspection and Office determination of claim meaning in subsequent proceedings.

name: Requirements for ex parte reexamination requests (35 U.S.C. 302 and 37 CFR)
description: A request for ex parte reexamination must meet formal requirements set by statute and regulation (content of request, fee, certification, representative information, showing of a substantial new question of patentability, copies of prior art, certificate of service, etc.).
guidance: The chapter enumerates required sections for ex parte requests: persons who may file, representative of requester, content of request, fee, showing of substantial new question of patentability, statement applying prior art to claims, copies of prior art, certificate of service, amendments included by patent owner, address, withdrawal, correspondence, timeliness, and initial processing. Each of those items must be included and comply with the detailed rules (see the specific MPEP sections referenced).

name: Showing a Substantial New Question of Patentability (SNQ)
description: A reexamination request must present a substantial new question of patentability as the basis for ordering ex parte reexamination.
guidance: The requester must explain how the cited prior art raises a SNQ as to at least one claim; the request should set forth comparisons and reasoning (e.g., how references read on claim limitations or render them obvious). Specific criteria and examples are provided in the chapter (see MPEP § 2242 and related subsections).

name: Statement Applying Prior Art in the Request
description: The request should include a statement applying the cited prior art to the patent claims (showing how each reference pertains to claim limitations).
guidance: Provide clear mappings of reference disclosures to claim limitations, including citations to figures/columns/lines where limitations are shown, and explain combinations relied on for obviousness arguments where applicable.

name: Amendments by the patent owner during reexamination
description: Amendments to claims or specification in the reexamination proceeding must be presented treating the changes made by any prior reexamination certificate as part of the original patent; italicized text in a certificate is considered originally present and bracketed text as not present.
guidance: Amendments that re-add text already italicized in a certificate or otherwise improperly present certificate text as a new change are informal and noncompliant with 37 CFR 1.530; the examiner should notify the patent owner of the defect using Form PTOL-475 or PTO-2311 and set a time period to correct.

name: Intervening rights resulting from reexamination (35 U.S.C. 307(b) / §252 analogy)
description: Any proposed amended or new claim determined to be patentable and incorporated into a patent following reexamination will have the same intervening-rights effect as specified in 35 U.S.C. 252 for reissued patents.
guidance: Persons who made, purchased, used, or imported items or who made substantial preparation for an invention prior to issuance of the reexamination certificate may have intervening rights; see cited case law and statutory provisions for scope and application.

name: Reexamination of a reexamination: basis for decision
description: A later reexamination request filed on a patent for which a reexamination certificate has already issued (‘reexamination of a reexamination’) must be considered based on the patent claims as modified by the previously issued reexamination certificate, not based on the original claims.
guidance: When received, CRU support staff will print the issued reexamination certificate and make it of record as a preliminary amendment. The examiner must ensure certificate changes are properly entered so the reexamination is conducted on the accurate specification and claims; checklists (Form PTO-1516, PTO-1517) and supervisory review are required.

name: Statutory application content requirement (Trademark Act § 1(a)(3)(D))
description: Every application claiming concurrent use shall (i) state exceptions to the claim of exclusive use; and (ii) specify, to the extent of the verifier's knowledge, (I) any concurrent use by others; (II) the goods and areas in which each concurrent use exists; (III) the periods of each use; and (IV) the goods and area for which the applicant desires registration.
guidance: In addition to these statutory elements, applicants should state the geographic area, goods/services, and mode of use sought, and identify other users by name/address and any registrations/applications they have. See TBMP § 1102.01 and TBMP § 1103.

name: Commitments and contingencies reporting
description: The USPTO is a party to various routine administrative proceedings, legal actions, and claims. Management discloses amounts that are reasonably possible and amounts where an adverse outcome is probable.
guidance: Provide estimates where reasonably possible (example: ~$900 thousand reasonably possible for labor relations claims in 2021 vs ~$600 thousand in 2020) and disclose probable adverse outcome claim amounts (e.g., $415 thousand in 2021; $300 thousand in 2020). State whether payments were made from the Judgment Fund and whether there are major long-term commitments.

name: Petitioner's burden to show unpatentability with particularity
description: In an inter partes review, the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable.
guidance: Cites Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech. and 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3). At institution the petitioner must present particularized arguments and evidence (e.g., declarations, argument mapping claim elements to references). Lack of particularity can defeat the petition at institution.

name: Obviousness legal standard (KSR / Graham framework)
description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Resolve obviousness based on underlying factual determinations: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claim and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations). Apply KSR's teaching, suggestion, or motivation and reasoned explanation, including motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success.

name: Claim construction standard (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
description: A claim 'shall be construed using the same claim construction standard that would be used to construe the claim in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b).'
guidance: Default is ordinary and customary meaning; parties can argue specific constructions. The Board may adopt constructions used by a district court in related litigation for purposes of institution, but such constructions are preliminary and the parties may develop the record further during trial.

name: Construction and interpretation of specific claim terms (example: 'situational network')
description: Example construction applied: 'situational network' = 'a network created in response to an event or situation.'
guidance: Board will interpret claim language consistent with the specification and prior constructions where appropriate. Parties' alternative constructions and related litigation constructions are considered; the Board notes the construction's preliminary nature and invites further record development.

name: Mapping claim limitations to prior art and combination rationale
description: To show unpatentability, the petitioner must map each claimed limitation to disclosures in the prior art and, when relying on combinations, explain why a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine references with a reasonable expectation of success.
guidance: Board reviews cited passages, figures, and expert testimony (declarations) showing where each limitation is taught. Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success may be supported by common industry practices and expert opinion. At institution, persuasive but preliminary showings are sufficient.

name: Preamble and whether limiting
description: Whether the claim preamble is limiting need not be decided at institution if parties have not argued it; the Board may proceed without resolving preamble limitingness.
guidance: If neither party presents arguments that the preamble is limiting, the Board may find sufficient support for the preamble's content in the cited art without deciding the limiting question; such issues can be developed further at trial.

name: Multiple petitions guidance (CTPG)
description: The Board has indicated that 'one petition should be sufficient to challenge the claims of a patent in most situations,' but recognizes circumstances where more than one petition may be necessary.
guidance: Factors: whether petitions are duplicative, whether they challenge substantially different claim scope, overlap of asserted prior art, burden on the Board and patent owner, and claim length. Overlap of prior art and claim differences can mitigate concerns that parallel petitions impose substantial unnecessary burdens.

name: Prior art status and effective filing date considerations
description: Determine whether cited references qualify as prior art under the applicable statutory regime (here, pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 103 because earliest possible effective filing date is before March 16, 2013) and whether references are §102(e) art based on their priority claims.
guidance: Establishing prior art status (e.g., §102(e)) and priority can be essential to grounds; petitioner must show the references' applicability (e.g., priority to an earlier provisional) in the petition and supporting evidence.

name: Treatment of arguments about timing of network formation and pre-existing data
description: Arguments that a prior-art system's connections were formed prior to an event (e.g., user subscriptions) do not necessarily defeat a showing that a 'situational network' is established 'in response to' an event; the claim language may permit use of stored information to facilitate establishment.
guidance: Board examines whether the claim language requires the connections to be created only after the event or whether stored preferences may be used at the time of the event to form the situational network. At institution, Board found stored subscription data can be used to facilitate formation in response to an event.

name: Fintiv Factor 4: Substantial overlap of issues and weight of Sotera stipulation
description: The petition and the parallel proceeding raise substantially overlapping issues, and Petitioner’s stipulation fails to quell concerns of inefficiency and inconsistent rulings.
guidance: Evaluate whether the same claims are challenged in both proceedings and whether the petition uses the same or substantially the same grounds, arguments, and evidence (including the same prior art). Substantial overlap favors denial. Consider the content and breadth of any Sotera stipulation: a narrow stipulation that only waives specific grounds or limits itself to "grounds that could reasonably have been raised" may be given little weight if petitioner reserves rights to assert product/system (unpublished) art or combinations not specifically disclaimed. Cite examples where overlapping claims/prior art and limited stipulations led to denial (e.g., Code200, Motorola/Stewart).

name: Fintiv Factor 6: Whether petition grounds render claims unpatentable (merits)
description: None of the grounds asserted by Petitioner render the claims unpatentable because they do not articulate the core limitations of the claims.
guidance: Factor 6 assesses the strength of the unpatentability challenge as expressed in the petition’s grounds — do the references and arguments actually teach the core claim limitations? Examples of failures: references that only show "relative movement" but not the claimed "sliding," fixation members that prevent sliding, or energy-absorbing structures that deform rather than permit the claimed sliding. Show how each asserted ground maps (or fails to map) to claim elements; where grounds do not articulate core limitations, Factor 6 favors denial. Use claim language citations and reference excerpts to show gaps.

name: Director’s factor: Settled expectations of the parties (length of time claims in force)
description: Settled expectations of the parties, such as the length of time the claims have been in force, are relevant to discretionary denial.
guidance: Long periods during which claims were in force and relied upon (e.g., years of maintenance fees paid, patents/licensing, prior public notice) weigh in favor of denial. Show petitioner’s prior knowledge (e.g., publications, IDS, related patent family) and long delay in challenging the patent despite notice. Cite precedents (e.g., iRhythm) where settled expectations supported denial.

name: Abbreviatures and abstracts as publications
description: Abbreviatures were prepared and published in accordance with the Notice of October 13, 1964. Each abbreviature contains a specific portion of the disclosure, preferably a detailed representative claim, and, where drawings exist, a figure. The publication of such abbreviatures was discontinued in 1965.
guidance: Abstracts and Abbreviatures are cited under 'Other References' and are prior art effective from their publication date in the Official Gazette.

name: Minimum content required for complete recordation of interview substance (A–H)
description: The complete and proper recordation of the substance of any interview should include at least the following applicable items: (A) description of any exhibit/demonstration; (B) identification of claims discussed; (C) identification of specific prior art discussed; (D) identification of principal proposed substantive amendments; (E) identification of principal thrust arguments of applicant and examiner; (F) general indication of other pertinent matters discussed; (G) general results or outcome; (H) for electronic mail, a paper copy of the e-mail contents must be placed in the file.
guidance: The identification of arguments need not be verbatim or highly detailed; it need only convey the general nature or thrust so the file context is clear.

name: PTOL-413 form information fields (A–L)
description: The PTOL-413 form provides for recordation of: (A) application number; (B) name of applicant; (C) name of examiner; (D) date of interview; (E) type of interview; (F) names of participants; (G) whether an exhibit was shown; (H) identification of claims discussed; (I) identification of specific prior art discussed; (J) whether an agreement was reached and description; (K) signature of examiner; (L) names of other USPTO personnel present.
guidance: The form also contains a statement reminding the applicant of responsibility to record the substance of the interview and instructions on distribution and placement in the file.

name: Specification must disclose sufficient directions (enablement)
description: The specification must disclose by sufficient and clear directions some practical means by which persons of competent skill in the art can apply the principle and produce the effect contemplated by the patentee.
guidance: Baron Parke in Neilson directed the jury to inquire whether a person of ordinary skill could construct an apparatus from the specification to produce some beneficial effect; if so, the patent was valid for that claim. Enablement is a factual inquiry for skilled artisans.

name: Broad/generic claim to a mode of applying a principle is permissible
description: A patentee may claim the mode of carrying a principle into effect generally, without confining the claim to a single form of apparatus, provided some mode of carrying it into effect is disclosed.
guidance: Lord Campbell: generality of claim 'is no objection whatever to the patent.' The ability to claim all modes of applying the principle, where the specification shows the principle applied to a special purpose, is seen as the merit of the invention.

name: Alice/Mayo test (two-part analysis)
description: The Alice/Mayo test is a two-part analysis: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon (judicial exceptions); (2) if so, assess whether any element or combination of elements in the claim infuses an 'inventive concept' that is 'significantly more' than the judicial exception.
guidance: Use this test as the framework for evaluating subject-matter eligibility. Draft claims with the two steps in mind: avoid language that reads as an abstract idea and include elements showing inventive concept or 'significantly more.'

name: Directed to a judicial exception (step 1)
description: First step: determine whether the patent claim is directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon (these are 'judicial exceptions' and not patentable by themselves).
guidance: Avoid drafting claims that merely state an idea or goal without specifics. Identify whether the claim, as worded, would be characterized as one of these exceptions and reword to emphasize concrete application.

name: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' (step 2)
description: 'Significantly more' requires that elements individually or as an ordered combination transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application. It is satisfied by an inventive concept beyond mere instruction to implement the abstract idea on a computer.
guidance: Show concrete technical improvements (improvement in another technology or functioning of the computer itself), meaningful limitations beyond generic computer implementation, novel/useful application, or a non-conventional/non-generic arrangement of known components.

name: Claim language must concretely define the invention
description: Claim language should concretely define the invention and demonstrate practical application rather than merely stating an abstract idea.
guidance: Use specific words/phrases that describe how the invention works and its tangible implementation; ground abstract ideas in real-world technical applications.

name: Differentiate abstract ideas from concrete applications by articulating specifics
description: A claim that merely states an idea or goal without specifics is likely to be seen as abstract; a claim that details a specific, inventive method or particular arrangement of components is more likely to be regarded as a concrete application.
guidance: Describe how the invention achieves its goal step-by-step or by specific structure; include technical detail that ties the claim to a practical application.

name: Avoid broad, sweeping language; tailor claims to specifics
description: Overly broad claims risk encompassing abstract ideas and being rejected under Alice.
guidance: Limit claim scope to the specific technical solution and distinguishing features of the invention. Use claim limitations that demarcate the concrete application and separate it from abstract characterizations.

name: Frame claims around technical problems and solutions
description: Post-Alice, drafters should emphasize the technical problem addressed and the specific technical solution provided by the invention.
guidance: In both claims and specification, explain the problem in the prior art and precisely how the invention solves it; tie claim elements to that technical solution.

name: Highlight improvement over existing technology and practical application (USPTO guidance)
description: USPTO guidelines advise that claims should clearly convey the invention's improvement over existing technology and highlight practical application of any judicial exception involved.
guidance: Explicitly state (in specification and where possible in claims) the technical improvement or functional enhancement and how it is achieved; eligibility depends on subject matter, not novelty/non-obviousness.

name: Use non-generic, non-conventional arrangements or ordered combinations
description: An inventive concept can be shown by a novel, non-conventional, non-generic arrangement or an ordered combination of elements that transform an otherwise abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
guidance: Draft claims that recite specific architectures, data flows, interactions, ordering, or other structural/functional details that are not merely conventional or generic computer implementation.

name: Cite and follow instructive case-law patterns (e.g., Diamond v. Diehr, Enfish, DDR Holdings)
description: Case law shows what courts consider patent-eligible: Diamond v. Diehr upheld practical application of a formula; Enfish held that a specific software implementation on a general-purpose computer can be eligible; DDR Holdings upheld claims 'necessarily rooted in computer technology.'
guidance: Study successful cases to identify patterns: claims that focus on solving a technical problem, are rooted in computer technology, or claim a specific implementation tend to fare better under Alice. Use these examples to model claim phrasing and specification support.

name: Emphasize technical nature rather than reliance on novelty/non-obviousness
description: Patent eligibility under §101 focuses on subject matter (technical nature / concrete application), not on novelty or non-obviousness.
guidance: While novelty and non-obviousness remain important for patentability overall, ensure claim drafting addresses subject-matter eligibility by showing technical contribution and concrete implementation rather than relying on novelty arguments alone.

name: Summary of claimed subject matter and identification of means/steps
description: For each independent claim involved and each dependent claim argued separately, the brief must provide a concise explanation of the subject matter, referring to the specification by page/line and to drawings by reference characters; every means-plus-function and step-plus-function element must be identified and the corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification set forth with references.
guidance: This requirement implements 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, and is mandatory for the summary section of the brief.

name: Argument format, waiver, and grouping of claims
description: Argument must state contentions for each ground of rejection with citations; any argument not included in the brief or reply will be refused unless good cause shown. Each ground must be treated under a separate heading. Claims may be argued separately or as a group; failure to separately argue grouped claims constitutes waiver of separate consideration.
guidance: If multiple claims are grouped, Board may select a single claim from the group to decide the appeal for that group; merely pointing out what a claim recites is not an argument for separate patentability.

name: Claims appendix requirement
description: An appendix containing a copy of the claims involved in the appeal must be included.
guidance: Claims appendix helps the Board and examiner quickly identify the contested claim language; follow appendix formatting rules in the MPEP/regulations.

name: Office procedure following Federal Circuit decision (mandate effect)
description: After the Federal Circuit decision and issuance of the mandate, the mandate is entered in the application/reexamination/interference file and marks the conclusion of the appeal; the application/file is returned to the appropriate PTO official for further proceedings consistent with the mandate.
guidance: If all claims stand rejected, proceedings are terminated on the issue date of the mandate; if some claims allowed, termination applies only to rejected claims; remand or reopening of prosecution may occur as directed by the court's decision.

name: Analyze examples under the 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility (IEG)
description: The examples should be analyzed under the 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility (IEG).
guidance: When performing the eligibility analysis for the example claims, apply the steps, concepts, and tests set forth in the 2014 IEG. Use the IEG framework as the primary analytical standard for determining abstract-idea/judicial-exception issues in these examples.

name: Use the Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheet (Abstract Idea Workshop) for claim analysis
description: Please analyze claim 1 using the attached Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheet (Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheet - Abstract Idea Workshop).
guidance: Both the original and amended claims provided in the examples are to be analyzed by completing the worksheet. The worksheet captures the stepwise analysis (identification of the abstract idea/judicial exception and evaluation of additional elements) that the workshop demonstrates.

name: Analyze original and amended claims independently using the worksheet
description: Please analyze claim 1 (original) and amended claim 1 using the attached Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheet (Separate Worksheet prompts are provided for original and amended claims).
guidance: Treat claim versions (original, amended/newly added) as separate analysis targets: apply the worksheet and Quick Reference guidance to each claim version to determine whether amendments affect the subject-matter-eligibility outcome.

name: Foreign priority / provisional benefit (35 U.S.C. 119)
description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or a provisional application filing date only if the corresponding earlier application supports the claims 'in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.'
guidance: Examiner should verify that the earlier-filed foreign or provisional application contains the requisite disclosure to support the claimed subject matter (see cases cited).

name: Support for claim corresponding to an interference count
description: A claim corresponding to a count in an interference must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: When seeking benefit of an earlier-filed U.S. application in an interference, the earlier application must meet 112(a) support for the subject matter of the count. Generic disclosures that do not specifically describe the claimed species may be insufficient.

name: Original claim adequacy (presumption and rebuttal)
description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description is present in the specification as filed, but an original claim may nonetheless lack written description support.
guidance: Typical failures include (1) claims defined in functional language specifying a desired result without identifying how the function is performed, and (2) broad genus claims when the disclosure only describes a narrow species without evidence that the genus is contemplated. Mere appearance of claim language in ipsis verbis in the specification does not necessarily satisfy the requirement. Examiner should consult MPEP § 2163 subsections for rebutting the presumption.

name: Indefiniteness of means-plus-function (112(f)) limitations
description: A means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents; if the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts that perform the entire claimed function, the limitation is indefinite.
guidance: Such a limitation also lacks adequate written description because an indefinite, unbounded functional limitation would cover all ways of performing a function and indicate lack of possession. See 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA 6th paragraph), 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 2nd paragraph), and MPEP § 2181. Cite In re Donaldson Co., en banc.

name: Examiner burden in challenging written description
description: The inquiry into whether the description requirement is met is a question of fact; the description as filed is presumed adequate unless and until the examiner rebuts that presumption with sufficient evidence or reasoning.
guidance: The examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy and has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the claimed invention. The examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting a lack of written description conclusion (see MPEP § 2163).

name: Changes to scope of claims must be supported
description: Failure to meet the written description requirement commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow breadth, alter a numerical range, or use terminology not synonymous with the original disclosure.
guidance: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and to be entitled to earlier priority dates (35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 365(c)), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure. See MPEP § 2163 for examples and guidance.

name: Broadening by omission of a limitation
description: Omission of a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits an element described as essential or critical in the specification does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: If the specification describes a feature as 'essential' or 'the only possible location', omitting it may render the broadened claim unsupported (see Gentry Gallery, Tronzo, In re Wilder). An omitted essential element can also cause enablement or indefiniteness rejections.

name: Genus claims and representative species (addition of generic claim)
description: Written description for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species; the 'representative number' must reflect the variation within the genus.
guidance: Where substantial variation exists within the genus, describe sufficient species to reflect that variation. Disclosure of only one species may suffice only if the disclosure indicates patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus. Courts have found both supporting and non-supporting outcomes depending on predictability and evidence (see AbbVie, Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis, In re Rasmussen).

name: Numerical range limitations
description: When changing numerical range limitations, analysis must consider which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
guidance: An example: original ranges of '25%-60%' and examples of '36%' and '50%' did not support a later claim to 'at least 35%' because 'at least' lacked an upper bound and covered embodiments outside disclosed range; however, 'between 35% and 60%' did meet the description requirement in that case. Courts differ by facts (see In re Wertheim, Purdue Pharma, General Hosp. Corp. v. Sienna).

name: Treatment when specification amended to add new matter
description: When specification is amended to add new matter (even if claims are not amended), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) should be made whenever any claim limitations are affected by the added material.
guidance: Examiner should still consider prior art rejections in view of the new matter since applicant may overcome new matter rejection. Applicant should specifically point out support for any amendments made to the disclosure, especially when filed in reply to an objection or rejection.

name: Types of AIA proceedings and core distinctions
description: Post-Grant Review (PGR), Inter Partes Review (IPR), and Derivation: PGR has a limited 9-month window and broader range of challenges; IPR can be filed after 9 months and is limited to grounds under 35 U.S.C. § 102 or § 103 based on prior art patents or printed publications; Derivation has a 1-year window from claim publication and alleges another derived invention from the correct inventor.
guidance: Use these distinctions to choose the correct proceeding and to understand timing and permissible grounds of challenge.

name: Common motions in AIA proceedings
description: Typical motions include: pro hac vice admission; to seal; to exclude evidence; to amend claims; for additional discovery; to terminate; to strike.
guidance: These are frequent procedural requests practitioners should expect and plan for during trials.

name: Possible outcomes in final written decisions
description: Final written decisions may: uphold all challenged claims (each and every challenged claim upheld); be mixed (at least one challenged claim, but not all, upheld); or hold all claims unpatentable (no challenged claim upheld).
guidance: Determine post-decision options and implications for appeals or further actions based on which outcome occurred.

name: Identifying the problem
description: The identification of the problem and the solution provided by the invention informs the purposive construction of the claims. An identification of the problem is guided by the description and the examiner's understanding of the common general knowledge in the relevant art. Examiners should bear in mind that an application may describe more than one problem to be solved. For diagnostic methods, it may be appropriate to consider that an inventor is generally looking to solve a data acquisition problem and/or a data analysis problem.
guidance: Look to the specification and the common general knowledge (CGK) of the person of ordinary skill (POSITA) to identify the problem. Recognize multiple problems may be present; for diagnostics, explicitly consider whether the problem is a data acquisition problem (practical means to obtain data about an analyte) and/or a data analysis problem (intellectual correlation/interpretation of data). Use the description's emphasis and CGK to guide which problem(s) are at issue.

name: Determining the solution to the identified problem
description: The solution is the element or set of elements that is essential to the successful resolution of the problem. If a claim includes solutions to more than one problem, examination should focus on one solution to a problem in performing the purposive construction. The initial choice of solution should be guided by the description, selecting the solution given the greatest emphasis by the inventors. If it becomes necessary to consider a different solution, the analysis should be undertaken anew.
guidance: Identify which claim elements provide the solution to the selected problem (the 'essential elements'). Where multiple problems/solutions appear, pick the one receiving greatest emphasis in the disclosure and analyse that; if later another solution must be considered, restart the purposive construction for that solution.

name: Representative examples of data acquisition elements
description: Where a data acquisition problem has been identified, the solution is provided by those elements that provide a means to acquire data about an analyte. The means by which the data is acquired may be represented by either a single step or by multiple steps within the diagnostic claim.
guidance: Representative claim steps that indicate data acquisition elements include: detecting protein X in a subject sample; measuring the concentration of substrate X; determining expression levels of genes A, B and C; contacting a urine sample with antibody A and determining optical density at 450 nm; incubating a sample with a nucleic acid probe (e.g., SEQ ID NO:1) and detecting hybridization to target sequence Z. These steps typically supply tangible, physical steps that supply statutory subject‑matter.

name: Representative examples of data analysis elements
description: Where a data analysis problem has been identified, the solution is provided by those elements that relate to the analysis of acquired data for the purpose of providing diagnostic meaning.
guidance: Representative claim steps that indicate data analysis elements include: relating presence of protein X from a test sample to a diagnosis; comparing expression levels of genes to a control standard (e.g., decrease indicates disease Y); conditional thresholds (e.g., if sample value >0.24 then disease Y suspected); interpreting hybridization as indicative of presence of disease Y. Such elements may be mental, conceptual, or interpretive in nature.

name: Purposive construction (interpretation and essentiality determination)
description: Having identified the problem and solution, a purposive construction of the claims involves: interpreting the meaning of the various terms used therein; and determining whether elements in the claims are essential (provide the solution to the identified problem) or non‑essential (do not provide the solution to the identified problem).
guidance: Perform claim term interpretation in light of the specification and CGK, then mark which elements are essential because they provide the solution. Use this construction to determine the inventive concept and to assess statutory subject‑matter, novelty and obviousness.

name: Relationship between data acquisition and data analysis elements (aggregation vs combination)
description: Recognizing that how data is analyzed or interpreted in a diagnostic method generally has no material effect on how the data needs to be physically acquired (and vice versa), the data acquisition elements and data analysis elements in the diagnostic method claim likely have a relationship reflecting an aggregation rather than a combination. Thus, the solution to a problem will be provided by either data acquisition elements or data analysis elements, but not both.
guidance: Treat acquisition and analysis steps as aggregated (co‑present) rather than synergistically combined for the purpose of determining which elements provide the inventive concept. Typically only one class (acquisition or analysis) will constitute the essential solution.

name: Determining whether a claim defines statutory subject‑matter
description: A diagnostic claim construed as being limited to essential elements that are disembodied (e.g., mental process, lacking physicality, no practical application, etc.) will be identified as defective for not complying with section 2 of the Patent Act because the subject‑matter does not fall within a category of invention as defined in section 2. By contrast, data acquisition elements likely define statutory subject‑matter since they usually relate to tangible (non‑disembodied) practical steps which fall within a category of invention as defined in section 2. Thus, where such a data acquisition element is identified as an essential element of the construed claim, the claimed subject‑matter will likely be statutory unless the claim includes excluded subject‑matter, such as a method of medical treatment.
guidance: If the essential elements are purely disembodied analysis/mental steps, conclude the claim may not be statutory under s.2. If essential elements are concrete acquisition steps, the claim will likely be statutory, but still check for other exclusions (e.g., medical treatment). Use the purposive construction to identify which side applies.

name: Use of the essential elements to define the inventive concept for novelty and obviousness
description: Once essential elements (the solution) are identified, the inventive concept of the claim includes those essential elements. Novelty and obviousness analyses should be performed with respect to that inventive concept: whether a single prior art disclosure discloses and enables the essential elements (anticipation), and whether the inventive concept would have been obvious to the POSITA in light of the prior art and CGK.
guidance: Compare the inventive concept (essential elements) to prior art documents. A prior art disclosure that discloses and enables the essential elements anticipates the claim. For obviousness, determine whether the POSITA, in light of CGK and prior art, would have arrived at the inventive concept without invention. Where data acquisition is the inventive concept, prior art that teaches the same means to acquire the specific data will defeat novelty/obviousness.

name: POSITA and Common General Knowledge (CGK) identification
description: The POSITA is defined relative to the field and may be a team (examples include combinations of clinicians, geneticists, molecular biologists, medical technologists, toxicologists, endocrinologists, microbiologists, etc.). The CGK consists of knowledge in the relevant field at the claim date (e.g., known genes, public sequence databases, known assay techniques, commercial microarrays, epidemiological links).
guidance: Explicitly define the POSITA team and the CGK for each case (use the specification and prior art to support this). Use CGK to determine whether elements (analytes, methods, correlations) were known or routine, which affects whether the identified problem is acquisition or analysis and how inventive the solution is.

name: Procedure when claims implicate both acquisition and analysis
description: Where claims include both data acquisition and data analysis elements related to medical diagnoses, the purposive construction analysis should identify which elements provide the solution to the identified problem; elements providing the solution are essential, others may be non‑essential.
guidance: If acquisition elements provide the solution, treat those as essential and evaluate statutory subject‑matter and patentability accordingly. If analysis elements provide the solution, be alert to statutory subject‑matter concerns (disembodied mental steps). Example guidance: in mixed claims, acquisition steps may be essential while the interpretive use of the acquired data might be non‑essential to the inventive concept.

name: Equitable right to withhold pending adjustment
description: Even absent a strict legal right of set-off for unliquidated claims, the Government has an equitable right to withhold money due (or to become due) to a contractor as security until the unliquidated claim can be judicially adjusted.
guidance: Withholding is discretionary and intended to protect public interest; advisable to refer unresolved amounts to Court of Claims or await judicial adjustment. Where a definite amount of damages has already accrued, it is a proper subject for set-off and may be retained.

name: Limitation periods for financial claims against the Organisation
description: Rights of the Organisation to payment of a fee to the EPO are extinguished after four years from the end of the calendar year in which the fee fell due; rights to refund excess fees are extinguished after four years from the end of the calendar year in which the right arose.
guidance: Interruption rules apply (e.g., by request for payment or reasoned claim); periods may be extended in case judicial proceedings are begun.

name: Grounds for revocation of a European patent
description: A European patent may only be revoked under the law of a Contracting State with effect for its territory on grounds including: (a) subject-matter not patentable under Articles 52–57; (b) patent does not disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art; (c) subject-matter extends beyond the content of the application as filed (or earlier application); (d) protection conferred has been extended; (e) proprietor is not entitled under Article 60(1).
guidance: If revocation grounds affect only part of the patent, revocation is pronounced as corresponding limitation; national law may permit limitation by amendment of claims/description/drawings.

name: Claims define precise boundaries
description: Patent claims are the heart of any patent. They define the precise boundaries of what an inventor owns.
guidance: A well-drafted claim survives examination, withstands invalidity challenges, and reads cleanly on competitor products. A poorly drafted claim invites office actions, narrowing amendments, and claim construction rulings that can gut commercial value.

name: Balance breadth and defensibility
description: Patent claims must balance breadth and defensibility, and medtech amplifies that tension.
guidance: Draft claims broad enough to capture market-relevant activity but defensible in view of prior art and prosecution. Overbroad claims increase risk of rejection or invalidation; overly narrow claims may be easy to design around.

name: Match claim scope to commercial reality
description: Match claim scope to what competitors will actually build and to what the market values, not merely what is theoretically possible.
guidance: For surgical instruments, focus on the specific geometry delivering clinical advantage; for diagnostics, protect the algorithm or workflow that makes the device useful. Use competitive intelligence and a clear understanding of clinical use case to inform scope decisions.

name: Use multiple claim types (apparatus, method, system)
description: Include a mix of independent and dependent claims spanning apparatus, method, and system formats.
guidance: Apparatus claims protect the physical device; method claims protect how the device is used (including clinical methods when appropriate); system claims tie the device into workflows or infrastructure. Each claim type provides a different theory of infringement, important when an accused infringer offers only one component.

name: Anticipate the examiner’s view and build fallback structure
description: Think like an examiner: anticipate likely prior art, predictable rejections, and appropriate fallback dependent claims.
guidance: Design a claim set with intentional fallback positions to speed prosecution and reduce the risk of estoppel. Consider which dependent claims can survive and serve as fallbacks if independent claims are narrowed.

name: Use examiner interviews proactively
description: Examiner interviews (phone/video) are underused in medical device prosecution and can dramatically accelerate allowance.
guidance: Engage examiners early to discuss application, clarify claim scope, and resolve issues that might otherwise result in protracted back-and-forth.

name: Invest in specification quality
description: The specification is the foundation that supports every claim.
guidance: Describe multiple embodiments, define key terms thoughtfully, and provide enough technical detail to support claim amendments later in prosecution. Skimping on the specification to save time usually costs more later.

name: Use functional language, broad genus terms, and supported dependent claims to limit design-arounds
description: Strong claims anticipate design-around tactics and use language to close off obvious avenues of escape.
guidance: Employ functional claim language, broad genus terms, and a suite of well-supported dependent claims so competitors cannot evade coverage by swapping materials, repositioning components, or adding inert intermediates.

name: Prepare for claim construction methodology (Markman framework)
description: Courts construe claims starting with the plain meaning to a person of ordinary skill, then consult the specification and prosecution history; extrinsic evidence is given less weight.
guidance: Draft claims and specification with foreseeability of judicial construction in mind. Avoid ambiguous terminology; provide clear definitions and characterizations in the specification to guide courts.

name: Recognize that medtech cases often turn on claim construction
description: In medical device litigation, claim construction frequently determines the case outcome.
guidance: A favorable construction can yield clear infringement of a broad claim; an unfavorable one may force reliance on doctrine of equivalents. Prepare for Markman early—consider likely disputed terms and supporting intrinsic record well before litigation.

name: Account for regulatory constraints and interdisciplinary complexity
description: Medical devices combine mechanical, electrical, software, and biological elements and are subject to regulatory pathways that can limit how the device is described.
guidance: Be mindful that regulatory materials (e.g., FDA submissions) can be prior art or reveal disclosures; also recognize that examiners' familiarity varies across subfields, which affects prosecution strategy and claim drafting choices.

name: Avoid imprecision; every word matters in medtech claims
description: An ambiguous word in medtech claims can become the focal point of costly Markman rulings.
guidance: Courts scrutinize specification, prosecution history, and contemporaneous inventor notes to determine meaning. Draft with discipline and precision from day one to avoid costly ambiguity later.

name: Protect commercially meaningful embodiments
description: Claims should be structured to capture the commercially meaningful embodiments of the invention.
guidance: Focus on elements that deliver the clinical or commercial advantage, and ensure those embodiments are described in the specification and supported by dependent claims to preserve enforcement value.

name: Step 1 — Statutory Category (35 U.S.C. §101)
description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
guidance: If the claim recites a process (series of acts), machine (device or set of devices), manufacture, or composition of matter, Step 1 is satisfied (Step 1: YES). Examples: method claims (process), system claims (machine), non-transitory computer-readable medium (manufacture).

name: Step 2A — Directed to a Judicial Exception?
description: Determine whether the claim is "directed to" a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).
guidance: Identify whether the claim recites concepts similar to those courts have found abstract — e.g., mathematical relationships/algorithms, fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, or an idea standing alone. If no judicial exception is present, the claim is not directed to an exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible.

name: Common Abstract-Idea Categories (examples)
description: Categories of concepts the Office treats as judicial exceptions: mathematical concepts, fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, and stand-alone ideas.
guidance: Use precedents and examples to map claim language to these categories (e.g., mathematical operations like generating a mask; business practices; data collection/organization concepts).

name: Identify Abstract Idea by Claim Language and Comparable Precedent
description: When rejecting, an examiner should point to the claim language that describes the abstract idea and explain similarity to court-found abstract concepts.
guidance: E.g., explain how a claim describing inventory management is similar to prior abstract-data-collection/management cases (Content Extraction, TLI Communications, Electric Power Group). Provide reasons showing the claim's recited information and operations embody an abstract concept.

name: Step 2B — Additional Elements Must Amount to 'Significantly More' (Inventive Concept)
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether any element or combination of elements adds significantly more such that the claim as a whole is patent eligible.
guidance: Consider whether limitations (individually or as an ordered combination) provide a meaningful technological improvement beyond the abstract idea. Positive indicators include improvements in the functioning of the computer itself or improvements to another technological field. Negative indicators include mere use of generic computer components to perform conventional functions.

name: Improvement in Computer Functioning or Other Technology Supports 'Significantly More'
description: Claim elements that show an improvement to computer technology itself or an improvement to another technical field can constitute significantly more than an abstract idea.
guidance: E.g., a halftoning method that uses a 'blue noise' mask requiring less memory and faster computation (improved functioning) or a GPS solution that increases signal-acquisition sensitivity (improvement to positioning technology) support eligibility (Step 2B: YES).

name: Claims 'Rooted in Computer Technology' vs. 'Apply Abstract Idea on the Internet'
description: Distinguish claims that are necessarily rooted in computer/network technology to solve a problem arising in that realm from claims that merely apply an abstract idea 'on the Internet.'
guidance: Merely stating 'apply the abstract idea on the Internet' is insufficient. When the claimed limitations are necessarily rooted in computer technology and address an Internet-centric technical problem (e.g., constructing composite web pages to retain visitors), they may amount to significantly more (per DDR).

name: Physical/Technical Limitation Examples That Can Negate Abstractness
description: Specific technical recitations tied to physical/technical structure or operations can show the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: E.g., reciting the physical isolation of data in a quarantine memory sector and routines that parse and extract flagged bytes (as in the malicious-code removal example) was analyzed as not describing an abstract concept because it is inextricably tied to computer technology.

name: Selection and Manipulation of Particular Information Alone Is Abstract
description: Claims that merely select, manipulate, store, or organize particular information are likely to be considered abstract absent meaningful technological limitations.
guidance: Cite cases where choosing particular data fields and storing/associating them (e.g., adding classification/location data to inventory records) was deemed an abstract data‑collection and management concept. Such recitations, plus generic computer use, typically fail Step 2B.

name: Evaluate Elements Individually and in Ordered Combination
description: Assess whether individual claim elements or their ordered combination provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
guidance: Even if individual elements are conventional, their particular combination may provide a technological improvement or meaningful limitation (and thus amount to significantly more). The examiner should explain why the combination is meaningful or why it remains conventional.

name: Examiner Remarks / Rejection Drafting Guidance
description: When issuing a rejection, explain (1) which abstract idea is identified and where in the claim it appears, and (2) why additional elements are only conventional computer components or generic steps.
guidance: Provide analysis comparing claim language to relevant Federal Circuit precedent and explain whether claim elements, alone or in combination, supply any technical improvement or meaningful limits that would convert the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.

name: Not All Internet-Centric Claims Are Eligible — Must Show More Than Internet Implementation
description: Claims addressing Internet problems are not per se eligible; they must recite additional limitations that are more than simply performing a known business practice on the Internet.
guidance: Use DDR as guidance: eligibility arose because the claim stored 'visually perceptible elements' and automatically generated composite pages to solve a problem particular to the Internet; the limitations were more than 'apply on the Internet.' Examiners should explain why similar Internet‑centric claims either do or do not amount to significantly more.

name: Priority — filing date and Convention/Exhibition priority
description: Filing date is date of receipt by the Patent Office of an application meeting Article 8(4) requirements; convention priority may be claimed if first-filed in a Paris Convention country and received within six months; exhibition priority may be claimed if first publicly demonstrated at official exhibitions and received within six months.
guidance: To enjoy convention/exhibition priority applicant must claim it when filing or within two months of receipt and enclose supporting documents (Article 9).

name: Person skilled must not be required to solve problems requiring undue burden or inventive ingenuity
description: The skilled person can be called upon to perform routine experiments, but must be able to practice the full scope of the invention without undue burden or the need to exercise inventive ingenuity; if undue burden or inventive step is required the description is insufficient and claims unsupported.
guidance: Routine testing to verify predictable characteristics is permitted; discovering unexpected, unpredictable properties is not routine. Examples: (1) defining a flange by ductility range is acceptable if skilled person can test or know suitable metals; (2) claiming a drug by a desirable release profile without guidance to other compounds that achieve it may be insufficient because identifying others may require inventive effort. The inquiry focuses on whether identifying suitable embodiments requires invention.

name: Functional limitations must be scrutinized for support and enablement
description: Functional language (in claims or description) is not per se objectionable but is used to provide breadth and must be considered from the perspective of the skilled person: can the skilled person practice the full breadth without undue experimentation or inventive ingenuity?
guidance: If means to effect the function are common general knowledge, functional limitation is less likely to be objectionable. If few or only one means is known, broad functional language may improperly claim speculative embodiments. Examples: a broad 'hair-growth activating compound' claim when only one compound is known is objectionable; defining a second component as 'NSAID' when that class and its members are well understood is acceptable; 'cutting means' can be acceptable if appropriate cutting means are known to skilled person.

name: Description must not state the invention by reference to the claims
description: It is improper for the description to state the nature of the invention by reference to the claims (e.g., 'the problem is overcome through the method of claim 1'). The description must correctly and fully describe the invention in the body of the specification itself.
guidance: Such cross-referential statements suggest the description does not correctly and fully disclose the invention and are objectionable under subsection 27(3). Amending the description to include language of originally filed claims in a non-divisional application can be compliant under subsection 38.2(2).

name: Definition of practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b))
description: Practice before the Office in patent matters includes preparing and prosecuting any patent application; consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the Office; drafting the specification or claims of a patent application; drafting an amendment or reply to a communication from the Office that may require written argument to establish patentability of a claimed invention; or drafting a reply to a communication from the Office regarding a patent application.
guidance: The Final Order cites this definition to show that non-practitioner employees performing searches, drafting patentability opinions, drafting applications, and communicating with clients were engaging in 'practice before the Office.' Any activity falling within this definition may require a licensed practitioner.

name: Reversal of burden of proof for process claims (presumption)
description: If patent subject-matter is a process for obtaining a new product, the identical product when produced without proprietor's consent shall, absent proof to the contrary, be deemed to have been obtained by the patented process; same applies where there is substantial likelihood and proprietor unable, despite reasonable efforts, to determine actual process used.
guidance: In adducing proof to the contrary, legitimate interests of defendant in protecting manufacturing/trade secrets shall be taken into account.

name: Orders to produce evidence and limits
description: At request of a party presenting reasonably available evidence supporting its claims and specifying evidence controlled by opposing party/third party, the Court may order production of such evidence, subject to protection of confidential information; such orders shall not result in obligation of self-incrimination.
guidance: Court may also order communication of banking/financial/commercial documents under same conditions.

name: Orders to preserve evidence and inspect premises (provisional measures)
description: At request of applicant presenting reasonably available evidence supporting claim that patent has been infringed or is about to be infringed, the Court may, even before merits proceedings, order prompt and effective provisional measures to preserve relevant evidence and order inspection of premises; measures may include detailed description (with/without samples), physical seizure of infringing products, materials, implements and documents.
guidance: Inspection conducted by person appointed by Court; applicant shall not be present but may be represented by independent professional practitioner named in order. Measures may be ordered without hearing where delay would cause irreparable harm or risk of evidence destruction. Notice and right to review exist; measures may be subject to lodging of adequate security; measures revoked if applicant does not bring action on merits within 31 calendar days or 20 working days (whichever longer). Revocation/lapse can trigger compensation to defendant.

name: Identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A)
description: Analyze whether the focus of the claim is on a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon) — i.e., whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea.
guidance: Compare the claim concept to categories/case law (e.g., abstract ideas like organizing human behavior, data collection/recognition/storage, intermediated settlement, risk hedging). If claim is similar to prior abstract-idea holdings, conclude Step 2A: Yes and proceed to Step 2B unless claim is readily seen as an improvement in computer-related technology.

name: Consider Enfish improvement-in-computer-technology exception at Step 2A
description: Check whether the claim is 'directed to' a specific improvement in computer-related technology (as in Enfish), in which case it may not be an abstract idea.
guidance: If the claim is clearly directed to an improvement in how computers operate or to computer functionality itself, the analysis can end at Step 2A with eligibility. If not readily apparent, proceed to Step 2B. Examples: Enfish claims were non-abstract because they improved computer functionality; BASCOM involved a close call where internet-centric/technology-improvement reasoning could end analysis at Step 2A.

name: Inventive concept/inventive-concept inquiry (Step 2B)
description: Determine whether any element or combination of elements in the claim is sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (i.e., provides an inventive concept).
guidance: Consider both individual limitations and the ordered combination. An inventive concept can arise from an unconventional, non-generic combination of known elements that yields a technology-based solution or improvement. If the additional elements, viewed individually or as an ordered combination, are insufficient, Step 2B: No (ineligible).

name: Assess whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity
description: Determine whether claim limitations reflect activity that was well-known, routine, or conventional at the time of invention.
guidance: Use the specification and, where appropriate, external evidence to evaluate conventionality.
