If limitations are well-understood, routine, and conventional, they do not contribute to a finding of 'significantly more.' The guidance notes examiners should consider whether the combination is 'not well-understood, routine or conventional.'

name: Assess whether the combination yields a technology-based solution or an improvement in the technological field
description: Determine if the ordered combination of claim elements provides a technical improvement or solves a technological problem in a particular technical environment.
guidance: If the claim's combination offers benefits or improvements over prior art technical systems (e.g., improvement in Internet content filtering, 3-D coordinate reconstruction from overlapping camera views), and is not merely an abstract-idea-based solution implemented with generic components, then the combination can amount to significantly more (eligible). BASCOM and certain inventory-camera-array examples illustrate technology-based solutions that confer eligibility.

name: Identify the abstract idea by mapping claim language to prior court-identified abstract concepts
description: When rejecting, explicitly identify the abstract idea reflected in the claim by pointing to claim language and analogizing to concepts courts have deemed abstract.
guidance: A rejection should state which claim language describes the abstract idea (e.g., fraud prevention by identity verification; inventory management; filtering content) and explain why that concept is similar to prior cases (CyberSource, Content Extraction, Digitech, etc.).

name: Use broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and plain meaning in examination
description: Claims under examination are given their broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification; claim terms default to plain meaning absent special definitions.
guidance: Apply BRI when analyzing the claim scope and the abstract-idea inquiry; the examples explicitly assume BRI when examining recently filed applications.

name: Use the specification and factual record to assess conventionality or inventive concept
description: Consider the specification's descriptions of technical problems/solutions and any record evidence when determining whether limitations are conventional or reflect inventive concept.
guidance: The specification can show that a claimed combination was not well-understood or routine and can support a finding that the claim provides a technological improvement. Examiners may add remarks or reasons for allowance if the record would benefit from clarification.

name: When a claim is a 'close call', consider internet-centrism or clear technological improvement
description: If it is a close call whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, determine whether the claim is internet-centric or clearly directed to an improvement in computer technology; if so, find not directed to abstract idea (end at Step 2A).
guidance: The BASCOM claim was described as a 'close call.' If an examiner skilled in the art recognizes the claim as internet-centric or as an improvement in the technology of filtering, it would be appropriate to find the claim not directed to the abstract idea and finish the analysis at Step 2A.

name: Drafting a proper rejection: explain why additional limitations amount only to generic computer functions
description: When issuing a rejection, explain clearly why the additional limitations are insufficient (e.g., mere generic computer components, conventional activities).
guidance: The rejection should identify the abstract idea, point to claim language describing it, and explain why the additional claim limitations amount to no more than generic computer functions or conventional activity in the particular technological environment (cite case analogies).

name: Office action/allowance remarks when claim is eligible but recites an abstract idea
description: If a claim recites an abstract idea but is nonetheless eligible because of inventive concept, examiners may add remarks to the Office action or reasons for allowance indicating both points.
guidance: Examiners can document that the claim recites the abstract idea yet explain why, after Step 2B analysis of the ordered combination (e.g., technology-based solution, unconventional combination), the claim is eligible; such remarks can help the record.

name: Claims reciting selection/manipulation of particular information remain abstract absent technical improvement
description: Merely selecting, recognizing, storing or manipulating particular information (e.g., image sequences, classification/location data) does not make the concept any less abstract without a meaningful technical improvement.
guidance: Electric Power Group, Digitech, Content Extraction indicate that information manipulation alone is abstract. To be eligible, the claim must integrate the abstract idea into a specific practical application that improves technology (e.g., 3-D reconstruction from overlapping camera views).

name: Distinction between invention information and additional information
description: Patent documents contain 'invention information' (technical information representing an addition to the state of the art, determined using claims, description and drawings in context) and 'additional information' (non-trivial technical information that does not itself represent an addition to the state of the art but may be useful for searching); rules for selection of classification symbols are the same for both.
guidance: Determine whether disclosed subject matter is an addition to the state of the art (invention information) or complementary (additional information); both are classifiable using the same rules.

name: ARIPO patent application unity and contents
description: An ARIPO patent application shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked that they form a single general inventive concept; it shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art, entirely effected by an enabling description read with drawings if any.
guidance: Applications must include a request for grant, description, claim(s), drawings (where necessary), sequence listing (where necessary) and an abstract; claims must be clear, concise and supported by the description.

name: Claims define protection; clarity and support
description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and shall be supported by the description.
guidance: Extent of protection is determined by the terms of the claims, but description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims.

name: Abstract purpose
description: The abstract shall merely serve for use as a source of technical information; in particular not for the purposes of interpreting the scope of the protection sought.
guidance: Applicants should draft abstracts as technical summaries only; abstracts do not limit claim scope.

name: Extent of protection determined by claims; use of description/drawings for interpretation
description: The extent of the protection conferred by an ARIPO patent or application shall be determined by the terms of the claims. Nevertheless, the description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims.
guidance: Claims are primary for scope; ensure claims are consistent with description and drawings for correct interpretation.

name: Utility model definition and requirements
description: A utility model is defined as a form, configuration or disposition of elements of some appliance, working tools and implements... in so far as they are capable of contributing some benefit or new effect or saving in time, energy and labour or allowing a better or different functioning; includes micro-organism or other self-replicable material, products of genetic resources, herbal as well as nutritional formulations which give new effects. A utility model shall be protected if it is new and industrially applicable.
guidance: Utility model applications must contain a request, description, claim(s), drawings and abstract, and are subject to formal and substantive examination; duration 10 years from filing; conversion to patent application allowed once before refusal/registration upon payment.

name: Act of 1839 §7 — prior purchaser/constructor rights and two-year limitation
description: The Act of 1839 provides that any person or corporation who purchased or constructed a newly invented machine, manufacture, or composition of matter prior to the inventor's application shall possess the right to use and vend that specific machine without liability; and no patent shall be invalid by reason of such prior purchase, sale, or use except on proof of abandonment to the public or that such prior purchase/sale/use was more than two years prior to the application.
guidance: After a patent issues the prior purchaser retains a right to use the specific machines they purchased/constructed. To claim protection under the statute one must be a purchaser or prior user by license or consent of the inventor — not a purchaser from a mere wrongdoer. If prior use/purchase was for more than two years before application, or there was abandonment, the patent may be invalid. (§58–60)

name: Purchasers from wrongdoers are not protected as prior users
description: A purchaser who acquired the invention from a wrongdoer (a pirate) cannot claim protection under the Act as a bona fide prior purchaser; a wrongdoer cannot confer valid title under the statute.
guidance: Even though the statute speaks broadly of 'purchasers,' courts will not interpret it to protect those who obtained the invention via fraud, piracy, or gross misconduct. Trace good faith and lawful acquisition when asserting prior-user rights. (Pierson v. The Eagle Screw Company; §60)

name: Parties' agreed-upon claim construction
description: When the parties have consistently advanced and litigated a particular claim construction before the Board, the Board may adopt that construction and evaluate the case accordingly.
guidance: If a petitioner and respondent both treated claim terms as having a particular meaning (e.g., that the claim requires a server and a network switch box 'as separate and distinct components'), the Board may properly adopt that understanding. The record (petition, reply, expert testimony, hearing statements) showing consistent advocacy of the construction supports the Board's use of it on review. Example: Apple repeatedly characterized its theory as relying on Ahopelto's 'logically distinct' GGSN functions, so the Board adopted the parties' understanding.

name: Three-tiered approach to assessing prior-art disclosure
description: When evaluating whether prior art discloses claimed elements, the Board may analyze (1) the prior-art disclosure itself, (2) testimonial (expert) evidence about how a POSITA would understand the disclosure, and (3) any additional cited references or evidence.
guidance: The Board's review is not limited to verbatim claim term recitations or architecture diagrams; it sequentially examines the text of the reference, assesses expert testimony about the skilled artisan's understanding, and then considers other cited references to determine whether the claimed elements are shown as distinct components. Example: the Board found Ahopelto did not expressly describe 'a server' and a separate 'network switch box', then looked at testimony and additional evidence.

name: Burden to show prior art discloses distinct claim elements
description: The petitioner must prove that the prior art would have been understood by a POSITA to disclose the claimed elements, including any requirement that elements be 'separate and distinct' (whether logically or physically).
guidance: If a claim requires separate and distinct components, petitioner must show the prior art teaches those components as separate/logically distinct entities. Merely pointing to different functions within an overarching process is insufficient unless the record supports that those functions would have been understood as distinct components. Example: petitioner failed to show Ahopelto’s GGSN included a server functionality separate from its routing functionality.

name: Treatment of logical vs physical separateness
description: Claims may require elements to be 'logically separate and distinct' rather than physically separate; whether that construction is appropriate depends on the parties' positions and record evidence.
guidance: A party can consistently argue for logical separate-and-distinctness (e.g., different logical/software entities on a shared platform), and the Board can adopt that construction; the Board acknowledged that physical separation is not required. However, the petitioner still must show the prior art teaches the logical separation. If a party wishes to challenge the appropriateness of a logical-separation requirement (e.g., 'box-drawing' problem in software), that challenge must be presented to the Board to avoid forfeiture.

name: Weight and credibility of expert testimony
description: The Board's credibility assessments of expert witnesses are entitled to deference, and the Board may give little weight to expert testimony that fails to point to supporting references or that concedes overlap with challenged disclosures.
guidance: The Federal Circuit defers to the Board on expert credibility. If an expert cannot point to references showing the asserted distinction or admits overlap (e.g., that claimed functionality overlaps with an overarching process in the prior art), the Board may reasonably discount that testimony. Example: the Board gave 'little weight' to Dr. Jensen because he could not point to any reference showing implementation of server and routing functionality as different logical entities.

name: Embedded/multi-function prior-art disclosures may not satisfy separate-element claims
description: If a prior-art reference describes multiple functions as part of an overarching process (rather than as separate modules or components), that reference may not satisfy claim elements requiring separate and distinct components.
guidance: When prior art embeds multiple functions within a single routing procedure or process, the Board may reasonably find that it does not disclose separate claim elements. Example: Ahopelto's routing procedure encompassed both the 'server' and 'routing' functionalities, so the Board found it did not disclose them as separate components.

name: Appellate reliance on the full record to evaluate Board findings
description: The Federal Circuit will consider the full administrative record (petitions, replies, expert declarations, hearing statements) when assessing whether the Board's factual findings and claim constructions were proper.
guidance: Statements and positions across the record (petition text, reply briefs, expert testimony, hearing responses) can bind parties' positions and justify the Board's chosen construction or assessment. Example: Apple's repeated descriptions in the petition/reply/hearing that its theory relied on 'logically distinct' GGSN functions supported the Board's adoption of that construction.

name: Protection against becoming generic (Article 12)
description: Registered appellations of origin and geographical indications cannot be considered to have become generic in a Contracting Party, subject to the agreed statement that elements with a generic character in the Contracting Party of Origin need not be protected in other Contracting Parties.
guidance: The Act preserves GI status against genericide claims across Contracting Parties, but recognizes existing generic elements and prior use exceptions.

name: Anticipation (novelty)
description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention is not new. For a claim to be invalid as not new (i.e., 'anticipated'), all of its requirements must have existed in a single prior art reference that predates the effective filing date (or the date of invention, as applicable). The alleged infringer must prove anticipation by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: The description in the written reference need not use the same words as the claim, but all claim requirements must be present—stated or necessarily implied—so that a person of ordinary skill could make and use the claimed invention from that single reference. Examples of ways to show lack of novelty include: (1) known or used by others in the U.S. before the date of invention (publicly accessible); (2) already patented or described in a printed publication anywhere in the world before the date of invention (a 'printed publication' is accessible to those interested in the field even if difficult to find); (3) already made by someone else in the U.S. before the date of conception (if not abandoned or secret); (4) described in another issued U.S. patent or published U.S. patent application filed earlier; (5) the named inventor learned the invention from someone else.

name: Obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103)
description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the relevant time (e.g., time of invention or effective filing date). The alleged infringer must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Determination requires consideration of (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the field, and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations). Do not use hindsight; consider only what was known at the relevant time. Existence of each claim element in the prior art does not automatically prove obviousness because inventions often build on prior art building blocks.

name: Factors bearing on motivation to combine / obvious-to-try considerations
description: When deciding whether a claimed invention would have been obvious, consider whether there was a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill to combine known elements in the claimed way.
guidance: Relevant considerations include: (1) whether the claimed invention was merely the predictable result of using prior art elements according to known functions; (2) whether the invention provided an obvious solution to a known problem; (3) whether the prior art teaches or suggests combining the claimed elements; (4) whether the prior art teaches away from the combination; (5) whether it would have been 'obvious to try' such combinations (e.g., finite, predictable solutions due to design need or market pressure); and (6) whether the change resulted primarily from design incentives or market forces. There must have been a reasonable expectation of success. 'Obvious to try' alone is insufficient in unpredictable technologies.

name: Differences between prior art and the claimed invention
description: Determine what differences, if any, exist between the prior art and the patented invention as a whole.
guidance: Do not focus solely on differences; the test is whether the invention as a whole would have been obvious in view of all prior art. If all elements are disclosed in separate items, consider whether it would have been obvious to combine them.

name: Damages – burden of proof and measure
description: If the jury finds infringement of any valid claim, it must determine monetary damages adequate to compensate the patent holder. The patent holder has the burden to prove the amount of damages by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not) and with reasonable certainty.
guidance: Damages should place the patent holder in approximately the financial position it would have been in absent the infringement, but must not be punitive and cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. The patent holder need not prove damages with mathematical precision but must avoid remote or speculative claims.

name: Scope of examination in inter partes reexamination (37 CFR 1.906(a))
description: Claims in an inter partes reexamination proceeding will be examined on the basis of patents or printed publications and, with respect to subject matter added or deleted in the reexamination proceeding, on the basis of the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Inter partes reexamination practice as to substance is the same as ex parte reexamination; however, procedure differs. Examiner must apply 35 U.S.C. 112 when subject matter is added or deleted.

name: Prohibition on enlargement of claim scope (37 CFR 1.906(b) and 35 U.S.C. 314)
description: Claims in an inter partes reexamination proceeding will not be permitted to enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent; no proposed amended or new claim enlarging the scope shall be permitted.
guidance: Examine presented claims under 35 U.S.C. 314 to determine enlargement. A claim that is broader than each and every claim of the patent is considered broadening; a claim is broadened if it is broader in any one respect even if narrower in others. See MPEP §1412.03 for guidance on what constitutes broadening.

name: Criterion for determining enlargement of scope
description: A claim presented in a reexamination enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent being reexamined where the claim is broader than each and every claim of the patent.
guidance: See MPEP §1412.03 for guidance on what is broadening. If a claim is considered broadening for reissue purposes, it is likewise broadening in reexamination.

name: Rejection procedure for claims that enlarge scope (35 U.S.C. 314(a))
description: Any claim which enlarges the scope of the claims of the patent should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 314(a).
guidance: Form paragraph 26.03.01 is employed when making the rejection. Examiner must identify and explain the claim limitations considered to broaden the scope (see bracket 2 in form paragraph and MPEP §2658).

name: Scope of reexamination limited to 'live' claims requested
description: The Office’s determination will generally be limited solely to a review of the 'live' claims (existing claims not held invalid by a final decision) for which reexamination has been requested.
guidance: Requester had the opportunity to include all claims in its request. 35 U.S.C. 311(b)(2) requires the requester to set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested; failure to do so generally precludes reexamination of that claim. The Office may in its discretion reexamine non-requested claims or initiate reexamination on its own (35 U.S.C. 303(a)).

name: Ancillary amendments necessary to patentability may be considered
description: Matters ancillary to reexamination which are necessary and incident to patentability will be considered; amendments may be made to the specification to correct, for example, an inadvertent failure to claim foreign priority or continuing status if necessary to overcome a reference.
guidance: Such amendments should be limited to those necessary to address patentability issues raised by prior art or other reexamination matters.

name: Requests for reexamination on patents after reissue
description: A request for reexamination filed on a patent after it has been reissued will be denied because the patent on which the request is based has been surrendered.
guidance: To reexamine a reissued patent, a new request based on the specification and claims of the reissue patent must be filed. Any amendment made by the patent owner during reexamination should treat changes made by the granted reissue patent as the text of the patent, including bracketing/underlining with respect to reissue changes.

name: Completeness of examiner's action and limitations
description: The examiner's action will be complete as to all matters, except that in appropriate circumstances (misjoinder, fundamental defects, etc.) action may be limited to such matters before further action is made; matters of form need not be raised until a claim is found allowable.
guidance: Where rejection is based on facts within personal knowledge of an Office employee, data shall be as specific as possible and may require supporting affidavit subject to contradiction/explanation by applicant affidavits.

name: Standards when rejecting claims (37 CFR 1.104(c))
description: If the invention is not considered patentable, the claims considered unpatentable will be rejected. In rejecting claims for novelty or obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his/her command and, when a reference is complex, designate the particular part relied upon 'as nearly as practicable.'
guidance: The pertinency of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified. Examiner may rely on admissions by applicant/patent owner and on facts within his/her knowledge.

name: Treatment of subject matter developed by another person (35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f),(g) and 103)
description: Subject matter developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) or (g) may be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103 against a claimed invention unless the entire rights to the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned or subject to obligation of assignment at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: For patents/applications on/after Dec 10, 2004, a claimed invention and subject matter are deemed commonly owned for purposes of this exception if (A) made by parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the claimed invention date, (B) made as a result of activities within the agreement's scope, and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. To overcome a 103 rejection based on 102(e)/(f)/(g) subject matter, applicant must provide a statement to that effect as required.

name: Reasons for allowance must be set forth when unclear (37 CFR 1.104(e))
description: If the examiner believes the record does not make clear his/her reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning; the applicant or patent owner may file a statement commenting on the reasons for allowance within a specified time.
guidance: Reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims or be the subject of a separate communication. Failure by the examiner to respond to any commenting statement does not give rise to any implication.

name: Form and content requirements for the first Office action
description: The examiner’s first Office action should be comprehensive and address all issues as to the prior art patents and/or printed publications, clearly setting forth each ground of rejection/objection and the reasons supporting them, and each determination favorable to patentability.
guidance: The action should respond to the substance of each argument raised by the third party requester pursuant to 37 CFR 1.915 and address any other issues proper for reexamination. If request includes a claim chart, examiner may incorporate it but must carefully review to ensure incorporated items clearly and completely address patentability. The first action should caution the patent owner that a complete response is required because the next action is expected to be an ACP and that 37 CFR 1.116(b) will be strictly enforced after an ACP; include form paragraph 26.05 and 26.73 as appropriate.

name: Specification showing how to apply a known substance can sustain a patent claim
description: If a patentee shows how a known substance (e.g., hydrated oxides of iron) is to be used in a particular way, an objection that it is merely the use of a known property may fail.
guidance: Court of Exchequer held that mere claim to use might be insufficient, but practical disclosure of method can render it patentable (Hills v. London Gas Light Co.; compare Ormson v. Clarke).

name: Substance-over-form inquiry for jury fact-findings
description: The legal determination of infringement depends on substance and result — juries decide on the evidence whether defendants' mode of working is in substance the same or essentially different from the specification.
guidance: Testimony of practical/scientific witnesses and comparisons of materials, proportions, modes, and results are critical. Single witnesses can determine outcomes; inconsistent testimony or lack of proof that defendants used the claimed mode may defeat infringement claims.

name: Include a broad claim that defines your invention in broad terms
description: First, include a claim that defines your invention in broad terms, leaving out any and all unnecessary options.
guidance: Broad claims should omit unnecessary options so they capture the generic invention. The author recommends creating at least one broad/generic claim at the initial filing stage to 'bookend' the invention with a generic version. It's acceptable if the claim isn't in perfect Patent Office format at first — scope matters more initially.

name: Include a highly specific claim listing every option
description: Include another claim that defines your invention with as much specificity and with every option you can think of.
guidance: Write dependent/narrow claims that add every possible optional feature or configuration you can imagine so you have specific fallbacks. Example: start with a generic peanut butter-and-jelly sandwich claim, then add a dependent claim listing bacon, lettuce, tomato and fluff. Having both broad and narrow claims 'bookends' the invention.

name: Start claims with 'A {title} comprising:' and list parts and connections
description: When drafting a claim you want to start with something like this: '1. A {insert title} comprising: {list the parts one by one} {then explain how each are connected}.'
guidance: The article gives a simple template and examples (peanut butter & jelly sandwich; shovel). Use 'comprising' and enumerate elements, then explain how elements are connected/interact. Don't worry about perfect Patent Office formatting at the drafting stage — focus on capturing parts and their relationships.

name: Describe how components are structured and interact (must be complete and distinguish over prior art)
description: When writing a claim it is important to describe how the various components are structured and how the various components interact and connect. It is necessary to describe the invention so that it is complete, so that it works, but also so that it is different than what is known in the prior art.
guidance: Claims should make clear 'what makes your invention different' from prior art. Describe structure, interconnections, and operation sufficiently to define the invention and to enable understanding of distinctions from known devices or methods.

name: Provide proper antecedent basis (introduce elements with 'a/an' then refer with 'said'/'the')
description: Introduce elements with either 'a' or 'an' and then when you subsequently refer to the element refer to it by either 'said' or 'the,' hence introducing 'a shovel head' and then later referring to 'said shovel head.'
guidance: Use internal reference points to make it easier to describe how to connect elements. Avoid referring to an element as 'said X' before it has been introduced; doing so signals an improper antecedent basis and causes problems (e.g., mentioning 'said neck' when 'neck' wasn't previously introduced). If you need to reference sub-parts later, introduce them in the earlier claim language.

name: Use dependent claims to narrow and add specific features
description: In dependent claims you build on a claim earlier to narrow the description to make it more specific.
guidance: Dependent claims should explicitly reference and add limitations to earlier claims (examples: adding 'a grip disposed around said second end' or specifying the grip material). Use dependent claims to create layers of fallback positions narrowing feature sets and specifying materials, attachments, and configurations.

name: When adding specific connectors or attachments, introduce the referenced sub-elements first
description: If you add a claim that depends on some sub-element (e.g., a neck) used to explain how a screw connects parts, you must first have introduced that sub-element in an earlier claim or modify the independent claim to introduce it.
guidance: Example: to claim 'a screw through said neck' you should either have introduced 'a neck' in claim 1 (e.g., 'a shovel head, which is made up of a neck leading up into a blade') or modify the independent claim so that the sub-element has antecedent basis. Otherwise an examiner will flag improper antecedent basis.

name: At the initial filing stage, include claims with appropriate scope even if not in perfect PTO format
description: At the initial filing stage what matters most is that claims are present and they have appropriate scope, with some being broad and some being narrow and quite specific.
guidance: It's more important to capture scope and alternatives than to have perfect formal language. Draft broad and narrow claims to 'bookend' the invention. Later you can refine to PTO-required formats, but failing to capture scope early can harm rights.

name: Provisional patent applications: focus on broadest disclosure; claims are not required
description: Provisional patent applications, however, do not need claims and can and should focus on providing the broadest disclosure possible.
guidance: A conscientious inventor can create a pretty good disclosure using a provisional, and then use that disclosure as the basis for later drafted claims. The author notes The Invent & Patent System™ helps create provisionals but does not try to create claims.

name: Iterative drafting: start writing, add elements as needed, and check antecedent introductions
description: Perhaps the best way to go about writing claims is to just start writing, then as you need to add elements to the invention to define ever more specific versions check to see if the pieces and parts being added have been introduced properly and result in a description of the version that is complete and describes what you have pictured in your mind’s eye.
guidance: Draft claims iteratively: begin with basic independent claim(s), then add dependent claims and modify independent claims as needed to introduce sub-elements. Continuously check for completeness, antecedent basis, and whether the description conveys the intended embodiment(s). Recognize that drafting claims is difficult and that professional assistance improves outcomes.

name: Remand by the Board for further consideration of a rejection (37 CFR 41.50(a)(1))
description: The Board may remand a case to the examiner for further consideration of a rejection (e.g., where pertinence of references is not clear) or for other examiner action.
guidance: A supplemental examiner’s answer written in response to such remand may set forth a new ground of rejection (see MPEP § 1207.03). If remand is for further consideration of a rejection, the appellant must, within two months of the supplemental examiner’s answer, either (A) reopen prosecution (file a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 with/without amendment or affidavits/evidence) or (B) maintain the appeal by filing a reply brief under 37 CFR 41.41; failure to do so may result in sua sponte dismissal of the appeal as to the remanded claims.

name: Remand by Board to consider amendment (1211.02)
description: The Board has no obligation to consider new or amended claims submitted while it has jurisdiction, but a proposed amendment filed after the filing of a brief that cancels claims (where cancellation does not affect scope of other claims) or rewrites dependent claims into independent form may be remanded for consideration by the examiner.
guidance: If the proposed amendment effectively abandons the appeal (e.g., cancels appealed claims), the amendment must be entered and the Chief Clerk notified so the case can be removed from the Board’s docket. See MPEP § 1206.

name: Board statement on how a claim may be amended to overcome a rejection (37 CFR 41.50(c))
description: The opinion of the Board may include an explicit statement of how a claim on appeal may be amended to overcome a specific rejection; when it does, appellant has the right to amend in conformity and such amendment will overcome that specific rejection.
guidance: An amendment in conformity with such statement will overcome the specific rejection but is not itself a guarantee of allowability—an examiner may reject the so-amended claim if the rejection constitutes a new ground (any such new ground must be approved by a TC Director and prominently identified). A remark by the Board that a feature does not appear in a claim is not to be construed as authority to amend unless the Board makes an explicit statement. Appellant’s right to amend under 41.50(c) may be exercised within the period allowed for seeking court review under 37 CFR 1.304.

name: Alice/Mayo framework (only analysis for 35 U.S.C. 101)
description: Use the Alice/Mayo two-step framework as the only analysis when examining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Prior tests (e.g., Alappat special purpose computer test, Bilski machine-or-transformation as a stand-alone test, State Street UCT test) are no longer to be used as the governing analysis.
guidance: Follow the two-step flowchart (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: diamonds 2A and 2B). The Alice/Mayo framework incorporates principles from earlier cases but supersedes prior stand-alone tests. Eligibility should be considered for every claim, but claims that clearly do not seek to tie up an abstract idea need not be exhaustively analyzed using the framework.

name: Step 2A — is the claim 'directed to' an abstract idea?
description: After Step 1, determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea by comparing the claimed concept to concepts the courts have previously identified as abstract ideas.
guidance: Use court-identified abstract ideas as comparators. Be familiar with court cases in technologies similar to your art. The Abstract Idea Quick Reference Sheet (QRS) groups common abstract idea types and links cases; the Case Law Chart lists litigated patents by title and classification. Examiners are not required to rely on the most similar or the most recent case—any court case identifying a similar abstract idea may be relied upon.

name: Step 2B — evaluate whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, evaluate whether any additional element or combination of additional elements transforms the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., whether they provide 'significantly more' or an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Considerations that may provide 'significantly more' include: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to the functioning of the computer itself; applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field; adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; and other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment. Considerations that may NOT provide 'significantly more' include: reciting a generic computer performing a generic computer function; words equivalent to 'apply the exception'; mere instructions to implement the judicial exception on a computer; insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering); generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use; and merely appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality.

name: Apply the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in view of the specification as it would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Interpret claim terms according to plain meaning unless the specification provides a special definition. When applying BRI, ask helpful questions: Does the method need to be performed by a computer or any particular device? What limits are imposed by the claim language on how information is obtained? How is the comparison accomplished? What is the result of a match (what happens when identity is verified)? These questions help define claim boundaries and whether elements are recited at a high level of generality.

name: Treat the claim as a whole; consider all recited limitations
description: Analyze the claim in its entirety and consider all recited limitations in making the eligibility determination.
guidance: Do not cherry-pick only certain elements—look at independent and relevant dependent claims and the specification. Also look beyond independent claims to other disclosed details that could be claimed in a manner that adds an inventive concept. The key inquiry: is the claim attempting to cover an abstract idea itself without significant limits on its application?

name: Hardware or machine limitations alone do not confer eligibility
description: The mere presence of a machine (e.g., a processor, memory, or a 'particular' machine) or software in a claim does not automatically render it eligible.
guidance: Applying the Alice/Mayo framework is required—do not rely on the machine-or-transformation (Bilski) or special purpose computer (Alappat) tests as standalone reasons for eligibility. A generic processor performing generic functions, or merely adding conventional hardware, is not 'significantly more.'

name: Practice compact prosecution—consider other statutory requirements
description: While determining eligibility, examiners should also fully examine claims under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 103, 112 and other related requirements.
guidance: Compact prosecution includes addressing utility, inventorship, double patenting, and non‑statutory double patenting along with 101. Point applicants to eligible subject matter in the specification when possible.

name: Specific, meaningfully integrated technical limitations can render claims eligible (Example-based guidance)
description: Reciting specific, detailed technical features and how they interact can add 'significantly more' to an abstract idea and render a claim eligible (illustrated by Example 35).
guidance: For Example 35, adding limitations such as generating a random code and transmitting it to a registered mobile device, a downloadable software module that generates an encrypted image including code data, reading/decrypting that image at the ATM, analyzing decrypted code data against the random code, or reciting a radio frequency reader and particular interactions between ATM and mobile device, were explained as adding significantly more. The training shows that these specific, discrete implementations present a practical application of fraud prevention and meaningfully limit the abstract idea, making the claim eligible at Step 2B.

name: Workload Management — permitted considerations parties may address
description: Parties are permitted (but not limited) to address specific considerations including: whether PTAB or another forum already adjudicated validity; changes in law/new judicial precedent since claim issuance; strength of the unpatentability challenge; extent of petition’s reliance on expert testimony; settled expectations of the parties (e.g., how long claims have been in force); compelling economic, public health, or national security interests; and any other considerations bearing on the Director’s discretion.
guidance: This non‑exhaustive list defines typical topics parties should address in discretionary briefing; it signals that factual, legal, policy, and equitable considerations can all bear on the Director’s exercise of discretion.

name: No fixed time standard — sufficiency of elapsed time
description: No specific lapse of time has been adopted as a standard; the general principle is that the time elapsed between granting the patent and the application for an injunction must have been sufficient to permit articles or machines to be constructed by the patentee in conformity with his claim and to be sold publicly and repeatedly.
guidance: Courts look to practical sufficiency: whether enough time has passed to allow public manufacture and sale under the patent so that enjoyment/possession evidence is meaningful; specific durations vary by case (examples range from one year to many years).

name: Box I — Top‑up searches and supplementary searches
description: Box No. I, item 6 must indicate whether top‑up searches have been carried out by the IPEA; if carried out, the date of the top‑up search and whether additional relevant documents were discovered must be indicated. If a document discovered in the top‑up search is used to support any negative statement with respect to claimed subject matter, it should be cited in Box No. V of the report. Documents that refer to an oral disclosure, use, exhibition or other means that occurred prior to the international filing date and documents that refer to an earlier patent document published on or after the international filing date should be cited in Box VI of the report. Box No. I, item 7 must be marked if the report is established taking into account the supplementary international search report(s) from the specified SISA(s).
guidance: Indicate dates and whether additional relevant documents were found; cite top‑up search documents in Box V if relied on for negative findings; distinguish documents to be reported in Box VI (non‑written disclosures or later publications of earlier filings). Mark use of SISA reports in the supplemental item.

name: Box II — Priority treated as not made; grounds
description: Box No. II informs the applicant that the report is established as if the priority claim had not been made. This may occur when: (A) the IPEA requested but was not furnished a copy of the earlier application whose priority is claimed (PCT Rule 66.7(a)); (B) applicant failed to timely comply with an invitation to furnish a translation of the earlier application (PCT Rule 66.7(b)); (C) the priority claim is found invalid or all claims are directed to inventions not described and enabled by the earlier application (PCT Rule 64.1); (D) the description, claims or drawings are so unclear that no meaningful opinion could be formed; (E) the claims are so inadequately supported by the description that no meaningful opinion could be formed; (F) no international search report has been established for the claims.
guidance: Specify which claims are affected if the report is not established only as to certain claims. Indicate withdrawal of the priority claim where applicable. Provide explicit reasons for treating the application as if priority not claimed.

name: Box III — Non‑establishment of opinion on novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability
description: Box No. III indicates that the report has not been established on questions of novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability as to some or all claims. The examiner must specify that the report was not established because, for example: (A) the application relates to subject matter which does not require international preliminary examination; (D) the applicant has neither restricted the claims nor paid additional fees; (E) the examiner considered the international application did not comply with unity of invention but decided not to issue an invitation to restrict or pay additional fees. Where less than all claims are examined, the examiner must indicate which parts were and which parts were not the subject of international preliminary examination.
guidance: Give precise reasons for non‑establishment and identify the exact claims or parts not examined. Use the enumerated grounds from PCT Rules and internal guidance.

name: Box IV — Lack of unity of invention and handling of additional fees/restrictions
description: If the applicant has paid additional fees or restricted claims in response to an invitation, or failed to respond, the IPR report shall indicate whether: (A) the claims have been restricted; (B) additional fees have been paid without protest; (C) additional fees have been paid by the applicant under protest; (D) the applicant has neither restricted nor paid additional fees. If additional fees were paid under protest and the applicant requested it, the text of the protest and the decision thereon must be annexed to the report by IPEA personnel.
guidance: State clearly whether restriction occurred or fees were paid and whether payments were protested; attach protest text and decision where requested by applicant; if indication under item (E) (examiner thought unity lacking but did not issue invitation), specify reasons.

name: Box V — Reasoned statement on novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability (Article 35(2))
description: The examiner must indicate whether each claim appears to satisfy novelty, inventive step (nonobviousness), and industrial applicability. Determinations should be made for each criterion separately and should be negative if the criterion is not satisfied for that claim. The examiner should always cite documents believed to support any negative determination as to novelty and inventive step. Any negative holding on industrial applicability must be fully explained.
guidance: Provide explanations referencing the cited documents and identify relevant passages (page/column/lines). Preferably provide a reasoned statement in all instances. Follow document citation procedure per Administrative Instructions Sections 503 and 611. If a statement is positive and the reason for citing a document is obvious, less explanation may suffice; otherwise give detailed rationale.

name: Box VI — Identification of certain cited documents (non‑written disclosures and later publications)
description: If the examiner or the international search report cites a relevant document referring to a non‑written disclosure and the document was published on or after the relevant date, the examiner must indicate: (A) the date the document was made available to the public; and (B) the date the non‑written public disclosure occurred. The examiner should also identify any published application or patent which would constitute prior art for purposes of PCT Article 33(2) and (3) had it been published earlier but was filed prior to, or claims the priority of, an earlier application filed prior to the relevant date. For each such published application or patent provide publication date, filing date, and claimed priority date (if any). The report may also indicate that the priority date of the document cited has not been validly claimed (PCT Rule 70.10).
guidance: Provide the dates precisely and follow Administrative Instructions Sections 507(c)–(e) and 508 for indicating special categories of documents and the claims to which the documents are relevant.

name: National stage (U.S. 35 U.S.C. 371) — identification and required submissions
description: When entering the U.S. national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371, once a U.S. application number is accorded, that number should be used in communications; include international application number, international filing date, and national stage entry date for cross‑checking. The national stage commences upon expiration of applicable time limits under Articles 22 or 39. The applicant shall file in the USPTO: (1) the national fee (section 41(a)); (2) a copy of the international application and an English translation if filed in another language (unless already communicated by the IB); (3) amendments to claims made under Article 19 (unless already communicated) and translations if made in another language; (4) an oath or declaration complying with section 115; and (5) an English translation of any annexes to the international preliminary examination report if the annexes were made in another language.
guidance: Use the U.S. application number for speedier processing. Ensure required fees, translations, and declarations are timely filed to avoid issues. Understand that the national stage differs from domestic filings in timing and that the prior art status is usually better known at national stage.

name: Reasonable royalty methods (B) - Established marketplace royalty
description: Established royalty based on marketplace licensing--the royalty may be based on other nonexclusive licenses of the patented invention if the claimed invention has been the subject of a nonexclusive license to a number of persons sufficient to indicate a general marketplace recognition of the reasonableness of the licensing terms, if the license was secured prior to the filing of the case, and if the infringer’s use is of substantially the same scope, volume and benefit of the rights granted under such license.
guidance: Court may rely on pre-existing nonexclusive licenses as a basis for reasonable royalty when licences demonstrate marketplace recognition and are comparable in scope/volume/benefit and were secured prior to filing.

name: Reasonable royalty methods (C) - Apportionment to claimed invention
description: If showings under (A) and (B) have not been made, the court shall conduct an analysis to ensure that a reasonable royalty is applied only to the portion of the economic value of the infringing product or process properly attributable to the claimed invention’s specific contribution over the prior art.
guidance: Requires apportionment: royalty must be limited to the economic value specifically attributable to the claimed invention over the prior art (avoid applying royalty to value from unclaimed/known features).

name: Willfulness route (A) - detailed written notice and continued infringement
description: The infringer received written notice from the patentee (i) alleging acts of infringement in a manner sufficient to give the infringer an objectively reasonable apprehension of suit on such patent, and (ii) identifying with particularity each claim of the patent, each allegedly infringing product or process, and the relationship of such product or process to such claim, the infringer, after a reasonable opportunity to investigate, thereafter performed one or more acts of infringement.
guidance: Notice must be particularized (claims, accused products/processes, claim-to-product relationship); continued acts after reasonable opportunity to investigate constitutes willfulness element A.

name: Sec.322 — Timing and basis of PGR petition (three circumstances)
description: A PGR petition may be filed in any one of three circumstances: (1) within 12 months of the patent’s issuance or reissuance (1st window); (2)(i) substantial reason to believe continued existence of the challenged claim is likely to cause the petitioner significant economic harm, and (ii) the petitioner files within 12 months after receiving notice (explicitly or implicitly) of infringement; or (3) the patent owner consents (2 and 3 are 2nd window).
guidance: Defines narrow 1st window and broader 2nd-window paths tied to economic harm/notice or owner consent; each path has distinct predicates.

name: Sec.323 — Requirements of petition
description: A petition must, inter alia, include the necessary fee, identify the real parties in interest, specifically identify each claim challenged, the grounds for challenging it, and the evidence that supports each challenge, including, where applicable, copies of relevant patents and printed publications, or supporting affidavits or declarations. The Director may, by regulation, require additional information. The petitioner must provide a copy of the petition with supporting documents to the patent owner or his designated representative.
guidance: Petitions must be detailed and supported by evidence; service on patent owner required; Director can require more info.

name: Sec.327 — Institution standard and timing
description: The Director may not authorize a PGR proceeding to commence unless the Director determines that the information presented in the petition raises a substantial new question of patentability for at least one of the challenged claims. The Director shall decide a petition within 90 days of its receipt, notify the petitioner and patent owner, and if granted shall publish notice including the date the PGR proceeding shall commence. The determination is not appealable. The Director shall assign a PGR proceeding to a panel of 3 Board judges.
guidance: High-level screening standard: 'substantial new question of patentability' required; 90-day decision clock; institution decisions are final (nonappealable); assigned to three-judge panel.

name: Sec.332 — Patent owner amendment in PGR (limits)
description: During a PGR, the patent owner may file one motion to amend the patent in one or more ways: (1) cancel any challenged claim; (2) propose a substitute claim for each challenged claim; or (3) amend the patent drawings or otherwise amend the patent other than the claims. Additional motions permitted only for good cause. An amendment may not enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new matter.
guidance: Narrow amendment rights: single primary motion allowed; no enlargement of claim scope or new matter permitted; additional motions require good cause.

name: Sec.335 — Effect of Board decision on patent record
description: If a final decision of the Board that is not timely appealed (or if that appeal is terminated), the Director shall publish a certificate canceling any claim determined unpatentable, and shall incorporate in the patent any new claim determined to be patentable.
guidance: Final PTAB decisions are implemented by certificate changing the patent's claims (cancellation/incorporation) when not appealed or appeal resolved against appellant.

name: Sec.337 — Effect of civil-action decisions on future PGR requests
description: If a final decision has been entered against a party in a civil action arising under section 1338 establishing that the party has not sustained its burden of proving the invalidity of any patent claim, that party may not subsequently request a PGR on that patent claim on the basis of any grounds under Sec.322. In addition, the Director may not subsequently maintain a PGR previously requested by that party.
guidance: Adverse civil-action final decisions preclude same party from later pursuing PGR on same grounds; Director must decline/terminate overlapping PGRs by that party.

name: Sec.338 — Collateral effects of favorable PGR final decision
description: If a final decision under Sec.334 is favorable to the patentability of any original or new claim of the patent challenged by the petitioner, the petitioner may not thereafter, based on any ground which the petitioner raised during the PGR, (1) request or pursue a derivation proceeding with respect to such claim; or (2) assert the invalidity of any such claim in any civil action arising in whole or in part under section 1338. If final decision results from a petition filed on basis of Sec.322(2), the prohibition extends to any ground the petitioner raised during the PGR.
guidance: Successful defense at PTAB creates estoppel preventing petitioner from later raising same grounds in derivation or civil actions (with extended scope for certain 2nd-window petitions).

name: Sec.12 — Inequitable conduct standard (Sec.298)
description: A party asserting that a patent should be cancelled or held unenforceable due to inequitable conduct shall prove independently, by clear and convincing evidence, that material information was misrepresented, or omitted, from the patent application with the intention of deceiving the USPTO. Information is material if a reasonable examiner would consider such information important in deciding whether to allow the patent application; any such information is not cumulative. Although intent to deceive may be inferred, it may not be done so based solely on the gross negligence of the patent owner or its representative, or on the materiality of the information misrepresented or not disclosed. The party asserting the defense shall comply with the pleading requirements set forth under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 9(b). If the court finds inequitable conduct, the court has discretion to (1) hold the entire patent unenforceable, (2) hold one or more claims unenforceable, or (3) hold that patentee is not entitled to an injunction.
guidance: Elevates and clarifies the elements (materiality + intent) and pleading standard for inequitable-conduct claims; bars inferring intent from mere gross negligence or materiality alone; provides remedies and requires FRCP 9(b) particularity.

name: Patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§ 101-103, 112)
description: Outlines the statutory conditions for obtaining a patent (sections 101-103, 112).
guidance: Mentioned as the baseline legal framework governing patents; these sections constrain what may properly be claimed and therefore affect claim drafting and claim-scope disputes.

name: 35 U.S.C. § 112 — written description/definiteness
description: Section 112 governs written description requirements and claim definiteness.
guidance: Invoked when discussing linguistic certainty and when broad claim language may increase risk of invalidation under § 112; connects to concerns about indefiniteness and ambiguity in claim drafting.

name: Ordinary and customary meaning as seen by a person of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA)
description: Claim terms should be given the ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field.
guidance: Cites cases (e.g., Ajinomoto; Multiform Desiccants) describing that PHOSITA reads the patent documents with understanding of field-specific usage; the PHOSITA perspective guides the interpretive baseline and points courts toward intrinsic resources (specification, prosecution history).

name: Specification (intrinsic record) is highly relevant to claim construction
description: The specification contains a written description of the invention and is always highly relevant to claim construction analysis.
guidance: Cites Vitronics and Phillips: courts should refer to the specification for linguistic context; authors stress using the specification for ordinary English usage conventions rather than to limit claims to the patentee's inventive contribution.

name: Prosecution history can provide relevant linguistic context
description: The prosecution history, though not physically attached to the claims, may sometimes supply linguistic context for claim meaning.
guidance: Examples (Liebel‑Flarsheim) show prosecution statements (e.g., deletions or amendments) can inform claim scope; but prosecution history is treated as a separate type of intrinsic evidence and has limits.

name: Dictionaries and extrinsic evidence vs. intrinsic record (weighting debate)
description: There is debate whether claim terms should be interpreted primarily by reference to dictionaries/extrinsic sources or by reference to the intrinsic record (specification and prosecution history).
guidance: Phillips and later cases resolved to give primacy to intrinsic evidence but discussed the role of dictionaries; the text canvasses the split between dictionary-dependent and specification-dependent methodologies and notes the practical implications for public notice.

name: Public notice and efficiency standard for determining patent scope
description: Patent scope should be judged by an efficiency/public notice paradigm balancing incentives to innovate against monopoly avoidance.
guidance: Cites Bonito Boats and the economic literature arguing the Patent Clause reflects a balance between encouraging innovation and avoiding monopolies; this policy lens informs normative views about how broadly claims should be read.

name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during PTO examination
description: PTO examiners use the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' standard when construing claim language in prosecution.
guidance: Cites In re Yamamoto and notes PTO's procedural posture calls for a different standard (BRI) than courts use in infringement litigation; this reduces patentee tricks by construing claims broadly during examination.

name: Deliberate ambiguity as a patentee strategy — incentives and limits
description: Patentees may intentionally use ambiguous or vague claim language to seek broader coverage, but the success of this strategy depends on PTO competence and enforcement incentives.
guidance: Discusses literature asserting deliberate ambiguity leads to overbroad patents (Bessen & Meurer; Burk & Lemley). Authors argue the patentee's incentive exists only in a 'Goldilocks' range where the PTO is competent enough to cause fear of rejection but not competent enough to detect deceit; remedy may be improved examiners rather than abolition of claims.

name: Judicial competence, cognitive difficulty, and reversal rates
description: Claim construction is cognitively demanding; high reversal rates at the Federal Circuit raise questions about judges' ability to resolve highly technical terms without institutional reforms.
guidance: Cites literature (Moore, Lee, Rai) and empirical work on reversal rates; suggests potential procedural responses (e.g., expedited appeals) and highlights selection effects and the difficulty of technical determinations for generalist judges.

name: Claim differentiation and related structural canons affect claim reading
description: Doctrines like claim differentiation can constrain how courts read claims relative to one another.
guidance: Cites Lemley and Phillips debates: claim differentiation sometimes used to argue against an interpretation that would render certain claims redundant or inconsistent with the claimed embodiments; commentators dispute proper weight and limits.

name: Genus-species rules when predictability is in question
description: Where generic claims have been rejected on a reference which discloses a species not antedated by the affidavit, the affidavit will not ordinarily be withdrawn unless applicant can establish possession of the generic invention prior to the reference date (i.e., affidavit must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to support a generic claim).
guidance: If the reference discloses a claimed species, overcome by showing prior completion of that species or a different species plus a showing the claimed species would have been an obvious modification. If the reference discloses several species of a genus, applicant must show prior completion of all species shown to overcome directly. Alternatively, applicant may show prior completion of one or more species sufficient to infer generic applicability — the test is whether the species completed provide an adequate basis for inferring generic applicability (examples: small genera like halogens vs large genera). Case law cited: In re Spiller; In re Stempel; In re Clarke; In re Plumb; In re Hostettler; In re Mantell; In re Rainer; In re Shokal; In re Schaub.

name: 37 CFR 1.131 ineffective against certain U.S. patents or publications claiming the same invention
description: A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or patent application publication claiming the same invention when the publication date is less than one year prior to presentation of claims — applicant's remedy must be by 37 CFR 1.608; where publication date is 1 year or more prior, rejection under 35 U.S.C. 135(b) should be made.
guidance: Where domestic reference and application/patent under reexamination are commonly owned and claims are not identical but not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (see MPEP §718). If claims are identical or not patentably distinct, the items claim the 'same patentable invention' (see 37 CFR 1.601(n)) and 1.131 cannot be used to avoid an interference; allowing 1.131 here would permit issuing two patents to the same invention. Form paragraphs (e.g., 23.14, 23.14.01) may be used for rejections under 135(b).

name: Effect of Claim Preamble Phrases: 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
description: Alternative 1: 'comprising' means 'including the following but not excluding others.' Alternative 2: 'consisting of' means 'including the following and excluding others.' Alternative 3: 'consisting essentially of' means 'including the following and possibly including unlisted components that do not materially affect the invention.'
guidance: If claim preamble uses 'comprising', accused product that includes all claimed elements literally infringes even with additional components. If 'consisting of', additional components negate literal infringement. If 'consisting essentially of', literal infringement exists if additional components do not negate an element or materially affect the basic and novel properties.

name: Limitations on DOE—Subject Matter Dedicated to the Public
description: If the Court determines that certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to the listed elements of the asserted claims.
guidance: This instruction is given only if the Court determines dedication applies as a matter of law. The Court will list elements; those elements must be literally present for infringement. Cited cases: SanDisk, Pfizer v. Teva, etc.

name: Infringement by Supply of All or a Substantial Portion of Components Abroad (§271(f)(1))
description: Plaintiff asserts Defendant infringed by supplying (or causing to be supplied) all or a substantial portion of the components of the patented product from the United States to another country and actively inducing the assembly of those components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the United States.
guidance: To show infringement under §271(f)(1), Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one claim; (2) Defendant supplied components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention; and (3) Defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into an infringing product. A 'substantial portion' is a quantitative (not qualitative) assessment; exporting a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability. Practice note: §271(f)(1) does not apply to method claims.

name: Infringement by Import/Sale/Offer/Use of Product Made by Patented Process (§271(g))
description: Plaintiff asserts Defendant infringed by importing, selling, offering for sale, or using a product that was made by a process covered by one or more claims of the patent.
guidance: To show infringement under §271(g), Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that: (1) Defendant imported into the U.S. or, within the U.S., sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the patent; (2) the product was made between the issue date of the patent and its expiration/date of trial; and (3) [further statutory elements as applicable].

name: 37 CFR 1.57(a) — inadvertent omission safeguard
description: If a portion of the specification or drawings was inadvertently omitted, incorporation by reference is allowed where (a) the application contains a claim under § 1.55 or § 1.78 for priority/benefit present on the filing date, and (b) the omitted portion is completely contained in the prior-filed application.
guidance: The application must be amended to include the omitted portion within any Office-set time period but no later than the close of prosecution (§ 1.114(b)) or abandonment. Applicant must supply a copy of the prior-filed application (except where the prior-filed application is filed under 35 U.S.C. 111), an English translation if needed, and identify where the omitted portion is found in the prior-filed application. Amendments to international applications under this paragraph are effective only as to the U.S. and do not affect international filing date; where no filing date is otherwise present, amendment must be by petition with fee (§ 1.17(f)).

name: Definition of 'essential material' (37 CFR 1.57(c))
description: 'Essential material' is material necessary to: (1) provide a written description of the claimed invention and enable one skilled in the art to make and use it and set forth the best mode (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph); (2) describe the claimed invention in terms that particularly point out and distinctly claim it (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph); or (3) describe structure, material, or acts corresponding to a claimed means or step for performing a specified function (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph).
guidance: In applications that are to issue as U.S. patents, essential material may only be incorporated by reference to a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that itself does not incorporate such essential material. Incorporation of essential material to unpublished U.S. applications, foreign applications/patents, or publications is improper under § 1.57(c).

name: Treatment of improper incorporations during examination (procedural consequence)
description: If incorporation by reference is improper (e.g., essential material incorporated from a foreign patent/publication or to an unpublished application), the incorporation is ineffective and the examiner should make the appropriate objection or rejection (for example under 35 U.S.C. 112) until applicant corrects it.
guidance: Applicants must timely correct improper incorporations (within the period set in § 1.57(g)). Correction usually requires an amendment that inserts the material and the § 1.57(f) statement that no new matter is included. Failure to correct can result in rejections and may require after-final practice (§ 1.116), RCE (§ 1.114), filing a reissue after grant, or revival procedures if abandoned. Certificate of correction is not appropriate to fix incorporation-by-reference issues that would impact claim scope.

name: Incorporation practice for benefit/priority (earlier effective filing date) applications
description: The limitations applicable to applications to issue as patents do not apply to earlier applications relied on solely to establish an earlier effective filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119 or 120.
guidance: An application may be entitled to rely on the filing date of an earlier application even if that earlier application incorporates essential material by reference. However, when benefit is claimed the applicant or patent owner may be required to supply copies (and translations) of material incorporated by reference so the Office can determine whether the earlier application discloses the invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112.

name: 37 CFR 1.125(a)-(c) — substitute (rewritten) specification required by Office
description: If amendments or poor legibility make the application difficult to consider or to arrange papers for printing/copying, the Office may require the entire specification (including claims) or any part thereof be rewritten.
guidance: A substitute specification required by the Office under § 1.125(a) must be submitted with markings showing changes relative to the immediate prior version: underline added text; strike-through deleted text (or double brackets for small deletions); an accompanying clean version without markings must be supplied. A statement that the substitute specification contains no new matter must also be supplied. Numbering paragraphs of the specification of record is not considered a change requiring marking.

name: 37 CFR 1.125(b) — voluntary substitute specification
description: Subject to § 1.312, an applicant may voluntarily file a substitute specification (excluding claims) at any point up to payment of the issue fee if accompanied by a statement that it includes no new matter.
guidance: Voluntary substitute specifications must also comply with the marking and clean-copy requirements noted in § 1.125(c). The Office will accept a voluntary substitute if § 1.125(b) requirements are satisfied.

name: Importance of claim construction and review of entire disclosure (BRI) before eligibility analysis
description: Before performing eligibility (Step 1 or Step 2A) examiners must determine what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: See MPEP §2106 subsection II and MPEP §2111 for BRI. Eligibility evaluation is dependent on properly understanding claim scope; examiners should point out BRI issues and suggest narrowing amendments where appropriate.

name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments fail Step 1
description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter (Step 1: NO).
guidance: When BRI encompasses non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable medium that covers carrier waves and physical media), a §101 rejection is appropriate. Best practice: point out the BRI on the record and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments if possible.

name: When claim is clearly not within the four categories — rejection practice
description: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four statutory categories (Step 1: NO), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01; see MPEP §2106.07(a)(1). If the disclosure indicates the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, continue analysis to determine whether such amended claim would be eligible and recommend amendment if possible.

name: Step 2A is a two‑prong inquiry (Prong One and Prong Two)
description: Step 2A consists of Prong One: whether the claim recites a judicial exception; and Prong Two: whether the recited exception is integrated into a practical application by additional elements.
guidance: Perform Prong One first; if an exception is recited, perform Prong Two to determine if the claim as a whole integrates that exception into a practical application. If the claim does not recite an exception, the claim is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B.

name: Step 2A Prong One — identifying whether a claim recites an exception (set forth or described)
description: Prong One asks whether the claim 'recites' (i.e., 'sets forth' or 'describes') an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon — meaning an identifiable judicial exception is stated or described in the claim language.
guidance: There are two ways an exception can be recited: 'set forth' (explicitly stated, e.g., a mathematical equation in Diehr) or 'described' (the concept is described but not named, e.g., intermediated settlement in Alice). Examiners should identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an exception and determine whether those limitations fall within judicial exceptions. Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception from claims that merely 'involve' an exception (the latter do not require further eligibility analysis).
