Examples: a claim reciting 'F=ma' sets forth a law of nature (Prong One YES); a teeter-totter claim merely involves the law of the lever (Prong One NO). See MPEP §2106.04(a)/(b)/(c) for detailed guidance.

name: Step 2A Prong Two — practical application/integration of the exception
description: Prong Two asks whether the additional elements in the claim integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application of that exception. If they do, the claim is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B; if they do not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and proceeds to Step 2B.
guidance: Additional elements must 'integrate' the exception into a practical application or otherwise transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (Alice: 'transform the nature of the claim'). Mere recitation of a judicial exception or mere addition of another judicial exception is insufficient. See RecogniCorp, Genetic Technologies and related case law. If no additional elements exist, the claim cannot be eligible and examiner should consider recommending amendment. For details on evaluating 'integration into a practical application' see MPEP §2106.04(d)(2).

name: Mere recitation vs. integration: additional elements cannot be another judicial exception
description: Where additional claim elements merely recite another judicial exception or are otherwise only the judicial exception itself, that is insufficient to integrate the exception into a practical application.
guidance: Examples: adding one abstract idea (math) to another abstract idea (encoding/decoding) does not render the claim non-abstract (RecogniCorp). The additional elements must do more — change the claim's nature or provide a practical application — either at Prong Two or in Step 2B (inventive concept).

name: Enumerated groupings of abstract ideas for examiner use
description: To facilitate examination, the Office has enumerated groupings of abstract ideas: (1) mathematical concepts; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) mental processes.
guidance: These groupings distill case law and shift examiners away from a strict case-comparison approach. Examiners should (1) identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an abstract idea and (2) determine whether those limitations fall within at least one enumeration. If they do, the claim requires further analysis in Prong Two. If they do not, the claim does not recite an abstract idea (subject to rare circumstances in MPEP §2106.04(a)(3)). Examples and subdefinitions: mathematical relationships/formulas/calculations; fundamental economic principles, commercial/legal interactions, advertising/marketing/sales activities; mental observations/evaluations/judgments. See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) for further discussion.

name: Software and business‑method clarifications
description: Software and business methods are not categorically excluded from §101 and are not automatically abstract ideas merely because they involve calculations or business practices.
guidance: Case law (Enfish, McRO, Thales Visionix, Content Extraction) shows that claims to software or business methods can be eligible if they do not recite or are not directed to judicial exceptions as a whole. Examiners should apply the enumerated groupings and the Prong One/Two analysis rather than blanket assumptions about software or business-method claims.

name: Absence of complete preemption is not dispositive of eligibility
description: While preemption is the underlying concern with judicial exceptions, the mere absence of complete preemption does not demonstrate that a claim is eligible.
guidance: The Alice/Mayo test must be applied; finding some non-preemptive scope does not obviate the need for the two-part analysis. Courts have rejected arguments that limited preemption implies eligibility (Diehr discussion). Several Federal Circuit decisions have noted lack of preemption where claims were found eligible, but preemption analysis should be resolved through the two-part test (steps 2A/2B).

name: If claim recites an exception and no additional elements exist, claim cannot be eligible
description: A claim that recites only a judicial exception without additional elements that integrate it into a practical application cannot be eligible under §101.
guidance: In such cases make the appropriate rejection (see MPEP §2106.07) and a best practice is to recommend an amendment, if possible, that would resolve eligibility by adding qualifying elements.

name: Completeness of inventions' features
description: Fine-tuning can enhance the completeness of inventions' features.
guidance: Evaluates whether generated claims include all salient technical features of the invention as described in the specification/description. The paper reports fine-tuning improves this dimension.

name: Feature linkage
description: Fine-tuning can enhance ... feature linkage.
guidance: Measures how well individual claim features are connected/related within the claim (logical linkage among elements) and across dependent claims.

name: Technical coherence
description: GPT-4 demonstrates the best performance ... with better ... technical coherence.
guidance: Evaluates internal technical consistency of the claim language and whether the claim's technical statements make sense together.

name: Quality of first independent claims vs dependent claims
description: LLMs can produce high-quality first independent claims, but their performances markedly decrease for subsequent dependent claims.
guidance: Separate evaluation of independent claim quality (often stronger) and dependent claim generation (linking back to and properly narrowing independent claims); highlights model weaknesses on dependent claims.

name: Model selection: patent-specific LLMs vs general LLMs
description: Current patent-specific LLMs perform much worse than state-of-the-art general LLMs.
guidance: Implication for evaluating/generated claims: choice of model architecture/training matters; off-the-shelf general LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) may outperform smaller or domain-specialized models in claim quality metrics used by experts.

name: Statutory enablement requirement ('make and use')
description: 35 U.S.C. § 112(a): the specification must contain a written description ... in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art ... to make and use the same.
guidance: The brief emphasizes that enablement is governed by the statute’s command to teach skilled artisans 'to make and use' the invention. The correct inquiry is whether the patent’s disclosure, viewed reasonably in light of the subject matter, teaches those skilled in the art how to practice the invention (Minerals Separation v. Hyde, Universal Oil, The Telephone Cases). The petitioner argues the statutory standard is practical and does not require enabling every conceivable variation of a claimed genus.

name: Undue experimentation
description: A claim is invalid for lack of enablement if a person of ordinary skill in the art would not be able to practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation (clear-and-convincing standard).
guidance: Courts assess whether following the patent's teachings would force artisans to engage in experimentation that is excessive (e.g., 'searching for a needle in a haystack'). Relevant precedents and factors include In re Wands, Atlas Powder, Consolidated Electric, and the Wands factors for undue experimentation (amount of guidance, working examples, routine nature of experimentation, predictability of the art, etc.). Where the number of inoperative combinations becomes significant or where success requires extensive time/failures, experimentation may be undue.

name: Clear-and-convincing evidence burden
description: Invalidity for lack of enablement must be proven by clear-and-convincing evidence.
guidance: Challengers bear the high burden to show by clear-and-convincing proof that a person of ordinary skill could not practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation. The brief notes that mere speculation about hypothetical embodiments is insufficient; challengers should present evidence (e.g., actual inability or post‑filing embodiments that demonstrate non-enablement) as in Consolidated Electric and related cases.

name: Treatment of genus claims (no special 'reach-the-full-scope' heightened rule)
description: Genus claims cover a group of structurally related products that incorporate the basic advance of the invention. The Federal Circuit imposed a 'reach-the-full-scope' test requiring artisans to 'reach the full scope of claimed embodiments' without 'substantial time and effort.'
guidance: The brief argues there should be no separate, heightened enablement test for genus claims demanding that skilled artisans be able 'to cumulatively identify and make all or nearly all embodiments' without substantial time and effort. Instead, genus claims are evaluated under the statutory 'make and use' enablement and undue experimentation framework; representative examples and a practical roadmap can suffice (see Consolidated Electric, Minerals Separation).

name: Whether examples are representative of the genus
description: A factor is whether the working examples disclosed in the specification are representative of the structural diversity of the claimed genus.
guidance: If the specification discloses working examples that reasonably represent the claim's structural diversity and provides a method/roadmap to obtain other embodiments, courts can find the genus enabled. District-court findings that disclosed examples were 'representative' carry weight; the Federal Circuit should not require every variation to be specifically exemplified so long as skilled artisans can make others by following the specification.

name: Roadmap / sufficiency of instructions to generate embodiments
description: Whether the patent provides a practical 'roadmap' — step-by-step methods, known techniques, anchor examples, assays, or high-throughput procedures — that enable skilled artisans to make claimed embodiments.
guidance: The brief emphasizes that a specification that supplies anchor exemplars (e.g., specific antibodies), assays/competition tests, immunization and screening schedules, and known techniques (phage display, conservative substitutions) constitutes a roadmap that enables artisans to produce embodiments 'every time.' The presence of routine, high-throughput methods reduces the likelihood that follow-up work constitutes undue experimentation (In re Wands).

name: Distinct mechanism / category non-enablement
description: A claim covering distinct categories of embodiments that operate by different mechanisms may be non-enabled if the specification fails to teach how to make embodiments that operate by a particular mechanism (e.g., mechanical vs. electronic sensors).
guidance: Enablement must encompass embodiments across distinct mechanisms; failing to teach one mechanism can render the claim non-enabled even if other embodiments are enabled. The concern is not the number of variants per se but the specification's inability to make distinct types that function differently (Auto. Techs. v. BMW example).

name: 'Needle in a haystack' / number of inoperative combinations
description: A claim is non-enabled when artisans must search among a vast number of inoperative combinations before finding operative embodiments — i.e., the specification leaves them 'searching for a needle in a haystack.'
guidance: If the number of inoperative combinations makes the required experimentation significant (billions of permutations, months/years of trial-and-error), the claim crosses into undue experimentation (Atlas Powder; Idenix; Wyeth & Cordis). Empirical evidence of large-scale failures or painstaking experimentation (as in Consolidated Electric) supports non-enablement; speculation about many theoretical candidates does not.

name: Preventing overbroad claims via the statutory standard
description: Concerns that patentees might claim more than they invented are addressed by §112(a): if a claim 'exceeds what the patent enables,' challengers can show skilled artisans cannot 'make and use' large areas of the claimed invention by following the patent's teachings.
guidance: The brief argues no new judicially invented 'reach-the-full-scope' test is necessary to police overbreadth; the statutory enablement/undue-experimentation framework (and cases like Consolidated Electric, Béné, Holland Furniture) already provides the mechanism to invalidate claims that overreach.

name: Written-description requirement (possession of claimed invention)
description: §112(a) has been construed by some courts to embody both an enablement requirement and a written-description requirement (Ariad): the specification must show that the inventor possessed the claimed invention.
guidance: Courts evaluate written description by asking whether the specification conveys to persons skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter. Representative examples, structural detail, and corroborating disclosures support written description. In this case the district court upheld written description based on examples and structural disclosures (26 example antibodies, atomic-level structures).

name: Novelty (for purposes of IPE)
description: Novelty — defined (for purposes of IPE); one of IPE criteria.
guidance: Declaration as to exceptions to lack of novelty; lack of novelty may be the subject of comment in the written opinion; relevant prior art assists in determining whether claimed invention involves novelty; statements and remarks in IPRP (Chapter II) as to novelty (see cross-references to industrial applicability and inventive step).

name: Inventive step / Obviousness
description: Inventive step (obviousness) — central substantive criterion for IPE/search.
guidance: Inventive step is treated as a distinct IPE criterion (see cross-references); prior art analysis assists assessment of inventive step (see PRIOR ART); see also references to rectification of unity and protests regarding unity which may affect claim scope considered for inventive step.

name: Prior art identification and use
description: Prior art — general rules and role in international search and examination.
guidance: Prior art is used to determine novelty and inventive step; claims must include statement of prior art (see 5.112); prior art relevant for IPE (10.058-10.059); treatment and effect of international applications as prior art in designated States (see national chapter references).

name: Requirements for claims (form and content)
description: Requirements for claims — form, content and numbering requirements.
guidance: Specific requirements for claims cited at 5.112-5.127; numbering of amended claims (9.005); requirements may include statements of prior art (5.112); rectification/amendment rules for claims (5.126, 11.033-11.044) and requirements for Art. 19/34 amendments (9.005, 10.071).

name: Physical requirements (paper/electronic) for filings
description: Physical requirements by RO and IPEA for papers and electronic media.
guidance: Physical requirements for IA regarding paper (5.177) and for specific elements (claims, description, drawings) are cited (5.105, 5.124, 5.131–5.159); IPEA and RO have separate physical requirements (10.044, 10.047(i), 6.001(ii)).

name: Request form and filing boxes (formal filing requirements)
description: Request form — required boxes and what information each box must contain.
guidance: Detailed guidance for Request Form: Box I Title of Invention (5.019); Boxes II/III Applicants/Inventors (5.020-5.039); Box IV Agent/Common Representative/Address for Correspondence (5.041-5.051); Box V Designation of States (5.052-5.055); Box VI Priority Claim (5.057-5.071); Box VII ISA (5.072-5.073); Box VIII Declarations (5.074-5.083); Box IX Check List/Language (5.084-5.087); Box X Signature (5.088-5.091). Continuation sheets, supplemental boxes and fee calculation sheet guidance provided (5.085, 5.093).

name: Time limits, priority periods and deadlines
description: Time limits for various PCT acts — priority periods, deadlines for demands, publication timing and national phase entry.
guidance: Specific periods referenced: 13, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 26, 28, 30 months from priority/filing for various actions (e.g., demand filing, availability of Art. 19/34 amendments, establishment of IPRP Chapter II, national/regional fees deadlines). Priority date established by priority claim (5.060); national/regional phase entry deadlines extended by IPE for certain DOs (10.002).

name: Claims lack an inventive concept
description: Whether the claims contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter — i.e., a meaningful limitation beyond the abstract idea.
guidance: Courts repeatedly hold claims ineligible where there is 'no inventive concept' or 'no meaningful limitation' to the abstract idea. Typical determinations find no inventive concept where the claim merely applies the abstract idea using existing or generic technology.

name: Whether claimed elements are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional' is a question of fact
description: Determination of whether elements recited in the claims are well-understood, routine, and conventional often presents a factual dispute.
guidance: Courts frequently find that whether claim elements are routine and conventional is a question for fact (with competing expert testimony) and therefore summary judgment or dismissal on §101 is inappropriate where genuine disputes exist.

name: Claim construction may be necessary before deciding eligibility
description: Whether claim construction has occurred and whether construing claim terms is required to resolve the §101 inquiry.
guidance: Multiple holdings deny motions to dismiss or for judgment on the pleadings because claim construction had not yet occurred and is necessary to determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea or possess an inventive concept.

name: High-level data/software recitations without detail are insufficient
description: Whether claims that recite high-level software/data processing (e.g., 'taking in and outputting data' with no detail on how data is manipulated) provide patentable subject matter.
guidance: A mere recitation of software at a highly abstract level—input, output, and generic manipulation—with no detail on how data is transformed typically fails to provide an inventive concept. Courts have struck down claims that provide no detail as to how data is manipulated between input and output.

name: Fundamental economic practices and longstanding commercial methods are abstract ideas
description: Whether the claimed subject matter embodies fundamental economic practices or long-prevalent commercial methods (e.g., auctions, payment processing, third-party intermediaries, financing applications).
guidance: Courts repeatedly treat fundamental economic practices as abstract ideas. Claims covering such practices typically require an additional inventive concept to be patent eligible; absent that, they are held ineligible.

name: Use of specialized database/analytics or unconventional technological detail can preserve eligibility
description: Whether the claim recites specialized databases, powerful data analytics, or other specific technological implementations that constitute an unconventional solution beyond generic components.
guidance: Some holdings indicate claims should not be dismissed when the complaint alleges 'unconventional technological solution through a specialized database permitting powerful data analytics' or when the specification expressly recites unconventional technical features—these factual allegations may preclude dismissal at early stages.

name: Invented mode requirement to secure broad protection
description: To claim protection against other means of carrying the same principle into effect, the patentee must have invented some mode of carrying the principle into effect.
guidance: If the patentee has not invented any mode of carrying the principle into effect, he cannot claim a monopoly over all modes (Jupe v. Pratt). But if he did invent a mode, he may be entitled to protection from 'all other modes of carrying the same principle into effect,' treated as piracy by imitating that original invention.

name: Claims cannot be unrealistically broad (no claim to an art in the abstract or all means)
description: A claim that purports to cover an art or method in the abstract or 'by any means' is invalid; patents must be limited to particular methods or machinery described.
guidance: Wyeth v. Stone: claim to 'cut ice ... by means of any other power than human' was 'unmaintainable.' A timely disclaimer narrowing the claim to particular methods can sometimes save a claim.

name: Combinations of known elements may be patentable if they produce a new/better/cheaper article
description: A new combination of materials or known means may be patentable where the combination produces a new article, or a better or cheaper article to the public than previously produced.
guidance: Example: combination of hot blast with anthracite coal in ironmaking — if the result is improved, the combination may be 'an invention or manufacture intended by the statute.' The specification must clearly express that it is the new combination or application being claimed.

name: Specification must clearly express the claimed new combination or application
description: When the invention is a combination or an application of known agents, the specification must clearly state that the claim is in respect of that new combination or application.
guidance: Failure to clearly express the combination or to disclaim separately claimed parts can lead to invalidity; courts examine whether the specification limits the monopoly to the inventive combination.

name: Validation test of quasi-random assignment (Righi and Simcoe style)
description: Under quasi-random assignment, the first-stage coefficient on the instrument should be invariant to including controls for application, applicant, and examiner characteristics.
guidance: Estimate first stage with progressively richer controls; show coefficient stability across specifications. Include proxies for applicant quality (log employees, log sales, growth), application quality (log independent claims), examiner specialization, experience, and seniority. Use subclass-by-year or art-unit-by-year fixed effects as suggested.

name: Process as transformation (Cochrane definition)
description: A process is 'an act, or a series of acts, performed upon the subject-matter to be transformed and reduced to a different state or thing,' provided it is new and useful.
guidance: This historical definition supports eligibility for processes that effect a physical transformation; it is a relevant factor when assessing manufacturing and treatment claims.

name: Mathematical formulas and algorithms require inventive application
description: Mathematical formulas, scientific truths, and algorithms are not patentable in the abstract; to be eligible they must be applied in a novel and useful structure or process.
guidance: Gottschalk v. Benson and Parker v. Flook: claiming a mathematical algorithm alone (or with known post-solution activity) risks ineligibility unless the claim integrates the algorithm into a novel, practical application or technical process.

name: Consider the claim 'as a whole'; avoid improper dissection
description: Claims should be considered in their entirety; courts warn against dissecting claims into old and new elements and ignoring the old elements.
guidance: Diehr cautioned that parsing claims to isolate a judicial exception while ignoring the overall combination can be inappropriate; the ordered combination may supply eligibility even if individual elements appear conventional.

name: Practical application / useful arts test (proposed alternative)
description: Some public and legislative proposals recommend replacing the Mayo/Alice framework with a 'technological' or 'useful arts' test that treats claims as eligible if they contribute to the technological arts or recite a practical application.
guidance: Proposals vary: some would expressly permit claims that recite a practical application of a law/phenomenon/idea while preventing claims that preempt all applications; proponents argue this aligns U.S. law with international norms and reduces unpredictability.

name: Overbreadth is often better addressed under §§112 or 103
description: Some judges and commentators argue that claims that are overly broad should be policed under disclosure (§112) or obviousness (§103) rather than by broadly applying §101 exclusions.
guidance: This view suggests using stricter claim construction, definiteness and enablement review, or obviousness analysis to limit overbroad claims instead of deeming subject matter ineligible at the threshold.

name: Technology-specific considerations (life sciences vs. computer-related)
description: The application of §101 principles varies by technology domain: life sciences cases often turn on whether claimed materials/diagnostics are natural products or merely isolated natural phenomena, while computer-related cases focus on abstract ideas implemented on computers and whether inventive technical improvements are claimed.
guidance: The report documents differential Federal Circuit outcomes: life sciences decisions emphasize natural-product and natural-phenomenon issues (e.g., Myriad, Ariosa), whereas computer cases emphasize abstract ideas and generic computer implementation (Alice). Examiners and drafters should tailor claims and arguments to technology-specific precedent.

name: Use of definitional statutory language in legislative proposals
description: Various public proposals include explicit statutory definitions (e.g., defining 'law of nature', 'natural product', 'abstract idea') and procedural rules (e.g., 'sole exception', or that eligibility be determined 'without regard' to §§102/103/112).
guidance: Examples in the appendix: IPO/AIPLA/NYIPLA/HIPLA proposals—some propose that a claim is ineligible only if it 'exists in nature independently of and prior to any human activity' or that 'abstract idea' excludes processes performed by computer programs. These definitions would materially alter eligibility analyses if enacted.

name: Substantial New Question (SNQ) of Patentability standard
description: Under 35 U.S.C. 312(a) (pre‑AIA SNQ standard), the Director determines whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim of the patent is raised by the request.
guidance: This was the standard applicable for inter partes reexamination requests filed prior to September 16, 2011. If SNQ is present, reexamination will be ordered; if ordered under SNQ, the SNQ standard continues to apply throughout that reexamination proceeding.

name: Scope of reexamination cannot enlarge patent claims
description: The scope of the patent claims cannot be enlarged by amendment during inter partes reexamination.
guidance: Amendments may confirm, cancel, or incorporate new/amended claims but cannot broaden claim scope beyond original claims.

name: Format and content of inter partes reexamination certificate
description: The inter partes reexamination certificate (titled 'INTER PARTES REEXAMINATION CERTIFICATE') will set forth the results of the proceeding, including canceling claims determined unpatentable, confirming patentable claims, incorporating amended/new claims determined patentable, listing changes in description, disclaimers, and identifying unamended claims held invalid or claims not reexamined.
guidance: New claims printed in italics; amended claims printed with italics and bracketing; certificate numbered with patent number + kind code suffix (C1, C2, etc.); certificate mailed to patent owner and copy to requester; bibliographic info similar to patent title page.

name: Intervening rights for amended or new claims
description: Amended or new claims determined patentable and incorporated into the patent after inter partes reexamination have the same effect for intervening rights as specified in 35 U.S.C. 252 for reissued patents.
guidance: This protects parties who made or prepared for use/import before issuance of the reexamination certificate; case law parallels noted (e.g., Fortel, Kaufman, Tennant).

name: Fees for requesting reexamination and for adding claims
description: A request for inter partes reexamination must be accompanied by the fee required (37 CFR 1.20(c)(2)); fees are required for adding claims in a reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Specific fee amounts and fee processing procedures are set out in the regulations and MPEP; see the relevant MPEP sections for payment, partial refunds, and fee codes.

name: Specification must distinguish new from old (identify improvement)
description: "if it be an improvement only upon an existing machine, he should distinguish what is new and what is old in his specification"
guidance: Patentee may not claim exclusive use of machinery already known. If the description mixes up old and new without clearly indicating what is claimed as new, the patent is void for covering too much or leaving uncertainty about what is claimed.

name: Disclaimer procedure to remove erroneously claimed parts (Act of 1837)
description: "any such patentee ... may make disclaimer of such parts of the thing patented, as the disclaimant shall not claim to hold by virtue of the patent ... which disclaimer shall thereafter be taken and considered as part of the original specification ... recorded in the patent office ... On payment ... of the sum of ten dollars."
guidance: A patentee who inadvertently claimed more than he had the right to claim may file a written, witnessed disclaimer recorded in the patent office (fee required). To obtain benefits (e.g., costs) in pending suits the disclaimer must be filed before suit commencement; unreasonable delay in filing can be a defense to the suit.

name: Invalidity-112 Indefiniteness (section 112(b))
description: Invalidity on grounds of indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) — recorded as “Invalidity-112-Indefiniteness--Any Stage.”
guidance: The paper documents that indefiniteness arguments succeeded at very different rates across technologies (e.g., nearly a quarter in software, a third in electronics, 0% in mechanical and biotech, ~3% in chemicals). It links higher indefiniteness success in software to particular definiteness rules that apply to means-plus-function claims and summarizes case law requiring disclosure of corresponding algorithms (Aristocrat, Function Media, ePlus, Ergo, Noah Systems, In re Aoyama, Typhoon Touch, Dell). The authors caution small sample sizes in some categories.

name: Technology and industry categorical variables
description: Use of technology-area categories (mechanics, electronics, chemistry, biotech, software, optics, etc.) and industry categories (pharmaceuticals, medical devices, computer & electronics, communications, consumer goods, transportation, construction, energy, industrial/business goods) as explanatory variables.
guidance: The paper distinguishes technology (the nature of the claimed technology) from industry (the industry deploying the patent) and presents outcomes by both. The analyses show significant differences across both axes and argue for interpreting technology- and industry-specific patterns separately (e.g., biotech technology vs biotech industry).

name: Patent and lawsuit covariates included in regressions
description: Patent and litigation characteristics included as covariates in multivariate regressions: inventor domestic/foreign status, number of claims, number of prior art references cited, number of other patents that cite this patent, patent age at filing of suit (how old when suit filed), number of defendants sued, and number of other patents asserted in the same case.
guidance: These variables were incorporated alongside technology and industry dummies in logistic regression specifications to control for patent and lawsuit heterogeneity. The paper reports multiple specifications (primary and alternative), and notes internal consistency across specifications. Appendices present full specifications.

name: Interpretation caveats: small sample sizes, selection, and representativeness
description: Cautions about small numbers in some categories, potential selection bias, and the non-representativeness of litigated-and-adjudicated patents versus all patents (or even all litigated patents).
guidance: Authors repeatedly warn that small cell counts can make percentages sensitive to a few cases (e.g., biotech small N), note that their dataset includes only a subset of filed suits (less than 10% of filed lawsuits in study years) and largely excludes settled cases (whose terms are confidential), and outline a 'selection story' whereby patents reaching judgment may not be representative of all patents. These caveats qualify causal or general claims from the observed associations.

name: Means-plus-function doctrine effect on software claim definiteness
description: Doctrinal rule: means-plus-function software claims require disclosure of the corresponding algorithm in the specification, failing which the claim can be invalid as indefinite.
guidance: The paper cites a line of Federal Circuit cases (Aristocrat, Function Media, ePlus, Ergo, Noah Systems, In re Aoyama, Typhoon Touch v. Dell) illustrating that algorithms must be disclosed for means-plus-function claims; this doctrinal feature likely contributes to higher indefiniteness success rates in software cases in the dataset. The authors note that many patents in the dataset were drafted before development of this case law, possibly explaining failures on indefiniteness grounds.

name: Language for submission of amendments
description: There are specific language requirements for amendments: amendments of claims under Article 19 and amendments under Article 34 must be submitted in specified languages (refer to paragraphs 9.004, 9.017-9.019, and 10.071).
guidance: See Rule 46.3 and Rule 55.3 and the referenced paragraphs for detail; translations may be required depending on whether a translation of the international application was transmitted for ISR, supplementary search, publication or IPE.

name: Filing of letters and documents — general formalities (Rule 92 and related)
description: Letters must be signed; any other document submitted must be accompanied by a letter. Letters/documents to RO, ISA, Authority for supplementary search, and IPEA must generally be in the language of the international application or in the language of a transmitted translation; communications to the IB must be in English or French and may be in the language of publication if submitted via ePCT.
guidance: Refer to Rule 12.1, Rule 55.2, Rule 92 and Section 104 for detailed requirements. Language of amendments to claims under Article 19 and demands/amendments under Article 34 have specific references.

name: Title must correspond with specification
description: The title of the patent must correspond with the description in the specification.
guidance: Claims in the title should neither be excessively extensive nor overly confined. Claiming one thing when another is really meant can vitiate the patent.

name: Claims must not appropriate old parts (originality of claimed parts)
description: Parts claimed must be original; must not, even unintentionally, appropriate any part that is old.
guidance: A specification should not claim old subject-matter as new. Describing old parts need not be unnecessary, but appropriating known features as new is incorrect and can invalidate claims.

name: Connection between patent and specification
description: There is a strict connection of the patent and specification; title and specification must correspond.
guidance: A patent's scope is tethered to its specification; discrepancies between the patent's title/claims and the specification invite invalidation or narrow construction.

name: Combination patents (union of two or more machines/articles)
description: Combinations or arrangements of known things may be patentable; specifications must show that parts are united and the operation of the combination.
guidance: When patenting a combination, the specification must explain how the parts operate together and, where old combinations are claimed, must show novelty in the particular arrangement or resulting function.

name: Handling obviously informal cases (MPEP §702.01)
description: Procedure when application disclosure is informal or insufficient so that a complete action on the merits is impractical.
guidance: Steps the examiner may follow: (A) make a reasonable search of the invention as it can be understood; if disclosure is so incomprehensible that a reasonable search cannot be made, inform applicant no search was made; (B) note informalities and drawing deficiencies via attachments to the Office action; (C) require that the specification be revised to conform to idiomatic English and U.S. patent practice; (D) reject claims as failing to define the invention per 35 U.S.C. 112 if they are informal (blanket rejection usually sufficient). If many informal claims, treat them as a single claim for fee/examination purposes. Encourage applicant to submit a preliminary amendment (preferably within 3 months) correcting obvious informalities; do not allow new matter in such amendments. Examiner should attempt to point out points of informality and may request correlation of terminology with art-accepted terminology (use form paragraph 7.01 where terminology prevents a proper search).

name: Search requirements (MPEP §704.01)
description: After reading specification and claims, the examiner searches the prior art; the invention should be thoroughly understood before searching.
guidance: Searching subject matter covered in MPEP Chapter 900 (esp. §§904–904.03). Informal or imperfectly understood cases are nevertheless given a search to avoid piecemeal prosecution. When assigned after another examiner's action, give full faith and credit to prior examiner's search and action unless there is a clear error or knowledge of other prior art—second examiner generally should not reorient the approach or perform a new search merely to find something different. See MPEP §719.05.

name: Requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 — authority and illustrative examples (MPEP §704.10)
description: An examiner or Office employee may require from inventors (37 CFR 1.56(c) individuals) or assignees such information as may be reasonably necessary to properly examine or treat a matter in a pending/abandoned application or reexamination proceeding.
guidance: Examples in 37 CFR 1.105(a)(1)(i)-(viii) include: (i) particularly relevant commercial databases known to inventors that could be searched; (ii) whether a prior-art search was made and what was searched; (iii) copies of non-patent literature/published applications/patents by any inventor relating to the claimed invention; (iv) copies of literature used to draft the application; (v) copies of literature used in the invention process (designing around/providing a solution); (vi) identification of what is being improved (for improvements); (vii) identification of any use of the claimed invention known to inventors at filing time; (viii) technical information known to applicant concerning related art, disclosure, claimed subject matter, or accuracy of examiner’s interpretation. Presentation formats may include a requirement for factual information, interrogatories (specific questions), or stipulations. A reply stating the information is unknown or not readily available may be accepted as a complete reply. Replies and failures to reply are governed by §§1.135 and 1.136.

name: Specific types/examples of information that may be reasonably required (MPEP §704.11(a) and (b))
description: Non-exhaustive list of particular factual items the examiner may request when reasonably necessary for examination or finding prior art.
guidance: Examples include: (A) name/citation of any particularly relevant indexed journal or treatise; (B) trade name(s) of goods/services embodying claimed subject matter; (C) citation/dates/copies of advertising/promotional literature for goods/services embodying claimed subject matter; (D) citation/copies of journal articles describing such goods/services; (E) trade names/providers of competing goods/services; (F) written descriptions/analyses prepared by inventors/assignees of competing goods/services; (G) identification of pending/abandoned applications filed by at least one inventor or assigned to the same assignee that disclose similar subject matter and are not identified in current application; (H) reply to matters raised in a 37 CFR 1.291 protest; (I) explanation of technical material in a publication (including inventor’s publications); (J) identification of changes in reformatted continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b); (K) a mark-up for a continuation-in-part showing added subject matter where there is an intervening reference; (L) comments on a new Federal Circuit decision that appears on point; (M) publication date of an undated document mentioned by applicant that may qualify as printed publication prior art; (N) comments on whether information of record raises derivation issues under 35 U.S.C. 102(f); (O) art related to applicant’s invention/disclosure/claimed subject matter; (P) other factual information pertinent to patentability; (Q) accuracy of the examiner’s stated analysis; (R) clarification/correlation for means-or-steps-plus-function claim support (35 U.S.C. 112); (S) interrogatories or stipulations about claim features/support/meaning/utility/public use facts etc. (specific interrogatory topics 1–9 are listed in the MPEP). These examples are illustrative, not exhaustive.

name: Timing for making a requirement for information (MPEP §704.11(b))
description: A requirement for information is discretionary and may be made when a necessity is recognized; timing affects utility of the response.
guidance: Optimum time is prior to or with the first action on the merits because examiner has maximum opportunity to consider and apply the response; ordinarily do not make a request with or after a final rejection. A requirement may be appropriate prior to first action (e.g., restriction requirement) when search/preliminary analysis shows claimed subject matter cannot be adequately searched by class/keyword or in emerging tech areas with minimal prior art. Factors to consider before a separate requirement prior to first action include: (A) claimed subject matter in newly established art area; (B) whether applicant submitted an IDS; (C) whether specification’s background adequately describes background; (D) whether related documents authored by inventor/assignee not submitted are found during search; (E) whether non-patent literature is referred to but copy not supplied; (F) whether background describes information as known/conventional but unfamiliar to examiner and not findable by search. Requirements may also be made in abandoned applications or patents in proceedings such as revivals, change of inventorship, or reexamination.

name: Objective evidence of nonobviousness and related evidentiary criteria (MPEP §716)
description: Criteria and considerations for objective (secondary) evidence of nonobviousness: nexus, probative value, weighing, and categories of evidence.
guidance: General applicable criteria include: (A) objective evidence of nonobviousness (categories listed), (B) nexus requirement and evidence of nexus between claimed invention and secondary considerations, (C) probative value of objective evidence, and (D) weighing objective evidence in overall obviousness analysis. Specific guidance: evidence must show unexpected results (716.02(a)); burden on applicant to provide such evidence (716.02(b)); examine and weigh evidence of expected results vs allegations of unexpected results (716.02(c)); unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention (716.02(d)); compare with closest prior art (716.02(e)); advantages may be disclosed or inherent (716.02(f)); use appropriate declaration/affidavit form (716.02(g)). Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention (716.03(a)) and derived from the claimed invention (716.03(b)). Other secondary considerations include long-felt need and failure of others, skepticism of experts, copying, inoperability of references, utility/operability of applicant’s disclosure, sufficiency of disclosure, and attribution. See MPEP §716 for tests and weighing guidance.

name: Petitions to expunge information from application file (37 CFR 1.59; MPEP §724.06)
description: Rules and procedure for petitioning to expunge information (other than original disclosure) from the application file under 37 CFR 1.59(b).
guidance: Information forming part of the original disclosure (specification including claims, drawings, preliminary amendments in executed oath/declaration) will not be expunged. An applicant may request expungement of other information by filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.59(b) with required fee (37 CFR 1.17(g)) and establishing to the Director’s satisfaction that expungement is appropriate. The decision on such a petition is typically held in abeyance until allowance, Ex parte Quayle action, or abandonment, at which time a Technology Center Director decides (subject to particular conditions). Expungement is appropriate when petitioner complies with criteria in MPEP §724.05 and the examiner determines the information is not material to patentability. If information was inadvertently submitted, specific factors (MPEP §724.05, II) apply. If petition is granted, expunged material must be retained by petitioner for life of any patent issuing on the application. Form paragraphs 7.204–7.213 provide sample grant/dismissal and specific dismissal reasons, including: lack of fee, information considered material to patentability, information made public, no commitment to retain information, no clear statement that information is trade secret/proprietary/subject to protective order or was unintentionally submitted, unclear identification of information to be expunged, or petition not submitted by/for the party in interest who originally submitted the information.

name: Completeness and clarity of examiner’s action and required content in Office actions (MPEP §707.07 et seq.)
description: Standards for the content and clarity of examiner’s actions (office actions) to ensure proper prosecution and record.
guidance: Examiner should provide complete action on formal matters, require new oath when appropriate, follow draftsperson’s requirements, use proper language when rejecting claims, note all outstanding requirements, and answer all material traversed by applicant. Piecemeal examination should be avoided. Each claim should be mentioned in each office action and the action should state when claims are allowable. Other procedural guidance includes numbering paragraphs, notifying inaccuracies in amendments, reviewer/assistant initialing, signing by authorized examiner, entry and mailing dates, and handling returned office actions. See the MPEP subparagraphs for form paragraph usage and more detailed instructions.

name: Continuation Vulnerability (post-grant marker)
description: Continuation patents drafted to capture later-developed competitor products show higher invalidation rates due to written-description and intervening-rights challenges.
guidance: Inspect continuations for broad claim scope not supported by the original specification and for possible intervening-rights issues; such structural prosecution choices raise invalidation risk.

name: Drafting: Build Multiple Defensible Claim Layers
description: Include independent and dependent claims at multiple levels of generality to preserve fallback positions.
guidance: Craft claim sets with layered scope so that narrower fallback claims remain if broader claims are invalidated; this reduces the chance the entire patent is lost.

name: Drafting: Avoid Functional Claiming Without Structure
description: Functional claiming without structural support invites 112(b) and 112(f) issues, which are common invalidation grounds.
guidance: Prefer concrete structural disclosure for claimed functions; ensure the specification provides adequate support for functional language or include structural equivalents.

name: Operative Quality Test (assessment checklist)
description: For any issued patent at risk of litigation, ask: How comprehensive was the prior-art universe considered during prosecution? What fraction of likely invalidating art was actually cited? How many substantive office actions did the application receive? Are there continuation-related vulnerabilities (intervening rights, written description, OTDP)? Are independent claims supported by clear specification structure? Is the prosecution history consistent across related applications?
guidance: Use these specific diagnostic questions as a practical scoring checklist; patents scoring high across these items are in the upper tier of the litigated-patent population.

name: Acknowledgment of specific alleged wrongful acts (unauthorized practice and related misconduct)
description: The affidavit details alleged acts including: forming/controlling The Inventors Network; permitting filing/prosecution of over 150 patent applications without involvement of a registered patent practitioner; charging fees representing that a registered practitioner would handle matters; failing to disburse fees to registered practitioners; preparing/signing documents in a registered practitioner's name; providing patent legal services and prosecution without being licensed; misrepresenting himself as a registered practitioner (including participating in telephone conferences with USPTO Examiners).
guidance: These factual allegations function as the operative misconduct claims that the respondent acknowledges awareness of; although respondent did not admit the allegations, he consents that they will be presumed true for reinstatement purposes.

name: ODP determinations when PTA is present
description: When a patent has patent term adjustment (PTA), obviousness-type double patenting (ODP) must be assessed based on the patent's expiration date after PTA has been added.
guidance: Because ODP is applied after adding PTA, a later-expiring patent with PTA may cause ODP against earlier family members. Terminal disclaimers can overcome ODP only if filed before the implicated patent expires. Practitioners should analyze family expiration dates and claim similarity when some family members have PTA and weigh the tradeoffs of filing terminal disclaimers (reduced term versus risk of future ODP).

name: Enablement requirement and undue experimentation (Amgen and Wands)
description: Claims that cover a broad genus (e.g., "all antibodies" performing a function) must be enabled across the full claim scope without requiring undue experimentation; the Wands factors remain the framework for assessing undue experimentation, and Amgen's guidance was reaffirmed by the CAFC.
guidance: If the specification only discloses a small number of exemplars while claiming millions of possible candidates, that disclosure may be insufficient. Patent drafters should disclose structural attributes common to the claimed members or explain why certain screened items meet the claim and others do not so that skilled artisans can make predictions without 'painstaking experimentation.' Relying on routine screening that is effectively trial-and-error risks invalidity for lack of enablement.

name: Pre‑AIA public use bar elements
description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), the public use bar is triggered when, before the critical date, the invention is (1) in public use and (2) ready for patenting.
guidance: The 'in public use' element is satisfied if the invention was publicly accessible or commercially exploited by the inventor; mere display at a public commercial event without confidentiality can qualify even if the public did not physically handle the device. The 'ready for patenting' element may be established by reduction to practice before the critical date or by enabling documentation describing the claimed invention. Practitioners should be alert to disclosures at industry events and ensure appropriate confidentiality or timing to avoid triggering the bar.

name: Translation requirement for abstract/text in drawings (Rule 26.3ter(a))
description: If the abstract or text matter in the drawings is in a language different from the language of the description and claims, the RO will invite the applicant to furnish a translation of the abstract or drawing text into the language in which the application is to be published.
guidance: No invitation if the abstract/text in the drawings is already in the publication language, or if a translation of the application is required for other reasons and will already be in the publication language.

name: Procedure when description and claims are not in a single language (Rules 12.3(c)-(e), 26.3ter(e))
description: The PCT requires description and claims to be filed in a language accepted by the receiving Office; if they are not in a single language but all languages used are accepted by the RO, the RO will invite the applicant to furnish a translation to provide description and claims in a single language within one month from receipt.
guidance: The single language must (i) be one of the languages used as filed; (ii) be accepted by the ISA that will carry out the search; and (iii) be the language of publication. The RO may refrain from inviting a translation if multiple languages assist comprehension (e.g., language-neutral terms, certain technical terms, citations, or translation-technology inventions). If the three criteria cannot be satisfied, the RO invites the applicant to furnish a translation under Rule 12.3 or 12.4. Time limits and late fees apply as described elsewhere.

name: Request must be in a language of publication accepted for filing the request (Rules 12.1(c), 26.3ter(c))
description: Whatever the language of the description and claims, the request must always be filed in a language of publication accepted by the receiving Office for filing the request.
guidance: If the request is not in such a language, the RO invites the applicant to file a complying translation.

name: Defects consisting of missing or erroneously filed parts (Article 14(2) / Rule 20.5 series)
description: If parts of the description, claims, drawings or parts thereof are missing or appear erroneously filed, the RO notifies the applicant and invites correction or confirmation of incorporation by reference. The time limit for furnishing missing parts or correct elements is two months from the date of invitation.
guidance: If missing parts or correct elements are furnished within the time limit, the date of their receipt becomes the international filing date unless incorporation by reference is confirmed and retains earlier date. If missing drawings referred to are not furnished within the time limit, references to drawings are considered non-existent and the original filing date remains.

name: Permitting incorporation by reference of missing/correct elements (Rule 4.18, 20.6)
description: Missing or correct elements or parts may be incorporated by reference into the international application where the missing/ correct element is completely contained in an earlier application of which priority is claimed as of the date when one or more Article 11(1)(iii) elements were first received by the RO.
guidance: Incorporation by reference will have the effect that the incorporated elements are considered received on the earlier date (so the international filing date can be retained), subject to compatibility notifications by ROs under Rule 20.8. If incorporation is needed after filing, applicant may request transmission to the IB as RO under Rule 19.4(a)(iii) which accepts incorporation by reference.

name: Requirements for the statement and confirmation of incorporation by reference (Rule 4.18, 20.6)
description: A statement of incorporation by reference must have been included in the international application on the date when one or more Article 11(1)(iii) elements were first received (Form PCT/RO/101 includes it automatically). If the statement was not contained in the request at filing, it can only be added if it was otherwise contained in or submitted with the application at filing. One or several priority claims that completely contain the missing/correct element must have been made at filing; adding such priority claims later is insufficient.
guidance: The applicant must confirm incorporation by written notice to the RO within the applicable time limit and attach: the sheet(s) embodying the entire element/part as contained in the earlier application; a copy of the earlier application if Rule 17.1 requirements not complied with; any required translations; and, for missing/correct parts, an indication where the part is in the earlier application and translations.

name: Defects that do not influence the international filing date (Article 14(1), Rule 26 series)
description: Certain defects do not affect the accorded international filing date and the RO will invite correction: (i) application not signed (or lacks seal where applicable); (ii) applicant name not presented in prescribed way (other than specified exceptions); (iii) no title; (iv) no abstract; (v) physical requirements non-compliance to the extent necessary for reasonably uniform publication; (vi) any element other than description and claims not in an admitted language.
guidance: RO invites correction with a two-month time limit; if corrected within the time limit (including any extension), the international filing date remains the original date; otherwise the application is considered withdrawn. Note some Offices have notified incompatibility with Rule 26.3ter(a) so all elements may need to comply with language requirements before a filing date is accorded at those Offices.

name: Reissue for defective or insufficient specification (Act of 1836 §13)
description: When a patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective or insufficient description or specification, or by reason of claiming more than the inventor had a right to claim as new, if the error arose by inadvertence, mistake, or accident and without fraudulent intention, the Commissioner may, upon surrender and payment, issue a new patent for the residue of the unexpired term in accordance with the corrected description.
guidance: Statutory procedure: surrender the patent, pay the fee (historically $15), and the Commissioner may issue new letters for the same invention for the unexpired period. The statute also contemplates adding subsequently-invented improvements by similar proceedings (and may require disclaimers or specification alterations per the Commissioner's decision).

name: Disclaimer for inadvertent overbroad claim
description: Specifications may be amended by filing a disclaimer when, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, the original claim was too broad (claiming more than the patentee was the original inventor of), provided some material and substantial part of the thing patented is truly the patentee's own.
guidance: A disclaimer may be filed in the Patent Office by the patentee, administrator, executors, or assigns, of the whole or of a sectional interest; the disclaimer will be thereafter taken and considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest and by those claiming under him subsequent to record.

name: Concepts relating to organizing or analyzing information analogous to human mental work
description: Claims that organize, analyze, or translate information in ways that mirror human mental activity (even if aided by computers) are abstract when the claim could be performed mentally or with routine tools.
guidance: Examples: Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics (translating a functional description into hardware component description), Content Extraction (data collection, recognition, and storage analogous to human review and record-keeping), FairWarning (collecting and analyzing access logs to detect misuse). Courts have rejected arguments that computer processing of bit streams alone avoids abstraction when the claimed steps are those humans have long performed.

name: Concepts relating to a mathematical relationship or formula (specific formulas)
description: Claims relying on a specific mathematical relationship or formula (e.g., Arrhenius equation for cure time) are judicial exceptions and can be non-statutory subject matter.
guidance: Example: Diamond v. Diehr noted that a mathematical formula is an exception (non-statutory) like a scientific principle or natural phenomenon. The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions have repeatedly treated specific formulas or algorithmic relationships as falling within the abstract-idea exception unless the claim contains inventive application.

name: Concepts relating to performing mathematical calculations (manipulating data)
description: Claims that amount to performing mathematical computations, manipulating numerical data, or organizing information through mathematical correlations are abstract ideas.
guidance: Examples: Bancorp (calculations/manipulation in life insurance policy valuation), Digitech (manipulating existing information using mathematical formulas to create new organized data). Courts look to whether claimed computations are merely mathematical operations or whether they are applied in an inventive manner tied to a specific technological improvement.

name: Company liability for goods damaged in transit
description: Our responsibility ceases when delivery is made to Carrier and Clear Receipt delivered to us. We do not guarantee delivery or make delivered price, but we allow freight at Tariff rate on Actual Weight; hence we are not responsible for errors, overcharges, shortage or damage to stock in transit.
guidance: Company will assist customers in collecting freight claims when possible provided damage is noted on freight receipt.

name: Examiner duty under 37 CFR 1.809(a): determine need and acceptability of deposit
description: The examiner shall determine pursuant to § 1.104 in each application for patent, reissue, or reexamination whether a deposit is needed, and if needed, whether a deposit actually made is acceptable for patent purposes.
guidance: If a deposit is needed and has not been made or replaced/supplemented according to regulations, the examiner, where appropriate, shall reject the affected claims under the appropriate provision of 35 U.S.C. 112, explaining why a deposit is needed and/or why a deposit actually made cannot be accepted.

name: Rejection ground: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — enablement when deposit needed
description: Rejection for lack of an enabling disclosure without access to a specific biological material where a person skilled in the art could not make or use the invention as claimed without access to the specific biological material.
guidance: The rejection should be accompanied by evidence of scientific reasoning supporting that conclusion (see MPEP § 2164.06(a)).

name: Rejection ground: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — written description when deposit absent
description: A rejection for lack of written description may arise where the application as filed does not contain a description to support an amendment to the specification or claims, or where amendment to claims/other application parts is not described in the application as filed.
guidance: Such situations may also give rise to objections under 35 U.S.C. 132 (new matter) and a requirement that the amendment be canceled. See MPEP § 2163 et seq.

name: Rejection ground: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — indefiniteness as applied to deposit issues
description: A rejection for indefiniteness may be applied where terms in the claims and/or scope of the invention are unclear because of an incomplete or inaccurate description or absence of reference to a biological material.
guidance: Examiner must provide reasons why claim terms are unclear due to deposit-related disclosure deficiencies.

name: Rejection ground: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) — claims must set forth what inventor regards as the invention
description: A rejection that claims do not set forth the subject matter that the inventor regards as the invention requires citation of evidence (not in the application as filed) supporting the rejection; disagreements between disclosure and claim scope should be addressed under 112(a).
guidance: Cite precedents (e.g., In re Prater, In re Ehrreich) when applicable.

name: Use of sequence identifiers (SEQ ID NO:) when referencing sequences in description/claims/drawings
description: Where the description or claims discuss a sequence set forth in the Sequence Listing XML, reference must be made to the sequence by use of the sequence identifier (preceded by 'SEQ ID NO:' or the like) in the text of the description or claims. For sequences in drawings, reference must be made by sequence identifier either in the drawing or in the Brief Description of the Drawings where correlation is clear.
guidance: Sequence identifiers in the disclosure must correspond to those in the Sequence Listing XML. Identifiers permit shorthand references (e.g., 'residues 14 to 243 of SEQ ID NO:23') and do not alter 35 U.S.C. 112 requirements; they merely permit discussion and claiming without re-enumerating the sequence.

name: Written description requirement for filing date
description: An application is entitled to a filing date only if it contains something that can be construed as a written description (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
guidance: If the application does not contain anything that can be construed as a written description, OPAP will mail a Notice of Incomplete Application indicating the application lacks the specification required by 35 U.S.C. 112. Applicant may (A) file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) with evidence to establish prior receipt, (B) submit the omitted specification (including at least one claim) with an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.63/1.64 and accept that submission date as the filing date, or (C) submit an amendment under 37 CFR 1.57(a). Petitions must be accompanied by sufficient evidence (37 CFR 1.181(b)) such as a date-stamped postcard receipt (MPEP § 503). The 2-month period for response (where applicable) is not extendable under 37 CFR 1.136.

name: Drawing requirement for filing date (35 U.S.C. 113)
description: An applicant must furnish a drawing where necessary for the understanding of the subject matter sought to be patented (35 U.S.C. 113, first sentence); an application is entitled to a filing date only if it contains at least one drawing figure when a drawing is necessary.
guidance: Applications filed without drawings are inspected to determine whether a drawing is referred to in the specification and whether a drawing is necessary for understanding the invention. The Office has practiced that process/method claims and many composition applications usually do not require drawings for a filing date. Specific situations where drawings are usually not necessary include: (A) coated articles/products where invention resides solely in coating unless structural details involved; (B) articles made from a particular material/composition unless structural details involved; (C) laminated structures limited to layer order unless significant structure/arrangement involved; and (D) articles/apparatus/systems distinguished solely by the presence of a particular material (examples given). If a TC determines drawings are necessary under 35 U.S.C. 113, the filing-date issue will be reconsidered and application returned to OPAP for mailing of a Notice of Incomplete Application.

name: Notice of Incomplete Application — procedures and applicant options
description: When an application lacks required content (e.g., written description, claim, or required drawing), OPAP will mail a "Notice of Incomplete Application" indicating no filing date has been granted and setting a period for applicant response.
guidance: Applicant options typically include: (A) filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) (with petition fee per 37 CFR 1.17(f)) asserting the missing item was submitted or that deposited papers contain an adequate written description, with sufficient evidence (37 CFR 1.181(b)); (B) submitting the omitted material (specification, claim, or drawings) accompanied by an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.63/1.64 referring to the submission and accepting the submission date as the filing date; or (C) submitting an amendment under 37 CFR 1.57(a). Petitions/filings must comply with the cited CFR provisions. The 2-month period specified is not extendable under 37 CFR 1.136.

name: Notice of Omitted Item(s) — when filing date accorded but figures missing
description: If an application is filed without all drawing figures referred to in the specification but contains something that can be construed as a written description, at least one drawing (if necessary under 35 U.S.C. 113), and at least one claim, OPAP will mail a "Notice of Omitted Item(s)" indicating the papers have been accorded a filing date but are lacking some drawing figures.
guidance: The "Notice of Omitted Item(s)" permits the applicant to: (A) within 2 months file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) with evidence establishing prior receipt of the drawing(s) (petition fee refundable if drawing(s) was received); (B) within 2 months submit the omitted drawing(s) in a nonprovisional application with an oath/declaration referencing the drawing(s) plus a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 requesting the later filing date (2-month period not extendable); or (C) accept the application as deposited by failing to file such petitions within 2 months (constructive acceptance), but must then amend the specification to cancel references to omitted drawings, renumber drawing figures via replacement sheets under 37 CFR 1.121(d), and correct references to drawing figures in the specification to correspond to any relabeled figures. Any petitions under 37 CFR 1.53(e) or 1.182 filed after the 2-month period may be dismissed as untimely (37 CFR 1.181(f)). The manual advises applicants to consider filing a new application as a cost-effective alternative to requesting a later filing date by petition, and notes that petitions under 1.182 will not be granted for provisional applications (applicants should file a new provisional instead).

name: Strict 2-month deadline for petitions regarding omitted items
description: Petitions under 37 CFR 1.181(f) or related provisions claiming prior receipt or requesting an alternate filing date in response to a Notice of Omitted Item(s) or Notice of Incomplete Application generally must be filed within the 2-month period specified in the notice; the 2-month period is not extendable under 37 CFR 1.136.
guidance: The USPTO may strictly adhere to the 2-month period and dismiss as untimely any petition not filed within the period. Strict adherence is justified because applications forwarded for examination at the end of the 2-month period or because according a later filing date may affect patent term and related rights. Applicants should consider filing a new application if appropriate rather than relying on late petitions.

name: Procedures when application located in a Technology Center (TC)
description: If an application located in a TC was filed without required pages or drawing figures and OPAP has not mailed a notice, the examiner should review the application to determine whether it is entitled to a filing date (i.e., contains something that can be construed as a written description, at least one drawing figure if necessary, and at least one claim).
guidance: If entitled to a filing date, the examiner should notify applicant in the next Office action and require the applicant to: (A) accept the application as filed without omitted pages/figures; (B) file omitted pages/figures with an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.63/1.64 and a petition under 37 CFR 1.182 requesting the submission date as filing date; or (C) file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) alleging that the omitted pages/figures were deposited with the application and include supporting evidence. Petitions filed in accord with items (B) or (C) should be filed with the TC which will match the petition to the file and forward to the Office of Petitions with a brief explanation. If the examiner determines the application is NOT entitled to a filing date, the examiner should forward the application to OPAP for mailing of a Notice of Incomplete Application.

name: Petition and evidence standards for establishing prior receipt
description: Petitions asserting that an omitted item (specification pages, drawing(s), or claims) was in fact deposited with the USPTO must be accompanied by sufficient evidence to establish entitlement to the requested filing date (37 CFR 1.181(b) and (f)).
guidance: Acceptable evidence examples include a date-stamped postcard receipt (MPEP § 503) or other documentation establishing prior receipt. Petition fees per 37 CFR 1.17(f) apply; petition fee will be refunded if it is determined the item was in fact received with the application papers deposited on filing. Failure to file within the 2-month period may result in dismissal as untimely.

name: Claims' form matters: information-focused vs chemical-composition-focused claims
description: Claims expressed in terms of genetic information (the informational content of DNA) are different from claims expressed in terms of chemical composition; the former may render isolation insufficient for patent eligibility.
guidance: If a claim focuses on the information encoded in DNA rather than on a novel chemical composition, courts will scrutinize whether the claim effectively covers the natural phenomenon itself. Myriad's claims focused on genetic information, undermining the argument that chemical changes from isolation made the claimed molecules patentable.

name: Chemical alteration/severing bonds is relevant but not dispositive
description: Severing covalent bonds (chemical alteration) when isolating DNA may be considered but is not necessarily sufficient to render the isolated material patent eligible.
guidance: Federal Circuit judges disagreed: some treated chemical alteration (cleaving covalent bonds) as creating a new molecule and thus dispositive; others rejected bond-breaking as 'magic' that creates a new product. Courts will analyze both the structural/chemical differences and whether claims depend on those differences.

name: Mayo two-step / inventive concept requirement
description: Under Mayo, after identifying a law of nature, courts look for an 'inventive concept'—an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent on the natural law itself.
guidance: If a claim recites a natural law plus only conventional, routine, or well-understood steps, it may fail §101. Courts ask whether the additional claim elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.

name: Machine-or-transformation test is not the sole test for process patentability
description: The machine-or-transformation test (tie to a particular machine or transformation of an article) is not the exclusive test to determine whether a claimed process is patent-eligible under §101.
guidance: Bilski rejected the machine-or-transformation test as the sole test; courts should use it as a useful clue but not as definitive. Process claims must still be analyzed for whether they claim an abstract idea, natural law, or application.

name: Computer functions recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
description: Courts have recognized certain computer functions as well‑understood, routine, and conventional when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra‑solution activity.
guidance: Representative examples (with case citations): (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (Symantec; TLI Communications; OIP Techs; buySAFE), (ii) performing repetitive calculations (Flook; Bancorp Services), (iii) electronic recordkeeping (Alice; Ultramercial), (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory (Versata; OIP Techs), (v) scanning/extracting data from documents (Content Extraction; OCR), and (vi) web browser back/forward functionality (Internet Patent Corp.). Note the listing is not exhaustive and does not imply that all computer functions or any generic computer implementation are necessarily conventional or ineligible — see DDR Holdings, Amdocs, BASCOM for distinctions where generic components in combination provided a technical improvement.

name: Laboratory techniques recognized as well‑understood, routine, conventional
description: In the life sciences, certain laboratory techniques have been recognized by courts as well‑understood, routine, and conventional when recited generically.
guidance: Representative examples (with case citations): determining a biomarker level in blood (Mayo; Cleveland Clinic), using PCR to amplify/detect DNA (Genetic Techs; Ariosa/Sequenom), detecting DNA/enzymes in a sample (Sequenom; Cleveland Clinic), immunizing a patient (Classen), analyzing DNA for sequence or allelic variants (Genetic Techs), freezing and thawing cells (Rapid Litigation Mgmt.), amplifying/sequencing nucleic acids (University of Utah v. Ambry), and hybridizing a gene probe (Ambry). When claimed merely at a high level, these techniques may be conventional or insignificant extra‑solution activity for eligibility purposes.

name: Other activities courts have found well‑understood or conventional
description: Courts have identified additional nontechnical activities as well‑understood, routine, or conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner.
guidance: Representative examples (with case citations): recording a customer's order (Apple v. Ameranth), shuffling/dealing a standard deck of cards (In re Smith), restricting public access by requiring viewing an advertisement (Ultramercial), presenting offers and gathering statistics (OIP Techs), determining an estimated outcome and setting a price (OIP Techs), and arranging/sorting information and determining price (Versata). These may be conventional or mere extra‑solution activity depending on claim specifics.

name: Rationale: teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art
description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention may support obviousness.
guidance: TSM is an acceptable rationale but should not be applied rigidly. KSR recognized TSM as a helpful insight and not inconsistent with Graham. See MPEP §2143 and related discussion.

name: Applicant's reply duty under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
