guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references; failure to distinctly and specifically point out errors may render applicant's response substantively inadequate.

name: Types of rebuttal evidence showing nonobviousness
description: Applicants may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods; (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the same functions they perform separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
guidance: Office must reconsider obviousness determinations in light of such evidence; examples illustrate how claims to combinations can be rebutted.

name: Burden to show 35 U.S.C. 103(c) conditions
description: An applicant who wants to avail of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) benefits has the burden of establishing that subject matter used in a 103 rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: For joint research agreement (JRA) protections (post-Dec. 10, 2004), applicant must show: (A) claimed invention made by/on behalf of parties to a JRA in effect on or before the invention date; (B) invention made as a result of activities within the scope of the JRA; (C) application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA. See MPEP §706.02(l).

name: Reference must be analogous art to be used in a 103 rejection
description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, it must be analogous prior art — either (1) from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor.
guidance: Examiner must determine analogous art (Bigio, KSR). 'Reasonably pertinent' requires the reference would have 'logically [] have commended itself to an inventor's attention' (In re Icon/Clay). Examiner should consider the problem as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support the determination.

name: Differences must be analyzed with the claimed invention 'as a whole'
description: The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
guidance: Interpret claim language and consider invention and prior art references as a whole (see MPEP §2111-§2116.01 and cases such as Stratoflex and In re Hirao). Do not ignore unobvious sub-combinations or previously admitted unobvious steps.

name: Do not distill invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' ignoring claim limitations
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the 'as a whole' requirement and improperly narrows or alters claim scope.
guidance: Avoid focusing only on a conceptual gist that omits express claim limitations; cases (W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb) illustrate that disregarding express limitations can lead to improper obviousness findings.

name: Abstract idea that is not computer- or network-specific remains abstract
description: If the claimed idea is not specifically tied to computer or network technology, courts treat it as abstract even if implemented on computers or networks.
guidance: Examples: presenting product iterations was held 'not computer or network specific'; an address directory and many business methods were 'neither novel nor specific to interactive television systems' yet implemented on generic computers. Applying an abstract idea to the Internet or web-based applications does not alone make it non-abstract.

name: Lack of inventive concept when claim elements are generic computer components
description: Claims lack an inventive concept if they merely recite generic computer hardware or software to perform conventional steps.
guidance: Numerous cases hold that reciting a 'processor, memory device, and computing device,' or 'sending a message over the internet,' or 'generic computer components' does not supply an inventive concept. Courts reject claims that 'merely employ generic hardware and software' or do not place meaningful limitations on hardware or software.

name: Claims not tied to a particular machine or specific technical implementation lack inventive concept
description: A claim that is not tied to a particular machine or does not describe specific hardware/software techniques is more likely to lack an inventive concept.
guidance: Courts noted that inventions 'not tied to a particular machine' or that 'do not recite how' functions are performed 'in a manner that generates [technical] data' fail to provide an inventive concept. Attempts to imply specific hardware from the specification without explicit tying have been found insufficient.

name: Human-performable tasks or processes that can be done mentally indicate abstractness
description: If the claim describes tasks that humans could perform mentally or in the human realm, courts treat the claimed subject matter as abstract.
guidance: Example holdings: digital matching processes that can be performed by humans confirmed abstractness; claims that 'can be performed by humans rather than computers' support finding an abstract idea.

name: Need for specific technical description of how steps are performed
description: A specification/claim that explains how steps are technically performed or claims an improvement in the means of performing the steps supports eligibility.
guidance: Courts criticized patents that 'do not disclose any technical description of how the steps in the process take place' or 'do not recite any improvement to technology.' By contrast, claims that disclosed 'innovative technology' (e.g., using engine frequency to measure run time) or solved a technological flaw were treated as eligible.

name: Concrete, tangible instruments or physical components can transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter
description: Claims directed to concrete physical devices or components that utilize specific techniques can be 'significantly more' than mere abstract concepts.
guidance: Example: infusion pump battery gauge and medication level controller claims were held not to be abstract because they were 'concrete, tangible instrument[s]' using a sampling detection technique and provided dynamic automatic adjustment, which went beyond mere calculation or improved speed/efficiency.

name: Claims that provide a technological improvement or solve a problem rooted in computer technology may be eligible
description: If the claimed invention addresses a technological problem and provides a concrete technological improvement (not merely a business or abstract solution), courts may find patent eligibility.
guidance: Examples: a judge found claims overcoming 'the inability to remotely install software on-demand without pre-installation' to supply inventive concept; claims that 'address specific problems and provided the necessary technological improvements' were held not directed to an abstract idea.

name: Claims that merely recite conventional activities like receipt, storage, processing, or data collection are likely abstract
description: High-level recitations of receipt, storage, processing, gathering, labeling, and delivering data are treated as abstract and lacking inventive concept when implemented with generic technology.
guidance: Several holdings labeled claims as abstract where they covered 'receipt, storage, and processing,' 'collecting and organizing information,' 'gathering and labeling information,' 'collecting delivery information,' 'sending and storing messages,' and similar conventional data-management activities.

name: Claims that lack meaningful limitations on hardware/software are generic
description: If claims do not meaningfully limit or specify hardware or software, they are treated as generic implementations and lack an inventive concept.
guidance: Court language: 'no meaningful limitations are placed on any of the hardware or software' supports ineligibility. Bare recitals of commonplace components without specifics were repeatedly rejected.

name: Claims must recite a novel and ordered combination of existing elements to show inventive concept
description: A mere aggregation of known elements will not provide an inventive concept unless the elements are combined in a novel, non-routine, and meaningful way that imposes limitations beyond the abstract idea.
guidance: Example: claims 'did not recite a novel and ordered combination of existing elements' and were therefore held ineligible. Courts look for an inventive interplay or particular arrangement that yields a technological improvement.

name: Benefits asserted in briefs but not recited in the claims do not support eligibility
description: Claims are judged by their actual recitations, not by hypothetical or asserted benefits not included in claim language.
guidance: Examples: a patentee's claim of large-scale tracking benefits or privacy advantages that were not recited in the claims were disregarded in the eligibility analysis.

name: Use of conventional third-party intermediaries or commonplace authentication techniques is abstract when implemented generically
description: Using a third party or a random time-sensitive code for authentication is treated as an abstract concept if nothing in the claims renders the implementation unconventional or technological.
guidance: Example holdings described claims as 'using a third party and a random, time-sensitive code to confirm identity' and concluded lack of inventive concept because they were implemented with generic computer components.

name: Claims that enable routine business or organizational tasks simply by digitization are abstract
description: Converting conventional business practices, organizational tasks, or administrative processes into a computerized form without inventive technological changes yields ineligibility.
guidance: Examples: membership discount programs, check financing systems, trucking manifests, and administering tests were held abstract when merely implemented on computers or networks with routine components.

name: Claims that describe novel technical measurement techniques or sensing tied to physical parameters may be eligible
description: Innovative uses of physical measurements or sensing (e.g., using engine frequency to measure run time, sampling detection techniques) that materially change how a device functions can supply an inventive concept.
guidance: Court examples: remote monitoring of fleet vehicles using engine frequency and certain imaging/sensing claims were found to involve 'innovative technology' or concrete techniques that support eligibility.

name: Claims that are premature to judge for inventive concept prior to claim construction or factual development
description: In some circumstances, courts decline to resolve inventive-concept issues at early stages (e.g., pre-claim-construction) because factual development may be necessary.
guidance: The page notes instances where courts sustained objections or found the inventive-concept determination premature, indicating eligibility analysis can depend on claim construction and factual record.

name: No concealment via obscure terms or misleading statements
description: A specification using obscure terms for the sake of concealment, or making misleading statements (e.g., claiming a preference for a material while concealing that no other will answer), is bad.
guidance: Avoid intentionally opaque language or misstatements that would induce belief that elaborate processes are necessary when simple ones suffice; such conduct misleads the public and risks invalidity.

name: Drawings as part of the specification
description: Where the nature of the case admits of drawings, the statute directs the patentee to accompany the specification with drawings and written references; drawings annexed constitute part of the specification and may be used to explain or help out an otherwise imperfect written description.
guidance: A specification may be partly in writing and partly in drawing; the combination must enable a skilled mechanic to perform the work and show what is claimed. Written description need not always reference the drawing explicitly if both together enable understanding.

name: Statutory protection for inadvertent overclaiming (§9 of 1837 act) and cost limitations
description: If a patentee by mistake claimed as original what he was not the original inventor of, the patent is deemed valid for so much as is truly and bona fide his own; the patentee may maintain suit for that part, but to recover costs he must have entered at the Patent Office a disclaimer of the part claimed without right and must not have unreasonably neglected to do so.
guidance: This provides a remedy rather than an outright invalidation for inadvertent overclaiming, but imposes procedural requirements (disclaimer filing) to obtain full benefits like costs. Courts will bar costs if disclaimer not timely filed.

name: Policy objective — prevent evergreening; require significant efficacy enhancement
description: Section 3(d) was enacted and interpreted to prevent 'evergreening' (repetitive patenting/extension of monopoly) by allowing only derivatives of known substances that demonstrate significantly enhanced efficacy to be patentable.
guidance: This policy frame distinguishes between impermissible attempts to extend patents through trivial modifications and permissible incremental innovation that yields meaningful therapeutic improvements. Drafting and prosecution strategies should therefore focus on claiming and evidencing genuine efficacy improvements.

name: Section 3(d) sets a 'second tier' of qualifying standards for chemical/pharmaceutical products
description: As described by the Supreme Court, the amended portion of Section 3(d) 'clearly sets up a second tier of qualifying standards for chemical substances/pharmaceutical products' to admit genuine inventions while checking spurious extensions.
guidance: For chemical and pharmaceutical claims, practitioners must meet both the general patentability requirements (e.g., novelty, inventive step where applicable) and the additional Section 3(d)-specific requirement that derivatives show enhanced efficacy where the statute or explanation applies.

name: Consequences of non-identical claims after merger
description: If an amendment to make the claims the same in each file is required by the merger decision but is not timely submitted, any claim that does not contain identical text in all merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 2, as indefinite.
guidance: Failure to place identical text in all files may trigger 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 2 rejections for indefiniteness (failing to particularly point out the invention).

name: Treatment of Federal Court decisions known at time of request determination
description: If a Federal Court decision on the merits is known to the examiner at the time the determination on the request for inter partes reexamination is made, the examiner follows guidelines: the existence of a final court decision does not necessarily preclude a substantial new question; the Office will make its determination independently of the court's decision except a final holding of invalidity/unenforceability is controlling.
guidance: The Office may accord deference to factual findings by the court but will make its own determination of SNQ (substantial new question). Non-final holdings are not controlling. Only a final holding (after all appeals) of invalidity/unenforceability will preclude a SNQ as to the claims held invalid or unenforceable (Ethicon v. Quigg).

name: Special rules when third-party requester was a party to prior litigation
description: When the third-party requester was a party to the prior litigation, the provisions of 37 CFR 1.907(b) apply: a final decision adverse to the requester as to claim validity precludes that party (and privies) from requesting inter partes reexamination on issues raised or that could have been raised in the civil action.
guidance: Examiner must determine: (1) was the decision adverse to requester as to at least one claim; (2) was the decision final after all appeals; (3) is the issue in the reexamination request the same or could have been raised in the civil action. If all three are yes for all claims requested, the reexamination prosecution must be terminated and CRU Director will vacate the proceeding. If yes for some claims, those claims will not be treated and reasons noted in examiner’s action. If questions (1) or (3) are no for all claims, examination proceeds.

name: Effects of final court holding of invalidity vs validity
description: A final holding of claim invalidity or unenforceability (after all appeals) is controlling on the Office; reexamination of those claims will continue until decision becomes final and then the claims held invalid/unenforceable will be withdrawn from consideration. Conversely, a final holding upholding validity where requester was a party may require discontinuance for affected claims under 37 CFR 1.907(b).
guidance: If all claims being examined are finally held invalid, CRU Director will vacate the reexamination as not containing a substantial new question. If a final holding upholds validity and 1.907(b) applies to all claims, the order to reexamine is vacated and reexamination terminated. Non-final court decisions have no binding effect.

name: Benefit of earlier filing date; specific reference rules
description: A request for a CPA is a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120 to every application assigned the application number identified in the request; 37 CFR 1.78(a)(2) provides that a request for a CPA is the specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120 to the prior application.
guidance: No further amendment to the specification of the CPA nor a reference in the CPA’s application data sheet is required by 35 U.S.C. 120 or 37 CFR 1.78(a) to identify or reference the prior application. Where an application claims a benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of a chain of applications, the application must reference the first (earliest) application and every intermediate application. In a chain of CPAs, each CPA by operation of 37 CFR 1.53(d)(7) contains the required specific reference to its immediate prior application and every other application assigned that application number. Any amendment to the specification or ADS attempting to add such a reference will not be entered; use form paragraph 2.34 to notify applicant.

name: Particulars of breaches — statutory requirement and amendability
description: By Patents Act 1883 s.29 the plaintiff must deliver particulars of the breaches with his statement of claim (or later by order); particulars may be amended by leave of the Court or judge and further/better particulars may be required if insufficient.
guidance: Particulars are sufficient if, together with the pleadings, they give the defendant full and fair notice of the case (Needham v. Oxley); the Court may order pointing to pages/lines of specification when necessary.

name: Pointing to specification pages/lines where required
description: Plaintiff may be ordered to point out by reference to pages and lines the parts of specification alleged to be infringed, but this is not required when the infringing articles are exhibits or when particulars and claims already enable defendant to know what he will have to meet.
guidance: Court exercises discretion based on what suffices to give clear notice (Lamb v. The Nottingham Manufacturers' Co.; Batley v. Kynock; Cheetham v. Oldham).

name: State-court jurisdiction for contract disputes under patents
description: But where the controversy at issue does not turn upon the letters-patent themselves, but rather upon the force of some contract under them, e.g. an assignment or license, which acknowledges their validity, in such cases the jurisdiction appertains ... to the State courts, and can only be brought into the United States courts on some other ground, e.g. that of citizenship or residence.
guidance: Disputes that are essentially contract claims (specific performance, breach of license) that implicitly accept patent validity belong in state courts unless another federal ground (diversity, federal question separate from validity) exists; litigants should frame or plead issues accordingly to obtain or avoid federal jurisdiction.

name: Equitable relief for interfering patents (act of 1836): scope of relief
description: The act of 1836 made provision for suits by bill in equity to declare void either of two interfering patents, or an existing patent where a subsequent applicant claimed the invention on the ground of priority ... The court was empowered, in the case of two interfering patents, to declare either of them void, in the whole or in part, or invalid or inoperative in any part or portion of the United States, according to the interest which the parties to the suit might possess in the inventions patented.
guidance: In interference suits courts can adjudicate priority and may partially or wholly void patents or limit their operation geographically or by claim; relief is tailored to parties' interests and the scope of the interference.

name: Operative identification checklist for issued patents
description: Practical steps to evaluate an issued patent using examiner signals: identify the examiner (name, art unit); collect examiner tenure and patent count; measure allowance rate vs art-unit median; measure litigation-upheld rate; examine examiner prior-art search pattern (cited art breadth).
guidance: Use this checklist as a standard workflow when performing patent-level quality assessment or valuation: combine these examiner-level signals with claim and prior-art characteristics in a validity/valuation model.

name: Timely SNQ determination (three-month requirement)
description: Within three months after the filing date of a request for supplemental examination, the Office will determine whether a substantial new question of patentability (SNQ) affecting any claim of the patent is raised by any of the items of information presented in the request.
guidance: The determination will generally be limited to a review of the item(s) of information identified in the request as applied to the identified claim(s) of the patent. The determination will be based on the claims in effect at the time of the determination and will become a part of the official record of the patent.

name: Reasons document must explain why each item does or does not raise an SNQ
description: For each item of information, the reasons document should explain whether the item, as presented in the request, raises an SNQ and identify the claims affected, or explain why the item does not raise an SNQ and identify the claims not affected.
guidance: Include: (1) statement that the item raises an SNQ and identification of claims; (2) where appropriate, statement that the item does not raise an SNQ and identification of claims; (3) a brief statement of the basis for the determination. Use form paragraphs 28.02 (no SNQ) and 28.03 (SNQ) as templates.

name: When an item raises an SNQ – required explanatory elements (A–E)
description: Where an item of information is determined to raise an SNQ, the reasons document should point out: (A) that the item raises an SNQ affecting specific claims; (B) the specific claim limitation(s) affected; (C) what the teaching(s) are and where in the item the teaching(s) are found; (D) why a reasonable examiner would consider the teaching(s) important to patentability of the specific claim(s); and (E) where appropriate, whether the item is prior art to specific patent claims and reasons why.
guidance: List the specific claims affected, recite specific claim limitations implicated, cite the exact portion of the item that discloses the teachings, explain the importance to a reasonable examiner, and discuss prior art status (issue/publication dates) and rationale when applicable.

name: When an item does not raise an SNQ – recommended explanatory elements (optional C–F)
description: For each item determined not to raise an SNQ, the reasons document should state that the item does not raise an SNQ affecting specific claims and recite the specific claim limitation(s) discussed; it may optionally include what the teachings are and where found; why a reasonable examiner would not consider them important (e.g., cumulative or not important); whether the item is available as prior art and reasons; and, if not prior art, a statement that the item does not raise any other issues of patentability.
guidance: When explaining why an item is not important, include reasons such as cumulativeness to previously considered teachings or that the teaching was previously considered. If an item is not deemed prior art, explain why and explicitly state it does not raise issues under 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, or 112 when applicable (example: foreign search report). Use form paragraph 28.02.

name: Identify claims for which SNQ is (or is not) raised with granularity
description: If an item raises an SNQ for some but not all claims to which the item was applied, the reasons document should identify those claims for which an SNQ was not raised and briefly state the basis for that determination.
guidance: If the SNQ is raised for an independent claim, it may serve as the basis for dependent claims that incorporate the independent claim's subject matter, provided the dependent claims were also requested to be examined. Form paragraph examples illustrate partial-claim findings (e.g., SNQ for claims 1–5 but not 6–10).

name: Only one SNQ need be identified per identified claim
description: For each identified claim, the examiner need only identify one SNQ (e.g., a teaching that would be important to a reasonable examiner when determining patentability).
guidance: The examiner may rely upon a single identified SNQ as the basis for the determination for that claim; no need to enumerate multiple alternative SNQs for the same claim.

name: Requests limited to correction of factual information must be supported
description: Where the request includes an item limited to the correction of factual information, the request should also include one or more additional item(s) of information (e.g., intervening references) that potentially provide evidence that patentability of the claims depends upon the factual information to be corrected.
guidance: If correction-only items are provided without additional supporting items, the examiner should explain that the correction does not raise an SNQ because no items were included that show patentability depends on the corrected fact. Examples illustrate scenarios with intervening references and how to explain whether the intervening reference raises an SNQ depending on whether the domestic benefit is corrected or deleted.

name: Processing, issuance, and public availability of certificate and reasons document
description: After preparation, the Supplemental Examination Certificate and reasons document are referred to the CRU Legal Instrument Examiner for clerical processing; they are made of record in the electronic file, copies mailed to the patent owner, and the certificate is electronically issued and viewable in Patent Center within three months of filing.
guidance: The electronically issued certificate will display the filing date, list each properly submitted item, state whether an SNQ affecting at least one claim is raised, and remain part of the public record. The reasons document will be labeled 'Reasons for SNQ Determination' in IFW and generally available at or shortly after the certificate issuance.

name: Supplemental examination concluding act — electronic publication
description: Supplemental examination is concluded by the electronic publication of the certificate; the Office procedure after publication depends on whether the Office determines an SNQ affecting at least one claim is raised in the request.
guidance: If an SNQ is raised, ex parte reexamination will be ordered; if not, the certificate will be published and refund rules applied. The certificate remains in the public record and may be published as an attachment to the patent.

name: PTAB/IPR and Parallel USPTO Proceedings
description: Impact of PTAB post-grant proceedings (IPR/PGR) on district-court patent litigation, including institution standards and interplay with co-pending litigation.
guidance: IPR institution requires a threshold 'reasonable likelihood' that the petition will succeed in whole or in part. The PTAB’s discretionary denial practice uses 'Fintiv factors' when litigation is co-pending (stay likelihood, proximity of trial date, overlap of issues, investment in district proceedings, party identity, and other circumstances). Historically ~60–70% of instituted IPRs resulted in invalidation of all claims at trial (2016–2019). Post-grant review (PGR) is rarer and may include broader issues (101, 112). IPRs can produce stays in district court and substantially affect venue attractiveness.

name: Machine infringement test — performs same service/effect in same way
description: A machine will be infringed by a machine which incorporates in its structure and operation the substance of the invention; that is, by an arrangement of mechanism, which performs the same service, or produces the same effect in the same way, or substantially in the same way.
guidance: Compare mode of operation and the substance of the claimed invention (Wyeth v. Stone example). Minor differences (e.g., double vs single series of cutters) may be immaterial if the substance and mode are substantially the same.

name: Improvement patents limited to the improvement; cannot claim prior inventions
description: If another person invents an improvement on such a machine, he can entitle himself to a patent for such improvement only, and does not thereby acquire a right to patent and use the original machine; and if he does procure a patent for the whole of such a machine with the improvement, and not for the improvement only, his patent is too broad, and therefore void.
guidance: An improver may obtain exclusivity for his improvement but cannot lawfully use the original inventor's discovery without license. The law awards exclusive property to each discovery but prevents one from invading the other's rights (examples: Read v. Perkins discussion).

name: Patents claiming application of a principle — focus on substantial identity of application
description: Wherever the real subject covered by the patent is the application of a principle, in arts or manufactures, the question, on an infringement, will be as to the substantial identity of the principle, and of the application of the principle.
guidance: Means, machinery, forms, or modifications of matter are material only so far as they affect the identity of the application of the principle. First form a clear idea of the object of the patent and what the specification properly points out as the patentee's claim (intro to §229–230).

name: Joint research agreement exception (Section 102(b)(3))
description: Subject matter and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment for purposes of paragraph (2) if— (i) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the effective filing date; (ii) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (iii) the application for patent for the claimed invention discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. 'Joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
guidance: Specifies conditions under which collaborative research negates certain prior‑art effects by treating the earlier subject matter and the claimed invention as commonly owned.

name: Patents and published applications effectively filed (Section 102(b)(4))
description: A patent or application for patent is effectively filed with respect to any subject matter described in the patent or application— (A) as of the filing date of the patent or application; or (B) if entitled to claim priority/benefit under specified sections, as of the filing date of the earliest such application that describes the subject matter.
guidance: Defines when a patent or application counts as 'effectively filed' for prior art comparisons (important for determining novelty and priority).

name: Derivation proceeding initiation requirements (Section 135(a)(1))
description: An applicant may request initiation of a derivation proceeding by filing a request that sets forth with particularity the basis for finding that another applicant derived the claimed invention and, without authorization, filed an application claiming such invention. Any such request— (i) may only be made within 12 months after the earlier of (I) the date on which a patent is issued containing a claim that is the same or substantially the same as the claimed invention; or (II) the date of first publication of an application containing such a claim; and (ii) must be made under oath, and must be supported by substantial evidence.
guidance: Establishes strict timing (12‑month) and evidentiary/oath requirements for initiating derivation proceedings to resolve disputes over who has the right to a patent.

name: PTAB determination and effect of final decision in derivation proceedings (Section 135(a)(2) & (4))
description: In any proceeding under this subsection, the Patent Trial and Appeal Board shall determine the question of the right to patent; in appropriate circumstances may correct the naming of the inventor; and shall issue a final decision on the right to patent. The final decision of the Board, if adverse to the claim of an applicant, shall constitute the final refusal by the PTO on the claims involved. The Director may issue a patent to an applicant who is determined by the Board to have the right to a patent. The final decision of the Board, if adverse to a patentee, shall, if no appeal or other review has been or can be taken, constitute cancellation of the claims involved, and notice of such cancellation shall be endorsed on copies of the patent distributed after such cancellation by the PTO.
guidance: Specifies the PTAB's authority to resolve derivation disputes, correct inventorship, issue final decisions that affect issuance and cancellation of claims, and the administrative effects of adverse determinations.

name: Box III — Non-establishment of opinion on novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability
description: Box No. III covers situations where claims are so unclear or inadequately supported by the description that questions of novelty, inventive step (nonobviousness), and industrial applicability cannot be considered, or where the claims relate to subject matter for which it is not required to establish a written opinion, or where no international search report has been established for the claims.
guidance: If some or all claims fall into these categories, check appropriate boxes, indicate which claim(s), and specify reasons (e.g., improper multiple dependent claims failing PCT Rule 6.4). If a ST.26-compliant sequence listing is required and not available or late fees unpaid, indicate that specific reason.

name: Box IV — Lack of unity of invention (notification and markings)
description: Box No. IV notifies applicant that lack of unity has been found. Mark item 1 and one of the four boxes under item 1 to indicate specifics (e.g., additional fees paid under protest, search based on first mentioned invention, etc.). Item 2 is used when unity lacking but no invitation to agree to a limited search or pay fees is issued. Item 3 can point to reasons set out in the ISR rather than repeat them. Item 4 indicates which parts of the application form the basis of the opinion after explaining lack of unity.
guidance: Because ISA/US does not require a protest fee, certain boxes will not be checked. When lack of unity exists, identify relevant claims/parts and, if applicable, whether additional fees were paid and whether the search was limited to the first-mentioned invention.

name: Box V — Reasoned statement re: Novelty, Inventive Step, Industrial Applicability
description: In Box No. V the examiner must list in summary form all claims with regard to novelty (N), inventive step (IS), and industrial applicability (IA). All claims without fatal defects are treated on the merits in Box No. V as to these criteria. Examiner statements can be positive or negative; positive statements should indicate how claims meet the tests; negative statements must provide specific reasons.
guidance: Do not use words 'rejection', 'patentability', or 'allowable' in a written opinion. Use the provided form paragraphs (18.04, 18.04.01, 18.01, 18.02, 18.02.01, 18.02.02, 18.03) to structure positive/negative statements and ensure completeness and clarity of reasoning.

name: Box VII — Certain defects in the international application (form/content defects)
description: Box No. VII identifies defects in form and content of the international application (e.g., misplaced/omitted drawing numerals, misspelled words, grammatical errors). Use form paragraphs such as 18.08 (drawing defects), 18.08.01 (drawing required), 18.09 (description defects), 18.10 (claims defects).
guidance: Specify the technical deficiency in the bracketed insertion fields. Use the appropriate form paragraph for the type of defect and be specific about the defect(s).

name: Box VIII — Observations on clarity/support/drawings (substantive objections)
description: Box No. VIII notifies applicant of observations as to clarity of claims, description, drawings, or on whether claims are fully supported by the description. If claims are so unclear or inadequately supported that no meaningful opinion can be formed, inform applicant in Box III. Otherwise, treat observations as objections in Box VIII (not rejections) and provide reasons.
guidance: When lack of clarity is limited to certain claims apply PCT Article 34(4)(a)(ii) to those claims only. Use substantive objection form paragraphs (e.g., 18.11, 18.12.01, 18.13.01, 18.14.01, 18.15) to explain objections and required reasons.

name: Claims Objectionable — Lack of Best Mode (Form para 18.14.01)
description: ¶ 18.14.01: 'Claim [1] objected to under PCT Article 6 because the claim [2] not fully supported by the description. The description fails to set forth the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the claimed invention as required by PCT Rule 5.1(a)(v) because: [3].'
guidance: Insert claim numbers, appropriate verbs, and explain why best mode not disclosed. Provide concrete examples of missing best mode information.

name: Claims Objectionable — Indefiniteness (Form para 18.15)
description: ¶ 18.15: 'Claim [1] objected to under PCT Article 6 as lacking clarity because claim [2] indefinite for the following reason(s): [3]'
guidance: Specify which claims and precisely why indefinite. Use clear technical reasons rather than conclusory language.

name: Claims Objectionable — Inadequate Written Description (Form para 18.12.01)
description: ¶ 18.12.01: 'Claim [1] objected to under PCT Article 6 because the claim [2] not fully supported by the description. The application, as originally filed, did not describe: [3]'
guidance: Identify subject matter not described in the application as filed; insert claim numbers and be specific about missing elements.

name: Claims Objectionable — Non-enabling Disclosure (Form para 18.13.01)
description: ¶ 18.13.01: 'Claim [1] objected to under PCT Article 6 because the claim [2] not fully supported by the description. The description does not disclose the claimed invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the claimed invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art as required by PCT Article 5 because: [3]'
guidance: Insert claim numbers and explain why the disclosure is non-enabling, providing technical reasons and examples.

name: Sequence listings requirement under WIPO Standard ST.26 (format & placement)
description: Patent applications that disclose nucleotide and/or amino acid sequences as defined in WIPO Standard ST.26 must present each sequence and associated sequence data in a standardized electronic XML format as a separate part of the specification. The sequence listing part must be an electronic file in WIPO ST.26 XML format. Sequences included in the sequence listing are not required to also appear in the main part of the description. In the description, claims or drawings, sequences shall be referred to by the sequence identifier preceded by 'SEQ ID NO:'.
guidance: It is advisable to submit a ST.26-compliant XML sequence listing together with the international application on the filing date rather than wait for an invitation. See MPEP §§2412–2419 for details.

name: Effect of traversing only linking claim nonallowance
description: An election of a single invention combined with a traverse of only the nonallowance of the linking claims is an agreement with the Office that restriction is proper if the linking claim is not allowable and improper if it is allowable.
guidance: If the Office allows the linking claim, it is bound to withdraw the restriction requirement and act on all linked inventions which depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of the allowable linking claim. But once all linking claims are canceled 37 CFR 1.144 would not apply since the record would be one of agreement as to the propriety of restriction.

name: Nonelected claims withdrawn from further consideration (37 CFR 1.142(b))
description: All claims that the examiner holds as not being directed to the elected subject matter are withdrawn from further consideration by the examiner in accordance with 37 CFR 1.142(b).
guidance: The examiner should clearly set forth in the Office action the reasons why the claims withdrawn from consideration are not readable on the elected invention. Applicant may traverse the requirement pursuant to 37 CFR 1.143 and may file a petition under 37 CFR 1.144 if a final restriction is made.

name: If examiner withdraws restriction after reconsideration, must specify rejoined groups and act on merits
description: If the examiner, upon reconsideration, is of the opinion the requirement is improper in whole or in part, he or she should clearly state in the next Office action that the requirement for restriction is withdrawn in whole or in part, specify which groups have been rejoined, and give an action on the merits of all the claims directed to the elected invention and any invention rejoined with the elected invention.
guidance: Form paragraphs such as 8.45, 8.46, 8.50, etc., are used to notify applicant of rejoinings and the specific claims rejoined; the examiner must act on the merits of rejoined claims.

name: Rejoinder eligibility requires dependence on all limitations of an allowable claim
description: In order to be eligible for rejoinder, a claim to a nonelected invention must depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim. A withdrawn claim that does not require all the limitations of an allowable claim will not be rejoined.
guidance: Where restriction was between product and process and the product invention was elected and found allowable, all claims to a non-elected process invention must depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim to be eligible for rejoinder. Applicant should amend nonelected claims during prosecution to require limitations of the elected invention to retain right to rejoinder.

name: Withdrawal of restriction removes 35 U.S.C. 121 protection and may create double patenting risk
description: In view of the withdrawal of the restriction requirement, the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 121 are no longer applicable. Any claim presented in a continuation or divisional application that is anticipated by, or rendered obvious over, claims of the parent application may be subject to a double patenting rejection when the restriction requirement is withdrawn.
guidance: Cite In re Ziegler and MPEP § 804.01. Examiner should advise applicant when rejoin occurs that continuation or divisional claims including limitations of an allowable claim may be subject to provisional statutory and/or nonstatutory double patenting rejections over the instant application.

name: Timing and entry of amendments relating to rejoined claims
description: An amendment presenting additional claims that depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim will be entered as a matter of right if presented prior to final rejection or allowance, whichever is earlier. Amendments submitted after final rejection are governed by 37 CFR 1.116; amendments after allowance are governed by 37 CFR 1.312.
guidance: If nonelected claim(s) which depended from or required all the limitations of an allowable claim were canceled by applicant, they may be reinstated by timely amendment in reply to the action; upon entry such claims will be examined for patentability under 37 CFR 1.104.

name: Use of specific form paragraphs to communicate election/traverse/rejoin actions
description: The MPEP prescribes specific form paragraphs (e.g., 8.22, 8.25, 8.25.01, 8.25.02, 8.05, 8.03, 8.24, 8.04, 8.26, 8.45, 8.46, 8.49, 8.50) to be used in Office actions to acknowledge elections, traverses, withdrawals, rejoinings, and to instruct applicant on required next actions.
guidance: Form paragraphs include prescribed language for acknowledging election with/without traverse, explaining why claims are withdrawn, advising on cancellation deadlines, notifying of non-responsive amendments, and warning about double patenting consequences; examiners should use the appropriate form paragraph in each factual situation.

name: When nonelected claims do not require all limitations of an allowable claim, explain why they remain withdrawn
description: When no claims directed to the nonelected invention(s) depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim, the examiner should explain why all nonelected claims are withdrawn from further consideration (use form paragraph 8.49).
guidance: The notice should state that the restriction requirement is withdrawn as to any claim that requires all the limitations of an allowable claim and identify the claims that remain withdrawn and the reasons (e.g., they do not all require the limitations of the allowable linking/generic claim).

name: Field of the invention
description: A statement as to the field to which the invention relates.
guidance: Start with a brief paragraph summarising the field, framed as broadly as possible to help readers appreciate the greatest extent of the invention as described and claimed.

name: Statements of invention (summary corresponding to claims)
description: Statements of invention which correspond in scope and content to the claims, including any statements of technical advantages achieved by the invention.
guidance: Include main statements corresponding to each independent claim (reciting essential features) and subsidiary statements corresponding to dependent claims (preferred or optional features). May include statements of advantage and possible variations/modifications. Sometimes a simple reference to the claims is used instead of separate statements.

name: Detailed description / specific examples (non‑limiting)
description: A description of specific examples of the invention, often with reference to any drawings; by convention non‑limiting as to the scope of the claimed invention.
guidance: Provide full technical details so a person skilled in the art is enabled to work the invention across substantially the entire claimed range. Include as many embodiments and practicable variations as possible. Give precise ranges and examples (e.g., showing a working temperature range and best values, and indicating values outside the range that fail) to support breadth and enablement.

name: Claims — format (numbered single‑sentence paragraphs)
description: The claims are a series of numbered paragraphs, each containing a single sentence.
guidance: Claims must be drafted as numbered, single‑sentence paragraphs. Independent and dependent claims form a nested structure; dependent claims usually refer back to earlier claims.

name: Claims — balance between novelty and breadth for independent claims
description: Independent claims must define something that is new and inventive compared with the prior art, yet also define the scope of protection as broadly as possible.
guidance: Independent claims serve two conflicting purposes: be specific enough to distinguish over prior art (possibly requiring added detail during examination) while being as broad as possible to maximise protection. Strike a balance so every feature in an independent claim is essential to the working of the invention.

name: Claims — dependent (subsidiary) claims as fallback and commercial coverage
description: Dependent claims recite preferred or optional features and form narrower, nested claims that provide fallback positions.
guidance: Use dependent claims to anticipate possible prior art, provide fallback positions if independent claims are unpatentable, and to cover expected commercial embodiments. Ensure subsidiary claims cover valuable technical alternatives not captured in the independent claims.

name: Claims — clarity, conciseness, and support
description: The claims must be clear and concise and supported technically by the description.
guidance: Claims must be supported so that the extent of the claimed invention is credible from the description and exemplification. Ensure the invention as defined in the claims is enabled across substantially the entire range of claimed features.

name: Enablement / sufficiency of disclosure
description: The invention must be disclosed in such complete terms that a person of average skill in the art can work the invention in substantially all the claimed areas without undue burden.
guidance: Routine trial and error to a reasonable degree is permissible but the skilled person must not face undue burden due to missing technical information. Counsel can suggest whether a specification might be sufficient but final factual judgment rests with technical experts; inventors should carefully review technical completeness.

name: Client review checklist — claims, objectives, sequences, drawings
description: Specific items applicants should check in a specification prepared by counsel before filing.
guidance: Clients should: verify prior art has been considered; confirm objectives and achievements are accurately stated; ensure the best mode is disclosed; check enablement and that the claims only recite essential features (think what a third party could omit to avoid infringement); flag technical features that could limit claims but still have commercial value and are not covered by dependent claims; ensure sequence listings are correct; and advise on better drawings if available.

name: Explain the 'principle' as the peculiar structure and mode of operation
description: By the principle of a machine ... is to be understood the peculiar structure and mode of operation of such machine; or, as the statute itself explains it, the character by which it may be distinguished from other inventions.
guidance: When invoking a 'principle' in a specification, tie it to a concrete structure and mode of operation so the claim reads as an application embodied in matter rather than an abstract idea.

name: Point out all modes of application claimed, but minute variations need not be described in detail
description: He is to state not only the peculiar device or construction which he deems the best ... but also all the other modes of producing the same effect, which he means to claim as being substantially applications of the same principle. In doing this, it is not necessary for him to enter into a minute description of the mode of producing those variations.
guidance: Indicate variations of application you intend to cover; you need not detail every minor structural variation, but you should indicate what sorts of variations are claimed beyond the preferred embodiment.

name: Do not claim mere abstract principles or laws of nature
description: A patent cannot be taken out solely for an abstract philosophical principle ... The mere discovery of such a principle is not an invention, in the patent law sense of the term.
guidance: If the subject is a scientific principle or law of nature, the specification must show its practical application to a special purpose by incorporation with matter so as to produce a practical result. Without that application, the claim is void. Cases cited: Barrett v. Hall; Househill Co. v. Neilson.

name: Describe some practical mode of carrying the principle into effect
description: It is essential that the specification should describe some practical mode of carrying the principle into effect; and then the subject-matter will be patentable, because it will be, not the principle itself, but the mode of carrying it into effect.
guidance: Provide at least one working embodiment or mechanical contrivance that applies the principle to a specified result so the invention is enabling and patentable; otherwise the claim risks being declared an abstract principle (Wyeth v. Stone example).

name: General claims may cover all forms of apparatus applying the same principle to a specified result
description: If you suggest and invent how [a principle] may be applied to a practical result by mechanical contrivance and apparatus, and show that you are aware that no particular sort or modification or form of the apparatus is essential, then you may take your patent for the mode of carrying the principle into effect ... and you are not under the necessity of describing and confining yourself to one form.
guidance: A broad claim directed to the application of a principle for a specified beneficial result can lawfully embrace multiple apparatus forms (Neilson hot-blast example). The generality of the claim is not per se fatal; it can be a merit, not an objection, provided the patentee has disclosed a practical application.

name: Claims of entire/absolute discovery must account for prior use; qualify as improvement if needed
description: So far, therefore, the application of lime is, in terms claimed as an improvement, and nothing is said of any previous use, of which the use proposed is averred to be an improvement; it is, therefore, in substance, a claim of entire and original discovery ... The recital should have stated, supposing a previous use to be proved in the case, that, 'whereas lime has been in part, but improperly, made use of, &c.' and then a different mode of application and use should have been suggested as the improvement claimed.
guidance: Draft recitals and claims to acknowledge prior uses and frame the invention as an improvement where appropriate; claiming sweeping 'discovery' of an effect when prior use exists can render the patent void.

name: When a combination is claimed, the patent is for the whole combination only
description: A patent for a combination of three things cannot at the same time be a patent for a combination of any two of them. If the subject-matter is the combination of any given number of things ... no portion of the combination less than the whole can be considered at the same time as being also the subject-matter.
guidance: If claiming a combination, be aware that subsets of the combination are not automatically covered as separate claims; if parts are not new, consider whether the claim can be sustained as a combination. Construction and validity depend on factual specifics.

name: Omit nothing material and avoid misleading the public
description: The rule ... requires the patentee so to describe his invention as to enable the public to know what his claim is, it of course imposes upon him the duty of not misleading the public, either by concealing anything material to the invention, or by adding any-
guidance: Do not conceal material elements, and avoid misleading statements or unnecessary verbiage that obscures what is claimed. Failure to disclose essential features is a serious defect; omission of only contributory non-essential details is less likely fatal.

name: Enablement: specification must enable others to apply the principle
description: The patentee must give [the discovery] a practical application to some useful purpose ... and his specification must show the application of the principle to such a special purpose, by its incorporation with matter in such a way as to be in a condition to produce a practical result.
guidance: Enablement requires enough detail for a person skilled in the art to carry the invention into practice and use the claimed principle for the stated purpose; even if best modes are not fully worked out, showing practical application suffices (Watt example).

name: Limit false patent marking damages
description: Limit the ability of a party to recover false patent marking to the amount of the party’s actual competitive injuries.
guidance: This narrows potential treble or statutory damages remedies for false marking claims; weigh deterrence benefits versus risk of excessive damages litigation.

name: Written Description Requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, ¶1)
description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention; this requirement is separate and distinct from enablement and must clearly convey that the applicant had invented the subject matter claimed.
guidance: Policy objectives: (1) demonstrate inventor possession of claimed invention; (2) put the public in possession of the claimed invention. Rejections will be based on substantive law and are appealable. See cited cases (e.g., Vas-Cath, Univ. of Rochester, Capon v. Eshhar).

name: Written Description for Biological Materials and Deposits
description: For biological materials, a deposit in accordance with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may help satisfy written description regarding a claimed material, but a deposit is not a substitute for a written description — the written description of the deposited material should be as complete as possible.
guidance: Deposits support verification and infringement questions but examination proceeds on the written description. Deposits made after filing cannot be relied upon to support additions/corrections except in limited circumstances; see 37 CFR 1.804 and MPEP references.

name: Insufficiency of Purely Functional Claiming (especially biomolecules)
description: An invention described solely in terms of a method of making coupled with its function, without a described or art-recognized correlation between structure and function, normally does not satisfy written description—functional characteristics alone are usually insufficient to identify biomolecule sequences.
guidance: E.g., a biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic without structural correlation is generally inadequate even if a method of obtaining it is provided. Citations: In re Bell, In re Deuel, Eli Lilly discussion.

name: Claim-as-a-Whole Analysis and Claim Construction
description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers; each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the written description.
guidance: Include preamble language and transitional phrase in analysis. Understand 'comprising' (open-ended), 'consisting essentially of' (middle ground), and 'consisting of' (closed). Consider how preamble weight and transitional phrases affect scope. See In re Morris, Genentech v. Chiron, PPG v. Guardian.

name: Evaluate Support for Each Claim Element
description: Review whether sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble; the entire claim must be supported to satisfy written description.
guidance: Absence of definitions or details for well-established terms should not alone trigger a written description rejection. Limitations should not be imported into claims from the specification without support. See Lockwood, Bell Communications Research, Corning Glass.

name: Omission of an Element That Was Described as Essential
description: Omitting matter which the specification describes as essential or critical to the invention may render later-claimed broader subject matter unsupported by the original disclosure.
guidance: If the specification makes clear that a particular understanding of a claim term is essential to the invention, claims that omit that element can fail written description (e.g., Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).

name: Examiner Initial Burden and Applicant's Duty to Point Out Support
description: After a thorough reading the examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasons why a skilled person would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims; applicant should specifically point out where the original disclosure supports any amendments.
guidance: If applicant amends and points out support but the examiner finds it lacking, the examiner must explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as supporting the amendment. See MPEP §§2163.04, 714.02.

name: Methodology for Determining Adequacy — Read and Analyze the Specification
description: Follow structured procedures: read/spec analysis, determine what each claim as a whole covers, review the entire application to find support for each element/step, and consider all possible forms of disclosure (words, drawings, examples, claims).
guidance: Claim construction is essential; evaluate preamble, transitional phrase, and body. Consider whether specification imparts sufficient detail about overall invention and each limitation; the inquiry is case-by-case. See MPEP guidance and cited cases.

name: Genus-Species and 'Laundry List' Disclosures
description: A broad genus claim may not be supported by mere listing of every possible moiety (a 'laundry list') or by a generic disclosure plus a single species if the disclosure would not reasonably lead skilled artisans to the claimed species.
guidance: Examples and caselaw: Fujikawa (laundry list insufficient), In re Ruschig, Purdue Pharma (broad disclosure not necessarily supporting later carved claims).

name: Effect of Transitional Phrases and Preamble on Written Description
description: Transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') and preamble language affect claim scope and thus the written description analysis; the claim as a whole including these parts must be supported.
guidance: 'Comprising' is open-ended; 'consisting essentially of' occupies middle ground and may be treated as comprising for prior art purposes unless specification defines what materially changes the invention. Applicant bears burden to show exclusions under 'consisting essentially of.'

name: Content limitation of 35 U.S.C. 301/37 CFR 1.501 submissions
description: Submissions under 35 U.S.C. 301 and 37 CFR 1.501 are limited to patents, printed publications, and/or patent owner written claim‑scope statements (and accompanying additional information) and an explanation of their pertinence and manner of applying to at least one claim.
guidance: Copies of all cited documents and necessary English translations must be included. Affidavits/declarations may accompany submissions to explain contents or pertinent dates (e.g., commercial success). Submissions cannot include issues not directed to patents/printed publications/written claim scope statements (for example, 35 U.S.C. 112 arguments, public use statements, conduct of the patent owner, or argument about references previously treated in prosecution or reexamination). If a submission contains such prohibited material it should not be entered and should be returned to the sender (see MPEP §2206).

name: Explanation requirement (pertinence and manner of applying)
description: A submission must include an explanation in writing of the pertinence and manner of applying any prior art or written statement to at least one claim of the patent for the submission to become part of the official file (35 U.S.C. 301(b); 37 CFR 1.501(b)).
guidance: The explanation should set forth, for at least one claim, how each cited item shows or teaches at least one limitation of the claim. Patent owners may also include explanations of how the claims differ from submitted prior art. Examples in MPEP show claim‑by‑claim mapping and references to figures/col/lines.

name: Required accompanying materials for written statements
description: Any statement submitted under 35 U.S.C. 301(a)(2) must be accompanied by any other documents, pleadings, or evidence from the proceeding in which the statement was filed that address the written statement (35 U.S.C. 301(c); 37 CFR 1.501(a)(2)).
guidance: Submissions of written statements must identify the forum and proceeding, the specific papers and portions containing the statements, and how each statement is a position on claim scope (37 CFR 1.501(a)(3)). If a submitted written statement or additional information is subject to a protective order, the submission must be redacted to exclude protected information.

name: What the submission must not include (prohibited content examples)
description: Submissions should not include issues not directed to patents, printed publications, or patent owner written claim scope statements and additional information—e.g., statements that claims violate 35 U.S.C. 112, statements about public use, or arguments about the conduct of the patent owner.
guidance: If a submission includes prohibited material it should be returned to the sender and not entered into the patent file even if it otherwise contains acceptable patents/printed publications and explanations (see MPEP §2206).

name: Identification requirements for section 301 written statements
description: A submission that includes section 301 written statements must identify (1) the forum and proceeding where the patent owner filed each statement, (2) the specific papers and portions containing the statements, and (3) how each statement is one in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim in the patent (37 CFR 1.501(a)(3)).
guidance: Identification of portions can be satisfied by citing documents and specific page numbers. Provide information about the status of the proceeding and the relationship of the proceeding to the patent to assist the Office in identifying the claim scope statement.

name: Office consideration limits for written statements
description: A written statement submitted under 35 U.S.C. 301(a)(2), and the additional information under 301(c), shall not be considered by the Office for any purpose other than to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim in a proceeding ordered or instituted pursuant to sections 304, 314, or 324 (35 U.S.C. 301(d)).
guidance: This limits how such statements and accompanying documents may influence Office activity—generally restricted to claim construction in ordered proceedings. Protective‑order redactions apply.

name: Examples and formatting of acceptable submissions
description: MPEP provides sample submission letters (Example I: third party; Example II: patent owner) that show how to list references, map references to specific claims and patent figures/columns/lines, and include a certificate of service.
guidance: Follow examples for structure: identify patent, list references with bibliographic info, explain pertinence to specific claims with citations to figures/cols/lines, sign the submission, and include certificate of service when required.

name: Reexamination of a reexamination (how to consider claims)
description: A request for reexamination filed on a patent for which a reexamination certificate has already issued (a 'reexamination of a reexamination') must be considered based on the claims in the patent as modified by the previously issued reexamination certificate, not the original claims.
guidance: CRU support staff must incorporate certificate changes into the reexamination specification before forwarding to the examiner. Examiners should verify the certificate changes are properly entered. Checklists (PTO‑1516, PTO‑1517) and supervisory reviews are required to ensure compliance.

name: Restrictions on patent owner amendments in reexamination of a reexamination
description: Amendments to claims/specification must treat the reexamination certificate changes as part of the original patent; re‑adding text already in the certificate (e.g., italicized text) as if newly added is improper.
guidance: Improper amendments will be treated as informal submissions; examiners should notify patent owner of defects (Form PTOL‑475) and set a one‑month period for correction. See MPEP §2266.02 for procedures.

name: Essential goal: demonstrate possession
description: The essential goal of the written description requirement is to clearly convey that the applicant had invented the subject matter claimed (i.e., to show possession).
guidance: Use authorities (e.g., In re Barker; Capon v. Eshhar) and emphasize public notice: the patent must describe the technology claimed so the public is put in possession of what is claimed.

name: Specification must describe claimed invention with all limitations
description: An applicant shows possession by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, or formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention (Lockwood).
guidance: Possession may be shown by reduction to practice, drawings, structural formulas, or distinguishing identifying characteristics. Lack of description of essential/critical features may render the claim unsupported.

name: Original claims: strong presumption of adequacy
description: There is a strong presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed (In re Wertheim).
guidance: Rejections of original claims for lack of written description should be rare; examiner has initial burden to present reasons or evidence why a skilled artisan would not recognize support in the disclosure.

name: No in haec verba requirement, but support required
description: There is no requirement that claim language appear verbatim in the specification, but newly added claim limitations must nevertheless be supported by the original specification.
guidance: Support can be through express disclosure, implicit or inherent disclosure; beware of adding subject matter beyond what the original disclosure conveys to skilled artisans.

name: Claim as a whole must be analyzed (claim construction)
description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers and give it its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
guidance: Include preamble and transitional language in the analysis; consider whether preamble language is a structural limitation; interpret transitional phrases (comprising, consisting essentially of, consisting of) per case law and MPEP guidance.

name: Omission of essential/critical feature undermines support
description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential or critical in the specification does not comply with the written description requirement.
guidance: If the specification explicitly indicates a narrow understanding or that a feature is essential, broadening claims to omit that feature can be rejected; such omissions may also raise enablement or definiteness issues.

name: Deposits of biological material are not a substitute for written description
description: A deposit of biological material may assist but is not a substitute for a written description of the claimed invention; written description of the deposited material must be as complete as possible.
guidance: Deposits made under 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. help verification but examination proceeds on written description; later deposits cannot support added matter unless regulatory conditions (e.g., 1.804) are met.

name: Examiner initial burden and applicant response obligations
description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasons why a skilled artisan would not recognize written description support; applicant should point out where the original disclosure supports amendments or claims.
guidance: If applicant points to support and examiner finds disclosure insufficient, examiner must present reasons; rejections should follow a thorough review and be based on substantive law and facts.

name: Claim drafting elements to be mindful of (preamble/transitional/functional language)
description: Preamble language, transitional phrases (comprising/consisting essentially of/consisting of), and functional claim language affect claim scope and written description analysis.
guidance: Interpret 'comprising' as open-ended; 'consisting essentially of' is middle-ground and may be treated as 'comprising' absent specification definition; functional language for software may be satisfied by disclosure of functions (Fonar) but examine whether undue experimentation is required to implement.

name: Standard: disclosure must reasonably convey possession to skilled artisan as of filing date
description: The fundamental factual inquiry is whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date, the applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed (Vas-Cath).
guidance: Use case law and the totality of disclosure (including examples, figures, sequence listings, deposits, and incorporated material) to determine whether possession is conveyed; this is the ultimate test for written description compliance.

name: Extend only specific heads of invention when appropriate
description: Where a patent comprises several heads of invention and only one head seems deserving of prolongation, the prolongation will be granted solely with reference to that head.
guidance: Authorities: Leaver's Patent, Lee's Patent, Napier etc. Practical implication: tailor any extension/new patent to the particular claims/parts meriting protection.

name: Oral_disclosure_and_silence_not_estoppel_without_harm
description: The fact that a patentee explained his invention orally to several persons, without written specification or model, and that another later described and perfected the same thing in the patentee's presence, and the patentee made no claim, does not bar an infringement action; silence works no estoppel unless it has misled another to his injury.
guidance: Courts require evidence that silence actually misled and caused injury before applying estoppel against the inventor.

name: Comprehensiveness of examiner's answer
description: The examiner should furnish each party with a comprehensive examiner's answer that provides a written statement in answer to each appellant brief and each respondent brief, containing a response to the allegations or arguments made in all of the briefs and calling attention to any errors in an appellant's copy of the claims.
guidance: May incorporate from any of the briefs the most accurate and comprehensive information. If a ground of rejection or reason for patentability is not addressed, the proceeding will be remanded by the Board. An answer should include rebuttal of any and all arguments presented in all of the briefs. An examiner should reevaluate positions in light of briefs and expressly withdraw rejections or determinations not adhered to (but reopening prosecution is required if a new ground or new finding is made).

name: Status of Claims
description: A statement of whether the examiner agrees or disagrees with the statement of the status of claims contained in the briefs; if disagreeing, set forth a correct statement of the status of all claims in the proceeding.
guidance: If there is disagreement, explain the area of disagreement and include a correct statement (use form paragraphs referenced). Remember a 'final rejection' is not made in reexamination—use 'Action Closing Prosecution' and 'Right of Appeal Notice' terminology where appropriate.

name: Explanation of rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the examiner's answer must explain how the first paragraph is not complied with, including how the specification and drawings do not describe the subject matter defined by each rejected claim or would not enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the subject matter without undue experimentation.
guidance: Include consideration of undue experimentation factors set forth in MPEP § 2164.01(a).

name: Explanation of rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner's answer must explain how the claims do not particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention.
guidance: Provide specific explanation tied to claim language and what is deficient in definiteness.

name: Explanation of rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, the examiner's answer must explain why the rejected claims are anticipated or not patentable under 35 U.S.C. 102, pointing out where all of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims are found in the prior art relied upon.
guidance: Point to specific locations in the prior art showing each claimed limitation.

name: Explanation of rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
description: For each rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner's answer must (a) state the ground of rejection and point out where each of the specific limitations recited in the rejected claims is found in the prior art relied on, (b) identify the differences between the rejected claims and the prior art relied on (the primary reference), and (c) explain why it would have been obvious at the time of the invention to modify the primary reference to arrive at the claimed subject matter.
guidance: If the proposed rejection is based on a combination of references, explain the rationale for not making the combination (when maintaining patentability) or, if making a rejection, explain why the combination would have been obvious.

name: Feature-by-feature comparison when correspondence unclear (102/103)
description: Where there are questions as to how limitations in the claims correspond to features in the art even after complying with the requirements for 102 and 103 explanations, the examiner must compare at least one of the rejected claims feature-by-feature with the art relied upon in the rejection.
guidance: The comparison should align the language of the claim side-by-side with a reference to the specific page/column/line number/drawing reference number and quotations from the reference as appropriate.
