name: Determinations of Patentability — general explanation
description: For each determination of patentability (i.e., each determination of inapplicability of a proposed rejection), provide a clear explanation of the determination.
guidance: Must address proposed-for-rejection claims and explain why they are not rejected; mirror the structure required for grounds of rejection (e.g., explain compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph, identify which limitations are not found in the art for 102/103, and explain rationale where combinations are involved).

name: Determination of inapplicability for 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph
description: For each determination that a proposed-for-rejection claim is not unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph, the examiner's answer must explain how the first paragraph is complied with, including how the specification and drawings describe the subject matter and would enable a person skilled in the art without undue experimentation.
guidance: Address enablement and written description with reference to specification/disclosure and undue experimentation factors.

name: Determination of inapplicability for 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
description: For each determination that a proposed-for-rejection claim is not unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph, the examiner's answer must explain how the claims do particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter.
guidance: Explain claim language and how it meets definiteness requirements.

name: Determination of inapplicability for 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103
description: For each determination that a proposed-for-rejection claim is not unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103, the examiner's answer must explain why the proposed-for-rejection claims are not anticipated (102) or are patentable over the art relied upon (103), pointing out which limitations are not found and identifying differences.
guidance: If the proposed rejection is based on a combination, explain the rationale for not making the combination; where correspondence is unclear, do a feature-by-feature comparison as required.

name: Select the closest naturally occurring counterpart
description: When comparing a claimed nature-based product to what occurs in nature, examiners should identify and compare the claimed product to the closest naturally occurring counterpart (not to other adjacent or broader natural material).
guidance: Do not confuse the counterpart with other material that may occur naturally with, or adjacent to, the counterpart (e.g., compare an isolated gene to the natural gene, not the whole chromosome). If multiple natural counterparts exist, select the counterpart most closely related to the claimed product based on examiner expertise (e.g., when a cloned animal combines material from two breeds, choose the most closely related breed(s)). For combinations that do not have a natural counterpart mixture, compare to the individual nature-based components (e.g., each bacterial species in a claimed inoculant). See Myriad; Ambry Genetics; Roslin; Funk Bros.; MPEP §2106.04(c), subsection II.C. If a claim is rejected as ineligible, it is a “best practice” for the examiner to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if the record is not already clear.

name: Characteristics compared must be possessed by the claimed product
description: Appropriate characteristics for the markedly-different analysis must be characteristics that are actually possessed by the claimed product, because the claim defines what may be patented.
guidance: Identify characteristics from what is recited in the claim language and from the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the nature-based product. A characteristic may be explicitly recited (e.g., the prefix 'deoxy' in 'deoxyribose' signals removal of a hydroxyl) or may be apparent from the BRI (e.g., nucleotide sequence or encoded protein in a claim to 'isolated gene B'). Unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute to eligibility. See Roslin.

name: Search for an inventive concept (Step 2B) — must be 'significantly more' than the judicial exception
description: After finding a claim directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, natural phenomenon, law of nature), evaluate whether the claim elements add an 'inventive concept' — elements beyond the exception that make the claim as a whole amount to significantly more.
guidance: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable exception itself. It is furnished by an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception and sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception. Evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination; consider all claim elements because an inventive concept may arise from a non-conventional combination. See Alice; Mayo; RecogniCorp; Rapid Litigation; BASCOM.

name: Do not conflate inventive-concept inquiry with novelty or obviousness
description: The search for an inventive concept under §101 is distinct from novelty (§102) and obviousness (§103) inquiries; lack of novelty or obviousness is not dispositive of the §101 inventive-concept analysis.
guidance: Courts have rejected substituting §§102/103/112 inquiries for the §101 eligibility test. Novelty of an element is of no relevance to whether the claim falls within §101 categories; a new abstract idea is still an abstract idea. Patentability under §§102/103 is neither required for nor a guarantee of patent eligibility under §101. See Mayo; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec; Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics; BASCOM discussion.

name: Limitations that courts have found to qualify as 'significantly more'
description: Certain types of claim limitations have been recognized by the courts as qualifying as 'significantly more' when recited with a judicial exception.
guidance: Non-exhaustive list (courts have found these to qualify): (i) improvements to the functioning of a computer (e.g., DDR Holdings); (ii) improvements to another technology or technical field (e.g., Diehr rubber-molding with thermocouple); (iii) applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine arranged in a particular way (e.g., Fourdrinier machine example); (iv) effecting a transformation/reduction of an article to a different state or thing (Diehr); (v) adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (e.g., non-conventional arrangement in BASCOM); (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a technological environment (e.g., an immunization step integrating data-comparison into a specific immunizing process as in Classen). See MPEP §2106.05(a)-(e) and cited cases.

name: Limitations that courts have found not to qualify as 'significantly more'
description: Certain additions or phrasing do not transform a claim directed to a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Non-exhaustive list (courts have found these insufficient): (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality (Alice; BASCOM discussion); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering in conjunction with an exception (CyberSource); (iv) generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (Bilski; Parker v. Flook). See MPEP §2106.05(d),(f),(g),(h) and cited cases.

name: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element is not enough
description: Physical or tangible implementation of a judicial exception (e.g., reciting a computer) is not itself an inventive concept and does not guarantee eligibility.
guidance: The fact that a computer is a tangible machine is beside the point; claiming a computer-configured implementation could allow drafting around §101 if mere physicality sufficed. Eligibility cannot depend on draftsman’s art. Courts emphasize that mere physicality/tangibility does not transform an otherwise ineligible claim into eligible subject matter. See Alice.

name: Quality of visual disclosure (drawings)
description: If the visual disclosure of the claimed design as originally filed is of such poor quality that its overall shape and appearance cannot be understood, applicant should be advised that the claim might be fatally defective (use form paragraph 15.65).
guidance: Advise applicant and consider form paragraph 15.65; poor drawings may make the claim fatally defective because overall shape/appearance cannot be determined.

name: Use of narrative description to supplement drawings
description: A narrative description in the specification can supplement the drawing disclosure to define the scope of protection sought; such description is incorporated into the claim by the use of language 'and described' therein.
guidance: If the description refers to embodiments or modified forms not shown in the drawing, or uses vague/nondescriptive words like 'variations' and 'equivalents', or states the claimed design is not limited to the exact shape and appearance shown, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, as nonenabling and indefinite. Form paragraph 15.21 may be used.

name: Undisclosed visible surfaces/portions not part of claimed design
description: Any part of the article not shown in the drawing or described in the specification forms no part of the claimed design (In re Zahn). Determination of patentability is based on the design shown and described.
guidance: When portions are not shown/described, they are excluded from the claimed design; use appropriate form language to indicate which surfaces/portions are not shown.

name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs) — general
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, when the claimed invention is not described in full, clear, concise and exact terms to enable one skilled in the art to make and use it and when it fails to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter.
guidance: Use form paragraph 15.21 and provide a complete explanation of the basis for the rejection in the Office action (bracket 1). Do not use this form paragraph when separate specific rejections under the first and/or second paragraph are appropriate.

name: Suggestions to overcome 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections
description: Applicant may submit large, clear informal drawings or photographs showing the unclear areas, or disclaim indefinite areas by converting them to broken lines and amending the specification to state those portions form no part of the claimed design.
guidance: Refer to 35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121; identify unclear areas in bracketed instruction. Alternative is to disclaim portions via broken lines and include a statement in the specification that those portions form no part of claimed design.

name: New matter prohibition and antecedent basis
description: New matter is subject matter which has no antecedent basis in the original specification, drawings or claim. An amendment to the claim must have antecedent basis in the original disclosure; otherwise it introduces new matter and must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
guidance: A change in configuration (including removal of three-dimensional surface treatment integral to configuration) introduces prohibited new matter (In re Salmon). Conversion of broken to solid lines or reduction to broken lines may be permissible only if the underlying configuration was fully disclosed and enabling in the original filing.

name: Permissible and impermissible amendments (examples)
description: Permissible amendments include preliminary amendments specifically identified in the original oath/declaration and disclaimers included in the original filing; impermissible amendments include claim changes without antecedent basis that change configuration or surface appearance by adding previously undisclosed matter (In re Berkman).
guidance: Examine whether the amendment departs from the original disclosure; permissible examples and impermissible examples are given in the MPEP. If impermissible, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — indefiniteness analysis
description: Defects in claim language give rise to a second paragraph rejection. Definiteness of claim language must be analyzed in light of prior art teachings and the application disclosure as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art (In re Moore).
guidance: Terms of degree or broad language are not per se indefinite; evaluate each claim in context of the disclosure and prior art (see MPEP § 2173.05(b)). Use appropriate form paragraphs when scope cannot be determined.

name: Use of broadening phrases (e.g., 'or the like')
description: Use of phrases in the claim such as 'or similar article,' 'or the like,' or equivalent terminology has been held indefinite (Ex parte Pappas).
guidance: If such a phrase appears in the claim/title and renders the claim indefinite, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph (form paragraph 15.22.02). However, similar language in the title directed to the environment of the article may not be the basis for rejection; see MPEP § 1503.01 subsection I. Examiner's amendment can remove such phrases (form paragraph 15.69.01).

name: Rejection when scope cannot be determined from drawings/specification
description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, should be made when the scope of protection sought by the claim cannot be determined from the designation of the design as shown in the drawing, referenced in the title and described in the specification.
guidance: Examples include unclear boundaries between claimed (solid lines) and unclaimed (broken lines) portions. Use form paragraph 15.22 and provide full explanation (bracket 1).

name: Title must specify a known article of manufacture
description: The title must identify an article of manufacture; if the title fails to identify a known article and the drawing does not inherently identify it, the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (Ex parte Strijland).
guidance: Attempting to clarify the title may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121). Use form paragraph 15.22.03 when appropriate.

name: Restriction practice under 35 U.S.C. 121 (single claim rule)
description: A design patent application may only have a single claim. More than one embodiment may be protected by a single claim only if they involve a single inventive concept; otherwise restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 when multiple patentably distinct designs are claimed.
guidance: The examiner will require restriction whenever an application contains more than one patentably distinct design. The search/burden issue applicable to utility restrictions (MPEP § 803) is not applicable when determining restriction for design applications.

name: Notice of non-compliance after filing (section 65)
description: After filing, the Office reviews whether required parts have been submitted and will issue a notice under section 65 if required parts (other than sequence listings or drawings) are missing.
guidance: The applicant has three months to respond in good faith to avoid abandonment under subsection 73(2). After required parts are submitted, specification, claims, abstract and drawings are not thoroughly assessed until examination and may receive defect reports then. PCT national phase translation requirements are assessed on national phase entry; notice under subsection 155.5(6) may be issued for missing translations.

name: Reissue for defective or insufficient specification (conditions)
description: Whenever a patent is inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective or insufficient description or specification, or by claiming more than the patentee had right to claim, and the error arose by inadvertency, accident, or mistake without fraudulent intention, the Commissioner may, upon surrender of the patent and payment of fifteen dollars, issue a new patent to the inventor for the same invention for the residue of the unexpired term in accordance with the corrected description and specification.
guidance: Reissue requires surrender of original patent and payment of $15; in case of death or assignment, executors/assignees have similar rights; reissued patent has same legal effect as though originally filed in corrected form.

name: Specific grounds of defense to be pleaded/proved
description: Defendant may rely on proof that the specification does not contain the whole truth, contains more than necessary, concealment/addition intended to deceive, that the patentee was not original inventor or first discoverer of the thing or a substantial part claimed, that it was described in a public work prior, or had been in public use or on sale with patentee's consent prior to application, or that patentee surreptitiously or unjustly obtained the patent.
guidance: If defendant relies on prior invention, knowledge, or use, he must state in his notice the names and places of residence of those he intends to prove possessed prior knowledge and where used; judgment for defendant when such defenses succeed.

name: Adjudication when plaintiff overclaims
description: When plaintiff fails to sustain action because his specification or claim embraces more than he was first inventor of, but defendant used or violated any part truly and justly specified and claimed as new, the court may adjudge costs as just and equitable.
guidance: Court has equitable discretion to apportion costs when partial rights are infringed despite overbroad claims.

name: Recording and re-recording of patents/assignments (pre-Dec 15, 1836)
description: Persons in possession of patents or assignments issued prior to December 15, 1836, may, without charge, present them to the Commissioner to be recorded anew in the Patent Office together with descriptions, specifications, claims, and drawings.
guidance: Commissioner must transcribe/copy into record books; where drawings were not originally annexed, a verified drawing may be transmitted and placed on file or copied; clerks of judicial courts must transmit authenticated copies; certified copies by Commissioner are prima facie evidence when recorded anew.

name: Applications to add newly discovered improvements are reviewed like originals
description: Applications to add a newly discovered improvement to an existing patent, or patents returned for correction/reissue, shall have their specifications and claims subject to revision and restriction in the same manner as original applications; Commissioner will not add the improvement or grant reissue until applicant has entered disclaimer or altered specification/claim per Commissioner's decision.
guidance: Applicant dissatisfied with Commissioner's decision has same remedies and privileges as in original applications.

name: Identify what applicant invented and review the disclosure (Section I)
description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I))
guidance: Use the disclosure to state what applicant invented (example language: 'a graphical user interface for dynamically relocating/rescaling obscured textual information ...'). This informs the analysis of additional elements and inventive concept in later steps. As every claim must be examined individually, use a separate worksheet for each claim. The worksheet use is optional.

name: Step 1 — Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, composition)
description: Does the claimed invention fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter)?
guidance: Choose A or B: A. Yes — continue SME analysis. B. No — make a rejection of the claim as being drawn to non‑statutory subject matter (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If an amendment could render the claim statutory, consider proceeding with the analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record; suggest potential amendments.

name: Step 2A — Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea
description: Identify whether the claim recites a concept similar to judicially identified abstract ideas (e.g., fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, mathematical relationships/formulae). 'A claim is “directed” to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited ... in the claim.'
guidance: Choose A, B, or C: A. No — conclude SME analysis. B. Yes, but streamlined analysis appropriate — eligibility is self‑evident; no full analysis needed (refer to February 2015 Training Slides). C. Yes — identify limitation(s) that recite the abstract idea and explain the similarity to court examples (refer to July 2015 Update Quick Reference Sheet). Provide explanation linking claim limitations to judicial exceptions (e.g., steps that calculate areas and a scaling factor are mathematical relationships/algorithms).

name: Identify claim limitations that correspond to the abstract idea
description: Point to the specific limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe the abstract idea and explain why they are abstract.
guidance: Explicitly identify the limitation text (for example: 'generating first and second data ... calculating a scaling factor proportional to the difference between the first data and the second data'). Explain how these recite mathematical relationships/algorithms or other judicial exceptions, and cite controlling cases (e.g., Benson, Flook, Diehr, Grams) as appropriate.

name: Streamlined analysis option when eligibility is self‑evident
description: Where the eligibility determination is self‑evident and the claim does not attempt to tie up an abstract idea, a full eligibility analysis may not be needed.
guidance: If using streamlined analysis (Step 2A choice B), state why the claim is not focused on the abstract idea and why it does not prevent others from practicing the abstract idea. Refer to February 2015 Training Slides for examples.

name: Evaluate significance of additional elements (search for inventive concept)
description: Consider whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the abstract idea (i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept').
guidance: Reasons that can support significance include one or more of the following: improves another technology/technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state; adds a specific limitation other than what is well‑understood, routine and conventional; adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; adds meaningful limitations beyond merely linking to a technological environment. Anti‑patterns: generic computer performing generic functions, merely adding the words 'apply it', appending well‑understood/routine/conventional activities at a high level, adding insignificant extrasolution activity (mere data gathering).

name: Consider claim preamble and 'computer‑implemented' limitations when construing scope
description: Treat computer‑implemented limitations (e.g., 'the computer', references in preamble) as giving 'life, meaning and vitality' to the preamble when appropriate (see MPEP 2111.02).
guidance: A preamble that is given weight can further limit the claim and may be relevant to whether additional elements amount to significantly more. However, simply stating 'computer‑implemented' or 'by the computer' is often akin to adding the words 'apply it' to a claim and may not be sufficient.

name: Conclude eligibility or issue § 101 rejection with articulated reasoning
description: If additional elements amount to significantly more, conclude SME analysis and continue with examination. If not, make a § 101 rejection.
guidance: If concluding ineligibility, use sample rejection language (examples provided), use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015, and clearly articulate why the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more. The examiner's burden is met by clearly articulating the reasons why the claimed invention is not eligible. Although factual evidence is not required for a prima facie rejection, examiners are encouraged to cite any additional resources that support their rejections.

name: Suggest possible claim amendments to confer eligibility
description: Identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to the claim that may make it eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant.
guidance: Provide concrete suggested claim elements or point to example claims in the application that demonstrate how added limitations produced eligibility (e.g., see Example 23 claim 4). Document such suggestions in the Office action record when appropriate.

name: Use of form paragraphs and recordkeeping guidance
description: When issuing rejections or following assumptions (e.g., assuming claim amended to fall within statutory category), use the specified form paragraphs and make the assumptions clear in the record.
guidance: References in the worksheet: use Form Paragraphs 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.015 available in Custom OACs for § 101 rejections or notices. If proceeding under an assumption that an amendment makes the claim statutory, state the assumption in the record and consider suggesting potential amendments to applicant.

name: Exclusion of laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas
description: ‘Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas’ are not patentable subject matter under §101.
guidance: Examples: a new mineral or plant, Einstein’s E=mc2, Newton’s law of gravity. The Court cites prior cases (Diehr, Chakrabarty, Benson, Funk Brothers) emphasizing that these are 'basic tools of scientific and technological work' and cannot be monopolized by patent. Use this exclusion as a threshold inquiry when claims recite such subject matter.

name: Requirement of additional features providing 'practical assurance' (inventive concept)
description: Claims that recite a law of nature must include additional features that provide practical assurance the claims are genuine applications rather than drafting efforts designed to monopolize the law.
guidance: These 'additional features' (sometimes called an 'inventive concept') can be elements or a combination that integrate the law into a patent-eligible application (as in Diehr). They must be more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity and must add something significant beyond the natural law itself.

name: Ordered combination must add significance beyond parts
description: Considering the claim steps as an ordered combination is insufficient if the combination adds nothing to the law of nature that is not already present when the steps are considered separately.
guidance: Diehr succeeded because the equation was integrated into a process that was not merely routine; by contrast, claims whose combined steps amount to nothing more than instructions to apply the law fail (the Mayo claim’s administering, determining, and wherein steps added nothing significant together).

name: Transformation/reduction-of-an-article is a clue for processes without specific machines
description: Transformation and reduction of an article 'to a different state or thing' can be a clue to patentability for a process claim that does not include particular machines.
guidance: Historical precedent (Cochrane/Deener, Benson) treats transformation as a useful indicator. But such transformations are irrelevant if they merely pick out a preexisting audience or can be satisfied without a meaningful transformation (e.g., administering a drug merely picks out doctors; blood analysis might be performed without transforming blood in some future method).

name: Claim steps that instruct to measure by any means are routine and insufficient
description: A 'determining' step that tells practitioners to measure a quantity 'through whatever process the practitioner wishes to use'—when measurement methods were well known—is routine and does not add inventive concept.
guidance: Where the patent concedes that methods for making the determination were well known, that step is treated as conventional/pre-solution activity (Mayo’s measuring metabolite levels).

name: Meritorious claims and use of legal procedure (§ 11.301)
description: Practitioner must present well-grounded positions and has a duty to use legal procedure for the fullest benefit of the client's cause, but not to abuse legal procedure; corresponds to ABA Model Rule 3.1, with USPTO deletion of certain criminal-law-specific language.
guidance: Prohibits frivolous claims or contentions; USPTO excludes ABA's criminal-defense-specific phrasing about requiring every element be established because it is limited to criminal practice.

name: Statutory ("Same Invention") Double Patenting
description: Where the same invention is claimed in two patents/applications.
guidance: Statutory double patenting cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer.

name: Nonstatutory ("Obviousness-Type") Double Patenting
description: Where claims are not patentably distinct from claims in another commonly owned patent/application (a judicial doctrine).
guidance: This type of double patenting can be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer that meets regulatory requirements.

name: Public Policy Rationale for Nonstatutory Double Patenting
description: The nonstatutory-type rejection is grounded in public policy and primarily intended to prevent prolongation of the patent term by prohibiting claims in a second patent not patentably distinct from claims in a first patent.
guidance: Also intended to prevent harassment by multiple assignees of patents covering essentially the same invention; these policy goals inform application of the doctrine.

name: Examples of fact patterns supporting discretionary denial
description: Representative fact patterns that weigh against referral (support denial).
guidance: Examples provided: unfair dealings when inventors advocate for unpatentability of their own patent (e.g., Tessell, Inc. v. Nutanix, Inc.); settled expectations based on length of time patent in force when petitioner provides no persuasive reasoning why IPR is appropriate (e.g., Dabico Airport Sols. v. AXA Power ApS); non‑exclusive examples that rebut a patent owner’s settled‑expectation claim (e.g., change in law or a patent that has not been commercialized).

name: PCT national phase entry requirements — fees, copy, translation
description: To enter the PCT national phase within 30 months: Fees — pay basic national fee and all annual maintenance fees for anniversary dates before national phase entry; Copy if not published by WIPO — provide a copy of the patent application (RO/101 part of application); Translation — if description and claims entirely in a language other than English or French (other than sequence listing), submit a translation into English or French.
guidance: Applicants should consult the PCT Applicant’s Guide and Canadian National Chapter for further details and guidance.

name: Reinstatement of rights for national phase entry (requirements)
description: If an international application does not enter national phase in Canada within 30 months, the applicant has 12 months after that to reinstate rights under subsection 154(3). Requirements: request reinstatement of rights; provide a statement that the failure was unintentional; pay fees (basic national fee, fee for reinstatement, and all annual maintenance fees for anniversaries before national entry).
guidance: If the international application is unpublished at national entry, provide a copy (RO/101 part). If description/claims entirely in a language other than English/French, submit translations.

name: Notice requiring translation of complete copy (three-month compliance)
description: If applicant does not provide a translation of the abstract or Article 4 PCT request (RO/101), or does not provide a complete copy of description, claims, text in drawings, or language-dependent free text in sequence listing, the Commissioner may by notice require the complete translation no later than three months after the date of the notice.
guidance: Failure to comply with the notice will result in the application being deemed abandoned under subsection 132(1)(h) of the Patent Rules.

name: Applicant‑attributable periods (what counts as applicant delay)
description: The period 'attributable to an act or omission of the applicant' includes numerous specific delays (without prejudice to generality), such as: the time to pay filing fees, time to make required observations, time to file earlier‑application documents, time to file claims, time to respond to formal requirements or invitations to amend, time to request and pay for search/examination/reports, time to respond to written opinions, time to apply for reviews, time to satisfy grant fee conditions, time to enter national phase, time to rectify failures to comply, and any extensions granted on applicant request.
guidance: A long detailed list (items a through u) enumerates typical applicant delays used to exclude from Registrar delay calculations; includes periods for prosecution actions, responses, and corrections.

name: Documentary certificate for marketing approval dates
description: The applicant should submit to the Registrar a certificate from the relevant authority stating the date the application for marketing approval was filed, the date marketing approval was obtained, and for each period attributable to an act or omission of the applicant for marketing approval the dates on which such periods started and ended.
guidance: This certificate supports pharmaceutical‑ground extension claims (Rule 51A(9)).

name: Application procedure for amendment after grant
description: To amend the specification after grant the proprietor may file Patents Form 17 together with supporting documents setting out reasons for amendments.
guidance: From 1 Apr 2017 both marked‑up amendments and clean copies of amended sheets are required; from 1 Dec 2019, if claims amended, a marked‑up and clean copy of the full set of claims must be submitted; amendments should be based on latest specification on record.

name: Prior patent publication vs unpublished patent for novelty
description: A published patent places all that it claims and discloses into the prior art relevant to the novelty determination, whereas an unpublished patent places only the material actually claimed into the prior art.
guidance: Material in a published patent counts to the extent it adequately describes the invention (i.e., enables one of ordinary skill in the field to make and understand the invention).

name: Graham framework — scope and content of the prior art
description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention.
guidance: Prior art includes the invention's own art and logically related arts (e.g., related manufacturing or material arts). Content generally includes items defined in §102 (printed publications, patents, prior US use/knowledge, earlier-filed US applications, another’s US-made invention not abandoned/suppressed/ concealed).

name: Graham framework — differences between prior art and claims
description: Determine the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
guidance: Do not mislead by examining only differences and treating them as the invention; the claimed subject matter must be considered as a whole in the §103 inquiry.

name: Avoiding hindsight in obviousness determinations
description: Decisionmakers must avoid hindsight reconstruction — using the claimed invention as a template to piece together teachings in separate prior art pieces.
guidance: Consider the totality of evidence and take the perspective of the hypothetical person of ordinary skill at the relevant time.

name: RPS may file DJ action if Applicant does not provide l(2)(A) (l)(9)(C))
description: If the Applicant does not provide the (l)(2)(A) application and information, the RPS may file a DJ action for any patent that claims Applicant's product or its use. (42 U.S.C. § 262(l)(9)(C))
guidance: Failure to make the initial statutory disclosure opens broader options for RPS to seek declaratory relief on patents claiming the product or its use.

name: Interest not payable absent express contractual or statutory authorization
description: Except where payment of interest is expressly stipulated by contract or specifically authorized by an act of Congress, the United States is not bound to pay interest on claims prior to rendition of judgment.
guidance: Authorities cited: multiple Comptroller opinions and the act of Mar. 3, 1911 reenacting 'No interest shall be allowed ... unless upon a contract expressly stipulating for the payment of interest.' Practical guidance: do not expect interest payments unless contract/statute allows.

name: Possible narrow exception for marine torts and Congressional appropriation practice
description: Although the general rule is nonliability, an exception has been recognized in some opinions for marine torts; even so, claims for marine torts are often not enforceable against the United States and are customarily referred to Congress for appropriation.
guidance: The Comptroller noted doubt about authorization to liquidate marine torts and that practice has been to refer such claims to Congress. Cite: XIII Comp. Dec. 349 and historical practice.

name: Teaching away does not automatically defeat an anticipation or obviousness rejection—specific evidence required
description: A reference's teaching away (e.g., showing an embodiment is less than optimal) does not vitiate the fact that it is disclosed and can still anticipate or render obvious the claimed invention (Celeritas; Merck; Gurley).
guidance: When an applicant argues that a reference teaches away, evaluate whether the reference contains explicit criticism/discouragement or whether there is additional discovery beyond the prior art. The mere showing that an embodiment is suboptimal or inferior does not remove it from consideration as prior art. Refer to MPEP §§2131.05 (anticipation) and 2145 (obviousness) for more detailed treatment of teaching away in each legal context.

name: Disclaimer form and effects
description: A disclaimer of parts of a patent must be in writing, attested by one or more witnesses, recorded in the Patent Office on payment of ten dollars, and thereafter is taken as part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest.
guidance: The disclaimer is effective as part of the original specification for claim scope of the disclaimant and those deriving under him; it does not affect any action pending at the time of filing except insofar as relates to unreasonable neglect or delay in filing the disclaimer.

name: Revision/restriction for adding improvements or reissue
description: When application is made to add a newly discovered improvement to an existing patent or when a patent is returned for correction/reissue, the specification and claim annexed shall be subject to revision and restriction in the same manner as original patent applications.
guidance: The Commissioner shall not add the improvement nor grant the reissue until the applicant has entered a disclaimer or altered his specification/claims in accordance with the Commissioner's decision; dissatisfied applicants have the same remedies and privileges as in original applications.

name: Primary examination objective: focus on prior art
description: The primary object of the examination of an application is to determine whether or not the claims are patentable over the prior art.
guidance: Do not relegate prior art consideration to a secondary position while giving undue emphasis to nonprior art or 'technical' rejections. Concentrate effort on truly essential matters; where a major technical rejection is proper (e.g., lack of proper disclosure, undue breadth, utility, etc.), state it with a full development of reasons rather than a mere conclusion or stereotyped expression.

name: 35 U.S.C. 101 statutory subject matter
description: The subject matter of the invention must come within the boundaries set forth by 35 U.S.C. 101, which permits patents only for 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.' The term 'process' as defined in 35 U.S.C. 100 means process, art or method, and includes a new use of a known process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or material.
guidance: Ensure claims define statutory subject matter; see related MPEP sections for patentability of microorganisms and algorithms (e.g., §§ 2105-2106.02). Use form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05 family where applicable.

name: Utility examination: determine what applicant has invented
description: Office personnel must determine what the applicant has invented and is seeking to patent by: (1) ensuring claims define statutory subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition), and (2) reviewing the complete specification including detailed description, embodiments, claims, and any asserted utilities.
guidance: Thorough review of the entire disclosure and claims is required before assessing utility; do not rely on partial or isolated statements.

name: Utility examination: credible specific utility standard
description: If the applicant has asserted that the claimed invention is useful for a particular purpose (a 'specific utility') and that assertion would be considered credible by a person of ordinary skill in the art, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility.
guidance: Credibility is assessed from the perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art in view of evidence of record (data, statements, opinions, references). An applicant must provide only one credible assertion of specific utility to satisfy the requirement.

name: Utility examination: no asserted specific utility -> 101 and 112 rejections
description: If the applicant has not asserted any specific utility for the claimed invention and it does not have a well-established utility, impose a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (lack of utility) and a separate rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (failure to teach how to use the invention due to lack of disclosure of a specific utility).
guidance: The 101 and 112 rejections should shift the burden to the applicant to (i) explicitly identify a specific utility for the claimed invention and (ii) indicate where support for the asserted utility can be found in the specification. Review subsequently asserted utilities under the credible-utility standard and ensure full support in the original disclosure.

name: Utility rejection: applicant rebuttal and examiner response
description: Once a prima facie showing of no utility has been established, the applicant bears the burden of rebutting it by amending claims, providing reasoning/arguments, or providing evidence (declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 or a printed publication).
guidance: Office personnel must review the original disclosure, evidence relied upon for the prima facie showing, claim amendments, and any new reasoning/evidence. Recognize, consider, and respond to each substantive element of any reply. Withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 and corresponding 112 rejections if the applicant satisfactorily rebuts the prima facie rejection. Treat as true a factual statement by applicant unless countervailing evidence provides legitimate basis to doubt credibility. Accept qualified expert opinions based on relevant facts unless the facts' accuracy is questioned.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: written description requirement
description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
guidance: Use ¶ 7.30.01 (statutory quotation) in first actions/final rejections. Use form paragraph 7.31.01 to reject when claimed subject matter was not described so as to reasonably convey that the inventor had possession at the filing date. In bracketed inserts identify by page/line/drawing where subject matter is missing and explain examiner's position, including unresolved examiner questions.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: enablement requirement
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, if the specification does not enable one skilled in the art to make and/or use the invention. (Form paragraph 7.31.02.)
guidance: Precede this rejection with form paragraph 7.30.01 or 7.103. Identify claimed subject matter not enabled and explain why the specification is not enabling, including any examiner questions not satisfactorily resolved. If the problem is scope-related, use form paragraph 7.31.03 instead. If an essential component or step is missing from the claims, use form paragraph 7.33.01.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: scope of enablement (commensurateness)
description: Claim rejected because the specification, while enabling for certain subject matter, does not reasonably provide enablement for other claimed aspects; the specification does not enable the invention commensurate in scope with the claims (form paragraph 7.31.03).
guidance: Use this when claim scope is broader than the enabling disclosure. Identify in bracketed inserts what is enabled (by reference) and which claim aspects are not enabled. Specify whether the deficiency is inability to 'make', 'use', or 'make and use', and explain why the specification is not enabling, including unresolved examiner queries.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: essential subject matter missing from claims
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as based on a disclosure which is not enabling because subject matter considered critical or essential to practice of the invention is omitted from the claims (form paragraph 7.33.01).
guidance: Precede with 7.30.01 or 7.103. Recite omitted subject matter and give rationale for considering it critical or essential, citing statements/arguments/drawings or other evidence showing the applicant considered the feature essential but it is not reflected in the claims.

name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph: indefiniteness (failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim)
description: Claim rejected as indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention (form paragraph 7.34.01).
guidance: Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103 and follow with specific form paragraphs (7.34.02-7.34.06) as applicable. Whenever possible identify particular term(s) or limitation(s) rendering the claim indefinite and explain why. If scope can be determined by one of ordinary skill, do not use this rejection.

name: Broad range and narrow range limitation in same claim
description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrower range or limitation that falls within the broad range in the same claim is considered indefinite because the claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the protection desired (form paragraph 7.34.04).
guidance: Identify the broader and narrower ranges/limitations and where they appear in the claim. Modify the paragraph to fit similar instances of indefiniteness and reference case law (e.g., Ex parte Wu). Precede with 7.34.01.

name: Use claims that merely recite a use without steps are indefinite / improper process claims
description: A claim that provides for the use of something but does not set forth any steps involved in the method/process is unclear what method/process is intended and is indefinite; such a claim may also be improper under 35 U.S.C. 101 as not a proper process claim (form paragraph 7.34.06).
guidance: Insert what is being used and explain the lack of active steps delimiting how use is practiced. Cite MPEP § 2173.05(q) and relevant decisions (Ex parte Dunki, Clinical Products v. Brenner). Precede with 7.34.01.

name: Claims are literal translations (narrative/indefinite)
description: Claims that are generally narrative and appear to be literal translations into English from a foreign document, with grammatical and idiomatic errors, are generally indefinite and fail to conform with current U.S. practice (form paragraph 7.34.07).
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01 and explain deficiencies. Recommend redrafting claims into standard U.S. claim format.

name: 'For example' renders the claim indefinite
description: Use of the phrase 'for example' in a claim renders it indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention (form paragraph 7.34.08).
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d).

name: 'Or the like' renders the claim indefinite
description: The phrase 'or the like' renders a claim indefinite because it includes elements not actually disclosed, making the scope unascertainable (form paragraph 7.34.09).
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01 and cite MPEP § 2173.05(d).

name: 'Such as' renders the claim indefinite
description: The phrase 'such as' renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention (form paragraph 7.34.10).
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01 and cite MPEP § 2173.05(d).

name: Modifier of 'means' lacks function (112, sixth paragraph issue)
description: When the word 'means' is preceded by words that do not convey a function (e.g., 'conduit means'), it is impossible to determine equivalents as required by 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, rendering the claim indefinite (form paragraph 7.34.11).
guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. The words which precede 'means' must convey a function (e.g., 'latch means' conveys 'means for latching'). If the phrase cannot be restated as 'means for ________' sensibly, it is indefinite. Cite Ex parte Klumb and provide the necessary explanation.

name: Essential steps omitted in method/process claims
description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, the omission amounting to a gap between the recited steps (form paragraph 7.34.12).
guidance: Identify the omitted steps, explain why omission creates a gap between steps, and precede with 7.34.01. See MPEP § 2172.01 for reasoning.

name: Claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought (Article 84 EPC)
description: Article 84 EPC: "The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description."
guidance: The claims must set out what is being claimed (the purported invention). This ensures the public can determine what is and is not covered by the patent, providing legal certainty for third parties (e.g., for licensing, designing around, or market entry).

name: Claims must define the invention in terms of technical features
description: Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought in terms of the technical features of the invention.
guidance: Technical features may be structural (e.g., a nail, screw, rivet) or functional (e.g., fastening means). The claimed features should convey a technical teaching so the scope of protection can be assessed.

name: Claims must be clear in themselves and not rely on the description to achieve clarity
description: Established case law: claims must be clear "in themselves" when read with normal skills; the skilled person's knowledge of the prior art may be used but not knowledge derived from the description to render an otherwise unclear claim clear.
guidance: If a claim is clear to the skilled person on its face, the description need not be consulted. Conversely, the description generally cannot be used to give a different meaning to a claim feature that has a clear technical meaning. Reference: decisions such as T 0908/04, T 454/89 and others.

name: Scope of claims must not be broader than justified by the description and the contribution to the art
description: The scope of the claims must not be "broader than is justified by the extent of the description and also the contribution to the art."
guidance: This reflects the legal principle that the monopoly conferred by the claims should correspond to the technical contribution disclosed. Over-broad claims that claim more than the disclosed contribution are contrary to Article 84.

name: Article 84 EPC is not a ground for opposition or revocation; clarity may be examined post-amendment (G 3/14)
description: Article 84 EPC is neither a ground of opposition under Article 100 EPC nor a ground for revocation under Article 138(1) EPC. However, Article 84 may be considered in opposition proceedings by virtue of Article 101(3) EPC if the patent proprietor amends the claims.
guidance: The Enlarged Board of Appeal in G 3/14 held that clarity of amended claims may be examined in opposition proceedings only when, and to the extent that, the amendment introduces non-compliance with Article 84. Prior lack of clarity in granted claims is not per se a ground for opposition/revocation.

name: Interpretation of claims: use of description for ambiguous terms; skilled-person standard and synthetical propensity
description: In opposition/examination, if claims are sufficiently clear to a skilled person, there is no reason to consult the description. The description can be used as the patent's "dictionary" to assess the correct meaning of ambiguous claim terms, but it cannot be used to give a different meaning to a term that has a clear technical meaning.
guidance: Claims must be interpreted through the eyes of the person skilled in the art, who should try—with synthetical propensity—to arrive at an interpretation that is technically meaningful and takes account of the whole disclosure. In case of discrepancy between clear claim wording and the description, the unambiguous claim wording is to be understood as the skilled person would without help of the description; description parts not reflected in the claims are generally not considered for novelty/inventive step assessments.

name: Plant patent applications
description: Special rules and content requirements applicable to plant patent applications.
guidance: Covers applicant and claim requirements, declaration, description, drawings, examination, fee structure, oath, specimens, rules applicable to plant patents, and specification arrangement (see 1.161–1.167, 1.162–1.166).

name: Treatment of software elements under Section 18
description: Patents that recite software elements are not automatically ineligible for Section 18 review; they are excluded only if the invention is 'novel as software' (i.e., a true software/technological invention).
guidance: If a claim merely includes software elements but does not assert novelty as software or does not colorably appear novel as software, it is not excluded from review solely on that basis. By contrast, an actual software invention whose novelty is technological falls within the 'technological invention' exclusion.

name: Definition of 'covered business method patent' and financial-product nexus
description: A 'covered business method patent' is one that relates to a financial product or service or to performing data processing/operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service.
guidance: To be eligible for Section 18 review the patent claims must be broad enough to cover a financial product or service. 'Financial product or service' is given a broad nonexclusive list of examples (extending credit, servicing loans, leasing, real estate services, payment instruments, check processing, financial data processing, benefits administration, fraud detection, financial advisory/management consulting, securities transactions, insurance, consumer reports, asset management, trust functions, annuities, brokerage, etc.). The provision covers patents claiming activities that are financial in nature, incidental to, or complementary to financial activities—claims need not recite a specific financial product.

name: One skilled in the art does not excuse disclosure of algorithm
description: The fact that one of ordinary skill in the art could write software to perform the claimed function does not relieve the patentee of the duty to disclose sufficient structure (i.e., the algorithm) in the specification to support means‑plus‑function claim terms.
guidance: Cite Blackboard, Biomedino, Atmel. Examiners should not accept arguments that POSITA knowledge supplants the required disclosure of corresponding structure/algorithm.

name: Adequacy of algorithm disclosure judged in view of ordinary skill
description: If the specification explicitly discloses an algorithm, the sufficiency of that disclosure must be determined in light of the level of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Examiner should determine whether one skilled in the art would know how to program the computer to perform the described steps (enablement) and whether the inventor was in possession (written description). Knowledge of POSITA can clarify how to implement a disclosed algorithm (AllVoice, Intel cases). The specification must disclose an algorithm sufficient for POSITA to implement the claimed function.

name: Examination procedure when §112, sixth paragraph is invoked
description: Once a limitation is determined to be a means‑plus‑function limitation invoking §112, sixth paragraph, the examiner should determine the claimed function and then review the written description (including drawings, figures, tables, sequence listings) for corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function.
guidance: Drawings can provide written description (Vas‑Cath). Corresponding structure cannot rely on material only incorporated by reference or on prior art references; the disclosure must come from the application specification itself. Review disclosure from POSITA perspective (Tech. Licensing, Med. Instrumentation).

name: Three common grounds for 112 second paragraph rejection when sixth paragraph invoked
description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph may be appropriate when: (1) it is unclear whether a claim limitation invokes §112, sixth paragraph; (2) sixth paragraph is invoked and there is no disclosure or insufficient disclosure of structure/material/acts; and/or (3) sixth paragraph is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link or associate the disclosed structure/material/acts to the claimed function.
guidance: If examiner cannot identify corresponding structure/material/acts, make a 112 second paragraph rejection. May issue a requirement for information under 37 C.F.R. 1.105 to require identification; failure to supply leads to rejection.

name: If corresponding structure disclosed, claim limited to that structure and equivalents
description: If the written description sets forth the corresponding structure/material/acts in compliance with §112, second paragraph, the claim limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Functional limitations not recited in the claim, or structural limitations in the written description unnecessary to perform the claimed function, cannot be imported into the claim (Welker Bearing, Wenger). Examiner should construe means‑plus‑function limitation consistent with disclosed corresponding structure.

name: Assessing §112 first paragraph support for means‑plus‑function limitations
description: In determining whether there exists §112, first paragraph support for the claim limitation, the examiner must consider not only the summary and detailed description but also the original claims, abstract, and drawings.
guidance: Cite Mott, Anderson, Hill‑Rom, Armbruster, Vas‑Cath, Wolfensperger: all parts of the original disclosure may provide support. Examiner may require applicant to clarify record per 37 C.F.R. 1.75(d) if antecedent basis is not clear.

name: 37 C.F.R. 1.75(d)(1) and the duty to provide antecedent basis/clarity
description: The terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description.
guidance: If the written description only implicitly sets forth corresponding structure/material/acts and POSITA would recognize it, the examiner should either have applicant amend the written description to expressly recite the structure/material/acts or state on the record what structure/material/acts perform the function. The PTO may require explicit antecedent basis even if implicit support exists (B. Braun, Wolfensperger).

name: Single means claims and enablement (Donaldson/Hyatt guidance)
description: Donaldson does not affect In re Hyatt: a single means claim does not comply with the enablement requirement of §112, first paragraph; Donaldson applies only to limitations drafted to correspond to §112, sixth paragraph (claims to combinations).
guidance: See MPEP §2164.08(a) for further context.

name: Ensure the record is clear in Office actions about invocation of §112, sixth paragraph
description: The examiner should specify in the Office action that a claim limitation has been interpreted under §112, sixth paragraph, and when non‑“means for” language invokes sixth paragraph, explain why (e.g., functional term coupled to non‑structural word such as “module for”).
guidance: Office action may also specify what the specification identifies as the corresponding structure. If corresponding structure is not clearly identifiable, the Office action should attempt to identify the structure most closely associated to facilitate prior art search, especially where implementation mode (hardware vs software) is unclear.

name: On allowance, state sixth paragraph interpretation and associated structure
description: When allowing a claim that was treated under §112, sixth paragraph, the examiner should indicate that the claim was interpreted under §112, sixth paragraph in the reasons for allowance and clarify the associated structure if not previously made of record.
guidance: This should be done if such an explanation has not been previously provided on the record.

name: Principle of broadest reasonable interpretation and scope of search (Donaldson)
description: Donaldson reaffirms that claim language should be given its broadest reasonable interpretation; prior art application to a means/step‑plus‑function limitation requires the prior art element perform the identical function specified in the claim. If a prior art reference teaches identity of function, examiner bears initial burden to show the prior art structure is the same as or equivalent to the structure disclosed in the specification as corresponding to the claimed means/step plus function.
guidance: Donaldson does not substantially alter search practice: examiner must show identity of function and equivalence to identify prior art anticipation or obviousness under means‑plus‑function limitations.

name: Two‑step Golight analysis for construing means‑plus‑function limitations
description: First, define the particular function of the claim limitation (include only limitations contained in the claim language). Second, look to the specification and identify the corresponding structure for that function; structure is “corresponding” only if the specification or prosecution history clearly links or associates that structure to the function recited in the claim.
guidance: Cite Golight, Budde, Cardiac Pacemakers, Med. Instrumentation & Elekta: exercise care if specification provides a special definition; absent definition, apply judgment to determine scope consistent with specification disclosure.

name: Making a prima facie case of equivalence for prior art elements
description: If examiner finds a prior art element (A) performs the claimed function, (B) is not excluded by an explicit definition in the specification for an equivalent, and (C) is an equivalent of the means‑/step‑plus‑function limitation, the examiner should explain and rationalize why the prior art element is an equivalent.
guidance: Factors supporting equivalence include: (A) performs identical function in substantially the same way and produces substantially the same results (Kemco, Odetics); (B) POSITA would recognize interchangeability (Caterpillar v. Deere, Al‑Site); (C) insubstantial differences between prior art element and corresponding element in specification (IMS, Warner‑Jenkinson). The overall structure corresponding to the claimed function is what matters; individual components of that overall structure are not claim limitations. Advantages unrelated to claimed function should not be considered in an equivalents determination.

name: Formal contents of a petition under 37 CFR 1.292
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.292 must be submitted in writing, must specifically identify the application by application number or serial number and filing date, and should include a listing of all affidavits or declarations and exhibits relied on.
guidance: The petition must contain a sufficient description of the subject matter alleged to have been in 'public use' or 'on sale,' including necessary photographs, drawings, diagrams, exhibits, or flowcharts to enable the examiner to compare the claimed subject matter to the alleged public use/on-sale matter. The petition and accompanying papers must either (A) reflect that a copy has been served upon the applicant or applicant's attorney/agent or (B) be filed in duplicate if service is not possible.

name: Examiner’s standard for prima facie showing
description: A prima facie case is established if the examiner finds that the facts asserted in the affidavits or declarations, as supported by exhibits, if later proved true by testimony taken in the public use proceeding, would result in a statutory bar to the claims under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) alone or in combination with 35 U.S.C. 103.
guidance: To determine this, the examiner must identify exactly what was in public use or on sale, whether it was in use/on sale in this country more than one year before the effective filing date, and whether the pending claims 'read' on or are obvious over the alleged matter. Compare all pending claims with the alleged matter, not just claims identified by petitioner.

name: Requirements for petitions alleging obviousness
description: When the petition alleges only that the claims are obvious over subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale, the petition should include prior art or other information on which it relies and explain how the prior art or other information in combination with the asserted subject matter renders the claims obvious.
guidance: The examiner is not expected to perform a prior art search when evaluating the petition; however, if the examiner is aware of prior art that renders the claims obvious in combination with the alleged public use/on-sale matter, the examiner may determine a prima facie case has been made out even if the petition alleged only anticipation.

name: Examiner memorandum/report to OPLA after prima facie determination
description: After making the determination, the examiner will forward a memorandum to the OPLA staff member stating findings and the decision as to whether a prima facie case has been established.
guidance: The findings should include a summary of the alleged facts, a comparison of at least one claim with the device alleged to be in public use or on sale, and any other pertinent facts to aid OPLA in conducting the preliminary hearing. The report should be prepared in triplicate and addressed to the OPLA staff member.

name: Scope limitation of testimony
description: In all public use proceedings, testimony will be limited to the issues of public use or on sale; no testimony will be received on whether the claimed subject matter would have been obvious over subject matter asserted to be in public use or on sale.
guidance: Obviousness questions may be addressed differently (e.g., via prior art and legal analysis) but are not proper topics for testimony in the public use proceeding itself.

name: Discovery of a new property of matter can support patentability when practically applied
description: When a newly discovered property of matter is made practically useful by applying a (possibly old) combination of machinery, the combination as applied may be patentable.
guidance: Example: discovery that lead, when recently set and still hot, will reunite perfectly under extreme pressure; substituting a short immovable core and bridge to exploit that property produced a new, patentable process/article even if parts of the machinery were old. Caveat: the claim must not be drafted so that novelty of the machinery becomes essential to the patentee's case.

name: Claims must describe the real invention; avoid claiming unrelated structure
description: A patentee who claims the structure of the machine itself (when the real invention is a new application or method) may hazard the patentable quality of his invention upon the novelty of that machine.
guidance: Example: the caisson case — the plaintiff claimed "the mode of constructing the interior of a caisson..." but by describing the caisson structure prominently, the patent turned on novelty of the caisson apparatus rather than the method of building foundations under water. Drafting guidance: claim the proper improvement (the method or developed use), and avoid unnecessarily making known apparatus the critical novel element.

name: Precision and skill in claim drafting affects scope and validity
description: The language of a claim can limit or change what the patentee is effectively claiming (e.g., claiming a combination "when used" in a particular manner may be construed to require novelty in the machinery).
guidance: Poorly phrased claims can be construed to make the novelty of old components essential; courts will read claims and may refuse the broader construction the patentee intended. Draft claims to manifest the patentee's true purpose and to avoid unintended limitations (use clear linkage of elements to the novel function or property).

name: Courts will compare specifications and constructions to determine novelty and coverage
description: Courts compare the respective specifications of competing patents (or prior uses) to declare what each covered and whether the claimed matter was new.
guidance: Judges may direct verdicts based on comparison of specifications; evidence of prior use of substantially the same combination may be fatal. Practitioners should draft specifications to clearly show the matter the patentee regards as novel and how it differs from prior art; be aware courts will parse claim language in light of the specification.

name: An old combination used for a genuinely new method can be patentable if properly claimed
description: The novelty of an invention may consist in the application of an old combination of machinery to a new end as part of a new process, provided the claim does not make novelty of the machinery essential.
guidance: Example: using an otherwise old machine combination as one element in a new process (e.g., spinning combined with prior maceration). Draft claims to capture the process or the novel application rather than gratuitously claiming old machinery elements standing alone.

name: Beware of overbroad claims that hinge on novelty of known parts
description: Claims which 'hazard the entire patentable quality' on a single issue of novelty of a known component (e.g., the caisson) risk invalidation if that component is shown to be old.
guidance: Avoid claiming too broadly (or for the whole apparatus) when the patentee's true inventive contribution is a specific application, method, or property exploitation. Narrow, focused claims on the improvement reduce the risk that prior art in unrelated parts will invalidate the whole patent.

name: Overall three-question subject matter eligibility process
description: After determining what applicant invented and establishing the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim (per MPEP §2103), walk through three questions in sequence to determine whether the claim is drawn to patent-eligible subject matter; if not, the claim is prima facie ineligible and should be rejected using revised form paragraph 7.05.13.
guidance: Question 1: statutory category. Question 2: does the claim recite or involve one or more judicial exceptions? Question 3: does the claim as a whole recite something significantly different than the judicial exception(s)? If at any point the answer dictates ineligibility, use form paragraph 7.05.13 and precede with form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05. For claims reciting abstract ideas continue to use MPEP §2106(II).

name: Question 2 — Judicial exception identification
description: Does the claim recite or involve one or more judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural principles, natural phenomena, natural products)?
guidance: If no, the claim is patent-eligible and analysis is complete. If yes or unclear, proceed to Question 3. Examples of natural products include chemicals derived from natural sources, foods, metals, minerals, natural materials, nucleic acids, organisms, proteins/peptides, and other substances found in or derived from nature. If any doubt whether the claim recites a judicial exception, treat it as requiring further analysis under Question 3.

name: Question 3 — 'Significantly different' inquiry
description: Does the claim as a whole recite something significantly different than the judicial exception(s)?
guidance: For abstract idea claims, analyze using only MPEP §2106(II). For other judicial exceptions use the factor-based 'significantly different' analysis set forth in Part II. If the claim as a whole is not significantly different, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 using revised form paragraph 7.05.13; if it is significantly different, the claim is patent-eligible.

name: Definition / examples of judicial exceptions
description: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural principles, natural phenomena, and natural products. These exceptions reflect the judicial view that fundamental tools of scientific and technological work are not patentable.
guidance: Also note other terms have been used (natural phenomena, products of nature, naturally occurring things, scientific principles, mental processes, mathematical algorithms/formulas). When a claim recites something similar to a natural product, proceed to the 'significantly different' analysis regardless of claim language like 'isolated', 'recombinant', or 'synthetic'.

name: Factor-based analysis for 'significantly different'
description: If a claim recites or involves a judicial exception other than an abstract idea, determine whether the claim as a whole is significantly different from the judicial exception by weighing multiple factors (a through l).
guidance: A significant difference can be shown by (1) elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception that practically apply it in a significant way (add significantly more), and/or (2) features or steps that demonstrate the claimed subject matter is markedly different from what exists in nature. Not every factor will be relevant to every claim; consider and weigh all relevant factors and evidence. On balance, if the totality of relevant factors weigh toward eligibility, the claim qualifies; if against, it should be rejected. The weight accorded each factor varies with the facts (analogous to Wands analysis).

name: Factor a) — Product claim markedly different in structure
description: Claim is a product claim reciting something that initially appears to be a natural product, but after analysis is determined to be non-naturally occurring and markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
guidance: To evaluate, identify differences between the recited product and naturally occurring products and assess whether differences together rise to the level of a marked difference in structure. A marked difference must be significant (more than incidental/trivial). Routine or conventional human manipulation that produced the marked difference does not prevent it from weighing in favor of eligibility (e.g., cDNA, hybrid plants).

name: Factor b) — Elements/steps that impose meaningful limits on claim scope
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that impose meaningful limits on claim scope, i.e., the elements/steps narrow the scope so that others are not substantially foreclosed from using the judicial exception(s).
guidance: Examples: specific dosage and treatment period in a medical treatment claim that prevent broad foreclosure of other uses. If satisfied, this factor weighs toward eligibility.

name: Factor c) — Elements/steps significantly related to the judicial exception
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that relate to the judicial exception in a significant way — more than nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related.
guidance: Examples: steps that manipulate, integrate, or materially interact with the natural product/principle (e.g., positioning and filtering light; manipulating a protein with a specific antibody). If satisfied, this factor weighs toward eligibility.

name: Factor d) — More than general instructions to apply the exception
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that do more than describe the judicial exception(s) with general instructions to apply or use them.
guidance: Claims that contain only high-level directives to 'apply' or 'use' a natural principle are less likely to qualify. Specific, particularized steps (dosage, times, filtering/positioning) satisfying this factor weigh toward eligibility.

name: Factor e) — Particular machine or transformation
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that include a particular machine or transformation of a particular article, where the machine/transformation implements or integrates the judicial exception(s) into a particular practical application.
guidance: See MPEP 2106(II)(B)(1) for explanation of machine-or-transformation considerations. Satisfying this factor supports eligibility; lack of a machine/transformation does not by itself make a claim ineligible.

name: Factor f) — Features more than well-understood, purely conventional or routine
description: Claim recites one or more elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that add a feature that is more than well-understood, purely conventional or routine in the relevant field.
