guidance: If additional elements are novel in the relevant art or not routine/conventional for the claimed application, this factor weighs toward eligibility. Conversely, if the additional elements are well-known and routine in the field, this factor does not favor eligibility.

name: Factor g) — Product claim not markedly different (weighs against eligibility)
description: Claim is a product claim reciting something that appears to be a natural product that is not markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
guidance: If the recited product is structurally indistinguishable in any meaningful way from what exists in nature (e.g., purified compound with same structure), factor g) weighs against eligibility. Mere isolation that changes bonds (e.g., isolated gene fragment) may not be a marked difference per Myriad.

name: Factor h) — Additional elements recited at a high level of generality
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) at a high level of generality such that substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception(s) are covered.
guidance: High-level recitations that effectively preempt substantial practical uses of the judicial exception weigh against eligibility. Specific limitations that narrow applications avoid this problem.

name: Factor i) — Additional elements are required to apply the judicial exception
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that must be used/taken by others to apply the judicial exception(s).
guidance: If the claim requires steps or elements that everyone must perform to practice the natural principle (thereby foreclosing others), this factor weighs against eligibility. If alternatives are available (different antibodies, methods), this factor may not be satisfied.

name: Factor j) — Additional elements are well-understood, purely conventional or routine (weighs against eligibility)
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that are well-understood, purely conventional or routine in the relevant field.
guidance: When the supposedly limiting steps are routine and conventional, they do not add significantly more to the judicial exception and thus weigh against eligibility.

name: Factor k) — Insignificant extra-solution activity
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that are insignificant extra-solution activity, e.g., are merely appended to the judicial exception(s).
guidance: If additional steps merely amount to post-solution activity or insignificant appendages, they do not make the claim significantly different and weigh against eligibility.

name: Factor l) — Mere field of use
description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that amount to nothing more than a mere field of use.
guidance: Limiting a judicial exception to a field of use (e.g., use of sunlight only for mood disorders) without more does not render claim eligible; such limitations weigh against eligibility.

name: Interaction with other statutes and compact prosecution guidance
description: §101 is not the sole tool for determining patentability; where a claim encompasses a judicial exception such as a natural product, sections 102, 103, and 112 provide additional tools for ensuring the claim meets patentability conditions. Under compact prosecution, Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
guidance: Use obviousness (103), novelty (102), and written description/enablement (112) rejections as appropriate in addition to §101. Ensure initial Office action is comprehensive as to non-cumulative grounds.

name: Claim interpretation prerequisite (MPEP §2103)
description: Before performing the three-question analysis, determine what the applicant invented and establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in accordance with MPEP §2103.
guidance: Accurate claim construction is a prerequisite to applying the eligibility questions and factor analysis; examination record and specification should be consulted to understand the claimed invention.

name: Abstract idea claims — continue to follow MPEP §2106(II)
description: There is no change to examination of claims reciting an abstract idea; such claims should continue to be analyzed for subject matter eligibility using existing guidance in MPEP §2106(II).
guidance: Even if a claim recites both an abstract idea and another judicial exception (e.g., a natural product), the analysis in MPEP §2106(II) controls eligibility for abstract-idea recitations.

name: Form paragraph 7.05.13 usage and explanatory content
description: Revised form paragraph 7.05.13 should be used when rejecting claims that recite or involve a law of nature/natural principle, natural phenomenon, or natural product for lack of subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101. It must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05.
guidance: Bracket 2 of the form must identify the judicial exception(s) recited and explain why the claim features do not result in the claim as a whole reciting something significantly different. Explain why features do not add significantly more and/or do not demonstrate a marked difference from nature; e.g., show additional elements are extra-solution activity, mere field of use, or well-understood/purely conventional/routine. The explanation must be sufficient to establish a prima facie case of patent ineligibility under §101.

name: English translation and accuracy statement for non‑English provisional
description: An English translation of the non-English language provisional application and a statement that the translation is accurate must be filed in provisional application No. [3]. See 37 CFR 1.78.
guidance: If missing, applicant must supply (1) the missing translation and statement in the provisional application and (2) in the present application, a confirmation that the translation and statement were filed in the provisional application. If not filed (or the benefit claim withdrawn) before the expiration of the Office action time period, the present application will be abandoned. Use the specified form paragraph to notify applicant.

name: Design applications cannot claim 35 U.S.C. 119(e) provisional benefit
description: Design applications may not claim the benefit of a provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e). See 35 U.S.C. 172.
guidance: If a design patent application claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 to an intermediate utility nonprovisional that directly claims a provisional, the design application still cannot claim the provisional's filing date. Cite statutory provision when informing applicant.

name: Copendency requirement for benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)/386(c)
description: When claiming the benefit of a prior nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), the later‑filed application must be copending with the prior application or with an intermediate nonprovisional similarly entitled to the prior filing date.
guidance: Copendency means the later application must be filed before the patenting, abandonment, or termination of proceedings in the prior application. If the prior application issues as a patent, filing on the same date or before the patent issues suffices. Best practice: file continuing applications before payment of the issue fee. If prior application is abandoned, the later application must be filed before abandonment to be copending.

name: Consequences and handling of non‑copendency
description: A later‑filed application that is not copending with the prior application is not entitled to the benefit of the prior filing date.
guidance: Applicant should not refer to such prior application(s) in an ADS and is not required to refer in the specification, but must call examiner’s attention under 37 CFR 1.56(b) if contents or prosecution are material to patentability. Use form paragraphs 2.09 and 2.11 to indicate improper benefit claim due to lack of copendency.

name: Identification of intermediate applications when relying on chain for provisional benefit
description: If a nonprovisional does not itself meet the 12‑month provisional filing requirement but claims benefit via an intermediate nonprovisional that was filed within 12 months and claimed the provisional, the intermediate application must be clearly identified as claiming the benefit of the provisional.
guidance: Where the benefit of more than one provisional is claimed, the intermediate nonprovisional(s) claiming the benefit of each provisional must be indicated. Failure to indicate the intermediate application will prevent Office recognition of the benefit claim.

name: Office recognition, filing receipt, and effect of missing/incorrect references
description: If a benefit claim is submitted without required indication of intermediate relationships or outside required periods, the Office will not recognize the benefit claim and will not include it on the filing receipt; petitions (37 CFR 1.78(c)) and fees (37 CFR 1.17(m)) may be required to correct such omissions.
guidance: If a benefit claim was present on the filing date but not in the correct location, and the Office recognized it as shown on the filing receipt, a petition/fee may not be required but applicant must still submit the reference in compliance (ADS/amendment). If not recognized by the Office, petition and fee are required for late correction. The Office may refuse to recognize benefit claims lacking necessary relationship information.

name: Where to place the specific reference (Application Data Sheet requirement)
description: For applications filed on or after September 16, 2012, the specific reference to the prior application must be included in an application data sheet (ADS) in compliance with 37 CFR 1.76. For applications filed prior to that date, the reference must be in an ADS and/or in the first sentence(s) of the specification following the title (Office prefers ADS).
guidance: If the reference is only in the ADS it will be included on the front page of any patent or publication but not in the first sentence(s) of the specification. For multiple prior applications included in the specification, the sentences must be continuous beginning as the first sentence after the title and any additional sentences stating benefit claims must immediately follow.

name: ADS/incorporation by reference and 37 CFR 1.57(b) (inadvertently omitted material)
description: For applications filed on or after September 21, 2004, a claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 present on the filing date is considered an incorporation by reference of the prior application as to inadvertently omitted material subject to 37 CFR 1.57(b).
guidance: Applicants are encouraged to provide an explicit incorporation by reference statement in the specification if they do not want the incorporation to be limited to inadvertently omitted material. An incorporation by reference statement cannot be added after filing because adding new matter after filing is prohibited (see 35 U.S.C. 132(a) and Dart Indus. v. Banner).

name: If reference was submitted but not in required location (timely recognition exception)
description: If applicant included the reference elsewhere (oath/declaration/transmittal letter) within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78 and the Office recognized the claim (shown on filing receipt), a petition under 37 CFR 1.78 and petition fee under 37 CFR 1.17(m) are not required to correct the claim.
guidance: Applicant is still required to submit the reference in compliance (ADS or amendment to first sentence(s) for pre‑Sep 16, 2012 filings). If the claim was not recognized on the filing receipt, a petition/fee will be required if correction is sought after the time period. Office may refuse to recognize benefit claims lacking relationship or intermediate identification.

name: Form paragraph 2.15 wording and time limits for submitting reference
description: Form paragraph 2.15 notifies applicant that if they desire to claim the benefit of a prior application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), the instant application must contain, or be amended to contain, a specific reference in compliance with 37 CFR 1.78; and it sets required submission time frames.
guidance: For utility or plant applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), the specific reference must be submitted during pendency and within the later of 4 months from the actual filing date or 16 months from the filing date of the prior application. For national stage applications under 371, similar later‑of timing (4 months from national stage commencement or initial submission, or 16 months from prior filing) applies. These time periods are not extendable; failure to submit is a waiver unless a petition to accept an unintentionally delayed claim is filed (37 CFR 1.78(c) for 119(e) or 1.78(e) for 120/etc.). Petitions must include reference, petition fee (1.17(m)), and statement the delay was unintentional; Director may require further info. Petition should be mailed to Mail Stop Petition, Commissioner for Patents, P.O. Box 1450, Alexandria, VA 22313‑1450.

name: Proper wording for referencing prior nonprovisional applications
description: For references to prior nonprovisional applications (allowed for pre‑Sep 16, 2012 placement in specification), an example of a proper benefit claim is: 'this application is a continuation of prior Application No. ---, filed ---.'
guidance: A statement that merely 'claims the benefit of Application No. ---' does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 because the relationship (continuation/divisional/CIP) is not stated. Similarly, saying 'this application is a continuing application of Application No. ---' is insufficient without specifying the type of continuing application.

name: Graham factor — differences between prior art and claimed invention
description: Ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claimed invention.
guidance: Make explicit findings comparing claim limitations to prior-art disclosures. Differences should be described with respect to the claim limitations at issue. See MPEP 2141.

name: Address each included claim explicitly
description: Each claim included in a rejection must be explicitly addressed.
guidance: Examiners must explain why the limitations of each included claim would have been obvious. It is not necessary to rewrite the entire rejection for every claim, but each claim's limitations should be tied to the factual findings and rationale. See MPEP 2143.

name: Overlapping/approaching/similar ranges, amounts, proportions
description: Overlapping, approaching, and similar ranges, amounts, and proportions in prior art can support an obviousness finding.
guidance: When claimed ranges overlap or are close to prior-art ranges, show why the claimed ranges would have been obvious (e.g., overlap, predictability). Explain overlaps/close proximity for each included claim and specifically address ranges in dependent claims as needed. See MPEP 2144.05.

name: Optimization within prior-art conditions / routine experimentation
description: Optimization within prior-art conditions or through routine experimentation can be a rationale, but differences in parameters (e.g., concentration, temperature) generally do not support patentability unless the optimization is shown to be more than routine.
guidance: Articulate why routine optimization would have led to the claimed parameter and why the skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success. Presence of a result-effective variable is one possible motivation; examiners must make findings of fact and present underpinning reasoning in sufficient detail. See MPEP 2144.05 (II).

name: Examiners must present factual findings and sufficient underpinning reasoning
description: Examiners are required to make findings of relevant facts and present the underpinning technical/legal reasoning in sufficient detail to support a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Factual findings include what each reference discloses, differences with the claims, the level of ordinary skill, and any objective evidence. The rationale must tie these facts to one or more acceptable lines of reasoning. See MPEP 2141, 2143.

name: Summary requirement — explain obviousness of claim as a whole and of each limitation
description: Obviousness rejections must explain why the invention as a whole would have been obvious and why the limitations of each claim included in the rejection would have been obvious.
guidance: Clear, explicit rejections allow applicants, examiners, and reviewers to understand the basis for the rejection; regardless of the rationale used, explain how it applies to the particular facts of the application and to each claim limitation. See MPEP 2141, 2143.

name: Practical examples illustrate adequate vs. inadequate rationales
description: Concrete examples (e.g., spray pressure in meat treatment; substitution of antibiotics; counterion selection; codon optimization) demonstrate what constitutes adequate factual findings and reasoning versus inadequate, conclusory rationales.
guidance: Use example patterns: simple combination, simple substitution, overlapping ranges, optimization within prior art, teaching-suggestion-motivation. Adequate rationales tie specific reference teachings to claim limitations and show reasonable expectation of success; inadequate rationales are conclusory and fail to explain why routine optimization or similarity would have led to the claimed invention.

name: Graham Factors (four-factor analysis)
description: The objective four-factor analysis announced in Graham v. John Deere: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (4) secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, etc.).
guidance: KSR followed this Graham framework; the guidance emphasizes applying these factors (and considering them together) when determining obviousness. The office reiterates that the Graham factors remain central to the analysis. Example citations: KSR, 550 U.S. at 406 (quoting Graham).

name: Analogous art determination
description: Prior art is analogous when it shares the 'same field of endeavor' with, and is 'reasonably pertinent' to, the claimed invention.
guidance: Determination of whether a reference is analogous art should take into account relevant evidence in the record cited by parties to demonstrate the knowledge and perspective of a PHOSITA (citing Airbus S.A.S. v. Firepass). Examine whether the reference would have been within the ordinary knowledge or concern of a PHOSITA such that it is reasonably pertinent.

name: Requirement for articulated reasoning and evidentiary support for rejections
description: Any legally proper obviousness rejection must 'identify facts and then articulate sound reasoning that leads to the conclusion that the claims would have been obvious to a PHOSITA.'
guidance: MPEP 2142 and the USPTO guidance require clear articulation of the reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious; examiners must provide adequate analysis based on evidentiary support. A mere conclusory statement without fact-based reasoning is insufficient. The guidance calls out the need for this as a frequent theme in post-KSR cases.

name: Definitions and scope for ex parte appeals
description: For Subpart B (Ex Parte Appeals), definitions specify applicant, owner, proceeding; an appeal to the Board in an inter partes reexamination is controlled by Subpart C.
guidance: Clarifies scope of Subpart B versus Subpart C; defines when ex parte reexamination owners may appeal depending on filing date and claim status (§ 41.30).

name: Amendments and affidavits/evidence after appeal filing
description: Amendments filed after filing an appeal and prior to filing a brief may be admitted as provided in § 1.116. Amendments filed on/after the date of filing a brief may be admitted only to cancel claims or to rewrite dependent claims into independent form; other amendments after appeal filing will not be admitted except as permitted by specified sections.
guidance: An affidavit or other evidence filed after appeal filing and prior to a brief may be admitted if the examiner determines it overcomes all rejections under appeal and that good and sufficient reasons exist why it was not earlier presented. Other affidavits/evidence are subject to other specific provisions (cut off in chunk) (§ 41.33).

name: Prior adverse Office decisions on same/substantially identical prior art
description: A prior decision adverse to the patentability of a claim by the Office based upon prior art patents or printed publications would usually mean that 'a substantially new question of patentability' is present.
guidance: Example: could arise from a reissue application abandoned after rejection of the claim and without disclaiming the patent claim. Examiner should consider such prior adverse Office decisions when determining whether SNQ is present.

name: Effect of federal court decisions on SNQ (final validity, nonfinal, final invalidity)
description: When considering whether prior art raises a SNQ, a final court decision of claim validity in view of the same or different prior art does not necessarily mean no SNQ is present because of differing standards of proof; factual findings may be accorded deference but the Office's determination is independent. A nonfinal holding of invalidity/unenforceability is not controlling. A final holding of invalidity or unenforceability after all appeals is controlling and a SNQ would not be present as to the claims finally held invalid or unenforceable.
guidance: Cases cited: In re Swanson, 540 F.3d 1368 (Fed. Cir. 2008); In re Baxter Int’l, 678 F.3d 1357 (Fed. Cir. 2012); Ethicon v. Quigg, 849 F.2d 1422 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Bring unclear situations to Office of Patent Legal Administration.

name: Claims considered in deciding the request (claims in effect at time)
description: The claims of the patent in effect at the time of the determination will be the basis for deciding whether a SNQ is present (37 CFR 1.515(a)). The Office's determination will generally be limited to review of the claim(s) for which reexamination was requested.
guidance: Requesters must set forth the pertinency and manner of applying cited prior art to every claim for which reexamination is requested (35 U.S.C. 302). If requester fails to apply the art to certain claims, requester is not statutorily entitled to reexamination of such claims. The Office may, in its discretion, reexamine claims not requested (35 U.S.C. 303(a)). If reexamination is ordered, the prosecution should be on the basis of the claims as amended by any copending reexamination or reissue proceeding.

name: Decision to order reexamination must identify claims/issues, art, and rationale
description: If a SNQ is found, the determination will include an order for reexamination and the examiner’s decision will (A) identify all claims and issues, (B) identify the patents and/or printed publications relied on, and (C) provide a brief statement of the rationale supporting each new question.
guidance: Examiner must identify at least one SNQ and explain how the prior art raises such a question. Examiner should, insofar as possible, indicate initial positions on all issues identified in the request to allow comment in the patent owner’s statement and requester’s reply. Prior art relied on should be listed on form PTO‑892 or equivalent; supply copies only where not previously supplied to the patent owner/requester.

name: Decision contents: six required points (A–F)
description: As to each SNQ identified, the decision should point out: (A) the prior art patents/printed publications which add some new teaching as to at least one claim; (B) what that new teaching is; (C) the claims that the new teaching is directed to; (D) that the new teaching was not previously considered nor addressed in the prior examination or a final court holding; (E) that the new teaching is such that a reasonable examiner would consider it important in deciding to allow the claim; and (F) where raised or unclear, why the patent or publication is deemed to be available against the patent claims.
guidance: See MPEP § 2247.01 for an example decision. In simple cases examiner may adopt requester’s reasons. If request indicates SNQ without stating claims unpatentable, language should state SNQ is raised as to specified claims rather than asserting unpatentability.

name: Patent owner statement and reply timing and procedural limits
description: When reexamination is ordered, the patent owner will be given a reasonable period, not less than two months from the date the determination is mailed, to file a statement on the SNQ, including any amendment and new claims to propose. The requester may file a reply within two months from service.
guidance: Extensions of time under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are not permitted (provisions apply only to 'an applicant'); ex parte reexamination proceedings are conducted with special dispatch (35 U.S.C. 305; 37 CFR 1.550(a)). Extensions in ex parte reexamination are provided in 37 CFR 1.550(c). For EFS‑Web transmissions, follow 37 CFR 1.8 filing/timeliness requirements including certificate of transmission.

name: Petition to vacate reexamination order as ultra vires (37 CFR 1.181(a)(3)) — appropriate circumstances
description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.181(a)(3) to vacate an ex parte reexamination order as 'ultra vires' should be rare and granted only where the USPTO acted in 'brazen defiance' of its statutory authorization. Appropriate circumstances include: (A) order is facially not based on prior art patents or printed publications; (B) all claims for which reexamination ordered were held invalid by a final decision of a Federal Court after all appeals; (C) reexamination was ordered for the wrong patent; or (D) reexamination was ordered based on a duplicate copy of the request.
guidance: There is no right to petition as ultra vires if SNQ is based on reasons other than those urged by the requester. Petitions to vacate are delegated to the Director of the Central Reexamination Unit; third‑party requester may file a single opposition submission (must file within two weeks of service) and should notify CRU support staff upon intention to oppose. File oppositions preferably by facsimile when possible.

name: Limitations on when P.R. practice is proper
description: Patentability Report practice is not proper where claims are directed to the same character of invention but differ in scope only.
guidance: Exemplary situations where P.R.s are ordinarily not proper include: (A) claims related as a manufacturing process and a product defined by the process; (B) claims related as product and a process which merely involves the fact that a product having certain characteristics is made; (C) claims related as a combination distinguished solely by characteristics of a subcombination and such subcombination per se.

name: Purpose and goal of rejections
description: After the application has been read and the claimed invention understood, a prior art search is made and the application reviewed to determine whether the claims define a useful, novel, nonobvious, and enabled invention that has been clearly described in the specification.
guidance: The goal of examination is to clearly articulate any rejection early so applicant can provide evidence of patentability; examiner then reviews all evidence, including arguments and evidence responsive to any rejection, before issuing the next Office action.

name: 37 CFR 1.104(c)(2) citation of best references
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command.
guidance: When a reference is complex or shows inventions other than that claimed, the particular part relied on must be designated as nearly as practicable; the pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified.

name: Choice of prior art: best available and avoid cumulative rejections
description: Prior art rejections should ordinarily be confined strictly to the best available art.
guidance: Exceptions may be made (e.g., when propriety depends on particular claim interpretation, when a reference meets a claim only in terms, or when a reference seems likely to be antedated by a §1.131 affidavit/declaration). Avoid merely cumulative rejections which would fall if the primary rejection is not sustained.

name: Determining the effective filing date (continuation/divisional/CIP rules)
description: The effective filing date may be the same as an earlier application where requirements of 35 U.S.C. 120 and 365(c) are satisfied; for continuation-in-part (CIP), claims not supported by parent have effective filing date equal to new application, whereas claims fully supported by the earlier parent have the parent's effective filing date.
guidance: Determine support under 35 U.S.C. 112 and applicable statutes to ascertain effective filing dates for claims.

name: Patent for application of a principle (generality of claim)
description: A patentee may claim the application of a newly discovered principle to a specified result; the patent may cover the mode of carrying that principle into effect rather than a single specific form of apparatus.
guidance: Examples: Minter v. Wells (self-adjusting chair): claiming a self-adjusting lever applied to the back of a chair — held to cover any chair constructed on that principle. Neilson (hot blast): patent construed as for the application of blowing with hot air by means of a vessel heating the air between blowing apparatus and furnace; the 'shape of the receptacle is immaterial' and the patent embraced all forms of apparatus effecting the same principle. The generality of claiming 'all modes of applying the principle to the purpose specified' is not in itself an objection; breadth may be the merit of the invention where the patentee has disclosed the principle and a mode of applying it.

name: Claiming a mode of carrying a principle into effect (broad claim when no particular form is essential)
description: If the inventor suggests the principle and also invents how it may be applied to a practical result by mechanical contrivance, and shows awareness that no particular form of apparatus is essential, he may claim the mode of carrying the principle into effect without confining himself to one form.
guidance: Court rationale: requiring a patentee to confine to one form would often prevent patents for valuable discoveries because the best form cannot be known at once. If any sort of apparatus applied in the stated way will produce the benefit, the patentee need not be tied to a specific form.

name: Determine whether patent claims a combination or distinct inventions
description: Courts must decide whether the patentee claims a combination of several things or distinct inventions of several things; if one or more elements are not new, the question becomes whether the patent can be sustained for the combination as claimed.
guidance: Principle: a patent for a combination of three things cannot at the same time be a patent for a combination of any two of them; if the subject-matter is the combination of a given number of parts, no portion less than the whole is, simultaneously, the subject-matter. Example: agricultural machine claims covering multiple interconnected parts — using a single part (knife) alone was held not to infringe because patent was for the combination.

name: Claims must not be mere claims for a result (no result-only claims)
description: A claim that merely states a desired result without claiming the means or construction to achieve it is bad; claims should be to the construction or arrangement 'in substantially the manner described.'
guidance: Coffin v. Ogden: first claim phrased as a result was held bad; the valid construction is a claim to dividing the hub or follower 'in substantially the manner described' and combining it with the reversible latch as described. Always tie the claimed result to the structural/operational features disclosed in the specification.

name: Claims and specification must be read together (interpretation in light of description and drawings)
description: Claims should be interpreted in the light of the specification and drawings; the whole claim, read with the specification, should disclose the organized mechanism which the inventor has patented.
guidance: Judge Shipman's instruction in Blake v. Stafford: alleged vagueness can be resolved by reading claims alongside the detailed description and drawings. The specification + drawings may plainly disclose the mechanism and cure objections of vagueness when considered together.

name: Construction: device vs process (claim language controls what is claimed)
description: Courts must construe claims to determine whether they are for a process or for a device/instrument; the same wording may be interpreted as a device when the claim describes an instrument to be employed in a process.
guidance: Railroad Co. v. Dubois: claim for 'building and setting piers by means of a floating coffer-dam, substantially as set forth' was construed as a claim to a device (floating coffer-dam) rather than to a process, and the court refused to require proof of use of a particular process. Drafters should be mindful of wording ('the use of the tube...','in combination with') and the court's likely construction.

name: Avoid mixing statutory categories or incompatible claim types
description: A patent should not contain claims that fall under different statutory regimes or that are essentially distinct types of subject-matter (e.g., a machine and a design protected under different acts) in a way that renders the patent void.
guidance: Clark v. Bousfield: the second claim was argued to be merely a design; court held the elastic bed in the machine (even if embodying designs) constituted an element of the machine and thus was within the machine patent. Nevertheless, drafters must avoid claims that improperly mix categories (which may have different protection terms) unless the specification clearly makes them part of the same invention.

name: Breadth of claim language will be interpreted in ordinary use
description: Broad terms in claims (e.g., 'iron frame') may be read to encompass whatever, in ordinary language, would be called by that term, not necessarily limited to a particular embodiment described elsewhere in the specification.
guidance: Example: English case where 'iron frame' in a broad claim was held to include any iron frame that would ordinarily be called such, not only the specific frame in another claim. Be cautious: breadth invites scrutiny for prior art that may anticipate the broad claim.

name: Read description before construing claims (claims not in isolation)
description: The proper approach is to read the inventor's description of the invention first so the drafter/reader is prepared for what the inventor then claims; claims should not be divorced from the preceding detailed description.
guidance: Lord Hatherly in Arnold v. Bradbury: read the description first to understand what is claimed; claims that appear broad may be limited in meaning by the specification's detail. Also, inventor may reserve right to make modifications 'substantially the same' as present invention — court will respect that if the description shows such intent.

name: Specification must enable a person skilled in the art to practise the invention
description: The specification must describe the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding the invention 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity' as to enable any person skilled in the art to make, construct, compound, and use the invention from the specification alone.
guidance: Statute requires explaining the principle and the several modes contemplated for application and to 'particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination' claimed. Whether the specification suffices is a question of fact for a jury; technical terms are permissible but may need explanatory evidence. The specification need not teach a layperson — it must enable a person of competent skill in the art.

name: Claims limited to what is novel and described (prior art limits scope)
description: Even where a patentee describes and claims broadly, if subsequent evidence shows that the claim 'takes in that which has already been invented' (prior art), the claim may fail — breadth cannot capture what is not novel.
guidance: Lord Hatherly's observation: a broad claim might be invalid not because it claims too much in form, but because it covers subject-matter already invented. Drafters should ensure novelty of what is claimed and be prepared that broad language invites challenge by prior art.

name: Types of technical illustrations required
description: Include appropriate figure types for the invention: exploded views, cross‑sectional views, perspective views, elevation views, flow charts, block diagrams, circuit diagrams, etc.
guidance: Select view types to make claimed features visible and unambiguous; multi‑figure sheets must be clearly labeled and organized for examiner review.

name: Understand and mitigate consequences of non‑compliance
description: Non‑compliant drawings can trigger WIPO formal deficiency notices, national phase drawing objections, prosecution ambiguity, and multiplied correction costs across jurisdictions.
guidance: Recognize that drawing deficiencies can delay or damage priority claims and prosecution strategy; invest in PCT‑standard drawings at filing to avoid compounded international correction costs.

name: Preemption concern as the driving consideration
description: The ‘driv[ing]’ concern of the eligibility exceptions is preemption — the prospect that a patent would render too much activity infringing; courts must scrutinize patents that would excessively preempt ideas because they risk impeding innovation rather than promoting it.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claim would ‘tie up’ or preempt the basic tools of scientific and technological work. Even if an invention involves ideas (as all do), ask whether the claim scope would ‘render too much activity infringing.’ Absence of total preemption is relevant but insufficient by itself to show eligibility (courts have held that absence of complete preemption does not demonstrate patent eligibility).

name: Step one — ‘directed to’ an abstract idea / claim ‘focus’ inquiry
description: At step one a court asks whether the claims are ‘directed to’ a patent-ineligible concept by looking at the ‘focus’ of the claims — whether they are aimed at an abstract idea or at a specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities or technology.
guidance: Determine whether the claim’s focus is a specific technological advance (which favors eligibility) or an abstract result/idea (which favors ineligibility). Interpret ‘directed to’ as more than mere presence/containment of an idea. Use precedent (Enfish, Bandai/McRO, Finjan, Elec. Power) to decide whether claims are focused on a specific technical improvement or merely automate a known manual/mental process or effect. Consider examples: McRO/Bandai (eligible because focused on a specific algorithmic rule set improving animation) vs. generic automation of loan applications or virus screening (treated as abstract).

name: Categories and limits of abstract ideas (as articulated)
description: Courts group abstract ideas into categories (e.g., fundamental economic practices; certain methods of organizing human activity; an idea ‘of itself’; mathematical relationships/formulas), and the USPTO (MPEP) later summarized categories as mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.
guidance: When assessing whether a claim recites an abstract idea, map the claimed subject matter to these categories. Be aware that the MPEP attempts to limit examiners to these categories and presumes against finding abstract ideas outside them — but courts have not held those to be the only possible categories. If an examiner contemplates treating an idea as an abstract idea outside these categories, supervisory approval may be required (per MPEP).

name: Three claim-types that almost always fail Alice step one
description: The Federal Circuit has identified three claim types that almost always fail step one: (1) claims that simply demand the production of a desired result (no limitation on how achieved); (2) claims to processes that can be performed in the human mind (or their automatic equivalents); (3) claims that gather and analyze information of a specified content and then display the results, when done in a conventional way.
guidance: Watch for broadly preemptive result-oriented claims, mental-process-equivalent claims, and conventional data-collection/analysis/display claims. These raise heightened preemption concerns and typically proceed to step two, where they often fail absent a transformative inventive concept. Use these categories as red flags during drafting/examination and argue specificity or technical solution if seeking eligibility.

name: Step two — ‘inventive concept’ requirement
description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea at step one, courts must search for an ‘inventive concept’ — claim elements beyond the abstract idea that ‘transform’ the claim into a patent-eligible application; token invocations of generic computer parts or instructions to ‘apply it’ will not suffice.
guidance: Look for claim elements that meaningfully limit the abstract idea so preemption is avoided. Factors supporting an inventive concept include: use of nongeneric or specially adapted technology; a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known components; absence of total preemption; presence of a technical improvement; and a technical solution to a problem unique to a particular technological context. Case law examples: BASCOM (claims eligible at step two due to specific location and customizable filtering features and lack of total preemption); Diehr (technical improvement via continuous temperature measurement). The bar is high; many claims fail at step two.

name: Technical improvement / ‘technical solution to a technical problem’ as the most important factor
description: Claims that represent a technical solution to a technical problem (i.e., a specific asserted improvement to computers or technology) are more likely to be found eligible at one or both steps of Alice.
guidance: When drafting or evaluating claims, emphasize how the invention improves computer functionality or solves a technology-specific problem (not merely makes a process more efficient by automation). Courts treat specificity of the improvement as important — mere novelty, brilliance, or general improvement is not enough; the claimed improvement must be specific and tied to limitations that reduce preemption concerns.

name: Streamlined (step-zero) analysis in USPTO guidance
description: The USPTO’s streamlined eligibility analysis is a fast track to eligibility where the invention ‘clearly’ does not preempt an idea or ‘clearly improve[s] a technology or computer functionality,’ allowing examiners to presume eligibility without full two-step analysis.
guidance: Under the 2019 MPEP changes, examiners may use streamlined analysis for claims showing clear technological improvement (citing Bandai and Enfish fact patterns). Be cautious: courts require detailed analysis of preemption and specificity; the mere appearance of an improvement does not guarantee eligibility. The Office’s adoption of broadened streamlined analysis departs in some respects from judicial precedent and can be contested.

name: MPEP’s addition of a second prong within step one: ‘integration into a practical application’
description: If a claim recites a judicial exception, examiners should consider whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (e.g., an apparent improvement to computers disclosed in specification/claims); if so, the claim may be eligible without proceeding to step two.
guidance: Integration requires more than conclusory assertions of improvement — the improvement should be apparent from the specification and claims. This is an MPEP-specific placement of the search for technological improvement at an earlier point in the analysis; courts typically look for technical improvements at step one, step two, or both. Emphasize specificity and reduced preemption when arguing integration.

name: Conventional computer automation / improved efficiency alone is insufficient
description: Efficiency gains that result only from computer automation — i.e., using a computer ‘merely as a tool’ to perform a known manual process more efficiently — do not amount to an improvement to computers themselves and are not enough to establish eligibility.
guidance: Differentiate between inventions that improve computer functionality/architecture and those that merely automate tasks. Claims that only capture improved speed or convenience of automating a manual process typically fail Alice. Use claim language to tie inventions to changes in computer operation or architecture where possible.

name: Specificity requirement and limits of ‘absence of total preemption’
description: Specificity in claimed improvements matters because it reduces preemption; conversely, absence of total preemption (i.e., not tying up the entire idea) alone does not establish eligibility.
guidance: When analyzing or drafting claims, identify precise means, methods, or structural limitations that limit the claim’s scope. Courts look for specific means or methods that improve technology rather than broad results. The MPEP’s emphasis on ‘improvement’ should be accompanied by claims and specification that demonstrate particularity and specific technical features to withstand eligibility scrutiny.

name: Limit preservation, disclosure, and discovery to relevant and necessary data
description: Preservation, disclosure, and discovery of Protected Data should be limited in scope to that which is relevant and necessary to support any party’s claim or defense in order to minimize conflicts of law and impact on the Data Subject.
guidance: Principle recognizes obligations of Data Controller, requesting party, and court to protect Data Subjects; parties and courts should cooperate, use stipulations or court orders, and avoid producing Protected Data beyond what is relevant and necessary.

name: Conform discovery scope to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) relevance and proportionality
description: Discovery obligation under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) extends only to information that is relevant to claims and defenses and proportional to the needs of the case; apply proportionality factors when weighing discovery of Protected Data.
guidance: Consider six proportionality factors: importance of issues at stake, amount in controversy, parties' relative access to information, parties' resources, importance of discovery in resolving issues, and whether burden/expense outweighs likely benefit. Courts may require information to be 'necessary', 'vital', or at least 'relevant' when foreign Data Protection Laws are implicated.

name: Fintiv Factor 4 — Overlap between issues raised in the petition and in the parallel proceeding
description: Explores the extent to which claims, grounds, arguments, and evidence in the petition overlap with those in the district court litigation, as overlap raises concerns of inefficiency and conflicting decisions.
guidance: Substantial or identical overlap of claims/grounds/evidence strongly favors discretionary denial. Overlap is highly fact-dependent. Petitioners can mitigate overlap concerns by stipulations (e.g., agreeing not to pursue the same grounds in district court if IPR is instituted). The PTAB has noted that broader stipulations (e.g., not pursuing any ground that could reasonably have been raised in an IPR under §102/§103 based on patents/printed publications) are more persuasive and can tip this factor toward permitting institution. Parties should consider and propose appropriate stipulations and explain the scope of overlap.

name: Compare claim to previously found-abstract claims
description: When determining whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it is appropriate to compare the claim to claims already found to be directed to an abstract idea in a previous court decision.
guidance: Use prior court decisions to identify whether the concept recited by the claim is similar to concepts previously held abstract. Examiners are to determine if the claim recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) a concept that is similar to concepts previously found abstract by the courts.

name: "Directed to" inquiry considers claim as a whole in view of the specification
description: The 'directed to' inquiry applies a filter to claims, when interpreted in view of the specification, based on whether their character as a whole is directed to a patent ineligible concept.
guidance: Interpret the claim in light of the specification to determine the focus of the claimed invention (its character as a whole), rather than isolating elements or ignoring specification teachings.

name: Avoid describing claims at a high level untethered from claim language
description: Caution against describing a claim at a high level of abstraction untethered from the language of the claim when determining the focus of the claimed invention.
guidance: Do not abstractly summarize the claim into overly broad categories; instead, focus on what the claim actually recites and how the specification characterizes the invention.

name: Claims directed to improvements in computer-related technology may be non-abstract
description: Certain claims directed to improvements in computer-related technology, including claims directed to software, are not necessarily abstract (Step 2A).
guidance: If a claim is directed to a specific improvement in computer functionality (analogous to chip architecture or an LED display), it can demonstrate the claim is not similar to previously identified abstract ideas and may be patent eligible at Step 2A.

name: Software can make non-abstract improvements like hardware can
description: Explaining that software can make non-abstract improvements to computer technology just as hardware can, the court noted that claims directed to software, as opposed to hardware, also are not inherently abstract.
guidance: Do not treat software claims as presumptively abstract; assess whether the software claim recites a specific technical improvement to computer capabilities.

name: Distinguish focus: improvement in computer capabilities vs abstract process using computers
description: Ask whether the focus of the claims is on the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities, or instead on a process that qualifies as an 'abstract idea' for which computers are invoked merely as a tool.
guidance: Use this distinction to decide whether the claim is directed to an improvement in existing computer technology (favoring eligibility) or to an abstract idea implemented on conventional computers (likely ineligible).

name: Look to specification to identify improvements and benefits
description: To make the determination of whether these claims are directed to an improvement in existing computer technology, the court looked to the teachings of the specification.
guidance: Identify specification teachings that show advantages over conventional systems (e.g., increased flexibility, faster search times, smaller memory requirements). The improvement need not be physical; logical structures and processes can define a technical improvement.

name: Improvement need not be defined by physical components
description: The improvement does not need to be defined by reference to 'physical' components. Instead, the improvement here is defined by logical structures and processes, rather than particular physical features.
guidance: Accept non-physical (logical/architectural/algorithmic) improvements as potentially demonstrating non-abstract character, provided the claim and specification support that characterization.

name: If claim is directed to a computer-technology improvement, Step 2B may be unnecessary
description: An examiner may determine that a claim directed to improvements in computer-related technology is not directed to an abstract idea under Step 2A (and is thus patent eligible), without the need to analyze the additional elements under Step 2B.
guidance: When Step 2A shows the claim is directed to a specific improvement in computer functionality, do not proceed to Step 2B if no abstract-idea finding is warranted.

name: Additional elements must add 'significantly more' beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activities (Step 2B)
description: If a claim is found to be directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A), the additional elements must add significantly more. Elements that are well-understood, routine, conventional activities do not add significantly more.
guidance: Evaluate whether elements such as using a telephone unit and a server are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' — if so, they do not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter under Step 2B (as in TLI).

name: Claims that merely implement abstract processes on conventional computers are likely abstract
description: Claims that are directed to generalized steps to be performed on a computer using conventional computer activity (e.g., recording, administration and archiving of digital images) can be directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: When the claimed steps are general organizational/classification activities implemented using routine computer components, treat them as more likely to be abstract absent a specific improvement in computer technology.

name: Purpose and scope of Supplemental Examination
description: This new 'Supplemental Examination' procedure encourages the voluntary and proactive disclosure of information that may be relevant to patent prosecution for the Office to consider, reconsider, or correct.
guidance: Voluntary disclosure by patentees serves to strengthen valid patents, while narrowing or eliminating patents or claims that should not have been issued. Both outcomes promote investment in innovation by removing uncertainty about the scope, validity or enforceability of patents, and thus the use of this new proceeding by patent owners is to be encouraged. The Director should implement this new authority in a way that maximizes this potential.

name: Weldon Amendment prohibition on patents 'directed to or encompassing a human organism'
description: None of the funds appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be used to issue patents on claims directed to or encompassing a human organism.
guidance: The prohibition limits the use of appropriated funds by the PTO to issue certain types of claims (specifically claims that encompass a human individual). It operates on patents that may issue on applications filed on or after the date of the legislation, does not create a cause of action, and does not alter rights associated with patents duly granted by the PTO. Because it addresses only appropriated funds, alternate funding (e.g., user fees) could affect its practical coverage unless codified into patent law.

name: USPTO policy and MPEP guidance rejecting claims that encompass humans
description: Longstanding USPTO practice: 'A claim directed to or including within its scope a human being will not be considered patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101.' (Quigg memo / MPEP §2105).
guidance: The Quigg memo and MPEP suggest including the limitation 'non-human' in claims that otherwise could be construed to encompass a human being to avoid a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection. If the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention as a whole encompasses a human being, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating that the claimed invention is directed to nonstatutory subject matter.

name: Scope of what Weldon does not affect (exceptions/clarifications)
description: The Weldon Amendment does not limit patent eligibility for many biotechnology inventions and does not prevent patents on human cells, genes, or other tissues obtained from human embryos or human bodies.
guidance: Specifically, nothing in this section should be construed to limit the PTO's ability to issue a patent containing claims directed to: (1) chemical compounds or compositions (including nucleic acids, polypeptides, proteins, antibodies and hormones); (2) cells, tissue, organs or other bodily components produced through human intervention (including stem cells, stem cell derived tissues, stem cell lines, and viable synthetic organs); (3) methods for creating, modifying, or treating human organisms (e.g., IVF, somatic cell nuclear transfer, medical or genetic therapies); or (4) a nonhuman organism incorporating one or more genes taken from a human organism (e.g., transgenic animals). Rep. Weldon and others clarified the amendment does not affect patents for non-human organisms even with some human genes, nor patents for human cells, tissues, organs, methods, drugs, or devices.

name: Recitation of specific numerical ranges generally not indefinite
description: Generally, the recitation of specific numerical ranges in a claim does not raise an issue of whether a claim is definite.
guidance: The mere presence of numerical ranges in a claim is not by itself a basis for a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection. Examiners should look to whether the claim's boundaries are discernible rather than treating numeric ranges as presumptively indefinite.

name: Narrow and broader ranges in the same claim can render claim indefinite
description: Use of a narrow numerical range that falls within a broader range in the same claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries of the claim are not discernible.
guidance: Description of examples and preferences belongs in the specification rather than in a single claim. If it's unclear whether the narrower range is a limitation or merely an example/preference, make a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection. Examiner should analyze whether the metes and bounds of the claim are clearly set forth. Examples of problematic language: (A) "a temperature of between 45 and 78 degrees Celsius, preferably between 50 and 60 degrees Celsius"; (B) "a predetermined quantity, for example, the maximum capacity."

name: Prefer narrower-range limitations in dependent claims or separate independent claims
description: Presenting a narrower range in a dependent claim (or another independent claim) is proper even if it falls within the broader range of the parent claim.
guidance: A dependent claim that sets forth a narrower range than its parent should not be rejected as indefinite merely because it falls within the parent's broader range. Example: claim 1 recites "resistance is 70-150 ohms" and claim 2 recites "resistance is 70-100 ohms" — claim 2 should not be rejected as indefinite for that reason.

name: Open-ended numerical ranges require careful definiteness analysis
description: Open-ended numerical ranges (e.g., "at least 20%") should be carefully analyzed for definiteness, particularly when dependent claims or other claim language appear to exclude the open-ended element.
guidance: Example caution: an independent claim recites "at least 20% sodium" while a dependent claim sets specific amounts of non-sodium ingredients adding to 100%, creating an ambiguity as to the 'at least' limitation unless percentages are expressly based on the weight of nonsodium ingredients. Examiners must resolve whether the claim language and specification make the scope clear.

name: Theoretical/impossible compositions do not automatically render claims indefinite
description: Claims that, in theory, could read on compositions impossible to formulate are not necessarily indefinite.
guidance: Court held that a composition claimed as 20-80% A, 20-80% B and 1-25% C was not indefinite merely because some combinations would total more than 100% (In re Kroekel). Subject matter that cannot exist in fact cannot anticipate or infringe, but that theoretical impossibility does not alone make the claim indefinite.

name: Maximum-only amount limits can be definite in context
description: A limitation specifying only a maximum amount (e.g., "maintained at less than 7 mole percent") does not automatically render a claim indefinite.
guidance: If the claim is clearly directed to a process or context where an upper limit makes sense, the absence of an explicit minimum does not necessarily mandate rejecting the claim as indefinite. Example: In re Kirsch held that imposing a maximum limit without a minimum does not require distorting the claim to preclude performance of the claimed process.

name: Meanings of certain open-ended phrases have been judicially defined
description: Some common phrases have been given specific meanings in reported cases (e.g., 'up to' and 'not more than X% by weight').
guidance: Case law: 'up to' includes zero as a lower limit (In re Mochel); 'a moisture content of not more than 70% by weight' can be read on dry material (Ex parte Khusid). Examiners and drafters should be aware of these interpretations when assessing or drafting claim language.

name: "Effective amount" requires assessment of disclosure support and function
description: The phrase 'an effective amount' may or may not be indefinite; the proper test is whether one skilled in the art could determine specific values for the amount based on the disclosure.
guidance: If the amount is not critical and the written disclosure (including examples) enables a skilled artisan to determine what is effective, the phrase can be definite (In re Halleck). Conversely, 'an effective amount' is indefinite if the claim fails to state the function to be achieved and more than one effect can be implied (In re Fredericksen). Recent decisions trend toward accepting 'effective amount' when read in light of supporting disclosure and absent prior art introducing uncertainty (Ex parte Skuballa). Examiners should consider whether the specification gives guidelines or intended utilities that permit determination of effective amounts.

name: Examiner procedure: apply 35 U.S.C. 112(b) when claim boundaries are unclear
description: When it is not clear whether a particular numerical expression is a claim limitation or merely an example/preference, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph) should be made.
guidance: Examiners should analyze the claim language and the specification to determine whether metes and bounds are set forth. Use case examples and the context of the disclosure to decide whether a limitation is definite; if not, issue a 112(b) rejection.

name: Data verification, validation, and reporting requirements
description: Performance data included in the PAR must be verified and validated; the Performance Information section describes key and supporting performance metrics and how results were verified/validated.
guidance: The PAR includes a Performance Data Verification and Validation subsection and uses audited financial statements and independent auditors' reports to support claims of data completeness, reliability, accuracy, and consistency. Performance audits and evaluations are documented in the report.

name: Examiner search and evidence resources
description: Examiners are expected to search both patent and non-patent literature and use available electronic databases and collections to compare claimed inventions to existing technical information.
guidance: PAR tracks use and growth of non-patent literature collections, full-text electronic journals/books, and databases available for searching; the agency emphasizes improving collections and machine/Manual translation resources for examiner support.

name: Liberal construction for inventions of exceptional merit
description: Even though an invention is not generic, if it is one of exceptional merit it is entitled to a liberal construction and a fair range of equivalents.
guidance: If a patented invention is especially meritorious, courts may construe its claims broadly and allow a wider range of equivalents than for ordinary patents. (Cited in text as a recognized rule.)

name: Evidential weight of a later patent
description: The grant of a subsequent patent is frequently said to raise a legal presumption of patentable difference from an earlier invention, but that presumption is limited and does not itself establish non-infringement.
guidance: Distinguish between improvements over prior structures and inventions of a different species. A later patent may embody things that are exclusive to the earlier patentee; Patent Office findings of patentable difference concern disclosure, not claim scope. The later patent is not evidence of non-infringement unless the earlier patent is shown to be specific (narrow) so that the later patent's claims neither improve nor embody the earlier claims. Cases (e.g., Kokomo, Herman v. Youngstown) illustrate limits and exceptions. The Commissioner’s interference determination may overcome or affect the presumption in some jurisdictions.

name: Structures made to evade the spirit but containing claimed elements infringe
description: Structures designed merely for the purpose of evading the spirit of the invention but which contain all the elements of the claims are infringements of the patent.
guidance: Adding an easily discarded part that may or may not be used by the purchaser will not avoid infringement if the accused device contains all claimed elements. Attempts to evade by artifice fail where the normal/easiest/effective use would infringe.

name: Normal/useful mode of use controls infringement analysis
description: A showing that the accused structure may occasionally be used in a manner that would not infringe does not avert infringement if the structure, when used in the normal, easiest, and most effective way, infringes.
guidance: Courts look at how the device is normally used; sporadic non-infringing uses are insufficient to defeat infringement where the ordinary use falls within the claims.

name: Infringement of composition patents depends on sameness/equivalence and proportions
description: Infringement of patents for compositions of matter depends upon sameness or equivalence of ingredients and upon substantial sameness of the proportions of those ingredients; omission of an ingredient avoids infringement; addition that substantially changes character avoids infringement.
guidance: Like mechanical combinations, omission of a claimed ingredient defeats infringement. Additions that materially alter character avoid infringement; trivial or insubstantial additions made to evade liability will not avoid infringement. Determination often requires chemical analysis.

name: Limits on monopolizing a claimed group via doctrine of equivalents
description: Where a patent states that each member of a group of substances can be used and some members cannot be so used, the patentee cannot later invoke the doctrine of equivalents to monopolize all members subsequently found suitable; a generic claim purporting to cover matter from any prescribed starting material is void if some members are unsuitable.
guidance: A specific claim limited to a particular suitable starting material may still be valid even if a generic claim in the same patent is not. The doctrine prevents patentees from claiming by equivalence what they expressly admitted was unsuitable.

name: Comparative utility alone is not determinative of infringement
description: The comparative utility of the plaintiff's and the defendant's process, machine, manufacture, or composition is not alone a criterion of infringement; constructing the patented thing imperfectly to diminish utility does not avoid infringement, nor does a defendant's superior machine that is nevertheless an addition to the claimed invention.
guidance: If a defendant's superiority results from an addition to the patented combination, that superiority does not avoid infringement even if the addition is patentable. However, if the defendant discovered an entirely different mode of construction/operation (a different species), it may avoid infringement. Comparative utility is relevant only when coupled with comparative character.

name: Species vs genus: different species do not infringe each other
description: A defendant's machine may be of a different species and thus cannot infringe a patent of a different species, though both might infringe a genus patent of which they are species.
guidance: Determine whether accused device and claimed invention are same species or merely species of a common genus; species-level differences can defeat infringement even if genus claims might read on both.

name: Original disclosure exclusion and petition under 37 CFR 1.183
description: Information forming part of the original disclosure (written specification including claims, drawings, and incorporated preliminary amendments) will not be expunged under 37 CFR 1.59 and requests to expunge such material must be filed under 37 CFR 1.183.
guidance: A petition under 1.183 must explain why justice requires waiver of the rules to permit expungement of original-disclosure material. Such petitions will ordinarily not be favorably entertained because original disclosures are scanned for record-keeping and changing the record may not be possible.

name: Definition of 'material to patentability' (materiality standard)
description: Materiality is defined as any information which the examiner considers as being important to a determination of patentability of the claims.
guidance: The examiner (or other appropriate Office official) is responsible for considering whether any portion or all of submitted information is material; if found material, petition to expunge will be denied and information becomes part of official file.

name: Do not make subsequent final rejection on prior art not of record against amended claims
description: A second or any subsequent action on the merits ... should not be made final if it includes a rejection, on prior art not of record, of any claim amended to include limitations which should reasonably have been expected to be claimed.
guidance: If claims were amended to add limitations that ought reasonably to have been claimed, the examiner should avoid making a subsequent Office action final when relying on prior art not of record; this protects applicants who amend to supply omissions that would prompt a reasonable new rejection.

name: Examiner caution where applicant fails to point out patentable novelty in amended case
description: In the consideration of claims in an amended case where no attempt is made to point out the patentable novelty, the examiner should be on guard not to allow such claims.
guidance: If applicant does not indicate the patentable novelty when amending, examiner should scrutinize and may finally reject claims if, in the opinion of the examiner, they are clearly open to rejection on grounds of record. See MPEP § 714.04.

name: Transitional after-final practice under 37 CFR 1.129(a)
description: An applicant in an application ... that has been pending for at least two years as of June 8, 1995 ... is entitled to have a first submission entered and considered on the merits after final rejection if the first submission and the fee set forth in § 1.17(r) are filed prior to the filing of an appeal brief and prior to abandonment of the application. The finality of the final rejection is automatically withdrawn upon the timely filing of the submission and payment of the fee.
guidance: A second submission and fee may be similarly filed prior to filing an appeal brief and prior to abandonment. The section does not apply to applications filed after June 8, 1995, or to reissue/design/reexamination proceedings. 'Submission' includes IDS, amendments to specification/claims/drawings, new substantive argument, or new evidence. Use form paragraph 7.41.01 to notify applicant that application qualifies under 37 CFR 1.129(a). Where an amendment was timely filed without the 1.17(r) fee, examiners may consider the amendment in expedited manner per MPEP § 714.13 and issue advisory actions about entry; applicant may pay fee later to obtain entry as a 1.129(a) submission. Form paragraph 7.42.01 should be used to notify applicant that finality has been withdrawn in transitional cases.

name: Partial refund conditions (search fees)
description: Partial refund applies where the EPO can make partial use of the earlier search report for drawing up the international search report.
guidance: Typical cases: where claims of the later application are broader than those of the earlier application (generalisation) or where later claims are limited by a feature not disclosed in the earlier application but relating to the same invention as that searched in the earlier application.

name: Objective of the international search
description: The objective is to discover the prior art relevant for determining whether the claimed invention is novel and involves an inventive step; results are communicated in an international search report.
guidance: The ISA may be exempted from searching some or all claimed subject-matter in cases (e.g., multiple inventions, excluded subject-matter). The ISA also formulates a preliminary, non-binding opinion on novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability and, where appropriate, on added subject-matter, unity, insufficient disclosure, clarity/support issues, and formal defects.

name: Basis for the search — interpretation of claims
description: The examiner should interpret claims consistently with EPO/ISPE guidance when determining the subject-matter to search.
guidance: Section B-III, 3.2 applies mutatis mutandis; see ISPE Guidelines for details on claim construction in searches.

name: Treatment of amended claims or incorporated missing parts/elements
description: Amended claims or claims incorporating missing parts/elements affect the basis and scope of the search and should be handled according to the relevant Guidelines (section begins in text).
guidance: Examiners should follow the guidance in subsequent sections (not fully included in this chunk) regarding searching amended claims and incorporated matter; informal clarification procedures may apply.

name: Means-plus-function claim construction scope
description: The recited “means” for performing the specified function shall be construed to cover the corresponding “structure or material” described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: By choosing to use a means-plus-function limitation and invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f), applicant limits that claim limitation to the disclosed structure, i.e., implementation by hardware or the combination of hardware and software, and equivalents thereof. Examiner should not construe the limitation as covering pure software implementation if corresponding structure is disclosed as hardware or hardware+software.

name: Insufficiency of corresponding structure -> indefiniteness
description: If there is no corresponding structure disclosed in the specification (e.g., limitation only supported by software and does not correspond to an algorithm and the computer or microprocessor programmed with the algorithm), the limitation should be deemed indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Such a limitation should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 112 second paragraph). Claims must be interpreted as a whole; a means-plus-function limitation lacking structural support is not necessarily directed to software per se unless other structural limitations are missing.

name: Interrelationship of indefiniteness, written description, and enablement
description: A claim limitation found indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for failure to disclose sufficient corresponding structure will also lack written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and may not be enabled to support the full scope of the claim.
guidance: Examiners should consider whether the disclosure contains sufficient information to enable one skilled in the art to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention (enablement) and whether written description support exists (see MPEP § 2161.01, § 2163.03, § 2164.08).

name: Requirement that disclosure clearly link structure to function
description: The structure disclosed in the written description is corresponding structure only if the specification or prosecution history clearly links or associates that structure to the function recited in the means- (or step-) plus-function claim limitation.
guidance: This 'clear link or association' is required to satisfy the quid pro quo for using 112(f). If one of ordinary skill cannot identify what structure/material/acts perform the claimed function, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is appropriate (cases: B. Braun, Medical Instrumentation & Diagnostics, Telcordia).

name: Three situations warranting 112(b) rejection when 112(f) invoked
description: (1) unclear whether a claim limitation invokes 112(f); (2) 112(f) is invoked and there is no disclosure or insufficient disclosure of structure/material/acts for performing the claimed function; (3) 112(f) is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link or associate the disclosed structure/material/acts to the claimed function.
guidance: If any of these situations exist, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 112 second paragraph) may be appropriate.

name: Three‑prong analysis and determination of invocation
description: Perform the 3-prong analysis to determine whether a claim limitation should be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f): examine claim language, the specification, and how those of ordinary skill would understand the claim in light of the disclosure.
guidance: If ambiguous words make the 3-prong analysis inconclusive, examiner should determine whether the words recite sufficiently definite structure that performs the claimed function; applicant may present arguments or amend to clarify whether 112(f) applies.

name: Single means claim problem and rejection
description: A 'single means' claim that recites a means-plus-function limitation as the only limitation cannot invoke 112(f) (which applies only to an element 'in a combination') and therefore such a claim will cover all means of performing the function and is likely non-enabling.
guidance: Single means claims often read on subject matter not enabled by the specification and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112 first paragraph). Distinguish claims that recite multiple functional limitations (each treated as separate elements) from true single element claims (In re Hyatt).

name: Record and Office action clarity when invoking 112(f)
description: When an examiner interprets a claim limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the Office action should specify that 112(f) has been applied and should specify what the specification identifies as the corresponding structure (or attempt to identify the structure to facilitate prior art search).
