guidance: A claim limitation that explicitly uses the term 'means' and includes functional language without corresponding structure is presumed to invoke 112(f). Examiners should state the presumption and the 3-prong analysis on the record; these presumptions are rebuttable.

name: Applicant rebuttal and amendment options
description: In response to an Office action determining 112(f) was invoked, applicant may (1) present a sufficient showing that the limitation recites sufficient structure to avoid interpretation under 112(f), or (2) amend the claim to recite sufficient structure to avoid 112(f).
guidance: If applicant does not want the limitation interpreted under 112(f), amendment can clarify structural content or arguments can establish structural content; see MPEP § 2187 for form paragraphs.

name: Allowance notation for claims treated under 112(f)
description: When allowing a claim that was treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the examiner should indicate that the claim was interpreted under 112(f) in the reasons for allowance and clarify the associated structure if not already of record.
guidance: This ensures the public and applicant understand the claim construction used during prosecution and helps avoid later confusion.

name: Two-step analysis for construing means-plus-function limitations
description: First, define the particular function of the limitation (construe the function to include the limitations in the claim language and only those limitations). Second, identify the corresponding structure in the specification that performs that function, where 'corresponding' means the specification or prosecution history clearly links that structure to the recited function.
guidance: Follow Golight/Budde/Cardiac Pacemakers framework. If the specification provides a definition for the limitation, interpret the limitation according to that definition; otherwise exercise informed judgment applying case law (B. Braun, Elekta).

name: Prior art application to means-plus-function and equivalence prima facie
description: Applying a prior art reference to a means-plus-function limitation requires that the prior art element perform the identical function specified in the claim, and the examiner must show that the prior art structure or step is the same as or equivalent to the corresponding structure described in the specification.
guidance: The examiner must provide a 'sound basis for believing' the prior art structure or acts could perform the claimed function (Spada). Factors supporting equivalence include performing the identical function in substantially the same way and producing substantially the same results (Kemco, Graver Tank concepts). The examiner should explain and provide rationale in the Office action when asserting equivalence (In re Bond).

name: Timing of ownership/invention — 'at the time the invention was made' / conception
description: Common ownership (or a joint research agreement) must have existed on or before the date the claimed invention was made (i.e., when conception was complete). Ownership obtained after the invention date cannot be used to disqualify prior art.
guidance: Invention timing follows case law (e.g., Mergenthaler, In re Tansel, Pfaff v. Wells Electronics) — invention is 'made' when conception is complete and the invention is ready for patenting (e.g., sufficient drawings or descriptions). Examine facts to determine whether ownership or JRA was in effect on that date; foreign/foreign filing issues noted (pre-AIA 104 interplay).

name: Definition and statutory requirements for 'joint research agreement' under pre-AIA 103(c) (CREATE Act)
description: For pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as amended by the CREATE Act, a 'joint research agreement' is a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. To qualify, (A) the claimed invention must have been made by or on behalf of the parties to the JRA that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention must result from activities within the scope of the JRA; and (C) the patent application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA.
guidance: The JRA need only be in effect on or before the date the later invention was made (not required to be in effect on or before the prior art date). The applicant must comply with the statute and rules of practice (including disclosure). The burden to prove JRA applicability rests on applicant once prima facie obviousness is established.

name: Effect on reissue and recapture doctrine considerations
description: The recapture doctrine may prevent presentation of claims in a reissue that were amended or canceled to overcome a 103(a) rejection based on prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) that could not be disqualified under 103(c) during original prosecution.
guidance: If an examiner determines recapture may apply in a reissue, consultation with the Office of Patent Legal Administration via the Technology Center Quality Assurance Specialist should be initiated. CREATE Act timing and prior prosecution history must be considered when evaluating reissue claims and disqualification.

name: Anticipation requires a single reference teaching every element
description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element of the claim is found, either expressly or inherently, in a single prior art reference under its broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: Elements must be arranged as required by the claim, but identity of terminology is not required (ipsissimis verbis test not required). If the claim covers alternatives, any known structure/composition within the claim scope can anticipate (Verdegaal; Brown v. 3M). See MPEP § 2114 for related guidance.

name: Extra references to show primary reference has enabled disclosure
description: When the primary reference discloses the claimed subject matter identically, extra references may be used to show the primary reference had an enabled disclosure (e.g., methods of making).
guidance: Motivation to combine is not required when the primary reference already teaches all claim elements; secondary patents/publications can be evidence that methods or enabling information were in the public’s possession (In re Samour; In re Donohue).

name: Reference expressly naming a species anticipates that species regardless of other species listed
description: When a reference clearly names the claimed species, that disclosure anticipates the species claim no matter how many other species are named in the reference.
guidance: Even comprehensive listings (e.g., Merck Index analogies) that include the specific compound are sufficient to anticipate (Ex parte A; In re Sivaramakrishnan). Unexpected properties of a species disclosed among many may not avoid anticipation unless the reference fails to describe the species as such.

name: Generic disclosure can anticipate a species if the species can be 'at once envisaged'
description: A generic disclosure will anticipate a claimed species when a person of ordinary skill would 'at once envisage' the specific species from the disclosure (i.e., be able to draw the structure or write the name immediately).
guidance: Consider factual aspects: size of genus, limitation/delineation of substituents, presence of preferred embodiments, and whether PHOSITA could immediately envisage the species (Sanofi; Kennametal; In re Petering; In re Schauman). If significant selection/combination from lists is required, anticipation may not be found.

name: Arguments about nonanalogous art or teaching away not germane to § 102 rejections
description: Claims that alleged anticipatory prior art is 'nonanalogous art' or 'teaches away' or is not recognized as solving the problem are not germane to a rejection under § 102.
guidance: Such arguments are relevant to obviousness (§ 103) but do not affect a § 102 anticipation rejection (Twin Disc; In re Self). Examiners should focus on whether the reference discloses the claimed elements, not whether it is analogous or teaches away.

name: Prohibited marketing/labeling practices
description: Each of the following acts, if performed in connection with the sale, offering for sale, or advertising of sexually or asexually reproducible plant material or tubers or parts of tubers, is prohibited: (1) Use of the words 'U.S. Protected Variety' or any word or number importing that the material is a variety protected under certificate, when it is not. (2) Use of any wording importing that the material is a variety for which an application for plant variety protection is pending, when it is not. (3) Use of either the phrase 'Unauthorized Propagation Prohibited' or 'Unauthorized Seed Multiplication Prohibited' or similar phrase without reasonable basis. Any reasonable basis expires one year after the first sale of the variety except as justified thereafter by a pending application or a certificate still in force. (4) Failure to use the name of a variety for which a certificate of protection has been issued under this chapter, even after the expiration of the certificate, except that certain grass and forage seeds may be sold without a variety name unless state law requires it (7 U.S.C. §2568(a)).
guidance: These labeling/advertising prohibitions can trigger PVPO cease-and-desist orders after hearing; they set specific limits on claims about protected status and the use of 'Unauthorized' legend language without a continuing reasonable basis.

name: Pay — who and what is payable
description: Rules on pay of adjutants general, heads of staff departments at state camps, officers authorized for pay at joint encampments, pay of disbursing officers, assistant surgeons; extra pay items (keeping horse), longevity pay, pay of officers on special duty preparing camp ground, pay of members of damaged property boards, pay of deceased soldier claims, and other enumerated entitlements.
guidance: Many specific holdings on eligibility and computation of pay; e.g., allotments under §1661 cannot be used to reimburse state losses in some cases (C. 20402). (Militia XI items.)

name: Is the claim directed to an abstract idea? (Step 2A)
description: Identify the claim limitation(s) that correspond to an abstract idea and explain how such is similar to concepts previously held by the courts to be abstract. A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim.
guidance: Courts have found certain concepts to be 'abstract ideas', for example fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. Identify limitations and explain similarity to judicial holdings (refer to the Quick Reference Sheet). Choose A, B, or C: A) No — conclude SME analysis. B) Yes, but streamlined analysis appropriate — eligibility self-evident; conclude SME analysis. C) Yes — identify limitations and continue to Step 2B.

name: Streamlined analysis applicability
description: When the eligibility determination is self-evident, a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
guidance: Use streamlined analysis (Step 2A choice B) where applicant's claimed invention is not focused on the abstract idea and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an abstract idea such that others cannot practice it. Refer to the February 2015 Training Slides for examples of a streamlined analysis.

name: Identify limitations that set forth the abstract idea and explain why
description: Explicitly identify the steps/limitations in the claim that 'set forth or describe the abstract idea' and explain why those limitations are abstract.
guidance: Explain how the limitations correspond to abstract-idea concepts (e.g., 'the steps of receiving, filtering, and generating describe manipulating information by comparing and sorting the information based on a subscriber’s preferences' — 'These steps describe the abstract idea of comparing and organizing information for transmission'). Note that 'specifying the type of information being manipulated' does not render the idea less abstract. Cite analogous cases (e.g., Cyberfone, SmartGene) as guidance. Remember: 'Judicial exceptions need not be old or long-prevalent.'

name: Identify additional elements beyond the abstract idea (Step 2B A)
description: Determine whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the abstract idea identified in Step 2A.
guidance: Choose 1 or 2: 1) No — conclude SME analysis by making a § 101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). Identify whether elements in the disclosure could be added to make the claim eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant. 2) Yes — list the additional claim elements (e.g., 'a transmission server with a memory that stores subscriber preferences and a microprocessor that performs the steps...'). Continue to evaluate significance under Step 2B.

name: Evaluate whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
description: Identify whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, provide an 'inventive concept' such that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.
guidance: Consider reasons supporting the significance of additional elements, which can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic computer functions); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending routine activities at a high level); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment. Anti-patterns: merely adding 'apply it' language, generic computer functions, field-of-use limitations, or mere data gathering do not amount to significantly more.

name: Consideration of elements individually and in combination; outcome determination
description: Complete the evaluation by deciding whether additional elements, taken individually or as a combination, result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the abstract idea.
guidance: If Yes — conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements (explain reasoning in Office action if helpful). If No — conclude the SME analysis by making a § 101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). Note: 'absence of complete preemption does not equate to eligibility.'

name: Suggesting claim amendments and identifying candidate disclosure elements
description: Identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to the claim that may make it eligible, and consider suggesting such amendments to the applicant.
guidance: Examples include disclosed elements that transmit the alert over a wireless communication channel to activate an application, cause display of the alert, and enable connection to a data source over the Internet — elements that may, in combination, provide meaningful limitations and solve an Internet-centric problem (analogous to DDR Holdings). Provide specific suggested claim language where appropriate.

name: Office action drafting and sample rejection language
description: When concluding the claim is ineligible, include a clearly articulated § 101 rejection in the Office action with supporting reasons and sample language.
guidance: Sample rejection language is provided (e.g., 'Claim 1 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception...'). Use appropriate form paragraphs (7.05, 7.05.015, 7.05.01) for Office Action text. If concluding eligibility, an explanation is not necessary unless clarification would benefit the record.

name: Examiner's burden and evidentiary guidance
description: Examiners must 'clearly articulate the reasons why the claimed invention is not eligible.'
guidance: While factual evidence that an idea is abstract is not required for a prima facie rejection, examiners are encouraged to cite any additional resources that support their rejections. Provide clear reasoning in the record; include citations to precedent or training materials as appropriate.

name: Burden of persuasion in IPR
description: In an IPR, the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable; this burden of persuasion never shifts to Patent Owner.
guidance: Cites Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech. and 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3). A petition must identify with particularity the evidence supporting each ground for each claim. The Board applies the preponderance of the evidence standard in the Final Written Decision (35 U.S.C. § 318(a)).

name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. §102
description: A single prior art reference must expressly or inherently disclose each claim limitation; the reference must describe the claimed invention with sufficient precision and detail to establish that the subject matter existed in the prior art.
guidance: Cites Finisar Corp. v. DirecTV Grp., Verve, LLC v. Crane Cams, Inc. and In re Preda. Inherency for anticipation requires that the missing descriptive material be 'necessarily present,' not merely probable. Consider not only explicit teachings but the inferences a POSITA would reasonably draw.

name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 (Graham/KSR framework)
description: Apply the Graham factual inquiries (scope/content of prior art; differences between the prior art and claims; level of ordinary skill; objective evidence) and KSR's expansive/flexible approach to obviousness.
guidance: KSR explains that combining old elements that perform their known functions in a predictable way can be obvious. A petitioner must show a POSITA would have been motivated to combine references and would have had a reasonable expectation of success. A precise teaching directed to the claimed subject matter is not necessary; any known need or problem can provide motivation to combine.

name: Enablement / sufficiency of prior art disclosure
description: A prior art reference must provide enough disclosure (precision, detail, and enablement) to teach or enable practice of the claimed invention for it to anticipate or to be used in an obviousness combination.
guidance: Patent Owner may argue a reference is non-enabling. The Board examines the reference's examples, claimed preferred embodiments, and whether a POSITA could practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Lack of enabling disclosure can defeat anticipation or reduce weight of a reference in an obviousness analysis.

name: Weight to be given to preferred embodiments and examples in prior art
description: When assessing a reference, the Board considers explicit disclosures, preferred embodiments, individual claims, and worked examples as stronger evidence of what the reference teaches.
guidance: The decision stresses that preferred embodiments and specifically-claimed variants (e.g., Stafford's explicit R338L and R338A recitations) materially affect whether a reference teaches a limitation. The Board will treat a reference 'for all that it teaches' and will not ignore adjacent or secondary statements (e.g., gene therapy discussion next to vector disclosure).

name: Priority/chain-of-priority and its effect on prior art dates
description: Establishing the correct effective filing/priority date is necessary to determine which prior art is available against the claims.
guidance: The Board considers the chain of continuation and priority claims (e.g., PCT and foreign filings) and accepts parties' unopposed assumptions where appropriate. The assumed priority date affects whether references are pre- or post-date for anticipation/obviousness analysis.

name: To preserve right to petition, applicant must traverse (37 CFR 1.144)
description: To preserve the right to petition a final restriction requirement to the Director, the applicant must have traversed the restriction (i.e., distinctly and specifically pointed out errors).
guidance: A petition from a requirement for restriction may be deferred until after final action on or allowance of elected claims but must be filed not later than appeal. A petition will not be considered if reconsideration (37 CFR 1.143) was not requested (see § 1.181). If applicant failed to distinctly and specifically point out errors, election treated as without traverse and right to petition is generally lost.

name: Treatment of claims held to be drawn to nonelected inventions (withdrawn under 37 CFR 1.142(b))
description: Claims held to be drawn to nonelected inventions are withdrawn from further consideration pursuant to 37 CFR 1.142(b); examiner should clearly set forth reasons why the withdrawn claims are not readable on the elected invention.
guidance: Applicant may traverse under 37 CFR 1.143. If a final restriction is made, applicant may petition under 37 CFR 1.144. Examiners should treat withdrawn claims as directed in MPEP §§ 821.01–821.04 and use the appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 8.05 for claims withdrawn with traverse; 8.06 for without traverse).

name: If examiner withdraws restriction (in whole/part), must state rejoin groups and act on merits
description: If examiner determines restriction is improper in whole or in part, the next Office action should clearly state the restriction is withdrawn, specify which groups have been rejoined, and give an action on the merits of all claims directed to the elected invention and any rejoined invention.
guidance: Use form paragraph 8.45 (and 8.46/8.47 variants as appropriate) to notify applicant when rejoining claims. Rejoined claims must be examined for patentability under 37 CFR 1.104.

name: Rejoinder eligibility: must depend from or require all limitations of an allowable claim
description: To be eligible for rejoinder, a claim to a nonelected invention must depend from or otherwise require all the limitations of an allowable claim (generic, linking, or subcombination claim). A withdrawn claim that does not require all the limitations of an allowable claim will not be rejoined.
guidance: Applicant should amend nonelected claims during prosecution to require the limitations of the elected invention to retain the right to rejoinder. Rejoinder between product and process claims requires that process claims depend from the allowable product claim limitations as appropriate (see MPEP § 821.04(b)).

name: Withdrawal of restriction removes 35 U.S.C. 121 protections; watch for double patenting
description: Once the restriction requirement is withdrawn, the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 121 are no longer applicable; claims presented in continuation/divisional applications that are anticipated by or include all limitations of an allowable claim may be subject to provisional statutory and/or nonstatutory double patenting rejections.
guidance: The examiner should call applicant's attention to potential double patenting and the possible need for a terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321(c)). See In re Ziegler and MPEP § 804.01 for guidance and case law.

name: Use of specific form paragraphs to communicate status and actions
description: Examiners should use the prescribed form paragraphs for various situations: e.g., 8.22 (Requirement for Election and Means for Traversal), 8.25/8.25.01/8.25.02 (election/traverse acknowledgments), 8.05/8.06 (claims withdrawn with/without traverse), 8.03/8.24 (in condition for allowance notices and replies to final), 8.04/8.26 (election by original presentation and nonresponsive amendment), 8.45–8.50 series (rejoinder/withdrawal notices).
guidance: Selecting the correct form paragraph communicates the legal/consequential status (e.g., preservation of petition rights, cancellation risk, rejoin outcome) and provides the applicant with proper instructions and time periods. Examiner notes in form paragraphs indicate bracketed fields to populate and contextual rules to observe.

name: Akamai's effect on divided performance liability
description: Akamai arguably made it easier for patent owners to hold a person liable for induced infringement of a method claim when no single person performed all the steps of the method.
guidance: While Akamai allows suits against those who induced collective infringement, litigators and courts must still grapple with how to weigh circumstantial evidence of intent in these more strained scenarios; understanding and applying the nexus/control/mitigating-evidence framework can help close the prior loophole without abandoning the specific-intent requirement.

name: Literal infringement vs. doctrine of equivalents
description: To determine literal infringement, the accused device is compared against the elements of the patent claim: if the device includes every requirement of the claim, it literally infringes. If it does not literally infringe, it may still infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if a component of the accused device that does not literally meet the corresponding requirement 'performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result.' Graver Tank & Mfg. Co. v. Linde Air Prods. Co., 339 U.S. 605.
guidance: Use the Graver Tank function-way-result test to assess whether non-literal components nonetheless infringe under equivalents; first attempt literal comparison element-by-element, then apply equivalents test only where literal infringement fails.

name: Prior art circumscribes doctrine of equivalents (ensnarement principle)
description: An important limitation on the doctrine of equivalents is that it is always circumscribed by the prior art: if the aspect alleged to infringe under equivalents would not have been patentable at the time the patent was sought because it would also cover the prior art, it cannot form the basis for a judgment of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. (Wilson Sporting Goods Co. v. David Geoffrey & Assocs., 904 F.2d 677).
guidance: When applying the doctrine of equivalents, evaluate the scope of prior art contemporaneous with the patent application; deny equivalents-based infringement if the asserted equivalent would have anticipated or rendered unpatentable a hypothetical claim of that breadth.

name: Plaintiff bears burden to show a patentable equivalent (no burden-shifting)
description: Because the plaintiff bears the burden of proving patent infringement, 'the burden of showing that there could exist a patentable equivalent to a claim also falls on the plaintiff.' Wilson Sporting Goods, 904 F.2d at 684.
guidance: Require the patentee/plaintiff to demonstrate that a hypothetical claim broadened to cover the accused device would have been patentable (i.e., would not have been anticipated or rendered obvious by the prior art); do not treat this as shifting the defendant's burden to prove invalidity.

name: Hypothetical claim used to test ensnarement must be properly broadened and patentable
description: In the district court, the patentee submitted hypothetical claims expanded to cover the accused device; the court concluded that neither hypothetical claim was proper 'because neither had been broadened in scope,' and therefore vacated the jury verdict of infringement.
guidance: When courts require a hypothetical claim for ensnarement analysis, the hypothetical must be a properly broadened claim that would literally encompass the accused product; the court then assesses whether that broadened claim would have been patentable over the prior art.

name: Evidence standard for enhanced efficacy (experimental/clinical data)
description: Enhanced/therapeutic efficacy must be validated by experimental data; mere demonstration of enhanced bioavailability is not sufficient unless it is specifically claimed and established that it leads to enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
guidance: Comparative data must directly show superior ability to treat a patient (e.g., improved clinical outcome). Data such as bioavailability, flowability, disintegration, dissolution, etc., may be insufficient in India unless connected causally and experimentally to improved therapeutic effect. The Novartis precedent requires research data linking the claimed property to therapeutic benefit.

name: Novelty determination as a way to avoid Section 3(d)
description: If the subject matter is considered novel by the Controller (or is made novel by amendment/argument), it cannot be treated as a known process/substance under Section 3(d).
guidance: When novelty can be established, submit a detailed and persuasive reply on novelty and inventive step together with supportive arguments related to technical effects/advantages of the claim features to rebut Section 3(d) objections.

name: Process/method claims—'mere use' prohibition and escape routes
description: Section 3(d) bars the 'mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus' unless such known process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant.
guidance: To overcome Section 3(d) for process claims, either (a) claim a process that results in a new product, (b) show the process employs at least one new reactant, or (c) demonstrate a significant improvement over existing prior art (with supporting data) showing the claimed method is more than a mere use of known method.

name: Judicial application—Novartis precedent
description: Novartis AG v. Union of India: the Court held that for pharmaceutical inventions the test of efficacy is tied to function/utility (therapeutic efficacy), and that enhanced bioavailability alone is not sufficient to meet Section 3(d).
guidance: Rely on Novartis when arguing what types of data and which endpoints are relevant: must specifically claim and establish that a claimed property increases therapeutic efficacy in treating disease.

name: Anti-evergreening principle and intent scrutiny
description: Section 3(d) is intended as additional scrutiny to prevent evergreening of chemical compounds and to provide fair competition rather than allowing minor modifications to extend monopoly.
guidance: Examiners and courts are alert to attempts to extend patent term by claiming trivial modifications; applicants should be prepared to show substantive, demonstrated improvements in therapeutic efficacy (for pharma) or genuine technical advances for other fields.

name: Prosecution strategy—what to include in replies
description: When faced with a Section 3(d) objection, applicants should assess novelty status and, if necessary, present arguments on novelty/inventive step and present technical effects/advantages shown by the claimed features.
guidance: If the claim falls within Section 3(d) categories, produce experimental/comparative data that directly demonstrate enhanced efficacy (therapeutic effect for drugs). If novelty can be established, argue that the subject matter is not a 'known substance/process' and therefore outside Section 3(d). Tailor responses to emphasize functional improvements tied to the statutory test of efficacy.

name: Eligibility to file an IPR
description: A person who is not the owner of the patent (the petitioner) may initiate an IPR, but an IPR is not available to: the owner of the patent; a petitioner or real party-in-interest who filed a civil action in federal district court challenging validity of a claim (with a limited exception for counterclaims); a petitioner/real-party-in-interest/party-in-privity who has not filed the IPR within one year of being served with an infringement complaint; or a petitioner/real-party-in-interest/party-in-privity who is estopped from challenging the claim(s).
guidance: See 35 U.S.C. §§312, 315, and 37 C.F.R. §42.101. Careful pre-filing clearance is required to ensure no prior civil action, timing, or estoppel bars the petition.

name: Statement of precise relief requested and per-claim requirements
description: For each claim challenged, the petition must state the precise relief requested and include: a construction of the claim (including references to the patent specification for some claim formats); the statutory grounds for the challenge (35 U.S.C. §102 and/or §103); and a discussion of the invalidity of the claim specifying where each claim element is found in the prior art.
guidance: Include clear claim constructions and tie each element to prior art; ambiguous or generalized arguments weaken the petition and risk exclusion of evidence. See 35 U.S.C. ¶312 and 37 C.F.R. §42.104.

name: Evidence citation and specificity requirements
description: The petition must include references to evidence by exhibit number, state the relevance of the evidence to the respective validity challenge, and reference the specific portions of the evidence that support the challenge.
guidance: The PTAB may exclude or give no weight to evidence where the petitioner fails to state its relevance or identify specific portions that support the challenge (35 U.S.C. ¶312(a)(3) and 37 C.F.R. §42.104(b)(5)). Be explicit about which document pages/lines support each claim element.

name: Use of claim charts (recommended evidence organization)
description: A two-column claim chart with claim elements in the left column and the corresponding quotation or specific reference in the right column is a useful guide for the Board in evaluating claims against prior art.
guidance: Adopt claim charts to clearly map claim elements to specific prior-art passages or exhibits; this improves clarity and helps prevent exclusion for lack of specificity.

name: Institution standard (35 U.S.C. §314)
description: The drafting goal is to convince the Director there 'is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner will prevail with respect to at least 1' of the patent claims challenged.
guidance: Target the petition to meet the §314 reasonable-likelihood threshold, but recognize that petitions should, when possible, be drafted to do more than just clear this bar to create a substantive trial record advantage.

name: Fourteenth Defence: Ambiguity / indefiniteness in the claims
description: Denial that the claim defines the invention with sufficient precision and completeness to distinguish it from other inventions — i.e., claim is ambiguous, uncertain, or unintelligible, rendering the patent void.
guidance: The claim is 'the life of the patent' and must clearly draw the line of monopoly. If a claim conveys no idea, is uncertain about essential characteristics, or expresses multiple inventions leaving the intended scope doubtful, it is inoperative. In multi-claim patents, defective claims do not invalidate other sufficient claims; each claim stands or falls on its own. Authorities and examples are cited.

name: Eighteenth Defence: Non-coverage of defendant's art (non-infringement)
description: Denial that the art or instrument employed by the defendant is covered by the patent (i.e., assertion that the defendant's product/process does not fall within the scope of the patent claims).
guidance: Introduces the non-infringement line of defence; further elaboration appears subsequently in the treatise. (In context this is the beginning of the group of defences attacking whether the defendant's practice is within the claimed monopoly.)

name: Inorganic compound with specific feature — claim and inventive-step review
description: For an inorganic compound, name and chemical formula alone may not specify the subject matter because physical property or configuration (microstructure, e.g., crystal form, unit surface area) can differ; therefore, review of specific property shall be included in the claim regardless of explicit statement.
guidance: Determine whether it can be expected that the compound with specific property stated in the specification is produced by adoption/combination of components given the level of technology; do not determine inventive step without taking account of specific property differences even when name/formula are the same.

name: Product-by-use (compound 'for ~') construction
description: In case of a chemical compound, use limitation stated by 'for~' (e.g. 'Chemical compound Z for Y') is considered as indicating only utility, and is construed as the chemical compound without the use limitation (e.g. 'Chemical compound Z').
guidance: If a claimed chemical compound is disclosed in the prior art, the chemical compound with a use limitation is deemed to lack novelty. Example: 'Chemical compound Z for killing insects' reads as 'Chemical compound Z' and lacks novelty if Z is in prior art.

name: Enantiomer novelty (disclosure from racemate)
description: If an enantiomer is specifically disclosed in the prior art while a racemate (racemic mixture) is stated, the enantiomer is considered to lack novelty. If the existence of the enantiomer can be found out from the disclosure or easily carried out by a skilled person, it may be deemed disclosed.
guidance: Court verdict examples: where prior art disclosed racemate and teaching allowed identification/preparation of individual enantiomers, the enantiomer claim was anticipated.

name: Alloy inventions — when alloy guidelines apply
description: Chapter applies to an invention relating to alloying technique (C22C). For other fields, apply if alloy structure/property/use are specified through alloying components and numerical limitation of each component.
guidance: If claims merely recite that a product comprises an alloy plating formed by a plating solution (without alloy structure/property/composition ranges), alloy guidelines may not apply. But a manufacturing method claim that includes specific alloy component ranges does trigger the alloy guidelines.

name: Description requirements — grounds and embodiment for numeric composition limits
description: If a numerical limitation to a composition range is stated in claims, grounds and embodiment should be described in the description; exception when it is recognized that the alloy can be specified and carried out easily.
guidance: Maximum and minimum limits must be clear; ambiguous terms not allowed. For every limited range state reasons for limits, significant effect across the whole span, and concrete reasons for synergy of elements. Failure to disclose may lead to cyclic tests/trial-and-error and not satisfy disclosure requirements.

name: Embodiment sufficiency criteria
description: Whether an embodiment is specified is determined: (1) at least one embodiment with a composition range consistent with the claims satisfies Article 42(3)i; (2) if an embodiment lacks essential alloying elements or includes non-claimed alloying elements (except inevitable impurities), it's not representative; (3) specific content of each alloying element should be specified in embodiment; (4) effects should be specifically stated (not abstract/subjective).
guidance: One representative embodiment may be enough for disclosure, but proving significant effect across a numerical range often requires more than a single example (esp. near range limits).

name: Manufacturing method disclosure for alloys
description: Even if the claimed invention is directed to a product alloy, the manufacturing method (melting, casting, heating, machining, etc.) should be stated in detail for a skilled person to reproduce the alloy.
guidance: A manufacturing method can be simply stated if the alloy can be manufactured by normal methods. Distinguish between smelting/refining methods and methods that alter structure/property of a parent metal (these can be distinct inventions).

name: Claim requirements — limitation of alloy composition
description: An alloy's composition that achieves intended properties or use should be specified; reciting only alloying elements without composition ranges typically fails to particularly point out the invention.
guidance: Specify composition ranges for each alloying element (e.g., C:a-b wt%, Si:c-d wt%, ...). When issuing a rejection for lack of particulation, state reasonable grounds in detail after reviewing full disclosure.

name: Claim requirements — overly broad composition ranges
description: If a composition range is too broad (e.g., constituents with 0-100% ranges), except special cases, the claim should be deemed not clearly described because the alloy's structure/property/use can change across the range.
guidance: Special cases include homogeneous solid solution, amorphous alloy, commercial alloy notifying its composition, and alloys included in industrial standards (KS, ASTM, JIS, DIN), where composition ranges may not need specification.

name: Impurity recitation and allowable ranges
description: An element in claims cannot be treated as an impurity unless defined as such in the specification or by common knowledge; allowable ranges of impurities should be stated in the description and upper limits specified in claims when impurities greatly impact property/use.
guidance: Allowable impurity ranges are typically given as an upper limit (e.g., '0.3 wt% or less'). When possible, state ranges in the description for publication clarity.

name: Amendment adding numerical range — new matter test
description: When claim is amended to include a new numerical range, if the new numerical range and the reasons for it are not disclosed in the original description, it is deemed an addition of new matter.
guidance: Examples provided: adding specific wt% ranges in amended claims when not present originally constitutes new matter.

name: Novelty — method to determine identity and selection exceptions
description: When comparing claimed alloy with prior art: if composition and structure are identical, effects cannot be different and inventions deemed substantially identical; partial overlap of composition ranges can still be identical unless selection of a specific range has critical meaning.
guidance: To establish patentability based on a selected composition range from prior art, the selection must have critical meaning (e.g., provide unexpected effect). Court case references illustrate application.

name: Defenses available under the general issue without notice
description: Of the ordinary defences open to defendants in infringement actions, nineteen may be set up and proved under the general issue, without notice or special plea.
guidance: Enumerated examples given in the text (as stated): (1) the alleged invention is not the product of inventive skill; (2) it does not fall within either of the protected classes of inventions; (3) it is not useful; (4) no such patent as the one declared upon has ever existed; (5) the plaintiff's patent was issued contrary to law; (6) the invention described in the patent is neither an art, a machine, a manufacture, a composition of matter, a design, or an improvement; (7) the specification is ambiguous; (8) the claim is excessive and has not been cured within reasonable time by a disclaimer; (9) the claim is ambiguous; (10) the patent in force at the date of the infringement has been surrendered; (11) the patent declared on has been repealed; (12) the plaintiff has no such title to the patent as enables him to sue at law; (13) [text numbering jumps but continues with other common defenses]; (14) that the invention practiced by the defendant is not identical with the one covered by the patent; (15) that the acts of the defendant in reference to the patented invention were not acts of making, use, or sale; (16) that the practice of the invention by the defendant occurred before the issue of the patent or after it had expired; (17) that the practice of the invention by the defendant was in pursuance of his lawful rights; (18) that the plaintiff is estopped by his own conduct from pursuing his action; (19) that the plaintiff's right of action has been released or extinguished or merged in a judgment.  (Text explains these cover most defences admissible under general issue; earlier authorities recognized slightly different scopes.)

name: Notice of fraudulent specification: requisites
description: A notice alleging that the patentee's specification is fraudulent must point out the concealment or redundancy relied upon and must aver specifically that it originated in an intention to deceive the public.
guidance: A general statement that the specification was fraudulently made too comprehensive or too narrow is not sufficient. Alleging the Description is vague/ambiguous or contains superfluous matter, or that the Claim is frivolous, without asserting an intention to deceive, is defective. The plaintiff must be forewarned both of the particular errors in his specification and that they were committed in pursuance of a design to mislead; otherwise the notice only gives matters that could be proven under the defence of ambiguity without notice.

name: Notice of prior use / prior knowledge: requisites
description: When alleging prior use or knowledge as a defence to novelty, the notice must be tailored to the nature of the defence and disclose the names and residences of persons who had knowledge of or used the invention before the patentee, and the localities in which it was used.
guidance: It is immaterial whether the first inventor is known or unknown; the critical fact is that the invention itself was known or used before the patentee. The notice must give such detailed information as the defendant possesses and can fairly impart without prejudicing his rights so the plaintiff can identify persons and places and resort to them. The persons named are those who had the knowledge or made the use (not merely expected witnesses). The locality must be alleged with reasonable certainty (naming only a county is insufficient; naming particular towns, villages, or establishments is proper). The date of such knowledge/use need not be stated except by a general averment that it preceded the patentee's inventive act. The notice must extend to the entire invention claimed, not merely to elements. A defective notice cannot be cured by presenting the prior publication/patent/rejected application as evidence of use without proper notice.

name: Obviousness (general test)
description: Question whether, before the filing or priority date, having regard to the art known at the time, it would have been obvious to the person skilled in the art to arrive at something falling within the terms of the claim; if so, the claim lacks inventive step.
guidance: ‘Obvious’ means following plainly or logically from prior art without exercise of skill beyond that expected of the skilled person. Construed in light of knowledge up to and including the day before filing/priority. Distinguish inventive step from novelty.

name: Problem-and-solution approach
description: To assess inventive step objectively and predictably, apply the problem-and-solution approach (deviation should be exceptional). The approach has three stages: (i) determine the closest prior art, (ii) establish the objective technical problem, (iii) consider whether the claimed invention would have been obvious starting from the closest prior art and the objective problem.
guidance: Follow the three-stage method to avoid ex post facto reasoning and to structure the inventive-step assessment.

name: Combination vs. juxtaposition or aggregation
description: A claimed invention must be considered as a whole. If a claim is an aggregation/juxtaposition of features without functional interaction it may be obvious even though individual features are known; a combination of features requires functional interaction producing a synergistic technical effect different from the sum of individual effects.
guidance: Look for synergistic interaction (example: transistors forming a microprocessor produce data-processing effects beyond individual transistor switching). If no synergistic effect exists, treating the claim as a mere aggregation may defeat inventive-step.

name: Dependent claims and claims in different categories
description: If an independent claim is new and non-obvious, generally there is no need to investigate novelty/non-obviousness of dependent claims, except where dependent claims have a later effective date requiring consideration of intermediate documents. Similarly, if a product claim is new and non-obvious there is no need to examine a process claim which inevitably results in the manufacture of that product, and vice versa.
guidance: Note that analogy processes that lack inventive step may still be patentable insofar as they provide a novel and inventive product. Where product, process and use claims have different effective dates, separate examination may be necessary.

name: Unity of invention (Section 2(9)(a), Rule 7(5))
description: An ARIPO application must relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept; the link must be a technical relationship expressed by the same or corresponding special technical features in the claims.
guidance: Special technical features are those defining the contribution over the prior art. Correspondence (e.g., different means achieving the same functional effect) suffices. A single general inventive concept may permit multiple independent claims in different categories (product/process/use); specified combinations (i)-(iii) are generally permissible, but multiple such sets are allowed only exceptionally and require the single-concept link to be present. Phrases like 'specially adapted' do not by themselves establish a single general inventive concept.

name: Permissible combinations of claim categories (examples)
description: ARIPO permits inclusion, as part of a single-concept linked group, combinations such as: (i) an independent product claim plus an independent process claim specially adapted to manufacture that product and an independent use claim for that product; (ii) a process claim and an apparatus or means specifically designed for carrying out the process; (iii) product + specially adapted manufacturing process + apparatus for the process.
guidance: A process is 'specially adapted' for manufacture of a product if it results in the claimed product and thus defines a technical relationship. A manufacturing process and its product do not lack unity merely because the process is not limited to making that product. Multiple sets of such combinations in one application are exceptional.

name: Distinction between claiming a material and claiming its qualities
description: Product patents typically claim a material that has particular qualities; they do not claim the qualities themselves.
guidance: The article stresses that a claim to 'conductivity of 4.23 siemens' or similar would be peculiar and properly fail as an abstract idea and be impossible to support in the specification. Courts focus on whether the claim is to a thing (composition) versus claiming a property or principle.

name: New uses / functional distinction as a metric for eligibility (Judge Moore’s approach)
description: Consider whether the isolated/claimed subject matter enables new uses that the native form could not serve.
guidance: Judge Moore’s concurring opinion in the Federal Circuit emphasized that isolated nucleotide structures had new practical uses (genetic testing, primers, probes) that native chromosomal structures could not serve. This 'new uses' metric supports eligibility by focusing on functional differences rather than mere structural similarity.

name: Materiality / tangibility / transformation (machine-or-transformation relevance)
description: The physicality of an end result or a transformation of matter can be relevant to eligibility: tangible material outcomes weigh in favor of eligibility.
guidance: Compare Flook/Benson (number/abstract) with Diehr (tire/cured product). Diehr’s emphasis on materiality and tangibility supported eligibility; Bilski recognized machine-or-transformation considerations as relevant but not dispositive. Courts will ask whether the claim is anchored to a material transformation or merely an abstract result.

name: Routine or conventional activity insufficient to convert a natural principle into a patentable application (Mayo/Alice concern)
description: Applying a natural correlation with only routine, conventional steps does not make the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Mayo held diagnostic method claims invalid because measuring metabolite levels and adjusting dosage were routine/conventional activities that did not add an inventive concept beyond a natural correlation. This test is used to examine whether additional claim elements meaningfully limit the scope and add inventive subject matter.

name: Preemption / breadth concern
description: Claims that effectively preempt all practical use of a natural principle or abstract idea create patentability problems.
guidance: The article notes that claims that read too broadly risk preempting downstream uses; this concern underlies many exclusions and causes courts to scrutinize whether claims monopolize basic tools of scientific and technological work.

name: Focus on Unique Advantages
description: When drafting claims, focus on the unique advantages and benefits of your invention.
guidance: Highlighting these aspects can help demonstrate the invention's novelty and non-obviousness.

name: Use Clear, Simple Language
description: Avoid technical jargon or complex sentence structures that might confuse the reader.
guidance: Each element of the claim should be clearly defined and easy to understand. If your invention involves specialized terminology, define these terms clearly within the claim or in the detailed description.

name: Balance Breadth with Specificity
description: Claims should cover a wide range of potential infringements but not be so broad that they lose enforceability.
guidance: Aim to cover as many potential infringing variations as reasonable while ensuring the claim remains supported, novel, and non-obvious — overly broad claims risk invalidation or rejection.

name: Avoid Limiting Language ("Patent Profanity")
description: Do not use words that unnecessarily limit the scope of claims.
guidance: Common 'patent profanity' to avoid includes: "necessary", "essential", "key", "every", "must", "never", "only", "absolutely", "critical", "important", "preferred" — these can be interpreted as limiting and shrink claim scope.

name: Consider Prior Art
description: Adequately consider existing patents and publications when drafting claims.
guidance: Failing to consider prior art can lead to claims that are not novel or are obvious. Such oversight might invalidate your patent or severely limit its scope; use prior-art searching to shape claim scope and distinguishing features.

name: Maintain Consistency
description: Be consistent in terminology throughout the patent document.
guidance: Using different terms to refer to the same component or feature can cause confusion and ambiguity; keep term usage uniform between claims, specification, and figures.

name: Use a Layered Claim Structure
description: Draft independent and dependent claims in a hierarchical (layered) structure.
guidance: Dependent claims provide variations and inherit all limitations of the claims they depend on. If the broadest independent claim is invalidated, narrower dependent claims can still provide protection — use dependent claims to capture fallback positions and preferred embodiments.

name: Get Professional Review
description: Have your claims reviewed by peers and patent professionals.
guidance: Fresh eyes (peers, patent attorneys/agents) can catch inconsistencies, ambiguities, and potential weaknesses that the drafter might have missed; professional review improves claim clarity, enforceability, and prosecution prospects.

name: Utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101
description: The Office must examine each application to ensure compliance with the 'useful invention' or utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101; to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 an applicant must claim statutory subject matter and show the claimed invention is 'useful' for some purpose either explicitly or implicitly.
guidance: Office personnel must keep in mind general principles controlling application of the utility requirement, including that utility ensures patents are granted only on inventions that are 'useful.' Application of this element is the focus of the guidelines. The examiner should determine whether the asserted utility is specific, substantial, and credible.

name: Inoperative or 'incredible' utility (total incapacity test)
description: An invention that is wholly inoperative (i.e., totally incapable of achieving a useful result) is not 'useful' under patent law; however partial success is sufficient—total incapacity must be shown to sustain a 101 rejection on inoperativeness grounds.
guidance: Rejections on inoperativeness are rare and fact-specific. Examples of inventions found inoperative include perpetual motion machines, claims inconsistent with known science, or claims that cannot possibly produce the asserted results. Office personnel should not label an asserted utility 'incredible' or 'speculative' unless it is clear that the invention cannot work as claimed based on the record.

name: Focus on the claimed invention (claim-by-claim evaluation)
description: Each claim must be evaluated on its own merits for compliance with statutory requirements; the claimed invention is the focus of the utility assessment.
guidance: Generally a dependent claim has utility if the independent claim from which it depends has utility and is in the same statutory class. Exception: where the dependent claim specifies a different utility than the independent claim. For genus claims where species within the genus may lack utility, a generic claim should be treated as sufficient unless it can be established that other species clearly encompassed by the claim do not have utility — in such cases encourage amendment to exclude species that lack utility.

name: One credible assertion of specific utility is sufficient
description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for a claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not credible, do not render the claimed invention lacking in utility.
guidance: Case law (e.g., Raytheon v. Roper, In re Gottlieb) supports that meeting at least one stated objective establishes utility. Thus do not reject claims merely because some asserted utilities are speculative if at least one credible utility is present.

name: Applicant statements are not alone sufficient basis for a lack-of-utility rejection
description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or during prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack of utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: Applicants may include nonessential statements of uncertain technical accuracy; the Office should not require striking such statements. Examiners should avoid reading unclaimed results, limitations, or embodiments into claims, which can inappropriately change the relationship of asserted utility to the claimed invention.

name: Procedural examination step: determine whether an asserted or well-established utility exists
description: Upon initial examination the examiner should review the specification to determine if there are any statements asserting that the claimed invention is useful for any particular purpose; a complete disclosure should identify a specific and substantial utility for the invention.
guidance: A statement of specific and substantial utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant asserts the invention is useful (i.e., purpose and how it may be used) and must enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the claimed invention is useful. Examiners should look for such enabling assertions in the specification at the outset of examination.

name: Definition of Covered Business Method (CBM) patent
description: “A covered business method patent is ‘a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a ﬁnancial product or service, except that the term does not include patents for technological inventions.’”
guidance: Requires a two-part analysis: (1) whether the patent claims involve 'the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service'; and (2) whether the patent is directed to a 'technological invention.' Legislative history indicates the definition will be construed broadly.

name: Two-part CBM eligibility analysis (financial nature and technological invention exclusion)
description: First, determine whether the claims are used in the practice/administration/management of a financial product or service; second, determine whether the patent is a technological invention (which would exclude it).
guidance: Whether a patent is for a technological invention is determined case-by-case, considering whether the claimed subject matter as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious over the prior art, and whether it 'solves a technical problem using a technical solution.' The Board has construed 'financial' broadly (activities financial in nature, incidental or complementary to financial activity).

name: CBM petition fee structure
description: Filing fee: $12,000 to challenge the validity of up to 20 claims and $250 per each additional claim beyond the twentieth. Post-institution fee: $18,000 for challenging up to 15 claims and $550 per each additional claim beyond the fifteenth.
guidance: Practice note: overall cost similar to PGR. Fees apply at filing and post-institution if review is granted.

name: Who may bring a CBM petition (eligibility/prerequisites)
description: A patent is eligible for CBM review only if the petitioner establishes: (1) petitioner has been sued for infringement of the patent in question; (2) the patent claims are directed to 'financial products or services'; and (3) the patent claims do not recite a 'technological invention.'
guidance: PTO comments suggest 'sued' likely includes parties served with cease-and-desist letters. The Board construed 'sued' to encompass litigation at any stage up to final judgment on appeal; a prior trial loss did not automatically preclude a petition if appeals were pending. Additional eligibility limits in fast facts: generally any non-owner unless petitioner/real party/privy previously filed an IPR/PGR/CBM that resulted in a final written decision, or previously filed a civil action challenging validity (a counterclaim does not bar CBM).

name: Statutory petition content requirements
description: By statute the petitioner must (i) identify all real parties in interest; (ii) identify all claims challenged and all grounds on which the challenge to each claim is based; and (iii) provide copies of evidence relied upon. The petition must be accompanied by a fee.
guidance: These are mandatory statutory elements — omission risks denial for failure to meet chapter 32 requirements.

name: Regulatory (rule) petition content requirements
description: By rule the petitioner must (i) identify the grounds for standing; (ii) provide a claim construction for each challenged claim; (iii) specifically explain the grounds for unpatentability; and (iv) specifically explain the relevance of evidence relied upon.
guidance: The rule-level requirements demand a specific, claim-by-claim showing and justification of evidence; the preliminary pleading must be sufficiently detailed to meet the 'more likely than not' threshold if not rebutted.

name: Evidentiary standard and claim construction during CBM
description: The default evidentiary standard is a preponderance of the evidence. The Office will apply the broadest reasonable construction standard to CBMs, and there will be no presumption of validity.
guidance: Preponderance is more favorable to petitioners than the 'clear and convincing' district court standard. Broadest reasonable construction (BRI) tends to favor broader claim readings for anticipation/obviousness analyses.

name: Limitations for pre-AIA first-to-invent patents (prior art availability)
description: A petitioner who challenges claims in a covered business method patent having an effective filing date prior to March 16, 2013 based on prior art will be limited to relying on prior art defined by pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §102.
guidance: This restriction narrows available prior art for first-to-invent patents and should inform prior-art strategy in CBM petitions against pre-AIA patents.

name: Practical takeaways from SAP v. Versata precedent
description: PTAB in SAP v. Versata held: (1) petitioner had demonstrated 'more likely than not' unpatentability under §101; (2) 'sued' can encompass litigation at any stage up to final judgment on appeal; (3) CBM definition construed broadly to include activities financial in nature, incidental to financial activity, or complementary to financial activity; (4) 'technological invention' exclusion was not met where claims required only generic computer/software and no specific unconventional software/equipment.
guidance: The decision suggests PTAB may be amenable to instituting CBM review in borderline cases; technological invention exclusion can fail where claims merely require routine computer implementation without specific unconventional technology.

name: Re-issue may claim elements described but not claimed in original
description: An element described but not claimed in the original patent may be claimed in the re-issue.
guidance: Example: Loring v. Hall (1879), 15 O. G. 471.

name: Re-issue may contain new claims founded on original description
description: The re-issue may contain new Claims founded on the original Description.
guidance: See Combined Patents Can Co. v. Lloyd (1882), Union Paper Bag Co. v. Nixon (1873). New claim language may be used provided it is supported by the original disclosure.

name: Re-issue may include new drawings based on original specification
description: The re-issue may contain new drawings based on the original specification; the drawings of the re-issue may contain features not shown in the drawings of the original.
guidance: See Union Paper Bag Co. v. Nixon (1873) and other cited cases. Drawings may be amended in matters outside the model if they do not affect claims (Pearl v. Appleton Co. (1880)).

name: Patentee may insert dependent/auxiliary inventions that were substantially indicated
description: Where the original specification described subordinate parts or additional inventions dependent on the principal one, and they were substantially indicated, the patentee (absent abandonment/estoppel) is permitted to insert such inventions in the re-issue if they could lawfully have been claimed in the original.
guidance: See §669 discussion and cited cases; the test is whether the inventor attempted to protect those dependent inventions as indicated in the original disclosure.

name: Re-issued combination patent cannot embrace a combination essentially distinct from original
description: A re-issued combination-patent cannot embrace a combination essentially distinct from that described and claimed in the original patent.
guidance: §670: identity of combination rests on identity of elements and the cooperative law under which they operate; adding new elements or substituting non-equivalents makes the re-issue invalid (see Washburn & Moen v. Fuchs and other cases).

name: Identity test for combinations: elements and cooperative law
description: The identity of the combination claimed in the re-issue with that described in the original depends upon the identity of their respective elements and of the cooperative law under which they are associated.
guidance: If the re-issue contains less than all elements described or substitutes a non-equivalent, it departs from the original combination and is void.

name: Inventor's opinion in re-issue is permissible if it does not affect claims
description: The opinion of the inventor, stated in the re-issue, as to the character of his invention is not improper if it does not affect the claims.
guidance: See Beed v. Chase (1885) and related cases: subjective statements are allowed so long as they don't alter claim scope.

name: Patent document structure and required sections
description: Patent documents normally include publication information, title, bibliometric information, patent classification, citations, abstract, background, detailed description, claims, and drawings.
guidance: For dataset curation and automated processing, segmenting documents into these sections (abstract, claims, description, etc.) is a recommended preprocessing step. Each section serves different analytical/generative roles (e.g., descriptions contain details; claims define legal scope).

name: Claims drafting rules
description: Claims define the legal scope of the patent; each claim is a single sentence describing specific features that make the invention novel and non-obvious.
guidance: Claims must be carefully and precisely crafted to define boundaries that can withstand legal scrutiny. Claim wording must be consistent with descriptions and reference numbers; small wording differences can dramatically change scope. Automated claim generation must prioritize precision and legal defensibility.

name: Detailed description completeness
description: The detailed description must provide comprehensive details about the invention and specific embodiments, typically discussing the drawings to support the claims.
guidance: Patent analysis and generation should prioritize full descriptions (not just titles or abstracts) because they contain essential technical details; training/evaluation datasets should include description sections when possible.

name: Information extraction from patents
description: Information extraction focuses on extracting desired structured information (entities, relationships, claims, figures) from patent texts for downstream tasks.
guidance: IE systems must account for idiosyncratic patent phrasing, self-defined terms, and noisy figures/metadata; high-quality labeled data is limited for some IE sub-tasks, requiring task-specific dataset creation or silver-standard labeling.

name: Quality assessment tasks (novelty, granting, litigation, valuation)
description: Quality assessment includes predicting novelty, whether an application will be granted, litigation likelihood, and patent valuation as proxies for patent quality and scope.
guidance: These tasks incorporate textual signals and metadata; e.g., unclear or ambiguous claims and scarce descriptions increase litigation risk. Granting prediction must consider formal/legal language and document completeness beyond novelty.

name: Litigation risk indicators
description: Patents with unclear or ambiguous claims or very scarce descriptions tend to have higher likelihoods of being subject to litigation.
guidance: Litigation-prediction models should include measures of claim clarity, description completeness, and possibly citation/network features to improve predictions.

name: Keystroke-based evaluation for generative patent tools
description: Keystroke-based evaluation measures the number of keystrokes saved by model autocomplete suggestions (a productivity metric for claim drafting).
guidance: Reported results are task- and model-dependent; this metric may not correlate with legal correctness or claim quality. Use alongside other quality/human-evaluation metrics.

name: Reporting and benchmarking practices
description: Because tasks and datasets vary widely, researchers should report dataset preprocessing steps, exact sections used (abstract/claims/description), evaluation metrics, and averaging methods to enable reproducibility.
guidance: Shared tasks and large curated datasets (e.g., HUPD) are recommended to standardize comparisons. Explicitly document proxies used for labels (e.g., novelty proxies) and limitations.

name: Inventorship determination
description: Under U.S. law an inventor is a person who takes part in the conception of the ideas in the patent claims; inventorship may change as claims change during prosecution.
guidance: Determination can require intricate legal analysis by the patent attorney prosecuting the application.

name: Provisional versus regular (utility) patent applications
description: A U.S. provisional application can preserve patent rights while temporarily reducing costs and providing time to prepare a regular application; a regular application must be filed within one year to claim the provisional's date.
guidance: Provisionals are not examined and do not require claims; applicants receive the benefit of the earlier date only for material adequately described and enabled in the provisional—patent counsel involvement may still be needed.

name: Foreign patent considerations and PCT/Paris Convention
description: Foreign patent protection is governed by each country; many countries bar patenting after public disclosure (no grace period); PCT provides a streamlined procedure and delays costly national filings (generally up to 30 months).
guidance: U.S. has a one-year grace period; PCT gives preliminary examination and delays foreign costs; use Paris Convention to claim earliest filing date when filing abroad within one year.

name: Relevancy determination for parts/materials-specialized businesses
description: The relevancy between parts·materials-specialized businesses and the claimed invention shall be determined based on proving documents (business license, and etc.) enclosed in the expedited examination request form, and if necessary, by referring to the total information network run by the Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology.
guidance: If the relevancy cannot be checked or confirmed, the examiner may order the requester to supplement the proving documents.

name: Start-up financial support thresholds for expedited acceptance
description: A patent application financially supported by the government with over 10 million won for technology development/commercialization, or filed by early-stage startups funded by venture capital/cloud funding/angel investors/accelerators with over 50 million won, shall be accepted for expedited examination without submission of proving documents, on the assumption that the claimed invention is being practiced or to be practiced.
guidance: This is pursuant to relevant domestic support acts (Support for SME Establishment Act; Business Start-up Support Act).

name: Eligibility when corresponding application has at least one claim indicated allowable
description: A patent application is eligible where the corresponding application filed with a participating patent office has at least one claim indicated allowable in a most recent office action for examination, and where the concerned KIPO application’s claims are identical to the allowable claims or narrowed by restricting or adding limitations.
guidance: This provision facilitates expedited examination when a foreign office has indicated allowability; claim correspondence must be demonstrated.

name: Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) basic eligibility
description: The PPH allows an applicant who received a positive decision on claims from the Office of First Filing (OFF) — that at least one claim is allowable — to request expedited examination at the Office of Second Filing (OSF) for the corresponding application that includes claims identical to the allowable claims or narrowed by restrictions/additions.
guidance: Participating country lists and program participation should be checked on KIPO homepage as participating countries can change; eased requirements since Jan 1, 2014 allow eligibility when earliest priority dates match.

name: PPH: all-claims correspondence requirement
description: All claims of the concerned patent application shall correspond to the claims decided allowable in a patent application filed in a participating country.
guidance: Correspondence means substantially identical claims or claims further limited by adding limitations. Differences only in translation or claim types (independent/dependent) may be treated as substantially same. Different claim categories count as non-corresponding. Claim correspondence is determined based on a claim correspondence table submitted by the requester.

name: PPH evidential documents (Annex Form and evidence list)
description: A PPH requester shall file a written explanation referencing Annexed Form no. 3 and submit: (a) copy of the claims including those recognized as allowable by the participating office; (b) copy of an examination-related notification on the corresponding patent application issued by the participating office; (c) copy of prior arts relied upon in that notification (non-patent docs must be submitted); (d) explanation on correspondence between each claim and the allowable claims (claim correspondence table) — the correspondence explanation must be submitted in any case.
guidance: If examiner can obtain documents via public networks (AIPN, PAIR, PVS online), submission may not be necessary. If documents are in non-Korean/English languages, translations must be submitted unless examiner can obtain translations via networks.

name: PCT-PPH evidential documents (Annex Form and evidence list)
description: A requester under PCT-PPH shall submit (using Annexed Form no. 6): (a) copy of patent claims decided to meet requirements in an international search/IPER/WO opinions; (b) copy of the written opinion(s) or international preliminary examination report; (c) copy of prior art documents cited in those international opinions/reports (non-patent docs must be submitted); (d) explanation on correspondence between all claims of concerned application and the claims recognized as meeting requirements (claim correspondence explanation must be submitted).
guidance: If 'opinions on an international application' (Box VIII) indicate ambiguity/unclear claims, the requester must explain that all claims are not affected (e.g., provide responses or amendments). If such explanations are not provided, examiner may order amendments.

name: Determination/redetermination instructions and amendment consequences
description: When determining expedited examination for applications agreed between KIPO and foreign offices, the result of determination is not notified to requester unless rejected. If an applicant amends claims after determination in ways not reflected in prior explanations (e.g., claims not included in prior comparison or not substantially identical), the examiner may order corrections and re-determine whether to permit expedited examination, granting up to one month to correct at examiner's discretion.
guidance: If the applicant submits comparison explanations covering amended claims or correspondence explanations for claims meeting international requirements, expedited examination shall proceed without re-determination.

name: Claim correspondence table requirement
