description: Whether claims correspond to each other shall be determined based on a claim correspondence table that a requester submits with a written explanation of request for expedited examination; an explanation on claim correspondence must be submitted in any case (PPH/PCT-PPH).
guidance: Grounds for correspondence must be indicated for each claim (e.g., statement that claims are literal translations or explain mere translation differences).

name: Pre-search and search responsibilities
description: Searches existing technology for claimed invention; reads and understands the invention set forth in the specification; determines whether the application is adequate to define the metes and bounds of the claimed invention; determines the scope of the claim(s).
guidance: On taking up an application the examiner must make a thorough study and investigation of available prior art (37 CFR 1.104). Proper characterization of the invention and claim scope is foundational to examination and any subsequent rejections.

name: Basis for rejection — 35 U.S.C. §112 (specification and claim requirements)
description: Specification requirements: written description, enablement, best mode. Claim requirements: content must 'particularly point out' (not vague) and 'distinctly claim' (not indefinite). Claim format: independent, dependent, multiple dependent.
guidance: Examiners must assess written description and enablement support for claimed subject matter, identify lack of best mode if applicable, and evaluate claim definiteness and proper claim format per §112.

name: Basis for rejection — 35 U.S.C. §102 (novelty / anticipation)
description: Novelty (new); Anticipation (no difference); defines what is 'prior' art.
guidance: Assess whether a single prior art reference anticipates a claim; determine what qualifies as prior art for the application under §102.

name: Basis for rejection — 35 U.S.C. §103 (non-obviousness)
description: Non-obvious is a legal determination that involves the concept of 'one of ordinary skill in the pertinent art'.
guidance: Examiners must articulate reasoning why claimed subject matter would have been obvious to a POSITA, using proper factual underpinnings and legal standards.

name: Final office action characteristics and consequences
description: A final office action may occur on second (or later) examination if there are claims that are not allowable; notifies applicant of examiner’s final patentability determination; could include objections, rejections, and/or indication of allowable subject matter; sets SSP for response; prosecution is considered closed; further amendment after final is restricted (37 CFR §1.113 & §1.116).
guidance: Final actions close prosecution and limit amendments; examiners should state grounds clearly and note available post-final options for applicants.

name: Appeal practice (PTAB)
description: A notice of appeal may be filed after any of the claims has been twice rejected, regardless of whether the claim(s) has/have been finally rejected; the 'twice rejected' limitation does not have to be related to a particular application. Guidance for filing a Notice of Appeal, Appeal Brief and appropriate fees are found in MPEP sections 1204 and 1205.
guidance: Examiners should follow MPEP procedures for appeals and recognize the procedural rule about 'twice rejected' claims.

name: NSDP based on anticipation (one-way genus-species test)
description: If the reference claims, when properly construed, provide coverage for an embodiment within the scope of the examined claims, the examined claims are anticipated by the reference claims and thus are patentably indistinct (a one-way test).
guidance: When a claim under examination is generic to a species or sub‑genus claimed in a conflicting patent/application, explain that the species/sub‑genus anticipates the genus and that a patent to the genus would improperly extend exclusivity. Use FP 8.34/8.35 as appropriate. MPEP 804 (II)(B)(1).

name: NSDP based on obviousness (Graham analysis applied to reference claims)
description: Obviousness-based NSDP uses only the claims of the reference patent/application as the basis, but the reference disclosure may be consulted to interpret those claims.
guidance: Perform the Graham v. Deere analysis: (A) scope/content of reference claim; (B) differences between reference claim and examined claim; (C) level of ordinary skill; (D) objective indicia of nonobviousness. Use appropriate FP paragraphs (8.36/8.37 for secondary references, 8.34/8.35 for no secondary refs). MPEP 804 (II)(B)(2).

name: Do not use "shortcut" rationales — full analysis required
description: NSDP rejections based on an obviousness analysis must carry out a full analysis for all examined claims; merely pointing out scope overlap or addressing all claims in a single sentence is generally insufficient.
guidance: Ensure each claim addressed has a reasoned Graham-type analysis; avoid one-line or conclusory rejections. See MPEP 804.01.

name: Consulting the reference specification
description: The reference's specification can be used as a dictionary to interpret the reference's claims and to confirm the scope of those claims when making an NSDP rejection.
guidance: Cite and explain how the specification construes the reference claim; use FP 8.34/8.35/8.36/8.37 as appropriate. MPEP 804(II)(B)(2)(a).

name: Genus/species: immediately envisage test
description: First determine whether a PHOSITA can immediately envisage the species from the genus claimed in the reference without consulting the reference specification; if yes, the genus anticipates the species.
guidance: If not immediately envisaged, search for a secondary reference that would render the species obvious over the genus and explain motivation/expectation of success. If no secondary reference, consider whether the species is obvious over the genus using the reference's own disclosures (or consider equitable principles if not obvious). Use FP 8.33 and appropriate FP 8.34/8.35/8.36/8.37; rare equitable rejections use FP 8.38/8.39 with supervisory approval. See MPEP 804 (II)(B)(1) & (2).

name: Drafting proper NSDP rejections — form paragraphs and explanations
description: Use the appropriate form paragraphs and include claim-by-claim reasoning: FP 8.33 (general), 8.34/8.35 (no secondary references), 8.36/8.37 (with secondary references / provisional language), 8.38/8.39 (equitable principles).
guidance: Ensure the rejection explains why each examined claim is patentably indistinct from each reference claim relied upon, performing the necessary Graham-type analysis for obviousness-based rejections or an anticipation explanation for anticipation-based rejections.

name: Overcoming NSDP rejections — applicant options
description: To overcome an NSDP rejection based on anticipation: (A) amend the examined claims so reference claims no longer anticipate, (B) cancel the relevant reference claims, or (C) obtain an approved terminal disclaimer in the examined application. Evidence of secondary considerations is NOT an option for anticipation-based NSDP; a promise to file a TD later is NOT an option.
guidance: For obviousness-based NSDP, options include claim amendment, cancellation, evidence of unexpected results (if properly presented), or an approved TD in the examined application. A TD is not effective until approved and only effective in the application in which it is filed. Examiners should confirm reference numbers on TDs but need not review TD compliance; contact Patent Legal Research Center if TD approval is unclear. See MPEP 804, 804.02.

name: Substantial new question of patentability required for subsequent requests
description: In order for a second or subsequent request for ex parte reexamination to be granted, a substantial new question of patentability must be raised by the art (patents and/or printed publications) cited in the second or subsequent request for reexamination.
guidance: See MPEP § 2240 for analysis of whether a substantial new question of patentability is raised. The second request is decided based on the claims in effect at the time of determination (37 CFR 1.515(a)).

name: Non-identical claims in merged proceedings treated as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112
description: Where an amendment to make the claims the same is required by the merger decision but is not timely submitted, any claim that does not contain identical text in all merged proceedings should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite.
guidance: This rejection is for failure to particularly point out the invention.

name: Reexamination based on reissue claims when reissue issues before determination
description: If a reissue patent issues on the patent under reexamination before determination on the reexamination request, the determination should be made on the claims of the reissue patent (the reexamination would be processed on the reissue claims rather than the original patent claims).
guidance: Reissue claims used as starting point must be presented in the reexamination proceeding as a 'clean copy' (bracketed words in reissue patent claims would not appear in reexamination clean copy). Form paragraph 22.05 may be used in the Office action.

name: Support requirement (Article 36(6)(i)) / claim must be supported by description
description: A claimed technical solution must be obtainable from the contents sufficiently disclosed in the description and must not go beyond the scope of the contents disclosed in the description.
guidance: Claims that generalize beyond concrete embodiments or facts disclosed in the description (e.g., claiming 'any feature value representing face shape' when only face-outline angle was supported) fail the support requirement. Remedy: narrow or amend claims to the supported embodiments.

name: Enablement requirement (Article 36(4)(i)) / ability to carry out
description: The description must provide a clear and sufficient disclosure so that a person skilled in the art can make and use the claimed invention.
guidance: If essential correlations, parameters, or production conditions are missing, or only model estimations (without verification) are given, the invention may be held not enabled. Examiner may require experimental evidence or deletion/narrowing of unsupported claims.

name: Claim scope must not exceed the disclosure (no unsupported generalization)
description: The scope of a claim cannot be expanded or generalized beyond the scope of the contents disclosed in the description. Generalizations that contain speculative content or unproven effects are not allowed.
guidance: Examples: (i) claiming an estimation model that accepts 'any feature value representing face shape' when only face-outline angle correlation is shown; (ii) claiming allergy incidence estimation for any allergic reaction when only contact dermatitis was supported. Antipattern: asserting broad functional results without specific enabling disclosure.

name: Experimental verification required when claimed effect is empirical
description: If the claimed technical effect depends on empirical results (e.g., curing strength, estimation accuracy), the description should include experiments or verified evidence supporting that effect.
guidance: Antipattern: relying solely on model-estimated results or speculative statements without any experimental data. Where only estimation results are disclosed, the examiner may find the disclosure insufficient unless estimation accuracy is validated and measurement methods are given.

name: Disclosure of measurement methods and conditions
description: Measurement methods and conditions for claimed measured outcomes should be specifically disclosed in the description when claims depend on those measurements.
guidance: Example: the description specifically disclosed how to measure curing strength within 5 minutes and after 24 hours. Including measurement method/conditions helps enable reproducibility; omission weakens enablement/support.

name: Limitations on extrapolating across biological/technical subtypes
description: Generalizing results across biologically or technically distinct subtypes (e.g., various allergic reactions, different facial features) requires disclosure because mechanisms may vary among types.
guidance: Example: experimental support for contact dermatitis does not automatically support claims for other allergic reactions. Applicants should limit claims to supported types or provide broader supporting evidence.

name: Compositions defined by component ranges require support for claimed functional effect
description: When a claim defines a composition by component ranges and asserts a functional performance (e.g., curing strength threshold within a time), the description must support that the claimed ranges achieve the asserted effect.
guidance: Antipattern: presenting a model prediction that a composition within specified ranges would meet the performance target without any experimental verification. The examiner may require actual embodiments or validated model accuracy.

name: Prosecution remedy: amend claims to overcome lack of support/enablement
description: An applicant can overcome a reason for refusal by amending or deleting unsupported claims (e.g., deleting an overbroad independent claim and leaving a supported dependent claim).
guidance: Guidance shown in cases: narrowing claims to embodiments actually disclosed (for example, keep Claim 2 supported by description and delete overbroad Claim 1). Applicants should consider targeted amendments rather than speculative generalizations.

name: Requirement of both positive and negative instances (Method of Difference)
description: Verification must supply both the affirmative instance (that from the hypothesis we can deduce the known facts) and the negative instance (that no other antecedent, except the one assumed in the hypothesis, would in conjunction with the background produce the same effect).
guidance: Without both instances one cannot claim the hypothesis is established; Newton's argument illustrated obtaining the negative instance by showing alternative hypotheses would give different results.

name: Fundamental economic practices (abstract idea grouping)
description: Claims reciting fundamental economic practices—e.g., hedging risk, managing insurance, intermediated settlement, offer-based price optimization—are directed to abstract ideas.
guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have characterized hedging and other core economic practices as 'fundamental economic practice' abstract ideas (e.g., Bilski; Alice; Bancorp). Examples listed include: mitigating settlement risk (Alice), rules for conducting a wagering game (In re Smith), financial instruments designed to protect against investment risk (In re Chorna), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs. v. Amazon), local processing of payments for remotely purchased goods (Inventor Holdings v. Bed Bath Beyond), using an external marking on mail to communicate sender/recipient/contents (Secured Mail Solutions v. Universal Wilde), and placing an order based on displayed market information (Trading Technologies v. IBG).

name: Point A: Claim limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind do not recite a mental process
description: If claimed limitations cannot practically be performed by a human (i.e., the human mind is not equipped to perform them), the claim does not fall into the 'mental process' abstract-idea grouping.
guidance: Examiner should identify whether the limitation requires capabilities beyond human mental performance (e.g., network-packet analysis, GPS pseudorange calculations, specific encryption steps, pixel-by-pixel digital-image halftoning). Cases: SRI Int’l v. Cisco (network monitors/packets), SiRF Tech. (GPS pseudorange calculations), Synopsys (specific encryption/data-manipulation), Research Corp. Techs. (halftoning images). The guideline gives concrete claim examples that were held not to be mental processes because they require non-mental technical operations.

name: Point C: A claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
description: Claims reciting steps performed on a computer can nonetheless be mental-process abstract ideas if the underlying concept can be performed mentally or with pen and paper.
guidance: Examiners must consider the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in view of the specification to see if the applicant is merely claiming a concept performed on a generic computer or using a computer as a tool. The guideline cites Benson and Mortgage Grader as examples where computer-implemented claims were nonetheless abstract because humans could perform the claimed concept. The examiner should review whether the specification describes the concept as being performed in the human mind and only claimed as computer-implemented.

name: Point C.1: Performing a mental process on a generic computer remains an abstract idea
description: If the claims merely recite performing a mental process on a generic computer (i.e., human cognitive actions implemented on general-purpose hardware), the claim can still be directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Examples: Voter Verified v. ESS (voting, verifying, and submitting performed on a computer were human cognitive actions and thus abstract); Versata (pricing implemented using general-purpose computer hardware still found to be an abstract idea). Examiners should rely on the specification and claim language to determine whether the computer elements are generic and the claimed invention is essentially a mental process.

name: Mental-process applicability to product and process claim types (Point D reference)
description: Both product (e.g., systems, computer-readable media) and process claims can recite a 'mental process' type abstract idea; the 'mental processes' label refers to the type of abstract idea, not the statutory claim category.
guidance: The courts have identified product claims (systems and computer-readable media) as reciting mental-process abstract ideas (e.g., Versata). Examiners should therefore evaluate product claims for mental-process content, not assume only method claims can be mental processes. (The guideline notes this concept and refers examiners to further discussion under point D.)

name: Outcome rule for claims that include nature-based products with marked differences
description: If the claim includes a nature-based product that has markedly different characteristics, then the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless the claim recites another exception.
guidance: For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, once a markedly different characteristic is shown, no further eligibility analysis is necessary (Step 2B is not necessary because the answer to Step 2A is NO). For claims including additional limitations, examiners should consider whether the claim recites another exception and thus requires further eligibility analysis.

name: Application to process claims
description: Generally, process claims are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process because process analysis focuses on active steps, not products used in those steps.
guidance: Examples where the markedly different analysis is not applied: claims to cryopreserving hepatocyte cells were not subjected to the analysis for the hepatocytes used in the process (Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect). Exception: if a process claim is drafted such that it is no different in substance from a product claim (i.e., focuses on the product), it is subject to the markedly different analysis (e.g., a claim that recites "a method of providing an apple" or claims effectively to detecting naturally occurring cffDNA because they are directed to the product).

name: Evaluating whether characteristics are "markedly different"
description: Compare the claimed product's characteristics to the naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to determine whether they are "markedly different."
guidance: To show a marked difference, a characteristic must be changed as compared to nature and cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change. The inventor must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart. If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product is a product of nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and the change was produced by the inventor's efforts, the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic and the claimed product is not a product of nature exception.

name: Duties of the Judge Advocate General (enumerated functions)
description: The work done in the office of the Judge Advocate General ... consists mainly of the following particulars: Reviewing and making reports upon proceedings of trials by court-martial ... making reports upon applications for pardon or mitigation of sentence; preparing and revising charges and specifications prior to trial ... drafting of contracts, bonds, deeds, leases, licenses, grants of rights of way, approvals of location of rights of way, approvals of plans ... framing of bills, forms of procedure, preparing opinions upon questions relating to the appointment, promotion, rank, pay, allowances ... the civil rights, liabilities and relations of military persons ... interpretation and effect of public contracts ... validity and disposition of claims against the United States ... execution of public works under appropriations by Congress; upon obstructions to navigation ... riparian rights ... and furnishing statements and information apposite to claims.
guidance: JAG office performs broad legal advisory, drafting, prosecutorial, and claims-related functions for the War Department; duties include confidential opinions and varied legal instruments for execution by the Secretary of War.

name: Disposition of found money on transport by officers
description: An officer took possession of found money ($15.65) as the finder, which was valid against all the world except the true owner. He could retain the money subject to claim by the true owner or he could turn it over to the transport quartermaster. The latter, upon the receipt of such money, should take it up as 'found on U. S. Army transport,' and turn it into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts.
guidance: Finders' rights limited by true-owner claims; turning found money into official quartermaster channels for Treasury receipt is proper practice.

name: Very demanding standard for judicial correction
description: Judicial correction of erroneous wording of a claim is proper only in narrow, demanding circumstances — e.g., when the intrinsic evidence clearly establishes that the error could only be reasonably understood in one way.
guidance: Court quotes precedent (Essex, Ultimax, CBT Flint, Novo, Group One, Pavo) and explains that correction is appropriate only when the construction is not subject to reasonable debate; the standard takes account of the public-notice function of patents and is applied de novo based entirely on intrinsic evidence.

name: Error must be evident from the face of the patent
description: "The error must be 'evident from the face of the patent'" — i.e., obvious as determined 'from the point of view of one skilled in the art.'
guidance: Evidence for obviousness comes from claim language, specification, and figures; if the claim grammar/logic plainly lacks antecedent or makes no sense, that supports evident error (example: backward reference to 'the connection profile of the second part' when no such antecedent exists).

name: Correction must not be subject to reasonable debate
description: Correction is appropriate only if 'the correction is not subject to reasonable debate based on consideration of the claim language and the specification and the prosecution history does not suggest a different interpretation of the claims.'
guidance: Court applies Novo/CBT Flint language: consider claim language and specification to determine whether only one reasonable correction exists; if reasonable parties could debate alternative constructions, judicial correction is improper.

name: Correction limited to minor typographical/clerical errors
description: A district court may correct 'obvious minor typographical and clerical errors in patents.'
guidance: The correction should be textually simple and minor (e.g., restoring an omitted word) and must not amount to remaking the claim or changing substantive claim scope; Essex example: adding omitted word 'rear.'

name: Correction must be textually simple and not change claim scope
description: The correction should be 'textually simple' and should not alter the scope or meaning of the claims in a substantive way.
guidance: Corrections that significantly change claim context or scope are disallowed; however, if multiple reasonable alternatives have the same scope and meaning, a court may correct to the version that captures the intended scope (CBT Flint).

name: Uniqueness of the reasonable correction (only one reasonable correction)
description: The proposed correction must be the only reasonable correction a person skilled in the art would adopt from the intrinsic evidence.
guidance: Court must show the correction (e.g., changing 'second' to 'first') is the unique reading that the claim language and specification compel; alternative corrections that would alter meaning are not acceptable.

name: Antecedent basis requirement as a trigger for indefiniteness/correction
description: Claims require proper antecedent basis; a missing antecedent (e.g., introducing 'the connection profile of the second part' without prior mention) can render a phrase indefinite or demonstrate an evident clerical error.
guidance: When a backward-referring 'the' lacks an antecedent in the claim, a skilled reader will note the anomaly; courts assess whether that anomaly evidences an obvious error correctable by construction.

name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence; limited role for extrinsic evidence
description: Claim interpretation and judicial correction depend on intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history); extrinsic evidence (experts) plays a limited role and cannot override clear intrinsic conclusions.
guidance: District courts should not rely on extrinsic evidence to alter intrinsic conclusions; expert testimony that merely repeats intrinsic points adds nothing. Teva/Phillips limits on expert evidence are invoked.

name: Avoid using correction to 're-make' the claim
description: Correction cannot be 'in any real sense ... a re-making of the claim'—it must give the claim the meaning intended by the applicant and understood by the examiner, not craft a new claim.
guidance: Essex principle: the correction must reflect what was intended and understood; courts must resist correcting into language that would supply substantive additions or omitted limitations beyond a simple textual fix.

name: Aggregate rule for judicial correction
description: If (1) the error is evident on the face of the patent, (2) the proposed correction is the only reasonable interpretation from intrinsic evidence, and (3) the change is minor/clerical/textually simple and the prosecution history does not compel a different meaning, then judicial correction is appropriate.
guidance: This aggregates the elements discussed by the court; the analysis is fact-specific and must be applied de novo using claim language, specification, figures, and prosecution history; court cited Scalia & Garner: correct when failing to do so would yield a disposition no reasonable person could approve.

name: Full, clear, and exact description
description: The goal in a patent application is to provide a full, clear, and exact description of the invention in a way that particularly points out and distinctly identifies what the inventor believes he or she has invented and wants the patent to cover.
guidance: Describe the invention comprehensively so a reader can understand what is claimed and what the inventor regards as the invention. This is the statutory requirement for a patent specification; the disclosure must 'particularly point out and distinctly identify' the invention. Omit nothing material to understanding the invention.

name: Choose wording to avoid literal misinterpretation (say what you mean)
description: You need to choose your words carefully to make sure your words are exactly what you mean — what you say will be interpreted literally.
guidance: Carefully proofread for literal errors or imprecise phrasing that could render a claim meaningless (e.g., 'heat the dough to 450 degrees' vs 'heat the oven to 450 degrees'). Antipattern: sloppy or colloquial phrasing that changes legal effect when read literally.

name: Include examples and embodiments to flesh out concepts
description: Consider providing an example or two to help flesh out what it is you are describing — while not required examples can be particularly helpful in a patent application.
guidance: Use worked examples, specific parameter values, exemplary materials, or implementation steps to illustrate embodiments. Examples help satisfy enablement and illustrate the breadth/scope of claimed concepts.

name: Claims define the invention / primary importance of claim language
description: ‘The claims of a patent define the invention to which the patentee is entitled the right to exclude.’ Claims themselves—not the patent specification, dictionaries or extrinsic evidence—are 'of primary importance' in defining a patent's scope.
guidance: Treat claim language as the starting point and primary authority for scope. Use other claims as a source of enlightenment only after construing claim language; specification and extrinsic evidence may inform but should not override clear claim language. (Cites Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303.)

name: Claim differentiation doctrine (negative and positive)
description: Presence of a dependent claim that adds a particular limitation gives rise to a presumption that the limitation in question is not present in the independent claim ('negative' differentiation). Conversely, independent claims are deemed broader than their dependents so that if one infringes a dependent claim, infringement of its independent parent automatically follows ('positive' differentiation).
guidance: Use differences among claims as a guide to meaning and scope. Claim differentiation can broaden independent claims based on dependent claim language, and is frequently relied upon by courts to construe claims more broadly (examples: Wright Med. Tech., Laitram, Robotic Vision). But be aware it is a presumption, not an absolute rule.

name: Statutory text of 35 U.S.C. §112(d) for dependent claims
description: Current provision: '(d) Reference in Dependent Forms.—Subject to subsection (e), a claim in dependent form shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed. A claim in dependent form shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.'
guidance: Treat §112(d) as a statutory requirement that defines when a claim is properly in dependent form and how it must be construed (i.e., incorpora­tion of parent claim limitations). Congress intended the provision to permit dependent claiming but also to set a procedural/substantive requirement for dependents.

name: Dependent claim must 'specify a further limitation' or be invalid (Pfizer)
description: A dependent claim that does not 'specify a further limitation of the subject matter of the claim to which it refers' fails §112(d) and can be invalidated (Pfizer v. Ranbaxy).
guidance: Ensure that each dependent claim both refers to an earlier claim and adds a further limiting element; failure to do so can render the dependent claim invalid. Courts will not rewrite claims to preserve validity. Example: Pfizer invalidated a dependent claim that merely recited subject matter outside the scope of its immediate parent and thus did not further limit it.

name: Dependency determined by substance, not form (Monsanto)
description: Whether a claim is dependent depends on the substance of the claim in light of §112(d), not merely on its customary dependent claim wording. A claim drafted in an unusual format can still be dependent if it refers to an earlier claim and adds a further limitation.
guidance: Evaluate the actual claim language and the statutory requirements to determine dependence; do not allow mere variations in wording or unconventional formatting to defeat a dependency that meets §112(d)'s substantive criteria (Monsanto Co. v. Syngenta Seeds).

name: §112(d) can prevent using dependent claims to broaden independent claims (Zircon)
description: Section 112(d) can limit a patentee’s attempt to use the language of a dependent claim to broaden an independent claim when such a reading would make the dependent claim fail to further limit the parent (Zircon v. Stanley Black & Decker).
guidance: Be cautious about arguing that independent claims should be broadened based on dependent claims if that reading would violate §112(d). Consult specification and prosecution history to determine the proper meaning (Zircon: 'ratio' meant division per specification/prosecution history; dependent claims could not be used to expand to subtraction).

name: Do not construe claims to preserve validity except where ambiguity remains
description: Courts should not construe claims to preserve their validity unless 'the court concludes, after applying all the available tools of claim construction, that the claim is still ambiguous' (Phillips).
guidance: Avoid constructions motivated solely by an intent to save validity; only where a claim remains ambiguous after full claim-construction analysis should courts select a construction that preserves validity. This principle supports applying §112(d) first rather than using claim differentiation as a 'golden ticket' to validate dependents.

name: PTO practice: §112(d) rejections are rare but possible
description: In PTO prosecution practice, rejections under §112 paragraph (d) (now §112(d)) are uncommon; examiners rarely perform substantive invalid dependent-claim analyses, though isolated rejections occur (e.g., scrivener's errors, dependent claims that merely restate properties).
guidance: Do not assume that lack of §112(d) scrutiny during prosecution insulates dependent claims from invalidity in litigation; courts may apply §112(d) even if the PTO overlooked the issue. Consider potential §112(d) vulnerabilities when drafting and prosecuting dependent claims.

name: District court jurisdiction for discrimination claims (5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2))
description: Federal district courts, not this court, have jurisdiction over '[c]ases of discrimination subject to the provisions of [5 U.S.C. §] 7702,' 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2)—i.e., where an employee has made a non-frivolous allegation regarding an action appealable to the Board and that the action was based, at least in part, on covered discrimination.
guidance: Cites Perry v. Merit Sys. Prot. Bd., 582 U.S. 420, 437 (2017). Apply this standard when an EEO complaint alleges discriminatory personnel actions (e.g., alleged termination) and the discrimination allegation is non-frivolous; such matters belong in district court rather than the Federal Circuit.

name: Role of prior art in infringement comparison (three-way comparison)
description: Comparison should consider the patented design, the accused design, and the closest or relevant prior art designs to determine whether an ordinary observer (familiar with the prior art) would be deceived.
guidance: Courts and factfinders should use the prior art as the frame of reference. Where the prior art is close or the field crowded, small differences between claimed and accused designs may be significant. The accused infringer bears the burden of production to introduce comparison prior art; the patentee retains the ultimate burden to prove infringement by a preponderance of the evidence.

name: Functional/utilitarian limitation (dictated by utilitarian purpose)
description: A patented design may be invalid if the appearance is dictated solely by utilitarian purpose (design governed by function rather than ornamentation).
guidance: Courts should assess and distinguish between ornamental and purely functional elements (see Oddzon). If a design's appearance is dictated by function (Seiko Epson cited), it may be invalid; functional features do not broaden claim scope for ornamental protection.

name: When verbal description is required for obviousness/invalidity
description: In determining obviousness (invalidity), trial courts must attempt to translate visual descriptions into words to communicate the reasoning behind the decision.
guidance: Translating visual elements into verbal descriptions is required for explaining invalidity analyses (Durling), but that requirement is distinct from and does not mandate detailed verbal claim construction for infringement inquiries.

name: Court guidance to factfinder without invading factfinding role
description: A trial court may point out features of the claimed design as they relate to the accused design and prior art, and describe conventions or prosecution history, but must avoid unduly invading the jury's fact-finding.
guidance: Permissible guidance includes pointing out that the patented design has pads on three sides while the accused product has pads on four; courts can describe conventions (e.g., broken lines), prosecution history effects, and functionality distinctions. Appellate courts should be cautious about over-prescriptive guidance that interferes with the trial court's discretion.

name: Role of drafting conventions and prosecution history
description: Features like broken lines and statements made during prosecution can affect the scope of a design patent claim.
guidance: Courts should assess the role of broken lines (37 C.F.R. § 1.152) and any representations in the prosecution history (see Goodyear) when construing the scope of the claimed design.

name: Commitments and contingencies disclosure standards
description: USPTO discloses routine administrative proceedings, legal actions, and claims, including threatened or pending litigation. Management assesses likelihood (probable, reasonably possible) and discloses estimated amounts when reasonably possible.
guidance: Examples: management expects it is reasonably possible that ~$2,400 thousand may be owed for awards/damages involving labor relations claims; discusses when adverse outcomes were probable and resolution details. Payments to the Judgment Fund and existence/absence of major long-term commitments are disclosed.

name: Possession standard for written description
description: The written description requirement is met when the specification “conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of” and “actually invented” the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Ask whether the disclosure would allow a person of ordinary skill to clearly conclude that the inventor invented the claimed invention as of the asserted priority date (Lockwood: must describe an invention in sufficient detail). The focus is on what the spec reasonably conveys to the artisan, not later inferences.

name: Written description of specific quantitative limitations (e.g., expression levels)
description: For limitations reciting particular expression levels or numeric ranges, the earlier application must disclose those levels or otherwise convey possession of those specific quantitative limitations.
guidance: General statements about low or higher activity are insufficient if no numerical levels or enabling examples are provided. The absence of gene therapy examples or numerical expression data in the earlier application supports a finding of inadequate written description for claimed expression-level limitations.

name: Written description must support specific vector/type limitations (e.g., AAV vs adenovirus)
description: A disclosure of dosing or particles/kg for one viral family (e.g., adenovirus) does not necessarily provide written description support for claims directed to a different viral family (e.g., adeno-associated virus, AAV).
guidance: Units or particles/kg alone do not bridge different vector families. The specification must convey that the inventor possessed administering the particular vector type claimed; expert testimony that dosing for one vector ‘does not inform’ dosing for another supports non-support.

name: Priority entitlement depends on adequate written description
description: If the earlier application does not provide adequate written description support for the claimed limitations, the claims are not entitled to the earlier filing date and instead take the later patent's filing date.
guidance: Legal consequence: lacking written description, earlier provisional cannot be relied upon for priority; this can render intervening references prior art under §102(a).

name: Nexus requirement for objective indicia
description: A patentee must establish a nexus between the objective evidence and the merits of the claimed invention; the patentee bears the burden of establishing that nexus.
guidance: Nexus means a legally and factually sufficient connection such that the objective evidence should be considered in determining non-obviousness. If the evidence is directed to something other than what is both claimed and novel, nexus is lacking (ClassCo; Merck & Cie).

name: Presumption of nexus and coextensiveness
description: A patentee is entitled to a presumption of nexus when the patentee shows the asserted objective evidence is tied to a specific product and that product ‘embodies the claimed features, and is coextensive with them.’
guidance: If the marketed product embodies the claimed features and is coextensive (i.e., product is the invention disclosed and claimed), nexus is presumed and the burden shifts to the party asserting obviousness to rebut. Coextensive means the product is essentially the claimed invention and unclaimed features are insignificant.

name: Commensurate-in-scope requirement for nexus
description: There is no nexus unless the evidence presented is ‘reasonably commensurate with the scope of the claims.’
guidance: Evidence directed to a narrow aspect (e.g., a single mutation) may fail to be commensurate with broad claims that cover many variants, capsids, promoters, or sequences. Courts equate coextensiveness with commensurate-in-scope in evaluating presumptions of nexus (Fox Factory, Zaxcom).

name: Alternative route to prove nexus without presumption
description: Even when a presumption of nexus is inappropriate, a patent owner may still prove nexus by showing the secondary-considerations evidence is the direct result of the unique characteristics of the claimed invention.
guidance: Patent owner must identify the unique characteristics and provide evidence linking the objective indicia directly to those characteristics (Fox Factory quoting In re Huang). Mere industry praise directed to an element already in the prior art will not suffice.

name: Claim construction influences validity analysis (e.g., definition of 'treating')
description: How claim terms are construed (for example, ‘treating’ construed to include partial alleviation of symptoms) materially affects anticipation/obviousness analyses and whether prior art discloses or renders the claim obvious.
guidance: Explicit claim constructions adopted in the proceeding should be applied consistently when assessing prior art teachings and whether those teachings satisfy claim limitations.

name: Required contents of a protection registration application
description: Application must include: (a) a declaration form made according to set form; (b) photos and technical declarations per set form; (c) power of attorney if filed through a representative; (d) documents evidencing registration right if registrant is transferee; (e) documents evidencing priority right where claimed; (f) vouchers of payment of fees and charges.
guidance: Applications and transactional documents must be in Vietnamese, except certain documents (power of attorney, documents evidencing registration right, priority right, other supporting documents) may be in another language but must be translated into Vietnamese at the agency's request. Documents evidencing priority include certified copies of first applications and transfer/inheritance papers. Each application must be for protection of one plant variety only.

name: Provisional rights between publication and grant
description: Provisional rights arise from date of publication of the protection registration application until grant; they do not exist if certificate is not granted. Registrants aware of commercial use by others may notify users of filing and publication dates; upon grant, the certificate holder may request compensation equivalent to licensing price for corresponding scope/duration for prior commercial use.
guidance: Notification in writing specifying filing and publication dates precedes compensation claims. Compensation claims apply after grant if prior use continued after notification.

name: Anticipation — every element in a single reference
description: A claimed invention may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 when the invention is anticipated (not novel) over a disclosure available as prior art. To reject a claim as anticipated by a reference, the disclosure must teach every element required by the claim under its broadest reasonable interpretation.
guidance: “A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference.” (Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil). The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the claim; elements must be arranged as required by the claim (but ipsissimis verbis identity of terminology is not required). See MPEP § 2131 and case law (e.g., Richardson v. Suzuki; In re Bond).

name: Not ipsissimis verbis test (terminology flexibility)
description: Elements must be arranged as required by the claim, but identity of terminology is not required; the test is not ipsissimis verbis.
guidance: In re Bond and related cases: identity of terminology is not necessary so long as the reference discloses the elements and arrangement required by the claim. Examiners should analyze whether the reference sufficiently describes the claimed elements, not whether it uses the exact words of the claim.

name: Use extra references to prove the primary reference contains an 'enabled disclosure'
description: An additional reference may be relied on to show that the primary reference has an 'enabled disclosure' when the claimed composition or machine is disclosed identically by the reference but methods or enabling details are missing.
guidance: Case examples: In re Samour; In re Donohue — publication teaching structure plus patents teaching methods of making the class. If the publication teaches all claim elements, motivation to combine is not required; patents may be submitted to show what was publicly known that would enable the primary reference.

name: Use extra references or extrinsic evidence to explain meaning of a term in the primary reference
description: Extrinsic evidence may be used to explain (but not expand) the meaning of terms and phrases used in the primary reference relied upon as anticipatory prior art.
guidance: Example: Baxter Travenol — extrinsic evidence (depositions, declarations, admissions) showed what 'commercial blood bags' meant. Actelion v. Mylan: where claims/specification/prosecution history do not clarify a term's precision, courts may consult extrinsic evidence to understand the meaning of the term to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time. Do not use extrinsic evidence to broaden a reference beyond what it teaches.

name: Genus-species: a species will anticipate a genus
description: A generic (genus) claim cannot be allowed if the prior art discloses a species falling within the claimed genus — the species will anticipate the genus.
guidance: Cited cases: In re Slayter; In re Gosteli. If a prior art reference discloses a specific species within a claimed genus, the genus claim is anticipated unless entitlement to an earlier priority date exists.

name: Species named in a reference anticipates the species claim regardless of how many species are listed
description: When the species is clearly named in a reference, the species claim is anticipated no matter how many other species are additionally named.
guidance: Example: Ex parte A — a compound specifically named among many compounds is still 'described' for anticipation purposes (Merck Index analogy). In re Sivaramakrishnan also supports this principle; unexpected properties of the species do not negate anticipation if the species was disclosed.

name: Anticipation of ranges — specific example within claimed range anticipates
description: A claim that covers several compositions by recitation of ranges is anticipated if one specific example within the prior art falls within the claimed range.
guidance: Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner: an actual prior art data point within a claimed compositional range anticipates the range. See also UCB, Inc. v. Actavis Labs. UT, Inc. If the prior art discloses a point within the claimed range, the prior art anticipates the claim.

name: Anticipation of ranges — overlapping/touching ranges require 'sufficient specificity'
description: When the prior art teaches a range overlapping or touching the claimed range but provides no specific examples within the claimed range, anticipation depends on whether the prior art range discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' (case-by-case).
guidance: Examiners must consider the narrowness of the claimed range and other facts; cases include ClearValue (anticipated where no evidence of criticality across range) and Atofina (not anticipatory where claimed narrow range was shown critical). If unclear, an examiner may make both a §102 and §103 statement and must explain reasons for anticipation and an obviousness analysis. See MPEP § 2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

name: Nonanalogous art or 'teaching away' does not prevent anticipation
description: Arguments that alleged anticipatory prior art is nonanalogous, teaches away, or addressed a different problem are not germane to a §102 anticipation rejection; a reference can be anticipatory even if it disparages the invention or is from a different field.
guidance: Twin Disc; State Contracting & Eng'g; Celeritas; Upsher-Smith Labs; Atlas Powder: the focus is whether the reference explicitly or inherently discloses every limitation in the claims, regardless of its field or whether it later disparages the invention.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) — sale of product made by secret process may be public use if process can be determined from product
description: The nonsecret use of a claimed process in producing articles for commercial purposes is a public use; secret use coupled with sale does not result in public use unless the public could learn the claimed process by examining the product.
guidance: If examination of the product would reveal the process, sale can create a public use; otherwise secret process + sale does not create a §102(a) bar.

name: Elements required to establish infringement
description: Patentee must prove ownership of the patent and that defendant has practiced the patent; defendant’s products or methods must fall within the scope of protection of the patent.
guidance: Scope of protection is determined by claim construction prior to infringement determination.

name: Principle that scope of protection is determined by claims
description: The scope of protection is the objective scope determined by what is stated in the claims; claims must be construed before determining infringement, novelty, or inventive step and claim construction is a legal evaluation, not factual confession.
guidance: Claims should be construed objectively and reasonably based on claim wording, reference to detailed description/drawings, and general technical knowledge at filing; prosecution history may be referenced but should not be used to broaden or narrow claim meaning.

name: Literal interpretation principle and reference to description/prosecution history
description: Main reliance is on wording of the claims (literal interpretation), but descriptions/drawings and general technical knowledge should be given weight (reference to description); prosecution history (specs, amendments, written arguments, examiner opinions) may be consulted but not used to broaden or narrow claims.
guidance: Use descriptions/drawings to accurately understand technical meaning of claim language; avoid using prosecution history to alter claim scope.

name: Infringement analysis by element-by-element comparison (all elements rule)
description: Plaintiff breaks down disputed claim into elements and compares them to corresponding elements of defendant’s product/process; defendant may dispute element identification and courts ensure common understanding; infringement requires every element and their organic combination to be present.
guidance: One-to-one comparison charts are often produced; if any element is missing, no infringement under literal all-elements rule.

name: Literal infringement standard
description: Established when all claim elements and their organic combination, as specified by literal interpretation of the claims, are found in the defendant’s product or process.
guidance: Literal matching of claim language and combination is required for literal infringement.

name: Infringement by equivalence (requirements and burdens)
description: Infringement by equivalence is established when defendant’s elements are not literally identical but are equivalent, requiring positive and negative requirements: (i) identity of solution principles (same principle to solve problem); (ii) substantial identity of effects; (iii) easiness of replacement (person skilled would easily conceive replacement); (iv) not free-to-practice technology in public domain; (v) replaced element not purposely excluded from claim scope during prosecution.
guidance: Patentee bears burden for positive requirements; infringer bears burden for negative requirements. Determination requires identifying the essence of the technical idea underlying the patented solution in light of description and prior art; superficial feature deductions are insufficient.

name: Claims as starting point for patentability assessment
description: The starting point and basis for assessing patentability under Articles 52 to 57 EPC is the claims.
guidance: The EBA referred to existing case law applying provisions analogously to examining patentability and extracted the principle that claims are the primary reference when assessing novelty, inventive step and other patentability requirements. This emphasises that claim language anchors the assessment even where other parts of the file are consulted.

name: Description and drawings must always be consulted when interpreting claims for patentability
description: The description and any drawings must always be consulted when interpreting claims, not just in cases of unclarity or ambiguity.
guidance: The EBA rejected prior Board of Appeal case law that saw no need to refer to descriptions and drawings where a claim appeared clear in isolation. The decision aligns EPO practice with national courts and the UPC and stresses consulting the description/drawings as a mandatory step in claim interpretation for patentability.

name: Consulting description is required but does not necessarily allow overriding clear claim language
description: The EBA orders that the description should always be consulted to interpret the claims, but consulting the description does not necessarily mean using it to override otherwise clear claim language.
guidance: Commentators note the nuance: the decision mandates consultation of the description/drawings but leaves open the extent to which a clear claim may be modified by descriptive definitions. Practitioners should expect examiners and tribunals to consult the description but not automatically accept descriptive definitions that contradict clear claim wording.

name: Harmonisation principle with downstream tribunals
description: The EBA underlined the importance of uniformly applying claim interpretation principles in granting patents as well as revocation and infringement proceedings, aligning EPO practice with national courts and the UPC.
guidance: The decision states it would be 'a most unattractive proposition that the EPO deliberately adopt a contrary practice to that of the tribunals that are downstream of its patents.' This supports convergence of interpretative practice across forums and may affect prosecution, opposition and litigation strategies.

name: Unresolved question on disregarding description definitions (question 3 inadmissible)
description: The EBA deemed the question of whether a definition in the description can be disregarded when interpreting claims to assess patentability inadmissible (considered encompassed by the second question), leaving this specific issue unanswered.
guidance: Because the EBA did not answer whether explicit descriptive definitions can be ignored, practical uncertainty remains. Practitioners report situations where examiners refuse to adopt a description-provided definition if it is not in the claim; the decision may not settle that examiner/tribunal practice. Expect debate and continued attention to how tribunals treat explicit definitions in the description.

name: Rejection of prior Board of Appeal practice that omits consultation where claim appears clear
description: The EBA rejected contrary BoA case law which held there was no need to refer to descriptions and drawings when interpreting a clear claim.
guidance: This entry emphasises the anti-pattern the EBA overturned: treating isolated claim language as sufficient without consulting the rest of the application. Practitioners should avoid relying on the idea that a claim read in isolation will be decisive; always ensure the description/drawings support the intended claim meaning.

name: Practical implication for prosecution and opposition strategies
description: Because descriptions and drawings must be consulted, applicants and opponents should ensure definitions, embodiments and drawings are drafted and relied on consistently to support claim interpretation across granting, opposition and litigation.
guidance: Practical steps include placing clear definitions and embodiments in the description that support intended claim scope, and being prepared to argue how the description informs claim meaning without improperly broadening or contradicting clear claim text. The decision signals that harmonised downstream practice may influence how examiners and tribunals assess claim scope.

name: Accuracy in description of the invention in letters-patent
description: It is most important that the invention be accurately pointed out in the letters-patent so that the inventor's rights are permanently established within precise limits required by the nature of the discovery and its position in the arts.
guidance: The Patent Office exists to secure this accuracy by examining novelty and utility, correcting language, and resolving rival claims; errors in description can produce serious injustice if not corrected.

name: Patent construction: first general rule — liberally construed in favor of inventor
description: Patents are to be liberally construed in favor of the inventor so as to give appropriate effect to the invention as claimed.
guidance: Liberal construction permits interpretation in accordance with the real nature of the invention unless the patent's language clearly forbids such interpretation.

name: Limitation on liberal construction
description: The rule of liberal construction does not authorize departure from the language of the letters-patent nor an equivocal or elastic interpretation of the claims.
guidance: Courts will not stretch patent language beyond its words; liberal construction must still respect clear language and limits set by the claims.

name: Patent construction: entire patent construed together as an indivisible instrument
description: An entire patent — claims, specification, drawings — must be construed together; different parts may clarify and restrict claims but may not enlarge them.
guidance: Other portions of the patent may be used to restrict the claims to their proper scope but cannot be used to broaden them beyond the claim language.

name: Special rules of construction for particular claim-types
description: Special rules apply to pioneer patents, re-issued patents, patents granted by act of Congress, claims for combinations, improvements, claims for principles/functions/effects, claims to an indivisible entirety versus separate devices, use of foreign words, 'substantially as described', 'generic', and terms admitting degrees.
guidance: These special rules modify general construction principles and address recurring interpretive issues; courts have developed specific doctrines for each category.

name: Entitlement to equivalents despite reformed claims
description: A patentee is entitled to equivalents though he may have reformed his claims under requirements of the Patent Office.
guidance: Case: Rodebaugh v. Jackson (1889). Principle: narrowing or amending claims during prosecution does not necessarily deprive the patentee of protection under the doctrine of equivalents.

name: Use for a different purpose can be infringement
description: Use of the invention for a different purpose is infringement.
guidance: Case: Thompson v. Gildersleeve (1888). Even non-ordinary uses that fall within claim scope may infringe.

name: Separate acts by different parties can infringe if common purpose
description: A patent may be infringed by the separate acts of different parties having a common purpose, though no one act is by itself an infringement.
guidance: Case: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. American Zylonite Co. (1887). Used in multi-actor scenarios where combined conduct achieves claim elements.

name: Combination not infringed unless all elements or equivalents used
description: A combination is not infringed unless all its elements or their equivalents are used.
guidance: Case: Perkins v. Eaton (1889). Defense: absence of one claim element or its equivalent defeats infringement of the combination claim.

name: Bond and account in lieu of injunction when infringement disputed and defendant claims ignorance
description: A bond and account may be ordered in lieu of an injunction when infringement is disputed, and defendant avers that he was ignorant of the patent until the suit was brought and derived no real aid from the invention.
guidance: Case: Eagle Mfg. Co. v. Chamberlain Plow Co. (1888). Fact-specific protective measures used when uncertainty exists.

name: Finality timing for grant/reject decisions
description: The time at which the decision to grant a patent becomes final and conclusive is when a certified copy of the decision to grant a patent is served to the applicant. The time at which the decision to reject an application becomes final and conclusive is when thirty days have elapsed from the date on which a certified copy of the decision to reject a patent is served to the applicant.
guidance: Examiners must use these timings to determine whether subsequent amendment or addition of priority claims is permitted.

name: Post 1 year 4 months limitation to clerical corrections only
description: Amendments of a priority claim after one year and four months has elapsed shall be permitted only when correcting clerical errors in the indication of the priority claim.
guidance: Changing the first application, specifying a first application not previously specified, or adding the first application after this period are not allowed. Withdrawal of all or part of priority claims remains allowed even after this period.

name: Formality examination requirements for priority
description: The requirements for formality examination on priority claim under the Treaty include: the identicalness of the applicants, the earliest filing date of the first application filed in one of the countries under the Treaty, the regularity of the first application, the compliance with the priority period, the description of the purport of priority claim and the submission of the evidential documents proving the priority claim.
guidance: Examiner must check each listed element when assessing formality; deficiencies in part of multiple priority claims may lead to partial invalidation (see Note1).

name: Use of Patent Net / WIPO records for evidential documents
description: The evidential documents certifying the priority in an international patent application can be checked through the evidential documents for priority claims posted onto the Patent Net. If not available, examiner can access attached documents via WIPO (http://www.wipo.int/pctdb/en). If still not confirmed, examiner shall request amendment and then determine whether to invalidate priority claim after considering submissions and opportunity to explain.
guidance: Examiner should exhaust electronic sources before requesting applicant submission; provide opportunity to explain before invalidating.

name: Consequences of invalidated priority claim for substantive examination date
description: If the examiner has invalidated priority claim since the claim is illegitimate based on the result of the formality examination and amendment to priority claim, the examiner shall examine the application ... based on the filing date of the application with a priority claim under the Treaty (the filing date in the Republic of Korea).
guidance: Invalidation of priority shifts applicable prior art cutoff and patentability determination to the local filing date rather than any earlier priority date.

name: Granting retroactive filing date by invention when priority legitimate
description: Where priority claim is found to be legitimate, the examiner shall determine whether to grant a retroactive filing date by invention when examining the patentability of the inventions. For inventions identical to those in the first application (specification/drawings), examine based on filing date of the first application; otherwise examine based on filing date of the claiming application.
guidance: Examiner may request translations of evidential documents to compare content. When delivering grounds for rejection without retroactive filing date, examiner must describe why the retroactive date was not granted.

name: Identicalness standard for retroactive priority
description: Requirements for identicalness do not mean claims must be identical; rather the invention described in the claims of the application claiming priority shall be identical to the invention in the specification or drawings of the first application. Determination uses the standard in Article 29(3) of the Patent Act.
guidance: Apply Article 29(3) standard; identity may be by invention (not necessarily claim language). Examples illustrate partial identity (e.g., subsets of compounds/elements take priority date for those subsets).

name: Determination of priority dates for multiple-first-application cases
description: Where a Korean patent application has priority claims for more than two first applications, the examiner shall examine the application based on the earliest filing date of each invention under the Treaty in accordance with Articles 29 and 36 of the Patent Act.
guidance: If an invention is based on one of the first applications, examine based on filing date of that first application. If an invention combines subject matter separately described in different first applications (e.g., a+b where a only in A and b only in B), examine that combined invention based on the filing date of the Korean application.

name: Effect of withdrawing earliest-filed priority among multiple claims
description: Where a priority claim in the first application having the earliest filing date has been withdrawn among more than two priority claims, the filing date of the earliest-filed remaining application shall be deemed to be the priority date.
guidance: Examiner must determine whether the newly earliest-filed application meets requirements to serve as basis of priority claim under the Paris Convention.

name: General instruction: accept evidential documents issued by other patent offices
description: Countries have various types of patent application systems; each patent office can determine whether their applications are regular national applications seeking priority claim and then issue evidential documents. Other patent offices can recognize priority based on those evidential documents.
guidance: KIPO examiners should rely on evidential documents issued by other offices as indicators of legitimacy, subject to further verification where necessary.

name: Treatment of priority claims based on US Continuation-In-Part (CIP)
description: Where priority claim is based only on a US CIP and only the CIP specification was submitted as evidential documents, examiner shall examine inventions based on the date to determine patentability without granting retroactive filing date. If original application spec/drawings are submitted, follow the guideline for original/CIP combinations.
guidance: If invention is described only in CIP, CIP filing date used. If invention described in both original and CIP and claiming app filed within one year of original, subject matter in both takes original filing date; subject matter only in CIP takes CIP filing date. If claiming app filed after one year from original, retroactive date may not be available for subject matter described in original and CIP.

name: CIP exception to being 'first application' under Paris Convention
description: CIP application is not recognized as the first application prescribed in Article 4C(2) of the Paris Convention; therefore, in principle a CIP's priority claim cannot be recognized. Exception: if a copy of the original application's specification/drawings (including application number) has been submitted and the claiming application is ensured to be claiming priority based on subject matter only in the CIP spec/drawings.
guidance: Examiner must confirm presence of original spec/drawings with application number to consider exception.

name: Treatment of priority claims based on US provisional and non-provisional applications
description: Provisional applications and converted provisional/non-provisional relationships affect which application can serve as basis for priority claim. Examiner shall determine legality based on which application the USPTO has issued evidential documents for; the priority period starts on filing date of the provisional recognized as the filing date of the legitimate application.
guidance: Normally, if non-provisional not filed after provisional, provisional serves as basis. If non-provisional filed claiming benefit of provisional, the provisional serves as basic application and priority period begins on provisional's filing date. Examiner relies on USPTO-issued evidential docs.

name: Scope of revocation suits (original disposition principle)
description: A revocation suit can generally only be filed against the original disposition (principle of original dispositions), except where the adjudication itself is legally flawed (exceptional adjudication).
guidance: Suits against adjudications are allowed only as prescribed by the Patent Act; you cannot sue claiming 'patent X shall become null and void' — the complaint must seek revocation of the IPTAB decision (specifying date and case number).

name: Claim construction as legal determination
description: The scope of protection is determined by the claims and claim construction is a legal evaluation (not fact-finding) to be performed before assessing infringement, novelty, or inventive step.
guidance: Claim construction should determine the objective scope the patent effects reach; it cannot be established by confession and must be based primarily on claim wording with reference to descriptions/drawings and technical knowledge.

name: Principles of claim construction
description: Claims are construed mainly by the literal wording (principle of literal interpretation), but descriptions/drawings (reference to description) and general technical knowledge at filing are used to ascertain technical meaning. Prosecution history may be referenced but must not be used to broaden or narrow claim wording.
guidance: Reference to applicant's arguments, amendments, written arguments, and examiner opinions is permitted for accurate understanding but cannot alter the claim's meaning beyond its wording.

name: Infringement analysis and all-elements rule
description: Infringement analysis breaks the disputed claim into elements and compares each element (and their organic combination) to the defendant’s product or process; all elements as confirmed by claim construction must be present for infringement.
guidance: Parties often prepare one-to-one comparison charts. If any element is missing, the defendant’s product/process falls outside the protected scope (all elements rule).

name: Infringement by equivalence (positive and negative requirements)
description: Equivalence is found when defendant’s elements are not literally identical but are equivalent to claim elements, subject to positive requirements (shared problem-solving principle; substantially identical effects; replacement is obvious to person skilled in art) and negative requirements (defendant's technology not free-to-practice/public domain; replaced element not intentionally excluded during prosecution).
guidance: Burden of proof: patentee proves positive requirements; infringer proves negative requirements. Determination requires substantive review of the underlying technical idea (essence of technical solution) with reference to detailed description and prior art.

name: Defensive categories and defendant disclosure obligations
description: Defenses are legally cognizable rebuttals (burden on defendant); denials challenge plaintiff’s proof (burden on plaintiff). A defendant denying infringement must disclose the product/process actually used; refusal without justification may lead the court to presume infringement.
guidance: Under amended Patent Act provisions, courts may draw adverse inferences if a defendant refuses to provide details of the product/process used. Denial examples include arguing the patent right doesn't exist or the defendant's technology does not fall within the claim scope.

name: Abuse of rights defense (review of inventive step in infringement suits)
description: When it is clear that the patented invention lacks an inventive step (or is invalid for novelty/description), claims for damages or injunctions may constitute an abuse of rights; courts handling infringement suits may review inventive step to assess this defense.
guidance: The Supreme Court permits the infringement court to decide inventive step when the defense is raised. The plaintiff may respond with a correction/reply to narrow or correct claims, provided the correction does not substantially alter the claimed subject matter.

name: Identify judicial exceptions in Step 2A
description: How to identify judicial exceptions in Step 2A (e.g., laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas).
guidance: Use the Step 2A analysis to determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception. The July 2015 Update graphic and the case law chart available on the website may be used as guides for identifying abstract ideas and other exceptions.

name: Evaluate additional elements in Step 2B, particularly combinations
description: How to evaluate additional claim elements in Step 2B to determine if they amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception, with particular attention to combinations of elements.
guidance: Assess whether the additional elements, alone or in combination, integrate the exception into a practical application or otherwise add significantly more than the judicial exception itself. Consider whether any claimed combination produces a new/markedly different result or merely applies routine, conventional techniques.

name: Satisfy burden to make a prima facie case of ineligibility when writing a rejection
description: How to write a rejection that satisfies your burden to make a prima facie case of ineligibility.
guidance: A rejection must explain why the claim is directed to a judicial exception (per Step 2A) and why the additional elements do not add significantly more (per Step 2B). Use the worksheets, claim construction, and appropriate case law to build the prima facie case.

name: Use the Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheets (generic and Nature-Based Products)
description: Which worksheet to use: generic Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheet vs Nature-Based Products Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheet.
guidance: Analyze claims using the appropriate worksheet: use the generic worksheet for general life-science claims (e.g., diagnostics/treatments) and the Nature-Based Products worksheet for claims reciting nature-based products and mixtures. Worksheets structure the Step 2A/2B analysis.

name: Determine whether claimed detection/diagnostic methods are routine and conventional
description: Identify when claim steps recite routine and conventional methods (e.g., physical biopsies, immunoassays) and the implications for Step 2B.
guidance: Example language: 'discloses detecting JUL-1 by routine and conventional methods such as (i) physical biopsies of skin, hair or nails, or (ii) immunoassays ... contacting the sample with an antibody ... and then binding between the antibody and the protein is detected using a laboratory technique such as fluoroscopy.' If elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional at the time of filing, they may not supply the 'significantly more' required in Step 2B.

name: Consider manufacturing/process features and specified parameters as potential inventive concept
description: Evaluate whether claimed manufacturing/process features (e.g., granulation to achieve X10/X90 particle sizes, crystallization controls, encapsulation for controlled release, addition of pectin) produce tangible, practical improvements beyond a natural product.
guidance: Example: 'Granular texiol having a particle size of X10 of 80 microns and X90 of 300 microns is preferred, because this particle size distribution results in a greatly increased (and consistent) dissolution rate ...' Such specific parameters and processing steps may support a finding of 'significantly more' if they produce new/markedly different properties as compared to the naturally occurring material.

name: Evaluate source and nature of biological materials (naturally occurring vs non-naturally occurring)
description: Determine whether claimed biological materials are naturally occurring, isolated, or non-naturally occurring (e.g., naturally occurring anti-JUL-1 antibodies vs porcine or monoclonal antibodies).
