guidance: Examples from the text: anti-JUL-1 antibodies that may be naturally occurring (isolated from a patient), non-naturally occurring (porcine anti-JUL-1 antibody created by injecting pigs), or a specific monoclonal antibody 'mAb-D33' created by applicant. Consider whether the material as claimed is merely a naturally occurring product or has been modified/isolated in a way that confers new characteristics or uses; also consider whether prior art use and routine application bear on whether the claimed material contributes 'significantly more.'

name: Registration and use of the ® symbol
description: If no opposition is encountered and the opposition term lapses, the trade mark registration certificate is issued electronically and should be checked for correctness. The ® symbol can only be used once the trade mark is registered in South Africa.
guidance: Verify the electronic certificate for errors and only begin using ® after registration. Use TM prior to registration to indicate claim of trade mark.

name: Check for linking/generic claims or rejoinder eligibility
description: In either traverse or no-traverse situations, examiners must determine if any allowable claims are linking and/or generic claims or if any nonelected inventions are eligible for rejoinder.
guidance: Treat linking/generic claims specially (see MPEP § 809) and consider rejoinder rules (MPEP § 821.04).

name: Clear, detailed record of how application is restricted
description: The examiner must provide a clear and detailed record of the restriction requirement to demarcate restricted inventions for future divisional/consonance and double patenting analysis.
guidance: The record should be detailed enough to determine whether inventions claimed in a divisional are consonant with the restriction requirement and therefore subject to double patenting prohibitions (citations: Geneva Pharms., GlaxoSmithKline). See MPEP § 804.01.

name: Species restriction specifics
description: When restricting between species, identify the species and reasons showing they are independent/distinct.
guidance: Follow MPEP § 809.02(a). Mention particular claim limitations and why such limitations support restriction to a particular disclosed species. Use form paragraph 8.01 or 8.02 to require election of species where appropriate.

name: Identify inventions other than species by grouping claims
description: Read all claims to determine what each claim covers and group claims directed to each separate invention with a short description of the extent of each invention.
guidance: State the type/relationship of each group (process, subcombination, product, etc.) and indicate classification or separate status of each group (class and subclass). While every claim should be accounted for, mis-grouping or omission won't affect propriety if correct disposition is clear. See MPEP § 817.

name: Election and required reply contents
description: A complete reply to a restriction requirement must include an election of one invention for examination and identification of claims encompassing the elected invention.
guidance: Election may be with or without traverse. To reserve the right to petition, the election must be made with traverse. If the reply does not distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors, the election is treated as without traverse. Traversal must be presented at time of election to be timely. If claims are added after election, applicant must indicate which claims are readable upon the elected invention.

name: Special considerations for AIA/FITF and common-assignee double patenting
description: Use specific AIA form paragraphs and include appropriate double patenting notices where claims are directed to same invention or not patentably distinct across commonly-assigned applications/patents.
guidance: Use paragraphs such as 8.27.aia, 8.28.aia and include nonstatutory/provisional double patenting rejections (form paragraphs 8.31–8.37) and appropriate 102/103 paragraphs (e.g., 7.21.aia) as needed. Insert patent/application numbers and explain why claims are patentably indistinct where applicable. Include form paragraph 7.03.aia when required.

name: Traverse required to preserve right to petition
description: To preserve the right to petition under 37 CFR 1.144, applicant must distinctly and specifically point out all errors relied upon in a timely traverse.
guidance: Petition may be deferred until after final action or allowance of elected claims but must be filed not later than the filing date of the notice of appeal. If errors are not distinctly and specifically pointed out, the election is treated as without traverse and form paragraph 8.25.02 should be used.

name: Traverse with linking claims — special rules
description: A proper traverse with linking claims must distinctly and specifically point out errors; treatment of linking claims affects preservation of the right to petition and finality.
guidance: If restriction is made final following traverse, the right to petition is preserved even if linking claims are canceled. If final restriction is contingent on nonallowability of linking claims, applicant may petition under 37 CFR 1.144 without waiting for final action on linking claims, or defer until linking claims are finally rejected (but not later than notice of appeal). An election coupled with argument that the linking claim is allowable is not a traverse (it concedes restriction proper if linking claim not allowable). If the linking claim is allowed, restriction must be withdrawn and all claims dependent from or containing the allowable linking claim must be acted upon.

name: Election other than express (origination/cancellation rules)
description: Elections may be made implicitly by originally presented claims acted upon, by optional cancellation leaving claims to one invention, or by cancellation lacking an express election statement.
guidance: Originally presented claims acted upon determine the invention elected for restriction purposes. If applicant cancels claims to all but one invention, the remaining invention is deemed elected even without express statement. Where only generic or only linking claims were first prosecuted, later species or multiple linked inventions presented may require election per MPEP § 818.02(b).

name: Withdrawal and treatment of claims found to be to nonelected inventions
description: Claims found drawn to nonelected inventions are withdrawn from further consideration under 37 CFR 1.142(b) and must be clearly explained in the Office action.
guidance: The examiner should clearly set forth reasons why withdrawn claims are not readable on the elected invention. Applicant may traverse. If final restriction is made and applicant timely traversed, applicant may petition under 37 CFR 1.144. If election results in withdrawal such that the C* classification picture is incorrect, the examiner should submit a C* classification challenge prior to action on the merits to reflect elected invention appropriately.

name: After election with traverse — finalization or withdrawal
description: If initial requirement is traversed and examiner remains of opinion restriction proper, maintain and make it final in next Office action and respond to traverse arguments; if examiner finds requirement improper, withdraw and reinstate groups as appropriate.
guidance: Use form paragraph 8.25 to make restriction final and use form paragraph 8.05 to indicate claims stand withdrawn with traverse. If restriction is withdrawn in whole or part, clearly state which groups reinstated and provide action on the merits for reinstated claims.

name: After election without traverse — examiner actions
description: Where initial requirement is not traversed (expressly or via incomplete reply), examiner should act on elected claims and determine whether restriction should be withdrawn in whole or part.
guidance: Use form paragraphs 8.25.01 or 8.25.02 to acknowledge election without traverse and proceed to examine the elected claims; consider eligibility for rejoinder per MPEP § 821.04.

name: Initial inspection to determine necessity of drawings
description: Applications filed without drawings are initially inspected to determine whether a drawing is referred to in the specification, and if not, whether a drawing is necessary for the understanding of the invention (35 U.S.C. 113 first sentence).
guidance: OPAP/examiner assesses spec references and whether drawings are necessary to understand claimed subject matter; if necessary, filing date entitlement and follow-up notices are handled as described in MPEP §601.01.

name: Categories where drawings usually not necessary
description: USPTO practice treats applications with at least one process/method claim, composition applications, coated articles/products, articles made from a particular material/composition, laminated structures (only order of layers), or articles whose sole distinguishing feature is presence of a particular material as usually not requiring drawings under 35 U.S.C. 113 (first sentence).
guidance: Examples: coated sheet where invention is the coating only; article distinguished solely by use of a particular hydraulic fluid; packaged sutures where package structure is conventional. If claims involve significant structural/arrangement details, drawings may still be necessary.

name: Treatment of applications filed without drawings that refer to drawing figures
description: A nonprovisional application (filed prior to 12/18/2013) or a design application having at least one claim, or a provisional application having at least some disclosure, that describes drawing figures in the specification but is filed without drawings will be treated as an application filed without all of the drawing figures referred to in the specification (see MPEP §601.01(g)).
guidance: Such applications will be processed only if they contain something that can be construed as a written description; OPAP will take further action (e.g., Notice of Incomplete Application) if drawings are necessary for understanding under 35 U.S.C. 113.

name: OPAP Notice of Omitted Items when drawing figures referenced are missing
description: OPAP reviews papers to determine whether all figures of the drawings mentioned in the specification are present. If an application (under 35 U.S.C. 111 prior to 12/18/2013, or a design app) is filed without all drawing figures referred to in the specification, and the application contains something that can be construed as a written description (and other minimal items), an OPAP notice (e.g., 'Notice of Omitted Item(s)') will be sent indicating the application has been accorded a filing date but is lacking some figures.
guidance: For applications filed on/after 12/18/2013 under 37 CFR 1.53(b) or (c), an OPAP notice will be sent if drawings are lacking but the application contains something that can be construed as a specification, with or without claims.

name: Options after OPAP mailing in nonprovisional applications (A: establish prior receipt)
description: An applicant asserting that the drawing(s) was in fact received with the application must, within two months from the date of the OPAP notice, file a petition under 37 CFR 1.53(e) with the petition fee and evidence of deposit; the petition fee will be refunded if it is determined the drawings were received.
guidance: The two-month period is extendable under 37 CFR 1.136. Provide documentary evidence (e.g., date-stamped receipt) to support prior receipt claims.

name: Options after OPAP mailing in nonprovisional applications (C: accept application as deposited by amendment)
description: Applicant may accept the application as deposited in the USPTO by filing an appropriate amendment (e.g., substitute specification excluding claims, replacement drawing sheets renumbered, or amendment relying on incorporation by reference) without adding subject matter that was in the omitted drawings.
guidance: If accepting as deposited, the application will maintain the original filing date. Amendments must comply with 37 CFR 1.121(d), 1.121(b)(3), and 1.125, and must not add new matter (35 U.S.C. 132(a)).

name: Step 2B: 'Significantly more' / inventive concept
description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., whether there is an inventive concept). (Step 2B: YES/NO)
guidance: Consider whether claim elements add meaningful limitations beyond the abstract idea (e.g., improvements to computer or other technology, unconventional components, specific application). Generic computer implementation, routine data-gathering, or limiting to a field of use typically do not supply 'significantly more.'

name: Improvement to computer or other technology can supply inventive concept
description: A claim that purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself, or to improve another technology or technical field, can provide the necessary inventive concept to make an otherwise abstract idea patent eligible.
guidance: Examples: claims that produce functional and palpable applications or specific technological improvements (e.g., improved halftoning algorithms that improve image quality, application of a mathematical formula to configure hardware such as an antenna) were found eligible (Research Corp.; Mackay Radio; DDR Holdings).

name: Organizing human activity / fundamental economic practices are abstract ideas
description: Claims that recite longstanding commercial practices or methods of organizing human activity are likely to be characterized as abstract ideas.
guidance: Examples provided: intermediated settlement, hedging/consumption risk management, contractual guaranty services, managing bingo games—these concepts are organizing human activity/fundamental economic practices and were treated as abstract ideas in case analyses (Alice, Bilski, buySAFE, Planet Bingo).

name: Tying to a specific machine or meaningful limitation can support eligibility
description: Including a specific machine or device that is essential to the claim and plays a significant part in permitting the claimed method to be performed can meaningfully limit claim scope and support eligibility.
guidance: Example: Presence of a GPS receiver in SiRF was interpreted to place a meaningful limit on the claim because the receiver was essential to perform the method; that contributed to eligibility.

name: Limiting to a particular technological environment is insufficient
description: Restricting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., 'on the Internet' or 'online') generally does not render the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Examples: Limiting to online transactions or the Internet (buySAFE, Ultramercial) was held insufficient because it is merely a field-of-use limitation and does not supply a non-conventional inventive concept.

name: Claims that effect a practical technological improvement can be eligible
description: Claims that produce a concrete technological improvement or solve a technological problem in a non-generic way can be patent eligible.
guidance: Examples: Research Corp. halftoning improved the generated halftoned image (practical application in computer technology); DDR Holdings claims addressing a specific Internet-centric problem were found to supply sufficiently inventive concepts under Alice.

name: Claims reciting mental steps performed by or with a computer are likely abstract
description: Claims that essentially recite familiar mental steps (even if performed by a computer) tend to be characterized as abstract and therefore ineligible absent additional inventive concept.
guidance: Example: SmartGene claims describing comparing new and stored information and using rules to select medical options were viewed as familiar mental steps and found ineligible.

name: Adding a 'computer-aided' limitation without more is insufficient
description: Merely adding that an abstract idea is 'computer-aided' or carried out by conventional computer components does not render the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Example: Dealertrack — reducing claim to receiving data, selectively forwarding, and returning decisions; calling this 'computer-aided' did not supply an inventive concept.

name: Organizing information into a new form needs a specific practical application
description: Processes that merely organize or manipulate information (e.g., combining data sets) are abstract unless the claim ties that organization to a specific structure, machine, or practical application.
guidance: Example: Digitech—combining two data sets into a device profile was treated as an abstract process of organizing information because the claim was not tied to a specific image processor or concrete application of the profile.

name: Routine, conventional activity recited at a high level fails to supply inventive concept
description: If claimed steps are conventional and specified only at a high level of generality, they do not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Examples: Ultramercial and buySAFE emphasized that generic, routine activities (even ordered combinations) recited at a high level fail Step 2B. Courts examine whether claim limitations are routine and conventional in the field.

name: Narrowing to a particular type of relationship may not cure abstractness
description: Merely narrowing an abstract idea to a particular type of relationship or particular form of agreement does not necessarily make it non-abstract.
guidance: Example: buySAFE dependent claim narrowing the guaranty to a surety bond, insurance policy, etc., did not change the analysis because it did not remove the abstract nature of creating a contractual guaranty.

name: Limiting to a field of use or adding token post-solution components is insufficient
description: Limiting an abstract idea to a field of use or adding post-solution activity that is token or conventional does not render the claim patent eligible.
guidance: Examples: Bilski dependent claims and other cases where field-of-use and post-solution components were added did not make the claims patentable; courts require more than token limitations.

name: Characterization of the abstract idea may vary; consider claim as a whole and ordered combination
description: Courts may characterize the abstract idea in different ways; examiners should consider the claim as a whole and whether the ordered combination of elements supplies an inventive concept.
guidance: Example: DDR Holdings discussed multiple possible characterizations of the abstract idea and concluded that, under any reasonable characterization, the claims satisfied step two by reciting a non-conventional solution. Examiners should assess both individual limitations and their ordered combination.

name: Claim statement requirements (JPO)
description: At the JPO the statement in the claims must comply with: an invention for which a patent is sought is disclosed in the description; an invention for which a patent is sought is clear; the statement for each claim is concise (Article 36(6)(i),(ii),(iii) JPA).
guidance: Claims must be consistent with the description; unclear or indefinite claim scope (e.g., when it's unclear whether 'module', 'model', 'neural network' mean 'program') can breach clarity.

name: Acceptable claim formats (JPO)
description: An applicant can claim as an 'invention of a method' (series of steps) or an 'invention of a product' (program, structured data, data structure, computer-readable recording medium).
guidance: Examples: a program 'for causing a computer to execute step A, step B ...'; structured data / data structure (whether stored or not) is acceptable; computer-readable medium claims are acceptable if the claim makes clear which of (a) program itself, (b) recording medium, (c) system into which program is read is meant.

name: JPO two-step approach to software-related eligibility
description: First determine under JP Guidelines Part III Chap.1 whether the claimed subject-matter is a 'creation of a technical idea utilizing a law of nature'; if that does not resolve eligibility, determine according to the 'idea based on the standpoint of software' (JPHB Annex B Chap.1,2.1).
guidance: If the invention utilises a law of nature as a whole it may be statutory without considering whether implemented in software. If not, examine whether information processing by software is specifically implemented by using hardware resources (cooperation of software and hardware). Examiner assesses the claim 'as a whole' irrespective of some recitations.

name: CNIPA factors for a 'technical solution'
description: When determining whether a claim is a technical solution (Article 2.2), consider technical means, technical problems, and technical effects as a whole.
guidance: Examples of technical solutions: (a) programs executed to solve technical problems by controlling/processing external or internal objects; (b) programs improving internal performance of computer systems (reducing storage/transmission, improving speed); (c) big-data algorithms that mine internal associations in data to improve reliability/accuracy in a specific application field.

name: Novelty examination principles (JPO)
description: Examiners should understand a software-related invention as a whole; do not specify it by arbitrary sub-division. When examining novelty, consider claims, description, drawings and common general knowledge at filing. For sub-combination inventions, consider elements relevant to another sub-combination only to the extent they specify structure/function of the claimed sub-combination.
guidance: If elements relevant to 'another sub-combination' merely specify that other sub-combination and do not affect the claimed sub-combination's structure/function, they may be disregarded; if they do specify structure/function then they contribute to novelty.

name: Inventive step assessment procedure (JPO)
description: Select the 'primary prior art' most suitable for reasoning; determine whether a person skilled in the art would easily arrive at the claimed invention from the primary prior art by using secondary prior art or common general knowledge, following steps (1)–(4) (JP Guidelines Part III Chap.2,3).
guidance: The examiner should not treat combination of multiple independent prior art items as the primary prior art. Steps include assessing factors supporting non-existence/existence of inventive step and comprehensively assessing supporting factors.

name: Inventive step assessment procedure (CNIPA)
description: Three-step approach: (1) determine the closest prior art; (2) determine the distinguishing features and the technical problem actually solved; (3) determine whether the claimed invention is obvious to a person skilled in the art by assessing whether the prior art provides technical motivation to apply those distinguishing features to the closest prior art.
guidance: Circumstances where technical motivation usually exists include: (i) distinguishing feature is common general knowledge; (ii) distinguishing feature is a technical means related to the closest prior art (e.g., disclosed elsewhere in same document with same function); (iii) distinguishing feature is a relevant technical means disclosed in another reference whose function is the same in solving the re-determined technical problem.

name: Enablement / Sufficiency of disclosure general requirement
description: Description must set forth the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete so that a person skilled in the art can carry it out (JPO Article 36(4)(i) / CNIPA Article 26.3 etc.). Claims must be supported by the description (support requirement, JPO Article 36(6)(i) / CNIPA Article 26.4).
guidance: Insufficient disclosure or lack of support for claimed scope can lead to refusal; examiners evaluate whether the description plus common general technical knowledge enable the claimed subject-matter.

name: AI-specific enablement requirements (training data / model disclosure)
description: For AI-related inventions, disclosure should include sufficient information about training data, model construction, and evidence of reliability/technical effect; model estimation results alone typically do not substitute for experimental verification unless the description enables a skilled person to reproduce and achieve the claimed effect.
guidance: Example: a trained model's estimation that a composition meets specified curing-strength characteristics is insufficient without experimental verification or clear instructions enabling reproduction; CNIPA and JPO both expect either concrete experimental data or disclosure that allows a skilled person to reproduce the model/result.

name: Support requirement / No undue generalization
description: Claims must not generalize beyond what the description discloses; broad generalizations unsupported by disclosed embodiments are not allowed (support requirement).
guidance: Example from CNIPA: Claim generalizing correlations beyond those recorded in description (different types of allergic reactions) was held unsupported. Remedies include amending claims to the specific disclosed mode (deleting broader claims).

name: Treatment of computer program products
description: Computer program products should be regarded as software products that implement the solutions primarily through computer programs.
guidance: JPO: program products are software products; CNIPA: program/product claims are acceptable if the program/instructions can carry out the recited steps when implemented by a processor. Examiners assess whether such claims constitute technical solutions under applicable law.

name: Claim drafting and unity considerations
description: More than one independent claim is acceptable as long as those claims meet the requirement of unity (JPO).
guidance: Draft claims to maintain unity and clarity; for software-related inventions ensure each independent claim meets unity and is supported by the description.

name: Partial protein structure plus identifying characteristics can suffice
description: A partial protein structure (e.g., a short N‑terminal amino acid sequence) combined with other identifying characteristics (ability to bind/activate a target, approximate molecular weight, purification/isolation method, HPLC elution fraction, etc.) and a working isolation example may show possession of the claimed protein.
guidance: When evaluating protein claims that lack full sequence disclosure, consider (1) the partial structural disclosure, (2) other identifying characteristics, and (3) whether a working isolation method is disclosed and exemplified. If these together would enable a skilled artisan to recognize the inventor had possession of the claimed protein, written description may be satisfied (see In re Wallach style fact pattern).

name: DNA claims based solely on partial protein information are generally inadequate
description: Disclosure of only partial protein sequence and identifying protein characteristics (without DNA sequence, deposit, or cloned DNA) generally fails to provide possession of the full scope of claimed DNAs that encode the protein.
guidance: Because many different DNAs can encode the same partial amino acid sequence (genetic code degeneracy) and the remainder of the DNA sequence is unpredictable, scholars should require disclosure of at least one DNA species or other identifying attributes sufficient to represent the claimed DNA genus. Prophetic examples for making DNA libraries are not dispositive where unpredictability exists.

name: Complete sequence disclosure supports claims to that nucleic acid species
description: When the specification discloses the complete chemical structure (e.g., SEQ ID NO: 1) of a nucleic acid and demonstrates reduction to practice, the specification can satisfy the written description requirement for a claim to that nucleic acid species.
guidance: A claim directed to a particular isolated nucleic acid sequence is supported when the sequence is fully disclosed even if no deposit is made — possession is shown by the complete sequence and exemplification.

name: Genus claims defined by hybridization under stringent conditions
description: A claim to nucleic acids that hybridize under highly stringent conditions to a complement of a disclosed sequence may be supported by the disclosure of that sequence plus an explicit definition of highly stringent hybridization conditions and the well‑known behavior of hybridization.
guidance: Because highly stringent hybridization requires high structural similarity, disclosure of a species sequence plus defined stringent conditions and knowledge in the art may place one in possession of the genus of sequences that would hybridize under those conditions. However, if the genus is further limited by function (e.g., encode a protein having a function) and no correlation between structure and function is provided, support may still fail for the function‑limited genus.

name: Broad functional genus claims require representative species or correlation
description: Claims to a broad genus defined only by function (e.g., 'isolated nucleic acids that encode a protein that binds to receptor X') are not supported by disclosure of a single species unless the specification or the art provides a correlation (structural or domain) that makes the single species representative of the genus.
guidance: Evaluate predictability and common structural features across the claimed genus. If receptor‑binding domains or common sequence motifs are known or disclosed such that a single species is representative, support may exist. If the proteins/nucleic acids can vary substantially and no common attributes or correlations are disclosed, the specification likely fails to show possession of the entire genus.

name: Allelic variant claims require more than a single allele disclosure
description: A specification that discloses only one allele sequence is generally insufficient to support claims to a broader genus of allelic variants (native alleles) because alleles are variant and unpredictable without disclosure of mutational sites or common attributes.
guidance: Unless the specification describes how known allelic variation relates structurally or functionally to the disclosed allele (or provides representative alleles), applicants should not be treated as having been in possession of the full allelic genus. The ordinary meaning of 'allele' and supporting authority may be used to interpret scope; the Office should cite references when relying on term interpretation.

name: Representative number / common structural attributes requirement for genus claims
description: To support a genus claim, the specification must either disclose a representative number of species or describe common structural features that identify the genus; the number of species required rises with the degree of variability in the genus.
guidance: When the genus is highly variable (many different possible structures/functions), a single species disclosure is less likely to be representative. Examiner should assess predictability in the art and whether common attributes are taught that unify the claimed genus.

name: Prophetic examples are weak evidence when unpredictability exists
description: Prophetic examples (e.g., proposed methods for making a library of DNAs) may not establish possession of claimed species or genus where the art is unpredictable; prophetic procedures that might eventually produce a species do not show possession at filing.
guidance: Do not rely solely on prophetic examples to support broad claims in unpredictable arts (e.g., isolating unknown DNA species). Consider whether the prophetic method is routine and predictable in the field; if not, written description support is lacking.

name: Use of general knowledge in the art to supplement disclosure
description: General, well‑known correlations or knowledge in the art (e.g., the genetic code's degeneracy, routine methods for protein modification, or standard bioinformatics practices) may supplement the specification to show possession of some claimed subject matter.
guidance: Assess whether knowledge in the art would allow skilled artisans to envision the claimed genus or species from the disclosure. Examples: genetic code allows predicting degenerately related DNAs encoding a disclosed protein; routine fusion protein methods may justify genus claims defined by additions/fusions.

name: Claims to highly variant product families (unlimited substitutions/deletions/insertions) often fail
description: A claim reciting variants generically (one or more amino acid substitutions, deletions, insertions, additions) without bounds or exemplified representative variants often fails written description when the genus is highly variant and no common identifying attributes are disclosed.
guidance: When variant scope is open‑ended and a representative number of species or common attributes are not disclosed, enter a written description rejection for the unsupported scope. Fusion/addition variants may be more predictable and supported, but substitution/deletion/insertion variants usually require more description.

name: High‑identity variant claims (e.g., ≥95% identity) can be supported by a single sequence
description: Claims to variants defined by a high percent sequence identity to a disclosed sequence (for example, at least 95% identical to SEQ ID NO: 3) can be supported by disclosure of that sequence because the high‑identity limitation identifies a concrete partial structure common to the genus.
guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed identity threshold and the disclosure enable one skilled in the art to identify and make sequences with the claimed identity. High percent identity narrows the genus and may render a single disclosed sequence representative; however, if function is additionally required and no guidance which residues can vary while retaining function is given, support for the function‑limited genus may still fail.

name: Product‑by‑function claims need structure‑function correlation or descriptive guidance
description: Claims that recite a product by its function (e.g., 'variant that catalyzes reaction A->B') require disclosure of which structural features are responsible for the function or sufficient descriptive guidance to show possession of variants that perform the function.
guidance: If the specification discloses only one species with the function and does not teach which portions of the structure can vary while retaining function, a broader claim to variants that have the function may be unsupported. Examiner should require correlation or representative examples showing which changes preserve function.

name: Bioinformatics/computer‑implemented method claims can be supported by method steps plus ordinary skill
description: A computer‑implemented method that recites steps (e.g., analyzing expression, inputting data, displaying axes and marks, selecting compounds based on plotted positions) may satisfy written description even if the specification does not disclose particular algorithms, devices, or example data, provided the steps and required physical steps are sufficiently described and the art makes their implementation routine.
guidance: Assess whether the specification teaches the steps of the claimed method and whether implementation is routine for one skilled in the art. If so, possession of the claimed method may be found despite the absence of detailed algorithms or exemplified data. Consider cited case law on programming microprocessors and routine implementation.

name: Office burden to cite authority for claim term interpretations
description: When the Office relies on a particular technical or ordinary meaning of a claim term (e.g., 'allele'), it should support that interpretation with citations to authoritative sources (practice note referencing MPEP 2163.04).
guidance: Examiners should cite authoritative glossaries, treatises, or case law when using such references to construe claim scope for written description analysis. This practice strengthens the Office's position and clarifies claim interpretation for applicants.

name: Patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101
description: The Supreme Court in Diamond v. Chakrabarty held that a live, man-made microorganism is patentable subject matter under Section 101 — summarized by the phrase 'anything under the sun that is made by man.'
guidance: Court concluded that the claimed microorganism constituted a 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter' within the meaning of the Patent Act; this decision opened the door to patent protection for a broad range of biotechnology-related inventions.

name: Categories of eligible subject matter: 'manufacture' and 'composition of matter'
description: Eligibility analysis asks whether the claimed invention falls within statutory categories such as a 'manufacture' or a 'composition of matter.'
guidance: In Chakrabarty the Court framed the microorganism inquiry in these terms; processes, compositions, and manufactured items (including engineered organisms) can fall within these categories and thus be §101-eligible.

name: Non-naturally occurring / 'made by man' requirement for living organisms
description: Living organisms that are non-naturally occurring or that do not occur in nature without human intervention are treated as patentable subject matter.
guidance: Ex Parte Allen found claims patentable where there was 'no evidence that the claimed polyploid oysters occur naturally without the intervention of man.' The PTO explicitly stated that 'non-naturally occurring non-human multicellular living organisms, including animals, [are] patentable subject matter within the scope of 35 U.S.C. 101' (PTO Notice, Apr. 7, 1988).

name: Claim drafting skill determines practical scope of patents
description: The ultimate breadth and protection afforded by biotech patents are largely a function of how well the patent claims are drafted.
guidance: The authors note that 'The patents for these innovations are limited only by the skill of the individuals drafting the claims,' highlighting claim-drafting as a practical determinant of patent value and enforceability.

name: Limitation on issuance of patents — human organism (AIA § 33)
description: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.
guidance: Absolute statutory bar: claims directed to or encompassing a human organism may not result in the issuance of a patent.

name: MPEP / Patent laws index (topics referenced)
description: The page includes the MPEP index listing numerous patent-law topics and headings (examples: novelty; nonobviousness/obviousness; patentability conditions under 35 U.S.C. 101; claims (independent/dependent); written description/description of invention; enablement/what to contain; priority/filing date; reexamination; inter partes review; post-grant review; infringement; damages; venue; appeals; assignments; fees; patent term adjustment/extension; design and plant patents; secrecy orders; confidentiality; provisional applications; international applications).
guidance: This index entry is a pointer to substantive rules and standards located elsewhere in the MPEP and statutory/regulatory texts. For concrete criteria (e.g., novelty, nonobviousness, enablement, written description, claim drafting rules), consult the referenced MPEP sections and the cited statutory provisions.

name: Nonpublication request and foreign-filing certification (35 U.S.C. 122(b)(2)(B))
description: If an applicant certifies upon filing that the invention has not and will not be the subject of an application filed in another country or under an international agreement that requires 18-month publication, the application shall not be published.
guidance: Applicant may rescind such request at any time. If applicant later files corresponding foreign/international application, applicant must notify the Director within 45 days or the U.S. application will be regarded as abandoned. If rescinded or notice given, the application will be published as soon as practical. Where foreign-filed applications are less extensive than the U.S. application, applicant may submit a redacted copy eliminating parts not contained in foreign filings; Director may publish only the redacted copy if received within 16 months after earliest effective filing date. Section 154(d) benefits do not apply to a claim if the redacted description does not enable a skilled person to make and use the claimed subject matter.

name: Categories when application records may be available to public (37 CFR 1.14(a)(1)(i)-(vii))
description: Records associated with patent applications may be available in specified situations: (i) patented applications/statutory invention registrations; (ii) published abandoned applications; (iii) published pending applications; (iv) unpublished abandoned applications that are identified or relied upon; (v) unpublished pending applications whose benefit is claimed; (vi) unpublished pending applications incorporated by reference or otherwise identified; (vii) when a petition for access or a power to inspect is required.
guidance: Each category has its own conditions and procedures (e.g., written request, payment of fees, identification criteria). For unpublished files, availability often depends on identification in another published document or benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c). Access to paper file of pending applications is normally not provided except under narrow exceptions (paragraphs (c) or (i)).

name: AFCP 2.0 program participation requirements and effects
description: AFCP 2.0 is a pilot program focused on obtaining agreement through after-final amendments. To opt into AFCP 2.0, applicants must file a request for consideration under the pilot and amend at least one independent claim that does not broaden the scope of the claim.
guidance: AFCP 2.0 participation substantially lowered the probability an applicant would file an RCE—holding other variables constant, participation lowers likelihood by almost 20 percentage points. Supervisors noted benefits (allows interviews to resolve issues) and limitations (applicants may not sufficiently narrow claims; examiners may lack time to review after-final amendments). Participation was tracked at 16,598 (May–Nov 2013) but underutilized.

name: Focus on technical specificity
description: Prefer concrete, application-specific claim language (instead of generic phrasing like 'a method for data analysis using machine learning').
guidance: Example substitution: use 'a method for predictive maintenance in industrial machinery, comprising training a neural network on historical sensor data to predict equipment failures'. Specificity helps avoid overlap with prior art and clarifies the practical application; tailor claims to the concrete domain and technical effect.

name: Separate training and execution (inference) claims
description: Draft separate independent claims for the training phase and for the execution/inference phase.
guidance: Training-phase claims should recite model architecture, training data, loss/objective functions, hyperparameters, etc. Execution/inference claims should recite deployment, prediction, output use, and how outputs are used in a technological context. Where the execution phase lacks independent substance, include training-phase details in passive clauses to support eligibility/enablement.

name: Distinguish multiple ML models clearly
description: When multiple models are involved, explicitly distinguish them in claim language so their respective roles are unambiguous.
guidance: Use ordinals and clear labels (e.g., 'first training data' / 'second training data', 'first output' / 'second output') and avoid ambiguous references about which model performs which function to prevent claim indefiniteness and enable precise claim scope.

name: Establish patent eligibility by showing technical improvements and real‑world application
description: AI inventions are more likely to be patent eligible when they solve concrete technical problems, provide measurable improvements, and explain how those improvements are achieved.
guidance: Draft claims and specification so they (1) identify a concrete technical problem, (2) describe measurable improvements (metrics, accuracy gains, latency reduction, resource savings), (3) explain the mechanism by which the improvement is achieved, and (4) reflect the technical improvement in claim language; ensure there is a real-world application.

name: Align claims with USPTO 2024 AI guidance and eligible examples
description: Follow USPTO 2024 Subject Matter Eligibility Update examples that identify specific AI applications in computer technology as potentially eligible.
guidance: Use precedent/examples in claim drafting: improving accuracy of speech recognition (eligible), anomaly detection methods tied to specific networks (eligible), AI-driven medical treatment selection (may be eligible if claims show practical application). Tie claims to specific computer/technological implementation details to mirror USPTO-identified eligible categories.

name: Avoid common pitfalls / anti-patterns
description: Do not draft claims that fall into patterns frequently rejected as abstract or non-enabling.
guidance: Avoid claims that simply recite 'using a machine learning model'; math-only claims with no technical use; claims describing only data manipulation; claims that are merely mental processes implemented 'on a computer'; and purely functional claims without enabling structural disclosure. These anti-patterns increase the risk of abstract-idea rejections or indefiniteness.

name: Provide sufficient disclosure / enablement (35 U.S.C. 112 / Article 83)
description: The specification must disclose enough detail for enablement and written description, particularly for AI/ML innovations.
guidance: Disclose model architecture (if novel), training data type and characteristics, loss/objective functions, hyperparameters or hyperparameter ranges, performance metrics, and sufficient detail to reproduce the technical effect. Ensure functional claim elements are supported by structural/algorithmic disclosure to avoid failing enablement or written description requirements.

name: Hindsight-Resistant Procedure
description: Construct prior art baseline before viewing the claimed invention; document specific reasons combining references would have been motivated absent hindsight; identify what teaching, suggestion, or motivation existed in the prior art at the time.
guidance: Procedural steps to reduce hindsight: (a) reconstruct the relevant prior-art landscape before disclosing the invention; (b) explicitly record why a POSITA would combine references (motivations) without reference to the invention; (c) identify teaching, suggestion, or motivation actually present in the art at the relevant time. Emphasizes that these steps should be done before or independently of the inventor's disclosure to avoid bias.

name: Graham v. John Deere Discipline (core obviousness factors)
description: Apply the Graham factors without invention bias: (1) scope and content of the prior art (without invention bias); (2) differences between prior art and claims (carefully delineated); (3) level of ordinary skill (calibrated to actual practitioners); (4) secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, etc.).
guidance: Maintain discipline in each Graham factor: do not let knowledge of the invention color the claimed 'scope and content' analysis; precisely delineate claim elements vis-à-vis references; calibrate the POSITA to realistic practitioners (not idealized or hindsight-amplified skill); preserve and evaluate secondary indicia as potentially dispositive evidence of nonobviousness.

name: KSR Application Limits
description: "Obvious to try" requires limited, identified, predictable solutions; "common sense" must be supported by evidence, not bare assertion; combination must be predictable to POSITA, not just possible in retrospect.
guidance: Under KSR, courts accept more flexible rationales but quality analysis should demand: (a) demonstration that the options were limited and that one of ordinary skill would have been reasonably expected to try the claimed solution with a reasonable expectation of success; (b) evidentiary support for any invocation of 'common sense'—not mere conclusory statements; (c) focus on predictability to a POSITA rather than post-hoc plausibility.

name: Quality Markers in the Patent Itself
description: Specification distinguishes the invention from each cited reference with technical reasons; claims include specific limitations the prior art does not teach; secondary-considerations evidence (commercial success, copying, etc.) is preserved in the record; prior-art search was thorough, leaving few blindspots.
guidance: Concrete signs of a robust nonobviousness showing: detailed specification explanations differentiating over cited art, claim drafting that incorporates technically substantive limitations (not merely formalistic language), preservation of secondary indicia in the file history and record, and documentation (or indicia) of a thorough prior-art search during prosecution to reduce unknown references.

name: Quality Defects Indicating Vulnerability
description: Claim differences from prior art are minor or framed in conclusory terms; no technical justification for novel limitations; prosecution history shows applicant arguments unsupported by specification; specification reads as a rationalization of the prior art combination.
guidance: Red flags that a patent is likely to be invalidated for obviousness: superficial or conclusory claim distinctions, absence of technical explanation for claimed features, reliance in prosecution on arguments not grounded in the specification, and specifications that appear to be post-hoc rationalizations rather than contemporaneous technical justification.

name: Operative Test — Claim Differentiation
description: Are the claim differences from prior art technically substantive, not merely formal?
guidance: Assess whether claim limitations correspond to concrete technical distinctions that the prior art does not teach or suggest; beware of sleight-of-hand claim drafting that purports to 'add' limitations without technical substance.

name: Post-KSR Quality Requirements
description: Post-KSR environment requires explicit teaching against the claimed combination (negative motivation); specific technical reasons the combination is non-trivial; documented unexpected results; and strong secondary-considerations evidence.
guidance: Because KSR permits 'common sense' and 'obvious to try' rationales, high-quality patents in the post-KSR era should: (a) identify any prior art teaching away from the combination, (b) provide technical explanations showing non-triviality, (c) document unexpected results when available, and (d) preserve secondary indicia to bolster nonobviousness.

name: Claim only the invention
description: Nothing more than the invention must be claimed.
guidance: Every old part which is essential and material in producing the intended effect will be considered as claimed if it be not designated as old. Do not claim more than what you actually invented; explicitly identify older elements to avoid implying they are claimed.

name: Do not claim whole when only an improvement
description: If the inventor has only invented an improvement of an old engine/manufacture, a specification claiming the whole will be bad.
guidance: If the invention is merely an improvement of an existing device (e.g., Heathcote's engine), the specification must not claim the entire prior machine as the inventor's; improvements should be limited to the newly invented part or combination.

name: Keep new combination or improvement distinct from the old manufacture
description: An improvement or new combination must be kept distinctly apart from the old manufacture.
guidance: Clearly distinguish and identify the invented features vs prior manufacture so the scope of the claim and the disclosure are not conflated.

name: Automated subject classification (task definition)
description: A multi-label classification task where the aim is to predict patents' specific categories or classes based on patent content (title, abstract, claims).
guidance: Patents may belong to multiple classes; classification assists database organization and examiner workflows. Input is a sequence of tokens x=[w1,...,wn], output label y in {y1,...,ym}.

name: Recommendations for future classification work
description: Focus more on detailed patent descriptions (not just titles/abstracts/claims) and investigate domain-adaptive methods adapting LLMs to the patent domain.
guidance: Descriptions contain more specific technical information; domain adaptation can improve performance over general pre-trained embeddings.

name: Legal definition of novelty and features (formal patent standard)
description: An invention is conceived as a combination of features; it is novel if there is no older document or disclosure that alone includes and/or describes all essential features of the invention. Features are outlined in the patent claims, and independent claims list the essential features. In many jurisdictions, features cannot be negative.
guidance: Novelty assessment critically relies on correct identification and comparison of features. The same feature may be named differently across documents; feature variability is a major challenge for examiners and automated systems. Some offices allow negative limitations only when clearly stated in the description.

name: §301(a)(2) & (c)-(d): Submission and use of patent-owner claim-scope statements
description: The AIA allows any party to submit to the USPTO 'statements of the patent owner filed in a proceeding before a Federal court or the Office in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim of a particular patent.' Submitters must include related documents, pleadings, or evidence from the proceeding that address the written statement. These materials 'shall not be considered by the Office for any purpose other than to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim' in reexamination, inter partes, or post-grant review.
guidance: This expansion helps the Office identify inconsistent claim constructions by patent owners across forums (e.g., district court vs. PTAB). The Committee emphasized these statements are not intended as a basis for initiating reexamination proceedings; reexaminations remain institutionable only on the basis of 'patents or printed publications.' The legislative history notes the scope of 'patent or printed publication' prior art for reexamination remains coextensive with section 102 prior art.

name: Statutory subject-matter categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
description: The four statutory categories of invention: Process, Machine, Manufacture, or Composition of Matter and improvements thereof. Process = "an act, or series of acts or steps"; Machine = "a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices"; Manufacture = "an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations"; Composition of Matter = "all compositions of two or more substances and all composite articles..."
guidance: A claimed invention must fall within at least one of these categories to be eligible. Identification of a single category is not necessary; a claim may satisfy more than one. Analyze based on the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). See MPEP 2106(I) for definitions.

name: Judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas)
description: The courts have interpreted the statutory categories to exclude 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas' (the 'judicial exceptions'). These terms cover the basic tools of scientific and technological work, such as scientific principles, naturally occurring phenomena, mental processes, and mathematical algorithms.
guidance: If a claim falls within a statutory category, the examiner must still analyze whether it is directed to a judicial exception. For example, a process that meets the statutory definition could be ineligible if it is directed to an abstract idea and does not recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.

name: 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance: examination principles
description: For examination of all claims the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance directs: use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim; analyze the claim as a whole; practice compact prosecution by fully examining under 35 U.S.C. §§102, 103, 112 and 101; and take a comprehensive view of subject matter eligibility incorporating relevant case law (Alice, Myriad, Mayo, Bilski).
guidance: If a claim falls within at least one statutory category, proceed to judicial exception analysis. Apply BRI and analyze the claim as a whole rather than dissecting in isolation. Consider the full body of case law in performing the eligibility determination.

name: Signals per se and computer-readable media (CRM) guidance
description: A transitory, propagating signal (e.g., a signal with embedded supplemental data) is not within one of the four statutory categories (In re Nuijten). Under BRI, computer readable media (CRM) will cover an ineligible signal per se unless the specification as filed provides a special definition distinguishing storage media from transmission media.
guidance: When the specification is silent, a claim to CRM or CRSM is ineligible unless amended to avoid the ineligible signal embodiment. It is acceptable to amend claims to exclude the signal embodiment by adding 'non-transitory' to modify the computer readable media ("non-transitory" is an option, not a requirement). It is not acceptable to merely add 'physical' or 'tangible' (Nuijten's ineligible signals were physical and tangible) nor acceptable to add 'storage' absent support in the original disclosure because BRI of CRSM commonly covers signals/carrier waves.

name: Utility requirement
description: 'Useful' — the invention must have a specific, substantial, and credible utility.
guidance: This is the utility requirement under §101; see MPEP 2107 for Utility Guidelines. Ensure that claimed subject matter satisfies utility requirements as part of §101 considerations where relevant.

name: Rejections and appropriate form paragraphs
description: If a claim under BRI covers non-statutory subject matter, the examiner must make a §101 rejection and use the appropriate form paragraphs.
guidance: Use Form ¶ 7.04.01 (reciting the statutory text), Form ¶ 7.05 ("Claim *** rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because …"), and Form ¶ 7.05.01 ("the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter because ***."). For human organisms use Form ¶ 7.04.03. For incorrect inventorship use Form ¶ 7.04.101.aia or 7.04.102.aia. Include explanatory specifics in the record for clarity.

name: Clarity of the record — examiner documentation practices
description: Clarifying the record benefits the Examiner, the Applicant, and the Public, places the Applicant on notice regarding the Office's position, and provides insight into the BRI for claim limitations.
guidance: Examples of clarifying actions: explain why the claim does not fit within one of the four categories (see MPEP 2106(I)), illustrate why the BRI of the claim encompasses a non-statutory embodiment (e.g., a signal per se), explain why the claim is interpreted to read on a human organism, and when the category is unclear add comments explaining the BRI. Clear recordation enables a more effective Applicant response.

name: Use of case law in eligibility determinations
description: Apply teachings from the full body of relevant case law (notably Alice, Myriad, Mayo, Bilski, In re Nuijten, In re Ferguson, Digitech) when conducting subject-matter eligibility analysis.
guidance: The 2014 Interim Guidance reflects Supreme Court and Federal Circuit developments; examiners should consider these precedents in determining whether claims are directed to judicial exceptions or include additional elements amounting to significantly more. Cite relevant cases to support eligibility findings or rejections.

name: Patent must claim new mode/process, not result alone
description: A patent can be for an effect produced in a given manner, or by a peculiar operation; it cannot be a patent for a result merely or for an effect only (e.g., admeasurement of time or expansive operations of steam are not patentable per se).
guidance: If an old machine in its unaltered state produces new effects, that alone does not support a patent — there must be a new mode, process, machinery, or specific manner of producing the effect. The patentee must show some new mode or means that produces the effect.

name: Statutory categories of patentable subject-matter: Machine
description: A machine must be a particular construction of mechanism containing the improved method of producing an old effect or the method of producing a new effect; it is a function embodied in a particular mechanism with its mode of operation and general structure pointed out.
guidance: Includes new combinations of machines and new organizations of mechanism for a single purpose. A machine patent may cover machinery entirely new in all its combinations, or mechanism whose principle or modus operandi is new. Example: a telescope combining convex and concave glasses. Claims construction determines whether the claim is to the combination only or to specific parts as well.

name: Combination patents protect the combination, not separate machines
description: Where the thing patented is a new combination of machines (whether the constituent machines be new or old), the patent is for the combination only; making the separate machines separately is not an infringement unless the whole combination is used.
guidance: If a patent is limited by its terms to a combination, the statute gives remedy only for violation of that combination. Where several distinct independent improvements are in the same machine, a patent may be taken for them in the aggregate and will protect each improvement. But a patent solely for a combination does not prevent others from making/use of the separate machines absent use of the claimed combination.

name: Improvement-of-machine patents limited to the improvement
description: A patent for an 'improvement' of a machine is the same as a patent for an improved machine, but the patent can only be for the improvement or new combination added, not for the whole old machine.
guidance: If a mere addition produces the same effects in a better manner, the inventor cannot claim the whole machine — only the actual improvement. Determining whether an alleged improvement is real and material (versus mere change of form) is key; this often requires assessing boundaries between known prior art and new mode of operation. Examples: patent lever in a watch — inventor's right limited to his actual improvement. If a specified improvement is pirated, that can be infringement; jury decides triviality vs materiality.

name: Overlapping patents and improvements in force
description: A patent that includes subject-matter of a still-in-force patent may be valid if only the improvement is claimed in the specification; the new patent comes into force after the old one expires or may be used under license/purchase while the old exists.
guidance: In infringement actions on an alleged improvement of a former patent, the specification of the former patent should be read; validity and remedies depend on whether the later patent claims only the improvement. Practical remedies while old patent runs include obtaining license or purchasing apparatus. Authorities cited support this practice.

name: Requirement to read prior patent in infringement of improvement cases
description: In an action for infringement of a patent professing to be an improvement on a former patent, the specification of that former patent must be read.
guidance: It is not material whether a machine constructed according to the first patent would be useful or not; if a machine constructed according to the subsequent patent is useful and claims only the improvement, the fact of utility of the first-specification machine does not bar consideration. This is part of evaluating novelty/priority of the improvement.

name: Benefit claim requirements under 37 CFR 1.78(d)
description: To obtain benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 365(c) of a prior-filed copending nonprovisional application or prior-filed copending international application designating the United States, the national stage application must comply with the requirements set forth in 37 CFR 1.78(d). The prior application must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the later-filed international application and disclose the named inventor’s invention claimed in at least one claim of the national stage application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
guidance: The national stage application must contain a reference to the prior nonprovisional or international application identifying it by application number (series code and serial number) or international application number and international filing date and indicating the relationship of the applications. If international filing date is prior to Sept 16, 2012, the reference must be in either an application data sheet (37 CFR 1.76) or in the first sentence(s) of the specification; if on or after Sept 16, 2012, the reference must be in an application data sheet. Presentation of the benefit claim in the PCT Request form or presence on the front page of the published international application may satisfy ADS requirement in certain circumstances (see 37 CFR 1.76(g)).

name: Unity of invention requirement (37 CFR 1.475 / 37 CFR 1.499)
description: A national stage application shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept (requirement of unity of invention). A group of inventions is considered linked where there is a technical relationship among the inventions involving at least one common or corresponding special technical feature.
guidance: The expression 'special technical features' means those technical features that define the contribution which each claimed invention, considered as a whole, makes over the prior art. The determination is made without regard to whether inventions are claimed separately or as alternatives within a single claim. See MPEP § 1850 for detailed discussion.

name: Definition and examples of 'special technical feature' and 'technical relationship'
description: A 'special technical feature' defines the contribution which each claimed invention makes over the prior art. A 'technical relationship' among inventions involves at least one common or corresponding special technical feature linking them into a single general inventive concept.
guidance: Examples: a key defined by certain structural characteristics corresponding to claimed features of a lock; a process 'specially adapted' inherently produces the claimed product; an apparatus 'specifically designed' is suitable for carrying out a claimed process. 'Specially adapted' and 'specifically designed' do not imply exclusivity (i.e., product could be made by other processes or apparatus could be used for other processes).

name: Examiner obligations when making lack of unity requirement
description: When making a lack of unity requirement the examiner must (1) list the different groups of claims and (2) explain why each group lacks unity with each other group, specifically describing the unique special technical feature in each group.
guidance: Such a requirement may be made before any action on the merits and at any time before final action at examiner's discretion. Review is provided under 37 CFR 1.143 and 1.144. The examiner may make a lack of unity requirement in a national stage application even if no such requirement was made by the ISA or IPEA.

name: Permitted combinations when claims are to multiple categories of inventions (37 CFR 1.475(b))
description: A national stage application containing claims to different categories of invention will be considered to have unity of invention if the claims are drawn only to one of specified combinations of categories.
guidance: Permitted combinations: (1) a product and a process specially adapted for the manufacture of said product; (2) a product and a process of use of said product; (3) a product, a process specially adapted for the manufacture of said product, and a use of said product; (4) a process and an apparatus or means specifically designed for carrying out the said process; (5) a product, a process specially adapted for manufacture of the said product, and an apparatus or means specifically designed for carrying out the said process. Otherwise unity might not be present (see 37 CFR 1.475(c)).

name: Rejoinder criteria for nonelected claims
description: If an examiner requires election and all claims drawn to the elected invention are allowable, the nonelected invention(s) should be considered for rejoinder.
guidance: Any nonelected product claim that requires all the limitations of an allowable product claim, and any nonelected process claim that requires all the limitations of an allowable process claim, should be rejoined. Nonelected processes of making/using an allowable product should be considered for rejoinder. Withdrawn process claims not commensurate in scope with an allowable product/apparatus claim will not be rejoined. Applicant is advised to amend process claims to require the limitations of the product/apparatus claim to preserve rejoinder. Rejoined claims must meet 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103 and 112; until all elected product/apparatus claims are found allowable, a restriction between product/apparatus and process claims may be maintained. Note prohibition against double patenting rejections of 35 U.S.C. 121 does not apply where restriction is withdrawn by examiner before patent issues (see MPEP § 804.01).

name: Election of species (form paragraph 18.20) and content of election replies
description: When application contains claims to more than one species of the generic invention, species are deemed to lack unity; applicant is required to elect a single species to which the claims shall be restricted if no generic claim is finally held allowable. Reply must identify claims readable on the elected species; argument that a claim is allowable or all claims are generic is non-responsive unless accompanied by an election.
guidance: Upon allowance of a generic claim, applicant entitled to consideration of claims to additional species written in dependent form or otherwise requiring all limitations of an allowed generic claim. Form paragraph usage instructions include identifying species in bracket 1 and generic claims in bracket 2 or NONE.

name: Election by original presentation and traversal requirements (form paragraph 18.21 & 18.22)
description: An election can be made by original presentation; newly submitted claims directed to invention that lacks unity with originally claimed invention may be treated as constructively elected by original presentation. To preserve right to petition, reply must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the restriction requirement (traverse).
guidance: Traversal must be timely; failure to timely traverse results in loss of right to petition under 37 CFR 1.144. If applicant traverses on grounds that inventions are not patentably distinct, applicant should submit evidence or identify evidence now of record showing inventions are obvious variants, or clearly admit such on the record; such evidence or admission may be used in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection of the other invention.

name: Scope limitation of automatic consideration of international-cited documents
description: The practice of automatically considering documents applies only to documents cited in the international search report relative to a national-stage application filed under 35 U.S.C. 371.
guidance: It does not apply to documents cited in an international preliminary examination report that are not cited in the search report, nor to applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) claiming the benefit of an international application filing date.

name: Computer-technology-specific claiming
description: Craft claims that are necessarily rooted in computer technology.
guidance: Where possible, draft claims tied to computer/website/technology specifics so that the invention is technically grounded rather than framed as an abstract idea implemented on a generic computer.

name: Avoid Group 3600 (and other high-101 groups)
description: Craft claims to avoid USPTO examining groups with high 101 rejection rates (notably groups 3600 and 3700).
guidance: Consider claim drafting and filing strategies (e.g., claim phrasing, choice of claim focus) that route examination to art units/examining groups less prone to §101 rejections. Be aware that allowance rates and rejection tendencies vary by art unit.

name: Name the specific technical benefit and define the problem solved
description: Tailor the application and claims to a specific technical benefit afforded by the claimed invention and include a clear definition of the problem solved and the specific technical solution.
guidance: Give concrete technical benefits (examples in the article: faster search times within a database, smaller memory requirements for a database, more dynamic or efficient information filtering, more accurate image-sound synchronization, producing more realistic expressions or movement in animated characters). Do not merely argue that the computer generally improves an existing system; instead, teach how the claimed invention improves the existing technology and include precise language delimiting the type of data and how it is handled (see Core Wireless example).

name: Explain how the invention is not abstract
description: Actively rebut the 'abstract idea' prong of the Alice analysis by showing the claims are directed to an improvement in computer functionality or are otherwise non-abstract.
guidance: Use Federal Circuit precedents (e.g., Enfish v. Microsoft) and their progeny to support arguments that software claims are not inherently abstract and can be analyzed under step one of Alice. Ask whether the claims are directed to an improvement to computer functionality and frame the disclosure and claims accordingly.

name: Include more independent claims of varying scope
description: Consider claiming the invention with additional independent claims that vary in scope and language.
guidance: Include broader and narrower independent claims, and consider using 'means for' language where helpful to avoid functional claiming traps. Varying claim scope can help identify allowable claim sets and provide fallback positions during prosecution or in continuations.

name: Recite the improvement steps in the claim language
description: Recite the specific steps or rules that produce the claimed improvement directly in the claims.
guidance: The USPTO and courts have pointed to cases (e.g., McRO, Finjan) where claims survived §101 review because they recited concrete steps/rules for improving computer functionality (e.g., rules for animation lip-sync or steps to generate and link a security profile). Draft claims to include those implementation steps rather than high-level outcomes.

name: Use continuations to refine claims over time
description: If needed, narrow claims to overcome a §101 rejection and file continuation applications to pursue alternative claim scopes later.
guidance: Continuations allow you to preserve multiple claim strategies while awaiting additional guidance from PTAB, Federal Circuit, or the Supreme Court. As new case law or PTAB decisions issue, continuation prosecution can be shaped to avoid §101 rejections based on evolving precedent.

name: Substitute/unverified specimen declaration
description: If checking the box that specimens are now being submitted or were previously submitted unverified, the form automatically adds declaration language asserting the specimen(s) was/were in use as claimed.
guidance: Willful false statements are punishable under 18 U.S.C. §1001; make truthful attestations only.

name: Accuracy and fraud warning for goods/services listings
description: Statements made in filings must be accurate; inaccuracies (e.g., lack of bona fide intent to use or lack of use on all goods/services claimed) could result in cancellation of the registration.
guidance: Do not exceed the scope of the current identification; modifications can clarify or limit but not broaden the listing.

name: Image and color claim requirements
description: For special form/stylized marks attach a JPG image; if claiming color you must submit a color image and list colors beginning with a lower-case letter and state the location of each color; if not claiming color, check the box and leave the color field blank.
guidance: Image size cannot exceed 5 megabytes; the image must include all elements of the mark; any literal element entered that is not in the image will not be considered part of the mark.

name: Permitted grounds for a trial for correction
description: A patent holder may pursue a petition for the correction of a granted patent or utility model for the reasons of narrowing a claim, correcting a clerical error, or clarifying an ambiguous description (Article 136 of the Patent Act).
guidance: Correction petitions are limited to specified grounds—requests outside narrowing/clerical/clarifying grounds likely to be dismissed. Draft correction requests narrowly to fit statutory reasons.

name: Factual Findings Relating to Obviousness and Anticipation (substantial evidence review)
description: The Federal Circuit reviews PTAB factual findings under the substantial evidence standard; although deferential, findings can be reversed when not supported by substantial evidence on issues such as disclosure of claim limitations, motivation to combine, reasonable expectation of success, and qualification of prior art.
guidance: On appeal, identify where the board's factual conclusions contradict claim language or rest on erroneous interpretations of the record. Show gaps in the evidentiary support, reliance on speculation/inherency without reasonable support, or failures to make necessary findings. Break down obviousness/anticipation analyses into discrete factual sub-issues (elements disclosed, motivation to combine, expectation of success, art qualification) and challenge each where evidence is deficient.

name: Failure to Disclose a Claim Limitation
description: Board determinations that a prior art reference disclosed a particular limitation are vulnerable when they contradict the plain language of the claim or rest on an erroneous reading of the reference.
