guidance: Argue that the PTAB mislabeled or misread prior art when: the disclosure was not expressly shown and relied instead on implied figures or on inherency without reasonable support; the board rewrote or narrowed a limitation to force a fit (e.g., treating 'substantially all' as satisfied by an inherency finding of 'greater than impurity levels'); or the record left the disclosure ambiguous such that the petitioner failed to meet its burden by a preponderance of evidence. Cite instances where the Federal Circuit required explicit support rather than implication or hindsight.

name: PTAB Consideration of Evidence and Arguments
description: The PTAB must consider material evidence and parties' arguments; failure to consider evidence or reliance on improper evidence can render PTAB decisions unsupported and subject to vacatur.
guidance: Argue that the PTAB erred by: refusing to consider an alternative single-reference ground presented in the petition; failing to separately construe different limitations and instead analyzing claims in a group; overlooking parties' proposed motivations or arguments; refusing to consider prior art for analogous-art analysis; failing to address arguments in reply or supplemental briefing; relying on evidence tied solely to non-instituted grounds; failing to notify parties of an unpatentability theory for substitute claims or provide opportunity to respond; disregarding factual findings such as copying; presuming nexus for secondary considerations; or making inconsistent findings across proceedings. Emphasize that these omissions can be reversible under substantial-evidence review.

name: PTAB-Specific Procedural/Legal Issues
description: PTAB practice and statutory interpretation questions (burdens of proof, time-bar and real-party-in-interest, motions/discovery, joinder, estoppel, scope of CBM) present distinct grounds for appeal and have produced Federal Circuit rulings altering practice.
guidance: Preserve and raise issues such as: petitioner bears burden to prove proposed amended claims unpatentable in IPRs; PTAB must consider real-party-in-interest relationships arising after filing for time-bar analyses; denying authorization to file for additional discovery can be an abuse of discretion; rejecting a patent owner's request to file a certificate of correction to amend priority chain can be error; same-party joinder is not authorized under the statute; Section 317(b) estoppel applies to reexamination; even if claims are held indefinite the board must still address anticipation/obviousness; and types of patents subject to CBM review. Use these as discrete appellate arguments where applicable and cite Federal Circuit holdings that clarify these PTAB-specific legal points.

name: Appellate Advocacy and Preservation of Arguments
description: To maximize chances on appeal, appellants should connect board decisions to erroneous claim constructions and preserve known arguments that could reflect later changes in the law so they are not waived.
guidance: On appeal and in the PTAB, preserve all arguments that might become relevant due to shifting law; clearly link reversible errors (e.g., improper claim construction) to the board's outcome; in claim construction disputes explicitly rely on specification, prosecution history, plain and ordinary meaning, POSITA understanding, claim language, relationships among claim terms, and definitional passages. Make sure to raise issues early (in administrative proceedings and opening appellate brief) to avoid waiver and to provide the Federal Circuit the opportunity to address PTAB legal errors.

name: Burden of proof for invalidity
description: The defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
guidance: This burden never changes regardless of whether a particular prior art reference was considered by the Patent Examiner. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i; Sciele Pharma v. Lupin.)

name: Prior art (AIA) — definition
description: Prior art includes anything patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public anywhere in the world before the effective filing date of the claim; and patents/applications naming another inventor filed before the effective filing date.
guidance: Includes AIA-specific statutory references (35 U.S.C. § 102 as amended by AIA; §100(i)). Practice Note: identify to the jury disputes over date/public availability and related issues.

name: Invalidity analysis for independent and dependent claims
description: Independent claims do not refer to other claims and must be read separately; dependent claims refer to and include all elements of the claim(s) they depend from. Each asserted claim must be evaluated separately for invalidity.
guidance: Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims are not automatically invalid; however, if a dependent claim is invalid, the independent claim from which it depends must also be found invalid. (Cites: Comaper v. Antec; Callaway v. Acushnet; Ormco v. Align Tech.)

name: Prior public knowledge (pre-AIA) — standard
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was publicly known by others in the United States before the date of invention (pre-AIA cutoff).
guidance: If the date of invention or priority is disputed, instruct the jury on how to determine the Cutoff Date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a) (pre-AIA); case law.)

name: Prior public use (pre-AIA) — elements
description: The invention was publicly used by others in the U.S. before the invention date or more than one year before U.S. filing date (pre-AIA), rendering the claim invalid.
guidance: An invention was publicly used in the U.S. if an embodiment was (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the U.S., and (2) ready for patenting. Factors: nature of activity, public access, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation, testing circumstances. Secret third-party use is not public unless public/employees had access. Ready for patenting = reduced to practice or sufficiently detailed drawings/descriptions enabling one of ordinary skill. (Cites: numerous Fed. Cir. cases.)

name: On-sale bar (pre-AIA and AIA)
description: A claim is invalid if, before the applicable cutoff/effective filing date, an embodiment of the claimed invention was the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (pre-AIA limited to U.S. sales), and the invention was ready for patenting at that time.
guidance: A commercial offer for sale exists if another party could make a binding contract by accepting the offer. The invention is 'subject of a sale or offer' if embodied in an actual product commercially sold or offered for sale, even if confidential; no actual sale required. Readiness for patenting requires reduced to practice or sufficiently specific drawings/descriptions. Practice Note: address §102(b) exceptions when factual disputes about inventor-origin disclosures exist. (Cites: Pfaff v. Wells Elecs.; Helsinn; Medicines Co.; others.)

name: Prior invention (pre-AIA) — anticipation by another's invention
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the U.S. before the patentee (and not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed).
guidance: Defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence either (1) the third party reduced to practice a product/method including all features of the claim before the patentee, or (2) the third party was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence to reduce to practice. Prior invention may be negated if abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If abandonment/suppression/concealment is at issue, define those terms for the jury. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(g) pre-AIA; Teva v. AstraZeneca; Rosco v. Mirror Lite; others.)

name: Prior patent (pre-AIA) — anticipatory effect
description: A claim is invalid if the invention was previously patented in the U.S. or a foreign country before the relevant cutoff (pre-AIA), e.g., before the patentee's invention date or more than one year before U.S. filing date.
guidance: If the date of invention or priority is disputed, instruct the jury on how to determine the date of invention or deliver the Cutoff Date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102 pre-AIA; Advanced Display; In re Carlson.)

name: Section 101 — Utility
description: Whether an application discloses a utility for a claimed invention is a question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence.
guidance: In re Fisher, 421 F.3d 1365, 1369 (Fed. Cir. 2005): utility is a factual determination subject to substantial-evidence review.

name: Section 103 — Obviousness
description: Whether a claimed invention would have been obvious is a question of law based on factual determinations (scope/content of prior art, differences between prior art and claims, level of ordinary skill, objective indicia). The Board's compliance with legal standards is reviewed de novo and underlying factual determinations for substantial evidence.
guidance: Randall Mfg. v. Rea, 733 F.3d 1355, 1362 (Fed. Cir. 2013): mixed question—legal review de novo for legal standard, substantial-evidence review for facts.

name: Section 112 — Written Description
description: Whether a claimed invention is supported by an adequate written description under § 112, ¶ 1, is a question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence.
guidance: In re Owens, 710 F.3d 1362, 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2013).

name: Section 112 — Indefiniteness (claim construction subset)
description: Indefiniteness, as a subset of claim construction, is a question of law reviewed without deference.
guidance: In re Packard, 2014 WL 1775996, *2 (Fed. Cir. May 6, 2014).

name: Section 112 ¶ 6 — Means-Plus-Function (whether claim is in MPF form)
description: Determining whether a claim limitation is written in means-plus-function form is a question of law reviewed de novo.
guidance: In re Aoyama, 656 F.3d 1293, 1296 (Fed. Cir. 2011).

name: Section 112 ¶ 6 — Function and corresponding structure for MPF claims
description: Determining the claimed function and the corresponding structure for a means-plus-function limitation are matters of claim construction presenting issues of law reviewed de novo.
guidance: In re Aoyama, 656 F.3d 1293, 1296 (Fed. Cir. 2011).

name: §112 written description / enablement / best mode
description: To enable a patent holder to know what he owns, and the public to know what he does not, the inventor must describe his work in 'full, clear, concise, and exact terms.' Section 112 requires that the application describe, enable, and set forth the best mode of carrying out the invention.
guidance: If §112 requirements are not satisfied, the patent should not issue and an applicant's failure could lead to invalidity in later litigation. Amendments made to comply with §112 can be cosmetic (clarifying ambiguous terms, improving translations, rewriting dependent claims as independent) or necessary; if the amendment is necessary and narrows the patent's scope, prosecution history estoppel may arise. Example: Festo's amendments adding sealing rings and a magnetizable sleeve were made to address §112 issues and were central to estoppel analysis.

name: Doctrine of equivalents (scope beyond literal claim)
description: A patent's scope is not limited to its literal terms but embraces equivalents to the claims described; the doctrine protects inventors against efforts to evade liability by making insubstantial changes to a patented invention.
guidance: Recognize tradeoff: doctrine preserves inventor incentives but creates uncertainty for competitors. Courts should apply the doctrine consistent with precedent (e.g., Graver Tank, Warner-Jenkinson) while being mindful of public notice and predictability. Literalism would undermine protection against insubstantial changes; equivalence remains entrenched unless Congress acts.

name: Amendments that can give rise to estoppel: 'substantial reason related to patentability'
description: Prosecution history estoppel applies to amendments made for a 'substantial reason related to patentability'—not limited to narrowing to avoid prior art but including amendments to satisfy any Patent Act requirement (e.g., §§101–103 and §112).
guidance: Warner-Jenkinson recognized the phrase but did not catalog every reason that might raise estoppel. Courts should evaluate whether the amendment was made to secure the patent and whether it narrowed the patent's scope; if both, estoppel may apply. Example: amendments to satisfy §112 (form/description) may still produce estoppel if they are necessary and narrow the claim.

name: Estoppel's reach: not an automatic complete bar
description: Prosecution history estoppel need not bar suit against every equivalent to a narrowed element; estoppel's reach requires examination of the subject matter actually surrendered by the narrowing amendment.
guidance: The Federal Circuit's 'complete bar' (all equivalents barred) departs from precedent and is rejected: courts should apply a flexible approach. By amending, the inventor is presumed to have disclaimed territory between original and amended claims, but that presumption can be rebutted for particular equivalents. Courts must ask what equivalents were reasonably surrendered, not impose per se literalism.

name: Claim construction starting point and role of prosecution history
description: Interpretation of a patent begins with its literal claims, and the prosecution history is relevant to construing those claims and determining what was surrendered by amendment.
guidance: Courts should construe claims in light of the prosecution record; amended claim language may be presumed composed with awareness of the estoppel rules. Prosecution history helps determine the scope of what was relinquished between original and amended claim language, informing whether a particular equivalent remains within the patent scope.

name: Patentability statutory requirements (§§101–103) relevant to amendments
description: Before a patent issues, claimed subject matter must be useful, novel, and nonobvious (35 U.S.C. §§101–103); amendments made to address these requirements may give rise to prosecution history estoppel.
guidance: Amendments to avoid prior art or to address obviousness are paradigmatic bases for estoppel. When an amendment is made to secure patentability under §§101–103, the patentee's narrowing may be treated as a concession about the scope of what can be claimed, supporting estoppel against asserted equivalents.

name: Translations of the International Application (required EPO language translation)
description: Translations in one of the EPO official languages (English, French, German) of the international application (description, claims, any published abstract and any indications under Rule 13bis.3 and 13bis.4 PCT regarding biological material) are to be submitted.
guidance: Provide full translations of the international application into an EPO language. Certain translations (e.g., priority application translations) may be required only upon invitation (Rule 53(3) EPC).

name: Argument requirements
description: The arguments of appellant with respect to each ground of rejection, and the basis therefor, with citations of the statutes, regulations, authorities, and parts of the Record relied on. The arguments shall explain why the examiner erred as to each ground of rejection contested by appellant.
guidance: Every ground of rejection stated by the examiner must be addressed; failing to address a ground waives challenge and Board may summarily sustain it unless withdrawn in the examiner's answer. Each ground contested must be argued under a separate heading that reasonably identifies the ground (e.g., claim number, statutory basis, applied reference). For grounds applying to multiple claims, claims may be argued separately, as a group, or as a subgroup; when grouped, appellant must still use subheadings to identify claim(s) argued separately/subgroups. A statement merely pointing out what a claim recites is not an argument. All arguments and authorities to be considered must be included in the appeal brief for the present appeal, except as provided in §§ 41.41, 41.47, and 41.52. Arguments raised first at oral hearing are generally not entitled to consideration.

name: Oppositional post-grant model with petitioner burden and deadlines
description: The bill uses an oppositional model for post-grant review (preferred by the PTO) where the burden is on the petitioner to show a claim is not patentable, not on the PTO; this model supports quicker adjudication and predictable deadlines.
guidance: Proposed section 329(b)(1) mandates completion of post-grant proceedings within one year of institution, with a possible 6-month extension for good cause or second-window joinder; this is intended to avoid interminable delays seen in inter partes reexamination.

name: When IPEA need not carry out international preliminary examination
description: If the IPEA considers that the international application relates to subject matter on which it is not required to carry out an international preliminary examination, or that the description/claims/drawings are so unclear or the claims so inadequately supported that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability, the authority shall not go into the Article 33(1) questions and shall inform the applicant of the reasons.
guidance: If the situation applies only to certain claims, the provision applies only to those claims. Such instances should be rare since most problems are discovered during the international search.

name: Unity of invention: determination before written opinion/IPER
description: Before establishing any written opinion or the IPER, the IPEA will determine whether the international application complies with the requirement of unity of invention (see 37 CFR 1.475).
guidance: If the IPEA considers unity lacking, it may: (1) issue a written opinion/IPER for the entire application indicating lack of unity and reasons without inviting restriction or fees; (2) invite the applicant to restrict the claims or pay additional fees (no extension of time); or (3) if applicant fails to comply, establish a written opinion/IPER on the main invention and indicate facts. Lack of unity may be evident before or after considering prior art.

name: Supplemental replies (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2))
description: A supplemental reply to a reply in compliance with 37 CFR 1.111(b) will not be entered as a matter of right except in limited circumstances.
guidance: The Office may enter a supplemental reply only if it is clearly limited to: (A) cancellation of claims; (B) adoption of the examiner's suggestions; (C) placement of the application in condition for allowance; (D) reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply was filed; (E) correction of informalities; or (F) simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply will be entered if filed within the period during which action by the Office is suspended under 37 CFR 1.103(a) or (c).

name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) — when to use
description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) where the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (for example, the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
guidance: The streamlined analysis is for efficiency; its results must match the full Alice/Mayo analysis. If there is doubt whether applicant is seeking coverage for a judicial exception itself, the full analysis should be conducted. A claim eligible under Step 2A (Pathway B) or Step 2B (Pathway C) would also be eligible under the streamlined analysis. The record may show eligibility simply by absence of an eligibility rejection or include clarifying remarks. See MPEP § 2106 (subsection III) and MPEP § 2106.06 for details.

name: Eligibility is self-evident — what qualifies
description: A claim is 'self-evidently' eligible when, viewed as a whole, it clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it.
guidance: Examples: complex manufactured industrial products or processes that recite meaningful limitations alongside a judicial exception (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system using certain mathematical relationships); nature-based products that do not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (e.g., artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral; cellphone with gold electrical contact; plastic chair with wood trim). If claims are a 'close call' as to whether they improve technology or computer functionality, perform the full eligibility analysis (BASCOM example). Only when clear improvement or self-evident eligibility exists should Pathway A be used.

name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and review the whole record
description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent, and examiners should review the entire record (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, prior art) before concluding eligibility.
guidance: Examination guidance, training, and examples discuss substantive law but do not themselves serve as a basis for rejection. Applicants may cite training materials or examples in arguments but should not be required to model claims after training examples. The substantive law on eligibility is discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.06. The evaluation of eligibility should be claim-by-claim because dependent claims may add limitations that change the analysis.

name: Formulating a prima facie case for ineligibility and examiner burden
description: If it is more likely than not that a claim does not satisfy eligibility criteria (Step 1 NO and/or Step 2B NO), the examiner should formulate an appropriate rejection that sets forth a prima facie case of ineligibility under the substantive law.
guidance: The prima facie concept allocates burdens: the initial burden is on the examiner to clearly and specifically explain why a claim is ineligible so the applicant has sufficient notice and can respond effectively. If applicant rebuts properly, the rejection should be withdrawn or the examiner must rebut in the next Office action. See MPEP § 2106.07(b) for response considerations.

name: Requirements for a Step 2A Prong One rejection (identify the judicial exception)
description: A Step 2A Prong One rejection must identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (e.g., identify the abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon and provide a reasoned rationale).
guidance: If the claim 'describes' but does not expressly set forth the exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why the described subject matter is a judicial exception. For abstract ideas, identify how the claim recites the abstract idea (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) as enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).

name: Requirements for a Step 2A Prong Two rejection (integration into a practical application)
description: For Step 2A Prong Two, the rejection should identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
guidance: The rejection must specifically point to claim features/limitations/steps beyond the identified judicial exception and explain that either (1) there are no additional elements, or (2) the claim as a whole (considering additional elements individually and in combination) does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two, even if they represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

name: Requirements for a Step 2B rejection (inventive concept / 'significantly more')
description: For Step 2B, the rejection must explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
guidance: When the examiner concludes certain claim elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III (e.g., factual findings, citation to evidence). The rejection should address both individual elements and their combination and explain why they fail to supply an 'inventive concept' that makes the claim eligible.

name: Establish invention and apply broadest reasonable interpretation when formulating rejection
description: Before rejecting, examiners should determine what the applicant invented and establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention (see MPEP § 2111), then evaluate eligibility of each claim as a whole using MPEP § 2106 analysis.
guidance: When making a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, the Office action must provide an explanation as to why each claim is unpatentable that is sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice and enable effective response. Subject matter eligibility rejections under Step 1 and Step 2 should follow the specific explanatory guidance for each step (see MPEP §§ 2106.03 and 2106.07(a)).

name: Compact prosecution — state all non-cumulative reasons and bases in first Office action
description: Regardless of whether a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection is made, examiners should perform a complete examination for every claim under other patentability requirements and state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
guidance: Complete examination should include consideration under 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and issues of utility, inventorship, and double patenting (including non-statutory double patenting). This supports compact prosecution and avoids piecemeal rejections.

name: Specification as best source for technical term
description: “The best source for understanding a technical term is the specification from which it arose . . . .” (Multiform Desiccants, Inc. v. Medzam, Ltd., 133 F.3d 1473, 1478 (Fed. Cir. 1998)).
guidance: Use the patent specification first when defining technical terms used in the claims; the specification provides authorial context and can be more reliable than general dictionaries for field-specific terminology.

name: PTO may construe claims differently during prosecution
description: The PTO has historically construed claims more broadly than courts do during infringement litigation; MPEP § 2111 and related commentary note this prosecutorial/litigation distinction.
guidance: Recognize that claim meaning in prosecution may not match litigation constructions; drafters and litigators should account for differences in contexts and incentives.

name: Claim construction presumes textual imprecision
description: “The process of claim construction itself presumes that the words of the claims are insufficiently precise to delineate those boundaries.” (Burk & Lemley).
guidance: Accept that claims may be indeterminate at their margins; construction is a method for resolving underdeterminacy rather than revealing a single pre-existing meaning in all cases.

name: Drafting goal: as broad as the PTO will allow
description: “The overall goal when drafting claims is to make them as broad as the Patent Office will allow.” (Merges & Duffy).
guidance: Claim drafters should aim for maximal breadth subject to statutory and examination constraints, while balancing enforceability and validity risk.

name: Breadth trade-off: broader claims increase invalidity risk
description: Broad claim language increases the likelihood of the claim being invalidated, but patentees tend to favor broader language because courts have a bias against invalidating claims (Giles S. Rich; Roger Allan Ford; commentary).
guidance: When choosing claim scope, weigh the commercial benefits of breadth against higher invalidity exposure; consider that litigation and institutional biases affect the practical desirability of broad claims.

name: Interpretation from viewpoint of skilled artisan
description: “A patent presumes a readership skilled in the field of the invention.” (Ajinomoto Co. v. Archer-Daniels-Midland Co., 228 F.3d 1338, 1347 (Fed. Cir. 2000)).
guidance: Assess claim language as it would be understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing; technical dictionaries and expert evidence may inform that understanding.

name: Use specification for linguistic context, not to rewrite claims
description: “We have no objection to looking to the specification as part of the interpretative process. But our reason to look at the specification—for linguistic context—is very different from Judge Newman’s.”
guidance: Consult the specification to provide context and clarify meaning, but do not allow specification-based readings to impermissibly narrow or rewrite claim terms unless the patentee clearly disclaimed scope.

name: Court role limited to interpretation, not rewriting for policy
description: Courts interpret, rather than author, legal texts and should not 'rewrite' claims for fairness or policy reasons (United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers’ Coop.; Autogiro Co. of Am. v. United States; Salvano v. Merrill Lynch).
guidance: Resist policy-driven reconstruction of claim language; when policy suggests changing scope, the proper remedy is legislation or administrative action, not judicial redefinition of claims.

name: Claim meaning often dispositive of dispute
description: “[T]o decide what the claims [legally] mean is nearly always to decide the case.” (Wang Labs., Inc. v. Am. Online, Inc., 197 F.3d 1377, 1381 (Fed. Cir. 1999)).
guidance: Recognize that claim construction is frequently the determinative issue in infringement/invalidity disputes; invest appropriate effort in rigorous construction analysis.

name: Temporal lens: assess meaning as of filing date
description: A claim’s meaning is assessed as of the filing date (Playtex Prods., Inc. v. Procter & Gamble Co.; related authority).
guidance: When construing terms, use the knowledge and usage prevailing at the time of filing, not later developments in the art or language.

name: Intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence debate (dictionaries, experts, usage)
description: Phillips en banc and associated commentary posed whether the public notice function of patent claims is better served by referencing primarily to technical and general purpose dictionaries and similar sources or by looking primarily to the patentee’s use of the term in the specification.
guidance: Follow the Phillips framework (intrinsic evidence primary) but acknowledge ongoing debate; use extrinsic sources (dictionaries, expert surveys, usage data) cautiously to confirm, not supplant, intrinsic meaning.

name: Reasons for nonentry of amendment (concise)
description: The reasons for nonentry should be concisely expressed. Examples given: (A) amendment would not avoid any of the rejections set forth in the last Office action and thus would not place the case in condition for allowance or better condition for appeal; (B) amendment would raise the issue of new matter; (C) amended claims present new issues requiring further consideration or search; (D) amendment presents additional claims without canceling any finally rejected claims.
guidance: Ordinarily the specific deficiencies need not be discussed but reasons should be concise and may use the example wordings (A)–(D). When an amendment is denied entry, follow with the appropriate explanatory form paragraphs (7.72–7.80) as applicable.

name: 37 CFR 1.312 amendments after allowance: timing and examples
description: No amendment may be made as a matter of right after mailing of the notice of allowance; any amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 must be filed before or with payment of the issue fee and may be entered on recommendation of the primary examiner approved by the Commissioner.
guidance: Examples of 'amendments' under 1.312 include: (A) an amendment to the specification, (B) a change in the drawings, (C) an amendment to the claims, (D) a change in the inventorship, (E) the submission of prior art. Primary examiners have delegated authority to recommend entry; supplemental reissue oaths are treated as amendments and must comply with 1.312.

name: Scope of primary examiner authority for 1.312 entries
description: After Notice of Allowance, the application is technically no longer under primary examiner jurisdiction, but the primary examiner may make examiner’s amendments and enter amendments that merely correct formal matters in the specification or drawing or formal matters in a claim without changing its scope, or cancel claims, without forwarding to the SPE.
guidance: Amendments other than trivial formal corrections require SPE approval. TC Director establishes policy on trivial informalities based on two vital formal requirements: (A) disclosure must be adequately clear, and (B) any invention present be defined with sufficient clarity to form an adequate basis for an enforceable contract.

name: Entry criteria for 1.312 amendments affecting disclosure, scope, or adding claims
description: Remarks accompanying an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 that affect the disclosure, change scope of any claim, or add a claim must fully and clearly state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: Prosecution continuation is not permitted by 1.312. If recommendation is against entry, a simple statement that the proposed claim is not obviously allowable and brief reason usually suffices. Provide detailed statement only when necessary.

name: Copied patent claims after allowance entry not matter of right (714.16(a))
description: When an amendment received after notice of allowance includes one or more claims copied or substantially copied from a patent, entry of those copied patent claims is not a matter of right.
guidance: Follow the specific procedure in MPEP § 2305.04 when such copied claims are received. Additional fee requirements may apply (see MPEP § 607 and § 714.16(c)).

name: Processing and notation of 1.312 amendments by examiner
description: Amendments under 37 CFR 1.312 affecting disclosure, adding claims, or changing scope are sent to Publishing Division which forwards them to the Technology Center that allowed the application; the examiner promptly considers the amendment and indicates 'Enter — 312', 'Do Not Enter' or 'Enter In Part' in red ink in the upper left corner.
guidance: If class/subclass transfers occurred after allowance, the amendment may be transmitted to another TC and the original examiner consulted. Prompt consideration and clear entry notation by examiner are required.

name: Claim construction — interpret each claim as a whole
description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers; give each claim its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description. Consider the entire claim including preamble language and the transitional phrase.
guidance: Evaluate preamble language and whether it constitutes a structural limitation by reviewing the entire application. Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims. Give weight to preamble language where the claim as a whole suggests it; resolve preamble importation by considering what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass.

name: Ways to show possession of the claimed invention
description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice, by clear depiction in detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas, or by disclosure of sufficiently detailed identifying characteristics that a skilled artisan would recognize applicant had possession of the claimed invention.
guidance: Examples include: construction of an embodiment or performance of a process meeting all claim limitations (reduction to practice); detailed drawings/structural formulas; deposits for biological materials per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; identifying characteristics such as sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length, restriction maps, expression data. The description need only detail what is new or nonconventional.

name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. §112, sixth paragraph) support and interpretation
description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. §112, para. 6, it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: Determine adequacy by: (1) whether the written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to the recited function; or (2) whether one skilled in the art would have known what structure/materials/acts perform the recited function based on the application (including original claims, abstract, drawings). A rejection under §112, para. 2 cannot stand where §112, first paragraph provides adequate description for means-plus-function recitations.

name: Claim drawn to a single embodiment/species — stepwise written description analysis
description: For a claim drawn to a single embodiment or species, determine whether the application (A) describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, whether there is reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed; (C) if not, whether distinguishing identifying characteristics are set forth that show possession.
guidance: Specifically: (1) If the application describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole, the written description requirement is satisfied. (2) If not, determine whether other identifying characteristics are disclosed in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms that a skilled artisan would recognize possession. Consider established correlations between structure and function; where present, function plus minimal structure may suffice; where absent, function alone is insufficient.

name: Factors to consider in assessing written description possession
description: Whether the specification shows possession is a factual determination based on multiple factors.
guidance: Factors include: level of skill and knowledge in the art; disclosure of partial structure; physical and/or chemical properties; functional characteristics coupled with a known/disclosed correlation between function and structure; and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one skilled in the art to conclude applicant was in possession is sufficient.

name: Varying disclosure requirements by technology maturity and predictability
description: The description needed to satisfy §112, first paragraph varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with existing scientific and technological knowledge; mature predictable arts require less detailed disclosure than emerging, unpredictable technologies.
guidance: In mature fields where knowledge/skill is high, a written description objection should generally not be raised for claims present in the original filing even if the specification only discloses a method and its function. In unpredictable/emerging technologies, more evidence (e.g., reduction to practice, detailed structure) is required. For product-by-process claims, the written description is satisfied where the process has actually been used to produce the product; otherwise disclosure of process alone may not support a product claim.

name: Eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 156(a)
description: The term of a patent which claims a product, a method of using a product, or a method of manufacturing a product shall be extended from the original expiration date if: (1) the patent has not expired before an application under subsection (d)(1) was filed; (2) the term of the patent has never been extended under subsection (e)(1); (3) an application for extension is submitted by the owner of record or its agent and in accordance with subsection (d) requirements; (4) the product has been subject to a regulatory review period before its commercial marketing or use; and (5) except as provided in (B) or (C), the permission for commercial marketing or use after such regulatory review period is the first permitted commercial marketing or use of the product under the provision of law under which such regulatory review period occurred.
guidance: This statutory checklist (35 U.S.C. 156(a)(1)-(5)) is the primary eligibility test: the applicant must demonstrate each listed element (timing, prior extensions, proper filer, regulatory review, and first permitted marketing/use). Subparts (B) and (C) provide limited exceptions (e.g., recombinant DNA manufacturing and certain animal drug approvals).

name: Application contents required by 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1)
description: The extension application must contain: (A) the identity of the approved product and the Federal statute under which regulatory review occurred; (B) the identity of the patent and each claim which claims the approved product or a method of using/manufacturing it; (C) information enabling the Director to determine eligibility, the rights to be derived from the extension, and enabling the Director and the Secretary to determine the period of extension; (D) a brief description of activities undertaken during the regulatory review period and significant dates; and (E) such patent or other information as the Director may require.
guidance: Provide detailed factual support (patent claims, dates, regulatory interactions). The Office may require additional documents. Failure to include required items can render the application noncompliant under §1.740.

name: 37 CFR 1.710 — Patents subject to extension (CFR product definition)
description: A patent is eligible for extension if it claims a product as defined in §1.710(b) (active ingredient of new human drug/antibiotic/human biological product including salts/esters; active ingredient of certain animal drugs not primarily manufactured via certain biotech processes; or any medical device, food additive, or color additive subject to FDA regulation) either alone or in combination or claims a method of using or manufacturing such a product, and meets other conditions of the subpart.
guidance: 37 CFR 1.710 restates the statutory 'product' boundaries in regulatory language used by USPTO; applicants should map claim language to §1.710(b) categories to assess eligibility.

name: 37 CFR 1.720 — Conditions for extension (CFR checklist)
description: The term of a patent may be extended if: (a) the patent claims a product or method as defined in §1.710; (b) the term has never been previously extended except for extensions per §§1.701,1.760,1.790; (c) an application is submitted in compliance with §1.740; (d) the product was subject to a regulatory review period as defined in 35 U.S.C.156(g); (e) the product has received permission for commercial marketing/use and meets first-permission rules (including special rules for recombinant manufacturing and certain animal drugs); (f) application filed within the sixty-day period beginning on date of first permission (with special timing for recombinant manufacturing/animal drug situations); (g) the patent term has not expired before submission in compliance with §1.741; and (h) no other patent term has been extended for the same regulatory review period for the product.
guidance: This CFR checklist operationalizes the statutory requirements and adds procedural conditions (filing compliance sections and expiration checks). Applicants must satisfy each listed subcondition and follow associated filing provisions (§1.740, §1.741).

name: Animal drug special rules for subsequent approvals (35 U.S.C.156(a)(5)(C) / 37 CFR 1.720(e)(3))
description: A patent directed to a new animal drug or veterinary biological product may be extended based on a second or subsequent approval of the active ingredient if: (A) the patent claims the drug/product; (B) the drug/product is not covered by the claims in any other patent that has been extended; (C) the patent term was not extended based on regulatory review for use in non-food-producing animals; and (D) the second/subsequent approval was the first permitted commercial marketing/use for administration to a food-producing animal. The application must be filed within sixty days of that first approval for food-producing animals.
guidance: This allows PTE for later approvals specifically for food-producing animals even if there was prior approval for non-food-producing animals, provided the listed conditions are met and filing timing is respected.

name: Scope of rights during the extended period (35 U.S.C.156(b))
description: The rights derived from extension under 35 U.S.C.156(a) are defined in 156(b) and are not limited to a claim-by-claim basis; the statute indicates that 'the term of a patent which claims a product, a method of using a product, or a method of manufacturing a product shall be extended.' However, if the patent claims other products in addition to the approved product, the exclusive patent rights to the additional products expire with the original expiration date of the patent.
guidance: Extension is attached to the patent term and the rights during the extended period are limited to the approved product (e.g., active ingredient, salts/esters). Case law (e.g., Biogen v. Banner) constrains scope (metabolites not covered), and Genetics Institute/other cases discuss claim scope implications. Applicants must identify which claims 'claim the approved product' to determine the rights conferred by the extension.

name: Resources for Examining Means-Plus-Function and Step-Plus-Function Claim Limitations
description: Resources for Examining Means-Plus-Function and Step-Plus-Function Claim Limitations — Federal Register notice, 89 FR 19817, March 20, 2024.
guidance: Accompanied by a Memorandum to the Examining Corps, March 18, 2024.

name: Level of Ordinary Skill
description: The level of skill in the art to which an invention pertains that is used in judging whether a disclosure or claim is enabling.
guidance: Used to assess enablement and obviousness (see: Enablement). MPEP 2141.03

name: Reduction to Practice
description: Completion of the inventive process by physical verification that the invention works for its intended purpose (actual reduction) or constructive reduction by filing a patent application that adequately discloses the invention.
guidance: Actual reduction requires verification of each claimed element; degree depends on invention complexity. Constructive reduction occurs upon filing. MPEP 2138.05

name: Prior Art (and Prior Art Reference)
description: The body of prior knowledge relevant to the claimed invention (publications, prior use, patent disclosures). A prior art reference is a specific cited document.
guidance: Material to novelty and obviousness determinations. See relevant MPEP sections (2126–2128).

name: New Matter
description: Information not present in the original specification, claims, or drawings which an applicant attempts to add; such additions are rejected for not being present explicitly or implicitly in the original disclosure.
guidance: Amendments cannot add new matter beyond original disclosure. MPEP 608.04 and subparts.

name: Means-Plus-Function / Means for Claim
description: A claim element recited as a means to accomplish a particular function (means-plus-function language).
guidance: Means claims are governed by specific rules (MPEP 2181); they are interpreted in view of disclosed structure that performs the function.

name: Markush Group
description: A claim reciting 'selected from the group consisting of …' creating a limited generic claim; members must share at least one property primarily responsible for the claimed function.
guidance: Use when claiming a set of alternatives sharing a common functional property.

name: Negative Limitation
description: A claim limitation that is exclusive (e.g., 'other than X', 'incapable of X'), also known as a negative claim limitation.
guidance: Treated specially in claim interpretation and indefiniteness analyses. MPEP 2173.05(i)

name: Prolix Claim
description: A claim containing long recitations or unimportant details that renders the claim indefinite.
guidance: Avoid excessive, unimportant detail in claims to prevent indefiniteness. MPEP 2173.05(m)

name: Preamble (of a Claim)
description: The formal introductory clause of a patent claim which may or may not define a narrowing element of the claim.
guidance: Preamble usually defines context; Jepson claim preambles imply admission of prior art and may affect claim scope.

name: Utility / New Use
description: Discovery of a new use for a previous invention can be patentable subject matter under U.S. law.
guidance: Claims to new, practical utility can support patentability when properly disclosed.

name: Reissue
description: An application filed by a patentee after grant to correct errors in the issued patent that render it wholly or partly inoperative, or to correct claims that are too broad or too narrow.
guidance: Applicant must surrender the issued patent provisionally; reissue patents keep original expiration date. MPEP 1401–1403

name: Prosecution History Estoppel / File Wrapper Estoppel
description: Doctrines limiting claim scope in litigation based on arguments or amendments made during patent prosecution.
guidance: Claims surrendered during prosecution may prevent recapture of scope in enforcement.

name: Patentability / Rationale for Patentability
description: The determination and reasoning whether a claimed invention meets legal requirements for patent grant (novelty, non-obviousness, utility, statutory subject matter, enablement).
guidance: Rationale often documented in office actions and MPEP guidance (e.g., MPEP 1302.14).

name: Defective initial reissue oath/declaration (37 CFR 1.175(a))
description: Where the reissue oath/declaration fails to comply with 37 CFR 1.175(a), the examiner will notify applicant in an Office action, rejecting the claims under 35 U.S.C. 251.
guidance: In reply to the Office action, a supplemental reissue oath/declaration should be submitted dealing with the noted defects. If the initial oath/declaration (1) failed to provide any error statement, or (2) attempted to provide one but failed to identify any error under 35 U.S.C. 251, the examiner should reject all claims as being based upon a defective reissue oath/declaration and point out the failure to comply with 37 CFR 1.175. A supplemental oath/declaration stating an error under 35 U.S.C. 251 must be submitted to support the reissue.

name: Form paragraph 14.05.02 use and content
description: Form paragraph 14.05.02 notifies applicant of requirement for supplemental reissue oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.175(b)(1) before allowance and rejects the claims as defective until the supplemental oath/declaration is submitted.
guidance: Includes sample acceptable language for the supplemental oath: e.g., 'Every error in the patent which was corrected in the present reissue application, and is not covered by a prior oath/declaration submitted in this application, arose without any deceptive intention on the part of the applicant.' Examiner notes specify bracket insertions (claims list; oath/declaration), and when not to use this paragraph: do not use if no amendments were made since last oath; cannot be used in Ex parte Quayle action; do not use in examiner's amendment; the supplemental oath must be filed prior to Notice of Allowability.

name: Post-allowance correction amendments governed by 37 CFR 1.312
description: Corrections of patent errors after allowance must be submitted in accordance with 37 CFR 1.312.
guidance: No amendment may be made as a matter of right after mailing of the notice of allowance. An amendment filed before payment of the issue fee may be entered on the recommendation of the primary examiner and approval of the supervisory examiner without withdrawing the case from issue. An amendment filed after payment of the issue fee must be accompanied by a petition including the fee (37 CFR 1.17(i)) and a showing of good and sufficient reasons, decided by the Group Director. Because such amendments affect disclosure or claim scope, the remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier. A supplemental reissue oath/declaration must accompany the amendment and must state that the errors arose without deceptive intention; it need only be directed to the errors being corrected after allowance and need not cover earlier errors.

name: Corrections that are not physical amendments (e.g., filing certified foreign priority) still governed by amendment rules
description: An error to be corrected after allowance that does not include an amendment of the specification or claims (for example, filing a certified copy of the original foreign application to obtain priority) still must comply with 37 CFR 1.312.
guidance: Even where no amendment is physically entered, the correction of the patent is an amendment and the same procedural requirements apply for supplemental oath/declaration and petitions when applicable.

name: Use of reissue to provoke an interference (limits and requirements)
description: A reissue application may be placed into interference, and a patentee may provoke an interference by filing a reissue application that (A) adds copied claims not present in the original patent, (B) amends claims to correspond to another patent/application, or (C) contains at least one error (not directed to provoking interference) appropriate for reissue.
guidance: Reissue error must be based upon applicant error; cannot be based solely on Office error for failing to declare an interference. When copying/amending claims to provoke an interference, the reissue oath/declaration must assert applicant erred in failing to include claims of the proper scope in the original application. The copied/amended claims' subject matter must be supported by the original patent disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. A reissue applicant cannot present added/amended claims to provoke an interference if the claims were deliberately omitted from the patent (e.g., described as undesirable). The issue date of the patent with which interference is sought must be less than 1 year prior to presentation of the copied/amended claims (35 U.S.C. 135(b)). If the reissue includes broadened claims, the reissue must be filed within two years from issue date of the original patent (35 U.S.C. 251 and MPEP § 1412.03). If a reissue is filed while the patent is in interference, notify the Board within 10 days (37 CFR 1.660(b)).

name: Restriction and election of species in reissue applications
description: The examiner may not require restriction in a reissue application (37 CFR 1.176 and MPEP § 1440); restriction may only be requested by applicant (37 CFR 1.177 and MPEP § 1451).
guidance: Even where the original patent contains claims to different inventions considered independent and distinct, the examiner should not require restriction in the reissue. If the reissue presents claims for the first time that are distinct and separate from those of the patent, follow In re Amos practice (MPEP § 1412.01). Failure to timely file a divisional application is not considered error correctable by reissue. If the original specification shows intent not to claim the invention, that invention cannot be added by reissue; added claims may be rejected for lack of defect in the original patent and lack of error in obtaining the original patent. When the original patent contains claims to multiple species and the reissue contains the same species, election of species should not be required even if no allowable generic claim exists; if reissue presents species not claimed in the original, election of species is still not required, but added claims may be rejected for lack of defect/lack of error.

name: Continuation reissue applications practice (In re Graff guidance)
description: Continuation of a reissue (continuation reissue) is permitted where it complies with reissue rules; parent and continuation should be examined together if possible.
guidance: Amend continuing data entries to identify parent-continuation relationship and provide notice. If parent issues prior to continuation examination, carefully review continuation claims for double patenting over the parent; where examined together, make provisional double patenting rejection in both cases for overlapping claims (see MPEP § 804). Terminal disclaimers filed to obviate obviousness-type double patenting ensure common ownership for the unexpired term. If the parent reissue issues without cross-reference to the continuation, require the continuation (or parent) be amended by Certificate of Correction to include cross-reference.

name: Amendments to reissue specification (37 CFR 1.121(b)(1))
description: Amendments to the specification, other than the claims, must be made by submission of the entire text of newly added or rewritten paragraph(s) with markings (underlining for additions, brackets for deletions) and must indicate the precise point where the paragraph is located; an entire paragraph may be deleted by a statement deleting the paragraph without presentation of its text.
guidance: All bracketing and underlining is made in comparison to the original patent (not prior amendments). Added paragraphs must be submitted completely underlined. Changes are handled as blocked paragraph insertions (assigned letter/number) with a caret indicating incorporation point, so applicants need not be concerned with page formatting. This section does not apply to claims or drawings amendments.

name: Amendments to reissue claims (37 CFR 1.121(b)(2))
description: Amendments to claims must present the entire text of each claim being amended and of each claim added, with markings; patent claims must not be renumbered and numbering of added claims must follow the highest numbered patent claim.
guidance: Use underlining for added subject matter and brackets for deleted subject matter. If a claim is amended, include a parenthetical such as '(amended)' or '(twice amended)' after the original claim number. Each amendment submission must set forth the status (pending or cancelled) as of the amendment date of all patent claims and added claims. Each amendment when originally submitted must be accompanied by an explanation of the support in the disclosure for the amendment and any additional comments on separate pages from the amendment text.

name: Disclosure correspondence and prohibition on new matter or enlargement beyond two years
description: The disclosure must be amended when required to correct inaccuracies and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings. No reissue patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from grant of the original patent. No amendment may introduce new matter or be made in an expired patent.
guidance: All amendments must be made relative to the patent specification, including claims and drawings, which is in effect as of the filing date of the reissue application. These provisions apply to amendments submitted on or after December 1, 1997; earlier amendments need not be re-submitted but will be entered if re-submitted unless directed otherwise by the SPE or SPRE.

name: Preamble as claim limitation
description: Whether preamble recitations are structural limitations or mere statements of purpose/use depends on review of the entire record and what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass; if the claim body fully and intrinsically sets forth all limitations, a preamble stating purpose/intended use is not a limitation, except where the preamble provides context or is relied on during prosecution to distinguish prior art.
guidance: Resolve by looking to the claim body, specification, and prosecution history. Examples/case law: Corning Glass Works (review entirety), Pitney Bowes v. Hewlett‑Packard (preamble stating purpose not limiting), Rowe v. Dror, Kropa v. Robie, STX LLC v. Brine. If preamble language forms the basis for distinguishing prior art in prosecution (clear reliance), it becomes a claim limitation (Metabolite Labs.; Catalina Mktg. Intl.). Also can be a limitation where preamble discloses a fundamental characteristic of the invention (Poly‑America). For method claims directed to treating people, preamble meaning (e.g., “a human in need thereof”) may be limiting (Jansen, Nantkwest, Cruciferous Sprout Litig.). During examination, evaluate whether recited purpose results in a structural (or manipulative) difference over the prior art; if so, it limits the claim (In re Otto; In re Sinex; In re Schreiber).

name: Transitional phrase: 'comprising' (open/including)
description: The transitional term 'comprising' (synonymous with including/containing/characterized by) is inclusive/open‑ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps.
guidance: Treat claims using 'comprising' as presumptively open‑ended; additional elements may be present without taking the subject matter outside the claim scope. Case examples: Mars Inc. v. H.J. Heinz; Invitrogen v. Biocrest; Genentech v. Chiron; Moleculon Research; In re Baxter; Ex parte Davis; Gillette v. Energizer (open‑ended example with razor blades). Note that context (e.g., 'group consisting of') can affect interpretation.

name: Clauses: 'adapted to/for', 'wherein', 'whereby' (potentially limiting)
description: Clauses such as 'adapted to/for', 'wherein', and 'whereby' may raise questions as to whether they are limiting; whether they limit the claim depends on the specific facts and how they give meaning/purpose to claim steps or structure.
guidance: Analyze whether the clause imparts a structural or required functional limitation. Examples: Griffin v. Bertina (wherein clause limited a process claim by giving meaning to steps); In re Giannelli (adapted to clause limited machine claim because specification showed narrower meaning); Hoffer v. Microsoft (whereby clause material to patentability cannot be ignored). Conversely, a wherein/whereby that merely states an intended result of an already‑recited step may be given no weight (Minton).

name: Contingent claim limitations (method vs system claims)
description: For method claims with contingent limitations, the broadest reasonable interpretation requires only steps that must be performed; contingent steps that depend on conditions not met are not required. For system/product claims, structure to perform a function (even if function is conditional) must be present irrespective of whether the condition occurs.
guidance: Apply contingent limitation analysis differently for method and system claims. Use factual analysis of conditions precedent. PTAB decision Ex parte Schulhauser illustrates that method claims do not require performance of contingent steps when condition not met, whereas system claims require structure to perform the function if condition occurs. For obviousness rejections of system claims, prior art must teach the structure that performs the contingent function along with other recited limitations. See also MPEP § 2143.03.

name: Printed matter doctrine: determine printed matter vs functional material
description: A limitation is 'printed matter' only if it claims the content of information. If a limitation is printed matter, it is given patentable weight only if there is a new and nonobvious functional relationship between the printed matter and the physical substrate; otherwise printed matter is given no patentable weight.
guidance: First determine if the limitation claims content of information (In re DiStefano). If so, evaluate whether the printed matter is functionally or structurally related to the substrate—if not, disregard for patentability (In re Gulack; Diamond v. Diehr). For method claims that add instructional limitations, analyze analogously whether a new and nonobvious functional relationship with the known method exists (In re DiStefano; In re Kao; King Pharm v. Eon Labs; In re Lowry; In re Ngai).

name: Evidence supporting a functional relationship for printed matter
description: Printed matter is given patentable weight when the printed matter performs some function with respect to the product (or the product performs a function with respect to the printed matter).
guidance: Examples: indicia on a measuring cup that indicate volume (In re Miller); a hatband arranged so that a string of numbers satisfies a claimed algorithm (Gulack example). Look for tangible interaction where printed matter affects product operation or product arranges printed matter such that a function is performed.

name: Evidence against a functional relationship for printed matter
description: No functional relationship exists where the product merely serves as support for printed matter or where the claim as a whole is directed to conveying a message/meaning to a human reader independent of the substrate.
guidance: Examples: decorative images on a hatband not arranged in sequence; deck of playing cards with printed images; instructions in a kit that are unrelated to that specific set of chemicals (In re Gwinn; In re Bryan; In re Ngai). If printed matter and product do not depend on each other, give no patentable weight.

name: Functional relationship must be new and nonobvious
description: Even where a functional relationship between printed matter and substrate is established, the relationship itself must be new and nonobvious for patentable weight; otherwise the claim may be anticipated or obvious over prior art.
guidance: Evaluate novelty/nonobviousness of the claimed functional relationship. Example: color‑coded indicia indicating expiration date may be a functional relationship but still be anticipated or obvious based on prior art.

name: Machine‑readable media claims: functional relationship test
description: When claims are directed to a computer‑readable medium containing programming, examine the relationship between the programming and the intended computer system: if the programming performs a function with respect to the computer, a functional relationship exists and may be given patentable weight; if the medium merely supports information for human consumption, no functional relationship exists.
guidance: Examples: attribute data objects that facilitate retrieval/addition/removal of information establish a functional relationship (Lowry). Memory sticks with tables of batting averages or music tracks merely support information for human readers and do not establish a functional relationship. Additionally, claims to computer‑readable media storing instructions/executable code that recite an abstract idea must be evaluated under 35 U.S.C. 101 (see MPEP § 2106).

name: Inherency in prior art rejections (general principle)
description: Express, implicit, and inherent disclosures of a prior art reference may be relied upon in rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103. Inherency is a question of fact and arises in anticipation and obviousness contexts.
guidance: Cite In re Napier; In re Grasselli. Examiner may rely on inherent teachings where a prior art embodiment necessarily possesses the claimed limitation, even if prior art did not recognize it. Use factual evidence to show inherency; inherency determinations can involve expert testimony.

name: Conversion to Utility Patent via Reissue
description: A design patent cannot be converted to a utility patent via reissue.
guidance: 35 U.S.C. 251 requires that the 'patent is, through error without any deceptive intention, deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid, by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than he had a right to claim in the patent'; however, the design patent (for which the reissue application would be filed) is not wholly or partly inoperative or invalid. There is no error in the design patent. Also, converting a design patent to a utility patent will, in most instances, involve the introduction of new matter into the patent. The disclosure of a design patent is not directed to how the invention is made and used, and the introduction of new matter is required to bridge this gap and provide support for the utility patent. Accordingly, the examiner should consider rejections based on the introduction of new matter under 35 U.S.C. 251 and lack of enablement and/or description under 35 U.S.C. 112, when a reissue application is filed to convert a design patent to a utility patent. Further, the term of a design patent may not be extended by reissue; a reissue that would extend the term should be rejected as failing to comply with 35 U.S.C. 251.

name: Certificate of Correction for Office Mistake (35 U.S.C. 254; 37 CFR 1.322)
description: The Director may issue a certificate of correction for a mistake in a patent incurred through the fault of the Office, where the mistake is clearly disclosed by the records of the Office.
guidance: The Director may act at the request of the patentee/assignee, sua sponte for Office-discovered mistakes, or on information supplied by a third party. The Office is not obligated to act on third-party submissions and will not make such papers of record nor retain them. The Office may decline to issue a certificate where the meaning is obvious from context and instead place correspondence in the patent file. Certificates should be requested only for errors of consequence; minor typographical errors that are readily apparent to one skilled in the art can be made of record by letter instead (no fee). It is strongly advised to submit the text of the correction on form PTO/SB/44 (PTO-1050) and to identify the location of the error by column and line number or claim and line number. Use the specified document description when filing electronically and address submissions to the Certificates of Correction Branch.

name: Expedited Issuance of Certificates of Correction (Office Error)
description: The Office will expedite processing and granting of patentee requests for certificates of correction where the request is accompanied by evidence showing the error is attributable solely to the Office and the matter is clearly disclosed in Office records.
guidance: Requirements for expedited consideration: submit text on PTO/SB/44 (not necessary in duplicate); identify location by column/line or claim/line; provide documentation unequivocally supporting patentee's assertion (e.g., relevant pages, photocopied correspondence dated and received by the Office, Examiners' responses regarding entry of amendments, receipts, manuscript pages) so the request can be processed without the patent file. Where only part of a request can be approved, patentee will receive a Notification of Approval-in-part and may request reconsideration. If determined the Office was not responsible, accelerated issuance cannot be anticipated. Use the prescribed document description when filing electronically and address submissions to the Certificates of Correction Branch.

name: Certificate of Correction for Applicant's Mistake (35 U.S.C. 255; 37 CFR 1.323)
description: A certificate of correction for an applicant's mistake may be issued where the mistake is clerical, typographical, or of minor character, was not the fault of the Office, was made in good faith, and the correction would not constitute new matter or require reexamination.
guidance: Two statutory requirements per In re Arnott: (1) the mistake must be clerical, typographical, or of minor character; (2) the proposed correction must not involve changes that would constitute new matter or require reexamination. Mistakes affecting claim scope (e.g., broadening a claim) generally are not 'minor' and should be corrected by reissue rather than certificate of correction. Clerical mistakes that are manifest from the patent file are typically correctable; errors requiring evidence outside the file are likely not manifest and not correctable. Benefit or foreign priority claim errors typically require petitions (37 CFR 1.78(e), 1.55(e)), not certificates. Fees for applicant mistake corrections are set in 37 CFR 1.20(a) (and for inventorship corrections 1.20(b)).

name: Element-by-element infringement proof
description: Patent infringement must be proven by showing that the product or service infringes each and every element of the asserted claims.
guidance: Claim charts must demonstrate alleged infringement on an element-by-element basis; failure to map any element means the infringement is not truly demonstrated.

name: Textual and graphical comparison (mapping)
description: Demonstrating an alleged unpermitted use is a textual and graphical comparison of the claims and the potentially infringing use. Because claim charts navigate the features of the product or service using claim terms, the explained potential infringement is often referred to as a 'mapping.'
guidance: Use both text and graphics to show how claim terms correspond to product/service features; structure mappings around claim term language so reviewers can follow the comparison.

name: Two-column claim chart format
description: A 'two-column' claim chart focuses on consistently mapping each claim element to a feature of the allegedly infringing product or service along with a citation to where that evidence can be found.
guidance: For each claim element include (1) the claim language and (2) the corresponding accused product/service feature plus a citation to supporting evidence (e.g., manual, spec, webpage, test result).

name: Three-column claim chart format (specification support)
description: A 'three-column' claim chart includes element-by-element cited support from the patent's specification that explains the interpretation of one or more of the claim terms and corroborates the rationale of why the cited evidence actually does demonstrate that claim element.
guidance: Include a column with patent specification citations and explanatory text that interprets claim terms and links spec language to the accused feature and external evidence; this corroborates why the evidence satisfies the element.

name: Cite evidence sources for each mapped element
description: Mapping each claim element must be accompanied by a citation to where that evidence can be found.
guidance: Cite documentation, manuals, webpages, test results, teardown findings, or other sources for every mapped element so the mapping is verifiable and defensible.

name: Identify and address mapping gaps
description: If a Claim Chart has a 'gap' in the mapping, the alleged infringement is not truly demonstrated.
guidance: Where documentation is limited, perform reverse engineering and testing to fill gaps; until presence is demonstrated by RE/testing/uncovered documentation, the chart must articulate a rationale for inferring the element's presence and propose a plan to complete the mapping.

name: Litigation-ready standard
description: Calling a claim chart 'litigation-ready' indicates that there is a high level of support in the patent specification and in the documentation of the targeted use case, but it does not typically mean it’s the streamlined version to be shown to the judge or jury.
guidance: A litigation-ready chart should have robust support and documentation for mappings and be suitable for driving litigation strategy (the backbone of a potential case), though it may include exhaustive detail rather than jury-presentable summary.

name: Collaborate with client and counsel to leave no element unmapped without plan
description: We work with the client and counsel to produce Claim Charts that demonstrate a likely case of infringement and aims to leave no claim element unmapped without a proper plan to complete the mapping.
guidance: Coordinate with counsel and the client to gather needed evidence, agree on claim term interpretations, and document any outstanding work and timelines to finish mapping every element.

name: Claim charts guide and drive litigation
description: Claim Charts are generally built to guide and drive the impending litigation. The demonstrated infringement is intended to be the backbone of a potential patent case.
guidance: Design charts not only to document mappings but also to inform litigation strategy, including which elements are strong, where proof is needed, and how to prioritize further investigation or expert work.

name: Replies and responses requirement (37 CFR 1.111) — specificity and bona fide attempt
description: If an Office action is adverse, the patent owner must reply and request reconsideration or further examination. The reply must be reduced to writing and must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the examiner’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. General allegations that claims are patentable without specific distinctions do not comply. Amendments in reply must clearly point out the patentable novelty and how amendments avoid cited references or objections. The reply must appear throughout to be a bona fide attempt to advance the proceeding.

name: Supplemental replies — limits on entry (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2))
description: A supplemental reply to a compliant reply will not be entered as a matter of right except where clearly limited to specific matters.
guidance: The Office may enter a supplemental reply only if it is clearly limited to: (A) cancellation of claims; (B) adoption of examiner suggestions; (C) placement of the proceeding in condition for allowance (or NIRC); (D) reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply; (E) correction of informalities (e.g., typographical errors); or (F) simplification of issues for appeal. A supplemental reply filed during a period when action is suspended under § 1.103(a) or (c) will be entered. If not entered, the contents must be included in a proper response to a subsequent Office action to be considered.

name: Conduct of ex parte reexamination proceedings (37 CFR 1.550)
description: Ex parte reexaminations must be conducted with special dispatch; patent owners are given at least 30 days to respond to any Office action; responses may include statements and/or proposed amendments or new claims to place the patent in condition where all claims, if amended as proposed, would be patentable.
guidance: If the patent owner fails to file a timely and appropriate response (or required interview summary) prosecution will be terminated and a reexamination certificate issued under § 1.570 per the last Office action. Late responses may be excused only under petition provisions of 37 CFR 1.137(a) (unavoidable delay) or 1.137(b) (unintentional delay).
