Documents filed must be served on the other party per § 1.248 or may be refused consideration. The reexamination requester will receive copies of Office actions; requester’s active participation ends after the reply under § 1.535. Third-party submissions after the date of order must meet § 1.501(a).

name: Role of the court in claim construction
description: The court determines the meaning of claim terms and provides definitions of certain claim terms; jurors must accept the court’s definitions as correct and apply them to decide issues such as infringement and validity.
guidance: "The law says that it is my role to define the terms of the claims and it is your role to apply my definitions to the issues that you are asked to decide in this case... You must accept my definitions of these words in the claims as being correct. It is your job to take these definitions and apply them to the issues that you are deciding, including the issues of infringement and validity." (Also: when the court has not defined a term, jurors should apply the common meaning.)

name: Claim interpretation by court and use of common meaning
description: The court will explain the meaning of some claim words; jurors must accept those definitions. For terms the court has not defined, jurors should apply the common meaning, based on a person of ordinary skill in the art where applicable.
guidance: "For any words in the claim for which I have not provided you with a definition, you should apply their common meaning... You should not take my definition ... as an indication that I have a view regarding how you should decide the issues... These issues are yours to decide." Authorities: Markman; Phillips (ordinary and customary meaning tied to person of ordinary skill in the art).

name: Infringement generally — claim-by-claim and types
description: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim; there are five possible types of infringement (direct infringement, active inducement, contributory infringement, infringement through supply of components from the U.S. to another country (§271(f)), and infringement through importation of a product made abroad by a patented process). Active inducement and contributory are indirect and require someone else to have engaged in direct infringement.
guidance: "Infringement is assessed on a claim-by-claim basis... The five types of infringement are called: (1) direct infringement; (2) active inducement; (3) contributory infringement; (4) infringement through the supply of components from the United States to another country; and (5) infringement through importation of a product made abroad by a patented process." Burden: preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: Warner-Lambert v. Teva; Seal-Flex.

name: Direct infringement — literal infringement of §112 ¶6 (means/step-plus) requirements
description: A product/process meets a means/step-plus-function requirement literally only if it (1) performs the identical function recited and (2) the structure/action performing it is identical or equivalent to the disclosed structure/acts; otherwise there is no literal infringement of that limitation.
guidance: "A product or a process meets a means-plus-function requirement ... if: (1) it has [a structure or set of structures/action or set of actions] that perform(s) the identical function recited in the claim, and (2) that [structure or set of structures/action or set of actions] is either identical or 'equivalent' to [one or more of] the described [set(s) of] [structure(s)/action(s)] ... If the [product] does not perform the specific function recited in the claim, the 'means-plus-function' requirement is not met." Authorities: §112 ¶6; Omega Eng'g; Allvoice.

name: Direct infringement — doctrine of equivalents (DOE) test
description: If an accused product/process does not literally meet all claim requirements, it may still infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if each requirement is met by an equivalent element/action; equivalency is judged by whether differences are insubstantial or whether the element/action performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, and the equivalence must have been known at the time of the alleged infringement.
guidance: "You may find that an element or step is equivalent ... if a person having ordinary skill ... would have considered the differences between them to be 'insubstantial' or would have found that the [structure or action]: (1) performs substantially the same function and (2) works in substantially the same way (3) to achieve substantially the same result... In order to prove infringement by 'equivalents,' [patent holder] must prove the equivalency ... by a preponderance of the evidence." Authorities: Graver Tank; Warner-Jenkinson; Festo; Interactive Pictures.

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — prior art / hypothetical claim
description: Prior art may preclude DOE: if a hypothetical claim that would literally cover the accused equivalent would have been invalid as anticipated or obvious in view of the prior art, there can be no DOE for that equivalence.
guidance: Two formulations given: (1) determine prior art and what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill; if a product with the allegedly equivalent feature was in prior art or would have been obvious, find no DOE; (2) use a 'hypothetical claim' broadened to cover the accused equivalent and decide whether that hypothetical claim would have been invalid for anticipation or obviousness. Authorities: Festo; cited cases.

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — patent disclosure preclusion
description: You may not find DOE if the allegedly equivalent alternative feature was described somewhere in the patent and that product/process is not covered literally by any claim of the patent.
guidance: "You may not find that a [product or process] infringes a claim under the doctrine of equivalents if you find that: (1) the allegedly 'equivalent' alternative feature(s) ... was/were described somewhere in the patent and (2) that [product or process] is not covered literally by any of the claims of the patent."

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — prosecution history estoppel (argument-based)
description: If during prosecution the applicant distinguished a claim requirement from the allegedly equivalent alternative, the patentee may be precluded from asserting DOE for that alternative.
guidance: "You may not find that a [product or process] infringes a claim under the doctrine of equivalents if you find that, during the patent application process, the applicant for the patent distinguished an unmet requirement from the allegedly 'equivalent' alternative aspect of that [product or process]."

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — prosecution history estoppel (amendment-based) — factors to overcome estoppel
description: If an alleged amendment during prosecution is asserted to limit DOE, the patentee can still show equivalence only if at least one specified factor is met (amendment substituted broader for narrower, reason not related to patentability, unforeseeability to a person of ordinary skill at time of amendment, amendment was tangential, or other good reason such as language shortcomings).
guidance: Listed factors jurors must find at least one of: (1) amendment substituted a broader requirement for a narrower requirement or replaced equal scope; (2) reason for amendment was not related to patentability; (3) person of ordinary skill would not have foreseen substitution of the allegedly equivalent alternative; (4) reason for amendment is tangential; or (5) other reason (e.g., language shortcomings) prevented broader claim language. If none found, estoppel precludes DOE. Authorities cited re: Festo and cases.

name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — vitiation
description: An alleged equivalent cannot be found to be equivalent if doing so would effectively eliminate or ignore an element or requirement of the claim (i.e., it would vitiate an element).
guidance: "You may not determine that an alternative aspect ... is equivalent to an unmet requirement of a claim if a finding of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents would effectively eliminate that requirement. Specifically, the alleged equivalent cannot eliminate or ignore an element or requirement of the claim." Authorities: Honeywell; Festo; Interactive Pictures.

name: Indirect infringement — active inducement (elements)
description: Active inducement requires proof, by a preponderance of the evidence, that (1) someone else actually carried out acts that directly infringe the claim; (2) the alleged inducer took action intending to cause those infringing acts during the patent term; and (3) the alleged inducer was aware of the patent and knew the acts would constitute infringement (or acted with willful blindness to a high probability of infringement).
guidance: "[Alleged infringer] is liable for active inducement ... only if [patent holder] proves ... that the acts are actually carried out by [another] and directly infringe ... that [alleged infringer] took action ... intending to cause the infringing acts ... and that [alleged infringer] was aware of the [ ] patent and knew that the acts, if taken, would constitute infringement..." Willful blindness language incorporated from Global-Tech. A good-faith belief that acts did not infringe or that the patent was invalid negates inducement intent. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §271(b); Global-Tech; DSU Med.; Lucent.

name: Obviousness / Inventive step
description: That the invention so far as claimed in any claim is obvious or does not involve any inventive step having regard to what was publicly known or publicly used in India or what was published in India or elsewhere before the priority date of the claim.
guidance: Obviousness means something 'easily perceived by the senses or grasped by the mind' or 'clearly or plainly evident' to a person having fair knowledge of the subject. The manner in which the invention was arrived at is relevant. The assessment is with reference to the 'state of art' and whether a skilled person could carry out the development without any substantial inventive step. If subject matter appears obvious it does not involve an inventive step and vice versa.

name: Complete specification not sufficiently and fairly describing the invention (sufficiency of disclosure)
description: The complete specification must describe an embodiment of the invention claimed in each of the claims and the description must be sufficient to enable those in the industry concerned to put it into effect without their making further invention; the description must be fair and not unnecessarily difficult to follow.
guidance: The instructions for working the invention must be sufficient for a person in India possessing average skill and knowledge of the art to work the invention. The specification should disclose the best method known to the applicant for performing the invention if entitled to claim protection for it. Sufficiency is judged on the merits of the specification; no hard and fast rule can be laid down.

name: Claim not clearly defined and not fairly based
description: (i) The scope of any claim of the complete specification is not sufficiently and clearly defined; and/or (ii) any claim of the complete specification is not fairly based on the matter disclosed in the specification.
guidance: ‘Fairly based’ means the patentee should get a monopoly exactly sufficient to protect his invention as disclosed, but must not claim more monopoly than is justified by the disclosure. A patent is granted in lieu of disclosure to the public, so claims must be commensurate with the disclosed matter.

name: Subject of claims not a patentable invention
description: The subject of any claim of the complete specification is not an invention within the meaning of the Act or is otherwise not patentable under the Act (e.g., exclusions under sections 3 and 4).
guidance: This ground captures statutory exclusions and other legal doctrines rendering claimed subject-matter outside patentable subject matter under Indian law.

name: Claimed invention secretly used before the priority date (secret prior use)
description: That the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification was secretly used in India, otherwise than as excepted, before the priority date of the claim.
guidance: Prior secret use will invalidate the patent except for certain conditions (see section 64(3)). Secret use done for trial or experimental purposes as specified may be excepted. No account is to be taken of personal documents or secret trial or secret use for some clauses.

name: Invention anticipated by traditional knowledge
description: A patent may be revoked if any detail claimed in the specification is anticipated by knowledge available orally or otherwise within any local or indigenous community in India or anywhere.
guidance: Traditional knowledge (oral or otherwise) that predates the priority date can be treated as anticipation and defeat patentability; this is explicitly recognized as a ground of revocation.

name: Exceptions to anticipation and secret use
description: No account shall be taken of personal documents or secret trial or secret use for certain anticipation and prior-use provisions; importation into India of a product made abroad by a claimed process may constitute knowledge/use in India of the invention on date of importation, except where importation has been for reasonable trial or experiment only.
guidance: The statute carves out exceptions where secret trials/uses and limited importations do not count as public knowledge or use; these exceptions must be considered particularly when applying clauses on novelty and obviousness.

name: Definition and tests for 'reasonable requirements of the public'
description: For the purposes of compulsory licensing, the reasonable requirements of the public shall be deemed not to have been satisfied if, by reason of the patentee's refusal to grant licences on reasonable terms: (i) an existing trade or industry or its development or establishment of new trade/industry in India is prejudiced; or (ii) the demand for the patented article has not been met to an adequate extent or on reasonable terms; or (iii) a market for export of the patented article manufactured in India is not being supplied or developed; or (iv) the establishment or development of commercial activities in India is prejudiced; or if by reason of conditions imposed by the patentee on grants of licences or purchase/use, manufacture/use/sale of materials not protected by the patent or establishment/development of trade is prejudiced; or if the patentee imposes exclusive grant-back, prevents challenges to validity, or engages in coercive package licensing; or if the patented invention is not being worked in India on a commercial scale to an adequate extent or to the fullest extent reasonably practicable; or if working is prevented or hindered by importation from abroad by the patentee or persons claiming under him or by persons purchasing from him, or other persons against whom the patentee is not taking proceedings for infringement.
guidance: This is a broad multi-factor test indicating circumstances where public requirements are unmet and justifying compulsory licensing or other remedies.

name: Revocation of patents: statutory list (section 64)
description: Subject to the Act, a patent may be revoked by Appellate Board/High Court on petition of any person interested or Central Government on grounds enumerated in section 64 clauses (a)–(q) (e.g., earlier valid claim, wrong applicant, not an invention, not novel, obvious, not useful, insufficiency, unclear scope or not fairly based, false suggestion, not patentable, secret prior use, failure to disclose foreign application info, contravention of secrecy directions/section 39, amendment obtained by fraud, wrong source/geographical origin disclosure for biological material, anticipated by local/indigenous knowledge).
guidance: Section 64 consolidates the statutory grounds for revocation; many of these are expanded elsewhere in the chapter (novelty, inventive step, sufficiency, disclosure obligations, secrecy, fraud, traditional knowledge). Procedural aspects (who may petition, notices) are also prescribed.

name: Improper Markush grouping (written description) — 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
description: The examiner should not suggest a grouping that meets the requirements for a proper Markush grouping, but would clearly lack adequate written description if presented in a separate claim.
guidance: Reject claims based on an improper Markush grouping under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) when the grouping would not meet written description requirements if recited in separate claims. Maintain the improper Markush grouping rejection until the claim is amended to correct the grouping or the applicant convinces the examiner that the members share the required similarity and common use.

name: Indefiniteness of Markush claim — 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
description: The claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) if one skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of the Markush claim due to an inability to envision all of the members of the Markush grouping. If a boundary cannot be drawn separating embodiments encompassed by the claim from those that are not, the claim is indefinite.
guidance: Apply 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) when the Markush grouping prevents a person of ordinary skill from drawing clear boundaries. See also MPEP § 2173.05(h).

name: When to withdraw improper Markush grouping rejection
description: The improper Markush grouping rejection should be maintained until (1) the claim is amended such that the Markush grouping includes only members that share a single structural similarity and a common use; or (2) the applicant presents convincing arguments why the members of the Markush grouping share a single structural similarity and common use.
guidance: Convincing arguments may show that alternatives are members of a physical, chemical, or art-recognized class that share a common use, or that chemical compounds share a substantial structural feature essential to the common use. Reconsider the rejection when all claims are otherwise in condition for allowance and the prior art and record support propriety.

name: Two-prong test for propriety of chemical Markush groupings
description: A Markush grouping is proper if the members share (1) a substantial single structural similarity and (2) a common use (utility) that flows from that structural feature.
guidance: For chemical compounds evaluate each claimed compound as a whole to determine whether both prongs are met. The common use should be tied to the substantial structural feature disclosed as essential to that utility.

name: Sufficient common structural proportion (prong 1 guidance)
description: When the claimed class shows a relatively large proportion of the structure common to the entire class, the prong 1 requirement for structural similarity may be met.
guidance: Evaluate whether a substantial portion of the molecules' structure is shared across the class (example: common coumarin core or phosphoric acid diester backbone). Breadth due to indices (e.g., repeating units) does not automatically defeat prong 1 if the common structure is substantial.

name: Common use requirement (prong 2 guidance)
description: All of the compounds must share a common disclosed use (e.g., being dyes, antimycotic activity) and that use should be related to the substantial structural feature.
guidance: Determine whether the disclosed utility is common to the claimed members and flows from the shared structural feature; mere potential multiple modes of application does not preclude a finding of common use if the compounds form a single invention/subgenus.

name: Choice of prior art — confine rejections to best available art
description: Prior art rejections should ordinarily be confined strictly to the best available art.
guidance: Exceptions are permitted (for claim-interpretation dependence, missing inventive concept, AIA-specific exceptions, or pre-AIA §102(e)/(f)/(g) qualification). Provide best backup rejections where appropriate, avoid merely cumulative rejections, and back up rejections with the best other art available to allow compact prosecution.

name: Determine effective filing date and reference date for applying 102
description: To determine which paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 102 applies, the effective filing date of the application and each claimed invention must be determined and compared with the date of the reference. The examiner must also determine the issue or publication date of the reference.
guidance: Use appropriate MPEP sections (e.g., §§2139.01, 2152.01, 2124, 2126, 2128–2128.02, 2152.02–2154.02(c)) to determine dates. Use form paragraphs 7.03.aia or 7.03.fti in Office actions to indicate AIA vs pre-AIA status and which 102 paragraph applies.

name: Interpretation limited to corresponding structure/material/acts and equivalents
description: A 35 U.S.C. §112, 6th paragraph "means or step plus function" limitation in a claim must be interpreted as limited to the corresponding structure, materials or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Effective immediately (per In re Donaldson), examiners shall not disregard the structure disclosed in the specification corresponding to means-plus-function language when rendering a patentability determination. This changes prior practice of reading such limitations to cover any prior art means that performs the function without regard to equivalence to disclosed structure.

name: Identify means/step-plus-function by functionally-defined claim language
description: A limitation falls under §112, 6th paragraph if the element in the claim is set forth, at least in part, by the function it performs as opposed to the specific structure, material, or acts.
guidance: There is no magic phrase required; examples include: 'jet driving device so constructed and located on the rotor as to drive the rotor' (means unnecessary), 'printing means'/'means for printing', 'force generating means adapted to provide...', 'call cost register means, including a digital display for providing a substantially instantaneous display for...', reducing the coefficient of friction of the resulting film (step-plus-function), and 'raising the pH of the resultant pulp to about 5.0 to precipitate...' (step-plus-function). If unclear whether a limitation falls within §112, 6th paragraph, a rejection under §112, second paragraph may be appropriate.

name: If specification defines limitation, give that meaning
description: If the specification defines what is meant by the limitation for the purposes of the claimed invention, the examiner should interpret the limitation as having that meaning.
guidance: If no definition is provided, examiners must exercise judgment in determining scope of the limitation; interpretation should be consistent with specification disclosure.

name: Scope of prior art search unchanged: prior art must perform identical function
description: Application of a prior art reference to a means- or step-plus-function limitation requires that the prior art element perform the identical function specified in the claim.
guidance: Donaldson does not substantially change the scope of the search; however, once identity of function is found, examiner carries initial burden to show that the prior art structure or step is the same as or equivalent to the structure, material, or acts described in the specification corresponding to the claimed limitation.

name: Make a prima facie case of equivalence when prior art performs claimed function
description: If a prior art element performs the function specified in the claim, and is not excluded by any explicit definition in the specification for an equivalent, the examiner should infer that the prior art element is an equivalent and conclude that the claimed limitation is anticipated by the prior art element.
guidance: Once the examiner makes this inference, the burden shifts to the applicant to show that the prior art element is not an equivalent of the structure, material or acts disclosed in the application (citing In re Mulder).

name: Even if non-equivalence proven, perform obviousness (§103) analysis
description: A showing of non-equivalence prevents anticipation but does not prevent the prior art element from rendering the claim limitation obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art.
guidance: Examiner must still make a §103 analysis to determine whether claimed means or step-plus-function is obvious in view of the prior art.

name: Apply §102/§103 rejections when equivalents scope uncertain
description: Because the exact scope of an 'equivalent' may be uncertain, it is appropriate to apply a §102/§103 rejection where the balance of the claim limitations are anticipated by or render obvious the claimed invention based on the prior art relied on.
guidance: Although best practice is to rely on the best prior art references, alternative grounds of rejection may be appropriate when prior art shows differing elements that nonetheless perform the claimed function.

name: Definition of 'equivalent' in §112, 6th paragraph
description: An 'equivalent' is generally interpreted as embracing more than the specific elements described in the specification for performing the specified function, but less than any element that performs the function specified in the claim.
guidance: The scope of equivalents depends on how the element is described in the supporting specification; the claim may or may not be limited to particular structure, material or acts depending on the specification's treatment. If the disclosure is so broad as to encompass any and all structures for the function, the limitation may effectively cover any element performing that function; conversely, a disclosure limited to a specific structure may constrict claim scope to the disclosed embodiments.

name: Weigh indicia; do not accept bare statements of non-equivalence
description: In determining whether arguments or Rule 132 evidence are persuasive, the examiner should consider and weigh as many indicia as are presented and determine whether, on balance, the applicant has met the burden of proof to show non-equivalence.
guidance: Under no circumstance should an examiner accept as persuasive a bare statement or opinion that the prior art element is not an equivalent embraced by the claim limitation.

name: Prevent improper narrowing by applicant without specification support
description: If applicant argues that 'means' or 'step' plus function language is limited to certain specific structural or additional functional characteristics where the specification does not describe the invention as being only those characteristics, the claim should not be allowed until amended.
guidance: Applicant must amend the claim to recite those specific structural or additional functional characteristics if they want the claim limited accordingly; otherwise claim allowance would provide inadequate public notice of true scope.

name: Amendment options to overcome rejections
description: Applicant may amend the claim by further limiting the function so there is no longer identity of function with prior art, or may replace the claimed means-plus-function limitation with specific structure, material or acts not described in the prior art.
guidance: Amendments are an available avenue during prosecution to meet statutory criteria for patentability.

name: Related §112, first and second paragraph rejections when no corresponding structure
description: If a means or step-plus-function limitation is not supported by corresponding structure, material or acts in the specification disclosure, consider rejections under: (1) §112, first paragraph (not enabled), (2) §112, second paragraph (indefinite), and (3) §102 or §103 where the prior art anticipates or renders obvious the claimed subject matter.
guidance: Theory: without corresponding structure in the specification to limit the limitation, an equivalent could be any element that performs the specified function. Note that block diagrams that describe function but not structure are not fatal under enablement if structure is conventional and determinable without undue experimentation.

name: Distinguish §112,6th 'equivalents' from doctrine of equivalents
description: An 'equivalent' for §112, 6th paragraph should not be confused with the doctrine of equivalents (DOE).
guidance: §112,6th limits the scope of means-or-step-plus-function language to structures, materials and acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof for claim construction during examination. DOE is an equitable doctrine applied in infringement litigation to expand exclusive rights beyond literal claim scope; DOE decisions should not unduly influence ex parte examination under §112,6th.

name: Statutory rule — 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
description: An element in a claim may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without recital of structure, material, or acts, and such a claim is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
guidance: If a claim limitation is held to invoke §112(f), the claim is limited to the structure (and equivalents) actually disclosed in the specification; function-only claiming therefore risks narrowing claim scope to examples in the disclosure.

name: Determination standard — whether a POSITA would understand the term as a name for structure
description: The key test is 'whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure' (Williamson).
guidance: In litigation, expert declarations/testimony about what a POSITA would understand can be decisive in whether §112(f) applies.

name: Avoid coinage / nonce words; use inventor/industry terminology
description: Many §112(f) problems arise when practitioners coin generic terms instead of using the names that the inventor or the industry uses for components.
guidance: Ask the inventor what the industry calls the component and use that terminology in claims to reduce the risk that courts will treat the term as a non-structural placeholder.

name: Avoid purely functional language; include structural detail
description: Purely functional recitations (statements of what something does without structural context) increase the risk of means-plus-function interpretation.
guidance: Each claim paragraph should do more than describe what something does — it should recite structure, connections, components, or location as appropriate.

name: Include structural language immediately after introducing a claim element
description: After introducing an element, describe what the element looks like, what it is connected to, what its components are, and/or where it is located so the element reads as structural rather than purely functional.
guidance: Examples given: 'a fluid conduit extending between an inlet end that is connected to a water source and an outlet end that is connected to the water cannon' or 'a pipe, hose, or tube connected to the water cannon to define a water supply passage.' These phrasings avoid means-plus-function treatment while covering varied embodiments.

name: Draft multiple independent claims reciting different variations
description: When uncertain whether a wording might invoke §112(f), draft multiple independent claims that recite different variations of the limitation (functional and structural variants).
guidance: This hedge increases the chance that at least some claims will be interpreted as structural and not limited to disclosed structures.

name: Consequences illustrated by practical example (water cannon / fluid delivery)
description: A claim reciting 'a fluid delivery system for supplying water to the water cannon' may be treated as means-plus-function and limited to the corrugated hose disclosed in the specification (and equivalents), whereas reciting 'a fluid conduit' or explicitly 'pipe, hose, or tube' is less likely to invoke §112(f).
guidance: Use concrete drafting alternatives that recite structure and connections; the example demonstrates how an apparently broad term can be narrowed by §112(f) unless structural language is included.

name: Courts' inconsistent application and case law examples
description: Courts have differed in treatment of the same or similar terms across cases (e.g., some treat 'system' as a nonce word invoking §112(f), others may not). Relevant cases and authorities include Greenberg, Williamson, DYFAN v. Target, TEK Global, and cited MPEP guidance.
guidance: Because judicial outcomes vary, practitioners should (1) prefer structural wording, (2) document how a POSITA would understand terms (inventor statements, expert input), and (3) consider claim drafting redundancy to survive diverse interpretations.

name: Timing of RCE filings relative to appeals and civil actions
description: An RCE may be filed after a decision by the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences but before filing a Notice of Appeal to the Federal Circuit or the commencement of a civil action; RCE practice is not available after the filing of a Notice of Appeal or commencement of a civil action unless the appeal/civil action is terminated and the application is still pending.
guidance: If an RCE is filed in an application that has undergone court review, the examiner should bring the application to the attention of the supervisory patent examiner or special program examiner to determine propriety. Termination of an unsuccessful appeal or civil action generally results in abandonment unless claims were allowed or the court's mandate directs further Office action.

name: Fee rules and patent term adjustment effects for CPA/URAA/RCE
description: The Office sets the RCE fee at an amount equal to the basic filing fee of a utility application (small entity reduction available); RCE fee need not include excess claims fees previously paid. Filing an RCE on or after May 29, 2000 will not cause an application to be entitled to patent term adjustment provisions of the AIPA; filing an RCE cuts off the applicant's ability to accumulate additional patent term adjustment against the three‑year pendency provision.
guidance: CPA and URAA fee rules and patent term adjustment entitlements differ: CPA fees must be statutory filing fee (basic filing fee plus excess claim fees) and CPA filed on/after May 29, 2000 is entitled to patent term adjustment provisions under the AIPA in specified circumstances.

name: Completeness of examiner's action and scope limitation
description: An examiner's action will be complete as to all matters, except that in appropriate circumstances (e.g., misjoinder of invention, fundamental defects) the action may be limited to such matters before further action is made. Matters of form need not be raised until a claim is found allowable.
guidance: Limitations on scope should be applied only in appropriate circumstances; supervisory review is expected in protracted prosecutions.

name: Rejecting claims: cite best references and explain pertinence
description: If the invention is not considered patentable, the claims considered unpatentable will be rejected. In rejecting claims for want of novelty or for obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references at his or her command and, when a reference is complex or shows inventions other than that claimed, designate the particular part relied on as nearly as practicable. The pertinence of each reference, if not apparent, must be clearly explained and each rejected claim specified (37 CFR 1.104(c)(2)).
guidance: When rejecting under 35 U.S.C. 103, the way in which a reference is modified or plural references are combined should be set out. Include particular figures/pages/paragraphs when necessary to inform applicant of the basis for rejection.

name: Reliance on admissions and Office employee knowledge
description: In rejecting claims the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant (or patent owner in reexamination) as to any matter affecting patentability and may rely upon facts within his or her knowledge under certain regulatory provisions.
guidance: When a rejection is based on facts within the personal knowledge of an Office employee, the data shall be as specific as possible and the reference must be supported, when called for by the applicant, by the affidavit of such employee; such affidavit is subject to contradiction or explanation by applicant affidavits.

name: Reasons for allowance: documenting examiner rationale
description: If the examiner believes the record of the prosecution does not make clear his or her reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning; the reasons shall be incorporated into an Office action rejecting other claims or be the subject of a separate communication. The applicant may file a statement commenting on the reasons for allowance within a specified time.
guidance: Failure by the examiner to respond to any statement commenting on reasons for allowance does not give rise to any implication.

name: Search practice regarding filing dates and patent term consequences
description: Examiners should search all applications based on the actual U.S. filing date of the application rather than on the filing date of any parent U.S. application for which benefit is claimed, because the 20-year patent term is measured from the earliest U.S. filing date for which benefit is claimed (Public Law 103-465 changes).
guidance: Cite material prior art having an effective filing date after the filing date of the U.S. parent application but before the actual filing date of the application being examined.

name: Statutory requirement: claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(b) / pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
description: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph requires that a patent application specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
guidance: Note that although pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph uses the phrase 'which applicant regards as his invention,' pre-AIA 37 CFR 1.41(a) provides that a patent is applied for in the name or names of the actual inventor or inventors.

name: Definiteness requirement of claim language
description: In patent examining parlance, the claim language must be 'definite' to comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph). Conversely, a claim that does not comply with this requirement is 'indefinite.'
guidance: The primary purpose of this requirement is to ensure that the scope of the claims is clear so the public is informed of the boundaries of what constitutes infringement of the patent. It is of utmost importance that patents issue with definite claims that clearly and precisely inform persons skilled in the art of the boundaries of protected subject matter.

name: Primary purpose: clear public notice of claim boundaries (infringement)
description: The primary purpose of the definiteness requirement is to ensure that the scope of the claims is clear so the public is informed of the boundaries of what constitutes infringement of the patent.
guidance: Optimizing patent quality by providing clear notice to the public of the boundaries of the inventive subject matter protected by a patent grant fosters innovation and competitiveness. Issuing patents with clear and definite claim language is a key component to enhancing the quality of patents and raising confidence in the patent process.

name: Secondary purpose: measure of what inventor regards as the invention (assessing patentability and written description)
description: A secondary purpose is to provide a clear measure of what the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention so that it can be determined whether the claimed invention meets all the criteria for patentability and whether the specification meets the criteria of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph with respect to the claimed invention.

name: Indefiniteness rejection requirement
description: Claims that do not meet the definiteness standard must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph) as indefinite.
guidance: Such a rejection requires that the applicant respond by explaining why the language is definite or by amending the claim, thus making the record clear regarding the claim boundaries prior to issuance.

name: Examiner obligation when making an indefiniteness rejection (identify language and explain reasoning)
description: An indefiniteness rejection must clearly identify the language that causes the claim to be indefinite and thoroughly explain the reasoning for the rejection.
guidance: Because an indefiniteness rejection requires the applicant to respond by explaining why the language is definite or by amending the claim, such rejections must make the record clear regarding the claim boundaries prior to issuance.

name: Oath/declaration must identify the application and affirm review
description: The oath or declaration must identify the application to which it is directed and state that the person making it has reviewed and understands the contents of the application, including the claims, as amended by any amendment specifically referred to in the oath or declaration.
guidance: This requirement appears in §1.63(b)(1)-(2) and ensures the signer is aware of the application content being attested.

name: Specification — improvements and scope of description
description: In the case of an improvement, the specification must particularly point out the part(s) of the subject matter to which the improvement relates and the description should be confined to the specific improvement and parts that necessarily cooperate with it or are necessary to a complete understanding.
guidance: This limits the required descriptive scope when claiming an improvement (§1.71(c)).

name: Specification formatting — separate sheet and exclusion of other parts
description: The specification must commence on a separate sheet. Each sheet including part of the specification may not include other parts of the application; the claim(s), abstract, and 'Sequence Listing' (if required) should not be included on a sheet including any other part of the application.
guidance: Formatting requirement per §1.71(f).

name: Abstract requirements (§1.72)
description: A brief abstract of the technical disclosure must commence on a separate sheet (preferably following the claims) under the heading 'Abstract' and must be as concise as disclosure permits, preferably not exceeding 150 words. Purpose: enable quick, cursory determination of the nature and gist of the technical disclosure.
guidance: Abstract sheets may not include other parts of the application (§1.72(b)).

name: Summary of the invention (§1.73)
description: A brief summary indicating the nature and substance of the invention, which may include a statement of the object of the invention, should precede the detailed description; it should be commensurate with the invention as claimed.
guidance: Any object recited should be that of the invention as claimed.

name: Claims — general requirement to particularly and distinctly claim (§1.75(a))
description: The specification must conclude with a claim particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention or discovery.
guidance: Fundamental statutory/formal requirement for claims placement and clarity.

name: Dependent claims and multiple dependent claim rules
description: Dependent claims may refer back to and further limit another claim; multiple dependent claims must refer to other claims in the alternative only and may not serve as a basis for another multiple dependent claim. For fee calculation, a multiple dependent claim is considered to be the number of claims to which direct reference is made, and any claim depending from a multiple dependent claim is considered to be that number of claims to which direct reference is made.
guidance: Original applications filed with or amended to include multiple dependent claims must include the fee set forth in §1.16(j). Dependent claims are construed to include all limitations of the claim incorporated by reference (§1.75(c)).

name: Claim drafting order for improvements
description: Where the nature of the case admits (e.g., improvement), an independent claim should contain: (1) a preamble of general description of conventional/known elements; (2) a phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises,' and (3) those elements/steps/relationships constituting the new or improved portion.
guidance: Suggested structure to clearly separate known elements from the improvement (§1.75(e)).

name: Claim numbering, order, and grouping
description: Claims shall be numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals; the least restrictive claim should be presented as claim number 1, and dependent claims should be grouped together with the claim(s) to which they refer to the extent practicable.
guidance: Organizational requirement to improve clarity and prosecution practice (§1.75(f)-(g)).

name: Claims formatting — separate sheet and element separation
description: Claims must commence on a separate physical sheet or electronic page; any sheet including a claim may not contain other parts of the application. Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step should be separated by a line indentation.
guidance: Formatting rules intended to make claims clear and machine-processable (§1.75(h)-(i)).

name: ADS — domestic benefit information
description: ADS must include domestic benefit information: application number, filing date, status (including patent number if available), and relationship of each application for which a benefit is claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) (§1.76(b)(5)).
guidance: Providing this in ADS constitutes the specific reference required by statute and §1.78.

name: Procedural/abstract steps contribute to technical character only if they serve a technical purpose; simulations can be technical if essential to production
description: A procedural step may contribute to the technical character of a claimed method only to the extent that it serves a technical purpose of the method. Simulation methods which form an essential part of the fabrication process and precede actual production, mostly as an intermediate step, cannot be denied a technical effect merely on the grounds that they do not yet incorporate the physical end product. (T 1227/05 / Schaltkreissimulation I / Infineon Technologies)
guidance: Evaluate whether the step or simulation serves a concrete technical purpose in a technical process (e.g., fabrication), not merely abstract modelling; being essential to a technical workflow supports technical character.

name: Contents of an international application (filing elements)
description: Filing includes a 'request' together with a description, one or more claims, one or more drawings (where required) and an abstract.
guidance: The 'request' must include certain data such as applicant, inventor, any agent and formal details like title and priority claims.

name: Written opinion primary and secondary objectives
description: The written opinion formulates a preliminary and non‑binding opinion on whether the claimed invention appears to be novel, to involve an inventive step and to be industrially applicable. Secondarily it identifies defects in form or contents and significant issues of clarity or support.
guidance: The written opinion should be produced according to the same criteria used in international preliminary examination.

name: On‑sale bar general rule (definition)
description: An impermissible sale occurs if there was a definite sale, or offer to sell, more than 1 year before the effective filing date and the subject matter of the sale/offer fully anticipated the claimed invention or would have rendered it obvious (Ferag; Pfaff).
guidance: Apply traditional contract law principles (look to UCC) to determine whether a commercial offer for sale occurred. Pfaff two‑prong test: (1) product is the subject of a commercial offer for sale not primarily for experimental purposes; and (2) the invention is ready for patenting. See Linear Tech., Group One, etc.

name: The invention must be 'ready for patenting' (Pfaff second prong)
description: The on‑sale bar applies when (1) a commercial offer for sale exists and (2) the invention is 'ready for patenting'—satisfied by reduction to practice before the critical date or by drawings/descriptions sufficiently specific to enable one skilled in the art to practice the invention.
guidance: Ready for patenting may be shown by detailed drawings/specifications used to produce the product (Invitrogen, Weatherchem). A product offered that inherently possesses each claim limitation triggers the bar even if parties did not recognize it (Abbott Labs, STX). Actual reduction to practice normally requires testing under working conditions demonstrating practical utility. 'Ready for patenting' does not require readiness for satisfactory commercial marketing.

name: Evidence standards / objective evidence of sale or offer
description: In determining if a sale/offer occurred, key question: did the inventor sell or offer for sale a product embodying the claimed invention? Objective evidence (contracts, correspondence, memoranda, drawings, abstracts) controls over uncommunicated seller intent.
guidance: Use objective documentation—orders, confirmations, abstracts identifying vendor and release/installation dates, descriptions, warranties, price terms—to establish a sale/offer. An order acknowledgement or order confirmation containing material terms prior to the critical date can trigger the on‑sale bar even if later delivery or payment occurred after the critical date (Weatherchem, Ferag).

name: Intent and notice in experimental scenarios
description: An inventor's secretly held subjective intent to experiment is insufficient when sales occur in an ordinary commercial environment unless objective evidence supports the claim; customers should be made aware of experimentation.
guidance: Where sales are made to ordinary customers and goods are placed outside the inventor's control, objective evidence (disclosures to purchasers, testing records, contemporaneous experimental documentation) is required to rebut a statutory bar. Secret claims of non‑durability or that units are for testing without customer notice are generally unavailing (LaBounty, Paragon).

name: Completeness of the invention and end of experimental use
description: Experimental use ends when the invention is actually reduced to practice; experimental use 'means perfecting or completing an invention to the point of determining that it will work for its intended purpose.'
guidance: If evidence shows the inventor considered the invention 'complete' prior to the critical date, awaiting external approvals (e.g., Underwriters' Laboratories) will not ordinarily overcome that conclusion. Lack of resulting modifications from alleged experimental activity is evidence (though not conclusive) that the activity was not experimental. Any modifications resulting from experimentation must be features of the claimed invention to be probative.

name: Consider the Express Teachings
description: If the prior art reference expressly teaches a particular reason to select the claimed species or subgenus, Office personnel should point out the express disclosure and explain why it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill to select the claimed invention.
guidance: Look for explicit statements such as recognized equivalence or co-administration examples (e.g., Merck & Co. v. Biocraft). If one reference specifically refers to another (In re Kemps), explain how the express teaching provides motivation to select the species/subgenus.

name: Make Express Fact-Findings and Determine Whether They Support a Prima Facie Case
description: Based on the whole evidence, make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors, focusing primarily on the prior-art teachings discussed, and specifically articulate what teachings or suggestions in the prior art would have motivated selection of the claimed species or subgenus.
guidance: Fact-findings should state which teachings/suggestions provide motivation and then determine whether, considered as a whole, they support a prima facie case of obviousness. Cite In re Bell, In re Kulling, Panduit. Explicitly tie teachings to the motivation/suggestion analysis.

name: Presence or Absence of Prior-Art Suggestion of Method of Making May Be Relevant
description: The presence—or absence—of a suitably operative, obvious process for making a composition may bear on whether that composition is obvious; absence of a known/obvious method to make a compound may overcome presumption of obviousness.
guidance: If prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making the claimed compound at the time of invention, the compound may not be in the public possession (Hoeksema, Maloney). Consider whether a disclosed method for a related compound would enable production of the claimed compound; methodology can be proper in rejecting product claims, depending on facts (Goldgaber, Payne).

name: If Prior-Art Compounds Have No Utility or Only as Intermediates, They May Not Render Claim Prima Facie Obvious
description: If the prior art does not teach any specific or significant utility for disclosed compounds, or discloses them only as intermediates, the prior art is unlikely to render structurally similar claims prima facie obvious absent a reason an ordinary artisan would make or investigate such compounds.
guidance: Assess whether prior-art compounds had recognized useful properties or were merely intermediates; if intermediates, an artisan would not ordinarily stop synthesis to investigate utility (Stemniski, Albrecht, Lalu).

name: Consideration of Applicant’s Rebuttal Arguments and Evidence
description: If a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut with arguments and/or evidence (specification, affidavits/declarations, counsel submissions), but arguments of counsel cannot substitute for factually supported objective evidence.
guidance: Consider all rebuttal evidence, including secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others), declarations from skilled artisans, evidence of copying, state of the art, level of skill, and methods of making. Require nexus between the evidence and the claimed invention for substantial weight; evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention. Examiners should weigh proffered evidence and avoid giving evidence no weight without reason (Soni, Piasecki, Beattie, GPAC, Huang, Kulling, Grasselli, Chupp, Hoeksema).

name: Infringement analysis based on claim scope (Article 41 LPI)
description: To determine infringement, verify whether the accused product/process has all the characteristics of a patent's independent claims; independent claims define essential characteristics and dependent claims help interpret terms.
guidance: Dependent claims don't limit scope but clarify terms; use dependent claims to detect infringement and see if infringement extends to narrower dependent claim terms.

name: Direct (literal) infringement (Article 42 LPI)
description: Direct or literal infringement occurs when each element of the infringing product coincides with the definition contained in the claim. Patent holder may prevent third parties from producing, using, selling, importing, etc., the patented product or processes.
guidance: Interpretation of claim expressions may be needed; once meaning established, correspondence is immediate. Protection covers both product and 'process or product obtained directly through a patented process'.

name: Infringement by equivalence
description: Infringement by equivalence is non-literal: an element of an accused product does not fall under the literal claim definition but is a technical equivalent of it.
guidance: Equivalence may be direct (extend claim scope) or inverse (restrict claim scope). Limitations include non-extension to subject matter within the state of the art and not recovering protection surrendered during prosecution. Jurists suggest interpreting claims by considering legal meaning, specifications, state of the art, prosecution history, and technical field meanings.

name: Amend disclosure to correct inaccuracies
description: The disclosure must be amended, when required by the Office, to correct inaccuracies of description and definition, and to secure substantial correspondence between the claims, the remainder of the specification, and the drawings.

name: Reissue enlargement time limit and new matter prohibition
description: No reissue patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent, pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 251. No amendment to the patent may introduce new matter or be made in an expired patent.

name: Amendments reference basis for reissue
description: All amendments must be made relative to the patent specification, including the claims, and drawings, which is in effect as of the date of filing of the reissue application.

name: Meaning of 'brackets' in claim amendments
description: The term 'brackets' set forth in 37 CFR 1.121(a) means square brackets, thus: [ ]. It does not encompass and is to be distinguished from parentheses ().
guidance: Any amendment using parentheses to indicate canceled matter in a claim rewritten under 37 CFR 1.121(a) may be held not fully responsive.

name: Exact instructions for insertions/deletions (37 CFR 1.121)
description: A claim may be amended by specifying only the exact matter to be deleted or inserted by an amendment and the precise point where the deletion or insertion is to be made, where the changes are limited to deletions and/or the addition of no more than five (5) words in any one claim.
guidance: If more than five words are added in at least one claim the amendment will not be entered; applicant is given one month (30 days) to supply an amendment in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121 (extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) may be granted).

name: Situations where 37 CFR 1.131 is inappropriate
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is not appropriate in many situations, including: (A) reference publication date more than 1 year prior (statutory bar 35 U.S.C. 102(b)); (B) reference U.S. patent claims the same patentable invention; (C) reference is a foreign patent to applicant issued prior to domestic filing from an application filed >12 months earlier (35 U.S.C. 102(d)); (D) applicant's parent/PCT effective filing date is prior to the reference date; (E) prior U.S. patent to same entity claiming same invention (double patenting); (F) disclosure of prior U.S. patent to same party not copending (dedication); (G) applicant has clearly admitted subject matter is prior art; (H) subject matter is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f); (I) subject matter is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(g); (J) lost count in an interference where doctrines bar use.
guidance: See cited MPEP sections and case law for specifics; 37 CFR 1.131 cannot overcome statutory bars or some 102(g) situations because those establish actual prior invention by others.

name: Furnishing PCT Article 19 claim amendments by 30 months
description: A copy of any amendments to the claims made under PCT Article 19, and a translation of those amendments into English, if they were made in another language, must be furnished not later than the expiration of thirty months from the priority date. Amendments under PCT Article 19 which are not received by the expiration of thirty months will be considered canceled.
guidance: Timely submission of Article 19 amendments and translations is required to preserve those amendments in the U.S. national stage.

name: Content and form requirements for an oath/declaration (pre-AIA wording)
description: An oath or declaration must: (1) be executed in accordance with §§ 1.66 or 1.68; (2) identify the specification to which it is directed; (3) identify each inventor and the country of citizenship of each inventor; and (4) state that the person making the oath or declaration believes the named inventor(s) to be the original and first inventor(s) of the subject matter claimed.
guidance: All actual inventors must make the oath except as provided in §§ 1.42, 1.43 or 1.47. If a non-inventor signs, the relationship and the facts 'upon information and belief' must be stated; legal representatives must state status and contact info.

name: What may be submitted to patent file under § 1.501 (citations and written statements)
description: At any time during the period of enforceability of a patent, any person may file a written submission with the Office directed to: (1) prior art patents or printed publications believed to have a bearing on patentability of any claim; or (2) statements of the patent owner filed by the patent owner in a proceeding before a Federal court or the Office in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim of the patent.
guidance: Submissions under (2) must be accompanied by other documents/evidence and submitted in redacted form to exclude protected information. Submissions may be anonymous if identity is to be excluded.

name: Contents required in a request for ex parte reexamination
description: Any request for ex parte reexamination must include: (1) a statement pointing out each substantial new question of patentability based on prior patents and printed publications; (2) identification of every claim for which reexamination is requested and a detailed explanation of the pertinency and manner of applying the cited prior art to every claim; (3) a copy of every patent or printed publication relied upon (with English translations of necessary parts); (4) a copy of the entire patent including front face, drawings, and specification/claims (double column format); (5) a certification that a copy of the request was served on the patent owner; and (6) a certification that statutory estoppel provisions do not prohibit the requester from filing the ex parte reexamination request.
guidance: The request must be accompanied by the fee set in § 1.20(c)(1). If incomplete, the requester will be notified and given opportunity to complete; failure results in no filing date and placement of the material in the file as a citation if it complies with § 1.501.

name: Examiner determination standard for ex parte reexamination requests
description: Within three months following the filing date of a request for ex parte reexamination, an examiner will consider the request and determine whether or not a 'substantial new question of patentability' affecting any claim of the patent is raised by the request and the prior art cited therein, with or without consideration of other patents or printed publications. A statement and any accompanying information submitted pursuant to § 1.501(a)(2) will not be considered by the examiner when making a determination on the request.
guidance: Determination is based on the claims in effect at the time; notice of the determination is mailed to patent owner and requester. Where no SNQ is found, a portion of the fee is refunded.

name: Patent owner statement timing and content in ex parte reexamination
description: Except as provided in § 1.510(e), no statement or other response by the patent owner shall be filed prior to the determinations made in accordance with § 1.515 or § 1.520. The order for ex parte reexamination will set a period of not less than two months from the date of the order within which the patent owner may file a statement on the new question of patentability, including any proposed amendments. Any statement shall clearly point out why the subject matter as claimed is not anticipated or rendered obvious by the prior art patents or printed publications.
guidance: Premature statements will not be considered and may be returned or discarded. If a third party requester exists, the patent owner’s statement must be served on the requester in accordance with § 1.248.

name: Requirements and formalities for proposed amendments in reexamination
description: A proposed amendment is made by filing a paper directing specified changes to the patent specification (including claims) or drawings. Changes to the specification (other than claims and certain appendices) must be made by submission of the entire text of an added or rewritten paragraph (identify precise point). Changes to claims must include the entire text of each claim being changed and each new claim; parenthetical 'amended', 'twice amended' etc.; markings per paragraph (f). Drawings changes submitted as a sketch showing proposed changes in red for examiner approval; amended figures identified as 'Amended', new as 'New', canceled figures bracketed and 'Canceled.' Formal requirements are in § 1.52.
guidance: Also: status of all claims as of amendment date and explanation of support in disclosure must be supplied on separate pages. 'Large Tables', program listings, sequence listings have their own rule references for changes.

name: Claim numbering and scope limitations during reexamination
description: Patent claims may not be renumbered; numbering of any claims added must follow the highest numbered patent claim. No amendment may enlarge the scope of the claims of the patent or introduce new matter. No amendment may be proposed for entry in an expired patent. Also, amendments are not effective until the reexamination certificate is issued and published.
guidance: Ensure proposed claim changes narrow or cancel claims, do not add new matter, and respect expiration limits; proposed amendments are treated as though entered during prosecution but become effective only upon issuance of certificate.

name: Continuation patents and terminal disclaimers enabling duplicative protection
description: U.S. continuation practice and the use of terminal disclaimers allow applicants to file slightly different-claimed patents repeatedly, effectively duplicating coverage and helping produce a patent thicket.
guidance: The USPTO permits this maneuver (terminal disclaimers) to link continuations to a common expiry; this duplicative strategy is unique to the U.S. and is disallowed as 'double patenting' in many other countries, enabling U.S. patent portfolio expansion post-approval.

name: Triage Toward High-Stakes Patents
description: Effective examination should concentrate scrutiny on patents most likely to be commercially valuable (e.g., pharmaceutical compositions, claims drafted with broad commercial reach). Ex post mechanisms (post-grant review, IPR) should bear the validity-determination burden for the rest.
guidance: Prioritize examination resources on patents where validity will have large social/commercial consequences; accept that exhaustive ex ante examination for every patent is socially wasteful. Use applicant election (fee/track) or triage criteria to allocate 'gold-plated' examination.

name: Disclosure-Based Quality
description: Even patents that will never be litigated must serve the disclosure function: examiner quality work includes ensuring claims are clearly tied to specification disclosure even when validity will not be tested.
guidance: Check that claim scope corresponds to the specification; look for written-description and enablement support. Examiner should reject or require amendment where claims reach beyond described embodiments.

name: Notice Quality
description: Claims must be clear enough that a competitor reading the patent can determine its scope without litigation. Failure of notice (vague boundaries, functional language untethered to structure) is a quality defect even if the patent is never enforced.
guidance: Evaluate claim clarity and boundaries; avoid untethered functional claiming. Prefer claim language that a POSITA can interpret without resort to costly litigation; use 112 doctrine to police indefiniteness and functional breadth.

name: First-action allowances of broad genus claims without examiner-cited art (marker of low-quality)
description: Allowing broad genus claims at first action without the examiner citing relevant prior art is a sign of poor examination.
guidance: Broad genus/claiming should trigger independent search and substantive rejections if art exists; absence of examiner-cited art for broad claims is an anti-pattern.

name: Allowance of claims using functional language without 112(f) treatment or written description support (marker of low-quality)
description: Permitting functional claim language that lacks proper 112(f) structure or written-description support indicates poor scrutiny of claim scope.
guidance: Apply 35 U.S.C. §112 standards: require corresponding structure, material, or acts for functional claiming, or treat such claims under 112(f)/means-plus-function rules. Reject or require narrowing where written description is missing.

name: Examiner-initiated claim amendments that narrow overbroad terms (marker of high-quality examination)
description: When examiners propose or require claim amendments that narrow overbroad claim language, it demonstrates active policing of claim scope.
guidance: Look for examiner-driven narrowing amendments during prosecution; this is evidence of quality work to align claims with patentability and disclosure.

name: Substantive 112 rejections rather than purely 102/103 (marker of high-quality examination)
description: Issuing substantive written-description, enablement, or indefiniteness rejections shows attention to disclosure and claim clarity beyond obviousness/novelty questions.
guidance: Prioritize 112 issues where claims appear untethered to the specification; substantive 112 activity indicates careful review of the disclosure function.

name: Final claim language that maps clearly onto specification disclosure (marker of high-quality examination)
description: High-quality examination yields issued claims whose language corresponds clearly to the patent specification and disclosed embodiments.
guidance: Assess issued claims for a clear mapping to specification terms and embodiments; absence of mapping indicates weaker quality.

name: Enablement (critical quality dimension for issued patents)
description: A POSITA could practice the full claim scope from the disclosure.
guidance: Evaluate whether the specification teaches how to make and use the full claimed invention across its full scope. Lack of enablement supports invalidity or narrowing.

name: Written Description (critical quality dimension for issued patents)
description: The applicant possessed the full claim scope at filing.
guidance: Check for demonstrable possession of claimed subject matter in the application as filed; claims that extend beyond the original disclosure should be scrutinized or rejected.

name: Notice (critical quality dimension for issued patents)
description: Claim boundaries are knowable without expensive claim-construction litigation.
guidance: Assess claims for definiteness and clarity from the perspective of competitors and POSITA. Ambiguous claim scope undermines the notice function of patents.

name: Claims clearly tied to specification disclosure (operative test question)
description: Are the final claims clearly tied to specification disclosure?
guidance: Examine claim language vs. specification to confirm a clear mapping; lack of mapping suggests weak examination.

name: Employer obligations for foreign patent applications upon worker's request
description: Upon the worker’s request; the employer shall be obliged to give their rights on the invention for the foreign countries in which they do not wish to obtain a patent; and to provide the worker with conditions for making an application to claim a patent in such countries. Releasing the invention shall be made in a reasonable time period in terms of keeping within time period of priority right.
guidance: Employer may reserve a non-monopolized right of tenancy (for a proper/decided fee) to continue using the invention in those foreign countries and may claim protection for interests generated from this reserved right.

name: Application of workers' invention provisions to higher education institutions
description: Provisions regarding workers’ inventions apply to inventions made as a consequence of scientific studies and research conducted in higher education institutions defined by the Law numbered 2547 and certain military/defense higher education institutions, without prejudice to special law/regulations.
guidance: Inventor must notify the higher education institution in writing without delay; if a patent application is filed, the institution must be notified. If the institution claims rights, it must file a patent application, otherwise the invention becomes an independent invention. The inventor may object; institution must specify written grounds or invention becomes independent. Articles 115, 116, 118 and para 4 of 119 do not apply to inventions made in HEIs. If institution renounces application or patent right it must first offer inventor takeover; if inventor accepts rights are transferred and documents delivered; HEI may reserve a non-monopolized tenancy for a decent fee. HEI must cover inventor losses caused by its fault. Revenue sharing: at least one third of revenue paid to inventor; institution’s share recorded as equity revenue and used for institutional research needs. Specific procedures determined by regulation.

name: Rules for inventions generated in state-supported projects
description: Inventions generated in projects supported by State institutions must be notified to the supporting institution per regulation. Within one year of notification, the beneficiary must notify the supporting public institution in writing of their decision on claiming right ownership; if not, the supporting institution may take over rights.
guidance: Beneficiary cannot make statements affecting patent/utility model until ownership process concludes. If beneficiary claims ownership they must file a patent application naming the supporting institution. The state institution may demand confidential commercial/financial updates and keep them private. Revenue-sharing form determined by agreement. State institution obtains a license at no charge for its own needs (renouncing this right only if specified in agreement). State institution may claim use or require third-party licensing in reasonable conditions if: (a) beneficiary does not use per Article 130; (b) product cannot cover public health or national security needs in other countries; (c) product cannot cover needs of the state institution. These license practices do not affect compulsory license provisions. Exceptions apply to certain R&D centers and technology development areas and to non-project-based state supports.

name: Confidential (classified) patent procedure for national security
description: If Office believes an application matters for national security it sends a copy to the Ministry of National Defense for opinion and notifies applicant. If Ministry decides confidentiality it must notify Office within three months; otherwise Office proceeds with normal processing.
guidance: If classified, Office registers application as a classified patent application and suspends other processing. Applicant cannot declare the invention to unauthorized parties. Ministry of National Defense may permit partial or full use of the invention. Applicant may claim compensation from the government for the classified period; if no agreement, court determines allowance considering invention significance and expected revenue. Annual fees are not payable while application remains classified. Office may declassify upon Ministry request; declassified application is processed from declassification date. If an invention made in Turkey concerns national security, no foreign patent application allowed without Ministry permission. Inventor domicile in Turkey is presumed until proven otherwise.

name: Liability for unauthorized transfers and malicious behavior in assignments/licensing
description: If it later emerges that the transferor of patent application/patent rights or the licensor was not authorized to make the transaction, that person is answerable to those concerned.
guidance: If application is withdrawn, rejected, or patent nullity declared and parties failed to prescribe broader responsibility in contract, Article 139 applies. Transferor/licensor acting maliciously are always responsible. Failure to inform the other party of documents/reports in Turkish or a foreign language related to preservability of the application or invention or omission to include such documents in the contract may be accepted as malicious intent. Time to claim compensation under this article begins on the finalization date of the court decision that the obligations case is based on.

name: Time for filing certified copy (37 CFR 1.55(f))
description: For an original application under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) filed on or after March 16, 2013, a certified copy of the foreign application must be filed within the later of four months from the actual filing date of the (U.S.) application or sixteen months from the filing date of the prior foreign application. For international applications entering the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371, the certified copy must be filed within the time limits set forth by the PCT, with specific later-of periods if not filed during the international stage.
guidance: The time period does not apply to design applications. If a certified copy is not filed within these periods and none of the exceptions apply (see 37 CFR 1.55(h),(i),(j)), the certified copy must be accompanied by a petition showing good and sufficient cause and the petition fee per § 1.17(g). If certified copy is filed after payment of the issue fee the patent will not include the priority claim unless corrected by a certificate of correction (35 U.S.C. 255; 37 CFR 1.323).

name: Interim copy permitted to satisfy timeliness (37 CFR 1.55(j))
description: An ‘interim copy’ of the original foreign application, clearly labeled 'Interim Copy', including specification and any drawings or claims, together with a separate cover sheet identifying the foreign application (application number, country, day, month, year) and stating the copy is a true copy as filed, may be filed to satisfy the time requirement.
guidance: The interim copy and cover sheet must be filed within the later of sixteen months from the prior foreign filing or four months from the U.S. filing (or corresponding national stage dates) or with an appropriate petition. A certified copy still must be filed within the period specified in 37 CFR 1.55(g)(1) (unless accompanied by an appropriate petition).

name: Required contents and labeling of interim copy
