description: The interim copy must be clearly labeled as 'Interim Copy,' include the specification and any drawings or claims upon which it is based, and be accompanied by a separate cover sheet identifying the foreign application by application number, country (or IP authority), day, month, and year of filing, and stating that the copy filed is a true copy of the original foreign application as filed.
guidance: When filing via USPTO electronic filing, applicants should select the document description 'Interim Copy of the Foreign Priority Application' to index the document. Parts submitted only as plain text (.txt) should be filed as text files and indexed appropriately ('Interim Copy of the Foreign Priority (text file)'). XML parts (e.g., ST.26 sequence listings) may be filed on a read-only optical disc as part of the interim copy. See MPEP § 502.05 and related sections for electronic filing details.

name: Accepted file formats and indexing for interim copy
description: If not provided as a single paper document, the main parts of an interim copy (Abstract, Drawings, Specification, Claims, sequence listings, large tables, program listings) may be filed as a single PDF image file via USPTO electronic filing, or as .txt for plain text parts, or as XML on a read-only optical disc for XML parts.
guidance: When filing online, select the appropriate document description to index each part. The PDF image file will be stored in the file wrapper and must be indexed as 'Interim Copy of the Foreign Priority Application' (or appropriate text/XML description).

name: Examiners' review of priority papers and entitlement to priority
description: When the claim and certified copy are received while the application is pending before the examiner, the examiner generally only checks for obvious formal defects and correspondence in number, date, and country with the application data sheet (or oath/declaration). The subject matter is not examined to determine entitlement to the priority date unless required for patentability reasons (e.g., intervening reference, interference/derivation).
guidance: If an intervening reference is found that raises priority entitlement issues, the examiner may reject claims and then require the foreign papers or translations to be filed to overcome the reference; form paragraphs (e.g., 2.19) may be used to request translation or further papers.

name: PDX and WIPO DAS specifics for design and PCT applications
description: USPTO will attempt retrieval of foreign applications to which priority is claimed in a U.S. design application where possible. The Spanish PTO deposits certain ES industrial design applications for USPTO access via WIPO DAS. USPTO will automatically attempt retrieval of PCT international applications where the receiving office is RO/AU, RO/DK, RO/ES, RO/FI, RO/IB, RO/MA or RO/SE and the applicant has provided the required WIPO DAS access code.
guidance: Applicants claiming priority to such foreign or international applications should provide WIPO DAS access codes and identify the foreign applications properly on the application data sheet to enable automated retrieval.

name: Definition/examples of 'amendment' under 37 CFR 1.312
description: The amendment of an application by applicant after allowance falls within the guidelines of 37 CFR 1.312. Examples of 'amendments' by applicant after allowance which must comply with 37 CFR 1.312 include: (A) an amendment to the specification, (B) a change in the drawings, (C) an amendment to the claims, (D) a change in the inventorship, (E) the submission of prior art, (F) a petition to correct the spelling of an inventor’s name, (G) a petition to change the order of the names of the inventors.
guidance: Any change in the file record broadly encompasses an 'amendment' and thus is subject to 37 CFR 1.312 and the related processing requirements (e.g., compliance with 37 CFR 1.121).

name: Post-Notice-of-Allowance examiner authority (formal corrections)
description: After the Notice of Allowance has been mailed the application is technically no longer under the jurisdiction of the primary examiner. The primary examiner can, however, make examiner's amendments and has authority to enter amendments submitted after Notice of Allowance which embody merely the correction of formal matters in the specification or drawing, or formal matters in a claim without changing the scope thereof, or the cancellation of claims from the application, without forwarding to the supervisory patent examiner for approval.
guidance: Formal matters may be entered by the primary examiner without supervisory approval. If the amendment affects disclosure or claim scope, supervisory approval is required.

name: Supervisory approval required for non-formal amendments
description: Amendments other than those which merely embody the correction of formal matters without changing the scope of the claims require approval by the supervisory patent examiner. The Technology Center Director establishes TC policy with respect to trivial informalities and whether they may be treated without supervisory review.
guidance: The TC policy balances (A) adequate clarity of disclosure and (B) sufficient claim definition for an enforceable contract when deciding treatment of trivial informalities.

name: Required remarks when amendment affects disclosure/scope/adds claim
description: For amendments affecting the disclosure, the scope of any claim, or that add a claim, the remarks accompanying the amendment must fully and clearly state the reasons on which reliance is placed to show: (A) why the amendment is needed; (B) why the proposed amended or new claims require no additional search or examination; (C) why the claims are patentable; and (D) why they were not presented earlier.
guidance: The requirements of 37 CFR 1.111(c) with respect to pointing out the patentable novelty of any claim sought to be added or amended apply in the case of an amendment under 37 CFR 1.312.

name: Additional fees required for added claims
description: If the amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 adds claims (total and independent) in excess of the number previously paid for, additional fees are required. The amendment is not considered by the examiner unless accompanied by the full fee required.
guidance: See MPEP § 607 and 35 U.S.C. 41 for specifics on claim fees; do not process additions without full payment or authorization to charge account/credit card.

name: Processing/routing and prompt examiner consideration
description: Amendments under 37 CFR 1.312 that affect disclosure, add claims, or change claim scope are sent by OIPE to the Publishing Division and forwarded to the Technology Center that allowed the application (or scanned in IFW and messaged to PUBS and the TC). The amendment is promptly considered by the examiner who indicates 'Enter — 312', 'Do Not Enter' or 'Enter In Part' in red ink on the amendment.
guidance: Hand-delivered amendments are no longer accepted in the TC (unless PUBS specifically requires). For IFW, print the first page and annotate before scanning. Prompt consideration and correct routing are required to resume issue processing.

name: Formality of entry and required signatures
description: If the amendment is favorably considered, it is entered and a Response to Rule 312 Communication (PTO-271) is prepared. The primary examiner indicates recommendation by stamping and signing; entry that affects scope of claims requires the signature of the supervisory patent examiner.
guidance: Use form paragraph 7.85 for entry and 7.87 for non-entry. The technical support staff mailing the PTO-271 does not officialize admission until supervisory approval where required.

name: List of amendments ordinarily denied entry — J: drawings alleged to contain new matter
description: Amendments to the drawing held by the examiner to contain new matter are not entered until the question of new matter is settled. This practice of nonentry because of alleged new matter does not apply to amendments to the specification and claims.
guidance: Resolve new matter questions before entry of drawing amendments.

name: List of amendments ordinarily denied entry — O: noncompliance with 37 CFR 1.121 (e.g., missing replacement paragraphs/claim listings)
description: An amendment including changes to the specification/claims which is not in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121, e.g., one which does not include replacement paragraphs or claim listings, is ordinarily denied entry.
guidance: See MPEP § 714 for treatment of amendments not in compliance with 1.121; require properly formatted replacement text or claim listings.

name: Amendments entered in part — examples and limits
description: To avoid confusion an amendment generally should not be entered in part; where strict observance would do more harm than good, acceptable portions should be entered and unacceptable ones denied entry. Examples: (A) unacceptable substitute specification with acceptable amendatory matter — enter in part; (B) amendment under 1.312 partly approved and partly disapproved — enter only approved part; (C) in Quayle action where formal defects cured but new claims unpatentable/would require search — enter only formal matter; (D) amendment accompanying a motion granted only in part — enter to extent motion granted.
guidance: Indicate entered portions with 'Enter' in red ink and initials. For IFW processing follow IFW Manual. Entry in part typically requires accompanying fees for any added claims.

name: Situations where 37 CFR 1.131 is inappropriate (statutory bars, same invention, admissions, 102(f), etc.)
description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is not appropriate in the following situations: (A) reference publication date more than 1 year prior to applicant's effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C.102(b)); (B) reference U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication claims the same patentable invention; (C) reference is a foreign patent for the same invention to applicant issued prior to the domestic filing date where an earlier foreign filing was made more than 12 months earlier (35 U.S.C.102(d)); (D) where applicant's parent application's effective filing date or PCT proved filing date is prior to the effective date of the reference (unnecessary); (E) reference is a prior U.S. patent to the same entity claiming the same invention (double patenting); (F) reference is disclosure of a prior U.S. patent to the same party not copending (dedication issues); (G) applicant clearly admitted on the record that subject matter is prior art; and (H) subject matter relied upon is prior art under 35 U.S.C.102(f).
guidance: Cite the pertinent case law (e.g., In re Hellsund, In re Garfinkel, In re Blout, In re Lopresti) and MPEP references when evaluating appropriateness of a 1.131 affidavit.

name: Detecting and objecting to new matter (35 U.S.C. 132(a))
description: In the examination of an application following amendment thereof, the examiner must be on the alert to detect new matter. 35 U.S.C. 132(a) should be employed as a basis for objection to amendments to the abstract, specification, or drawings attempting to add new disclosure to that originally disclosed on filing.
guidance: If new matter is added to the specification, it should be objected to by using Form Paragraph 7.28. If new matter is added to the claims, or affects the claims, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, using form paragraph 7.31.01 should also be made. If subject matter capable of illustration is originally claimed and it is not shown in the drawing, the claim is not rejected but applicant is required to add it to the drawing (see MPEP § 608.01(l)). Examiner should identify new matter by page and line numbers/drawing figures and provide an explanation addressing applicant's support arguments and any unresolved questions about possession at time of filing.

name: Form Paragraph 7.28 — Objection to New Matter Added to Specification
description: Template objection: 'The amendment filed [1] is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132(a) because it introduces new matter into the disclosure... The added material which is not supported by the original disclosure is as follows: [2]. Applicant is required to cancel the new matter in the reply to this Office action.'
guidance: This form paragraph is not to be used in reissue applications (use form paragraph 14.22.01 instead). In bracket 2, identify the new matter by page and line numbers and/or drawing figures and provide an appropriate explanation of your position. The explanation should address any applicant statement supporting possession at filing and include any unresolved questions raising doubt. If new matter affects claims, also make a 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph rejection (form paragraph 7.31.01).

name: Rejection of previously-allowed claims — examiner caution and approval
description: A claim noted as allowable shall thereafter be rejected only after the proposed rejection has been submitted to the primary examiner for consideration of all the facts and approval of the proposed action.
guidance: Great care should be exercised in authorizing such a rejection. Full faith and credit should be given to the search and action of a previous examiner unless there is clear error or knowledge of other prior art. In general, an examiner should not take an entirely new approach or make a new search merely in hope of finding something. Because unusual to reject previously allowed claim, point out in office action that the claim was previously allowed by using Form Paragraph 7.50.

name: Final rejection practice — when a rejection may be made final (37 CFR 1.113)
description: (a) On the second or any subsequent examination or consideration by the examiner the rejection or other action may be made final, whereupon applicant’s reply is limited to appeal or to amendment as specified. Reply must comply with §1.114 or paragraph (c). (b) In making such final rejection, the examiner shall repeat or state all grounds of rejection then considered applicable to the claims, clearly stating the reasons in support thereof. (c) Reply must include cancellation of, or appeal from, each rejected claim.
guidance: Before final rejection, develop a clear issue between examiner and applicant where possible. Claims should be thoroughly searched and references fully applied in the first action where possible. Avoid hasty final rejections. If a single previous Office action contains a complete statement supporting the rejection, the final may refer to it but should include rebuttal of applicant arguments. The applicant is entitled to a full and fair hearing; prosecution should be confined to as few actions as consistent with thorough consideration. Use Form Paragraph 7.39 to conclude final rejection letters.

name: When final rejection is proper on second or subsequent action and exceptions
description: Under present practice, second or any subsequent actions on the merits shall be final, except where the examiner introduces a new ground of rejection that is neither necessitated by applicant’s amendment nor based on information submitted in an IDS filed during the period set forth in 37 CFR 1.97(c) with the required fee. Where information is submitted in an IDS with the fee, the examiner may use the information and make the next Office action final whether or not claims have been amended, provided no other new ground of rejection not necessitated by amendment is introduced.
guidance: A second or subsequent action should not be made final if it includes a rejection on prior art not of record of any claim amended to include limitations which should reasonably have been expected to be claimed. If applicant files a statement averring common ownership disqualifying a 102(e) reference, the examiner may not make the next action final if a new rejection is made. Note special rules for reexaminations. See MPEP §706.07(a) and §609.04(b).

name: Claim construction by the Court
description: It is the judge's job to provide to you the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted. You must accept the meanings the judge gives you and use them when you decide whether any claim has been infringed and whether any claim is invalid.
guidance: [READ STIPULATIONS AND COURT’S CLAIM CONSTRUCTIONS]. Use these constructions when comparing accused product/method to the claims.

name: Means-plus-function claim interpretation (35 U.S.C. §112(f))
description: When a patentee expresses an element as a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, the clause is a means-plus-function element and requires special interpretation: it does not cover all means that perform the recited function; instead the claim covers the recited function and the structure/step described in the specification and equivalents.
guidance: The court will determine the recited function and the structure/step described in the patent specification and drawings that perform the recited function; the jury must use that interpretation in deliberations. Give Instruction 2.2 only if the case involves means-plus-function claims; consider whether 2.2 is unnecessary when §112(f) governs but the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' is not used.

name: Direct literal infringement—all claim elements required
description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the defendant’s product/method includes each and every element/method step recited in that patent claim. If the defendant’s product/method does not contain one or more elements/method steps recited in a claim, the defendant does not literally infringe that claim.
guidance: Determine literal infringement for each claim individually, using the court's constructions of claim terms. The same element of the accused product/method may satisfy more than one claim element.

name: Literal infringement of means-plus-function/step-plus-function claims
description: To establish infringement of a means-plus-function or step-plus-function claim, the plaintiff must prove that (1) the accused part/step performs the recited function, and (2) it is identical or equivalent to the structure/step described in the specification and drawings for performing that function.
guidance: First determine whether the accused product/method has any structure/step performing the specific function. If not, the claim is not infringed. If yes, decide whether that structure/step is the same as or equivalent to the structure described in the specification. Equivalence is judged from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art: differences are equivalent if insubstantial (e.g., performs same function in substantially same way to achieve substantially same result). Both prongs must be met for infringement.

name: Meaning and effect of 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
description: 'Comprising' means including the following but not excluding others. 'Consisting of' means including the following and excluding others. 'Consisting essentially of' means including the following and possibly unlisted components/steps that do not materially affect the invention.
guidance: If a claim uses 'comprising', additional components do not avoid literal infringement if all claim elements are present. If a claim uses 'consisting of', presence of additional components means no literal infringement. If 'consisting essentially of', literal infringement exists if additional components do not negate an element or materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention. Practice note: if the claim is literally infringed, no need to resort to doctrine of equivalents.

name: Doctrine of equivalents (DOE) test
description: If the accused product/method does not literally infringe, determine whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents: the product/method can infringe if it includes components/steps that are equivalent to those claim elements not literally present.
guidance: Examine each individual claim element and decide whether the accused product/method has an equivalent component/step for that element. An equivalent is insubstantially different—one way to show this is demonstrating it performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result. Consider whether persons of ordinary skill at the time would have known of interchangeability; known interchangeability is not required. The same accused component may satisfy more than one element, and two accused components may satisfy a single claim element. If any claim element lacks an equivalent in the accused product/method, DOE infringement cannot be found.

name: Limitation on DOE—Prosecution history estoppel
description: If the patentee made a representation/argument or amended a claim for reasons related to patentability, there is a presumption that equivalent subject matter has been surrendered and DOE cannot be applied to those elements.
guidance: The court determines whether prosecution history estoppel applies as a matter of law. If it applies, the court will instruct the jury which claim elements (by claim) cannot be the subject of DOE; those elements must be literally present for infringement. Remaining elements may be analyzed under DOE.

name: Active inducement of infringement (§271(b))
description: To find that the defendant actively induced another to directly infringe, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/steps), and (2) the defendant actively induced those acts.
guidance: Specifically, the plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with intent to cause acts by the alleged direct infringer that would constitute direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent or showed willful blindness to its existence; (3) the defendant knew or showed willful blindness that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one claim. Willful blindness requires (i) subjective belief of a high probability a patent existed covering the accused product/method, and (ii) deliberate actions to avoid learning of the patent.

name: Infringement by supply of components abroad—§271(f)(1)
description: To show infringement under §271(f)(1), plaintiff must prove: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one claim; (2) the defendant supplied (or caused to be supplied) components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention of a claim; and (3) the defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the U.S.
guidance: A 'substantial portion' requires a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment—export of a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability under §271(f)(1).

name: Infringement by supply of specially made components abroad—§271(f)(2)
description: To show infringement under §271(f)(2), plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant actually supplied components from the U.S. into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied; (2) the defendant knew or should have known the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) the defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
guidance: It is not necessary to find that the components actually were combined into an infringing product, as long as the defendant intended the components to be combined into a product that would have infringed a claim if combined in the U.S.

name: Refund when additional species embraced by allowable generic claim (transitional applications)
description: Whenever claims drawn to an additional species in a transitional application for which applicant paid the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(s) are no longer withdrawn from consideration because they are fully embraced by an allowable generic claim, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional species.
guidance: The determination of when claims to nonelected species would no longer be withdrawn from consideration should be made as indicated in MPEP § 806.04(d), § 821.04, and § 821.04(a).

name: Nucleotide sequences normally independent and distinct inventions
description: Polynucleotide molecules defined by their nucleic acid sequence that encode different proteins are structurally distinct chemical compounds and are thus deemed to normally constitute independent and distinct inventions within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 121 and 37 CFR 1.141 et seq.; absent evidence to the contrary, each such nucleotide sequence is presumed to represent an independent and distinct invention, subject to a restriction requirement.
guidance: To aid biotechnology industry, Director partially waived 37 CFR 1.141 et seq. to permit a reasonable number of such nucleotide sequences to be claimed in a single application (Examination of Patent Applications Containing Nucleotide Sequences, 1192 O.G. 68 (Nov. 19, 1996)). See MPEP § 1850 for international/PCT treatment.

name: Exceptional cases and petition for additional nucleotide sequences
description: In some exceptional cases, the complex nature of the claimed material may necessitate that the reasonable number of sequences to be selected be less than ten. Applicants may petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.181 for examination of additional nucleotide sequences by providing evidence that the different nucleotide sequences do not cover independent and distinct inventions.
guidance: Use 37 CFR 1.181 petitions and provide supporting evidence demonstrating lack of independence/distinctness among sequences.

name: Doctrine and public policy of double patenting
description: The doctrine of double patenting seeks to prevent the unjustified extension of patent exclusivity beyond the term of a patent. Double patenting results when the right to exclude granted by a first patent is unjustly extended by the grant of a later issued patent or patents; the focus of any double patenting analysis is on the claims in the multiple patents or patent applications involved.
guidance: Double patenting analysis considers common inventorship/ownership/joint research agreements (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3)). See cited case law (e.g., In re Zickendraht; In re Van Ornum) and MPEP § 804.03 for ownership treatment.

name: Statutory double patenting test (same invention / literal infringement test)
description: A reliable test for double patenting under 35 U.S.C. 101 is whether a claim in the application could be literally infringed without literally infringing a corresponding claim in the patent. If an embodiment falls within the scope of one claim but not the other, identical subject matter is not defined by both claims and statutory double patenting does not exist.
guidance: If it is determined that the same invention is being claimed twice, 35 U.S.C. 101 precludes the grant of the second patent regardless of the presence or absence of a terminal disclaimer. Examples: 'halogen' vs 'chlorine' and '36 inches' vs '3 feet' illustrate scope considerations. Use form paragraphs 8.30–8.32 as headings/paragraphs for statutory rejections.

name: Procedures for provisional ODP rejections between copending applications (terminal disclaimer rules)
description: A 'provisional' obviousness-type double patenting (ODP) rejection may be made between copending applications. If a provisional ODP rejection is the only rejection remaining in the earlier-filed application while the later-filed application is rejectable on other grounds, the examiner should withdraw that rejection and permit the earlier-filed application to issue without a terminal disclaimer. If the ODP rejection is the only rejection remaining in the later-filed application while the earlier-filed application is rejectable on other grounds, a terminal disclaimer must be required in the later-filed application before the rejection can be withdrawn.
guidance: If ODP rejections exist in two applications where both are otherwise free of other rejections, withdraw ODP in the earlier-filed app to allow it to issue; require terminal disclaimer in later-filed before withdrawal. If applications filed same day, determine base vs improvement claims; base application's ODP can be withdrawn without a terminal disclaimer; improvement application cannot. For three conflicting applications, terminal disclaimers must be filed in at least two to link all three.

name: Nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting analysis parallels 35 U.S.C. 103 Graham factors
description: A nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting rejection is appropriate where conflicting claims are not identical but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined claim is anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s). The analysis parallels the guidelines for analysis of a 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness determination.
guidance: Use Graham factual inquiries: (A) determine scope and content of the patent claim relative to the application claim; (B) determine differences between them; (C) determine level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (D) evaluate any objective indicia of nonobviousness. The patent principally underlying the double patenting rejection is not considered prior art in this analysis.

name: Antibody claim distinguishing features
description: An antibody claim may be novel and non-obvious where the claimed antibody is additionally defined in the claim by properties that distinguish the antibody from both generic and prior art antibodies, which may include: its structure (nucleotide or amino acid sequences); reference to a novel hybridoma which produces the claimed antibody and which was deposited in accordance with the Patent Rules; and/or a specific and supported binding activity, such as an affinity that exceeds the threshold affinity expected from a generic antibody.
guidance: Use structural sequence data, a proper hybridoma deposit, or specific binding/activity data to limit claim scope and distinguish from generic/prior-art antibodies; each basis carries different support/enablement considerations.

name: Monoclonal antibody utility requirement
description: A monoclonal antibody invention must be useful in order to satisfy section 2 of the Patent Act.
guidance: See 23.07.05 for details on levels of utility evidence (mere scintilla for some in vitro uses; demonstration or sound prediction needed for therapeutic/in vivo uses and claims requiring functional activity).

name: Support requirement for antibody-related nucleic acids/polypeptides
description: Where an application claims nucleic acids or polypeptides relating to antibodies of the invention (e.g., light and heavy chains, variable regions, CDRs), the nucleic acids and polypeptides must be fully supported by the description.
guidance: Deposits of biological material are not a substitute for a full and correct description of a polynucleotide molecule itself (see section on deposits and 23.05). Provide sequences or other structural disclosure sufficient to satisfy paragraph 27(3)(a).

name: Novelty and inventive step linked to full characterization
description: A claimed protein or antibody may be novel and non-obvious where the prior art does not disclose or suggest any protein/sequence with significant identity; a complete amino acid (and corresponding nucleic acid) sequence and characterization can support novelty and inventive step.
guidance: Full characterization supports compliance with subsection 27(3) (enablement/written description) and subsection 27(4) (distinct and explicit definition). Examiners rely on sequence and characterization to determine novelty and enablement.

name: Enablement and written description (subsection 27(3)) and distinct definition (subsection 27(4))
description: Claims must be supported by a specification that satisfies subsection 27(3) of the Patent Act (enablement and correct/full description) and comply with subsection 27(4) (subject-matter distinctly and explicitly defined).
guidance: Enablement analysis asks whether a person skilled in the art, with common general knowledge and the specification, could make or use the invention without undue experimentation or inventive ingenuity as of the filing date.

name: Generic antibody claims may be obvious if target known and methods routine
description: A claim to a generic monoclonal antibody that encompasses any monoclonal antibody specific to a known antigenic protein may be obvious where techniques for preparing monoclonal antibodies were well established and no inventive ingenuity is required to prepare an antibody specific to a known antigen.
guidance: If the antigen is known and routine antibody methods are available, claiming all antibodies to that antigen risks being rejected under obviousness (section 28.3 and common general knowledge). Narrow claims to particular antibodies or deposited hybridomas may be needed.

name: Hybridoma deposit can support claim to a particular antibody
description: A claim that defines an antibody by reference to a deposited hybridoma (made in accordance with the Patent Rules) can be novel and non-obvious and may be supported by the specification because the deposit serves to provide a correct and full description of the specific antibody produced by that hybridoma.
guidance: Ensure the hybridoma deposit complies with Patent Rules (timing, IDA, accession number, description in specification) so the deposit can be relied upon to satisfy paragraph 27(3) and to limit scope to the specific antibody.

name: Claims defined by competition (competing antibodies)
description: An antibody defined as one that competes for specific binding to a target with a particular deposited monoclonal antibody may be distinctly and explicitly defined and, if the competitor relationship is to a novel/non-obvious deposited antibody, may be novel and enabled.
guidance: Enablement may rest on routine competition binding assays; if a skilled person could identify competing antibodies without undue experimentation, the claim can be supported. A properly deposited reference antibody strengthens support.

name: Utility thresholds for antibodies and functional claims
description: An antibody invention must be useful (section 2). The threshold is generally low (a 'mere scintilla' may suffice) for many uses; if therapeutic/in vivo utility or specific functional activities (antagonist/agonist/neutralizing) are required, utility must be demonstrated or soundly predicted as of the filing date.
guidance: In vitro uses: binding to antigen often suffices. In vivo therapeutic claims or claims requiring a functional activity typically require working examples or in vitro/in vivo data, or a sound prediction supported by the specification.

name: Reach-through claims invalid (unsupported)
description: A 'reach-through' claim that seeks to encompass subject-matter extending beyond the described invention (i.e., products not yet identified but discoverable by future use of the invention) is not supported by the specification and fails the written description/enablement requirements.
guidance: Examples include product claims directed to unidentified substances defined solely by the process used to identify them or by their ability to modulate a biomolecule, and method/use claims relying on unidentified substances. Such claims fail section 60 of the Patent Rules and subsection 27(3) disclosure/enablement.

name: Claiming benefit of prior application (35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c))
description: If applicant wishes to claim the benefit of a prior application under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c), applicant must include a reference to the prior application in compliance with 37 CFR 1.78(a) in the first sentence(s) of the specification or in an ADS.
guidance: Examiners should review the front page identifying data to ensure accuracy of all prior applications for which benefits are claimed.

name: Amendments in inter partes reexamination and timing limits
description: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.116(d)(1), no amendment other than canceling claims (that does not affect scope of other pending claims) can be made in an inter partes reexamination proceeding after the RAN except as provided in 37 CFR 1.981 or permitted by 37 CFR 41.77(b)(1).
guidance: Various reexamination sections updated to reflect transfer procedures, CRU processes, forms, and co-pending proceedings with reissue.

name: Statute of Limitations and limits on damage claims (patents)
description: There is no statute of limitations for infringement generally, however there is a two-year limitation period to pursue a civil action for damages.
guidance: Civil law (suppletory) timing to claim damages must be considered when deciding when to file infringement actions.

name: Trademark infringement — statutory definitions
description: Acts constituting infringement include: I) distributing/placing products on sale or offering services with indication they are protected by a registered trademark when they are not; II) using a trademark confusingly similar to another registered mark for identical/similar products or services; III) using names, signs, symbols, abbreviations or emblems prohibited by law; IV) using combinations of distinctive signs and operating elements/images to induce confusion (unfair competition).
guidance: Claims before IMPI begin with a formal written claim; both parties must produce supporting evidence at filing/answer stages.

name: Software patents (Paraguay)
description: Claims comprising embedded software in a system or in a specific step of a method are usually accepted; 'software per se' is excluded from patentability and protected by copyright.
guidance: Draft claims to tie software functionality to technical apparatus or method steps to improve patentability prospects.

name: Markush claims (Paraguay pharmaceutical practice)
description: Compounds represented by a Markush formula may be admitted if they meet novelty, inventive step and industrial application, present sufficient support in the specification, and properly characterize representative compounds of the various embodiments.
guidance: Ensure sufficient support and representative examples in the specification when filing Markush-style claims.

name: Expectation of consistent, reasonable examination
description: Applicants should expect that multiple examiners examining the same application will identify art of comparable quality, cooperate with applicants to a similar degree, and interpret patent law in a similar manner.
guidance: This is the baseline desideratum: examination should be both consistent across examiners/art units and reasonable in application of law. Variability that prevents applicants from reasonably predicting outcomes (e.g., allowance likelihood, degree of claim narrowing) is unacceptable and should prompt review.

name: Avoid Pure Math Claims
description: Claims that recite only mathematical operations without anchoring to a technical use case are textbook abstract ideas.
guidance: Anchor every AI claim to (a) what the model does in operational terms, (b) what hardware/system it runs on, and (c) what technical improvement it provides. Avoid claims that merely recite matrix multiplications, activation functions, or other raw math.

name: Recite Specific Architectural Choices in Claims
description: Claims should recite concrete architectural elements rather than high-level descriptions.
guidance: Example: a claim reciting 'a transformer with 12 layers and 768-dimensional embeddings, where attention is computed using a sparse pattern that...' is more eligible than 'a neural network that predicts X.' Specific architecture details buy eligibility and help distinguish prior art.

name: Disclose Training Data Characteristics
description: The specification should disclose characteristics of the training data rather than simply naming datasets.
guidance: Include size, modality, label distribution, augmentation strategy, and other characteristics. Training data choices can be inventive and therefore support claim limitations; full dataset disclosure is not required but meaningful characteristics should be described.

name: Address Enablement/'Black Box' Risks (§112)
description: Claims that merely state 'a model trained to determine X' may face §112 enablement problems if not reproducible.
guidance: Disclose the training objective, loss function, and key hyperparameters. Provide sufficient procedural detail about training to avoid enablement rejections when outcomes depend on training choices or stochastic factors.

name: Draft for Federated and Distributed Training with Single-Actor Claims
description: For federated or distributed learning, structure claims to reflect enforceable single-actor steps.
guidance: Draft method claims with single-actor architecture: have the orchestrator perform the steps that combine data even if underlying gradients come from multiple clients. This helps avoid multi-actor/non-infringement issues.

name: Consider Foreign Filing Regimes and Tailor the Spec
description: Different patent offices treat AI differently; tailor disclosures and claim framing for target jurisdictions.
guidance: EPO is generally more favorable to AI patents than USPTO post-Alice; CNIPA has its own AI-specific guidance. Support both 'technical improvement' framing (US/EPO) and the EPO-specific 'further technical effect' framework when drafting to multiple jurisdictions.

name: Examinations conducted in accordance with Examination Guidelines
description: Examinations are conducted in accordance with the Examination Guidelines for Patent and Utility Model in Japan prepared by the JPO to ensure consistent decisions and transparent processes.
guidance: Guidelines address principles/procedures of examination, requirements for patentability, descriptions and claims, priority, foreign-language applications, and patent term extension; an English version is available on the JPO website.

name: Ex officio proceedings authority
description: Panels may conduct ex officio proceedings, allowing them to investigate facts and examine evidence on their own authority, including grounds not pleaded by parties (subject to limits).
guidance: Ex officio examination is permitted because trials serve broader public interests; when ex officio proceedings are invoked, panels must provide notice of reasons and allow formal responses. Panels cannot examine any claim not claimed by a demandant.

name: Opposition — scope of examination and panel practice
description: A panel will examine only the claims to which an opposition is filed and will conduct examination based on the reasons and evidence pleaded by the demandant, although it may examine unpleaded reasons via ex officio proceedings under certain considerations.
guidance: A decision to invoke ex officio proceedings must take into account public interest, purpose of the process, delay, and whether ex officio examination will produce a more accurate determination.

name: Trial for correction — permissible corrections (Article 126(1))
description: Corrections that may be requested in a trial for correction are limited to: restriction of the claims, correction of errors or mistranslations, clarification of any ambiguous statement, or rewriting a claim that cites the preceding claim so that it does not cite the preceding claim.
guidance: A correction is usually preventive to guard against invalidation or to clarify ambiguity; requests for correction cannot be filed while an invalidation trial is pending and until its final resolution, except at prescribed times; a correction request may not add new matter or change gist of a request without prohibition; chief administrative patent judge must notify reasons for rejection and provide opportunity to submit written opinion.

name: Trial for invalidation — inter partes requirement and interested person standing
description: Trials for invalidation are inter partes proceedings involving a demandant (interested person) and the demandee (patentee); only an 'interested person' may file a request for invalidation, and whether a person is interested is determined case-by-case.
guidance: Examples of interested persons include those sued for infringement, manufacturers of the same product, or persons claiming a legitimate right to obtain a patent (co-owners, transferees).

name: Trial for invalidation — grounds for invalidation (Article 123(1) exhaustive list)
description: Reasons for invalidation are limited to statutory reasons under Article 123(1)(i)–(viii), including (inter alia): patents granted on amendments beyond the original disclosure; grants in violation of Articles on enjoyment of rights, conditions for patentability, unpatentable inventions, joint applications; grants in violation of a treaty; failure to comply with requirements for statements of detailed explanation/claims; foreign-language application matters exceeding scope; grants to persons without right; post-grant disqualifying events; improper corrections in violation of Article 126 provisos.
guidance: No other reasons outside statutory provisions constitute grounds for invalidation; requests may be filed claim-by-claim where multiple claims are involved.

name: Strategic patenting motives
description: Identify the firm's motive(s) for patenting: prevention of copying; patent blocking; use in cross-licensing; prevention of suits; reputation/financing signaling.
guidance: Evaluate whether the stated or inferred motive aligns with claim scope and filing strategy. Motives that match claim drafting (e.g., blocking patents with broad families to prevent competitor filings) suggest coherent strategy; motives that are purely signaling or opportunistic may indicate lower appropriability value.

name: Claims map onto products the firm sells or expects to sell
description: Check whether patent claims are written to cover the firm's own commercial products or planned offerings rather than only broad external possibilities.
guidance: Claims that closely map to the firm's commercial output indicate coherent appropriability use—facilitating enforcement and licensing. Claims that do not relate to the firm's product portfolio may signal nuisance, blocking-only, or rent-seeking patents.

name: Continuation strategy preserves options for capturing competitor designs
description: Consider whether the firm uses continuation/divisional filings strategically to maintain flexibility in claim scope as competitor designs evolve.
guidance: A continuation strategy that preserves later claim amendments can be a marker of strategic, high-quality patenting (allowing capture of emergent competitor designs). Lack of such a strategy may reduce the patent family's strategic value.

name: Cross-license potential recognized in claim drafting
description: Assess whether patents are drafted with potential cross-licensing value in mind (e.g., claiming technologies likely to be complementary or contested in negotiations).
guidance: Patents intended as cross-license currency should have claims that intersect with competitors' technologies and are clear enough to be bargained over. If claim drafting ignores cross-license opportunities, the patent's strategic exchange value is reduced.

name: Pharmaceutical / biotechnology-specific quality criteria
description: In pharma/biotech, patents are primary appropriability mechanisms; quality requires structural specificity, robust claim layering, and defenses against generics.
guidance: Evaluate patent quality for structural specificity (precise molecular/structural claims), claim layering (families and continuations creating multiple claim scopes), and legal/market defenses (regulatory exclusivities, formulation/usage claims) to deter generics. In this industry, patent quality heavily determines commercial value.

name: Discrete mechanical industries criteria
description: In discrete mechanical industries patents are important; quality requires clear scope and resistance to design-arounds, though lead time and brand often matter more than mere claim breadth.
guidance: Assess whether claims are drafted to resist simple design-arounds and whether the patent complements lead-time and branding advantages. Broad but vague claims may be less valuable than narrowly tailored, design-around-resistant claims.

name: Complex-product industries criteria (semiconductors, software)
description: In complex-product industries patents tend to be defensive (cross-license currency); quality emphasizes standard-essential or design-essential coverage and scope clarity over breadth.
guidance: High-quality patents in these industries often claim features that are essential to design or standards, or otherwise are clear and enforceable in cross-licensing contexts. Vague, overly broad patents are less useful when products are complex and modular.

name: CNW Quality Test (synthesis of evaluative questions)
description: A concise checklist: Does the firm's industry rely on patents as a primary appropriability mechanism? Does the patent cover the firm's actual or planned commercial products? Is the strategic motive consistent with claim drafting? Does the disclosure preserve trade-secret value where applicable? Does the patent fit the firm's broader IP/competitive strategy?
guidance: Use this checklist as a quick, synthesized test of appropriability coherence. A patent that answers these questions positively is deemed higher-quality in the CNW framework even if it merely meets formal patentability standards.

name: Grounds for opposition / revocation
description: Opposition may only be filed on the grounds that the patent’s subject matter is not patentable (e.g., lack of novelty, lack of inventive step, excluded subject matter), that the patent does not disclose the invention clearly and completely for a person skilled in the art, or that the patent’s subject matter extends beyond the content of the earlier application as filed.
guidance: These grounds are exhaustive under the EPC (art. 100). In opposition proceedings the Opposition Division examines whether the grounds prejudice maintenance of the patent and may invite written observations; proprietor may file amended description/claims/drawings but late-filed proposals may be disregarded.

name: Novelty (no prior public disclosure / anticipation)
description: Novelty generally requires that the claimed invention must not have been 'made available to the public' before the filing date (or priority date). The claimed invention is not novel if all of its elements are found in a single prior art reference (anticipation).
guidance: Key points and examples: a single reference must contain every claimed element to anticipate; examiners may not combine multiple references to destroy novelty (but can for obviousness). 'Made available to the public' includes oral disclosure, publications, use/display, exhibitions, social media. Use NDAs to preserve novelty when disclosing pre-filing. Jurisdictional notes: many countries treat worldwide disclosure as prior art; treatment of prior-filed but later-published patent applications (secret prior art) and grace periods varies by country (e.g., US/Japan have a one-year comprehensive grace period; Europe/China are more restrictive). Generic-versus-specific claims: a prior disclosure of a specific a1 can destroy a later generic claim A (if a1 ∈ A); the converse depends on distinguishing technical features.

name: Inventive step / Nonobviousness
description: The invention must not have been obvious to a person skilled in the art. Nonobviousness means a person of ordinary skill could not have combined existing knowledge to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Conceptual differences from novelty: obviousness can be based on combining multiple prior art references. Typical analytical approaches: U.S. style — determine scope & content of prior art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, and the level of skill in the art; EPO problem–solution approach — identify closest prior art, establish distinguishing features, formulate the objective technical problem, and assess obviousness of the solution. Beware impermissible hindsight/ex post facto analysis. Consider 'teaching away' (if prior art discourages the claimed route, that supports nonobviousness) and secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others) as supporting evidence—though they rarely overcome a clear primary obviousness finding.

name: Patentable subject matter / Subject-matter eligibility
description: The claimed invention must fall within patent-eligible subject matter in the jurisdiction (e.g., US: process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter; Japan: creation of a technical idea utilizing a law of nature) and must not be an excluded category (laws of nature, abstract ideas, natural phenomena, etc.).
guidance: Differences by jurisdiction: some systems positively define eligible matter (US, Japan), others list nonpatentable categories (EPC). The EPC lists nonpatentable examples such as discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, aesthetic creations, schemes/rules for mental acts, business methods and computer programs 'as such', and presentations of information. Exclusion applies when claims are directed to such subject matter 'as such'; courts/boards test 'technical character' to distinguish eligible inventions. Field-specific examination guidelines may apply (software, business methods, biotech). Also note public-order/morality exclusions (ordre public), and special rules for diagnostic/therapeutic/surgical methods and plants/animals in some jurisdictions; products for use in medical methods may still be patentable. U.S. case law further refines exclusions (laws of nature, abstract ideas, natural phenomena).

name: Improvement patents and territoriality
description: An improvement patent covers an improved or enhanced effect compared with an earlier patent; however, practicing the improved invention may still require permission if it falls within the scope of earlier patent claims. Patents are territorial — protection applies only in the granting jurisdiction.
guidance: Example: Inventor B obtains a patent for a faster filling machine with less spillage, but may need a license from Inventor A if A's claims cover B's embodiments. Licensing, cross-licensing and negotiation are common. Territorial implication: if Inventor A has rights only in Country X, Inventor B may practice the invention in other countries where A has no patent, subject to other patents in those countries. Consider patent mapping to identify blocking patents when planning exploitation.

name: Disclosure requirement (public disclosure in exchange for exclusivity)
description: In return for exclusive rights, patent holders must sufficiently disclose technical information about the invention so that the public benefits and others can practice the invention after patent expiry. The disclosure requirement typically includes a support (written description) requirement, an enablement requirement, and a clarity requirement; some jurisdictions also require disclosure of the best mode known to the inventor.
guidance: Objectives: ensure the scope of claims is justified by the description/drawings and enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention. Practical consequences: you cannot add new subject matter after filing; inadequate disclosure can invalidate claims. Professional tip: assess disclosure carefully before filing to ensure claims are supported and enabling.

name: Enablement, clarity, and best mode (components of disclosure)
description: Enablement requires sufficient information for a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention; clarity requires that the claims and description clearly define the invention; best mode (in some jurisdictions) requires disclosing the best-known way of practicing the invention at filing.
guidance: Enablement and clarity are prerequisites to allow third parties to practice the invention and to delimit claim scope. Best mode is required in some countries (not universally) and failure to disclose it can be problematic in those jurisdictions. The manual points to later modules for practical drafting techniques to satisfy these requirements.

name: Findings regarding properties, utilities, and limitations of the prior art genus
description: Office personnel should make findings as to any physical or chemical properties and utilities disclosed for the genus, as well as any suggested limitations on the usefulness of the genus, and any problems alleged to be addressed by the genus.
guidance: Document disclosed utilities, known problems, and any language in the reference that limits usefulness — these inform motivation and whether the prior art would prompt selection of a claimed species.

name: Compare claimed species to the closest disclosed prior art species/subgenus
description: Once the structure of the disclosed genus and any expressly described species/subgenus are identified, Office personnel should compare them to the claimed species/subgenus to determine the differences and identify the closest disclosed species or subgenus.
guidance: Make explicit findings on similarities and differences including structure, properties, and utilities; identify the closest prior art species of record and analyze whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious (see Stratoflex).

name: Determine level of ordinary skill in the art
description: Office personnel should evaluate the prior art from the standpoint of the hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the claimed invention was made.
guidance: Resolve level of skill to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry. Facts of record about skill are commonly found in the prior art; consider applicant evidence as appropriate (see Ryko, Uniroyal, MPEP §§2141, 2141.03).

name: Consider the size of the genus as a motive factor
description: Consider the size of the prior art genus, bearing in mind that size alone cannot support an obviousness rejection; however, a genus may be so small that it would anticipate the claimed species or subgenus.
guidance: Do not apply a per se rule; evaluate ‘total circumstances’ including number of permissible variations. Small, narrowly varying genera (e.g., Petering) can render selection foreseeable; large diverse genera may not.

name: Consider teachings of structural similarity (typical/preferred species)
description: Consider any teachings of a 'typical', 'preferred', or 'optimum' species or subgenus within the disclosed genus; if such species is structurally similar to the claimed species, its disclosure may provide a reason to choose the claimed species based on expectation of similar properties.
guidance: Structural relationships (homologs, adjacent homologs, isomers, stereoisomers, etc.) can suggest motivation to select claimed compounds because similar structure often implies similar properties (see Dillon, Deuel, and examples cited).

name: Consider the predictability of the technology when assessing motivation
description: Consider the predictability of the technology: if the technology is unpredictable, structurally similar species are less likely to render a claimed species obvious because properties may not be inferred from structure.
guidance: Assess whether a reasonable expectation of success exists (obviousness requires reasonable expectation, not absolute predictability). Use case law examples (Dillon, May, Schechter, O’Farrell).

name: Make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors
description: Office personnel should make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors and specifically articulate what teachings or suggestions in the prior art would have motivated one of ordinary skill to select the claimed species or subgenus.
guidance: Explicitly tie fact-findings to motivation and assess whether those findings, considered as a whole, support a prima facie case of obviousness. Cite precedent (Kulling, Panduit) when appropriate.

name: Obviousness rejection based on close structural similarity
description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be made when chemical compounds have very close structural similarities and similar utilities; the rejection is founded on the expectation that compounds similar in structure will have similar properties.
guidance: Use structural-and-functional similarity to establish motivation to make a claimed compound in expectation of similar properties (see In re Payne, Papesch, Dillon).

name: Account for homology and isomerism as facts (not conclusive) in obviousness
description: Homology and isomerism are facts which must be considered with all other relevant facts in determining obviousness; such relationships often create a presumption of similar properties but are not automatically dispositive.
guidance: Position isomers, homologs, stereoisomers often carry a presumption of similar properties, but divergent homologs or isomers may not. View claims and references 'as a whole' (see Wilder, May, Mills, Langer).

name: Prior art compounds lacking utility or disclosed only as intermediates may not render claimed compounds obvious
description: If the prior art does not teach any specific or significant utility for the disclosed compounds, or only discloses them as intermediates, then structurally similar claimed compounds may not be prima facie obvious.
guidance: Lack of disclosed utility undermines motivation to make related compounds; intermediates shown only as synthesis steps are unlikely to be investigated for other utilities (see Stemniski, Albrecht, Lalu).

name: Prima facie obviousness rebuttable by evidence of unexpected results and secondary considerations
description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties and by secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, copying, etc.).
guidance: Rebuttal evidence must be factual (data, declarations, comparative results); arguments alone are insufficient. Consider types of rebuttal: unexpected results, commercial success, copying, expert declarations on level of skill/state of art, and evidence that no method of making was known (see Papesch, Soni, Piasecki, Dillon, Mayne, GPAC, Hybritech). Ensure comparisons are supported by evidence, not conclusory statements.

name: § 101 as a threshold test / 'first door' inquiry
description: The § 101 patent-eligibility inquiry is a threshold test or 'first door' an invention must pass before other patentability requirements are considered.
guidance: Courts and commentators describe § 101 as a 'coarse eligibility filter' that can exclude broad categories of subject matter before examination of novelty (§ 102), nonobviousness (§ 103), and written description/enablement (§ 112). However, the Federal Circuit recognizes there is no rule that § 101 must always be considered first; examiners may dispose of claims on other grounds if appropriate. The threshold framing supports using § 101 to economize administrative costs but raises risks of over- and under-inclusiveness.

name: Physical elements and functional applications weigh against 'abstract' characterization
description: Presence of concrete physical elements (e.g., 'high contrast film,' 'film printer,' 'memory,' 'printer and display devices') and 'functional and palpable applications' support finding a claim non-abstract and § 101-eligible.
guidance: Judge Rader observed that such tangible elements 'confirm' a holding that an invention is not abstract; courts may look to claimed physical components or clear technological improvements when assessing abstractness.

name: Practical application / putting knowledge to use
description: Claims that 'put knowledge to practical use'—i.e., that implement or use the discovered principle in a concrete, practical way—are more likely to be patent-eligible than claims that merely assert an idea or principle.
guidance: Judge Newman (Classen) upheld patents that included the physical step of immunizing patients according to a chosen schedule as being 'directed to a specific, tangible application.' Conversely, claims that merely involve reviewing or comparing results without practical application may be considered too abstract.

name: Post-solution activity is insufficient to confer eligibility
description: Addition of insignificant 'post-solution activity' or mere data-gathering steps to a claimed principle does not transform an otherwise unpatentable idea into a patentable process.
guidance: Judge Moore argued that immunizing steps that are merely data-gathering or post-solution activity cannot save a claim from ineligibility. Courts should examine whether added steps are meaningful technological or transformative limitations or merely token activities.

name: Use of other statutory sections to police claim scope (§§ 102, 103, 112)
description: Even if a claim passes the § 101 threshold, other patentability doctrines—novelty (§ 102), nonobviousness (§ 103), and written description/enablement/definiteness (§ 112)—provide mechanisms to restrict overly broad or vague claims.
guidance: Some panels (Research Corporation, Newman opinions) favor treating § 101 as a 'coarse filter' and using §§ 102/103/112 to 'weed out' claims that are indefinite, overly broad, or conceptually abstract. The text explicitly notes using § 112 to invalidate claims that are not clear and concrete rather than relying solely on § 101.

name: Clarity and fidelity to claim language in § 101 analysis
description: Courts should interpret claim language carefully; reading limitations out of claims (e.g., ignoring explicit immunizing steps) can distort § 101 analysis and lead to questionable results.
guidance: Criticism in the text highlights that judicial reinterpretation of claim scope to reach § 101 conclusions (e.g., treating an immunizing claim as merely 'gathering published data') is suspect. Proper claim construction is essential before applying § 101 doctrine.

name: No absolute sequencing requirement for § 101 during examination
description: Although § 101 is a threshold inquiry conceptually, there is no absolute rule that examiners must address § 101 before other patentability grounds.
guidance: The Federal Circuit clarified that examiners may reject claims on other grounds without addressing § 101 when expedient. Thus administrative practice can prioritize other deficiencies (e.g., novelty, obviousness, indefiniteness) over subject-matter analysis where appropriate.

name: Technology-area assignment procedure
description: Assigned each patent in the study to a single, primary technology area (six primary areas) and, in about one-third of patents, one or more secondary technology areas when another area clearly formed an additional but integral part of the claims.
guidance: Place emphasis on the claims, aided by written descriptions and drawings to explain ambiguous claim terms; consult technical dictionaries/encyclopedias/Internet only when further interpretation is required; primary areas are mutually exclusive while primary-plus-secondary are not.

name: Industry-category assignment procedure
description: Industry categories focused on the business use of the patent; assignment paid attention to claim language but relied more on the written description and extrinsic evidence (especially from the Internet).
guidance: Industry categorization may require consulting extrinsic sources to determine the patent owner's industry or the way the technology is put to use.

name: Independent and Dependent Claims; Clarity and Support (Rule 416(b–d))
description: Application may contain one or more independent claims in the same category; each claim shall be clear, concise, and supported by the description. Dependent claims may refer back and further limit another claim; multiple dependent claims must refer in the alternative only and cannot serve as a basis for other multiple dependent claims.
guidance: Claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the description; terms and phrases used in claims must have clear support/antecedent basis in the description so their meaning is ascertainable by reference to the description; claims shall not, except where absolutely necessary, rely on reference to the description or drawings (avoid 'as described in part xxx').

name: Claims for Improvements (Rule 416(e))
description: If invention relates to an improvement, claims should specifically point out and distinctly claim the improvement in combination with a preamble indicating prior art features necessary for the definition.

name: Form and Contents of Claims — Structure (Rule 417)
description: Claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought in terms of technical features. Where appropriate, claims shall contain: (a) a statement indicating designation and prior art technical features necessary for definition; (b) a characterizing portion preceded by 'characterized in that' or 'characterized by' stating the technical features to be protected; (c) if drawings present, technical features may be followed by reference signs in parentheses (not construed as limiting).

name: Presentation of Application Documents — General (Rule 419(a–j))
description: All papers for an application must be original copy only, legibly written/typewritten/printed in permanent ink on one side; typing 1½-spaced; capital letters not less than 0.21 cm and in dark indelible color. Documents on A4 (29.7 x 21 cm) paper, pliable, strong, white, smooth, matte, durable. Abstract, description and claims lines must be numbered in sets of five restarting each page (numbers on left margin). Each document commences on a separate sheet. Margins specified and must be blank. Abstract/description/claims/drawings/sequence listings filed online may be in separate files per system; copies required if voluminous.
guidance: Tables and chemical/mathematical formulas allowed; may be presented sideways if necessary with top at left side. Physical values in SI units where appropriate; use technical terms/signs/symbols generally accepted in the field. Page numbering rules: abstract/description/claims pages numbered consecutively with Arabic numerals in central top or bottom margins.

name: Requisites for the Working Model (Rule 420.1)
description: When required, working model must clearly exhibit every feature of the machine which forms the subject of the claim(s) of the invention.
guidance: Model should not include other matters beyond the actual invention unless necessary to exhibit the invention.

name: Filing Date Requirements (Rule 600)
description: Filing date shall be the date on which the Office received the following elements in English or Filipino: (a) a duly accomplished request expressly indicating a Philippine patent is sought; (b) an abstract; (c) description; (d) at least one claim; (e) drawings, if necessary; (f) payment of required fees at time of filing; (g) appointment of agent if applicant is non‑resident.

name: Formality Examination Scope (Rule 602)
description: If application accorded filing date and required fee paid in full, application shall be evaluated for formality requirements such as: (a) contents of request for grant; (b) priority documents if claiming convention priority; (c) proof of authority, if applicant not inventor; (d) deed of assignment; (e) full payment of other fees (e.g., deficit claims fees); (f) signature; (g) identification of the inventor; (h) formal drawings; (i) complete and clear description.

name: Requirements for Unity of Invention — Technical Relationship (Rule 605)
description: Unity requirement fulfilled only when there is a technical relationship among those inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding special technical features. 'Special technical features' mean those features that define a contribution which each claimed invention makes over the prior art.
guidance: Determination of single general inventive concept made without regard to whether inventions are claimed separately or as alternatives in a single claim. Plurality of independent claims in different categories (product/process/apparatus/use) may constitute a group linked as a single general inventive concept. Examples provided for permissible different specific combinations of claims.

name: Post-retirement solicitation and prosecution under section 5498 R.S.
description: A retired post quartermaster sergeant who solicited claims by printed circular was not prohibited by statute from assisting in prosecution of those claims, nor was it improper for claimants to turn claims over to him; not criminal under section 5498 R.S. as applied.

name: GATT-TRIPs (Uruguay Round) — trade-related IP standards
description: TRIPs (under GATT Uruguay Round) requires GATT signatory countries to provide certain patent protections and enforcement mechanisms.
guidance: Significant provisions include: patent term of 20 years from earliest filed application (with limited extensions for special circumstances); ability to use provisional applications (establish priority without claims); patent rights include exclusive right to offer for sale and to import patented goods; rules affecting interference proof of invention date across signatory countries.

name: Reexamination reforms (AIPA) — third-party participation and estoppel
description: AIPA reformed reexamination procedures to allow a third-party requesting reexamination (for patents issuing from applications filed on or after Nov 29, 1999) to participate to a limited extent.
guidance: Third-party requestor can file one written comment on each PTO action and applicant response, can appeal to the Board of Appeals of the PTO (but not directly to federal circuit), and is estopped from later raising issues they 'raised or could have raised' in the reexamination. Requestor is estopped from later challenging any fact determined in reexamination. Patent owner may appeal final rejection of claims to the Board or federal court and can seek a stay in certain cases.

name: Availability of AIA trials (timing and CBM definition)
description: IPR: from 9 months after patent grant throughout the life of the patent. PGR: from patent grant through 9 months. CBM: same as PGR, but must be a 'covered business method' patent (claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service) and does not include 'technological inventions'.
guidance: Use the specified time windows to determine availability; CBM has subject-matter eligibility limitations (financial/business-method focus, excludes tech inventions).

name: Appeal Brief argument formatting and content (37 C.F.R. § 41.37(c)(iv))
description: Arguments of appellant with respect to each ground of rejection, and the basis therefor, with citations of the statutes, regulations, authorities, and parts of the Record relied on. The arguments shall explain why the examiner erred as to each ground of rejection contested by appellant. Except as provided in §§ 41.41, 41.47 and 41.52, any arguments or authorities not included in the appeal brief will be refused consideration by the Board for purposes of the present appeal. Each ground of rejection contested by appellant must be argued under a separate heading, and each heading shall reasonably identify the ground of rejection being contested (e.g., by claim number, statutory basis, and applied reference, if any).
guidance: Structure arguments under separate headings, include full citations, and anticipate that the Board will refuse to consider anything not included.

name: Paper A syllabus: Specification drafting substantive criteria and marks allocation
description: Paper A requires drafting a specification for filing in Singapore that complies with the Patents Act and Patents Rules. The specification must (a) disclose the invention in a manner clear and complete for a person skilled in the art to perform the invention; and (b) include claims that (i) define the matter for which protection is sought; (ii) are clear and concise; (iii) are supported by the description; (iv) relate to one invention or a group linked as a single inventive concept; (v) have at least one independent claim offering the broadest possible protection and being novel, inventive and industrially applicable; and (vi) include dependent claims for fallback positions.
guidance: Time allowed: 4 hours including reading time. Broad allocation of marks: Independent Claim(s) 50–60 marks; Dependent Claims 20–30 marks; Description 20 marks. References include specific sections of the Patents Act and Patents Rules (listed in Annex A). Candidates are to assume receiving a client letter and pertinent prior art when drafting.

name: Paper B syllabus: Amendment tasks, assumptions and marks allocation
description: Paper B tests amendment of a patent specification: candidates may be required to review the client's reply and draft a response to a Written Opinion (including prior art analysis & argument), provide amended claims and the basis for amendments, and draft a client advice letter.
guidance: Time allowed: 4 hours including reading time. Broad allocation of marks: Draft response to Written Opinion 35 marks; Claim Amendments 35 marks; Client Advice Letter 30 marks. Candidates must accept facts given, assume prior art provided is exhaustive, not use special knowledge, and in some situations may not need to amend the description. Relevant Patents Act/Rules and case law references are provided in Annex A.

name: Paper C syllabus: Infringement and validity advisory criteria and marks
description: Paper C requires advice on infringement and validity of a Singapore patent: claim construction, infringement analysis, validity (including internal validity issues such as sufficiency), and drafting a letter to the client. Candidates must advise on how the patent may be amended to improve the patentee's position and the impact of amendments on prior advice.
guidance: Time allowed: 4 hours including reading time. Broad allocation of marks: Claim Construction 35 marks; Infringement 25 marks; Validity 25 marks; Letter 15 marks. Advice must give clear, logical reasons, cite and apply relevant laws and cases. Candidates must accept facts and provided prior art as exhaustive. Extensive Singapore case law and some UK authorities are listed as references.

name: Confirmation of incorporation by reference (what to submit)
description: The applicant may submit to the receiving Office, within the applicable time limit under Rule 20.7, a written notice confirming that an element or part is incorporated by reference under Rule 4.18, accompanied by: (i) a sheet or sheets embodying the entire element as contained in the earlier application or embodying the part; (ii) where required, a copy of the earlier application as filed; (iii) where language differs, a translation of the earlier application into the language of the international application or into both that language and the language of any required translation; and (iv) for a part of description/claims/drawings, an indication where that part is contained in the earlier application and any translation.
