guidance: Submissions must comply with Rule 4.18 and include complete material or translations as needed to permit the receiving Office to determine whether the element/part is completely contained in the earlier application.

name: Invitation to translate abstract/text matter of drawings (Rule 26.3 ter)
description: Where the abstract or text matter of the drawings is filed in a language different from the language of the description and claims, the receiving Office shall, unless a translation is otherwise required or the abstract/text matter is in the publication language, invite the applicant to furnish a translation into the language of publication. Rules 26.1, 26.2, 26.3, 26.3 bis, 26.5 and 29.1 apply mutatis mutandis.
guidance: There are compatibility exceptions with national law; invitation procedure mirrors other correction invitations. If request does not comply with Rule 12.1(c) the RO shall invite the applicant to file translation to comply.

name: Petitions and matters decided by Supervisory Patent Examiners (SPE)
description: Various authorities delegated to Supervisory Patent Examiners including entry of certain amendments, approval of reopening prosecution after filing appeal brief for new ground entry, certificates of correction requests (except clearly minor clerical errors handled by Certificates of Correction Branch), correction of inventorship errors for patents not in interference, disapproval of certain preliminary amendments and second supplemental amendments, suggested claims for interference purposes, and other specified matters.

name: Petitions decided by Director of International Patent Legal Administration (PCT matters)
description: A broad set of petitions and requests in PCT/international matters: withdrawal of Notice of Acceptance/filing receipt for national stage 35 U.S.C. 371 matters; withdrawal of attorney in PCT Operations; petitions for access to international/national stage applications; fee refund requests; conversion petitions between 35 U.S.C. 371 and 111(a); petitions to withdraw holding of abandonment in PCT Operations; petitions under 37 CFR 1.137 to revive PCT-filed applications; pre-AIA signature acceptance under 1.47/1.42; requests under 1.48/1.28 for inventorship/small entity changes prior to national stage entry; petitions relating to priority claims, filing date matters, drawing problems, Chapter II demands, obvious mistakes, withdrawal; decisions withdrawing examiner’s actions for PCT noncompliance; petitions under PCT Rule 26bis.3 or 37 CFR 1.55/1.78 to restore priority or domestic benefit; petitions to accept delayed priority/domestic benefit claims in national stage applications; PCT-related issues in 111(a) applications; petitions for time extensions under 1.136(b) before International Patent Legal Administration; other PCT matters and requests for PPH participation or Make Special under international agreements.
guidance: Multiple 37 CFR and MPEP citations (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 371, 37 CFR 1.26, 1.181, 1.182, 1.183, PCT Rule 26bis.3); see MPEP § 1002.02(p) and related subsections for details and delegation.

name: ¶ 7.06 Notice re prior art available under both pre-AIA and AIA
description: In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA to pre-AIA) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This form paragraph must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013, that claims priority to, or the benefit of, an application filed before March 16, 2013. (2) This form paragraph should only be used ONCE in an Office action.

name: ¶ 7.20.02.fti Joint Inventors, Common Ownership Presumed
description: When an application names joint inventors, the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were made absent evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and invention dates of each claim not commonly owned so the examiner can consider applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e),(f) or (g) prior art.
guidance: Examiner Note: This paragraph must be used in all applications with joint inventors (unless the claims are clearly restricted to only one claimed invention, e.g., only a single claim is presented in the application).

name: ¶ 7.21.fti Rejection, Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a)
description: Template rejection language: 'Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2].' An explanation of the rejection must follow this form paragraph.
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This paragraph must be preceded by either form paragraph 7.20.fti or form paragraph 7.103. (2) An explanation of the rejection must follow; see MPEP § 2144. (3) If rejection relies upon prior art under pre-AIA 102(e), use pre-AIPA 102(e) as amended by AIPA to determine reference's prior art date unless reference is a US patent issued from international application with filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000; see related form paragraphs (7.12.fti, 7.12.01.fti). (4) If applicability of rejection prevents disqualification under 103(c), form paragraph 7.20.01.fti must follow. (5) If this is a provisional rejection based on a copending application that would comprise prior art under 102(e) if patented/published, use 7.21.01.fti instead. (6) In bracket 1 insert claim numbers; (7) in bracket 2 insert prior art relied upon.

name: ¶ 7.21.01.fti Provisional Rejection, Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), Common Assignee, Common Applicant, or at Least One Common (Joint) Inventor
description: Template stating claim(s) are provisionally rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over copending application No. [2] which has a common [3] with the instant application; the copending application would constitute prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) if published or patented. The provisional rejection is based on presumption of future publication or patenting of the copending application. Applicant may overcome by showing derivation under 37 CFR 1.132, antedating under 37 CFR 1.131(a), or showing disqualification under 103(c).
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) Used to provisionally reject claims not patentably distinct from disclosure in a copending application that would be prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) if published/issued and also has a common assignee, common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118), or at least one common inventor. Should not be used when copending application is disqualified under pre-AIA 103(c). See MPEP § 2146.03(a). (2) Use pre-AIA 102(e) as amended by AIPA to determine copending application's prior art date unless copending application is based on an international application with filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000. (3) If claimed invention is fully disclosed in copending application, use paragraph 7.15.01.fti. (4) In bracket 1 insert claim numbers; bracket 2 application number; bracket 3 --assignee--, --applicant--, or --joint inventor--. (5) In bracket 4 insert an explanation of obviousness; see MPEP § 2144. (6) If not patentably distinct from invention claimed in copending application, add provisional obviousness double patenting rejection using form paragraphs 8.33 and 8.37. (7) Additionally make a rejection under 103(a) using 7.21.fti if evidence indicates copending application is also prior art under 102(f) or (g) and copending application not disqualified under 103(c).

name: ¶ 7.21.02.fti Rejection, Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), Common Assignee, Common Applicant, or at Least One Common (Joint) Inventor
description: Template: 'Claim [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over [2]. The applied reference has a common [3] with the instant application. Based upon the pre-AIA 102(e) date of the reference, it constitutes prior art.'
guidance: This rejection might be overcome by: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that any invention disclosed but not claimed in the reference was derived from the inventor of this application; (2) showing a date of invention for the claimed subject matter corresponding to subject matter disclosed but not claimed in the reference under 37 CFR 1.131(a); or (3) an oath/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) stating that the application and reference are currently owned by the same party and that the inventive entity named is the prior inventor under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 104 (as in effect Mar 15, 2013), together with a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c). This rejection might also be overcome by showing the reference is disqualified under pre-AIA 103(c). See MPEP § 2146 et seq. Examiner Notes: (1) Use when rejecting over a reference that discloses the claimed invention and only qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e). Do not use if the reference qualifies under 102(a) or (b) (use 7.21.fti instead). Reference must have common assignee, common applicant, or at least one common inventor. (2) Guidance on applying pre-AIA vs pre-AIPA 102(e) dates and related bracket insertions: bracket 1 = claim numbers; bracket 2 = prior art references; bracket 3 = --assignee--, --applicant--, or --joint inventor--; bracket 4 = explanation of obviousness (see MPEP § 2144).

name: ¶ 7.22.fti Rejection, Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), Further in View Of
description: Template: 'Claim [1] rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2] as applied to claim [3] above, and further in view of [4].'
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21.fti. (2) An explanation of the rejection must follow; see MPEP § 2144. (3) If the rejection relies upon prior art under pre-AIA 102(e), apply pre-AIPA 102(e) rules to determine reference's date as described elsewhere (see form paragraphs 7.12.fti and 7.12.01.fti). Insert appropriate claim/reference identifiers in brackets.

name: ¶ 7.23.fti Test for Obviousness
description: Summarizes the factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a): (1) Determining the scope and contents of the prior art. (2) Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue. (3) Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. (4) Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
guidance: Examiner Note: This form paragraph may be used, if appropriate, in response to an argument regarding the applicability of the factors for determining obviousness. These four Graham factors form the core factual inquiries supporting a prima facie case of obviousness and must be addressed in the explanation of rejections (see MPEP § 2144 for supporting rationale).

name: ¶ 7.27.fti Rejection, Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a)
description: Template allowing a combined rejection: 'Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 ([2]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over [3].'
guidance: Examiner Note: (1) Not intended to be commonly used as substitute for a rejection under 102; prefer single rejection under either 102 or 103(a) when possible using appropriate form paragraphs. (2) Examples where paragraph may be used: dispute in claim interpretation (different interpretations lead to 102 vs 103), reference discloses all limitations except a property/function where inherent possession unclear (In re Fitzgerald), genus-species situations where species may be obvious even if genus not anticipatory (In re Schaumann), product-by-process issues (In re Marosi, In re Thorpe), means-plus-function uncertainty, overlapping ranges. (3) If claim interpretation renders claim indefinite, consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). (4) Bracket instructions: bracket 1 = claim numbers; bracket 2 = appropriate paragraph letters; bracket 3 = prior art reference relied upon. (5) A full explanation should follow. (6) If relying on pre-AIA 102(e), apply pre-AIPA rules as described elsewhere. (7) Must be preceded by 7.07.fti and appropriate supporting form paragraphs (7.08.fti-7.14.fti) and form paragraph 7.20.fti or 7.103. (8) For transition applications with filing/priority complexities, include form paragraph 7.06 when required.

name: Burden and standard for damages
description: The patent holder must prove each element of its damages claim, including the amount of damages, by a 'preponderance of the evidence.' Damages must be adequate to compensate the patent holder and put it in approximately the same financial position it would have been in absent infringement.
guidance: Damages need not be proven with mathematical precision but must be shown with reasonable certainty. Damages must compensate, not punish; the jury may not add anything to penalize the infringer or to set an example. (Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §284; Lucent; Aro; Riles; Ericsson v. D-Link.)

name: Factor One — Incremental value contributed by the claimed invention
description: The patent holder is entitled to recover damages not greater than the cost to the accused infringer of its best alternative to the claimed invention at the negotiation time, plus the value of any additional benefit the claimed invention contributes over that best alternative.
guidance: Determining incremental value requires a baseline: consider whether a commercially acceptable non-infringing alternative was available at the time. If a non-infringing alternative existed, the royalty cannot exceed the invention's incremental value over that alternative. Do not include 'switching costs' (e.g., redesign, retooling, inventory elimination) because the hypothetical negotiation is before the infringer invested in the technology. Authorities: Garretson; Minco; Ericsson; Microsoft v. Motorola; AstraZeneca.

name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR) — narrow application
description: The entire market value rule allows a patentee, in rare circumstances, to recover a royalty based on the value of an entire multi-feature product even when the asserted patent covers only one feature or technology.
guidance: EMVR applies only if the patentee proves the claimed invention is the sole basis driving customer demand for the entire product (or, if modified, that the novel elements in the asserted claim are the sole basis driving demand). If the patentee cannot make that proof, damages must be based on the smallest saleable unit. Authorities: VirnetX; Uniloc; Lucent.

name: Comparability factors to evaluate prior licenses
description: When deciding whether a license agreement is technologically and economically comparable, consider multiple dimensions of similarity between the prior license and the hypothetical license.
guidance: List of factors provided: (1) similarity of negotiating circumstances (arms-length, no litigation threat); (2) similarity of license structure to hypothetical license; (3) similarity of patents covered; (4) similarity of products covered; (5) whether other product features/technologies affect comparability; (6) whether other relationships or consideration exchanged affected terms; (7) similarity of relationship between the parties; (8) timing of the agreement relative to when the licensee adopted the technology or standard (post-adoption may reflect lock-in and should be adjusted); (9) whether market circumstances at license time differ from the hypothetical negotiation time. Also: if a license bases royalty on an entire multi-component product, the jury should admit it only if comparable and must apportion out value not attributable to the claimed invention. Authorities: Apple v. Motorola; Ericsson; LaserDynamics; ResQNet; Finjan; Lucent; Wordtech.

name: Redetermination when applicant amends after expedited determination
description: If applicant amends claims after a determination on expedited examination so that claims differ from prior explanations/foreign-recognized claims/international search conclusions, examiner may instruct corrections and re-determine eligibility.
guidance: If an applicant amended a specification with claims not included in the explanation on comparison with prior art, or claims not substantially identical with claims a foreign patent recognizes to be patentable, or claims not substantially identical with claims decided to meet novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability in international search/examination, the examiner may instruct corrections for the expedited-exam request and re-determine whether to permit expedited examination. Examiner may grant a correction order designating a period up to one month at his discretion.

name: Expedited examination without redetermination when full correspondence provided
description: If applicant submits a comparison explanation covering all claims (including amended ones) against prior art cited by a foreign office, or correspondence with claims recognized patentable by a foreign office, or claims meeting requirements in international search/examination, expedited examination shall proceed without redetermination.
guidance: Where applicant submits explanation on comparison between all claims (including amended) and prior art cited in foreign examination notifications; or correspondence with claims recognized to be patentable by a foreign office; or correspondence with claims meeting novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability in international search/examination, expedited examination shall be conducted without undertaking re-determination.

name: Determination based on authorized prior-art search report
description: Where a prior-art search report is submitted by an authorized institute, the examiner shall make a determination on expedited examination; identical claims between the application and the search report support recognition of the request.
guidance: If the authorized institute fails to meet the guideline for writing the report and the report cannot be used, the examiner shall issue a correction order within the designated period and may reject the expedited-exam request if the search report is not corrected. A written explanation for the request must be attached unless the application is marked as having requested prior-art search and the written request includes institute name and date.

name: Use of parent prior-art search report for divisional expedited requests
description: If expedited examination was determined for the parent based on authorized prior-art search reports and all claims of a divisional were already examined in that parent report, a request for expedited examination on the divisional can be filed without additional prior-art search, subject to showing claims identity and inclusion in the parent's search report.
guidance: Applicant should submit a contrastive explanation indicating claims of divisional are identical to parent claims and a written explanation that the divisional's prior-art search results are included in the parent's report. If examiner finds that search results do not cover all divisional claims, a correction order is issued; if deficiencies persist, the expedited-exam request may be rejected; deficiencies addressed (e.g., by submitting additional authorized search report) allow the examiner to decide on expedited examination.

name: Handling cases where specification amended after commission of prior-art search
description: If a prior-art search was conducted based on pre-amended claims and the specification was amended before filing the expedited request, a re-submitted search report at the time of filing may affect determination.
guidance: Where prior-art search was commissioned to an authorized institute, a request for expedited examination is filed after amendment to the claims, and the institute conducted search on pre-amended claims, resubmission of the search report at filing after correction order allows the examiner to make a determination on expedited examination.

name: Evaluation criteria for appropriateness of amendments submitted with appeal
description: Amendments filed within 30 days must correspond to those necessitated by final rejection; must be within the scope of originally filed specification/drawings, and claim-scope amendments should be narrowing, clerical corrections, clarifications of ambiguity, or permissible reinstatements per statutory exceptions.
guidance: Specifically: (i) amendments must be within the scope of originally filed specification/drawings; (ii) claim-scope amendments count as: 1) narrowing by restriction/deletion/adding an element; 2) clerical error correction; 3) clarifying ambiguous description; 4) amendments beyond scope of paragraph 47(2) to reinstate earlier claims or amend in accordance with listed subparagraphs. If amendments do not satisfy requirements or give rise to new grounds for rejection, the amendment shall be refused entry. Criteria for evaluating requirements and scope refer to Chapter 2 Part 4 of the Examination Guidelines.

name: Refusal to enter illegitimate amendments and comparison rules
description: Amendment may be refused entry where it does not comply with Article 47(2)-(3) or where new grounds for rejection arise; evaluation of new matter and scope uses comparisons to specific prior versions of the specification/drawings depending on procedural posture.
guidance: Notes: If previously notified grounds for rejection are not overcome but no new grounds arise, the amendment may be accepted but the original rejection stands. If new grounds arise from the amendment, the amendment shall be refused entry and review proceeds based on the specification prior to amendment. For purposes of assessing introduction of new matter (Article 47(2)), compare with the originally filed specification/drawings; for Article 47(3) requirements compare with the specification/drawings of the immediately prior amendment (amendment II). Whether claim scope is narrowed is determined by comparing corresponding claims between the prior amendment and the new amendment. Several scenarios (amendments I/II/III/IV, refusal to enter, timing of notices) govern which comparison baseline applies.

name: Claims — form and types
description: Claims are the operative part of a patent; claims may be in varied forms depending on subject matter (machine, manufacture, composition, process, design). Particularity in descriptions and claims is a condition precedent to validity.
guidance: Includes claims in machine patents, methods of specifying parts, claims in manufactures/compositions/processes, design claims; generic vs specific claims; plurality of inventions in one patent; double patenting; particularity and sufficiency are factual questions.

name: Construction of letters patent / claim construction principles
description: Claims must be construed to determine their scope; construction involves legal rules and takes into account specification, drawings, application papers, contemporaneous statutes, prior art, and usage.
guidance: Claims construed in light of the descriptions and prior state of the art; functional claims, claims with reference letters/numerals; proper liberality vs proper strictness of construction; breadth governed by extent of use; construction in light of application papers and Patent Office limitations; questions of construction are issues of law.

name: Particularity and sufficiency of description
description: The description (specification) must be sufficiently particular and full to support the claims and to enable skilled persons to carry out the invention.
guidance: Particularity and sufficiency are conditions precedent to validity; sufficiency and particularity are questions of fact; claim language 'substantially as described' and how implied; deceitfully lacking or excessive specification and remedies and pleading in law and equity.

name: Disclaimers — statutory authorization and proper use
description: Statutory authorization exists for filing disclaimers to correct errors in patents; disclaimers affect scope and ownership interests.
guidance: Explains errors that justify disclaimers (mistakes of fact relevant to novelty, mistakes of law relevant to invention), proper vs improper disclaimers, reissue claims, fraudulent or deceptive intention, effect of unreasonable delay in filing disclaimer, construction of a patent after disclaimer, disclaimers filed during litigation, and disclaimers required by judicial decisions.

name: Reissues — grounds and limits
description: Reissue of a patent is available to correct defects (insufficiency, errors) but must comply with statutory and judicially imposed limits (same invention, no new matter, etc.).
guidance: History of reissue statutes; subjects of reissue; definitions of 'specification', 'defective', 'insufficient'; faults justifying reissue; broadened and narrowed reissues; inadvertence, mistake and delay doctrines (e.g., Miller v. Brass Co.); same-invention requirement, new matter prohibition; reissues as construed liberally in some respects; reissues may be valid as to some claims and void as to others.

name: Doctrine of equivalents and equivalents in compositions/processes
description: The doctrine of equivalents applies to determine infringement when accused device/process does not literally practice all claim elements but performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain the same result.
guidance: Discusses equivalents in processes and machines, substitution of equivalents, primary and secondary inventions, necessity of change in equivalents, secondary patents, disclaimers of particular equivalents, substitution of ingredients in compositions (equivalent and non-equivalent ingredients), and cases such as Giant-Powder.

name: Standards for sufficiency of claim breadth and plurality of inventions
description: Limits on claiming multiple inventions in a single patent and on claim breadth; double patenting issues and when plural inventions may be improper.
guidance: Plurality of inventions in one patent is addressed; double patenting doctrine; reissues and sub-combination claims; when sub-combinations may be properly claimed.

name: RCE not available after filing of notice of appeal to Federal Circuit or commencement of civil action (unless terminated)
description: 37 CFR 1.114 is not available in an application after filing of a Notice of Appeal to the Federal Circuit or commencement of a civil action in district court unless the appeal/civil action is terminated and the application is still pending.
guidance: If an RCE is filed after court review, examiner should bring the application to SPE or special program examiner to determine propriety. Unless application contains allowed claims (or court mandate indicates Office action), termination of unsuccessful court review results in abandonment. See MPEP § 1216.01.

name: When rejecting claims for novelty/obviousness, cite best references and explain pertinence
description: In rejecting claims for want of novelty or obviousness, the examiner must cite the best references available. When a reference is complex or shows other inventions, designate the particular part relied on as nearly as practicable and clearly explain the pertinence of each reference and specify each rejected claim.
guidance: For rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, set out how a reference is modified or how plural references are combined. Include particular figures/pages/paragraphs when necessary to provide adequate information.

name: Examiner may rely on applicant admissions and facts within examiner's knowledge
description: In rejecting claims, the examiner may rely upon admissions by the applicant (or patent owner in reexamination) and, for applications, may rely upon facts within the examiner's knowledge pursuant to 37 CFR 1.104(d)(2).
guidance: When a rejection is based on facts within an Office employee's personal knowledge, the data shall be as specific as possible and, when called for by the applicant, supported by an affidavit of such employee, subject to contradiction/explanation by applicant affidavits.

name: Use of 102(e)/(f)/(g) subject matter as prior art and joint research agreement exception
description: Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) may be used as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103 unless the entire rights were commonly owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment at the time the claimed invention was made; joint research agreement conditions can establish common ownership.
guidance: To overcome a 103 rejection based on such prior art via 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2), the applicant must provide a statement that the prior art and claimed invention were made by parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date of invention and that the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of that agreement.

name: Reasons for allowance must be documented and may be communicated
description: If the examiner believes the record does not make clear reasons for allowing claims, the examiner may set forth such reasoning, incorporate it into an Office action rejecting other claims or communicate it separately to applicant. Applicant may file a statement commenting on the reasons for allowance within a specified time.
guidance: Failure by the examiner to respond to any statement commenting on reasons for allowance does not give rise to any implication.

name: Particularity requirement for petitions (35 U.S.C. §312(a)(3))
description: "the petition identifies, in writing and with particularity, each claim challenged, the grounds on which the challenge to each claim is based, and the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim."
guidance: A petitioner must explain specifically how the references would be combined to produce the claimed invention; merely reciting individual teachings without tying them to particular limitations is insufficient. (Text cites §312(a)(3) and Lowe’s v. Epistar.)

name: Clear, evidence-supported account of the contemplated workings of the combination
description: A 'clear, evidence-supported account of the contemplated workings of the combination is a prerequisite' to adequately explain and support a conclusion that a skilled artisan would be motivated to combine and reasonably expect success (Personal Web Techs.).
guidance: Petitioners should explain which portions of each reference correspond to which claim limitations and how the combined system would operate. Anti-pattern: describing references individually without showing how their teachings interact to meet claim limitations.

name: No pick-and-choose / mix-and-match approach
description: A petitioner cannot merely show that elements of a claim were independently known in the prior art; the Board disfavors an approach that asks the factfinder to interpret which parts of multiple references would be combined without a clear roadmap.
guidance: Cite specific passages showing which reference supplies each limitation. Avoid broad citations spanning many columns/pages and then asking the Board to infer the combination. Case cites: KSR, Personal Web, Trend Micro, Lyft.

name: Specificity for showing discrete claim limitations
description: For each limitation, the petitioner must tie claimed language to specific disclosure in the prior art or show obviousness of the limitation with reasoning.
guidance: Patent Owner criticized petitions that assert Kaplan-Bryant combinations but fail to state which reference supports which limitation (illustrated by the PO's table mapping limitations to petition discussion). The Board looks to the petition plus any roadmap pages to determine sufficiency.

name: Use of pointers/indexed databases supports certain functional claim effects
description: Disclosures showing an indexed database with pointers to a single physical file support claim limitations concerning representation of the same object in multiple collections and deletion semantics (i.e., deleting a pointer vs physical file).
guidance: Kaplan's ¶44 (indexed file stores a pointer) was persuasive to the Board to show limitation 1[l]/9[j] where a single physical file can be represented in multiple collections such that deleting from one collection need not delete the file from another.

name: Petition roadmap can cure apparent pick-and-choose gaps
description: A petition's general roadmap pages that explain the proposed combination can supply the detail missing from per-claim explanations, and the Board will read specific claim analyses in light of that roadmap.
guidance: Patent Owner argued the petition inconsistently relied on Kaplan or Bryant for various limitations; the Board found the petition's pages 66–70 provided a sufficient roadmap tying references together for the per-claim analyses.

name: Include claim variants at filing/first reply
description: Applicants are encouraged to include, at the time of filing or no later than the first reply, claims varying from the broadest to the most detailed that the applicant is willing to accept.
guidance: Providing claim variations early can alleviate prosecution difficulties and is beneficial for both Office and applicant.

name: Showing required for amendments after final (37 CFR 1.116(c))
description: Except where an amendment merely cancels claims, adopts examiner suggestions, removes issues for appeal, or otherwise requires only cursory review, compliance with the requirement of a showing under 37 CFR 1.116(c) is expected in all amendments after final rejection.
guidance: Failure to provide the proper showing will support refusal to enter the amendment; refusal should not be arbitrary and should be concisely stated.

name: Grounds for specific advisory paragraphs refusing entry
description: Specific form paragraphs address grounds for refusing entry, including: lack of showing why amendment necessary and not earlier presented (7.72); raises new issues requiring further consideration/search (7.73); amendment not improving form for appeal (7.75); additional claims without canceling corresponding finally rejected claims (7.76); proposed new claims would be allowable only if filed separately (7.78); affidavits/exhibits considered but do not overcome rejection (7.79); affidavits/exhibits not considered for failure to show earlier presentation (7.80).
guidance: When using these paragraphs, follow the examiner notes to identify claims, provide explanations, and include transitional provisions if applicable (e.g., 37 CFR 1.129(a)).

name: 37 CFR 1.312 amendments after allowance (requirements)
description: No amendment may be made as a matter of right after mailing of the notice of allowance. Any amendment under 37 CFR 1.312 must be filed before or with payment of the issue fee and may be entered on recommendation of the primary examiner, approved by the Commissioner.
guidance: Examples of amendments that fall within 1.312 include amendments to the specification, changes in drawings, amendments to the claims, changes in inventorship, submission of prior art, etc. The amendment must be filed on or before the date the issue fee is paid. Approval authority for recommendations under 1.312 is delegated to SPEs.

name: Characteristic Feature Statement (permissible form)
description: A 'characteristic features' statement describing a particular feature of novelty or nonobviousness in the claimed design may be permissible in the specification. Such a statement should be in terms such as 'The characteristic feature of the design resides in [1],' or if combined with one of the Figure descriptions, in terms such as 'the characteristic feature of which resides in [2].'
guidance: May serve later to limit the claim (McGrady v. Aspenglas). Examiner Note: insert brief but accurate description of the feature of novelty or nonobviousness in brackets 1 and 2.

name: Feature Statement Caution — overall appearance controls
description: Inclusion of a feature statement in the specification is noted. However, the patentability of the claimed design is not based on the specified feature but rather on a comparison of the overall appearance of the design with the prior art.
guidance: Cite In re Leslie. Do not treat a characteristic feature statement as determinative of design patentability; assess total/overall appearance against prior art.

name: Necessity for Good Drawings
description: The drawing constitutes the whole disclosure of the design; it must be so well executed in clarity and completeness that nothing regarding the design sought to be patented is left to conjecture.
guidance: Insufficient drawings may be fatal to validity (35 U.S.C. 112(a)) and may negatively affect effective filing date of continuations. Emphasize clear, complete drawings showing claimed subject matter.

name: Required Description Statement for Broken Lines
description: A statement similar to: 'The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design.' should be inserted in the specification preceding the claim.
guidance: In bracket 1 insert name of structure. In bracket 2 insert 'portions of the “article”' or 'environmental structure.' Do not use in international design applications. Ensure proper tense in bracket 3 ('must be' or 'has been').

name: Separate Figure When Broken Lines Obscure Full-Line Disclosure
description: Where superimposed broken lines showing environmental structure obscure the full line disclosure of the claimed design, a separate figure showing the broken lines must be included in the drawing in addition to the figures showing only claimed subject matter.
guidance: This avoids obscuring the claimed design and ensures clarity of what is claimed in solid lines (35 U.S.C.112(a)).

name: Rejection for New Matter — 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (Design)
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as failing to comply with the description requirement since the [1] introduces new matter not supported by the original disclosure. The original disclosure does not reasonably convey to a designer of ordinary skill that applicant was in possession of the design now claimed at filing.
guidance: Cite In re Daniels; In re Rasmussen. Specify in bracket 1 whether new drawing or amendment to drawing/title/spec. In bracket 2 specifically identify the new matter. Suggest ways to overcome (e.g., correct bracket in figures or delete descriptive statement).

name: Trademark Material in Drawing — Specification Amendment Required
description: If trademark material forms part of the claimed design, the specification must be amended to include a statement preceding the claim identifying the trademark material and the name of the owner of the trademark.
guidance: Examiner Note: identify trademark material in bracket 1 and trademark owner in bracket 2.

name: Claim Wording Requirements — 'As Shown' and 'As Shown and Described'
description: For proper form (37 CFR 1.153 or 1.1025), claims should read: '[I/We] claim: The ornamental design for [article] as shown.' or '... as shown and described.'
guidance: In bracket 1 insert 'must be' or 'has been' as appropriate; bracket 2 insert 'I' or 'We'; bracket 3 insert title of article. Use correct statutory/formal wording to avoid rejection under 35 U.S.C.112(b) or form rejections.

name: Rationale for 35 U.S.C. 103 Rejection (Single Reference)
description: It would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill not later than the effective filing date of the present claimed invention to [1] (or pre-AIA wording: 'at the time the invention was made to [1]').
guidance: Insert explanation of the use of the reference in bracket 1. For design patents, explain how the primary reference teaches the claimed appearance and why it renders claims obvious.

name: Remove Indefinite Language ('or the like') by Examiner’s Amendment
description: The phrase [1] in the claim following the title renders the claim indefinite. By authorization of [2] in a telephone interview on [3], the phrase has been cancelled from the claim and at each occurrence throughout the papers.
guidance: In bracket 1 insert objectionable phrase (e.g., 'or the like'). Use Ex parte Pappas precedent. Note exemptions for oath/declaration per 35 U.S.C.112(b) and 37 CFR 1.153.

name: Plant Patent — Rejection for Non-Support for Colors (35 U.S.C.112(a))
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C.112(a) as being unsupported by a clear and complete disclosure with regard to [1] colors, for the following reasons: [2].
guidance: Specify color-related deficiencies and reasons in brackets.

name: Generic 35 U.S.C.112 Rejection Form — 35 U.S.C.112 Rejection Paragraph
description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C.112 [1] because [2].
guidance: Use to state specific statutory deficiency and reasoning in bracket 2; add detailed reasoning in bracket 3 as needed.

name: PCT — Unity of Invention Requirement
description: An international application shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept. 'Special technical features' are those technical features that define a contribution which each of the claimed inventions makes over the prior art.
guidance: Determine unity without regard to claim format. For multiple categories, unity present only for permitted combinations (product+manufacture process, product+use, product+process+use, process+apparatus, product+process+apparatus). Follow with lack-of-unity form paragraphs (18.06 etc.) when not met. Use PCT Rule 13.1/13.2 and 37 CFR 1.475.

name: PCT — Markush Group Alternatives of Chemical Compounds Not of Similar Nature (unity test for Markush)
description: When a single claim defines alternatives of a Markush group of chemical compounds, alternatives are of a similar nature if: (A) all alternatives have a common property or activity; AND (B)(1) a common structure is present (a significant structural element shared by all alternatives); OR (B)(2) if common structure cannot unify, all alternatives belong to a recognized class of chemical compounds in the art.
guidance: Use this two-part test to determine if Markush alternatives meet unity; if not, lack of unity applies.

name: Suggestion/motivation and expectation must be founded in prior art, not applicant's disclosure
description: "Both the suggestion and the expectation of success must be founded in the prior art, not in the applicant’s disclosure." In re Dow Chemical Co., 837 F.2d 469, 473 (Fed. Cir. 1988).
guidance: Arguments that rely on the patent specification or the patentee's own work to supply the reason to combine or the expectation of success are improper. The rationale for combining references and any claimed predictability must be supported by the prior art record.

name: Anticipation requires every element in a single reference (express or inherent)
description: For a claim to be anticipated, each claim element must be disclosed, either expressly or inherently, in a single prior art reference, and the claimed arrangement or combination of those elements must also be disclosed, either expressly or inherently, in that same prior art reference. Therasense, Inc. v. Becton, Dickinson and Co., 593 F.3d 1325, 1332–33 (Fed. Cir. 2010); Sanofi‑Synthelabo v. Apotex, Inc., 550 F.3d 1075, 1082 (Fed. Cir. 2008).
guidance: Anticipation is a strict, four-corners test: every limitation must be found in a single prior art reference. Where an element is not expressly disclosed, analyze whether it is inherently disclosed (see inherency standard).

name: Inherency standard for anticipation: 'necessarily present' / 'unavoidably teaches'
description: A reference may anticipate inherently if a claim limitation that is not expressly disclosed 'is necessarily present, or inherent, in the single anticipating reference.' The very essence of inherency is that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize that a reference unavoidably teaches the property in question. Verizon Servs. Corp. v. Cox Fibernet Va., Inc., 602 F.3d 1325, 1337 (Fed. Cir. 2010); Agilent Techs., Inc. v. Affymetrix, Inc., 567 F.3d 1366, 1383 (Fed. Cir. 2009).
guidance: Inherency requires inevitability — the missing limitation must be necessarily present, not merely possible or likely. If the reference allows alternative implementations that would not include the limitation (e.g., multiple injections instead of a single-device 162 mg dose), inherency is not satisfied.

name: Claim construction principle: do not import limitations from the specification
description: A claim should not be limited by reciting unclaimed specifics from the specification (e.g., importing a particular disease into a claim that does not recite it). Acceleration Bay, LLC v. Activision Blizzard Inc., 908 F.3d 765, 771 (Fed. Cir. 2018).
guidance: When evaluating prior art or claim scope, assess the claim language itself; avoid reading examples or preferred embodiments in the specification into the claim unless the claim expressly includes those limitations.

name: Section 2A: Is the claim directed to a product of nature?
description: Section 2A requires the Examiner to analyze whether or not the claim is directed to a natural product. If there is more than one claim element that could be a natural product, they are to be evaluated to see if they occur together in nature. If they do not, the components are each compared to their closest naturally occurring counterpart to see if any of the components is clearly not a product of nature.
guidance: Evaluate each potentially nature-based claim element independently and in combination; determine whether the claimed combination or each component as claimed has a counterpart in nature. Use factual comparisons to closest natural counterparts; do not shortcut by conflating with anticipation/obviousness analysis.

name: Markedly different characteristics requirement (2A analysis)
description: If none of the claim elements is clearly not a product of nature, the nature-based combination is examined to see if the combination of components has 'markedly different' characteristics due to the interactions in the combination.
guidance: Marked difference typically requires evidence of some change in physical or chemical properties (for a single nature-based product) or evidence of interaction between multiple natural products. Examples: changes in oxidative stability when ratios change; functional/structural changes attributable to formulation or delivery form.

name: Carriers/non-natural components can render claim patent-eligible
description: Carriers for a natural product that is the active ingredient, which are not themselves natural products (e.g., nanoparticles), will often have structural and physical characteristics that distinguish them from their closest natural counterparts and therefore can render a claim patent-eligible.
guidance: Identify whether claimed carriers or excipients possess structural/physical properties not found in nature. If so, the inquiry under 2A can end in favor of eligibility. Cite Examples 3 and 4 of the Interim Examination Guidelines as support.

name: Step 2B "inventive concept" standard
description: Under Step 2B the claim must possess a further 'inventive concept' that renders it 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (the nature-based product).
guidance: The PTO Guidelines say inventive-concept questions should not be decided on the basis of §§102/103 analysis, but in practice courts/boards often rely on prior-art style reasoning. Be prepared to show functional/structural features that add significantly more than mere natural phenomena or routine activity.

name: Plain-words claim construction in §101 context
description: Claims must be examined by the plain words of the claims in context of surrounding words (e.g., 'contained in one or more complementing casings providing controlled delivery of the formulation to a subject' should be treated as recited).
guidance: Do not collapse or paraphrase a detailed claim limitation into a generic term (e.g., reducing the quoted casing language to 'casing') when assessing whether a limitation is a non-natural element or imparts structure/function for §101 purposes.

name: Anticipation requires same part-to-part relationship; 'intermixtures' must be disclosed
description: Anticipation law requires the same part-to-part relationship; references that do not disclose the claimed intermixtures or specific ratios do not anticipate.
guidance: When arguing against an anticipation rejection, show that prior art does not disclose the claimed combination or the particular quantitative ranges/ratios and that the references fail to disclose intermixtures in the claimed manner.

name: Dosage and controlled-delivery limitations can be non-natural, functional/structural additions
description: Limitations reciting 'dosage' and 'casings providing controlled delivery' may not exist in nature and can change characteristics of natural products (e.g., avoid concentrated delivery of specific phytochemicals that may be harmful).
guidance: Use evidence showing natural products lack predictable dosages or controlled delivery (e.g., lipid profiles in natural sources are variable) to support that claimed dosage/delivery limitations add 'significantly more' or at least satisfy 2A marked-difference analysis.

name: Claimed specific ratios/concentrations support non-nature and patentability if not found in nature
description: Claims reciting specific ratios of polyunsaturated, monounsaturated, and saturated fatty acids (or specific omega-6/omega-3 ranges) that are NOT known in nature can distinguish the claims from natural products.
guidance: Point out examiner failures when no prior product or oil is cited that meets the claimed ratios; provide comparative compositional data to show claimed ranges are novel relative to natural sources such as olive or walnut oil.

name: Collecting/analyzing/displaying/manipulating information (abstract idea)
description: Claims directed to concepts such as collecting, displaying, manipulating, analyzing, recognizing, and storing information are abstract ideas (e.g., data collection, recognition and storage).
guidance: Court examples: Alice (claims requiring a computer that processed streams of bits found abstract); FairWarning (collecting access information, applying rules to detect misuse, and notifying users found to be an abstract idea); other cited examples include: (i) collecting, displaying, and manipulating data (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One); (ii) collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying results (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); (iii) creating an index and using it to search/retrieve data (Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem.); (iv) determining a price using organizational/product hierarchies (Versata v. SAP); (v) encoding and decoding image data (RecogniCorp v. Nintendo); (vi) organizing information through mathematical correlations (Digitech Image Techs. v. Electronics for Imaging); (vii) relaying mailing address data (Return Mail, Inc. v. USPS); (viii) retaining information in navigation of online forms (Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). The Office treats these kinds of information-processing concepts as abstract ideas in Step 2A.

name: Concepts having no particular concrete or tangible form (idea abstraction)
description: Claims that recite a combination of steps constituting an idea with no particular concrete or tangible form are directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Examples: Ultramercial (an eleven-step method for displaying an ad in exchange for access to copyrighted media — characterized as 'an idea, having no particular concrete or tangible form' described as 'using advertising as an exchange or currency'); Versata (determining price using hierarchies described as a building block/basic conceptual framework); In re Brown (method of allocating hair weight described as the abstract idea of assigning hair designs to balance head shape). Such claims are treated as abstract ideas and evaluated under Step 2A.

name: Performing mathematical calculations (abstract idea)
description: Claims that are essentially directed to performing mathematical calculations or manipulating mathematical results are considered directed to an abstract idea.
guidance: Examples: Bancorp (claims for managing life insurance policies by performing calculations and manipulating results were seen as the abstract idea of managing such a policy by computation); Digitech (claims generating and manipulating data using mathematical formulas and organizing the information into a new form were directed to organizing information through mathematical correlations). The Office looks to the specification and claimed steps to determine whether the claimed subject matter is mere mathematical computation and thus an abstract idea under Step 2A.

name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena (judicial exceptions)
description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena (including naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that do not have markedly different characteristics) are judicial exceptions and are not patentable by themselves.
guidance: The courts view basic tools of scientific and technological work as not patentable. Examples identified as laws of nature/natural phenomena include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), correlations between genetic variations and alleles, metabolic correlations (Mayo), presence of biomarkers correlated with disease (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), electromagnetism (O’Reilly v. Morse), qualities of bacteria (Funk Bros.), primers (Ambry Genetics), chemical principles (Tilghman v. Proctor), and existence of cffDNA (Ariosa v. Sequenom). The guidance notes that not every claim describing a natural ability or response is directed to a law of nature (e.g., treatment methods applying a principle may be eligible). A claim that recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon is Step 2A: YES and requires Step 2B analysis to determine whether there is a patent-eligible application.

name: Products of nature (judicial exception)
description: Physical products that are naturally occurring, or non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from naturally occurring counterparts, are products of nature and are exceptions to patent-eligible subject matter.
guidance: Court examples: isolated DNA and cDNA (Myriad), cloned farm animals (Roslin), primers (Ambry), and similar illustrations. The guidance emphasizes that synthetic or human-made products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts remain products of nature. The Office treats 'product of nature' exceptions inclusively under Step 2A and instructs examiners to use the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to determine whether a claimed nature-based product limitation is an exception. If a claim to a nature-based product is broad enough under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to encompass unmarkedly-different embodiments that are products of nature, examiners should consider pointing out the BRI and recommending narrowing amendments where appropriate.

name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (how and when to apply)
description: The markedly different characteristics analysis compares a claimed nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to determine whether the product possesses markedly different characteristics (structure, function, and/or other properties). This analysis is part of Step 2A to identify product-of-nature exceptions.
guidance: Key points and procedures: - Purpose: If a nature-based product has markedly different characteristics, it is not a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: NO) and may not require Step 2B unless another exception is recited. If it lacks markedly different characteristics, it is a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: YES) and Step 2B is required. - Scope: Apply the analysis only to nature-based product limitations in the claim (not to non-nature-based claim elements). For claims to a nature-based product by itself, analyze the entire product. For a nature-based combination (multiple components), analyze the resultant nature-based combination. For a claim including a nature-based product plus non-nature-based elements, analyze only the nature-based product limitation; additional elements are evaluated in Step 2B. - Product-by-process: Determine whether the claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart (see MPEP §2113). - Process claims: Generally, do not apply the markedly different analysis to process claims because the focus is on active process steps, not products used; however, if a process claim is drafted such that it is substantively indistinguishable from a product claim (i.e., effectively claims the product), then apply the analysis to the recited nature-based product. - Selecting counterparts: Compare the nature-based product to the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state (e.g., for a derivative chemical, compare to the original natural chemical; for a nucleic acid derived from a gene, compare to that gene strand). When multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart. - Characteristics for analysis: Consider structure, function, and other properties; evaluate on a case-by-case basis using what is recited in the claim and the specification. - Practical note: If the claimed nature-based product is by definition naturally occurring, no analysis beyond recognizing it is necessary. Examiners should consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106.06) is appropriate for claims that recite nature-based products but clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception.

name: Non-technical features may be included in the problem only if known or obvious
description: Novel non-technical features should not be incorporated into the statement of the problem unless their inclusion is known or would have been obvious from what was made available to the public before the priority date.
guidance: This is the proposed modification of the Comvik 'second rule': the mere presence of a non-technical aim in a claim does not justify adding it to the problem unless it is part of the prior art. Legal consequence: findings of obviousness cannot be based on features not in the state of the art. Examples/contrast: decision T 2063/09 (BlackBerry) where a non-technical data-limit feature was added to the problem; guidelines' earlier comment that 'requirements specification is not prior art' is inconsistent with Article 56 and has been removed.

name: Problem formulation must avoid pointers to the solution (no hindsight)
description: The problem should not contain matters of which the skilled person would only have become aware by knowledge of the claimed solution; it must not include pointers to or partially anticipate the solution.
guidance: This principle prevents hindsight and is fundamental to ensuring inventive step is judged against the prior art alone. Comvik part 7 expresses this as a general rule, but the article argues that it must apply to all aspects of the problem (technical and non-technical) unless those aspects are themselves in the prior art. Anti-pattern: including elements in the problem that derive solely from the claimed invention.

name: Patentability should depend only on technical features, not on recited non-technical aims or inventor's motivation
description: The patentability of technical features should not be affected by why the inventor made the invention or by which non-technical aims are recited in particular claims.
guidance: Including novel non-technical aims in the problem makes patentability depend arbitrarily on claim drafting or inventor motivation (the same technical features could be patentable or not depending on which non-technical aim is claimed). The refined approach prevents this anomaly by requiring non-technical aims to be prior art before they can be used in the problem formulation.

name: Refined Comvik approach for practical application
description: When a claim includes non-technical features, assess inventive step by: (a) considering only those features that contribute to a technical effect as part of the invention/solution; and (b) including non-technical features in the problem only if they were known or would have been obvious from the prior art.
guidance: This reconciles Articles 52, 54(2) and 56 with Comvik practice: (i) technical features (or combinations producing a technical effect) supply inventive step; (ii) non-technical features may be part of the problem only if in prior art. Example: T 1784/06 supports (i); T 0641/00 Comvik historically supported (ii) in a problematic way; the article cites T 2063/09 as a case where the modified approach would alter the reasoning. Practical effect: examiners/boards should show that any non-technical constraint included in the problem was known/obvious in the prior art rather than inferred from the claim.

name: Simultaneity of action not required for a valid combination
description: "To make a valid claim for a combination, it is not necessary that the several elementary parts of the combination should act simultaneously. If those elementary parts are so arranged that the successive action of each contributes to produce some one practical result, which result, when attained, is the product of the simultaneous or successive action of all the elementary parts, viewed as one entire whole, a valid claim for thus combining those elementary parts may be made."
guidance: Nor is it necessary that all parts of a machine combination co-operate all the time; "it is enough that, in the normal and progressive use of the machine, they do so some of the time." (cases cited in support).

name: Design applications may not claim provisional benefit (35 U.S.C. 119(e) / 35 U.S.C. 172)
description: Design applications may not claim the benefit of a provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e).
guidance: See 37 CFR 1.55 and MPEP § 213–216 for related formal requirements. Because a design application cannot claim the benefit of a provisional, a design application cannot obtain the provisional filing date via an intermediate utility application that directly claims provisional benefit.

name: Certified copy requirement for foreign priority (37 CFR 1.55)
description: A certified copy of the foreign application is required to support a claim to foreign priority under 37 CFR 1.55.
guidance: For design applications, the certified copy must be filed during the pendency of the application unless filed with a petition under 37 CFR 1.55(g) together with the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(g) and a showing of good and sufficient cause for the delay. If the certified copy is filed after the date the issue fee is paid, the patent will not include the priority claim unless corrected by a certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323. Examiner notes indicate where to insert foreign application number, country, and filing date in form paragraphs.

name: Benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 — specific reference requirement
description: To claim the benefit of an earlier‑filed U.S. application under 35 U.S.C. 120, the later‑filed application must contain a specific reference to the earlier‑filed application (i.e., identify the prior application and relationship).
guidance: For applications filed on or after Sept 16, 2012 the specific reference must be in the application data sheet (37 CFR 1.76). For applications filed prior to Sept 16, 2012, the specific reference must be in the first sentence(s) of the specification or in an application data sheet. The Director may consider failure to submit such an amendment within the required time as a waiver of any benefit; the Director may establish procedures (including payment of fee under section 41(a)(7)) to accept an unintentionally delayed submission.

name: Failure to timely submit reference is waiver of benefit (37 CFR 1.78(d)(3)(iii))
description: Except as provided in 37 CFR 1.78(e), the failure to timely submit the reference required under 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 in a design application during its pendency is considered a waiver of any benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c) or 386(c).
guidance: If a waiver occurs, applicant may be required to change the relationship of the continuing application (e.g., to continuation‑in‑part) or delete the benefit claim. For post‑Sept 16, 2012 filings, applicant can delete or change the benefit claim by filing a corrected ADS in compliance with 37 CFR 1.76(c); for pre‑Sept 16, 2012 filings, by amending the specification or submitting a supplemental ADS per pre‑AIA 37 CFR 1.76(c). See MPEP § 211 for additional information.

name: Continuation and divisional application requirements and examiner responsibilities
description: A continuation or divisional application (other than a continued prosecution application under 37 CFR 1.53(d)) must include a specific reference to the prior‑filed application in compliance with 37 CFR 1.78 to claim benefit. The prior application must disclose the claimed design in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
guidance: In all continuation and divisional applications, the examiner must determine whether conditions for priority under 35 U.S.C. 120 have been met. If not met, the examiner should notify applicant, specify reasons why benefit is not allowed, and may require applicant to change the relationship or delete the benefit claim. Form paragraphs (e.g., 2.09, 2.10, 2.10.01, 15.26) may be used followed by a specific explanation.

name: When foreign priority in parent affects CIP — foreign app as prior art (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172)
description: Where a CIP claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 and the parent also claimed foreign priority, and the CIP is not entitled to benefit of the parent (e.g., insufficient disclosure), the foreign application may qualify as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172 if the foreign application was filed more than six months before the CIP filing date and matured into a form of patent protection prior to the CIP filing date.
guidance: Examiner should use charts in MPEP § 1504.02 to determine the status of the foreign application. If the foreign application qualifies as prior art and its design anticipates or renders the CIP claim obvious, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102/103 using appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 15.74.01 followed by rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/103(a)). If the status is unknown, use the C‑I‑P caution form 15.75.01.fti and request applicant to inform the Office of the foreign application's status.

name: Burden of proof in disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. Respondent must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
guidance: Standard of proof for both proving violations and asserting affirmative defenses is clear and convincing evidence; adjudicators must apply this burden when assessing claims and defenses.

name: Thorough description of the omitted rejection(s) (general requirement)
description: A complete proposed rejection for each of the claim(s) listed must be provided.  For each claim the statute, sub paragraph and evidence supporting the rejection must be clearly identified.  The proposed rejection should not be personalized, and should reflect a thorough analysis.
guidance: Provide a complete proposed rejection for each listed claim, identify the statute and the evidence supporting the rejection, avoid personalization, and analyze how the prior art or disclosure supports the legal conclusion (anticipation, obviousness, lack of enablement/written description, indefiniteness, ineligibility, lack of utility, double patenting, etc.).

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: 35 U.S.C. 103 (Obviousness)
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 when the invention is obvious subject matter. To support the conclusion that the claimed invention should have been rejected as directed to obvious subject matter, the proposed rejection should articulate a prima facie case of obviousness.
guidance: Findings of fact must be supported by sufficient evidence in the prior art. The rejection must articulate how the prior art is to be modified to arrive at the claimed invention. The reasoning/rationale should be taught by the prior art applied or provided by the reviewer in a convincing line of reasoning as to why the artisan would have found the claimed invention obvious in light of the applied prior art. Also: list each claim for which an omitted 103 rejection is proposed; do not list claims that already have a compliant rejection even if covered by the omitted combination (see provided example). Indicate whether omitted rejection applies to independent claims, dependent claims, or both.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) Enablement
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) Enablement if the disclosure, when filed, does not contain sufficient information regarding the subject matter of the claims as to enable one skilled in the pertinent art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
guidance: List each claim for which an omitted 112(a) Enablement rejection is proposed (including dependent claims that inherit deficiencies). Indicate whether omission applies to independent claims, dependent claims, or both. Check applicable boxes for specifics (112(a) related to 112(f); insufficient reference to deposit of biological material; dependent claims inheriting deficiencies). Provide a complete proposed rejection for each listed claim, identify statute and evidence, avoid personalization, and analyze why the disclosure fails to enable without undue experimentation.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) Written Description
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) Written Description if there is not sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at the time the application was filed. For newly added or amended claims, applicant should show support in the original disclosure.
guidance: List each claim for which an omitted written-description rejection is proposed (including dependent claims inheriting deficiencies). Indicate whether omission applies to independent claims, dependent claims, or both. Check basis boxes (new matter; original claims; 112(a) related to 112(f); lack of sufficient algorithm for computer-implemented inventions; insufficient deposit reference for biological material; dependent claims inheriting deficiencies; or none). Provide a complete proposed rejection identifying statute and supporting evidence, explaining why the disclosure does not show possession of the claimed invention as a whole at filing.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (Indefiniteness / Particularity)
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) when the claims do not particularly point out and distinctly claim that which the inventor regards as the invention.
guidance: List each claim proposed for an omitted 112(b) rejection (including dependent claims inheriting deficiencies). Indicate whether omission applies to independent claims, dependent claims, or both. Check all applicable bases from: relative terminology; ranges and amounts limitations; exemplary language (e.g., 'for example'); lack of antecedent basis; alternative limitations (e.g., Markush); unclaimed/omitted essential subject matter; relation to 112(f); unbounded functional claiming; dependent claims inheriting deficiencies; or 'Other'. Provide a complete proposed rejection per claim, identifying statute and evidence, and analyze how claims fail to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: 35 U.S.C. 112(d) (Improper Dependent Claim)
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) as being directed to an improper dependent claim when the claim contains a reference to a previous claim and does not specify a further limitation and include all limitations of the previous claim.
guidance: List each claim for which an omitted 112(d) rejection is proposed (including dependent claims inheriting deficiencies). Provide a complete proposed rejection for each listed claim, identify statute and evidence, and analyze how dependent claims fail to specify a further limitation and include all limitations of the referenced claim.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: 35 U.S.C. 101 Subject Matter Eligibility (SME)
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 if it is not directed to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) or if the claim is directed to a judicial exception and the claim as a whole does not include additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
guidance: List each claim for which an omitted 101 SME rejection is proposed and indicate whether omission applies to independent/dependent/both. For Step 1 failures, check applicable categories (Transitory Signal/Signal per se; Program/Software per se; Human Organism; Use Claim; Information/data per se; Other). For Step 2, follow structured checks: 2(b)(1) identify judicial exception (product of nature, law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea). If abstract idea, select subcategory (mathematical concept; certain methods of organizing human activity; mental process; tentative abstract idea per 2019 guidance). 2(b)(2) evaluate integration into a practical application (no additional elements; merely 'apply it'; adds insignificant extra-solution activity; merely links to a technological environment; or Other with explanation). 2(b)(3) evaluate inventive concept (no additional elements; merely 'apply it'; adds insignificant extra-solution; links to environment; appends well-understood routine/conventional activities — if last, support per Berkheimer options: Applicant statement, court decision, publication, or official notice). Provide a thorough proposed rejection for each claim, identify statute and evidence, and analyze why claims are not patent eligible.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: 35 U.S.C. 101 Utility
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 Utility when there is no assertion of a specific and substantial credible utility by the applicant, and the claimed invention does not have readily apparent well-established utility.
guidance: List each claim for which an omitted 101 Utility rejection is proposed (identify independent/dependent/both). Provide a complete proposed rejection for each claim, identify statute and supporting evidence, and analyze how the claims lack a specific and substantial credible utility.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: 35 U.S.C. Statutory Double Patenting
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under Statutory Double Patenting when the claimed invention is directed to the same invention (identical subject matter) claimed in a patent or co-pending application with at least one common inventor/assignee/applicant or under a Joint Research Agreement.
guidance: List each claim for which an omitted statutory double-patenting rejection is proposed (identify independent/dependent/both). Must check basis (Provisional or Non-provisional). Identify conflicting patent/application relied on: complete columns including Name, Document Identifier, US(F) CPC Classification Symbol, Found by (Reviewer Search, 892, 1449, ISA, Other) and Reference Type. Ensure US patent/application numbers formatted correctly. Answer whether the omitted rejection is based on a rejection previously made during prosecution and improperly withdrawn in response to filing of a Terminal Disclaimer (Yes/No). Provide a complete proposed rejection per claim with statute and evidence, analyzing identical subject matter.

name: MRF Omitted Rejection: Nonstatutory Double Patenting
description: A claimed invention should have been rejected under Nonstatutory Double Patenting when the claimed invention is not patentably distinct from an invention claimed in a patent or co-pending application with at least one common inventor/assignee/applicant or under a Joint Research Agreement.
guidance: List each claim for which an omitted nonstatutory double-patenting rejection is proposed (identify independent/dependent/both). Indicate basis (Provisional or Non-provisional) and type of omitted rejection (Anticipatory Type and/or Obviousness Type). Identify conflicting patents/applications and any modifying references; specify for each whether it is the conflicting patent/application or a modifying reference, provide Name, Document Identifier, US(F) CPC symbol if applicable, Found by, Reference Type, and provide search explanation if found by Reviewer Search or Other. Indicate whether omission is based on a rejection dropped during prosecution because of a terminal disclaimer not accepted by the Office (Yes/No). Provide a complete proposed rejection and analysis of lack of patentable distinctness.

name: Office Action Characteristics: Allowable Subject Matter (questions & best practices)
description: Evaluate whether the examiner indicated allowable subject matter and related prosecution characteristics: Did the examiner indicate allowable subject matter? Was rejoinder properly practiced? Is a reason for allowance present? Optional comments; check best-practice characteristics.
guidance: Q1: Answer 'Yes' only when examiner affirmatively allows a claim or indicates a claim as containing allowable subject matter (including allowances). 'No' if examiner simply does not reject/does not address claim. Q2: Rejoinder: answer Yes/No/N/A — apply MPEP 821.04 and appropriate form paragraphs; if 'No' provide details. Q3: Is there a reason for allowance (an explanation for how claims distinguish over prior art)? If Yes, indicate whether reasons add substance to the record. Q4: Optional comments/suggestions/best practices. Q5: Check all applicable best-practice boxes — presence of characteristics (does not require accolade-worthiness): (a) Office action identifies specific allowable subject matter and demonstrates how prior art neither anticipates nor renders obvious that allowable subject matter; (b) Check only when specific allowable subject matter is identified and there is an explanation as to how prior art does not anticipate/render obvious; (c) An Examiner’s Amendment was completed to place the case in condition for allowance; (d) Office action cites pertinent applicant arguments persuasive in overcoming a previous rejection; (e) Office action cites newly discovered prior art providing a brief description why it was cited but not applied; (f) Reasons for Allowance addresses each independent claim separately; (g) None of the above.
