Q6: Is there an accolade related to Allowable Subject Matter? — Only available if at least one of the above best-practices boxes is checked; follow current accolade procedures and guidance; when indicating an accolade, complete the specified sentence per procedures.

name: Claim construction can be dispositive for Section 101 at the motion stage
description: Courts denying Section 101 motions often determine that claim construction — defining the scope and meaning of a patent — is necessary to resolve the Section 101 challenge, or they dismiss without prejudice to developing Section 101 arguments later.
guidance: Plaintiffs can try to persuade courts to require claim construction to sidestep Alice; doing so requires showing a genuine dispute over claim scope and may benefit from specific, detailed constructions supported by expert testimony.

name: Best practices for plaintiffs relying on claim construction
description: The best chance of success for patent owners tends to be portraying a fundamental dispute over the basic character and coverage of the patent claims and/or adopting a specific and detailed claim construction argument based on expert testimony.
guidance: Plaintiffs should propose concrete constructions and tie them to factual disputes and expert support; avoid vague assertions that construction is needed without particulars.

name: Defendant strategy: minimize claim construction and emphasize factual distinction
description: Infringement defendants should focus on minimizing issues of claim construction and instead factually distinguish the asserted claims from those in Federal Circuit opinions that found eligibility.
guidance: Avoid giving plaintiffs an opportunity to convert the motion into a claim-construction dispute; instead press factual differences and abstract-idea character to support invalidity.

name: Determine prior art content as of the time the invention was made (avoid hindsight)
description: Content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
guidance: Decisionmakers must 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made' and avoid using knowledge of the claimed invention to read back into the prior art. See cases such as W.L. Gore & Associates v. Garlock for the admonition against hindsight. See MPEP §2145 for discussion of rebutting hindsight-based applicant arguments.

name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — evidence and burdens to avail benefits
description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to avail of benefits of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) bears the burden of establishing that subject matter used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
guidance: To avail joint research provisions, applicant must establish (A) the invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement effective on or before the invention date, (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement, and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the agreement. See MPEP §706.02(l)(1)-(2) and cases such as In re Bartfeld.

name: Analogous art requirement for 35 U.S.C. 103
description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
guidance: A reference is analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would logically have commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering the problem. Examiner may consider the problem as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support pertinence. If the problem is perceived too narrowly inconsistent with the specification, available prior art may be improperly limited; examiners should explain why an inventor seeking to solve the identified problem would have looked to the reference. See KSR, In re Bigio, In re ICON, In re Clay, and In re Klein.

name: Analogous-art analysis is technology-specific (chemical/mechanical/electrical/design examples)
description: Analogy may be determined differently in various arts; examples illustrate how courts have treated analogous art in chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts.
guidance: For chemical arts, teachings concerning absorbing biologically active materials on carriers or dye chemistry may be pertinent; for mechanical arts, a broad spectrum of prior art is appropriate when similar problems exist; for electrical arts, solutions to rate-limiting problems in different high-frequency devices may be pertinent; for design arts, a prior design is of the type claimed if it has the same general use as that claimed. See cited cases (Ex parte Bland; Stratoflex; In re Mlot-Fijalkowski; Stevenson; Medtronic; In re Rosen; Ex parte Pappas; In re Butera). Use these precedents to inform analogous-art determinations.

name: Interpreting claims and determining differences between prior art and claims
description: Ascertaining differences between the prior art and the claims requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole.
guidance: Examiners should consult MPEP §§2111–2116.01 for claim interpretation law and MPEP §2143.03 for examples of claim language issues. The analysis must consider all claim limitations and the references as complete disclosures, not isolated features.

name: Do not distill to a 'gist' or 'thrust' of an invention (avoid improper abstraction)
description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the statutory requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
guidance: Restricting consideration to a single feature or purported advantage and disregarding express claim limitations is improper (see W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind/Hydrocurve; Jones v. Hardy; Panduit). Examiners must apply the full scope of claim limitations in the obviousness analysis.

name: Discovery of the source/cause of a problem is part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
description: Discovery of the source of a problem can itself be the patentable inventive contribution, even if the remedy would be obvious after that discovery.
guidance: Determining whether discovery of a problem's cause renders the claimed invention patentable requires analyzing the invention as a whole. However, if the prior art already contains the same solution for a similar problem, discovery may not result in patentability. See In re Sponnoble and In re Wiseman for examples and limits of this principle.

name: Characteristics to identify for markedly different analysis must be possessed by the claimed product
description: Appropriate characteristics for comparison must be characteristics possessed by the claimed product — the claim defines the invention and thus the characteristics to be evaluated.
guidance: Examiners identify characteristics by reading the claim language and using the broadest reasonable interpretation of the nature-based product. A characteristic may be explicitly recited (e.g., chemical name indicating structural detail) or inferred from the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., what nucleotide sequence an 'isolated gene B' encompasses). Unclaimed characteristics cannot be relied upon (Roslin).

name: Compare claimed product characteristics to counterpart in its natural state
description: To determine if characteristics are 'markedly different,' compare the claimed product’s characteristics to those of the naturally occurring counterpart in the counterpart's natural state.
guidance: The courts emphasize comparison to the natural state; a characteristic must be changed as compared to nature and cannot be merely inherent or incidental in the counterpart (Myriad).

name: Marked difference requires applicant-caused change (not inherent or incidental)
description: A characteristic is 'markedly different' only if it has been changed relative to the natural counterpart, and that change was caused or produced by the applicant’s efforts or influences.
guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product is a product of nature exception. If there is at least one changed characteristic produced by the applicant, that change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic and support eligibility.

name: Unclaimed characteristics and incidental changes do not support eligibility
description: Changes that are incidental to isolation or characteristics that are unclaimed/innate to the natural counterpart cannot be relied upon to show a marked difference.
guidance: Examples: Myriad — incidental structural differences from isolation (loss of covalent chromosomal bonds) were not enough where genes were otherwise structurally identical; Ambry — primers' single-stranded creation and their use as starting materials did not create a new function because binding ability was innate; Marden — inherent ductility cannot be treated as a change given by invention; Roslin — phenotypic differences not claimed cannot establish marked difference.

name: Claim language controls what characteristics can be evaluated
description: Only characteristics that are recited in the claim or are encompassed within the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim may be considered in the markedly different characteristics analysis.
guidance: Courts have rejected reliance on characteristics not claimed. Examiners should look at explicit claim recitations and at what the claim reasonably encompasses to determine characteristics (e.g., 'deoxyribose' indicates a structural removal of hydroxyl).

name: Inventive concept: additional elements must supply 'significantly more' than the judicial exception
description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon), an inventive concept requires elements beyond the exception that, individually or in combination, ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception itself.
guidance: An inventive concept cannot be the judicial exception itself. It is furnished by an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the exception (Alice/Mayo). The search for an inventive concept asks 'what else is there in the claims' beyond the exception.

name: Apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
description: The USPTO must apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) in appropriate cases, and give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), in light of and consistent with the written description of the invention in the application.
guidance: In determining the BRI, establish the meaning of each claim term consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art, including identifying and construing functional claim limitations. The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim limitation that invokes 112(f) is the structure, material or act described in the specification as performing the entire claimed function and equivalents to the disclosed structure, material or act. Absent a determination that a claim limitation invokes 112(f), the BRI is not limited to corresponding structure and equivalents.

name: Three-prong analysis for invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
description: A claim limitation will be treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) if it meets the following three-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the term “means” or “step” or a term used as a substitute for “means” that is a generic placeholder; (B) the term is modified by functional language (e.g., linked by "for" or wording like "configured to"); and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
guidance: All three prongs must be considered. The determination should be explicitly stated in the examiner's Office action. If the limitation uses “means” or “step” but the examiner determines the second or third prong is not met, the Office action must explain why the limitation is not being treated under 112(f).

name: Prong A — presence of “means”/“step” or generic placeholder
description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term “means” or “step” and includes functional language. A limitation that does not use “means” or “step” triggers a rebuttable presumption that 112(f) does not apply.
guidance: The presumption that 112(f) applies (when 'means'/'step' is used) is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure, material or acts necessary to perform the recited function. Conversely, the presumption that 112(f) does not apply (when 'means'/'step' is absent) may be overcome if the claim uses a generic placeholder (a substitute for 'means') or otherwise fails to recite sufficiently definite structure and instead recites function without sufficient structure. There is no fixed list of generic placeholders; examples include “mechanism for,” “module for,” “device for,” “unit for,” “component for,” “element for,” “member for,” “apparatus for,” “machine for,” and “system for,” but every case is fact specific.

name: Prong C — absence of sufficient structure, material, or acts
description: The limitation will invoke 112(f) only if the term "means"/"step" or generic placeholder is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function.
guidance: If the claim limitation itself recites sufficient acts or structural modifiers that denote the type of structural device (e.g., 'filters', 'circuit', 'detent mechanism', 'baffle'), then 112(f) does not apply. Examiners should consider whether the modifier is defined in the specification, is known by one skilled in the art, or otherwise imparts structure. There are fact-specific outcomes; e.g., 'spring means' invoked 112(f) in one case, while 'perforation means' did not in another because the claim described the supporting structure.

name: Generic placeholders may invoke 112(f) if non-structural
description: A substitute term acts as a generic placeholder for 'means' and may invoke 112(f) when it is a non-structural, black-box term not understood by a person of ordinary skill as denoting structure.
guidance: Even if the term is not literally 'means', words like 'module', 'mechanism', 'element', 'member', 'component', or 'device' may be treated as generic placeholders if they fail to connote sufficient structure in the art. The standard is whether the words are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure (Williamson). If the term, in view of the specification, would be understood to denote structure (even broadly), 112(f) will not apply. No per se list — every claim turns on its facts.

name: Process-claim special consideration — 'step' vs 'step for' and acts requirement
description: For method claims, 112(f) (step-plus-function) is implicated only when the element sets forth a step for reaching a result without reciting the specific technique or acts used to achieve the result; mere 'ing' verbs in steps do not automatically create step-plus-function clauses.
guidance: If a method claim uses 'step for' with only functional recitation (no acts), it tends toward invoking 112(f). By contrast, the term 'step' alone or the phrase 'steps of' tends to show that 112(f) does not govern that limitation. Examiners must distinguish between 'what' is accomplished (the underlying function) and 'how' it is accomplished (acts).

name: Presumption and burden: applicants may rebut or choose 112(f) treatment
description: Application of 112(f) is driven by claim language, not applicant intent. If a limitation is found to invoke 112(f), applicant may either present a sufficient showing that the limitation recites sufficient structure to avoid 112(f) or amend the claim to avoid 112(f) (e.g., by reciting sufficient structure).
guidance: If the examiner has not interpreted a claim limitation as invoking 112(f) and applicant wishes 112(f) treatment, applicant must either amend to include 'means'/'step' or rebut the presumption by showing the limitation is purely functional and lacks structure/acts. Applicants have the opportunity and obligation to define their inventions precisely during prosecution.

name: Office action and procedural requirements when invoking or declining 112(f)
description: A determination that a claim is being interpreted according to 112(f) should be expressly stated in the examiner’s Office action. If a claim limitation uses 'means'/'step' but the examiner determines that 112(f) does not apply (second or third prong not met), the Office action must explain the reasons why.
guidance: If it is unclear whether the claim limitation falls within 112(f), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be appropriate. The Office action should set forth the basis for the interpretation and advise applicant of options (showing of structure or claim amendment).

name: Element-by-element application and limits of 112(f) scope
description: It is necessary to decide on an element-by-element basis whether 112(f) applies. 112(f) applies only to the interpretation of the means or step that performs the recited function; not all terms in a clause are limited to what is disclosed in the written description and equivalents thereof.
guidance: Some claim terms in a means/step clause may not themselves be the means performing the function and thus may not be limited to disclosed embodiments and equivalents (see IMS Technology example). Examiners should analyze whether a particular term performs the recited function and whether its meaning is tied to corresponding structure in the specification.

name: Use of examples and case law: apply fact-specific precedents, not per se rules
description: There is no absolute or exhaustive list of terms that always invoke or avoid 112(f); courts' holdings are fact-specific and should be used as guidance rather than bright-line rules.
guidance: Examples from case law illustrate outcomes (e.g., 'module' found non-structural in Williamson; 'code'/'application' found structural in Dyfan/Target and Zeroclick/Apple given context). Examiners should rely on specification disclosure, dictionary and art usage, and prior decisions as instructive but evaluate each claim in its own factual context.

name: Declaration requirement in application
description: An application must contain a declaration that the applicant is in possession of an invention and that he (or one or more joint applicants) claims to be the true and first inventor and desires to obtain a patent; the application must be accompanied by either a provisional or a complete specification.
guidance: The declaration must be signed (see rules re: statutory declarations if made abroad or before certain officers). Failure to include the declaration or required specification will render the application defective. (Sect. 5 sub-s. (2), statutes and Patents Forms cross-referenced.)

name: Provisional specification content
description: A provisional specification must describe the nature of the invention; it need not contain all minute directions or enable a workman of ordinary skill fully to make the invention, but must disclose what the invention really is.
guidance: Provisional spec must commence with a title; a claim is not necessary. It suffices if it shows the invention in a rough state (cases: Stoner v. Todd; Bailey v. Roberton; In re Newall and Elliott). Provisional spec requires no stamp. Drawings should accompany when required. Omitting essential information can be fatal later when comparing with the complete specification.

name: Complete specification core requirement
description: A complete specification must particularly describe and ascertain the nature of the invention and in what manner it is to be performed; it must begin with a title and end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed.
guidance: Complete spec must be supplemental to any provisional spec and should not go beyond or vary from the nature of the invention disclosed in the provisional. It requires a stamp. Failure to describe the invention particularly or to state how to perform it can render the patent void. (See sect. 5 and attendant notes.)

name: Claim requirement and relation to title
description: A complete specification must end with a distinct statement (claim) of the invention claimed; the claim ought not to exceed the title.
guidance: Historically claims were used mainly to disclaim old matter, but under the Act the complete specification must include a distinct claim. Overly broad claims exceeding the title risk invalidity. The claim should properly delimit what is new and claimed as the inventor's invention.

name: Distinguish new from old (novelty in specification)
description: The specification should, where necessary, carefully distinguish what is new from what is old; otherwise the patent may be held to claim what is old and be void for want of novelty.
guidance: This applies especially to improvements on existing patents and machines; old matter should be disclaimed (usually in the claim). Incidental references to universally known old things need not be treated as part of the invention. Methods of disclaiming old matter (claims, drawings) discussed in cases (Crane v. Price; Netvall v. Elliott; Daw v. Eley).

name: No material variation between provisional and complete specifications
description: The complete specification ought not to vary materially from the provisional specification so as to claim a different invention; substantial variation may invalidate the patent.
guidance: The examiner compares provisional and complete specs to ascertain substantial identity; favourable examiner report is not conclusive and courts may still consider variation (Bailey v. Roherton; Penn v. Bibby; Thomas v. Welch). Parts of provisional may be omitted in the complete spec if there is no fraud and the remaining effect is not altered (Thomas v. Welch).

name: Claims define the patent's scope
description: Nothing described in letters patent, is secured thereby, unless it is covered by a claim, and no element not mentioned in a claim can be read into it even though the element appears in the specification.
guidance: A patent secures only what its claims cover. Do not import unclaimed elements from the specification into the claim. Example/anti-pattern: attempting to assert protection for a feature present only in the description but not in any claim.

name: Claims control construction of the patent
description: The construction of letters patent depends therefore upon the construction of their respective claims.
guidance: Interpretation work should begin with the claims; the established rules for construing claims govern the meaning and scope of the patent.

name: Effect of a claim narrower or broader than the invention
description: A claim which is clearly narrower than the invention which it was designed to cover, cannot be broadened by construction... Nor can a claim, which is broader than the state of the art will allow to the invention described, be narrowed by a construction out of harmony with its language.
guidance: Courts must respect the literal language of the claim: they cannot judicially broaden an unduly narrow claim, nor artificially narrow a broadly worded claim contrary to its language. Balance must be kept with prior art and validity concerns.

name: Meaning and import of 'substantially as described' / 'as specified'
description: The phrase 'substantially as described,' or its equivalent, when such a phrase occurs in a claim, throws the investigator back to the description for means of construction; and that phrase is always implied in claims wherein it is not expressed.
guidance: Such phrases (expressed or implied) direct construction toward the specification and drawings with respect to the particular matter claimed, but they will not import into a claim any unessential feature or unnecessary detail. Some courts have given special narrowing effect to the phrase; Supreme Court decisions caution not to add elements not already in the claim.

name: Uncommon claim terms construed in light of specification
description: An uncommon word in a claim is to be construed in the light of the description, rather than in the light of the dictionary;
guidance: Where a patentee used an unusual term, presume the reader will consult the specification; interpret such terms according to the patentee's description, not solely by dictionary meaning.

name: Do not imply 'for the purpose set forth' in claims
description: The phrase 'for the purpose set forth' is never implied in a claim, because an inventor is entitled to the exclusive use of his invention for all purposes, whether he sets them all forth in his specification or not.
guidance: Avoid drafting or interpreting claims as limited to stated purposes; including such a phrase is discouraged because it cannot validate an otherwise void claim and may enable design-arounds.

name: Effect of limiting words like 'in mechanism'
description: The phrase 'in mechanism' is used in many claims, with a purpose to limit the claim ... to the subject of that claim where that subject is employed as a part of a particular mechanism. Such a limitation is effective to exclude later employment ... in other mechanism, and thus to negative infringement; but such a limitation is not effective to exclude earlier employment ... and thus to avert negation of novelty.
guidance: Limiting a claim to use 'in mechanism' narrows infringement scope (environment-dependent) but does not change novelty determinations; novelty depends on the character of the invention, not environment.

name: Role of drawings in claim construction
description: The drawings attached to letters patent may be referred to for explanation of anything which the description leaves obscure, but not to supply a total omission of description, or to contradict any plain statement therein.
guidance: Use drawings to clarify obscurities only. Do not use drawings to fill in a complete missing description or to contradict explicit specification text.

name: Neither drawings nor descriptions can enlarge claims
description: And neither drawings nor descriptions can enlarge claims.
guidance: The specification/drawings cannot be used to broaden the express scope of the claims. They may, however, justify narrowing a claim by showing necessary elements for operativeness/novelty.

name: When description may narrow a claim
description: Claims may be narrowed by limitations in the description, and also by importation by construction of described elements which are necessary to invention or novelty as well as operativeness; or are necessary to operativeness alone; but not such as are necessary only to invention or novelty.
guidance: Courts may construe a claim narrowly by importing elements from the description if those elements are necessary for the invention to operate or to distinguish over the prior art; but do not import elements that are only incidentally described.

name: Reference letters/numerals do not automatically limit claims
description: Reference letters or numerals, when used in a claim to indicate, or to help indicate, a part or combination covered thereby, do not limit that claim to the specific mechanism shown in the patent; unless the claim must be thus limited by the prior state of the art.
guidance: Using reference numerals in claims is generally illustrative, not limiting. However, if novelty resides exclusively in the particular characteristics shown and identified, the claim will be limited to those particular characteristics to avoid lack of novelty.

name: Specific references imply materiality of referenced parts
description: Every part specifically referred to by a letter is deemed material according to the well known doctrine...
guidance: If the specification labels parts (e.g., vessel A, A', C, C'), those labeled characteristics are deemed material; a reader must assume those characteristics (or equivalents) are required for the part in the claim.

name: Functional claims limited to means that produce the result
description: Claims which are functional in form; that is to say, claims which literally purport to cover a result rather than a process or a thing, are properly construed to cover only the process or the thing which produces that result, for otherwise such claims would be void.
guidance: A claim phrased by result must be read as covering the specific means/process/thing disclosed that achieves the result; purely result-oriented claim language will not be permitted to stand if it would otherwise be indefinite or void.

name: Claims that mix machine and process - constraints
description: It has ... been held that if a process claim be combined with a claim for a machine the process must be capable of being carried out by other means than the machine of the patent and such means must be known, otherwise the process claim will be regarded as a claim for the function of the machine and hence invalid.
guidance: When drafting/reading both machine and process claims, ensure the process is not limited to the machine unless alternative means are known; otherwise the process claim risks invalidity as an attempt to claim the machine's function.

name: Ascribing a function to an element limits the claim
description: Where a claim ascribes a function, to any of the things which it specifies, that ascription is a limitation of that claim.
guidance: If a claim element is defined by the function it performs, this functional language narrows the scope to elements performing that function (and may affect equivalents analysis).

name: Material-based article claims limited by specific material in description
description: A claim for an article of manufacture ... which designates its distinguishing thing by naming the material of which it is made, but which uses a generic name for that purpose; will be limited by construction, to the specific material specified in the description.
guidance: Using a generic material name in a claim will be construed in light of the specific material(s) disclosed—do not assume broad coverage over all materials unless the specification supports it.

name: Prior art and state of the art must inform claim construction
description: The prior state of the art, to which an invention belongs, must be considered in construing any claim for that invention, although the art may have been advanced to that stage, by a prior invention of the same inventor.
guidance: Interpret claims against the background of the relevant prior art (patents, uses, printed publications, drawings). The state of the art narrows the territory available to the patentee and affects how claims are given meaning.

name: Prior art in other fields may be considered with caution
description: The prior state of other arts, may also be considered in construing a claim; because that construction may depend on the area of the territory which was open to the claimant to cover; ... But an invention which was not designed by its maker, nor actually used, nor apparently adapted to perform the function of the claimed invention, but which was used in a remote art, under radically different conditions, to perform another function, does not limit the scope of the invention as claimed.
guidance: Cross-field prior art can be relevant to construction where it meaningfully reduces the patentee's available territory; remote art under different conditions typically should not restrict claim scope.

name: Patents entitled to liberal construction to preserve inventor's rights
description: Patents for inventions are to receive a liberal construction ... are, if practicable, to be so interpreted as to uphold and not to destroy the right of the inventor. ... In a case of doubt, where the claim is fairly susceptible of two constructions, that one will be adopted, which will preserve to the patentee his actual invention.
guidance: When a claim admits two reasonable constructions, prefer the one that preserves the inventor's actual invention, so long as it is consistent with the claim language. Liberality should not interpolate or add matter not present.

name: Construction may be narrow to preserve validity
description: That liberality as often shows itself in a narrow construction as in a broad one; for narrow construction may be as necessary to establish the validity of a patent, as a broad construction is to lay the foundation for proof of its infringement.
guidance: Courts will construe claims narrowly where needed to avoid anticipation or invalidity from the prior art; interpretive choice depends on preserving validity or enabling infringement proof.

name: Commercial success and public use affect construction
description: It has been held ... that when no practical use has been made of the patent the claims will be narrowly construed, the reason for so holding being that in such a case the patent lacks the support that comes from public acquiescence. And ... where the invention is a practical success and constitutes a distinct advance in the art the claims are entitled to a liberal construction.
guidance: Consider commercial success/practical adoption as a factor: practical success supports broader (liberal) construction; absence of public use supports narrower construction.

name: Prosecution history and PTO actions can preserve breadth
description: Nor will claims be narrowed where the proceedings in the Patent Office clearly show that the inventor intended to claim and the Patent Office intended to grant the broader monopoly.
guidance: If the prosecution record demonstrates both applicant and PTO intended broader coverage, courts should not construe the claim narrowly in contradiction of that record.

name: Best mode/expressed alternatives may affect construction
description: While it is true that by statutory provision an inventor ... 'shall explain ... the best mode' ... it is not clear how this requirement has any bearing on the scope of his claims. The court has apparently given a broader construction to a patent in which the inventor has stated as a conclusion that there might be alternatives for the device described and shown by him, than it would have done had that statement been absent.
guidance: An explicit statement in the specification that alternatives exist may support a broader claim construction; absence of such disclaimers may weigh against reading alternatives into the claim.

name: Effect of Myriad decision on isolated genetic/natural products
description: Myriad held that an isolated DNA molecule with an identical sequence to a natural gene is not patentable as it is a naturally-occurring product; complementary DNA (cDNA) with introns removed can be patentable, though short strands indistinguishable from natural DNA may not be.
guidance: The Court found that severing chemical bonds to isolate DNA did not create 'markedly different characteristics' and emphasized that claims focused on genetic information (naturally occurring) are not created by patentees. Apply analogously to other isolated natural molecules: structural identity to natural counterpart weighs against eligibility.

name: USPTO 2014 guidance: weighting factors and 'marked difference' standard
description: USPTO guidance provides a list of factors for and against patent eligibility of claims involving natural principles/products and determines eligibility principally by whether the claim recites something 'significantly' or 'markedly' different.
guidance: Key points from guidance: 'a marked difference must be a significant difference, i.e., more than an incidental or trivial difference.' Structural differences are a primary (but not sole) criterion; functional differences can be considered when structural differences are absent; words like 'isolated', 'recombinant', and 'synthetic' add no weight. Examples: synthetic derivative 5-methyl amazonic acid is patent-eligible (structural difference); purified amazonic acid is not (no marked difference).

name: Structural difference favored over mere functional difference
description: A structural difference is deemed sufficient for patent eligibility, whereas a functional (utility) difference is not mandatory and may or may not weigh in chemical/natural product cases.
guidance: When structural difference is absent or insignificant, the claimed natural product must exhibit new functions/characteristics that rise to the level of 'marked' differences. Functional differences alone do not guarantee eligibility; assess whether they are 'marked' beyond routine or incidental benefits.

name: Composition/combination claims of natural products
description: Compositions combining multiple natural products remain products of nature if the combined products show no marked difference from the natural products.
guidance: Compositions may be patent-eligible if they include additional element(s) that make the combination 'something significantly different than the natural products by themselves' — e.g., enhanced efficacy at a lower dosage. Draft and support combination claims with evidence of markedly different properties.

name: Method-of-use claims must recite practical, specific, significant application
description: A method of using natural products should involve a practical, specific, and significant application so the claimed method would not foreclose others from using the same natural product in other ways.
guidance: Avoid claims that merely recite: (i) a general instruction to apply or use the natural products; (ii) well-understood, purely conventional, or routine steps; or (iii) steps that need to be used by anyone who applies the natural products. Include additional steps such as regimen and dosage (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid for 10–20 days at a daily dose of 0.76–1.25 teaspoons') to satisfy the requirements.

name: Table summary: likely patentability outcomes under USPTO policy
description: Under the USPTO policy, extracts and isolated products from natural materials are likely to be unpatentable; formulations of combined extracts may be patentable if 'markedly different'; manufacturing methods are patentable if they meet novelty and non-obviousness.
guidance: Use this high-level mapping to prioritize claim drafting: focus less on isolated per se claims and more on derivatives, formulations, methods, and applications that can be shown to be different in kind or provide marked advantages.

name: Product-by-process claim constraints in the US
description: 'Product-by-process' claims define a product by the process used to make it (e.g., “product X obtained by process Y”) and are allowed when products cannot otherwise be adequately defined, but US patentability of such claims is determined solely on the product itself, not the process.
guidance: A product identical or similar to a known product is not patentable even if made by a new method. Process steps are considered only if they imply distinctive structural characteristics. Product-by-process claims may be limited in enforcement (they only cover products produced by the recited process) and may not cover equivalents made by different processes; accused products made by a different process may not infringe. Recommended practice: include all available characterization in the specification and draft separate product and process claims for broader protection.

name: Burden of proof on novelty/non-obviousness for claimed product similar to known products
description: If the claimed product is identical to, or similar to, a known product, applicants bear the burden of proof on novelty and non-obviousness to show the claimed product is distinguishable from known products.
guidance: Provide structural/functional evidence and characterization to meet this burden. If such proof is available, the product may be adequately defined (which paradoxically undermines the need for product-by-process language).

name: Enforcement/infringement limitations for product-by-process claims
description: 'Product-by-process' claims only cover products that are produced by the process recited in the claim; an accused product made by a different process does not infringe such a claim.
guidance: This limits the scope of protection from product-by-process claims. Consider drafting both process claims (to capture infringers using the claimed method) and product claims (if possible) and include detailed characterization to avoid reliance solely on product-by-process.

name: Sufficiency of disclosure / written description and enablement
description: US patent law requires sufficient description so that one skilled in the art would recognize the inventions; a claim reciting a general formula is not patentable if only a few species of the general formula are disclosed in the application.
guidance: A claim to a general formula (e.g., CnH2n+2) may be limited to species explicitly described (e.g., CH4, C3H8) if only those were disclosed. To obtain broader scope, disclose as many embodiments, substitutions, and variations as possible; include experimental conditions and technical features (temperature, pH, reagents). Claims should be drafted to include all enabling and foreseeable embodiments.

name: Claim drafting: scope, significance, and specificity
description: Claims should be drafted within a reasonable scope and be of sufficient significance so they do not appear to be a general application of the natural products.
guidance: Avoid overly broad claims that merely apply a natural product generally. Add technical limitations, specific regimens, dosages, modified structures, or unique manufacturing steps to show significance and limit scope. Identify and characterize individual embodiments and combinations for broader coverage.

name: Recommended patenting strategy for natural products
description: Focus patenting efforts on derivatives with enhanced properties, optimized formulations and dosages, new uses or applications, and advanced methods for preparing natural products; disclose detailed information to meet written description and enablement.
guidance: Identify and characterize individual embodiments and/or combinations to support broader claim coverage. Frequently review developments in patenting policy and adjust strategy. Include detailed descriptions in the specification and draft multiple claim sets (product, product-by-process, process, method-of-use) as appropriate.

name: Manufacturing/process claims remain viable
description: Manufacturing methods such as extraction and preparation of drugs/supplements using natural products are patentable if they satisfy statutory requirements like novelty and non-obviousness.
guidance: Even when product claims are vulnerable under the product-of-nature doctrine, well-drafted process claims can provide meaningful protection. Ensure processes imparting distinctive structural characteristics are well-supported in the specification.

name: Overlapping, Approaching, and Similar Ranges — prima facie obviousness
description: If claimed ranges, amounts, or proportions overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art, a prima facie case of obviousness exists; ranges that are merely close (approaching) may also create a prima facie case if a skilled person would expect similar properties.
guidance: Examples: In re Wertheim, In re Woodruff (overlap of 'about 1-5%' and '>5%'), Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner (very close alloy proportions deemed prima facie obvious). A prior art range that is extremely broad may present genus/species issues—see MPEP § 2144.08. Multiple prior art references together can supply a 'range' (Iron Grip Barbell). Cases and citations include Peterson, Harris, Baird, Jones, and others.

name: Routine Optimization
description: Optimizing within prior art conditions or discovering the optimum/workable ranges by routine experimentation is not inventive where the prior art discloses the relevant conditions, unless evidence shows the claimed concentration/temperature/etc. is critical.
guidance: General principle: mere differences in concentration or temperature typically will not support patentability absent evidence of criticality. Examples: In re Aller, Peterson, In re Hoeschele, Merck v. Biocraft, In re Kulling, In re Geisler. History: changes in form, proportions, or degree generally do not sustain a patent absent criticality or unexpected results.

name: Obviousness of Species — Graham three-step process and required findings
description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness for species under a genus disclosure, apply the Graham factors: (A) determine scope and contents of the prior art; (B) ascertain differences between the prior art and claims; (C) determine level of ordinary skill in the art; and (D) evaluate evidence of secondary considerations. If prima facie made, burden shifts to applicant to rebut.
guidance: Specific examiner actions: 1) determine scope/content of relevant prior art and whether references qualify under 35 U.S.C. 102 and are analogous; 2) for a prior art genus, make findings on (A) genus structure and any species described, (B) physical/chemical properties/utilities and suggested limitations/problems addressed, (C) predictability of the technology, and (D) number of species encompassed by the genus; 3) identify and compare the closest disclosed prior art species/subgenus and make explicit findings on similarities/differences in structure, properties, and utilities; 4) evaluate level of ordinary skill in the art from the prior art standpoint and any applicant evidence; 5) determine whether one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to select the claimed species/subgenus. Case citations: Graham v. John Deere; In re Bell; In re Rijckaert; In re Oetiker; Stratoflex; In re Dillon.

name: IFW waiver for pending U.S. application copies
description: The requirement for a legible copy of the specification, including claims, and drawings of each cited pending U.S. patent application is sua sponte waived where the cited pending application is stored in the USPTO’s Image File Wrapper (IFW) system.
guidance: The waiver is limited to the specification, claims, and drawings. If other material in the file is being cited, copies of that material are required.

name: Problem‑solution approach (overview)
description: EPO's problem-solution approach is used to assess inventive step objectively and to avoid hindsight: (A) determine state of the art and closest prior art; (B) establish the objective technical problem; (C) consider whether the prior art would have prompted PSA to modify the closest prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Derived from Rule 42(1)(c) EPC; requires formulating distinguishing features, then an objectively framed technical problem that does not anticipate the solution.

name: Step A — determine closest prior art / state of the art
description: Determine the state of the art including neighbouring fields and then identify the closest prior art which corresponds to a similar use and requires minimal structural/functional modifications to arrive at the claimed invention.
guidance: Closest prior art selection can be replaced by a 'reasonable selection' of prior art; examiners should consider relevant neighbouring fields where the same or similar problems arise.

name: Combination inventions — synergy vs aggregation
description: A combination claim may involve an inventive step if the functional interaction between features achieves a synergistic effect; if the claim is merely an aggregation of individually obvious features with no greater synergistic effect, there is no inventive step.
guidance: Consider whether the prior art suggested precisely the claimed combination. If it was 'obvious to try' but there was no reasonable expectation of success, the invention may still be inventive. 'Reasonable expectation of success' is distinct from mere hope.

name: Submission of evidential documents or written statement for priority (Article 54(4))
description: A person who claims priority shall submit certified copies of the specification and drawings of the relevant invention certified by the government of the state in which the first application was filed, or a written statement specifying details (only for states specified by Ordinance).
guidance: The written-statement option is limited to states specified by Ordinance of the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy; certified copies are the standard.

name: Regularity of first application not affected by later status
description: The first application filed must be regular as determined by the relevant law of the country; whether the first application is pending does not influence the effects of the priority claim—even if withdrawn, abandoned, invalidated or rejected, priority claim remains effective.
guidance: Even if the first application later fails to produce a patent in its country, priority effects under the Convention persist.

name: Submission of evidential documents within one year and four months
description: A person who has made a priority claim shall submit to the Commissioner of KIPO the documents containing the application date recognized by the government of the country where the first application was filed as well as the copy of the specification or drawing(s) within one year and four months from the priority date.
guidance: In countries designated in the Enforcement Decree, submission may be replaced by submitting application numbers; failure to submit within the period causes loss of priority effects.

name: Examiner may require Korean translation of evidential documents
description: Where an examiner requires the applicant to submit the Korean translation of the evidential documents claiming a priority within the designated time period in order to determine patentability (e.g., when prior art exists between priority and filing date), the applicant shall submit the Korean translation within the designated time period.
guidance: Allowed period is two months, extendable. Failure to submit translation may invalidate the proceedings for the concerned priority claim.

name: Limitations of priority effect for disclosure-exception timing
description: Except for certain cases, the filing date of an application claiming priority shall be deemed to be the actual filing date; e.g., for applying the disclosure-exception provisions, if the applicant did not file within twelve months of disclosure, novelty or inventive step may be lost even if application was filed within one year from the first filing.
guidance: Practical warning that other timing rules (like disclosure exceptions) can make the effective filing date the actual filing date for some analyses.

name: Eligibility requirement to amend/add priority claim
description: To amend or add a priority claim, an applicant shall have made a priority claim at the time of filing an application and at least one of the priority claims made at filing shall meet the requirement specified in Article 54(2).
guidance: Whether an applicant has made a priority claim is determined by the indication in the 【Priority Claim】 column of the written application at filing.

name: Acceptable replies for abandonment to a final action
description: For abandonment for failure to reply to a final Office action, the reply required for consideration of revival must be one of: (A) a Notice of Appeal and appeal fee; (B) an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 that cancels all rejected claims or otherwise places the application in condition for allowance; (C) filing an RCE under 37 CFR 1.114 accompanied by a submission meeting 37 CFR 1.111 and the requisite fee; or (D) filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) for design applications).
guidance: If a proposed amendment under 1.116 is filed as the reply, the Office of Petitions normally routes the application to the Technology Center to determine whether it places the application in condition for allowance. If the amendment does not place the application in condition for allowance, the examiner completes PTOL-303 and returns it to Office of Petitions (petition will not be granted). If the reply places the application in condition for allowance, the examiner should mark 'OK to enter upon revival.' Time for filing appeal brief will be set by Director if notice of appeal is used as reply.

name: Intentional or deliberate abandonment precludes unintentional/unavoidable finding
description: An abandonment that resulted from an applicant's deliberately chosen course of action (e.g., deciding claims are unpatentable, not cost-justified, or intentionally deferring fees) is not 'unintentional' under 1.137(b) nor 'unavoidable' under 1.137(a). A change of mind after deliberate abandonment does not render the prior delay unintentional.
guidance: Examples listed: (A) applicant considers claims unpatentable; (B) allowed/patentable claims not of sufficient breadth; (C) patent not worth expense; (D) not worth maintaining interest; (E) applicant seeks to defer fees and prosecution costs. Case law (In re Application of G; In re Maldague) supports this.

name: Accelerated examination procedural steps after grant
description: When special status is granted for accelerated examination, the examiner will take up the application ahead of most others and give a complete first action covering all claims; the examiner's search is restricted to the subject matter encompassed by the claims.
guidance: A first action rejection sets a 3-month shortened period for reply. During that period applicant is encouraged to arrange an interview; applicant or representative should deliver a copy of proposed amendment at least one working day before the interview (that paper won't become part of the file). The formal 'record' reply must be restricted to the rejections, objections, and requirements made; any amendment broadening the search field is treated as improper. The examiner will, within 1 month from receipt of applicant's formal reply, take up the application for final disposition (final action terminating with a 3-month period for reply, or notice of allowance). Examiner may use telephone for minor issues. Personal interviews after a final Office action are not permitted unless requested by the examiner; telephonic interviews may be allowed for correcting minor matters. After allowance these applications receive top priority for printing (see MPEP §1309).

name: Overlapping applications (same applicant or same assignee) — handling during inter partes proceedings and interferences
description: Examiners should not consider ex parte questions pending before the Office in inter partes proceedings involving the same applicant; related applications with overlapping claims and interference issues have special handling.
guidance: Where one application with overlapping claims is in an interference, better practice is to reject claims in the related application over the interference counts and suspend prosecution pending final determination of priority. If applicant wishes to prosecute the outside application and presents good reasons, prosecution may be continued. Cases and authorities cited (Ex parte Jones, Ex parte McCormick, In re Seebach, In re Hammell) provide precedent; see MPEP §804.03 for more detail.

name: Petition to Expunge — Conclusion: Material to Determination of Patentability (¶ 7.208)
description: This is a decision on the petition under 37 CFR 1.59(b) to expunge information. The petition is dismissed. 'Materiality' is defined as any information which the examiner considers as being important to a determination of patentability of the claims. The petition is deficient because: [8]
guidance: If information is considered material to patentability, explain basis for conclusion in bracket 1. A Technology Center Director decides only if submitted pursuant to MPEP § 724.02 or in an IDS. Petition should not be granted until application allowed/abandoned or Ex Parte Quayle action mailed. Send to Office of Petitions in specified circumstances. Identify the document requested to be expunged in bracket 6 (author/title).

name: Ready for Allowance, Non-elected Claims Withdrawn Without Traverse (¶ 8.07)
description: This application is in condition for allowance except for the presence of claim [1] directed to [2] nonelected without traverse. Accordingly, claim [3] has been canceled.
guidance: In bracket 2 insert appropriate wording (an invention/inventions/a species/species). Use when ready for allowance but non-elected claims canceled due to election without traverse.

name: Restriction, Linking Claims (¶ 8.12)
description: Claim [1] link(s) inventions [2] and [3]. The restriction requirement [4] the linked inventions is subject to the nonallowance of the linking claim(s), claim [5]. Upon the indication of allowability of the linking claim(s), the restriction requirement as to the linked inventions shall be withdrawn and any claim(s) depending from or otherwise requiring all the limitations of the allowable linking claim(s) will be rejoined and fully examined.
guidance: Insert 'between' or 'among' in bracket 4 and the linking claim numbers in bracket 5. Claims that require all limitations of an allowable linking claim will be entered as a matter of right if amendment presented prior to final rejection or allowance. Amendments after final governed by 37 CFR 1.116; after allowance by 37 CFR 1.312. Warn applicant about potential provisional statutory/nonstatutory double patenting for continuation/divisional claims anticipated by allowable linking claim. Where restriction withdrawn, 35 U.S.C. 121 no longer applies (In re Ziegler).

name: Intermediate–Final Product Distinctness (¶ 8.14)
description: Inventions [1] and [2] are related as mutually exclusive species in an intermediate-final product relationship. Distinctness is proven if the intermediate product is useful to make other than the final product and the species are patentably distinct.
guidance: Use when claims presented to both an intermediate and final product (MPEP § 806.05(j)). Provide example of intermediate product utility and conclude restriction with form paragraph 8.21.

name: Distinct Products or Distinct Processes (¶ 8.14.01)
description: Inventions [1] and [2] are directed to related [3]. The related inventions are distinct if: (1) not capable of use together or can have materially different design/mode/function/effect; (2) do not overlap in scope (mutually exclusive); and (3) are not obvious variants.
guidance: Use for related product inventions or related process inventions where inventions as claimed are mutually exclusive. If a generic or linking claim is present see MPEP §§ 809–809.03. Explain why inventions are not capable of use together or can differ materially. Conclude restriction with 8.21.

name: Combination–Subcombination Distinctness (¶ 8.15)
description: Inventions [1] and [2] are related as combination and subcombination. They are distinct if (1) the combination as claimed does not require the particulars of the subcombination for patentability, and (2) the subcombination has utility by itself or in other combinations.
guidance: Specify limitations of the claimed subcombination not required by the combination, or evidence supporting that conclusion. Suggest separate utility for the subcombination. Conclude restriction with 8.21. Warn about rejoining and double patenting issues; see MPEP § 821.04(a).

name: Subcombinations Usable Together (¶ 8.16)
description: Inventions [1] and [2] are related as subcombinations disclosed as usable together in a single combination. Subcombinations are distinct if they do not overlap in scope, are not obvious variants, and at least one subcombination is separately usable.
guidance: Identify the subcombination and suggest separate utility other than with the other subcombination. Conclude restriction with 8.21. See MPEP § 806.05(d); warn of double patenting for continuation/divisional claims.

name: Process and Apparatus Distinctness (¶ 8.17)
description: Inventions [1] and [2] are related as process and apparatus for its practice. They are distinct if either: (1) the process can be practiced by a materially different apparatus or by hand, or (2) the apparatus can be used to practice a materially different process.
guidance: Use when claims are presented to both a process and apparatus for its practice (MPEP § 806.05(e)). Provide factual showing (bracket 3) and conclude with paragraph 8.21. Notify applicant that if a product claim is allowable, process claims depending from or requiring all limitations of the patentable product may be rejoined (see form paragraph 8.21.04).

name: Moral rights (core)
description: Independently of economic rights and even after assignment, the author has the right to: (i) claim authorship, have name affixed to copies and, where possible, in relation to public use; (ii) remain anonymous or use a pseudonym; (iii) oppose any distortion, mutilation or other modification or action derogatory to the work prejudicial to his honor or reputation.
guidance: Moral rights are vested in the person of the author, perpetual, inalienable, not subject to time limitations, indefeasible, and transferable after death to heirs; exercise may be transferred testamentary.

name: Petition particularity requirement (burden from onset)
description: “In an [inter partes review], the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable.” (citing Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech., Inc.; 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3); 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)).
guidance: A petition must identify with particularity the evidence supporting each ground and where each claim element is found in the cited patents/printed publications. This particularity requirement is described as 'of the utmost importance.' Failure to identify grounds/evidence with particularity can be a basis to deny institution. Provide clear citations, explicit mapping of elements, and direct evidentiary support (e.g., attested captures for web pages).

name: Design-patent obviousness standard post-LKQ (apply Graham factors)
description: Following LKQ Corp. v. GM Global Tech. Operations LLC (en banc), obviousness of a design patent is determined using factual criteria similar to those for utility patents under § 103 — application of the Graham factors adapted for designs: (1) scope and content of the prior art (identify a primary reference), (2) differences between claimed design and prior art (visual comparison from perspective of an ordinary designer), (3) level of ordinary skill in the art (ordinary designer), and (4) objective evidence (secondary considerations) when in evidence.
guidance: Apply each Graham factor explicitly in the design context: identify the primary reference (closest/most visually similar), compare overall visual appearance from an ordinary designer's perspective (not isolated features), resolve the ordinary designer skill level, and address any secondary considerations (commercial success, praise, copying) if present. Cite the 2024 Updated Guidance and LKQ for methodology.

name: Overall visual appearance comparison (avoid feature cherry-picking)
description: Compare the visual appearance of the claimed design with prior art 'from the perspective of an ordinary designer in the field of the article of manufacture.' Do not compare only selected features; consider the overall visual impression of the designs as a whole (citing In re Harvey and LKQ).
guidance: Do not selectively choose discrete features to the exclusion of other features that materially affect overall impression (dimensions, corner radii, positions, counts of elements, presence/absence of closures/mounts, etc.). Demonstrate how the overall impression of the prior art is visually similar to the claimed design. Explicitly address differences and explain why they would not change the overall impression.

name: Claim construction standard in IPRs and design-specific guidance
description: Claims in an IPR proceeding are construed 'using the same claim construction standard that would be used to construe the claim in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. [§] 282(b).' (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b)). For design patents, tribunals should not treat claim construction as requiring a detailed verbal description; 'a design is better represented by an illustration.' (Egyptian Goddess).
guidance: Rely primarily on the drawings for design claim scope. A verbal description is not required but can be helpful to point out particular features relative to the prior art; if provided, ensure it accurately captures the overall visual impression rather than creating a narrow hindsight-focused description.

name: Printed-publication/public-accessibility standard for web references
description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 311(b), IPR petitions may only rely on patents or printed publications. The petitioner bears the burden to identify with particularity evidence sufficient to establish a reasonable likelihood that a reference was publicly accessible before the critical date; whether something is a 'printed publication' is a case-by-case factual inquiry into accessibility (citing Acceleration Bay, In re Lister, Samsung Elecs. v. Infobridge).
guidance: Provide concrete evidence that an ordinary designer could have reasonably found the specific webpage before the critical date (e.g., reliable archived captures, attestation showing the specific URL/page). Indexing is not required, but some evidence of discoverability is critical. Be mindful that discrepancies between an asserted exhibit and an attested archive (differences in content, quality, presence of later-date comments or links) can undermine public-accessibility claims.

name: Secondary considerations (Graham factor four) — objective evidence
description: Secondary considerations (when in evidence) are objective indicia of nonobviousness, such as commercial success, industry praise, and copying.
guidance: Address secondary considerations where the record contains relevant evidence. If none are presented, state that the record lacks such arguments (as in this decision). When present, tie the evidence (sales, awards, direct evidence of copying) to the claimed design and explain whether it supports nonobviousness.

name: No new matter in corrections
description: Any amendment used to correct an improper incorporation by reference must not introduce new matter.
guidance: A statement that the material being inserted is the material previously incorporated by reference and that the amendment contains no new matter is required (37 CFR 1.57(g)). If correction would alter scope of the claims (e.g., by adding omitted equivalent means), such changes should be made via the reissue process rather than correction under 1.57.

name: Examiner response to improper incorporation of essential material
description: If essential material is improperly incorporated by reference, the examiner should object to the specification and/or reject the claim(s) (e.g., under 35 U.S.C. 112) until corrected.
guidance: Example: if essential material from a foreign patent was incorporated improperly, examiner may require applicant to amend the specification to include that essential material in reply to a non-final Office action, and applicant must file the amendment and required statement within the reply time. If applicant later adds claim limitations supported only by the foreign patent, examiner may reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and treat the Office action as final; applicant may then use after-final amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 or file an RCE under 37 CFR 1.114 with a 1.57(g) amendment.

name: Incorporation by reference as a safeguard for priority/benefit claims
description: An incorporation by reference statement filed at the time of filing a later application may permit inclusion of subject matter from the prior application without it being considered new matter.
guidance: To serve as an effective safeguard, the incorporation statement must be filed at time of filing the later application; adding such statement after filing is not effective because no new matter can be added after the filing date (35 U.S.C. 132(a)). An incorporation statement will not substitute for the specific reference requirements of 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 or 37 CFR 1.78.

name: Use of prior applications to establish an earlier effective filing date
description: Limitations on incorporations in U.S. applications that issue as patents do not apply where an earlier application is relied upon solely to establish an earlier effective filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119 or 120.
guidance: An application is entitled to rely upon the filing date of an earlier application even if that earlier application itself incorporates essential material by reference. However, when benefit/priority is claimed, the applicant may be required to supply copies (and translations if necessary) of incorporated material so the Office can determine whether the earlier application disclosed the invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a).

name: Substitute specification requirements (37 CFR 1.125)
description: The Office may require the entire specification or part thereof be rewritten if the number/nature of amendments or legibility renders the application difficult to consider or arrange for printing/copying (37 CFR 1.125(a)).
guidance: A substitute specification (excluding claims) may be voluntarily filed up to payment of the issue fee if accompanied by a statement that it includes no new matter (37 CFR 1.125(b)). A substitute filed under 1.125 must be submitted with markings showing all changes relative to the immediate prior version (underline added text; strike-through or double brackets for deleted text) and an accompanying clean version without markings. Substitute specs are not permitted in reissue applications or reexamination proceedings (37 CFR 1.125(d)).

name: Formatting and marking of substitute specifications
description: A substitute specification submitted under 37 CFR 1.125 must show changes relative to the immediate prior version with specified conventions and include a clean copy.
guidance: Added subject matter shown by underlining; deleted matter shown by strike-through or double brackets (for deletions of five or fewer characters or when strike-through is hard to perceive). Paragraph numbering of the specification of record is not considered a change that must be shown. Paragraphs of substitute spec (other than claims) should be individually numbered in Arabic numerals to facilitate replacement paragraphs under 37 CFR 1.121(b)(1).

name: Permissible use of marks and trade names in patent applications
description: A mark or trade name may be used in a patent application to identify an article, product, service, or organization only if (A) its meaning is established by an accompanying definition in the specification that is sufficiently descriptive, enabling, precise and definite to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112, or (B) its meaning is well-known to one skilled in the art and satisfactorily defined in the literature.
guidance: Condition (A) or (B) must be met at the time of filing. Identification introduced by amendment must be restricted to characteristics known at the time of filing to avoid new matter. If proper identification is omitted and necessary, the examiner should reject claims that merely rely on identification by mark/trade name as insufficient disclosure. Arbitrary marks liable to mean different things do not constitute definite language.

name: Use of empirical studies of industry license agreements
description: Empirical study of industry license agreements can provide observed industry average royalty rates that inform the hypothetical negotiation construct.
guidance: Results from such studies provide useful context within which rates for specific patent claims can be assessed, but they are contextual evidence rather than determinative on their own.

name: Certain Methods of Organizing Human Activity (abstract-idea grouping)
description: Abstract-idea grouping limited to specific sub-groupings such as fundamental economic principles, commercial/legal interactions, and managing personal behavior/interactions.
guidance: Do not expand this grouping beyond the enumerated sub-groupings in MPEP 2106.04(a)(3) except in rare circumstances. Evaluate whether the claimed activity fits one of the enumerated sub-groupings before categorizing it here.

name: Improvement to Computer or Technological Field
description: A claim can be eligible if, as a whole, it provides an improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technological field.
guidance: Show technical explanation in the specification and ensure the claim reflects the asserted improvement. Example: steps that act in real time to drop malicious packets and block future traffic can reflect an improvement to network security and thus integrate the abstract idea into a practical application.

name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Test
description: Assess whether claimed additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
guidance: If background or common knowledge shows elements are routine (e.g., devices already equipped with microphones to receive audio), those elements cannot supply the inventive concept in Step 2B.

name: Dependent Claims Inherit Parent Limitations and Abstract Ideas
description: A dependent claim includes all limitations of its parent claim and thus inherits the abstract ideas recited in the parent.
guidance: When analyzing a dependent claim, consider the parent claim's abstract-idea findings; dependent limitations may add further elements but do not negate inherited abstract ideas unless they add significantly more.

name: Cannot Be Practically Performed in the Human Mind
description: If a claim limitation cannot be practically performed in the human mind (or via pen-and-paper), it is not a 'mental process' abstract idea.
guidance: Evaluate whether the limitation could be practically done mentally. Steps such as synthesizing audio waveforms or converting masked clusters into time-domain signals are technical operations that cannot be performed in the human mind and thus fall outside the mental-process grouping.

name: Use the Specification/Background to Support Claimed Improvements
description: Evaluate the specification and background to determine if they describe a technical improvement and whether the claim reflects that improvement.
guidance: Where the background explains an advantage (e.g., improved speech separation that does not require speaker-specific training and uses temporal/spatial features), that description can support finding the claim integrates an abstract idea into a practical application if the claim elements reflect those improvements.

name: Claim Drafting Guidance to Demonstrate Technical Improvement
description: Draft claims to recite technical details showing how components (e.g., a DNN) achieve the asserted improvement, rather than merely stating 'using' generic components.
guidance: Include limitations that show how the algorithm/structure operates and how it modifies computer functionality (e.g., details of how the DNN aids cluster assignments, how masked clusters are synthesized into separate waveforms, real-time packet dropping/blocking), so the claim is more likely to be found to integrate the exception into a practical application or include an inventive concept.

name: Exclusive/partially exclusive license: public_served_and_scope_limit (35 U.S.C. 209(a)(2))
description: The Federal agency finds that the public will be served by the granting of the license, as indicated by the applicant’s intentions, plans, and ability to bring the invention to practical application or otherwise promote the invention’s utilization by the public, and that the proposed scope of exclusivity is not greater than reasonably necessary to provide the incentive.
guidance: Assessment based on applicant's stated intentions/plans/ability; scope of exclusivity must be no greater than necessary to provide the incentive claimed.

name: Reissue of defective patents: grounds and prohibition on new matter (35 U.S.C. 251)
description: Whenever any patent is, through error, deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than he had a right to claim, the Director shall, on surrender of the patent and payment of the fee, reissue the patent for the invention disclosed in the original patent; no new matter shall be introduced into the application for reissue.
guidance: Reissue corrects defects in specification/drawings or incorrect claim scope; reissue cannot add new matter beyond original disclosure.

name: Limitation on enlarging claim scope in reissue (35 U.S.C. 251(d))
description: No reissued patent shall be granted enlarging the scope of the claims of the original patent unless applied for within two years from the grant of the original patent.
guidance: To broaden claim scope via reissue, application must be filed within two years of original grant (statutory time limit).

name: Disclaimer and dedication requirements (35 U.S.C. 253)
description: A patentee may, on payment of the required fee, make disclaimer of any complete claim, stating the extent of his interest; such disclaimer shall be in writing and recorded in the Patent and Trademark Office and shall thereafter be considered as part of the original patent; likewise a patentee may disclaim or dedicate to the public the entire term or any terminal part of the term.
guidance: Disclaimers must be written, recorded, and are effective as part of the patent; dedication of term possible.

name: Effect of reissue on prior actions and prior users (35 U.S.C. 252)
description: Surrender of the original patent takes effect upon issue of the reissued patent; every reissued patent has same legal effect as if originally granted in amended form. Reissue shall not abridge or affect the right of any person who, prior to the grant of a reissue, made, purchased, offered to sell, used, or imported the patented thing to continue such activities unless doing so infringes a valid claim of the reissued patent that was in the original patent; courts may provide equitable terms protecting investments begun before reissue.
guidance: Reissue generally continues patent effect retroactively, but prior users are protected from being suddenly barred except to extent they would infringe valid original claims; courts have equitable powers to protect pre-existing investments.

name: Submission of certain drug applications may be act of infringement (35 U.S.C. 271(e)(2))
description: It shall be an act of infringement to submit — (A) an application under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or described in section 505(b)(2) for a drug claimed in a patent or the use of which is claimed in a patent; (B) an application under section 512 or under the Act of March 4, 1913 for certain drugs or veterinary biological products claimed in a patent — (text truncated in source).
