guidance: Statute addresses specific situations where submission of regulatory applications can implicate infringement; full statutory text should be consulted for scope and exceptions (source chunk truncates complete provision).

name: 101(a) Eligible Subject Matter
description: Proposed statutory text: "Whoever invents or discovers, and claims as an invention, any useful process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or any useful improvement thereto, shall be entitled to a patent for a claimed invention thereof, subject only to the exceptions, conditions, and requirements set forth in this Title."
guidance: Expresses the broad, technology-neutral categories of patentable subject matter intended by Congress in the 1952 Act; frames eligibility as categorical (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or useful improvement).

name: 101(c) Sole Eligibility Standard — exclusion of §§102, 103, and 112 and inventive concept
description: Proposed statutory text: "The eligibility of a claimed invention under subsections (a) and (b) shall be determined without regard as to the requirements or conditions of sections 102, 103, and 112 of this Title, the manner in which the claimed invention was made or discovered, or the claimed invention's inventive concept."
guidance: Expressly prohibits importing novelty, nonobviousness, written description/enablement, manner of making, or the 'inventive concept' inquiry into the §101 eligibility analysis. Intended to preserve the separation between categorical eligibility (§101) and patentability/merits ( §§102/103/112 ).

name: Evaluate eligibility for the claimed invention 'as a whole' (no point-of-novelty dissection)
description: Guidance repeatedly emphasizes that eligibility must be assessed for the invention "as a whole" and not by dissecting claims into old and new elements or isolating a 'point of novelty' (cites Diehr and critical discussion of Flook/Benson).
guidance: Disapproves of claim dissection into old/new elements to determine eligibility; rejects the 'point-of-novelty' approach and directs courts/examiners to consider the entire claimed invention in context rather than isolating individual limitations.

name: Exclude novelty/nonobviousness/enablement considerations from §101 analysis
description: Repeated explanation that the §101 inquiry should not consider the conditions or requirements of §§102, 103, or 112 (novelty, non-obviousness, written description/enablement), nor be influenced by whether elements are 'conventional, routine, well understood.'
guidance: Addresses and rejects the practice (in Mayo/Alice line) of treating lack of novelty or conventionality as evidence that a claim is merely 'something more' or not 'significantly more.' Such determinations belong to §§102/103/112; using them in §101 conflates distinct statutory functions.

name: Ineligibility if the claimed invention 'exists in nature independently of and prior to any human activity'
description: Interpretive guidance: this ineligibility criterion targets laws of nature and natural products — anything that existed in nature independently of human activity is not eligible. The requirement of 'independently of any human activity' captures the idea that inventions must be the result of some human act upon nature (i.e., 'made by man').
guidance: Explains the distinction with Myriad (cDNA vs genomic DNA): cDNA did not exist in nature independently of human activity and therefore could be patent eligible; notes ambiguity around 'isolated' gDNA and explains why 'activity' was chosen over alternative phrasing (effort, agency, contribution).

name: Ineligibility if the claimed invention 'exists solely in the human mind' (abstract ideas / mental processes)
description: Interpretive guidance: this ineligibility criterion is directed to abstract ideas and purely mental phenomena — ideas that do not have physical or tangible aspects (e.g., purely mental processes).
guidance: Returns the abstract idea exception to its original focus on purely mental phenomena (per Benson/Diehr) and states that claim limitations requiring some external involvement with the physical world or a representation thereof (e.g., data in a computer) should be considered eligible. Cites policy reasons (proof problems, First Amendment) for excluding purely mental phenomena from protection.

name: Use of the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) in eligibility analysis
description: The proposed statute and notes specify that eligibility is assessed 'as understood by a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains' (POSITA).
guidance: Argues that applying a POSITA standard makes §101 analysis objective, technology-neutral, and consistent with other patent doctrines (enablement, obviousness, claim construction). A limitation that appears 'abstract' to a court may have technical meaning to POSITA; POSITA evolves with technology.

name: No-response: Issue Action Closing Prosecution (ACP) when at least one claim patentable
description: If the patent owner does not respond and at least one claim is free of rejection/objection, issue an Action Closing Prosecution (ACP) limiting the proceeding to those patentable claims and to claims added or amended which do not expand scope of the patentable claims.
guidance: ACP will state that claims under rejection/objection are withdrawn from consideration and will be canceled upon issuance of an NIRC; see MPEP § 2666.10 for entry of new claims that do not expand scope.

name: When an Office action will not close prosecution (non-ACP issuance criteria)
description: An action will not normally close prosecution if it includes a new ground of rejection not previously addressed by the patent owner, unless necessitated by an amendment; examiner may also issue a non-ACP when issues are not clearly defined.
guidance: This preserves the patent owner’s right to amend claims prior to closure. Examiner discretion to issue a non-ACP is appropriate when more development or clarification of issues is needed (see 37 CFR 1.949 and MPEP § 2671.01).

name: Withdrawal of a rejection must be clearly stated as favorable to patentability
description: When the examiner withdraws a ground of rejection originally initiated by the examiner, that withdrawal should be clearly stated in the Office action as a decision favorable to patentability with respect to the withdrawn rejection.
guidance: If withdrawn rejection was originally proposed by third party and claims were not amended, treat as a third-party-proposed rejection that the examiner refuses to adopt and state reasons. If withdrawn rejections relate to amended claims, normally they are not treated as refusals to adopt since the original rejection was not proposed against amended claims; explain treatment and appellate consequences (37 CFR 41.61(a)(2)).

name: No response by patent owner and claims patentable: issue ACP and limit proceeding
description: If the patent owner fails to respond to an action and claims have been found patentable, the examiner will issue an ACP which repeats determinations of patentability and limits the proceeding to the claims found patentable and to new claims which do not expand scope.
guidance: ACP should incorporate by reference reasons for determinations and include more explanation if helpful. A panel review conference will be held per MPEP § 2671.03.

name: Apportionment and reliable allocation of damages
description: Damages testimony should be reliably apportioned to the patented contribution; apportionment arguments are a recognized constraint on reasonable royalty opinions (i.e., experts must show their royalty applies to the infringing contribution, not improperly to unpatented features).
guidance: Although apportionment was not the focus of the en banc grant in this case, courts routinely scrutinize whether expert calculations properly apportion value to the claimed invention and whether methods for apportionment are supported by facts and reliable methodologies.

name: Presumption of patentability and prima facie burden
description: Claimed inventions are presumed to be patentable unless the examiner is able to establish a prima facie case that one of the patentability requirements is not met.
guidance: A prima facie case is one that at first sight presents sufficient evidence to support the conclusion. An examiner's evidence is prior art (e.g., publications, patents, admissions, on-sale items). Anticipation (35 U.S.C. §102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103) are most frequent. If examiner establishes prima facie case, burden shifts to applicant to rebut or supply evidence.

name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. §102 (single-reference test)
description: Anticipation occurs when a single prior art reference describes, either expressly or inherently, each and every limitation of a claim.
guidance: A single prior art reference anticipates the claimed invention by describing every limitation in the claim; limitations can be expressly set forth or inherently present in the reference. If conditions of §102(a)(1) are met, claims lack novelty and should be rejected under §102(a)(1).

name: Statutory categories of §102(a)(1) prior art
description: §102(a)(1) enumerates categories of prior art that negate novelty.
guidance: The statute states: (1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or (2) in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date. Examiners determine these conditions after a complete search.

name: Complete search and novelty determination
description: Novelty determination under §102(a)(1) is made after a complete search for the claimed invention is done.
guidance: If the conditions are met (novelty lacking), reject claims under §102(a)(1). If not, no §102(a)(1) rejection is made, but other statutes (e.g., §101, §102(a)(2), §103, §112) may still apply.

name: Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries (framework for obviousness)
description: Four factual inquiries must be addressed to determine obviousness.
guidance: 1) Scope and content of the prior art; 2) Differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; 3) Relevant level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; 4) Any objective evidence of non-obviousness. See MPEP 2141; KSR affirmed continued use of this framework.

name: Prima facie obviousness — examiner's initial burden
description: The examiner must establish a prima facie case that the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the pertinent art before the effective filing date.
guidance: The examiner must supply facts and reasoning supporting a prima facie conclusion of obviousness (see MPEP 2142-2144). Mere conclusory statements are inadequate.

name: Articulation of rationale — required reasoning underlying 103 rejections
description: A clear articulation of the rationale or reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious is essential to support a §103 rejection.
guidance: Mere conclusory statements are inadequate; there must be some articulated reasoning with rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness (In re Kahn). If the office action does not explain WHY the combination or modification would have been made, the examiner has failed to set forth necessary rationale and cannot shift the burden to applicant.

name: Consideration of all claim limitations when asserting obviousness
description: All claim limitations must be considered when establishing a prima facie case of obviousness, including indefinite limitations and limitations lacking specification support.
guidance: "All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art" (In re Wilson). See MPEP 2143.03.

name: Remedy when assignee refuses to accept conveyance
description: If an assignee refuses to accept the conveyance when duly tendered, the assignor's remedy is generally a suit at law for damages; specific performance in equity is only available in special cases.
guidance: Equity will compel execution only when obligations are such that justice cannot be done at law—for example when consideration is conveyance of real property or surrender of essential rights. In such peculiar circumstances, specific performance may be ordered to require transfer or release of stipulated property or claim.

name: Patent invalidity as defense to recovery of purchase money
description: An assignee may defend an action for the purchase money by showing that no patent corresponding to the assignment ever issued or that the patent is void (for want of novelty or utility, abandonment, defective specification, excessive claims, or substantial variations in a re-issue).
guidance: Invalidity is a defense on ground of failure of consideration. Courts distinguish lack of pecuniary market value (not a defense absent fraud/warranty) from lack of utility or patent-invalidating defects (which are defenses). Utility is presumed from existence of patent but can be disproved; if patent wholly void for want of utility, price cannot be recovered; if partially void as to some claims and apportionment possible, assignor can recover for valid portion. When assignee has used or profited from the patent, he should offer to return it and account for profits; if patent is void no actual return necessary. Evidence of invalidity may be collateral and certain procedural requirements (e.g., spreading equity on record) may be necessary.

name: Claim indefiniteness standard
description: To avoid invalidity for indefiniteness, a claim, read in light of the specification, must “reasonably apprise those skilled in the art both of the utilization and scope of the invention.” Shatterproof Glass Corp. v. Libbey-Owens-Ford Co., 758 F.2d 613, 624 (Fed. Cir. 1985).
guidance: If a claim 'is subject to construction, i.e., it is not insolubly ambiguous, it is not invalid for indefiniteness.' Bancorp Servs., L.L.C. v. Hartford Life Ins. Co., 359 F.3d 1367, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2004). A claim will not be held invalid if its meaning is discernible even though reasonable persons may disagree; courts look to specification and figures to supply sufficient basis for construction.

name: Using specification and figures in claim construction
description: The specification and the figures provide a sufficient basis for differentiating 'sides' from 'corners' (e.g., 'sides' contain only lateral string ends; 'corners' contain both lateral and longitudinal string ends).
guidance: Court may construe terms by reference to the written description and figures when they instruct how to differentiate portions of the claimed device; ordinary-language terms that are not used in a specialized sense ('region') may be interpreted by their plain meaning as used in the spec.

name: Anticipation and inherency (what prior art must disclose)
description: A reference that is silent about a limitation (e.g., direction in which opposite ends of a string are splayed) does not necessarily anticipate; inherency requires that the asserted limitation be necessarily present in the prior art disclosure.
guidance: If prior art does not inherently disclose every limitation (e.g., does not disclose whether splay is in opposite directions or number of main strings), it may not anticipate the claim; board/examiner analysis on anticipation focuses on presence or absence of explicit or necessarily present disclosure.

name: Teaching away concept in obviousness
description: AAI argued Martel teaches away from the claimed invention because it calls for a racquet design that limits twisting, which AAI says an even number of strings would cause.
guidance: A teaching-away argument can defeat an obviousness combination, but the party asserting teaching away must explain why the prior art discourages the claimed modification; unsupported assertions are insufficient.

name: Sufficiency of claim language when term is not specialized ('region')
description: The specification makes clear that the term 'region' is not used in a specialized sense, but merely refers to a portion of the edge of the racquet, so the claim language 'in the regions where the length of said ends is greater' equates to 'where the length of said ends is greater.'
guidance: Ordinary words used in their plain sense in the specification do not introduce fatal ambiguity; courts may simplify or equate such language to its plain counterpart for construction.

name: Continuing-breach doctrine and trade-secret-related contract claims
description: The continuing-breach theory does not apply to breach of a contract covering trade secrets; where contract claims 'consist entirely of the same acts of misappropriation . . . that would be barred by the statute of limitations applicable to trade secret claims,' they cannot be revived by treating each act as a continuing breach.
guidance: Under Arizona law (as applied here), misappropriation of trade secrets has a 3-year statute of limitations and 'a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim'; plaintiffs cannot extend contract claims beyond the statutory period by recasting them as continuing breaches when they are essentially trade-secret misappropriation claims.

name: Statute of limitations tolling during related litigation
description: AAI argued the statute should be tolled during the pendency of an earlier lawsuit because the action involving the ’731 patent was stayed; the court rejected this because AAI's trade secret claim had been voluntarily dismissed earlier and AAI pointed to no authority for tolling under these facts.
guidance: Tolling during earlier litigation is not automatic; a party must identify legal authority supporting tolling and the factual predicate (e.g., an actual stayed claim) to justify tolling.

name: When a claim 'is subject to construction' it is not fatally indefinite
description: If the claim 'is subject to construction, i.e., it is not insolubly ambiguous, it is not invalid for indefiniteness.' Bancorp Servs., L.L.C. v. Hartford Life Ins. Co., 359 F.3d 1367, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2004).
guidance: Even difficult claim-construction tasks do not equate to indefiniteness; discernible meaning suffices—courts must attempt construction before finding invalidity for indefiniteness.

name: Pressman drafting approach (overview)
description: Emphasizes thorough invention documentation, careful prior art search, clear and detailed specification, and methodical claim drafting.
guidance: Treat drafting as a multi-step process: document the invention well, evaluate patentability before drafting, search prior art to shape claim strategy, write a full specification that supports multiple claim scopes, and draft claims methodically to provide fallbacks.

name: Prior art search (patentability search)
description: Conduct a 'patentability search' before filing by searching patent databases, technical literature, products on the market, and trade shows. The closest art shapes claim strategy.
guidance: A thorough search informs whether the invention is novel/non-obvious and helps identify the closest references to distinguish over; use searches to tailor claim scope and anticipate likely examiner rejections.

name: Drafting the specification (required components and depth)
description: The specification should: describe the technical field briefly; provide background sufficient to understand the invention; summarize the invention at a high level; describe the drawings; detail the invention with reference to drawings; and disclose multiple embodiments and alternatives.
guidance: Provide enough detail to enable one skilled in the art to practice the invention and to support the breadth of the claims. Disclose variations and alternatives to preserve fallback claim support. Avoid minimal or vague backgrounds that fail to support claims.

name: Claim drafting structure and strategy
description: Use the structure: preamble, transition phrase, body. Use 'comprising' for open scope. Provide proper antecedent basis. Recite each element clearly. Draft 3-4 independent claims of varying scope and add dependent claims as fallback positions.
guidance: Follow formal claim structure and use open transition language ('comprising') to keep scope broad unless closed scope is intended. Ensure each term has antecedent introduced in the spec or earlier claims. Prepare multiple independent claims at differing scopes to increase chances of allowance and add dependent claims to preserve fallbacks.

name: Filing the application (procedural requirements)
description: File electronically via Patent Center. Include all required components and pay the fees. Confirm receipt and docket all relevant deadlines.
guidance: Prepare and submit the complete application package (specification, claims, drawings, oath/declaration, transmittal forms, and fees). Use electronic filing, verify filing receipt, and calendar subsequent deadlines such as provisional-to-nonprovisional dates, priority claims, and maintenance of IDS obligations.

name: Responding to office actions (post-filing prosecution)
description: Most applications receive office actions. Read the office action carefully, identify each rejection and the grounds, pull the cited references and analyze them, decide whether to argue, amend, or both, respond within the deadline, and consider an examiner interview for complex issues.
guidance: Address every rejection and ground raised, compare cited prior art to claim scope, and choose a response strategy (argument vs amendment) that balances preserving claim scope and obtaining allowance. Timely responses and examiner interviews can materially affect outcomes; consider counsel for complex rejections.

name: Common pro se pitfalls
description: Frequent mistakes include: filing too thin a provisional; drafting claims in lay English instead of patent format; failing to do a thorough prior art search; over-disclosing in a way that creates 102/103 admissions; missing deadlines; and failing to file IDS.
guidance: Avoid these anti-patterns by providing substantive disclosure in provisionals, using proper claim language and format, performing thorough searches, being careful what is admitted in the specification, docketing deadlines, and timely submitting information disclosure statements for known prior art.

name: Recommendation on hiring patent counsel
description: Even for a pro se approach, consult a patent attorney for complex inventions or for the office action response phase; the cost of professional help often exceeds DIY savings when the application is rejected on technical drafting grounds.
guidance: Recognize limits of DIY filing: use counsel when claim drafting or prosecution issues are complex, when important commercial value is at stake, or when confronted with difficult office actions where technical legal arguments and sophisticated amendments are needed.

name: Patent Claims Variables: Number of Independent Claims
description: Count of independent claims in the patent; included as a claims-structure predictor.
guidance: Number of independent claims is a significant predictor in models (odds ratios reported). Report effect size and statistical significance.

name: Patent Claims Variables: Functional Claim Indicator
description: Indicator for whether the claims are functional in nature.
guidance: Included in logistic models; report odds ratio and significance.

name: Reviewer Questionnaire: Six Prosecution-History Aspects (A–F)
description: Questionnaire designed to gather information about six aspects of the prosecution history: A. sources of prior art relied on in the PTAB decision; B. examiner’s prior art search; C. examiner’s handling of prior art rejections; D. examiner’s handling of application continuity; E. substantive interviews between the examiner and the applicant; F. claim interpretation issues.
guidance: Assign reviewers by technical competence; a single reviewer completed all facets for each patent in the study. The questionnaire prompts reviewers to comment about reasons for examiner/PTAB differences. The design should be trialed and revised for clarity; consider blind review to reduce hindsight bias.

name: Recharacterization of prior communications limited by wording and conduct
description: A practitioner's later attempt to recharacterize earlier correspondence (e.g., claim it was only a name-change notification rather than a request for removal) is disallowed when inconsistent with the original wording and the practitioner's conduct.
guidance: Subsequent reinterpretations will not override contemporaneous textual evidence and behavior; courts/agency will rely on original text and actions.

name: Referral of requests beyond reconsideration to OED Director
description: Requests for relief other than reconsideration or stay of the Final Decision are referred to the OED Director.
guidance: If a petitioner seeks forms of relief outside the narrow reconsideration remedy, those claims are not decided under §11.2(d) but forwarded to the OED Director for appropriate action.

name: Commissioner must notify reasons for claim rejection
description: Whenever any claim for a patent is rejected for any reason whatever, the commissioner shall notify the applicant, giving him briefly the reasons for such rejection, together with such information and references as may be useful in judging of renewing his application or altering his specification; persistence shall prompt re-examination.
guidance: Section 41. Rejection notice must include brief reasons and useful references; applicant's persistence leads to ordered re-examination.

name: Reissue for inadvertent defects or over-claiming
description: When a patent is inoperative or invalid due to a defective or insufficient specification, or because the patentee claimed more than his right, if the error arose by inadvertence, accident, or mistake without fraudulent intention, the commissioner shall, on surrender and payment of duty, cause a new patent to be issued in accordance with the corrected specification for the unexpired part of the term; specifications and claims shall be subject to revision and restriction as original applications; no new matter shall be introduced.
guidance: Section 53. Reissue available for inadvertent errors; surrender and payment required; cannot add new matter.

name: Disclaimer of over-claimed parts
description: When through inadvertence a patentee has claimed more than he was the original inventor of, his patent shall be valid for what is truly his; such patentee may, on payment of duty, make disclaimer of parts he does not choose to claim, stating extent of his interest, attested and recorded, and it shall be considered part of the original specification to that extent; disclaimers do not affect pending actions except for unreasonable neglect or delay in filing them.
guidance: Section 54. Formal disclaimer procedure protects valid portions and must be recorded; timing can affect litigation costs.

name: Innocent overclaim does not bar suit for bona fide part
description: If a patentee innocently claimed to be original inventor of more than he was, he (or his representatives/assigns) may maintain suit for infringement of the part bona fide his own if it is a material and substantial part and definitely distinguishable; however, no costs shall be recovered unless a proper disclaimer has been entered at the Patent Office before suit, and not entitled if unreasonably neglected or delayed to enter disclaimer.
guidance: Section 60. Protects enforcement rights for rightful portions of a patent even when other parts were erroneously claimed, but requires timely disclaimer to recover costs.

name: Lead compound/structural similarity as basis for obviousness
description: Obviousness based on structural similarity can be proven by identification of some motivation that would have led one of ordinary skill in the art to select and then modify a known compound (a lead compound) in a particular way to achieve the claimed compound; an expectation of similar properties in light of the prior art can be sufficient even without an explicit teaching.
guidance: The requisite motivation can come from any number of sources and need not be explicit in the art. Structural similarity may create an expectation that the new compound will have 'similar properties' to the old in light of the totality of the prior art (Eisai, Aventis). Office personnel should look for a reason to select and modify the prior art compound; explicit motivation in the reference is not required, but there must be some articulable reason to start with that compound other than its mere existence.

name: Need for a reason to select and modify a lead compound
description: To support an obviousness rejection based on a lead compound, there must be some reason for selecting that particular compound and for modifying it to arrive at the claimed compound.
guidance: The reason need not be explicitly stated in the prior art but must be articulable from the totality of the prior art, common knowledge, or other sources. Mere structural similarity or existence of the compound is insufficient without a reason to select and modify (Altana Pharma AG v. Teva; Eisai; Ortho-McNeil).

name: Obviousness without identifying a single lead compound
description: A claimed chemical compound may be obvious even without identifying a single lead compound if the prior art suggests formulating a compound having certain structurally defined moieties or moieties with certain properties, and one of ordinary skill would have known how to synthesize such a compound and predict the structural/functional result.
guidance: Examples: when a claim can be viewed as two known compounds linked by a chemical linker, an obviousness finding may be proper if there is a reason to link them, a person of ordinary skill knows how to do so, and the resulting compound would have been a predictable result of the linkage. Office personnel should consider teachings that suggest classes of moieties or linking strategies, not only single lead compounds.

name: Rationale: Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods or products) — required findings
description: To reject a claim on the ground of applying a known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate specific findings: (1) prior art contained a 'base' device; (2) prior art contained a 'comparable' device that has been improved in the same way; (3) one of ordinary skill could have applied the known improvement technique to the base device and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
guidance: This rationale rests on the proposition that an enhancement technique recognized in other situations becomes part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art. If any of the findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness conclusion. See examples such as Intel v. PACT XPP and Nilssen.

name: Attack the identification of the abstract idea
description: Attack the identification of the abstract idea: As instructed in the May 4, 2016 Memorandum at page 3: Examiners should be familiar with any cited decision relied upon in making or maintaining a rejection to ensure that the rejection is reasonably tied to the facts of the case and to avoid relying upon language taken out of context. Examiners should not go beyond those concepts that are similar to what the courts have identified as abstract ideas.
guidance: Challenge the examiner's characterization of the claims; show the cited cases are not reasonably tied to the facts of the application and that language was taken out of context.

name: Use Enfish, McRo, and Berkheimer memos/analogs
description: Use the McRo, Enfish, and Berkheimer memos
guidance: Frame arguments using these precedents/memos: emphasize claim elements that show improvements in computer technology (Enfish), that create technical solutions to technical problems (McRo), and factual disputes about conventionality (Berkheimer).

name: Argue a technical solution to a technical problem
description: Argue a technical solution to a technical problem, clearly identifying why the problem and the solution are technical in nature.
guidance: Explicitly identify the technical problem being solved and explain how the claimed features provide a technical solution (not merely a business/abstract one). Demonstrate how elements improve computing or other technological functionality.

name: Recite and emphasize generation of new information
description: Recite and emphasize generation of new information that did not previously exist, which sets up an analogy to Enfish.
guidance: Show the claims produce or derive new data/metrics/information (not merely reorganize or present known information) to support eligibility analogies to cases like Enfish.

name: Avoid characterization as merely 'collecting, analyzing, and displaying' information
description: Argue that the claims have been over simplified and improperly characterized broadly as 'collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying certain results of the collection and analysis' in an attempt to compare the claims to Electric Power Group.
guidance: Demonstrate concrete claim elements beyond the caricature; show the combination of limitations as a whole provide technical improvements or specific inventive technology.

name: Not merely presenting results of collection and analysis
description: "merely presenting the results of abstract processes of collecting and analyzing information, without more (such as identifying a particular tool for presentation), is abstract as an ancillary part of such collection and analysis."
guidance: Include claim elements that identify specific presentation tools or techniques (not generic 'displaying') to avoid being characterized as mere presentation of results.

name: Argue Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) is unreasonable if overbroad
description: Broadest reasonable interpretation: Argue that the interpretation of the claims is unreasonable.
guidance: When the examiner's characterization stretches claim language beyond reasonable meaning, argue against that BRI to prevent over-generalization to abstract concepts.

name: Identify claimed improvement to computer-related technology (Enfish guidance)
description: Identify the improvement offered by the claimed invention and inquire whether that improvement represents a specific improvement to the technology itself.
guidance: Show how the claim's 'character as a whole' is directed to technological improvement (example: Enfish's self-referential table improving database operation). Describe concrete technical benefits and how they differ from routine computing.

name: Support unconventional measurement/algorithm with specification and facts (Exergen guidance)
description: Even if a claim employs a natural law, if the measurement method is not conventional, routine, and well-understood, it can supply an inventive concept under Alice/Mayo step two.
guidance: Include in the specification mathematical equations, derivations, experimental results, and factual support showing the method is unconventional and not routine. Assert and support factual findings (per Berkheimer) where relevant.

name: Claim specific steps and new data structures, not just results (Finjan guidance)
description: Creating a new data structure based on conventional activity (virus scanning) can satisfy the Alice test provided your claims recite more than just the result.
guidance: Include specific steps that accomplish the result and clear description in the specification so that claim construction supports a narrower, technology-improving reading.

name: Avoid wholly functional/generic claim language (Glasswall guidance)
description: Claims framed in wholly functional terms without how the invention performs the functions are vulnerable; the court found claims similar to Intellectual Ventures I (Symantec) which 'simply require generic computer-implemented steps.'
guidance: Recite how the computer receives files, determines types, parses content, extracts allowable data, creates substitutes, and authorizes forward — show concrete mechanisms and improvements in computer functioning.

name: Show claimed improvement to a specific platform or computer technology (Downing guidance)
description: Unlike in McRo and DDR Holdings, the claims did not include an improvement and did not claim an improvement in Excel spreadsheets or an improved resource planning computer technology.
guidance: If claiming an implementation on a platform (e.g., Excel), include improvements to that platform or claim features that change how the platform operates rather than simply running an idea on a known platform.

name: When claiming mathematical concepts, claim improvement to technology (Gitlin guidance)
description: Practitioners need to claim an improvement to a computer or some other technology when claiming a mathematical algorithm.
guidance: Do not claim pure mathematical interpolation/algorithm alone; tether the algorithm to a technological improvement or specific implementation that changes operation of a device or system.

name: Avoid claiming fundamental economic practices (Villena guidance)
description: Claims directed to fundamental economic practices long prevalent in commerce (e.g., property valuation) are abstract under Alice step one.
guidance: Avoid drafting claims that recite longstanding commercial practices; instead, add technological features or inventive concepts that transform the abstract economic practice into a technological application.

name: Avoid result-oriented display claims lacking technical detail (Interval Licensing guidance)
description: An abstract idea was found because the claims were result oriented, without technical detail. The abstract idea was 'displaying a second set of data without interfering with a first set of data.' At step 2, the claims were found to not recite a technical solution.
guidance: Include technical details about how the display is implemented, scheduling, acquisition, update, and specific mechanisms rather than high-level result-oriented language.

name: Draft claims with concrete technical elements (example: dynamic stability metrics claim features)
description: Claims that recite technical elements such as frequency instability, voltages, power flows, phase angles, damping, oscillation modes, derived from phasor measurements, displaying event analysis results in visuals/tables/charts, concurrent visualization of measurements and dynamic stability metrics, real-time accumulation and updating of measurements, and deriving a composite indicator of reliability that uses real time measurements and non-grid data.
guidance: When possible, include concrete sensor/measurement sources, derived metrics, real-time processing, visualization modalities, and how those elements combine technically to produce a new capability (e.g., power grid vulnerability indicator) rather than high-level data collection/display descriptions.

name: Provide detailed specification support and factual evidence
description: The Exergen and related entries stress that factual findings and specification support (e.g., mathematical equations, experimental testing/results) can be decisive in showing claims are not conventional or routine.
guidance: Populate the specification with equations, derivations, test data, descriptions of unconventional steps, implementation details, and any empirical evidence to support non-conventionality and enable meaningful claim construction and rebuttal of examiner assertions.

name: Effect when all claims are rejected after court mandate
description: If all claims in the case stand rejected, proceedings are considered terminated on the mandate issue date; the case is ordinarily not open to subsequent amendment and prosecution. An applicant wishing to continue prosecution must file a continuation prior to the court mandate entry.
guidance: No revivability by USPTO petition for abandonment caused by outside proceedings; failure to file continuation prior to mandate prevents co-pendency with parent application.

name: Effect when some claims are allowed after court mandate
description: If one or more claims are allowed (including those reversed by the Board/court), proceedings are considered terminated only as to claims still rejected; claims indicated as allowable but objected to due to dependency from rejected claims will be treated as rejected.
guidance: Examiner should either convert dependent claims to independent form via examiner’s amendment and issue the application or set a 2-month shortened statutory period for appellant to rewrite dependent claims in independent form (extensions available under 37 CFR 1.136(a)). If no timely reply, application is abandoned.

name: Inventive step for dosage regimen/dose as element
description: “invention shall be evaluated, considering dosage regimen or dose as its element. Inventive step may be acknowledged only for a specific dosage regimen and dose which are deemed to be worthwhile to be protected as a patent due to prominent or heterogeneous effect for which a person skilled in the art cannot expect.”
guidance: Examples: (Ex1) claim of composition with Compound A 0.5–1.0 mg once a day — closest prior art disclosed 0.5–2.5 mg orally and optimization of administration is a general technical issue, so expected efficacy means inventive step denied. (Ex2) monthly high-dose administration may be found obvious if a skilled person could easily select that regimen, unless an unexpectedly striking difference (e.g., bioavailability or long-term bone density improvement) is shown. In short: dosage/regimen can support inventive step only when an unexpected/prominent effect unpredictable to skilled person is demonstrated and supported by evidence.

name: Physiochemical/mechanical analysis details
description: “The method, device, requirements, etc. should be stated specifically in the description of the invention for a skilled person in the art to understand and reproduce the invention. The detailed statement is needed to fully support sensory feature in accordance to the result of analysis.”
guidance: Describe measurement methods, devices and parameters. Link analytical results to claimed sensory effects (e.g., Brix change for sweetness). Without specific analytical details the sensory claim may be unsupported.

name: Claims for health functional foods — usage treated as claim element
description: “If the subject matter recited in a claim is a health functional food, the usage limiting the food is considered as a claim element.”
guidance: Using a usage limitation in a claim to restrict a food may be treated as an element; however, merely stating a different usage for the same composition as prior art does not automatically impart novelty (see note referencing case law).

name: Claims for health functional foods — describe usage by objective
description: “For a use invention of a health functional food, its usage shall be specifically described by not its quality itself but its objectives to be achieved through the quality.”
guidance: State specific objectives (e.g., improvement of hyperlipidemia, reduction of blood sugar) rather than ambiguous quality terms. Quality terms that describe mechanism/function rather than use may not be accepted as a use-limitation.

name: Claims for health functional foods — permitted scope of usage expression
description: “Contrary to a medicinal use invention stating a usage for cure of specific diseases or symptoms, the usage may be stated with the type of function which is helpful to human body.”
guidance: Avoid claiming food as a medicinal treatment (e.g., 'to treat disease'); such phrasing is unclear/ improper because food is not a medicinal object. Use appropriate wording that reflects health-promoting function rather than treatment of disease.

name: Functional drinking water: description and evidentiary requirements
description: “it is necessary to satisfy requirements for description including statement of medical effect of functional drinking water, statement of maintaining magnetic state of magnetized water, etc.; subject matter eligibility of invention, and determine whether the invention is possibly harmful to public health or not pursuant to Article 32 of Patent Act.”
guidance: For electrolyzed reduced water, state process parameters and beneficial effects; for hexagonal water and magnetized water, submit objective tests and measurement methods to support production principle and claimed states. If medical effects are asserted, provide objective data unless the effect is part of technical common knowledge.

name: Industrial applicability / completed invention requirement for functional water
description: “Since manufacturing device or manufacturing method of hexagonal water made by Hyranya (hexagonal pyramid) model has no test reports or evidence to prove that hexagonal water is just made by Hyranya model, it is considered as uncompleted invention which is impossible to be accomplished.”
guidance: Processes that are theoretical without scientific proof or lacking evidence to show the claimed result are uncompleted and may be ineligible. Demonstrate practicability with test data or reproducible methods.

name: Chemical compound: requirement to disclose representative embodiments
description: “For an invention relating to a new chemical compound, embodiment specifying technical means shall be disclosed. Where the claim is recited genetically, representative embodiment shall be disclosed by a group except for a case that the specific content of invention can be recognized to a person skilled in the art based on the disclosure of the specification and the level of skill in the art.”
guidance: When using broad/Markush-type claims, disclose representative examples and embodiments to support the claimed genus; failure to do so may lead to a finding that the claim is not supported by the description.

name: Clarity of chemical compound claims (naming, formulae, properties)
description: “If a new chemical compound is specified by its name, or structural formula, the claim shall be deemed clear. ... If structural formula is simple, it will be possible to state only the name ... if physical or chemical property can specify it, it is allowed to define the invention with the properties.”
guidance: Specify name, structural formula, and crystal structure when needed. Use property-based definitions only when they uniquely identify the compound. Avoid ambiguous terms like 'substituted …' without specifying substituents, and be cautious using generic labels ('alkyl', 'aryl') if carbon-number range or embodiments require specification.

name: Novelty rules for chemical compounds (specific characteristics, salts, purity)
description: “Chemical compound defined by specific characteristics ... if the claimed compound is identical with the well-known compound specified by name or structural formula, the claimed compound is deemed to lack novelty. A chemical compound and its conventional salt are substantially identical. Hence the salt of the known compound is deemed to lack novelty. A known chemical compound with simply improved purity lacks novelty.”
guidance: Avoid claiming known compounds by only changing naming conventions, salts, or marginal purity improvements unless distinctive properties or structure are shown.

name: Novelty of preparation method (method claims)
description: “Where the claimed preparation method is the same with that of the prior art, and merely the use is limited, it is deemed to lack novelty since both are preparations for producing the substantially same compound.”
guidance: Method claims that are identical to prior art except for a use limitation will generally lack novelty. Using a starting material produced by a particular prior preparation may also render the method non-novel if other conditions are equivalent.

name: Inventive step for chemical compound inventions (structure + special effect)
description: “Inventive step of a chemical compound invention is determined by two features: i) structural formula ii) technically special effect of the chemical compound. ... improved effects accomplished by the claimed compound compared to that of a prior art reference is very important ... An examiner should not deny the inventive step because of similar structure ... if the claimed compound has unexpected or extraordinary characteristic, it is recognized as involving inventive step.”
guidance: Assess whether the claimed structural differences and/or unexpected technical advantages (final result, chemical feature, purpose or use) would have been predictable to a skilled person. If effects are predictable, inventive step may be denied despite favorable results.

name: Inventive step for inorganic compounds with specific features
description: “For an inorganic compound, even though the name and the chemical formula are same, it is common that physical property or its configuration, including microstructure such as crystal form, a unit surface area of particles, etc. is different. ... to determine inventive step of the invention of preparation of inorganic compound with specific feature, the review of specific property shall be included in the claim regardless of statement of the property.”
guidance: Claims should specify the specific properties (microstructure, particle surface area, etc.) that distinguish the inorganic product; the claim should allow review of whether those properties are produced by the claimed combination of components and conditions.

name: Product-by-use claims (use limitation construed as utility, not novelty)
description: “In case of a chemical compound, use of which is limited by stating ‘for~’ (e.g. Chemical compound Z for Y), since the limitation is just to indicate its utility, so it is considered as a chemical compound without use limitation (e.g. Chemical compound Z). If a claimed chemical compound is disclosed in the prior art, the chemical compound with use limitation is deemed to lack novelty.”
guidance: A claim of product 'for' a use will typically be read as the product per se for novelty purposes. To obtain novelty for a new use, consider use-limited method claims or other claim drafting strategies; be aware of local case law.

name: Integrative mechanistic interpretation linking behavioural and neurochemical pathways
description: These results suggest that the strain differences observed in (non)adaptive anxiety behaviour are at least in part mediated by differences in gamma-aminobutyric acid-A and mGluR5 mediated transmission.
guidance: Synthesize behavioural, endocrine and molecular findings to propose mechanistic explanations (e.g., implicating GABA-A and mGluR5 systems). Be cautious about causal claims and support mechanistic interpretations with converging evidence from multiple outcome measures.

name: Language(s) for filing
description: Applicants must file their patent application, including the specification, in the official language of the country of filing (for Cambodia, Lao PDR, Indonesia, Thailand and Viet Nam) and English (for Brunei Darussalam and Singapore). In Malaysia, Myanmar and the Philippines, applicants can choose between the official language of the country of filing and English. The language in which the patent is filed is also used as the language of the proceedings, and any amendments made to the application, or the patent must be drawn up in that language.
guidance: If filed in any language other than an official/authorized language, a translation of the specification (title, abstract, claims, description and drawings) in the required language must be filed within a specified period or upon request of the patent office/registrar. Note: in Myanmar, even if English is selected the proceedings of office communication are in the country’s official language.

name: Formalities examination — scope and timing
description: All patent applications undergo a formalities examination in-house before substantive examination. The formalities examination checks compliance with formal requirements and results in acceptance for further examination, acceptance subject to amendment(s), or refusal.
guidance: Formalities examination typically requires identifying presence of request form, applicant/inventor identification, title, description, claims, drawings (if necessary), abstract, representative details, and priority claim. The contents of abstract, description, drawings, title and claims are not closely scrutinized in formalities per se; it is sufficient that documents identifiable as description and claims exist. However, some AMS perform initial checks on clarity, multiple dependency, claim(s) evaluation for priority (Philippines), exclusions/exception to patentability and initial clarity (Thailand), and unity 'a priori' in some cases. Supporting documents may be filed within prescribed periods after filing; extensions may be allowed per national provisions.

name: Grounds for rejection during formalities examination
description: An examiner identifies deficiencies and invites remedy within a defined (possibly extendable) period; failure to remedy can lead to abandonment or rejection.
guidance: Grounds for abandonment/rejection include: required filing documents missing/erroneous/incomplete/non-compliant with format; missing title, abstract, description and/or claim(s); specification not translated timely into official language; foreign applicants not represented by professional representative where required; inventor designation not made or deed of assignment not submitted; filing/supporting documents not filed in due time; prescribed fees not paid on time; non-patentable subject matters (Thailand, Viet Nam).

name: Amendment before and during formalities examination
description: Applicants may, of their own initiative or at the request of the patent office/registrar, amend or correct the application including the specification without impacting the filing date, subject to procedural requirements.
guidance: Amendments must be requested in the prescribed manner, within prescribed periods, and accompanied by prescribed documents/fees if applicable. Amendments accepted are entered in the application and considered for publication. New matter extending beyond the original disclosure will be rejected. There is no restriction on broadening claims as long as the amendment does not include matter extending beyond the originally filed disclosure; substantive examination will inform applicant if amendments constitute new matter and allow amendment within a prescribed time.

name: Assessment of unity of invention
description: A patent application must relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept. Assessment uses both a priori and a posteriori approaches.
guidance: Link between group must be a technical relationship expressed in the claims in terms of same or corresponding special technical features. Lack of unity must be determined from the language of the claims as properly construed and, where appropriate, by regard to relevant prior art. Unity may be lacking a priori (from claim language) or a posteriori (after considering prior art). Example: independent claims to A+Z, A+Y, Z+Y lack unity a priori absent common subject-matter to all three; A+Z and A+Y have unity a priori since A is common, but if A is found to be prior art after search, lack of unity a posteriori can arise. Assessment best during substantive examination but should be considered early to avoid unnecessary costs. Lack of unity should not be raised/maintained based on narrow or literal approach; adopt broad, practical consideration of interdependence of alternatives in relation to state of the art. Assessment should ensure efficient use of examination resources.

name: Limitations on third-party participation in inter partes reexamination
description: Under AIPA, on patents issuing from applications filed on or after November 29, 1999, a third party requesting reexamination can participate to a limited extent in the reexamination process.
guidance: Specific limitations include: the third-party requestor can file one written comment on each PTO action and applicant response; the third-party requestor can appeal to the Board of Appeals of the PTO but not to the federal circuit court; the patent owner may appeal a final rejection of claims to the Board of Appeals of the PTO or to the federal court of appeals and can seek a stay of any pending litigation involving any claim subject to inter partes reexamination. Also, a third-party requestor is estopped from later (e.g., in litigation) raising issues they 'raised or could have raised' in the reexamination, and any requestor is estopped from later challenging 'any fact' determined in the reexamination.

name: State disciplinary findings and applicable professional conduct rules
description: State findings of professional misconduct (here, the Maryland Court of Appeals order) that identify violations of specific state professional conduct rules can predicate USPTO reciprocal discipline.
guidance: The Order cites the Maryland findings that respondent violated Maryland Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct rules 1.2 (Scope of Representation); 1.4 (Communication); 1.6 (Confidentiality of Information); 1.9 (Duties to Former Clients); 1.16(d) (Termination of Representation); 3.1 (Meritorious Claims and Contentions); 4.4 (Respect for Rights of Third Persons); and 8.4 (Misconduct). Those state-rule violations were the predicate for the USPTO action.

name: Resolving ambiguity of functional limitations
description: During prosecution, applicant may resolve ambiguities of a functional limitation by: (1) using a quantitative metric (e.g., numeric limitation) rather than a qualitative functional feature; (2) demonstrating that the specification provides a formula for calculating a property along with examples that meet and do not meet the claim limitation; (3) demonstrating that the specification provides a general guideline and examples sufficient to teach a person skilled in the art when the claim limitation was satisfied; or (4) amending the claims to recite the particular structure that accomplishes the function.
guidance: These are example remediation routes; examiners should consider these approaches when determining whether language is ambiguous. The primary inquiry is whether the language leaves room for ambiguity or whether the boundaries are clear and precise. Other relevant factors may vary by art.

name: Markush group treatment (general)
description: A claim reciting a list of alternatives (Markush claim) is an acceptable claim construction and should not necessarily be rejected as confusing under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Treatment is not governed by particular format (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C' or 'A, B, or C').
guidance: See MPEP § 2117 and § 706.03(y) for additional guidance. Evaluate Markush groupings on their facts; the listing (Markush group) is a recognized drafting technique.

name: Closed vs open Markush groups (indefiniteness risk)
description: A Markush grouping is a closed group of alternatives when selection is from a group 'consisting of' the recited alternatives. If a Markush grouping requires selection from an open list (e.g., 'comprising' or 'consisting essentially of'), the claim should generally be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite because it is unclear what other alternatives are intended to be encompassed.
guidance: If combinations or mixtures are intended, include qualifying language (e.g., 'at least one member selected from the group' or 'or mixtures thereof'). Cite Abbott Labs. v. Baxter and MPEP § 2111.03 as relevant authority.

name: Markush breadth and indefiniteness (when excessive breadth causes rejection)
description: A Markush group may include many alternatives, and breadth alone is not indefiniteness; however, if the grouping is so expansive that persons skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of the claimed invention (e.g., massive number of distinct chemical alternatives that cannot be envisioned), the claim may be indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
guidance: Evaluate whether skilled artisans can determine the scope; if not, a rejection for indefiniteness under 112(b) is appropriate. Breadth ≠ indefiniteness per se (In re Gardner).

name: Diminishing scope and double inclusion in Markush groups
description: Use of Markush claims of diminishing scope or double inclusion of an element by members of a Markush group is not, by itself, a sufficient basis for objection or rejection. The facts of each case must be evaluated to determine whether multiplicity or indefiniteness results.
guidance: Assess whether the practice renders claims indefinite or results in undue multiplicity. Redundancy (e.g., generic and specific terms both listed) does not automatically render a claim indefinite (Eli Lilly v. Teva example).

name: Negative limitations (exclusionary provisos)
description: Negative limitations or exclusionary provisos are not inherently ambiguous or uncertain; they comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) so long as the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely. However, any negative limitation must have basis in the original disclosure; lack of basis may require rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description).
guidance: Older skepticism about negative limitations may be distinguished by facts; if alternative elements are positively recited in the specification, they may be excluded in the claims. Lack of literal basis for a negative limitation is not necessarily sufficient to establish lack of descriptive support—evaluate facts and precedent (In re Johnson, Ex parte Parks; MPEP § 2163.07(b)).

name: Aggregation is not a statutory ground for rejection
description: A claim should not be rejected on the ground of 'aggregation' as non‑statutory. If a claim omits essential matter or fails to interrelate essential elements as defined by the specification, see MPEP § 2172.01 for proper treatment.
guidance: Ensure rejections are tied to statutory grounds (101/102/103/112) rather than non‑statutory 'aggregation' theory.

name: Prolix claims (long recitations)
description: Claims should be rejected as prolix only when long recitations or unimportant details render the scope of the claimed invention indefinite and the metes and bounds cannot be determined.
guidance: Reject for prolixity only when the claim's long recitations make the subject matter indefinite; provide reasoning about how claim language clouds metes and bounds.

name: Double inclusion: fact‑specific evaluation
description: No per se rule that double inclusion is improper; whether multiple inclusion of an element gives rise to indefiniteness must be evaluated on the facts of each case.
guidance: Consider reasonable claim construction (In re Kelly) and examine whether double inclusion leads to ambiguity (e.g., device claims that can read the same element twice may be indefinite).

name: Product‑by‑process claims are permissible
description: Product‑by‑process claims, which define the claimed product in terms of the process by which it is made, are proper so long as it is clear that the claim is directed to the product and not the process.
guidance: Applicants may present claims of varying scope using product‑by‑process language. Cite Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma and In re Luck for supporting precedent.

name: Claims combining product and process in the same claim (improper)
description: A single claim that claims both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b); such claims create confusion as to when infringement occurs.
guidance: Examples: Katz (system claim with user actions) and IPXL Holdings v. Amazon. Avoid claims mixing statutory classes which create ambiguity about direct infringement.

name: 'Use' claims and process claims lacking steps
description: Attempting to claim a process without setting forth any steps generally raises an indefiniteness issue under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Such 'use' claims may also be improper under 35 U.S.C. 101; examiners should consider rejecting under alternative grounds (101 and 112).
guidance: Decide based on authority and facts; sometimes recited steps like 'utilizing' have been held not indefinite (Ex parte Porter). If ambiguous, reject under both 101 and 112 to preserve grounds.

name: Chemical formula and structure claims
description: Claims to chemical compounds and compositions using chemical formulas should not be considered indefinite or speculative merely because a structure is not fully presented or because corroborating spectroscopic data is absent.
guidance: Absence of corroborating data cannot be the basis for indefiniteness. Partial structures or claims by name/physical‑chemical characteristics or by making process are acceptable where a skilled artisan can identify the compound (see In re Fisher, Martin v. Johnson, Ex parte Brian).

name: Mere function of a machine does not bar process claims
description: Process or method claims should not be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) solely because they define the inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus; an otherwise patentable process should not be rejected merely because the application discloses an apparatus which will inherently carry out the recited steps.
guidance: Follow In re Tarczy‑Hornoch: do not use inherent machine function alone as basis for indefiniteness rejection of process claims.

name: Practice compact prosecution (examine claims thoroughly early)
description: Examiners should review each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review and identify all applicable grounds of rejection in the first Office action to avoid unnecessary delays (compact prosecution). When a term renders a claim indefinite, make a 112(b) rejection and also rejections over the prior art under 102/103 where applicable, stating how the indefinite term is being interpreted.
guidance: Avoid piecemeal examination by rejecting each claim on all valid grounds available; when claiming indefiniteness, state on the record the interpretation applied with respect to prior art rejections (see 37 CFR 1.104(a)(1), In re Packard, and MPEP § 707.07(g)).

name: Prior art rejection when claim is indefinite (two approaches)
description: When a claim is indefinite relative to prior art, two examination approaches are possible: (1) if uncertainty is limited and at least one interpretation renders the claim unpatentable, enter both (A) a 112(b) indefiniteness rejection and (B) a prior art rejection based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable (stating how the claim is being interpreted); (2) if there is great confusion as to proper interpretation, do not base a 103 rejection on substantial speculation about claim meaning.
guidance: The first approach is recommended to avoid piecemeal prosecution and to give applicant better appreciation of relevant prior art (see Ex parte Ionescu and In re Steele). Examiners must state how the claim is interpreted when making prior art rejections in these circumstances.

name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C.112(a) and (b)
description: The requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enabling) and 112(b) (definiteness) are separate and distinct. A specification disclosure not commensurate in scope with the claim does not by itself render the claim indefinite (112(b)) but indicates insufficient disclosure under 112(a).
guidance: If the specification discloses a feature as critical or essential and the claims fail to recite it, a 112(a) rejection (lack of enabling/descriptive support) may be appropriate (In re Borkowski, In re Mayhew). Distinguish insufficiency of disclosure from indefiniteness.

name: Amendments adding subject matter not described (new matter)
description: If a claim is amended to include an invention that is not described in the application as filed, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA first paragraph) as directed to subject matter not described in the specification may be appropriate.
guidance: Evaluate changes for written‑description support; see In re Simon and In re Panagrossi for examples where claims to a subcombination lacked description in the filing.

name: Interpreting 35 U.S.C.112(f) / pre‑AIA sixth paragraph (means‑plus‑function)
description: A 'means or step plus function' limitation should be interpreted under the broadest reasonable interpretation that is statutorily mandated in paragraph six; the PTO may not disregard the structure disclosed in the specification corresponding to such language when rendering a patentability determination.
guidance: Follow the en banc In re Donaldson holding: identify corresponding structure/steps in the specification and limit the means‑plus‑function claim accordingly. These are guidelines consistent with binding precedent; they do not have the force of rulemaking.

name: Affidavit/deposition limits under Equity Rule (SDNY)
description: If expert testimony in patent causes is taken by affidavit, witnesses shall not give opinion as to the meaning of any patent claim or specification; testimony must be strictly confined to explanation of the operation of the relevant arts, processes, machines, manufactures or compositions.
guidance: Affidavits or depositions containing matter forbidden by the rule or irrelevant/immaterial matter shall not be answered by the opposite party nor be the basis of cross-examination; the court may strike such matter at any stage.

name: Evidence for defence that patent claims unpatentable subject-matter (Defense 1)
description: Evidence may be required to show that terms of art/science in the patent require the court to construe the patent as claiming a principle or other unpatentable subject rather than a patentable process, machine, manufacture, composition, or design.
guidance: Where the patent plainly claims only a peculiar function of a described machine, this defense may be maintained without evidence outside the patent.

name: Indefiniteness / uncertainty in claim embodiment (Defense 13)
description: May sometimes be sustained without evidence outside the letters patent, but prudence suggests fortifying the defense with expert testimony showing the outward embodiment of the claim is uncertain in character or extent.
guidance: Expert testimony is advisable to show claim terms are uncertain; in some cases the patent alone may suffice.

name: Delay in applying for reissue (Defense 16)
description: Can be supported by comparing the original patent with the reissue: if the reissue claims something the original did not and was applied for long after the original, this supports the defense.
guidance: How long is ‘long’ depends on circumstances; different times have been held sufficient and are collated elsewhere; the burden is on the plaintiff to excuse delay beyond two years.

name: Substantial difference between reissue and original (Defense 17)
description: Always requires the original patent and generally expert testimony showing that the outward embodiment of something claimed in the reissue is substantially different from anything described in the original and apparently intended to be claimed.
guidance: Judge will not reject such expert testimony unless the case is so clear he would have decided it on demurrer.

name: Prior patent by same inventor (Defense 18)
description: Requires introduction of the prior patent granted on the same inventor's application; usually does not require expert testimony unless phraseology renders understanding difficult.
guidance: To prevail, the claim of the prior patent must be so clearly coextensive with the claim in suit that coextensiveness is apparent on the face of the documents; experts may be needed where claim language is obscure.

name: Narrowly bounded product claims in synthetics keep technological progress competitive
description: In synthetic materials, product patent claims tend to be narrowly bounded and, because of that, they keep advance of synthetic material technology competitive rather than monopolized.
guidance: Examples: Du Pont licensing Rayon and Cellophane; Nylon licensed to ICI and IG Farben with subsequent variants patented by others. Narrow product claims allow competing variants (e.g., Dacron, Orlon) and avoid long-term exclusion of improvements.

name: Product vs. process patenting in pharmaceuticals: new-use discoveries rewarded via process patents
description: When someone discovers a new use for an established product, the general solution has been to award a process patent to the discoverer of the new use, rather than a product patent covering the substrate.
guidance: This doctrine (e.g., Rohm & Haas v. Roberts Chemical) rewards important inventive work in discovering new uses while not giving absolute control over the product itself; process claims limit scope to the new application, balancing incentives and access.

name: Patent doctrine and enforcement outcomes (validity, infringement) materially shape incentives and industry trajectories
description: Court decisions upholding or invalidating patents (and injunctions enforcing them) changed market structure and innovation incentives in concrete historical cases (Edison, Brush, Marconi, Wright, Selden).
guidance: Those drafting patent claims, litigating, or formulating policy should recognize that doctrinal outcomes (scope, validity, remedies) have tangible economic effects; thus legal standards for claim breadth and validity must be informed by their likely industrial consequences.

name: Grave injustice (Selling element (iii))
description: Reciprocal discipline may be avoided if the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates that imposition of the same discipline by the USPTO would result in grave injustice.
guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii) quoted. The Office will evaluate claims (e.g., delay, mitigation, mistaken factual findings) but requires clear and convincing proof that accepting the other jurisdiction's sanction would be gravely unjust.

name: Scriptural and patristic authority central to theological proof
description: Doctrinal claims are supported and justified by extensive citation of Scripture, Church Fathers, and Councils; patristic quotations serve as primary evidence for dogmatic positions.
guidance: Numerous quotations (Augustine, Chrysostom, Councils like Trent, scriptural passages) used throughout to ground arguments about grace and predestination.
